## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the times of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the very extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indices following each volume and each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority and influence in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indices: the first, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in which places of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.**

**A most accurate edition, and one easily to be preferred above all others if the following features are properly considered: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the whole work, the modest price, and above all this collection, unified, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and short works previously scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the various branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eighteen hundred. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of Our Lord 1054

## Hermann the Lame, Monk of Reichenau

[Column 0009]

# Historical Notice concerning Hermann the Lame

*(From John Egon’s book On the Distinguished Men of Reichenau, in Pez, Treasury, I, III, 688.)*

[Column 0009A]

Hermann the Lame—so called from the weakness of his limbs—was the singular glory of the monastery of Reichenau and the most radiant light of the entire Benedictine order. In the year of Christ 1013, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August [18 July], he was born to his father Wolferad, count of Veringen, and his mother Hiltrude.

As a boy he was brought to Reichenau. Although he was indeed of good natural disposition, his intellect was found to be somewhat dull and less suited to the acquisition of letters. Therefore he began to call upon the assistance of the Blessed Virgin, to whose singular protection he had already long before devoted himself; and she obtained for him, very soon, a more capable intellect.

Within a short time he learned Latin, Greek, and Arabic so perfectly that he pronounced each of them as though it were his native language. He was an outstanding poet of his time, an excellent historian, a distinguished musician, an eminent philosopher and theologian, and an exceptionally learned and gifted mathematician, so that no one at that time seems to have surpassed him in reputation.

Indeed, he wrote about the astrolabe with such remarkable intellectual skill that many considered him its inventor. First, with great diligence, he composed a concise and very clear *Chronicle*, which he brought from the beginning of the world down to his own age, namely to the year of Christ 1054. It was printed several times and published in an enlarged form by Henry Canisius in volume I of his *Ancient Readings*, and was also inserted in volume XI of the *Library of the Fathers*.

He wrote one book *On Music*; one book *On the Monochord*; one book *On Eclipses*; one book *On the Squaring of the Circle*; one book *On Computation*; one book *On Physiognomy*; one book *On the Contest of Rithmomachy*; a commentary on astronomy; three books *On the Construction of the Astrolabe*; one book *On the Usefulness of the Astrolabe*; one book *On the Lives of Several Saints*; histories, or offices, of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin and of Saint Mary Magdalene; also a history of the holy angels; sequences on the Lord’s Ascension, “Almighty King,” and others; *On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin*, “Hail, glorious Star of the Sea,” and others; *On the Holy Spirit*, “Come, Holy Spirit, and send forth from heaven”; the responsory “Simon Bar-Jona,” and others.

He also dictated many sequences, responsories, and songs, among which are the celebrated antiphons useful and pleasing to the entire Church: “Hail, Queen,” and others; “Loving Mother of the Redeemer,” and others.

In addition to all these works, he translated Aristotle’s *Rhetoric* and *Poetics* from Arabic into Latin, and wrote many other things clearly and elegantly. Finally, after he had grown greatly in every virtue, while his body could scarcely sustain his feeble limbs, he rendered his soul to its Creator, whom alone he had striven to please in this life. This took place in the year 1054 after the Virgin’s childbirth, and he was transferred to his parents’ estate at Adelshusen.

Although I would willingly refrain from unnecessary controversies, because one group after another is continually writing new histories in which, according to its own discretion, it sells all sorts of opinions—even plainly false ones—to win the gossip and applause of the people, I think it will be preferable to refute, however briefly, at least those things that they have falsely asserted about our Hermann. Otherwise, if I remained silent, no one might believe that our arguments possessed any force with which we could defend ourselves along with the Lame.

[Column 0010B]

Trithemius, therefore, unjustly hostile to the monks of Reichenau, wrote in several places that our Hermann was from Saint Gall. Others followed his error and fell into even more disgraceful mistakes. For, in order to defend an opinion once conceived in their minds, they dared to assert that Helpericus of Saint Gall—otherwise a very learned monk—had been Hermann’s teacher and master, and that when Helpericus departed this life Hermann had been installed in his place at the school of Saint Gall. Thus, if everything fitted together and cohered so neatly, no one would any longer dare to call Hermann’s monastic profession at Saint Gall into question, much less attack it.

Lest I seem unable to cite any author of this invention, I direct the reader to the booklet of Jacob Meckius, *On the Bishops of Constance*, published in the German language. There he relates this story bluntly and, unconcerned about its truth, considers it so certain and well known that he adduces neither argument nor authority on its behalf.

From where he derived this error is not yet clear to me. I should wish writers and such little historians to pass over in silence what they do not know, rather than strive, to the great prejudice of others, to purchase a high reputation for empty honor and applause among ignorant people.

Why, then, does the writer cited first say that Helpericus of Saint Gall was Hermann’s teacher, without adducing any evidence from antiquity? Did he derive this from some writings of Helpericus, of Hermann himself, or from some other ancient and authentic document? Let him produce it, if he has found anything of the kind, and not begrudge us a ray of truth, so that we too may give credence to it, as is fair. But if—as I believe—he found nothing of the sort, why does he so boldly affirm what he does not know?

But why am I attacking a man so harshly, when I suppose that his error will do us no harm but rather prove greatly beneficial? If I demonstrate that Helpericus died long before Hermann was born, will not his entire foundation collapse? And when I have proved that Hermann was not Helpericus’s disciple, will not the opinion that Hermann was a monk in the monastery of Saint Gall also weaken, if it is not extinguished altogether?

That is certainly what will happen. For the more fragile and weak that opinion becomes, the stronger and more certain ours will grow. Once it becomes clear that Hermann did not succeed Helpericus at the school of Saint Gall, it will appear still less likely that he was a religious at the monastery of Saint Gall.

To detect this error more quickly, we must first investigate the age in which each of the two men—Helpericus and Hermann—flourished. As for Helpericus’s age, I can write nothing more certain than what the writers of Saint Gall themselves transmit, especially the Reverend Father Jodocus Mezler, an excellent writer and interpreter of the antiquities of his monastery. In his book *On the Distinguished Men of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, where he treats of Walafrid Strabo, he says:

“We certainly know that our fathers Helpericus and Werembert were disciples of that same Rabanus, and so forth.”

If Helpericus was a disciple of Rabanus, he must have been alive before the year 847, in which, as Hermann the Lame in his *Chronicle* and Baronius in volume X of the *Annals* at the entry for that year of Christ teach us, Rabanus was appointed to the archbishopric.

From this it may further be inferred that Helpericus was born before the year 828. For it is probable that, when he was sent from Saint Gall to Fulda for the sake of study, he was at least seventeen years old, and that he listened there for approximately two or three years to Rabanus expounding the sacred Scriptures. This, as I have said, must have occurred before 847. It is not credible that Rabanus, already an archbishop and burdened with the gravest responsibilities, continued to maintain schools.

[Column 0011D]

With this as our foundation, we shall further see at what time Helpericus, if he was Hermann’s teacher, ought to have taught. Hermann himself writes in his *Chronicle* that he was born in the year 1013, but was handed over to the study of letters at the age of seven, in the year 1020.

Helpericus therefore remained alive after 1020, and indeed longer, since the writer mentioned above says that Hermann was made Helpericus’s assistant at the school of Saint Gall. Hermann could not have presided over that school while still a seven-year-old boy; rather, he must have done so when he already possessed good judgment and was sufficiently mature—a condition that, it is reasonable to believe, could scarcely have occurred before his twenty-fourth year.

If, therefore, we allow Hermann twenty-four years before he was appointed schoolmaster of Saint Gall, we shall find that this could not have happened before the year of Christ 1037. Since, as the reader may recall, we have proved above that Helpericus was born around the year of Christ 827, it follows that he would have had to extend his life beyond two hundred years, so that Germany might now boast of having a new Nestor and need not envy Greece its own.

Although the writer so often cited assigns a sufficiently long life to Hilpericus and says that he reached the age of ninety-seven—perhaps so that what he fabricated concerning Hermann’s discipleship under Helpericus might appear more plausible—he nevertheless has not fabricated enough. If he wants his story to stand, he must add another 114 years to the age of ninety-six.

Let the authors of the opposing opinion therefore consider into how many errors they fall while they cling stubbornly to the view they once adopted concerning Hermann’s profession.

Nor is it plausible that anyone could suppose there were perhaps two men named Helpericus at Saint Gall, one flourishing under Rabanus and the other flourishing with Hermann and able to be his teacher. I say this because I have not yet read anyone who makes two learned men of this name.

Trithemius also—whose reliability our opponents here extol with extraordinary enthusiasm—mentions only one Helpericus. He generally makes him Hermann’s equal in age, or even somewhat younger, especially in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, which he wrote after his book *On the Distinguished Men of Our Order*.

There he says that Hermann lived under the emperor Henry II, around the year of the Lord 1040, while Helpericus lived around the year 1069, under the emperor Henry III.

See, then, that even according to Trithemius’s opinion—which elsewhere our opponents willingly embrace as altogether true concerning Hermann’s monastic profession—Hermann could not have been Helpericus’s replacement at the school of Saint Gall.

But why should I linger longer over these inventions, already sufficiently refuted? Let us finally explain why we attribute Hermann’s monastic profession to Reichenau and deny it to Saint Gall.

As for ourselves, we say that stronger arguments cannot be produced to prove that he made his profession at Reichenau than those that Arnold Wion, Christian Urstisius, and other lovers of truth have already drawn from Hermann himself. Such is the passage he has in his *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 1048, where he says:

“The emperor [Henry II], having departed from Regensburg, where he had celebrated Easter, returned to Alemannia. Entering our Reichenau on the eighth day before the Kalends of May [24 April], he caused the new basilica of Saint Mark the Evangelist, our patron, constructed by Lord Berno the abbot, to be dedicated in his presence by Theoderic, Bishop of Constance. At the feast of that saint he celebrated eight days with us; the Ascension of the Lord at Zurich; Pentecost at Solothurn; and so forth.”

Thus far Hermann. We have listened all the more willingly to him speaking at length about Reichenau because here he has provided us with a greater light by which to discover the place of his profession.

He wrote so clearly that the things we have adduced need no elucidation from our notes and are too plain to require any other interpreter. What could he have said more explicitly to assert that he was a man of Reichenau than when he said: “The emperor entered our Reichenau and caused the basilica of Saint Mark, our patron, to be dedicated”? Did he not celebrate the feast of Saint Mark at Reichenau among us?

If the monks of Saint Gall wished to relate that the emperor had celebrated at Reichenau the feast of Saint Mark the Evangelist, patron of that place, would they say: “The emperor celebrated the feast of Saint Mark, our patron, among us”? If they said this, who, I ask, would not think that the emperor had celebrated the feast of Saint Mark at Saint Gall, when Hermann, on the contrary, says that it happened at Reichenau?

Who also would not infer from this that Saint Mark the Evangelist was the patron of the monks of Saint Gall and that his sacred relics were preserved by them, whereas Hermann, under the year 830, reports only that they were brought to the monastery of Reichenau?

Since all these things are highly absurd and utterly foreign to the truth, it follows that no one other than a monk of Reichenau could have written this *Chronicle*. Since it is established that Hermann was the author of this *Chronicle*, it follows clearly that he was a monk of Reichenau.

Nevertheless, even if these things are entirely true, let us hear what the Reverend Father Jodocus Mezler replies and how he explains the words cited from Hermann. In chapter 26 of book *On the Distinguished Men of Saint Gall*, where he treats of Hermann, he writes:

“They are mistaken who think that Hermann was not a monk of Saint Gall. For from the fact that Hermann, when he names Reichenau, calls it ‘our Reichenau’—‘the emperor entered our Reichenau and celebrated Saint Mark with us’—and uses similar expressions, nothing more can be inferred than that Hermann was at Reichenau at the time when the emperor arrived, or at most that Hermann had by then been received into Reichenau and perhaps established his stability there. For Hermann could well have made his religious profession at Saint Gall in the beginning and then afterward moved to Reichenau, and so forth.”

Thus far Mezler.

Do you see, reader, how he attempts to pierce this knot with a twofold weapon? After noticing that the first weapon was weaker, he employed a second as well.

At first he thought that Hermann had perhaps been staying at Reichenau at that time and had attended the dedication with other outsiders. But even if we imagine that this happened, Hermann could not immediately on that account have called Reichenau “our” Reichenau, nor Saint Mark “our patron.”

No guest or newcomer, merely because he had crossed the threshold of another monastery, would immediately acquire such a right over it that, having forgotten his own monastery, he would call the place where he was lodging his own. Who, then, does not see that Hermann, when he described Reichenau in such terms, counted himself among the monks of Reichenau?

When Mezler therefore perceived that his first response had not yet weakened the force of the argument, he added a second. He conjectured that Hermann might first have made his profession among the monks of Saint Gall and then, when he moved to Reichenau, renewed his profession there and established his stability.

But since this lacks proof, it is asserted without basis. Although he attempts, by examples he adduces, to prove that before and after Hermann certain monks of Reichenau had transferred to Saint Gall and made a new profession there, it does not follow that Hermann and others likewise did so. Reasons may be supplied for affirming this in one case and not in another.

But even if we granted that this had happened, Hermann would nevertheless belong more to the monks of Reichenau than to those of Saint Gall. For it is certain that, if he transferred from Saint Gall to Reichenau and established his stability there, he had first renounced the right he possessed in relation to that monastery, and, in turn, the abbot of Saint Gall with his community had released him from their obedience and dismissed him as a free man.

If the matter is so, why do the monks of Saint Gall, who then willingly dismissed Hermann, now reclaim him and call him back against his will? Was not Mezler compelled shortly before to concede that Hermann, after transferring from Saint Gall to Reichenau, established his stability there? How can one be called back who has sworn that he would remain permanently at Reichenau?

He is therefore ours, and after such a long passage of time it is pointless to reclaim him through prescription. Six hundred years ago, with the permission even of the monks of Saint Gall, he freely bound himself to Reichenau with an indissoluble bond.

Finally, when Mezler noticed that even this second response did not support the cause of the monks of Saint Gall, he was at last led to the opinion that Hermann had indeed been at Reichenau when he wrote those words, but could nevertheless have returned to Saint Gall. He claimed that, according to Trithemius, monks were formerly sent to different monasteries in order to acquire fuller learning; and since this is certain of disciples, it was far more certain of teachers.

Thirdly, he supposes that Hermann had been sent from Saint Gall to Reichenau to instruct the young in good literature.

But this response too is wholly implausible and in no way consistent with the truth. Apart from the fact that it was devised merely to evade the force of our argument and cannot be supported by any evidence, it is also incredible that this happened.

First, the monastery of Reichenau at that time had no need of a teacher from elsewhere. Under Abbot Berno, who was celebrated for his published works, it flourished with men so learned that it surpassed the summit and pinnacle of every branch of knowledge.

Second, even if we grant that a teacher from Saint Gall was sent to assist the school at Reichenau, Hermann could not have been the one sent. His body and health were always weak, and he was almost entirely deprived of the use of his limbs. Another man, stronger in body and better suited to endure all such burdens, should have been sent.

Finally, I do not think that Hermann—easily the most learned and educated man of his age—would have been sent away from his own monastery to another, since we know that even today precious and rare treasures are guarded with greater care.

But let the reader attend to what Mezler finally throws against our arguments. When he had examined their strength more carefully and felt them pressing heavily upon his shoulders, with no door open through which he could escape, he anxiously turned in every direction to shake the heavy yoke from his back.

At last, thinking he had found a sure means of escape, he began to deny that the words we cited from the aforementioned *Chronicle* had been written by Hermann. He says that they were added by someone else as part of an appendix, and claims that he demonstrated this in his *Annals*, which I have neither seen nor read.

But if we were ultimately to come to this, I could have omitted everything we have proved so far. Mezler too could have spared himself the three responses he devised with such great effort and, with a single word of denial, overthrown the whole force of the argument and settled the entire dispute.

For it is true that, if those words are not Hermann’s, we have so far proved little; but if they are—as I have no doubt they are—it is equally true that Hermann has clearly asserted himself on our side.

Although Mezler says that he demonstrated this in his *Annals*, I nevertheless wonder where he obtains his proof. If I may conjecture, I suspect that he wishes to infer it from the fact that in the fuller *Chronicle* published by Henry Canisius there are many passages inserted by others.

Although I do not deny that this is entirely true, it is certain that the words we quoted above are Hermann’s. For they are found in every edition that I have happened to see, both ancient and recent, both fuller and shorter—not to mention the various manuscripts.

In my very ancient copy—which I possess, and which some believed to be the autograph itself, and so forth—although several passages have been added by a more recent hand and have also entered Canisius’s edition, the words written above can nevertheless be seen in their proper place, written continuously in a character very similar to the old script.

Let our opponents produce, if they possess one, an old manuscript in which these words are not found. Even if they had such a manuscript and could produce it, they would not thereby prove that the words mentioned above were added by someone else. It is plausible that Hermann did not compose his *Chronicle* only once, but corrected it after some years and enlarged it with additional material, as Urstisius and Canisius also clearly indicate. They assert that the variety and difference among the many editions arise solely from this process.

We have discussed these matters at length up to this point in order to show that the passage in which Hermann indicates in his *Chronicle* that he was from Reichenau must not be passed over negligently as obscure, or as something newly attached to the *Chronicle* and adulterine. Rather, it must be recognized as especially clear, lucid, and genuine, so that, even if no other argument were available, it could rightly be established that Hermann has attached himself to our side.

It is therefore surprising that Mezler asserts that nothing against the monks of Saint Gall can be proved from that passage. To pass over what I treated more fully above, this one point—that Hermann called Saint Mark “our patron”—could have been sufficient to persuade Mezler that he was a monk at Reichenau.

He ought to have remembered that earlier he had proved by an almost identical argument that Walafrid had lived under the discipline of the abbot of Saint Gall, because in the prologue to the *Life of Saint Gall* he had called that same saint “our patron.”

If Mezler was permitted to infer that no one could have called Saint Gall “our patron” who had never possessed any share in its patrimony, why may I not likewise assert that no one could have called Saint Mark “our patron” who had never possessed any share in his patrimony?

Indeed, it should have followed from this—which we refuted above in chapter 12—that Walafrid was a man of Saint Gall. Much more strongly, it should follow that Hermann was a man of Reichenau, since he indicates this so clearly, in one and the same place, by several different expressions.

Now let our opponents produce some passage from the *Chronicle* by which they may prove that Hermann was from Saint Gall. Perhaps, just as he called Saint Mark “our patron,” he also called Saint Gall “our patron”; or perhaps it may be inferred from other words that he was from Saint Gall.

But nowhere do I find anything of the kind. Indeed, I infer something rather contrary, though not obscurely, from the fact that under the year of Christ 977 he writes:

“At Saint Gall, Ymmo was abbot for eight years; he labored to adorn the church of his patron, and so forth.”

Who, I ask, could believe that Hermann was from Saint Gall, when here he deliberately refrains from calling Saint Gall “our patron,” although, if he had been from Saint Gall, there would have been no reason for him to refrain?

Why did he call Saint Gall only the patron of Abbot Ymmo and omit calling him his own? Certainly for no other reason than that he knew he was a monk of Reichenau and a son of Saint Mark.

Thus far, therefore, we have demonstrated clearly from Hermann himself that he was from Reichenau, not from Saint Gall. It is therefore futile to thrust upon us the authority of Trithemius, who, overwhelmed by the variety of very diverse histories [Col. 0016C], could devote little effort to examining such particular questions. For, besides Hermann himself, we oppose to him Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Antonio Possevino in the *Sacred Apparatus*; Antonio de Yepes of Spain in the *General Chronicle of the Order of Saint Benedict*; Arnold Wion in the *Lignum Vitae*; Henricus Canisius; Carolus Stengelius; Christian Urstisius; and countless others, all of whom unanimously assert that Hermann was a monk of Reichenau. Many of them further suspect that Trithemius’s error arose because the first and widely circulated edition of Hermann was perhaps transcribed from a Saint Gall manuscript.

Here too, I think it should not be left unmentioned that Hermann is everywhere called a monk of Reichenau in old manuscript copies [Col. 0016D], and never a monk of Saint Gall, as Arnold Wion explicitly testifies. Hence those who call our view of Hermann’s Reichenau monastic profession new, and suppose that it was first discovered by the person who promoted the Frankfurt edition, are far from the truth. Nothing refutes this more effectively than an examination of the old copies, written several hundred years before the Frankfurt edition, which bear the name “Hermann, monk of Reichenau” inscribed at their head. Such a copy is found at Augsburg, at Saint Ulrich’s, from which Henricus Canisius transcribed his edition. There was also the copy used by Urstisius; such were the copies Arnold Wion says that he saw or read; and such are many others preserved here and there in various libraries. How, then—as someone claimed—could no one ever have doubted that Hermann was a monk of Saint Gall before his *Chronicle* appeared at Frankfurt?

I would therefore state more truly that, before Trithemius’s time, no one existed who did not believe Hermann to have been a monk of Reichenau, as the ancient copies just mentioned can demonstrate. Moreover, to bring this controversy at last to an end, it may be useful finally to hear what arguments, reasons, and ancient manuscripts the people of Saint Gall produce on their side, by which they claim Hermann for themselves. Up to now, nothing has been brought forward by which he might be proved to have been from Saint Gall. Thus, even if it were known that he was not from Reichenau, it would still not be established that he was from Saint Gall. You may therefore judge that their method of argument is backward: they boldly attack another’s opinion, however well supported, while neglecting their own and fortifying it with no arguments [Col. 0017B]. If, then, we should at some point find the arguments of the people of Saint Gall more effective than ours, let no one doubt that we shall gladly make room for the truth and immediately bury the whole dispute. Nevertheless, until they discover something more certain, let our Hermann remain ours for the time being; and since we hope that they will scarcely find anything more certain, he will remain with us forever.

## APPENDIX

My dispute concerning Hermann’s monastic profession had already ended and had been sent to the frequently mentioned Reverend Father Mezler, a man of Saint Gall, so that, if anything in it seemed less firm or sound, he might point it out and refute it with contrary arguments, should he possess stronger ones [Col. 0017C]. But he did nothing except reheat that old, oft-repeated dish of his: he asserted that the words of the *Chronicle* which, as reported above at greater length, we had used to prove that Hermann was from Reichenau were not Hermann’s own production. He added that the entire remaining part of the *Chronicle*, from the year 1040 onward, was spurious and had been added by someone else as an appendix. He evidently thought he had demonstrated this from the fact that, in the older *Chronicle*, Hermann’s death and praises are found described under the year 1054.

Certainly, Hermann could not possibly have composed this; it must have been done by someone else. I have no doubt of that and readily admit that his death was described by another, as were the events that followed his death [Col. 0017D]. But I cannot understand on what grounds everything preceding his death—from the year 1040, that is, through the year 1054, in which he died—should immediately be attributed to Hermann. I suspect that this was devised for no other reason than to make those words placed under the year 1048, by which we had plainly proved Hermann to have been from Reichenau, appear spurious and uncertain. If nothing else remained, the entire foundation of our position would collapse, and consequently the opinion of the people of Saint Gall would become stronger.

If you say that the difference of style and method indicates a different author, I shall say that the style and method are the same and proclaim the same author. This is absolutely certain, as is plainly evident both in the fuller *Chronicle* edited by Canisius and now also included in volume IX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, as fair and prudent judges of these matters—whose judgment we willingly submit to—can perceive. It is true that, from the year 1040 to the end, the order in that older *Chronicle* appears greatly different: partly because this version is much fuller and longer, and partly because in the preceding portion it also adds each individual year of the reigns of the Roman emperors, whereas in the later portion those years are omitted and only the years of Christ are marked.

In reality, however, the new and expanded *Chronicle* now published, which must be regarded as Hermann’s genuine and legitimate work, is entirely consistent with itself throughout. The reason why the latter portion is more extended is undoubtedly that he judged events which were more recent and had occurred in his own lifetime worthy of being written with greater detail and care than events which had taken place from the creation of the world down to his own times. In order that his chronological work might appear complete in every respect, he sought rather to touch upon those earlier events as briefly as possible than to expound them, knowing that others had treated them more fully, whereas the later matters had not been so treated.

Besides this, I cannot help wondering why Hermann, who brought his history down to his own times—succinctly indeed, but accurately—is said to have omitted the events that occurred during his own age. Who could persuade himself that a man eager for work and devoted to history ceased writing and lived in idleness for the entire fourteen years during which, from the year 1040, he was still alive? [Col. 0018C]

But, leaving other conjectures untouched, another inseparable source of strength for our argument presents itself, by which we can very easily overthrow our opponents’ poorly supported opinion. I believe they concealed this rather than failed to notice it. It is so obvious that even someone moderately acquainted with history cannot fail to detect it. “And what is it?” you ask. This, certainly: in the latter part of the *Chronicle*—which they deny to be Hermann’s work—the death of Countess Hiltrude, Hermann’s mother, is described under the year 1052 in words of a kind that no one except Hermann, as her son, could have used. It consequently becomes perfectly clear that this part of the *Chronicle* can be attributed to no one but Hermann.

The words are these:

> At that time, on the fifth day before the Ides of January, my mother Hiltrude, a most devout woman and the wife of Count Wolferad, closed her final day, etc.; and I wished to write these verses for her as an epitaph:
>
> Mother of the needy, hope and help of her own, etc.

So they must admit that this epitaph is Hermann’s work, as are the words spoken under the year of Christ 1052 about Hiltrude’s death. Once they are compelled, whether they wish it or not, to acknowledge this, who does not see that the words repeatedly cited above, by which we made him a man of Reichenau, must likewise be attributed to Hermann, since what follows and what precedes are, without any dispute [Col. 0019A], judged by everyone to be Hermann’s?

It is not my task to determine at what point Hermann ended his history, since this can contribute nothing toward resolving our little dispute. Nevertheless, it must be certain that he had begun the year 1052, as can be understood from the death of Hiltrude described there, but did not complete the year 1054; this likewise follows from the fact that he is said to have died in that year. By whom his death was recorded, and by whom the subsequent appendix was attached, I do not know. For the present, it is enough to know that everything preceding the year 1054 is genuinely Hermann’s own work, and that it plainly reveals its author to have been a monk of Reichenau.

It would remain to refute yet another error of a certain Crispinian, were it not rejected by its very absurdity from every school of learned historians [Col. 0019B]. For this author invents that our Hermann was not only a monk of Saint Gall but also became abbot of that same monastery of Saint Gall and afterward bishop of Constance. Thus Augustine Wickman of Antwerp, a Norbertine canon, reports and follows him in his recently printed *Marian Sabbath*.

Are things alleged in nocturnal dreams, or fabricated in the ramblings of some old woman, really to be sold at once by historians as sheer truth and unquestionable oracles? Is this the practice of good authors: that whatever is circulated after being fashioned in the trivial brain of some blockhead should immediately be approved by their own vote and proclaimed by everyone’s mouth? By no means is this customary among good men. They examine what is uncertain, approve what is true, and eliminate and expel what is false from their writings.

But I am ashamed to linger any longer over such funeral songs and ravings, which lack every reason and foundation, and of which none of the ancient writers ever wrote or dictated anything similar. Let those who have written about the affairs of Saint Gall be read; let those who composed catalogues or histories of the bishops of Constance be examined with the greatest care; let them be searched most thoroughly from beginning to end. I shall be lying if they have spoken or written a sentence, a word, or a letter about this invention. Since the people of Saint Gall themselves, who know their own affairs best, mention nothing about a Saint Gall or Constance episcopate administered by Hermann, and exclude him from the list [Col. 0020B] of their abbots, what outsider could be so stupid as to dare claim that he knows this better?

It therefore remains firmly established, to bring the whole matter to an end at last, that Hermann was never made either abbot or bishop, but remained simply a monk of Reichenau. If someone should prove, by arguments brought forward, that he also spent some time in the monastery of Saint Gall—as I know certain people, including Martin Crusius in the *Swabian Annals*, have believed—he will find me not contradicting the truth but strongly supporting him. Since, however, up to now, as I have also noted above, nothing has been found or devised that could establish their opinion, Hermann will remain the foster son and son of Saint Mark, the patron of the monks of Reichenau, whom he himself acknowledges, names as his patron, and venerates as a suppliant.

[Col. 0019]

## LITERARY NOTICE

(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini*)

Hermann, called “the Lame” (*Contractus*) because of the weakness of his limbs from which he suffered from childhood, was the son of the Count of Veringen and Sulgau in Swabia. He was first a monk of Saint Gall and afterward of Great or Rich Reichenau, of the Benedictine Order. Outstanding in intellect, he knew the Latin, Greek, and Arabic languages and cultivated his mind with various sciences. He died in the year 1054 on his estate at Aleshusen [Note: [Col. 0019D] See Pagi under the year 1054, no. 10.].

Trithemius discusses him in chapter 321 of *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, in II.84 of *Illustrious Benedictines*, and in chapter 41 of *De scriptoribus Germaniae*. Among more recent writers, to pass over countless celebrated names, are Nicolaus Hieronymus Gundlingius in volume I of the *Gundlingiana*, pp. 51 ff., and our own Blessed Johannes Hübner in the third century of the *Historical Library*, pp. 71 ff.

Among his works the chief is the *Chronicle of the Six Ages of the World*, which he brought down from the origins of things to the year of Christ 1054. Various editions exist, some fuller than others, since the author himself seems, as time passed, to have revised or expanded his work.

The first edition appeared from a manuscript of Saint Gall, edited by Johannes Sichardus [Col. 0020C] at Basel in 1529–1536, together with the *Chronicle* of Eusebius and Jerome, which Hermann carefully followed, as he also followed those of Prosper, Jordanes, and Bede, the latter ending in A.D. 726.

It was then printed in a single volume by Johannes Pistorius at Frankfurt, 1583–1613, and, under the care of the distinguished Burchard Gotthelf Struvius, at Regensburg in 1726, folio, with a continuation from 1054 to 1065.

From a better manuscript of the monastery of Saint George near Rottweil, Christian Urstisius published it among the German historical writers at Frankfurt in 1584 and 1670. In the first volume he published a fuller *Chronicle* of Hermann, placing the old edition in facing columns and adding, besides the continuation by an Anonymous from 1054 to 1065, another by Berthold, priest of Constance, from 1053 to 1100.

Finally, Henricus Canisius published this *Chronicle* more accurately and fully from a manuscript of the library of Saint Afra and Saint Ulrich at Augsburg, at Ingolstadt in 1601, quarto, in volume I of the *Antiquarian Readings* (volume III of the new edition, p. 193), with the earlier continuation extending to 1066. The editors of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, both the Cologne edition, volume XI, and the Lyon edition, volume XVIII, followed Canisius’s edition.

Daniel Nessel also promised, from an imperial manuscript, a continuation of this *Chronicle* up to the year 1347. Lambecius, volume II, p. 3, noted that the continuation from 1279 to 1310 was attributed to Wichard of Polheim, archbishop of Salzburg; he also mentions the continuation to 1347 on p. 70.

The rest of Hermann’s writings are recorded by the Anonymous of Melk, chapter 91, as follows:

1. *Deeds of Conrad and Henry.*

2. A poem *On the Contest between the Sheep and the Flax*, and another in the manner of Theodulus. Also another *On Contempt of the World*. For the poem *On the Virtues*, see Eckard, volume II of the *Corpus of the Middle Ages*, p. 6.

[Col. 0021B]

3. A book *On the Principal Rules of Computus*.

Trithemius adds to these:

4. *Lives of Several Saints.*

5. *On Physiognomy.*

6. *On the Construction or Measurement of the Astrolabe and on Its Usefulness*. Bernard Pez first published these two works in volume III, part II, of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, pp. 95 and 109. Because of these books, Hermann was regarded as the inventor of the astrolabe by William Durand, IV.22, and others. See the preface to the aforementioned work of Pez, p. IX. But it is known that the use of the astrolabe was already widespread before the time of Ptolemy.

7. *On Eclipses.*

8. *On the Squaring of the Circle.*

9. *On the Contest of Rhythmomachy.*

[Col. 0021C]

10. Honorius, IV.12, writes that he composed sweet-sounding song. The Anonymous of Melk says that in music he was more subtle than almost all modern writers and that he published many songs on music and sufficiently authoritative chants concerning the saints. [Col. 0022A] Trithemius says that, besides a work *On Music* and another *On the Monochord*, he composed beautiful chants and sequences in a sweet and orderly melody.

Among these are the very sweet song to the Blessed Virgin, *Salve, Regina* (“Hail, Queen”) [Note: [Col. 0021C] Others, less plausibly, attributed this to Ademar, bishop of Le Puy; hence “the Antiphon from Le Puy” in Alberic’s *Chronicle* under the year 1130, p. 263. Others attributed it to Peter of Monsoncio, bishop of Compostela around the year 960. [Col. 0022C] See Nicolaus Antonius, VI.14, *Bibliotheca Vetus Hispanica*, p. 579; *Works of Saint Bernard*, volume II of the new Mabillonian edition, Paris 1719, folio, pp. 738, 749.] and *Alma Redemptoris Mater* (“Kind Mother of the Redeemer”), as well as the others, of which there is a great number.

The sequence *Veni, Sancte Spiritus, et emitte caelitus lucis tuae radium* (“Come, Holy Spirit, and send down from heaven a ray of your light”) is also attributed to Hermann as its author. See Johannes Egon, *On the Illustrious Men of Rich Reichenau*, chapter 28, p. 689; volume I, part III, of Bernard Pez’s *Anecdotes*, p. 68; and Possevino in the *Sacred Apparatus*.

Much more is added both by the same Egon and by Johannes Metzler in chapter 47, *On the Illustrious Men of Saint Gall*, volume I, part III, of the same work by Pez, p. 582: *Ave, praeclara maris Stella* (“Hail, illustrious Star of the Sea”); the history, or offices, of the Annunciation and of Saint Mary Magdalene; the responsory *Simon Barjona* (“Simon Bar-Jonah”); and the sequence *Rex omnipotens* (“Almighty King”), for the Ascension of the Lord; as well as a history of the angels.

Finally, according to Trithemius, he translated into Latin several volumes of Greek philosophers and Arab astrologers. Among these Johannes Metzler names Aristotle’s rhetoric and poetry, translated from Arabic.

*He also wrote a hymn or rhythm in praise of the glory of Emperor Henry II, when, after expelling Obbo, the invader of the kingdom of Hungary, he restored Peter, the rightful prince. This song begins: “Let this voice strike up a melody.” See Alberic in his *Chronicle* under the year 1045.*

Muratorius published a historical encomium of this Hermann, perhaps written by one of his associates in the year 1054, from a Viennese manuscript, in *Antiquities*, volume III, p. 933. In it, besides the works of Contractus listed here [Col. 0022C], a little book is mentioned *On the Eight Capital Vices*, “playful in metrical variety, lyrical poetically” [sic].

## [LIFE OF HERMANN]

[Col. 0021]

## USSERMANN’S PROLOGUE TO THE LIFE OF HERMANN THE LAME

(*Sacred Germany: Preliminary Work*, volume I, at the end of Hermann’s *Chronicle*)

The manuscripts mentioned at the beginning of our work commence their continuation of Hermann’s *Chronicle* with his *Life*, written by Berthold, his disciple, as the Anonymous of Melk testifies (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, book 92), as does the manuscript of Muri, which notes at the end of Hermann’s *Chronicle*: “From here Berthold begins, and shortly afterward begins the *Life of Hermann*.” We have already spoken of this Berthold in the preliminary dissertation to the work.

We therefore judged that this *Life* ought to be placed before that continuation from our manuscripts, both so that we might possess in full the writings of this Berthold, which the Anonymous of Melk indicates, and also so that nothing concerning Hermann might be lacking here [Col. 0022D]. Ludovico Antonio Muratori did indeed publish it—quite similar to ours and communicated to him by the distinguished Garelli from the Imperial Viennese Library—in volume III of the *Italian Antiquities*, p. 933, under the title *Encomium of Hermann the Lame, Written by One of His Associates*. But these volumes are in the hands of very few people.

Indeed, this *Life* more appropriately deserves the name “brief encomium,” since, apart from very few circumstances of his life, praise of his virtues, and a short catalogue of his works, it contains scarcely anything of the particulars that the writers of other lives usually record [Col. 0023A]. We have therefore thought it worthwhile to present here, in summary, certain matters drawn from his own *Chronicle*.

Hermann himself reveals his birth and ancestry in various places. Under the year 1009, when he mentions the marriage of the younger Count Wolferad and Hiltrude, he declares himself their son and the brother of fourteen other children. Shortly afterward, under the following year, 1010, he reports the death of the elder Count Wolferad, his paternal grandfather, although he omits the family name. Everyone traces that family to the Counts of Veringen, among whom most writers require this elder Wolferad to be supplied.

Crusius (*Swabian Annals*, part II, book VI, chapter 9) extends that once very extensive county in Swabia from the Swabian Alps beyond the Danube. When the earlier line died out, it passed partly to the stewards of Waldburg and partly to the Zollerns [Col. 0023B].

The wife of this elder Wolferad, and Hermann’s grandmother, was Bertha, whose death he records under the year 1032. He writes that Bertha’s uncle was Reginbald, or Reginbold, who was killed in battle against the Hungarians near Augsburg under the year 955. He assigns to her as mother a sister of Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, whom under the year 971 he calls Luitgard. She was also the mother of Adalbero, whom his uncle Ulrich had designated as his successor in the episcopate.

Her third son, who was also Bertha’s father, is identified from chapter 15 of the *Life of Saint Ulrich* in Velserus as Manegold, the brother of the aforementioned Adalbero. It is therefore beyond doubt that all these men must be assigned to Luitgard, the sister of Saint Ulrich, who, according to the genealogical table in the same Velserus [Col. 0023C], p. 589, had only one such sister.

There is, however, greater difficulty in determining their father, or Luitgard’s husband. In the aforementioned genealogy this Luitgard is called the first wife of Burchard II, or the younger Burchard, duke of Swabia or Alemannia, who held the duchy from 957 to 973, as Hermann writes under those years. Yet nowhere in the entire *Life of Saint Ulrich*, nor in Stumpf (*Swiss Chronicle*, book IV, chapter 38), are children born to the said Luitgard by him mentioned.

Crusius (*Swabian Annals*, part II, book III, chapter 11) assigns Adalbero and Reginbold, along with others, to Burchard as sons by Luitgard, but does so rather fabulously, making Reginbold the first abbot of Saint Afra at Augsburg in 1012, although he had already fallen in battle in 955 [Col. 0023D]. Nor do I recall having read elsewhere about any sons of this Burchard. Indeed, in the new edition of *The Art of Verifying Dates*, volume III, p. 67, under the year 973, he is said to have died entirely without male offspring, as also in the *Chronicle of Petershausen*, published below.

According to Widukind of Corvey (*Annals*, book III, in Meibom, volume I of the *Writers*, p. 656), Burchard had already married by at least the year 955 the daughter of the king’s brother—namely Hadwig, daughter of Henry, duke of Bavaria and brother of King Otto I—whom writers commonly regard as the second wife of Duke Burchard. Thus Luitgard, his first wife, had already died, and he appears to have married her as a widow and mother of the sons mentioned, born from an earlier marriage.

Hermann, who knew his own ancestry as well as anyone could, reveals this man as her first husband under the year 971, when he calls Adalbero—apparently the younger one, brother of her earlier sons—the son of Peiere, Count, and of Luitgard, Saint Ulrich’s sister. But who was this Count Peiere? His name is certainly surrounded by profound silence among all the genealogists of that period. An ancient catalogue of proper names once used in Germanic Alemannia does record the name *Peir* (Goldast, volume II of the *Writers*, p. 105), which is quite close to this, but it does not add its Latin form.

I can scarcely avoid suspecting that Peringer or Peringerius lies hidden here. Herrgott produces him from the charters of the traditions of Saint Gall among the counts of Zürichgau, which was part of the duchy of Alemannia [Col. 0024B] (*Habsburg Genealogy*, volume II), under the years 942, 948, and 950. In the final instance he appears together with Duke Burchard himself. I do not know how Burchard could already have been called duke at that time, since Ludolf, son of King Otto, still held the duchy at least until 954, unless this is to be understood of Swabia alone or of another part of the Alemannian duchy—especially Zürichgau, where, as the son of the elder Duke Burchard, he perhaps obtained the title and authority together with his father’s possessions.

But these matters belong elsewhere. If, as we conjecture, this Peringer, count of Zürichgau, was Luitgard’s first husband, his marriage with Burchard must have been very brief, since according to what has been said it lasted only between the years 951 and 955. But these must not exceed the limits of conjecture. We shall be grateful to anyone who informs us more certainly about this Count Peiere [Col. 0024C].

Setting these matters aside, let us continue with the rest from Hermann. Of the three children of Luitgard mentioned above, Adalbero was a cleric and unmarried, and therefore could not have been Bertha’s father. Since Reginbald, who is called Bertha’s uncle, fell in battle as early as 955, he must have had another brother, Bertha’s father. This man necessarily must have been their brother Manegold.

The name Manegold, common in the Dilingan family, seems to have been introduced by Luitgard, through her son Manegold, into other families as well; at least it appears frequently afterward in the Veringen family.

Of this Manegold himself—certainly Luitgard’s son and the father of Bertha, Hermann’s grandmother—little or nothing recurs in the records. Manegold and Wolfrad are listed among the counts in a charter of Otto I for the church of Chur in 972, in Herrgott, cited work, no. 141. Of these, Wolfrad could easily have been Hermann’s grandfather, while Manegold could have been Bertha’s father and subsequently Wolfrad’s son-in-law.

The county of this Manegold, as it seems, in the district of Zürichgau is revealed by another charter of the same Otto for the cell of Meginrad, dated 975 (Herrgott, cited work, no. 143). We therefore suppose that Bertha, who died in 1032, was born from him, with the chronology by no means objecting; for she had already had a marriageable son in 1009 and must have been born around this time.

We consequently think that our conjecture about Peringer, likewise count of Zürichgau and Manegold’s father, is thereby all the more strengthened. But what the interpolator of the fourteenth-century Reichenau manuscript conjectured when he enrolled Luitgard, together with her sons, among the family of Helfenstein, we at least do not understand—unless he thought that their father too belonged to the same family, although one later than these times, or that their descendants derived their origin from it. To investigate this, however, is not part of our undertaking.

Thus far we have elucidated from Hermann’s *Chronicle* what we possess concerning the paternal line of our Hermann. From it we receive no comparable light by which to bring his maternal ancestry into view. Hermann reveals only this about it: under the year 1009 he calls his mother Hiltrude, the daughter of some Piligrin and Bertrada; in 1052 he mourns her death at approximately sixty-one years of age, saying that she was descended from a noble line [Col. 0025B].

Bucelinus, in the *Benedictine Menology* under 19 May, traces this maternal ancestry to the Counts of Thierstein, but, as is his custom, he produces no guarantor for his assertion. Nor do the documents so far recovered permit the origin of this family to be traced back to the tenth century, when Hiltrude was born. But there is no time to linger longer in speculation amid such great uncertainties.

We likewise learn from Hermann that Hiltrude’s marriage with the younger Wolferad was quite fruitful. Under the same year, 1009, he writes that fifteen children were born from it, although of these he mentions only one by name, Werinharius, born in 1021 and dead in Palestine before him in 1053. Of all the children, only seven are said to have survived their mother when she died in 1052 [Col. 0025C].

Among them must be counted Wolferad III, founder of the monastery of Isny in Allgäu [Col. 0026A], and his brother Manegold, together with their widowed sister Irmengard, about whom see the *Chronicle of Isny* (in P. Hess, *Preliminary Work for the Guelph Monuments*, p. 275). From this we also learn that Wolferad II, Hermann’s father, died in the year 1065, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, although others postpone his death to the year 1069, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November.

Among Hermann’s full brothers, the aforementioned Manegold shone most brightly. During the disastrous schism between priesthood and empire, in 1077 he was sent by the princes of the realm as envoy to Pope Gregory VII and also took part in the assembly at Forchheim. For this reason he is called a great lover of truth by Paul of Bernried in his *Life of Gregory VII*, who honors him with an extensive encomium (same work, no. 81) as a faithful follower and propagator of apostolic teaching:

> He was born from the noble and religious lineage of Blessed Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, and was instructed with exactness in every observance of the Christian religion by his most wise brother, namely Hermann the Lame. He advanced so far that, before his end—which he reached old and full of days—he shone forth through certain signs of virtue and was venerably distinguished by the gift of prophecy, as became evident in the killing of his son. For earlier he had written of him that, although far removed in place, he miraculously recognized through the Spirit that one of his sons, living in celibacy, had been killed, and even knew the day of his killing.

So much seemed worth saying about Hermann’s family, mostly from Hermann himself. Let readers add the rest [Col. 0026C]; we shall also provide several further details in the notes that follow.

[Col. 0025]

## THE LIFE OR ENCOMIUM OF HERMANN THE LAME, WRITTEN BY BERTHOLD, HIS DISCIPLE

(From Ussermann, cited above, p. 145)

Hermann—also a great hero—was the son of the religious Count Wolferad. From early childhood, in his outward person, he was afflicted with paralytic suffering and was helplessly contracted in all his limbs; but inwardly, in the vein of his intellect, he was wonderfully enlarged beyond all the men of his age. By his own understanding he grasped almost unaided the intricacies of every art and the subtleties of meter.

Always, from his earliest years [Note: [Col. 0025D] Hermann was born, according to his own testimony, on 18 June 1013, and was given over to letters on 15 September 1020, at the age of seven. He does not specify the place, which was one or the other of the monasteries of Reichenau or Saint Gall, both of which at that time were highly renowned for their schools. Trithemius adopts the latter (Hirsau Annals, volume I, p. 148), but with an obvious anachronism, when he says that our Hermann undertook the teaching office there after Helperic the scholastic, his teacher, who died in 1005—at which time Hermann had not yet been born. As to the place, at least, the writer of the *Chronicle of Melk* agrees with Trithemius (Pez, *Austrian Writers*, volume I, p. 224), recording the following under the year 1044: “Hermann the Lame was the son of the most noble Count of Veringen and first studied at the monastery of Saint Gall.” Hence Gundlingius reasonably believes that Hermann was first educated in the monastery of Saint Gall, then brought to Reichenau, and there made a monk. In the *Chronicle* he himself repeatedly presents himself as such, not as a monk of Saint Gall, especially under the year 1048. See the following note (5).] [Murat.: “devoting himself to this study and leisure, and becoming great through complete mastery of divine and secular letters, he was held in wonder and admiration by all who flocked from every direction to his instruction and teaching.”]

He was so horribly crippled throughout the joints of his limbs that, without someone to help him, he could not move himself in any direction from the place where he had been set down, nor even turn onto another side. Rather, once placed by his attendant in a certain carrying chair, he could scarcely sit in a bent position to perform any task [Col. 0027A].

In this condition, although his mouth, tongue, and lips were impaired, and he could somehow produce broken and scarcely intelligible sounds of words only with difficulty and slowly, he nevertheless did not fail his students. To them he was eloquent and diligent in teaching, cheerful with complete liveliness, prompt in disputation, and accommodating in answering their questions. At times he laboriously wrote something new with his fingers, which were likewise impaired [Note: [Col. 0027C] Thus Hermann was not so completely contracted that he could not use his hands, at least to some extent, in writing, although his *Chronicle*, and perhaps other works as well, seem to have been transcribed by his disciples from Hermann’s tablets]. At other times he read—either to himself or to others—or was always intensely occupied with exercises of usefulness or legitimate necessity.

A man truly without reproach, he considered nothing human alien to himself. Indeed, as an industrious executor of the humblest charity and charitable humility, an extraordinary guardian of patience [ed., *cultor sapientiae*, “cultivator of wisdom”], a most ready attendant of obedience [Col. 0027B], a lover of chastity, a preserver of virginal purity, a most cheerful cultivator of mercy [al., “of Mary”], an unconquerable champion and defender of true Catholic truth [ed., “a truly Catholic exponent of the most unblemished faith, a defender of truth, etc.”], and a highly approved teacher of the Christian religion, he was a man of no little modesty, sobriety, and continence—for from childhood he never ate meat. He was sufficiently devoted to psalmody, prayer, and the divine praises in the exercise of his office, both before and after he undertook the clerical state, which he had entered around his thirtieth year at the urging of the holy and wise man Bern, abbot of Reichenau [Auga] [Note: [Col. 0027C] From this single mention of Bern or Bernhard, abbot of Reichenau, Hermann’s monastic profession at Reichenau is abundantly confirmed; he himself also makes this clear enough in his *Chronicle*, writing, among other things, under the year 1048: “The emperor entered OUR REICHENAU on 24 April and caused the new basilica of Saint Mark, OUR PATRON, to be consecrated … and on the feast of that saint, a Litany Major was celebrated AMONG US,” etc. What Berthold writes here about Hermann’s clerical state plainly seems incapable of applying to a man so severely contracted and wholly unfit for the ministry of the altar. I therefore rather believe that these words should be understood of the monastic profession he undertook, which Mabillon frequently shows in the *Annals* and the *Acts of the Saints* to be designated by the term “clerical state” because of the tonsure. His Eminence Gerbert likewise published, from a ritual manuscript of Reichenau contemporary with this period, an order “for making a cleric or monk,” *Liturgia Alemannica*, vol. II, p. 93. Those who have written that Hermann was a canon are consequently easily shown to be mistaken, since there had certainly never been canons at Rich Reichenau. See Pagi, *Criticism of Baronius*, under the year 1054.] [Note: [Col. 0027D] Muratori reads “his thirty-eighth year,” which cannot refer to his age: for Bern had already died in 1048, when Hermann, born in 1013, was only thirty-five years old. It must therefore mean the year of Christ 1038. Which reading here is genuine cannot be determined.]—and he proved himself an orthodox administrator of an entire holy and honorable life.

Displaying himself to everyone as obliging and suitable, through every kind of effort, with extraordinary goodwill, affability, cheerfulness, and humanity—for he became all things to all people—he was loved by everyone. But as an opponent and indefatigable assailant of iniquity, injustice, every kind of depravity and wickedness, and whatever is done against God, he continued happily to the end of his life.

## HERMANN’S STUDIES

He therefore composed and arranged, with considerable clarity, an account of computation, its rules, and several arguments, in which he surpassed all his predecessors by no small degree. Among other things, he also established [ed., “discovered”] highly reliable rules concerning the moon’s natural illumination, by which it may be known with complete certainty at what hour of the day or night it is illuminated by the sun.

[Col. 0028B] He likewise devised highly reliable rules for determining a lunar eclipse, and he also wrote, by natural reasoning and orderly treatment through numbers and figures, a certain geometry of no small usefulness, so far as that art is concerned. No one among his predecessors possessed equal knowledge and subtlety in this field.

He also composed and set to music complete historical chants—for there was no more accomplished musician—concerning Saint George; Saints Gordian and Epimachus; Saint Afra the martyr; Saint Magnus the confessor; and Saint Wolfgang the bishop. He rendered and composed them in euphonious settings of remarkable sweetness and elegance, besides very many other works of this kind. [Note: [Col. 0027D] By these are meant rhythmic compositions, prose pieces, or even sequences fashioned in honor of these saints, of which, according to Trithemius under the year 1005, he published several without a fixed number. His book on the monochord, which the same Trithemius cites in book 3 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 321, was published by His Eminence Gerbert among the musical writers, vol. II, p. 124, from a Viennese manuscript. [Col. 0028C]]

He laboriously compiled this little book of chronicles, from the Incarnation of the Lord down to his own year, from sources of every kind. [Note: [Col. 0028C] We discuss this below in the preliminary Dissertation. Since he calls it “this book,” we rightly conjecture that this *Chronicle* was indeed collected by Hermann from other writers, but was written out by Berthold from his notes down to the year of Hermann’s death, 1054; Berthold then added this *Life*, together with its continuation, from his own material. Moreover, the writer himself indicates that this catalogue of Hermann’s works is incomplete, when he says that he composed very many other works besides. Trithemius certainly enumerates more in the passages cited just above. The writer of the *Chronicle of Melk*, in Pez (*Scriptores Austriaci*, vol. I, under the year 1044), adds several others. Father Bernhard Pez (*Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, part II, p. 951) published a book written by Hermann the Contracted, *On the Measurement of the Astrolabe*, found in the library of Saint Peter at Salzburg; from its opening it is plainly recognized as the very work indicated by Trithemius, chapter 321 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers* [Col. 0028D]. There, however, Trithemius attributes to Hermann three books *On the Construction of the Astrolabe* and only one *On the Usefulness of the Astrolabe*; Pez, on the other hand, has two books on the latter subject (*loc. cit.*, p. 107), as Trithemius also corrected himself in the *Annals* under 1035. Hermann dedicated the former work, *On the Measurement of the Astrolabe*, to one of his friends designated only by the initial B., who is undoubtedly this same Berthold, whom there likewise, as shortly below, he addresses as his “soul.” In the preface to volume I of the same work, fol. XXXVIII, Pez further states that he saw another codex in the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, containing a little book of Hermann’s poems—undoubtedly the Contracted’s—addressed to nuns; perhaps Trithemius mentions it only generally among his poems. It is, however, highly credible that, as commonly befalls learned men, several little works were falsely attributed to him although he was not their author, since he died already in his forty-first year and was moreover so severely contracted.] [Col. 0029A] He also described most beautifully the deeds of the emperors Conrad and Henry. [Note: [Col. 0029C] The Anonymous Mellicensis and Otto of Freising likewise attest this in the *Chronicle*, book VI, chapter 33: “Moreover, Hermann the Contracted discussed quite brilliantly the deeds and virtues both of Henry [III] and of his father Conrad [II] in a certain little book that he dedicated to them.” From this work was taken what the same Otto has in the same place, chapter 32: hence comes Hermann the Contracted’s poem on the aforementioned triumph of Henry III over the Hungarians, which begins: “Let this voice strike up its melody.” Would that some diligent librarian might one day search carefully through his repositories and bring it to public light for the benefit of the history of our homeland.]

In addition to these works, he composed a charming little book on the eight principal vices, lyrical in its metrical variety and sufficiently elaborated in poetic form. In constructing horological, musical, and mechanical instruments, he was inferior to no one. In these and in very many similar pursuits, which it would take considerable time to enumerate, he devoted himself continually and wholly, as far as his bodily weakness allowed.

At last, when the mercy of God deigned to free his holy soul from the wearisome prison of this world, he was seized by pleurisy and, wasting away for ten days, suffered almost continuously and terribly under this fatal attack. Then one day, very early in the morning, after the morning office had been celebrated, I—whom he regarded as more intimate than the others—approached the sick man’s bed and asked him whether he was somewhat better. He replied:

“Do not, I say, do not ask me about that; rather, pay close attention to what I am going to tell you, since I place no little confidence in you. I shall certainly die shortly; I shall neither live nor recover. Therefore I commend my sinful soul uniquely and exceedingly to you and to all my others. For throughout this entire night I had been carried away in a kind of ecstasy, and it seemed to me that, with the memory and knowledge by which we are accustomed to run attentively through the Lord’s Prayer, reading and immediately rereading it, I was likewise reading through the *Hortensius* of Tullius Cicero, and then the sense and wording of the material that I had proposed to dictate concerning the vices, as though I had already written it out, and many other things of that kind. Under the impulse and prompting of this reading, the whole present world, with all that belongs to it, and this mortal life itself, have become so contemptible and wearisome to me; and, conversely, that future and non-transitory world, and that eternal and immortal life, are objects of such ineffable desire and love, that all these transitory things are reckoned by me as entirely worthless and empty, and are treated as trifles. I am weary of living.”

I was greatly astonished at the oracle of this vision and speech, and, as was fitting at the departure of so dear a friend and such a teacher, I could scarcely restrain myself, overwhelmed in tears and shaken by lamentation, though in a sufficiently unbecoming manner. Immediately he rebuked me, as though zealously correcting me, turning a trembling and reproachful gaze upon me in my foolishness:

“Do not, my dear soul, do not weep over me; rather, rejoice with me and congratulate me with dancing. Please take my tablets, and whatever remains to be written in them, carefully correct first of all; then entrust what has been written to those who may deem it worthy. As for yourself, thinking every day that you will die, prepare yourself with all your strength and reflection for that same journey, because you do not know on what day or at what hour you will follow me, your dearest friend.”

With these words he fell silent.

Thereafter, as happens, his weakness grew worse from day to day, and, alas, he was brought to the end. Already wholly suspended toward heavenly things, after a most pure confession of sins from his entire heart and after receiving the Eucharist of Christ with the greatest devotion, while many brothers, friends, and familiars who had gathered to visit him were psalmodizing, praying, and weeping together, that happy and incomparable man of God, happy in the consummation that alone he had always desired above all else, breathed his last in complete blessedness on 24 September. [Note: [Col. 0029D] This day is 24 September. The Bollandists record Hermann among the saints passed over on that date, as they also do on 19 July, the day after his birth, on which Bucelinus records him in the Benedictine *Martyrology* with the title “blessed,” although he has nowhere yet received ecclesiastical cult. The author does not explicitly state the year of his death, being content to note that he brought his *Chronicle* down to the year of his death; as shown in the Dissertation, this indicates 1054. As for what Trithemius writes under the year 1043 (*Annals*, vol. I, p. 181): “In the aforesaid year Hermann the Contracted, a monk of our order from the counts of Veringen and of the monastery of Saint Gall in Swabia, a man most learned in every branch of literature, dies with a reputation for sanctity … he gloriously presided over the school of the monks in that place for more than thirty-eight years”—the statements thus far made prove that this is erroneous both concerning the place of his residence and the year of his death, as well as the years of his direction of the schools, especially since Hermann died at the age of only forty-one in his monastery at Reichenau and was afterward buried in the monument of his ancestors at Alleshausen. His Reichenau monastic profession, against Trithemius, was ably defended by Joannes Ego in his book *On the Illustrious Men of Reichenau*, chapter 28, in Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, part III, p. 683, where further material concerning his *Chronicle* is given. [Col. 0030C]]

He was buried with solemn and dutifully lamentable rites and rested in peace, leaving all his people to grieve greatly at his estate near Alleshausen. [Note: [Col. 0030C] Hermann himself calls the place “the villa Aleshusin” under the year 1052, writing that he had buried his mother there beneath the chapel of Saint Ulrich, in a tomb that she had prepared for herself. Since that place was his estate, as it was Hermann’s, it was doubtless situated in the county of Veringen. If the former very extensive boundaries of this county were known with certainty, there would be no reason to doubt the location of this place. For two villages bearing almost the same name occur in this part of Swabia. One, now called Alschausen or Altznhausen, is the seat of the provincial commander of the bailiwick of Alsace and Burgundy, which passed to the Teutonic Order in 1264; it lies nearer Lake Constance, in the rural deanery of Saulgau. The other is Aleshausen, near Lake Plumbarium or Buchau, in the rural deanery of Biberach. This very similarity of names may have led writers astray, so that they substituted one place for the other. Bruschius distinguishes the two places. Writing about the bishoprics of Germany, he assigns the former to Hermann’s burial and testifies that in 1548, at Lambert, bishop of Constance, he was shown Hermann’s tender bones, already beginning to crumble into ashes. When consulted on this matter, the noble D. Ignatius Depra of Plain, counselor of the aforementioned commandery, replied that, apart from the common tradition that Hermann was buried there, he had found nothing in its archives except two copied documents concerning the transfer of certain of Hermann’s relics. According to these, in 1631 three bones of the body of Blessed Hermann the Contracted were transferred from his tomb, preserved at Altschausen, to the monastery of Ochsenhausen; likewise, on 18 May 1626, others were transferred to Weingarten, namely the sacred crown of his head with an arm and several other holy bones, which Bucelinus lists in his *Martyrology*. It therefore seems impossible to doubt the existence of Blessed Hermann’s tomb at Altschausen. Yet the same Bruschius writes that Hermann’s mother Hiltrude was buried at Alleshausen, in the *Chronology of the Monasteries of Germany*, in his history of the Premonstratensian canons’ monastery at Marchtal. There it is reported that Abbot Jodocus, elected in 1461, purchased Alleshausen near Lake Buchau or Plumbarium, “where the mother of Hermann the Contracted lies.” Bucelinus likewise notes this in his own hand in the margin under Hermann in 1052, distinguishing Alleshausen, under the rule of the abbot of Marchtal and the burial place of Hiltrude, from the knightly estate of Altschausen. But after letters were sent there, I learned that no trace of this tomb or of the chapel of Saint Ulrich beneath which she was buried, nor even any memory of the event, could be found. Although this place certainly belonged to the county of Veringen and was not very far from its principal town of that name, it was not as distant as Altschausen in the Allgäu. For the present, however, let the statements of these writers retain their authority. At least we cannot persuade ourselves that Hermann, who died at Reichenau, wished to be buried in another place outside it rather than where he knew his mother had been buried—namely, at the place called Alleshausen in both accounts, from which Alleshausen and finally Altschausen could easily have been formed. We judge that this place, as the more famous one, should be preferred to the other, which is obscure and merely a filial church under the parish of Seekirch, as the burial place of both mother and son. But enough concerning Hermann for the present. [Col. 0032D]]

# [CHRONICLE]

[Col. 0031]

# USERMANN’S PRELIMINARY DISSERTATION ON HERMANN THE CONTRACTED’S CHRONICLE, ITS EDITIONS, MANUSCRIPT COPIES, AND THE METHOD OF THIS NEW EDITION

(*Sacred Germany: Preliminary Work*, vol. I, p. 10)

[Col. 0031A] It is universally acknowledged among scholars that Hermann, commonly called “the Contracted” because almost all his limbs were paralyzed, is too well known to require much commendation. He is everywhere celebrated in the praises of learned men. Among them, Joannes Trithemius, in the *Annals of Hirsau* under the year 1005, calls him “among all the doctors of Germany, the most celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, astronomer, poet, musician, and theologian of his age.” In the same author’s *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, Hermann is described as “a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and, in secular literature, the most learned of all the learned men of his time; highly skilled in three languages, Greek, Latin, and Arabic, and not ignorant of Hebrew; in life and conduct also most devout.” Yet in neither place does Trithemius list among Hermann’s compositions a certain *Chronicle*. He does so correctly in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he attributes to Hermann a book *On the Six Ages of the World*—the title under which it is still designated in printed editions, although incorrectly, as we shall explain below.

Even before Trithemius, the author of the Augsburg *Chronicle*, who died toward the end of the eleventh century, in which period Hermann died, calls him under the year 1054 “the wonder of his age and pre-eminent over all in acuteness of intellect.” The Anonymous Mellicensis, an author of approximately the same period, says in chapter 91, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “Hermann the Contracted, a Swabian, proved himself an exceptionally subtle philosopher in computation.” After listing several of his works, he adds: “He also composed a chronicle and the deeds of Conrad and Henry [the emperors], in all of which his excellence shone forth sufficiently.”

This *Chronicle*, just as it deservedly surpasses his other works because of its usefulness for the history of his homeland, especially that of the Middle Ages, is also almost the only one among all of them—apart from a few exceptions—to have survived. It provided later historians, and especially chroniclers, with a kind of foundation and source for their annals. From it they generally drew what belonged to earlier times, and they either inserted their own material, better known to them according to differences of place and time, into the same work, or omitted particular matters less suited to their regions. It would be immense as well as superfluous to list here chronicles constructed in this way upon Hermann, since the matter can be observed everywhere in collections of chronicles.
