Just as those before Hermann generally placed the Venerable Bede’s book *On the Six Ages of the World* in the position of a foundation, so those after him—at least in our regions—undertook to build their chronicles upon Hermann. And rightly, it seems. For whether we consider events nearer to or contemporary with his own age, many things would surely be unknown to us today if his industry had not preserved them for the memory of posterity; or whether we attend to the reckoning of time, his is generally more accurate than the others, except when a scribe’s errant pen has prefixed a false date or year. Finally, by embracing much in a brief and concise narrative, Hermann, above all, upheld the true fathers of chronography, if anyone did.

But let others judge these matters. For the present, our task is to offer a brief preliminary discussion of the editions of this *Chronicle*, its manuscript copies, and the method of this edition.

## § I.—Editions of Hermann’s Chronicle

**I.** Several editions of this celebrated Hermannian *Chronicle* have appeared to date, but they differ so greatly from one another—being interpolated or abridged—that it is entirely uncertain and doubtful which of them presents Hermann’s genuine work. We shall explain later the principal source of this great diversity, after first saying something about the individual editions.

**II.** The first to publish Hermann, together with other writers, was Joannes Sichardus at Basel in 1529, apparently from a manuscript of Saint Gall. Much proves, however, that this manuscript had been altered and repeatedly interpolated. It begins with the creation of the world, and the entire work, entitled *On the Six Ages of the World*, was copied almost word for word from the Venerable Bede down to the time of Christ’s birth. Hermann is said in his *Life* to have begun his *Chronicle* from that point; this is also clear from the fact that from then onward he differs considerably from Bede. Those who regard Hermann merely as Bede’s compiler therefore depart greatly from the truth, as we shall see below. Although Sichard’s edition subsequently agrees in most respects with the Reichenau manuscript, it nevertheless contains many interpolations, records events under other years, and repeatedly omits considerable material [Col. 0033C] down to the year 1040, where it again agrees with the Reichenau manuscript.

**III.** Joannes Pistorius reproduced this first edition of Sichard word for word in his *Collection of Writers*, likewise at Basel in 1536, and again in the edition printed at Frankfurt in 1613. He too was without the assistance of any manuscript copy. The same judgment must therefore be passed on both editions; Gundling rightly assigned them little value. They also agree in carrying Hermann’s *Chronicle* from the creation of the world down to the year 1066 from the birth of Christ, immediately appending Berthold’s continuation to Hermann without any mention of Berthold, although Hermann had ceased to write and live in 1054.

**IV.** Burchard Gotthelf Struve later published at Regensburg, in 1726, a Hermann corrected through new labors and enlarged from the editions of Urstisius and Canisius. Its value must be assessed from the editions cited and shortly to be indicated. This edition too, like the earlier one of Pistorius, runs from the creation of the world to the year 1066, without any mention whatsoever of a continuation.

**V.** The third edition, and a better one—indeed, the best of Hermann’s editions to date—is owed to Christoph Urstisius. He inserted it in volume I of his *German Writers*, published at Frankfurt in 1587 and 1670. There he presented Hermann as printed by Sichard from an ancient exemplar of the monastery of Saint Gall, as he himself believed, doubtless led to this conclusion by Sichard, who incorrectly asserted in his preface that Hermann’s annals had been written in the monastery of Saint Gall. Urstisius achieved one unusual thing: alongside the earlier text, he added in a second column a different text beginning with the year 378 after Christ, taken from a twelfth-century manuscript of the monastery of Saint George, now at Villingen, which perished in the fire together with our monastery of Saint Blasien in 1768. Urstisius judged this manuscript worthy of simultaneous publication because it was much fuller than the printed texts and more carefully corrected. In this judgment, however, he was considerably deceived, since it is merely a certain abridgment of the genuine Hermann, and neither complete nor sufficiently consistent with the *Chronicle* itself in various places, as we shall demonstrate below when discussing the manuscripts. Urstisius’s edition does, however, have the advantage of appending two continuations of Hermann: one shorter, extending from 1054 to 1066, and another fuller one extending to 1100. We shall discuss these in what follows.

**VI.** Hermann’s *Chronicle* could therefore hitherto appear defective, or at least insufficiently exact in the printed editions, until Heinrich Canisius suddenly published a much enlarged and more complete version in volume I of the old edition of his *Ancient Readings* in 1601. From Canisius’s edition it subsequently passed into the Cologne *Library of the Fathers*, volume XI, and the Lyons edition, volume XVIII; it was reprinted by Jacques Basnage in volume III of the new edition in 1725, from which P. Bouguet, a Maurian monk, recently published excerpts in his extensive *Collection of Writers on Frankish Affairs*, volumes III and following.

Canisius himself had drawn his *Chronicle* from a manuscript of the Augsburg monastery of Saints Ulrich and Afra. On its title page he asserts that it is very different from and much richer than the Urstisian edition. This was also why it was initially received with the common applause of scholars. Nor was this undeserved, since it contained very much that was missing from the printed editions then available. But the more perceptive soon noticed that the much-praised bulk had grown so large chiefly through interpolations inserted into the Augsburg manuscript without any discrimination and then published without textual criticism; many of these additions were either later than Hermann or at least foreign to his hand. Hence a number of learned men, including the Bollandist hagiographers in volume I of the September *Acta Sanctorum*, p. 540, and volume VI of the June volume, appendix, p. 89, judged that Canisius’s edition—beset, moreover, by countless errors—was less trustworthy, and that the earlier editions, although less extensive, should be preferred to it as more genuine and less exposed to so many errors. A review of the manuscript copies, which we undertake here, will make this clearer.

## § II.—Manuscript Copies

**VII.** Setting aside the Schardian manuscript, about which we have already spoken, we shall examine the others, especially the shorter manuscript of Saint George, from which Urstisius partly prepared his edition, and the fuller Augsburg manuscript, from which Canisius fashioned his complete edition.

Regarding the former, since it has now been lost and was not copied with sufficient care by Urstisius, it would be impossible to form a judgment unless a comparison instituted between Urstisius’s edition and another manuscript—now preserved in the Electoral Library at Munich and almost entirely similar to the former—provided us with more reliable information. The learned Oefelius describes this manuscript (vol. I of the *Bavarian Writers*, p. 652) as a parchment codex in quarto format which, besides Hermann’s *Chronicle*, also contains the continuation of his continuator Berthold of Constance—called Bernoldus in the manuscript—from the year 1053 to 1100.

It is contemporary with its authors and was written by Bernold himself. The script and erasures, as well as the parchment repeatedly scraped clean, all seem clearly to indicate that the text was produced by the same hand, though expanded, altered, and corrected with ink of a different kind and at a different time. This is the same judgment that Urstisius passed on his Saint George manuscript as on the Munich manuscript of Bernold: that the author, by repeatedly polishing the work—like a fetus initially formed in some fashion and afterward licked into shape—made it more refined and exact.

Oefelius continues his discussion of his manuscript:

“The illuminated title of the codex further confirms the conjecture. It reads: ‘THESE ARE THE CHRONICLES OF BERNOLD, WHICH HE HANDED OVER TO THE MONASTERY OF THE LORD SAVIOR,’ namely, Schaffhausen. What those chronicles written by Bernold are is sufficiently shown by what is written there in very small letters in the margin: ‘Contained are the authors of the chronicles: Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Dionysius, Jordanes, Bede, and Hermann of our own time—that is, the eleventh century—and thereafter OUR [book], written in the hand of Bernold himself, describing his own time.’”

All these works appear under the name of Bernold’s *Chronicles* in this autograph manuscript, partly because they were written by him in one volume, but partly and principally because he reduced them, as it were, into a compendium from Hermann. Bernold did not reproduce Hermann’s *Chronicle* itself, but only its epitome; to this he then attached his own continuation—or rather his own *Chronicle*—in a single continuous narrative, which he identifies here under the designation “OUR BOOK.” More will be found about this in the preliminary investigations concerning Bernold, where he will be vindicated for the monks of Saint Blasien.

**VIII.** From this Munich manuscript, Oefelius gave variant readings for Urstisius’s Saint George manuscript, beginning with the year 378, at which point Urstisius began his text. He was doubtless guided by what is written in Bernold’s autograph manuscript after the year 377, and perhaps was also found in the Saint George manuscript:

“Thus far Eusebius and Jerome brought their chronicles. From here to the year 1054 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Lord Hermann brought his *Chronicle*.”

But since, according to the author of Hermann’s *Life*, Hermann began his *Chronicle* from the Incarnation of the Lord, even though he drew most of it from Eusebius and Jerome, there can be no doubt that the material extending from there to the year 378 also belongs to this *Chronicle*, in the same way that what follows the year 378 is attributed to Hermann, although it was taken from Prosper and other chroniclers.

[Col. 0036A] Therefore, in order to possess the complete shorter Hermann derived from Bernold, we also took care to obtain the variant readings preceding the aforementioned year. The most reverend and learned D. Hart, serving as deputy director of the Electoral Library at Munich, most courteously sent these excerpts, which he had made with the utmost diligence and checked against Urstisius’s ancient manuscript. We publicly offer him our thanks here.

From his letters we further learn that Bernold’s manuscript, like Sichard’s, begins with the six ages of the world, which belong to the Venerable Bede, but that from the birth of the Lord to the year 378 it differs considerably from Bede, as will be apparent to the reader from our edition.

The same Saint George manuscript also contained another small *Chronicle*, extending from the birth of Christ to the year 1153, written by the same original hand and thereafter continued by various hands to the year 1627. Its earlier part, subsequently interpolated by later hands, was only a summary or epitome, chiefly of Hermann the Contracted. We found several fragments of it still gathered among our notes; insofar as they concern the history of the homeland, they will be inserted in their proper places under the title *Chronicle of Saint George*.

**IX.** Having now discovered the source of the Saint George manuscript—which, apart from a few interpolations, is Bernold himself, whom we are preparing to publish—we also seem to have detected the origins of the Muri and Engelberg manuscripts. These two celebrated monasteries of the Swiss Benedictine Congregation are rightly counted among the religious colonies of our monastery of Saint Blasien. The records of Muri itself do not deny its origin from Saint Blasien (*History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, p. 247). According to them, under Gisilbert, abbot of Saint Blasien, Luitfrid, a monk of that monastery, was made abbot of Muri; Bernold reports his death in the *Chronicle* under the year 1096.

This manuscript appears to have been copied at Saint Blasien under that abbot and then sent from there to the brothers at Muri. For it ends at the year 1091, around which time the colony was transferred from Saint Blasien to that place, and there is no mention whatsoever in it of the monastery of Muri. A writer would certainly not have omitted such a reference had he written the manuscript at that location.

To speak accurately, however, the *Chronicle* contained in this manuscript should be regarded less as Hermann’s than as a compilation gathered from various chroniclers. Its beginning with the year 144 after Christ seems to point to Bernold, since the earlier years are absent down to 378; from that point onward it generally agrees with him so exactly that the material occasionally noted in the margin of the Munich Bernold manuscript is usually inserted into the text of the Murau manuscript, which also records, under the relevant year, Bernold’s words:

“Thus far Eusebius and Jerome brought their chronicles; from here to the year 1054 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Lord Hermann brought his *Chronicle*.”

Who would not, after this, expect the text of Hermann—either the shorter version from Bernold, as far as this point, or the fuller and genuine version from the Augsburg manuscript, as occurs from the year 1045 to the end? Yet from this point onward Hermann is more heavily interpolated than anywhere else, especially from Regino of Prüm, and sometimes from other sources as well, apparently by different writers. The same event is often attached to different wording and different years, with no regard whatsoever for the sequence of events or the order of time.

After the year 906, an illuminated heading does indeed read: “Thus far the chronicles of Regino,” followed by “The chronicles of Hermann.” But this is the same empty promise: what follows that year is no more Hermann’s than what precedes it, but belongs to that anonymous writer whom Pistorius appends to Regino as his continuator. Nor does the manuscript present even this work complete, for in the middle of the text it breaks off under the year 939 and thereafter presents Hermann beginning with the year 940, in an even more contracted form, as will shortly be described in the Gottweig manuscript.

The Engelberg manuscript has exactly the same character as the Murau manuscript and appears to have been copied from that very manuscript. Neither could serve our purposes in this edition except in the final decade of Hermann’s work, with which they agree for the first time. In this way they preserved Hermann for us complete through the final three years, whereas he is defective at that point in the Augsburg manuscript and in the other copies transcribed from it.

**X.** The material found in both manuscripts under the year 741 deserves notice, although according to Pagi it belongs under the year 725:

“Thus far the Venerable Bede the priest brought his *Chronicle* in the larger book *On Times* … But many things have been interwoven from the chronicles of a certain Regino, abbot of Bremen [read: Prüm], who began from the Incarnation of the Lord and extended his work to 906. From this point onward—that is, from the year 727—the material that follows was taken from the writings of FOUR AUTHORS, namely, the aforementioned abbot Regino of Prüm, Lord Hermann the Contracted, his disciple Berthold, and Lord Bernold, priest of Saint Blasien.”

Here the sources from which the compilers of this manuscript drew their material are indicated together, and the distinction between Hermann’s two continuators is clearly noted: Berthold, his disciple, and Bernold, priest of Saint Blasien. Until now, the two have been wrongly confused into one Berthold of Constance.

**XI.** Finally, these manuscripts append what is read at the end of the first book of Regino’s *Chronicle* under the year 741:

“Thus far the reckoning of the Romans; from this point onward that of the Franks.”

These words seem more properly to belong under this year, when, after the death of his father Charles, Pippin, the founder of the second line of Frankish kings, began to rule the Franks, first in fact and then, in 752, also under the royal title. They are assigned in most printed editions to the year 726, however, a date entirely unsuitable to the time—namely, the period of Charles Martel, when the Merovingian kings of the first line were still ruling.

Although the Roman kingdom had otherwise already come to an end in Gaul in 484, after Clovis defeated Syagrius and transferred the kingdom from that point to the Merovingians.

Moreover, at the front of this Muri codex there is bound another brief Chronicle, written by a different hand but in a script of the same twelfth century, extending from the year 398 to 1175. It is arranged in such a way that it contains, as it were, an epitome first of Hermannus Contractus down to the year 1054, then of Bernold down to 1100, whom it subsequently continues down to 1175.

It was inserted into [or: written in] chronological tables [the reading *opactarum* is uncertain]. Hence it often happened that, when the space allotted to a given year was insufficient, the remainder was entered under other vacant years, either before or after it. We have therefore extracted these entries from there and placed them in their proper locations. We have entitled that Chronicle the Chronicle of St. Blaise, because it frequently reports matters especially concerning this monastery after Hermannus’s time, usually without mentioning its name; this fact itself sufficiently proves that its author was a member of that monastery and wrote his Chronicle there. For when he discusses other monasteries, he identifies them by their proper names.

The illustrious Gerbert discusses it at length in his *History of the Black Forest*, volume I, pp. 390 ff. Following the distinguished Father Mauritius Van der Meer, historiographer of the monastery of Rheinau, he conjectures that its author was Blessed Frowin, formerly a monk of St. Blaise who was appointed abbot of Engelberg around the year 1147. There, as is also recorded in the same work, p. 421, he died in 1178, leaving behind codices written in his own hand. The learned author believed that he had detected that same hand in this Chronicle as well.

[Col. 0038C] Yet although the monasteries of Einsiedeln and St. Blaise may both claim this Frowin as their own, since he may successively have belonged to both, it may still remain doubtful whether he was the author of this Chronicle. For what reason would he have made no mention whatsoever of his own monastery, of which he had been requested to become abbot, but only of his St. Blasian monastery?

He does indeed appear there under the year 1120, but in a note added by a later hand we read:

> In that same year this cell was begun by Abbot Adschelinus, or more correctly Adelhelmus, who in the year 1124, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, received from Callistus II a privilege of confirmation, and likewise in the year 1125 from the Emperor Henry V.

(See Herrgott, *Genealogia Habsburgica*, volume II, p. 143.) In that emperor’s charter this monastery is said to have been honorably constructed during the time of Henry IV, king of the Romans. Since Henry had already died in 1106, this cell must already have been constructed by then, and therefore cannot have been begun only in 1120, as the interpolation just mentioned incorrectly states. That interpolation is also absent from the Engelberg copy of this Chronicle itself. There, however, other entries have been inserted by a second hand, such as: under 1125, the death of Conrad of Seldenburen, the founder; under 1131, the death of Blessed Adelhelmus; under 1178, “Lord Frowin, our venerable abbot, the second, died”; likewise under 1197, the death of Blessed Berthold; under 1125, Henry I; under 1241, Henry II; and under 1250, Werner, celebrated abbots of that monastery.

These entries, therefore, seem to have been added later to the Chronicle of the St. Blasian author by some Engelberg monk, whether after Frowin’s death or after Frowin had been appointed to the Engelberg abbacy. Certainly, in the Chronicle mentioned above, the last reference to St. Blaise occurs under the year 1143. From their domestic records, especially their Necrology, our highly learned Einsiedeln colleagues infer that Frowin then assumed the governance of the monastery of Engelberg; in that Necrology the Frowinian, or earlier, hand ends under the year 1143.

### XII

Among the codices of Hermannus’s Chronicle that have so far been surveyed, so to speak, as domestic copies, the Gottweig codex must also be counted. It was found in the famous monastery of that name in Lower Austria, into which likewise the first colony of brothers was sent from St. Blaise, under the leadership of Abbot Hartmann, as Bernold relates in his Chronicle under the year 1094.

This codex has the particular feature that it begins with the year 726 and presents a much shorter compendium of Hermannus than Bernold’s, while from the year 940 to 1052, where it ends, it agrees almost word for word with the Muri and Engelberg codices. Unless I am mistaken, the Melk codex published by Father Hieronymus Pez, volume I of the *Scriptores rerum Austriacarum*, p. 163, was transcribed from this one. Hermannus’s Chronicle is likewise contained there from the Incarnation of the Lord.

For from the year 726 to 1040, where the Gottweig codex begins to become fuller, it agrees with it exactly, except for certain details concerning the monasteries of Reichenau and St. Gall. The Melk codex frequently omits these and inserts in their place particular events from its own Austria, while the rest of the text remains unchanged. Another Gottweig codex, containing a fuller version of Bernold, will be discussed elsewhere.

[Col. 0039C] ### XIII

Since all the codices of Hermannus that we have so far reviewed agree so closely with one another—not merely in general matters, but especially in their accounts of particular affairs of the diocese of Constance—they clearly seem to have been written in that same diocese. Indeed, as we may reasonably conjecture from what has already been said, they were written in our monastery of St. Blaise and by several authors, with Bernold leading the way by reducing Hermannus’s Chronicle to a kind of abridgment. Later writers either abbreviated it still further, interpolated it to some extent from other chronicles, or copied it in the form in which Bernold had abridged it.

For at that time monks devoted themselves almost exclusively to copying books, and especially chronicles; hence there arose such a mass of chronicles, most of them composed by monks. From this literary storehouse, brothers sent out to establish monasteries abroad were supplied, among other necessities, with codices, which they carried with them to these new colonies. Since the monasteries mentioned above were colonies from St. Blaise, they must be considered to have received their codices from there, especially since all of them bear the age of the monasteries’ foundations. Thus what the mother-house lost through adverse circumstances and frequent fires, the diligence of her daughters preserved and later generously returned to her.

### XIV

After these domestic codices and the brief abridgments of Hermannus comes the fuller Augsburg version, whose publication Canisius undertook. It is written on paper and was copied from a Reichenau codex only toward the end of the fourteenth century. This is evident partly from the script itself, but chiefly from the very frequent interpolations, much later than Hermannus, which successively crept into the Reichenau codex, both in the margins and in the remaining blank spaces, and from there all migrated together into the Augsburg copy and thence, without any critical examination, into Canisius.

The Augsburg copy also frequently differs from its Reichenau exemplar. In it events are often assigned to a different year, entire clauses are sometimes omitted, and sometimes they are even transcribed incorrectly. One example will suffice, at least as it appears in Basnage’s edition.

Under the year 1021, the Reichenau codex reads:

> Irmentrudis, the venerable abbess of Buchau, died, and Abarhild the abbess succeeded her.

In its place, the Augsburg manuscript, and Canisius from it, give a statement with the opposite meaning:

> Irmentrudius, abbot of Rrdchau, died, and Abarhild the abbot succeeded him.

This led Mabillon—and what a man!—so far astray that in volume IV of the *Annales Benedictini*, p. 279, he conjectured from it an otherwise unknown monastery whose memory had already vanished.

Nor was he content to have committed this same error only once. Under the year 1027, where the Reichenau codex has “Hildegard, abbess of Buchau,” gross negligence once again produces: “Hiltigart, abbot of Buchau.”

Several further errors of this kind, which cannot be tolerated, are noted below in § III, no. 19; nevertheless, readers will easily detect them all. To the accumulation of error and deception was added the fact that Canisius published his codex—already sufficiently corrupt from elsewhere—with still greater errors scattered through it by his own hand. Thus he imposed upon the literary world a Hermannus of greater bulk but lesser reliability.

### XV

If one excepts its errors, the oldest principal codex of the monastery of St. Emmeram at Regensburg agrees with the Augsburg codex more than with the other editions. It was written there in the eleventh century, not long after Hermannus’s time, as is clear from the passages concerning St. Emmeram and Regensburg, while it sometimes omits matters concerning Hermannus’s diocese of Constance. It begins with the year 378, like Urstisius’s St. George codex, and ends with the year 1054.

### XVI

The Einsiedeln codex also flowed from the same Reichenau source as the Augsburg codex. It was written in the monastery of Pfäfers in the middle of the fourteenth century, as is recorded at its beginning by another hand:

> Hermann, by birth from Arbon, abbot of this monastery of Pfäfers, arranged for this book to be made; it was written in the same monastery in the year of the Lord 1356.

This Hermann, an abbot from the Hermitage who had been requested by the monks of Pfäfers, asked the monks of Einsiedeln to have the Reichenau codex copied, since at that time—by some unknown turn of fortune—it was in their possession. He later sent them the transcript, retaining the original codex for himself, as is recorded there in a distinct script:

> I, Brother Henry of Ligritia, humble treasurer of the monastery of the Hermitage, lent the exemplar of this book in the same year—that is, 1356—to that venerable abbot, Hermann, for copying; he retained our most ancient book and gave us this new one.

The Reichenau codex does not seem to have remained long at Pfäfers. It may already have returned to its place of origin by 1361, when Pfäfers was destroyed by fire. At any rate, it had certainly been restored to Reichenau before the end of the fourteenth century. The interpolations made at Reichenau from that time onward provide evidence of this. They are absent from the Einsiedeln copy made at Pfäfers, but present in the Augsburg codex, which is therefore later than the Einsiedeln one.

For example, before the year 882, in the vacant upper margin, the Reichenau codex contains:

> Note: Bishop Burkhard of Hewen was installed at Constance on the Wednesday before the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin in the year [1388] from the Incarnation of the Lord. And on the preceding Tuesday he transferred to me, Henry Leman, and to … John, Caspar, and Ulrich the fiefs commonly called the *Mantelars lehen*. And our father, Henry Leman of pious memory, died in the year 88 during the fast when “Those who thirst” is sung; he had purchased the aforesaid fiefs for William Gochan.

Another note, written by the same hand in the blank spaces under the years 988 and following, reads:

> Note that the year [1388] from the Incarnation of the Lord was very remarkable. In Alamannia there were many quarrels. First, the League marched into Bavaria and destroyed many villages there. Second, Württemberg waged war against the League. In the same year the two dukes of Bavaria also gained a victory on the Sunday before the feast of the Apostle Bartholomew, and four thousand men of the League were killed. One escaped from Constance, none from Lindau, one from St. Gall, and two from Basel. That war took place near Richenwil.

We have thought it worthwhile to include these passages because such scraps occasionally contribute to the elucidation of the history of the homeland.

The Einsiedeln copy, written on parchment in quarto format, is much more accurate than the Augsburg codex, though it too is not free from chronological errors and additions that are plainly not contemporary with Hermannus’s genuine work. By an entirely remarkable coincidence, at almost the same time both of the Hermannus codices that we are publishing came to the monastery of Pfäfers: the Reichenau codex, as we have just seen, and the Munich codex of Bernold. This itself proves that letters were still cultivated there with great distinction in the fourteenth century.

### XVII

From these descriptions of the codices of Hermannus’s Chronicle it will now be easy to determine the origin of the great diversity among the printed editions: it arose simply from the variety of the codices used by the editors.

We believe that this variety must be attributed to several causes. First, to the excessively scrupulous diligence of the copyists, who, impelled by a desire for improvement, repeatedly revised what they had previously written and labored to make it increasingly accurate. This is the judgment of Oefelius and Urstisius concerning Bernold’s codex; consequently, the earlier copies made from it had to differ from later ones and from the source itself after it had been corrected.

Second, learned men who used these chronicles added or altered many things in them, either for their own use or to inform others. Basnage expresses this view in the preface to his Canisius.

Finally, and above all, copyists living in different places retained or abridged general events, or those that pleased them more, omitted particulars concerning foreign places and regions, and inserted in their place matters that seemed more proper to the provinces where they were writing. A very clear example of this is provided by Bernold alone when compared with Hermannus.

Thus, while some added to their copies items from their own knowledge, and others adopted numerous passages from different chronicles in order to enlarge their work, a new kind of chronicle compilation necessarily emerged, although it was often attributed to one and the same author, as we observed above in the Muri codex.

The editors—or more often the copyists—also increased the evil and confusion. Whatever they found stitched into their codices from whatever source, including marginal notes and all kinds of interpolations, they published under the name borne by the codex as though it belonged to the original author. They exercised little or no discrimination and applied no sober criticism, being concerned more with bulk than with truth and authenticity. This unfortunate fate befell our Hermannus above all.

But what good did all this ultimately accomplish? Only that Hermannus is sought in Hermannus in vain, that the genuine cannot readily be distinguished from the spurious, and that—greatly to the detriment of the history of the homeland—even the otherwise most penetrating investigators are led into various errors or at least confusion.

We have already demonstrated this above in the case of Mabillon and the Bollandist hagiographers. We have another example in Hartmann’s *Annals of the Hermitage*. The interpolations of Canisius’s edition under the year 947 concerning Abbot Thietland, and under the year 949, “Gregory II the Father,” greatly perplexed him, although the Reichenau codex reads: “Gregory, the holy Father.”

But enough has now been said about the printed editions and manuscript codices of Hermannus’s Chronicle. From this the necessity of preparing a new edition from a genuine codex is simultaneously evident; this must now be discussed in greater detail.

## § III. Plan and Sources of the New Edition

### XVIII

It is especially surprising that none of those who undertook to publish Hermannus ever thought of the primary Reichenau source. They were all content merely with the streams derived from it, which, the farther they move from their spring, the more they swell with foreign and sometimes muddy inflows.

The first to undertake to satisfy the wishes of scholars in this matter, in keeping with his indefatigable devotion to the history of his homeland, was the distinguished Father Mauritius Van der Meer of Hochenbaum, the exceptionally industrious polymath of the monastery of Rheinau. He had already prepared numerous aids for this purpose.

For several years the illustrious Martin Gerbert, prince-abbot of St. Blaise, had also been engaged in examining literary repositories everywhere, with the aim of preparing a new edition of the works of our Bernold—or, as he is commonly called, Berthold, the priest of Constance—and especially of that author’s Chronicle. The very gracious Father Mauritius therefore allowed us to place Hermannus before his continuator, although other labors had somewhat hindered him from publishing it himself.

This happened most opportunely, so that Hermannus, from the Reichenau codex as though from the primitive soil of his birth, and Bernold, his epitomator and continuator, from his own Munich autograph, might once again emerge into the light, joined by a kind of friendly bond.

Since we have already said much about the latter above, some remarks must now be made here about the former, insofar as careful examination of it has enabled us to discover.

This Reichenau codex is written on parchment in a smaller folio format, in a clear and elegant script that unquestionably belongs to the eleventh century and to Hermannus’s age. Some believe that it was written by Hermannus’s own hand. Nevertheless, serious doubts arise especially from the many slips of the pen, the orthography that is neglected in places, the frequent rendering of the same proper names in different forms, and, above all, the words that are often joined or divided incorrectly. It is difficult to persuade oneself that all this flowed from Hermannus’s skilled pen.

To us it seems highly probable that the codex was taken either from notes or from Hermannus’s own autograph, if such an autograph ever existed. The statement “I, Hermannus, was born,” together with the other things he relates about himself, sufficiently indicates this. Yet it appears to have been copied not from direct inspection but from hearing—someone else dictating it—in accordance with the practice then customary in monasteries. Because books were scarce and monks were numerous, one person would dictate while several scribes simultaneously produced several copies.

Among so many scribes there were doubtless some who were less experienced, and it was easy for many things misunderstood by them to be recorded incorrectly. We therefore judge that this is also the origin of the many errors that the carelessness or incompetence of those scribes first introduced into the codices and eventually into the printed editions, since their editors thought that everything contained in the codices had to be religiously retained.

There is another circumstance concerning Hermannus that has not been sufficiently observed. Berthold, Hermannus’s disciple, says in his *Life* that this book of chronicles was collected everywhere by his master. Rather, Berthold himself seems to have composed it from Hermannus’s notes, not Hermannus. Nor can the elegant script of this codex be attributed to Hermannus, who was so physically contracted that he could scarcely write anything new even with fingers stiffly spread. One may therefore reasonably doubt whether any autograph of Hermannus existed, apart from the one written by his disciple.

### XIX

Besides the defects of this codex mentioned above, it is also far from free of interpolations. These were inserted by different hands, at different times and in different places, partly in the margins and partly in the spaces left blank either under years for which no event had been recorded or, as was usually the case, between one year and another, where two or more lines had been left vacant. They can easily be recognized as the work of different hands or scripts.

Since we wish these additions to be absent from the text of our edition, we have thought it useful to append the more notable ones separately here, for historical information, in addition to those noted above.

Under 838, after what had been written by the original hand was erased, another entry was substituted by a fourteenth-century hand:

> Saint Meginrad came to the Reichenau site.

Under 861, a later marginal note concerning the same Meginrad reads:

> Saint Meginrad, our patron, count of Sulgen, son of the count of Sulgen.

Under 871, after “Bishop Salomon died,” a fourteenth-century hand adds at the edge of the margin:

> Patecho succeeded him and ruled for three years.

Concerning him, in the same manner, the lower margin under 875 reads:

> Patecho, bishop of Constance, died in the year 875; Gebehard ruled in his place for ten years.

Under 911, after “he invaded the duchy,” a recent fifteenth-century marginal note adds:

> Burkhard himself was count of Veringen.

[Col. 0044B] After 924, some material is inserted below concerning bells cast at Reichenau in 1393; thus the codex must already have returned from Pfäfers by that time.

Under 934, beside “Eberhardus, etc.,” a fourteenth-century marginal note reads:

> Saint Eberhard, our Father.

This indicates that the remaining text has not been interpolated.

Under 941, in the blank space for that year, the following chronologically false entry has been placed:

> Note that Duke Luitpold of Austria was killed with many soldiers in the year 1385 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June. The forest cities, which are called Walstet, did this. Later, in the year 1388, many peoples wished to destroy that province called Glarus, and they came through the passes. Afterwards the people of Glarus came with eighty men and killed about three hundred, who disgracefully took flight.

These words are not read in the Einsiedeln codex, but they are found in the Augsburg codex, written by the original hand. Who could tolerate Canisius’s inserting them into his edition under the year 941?

Under 945, a thirteenth- or fourteenth-century hand adds:

> Thietland, our Father, came—the first abbot of this place.

Canisius miserably printed this as “Tietlandus Patuen.” In the margin appears:

> Thietlandus, abbot of the monastery of the Hermitage, who composed a gloss on the Epistles of Saint Paul.

Canisius included this under 947 in his edition, together with the following words noted in the Reichenau codex under 947 in the lower part of the leaf, although they are not found even in the Einsiedeln codex:

> Note: In the year 1390 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the Wednesday after the Nativity of the Lord, there were flashes of lightning and thunder around midnight.

Here he also incorrectly read *tetra* instead of “around.” What an editor of Hermannus, to dare to scatter such things throughout his Chronicle! But this is not yet the end.

Under 949, in a hand of the thirteenth century or shortly thereafter, appears:

> Gregory, the holy and most noble Father, came—to Einsiedeln, that is.

Canisius, however, once again, contrary even to the testimony of his own Augsburg codex, has:

> Gregory II the Father.

Under 950, in the same earlier hand:

> The scribe Vigilius died.

This is entirely absent from the other codices.

Under 955, beside Reginbald, a fifteenth-century marginal note concerns Helfenstein.

Under 960, in a hand dating from around the thirteenth century:

> Gregory became abbot.

This refers to Einsiedeln and was inserted into Canisius’s edition.

Under 971, beside Adalbero, a fifteenth-century hand writes:

> of Helfenstein.

Under 972, another hand, nearly contemporary with the text, adds:

> At Regensburg Saint Wolfgang was made bishop.

A more recent fifteenth-century hand adds:

> Here was born the count of Pfullingen; the nobleman of Ridenfels was born near Schwebeswerd.

In the lower margin:

> On his mother’s side, from Veringen.

Under 973, a fifteenth-century hand or one shortly thereafter adds:

> Note: That Burkhard was the founder of the monastery of Mount Duel. Then, in 1005, that monastery was transferred by the divine Henry, Roman emperor, to a place called Stain. See below, the Chronicle of Petershausen.

Under 979, beside Gebehard, a fifteenth-century marginal note reads:

> Count of Zähringen.

This is false, since he was from Bregenz.

Under 987, in a thirteenth-century hand:

> The church of the cell of Saint Meginrad was enlarged.

In the other codices derived from this one, these words are written by the original hand, as is also the entry under 996:

> Gregory, the holy abbot, died.

In the Einsiedeln codex, a later hand added:

> namely, of the monastery of the Hermitage.

Under 997, after “he left behind daughters,” a fifteenth-century hand adds in the margin:

> one, Gisela.

Under 1008, beside “the monastery of Reichenau,” a fourteenth-century note reads:

> The year of requital of the wicked abbot has come—namely, of Immo, who had then been deposed.

This is also found in the Einsiedeln codex, written by the original hand.

Under 1009, beside Wolferad, Hermannus’s father, a fifteenth-century marginal note reads:

> Count of Veringen.

Here again Canisius concocted I know not what, reading “Piligrim and daughter of Bernhard” instead of “daughter of Piligrinus and Bertrada.” In the following year, in place of “my paternal grandfather Clemens,” he likewise, with an intolerable error, gives “my paternal grandfather in the censuses, Clemens.”

Under 1031, a thirteenth-century marginal addition reads:

> The first stones of the church of the cell of Saint Meginrad were laid on the sixth day before the Ides of May.

In the other codices, Canisius presents this material, written by the original hand, in mutilated form.

Under 1032, beside Bertha, a fifteenth-century hand writes:

> Born of Helfenstein.

In the same place, a fourteenth-century marginal hand adds:

> Warmannus, bishop of Constance, formerly a monk of this place—that is, of the Hermitage.

There is still a dispute between the monks of Einsiedeln and Reichenau concerning him. We supplied the lacuna under this year, which is found in the Reichenau codex and the copies derived from it, from Bernold’s Munich codex.

Under 1034, the Augsburg codex and Canisius depart from the Reichenau codex. Instead of “Brun, the emperor’s cousin, namely Mathilda’s son,” they read:

> Brun, the emperor’s cousin, the son and daughter.

And shortly afterward, corruptly:

> He received the bishopric on Easter Day at Saint …; likewise, Theobald, etc.

Instead of:

> He received it. At Saint Gall likewise, Theobald, etc.

Under 1039, a thirteenth-century hand adds:

> The church of the cell of Saint Meginrad was dedicated on the third day before the Ides of October, and the relics of Saint Meginrad’s body, hitherto retained by the monks of Reichenau, were returned.

The same words are found in the Einsiedeln codex in the original hand. In the Reichenau codex, however, the word “from” has been deliberately erased, indicating that a controversy had already arisen between the two monasteries concerning possession of Saint Meinrad’s body.

Canisius presents similar material from the Augsburg codex at the end, but in this corrupt and mutilated form:

> And the relics, the body of Saint Meginrad.

To produce more of the monsters of error found in this edition, which we have elsewhere praised, would be excessively laborious. These few examples, however, are more than sufficient for anyone to form a sound judgment of its value.

These additions, insofar as they concern the monastery of Einsiedeln, were for the most part inserted into the Reichenau codex in the fourteenth century, when it was kept there. This is shown both by the much more recent character, which is nearly always the same, and by the frequent omission of the place-name. Genuine Hermannus always gives the place-name, even when he is discussing Reichenau itself, where he was writing.

A different judgment must be made concerning the entries under 948 and 964 about the divine consecration of the chapel of the Blessed Virgin and its confirmation. These are found not in the margin but in the body of the text. They appear to be older and do not differ so greatly from the original hand of the codex. The script has been formed in imitation of that of the rest of the text, although it appears somewhat more compressed, and it leaves no blank space between the two years, as is usually observed elsewhere. The ink is also somewhat more recent and darker.

We do not dare to establish with certainty from this alone that these entries are interpolations. Even if they were, they would be sufficiently old and almost contemporary with the codex. We believe the same judgment should be applied to the entries under 934 and 958 concerning Eberhard; we have therefore left them intact in their proper places. The same does not apply to the entries under 949, 960, and 996 concerning Gregory the abbot. Although they retain some features of an ancient script, they appear to be interpolations, since the place-name, or the cell of Meginrad, is not expressed there. These additions seem attributable to the Einsiedeln scribe. Likewise, we consider those entries to have been written at Reichenau whenever that designation is added, unless a more recent script reveals otherwise.

### XX

The Reichenau codex begins with the Nativity of the Lord, without any further title except one added by a fourteenth-century hand, which we have recorded in our edition. It proceeds in continuous sequence to the year 1051, where it ends—not because Hermannus ceased writing there, but because the codex is defective at that point, several leaves containing the later years having been cut away.

The same defect is found in the Einsiedeln and Augsburg codices copied from it. This unfortunate fate must therefore have befallen the Reichenau codex at least by the fourteenth century, when those copies were made from it. The loss would be regrettable if this lacuna of three years, down to 1054, could not be supplied from the Muri and Engelberg manuscripts, which agree with the Reichenau codex from earlier years. Hermannus’s Chronicle extends to 1054, as Berthold, his disciple, attests in the *Life* given above; the codices of Bernold and Muri likewise begin at the year 378.

Although the Muri codex continues through the years 1052, 1053, and 1054, where the Reichenau codex is defective, it nevertheless differs somewhat in those three years from Urstisius’s printed edition. We have therefore thought that both should be published, since we are uncertain which contains Hermannus’s genuine reading. This is especially so because Urstisius’s St. George codex ends after the year 1052; we likewise end Bernold there, intending to continue him from the year 1053 in volume II.

### XXI

Nor is the conjecture of Gundling and Vossius (*De historia Latina*, book II, chapter 44, § 19) thereby confirmed: namely, that Hermannus brought his Chronicle only to the year 1053 because Berthold of Constance began his continuation in that year.

Urstisius does indeed present the matter this way in his edition. But in the Bernold autograph, the earlier and later events of the year 1053 continue to be narrated in a single sequence, without any mention of a continuation. It therefore cannot be determined from this point at what year the continuation should begin; more will be said about this in its proper place.

That the year 1053 still belongs to Hermannus is shown by Hermannus himself when he writes:

> Werinharius, my brother.

At least, that is what Urstisius has.

Trithemius went much further astray, assigning Hermannus’s death as early as the year 1043 in volume I of the *Annals of Hirsau*. Those too are mistaken who persuade themselves that what follows under the year 1040 in that Chronicle was added by another writer because it is written at greater length. Surely Hermannus could have described events nearer to the time of writing, and therefore better known to him, with a more expansive pen.

Indeed, the events of that period identify him even more clearly as the author, since it was then that he first became a cleric or monk at Reichenau, around the thirtieth year of his life, as the author of his *Life* testifies. He even wrote his mother Hiltrud’s epitaph under the year 1052, to say nothing of the other testimony already cited.

Only one question might remain: whether the year 1054, to which he is said to have brought his Chronicle, should be included in this calculation or excluded from it. Some codices seem to favor the contrary view, though we have just discussed them; and the miracles of Pope Leo IX, who died on 19 April of that same year, could scarcely have reached Hermannus’s knowledge after five months and after a long illness, so that he himself could still have written about them.

From this one might perhaps conjecture only that the events of the earlier part of the year 1054 were noted by Hermannus and later supplemented by his disciple, while the year as a whole was nevertheless attributed to Hermannus. The Muri codex expressly does this, and we have decided to follow it in this matter.

### XXII

From what has been said we learn when Hermannus began his Chronicle and when he brought it to an end. The Chronicle of the Old Testament, therefore, prefixed to it in the other codices, with the exception of the Reichenau codex, must be attributed not to Hermannus himself but to the copyists. Following the taste of the Middle Ages, they did not think that they could write chronicles unless they first placed before them the venerable name of Bede and his book *On the Six Ages of the World*, perhaps in order to compensate for the scarcity of codices.

Although the copyists may be excused for this, we believe that the editors cannot be forgiven for repeatedly forcing Bede’s Chronicle, reheated again and again, upon the public without justification.

### XXIII

The Reichenau codex has the special feature that it does not calculate the events it narrates according to the years of the reigns of emperors or kings, as the other codices do and as is also customary in the Munich family. It therefore easily happened that, while one writer counted the first year of a particular king from the death of his predecessor and another counted it only from the following year, they did not agree among themselves even about the years of the reigns. Consequently, they also differed from one another in assigning events to each year and in calculating the times.

Hermannus, however, undertook to connect events with the years from the Incarnation of the Lord. But, as Bouquet notes in volume III of the *Scriptores rerum Francicarum*, p. 319, he did so with little success, at least as regards the events that took place under the first dynasty of the Frankish kings. In fact, he often failed elsewhere as well, clearly because he followed earlier authors.

Bouquet adds:

> We shall record the true years, insofar as this can be done, without regard to the years noted by Hermannus.

In this edition we partly follow the same practice: while retaining Hermannus’s order, we place the genuine date of each event below it in a different type, insofar as it could be established from more recent and more accurate chronologists.

Among these we especially count Father Stephan Clement, an outstanding ornament of the Benedictine-Maurist congregation in France. In his excellent work *The Art of Verifying Dates*, printed and enlarged in Paris from 1783 onward in three large volumes to date, he arranged the sequence of times with exactness—if anyone has done so. Yet he, like us, may sometimes be corrected by others:

> At times even good Homer nods.

Those who have read the most celebrated chronologists to date—Scaliger, Petavius, Calmet, and others—know very well how much labor and difficulty are still involved in establishing a chronology that is always orderly and accurate.

The writers of the Middle Ages deserve even greater indulgence if they occasionally went astray in their calculations. They were often more intent on narrating events than on examining chronology, and therefore, so as not to interrupt the thread of their narrative, they gathered the events of several years together under one year.

Moreover, one and the same ancient author is not always consistent with himself in establishing chronology. This is clear even from Eusebius, who arranged the times differently in his *Chronicle* and in his *History*. How much less should one expect exact agreement among so many and such diverse authors?

This is especially true of our Hermannus, who compiled his Chronicle from such a variety of writers.

Another explanation for such divergent calculations of time arises from the negligence or incompetence of copyists, who often either failed to mark the year or entered it in an inappropriate place. As a result, several events belonging to different times are joined to a single year, or the events of one year are distributed among several; hence an error once admitted spreads through the subsequent years. We have observed this more than once in our Chronicle. This happened frequently both in the manuscripts of Bernold and in those of Hermann, as comparison will show; and it is proved still more clearly by the Canisian edition, which, although prepared from a manuscript copied from the Augian codex, nevertheless often disagrees with it in the years it records. Since, therefore, reconciling those discrepancies and restoring the genuine reckoning corrupted by the scribes would have been extremely difficult, not to say impossible, we judged it more prudent to retain the years as they appear in our manuscripts than rashly to alter them, while nevertheless taking care to point out the error wherever it is clear.

Finally, it will suffice to observe once for all that Hermann, like the other German chroniclers of his time, reckons the beginning of the year not from the first day of January but from the feast of the preceding Nativity of the Lord. Hence it often happens that events occurring around Christmas are assigned sometimes to the preceding year and sometimes to the following year, as happened with the coronation of Charlemagne as emperor, which is now assigned to the year 800 and now to 801.

### XXIV. On the Sources of Hermann’s Chronicle

That chronicles can be composed not from the authors’ own invention but from the testimony of earlier writers is self-evident. The only question here is from what source one draws and with what fidelity events are narrated. Hermann’s biographer testifies that he laboriously gathered his little book of Chronicles from everywhere. The principal sources are indicated by the Munich manuscript of Bernold in these words: “The authors of the Chronicles are Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, Dionysius, Jordanes, and Bede.” Accordingly, as the work proceeds, the year in which each of them completed his Chronicle is cautiously recorded.

Besides these, however, there are still many others from whom Hermann drew his material, as we shall see, each noted in its proper place both below and in the Chronicle. A few words may now be said about the principal ones.

The first is Eusebius of Caesarea, specifically his Chronicle, extending from the birth of Christ to the year 327. Jerome translated it into Latin and continued it to the year 379, as found in Scaliger’s *Thesaurus temporum*, Leiden edition, 1606. Hermann did not simply copy it, however, but excerpted only what seemed more important to him and occasionally inserted other material, chiefly from Bede’s Chronicle. Eusebius’s chronology has nevertheless often been altered here, advanced or postponed by one year or another. On this subject see Petavius, *De doctrina temporum*, book IX, chapter 1. It is also clear from many passages that, besides Eusebius’s Chronicle, Hermann used his *Ecclesiastical History*. It appeared in the recension of Henri Valois at Turin in 1746.

The second is Prosper of Aquitaine, who continued the Chronicle from the year 379, where Jerome stopped, to 435. It is found in the same Scaliger edition and in du Chesne, *Scriptores Francici*, vol. I, p. 196, as well as in Graevius’s *Thesaurus Antiquitatum Romanarum*, vol. XI, p. 312, and especially in Prosper’s works, Venice edition, 1744.

Prosper had as continuator, up to the year 565, Victor, bishop of Tunnuna in Africa; together with the continuation of John, abbot of Biclaro, extending to 590, he is found in the same Scaliger edition. Likewise there is Marius, bishop of Aventicum or Lausanne, from 455 to 591, in du Chesne, cited work, p. 210, and in P. Bouquet’s latest *Collection of the Frankish Writers*, vol. II, p. 12.

Among Jerome’s continuators also belongs Hydatius, bishop of Lemica in Gallaecia, whose Chronicle, from 379 to 467, is included in the cited works. Likewise Marcellinus Comes of Illyricum, from 379 to 566, in Scaliger and Bouquet. Cassiodorus must not be omitted either: his Chronicle, extending to 519, is read among his works, vol. II, p. 354, Venice edition, 1729. Nearly all these authors also appear in Roncalli’s new edition of the chronicles, Padua, 1787.

We have repeatedly noted that Hermann used all these writers, but especially Marcellinus, from whom he inserted entire sections verbatim into his Chronicle.

The third mentioned by Bernold is Dionysius, surnamed Exiguus, who began reckoning the years from the Nativity of Christ and thus became the author of the common era, beginning his Paschal cycle with the year 531. In 527 he also wrote a collection of ecclesiastical canons translated from Greek into Latin, found in Justellus’s *Bibliotheca Juris Canonici*, vol. I, p. 97. I find no evidence that he wrote a Chronicle, nor does Hermann mention anything of his except his Cycle.

The fourth is Jordanes, called Jornandes by others, a bishop, as some hold, of Ravenna. He wrote *On the Succession of Kingdoms and Times* up to the year 560, and also a *History of the Origin of the Goths* up to the year 540. These works appear in Muratori’s *Scriptores Rerum Italicarum*, vol. I, pp. 187 and 202.

Finally, the Venerable Bede, besides his work *On the Six Ages of the World* extending to the year 624 after the birth of Christ (*Works*, vol. II), also wrote an *Ecclesiastical History of the English People* (*Works*, vol. III). Under his name there is also a brief Chronicle extending to 810, in du Chesne, cited work, vol. III, p. 125.

Bernold did not, however, identify all the writers from whom Hermann’s Chronicle was drawn. We have discovered still others whose works he used. Of these we note especially the following.

Gregory of Tours’ *History of the Franks*, extending from 458 to 591, was published at Paris in 1699 by Theodoric Ruinart. Ruinart appended to it the epitome made by Fredegar the Scholastic, together with Fredegar’s continuation and those of others up to 768. All these are also found in Bouquet’s cited *Collection*, vol. II, pp. 74 ff., although the chronology is calculated somewhat differently.

The Chronicle of Isidore of Seville, extending to 626, appears among his works, vol. I, Madrid edition, 1778.

Procopius of Caesarea’s *History of the Gothic War*, from 489 to 552, is found in Muratori’s *Scriptores Rerum Italicarum*, vol. I, p. 143, as are the six books of Paul the Deacon *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, from 568 to 744, in the same work, p. 396, and the *Miscellaneous History* circulated under his name, extending to 813, ibid., p. 1.

Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, is believed to have written in the ninth century the lives of the Roman pontiffs. These were published several times, but most excellently at Rome in 1718 by Francesco Bianchini.

The annals of Hepidanus, a monk of St. Gall, from 709 to 1041, seem to be counted, if not among Hermann’s sources, certainly among his aids, since they approach closely both his period and the vicinity of his place, although Hepidanus outlived him. They are presented by du Chesne, vol. III, and by Goldastus, book I of the *Scriptores Rerum Alemannicarum*, together with the writings of other monks of the same monastery that serve to illuminate or confirm Hermann.

The principal source of Hermann’s Chronicle from 614 to 900 is easily identified as the *Annals of Fulda*, so called after their anonymous author, a monk of Fulda. Hermann follows them closely and sometimes abridges them while changing their style. When they fail or come to an end, Hermann likewise becomes more concise again, and he frequently reproduces the continuator of Regino up to 972 so closely that it is scarcely possible not to suspect that Hermann himself is concealed under the name of that continuator; for most of the particulars concern our neighborhood and the diocese of Constance.

Hermann did the same when he excerpted the *Annals of Fulda*: he added to them, whether from his own material or from elsewhere, a succession of the Roman pontiffs and bishops of Constance, as well as of the abbots of Reichenau and St. Gall. These annals were edited by Freherus, Pithoeus, and du Chesne, and best of all by P. Martin Bouquet in the often-mentioned *Collection*, parts of vols. II, V, VI, and VII, where he also corrected the frequently corrupt chronology.

### § IV. The Plan of the New Edition

**XXV.** From these points, we think, the plan of the new edition undertaken by us is already sufficiently clear. We resolved to prepare it from the Augian codex—not, if not Hermann’s own autograph (which cannot properly be asserted, since no work of his written in his own hand has yet been found by which the similarity of the script could be judged), at least from the primary and, of all copies so far discovered, the oldest; and, most importantly, from a manuscript hitherto unpublished—supported also by the assistance of nearly all the other contemporary codices.

We placed this manuscript first as the foundation, removing from it all additions or interpolations demonstrably made by a later hand, while retaining only those that remain doubtful and have already been discussed above. For each year or event, insofar as possible, we add the sources from which Hermann can be shown to have drawn. On the upper page we identify it by the words **AUGIAN CODEX**. Beneath it, in a different type, we place Hermann’s abridgment from the Munich codex of Bernold, marked by that name, which may serve as a record of variant readings. In it, moreover, the omitted years either contain the same material as the Augian codex or are for the most part blank.

We did not think it necessary to identify the other manuscript codices mentioned above, since some abound in innumerable interpolations, while others agree, at least in the principal matters, with those we publish. Only for Hermann’s final decade, in which they agree with the Augian manuscript or supply what is defective, do we identify the Gottweig and Muri codices by their initial letters.

We preserve everywhere the chronology observed in the codices, as explained above, adding beneath it the genuine year of the events wherever the recorded year is certainly wrong. We have adopted an orthography suited to our own time, especially in proper names, rather than the forms that differ so greatly among the various codices and often arise from the ingenuity of incompetent scribes. We have done this so that readers may not be wearied by the many solecisms that would otherwise be inserted into the text and then corrected through the appended variants.

For the same reason, we have omitted the variations found in editions published hitherto, since they burden or obstruct readers and needlessly increase the bulk of the book. Those who possess the printed copies can easily detect them by comparing our edition; those who lack them will not greatly regret their loss, since a genuine narrative of events drawn from a pure source will benefit them more than a confused mass of highly divergent readings and errors accumulated from various editions.

Finally, notes are occasionally added at the foot of the page wherever they are needed either to correct or to illuminate Hermann’s work. These notes are kept as concise as possible, lest, by enlarging the text excessively with observations, we seem not so much to be editing another person’s Chronicle as composing a new one from various materials. We hope that our edition will be useful; if we have achieved this, the wishes both of ourselves and of scholars will have been sufficiently fulfilled.

### § V. Berthold, Continuator and Disciple of Hermann

**XXVI.** We should now discuss Hermann himself, the author of the Chronicle, at greater length. To avoid frequent repetition, however, we think this should be deferred to his *Life*, which we presented above, written by Berthold, his disciple and first continuator. Berthold’s continuation, from 1054 to 1066, is also immediately appended to Hermann in the printed editions, though his *Life* is omitted and replaced by a brief eulogy.

Only Urstisius, having ended Hermann’s Chronicle after 1054, distinguishes the following continuation in his edition, although he is mistaken in hesitantly attributing it to Berthold of Constance, whose different Chronicle he immediately added in vol. I of the *Scriptores Germanici*, p. 339. We are surprised that a man otherwise so perceptive could have fallen into this error: although he had two continuations so plainly different before him, he nevertheless considered, even if tentatively, that both had the same author.

That the authors were different is shown, apart from the fact that almost every event up to 1066 is narrated differently, by one point alone, which places the matter beyond doubt: the earlier continuation calls Alexander II a usurper of the Apostolic See in 1061, while regarding Honorius, or Cadolaus, as the legitimate pope. We do not therefore count this Berthold among the schismatics, since he wrote from the report of events that had taken place at nearby Basel during his own time. He would surely have held a different view if he had extended his continuation to 1067, when Alexander was recognized as the legitimate pope at the synod of Mantua. This is clear evidence that this Berthold ceased writing in 1066, since thereafter he could no longer correct what he had previously written incorrectly.

Bernold, although writing later in the same period, understood the truth of the matter more clearly from the outcome. He therefore praises the same Alexander as the true pontiff and declares himself, throughout the whole course of his Chronicle, a sworn enemy of the schismatics. What sane person would attribute such devotion to opposing parties to one and the same author?

The Muri codex attributes that first and shorter continuation to Berthold, writing at the end of Hermann’s year 1054: “Thus far, the chronicle is Hermann’s. From this point onward, Berthold’s.” But who is this Berthold? Certainly no other than the man who appends Hermann’s *Life* together with the said shorter continuation, and from whom the scribe of that codex admits that he drew his material, above all, up to the year 741: namely Berthold, Hermann’s disciple. The same scribe expressly distinguishes him there from Berthold, priest of St. Blasien, the author of the longer continuation. Other writers have so far wrongly conflated both men into one Berthold, priest of Constance; the contrary can be demonstrated from the points just mentioned alone, quite apart from what will be explained more fully concerning Berthold in volume II.

The same Berthold is also clearly indicated by the Anonymous of Melk, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 92 (*Miraei Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica*, p. 155), who writes: “Berthold, who was his [Hermann’s] hearer and disciple, wrote the Life of his master and the Chronicle.” From this the author of that *Life* also becomes known, although his name is not given in it.

The Muri codex appends that *Life* immediately after the words “From this point onward, Berthold,” and it is also found in the Gottweig codex. In those manuscripts it is immediately followed by what appears under the name of the continuation after Hermann in Urstisius. The passages are nearly identical, except that some material is occasionally inserted from the other continuation of Bernold. Both continuations are there confused into one, as is evident, among other things, from the fact that the scribes of those codices favor Alexander II as pope in 1061 and thus follow Bernold in that matter, not Berthold.

**XXVII.** From what Berthold himself relates about his own life in that *Life*, it can easily be concluded that he was a monk of Reichenau and especially close to Hermann. Moreover, during Hermann’s final illness Hermann wished Berthold to remain constantly at his side as his assistant, and at his death he entrusted his papers to him, so that he might carefully correct whatever still remained to be written in them and recommend the written material to others. This may have been the occasion for continuing the Chronicle.

When Berthold calls Hermann his master, this should be understood not as a teacher of boys but as a teacher of men being instructed in the higher disciplines over which Hermann presided. The details we have just mentioned certainly show that Berthold was a man, not a youth. Nor does the fact that Hermann dedicated to him his book *On the Measurement of the Astrolabe*, in Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, part II, p. 95, indicate that he was still young; Hermann composed that work chiefly at Berthold’s urging.

Indeed, from these facts he might already seem to have been a priest, if he ever was one, since neither the Anonymous of Melk, nor the cited codices, nor Hermann himself bestow on him the title of priest, although they do so in Bernold’s case. The conjectures made by others are examined below under Bernold.

**XXVIII.** How far this Berthold continued his work cannot be established with certainty from the codices. Those who recognize only one continuator of Hermann must admit that it was carried down to the year 1100, although, among other objections, his death is recorded in Bernold’s Chronicle under the year 1088. We judge this to be the very man of whom Bernold writes in the cited passage: “Berthold, an outstanding teacher, exceptionally learned in sacred letters, full of days in a good old age, departed to the Lord on the fourth Ides of March.” These words seem to agree perfectly with what was said above.

All the printed editions we possess go no further than 1066; after that year our codices agree with the other continuation of Bernold.

Thus the conjecture is not unfounded that the codices used by the editors likewise did not proceed beyond the year 1066 in Berthold’s work. This is further confirmed by the difference in the opinions of the two authors cited above (§ 26). Even if we grant that Berthold later changed his view, he would at least have corrected what he had written in 1061 against the legitimate pope if he had extended his continuation into the later period of the schism.

This will suffice concerning Hermann’s Chronicle. For anyone desiring more, John Ego’s treatise *On the Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Rich Reichenau*, written in 1630, chapter 28, in Pez’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, part III, p. 688, will provide ample material.

# THE CHRONICLE OF HERMANN THE CONTRACTED

[Note: The Augian codex lacks a title; a later fourteenth-century hand supplied this one: “The Chronicle of Hermann, a noble man, count of Veringen and most devout monk of the monastery of Reichenau; and he wrote up to the time of Pope Victor II and the emperor Henry, to the year 1053 from the Incarnation, and died in the forty-fourth year of his age, on the eighth Ides of October.” Canisius prefixed a nearly identical title to his edition, which he traced from the creation of the world; but there Victor XXI is wrongly read instead of Victor II, and in both places Hermann’s date of death is wrong: his *Life* records that he died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, in the forty-second year of his age.]

FROM THE HITHERTO UNPUBLISHED AUGIAN CODEX, TOGETHER WITH HIS LIFE AND THE CONTINUATION WRITTEN BY BERTHOLD, HIS DISCIPLE. THE UNPUBLISHED PETERSHAUSEN CHRONICLE IS APPENDED. Collected from manuscript codices and illustrated with notes and observations by P. AEMILIAN USSERMANN, monk and librarian of the Congregation of St. Blasien.

(*Prodrome of Sacred Germany*, vol. I.)

## AUGIAN CODEX

[Note: The following divisions should be read in parallel.]

**1.** In the forty-second year of Augustus Caesar, and in the twenty-eighth year after Egypt had been reduced to a province and Cleopatra had been defeated together with Antony; in the 752nd year from the founding of the City; in the third year of the 193rd Olympiad, our Lord Jesus Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judea. From the beginning of the world, 3,952 years had elapsed according to the Hebrew truth, but 5,199 according to the Seventy Interpreters.

[Note: To linger longer over the chronology here and below would be excessively laborious, given the great disagreement among the authors. Readers are therefore referred to the authors noted beneath each event, insofar as this has been possible; we have been content to record the years in which they assign each event.]

**2.** The codices are blank.

[Note: To avoid empty spaces, we henceforth omit those years that contain no noteworthy event.]

**3.** Infants are slaughtered by Herod for the Lord. Eusebius.

**5.** The orator Asinius Pollio dies. Eusebius.

**6.** Herod, king of Judea, dies in great agony; Archelaus reigns in his place for nine years.

[Note: Eusebius assigns Herod’s death to the fourth year, but assigns Archelaus’s reign to this year. See Petavius, book XI, chapters 2 ff.]

**7.** A great famine occurs at Rome. Eusebius.

**9.** Tiberius Caesar subdues the Dalmatians and Sarmatians. Eusebius, Dio.

**12.** The gates of Janus, which had already been closed for twelve years by Augustus, are opened. Suetonius; Orosius.

**13.** The orator Messalla Corvinus dies. Eusebius.

**14.** An eclipse of the sun occurs.

[Note: This occurred on 18 April.]

**15.** *(In the margin: Tiberius, Augustus’s stepson, reigned twenty-three years.)* Archelaus is banished by Augustus to Vienne, a city of Gaul, and Augustus dies in the seventy-sixth year of his age and the fifty-sixth of his reign. Tiberius reigns in his place for twenty-three years. Eusebius, previous year.

**16.** Herod the tetrarch holds the kingdom of the Jews for twenty-four years. Eusebius, year 14.

**17.** The mathematicians are expelled from the city. Dio.

**18.** The historian Livy dies. The poet Ovid dies in exile. Eusebius, year 17.

**19.** Germanicus, sent by Tiberius, defeats the Germans. Tacitus, year 16.

**20.** Thirteen cities collapse in an earthquake. Eusebius, previous year; Dio, year 17.

**21.** The historian and poet Fenestella dies. Eusebius, previous year.

**22.** Tiberius never sends back many kings whom he had summoned to him by deceit. Eusebius, previous year.

**23.** The theater of Pompey burns. Eusebius, previous year.

**24.** Tiberius makes Drusus his associate in the kingdom; Drusus dies by poison in the same year. Eusebius, previous year.

**27.** Pilate is sent by Tiberius as governor of Judea. Eusebius.

**30.** Our Lord Jesus Christ is baptized by John as he begins the thirtieth year of his age according to the flesh, and begins to preach.

**31.** John the Baptist is beheaded by Herod the tetrarch.

**33.** The Lord suffers and rises again in Jerusalem. An eclipse of the sun and very great earthquakes occur.

[Note: Only one eclipse is recorded, on 12 September. Eusebius relates from Phlegon that the eclipse occurring at the Lord’s death took place unnaturally at the full moon.]

Eusebius.

**34.** James, the brother of the Lord, is ordained by the apostles bishop of Jerusalem and holds the office for thirty years. Eusebius.

**35.** Pilate causes a riot by setting up an image of Caesar in the temple. Eusebius, year 32.

**36.** Pilate comes to Rome and reports the Lord’s miracles to Caesar. Eusebius.

**37.** Tiberius reports to the Senate what he had heard from Pilate, but the Senate rejects it. Eusebius, previous year.

**38.** Tiberius severely afflicts the Roman people and himself dies by poison. Eusebius, previous year.

*In the margin: Gaius, three years, ten months, eight days. A most wicked man.*

**39.** Herod Agrippa is appointed king of Judea by Gaius and reigns for seven years. Eusebius, previous year.

**40.** The Jews are defeated at Alexandria; Philo, a most distinguished writer, appeals to Gaius on their behalf, but without effect. Eusebius, year 38; Josephus, book XVIII, chapter 9.

**41.** Pilate kills himself, overwhelmed by great calamities inflicted by Gaius. Eusebius, Chronicle.

**42.** Matthew writes the Gospel in Hebrew. Gaius is killed by his own men.

*In the margin: Claudius, thirteen years, eight months, twenty-eight days. Alternatively, previous year.*

**44.** The apostle Peter comes to Rome and, preaching there for twenty-five years, holds the episcopate. Eusebius, previous year.

**45.** Herod Agrippa is struck by an angel and expires; his son Agrippa reigns in his place for twenty-six years. Eusebius; Josephus, year 40. The evangelist Mark preaches in Egypt.

**46.** Claudius subdues Britain. Eusebius, previous year; Dio, year 43. A great famine occurs. Acts 11:28; Dio, year 42.

**47.** A new island, thirty stadia in extent, appears in the sea. Eusebius, year 45.

**48.** The Roman citizens counted by Claudius are found to number 6,944,000. Eusebius, year 46; Tacitus.

**49.** Thirty thousand Jews are killed during the uprising on the days of Unleavened Bread. Eusebius, previous year.

**51.** Claudius expels the Jews from the city. Bede, year 49; see Acts 18:2.

**52.** A great famine occurs at Rome. Eusebius, previous year.

**53.** Claudius appoints Felix procurator of Judea. Eusebius, previous year.

**54.** At this time Simon Magus becomes the author of the Simoniac heresy.

**55.** A certain Egyptian false prophet, leading many Jews astray, is suppressed by Felix. Eusebius, previous year; see Acts 21:38.

**56.** Claudius dies from poison in the sixty-fourth year of his age. Eusebius, previous year.
