**57.** *(In the margin: Nero, thirteen years, seven months, twenty-eight days.)* Nero, a man of disgraceful conduct, launches the first persecution against Christians. A riot arising at Caesarea destroys many Jews. Bede.

**58.** The apostle Paul is sent to Rome by Festus the governor. Eusebius, Chronicle, year 56.

**59.** Up to this point the evangelist Luke brought the book of the Acts of the Apostles, which covers twenty-seven years from the Lord’s Passion.

**60.** The poet Statius is famous. Eusebius, year 58.

**61.** Nero kills his mother Agrippina and his father’s sister. Eusebius, previous year.

**62.** Nero revels in boundless luxury, wantonness, and sloth. Eusebius, previous year.

**63.** James, the brother of the Lord, is stoned by the Jews. Eusebius, Chronicle, year 61.

**64.** The evangelist Mark suffers martyrdom at Alexandria. Eusebius, previous year.

**65.** Nero builds the Neronian Baths. Eusebius, year 63.

**66.** So that he might see a likeness of burning Troy, Nero sets fire to a large part of the City. Eusebius, previous year; Tacitus, year 64.

**67.** Nero kills Seneca, his teacher. Eusebius, previous year.

**68.** Vespasian is sent by Nero against the Jews in revolt. Eusebius, following year; Josephus, year 66.

**69.** Peter and Paul are slaughtered by Nero because of Simon Magus, a plague occurs at Rome, and Nero kills himself. Suetonius, year 68; alternatively, year 66.

Linus, the first after blessed Peter, holds the episcopate for twelve years.

At Antioch, Ignatius is ordained the second bishop [Note: Namely, after Peter; elsewhere he is called the third, successor of Evodius.] Alternatively, year 68.

**70.** Galba, seven months; Otho, three months; Vitellius, eight months. Vespasian, while fighting in Judea, is proclaimed emperor by the army, a man outstanding in military valor. Eusebius; Suetonius, previous year.

**71.** *(In the margin: Vespasian, nine years, eleven months, twenty-two days.)* Titus besieges the Jews, who are afflicted by an indescribable famine. Eusebius.

**72.** Jerusalem is stormed and destroyed by Titus, forty years after the Lord’s Passion and 1,089 years after the original construction of the Temple under Solomon. Bede; alternatively, year 70.

**75.** At this time the historian Josephus is considered distinguished.

**77.** The Colossus is erected, 107 feet high. Dio, year 75.

**79.** A plague occurs at Rome, and an earthquake destroys three cities of Cyprus. Eusebius, previous year.

**80.** Vespasian dies from a flux of the bowels at a villa near the Sabines. Eusebius, previous year.

*In the margin: Titus, three years, two months.*

**81.** Titus was a man remarkable for virtues of every kind, so that he was called wealth and love of the human race. He built an amphitheater at Rome, at the dedication of which five thousand wild beasts were killed. Eusebius; Dio, previous year.

**82.** Pope Cletus, the second, holds office for twelve years. Eusebius, previous year; alternatively, year 78.

Titus dies in the same villa as his father, in the forty-second year of his age. Eusebius, previous year.

*(In the margin: Domitian, Titus’s brother, fifteen years, five months.)*

**83.** Domitian, infected with every crime, persecutes Christians for the second time. Eusebius, previous year.

He also forbids people to be made eunuchs. Eusebius, following year.

**84.** By decree of the Senate, Titus is enrolled among the gods. Eusebius, previous year.

**85.** Three Vestal virgins are condemned for unchastity. Suetonius, year 83.

**86.** Anianus, the first bishop of Alexandria after the evangelist Mark, dies after twenty-two years; Abilius holds office in his place for thirteen years. Eusebius, previous year.

**88.** Domitian orders himself to be called God and Lord. Eusebius, previous year.

**90.** Quintilian the rhetorician is famous at Rome. Eusebius, previous year.

**91.** At this time the heresies of Menander the magician, the Ebionites, the Cerinthians, and the Nicolaitans arise.

**92.** The Romans suffer very many evils from Caesar and from their enemies. Eusebius, year 89.

**93.** Domitian celebrates a triumph over the Dacians and Germans. Eusebius, previous year.

**94.** Pope Clement III holds office for nine years. Eusebius, year 91.

Cornelia, a Vestal virgin, is buried alive for adultery. Eusebius, year 92; alternatively, year 91.

**95.** Domitian kills many nobles. Eusebius, previous year.

[Note: Eusebius assigns the second persecution to this year, whereas Pagius places its beginning in his *Critica* under the year 93, observing at the same time, under the year 90, that in Eusebius’s Chronicle events are often assigned to years other than those in which they occurred.]

**96.** At this time the apostle John, sent by Domitian into exile on the island of Patmos, writes the Apocalypse. Eusebius, previous year.

**97.** Domitian sends Flavia Domitilla and many others into exile for the faith of Christ. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, this year.

**98.** After doing many evil things, Domitian is cruelly killed by his own men, in the thirty-fifth year of his age.

[Note: According to Suetonius, this occurred in the year 96, when he was forty-five years old.]

Eusebius, year 97; see Pagius, *Critica*.

**99.** *(In the margin: Nerva, one year, four months, eight days.)* In his first edict Nerva recalls all exiles. The holy apostle John, returning from exile, writes the Gospel. Irenaeus, year 97.

Nerva dies, worn out by illness; Trajan reigns in his place. Eusebius, previous year.

**100.** *(In the margin: Trajan, nineteen years, six months, fifteen days.)* Trajan, a Spaniard by birth and a man useful to the state, but misled by error, persecutes Christians for the third time. Bede.

Cerdo, the third bishop of Alexandria, holds office for twelve years. Eusebius, year 97.

The apostle John falls asleep in peace at Ephesus, sixty-eight years after the Lord’s Passion. Bede; Eusebius, following year; Jerome, previous year.

**103.** Pope Evaristus holds office for eight years. Eusebius, year 100.

Trajan celebrates a triumph over the Dacians and Scythians. Eusebius.

**104.** Trajan subjects many peoples to Roman rule. Eusebius, previous year.

**106.** Nero’s Golden House is consumed by fire. Eusebius, previous year.

**107.** Many cities are destroyed by an earthquake. Eusebius, previous year.

**108.** Primus is ordained the fourth bishop of the Alexandrian Church. Eusebius, previous year; alternatively, year 109; Pagius, this year.

**109.** Simon, son of Clopas, who held the episcopate at Jerusalem, is crucified at the age of 120; Justus succeeds him. Eusebius, year 107; Pagius, year 116.

**110.** Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, is brought to Rome and handed over to the beasts. Heron is appointed third bishop in his place.

[Note: Eusebius and others call him Heron or Heros, as does the Roman Martyrology on 17 October.]

Eusebius, year 108; Pagius, year 116.

**111.** Pope Alexander V holds office for ten years. Eusebius, year 109.

**112.** The Pantheon at Rome is burned by lightning. Eusebius, year 111.

**113.** After Justus, Zacchaeus becomes the fourth bishop of Jerusalem.

[Note: Epiphanius calls him Zacharias.]

Eusebius, previous year; alternatively, year 110.

**114.** An earthquake almost completely destroys Antioch. Eusebius, this year.

**115.** Trajan makes Assyria, Armenia, and Mesopotamia provinces. Eusebius, year 113.

**117.** The Jews, having risen in revolt, carry out great massacres; but after being defeated at Alexandria, they are slaughtered everywhere by all peoples. Eusebius, year 115.

**118.** Trajan dies at Seleucia from a flux of the bowels, in the sixty-fourth year of his age. Eusebius, previous year.

**119.** Hadrian, twenty-one years.

Through Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, and Aristides, a wise man, who instructed him by apologetic books, Hadrian becomes mild toward the Christians. Jerome.

Hadrian restores Alexandria at public expense. Eusebius, previous year.

**120.** Hadrian again defeats the Jews. Eusebius, previous year.

**121.** Pope Sixtus VI holds office for twelve years. Eusebius, previous year; alternatively, year 119.

**122.** Hadrian wages war against the Sarmatians. Eusebius, year 120.

An earthquake occurs. Eusebius, previous year.

**123.** Hadrian establishes colonies in Libya, which had been devastated by the Jews. Eusebius, previous year.

**124.** Justinus [Note: Eusebius calls him Justus, under the year 120.], bishop of Alexandria, holds office for eleven years; alternatively, year 122.

Hadrian gives a law to the Athenians. Eusebius, previous year; lacking in B.

**125.** After Philip, Seneca is appointed the tenth bishop of Jerusalem.

[Note: After Zacchaeus came Tobias, Benjamin, John, Matthias, Philip, Seneca, then this Justus II; Levi, Ephrem, Joseph, Judas II—all of them Jews.]

Eusebius, this year.

**126.** At this time Aquila is regarded as an interpreter. Jerome, year 128.

**127.** After receiving the Christians’ apologetic writings, Hadrian sends a letter on behalf of the Christians. Eusebius, this year.

**129.** At this time Saturninus, Basilides, and Carpocrates establish heresies. Eusebius, year 123.

**130.** Hadrian is first called “Father of his Country.” Eusebius, year 127.

**131.** Cornelius is ordained bishop at Antioch. Eusebius, year 129; alternatively, year 136.

Nicopolis and Caesarea collapse in an earthquake. Eusebius, year 129.

**133.** Pope Telesphorus VII holds office for seven years. Eusebius, year 129; alternatively, year 127.

**134.** The Jews take up arms and devastate Palestine. Eusebius, previous year.

**135.** Eumenes is bishop of Alexandria for thirteen years.

[Note: Eusebius calls him Hymenaeus under the year 131.]

**136.** The Jews rise again and are killed everywhere in great massacres; alternatively, years 132 and 135.

**137.** Jerusalem is restored by Aelius Hadrian, called Aelia after him, and entry is forbidden to the Jews. Eusebius, year 135 and this year.

**138.** Mark is ordained the first bishop of Jerusalem from the Gentiles, after fifteen bishops of Jewish origin had already died. Eusebius, years 125 and 136.

**139.** Hadrian dies from dropsy, being more than sixty years old. Eusebius, previous year.

**140.** *(In the margin: Antoninus, twenty-five years, three months.)* Antoninus, surnamed Pius, instructed through the apology of Justin, a Christian philosopher and later martyr, becomes merciful toward our people. Bede; Epiphanius.

Pope Hyginus VIII holds office for four years. Eusebius, this year; alternatively, year 139.

**141.** Antoninus is called “Father of his Country.” Eusebius, previous year.

**142.** Valentinus and Cerdo, and afterward Marcion and Marcus, attack the Church with heresy. Eusebius, previous year.

**143.** Justin the philosopher writes an apology for the Christians to Antoninus. Eusebius, previous year.

**144.** Pope Pius IX holds office for fifteen years. Eusebius, previous year; alternatively, year 142.

**145.** Heros is appointed bishop at Antioch.

[Note: Heros or Heron is mentioned above under the year 110; he died in 136. This is therefore another man of the same name, the earlier man’s successor after Cornelius, around the year 150.]

Eusebius, year 143.

148 Mark, the seventh bishop of Alexandria, held office for ten years. [Col. 0064C] Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 144.

149 Valentinus the heretic became known. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 144.

152 Apollonius and Basilides were regarded as distinguished philosophers. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 147.

156 Crescens, the Cynic philosopher, stirred up persecution against our Justin; in it he gloriously shed his blood for Christ. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 151; elsewhere, year 167.

[Col. 0065A] 157 Celadion, the eighth bishop of Alexandria, held office for fourteen years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 150; elsewhere, year 154.

158 Anicetus, the tenth pope, held office for thirteen years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 154; elsewhere, year 157.

12 159 At Jerusalem, after Mark, Cassianus was made the seventeenth bishop. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 157.

160 Antoninus Pius died at Lorio in the seventy-seventh year of his age. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

161 Marcus Antoninus Verus and his brother Lucius Aurelius Commodus administered the empire with equal authority. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year. (In the margin: Marcus and Lucius, nineteen years and one month.)

162 While Lucius Caesar was sacrificing at Athens, a fire was seen in the sky being carried from the East to the West. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

[Col. 0065B] 163 Fronto was regarded as a distinguished orator. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

164 The Caesars celebrated a triumph over the Parthians. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 166.

165 The fourth persecution, which arose in Asia, crowned Polycarp with many others, and in Gaul many saints. [Note: [Col. 0065D] According to Sulpicius Severus, book II of the *Sacred History*, chapter 46, martyrdoms were first witnessed in Gaul in the year 177; Paul Orosius agrees with him in book VII, chapter 15 of his *History of the Pagans*.] Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 168.

167 A very great pestilence devastated many provinces and nearly destroyed the Roman army. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 169; Capitolinus, year 168.

168 Soter, the eleventh pope, held office for eight years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 169; *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

169 Theophilus, a wise man, was ordained bishop of Antioch. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year; elsewhere, year 176.

170 Lucius Caesar was killed by apoplexy. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year. — Agrippinus held the office of bishop of Alexandria for twelve years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 167.

[Col. 0066A] 13 171 At this time Hegesippus, Dionysius bishop of Corinth, and Pynitus bishop of Crete were regarded as distinguished men. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 172.

173 The heresy of the Cataphrygians arose. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 172.

174 At this time Tatian founded the heresy of the Encratics. [Note: [Col. 0066D] Read “Encratites.”] Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 172.

175 There was a very great pestilence throughout the whole world. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 173.

176 Antoninus waged many wars personally and through his generals. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 174. — Eleutherius, the twelfth pope, held office for fifteen years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 177.

177 Antoninus made his son Commodus his partner in the kingship. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 178.

178 The emperors distributed gifts, remitted debts, and moderated the harsher laws. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 179. — Lucius, king of Britain, was made a Christian by Pope Eleutherius. Bede.

179 Antoninus perished of illness in Pannonia, and Commodus was called Augustus by the Senate. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 180.

180 After his father’s death, Commodus successfully defeated the Germans. He was obscene and depraved. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 181. — (In the margin: Commodus XV, year XIII.)

181 The temple of Serapis at Alexandria was burned. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 182. — 14 Julian, the tenth bishop of Alexandria, held office for ten years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 180.

182 Irenaeus, bishop of Lugdunum, was regarded as distinguished. Eusebius, year 183. — Pantaenus and Clement were regarded as distinguished men at Alexandria. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 195.

183 The Baths of Commodus were built at Rome. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 184.

[Col. 0067A] 184 Commodus named the month of September after himself. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 185.

185 At Jerusalem Maximus was ordained the twenty-sixth bishop. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 186. — Origen was born at Alexandria. The *Defensor* in B., same year.

186 A certain Montanus founded the heresy of the Cataphrygians. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 172.

188 The Capitol and the library at Rome were burned by lightning. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 189.

189 Demetrius held the office of bishop of Alexandria for forty-three years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year. — Commodus ordered the head of his own image to be placed on the Colossus after its original head had been removed. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 190.

190 Commodus killed many nobles. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 191. — Serapion was ordained the eighth bishop of Antioch. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year; elsewhere, year 199.

[Col. 0067B] 191 A controversy concerning Easter arose, and it was ordered that it be celebrated on the Lord’s Day. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 197. [Note: [Col. 0067D] There is no single agreement among all authorities concerning the date of this Roman council; most assign it to the year 196 or the following year. Pagi.]

192 Commodus, troublesome to everyone, was strangled in the house of Vestalis. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 193; but the reading is “Vestiliani.”

193 Pertinax, more than seventy years old, was ordered by decree of the Senate to rule. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year. (In the margin: Pertinax XVI, seven months.) 15 Victor, the thirteenth pope, held office for ten years. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year. — Julian, a jurist, killed Pertinax in the palace and ruled in his place for seven months. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

194 Severus, an African by origin, killed Julian at the Milvian Bridge and, in honor of Pertinax, whom that same Julian had killed, ordered himself to be called Pertinax. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year. In the margin: Severus XVII, year XVII.

196 At this time Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, Theophilus of Caesarea, Polycarp, [Note: [Col. 0067D] Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*, more correctly calls him Polycrates.] [Col. 0068A] Bachylus of Asia, and other bishops were regarded as distinguished. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

198 A Jewish and Samaritan war broke out. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

199 Severus defeated the Parthians, the Adiabenians, and the Arabs. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

201 The Severan Baths were built near Antioch. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

202 Zephyrinus, the fourteenth pope, held office for eighteen years. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

203 In the fifth persecution Severus crowned very many saints with martyrdom; among them Leonides, the father of Origen, was martyred with many others. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

205 Perpetua and Felicity were condemned to the beasts at Carthage in this persecution.

[Col. 0068B] 206 Symmachus and Theodotion were regarded as translators at this time.

16 207 Severus built a wall among the Britons for 132,000 paces, from sea to sea. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year; Spartianus, year 209.

208 Tertullian, an African, was regarded as very distinguished. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

209 Origen was educated in Alexandria. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

210 Severus died in Britain. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 211.

211 Asclepiades was ordained the ninth bishop of Antioch. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 212. (In the margin: Antoninus XVIII, year VII.)

212 Alexander was ordained the thirty-fifth bishop of Jerusalem while Narcissus was still alive, at God’s command through a vision. [Note: [Col. 0067D] This Alexander had previously been bishop of Cappadocia, in the year 212. He was appointed successor to Narcissus of Jerusalem; concerning him, see Bollandists, 18 March, volume II. Narcissus, however, is commemorated on 29 October.] Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 213.

[Col. 0068C] 213 Antoninus Caracalla received his surname from the type of garment that he distributed at Rome. [Note: [Col. 0068D] The *caracalla* was a type of clothing reaching down to the ankles. See Sextus Aurelius on Antoninus.] Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 214; Sextus Aurelius Victor, preceding year.

[Col. 0069A] 214 The Antonine Baths were called Caracalla’s, after the name of Antoninus.

215 Antoninus built at Rome baths bearing his own name. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 216.

216 Antoninus, unable to restrain his lust, married his stepmother Julia. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 217.

217 Antoninus was killed in the forty-third year of his life. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

218 (In the margin: Macrinus, one year.) The amphitheater at Rome was burned. Eusebius. — Philetus was appointed the tenth bishop of Antioch. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year; elsewhere, following year. — Macrinus was killed with his son Diadumenian in Archelaïs. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

17 219 (In the margin: Aurelius Antoninus, four years.) Aurelius Antoninus lived so indecently during his reign [Col. 0069B] that he omitted no form of obscenity. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year. Callistus, the fifteenth pope, held office for five years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 220; elsewhere, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

220 Hippolytus was regarded as distinguished as a bishop. Bede.

221 Nicopolis was founded in Palestine; previously it had been called Emmaus. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

222 Aurelius was killed at Rome in a military uprising. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

223 (In the margin: Alexander, twenty-one years and thirteen years.) Alexander defeated Xerxes, king of the Persians. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

224 He was a strict reformer of military discipline. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

225 Urban, the sixteenth pope, held office for nine years. He converted many nobles to the faith of Christ. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year; elsewhere, year 223.

[Col. 0069C] 226 Ulpian, a distinguished legal scholar, was regarded as eminent. Eusebius, [Col. 0069C] *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

227 The Alexandrian Baths were built at Rome. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

228 Geminus, a presbyter of Antioch, Hippolytus, [Col. 0070A] and Beryllus, bishop of Bostra, were regarded as distinguished writers. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year. [Note: [Col. 0069D] Eusebius calls this man Geminianus.]

229 Zebennus was ordained the eleventh bishop of Antioch. [Note: [Col. 0069D] Others call him Zibenus at the year 230.] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

230 Mammaea, the mother of Alexander, listened to Origen, the most famous teacher, after he had been summoned to her. Eusebius, *History*. — Heraclas held the office of bishop of Alexandria for sixteen years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

231 Alexander was exceptionally devoted to his mother Mammaea, and for that reason was beloved by everyone. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

232 Origen moved from Alexandria to Caesarea in Palestine. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

233 Pontian, the seventeenth pope, held office for five years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year; elsewhere, year 230.

234 Alexander was well regarded at Rome.

[Col. 0070B] 235 Alexander was killed at Mainz in a military uprising. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year; Paul Orosius.

236 (In the margin: Maximinus, twenty-two years and three years.) Maximinus persecuted Christians, especially the leaders of the Church, as the sixth persecution after Nero. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

237 Maximinus successfully waged war against the Germans.

238 Maximinus was killed at Aquileia by Pupienus. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

239 (In the margin: Gordian XXIII, six years.) Anterus, the eighteenth pope, held office for one month; after him Fabian, the nineteenth, for thirteen years. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year; elsewhere, year 236.

240 Pupienus and Albinus, who had seized the empire, were killed in the palace by Gordian. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

[Col. 0070C] 241 At this time Julius Africanus, the chronographer, was regarded as distinguished.

242 At this time Origen imbued Theodore [Note: [Col. 0069D] The Murensis manuscript adds “surnamed Gregory,” namely the later bishop of Neocaesarea. See the year 266.] and Athenodorus, brothers who later became distinguished bishops, with divine philosophy. Eusebius, *History*.

[Col. 0071A] 19 243 Gordian, while returning victorious from the Parthians, was killed not far from Roman territory. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

244 The soldiers built Gordian a tomb and carried his bones back to Rome. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year. (In the margin: Philip XXIV, with his son, seven years.)

245 Philip was the first of all the emperors to be a Christian. He made his son Philip his partner in the kingship. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

246 During the reign of the two Philips, the thousandth year of the city of Rome was completed. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

247 The thousandth year was celebrated by the Christian emperor with various games. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

248 Pompey’s Theater at Rome was burned. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 246.

[Col. 0071B] 249 Philip built in Thrace a city bearing his name. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, preceding year. — At this time Origen wrote many works.

250 Dionysius, the thirteenth bishop of Alexandria, held office for seventeen years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, preceding year.

251 The elder Philip was killed at Verona, while the younger was killed at Rome. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year. (In the margin: Decius, one year and three months; elsewhere, year 249.)

20 252 Decius, after killing Philip father and son, began a persecution against Christians out of hatred for them. — Antony was born in Egypt. Decius was killed with his son. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year. — Fabian was martyred; Cornelius, the pope, held office in his place for three years. [Note: [Col. 0071D] Perhaps in the letter to Paula, in which he states that he compiled a catalogue of Origen’s works, chapter 54 of *On Illustrious Men*, though that work has been lost.] He too was crowned with martyrdom. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year; elsewhere, preceding year.

253 (In the margin: Gallus with Volusian, two years and three months.) Origen died in the seventieth year of his life. Novatus, a presbyter, became the author of a heresy. There was a very great pestilence. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

254 Lucius, the twenty-first pope, held office for eight months; after him Stephen held office for two years. Gallus was killed with his son. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

255 (In the margin: Valerian and Gallienus, fifteen years.) Valerian carried out the eighth persecution against Christians. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 257.

[Col. 0072B] 257 Cyprian, an outstanding teacher and bishop of Carthage, was crowned with martyrdom. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year; others assign it to the following year.

258 Valerian was captured by Sapor, king of the Persians. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year. 21 Xystus, the pope, held office for seven years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 256, for eight years.

259 After Valerian had been led away to the Persians and deprived of his eyes, Gallienus restored peace to our people. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

261 Gallienus gave himself over to every kind of dissipation. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

[Col. 0073A] 262 The Germans ravaged Italy; the Alamanni, Gaul and Italy. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year; Eutropius, year 264.

263 Macedonia, Greece, Pontus, Asia, and the other provinces were devastated by the Goths. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, preceding year.

265 Dionysius, the pope, held office for nine years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year; elsewhere, year 259.

266 At this time Theodore, also called Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, became distinguished for his miracles.

267 Hymenaeus was ordained bishop of Jerusalem. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

269 Gallienus was killed at Milan. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

270 (In the margin: Claudius, one year and nine months.) Claudius defeated the Goths, who had been ravaging Illyricum and Macedonia for fifteen years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year. — Paul of Samosata was convicted of being a heretic as bishop of Antioch. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 267. 22 Claudius died at Sirmium; his brother Quintillus ruled in his place for seventeen days and was killed at Aquileia. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

271 (In the margin: Aurelian, five years and six months.) Aurelian was useful to the state: at first he was merciful toward Christians, later a persecutor. Trebellius, preceding year.

272 Zenobia, queen of the East, was defeated. Eusebius of Laodicea was regarded as a distinguished bishop. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

273 Tetricus and Zenobia, captives, preceded Aurelian in his triumph at Rome. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

274 The emperor built a temple to the sun and became the ninth persecutor of Christians. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

275 (In the margin: Tacitus, six months.) Aurelian, terrified by a divine thunderbolt, was killed by the soldiers; Tacitus ruled in his place for six months. When Tacitus was killed in Pontus, Florian ruled for eighty-eight days and was then killed. Eusebius, [Col. 0074A] *Chronicle*, following year.

276 Felix, the twenty-fifth pope, held office for five years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year; elsewhere, year 269.

277 (In the margin: Probus, six years and four months.) Probus restored Gaul, which had been occupied by the barbarians, with immense courage. Eutropius.

278 Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, was regarded as distinguished. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

279 A certain Manes, a Persian by birth, founded the insane heresy of the Manichaeans. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, preceding year.

23 280 Quirillus was appointed the eighteenth bishop of Antioch. Eusebius, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, calls him Cyrillus.

281 Eutychian, the pope, held office for eight months. [Note: [Col. 0073D] He held office for eight years and eleven months; Gaius, however, for twelve years and four months.] Pope Gaius succeeded him and held office for sixteen years. [Col. 0074B] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

282 Probus was killed at Sirmium in a military uprising. Theonas held the office of bishop of Alexandria for nineteen years. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

283 (In the margin: Carus with his sons Carinus and Numerian, two years.) Carus, victorious over the Parthians, died after being struck by lightning over the Tigris. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

284 Numerian was killed through the treachery of his father-in-law Aper. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year. — Carinus, defeated in battle by Diocletian near the Margus, was killed. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year. — Up to this point, according to Dionysius, 284 years are reckoned from the incarnation of the Lord.

285 (In the margin: Diocletian, twenty years.) From this year the Greeks began their Easter cycles. [Note: [Col. 0073D] This is the celebrated Era of Diocletian, or of the Martyrs, whose beginning is reckoned from 29 August of the year 284.] [Col. 0075A]

286 Diocletian took the Herculius Maximian into partnership in the kingship. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 288.

287 Maximian defeated Amandus with his peasants in Gaul. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

24 288 At this time Carus [Eusebius: Carausius] harassed Britain; Narseus, king of the Persians, the East; Achilleus, Egypt; and the Quinquegentiani, Africa. For this reason Constantine [read: Constantius], Galerius, and Maximian were elevated to the kingship. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

290 The emperor made Constantius, the father of Constantine, Caesar; he ruled for sixteen years. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, preceding year.

291 The emperor made Galerius Maximian Caesar. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 289.

292 At this time the presbyter Pierius, and Achillas [Col. 0075B] and Melitius, became distinguished at Alexandria.

293 At this time various enemies were defeated in diverse and numerous battles. Eusebius.

295 Diocletian ordered himself to be worshiped as a god. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year; elsewhere, year 293.

296 After Pope Gaius was crowned with martyrdom, Marcellinus, the twenty-eighth pope, succeeded him. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

297 After defeating Achilleus, Diocletian recovered Alexandria and Egypt. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

298 The same man condemned very many people throughout Egypt to confiscation and exile. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

299 Constantius killed sixty thousand Alamanni near Langres. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 301; Eutropius, year 297.

[Col. 0076A] 25 300 Galerius Maximian, defeated by Narseus, ran in purple before Diocletian’s chariot. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 301.

301 Maximian defeated Narseus and took his wife and children captive. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 303; Eutropius, year 297.

302 Diocletian and Maximian celebrated a magnificent triumph over the enemies. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

303 Diocletian and Maximian overthrew the churches, burned the sacred books, and tortured Christians. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

304 Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid down the purple and the rule. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year. — Pope Eusebius held office for eight months, after whom Miltiades held office for four years. [Note: [Col. 0075D] Marcellinus indeed died in this year, but not Eusebius: Marcellus succeeded him after an interruption of three years in the pontificate, in the year 308. Pagi.] Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

[Col. 0076B] 305 Maximinus and Severus were made Caesars. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year. — Constantius Augustus died; after him came his son Constantine. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 307. — Constantine, the son of Constantius by his concubine Helena, was the first Christian emperor apart from Philip, and from him Christian emperors began. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 307.

306 (In the margin: Constantine, thirty years and ten months.) Maxentius, the son of Maximian Herculius, was called Augustus. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 308.

26 307 Maximian was disgracefully killed at Massilia. Eutropius, year 310.

[Col. 0077A] 308 After Severus was killed, Licinius was made Caesar. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year. — Galerius Maximian died. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 311.

309 Silvester, the pope, held office for twenty-five years. [Note: [Col. 0077D] The beginning of Silvester’s pontificate belongs to the year 314, when he succeeded Melchiades or Miltiades. Pagi.] Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 312. — Maximinus persecuted Christians and died at Tarsus. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 312.

311 Maxentius was defeated and killed by Constantine near the Milvian Bridge. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 313.

312 The persecution finally ended after ten years.

314 Diocletian died on his estate and alone among all private citizens was enrolled among the gods. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 317; elsewhere, year 313.

315 Very many persecutors and magicians were slaughtered.

[Col. 0077B] 318 Licinius drove Christians from his palace and persecuted them. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 321.

27 319 At this time Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, founded the abominable heresy of the Arians. Epiphanius, year 361.

320 Alexander was ordained bishop of Alexandria. [Note: [Col. 0077D] Alexander began his pontificate in the year 312.] Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 322.

321 The presbyter Arius, expelled from the Church by his bishop Alexander, brought many over to his impiety. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

322 A council of 318 bishops assembled at Nicaea under Pope Silvester. [Note: [Col. 0077D] By universal agreement this council was held in the year 325.]

[Col. 0078A] 323 Constantine [Note: [Col. 0077D] Eusebius more correctly has Constantius. Constantine the younger had already been appointed Caesar in the year 318.] the son of Constantine, was made Caesar. — Licinius was killed. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

324 At this time the Lord’s cross was discovered at Jerusalem by Helena, the mother of Constantine, under Macarius, bishop of that city. Saint Paulinus, letter 11; elsewhere, year 326. — Nazarius, a distinguished rhetorician, was regarded as eminent. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, following year.

325 Constantine’s twentieth-anniversary celebrations were held at Nicomedia and, in the following year, displayed at Rome. Eusebius, *Chronicle*, year 327.

326 Up to this point Eusebius writes his history. From here Jerome continues it; elsewhere, the following year.

327 28 Constantine, while restoring Drepana, a city of Bithynia, named it Helenopolis in honor of his mother Helena. Jerome, following year.

328 Arian bishops obtained control of the Church. Their periods are not arranged, because they are judged to be enemies of Christ. [Col. 0078B] Jerome, following year.

329 The presbyter Juvencus became distinguished. The heretic Porphyry was released from exile by Constantine. Jerome, following year.

330 Athanasius was ordained bishop of Alexandria. Constantinople was dedicated. Jerome, following year.

331 By an edict of Constantine the temples of the pagans were overthrown. Jerome, following year.

332 At this time Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, and many other teachers became distinguished.

333 Antony the monk was regarded as distinguished.

[Col. 0079A] 334 Constantine sent honorable letters to Antony with his sons. Jerome, year 337.

335 At Constantine’s thirtieth-anniversary celebrations, Dalmatius was called Caesar. Jerome, year 337.

29 336 Constantine died at Nicomedia while preparing for war against the Persians, in the sixty-sixth year of his age. Elsewhere, year 337.

337 (In the margin: Constantius, thirty-five years; Constantine and Constans, twenty-four years, five months, thirteen days.) Dalmatius Caesar was killed through the faction of his cousin Constantius and a military uprising. Jerome, year 339.

338 Constantius, polluted by the Arian heresy through the presbyter Arius and Eusebius of Nicomedia, persecuted Bishop Athanasius and all bishops who did not belong to his party. Jerome, year 340.

[Col. 0079B] 339 Constantine, making war against his brother Constantius, was killed near Aquileia. Jerome, year 341; elsewhere, year 340.

340 Earthquakes overthrew many cities. Jerome, year 342.

341 The Franks, subdued by Constans, were received into peace. Jerome, following year.

342 After the Arians expelled Paul, bishop of Constantinople, Macedonius, the arch-heretic, was substituted in his place. Jerome, year 343.

343 At this time Maximinus, bishop of Trier, became distinguished; he received Athanasius when Athanasius was a fugitive from Constantius. Jerome, following year.

344 Athanasius returned to Alexandria in response to a letter from Constans. Jerome, year 346.

[Col. 0080A] 345 There was an eclipse of the sun, and earthquakes overthrew many cities. Jerome, following year and year 348.

30 346 For three days and nights Rome floated, and the cities of Campania were afflicted. Jerome, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year; he reads “swayed” (*nutavit*).

347 War was waged against the Persians, with heavy losses for the Romans. Jerome, year 349.

348 Liberius was ordained at Rome; after he was expelled by the Arians, Felix was substituted in his place. [Note: [Col. 0079D] The ordination of Liberius occurred in the year 352, and the substitution of Felix in 355. Pagi.] Jerome, year 350.

349 Constans was killed in the thirtieth year of his age. Magnentius and many others threw the state into confusion. Jerome, year 351.

350 At this time the bones of the apostles Timothy and Saint Andrew, and of Luke the evangelist, were brought to Constantinople. [Col. 0080B] Jerome, years 357 and 359.

351 Gallus, the cousin of Constantius, was made Caesar. Magnentius killed himself. Jerome, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

352 Antony the monk died in the desert in the 105th year of his life. Many hermits became distinguished. Elsewhere, year 356.

353 Gallus Caesar was killed. Victorinus the rhetorician and Donatus the grammarian were regarded as distinguished. Jerome, year 355.

354 Julian was made Caesar by Constantius. Eusebius of Vercelli and Dionysius of Milan were exiled with others. Jerome, year 356.

355 Great forces of the Alamanni were destroyed at Argentarium [Note: [Col. 0079D] This is present-day Strasbourg. See Ammianus Marcellinus, book XVI, chapter 12; Eutropius, book X.] by Julian Caesar. Zosimus, year 357.

[Col. 0081A] 31 356 Julian defeated the Germans on the Rhine. Ammianus. Hilary of Poitiers and Athanasius of Alexandria suffered many evils at the hands of the Arians.

357 A synod of Arians was held at Rimini against the faith. Jerome, year 360. — Paulinus, bishop of Trier, died in exile. Jerome, year 359.

358 Julian usurped the title of Augustus. Constantius prepared for war against the Parthians. Ammianus, year 360.

359 Constantius, abandoning the Parthian war, took up arms against Julian. Ammianus.

360 Constantius died in the forty-fifth year of his age. Jerome, year 362.

361 (In the margin: Julian XXXVI, one year and eight months.) Julian, having been made a pagan from a Christian reader, persecuted Christians. Athanasius, Eusebius, and Lucifer returned from exile. Jerome, year 363. — Pagans attacked the tomb of Saint John the Baptist at Sebaste.

32 362 Julian, having departed for the Parthian war and vowed the blood of Christians to his gods, was killed and died by the judgment of God at the hands of a certain enemy, in the thirty-second year of his age. After him Jovian was made emperor, and with the whole army returned to Christianity. Ammianus, year 363. — A heretical synod was assembled at Antioch. Jerome, year 365; elsewhere, year 361.

363 Jovian, lying in a new house, died after being suffocated by the odor of burning coals and lime. Valentinian ruled in his place; Julian had deprived him of his military tribunate because of his faith in Christ. Jerome, year 365. — (In the margin: Jovian, thirty-seven years and eight months.)

364 (In the margin: Valentinian XXXVIII, eleven years.) Valentinian gave his brother Valens the empire of the East. Jerome, year 365.

365 Pope Damasus was ordained at Rome. [Note: [Col. 0081D] This happened in the year 366. Pagi.] Jerome, year 367. — Valens, baptized by Eudoxius, the Arian bishop, persecuted Christians. Jerome, year 368.

366 Gratian, the son of Valentinian, was made emperor. True wool mixed with rain flowed from the clouds. Jerome, year 368.

367 Athanaric, king of the Goths, persecuted Christians. [Note: [Col. 0081D] The persecution of Athanaric, who first began to reign in the year 369, belongs to a later date.] Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, died. Jerome, following year. Nicaea collapsed in an earthquake. Jerome, year 369.

[Col. 0082B] 33 368 Eusebius of Vercelli died. Jerome, year 371. — At this time the bishop Apollinaris founded a heresy. Jerome, year 376.

369 There was a great famine in Phrygia. Jerome, year 371.

370 On these days, after the death of Auxentius the Arian, Ambrose was ordained bishop of the Milanese. [Note: [Col. 0081D] The ordination of Ambrose belongs to the year 374.] Jerome, year 376.

371 Didymus the blind became distinguished at Alexandria. Jerome, year 373. — Valentinian subdued the Saxons by slaughter. Jerome, year 374; Ammianus, year 370.

372 Eunomius became known, from whom came the Eunomian heresy. Jerome, year 373. — The Burgundians settled near the Rhine.

[Col. 0083A] 373 At this time, through the teaching of Ambrose, Italy was converted to the faith of Christ. Jerome, year 376.

374 Valentinian died from a sudden bursting of blood; his son Gratian then ruled with his uncle Valens. Jerome, year 376.

375 (In the margin: Valens with Gratian and Valentinian, four years.) Gratian destroyed thirty thousand Alamanni. Ammianus, year 378. Orosius.

376 Valens issued a law that monks should serve in the army; those unwilling were ordered to be killed with clubs. Sozomen, year 375; Jerome, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

377 After Valens provided them with Arian teachers, the Goths became Arians. Gothic Chronicle.

34 378 Valens, the Arian emperor, after his many evil deeds, when the Roman army had been slaughtered in Thrace by the Goths, was himself wounded by an arrow and fled. Since he repeatedly fell from his horse, he was brought into a poor hut; when the pursuing enemies arrived, he was burned alive in that very hut and was denied even burial. After him Gratian, the thirty-ninth emperor and his brother’s son, ruled with his brother Valentinian for six years. Jerome, year 379; elsewhere, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year. — Up to this point Jerome brought the Chronicle of Eusebius. From here Hermann continues it. [Note: [Col. 0083D] From this point begins the new manuscript of the Urstisian edition, or the San-Georgian manuscript, which agrees word for word with the Bavarian autograph of Bernold. The San-Emmeram manuscript likewise begins here, though it is more exact in relation to the Augian manuscript. The reason why the manuscripts mentioned above begin chiefly at this point seems to be no other than that Hermann is remembered as having begun his Chronicle from here, although he collected the earlier material no less than the later from the Chronicles of other writers.]

379 Because of the disturbed condition of the empire, the emperor Gratian appointed Theodosius, a Spaniard distinguished in arms, faith, [Col. 0084A] and religion, emperor of the East. Reigning for seventeen years, he restrained the Goths, Huns, Alans, and many other peoples, and often recovered the empire from Roman tyrants. Idatius. — At this time Priscillian, a bishop from Gaul, [Note: [Col. 0083D] The manuscripts indeed read this way, but Prosper more correctly has “from Galicia”; Priscillian was not a Gaul but a Spaniard.] founded the heresy named after himself. Orosius; Prosper.

380 From this year Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, began the Easter cycles. [Note: [Col. 0083D] See Leo the Great, letter 44.] At this time Ambrose, archbishop of Milan, wrote many elevated works. Prosper, *Ecclesiastical History*, same year.

35 381 The second universal synod of 150 bishops was held at Constantinople against Macedonius, the arch-heretic and bishop of that city, under Theodosius Augustus and Pope Damasus. Prosper; Idatius. [Note: [Col. 0083D] Both the new and the old editions of Prosper number 180 bishops; all the others generally agree with our text. See Labbe, *Collection of Councils*, volume II, p. 911.]

382 Athanaric, king of the Goths and persecutor [Col. 0084B] of Christians, was received at Constantinople by Theodosius and died. [Note: [Col. 0083D] Prosper has “was killed.” Idatius and Marcellinus assign this to the preceding year, while the latter writes that he died a natural death.]

383 Arcadius, the son of Augustus Theodosius, was taken into partnership in the kingship by his father and ruled for twenty-six years. Prosper.

384 Honorius, the son of Augustus Theodosius, was born. At Rome, after Pope Damasus, Siricius—called Ursinus in Prosper’s Chronicles [Note: [Col. 0084D] This reading occurs only in certain manuscripts; in the new edition of his works he is likewise called Siricius. The differing manuscript reading seems to have arisen because Ursinus or Ursicinus attempted to occupy the Roman see at the same time as Siricius; hence both were conflated into a single person. Siricius presided from 22 December 384 until 25 November 398, nearly fourteen years, although Prosper assigns him fifteen years of pontificate. In addition, the Murensis manuscript rightly notes here that the succession of Roman bishops and their years are found written very differently in certain books.]—was the fortieth pope and held office for fourteen years. Prosper; Cassiodorus.

[Col. 0085A] 385 Maximus was made emperor by the soldiers in Britain. Crossing over to Gaul, he drove Gratian Augustus—betrayed by his own men and defeated in battle—into flight, captured him at Lyon, and killed him. He drove his brother Valentinian Augustus from Italy to Theodosius in the East and made his own son Victor his partner in the empire. [Note: [Col. 0085D] Marcellinus and Socrates record the death of Gratian in the year 383; Valentinian’s expulsion belongs to the year 387.] Marcellinus, year 383.

36 388 The tyrant Maximus was defeated and captured by the Augusti Theodosius and Valentinian near Aquileia; stripped of the purple, he was beheaded. His son Victor was killed in Gaul by Arbogast, master of the soldiers, and Valentinian was restored to the empire. Prosper; Idatius.

389 The bishops Ithacius and Ursacius were deprived of communion with the Church because of the killing of Priscillian, whom they had accused. Prosper; Isidore, *On Illustrious Men*.

392 Valentinian Augustus, wearied—as they say—by the excessive harshness of Arbogast’s conduct, ended his life by hanging at Vienne. Thereupon Arbogast, having been accused, made Eugenius emperor in Gaul. Prosper. — Jerome brought to this point the book that he wrote *On Illustrious Men of the Church*. Marcellinus.

393 The emperor Theodosius ruled for three years with his sons Arcadius and Honorius. Prosper.

[Col. 0086A] 394 John the anchorite, whose life Jerome published, [Note: [Col. 0085D] See Saint Augustine, book V of *The City of God*, chapter 26, and Rufinus, book II of his *History*, chapters 19 and 32. I do not find the life indicated here among the works of Saint Jerome. Baronius indeed says in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, 27 March, that it was written in the letter to Ctesiphon (*Works*, volume IV, p. 476); but the editor Martianaeus maintains that the John praised there is Chrysostom. Compare volume III of the Bollandists’ *March*, 27th.] foretold that Theodosius the emperor would be victorious against the tyrant Eugenius. Prosper.

395 The emperor Theodosius, aided by God, defeated and killed the tyrant Eugenius in battle. In that same year he himself died at Milan and was buried at Saint Laurence; his son Arcadius then ruled with his brother Honorius for thirteen years. Prosper. — Augustine, the most eloquent defender of the Church, was ordained bishop—although unwilling—of Hippo in the African region, while the city’s bishop Maximus was still alive. [Note: [Col. 0085D] This passage contains an error. Although Saint Augustine was ordained bishop in this year, it was by no means Maximus, but Megalius, primate of Numidia, who did this, as Augustine himself reports in the brief account of the third day’s conference, chapter 7 (*Works*, volume IX, p. 558).] Possidius. The poet Claudian became distinguished. John the hermit departed to the Lord. — Up to this point Rufinus brought the ecclesiastical History of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, which he had translated.

[Col. 0086B] 396 Gildo, count of Africa, seized tyranny there, daring to usurp it for himself. Zosimus.

397 After a council had been held at Carthage, the council of Hippo was confirmed. Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, departed to the Lord after many virtues, in the eighty-first year of his age and the twenty-sixth of his episcopate; Sulpicius Severus published his life and virtues in an excellent style. [Note: [Col. 0085D] See Petavius, book XI, chapter 47. Pagi, however, argues in a separate dissertation that Martin died in the year 400.] Gregory of Tours.

[Col. 0087A] 398 Saint Ambrose of Milan, archbishop and a marvelous teacher of the Church, departed to the Lord. Marcellinus. — At Rome Anastasius, the forty-first pope, held office for four years. The same author. — 38 In Africa Gildo, the count, was defeated in battle by his brother Mascezel, with God’s help, and perished. Marcellinus; Jordanes.

399 By order of the emperors, temples of idols were destroyed in various parts of the world, and gladiatorial games were abolished. Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, final chapter. The eunuch Eutropius, who in this year had usurped the consulship with Theodorus, died deprived of both his honor and his life. Prosper; Marcellinus.

400 The Goths, entering Italy under their kings Alaric and Radagaisus, devastated it. Prosper; Cassiodorus. — At this time Pope Anastasius also established his decrees, discovered and condemned Manichaeans in the City, and built the basilica called Crescentiana on the Mamurtine Way. Anastasius.

401 John of Constantinople and Theophilus were regarded as very distinguished bishops, but they were so opposed to one another that, through Theophilus’s machinations, John was banished into exile in Pontus. Prosper.

402 The Romans at Pollentia, fighting under the command of Stilicho against the Goths with heavy losses on both sides, were finally defeated and turned their backs [Note: [Col. 0087D] Claudian, in his *Sixth Consulship of Honorius*, and Clarius, Book IV of *The Gothic War*, write that the Goths were routed by Stilicho. This battle, however, took place on 29 March 403, although Prosper and several others assign it to this year.]. Cassiodorus; Jordanes; Orosius. — At Rome Pope Innocent XLII held the see for fourteen years.

403 A council was held at Carthage against the Donatists.

39 404 In these times Pope Innocent established many decrees in the Church [Col. 0088A], dedicated at Rome the church constructed for the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius, and established a titular church in the City. Anastasius; Bede.

405 While the Romans were fighting in Tuscany under the command of Stilicho, Radagaisus [Note: [Col. 0087D] The reading of the Augiensis manuscript, corrupted in the Bavarian manuscript, should be restored as *Radagaisus and thousands*.], together with thousands of Gothic soldiers, was defeated and captured, by God’s favor, in an easy victory. Marcellinus; Prosper.

406 The Vandals, Sueves, and Alans, having crossed the Rhine on 3 Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 0087D] Prosper has “the day before the Kalends of January” and omits the Sueves, as does Cassiodorus.], entered Gaul in a hostile manner. Gothic Chronicle.

407 Constantine, having seized tyrannical power in Britain, crossed over to Gaul. Prosper.

408 The emperor Arcadius died at Constantinople, leaving his son Theodosius as his successor; with him his uncle Honorius thereafter ruled for fifteen years. Cassiodorus; Prosper. — The brave commander Stilicho, together with his son Eucherius, was killed by Honorius Augustus. Orosius; Marcellinus.

409 The Vandals, Alans, and Sueves occupied Spain on the day of October [Note: [Col. 0087D] In the manuscript, *III* appears to be read instead of *in*, yielding the same reading found in Bernold and genuinely derived from Hydatius, who says that this invasion occurred on a Tuesday; neither the fourth day before the Kalends nor the third day before the Ides of October assigned by Hydatius can apply to this year, whereas the third day of that month does.]. Hydatius. Attalus, made emperor at Rome by tyranny and soon expelled, joined the Goths. Prosper.

40 410 Alaric, king of the Goths, besieged Rome and, after inflicting many massacres and carrying off much plunder there, spared only the sacred places and those who had fled to them, because he was a Christian, in the 1,164th year from the founding of the City. Placidia, sister of Honorius Augustus, was captured by the Goths in the City among others. Hydatius. A part of the Goths occupied Venetia after its capture; they were later called Ostrogoths and entered into alliance with the Romans. Jordanes, under the year 409.

[Col. 0089A] 411 The tyrant Constantine was defeated and captured by Honorius at Arles; his son Constans was killed in Spain by the count Gerontius, and Maximus was raised by him to the throne. Prosper; Marcellinus. — Constantius was appointed commander by Honorius. When Alaric, king of the Goths, died, Ataulf succeeded him and took the captive Placidia as his wife. Pestilence, famine, wild beasts, and the barbarian sword spread misery and devastation widely throughout the world. Zosimus; Hydatius, and others, under the year 414.

412 Maximus was deprived of his kingdom in Spain but allowed to live. Most of the Goths entered Gaul under their king Ataulf. Prosper. — Heros, a disciple of Saint Martin and holy bishop of Arles, was unjustly driven from his see, and Patroclus was appointed in his place. Prosper. — The Vandals and Sueves obtained Gallaecia, the Alans Lusitania and the provinces of Carthaginensis [Col. 0089B], and the Silingi Baetica, by lot. Hydatius, under the year 411.

413 Herodianus, consul of this year with Lucius, was accused of revolutionary activity in Africa and deprived of his office and life. Prosper, however, calls him Heraclianus. The Burgundians obtained the part of Gaul adjoining the Rhine [Note: [Col. 0089D] From Olympiodorus it may be inferred that this incursion of the Burgundians into Germania Prima had already taken place in 411.]. Prosper. The brothers Jovinus and Sebastianus, tyrants of Gaul, were killed at Narbonne by Honorius. Prosper; Hydatius. — In these times Pelagius the Briton, with the support of Coelestius and Julian, excessively exalting free will and asserting that a human being could become perfect by his own effort without the help of God’s grace, disturbed the faith of the Church. Saint Augustine opposed his heresy more particularly than all others, and Pope Innocent condemned it along with the other heretics. Prosper.

[Col. 0089C] 414 Attalus, at the instigation of the Goths, seized tyrannical power in Gaul. Prosper.

415 The Goths set out for Spain. Attalus, deprived of their support, was captured by the Romans [Note: [Col. 0089D] Philostorgius more correctly assigns this to the following year.]. Marcellinus. — Ataulf, king of the Goths, died after being wounded by one of his companions, and Wallia assumed the royal title in his place. Prosper. — At Jerusalem, the bodies of Saint Stephen the protomartyr, Gamaliel, and Nicodemus, divinely revealed to the presbyter Lucian, were discovered and glorified by countless miracles. Hydatius.

416 Wallia, king of the Goths, desiring peace, returned Placidia, Ataulf’s widow, to her brother Honorius Augustus. The commander Constantius won her marriage [Note: [Col. 0089D] Olympiodorus also places this first in the following year.]. Prosper; Marcellinus. — At Rome Pope Zosimus XLIII held the see for three years; he also promulgated decrees concerning the condition of the Church. Anastasius, and others, under the year 417.

417 Honorius Augustus entered Rome in triumph, with Attalus preceding his chariot and afterward being sent into exile. Prosper. — A dispute and disagreement arose concerning the Easter of this year [Col. 0090B] under Pope Zosimus at Rome [Note: [Col. 0089D] According to Marcellinus, Zosimus succeeded Innocent on 18 March of the following year; Innocent died on the 12th of that same month. Only one year of his pontificate, together with nine months and as many days, is therefore assigned to him. The “Ysicius” mentioned here is in fact Hesychius, bishop of Salona. See Labbe, *Collection of the Councils*, vol. II, p. 1556.]. Constantius captured Fredibalus, king of the Vandals, by stratagem without a battle and sent him to the emperor Honorius. Hydatius, under the year 415.

418 At Carthage, a council of 217 bishops was assembled and confirmed by Pope Zosimus; Pelagius and the other heretics were condemned. Prosper. — An eclipse of the sun occurred on 14 Kalends of August [Note: [Col. 0090D] Hydatius incorrectly assigns it to 417, when 19 July was a Thursday; but according to the Alexandrian Chronicle the eclipse occurred on a Friday, and therefore in this year, 418.], and a comet was visible thereafter until September. Marcellinus. — A battle took place between Gunderic, king of the Vandals, and Hermeric [also Ermenric], king of the Sueves. Hydatius, under the following year.

419 Honorius Augustus took the commander Constantius into partnership in the imperial power. Hydatius, under the year 421. — At Rome Pope Boniface XLIV held the see for four years; during his pontificate Eulalius was also ordained pope by some. After Eulalius was expelled by the emperors, Boniface was firmly established in the see, issued his own decrees, and built in the City the church of Saint Felicitas and Saint Silvanus [Note: [Col. 0090D] Boniface was ordained in 418, on 29 December.]. Anastasius; Prosper. — The emperor Constantius established peace with Wallia, king of the Goths, granting him Aquitania Secunda, together with several cities, for settlement. Prosper; Hydatius.

420 When Wallia, king of the Goths, died, Theoderic succeeded him. Isidore, under the year 419. — At Bethlehem the presbyter Jerome, incomparable teacher and interpreter of the Scriptures, died in the ninety-first year of his age. Prosper; Bede. — The Alans were so thoroughly subdued by the Goths through slaughter that, abandoning their royal title, they submitted themselves for protection to Gunderic, king of the Vandals. Gregory of Tours; Hydatius, under the year 418.

43 421 The emperor Constantius died at Ravenna. Hydatius; Prosper. — War arose between the Vandals and the Goths. Hydatius.

422 An army under the command of Castinus was sent against the Vandals in Spain, with Gothic assistance. Boniface, a warlike man, offended by this, withdrew and went to Africa. The Vandals, however, driven to desperation, became victorious when Castinus imprudently engaged them in battle. Prosper; Hydatius.

423 Placidia Augusta, expelled by her brother Honorius, went with her son Valentinian to the emperor Theodosius in the East. Prosper. — At Rome Pope Coelestine XLV held the see for nine years; he established many ordinances in the Church and dedicated the basilica of Julius, constructed in the City. Anastasius; Marcellinus, more correctly under the year 421. — Honorius, emperor of the West, died at Ravenna, and the tyrant John seized his kingdom. The emperor Theodosius of the East ruled for twenty-six years after the death of his uncle Honorius. Prosper, under the twenty-seventh year.

424 Theodosius made Valentinian, the son of his aunt Placidia, Caesar and sent him back with his mother to possess the kingdom of the West [Col. 0091C]. Prosper; Cassiodorus. — The tyrant John set out for Africa against Boniface. Hydatius.

425 Valentinian, together with his mother, overcame John, who was killed by his own men, and assumed the kingdom of the West. He condemned Castinus, who had favored John, to exile, but pardoned the patrician Aetius because he had caused the summoned Huns to return. Prosper; Marcellinus.

426 Patroclus, bishop of Arles, was innocently murdered by a certain barbarian tribune. Prosper. — Gunderic [Col. 0092A], king of the Vandals, died, struck down by divine judgment; the tyrant Geiseric [also Genseric], an Arian heretic and cruel persecutor of Catholics, succeeded him. Hydatius, under the year 428.

44 427 Boniface, powerful in Africa, killed certain commanders who were fighting against him. Against him, barbarians having been summoned, the sea, previously unknown to them, was made passable for this purpose. Thus the savage nation of the Vandals, driven from Spain by the Goths, crossed the strait and invaded Africa, raging miserably with sword, plunder, and fire, after first killing Ermengarius [Hydatius has Hermigarius], king of the Sueves, following nineteen years of devastation in Spain. Hydatius, and others, under the year 429.

428 Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, teaching that there were two persons in Christ and asserting that a mere human being had been born from the Virgin and had afterward received divinity, was accused of heresy by Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and by Pope Coelestine. Prosper. — Aetius, a Roman count, after slaughtering many Franks, recovered the part of Gaul that they had occupied and held. Prosper; Hydatius.

429 Aetius was made master of the soldiers and patrician. Prosper. — The Pelagian heretic Agricola infected Britain with his error. Consequently Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, sent there by Pope Coelestine, defeated the heresy and brought salvation to very many. Prosper; Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*.

430 Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, the most invincible champion and defender of the Church of Christ and of the Catholic faith, was besieged by barbarians in his own city. In the midst of the hardships of the siege, concerned for the Church, he had replied to Julian’s sophistries while contending for the grace of God. He was taken away by that same divine grace, lest he should see the ruin of his people, and departed to the Lord on 5 Kalends of September, in the seventy-sixth year of his age and the fortieth of his episcopate or priesthood. Prosper; Bede, *Chronicle*.

431 The third universal synod, of 200 bishops, was assembled at Ephesus under Pope Coelestine; there, among other heresies, Nestorius and his sect were condemned.

[Col. 0093A] 45 Palladius was sent by Pope Coelestine as the first bishop to the Scots who believed in Christ [Note: [Col. 0093C] Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, Book I, chapter 13, assigns this to the eighth year of Theodosius the Younger, which should be understood as the eighth year from the death of his father Honorius. Others maintain that Palladius was sent to the Irish. On this matter see Ussher, *On the Antiquities of the British Churches*, chapter 16, and other English writers.]. Prosper; Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*.

432 At Rome Pope Xystus XLVI held the see for eight years. When accused by a certain Bassus, he was acquitted by fifty-six bishops after the case had been examined in a synod, and Bassus was condemned. Boniface, having returned from Africa and been made master of the soldiers, fought against and defeated Aetius, but a few days later died of illness. Aetius, fleeing his enemies, went to Dalmatia and Pannonia and, with the help of the Huns, recovered the favor of the imperial rulers and his former rank. Prosper; Marcellinus.

433 The Burgundians were defeated in battle by Aetius. Hydatius, under the year 436. — At this time Pope Xystus built in the City the church of Saint Mary called that of Liberius and the church of Saint Laurence [Col. 0093B]; he also embellished the confession of Saint Peter and that of Saint Laurence. Valentinian Augustus likewise gave many gifts to the churches and built the confession of Saint Paul. Peter, bishop of Saint Sabina, also built a church. Bede, *Chronicle*; Anastasius.

434 The Vandals, now harassing Africa for the ninth year, requested a treaty from the Romans. Prosper.

435 Peace was made with the Vandals, and a portion of Africa was given to them for habitation. Aetius defeated Gundicharius, king of the Burgundians, in war and granted peace when he begged for it; but he did not enjoy it long, for he was killed by the Huns together with his people. Prosper.

436 The Goths disturbed the peace and, among their other evils, pressed Narbonne, which they had besieged, with famine [Col. 0093C]. But the Roman commander Litorius arrived, drove back the enemy by force, and freed the city from famine by bringing in grain. Prosper.

437 The Romans waged war against the Goths with the Huns [Col. 0094A] as auxiliaries. Geiseric, king of the Vandals and an Arian, persecuted the Catholics in Africa: he drove some from their churches, condemned others to exile, and subjected still others to various punishments, crowning them with martyrdom. The barbarians began to practice piracy. Prosper. — Valentinian Augustus, coming to Constantinople to visit the emperor Theodosius, his maternal uncle’s son, took his daughter as his wife. Prosper. — Hermeric, king of the Sueves, overcome by illness, appointed his son Rechila king in his place. Hydatius, under the year 438.

438 The Goths defeated Rechila, king of the Sueves, in battle and stripped him of his treasures. Hydatius.

439 Julian, bishop of Eclana, an exceedingly boastful Pelagian, attempting to insinuate himself into the communion of the Church [Note: [Col. 0093C] The Canisian edition reads *subrepere* (“to creep in”) instead of *subripere* (“to steal away”).], was again condemned by Pope Xystus. The Romans, with the Huns as auxiliaries, fought an unsuccessful battle against the Goths and King Theoderic in Gaul; the Roman commander Litorius was wounded and afterward captured and killed by them. Nevertheless, not long afterward, when they humbly requested it, peace was arranged between them and the Romans. Prosper. — In that same year, while Aetius and the Romans were engaged against the Goths [Note: [Col. 0093C] For *et*, read *cum* (“with”).], Geiseric, king of the Vandals, who was thought to be faithful and friendly toward the Roman people, treacherously captured Carthage under the pretext of peace on 14 Kalends of November. He massacred the citizens, especially the nobles; plundered all their wealth; killed and expelled the priests; converted the churches to the use of his own people; and confused every divine and human right. There he held the kingdom for thirty-seven years, during which very many saints were crowned with martyrdom for the Catholic faith. Prosper.

[Col. 0094C] 47 440 After Xystus died at Rome, Leo, a man distinguished in learning and character, became Pope XLVII and held the see for twenty-two years. He wrote and established many things of great importance for the benefit of the Church [Col. 0095A]; he condemned the Eutychian and Nestorian heresies. In his time Demetrias, a servant of Christ, built the church of Saint Stephen at Rome. — Geiseric, severely afflicting Sicily after overrunning it, returned to Carthage out of fear of the commander Sebastian. Rechila, king of the Sueves, captured the province of Baetica and Carthaginensis Spain. Prosper; Marcellinus; Anastasius; Hydatius.

441 The emperor Theodosius began a war against Geiseric and the Vandals through his commanders; but because they delayed and postponed the undertaking, they were more a burden than a defense to Sicily. Prosper; Cassiodorus.

442 While the Huns were devastating Thrace and Illyricum with savage plundering, the army sent against the Vandals was recalled to defend the Eastern territories. The emperor Valentinian established peace with Geiseric, king of the Vandals, Africa being divided between them by fixed boundaries. Prosper; Cassiodorus.

443 Saint Brictius, bishop of Tours, died, and Saint Eustochius succeeded him. Gregory of Tours. Pope Leo, finding many Manichaeans in the City, exposed them publicly and burned their books. Prosper.

444 Attila, king of the Huns, killed his brother Bleda, king and partner in the rule, and subjected his kingdom and people to himself. Proterius and Paschasinus wrote to Pope Leo concerning the Easter of this year [Note: [Col. 0095D] This letter exists among those written by Saint Leo in the preceding year concerning the celebration of Easter in this year, 444, on 23 April.]. Prosper.

48 445 In these times Pope Leo, among his other good works, restored the basilicas of the apostles Peter and Paul and built the church of Saint Cornelius, pope and martyr, on the Appian Way [Col. 0095C]. Anastasius.

446 The Britons implored aid from Aetius and the Romans against the Scots and Picts, but did not obtain it. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*. — At Ephesus the Seven Sleepers, who under Decius had suffered many torments for Christ and fallen asleep in a certain cave [Col. 0096A], awoke after 196 years; having confirmed the faith in the resurrection of the dead, they fell asleep again [Note: [Col. 0095D] This account, taken from Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 95, is also found among the Greeks: Nicephorus, *History*, Book XIV, chapter 45; Cedrenus, *Compendium*, in the twenty-third year of Theodosius. It should, however, more probably be understood as referring to the discovery of their bodies. See the Bollandists [Col. 0096D] at 27 July, vol. VI.].

447 Eutyches, presbyter and abbot of Constantinople, confusing the substance of divinity and humanity in Christ and teaching that there was one nature in him, with the support of Theodosius Augustus and Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, expelled Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople, who resisted him, and persecuted him until his death. Against this heresy Pope Leo sent legates. Prosper, under the year 449. — Rechila, king of the Sueves, died, and his son Rechiar [Note: [Col. 0096D] Hydatius, under the year 448, calls him *Rechiarius*; other writers call him *Richiarius*.] succeeded him.

448 The emperor Theodosius summoned Pope Leo to appear before him in defense of Eutyches. Prevented by the Roman people from going, Leo sent legates in his place [Col. 0096B]. Rechiar, king of the Sueves, having married the daughter of Theodoric [Note: [Col. 0096D] Some copies of Hydatius read “Theodoris, king”; others have “Theodora, daughter of the king of the Goths.” The more correct manuscript reading is nevertheless preferable, although *Theodoricus* must be substituted for *Theodorus*, even though the latter is occasionally used for him.], king of the Goths, devastated Vasconia. Hydatius, under the following year. — At this time the Anglo-Saxons, summoned by the Britons to assist against the Picts and Scots, came to the island; after routing the enemy, they turned their arms against their allies and, after many wars, gained possession of most of the island, having subdued it. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*.

449 Again the Catholics were summoned by the emperor Theodosius to a hearing. 49 Attila, king of the Huns, devastated Gaul and the surrounding provinces. By a stratagem of Aetius, a great battle was provoked between him and the Goths; Theodorus, king of the Goths, fell, and his son Thorismund [also Torismodus] succeeded him. Hydatius, under the year 451; Jordanes.

[Col. 0096C] 450 Pope Leo took care to send legates to refute the heresy. The emperor Theodosius died and was carried with immense ceremony by the empress Placidia, Leo, and the entire Senate, and buried in the Mausoleum near Saint Peter. In his place Marcian obtained the empire of the East; reigning for seven years [Col. 0097A], he condemned Eutyches and his followers. The empress Placidia died. — The Romans [Note: [Col. 0097D] The printed editions assign this battle to 451, as they do many subsequent events, advancing them by a full year. Perhaps it ought here to have been assigned to 451, and so on; nevertheless, we have not wished to alter the manuscript evidence.], under the command of Aetius and with the Goths as auxiliaries, fought against Attila, king of the Huns, with great slaughter on both sides, and defeated him in battle on the Catalaunian plain, compelling him to flee into upper Gaul. He returned fearfully to his kingdom, but not long afterward took up arms against Italy. Prosper; Cassiodorus; Hydatius; Jordanes, under the following year.

451 Attila, having gathered his forces, captured Aquileia, which had long been besieged with great violence, and raged furiously throughout the surrounding region with plunder and slaughter. The emperor Valentinian sent Pope Leo to him and made peace with him; but his army, weakened by famine, pestilence, illness, and slaughter, and further worn down by Aetius, forced him to withdraw. Prosper; Marcellinus, under the following year.

[Col. 0097B] 452 Attila, king of the Huns, died in his own territory. After Thorismund, king of the Goths, was killed, his brother Theodoric succeeded him. Prosper; Hydatius, under the following year. — At this time the fourth universal synod, of 630 bishops, was assembled at Chalcedon against Eutyches and all heretics [Note: [Col. 0097D] Evagrius and others correctly assign this Council of Chalcedon to the year 451.]. Prosper, under the following year.

50 453 The emperor Valentinian deceitfully killed the patrician Aetius with his own hand in the palace, although Aetius had labored greatly for the commonwealth; and the prefect Boethius, his friend, was killed by those standing nearby. Prosper and the others, under the following year.

454 The emperor Valentinian was killed in the Campus Martius by Aetius’s friends. Maximus seized the empire in his place but was killed by the soldiers within two months and thrown into the Tiber. Prosper, under the following year [Col. 0097C]. — After him Avitus seized the empire in Gaul, relying on the support of the Goths. In that same year Geiseric, king of the Vandals, crossed from Africa and invaded Rome, since it had no emperor, stripping it of all its wealth. Up to this point Prosper brought his chronicle. Hydatius; Marcellinus, under the following year.

[Col. 0098A] 455 While Rechiar, king of the Sueves, was pressing Spain with devastation, Theodoric, king of the Goths, at Avitus’s advice, marched against him, entered battle, crushed him with heavy slaughter, and put him to flight after wounding him; afterward he captured and killed him. Having impiously and cruelly devastated Spain and the province they had occupied, he subjected the Sueves to himself. Hydatius, under the following year. — Avitus, deprived of Gothic support, laid down the empire at Placentia by order of Augustus Marcian. Marius of Aventicum, under the following year. — At this time among the Franks, after King Meroveus died [Note: [Col. 0097D] Here the first mention of the kingdom of the Franks occurs in Hermannus, beginning with Meroveus, who gave his name to the first royal dynasty [Col. 0098D]. Fredegar. We shall henceforth note these in the margin.], his son Childeric ruled for twenty-four years. Driven from the kingdom on account of his extravagance, he fled to Thuringia, but was recalled through the stratagem of his friend Viomad. Gregory of Tours, under the following year; *Deeds of the Kings of the Franks*.

456 From this year Victorius began his Easter cycles, at the command of Pope Hilary [Col. 0098B] [Note: [Col. 0098D] Here Pagi notes Baronius, who assigns this to 463, although it occurred under the consulship of Constantine and Rufus, as is clear from Victorius’s preface, and therefore in 457, when Hilary was still an archdeacon.]. Bede, *Chronicle*. — After the emperor Marcian died in the East, the emperor Leo ruled for seventeen years, and at Rome the emperor Majorian ruled for four years. Cassiodorus, under the following year. — Theodoric, king of the Goths, after devastating many churches and cities in Spain, besieged the city of Emerita. The Sueves chose Maldras as their king. Hydatius.

457 The emperor Majorian prepared to march against the Vandals in Africa. Cassiodorus, under the following year. — Theodoric, terrified by messengers, abandoned Emerita and returned to Gaul. With peace abandoned [Note: [Col. 0098D] Hydatius reads *pace fucata* (“peace having been feigned”) for this year.], he raged with slaughter, devastating and burning churches, cities, and estates. Jordanes, under the following year; Hydatius, under this year.

458 The Sueves devastated Gallaecia, and the Goths the provinces of Baetica. Hydatius.

[Col. 0098C] 459 Likewise, some of the Sueves, with King Maldras, plundered Lusitania, while others, with Richmundus [Note: [Col. 0098D] Hydatius calls him Remismundus], plundered Gallaecia.
