The Heruli invaded Baetica. The emperor Majorian, having made peace with Theodoric and the Goths, enlisted them as auxiliaries against the Vandals and Sueves. Hydatius, under the following year.

[Col. 0099A] 460 Maldras, king of the Sueves, was killed. The Sueves, plundered by the Goths, requested peace. The emperor Majorian, setting out for Spain, prepared a fleet against the Vandals; but the Vandals attacked and captured it. When he again prepared to cross to Africa against them, Geiseric, terrified, requested peace. Majorian returned to Rome and, while arranging the affairs of the state, was killed through the treachery of the patrician Ricimer, aided, as they say, by the counsel of the Sueves. Cassiodorus; Hydatius, under this and the following year.

461 Severus was made emperor at Ravenna by Ricimer and ruled for four years. Cassiodorus; Hydatius. In Gaul, the count Agrippinus [Note: [Col. 0099D] The same author, under the year 463, calls him Atrepennum or Agrippinus], allied with Theodoric, king of the Goths, handed Narbonne over to him. Hydatius. — 52 At Tours the blessed Perpetuus became bishop. After enlarging the basilica of Saint Martin [Col. 0099B], he carried out the translation of his body. Gregory of Tours, under the year 460. — In Gallaecia, estates, people, and flocks were burned after being struck by lightning in a remarkable manner, and two young men were found whose corpses had been burned together into a single mass.

462 At Rome Pope Hilary [Note: [Col. 0099D] Hilary, or Hilarus, had already been ordained pope in the preceding year, on 22 November.] held the see for six years and three months. He issued and established several measures for the welfare of the Church; condemned the Eutychian and Nestorian heresies; adorned many basilicas in the City with various marbles; built a monastery of Saint Laurence at the baths [Note: [Col. 0099D] In the *Book of the Pontiffs*, from which this account is taken, the reading is: “He built monasteries at Saint Laurence, and a bath, etc.”]; built another at Luna; and founded two libraries in the City. Anastasius.

463 Beorgor, king of the Alans, while heading toward Italy, was defeated in battle near Pergamum by the patrician Ricimer and died. [Col. 0099C] Cassiodorus, under the following year; Jordanes.

464 The emperor Severus died at Rome in the palace by poison through the treachery, as they say, of Ricimer. Cassiodorus, under the following year; Jordanes.

465 The Vandals were defeated, slaughtered, and routed in Sicily by Marcellinus. Hydatius.

[Col. 0100A] 466 The emperor Leo sent Anthemius from Constantinople to govern the empire of the West at Rome; having assumed the empire, he ruled for six years. Marcellinus, under the following year; Hydatius, under the preceding year.

467 Marcellinus was killed in Sicily. At Toulouse, where the kingdom of the Goths was located, blood burst forth from the earth in the middle of the city and flowed for an entire day. Hydatius; Fredegar, under the following year.

53 468 Arabundus [Note: [Col. 0100D] Cassiodorus calls him Ardaburius.] attempted to seize the empire and was transported into exile by order of the emperor Anthemius. Cassiodorus. — At Rome Pope Simplicius XLIX held the see for fifteen years and three months. He dedicated the basilica of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. He also built the basilica of Saint Andrew beside Saint Mary, and the basilica of Saint Bibiana [Note: [Col. 0100D] The *Book of the Pontiffs* has “of the blessed martyr Bibiana”] beside the Licinian Palace. Anastasius.

[Col. 0100B] 469 The Roman patrician, aspiring to the empire, was punished capitally. Cassiodorus, under the following year.

470 At Constantinople Aspar, having attempted tyranny, was ordered killed by the emperor Leo. Marcellinus, under the following year. — In Gaul Saint Remigius, foretold from heaven before his birth by the cell in which, as a young man serving God, he had shut himself away, was forcibly taken from it and ordained archbishop of Rheims [Note: [Col. 0100D] *Gallia Christiana*, vol. X, p. 10, already assigns this to 459, specifically to the twenty-second year of his age, as the Murensis manuscript reads.].

471 At Rome the patrician Ricimer, having made Olybrius emperor, killed the emperor Anthemius contrary to the law of kinship [Note: [Col. 0100D] For he had been his son-in-law, according to Marcellinus.] and of the empire, with grievous destruction inflicted on the City. But he did not long enjoy his crime: he himself ended his life forty days later, and Olybrius after seven months. Marcellinus, under the following year; Jordanes.

[Col. 0100C] 472 At the urging of Gundobad, Glycerius assumed the empire at Ravenna. Jordanes, under the following year. — At Constantinople the emperor Leo made his nephew Leo his partner in the empire. Cassiodorus, under the following year.

[Col. 0101A] 473 At Constantinople the elder emperor Leo died. After him the younger Leo ruled for a few months and also died; after him Zeno became emperor and ruled for seventeen years. At Rome as well, Glycerius was succeeded in the empire by Nepos. Marcellinus, under the following year.

474 At Rome the patrician Orestes, after driving the emperor Nepos into Dalmatia, made his own son Augustulus emperor. Cassiodorus, under the following year; Jordanes.

475 Odoacer, king of the Torcilingi and Rugians, having invaded Italy with many barbarian auxiliaries, took Rome in the 1,230th year from its foundation. He killed the patrician brothers Orestes and Paulus, condemned the emperor Augustulus to exile, and seized the title of king in his place, although he used neither the purple nor the insignia of kingship. Cassiodorus and others, under the following year.

[Col. 0101B] 476 Odoacer, having taken possession of Rome, subjected most of Italy to himself.

477 Geiseric, king of the Vandals, after thirty-seven and somewhat more years from his invasion of Carthage, finally died, bringing an end to his tyranny. After him his no better son Hunneric ruled for nearly eight years. Procopius; Victor, under the preceding year.

478 During the reign of the emperor Zeno, the body of the apostle Barnabas and the Gospel of the evangelist Matthew, written in Matthew’s own hand, were discovered through his own revelation [Note: [Col. 0101D] Baronius discusses this under the year 485, whereas Cedrenus places it under 477.].

479 In these times [Note: [Col. 0101D] Pagi, with Bernold, assigns this to the preceding year.] Pope Simplicius condemned Peter, the heretical Eutychian bishop of Alexandria, after he had been accused by Acacius of Constantinople. Anastasius.

[Col. 0101C] 480 At this time, after Childeric, king of the Franks, died, his son Ludovicus, whom they call Clovis, ruled for thirty years. Gregory of Tours, under the following year. 55 — In that same year Odoacer, ruling at Rome, defeated and killed Odiva, king of Dalmatia. Cassiodorus; Jordanes.

482 Theodoric, son of Theodemir [Note: [Col. 0101D] From Jordanes and Paul the Deacon, it is established that this Theodoric was the son of Triarius, a noble Goth.], king of the Ostrogoths—that is, of the Goths who had formerly remained in Italy—became a close associate of Zeno Augustus and served him with his Goths. Marcellinus, under the following year.

[Col. 0102A] 483 Zeno Augustus made Theodoric consul of this year [Note: [Col. 0102D] Theodoric was consul in 484, so this belongs to the following year.] and master of the soldiers. Cassiodorus, under the following year. — At Rome Pope Felix III, L, held the see for nearly nine years. He built the basilica of the blessed Agapitus beside Saint Laurence. Anastasius. — In Africa, the Arian bishop Cyrola, moved by zeal against Eugenius, archbishop of Carthage, and the other Catholics renowned for miracles, ordered one of his own men, whom he had bribed with money, to pretend blindness so that, when he invoked Cyrola before the king, Cyrola might appear to restore his sight through his faith. But when Cyrola laid hands on him before everyone, he was immediately struck by genuine blindness through divine power, exposed the fraud, and, after being converted by the holy bishops Eugenius, Vindemialis, and Longinus [also Longuinus], deserved to be illuminated again. Instigated by this Cyrola, King Hunneric persecuted the Catholics [Col. 0102B]; after very many had been crowned with martyrdom, he sent Eugenius himself, together with 324 bishops, into exile and closed the Catholic churches. Gregory of Tours, under the following year; Marcellinus.

484 Hunneric, king of the Vandals, struck by divine judgment, breathed his last, swarming with worms. After him his brother’s son Gundamundus ruled for nearly twelve years; not long afterward he recalled Bishop Eugenius. Jordanes. — King Ludovicus of the Franks, aided by his kinsman Raganharius [also Ragnacharius], defeated Syagrius, king of Gaul and son of Aegidius, in battle, drove him to flee to Alaric, king of the Goths, had him handed over, and killed him. He subjected his entire kingdom and its treasures to himself. Gregory of Tours, under the year 486.

485 At this time Acacius of Constantinople, favoring the heresy, recalled Peter of Alexandria [Col. 0102C]. When Felix the pope heard this, he condemned both men and their followers in error [Note: [Col. 0102D] This occurred at the Roman council of 484. Pagius.]. Letter 5 of Felix.

486 Odoacer defeated and captured Feva [also Phoeba or Foeba], who was also called Feletheus [Note: [Col. 0102D] Eugippius discusses him at greater length in the *Life of Saint Severinus, Apostle of Noricum*, in the Bollandists, vol. I, January, 8th day; and Paul the Deacon in *History of the Lombards*, Book I.]. Cassiodorus, under the following year.

487 Gundamundus, king of the Vandals, at Carthage restored the church of Saint Agileus to the Catholics at the request of Saint Eugenius the bishop. Appendix to Prosper.

[Col. 0103A] 488 Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, with the permission of Zeno Augustus, set out for Italy. Odoacer met him near the Isonzo, engaged him in battle, and, after being defeated, fled. Having gathered his strength again, he met him in battle at Verona and was once more defeated and routed. Jordanes, under the following year; Marius.

489 Theodoric defeated Odoacer for the third time at the Adda River and besieged him, as he fled, at Ravenna. Jordanes, under the following year; Marius. — Ludovicus, king of the Franks, marching against the Thuringians, struck them down with heavy slaughter and subjected both them and their land to himself. Gregory of Tours, under the year 491.

490 Odoacer, emerging by night from Ravenna with the Heruli, gathered his forces and engaged Theodoric for the fourth time; likewise defeated, he was captured by him [Note: [Col. 0103D] Cassiodorus describes the affair at greater length in *Variarum*, Book IV, Letter 2; also the *Miscellaneous History*, Book XV, and Ammianus.]. [Col. 0103B] The references cited belong to the following year. — In that same year Gundamundus, king of the Vandals, made peace with the Romans. At Constantinople the emperor Zeno died; after him Anastasius held the empire of the East for twenty-eight years. Cassiodorus, under the following year. — At this time Ludovicus, king of the Franks, through his envoy Aurelianus, took as his Christian wife Hruodhild [also Chlotild or Crotild], namely the daughter of Hilperic [Note: [Col. 0103D] That is, Chilperic, king of Burgundy, who was killed around 491 by his brother and successor Gundobad.], whom his brother Gundobad had massacred together with his wife and children. Gregory of Tours, under the year 493.

57 491 After Pope Felix died at Rome, a council was conducted by the priests and deacons [Note: [Col. 0104D] Felix died in 492, according to Anastasius; concerning this council or decree, see Baronius under the year 492.].

492 Theodoric killed Odoacer at Ravenna while Odoacer was plotting an ambush against him, and Theodoric himself held the empire of the West for thirty years. Cassiodorus; Marius, under the following year. — At Rome Pope Gelasius LI held the see for four years and seven months. A learned and devout man, he made several decrees concerning the condition of the Church, wrote many lofty works, condemned heretics, increased the Roman clergy, and loved the poor. [Col. 0103C] He dedicated the church of Saint Euphemia in the city of Tibur, as well as other basilicas of the saints Nicander, Eleutherius, and Andrew on the Lavican Way. He also built the basilica of Saint Mary on the Laurentine Way. Anastasius.

### 493

At this time in Africa the blessed bishop Fulgentius, who governed the Church of Ruspe for twenty-six years, shone forth, distinguished in teaching and conduct. He too endured very many hardships and exiles among the other Catholics. Victor of Vita; Isidore.

—At this same time Chlodovic, king of the Franks, brought under his rule the Gallic territories as far as the Seine and thereafter as far as the Loire. His wife Chrodhild strongly urged him toward faith in Christ. Gregory of Tours, under the following year.

### 494

Gundamund, king of the Vandals, at the urging of Archbishop Eugenius, finally, after ten years, recalled all the Catholic bishops from exile and, peace having been restored, reopened the churches that had long been closed. Procopius, under the following year.

—Chlodovic, king of the Franks, fighting against the Alamanni, when his army was in danger, invoked the God of heaven and vowed his faith to Christ; with Christ’s help he won and subjugated the Alamanni. Gregory of Tours, under 496.

### 495

Chlodovic, or Clovis, king of the Franks, at the insistence of his wife Hrodhild [Note: See the Life of Saint Chlotild in Mabillon, *saec. I, Bened.*, p. 98, and in the Bollandists, vol. I, June, under the third day], having been instructed in the faith of Christ by Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims, was baptized together with his people. Gregory of Tours, under the following year.

### 496

After Gundamund, king of the Vandals, had died, Thrasamund reigned in his place for a little more than twenty-six years. He too, hostile to the Catholics, closed the churches after several years and, among the other hardships of the persecution, afflicted 240 bishops with exile in Sardinia and the other islands. *Miscellaneous History*; Procopius, under the following year.

### 497

Boethius, patrician and consul, published at this time many outstanding monuments of his intellect in secular philosophy [Col. 0105A].

At Rome Pope Anastasius II [Note: Pope Anastasius was ordained on 24 November 496] occupied the see for nearly two years. He embellished the confession of Saint Lawrence; and because he seemed willing secretly to restore communion to certain heretics, some people separated themselves from communion with him. Anastasius, under 496.

### 498

The Isaurians, after killing their own commander Lilingus, were defeated and massacred by the emperor Anastasius. Marcellinus.

—At this time Chlodovic, king of the Franks, defeated in battle and put to flight the brothers Gundebald and Gondegisel, kings of the Burgundians. He besieged Gundebald at Avignon, made him tributary, and returned with great booty. Gregory of Tours; Marius, under 500.

### 499

King Theodoric built many remarkable structures at Rome and elsewhere during this period. Cassiodorus, under the following year.

—At Rome Pope Symmachus LIII occupied the see for fifteen years and nearly eight months. Alongside him, through excessive dissension, Laurentius was also ordained [Col. 0105B] [Note: Symmachus was ordained on 22 November 498; he had as his rival Laurentius, suborned by the patrician Festus. See Pagius in his Life]. A great disagreement arose at Rome between the clergy and the people, until Symmachus was confirmed in the see by the judgment of King Theodoric and of the greater number. Anastasius; Victor of Tunnuna, under 498.

### 500

Pope Symmachus, after a synod had been held at Rome, among other acts appointed his rival Laurentius bishop of Nocera. Anastasius; Pagius, under this year.

### 501

King Theodoric constructed an aqueduct at Ravenna. Cassiodorus, under the following year.

—At this time Saint Mammertus, archbishop of Vienne, became famous for his miracles. Because of the ferocity of wolves and bears and other calamities, he was the first to institute three-day litanies before the Ascension of the Lord, and thereby obtained the Lord’s mercy and the cessation of the calamities [Note: Ado of Vienne already places this under 452, whereas the common opinion, together with Sigebert of Gembloux, assigns it to 468. See the Bollandists under 11 May, and Baronius under 475, as well as Mabillon, book II, *On Gallican Liturgy*].

### 502

King Theodoric, after defeating the Bulgarians [variant: the Bulgar[ians]], restored Sirmium to the kingdom of Italy. Marcellinus, under 504.

### 503

Certain Romans, falsely accusing Pope Symmachus and denouncing him before the king, and recalling Laurentius [Col. 0106A], created a great schism at Rome; and Peter, bishop of the city of Altinum, with Theodoric’s permission, invaded the apostolic see. Anastasius; Pagius.

### 504

After a synod of 115 bishops had been assembled, the blessed Pope Symmachus was cleared of the charges brought against him and restored with glory to his see; and the usurpers of his see, Laurentius of Nocera and Peter of Altinum, were condemned. Anastasius, under the preceding year.

—King Chlodovic of the Franks, imploring divine assistance through the intercessions of Saint Peter, Saint Martin, and the other saints, attacked the Goths. Near the city of Poitiers, in the field of Vouillé [Note: In Gregory of Tours, book II, chapter 37, under 507, the field is called Vogladensis], he defeated them in battle and killed their king Alaric, who had already reigned for twenty-two years. He took both the kingdom that Alaric possessed in Gaul and its treasures. Alaric’s son Amalric [variant: Amalaric], however, fled and received his father’s kingdom in Spain. Procopius, *On the Gothic War*, under 507; Jordanes.

### 505

King Chlodovic of the Franks built the basilica of Saint Peter at Paris. Gregory of Tours, under 508.

### 506

At this time King Chlodovic of the Franks, having obtained many victories and possessing nearly all Gaul, defeated and put to flight his kinsman Ragnacharius [Note: Ragnacharius was the petty king of Cambrai. See under 484; his brother Richiarius was killed together with him], who had been made a partner in the kingdom but was cowardly and dissolute and had been betrayed by his own men. After capturing him, he killed him with his own hand together with his brother Richiarius, and subjected his people to himself. Gregory of Tours, under 509.

—King Theodoric of Italy sent an army against the Franks into Gaul. Cassiodorus, under 508.

### 507

At this time, when dissension again arose at Rome against Pope Symmachus and the Church, some of his party were afflicted with clubs and various blows, others were slaughtered and killed, and many disgraceful and wicked acts were committed against the Church and religion. Anastasius.

### 508

This year [Note: According to the consular Fasti, Boethius was consul in 510; thus the years here, as also in the preceding and following entries, are marked with less accuracy], at Rome the most learned Boethius held the consulship. Cassiodorus.

### 509

King Chlodovic, also called Clovis the Great, king of the Franks, possessing almost all Gaul after many victories, died at Paris, where he had established the seat of his kingdom, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter that he himself had built, in the thirtieth year of his reign, after the passing of Saint Martin, as is stated in the *Deeds of the Franks*, in the year 112 [Note: The thirtieth year of Clovis’s reign, counted from 481, is the year 511, in which he also died; although the 112th year from the death of Saint Martin, who died in 397, would correspond to the year 509 recorded here].

After him, his four sons divided the kingdom. Theoderic, whose seat was at Metz, reigned for twenty-three years together with his vigorous son Theodebert; Chlodomer had his seat at Orléans; Childebert at Paris; and the fourth, Chlotar, establishing his seat at Soissons, reigned for fifty-one years. Their sister Hrodhildis, sharing the name of her mother and equally devout, married Amalric, the Arian king of the Goths in Spain; and their mother, a widow, remained at Saint Martin’s in Tours in prayer and almsgiving. Gregory of Tours; Aimoin; the others correctly place these events under 511.

### 510

At this time Pope Symmachus, among his other good works, condemned the Manichaeans found in the city. He built the church of Saint Andrew at Saint Peter’s; the oratory of Saint Thomas; the confession of Saint Cassian and likewise those of Saints Protus and Hyacinthus; the oratory of Saint Apollinaris and likewise that of Saint Sosius; also those of the Holy Cross, Saint John the Baptist, and Saint John the Evangelist; the basilica of Saint Peter; and he paved the portico with marble and adorned it in many ways. He established hospices and every year supported with food and clothing the Catholics whom Thrasamund, the Arian king of the Vandals, had scattered through exile. He also built the basilica of Saint Agatha on the Via Aurelia; likewise those of Saint Pancratius, Saint Sylvester, Saint Martin, and Saints Cosmas and Damian; and several others he built, renewed, and adorned. Anastasius; Bede, *Chronicle*.

### 511

At this time the Frankish kings Chlodomer, Childebert, and Chlotar attacked the Burgundian kings Sigismund and Godomar and put them to flight after defeating them in battle. Sigismund, one of them, a devout king, fled to the saints of Agaunum [Note: These events, drawn from Gregory of Tours and Marius of Avenches, belong to a later period. The monastery at Agaunum was built in 515 by Sigismund, who became king in 516 after the death of his father Gundebald; he was defeated in 523 and finally killed in 524 by Chlodomer, who himself also died in battle. See the Bollandists under 1 May], but while Chlodomer pursued him he was captured there and sent to prison at Orléans. He was slaughtered together with his wife and sons. Later Chlodomer again attacked the Burgundians and put them to flight in battle; but he himself, carried on horseback among the enemy, was killed by them, and Burgundy was subjugated by the Franks. Gregory of Tours; Marius of Avenches, under 515 and following.

### 512

Amalric, the Arian king of the Goths in Spain, afflicted his Catholic wife Hrodhild in many ways. Later he was defeated and killed in battle by her brother Childebert; and Theuda reigned in his place [Note: See Procopius, *On the Gothic War*, and Jordanes, *On the Origin of the Goths*]. Gregory of Tours, under 531.

### 513

Cassiodorus was consul in this year. Later he converted, became a monk, and built a monastery; he shone forth in secular and divine literature. He expounded the Psalms and composed books of the *Institutions* and a chronicle. At Rome, when the dissension between clergy and people had finally ceased, the desired harmony returned, and the blessed Pope Symmachus died [Note: These events belong to the year 514, in which Cassiodorus was also consul]. Anastasius; Cassiodorus.

### 514

King Theodoric of Italy gave his daughter Amalasuntha in marriage to Eutharic the Cilligan (Cillicae). Cassiodorus, under the following year; Jordanes.

—At Rome Pope Hormisdas LIV occupied the see for nine years. Among his other good works, he condemned the Eutychians and the Manichaeans, instructed the clergy, and adorned the basilicas. Anastasius.

### 515

At this time a certain Vitalian, a slave raised to positions of distinction, rebelled against the emperor Anastasius. Joining himself to the Scythians, he repeatedly defeated and routed the emperor’s soldiers in battle, bringing great disgrace and loss upon the state. Marcellinus.

### 516

In these days Pope Hormisdas, sending legates to the emperor Anastasius at Constantinople on behalf of the Catholic faith and achieving nothing, sent other legates likewise with letters [Col. 0108C]. When Anastasius could not corrupt them, he condemned them to exile. Among other things he wrote back to the lord pope: “We wish to give orders, not to have orders given to us.” Anastasius.

### 517

At this time King Theoderic of the Franks, through his son Theodebert, utterly destroyed the Danes who had invaded them, together with their king. Gregory of Tours, under the preceding year; variant: around 515.

### 518

When the emperor Anastasius, who had favored the heresy of Eutyches and persecuted the Catholics, was struck by lightning, he died, being more than eighty years old. In his place the Catholic emperor Justin reigned at Constantinople for eight years. He killed certain men who coveted the empire and, after first making peace with the tyrant Vitalian, later killed him. Marcellinus.

### 519

Augustus Justin received with the highest honor the legates of the apostolic see whom Pope Hormisdas had sent to Constantinople on behalf of the faith. Entirely agreeing with them in the condemnation of heresy, he sent many gifts through them to Rome. Anastasius.

### 520

At this time King Theoderic of the Franks, attacking the Thuringians with his son Theodebert, crushed them in an immense slaughter and put their king Ermenfrid to flight [Col. 0109B]. Later, when Ermenfrid came to him after having been given a pledge of faith, Theoderic received him and then threw him from a wall; he also had his sons killed. Gregory of Tours, under 530.

### 521

Augustus Justin, hostile to the heretics, also persecuted the Arians at Constantinople. Angered by this, the Arian King Theodoric of Italy threatened the Catholics in Italy with destruction. *Miscellaneous History*.

### 522

In Africa, after Thrasamund, the Arian king of the Vandals, finally died, Hilderic reigned in his place for eight years. At the beginning of his reign he immediately reopened the churches that had long been closed, sought to recall all the Catholics from exile, and restored the Church’s desired peace. Procopius; Victor of Tunnuna, under the following year.

### 523

At Rome Pope John LV occupied the see for two years and nine months. Restoring the cemeteries in the city and devoting himself to other good works, he was sent as a legate by Theodoric to Constantinople. Received with the highest honor and joy at the gate called the Golden Gate by Augustus Justin and all the citizens, he gave sight to a blind man. After crowning Augustus Justin himself, obtaining what he had come to request, and receiving gifts and presents, he returned. Marcellinus, under 525.

### 524

Theodoric, king of the Goths and tyrant of the Romans, among his other evils, killed Boethius, the patrician and philosopher, after keeping him imprisoned for a long time. Not long afterward he likewise killed his father-in-law, the patrician Symmachus. He also killed the blessed Pope John, who had returned from Constantinople, at Ravenna, together with his companions, by the hardship of imprisonment, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June. Not long afterward John was taken back to Rome and buried at Saint Peter’s [Note: Marius of Avenches likewise assigns Boethius’s death to this year, but Symmachus’s to 525. Pope John died only in 526]. Bede; *Miscellaneous History*.

### 525

The tyrant Theodoric, three months after the death of Pope John, after his many crimes, died suddenly at Ravenna by God’s judgment. As was revealed to a certain solitary, he was thrown by Pope John and the patrician Symmachus into Vulcan’s cauldron, in the thirty-second year of his Italian reign. After him his nephew Atharic [Athalaric], a child, reigned with his mother Amalasuntha for eight years. *Miscellaneous History*; Procopius; Jordanes.

—At Rome Pope Felix IV, the fifty-sixth pope, occupied the see for four years and two months. He built the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian on the Via Sacra and that of Saint Saturninus on the Via Salaria [Note: Everything recorded under this year belongs to the following one]. Anastasius.

### 526

At Constantinople the emperor Justin died after making Justinian, his sister’s son, his partner and successor in the kingdom. Justinian then ruled for thirty-eight years, conspicuous for great piety and prudence, except that he favored certain heretics. Marcellinus, under the following year.

### 527

Augustus Justinian appointed his friend Belisarius commander-in-chief. Through him he triumphed over the Parthians and recovered a large part of the state. *Miscellaneous History*.

—The nation of the Winnili, or Lombards, under King Odwin [variant: Audoinus], invaded Pannonia and began to dwell there. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*; Procopius.

### 528

At this time the blessed abbot Benedict shone forth with immense glory for his virtues. The grammarian Priscian also lived in these times. Bede, *Chronicle*.

### 529

The Roman army was defeated by the Parthians on Holy Saturday.

### 530

In Africa, after the Catholic king Hilderic had been wickedly killed, Gelimer invaded the kingdom and raged with such savagery against the Catholics and everyone else that he spared not even his own relatives. Procopius; Victor of Tunnuna.

—At Rome Boniface II, the fifty-seventh pope, occupied the see for two years and about one month. Alongside him, through dissension, Dioscorus was ordained; he died a few days later. Boniface nevertheless attempted to condemn him by assembling a synod. Anastasius.

### 531

Pope Boniface decreed in a written undertaking that the deacon Vigilius should be elected pope after him. Later, however, recognizing that this was contrary to the canons, he revoked the decree and burned it. When famine threatened, he supplied food to the clergy and the poor. Anastasius.

### 532

Beginning with this year, namely the sixth year of the emperor Justinian, Dionysius the Roman abbot, highly skilled in both languages, began his great Paschal cycle. Since 532 years had already elapsed from the Incarnation of the Lord, this cycle likewise contains 532 years. It begins with the first year of Diocletian, from which the Greeks began their cycles, after thirteen nineteen-year cycles had been completed, that is, in the year 247. Bede, *Chronicle*.

—At Rome John II, also called Mercury, the fifty-eighth pope, occupied the see for two years and four months. To him Augustus Justinian sent letters concerning his faith and gifts to Saint Peter [Col. 0111C]. Anastasius, under 533.

—King Theodoric of the Franks died in the twenty-third year of his reign and was buried at Metz. His son Theodebert reigned in his place for fourteen years. Gregory of Tours, under 534.

### 533

At Rome, after the Gothic king Athalaric died, Amalasuntha took Theodahad into partnership in the kingdom. Not long afterward he ordered her to be killed and usurped the kingdom for himself. Marcellinus, under the following year.

### 534

The patrician Belisarius, sent by the emperor Justinian, defeated and destroyed the nation of the Vandals in Africa. He captured their king Gelimer and led him to Constantinople, and restored Carthage to the state, ninety-four years after it had been captured by Geiseric. After several years Gelimer too was made a count by Augustus Justinian and stationed on the Parthian frontier to repel them. Marcellinus; Marius; Procopius.

### 535

At Rome Pope Agapetus LIX occupied the see for nearly one year. The tyrant Theodahad sent him to Constantinople to seek the favor of Augustus Justinian, who was hostile to Theodahad because he had killed Amalasuntha. There he steadfastly contended with the emperor for the faith of Christ. He convicted and condemned Anthimus, the bishop of that city, as a heretic, and, with the emperor’s support, appointed Mennas [variant: Moenas] in his place. Agapetus himself was struck by illness there and died; he was brought back to Rome in a leaden coffin and buried at Saint Peter’s. Anastasius; Marcellinus; Victor of Tunnuna.

### 536

At Rome Silverius, formerly the son of Pope Hormisdas, was violently promoted as the sixtieth pope against the will of the clergy, after the tyrant Theodahad had been bribed with money [Note: Pagius, in *A Brief History of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, p. 284, has convincingly cleared Silverius of this accusation]. He occupied the see for one year and five months. Marcellinus; Anastasius.

—The tyrant Theodahad was killed by Witigis two months later, and Witigis [variant: Witiges] became king of the Goths. Aimoin.

—The patrician Belisarius, sent by Augustus Justinian to Italy against the Goths, passed through Sicily, defeated its commander Sunderas, and rescued Africa from its tyrants. He crossed to Naples, which resisted him, besieged it, and captured it by force; sparing no one, he slaughtered both citizens and Goths. From there, when he had entered the city of Rome, all the Goths who had been there went out by night and fled toward Ravenna. Pursuing them, he joined battle and killed seven thousand of them. Witigis, however, gathering a large army, besieged Belisarius and the city of Rome for one year. Laying waste to everything around it, he grievously oppressed the city by war and famine. Later, when Belisarius had gone out and was defeated in battle, he fled to Ravenna. Procopius; Marius; Jordanes.

—Such a great famine occurred that in Liguria certain women ate their own children. Marcellinus, under this year.

### 537

When Pope Silverius refused to obey the emperors concerning the restoration of Anthimus and communion with heretics, he was falsely accused by the patrician Belisarius at their command, secretly confined, and dressed in a monk’s habit. In the fifteenth indiction he was afflicted by exile at the hands of the deacon Vigilius, and, wasting away, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July. After his death he also became renowned for miracles. Vigilius himself, ordained the sixty-first pope, occupied the see for seventeen years and seven months. Anastasius; Aimoin.

—In those days Belisarius defeated Theodebert, king of the Franks, who had entered Italy with a large army, and forced him to return from there [Note: Gregory of Tours, under 539, attributes the victory to Theodebert, as does Procopius, although one-third of his army died of dysentery, forcing him to return]. He offered gifts to Saint Peter at Rome. Marcellinus; Victor of Tunnuna; Procopius.

### 538

The patrician Belisarius, having again defeated the Goths in battle, captured their king Witigis while he was fleeing, through John the Bloodthirsty, master of the soldiers, and brought him to Rome. Belisarius and Pope Vigilius then took him, together with his wife and treasures, to Constantinople to Augustus Justinian. There he was made patrician and count and stationed in the East against the incursions of the Parthians or Persians; he ended his life there. The Goths remaining in Liguria raised Helebad [variant: Heldebad] as their king and again rebelled against the Romans. Procopius; Marius; *Miscellaneous History*, under 540.

### 539

The Parthians, breaking the peace, invaded and devastated Antioch and all Syria, until at last they were driven back by Belisarius and returned to their own borders. Later a peace was made with them by the commander Martin, when Belisarius had been recalled to Italy against Totila. Marius, under the following year.

—After Helebad had been killed one year later, the Goths made Eraric their king. Procopius, under 541 and following.

### 540

After King Eraric had been killed one year later in Italy, the Goths established Totila, also called Baduilla, as their king. Trusting in his successes in war, he defeated the Roman army and its commanders several times. For many years he afflicted and devastated all Italy, and Rome itself after capturing it, with numerous calamities. Procopius, under 541.

### 541

During this period Totila defeated the Roman army near the town of Faventia in Aemilia. Not long afterward, again putting the Roman commanders to flight, he joined part of the army to himself by force and part by gifts. Persisting in his tyranny, he devastated Rome itself and Campania. *Miscellaneous History*; Procopius; Marcellinus, under 543.

### 542

In the time of this Justinian, the body of Saint Antony the monk was revealed by divine disclosure, transferred to Alexandria, and buried in the church of Saint John the Baptist. Bede, *Chronicle*; Victor of Tunnuna.

—At this time the Fifth Ecumenical Council was assembled at Constantinople under Pope Vigilius against Theodore and all the heretics [Note: This council is wrongly placed here, since it was held only in 553, although the matter of the Three Chapters had begun around this period. See Norisius, *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter 3, and Pagius, *Brief History*, vol. I, p. 292].

### 543

During this period, when Belisarius had been recalled from the Parthian frontier to aid Italy and had been delayed for a long time, he finally entered Rome, already almost devastated, with a small fleet. He engaged Totila’s attacking army in battle, routed it, and drowned it in the Tiber, driving Totila himself back into Campania. Marcellinus, under 547.

—At this time, after Abbot Benedict had sent his disciple Maurus to Gaul, Benedict himself, after many virtuous deeds, departed to the Lord. Leo of Ostia; variant: under 544.

### 544

Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims and apostle of the Frankish nation, in the seventy-fourth year of his episcopate, full of virtues, departed to the Lord on the Ides of January [Note: This is correct according to Hermann’s reckoning, which states that Remigius was ordained bishop in 470; but according to the calculation of *Gallia Christiana*, where he is already said to have been ordained in 459, his death should be assigned to about 533 or 530].

The Roman subdeacon Arator publicly recited, with great acclaim, before Pope Vigilius the book he had composed on the Acts of the Apostles in heroic meter and presented to him [Note: Gallandius discussed this in his new *Library of the Fathers*, vol. XII, chapter 5 of the prolegomena, and on p. 93 presents the work divided into two books]. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book I, chapter 25.

### 545

At this time, when Belisarius had been recalled from Sicily to Constantinople by order of the emperor, Totila, now secure, again invaded Rome. Later, gathering his forces, he also invaded and captured Sicily; and, mocking the Romans who had been withdrawn on various occasions, he devastated all Italy. Procopius; Marius, under 547.

### 546

Theodebert, vigorous and brave king of the Franks, died. His son Theudebald, much worse and more sluggish than his father, reigned in his place for seven years. Marius; Gregory of Tours, under the following year.

### 547

At this time Pope Vigilius, since he could not in any way be brought to agree to the heresy or to the restoration of the bishop Anthimus, was seized by force at Rome by imperial order and taken to Constantinople. Because he steadfastly persisted in what he had begun and would not yield to the emperor, he was subjected, together with his companions, to [injuries] and condemned to exile; he was grievously afflicted for several years [Note: Anastasius does report these things concerning Vigilius’s captivity, but Baronius and Pagius demonstrate that they are false. His exile, however, should be assigned to 553]. Marcellinus.

### 548

During this period Augustus Justinian, among his other magnificent works, constructed at Constantinople, with incomparable craftsmanship, the basilica of the Savior, which is called Hagia Sophia. He also collected and abridged countless Roman laws and composed the laws called Justinian’s. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book I, chapter 25.

### 549

At this time the nation of the Gepids [Gepidarum] was defeated in battle and almost destroyed by King Alboin and the Lombards, who were then dwelling in Pannonia; their king Cunimund was killed. From his head, enclosed in gold, Alboin made himself a drinking cup [Note: Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book I, chapter 27, has *poculum*, which is called *scala*, whence the German *Schalen*, or *patera*. See Muratori, *Italian Historical Writings*, vol. I, part II, p. 424]. He took his daughter Rosamund [variant: Rosamunda] captive, among many others, and later, after the death of his wife, the daughter of Lothar, king of the Franks, married her to his own destruction. Variant: under 547; others, under 568.

### 550

The bishop Victor of Capua, writing about this year’s Easter [Note: This work of Victor has perished; Bede mentions it in *On the Reckoning of Time*, near the end of chapter 49, concerning the disputed Easter of the year 550], criticized the erroneous cycles of Victorius. Bede, *Chronicle*.

—At this time Totila, king of the Goths, again captured Rome after it had been besieged and severely oppressed by famine. When certain senators fled to Constantinople [Col. 0116A], he possessed the city without fear. Procopius, under 549.

### 551

Up to this point Jordanes had brought his abridged *Chronicle of the Deeds of the Romans* [Note: We discussed Jordanes, or Jornandes, in the preliminary dissertation].

At this time in Africa the Moors were subdued by the patrician John. Marcellinus.

### 552

At this time Augustus Justinian made Narses, his eunuch, chartularius and chamberlain, commander-in-chief and sent him to Italy. After engaging in battle, by God’s grace he won and killed King Totila, and, with the Lombards also assisting, exterminated the Gothic nation in Italy. Marcellinus, appendix.

—During this period, when Count Buccelinus, sent some time earlier by King Theodebert of the Franks together with his associates, had harassed Italy and Sicily for several years and often defeated the Roman army, his army was finally weakened and exhausted by dysentery, defeated and routed in battle by Narses, and the commander himself was killed. Not long afterward his associate, the commander Ammingus [Note: Marcellinus calls him Omnirugus; Hermann copied almost everything from him verbatim up to 558], was killed together with the remaining Goths who had joined him. Marcellinus, appendix, under the following year.

### 553

King Theudebald of the Franks died, and King Chlotar, the paternal uncle of Theodebert, took possession of his kingdom and his wife Wanderada [variant: Vuldetrada]. Chlotar had already been reigning for forty-four years. In that same year Chlotar himself subdued the rebellious Saxons near the River Weser with great slaughter and devastated Thuringia after overrunning it. Marcellinus, appendix.

### 554

Pope Vigilius, finally released from exile through the efforts of the Romans and Narses, had begun to return to Rome when he died in Sicily from a disease of the stone [Col. 0116C] [Note: Vigilius died at Syracuse on 10 January 555]. Nevertheless, he was taken back to Rome and buried at Saint Marcellus on the Via Salaria.

In his place Pope Pelagius LXII was ordained and occupied the see for eleven years and ten months. Accused by the Roman people of being part of the faction against Vigilius, he cleared himself under oath of the charge after celebrating litanies with Narses at Saint Peter’s, ascending the ambo, and placing the Gospel upon his head. Marcellinus, appendix.

### 555

At this time the Saxons again rebelled against Chlotar. When he attacked them and they offered him half of their possessions as satisfaction, the Frankish army rejected the offer and, against his wishes, began the battle. It was severely defeated by them and sought safety in flight. Marcellinus, appendix.

### 556

In these days Chramn, rebelling against his father Chlotar with the support of his uncle Childebert, disturbed the Frankish kingdom by domestic sedition. The Saxons, through Childebert’s faction, carried out raids in Francia. Childebert ravaged the Campania of Reims. Marcellinus, appendix.

### 557

In Britain Bridius [variant: Bridus] became king of the Picts.

About this time Childebert, king of the Franks, died and was buried at Paris in the basilica of Saint Vincent, which he himself had built. His brother Chlotar took over his kingdom and obtained the monarchy of the entire paternal realm. Marcellinus, appendix; variant: under the following year.

### 558

At this time Chramn, having offended his father Chlotar in many ways, fled to Britain. Chlotar pursued him there together with King Conobrus; Chramn was defeated and captured in battle, and was burned alive together with his wife and daughters [Note: According to Gregory, book IV, chapter 20, these events occurred one year before the death of his father, and therefore in 560].

At the same time, the basilica of Saint Martin at Tours was burned by fire, because rebels had fled to it. Marcellinus, appendix.

### 559

King Chlotar, doing penance for his crimes and sins, diligently repaired the basilica of Saint Martin at this time and roofed it with tin. Gregory of Tours, under the following year.

Saint Medard, bishop, full of virtues, departed to the Lord and was buried with great glory at Soissons by Chlotar, king of the Franks. Gregory of Tours, under the following year.

### 560

Chlotar the Elder, son of Clovis the Great and king of the Franks, died at Compiegne in the fifty-first year of his reign and was buried at Soissons beside Saint Medard [Col. 0118A].

After him his four sons divided the kingdom. Sigibert, whose seat was at Metz and Reims, reigned for fourteen years; Charibert at Paris; Chilperic at Soissons for twenty-five years; and Guntram at Orléans and in Burgundy for twenty-three years. Marius; Gregory of Tours, under the following year.

### 561

In Britain Æthelbert, king of the English, reigned for fifty-six years. Bede, *History of the English*, under 560.

The Huns, advancing into Gaul with their king Chagan, were defeated and humbled in battle by King Sigibert. Having obtained peace only with difficulty and concluded a treaty, they returned. Gregory, under the following year.

### 562

King Chilperic invaded the kingdom of his brother Sigibert and the city of Reims, and devastated the Campania. When Sigibert heard this, he returned from the Huns, captured the city of Soissons in turn, and sent Theodebert, Chilperic’s son, who had been captured there, into exile. He defeated Chilperic in battle, put him to flight, and recovered his cities. Later, after receiving an oath of peace from him, he returned his son and established peace with him. Gregory of Tours, under 563, book IV, chapter 23.

### 563

King Charibert, devoted to lust, repudiated his wife Ingoberga and married two maidservants who were sisters. He was excommunicated by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, and died not long afterward [Note: Gregory of Tours assigns Charibert’s death to 567; he also discusses it in chapter 19 of *On the Glory of the Confessors*].

At the same time King Sigibert took Bruna, also called Brunhildis, daughter of Athanagild, king of the Goths in Spain, as his wife [Note: This occurred in 566, as did the marriage mentioned below in 567]. Later his brother Chilperic took Bruna’s sister Gielswinda [variant: Gailesuintha] as his wife. He afterward strangled her at night at the urging of his concubine Fredegund; through Fredegund’s artifice he also repudiated Queen Audovera, who had become his spiritual co-mother, and committed many evils. Gregory of Tours, under 566 and following.

### 564

At Constantinople the emperor Justinian died in the thirty-eighth year of his reign. Justin the Younger reigned in his place for eleven years, an unjust man excessively devoted to avarice. Evagrius, book V, chapter 1, under the following year.

At this time an immense plague and mortality devastated all Italy, and especially Liguria, in an unbelievable manner. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*.

### 565

Saint Columba, priest and abbot, coming from Ireland, preached the word of God to the Britons. Epitome of Bede.

At this time the patrician Narses defeated in battle and captured Sindwald, a king of the remnants of the Heruli who had rebelled against him in Italy, and suspended him from a high beam. Marius of Avenches, under the following year.

Having become wealthy, Narses suffered great envy from the Romans. He was accused before Augustus and brought to the point that, leaving Rome, he withdrew to Campania after some time [Note: Read “after the passage of time”]. Longinus was sent to Italy as his successor. Paul the Deacon; Marius, under 568.

### 566

At Rome Pope John III, the sixty-third pope, occupied the see for fourteen years [the text reads *ere*]. He completed and dedicated the church of the apostles Philip and James, which his predecessor Pelagius had begun [Note: This John had already been substituted for Pelagius in 560]. Anastasius; Bede.

### 567

The eunuch and patrician Narses, who had liberated Italy from the Goths and other enemies and had labored greatly for the state, was provoked by insults from Augustus Justin and his wife Sophia. He invited the Lombards, who were dwelling in Pannonia, to invade and possess Italy, sending them samples of Italy’s agricultural abundance and gifts. Paul the Deacon, book II, chapter 5.

—Many prodigies, and especially fiery armies seen in the sky, as well as flashing blood, terrified Italy. Gregory the Great, book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 38.

### 568

In April, the Lombards, under King Alboin, entered Venetia and its territories. Except for a few cities, they captured and subjected it; at Aquileia, or Forum Julii, they left a chosen part of their forces with the commander Gisulf and turned their attention to conquering all Italy. Paul the Deacon, book II, chapter 7.

—A great snow fell this year, followed by an extraordinary abundance of crops. Paul the Deacon.

### 569

At this time the Huns, having broken the peace and again advancing into Francia, used treachery to defeat King Sigibert and the Franks in battle and put them to flight. Gregory of Tours, 566.

—King Alboin invaded Liguria with the Lombards, captured Milan and most of the other cities, and, raging everywhere with plunder and slaughter, besieged Pavia for more than three years. Paul the Deacon.

### 570

Alboin captured most of the cities in Tuscany and on this side of it, except Rome, Ravenna, and a few fortified places. After Italy had enjoyed abundance, a great famine also invaded it, following upon a pestilence that had worn it down. Marius.

—Saint Vedastus, bishop, died. Paul the Deacon.

571 The citizens of Pavia, no longer able to resist, surrendered themselves to King Alboin. When he entered the city, his horse stumbled and fell inside the gate; thereby divinely softened, he spared the citizens, contrary to the vow by which he had threatened to punish them all. Establishing the seat of his kingdom there, he ruled in Italy for three years and six months. At that same time the patrician Narses, after returning from Campania to Rome, died not long afterward and was carried back to Constantinople in a leaden coffin with his treasures. [Note: Muratori proves in his notes on Paul the Deacon, vol. I of *Italian Writers*, p. 430, that the death of Narses belongs to the year 569.] Paul the Deacon.

[Col. 0120B] 572 At this time King Chilperic sent his son Clovis hostilely into the kingdom of his brother Sigebert. While Clovis was staying near the city of Bordeaux, the duke Sigulf, on Sigebert’s side, fell upon him; and when he fled, Sigulf pursued him all the way to Paris, where his father had been, shouting with trumpets and horns as though he were pursuing a stag. Gregory of Tours.

573 In these days Chilperic sent his son Theudebert likewise across the Loire to ravage Sigebert’s kingdom. When Theudebert pressed on with the utmost cruelty in his devastation and had captured some cities, he finally rashly engaged in battle with Sigebert’s commanders, was cut down, and perished. Gregory of Tours, year 575.

574 Alboin, king of the Lombards, was killed near Verona through the treachery of his wife Rosamund by his armor-bearer Helmichis. Helmichis himself, attempting unsuccessfully to seize the kingdom, fled to Ravenna when he was sought for execution, together with his wife Rosamund, his treasures, and the royal daughter Albsuinda. There, after receiving poison from Rosamund, he forced her also to drink it, and died together with her. Paul the Deacon, book II, chapter 29.

[Col. 0120C] King Sigebert of the Franks, while avenging his wrongs, had invaded the kingdom of his brother Chilperic and, contrary to the prohibition of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, was pursuing Chilperic, who was fleeing in deadly hatred. Fridegund, now queen, deceitfully sent two young men; they killed Sigebert, and were themselves immediately put to death. His wife Brunhild and their son Childebert were captured and consigned to custody. But the boy Childebert was secretly rescued by his supporters, raised to the kingship in his father’s place, and ruled for twenty-three years, a very brave and energetic king. His sister Ingund married Hermenegild, son of Leovigild, king of the Goths. Gregory of Tours, book IV, chapter 46, year 575.

575 At Constantinople, after many evils and his own desires had driven him mad, the emperor Justin died. Tiberius Constantine succeeded him; while Justin was mentally incapacitated, Tiberius had already governed the palace. He ruled for seven years, a man devoted to God and exceptionally generous in alms to all the poor, and, in acquiring wealth, the most fortunate of all. [Note: Justin, in 574, having become insane, created Tiberius Caesar; he himself died only in the year 578. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book III; Evagrius, book V, chapter 13.]

In Italy Cleph (Clepho), king of the Lombards, who had been chosen in succession to Alboin, ruled cruelly for one year and one month and killed many Romans; then he was killed by one of his own servants. After him the Lombards remained without kings for ten years, serving under dukes, and raged throughout Italy with many crimes. They also entered Burgundy—as the holy recluse Hospitius had foretold—killed Amatus, commander of King Guntram, after defeating him in battle, and, having enriched themselves with plunder after much slaughter, returned to Italy. Gregory of Tours, Paul the Deacon, and Marius, year 576.

[Note: He is commemorated on 21 May. See Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book VI, chapter 6.]

[Note: Amatus, duke of King Guntram, had already been killed by the Lombards in 570 or the following year, while King Cleph was still alive.]

576 At this time Meroveus, son of Chilperic, sent by his father against the people of Poitiers and returning from there, took Brunhild as his wife. His father immediately separated him from her, regarding him with suspicion; not long afterward Meroveus was tonsured and ordered to be ordained a priest. Gregory of Tours, book V, chapters 2–3.

At about the same time Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, departed to the Lord. Around this time the Lombards again entered Burgundy but were surrounded by the patrician Mummolus, who had succeeded Amatus on behalf of Guntram. After many had been killed and captured, they barely escaped. Gregory of Tours and Paul the Deacon.

577 In these days Chilperic sent his son Clovis and the duke Desiderius against his brother Guntram, but they were defeated in battle by Guntram’s patrician Mummolus and turned their backs in flight. Gregory of Tours; Paul the Deacon, year 572.

At this same time the Saxons who had entered Italy with Alboin invaded Gaul. Mummolus defeated and humbled them, and they returned after obtaining peace. A year later, wishing to return again to their homeland, they went toward Gaul; terrified at the sight of Mummolus, they bought themselves off with gold. Finally they were defeated in battle by the Suebi, who had taken possession of their territory, and were almost annihilated. Paul the Deacon, book III, chapter 5; another account assigns this to 572.

578 At Rome Pope Benedict, the sixty-fourth pope, held the see for four years and two months. [Note: Pope Benedict died in this year, having been elected in 574. What is said here about Gregory’s ordination must not be attributed to Benedict, but to Pelagius, his successor in this same year.] Through him blessed Gregory was taken from the monastery, ordained a deacon, and sent to Constantinople as papal representative. In the presence of Tiberius Augustus, Gregory proved Eutychius, bishop of that city, mistaken in his teaching concerning the resurrection. There also, when his monks came to him, Gregory was compelled to write his outstanding work *Moralia on Job*. Bede.

At this time Guntram Boso, one of the nobles of King Chilperic, killed Duke Dracolenus, who proudly threatened him with chains, after defeating him in battle. Gregory of Tours. [Note: This Guntram was not king of the Franks, but Guntram Boso, one of the nobles of King Chilperic. Aimon.]

579 King Chilperic of the Franks oppressed his people with unheard-of exactions and assessments. But his tax collector was killed, and the tax registers were burned. Gregory of Tours, the following year.

A great flood and deluge, lightning, earthquakes, and a pestilence that followed afflicted Gaul and other provinces.

Three sons of Chilperic died of dysentery; a fourth, whom his father had placed in custody, was killed by a sword through the plotting of his stepmother Fridegund. Gregory of Tours, abbreviated history, the following year.

In Spain Leovigild, the Arian king of the Goths, at the instigation of his wife Goiswinth, persecuted the Catholics.

In these days a large Lombard army entered Gaul with three commanders. Mummolus exhausted it by various means and battles, and at last it barely escaped back into Italy. Paul the Deacon, book III, chapter 8; another account assigns this to 576.

580 A comet was seen on Easter Day. At Soissons the sky appeared to be burning. At Paris blood flowed from the clouds. A great pestilence and mortality occurred. Gregory of Tours, year 582.

King Leovigild pursued his Catholic son Hermenegild with an army. The same source, at the preceding year.

The duke Rodinus [elsewhere Chrodinus], pious and religious, died. Aimon, year 582.

[Col. 0123A] 581 At this time the army sent by the emperor Tiberius decisively defeated the Persians and returned twenty elephants to the emperor amid an immeasurable quantity of booty. The emperor himself, while Italy and Rome were suffering severely from the war with the Lombards, pestilence, and, in addition, famine, sent ships laden with grain to Rome and supplied the people with abundant provisions. Paul the Deacon, book III, chapter 12.

582 At Constantinople the emperor Tiberius, deserving of every praise, stricken by illness, handed over his daughter and the empire to Maurice and himself departed happily from this life. Maurice, a Cappadocian by origin, succeeded him and ruled for twenty-one years. Gregory of Tours.

At Rome Pelagius II, the sixty-fifth pope, held the see for ten years and two months. He covered Saint Peter’s church with gilded silver panels, made his own house into a hospice, built the basilica of Saint Lawrence, and adorned its tomb with silver panels. Anastasius.

[Note: Pelagius II had already been elected pope in 578.]

583 King Childebert of the Franks, having received fifty thousand gold solidi from the emperor Maurice so that he might drive the Lombards from Italy, set out for Italy with a powerful army. But when the Lombards requested peace and offered gifts, Childebert made peace and confirmed an agreement with them, then returned without battle and gave no answer when Maurice demanded the money back. Gregory of Tours; Paul the Deacon, year 584.

584 King Guntram, building with the greatest zeal a monastery of Saint Marcellus in the suburb of Chalon, established it on the model of Agaunum. Gregory of Tours.

A certain Gundoald, with the help of Mummolus and Desiderius, aspiring to the kingdom, seized power tyrannically against Guntram. But after being driven away by Guntram’s commanders Leudegisel and Aegila, he took refuge in the city of Comminges. There he was thrown from a cliff by Boson and perished. Gregory of Tours.

[Note: This was Gundobald, the pretended son of King Clothar; Gregory of Tours discusses him more fully in *History of the Franks*, book VI, chapters 24 and 26; book VII, chapters 36 and 38; and elsewhere, as do Aimon in his *History of the Franks* and others.]

[Note: Gregory of Tours calls it the city of Comminges. He also calls Guntram’s commanders Leudegisel and Aegila, and substitutes Ollon for Boson, book VII, chapter 38.]

585 After Chilperic, king of the Franks, had been killed by treachery following his many crimes and evils [Note: Gregory of Tours assigns Chilperic’s death to the year 584] and buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent at Paris, his young son Clothar was ordered to be baptized by his uncle, King Guntram, and was received from the sacred font. Raised to his father’s kingdom, he ruled for forty-five years, while his mother Fridegund and Landeric, mayor of the palace, governed. Gregory of Tours, the preceding year.

[Note: Clothar was not baptized until 590. Gregory of Tours, book X, chapter 28.]

The patrician Mummolus, convicted of treason, was killed by order of King Guntram, and his treasures were transferred to the treasury. Gregory, the same year.

586 In Italy, after the ten years during which the dukes had ruled, the Lombards established Authari Flavius, son of Cleph, as king. Famous for his military valor, he ruled for six years. Among other deeds, he destroyed the city of Brescello and afterward traversed almost all Italy in war. Paul the Deacon.

Leovigild, the Arian king of the Goths in Spain, ordered his son, King Hermenegild, to be killed with an axe on the holy day of Easter, eighteen days before the Kalends of May. [Note: These chronological indications point to the year 586, although others place the event earlier.]

King Guntram sent an army into Spain, but it fell ill and immediately returned. Gregory of Tours, year 585.

587 Leudegisel [Leudisolus] was promoted by Guntram to the rank of patrician. Gregory of Tours, year 586.

A great flood occurred. A sparkling and apparently roaring ball of fire fell from the sky to the earth. The same source, the same year.

In Spain Leovigild, king of the Goths, died, and his son Reccared became king in his place. At the urging of Leander, bishop of Seville, through whom his brother Hermenegild had been converted, Reccared not long afterward converted to the Catholic faith together with the entire Gothic people. Gregory of Tours, years 586 and 588.

588 Kings Guntram and Childebert mutually confirmed peace and an agreement between themselves, and Guntram’s kingdom was promised to Childebert after Guntram’s death. Some of Childebert’s princes and dukes, convicted of conspiracy against him, were punished. Fredegar, year 587.

In Spain heresy was destroyed and a synod was convened at Toledo through the efforts of Bishop Leander and King Reccared. [Note: This synod was held in the Spanish era 627, that is, in the year 589.]

Caesara, queen and wife of Aunulf, king of the Persians, came as a refugee to Constantinople, concealing her royal name, and obtained baptism. Later, when her husband found her, she induced him also, when he came to Antioch with many of his people, to be baptized and embrace Christianity. Fredegar.

[Note: This account, drawn from the *Miscellaneous History* and Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*, book IV, chapter 52, is counted by Muratori among the fables. See the notes of Ruinart on this passage of Fredegar.]

589 Guntram’s army, sent into Spain, was severely slaughtered by the Goths through the negligence of its commander Boson. Fredegar.

At this time King Childebert gave his sister, whom he had promised to Authari, king of the Lombards, in marriage to the king of the Goths, who had recently become Catholic. [Note: That is, to Reccared in Spain, who requested Clodosuinda, according to Gregory of Tours, book IX, chapters 16 and 25. Either this marriage was brief or it did not take place; for in this same year Queen Baddo is named in Reccared’s profession of faith. Unless, with Mariana, *History of Spain*, book VI, chapter 1, we say that Clodosuinda was first married to the king after Baddo had died.]

Paul the Deacon, book III, chapter 27; another account assigns this to 588.

590 The tunic of the Lord and Savior, pointed out by a certain Jew named Simon after he had been compelled by torture, was found in a marble chest at the town of Zaphad, after a three-day fast had been observed by Gregory of Antioch, John of Constantinople, Thomas of Jerusalem, and many other bishops. It was brought to Jerusalem with the highest honor. Gregory of Tours; Fredegar.

[Note: At this time there was no Thomas bishop of Jerusalem, but John IV held that office from 574 to 594, as Le Quien proves in *Christian East*, vol. III, p. 242, adducing this very narrative. See Pagi under the year 593.]

[Note: Also called Saphad, which is now Jaffa and was formerly Joppa.]

A battle was fought between the Franks and the Britons. Fredegar.

At this same time, at the request of the emperor Maurice, Childebert again marched with an army against the Lombards in Italy. But after his army was defeated and severely cut down by King Authari, he returned with only a few men. Paul the Deacon; Gregory of Tours; another account assigns this to 588.

591 In these days the king of the Lombards took as his wife Theodelinda, daughter of Garibald, king of the Bavarians, a woman beautiful, prudent, and pious. Paul the Deacon, year 590; another account assigns this to 589.

[Note: King Authari, who died in 590, must already have entered into this marriage. See Paul the Deacon, book III, chapter 34. A letter of Saint Gregory concerning his death exists, dated in the ninth indiction, that is, in the year 591.]

At that time a great Frankish army, sent by King Childebert against the Lombards with twenty commanders, suffered through various misfortunes, especially illness. It was scarcely able to harm the enemy enclosed within their fortifications, and, afflicted by hunger with little result achieved, finally returned with difficulty. Paul the Deacon; Gregory of Tours, year 590.

592 An immense flood and deluge caused by rains occurred, followed by a great mortality. Another account assigns this to 590. [Note: Pelagius was carried off by the plague on 8 February 590; Gregory succeeded him on 3 September of the same year. Thus this passage applies to Gregory, as does the death of King Authari or Autharis.]

First Pelagius the pope, and then countless people, died in groups. Blessed Gregory, then archdeacon of the Roman Church, established litanies; when the plague ceased, he was ordained the sixty-sixth pope. He was deservedly superior to all in doctrine and conduct worthy of the apostles, and held the see for thirteen years, six months, and ten days. Immediately, among his other good works, he produced the book *Pastoral Care* in an outstanding style. He also made a canopy over the body of blessed Peter and instituted the celebration of Masses there; he did likewise at Saint Paul’s. Paul the Deacon; Anastasius.

In Italy, when King Authari had sent an embassy to the Franks to seek peace, he died, as they say, by poison. His widowed queen Theodelinda chose Agon, also called Agilolfus [elsewhere Agilulfus], as her husband and king. Having become king of the Lombards, he ruled for twenty-two years. The Lombards made peace with the Franks. Fredegar, year 591; Paul the Deacon.

593 Guntram, king of Burgundy, outstanding in every virtue, died in the thirty-third year of his reign, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Marcellus, which he himself had built. Childebert, son of his brother Sigebert, received the kingdom and held it afterward for four years. Fredegar.

In Britain King Edilfrid was established over part of the Angles. Great drought and famine occurred, together with an unusual multitude of large locusts. Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 2.

594 The duke Quintrio, having entered the kingdom of Clothar, son of King Chilperic, with hostile intent, was defeated by Clothar in a bloody battle on both sides and fled. Fredegar, year 593.

A multitude of locusts likewise damaged the crops. Paul the Deacon.

595 Pope Gregory assembled a synod of twenty-four bishops at Saint Peter’s for the benefit of the Church, in the fourteenth indiction. [Note: Bede’s *Chronicle* more accurately reads “in the thirteenth indiction,” which agrees with July of this year.]

The Franks and Britons engaged in battle, with heavy slaughter on both sides. In these days Tassilo was established by Childebert as king of the Bavarians. He soon defeated the Slavs and carried away great booty from them. Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapters 4, 7, and 42.

596 Saint Columba, priest and abbot, after many miracles on the island of Iona near Ireland, departed to the Lord in the seventy-third year of his age. Bede, *History of the English*.

At this time blessed Pope Gregory ordered the teachers Augustine, Mellitus, John, and other servants of God to preach the word of life to the English people in Britain; with God’s grace cooperating, through them he converted that people to the faith of Christ. The same source.

A comet and many signs appeared in the sky. Childebert’s army almost destroyed the rebellious Varni in battle. Fredegar, year 595.

597 Childebert, king of the Franks, strong and energetic, son of Sigebert, died in the twenty-third year of his reign and the twenty-fifth year of his age, having, as they say, received poison from his wife. [Note: Others report the event in the twentieth year of his reign and the twenty-sixth year of his age, and say that he was killed together with his wife, not by her poison. Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 12.]

[Note: Gregory the Great praises him further in *Letters*, book VI, letter 6.]

His two sons succeeded him: Theudebert ruled in Austrasia for seventeen years, and Theoderic ruled in Burgundy with their grandmother Brunhild for eighteen years. In that same year Fridegund invaded their kingdom with her son Clothar and, after crushing and routing them and their resisting army in a severe slaughter, put them to flight. Fredegar, year 596; Paul the Deacon.

598 Queen Fridegund, mother of King Clothar, died. Fredegar, the preceding year.

In these times, when the patrician Romanus had recovered by surrender several cities previously captured by the Lombards, King Agilolfus sought to avenge this and threatened Italy and Rome itself with a hostile army. Through the efforts of holy Pope Gregory and the support of the devout Queen Theodelinda, peace was established between the two sides. Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 8 and following.

599 The duke Quintrio (Wintrio) was killed at the instigation of Brunhild. Fredegar, the preceding year.

Around this time King Agilolfus killed some Lombard dukes who rebelled against him and subdued others by various means. He also made a perpetual peace with Theoderic, king of the Franks. Paul the Deacon; Fredegar, year 598.

Around this same time the monastery of Saint Benedict, situated in the fortress of Monte Cassino, was completely destroyed and left desolate by the Lombards after the monks had fled from it. [Note: We omit here the opinions of the authors concerning the date of this destruction, which Muratori discusses at length in his notes on Paul the Deacon. Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. I, p. 176, proves that it should be placed around 580, although the more common opinion has hitherto adopted the year 589.] Paul the Deacon, chapter 18.

600 Pope Gregory decreed that the bishops of London and York in Britain should be metropolitans, sending them the pallium, in the fourth indiction. Gregory, letter 65, assigned to the year 601.

A glandular disease severely afflicted Marseille, other cities of those regions, and Italy. Another account assigns this to 599.

In Lake Geneva the water suddenly boiled and became hot, cooking a large part of the fish. Warinharius [elsewhere Warnharius], mayor of the palace of Theoderic, died after distributing all his possessions. Fredegar, the preceding year.

601 Brunhild, expelled from Theudebert’s kingdom because of her crimes, was found alone by a certain poor man. At her request he brought her to King Theoderic, who received her kindly; in return, she obtained for that poor man the bishopric of Auxerre. Aimon, book III, chapter 87; another account assigns this to 599.

[Note: This account, taken from Fredegar under the year 599, is attributed in the new manuscript *Bibliotheca* of P. Labbe to Desiderius, bishop of Auxerre. Yet in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XII, p. 168, he is called a man of the highest nobility and a relative of Brunhild; hence Cointius rejects this narrative as fictitious under the year 599.]

602 The emperor Maurice appointed Phocas commander of the army, useful to the state, and sent him with an army; Phocas triumphed over the Persians and several other peoples. *Miscellaneous History*.

Fiery globes and other signs were seen in the sky. Fredegar, year 600.

The brothers Theudebert and Theoderic defeated King Clothar in a great battle, slaughtered and routed his army, seized his kingdom, and divided it between themselves. Only a small part was left to Clothar—twelve counties along the ocean coast—under a peace agreement. Fredegar, year 600; Paul the Deacon.

603 At Constantinople Phocas, returning victorious from the Persians, shamefully killed the emperor Maurice, who was said always to have prayed to expiate his sins in the present life. Phocas seized the empire and held it for eight years. Fredegar, year 602.

The duke Aegilan [elsewhere Aegila] was killed without cause, solely because of his wealth, at the instigation of Brunhild. Fredegar, year 602.

Theudebert and Theoderic sent an army and brought the defeated Vascones under their authority. The same source.

The body of Saint Victor the martyr, who had suffered at Solothurn with blessed Ursus, was found by divine revelation near the city of Geneva [or Genava], in a silver coffin, and was made famous by many miracles. Fredegar, year 602.

[Note: The Bollandists discuss this discovery at length, vol. VIII of the September volume, under 30 September, beginning on p. 272.]

Adaloald, son of King Agilolfus, was baptized and received from the font by Secundus, a servant of God and bishop of Trent. Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 28.

[Note: Secundus or Secundinus, famous in the testimony of Saint Gregory the Great, is nowhere else recorded among the bishops of Trent; he is called only “the servant of Christ from Trent.” See Muratori, vol. I of *Italian Writers*, p. 461, in the notes on Paul the Deacon. Others say that he was an abbot.]

604 In Britain Edilfrid, king of the Angles, defeated Aedan, king of the Scots, who had invaded the island, in a fierce battle and routed his army. Bede, *History of the English*.

Etherius, bishop of Lyon, died, and Secundinus succeeded him; Aridius then succeeded Secundinus. Fredegar, year 602.

[Note: Etherius, or Aetherius, died in 602; Secundinus in 603, and Aridius or Aredius succeeded him in the same year. Fredegar.]

King Agilolfus destroyed Cremona and Mantua after capturing them, and ravaged other cities and provinces. When the Romans returned to him his daughter, who had previously been captured, they received peace from him for a time. Paul the Deacon.

605 Blessed Pope Gregory, the most holy teacher, departed to the Lord in the eighth indiction. [Note: From Anastasius, Pagi, and others it is certain that Gregory died on 12 March 604, while the seventh indiction was still current; therefore this must be referred to the preceding year.] After the episcopate had remained vacant for more than five months, Fabianus [read: Sabinianus], the sixty-seventh pope, was ordained and held the see for one year and five months. After him the episcopate again remained vacant for nearly a year, because an imperial embassy from Constantinople was being awaited. Anastasius.

In this year also the wicked synod of Chalon was convened. [Note: The synod of Chalon is gathered from Fredegar and Aimon under the year 603; it was convened by Aridius of Lyon against Saint Desiderius.] Blessed Desiderius, archbishop of Vienne, because he denounced Brunhild’s crimes, was deposed and assigned to exile through her plotting, and Domnulus was appointed in his place. The sun was darkened. A severe winter destroyed a large part of the vineyards. Fredegar, year 603.

606 Famine occurred at Rome, and peace with the Lombards was arranged for one year at the price of twelve thousand solidi. Paul the Deacon.

Protadius, who had committed adultery with Brunhild among many others, became duke. Clothar’s army, contrary to the agreement, invaded Theoderic’s kingdom and, after putting Berthoald, mayor of the palace, a brave and devout man, to flight, besieged him at Orléans. Fredegar, year 604.

Adaloald, son of Agilolfus, was elected king by the Lombards in his father’s presence. After he was betrothed to the daughter of Theudebert, perpetual peace was made with the Franks. Paul the Deacon, year 604.

In April and May a comet was seen.

607 Theoderic defeated and routed Clothar’s army in battle. In that battle, however, Berthoald, mayor of the palace, advanced too boldly among the enemy and was killed. In his place Protadius was promoted through Brunhild’s plotting. When Theudebert and Clothar came hostilely together with their assembled armies, they departed after making peace with one another. Fredegar, year 605.

Theoderic, at the instigation of Brunhild and Protadius, took up arms against his brother Theudebert. When they were preparing to meet with hostile armies, everyone else urged peace, but Protadius alone resisted. In the resulting fury of the soldiers, he was killed in the king’s tent, and the brothers withdrew from one another after making peace. Fredegar, year 605.

608 At Rome Boniface III, the sixty-eighth pope, held the see for about nine months. After him the episcopate again remained vacant for ten months. Because the Church of Constantinople claimed in its correspondence to be first, Boniface obtained from the emperor Phocas a decree that the Roman Church should be declared the head of all the Churches. He also assembled a synod of seventy-two bishops at Rome. Bede, *Chronicle*; Paul the Deacon, assigned to 607.

In Theoderic’s kingdom Claudius, a prudent and devout man, became mayor of the palace in place of Protadius. Fredegar, year 606.

609 At Rome Boniface IV, the sixty-ninth pope, held the see for six years and eight months; after him the episcopate remained vacant for seven months. From the emperor Phocas he obtained the temple of all the idols, called the Pantheon, and dedicated it in honor of Saint Mary and all the saints on the third day before the Ides of May. He called it Saint Mary of the Martyrs and established the celebration of All Saints on the Kalends of November. [Note: This applied only at Rome; in the universal Church the feast was instituted under Gregory IV. See Sigebert, *Chronicle*, under the year 835.]
