During his pontificate famine, pestilence, and an immense flood occurred. Anastasius; another account assigns this to 608.

At Brunhild’s instigation, Duke Uncilenus had his foot cut off by Theoderic and was stripped of his possessions because of Protadius’s death. The patrician Volfus was likewise killed. Fredegar, year 607.

[Note: This Uncilenus must not be confused with the man who was appointed duke of the Alamanni by King Childebert in 588, according to Fredegar, chapter 8.]

The same Theoderic brought Ermenberga from Spain, the daughter of Vittericus [elsewhere Bettericus], king of the Goths, intending to make her his wife. At Brunhild’s urging—for she ambitiously detested queens, fearing that her own honor would be diminished—he did not accept her as his wife, but sent her back the following year after repudiating and stripping her. Fredegar, year 607.

Blessed Desiderius, archbishop of Vienne, recalled from exile, was stoned and crowned with martyrdom through the faction of Brunhild, Theoderic, and Aridius of Lyon. He became famous after death through many miracles. The same source.

[Note: Jonas says nothing about Aridius; hence Cointius absolves him of this crime, although contemporary or nearly contemporary writers, Fredegar and Aimon, report the matter quite differently under the year 605. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 40. Concerning Saint Desiderius, see the Bollandists, May volume, vol. V, under 23 May.]

610 Vittericus, king of the Goths, having enlisted three other kings as allies, prepared for war against Theoderic. Fredegar, the preceding year.

In these times the Persians, raging in war, took many provinces from the Romans. Among them they seized Jerusalem itself and destroyed the holy places; along with other ornaments and treasures of the churches, they carried away the Lord’s cross. Paul the Deacon; but Theophanes assigns this to 614.

611 Heraclianus, who governed Africa, rebelled against the emperor Phocas. Coming with an army, he deprived Phocas of both kingdom and life, and raised his son Heraclius to the imperial office. Heraclius ruled for twenty-six years. Paul the Deacon, year 610.

Blessed abbot Columbanus, who had come from Ireland with his disciples Saint Gall and others during the reign of King Sigebert and was building the monastery of Luxeuil, shining with many virtues, often rebuked Theoderic for his crimes, especially his adulteries, and urged him to enter a lawful marriage. Through the plotting of Brunhild, who bitterly opposed this, he was expelled from there by order of King Theoderic and left Saint Eustasius there as abbot in his place. Fredegar, year 609; Marius of Avenches.

[Note: This occurred in 610. See the *Life of Saint Columbanus*, *Acta Sanctorum of the Order of Saint Benedict*, section II, p. 22.]

612 Around this time blessed Augustine, apostle of the English, archbishop, and remarkable teacher, departed to the Lord. [Note: Mabillon, in his notes on Augustine’s life, first Benedictine century, p. 532, places his death around 607; others assign it to 609.]

Saint Columbanus, expelled from Luxeuil, went to King Clothar and from there to Theudebert. When Theudebert gave him the choice of remaining in his kingdom, Columbanus finally came to Brigantium in Alamannia and stayed there for three years.

When a dispute arose between Theudebert and Theoderic over the kingdom, Theudebert violently seized Alsace. The Alamanni, making their way to the district of Aventicum and beyond the Jura, returned victorious with booty.

Theudebert killed his wife and took another. Fredegar, year 610.

[Note: Brigantium is recorded as a military station at the headwaters of the Rhine in the itinerary of Antoninus Pius, and likewise in Strabo and Ptolemy.]

[Note: Concerning this formerly famous district of the Helvetii, now called Uchtlandia according to Guillimann, see Paulinus’s commentary on the districts of ancient Germany.]

613 In Spain, after Vittericus had died, Sisebut became king of the Goths. [Note: Gondemar succeeded King Vittericus when he was killed in 610, and Sisebut succeeded Gondemar in 612.] He was a brave and pious man who, often victorious in engagements with Roman soldiers, spared them and nobly enlarged the Gothic kingdom after capturing many cities. Fredegar, year 607; another account assigns this to 613.

Theoderic, preparing for war against his brother Theudebert, attempted to draw King Clothar, his cousin, away from aiding Theudebert by promising him a certain province. Fredegar, year 611.

Around this time the Huns, also called Avars, attacked Venetia. They devastated the entire province with sword, fire, and plunder; they destroyed Forum Julii itself, which had been betrayed to them by Romhilda, widow of Gisulf; then, after laying waste the province, they returned. Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 38; another account assigns this to 610.

614 The emperor Heraclius made his son Constantine his associate in the empire. Another account assigns this to 613.

Theoderic and Theudebert fought a fierce battle with hostile armies in the territory of Toul. After great slaughter on both sides, Theudebert was defeated and fled to Cologne. Theoderic pursued him out of hatred and also at the instigation of the venerable Leunisius, bishop of Mainz. Theudebert again gathered forces from every direction, met Theoderic at Tolbiac, and engaged him; after an immense slaughter of men, he was again defeated and fled. Theoderic entered Cologne, seized Theudebert’s treasures and kingdom, ordered his little son to be killed, captured Theudebert himself, had him tonsured, and sent him to Chalon. Not long afterward, suspecting him, he ordered him killed at Brunhild’s instigation. Fredegar, year 612; Marius of Avenches.

[Note: This man is called Leonisius by others. Trithemius calls him “a man of great virtues in Christ.” For the deed narrated here, see Aimon, *History of the Franks*, book III, chapter 98.]

In those days blessed Columbanus was expelled from Brigantium. He left the fever-stricken Gall there, came to Italy, and was kindly received by King Agilolfus and Theodelinda. He built the monastery of Bobbio. Jonas in the *Life*; Mabillon, second Benedictine century; another account assigns this to 612.

Saint Gall likewise began to inhabit the solitude of his cell. Ratpert; Strabo.

[Note: The cell was situated in the forest between the Rhaetian Alps and Lake Constance; it later grew into the celebrated monastery bearing his name.]

615 Theoderic, preparing to take up arms against Clothar, died at Metz from a flux of the bowels and, as some say, through Brunhild’s treachery by poison. His son Sigebert, born of a concubine, was made king in his place by Brunhild and the nobles. Not long afterward King Clothar invaded his kingdom, in the thirtieth year of his own reign. Fredegar, year 613; Marius of Avenches; Paul the Deacon.

616 In Britain Ethelbert, the first Christian king of the English, died in the fifty-sixth year of his reign. Eadbald [elsewhere Eatpolt] succeeded him and ruled for twenty-four years. Bede, *History of the English*, assigned to 613.

At this time Isidore, bishop of Seville, was renowned in Spain. He carried his abridgment of the history of the ages down to this point [Note: That is, to the fifth year of Heraclius and the Spanish era 654, which is the year of Christ 616. A work entitled Isidore’s *Chronicle* is found in the new edition of his works, Madrid, 1778, vol. I, part II, p. 121], and published many excellent short works.

In Italy Agilolfus, king of the Lombards, died. His son Adaloald ruled with his mother Theodelinda for ten years. Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 93.

Among the Franks, when King Sigebert had assembled an army against Clothar, he was abandoned by his own men and captured by the enemy. Together with his brothers, he was killed by order of Clothar. Brunhild herself was ordered by Clothar to be tied to wild horses and torn apart by them; thus she perished at last by a fitting death, and Clothar obtained sole rule of the kingdom. Fredegar, year 613; Marius of Avenches.

[Column 0134A] **617** In Rome, Pope Deusdedit, the seventieth pope, occupied the see for three years and nearly one month. [Note: [Column 0134D] Deusdedit had succeeded Pope Boniface IV no later than 615.] He loved the clergy and priests and increased their allowances. During his pontificate, the patrician Eleutherius came to Ravenna and killed the slayers of the patrician John. Likewise, after tyrants had been killed at Naples and elsewhere, he restored peace to Italy. Anastasius, under 615. — In Britain, after Edwin had killed Æthelfrith and his sons had been driven into Ireland, he ruled his kingdom splendidly for seventeen years. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*.

**618** A great earthquake occurred, and an ensuing scabrous plague afflicted the people with a loathsome death, so that the dead could not be recognized. Anastasius. — Jerusalem, among the other cities of Palestine, was captured by Chosroes, king of the Persians, and the Lord’s Cross was carried away into Persia. [Note: [Column 0134D] See the year 610; but this belongs to neither year, for it occurred, according to the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, in the second indiction, that is, in the year 614.]

[Column 0134B] **619** King Clothar, receiving Warnhar[ ius ] [alternative: Warnacharius], against whom he had been somewhat hostile, back into favor with the support of many, confirmed him in the office of mayor of the palace. Fredegar, under 613.

**620** In Rome, Boniface V, the seventy-first pope, occupied the see for five years; he was a very gentle and pious man. Anastasius, under 618, correctly. — The patrician Eleutherius, aspiring to tyranny and kingship in Italy, was killed by the soldiers, and his head was sent to Constantinople. Another source, under 619. — In Britain, after Archbishop Laurence died, Mellitus succeeded him. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*. — Magundat the Magian, a Persian by birth, converted to the faith of Christ and called Anastasius, became at Jerusalem a monk of extraordinary holiness.

**621** King Clothar, at the request of the Lombards, relinquished the twelve thousand gold solidi which they had annually paid to the Franks as tribute for Burgundy, once invaded, after certain advisers had urged him to do so. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 618.

**622** Queen Bertrude, wife of King Clothar, exceedingly beloved by him and by everyone because of her piety and excellence of character, died. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 619.

**623** In these times the blessed Attala, and after him Bertulf, abbots of Bobbio, and also the most blessed Gallus in Alamannia, became renowned for their virtues. Jonas.

[Column 0135A] **624** In Britain, after Archbishop Mellitus died, Justus was appointed in his place. In the following year he ordained the blessed Paulinus bishop and sent him as preacher and teacher to those English who were still pagans. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*. King Clothar of the Franks, in the thirty-ninth year of his reign, made his son Dagobert his associate in the kingdom and, entrusting him to the blessed man Arnulf [Note: [Column 0135D] We have already prefixed to Hermann’s work the genealogy of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz. Pippin, however, was duke of Austrasia and mayor of the palace, surnamed of Laon.] and to Duke Pippin, sent him to govern the kingdom of Austrasia. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 622.

**625** In Rome, Pope Honorius, the seventy-second pope, occupied the see for thirteen years. Devoted to many good works, he adorned, restored, and built several churches. He built the basilica of Saint Agnes on the Nomentan Way; likewise that of Saint Apollinaris in the portico of Saint Peter; likewise that of Saint Quiriacus on the Ostian Way; likewise the church of the Four Crowned Martyrs; likewise that of Saint Severinus in the city of Tibur; likewise that of Saint Pancras on the Aurelian Way; likewise that of Saint Lucy; likewise that of Saint Hadrian; and he accomplished many other praiseworthy works. Anastasius.

**626** A certain Samo, a Frankish merchant, had come with others to the Slavs and had fought most bravely in their support against the Huns, who are also called Avars, when they made war upon them. After obtaining victory, the Slavs chose him as their king. Celebrated for many victories, he ruled successfully for thirty-five years. There he took twelve wives and had by them twenty-two sons and fifteen daughters. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 623. — In Italy, Adaloald, king of the Lombards, after being driven insane by the malicious potion of a certain Greek envoy and killing some of the nobles, was deposed from the kingdom and not long afterward destroyed by poison. After him Hariald [alternative: Arioald] became king and reigned for seven years. He had Gundiberga, daughter of Agilulf, as his wife. Paul the Deacon, under 625; another source, under 623.

**627** In Britain, King Edwin of the English was converted by Bishop Paulinus and baptized with his people, about 180 years after the arrival of the English in Britain. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*. — A dispute that had begun between King Clothar and his son Dagobert was calmed through the mediation of the blessed Arnulf and other nobles. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 625.

**628** The blessed monk Anastasius, after suffering many torments for Christ, was finally strangled in Persia by King Chosroes together with seventy others and completed his martyrdom. Bede, *Chronicle*. — In the same year Emperor Heraclius marched into Persia and, after defeating and killing Chosroes, triumphantly brought the Lord’s Cross back to Jerusalem with immeasurable booty. Theophanes, *Chronicle*. — Among the Franks, Warnharius [or Warnacharius], mayor of the palace, died. His son Godinus, after taking his stepmother as his wife, fled from place to place while Clothar pursued him, and was eventually killed. Fredegar, under 626.

**629** King Clothar held a great assembly at Clichy from throughout his kingdom. There a great disagreement and tumult arose, which was scarcely calmed at last through the king’s efforts. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 627.

**630** The strong, pious, and devout King Clothar of the Franks died in the forty-fifth year of his reign and was buried at Paris in the basilica of Saint Vincent. His son Dagobert received the kingdom; although he had already been reigning for six years, he governed it for another ten, granting only a small portion near the Vascones and the Pyrenees to his brother Charibert. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 628.

**631** King Dagobert, using as advisers Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz; Duke Pippin, mayor of the palace; and Chunibert, archbishop of Cologne, burned with an excessive love of justice and proved in every respect a praiseworthy king. Later, however, following his own counsels, he began to decline greatly into worse things. After repudiating his wife Gomatrude, he took as his wife a certain girl named Nanthild from a monastery. [Note: [Column 0135D] Fredegar, in chapter 58 of his *Chronicle*, has the better reading, *de ministerio*, that is, from the palace service or queen’s household.] Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 629.

**632** Charibert, the petty king and brother of Dagobert, invaded Vasconia and added it to his own kingdom. Dagobert fathered a son, Sigebert, by a certain concubine. [Note: [Column 0136D] Fredegar calls her Ragintrude.] Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 630. — Through the mediation of envoys, perpetual peace was made between Emperor Heraclius and Dagobert. At the emperor’s request—for he had foreseen that his empire would be devastated by the circumcised people—many Jews in the Frankish kingdom, as also elsewhere in the Roman Empire, were driven out. [Note: [Column 0136D] The same author says that Dagobert compelled the Jews to undergo baptism.] Not long afterward, in the ensuing times, the most savage people of the Saracens, themselves also circumcised, inundated and devastated many provinces, and the Roman army, repeatedly slaughtered in battle, was severely weakened. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 630.

**633** In Britain, Edwin, peaceful and pious king of the English, was defeated and killed by the pagan kings Ceadwalda [alternative: Cedowalla] and Penda. After his death, the sons of Æthelfrith returned from the Scots and seized their father’s former kingdom. Two of them, however, apostatizing from the faith of Christ which they had learned among the Scots, perished within one year. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*. — [Page 95] Among the Franks, Charibert, the petty king and brother of Dagobert, died, and his brother Dagobert received his kingdom and treasures. Dagobert sent three armies against Samo and the Slavs by different routes: one Frankish army was defeated, while two armies of Suevi and Lombards returned victorious. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 631.

**634** This was a disastrous year for the English, both because of the apostasy and destruction of their kings and because of the barbarous and cruel devastation they suffered at the hands of Ceadwalda. But immediately Oswald, the third son of Æthelfrith, a most Christian man, trusting in the Lord with a small force, and having worshiped the wooden cross which he had raised, boldly entered battle with Ceadwalda. After defeating him and recovering the province and his brothers, he ruled his father’s kingdom nobly and with great piety for eight years. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*. — Samo ravaged Thuringia with the Slavs. The Saxons, promising to resist the Slavs, were released by Dagobert from the tribute of five hundred cows which they annually paid to the Franks. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 631. — In Italy, after Hariald, king of the Lombards, died, Rotharius [alternative: Rotharis], husband of Gundiberga, was chosen and became king; he reigned for thirteen years. Paul the Deacon, under 636.

**635** In these times, when Sergius of Constantinople, with the support of Cyrus of Alexandria, was restoring the heresy of the Acephali and had taught as doctrine that there was one will and one operation of divinity and humanity in Christ, and had led the emperor astray, he was condemned by the Apostolic See. Bede, *Chronicle*; another source, under 634. — While the Slavs, together with Samo, were raiding Thuringia and the neighboring districts, Dagobert made his young son Sigebert king of Austrasia, entrusting him to the dukes Pippin and Adalgis and to Chunibert, archbishop of Cologne. He gave him Metz as his seat and persuaded the nobles thereafter to defend the borders of the eastern kingdom. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 633.

**636** To King Dagobert, Clovis, also called Louis, was born by Queen Nanthild. Not long afterward Dagobert designated and confirmed him for his western kingdom. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 633. — Ratolfus [alternative: Radulfus], duke of Thuringia, often engaging the Slavs, drove them away victorious. Consequently, puffed up and attempting to rebel against his king, he gradually began to raise his ambitions. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 633.

**637** In Constantinople, Emperor Heraclius, previously induced into heresy, as they say, by Sergius, bishop of Constantinople, died. His son Heraclonas [alternative: Heracleonas], together with his mother Martina, ruled for two years. Theophanes; another source, under 641; see under 639. — During these times Rotharius, king of the Lombards, although an Arian, was nevertheless a lover of justice and wrote down the laws of the Lombards. He also captured several Roman cities, and, engaging the people of Ravenna in battle, killed eight thousand of them and put the rest to flight. Paul the Deacon, under 643.

**638** In Rome, after Pope Honorius died, the Apostolic See remained vacant for one year, seven months, and fourteen days, because imperial authority at Constantinople was wavering amid the deaths of the rulers. [Note: [Column 0137D] Since Honorius died nearly three years before Heraclius, the reason for the consecration’s having been delayed so long seems to lie not in the death of the rulers but in the fact that Severinus, though elected, was unwilling to approve Heraclius’s *Ecthesis*, as Anastasius records in the collections edited by Sirmond.] Anastasius. — At this time the Lateran treasury was plundered and dispersed by Maurice the chartularius and Isaac [alternative: Isaak], patrician and exarch of Italy. — The Vascones attempted rebellion but were subdued after Dagobert sent an army. The king of the Britons came to Dagobert, humbly satisfied him, and returned after obtaining peace. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 635.

**639** In Constantinople, after the emperor Heraclonas died, his brother Constantine reigned for six months. [Note: [Column 0137D] Hermannus derived this from Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book IV, chapter 41, but was misled by him. For from Nicephorus we learn that, after Heraclius died on 11 February 641, his elder son Constantine succeeded him; he died, however, after 103 days, that is, on 25 May, making way for his brother Heraclonas, Heraclius’s son by Martina. After six months of rule, Heraclonas was driven into exile with his mother and was succeeded by Constans, his nephew, the son of his aforesaid brother Constantine. Accordingly, the statements above under 637 and those that follow shortly must also be corrected.] [Column 0138C] Paul the Deacon. In Britain, Eadbald, king of the Kentish English, died, and his son Erchanbert succeeded him for twenty-five years. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*. — The Vascones begged forgiveness from Dagobert for their rebellion and obtained it. Fredegar, under 636.

[Page 97] **640** In Constantinople, after the death of Emperor Constantine, his son Constantine, also called Constans, reigned for twenty-eight years, beginning with the following year. — In Rome, Pope Severinus, the seventy-third pope, occupied the see for two months and four days. He was a holy, gentle, and pious man. After him the bishopric remained vacant for five months. Anastasius. — King Dagobert died in the sixteenth year of his reign and was buried in the Parisian suburb, in the monastery of Saint Denis, which he himself had built, adorned, endowed, and arranged according to the institution of the monastery of Agaune. With him, the strength and dignity of the Frankish kingdom gradually collapsed and declined; in his place his two sons, Sigebert and Louis, obtained their father’s kingdom. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 638.

**641** In Rome, John IV [Note: [Column 0139D] John was ordained on 24 December 640.], the seventy-fourth pope, occupied the see for one year and nearly ten months. After spending a large sum of money, he redeemed many captives from the barbarians in Istria and Dalmatia, and built and adorned the basilica of the holy martyrs Venantius, Anastasius, and Maurus. Anastasius. — Louis, or Clovis, still a child, was placed over the western kingdom while his mother Nanthild reigned. Fredegar, under 638. — In Spain, Sentila [alternative: Chintila], king of the Goths, died, and the boy Tolga received the kingdom. After he was deposed and tonsured not long afterward, Chindasind [alternative: Chindasuind] assumed the kingdom and, by slaughtering the leading men, excessively humbled the pride of the Goths. Fredegar, under 640 and following years.

**642** In Rome, Pope Theodore, the seventy-fifth pope, occupied the see for six years and nearly six months. He raised the bodies of the saints Primus and Felician and buried them in the basilica of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr. He built the church of Saint Valentine on the Flaminian Way, the oratory of Saint Sebastian at the Lateran, and the oratory of Saint Euplus before the gate of Saint Paul; among other good works, steadfast in the faith, he condemned the heretics. Anastasius. — [Page 98] In Britain, Oswald, the most pious king of the English, fell while fighting for his country against Penda, the pagan king of the Mercians, and became renowned after his death through many miracles. His brother Oswi succeeded him and reigned for twenty-eight years. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*.

**643** At this time Maurice the chartularius, aspiring to tyranny, was seized in Rome by soldiers sent by the patrician Isaac [alternative: Isaak], carried away, and beheaded near Ravenna. Not long afterward Isaac himself died at Ravenna, and in his place Theodore was sent by the emperor as exarch of Italy. [Note: [Column 0139D] According to the succession of the exarchs of Ravenna, Isaac died in 638, and Plato succeeded him; after Plato came, in 648, Theodore Calliopa, who will recur below.] Aega, mayor of the palace of Louis, a vigorous and religious man, died. After him Erchonald [alternative: Erchinoald], likewise a praiseworthy man, became mayor of the palace. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 640.

**644** Saint Paulinus, bishop of York and teacher of the English, departed to the Lord on 10 October, in the twentieth year of his episcopate. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*. — Pippin [Note: [Column 0139D] Namely Pippin of Landen, father of Saint Gertrude, who is commemorated under 646 and is venerated among the saints. See Bollandus, volume III, February 21], mayor of the palace and duke of Sigebert, an outstanding lover of justice and piety, died. After him his son Grimoald became mayor of the palace. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 639.

**645** At this time Pyrrhus of Constantinople, successor of Sergius both in office and in heresy, came from Africa to Rome, having long before been condemned by Pope Theodore. After pretending to repent and to make satisfaction, he was kindly received and reconciled. Later, however, after returning home and resuming his error, he was again deposed, condemned, and anathematized by that same pope. [Note: [Column 0139D] Pyrrhus’s renunciation belongs to the year 646; his condemnation, carried out in a synod at Rome, belongs to 648.] Bede, *Chronicle*; Paul the Deacon.

**646** In these times the blessed virgin Gertrude, daughter of Pippin and sister of Grimoald, mayor of the palace, and mother of the monastery of Nivelles [alternative: Niviala], became renowned for her virtues. Her sister Begga, herself also a religious woman, married Ansegisus, son of Saint Arnulf, and bore him Pippin the Younger. [Note: [Column 0140D] Surnamed of Herstal, father of Charles Martel. See the *Life of Saint Gertrude*, *Acta Sanctorum*, second century of the Benedictines, p. 462, and Bollandus, volume II, March 17; Saint Begga is commemorated on 17 December.] *Life of Saint Sigebert*, volume II of the Frankish writers; another source, under the following year.

**647** In these times, when Paul of Constantinople, successor of Pyrrhus, not only refused to abandon the heresy but increased it, and led the emperor and others astray, and did not repent when admonished and rebuked by the lord pope, he too was repeatedly condemned. Bede, *Chronicle*; Anastasius, under 648. — In Italy, after Rotharius, king of the Lombards, died, his son Rodoald reigned for five years. [Note: [Column 0140D] Rotharius did not die until 652, and his son Rodoald reigned for only five months, not years, as stated in the ancient *Chronicle of the Lombards*, edited by Muratori, volume II of the *Italian Writers*, part I, p. 270.] Paul the Deacon.

**648** During the reign of the emperor Constans [Note: [Column 0140D] Rather, Jerusalem had already been captured by them under Heraclius in 637], the most savage people of the Saracens devastated and plundered Palestine itself and Jerusalem, both Egypts, the city of Alexandria, a large part of Africa, and many other provinces of the Roman Empire. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 639.

**649** In Rome, Pope Martin, the seventy-sixth pope, occupied the see for six years and nearly two months. At that time Paul of Constantinople, after leading the emperor Constans astray, afflicted envoys of the Apostolic See who accused him of heresy with imprisonment, exile, and various other punishments; wherever he could, he stirred up considerable persecution against Catholics. Anastasius.

**650** In the ninth indiction [Note: [Column 0141D] Bede records the eighth indiction, and therefore the preceding year], Pope Martin convened at Rome a synod of 105 bishops. In it he condemned Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul, together with their followers in error. Bede, under 649.

[Column 0141B] **651** In Britain, the pious King Oswin was put to flight in battle by King Oswi and came to one of his own men, in whom he trusted. He was immediately betrayed by that man and ordered to be killed by King Oswi, his kinsman. In the same year the blessed Aidan the Scot, bishop and teacher of the English, died on the second day before the Kalends of September. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*. — In Italy, after Rodoald, king of the Lombards, died, Haribert [alternative: Aripert], son of Gundoald, brother of Queen Theodelinda, reigned for nine years. Paul the Deacon; another source, under 653.

**652** At this time the exarch Olympius, sent to Italy by the emperor Constans, was unable to corrupt or harm the lord pope and the others united with him in the Catholic faith. Having vainly laid plots against the pope, who was divinely protected, he was finally reconciled with him, assembled an army, and entered Sicily against the Saracens. There, after his Roman army had been defeated and slaughtered by them, he died, worn out by grief and illness. Anastasius; Paul the Deacon.

**653** In Britain, Honorius, archbishop of the English, died, and Deusdedit presided in his place for ten years. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*.

**654** In Britain, the inland English were converted to the faith of Christ. [Note: [Column 0141D] Thus the manuscript reads, but *Mediterranei* should be read.] The blessed Pope Martin, by order of the heretical emperor Constans, was seized at Rome by the exarch Theodore, who had been sent for this purpose, in the basilica of the Savior called the Constantinian, and was brought to Constantinople. Since he could in no way be bent, he was condemned to exile in Cherson. Bede, *Chronicle*; Anastasius; another source, under 653.

**655** Pope Martin departed to the Lord in exile and was buried there; afterward he became renowned through many miracles. In his place Pope Eugenius, the seventy-seventh pope, was ordained at Rome [Note: [Column 0142D] This occurred on 8 September 654, although he had already governed the Church in Martin’s absence] and occupied the see for two years and nearly ten months. He was a kind, gentle, and pious man. Anastasius. — In Britain, Penda, the pagan king of the Mercians, was defeated and killed in battle by Oswi, brother of Saint Oswald, and the people of Mercia accepted the faith of Christ. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*.

[Page 101] **656** Peter of Constantinople, as though making satisfaction on behalf of his faith, sent to Rome a very obscure and doubtful synodal letter, but it was not accepted by the lord pope or the Roman Church. Anastasius.

**657** In Rome, after Pope Eugenius died, the bishopric remained vacant for two months. Anastasius.

**658** In Rome, Pope Vitalian, the seventy-eighth pope, occupied the see for fourteen years and six months. Confirmed in office after letters had been sent to Constantinople according to custom, he governed the Roman Church with distinction. Anastasius, under 657.

**659** In Britain, Vulfhere [alternative: Wolpher], son of Penda, became king of the Mercians and reigned for seventeen years. Constantine, also called Constans, the emperor, sent precious gifts to Rome to Saint Peter. Anastasius.

**660** In Italy, after King Haribert of the Lombards died, his two sons, Godabert and Pertharich, divided the kingdom between them, establishing Godabert’s kingdom at Pavia and Pertharich’s at Milan. Not long afterward, however, through the faction of wicked men, desiring with unspeakable hatred to drive one another from the kingdom, they quarreled. Godabert, sending the most treacherous Duke Gunbald [Note: [Column 0142D] He was Garibald, duke of Turin], called upon Grimoald, a vigorous man who had already been duke of Benevento for twenty-five years, for aid against his brother. At the instigation of Gunbald himself, Grimoald killed Godabert, while Pertharich, driven into flight by the terror of the event, withdrew to the Huns. After one year and three months of his reign, Grimoald seized the kingdom of the Lombards and ruled it vigorously for nine years. Paul the Deacon, under 661 and following.

**661** At this time Pertharich, formerly king of the Lombards, returned from exile and sought the favor of King Grimoald. Although he was kindly received, through the faction of wicked men he was ordered by the king to be watched during the following night, to be killed the next day. But through the ingenuity—or rather the loyalty—of his friend Hunold and of a faithful wardrobe attendant of his, he was brought out of the city of Pavia and fled to the Franks, where he remained concealed. Paul the Deacon, under 664. — At this same time a Frankish army entered Italy. While it was feasting in the camp of King Grimoald, which he had apparently abandoned in a simulated flight, he fell upon it and destroyed it utterly. The same author; another source, under 665.

[Column 0143B] **662** Constantine, also called Constans, the emperor, marched into Italy against the Lombards. After capturing some of their towns, he besieged at Benevento Rumoald, son of King Grimoald. But when Grimoald approached with an army, Constantine was terrified and returned to Naples. A large part of his army, under the command of Saburrus, engaged Rumoald in battle, but was defeated and slaughtered; thus he accomplished nothing against the Lombards. Paul the Deacon, under 663.

**663** Emperor Constantine came to Rome and was honorably received by Pope Vitalian. With his entire army entering the church bearing candles, he offered Saint Peter a pallium woven with gold. After spending twelve days there, he removed nearly all the ornaments of the City. Among other things, he tore away the bronze tiles with which the basilica of Saint Mary at the Martyrs—the building anciently called the Pantheon—had been roofed and sent them ahead to Sicily. Then, after his men had plundered Italy, he himself entered that island in the seventh indiction. [Note: [Column 0143D] This indiction indicates the year 664.] There he remained for five years, notorious for great avarice and wickedness. Bede, *Chronicle of the English*.

**664** An eclipse of the sun occurred on 3 May at about the tenth hour, in the seventh indiction. [Note: [Column 0143D] The seventh indiction does indeed indicate this year, but the eclipse occurred not on the third day of May but on the first.] Bede, *Chronicle*. In Britain, at an assembly held by the English and Scots, the question of Easter was debated, and the Scots were reasonably defeated by the priest Wilfrid. A savage plague and pestilence devastated Britain and Ireland excessively. Deusdedit, archbishop of the English, died. Cridla [alternative: Ceadda] and Wilfrid were ordained bishops of the Northumbrians. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*.

**665** In Britain, after Erchanbert, king of Kent, died, his son Egbert reigned for nine years. The English sent to Pope Vitalian, asking that a bishop and teacher be provided for them. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*. — In these days among the Franks, Clovis, also called Louis, the sluggish and infamous son of Dagobert and brother of Sigebert, was staying at Paris. When he dared to remove the arm of Saint Denis, he was driven insane. Fredegar, *Chronicle*, under 654.

**666** At this time, when Lupus, duke of Friuli, rebelled against King Grimoald, the Huns, also called Avars, invited by the king himself, marched into Venetia. They were defeated in three battles but victorious in the fourth; after Lupus and his men had been killed, they ravaged Provence until, terrified by Grimoald’s strategy, they were finally forced to return. Paul the Deacon, under 665.

**667** About this time, the Slavs from Caruntum, which we call Carantania [Note: [Column 0143D] Today Carinthia, the province of ancient Noricum], were ravaging Venetia with an army. Duke Nuectarius, attacking them with twenty-five of his men, left scarcely any survivors out of five thousand. Paul the Deacon.

**668** In Sicily, Emperor Constantine, also called Constans, after imposing many exactions and carrying out plundering throughout the provinces, was finally killed by his own men in a bath and died, in the twelfth indiction. [Note: [Column 0143D] He was killed toward the end of September, when the twelfth indiction was already in progress.] After him Mezecius [alternative: Mizizius] seized the imperial power there but was killed, together with his accomplices, by the army from Italy. Constantine [Note: [Column 0144D] Surnamed Pogonatus] son of Constans then became emperor at Constantinople and reigned for seventeen years; he was, in truth, a Catholic and pious emperor. Paul the Deacon. — In this year Theodoricus [read: Theodorus] was ordained archbishop by Pope Vitalian and sent with the abbot Hadrian to the English. He benefited many both by his preaching and by his example. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*. — Among the Franks, after the death of Clovis [Note: [Column 0144D] Clovis II had already died in 656, and was succeeded by his son Clothar, then four years old, who reigned for fourteen years], or Louis, the infamous king, his son Clothar, still a child, reigned for four years. Fredegar, under 656.

[Column 0145A] **669** The Saracens, who already held Egypt after devastating many provinces, invaded Sicily at this time, caused great slaughter, plundered the island, seized the things which the emperor Constans had gathered there, and returned to Alexandria. Paul the Deacon.

**670** In Britain, Oswi, king of the English and brother of Saint Oswald, died; Egfrid succeeded him and reigned for fifteen years. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*. — In Italy, after Grimoald, king of the Lombards, died, Pertharich returned from exile, recovered his father’s kingdom with the great favor of the Lombards, and held it for seventeen years, distinguished by great piety. Paul the Deacon, under 671.

**671** During these times in Italy, Pertharich governed the Lombard kingdom in the greatest peace and uprightness. At this time Childeric, brother of King Clothar and son of Louis, had been summoned to the kingdom of Austrasia. Because he behaved there frivolously and cruelly, the Franks slaughtered him together with his wife and children. Fredegar, under 673.

**672** In Rome, after Pope Vitalian died in the fifteenth indiction, Pope Adeodatus, the seventy-ninth pope, was installed after two months and occupied the see for four years and two months. He was a very gentle and pious man. He restored and adorned churches and built new structures. Anastasius. — Among the Franks, after the child Clothar, his brother Theodoric reigned for nineteen years; under him Ebroin exercised tyranny. Fredegar, continuation, under the following year.

**673** In Britain, after Egbert, king of Kent, died, his brother Luthere [alternative: Lotharius] reigned for eleven years and four months. In that year Archbishop Theodore of the English convened a useful synod. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*.

[Page 105] **674** About these times Alachis, duke of Tridentum, became elated after gaining a victory over a certain count of Noricum and rebelled against his king Pertharich. But through the king’s son Chunibert he was repeatedly reconciled and advanced in honors. Paul the Deacon; another source, under 680.

**675** In Britain, Vulfhere, king of the Mercians, died; his brother Edilred succeeded him and reigned for thirty-five years. In the following year he ravaged Kent. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, under 677.

**676** In Rome, after Adeodatus died, Pope Donus, the eightieth pope, was installed after four months and occupied the see for one year and five months. Among other good works, he paved the portico of Saint Peter with marble. That summer an immense force of thunder and rain afflicted the people. Legumes, which could not be gathered because of the rain, sprouted again in some places and were brought to maturity. A comet was seen for three months, and a great pestilence among the people followed in the East. Anastasius; Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, under 678.

**677** In Italy, King Pertharich of the Lombards made his son Chunibert his associate in the kingdom; together with him he afterward reigned for ten years. — The Church of Ravenna, which had separated from the Roman Church by usurping autocephaly for itself, submitted again to Pope Donus. Anastasius.

**678** In Rome, after Donus died, Pope Agatho, the eighty-first pope, was ordained after two months and occupied the see for two years and six months. He was a gentle and kindly man. Anastasius. — Wilfrid, bishop of the English, driven from his see by King Egbert, converted many to the Lord by preaching during his pilgrimage. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*.

**679** Constantine Augustus sent an embassy to Rome and requested that, by apostolic authority, a synod be held at Constantinople for the refutation of the heretics. Pope Agatho convened a synod of 120 bishops at Rome and condemned the heretics who taught that there was one operation in Christ. Bede, *Chronicle*; another source, under 680.

[Column 0147A] **680** A lunar eclipse [Note: [Column 0147D] Namely, on 17 June and 11 December] and a great mortality occurred at Rome during the summer months. Anastasius. — Pope Agatho sent envoys to Constantinople in the ninth indiction. [Note: [Column 0147D] The papal envoys reached Constantinople on 10 November, when the ninth indiction was already being counted; the synod was held during that indiction, extending through this and the following year.] Received and treated honorably by the Emperor, they presided over the Sixth Ecumenical Council of 150 bishops and, after the heretics who asserted one will and one operation in Christ had been reasonably convicted, condemned them. Anastasius. — Archbishop Theodore of the English likewise convened a synod. [Note: [Column 0147D] Labbe presents the canons of this synod in his collection, volume VI, p. 1875. See Spelmann, *English Councils*, volume I, p. 168.] Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*.

**681** At Constantinople, the Sixth Council, consisting of 150 bishops, was held in the ninth indiction, in February, and Macarius of Antioch and the followers of his error were condemned. After their condemnation, suddenly very many spiders’ webs fell in the basilica before everyone, signifying that the heretical trifles had been cast down. Anastasius.

**682** In Rome, after Pope Agatho died, the bishopric remained vacant for one year and seven months. [Note: [Column 0148D] Pagius proves that the see of Leo II was vacant for only seven months and assigns both Agatho’s death and Leo II’s ordination to the same year, 682.] Anastasius.

**683** In Rome, Leo II, the eighty-second pope, occupied the see for nearly eleven months. He was in every respect a most learned, eloquent, and pious man. He restored, dedicated, and adorned several churches; issued his own decrees; and wrote, taught, and established many things with great distinction. Anastasius. — In this year, on 16 April, during Good Friday, the moon suffered an eclipse for nearly the entire night. [Note: [Column 0148D] Easter fell on 19 April that year, and Good Friday on 18 April; therefore the eclipse occurred on the night following 17 April, although elsewhere it is recorded as having occurred on 16 April.] King Egfrid of the English sent an army and cruelly ravaged the island of Ireland without cause. Saint Cuthbert [alternative: Cudberht], bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne [alternative: Lindufarne], was ordained; he adorned Britain with very many virtues. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*.

**684** In Rome, after Leo died, the bishopric remained vacant for nearly one year. After him Benedict II, the eighty-third pope, occupied the see for ten months. He was a learned man, pious and beneficent toward all, restoring and embellishing churches and constantly pursuing good works. Anastasius. — Comets appeared, and Mount Bobius in Campania, spewing flames beyond measure, burned the surrounding areas. Paul the Deacon. — In Britain, King Egfrid, against the advice of Saint Cuthbert, rashly attacked the Picts in war. He was defeated and killed by them; Aldfrid, a pious and prudent king, succeeded him and reigned for nineteen years. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*.

**685** In Rome, after Benedict died following Easter, Pope John V, the eighty-fourth pope, occupied the see for one year after an interval of more than two months. He too was a learned and discerning man; previously he had been archdeacon and an envoy of the Apostolic See at the Sixth Synod. Anastasius. — At Constantinople, after Emperor Constantine died, his son Justinian reigned for ten years. Tainted by heresy, he was hostile and harmful to the orthodox. When the Saracens were devastating many provinces, he made peace with them for ten years by giving them a large sum of money. Paul the Deacon. — In Britain, Luthere, king of Kent, died. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*.

**686** In Rome, after John died, Pope Conon, the eighty-fifth pope, was ordained after three months and occupied the see for eleven months. He was advanced in age, supremely innocent, and of holy simplicity. When the clergy and people were divided in the election of two priests, he was finally chosen by both sides as a third candidate. Anastasius. — In Britain, Saint John was ordained bishop of the Church of Hexham and became renowned for many virtues. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*.

**687** In Rome, after Conon died, Pope Sergius, the eighty-sixth pope, occupied the see for thirteen years and nearly nine months after an interval of almost three months. Here too, when the factions were divided over the election of two candidates, a third was elected by God’s will. Strong in the Catholic faith, he suffered persecution from the Emperor Justinian. He built, restored, adorned, and endowed many churches; he was a holy man, intent upon every good work. Anastasius. — In Italy, after Pertharich, king of the Lombards, died, his son Cunibert, a vigorous, gentle, and good king, reigned for twelve years. Paul the Deacon, under 686.

688 Ceadwald, king of the West Saxons, converted to the faith of Christ, came to Rome, and on Holy Saturday of Easter was baptized by Pope Sergius and called Peter. He died there in his white baptismal robes, was buried by the supreme pontiff with the highest honors, and was commemorated with an epitaph. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, under 689. — In the Frankish kingdom, Pippin, son of Ansgisus, son of Saint Arnulf, defeated Theoderic, son of King Louis, in battle at Testri; having obtained control of the Frankish kingdom, he ruled as duke and mayor of the palace for twenty-seven years, while Louis, Childebert, and Dagobert meanwhile possessed the royal title but not the authority. Continuation of Fredegar, under 687. [Col. 0149B] Annals of Metz.

689 Around this time in Italy, the duke Alachis seized tyrannical power. After occupying Pavia, and while King Cunibert, because he was inferior in the number of his soldiers, fortified himself on the island of Comacina, Alachis cruelly pursued everyone, especially clerics. Paul the Deacon, under 690.

690 The venerable Theodore, archbishop of the English, died in the twenty-third year after his arrival in Britain, and in the eighty-eighth year of his age. Among his other good works, he composed a penitential book with great discernment. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*.

691 Among the Franks, King Theoderic died in the nineteenth year of his reign. In his place his son Louis, still a child, was made king in name only by Pippin and the Franks; he reigned for two years. [Col. 0149C] [Note: Fredegar’s continuation correctly gives four years, since he died in 695.] Continuation of Fredegar; Annals of Metz.

692 At this time Cunibert, king of the Lombards, having recovered his kingdom by the grace of God, defeated and killed the tyrant Alachis in accordance with everyone’s wishes, and thereafter ruled his people in the desired peace. Paul the Deacon, under 690.

693 Among the Franks, after Louis his brother Childebert obtained the royal title and reigned for seventeen years. Continuation of Fredegar, under 695. Annals of Metz.

694 In these days two English priests, the black Hewald and the white Hewald, inflamed with zeal for the divine word, were preaching to the Saxons when they were crowned with martyrdom by certain peasants and glorified by divine miracles. They were buried at Cologne by Pippin. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*.

695 At Constantinople, the heretical emperor Justinian, ill-treated by Leo, Tiberius, and other conspirators, was expelled from the kingdom after his nose had been cut off. He withdrew as an exile to Pontus, while Leo seized the imperial power and held it for three years. Paul the Deacon. — The holy man Wilibrord was ordained archbishop by Pope Sergius and called Clement. Preaching the word of life to the Frisian people, he benefited very many by bringing them to salvation. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, under 690; Alcuin.

696 In the province of Britain, a certain Northumbrian named Truthelinus was carried away bodily and, after terrifying and joyful visions, restored to life. Thereafter he led a most rigorous and holy life. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*. — At this time Pope Sergius, by revelation from the Lord, found a chest containing a portion of the Lord’s cross. [Col. 0150B] Anastasius; Bede’s *Chronicle*.

697 In Britain, Saint Cuthbert, who had been an anchorite and then became a bishop, departed to the Lord after many miracles. The priest Bede composed his life both in prose and in hexameter verse. Bede’s *Chronicle*. — In that same year Queen Ostric [variant: Ostrida] was killed by her own people. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*.

698 At Constantinople, Tiberius, seizing the imperial power, kept the emperor Leo in prison for seven years, during which Tiberius himself reigned after him. Paul the Deacon.

699 At this time a synod was held at Aquileia, and certain people who had refused to accept the Fifth Ecumenical Council were corrected by Pope Sergius. Bede’s *Chronicle* [Col. 0150C], under 698.

700 In Italy, the strong and devout Lombard king Cunibert, dying, left the kingdom to his little son Luitpert and appointed as his guardian Asprand, a prudent and vigorous man. But after eight months the duke Raginbert, son of the former king Gotabert [variant: Godebert], defeated Luitpert and his supporters in battle and usurped the kingdom, though he died that same year. His son Haribert [variant: Aripert] then held the kingdom received from his father for nearly twelve years. He again defeated Luitpert and his followers in battle, put them to flight, captured him, and killed him. Paul the Deacon.

[Col. 0151A] 701 At Rome, after Sergius died, John VI, the eighty-seventh pope, held office for three years and two months. Anastasius.

702 In Italy, at this time, when Haribert, after defeating and subduing the remaining enemies, was aggressively pursuing Asprand, Asprand, unequal in strength, first fled to Ravenna and then to Theodebert, duke of Bavaria, and remained there for nine years. Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 22.

703 The English priest Bede, a learned man, brought his *Shorter Chronicle, On Times*, down to this point. [Note: His book is entitled *On Times*.] — At this time, when Gisulf, duke of Benevento, was ravaging Campania and carrying away captives, and no one resisted him, he accepted gifts from Pope John, who requested peace, returned the captives, and made peace. Paul the Deacon; Anastasius.

704 In Britain, Edilred, king of the Mercians, handed over his kingdom to Coenred and himself became a monk. [Col. 0151B] Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*.

705 At Constantinople, the emperor Justinian, recovering the empire with the help of Terbel, king of the Bulgarians, killed Leo and Tiberius, usurpers of the empire, along with many others. He sent the blinded patriarch Gallicinus [variant: Gallinicus] to Rome and promoted in his place the abbot Cyrus, who had supported him while he was an exile in Pontus. It is said of this emperor that whenever he wiped away the discharge flowing from his mutilated nose, he almost always ordered one of his enemies to be killed. Paul the Deacon. — At Rome, Pope John VII, the eighty-eighth pope, held office for two years and nearly eight months; he was eloquent, learned, and well educated. Anastasius. — In Britain, Aldfrid, king of the Northumbrians, a devout and prudent man, died, and his son Osred reigned in his place for eleven years. The holy bishop Heddi of the West Saxons died; Daniel and Aldhelm were made bishops in his place. [Col. 0151C] Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*.

706 Pope John built and adorned an oratory of Saint Mary at Saint Peter’s and furnished several churches with ornaments. Bede’s *Chronicle*.

707 At this time Haribert, king of the Lombards, returned to Saint Peter and Pope John the possession of the Cottian Alps, formerly seized and held by the Lombards, by means of a privilege written in golden letters. Paul the Deacon.

708 At Rome, Pope Sisinnius, the eighty-ninth pope, was ordained. As his gout grew worse, he survived for only twenty days. After him Pope Constantine, the ninetieth pope, was appointed and held office for seven years and fifteen days. He was a very gentle and devout man, devoted to and steadfast in every good pursuit. Anastasius. — The bishop Aldhelm, a learned and eloquent man, witty in both prose and verse, died. Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century III, part I; Bollandists, 25 May.

709 Coenred, king of the Mercians, and with him Offa, a royal youth, son of King Sigher, abandoned their kingdoms, came to Rome, and there became monks. Not long afterward they ended their mortal lives. Bede, *Epitome*. — The venerable bishop Wilfrid died in the forty-fifth year of his episcopate, after exiles and many hardships; Acca succeeded him in the bishopric of Hagustald. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*; Mabillon, cited above; Bollandists, 24 April.

710 The venerable Adrian, abbot, died in the forty-first year from the time when he had been sent to Britain by Pope Vitalian with Archbishop Theodore. King Childebert of the Franks, son of Theoderic, died in the seventeenth year of his reign; Dagobert, his son, succeeded him for five years. Continuation of Fredegar; Annals of Metz, under the following year.

[Page 113] 711 At Constantinople, after becoming emperor, Philippicus killed the emperor Justinian and reigned for one year and six months, persecuting Catholics and favoring heretics. Bede’s *Chronicle*; Paul the Deacon.

[Col. 0152C] 712 Haribert, king of the Lombards, died; after him Luitprand [Note: According to Paul the Deacon, Ansprand succeeded Haribert, and when Ansprand died that same year, his son Luitprand succeeded him.] Paul the Deacon.

713 At Constantinople, Anastasius deprived Philippicus of his sight and his kingdom, and himself reigned for three years. Paul the Deacon.

714 The emperor Anastasius, sending a letter to Pope Constantine, declared himself a supporter of the Catholic faith. Bede’s *Chronicle*. — Pippin, son of Ansgisus and grandson of Saint Arnulf, mayor of the palace and duke of the Franks, died in the twenty-seventh year of his rule. [Col. 0153A] [Note: In this year the Annals of Fulda begin with Charles Martel; Hermann drew much of his material from them and also inserted events concerning his own homeland, as well as much from Hepidanus, who begins his brief annals with 708.] His son Charles, born to his secondary wife [Note: Pippin, around 688, repudiated Plectrudis, his legitimate wife, and married Alpaida. Continuation of Fredegar; Mabillon, *Annals*, book XVII, chapter 70], reigned in his place for twenty-seven years. Annals of Fulda. — At Rome, after Pope Constantine died, Gregory II held office for fifteen years and nine months. [Note: Constantine died in the following year, which is also the year in which Bernold records his death.] Anastasius.

715 Charles, freed by divine aid from the custody into which Plectrudis, the widow of his father, had cast him, fought against Radbod, king of the Frisians, with losses to his army. Annals of Fulda, under this and the following years. — Dagobert the Younger, son of Childebert and king of the Franks, died. Chilperic, also called Daniel [Note: He was the son of King Childeric, who was killed in 672; in the meantime he had remained concealed in a monastery. Mabillon, third century, part III, p. 564], succeeded him. Continuation of Fredegar; Annals of Metz.

[Page 114] 716 The holy man Egbert, an Englishman by birth, among his other good works, taught the Scots to celebrate Easter correctly. Bede’s *Chronicle*. — At Constantinople, Theodosius became emperor and reigned for one year. He had the defeated emperor Anastasius ordained a priest. Paul the Deacon. — King Chilperic and Reginfrid [variant: Raginfred], mayor of the palace, were ravaging the regions adjoining the Rhine when they were drawn away by gifts from Plectrudis, the widow of Pippin. Annals of Fulda. — Among the English, Osred, king of the Northumbrians, fell in the eleventh year of his reign. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*.

717 At Rome, the Tiber, overflowing beyond measure, overturned many buildings. Paul the Deacon. — Charles defeated Chilperic and Reginfrid in battle at Vincy on Palm Sunday and put them to flight. [Note: According to the continuation of Fredegar, this battle occurred on a Sunday in Lent, on 21 March; in that year it was not Palm Sunday but Passion Sunday. Annals of Petau.] Annals of Fulda. — At this time Winfrid, later also called Boniface, an Englishman by birth, preached the word of salvation to the peoples of Germany by the authority of Pope Gregory. [Col. 0153C] Annals of Fulda; Othlon; Pagi, under 716.

[Col. 0154A] 718 At Constantinople, the emperor Leo reigned for nine years. During his reign the Saracens, who had already overrun many provinces, besieged the city itself for three years, but were finally driven back by divine aid through hunger, pestilence, the sword, and shipwreck. Paul the Deacon, elsewhere under 717. — Charles, having recovered the treasures of his father from Plectrudis, appointed a certain Chlothar king for himself [Note: This occurred in 717, but the victory over Chilperic occurred in 719. This Chlothar is said to have descended from the line of Dagobert II. See the *Brief Register of the Kings of the Franks*], and, renewing the battle, put Chilperic and Reginfrid to flight, together with Duke Eudo of Aquitaine, who was bringing them aid. Continuation of Fredegar; Annals of Fulda, under 717.

[Page 115] 719 Chilperic, who had fled to Eudo, was handed over by Eudo to Charles, who demanded him, and King Clotarius died. Annals of Fulda and Metz, under 719 and 720. — Saint Boniface, ordained archbishop of Mainz by Pope Gregory [Note: Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century III, part II, assigns this ordination to 722; but Gregory’s own letter, dated in the sixth indiction, makes it clear that it occurred in 723, and that Boniface was then ordained not for the church of Mainz but as a bishop not yet attached to any particular see], benefited many peoples and nations by word and example. Annals of Fulda.

720 After Chilperic died, Theoderic, son of Dagobert, was appointed king by Charles. Annals of Fulda. — Saint Othmar, appointed the first abbot of the cell of Saint Gall, established monastic life there and governed it nobly for forty years. Hepidanus; Walafrid, *Life*.

721 Charles likewise defeated Reginfrid, captured the city of Angers by force, and overcame the Saxons in war. Annals of Fulda, under 724. — Saint John, bishop of Hagustald, died. Bede.

722 Charles subdued Alamannia and Bavaria by arms. Annals of Fulda, under 725.

723 The Alamanni and Bavarians again rebelled against Charles. Annals of Fulda; Fredegar, under 728 and 730.

[Col. 0154C] 724 Charles crossed the Loire and ravaged Aquitaine; he defeated Duke Eudo in battle and put him to flight. Annals of Fulda [Col. 0155A], p. 31. — Saint Pirmin, abbot and chorepiscopus [Note: That is, a regional bishop, called “of Meltis” in his *Life*, from the castle of Melteshem near Gemünd in the duchy of Zweibrücken, where he ended his life. Gerbert, *Disquisitions on Alemannic Liturgy*, vol. I, p. 37; *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, p. 75], was brought to Charles by the princes Berthold and Nebi [Page 116]. Charles appointed him head of the island of Reichenau [Note: This island was first called Sintlacis Augia after its possessor, and then Augia dives (“rich island”) because of its extensive donations.]. From there he drove away snakes and established monastic life there [Note: A later hand added “for three years,” whereas Bernold has “in the third year,” namely, from Saint Pirmin’s entry into Alamannia around 722. Although elsewhere Hermann makes it certain that Pirmin remained at Reichenau for only three years, from 724 to 727, after which he was expelled by Theodebald, Bouquet may seem to have understood otherwise, since in his excerpts from Hermann (vol. III of the collection, p. 330) he altered the chronology and placed 733 in the margin for Pirmin’s expulsion. But the chronological index prefixed to this volume shows that this alteration of the years concerns only the deeds of Charles Martel: the events relating to Pirmin and his successor Eton or Hetton are dated to the same years as in Hermann. The learned Grandidier failed to notice this and thought that Bouquet had placed the beginning of the episcopate of the said Hetton at Strasbourg in 739 (*History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. I, p. 270), although this Addas is already mentioned in a letter of Gregory III (Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. IV, p. 42, under 738). The Theodebald mentioned here was the son of Gothefrid, duke of the Alamanni, who died in 709—not, as Hepidanus writes in his *Annals*, the son of Luitfrid or Lantfrid. Whether he expelled Pirmin from Reichenau by his own authority or by that of Landfrid, then duke, who died in 730 according to Hermann, is disputed among writers. Cointius, in his *Frankish Annals*, assigns the event to 730, when Theodebald succeeded the deceased Lantfrid in the duchy and in hostility toward Charles Martel; consequently he gives Pirmin six years of governance and Hetton only four. But Cointius would have needed other arguments to act against the common view of Hermann and others. Theodebald could have conspired with Lantfrid, who was then rebelling against Charles, even if he was not yet duke, except insofar as he was the duke’s son. It may perhaps be in this sense that Berthold and Nebi, whom others incorrectly call Vehi, are called “princes” by Hermann, as rulers over some district of Alamannia. Berthold is certainly called “the most noble duke of the Alamanni” by Berno in the *Life of Saint Meginrad* (Mabillon, fourth century, part II). Nebi, as Thegan records in his *Life of Louis the Pious*, chapter 2, was the son of Houching, who likewise had Gothefrid the duke as his father. Thus Nebi was Theodebald’s cousin: Nebi brought Pirmin into Reichenau, while Theodebald expelled him. Nebi is also called duke by Walafrid in *Miracles of Saint Gall*, book II, chapter 2.] Hepidanus.

725 The Saracens, summoned by Eudo to his aid, ravaged Gaul with plunder and fire. Annals of Fulda, under 732.

726 Charles, having joined battle, victoriously struck down a great multitude of Saracens together with their king. Annals of Fulda, under 732.

[Page 117] 727 Charles, marching into Burgundy, subjected it to himself. Annals of Fulda, under 733. — Saint Pirmin, expelled from Reichenau through hostility toward Charles by Theodebald, son of the duke Gothefrid, appointed Eton abbot in his place [Col. 0155B] and himself went to Alsace to establish other monasteries. Fragment of an anonymous writer in Urstisius, part II, p. 76.

728 Duke Eudo died, and Charles recovered Aquitaine without a battle. Annals of Fulda, under 735.

729 Charles invaded Frisia, defeated and killed Duke Poppo in battle, burned the temples, and returned victorious. Annals of Fulda, under 733 and following. — Saint Egbert, an English priest, died at the age of ninety on Easter Day, that is, 24 April. See his *Life*, in Mabillon’s *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century III, part I.

730 The Saracens, having gathered an army, captured the city of Avignon and devastated the surrounding regions; elsewhere under 737. — Duke Lantfrid [Note: This is the same Lantfrid whom Charles defeated in 725 and in the present year, as Alberic the monk testifies in his *Chronicle* in Leibniz’s historical additions. Others call him Luitfrid, son of Duke Adalbert.] of Alamannia died. Annals of Nazarus, under this year.

731 Charles, having defeated and slaughtered the Saracens, recovered Avignon after storming it by force. Annals of Fulda; elsewhere under 739. — The priest and monk Bede, an Englishman by birth and a remarkable teacher, died. Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis S. Benedicti*, century III, part I. At Rome, Pope Gregory III held office for ten years and nine months. Anastasius. — Three monasteries—Altaha, Morbach, and Favarias—were supplied with monks from Reichenau: twelve brothers were assigned to each, and the same number remained at Reichenau.

[Page 118] 732 Charles invaded Gothia and besieged the Saracen king, who was shut up at Narbonne. Frankish Annals, elsewhere under 737. — Eton, abbot of Reichenau, was exiled by Theodebald, because of his hostility toward Charles, to Uri [Note: A district or valley in the larger Alamannic district of Thurgau in Switzerland, today the canton of Uri], but in that same year, after Theodebald was expelled, Charles restored him.

733 The Saracen army arriving from Spain at Narbonne was annihilated by Charles in a battle. Frankish Annals, under 737.

734 The Saracens were again defeated by Charles and, while fleeing, perished in a shipwreck. Frankish Annals, under 739. — After seven years, Eton [Note: Here he is called Adda in Letter 129 of Gregory III among the Bonifacian letters, and Eddanus in the preface to the German council of 742: *German Councils*, vol. I, p. 48.] of Reichenau left Keba as his successor; he himself was promoted by Charles as bishop of the church of Strasbourg and not long afterward built a monastery bearing his name, namely Ethenheim [Note: In the marches of Breisgau and Ortenau at the foot of the Black Forest. *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, pp. 56 ff.].

735 Charles likewise returned victorious, after defeating and crushing the Saracens, with great booty and a multitude of captives. Frankish Annals, under 739.

736 Charles marched against the Goths, destroyed some of their cities and fortresses, and returned victorious. Frankish Annals, under 737. — Bishop Audoin died [Note: Here Hermann begins the succession of the bishops of Constance. In *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 894, Bishop Radottus is placed between Audoin and Ernfrid; he is mentioned in a letter of Gregory III to Boniface in 738.]. After Keba of Reichenau died two years later, the monk Ernfred became abbot of Reichenau and bishop of Constance, and governed for ten years.

737 Charles made the defeated Saxons tributaries. Annals of Fulda of Metz, under 738.

[Page 119] 738 Charles marched into Provence and put to flight Duke Maurontus, who had invited the Saracens. Annals of Fulda, under 739.

739 Charles subjected all Provence to his rule. Annals of Fulda; Nazarus.

740 After the enemies all around had been defeated, Charles brought peace and quiet to the Frankish kingdom. Annals of Fulda.

[Col. 0158A] 741 At Rome, Pope Zacharias held office for ten years and four months. Anastasius. — After accomplishing many brave deeds, Charles died at Quierzy and was buried at Saint-Denis. His sons, having divided the Frankish kingdom between them, governed as mayors of the palace: Carloman for six years and Pippin for ten. Annals of Fulda; continuation of Fredegar, chapter 110.

742 Carloman and Pippin quickly suppressed Hunald of Aquitaine and Theodebald, duke of Swabia, when they attempted to rebel. Annals of Fulda.

743 The same brothers defeated Duke Odilo of Bavaria in battle when he rebelled against them. Annals of Fulda.

744 Carloman made peace with Duke Odilo. The monastery of Fulda was founded in the Bochonia forest by Saint Boniface, archbishop. Annals of Fulda.

[Col. 0158B] 745 Carloman ravaged Saxony, which had rebelled, together with his brother. He captured the fortress of Hoseburg [Note: Authors give various forms of this fortress’s name. Most think it was Osnabrück; others understand it as the fortress of Hochsiburg in Minden on the Weser. Fabricius, *Origins of Saxony*, book I]. Annals of Fulda, elsewhere under 743.

746 Carloman suppressed the Alamanni, who were again attempting to rebel. Annals of Fulda, under 745. — Saint Boniface, with Carloman’s approval and by the authority of Pope Zacharias, established two bishoprics in his province: the bishopric of Würzburg, appointing Saint Burchard as its first bishop, and that of Eichstätt, appointing Saint Willibald as its first bishop—both men his fellow countrymen [Note: The establishment of these bishoprics was somewhat earlier, since Burchard and Willibald had already attended the German synod celebrated by Saint Boniface on 21 April 742.] Annals of Fulda. — Sidonius, a monk of Reichenau, its fifth abbot, became bishop of Constance and governed for thirteen years [Note: Pistorius, on the basis of an ancient manuscript, places this under 748, as does the Gottwic manuscript. That is correct if Ratold succeeded Ernfrid in 738. But where then are Sidonius’s thirteen years of rule, since he had already died in 759? The dates are correct if, with the Gottwic manuscript, his death is assigned to 761.] He also claimed the cell of Saint Gall and consented, with wicked rulers, to the condemnation of Saint Othmar the abbot. [Col. 0158C] Hepidanus.

[Col. 0159A] 747 Carloman, touched by divine love, renounced the world and, going to Rome, changed his clothing and became a monk at the monastery of Cassino, at Saint Benedict’s [Note: The Gottwic manuscript says that this happened on Mount Soracte, as does Regino; but shortly afterward he went from there to Cassino]. Annals of Fulda.

748 Gripho, Pippin’s half-brother, aspiring to tyrannical power, withdrew to the Saxons; when Pippin arrived and Gripho refused to make peace with him, he fled to Bavaria. Annals of Fulda.

749 Pippin went to Bavaria and appointed Tassilo, the son of his sister Hiltrudis, duke there. Gripho and Lantfrid were taken away from that region [Note: Schoepflin and others assert that this Lantfrid was the son of the first Lantfrid, who died in 730, and was duke of Alamannia. See *Illustrated Alsace*, p. 751; Eccard, *Frankish Affairs*, vol. I, p. 487; Calles, *Annals*, vol. II, p. 310]. Annals of Fulda; continuation of Fredegar.

750 Pippin gave Gripho twelve counties in the regions of Neustria, but Gripho, again growing distrustful, fled to Duke Waifarius of Aquitaine. Annals of Fulda, under 749.

751 Pippin, having sent envoys to Rome [Note: Cointius, for serious reasons, considers this embassy at least suspect in authenticity, since it was derived from Einhard’s account, which was excessively partial to Pippin, into other annals; he likewise questions the coronation of Pippin by Saint Boniface. See Pagi, under 751], consulted Pope Zacharias concerning the kingdom of the Franks and its worthless Merovingian kings, who ruled in name only. Annals of Fulda. — Lantfrid died. Annals of Nazarus.

[Page 121] 752 By the authority of Pope Zacharias and, not long afterward, of Stephen, who succeeded him in the pontificate for six years, King Childeric, the last of the Merovingians, was deposed and tonsured. Pippin was elected king of the Franks and anointed and consecrated at Soissons by Saint Boniface, archbishop; he reigned for seventeen years. Annals of Fulda; *Deeds of the Kings of the Franks*. — Audogarius, first founder and abbot of the monastery of Kempten, began to inhabit that place [Note: See Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. II, pp. 159, 229].

753 King Pippin again ravaged treacherous Saxony, [Col. 0159C] and there Hildigarius, archbishop of Cologne, was killed. Annals of Fulda. — When Gripho was preparing to march to Italy, Pippin’s counts killed him in the valley of Maurienne. The same source. — Pope Stephen came to Francia to King Pippin seeking aid against Haistulf, king of the Lombards, and at Paris anointed his sons Charles and Carloman as kings [Note: This coronation took place the following year, on 5 August, at Saint-Denis. Anonymous writer in Henschen, *Preliminary Study*, II, to volume III of March, chapter 4, no. 35]. Annals of Fulda of Metz.

754 Saint Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, was preaching the gospel among the Frisians when they crowned him with martyrdom in the thirty-sixth year of his episcopate. He was buried at the monastery of Fulda; Lullus succeeded him as archbishop and governed for thirty-two years. Annals of Fulda, under 755. — Carloman, Pippin’s brother, died at Lyons when he was coming to Pippin to dissuade him from the Italian expedition. Elsewhere under 754. — Pippin marched into Italy with an army and compelled the defeated King Haistulf, besieged at Pavia, to give hostages and to return by oath the possessions of Saint Peter. Anastasius; continuation of Fredegar, appendix. — Pope Stephen returned to Rome with Pippin’s brother Jerome as his guide. Annals of Fulda.

[Page 122] 755 Haistulf, disregarding his oath, besieged Rome and devastated everything around it with sword and fire. For this reason the pope sent envoys by sea to Pippin to complain and again implore aid. Annals of Fulda.

756 King Pippin, marching into Italy for a second time, besieged Haistulf, shut up at Pavia, and compelled him, through his envoy Folrad, to return to Saint Peter and the lord pope Ravenna, the Pentapolis, and the other territories he had seized. Annals of Fulda; continuation of Fredegar, under the preceding year.

757 King Haistulf died after falling from his horse while hunting; Desiderius succeeded him [Note: Paul the Deacon records Haistulf’s death in the previous year, as does the Gottwic manuscript]. The emperor Constantine sent King Pippin, among other gifts, an organ. Annals of Fulda.

[Col. 0160C] 758 Pippin, having again defeated the Saxons, imposed upon them an annual tribute of three hundred horses. Annals of Fulda. — At Rome, Paul succeeded Pope Stephen and held office for ten years. Anastasius, under 757; likewise the Gottwic manuscript.

[Col. 0161A] 759 Waifarius, exercising tyrannical power in Aquitaine, oppressed churches and carried out plundering and the burning of villages. Annals of Fulda, under this year; elsewhere under the following year. — Saint Othmar the abbot, unjustly condemned with the consent of Sidonius, bishop, by Warinus and Rudhardus [Note: Goldastus says that these men were officials of the royal chamber, on the authority of Ekkehard’s *On the Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, chapter 1; according to Walafrid in the *Life of Saint Othmar*, they then administered the affairs of all Alamannia. See Gerbert, *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, pp. 58 ff.], and exiled to the Rhine island of Stein, departed to the Lord [Note: See Iso, *On the Miracles of Saint Othmar*, book I, chapter 5]. When Bishop and Abbot Sidonius had invaded his abbey with reckless audacity, he was struck by a flux of the bowels before the altar of Saint Gall and died [Note: Walafrid writes that Sidonius was indeed struck in this way, but not there; he died at Reichenau in 761. According to Iso, in the passage cited, Saint Othmar’s death belongs to 760. See under 720]. John, also a monk of Reichenau, then received the episcopate and both abbeys and governed for twenty-one years. He was the first to obtain from Pope Hadrian a privilege of the Roman see for Reichenau. Hepidanus, under 758; Gottwic manuscript, under 760.

760 Pippin invaded Aquitaine, or Gascony, and compelled Waifarius to return by oath what he had unjustly seized. Annals of Fulda.

761 Waifarius, setting his oaths aside, ravaged everything he could reach as far as Chalon with sword, plunder, and fire. Annals of Fulda.

762 Pippin, marching again into Aquitaine with his son Charles, captured many cities and subdued many who rebelled against him. Annals of Fulda.

763 Duke Tassilo withdrew from the army and returned to Bavaria. Annals of Fulda.

764 A winter severe with cold and unusually long occurred in this year. Pippin held a great assembly at Quierzy [Note: Regino has an assembly at Worms, which was also of this kind. See *German Councils*, vol. I, p. 123, and the *Life of Saint Chrodegang*].

765 Roudgangus [variants: Hruodhgangus or Chrodegangus], archbishop of Metz [Note: Anastasius writes that he had already been ordained in Gaul in 753, while Pope Stephen II was present there, and had received the use of the pallium. Concerning this translation, see Baronius under 764 and Pagi, who thinks it should be assigned to this year], obtained from Pope Paul the bodies of Saints Gorgonius, Nabor, and Nazarius. Annals of Fulda; Notker, *On the Martyrs*.

766 The body of Saint Gorgonius was placed in the monastery of Gorze [variant: Gorzia], that of Saint Nabor in Novacella, and that of Saint Nazarius in Lorsch [Note: An anonymous monk of the monastery formerly known as Gorze in Lorraine wrote the history of this translation; it can be read in Mabillon, third century, part II, p. 204. Novacella was the monastery of Hilaire, on the Moselle, founded by Saint Fridolin; in ancient documents it is also called Saint Nabor’s. Likewise Lorsch is Saint Nazarius’s, and Gorze is Saint Gorgonius’s.] Annals of Fulda; elsewhere under the preceding year.

767 Pippin captured the city of Limoges in Aquitaine after storming it. Annals of Fulda. — At Rome, Pope Paul died, and Stephen succeeded him for four years.

768 Pippin, returning victorious after Waifarius had been killed and Aquitaine subdued, died at Paris on 24 September and was buried there in the fifty-fourth year of his age. His sons divided the kingdom: Charles the Great reigned for forty-six years and Carloman for four. Annals of Fulda. [Note: After 768, the Murensian and Engelberg manuscripts insert the genealogy of Saint Arnulf, as we have prefixed it to Hermann’s work.]

769 Charles and Carloman captured Hunold, duke of Aquitaine, after defeating him in war. Annals of Fulda. — The body of Saint Othmar the abbot, found incorrupt after ten years on the island where he had died, was transferred to the monastery of Saint Gall. Hepidanus, under 768; elsewhere under 770; Walafrid Strabo.

770 Charles married the daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, who was brought to him by his mother Bertha, but he immediately repudiated her. Annals of Fulda; Einhard, in his *Life of Charles*.
