771 King Carloman died and was buried at Rheims. Charles summoned a great assembly [Note: This was the assembly of the princes at Valenciennes]. Einhard; Annals of Metz; Frankish Annals.

772 Charles marched against the Saxons, captured the fortress of Eresburg [Note: Others call it Herisburg in Westphalia. See Meibom, *On the Saxon Irminsul*, vol. III of *German Affairs*], destroyed their idol called Irminsul, and, when his army was suffering from thirst, deserved to refresh it when God miraculously supplied water in a certain dry streambed. Having received twelve hostages in exchange for peace, he returned. Annals of Fulda. — At Rome, after Stephen, Pope Hadrian held office for twenty-four years.

773 Charles, asked by Pope Hadrian to defend the possessions of Saint Peter, marched into Italy. Having forcibly occupied the Alpine passes, he besieged Desiderius, who was fleeing, at Pavia. He himself went to Rome to pray and celebrated Easter there [Note: This last event belongs to the following year]. Annals of Fulda.

774 The Lombards, together with their king Desiderius, surrendered to Charles, 205 years after they had entered Italy with King Alboin. Charles took possession of their kingdom and treasures, carried away the king with his wife, and returned victorious. Annals of Fulda of Metz.

The Saxons, breaking their treaty, marched against the Hessians; but, God forbidding it, they were unable to burn the church at Fritzlar, which had been dedicated by Saint Boniface. Elsewhere under the preceding year. — The bodies of Saints Gordian and Epimachus were transferred from Rome to Alamannia [Note: The Gottwic manuscript identifies the place as Kempten. See the Bollandists, vol. II of May, under 10 May, and Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. II, pp. 228 ff.; also vol. IV, p. 448]. — The church of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch was dedicated. Annals of Fulda.

775 Charles ravaged the lands of the Saxons far and wide and defeated them in two battles with great slaughter. The Lombard Roudgaud [Note: Rotgaud or Rotgausus was duke of Friuli. See Cointius, *Annals*, under this year] aspired to the kingdom of Italy. Annals of Fulda; *Royal Register*.

776 Charles again marched into Italy and killed Roudgaud after defeating him. The Saxons, again in rebellion, attacked Charles’s garrisons in battle. Annals of Fulda.

777 The Saxons, finally subdued after much slaughter, surrendered to Charles and became Christians, handing over themselves and all their possessions should they thereafter violate their pledge. Annals of Fulda.

778 Charles marched into Spain and returned after receiving hostages and subduing the Gascons and the Narbonese [Navarrese]. Annals of Lorsch. — Meanwhile, the Saxons again rebelled under their leader Widukind and ravaged the Frankish territories as far as the Rhine; but when the king’s army pursued them, they were killed in large numbers and fled. Annals of Fulda.

779 Charles again defeated and subdued the Saxons in battle and received hostages. At Fulda, Abbot Sturm died, and Bagolf [variant: Baugulfus] succeeded him. Annals of Fulda; Annals of Lorsch.

780 Charles held an assembly in Saxony and arranged both Saxon and Slavic affairs; he himself then went to Rome to pray. Annals of Fulda.

781 Pippin, Charles’s son, was baptized at Rome by Pope Hadrian and anointed king together with his brother Louis. Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, confirmed his oath of submission to Charles by an oath and hostages. Annals of Fulda. — John, bishop of Constance and abbot, died. Egino succeeded him as bishop for thirty-two years, Peter as abbot of Reichenau for five years, and Roudpert as abbot of Saint Gall for one year. Hepidanus. — Among other prodigies, crosses appeared on many garments. Blood was said to have flowed from the earth and from the air. Annals of Fulda.

782 Charles, likewise holding an assembly in Saxony, heard envoys of the Danes and Huns. On his return, the Saxons, persuaded by Widukind, attacked and killed the envoys whom Charles had sent with an army against the Slavs, not without suffering heavy losses themselves. In revenge for this, Charles ordered four thousand five hundred Saxons to be beheaded. *Annals of Fulda; Metz.*---

At Saint Gall, Abbot Waldo held office for one year and six months. Hepidanus.

783 Queen Hildegard, wife of Charles, died on 30 April [Note: [Col. 0164D] See the Bollandists, 30 April], and his mother Bertrada on 12 July. Charles, likewise engaging the Saxons twice in battle, defeated them with great slaughter, and in that year married Fastrada. *Annals of Fulda and Metz.*

[Col. 0164C] 784 The younger Charles, sent by his father into Saxony, defeated and subdued the Westphalians in battle. *Annals of Fulda.*---At Saint Gall, Abbot Werdo held office for twenty-five years. Hepidanus.

785 The Saxon Widukind, coming to Charles to surrender, was baptized, and all Saxony was subdued. A conspiracy of the Eastern Franks against Charles arose and was suppressed. *Annals of Fulda; Einhard.*

[Col. 0165A] 786 Charles, having sent an army under Autulf [variant: Audulf], subdued the Britons, and himself went to Rome for the sake of prayer. The authors of the conspiracy against Charles were punished with various penalties. Richulf succeeded Lullo as archbishop of Mainz and held office for [supplement: twenty-seven] years. At Reichenau, Waldo was the eighth abbot after Peter and held office for twenty years. *Annals of Fulda.*

787 Charles, marching against Benevento, received hostages. His daughter Ruoddrud [variant: Rotrudis] was betrothed to the emperor Constantine. An eclipse of the sun occurred on 17 September. *Annals of Fulda.*

788 Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, convicted of disloyalty and perjury, was deprived of his duchy by Charles. The army of the Greeks was defeated by the Franks and Italians. Likewise, the Huns, who are also called Avars, were defeated by Charles’s army. *Annals of* [Col. 0165B] *Fulda; Nazarius.*

789 Charles, having gathered a powerful army from every side, crossed the river Elbe and subdued the Slavs called Wilzi, after crushing them in battle. *Annals of Fulda; Einhard.*

790 Charles spent this year quietly at Worms, without war. *Annals of Fulda.*

791 Charles, entering the land of the Huns with his army divided into three parts, devastated it with sword and fire. *Annals of Fulda; Loisel.*

128 792 A synod having been convened at Regensburg, the Felician heresy was condemned. *German Councils*, vol. I, p. 287.---The conspiracy of Pippin against his father Charles was discovered, and its authors were punished. *Annals of Fulda; Einhard.*

793 A battle between the Saracens and the Franks was fought in Gothia, with the Saracens victorious. The Saxons likewise rebelled in their customary manner. *Annals of Fulda.*

[Col. 0166A] 794 At a great synod held at Frankfurt, the Felician heresy was again condemned. *Annals of Lorsch.*---Queen Fastrada died and was buried at Mainz. The pseudo-synod of the Greeks [Note: [Col. 0165D] This refers to the Second Council of Nicaea, held in 787 in support of the veneration of the holy images, and wrongly understood by the Fathers at Frankfurt. *German Councils*, vol. I, p. 288], held in favor of the worship of images, was condemned by the bishops. Charles likewise, after subduing the Saxons, transferred a third part of their men. At this time Alcuin, also called Albinus, was held in esteem by the king and everyone else for his life and learning. *Annals of Fulda; Einhard.*

795 After the Saxons had killed Witzan, duke of the Abodrites, while he was coming to King Charles, they were punished by the devastation of their territory and handed over hostages. The Huns too, having sent envoys, surrendered themselves and their land to him; they promised to become Christians. *Annals of Fulda; Einhard.*

129 796 At Rome, after Pope Adrian’s death [Note: [Col. 0165D] Namely, on 25 December; Leo succeeded him the very next day, so that this still belongs to the end of the preceding year according to the present reckoning], Pope Leo III occupied the see for twenty years. After the princes of the Huns, Cagan and Jugur, had been killed in civil war, Charles gained possession of their land and all its treasures through Eheric, duke of Friuli, and his son Pippin. Their prince Tudun likewise came to him and was baptized with his people, then was honorably sent back to his own country. Saxony, again in revolt, was also invaded and devastated by him. *Annals of Fulda; Einhard.*

797 The city of Barcelona in Spain was restored to Charles. At Constantinople, the emperor Constantine was blinded by the Greeks. Saxony was likewise devastated by Charles as far as the Ocean and received into submission through hostages. *Annals of Fulda; Theophanes.*

798 Charles wintered in Saxony with his army and extensively ravaged the Trans-Elbian Saxons who had seized his envoys; through his envoys, after joining battle, he killed four thousand of them and compelled the rest to ask for peace and give hostages. Alfonso [variant: Hadefuns], king of Galicia, first sent Charles costly gifts and likewise his spoils as a present. Helena [variant: Irene], mother of the blinded emperor Constantine, sent envoys to Charles to seek peace. The Moors began practicing piracy. *Annals of Fulda; Lorsch.*

799 Pope Leo, as the report has it, was attacked by the Romans during the greater litany, had his tongue cut out, and was blinded; but he was rescued by Abbot Wirundus and Winigis, duke of Spoleto, and brought through to Charles in Saxony. Anastasius; Metz.---Eheric, duke of Friuli, was treacherously killed by the people of Liburnia. *Annals of Metz; Einhard.*---

[Col. 0167C] Gerold likewise, prefect of Bavaria, Charles’s pious and religious standard-bearer and counselor, fell while fighting against the Huns and was buried at Reichenau, which he had greatly enriched with gifts and estates.

[Note: [Col. 0167C] The Codex Gottwicense reads: “Gerolt Pussinius, Charles’s standard-bearer, is killed in battle by the Huns.” I suspected that the scribe, deceived by the similarity of the letters, had written *Pussinius* for *piissimus*, which is the reading of the Melk manuscript. Martinierius, however, states in his *Lexicon* that this Gerold, the brother of Queen Hildegard and prefect of Bavaria and Swabia, possessed a fortress on Mount Bussen and called himself count of Bussen, or Bussinius.

This seems to be confirmed by a certain charter of Charles the Great for the monastery of Reichenau, issued at Worms in 811, in which Berthold, count of Bussen, the son of our Gerold, is mentioned. He held the prefectures of Tirmendingen, Oeffingen, Unlingen, Altheim, and other places belonging to them, or situated in that region of Mount Bussen. Queen Hildegard, Gerold’s sister, was the great-granddaughter of Godefrid, duke of the Alemanni, according to Thegan’s *Life of Louis the Pious*, chapter 2 (Duchesne, *Scriptores Francici*, vol. II, p. 274). She was therefore the daughter of Imma, whom Nebi, the prince mentioned above under the year 724, fathered; Nebi had as his father Punching, son of Godefrid, duke of Alemannia. Hence contemporary writers say that she came from the noblest family of the Suevi, although they do not name her father.

That Gerold was her brother is established by the vision of Wetti, the monk of Reichenau, written by Walahfrid Strabo in 825 (*Canisius, Lectures on Antiquity*, vol. II, book II, p. 73), where his epitaph is also found; it records that he was killed on the Kalends of September. An anonymous monk of Saint Gall, in book II of *The Deeds of Charles the Great*, year 14 (Duchesne, vol. II, p. 107; Bouquet, vol. V, p. 104), also presents another brother of Queen Hildegard, Uldaric or Pulderic, though without specifying his rank. Adlzreitter calls him a prince of the Suevi (part I, book VIII, no. 23), increased, according to the cited anonymous author, in wealth and honors in both East and West. Perhaps he is the same as Count Odalrih, noted on 3 February in the Reichenau Necrology. Raderus also names Gerold Pussinius as count from the Reichenau Annals (*Bavaria Sancta*, p. 76). Cointius provides further information about him (*Frankish Annals*, vol. VI, p. 22).

As for the father of Gerold and Hildegard, the writers are entirely silent; all that can be established from them is that he was a very noble Suevian or Alemannian. The only writer known to me who calls him Hildebrand is Bruschius (*Chronology of the German Monasteries*, p. 65), describing him as the most powerful duke of the Suevi, father of Hildegard, wife of Charles the Great, and of Adelinda, who founded the convent of Buchau. Since, according to Hermann under the year 902, this nunnery was first founded by Adelinda at the beginning of the tenth century, that assertion collapses by its own contradiction.]

The Balearic Islands, after the Moors and Saracens had been defeated with Charles’s help, were liberated. Lesser Cismarine Britain was subjected to Charles by Duke Wido. The patriarch of Jerusalem sent Charles relics from the Lord’s tomb, and Azan, prefect of the city called Huesca, sent him the keys of the city and other splendid gifts. *Annals of Fulda; Einhard.*---

[Col. 0168A] At Reichenau, the basilica of Saint Peter was built and dedicated by Egino, bishop of Verona [Note: [Col. 0168C] Mabillon (*Annals*, vol. II, p. 390) consequently suspects that Egino had previously been a monk of Reichenau; Ughellus, however, has nothing about him apart from his name (*Italia Sacra*, vol. V, p. 740). Since Charles the Great was then ruling the Lombards, Egino could easily have been made bishop of Verona by Charles from the Reichenau he loved so much. It remains uncertain whether he came to Reichenau in this year after giving up the episcopate and founded the lower cell there, as D. Wendenthal asserts (*Austria Sacra*, part I, p. 106). Cointius at least testifies that he attended the synod of Friuli in 796 (*Annals*, vol. VI, p. 546). Nevertheless, according to Panvinius, around the year 800 the bishop was already Ratold, or Ratoldus, under whose direction King Pippin of Italy either built or at least restored the basilica of Saint Zeno.]

800 Charles sent splendid gifts to Jerusalem for the holy places. 131 Having arranged garrisons along the shores of the Gallic Sea against pirates, he came to Saint Martin’s for the sake of prayer and there buried his deceased wife Luitgard [Note: [Col. 0168D] The Gottwicense adds the day of her death: 4 June]. From there, proceeding to Rome, he restored Pope Leo to his see after the pope had cleared himself by oath of the accusations brought against him but not proved, and he wintered there, having sent his son Pippin to plunder Campania. *Annals of Fulda; Einhard; Anastasius.*

801 On Christmas Day [Note: [Col. 0168D] This still belonged to the preceding year according to our manner of reckoning], after Pope Leo had placed the crown upon him, Charles was proclaimed the first emperor among the kings of the Franks, Caesar Augustus, while the Romans acclaimed him with praises. Later, according to Roman law, he condemned the perpetrators of violence against Pope Leo to capital punishment; but, at the same pope’s request, he spared their lives and banished them into exile. A great earthquake occurred on 30 April. *Annals of Fulda.*

802 The empress Helena [Irene] of Constantinople again sent envoys to the emperor Charles to seek peace, and he in turn sent Bishop Jesse of Amiens [Col. 0169A] and Count Helingaud to her and confirmed peace through them. Among other gifts, Aaron, king of the Persians, sent the emperor Charles an elephant. The Franks ravaged the Trans-Elbian Saxons. At Fulda, Ratgar succeeded Abbot Baugulf. Paulinus, patriarch of Friuli, or Aquileia, died. *Annals of Fulda.*---Egino, bishop of Verona, also departed this life and was buried at Reichenau in the basilica of his cell [Note: [Col. 0169D] His tomb, with its epitaph, is still visited in the parish church of the lower cell; a reproduction of his sandals is displayed with it in Gerbert’s *Itinerary*. His death is recorded in the Reichenau Necrology on 27 February].

803 At Constantinople, Helena was deposed and Nicephorus [variant: Niciferus] became emperor. He sent back the envoys of Emperor Charles together with his own, and peace was confirmed. Charles received them, made an agreement of peace in writing, and sent them away. *Annals of Fulda.*---The emperor was informed that the blood of the Lord had been found at Mantua; he entrusted Pope Leo with investigating the truth of the matter. Taking this as his occasion, the pope undertook the journey to the emperor and celebrated Christmas with him at Quierzy. *Annals of Fulda*, under 804.

132 804 The lord pope, loaded with great gifts by the emperor, returned through Bavaria. Emperor Charles transferred the Trans-Elbian Saxons, with their women and children, into Francia and gave their districts to the Abodrites. Richpot, archbishop of Trier, died. *Annals of Fulda.*

805 Charles the Younger, sent by his father, subdued Bohemia after killing its king Lech. The emperor restored Caganus to his former honor among the Huns. *Annals of Fulda.*

806 Emperor Charles divided the kingdom among his three sons [Note: [Col. 0169D] Charles’s charter of the division of the kingdoms is to be consulted in Du Chesne and Baluze]. Charles the Younger ravaged the Sorbs and killed their duke Miliduch. An army was likewise sent out and Bohemia was devastated [Col. 0169C]. King Pippin, Charles’s son, drove the Moors from the island of Corsica. *Annals of Fulda.*---At Reichenau, after Abbot Waldo had been transferred to govern the monastery of Saint-Denis, Hetto [Note: [Col. 0169D] From Hepidanus under the year 802. Heitto is regarded as prominent in Charles’s council. Thus he seems already at that time to have been appointed to the see of Basel. The Sammarthani at least infer this from Walahfrid (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 983): Hetto was first a bishop before becoming abbot, as the Gottwicense also records. Hetto, bishop of Basel, succeeded Abbot Waldo] became the ninth abbot and held office for seventeen years.

807 Aaron, king of the Persians, among many other costly gifts, sent the emperor Charles a sufficiently ingenious clock [Col. 0170A]. The fleet sent by Emperor Charles defeated the Moors in a battle in Corsica, killing many of them and putting the rest to flight. *Annals of Fulda.*

808 Godafrid, king of the Danes and Northmen, engaged the Abodrites in war and defeated them, though at great cost in his own soldiers. Charles the Younger ravaged the Linones and Smeldingi, who had defected to Godafrid. Eardwulf, king of the Northumbrians, driven from his kingdom, came first to Emperor Charles and then to Rome to lodge his complaint. *Annals of Fulda.*

809 Louis, the emperor’s son, marched against Spain. Eardwulf was restored to his kingdom through the legates of the pope and emperor. The question of the procession of the Holy Spirit was debated in a synod [Note: [Col. 0169D] This was the synod held at Aachen in November [Col. 0170D]. *German Councils*, vol. I, p. 390]. The emperor built the fortress of Esesfeld across the Elbe against Godafrid [Note: [Col. 0170D] Also called Essenfeld; it is now the town of Itzehoe in Holstein]. Trasico, duke of the Abodrites, after doing much with courage against Godafrid’s fugitives and his own deserters, was treacherously killed by Godafrid’s soldiers. *Annals of Fulda.*---At Saint Gall, Abbot Wolfleo [Note: [Col. 0170D] In Ratpert, Wolfleoz is nowhere called abbot, although, after being made bishop following Egino, he plotted against this abbey and forcibly claimed it for himself against Gozbert, elected after Werdo’s death in 816, until he was compelled by order of Emperor Louis to renounce it. Goldast, *Writers*, vol. I, p. 5] held office for four years.

810 Ruoddrud, the emperor’s daughter, died on 6 June. Godafrid, having sent a great fleet against the Frisians, imposed tribute on them after defeating them in battle three times. When Emperor Charles was already advancing against him with an army, the elephant that Aaron had sent suddenly died; the fleet returned, and it was announced that Godafrid, who had threatened to engage the emperor himself in battle, had been killed at home by his own men. The fortress of Hochbuoch, situated above the Elbe, was also captured by the Wilzi together with its garrison [Note: [Col. 0170D] In Einhard it is called Hochbucki and Hochbocki, and is thought to be present-day Hamburg, where Amalarius of Trier dedicated a church in the following year]. He also learned that his son Pippin, king of Italy, had died on 8 July. The Spaniards and likewise the Greeks confirmed peace with him through envoys. A very severe cattle plague occurred this year. Hemming, king of the Danes and son of Godafrid [Note: [Col. 0170D] In the Annals of Fulda and Metz he is said to have been the son of Godafrid’s brother], made peace with the emperor. *Annals of Fulda.*

[Col. 0171A] 811 Hetto, abbot of Reichenau and bishop of Basel, was sent to Constantinople with Counts Hugh and Haio [Note: [Col. 0171D] Namely, the count of Tours and the duke of Friuli. Hetto subscribed Charles the Great’s testament, made in this year. According to Einhard (Baluze, *Capitularies*, vol. I, p. 487), this testament was written in 811. Hetto’s *Hodoeporicon* has perished; the embassy of Michael took place in the following year. Einhard], and wrote his *Hodoeporicon* [account of his journey]. Meanwhile Emperor Nicephorus, fighting against the Bulgars, was killed. At last Michael became emperor and sent back the envoys of Emperor Charles. Three armies were sent by the emperor under a favorable omen against the Linones, into Pannonia, and against the Britons. Charles, the emperor’s son and king, died on 4 December. *Annals of Fulda.*

812 After King Hemming’s death, a battle arose among the Danes over precedence in the kingdom, in which 10,940 are said to have fallen. Emperor Michael, having sent back Charles’s envoys, also sent his own to confirm peace. The Beneventans paid Charles a tribute of twenty-five thousand gold solidi [Col. 0171B]. The Danish fleet, invading Ireland, was defeated by the Scots. *Annals of Fulda.*

813 Emperor Charles again sent Amalarius, archbishop of Trier, and Peter, abbot of Nonantola, to Constantinople; an account of their journey is likewise said to have been written [Note: [Col. 0171D] This *Hodoeporicon* is not found published anywhere]. He made his son Louis a partner in the empire, and also made his grandson Bernard [Note: [Col. 0171D] This had already been done in the preceding year], son of Pippin, king of Italy. Thegan.---He ordered five very great councils to be held for the condition of the churches, at Mainz, Reims, Tours, Chalon, and Arles [Note: [Col. 0171D] Labbe lists all these councils in sequence in his collection, vol. VII, p. 1239; Harzheim places Mainz in the *German Councils*, vol. I, p. 404]. The bridge over the Rhine at Mainz, built by Charles, was destroyed by fire. *Annals of Fulda.*---At Constance, Bishop Egino died. After him, Wolfleoz was made bishop; he had also already governed the monastery of Saint Gall for four years [Note: [Col. 0171D] See under 809. According to Ratpert, Gozbert was first elected abbot in 816, but according to Hepidanus in 815 [Col. 0172D]]. At Saint Gall, Abbot Gozbert held office for twenty-seven years.

814 Emperor Charles the Great, after first distributing his treasures among the twenty-one archbishoprics of his kingdom, the other bishoprics, and the churches, was stricken with fever [Col. 0172A] and pleurisy. He died at Aachen on 28 January and was honorably buried there, in the seventy-first year of his age, the forty-seventh of his reign, the forty-fourth since the subjection of Italy, and the fourteenth of his empire, in the seventh indiction. His son Louis, called the Pious, succeeded him and reigned for twenty-seven years. Immediately, after hearing and dismissing the envoys of various peoples, he held a general assembly at Aachen and corrected many abuses throughout the kingdom. *Annals of Fulda; Einhard; Thegan.*

815 The army sent by King Louis to assist the Danish king Heriold received forty [Note: [Col. 0172D] The Annals of Fulda count sixty hostages] hostages from the enemy. Certain leading Romans who had conspired for the death of Pope Leo were punished. *Annals of Fulda; Lorsch.*

816 The Sorbs and likewise the Wascones, who were attempting to rebel, were suppressed [Col. 0172B]. After Pope Leo died on 25 May [Note: [Col. 0172D] The Annals of Fulda give 24 June, plainly in error, since his successor Stephen had already been ordained on 22 June; Leo died on 11 June], Stephen occupied the see for seven months. Coming to King Louis in Francia, he crowned him emperor at Reims, and, joined to him by mutual gifts and friendship, returned to Rome. The emperor, having convened a synod [Note: [Col. 0172D] This was the synod of Aachen. *German Councils*, vol. I, p. 430], made many sound arrangements concerning the condition and discipline of monasteries. *Annals of Fulda.*---At Reichenau, the basilica of Saint Mary, built by Abbot and Bishop Hetto, was dedicated.

817 After Pope Stephen died on 25 January, Paschal occupied the see for seven years. An eclipse of the sun occurred on 5 February [Note: [Col. 0172D] The eclipse on this date was lunar; the solar eclipse occurred on 19 February], and a comet was seen. Envoys of Emperor Leo came from Constantinople to Emperor Louis concerning peace. Emperor Louis appointed his eldest son Lothar co-ruler of the empire [Note: [Col. 0172D] See the charter of division in Baluze, *Capitularies*, vol. I, p. 573], and his sons Louis and Pippin as kings of Bavaria and Aquitaine [Col. 0172C]. Sclaomir, duke of the Abodrites, rebelled. King Bernard of Italy, after attempting to rebel and despairing of his affairs, came to his imperial uncle to surrender. Ratgar, abbot of Fulda, was accused and convicted by the brothers and deposed. *Annals of Fulda.*

136 818 King Bernard, likewise convicted of rebellion, was blinded by judgment of the Franks and died; his accomplices were punished in various ways and the bishops were deposed. Emperor Louis subdued the rebellious Cismarine Britons after killing their duke Morman. A solar eclipse occurred on 8 July [Note: [Col. 0173D] This eclipse belongs to 7 July, not the eighth]. Empress Irmingard died on 3 October. At Fulda, Eigil was appointed abbot. *Annals of Fulda; Thegan.*

819 Sclaomir, duke of the Abodrites, was condemned to exile, and his kingdom was given to Ceaddrago, son of Trasico. At the synod held at Aachen [Note: [Col. 0173D] *German Councils*, vol. II, p. 11], many matters concerning the condition of the churches and monasteries were discussed. The emperor married Judith, daughter of Count Welf, by whom he fathered Charles. An army was sent into Pannonia against the rebellious Slav Liudewit [variants: Liutwitus and Liutulfus], but with little success. Pippin, the emperor’s son, subdued the rebellious Wascones. At Fulda, the church of Saint Boniface was dedicated by Archbishop Heistolf. *Annals of Fulda.*

820 Three armies sent from different directions against Liudewit devastated much of Pannonia. Bera, count of Barcelona, accused of treason, was convicted by single combat and condemned to exile. Excessive flooding from the rains produced a great pestilence and famine. *Annals of Fulda.*

821 Emperor Louis divided the kingdom among his sons, released those in exile, remitted everyone’s debts, and restored properties that had been brought into the royal treasury. His son Lothar took a wife. Thegan.---Ceaddrago, duke of the Abodrites, having been charged with treachery, Sclaomir was recalled from exile, fell ill, received baptism, and died. *Annals of Fulda.*

822 In Thuringia, a block of turf fifty feet long, fourteen feet wide, and eighteen feet high was found intact after being moved twenty-five feet from its place. In eastern Saxony, on one night, near Lake Arnseo [Note: [Col. 0173D] The town of Arntsee, or Arensee, in the old Brandenburg March, adjacent to this lake, takes its name from it], the earth swelled up for the distance of one league in the form of an embankment.

137 Emperor Louis performed public penance for his public sins and corrected whatever required correction in his kingdom. Lothar was sent to Italy, and Pippin, after taking a wife, was sent to Aquitaine as kings. At Fulda, Abbot Eigil died, and Rabanus succeeded him, a learned man and an excellent interpreter of the divine books. *Annals of Fulda.*---At Reichenau, after Abbot and Bishop Hetto had adopted a private and quiet life, Erlehald, the tenth abbot, held office for thirteen years. Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, preached the word of God to the Northmen. *Annals of Fulda.*

823 Lothar, king of Italy, was crowned emperor at Rome by Pope Paschal at the pope’s request. Liudewit, tyrant of Pannonia, having fled to Dalmatia, was killed through the treachery of the duke of Provence [Col. 0174B]. Among other prodigies, an earthquake shook the palace at Aachen. In the territory of Toul, a twelve-year-old girl remained for nearly three years [Note: [Col. 0173D] The Annals of Fulda give only ten months, as do the Annals of Einhard; but under 825 they give three years], healthy and working with her hands, almost without food or drink. In the district of Saxony called Firihsazi [Note: [Col. 0173D] This district, called Frisazi by others, is commonly placed near the borders of Saxony in Westphalia [Col. 0174D]; the *Gottwicense Chronicle*, p. 600, should be consulted. From this passage, however, Paulinus is proved to be in error when he places the same district in the Brandenburg March], twenty-three villages, and in other provinces more than usual, were burned by lightning. Thunderbolts frequently fell from a clear sky; many fields were devastated by hail more than usual, even in spring itself, and in some places large stones fell. A great pestilence also occurred. *Annals of Fulda.*

824 Omurtag, king of the Bulgars, sent to Emperor Louis to seek peace. At Rome, Pope Eugenius succeeded Paschal and occupied the see for three years. The winter was unusually cold and prolonged. In the territory of Autun, ice is said to have fallen from the air, fifteen feet long, seven feet wide, and two feet thick [Col. 0174C]. Emperor Louis sent his son Lothar to Rome to correct certain matters. He himself subdued rebellious Britain, ravaging it with sword and fire. *Annals of Fulda.*---At Reichenau, the monk Wetti, carried out of his body and brought back again, died after three days. Bishop Hetto wrote his visions in prose, and Walahfrid wrote them in heroic verse [Note: [Col. 0174D] Hetto’s prose account is not extant; Walahfrid’s poem survives in Canisius, *Lectures on Antiquity*, vol. II, part II, p. 204, new edition. See Cointius, *Annals*, vol. VII, p. 733].

[Col. 0175A] 825 The king of the Bulgars again sent envoys to the emperor to settle the boundaries of the kingdoms. Wiomarcus the Breton, harassing the borders of the Franks, was killed in his own house by the soldiers of Count Lantpert. The emperor made peace with the sons of Godafrid. *Annals of Fulda.*

826 The king of the Bulgars again sent envoys to the emperor, this time more insolently, demanding that the boundaries be fixed without delay; the emperor sent them back with insufficient attention. Heriold, king of the Danes, was baptized at Mainz with his wife, his sons, and a great multitude of his people [Note: [Col. 0175C] Nigellus and Theganus say that this took place at Ingelheim]. A certain Venetian priest named Georgius made a hydraulic organ at Aachen. Rizo the Goth, going from the palace to the Saracens, attempted to rebel. Abbot Hidowinus of Saint-Denis obtained from Pope Eugenius the bones of the blessed martyr Sebastian; placed in the basilica of Saint Medard at Soissons, they shone forth with varied and countless miracles. *Annals of Fulda; Lorsch.*

827 An army of Saracens sent to aid Rizo, while King Pippin resisted too slowly, ravaged the territories of Barcelona and Girona. When peace with the Bulgars had been disturbed, they invaded Pannonia by ships through the river Drava, ravaged it, and subjected it to themselves.---The bodies of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter were transferred to Francia in November [Note: [Col. 0175C] See Einhard’s account of this translation, vol. I of the Bollandists’ June]. At Rome, after Eugenius [Note: [Col. 0175C] Paschal died in 823; Eugenius succeeded him in 824, and in 827 Valentinus and Gregory succeeded Eugenius. Pagius] Pope Valentinus occupied the see for forty days [Col. 0176A], and after him Pope Gregory IV occupied it for sixteen years. *Annals of Fulda.*

139 828 The relics of Saint Marcellinus were brought to Aachen and glorified by many miracles. The emperor sent his son Lothar with an army to the borders of Spain against the Saracens, and Louis against the Bulgars into Pannonia. After the treaty with the Northmen had been imprudently broken, our camps were plundered by them. *Annals of Fulda; Lorsch.*

829 An earthquake occurred at Aachen on Holy Saturday of Easter. In August the emperor held a general assembly at Worms. The Bulgars, likewise entering by ships through the Drava, ravaged Pannonia. Lothar, the emperor’s son, departed for Italy. Count Bernard of Barcelona was made chamberlain of the emperor against the will of the Franks. *Annals of* [Col. 0176B] *Fulda.*

830 A disagreement among the princes against the emperor, stirred up on Bernard’s account, was calmed for a short time after Bernard was expelled. *Annals of Fulda; Life of Wala.*---Ratold, bishop of Verona, obtained the body of Saint Mark the Evangelist from the duke of Venice under the name of the martyr Valens, and brought it with the body of the martyr Genesius to the island of Reichenau [Note: [Col. 0175D] This account is suspected of being an interpolation, perhaps added later from the manuscript of Saint George or Bernold; certainly the handwriting seems to depart from that of the original hand. The ancient manuscript cited by Urstisius has only: “The bodies of Saints Valens and Sinesius are brought to the island of Reichenau”; or, as the brief Chronicle of Saint Gall has it (Duchesne, vol. III), “The bodies of Saints Valens and Sinesius came to Reichenau.” The Reichenau Chronicle already assigns this to 829: “The precious bodies of Saint Valentinus and Saint Senesius came to the island of Reichenau on 9 April.” The Saxon Annalist, under 831, says: “The bodies of Saints Valens, Sinesius, and Theopontius were brought to the island of Reichenau.”

As for Valens, I would rather be persuaded that he was the bishop of Verona who died on 26 July 531, on which day he is still venerated. Since his body was buried at Verona, Ratold, who was likewise bishop of that city, could certainly have obtained and sent it to Reichenau more easily than the body of Saint Mark, which had first been transferred from Alexandria to Venice only two years earlier (Pagius, *Critical Remarks*, under 820); Cointius nevertheless grants the people of Reichenau part of it (*Frankish Annals*, vol. VIII, pp. 164 ff.), where he also discusses at length Saints Senesius and Theopompus, whose relics likewise may on the same occasion have first been brought to Reichenau and then to Ratold’s cell. He writes that these had been brought from the East and deposited in the monastery of Saint Fusca in 807, where a portion had come into Ratold’s possession long before they were transferred from there to Nonantola in 911, as Ughellus fully describes (*Italia Sacra*, vol. V, pp. 491 ff.). Both are noted in the Roman Martyrology on 21 May, but in the Petershausen Calendar on 19 April and in the Reichenau Calendar on 20 April. See Gerbert’s *Alemannian Itinerary*, “Ratold’s Cell,” and vol. I of *Alemannian Liturgical Monuments*, pp. 404, 472; Tillemont, vol. II, *Ecclesiastical Observations*, pp. 98 and 513.]

The basilica of Saint Gall was begun by Abbot Gozbert.

140 831 The emperor, having held an assembly at Nijmegen [Note: [Col. 0176D] According to Thegan, this took place at the assembly at Aachen], deprived of their honors all who had opposed him; he also stripped some of their estates and sent others into exile, thereby seriously embittering the minds of both his sons and the others against himself and his wife Judith. *Annals of Fulda.*

832 The emperor came with an army against his son Louis at Augsburg. When Louis resisted, he turned against his other son Pippin in Aquitaine and deprived him of his kingdom. But, returning from there, he repudiated his wife through fear of his sons [Note: [Col. 0177D] Others assign this to the year 830; *Life of Louis the Pious*] and with difficulty regained the palace at Aachen. A solar eclipse occurred on 6 May and a lunar eclipse on 20 May. *Annals of Fulda.*

833 The emperor, having taken back his wife, took up arms against his sons, who were intending to come to him, gathering an army in Alsace [Col. 0177B]. When Pope Gregory came there with his sons, the emperor was betrayed and abandoned by his own men and fell into the power of his sons. *Annals of Fulda.*

834 The emperor, having laid down his arms by judgment of the bishops, was confined to perform penance [Note: [Col. 0177D] The deeds of his deposition reveal that this crime was committed in the preceding year; see Duchesne, vol. II, p. 332, where Louis the Pious’s complaint about it is also found], and his wife was banished to Italy. But soon, in the summer, having recovered his wife and taken up arms, he drove his son Lothar back into Italy [Note: [Col. 0177D] When Lothar fled, Louis had already been restored to the empire during Lent. Astronomus, under 834]. Nithard; Thegan.---In the same year a battle was fought against Matfrid and Lantpert, in which, among many others, Odo, count of Orléans, and Theodo, abbot of Tours, fell. *Annals of Fulda.*

835 The emperor held a great assembly with his sons Pippin and Louis at Lyon [Note: [Col. 0177D] This seems to refer to the assembly held at Worms in the following year. Appendix to Thegan, Lambecius, *Imperial Library*, book II, chapter 5]. The Northmen ravaged Dorestad [Note: [Col. 0177D] Now Wijk bij Duurstede, a town of the Netherlands in the province of Utrecht]. *Annals of Fulda.*---The basilica of Saint Gall was dedicated. Hepidanus.

[Col. 0177C] 836 The emperor held an assembly at the palace of Theodenhove [Note: [Col. 0177D] This is Theodon’s villa, or Toton’s villa, now Diedenhofen, a city of the duchy of Luxembourg on the Moselle. This assembly actually belongs to the preceding year. Thegan; *Annals of Bertin.*---This assembly must be replaced by the assembly at Aachen. *Annals of Bertin*], but his son Lothar, detained by serious illness, could not come to it [Note: [Col. 0178D] This relates to the assembly held at Worms in this year]. The Northmen burned the city of Antwerp and Witlam [variant: Witham], a trading center situated at the mouths of the Meuse, and received tribute from the Frisians. *Annals of Fulda.*---At Reichenau, Hetto, bishop of Basel, died and was buried [Note: [Col. 0178D] Sudanus says in *Sacred Basel* that he had already died in 830].

837 It is said that Ticinum trembled eight times during the night of 30 December. Many of the leading men of Italy died of illness. A comet was seen in the sign of Libra [Note: [Col. 0178D] The Astronomer places it in the sign of Virgo]. On 17 June, the Northmen engaged in battle on the island of Walcra [variant: Walacria] and killed many; likewise, while ravaging Dorestad, they received tribute from the Frisians. *Annals of Fulda.*
838 An earthquake occurred in the evening of the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February. Ships were built against the Northmen. The emperor gave the better part of the kingdom to his younger son Charles. Annals of Bertin, for the preceding year.—Lotharius and his brother Louis held a conference with one another in the valley of Trent. Annals of Bertin, for the preceding year.—The emperor, having held an assembly at Nijmegen, deprived his son Louis, on the advice of certain men, of the kingdom of the Eastern Franks, which he had received from him. Knowing that this had been done through the envy of wicked men, Louis invaded the same kingdom; whereupon the emperor, having gathered an army, resolved to expel him by force. King Pippin of Aquitaine, the emperor’s son, died in November [Note: Others assign his death to June. See Pagi, *Critical Remarks*, under 838, and Bünau, *Reichshistorie*, III, p. 175 ff.]. Annals of Fulda.—At Saint Gall, Bernwicus succeeded Gozpert as abbot. Ratpert.—At Reichenau, when Abbot Erlebald resigned, Ruodhelm, the eleventh abbot, served for four years.

142 839 Louis, thinking that he ought to yield to his father the emperor, returned to Bavaria. After celebrating Easter near Lake Brigantinus [Note: Namely, at the royal palace at Bodman. Annals of Bertin], the emperor later held an assembly at Worms, was reconciled with his son Lotharius, who was arriving from Italy, [Col. 0178C] and divided the kingdom between him and his son Charles. Annals of Bertin.—Only Bavaria was left to Louis, because he had offended his father; and when Lotharius returned to Italy, the emperor himself [Col. 0179A] set out with his son Charles to organize Aquitaine. A comet appeared in the sign of Aries; the sky was red like blood, and little sparks were seen darting through the air. Annals of Fulda.

840 Louis, grieving that he had been deprived of his position, gathered many men to himself throughout Alamannia and, as though reclaiming what was owed him, came to Frankfurt. Against him his father, Emperor Louis, left Aquitaine and gathered forces; he drove Louis through Thuringia to the barbarians and compelled him, with difficulty, to return to Bavaria through the lands of the Slavs. Annals of Bertin, Nithard.—The air appeared red, as though blood had coagulated, at Easter. A solar eclipse occurred on the seventh day before the Ides of May, after the sixth hour [Note: The Annals of Fulda give the fourth day before the Ides of May, on the vigil of the Ascension, which in that year fell on the third day before the Nones of May, that is, on 5 May, when this eclipse occurred; the Bertinian annalist likewise has this date].—Emperor Louis, seized by illness and taken to an island in the Rhine near Ingelheim, designated his son Lotharius as emperor, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, and was buried at Metz in the church of Saint Arnulf. Lotharius, returning from Italy, took possession of the kingdom. Since his brothers Louis and Charles could not endure this, Louis was the first to meet him near Mainz with forces from the Eastern Franks. When battle was scarcely postponed, and Lotharius was heading toward Gaul against Charles, Louis allied the Eastern Franks, Saxons, Thuringians, Alamanni, and Bavarians to himself. Annals of Fulda, Nithard.

841 After Louis had occupied the eastern bank of the Rhine with garrisons, Lotharius returned, abandoning his pursuit of Charles. In April, secretly crossing the Rhine with his army near Worms, Louis was almost betrayed by some of his own men and was outmaneuvered by his brother; he was compelled to return to Bavaria. Lotharius, however, leaving part of his forces to guard the Rhine, returned to pursue Charles. Nithard, Annals of Bertin.—Meanwhile Louis, recalled by messengers to assist Charles, encountered the forces of Lotharius that had been left behind in the territory of Rhaetia. On the third day before the Ides of May he engaged them in battle and, victorious, defeated Count Adalbert and many others. He then crossed the Rhine and, joining his forces with those of his brother Charles, could not agree with Lotharius, who sought sole rule, on the division of the kingdom. Thus, near the village of Fontenay [Note: The Annals of Fulda have *Fontaniacum*; it was Fontenay in the district of Auxerre], they met in battle on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, and after an immeasurable slaughter Louis and Charles gained possession of the camp. Lotharius, fleeing, sought the palace at Aachen and, gathering forces from everywhere, labored in vain to pursue his brothers after they had separated from one another—Louis first in autumn and winter, and Charles in Gaul. A comet was seen in the sign of Aquarius on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. Annals of Fulda, Nithard.—Grimald, archchaplain of Louis, received from him the monastery of Saint Gall as a benefice and held it for thirty-one years. Hepid.

842 Seeing his brother’s obstinacy, Louis and Charles gathered their forces at Strasbourg [Note: The Annals of Fulda have *Argentoratum*], resolved to pursue him. They found him at the village of Sentiacum (Sinzig), and, when he was abandoned by his own men, compelled him to flee on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April. They divided his kingdom between themselves on this side of the Alps. He, however, again gathered an army and awaited them at Mâcon, a city of Gaul. Finally, since all preferred peace to war, they ordered that the kingdom be divided into three parts on the appointed day, after three groups of forty nobles had sworn an oath. Nithard.—In Saxony Louis suppressed a conspiracy of freedmen against their masters, executing the leaders. Since the legates could not reach agreement on the appointed day, the partition was postponed to another time. Annals of Fulda. 144 At Reichenau the learned Walafrid Strabo served as abbot for seven years; he left many monuments of his talent in verse and prose.

843 After the kingdom had been surveyed and divided into three parts, and the brothers had met at Verdun, Lotharius received, together with the imperial title, Italy and Belgic Gaul, which is still called the kingdom of Lotharius after him [Note: Or Lotharingia. This is the famous Treaty of Verdun, from which Louis the German customarily counted the years of his reign in several charters]; Louis [Col. 0180C] received Germany, Pannonia, Noricum, and Alamannia; Charles received the remaining provinces of Gaul. After peace had been confirmed by oath, they departed. Annals of Bertin, Fulda.—Charles, attempting to take Aquitaine from Pippin, his brother’s son, and harassing him, suffered very serious losses to his own army. Empress Judith died. Annals of Fulda.—At Rome, after Pope Gregory’s death, Sergius II occupied the see for three years [Note: Gregory died on 25 January of the following year. Anastasius; Pagi]. The Moors occupied Benevento. Another source, under the following year.

844 King Charles of Gaul killed Bernard, duke of Barcelona, who suspected no evil. His army [Col. 0181A] was defeated in battle by Pippin’s commanders on the seventh day before the Ides of June, and his standard-bearer Rhaban fell with many other nobles, as did the abbots Hugh and Richboto [Note: According to the Annals of Bertin, Hugh, abbot of Saint-Quentin, was a natural son of Charles the Great, and Richboto, abbot of Centula, was Charles’s grandson through his daughter].—King Louis of Germany subdued the Abodrites, who were plotting rebellion, killing their king, and organized them under dukes. Fulda, Pith.—Rhaban, abbot of Fulda, sent to Pope Sergius the book that he had composed *On the Praise of the Holy Cross*, in verse and with various figures [Note: Rather, to Pope Gregory; but when Gregory died, these two books were delivered to his successor Sergius. See Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, century IV, part II, p. 40]. Annals of Fulda.—At Rheims, after Ebbo, Hincmar, a learned man, was ordained archbishop [Note: This ordination took place in the following year]. Flodoard, Hincmar.

145 845 The Northmen, ravaging Charles’s kingdom, sailed up the Seine as far as Paris and, after receiving a large sum of money from him for peace, departed. Annals of Bertin.—Likewise in Frisia, after being defeated once and victorious twice, they inflicted great slaughter on the population. Likewise in Saxony, after ravaging Hamburg [Note: It is called *Hammaburgum* in the Annals of Fulda and Metz], they returned, though not without losses.—King Charles, having engaged the Bretons in battle, lost many men and barely escaped with a few. Annals of Bertin.—King Louis had fourteen Bohemian dukes who had converted to the faith baptized. Emperor Lotharius compelled the Burgundians, who were attempting rebellion, to surrender. Annals of Fulda.

846 Gisalbert, a soldier of Charles, carried off by force the daughter of Emperor Lotharius. Angered by this, Lotharius refused to be reconciled with Charles, although Louis exerted himself to bring it about. Nithard, Annals of Metz.—Louis, having subdued the Slavs of Moravia [Note: The Moravians are the people now called Moravians], appointed Rastiz as their duke and returned through Bohemia with heavy losses to his army. Annals of Metz.—The Moors, when they could not capture Rome itself while marching against it, ravaged the church of Saint Peter. Annals of Fulda.—At Rome Leo IV occupied the see [Col. 0182A] for nine years and three months. He built the fortress called Leonine to strengthen the church of Saint Peter [Note: Leo’s predecessor Sergius did not die until 27 January of the following year. Anastasius]. Annals of Bertin, under 851.

847 Lotharius and Louis, inviting one another in turn, enjoyed royal banquets and gifts exchanged between them. The Northmen again burned Dorestad. At Mainz Archbishop Otgar died; in his place Rhaban, abbot of Fulda, a most learned man, was promoted to the archiepiscopate and held it for nine years. Soon, at Louis’s command, he assembled a great synod [Note: The acts of this synod are found in *Councils of Germany*, II, p. 151] at Mainz. Among other matters, Thiota, a false prophetess from the parish of Salomo, bishop of Constance, was arrested and publicly scourged; at last she ceased prophesying for those who sought profit from her predictions. Annals of Fulda.

848 King Louis, sending his son Louis, subdued the Bohemians [Col. 0182B] and compelled them to give hostages.—A certain presbyter named Goteschalcus, teaching as a dogma that some people were inevitably predestined by God to life and others to death, was convicted at an assembly of bishops at Mainz [Note: On this synod see *Councils of Germany*, II, p. 163. Mabillon discusses Goteschalcus more fully in *Benedictine Annals*, book XXX, chapter 3; book XXXIII, chapter 70, etc.; also Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, dissertation 5; Bernini, *History of Heresies*, II, chapter 7; the Annals of Bertin under 849; and Hincmar, *Against Goteschalcus*, in Labbe, *Councils*, IX]. He was expelled from Louis’s kingdom and sent to Rheims to his bishop Hincmar. Annals of Fulda, Hincmar.

849 The army sent by King Louis against the Bohemians, who were again in revolt, refused to accept the treaty and hostages requested by the enemy for peace. It was shamefully defeated and plundered by them, gave hostages, and returned in disgrace. Annals of Fulda.—An earthquake occurred. At Reichenau [Note: Ermenric, a monk of Reichenau and his disciple, testifies that Walafrid died not at Reichenau but in Gaul: “As my most blessed teacher Walahfrid was traveling to Charles the German to deliver a response from our lord King Louis, and died there,” etc.], Abbot Walafrid Strabo died; in his place Folcwin presided as thirteenth abbot for nine years.

850 The Northmen, advancing up the Seine under their leader Gotefrid, ravaged Charles’s kingdom [Col. 0182C] 147. Emperor Lotharius was summoned to help against them; but when Charles, believing that he would fight the enemy, was struck with fear, he accepted Gotefrid and his men into an alliance with the kingdom and gave them land to inhabit. A great famine oppressed Germany, especially the region around the Rhine, and Archbishop Rhaban fed many poor people. Annals of Fulda.

851 King Louis subdued the Sorbs, who were harassing the Frankish borders, after ravaging their territory. King Pippin was captured by his own men and handed over to his uncle Charles, who had him tonsured and confined in the monastery of Saint Medard at Soissons [Note: According to the Bertinian annalist, this happened in the following year]. Likewise his younger brother Charles, when he wished to go to him, was captured by Charles’s counts and, on Charles’s order, tonsured and placed under guard in the monastery of Corbie [Note: The Chronicle of Fontenelle assigns this event to 849]. Annals of Fulda.

[Col. 0183B] 852 A great and general synod was held at Mainz by Archbishop Rhaban and King Louis, and many matters were corrected. *Councils of Germany*, II, p. 165.—Heriold the Northman, long treated well by Louis, was killed by certain Franks on suspicion of treason. Annals of Fulda.—The translation of Saint Remigius, archbishop of Rheims, was carried out by Hincmar, archbishop of that city, on the Kalends of October. Bollandists, I, October 1.

853 The Northmen, sailing up the Loire and ravaging Gaul, also burned the basilica of Saint Martin at Tours. The Aquitanians, complaining of Charles’s injuries, urged Louis either to rule over them or to give them his son as king. Annals of Fulda.

854 Louis sent his namesake son into Aquitaine [Col. 0183C]; but, perceiving the instability of their minds, he disregarded them. The Northmen, gathered from the various regions that they had already been ravaging for twenty years, slaughtered an innumerable multitude and the entire royal line, down to a single boy, in mutual massacre. Annals of Fulda, Bertin.

855 It is reported that the earth shook twenty times at Mainz [Col. 0184A]. Unusual storms, hail, lightning, and thunder occurred. The church of Saint Kilian [Note: This is the cathedral of Würzburg. See Eccard, *Eastern Frankish History*, II, p. 442] 148 was burned by lightning on the fifth day before the Nones of June, and later its walls were destroyed by a storm. Gozpald, bishop of that city, died, and Arn became his successor. Annals of Fulda.—King Louis attacked Rastiz, duke of the Moravian Slavs, but, after partially ravaging the region, was unable to subdue him. When he had returned, the Moravians followed and ravaged the neighboring places beyond the Danube. Emperor Lotharius, having abandoned the world and divided his kingdom among his sons, became a monk at Prüm and not long afterward, on the third day before the Kalends of October, departed to the heavenly kingdom. After him his sons Louis the emperor held Italy, and Lotharius held the portions of the kingdom on this side of the Alps. Frequent little fiery objects, like darts, were seen being carried through the air from east to west on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, throughout the entire night. Annals of Fulda, Bertin.

856 After Rhaban, archbishop of Mainz, died on the second day before the Nones of February, Charles, son of King Pippin of Aquitaine, who had escaped from the custody of the monastery of Corbie to his uncle Louis, was promoted by him to the archiepiscopate and presided for eight years. Queen Hiltigart [Note: She was called Queen Hildegard because she was the daughter of Louis, king of Germany. Around 853 she was placed over the convent of women at Zurich, as is clear from a charter of that same king (Guillimann, *Helvetia*, book III, chapter 5). Her death is recorded by the Saxon Annalist under 857 and by the Chronicle of Saint Pantaleon under 859. Yet she was still alive in 858, when Louis issued another charter on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May. She died on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, as Mabillon inferred from an ancient manuscript of Saint Gall, *Benedictine Annals*, III, p. 63] died. At Fulda Abbot Hatto died, and Thioto succeeded him. King Louis, passing through the Sorbs and taking auxiliaries from them, defeated the Dalmatian people [Note: Others understand the Daleminci in Meissen] in war and made them tributary; he accepted the submission of some of them through the Bohemians and returned. Annals of Fulda, Bertin.—At Rome, after Leo’s death, Pope Benedict occupied the see for two years and six months [Note: The death of Pope Leo belongs to the preceding year. Later writers introduce here the female pope Joan; she has been refuted by Labbe, *Councils*, IX, p. 1173; Eckart, *Würzburg Antiquities*, book XXX, chapter 117; and others]. Anastasius.

857 An army again sent by King Louis into Bohemia drove the tyrant Sclavitag [Note: He is called *Scalajugatus* in the Annals of Fulda] 149 into the Moravian country. A synod was assembled at Mainz by Archbishop Charles [Note: See *Councils of Germany*, II, p. 243, although that work places this council around 859. Mansi nevertheless distinguishes it from another held in 857, in *Supplement to the Councils*, I, p. 979]. A very terrible storm occurred at Cologne on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October. Lightning in the form of a fiery dragon penetrated the church of Saint Peter, killing three men in different places and knocking down many more. Annals of Fulda.

[Col. 0185A] 858 A great earthquake occurred on the Kalends of January. King Lotharius, son of Emperor Lotharius, conspired against his uncle, King Louis, with his other uncle, King Charles. King Louis, summoned by a delegation of the people, who lamentably complained of Charles’s tyranny, hesitated for a long time but at last entered Gaul with an army; almost everyone turning to him, Charles fled. Louis, overly confident, dismissed his own army and organized that kingdom as he wished. But the treachery of certain men and the cunning of his brother Charles would have ensnared him there, had not news of the rebellious Sorbs recalled him more quickly to aid his own kingdom. When he returned, Charles recovered his kingdom. Annals of Fulda, Pith.—At Reichenau Abbot Folcwin was succeeded by Walther, the fourteenth abbot, who served for six years. A certain village near Mainz and the Rhine, called Cammunti [Note: In the annals cited this place is called *Caput montium*, from which the common people corruptly made *Cammunzi*. It was near Bingen], was infested for three years by an evil spirit. At first it gave answers invisibly and exposed thefts; afterward it also persecuted people by throwing stones and setting houses on fire, and made the place desolate. Annals of Fulda, Metz.—At Rome, after Benedict, Nicholas occupied the see for nine years. Anastasius.

859 King Louis, repeatedly sending envoys and striving to be reconciled with his brother Charles and with his cousin King Lotharius, finally came with the named men to a private conference and arranged a day for reconciliation. He also sent envoys to Pope Nicholas and to his cousin, Emperor Louis, to explain himself concerning his invasion of his brother’s kingdom. Frequent earthquakes shook Mainz [Col. 0185C]; there the devout and holy presbyter Probus died on the seventh day before the Kalends of July [Note: Some copies of the Annals of Fulda have the seventh day before the Kalends of June, or 26 May; Mabillon also discusses Probus on that day, *Benedictine Century IV*, part II, p. 56, as do the Bollandists among the saints omitted from the calendar]. Annals of Fulda, Pith.

860 A winter excessively severe and prolonged, harmful to the crops, occurred, so severe that even the Ionian Sea froze as far as Venice and became passable for horses and carts [Col. 0186A]. Kings Louis, Charles, and Lotharius met at the fortress of Confluence and were reconciled, confirming their mutual agreement by oath. Annals of Fulda.

861 King Louis, having held an assembly at Regensburg, deposed several of his leading men who had been accused of infidelity. He was also angered against his elder son Carloman, duke of Carinthia, as though he were plotting revolution against him. A very severe famine occurred that year. Annals of Fulda.—The monk Meginrad of Reichenau, the first inhabitant of the wilderness adjoining Lake Zurich, was killed there by certain robbers on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February. After his death he became renowned for miracles and was buried at Reichenau. From that time until today, the wilderness itself, cultivated by holy and devout men, has grown into a noble and famous monastery [Note: This is the celebrated Benedictine monastery of Einsiedeln in Switzerland, also called in ancient records the wilderness of the Blessed Virgin Mary and the cell of Meginrad. The Life of Saint Meginrad, written by Berno of Reichenau, is found in Mabillon, *Benedictine Century IV*, part II. See Eckart, *Eastern Frankish History*, book XXXI, chapter 80]. Hepid. Chronicle of Saint Gall.

862 King Lotharius, with the support of the archbishops Gunthar of Cologne and Theutgaud of Trier, repudiated his legitimate wife, Tiothpirga [also Thietberga], and joined his concubine Waldrada to himself. A synod was assembled at Metz [Note: This synod was held not at Metz but at Aachen, already in 860; another synod in the same matter was held there this year on the third day before the Kalends of May, and Lotharius was permitted to enter another marriage. Bouquet, VII, p. 79. See Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, dissertation IX, VI; Labbe, *Councils*, X, p. 206; *Councils of Germany*, II, p. 246 ff. The synod of Metz belongs to the following year; ibid., p. 283] to contrive this almost as though by right. Carloman, excusing himself from the charges brought against him, was reconciled with his father. King Louis attacked the rebellious Abodrites and compelled them to give hostages. Annals of Metz, Hincmar.

863 Carloman was likewise accused before his father so baselessly that, when his father came against him, he was betrayed by his own men and deprived of his duchy; scarcely proving his innocence, he appeased his father.—A synod was held at Metz in the presence of Arsenius [Note: Not Arsenius, but Rodoald and John were the legates of the pope, having been bribed by King Lotharius. Annals of Bertin] [Col. 0186C], the legate of Pope Nicholas. Gunthar and Theutgaud, the archbishops, were sent to Rome to strengthen the cause they had contrived for King Lotharius. At Rome, in a synod [Note: See *Councils of Germany*, loc. cit., p. 287 ff.] assembled by Pope Nicholas, they were deposed from office and anathematized together with their synod [Col. 0187A]. King Lotharius was excommunicated unless he repented. At Mainz, after Archbishop Charles died, Luitpert succeeded him. Annals of Fulda, Bertin.—Some of the Huns became Christians.

864 Gunthar of Cologne, because he had written insultingly to the lord pope [Note: His letter to Pope Nicholas is found in the Annals of Fulda under 863 and in the Bertinian Annals under 864] and had usurped episcopal office contrary to his prohibition, came to him at Rome, moved by repentance; but he did not deserve to be reconciled. Annals of Fulda, for the preceding year.—King Louis of Germany attacked Rastiz, duke of the Moravians, and besieged him at the fortress of Dowina. He compelled him to give the hostages demanded and to renew his oath of submission. Louis himself and his brother Charles, king of Gaul, also met, released one another from obligations owed, and renewed and confirmed their treaty and alliance [Note: This was first done in the following year. Baluze, *Capitularies*, II, p. 201]. [Col. 0187B] Annals of Fulda.—At Reichenau, after Waldkar, Hetto served as the fifteenth abbot for seven years. The translation of Saint Otmar to the basilica of Saint Gall [Note: The monastery of Gottwie likewise has this account. On this second translation see *Councils of Germany*, II, p. 293]. Hepid.

865 Ruodolf, a presbyter and monk of Fulda, a sufficiently learned teacher, poet, and historian, died on the eighth day before the Ides of March [Note: Peter the Librarian assigns Ruodolf’s death to the following year. Louis the German calls him his ambassador and confessor and prefect of the schools at Fulda, according to Brower, *Antiquities of Fulda*, book II, chapter 14]. Bishop Arsenius, the legate of Pope Nicholas, restored peace between King Louis and his cousins, Louis, emperor of Italy, and Lotharius. When Lotharius promised by the oaths of twelve of his nobles to uphold marital fidelity, Arsenius restored his reconciled wife, Tiothpirga, to him; he banished his concubine Waldrada to Italy. After arranging many matters with Charles throughout Gaul, he returned to Rome honored and rewarded by the kings. Annals of Fulda, Bertin.

[Col. 0188A] 866 Louis the Younger, because certain benefices of his had been given to his brother Carloman, made a determined attempt to rebel against his father, King Louis. Easily defeated, he was finally reconciled to his father through the mediation of Archbishop Luitpert. The soldier Gundpald [also Guntpoldus], who had dared to fight against Carloman, was defeated after losing his forces and barely escaped. The Bulgarians, sent preachers by Pope Nicholas and King Louis, accepted the faith of Christ. Annals of Fulda.

867 King Lotharius, disregarding his promises and the oaths of his nobles, again injured his wife Tiothpirga and secretly resumed relations with the recalled Waldrada. For this reason Pope Nicholas was moved and, sending letters to various people, excommunicated him together with all his accomplices [Note: According to the Annals of Fulda and Metz, the pope excommunicated not Lotharius but Waldrada. See the letter of Pope Nicholas dated 866, Labbe, *Councils*, IX, col. 1513]. Ruopert [Note: This Robert, surnamed the Strong, descended from Saint Arnulf through his son Robert and later became the founder of the third dynasty, that is, the Capetians. Mabillon, book XXXV, *Benedictine Annals*, no. 154], the strongest count of King Charles’s realm [Col. 0188B], another Maccabee of his age, who had often crushed the Northmen and Bretons in great battles, fell while fighting bravely against the Northmen by the Loire River. A great earthquake occurred on the seventh day before the Ides of October. Annals of Fulda.

868 A great synod was assembled at Worms in the presence of King Louis, and many decrees were issued there for the condition of the Church. *Councils of Germany*, II, p. 307.—In May [Note: Nicholas had already died in November of the preceding year, and Adrian had succeeded him], Pope Nicholas died at Rome and Adrian II occupied the see for five years. When King Lotharius came to him and, with the unsuccessful assistance of his brother, Emperor Louis, sought to obtain permission for his marriage to Waldrada, he achieved nothing. A comet appeared; a great flood and inundation occurred, followed by famine and a severe pestilence. Annals of Fulda.

[Col. 0189A] 869 The Bohemians harassed the borders of Bavaria. The Sorbs, the Suisli, and likewise the Bohemians ravaged Thuringia. Carloman twice engaged Rastiz with numerically superior forces, defeated him, and carried off enormous booty; he also killed Gundacar [Note: Gundacar had recently been appointed governor of Carinthia by Louis, but afterward joined the enemy], his perjured deserter, who had been divinely weakened in battle. Annals of Fulda.—King Lotharius, excusing himself before Pope Adrian for the crimes laid against him and rashly receiving the Lord’s Body from him, returned home and died at Piacenza in July [Note: The Annals of Metz give the sixth day before the Ides of August; others, the day before the Nones of June. See Pagi, *Critical Remarks*, under this year]. Almost all the supporters of his crime also died [Note: Read *obitu*, “in death,” as in Bernold]. His uncle Charles invaded his kingdom, ordered himself crowned at Metz, and commanded that he be called emperor. Annals of Metz and Fulda.—Meanwhile King Louis, ill at Regensburg to the point of desperation and distributing his treasures among churches and the poor [Col. 0189B], had sent his three sons with three armies against different enemies. Charles, the youngest of them, captured all the fortifications of Rastiz and ravaged the entire Moravian region with sword, fire, and plunder. Carloman likewise ravaged the kingdom of Zuentibald, Rastiz’s nephew. Louis, however, defeated the Sorbs and their allies twice and compelled them to submit. A severe famine and pestilence occurred. Annals of Fulda.

870 King Louis, recovering from his illness, received many men from Lotharius’s kingdom who came to him. Later, when he was going to meet his brother Charles for a conference, he fell from a certain upper gallery when the building collapsed [Note: The Annals of Bertin call the place *Flamereshem* in the Ripuarian district; the Annals of Metz call it a royal estate, now in the duchy of Jülich near Münster-Eifel]. He fell with many others, severely bruising his body and breaking his ribs. Nevertheless, concealing his pain, he came the next day [Col. 0189C] at the appointed time and divided Lotharius’s kingdom equally with his brother [Note: The document of division is preserved in Baluze, *Capitularies*, II, chapter 221]. Zuentibald surrendered himself and his kingdom to Carloman. Rastiz, angered by this, first resolved to destroy him by treachery; when this failed, he decided to pursue him openly. Zuentibald gained the upper hand, captured the defeated Rastiz, and handed him bound to Carloman. After the latter had overrun the kingdom, Rastiz [Note: The Annals of Fulda show that *Gazissius* should be read as *Rastizes*] [Col. 0190A] was sent to prison and presented to King Louis. Condemned to death by the judgment of the Franks, he was ordered to be deprived only of the sight of his eyes. In the same year Willibert, archbishop of Cologne, was ordained by Liutpert of Mainz [Note: This ordination took place on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, according to the Cologne Annals in Eckart, *Eastern Frankish History*, II, p. 918]. A great synod was assembled at Cologne [Note: Two Cologne councils held at different times are wrongly confused here: one in this year for the consecration of Archbishop Willibert, and another in 873 for the dedication of the church, as is noted in the acts themselves, *Councils of Germany*, II, p. 355 ff.], many decrees were issued for the condition of the Church, and the church of Saint Peter was dedicated. Among other prodigies, earthquakes occurred, and two red clouds, seeming to discharge fiery weapons against one another, appeared to mingle like combatants. Annals of Fulda, Pith.

871 Louis and Charles, attempting to rebel against their father, King Louis, because certain benefices had been granted to their brother Carloman, were at last scarcely persuaded by him to become reconciled and make peace. Zuentibald [Col. 0190B], accused of treachery, was placed under guard by Carloman. But when the charge was not proved, Carloman released him, gave him gifts, and sent an army to assist him against the presbyter Sclagamar, whom the Moravians had unwillingly made their duke in his place. Sclagamar, however, returning treacherously and taking refuge in the city, deceitfully surrounded the army that had come to aid him and utterly destroyed it, with only a few escaping or being captured. The Bohemians, attempting an incursion, were held back by the garrisons [read: defenses] stationed against them. Annals of Fulda.—At Constance Bishop Salomo died. At Reichenau, after Abbot Heito, Ruodho, the sixteenth abbot, presided for seventeen years. At Saint Gall the teacher Yso died. Hepid.

872 Emperor Basil of the Greeks sent King Louis, among other gifts, a large crystal containing a considerable portion of the Lord’s Cross, decorated with gold and precious gems [Col. 0190C]. King Louis, having reconciled his sons with himself and with one another, arranged the division of the kingdom after his death. An army sent against the Moravians, disagreeing among themselves because they lacked a leader, was defeated by the enemy, cut down, mocked, and disgracefully fled. Archbishop Liutpert, sent with an army against the Bohemians, defeated five of their dukes in battle and partially ravaged their territory. Carloman ravaged the Moravians; but his ship-guards were slaughtered by the enemy, while Bishop Embricho of Regensburg barely escaped by flight.—Almost the entire summer was made dreadful by lightning, thunder, and hail, destroying many people and crops. The church of Saint Peter at Worms was burned and destroyed by lightning. A great earthquake occurred on the third day before the Nones of December and destroyed Mainz. Annals of Fulda.—At Saint Gall, after Grimald’s death, Hartmuot served as abbot for twelve years. Hepid.

156 873 At an assembly held by King Louis at Frankfurt, his son Charles was seized by a demon and severely tormented [Note: The Annals of Bertin relate the same event under different circumstances and say that it happened as punishment for his rebellion against his father, according to the Fulda annalists. This Charles was surnamed the Fat and later became emperor]. King Charles of Gaul ordered his son, the deacon Carloman [Note: The Annals of Bertin describe the matter more fully, as does the Chronicle of Echternach in Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, IV, col. 509], who was exercising tyranny, to be blinded. Annals of Bertin. [Col. 0191B] Peace was established with the Danes, who had requested it, by King Louis. The Northmen, proudly sailing to Frisia with a fleet and demanding tribute, were defeated in battle; their leader Rudolf was killed with eight hundred men, and they were fined all their money. They returned in disgrace.—A great famine occurred. An immense and unprecedented multitude of locusts came in swarms from the East like armies and passed through these regions. For two continuous months they often obscured the rays of the sun while flying over an area of one mile, and within a single hour devoured whatever green vegetation they found in a hundred or more *jugera*. Finally, driven by the wind into the sea and thrown back by the waves, they produced a considerable pestilence through the foulness of the corrupted air. In the district of Brescia in Italy, it is reported that blood rained for three nights. Likewise, the Greeks, sending gifts through Archbishop Agatho, confirmed their friendship with King Louis. At Rome, after Adrian’s death, Pope John occupied the see for ten years [Note: Pope John VIII had already been ordained on 14 December of the preceding year]. Annals of Fulda, Bertin.

874 A very long, severe, and snowy winter killed many people and animals by the cold. The Sorbs and Suisli, attempting rebellion, were easily suppressed by Archbishop Liutpert.—During Lent, King Louis, warned by a vision, performed many almsgivings and prayers for the liberation of the soul of his father, Emperor Louis [Col. 0192B]. He likewise came to Italy and held a conference with Pope John and with Louis, emperor and son of his brother. He likewise made peace with Zuentibald, duke of the Moravians, who through envoys promised submission and pledged faith and an annual tribute; he also received the Bohemians who made the same agreement. He likewise held a conference with his brother Charles. A great famine and pestilence occurred throughout Gaul and Germany, and nearly a third of the people perished. Annals of Fulda.—Ratolfus [Note: [Col. 0191C]

This death is recorded in the Augian Necrology in Gerbert, *Monumenta Liturgica Alemannica*, vol. I, p. 489, under 13 September. He appears to have succeeded Eginon, who, according to Hermann, dedicated the Augian church in 799 and died and was buried at Augia in 802. Ughelli (*Italia sacra*, vol. V, p. 704) calls him Rotaldus, who, together with King Pippin of Italy, who died in 810, restored the monastery of Saint Zeno and transferred the saint’s body there in 807; hence his relics were later transferred to Ulm, then subject to the Augian monastery, as Hermann reports under 830. Ughelli also produces several charters of Rotaldus dated 814 and says that his last recorded appearance was at the Synod of Mantua in 824, or rather, according to Mansi, in 827 (*Supplementum Conciliorum*, vol. I). But he is quite mistaken: Rotaldus is still mentioned in 830 above by Hermann and in an imperial charter of Lothair from 834, which the same Ughelli (*loc. cit.*, p. 717) presents, attributing it to a second Rotaldus. This is nevertheless incorrect, as his editor Coletus notes, maintaining that there was only one Rotaldus, bishop of Verona. Thus this seems to be that same Bishop Ratholdus who, according to the Annals of Bertin, brought Judith, wife of Emperor Louis the Pious, who had been banished to Italy by her sons, back to Aachen in 834, and in the following year took part in the assembly at Thionville for the restoration of that emperor; Rothaldus subscribes the document (*Concilia Germaniae*, vol. II, p. 65). This also beyond doubt is the Bishop Rothaldus who first disclosed to Louis the Pious the conspiracy of Bernard, King of Italy, in 817, as his emperor’s *Life* relates (Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 101). Indeed, Perotus still calls him Rotaldus, bishop of Verona, in 840 (Cointius, vol. VIII, p. 375). Then, in 844, Anastasius, in his *Life of Sergius II*, presents Aginus or Agnimus, or Eginon, bishop of Verona, at the coronation of King Louis (Cointius, *loc. cit.*, p. 710).

Ratoldus, therefore, by this time already weighed down by old age, appears to have resigned his bishopric and, following the example of his predecessor Eginon, withdrawn to his own monastery at Augia. Certainly Mabillon argues that both were alumni, or monks, of Augia (*Annales Benedictini*, vol. II, pp. 390 and 531); for there would scarcely be any other reason why both these Veronese bishops should have shown such affection for this monastery and wished to end their lives there. By calculating the years, Ratoldus must have died at least a hundred years old in 874, if he succeeded Eginon in 802. The same year, 874, is also given as Ratoldus’s year of death in the Annals of Weingarten (Mabillon, *Annales*, *loc. cit.*, p. 368), which, since they end after 877, place this death beyond doubt. The same year is also found in the Chronicle of Saint Gall in Duchesne, vol. III.

It is therefore surprising that the booklet of the Fraternities of Saint Gall (Goldast, vol. II, part II, p. 152) reads:

> In the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 880, indiction II (III), Ratholdus, the most noble bishop of the Alamanni and of the Church of Verona, came to the monastery of Saint Gall and celebrated the feast of his deposition …; and Abbot Bernhard received him into the fellowship of his prayer.

This certainly cannot be understood of the earlier Ratoldus, since he had already been dead for a decade; moreover, his very advanced age makes it impossible. Nor would he himself have needed the fellowship of the people of Saint Gall, since, as an Augian monk, he was already a participant in it. At that time there was also no bishop of this name at Verona, but Adelardus—unless this is to be understood of a second Rotaldus, whom Ughelli, following Perotus, numbers among the bishops of that Church under 840. But since other bishops presided there from 844 onward, I do not see where this second Rotaldus could have remained hidden for forty years. Thus either the year and the abbot in the cited text are corrupt, or the name Ratoldus is erroneous.
