[Note: [Col. 0193D] What Ussermann had said here about Ratoldus, he repeated in his *Addenda and Corrigenda* in these words: “Hermann recorded under 874 the death of Ratolfus, bishop of Verona; yet we said that from the appended notes it appeared that he was still alive in 885, according to the booklet of the Fraternities of Saint Gall, and at the same time conjectured that some corruption lay in the passage; this has meanwhile also been discovered from another source. Among the ancient documents of the confraternities of the monastery of Saint Gall, a copy of the confraternity agreement made between that monastery and the bishops Ratpoltus of Trier and Luitwardus of Como in 886, under Abbot Bernard, is recorded in an old parchment manuscript of the Rule. Hence either the manuscript, or its editor Goldast, seems to have read *Rutholtus Veronensis* for *Ratpoldus* or *Ratbodus Trevirensis*. This is all the more probable because immediately afterward Goldast records, under 8 Kalends of July 885, the death of Liuchwardus, bishop of Como, who was confederated with the people of Saint Gall; and I find no difficulty either in the year or in the name. For in Roman numerals the unit I could easily have been added or omitted. Likewise, the man who is here called Ratpoldus is called Rabodus in the *Gallia Christiana*, vol. XIII, simply because proper names related to one another were expressed in different ways. Moreover, this Liutwardus should be added to the list of the bishops of Como in Ughelli’s *Italia sacra*, vol. VI.”]

The last point, however, seems to me quite plausible in light of Ekkehard the Younger, who, in chapter 11 of the *Life of Blessed Notker the Stammerer* (Goldast, vol. I, p. 231), writes that Peter, bishop of Verona, unexpectedly came to Saint Gall, and indeed in the same manner in which, as he relates in the preceding chapter, Adalbero, bishop of Augsburg, visited the place of Saint Gall on its feast day for the purpose of prayer. The booklet of the Fraternities assigns this to the year 908, although what is related about Peter could have happened earlier; for Ekkehard does not always observe chronological order. Immediately afterward, in chapter 13, he reports an event under the new abbot Bernard in 883, when, according to Hermann, Charles the Fat was at Saint Gall. For, as is clear from the whole sequence of the narrative, the events described here occurred in the time of Notker the Stammerer, who, according to Hermann, died in 912. Since Peter of Verona therefore visited Saint Gall around this period, while Ratoldus was already dead, perhaps the person who said that Ratoldus had been placed in Peter’s position did not greatly err. But here too the earlier difficulty returns: no Peter is recorded in the catalogue of the bishops of Verona, either before or after this period—unless one is willing to maintain that Peter succeeded Bishop Adelardus, who was excommunicated by the pope in 877; yet there is no other record of him.]

[Col. 0193A] 158 The bishop of Verona died; he had built a cell bearing his name beside the island of Augia. Queen Hemma [Note: [Col. 0194C] She was the wife of Louis the German, king.] was struck down by paralysis.

### 875

A revolt between the Franks and Saxons, almost reaching mutual slaughter, was suppressed by Louis the Younger. *Annals of Bertin.*—A comet, sparkling more brightly than usual, was seen on 8 Ides of June. A certain village in the district of Nitense [Note: [Col. 0194C] The Nitense district, also called Niddegowe, lay in Wetterau; see Besselius, *Chronicon Gottwicense*, vol. II, p. 709. In it stood Ascabrunnon or Aschenbrunnon, as it is called in a charter of Emperor Henry II from 1008; today it is Eschborn, between Frankfurt and Cronberg Castle.] called Ascabrunno was so suddenly consumed and destroyed at night, on 5 Nones of July, by a storm and rainburst, with eighty-eight people killed, that not even a trace of it remained.—The Emperor Louis of Italy died at Milan and was buried in the basilica of Saint Ambrose, in the twentieth year of his reign. His uncle, King Charles of Gaul, invaded and plundered his treasures and kingdom as though they were owed to him alone. Consequently, his brother Louis, king of Germany, sent his son Carloman [Note: [Col. 0194C] The cited annals state that Charles, the son, was first sent by his father to Italy, and that Carloman was subsequently sent to assist him. The Annals of Fulda and Bertin, however, relate the whole matter differently according to the interests of their respective parties. Andreas the priest of Ravenna, a contemporary, takes a middle position in his *Chronicle*, in Mencken, vol. I.] against him into Italy, while he himself invaded his kingdom in Gaul together with his namesake. But Charles, fearing to engage in battle, drove Carloman out of Italy by treachery, money, and lies, swearing that he too would soon depart and would await his brother Louis concerning the division of that kingdom. When Louis, believing him, had returned, Charles himself proceeded to Rome and, having won the Romans over by deceit and money, had himself crowned emperor by Pope John; he then arranged Italy as he wished, as though it were his own. *Annals of Fulda.*

### 876

King Louis, yielding to the people’s pleas, returned from Gaul so as not to devastate it. Queen Hemma died at Regensburg and was buried in the basilica of Saint Emmeram. The Frisians likewise defeated the Northmen in battle and seized very considerable spoils. *Annals of Fulda.*—The fraudulently crowned Emperor Charles, returning from Italy to Gaul, used a new style marked by vanity in dress, actions, and words, by boastfulness, and by frivolity; he insolently and foolishly threatened his brother Louis. But when Louis gathered an army, Charles was terrified and sent him frequent, suppliant envoys to seek peace. *The same.*

Meanwhile King Louis himself, a strong and religious man, stricken by illness at Frankfurt, died on 5 Kalends of September, in the thirty-sixth year of his reign, and was buried at the monastery of Lorsch. His kingdom was received by his three sons: Carloman received Bavaria, Louis Germany, and Charles Alemannia, each with the neighboring provinces; and they confirmed peace among themselves by oath.

But Charles, the tyrant of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0195D] The Annalist of Fulda, a German writer, regularly calls Charles the Bald this; the writer of the Annals of Bertin judges more mildly. Thus, in the writers of this period, one may rightly miss the primary quality of a true historian—namely, a mind free from partisan attachment.], rejoicing when he learned of his brother’s death, immediately gathered an army and invaded the part of his kingdom adjoining the Rhine. When Louis the Younger had unsuccessfully demanded through envoys that he return and preserve the peace, and had discovered that Charles was treacherously plotting an ambush against him, Louis crossed the Rhine and defeated him in battle in Ribuaria [read: Ripuaria] on 8 Ides of October [Note: [Col. 0195D] Concerning this once very extensive district of Austrasia or Lotharingia, Ripuaria, see *Chronicon Gottwicense*, vol. II, p. 749.]. After killing and capturing many, he forced Charles to flee shamefully, almost naked and with only a few companions, and plundered his camp with innumerable spoils. *Annals of Fulda and Bertin.*

### 877

The Linones, the Suisli, and their neighbors, while plotting revolt, were easily suppressed by envoys sent by Louis. *Annals of Fulda.*—The tyrannical Emperor Charles of Gaul likewise entered Italy in summer. When he learned that Carloman, his brother’s son, had crossed the Alps against his will and wished to engage him in battle, he fled, as was his custom; while fleeing, he was seized by dysentery and died in the thirty-seventh year of his reign. He was buried in Burgundy at Agaunum [Note: [Col. 0195D] Rather, in the monastery of Nantua.]. *Annals of Bertin.*—After him, his son Louis the Stammerer received the kingdom of Gaul. He excused himself to his cousins through envoys concerning all the injuries inflicted by his father and made peace with them. Carloman, having arranged Italy as he wished, returned to Bavaria and restored to his brother Louis his share of the kingdom of Lothair. Italian fever, cough, pain in the eyes, and pestilence severely afflicted and killed many. *Annals of Fulda.*

### 878

King Louis of Germany divided the kingdom of Lothair with his brother Charles. Counts Lambert [Note: [Col. 0195D] Lambert was duke of Spoleto; Adalbert was margrave of Tuscany.] and Adalbert, advancing on Rome with a strong force and keeping Pope John under guard, compelled the Roman leaders to confirm their allegiance to Carloman by oath. The pope, angered by this, closed the church of Saint Peter, after transferring all the treasures to the Lateran, and prohibited the celebration of divine offices there. He himself went by sea across the Tyrrhenian Sea to Gaul and remained there for almost an entire year.

Then, taking with him a certain Boso—who, after poisoning his own wife, had forcibly abducted the daughter of Louis, emperor of Italy, and whom Charles had placed in charge of Provence—he returned to Rome and attempted to subject the kingdom of Italy to Boso and take it away from Carloman. A solar eclipse occurred on 7 Kalends of November after the ninth hour [Note: [Col. 0196D] The Annals of Fulda more correctly give 4 Kalends of November.], and there was a great pestilence among humans and cattle. *Annals of Fulda.*

### 879

Carloman, king of Bavaria, struck by paralysis, lost the use of speech. His brother Louis came to visit him and arranged the affairs of the kingdom of Bavaria. *Annals of Fulda.*—Louis the Stammerer, son of Charles, king of Gaul, died at Compiègne on 3 Ides of April [Note: [Col. 0196D] Others give 4 Ides of April, or 10 April, which was Good Friday, as recorded in the Annals of Vedastinus.], and was buried there. He left a posthumous son, together with two other sons born to a non-legitimate wife, namely Louis and Carloman, who succeeded him in the kingdom. *Annals of Bertin.*—After his death, King Louis of Germany immediately made for the neighboring Belgic Gaul. From there, summoned again by certain people to Bavaria, he arranged matters as seemed appropriate; he visited his sick brother Carloman, who, unable to speak, committed his affairs to him in writing, and appointed several nobles to serve him. He also sent troops against Hugh, son of King Lothair by Waldrada, who was exercising tyranny in Belgic Gaul, and suppressed him and his followers. Boso exercises tyranny after invading Burgundy. *Annals of Fulda and Metz.*

### 880

A long and excessively cold winter occurred. King Louis of Germany came into Gaul, received the sons of Louis the Stammerer when they came to him, made peace with them, and subjected the entire kingdom of Lothair to himself. He himself engaged in battle with the Northmen who were settled on the river Scheldt [Note: [Col. 0196D] The Annals of Fulda give *Scalta*, which is now the river Scheldt.], killed more than five thousand of them, and there his son Hugh, born of a concubine, fell.

The Northmen likewise fought the Saxons and, victorious, killed two bishops [Note: [Col. 0196D] Namely, Theodoricus of Minden and Marquardus of Hildesheim. All these men are venerated as the Ebbekestorpian martyrs, named from the place of the battle. Their acts, however, are fictitious (Leibniz, vol. I, *Scriptores Brunsvicenses*). See vol. I of the Bollandists, 2 February.], twelve counts, and eighteen royal soldiers, together with a great multitude who followed them, and led many captives away. The Sorabi, Dalmatians (Daleminci), and Bohemians, Slavic peoples, gathered an army and ravaged Thuringia beside the river Saale. They were surrounded by Margrave Poppo and all killed.

Carloman, king of Bavaria, strong, prudent, and devout, died on 11 Kalends of April [Note: [Col. 0197C] Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, vol. II, p. 145, presents a charter of King Carloman dated 5 Ides of May in the year of the Incarnation 872, but in the fourth year of Lord King Carloman’s reign in Bavaria and the third in Italy, indiction V. It was issued at the royal court of Huotinga. The regnal year there indicates 880, although the indiction is incorrect. From this it is inferred that Carloman was still alive on 11 May 880 and therefore did not die on 22 March. His son, King Arnolfus, records the death-day of this same Carloman, his father, in a charter of 889 by which he grants the abbey of Lobbes to Francho, bishop of Liège, on condition that a commemoration be held on the Kalends of October, the day on which “Carloman, the most pious king of venerable memory and our father, ended his present life” (Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, p. 650; compare Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. III, p. 273). He therefore died on 22 September 880 and was buried at Hodingas (*Annals of Metz*). This place is the same as Huotinga or Otinga, now Octinga, formerly a royal estate in Bavaria (*Chronicon Gottwicense*, vol. II, p. 500).] at the village of Otinga and was buried there. His brother, King Louis of Germany, also sent troops against Hugh into Gaul and won a bloody victory. Supported by his aid, the sons of Louis the Stammerer pursued the tyrant Boso beyond the Rhône, drove him into Vienne, and captured and subjected the city of Mâcon.

The Northmen, ravaging Gaul and Frisia with fire, plunder, and slaughter, finally fortified Nijmegen and prepared to winter in the royal palace. Against them Louis took the field, but because of the winter he could accomplish little. A great failure of crops afflicted Germany. *Annals of Fulda; Regino, following year.*

### 881

There was again a harsh and prolonged winter and a great famine. King Louis of Germany kindly received Hugh, who came to submit, but when Hugh rebelled again, Louis pursued him and drove him into Burgundy.

King Louis of Gaul fought the Northmen and, victorious, struck down nine thousand horsemen. The Northmen, having gathered their forces again, attacked the kingdom of King Louis of Germany. They ravaged Cambrai, Utrecht, the district of Hasbania [read: Hasbanicum], all Ripuaria, Prüm, Stavelot, Malmedy [read: Malmundarium], Inda, and many other places. At Aachen they stabled their horses in the king’s chapel. They burned Cologne and Bonn, together with their churches. Since King Louis was unable to come against them because he was ill, he sent an army. Meanwhile, a great earthquake occurred at Mainz on 3 Kalends of January.

In the same year, King Charles, Louis’s brother, went to Italy and came to Rome; together with Queen Richgarda, he was crowned by Pope John with the imperial anointing [Note: [Col. 0197D] The Annalist of Fulda adds the day of the Lord’s Nativity under 880; Hermann, who begins the year from that feast, consequently assigned it to 881. John VIII himself already calls Charles emperor in a letter addressed to him on 4 Kalends of April, indiction XIV, which belongs to the year 881 (Letter 269 in Labbe, *Collectio Conciliorum*, vol. IX, p. 194). Muratori (*Antichità Italiane*, vol. I, p. 436, and vol. III, p. 753) proves from charters that Charles the Fat had not been crowned emperor before the middle of March 881. Eccardus (*Rerum Francicarum*, vol. II, p. 654), from a charter of Cadoldus, bishop of Novara, establishing at Augia an annual commemoration of that Caesar on the day of his consecration—that is, on Epiphany—thinks that this very day should be assigned as the day of his coronation, especially since Charles himself, in a charter for the Church of Fulda dated 9 Kalends of October 885 (Schannat, *Traditiones Fuldenses*, p. 212), calls that same day the annual day of his consecration. Saxius, however, in his notes to Sigonius on the kingdom of Italy, p. 344, doubts which of his coronations is meant here: the Italian, Roman, or German one, especially since on 6 January 880 he was crowned king of Italy at Milan. See above in the *Brief Chronicle of the Frankish Kings*, at the end.]. *Annals of Fulda, previous year.*

### 882

A comet spreading its tail beyond measure was seen on 15 Kalends of February. King Louis of Germany, as his illness increased, died on 13 Kalends of February [Note: [Col. 0198C] The Annals of Fulda and the Fulda Necrology assign 20 January as Louis’s day of death, but the Pithoean annals and Regino incorrectly give 19 November, and the Annals of Metz 20 August.], and was buried at Lorsch beside his namesake father. When this was heard, an army sent against the Northmen returned without accomplishing its task. The Northmen, meeting no resistance, ravaged the remaining regions all around. They killed Walach [Note: [Col. 0198D] Alternatively, Walo or Wala.], bishop of Metz, who rashly encountered them; among other places, they also burned the city of Trier on 5 Nones of April [Note: [Col. 0198D] This was Maundy Thursday according to the Annals of Metz.], after driving out and killing its citizens. Having devastated and burned the region, they returned to their fortification, called Ascaloha [Note: [Col. 0198D] The Annals of Fulda have *Ascloba*, Regino *Haslou*. Struvius understands this as Hassfeld; others more plausibly identify it with Hasla, a city on the Meuse, fourteen miles from the Rhine according to the cited annals.], beside the river Meuse. *Annals of Fulda.*

The Emperor Charles, returning from Italy, held an assembly at Worms and, having received his brother’s kingdom, gathered a large army and besieged the Northmen with their kings for twelve days. When they were afflicted by great heat and stench, in addition to mutual missiles, and were disturbed by immense storms and terrifying hail that arose on 12 Kalends of August, he saw that the fortress would be difficult to capture. The enemy therefore requested peace and promised thereafter by oath to submit to his kingdom. After hostages had been given, he held a mutual conference with their king Sigefridus [Note: [Col. 0199D] The other annals call the king Godefridus.], received him from baptism after he had professed Christianity, and, after exchanging gifts and confirming their friendship, they departed.

War broke out between the Saxons and Thuringians, and the Saxons prevailed. A great pestilence occurred in Bavaria. *Annals of Fulda, Bertin, Metz, and Regino.*

### 883

After celebrating Christmas in Alemannia, Emperor Charles also came to the monastery of Saint Gall. At the request of the aged Abbot Hardmot, he appointed Bernhard abbot in his place; Bernhard presided over that community for seven years. Charles himself celebrated Easter at Regensburg. *Ratpert.*

At Rome, Pope John was given poison by one of his relatives. While he was still thought likely to live, he expired after being struck on the head with a hammer. His attacker, when a crowd rushed together, fell dead at the same hour, though no one had harmed him. The archdeacon Martinus [Note: [Col. 0199D] The Annals of Fulda correctly have Marinus, and assign the event to the preceding year.] was made pope, the 110th, and presided for one year and six months.

Emperor Charles again went to Italy to meet the pope and ordered the pursuit of Duke Wido, who had been accused of treason and had fled. Pestilence afflicted the army. The Saxons likewise fought the Thuringians and defeated them together with Poppo [Note: [Col. 0199D] Duke of Thuringia.]. The Northmen, likewise advancing against Prüm, were massacred by Margrave Henry, the brother of Poppo.

King Louis of Gaul, after ruling and defending the kingdom vigorously, died and was buried at Paris in the sixth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0199D] According to the Annals of Bertin, Louis, king of France, had already died in August of the preceding year.]. Duke Zuentibald of the Marahenses cruelly ravaged Pannonia, which was governed by Arnolfus, duke and son of King Carloman. *Annals of Fulda.*

### 884

Bavarians were sent into Italy against Wido. Zuentibald likewise ravaged Pannonia most savagely. He defeated some Bavarians who had rashly engaged him near the river Rába [alternative: Raab], killed some, and captured others.

Carloman, king of Gaul and son of Louis the Stammerer, after paying the Northmen a large sum of money for peace, was struck by a boar while hunting and died in the seventh year of his reign. The kingdom of Gaul returned to Emperor Charles. *Chronicle of Normandy; Regino.*

Emperor Charles, holding an assembly in Nearer Pannonia, received Duke Zuentibald of the Marahenses, who surrendered himself into his power and promised peace and service. He likewise accepted Duke Brazlavus, who governed the region between the rivers Drava and Sava in Pannonia and who likewise surrendered himself. Charles came through Carantania into Italy and celebrated Christmas at Pavia. *Annals of Fulda.*

### 885

Emperor Charles held an assembly in Italy and received Duke Wido of Spoleto, who offered his defense and submitted himself. From there he went to Gaul, received its leading men, and, as it seemed, arranged that kingdom. He then came to Worms for the agreed meeting with the pope. But the pope died while setting out to come to him [Note: [Col. 0200D] The pope who died on the journey was Adrian, not Marinus, his predecessor, who had already died in May 884.]. At Rome, Adrian III, pope number 111, was ordained in his place and presided for one year and four months. *Supplement of Lambecius.*

King Gotafridus of the Northmen, accused of treachery against the Frankish kingdom, was killed by the very accusers through deceit. Hugh, the illegitimate son of King Lothair, was also deprived of his eyesight when he acted rashly against the emperor. *Regino.*

Peace between Arnolfus, duke of Carantania and Pannonia, and Zuentibald, duke of the Marahenses, was confirmed. *Annals of Fulda.*

### 886

After celebrating Christmas at Regensburg, the emperor, invited by the pope, went to Italy and sent Liutwardus, bishop of Vercelli, to Rome to investigate certain matters. A tumult broke out at Pavia between the citizens and the royal soldiers, causing serious losses on both sides.

After Easter, the emperor held an assembly at Pavia and proceeded through Burgundy into Gaul against the Northmen. When the battle against them went badly and Henry, margrave of Neustria, fell, he departed after affairs had turned out less favorably. Duke Peringarius [alternative: Berengarius] of Friuli, in conflict with Bishop Liutwardus, plundered the city of Vercelli.

An extraordinary flood occurred in autumn. The waters overflowed, destroyed many villages, demolished roads in the mountains, and inflicted many losses upon mortals. At Rome, Stephen V, pope number 112, was ordained after Adrian [Note: [Col. 0200D] Stephen V had already been appointed in September of the preceding year, in succession to Adrian.]. He presided for six years. *Annals of Fulda.*

### 887

Emperor Charles lay seriously ill in Alsace and, after recovering only slightly, underwent an incision of the head [Note: [Col. 0201C] At the palace of Bodoma, beside Lake Constance.]. After holding an assembly in Alemannia at the village of Weiblinga [Note: [Col. 0201C] Weiblinga appears as a royal estate in the Annals of Fulda under 894. It is also mentioned in a charter of this same Emperor Charles the Fat from 885, issued at Weihelinga, and in another of his charters dated 9 Nones of May 887, indiction IV, in the eleventh year of the reign of Lord Charles and the seventh of his empire: “Issued at the village of Weiblinga.” Learned men differ concerning its location. Besselius, in *Chronicon Gottwicense*, vol. II, p. 520, thinks it was the modern monastery of Wiblingen in the duchy of Swabia, formerly belonging to the district of Albegowe, at the confluence of the Danube and the Iller. Others understand Waiblingen in the duchy of Württemberg, in the Rems valley near the river Neckar, famous as the seat of the Hohenstaufen dukes of Swabia and as the origin of the Ghibellines. The latter view seems preferable, since it is scarcely credible that Charles held an assembly at a place so close to Ulm as the monastery of Wiblingen, rather than at Ulm itself, a royal village, as it is called in a charter of Charles the Great for the Augian monastery from 813.

We do not think either of the villages just mentioned is meant here, but rather another Wibelinga in the Lower Palatinate, likewise on the Neckar between Heidelberg and Mannheim, in the district of Lobodunum, which is frequently mentioned in the Lorsch records. This seems confirmed by the fact that, according to the Annalist of Fulda, after the assembly at Weiblinga the emperor received Boso at the Rhine, in the village of Chircheim or Kircheim, situated in the same district. I also think that the above-mentioned charter of Charles the Fat for the monastery of Otinga, dated 8 Kalends of September 885 and issued “at Weibelinga,” was given there. This is suggested by another charter of the same emperor, issued three days later, on 5 Kalends of September in the same year, at the monastery called Lorsch. It appears in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, among the instruments, p. 133; the short interval between the two documents indicates the proximity of the places and thus strongly supports the Palatine Wibelinga.]

He received Duke Berengarius, who came to submit, and who satisfied Bishop Liutwardus. After Boso died, his son, the young Louis, born of the daughter of Louis, emperor of Italy, came to Emperor Charles, who received him kindly and adopted him as a son. *Annals of Fulda.*

Empress Richgarda [alternative: Richarda] was accused by the emperor and others of adultery with Liutwardus, bishop of Vercelli, who enjoyed intimate influence in the palace with her and the emperor. By divine judgment she proved herself untouched by intercourse with any man and a virgin up to that point, although she had already appeared in the emperor’s marriage for twelve years. She was soon separated from him and withdrew to the convent of virgins that she herself had built at Andelau [Note: [Col. 0202C] This was a celebrated college of noble virgins in Alsace, founded by Queen Richgarda around 880.]. There she remained as a virgin queen, assiduous in divine service. *Annals of Metz and Regino.*

Then Emperor Charles became seriously ill and, as it seemed, also lost the strength of his mind. All the leading men of the kingdom, already alienated from him, held an assembly at Frankfurt and unanimously deserted him. They established as king over themselves Arnolfus, the son of his brother Carloman, born not of a legitimate wife but nevertheless of a noble woman [Note: [Col. 0202C] Writers call her Luitswinda, a noble woman from Carinthia.], and duke of Carantania.

When Charles saw that he had been entirely deserted by all his officials and even by his servants, and that only Liutpertus, archbishop of Mainz, still supported him, he humbly sent gifts to Arnolfus and obtained from him a few estates in Alemannia for the remainder of his life. *Annals of Fulda, Metz, and Regino.*

### 888

Charles, already deprived of the empire, became ill while devoutly serving God at the Alemannian village of Nidinga [Note: [Col. 0202C] Nidingen, Nydingen, or Neidingen, a village in the ancient Alemannian district of Bertoldsbaar, or in the modern landgraviate of Baar, and the burial place of the noble Fürstenberg family.]. Some say that he was strangled by his own men. He died from mortal life on the Ides of January. With certain people looking on, heaven opened and a light appeared above him; he was carried to Augia [Note: [Col. 0202D] Namely, the monastery of Reichenau, where Cadoldus, bishop of Novara, formerly a monk of that monastery and the brother of Bishop Liutwardus of Vercelli, established a solemn annual commemoration of this emperor.] and buried beside the altar of Saint Mary. *Annals of Fulda.*

While King Arnolfus was spending Christmas and Easter at Regensburg, numerous petty kings emerged. Peringarius, son of Eberhard, made himself king in Italy; Ruodolfus, son of Conrad, in Burgundy; Louis, son of Boso, and Wido, son of Lambert, in Belgic Gaul and Provence; Odo, son of Ruodpertus (Rotbertus), in Gaul as far as the Loire; and Ramnolfus [Note: [Col. 0202D] This Ramnulfus was count of Poitou and duke of Aquitaine; after invading Aquitaine, Septimania, and the Spanish March, he claimed the royal title for himself.], in Aquitaine and farther Gaul, likewise usurped the royal title [printed: *nihil*, perhaps *nihilominus*, “nonetheless”]. Of these, Odo humbly approached King Arnolfus when he came into Gaul and was kindly received; with Arnolfus’s permission, he retained the kingdom he had invaded. Likewise, Rodolfus came to him at Regensburg and, through his favor, obtained the Burgundy he had seized [Note: [Col. 0203D] Not everything listed here belongs to this year; Louis was first made king of Arles in 890.].

Nevertheless, when King Arnolfus wished to go to Italy, he met Peringarius, who shortly before had fought the tyrant Wido in battle, and, with few exceptions, granted him the whole of Italy. During this expedition a severe pestilence among horses occurred. *Annals of Fulda and Regino.*

At Augia, Hatto succeeded Abbot Ruodhoho and presided for twenty-five years. He built the cell and basilica of Saint George on the island.

### 889

Liutpertus, the venerable and wholly praiseworthy archbishop of the see of Mainz, died; Sunderold succeeded him.

This was a disastrous year, marked by diseases and pestilence, floods, extraordinary storms, whirlwinds and many hailstorms, famine, plague, and civil wars among fellow provincials on every side. In Thuringia, a rainstorm pouring down like a torrent suddenly destroyed three villages and killed three hundred people together with many animals. *Annals of Fulda.*

King Arnolfus scarcely succeeded in obtaining from the Franks a promise of submission to his sons, Zuentibald and Ratoldus, born of a concubine, unless no legitimate son should be born to him. He undertook a major expedition against the Abodrites, but with little success. *Annals of Fulda and Metz.*

### 890

At an assembly held in Pannonia concerning various matters, King Arnolfus was earnestly asked by Zuentibald, duke of the Marahenses, on the basis of the apostolic’s words, to come to Rome and, while retaining Italy under his authority, rescue it from so many tyrants. Arnolfus, prevented by other matters, postponed doing this for the time being.

Again, after an assembly had been held at Forchheim, he kindly received the daughter of Louis, emperor of Italy, Boso’s widow, who came to him with gifts. From there he visited Constance and Augia for the sake of prayer, and then returned to Regensburg. *Annals of Fulda.*

At Saint Gall, after Bernhard, Salomon presided as abbot for thirty years. Salomon II, the venerable bishop of Constance, died. In his place Salomon III, an abbot from the monastery of Saint Gall, was promoted to the episcopate and presided for thirty years. *Hepid.; Annals of Metz; others, following year.*
[Col. 0203D] **891** Embricho, bishop of Regensburg, venerable in life and age, died; and the city itself, except for the churches of Saint Emmeram and Saint Cassian, which were spared by divine providence, was entirely consumed by fire on 10 August. The Northmen [Col. 0204A] likewise ravaged Francia along the Rhine. An army was sent against them, but after an incautious engagement, Sunderolt, archbishop of Mainz, fell dead with many others, while the rest fled (Regino). In his place Hatto, abbot of Reichenau, an ingenious man, was advanced to the archbishopric. Annals of Fulda. — King Arnulf, pursuing the Northmen, elated by victory and ravaging the kingdom of Lothar, with an army, encountered them near the river Dila [Note: [Col. 0203D] The annalist of Fulda calls it the river Clyla, at a place called Lovonnium; others interpret this in various ways. More probably it was the river Dyla or Thylia in Brabant, which flows through the city of Leuven, as it is also called in the Annals of Metz.], where they were fortified in marshy places and were afraid to join battle. Having encouraged his soldiers, he dismissed the horses because of the difficulty of the terrain and attacked them on foot. A shout arose; then the struggle was conducted with swords at close quarters. With only one of our soldiers killed, two Northmen kings, Sigifrid and Godafrid, and their entire army, numbering many thousands, were slaughtered by the sword and drowned in the river, which blocked their flight, and were annihilated. On the same day the king, after celebrating the litanies and rendering praises to God, and after plundering much booty from the enemy, entered Alamannia and celebrated Christmas at Ulm. Annals of Fulda and Metz.

**892** In Gaul, Charles, the posthumous son of Louis the Stammerer, a youth who had been made king by certain nobles, subsequently inflicted many evils upon Odo and in turn endured them from him. Flodoard, following year. — King Arnulf, entering Pannonia, learned that Duke Zuentibald of Moravia had again rebelled against him. After conferring with Braslav, duke of Lower Pannonia, he devastated the region of Moravia in three divisions with three armies, including Hungarian auxiliaries who had recently come from the north into those regions, for an entire month. At the same time he also renewed his former friendship with the Bulgarians. Poppo was deprived of the duchy of Thuringia. Annals of Fulda. — At Rome, after Stephen, Formosus, formerly bishop of Porto, pope 113, occupied the see for four years and seven months [Note: [Col. 0204D] This belongs to the preceding year.].

**893** Engilscalc, margrave of Pannonia, was blinded by judgment of the Noricans, and his cousin William was beheaded. King Arnulf again ravaged the region of Moravia. A son, Louis, was born to the king himself by Queen Vota [Note: [Col. 0204D] Others call her Oda or Uta], and was baptized and anointed with sacred chrism by Hatto, archbishop of Mainz, and the noble Adalbero, bishop of Augsburg. — Pope Formosus, sending letters and envoys, earnestly urged King Arnulf to undertake Italy and free it from its tyrants, especially Guido. [Col. 0205A] Arnulf agreed and sent the envoys back with gifts. A severe and prolonged winter occurred this year. Annals of Fulda.

**894** A great thunderclap occurred on 28 January. Annals of Fulda. — After Guido, tyrant of Italy, died, his widow Angiltrude [also Agiltrude], together with her son Lambert, seized the tyranny. Regino; Liutprand. [Note: [Col. 0205D] Gottwicensis: “Arnulf subjected Italy and Burgundy to his kingdom”; the Annals of Metz and Fulda, restored by Bouquet, report the same. In the printed editions an entire folio is missing, evidently from a defective manuscript, such as Hermann also seems to have used, since he says very little for this year and entirely passes over Arnulf’s Italian expedition.]

**895** King Arnulf condemned to exile Hildegard, daughter of King Louis, his paternal uncle, chiefly through whose efforts he had been made king after Charles was deposed. Annals of Metz, preceding year. A great synod was convened at Tribur. German Councils, vol. II, p. 388. King Arnulf made peace with Odo, then king of Gaul, who came to him; and not long afterward he denied aid to Charles, son of King Louis the Stammerer, when Charles came and offered gifts. He also had his son by a concubine, Zuentibald, anointed king over the kingdom of Lothar. Likewise, urged by Pope Formosus through letters, he went to Italy in autumn, received Berengar, who came terrified to surrender and restored to him the kingdom he had seized, and distributed Italy on this side of the Po among the counts Waltfred and Meginfred. After ravaging everything and crossing with forces divided toward the Upper and Lower Seas, he himself celebrated Christmas at Lucca [perhaps “Luca”]. Annals of Metz and Fulda.

**896** After the army had been exhausted by a great inundation of rain and many horses had been lost, and after Berengar had also defected from his allegiance and gone over to Lambert, King Arnulf at last came to Rome. [Col. 0205C] Finding it blockaded through the machinations of Angiltrude, Guido’s widow, and her son Lambert, he attacked it at the command of Pope Formosus, who was shut inside, after the litanies had been celebrated at Saint Pancras. Having quickly conquered the city and entered it, he was honorably received by the lord pope and crowned emperor. [Note: [Col. 0205D] Some write that this occurred in April, which is scarcely credible, since Pope Formosus had already died on the fourth day of that month, so that this solemnity would have had to take place during the sacred three-day period. But since Arnulf, in a charter issued at Rome for the monastery of Amiata on 26 February in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 896 (Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. III, p. 614), already calls himself Emperor Augustus, he must have been crowned before 27 February.] After arranging matters there and binding the leading men by oath, he resolved to pursue Angiltrude but began to fall ill. Fearing a more serious illness, he hastened to return immediately from Italy. After his return, Berengar and Lambert divided the kingdom of Italy between them and exercised tyranny; Lambert ordered Count Meginfred to be beheaded. Annals of Fulda. — Pope Formosus died on Easter Day. In his place Boniface VI, pope 114, was ordained but died of gout on the fifteenth day. Stephen VI, formerly bishop of Campania, pope 115, succeeded him and occupied the see for one year. Favoring the tyrants and hating Arnulf, he had Pope Formosus exhumed eight months after his death and placed in a chair. With a deacon speaking for him, he accused and degraded him as though convicted, then ordered him dragged by the feet and thrown into the Tiber. But the Roman citizens, terrified by divine miracles worked through Formosus’s merits, not long afterward expelled Stephen, who had been deservedly tortured, and restored Formosus to his tomb. Annals of Fulda; Liutprand. — In the same year, when the Greeks made peace with the wandering Hungarian enemies, the Bulgarians, angered, invaded Greece and ravaged it as far as Constantinople. Meanwhile, deceived by Greek cunning, the Hungarians laid waste to the land of the Bulgarians with sword, plunder, and fire. When the Bulgarians returned, they were twice defeated and beaten in battle by them and turned their backs. Only at the third attempt, after praying more fervently for divine grace, did they win a bloody victory, having lost twenty thousand of their own and barely routing the enemy. There was also such a famine this year that innumerable people perished from hunger, and some Christians even ate one another. Emperor Arnulf fell when a building collapsed, severely crushing his body together with many others. Annals of Fulda.

**897** A great famine consumed many in Bavaria. The Bohemians sought aid from Emperor Arnulf against the Moravians. — At Rome, after the death of Stephen, Romanus, pope 116, occupied the see for a little more than four months. After him Theodore II, pope 117, occupied it for twenty days. After Theodore, John IX, pope 118, was ordained and occupied the see for two years [Note: [Col. 0206D] This partly belongs to the following year]. Emperor Arnulf, after holding an assembly, trusting no one, demanded anew from everyone an oath of fidelity to himself and to his young son Louis. Annals of Fulda.

**898** A deadly quarrel arose between the brothers Zuentibald and Moymar [also Moymirus], dukes of Moravia. Margrave Luitpold [Note: [Col. 0206D] Namely, Luitpold, margrave of Austria], together with others, ravaged the Moravians, who were in rebellion against the emperor. Annals of Fulda.

[Col. 0207A] **899** The Bavarians likewise ravaged the borders of the Moravians in winter. Queen Oda, accused by rumor of adultery with certain men, was acquitted at an assembly in Regensburg by the oath of seventy-two nobles [Note: [Col. 0207C] Others count eighty-two nobles]. Emperor Arnulf was crippled by paralysis, and some people were consequently accused and punished for poisoning or sorcery. The Bavarians again ravaged the land of the Moravians. Isanric [Note: [Col. 0207C] He was the son of Arbo, margrave of Austria], rebelling against the emperor and being besieged and forced to surrender, likewise fled to the Moravians. At Rome Benedict IV, pope 119, occupied the see for three years and five months [Note: [Col. 0207C] The election of Benedict IV first took place toward the end of the following year]. Annals of Fulda.

**900** Emperor Arnulf, while ill at Regensburg, where he stayed most frequently, died [Note: [Col. 0207C] Regino, the Annals of Metz, and others place his death on 29 November of the preceding year. [Col. 0207D] The same year is assigned by the Fulda Necrology in Leibniz, *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium*, vol. III, p. 763] and was buried in the basilica of Saint Emmeram, in the twelfth year of his reign. His son Louis, a child, was established in the kingdom. [Col. 0207B] His brother by a concubine, Zuentibald, king of Belgian Gaul, acted cruelly and recklessly, coveted the property of the churches, and even struck Ratpot, archbishop of Trier, on the head with a staff. Despised and abandoned by his own men, he rashly attempted to engage them in battle with inadequate forces and was killed. Regino, chronicle; Annals of Fulda. — The Bavarians, passing through Bohemia and taking the Bohemians with them, again devastated the region of Moravia. The Hungarians, new enemies, ravaged much of Italy and, having joined battle, killed twenty thousand Italians in one day. Invading Bavaria, which they had reconnoitered, they carried away much booty around the river Anesus [also Anasus, Ens]. They likewise occupied Pannonia after devastating it. — Margrave Luitpold [Note: [Col. 0207D] Luitpold, margrave of Austria], engaging some Hungarian forces with a few Noricans [Col. 0208A], killed 1,200 of them, losing only one of his own men [Note: [Col. 0207D] Here the Annals of Fulda end, and from this point Hermann becomes briefer]. Annals of Fulda.

**901** The Hungarians, making for Carantania, joined battle, were defeated and beaten, and fled. In the same year Moymar, duke of Moravia, and Isanric, count of Noricum, [174] who had defected to him, were reconciled with King Louis. Supplement to the Annals of Fulda.

**902** The Hungarians attacked the Moravians, but, defeated in battle, turned their backs. Annals of Saxony. — In the same year, the noble German brothers Beringer, Reginolf, and Gerhard, sons of Count Ato and Adellinda, were near the convent of virgins at Buchau, in the Alamannian district of Erichgewe [Note: [Col. 0207D] A district of nearly the same name appears in the charters of Saint Gall in Goldast, namely Argangawe and Arguna; it should not be confused with the Swiss district of Aargau], in a monastery built by their mother at that very time [Note: [Col. 0207D] This is a more credible, though later, origin of this famous nunnery than the fabulous account traced by Brusch and Bucelinus all the way back to Charlemagne. See Brunner, *Annales Boici*, part I, p. 305. Also Crusius, *Annales Suevici*, part I, book XI, chapter 8, p. 307, whose credibility on this point has now become suspect. The Bollandists treated all this more fully, though not sufficiently carefully, in vol. VI of the August collection, 28 August, in the Life of Blessed Aldelinda, abbess, p. 492. See the year 799. Ato, or Hatto or Otto, count of Kesselburg, is said to have been in the region of Lake Plumbarius.] out of devotion to Saint Cornelius and Saint Cyprian, martyrs. As they were secretly taking their virgin sister away in order to give her in marriage [Col. 0208B], they were surrounded and killed by their enemies and buried by their mother near the same convent. She too, after visiting Jerusalem and other holy places for the sake of prayer and returning, devoted to divine service and eager for the salvation of souls, happily ended this life and was buried there. Her virgin daughter, bearing the same name, was appointed abbess of the place.

**904** At Rome, after Benedict, Leo V [Note: [Col. 0208D] This occurred in the preceding year], formerly a priest of the Forum, pope 120, occupied the see for approximately two months. After him, as I have found in certain sources, Christopher, formerly a cardinal, pope 121, occupied it for four months; he was deposed and made a monk [Note: [Col. 0208D] That is, he was thrust into a monastery].

**905** At Rome Sergius III, pope 122, occupied the see for seven years and four months; elsewhere, the preceding year.

[Col. 0208C] **906** Adalbert, a noble and warlike Frank of Babenberg [Col. 0209A] [Note: [Col. 0209C] Son of Henry, duke of Eastern Francia. See the years 883 and 886. Conrad, count of Hesse or Wetterau. Regino], joined battle with his rival Conrad, defeated him, and killed him with many others [Note: [Col. 0209C] The Annals of Metz place the death of the elder Count Conrad, father of Conrad who later became king, in the year 905, on 27 February at Fritzlar]. Regino, preceding year.

**907** When Adalbert’s estates, because he was in rebellion, were being ravaged by King Louis and his castle was being attacked, he was brought, as rumor has it [Note: [Col. 0209D] Hermann writes “according to rumor,” but Ekkehard, in *The Disasters of Saint Gall*, says that the story was commonly embellished and sung. See Eccard, *Rerum Francicarum*, vol. II, p. 811, where he denies this event together with others. The Annals of Metz likewise say nothing of it; they call this castle Terassa, while others call it Babenberg. Marianus and Sigebert likewise mention the treachery, as does Liutprand, *History*, book II, chapter 3, and especially Otto of Freising, book VI, chapter 15. See Calles, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 33 ff.], to King Louis in the hope of an agreement through the treachery of Archbishop Hatto and a certain Luitpold, in whom he placed great confidence, and was ordered to be beheaded. Regino, year 905; elsewhere, year 996. — The Bavarians were defeated in battle against the Hungarians. Annals of Metz.

**908** The Hungarians widely ravaged Saxony and Thuringia. Annals of Saxony; year 996. Luitpold was killed [Note: [Col. 0209D] Namely, in battle against the Hungarians. This Luitpold was duke or count of the Bavarian frontier and seems to be the same man mentioned in the preceding year. Aventinus, book IV, chapter 21].

**909** The Hungarians invaded and ravaged Alamannia. Continuation of Regino; Hepidanus.

[Col. 0209B] **910** The Hungarians, making for Francia [Note: [Col. 0209D] Eastern Francia, or Franconia, is meant here], joined battle and prevailed. Hepidanus; continuation of Regino. — The venerable and famous Adalbero, bishop of Augsburg, died; after him Hiltine presided for thirteen years. Hepidanus.

**911** King Louis, a young man, died and was buried at Regensburg. Hepidanus. After him, since the royal line had failed in our regions, Conrad, son of Conrad [Note: [Col. 0209D] Son of the count of Franconia who was killed by Adalbert in 905, and of Glismoda, daughter of Emperor Arnulf], was elected king, anointed, and reigned for seven years. [Col. 0210A] Continuation of Regino. — Burchard, duke of Alamannia, was killed when a disturbance arose at his assembly; in his place Erchanger seized the duchy [Note: [Col. 0209D] Two dukes named Burchard are reported as having been killed around this time, and writers sometimes confuse them. The first was Burchard, duke of the Thuringians, or prefect of the Thuringian frontier, killed with others by the Hungarians in battle, as the Saxon chronicle reports under 908 and Eccard proves, *Rerum Francicarum Orientalium*, vol. II, p. 819. The other was Burchard I, duke of Alamannia, who, according to Hermann, was killed this year, 911, at his assembly; after him Erchanger seized the duchy. Ekkehard the Younger, *The Disasters of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, chapter 1, calls him, together with his brother Berthold, who were both beheaded in 917, “the chamberlains’ envoys in Swabia.”].

**912** The Hungarians likewise attacked Bavaria. The Bavarian and Alamannian forces assembled and engaged them near the river Ine [Note: Namely, the Inn]; the Hungarians were routed with great slaughter. Chronicle of Augsburg, year 913; Hepidanus. — Comets were seen this year. King Rudolf of Burgundy died, and his son Rudolf administered the rights of that kingdom for twenty-five years. Elsewhere, 911. — At Rome Anastasius [Note: [Col. 0209D] This is Anastasius III, elected the preceding year], pope 123, occupied the see for two years and two months. At Saint Gall the learned master Notker died [Note: [Col. 0209D] Surnamed Balbulus, “the Stammerer.” Ekkehard the Younger wrote his Life]. Bishop Otpertus was killed. Einhard was blinded. Continuation of Regino; Annals of Saxony.

**913** The Hungarians again came out and ravaged Alamannia. [Col. 0210B] At Mainz, after Archbishop Hatto [Note: [Col. 0210D] According to the continuation of Regino and the chronicle of Würzburg, Hatto died in 912] and the abbot of Reichenau had died, Heriger succeeded to the bishopric for fourteen years, while Abbot Hug, the eighteenth abbot, presided for one year. Chronicle of Augsburg.

**914** Salomon, bishop of Constance and abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, was captured by a certain insolent man and imprisoned [Note: [Col. 0210D] Ekkehard the Younger, *The Disasters of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, chapter 1, says that this was done by Erchanger and Berthold, the chamberlains’ envoys, who had seized the duchy of Swabia]. At Reichenau, after Hugh, Thietingus presided as nineteenth abbot for three years.

[177] **915** At Rome Lando, pope 124, occupied the see for five months; after him Leo VI, pope 125, for approximately two months; and after him John X, pope 126, for fourteen years and two months [Note: [Col. 0211C] This order is reversed. Lando died in 914 and John X succeeded him in the same year; Leo VI first succeeded John in 928, and ruled not for two months but for seven].

**916** The Hungarians again came out and, among their other evils, pitiably ravaged nearly all Alamannia with fire and sword. Annals of Saxony, year 915. — In the same year a synod was held at Altheim in the presence of a papal legate. — At Reichenau, after Abbot Thietingus had died, Heribraht became the twentieth abbot and presided for ten years. At Saint Gall the blessed virgin Wiborada was enclosed more strictly. Hepidanus.

**917** After invading Alamannia as they had begun to do, the Hungarians destroyed the city of Basel. Then, having ravaged Alsace, they invaded the kingdom of Lothar, inflicting much harm. Continuation of Regino. — Erchanger, who had seized the duchy of Alamannia, and his brother Berthold rebelled against King Conrad. At last they came to him in the hope of an agreement to surrender, and by his command were beheaded at the village of Adinga on 21 January [Note: [Col. 0211C] I have not found it noted which village Adinga this was. It seems, however, to have been the village of Ottingen in the same district of Rhaetia, on the river Wörnitz]. Chronicle of Augsburg; Ekkehard the Younger.

**918** Burchard [Note: [Col. 0211D] With the assent of the leading men of Swabia, Burchard, the first duke of the Alamanni, a man of the highest nobility and distinguished by the endowment of virtues, was appointed; these are the words of Ekkehard the Younger, p. 19. See Tentzelius, *Vindications*, pp. 218, 228], having been made duke of Alamannia, seized the tyranny. King Conrad died [Note: [Col. 0211D] On 23 December, according to Marianus Scotus and the Fulda Necrology]. Continuation of Regino.

[178] **919** Henry, a count by birth a Saxon, was elected to the kingdom and reigned without royal anointing for eighteen years. Widukind. — A battle was fought at Winterthur between Rudolf, king of Burgundy, and Burchard, duke of Alamannia; the king was defeated and put to flight by the duke. Hepidanus. — After Salomon, bishop of Constance and abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, died, Notingus succeeded him in the bishopric for fifteen years, and Hartmann in the abbey for nearly four years. Elsewhere, 920.

**920** King Charles of Gaul came into Francia [Note: [Col. 0211D] Charles the Simple, king of Gaul, marched against Henry into the district of Worms. Flodoard; Widukind]. At Saint Gall Rachildis was enclosed as a virgin. Hepidanus.

**922** Liuthard, appointed provost of Reichenau by Duke Burchard after Heribert had been oppressed [Note: [Col. 0211D] This abbot of Reichenau is called Heribraht under the year 916. See Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictines*, vol. III, p. 371], and the brothers were sent into exile.

**923** The blood of the Lord was brought to the island of Reichenau by a certain matron, as is contained in a written historical account preserved there [Note: [Col. 0211D] Mabillon published the history of this translation from a Reichenau parchment manuscript, cited above. The Engelberg codex records 8 November. See the Annals of Saxony]. At Saint Gall Engelbert was appointed abbot and presided for nine years [Note: [Col. 0212C] Hepidanus assigns this to the following year].

**924** Saint Voldaric was ordained bishop of Augsburg [Note: [Col. 0212C] Namely, on 28 December 923. See the entry for 924] and presided with remarkable piety and devotion [Col. 0212B] for fifty years.

**925** As the Hungarians roamed through Alamannia ravaging it and also reached the monastery of Saint Gall, the enclosed virgin Wiborada was killed by one of them and crowned with martyrdom after her cell had been broken open, while Rachildis, her fellow recluse, was miraculously preserved unharmed by divine power [Note: [Col. 0212D] See the younger Hepidanus, *On the Life and Miracles of Saint Wiborada*, in Goldast, *German Affairs*, vol. I, p. 206].

[179] **926** After ravaging Alamannia, the Hungarians traversed all Francia, Alsace, and Gaul, raging with fire and sword. Continuation of Regino. — Duke Burchard was killed [Note: [Col. 0212D] Namely, while bringing aid in Italy to Rudolf, king of Burgundy. Saxon Chronicle. In the book of fraternities of Saint Gall (Goldast, vol. II, p. 153), where a solemn commemoration was also established for him, his day of death is recorded as 3 November 925. But the Chronicle of Saint Gall (Duchesne, vol. III, p. 471) says that he died after falling from his horse in 926, on 2 May, a Monday; this date indicates the preceding year]. Liutprand; Hartmann. — King Henry [Col. 0213A] held a great assembly at Worms. Hermann [Note: [Col. 0213D] This Hermann was the son of Gerard, or Gebhard, duke of Eastern Francia and kinsman of King Conrad I. Clem.] was advanced as duke of Alamannia. Continuation of Regino. — At Reichenau Liuthard became the twenty-first abbot and presided for eight years.

**927** Heriger, archbishop of Mainz, died, and Hildibert received the archiepiscopal office in his place [Note: [Col. 0213D] Gallia Christiana assigns this, with certain chronicles, to 924. But the Fulda Necrology and the Chronicle of Würzburg more correctly assign it to this year].

**929** At Rome Stephen VII, pope 127, occupied the see for two years and one month. Flodoard.

**930** King Henry attacked Bohemia. Annals of Saxony, year 928.

**931** At Rome John XI, pope 128, occupied the see for four years. Liutprand. — King Henry compelled the kings of the Abodrites and Northmen to become Christians, and himself went into Gaul. Chronicle of Augsburg; continuation of Regino.

**932** As the Hungarians made for the province of the Sorbs, they were routed with slaughter by King Henry’s army; many of them were captured. Flodoard, following year; continuation of Regino, year 934.

**933** At Saint Gall Thieto presided as abbot for approximately ten years.

**934** At Constance, after Bishop Notingus died, Conrad, a prelate distinguished by birth and life, was ordained and nobly governed that church for forty-one years [Note: [Col. 0213D] His Life is in Pistor, vol. III, and Leibniz, vol. II; Hepidanus assigns it to the following year]. At Reichenau, after Liuthard, Alawicus, a venerable abbot, presided as the twenty-second abbot for twenty-five years. Eberhard, provost of Strasbourg, the first occupant [Note: [Col. 0213D] [ [Col. 0213D] The callout number for this note is printed in the text as (455).] Others assign this to the preceding year] of the cell of Meginrad, arrived [Note: [Col. 0213D] Life of Saint Udalric, chapter 50, and Guillimann, in his account of Ruthard, bishop of Strasbourg].

**935** At Rome Leo VII, pope [Note: [Col. 0214D] He was ordained at the beginning of the following year] 129, occupied the see for three years and six months. Flodoard.

[Col. 0213C] **936** King Henry died and was buried in Saxony at Quedlinburg [Note: [Col. 0214D] Quedlinburg, where he had begun to build a convent of virgins]. His son Otto, receiving the governance of the kingdom, ruled it vigorously for approximately thirty-eight years. Chronicle of Augsburg; Liutprand.

**937** The Hungarians roamed through Bavaria, Alamannia, and Eastern Francia, raging with plunder, sword, and fire. After crossing the Rhine at Worms, they ravaged Alsace, the kingdom of Lothar, and the neighboring regions of Gaul as far as the Ocean; then, passing through Burgundy and Italy, they finally returned to Pannonia. Widukind; Flodoard. — The monasteries of Saint Boniface and Saint Gall were consumed by fire. Continuation of Regino; Ekkehard the Younger. — In the same year Rudolf, king of Burgundy, died and was buried at Agaunum near Saint Maurice. His son Conrad [Note: [Col. 0214D] Surnamed “the Peaceful,” brother of Adelheid, later the wife of Otto I] succeeded to the kingdom. When Arnulf, duke of Bavaria, also died, his duchy was received by Berthold [Note: [Col. 0214D] Brother of Arnulf the Bad]. Fulda Necrology; continuation of Regino. — The Bavarians and many others rebelled against King Otto.

[181] **938** King Otto marched out against the Bavarians. Meanwhile his brother Henry was captured by Eberhard [Note: [Col. 0214D] Eberhard was duke of the Franks and brother of King Conrad I]. After Henry was freed and Eberhard was banished into exile, Otto again invaded Noricum with an army and subdued everyone except Arnulf, son of Duke Arnulf. Meanwhile the Hungarians invaded Saxony, but were defeated in battle by the Saxons, beaten, and put to flight. Widukind. — At Rome Stephen VIII, pope 130, occupied the see for three years and four months [Note: [Col. 0214D] This belongs to the following year].

**939** King Otto, attacking the rebellious Lotharingians, came with an army as far as Caprimons. Continuation of Regino. — Meanwhile Louis, king of Gaul and son of Charles, invaded Alsace. But when Otto learned of this and returned, Louis was terrified and withdrew to his own kingdom. While the castle of Breisach, besieged by King Otto, was being attacked, the leaders of the rebellion, Duke Eberhard, were killed, and Duke Giselbert [Note: [Col. 0214D] Giselbert, duke of Upper Lotharingia, had married Gerberga, sister of Otto the Great] was drowned and died in the Rhine. The bishops and others who had come with them against the king were put to flight and scattered. King Otto, after the castle surrendered, returned to the kingdom of Lothar and subdued all the rebels except the bishop of Metz. Widukind; continuation of Regino. — His brother Henry also laid down his arms and submitted to him. Flodoard; continuation of Regino.

**940** King Otto, marching into Gaul against King Louis, ravaged a great part of the province as far as the river Seine and received Hugh and Heribert, nobles who came to him. Flodoard. — A severe winter occurred this year, followed by a pestilence among the animals. Hugh, son of Richard, died [Note: [Col. 0215D] Hugh, surnamed “the Black,” son of Richard, duke of Burgundy, and brother of Rudolf, king of Gaul, first died in 951].

**942** King Otto was reconciled with Louis, king of Gaul. Flodoard. — A comet was seen for fourteen nights, and an immense pestilence among the animals occurred. Continuation of Regino. — At Rome Marinus II, pope 131, occupied the see for three years and six months.

[182] **943** The Hungarians again invaded Bavaria, joined battle with the Bavarians, were defeated, and turned their backs. At Saint Gall Gralo [also Cralo] presided as abbot for seventeen years. Hepidanus; Chronicle of Salzburg.

**944** An earthquake occurred on 16 April. Hepidanus.

**945** At Rome Agapetus II, pope 132, occupied the see for approximately ten years. Elsewhere, the following year. — King Otto marched into Lower Gaul. Flodoard, following year.

**946** At Saint Gall Rachildis, the enclosed virgin, departed to the Lord. Hepidanus.

**947** After Berthold, duke of Bavaria, died, Henry, brother of King Otto, received that duchy. Continuation of Regino, year 945 [Col. 0215C]. — Luitolf, the king’s son, married Ita, a praiseworthy woman [Note: [Col. 0215D] Daughter of Hermann, duke of Alamannia]. Mimidona [Note: [Col. 0215D] Namely, the city of Münster, unless one wishes to understand Minden, since at the synod of Ingelheim in 948 Eberisus, bishop of Mimidona, or Minden, is mentioned. Perhaps, therefore, Mimidona should be read here] was consumed by fire. Annals of Saxony, following year.

**948** Hermann, duke of Alamannia, who, as is reported, had greatly improved the worship, dress, customs, and institutions of the province entrusted to him, died and was buried at Reichenau in the chapel of Saint Kilian. Luitolf, son of King Otto, a man more beloved by the whole people than anyone else of his time, was appointed duke in his place by his father. Widukind; Hepidanus. — A great synod of thirty bishops was held at Ingelheim in the presence of Otto and Louis, kings [Note: [Col. 0215D] See German Councils, vol. II, p. 610. Canisius published its acts from the Weingarten codex, *Ancient Readings*, vol. III, part I, p. 8]. In the same year Lindau was consumed by fire. Hepidanus. — A chapel in the monastery of Saint Meginrad was consecrated from heaven on 14 September [Note: [Col. 0215D] We noted in the preliminary dissertation that this addition, if it is genuine, appears sufficiently ancient and contemporary with the codex].

[183] **949** After Lothar, king of Italy, died [Note: [Col. 0216D] Lothar actually died only at the end of 950. Muratori, *Antiquities of Italy*, under 949 and the following years], Berengar seized the kingdom and afflicted and confined his widow Adelheid, daughter of Rudolf II, king of Burgundy, with many injuries. She escaped only with difficulty and awaited King Otto’s arrival amid many hardships. [Col. 0216B] Leo of Ostia; Sigonius, year 951.

**950** King Otto went to Italy, subjected it to himself, drove out King Berengar, who was unable to resist, and freed the lady Adelheid, his future wife. Continuation of Regino, following year.

**951** A synod [Note: [Col. 0216D] Both the Synod of Augsburg and the other events related here belong to the following year. See German Councils, vol. II, p. 622. Thus these two years seem to have been largely transposed. See the continuation of Regino under 952. Canisius presents the acts of this synod from the Weingarten codex, *Ancient Readings*, vol. III, part I, p. 2] of twenty-five bishops and a great assembly of all the nobles of the kingdom was convened at Augsburg. There Berengar came to King Otto to surrender and promised submission. Widukind. — Among other portents, a fiery stone, like a mass of glowing iron, came through the air from the west, and a dragon was seen walking.

**952** King Otto marched toward Bohemia, and his son Duke Luitolf toward Italy [Note: [Col. 0216D] This belongs to the year 950. Continuation of Regino, years 950 and following]. King Otto entered Italy again together with his son Luitolf, and a royal marriage was celebrated at Pavia. A quarrel arose between Duke Luitolf and his uncle, Duke Henry. Widukind. — Frederick, archbishop of Mainz, and Hardpert, bishop of Chur, were sent by the king to Rome.

[Col. 0217A] **953** King Otto, favoring his brother Henry, stirred up his son Luitolf against himself, and great disturbance arose throughout the kingdom from the competing zeal of rival parties. Continuation of Regino; Widukind. — [184] Arnulf, son of Arnulf, formerly duke of the Noricans, joining Luitolf’s party against the king, plundered the city of Augsburg and its bishopric. He attempted to capture or kill the blessed Bishop Vodalric, who was loyal to the king, after besieging him in the castle of Mandichingen [Note: [Col. 0217C] In the Life of Saint Udalric, vol. II of the July Bollandists, p. 108, this castle is called Monichingen; today it is Schwabmünchingen, on the borders of Bavaria, not far from Augsburg]. But when Adalbert, count of Marhtal, arrived with troops [Note: [Col. 0217C] He seems to have been Adelbero, son of Berthold, who, according to Hepidanus, was killed this year. Eckhart, vol. II of *Eastern Frankish Affairs*, p. 813, makes Berthold, father of Adalbert [Col. 0217D], the son of Henry, brother of Adalbert of Babenberg, who was beheaded in 905. This Henry had his principal seat at Martala, Mertela, or rather Amardela, near Sulzbach; hence his nephew Adalbert was called count of Marhtal], and Theodpald, the bishop’s brother, also a count, Arnulf was defeated in battle and shamefully driven back. Not long afterward he and all his supporters were deservedly punished by divine vengeance. In that encounter Count Adalbert died from a minor wound and was honorably buried by the holy bishop at Augsburg [Col. 0217B]. Life of Saint Udalric. — Later, when the quarrel grew stronger and King Otto and his son Duke Luitolf had gathered armies against one another, they encamped near the river Hilara [Note: [Col. 0217D] The Hilara or Ilarus is a river of Swabia, from which the district of Ilargau is named; the town of Tussen, also called Tüssen or Illertissen, lies beside it] and a village called Tussa, on the very point of joining battle. But, through the intervention of the holy bishops Vodalric of Augsburg and Hardpert of Chur, by God’s gift they were reconciled and formed an alliance. Flodoard, year 954.

**954** The Hungarians again came out and ravaged Francia, Bavaria, and Italy. Continuation of Regino; Flodoard.

### 955

The Hungarians, with forces such as had never before been seen, traversed Bavaria, crossed the river Lech, and burned the basilica of Saint Afra at Augsburg. They surrounded the holy bishop Udalric, who was earnestly imploring divine assistance, together with his men at Augsburg, making a din with their weapons. But when King Otto arrived with his army, on 10 August, an exceedingly fierce battle was fought. Much human blood was shed; an immense slaughter of the Hungarians followed; the riverbed was filled with the corpses of those fleeing and dying; and, with only very few escaping by flight, their innumerable army was destroyed to the last man. Those who were then able to escape were afterward captured and killed throughout Bavaria wherever they were found. Among them their kings were seized and hanged on gallows at Regensburg.

In that battle, on our side, among many others, fell Duke Conrad, a warlike man and pious royal son-in-law [Note: This was the duke of Worms, in Franconia and Lotharingia, husband of Luitgard, daughter of Otto I, formerly a rebel against the king. Otto of Freising.], and the holy bishop’s brother, Count Theodpald [Note: Namely, of Kiburg and Dillingen.], as well as Count Reginbald, the son of his sister [Note: That is, of Luitgard, the first wife of Burchard III, or the Younger, duke of Alemannia.] and the paternal uncle of my grandmother Bertha [Note: Here Hermann makes the first mention of his own family, about which he will say more below in the account of his life.]. Regino’s Continuation; Hepidanus; Frodoard; Widukind.

At Rome John XII, also called Octavian, the 130th pope, occupied the see for eight years and four months. Forgetful, alas, and most grievously so, of the dignity of his office, he led his life devoted to vanity and filth. Another annal.

At Mainz Archbishop Frederick died, and Hatto succeeded him [Note: This is an anachronism. For when Frederick died in 954, not Hatto but William succeeded him, as the author himself admits at the end of the Chronicle of Reichenau (vol. I of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*) in these words, which also help to clarify the preceding events: “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 954, indiction XII, the venerable lord Frithuric, archbishop of the holy church of Mainz, died on 25 October. In that same year I, William, unworthy of so great a succession, was elected in his place, with the consent of the clergy and people of that holy see, on 17 December, on the very day on which peace was made between King Otto and his son Liudolf at Arnstadt; and on 24 December I was ordained at Mainz.”” Concerning this assembly at Arnstadt, see *Concilia Germaniae*, vol. II, p. 624.]. Henry also, duke of Bavaria and the king’s brother, died and left behind a son of the same name as his successor. Regino’s Continuation.

### 956

Duke Liudolf invaded Italy in a hostile manner. After putting Berengar and his son to flight, he took possession of the city and province of Pavia. Regino’s Continuation.

### 957

Duke Liudolf, having engaged Adalbert in battle, defeated him and subjected everyone, together with the kingdom of Italy, to himself. In that same year, however, he died prematurely at Plumbino [Note: Plumbinum, or Piombino, a city of Italy in Etruria.] and was buried at Mainz amid the great grief of many, leaving his son Otto, still a small child, as his survivor. Burchard also received the duchy of Alemannia [Note: We shall discuss this Burchard III below, in the Life of Hermann.]. Regino’s Continuation; Widukind.

### 958

After Alawic, abbot of Reichenau, had died, Eggehard, the twenty-third abbot, presided for fifteen years. He built there the church of Saint John the Baptist with beautiful workmanship. Hepidanus, under the year 959.

Some people displayed signs of the cross on their garments. Eberhard, provost of Strasbourg, came with a great retinue to the cell of Saint Meinrad and established a regular life there. In the twenty-fifth year after his entry, he departed to the Lord [Note: See Hermann under the year 934 and the *Annals of Einsiedeln* in Mabillon, *Vetera Analecta*, p. 368, and vol. III of the *Annales*, p. 539, as well as *Acta Sanctorum*, Benedictine century V, p. 241.].

### 959

At Saint Gall, Abbot Anno presided for a little more than one year [Note: He had already died in 954; after his brother and predecessor Cralo, he was restored to office and died in 959.].

### 960

At Saint Gall, Abbot Burchard presided for thirteen years [Note: This belongs to the preceding year, according to Hepidanus.

In the Reichenau manuscript, an interpolator added: “Gregory becomes abbot.” For this, the Chronicle of Saint Blasien says: “Gregory is appointed first abbot of the cell of Saint Meinrad,” but this is erroneous. For already under the year 945 another hand in the same Reichenau manuscript records: “Father Thietland came, the first abbot of this place.” Yet this note too is misplaced, since Eberhard is already called abbot in a diploma of Emperor Otto I from 946 (Hartmann, *Annals of Einsiedeln*, p. 46). When Eberhard died in 958, Thietland succeeded him; he is named the abbot then governing in another diploma of the same Otto from 961 (ibid., p. 63). Thus Gregory could have been neither the first abbot nor abbot in 960.].

### 961

King Otto caused his son of the same name, by Queen Adelaide, to be elected king, and he himself set out for Italy with an army. A sign appeared in the sun.

### 962

King Otto came to Rome and was crowned emperor by Pope John, or Octavian, with an imperial anointing. He reproached the pope for the crimes that rumor was spreading about him, but was unable to correct his disgraceful conduct.

### 963

Emperor Otto spent Christmas at Pavia. In that same year, partly for other reasons but especially to judge the crimes of Pope John, which he heard were being increasingly denounced, he came to Rome. When the pope learned this, he fled toward Campania and hid there in the forests and mountains. In his place, the Romans and the emperor elected the venerable Leo VIII, who was ordained the 134th pope [Note: The Continuator of Regino likewise recounts the matter under this year, though Frodoard in his Chronicle under the year 965 differs from him in some details. The synod at which John was deposed was held at Rome from 6 to 22 November; some of its acts are preserved at the end of Liutprand’s *History*. Baronius considers this synod and its acts illegitimate, whereas Fleury, Turrecremata, and other earlier authorities regard them as legitimate. See Liutprand, *History*, book VI, chapters 6 and following.].

### 964

Emperor Otto celebrated Christmas at Rome. While he was afterward visiting other parts of Italy, the Romans rose not long afterward against Pope Leo and attempted to kill him and restore John. The pope, however, fled from the city into the region of Spoleto and came to the emperor, complaining to him of his injuries. When the enraged emperor returned to Rome with a hostile army, the death of the wicked John was announced to him, and the Romans asked that the deacon Benedict be made pope. Although the emperor refused, this same Benedict, the fifth of that name and the 135th pope, was ordained against the emperor’s wishes and occupied the see for two months. The city was besieged by the emperor and oppressed by such famine that a bushel of bran sold for thirty denarii. Not long afterward, when the Romans had been afflicted and subdued, the emperor took possession of the city, received Benedict into his custody, restored Pope Leo, and compelled the Romans by oath to promise Pope Leo submission and fidelity. Yet this pope was afterward subjected to many injuries by those same Romans. Continuation of Regino; Liutprand, *History*, book VI, chapter 2.

In the same year, while the king was staying at Rome with the other princes, the same pope confirmed in writing before the princes the consecration of the chapel at the monastery of Saint Meinrad, which had been accomplished by heavenly intervention [Note: Hartmann prints this bull, dated 11 November 964, in his *Annals of Einsiedeln*, p. 71. Critics have raised many objections to it, examined in the new *Chronicle of Einsiedeln*, part II.].

### 965

Emperor Otto, remaining at Pavia for Christmas, returned from Italy by way of Mount Cenis and celebrated the octave of Epiphany at Chur. Duke Burchard of the Swabians, however, invading Italy in a hostile manner, defeated Adalbert in battle and put him to flight, killed his brother Wido, and returned victorious to the emperor.

In that same year Bruno, the venerable archbishop of Cologne, brother of Emperor Otto, died. His Life has been published in writing by certain authors [Note: The first to write this Life of Saint Bruno, at the command of Folcmar, his successor, was Rotger, or Roger, a monk of Saint Pantaleon at Cologne. It is found in volume V of the Bollandist October, p. 698, and in Leibniz’s *Scriptores Rerum Brunsvicensium*, vol. I, p. 273.].

### 966

After Leo died at Rome, John XIII, previously bishop of Narni, the 136th pope, occupied the see for approximately seven years [Note: This had already occurred in the preceding year.].

### 968

A solar eclipse occurred on 21 November [Note: No solar eclipse occurred this year on 21 November; one did occur on 22 December, or 11 days before the Kalends of January, as it also seems that our manuscripts should be corrected. Hepidanus gives the day correctly but is mistaken in assigning it to the year 970.].

### 969

At this time Count Rodfred and the prefect Peter, together with certain other Romans, seized Pope John, confined him in the Castle of Saint Angelo, and finally sent him into exile in Campania. They mistreated him for ten months or more, until, after Rodfred had been killed by a certain John, son of Crescentius, he was at last scarcely released and returned to his own see [Note: Pagi, together with the Continuator of Regino, assigns all these events, as well as those of the following year, to 965 and the year immediately following.]. Continuation of Regino under 965.

### 970

Emperor Otto again invaded the Italian provinces. Coming to Rome, he severely avenged the injuries inflicted upon the lord pope by the authors of the crime—some by exile, some by the gallows, and others by various punishments and acts of disgrace. Another annal, 967.

### 971

While Emperor Otto was staying in Italy, blessed Udalric, bishop of Augsburg, now very old and infirm, went to Rome for the sake of prayer. He approached the emperor and obtained from him that his episcopal see should be assigned to Adalbero, a cleric, son of his sister Luitgard and of Count Peiere [Note: Otto moved against the Greeks in Calabria in 969 and finally returned to Germany in 972. The events here related about Saint Udalric, however, are said by the author of his Life to have taken place at Ravenna, chapter 9; likewise, chapter 10 identifies the events soon to be related concerning the council at Ingelheim. See volume II of the Bollandist July, p. 115 and following. Count Peiere, or Adalbero’s parentage, will be examined more fully below in the Life of Hermann.]. A sign of fiery color appeared in the sky.

### 972

At Reichenau, after Abbot Eggehard had been accused of reducing the church’s resources to poverty and had been deprived of office by Emperor Otto, Provost Ruodmann was promoted as the twenty-fourth abbot. He presided for twenty-four years and enriched the monastery excessively.

A synod was assembled at Ingelheim by the bishops. There blessed Bishop Udalric and Adalbero, his sister’s son, were accused of violating the canons. After presenting and defending their case, they were acquitted and returned [Note: *Concilia Germaniae*, vol. II, p. 654.].

At Rome Benedict VI, the 137th pope, presided for one year and ten months. At Saint Gall, Abbot Notker presided for four years.

### 973

When blessed Bishop Udalric was celebrating Easter at the castle of Dillingen with Count Richwin, the son of his brother Theobald, Adalbero the cleric—who was expected to become bishop after him—was there subjected to bloodletting and died suddenly. He was buried at Augsburg in the basilica of Saint Afra by his uncle, the holy bishop. Among his other good works, the blessed bishop obtained from Emperor Otto, by a privilege of exemption, that the monastery of Ottobeuren, which was subject to him, should be freed from his jurisdiction [Note: Ottobeuren, a monastery of Saint Benedict in the Günz valley, had been granted to the aforesaid Adalbero. After his death, the holy prelate obtained it for himself and later restored it free to the monks. See chapter 10 of his Life, volume II of the Bollandist July.].

At about the same time, on the Nones of May, Emperor Otto died suddenly. He was buried at Magdeburg, called Parthenopolis, where he had established an archbishopric with the greatest zeal. His son Otto II assumed the rights of the kingdom in his place.

Saint Udalric, bishop of Augsburg, worn down by a long illness, died happily and departed to the Lord in the eighty-third year of his life and the fiftieth of his episcopate, on Friday, 4 July.
