He was buried in the basilica of Saint Afra the martyr by the venerable Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg, and to this day he shines forth through innumerable miracles. After him, Henry became bishop of Augsburg and presided for nine years.

Duke Burchard of Alemannia also died and was buried at Reichenau in the chapel of Saint Erasmus. Otto, the son of Liudolf, received his father’s duchy in his place [Note: A later hand adds: “This Burchard was the founder of the monastery on Mount Duelli; afterward, in 1005, that monastery was transferred by the divine Henry, Roman emperor, to Stein, as it is called.” See concerning this Burchard above under the year 957 and below in the Life of Hermann.].

### 974

At Rome, Pope Benedict was accused by the Romans and handed over by Crescentius, son of Theodora, to custody in the Castle of Saint Angelo, where he was strangled. While he was still alive, Boniface, son of Ferrucius, was ordained pope, but after one month he was expelled and later went to Constantinople. Benedict VII, previously bishop of Sutri, was ordained the 138th pope and occupied the see for nine years [Note: Pagi and others place Donus II before him; Donus died in the same year after three months of pontificate, and Benedict VII succeeded him.].

At Constance, Conrad, a bishop of holy memory, died on 26 November, and Gamenolf presided in his place for approximately four years [Note: His Life was written by Udalric I, likewise bishop of Constance, who died in 1028. It is found in Pistor’s volume III and elsewhere in Leibniz’s *Scriptores Rerum Brunsvicensium*, vol. II.].

### 976

A dispute arose between King Otto and his paternal cousin Henry, duke of Bavaria [Note: Henry the Quarrelsome, son of Henry, brother of Otto I, and father of Henry the Saint, later emperor. *Saxon Annals*.].

### 977

At Saint Gall, Abbot Immo presided for eight years. He strove with all his strength to adorn the church of his patron, in accordance with the following distich written on the church’s arch [Note: Burchard records this in *On the Calamities of the Monastery of Saint Gall* (Goldast, vol. I, p. 66): “Abbot Immo adorned this with paintings and gold.”].

A dispute was stirred up between Otto, duke of the Swabians [Note: Otto, son of Liudolf, duke of Alemannia. See the year 973.], and Henry, duke of Bavaria.

### 978

Emperor Otto led an army into Gaul against King Lothar. Henry, duke of Bavaria, another Henry, duke [Note: Henry, called the Younger, duke of Carinthia, son of Berthold and Eila. *Saxon Annals*.], and also Henry, bishop of Augsburg, were captured as rebels against the emperor and consigned to exile. Otto, duke of the Swabians, received the duchy of Bavaria.

### 979

At Constance Bishop Gamenolf died, and Gebehard, a noble and venerable prelate, succeeded him. He governed the Church for sixteen years and built, from his own estates, the basilica of Saint Gregory on the bank of the Rhine and the monastery [Note: Also called Peter’s House, or Petershausen. We shall give the chronicle of this monastery below, after Hermann.].

### 981

After traversing Italy, Emperor Otto entered Campania and the territory of the Calabrians with his army.

### 982

The Greeks, with large forces and with Saracens also hired for money, undertook to defend Calabria against Emperor Otto. In a battle joined with great strength on both sides [Note: Read “a battle was joined.”], they were initially defeated; then, when the Agarenes came to their aid with a fresh force, they destroyed or captured our army. The emperor himself, fleeing by swimming in the sea, was captured by the enemy. Since they did not recognize him, they brought him, at his own request, to a certain coastal fortress for a ransom, and he was redeemed by his own people.

In that disastrous conflict for our side, among countless others, Henry of Augsburg was also captured and disappeared [Note: More about this and the other vicissitudes of this bishop may be read in the final chapter of the Life of Saint Udalric.]. Etich succeeded him in the episcopate.

In the same year Otto, duke of the Swabians and Noricans, died. Conrad then became duke of Alemannia [Note: This Conrad was the son of Udo, or Otto, brother of Hermann I, duke of Alemannia in 926.], and Henry received the duchy of Bavaria. *Saxon Annals*.

### 983

Emperor Otto fell ill at Rome and died on 8 December. He was honorably buried there in the portico of Saint Peter. *Saxon Annals*.

### 984

Otto III, son of Otto II by a Greek wife, was established as king while still a child, in place of his father, despite the opposition of certain leading men. He was carefully educated and grew up with outstanding natural ability.

At Rome John XIV, also called Peter, previously bishop of Pavia and the 139th pope, occupied the see for eight months. Boniface, son of Ferrucius, who had previously driven Benedict into exile and had been improperly ordained, returned from Constantinople, where he had fled, seized John, confined him in the Castle of Saint Angelo, and killed him by hunger and, as they report, poison. He then usurped the papal see as the 140th pope.

### 985

At Rome Boniface VII, after occupying for eleven months the see he had wrongly seized [Note: Others count only seven months.], died suddenly. After his death, his own followers beat and stabbed him and dragged his body through the streets by the feet; only after this, when the clergy took pity on him, was he finally buried.

At Reichenau, after Abbot Ruodmann died, Witegowo, the twenty-fifth abbot, presided for twelve years. At Saint Gall, after Immo, Abbot Udalric presided for five years.

### 986

At Rome John XV [Note: Others call him John XVI; they say that another John, elected shortly after the death of John XIV, died soon afterward. Pagi, *Critical Notes* under 985.], the 141st pope, occupied the see for ten years and seven months. Because he held his clergy in contempt, he was hated by them.

### 987

There was a great famine this year.

### 990

At Saint Gall, Abbot Udalric and the learned master Eggehard died, and Gerhard became abbot and presided for eleven years.

### 991

The Greek empress Theophano, mother of King Otto, died in the ninth year of her widowhood. At Saint Gall the learned Scot Foillan departed this life.

### 994

After Conrad, king of Burgundy, died [Note: Others say that he died in 993.] and was buried at Saint Maurice, his son Rudolf, although ineffectual, occupied the royal title there for approximately thirty-eight years. Under him, since law had ceased to operate, violence and robbery grew so strong in that kingdom that they could not easily be driven out; there they obtained the kingdom, as is evident today, together with their accomplices.

### 995

Henry, duke of Bavaria, died. His son by Gisela, daughter of King Conrad of Burgundy—also named Henry, and later to become emperor—obtained the duchy in the meantime. His sister Gisela was given in marriage to Stephen, king of the Hungarians, when he converted to the Christian faith, as a kind of pledge of faith, truly in accordance with her name [Note: Hermann alludes to the German word *Geisel*, which also denotes a hostage or pledge.]. She grew old there, devoted to almsgiving and other good works.

At Constance the venerable Bishop Gebehard died and rests buried in the basilica of Saint Gregory the pope, which he himself had built. Lantpert, a monk by habit and profession, succeeded him in the episcopate and presided for twenty-three years. He enlarged the church of Saint Mary by partly demolishing it.

### 996

King Otto went to Italy with an army and suppressed the rebels.

### 997

After subduing the rebels, King Otto gained control of Italy and Rome.

Gregory V, also called Bruno, son of Duke Otto [Note: Guillimann, together with many others, consistently considered this Otto the duke of Alemannia, son of Liudolf, who was descended from Otto the Great. But the Annals of Hildesheim under this year and the *Saxon Annals* (in Leibniz’s *Scriptores Rerum Brunsvicensium*, vol. I) call Bruno the son of Otto who governed the March of Verona. According to the same Saxon source under the year 902, this Otto was the son of Conrad, duke of Worms and Franconia, who was killed by the Hungarians in 955 and whose wife was Luitgard, daughter of Otto I (see above, 955). Their son Otto was duke of the Carentani and count of Verona. This Otto issued a charter in 977 in which he founded the monastery of Grävenhausen, saying that he did so at the urging of “Judith, my wife,” with the consent of his three sons Henry, Bruno, and Cuno. The district of Speyer, however, belonged not to Alemannia, whose duke was the son of Liudolf, but to the duchy of Franconia. See Pagi, *Critical Notes* under 1024, and Gregory V’s epitaph in Leibniz, ibid., p. 576, where it says:

“Yet Bruno, offspring of the royal Franks,
Son of Otto by his mother Judith.”

Thus Gregory V was Emperor Otto III’s nephew, not through his paternal uncle Liudolf but through his aunt Luitgard, Liudolf’s sister. See Wipo, *Life of Conrad the Salian*, and Hermann under 1012.], was ordained the 142nd pope, and Otto was crowned emperor by him. This venerable pope, striving to restore canonical discipline there, occupied the see for three years and nine months.

At Reichenau, after Abbot Witegowo had been deprived of office, Alawic was promoted as the twenty-sixth abbot. He was consecrated at Rome by the pope himself and received a privilege from him.

Conrad, duke of the Alemanni, died, and Hermann succeeded him in the duchy [Note: The Saxon Annalist under 1002 says: “This Hermann was the son of Duke Udo, who died with many others in Calabria when Emperor Otto II fought against the Saracens,” namely in 982. In that year two dukes named Otto died in Italy: one was Liudolf’s son, duke of Alemannia, but since he died without male children he cannot be meant here. The other, therefore, was Udo, or Otto, duke of Franconia, and Hermann II.], and he too married Gerbirga, daughter of King Conrad of Burgundy. By her he left one son of the same name and three daughters.

### 999

Emperor Otto again visited Italy with an army.

### 1000

After Widerold, bishop of the Church of Strasbourg, died [Note: According to the Fulda Necrology, in Leibniz’s *Scriptores Rerum Brunsvicensium*, vol. III, p. 766, he had already died in the preceding year. See the *Life of Saint Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne*, chapter 2, no. 8, under 16 March, in the Bollandists.], Alawic, abbot of Reichenau, was appointed bishop in his place by the emperor, and Werinharius was appointed the twenty-seventh abbot of Reichenau. He presided for six years.

At Rome, after Pope Gregory died, Silvester II, also called Gerbert, formerly archbishop of Reims and afterward of Ravenna, was ordained the 143rd pope. Excessively devoted to secular learning, he was therefore greatly loved by the inquisitive emperor and occupied the see for five years. *Saxon Annals*, under the preceding year.

### 1001

Emperor Otto toured Italy, which was everywhere subject to him. At Saint Gall, Abbot Burchard presided for twenty-three years.

### 1002

Emperor Otto died prematurely in Italy, at the castle of Paterno [Note: Read *Paterno*, a fortress in the Romagna, according to the *Saxon Annals*], in the nineteenth year of his reign, on 23 January. His body was carried from there; his intestines were buried at Augsburg, and he himself was buried at Aachen.

Henry, duke of Bavaria, assumed the insignia of kingship and ruled as king in his place for twenty-three years. Thietmar.

### 1003

King Henry set out against Henry the margrave, who was rebelling against him, and destroyed many of his castles. Ernest was captured, while Bruno, the king’s brother, and Henry barely escaped by flight. Strasbourg was plundered while Hermann, duke of Alemannia, was rebelling against the king [Note: The Saxon Annalist under 1002 calls him duke of Alemannia and Alsace, a deeply religious and humble man, but led astray by those who approved of his leniency. There he also describes the plundering of Strasbourg by his troops and the restitution of the damage he had caused.]. Divine vengeance severely punished the authors of the crime, and the duke himself made satisfaction in a sacred place. Thietmar.

### 1004

King Henry, traveling through Verona into the part of Italy this side of the Po, subjected all the cities of those regions to himself. On the very day on which he was crowned, he burst into Pavia and subdued it by sword and fire. After taking hostages, he returned to Saxony; a few days later he turned his arms against the Slavs. He reduced the Bohemians to their former servitude and tribute, and also subjected Bolizlaus, duke of the Slavic Polabians, together with his entire people. He returned victorious to Saxony. Thietmar.

Duke Hermann of Alemannia died, and his son Hermann, a boy pleasing to all the people [Note: As the Saxon chronicler reports, Duke Hermann of Alemannia had already died in the preceding year. After returning from Italy in 1004, King Henry entrusted the borders of Alemannia to his still very young son between Pentecost and the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; the son was likewise named Hermann.], succeeded him in the duchy. Another annal, 1003.

### 1005

There was a great famine. At Rome, after Gerbert, John XVI, the 144th pope, occupied the see for one year [Note: This John was elected in 1003 and died after five months and twenty-five days, according to Pagi.].

### 1006

At Reichenau, after Abbot Werinharius died, the brothers elected the monk Henry. But King Henry, detesting his insolence, although he had received money from him, and angered by the brothers’ accusations against him, placed over them against their will a certain Immo, an abbot of Gorze who at that time also held Prüm, an austere man [Note: This is altogether different from the praise bestowed upon this Immo by the author of the Life of Adalbero II, bishop of Metz (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 986, and vol. XIII, p. 887). Yet Hermann, a writer of this period, cannot be denied all credibility, since in the manuscripts of Göttweig and Murano Immo is also called a destroyer of the monastery and an expeller of the brothers. Perhaps austerity was needed at Reichenau, though Immo exceeded its limits. The charge of simony is also imposed upon Saint Henry with excessive illiberality; if there was any such offense, it might have been attributed to certain courtiers.].

As a result, some of the brothers voluntarily left that place, while others were severely afflicted by him with fasts, beatings, and exile. Thus the noble monastery, rich in distinguished men, books, and ecclesiastical treasures, suffered a grave loss, as Ruodpert, a noble and learnedly witty monk, my mother’s uncle [Note: See below, the Life of Hermann.], mournfully laments in prose, rhythm, and meter [Note: The title of the lost work was *On the Ruin of the Monastery of Reichenau through Fire*.].

At Rome John XVII, also called Fasanus, was ordained the 145th pope [Note: He was ordained on 26 December 1003 and occupied the see for five years and five months.].

### 1007

King Henry, with the greatest zeal, established a noble and wealthy bishopric at his castle of Bamberg. Eberhard was first promoted as its bishop in this year.

### 1008

After Luitolf, the learned archbishop of Trier, died, Megingaud was promoted archbishop in his place by the king. But Adalbero the cleric, the brother of Queen Cunegund [Note: Cunegund, wife of Henry II, was the daughter of Siegfried, count of Luxembourg, and Hedwig. See the Bollandists, volume I of March, 3 March.], striving, with the support of certain men, to obtain the archbishopric as though it were owed to him by a royal promise, occupied the palace of Trier with garrisons. Together with his brothers Theodore, bishop of Metz, and Henry, duke of Bavaria [Note: Henry Hezelo was given the duchy of Bavaria in 1004 because of his sister Cunegund and was later restored.], and with Count Frederick [Note: Frederick, count of the Moselle region and his father’s successor, brother of Cunegund and of the persons mentioned above, died in 1019. *Saxon Annals*.], and with the further support of Count Gerhard, along with many others [Note: This seems to have been Gerhard, count of Metz, who was appointed by Saint Henry in 1002 and was the uncle of Conrad the Salian. See the year 1017.], he rebelled against the king. After some time, however, all of them were subdued by the king, and Henry himself was deprived of the duchy of Bavaria. Thietmar.

In the same year, when King Henry finally learned of Immo’s cruelty after two years, he removed him and appointed Bernard, a learned and pious man, a monk of Prüm, abbot of Reichenau. Bernard was gladly received, gathered the scattered brothers together, and, consecrated abbot of that place—the twenty-ninth—by Lantpert, bishop of Constance, presided for forty years, distinguished by great learning and piety.

### 1009

Count Wolferad married Hiltrude, daughter of Piligrim and Berhtrada [Note: Compare the Life of Hermann.]. By her he later fathered fifteen children, counting me, Hermann, among them.

### 1010

The elder Count Wolferad, my paternal grandfather, a merciful man, steadfast in justice, and distinguished among his own people, died already an old man on 4 March [Note: This appears to be the same Count Wolverad who was the emperor’s envoy in the election of Saint Udalric’s successor in 973. Bertha, the wife of this Wolferad and Hermann’s grandmother, was his niece through his sister. See the year 955 and below in the Life.].

### 1011

Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, died, and Erchenbald succeeded him.

Theodoric, duke of Upper Lotharingia [Note: “Upper”], was captured and carried away almost in the king’s presence by Henry, formerly duke of Bavaria, and certain Lotharingians. After he was later released, Henry himself recovered the king’s favor and his duchy. Thietmar.

### 1012

Conrad, duke of Carinthia, son of Duke Otto and brother of Bruno [Note: He was Gregory V, son of Otto, duke of Rhenish Franconia and Carinthia, and of Luitgard, daughter of Emperor Otto I, as stated above under the year 997.], the former pope, died. His son Conrad, still a boy, having been deprived of it, Adalbero [Note: Count of Mürz Valley and Aflenz, later also duke of Istria.] received it. Another annal, preceding year.

Hermann the Younger, duke of Alemannia, also died, and Ernest, the husband of his sister Gisela, succeeded him. Thietmar.

### 1013

At Rome, after Pope Sergius died, Benedict VIII, the 147th pope, occupied the see for approximately twelve years. Another annal, preceding year.

I, Hermann, was born on 18 July.

King Henry set out for Italy with an army.

### 1014

At Rome King Henry was crowned emperor by Pope Benedict with an imperial blessing. Thietmar.

### 1015

Ernest, duke of Alemannia, died after being wounded by an arrow from Count Adalbero while the latter was pursuing a wild animal. His son of the same name received his duchy, while Conrad, son of Henry, son of Duke Otto, later to become emperor, married his widow Gisela. Thietmar.

Megingaud, archbishop of Trier, died, and Poppo, a venerable man and brother of Duke Ernest [Note: Namely, of the Elder and the Younger, or the paternal uncle of Ernest II.], succeeded him.

### 1017

Godefrey, duke of Lower Lotharingia [Note: Godefrey III, duke of Lower Lotharingia.], defeated in battle Count Gerhard [Note: Gerhard, count of Egisheim in Alsace, whose daughter Adelaide was the mother of Emperor Conrad the Salian through Henry, duke of Franconia. Calmet, *History of Lotharingia*, book XVIII, chapter 69. P. Clement calls Adelaide Gerhard’s sister, daughter of Eberhard IV, count of the Nordgau or Lower Alsace; in that case, according to Hermann, he was truly Conrad the Salian’s maternal uncle.], the maternal uncle of Conrad, later emperor. Thietmar.

### 1018

At Constance Bishop Lantpert died, and Ruodhard received the episcopate and presided for approximately five years. Thietmar.

### 1019

Conrad, a young man and son of the former Duke Conrad of Carinthia, with the assistance of his paternal cousin Conrad, later emperor, defeated Adalbero, then duke of Carinthia, in battle near Ulm and put him to flight. See above, under 1012.

### 1020

Invited by the emperor, Pope Benedict came to Bamberg and dedicated the church of Saint Stephen there [Note: See the Life of Saint Henry and Leo of Ostia, book II, chapter 46.].

Werinharius, bishop of Strasbourg, with the assistance of certain Swabians, invaded the Burgundians and defeated them in a battle that was joined. *Saxon Annals*, under 1019.

I, Hermann, was committed to the study of letters on 15 September.

### 1021

A great earthquake occurred on 12 May, a Friday. Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, a man of great holiness, departed this life and became renowned through many miracles. Piligrim succeeded him. After Erchenbald died, Aribo became archbishop. Fulda Necrology.

After Wolbod [Wolbodo], Durand was promoted as bishop of Liège [Note: See the monk Reiner of Saint Lawrence at Liège in his Life, in the Bollandists, volume II of April, 21 April.].

The venerable Irmendrud, abbess of Buchau, died on 20 February, and Abbess Abarhild succeeded her. From that time onward, that place began increasingly to decline.

Emperor Henry undertook an expedition into Italy.

Werinharius, my brother, was born on 1 November.

### 1022

Emperor Henry, heading for Campania, entered Benevento, besieged and captured Troia, and received Naples, Capua, Salerno, and all the other cities in those regions into submission. He also granted, as is reported, a certain territory in those parts to some Normans who had gathered there during his reign; and thus, passing victoriously through the city of Rome, he returned to Germany. *Hepidanus; Leo of Ostia, Book II.*

A pestilence arose in the army and killed many; among them died Ruodhard, bishop of Constance, and Burchard, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall. *Necrology of Fulda; Hepidanus; Burchard, On the Disasters.* In their place Bishop Heimo presided for nearly four years, and Abbot Theodebald for eleven years. Notker, the teacher—also called Labeo, some of whose works survive in Schilter’s *German Antiquities* [Note: Labeo was his surname; some of his works survive in Schilter’s *German Antiquities*. See Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 287.]—and other distinguished brothers likewise died at Saint Gall.

### 1023

At Regensburg, after Bishop Gebehard—an abstemious man, famous for certain singular customs, for an unusual love of purity and adornment, and for excessive diligence in the divine offices—had been taken from this life, another Gebehard, a canon of Augsburg, succeeded him. [Note: See Conrad of the Mount of Maidens; the *Chronicle of the Bishops of Regensburg*; and Eccard, *Corpus of the History of the Middle Ages*, vol. II.]

### 1024

At Rome, Benedict having died, his brother John XVIII was ordained pope, the 148th, though previously a layman, and sat for nearly nine years.

Emperor Henry also died without sons on the third day before the Ides of July. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter at the episcopal see of Bamberg, which he himself had built and to which he had left all his estates and treasures as heir. *Life.*

Then, since Conrad the Elder [Note: See under the years 1017 and 1019.], son of Henry and Adelheid, and his cousin Conrad, son of Duke Conrad [Note: See under the years 1012 and 1019.] by Mathilda [Note: Daughter of Hermann II, duke of Alemannia.], were striving above all others for the kingship, a gathering of the princes was held at the village of Kamba [Note: Between Mainz and Worms. Wipo.]. Conrad the Elder was advanced as king and anointed by Archbishop Aribo at Mainz on the sixth day before the Ides of September. Not long afterward, his wife Gisela was likewise blessed as queen by Piligrin, archbishop of Cologne, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. [Note: The *Quedlinburg Chronicle* likewise asserts that this was done at Mainz by Aribo. See Schaten, part I, book V, p. 461.] *Wipo.*

### 1025

Much rebellion and discord arose against King Conrad, caused by his cousin Conrad and by Duke Ernest of Alemannia, his stepson [Note: For Gisela, Ernest’s mother, had married King Conrad.]; also by Count Welf, a Swabian [Note: This is Welf II, count of Altdorf in Swabia, called Welfhard by Hepidanus.], and by many others. *Hepidanus.*

### 1026

King Conrad, having partly pacified the rebels, went to Italy with an army around the time of Lent. After celebrating Easter at Vercelli, he brought all Italy on this side of Rome under his control, except the city of Lucca.

Duke Ernest of Alemannia, having been reconciled with him that same year at his mother’s intervention, received the abbey of Kempten as a benefice and distributed it among his soldiers; but not long afterward, turned aside by evil counsel, he rebelled again. *Wipo.*

That same year, Bishop Heimo of Constance died suddenly from pleurisy, and Warmann succeeded him, serving for nearly eight years. Burchard, abbot of Kempten and Reichenau, also died, and at Reichenau Abbot Pirhtilo was substituted for him. Bishop Brun of Augsburg and Count Welf ravaged one another with plunder and arson. *Wipo.*

### 1027

King Conrad, having celebrated Christmas at Ivrea [Note: *Eporegia*, now called Ivrea.], advanced farther, received Lucca into submission together with Marquis Reginher, and, reaching Rome, was crowned emperor by Pope John on holy Easter Day. After subduing all Italy, he returned and held a judicial assembly at Ulm in Alemannia. There he received into submission Duke Ernest, his stepson, and Count Welf, together with other men, and assigned them to exile for a time. *Wipo; Hepidanus.*

The castle of Kyburg, belonging to Count Werinharius, who was still resisting, and several other castles of the rebels were captured. His cousin Conrad likewise surrendered himself to the emperor but was nevertheless sent into exile. *Hepidanus under the year 1033.*

Werinharius, bishop of Strasbourg, was sent to Constantinople as the emperor’s envoy; he died there in the following year, and Wilhelm succeeded him. Hiltegart became abbess of Buchau.

### 1028

Henry, the emperor’s son, still a boy, was elected king by all the princes at Aachen on holy Easter Day and was anointed by Piligrin, archbishop of Cologne. [Note: The election had already taken place in 1026, but the coronation occurred this year at Easter.] *Wipo.*

### 1029

While the emperor was celebrating Easter at Regensburg, Bishop Brun of Augsburg, his chief fellow-officiant, died there. He was buried at Augsburg in the basilica of Saint Maurice, whose construction had begun, and Eberhard was appointed his successor. *Wipo.*

### 1030

Duke Ernest, after being released from exile and recovering his duchy, followed the counsel of wicked men and again opposed the emperor. He was deprived of the duchy, and his younger brother Hermann was made duke of the Swabians. *Hepidanus.*

Emperor Conrad, who had long been embroiled in enmity with Stephen, king of the Hungarians, went to Pannonia and ravaged the country as far as the Rába, insofar as the rivers and marshes did not prevent him. *Wipo.*

Meanwhile, in Alemannia, Ernest, formerly duke, and his accomplices, acting against the emperor with small forces, were harassing the inhabitants by plundering around the Martian Forest [Note: Under the year 1036, Hepidanus calls the castle occupied by Ernest Flackenstein, which is Falckenstein itself. Its ruins can still be seen on the borders of the Martian, or Black, Forest; the matter is discussed in the history of that forest.]. They were observed by Count Manegold [Note: This Manegold seems to have been count of Veringen, either the brother or the son of Welfrad the Elder. See above, under the year 1010. The place of his burial at Reichenau supports this. For the Manegold of Dillingen, count and founder of the monastery of Donauwörth, whom Calles, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. V, p. 298, investigates, is disproved by Brusch, who writes that he, like the other Manegolds of the same family, was buried in the monastery he had founded and endowed. See Crus, *Swabian Annals*, part II, book III, chapter 2.], with troops from Reichenau; they were defeated in battle on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September. Manegold himself was killed there, as were Ernest, formerly duke, and Count Werinhere, the leaders of the rebellion, together with the noble warriors Adalbert and Werin and many others. Ernest was buried at Constance, and Manegold at Reichenau. *Wipo.*

Burchard, a monk of Reichenau, was promoted to abbot at Saint Emmeram in Regensburg.

### 1031

Peace with Stephen, king of the Hungarians, was restored. [Note: Wipo assigns this event to the preceding year.] Aribo, archbishop of the see of Mainz, died while traveling to Rome to pray. Bardo, venerable in life and monastic habit, succeeded him in the archiepiscopate. *Wipo.*

### 1032

Rudolf, the feeble little king of Burgundy, died, and his crown and the insignia of his kingdom were brought to Emperor Conrad by Seliger.

While the emperor was leading an army in those days against Misicon, king of the Slavs called the Boles, Odo, son of Rudolf’s sister and prince of the French Champagne, invaded the kingdom of Burgundy. After capturing the castles of Neuchâtel and Murten, he placed garrisons of his own in them. *Hepidanus; Wipo.*

Bern, abbot of Reichenau, sent the privileges of his monastery to Rome and received from Pope John another privilege [Note: This appears to be the first example of a privilege of this kind being granted.], allowing him to celebrate Mass wearing sandals as episcopal vestments. Bishop Warmann of Constance was therefore disturbed and accused Bern before the emperor as an intruder upon his office and honor. Bern was constrained by both parties to such a point that the same privilege was to be burned on Maundy Thursday of the following year—[Bern adds: “when he had handed the privilege, with the sandals, to the bishop himself publicly in his synod, that is …”].

That same year the monastery of Buchau was ablaze in a fire on the third day before the Ides of January. My grandmother Bertha, a woman sufficiently devout, died in the twenty-third year of her widowhood, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.

### 1033

After Christmas, the emperor went to Burgundy and besieged Murten; but, because of the winter cold, he was unable to accomplish anything worthy of mention there. Therefore, in the summer, invading Odo’s province, French Champagne, he again devastated it with plunder and fires, until Odo himself came to him as a suppliant and, received mercifully, promised to make amends, although insincerely. *Hepidanus; Wipo.*

At Rome, after John’s death, Benedict IX, also called Theophylact, was ordained the 149th pope. Although his character and actions were unworthy of so great an office, he remained in office for more than twelve years.

An eclipse of the sun occurred on the third day before the Kalends of July, around the seventh hour of the day. [Note: See Bernold’s *Chronicle*, below, under the year 1093.]

### 1034

The emperor again went to Burgundy with a large force and brought under his authority all the castles on this side of the Rhône. He destroyed Murten, entered the city of Geneva, and received into submission, together with many other princes, Burchard, archbishop of Lyon [Note: This is not Burchard the archbishop who had already died around 1031 (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 83), but his namesake nephew. The latter, having abandoned the episcopal see of Augsburg, had seized Lyon; after perpetrating many crimes, he was captured by the emperor’s soldiers and condemned to perpetual exile, as Rodulfus Glaber reports, *History*, book V, chapter 4.]. He was a man noble by birth and vigorous, but in every respect wicked and sacrilegious. Having subdued the kingdom of Burgundy, the emperor returned. *Wipo.*

That same year, after Warmann, bishop of Constance, died [Note: The writer of the *Chronicle of Petershausen* says that Warmann died on a journey to Rome with his companions.], his brother Eberhard succeeded him and presided for more than twelve years. When Megenbard, bishop of Würzburg, also died, Brun—cousin of the emperor, namely the son of Duke Conrad by Mathilda—received the bishopric on Easter Day.

At Saint Gall, too, when Abbot Theobald died, Nordpert succeeded him. Pagan Slavs called Liutizi harassed the borders of Saxony. *Annals of Hildesheim.*

### 1035

In Italy, the lesser knights rose against their lords, wishing to live according to their own laws and to oppress them, and formed a powerful conspiracy. When the leading men united to restrain them and entered battle, many fell on both sides. Among them the bishop of Asti was wounded and died. *Hepidanus.*

Duke Adalbert of Carinthia and Istria, having lost the emperor’s favor, was also deprived of his duchy. [Note: See above, under the year 1012.]

The Liutizi secretly betrayed and captured the castle of Wirbin and killed many of our men or carried them away as prisoners. The emperor, crossing the Elbe by force, entered their province and laid it waste far and wide. *Annals of Hildesheim.* [Col. 0237B] *Wipo.*

A great synod was convened at Tribur by the emperor. [Note: *German Councils*, vol. III, p. 103, cites the *Annals of Hildesheim* and Saxon annals under the following year; Pagi, however, assigns it to this year.]

### 1036

Piligrin, archbishop of Cologne, died, and Hermann, grandson through his daughter of Emperor Otto II, succeeded him. *Wipo.*

Gebehard II, bishop of Regensburg, died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March. In his place Gebehard III, brother through his mother Adelheid of Emperor Conrad, was ordained bishop. *Chronicle of Augsburg; others under the preceding year.*

King Henry, the emperor’s son, took Chunihild, daughter of Chuton, king of the Danes and English, as his wife in a royal marriage at Nijmegen. *Annals of Hildesheim.*

Conrad, the emperor’s cousin, received from the emperor his father’s duchy in Carinthia and Istria, which Adalbero had held. *The same source.*

Hermann, duke of Alemannia, likewise received from the emperor in Italy the march of his father-in-law Meginfrid. [Note: Meginfrid was margrave of Susa, whose daughter Adelheid Hermann IV had married.]

The Slavic Liutizi became tributaries of the emperor.

Burchard, archbishop—or rather tyrant—of Lyon, a sacrilegious plunderer of churches, adulterer, and incestuous man, went to war against Vodalric, son of Seliger. He was defeated and captured by Vodalric, brought before the emperor, shackled in irons, and confined in custody, where he was held in chains for many years. *Glaber.*

The emperor went to Italy in winter.

Nuns were gathered at Altdorf by Lady Irmingard, widow of Count Welf, in place of clerics. [Note: Earlier, the counts Welf had founded a Benedictine monastery for men at Altenmünster in Bavaria and another for virgins at Altdorf in Swabia, later called “At the Vines.” Around this time they exchanged their sites with one another; Hess records this in his *Introduction to the Welf Monastery* under the year 1047.]

### 1037

After celebrating Christmas at Verona, the emperor reached Milan by way of Brescia and Cremona. From there, going to Pavia, he ordered Heribert, archbishop of Milan, arrested on a charge of disloyalty and entrusted him to Patriarch Poppo of Aquileia for safekeeping. Heribert escaped by flight and attempted with all his strength to rebel against that same emperor. *Wipo; Otto of Freising.*

After celebrating Easter at Ravenna, the emperor returned to the territory of Milan, besieged the city, and devastated the castles, villages, and everything around them belonging to the rebels. He easily suppressed the conspirators and confirmed in writing the law they had also possessed in earlier times. *Hepidanus.*

Pope Benedict came to Cremona to meet the emperor. The bishops of Piacenza, Cremona, and Vercelli were accused by the emperor, captured, and sent into exile. *Annals of Hildesheim; Wipo.*

That same year a battle was fought between Odo, prince of French Champagne, and Gozzilo, duke of the Lotharingians [Note: Gozzilo, or Gothelo I, duke of both Lotharingias, appointed by Emperor Conrad.]. Odo was defeated and put to flight with his men; he was killed and died during the flight. *Rodulfus Glaber, History*, book III, chapter 9.

### 1038

While the emperor was celebrating Christmas at Parma, a tumult arose between the citizens of Parma and the army. Many fell, and after numerous citizens had been slaughtered, the city itself was consumed by fire. *Wipo; Otto of Freising.*

The pope excommunicated the archbishop of Milan, who was still rebelling against the emperor. *Wipo.*

After the emperor had traveled through the lands beyond Rome and was returning along the shores of the Adriatic Sea, a great pestilence attacked the army in July and killed very many throughout the region. Among them Queen Chunihild, wife of King Henry, died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August [Note: Wipo gives the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August. The castle of Lindburg, which is called a provostship here, lies near Speyer.]. She was carried to the castle of Lindburg and buried there. *Wipo.*

Hermann, duke of Alemannia, also died a very grievous death on the tenth day before the Kalends of August [Note: Guichenon attempts here to undermine Hermann’s credibility by placing the duke’s death earlier, but incorrectly, as we shall say under the year 1092 in Bernold.]. He was buried at Trent. *Otto of Freising; Wipo.*

After returning from Italy, the emperor held a conference at Solothurn and compelled many of the leading Burgundians to confirm by oath their submission both to him and to his son.

That same year, King Stephen of the Hungarians—who many years earlier had converted himself and his entire people to the Christian faith, had established many churches and bishoprics [read: “had built”], and had, with the utmost gentleness, devoted effort to his kingdom (*probis*, sic)—died after appointing as king in his place Peter, born in Venice, the son of his sister. [Note: Aloldus, in his *Chronicle*, calls this sister of Stephen Gisela and says that she was married to Count William of Poitiers. Yet she cannot be found in the succession of those counts (*The Art of Verifying Dates*, vol. II, pp. 348 ff.), nor in the chronology of the kings of Hungary (ibid., p. 49), where only two sisters are attributed to King Stephen: one, Sama, married to Aba, or Owon, Peter’s successor; and another unnamed woman, wife of Otto Orseolo, duke of the Venetians, by whom Peter would therefore have been born, if he came from Venice, as Hermann and the Melk manuscript assert. See Pray, *Annals of the Kings of Hungary*, part I, p. 40. Others maintain that Peter was born from William of Burgundy and Saint Stephen’s sister, and that he was therefore called a German. Calles, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. V, p. 351.]

### 1039

Emperor Conrad, while celebrating Pentecost at Utrecht, city of Frisia, suddenly died an unexpected death on the third day before the Nones of June. [Note: The Saxon Chronographer more correctly gives the second day before the Nones of June, as do the *Annals of Hildesheim*. Wipo.] He was brought to Speyer and buried there, and his son, King Henry, assumed the government of the kingdom.

Reginbald, bishop of Speyer, a man venerable for his life and monastic habit, also died on the third day before the Ides of October. [Note: The Saxon annals give the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September.] Sibicho, very different from him in reputation, succeeded him.

Conrad, duke of Carinthia, and his rival Adalbero, who had previously held the duchy, both died that year. *Annals of Hildesheim.*

King Henry launched an expedition into Bohemia. When the duke of that people, Břetislav, had sent his son to him as a hostage and promised—although insincerely—that he himself would come and do what was commanded, Henry immediately returned.

In winter, King Peter of the Hungarians invaded the borders of his kingdom and devastated them with plunder, fires, and captivity. *Other source under the following year.*

### 1040

King Henry, marching against the duke of Bohemia, who had rebelled again, sent a detached part of his army by the trackless paths of the forests into the province, to attack the fortifications or defenses of the forest on both sides. But when, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, the soldiers entered by one route, and on the following day by another, they became exhausted by their fruitless labor in wooded, difficult, and obstructed places. They then attempted in vain to attack a certain extremely strong fortress. The Bohemians attacked them from every side, and they were slain, captured, and put to flight. Those of our men who still remained in the province were brought out unharmed through the intervention of Gunther the Hermit [Note: Wolfher, a monk of Altaich in the eleventh century, wrote the life of Saint Gunther, monk and hermit; it appears in Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, vol. III, part I, p. 185.] and returned.

The king, having meanwhile lost very many soldiers and nobles, withdrew without accomplishing his purpose. *Saxon Annals; Hepidanus.*

Eberhard, the first bishop of the Church of Bamberg, died in the thirty-third year after his promotion. Suideger, a Saxon by birth and a praiseworthy man, succeeded him. *Necrology of Fulda.*

### 1041

After King Henry returned the duke of Bohemia’s son, who had been held hostage, to him, he redeemed the captives taken in the forest. The following summer, having gathered a large army, he entered the province by difficult routes and devastated everything with plunder and fires, until the duke, overcome by his misfortunes, asked for peace. He promised, after summoning the king’s faithful men to him, that he would surrender himself and his entire people, come to the king at Regensburg, and do what was commanded. When the king departed, he soon fulfilled these promises by his actions. *Hepidanus.*

That same year the treacherous Hungarians, appointing a certain Owon as king, plotted to kill their own king, Peter. Peter barely escaped by flight and first fled to our margrave Adalbert, his sister’s husband [Note: This Adalbert was margrave of Austria, brother of Ernest I, duke of Alemannia and Swabia, and also of Poppo, archbishop of Trier (see under the year 1015). Some call his wife Adelheid, whereas King Henry, in a charter of the year 1051, calls her Troiza. Whether she was one woman or two different women we do not investigate; at least one or the other is certainly shown to have been King Peter’s sister. See above under the year 1038; Calles, *German Annals*, vol. I, p. 330, and Pray, *Annals of the Kings of Hungary*, part I, p. 44.]. From there he came to King Henry, fell at his feet, and begged for pardon and favor, which he obtained. *Hepidanus; Annals of Hildesheim.*

### 1042

King Henry invaded Burgundy in winter and received many of the princes who submitted to him; he also settled several matters by lawful judgment.

The Hungarian tyrant Owon, because our king had received Peter, divided his army into two. He ravaged and burned the borders of Bavaria on both sides of the Danube. But one part of his army was annihilated on the northern side of the Danube by Margrave Adalbert and his son Luitpold. *Chronicle of Augsburg.*

In autumn, Henry also went to Pannonia, overthrew Heimenburg and Brezesburg, and devastated or brought into submission the northern bank of the Danube as far as the river Gran, since rivers and marshes had fortified the southern bank. One division of the army, meeting the Hungarians when they invaded twice, inflicted great slaughter. After the Hungarians of those regions had been subdued, and since they refused to receive Peter, Henry appointed as their leader another man from among them who was likewise an exile among the Bohemians. Yet immediately after the king’s departure, Owon drove this man back into Bohemia because he was unable to resist. *Annals of Hildesheim.*

Patriarch Poppo of Aquileia died, and Eberhard, a canon of Augsburg promoted by the king, succeeded him.

### 1043

At Goslar, Empress Gisela, though deceived by fortune-tellers who sometimes foretold the truth to her and therefore believing that she would outlive her son the king, died of dysentery on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March. She was buried at Speyer beside her husband the emperor.

A rainy summer caused a shortage of crops and grapes.

King Henry, going again to Pannonia, obtained from Owon, though only with difficulty, a treaty, satisfaction, hostages, gifts, and part of the kingdom as far as the river Litha; then he withdrew.

From there he came to Alemannia. At the synod of Constance, he first himself remitted every debt to all who had offended against him. Then, through prayers and exhortations, he reconciled all the Swabians present to one another by remitting debts and enmities, intending that the same should afterward be done in the other provinces of his kingdom. He established peace—unheard of for many ages—and confirmed it by edict.

After this he received the daughter of William of Poitiers as his betrothed, had her anointed queen at Mainz, and celebrated a royal wedding at Ingelheim. He set forth a useful example to everyone by disregarding the empty applause of actors, treating it as worthless, and dismissing them empty-handed and sorrowful. *Chronicle of Augsburg.*

There also Luitpold, son of Margrave Adalbert, a young man of great courage and piety, was promoted by the king as margrave. He died a few days later and was buried at Trier by his uncle, Archbishop Poppo. *Hepidanus.*

### 1044

*M. G.* The greatest pestilence among cattle occurred. A sufficiently severe and snowy winter destroyed a large part of the vineyards through frost, and the failure of the crops caused no small famine. [Note: M. G. reads: “The great force of famine persuaded people to eat unclean animals. Heribert, archbishop of Milan, brought this life to an end, and Wido assumed his dignity. Beggelnheim, Godefrid’s castle, was captured and destroyed by the king.”]

Gozzilo, duke of the Lotharingians [Note: Namely, of Lower and Upper Lotharingia.], dying, intended to leave his duchy to his son Gozzilo, although the latter was indolent, since King Henry had promised it to him. But his other son Godefrid, already duke [Note: Of Upper Lotharingia together with his father. See Calmet, *History of Lotharingia*, book XVIII, chapter 67.], having been unable to obtain from the king, against justice, the duchy owed to his brother, set aside oath and loyalty and dared to rebel against the pious king.

King Owon, having broken his oath and treaty, faced King Henry, who went to Pannonia with a very small force. Owon, who had prepared a very large army, despised him so greatly that he allowed him to enter the province as though he could easily be killed or captured. But Henry, trusting in divine aid, rapidly forded the river Rába with part of his forces, entered battle while all the soldiers hurried forward from every side, and at the first encounter routed and struck down the countless Hungarian army. Having lost very few of his own men, he himself fought with the greatest courage and won a most glorious victory on the third day before the Nones of July.

King Owon barely escaped by flight, and all the Hungarians flocked in groups to King Henry to surrender, promising submission and service. Since Henry was in every respect most merciful, he restored Peter, long expelled, to his kingdom. He granted the Hungarians the Bavarian law at their request and himself returned in triumph to his kingdom. Not long afterward, Owon was captured by King Peter and paid the penalty for his crimes by execution. [Note: Hepidanus, who concludes his annals here. See Rodulfus Glaber, *History*, book V, chapter 4.]

That same year Count Louis [Note: This Louis was count of Montbéliard; Reginald, or Renald, was the first duke of Burgundy of that name.] was preparing to attack with a large force a certain castle belonging to Reginbold, a prince who was Queen Agnes’s uncle but an enemy of King Henry. The castle was called Mount Piligard. Louis entered battle with a small force of his soldiers, defeated Reginbold, and, after killing many, put the rest to flight.

The Romans drove Pope Benedict, accused of many crimes, from his see and installed a certain Silvester in his place. Benedict later, with the support of some partisans, expelled Silvester, who had been excommunicated, and was restored to his see. He subsequently deprived himself of it and, out of greed and contrary to the canons, ordained another in his place. [Note: Benedict IX had already been expelled from his see by the Romans in 1038 but was restored by Emperor Conrad, as Pagi proves from Glaber, book IV, chapter 8, in his *Critical Studies*. In 1044, however, he was expelled again, and John, bishop of Sabina, was substituted for him under the name Silvester III. After John was driven out three months later, Benedict returned to the see. Finally, after receiving money from John Gratian, archpriest, he ceded the pontificate to him; John became Gregory VI. Pope Victor III tells the story in this way in book III of the *Dialogues*.]

Heribert, archbishop of Milan, died. Godefrid’s castle of Beggelinheim was destroyed by the king. Archbishop Gebehard of Ravenna died, and Wideger was appointed in his place. [Note: From this year the two codices, those of Göttweig and Muri, agree almost word for word with the Reichenau manuscript.]

### 1045

Reginolt [Note: This is Renald, duke of Burgundy, previously in rebellion, mentioned shortly before under the preceding year.] and Gerolt, Burgundians, came to King Henry at Solothurn to submit.

Count Otto the palatine [Note: He was born to Ezo, count palatine on the Rhine, also called Ehrenfrid, and Mathilda, daughter of Emperor Otto II.] was appointed duke of Alemannia by the king at Goslar during Easter week.

King Peter received King Henry, whom he had invited to him on the feast of Pentecost, with great ceremony and gave him magnificent gifts. He restored to him the kingdom of Pannonia, while the Hungarian princes confirmed by oath their loyalty to Henry and his successors. Henry nevertheless received it from Peter to be possessed by Peter himself for as long as he lived.

On this journey, the king climbed an old upper story [Note: Aventine and other Bohemian writers call it the castle of Bosenbeug, situated in Upper Austria.] with many others. When the building collapsed, he fell with them. By God’s protection he himself escaped unharmed, but Bishop Brun of Würzburg fell lethally with the others and died one week later, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June. [Note: The manuscripts of Muri and Göttweig place the death there.] He was carried back to his see and buried there, and Adalbero succeeded him. *Aventine; Brunner.*

Duke Godefrid [Note: Namely, the duke of Lotharingia mentioned under the year 1044.], despairing of his rebellion and coming to submit to the king, was placed in custody. [Note: The Muri manuscript adds the place: Klingenstein.]

Wido was appointed archbishop of Milan.

The Slavs called Liutizi [Note: Some think that these were Lusatians.] were disturbing the borders of Saxony. When the king came against them with an army, they surrendered to him and promised the customary tribute.

In autumn, the hermit Guticharius [other reading: Guntharius] [Note: The Muri and Göttweig manuscripts read: “The hermit, released from the bonds of the flesh, migrated to Christ and rests buried at Braga, among the holy martyrs Adalbert and Wenezianus,” and so forth. This is Gunther, mentioned above under the year 1040.] migrated to Christ and rests buried at Braga, a city of Bohemia.

At the same time, the royal conference appointed to be held at Tribur was prevented by the king’s serious illness.

At that time Queen Agnes gave birth to a daughter for the king.

[Col. 0245A] 215 1046 M. G. The king celebrated Christmas in Saxony at Goslar. A great mortality destroyed many people everywhere. The exceedingly wealthy Margrave Eggehardus, dying suddenly, left the king heir to his estates [Note: [Col. 0245C] Ekkard II, margrave of Meissen, one of the few dear to Emperor Henry III; on him see Eccard, *Genealogical History of the Princes of Upper Saxony*, p. 229.]. *Annals of Saxony.*

The king celebrated Easter at Utrecht, a city of Frisia, and in the days that followed, crossing the channel by a naval expedition into Vlaardingen [Note: [Col. 0245C] Now Vlaardingen, a village of Holland on the Meuse, formerly the seat of the counts of Holland, among whom Theodoric IV, of that name, is recorded here.], he seized from Margrave Theodoric a certain district that Theodoric had usurped for himself; consequently, Theodoric later took this as the pretext for rebellion. Celebrating Pentecost at Aachen, he released Duke Godefrid from custody and, moved by pity, restored his duchy [Note: [Col. 0245C] Namely, Lower Lorraine.] to him after Godefrid had prostrated himself on the ground before the advancing king. During those same days he summoned Widgerus, who for two years had incompetently and cruelly held the see of Ravenna, still unconsecrated, and deprived him of the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0245D] Baronius therefore criticizes Henry, whereas Blessed Peter Damian praises him, book VII, letter 2, addressed to the same man.]. Shortly thereafter the king prepared an expedition into Italy. Frideric, brother of Duke Henry of Bavaria and Duke of the Lorrainers, was appointed in place of Godefrid’s brother, the incapable Gozzilo, as duke [Note: [Col. 0245D] P. Clement writes that, after Gozzilo II—called “the Incapable”—had died this year in the duchy of Upper Lorraine, the emperor appointed Albert the Alsatian, from the counts of Egisheim, who was killed in battle by Godefrid in 1048. Thus, when Godefrid was again deprived of his office because of rebellion in 1048, Frideric of Luxembourg was substituted in Lower Lorraine; Hermannus speaks of him.].

In the following autumn the Hungarians, remembering their former treachery, set up a certain Andrew as king for themselves. After killing many foreigners who had fought for King Peter, they mistreated Peter in various ways together with his wife [Gott.: “and finally deprived him of his eyes” [Col. 0246A] and assigned him, together with that same wife, to be maintained in a certain place], while during the same period many pilgrims were stripped of their possessions, driven into exile, and killed. When King Henry learned this—he had already assembled a powerful army and begun his march into Italy—he was deeply distressed; nevertheless, he did not abandon the expedition. Accordingly, after assembling his army, he held a synod at Pavia [Note: [Col. 0245D] Nothing concerning the Pavia synod of this year appears in Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*. Yet that it was truly held is clearly demonstrated by an old document from the Verona archives. It survives in Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, p. 760, taken from an ancient manuscript of the *Decrees* of Burchard, bishop of Worms, in the Vatican Library, publicly authenticated in 1583. It reads as follows: “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1046, indiction XV [that is, at its beginning], on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, while our most invincible lord, King Henry III, was reigning, a general synod was assembled at Pavia by the command of that glorious king; and while many matters were being treated in that synod justly and reasonably in the presence of that glorious king, and of his archbishops and bishops, etc.” The names of all the bishops who attended the council follow, both Italians [Col. 0246D] and Germans; Calles, *Ecclesiastical Annals of Germany*, vol. V, p. 422, lists the latter. See also Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book VIII.]. From there he came to Piacenza and honorably received Gratianus, whom the Romans had made pope after expelling his predecessors [Note: [Col. 0246D] Under the name Gregory VI.], when Gratianus came to meet him. Since everything was proceeding favorably, shortly before Christmas another synod was held near the city of Rome, at Sutri [Note: [Col. 0246D] What was done in this Council of Sutri is reported by one contemporary writer, Hermannus; Victor III later recounts it at greater length, book I, chapter 3 of the *Dialogue*.]. There the case of the erroneous pontiffs was examined with great care, and, having convicted Pope Gratianus, he deprived him of the pastoral staff [Note: [Col. 0246D] Rather, according to Bernoldus, later Victor III, at the place cited, he voluntarily resigned the pontifical dignity. As for where the new election of Clement took place, the writers disagree: Hermannus says that it was still done at Sutri, whereas the aforementioned Pope Victor, as well as Leo of Ostia (*Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book II, chapter 79), affirm that it first occurred at Rome. From Victor himself it is certain that this election was carried out by the same bishops who had assembled for the synod at Sutri, wherever it was ultimately conducted.]. Then, with the assent of all—Romans and others alike—they elected Bishop Suidgerus, who, after Eberhardus, had been the second Babenberger to govern the Church for six years, as supreme pontiff of the Roman Church, although he was extremely reluctant. Thus, around the vigil of Christmas, they entered the city itself. On that same night Eberhardus, bishop of the Church of Constance and a man of blessed memory, died in the thirteenth year of his episcopate; he was to be buried there in the portico of Saint Peter.

[Col. 0247A] 217 1047 M. G. On Christmas Day itself [Note: [Col. 0248D] Hermannus, following his usual practice, begins the year from the Christmas of the preceding year; these events therefore belong to that earlier date.] the aforementioned Suidgerus, a Saxon by nation, was consecrated pope in the customary manner at the apostolic see and, taking the name Clement II, was so called. On that same day he immediately elevated King Henry and his wife Agnes with the imperial blessing. After the solemn celebration of Mass, the lord pope and the emperor, together with the empress, proceeded in their coronation garments to the Lateran palace with immense glory, while all the Roman citizens marvelled, and they bestowed honours upon each person, as opportunity allowed, while passing by. After spending several days in Rome in complete peace, the emperor allowed a large part of his army to return home, while he himself, with the remainder, pressed onward.

218 Around this time the emperor appointed several prelates. Among them were Hunfridus, his chancellor in Italy, to the Church of Ravenna; Theodericus, his chancellor in the other provinces, archchaplain, and provost of Aachen, to the Church of Constance; Herandus, provost of Speyer, to Strasbourg, in place of Willehelmus [Note: [Col. 0248D] He was the brother of Gregory V, formerly pope, who died on 6 November of the preceding year.], who had died in the autumn; and Theodericus, provost of Basel and his chaplain, to Verdun. The emperor, after leaving Rome, captured several castles that were in rebellion against him, arranged the provinces as seemed appropriate, and appointed dukes for the Normans who lived in those regions and for other cities there. But when the emperor’s mother-in-law [Note: [Col. 0248D] She was Agnes, daughter of Otto William, duke of Burgundy; she was the third wife of William the Great, count of Poitiers and duke of Aquitaine, who had already died in 1030, and the mother of the Empress Agnes, wife of Henry III. Clement.] returned from Mount Gargano to Benevento, the citizens of Benevento, in a disturbance that arose, inflicted various injuries upon her [Col. 0248A]. Fearing severe vengeance from the emperor and not daring to submit to him, they therefore began a rebellion [Note: [Col. 0248D] For this reason they were placed under papal interdict. Leo of Ostia.]. But the emperor, who, as has been said, had already sent home a large part of his army and was now making for his homeland with his mind occupied by other matters, postponed attacking such a great city at that time; leaving the matter unfinished, but with the rest of Italy obedient and pacified, he decided to return. Meanwhile the Empress Agnes, who had separated from the emperor at Rome, gave birth to a daughter in the territory of Ravenna.

As the emperor continued his journey homeward, he spent Easter at Mantua, lying there in a very serious illness. Later, when he had recovered, he brought back with him from Italy, with great honor, the body of blessed Wido, abbot of the monastery of Pomposa, who had died less than a year earlier, had been glorified by many miracles, and had been buried in the city of Parma, to be transferred to the city of Speyer. On this journey, coming to Augsburg in the litany before the Ascension of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0248D] The Rogation days fell on 25 May in this year.], he appointed Henry, his chaplain, as the successor of Eberhardus, bishop of that city, who had died upon his arrival. After celebrating the same feast there, he celebrated Pentecost at Speyer, where he held an assembly with the princes of the realm and had the body of the aforementioned abbot buried in the basilica begun outside the city [Note: [Col. 0248D] This church later became collegiate and took its name from the same Saint Guido. See Bollandus, vol. III, 31 March.].

At that time he advanced Welf, count of Swabia [Note: [Col. 0248D] Namely, Welf III, son of Welf II.], the son of the former Count Welf, as duke of Carinthia. He also appointed his maternal uncle Adelbero—the brother of the dukes Henry and Frideric [Col. 0249A] [Note: [Col. 0249D] Namely, Henry VI, duke of Bavaria, and Frideric, duke of Lower Lorraine, sons of Frideric I, count of Luxembourg; their sister was Judith, wife of Welf. Clement.]—bishop of the Church of Metz, after Theodericus, who had recently died. Likewise, after Archbishop Poppo had died during those days, he placed Eberhardus, provost of Worms, over the city of Trier as archbishop.

At the same time, while he was preparing an expedition into Pannonia to avenge Peter, it was reported that Duke Godefrid had renewed his rebellion together with Baldwin [Note: [Col. 0249D] Baldwin V, count of Flanders.] and had prepared a war after gathering troops; it was also reported that Margrave Theodoric of Vlaardingen had rebelled and had ravaged the neighboring episcopal territories to the emperor’s injury. Moreover, Andrew, who had obtained Peter’s kingdom, had repeatedly sent humble envoys, asserting that he had accepted the kingdom under compulsion from the Hungarians, excusing himself for Peter’s injuries, and declaring that those who had conspired against Peter had been partly killed by him and partly destined to be handed over to the emperor. He also conveyed to the emperor his submission, an annual tribute, and devoted servitude if the emperor allowed him to retain the kingdom. For these reasons the expedition was postponed. Since Duke Godefrid was also concealing his rebellion through cunning embassies, the emperor, in the autumn, gathered a naval army and took up arms against Theodoric in Vlaardingen.

Meanwhile Otto, duke of the Swabians, who had governed the province entrusted to him piously and energetically for three years, ended his life by an untimely death. During those same days Duke Henry of Bavaria died and was buried at Trier. Clement, also called Pope Suidgerus, died in the Roman region in the ninth month [Col. 0249C] of his elevation [Note: [Col. 0249D] Lambert of Hersfeld, together with Bernoldus, places it on 9 October, or the ninth day of that month, which Blessed Leo IX wished to be celebrated throughout the entire bishopric of Bamberg. After Clement’s death, Benedict IX again seized the see and held it for eight months, after which he returned to private life.], and was buried after being carried back to his bishopric of Bamberg.

220 After the emperor had crossed into Vlaardingen, he was able to accomplish little because of the flooded terrain. On his return, the enemy followed him by sea in light boats like pirates, repeatedly attacking and cutting down the stragglers; thus he suffered a considerable loss in his army. At the same time Godefrid, among the other actions he undertook against the king, captured the city of Verdun by treachery, burned it, and destroyed it. The emperor entrusted its duchy to a certain Adelbertus [Note: [Col. 0249D] This is Albertus, who had been made duke of Upper Lorraine in the preceding year.]. *Deeds of Verdun*, letters in Calmet.

### 1048 M. G.

The emperor, having spent Christmas in Saxony [Note: [Col. 0250D] The events of this year are described almost exclusively by Hermannus.], immediately came through Würzburg into Alemannia. Holding an assembly at Ulm, he appointed Otto of Schweinfurt, margrave, duke of the Swabians. From there he came into Bavaria and spent the Lenten and Easter seasons there. During that same Lent, the blood of the Lord was discovered near the city of Mantua, as was believed, through a divine revelation given to a certain blind man, and was attested by many miracles. The emperor departed from Regensburg, where he had celebrated Easter with Dukes Otto and Břetislav and many other princes, returned to Alemannia, and entered our Reichenau on 24 April [Note: [Col. 0250D] These words, which are also found in the Gottweig and Muri manuscripts, make it clear that both were copied from the Reichenau manuscript for the later years in which they agree with one another.]. In his presence he had the new basilica of Saint Mark the Evangelist, our patron, constructed by Lord Bern, the abbot, dedicated by Theodericus, bishop of Constance. After celebrating the feast of that saint among us during the greater litany, he celebrated the Ascension of the Lord at Zurich and Pentecost at Solothurn. Having held an assembly there with the Burgundians, he returned through eastern Francia to Saxony.

At the same time Lord Bern, abbot of Reichenau, a man distinguished in learning and conduct, in the eleventh year of his advancement, worn out by illness in a good old age, ended his last day on 8 June and was buried in the basilica of Saint Mark, where he rests. In his place the brothers elected Vodelricus, the dean, whom the emperor appointed abbot.

221 [Col. 0250C] When the learned Wazo [Note: [Col. 0250D] Anselm praises the merits of Bishop Wazo at length in his *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*.], bishop of Liège, had died, Dietwinus succeeded him. In the following July Poppo, bishop of Brixen [Note: [Col. 0250D] Poppo was bishop of Brixen, or Säben.], elected by the emperor, was sent to Rome, honorably received, and ordained pope CLII at the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0250D] Damasus was ordained on 17 July and died on the following day, 8 August.]. Having changed his name, he was called Damasus II. But after only a few days he died and was buried at Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls.

In the autumn Emperor Henry and Henry, king of the Gauls, met in the territory of Metz [Note: [Col. 0251C] The *History of the Monastery of Andage* identifies the place of this meeting as Yvois, a town in the diocese of Trier, two leagues from Mouzon.], and made peace, confirming their agreement to one another by oath. During those days a great earthquake occurred on the night of 13 October. During those same days the Empress Agnes gave birth to a daughter for the emperor.

At the same time Godefrid pursued Duke Adelbertus, who was plundering him, and, after dismissing the larger force, found him with a few companions and killed him together with the others who attempted to resist. After him the emperor appointed Duke Gerhardus [Note: [Col. 0251C] Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, vol. I, book XVIII, chapter 69, identifies Gerhardus as the count of Alsace and duke of Upper Lorraine, and makes him the ancestor of the present house of Lorraine.]. During those days the emperor came to Strasbourg and from there, shortly before Christmas, to Ulm; thus he proceeded into Bavaria.

### 1049 M. G.

The emperor celebrated Christmas at Freising and the Purification of Saint Mary at Regensburg, appointing Conrad as duke of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0251D] He was the son of Luidolfus, whose father was Ezo, or Ehrnfridus, count palatine of the Rhine, and whose mother was Mathilda, daughter of Emperor Otto II.]. Around the beginning of Lent he withdrew from there into Saxony. Godebaldus, provost of Speyer [Note: [Col. 0251D] The Gottweig manuscript more correctly reads “of Metz.”], was promoted by the emperor as patriarch of Aquileia after Eberhardus, who had died during those days.

222 Meanwhile, with a freezing winter providing the opportunity, several soldiers and princes from the coastal regions, together with the bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 0251D] Namely Theoduinus, Bernoldus or Bernulfus of Utrecht, and Adalbero.], and with the bishops of Utrecht and Metz, gathered and set an ambush for Theodoric at Vlaardingen. After battle had been joined, they killed him when he was defeated [Note: [Col. 0251D] This occurred on 14 January, according to Clement, which agrees better with the winter season than 15 May, the date on which the *Chronicle of Holland*, cited by Antonius Matthaeus, vol. V, says that he died.], and subjected that province to the emperor. Not long afterward, however, Godefrid occupied it; when attacked and defeated in battle by those same men, he barely escaped.

At the same time Brun—that is, the bishop of Toul among the Leuci—was elected by the emperor and sent to Rome, where he was received with the greatest honor. During Lent [Note: [Col. 0251D] Namely, on 12 February, the first Sunday of Lent, as Wibertus states in his *Life*.] he was ordained pope CLIII and took the name Leo IX. At the following Easter he consecrated Udalricus, administrator of the monastery of Reichenau, who had come to Rome, with the abbatial blessing, and confirmed and renewed by his authority the privileges of that monastery, anciently granted by the apostolic see, in the second indiction, on 26 [al.: 25] March. The same pope held a synod at Rome during the week after Low Sunday with the bishops of Italy, chiefly against the heresy of simony [Note: [Col. 0251D] Wibertus and Blessed Peter Damian report some of its acts, *Opusculum* VI, chapters 25 and 37.]. During Pentecost week the same pope convened another synod at Pavia; from there, by way of Mount Jovis, he came down into Cisalpine territory with many Romans. After that period had passed, Odilo, venerable head of the monastery of Cluny and father of many monasteries, departed to the Lord on 2 January [Note: [Col. 0252C] Muri: “He departed to the Lord on 30 December, and Hugo, a brother of the same monastery, succeeded him in good conduct.”].

223 In the following summer, while the emperor was preparing an expedition against Godefrid and Baldwin, who had been excommunicated by the lord pope, Godefrid, fearing both the emperor’s power and the pope’s excommunication, came to Aachen to surrender and, with the pope’s assistance, obtained the emperor’s favor. Baldwin, however, despising both, after his province had been largely devastated by the army, finally gave hostages and made an agreement with the emperor.

In the autumn [Note: [Col. 0252C] Namely, on 3 October. Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, p. 1028.] the lord pope held a great synod at Reims with the bishops of Gaul. From there he came to Mainz and held another synod of eleven bishops in the presence of the emperor and the princes of our realm [Note: [Col. 0252C] Muri: “There, among other matters, Bertholdus, archbishop of Besançon, who had been driven from his see by many people for years, was finally canonically convicted and deposed.” But this appears to be mistaken. In this year Hugo, bishop of Besançon, was present at the council, as Wicbertus attests; he presided over that see from 1031 until 1071, and nothing about the matter is recorded in the acts of the council, vol. III of the *German Councils*, p. 112. Perhaps it should instead be understood of Bertaldus, who in the catalogue of the archbishops of the Church of Besançon (*Chifflet, Illustrations of the Claudian*, vol. I, June, Bollandus, p. 693) is called, before this Hugo, an intruded pseudo-bishop, but not accepted.]. Afterwards, visiting Alemannia, he celebrated the feast of Saint Clement at Reichenau and the Sunday before Advent, 26 November, and, passing through Augsburg and Bavaria, celebrated Christmas at Verona.

### 1050

The emperor, however, spent that same feast in Saxony. During the winter, while Gebehardus, bishop of Regensburg, who had recently received the abbey of Kempten from the emperor as a benefice, was staying on the borders of Pannonia, he entered the Hungarians’ territory as they withdrew and carried off booty from it. But after he had departed, a very large Hungarian army invaded our borders, taking many captives, burning, and ravaging a large part of the country.

The emperor spent Easter at Utrecht. After Easter the lord pope again convened a synod at Rome. Later, advancing beyond Rome, he subjected several princes of the region [Col. 0253B] and cities by oath both to himself and to the emperor, and excommunicated the Beneventans, who were still in rebellion [Note: [Col. 0253D] Leo of Ostia, book II, chapter 84, says that the Beneventans had then been absolved from Clement II’s excommunication; perhaps they were soon afterward bound by Leo X because of a new rebellion.]. Several princes of foreign peoples also sent envoys to him, as to an apostolic man, and promised him their submission.

The emperor prepared an expedition against Gazmerus [Note: [Col. 0253D] This is Casimir, who, having been a Cluniac monk and a deacon, became king of Poland through a dispensation granted by Pope Benedict IX.], duke of the Poles, who was plotting rebellion. Detained by a serious illness, he accepted Gazmerus when he sought peace and an agreement, and withdrew.

Gebehardus, bishop of Regensburg, together with Conrad, duke of Bavaria, Margrave Adelbertus, and certain other bishops and princes of Bavaria, rebuilt Heimenburg. They overthrew a large force of Hungarians invading them and pursued them as far as the presence of their innumerable armies, which were in flight. When all the Hungarian troops turned their backs, seized by a divinely sent terror, they returned to their camp giving thanks to God [Note: [Col. 0253D] See Aventinus, book V, chapter 8, and Brunnerus, part II, book V.].

That autumn the lord pope convened a synod at Vercelli [Note: [Col. 0253D] See Lanfrancus, book IV, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 4.] and suspended Archbishop Hunfridus from office because of a dispute between the Church of Ravenna and the Roman Church. From there he revisited Gaul and his own episcopal city among the Leuci. At that same time the Empress Agnes finally gave birth to a son for the emperor.

### 1051 M. G.

The emperor celebrated Christmas in Saxony at Goslar and made many of the princes swear an oath promising loyalty and submission to his son. Not long afterward he and the lord pope, together with many bishops and princes, met at Augsburg and celebrated the Purification of the Mother of God. The archbishop of Ravenna, having been reconciled there with the pope [Note: [Col. 0253D] Wibertus writes somewhat differently about this disagreement between Saint Leo and the archbishop of Ravenna in his *Life*, chapter 7.], they departed from one another in charity. The pope returned to Rome, while the emperor spent part of Lent at Speyer and Easter at Cologne, where his son Henry was baptized by Archbishop Hermannus.

After Easter the lord Pope Leo again convened a synod at Rome. Among other matters, he excommunicated Gregory, bishop of Vercelli, in his absence and without his knowledge, on account of adultery committed with a certain widow who was the betrothed of his uncle, and because he had committed perjury. Yet not long afterward, when Gregory came to Rome and promised satisfaction, Leo restored him to his former office.

At the same time the emperor compelled Count Lantpertus [Note: [Col. 0253D] We leave this count for others to investigate.] to surrender when he attempted rebellion. That summer Bardo, the venerable archbishop of the see of Mainz, formerly a monk, remarkable for every form of piety and holiness, was taken from this life on 11 June [Note: [Col. 0254D] The anonymous author of his life (*Mabillon, Benedictine Centuries*, sixth century, part II) associates 11 June with a Friday; Papebrochius therefore postpones his death to the year 1053, when 2 June was a Friday. Yet the authority of so many contemporary writers scarcely permits us to depart from the year 1051.]. Many miracles made him illustrious after his death. In his place the emperor appointed Luitpaldus, provost of Bamberg. Likewise, in place of Theodericus, bishop of Constance, who died on 22 June, in the fifth year of his episcopate, after a long illness, he promoted Rumaldus. Archbishop Hunfridus of Ravenna also suddenly died, as they say, from poison.

In the following autumn the emperor, with a large army, refused to accept the agreement of King Andrew as it was offered through envoys and marched into Pannonia. He sent Gebehardus, bishop of Regensburg, and Dukes Welf and Břetislav to ravage the northern bank of the Danube. He himself, transporting from the ships as much supplies as could be carried on horses, made a long circuit through the territory of Carinthia because of the flooding of the rivers. Invading the perjured kingdom, he found the Hungarian army fleeing here and there like brigands, never daring to engage in an even battle. He laid waste everything all around, as far as the army’s supplies permitted.

But when the Hungarians, already exhausted by scarcity and hunger, prepared to prevent the army’s return, placing their forces along the riverbanks at fortified and shallow marsh crossings, and threatening either to force everyone to surrender or to destroy them by starvation, the undaunted soldiers drove back the enemy. They crossed without hesitation through the rivers where the enemy resisted and soon captured a very strong fortification built at the bridge of the Rába River, in which the enemy had placed its greatest confidence. Certain soldiers from Burgundy, Saxony, and Poland crossed the river at no small danger to themselves and quickly captured it, having slain and scattered the Hungarians, for the rest of the army. [lacuna]

[Col. 0255] (Here the Reichenau manuscript is truncated, its final leaves having been cut away; the Einsiedeln and Augsburg manuscripts copied from it are likewise truncated. The Gottweig and Muri manuscripts continue.)

## GOTTWEIG AND MURI MANUSCRIPTS

[Col. 0255B] They open a way which, after nearly everyone had crossed, was set on fire and, with several of the last men being pursued by the enemy in great danger, closed off the passage [supplement: “the entrance”]. Thus, when the emperor returned, and those whom he had sent beyond the Danube had already returned some time before after successful operations, Andrew sent to request peace from our margrave Adelbertus, and in turn granted it.
