During those days, when the abbesses of Lindau and Buchau died at the same time, the noble, prudent, and religious widow Tuta was appointed by the emperor to restore both places.

### 1052

The emperor celebrated Christmas at Goslar. There he ordered certain heretics to be hanged on the gallows, with the consent of everyone, lest the heretical infection spread farther and infect more people. Among their other doctrines of wicked error, they condemned the eating of every animal according to the Manichaean sect [Col. 0256B] 227.

At the same time, on 9 January, my mother Hiltrudis, wife of Count Wolfradus [Note: [Col. 0255C] See above under the year 1010.], a very devout, gentle, generous, and religious woman, died her last day. Her husband and seven children survived her. Her end, as it appeared to human beings, was devout and blessed. She was about sixty-one years old and had been married for forty-four years. She was buried near the village of Alleshusan, beneath the chapel of Saint Ulrich, which she herself had built, in a tomb that she had prepared for herself. [lacuna]

[Col. 0255] (Here the small Gottweig manuscript ends; the Muri manuscript continues.)

## MURI MANUSCRIPT

[Col. 0255]

[Col. 0255B] As though for her epitaph, I wished to add these verses:

Mother of the needy, hope and aid of her own,

Here Hiltrud renders what she owes to the earth in the tomb.

She ennobled parents of a noble and powerful line,

Raising them up by her illustrious studies,

And, reverently cherishing chaste monogamy,

She lived inclined toward divine service.

228 Striving to remain in Martha’s good portion,

She studied to follow what practical life taught.

In clothing, food, speech, and step, with every effort,

She showed herself generous and devout toward the wretched.

In religion she cherished her pious friends above all others;

Toward everyone she made herself well-mannered and gentle.

Remaining gentle, patient, and ignorant of strife,

She pleased the world—oh, may she also have pleased the Lord.

Chastising the flesh and frequenting holy places in prayer,

She diligently sought heavenly aid.

Believe that I do not invent these things in empty praise,

Nor exalt my mother with deceitful words.

Consult the popular report everywhere,

And, made certain by the few things said by truthful people, you will be certain.

Finally, after pure confession had often cleansed her,

And she had been devoted to the Lord with a pious heart,

Strengthened by faith, secure in hope, and vigorous in devotion,

She happily departed this wretched life,

When January was rolling toward its fifth day before the Ides;

Her death moved very many tears.

For her, reader, I ask, pray, entreat, request, and implore you

To assail the Lord with humble prayers,

So that, in his compassion and by his own mercy,

The gentle Lord may wash her clean of every stain;

And in the happy lot of his blessed ones,

In his generosity, may he grant her lasting rest.

In the following Lenten season the emperor promoted Henry as archbishop of Ravenna. Nitzo [al.: Nitherus], bishop of Freising, who had first been converted from the manner of a supremely proud life to the appearance of humility and religion, but had then returned to the insolence of his former conduct, after conducting him to Ravenna at the emperor’s command, died there suddenly [Note: [Col. 0257D] Wibertus tells this story very differently in the *Life of Saint Leo*, book II, chapter 4, vol. II, April, Bollandus, under 19 April. See Pagi, *Critical Commentary*, vol. IV, p. 190, and Meichelbeck, *History of Freising*, vol. I, part I, p. 247.].

The emperor celebrated Easter at Speyer and from there, as they say, departed increasingly despising that place, which contained the burial of his father and mother [Col. 0258A], growing angry and hostile toward the bishop of that place.

During those same days Boniface, the wealthiest margrave of Italy [Note: [Col. 0257D] Namely, of Tuscany. He married Beatrice, daughter of Frideric II, duke of Upper Lorraine, in a second marriage in 1036, and had by her the famous Matilda. [Col. 0258D] Clement.], indeed a tyrant, was ambushed by two soldiers, wounded by arrows, and killed; he was buried at Mantua.

When the emperor was holding an assembly at Solothurn around the time of the litanies, certain Burgundians, offended, departed from there. Not long afterward some of them returned to his favor. From there, after celebrating Pentecost at Zurich, he likewise set out on an expedition into Pannonia [Note: [Col. 0258D] From here to the end the Muri manuscript differs somewhat from the edition of Urstisius; we have therefore appended it here.].

There, when Andrew, king of the Hungarians, treated the peace agreement with contempt, the emperor besieged the fortress of Brezzisburg and attacked it with many engines, but could not capture it by any means. Meanwhile, the lord Pope Leo, summoned by Andrew, labored to arrange peace and called the emperor away from the siege, since he was entirely in agreement with him. But, discovering that Andrew was mocking him by his counsels and trickery, he threatened to excommunicate him [Note: [Col. 0258D] In the *Life*, chapter 8, Wibertus places the blame for the peace not being achieved not on Andrew but on the emperor’s courtiers. See both Pagis.]. Thus he departed from there with the emperor and remained with him for some time. During those days the empress again gave birth to a son for the emperor, who was later called Conrad.

[Col. 0258C] 230 A dispute arose and was contested between Gebehardus, bishop of Regensburg, and Conrad, duke of Bavaria. The relics of Saint Zeno were transferred from Verona to Ulm and, as fame spread, shone forth through many miracles. At Constance the basilica of Saint Mary collapsed.

[Col. 0257] (Here another Gottweig manuscript begins, agreeing with the Muri manuscript through these two years, although it attributes this material to Bertholdus; the same attribution is found in Urstisius, who begins from this year the continuation of Bertholdus, or rather Bernoldus. See the preceding year, p. 127. Bernoldus writes of this year as follows: “The emperor, together with the lord pope . . . was detained for some time,” as in Muri. “Emperor Henry, having held . . . caused submission to be promised,” as in Muri. “Hazilinus, also bishop of Bamberg, died infamous.”)

[Col. 0259A] **1053** The emperor spent Christmas with the lord pope at Worms. There, when the pope had demanded from the emperor, as he had begun to do some time before, the abbey of Fulda and several other estates and monasteries allegedly donated to St. Peter in ancient times, [Col. 0260A] the emperor at last handed over to him, as though in exchange for the lands beyond the Alps, most of the possessions in the regions beyond Rome that belonged to his own jurisdiction, and assigned him aid to repel the violence of the Normans. [Col. 0261A] That people had flocked into the regions of Calabria, Samnium, and Campania since the time of the earlier King Henry [Note: [Col. 0261D] Namely, Henry II. See under the year 1022.]. Since they boldly assisted the natives in fighting against the incursions of the Greeks and Saracens, they were at first gladly received. Later, however, when more of them gathered in the fertile land and their strength had increased, they violently seized the natives themselves and their possessions. Leo of Ostia, Book II, chapter 84. Hence the lord pope, returning to Rome with many Germans, moved an army against the Normans after Easter. But when part of his army had been put to flight and part killed by the Normans, the pope himself was besieged by them in a certain fortress. Since the fortification had already been reduced and he was compelled by necessity to restore to them the communion previously forbidden them, he was accepted by them, but was nevertheless escorted honorably back to Benevento and detained there for some time so that he would not return. Otto of Freising.

In those same days, certain lakes which Julius Caesar was said to have blocked permanently with masonry, as people believed, were broken through by an excessive flood of water and caused the Nera and the Tiber to overflow beyond measure. A sudden inundation destroyed many buildings, the bridge of Narni itself collapsed, and many people were swept away. [Col. 0261B] The emperor spent Easter in Saxony at Merseburg, while the king of the Danes stayed with him. During those same days he deprived Conrad, duke of Bavaria, against whom he had already been hostile, of his duchy after the accusation had been brought against him and certain princes had judged the case. At that time both the greater and the lesser men of the kingdom complained that the emperor was much worse than the duke himself. A considerable shortage of crops occurred both this year and [Col. 0261C] the preceding year.

[Page 231] Werinharius, a very learned monk of Reichenau and one truly devoted to religion, burning with zeal for a more perfect life, set out as a pilgrim to Jerusalem for Christ’s sake; there, in the field of Acheldemach [Col. 0262A] [Haceldama], he died and was happily buried. Many others eventually followed his example. The emperor Henry, after holding an assembly at Tribur, had his son, who bore the same name, elected king by everyone, and secured a promise that after his death they would submit to him, provided that he should prove a just ruler. Conrad, formerly duke of Bavaria, did not come there and attempted to join the Hungarians; consequently the emperor deprived him of some of his possessions. There too the envoys of Andrew, king of the Hungarians, who had come to arrange peace, were sent back by the emperor after the peace had been [restored]. [Page 234] Hacilinus, the infamous bishop of Bamberg, died and made room [Note: [Col. 0261D] These statements about a bishop otherwise by no means lacking in praise appear to have been made without evidence.].

**1054** The emperor, coming into Bavaria, handed the duchy of that province over to his son, who bore the same name. [Col. 0262B] While remaining in that province, he celebrated Christmas at the villa of Ötting. There he bestowed the bishopric of Bamberg upon his cousin Adalbero [Note: [Col. 0261D] Namely, the son of Matilda, who was the sister of Henry’s mother, Gisela, and was married to Conrad, duke of Carinthia.]. Then, passing through Alemannia, he began Lent at Turgi. He celebrated Easter at Mainz, where Theobald, son of Odo, who had come to him from Gaul, became his knight.

At last the lord pope returned to Rome as Easter approached. He fell ill, and as his illness grew stronger day by day, he died a glorious death: first blessing everyone, taking leave of them after giving them admonitions, confessing his sins to St. Peter, and commending himself to him with the greatest devotion. He died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May and was buried in the basilica of St. Peter beside the tomb of St. Gregory; he is remembered as having become renowned there through miracles.

Duke Gotifrid again attempted to rebel against the emperor. Entering Italy secretly, he there took the lady Beatrice [Note: [Col. 0261D] Concerning this Beatrice, see below, under the year 1052.], widow of the margrave Boniface after her husband’s death, as his wife. Baldwin rebelled against the emperor.

[Col. 0261] **THUS FAR THE CHRONICLE OF HERMANN. FROM THIS POINT BERCHTOLD.** [Note: [Col. 0261D] In this way the Murensis and Engelbergensis codices close Hermann’s Chronicle. They alone among the others carried it through to the end, namely to the year 1054, in which Hermann died on 24 September; from that point his continuator, Berthold, his disciple, continues it.].

## COMPENDIUM FROM THE CODEX OF BERNOLD

[Col. 0055]

[Col. 0055B] **15** Archelaus is banished by Augustus to Vienne, a city of Gaul; Judaea is entrusted to tetrarchs; and Augustus dies at the age of seventy-six. Tiberius the second, Augustus’s stepson, reigned twenty-three years.

**20** He adds: Germanicus Caesar dies. Tacitus, *Annals*, Book 16.

[Col. 0057D] **29** The Lord Jesus Christ, etc., as in Augustine, under the following year.

**34** He adds: Stephen is stoned. Paul is converted.

**38** He adds: Gaius Caligula, the third, [reigned] four years, six months, and eight days. A most wicked man.

**45** Marcus, etc.; this is lacking in B.

[Col. 0058D] **56** He adds: Nero, the fifth, [reigned] thirteen years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. In every respect he was disgraceful; he initiated the first persecution of Christians.

**57** Sedition in Caesarea, etc., as in Augustine.

**59** Up to this point the Book of Acts of the Apostles contains twenty-seven years from the Lord’s Passion.

[Col. 0059C] **67** Nero, etc., as in Augustine. In the margin, in an early hand, the following is written: Jerome, in *On Illustrious Men* (chapter 12): “Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Cordoba, a disciple of the Stoic Sotion [Note: [Col. 0059D] In Letter 49 Seneca calls Sotion his teacher, as does Eusebius in the *Chronicle*. Jerome here otherwise indicates Seneca’s eleventh letter, which is the sixth to Paul, whom he addresses as follows: ‘What place is mine with you, and yours with you? I wish that yours might be mine.’ See Fabricius, *Apocryphal Codex of the New Testament*, part II, p. 880, [Col. 0060D] and part III, p. 710.], uncle of the poet Lucan, wrote many letters to the apostle Paul, and Paul to him; he wished to be among his own people such a person as Paul was regarded among Christians.” *Works*, vol. IV, part II, p. 106 of the new Maurist edition.

**68** Vespasian, commander of the army against [lacuna], etc., as in Augustine.

**69** Peter and Paul are slaughtered on the third day before the Kalends of July; the rest as in Augustine. Linus, the first after St. Peter, held office for twelve years and suffered martyrdom on the sixth day before the Kalends of December at Antioch, etc., as in Augustine. Galba, the sixth, [reigned] seven months. Otho, three months. Vitellius, eight months. Bernold’s marginal note: “In the succession of the Roman pontiffs this chronicle follows Eusebius, not the pontifical book, although the latter ought rather to be trusted in this account, as being the work which Pope Damasus, at the request of St. Jerome, described with the greatest care” [Note: [Col. 0060D] Critics think quite differently. See Pagius on Damasus.].

[Col. 0060C] **70** Vespasian [lacuna] is appointed. Vespasian, the seventh, reigned nine years, eleven months, and twenty-two days. A man outstanding in military valor.

**71** Titus [against] the Jews, etc., as in Augustine.

**72** Jerusalem [lacuna], forty-two years from the Lord’s Passion, from the first [lacuna], etc., as in Augustine.

**80** Vespasian dies from a flux, etc., as in Augustine. Titus, the eighth, son of Vespasian, [reigned] two years and two months; a man remarkable for every kind of virtue, so that he was called “the delight” [Note: [Col. 0060D] This is the reading to be adopted from the printed editions, although the codices have *divitiae*, “wealth.”] and love of the human race.

**81** Titus [builds] the amphitheater, etc., as in Augustine.

**82** Anacletus, the second pope, held office for twelve years and suffered martyrdom on the sixth day before the Kalends of May. Titus, in the same villa, etc., as in Augustine. Domitian, the ninth, brother of Titus, [reigned] fifteen years and five months. Tainted with every crime, he persecuted Christians for the second time. Bernold’s marginal note: “After Pope Linus some books have Cletus, and after Clement, Anacletus; but Eusebius’s history entirely passes over Pope Cletus” [Note: Namely, because in Eusebius’s and the Greek view he was the same person as Anacletus, whereas Epiphanius and most Latins distinguish them.].

**83** Domitian prohibited the making of eunuchs.

[Col. 0061B] **92** At this time the Romans suffered many evils, etc., as in Augustine.

**94** As in Augustine. Bernold’s marginal note: “The statements appear contradictory: Clement is said to have been enthroned in the apostolic see in the thirty-second year after the death of James, the Lord’s brother, and to have issued certain decrees to him” [Note: The reference is to Clement’s decretal letter, said to have been written by him to James. It appears in Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*, vol. I, p. 82.].

**98** He adds: Nerva, the tenth, an old man, [reigned] one year, four months, and eight days. By his first edict he recalled all exiles.

**99** St. John, etc., as in Augustine. Nerva died worn out by illness. Trajan, the eleventh, of Spanish origin, [reigned] nineteen years, six months, and fifteen days. A man useful to the state, but deceived by error, he persecuted Christians for the third time [Note: Idatius, in the *Fasti*, under the year 112; Eusebius, under the year 108.].

**100** The third [bishop] of Alexandria, etc., as in A.

**101** The apostle John at [lacuna], etc., as in A., under the preceding year.

**102** Jerome’s *On Illustrious Men* [Note: Namely, chapter 15, where he is said to have died in Trajan’s third year, or this year, although the day is not given. Cotelerius, among others, investigates how many in succession Clement was from St. Peter, in his notes on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book VII, chapter 46, vol. I, p. 383. See Pagius, critical notes, under the year 100.] asserts that Pope Clement died here on the eighth day before the Kalends of December [Col. 0062B] and was fourth from St. Peter. Eusebius, under the year 100.

**103** Evaristus, the fourth pope, held office for eight years and suffered martyrdom on the sixth day before the Kalends of November. Trajan, etc., as in Augustine.

Eusebius, under the year 107. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, is regarded as a distinguished teacher.

**107** A great earthquake. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and disciple of the apostles, was still flourishing.

**108** At this time Pliny the Younger, a distinguished philosopher, softens Trajan’s attitude toward the Christians; elsewhere under the year 102 [Note: See his Letter 98, Book X; compare Pagius’s critical notes under the year 102.].

**109** An earthquake overturns many cities; Nero’s golden house is destroyed by fire; and the Pantheon is burned by lightning. Eusebius, under the year 111.

[Col. 0063C] **116** Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, suffers martyrdom. Pagius, under this year.

[Col. 0063D] **132** Pope Sixtus suffered under the emperor Hadrian on the eighth day before the Ides of April; elsewhere under the year 127.

[Col. 0065C] **158** Pope Anicetus, the tenth, held office for eleven years and was crowned with martyrdom on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May. In his time Hegesippus records that he came to Rome and remained there until the time of Pope Eleutherius. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*.

**160** At Jerusalem, etc., as in Augustine, under the preceding year.

**161** Antoninus Pius, etc., as in A., under the preceding year.

**164** Lucius Caesar, etc., as in Augustine, under the year 162.

**165** Fronto the orator, etc., as in A., under the year 163.

**166** The Caesars, etc., as in Augustine, under the year 164.

**167** Under these emperors occurred the fourth persecution, etc., as in A., under the year 165.

[Col. 0065D] **169** At this time there was a very great pestilence, etc., as in A., under the year 167.

**183** The temple of Serapis, etc., as in A., under the year 181.

He also asserted that Christ was a human being of ordinary nature. When he refused to leave the church after being condemned, he was expelled from the church by public authority, to increase his disgrace, as the *Ecclesiastical History* relates” [Note: Eusebius, Book VII, chapters 23–24. Bernold’s marginal note: [Col. 0075D] “Up to this point Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* appropriately describes the successions of the Roman and Alexandrian bishops, just as they are described here” [Note: In the Murensis codex this note is read as inserted into the text.].

Marcellus, the twenty-ninth [Note: Pope Marcellus, elected in 308, died the following year, 310; his successor was Eusebius, who held the papacy for only four months.], held office for five years and suffered martyrdom on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February.

[Col. 0077C] **308** Maximianus Herculius, etc., as in A., under the preceding year.

**309** After Severus had been killed, etc., as in A., under the preceding year.

**310** Galerius Maximianus, persecutor of Christians, struck by divine vengeance, ordered that Christians be spared.

**315** Maximinus Caesar dies miserably and deservedly in great agony; elsewhere under the year 313.

**316** Many [things], etc., as in A., under the preceding year.

[Col. 0077D] **318** Licinius Caesar, initially good and a defender of the Christians, plotted wickedly against Constantine and persecuted Christians; defeated in war, he perished [Note: Licinius’s persecution began in this year, but his death occurred in 324.]. Pope Melchiades, the thirty-first, held office for four years and died on the fourth day before the Ides of January [Note: Melchiades was elected in 311 and died in 314.].

**320** At this time Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria, founded the abominable heresy of the Arians under Bishop Alexander, who succeeded Achillas.

[Col. 0078C] **321** Pope Silvester, the thirty-second [Note: He had already become pope in 314.], held office for twenty-three years and ten months; he died on the day before the Kalends of January.

**322** A council of 318 bishops is assembled at Nicaea under Pope Silvester. Arius is condemned there, and seventy chapters are established, as Athanasius says, who took part in that synod. Bernold’s marginal note: “There are seventy decrees from Nicaea, as Athanasius and Pope Mark alike write.”

**325** Constantine’s twentieth anniversary of accession is celebrated at Rome.

**327** Constantine subjects the Sarmatians, Goths, and many nations to Roman rule; elsewhere under the year 332.

**328** Constantine restored the city of Byzantium, called it Constantinople after his own name, and wished it to be the seat of the Roman Empire; elsewhere under the year 329.

**329** Athanasius is ordained bishop of Alexandria [Col. 0078D]; elsewhere under the year 328.

**330** At this time the Indians and Iberians become Christians. Socrates, under the year 327.

**331** In these times Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, the poet Juvencus, and many other teachers became renowned.

**332** Antony, as in A., under the following year.

**333** Constantia, sister of Constantine and wife of Licinius, dies.

[Col. 0079C] **334** Constantine lapses into the Arian doctrine [Note: Pagius and others vigorously defend Constantine against the charge of this heretical stain, which St. Jerome wrongly impressed upon him in the *Chronicle* because he received baptism at the end of his life from the Arian Eusebius of Nicomedia. See Pagius, *Critique of Baronius*, under the year 324, no. 14.].

**335** Constantine, while preparing war against the Persians, dies at Nicomedia at the age of sixty-six. Jerome, under the year 338. Constantius, son of Constantine, with his brothers Constantine and Constans, reigned twenty-four years, five months, and thirteen days.

**336** Constantius is made an Arian through the Arian presbyter and Eusebius of Nicomedia and persecutes the Catholics.

**337** James of Nisibis became renowned for his virtues. Jerome, under the year 339. Dalmatius Caesar is killed.

**339** An earthquake destroys many cities.

**340** The Franks, etc., as in Augustine, under the following year.

**341** At Constantinople [lacuna] is appointed, as in A., under the following year.

**342** At this time Maximinus, bishop of Trier [Col. 0079D], is regarded as distinguished. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, having fled from Constantius, is honorably received by him.

[Col. 0080C] **343** Pope Mark, the thirty-third [Note: Mark succeeded Silvester in 336; after seven months he was succeeded by Julius in 337.], held office for two years and died on the Nones of October.

**345** He adds: Julius, the thirty-fourth pope, [held office] fifteen years; elsewhere under the year 337.

**346** The war, etc., as in A., under the following year.

**347** Constans is killed not far from Spain at the age of thirty; elsewhere under the year 350.

**349** In these times the bones [lacuna] were brought, as in Augustine, under the following year.

**351** The monk Antony dies in the desert in the 105th year of his life. At that time many hermits became renowned for their virtues. Jerome, under the year 358.

**352** The rhetorician Victorinus and the grammarian Donatus are distinguished at Rome. Jerome, under the year 355.

**353** Julian, etc., as in A., under the following year.

[Col. 0080D] **354** Great [events], etc., as in Augustine, under the following year.

**355** Julian defeated the Germans on the Rhine.

[Col. 0081C] **356** At this time Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, Athanasius of Alexandria, and all the Catholic bishops suffered many evils from the Arians. Jerome, under the following year.

**357** At Rimini a synod of 400 Arian bishops was held against the faith; elsewhere under the year 359.

**358** Julian, elated by success in war, usurps the name of Augustus. Constantius prepares war against the Parthians. Bernold’s marginal note: Pope Liberius, the thirty-fifth, held office for six years. After he was expelled, Pope Felix, the thirty-sixth, occupied his place for one year, and Liberius was restored to his see. Jerome, under the preceding year. St. Felix, declaring the emperor Constantius a heretic, was martyred on the fourth day before the Kalends of August [Note: Concerning this condemnation and the martyrdom of Felix II, see Pagius, *Brief History of the Roman Pontiffs*, and the Bollandists, vol. VII of July, under the 24th; concerning Liberius, vol. VI of September, under the 23rd.].

**359** Constantius [lacuna] taking, dies. Jerome, under the year [Col. 0081D] 362. Julian, the thirty-sixth, the Apostate, [reigned] one year and eight months. Having become a pagan from a Christian reader, he persecuted Christians.

**360** The pagans [lacuna] invade, as in Augustine, under the following year.

**361** Julian goes to war [lacuna] in the thirty-second year of his life, as in Augustine, under the following year. Jovianus, the thirty-seventh, [reigned] eight months. He returned again to Christianity with his entire army. Jerome, under the year 364.

[Col. 0082C] **362** A heretical synod is held at Antioch. Jovianus [lacuna] dies, as in Augustine, under the following year. Valentinianus, the thirty-eighth, reigned eleven years. He [did something], etc., as in A., under the following year.

**363** Valentinianus and Valens, as in A., under the following year.

**364** Valens, seduced and baptized by Eudoxius, the Arian bishop, persecuted the orthodox after his brother’s death.

**365** Gratian, son of Valentinianus, is made emperor at Amiens. True wool [lacuna], etc., as in A., under the following year.

**366** Athanaric, king of the Goths, persecutes Christians among his people. Jerome, under the year 370. Pope Damasus, the thirty-seventh, held office for eighteen years.

**367** At this time Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, wrote many things, but later founded a heresy.

[Col. 0082D] **368** A great famine in Phrygia.

**369** In these days, after Auxentius [lacuna], etc., as in Augustine, under the following year.

**370** Valentinianus subdued the Saxons in the region of the Franks by slaughter.

**371** Nearly eighty thousand Burgundians settled beside the Rhine. Ammianus, under the year 372; Jerome, under the year 374.

**372** After Auxentius the Arian, when Ambrose had been ordained, Italy returned to the true faith.

[Col. 0083C] **373** Valentinianus, preparing war against the Sarmatians, dies of apoplexy. Valens, the thirty-ninth, after his brother’s death reigned four years with Gratian and Valentinian; elsewhere under the year 375.

**374** Gratian destroyed thirty thousand Alamanni. Jerome, under the year 378.

**375** Valens issued a law, etc., as in Augustine, under the following year. The Goths, after being given [something], etc., as in Augustine, under the year 377.

**377** Valens, fleeing after his army had been killed by the Goths, is burned alive in a certain house; elsewhere under the following year.

**378** After the death of Valens the Arian emperor, Gratian with his brother Valentinian reigned six years. Up to this point Jerome brought Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. [Col. 0084C] From here the lord Hermann brought his own *Chronicle* down to the year 1054 from the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 0084D] In the Bavarian codex this clause appears after the year 377, consistently with the earlier years, where he generally follows the Reichenau chronicle by a full year, although from the year 379 onward his reckoning again agrees with it. From this we nevertheless learn how far Hermann wrote his *Chronicle*.].

**379** The emperor Gratian appointed Theodosius emperor of the East. Priscillianus, etc., as in Augustine.

**380** From this time [lacuna] begins the Easter cycles.

**381** The second synod [lacuna] under Pope Damasus; after the condemnation of the aforementioned heretic, three canons are established.

**384** Maximus, usurping the kingdom for himself, killed Gratian at Lyons [Note: Socrates and Prosper likewise assign this to this year, but Marcellinus and the others assign it to the preceding year.].

[Col. 0085C] **385** Jerome the presbyter, now living at Bethlehem, is regarded as distinguished. Prosper, under this year. Priscillian the heretic, condemned at the synod of Bordeaux, fled, but was killed at Trier by the prefect Evodius [Note: St. Jerome, Sulpicius, and Prosper write that Priscillian was indeed examined by Evodius, but condemned to the sword by Maximus.]. Prosper, under this year.

**386** At this time Pope Siricius wrote fifteen chapters of decretal letters to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona [Note: This decretal letter was written on the fifth day before the Ides of February, in the consulship of Arcadius and Bauto, and therefore belongs to the preceding year. Scholars generally regard it as the first authentic decretal letter, although P. Constant disagrees, presenting still earlier genuine letters beginning with St. Clement in his collection, published at Paris in 1721.].

**388** Theodosius Augustus killed the tyrant Maximus at Aquileia.

**389** As in Augustine.

**390** At this time St. Martin, Ambrose the bishop, Jerome the presbyter, John Chrysostom, Augustine, Severus, and many other teachers became renowned.

[Col. 0086C] **392** Valentinianus ended his life by a noose through the treachery of Arbogastes [Note: The manner of this death is uncertain: Zosimus tells it differently from Epiphanius and the others. See St. Ambrose’s Letter 34 and his funeral oration for Valentinianus, from which it appears that death was violently inflicted upon him.]. Jerome, etc., as in Augustine.

**393** As in Augustine.

**394** John [lacuna]. Jerome described [it], etc., as in Augustine.

395 Emperor Theodosius defeated the tyrant Eugenius, and in that same year himself peacefully rested at Milan; in his place his sons Arcadius and Honorius ruled for thirteen years. Augustine was ordained bishop at Hippo. John the hermit departed to the Lord.

396 The count Gildo tyrannically usurped Africa for himself.

397 Saint Martin of Tours . . . Severus composed admirably.

[Col. 0087C] 398 Saint Ambrose of Milan, archbishop and outstanding teacher, departed to the Lord on the fifth day before the Kalends of May. [Note: [Col. 0088D] Marcellinus has “the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May,” but one should read “the day before the Nones of April”; this day was Holy Saturday, on which, according to Paulinus, Saint Ambrose died. This chronological note indicates the preceding year. See his Life, vol. II of the works, Maurist edition.]—At Rome Anastasius, etc., as in Aug.—The count Gildo was defeated in battle and perished.

399 The temples of the idols were destroyed, and the gladiatorial games were abolished.

400. The Goths ravaged Italy. At this time Pope Anastasius established his decrees and condemned the Manichaeans found in the City. The bodies of the prophets Habakkuk and Micah were revealed by the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0088D] According to Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History, book VII, final chapter, this happened under Theodosius the Elder; it is therefore incorrectly assigned to this year. See Bollandists, 15 January, vol. I.]

401 John . . . Theophilus are regarded as men of the highest distinction, but so discordant that, etc., as in Aug.

402 The Goths put to flight the commander Stilicho together with the Roman army. Pope Innocent, the forty-second, occupied the see for fourteen years. [Note: [Col. 0088D] Pagi rejects Innocent’s ordination as belonging to 21 December 401.] He wrote fifty-seven decretal chapters. Prosp. Marc.

[Col. 0088C] 403. At Carthage . . . is regarded. African Church Code.

404 In these years Pope Innocent issued many decrees. The presbyter Orosius was held in high regard. Prosp. a. 396.

405 At this time Radagaisus, with two hundred thousand Goths, was defeated by God’s favor.

406 The Vandals . . . entered.

407 Pope Innocent excommunicated the emperor Arcadius, who had consented to the expulsion of John Chrysostom. [Note: [Col. 0088D] The letter of Innocent to Eudoxia, and two letters of Arcadius to Innocent, from which Bernold derived this statement, are judged spurious by learned authorities. See Pagi in the Life of this pontiff, *Brief History of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, no. 28.]

408 Arcadius . . . ruled for fifteen years.—The brave commander Stilicho was killed by the emperor Honorius.

409 The Vandals, Alans, and Sueves, on the third day of October, etc., as in Aug.

[Col. 0089C] 410 Alaric, king of the Goths, besieged and entered Rome, in the year 1164 from the foundation of the City; and because he was a Christian, he spared only the sacred places and those who had fled to them.

411 Pestilence, famine, and the barbarian sword laid waste the wretched world far and wide. [Col. 0089D]

412 Most of the Goths entered Gaul.—Heros . . . was ordained, as in Aug.

413 At this time Pelagius, etc., as in Aug.—The Burgundians . . . took possession, as in Aug.

414 As in Aug.

415 The Goths . . . was captured, as in Aug.—The bodies of the saints . . . were found in Jerusalem. [Col. 0090C]

416 At Rome Zosimus [Note: [Col. 0090D] See the letter of Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, to Pope Leo among the latter’s works under the year 443.] the forty-third pope, occupied the see for three years. He also promulgated decrees concerning the state of the Church to Bishop Hysicius, in four chapters.

417 Honorius . . . and later sent into exile.—The question . . . under Pope Zosimus, as in Aug. [Col. 0090D]

418 At Carthage . . . are condemned, as in Aug.—A solar eclipse occurred on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August.

419 The emperor Honorius made the commander Constantius his associate in the empire. At Rome Boniface, the forty-fourth pope, occupied the see for four years; he also made four decrees. Alongside him, Eulalius was ordained pope by another party, but was subsequently deposed by the emperor.

[Col. 0091D] 420 At Bethlehem the presbyter Jerome, an outstanding interpreter, died at the age of ninety-one. [Note: [Col. 0091D] Writers disagree about the age of Saint Jerome; among them, Baronius in his *Ecclesiastical History* under the years 372 and 420 assigns him only seventy-eight years. Fleury, Pagi, and others generally attribute approximately ninety years of life to him. Moreover, for this year Prosper, in the Chronicle published by Pithou, places the beginning of the Frankish kingdom under Pharamund, its first king. [Col. 0092D]]

421 The emperor Constantius died at Ravenna.

423 At Rome Celestine, the forty-fifth pope, occupied the see for nine years. He wrote twenty-two decretal chapters to the bishops of Gaul.—The empress Placidia, expelled by her brother Honorius, departed for the East, to Theodosius. The emperor Honorius of the West died, and the tyrant John seized his kingdom.

424 Theodosius . . . sends back, as in Aug.

425 Valentinianus, together with his mother, overthrew the tyrant John at Ravenna.

[Col. 0092D] 426 Patroclus . . . was slaughtered, as in Aug.

427 Boniface . . . was made accessible, as in Aug.; the rest are missing.

428 Nestorius . . . is accused, as in Aug.

429 Agricola . . . infects [others] with error.

430 Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, while his city was besieged by barbarians, being concerned for the Church amid the very straits of the siege and fighting for the grace of God against Julian’s sophistries, etc., as in Aug.

431 The Third Synod . . . is condemned, and twelve chapters are written against the same.

[Col. 0093C] 432 At Rome Xystus, the forty-sixth pope, occupied the see for eight years.

433 The emperor Valentinian gave many gifts to the churches.

434 The Vandals had now held Africa for nine years, etc., as in Aug.

435 Peace was made with the Vandals.

436 The Goths pressed the besieged city of Narbonne by famine.

437 A war was waged by the Romans against the Goths.

438 At this time Saint Prosper, bishop of Reggio, wrote against Cassian’s book *On the Protection of God*, in which he proved that Cassian had excessively exalted free will. [Col. 0094C] [Note: [Col. 0093C] Saint Prosper of Reggio in Lombardy, a bishop, is here confused with Saint Prosper of Aquitaine, who was never a bishop and whose book against Cassian is extant in his works, Venice edition, 1744. See the preface there, p. XXI. [Col. 0094C]] Marcellinus.

439 Julian, bishop of Arles [Note: [Col. 0094C] There was no Julian who was bishop of Arles at that time. The latest editors of Saint Prosper’s works restore “of Eclanum,” as Cardinal Noris also calls him in his *History of Pelagianism*. See Baronius under the years 439 and 444, and also Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. VI, p. 302. Nevertheless, the reading of the Augian codex is preferable, so that he may be understood as the bishop of Atella, an ancient episcopal see in Campania Felix. Ughelli lists several bishops of that see in the cited work, vol. X, p. 16; this Julian also appears to belong among them, after Saint Elpidius.]—a most boastful Pelagianist, attempting to insinuate himself into communion with the Church—was again condemned by Pope Xystus. Prosp.

440 After Xystus died at Rome, Leo, a man distinguished in learning and morals, occupied the papal see as the sixty-seventh pope for twenty-two years. He condemned the Eutychian and Nestorian heresies and composed forty-nine decrees.

[Col. 0095C] 441 The emperor Theodosius launched a war against the Vandals through his commanders.

443 Saint . . . succeeded. Pope Leo exposed many Manichaeans in the City and burned their books. He also decreed that a nun should in no way receive a head-covering blessed by a bishop unless her virginity had first been proved. Hence Augustine likewise asserts that a woman was not to be consecrated among the virgins if she had been corrupted before baptism. [Col. 0095D] Anastasius.

444 Attila, king of the Huns, killed his brother and fellow ruler, Bleda. Concerning the Pascha of this year, etc., as in Aug.

445 At this time Pope Leo, among his other good works, renovated the basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul.

[Col. 0096C] 446 At Ephesus the Seven Sleepers, etc., as in Aug.

447 Eutyches . . . sent legates to the emperor Theodosius the Younger, etc., as in Aug.

448 The emperor Theodosius . . . sent on his behalf.

449 Once again the Catholics were summoned by the emperor Theodosius to a hearing.

450 Pope Leo . . . took care. The emperor Theodosius died; [Col. 0096D] in his place Marcian obtained the empire of the East and, ruling for seven years, condemned Eutyches and his followers. The empress Placidia died. The Romans, under the leadership of Aetius and with the Goths as auxiliaries, defeated Attila, king of the Huns.

[Col. 0097C] 451 Attila, having gathered his forces, captured Aquileia with great violence. The emperor Valentinian sent Pope Leo to him and made peace with him.

452 Attila, king of the Huns, died in his own territories. At this time the Fourth Synod . . . was convened, and there [Col. 0097D] they established twenty-seven canons after condemning the heretics.

453 The emperor Valentinian deceitfully killed the patrician Aetius with his own hand in the palace.

454 The emperor Valentinian was killed in the Field of Mars by Aetius’s friends. Maximus seized the empire in his place but was killed by the soldiers within two months. After him [Col. 0098C] Avitus assumed the empire.—In that same year Genseric, king of the Vandals, stripped Rome of all its wealth.

455 Avitus laid down the empire at Piacenza; in his place Majorian ruled for four years.

[Col. 0098D] 456 The emperor Marcian of the East died; in his place Leo ruled as emperor for seventeen years. From this year Victorius began his Paschal cycles, though they were full of errors, at the command of Pope Hilary.

457 The emperor Majorian of the West prepared an expedition into Africa against the Vandals.

[Col. 0099C] 460 The emperor Majorian was deceitfully killed by the patrician Ricimer.

461 Severus . . . ruled at Ravenna.—At Tours, Blessed Perpetuus was made bishop and transferred the body of Saint Martin.

462 At Rome Hilary, the forty-eighth pope, occupied the see for six years and three months. He condemned the Eutychian and Nestorian heresies and, among his other good works, founded two libraries [Col. 0099D] in the City and established six synodical chapters.

463 The king of the Alans, advancing toward Italy, perished in battle near Pergamum at the hands of the patrician Ricimer.

464 The emperor Severus died by poison through Ricimer’s treachery, as they say.

[Col. 0100C] 466 The emperor Leo sent Anthemius . . . who ruled for five years.

467 At Toulouse . . . flowed forth all day.

468 Arabundus . . . was deported. At Rome Simplicius . . . for three months; he promulgated two decrees.

469 The patrician Romanus, aspiring to the empire, was beheaded.

470 In Gaul Saint Remigius . . . was made archbishop.

[Col. 0100D] 471 Ricimer killed the emperor Anthemius, causing great destruction to the city of Rome, and himself established Olybrius as emperor; he himself then perished. Jornandes.

472 Glycerius assumed the empire at Ravenna. At Constantinople Leo made Leo his associate in the kingdom, since he was his nephew.

[Col. 0101C] 473 The senior emperor Leo died. After him Leo [Col. 0101D] the Younger ruled for a few months and then also died. After him the emperor Zeno ruled for seventeen years. At Rome Nepos succeeded Glycerius in the empire.

474 The patrician Orestes drove out the emperor Nepos and gave the empire to his own son Augustulus.

475 Odoacer, king of the Torcilingi and Rugians, after overrunning Italy . . . and killed the patrician Paul, and condemned the emperor Augustulus to exile.

476 Odoacer ruled at Rome, despite Zeno’s opposition.

477 In the time of Zeno . . . were discovered through his own revelation, as in Aug., following year.

[Col. 0102D] 478 Pope Simplicius condemned Peter . . ., as in Aug., following year.

480 After Hilderic, king of the Franks, died . . . ruled for thirty years.

482 Theodoricus . . . became his associate and served with his Goths. The emperor Zeno made Theodoricus . . ., as in Aug., following year.

483 At Rome Felix III, the fiftieth pope, occupied the see for nearly nine years and established twenty-seven canonical chapters.

485 At this time . . . recalls the man whom he had once accused; when this was heard, etc., as in Aug.

[Col. 0103C] 488 King Theodoricus . . . set out: Odoacer encountered him and engaged him in battle, but, defeated, fled.

489 Theodoricus defeated Odoacer for the third time, routed him, and besieged him at Ravenna.

490 Odoacer, engaging Theodoricus for the fourth time, was defeated and captured. At Constantinople the emperor Zeno died; after him Anastasius ruled the Eastern Empire for twenty-eight years.

491 At Rome, after . . . died, the matter was conducted by . . . and deacons.

[Col. 0103D] 492 Theodoricus killed Odoacer at Ravenna when the latter was plotting against him . . . took possession. At Rome Pope Gelasius, the fifty-first, occupied the see for four years and seven months. He was a learned and devout man who condemned all heretics, increased the Roman clergy, [Col. 0104C] and issued many decrees.

493 At this time the blessed Fulgentius, bishop in Africa, shone forth in learning and well-ordered conduct.

494 King Ludovicus of the Franks, with God’s help, defeated the Alamanni in battle; when he was in danger in that same war, he promised that he would believe.

495 Ludovicus . . . was baptized with his Christian wife . . .

496 Trasamundus, king of the Arian Vandals in Africa and hostile to the Catholics, closed the churches and inflicted exile in Sardinia upon two hundred forty bishops.

497 The patrician Boethius . . . published. At Rome Anastasius . . . for nearly two years and issued eight decretal chapters.

[Col. 0105C] 498 The Isaurians, after killing their own leader Lilingus, were slaughtered by the emperor Anastasius.

499 King Theodoricus . . . buildings. At Rome Symmachus . . . until, by the judgment of King Theodoricus, Symmachus was confirmed in the see.

[Col. 0105D] 500 Pope Symmachus, after a synod had been held at Rome, ordained his rival Laurentius bishop of Nocera.

501 King Theodericus . . . did. At this time . . . earned favor, as in Aug.

503 Certain Romans, etc., as in Aug.

[Col. 0106C] 504 At a synod of one hundred fifteen bishops, etc., as in Aug.

505 King Ludovicus, etc., as in Aug.

506 King Theodericus . . . moved his army.

507 Dissension again arose between Pope Symmachus and the Church.

[Col. 0106D] 508 In this year at Rome, etc., as in Aug.—At this same time Avitus, abbot of Orléans, shone forth through his virtues and spirit of prophecy. Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 99.

[Col. 0107D] 509 Ludovicus, also called Clodoveus, king of the Franks, died at Paris, where he established the seat of his kingdom.

510 At this time Pope Symmachus, among his other good works, condemned the Manichaeans found in the City; he paved the basilica of Saint Peter and its portico with marble, and carried out other works of this kind.

513 Cassiodorus completed his . . . chronicle and arranged a tripartite history. At Rome, when the dissension had finally ceased, Pope Symmachus died in peace.

[Col. 0108D] 514 At Rome Hormisdas . . . adorned [it] and issued four decrees.

515 A certain slave named Vitalianus rebelled against the emperor Anastasius with the Scythians.

516 Pope Hormisdas sent legates to Constantinople to the emperor Anastasius on behalf of the Catholic faith. Among other things, the emperor replied to him as follows: “We wish to command, not to be commanded.”

[Col. 0109C] 518 The emperor Anastasius, favoring the heresy of Eutyches and persecuting the Catholics, was struck by lightning and perished; he was more than eighty years old. In his place the Catholic emperor Justin ruled at Constantinople for eight years and made peace with the tyrant Vitalianus, whom he nevertheless later killed.

519 The emperor Justin Augustus honorably received the legates sent by Pope Hormisdas on behalf of the faith; agreeing with them in the condemnation of the heresy, he sent many gifts through them to Rome.

[Col. 0109D] 521 Justin Augustus . . . threatened ruin to the Catholics in Italy.

522 In Africa, after Trasamundus, the Arian king of the Vandals, died, Hilderic ruled in his place for eight years. He immediately reopened the churches that had long been closed and recalled all the Catholics from exile.

523 At Rome Pope John, the fifty-fifth, occupied the see for two years and nine months. Sent by Theodoricus to Constantinople, he was honorably received by the emperor Justin Augustus and all the citizens; at the gate called the Golden Gate he restored sight to a blind man. After crowning Justin Augustus, he returned with many gifts. [Col. 0110C]

524 Theodoricus, king of the Goths and tyrant of the Romans, killed Boethius . . . likewise. He also killed the blessed Pope John by the affliction of imprisonment, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

525 Theodoricus . . . suddenly died at Ravenna [Col. 0110D] after the death of Pope John, and, just as . . ., was cast down. After him his nephew Athalaricus, a boy, ruled with his mother for eight years.—At Rome Felix . . . for two months.

526 At Constantinople the emperor Justin died; in his place his nephew Justinian ruled for thirty-eight years.

527 Justinian Augustus . . . appointed to military service. The people of the Winili . . . invaded [the land] and settled there.

[Col. 0111D] 528 At this time, etc., as in Aug.

530 In Africa, after Hilderic was killed, . . . seized power and raged against the Catholics and everyone else. At Rome Boniface II, the fifty-seventh pope, occupied the see for two years and approximately one month.

531 Pope Boniface . . . burned Vigilius.

532 From this year . . . the abbot Romanus [began] a cycle . . . containing within itself [a number of] years. At Rome John . . . occupied the see for two years and four months. The emperor Justinian Augustus sent him a letter concerning his faith.

533 At Rome, after Athalaricus, king of the Goths, died, his mother Amalasuntha took Theodahad into partnership in the kingdom. He later ordered her to be killed and ruled alone.

534 The patrician Belisarius, sent by the emperor Justinian, defeated and destroyed the nation of the Vandals in Africa; after capturing their king Gevamerus (Gelimer), he restored Carthage to the Roman people. [Col. 0112D]

535 At Rome Pope Agapitus, the fifty-ninth, occupied the see for nearly one year. Sent by the tyrant Theodahad to Constantinople for the favor of the emperor Justinian Augustus, he condemned Anthimius, the heretical bishop of that city; after appointing another bishop, namely the Catholic Mennas, he himself died there, being exceptionally learned in ecclesiastical regulations.

536 At Rome Silverius, the son of Hormisdas, formerly pope, was violently advanced as the sixtieth pope against the will of the clergy by the tyrant Theodahad, who had been corrupted by money. He occupied the see for one year and five months.

[Col. 0113D] 537 Pope Silverius . . . falsely accused, was afflicted with exile by the deacon Vigilius and died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July; afterward he became renowned for miracles. Vigilius himself was ordained the sixty-first pope and occupied the see for seventeen years and seven months.

538 The patrician Belisarius and Pope Vigilius brought Vitigis, king of the Goths, defeated in battle, to the emperor Justinian at Constantinople.

539 The patrician Belisarius forced the Parthians, who were ravaging Antioch and Syria, to withdraw.

541 Totila, king of the Goths, ravaged Rome and Campania. [Col. 0114D]

542 In the time of this Justinian, the body of Saint Antony the monk, divinely revealed, was transferred to Alexandria.

At this time the Fifth Synod . . . was convened and established fourteen chapters.

543 At this time the abbot Benedictus, when . . ., departed to the Lord. Saint Remigius . . . departed to the Lord, as in Aug., following year.

544 The subdeacon Arator . . . publicly recited the work that had been offered.

545 King Totila again invaded Rome.

[Col. 0115C] 546 At this time Liberatus [Note: [Col. 0116D] Gallandius likewise published Liberatus’s *Brief Account of the Cause of the Nestorians and Eutychians*, book VI, p. 119; he discusses it at greater length in the prolegomena, chapter 7.] was archdeacon of Carthage. He wrote many useful things concerning the authority of the Council of Chalcedon and demonstrated that Pope Vigilius had at one time favored the heretics.

547 Since Pope Vigilius could in no way be brought to consent to the heresy and the restoration of Bishop Anthimius, he was forcibly taken to Constantinople and severely afflicted by exile.

[Col. 0115D] 548 The emperor Justinian Augustus built in Constantinople the basilica of the Savior, called Saint Sophia, with incomparable workmanship. He composed the laws called the Justinian laws.

550 Victor . . . criticized the cycles.

551 Up to this point Bishop Jordanes . . . carried [the account].

[Col. 0116C] 552 At this time the emperor Justinian Augustus, appointing the eunuch Narses commander-in-chief, sent him to Italy.

554 Vigilius . . . died in Sicily from a disease of the stone. In his place Pelagius . . . accused of wrongdoing against Vigilius, mounted the ambo at Saint Peter’s, placed the Gospel upon his head, and cleared himself under oath of the charge brought against him. [Note: [Col. 0116D] These matters belong to the following year.] He was ordained by the bishops of Perugia and Ferentino and by the archpriest of Ostia, Andrew. For this is the privilege of the Church of Ostia: its bishop and archpriest (if its bishop is not present) must perpetually take part in the ordination of the Roman pontiff. Moreover, if the bishop is present, he will thereafter have the privilege of wearing the pallium, which no other cardinal-bishop may do. Anastasius.

[Col. 0117B] 557 Hildebert, king of the Franks, died and was buried at Paris in the basilica of Saint Vincent . . . obtained possession.

558 At this time at Tours the basilica of Saint Martin, when rebels fled to it, was burned by fire; another account places this in the year 560.

559 King Lotharius, doing penance for his sins, repaired the basilica of Saint Martin and covered it with tin. Saint Medardus . . . was buried with great honor. Fortunatus, [Col. 0118B] in the Life.

560 King Clotharius, son of Clovis the Great, died at Compiègne in the fifty-first year of his reign.

563 King Charibert, devoted to lust, died excommunicated by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris. Gregory of Tours, under the year 557.

564 At Constantinople . . . Justinian the Younger, an unjust and avaricious man, ruled for eleven years.

[Col. 0119C] 565 At this time an immense pestilence and mortality devastated all Italy, especially Liguria. The patrician Narses, enriched by wealth and consequently becoming an object of Roman envy and being accused before the emperor, withdrew from Rome to Campania; his successor Longinus was sent to Italy. Saint Columba . . . preached.

566 At Rome John, etc., as in Aug.

567 The patrician Narses, who had labored greatly for the commonwealth, being provoked by injuries from the emperor Justin Augustus, invited the Lombards living in Pannonia to ravage and possess Italy.

Many prodigies, and especially fiery armies, were seen in the sky.

[Col. 0120C] 568 The Lombards, under King Alboin, entered Venetia in April and subjected it to themselves, except for a few cities.

569 King Alboin invaded Liguria with the Lombards, captured Milan and most of the other cities, and besieged Pavia for more than three years. [Col. 0120D]

570 Alboin captured most of the cities in Tuscany. Saint Vedastus, bishop, died.

571 The people of Pavia surrendered to King Alboin.

572 The patrician Narses died.

574 Alboin, king of the Lombards, was killed by his own arms-bearer through the treachery of his wife.

[Col. 0121D] 575 At Constantinople the emperor Justin, having turned insane after his many misdeeds, died. In his place Tiberius Constantine, who had governed the palace while Justin was mentally incapacitated, ruled for seven years; he was a man devoted to God.

576 Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, departed to the Lord.

578 At Rome Pope Benedict, the sixty-fourth, occupied the see for four years and [Col. 0122D] two months . . . he convicted in the presence of . . .; there too, when bishops came, he was compelled to [write] the *Moralia on Job* . . .

579 A great inundation and flood of waters, lightning, and earthquakes terrified people. Marcellinus; Gregory of Tours, following year.

580 A comet was seen on Easter Day. At Soissons the sky appeared to burn. A great pestilence arose.

[Col. 0123C] 581 At this time the army of the emperor Tiberius powerfully defeated the Persians.

582 At Constantinople Tiberius, most worthy of all praise, died; in his place Maurice ruled for twenty-one years. At Rome Pelagius II, the sixty-fifth pope, occupied the see for ten years and [Col. 0123D] two months. He roofed the temple of Saint Peter with gilded silver panels and performed many other good works.

583 Childebert, king of the Franks, having received fifty thousand gold solidi from the emperor Maurice to expel the Lombards from Italy, made a treaty with those same Lombards and gave no answer when the emperor demanded his money.

584 King Guntram built the monastery of Saint Marcellus in the suburb of Chalon.

[Col. 0124C] 585 King Chilperic of the Franks, killed by treachery, was buried at Paris.

586 The Lombards appointed Authari as their king.

587 A globe of fire . . . fell. In Spain Reccared, the son of Leovigild, the Arian king of the Goths, after his father’s death became king and was converted to the Catholic faith by Leander, bishop of Seville, together with the entire Gothic people. [Col. 0124D]

588 In Spain the Arian heresy . . . of the king. Queen Caesara, wife of Aunulfus, king of the Persians, was secretly baptized and later persuaded her husband also to be baptized at Antioch with his entire people.

[Col. 0125C] 589 King Childebert gave his sister, who had been promised to Authari, king of the Lombards, in marriage to the king of the Goths, who had recently become Catholic.

590 The tunic . . . was brought, together with several other bishops . . .

591 The king of the Lombards took Theodelinda, daughter of the king of the Bavarians, a beautiful and devout woman, as his wife. [Col. 0126C]

592 A great mortality occurred. In it, first . . . for ten days; he immediately, among many other things, wrote a book . . . as well as one concerning Saint Paul, and six synodical chapters.

593 A great drought, etc., as in Aug.

594 Likewise concerning the locusts, etc., as in Aug.

[Col. 0127C] 595 Gregory convened a synod of twenty-four bishops at Saint Peter’s, in the fourteenth indiction.

[Col. 0127D] 596 Saint Columbanus, presbyter and abbot, after many miracles . . . at the age of seventy-two. At this time Blessed Pope Gregory, having sent . . . John and others, converted the people of the Angles in Britain to the faith of Christ.

597 King Childebert died.

598 At this time, when Romanus . . . had recovered the cities captured through surrender, King Agilulf of Italy and [Col. 0128C] the Romans themselves . . . peace was made between both sides.

599 At this time the monastery, etc., as in Aug.

[Col. 0128D] 600 Pope Gregory at London . . . in the fourth indiction. A glandular plague afflicted many cities.

602 The emperor Maurice made Phocas, useful to the commonwealth, commander-in-chief. Fiery globes were seen in the sky.

603 At Constantinople Phocas disgracefully killed the emperor Maurice and ruled in his place for eight years. The body of Saint Victor . . . and was made manifest through miracles.

[Col. 0129C] 604 Etherius, archbishop of Lyon, died, and Secundinus succeeded him.

605 Blessed Pope . . . for months. Pope Sabinian, the sixty-seventh, occupied the see for a year . . . was expected. In this year the wicked synod of Chalon was convened, and Blessed Desiderius, [Col. 0129D] archbishop of Vienne, was unjustly deposed and condemned to exile.

606 Famine occurred at Rome, and a one-year truce was made with the Lombards. A comet was seen in April and May.

607 At Rome Boniface III, the sixty-eighth pope, occupied the see for [Col. 0130C] nearly nine months. After him the episcopate again remained vacant for ten months. Another account assigns this to the year 606.

608 Pope Boniface, because of the Constantinopolitan . . . gathered [them] at Rome.

609 At Rome Boniface . . .; after him the episcopate remained vacant [Col. 0130D] for nearly seven months. He established at . . . and in honor of Saint Mary . . .—Blessed Desiderius, archbishop of Vienne, recalled from exile, was stoned to death through the faction of Brunhild and Theodoricus; after his death he became renowned for miracles.

[Col. 0131C] 610 At this time the Persians, taking many provinces from the Romans, stripped Jerusalem of the Lord’s cross.

611 Heraclius’s father, Heraclanus, deprived Phocas Augustus of the kingdom and granted it to his own son Heraclius, who ruled for twenty-six years.—The blessed abbot Columbanus, teacher of Saint Gall, was driven from the monastery of Luxeuil, which he himself had built, through Brunhild’s machinations; he left Saint Eustasius there as abbot in his place. [Col. 0131D]

[Col. 0132C] 612 Blessed Augustine, archbishop of the Angles, departed to the Lord. Saint Columbanus, driven from Luxeuil, came by permission of King Theudebert to Brigantium, where he remained for three years.

613 In Spain, after Bettericus died, Sisebut became king of the Goths.

[Col. 0132D] 614 Heraclius . . . made [him] his associate. Blessed Columbanus, received by the king at Brigantium . . ., began to inhabit the monastery . . .

[Col. 0133D] 616 At this time Isidore was held in high regard as bishop of Seville. The most wicked Brunhild, bound to untamed horses, suffered a fitting death at the command of King Sigebert of the Franks. [Note: [Col. 0134D] This was not done by Sigebert, but by Clotharius, as Aug. correctly states.] The aforesaid Isidore brought his abbreviation of the ages down to this point.

617 At Rome Pope Deusdedit, the seventieth, occupied the see for three years and nearly one month.

618 At this time Jerusalem . . . was carried away.

[Col. 0134D] 620 At Rome Boniface, etc., as in Aug.—In Britain, etc., as in Aug.—The magician Magundat . . . became a monk.

622 Queen Gertrude [Note: [Col. 0134D] The Canisian edition likewise has this, but one must certainly read “Bertrude.”], the most devout wife of Lotharius and a woman of blessed memory, died.

623 At this time . . . abbots, and Saint Gall flourished.

[Col. 0135D] 624 In Britain, after Archbishop Mellitus died, Justus succeeded him, etc., as in Aug.

625 At Rome Pope Honorius, the seventy-second, occupied the see for thirteen years; he abounded in many good works.

627 In Britain . . . into Britain almost in the one-hundred-eightieth [year].

628 Blessed Anastasius . . . became a martyr. In that same year Heraclius . . . after defeating and killing Chosroes, brought the Lord’s cross back to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0136D] 630 Lotharius, a brave, devout, and religious king of the Franks, died in the forty-fifth year of his reign.

631 King Dagobert, using Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, and Pippin, mayor of the palace, as his counselors, burned with an extraordinary love of justice.

632 Perpetual peace was established between the emperor Heraclius and Dagobert through the mediation of legates.

633 In Britain Edwin, a peaceful and devout king of the Angles, was killed by pagan kings.

[Col. 0137C] 634 Oswald, the most Christian son of Æthelfrith, having gathered a small force and worshiped the cross that he had erected, defeated the killers of King Edwin and himself ruled for eight years. [Col. 0137D]

635 At this time, when Sergius . . . was condemned.

637 At Constantinople Heraclius . . . died after being led into the Acephalian heresy by a bishop. In his place Heraclonas [Col. 0138C] ruled with his mother Martina for two years.

638 At Rome, after Honorius died . . . was wavering. At that time the Lateran treasury was dispersed.

[Col. 0138D] 639 At Constantinople . . . six months.

640 At Constantinople . . . for twenty-eight years. At Rome Pope Severinus . . . [held the see] for four days; after him the episcopate remained vacant for five months.

[Col. 0139C] 641 At Rome John IV, the seventy-fourth pope, occupied the see for one year and nearly ten months. Having sent money, he redeemed many captives from the barbarians in Istria and Dalmatia.

[Col. 0139D] 642 At Rome Pope Theodore, the seventy-fifth, occupied the see for six years and nearly six months. He raised the bodies of Saints Primus and Felicianus and condemned the heretics. In Britain, Oswald, the most devout king of the Angles, against the pagan king Penda, etc., as in Aug.

[Col. 0140C] 644. Saint Paulinus . . . on the sixth day before the Ides of October.

645 At this time Pyrrhus . . . was deposed and anathematized.

646 At this time . . . and the devout Angiso herself . . . gave birth.

647 At this time, when Paulus . . . was condemned.

648 In the time of the emperor Constans the most savage people of the Saracens ravaged many provinces.

[Col. 0141C] 649 At Rome Pope Martin . . . afflicted him with prisons and exiles when they accused him of heresy, and wherever he could, he stirred up persecution against the Catholics.

650 Martin . . . convened [a synod], at which . . . he condemned.

651 Blessed Aidan . . . died.

[Col. 0141D] 652 At this time Olympius . . . could not cause harm; at last he was reconciled with the pope.

653 In Britain . . . governed for ten years.

654 Blessed Pope Martin, by order of the heretical emperor Constans, was brought to the basilica . . . and, when he could not be bent . . ., was condemned in Cherson.

655 Pope Martin . . . was buried and became renowned through miracles . . . occupied the see for two years and nearly ten months; he was a kind [Col. 0142C] and devout man. In Britain . . . perished, defeated by his brother . . . received.

656 Peter, etc., as in Aug.

657 At Rome . . . for six months, incorrectly derived from Anastasius.

[Col. 0142D] 658 At Rome, etc., as in Aug.

659 Constantine, etc., as in Aug.

660 In Italy, after Haribert, king of the Lombards, died, his two sons Godabertus and Pertarich divided the kingdom between themselves. When one of them, namely Godabertus, was killed and the other fled to the Huns, the duke Grimoald of Benevento obtained their kingdom.

[Col. 0143D] 661 At this time Pertarich, returning from exile, was compelled to go into exile again.

662 Constantine, also called Constans, came to Italy against the Lombards, but accomplished nothing.

663 The emperor Constantine came to Rome and was honorably received by Pope Vitalian. He offered Saint Peter a pallium woven with gold, but he carried off nearly all the ornaments of the City.

664 A solar eclipse occurred on the fifth day before the Nones of May. In Britain a dispute concerning Easter was debated by the Scots and the Angles, [Col. 0144D] and the Scots were reasonably defeated by the presbyter Wilfrid, who was later ordained bishop.

665 The Angles sent to Rome to Pope Vitalian, requesting a bishop and teacher.

668 In Sicily the emperor Constantine, also called Constans, after widespread plundering throughout the provinces, was finally killed by his own men in a bath. In his place his son Constantine ruled for seventeen years, a truly Catholic and devout emperor. In this year Theodorus . . . and by example.

[Col. 0145C] 669 The Saracens ravaged Sicily.

670 In Italy, after Grimoald, king of the Lombards, died, Pertarich held his ancestral kingdom for seventeen years.

672 At Rome Vitalian . . . gentle and devout, built many structures at Rome.

673 In this year Theodorus . . . convened [a synod].

674 King Dagobert, an outstanding venerator of the churches of God, died. He had ruled for forty-four years. [Col. 0145D] He was buried at Paris. [Note: [Col. 0145D] These matters are confused and do not belong to this year. For Dagobert I, of whom the account here speaks, died in 638 after sixteen years of rule; whereas Dagobert II, recalled from Scotland in this year, 674, began to reign and died in 679. This is an error found in many ancient writers, who conflated the two Dagoberts into one. [Col. 0146D]]

676 At Rome, after Pope Adeodatus died after four months, Pope Donus, the eightieth, occupied the see for one year and five months. He paved the portico of Saint Peter with marble. [Col. 0146C] A comet was seen for three months.

677 The Church of Ravenna . . . again subjected itself.

678 At Rome . . . occupied the see as the eighty-first pope for two years and six months. This pope obtained from the emperor a reduction of the sum customarily paid for the ordination of a pontiff, but only on condition that a general decree concerning the election first be sent to the emperor before the candidate was consecrated. [Note: [Col. 0146D] The Bernold codex assigns this in the margin to Pope Donus under the year 676; Urstisius, however, more correctly refers it to Agatho.] Anastasius.—Wilfrid, bishop of the Angles, [Col. 0146D] driven from his see by King Guibert [another reading: Ecbert], converted many people to the Lord while in exile.

679 Constantine, etc., as in Aug.

[Col. 0147C] **680** An eclipse of the moon, and a great mortality occurred at Rome. Pope Agatho … presided over the sixth … session, and condemned all the heretics … and composed nine chapters. Theodore, etc., as in Aug.

**681** At Constantinople, the Sixth Synod … portending …. Pope Agatho died. In the following year.

**682** At Rome, Agatho having died, etc., as in Aug.

[Col. 0147D] **683** At Rome Leo II, pope LXXXII, sat for nearly eleven months, a man in every respect most learned and devout; he issued his own decrees and wrote, taught, and established many things excellently. Saint Gudbert, bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne, adorned Britain with many virtues.

[Col. 0148C] **684** At Rome, after the death of …, [he] … for nearly one year … ten months, a sufficiently praiseworthy man. Comets appeared.

**685** At Rome, after Easter, … sat for one year; he had previously been archdeacon and legate of the Apostolic See at the Sixth Synod. At Constantinople, after the death of the emperor Constantine, his son Justinian reigned for ten years. Polluted by heresy, he was hostile to the orthodox.

[Col. 0148D] **686** At Rome, after the death of …, [he sat] eleven months, likewise a praiseworthy man. In Britain Saint John, bishop of Hexham, was held in high esteem.

**687** At Rome, after the death of …, [he sat] nearly nine [months], a man strong in the Catholic faith who suffered persecution from the emperor Justinian, a holy man indeed and devoted to every good work.

[Col. 0149D] **688** Ceadwalla … was adorned with …

**689** In Italy Duke Alachis seized tyrannical power and persecuted the clergy above all.

**690** Theodore … died; he composed a quite useful penitential book.

**694** In these days two English priests, while preaching to the Saxons, were crowned with martyrdom and distinguished by miracles; they were buried by Pippin at Cologne. Bolland, 3 October.

**695** At Constantinople the heretical emperor Justinian, after the cutting off of noses by Leo and Tiberius, was expelled from the kingdom, and Leo himself held the kingdom for three years. The holy man Willibrord, preaching among the Frisians, became renowned for his virtues. His life is in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, third century, part I, p. 601.

**696** Pope Sergius … discovered …

**697** In Britain …, after many virtues, [departed] to the Lord; the priest Bede wrote his life.

**698** At Constantinople, etc., as in Aug.

**699** At this time the Synod of Aquileia, etc., as in Aug.

[Col. 0151C] **701** At Rome, after the death of …, etc., as in Aug.

**703** Bede … brought to completion. At this time … when he was carrying off captives, he received gifts from Pope John, who requested peace, and returned the captives.

[Col. 0151D] **704** In Britain King Æthelred of the Mercians, abandoning his kingdom, made himself a monk.

**705** At Constantinople … he killed the invaders of the king of the Bulgarians. He ordered the patriarch Gallicinus … that as often as he wiped away the flow of blood from mutilated noses, so often he should … someone …. At Rome John … and learned. Saint Heddi, the bishop, departed to the Lord. His life is in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, third century, part I, and in Bolland, 7 July.

**706** Saint John, pope, … built … and adorned many churches.

**707** At this time Charibert, etc., as in Aug.

[Col. 0152C] **708** At Rome Sisinnius … [sat] fifteen days.

**709** King Coenred … died not long afterward. Wilfrid, bishop of the English, died, and Acca succeeded him.

[Col. 0152D] **710** Abbot Adrian … died. In the *Life of Saint Theodore*, second century, Benedictine collection. King Childebert of the Franks died, and Dagobert [reigned] in his place for five years.

**711** At Constantinople … favoring [heresy]; for this reason he was anathematized by Pope Constantine. Consequently, when the leading men of the kingdom shunned him as excommunicated, he was compelled to lay aside the royal diadem.

**712** Charibert, etc., as in Aug.

**714** Anastasius … declared himself Catholic. Pippin …; Charles reigned for twenty-seven years.

[Col. 0153C] **715** At Rome, after the death of Pope Constantine, Gregory II, pope XCI, sat for fifteen years and nine months; he composed seventeen chapters. Dagobert, also called Daniel.

**716** Egbert, a holy man of English nationality, taught the Scots to celebrate Easter correctly. At Constantinople … caused to be ordained.

**717** At Rome … overturned buildings. At this time Winfrid, also called Boniface, … of Pope Gregory.

**718** At Constantinople the emperor Leo reigned for nine years. During his reign the Saracens besieged Constantinople for three years, but at last, by divine assistance, they were driven back by famine, plague, and the sword.

**719** Saint Boniface … at Mainz … benefited many peoples [Col. 0154C] by his words and examples.

**720** After Chilperic had died … was appointed. Saint Othmar, appointed the first abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall, governed it for forty years.

**721** Charles … captured by force. Saint John, etc., as in Aug.

**722** Charles subdued Alemannia and Bavaria.

**723** At this time the body of Saint Augustine was transferred from Sardinia to Pavia by Liutprand. Bede, *Chronicle*.

**724** After crossing the Loire, Charles ravaged Aquitaine. Saint Pirmin, a chorepiscopus, appointed by Charles as governor of the island of Reichenau, drove the serpents from it and established monastic life there in his third year.

[Col. 0155B] **725** The Saracens ravaged Gaul through plunder and fire. Hepid.

**726** Charles defeated the Saracens together with their king [Col. 0156D].  

Here the shorter Gottweich manuscript begins, with these words, which also appear in the printed editions: “Up to this point the reckoning is of the Roman kingdom; from here onward it is reckoned by that of the Franks, namely, of the second dynasty.”

Charles, son of Pippin, after having held the office of mayor of the palace for twelve years, thereafter held the same office for fifteen years, while kings continued to reign in Francia, though with little authority.

**727** Charles, marching into Burgundy, subdued it for himself. Saint Pirmin, expelled from Reichenau, went to Eton … In the *Life*, third century of the Benedictine collection, part II.

[Col. 0156B] **728** Charles recovered Aquitaine without a battle.

**729** Saint Egbert … on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

**730** The Saracens captured the city of Avignon and ravaged the surrounding regions.

**731** Charles recovered Avignon, which had been stormed by force after the Saracens had been slaughtered [Col. 0156C]. The priest and monk Bede, an Englishman and an outstanding teacher, died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June [Col. 0156D]. The Gottweich manuscript adds: “in the fourteenth indiction,” which identifies this year. At Rome Pope Gregory III sat for ten years and nine months. Three monasteries—Altaich, Murbach, and Pfäfers—were supplied with monks from Reichenau.

**732** Charles invaded Gothia.

[Col. 0157C] **733** Charles destroyed the army of the Saracens coming from Spain. Roderic, *Arabian History*, under the year 732.

**734** At Reichenau, Abbot Eto, leaving Keba as his successor, was himself promoted to be bishop of Strasbourg; not long afterward he built at Ettenheim a monastery bearing his name.

**735** Charles likewise returned victorious after destroying the Saracens.

**736** Charles marched against the Goths and returned victorious from there. Bishop Audoin died. At Reichenau, after Keba had died two years later, Ernfrid became abbot of Reichenau and bishop of Constance and presided for ten years.

[Col. 0158C] **737** Charles made the defeated Saxons tributaries.

**739** Charles, etc., as in Aug.

**740** After the defeat of …, it was accomplished by Charles.

**741** At Rome Zacharias … [sat] four months. Charles died at Quierzy … [after reigning] ten years.

**742** Carloman and Pippin quickly suppressed the rebel dukes of Aquitaine and Swabia.

**744** The monastery of Fulda … was founded.

**745** Carloman … ravaged.

**746** Saint Boniface, with the consent of …, ordained bishops. Sidonius of Reichenau, etc., as in Aug.

[Col. 0159C] **747** Charles, renouncing the world for the love of God, made himself a monk at Monte Cassino.

**750** Pippin gave Grifo … Neustria.

**751** Pippin, having sent …, consulted concerning his inactive kings. The same Pippin, having become king, reigned for seventeen years.

[Col. 0159D] **752** By the authority of …, Pippin … was anointed in place of Childeric and reigned for seventeen years. Audogarius … began to inhabit …

**753** King Pippin … Saxony … was killed. Pope Stephen … anointed the kings.

**754** Saint Boniface of Mainz, while preaching to the Frisians, was martyred by them … [after] thirty-two years. Carloman … died at Lyons. Pippin, marching into Italy with an army, compelled King Aistulf, besieged at Pavia, to give hostages and to restore under oath the property of Saint Peter. Stephen … returned.

**755** Aistulf … ravaging; for this reason the pope sent envoys by sea to Pippin to ask for assistance.

[Col. 0160D] **756** Pippin … besieged Pavia and compelled him, through an envoy, to restore to Saint Peter and the lord pope Ravenna and the other cities he had occupied.

**757** The emperor Constantine … sent.

**758** At Rome … [sat] ten years.

[Col. 0161C] **759** Waifarius exercised tyrannical power in Aquitaine. Saint Othmar … had rashly seized …; he died of a stomach ailment, etc., as in Aug.

**760** Pippin … invaded and compelled Waifarius to restore under oath what he had unjustly usurped.

**761** Waifarius again exercised tyrannical power.

**762** Pippin … marching against it, captured many cities there.

**764** Pippin … possessed.

**765** Rudgang, bishop of Metz, etc., as in Aug.

**766** The body of Saint Gorgonius at Gorze, etc., as in Aug.

**767** At Rome Paul … [sat] four years [Col. 0162D]. The election of Stephen took place on 5 August 768.

[Col. 0162C] **768** Pippin, after subduing Aquitaine, died on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, in the fifty-third year of his age …; he had reigned four years.

**769** The body of Saint Othmar … was found … and transferred.

**770** Charles … of the Lombards, married his wife, but afterward repudiated her.

**771** Carloman died … gathered together.
