**772** Charles marched against the Saxons and returned after receiving hostages. At Rome, after Stephen, Adrian I sat as pope for twenty-four years.

[Col. 0163C] **773** Charles … marched against …, and, after King Desiderius had been besieged at Pavia, he himself went to Rome … and celebrated there.

**774** The Lombards, together with their king Desiderius, surrendered to Charles, in the two hundred and fifth year since they had entered Italy with King Alboin [Col. 0163D]. The bodies of the saints … were transferred.

**775** Charles ravaged Saxony, which had rebelled again.

**776** Charles killed Rudgaud, who was aspiring to the kingdom of Italy.

**777** At last the Saxons, after many …, were made …

**778** Charles marched into Spain and returned after subduing it. The Saxons rebelled again.

**779** Charles again defeated the Saxons.

[Col. 0164C] **780** Charles, having arranged the affairs of the Saxons and Slavs, himself … went to …

**781** Pippin, Charles’s son, was baptized at Rome by Pope Adrian, who also received him from the baptismal font; and together with his brother Louis he was anointed king [Col. 0164D]. At Constance … presided. At this time crosses appeared on many garments. Blood … is said.

**782** Charles ordered 4,500 Saxons to be beheaded. At Saint Gall Abbot Waldo presided for one year.

**783** Hildegard … died in July.

**784** The younger Charles subdued the Westphalians in war.

**785** Widukind … was baptized.

[Col. 0165C] **786** Charles again went to Rome for the sake of prayer. At Reichenau … for twenty years.

**787** Charles’s daughter Rothrude … was betrothed.

**789** In this year Charles sent nearly eighty-three chapters of canons to the bishops of his entire kingdom, so that with his help they might correct what needed correction [Col. 0165D]. These are the capitularies of Aachen from this year, which survive in the Baluze edition and are found throughout collections of councils.

**790** Charles spent this year quietly at Worms.

**791** Charles ravaged the land of the Huns.

**792** At the synod … was condemned.

[Col. 0166C] **793** The Saxons … rebelled.

**794** At the synod … the Felician [heresy] was condemned. The pseudo-synod … was condemned. In these times Alcuin … was held in esteem.

**795** The Huns, having sent envoys, surrendered themselves and their land to Charles and promised Christianity [Col. 0165D].

Around this time the following note appears in the margin of the Bavarian manuscript, written, as it seems, by an early hand:

“It should be known that Pope Adrian gave Charlemagne at Rome a book containing the Canons of the Apostles together with the councils of Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople, Chalcedon, and Sardica, as well as a certain excerpt from the African councils containing [Col. 0166D] the decrees of the holy Roman pontiffs Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Gelasius, Anastasius, Symmachus, Hormisdas, and Gregory. Some call this book the Adrianic book.”

Harzheim included this manuscript in volume I, p. 191, of his collection of the Councils of Germany. It does not, however, contain the decrees of the pontiffs; what it does contain appears among the papal letters sent to the Churches of Germany.

The quoted note continues:

“The same Charles collected two books from the treatises or sermons of the holy Fathers through his deacon Paul, because he did not wish anything apocryphal to be read in church. For the aforesaid two books, together with the Bible, can supply nearly all the nocturnal readings throughout the year, on individual feasts and fasts. Those two books were completed in the year of the Lord 808.”

This *Homiliary of Paul the Deacon* has been printed in various places.

**796** At Rome, after the death of …, [he sat] twenty years.

**797** At Constantinople … was blinded.

**798** Helena, the mother … sent in peace.

[Col. 0167B] **799** Pope Leo … was blinded and, after being freed by certain men, was brought to Charles in Saxony. The prefect Gerold … was buried. The patriarch … of the Lord sends [something] to King Charles.

**800** Charles sent splendid gifts to Jerusalem and, marching to Rome, restored Pope Leo, who had been … because of the charges brought against him [Col. 0168B].

**801** Charles … banished them. An earthquake occurred on the second day before the Kalends of May.

**802** Aaron, king of the Persians, sent among other gifts an elephant to the emperor Charles.

[Col. 0169C] **803** The blood of the Lord … celebrated.

**804** The lord pope, presented with great gifts by the emperor, returned to Rome.

**805** Charles the Younger, sent by his father, subdued Bohemia.

**806** The emperor Charles divided the kingdom among his three sons.

**807** Aaron, king of the Persians, sent Charles, together with other gifts, an ingenious clock [Col. 0170C].

**808** King Eardwulf of Northumbria, expelled from his kingdom, came to the emperor Charles to lodge a complaint.

**809** The question concerning … was debated.

**810** The Spaniards and Greeks confirmed peace with him through envoys. He learned that his son Pippin, king of Italy, had died.

[Col. 0171C] **811** Hetto, abbot of Reichenau and bishop of Basel, sent to Constantinople, wrote his own travel account.

**812** The emperor Michael, having sent back Charles’s envoys, also sent his own to confirm peace. The people of Benevento paid Charles a tribute of 25,000 gold solidi.

**813** The emperor Charles … sent [envoys], whose travel account, likewise written, is preserved. He made his son Louis [Col. 0171D] his associate in the kingdom. After the death of his son Pippin, king of Italy, he made Pippin’s son Bernard, his own grandson, king of Italy. He ordered very large councils to be held at Mainz, Rheims, Tours, Chalon, and Arles for the condition of the Churches [Col. 0172C].

**814** The emperor Charles … who immediately held a general assembly at Aachen and corrected many things improperly done throughout the kingdom.

**815** Certain leading Romans … were punished.

**816** After Pope Leo had died on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, … crowned … and then returned to Rome. The emperor arranged the synod … well [Col. 0172D].

**817** Pope Stephen … [sat] seven years. Leo’s envoys … came to the emperor.

[Col. 0173C] **818** The emperor Louis subdued the Cismarini Britons.

**819** After a synod had been held at Aachen, many matters concerning the condition of the Churches were arranged.

[Col. 0173D] **820** A great pestilence arose from excessive rains and flooding.

**821** The emperor Louis divided the kingdom among his sons, released exiles, and remitted everyone’s debts.

**822** Louis … succeeded, an outstanding man. At Reichenau, when Abbot and Bishop Hetto adopted a life of retirement, Erlebald, the tenth abbot, succeeded him [Col. 0174C].

**823** King Lothair … was crowned at Rome. Many fields were devastated by hail beyond what was usual, with large stones falling in some places [Col. 0174D].

**824** At Rome Pope Eugene sat after Paschal for three years. At Reichenau Wettin, a monk, was taken from the body after three days … Hetto … wrote.

[Col. 0175C] **826** Heriold … was baptized. Abbot Hilduin of Saint-Denis … placed [the relics] of Saint Medard.

**827** The bodies … were transferred. In this year Abbot Ansegis collected into four books both secular and ecclesiastical laws promulgated by the emperors Charles the Great, Louis, and Lothair [Col. 0176D]. This collection, contained in seven books, appears in the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings* in the Baluze edition.

**828** At Rome, after Eugene, Pope Valentine sat [Col. 0176C] for forty days; after him Pope Gregory sat for sixteen years. Relics … by miracles.

**829** At Aachen an earthquake occurred on Holy Saturday of Easter.

**830** The body of Saint Mark … brought to the island.

**831** The emperor, depriving all who opposed him of their honors, provoked against himself the hostility both of his sons and of the others.

[Col. 0177C] **832** The emperor raised an army against his sons; through fear of his sons he repudiated his wife.

**833** The emperor again came against his sons, into Alsace. When Pope Gregory came there with the emperor’s sons, the emperor was abandoned by his own men and fell into the power of his sons.

**834** The emperor, by judgment … was confined.

**835** The emperor … held a great assembly.

[Col. 0178C] **837** It is said that Pavia trembled eight times during the night on the third day before the Kalends of January.

**838** At an assembly held at Nijmegen, the emperor prohibited his son Louis from the kingdom of the Franks. Puoto [elsewhere Bodo], a palace deacon, fell into Judaism. *Annals of Bertiniani*, under the year 839.

**839** The emperor was reconciled with his son Lothair. Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, was degraded [Col. 0178D]. Pagi, in his *Critique of Baronius*, refers this deposition to the year 835. See *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IX, p. 36.

[Col. 0179D] **840** The emperor, having designated his son Lothair for the empire, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July and was buried at Metz.

**841** Louis the Younger, having joined forces with his brother Charles, fought Lothair, who was seeking sole rule, near the estate of Fontenay on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, since they could not agree concerning the division of the kingdom. Louis and Charles gained possession of the camp, and Lothair was put to flight.

**842** At last, since everyone desired peace, they decided to divide the kingdom into three parts [Col. 0180D]. At Reichenau, Walafrid … presided; he wrote many works in verse and prose.

**843** Lothair received Italy, together with the imperial title, and Belgic Gaul, which to this day is called the kingdom of Lothair after him; Louis obtained Germany, and Charles received Gaul.

**844** After Pope Gregory had died, Sergius II sat for three years [Col. 0180D]. The authors give differing accounts of the death of Gregory IV, whom Sergius succeeded this year.

[Col. 0181C] **845** Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, sent a book which he had written about the holy cross … as in the previous year.

**846** The emperor Lothair compelled the Burgundians, who were preparing to rebel, to surrender. As in the previous year.

**847** At Rome Leo IV, pope CV, sat for nine years and three months. He built the fortification at Rome called the Leonine City, dedicated it with an apostolic blessing, and confirmed it perpetually under anathema. At Mainz Rabanus, the most learned abbot of Fulda, was ordained archbishop; soon afterward, at Louis’s command, he convened a great synod at Mainz [Col. 0181D]. These two Mainz synods must not be confused: the first belongs to this year, while the second, against the Predestinarians, belongs to the following year [Col. 0182D].

During the time of Pope Leo and Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, at an assembly of bishops in Mainz, the heresy of the Predestinarians was refuted; Saint Augustine had already shattered and crushed its principal teachings in his book *On Rebuke and Grace and on the Predestination of the Saints* [Col. 0182C].

**848** A certain Gottschalk …, having been convicted, was expelled from the kingdom.

**849** At Reichenau Abbot Walafrid Strabo died; in his place Folcwin, the thirteenth abbot, presided for nine years.

**850** There was a great famine around the Rhine, during which Archbishop Rabanus fed many poor people [Col. 0182D].

[Col. 0183C] **852** A great synod … was held.

**853** The Northmen burned the basilica of Saint Martin at Tours.

[Col. 0183D] **855** The emperor Lothair … held the parts of the kingdom.

**856** After Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, had died [Col. 0184C], Charles, son of King Pippin of Aquitaine, succeeded him. At Rome, after Pope Leo had died, Pope Benedict III sat for two years and six months.

[Col. 0184D] **857** A synod was convened at Mainz by Archbishop Charles.

[Col. 0185C] **858** A certain village near Mainz and the Rhine, called Camuntum, was devastated by an evil spirit that afflicted people in many ways. At Rome, after Benedict, … sat for nine years.

**859** Frequent earthquakes [occurred] at Mainz … died.

**860** A very severe winter made even the Ionian Sea as far as Venice passable on horseback because of the ice.

**861** Meginrad … became renowned and was buried at Reichenau. From him onward, that wilderness, cultivated by holy and religious men down to the present day, grew into a noble monastery [Col. 0185D–0186C].

**862** King Lothair … repudiated his lawful wife Tithberga at Trier, after a synod had been convened for the purpose of contriving this.

**863** At a synod convened at Rome, the archbishops Gunthar and Theutgaud, who had been sent there, were deposed by Pope Nicholas and anathematized together with their synod. King Lothair was excommunicated unless he repented [Col. 0186D].

[Col. 0187C] **864** Gunthar, bishop of Cologne, usurped his episcopal office after the prohibition; but afterward, moved to repentance, he came to Rome, though he did not deserve reconciliation.

**865** Bishop Arsenius, legate of Pope Nicholas, restored Tithberga as wife to Lothair himself, after Lothair had promised by the oaths of twelve of his leading men to observe the marriage bond. *Annals of Fulda*.

**866** The Bulgarians, having sent …, received Christ.

**867** King Lothair, disregarding the oaths of his nobles, repudiated Tithberga and again joined himself to his former concubine. Therefore Pope Nicholas excommunicated him and his accomplices, sending letters to various people.

[Col. 0188C] **868** A great synod was convened at Worms in the presence of King Louis. At Rome, after Pope Nicholas had died, Adrian II sat for five years. To him … having dealt sufficiently concerning the marriage of his concubine Waldrada, it accomplished nothing. This condition was indeed imposed upon him: if he were innocent, he might confidently receive the Lord’s Body; but if he were not, he should in no way presume to receive it. Yet the rash man approached, and, with his accomplices, received an unavoidable judgment for himself and his kingdom—alas, in his excessive madness! For so great a disaster followed this presumption by divine judgment that in the kingdom of that same Lothair all its strength and nobility seemed to have been destroyed, not by plague but almost by an enemy’s sword. *Annals of Bertiniani*, *Metenses*, under the following year.

[Col. 0189C] **869** King Lothair … rashly receiving [something] from him, died at Piacenza while returning home; nearly all the supporters of his crime also died, and his uncle Charles invaded his kingdom.

**870** A great synod was convened at Cologne, and many decrees were issued concerning the condition of the Church [Col. 0189D].

**871** The emperor Louis was reconciled by oath with the tyrant Adalgis [Col. 0190C]. Nevertheless, Pope John absolved him from that oath [Col. 0190D] and incited him to wage war against the same tyrant. *Annals of Fulda*, under the following year.

**872** The emperor Basil of the Greeks sent King Louis a portion of the Lord’s cross [Col. 0190D].

[Col. 0191B] **873** At Rome, after Adrian had died, Pope John sat for ten years. At his command John the deacon of the Roman Church authentically described the *Life of Saint Gregory*.

[Col. 0192B] **874** Ratolf, bishop of Verona, died; he had built a monastery bearing his name near Reichenau.

[Col. 0193B] **875** The emperor Louis, having died in Italy, was buried at Milan in the twentieth year of his reign. His uncle, King Charles of Gaul, invaded his kingdom and had himself crowned emperor by Pope John.

**876** Louis, the religious king, died at Frankfurt on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the thirty-sixth year of his reign [Col. 0194B]. His kingdom was received by his three sons: Carloman received Bavaria, Louis Germany, and Charles Alemannia, each with the neighboring provinces.

[Col. 0195C] **877** Charles, king of Gaul, died in the thirty-seventh year of his reign. After him his son Louis the Stammerer received the kingdom of Gaul.

**878** Louis, king of Germany, divided the kingdom of Lothair with his brother Charles.

[Col. 0196C] **879** Louis the Stammerer, son of Charles and king of Gaul, died at Compiègne on the third day before the Ides of April.

**880** King Carloman of Bavaria died at the estate of Öttingen on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

[Col. 0197B] **881** The Northmen ravaged many provinces in Gaul. King Charles, the brother of Louis, coming to Rome, was crowned emperor by Pope John together with Queen Richarda, with imperial anointing; and all the bishops of Italy, except the pope, were subjected to the emperor by oath. In the preceding year.

[Col. 0198B] **882** Louis, king of Germany, died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February. The emperor Charles compelled the Northmen, who were ravaging the surrounding regions, thereafter to confirm peace with his kingdom by oath. He received their king, who had professed Christianity, from baptism; thus, with friendship confirmed, they departed.

[Col. 0199D] **883** At Rome Pope John was poisoned by one man and also struck with a hammer by another; immediately afterward his attacker died untouched by anyone. Marinus, archdeacon and pope CX, succeeded him and presided for one year and six months. King Louis of Gaul died.

**884** Carloman, son of Louis the Stammerer and king of Gaul, died, and the emperor Charles obtained the kingdom of Gaul.

[Col. 0200D] **885** Pope Marinus died; Adrian III, pope CXI, succeeded him and sat for one year and four months.

**886** Invited by the pope, the emperor came to Italy. At Rome Stephen V sat after Adrian for six years.

[Col. 0201B] **887** The empress Richarda, accused of adultery with Luitward, bishop of Vercelli, proved by the ordeal of water that she was untouched by intercourse with any man and remained a virgin … and queen. But the emperor was abandoned by everyone [Col. 0201C], and Arnulf, son of his brother Carloman, was chosen king [Col. 0202B].

**888** The emperor Charles, already deprived of power and, as some say, devotedly serving God, was strangled by his own men and died on the Ides of January; he was buried at Reichenau [Col. 0202D].

A note in the necrology of Saint-Germain at Paris records the deposition of the lord emperor Charles on the fifth day before the Nones of December. The Palatine Associates, in Muratori’s *Scriptores rerum Italicarum*, vol. II, part I, p. 416, interpret this as his deposition from the kingdom. It is better understood, however, as referring to his burial at Reichenau, which first took place then, since his name appears on 5 December in the Reichenau necrology, while he had been deposed from the kingdom on 2 November of the preceding year.

[Col. 0203D] **890** King Arnulf was asked by the apostolic see to come to Rome and defend Italy for himself against the tyrants.

**891** King Arnulf destroyed the Northmen utterly.

[Col. 0204D] **892** At Rome, after Stephen, … [sat] seven months.

**893** Pope Formosus invited King Arnulf to receive Italy and rescue it from the tyrants.

[Col. 0205D] **896** King Arnulf at last came to Rome and was crowned emperor by Pope Formosus. Pope Formosus died on Easter Day. In his place Boniface VI, pope CXIV, was ordained and died of gout on the fifteenth day. Stephen VI, pope CXV, succeeded him and sat for one year; he favored the tyrants.

[Col. 0206D] **898** At Rome, after Stephen’s death, Pope Romanus, pope CXVI, sat for a little more than four months. After him Theodore II, pope CXVII, sat for twenty days. After Theodore, John IX, pope CXVIII, was ordained and sat for two years.

[Col. 0207C] **899** Queen Uta, accused of adultery, was acquitted by the oath of eighty-two nobles. At Rome Benedictus … [sat] five months.

**900** The emperor Arnulf died at Regensburg, where he most frequently resided, on the sixth day before the Ides of December [Col. 0208D]. Most writers likewise assign the sixth of December, as does the lead tablet found in 1671 in his open tomb at the monastery of Saint Emmeram, although Regino records that he was buried at Öttingen. See Otto of Freising, book VI, chapter 13. Moreover, that this should be understood of the preceding year is also shown by the charter of his son Louis, dated the fourth day before the Ides of October in the year 900, in Schatten, *Annals of Paderborn*, book III, p. 236. In the twelfth year of his reign; his son Louis, still a child, reigned in his place.

**902** Beringer, Reginolf, and Gerhard, noble Germans, sons of Count Ato and Adellinda, were killed and buried at the monastery of Buchau for virgins, founded by the aforesaid Adellinda; their mother herself was afterward buried there.

**904** At Rome, etc., as in Aug.

**905** As in Aug.

**906** Adalbert of Babenberg, a noble and warlike man, killed Conrad, his rival, in battle together with many others [Col. 0209C].

**907** Adalbert, through the treachery of Archbishop Hatto and Luitpold, was brought to King Louis in the hope of an agreement and was ordered to be beheaded.

**908** The Hungarians ravaged Saxony and Thuringia. Luitpold was killed. Regino, under the year 907.

**909** The Hungarians ravaged Alemannia.

**910** The Hungarians defeated the Franks.

**911** Louis … [reigned] seven years. Duke Burchard of Alemannia was killed at his own assembly [Col. 0210C].

**912** The Hungarians were killed by the Bavarians and Alemannians near the river Inn. Rudolf, king of Burgundy, died; his son Rudolf reigned in his place for twenty-five years. At Rome Anastasius II, pope CXXIII, sat for two years and two months. At Saint Gall the learned teacher Notker died.

**913** The Hungarians ravaged Alemannia.

**914** Solomon, bishop of Constance, was captured.

**915** At Rome, etc., as in Aug.

[Col. 0211B] **916** The Hungarians ravaged all Alemannia by fire and sword. A synod was held at Atheim before Peter, the bishop and legate of the apostolic see [Col. 0212D]. In this general synod it was decreed that anyone who thereafter violated a ban imposed by a bishop should expiate the offense by a forty-day fast, taking only bread, water, and salt.

See concerning this synod *Concilia Germaniae*, vol. II, p. 588, and Pagi in his *Critique* under this year. The decree cited in the Bavarian manuscript is not found there; there too *Ostiensis* should be read *Ortensis* or *Hortanus* [Col. 0213D], in Etruria (Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 733). Altheim is a place in the Rhaetian district, or Riesa, in the duchy of Neuburg. See Eccard, *Rerum Francicarum*, vol. II, p. 850.

At Saint Gall … was enclosed.

**917** Basel was destroyed by the Hungarians. Duke Erchanger and his brother were beheaded.

**918** Burchard was appointed duke of Alemannia, etc., as in Aug.

**919** Count Henry … reigned for eighteen years. Duke Burchard defeated Rudolf, king of Burgundy [Col. 0212B].

**920** King Charles … was confined.

**923** The blood of the Lord … as is made clear by the letters displayed there.

[Col. 0212C] **924** Saint Ulrich presided as bishop of Augsburg for fifty years.

**925** While the Hungarians were again ravaging Alemannia, … a confined virgin, killed by one of them, was crowned with martyrdom … was preserved.

**926** After ravaging Alemannia, the Hungarians raged throughout Francia, Alsace, and Gaul by fire and sword. Duke Burchard was killed, and Herimann was made duke of Alemannia in his place.

[Col. 0213C] **927** Heriger, archbishop of Mainz, died; Hildebert succeeded him.

**929** At Rome Stephen … [sat] two years and one month.

**930** As in Aug.

**931** As in Aug.

**932** Henry killed the Hungarians in Swabia.

**934** At Constance Conrad, distinguished by birth and life, was ordained bishop and presided for forty-one years.

**935** At Rome … [sat] two months.

[Col. 0213D] **936** Henry … was buried at Quedlinburg; his son Otto reigned in his place for nearly thirty-eight years.

**937** The Hungarians, ravaging Francia, Alemannia, and Burgundy [Col. 0214C], eventually returned through Italy to Pannonia. The monasteries of Saint Gall and Saint Boniface were burned. Rudolf, king of Burgundy, died, and his son Conrad received the kingdom. Duke Arnulf of Bavaria died, and Bertolf received his duchy. The Bavarians, together with many others, rebelled against King Otto.

**938** King Otto marched against the Bavarians and subdued nearly all of them. At Rome Stephen … [sat] four months.

[Col. 0214D] **939** King Otto subdued all who rebelled against him, except the bishop of Metz.

[Col. 0215C] **940** King Otto marched into Gaul against King Louis. A severe winter and a mortality among animals.

**942** Otto and King Louis were reconciled. At Rome Marinus … [sat] six months.

**943** The Hungarians, invading Bavaria, were defeated.

**944** An earthquake, etc., as in Aug.

**945** At Rome … [sat] nearly ten [months]. King Otto entered Gaul.

**946** At …, etc., as in Aug.

**947** Bertolf, duke of Bavaria, died; Henry, the brother of King Otto, succeeded him in the duchy.

[Col. 0216C] **948** Duke Hermann of Alemannia died, and his duchy was received by Liudolf, son of King Otto. A great synod … was held.

**949** King Lothair … afflicted him with injuries.

**950** King Otto marched into Italy and subjected it to himself; after expelling Beringer, he freed the lady Adelheid.

**951** The synod … came to surrender. Among other things … walking over something like glowing iron …

**952** King Otto entered Italy with his son Liudolf, and a royal wedding was celebrated at Pavia.

[Col. 0217C] **953** Duke Liudolf rebelled against his father Otto, but they were reconciled by the holy bishops.

**954** The Hungarians, etc., as in Aug.

**955** The Hungarians, having devastated all Bavaria, were defeated in battle by King Otto near Augsburg, a city of Alemannia, with God’s help, and were killed in an immense slaughter on the fourth day before the Ides of August. On our side Duke Conrad also fell with many others. The Hungarians who were then able to escape were slaughtered throughout Bavaria. Their kings were hanged on gallows at Regensburg. At Rome John … was devoted to vanity and filthiness.

**956** Duke Liudolf invaded Italy in a hostile manner and drove Beringer away with his son.

**957** Duke Liudolf defeated Adalbert in battle; he himself died that same year, and Burchard received his duchy.

[Col. 0219C] **958** Crosses appeared on certain garments.

**961** King Otto … his son Otto … appeared.

**962** King Otto, coming to Rome, was crowned emperor by Pope John, or Octavian. He himself reproached the pope for his crimes but was quite unable to correct him.

### 963

Emperor Otto, having spent Christmas at Pavia, came to Rome again to investigate the crimes of Pope John. But when that same John fled before the emperor into Campania, a certain man . . . was appointed in his place by the Romans and the emperor.

[Note: Chronicon of St. Blasien: “In this year an edict of Otto was issued, in the twenty-seventh year of his reign but the second of his empire, in the sixth indiction, enacted at Verona on the Nones of June. The chronicler seems to have referred to the diploma of Emperor Otto by which he confirmed the cell of Reginbert, from which the monastery of St. Blasien later arose; Celsus Gerbert proved that this diploma was issued in 983, *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, pp. 179 ff. The diploma itself is reproduced there, vol. III, p. 15.”]

[Col. 0220C] ### 964

The Romans expelled Pope Leo. After the death of the former Pope John, the deacon Benedict was appointed by the Romans, against the emperor’s wishes, as the fifth pope of that name, the 135th pope; he sat for two months. The city was besieged by the emperor and oppressed by such great famine that a bushel of bran sold for thirty denarii. Not long afterward, when the city had surrendered and Benedict had been handed over, the emperor restored Pope Leo and compelled the Romans to promise him loyalty by oath.

[Col. 0221C] ### 965

The emperor returned from Italy, and Burchard, duke of the Suevi, defeated in Italy those who had rebelled against the emperor.

### 966

After Leo’s death at Rome, John XIII, formerly bishop of Narni, was appointed.

### 968

As in Augia.

### 969

At this time Pope John, having been severely afflicted by certain men and sent into exile, was at last restored to his see by a certain John.

### 970

When Emperor Otto came to Rome, he severely avenged the injuries done to the lord pope upon the authors of the crimes.

### 971

St. Udalric, bishop, obtained from the emperor for Adalbero, the son of his sister, his episcopate.

[Col. 0221D; Col. 0222C]

### 972

A synod, etc., as in Augia. At Rome Benedict . . . for ten months.

### 973

Adalbero the cleric, who was expected to become bishop, died. Emperor Otto suddenly died on the Nones of May at Parthenopolis, that is, Magdeburg, where he himself had established an archbishopric; he was buried there, and his son Otto reigned in his place. St. Uldaric, bishop of Augsburg, departed to the Lord in the eighty-third year of his age and the fiftieth of his episcopate, on the fourth of the Nones of July. Burchard, duke of Alemannia, died, and Otto, Luitolf’s son, received his father’s duchy in his place.

[Col. 0223C] ### 974

At Rome Pope Benedict was accused by the Romans and strangled; while he was still alive, Boniface, pope . . ., sat for nine years. At Constance, etc., as in Augia.

### 976

There was dissension between King Otto and Henry, etc.

### 977

Discord . . . was stirred up, as in Augia.

### 978

Emperor Otto . . . led out an army.

### 979

At Constance, etc., as in Augia.

### 981

Emperor Otto, having traversed Italy, entered Calabria with his army.

[Col. 0224C] ### 982

King Otto, when his army had been slain by the Greeks and Saracens in Calabria, leapt from the ship in which he had been captured and escaped. Otto, duke of the Suevi, died, and Conrad succeeded him.

### 983

The emperor, etc., as in Augia.

### 984

At Rome John . . . invaded the papacy. Otto III, the son of Otto II by a Greek wife, still a boy, reigned as king in his father’s place.

[Col. 0225C] ### 985

At Rome Boniface . . . was buried.

### 986

As in Augia.

### 987

As in Augia.

### 991

The Greek empress Theophania, mother of King Otto, died.

### 992

At Aachen, in a general synod, [Note: *German Councils*, vol. II.] in the presence of legates of Pope John, it was decreed that no one should presume to conduct secular legal proceedings or contract a marriage during the four weeks before Christmas, from Septuagesima until Easter, or during the fourteen days before the feast of St. John the Baptist.

### 994

When Conrad, king of Burgundy, died, his son Rudolf succeeded him in the kingdom.

[Note: The Chronicle of Verdun, together with others, assigns this to the preceding year.]

### 995

At Constance Gebhard . . . presided in the twenty-third year. Henry, duke of Bavaria, died, and his son, of the same name, obtained his duchy.

### 996

As in Augia.

[Note: The interpolated Augian text reads: “The holy abbot Gregory died.” In place of this, the Chronicle of St. Blasien has: “Gregory, first abbot of the cell of St. Meinrad, died; Wern succeeded him in its government.” Elsewhere he is called Wirandus. See above under the year 960.

[Col. 0227D] [Lacunose fragment:] “… father of Duke Hermann II and brother of Hermann I of Alemannia and of Conrad, duke of Lorraine,” the latter having fallen at Augsburg in 955 (*Hermann* under 955; Liudprand, book IV, chapter 10). Ditmar mentions this Duke Udo, maternal uncle of his mother, as having been killed by the Greeks in Calabria in 982, while Emperor Otto was fleeing to the sea with Otto, son of his brother Luitolf; by this account these two Ottos, both dukes, are clearly distinguished. Moreover, Gerbirga, wife of Hermann II, duke, was the daughter of Conrad—not Rudolf II, as Guillimann writes—king of Burgundy and brother of Adelaide, wife of Otto the Great.]

### 997

King Otto . . . for nine months. At Augia Alawicus [Col. 0227C] was appointed abbot . . . Conrad . . . received the duchy.

### 999

Emperor Otto . . . invaded.

### 1000

After Gregory’s death at Rome . . ., he sat for five years.

### 1001

Emperor Otto . . . made a circuit.

### 1002

Emperor Otto died in Italy on the tenth day before the Kalends of February. His intestines were buried at Augsburg, while the rest of his body was buried at Aachen. Henry, duke of Bavaria, was made king in his place and reigned for twenty-three years.

[Col. 0228C] ### 1003

At Strasbourg, through Hermann, . . . satisfaction was made. King Henry marched with an army against the margrave Henry and others who resisted him.

### 1004

King Henry, going to Italy, subjected it to himself. On the very day on which he was crowned, he burst into Pavia and subdued it with sword and fire. Returning from there to Saxony, he subjected Bohemia and Duke Boleslav of the Slavs, together with his entire people.

### 1005

As in Augia.

### 1006

At Rome John XVII, also called Phasanus, was appointed pope, the 145th pope, and sat for six years.

[Col. 0229C] ### 1007

Henry . . . built an episcopal church in honor of St. George the martyr . . . Eberhard.

### 1008

At Augia, after the cruel abbot Immo had been removed, Bernard, a learned and pious man, a monk of Prüm, was appointed abbot of Augia. He was gladly received, consecrated abbot of that place, the twenty-ninth, by Lambert, bishop of Constance, and, distinguished for piety and learning, presided for forty years.

### 1009

At this time Count Ebbo of Nellenburg [Col. 0230C] took Hedwig, a cousin of King Henry, as his wife from the king’s court.

[Note: These details were doubtless added by Bernold while he was living in the monastery at Schaffhausen, founded by the Nellenburg family. See under the year 1052. This Ebbo was the father of Eberhard, who founded that monastery.]

### 1010

At Rome Sergius IV, the 146th pope, was appointed. Alternatively, the preceding year.

### 1011

Willigis succeeded . . .

### 1012

When Conrad, duke of Carinthia, died, he left the duchy to Adalbero. Hermann, duke of Alemannia, died, and Ernest received his duchy.

### 1013

After the death at Rome . . . almost twelve.

[Col. 0231C] ### 1014

Henry, etc., as in Augia.

### 1015

Duke Ernest . . . received. Megingod . . . in whose place Poppo.

### 1017

Godfrey, duke of the part of Lorraine, defeated Count Gerard in battle.

### 1018

At Constance, etc., as in Augia.

### 1019

Conrad . . . of the duke of Carinthia drove Adalbero . . . defeated, into flight.

### 1020

Pope Benedict . . . dedicated.

### 1021

Heribert . . . was made archbishop. Emperor Henry set out on an expedition into Italy.

[Col. 0232C] ### 1022

Emperor Henry, going into Campania, . . . the cities of Troia, Naples, and Capua . . . into Germany. Ruothard, bishop of Constance, died; in his place Heimo presided for nearly four years. Notker, the master of St. Gall, also died.

### 1023

At Regensburg, after the highly praiseworthy Gebhard, another Gebhard was enthroned. In this year a synod met at Mainz.

[Note: Volume III of *The Councils of Germany*. This council is said to have been held at Seligenstadt in 1022, where the canon cited here appears first.]

It decreed that the Christian people should abstain from flesh and blood for fourteen days before the feast of St. John the Baptist, except when illness compelled otherwise or when there was a festival celebrated in that bishopric; likewise for fourteen days before Christmas. It was also decreed there that fasting should be observed on the vigils of Epiphany, All Saints, the Assumption of St. Mary, and St. Lawrence, with one hour allowed for a meal.

[Col. 0233C] ### 1024

At Rome, after the death of . . . nearly nine. Henry also . . . was buried at St. Peter’s. After an assembly had been held at the village of Kamba, Conrad the Elder, Henry’s son, was promoted to the kingship by Archbishop Aribo . . ., and was blessed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October.

### 1025

A rebellion against King Conrad was raised by his cousin Conrad, by Ernest, duke of Alemannia, and by many others.

### 1026

King Conrad, going into Italy, subdued nearly all the territory on this side of Rome. At Constance, after Bishop Heimo, Warmann presided for nearly eight years.

[Note: The Chronicle of St. Blasien: “Wern, abbot of St. Meinrad, died.”]

[Col. 0234C] ### 1027

When King Conrad reached Rome, Pope John crowned him emperor on Holy Easter Day. Returning from there to Alemannia, at Ulm he assigned Duke Ernest and Conrad, who had surrendered to him, to exile.

### 1028

Henry, son of . . ., was elected king and anointed by Piligrim . . .

### 1029

Bruno, bishop of Augsburg, died, and Eberhard succeeded him.

### 1030

Duke Ernest, released from exile and rebelling against the emperor once more, was killed with many others on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.

[Col. 0235C] ### 1031

Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, died, and Bardo, a monk venerable in life and habit, succeeded him.

### 1032

Bernard at Augia . . . to be burned. In that same year the monastery of Buchau was destroyed by fire on the second day before the Ides of July.

[Note: Some published texts have “the day before the Ides of January”; Bruschius and Crusius, however, agree with Bernold in asserting that this occurred in July.]

Rudolf, the ineffective king of Burgundy, died and transmitted his diadem to Emperor Conrad. His kingdom was invaded by Odo, his sister’s son, prince of the French Champagne.

[Col. 0236C] ### 1033

The emperor, invading Odo’s province, French Champagne, laid it waste until Odo himself came humbly and promised satisfaction, although insincerely. At Rome . . ., although unworthy of so great an office, sat for more than twelve years.

### 1034

The emperor went into Burgundy and subjected it to himself. After Bishop Warmann of Constance died, Eberhard succeeded him. Brun, son of Matilda, succeeded Megingod as bishop of Würzburg.

[Col. 0237C] ### 1035

A great synod was convened at Tribur by the emperor. Alternatively, the following year.

### 1036

Hermann succeeded Piligrim as archbishop of Cologne and Gebhard III succeeded the second Gebhard as bishop of Regensburg. King Henry . . . took a wife. The Luticians . . . became tributaries, as in Augia. The emperor went to Italy in winter.

### 1037

When the emperor came to Pavia, he sent Heribert, archbishop of Milan, accused of infidelity, into custody. He escaped and attempted to rebel against the emperor with all his strength. The emperor besieged Milan and devastated everything around it that belonged to the rebels.

Prince Odo of French Champagne was defeated in battle by Gozzilo, duke of Lorraine; while fleeing, he was killed by a certain soldier.

[Col. 0238C] ### 1038

While the emperor was spending Christmas at Parma, a riot arose between the Parmans and the army. Many fell on both sides, but more among the Parmans, and the city itself was consumed by fire. The pope excommunicated the archbishop of Milan, who had rebelled against the emperor.

Queen Chunihild, Henry’s wife, died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August.

[Note: She is also called Elifdrud or Cunigunt by others, her name having been changed at the coronation. Wipo.]

[Note: The Murensis and Gottwicensis manuscripts more correctly read “the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.”]

Hermann, duke of Alemannia, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, together with many others in Italy. King Stephen of Hungary, of good memory, died; he had converted himself and his entire people to the faith of Christ. Peter reigned in his place.

[Col. 0239C] ### 1039

Emperor Conrad died on the third day before the Nones of June, and his son, King Henry, reigned in his place.

### 1040

King Henry attacked the duke of Bohemia in battle, but, after many nobles and soldiers had been killed or captured in the forest barricade on both sides of it, he could accomplish nothing worthy of note.

[Note: The Gottwicensis and Murensis manuscripts add: “King Peter of Hungary also sent auxiliaries to that duke against King Henry.”]

After Eberhard I, bishop of Babenberg, died, Suidger succeeded him.

### 1041

The Hungarians, setting up a certain Ovo as their king, expelled their king Peter.

As an exile and fugitive, Peter sought and obtained the favor of King Henry, against whom he had rebelled the previous year. King Henry entered Bohemia with an army, devastating everything with fire and plunder. He compelled the rebellious duke to give hostages, to come humbly after him to Regensburg and surrender, and to confirm his loyalty and service to him by oath. Thus also the Murensis and Gottwicensis manuscripts.

[Col. 0241C] ### 1042

When Ovo, tyrant of the Hungarians, was devastating the borders of Bavaria, the greater part of his army perished, defeated in battle by Margrave Adalbert.

King Henry, going into Pannonia, destroyed fortified cities and subjected many through surrender. When they refused to receive their king Peter, he placed a certain duke over them; immediately after Henry’s departure, Ovo drove this duke into Bohemia.

[Note: The Gottwicensis and Murensis manuscripts agree substantially with the Augian text, as they do under the year 1043.]

### 1043

King Henry, going into Pannonia again, accepted a treaty from Ovo, who scarcely obtained it, and, after receiving satisfaction and gifts, withdrew. From there he came into Alemannia and, at the synod of Constance, personally remitted every debt owed by all who had wronged him. He urged others to do the same for their debtors and thereby established a peace unprecedented for many centuries.

Afterward, he took Agnes, daughter of William of Poitiers, and had her anointed queen at Mainz; he celebrated a royal wedding at Ingelheim. There Luitpold, son of Margrave Adalbert, died.

### 1044

When Gozzilo, duke of Lorraine, died, he left his duchy, which King Henry had promised to his son Gozzilo, although that son was ineffective. But his other son Godfrey, already duke for some time, was unable to obtain from the king the duchy owed to his brother and presumed to rebel against the pious king.

King Henry fought bravely with a small army against the exceedingly powerful people of Hungary and defeated them. He put the tyrant Ovo to flight and restored the expelled Peter to his former dignity. Later, when Peter had been strengthened in the kingdom, he captured and beheaded that same Ovo, together with his wife and sons.

A great famine compelled people to eat filthy animals.

The Romans expelled Pope Benedict for his crimes and rashly established a certain Sylvester as pope, the 150th. Benedict nevertheless expelled him with the help of certain men; restored to his see, he voluntarily withdrew from the papacy and allowed Gratian, named Gregory, to be appointed pope in his place, the 151st pope, in the year of the Lord 1046.

[Col. 0243C] ### 1045

Otto, count palatine, was made duke of Alemannia. King Peter of Hungary, having invited King Henry to him, handed over the kingdom of Pannonia to him, though he received it back from him to possess during his own lifetime.

Brun, bishop of Würzburg, died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June. Duke Godfrey, coming to the king to surrender, was placed in custody. The Luticians surrendered to the king and promised their customary tribute. The hermit Gunther departed to Christ and rests buried at Prague in Bohemia.

[Col. 0245C] ### 1046

At Aachen, on Pentecost, the king released Duke Godfrey from custody and restored his duchy to him. He removed from office Widger, bishop of Ravenna, excessively cruel and not yet consecrated.

The Hungarians deprived their king Peter of his sight and set up a certain Andrew as king in his place. When King Henry was coming on campaign into Italy, Pope Gratian, whom the Romans had established after expelling the former popes, met him at Piacenza and was honorably received. Later, however, at a synod at Sutri, he laid down the pastoral office not unwillingly. In his place Suidger, bishop of Babenberg, was elected by common consent, although he resisted greatly.

During the time of this pope innumerable earthquakes, and very great ones, occurred in Italy. This perhaps happened because this pope had not been canonically substituted for his predecessor, who had not been canonically deposed: that is, the predecessor had been removed by no fault, but simple humility had persuaded him to withdraw from office.

[Note: Victor III himself counts Gregory VI among the unjust invaders of the Apostolic See. See both Pagis on Gregory VI. He therefore withdrew justly and canonically, and Suidger was legitimately substituted for him by synodal judgment, contrary to the opinion of our Bernold, Baronius, Otto of Freising, and others. Angelo de Nuce, abbot of Monte Cassino, occupies a middle position in his dissertation on the *Cassino Chronicle*, book II, chapter 79. He defends both the abdication of Gregory VI and the election of Clement II, as well as the action of Emperor Henry; Muratori compares this with the praiseworthy efforts of Emperor Sigismund in a similar case, *Italian Annals*, under the year 1046. Peter Damian himself, *Opusculum* VI, chapter 27, *Works*, vol. III, p. 54, praises Henry highly for his tireless zeal in abolishing simony. Since suspicion of this vice fell upon Gregory VI because of the agreement he had made, although with the best intention, with the other two pontiffs, he preferred to surrender his dignity voluntarily rather than be deposed by synodal judgment for that reason or give occasion for a schism. Moreover, Henry III himself, in a diploma of 1047, on the third day before the Nones of January, by which he confirmed the privileges of the monastery of Perugia, counts Gregory VI, just as Benedict IX, among the legitimate pontiffs (*Cassinese Bullary*, vol. II), namely, until his voluntary abdication.]

Eberhard, bishop of Constance, died at Rome, and Theoderic succeeded him.

[Col. 0247C] ### 1047

On Christmas Day itself, Suidger, the 152nd pope, was consecrated according to custom and was called Clement II; he sat for nine months. Immediately, on that same day, he raised King Henry and his wife Agnes to imperial dignity by an imperial blessing.

Hunfrid was made archbishop of Ravenna. The citizens of Benevento rebelled after treating badly the emperor’s mother-in-law, who was returning from Mount Gargano.

The emperor transferred with him from Parma to Speyer the body of Blessed Wido, abbot of Pomposa. Poppo, archbishop of Trier, died, and Eberhard succeeded him.

Duke Godfrey and Baldwin of Flanders rebelled against the emperor. Likewise the margrave Theoderic of Phladirtingen rebelled against the emperor. The emperor led an army against him but accomplished little.

Clement, also called Suidger, died on the seventh day before the Ides of October. Among the other things Duke Godfrey did against the king, he burned the city of Verdun; the emperor gave his duchy to a certain Adalbert.

[Col. 0249C] ### 1048

The emperor appointed Otto of Schweinfurt duke of the Suevi. The Blood of the Lord was discovered near the city of Mantua through a divine revelation to a certain blind man.

Bernard, abbot of Augia, a man distinguished in learning and morals, died; Udalric succeeded him.

Poppo, bishop of Brescia, elected by the emperor, was sent to Rome and honorably received. He was appointed pope, the 153rd, under the name Damasus, and sat for thirty days [in other copies, twenty-two].

Emperor Henry and Henry, king of the Gauls, met in the territory of Metz and confirmed peace between themselves by oath. Godfrey killed Duke Adalbert, and the emperor gave his duchy to Gerard.

[Col. 0251C] ### 1049

The emperor appointed Conrad duke of Bavaria and promoted Godebald to the patriarchate of Aquileia after Eberhard, recently deceased.

Certain princes and bishops entered Phladirtingen, defeated and killed Theoderic in battle, and subjected that province to the emperor.

Brun, bishop of Toul, elected by the emperor, was sent to Rome and was called Pope Leo IX, the 154th pope. He sat for five years. At the following Easter he consecrated Udalric of Augia abbot at Rome and confirmed and renewed the privileges of his monastery, granted by the Apostolic See.

That same pope held a major synod at Rome, especially against the heresy of simony. In a plenary synod he decreed that from then on and thereafter the concubines of Roman priests should be assigned as servants to the Lateran palace. He prohibited, under anathema, the buying and selling of altars.

Imma died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1049, on the second day before the Nones of April.

[Note: We entirely do not know who this Imma was.]

Odilo, venerable abbot of Cluny, departed to the Lord on the fourth day before the Nones of January. Godfrey and Baldwin were reconciled to the emperor.

[Col. 0253C] ### 1050

The lord pope convened a synod at Rome after Easter, at which he condemned the Berengarian heresy, recently brought before the Apostolic See.

[Note: Bernold treats this same subject more fully in his *Treatise on the Multiple Condemnation of Berengar*, which we shall publish below among his minor works; until now others have cited it under the name of the anonymous author called Chifflet.]

In the autumn he also convened a synod at Vercelli, at which he anathematized the same heresy.

[Note: Lanfranc likewise asserts this against Berengar in book four of *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*.]

At this time Empress Agnes gave birth to a son by the emperor.

### 1051

The emperor spent Christmas at Goslar and made many of the nobles promise allegiance to his son by oath.

Hunfrid, archbishop of Ravenna, was reconciled with the lord pope at Augsburg.

After Easter Pope Leo convened a synod at Rome, where he excommunicated Gregory, bishop of Vercelli, on account of a certain adultery and perjuries he had committed. Later, however, when Gregory came to Rome and promised satisfaction, Leo restored him to his former office.

That same summer Bardo, the venerable archbishop of Mainz, died on the third day before the Ides of June and is renowned for many miracles; Luitpold succeeded him. At Constance, after Bishop Theoderic died, Rumald succeeded.

In the autumn the emperor devastated the kingdom of Hungary.

At this time Tuta, a noble and religious widow, was appointed by the emperor abbess of the monasteries of Buchau and Lindau.

[Col. 0255B] ### 1052

The emperor spent Christmas at Goslar and, with everyone’s agreement, had certain Manichaean heretics—who condemned the eating of every kind of animal—hanged, lest the heretical contagion spread to many.

In those days Boniface, the very wealthy margrave of Italy and husband of the most noble Countess Beatrice, was wounded by two soldiers with poisoned arrows, died, and was honorably buried at Mantua.

The relics of St. Zeno the confessor, brought into Alemannia to the village of Ulm by Waltharius, bishop of Verona, shone forth through many miracles.

[Note: Walther, a German by nationality, was appointed bishop of Verona by Emperor Conrad in 1036. He transferred the relics of St. Zeno, formerly bishop of that city, to Ulm, as Ughellus also reports (*Sacred Italy*, vol. V, pp. 680 and 754), and from this he suspects that Walther himself originated from Ulm. Since Ulm at that time was subject to the monastery of Augia, the donation could equally have been made with regard to that abbey, especially since it had already had two benefactor bishops of Verona. Baronius discusses St. Zeno in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology* under 12 April, as does the Bollandist under the same day, where this very translation is also discussed.]

[Note: Here, in Urstisius, the small-letter copy of the St. Georgian manuscript ends; with it, up to this point, the autograph Bavarian manuscript of Bernold agrees almost word for word. In that manuscript, however, there is no indication either of Hermann’s ending or of Bernold’s beginning; everything runs on in a continuous sequence. Since Hermann, according to the author of his Life, carried his Chronicle up to the year 1054, it seemed appropriate to supply the following two years from the Murensis manuscript, until Hermann’s work was brought to an end.]

This year Blessed Eberhard, count of Nellenburg, began to build the monastery of Schaffhausen. There Pope Leo IX consecrated an altar in honor of the Lord’s Resurrection on the tenth day before the Kalends of December and inaugurated and confirmed the place with his holy blessings.

[Note: These details concern the once-famous monastery of St. Saviour at Schaffhausen and were added by Bernold himself, who, dying there, had given his manuscript to the monastery, as was already observed under the year 1009. That Pope Leo was in Germany with the emperor this year is certain from Hermann and others.]

When Andrew, king of the Hungarians, pleaded and promised less and less in asking for the agreed peace, the emperor besieged the fortress of Bratislava. It was attacked for a long time with various engines of war, but, since God helped the besieged as they anxiously called upon him, all efforts were repeatedly frustrated, and the emperor could not capture it in any way.

Meanwhile, when the Lord Pope Leo, summoned by Andrew, had intervened to arrange peace, he recalled the emperor from the siege. Finding him entirely agreeable to himself but, on the contrary, discovering that Andrew was less obedient to his counsels, he departed offended, threatening him with excommunication because the Apostolic See had been mocked, and left with the emperor, remaining with him for some time.

In those days the empress gave birth to a son by the emperor, later named Conrad. Discord arose and was stirred up between Gebhard, bishop of Regensburg, and Conrad, duke of Bavaria.

The relics of Blessed Zeno the confessor, brought by Waltharius, bishop of Verona, into Alemannia to the village of Ulm, became famous through many miracles during this period. The basilica of St. Mary at Constance collapsed.

### 1053

The emperor spent Christmas at Worms with the lord pope and many bishops and princes, where with the pope he . . . handed over to him in exchange.

When that same pope had complained at length about the violence and injuries of the Normans, who were forcibly retaining the property of St. Peter against his will, the emperor assigned him auxiliaries to drive them out as well.

That people had gradually begun, from the time of the former Emperor Henry, to flow into the regions of Calabria, Samnium, and Campania from the shores of the Gallic Ocean, where they had arrived as foreigners. Because they seemed more warlike than the Italian peoples, they were initially welcomed gladly and often assisted the natives by fighting boldly against the attacks of the Greeks and Saracens.

Later, however, when more and more of them rushed toward that fertile land and increased their strength, they began to oppress the natives in war; to seize an unjust dominion; to take castles, estates, villages, houses, and even wives by force from their lawful heirs, to plunder church property, and finally to confuse all divine and human rights as far as their strength allowed. They no longer yielded either to the Apostolic Pontiff or to the emperor, except in words.

Therefore, intending to remove these wicked and insoluble crimes from those regions and free the natives from them, the lord pope set his mind to the task and, with the greatest affection, departed from the emperor as he returned to Rome.

Many Germans followed him, some at the command of their lords, others drawn by hope of profit; many were also wicked and insolent men, expelled from their homeland for various offenses.

He received all of them kindly and gladly, both from the excessive compassion of his customary mercy and because their services seemed necessary for the war that was impending.

[Note: Unless I am mistaken, the unhappy outcome of the later expeditions of the Crusades against the unbelievers should be traced back to this unfortunate beginning.]

Passing through Alemannia, he spent the Purification of St. Mary at Augsburg. After celebrating Quinquagesima at Mantua, where a disturbance arose and some of his men were killed, he reached Rome within the days of Lent.

Wibert.

In those days certain lakes in Italy, which Julius once . . . mortals were swallowed up.

While the emperor was residing in Saxony at Merseburg, he spent Easter with the king of the Danes . . . deprived him of his duchy.

At this time both the leading men and the lesser people of the kingdom were increasingly muttering against the emperor. They claimed that he had gradually declined from the course of justice, peace, piety, divine fear, and manifold virtue which he ought to have followed and in which he should have advanced from day to day, turning instead toward profit and a certain negligence, and that he had become much worse than he had been.

The monastery of Altdorf was consumed by fire.

[Note: See under the year 1036. The burned monastery was later transferred to the hill overlooking Altdorf, as though to the ancient seat of the princes. P. Hess.]

After Easter the lord pope held a synod and, as he had proposed, led an army against the Normans.

[Note: See Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, p. 1240.]

When they asked for peace and promised submission and service, saying that they wished to retain by his favor and grace the things they had previously seized and occupied unjustly, the pope refused this and demanded the property of St. Peter, taken by force and injury. He ordered them to withdraw from the place they had wrongly occupied.

But because they were far superior in number, they rejected the demand as though an impossible task had been imposed upon them. They declared that they would rather meet him in battle, defend by arms the homeland they had acquired, or die.

Thus, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, they fought a fierce battle. In the first engagement they were almost defeated by the Germans. But, when they surrounded our men with troops brought up from ambush, the Italians quickly turned their backs, and the Germans, for the most part, fell, though not unwillingly.

By the hidden judgment of God, whether because such a great priest ought to have engaged in a spiritual rather than a carnal battle for perishable things; or because he was leading against equally wicked men so many wicked people who had flocked to him either for impunity in their crimes or out of greedy desire for profit; or because divine justice was chastising our men for other causes known to itself, the enemies gained the victory, although it was excessively bloody.

The lord pope himself, besieged in a certain castle by them, was compelled by necessity, when the fortification was already on the point of being stormed, to restore to them the communion that had previously been denied them. They received him and led him honorably back to Benevento, where they detained him for some time and did not permit him to return.

There was also a considerable shortage of crops in this and the preceding year.

My brother Werinharius, a monk of Augia, a very learned young man devoted to true religion, burning with zeal for a more perfect life, secretly undertook a pilgrimage for Christ with another monk, Luitharius. He sent a letter requesting and obtaining the abbot’s permission.

Later, Richard, abbot of Reichenau, and Henry, likewise a monk of Augia, followed this example. Leaving everything behind, they undertook the same purpose.

Emperor Henry held a great assembly at Tribur. He had his son of the same name elected by everyone and had them promise submission to him after his own death, provided that he should prove a just ruler.

Conrad, formerly duke of Bavaria, unwilling to come to this assembly, attempted to rebel against the king with a force of soldiers and tried to join the Hungarians. The emperor deprived him of certain possessions which he had previously held, acquiring them as though by lawful right.

At the same assembly the envoys of Andrew, king of Hungary, seeking peace and a treaty, promised—with the support of the bishop of Regensburg—a vast sum of money and part of their province, as well as that their men would march on every expedition except an Italian one. The emperor promised, on his pledged word, to accept these terms and sent them back.

Hadamuta, venerable abbess of Neuburg,

[Note: Bruschius calls her Hademodis. She was the fourth abbess of the convent of Neuburg near Ingolstadt, built around the year 1007 by Emperor St. Henry.]

had restored her nearly ruined establishment within and without and brought it laudably into an excellent condition. After designating another woman to succeed her and piously bidding farewell to the sisters, she died happily—if only that were so—on the fourth day before the Kalends of November. Hazelinus, also, the infamous bishop of Bamberg, died and made room for another.

### 1054

At this time Conrad, formerly duke, was gladly received by Andrew, king of Hungary. He dissuaded him from fulfilling the treaty he had alleged with the emperor and, with his help, invaded and seized part of Carinthia, by the plotting of certain leading men who possessed it, after expelling other nobles.

The emperor, however, coming into Bavaria, gave the duchy of that province to his son of the same name. While remaining in that province, he spent Christmas at the village of Ötting and there granted the bishopric of Bamberg to his cousin Adalbero.

Afterward, having held a conference at Regensburg, he crossed Alemannia. Because the region was infested with thieves, he ordered several of their gatherings to be burned. He began Lent at Zurich and, gradually descending through the cities along the banks of the Rhine, celebrated Easter at Mainz.

There Theodbald, son of Otto, who had come to him from Gaul and had become his soldier, promised him his assistance.

When the lord pope, after spending a long time at Benevento devoted to divine service, finally returned to Rome in poor health as Easter approached, his weakness grew stronger day by day. He died a glorious death on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, after blessing everyone, bidding farewell to those whom he had admonished, confessing his sins to St. Peter, and devoutly commending himself to him. He was buried in the basilica of St. Peter beside the tomb of St. Pope Gregory and is said to have shone forth through miracles.

Godfrey again seized power as a tyrant against the emperor. He secretly entered Italy and took Beatrice, widow of the former Margrave Boniface, as his wife.

[Col. 0263] HERMANNUS URSTISIUS ENDS.

[Col. 0263]

CONTINUATION OF HERMANN’S CHRONICLE FROM THE YEAR 1054 TO 1066, TOGETHER WITH HIS LIFE WRITTEN BY BERTHOLD, HIS DISCIPLE

[Note: [Col. 0263B] We gave this Life above, in the preliminary material to Hermann.]

(Collated from the manuscript codices of Muri, Engelberg, and Göttweig with Urstisius.)

236–251 NOTICE.

Urstisius himself does not indicate where he obtained this continuation, although there is no doubt that he took it from earlier editions. Certainly it is not found in Bernold’s autograph codex, with which the San Georgian manuscript had hitherto agreed completely. Our codices likewise do not present it separately, but mix it with another continuation of the aforementioned Bernold in such a way that the sequence of the narrative itself makes clear what belongs to the first and what to the second continuator. We therefore place Urstisius’s text first, with the codices identified below in the customary manner. As for Berthold, its author, we have spoken in the dissertation on Hermann.

EDITION OF URSTISIUS.

[Note: [Col. 0263] The following divisions should be read in parallel.]

[Col. 0263B] 1054. Hermann, son of Count Wolferad, contracted in all his limbs from childhood, but surpassing all the men of his time in wisdom and virtues, died at his estate in Aleshusen

[Note: [Col. 0263C] He was indeed buried there, but died at Reichenau, according to the other source.]

and was buried there.—Werinher

[Note: [Col. 0264B] He was the brother of Hermann the Lame. See above, under the year 1053.]

and Liuther died on the journey to Jerusalem.—A council was held by the emperor at Mainz. At it Gebehard, elected bishop of Eichstätt by the bishops and sent to Rome, was received there with honor and, during the following Lent,

[Note: [Col. 0264B] The anonymous writer of Hasenried explains the reason for the long-delayed ordination in his Life of Gebehard, in Gretser, Works, vol. X, p. 847 ff. Gebehard was born of his father Hartwig and his mother Biliza, and was of Swabian origin; he also belonged partly to royal lineage, as Emperor Henry himself admitted. He was the brother of Adalbert II, Count of Calw, about whom more will be found below in Bernold, under the years 1093 and 1099.]

was ordained the 154th pope on Maundy Thursday and took the name Victor II.

[Col. 0265A] 1055. The emperor celebrated Christmas at Goslar, and afterward prepared an expedition into Italy. He spent Holy Easter Day at Mantua and Pentecost at Florence. There, in his presence, the lord pope held a general synod, at which many matters were corrected.

[Note: [Col. 0265C] Peter Damian mentions this council in Book IV, Letter 12, and Lanfranc in his book On the Body and Blood of the Lord, chapter 4; from these sources it may be inferred that, among other matters, the heresy of Berengar, simony, and the alienation of ecclesiastical property were treated there. Labbe, Councils, vol. X, p. 1079.]

The emperor released Adalbert, who had been condemned to death, through the intervention of the bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0265C] The writers do not reveal who this Adalbert was.]

At the same time, fifty or more armed soldiers secretly crossed the sea from Normandy, wishing to provide assistance to the Normans against the emperor. They were captured by the citizens of Picenum and brought before the emperor.

The emperor sent Bishop Otto of Novara to Constantinople. There, in place of Michael, who had recently died, he found a certain woman

[Note: [Col. 0265D] It was not Zoe, as the Göttweig manuscript has it, for she had died the previous year, but her sister Theodora. The latter died the following year and was succeeded, not preceded, by Michael Stratiotikos.]

holding the sole rule of the entire empire. The following year she sent him back to the emperor, together with her own ambassadors, to confirm friendship and a treaty.

[Col. 0265B] Beatrice came to the emperor to surrender herself on behalf of her husband. Although she had given her pledge, she was detained, and her son, the boy Boniface,

[Note: [Col. 0265D] He is also called Frederick by some.]

was afraid to come for this reason. But after only a few days had passed, while the emperor was still staying there, the same boy died.

253. Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg, and Duke Welf had obtained permission to return from Italy, and their soldiers, they say without their knowledge, conspired against the emperor. At that time Duke Welf, overtaken by a most grievous death, to the great grief of his retainers and of the entire people, was buried at the monastery of Altdorf.

[Note: [Col. 0265D] See P. Hess, Monuments of the Welfs, p. 16, from the Anonymous Writer of Weingarten. This was Welf II, previously duke of Carinthia, buried in the monastery of Weingarten. See below in Bernold’s Chronicle, under this year.]

Bishop Arnold of Speyer died.

[Col. 0266A] 1056. The emperor returned from Italy through Bavaria. He celebrated Christmas at the castle of Zurich, and there betrothed the daughter of Margrave Otto

[Note: [Col. 0265D] According to the Swabian Chronicle, she was Bertha, daughter of Otto, the Italian margrave, and Adelaide, countess of Turin. Henry later married her, in 1066. See below, vol. II, in Bernold, under the year 1092.]

to his son, who bore the same name.

Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg, defeated by the emperor because of the conspiracy made against him, was held first under guard in the castle of Ulfilingen

[Note: [Col. 0265D] Calles, Ecclesiastical Annals of Germany, vol. V, p. 505, understands this as the fortress of Wilfelinga near the Danube. But it is certain that the event took place in the castle of Wulflingen in Burgau, or Thurgau, below Winterthur. It came by matrimonial right through the marriage of Adelaide, daughter of Liuthon of Wulvelingen, to Count Rudolf of Achalm, one of the founders of the monastery of Zwiefalten. See Ortlieb, On the Foundation of the Monastery of Zwiefalten, in P. Hess, Preliminary Monuments of the Welfs, pp. 169 and 177; and Leu, Swiss Lexicon, part XIX, p. 601. Compare Crus, Annals, part II, book VI, chapter 12.]

and afterward in Stofola

[Note: [Col. 0266D] There are two fortresses of this name in Hegau, on the borders of Mount Duellius, called Stofelen.]

for some time.—Conrad was appointed by the emperor at Speyer in place of Bishop Arnold.—Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, died. Hanno, previously provost at Goslar, succeeded him in the archiepiscopate.—The emperor celebrated Holy Easter Day.

[Note: [Col. 0266D] Writers sometimes, being unaware of the places where kings celebrated festivals, left a blank. Here the place should be supplied from Lambert: Paderborn.]

254. In the same year the Slavs, also called Lutici, attacking the borders of the Saxons, killed very many of their leaders together with Margrave William.

[Col. 0266B] [Note: [Col. 0266D] The Saxon Annalist gives further information about this northern margrave William under this year.]

When the lord pope had been invited to come to him in Saxony during the autumn, Emperor Henry, while staying at Bothfeld,

[Note: [Col. 0266D] This place lies halfway between Quedlinburg and Halberstadt, in the district of Harthega. See the Göttweig Chronicle, p. 461.]

fell ill as his disease grew worse and died in the thirty-ninth year of his life, the eighteenth of his reign, the fifteenth of his empire,

[Note: [Col. 0266D] The codices more correctly read “the tenth year of his empire.” According to the Saxon Annals he died on 5 October, and according to Lambert was buried at Speyer on the 28th of the same month.]

in the tenth indiction. From there his body was carried to Speyer and buried in the church of Saint Mary, which he himself had built but which was still unfinished, beside his father and mother. His son Henry IV, seven years old, assumed the government of the kingdom in his place and was entrusted by the nobles to the care and upbringing of his mother, the empress.

1057. King Henry celebrated Christmas at Regensburg.—On 25 April, an immense snowfall and frost destroyed a large part of the vineyards.—At Rome Victor II died. In his place Frederick, brother of Duke Godefrid

[Note: [Col. 0267C] That is, of Godefrid the Bearded, duke of Lorraine and husband of Beatrice.]

and formerly archdeacon of the blessed Pope Leo,

[Note: [Col. 0267C] Others call him archchaplain and chancellor. See Leo of Ostia, Book II, chapter 96 ff.]

but at that time abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict, was ordained the 155th pope and was named Stephen IX.—Otto, duke of the Alemanni, died, and Rudolf

[Note: [Col. 0267C] Count of Rheinfelden, who had betrothed Mathilda, the sister of Henry IV, to himself and afterward became his rival for the empire. See the Saxon Annalist under this year.]

received his duchy.—This year stones of astonishing size, mixed with hail, fell from heaven, and several people were killed by lightning.

1058. Pope Stephen died at Rome. The Romans, having accepted money, elected a certain John

[Note: [Col. 0267D] John, bishop of Velletri, under the name Benedict X. See Blessed Peter Damian, Works, vol. I, Book III, Letter 4, and Leo of Ostia, Book III, chapter 13.]

against the canons. After occupying the see for several days without consecration, he was expelled by Duke Godefrid, and the bishop of Florence was appointed the 156th pope and called Nicholas II.

[Note: [Col. 0267D] See Leo of Ostia, Cassinian Chronicle, Book III, chapter 13; and Lambert under the year 1059.]

At the same time

[Col. 0267B] Bishop Henry of Augsburg held the highest position in the empress’s council. This greatly displeased certain princes of the kingdom, who could not tolerate his arrogance.

1059. This year there was a great mortality among human beings and a pestilence among cattle. When war broke out between the Milanese and the people of Pavia, many fell on both sides. Rudolf, duke of the Alemanni, married Mathilda, the sister of King Henry.—At Fulda Abbot Eberhard died, and Siegfried succeeded him.

[Note: [Col. 0267D] Lambert, under the preceding year.]

Andrew, king of Pannonia, after he had first confirmed peace and a treaty with King Henry through ambassadors, also obtained his younger sister

[Note: [Col. 0267D] Namely Judith, or Sophia.]

as a bride for his own son, who was still a boy.

[Note: [Col. 0267D] Solomon.]

1060. Henry, king of the Gauls, died, and his son,

[Col. 0267C] still a boy,

[Note: [Col. 0267D] Philip I, then eight years old.]

undertook the government of the kingdom together with his mother.—Lupald, archbishop of Mainz, died.

[Note: [Col. 0267D] According to Lambert, he died on 7 June of the preceding year.]

Siegfried, abbot of Fulda, succeeded him. Conrad,

[Col. 0268A] bishop of Speyer, died, and Einhard was promoted in his place. Mathilda, the king’s sister, died.

[Note: [Col. 0267D] That is, the wife of Duke Rudolf.]

Count Henry the Palatine

[Note: [Col. 0267D] Namely, of the Rhine, called “the Madman” or “the Monk.” Having entered the monastery of Gorze in 1057 and left it after three years, he killed his wife Mathilda, or Adelaide, daughter of Gothelon I, duke of Lorraine. He was therefore confined to the monastery of Echternach, where he wasted away in 1061. Lambert, under 1057; Clement, vol. III, p. 319. Others have wrongly confused him with his son Henry of Laach up to this point.]

having fallen into madness, when, under the appearance of religion and as if abandoning the world, he had withdrawn to the monastery of Echternach, was taken from it and killed his wife.

256. This year too, as in the preceding year, mortality carried off many people. The winter was severe, snowy, and longer than usual, and caused enormous damage to grain and wine. Andrew, king of the Pannonians, after suffering many injuries from his brother, who was devastating the kingdom all around him, was at last struck by a fever. He sent all his treasures to the castle of Medilhecka

[Note: [Col. 0268D] This castle of Medilhecka was in Austria and is now the monastery of Melk.]

and also sent his son to King Henry through Count Tiedbald.

[Note: [Col. 0268D] Lambert and others assign this event to the following year.]

1061. A great famine consumed many people.—Gebehard, bishop of Regensburg,

[Note: [Col. 0268D] This brother of Conrad II had already died in the preceding year.]

died, and Otto succeeded him.—Conrad,

[Note: [Col. 0268D] Lambert, under 1057, calls him Canon and identifies him as the brother of Henry the Palatine mentioned in the preceding year.]

who had ruled the Carinthians in name only as duke, died and made way for another; Berthold

[Note: [Col. 0268D] This was Berthold of Zähringen.]

of Swabia received his duchy.—At Rome, after Pope Nicholas had died, the Romans sent the crown and other gifts to King Henry and appealed to him to choose the supreme pontiff. He summoned all the bishops of Italy and held a general assembly at Basel. After placing the same crown upon him, they called him patrician of the Romans. Then, with the common agreement of all, he chose the bishop of Parma as pontiff of the Roman Church.

[Note: [Col. 0268D] On this election see the anonymous writer of Zwettl in Pez, Anecdotes, vol. I, part III, p. 384, and Peter Damian, vol. III, tractate IV, p. 25; Pagi and others. Berthold, moreover, is excessively hostile to Alexander II, whom he calls a usurper; in this alone he sufficiently distinguishes himself from Bernold, who held a different view. See the preliminary dissertation.]

Meanwhile, while these events were taking place, Bishop Anselm of Lucca, with the support of certain Romans, usurped the apostolic see for himself.—Burkhard and Wezil of Zolorin were killed. The church of Speyer was dedicated, and the empress Agnes, having laid aside her royal garments, was clothed in the sacred veil.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] It is clear from Lambert under 1062 and the Saxon Annalist under 1063 that this happened later. See Mabillon, Annals, Book LXI, no. 101 ff.]

257. 1062. On 8 February there were earthquakes, flashes of lightning, and thunderclaps; pestilence and mortality followed and destroyed many people. King Henry celebrated Easter Day at Utrecht in Frisia with his mother, the empress.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] Therefore she had not yet been veiled in the preceding year.]

In these days Hanno, archbishop of Cologne,

[Col. 0269D] with the support of certain princes of the kingdom, forcibly snatched King Henry away from his mother the empress with a lance and the other insignia of the empire and brought him with him to Cologne.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] Lambert describes this at greater length under this year.]

The bishop of Parma, who had long since been elected, went to Rome to be consecrated. When armed Romans met him and prevented his entrance, his soldiers killed many of them and drowned them in the Tiber;

[Col. 0269B] the rest were put to flight.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] See Lambert under the year 1064.]

1063. In the spring, in the middle of April, a fierce, windy, snowy winter lasted four days and killed birds and cattle with the cold. It also destroyed a very large part of the trees and vineyards.—Bishop Engilhard of Magdeburg died, and the brother of the archbishop of Cologne succeeded him.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] Others call him Wezilo or Wernher.]

Bishop Henry of Augsburg died.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] The necrology of Fulda and the Augsburg Chronicle likewise assign his death to this year, in September; Lambert assigns it to the following year.]

Imbricus succeeded him.—In the same year a woman near Constance gave birth to a child with two heads and with the other limbs likewise doubled as far as the thighs.

1064. King Henry celebrated Christmas at Cologne, but Easter Day at Liège.

Synod of Mantua

[Note: [Col. 0269D] Writers dispute the date of this synod. Some, with Baronius, assign it to this year; others, with Pagi, to 1067; and still others, with Mansius, Supplement to the Councils, vol. I, place it first in 1072. Calles presents their arguments in summary in Ecclesiastical Annals of Germany, vol. V, p. 566 ff.; there he inclines more toward the view of Pagi, who places it in 1067. Yet I do not see how it could have been mentioned in this continuation, which was already completed in 1066 and therefore before this synod was held, unless we wish to say that the passage was interpolated here from another source. This would explain why Berthold, the writer of this continuation, treated Alexander in 1061 as a usurper, although he was recognized as the legitimate pontiff at the said synod in 1067, one year after Berthold had ceased writing.]

1065. King Henry celebrated Christmas at Goslar and Easter Day
