[Col. 0269C] at Worms.—The royal residence at Goslar was burned.

[Note: [Col. 0270D] In this passage of Urstisius one or two lines have been omitted, either in the manuscript or by the editor. The correct text is found below in Bernold under this year.]

This occurred on 27 March, in the third indiction. There Henry was girded with the sword, in the ninth year of his reign and the fourteenth year of his life, and Duke Godefrid was chosen as his shield-bearer.

[Col. 0270A] The bishop of Passau died, and Altmann, the empress’s chaplain, succeeded him. At this time Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz,

[Note: [Col. 0270D] Lambert gives a fuller account of these events under this year.]

William, bishop of Utrecht, and Gunther, bishop of Bamberg, together with Bishop Otto of Regensburg, set out for Jerusalem with a large retinue and company. On that journey they suffered much at the hands of the pagans, and were even compelled to engage them in battle. Gunther died on the same journey, and Ricimannus

[Note: [Col. 0270D] Lambert and others call him Hermann.]

succeeded him by simony. Many nobles perished in civil war.

1066. King Henry celebrated Christmas at Goslar and Easter at Utrecht.—Eberhard, archbishop of Trier, on Holy Saturday, 15 April, after completing the offices of that day, died in peace clothed in the very vestments of the priesthood. Conrad, provost of Cologne, elected by the king, was supposed to succeed him, but was rejected by the clergy and citizens of Trier. Therefore a certain count from the military class of Trier, named Theodoric, seized this Conrad while he was making his way to Trier and, after tormenting him in custody for a long time, entrusted him to four soldiers to be killed.

When they had thrown him three times from a certain precipice and could injure nothing but his arm, one of them, moved by repentance, obtained his forgiveness. Another, wishing to behead him, cut off only his jaw. Thus, worthy martyr of God, he departed to the Lord on the first of June and was buried at a certain abbey called Doleia. Later a fitting vengeance overtook the three soldiers responsible for his death: one of them was unable to swallow the food he had taken, while the other two, tearing their own hands, descended to the prison of hell.

CODICES.

[Col. 0263]

1054. A council was held by . . . Gebehard, bishop of Augsburg . . . received the name.

[Col. 0265C] 1055. The emperor celebrated Christmas . . . many matters were corrected.—The emperor released Adalbert . . .—The emperor sent Otto back.—Beatrice . . . the boy died.—Gebehard . . . overtaken by death, and truly dedicating himself to God through a vow of holy monastic life, was buried at the monastery of Altdorf.—Bishop Arnold of Speyer died, and Conrad succeeded him.

[Col. 0266C] 1056. The emperor, returning from Italy, celebrated Christmas at Zurich . . . and betrothed her.—Gebehard . . . defeated, was held under guard for some time.—The emperor celebrated the day . . .

1057. King Henry . . . celebrated.—Duke Otto . . . received.—This year stones . . . fell from heaven.

[Col. 0267C] 1060. Henry, king of the Gauls, died, and his son Philip . . . assumed the government. Lupald of Mainz . . . succeeded him. In this year too . . . destroyed many. Henry the Palatine . . . killed.

[Col. 0268C] 1061. A great famine killed many. Gebehard . . . succeeded him. Conrad . . . died . . . a Swabian count assumed the duchy.

[Col. 0269C] 1062. On 8 February . . . destroyed many, and a great famine occurred. King Henry . . . celebrated. In these days Hanno . . . brought him to Cologne.

1063. In the same year a certain woman . . . gave birth.

1064. As in Urstisius.

[Col. 0270C] 1065. King Henry celebrated . . . at Worms. The royal residence . . . was burned. The bishop of Passau . . . succeeded him. At this time Siegfried . . . succeeded him by simony. Many . . . perished.

1066. King Henry . . . celebrated.

CHRONICLE OR ANNALS OF THE MONASTERY OF PETERSHAUSEN, FROM A MANUSCRIPT CODEX OF THE TWELFTH CENTURY BELONGING TO THAT IMPERIAL MONASTERY, NOW PUBLISHED FOR THE FIRST TIME.

(Ussermann, Sacred Germany: Preliminary Material, vol. I, part II.)

[Col. 0271]

PREFACE.

[Col. 0271A] We append here to the Chronicle of Hermann, taken from the Reichenau codex, another chronicle from the neighboring monastery commonly called Petershausen, situated outside the walls of Constance on the Rhine. It is indeed a particular work, presenting chiefly the origin and early fortunes of that place, but it also contains much else through which the history of the medieval homeland may be greatly illuminated with regard to the noble families of the Bodensee region, geography, and knowledge of the districts of Alemannia. The same subject is treated in the Diplomatic Codex of Alemannia and Transjurane Burgundy within the boundaries of the diocese of Constance, which our fellow religious, Father Trudpert Neugart, has just now sent to the press as a preliminary work for the history of that bishopric.

We therefore consider this Chronicle worthy of being brought into the public light. Until now, only certain excerpts concerning Saint Gebehard, its founder, have appeared in Manlius’s Chronicle of the Bishopric of Constance, in Pistorius (German Historical Writers, vol. III, p. 685). It is preserved in a parchment manuscript in folio, though it is marred here and there by many erasures. The highly worthy abbot Joseph of that monastery graciously shared it with us so that it might be included in our collection; for this reason we publicly offer him our thanks.

It does contain occasional narratives of lesser importance, which reveal the character of the age in which it was written and the disposition of its author, but knowledge of which is of no great public interest. Nothing, however, prevents their omission, since our sole concern is that nothing remain hidden that might in any way serve the history of the homeland.

[Col. 0271C] We, who for several years have been contributing our common labor to the preparation of Sacred Germany and searching everywhere for monuments hitherto concealed, have not thought it sufficient to turn them only to our sacred uses unless we also presented them to others, so that they might shed some light upon secular history.

262. Moreover, the writer of this Chronicle nowhere gives his name, yet he reveals himself as a monk of that monastery around the middle of the twelfth century. Thus, in Book IV, chapter 12, he says that he stayed for some time in the cell at Wagenhausen around the year 1126. In the same place, no. 3, he was present at Petershausen when, in 1134, the body of Saint Gebehard was raised; he also attributed his own recovery of health to the saint. Finally, in no. 16, while describing King Conrad’s expedition against the Saracens in 1147, he testifies that those who had set out from his own place for that expedition had not yet returned. Nevertheless, from various circumstances to be noted in their proper places, we shall see that this Chronicle was compiled not by one writer alone but by several, as we have already observed elsewhere concerning works of this kind.

The first writer of these annals composed them not merely from the reports of others, from which many fables ordinarily arise, but for the most part from authentic records,

[Col. 0272B] charters, and other contemporary documents of that monastery, as becomes clear from comparison with other writers, who themselves sometimes receive no small illumination from these materials.

To speak plainly, however, the credibility of our Chronicle is made considerably suspect by what appears at its beginning concerning the origin of the counts of Bregenz. This account is supported by the testimony of none of the ancient writers and is, moreover, contrary in several respects to the historical circumstances of those times. For this very reason Wilhelm Ernst Tenzelius, in his Historical Vindication in Defense of Conring’s Criticism of the Charter of the Monastery of Lindau, p. 270, after reporting from Manlius the material found below in Book I, nos. 2, 3, and 4, concerning this genealogy, finally added:

“It was worthwhile to quote the entire passage, so that the reader might more easily judge the fabulous origin of the counts of Bregenz described there.”

He then offers the following reasons for his severe criticism.

1. “Who could tolerate the claim that, in Gallia Togata during the time of the Frankish emperors, there was a particular king?”

Yet if the reference is to the true Gallia Togata, that is, Italy, then certainly, according to Hermann’s testimony under the year 888, many petty kings arose there after the death of Charles the Fat. If, however, by the name Gallia Togata our writer means Gaul Belgica or Celtica, as we shall say below,

263 [Col. 0273A] then Charles the Bald held a kingdom there under the Frankish emperors Lothair I and Louis II.

2. He asks: “How can it be proved from other genuine writers that any Frankish emperor gave his daughter in marriage to a nobleman from Gallia Togata?”

Tenzelius must have read little. For what he did not know we shall prove below not only from genuine writers but also from authentic documents.

3. He objects: “Is it not established by so many charters and writers that Potamum was a royal palace both in the time of the preceding Frankish emperors and in the time of Charles the Fat? How, then, could it have been given by one of the Frankish emperors to the count of Bregenz?”

Here Tenzelius himself answers his own question (in the cited work, p. 271), writing as follows:

“Nor did the emperors of those times consider it new or unusual to bestow royal estates also upon counts who had rendered good service.”

If, therefore, this was neither new nor unusual in the time of Charles the Fat, it must already have happened earlier, so that Louis the German, father of Charles the Fat, could have granted a royal estate such as Potamum—not merely to a deserving count but to his own nephew Udalric—as private property.

Despite this grant, Potamum could still have remained a royal estate in the sense that justice was administered there in the king’s name. Lustenowa, or Lustinava, likewise remained a royal estate. Concerning it Tenzelius writes as follows (in the cited work, p. 272):

“Just as Emperor Arnulf gave the estate of Lustenowa to Count Udalric of Linzgau as private property, according to a charter of the year 891 preserved by Herrgott, so I do not object if it is said that either Arnulf or another gave the estate of Lintowa to the count of Bregenz. Indeed, I would not object if someone wished this Count Udalric to be the same man whom the Petershausen Chronicle presents as rewarded at Bregenz and elsewhere (Book I, no. 3), provided that what is closer to fable and what notoriously belonged for a longer time to the imperial fisc—such as Potamum—or served other counts, such as Buchhorn, be removed.”

Finally he concludes:

“At least the more recent character of this Petershausen Chronicle is revealed by its mention of the ruins of an ancient residence inhabited by Uzo, father of Gebehard, founder of Petershausen (Book I, no. 5).”

Indeed, as we have seen, the author of the Chronicle wrote almost two centuries after Uzo, at a time when the old Bregenz fortress had already become a ruin. Hermann the duke had captured and destroyed it in 948. Yet the author could have drawn Gebehard’s lineage from the same sources, and from them he also described his deeds with such fidelity. A sincere writer should not therefore be denied all credibility in what he reports about periods distant from his own, especially when the testimony of others supports him, even if he errs in certain circumstances of the events.

[Col. 0274A] Tenzelius later proves himself a somewhat fairer judge of these annals (p. 275), writing:

“Although we have previously shown”—he asserted, but did not prove—“that they earlier contaminated the origin of the counts of Bregenz with fables, we nevertheless do not reject what they relate concerning the parent of Gebehard the founder, Uzo or Udalric. For, being closer to the beginnings of the monastery of Petershausen, these matters were undoubtedly preserved with greater diligence and sincerity. We know from the assertions of the Bregenz family itself . . . that they derive the entire lineage of their counts, as from a root, from the father of Gebehard II, bishop of Constance, born of the most distinguished Alemannic stock.”

If, then, by Tenzelius’s admission, those portions of these annals that concern the times nearer to Saint Gebehard are more sincere, the material they contain about that bishop’s relationship with Hedwig, duchess and wife of Burchard II, duke of Alemannia, should likewise be considered genuine. Tenzelius himself cannot explain this unless he accepts the genealogical system of these annals that we propose below in section 14. It is therefore not so fabulous as this writer considers it.

The Bollandist hagiographers judge our Chronicle somewhat more mildly. In their preliminary commentary on the Life of Saint Gebhard (August, vol. VI, p. 106), they pronounce as follows:

“The Constance Chronicle”—namely that of Manlius, who, as we said above, extracted this most noble lineage from these Annals of Petershausen—

[Col. 0274C] “rendered excellent service to the illustrious pedigree of this man, provided that what it relates is as true as it is splendid. But the age of this author, so recent in comparison with the antiquity of the lineage he reports, gives him little authority.”

Yet these learned associates should have noticed that this genealogy does not belong to Manlius, who wrote in the sixteenth century, but to the Petershausen Annals of the twelfth century. They correctly add:

“He gives neither the name of the emperor, nor that of his sister, nor that of the slain king.”

We too miss these details in the same passage, but will investigate them below. From that inquiry it will become clear that they rightly add:

“If, however, one considers the time, the account seems to refer to the family of Charlemagne, or to others who, being of the Frankish nation, held the empire of the West in the ninth century.”

This preliminary discussion of our Chronicle is sufficient. More will recur here and there in what follows, especially in the appended investigation in which we have attempted not to defend the disputed genealogy of Saint Gebhard but to examine it, leaving to others the freedom of judgment that we have claimed for ourselves.

[Col. 0275]

AN INQUIRY INTO THE LINEAGE OF THE COUNTS OF BREGENZ

From the genealogical system of the Petershausen Chronicle

[Col. 0275A] § I. 266 The origin of this once exceedingly powerful family, from which many others arose, is traced by Lazius, Crusius, Stumpf, and others to the ancient counts of Chur-Raetia. We do not examine this as the earliest origin of the lineage, but intend here to elucidate only the later genealogy, since the writer of our Chronicle deals with that later descent and brings those counts from Gallia Togata into these lands.

But he immediately goes astray at the outset. In his division of Gaul, contrary to the testimony of other writers, he places Gallia Comata in Cisalpine Gaul, or Italy, although that region is called Togata by the others. It follows by itself, therefore, that in the mind of our author Gallia Togata is the land that others call Comata, Celtica, or Belgica. Since those who have treated this Chronicle failed to notice this, they fell into further errors, as we have just observed in the case of Tenzelius.

## § II

The same thing happened to Jo. Conr. Fuesslin, who, although he recognized the error of our author (in *Staats- und Erdbeschreibung der Schweitz*, vol. IV, p. 173), nevertheless himself also sought this origin in Italy, as Gaul in the proper sense, namely, Gaul Togata. He believes that the regicide mentioned by the chronicler in Book I, ch. 2, should be placed after the death of the emperor Charles the Fat, when new petty kings emerged everywhere. Among these, for the year 895, he particularly lists Berengar, son of Everard, duke of Friuli, and Guido, duke of Spoleto, together with his son Lambert, who were contending with one another for the kingdom of Italy.

Lambert was killed in 898 by Hugh, son of Meginfred, whom the emperor Arnulf had appointed duke of Milan to defend his rights in Italy, while Lambert had ordered him to be executed, as Liutprand writes (*History*, Book I, ch. 12) [MURATORI, *Script. Ital.*, vol. II]. Fuesslin derived his opinion from Hermann Conring’s critique of the Lindau diplomas, p. 270, where he reports as follows:

> “While Conrad I was reigning, Hugh of Milan, after killing Lambert, king of Italy, according to Baronius, fled to that King Conrad, his maternal uncle; and he is believed to have been the first of all to receive the county of Bregenz.”

This opinion would fit very closely with the account of our Annals if, as Tenzelius desires (p. 282), he had cited the authorities and reasons for his assertion. But, apart from the objections which this same author brings against Conring in the cited passage, there are still other considerations which seem to stand in the way of this conjecture.

Baronius indeed assigned Lambert’s murder to the year 910, but incorrectly, since it is certain that it had already been perpetrated in 898, when Arnulf was still ruling as emperor over Germany and Alemannia. Accordingly, this murderer ought to have fled to him, not to Conrad, who was elected thirteen years later. Moreover, the murderer is called not Udalricus but Hugh, and is described as the only son of Meginfred, duke of Milan (LIUTPRAND, cited above, ch. 12), where there is also no mention of his flight.

But by what reasoning can it be proved that a daughter of some emperor or Frankish king—the mother of that first count of Bregenz, in whose relation Arnulf could be called his maternal uncle—was married to this Meginfred, when Arnulf did not even have any sisters? The matter could fit Conrad I, if Hugh’s name did not stand in the way. For some sister of King Conrad could easily have been the wife of this Meginfred; hence it also seems that he was appointed prefect of Milan by the emperor Arnulf, since Conrad’s grandmother was the daughter of Gisela, who was the sister of Louis the German, Arnulf’s father, as we shall shortly see.

This would explain why Meginfred’s son killed Lambert, since Lambert was a rival of Berengar in the kingdom of Italy, and Berengar was Gisela’s son and therefore related to him. When, however, his maternal uncle Conrad was raised to the kingship, he may have gone to him in Alemannia in hope of better fortune rather than because of the regicide, and may have received the county of Bregenz from him.

Even if we accepted the regicide, many difficulties would still remain, scarcely reconcilable with the account of our Chronicle. For in this system, who would have been the sister of the king of the Franks and the Roman emperor, the wife of the father of Udalricus of Bregenz, except the sister of Conrad, king of the Germans or of the Eastern Franks, from whom he was born, although Conrad was never emperor?

Furthermore, one of the regicides is here called Udalricus, whereas Conring calls him Hugh. Perhaps Liutprand, writing in Italy, did not know the name of one brother who had remained in Alemannia, and Conring substituted “Hugh” for Uzo or Huzo, which was also the name of Udalricus. If, then, these events occurred under Conrad and therefore after the year 911, Udalricus could easily have fathered in Alemannia Uzo, or a second Udalricus, the father of Saint Gebhard and of Udalricus III, who could have taken part in the battle of Augsburg in 935.

## § III

Thus far we have attempted the first method of explaining our Annals, although it is not yet sufficiently straightforward, retaining the story of the regicide, which cannot be admitted under the Carolingian kings or emperors except in the manner and at the time just described. We shall now attempt a second explanation, which, if the regicide is removed, is more compatible with the account of our Chronicle.

The principal foundation for this discussion is provided by a diploma of Louis the German issued in 867 (HERGOTT, no. 117), in which the same king calls Count Udalricus in the Argengau his beloved nephew. If his lineage could be established, the genealogy of the counts of Bregenz might perhaps be clear, as we shall presently explain.

[Note: The genuine genealogy of the counts of Bregenz seems to be established as follows, both from charters and from nearly contemporary writers. [We have the former as the son of the earlier man from the charter cited above, from the year 805; the following Udalricus in the charter of 867 must have been the son of either him or his brother Rodpert, if his kinship with Louis the German is to be maintained.]].

For we have no doubt that this is the very Udalricus mentioned in our Chronicle, whose son Uzo began to live at Bregenz after it had once again been restored following the destruction remembered by Walahfrid; hence his father also lived in the neighboring county of the Argengau or Linzgau.

Leaving our Chronicle aside for the moment—and we do not undertake to defend it in this matter—we seem to have discovered the ancestor of this kinship from two sources.

One is indicated by Thegan, chorepiscopus of Trier and a contemporary writer, in his *On the Deeds of the Emperor Louis the Pious* (BOUQUET, vol. VI, p. 73), where in chapter 2 we read:

> “Charles, later called the Great, while still young, took to himself a girl of the most noble Swabian lineage named Hildegard. She was of the family of Gothefrid, duke of the Alemanni. Duke Gothefrid begot Houching; Houching begot Nebi [see above in the notes to Hermann, year 724]; Nebi begot Imma; and Imma gave birth to the most blessed Queen Hildegard.”

Cointius and the Bollandists investigate more fully this lineage in the *Life of Blessed Hildegard*, vol. III for April, p. 790 and following; but those matters do not concern our present purpose.

More directly relevant are the statements of Wetti, a monk of Reichenau, in his visions concerning Count Gerold, the brother of Hildegard, Queen and wife of Charlemagne, who was killed in the Hunnic war in 799. Hermann mentions the same man under that year; we have also noted that he was called Pussinius because of his estates in Swabia and near Mount Bussen, in the present district of the chapter of Saulgau.

The anonymous monk of Saint Gall offers us a second path in his *Deeds of Charlemagne* (BOUQUET, vol. V, p. 111), when he introduces yet another brother of that same Queen Hildegard, Udalricus, to whom Charlemagne had granted very extensive possessions in the east and west—namely, in Swabia or Alemannia. When, after Hildegard’s death in 783, he was deprived of these honors by Charlemagne because of some offense, the king, once warned, immediately restored his former honors to him.

The fact that Hildegard’s estates were situated chiefly in the Allgäu is demonstrated even by the monastery of Kempten, which he founded. Consequently, her brothers’ possessions must be sought entirely in that region of Alemannia, as we have already seen in the case of Gerold.

We believe that this Udalricus was the count of Thurgau whom Father Herrgott records in his charters from 787 through 800. He also seems to have been count in the Argengau, according to Father Neugart’s *Old Alemannic Diplomatic Code*, no. 144; the fortress of Bregenz was situated within his county. Indeed, he was also count in the Linzgau, where he is recorded, in the cited work, no. 150, with his two sons Udalricus and Rodpert in a charter of 805, and in another charter of 804 he is additionally recorded in the Breisgau.

This perfectly explains the words of the cited anonymous writer concerning the east and west of the Alemannic duchy, where Udalricus, the brother of Queen Hildegard, possessed his estates.

Since Hildegard, through her son Louis the Pious, was the grandmother of Louis the German, Udalricus, her brother, being likewise the grandfather of the count of the same name in the Argengau in 867, the latter Udalricus and Louis the German ought properly to be called cousins rather than true nephews. This, however, does not prevent that count from having been called, at least improperly, Louis’s nephew or kinsman. Like his grandfather, he held the fortress of Bregenz, where his son or grandson, the father of Saint Gebhard, also lived.

I do not know whether the foundation of the entire account of our Chronicle may not lie hidden in the words of that anonymous writer, although it has been clothed in circumstances that do not suit this system. It is clear from the anonymous source that Udalricus committed some offense, for which Charlemagne, the husband of his sister, deprived him of his goods and later restored them to him.

Remove the regicide, Gaul, and the flight, and substitute a brother-in-law for the maternal uncle: you will have almost exactly what is narrated in Book I, no. 3, of the Annals, including the estates enumerated in the counties of the Argengau, Linzgau, and elsewhere.

This also explains why several men, especially Udalrici in these regions, are said to have descended from the lineage of Charlemagne: namely, through blood relationship with Hildegard, his wife and the mother of Louis the Pious. The name then passed from her brother Udalricus to other families as well, through newly contracted marriages. Examples of this are found everywhere in genealogies—not only among the Udalrici, but also among the Hartmanni, Manegoldi, Burchardi, and others, whose names were implanted in other families through marriage.

## § IV

The foregoing conclusions concerning the lineage of Saint Gebhard are taken from the Petershausen Chronicle. We shall now examine its system together with all its accompanying details. Although it is not without its difficulties, it nevertheless contains much that contributes to the clarification of the history presented in it.

We certainly do not deny that some things occur here which, if not fables, at least bear the character of traditions or sources that, although not always genuine, nevertheless report many true matters mixed at times with false ones, in accordance with the spirit of the age.

Scholars know that this frequently happens: when more remote events are being narrated, circumstances are sometimes added which, although of doubtful credibility or entirely false, do not thereby overturn the substance of the historical account itself. Otherwise the situation would be hopeless for many Frankish annals, which nevertheless have until now been sought out and elucidated with such great zeal even by the most learned men.

For even in these rather defective monuments one often finds something that is sought in vain elsewhere, yet is of great assistance to history. We trust that our effort in this matter will not be condemned. We put forward our opinions with the same freedom with which we take pleasure in examining the views or conjectures of others concerning similar matters. We grant this indulgence, and ask it in return.

## § V

To approach, then, the third method of reconciliation more closely: according to the account of our Annals, that most noble man in Gaul Togata—or rather, according to the system of the author (§ 1), in Belgic or Celtic Gaul—who was the father of Udalricus of Bregenz had married the sister of the king of the Franks, who was also afterward emperor of the Romans.

This alone points to the ninth century, not the tenth, when the Carolingians had already died out and Conrad was king (§ 2). But who was this emperor? Certainly, we do not read that any sisters of Charlemagne or Louis the Pious were married, except for Bertha, the wife of Saint Angilbert.

Thus we must understand daughters of Louis the Pious, sisters of the emperors Lothair I and Charles the Bald and of Louis the German. Four of these are found married to different men: Adelheid to Conrad, count of Auxerre; Alpais to Beggo, count of Paris; Hildegard to a certain Count Theodoric; and Gisela to Count Everard of Cisoing in Flanders and later duke of Friuli. Gisela was the maternal sister of the aforementioned Charles the Bald, being born of Judith.

One of these women must, in this system, have been the mother of the aforementioned Count Udalricus, who, as the nephew of Louis the German through his sister, is therefore called his maternal uncle in our Chronicle. Even if this maternal uncle is called “Emperor Augustus,” he can nevertheless be understood as no one other than Louis the German: for both of Louis’s brothers were emperors, but neither possessed any rights in Alemannia by which he could have granted estates to his nephew.

Which of these women gave birth to Udalricus must be determined more by conjecture than by certain arguments, since few of their deeds were committed to writing, and women are mentioned extremely rarely in the charters of this period.

Among Adelheid’s three sons by Conrad, none is called Udalricus. Two were abbots, and the third succeeded his father, whose name he shared. Accordingly, she cannot be meant here; nor can Alpais, whose two sons, Letard and Ebrard, are named by Flodoard in his *History of Reims*, Book IV, ch. 46.

Hildegard and Gisela therefore remain.

The husband of the former, Theodoric, is identified by Cointius only by name (*Annals*, vol. VIII, p. 605) and in *The Art of Verifying Dates* (vol. I, p. 555); the ancient writers of Frankish history do not reveal where he was count. From Nithard’s *History*, Book III, no. 4 (BOUQUET, vol. VII, p. 25), it seems possible to infer only that Hildegard, the sister of Charles the Bald, who had married Theodoric, had her residence in the city of Laon, and therefore in Belgic Gaul, and that in 842 she obtained pardon from Charles for having supported Lothair the emperor, her other brother, against him.

There is no mention there of her husband, whether he had already died or whether Charles, for the same reason, had driven her out with her sons, if she had any. If the ancient monuments contained more information about him, it might perhaps be established that this very man was the father of our Udalricus by Hildegard. Our Chronicle would not contradict this, provided that rebellion raised against the king were substituted for the regicide. We shall discuss below, in § 12, whatever further obstacles might arise here.

## § VI

We have now reached Gisela, the last daughter of Louis the Pious and the maternal sister of Charles the Bald. She had married Everard, or Evrard, at that time count of Cisoing in Flanders and later duke of Friuli. We have thought it appropriate to elucidate her more fully, if not for establishing this genealogy, at least for illuminating the history of our sacred Germany.

Hermann the Lame, under the year 799, records that Eheric, whom others call Henry, was appointed duke of Friuli by Charlemagne and was killed by the Liburnians. Eccard (*Eastern Francia*, vol. I, p. 796) identifies his son as Hunroc or Hunrog, the count who subscribed the will of Charlemagne in 811, preserved by Einhard in his *Life*, and who was also among the Frankish envoys sent to negotiate peace with the Danes (*Annals of Saint-Bertin*, 811).

Earlier, as an envoy of Charlemagne, he had already carried out an exchange with Bernwulf, bishop of Würzburg, who died in 800, as is clear from a diploma of Louis the Pious from 837 (ECCARD, *Eastern Francia*, vol. II, pp. 303 and 884). The same Unroch, or envoy of Charlemagne, is recorded in a capitulary of uncertain date preserved by Martène (*Amplissima Collectio*, vol. VII, p. 12). It is therefore beyond doubt that he was Frankish by birth and very dear to the emperor Charles.

According to Eccard (cited work, p. 196), this Unroch was the father of Everard, count of Cisoing and later duke of Friuli, and of Berengar, count in Lower Germany and afterward duke of Toulouse and Septimania.

Certainly, in the capitulary of Louis the Pious from 825, Count Berengar is listed among the royal envoys in Belgic Gaul, over the four dioceses of Noyon, Amiens, Thérouanne, and Cambrai. He is likewise listed in 834 among the envoys of Louis the Pious to his rebellious son Lothair, in Thegan, chapter 54, where he is called “Berengar the wise, a kinsman of Louis.” Concerning him the same writer says in chapter 58:

> “In that same year, 836, Berengar died on the very journey, a faithful and wise duke, whom the emperor mourned for a long time together with his sons” (BOUQUET, vol. II, pp. 84 and following).

Finally, the Astronomer, in his *Life of Louis the Pious*, calls Berengar count of Toulouse in 819, chapter 57, and says that he was taken away by premature death. He calls him “the son of Huron, once count” [DU CHESNE, vol. II, p. 315], whereas Bouquet (cited work, p. 120) reads “the son of Hugh, once count of Tours”; but this is incorrect, for even in the French version of the deeds of the same emperor (cited work, p. 164), Berengar is called “the son of Count Huron.”

This explains why Berengar is called a kinsman of Louis: his brother Everard had Louis’s daughter as his wife. Everard also gave his two sons, Unroch and Berengar, the names of their father and their uncle.

For the rest, Eccard attributes still other brothers by Hunroch to this Everard and Berengar (*Ancient Monuments*, quarto, p. 40): Henry or Hunric, Adalard, abbot of Saint-Bertin, and Count Albigar. But they are not relevant here.

## § VII

When Balderic, duke of Friuli, was deprived of office by Louis the Pious in 828, his march was divided among four counts (EINHARD, *On the Deeds of Louis*, under that year). One of them seems to have been the faithful Everard, who in 836 was sent from Italy among the envoys of the emperor Lothair to Louis his father, as recorded in the appendix to Thegan (BOUQUET, cited work, p. 85).

To this same Count Everard, in an uncertain year, Rabanus wrote a letter against Gottschalk, who, stopping with him during his journey to Rome, was attempting to spread his errors there. See Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, vol. III, p. 608; Sirmond, *Works*, vol. II, p. 1291; and Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, ninth century, dissertation V, p. 264.

It is not known in what year he obtained the duchy of Friuli and the march of Treviso. Andreas the priest, writing in his *Chronicle* about the emperor Louis II, says:

> “The Lombards endured much hardship and oppression from the Slavic people, until the emperor appointed Everard as prince of the people of Friuli; after his death, his son Unroch assumed the principate” (MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, vol. I, p. 47).

Others, by contrast, assign this event to 846 and to the emperor Lothair. Everard himself calls himself only a count in his will, issued in 867, which we shall discuss below.

In reality, he was count of Cisoing in Flanders, enriched with very extensive possessions in Belgic Gaul, both hereditary and received as a dowry from his son-in-law and father-in-law, in addition to those which he possessed in Italy, as is clear from his will.

Everard is also recorded with Notting, bishop of Verona, as having been sent by the emperor Louis II to Louis the German in the *Annals of Fulda* under 858. Likewise, Count Evrard is among the witnesses who took part in the agreement of the three kings at Conflans in 860 (ECCARD, *Eastern Francia*, vol. II, pp. 474 and following). There pardon was also granted to those who had defected from the kingdom of Charles the Bald to Louis the German; this deserves notice for what will be said shortly afterward.

## § VIII

Agnellus, a writer of this period, reports the following concerning Everard’s marriage in his *On the Bishops of Ravenna* (MURATORI, *Italian Historical Writers*, vol. II, p. 185):

> “Before the Augustus died—that is, Louis the Pious, in 840—he divided his empire among his royal sons. He bestowed upon Charles the more fertile and prosperous portion, and gave his daughter Gisela in marriage to a man named Curado [corrected to Evrado]. This Charles and this Gisela were borne by the empress Judith.”

This removes the objections raised against Gisela as the daughter of Louis the Pious by Adrian Valesius in his preface to the *Panegyric on the Praises of Berengar*, her son and later emperor of Italy (MURATORI, cited work, p. 374 and following).

Indeed, Charles the Bald himself calls Gisela his dearest sister in a charter for the monastery of Donon on the Scheldt, issued in 877, to which, among others, his nephew Rudolph subscribed—namely, Gisela’s son and abbot of Cisoing (MIRAEUS, *Diplomatic Works*, vol. I, p. 249).

Both points are confirmed by a charter of Gisela herself from 870 (DACHERIUS, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 879), in which she calls the noble Everard the elder her husband and Charles her once-germanus, or full brother; she does the same in another charter from 868 and a third from 874.

## § IX

Furthermore, in the charters just mentioned, the same Gisela refers to only four of her sons, although she may have been the mother of more: namely, Unroch, her associate in the Italian regions, who succeeded his father Everard in the duchy of Friuli after his death; Adalard and Rudolph, to whom she gave certain properties of hers in Gaul or Belgic Gaul in 874, as she had already done in 868; and another son, Berengar, who is also recorded in the latter year.

In 870 she assigned certain property with her son Rudolph to the monastery at Cisoing, which she had founded, for the burial there of herself and of her daughter Ingeltrude. We shall say something about this daughter below.

This charter of donation, issued at the Cisoing fisc, was signed by Adelardus, apparently Gisela’s son. In another charter issued by the priest Walgarius at the command of Lord Everard, likewise at Cisoing (cited work, p. 880), he is signed as Adelardus the elder of that place. His father had bequeathed to him by will his estate at Cisoing together with other goods.

By that will Everard distributed his possessions among the four sons mentioned above—“what he held both in Francia and in Lombardy or Alemannia, whether as his own property or as a benefice”—although he did not specifically mention any possessions in Alemannia.

That will of Everard was issued in the county of Treviso in the twenty-fourth year of the reign of Louis Augustus. Miraeus (cited work, vol. I, p. 19) and others understand this of Louis the Pious, or the year 837. But since Louis had first married Judith, Gisela’s mother, only in 819, she could scarcely have been betrothed by 837, much less the mother of as many children as appear in the cited will.

The document therefore belongs to the twenty-fourth year of the emperor Louis II, that is, 867. In this way the Sammarthani defend the authenticity of the will against Valesius and others (*Gallican Church*, vol. III, p. 285); Muratori should be added to their number (*Italian Historical Writers*, vol. II, p. 378).

In that same year, 867, on 16 December, Everard, this count or duke, seems to have died in Italy. He was venerated at Cisoing as a saint with a liturgical feast, and his body was transferred by his son and successor Unroch to the monastery at Cisoing, founded by himself and his wife Gisela, as Gisela herself testifies in a charter preserved by Miraeus (vol. III, p. 389) from 874.

Perhaps this led the Maurist scholars (*Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 446) and Mabillon (*Annals*, Book I, § 37, no. 71) to assign Everard’s death to 874. They evidently failed to attend to another charter of the same Gisela, dated 15 April, in the first indiction, in the twenty-ninth year of the reign of King Charles—that is, 868—in which she testifies that she was already a widow.

Nothing certain is known about Gisela’s death, except that, from the diploma of her brother Charles cited above, it is clear that she was still alive in 877.

## § X

Of the sons of Everard and Gisela, the elder, Unroch, succeeded his father in the duchy of Friuli after his death. According to some writers, he died as early as 872 without a male heir; but it is proved by Gisela’s charter cited above that he was still alive in 874.

His daughter, a nun who was related to the emperor, was abducted from her monastery by Luitward, bishop of Vercelli and chancellor of Charles the Fat, and married to his nephew. The *Annals of Fulda* complain of this under the year 887.

Berengar, the second of the sons, obtained his father’s duchy in Italy after the death of his brother Unroch. He became king because of his mother and finally emperor.

In a diploma for the monastery of Farfa from 920 (DU CHESNE, vol. III, p. 670), he calls Charlemagne his great-grandfather; and in another diploma for the monastery of Casauria from 917 (MURATORI, *Italian Historical Writers*, vol. II, p. 413), he calls the emperor Louis II, who was born from the emperor Lothair, the brother of his mother Gisela, his cousin.

Rudolph, apparently the younger of the sons, became abbot of the monastery at Cisoing in Flanders, founded by his parents:

> “After his father’s death he held those possessions throughout the days of his life; and, when he was about to depart from the world, he transferred those same possessions to the church of Reims together with the monastery and appointed that church heir to all his property. Then a certain Hucbald—still unknown to us—the husband of this Rudolph’s sister, accused him concerning the office of the same abbacy and attempted to remove it from the right of the church,”

as Folco, archbishop of Reims, writes to Pope Formosus, as reported by Flodoard in his *History of Reims*, Book IV, ch. 1 (Library of the Fathers of Lyons, vol. XVII, p. 595).

Formosus was pope from 891 through 896. He replied to Folco in the tenth indiction, when Lambert was already emperor (FLODOARD, cited work, ch. 2), which indicates the year 892. Rudolph, therefore, had already died in that same year.

A difficulty arises, however, because Flodoard, in the same passage, writes that the estate where Everard the margrave built the monastery passed after his death by hereditary right to his son Rudolph the abbot. Yet in the actual tablets of Everard’s will, written in 867, the estate at Cisoing together with the possessions of that church or monastery is transferred not to Rudolph but to his brother Adalard.

If, then, Rudolph received them by hereditary right, it must be said either that Adalard had died in the meantime or that he had voluntarily ceded his hereditary possessions in Belgic Gaul to his brother.

We have just seen above that Adalard was called the elder or lord of Cisoing in Walgarius’s charter of donation, from about 868. He also appears in Gisela’s charter from 874. Afterward, however, there is complete silence about him, and nothing is known concerning his later fate.

Certainly he was no longer living in Belgic Gaul when his brother Rudolph the abbot died; otherwise the husband of their sister could not have claimed any right in Cisoing. Therefore, if Adalard had not yet died, he must meanwhile have established himself elsewhere, where he possessed estates granted to him by others, rather than possessions acquired by inheritance.

## § XI

From these facts, and also from at least a partial similarity between the names Adalard and Adalrich or Udalrich, a considerable suspicion arises that this Udalricus, the ancestor of the counts of Bregenz, may himself have been Adalard: the son of Everard, duke of Friuli and count of Cisoing in Flanders, and by this route the true nephew of Louis the German through his sister.

Nor would it be impossible to attribute a fifth son, Udalricus, to Everard, even though no mention of him appears in any of the charters cited thus far. Such a mention was not necessary, since already in 867, before those charters were written, he had been endowed by his maternal uncle with his own county in the Argengau and with other estates in Alemannia. He therefore had no need to share in his paternal or maternal possessions in Belgic Gaul; hence his name, as that of someone long absent, would have been inserted into those documents in vain.

This final conjecture might therefore seem the more probable. Whatever the truth may be, we shall now examine the account of our Chronicle point by point.

> “In Gaul, which we have said was called Togata, there was a certain man adorned with the noblest lineage.”

We have already shown that the writer confuses Gaul Togata with Gaul Comata. Hence, under the name Togata, Gaul Comata—or Belgic Gaul—must be understood. Everard was count of Cisoing in that region, and we have traced his very noble lineage thus far.

> “The king of the Franks, and afterward, namely, the emperor of the Romans, had given him his sister in marriage.”

These words plainly designate Charles the Bald, after whom no one simultaneously held the kingship of the Franks and the Roman Empire whose sister was given in marriage. Both sisters of Charles the Fat were abbesses at Zürich.

It makes no difference whether the daughter of Louis the Pious or the sister of Charles the Bald is said to have been given in marriage. The Chronicle continues:

> “By her he had two sons,”

namely, as many as had come to Alemannia; the others, being farther away, were unknown to the writer in these regions.

What is subsequently narrated about the killing of the king of the Franks by these two brothers contradicts the history of the entire period. If it is to possess any appearance of truth, it must be understood only of some rebellion or defection from their king Charles the Bald, such as his other sister Hildegard, married to Count Theodoric, had already attempted against him in 842, as we said above.

What wonder, then, if her father-in-law and nephews also dared something of the kind? Nor are we relying here on conjecture alone. Gisela herself, the wife of Everard, reveals the matter sufficiently clearly in the two charters already cited, from 868 and 870, when she professes that the possessions lost by her elder, or husband, Evrard, and reduced to the king’s ownership, had been restored to her by Charles the Bald, her brother. This evidently indicates some crime or felony, at least on the part of her husband or sons.

Perhaps these two brothers themselves were among those nobles of Charles who, having long since grown weary of him, in 858 formally sought the aid of Louis, king of Germany, against the tyranny of their own king Charles. When Louis arrived in Gaul with an army, they abandoned Charles and went over to him, as the *Annals of Fulda* report under that year.

This agrees with the account of the Chronicle (Book I, no. 3), that noblemen came with these brothers and that the brothers themselves distributed among them the estates which their maternal uncle had granted them in Alemannia. We have already established above that this maternal uncle was none other than Louis the German, to whom Alemannia was subject.

What we have said thus far also seems to be confirmed by the fact that, according to the same *Annals of Fulda* under 858, Count Everard—undoubtedly the duke of Friuli and the father of these two German exiles—came from Italy, as an envoy of the emperor Louis II, to Louis the German at Ulm for a conference.

From this arises another conjecture: Everard, like his wife’s sister Hildegard, had previously supported the cause of the emperor Lothair. For that reason Charles the Bald deprived him of his territories in Charles’s kingdom, and he withdrew to Italy to Lothair. Lothair, or his son, the emperor Louis II, then appointed him duke of Friuli.

When Everard’s two sons resented this dispossession of their father, they rebelled against Charles together with other nobles and surrendered themselves to their maternal uncle Louis the German.

The events that follow in the Chronicle—the calming of the fury of the Gauls and the recall of these brothers to their homeland—should, in our opinion, be assigned to the year 860. In that year, when peace between Charles and the aforementioned Louis was confirmed at Conflans, Charles the Bald declared:

> “As for those men who acted against me, as you know, and came to my brother . . . I forgive them everything that they did wrongly against me; and I grant them their allodial possessions—those inherited, those acquired, and those received by donation from our Lord, that is, our father Louis the Pious—except what came from my own donation, provided that they give me assurance that they will remain peaceful in my kingdom,”

as is read in Baluze (*Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, vol. II, p. 144). This agrees perfectly with what Gisela, his sister, recalls in the charters cited above concerning the possessions taken from her and restored to her by her brother Charles.

All these considerations, at least in our view, may suffice to vindicate the reliability of our author, provided that the regicide is removed and a rebellion raised against the king substituted for it.

The writer could easily have been mistaken in assigning the true cause of the brothers’ departure without their arrival in Alemannia, or the genealogy constructed upon it, thereby being fictitious, as Tenzelius maintains. The arguments brought forward thus far may not establish both points beyond doubt, but they do not bear the character of fables. At the same time, they explain why both brothers came to Alemannia and the time at which each was recalled to his homeland—namely, after Charles the Bald, the king, granted pardon for the rebellion they had committed, with their father Everard acting chiefly as mediator. Everard is recorded among the witnesses to that peace in Eccard (*Eastern Francia*, vol. II, p. 476 and following).

## § XII

When, therefore, peace had been made and one of the brothers, whoever he was, had returned to his homeland, Udalricus alone remained in Alemannia, now the possessor of all the estates in Alemannia that had previously been granted by their maternal uncle to both brothers.

At least in 867, a date consistent with this account, Udalricus appears as the nephew of Louis the German and count in the Argengau, and perhaps also in the Linzgau in the years 879, 881, and 902 (HERGOTT, vol. II, p. 48).

As we observed above in the preface from Tenzelius, he may also easily have been the same man to whom the emperor Arnulf granted the estate of Lustenau as his property, as is established by a charter from 891 (HERGOTT, cited work, p. 57), which is also printed in full in Schardius’s *Writers* (vol. I, p. 534).

Nothing certain can be established here, however, since so many Udalrici occur in the various neighboring districts of Alemannia—especially in the Argengau, Linzgau, and Thurgau, and later also at Bregenz—that it always remains doubtful whether they were the same men or different individuals who bore the same name, which, as commonly happened, was also propagated into other families through marriage.

§ XIII. Having meanwhile submitted these matters to the examination of learned men, it is now worthwhile to consider what is found further on in our Chronicle concerning this genealogy of the counts of Brigantium, which is entirely consistent with the earlier evidence. Thus, in Book I, no. 36, it states:

> “There was a certain count named Adilhardus . . . a kinsman of the blessed man Gebhard according to bodily consanguinity, yet by no means a Swabian, but dwelling in a distant land. By hereditary right, great and numerous estates in Ilrigove”—or rather, perhaps, Hargove—had fallen to him, from which he later transferred an estate at Steinbach to his Brigantine kinsmen and several others to his nephew, Bishop Gebhard.

Who, then, was this Adilhardus, or Adalardus, the nephew or blood-relative of the counts of Brigantium? For this cannot refer to the earlier Adalard, son of Eberhard, since he lived a full century earlier. We seem to have discovered him in Ekkehard the Younger’s *On the Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, chapter 10 (Goldast, *Scriptores*, vol. I, p. 42), where he writes:

> “A certain count Uodalricus, descended from the lineage of Charles, took Wendilgarda, granddaughter of King Henry through his daughter, as his wife, and by her begot Adalhart, who later gave [his estate] to Saint Gall at Altstätten, and also a daughter. When this man, having received news at Buochorn, where he lived, that the Hungarians had invaded Noricum, where he possessed estates, he attacked the enemy together with the others; defeated, he was captured and carried away as a prisoner into Hungary.”

He then relates that Udalricus, returning from captivity after four years, fathered another son, Burchard, surnamed *Ingenitum* (“the Inborn”), whom Emperor Otto I, as his nephew, while still a young man, placed over the abbey of Saint Gall around the year 959.

From Hepidannus’s *Annals* under the year 913, and from excerpts of the Frankish Annals (above, p. 109), we learn that in that year Count Udalricus routed the Hungarians at the River Inn together with Erchanger and Berthold, who had invaded the duchy of Alemannia; yet after some time, around the year 915, he was carried off by them into captivity during another expedition. See Calles, *Annales Ecclesiastici Germaniae*, vol. IV, under the years 917 and 920, and Crusius, *Annals*, part II, book III, chapter 8.

Released after four years, he returned home while Solomon III, bishop of Constance—who died at the beginning of the year 920—was still alive. At the Synod of Constance, around the year 919, Solomon restored Wendilgarda to him as his wife, though she had meanwhile been veiled [as a religious] (*Concilia Germaniae*, vol. II, p. 591).

This Udalricus is plainly different from the count surnamed Brigantinus, as both the chronology and the different sons of the two men demonstrate. He appears to have been the son of one of those very noble men who, as our Chronicle testifies, fled with the Brigantine into Alemannia. The Brigantine bestowed gifts upon them and also joined himself to them by marriage alliances; to one of them he gave Buochorn, and perhaps also a daughter, later the mother of this Udalricus, from whom he inherited both the name and the lineage of Charlemagne.

Lazius, *On the Migration of Peoples*, p. 559, says that this man founded the castle of Buochorn with his brother Adelbert in the time of Charlemagne, under whom, after receiving lands in Noricum, he was captured by the Huns; yet he also writes that his wife Wendilgarda was enclosed at Saint Gall a full century later, in the year 916.

Here it should be noted that writers sometimes also bestowed the name of Charlemagne upon Charles the Fat, because, like his predecessor, he alone held the entire Frankish monarchy together with the empire. Mabillon proves this in *On Diplomatics*, book V, p. 408. Lazius should be understood in this sense, although even so an error remains: the captivity of Udalricus occurred not under Charles the Fat but under Conrad I.

He is also mistaken in saying that Hedwig, the wife of Burchard, duke of Alemannia, was the daughter of Henry the Fowler and the mother of Wendilgarda. She died childless and was not the daughter of Henry the Fowler, but his granddaughter through his son Henry, duke of Bavaria. Saint Gebhard is likewise called her grandson below, in Book I, no. 39.

Ekkehard does not name Wendilgarda’s mother, but merely says that she was the daughter of King Henry, that is, the Fowler. Crusius (*Annals*, part II, book III, chapters 8 and 12, and book IV, chapters 3 and 9) and others call her Hedwig, or Hatwig, although it is otherwise certain that she became the wife of Hugh the Great, duke of France, and the mother of King Hugh Capet.

§ XIV. Whatever her name may have been, she was certainly the daughter of Henry the Fowler, whose mother was Hedwig, or Hatwig, married to Otto the Illustrious, duke of Saxony. This Hedwig, in turn, was the daughter of the aforementioned Eberhard, duke of Fréjus, by Gisela, daughter of Louis the Pious. Hence her son Henry, with the Carolingian line extinguished in Germany, possessed a certain claim to this kingdom.

In her father’s testament she is called Heilwick, sister of Adalard, or Udalricus, the ancestor of the counts of Brigantium, and also of Judith, grandmother of King Conrad I, as Eccard proves (*Frankish Origins*, vol. II, p. 821; *Ancient Documents*, quatern. p. 40). Thus the following genealogy emerges.

**GENEALOGICAL SYSTEM OF SAINT GEBHARD**  
From the Chronicle of Petershausen and Eccard.

As for Hedwig, wife of Otto of Saxony, the writers diverge greatly. Hübner, in his *Genealogy*, makes her the daughter not of Gisela, sister of Louis the German, but of Louis the German himself, though the ancients know nothing of this. In *The Art of Verifying Dates*, Hedwig is called the daughter of Emperor Arnulf and is named Luitgarda by Tenzel.

Eccard, however (*Frankish Origins*, vol. II, p. 609), establishes by numerous arguments that Otto’s wife was the daughter of Gisela and Everard, especially from the *Life of Hathumoda*, abbess and sister of that same Duke Otto, where he is said to have had a granddaughter of kings in marriage, and therefore not a daughter.

The Fulda Necrology records that a Countess Hadawiga died in the year 903; we believe her to have been this same woman. Her elder sister is identified in their father’s testament as Judith, grandmother of King Conrad I, according to Eccard (*ibid.*, p. 824). Thus Conrad too obtained the kingdom of Germany as the nearest kinsman of the Carolingian family.

Eccard believes that a third sister, Ingiltrud, mentioned in the same testament, was a nun in the same monastery of Cison from a charter of their mother Gisela dated 870 (*ibid.*, p. 610). This cannot be accepted, however, since above, in § 10, it appears from Flodoard that a certain Hucbold was the husband of the sister of Rudolf, abbot of Cison. Since, therefore, the two sisters mentioned above—daughters of Gisela—had other husbands, one of two conclusions follows: either Ingeltrud, the third sister, was not a nun, or we must admit a fourth sister who was omitted from the testament, just as above (§ 11) we conjectured the existence of a fifth brother, Udalricus.

From the foregoing genealogy it is clear why our Chronicle calls Saint Gebhard the nephew both of Duchess Hedwig and of Count Adalard of Buochorn, reckoning only consanguinity and not degrees of relationship. Although that distinction of degrees was generally observed, at least in charters and especially in diplomas, the practice of medieval chroniclers was different. Following a custom still in use, their writers habitually called all those “nephews” who were related by blood or even by affinity in any manner, being descended from the same stock.

Whether another generation must still be inserted between Udalricus I, count of Brigantium, and Uzo, the father of Saint Gebhard, we shall discuss shortly, in § 16.

Another difficulty nevertheless remains from our Chronicle: it says that Count Udalricus in Buochorn, where he also had his residence, was not a Swabian by origin but had lived in a distant land. How could he not have been a Swabian when he lived at Buochorn?

This can be resolved only by saying that he was not originally a Swabian, but had arrived in these lands with the Brigantine from a distant country where he had previously lived. He did not always remain at Buochorn, where he had his seat, but also stayed in Noricum, where he was enriched with estates; while returning to defend them a second time against the Hungarians, he was captured. Perhaps his son Adalard was also born there; this was the man who later granted his property in Hargove to his Brigantine kinsmen, perhaps before Gebhard had become a bishop. In terms of age this presents no difficulty, even if he had already been born around the year 913. I willingly leave the investigation of another possibility to anyone who wishes to pursue it.

§ XV. Up to this point we have spent considerable effort illuminating the earliest origin of the counts of Brigantium in our Chronicle, although we do not claim to be guarantors of everything we have advanced. Let the arguments brought forward decide the matter; learned men may refute them or bring them into greater light by producing new documents, just as we present our views and opinions to them, without prejudice, in the interest of investigating history alone. We do not undertake to defend everywhere the narrative of our author, especially not at its beginning.

At least we cannot persuade ourselves that he either wished or was able to invent such matters without foundation or fabricate them from his own imagination, whether through ignorance or in order to flatter a family that still flourished in his time, without exposing himself to the guilt of admitted falsehood. This was a period when the same family, though divided into several branches, was still vigorous, and therefore its true origin ought to have been better known than it is now.

The blood relationship of the counts of Brigantium to the Carolingian kings is placed beyond doubt, at least, by the frequently cited diploma of Louis the German dated 867, in which he calls Udalricus, count of those regions, his nephew. We have so far attempted to investigate the basis of this relationship by two lines of inquiry.

Nor can that once-famous genealogy, and the others descending from it, be adequately examined, especially because of the many Udalrici bearing the same name. That name appears to have passed from one family into another through contracted marriages, until genuine documents yet to be produced bring the matter into the light. This is easier to wish for than to hope for, since the archives of ancient Alemannia are still too heavily closed in various places, and have been partly plundered, scattered, and dispersed by the disastrous events of wars and civil disturbances.

§ XVI. “From the seed of this Udalricus,” the Chronicle continues, “was born Uzo, a pious and venerable count, who lived at Brigantium, in a place that still has the ruins of an ancient dwelling.”

From this point the second genealogical system proposed above, in § 3, also enters the discussion. According to it, however, this Udalricus of the year 867 would have been only the grandson through a son of Udalricus I, count in Argengau in 802 and brother of Queen Hildegard, in accordance with the genealogy displayed there.

From the further narrative of our Chronicle it is uncertain whether this Udalricus was Uzo’s immediate father or merely his grandfather through a son, since our Annals can be understood in either way. Nothing seems to prevent Uzo from having been the son of Count Udalricus in Argengau mentioned in Louis the German’s diploma of 867—especially if he was the same as Count Udalricus in Linzgau, who appears in charters preserved by P. Herrgott down to the year 902.

The latter possibility might be supported by the estates listed below in Book I, most of which Gebhard inherited from his parents and which were situated in the district of Linzgau. His ancestors therefore appear to have been counts both of that district and of neighboring Argengau. In the latter, Uzo, the father of Saint Gebhard, is said in Book I, no. 6, to have nobly enriched the monastery of Lindau from his own estates; he was also buried there, a fact I do not recall having read anywhere else.

The endowment of that monastery appears to have been made after the year 948, when, according to Hermann, Lindau was consumed by fire by Hermann, duke of Alemannia. Uzo contributed his estates toward its restoration and, after his death, obtained burial there. He must have died not long afterward, since his sons, as recorded in the same place, no. 7, divided the inheritance among themselves after their parents had already died, and Gebhard at least already had dominion over his property and his own advocate by the year 958.

In that year or the following, Alawicus, abbot of Reichenau, certainly died; according to no. 11, Gebhard had entered into an exchange with him. Uzo’s elder son Udalricus took part in the battle fought against the Hungarians near Augsburg in 953, from which it is possible to judge the age of his father Uzo.

Lazius calls this man Etho, while Crusius calls him Utho, evidently from having misread or misunderstood the name Uzo. Tenzel rightly judges otherwise; in his view, Uzo, Uozo, and Huzo are synonymous with the name Udalricus.

The wife of this Uzo, or the mother of Saint Gebhard, is called Dietburga, a woman of the highest nobility, in the Chronicle, although her lineage is nowhere stated. It may perhaps be sought in the Swabian and Dillingen family because of the mother of Saint Udalricus, bishop of Augsburg, who bore the same name, or even in Alemannia or Turgau. What if she had been the daughter of Adelbert the Elder, count of Turgau?

§ XVII. Once again our annalist alone reports that Uzo had four sons. Lazius and the others, by contrast, attribute only one son, Gebhard, to Etho or Uzo; they entirely omit Udalricus, the firstborn, and make Lantfrid, father of Marquard, the son of Uzo’s or Etho’s brother Hugh. Tenzel too rejects all this as fictitious (p. 276) and considers that we must stand by our author.

For Gebhard’s brothers are explicitly assigned by the charter of his donation itself, Book I, no. 9, in which he transferred to the Church of Constance, with the consent of his brothers, the property rights that he had inherited from his parents in Linzgau and elsewhere.

The author records nothing about Udalricus, Uzo’s firstborn son, apart from the battle near Augsburg, in which he took part in 855. Yet he appears to have succeeded his father in the county, since, as we shall see, the other son, Marquard, was count in Goldineshuntare, while Luitfrid was count in Winterthur. Perhaps this is the same Vodalricus whom Hepidannus writes in his *Annals* died in the year 978.

§ XVIII. Marquard, the second son of Uzo, exercised considerable influence in the friendship of Emperor Otto. By Otto here I understand Otto III, a kinsman of the Brigantines according to the genealogy presented above. Through Count Marquard’s intervention, Otto donated certain estates in 993 to Saint Gebhard in the district of Goldinneshundere, which is called Marquard’s county in the diploma of Book I, no. 26.

Besselius, in his *Chronicle of Gottweig*, calls this district part of the district of Hegau, in the duchy of Alemannia and the territory of Mösskirch. The small district of Goldineshuntare is noted as being in the county of Count Udalricus in Louis the German’s diploma of 854, preserved by P. Herrgott, no. 56. Hence Marquard appears to have obtained this district from the paternal inheritance of Uzo and the grandfather Udalricus.

We have been unable to discover anything further about him. His date, or the year 993, agrees perfectly with that of his brother Saint Gebhard, who died in 996.

This Marquard is proved to be different, both by his own county and by chronology, from the Marquard who is recorded as count of Chur in Rhaetia in Emperor Conrad II’s diploma for the monastery of Pfäfers, dated 1032 and preserved by the same P. Herrgott, no. 171.

Lazius makes this latter man the son of Luitfrid, brother of Saint Gebhard, and perhaps not entirely wrongly. Although our author mentions only one son of that Luitfrid, Adelbert, there is nothing to prevent him from having had others. Indeed, according to Lazius, this Adelbert, or Albert, who fell in Apulia, was not the son of Luitfrid but his grandson through Marquard.

In view of the chronology, it is very difficult to call that Adelbert the son of Luitfrid, whose brother Udalricus was already serving in the army in 955. How, then, could Adelbert, his nephew through that brother, undertake so distant an expedition almost a full century later, namely in 1053, when, according to Hermann, that ill-fated war of Leo IX against the Normans was undertaken and the best men from Swabia and Noricum fell on 18 June?

On this subject see also the frequently cited Tenzel, p. 284, where he again follows our Annals, adopting the genealogy of Luitfrid established there.

A third Marquard, from the Brigantine line, also appears to belong to this same family. Burckard, in *On the Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, chapter 7, writes the following concerning Udalricus III, abbot of Saint Gall (Goldast, vol. I, p. 72):

> “The abbot, stirred up, stormed and burned a fairly well-fortified castle called Marchtorf together with Count Otto . . . He burned the town of Brigantium after capturing Marquard, a most noble Swabian.”

This occurred in the year 1079 or the following year. This Marquard, count of Brigantium, may belong to the descendants or perhaps the grandsons of Udalricus, brother of Saint Gebhard.

From Burckard’s testimony we infer that Count Otto of Brigantium adhered to the party of the pope in the schism; otherwise he would not have suffered this destruction at the hands of Abbot Udalricus, a supporter of the emperor. From the fuller account of Bernold (below, vol. II, under the year 1077), however, it may be conjectured that in that year Otto still adhered to King Henry, since he gave the schismatic Bishop Otto of Constance, who had fled from Constance, refuge in his castle. Shortly afterward, however, he may have changed his mind out of fear of the anti-emperor Rudolf. His son Udalricus likewise followed in his footsteps, as we shall see below, in §§ 23 and 24.

§ XIX. Our author has also rendered distinguished service to history by revealing the origin of the counts of Winterthur, hitherto sufficiently obscure; for this he was deservedly praised by Füesslin, vol. IV, p. 186 ff.

From him we learn that this once-famous castle of Turgau, together with its appurtenances, passed into the possession of the counts of Brigantium and, in the division of the estates, fell to Luitfrid, brother of Saint Gebhard. He was therefore the first count of Winterthur in the tenth century, from whom the counts of Kyburg later descended as well.

We also have Hartmann as a witness to this matter in his *Annals of Einsiedeln*. Concerning Hermann, abbot of Einsiedeln from 1053 to 1065, he reports the following from the domestic records:

> “He was descended from the counts of Vitodurum, who also founded Kyburg, and from whom the Kyburgs received their name. He had brothers, Luitfrid, who had preceded him in death, and Adelbert, who was then administering the county.”

It is not known which of the Vitodurans was the first founder of Kyburg Castle. Nevertheless, one may perhaps not be far wrong in attributing it to one of the sons of Luitfrid, the first count of Winterthur, or even to Luitfrid himself, “who amassed considerable wealth.”

Stumpf, in his *Chronicle* (book V, chapter 30), and others reject this, referring the origin of the castle and counts of Kyburg as far back as the ninth century. P. Herrgott, however, considers the matter insignificant (*Habsburg Genealogy*, vol. I, book I, chapter 9), since the name Kyburg scarcely, if at all, occurs in the older records before the beginning of the twelfth century.

I think this was said only of charters. For already under the year 1027 Hermann the Lame writes that the castle of Cuynburg, belonging to Count Werenhar, was captured by Emperor Conrad II. Under the year 1030 he calls Werinhar the leader of the rebellion against the emperor; in that same year Werinhar fell in battle near our Martian Forest together with Ernest, duke of Alemannia.

Hepidannus, anticipating the event by six years in his customary manner, writes under the year 1033:

> “The castle called Chiburch, having been besieged for three months while Count Werinher stubbornly resisted for a long time, was finally captured by the king himself.”

Under the year 1036 he likewise writes that Count Werinher, a soldier of Duke Ernest, fell with him in battle.

We believe that this Wernher, count of Kyburg and perhaps also its founder, should be counted among the sons of Luitfrid, and that he was the brother of Marquard (§ preceding), whom he succeeded in the county. Lazius calls him the father of Adelbert, who was killed in Apulia, and perhaps also of the younger Luitfrid and of Hermann, abbot of Einsiedeln, as we noted shortly above from Hartmann.

This is suggested by the mention there of Adelbert, who was then administering the county—namely in 1053, when Hermann became abbot on 15 February. Adelbert, however, fell in Apulia shortly afterward, on 18 June.

These words can scarcely refer to another Adelbert, count of Winterthur or Kyburg. The Adelbert mentioned by our annalist—the grandson through a daughter of the earlier Adelbert and heir of the entire patrimony—could scarcely have been born by 1065, the year in which Abbot Hermann died, since he was still alive around 1139, when the author wrote.

This would remove the difficulty raised in the preceding section if the earlier Adelbert were called the son of Luitfrid, as our chronicler states. Yet he seems to have passed over one generation—that of the elder Luitfrid—omitting his sons and contenting himself with indicating his grandson Adelbert, who in his own time administered the county. He likewise passed over Adelbert’s other brothers, since they had no bearing on the genealogy that he proceeds to trace.

§ XX. Adelbert, or Albert, whether son—or, more probably, grandson—of Luitfrid, the first count of Winterthur, was at once the last count of Winterthur and Kyburg from the Brigantine line. He left only a daughter, Adelheid.

Lazius makes her the paternal aunt of Adelbert, that is, the sister of Marquard, his father, and therefore the daughter of the aforementioned Luitfrid. Yet, considering the chronology, she cannot have been so.

I do not know whether our author may not here have confused certain persons, making a single individual out of two Marquards—one the brother and the other the son of Luitfrid, as we suspected above—and likewise making one Luitfrid out of two: the father, or elder Luitfrid, and the son, or younger Luitfrid, brother of Adelbert and of Hermann the abbot, whom we have mentioned above.

Whatever the truth may be, Lazius is entirely correct in adding:

> “Adelheid was married to Count Hartmann of Dillingen, to whom she brought Winterthur and the county of Kyburg as her dowry; for previously it had belonged to the counts of Brigantium.”

Thus, through this marriage, the counts of Dillingen first became, in the eleventh century, also counts of Kyburg. This is contrary to the usual claim in the genealogical family tree of those counts; and there, moreover, the mention of so many Hartmanns has introduced the same confusion that above we lamented in the case of the Brigantines because of the numerous Udalrici.

§ XXI. The annalist accordingly assigns to Count Hartmann the Elder of Dillingen, who took Adelheid, heiress of the county of Winterthur or Kyburg, in marriage, three sons by her:

> “She bore him Hartmann the Younger and Adelbert, who still survives and has become heir of the whole patrimony and marriage-alliance”—that is, of the counties of Dillingen and Kyburg—“and Udalricus, who became bishop at Constance,”

as the Chronicle states in Book I, no. 8.

If we examine the genealogies of the counts of Kyburg or Dillingen published thus far, we find various Hartmanns designated as elder or younger. We believe this is entirely due to the writers, who, without reference to earlier men of the same name, called “elder” the one who was more prominent in their own time, while they called his namesake son or successor “younger,” according to the ancient custom and with regard to the times and persons involved. We have already observed the same practice concerning Pippin of Herstal, who was called sometimes elder and sometimes younger.

Thus Crusius (*Annals*, part II, book III, chapter 11) calls Hartmann the Elder the son of Richwin, whose father was Theobald, brother of Saint Udalricus, bishop of Augsburg, who had already been killed in the battle near Augsburg in 955. Who could call that Hartmann the husband of Adelheid, who lived more than half a century later?

Pistorius goes even further astray (*Scriptores*, vol. III, p. 740), saying that Hartmann the Elder was altogether the brother of Saint Udalricus, and that Adelheid, daughter of Adelbert and granddaughter of Luitfrid, was married to him. That man would certainly have been no other than our count of Winterthur.

But this is again manifestly erroneous. Who could believe that the brother of Saint Udalricus, who died in 973, had as his wife the daughter of Adelbert of Winterthur, who first died in 1053? Nor, content with having erred once, does he also make Hugbald, count of Dillingen, who died in 1170, the father of Udalricus I, bishop of Constance, who had already died in 1127—forty-three years before his alleged father.

Which Hartmann he means here, the author himself reveals in Book II, no. 36, where he calls Hartmann the Elder “that count of Dillingen who founded the monastery of Neresheim in 1095.”

According to Bruschus, in the history of that monastery, and Stengelius, in his *Monasteriology* (see Franciscus Petrus, *The Church of Swabia*, p. 634), this man was the son of the fourth Count Hugbald of Dillingen, husband of Adelheid, countess of Kyburg, father of Udalricus, bishop of Constance, and of Hartmann the Younger. All of this agrees with our annalist.

Velserus too, in his *Life of Saint Udalricus* (*Works*, p. 589), dates Hartmann, husband of Adelheid, to 1073 and calls him the father of Hartmann and Udalricus, bishop of Constance, and the grandfather of Albert. This likewise agrees with our Chronicle.

Burckardus presents us with both Hartmanns. Concerning Udalricus III, abbot of Saint Gall, he writes in *On the Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, chapter 7:

> “He destroyed by fire a well-fortified castle of a certain very wealthy Count Hartmann of Kyburg, the bitterest enemy of King Henry, together with much booty, after capturing his son.”

This occurred in 1079 under Emperor Henry IV.

We therefore conclude that Hartmann was already count of Kyburg at that time through his wife Adelheid, heiress of her father Adelbert, who died in 1053 without a male heir. He was the father of Hartmann the Younger and Adelbert, who succeeded his brother—after the latter had become a monk and died in 1134—in both counties, becoming heir of the entire patrimony and marriage-alliance.

Lazius, pp. 535 and 559, wrongly confuses him with another Adelbert of Achalm, whom our author says was born of one of Hartmann’s daughters, as we shall shortly see.

§ XXII. In addition to the three sons of Hartmann the Elder already mentioned, the annalist assigns to him by Adelheid of Winterthur or Kyburg three daughters:

> “who now remain in the habit of nuns. One of them bore Udalricus, count of Gamertingen, and Adelbert of Achalm; both of them still enjoy life.”

Our author does not state the name of their mother. Crusius (*Annals*, part II, book IV, chapter 20) calls her Adelheid, daughter of Hartmann of Dillingen and sister of Udalricus, bishop of Constance. He says that she was the wife of Count Udalricus of Gamertingen, by whom she had another Udalricus, and that in 1101, with her husband’s consent or after his death, she became a nun at Zwiefalten and died thirty years later, in 1131, as P. Arsenius Sulger reports in his *Annals of Zwiefalten*, vol. I, pp. 57 and 77.
