He adds another nun there, Hedwig or Hadewig, and finally, on Sulger’s authority, an abbess at Edelstetten who died on 13 November 1131.

Ortlieb also discusses these sisters in *On the Foundation of the Monastery of Zwiefalten*, chapter 19, in P. Hess (*Guelphic Monuments*, p. 192). It is not known where the third sister assumed the monastic habit; Sulger is silent about her, at least when he discusses the counts of Gamertingen, who also held the county of Achalm (*ibid.*, p. 79), making no mention of this Adelbert of Achalm.

Lazius customarily calls him Albert, but wrongly, as we have already noted, makes him the son of Hartmann IV of Dillingen and places him under Emperor Otto II, as the brother or nephew of Saint Wolfgang. He was not that Hartmann’s son but his grandson through a daughter; nor did he flourish in the time of Saint Wolfgang of Regensburg, who had already died in 994, but only in the twelfth century. He was still alive around 1131, when the author wrote, as was also his brother Uldaricus of Gamertingen.

I believe this is the man of whom Burckardus writes in *On the Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, chapter 9:

> “A certain advocate of this Church, named Udalricus of Gamertingen, died, and his son, still a boy, was likewise snatched away by death under the same law. The abbot Wernher, who died around 1166, appointed Count Rudolf of Pfullendorf in his place.”

We shall return to Count Rudolf of Pfullendorf below, in § 24.

In the Zwiefalten Necrology this Udalricus is recorded under 3 October, as is his father under 18 September:

> “Count Ulricus of Gamertingen; he was buried with his father, Count Arnold, in our chapter.”

§ XXIII. Let us now return to the counts of Brigantium, where Uzo, or Udalricus, the father of Saint Gebhard, first established his seat and where his descendants still flourished in the author’s time, in the twelfth century.

We said something above, in § 17, about his elder namesake son and successor in the county, conjecturing that he died in 978.

In a charter of Eberhard, bishop of Constance, dated 1043 (below, Book II, § 10), Udalricus Brigantinus appears first among the witnesses. He seems to have been his son and may perhaps be the same man mentioned below, in Book II, § 20, as “Udalricus the Elder, count of Brigantium,” buried in the cloister at Petershausen.

He is called “the Elder” in relation to another man, perhaps his son, or rather his grandson (see the genealogical chart), who died in 1097, according to Berthold of Constance in his *Chronicle*. Berthold commemorates him with this eulogy:

> “Udalricus, a most distinguished count, a most ardent defender of Saint Peter’s cause against the schismatics, alas, closed his final day by a sufficiently untimely death, but with a good confession; and he was honorably buried at Brigantium, where he himself had established monastic life, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.”

On the day before this date, the Zwiefalten Necrology cited above records an Ulricus, count of Brigantium, who is entirely omitted at Petershausen.

Our Chronicle describes the manner of his death in Book III, § 23, where his sons, Rudolf and Udalricus, are also listed. Their mother was Bertha, daughter of Rudolf the anti-emperor and count of Rheinfelden, who is recorded in both of the aforementioned necrologies under 20 January; her marriage is also related in Book III, § 21.

The same Berthold of Constance writes the following about this Udalricus under the year 1093:

> “Duke Welfo and Count Udalricus of Brigantium, together with many others, began to ravage one another in every manner by setting fires.”

He does not disclose the cause of the dispute. It may perhaps have arisen because Welfo had already inclined toward the emperor’s party, as Berthold reports of him under 1095, whereas Udalricus, devoted to the pope, opposed that party.

P. Hess offers another explanation (*Guelphic Monuments*, p. 159): that Otto, the last count of Buochorn, ceded his inheritance to Welfo, as the anonymous author of Weingarten relates, chapter 8, § 3 (*ibid.*, p. 18), while Udalricus Brigantinus believed that it belonged to him by right of kinship.

Whether this Udalricus should be called the son of Udalricus the Elder, or rather the grandson through Otto’s son, as we reasonably suspect in the following genealogical chart, we leave to others to investigate.

§ XXIV. Our chronicler, together with Berthold, testifies that Udalricus established monastic life in the greater Brigantine Augia, or Mehrerau, where he was buried, in Book III, § 19 ff. Bruschus and others who followed him say the same, although they rightly understand this as a second foundation, or the restoration of the first foundation, which had been made earlier.

They err, however, in assigning it to the year 1098, when Udalricus had already died. They also make him count both of Brigantium and of the Rhaetians, because his county extended as far as Rhaetia, as is clear from Henry IV’s diploma for the monastery of Pfäfers dated 1095, preserved by P. Herrgott, no. 191. In it, Curvalia is said to lie in the county of Count Odalricus of Braganica.

This restoration is dated to 1097 in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 972. That may perhaps refer to the church begun by Udalricus, built of stone (Book II, § 22), which was later completed by Rudolf, son of Udalricus and Bertha, and consecrated in 1125 by Udalricus, his kinsman and bishop. A wooden cloister and oratory had already been built there around 1090 (Book III, no. 20).

Two count Rudolfs must be distinguished here. Otto of Saint Blaise writes in chapter 21, under the year 1167:

> “Count Rudolf of Pfullendorf, the nephew of Count Rudolf of Brigantium, handed over all his estates to the emperor [Frederick I] in the place of an heir.”

What he means by “nephew” he explains in the immediately preceding passage, where he calls the same emperor Welfo’s nephew—namely, the son of Welfo’s sister Judith, daughter of Henry the Black, duke of Bavaria.

Therefore this Rudolf of Pfullendorf was the son of Rudolf of Brigantium’s sister. Hence Bruschus rightly calls Udalricus, count of Brigantium, who died in 1097, the grandfather of Rudolf of Pfullendorf in the *White Augia of Brigantium*: he was the father of Rudolf’s mother, whom Bruschus calls Elisabeth, sister of Rudolf of Brigantium.

This fact alone makes untenable what the same Bruschus asks in the same place concerning that Rudolf of Pfullendorf as the second founder of the monastery as early as 1102.

For Bertha, his maternal grandmother, could then scarcely have been forty years old, since her father, Rudolf the anti-emperor, had entered his second marriage with her mother Adelheid only in 1061. Consequently, in that year, 1102, Bertha, the daughter of that Rudolf, could hardly already have had a grandson who was an adolescent.

What Bruschius therefore writes in the cited passage is by no means to be understood of Rudolf the brother-in-law, or of Pfullendorf, but of Rudolf of Bregenz himself, Bertha’s son (below, Book III, § 23): 294 who, as Lazius fancifully imagines (p. 557), became count of those territories after marrying the daughter of the last count of Pfullendorf and Sigmaringen. For how could the Bregenz count have married the daughter of the last Pfullendorf count, when his sister, married to a Pfullendorf, bore another count of that same family? Nor have I anywhere found this Rudolf of Bregenz also called count of Pfullendorf; rather, through the error of more recent writers, the two were merged into a single person. This happened especially [Col. 0298B] after Rudolf of Bregenz died—in what year is uncertain—and his possessions devolved upon Rudolf of Pfullendorf, as his sister’s son. From that time the latter is sometimes called count of Bregenz and sometimes of Pfullendorf, as heir to both counties.

All this is clearly confirmed by a charter of the Emperor Frederick I from the year 1170 (in P. Herrgott, no. 240), in which he granted to Frederick, Duke of Swabia, the advocacy of Chur, received from Egino, Bishop of Chur, with the same right “by which Count Rudolf of Bregenz, and afterward Count Rudolf of Pfullendorf, are known to have held it.” The latter is also subscribed here, as likewise in another charter of the year 1152 (cited work, no. 233); but Rudolf of Chur, or of Bregenz, is still recorded in the year 1127 (ibid., no. 208).

After the latter’s death, [Col. 0298C] and the male line of the Bregenz family had died out, all their possessions passed to the Pfullendorf family through the daughter of the last Bregenz count, and likewise through the son-in-law Count Albert, to whom Ita, daughter of the last Rudolf, was married. In the same way, all those possessions eventually came to the Habsburgs, just as the Dillingens had earlier succeeded, through Adelheid, the last heiress, to the other branch of the counts of Winterthur and Kyburg—possessions that ultimately also came to the Habsburgs.

Moreover, this Rudolf of Bregenz, son of Ulrich, is the very man between whom and Ulrich II—elected bishop in 1127 after having been a monk of St. Blasien—a dispute arose over certain possessions that St. Gebhard had once donated from his Bregenz inheritance to the monastery of Petershausen, as Manlius writes in his *Chronicle*; our author also mentions the matter below, Book IV, [Col. 0298D] § 20. What became of Ulrich, Rudolf’s brother, is unknown to us; but we suspect that he died early. Otherwise this county would not have passed to another family had he survived, or at least left a male heir.

This is the final mention in our *Chronicle* of the counts of Bregenz, from whom St. Gebhard arose. Since their line appears to have ended with Rudolf, we do not pursue it further. We have carried the investigation this far only to illuminate the identity of the author of the *Chronicle of Petershausen*, often indeed by conjectures alone, though supported by their own arguments; we shall gladly subscribe to the production of firmer evidence. To make the whole structure of this genealogy clear, we now present the following genealogical table of these counts, beginning with St. Gebhard’s father and omitting what has already been noted above in § 14.

[Col. 0299] **GENEALOGICAL TABLE OF THE COUNTS OF BREGENZ, FROM THE FATHER OF ST. GEBHARD IN THE TENTH CENTURY TO THE END OF THIS LINE, FROM THE *CHRONICLE OF PETERSHAUSEN*.**

[Note: [Col. 0299B] This generation seems to require insertion, lest the lifespan of Count Ulrich be extended too far. His namesake father had already died in 978, while his son could scarcely have been Bertha’s husband, who died only in 1097—and then an untimely death—for, on the evidence given, he could not have married Bertha before 1080. This is supported by the fuller account of Bernold, who under the year 1079 records that Duke Welf invaded Chur and subdued the son of Count Otto. That son could scarcely have been anyone other than this younger Ulrich. Otto was certainly recorded as a provincial official [Col. 0300B] and count in the Rhaetian court in a charter of the Emperor Henry III from the year 1050 for the monastery of Pfäfers, situated in that county—namely, in the county of Count Odalric of Bregenz, as the charter of the Emperor Henry IV from 1095 has it, in P. Herrgott, no. 191. This last Ulrich is therefore rightly judged to have been the son of that Otto.]

[Note: [Col. 0300B] This generation has been inserted not from our *Chronicle*, but from Lazius.]

[Col. 0299A] **296 § XXV.** Before we bring this inquiry to an end, we must discuss Fuesslin’s assertion concerning Count Cuono. In our *Chronicle* (Book III, no. 3), Cuono is said to have been the father, by a concubine, of Theoderic, abbot of Petershausen in 1086, and of Luitold and Marquard. The author says that these last two, after their father’s death, passed under the authority of Count Hartmann of Dillingen because they had been born of a bondwoman.

I think this should be understood as follows: those sons, being illegitimate and, moreover, born of a bondwoman—certainly a subject of Hartmann’s—lost their right to their paternal inheritance, which passed to the count of Dillingen. Their father Cuono was perhaps that count’s miles, or vassal. This is evident from what follows: one of the two sons, Luitold, obtained from King Henry IV a privilege of freedom for himself and his descendants. He must therefore previously have lost that freedom when he passed under Hartmann’s authority.

Since these matters are clear, I do not know how Fuesslin, vol. IV, p. 191, could have interpreted the cited words of the *Chronicle* as though both sons had succeeded the Count of Dillingen in the county, and therefore counted this Cuono among the counts of Winterthur, or Kyburg. Or did they succeed Hartmann because they were born of a bondwoman, and thus lose their own inheritance rather than acquire another? But this assertion cannot be maintained on other grounds either. On this reasoning, Cuno would have had to be the father of Luitfrid, whom Fuesslin himself first calls count of Winterthur, since his son Theoderic was already abbot in 1086. In that case, the Dillingens would have inherited the Kyburg county, not the Kyburgs the county of Dillingen.

Or how can these brothers be called successors of Hartmann of Dillingen? Hartmann himself had married Adelheid, daughter of Adelbert, the last count of Winterthur, and by her fathered Hartmann the Younger and Adelbert as his immediate successors. At least the latter was still alive in 1131, heir to the entire patrimony and marriage portion. Thus no place remains for Cuono and his sons among either the counts of Winterthur, or Kyburg, [Col. 0300B] or the counts of Dillingen. They must be sought elsewhere in Swabia, though it is no concern of ours to investigate their family.

The counts and other nobles who occur here and there in the *Chronicle* we shall briefly elucidate in the notes appended in their proper places, insofar as information about them can be obtained. We shall do the same with the names of places, though these can often be extracted by guesswork rather than determined with certainty.

[Col. 0301]

# THE EVENTS OF THE MONASTERY OF PETERSHAUSEN, OR THE CHRONICLE OF PETERSHAUSEN, BEGIN.

## BOOK ONE

### 297 § 1. On the divisions of Gaul

[Col. 0301A]

It is recorded that there are three divisions of Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 0301C] Among others, Aegidius Tschudius may be consulted on this ancient triple division of Gaul in his description of Comata Gaul. The author of the *Chronicle*, however, has instituted it incorrectly. Comata Gaul was what the Romans called Transalpine Gaul, namely Celtic and Belgic Gaul. Braccata Gaul consisted of Narbonese Gaul. Togata Gaul was called Cisalpine Gaul, or the territory on both sides of the Po, and thus comprised almost all of Lombardy, whose inhabitants wore the Romans’ long togas.]

One is Comata Gaul, which is also called Italy, inhabited by the Lombards and Romans. It is so called because in ancient times the Italians carefully cultivated their hair more than other nations; or it is called *Comata*, that is, “adorned,” because it is beautified by the Roman city, which held the summit of the empire of the entire world.

Another is Braccata Gaul, inhabited by the Germans. It is so called because the Germans use breeches, or trousers, more than other peoples.

The third is Togata Gaul, which received its name because the inhabitants of this province wear togas—that is, garments of different colors reaching to the ankles—so extensively that by this custom they have infected the neighboring nations as well. [Col. 0301B] These customs, as we have said, once belonged specifically to the individual provinces, but now they are common to all of them.

### § II. The origin of the counts of Bregenz

In this Gaul, which we have said is called Togata, there was a certain man distinguished by the nobility of his lineage. The king of the Franks, who was also emperor of the Romans, gave him his sister in marriage. By her he fathered two sons, both of whom were [Note: [Col. 0301C] The edition reads: “became.”] as illustrious in birth as they were outstanding in courage.

When they had grown up and had become wealthy, exceptionally strong, and highly skilled in arms, it happened that the poison of enmity entered between them and the king of that province and so infected their hearts that it could not be restrained until their hands deprived the king of life by the sword. [Col. 0301C–0302A]

### § III

After the king had been killed, the two men, fearing a conspiracy by their fellow provincials, went to their uncle, the august emperor. They were received by him with pleasure and were granted many places of residence in Alemannia, both numerous and excellent.

He gave them Potamum [Note: [Col. 0301C] This royal estate may perhaps have come to the Bregenz family only later. It was already within their district, although it still remained subject to the royal fisc.], Brigantium [Note: [Col. 0301C] A town or castle on the shore of Lake Constance; according to a charter of 802, it lay in the district of Argengewe. Walafrid already says that it had collapsed through age in the seventh century, though it was later restored.], Überlingen [Note: [Col. 0302C] Formerly a royal estate in the district of Linzgau.], and Buchhorn [Note: [Col. 0302C] In the same district; both are now imperial cities], Ahausen [Note: [Col. 0302C] Ahausen, in the same area], and Thüringen [Note: [Col. 0302C] Thüringen, in the same region, from which the rural chapter takes its name], as well as the district of Heistirgau [Note: [Col. 0302C] Haidgau, between the towns of Waldsee and Wurzach], and also Winterthur [Note: [Col. 0302C] Winterthur, a castle in Thurgau], with all their appurtenances. In Rhaetia of Chur they received Mesouch [Note: [Col. 0302C] Misax or Mesax, Latin *Mesaucum*, whence the Mesaucine valley, Italian Misocco], along with many other places whose memory has been erased by the passage of time.

Endowed with such gifts by the emperor, they went to these places and brought them under their own authority. They distributed gifts from them to the most noble men who had come with them. To one they gave Thüringen, to another Überlingen, and to another Buchhorn. These men afterward intermarried with the two brothers and became related to them by marriage.

### § IV

After the fury of the Gauls, which had blazed against these two brothers, had been calmed, their relatives and friends sent messengers and asked them to return to their homeland. One of them, overcome by earnest entreaties, returned home; but the other, named Odalric, remained in the land of the Alemanni. He retained everything that had been given by the emperor, and so did his descendants down to the present day.

### V. Uzo, father of St. Gebhard

[Col. 0303A]

From this man’s seed was born Uzo, a pious and venerable count, who lived near Bregenz, in a place that still displays the ruins of the ancient settlement.

[Note: [Col. 0303D] According to Sprecher, *Pallas Rhaetica*, in 948 Hermann, Duke of Alemannia, captured the castle of Bregenz at the command of the Emperor Otto and perhaps also destroyed it; hence these ruins.]

He took as his wife a woman named Dietpurga, very devout according to God and, in worldly terms, of the noblest birth.

Uzo was so pious and meritorious that even the birds sensed his holiness. They flew fearlessly to his table, took food from his hand, and when some had eaten their fill and departed, others came to be fed in turn.

On another occasion, at dawn, a hind came from the forest to the door of his bedchamber and struck it with her hoof. When the doorkeeper opened the door, saw the animal, and reported that she was standing there and had knocked, Uzo, foreseeing through piety that some need had brought the creature there, said to his servant: “Come, follow her and see whether she perhaps wants something.”

The servant immediately followed the hind as she went ahead. She led him into the forest and showed him her fawn, whose foot was caught in a fetter. Standing there with her head lowered, she began, by the movement of her ears, to plead for help. As soon as he freed the fawn’s foot from the fetter, the joyful hind departed into the forest with her young, while the servant returned to his master and reported what had happened.

In such ways, and in many similar ones, God seemed often to play with this venerable man, because “the cheerful man who shows mercy in the Lord will not be shaken forever.”

At another time, when the same venerable Count Uotzo was staying in the emperor’s palace, it happened one day that a lion escaped from its cage and, as was its nature, tore apart whatever it could attack. Since no one dared approach it and everyone fled before it, certain people suggested to the emperor that he should tell the aforementioned man of God, Count Uotzo, to mitigate the lion for a while through the power of God. They said that experience had taught them that he possessed such power in the Lord that, if he wished, he could easily calm the lion’s ferocity.

When the emperor heard this, he immediately summoned Uotzo and humbly asked him to intervene in the present emergency. At first, out of humility, Uotzo excused himself, saying that he could not attempt so great a deed. Finally, however, when all those present, together with the emperor, urged him, he agreed and went to meet the raging lion.

As soon as the lion saw him, it rushed forward with all its ferocity, as though it would tear him completely apart. But when Uotzo received it with outstretched hands, the lion suddenly forgot its fierceness, threw itself down at the man of God’s feet, and began to lick them. Uotzo stroked it with his hand and ordered its keepers to take hold of it without fear and lock it up.

When the emperor saw this, he was astonished and reverently offered him a gift, saying: “Since I see that you deal with God, I willingly release you from every royal service from now on.”

[Note: [Col. 0303D] The emperor appears to have been Henry the Fowler, or his son Otto, who was related to him by blood, as is clear from the preceding inquiry in § 14.]

### § VI. The descendants of Uzo

He fathered four sons: the first named Ulrich, the second Marquard, the third Luitfrid, and the fourth, the glory of the entire family, Gebhard.

They called Ulrich himself Uzo because of his gracefulness. His son was Ulrich, who fought in the battle in which the Emperor Otto engaged the Hungarians near Augsburg in Vindelicia. His father nobly enriched the monastery of Lindau from his own estates, where he also lies buried in honor; his descendants still flourish at Bregenz. Marquard, his son, became a count and enjoyed considerable influence through his friendship with the Emperor Otto.

### § VII. Luitfrid, Gebhard’s brother

[Col. 0304B]

When these four brothers, their parents already dead, wished to divide the inheritance among themselves, one of them, the Luitfrid mentioned above, was sluggish and unwarlike and held in less esteem than the others. Fearing that his brothers might despise him in the division because of his cowardice, he began to consider by what strategy he could deceive them so that they would not deny him his share of the inheritance.

After turning many matters over in his mind and finally finding a plan useful to himself and his descendants, he addressed one of his brothers secretly, without the others’ knowledge:

“Brother, you know that I am unequal to you, my brothers, and plainly unfit for worldly affairs. But if you follow my advice, you will provide no small advantage for yourself and your descendants. I love you more than my other brothers and wish to live with you. Therefore, when we come to divide our inheritance, make every effort to ensure that Winterthur [Note: [Col. 0304D] From this we learn that Winterthur, a castle and town in Thurgau in the duchy of Alemannia, belonged to the counts of Bregenz. From these counts Luitfrid established a county of his own, which afterward passed to the Dillingens. See Lew, *Lexicon*, s.v.] with all its appurtenances falls to my share. You may be certain that, if these possessions come into my ownership, I shall hand them over to you, and thereafter remain with you and serve you in whatever way you command. Therefore look to your own advantage and strive to comply with my wishes.”

He spoke secretly in the same way to the second brother, and then to the third. Each believed that he was speaking out of affection for him, and by this hope he made them all eager to carry out his will.

When the division took place and each received his lot, they hastened individually to fulfill Luitfrid’s request because of the promise just described. None of them knew that he had made the same promise to each. Since they all had the same intention, what they unanimously desired was easily accomplished, and they confirmed Winterthur with all its appurtenances to Luitfrid.

He, accordingly, rejoicing as was only proper, went to the excellent estates entrusted to him and brought them all under his authority. By such cunning he deceived his brothers, applied himself to agriculture, and accumulated much livestock. After taking a wife, he fathered by her a son named Adelbert. This son crossed into Apulia with Pope Blessed Leo and died there fighting for the cause of St. Peter against the Normans, who had invaded Apulia.

Adelbert’s daughter was Adelheid, whom Count Hartmann the Elder of Dillingen took in marriage. She bore him Hartmann the Younger and Adelbert, who was still living and became heir to the entire patrimony and marriage portion; and Ulrich, who became bishop of Constance, concerning whom we may perhaps say something later. She also bore three daughters, who now live in the religious habit. One of them gave birth to Count Ulrich of Gamertingen and Adelbert of Achalm, both of whom are still alive.

### 302 § VIII. How Gebhard acquired the inheritance

Gebhard, the youngest of the brothers mentioned above but their ornament, was cut from the womb of his deceased mother Dietpurga and wrapped in certain coverings until the time of his birth, God reserving his life for the salvation of many. Writings testify, however, concerning those cut from the womb in this manner that, if life accompanies them, they will be fortunate in the world.

He was brought up, entrusted to learning, and educated at Constance, where he became a canon. Since we have treated his life in another work as fully as we could, we shall touch on it here only briefly.

When his brothers, as we related above, were distributing the lots of the inheritance among themselves, they said that he was a cleric and had no need of their inheritance, since he was sufficiently wealthy from the resources of the Church.

When he heard this, he demanded his portion with deep indignation. Since he was highly eloquent and effective in speech, he finally threatened them that, if they were unwilling to give him his hereditary right voluntarily, he would take up arms and defend himself with the sword.

When they heard this, they unwillingly did what they had refused to do willingly and handed over his full share to him.

### § IX. What he gave to Constance

Because the law of God was in his heart, his steps were not led astray by earthly riches. He gave a portion of his estates to the church of St. Mary of Constance during the episcopate of Bishop Kuonrad, of blessed memory.

[Note: [Col. 0305D] At that time the canons of the cathedral church of Constance lived a common life, which is why they were called brothers and their residence a monastery. (Gerbert, *Historia Silvae Nigrae*, vol. I, p. 154.)]

For these estates he had the following privilege drawn up:

[Col. 0306A] **Privilege concerning Oberndorf**

“Let all present and future persons know that I, Gebehart, an unworthy brother of the holy Church of Constance, considering the remedy of my soul and following the examples of the Gospel and the apostles, with the consent of my brothers [Note: [Col. 0305D] Thus he did have the brothers named above, contrary to the view of Lazius and others; perhaps his advocate Ulrich himself was among them.] and by the hand of my advocate Ulrich, transfer to the monastery of the aforesaid holy Church of Constance, for the brothers who continually serve God there, the property belonging to me by right and inherited from my parents in the places Oberndorf [Note: [Col. 0306D] Oberdorf, in the rural chapter of Lindau.], Hackelinbach [Note: [Col. 0306D] This seems to be Heggelbach in the rural chapter of Isny; § 34 has *Hagilimbach*.], Billafingen [Note: [Col. 0306D] Billafingen, in the rural chapter of Linzgau.], and Luitefestorf [Note: [Col. 0306D] Liggerstorf, in the rural chapter of Stockach. These places lie in the districts of Linzgau, Hegau, and Allgäu, where the paternal possessions were located. See below, § 34.]—with all appurtenances belonging to those places, buildings, dependents, pastures, forests, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, and everything belonging to those places—which I am recognized as possessing.

“I transfer it to the monastery of the holy Church of Constance mentioned above, for the brothers there who continually serve God, under the spiritual governance of the most religious and learned man, Bishop Chuonrad. [Note: [Col. 0306D] St. Conrad died in 974; therefore this charter had already been issued before then.]

“The condition is that I, receiving the same property back to myself, or another member of that brotherhood whomsoever I may choose, shall pay the rent from it. That is, in each year henceforth, on the feast of our holy and venerable father, Pope Gregory, the aforesaid brothers shall be served according to the canonical rule. [Note: [Col. 0306D] See below, § 34.] Done at Constance, on the fourth day before the Ides of March, in the presence and with the approval of my aforesaid advocate Ulrich, and also of the other witnesses whose names are subscribed: Eberhard, Luitfred, Hildibold, Chuzzo, Cozpret, Adelpret, Mereboto, Liutpret, Sigibert, Hadepert, Dietger, Wern, Adelgoz.”

### § X. How he sought a place on which to build the monastery

[Col. 0306C]

When it pleased Him who had separated him from his mother’s womb in a wondrous manner and called him by His grace to be a burning and shining lamp in the house of the Lord, Gebhard did not immediately give way to flesh and blood by indulging in idleness or pleasure. Rather, reflecting that he had been called to labor in the Lord’s vineyard, cultivate it, and improve it, he began, following the counsel of the Holy Spirit, to seek by what means he might shake himself free, like a doe, from the snare of this world, so that, like a Hebrew servant in the seventh year—that is, after the labors of this world had been completed—he might keep Sabbaths free throughout the ages.

Finally, with complete dedication, he sought how he might offer Christ, in the most acceptable manner, whatever he had or could acquire. At last he found the following counsel: nothing would benefit his salvation more than building a monastery. He therefore began to search for a place suited to this plan, where he could fulfill his desire.

Once, for this reason, he spent the night in a certain place. The frogs of a marsh disturbed him throughout the night with their croaking. When day came, he inspected the site to see whether it was suitable for his wish and is said to have asked what name it ought to bear if a cell were built there.

One of his attendants immediately replied that it should be called “the Frogs’ Cell,” because their racket had disturbed them during the night.

But Gebhard said: “By no means shall anything be built in this place if it is to be rejected under such an ugly name.”

### § XI. How he acquired the place itself

Since it is written of God, “He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him and will hear their prayer” (Psalm 144), he soon showed his servant, as we believe, the place in which He was pleased that his desire should be fulfilled.

The opposite bank of the Rhine from the city of Constance pleased Gebhard’s intention, and he judged it suitable for building a cell: not especially useful, but attractive. This same place belonged to the monastery of Reichenau, both above and below it, and at that time was uninhabitable because it was wet like a marsh.

The man of God gave his own property at Zurzach in exchange for this little place.

[Note: [Col. 0307C] Zurzach is now a town on the Rhine, with a distinguished collegiate church. It was formerly a Benedictine abbey, donated by Charles the Fat to the monastery of Reichenau in 881. Gerbert, *Historia Silvae Nigrae*, vol. III, p. 14, presents a charter of exchange dated 983 with Alawic, abbot of Reichenau, in which this year is called the first year of the monastery of Petershausen. It should nevertheless be noted that at that time no abbot of that name existed at Reichenau. [Col. 0307D] Alawic I had already died in 958 or shortly thereafter, while the second Alawic was not made abbot until 997. Perhaps Gebhard, still a canon, made this exchange with the earlier Alawic and first had it confirmed by Otto II in 983, when he had already begun to build the monastery as bishop.]

The monastery of Reichenau did not receive from the man of God everything it now possesses at Zurzach, but only the portion that belonged to him and was of equal value for the exchange of that place.

After this exchange had been legally confirmed, the man of God divided the little estate into three portions. He assigned one to himself and his successors, the bishops of Constance; another to the canons of the same church; and the third to the construction of a cell.

### 305 § XII. On the rights of the inhabitants of that place

Since the people whom he established there [Note: [Col. 0307D] All this is found in the charter of exchange cited immediately above.] possessed nothing except the dwellings in which they lived together, and could have neither fields, wood, nor pastures, he granted them and their descendants the following right for their support: the belongings of the dead were not to be taken away, but their descendants were to possess in full whatever had been left behind. They were to sail only for the common needs of their lords and, where they possessed the skill, to fish for them.

He established the same right for the monastery’s servants, except that they, since they possessed a little land and meadows, were required to serve their lords daily and receive their grain allowance from them.

### § XIII. The chapel of St. Michael. Abbot Pezilinus

He first built a small chapel there and dedicated it in honor of St. Michael on the fourth day before the Kalends of August. In it he also restored a dead person to life through prayer.

At this beginning he had a certain Pezilinus as abbot.

[Note: [Col. 0307D] Bruschius and Bucelinus designate Pezelinus as the second abbot of Petershausen, although he never held that office; alternatively, he must be regarded as the first. It is certainly established that he was abbot of another monastery from the following charter of exchange, which Gebhard made with Abbot Pezilinus. In exchange, Gebhard granted him another estate in Hegau and in Para, so that he might receive from him possessions that the monastery he governed held elsewhere. Since below, in § 39, the monastery of Stein is said to possess a quarter of the village of Epfendorf, this appears to be the very village it acquired through this exchange. Pezilinus should therefore be called Abbot of Stein, a monastery situated near Petershausen, where he could supply “the duties of the holy bishop, who was often occupied with episcopal functions,” while “the principal administration nevertheless remained with the holy bishop Gebhard,” as stated in *Gallia Christiana* (vol. V, p. 1033), where this Pezelinus must also be supplied at p. 933.]

Under him Gebhard exchanged with the Church of Constance an estate at Togingen and a small holding at Epfendorf. Concerning this exchange he had the following privilege written:

### § XIV. Privilege concerning Togingen

[Note: [Col. 0308C] Herrgott published this charter in *Genealogia Habsburgica*, vol. II, p. 88, but incorrectly assigned it to the year 985.]

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Let it be known to all, present and future, how I, Gebhard, an unworthy bishop of the Church of Constance, with the hand of my advocate Chuzo [Note: [Col. 0308D] Chuzo, or Uzo, seems to be the same advocate Ulrich already mentioned above in § 9 in Gebhard’s charter, perhaps a count of Bregenz and St. Gebhard’s brother. Herrgott incorrectly counts Chuzo among the counts of Winterthur, since none of the sons of Luitfrid, the first count of Winterthur, bears the name Chuzo or Ulrich.], and with Abbot Pezilinus, considering the common advantage of the monastery of St. Gregory, have made the following exchange:

“I have transferred to him and his monks, to possess with full authority, an estate that the Church over which I appear to preside is said to hold in the village of Togingen [Note: [Col. 0308D] Perhaps Tengen in Hegau.] in the district of Hegau, and in the village of Epfendorf [Note: [Col. 0308D] See below, § 40.] in the district of Para. The arrangement is that they, by the hand of their advocate Eberhard, should in turn transfer to me and my successors, to be held firmly, whatever lawful property the monastery he governed possessed in Lutwangen [Note: [Col. 0308D] Langenwangen, in the parish of Fischen, in the rural chapter of Stiefenhofen, in Allgäu.] in the district of Allgäu, and in Rapirgahusa [Note: [Col. 0308D] I believe the district of Erreggau to be the same as that elsewhere called Erichgewe, Eritgewe, or Herekewe, extending formerly around Buchau. I therefore take Rapirgahusum to be Riedhausen, a parish not far from there, on the Ostrach. [Col. 0309D]].

“This exchange was made and confirmed at Constance in the presence of both advocates—my own and the abbot’s—who actively approved it, in the presence of the following witnesses, whose names are recorded in the subscription: Meginzo [Note: [Col. 0309D] The witnesses subscribed here belong to the cathedral church of Constance.], archpriest; Sigiboto, dean; Irinc, archdeacon; Gerhart, archdeacon; Albrich; Gunderic; and many others (so the text reads). Publicly enacted in the holy synod of the Church of Constance, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 995, on Wednesday, indiction VII.”

[Note: [Col. 0309D] In the year 995, the indiction was VIII.]

### § XV

Ruodpert the monk was the first to come to this monastery for conversion. Gebhard also decided that his monks should receive their rule of life and governance from the cell of St. Meginrad, which is called “of the Solitaries.”

[Note: [Col. 0309D] From this we learn where St. Gebhard obtained the first settlers of his monastery: namely, from the monastery of Einsiedeln. Pericherus, the first abbot of Petershausen, also appears to have been a member of that community, whose monks at that time were exceptionally devout.]

### 307 § XVI. When he founded the church

[Col. 0309B]

In the year 983 of the Lord’s Incarnation he laid the foundations of the basilica. He made drainage ditches throughout the site to dry the moisture and offered four gold pieces, which he placed beneath the four corners of the church.

On the western side he built a crypt, in which he dug a well and placed an altar in honor of St. Martin. Gebhard III later demolished it because of the dampness. Above the crypt he built the sanctuary, where he established the principal altar in honor of Pope St. Gregory, over which he constructed a ciborium of exceptional beauty.

### § XVII

After making four columns of holm-oak and having vine figures carved upon them, he gathered the citizens of Constance together and addressed them as follows:

“I have four daughters whom I ought to give in marriage, but I cannot adorn them without your assistance. For this reason I have summoned you and ask you to provide me, according to your ability and willingness, with some help toward obtaining their adornments.”

When they all replied that they would gladly do whatever he commanded, he ordered the columns to be brought out and said that he wished to clothe them in silver. He then began to ask them to assist him in this. They all did so with the greatest eagerness.

With their assistance he covered the columns with the finest silver and set them upon beautifully carved stone bases. Above the columns he placed four arches, covering them on one side with gilded silver and on the other with gilded copper.

Above the arches and columns he placed a panel large enough to cover the entire ciborium. In its center was a round window, itself covered on the inside all around with gilded copper. Beneath it was a projecting border, which he covered with silver; one of the abbots later removed this and attached lead in its place.

The entire underside of the panel was elegantly covered with gilded copper. It bore raised images of the four Evangelists and many other figures. Across it, silver plates were attached in four sections, and on each side one verse was inscribed in golden letters, as follows:

> This modest work, enriched by diverse arts,  
>
> bears you, Gregory, the suppliant devotion  
>
> of an unworthy bishop whom you, with the faithful people, ...

May you, gracious Father, join [me] to the heavenly companies by prayers.

## § XVIII

Above the opening of the panel was placed an angular, gilded structure set upon turned wooden columns; and above this was an image of a white lamb looking toward the people. The altar itself was hollow, having on its eastern side a panel decorated with the finest gold and precious stones [Col. 0310B]; on the western side there was another panel covered with silver, bearing in its center, in raised work, an image of Saint Mary made of the finest gold and weighing a talent of gold. Abbot Berthold removed this image during a famine, broke it up, and sold it for grain.

Various reliquaries of the saints hung above the altar. One ascended to that altar from the choir by several steps, which Abbot Theoderic removed when he enlarged the choir. At the top of those steps, in the middle, there was a lowered space as wide as the altar, surrounded by square stones and extending to the altar, where those praying might kneel; and beside the altar a marble panel of green color was set into the pavement, which those kneeling would kiss.

The choir itself [Col. 0310C] was very small, since its space had been reduced by the ascent of the steps. The walls of the basilica, too, were most beautifully painted on every side: on the left they displayed scenes from the Old Testament, and on the right scenes from the New Testament. Wherever an image of the Lord appeared, it had a golden circle around its head.

For the bishop of Venice [Note: [Col. 0310D] The Bollandists think that this bishop was Ursus of Venice, who, according to Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, p. 1200, governed from 981 to 992. But from Dandolo it is certain that at that time Marinus occupied the Venetian see, p. 1212.] had freely given him, out of charity, a full measure of the Greek pigment called *Lazur*. This exceptionally fine pigment was applied in great abundance to the walls everywhere, as we ourselves saw. Abbot Kuonrad had entirely removed this painting, because age had already taken away its beauty. He made doors of incomparable beauty, and in front of the church a very small portico, which Abbot Theoderic enlarged and improved.

## 309 § XIX. Concerning the spring.

[Col. 0310D]

While the church was being painted with great care in various colors, it happened that one day the blessed man withdrew from that place and delayed returning for some time. Meanwhile, the treacherous painters fraudulently taking away the finest colors went into a neighboring grove, where they secretly dug into the earth and hid them.

When the holy bishop had returned, the painters began insistently demanding colors, saying that the work was being negligently delayed because of the scarcity of colors. Hearing this, the blessed man remained silent for a little while, and then said:

“Even if we are presently lacking them, it is necessary that they be obtained. Come, then, follow me; perhaps the Lord in his kindness will give us what you seek, so that you may be able to bring the work to completion.”

He led them without a guide to the place where they themselves had hidden the colors. There he planted his staff in the earth and said:

“Dig here in the name of God, and see whether you find anything.”

Terrified by their guilty consciences, they dug into the earth and uncovered the colors they had hidden, bringing them forth, though unwillingly. The man of God said to them with a joyful countenance:

“Now go on, beloved sons, and work all the more diligently with this very thing that the Lord has revealed.”

Terrified, they departed, marveling among themselves at what had happened. From that very place a spring of crystal-clear water immediately burst forth, and it has not ceased flowing to the present day.

The next day, while the man of God was seated at table and the aforementioned painters were laboring anxiously at the work, they suddenly collapsed and lay there as though lifeless. When this was reported with a great uproar to Blessed Gebehard, who was still sitting at dinner, he said calmly:

“Let them be; they had to suffer for a while what they had done wrong against holy things.”

After saying this, he remained undisturbed until he cheerfully left the table. Then he climbed onto the scaffolding where they lay like dead men and, touching them with the staff he held in his hand, said:

“I am not, I say, going to pay you wages for lying here in a stupor of sleep. So get up and work.”

They immediately lifted their heads and rose up healthy, and, as though they had suffered nothing, began to work.

## 310 § XX. At what time he dedicated the church.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 992, indiction V, in the tenth year after he had begun to build it, Blessed Gebehard, bishop, himself dedicated the church he had built, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, in honor of Blessed Pope Gregory, with great splendor.

## § XXI. How he obtained the privilege.

Finally, when he came to Rome, he was honored by Pope John with such extraordinary reverence that the pope not only granted him the privilege he had requested [Col. 0312A], but also permitted him to lay his hand upon the body of Blessed Pope Gregory. This was allowed on the condition that whatever he could lift with one touch from the sound bones, he might unquestionably carry away with him.

Thus, by the grace of God, he took away Gregory’s head [Note: [Col. 0311D] Manlius gives a fairly remarkable account of the translation of this head in his *Life of Saint Gebhard*, chapters 15 and 16, although he does not specify whether it was the head of Gregory the Great or of another Pope Gregory. Certainly, in the *Chronicle of Saint Peter of Viviers* (d’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 467, new edition), it is recorded that around the year 876 Pope John VIII gave Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens, the head of Blessed Gregory, the universal pope and son of Gordianus, enclosed in lead; Ansegisus carried it with him to Gaul. Indeed, even earlier, in 826, the body of Saint Gregory is said to have been translated to the monastery of Saint Medard at Soissons. See the Bollandists, vol. II, March, pp. 126 ff. Yet according to Anastasius, Gregory IV later first raised that same body at Rome, where it is said still to be located today (p. 125). Accordingly, as commonly happens in translations of relics of this kind, either several persons of the same name were confused into one, or the whole was understood in place of a part. This seems to be indicated by what is said in § 22: that this head was found in a reliquary broken into fragments [Col. 0312D]. In the Prague manuscript martyrology (p. 130), under 12 March, we read: “The head of this saint [Gregory], obtained by the most serene prince Charles IV, Roman emperor, in the monastery of Saint Gebhard in the city of Constance, and adorned with gold and silver, he gave to the church of Prague.” Indeed, in the catalogue of the relics of that church (Bollandists, vol. I, January, p. 1084), the head of Saint Gregory the Great is listed; this, too, must be understood as referring only to some part of it. This does not, however, prevent some portion of the same head from still being preserved at Petershausen, since it is scarcely credible that its monks deprived themselves entirely of so great a treasure, even if they granted some part of it to Emperor Charles IV.] together with other magnificent relics of his body. Having obtained everything he desired according to his wishes, he returned joyfully.

## § XXII

311 We found this beloved head in a reliquary that had once been very firmly joined together, but which had now, through age and carelessness, completely come apart. In ancient times, as we heard, it had been kept in the altar of Saint Peter on the southern side; it is known that Gregory’s tomb was also located in that part of Rome. [Col. 0312B] But it had since been removed from there and placed above the altar of Saint Mary. Therefore, the aforementioned altar of Saint Peter had remained empty and violated; for this reason it was later renewed and dedicated by Kuonrad, bishop of the Church of Chur [Note: [Col. 0312D] He governed from 1122 to 1150.].

Finally, when we opened the reliquary, we found within it a red-painted container filled with the ashes of saints. Among them we discovered the most beloved treasure, namely the head of the most holy Pope Gregory, but broken into fragments. We grieved that we have never yet been able to learn how this had happened.

We also found many other relics in the same reliquary, which we hope belong to the same holy Father Gregory, since we found with them only one brief written statement, and since their whiteness resembled that of the other bones. We collected the intact bones [Col. 0312C] and transferred them elsewhere; but we returned the ashes to the place where we had first found them. This reliquary was given to Mimminhusin [Note: [Col. 0312D] A parish in the district of Linzgau.] when a chapel was being built there.

## § XXIII

This is the privilege that Blessed Gebehard received from Pope John of Rome concerning the place itself [Note: [Col. 0312D] It also appears in Lunig, *Archivum Spicilegii Ecclesiastici*, part II, p. 154, and part III, p. 399, though not without errors.]. The monastery’s privilege was originally written in *biblis* [reading uncertain] and has also been preserved in the monastery to the present day.

“JOHN, bishop, servant of the servants of God. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

“We wish it to be known to all the faithful of Christ [Col. 0313A] how Gebehard II, beloved bishop of the holy Church of Constance, our most beloved brother, came to Rome for the sake of prayer, to the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul, the princes of the apostles, and appeared before us. He reported to us that, compelled by God’s will, he had built a church of cenobites on the bank of the river called the Rhine, in honor of Blessed Gregory, confessor of Christ. In that place he would establish with the greatest splendor the rule of Saint Benedict, abbot, and of the monk-brothers. With the greatest devotion he offered for their support and maintenance his own estates, which had come to him from his parents, as well as a portion of the possessions of his holy Church—namely, for those monks who in that holy monastery diligently and without ceasing offer the praises of Christ day and night.

“For these reasons he implored the clemency of our humility that the aforesaid place should remain forever under the protection and defense of Saint Peter, and of us and our successors in the pontificate. Yet no king, duke, margrave, or bishop who at any time governs that bishopric, nor any other person, should dare to alienate from it any of the possessions granted there by the aforementioned Gebehard, or to remove them in any manner from that holy monastery. We grant that these provisions, established and confirmed, shall remain firm into future times.

“Moreover, at the request of our aforementioned brother, we prohibit by apostolic command, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that anyone be placed over that monastery [Col. 0313C] except one whom the brothers serving Christ diligently there have elected by common consent, and whom the bishop shall undertake to confirm with the title of blessing. We have likewise decreed that the same rule shall apply to the election of the advocate.

“But if—God forbid—it should ever happen that the bishop of that holy Church is a heretic or schismatic, the brothers of the aforesaid monastery shall have authority, by that of the apostolic see, to seek ecclesiastical orders wherever they know a Catholic bishop to be found; nor shall that wicked man presume to inflict any injury upon them on this account.

“For if anyone of whatever rank or power—which we do not believe—should attempt in any way to violate [this privilege], or wish to remove from the right and jurisdiction of that monastery the things granted to it by our aforementioned brother [Col. 0313D], unless he repents, let him remain excommunicated from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and anathematized by all the holy Fathers and by us. At the hour of death, let him not receive communion; and even after his death, let his name in no way be recited during the solemn celebration of Masses [Col. 0314A].

“But whoever, moved by pious regard, proves to be the guardian and administrator of this our command, may he deserve to obtain from the Lord God himself, our Savior Jesus Christ, the grace of blessing and eternal life, forever and ever. Amen.

“Written by the hand of John, notary, regional officer, and keeper of the records of the sacred Lateran palace, in the month of April and in the second indiction. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Gregory, bishop of the holy Church of Porto and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the fourth year of the pontificate of our lord John, most holy pope.”

[Note: [Col. 0313D] The fourth year of the pontificate of John XVI, together with indiction II and the month of April, indicates the year 989, as do the fifteen years mentioned below in § 24 after the death of Saint Ulrich, whom the same pope later enrolled among the saints in 993.]

## § XXIV. How he prayed at the tomb of Saint Ulrich.

Thus Blessed Bishop Gebehard, having received the privilege and the relics of the saints at the thresholds of the apostles, as related above, crossed the Alps and reached Alemannia. He came to Augsburg and approached the tomb of the most blessed Ulrich, bishop of that city, who had passed from the world to the Lord nearly fifteen years earlier, in order to pray there.

While he was praying there with deep attention, he heard a voice sounding as if from the tomb and saying to him:

“What do you seek, or what do you ask, Gebehard?”

As though he were hearing a familiar voice, he replied without fear:

“Because I have recently built a place to be dedicated to the Lord, I ask that this place be made illustrious by your patronage, and that, out of your piety, some relics of your most sacred body be granted to be carried there.”

Again, as if from the tomb, he received this answer:

“This can in no way be done, for I wish my little body to await the final day intact in this place. And because you have presumed to assail and disturb me with your prayers, as soon as you set foot on the land of your monastery, you will suffer punishment for it.”

Having received this oracle, he departed and returned home. When he had reached the farthest edge of the field belonging to the monastery, behold, a thorny bramble hanging over the road caught the passing bishop’s shoe and wounded his leg. When he felt the pain of the wound, he said in a clear voice:

“Behold what Saint Ulrich foretold in words, he has fulfilled in deed.”

This wound then grew worse day by day and could never afterward be healed by any medicine until the end of his life.

## § XXV. Concerning the arm of Saint Philip the Apostle.

Emperor Otto also gave him a reliquary covered with silver, in which was kept the arm of Saint Philip the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0313D] The associates of the Bollandists discuss the arm of Saint Philip transferred from Jerusalem to Florence in 1204 in vol. I, May, pp. 11–15. They also say that his body was brought to Rome, from which Emperor Charles IV received another arm. Relics of the same apostle are also said to have been in Constantinople; from there Theophanu, daughter of Romanus II, emperor of the East, could easily have brought them—and perhaps also part of the arm—with her to her husband, Emperor Otto II. Their son, Emperor Otto III, later gave it to Saint Gebehard; this account deserves greater credence because of its greater antiquity. Perhaps in one of the translations mentioned, the Apostle Philip was confused with Philip, one of the seven deacons, whose feast is celebrated on 6 June.] together with many other magnificent relics of the saints.

That arm was found in the time of Abbot Theoderic, but broken into pieces. Later, in the time of Abbot Berthold, it was adorned with gold, silver, and gems by Kuonrad, then his chaplain but later abbot, and by the other brothers. In its base one joint of the fingers of Pope Saint Gregory was placed, together with many other relics.

For the mother of the aforementioned prince Otto had been brought from Greece, and she had brought that arm with her.

## 314 § XXVI. The privilege concerning Worndorf.

At the request of Count Marquard, namely, the brother of Blessed Gebehard [Note: [Col. 0315D] Concerning this Count Marquard of Bregenz, see the discussion above in *Disquisitio*, § 18, p. 286. Lunig likewise presents this charter of donation, *Spicilegium Ecclesiasticum*, part III, p. 400.], the same emperor granted a small estate to the monastery and caused the following privilege to be written concerning it:

[Col. 0315B]

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. OTTO, by the gracious favor of God, king.

“Let the pious devotion of all our faithful, present and future, know how, at the petition and intercession of Count Marquard, and out of love for our faithful servant Gebehard, venerable bishop of the Church of Constance, who has often rendered devoted service to us, we have given to the Church of Saint Gregory, honorably built in the place called Petershausen, where the venerable and first abbot Bericherus now presides [Note: [Col. 0315D] Bericherus, Perriggerus, or Beringerus, appointed first abbot in 993 (below, § 44), was undoubtedly a monk of Einsiedeln, since Saint Gebehard had decided that from there his monks should receive “their way of life and governance” (§ 15). Since Beringerus is called the first abbot of Petershausen, Pezelinus must necessarily not be included in this list. See above, § 13.], whatever property we possessed in the villages called Worndorf and Crumacha [Note: [Col. 0315D] Worndorf and Krumbach are now in the district of the chapter of Mößkirch.], situated in the district called Goldinneshundere [Note: [Col. 0315D] In the Chronicle of Gottwic, this district is said to have been part of the district of Hegau, in the Mößkirch area.] and in the county of the aforementioned Count Marquard [Col. 0315C].

“We transfer this same property to the aforesaid church, with all the equipment properly belonging to it: courtyards, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, fields, meadows, open country, pastures, woods, hunting rights, waters and watercourses, fisheries, mills, roads and trackless ways, outgoings and income, things acquired and to be acquired, and all other appurtenances that can still be named. This is on the condition that henceforth the same property shall remain perpetually under the right of that church, without contradiction from any person.

“And so that this gift of our majesty may remain inviolate through the succession of future times, we ordered this charter to be written and marked with the impression of our seal, and, as appears below, confirmed it with our own hand. I, Hiltiboldus, bishop and chancellor, have verified it in the place of Archbishop Willigis. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of June, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 993, indiction VI, and in the tenth year of the reign of the third Otto. Done at Birgila.”

## § XXVII. How Blessed Gebehard gave his soldiers to the churches.

Whatever Gebehard possessed or was able to acquire, he faithfully offered to God for his monastery, except for certain men among his ministerials who were richer and more powerful. He did not wish to transfer them there, prudently judging that they might perhaps be more a burden than a support in a poor place.

## § XXVIII. Concerning Nuiheim.

The blessed man exchanged with the people of Markdorf a sufficiently honorable possession at Nuiheim [Note: [Col. 0316D] This seems to be the village now called Neuhaus, not far from Markdorf in Linzgau. Since wood had to be transported from there to the monastery (§ 29), it could not have been very far away; it was acquired from the people of Markdorf.].

## § XXIX. Concerning Tegirwilare and Gottliubon.

[Col. 0316B]

A certain noble matron also gave him her estate at Tegirwilare [Note: [Col. 0316D] Tägerwilen below Constance in Thurgau, not far from Gottlieben, near which Ottenberg is also located.] and Gottiliubon. From that time it was enlarged on various occasions. For two vineyards there were exchanged two manors, which Lord Adilgoz of Marstettin [Note: [Col. 0316D] Marstetten was a noble dynasty near Memmingen, now represented by the counts of Königseck; another Marstetten is in Thurgau.] had given to the monastery at a place called Ottinberch.

This estate was acquired in the time of Bishop Ulrich II, in exchange for which another excellent manor was given at Stalringen [Note: [Col. 0316D] Perhaps Stahringen in the district of Stockach.]. Likewise another manor, whose inhabitants he established as serfs, so that every day in that cell they might serve the brothers wherever necessary, as did those who lived in that place; and so that they might bring dried wood from Nuiheim and always be ready for every service.

## § XXX. Concerning the ministerials.

[Col. 0316C]

And to speak more fully about the vassals, that is, the ministerials: he gave to the Church of Constance a certain Makko, an ancestor of Rudolf of Arbon [Note: [Col. 0316D] Stumpf, in *Chronicle*, book V, chapter 9, mentions nobles of Arbon, as does Guillimannus in his *Habsburgica*. See Löw, *Lexicon*.] and of his line, and the ancestors of Hacho and of his kin from Bollingin, with everything they possessed.

The aforementioned Makko later went to Jerusalem and redeemed himself by giving certain gifts to the monastery, saying that perhaps he might otherwise be liable there for some service, because he had been the blessed man’s personal servant.

He also gave to the monastery a certain man named Turlandus, of the same family, nobility, and wealth; his descendants still flourish at Owingen [Note: [Col. 0316D] A village in the district of the chapter of Haigerloch; below, in the following section, it is called Uowingen.].

He also transferred many poorer men to the monastery, establishing this right for all of them [Col. 0317A]: that they should ride with the abbot, serve him at home and abroad, provide their horses to both the abbot and his brothers wherever they were needed, defend the monastery to the best of their ability, and be subject to no one’s service whatever except that of the abbot and his monks.

## § XXXI. Concerning the endowment of the monastery.

These are the properties that Blessed Bishop Gebehard gave to his monastery from his parents’ inheritance or acquired elsewhere: Uowingen, Suldorf [Note: [Col. 0317D] Sauldorf, in the district of the chapter of Mößkirch.], Anslechiswilare [Note: [Col. 0317D] Perhaps Andwil, in the district of Saint Gall.], Rinisgemunde, and at Hogste [Note: [Col. 0317D] Hochst, in the same district, as is Bruggen.], and Brugg, Rode [Note: [Col. 0317D] Roth near Sauldorf.], Stettin [Note: [Col. 0317D] Mühlheim with its filial church of Stetten, in the district of the chapter of Wurmlingen.], Mülheim, Wanhartiswilare [Note: [Col. 0317D] Perhaps Walpertsweiler, in the district of Mößkirch.], Slate [Note: [Col. 0317D] Perhaps Schlatt, in the district of Engen.], Rinhard [Note: [Col. 0317D] Renartsweiler in the district of Saulgau. See § 14.], a fourth part of the property at Epfindorf, and Togingen, which he acquired from the Church of Constance [Col. 0317B], giving it in return some of his own estates, namely Luitwanga and Ratpirgahusin, Eichstetten [Note: [Col. 0318D] Aichstetten, in the district of Isny. See § 36.], Epfindorf, Nuiheim, Tegerwilare, Gottiliubon, Tuscinanc [Note: [Col. 0318D] Tusnang, in the district of Steckborn, as is Wengen. See Book II, § 3.], and Oberwangin. Of these, he acquired one from the possessions of the bishopric and another from those of the monastery; he granted Obirndorf from the possessions of the bishopric.

## § XXXII. Concerning the freedom of the monastery.

Blessed Gebehard established that this monastery should render no service, tax, toll, embassy, or performance of any kind of official duty either to the Roman pontiff or to the emperor, nor to the bishop of Constance, nor to any person whatsoever, regardless of power or rank, but to God alone. For this reason the place has remained inviolate to the present day, so that no one dares to violate it [Col. 0317C].

## § XXXIII

Other monasteries, which are called free, must pay at Rome each year a gold coin worth five solidi. But the place of Petershausen owes nothing—to Rome, Constance, Mainz, king, or duke—nor does it owe anything to anyone else, except that it must devote itself wholly to regular religion.

## § XXXIV. Concerning the service on the feast of Saint Gregory.

Some people are accustomed to charge us with owing a provision to the brothers of Constance on the feast of Pope Saint Gregory. Let them know that this was established before this monastery had even been begun.

As we related above [Note: [Col. 0318D] Above, § 9.], before he became bishop, Blessed Gebehard gave to the Church of Constance what he personally possessed at Obirudorf, Pilolfingin, Hagilimbach, and Luitheresdorf. He himself received these properties back as a benefice, on the condition that both he and whoever afterward held this benefice should provide the brothers of the aforesaid church with a full service on the feast of Saint Gregory [Col. 0318A].

After he became bishop, however, he founded the monastery and granted the aforesaid estates to it under the same condition just described. In return, he established for those same brothers that they should come together to the monastery in solemn procession three times a year, sing Mass there for his soul on each occasion, and, in addition, on the feast of Saint Gregory celebrate a public Mass for him solemnly with the brothers; the monks were to direct the choir and minister at the altar, and on that day two talents and four solidi were to be given to the clergy for their service from the aforesaid estates.

## § XXXV

The form of that service is as follows: first, three measures of grain for making bread; then, from the western table in the refectory, fish; half a measure of millet pounded in a mortar; three urns of wine; and five solidi in money.

This is the service owed each year from the estates mentioned above. But Abbot Conrad reduced it to this: that they should be given two talents and five solidi.

## § XXXVI. Concerning Eichstettin.

There was a certain count named Adilhardus [Note: [Col. 0318D] See *Disquisitio*, § 13, p. 280.], a pious and religious man who feared God and was related to the blessed man Gebehard by blood, though by no means a Swabian. He lived in a distant land, where by hereditary right large and numerous estates had fallen to him in the district of Ilrigove [Note: [Col. 0318D] Hargau, a district of the duchy of Alemannia named from the river Iller, in the area of the rural chapter of Isny; the villages mentioned here—Aichstetten, Breitenbach, Ried, Hausen, and Steinbach—are situated there.], namely at Eichstatt, Breitinbach, Riedin, Husin, and Steinbach.

Whenever he came from his own land and visited these estates—which he did very rarely—all the inhabitants hurried to visit him with their little gifts, as all servants commonly do for their lords. But because he was kind and merciful, he asked what they wanted by doing this. When they replied that they were his people and had come with the customary greeting to visit him, he added:

“Let each of them keep his little gifts with him for the time being, until after dinner, when I myself can inspect them.”

Then, after they had all been fully and abundantly fed, he added gifts of his own to theirs, taking nothing from them, and dismissed them to leave, so that they rejoiced that they had come there.

This man therefore gave to his kinsmen of Bregenz the estate at Steinbach [Col. 0318D], which later, through a marriage settlement, came into the power of the lords of Kirchberg.

## § XXXVII. Adilhard gave Eichstetin, Breitinbach, and Riedin as a gift to Gebehard.

The pious Count Adilhard himself gave to his nephew, Blessed Bishop Gebehard, everything he personally possessed at Eichstetin, Breitinbach, Riedin, and Husin—forty manors and more—with cultivated fields and meadows, except only very extensive woods, together with the parish church, many tithes, pastures, fisheries, mills, and many tributary tenants, with all the equipment that can be possessed or named.

The aforementioned Count Adilhard lawfully transferred all this property into the ownership of his nephew, the venerable Bishop Gebehard. The blessed man then, with the readiest devotion and without any opposition, publicly gave it in perpetuity to his monastery, which he had built in honor of Pope Saint Gregory, for the benefit of the brothers serving God there, before suitable witnesses.

## § XXXVIII. Concerning Duke Burchard.

At the same time, the religious Duke Burchard [Note: [Col. 0319C] See Hermann, year 973, and the preliminary notice to his *Life*, above, p. 240.] and his wife Hadiwich, since they had no child of the flesh, chose Christ as their heir. Accordingly, in their castle on Mount Duello [Note: [Col. 0319C] Now Hohentwiel, a very strongly fortified castle in Hegau belonging to the dukes of Württemberg. Bucelinus discusses this monastery in *Germania Sacra*, vol. II, as does Crusius, *Annals*, book IV, part II, chapter 9. Bucelinus is nevertheless mistaken in saying that Hadwig was the daughter of Rudolf, king of Burgundy, since she was the daughter of Henry, duke of Bavaria and brother of Emperor Otto I. Her husband, Duke Burchard, died in 973; this establishes the period in which the monastery was founded. Yet it must be older if Mabillon is correct (*Annals*, vol. III, p. 277) in saying that Walfrid or Waldfred, who is called its first abbot here, had already died in 880. Certainly, the very ancient book of the Reichenau associations mentions “Lord Abbot Walfred of Duello.” Gallia Christiana, vol. V, p. 933, lists six of his successors as abbots, down to Trudewingus, under whom, in 1005, that monastery was transferred to Stein. Thus what Ekkehard writes in chapter 10 of *On the Affairs of Saint Gall*—that after her husband Duke Burchard’s death in 973, Hadwig began to establish a monastery on Mount Duello—seems to refer to the restoration of the earlier monastery; other authors should likewise be interpreted in this sense. Moreover, among these abbots, the younger Ekkehard writes that Watzemann, abbot of Duello, was a close friend of the elder Ekkehard around 973, in the same work, chapter 11, p. 53.], they established a monastery. There they gave estates and other equipment in very ample measure for the support of the monks, while distributing the rest among other monasteries.

A holy and venerable man named Walfridus was the first abbot of this monastery. Later, the monastery was transferred by Emperor Henry from Mount Duello and established on the bank of the Rhine, at a place called Stein. Since that same king had claimed all the possessions of Duke Burchard for himself by hereditary right, he took much away from the monastery and left only enough to support a few brothers [Note: [Col. 0320C] This contradicts what is stated in *Gallia Christiana*, cited above, where the monastery of Stein is said to have been generously endowed by Saint Henry the Emperor. Its subjection to the Church of Bamberg is also demonstrated by a letter of Bishop Otto to the abbots subject to him around 1123; among them is Otto, abbot at Stein, sent from Saint Blaise. See Gerbert, *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, p. 433.]. Finally, he subjected both the abbey itself and everything belonging to it—including what he had taken away—to the bishopric of Bamberg, which he himself had then first established.

## § XXXIX. How he acquired Epfindorf.

Thus the aforementioned Hadewic, widow of Duke Burchard, after his death gave to the blessed man, her nephew, Bishop Gebehard [Note: [Col. 0320D] See *Disquisitio*, § 14, p. 282.], the estate called Epfindorf, for the support of the brothers serving God in his monastery, which is called Petershausen. By the authority and privilege of Emperor Otto, the monastery has possessed it to the present day; the monastery of Stein, however, possesses a fourth part of the same village.

## § XL

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity [Note: [Col. 0320D] This diploma appears in Gerbert’s *History of the Black Forest*, vol. III, p. 17, and in Lunig’s *Spicilegium Ecclesiasticum*, part III, p. 401, although the latter text is quite corrupt.], OTTO, by the gracious favor of God, king.

“If we have graciously lent an ear to the pious petitions of priests, which they pour into our ears on behalf of the churches entrusted to them, we undoubtedly believe that this will be beneficial both to the present condition of our kingdom and to the reward of eternal blessedness. Therefore, let the diligent concern of all our faithful, both present and future, know how the lord Gebehard, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Constance, approaching [Col. 0320B] our royal majesty, earnestly begged that we might wish to transfer and confirm by our royal charter to the monastery of Saint Gregory—which the aforementioned bishop Gebehard, beloved by God and men, built from the foundations for the use of the monks serving God there under the Rule of Saint Benedict, for the salvation of his own soul and those of his parents—a certain estate called Epfindorf, with its appurtenances, situated in the places and villages of Bosinga [Note: Bosingen, in the chapter of Rottweil], Mesinga [Note: Hoch-Mossingen, in the same district], Ancencimbra [Note: Zimmeren, likewise; or Herrenzimmeren], Harthusa [Note: A dependent estate under Epfindorf, in the same district], and Ursilinga [Note: Urslingen, below Rottweil], in the district of Para and in the county of Count Hiltibald [Note: Hiltibald must be counted among the counts of Bertholdsbara, whom Herrgott displays in various documents, volume II, under the eighth and ninth centuries, though none bears this name. See Gerbert, cited work, volume I, page 150]. For, as we have learned from the report of our faithful, the aforementioned estate of Epfindorf, with everything belonging to it [Col. 0320C], lawfully belongs to the aforesaid monastery of Gregory through the transfer of the lady Hadewiga, duchess [Note: She had already died by this year. In the Petershausen Necrology, under 28 August, Hadewic the duchess is recorded].

Therefore, following the wishes and petitions of so good and beloved a man, we give and grant the aforesaid estate of Epfindorf and all its appurtenances—namely, with plots, buildings, serfs of both sexes, cultivated and uncultivated lands, fields, meadows, open country, pastures, vineyards, vine-plots, woods, waters and watercourses, fisheries, mills, roads and trackless ways, exits and entrances, things acquired and things to be sought, and all other implements that can still be stated or named [Col. 0321A]—to the aforesaid monastery built in honor of Saint Gregory, and likewise to the monks serving God there under the Rule of Saint Benedict; and we transfer them in their entirety from our right into their right. Moreover, by our royal authority we confirm everything that has already been transferred, or shall be transferred, to that same monastery by our beloved bishop Gebehard or by any other person, great or small, so that these things may remain firm and unshaken and perpetually free from all violation, and so that no annoyance may be inflicted upon the sacred place through the importunity of malicious persons. And, so that this transfer of our royal donation may remain firm from this hour and henceforth as before, we ordered this charter of our donation [Col. 0321B] to be written and sealed with the impression of our seal, and we have strengthened it with our own hand, as appears below.

Sign of the most glorious lord Otto, king. I, Hiltibold, bishop and chancellor, have reviewed this in place of Willigis, archbishop.

Given on the second day before the Nones of November, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 994 [Note: Therefore this transfer was not first made in the year 1007, as Crusius writes, part II, book V, chapter 2, and Bruschius; Gallia Christiana, volume V, page 1033, was likewise led astray by this error, assigning it to the time of Abbot Erlembold], indiction VII, and in the eleventh year of the reign of Otto III. Done successfully at Ingelheim.”

§ XLI. On the church’s ornaments

The blessed Gebehard acquired for the place he loved many splendid and honorable movable ornaments, most of which the wickedness of certain people scattered . . .

§ XLII.

[Col. 0321C]

Indeed, Bishop Gebehard had made two silver crowns, one of which he had suspended in the choir and the other before the cross in the vestibule . . .

§ XLIII.

He adorned the ceiling of the basilica throughout, at intervals, with gilded bosses. Above the choir, on a separate panel, he had an image of Saint Mary, the Mother of God, painted in gold and the finest colors, and around it the images of the twelve apostles in the form of a cross. All these things, however, the passage of time in the present age has compelled to cease to be what they once were . . .

§ XLIV.

[Col. 0322A]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 993, in the second year after the monastery’s consecration, Periggerus [Note: Concerning this abbot, see above, § 26] was appointed its first abbot.

§ XLV. When the blessed Gebehard ended his life

Afterward, in the fourth year—that is, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 996 [Note: Hermann gives the year 995, but the indiction conflicts with this]—and in the sixteenth year of his ordination, the blessed and venerable Bishop Gebehard ended his temporal life and passed into eternal life, in the twelfth year of the reign of Otto III, indiction IX.
