He was buried in the church that he himself had built, in the southern apse, happily and gloriously. Finally, we saw his tomb most beautifully adorned with splendid ornaments. At its head stood an altar dedicated in honor of Saint Benedict, where the first Mass was sung daily [Col. 0322B]. Attached to that altar was a panel bearing, in its lower part, an image of the Lord; to its right was an image of Saint Gregory, and on the left one of Saint Gebehard. In the upper part of the same panel were affixed sheets made of copper, on which this epitaph was written in golden letters:

> Earth’s due portion, spurn the deceiving seasons,  
>   
> and remember your own, as this ash bears witness.  
>   
> Here lies the honor of our people, and the grief of our people;  
>   
> here he presided over the city, yet benefited the whole world,  
>   
> and founded for God this temple and this dwelling.  
>   
> God, forgiving, have mercy on the earthly portion;  
>   
> repay the due return, because this man had loved you.

[Note: Another epitaph is added from an old book of the Stein monastery, in which he is said to have died on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, that is, 27 August.]

§ XLVI. On the adornment of the tomb

Around the tomb, set into the wall, were five columns made of plaster; their capitals and arches were decorated with elegant sculpture, and above them were vines, birds, and four-footed animals, all finely fashioned. At his head was an image of the Crucified, and on the right side of the man lying there was an image of him himself, in the middle, as though prepared for the service of the altar in pontifical vestments. On his right and left stood figures of his attendants, one holding a book and the other a linen cloth; the whole was excellently formed in plaster. The tomb itself stood beside the entrance to the crypt, raised above the ground on four wooden panels and continually covered with a carpet. There, to demonstrate the greatness of his merits, the merciful and compassionate Lord, in his goodness, frequently heals people afflicted with various illnesses, even to the present day [Note: In an old manuscript missal of the same monastery the following is read; it is also found in Gerbert’s History of the Black Forest, volume III, page 120, although through inadvertence the year 1224 is given there. The first elevation of his body is discussed below, book V, § 1 and following: “In the year of the incarnate Word 1239, indiction XII, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, a Saturday, the relics of our founder and patron, the holy and God-beloved confessor and bishop Gebehard, were revealed and placed in a new sarcophagus covered with silver and gold, with devotion and reverence and spiritual songs, while many prelates, monks, canons, and other learned persons, as well as many laymen and women, were present. The relics of the eleven thousand holy virgins and of many other saints were also placed in the same sarcophagus, to the praise, glory, and honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who with the Father,” etc.].

## THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0321]

### § I. How Tuscinanc was acquired

After the blessed bishop Gebehard passed from this world [Col. 0322D] to the heavenly realms, the monk Lampert succeeded him in the episcopate, and Periggerus became abbot in the monastery of Saint Gregory [Col. 0323A], which is called Petershausen, and took up its administration [Note: Thus, in the meantime, he acted almost as the deputy of Saint Gebehard. Bishop Lambert of Petershausen appears to have been a monk, according to the Annals of Einsiedeln; his death, in the year 1018, is omitted in this Chronicle. See Hermann under that year].

### § II

At about the same time, a certain noble and wealthy man named Siggerus sold to the aforesaid monastery his own estates at Tuscinanc and Oberwangin [Note: Tuscinanc, or Tuzzinananc, is now called Tusnang, in the chapter of Frauenfeld in Thurgau, as is Oberwangen, which in the following section is called Wengin or Wengen], with their appurtenances—namely, churches, tithes, and everything else belonging to those places. After Siggerus had received what had been agreed upon and had confirmed the aforesaid transfer according to Alemannic law, Bishop Lampert, with the assistance of Emperor Otto III, obtained from Gregory V, also called Bruno, a privilege concerning both the monastery itself and everything that had been, was, or would thereafter be transferred to it [Col. 0323B] [Note: Herrgott printed this bull, composed in an entirely distinctive style, in a corrupt form, assigning it to the year 997].

### § III

“ In the name of the holy and divided Trinity, Gregory, also called Bruno, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church, and servant of the servants of God.

“Desire that is shown to pertain to a religious purpose and to the stability of holy places must, with God as its author, be fulfilled without any delay. And whenever our assent and the customary protection of apostolic authority are sought for some benefit or advantage of the holy Church, it is fitting for us readily to help, with a view to kindness, and to strengthen an approved purpose with reason for complete security, so that from this the veneration of holy places, safety, and freedom from harm may be *profligatur* [reading uncertain; Note: Perhaps it should read *praefigatur et praescribatur*], and so that a most profitable reward may likewise be assigned to us by the Creator of all.

“Therefore, at the will and request of the august Emperor Otto III and of Lampert, bishop of the holy Church of Constance, we place under apostolic protection a certain monastery on the bank of the Rhine near Constance, in a village called Petershausen, built by the late Bishop Gebehard in honor of Saint Gregory. We adorn it with the commands of the Roman Church in such a way that this same monastery, now governed by Abbot Pericherus, together with all the various estates belonging to it, cultivated and uncultivated, colonists and households, and whatever Bishop Gebehard transferred to the same monastery by hereditary right or by any acquisition [Col. 0323D], or whatever he exchanged from the episcopal estate, or permitted without an exchange, as well as whatever the aforesaid Bishop Lampert granted to the same monastery in any transaction, together with Siggerus’s estates called Tuzzinananc and Wengin, situated in the district of Thurgau, in the county of Count Berthold [Col. 0324A] [Note: Berthold therefore belongs among the counts of Thurgau, perhaps the father of Berthold, who is also called count of Thurgau in a diploma of Henry III from the year 1044, in P. Herrgott, cited work, page 120]—one of these estates having been acquired from episcopal property through Bishop Gebehard, and the other from the property of the same monastery through Abbot Pericherus—and whatever is or shall be granted to that pious place by any person who fears God, or has already come to it as a grant, shall remain established and unshaken under the apostolic protection and guardianship of blessed Peter, with Christ as witness.

“Moreover, by this apostolic command, with the consent of the august Emperor Otto III and of the aforementioned Bishop Lampert, who requested that this be done, we absolutely prohibit anyone from being appointed over the same monastery unless chosen by the common agreement of the brothers serving God there; it shall belong to the bishop only to confirm the person so elected. We decree the same concerning the election of an advocate. Once elected, the abbot or the monastery’s advocate shall take care to administer the monastery’s property and to resist those who dissipate it. But if anyone in the meantime—which we do not believe—should dare rashly to oppose what has been piously and firmly established by this authority of ours through this privilege, or to resist or in any way transgress what we have ordained for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose office we exercise even though unworthy, he is bound by the chain of anathema and shall be burned with the devil and Judas, the betrayer of Christ, in everlasting fires. But whoever, with pious regard, proves himself an observer of our saving command shall receive manifold grace from the Lord, the just retributor [Col. 0324C], and shall merit becoming a participant in eternal life, world without end. Amen.”

### § IV. On King Henry and Bishop Lampert

After this, when Emperor Otto had died and Henry had assumed the empire and founded the bishopric of Bamberg, he brought under his own authority, as though by hereditary right, everything that had belonged to the former Duke Burchard and his wife Hadiwiga, concerning Mount Duello [Note: See above, book I, § 38]. For this reason, the monastery of Stein came under the authority of that church. But our monastery, that is, Petershausen, retained Epfindorf through the privilege of Emperor Otto, which the aforementioned Hadewic had long before transferred as property to the blessed bishop Gebehard. But since the aforementioned King Henry was collecting with the greatest zeal, from other churches wherever he could, whatever was necessary to enrich and adorn the place he had built, he despoiled many places by entreaty until he had enriched his own foundation beyond measure. It therefore happened that he also asked Lampert, bishop of the Church of Constance [Col. 0325A], to provide him, like the other bishops, with some assistance from his church. As a result, Lampert forcibly removed from the monastery built by the blessed Gebehard much of the treasure that the same Gebehard had given to God and to blessed Gregory, in order to satisfy the emperor’s will.

### § V

This is the treasure of Gebehard, bishop of Constance, of blessed memory, which he gave to the place he had built in honor of blessed Pope Gregory, and which Bishop Lampert, his successor, took away [327]. One gold-adorned bowl. Two silver basins. Two additional silver basins. One silver dish, two silver spoons, and two silver candlesticks: twenty-eight pounds of silver by weight. Two back-hangings. Two basins. One ivory comb, fitted with gold. Seven tablecloths, one handcloth, and one small carpet. One silver goblet. One golden stole and a napkin of the same workmanship, whose fringe one of the monks stole and hid; it is still kept there and is of very costly workmanship.

### § VI

Abbot Ellimboldus [Note: In *Gallia Christiana* he is called Erlemboldus, and by Bucelinus Elenboldus; his dates and deeds are uncertain], who succeeded Periggerus, left us a memorial of himself. (There is a lacuna in the manuscript here.)

### § VII

[Col. 0325C]

In the second year of the reign of King Henry, Abbot Waltharius [Note: In *Gallia Christiana* he is said to have been made abbot in 1021 from a monk of Einsiedeln; this is erroneous, however, if the places mentioned here were acquired in the second year of Henry’s reign, that is, in 1016. They are situated in the Raetia Curiensis: Campis or Gams; Essanc or Eschen; Quarabilis or Grabs; and Lindinis, that is, Upper and Lower Lienz. See Lew’s lexicon] acquired for the monastery an estate at Campis and Essanc, and Quarabilis by exchange from a certain Burchard. In return, the monastery gave him property of its own at Burron, at Berge, and at another Berge, as well as a church at Lindinis. That estate had previously been acquired in portions by a certain priest named Diethere during the time of Emperor Otto. Several privileges concerning it exist, but they are not worded in such a way that we wish to insert them here.

### § VIII

[Col. 0326A]

Sigifridus, first a canon of Constance, then a monk at the cell of Saint Meginrad, and finally appointed abbot at Saint Gregory’s.

### § IX

Abbot Erchinboldus [Note: Concerning both of these abbots, no information is found elsewhere except their names] left nothing worth recording.

### § X. Privilege concerning the estate of Rietilinis

Abbot Folmarus acquired Rietilinis and Wegefaza for the monastery, as the following privilege testifies [Note: This charter is also read in Lunig, *Spicilegium ecclesiasticum*, part III, page 402].

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Let it be known to all Christ’s faithful, present and future, that I, Erimbreth, at the request of Eberhard, bishop of the Church of Constance, have transferred, with the hand of my wife Irmingard and without any opposition, to God and Saint Gregory, at the place called Petershausen, and to the monks serving God there, by an authoritative act, such an estate as I appear to possess in the district of Nibelgewe [Note: The location of the district Nibilgewe, Nibalgow, or Nibalgauge has not yet been sufficiently determined. Goldastus, no. 10, and after him Besselius in the *Chronicle of Gottweig*, following Tschudi, *On Raetia*, chapter 24, place it in Raetia Curiensis, on the right bank of the Rhine between the districts of Brechtagow, Walgow, and Ringow, or in the present county of Montfort, in which, according to Münster’s *Cosmography*, book III, and Zeiler, the estate of Feldkirch was situated, as Besselius interprets it. P. Neugart, however, in the *Ancient Alemannic Diplomatic Code*, in his notes on charter XLV, thinks it should be sought around the imperial city of Leutkirch, as the places sometimes attached to it in the Saint Gall charters indicate, although that city is otherwise counted within the district of Algovia, of which the smaller district of Nibilgewe may perhaps have been a part. Certainly, in the charter below, book III, § 41, the island of Rotse, donated to Petershausen, is said to lie in the district of Nibilgouwe; yet that place is recorded as Rottsee in the rural chapter of Isny, to which the town of Leutkirch likewise belongs. Besselius, deceived here by Lunig, reads Rethe instead of Rotsee and, following his own system, seeks this name in Rottis near Montfort. But the reading Rotse is constant in our manuscript, and it also better suits the designation of an island. See below, book V, § 6. Near Rottsee and Arnach lies the village of Riedlings, here called Ritilenes; Wegesaza may perhaps also be the same region, although no place with that name is now found], in the places called Ritilines and Wegesaza, with farmsteads, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated land, ways in and out, and in the forest of Arinane, from my estate, as much as is sufficient on these plots in the aforesaid places for building and cutting timber, together with pastures, ways, and exits. Moreover, I wish it to be known that Bishop Eberhard, together with Folmar, abbot of the same place, and Heremann, the advocate, received that estate in the aforesaid places of Rietilines and Wegesaza [Note: Read *suscepit*, ‘he received’], and granted me and my wife fourteen manses at Eichstat [Note: See book I, § 36] as a benefice for the whole of our lives.

“These things were done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1043, indiction XI, with seven epacts and five concurrents, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, on the fifth day of the moon [329], in the presence of these witnesses: Udalricus of Bregenz [Note: He appears to have been the son of Udalricus, brother of Saint Gebehard; he is not found in Lazius. See below, § 20, and above in the inquiry, § 24], Switker, Wezel, Swigger, Ernest, Gerolt, Ruger, Landolt, Otgoz, Lutpreht, Sigipreth, Hartnit, Engilscalch, Enceli, Simpreht, Hunolt, Eppo, Ello, and Alberich [Col. 0327A]. Bishop Eberhard ordered this charter to be made.”

### § XI

It is also reported that the gold which had been on the small doors of that panel attached to the principal altar was then removed and given in exchange for the aforesaid estate, and that gilded silver was affixed to the panel.

### § XII. Privilege concerning Ouwiltingin

In the time of Abbot Adelbert [Note: Adelbertus was formerly a monk of Einsiedeln and died a sudden death at Buchau in the year 1060; see below, book IV, § 19], Swiggerus gave an estate at Ouwiltingin, concerning which the following privilege is preserved [Note: It is also found in Lunig, cited work, page 403, but in corrupt form]:

“Let all present and future people know how I, Swiggerus, with the hand of my wife Adelheida and my son Godeshalch, transfer to the monastery of Saint Gregory situated on the bank of the Rhine, into the hands of Abbot Adelbert and his advocate, Count Eberhard [Note: I believe this must certainly be the count of Nellenburg who founded the monastery of Schaffhausen in 1052. See above, under that year], one half of such an estate as I appear to possess with full authority in the village called Oweltinga [Note: Lunig and the *Chronicle of Gottweig* corruptly read Suiltinga. It appears to be Ober-Ultingen or Unter-Ultingen, not far from the episcopal castle of Meersburg], in the district of Linzgau, in the county of Count Otto [Note: Of Raetia Curiensis, in a charter of 1050 in Herrgott, and of Bregenz. See the inquiry, § 24]. The arrangement and agreement are that, for as long as my aforesaid wife and I live, whenever it pleases us to be present, we shall share in the buildings and in every communal benefit of the brothers. After our death, however, let our memory always be celebrated as that of one of the brothers; and, if it can be done, on the anniversary day of both of us—or, if that cannot be done, of the one whose soul first departs from the body—let the brothers make provision according to the constitution of the aforesaid venerable abbot.

“This was done in the same church of Saint Gregory in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1058 [330], in the presence of those whose names we have subscribed: Count Ruodolf [Note: He is recorded in charters of 1048 and 1050 together with the Otto mentioned shortly afterward in Herrgott, volume I, page 75; perhaps he was count of Montfort or Pfullendorf], Eberhart, Uodalrich, Adelbret, Hezo, Hezil, Adelolt, Gerolt, Hereman, Alwich, Adelbero, Ratolt, Hezel, Ruodolf, and Marcwart. I, Bernhardus the deacon, wrote and subscribed this, while the child Henry IV was reigning as king, in the second year after his father’s death, but in the seventh year of the ordination of Rumoldus [Note: Rumoldus was first made bishop of Constance in 1051 and died in 1069; therefore the words ‘of blessed memory’ appear to have been added by our author] of blessed memory, the bishop, indiction XII [Note: This indiction ran from September of the year 1038].”

### § XIII

There was also an Adelbertus, noble by birth and handsome in body [Col. 0328A]. He died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1060 [Note: According to the Necrology, on 23 April].

### § XIV

Siggo [Note: Below, book IV, § 19, he is said to have died with a broken back in the second year of his ordination, and therefore around the year 1062] succeeded Adelbertus [Note: There is a very large lacuna in the manuscript here]. When he died, Arnoldus succeeded him; Arnoldus was deposed and Meginradus was substituted.

### § XV

For some time, while Meginradus was abbot, the bishop of Constance had to hurry to royal service. He began importunately to demand a traveling allowance from the aforesaid abbot, saying that by right he was owed from that monastery a *spado* [Note: Italian *spadone*, a military sword, a broad sword] together with a *limbo* [Note: Or *limbus*, the border of a military cloak, a military mantle, a surcoat]. When Abbot Meginradus strongly resisted, saying that the bishop was owed absolutely nothing from it by right, and the bishop obstinately insisted that it be given, Meginradus cast away from him the staff of governance, saying that he would never consent to the sacred place being compelled by force to lose its freedom; and, since, as he said, he was no longer able to resist, it was better for him to relinquish the abbacy. Thus he relinquished the abbacy, and the bishop acquired nothing there. Nevertheless, afterward, when he had been restored to his office, the bishop again wished one day to sing Mass in the same monastery without Meginradus’s request. Meginradus threw his pastoral staff upon the altar and departed.

### § XVI. On the chapel of Saint John the Baptist

[331] About this time, Wolueradus [Note: He is recorded in the Necrology on 4 January, where his wife is called Gotistiv and the estates Uoldishusin and Judintunberch are mentioned. This noble family is otherwise unknown], a nobleman of Wilare, and his wife, named Gotistric, while Rumoldus presided over the Church of Constance, built a chapel in the monastery cemetery in honor of Saint John the Baptist, Saint Nicholas, and other saints [Col. 0328C]. He transferred Uodilshusin [Note: Oggelshausen, near the Feather Lake, in the rural chapter of Biberach] and Lucintunberch [Note: Ittenberg, in the parish of Burgweiler, where the nobles of Wilare perhaps had their seat, in the rural chapter of Mengen] to it as an endowment, and established that the chapel should have its own priest. He and his wife are also buried there before the sanctuary, each in a separate tomb, one (sic) in the right wall and the other in the left. Sigifridus, son of the aforementioned Wolueradus, also added to the chapel, in the time of Bishop Otto [Note: Otto was appointed bishop of Constance in 1071], an oratory of Saint James the Apostle, and gave Bozze, Gisilmarisruti, and Swabirichishusin to it as an endowment. He established a tomb for himself in that oratory. But while traveling to Rome, he was overtaken by death on the return journey at Clavine [Note: Perhaps Chiavenna in the diocese of Como, now belonging to the Grisons] [Col. 0329A] [Note: From the Necrology, 15 April], and was buried there. He too loved our place exceedingly, often visited it, and stayed there. It therefore happened that, when he wished one night to leave the church after the morning vigils had been completed, he fell in the darkness of night down the steps by which one then descended from the church door into the cloister. These steps have since been moved somewhat farther from the door by my uncle Gebino. Immediately after his fall, Sigifridus gave an estate at Maginbuoch [Note: Magenbuech, in the chapter of Mengen], on the condition that every night during the morning vigils a light should continually burn before that door.

### § XVII. The arm of the Theban martyrs

To return briefly to earlier times: Herimannus the elder of Hirzisegga [Note: See below, § 21. The village of Hirschegg, in the parish of Mittelberg and the rural chapter of Stiefenhofen, appears to preserve the name of this noble family], in the time of Emperor Conrad II, acquired at Agaunum an arm of one of the fellow soldiers of Saint Maurice. He brought it to the Fathers with due reverence, enclosed it in a small but silver-adorned sarcophagus, and gave it to the monastery. Herimannus himself and his brother gave two estates at Alminishus and Winiden [Note: Althausen and Wengen, or Winingen, in the chapter of Frauenfeld in Thurgau]. . . .

### § XVIII. On Gebino and his estate

There was a certain nobleman, Gebino of Pfruwangin [Note: Pfruewangen, today Pfrungen, in the district of Linzgau and the chapter of Thuringen. See below, book IV, § 5], who had begun to cultivate a relationship with the holy place. He gave it estates of his own at Ringginwilare [Note: Ringenweiler, in the same district], Firmanniswilare, and Tanchiratiswilare [Note: Danketschweiler, likewise], and had made a dwelling for himself at the monastery, where he continually lived for the sake of divine service . . . He gave a splendid chasuble of saffron color [Col. 0329C]. He was buried in the portico before the basilica [Note: There is a lacuna of five lines in the manuscript here].

### § XIX

After Abbot Meginradus, as we said above, had renounced his authority, Luitoldus was substituted [Note: He was later deposed and withdrew to Reichenau. See below, book III, § 2].

### § XX. On the nobles buried in the same monastery

[Col. 0330A]

At this time many nobles maintained a relationship with the same monastery and rejoiced to have a burial place there. Among them was Count Eberhard of Potamo [Note: He appears to be the same man who is recorded above in § 12 in the charter; he is listed in the Necrology under 8 February], who gave it the estate of Huedewanc and rests in the basilica before the Lord’s cross. Udalricus the elder, Count of Bregenz [Note: See above, § 10. He is called ‘the elder’ in relation to his son, or perhaps grandson, of the same name, who died in 1097 according to Berthold of Constance], who gave Briginhusin [Note: Perhaps Bichishausen, in the chapter of Mösskirch, or in Hegau], rests in the cloister. Count Gero of Pfullendorf [Note: This Gero is sought in vain in Lazius and in Lucae, *Grafensaal*, page 382; he should doubtless be counted among the ancestors of Count Rudolf, who later obtained Bregenz. See the inquiry, § 24], who gave a small estate at Adelberinwilare [Note: Perhaps Alberweiler in the chapter of Biberach, or Almenschweiler in the district of Saulgau], lies before the church door . . .

### § XXI

[333] Eppo of Sanctomonte and his wife Tuotta [Note: They appear to have been the parents of the brothers Henry and Arnold, discussed below in book III, §§ 26–27] also lie buried at Saint Peter’s in the same church. Their images are painted on the wall above the altar, and the following verses are inscribed beside the man’s image:

> Here lies good Eppo, patron of Saint Mountain;  
>   
> he himself died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

Above the woman’s image the following verses are written:

> Here Tuta lies, safe from evils, his companion;  
>   
> she was buried on the sixth day before the Kalends of December.

On the side of the same wall there is also this epitaph above Herimannus of Hirzisegga [Note: See above, § 17. The Necrology records him on 1 March] and his wife Pertherada:

> Pertherada and Herimannus, receive through the prayers of Peter and Gregory  
>   
> the everlasting blessings of the heavenly kingdom;  
>   
> you and your worthy offspring, after the Sabbath’s due observances,  
>   
> hope from here to attain the blessed octave.

On the other side of the church, at Saint Stephen’s, lie four noble men who were killed together: Wernherus, Burchardus, Herimannus, and Wolfarnus [Note: Among the nobles who died or were buried at the Petershausen monastery, John of Seinsheim should also be mentioned. In his Necrology, under the 28th day, the following was inserted by another hand: “In the year of the Lord 1461, on the Thursday after Pentecost, the noble young lord John of Sanshein, Baron of Schwarzenberg, died in our monastery. His annual commemoration is to be held on the prescribed day at night with a vigil and *Placebo*, by visiting his tomb, and on the following day with a Mass for the dead, and afterward with *Placebo*, as is customary for such noblemen to celebrate anniversaries in our monastery. Therefore, for us and our successors, he established one pound of annual census money from the ferry at Amlikain, according to the tenor of the charter drawn up concerning this by his noble widow, Lady Cunigunda, Countess of Nellenburg.” According to Rittershusius, Cunigunda, daughter of Conrad of Nellenburg, first married the Count of Lupfen and Landgrave of Stühlingen, and afterward John, Baron of Schwarzenberg. Yet I do not find him in Imhof’s *On the Princes of Schwarzenberg*, nor in the Seinsheim family].

### § XXII

At about the same time, Geroldus and his brother Herimannus gave estates at Miminhusin, Ruti, Estrichiswilare [Note: It is called Escherichiswilare in the Necrology under 14 January and may perhaps be Esseratschweiler in the chapter of Lindau], and Niwiron [Note: Perhaps Neuffen in the chapter of Rottweil, or in the district of Para]. Geroldus himself lived most devoutly in the same monastery until his death, in the time of Abbot Theodoricus [334], first in the garb of the *barbati* (bearded lay brethren), and afterward in that of a monk.

### § XXIII. On King Henry IV
Anno from the Lord’s Incarnation 1057 [1056], Emperor Henry III died, and his son Henry IV succeeded him while still a boy, namely nine years old [Note: [Col. 0331D] Read “seven.”], who for forty-eight years, as though smoking like a brand, pierced the eyes of the faithful. For after receiving the most serene and fortunate Roman Empire, he made it altogether most shameful and turbulent. . . He broke out into such madness that he sold all ecclesiastical offices by simony, and, whenever he discovered religious bishops who execrated his crimes, he deprived them of their own sees; then he himself promoted others, who favored his disgraces, to the churches, and confused all rights, both ecclesiastical and secular. For at that time there came upon the Roman Empire that curse which is read as having been written by Solomon: “Woe to the land whose king is a child” (Ecclesiastes 10); and in Job: “Who makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people” (Job 34).

§ XXIV.

In the year 1069 Rumald, bishop of Constance, died, and a certain Charles was sent by King Henry to that Church as bishop through simony [Note: [Col. 0331D] See Berthold of Constance, in the Chronicle under this year.]. But, having been caught in the aforesaid heresy, he was rejected by the clergy of Constance in the king’s presence and condemned, although the king himself was raging excessively. Then the king, moved by anger, said: “Since they have rejected a suitable man, let them receive an incompetent one”; and then he gave them as bishop a certain Otto, a Saxon by birth.

§ XXV.

In the year 1075, while King Henry was living tyrannically in every respect, fearing neither God nor human beings, and distributing the investitures of bishops and abbots according to his own will, and although he had often been admonished on this account by legates of Pope Gregory and was unwilling to reform, the aforesaid Pope Gregory, who was also called Hildebrand, having convened a synod [Note: [Col. 0331D] The year 1076, according to Berthold of Constance, in the Chronicle below.], excommunicated him and all his followers, absolved those who had sworn allegiance to him and were bound to him by treaty, detached them from him, and forbade anyone to receive from him an ecclesiastical office or investiture. Moreover, he forbade clerics marriage under the bond of anathema [Col. 0331D]. Because of this, so great a storm battered the Church that it overturned countless people, and up to the present—even, as we believe, not until the end—it does not cease to flood and beat against the ship of God. . .

§ XXVI.

In the year 1077 Rudolf, duke of the Suevians [Note: [Col. 0331D] See below, § 30.], was established as king at the town of Forchheim by order of Pope Gregory and on the advice of Duke Berthold, Duke Welf of Bavaria, and very many other Catholics. He held the kingdom against Henry for three and a half years. This was the beginning, indeed the increase, of sorrows; for from it arose battles and revolts, many shedings of blood, and, what is worse, the destruction of many souls.

§ XXVII.

In the year 1080, King Henry, under anathema, advanced toward Rome with a large army favoring him, besieged the city, which was not unjustly resisting him, and captured it by force of arms [Note: [Col. 0331D] This belongs to the year 1084. See below, §§ 32–33.]. He drove Pope Gregory from the apostolic see into exile with considerable impiety, installed Wibert, archbishop of Ravenna, who had already been excommunicated for seven years on account of his crimes [Note: [Col. 0331D] Berthold, under the year 1084.], in the apostolic see, and had him place the imperial crown upon his own head. This most abominable heresiarch harassed holy Mother Church for more than nineteen years. Nevertheless, he was exceedingly learned in letters and most eloquent in speech; and, had he been just, he would have been quite suitable for this office.

§ XXVIII.

Since, then, King Henry was treating ecclesiastical offices perversely, as we have said, and since, by divine judgment, ruin and misfortune were already drawing near his ways, he began to disturb the path of peace, neither keeping the fear of God before his eyes nor rendering human beings what was just. To mention only a few matters among many, he took the duchy of Bavaria from Duke Otto and gave it to Welf of Ravensburg [Note: [Col. 0331D] On the counts of Altdorf and Ravensburg, see the *Guelphic Origins*, from which it appears that Welf IV was appointed duke of Bavaria in 1071. Berthold.]. He also deprived Bertolf [Note: [Col. 0331D] Elsewhere Bertold. See Lambert of Hersfeld, under the year 1072.] of the duchy of the Carinthians at Zähringen and gave it to Luitold of Genoa [Note: [Col. 0332D] Rather, to Marquard, father of Luitolf, count of Mürz Valley and Avelanz in Upper Styria, a relative of King Henry IV. Why he is called “of Genoa” is unknown to us.].

Furthermore, since he often stayed in Saxony, because that province is said to be the emperor’s kitchen, he began to violate the wives and daughters of the princes and to place no restraint upon such crimes. The Saxons, unable to endure these disgraces, were provoked to rebellion, and thereafter experienced grave battles and revolts.

§ XXIX.

And, to return briefly to the earlier period [Col. 0332D], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1074 [Note: [Col. 0332D] Berthold under the year 1075, as does Lambert. Ernest, margrave of Austria and son of Ernest II, duke of Alemannia, had been killed in this battle. The *Chronicle of St. Blaise* names the sons of Eberhard of Nellenburg as Henry and Eberhard, whom Lucas, p. 1052, calls Albert and Theobald.], King Henry, having gathered an army, entered hostilely into Saxony, which had rebelled against him, and fought with them beside the waters of the Unstrut. He defeated them, killing many and putting very many to flight, while some also surrendered to him unconditionally. He gained the victory not through his own merit but, as we believe, because God was honoring the fortunate Roman commonwealth. In this war the dukes of the Suevians were with the king: Rudolf, later king, and Welf and Berthold, although they were suspect to him. On the king’s side there were killed Ernest, margrave of the East, and two sons of Count Eberhard of Nellenburg, who founded the monastery of Schaffhausen.

§ XXX.

Therefore the aforesaid dukes of Alemannia immediately began to rebel against the king after this battle. After deliberating among themselves for a long time, they finally, with the consent of Pope Gregory, also called Hildebrand, assembled at the town called Forchheim with the Saxons and established Rudolf, duke of the Suevians, as king, while Henry was still alive but excommunicated. This took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1077, in March.

Rudolf celebrated the following Easter at Augsburg; but Imbrico, bishop of that city, refused even to see or greet him, although he ordered the necessities to be supplied to him abundantly. Departing from there, King Rudolf besieged the castle called Sigmaringen [Note: [Col. 0333D] Burchard, *On the Disasters of St. Gall*, chapter 7, likewise calls this castle Sigmaringen; it is now the seat in Swabia of the princes of Hohenzollern.]. But when he learned that King Henry was approaching [Col. 0333B], coming with an army over the Alpine passes to liberate the stronghold, he fled and went to Saxony. King Henry, however, gave the duchy of the Suevians to Frederick of Staufen and joined his daughter to him in marriage; she bore him Frederick [Col. 0333C] and Conrad, later king.

§ XXXI.

King Henry again gathered an army and marched against Saxony to attack Rudolf. But the opposing forces, having gathered, met him in the province of Bavaria, at the place of the river called the Strow [Note: [Col. 0333D] Berthold, in his expanded account, under the year 1078.], saying that they did not wish to weary the king any farther. There a most violent battle took place. King Henry, with his men, turned his back and fled, and there he lost Margrave Diepold of Giengen [Note: [Col. 0333D] Giengen is known as an imperial town of Swabia, but no counts of it are known, much less margraves. Perhaps the counts of Lechsgemünd formerly held dominion there; Bruschius writes that some of them were princes and dukes, and that they founded the monastery of Kaisheim. Certainly the annalist of Saxony and the *Chronicle of Magdeburg* testify that Theobald and Henry of that family fell in this battle (*Meibom, Scriptores*, vol. II, p. 313); this seems to be the same Margrave Diepold mentioned here [Col. 0334D].] and many others.

The victorious Saxons therefore lifted up their wounded and dead and departed hurriedly. But on that same day, when the duke of Bohemia arrived with a strong force after the flight, King Henry returned to the place of battle, sought the Saxons, and wished to fight them again. When he found that they were nowhere to be seen, each of his men lifted up his dead and wounded and departed; then they devastated everything around with plunder, sword, and fire [Note: [Col. 0334D] The margin adds: “The third battle was at Mäderichstadt, in which King Rudolf was again victorious with the Saxons, while Henry fled.”].

§ XXXII.

[Col. 0334A]

After this, King Henry went to Italy [Note: [Col. 0334D] See above, § 27; this concerns the year 1084.]. He came to Rome with an army, captured it by force of arms because it was rebelling against him, and expelled Pope Gregory after the many injuries which his supporters had previously inflicted upon him.

For when, at one time, on the holy night of the Nativity of the Lord, he was celebrating Mass in the city of Rome at cockcrow, as is customary, he was attacked with a sword by a certain Crescentius [Note: [Col. 0334D] Berthold, in his expanded account under the year 1076, describes this incident at length; there, however, he names the author of the crime not Crescentius but Quintius, or Cincius.], a Roman citizen and supporter of the king, and struck on the head by a powerful blow, so that he fell to the ground [Col. 0334B]. Then, to add to his madness, he reduced him to captivity and thrust him into his own tower. But on that same day the faithful destroyed the tower itself, and before evening piously restored the pope to the altar from which he had been impiously dragged away. Still fasting and supported by others, he completed in the evening the Mass which he had begun at cockcrow; for he had already carried it through to Communion.

§ XXXIII.

After the Catholic Pope Gregory had been expelled and thrust into exile with considerable impiety, King Henry unworthily placed a certain schismatic named Wibert—formerly archbishop of Ravenna, but already excommunicated by the pope for seven years because of his crimes—in the apostolic see. From him Henry received an imperial consecration entirely befitting his wickedness; for this should be called not consecration but rather execration. We have also reported this above [Note: [Col. 0334D] Number 27. See Berthold’s Chronicle under the year 1084.].

§ XXXIV.

Meanwhile King Rudolf gathered an army and wished to enter Bohemia and devastate it [Note: [Col. 0334D] Other writers are silent about this plan of King Rudolf under the year 1080, when these events occurred.]. But the duke of Bohemia, with the Slavs and with other accomplices of King Henry added to his forces, met him at the river called the Elster. There a fierce battle took place, and many fell on both sides.

King Rudolf himself was seriously wounded in the river by a lance and fell from his horse into the water. But his men raised him up and carried him onto the field; when the bishops arrived, he received penance and the viaticum. When he was already near death, he is said to have raised his head and said: “Who, I ask, has the victory?” When those standing around replied, “You, lord,” he lowered his head again and said: “Now I do not care about my death, if I meet it with the honor of triumph.”

Thus King Rudolf ended his life that same day at the Elster [Col. 0334D]. His men carried him to Merseburg, where he was honorably buried in the very choir of the basilica; an image of him, cast in bronze and gilded, was placed above his tomb [Col. 0335A]. In this battle the victory was uncertain, since both sides fled; nevertheless, the Slavs defended their own region from the Saxon invasion. This took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1080, on the Ides of October.

§ XXXV.

339 Thereafter, in the following year, the nobles of the Saxons and Suevians assembled at the place called Ohsonefurt and established as king Hermann, a noble, handsome, vigorous, and capable man, a Frank by birth from Glichberg [Note: [Col. 0335C] Historians count King Hermann among the family of the counts of Luxembourg. According to their testimony, his father was Count Giselbert, who was the son of Frederick, count of Luxembourg. The anonymous writer of Weingarten’s account of the Guelph princes, chapter 5, reports the following (*Leibniz, Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium*, vol. I, p. 783): “Welf—son of Rudolf, brother of Saint Conrad, bishop of Constance—took as his wife a woman of Salian lineage, from the castle of Glihberg, named Judith, sister of Henry, duke of the Norici, and, notably, of Frederick, duke of Lorraine, etc.” This Frederick was also duke of Lower Lorraine, having been appointed by Emperor Henry III in 1048; Hermann discusses him in the Chronicle under the year 1046 and following.

The same anonymous writer explains the matter more clearly in the corrected Weingarten manuscript (*Hess, Monumenta Guelphica*, p. 12), where the same castle is called not Glihberg but Glizberch, and where Judith is called Imiza. Scheidius notes in his remarks on the *Guelphic Origins* (vol. II, p. 222) that, under both names, Glitzberg and Luxembourg, the same counts of Luxembourg are meant.

But when he there appeals to our Berthold, or Bernold, of Constance, and to Lambert of Hersfeld, I fear that Scheidius was misled by the similarity of the name. Bernold, under the year 1059, writes: “Frederick and his brother” (or, according to other manuscripts, “his brothers”) “from Glichberg rebelled against King Henry”; but we shall explain this shortly afterward.

The case of Lambert is different. Under the year 1075 he writes that Hermann, count of Gilzberg, restored the wavering royal line in Henry’s battle against the Saxons; Scheidius thinks this was the same man who later became king. Although at that time he stood on Henry’s side, just as Duke Rudolf and Welf—related to Hermann through affinity—did, he could nevertheless later have defected from him with them. This might even seem to explain why, after Rudolf’s death in 1081, the princes made him king, namely because his military valor had been proven.

When Hermann is here called a Frank by birth, this agrees with the anonymous writer of Weingarten, who says that Frederick, Hermann’s grandfather, was of Salian lineage. This also distinguishes the castle of Glizberg, or Luxembourg, from another castle of the same name, formerly situated in Thuringia near Jena.

From this place perhaps came Frederick and his brother of Glichberg, who, according to Bernold, rebelled against the king in 1059 [Col. 0336D]. But this cannot be understood of our Hermann, who had no brother Frederick and who, according to Lambert, was still serving vigorously in Henry’s army in 1075.] and he reigned for seven years.

§ XXXVI.

After this, Frederick, duke of the Suevians, and Conrad, count palatine of Vohburg [Note: [Col. 0336D] Berthold refers this event to the year 1081, as does the Saxon annalist, who calls this Conrad the son of Conrad, count palatine—namely, the Bavarian count palatine of Vohburg. Neither of them, however, can be found in Lucas, p. 1138, nor in Lazius.], together with the other retainers of King Henry, gathered and captured certain strongholds in Bavaria. They advanced as far as the stronghold called Werde [Col. 0335B], and captured it.

As they were departing from there, behold, King Hermann arrived with an army of Suevians and seized them at the place called Hoste. Battle having been joined, they fought fiercely on both sides. Since they fought courageously and neither side wished to yield, one man from the Alemannian side is said to have shouted loudly: “Come, Suevians, fight bravely! Look, the Bavarians are fleeing; do not let any of them escape.”

When the Bavarians heard this voice and thought that what the malicious man had said was true, they all turned their backs together, and each tried to outstrip the other in flight. Many fell there. Among them fell Conrad, count palatine of Vohburg [Col. 0335C], with many others.

§ XXXVII.

King Henry again sought to win Pope Gregory over with many flattering words [Note: [Col. 0336D] Berthold, under the year 1083], so that he might reconcile himself with him; but Gregory, steadfast in justice, could in no way be turned aside unless Henry repented of his impiety. Therefore, driven from his homeland, he went to Salerno, where he convened a synod [Note: [Col. 0336D] See below, § 42, and Berthold under this year, where this synod at Salerno is asserted against almost all other accounts. What is said here about those excepted from excommunication belongs to the synod of 1078.]. He again sharpened the sword of excommunication against Wibert and Henry, and against all their supporters and those who consented to their errors. He excepted peasants, children, and women who did not assist them either with weapons or with counsel.

In that same city, overtaken by the end of his life, he is reported to have said this memorial statement before his death: “Because I loved justice and hated those who commit transgressions, therefore I am dying in exile.” He died in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1081 [Note: [Col. 0336D] According to § 42, the year 1085 must be substituted.].

As King Henry was returning from Italy to the German regions, he found Duke Welf besieging Augsburg because of his hatred for Bishop Siegfried [Col. 0336B], and he drove him away from there [Note: [Col. 0336D] See the *Chronicle of Augsburg* under the years 1081 and 1084; Berthold should also be consulted for the latter year.].

§ XXXVIII.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1086 [Note: [Col. 0336D] Compare Berthold under this year, from whom our chronicler copied this almost word for word.], the faithful of Saint Peter held a general assembly after the feast of the apostles near Würzburg. Wishing to disturb it, King Henry arrived with an army; but when a multitude of Suevians with their princes arrived, he yielded the place for a time.

When the Suevians had joined Herbipolis and the Saxons had surrounded it, King Henry, having gathered an army of twenty thousand, drew up his battle line to liberate the city. But they advanced to meet him, carrying an upright cross, relying not so much on weapons as on the mercy of God, and halted two miles away. Very many of the king’s side having been killed, the Suevians [Col. 0336C] and Saxons emerged victorious; from their own army they lost only three men.

They carried away not only chests containing the royal garments but also the bishops’ mitres of those who had been with him in the battle [Col. 0337A]. That night they pitched their camp in the same field among the corpses of the slain. Then, returning to the siege, they captured the city without bloodshed.

§ XXXIX.

King Hermann [Note: [Col. 0337D] Our author gives here particular details about the final fate of King Hermann, which are absent from Berthold under the year 1088 and should be added to what is related by Calles, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. V, pp. 836 ff.], while staying in Alemannia and lacking the royal revenues by which he could have lived according to royal dignity—for none of the bishops wished to submit to him—came to the city of Constance and remained there for several days. From there he crossed the Rhine and spent nearly a week in the monastery of Petershausen.

Afterward he went to Saxony. As he was passing near a certain castle one day, someone on the fortress accidentally threw a stone and struck the king unexpectedly on the head [Col. 0337B]; from this injury he died not long afterward.

§ XL.

Then, after approximately six years [Note: [Col. 0337D] Namely, in 1093; according to Berthold, he died in 1101, as the *Saxon Annals* testify.], Conrad, the son of King Henry, crossing into Italy—as he himself admitted, to flee his father’s crimes—reigned there for a short time, and ended his life by poison. He lies buried at rest near the city of Florence.

§ XLI.

After these varied struggles, many calamities, immeasurable bloodshed, and the destruction of very many souls, Henry at last obtained the monarchy alone. Almost all the princes were reconciled to him and acknowledged him as the legitimate emperor. He always had all the cities adjoining the Rhine, as well as other powerful and metropolitan cities, allied with him; and many of the bishops were so closely bound to him that they could in no way be separated from him [Col. 0337C]. Among them was Otto, bishop of Constance. Since he was wholly unwilling, at the command and authority of the apostolic see, to break the oaths he had sworn to Henry, he was rejected by religious Catholics.

§ XLII.

In the year 1085 from the Incarnation, Pope Gregory, also called Hildebrand, while an exile at Salerno, convened a synod and again pronounced the sentence of anathema against the schismatic Wibert, against the said King Henry, and against their supporters [Col. 0337D]. The legates of the apostolic see—namely, Peter, bishop of Albano, in France, and Otto, bishop of Ostia, later pope, throughout the German lands—spread this sentence everywhere.

§ XLIII. On Hirsau and Gebhard III, bishop of Constance.

[Col. 0338A]

At that time the fervor of spiritual discipline was burning most intensely at the monastery called Hirsau. Many nobles and commoners, clerics and laymen, as well as monks from other places, flocked there. Emerging as if from a great shipwreck amid the storm of anathema that was then violently battering the ship of the Church, they took refuge there as though in a harbor and rejoiced that they had found the peace of the salvation they desired.

Among them was Gebhard, a most noble man, brother of Berthold II, duke of Zähringen. He had been provost at Xanten; abandoning worldly affairs, he withdrew to the aforesaid monastery [Note: [Col. 0337D] Trithemius, *Annals of Hirsau*, under the year 1085, although in attributing the foundation of the monastery of Petershausen to this man he wrongly confuses him with Gebhard II. Xanten, where he had previously been provost, is a town of Cleves with a once-prominent collegiate church in the diocese of Cologne.], and, just as he had changed his habit for a religious purpose, so he also took up the dignity of virtuous conduct [Col. 0338B].

§ XLIV.

When Otto, bishop of Ostia, had arrived at Constance on an apostolic mission [Note: [Col. 0338D] See Berthold’s Chronicle under the year 1084.] and had found that the Church itself was deprived of a shepherd because of the condemnation of Otto, who had been its bishop, he took counsel with venerable Fathers and religious Catholics about how he might provide for the government of that Church [Col. 0338D]. At that time William, abbot of Hirsau, happened to be present—a man, I say, acceptable to God and human beings, because he was exceedingly learned in letters and most devoted to regular discipline, humble, gentle, a despiser of the world, and an exceptionally diligent lover of monks and of all holiness.

§ XLV.

[Col. 0338C]

When he was present at the assembly and had the aforementioned Gebhard with him, they began to discuss the election of a Catholic bishop, since there was no hope concerning the condemned Otto. During these discussions, the monk Gebhard withdrew behind the altar of Blessed Mary and devoted himself there to prayer in greater secrecy.

Why say more? They elected this same Gebhard bishop of the Church of Constance. After everyone had agreed, and while he himself knew absolutely nothing of the matter, they approached him and said: “By God’s grace, this Church has today chosen you as its bishop.”

When he heard this, his spirit departed from him, so that he fell to the ground and lay there as if dead. Nevertheless, after his spirit returned, they compelled him against his will on that same day—namely, on the feast of Saint Thomas—to become a priest, and on the following day ordained him bishop [Col. 0338D] [Note: [Col. 0338D] Berthold likewise places this under the year 1084; therefore Manlius should be corrected, since he says it happened on 13 December.].

Otto, however, having been driven from possession of the same Church, which is called Colmbra [Note: [Col. 0338D] Otto, deposed in the following year, 1085, was again struck with anathema at the Council of Quedlinburg; and, according to Manlius, he died excommunicated in 1086 and was buried at Basel. Bucelinus asserts the same in his *Chronology of Constance*. It therefore seems quite likely that Colmbra is none other than Columbra, or Columbarium, or Colmaria, in Upper Alsace and the diocese of Basel.], went there and, after spending almost a year in that place, ended his life.

INCIPIT LIBER TERTIUS.

[Col. 0339]

§ I. How the monks of Hirsau came to the House of Peter.

[Col. 0339A]

Since the vigor of regular life was already failing at the monastery of Saint Gregory the Pope, which is called the House of Peter, and was neither flourishing effectively nor entirely absent, and since Gebhard III held the pontifical see of the Church of Constance by apostolic authority, he grieved that the deficiency of divine service had grown in the monastery adjoining his church. He therefore appealed to the venerable William, abbot of Hirsau, asking him to send regular men from his monastery to Petershausen, through whom the monastic order might revive there.

William, who was ready to accomplish every good work, sent distinguished and very religious men, together with a certain Otto, who was to be their abbot if, after a period of testing, his life and conduct pleased them [Col. 0339B]. But shortly afterward this same Otto displeased his brothers, and they were unwilling in any way to submit to his direction; therefore he was ordered to return to his own monastery.

§ II.

Luitold, likewise the abbot of that monastery, and Rupert the schoolmaster, together with certain other senior brothers, yielded their place to the monks arriving from Hirsau and withdrew to the monastery of Augia. Some also adopted clerical dress.

The aforementioned Rupert was an outstanding master in all the liberal disciplines. Bernard likewise, a monk of the same monastery and a man of the highest wisdom and learning, had at that time, together with Rupert, brought up a large number of students in that same place [Col. 0339C], since they presided over the schools and advanced many to the best education.

This Bernard [Note: [Col. 0339D] He may easily have been the author of the *Apologeticus on the Excommunication of Gregory VII*, which Gretser published among Bernard’s works, vol. VI, p. 29, and which Bernold says was brought from Hirsau in his letter to Adalbert, provost of Strasbourg (to be published below, vol. II). Perhaps Gretser’s own manuscript preferred the name Bernard, or Bernald. Since this Bernard had already withdrawn to Hirsau before the year 1085, he must be distinguished from another man of the same name, a teacher of the schools of Constance and later a monk of Corvey, to whom letters of our Bernold survive [Col. 0340C], to be published below, vol. II. This should be noted for the *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, p. 274, where the conjecture concerning this Bernard must be corrected in light of these statements.], as well as Wernhar, who possessed almost equal learning, had already joined himself to the monastery of Hirsau, fleeing the anathema.

§ III. How Theodoric arrived, and concerning his lineage and way of life.

Therefore the monks of Hirsau sent by Abbot William—very religious men—entered the monastery of the House of Peter and vigorously practiced the spiritual warfare for which they had been assigned. When, within a short time, they discovered that Otto, appointed as their superior, was blameworthy in certain matters [Col. 0340A], they immediately sent him back to his own people and asked that another man worthy to preside over them be assigned with the support of Bishop Gebhard.

Accordingly, Abbot William, employing excellent counsel, sent the most venerable Theodoric [Note: [Col. 0340D] Trithemius composed an extensive eulogy of this Theodoric (*Annals of Hirsau*, vol. I, p. 267), although he says nothing about his lineage; nor can we affirm anything certain about it. Nevertheless, as can be gathered from what follows, he is to be sought in Swabia. See the preliminary inquiry, § 25.], thoroughly instructed in both secular and monastic learning and entirely suitable for this government.

§ IV.

His father, Count Conrad, had a concubine named Bertha, whom he loved greatly, and he had taken no other wife besides her. She bore him three sons, very handsome in body and no less acute in mind: namely, Luitold, Marquard, and Theodoric.

But Luitold and Marquard, after their father’s death, passed into the jurisdiction of Count Hartmann of Dillingen [Col. 0340B], because they had been born of a servant woman. Nevertheless, they became extremely capable and exceedingly bold in every military matter, so much so that King Henry admitted Luitold among the twelve men whom he always kept with him as confidants and supporters of his crimes, since he was strong, very swift, and conspicuous for every military excellence. For this reason he also earned from that same king a privilege of freedom, both for himself and for all his descendants.

§ V.

Theodoric, however, in the first bloom of youthful age indulged the allurements of the flesh as his mind prompted him. But he restrained his mind from this inclination at a more mature age, for he was thoroughly trained in letters. A man of excellent bearing, eloquent in speech, and sufficiently venerable in appearance, he sought the monastery of Saint Ulrich at Augsburg and there first made himself a monk.

But since the poison of anathema at that time infected not only clerics and laymen but also very many members of monasteries, the venerable Theodoric withdrew from this danger and went to Hirsau. Joining himself to that monastery, he submitted to the direction of the abbot William, worthy of God, and under him grew so greatly within a short time in every discipline of regular life that it seemed he ought not merely to be subordinate but rather to preside.

Then he was placed in charge of a certain cell called Augia Leporis [Note: [Col. 0340D] This name seems to indicate the cell of Hasenau, or rather Hasungen, in Hesse and the diocese of Mainz. In 1070 Giselbert was appointed abbot there from Hirsau; after being expelled in 1085 (*Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 581), Theodoric may perhaps have served under him as prior, and was then recalled to Hirsau to administer the same office, as Trithemius writes in the cited passage, p. 289. See Gerbert, *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, pp. 272 and 293. It is indeed noted below, § 17, that Hasuunouwa was donated by Count Ulrich of Bregenz to the monastery of Petershausen; this may likewise be Hasenau, although I find no cell there.], and afterward was recalled to the monastery and appointed prior of the entire congregation. He presided vigorously for some time [Col. 0341A].

§ VI. How Theodoric was ordained.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1086, the reverend Bishop Gebhard III of Constance, the third of that name, obtained through exceptional prayers from William, abbot of Hirsau, of blessed memory, that he send the venerable man Theodoric to the monastery of Saint Gregory, called the House of Peter, so that he might preside over it and establish regular life there according to the rule of his monastery.

After he had obtained this request and Theodoric had arrived, the aforesaid bishop, at the unanimous petition of all the brothers, ordained him abbot of that monastery on the feast of Saint Barnabas the Apostle [Col. 0341B] [Note: [Col. 0341D] The administration of Abbot Theodoric therefore begins on 11 June 1086; thus Gebhard was still at Constance. [Col. 0342D]]. He loved and encouraged him and was always a source of assistance to him whenever he could be.

§ VII.

After his ordination, he devoted himself to every form of religious observance. He cared for the souls and bodies of his subjects with every diligence, educated them with the strictest discipline, and increased the number of his disciples, so that within a short time he had more than forty monks and more than fifty bearded brothers. He provided them with complete abundance of food and clothing, while restraining their life with great strictness.

§ VIII.

Because the choir was small—the steps by which one ascended into the sanctuary occupied the space—he reduced the number of the stone steps and enlarged the space for the singers. He removed the stones and set men in their place, making the choir almost equal to the sanctuary, the sanctuary rising above it by only one step. Thus he enlarged the space for those standing in the choir. . .

§ IX.

347 He used the very steps that he had removed from the choir to adorn other buildings thereafter. He constructed a washroom, placing part of those same steps there, and renovated the chapter house and the entire cloister surrounding it. He also enclosed the precinct of the cell with a wall and built a portico over the tombs of his predecessors, the abbots.

He completed all these works, as well as the others to be narrated below, not from the revenues or wealth of that place but from the donations of the faithful. Because of the novelty of the pure life that he had recently introduced into this region, everyone honored and loved him, and many entrusted themselves and their possessions to him.

Bishop Gebhard of Constance also assisted him greatly by making gifts, by entrusting to him both clerics and laymen who were answerable to him because of their faults, and, since this Father was eloquent in speech, by lending a gracious ear to him in all matters [Col. 0342A].

It also contributed to this that he was excessively generous to everyone and sparing toward himself. He weakened his body with extreme fasts, while granting complete abundance to all who lived with him and to those who came to him. Therefore he was always in the greatest anxiety, since he was continually bound by enormous debts; nevertheless, because he trusted in the Lord, he easily repaid everything through his generosity.

§ X.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, the venerable Abbot Theodoric built a chapel on the southern side of the basilica, beside the sanctuary and on elevated ground, in honor of Saint Ulrich the bishop, Saint Nicholas, Saint Afra, and Saints John and Paul. He had it dedicated on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June] [Col. 0342B]. He placed the relics of the saints there. . .

§ XI.

In the following year, that is, in the year 1093 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction 1, he built a chapel on the northern side of the sacristy and had it dedicated on the fifth day before the Ides of September in honor of Saint Mary, the Mother of God, and of the other saints whose relics are kept there. . . . Every day after Vespers and Matins, the community solemnly processes to this chapel in honor of Saint Mary; there, after singing her canticle, antiphon, and prayer, they sing Vespers or Matins for all the saints and for the dead.

§ XII.

348 Likewise, in the year 1094 of the Lord’s Incarnation, indiction 2, [Col. 0342C] Abbot Theodoric renovated and enlarged the chapel of Saint Michael; for it was exceedingly small, so that it could scarcely hold twelve men. It is situated beside the infirmary, and between the infirmary and the aforementioned chapel there was a small building in which the sick often lay. The aforesaid abbot demolished this building and added it to the chapel, and constructed a new altar. He had the chapel dedicated by the venerable Bishop Gebehard, the third of that name, as were the preceding chapels, [Note: [Col. 0342D] It is clear from this that Gebehard, although driven from his see, nevertheless returned from time to time to Constance.] on the Nones of July in honor of the Lord and of the Holy Cross, and especially in honor of Saint Mary, the Mother of the Lord, Saint Michael the Archangel, and all the saints.

§ XIII.

He also enlarged the chapel of Saint Andrew and assigned to the bearded brothers the buildings added to it, which [Col. 0342D] had previously been the dwelling places of the abbots of that place. The chapel itself, however, was very small, and so forth. . . .

§ XIV. What Sort of Disciples He Had

At that time the same venerable Father had under his care outstanding men, very religious and of excellent appearance and learning. Among them were Meinrad, formerly abbot, about whom we have spoken above [Note: [Col. 0342D] Book II, § 15, and below §§ 18, 20.], Bernhard the schoolmaster, Cuono, Wernharius of Alshusin, whose eyes were dim, Gozhalmus and Eberhardus, and also Heinricus the scribe. All these were from among the older brothers; but there were also Sigiherus the schoolmaster, Eppo, and Gebehardus, my grandfather. . . .

Bernhard, whom we also mentioned above, was an exceptional teacher and proved himself an exceedingly diligent guardian of monastic discipline. One night he saw a vision, which he himself committed to writing. . . .

§ XV.

There was another priest in the monastery itself, named Cuono, whom we also mentioned earlier. He was, I say, a very handsome man, one of the former monks, who had also earned the administration of the monastery of Rheinau [Note: [Col. 0343D] Cuno Gerungi became the first successor there in the abbacy of Rheinau around the year 1090 and introduced the customs of Hirsau from his own monastery. After accidentally committing homicide, however, he abandoned his dignity and secretly departed elsewhere, also usurping episcopal functions for himself. The writer calls the province Riez; it is uncertain whether this means Riesa or Riezza, a district in Raetia in the Nordgau, or Regio in the province called Rieze. In the meantime, when Pope Urban II was consulted by Bishop Gebehard about whether he might retain his dignity with a dispensation, he replied in writing that he could. See *Canon Clerico*, distinction 50, canon 37, where Gebehard of Constance seems to have to be substituted for Gwarnerius of Narbonne, especially since at the time of Urban II there was no Quarnerius bishop of Narbonne—although that passage speaks of throwing a stone and says nothing about dignity.]—for he had been appointed abbot there. But one day, angered against a servant, he struck him carelessly with the bolt of a door, [Col. 0343B] and from that blow the man began to fall ill and eventually died. Because of this offense he was deprived not only of the honor of the priesthood but also of the dignity of governance.

He therefore left that place and went to the province called Riez. In those parts he fraudulently usurped for himself the office of a bishop, dedicated churches, deceitfully anointed people with the oil of confirmation, performed other episcopal functions, and thereby amassed no small amount of money. When he had fully satisfied his desire in this matter, he laid aside the insignia of his vanity, returned to his former monastery—that is, Domus Petri—and submitted himself to the instruction of the venerable Abbot Theodoric.

Although he was legally excluded from the altar’s ministry, he was nevertheless a very capable man. Abbot [Col. 0343C] Theodoric, therefore, obtained through urgent petitions to Bishop Gebehard that he should finally be permitted to celebrate Mass. . . .

§ XVI. On Udalric of Bregenz

Around this time many people enjoyed the great favor of familiarity with the venerable Theodoric, because he was himself a religious and prudent man, useful in action and counsel. For this reason, noblemen and wealthy men came to him from every direction, wishing to advance through his example and advice. Among them was Count Udalric of Bregenz [Note: [Col. 0344D] See above, Book II, § 20. Here the reference is to the younger Udalric, who is named in a charter of Henry IV in 1095 as Odalric, count of Bregenz; his county was situated in Churwalchen. See Herrgott, vol. II, p. 130; see also the preliminary dissertation, § 24.], a man of the highest nobility and handsome appearance, who enjoyed the greatest friendship and intimacy with him.

§ XVII.

There was also a certain solitary, named Diedo, who had made for himself an oratory and dwelling in a forest called Andoltisbuoch [Note: [Col. 0344D] This seems to be Andelspuech in the chapter of Lindau.]. He had brought new land under cultivation around it, and the place appeared suitable for the service of the Lord.

After this solitary had fallen asleep in the Lord, Count Udalric asked the venerable Theodoric to build a cell there and establish a regular life in it. Theodoric absolutely refused to do so unless the count transferred the same place to his monastery as property, so that, if he labored there, he might also receive some benefit from it. After lengthy deliberation, the count finally agreed. He sent to the monastery of Saint Gregory the relics of the saints that the aforementioned servant of God had possessed in his oratory at the place of solitude. Later, before suitable witnesses and without any opposition, he transferred to the monastery of Petershausen, as perpetual property and for the service of the brothers who would serve God there continually through the succession of time, the place called Andoltisbuoch and another possession called Hasuunouwa [Note: [Col. 0344D] Could this perhaps be Augia Leporis, which above, § 5, is now simply called Auw in the same chapter of Lindau?], on the condition that a cell be built there and that a dwelling for monks be maintained there continually, according to the resources of the place.

§ XVIII.

After this donation had been completed, Abbot Theodoric began to inhabit the place. With much labor and expense he built there an oratory and cloister of wooden boards, had them dedicated in honor of Saint Peter the Apostle, and, assigning suitable brothers to the place, appointed Meinrad [Note: [Col. 0344D] This is Meginrad, formerly abbot of Petershausen. See above, § 14. He is called the first abbot of Augia Alba Brigantina after its restoration in 1087 in Gallia Christiana, vol. V, p. 972.], about whom we have also spoken above, [Col. 0344C] over them.

When they had remained there for some time, and the number of brothers had begun to increase, they found that they could scarcely transport provisions and other necessities there because of the length and difficulty of the journey, since the place lay deep in the forest. They therefore took counsel to move the cell to Bregenz, where the brothers could obtain what they needed more easily and conveniently.

§ XIX.

Accordingly, Abbot Theodoric came to the place called Bregenz, bringing with him Bishop Gebehard, Meinrad, Count Udalric, and others necessary for this undertaking, so that they might see where the cell ought to be built, since it had been decided to move it out of the forest.

After lengthy deliberation, they decided that it should be built beside the church [Col. 0345A] of that place, if Count Ludewicus [Note: [Col. 0345D] From the context it is clear that this Ludovicus was the Count of Pfullendorf, who may also have been of Helfenstein. He was perhaps the very man whose wife Count Otto, apparently of Montfort, abducted, according to Lazius, p. 553. See Berthold’s *Chronicle*, under the year 1089.] were willing to permit his share of that church to be used for the purpose. For there is a baptismal church there, half of which, together with the forests and all the revenues of those regions, belongs to the nobles of Pfullendorf, just as the other half belongs to the people of Bregenz.

Count Ludewicus, however, by no means agreed to surrender his share. Therefore, abandoning their earlier plan, they turned elsewhere. Since the earlier cell possessed a small house nearby, they approached it and searched all around among the thickets for a suitable place, which they found by the Lord’s direction. For while the venerable Gebehard was walking around praying, inspecting and examining the surrounding places, he suddenly stopped at one spot and judged that a cell should be built there.

§ XX.

[Col. 0345B]

When everyone had agreed unanimously to this, Theodoric began to build a cell there. At the expense and from the resources of his monastery, to which this place had been transferred as property, just as the earlier one had been, he first built an oratory and then a cloister [Note: [Col. 0345D] From this we learn that a monastery built there long before had been almost completely destroyed to its foundations. See *Gallia Christiana*, cited above; Bruschius, on Alba Augia.], everything constructed of wooden boards, and had them dedicated in honor of Saint Peter.

He appointed Meinrad abbot there, just as he had once been at Domus Petri. Theodoric himself, however, frequently visited the place and attended to its needs. For nearly five years he spent on the construction of these two cells whatever was supposed to come from Eichstätt to Petershausen. In addition, he contributed sacred vestments, books, and relics of the saints, both those that had originally been sent [Col. 0345C] from Andoltisbuoch and many others, numerous and splendid.

§ XXI.

When the place had begun to prosper and grow wealthy, they began to consider how it might be granted liberty. After lengthy deliberation, they found that this could in no way be done better than by Count Udalric’s returning to the monastery of Petershausen the estate called Biginhusin [Note: [Col. 0345D] Bichishausen in the chapter of Munderkingen.], which his father had once donated, and by his receiving Bregenz from the monastery in exchange.

The same count, while still a young man, had become betrothed to the daughter of Count Wernher of Habichisburc [Note: [Col. 0345D] This must have been Wernher II, Count of Habsburg, who died in 1096. Hergott, vol. I, p. 142, gives him one daughter, later married to Rudolph of Tierstein.], and had confirmed the betrothal by oath. Before he took her as his wife, however, he went with Duke Welf to Chalaminza [Col. 0345D] [Note: [Col. 0345D] In the Upper Palatinate, or the duchy of Neuburg, which at that time was subject to Duke Welf.], and secretly slept with Bertha, daughter of King Ruodolf [Note: [Col. 0346D] Most people identify this Bertha as the daughter of Count Rudolph of Rheinfelden, later anti-king, by his second wife, Adelheid. For a fuller account of them, see His Highness Gerbert, *Treatise on Rudolph the Anti-King*, pp. 118, 143 ff.]. He wanted the matter to remain hidden, but the girl made it public. Thus the power of her relatives compelled him to take her in marriage. He made amends for the oath he had sworn to Wernher’s daughter and returned from his own possessions everything he had promised her.

Consequently, when he gave the revenues and benefices of some of his ministeriales there and assigned them elsewhere, he also transferred some of them to Biginhusin, where their descendants still flourish. Therefore, as I think, this was the occasion on which the estate was taken away from the monastery.

§ XXII.

Accordingly, as was said above, in order to receive Bregenz, Count Udalric restored Biginhusin to the monastery of Petershausen; nothing was done concerning Andoltisbuoch and Hasuunouwa. The original arrangement, however, remained untouched. Through the negligence of our people it passed into the use of the men of Bregenz, although the Bregenz exchange was not legally valid: Biginhusin had previously belonged to the monastery, and under the law of that time it was restored without purchase as something that had been taken away by fraud.

For the ornaments and ecclesiastical utensils—sacred vestments, metal objects, books, and relics of the saints—that had been sent there from the monastery so that they might remain there, thirty talents were given. After these matters had been settled, they began to build the church out of stone.

§ XXIII.

At the same time Count Udalric went to Bretingen and stayed there for several days with [Col. 0346C] a large number of his men. One day, after dinner, some young men climbed nearby to the ridge of a high mountain and began rolling rocks down into the valley for amusement. One of them, named Opertus, rolled down a rock and shouted a warning to those below in the valley.

It happened that Count Udalric was walking in the opposite direction. He did not wish to avoid the stone’s blow but tried to leap over it. The stone struck him in the shin and shattered it. Soon afterward a malignant swelling developed, and it killed him within a short time [Note: [Col. 0346D] Berthold of Constance briefly describes his death under the year 1097 and relates that he was buried on 27 October in the monastery he had founded. His death is also recorded on that day in the ancient necrology of that monastery, as is that of his wife Bertha on 20 January in the Zwiefalten entry, “Bertha, countess of Bregenz.”].

He was therefore carried to Bregenz. Since the church had not yet been dedicated, his body was kept unburied until the bishop could be summoned to dedicate the oratory. When Abbot Theodoric heard them murmuring that they wanted to reclaim Biginhusin for their own right, he absolutely refused to permit the bishop to dedicate the church before Bertha, Udalric’s widow, with her sons Rudolph and [Col. 0347A] Udalric [Note: [Col. 0347C] In discussing the sons of Count Udalric of Bregenz by Bertha, Lazius contradicts himself. In the Counts of Bregenz, p. 557, he asserts that Udalric was Count of Bregenz and Rudolph was his brother, Count of Pfullendorf, the founder of the monastery of Auw above Bregenz; earlier, however, on p. 51, he counts this same Udalric among the counts of Sulgau, Sigmaringen, and Pfullendorf, and then gives an account of his descendants. See the preliminary dissertation, § 24.]—should confirm Biginhusin before many witnesses, both freedmen and serfs, as a perpetual possession of Saint Gregory.

Thus Bregenz was left free, on the condition that those living there should always maintain regard for Domus Petri, receive counsel and assistance, governance and an abbot from there, and remain one and the same community. At last the oratory was dedicated, and Udalric’s body was buried there.

§ XXIV. On Wagenhausen

There was a nobleman named Tuoto who offered his estate at Wagenhausen [Note: [Col. 0347D] Wagenhausen on the Swiss bank of the Rhine, opposite the town of Stein. There was formerly another Benedictine monastery there as well, belonging to the same order. Some information about it is given in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 932, and by Franciscus Petri in *Ecclesiastical Swabia*, p. 846, as well as by His Highness Gerbert, *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, p. 436.
