Its founder seems to have been this same Tuto, whom Berthold mentions under the year 1092 and whom Dudo calls him under the year 1094. His account, however, does not agree sufficiently with our chronicle, since the monastery is said to have been assigned to Abbot Sigifrid in 1094 by Bishop Gebhard himself, who is reported to have entrusted it a few years later to the monks of Petershausen under Adalbert, elected abbot of Schaffhausen in 1099. From there, too, it received its first abbots.], together with everything else he possessed, and offered himself to Schaffhausen. For some time he lived there in a holy vocation.

Later, withdrawing himself and everything he had transferred there, he afflicted them with such great troubles that they finally handed over three estates to him and renounced him—namely Wagenhausen, where they had already built a cell, Capella, and Honstetin—so that at least they themselves might possess the rest in peace.

After this had been done, Tuoto transferred the aforementioned cell of Wagenhausen, with all its appurtenances, to the church of Constance, in the presence of Adalbert, abbot of Schaffhausen, his advocate Adalbert, Count of Morisberch [Note: [Col. 0348D] Nobles of Morsperg or Mersperg in Alsace occur in various thirteenth-century charters in P. Herrgott. See *History of the Black Forest*, vol. II, p. 229.], and several of the brothers, none of whom objected. The transaction took place in a public synod at Constance before many suitable witnesses.

Bishop Gebehard entrusted the place that had been given to him to Abbot Theodoric, and Theodoric himself brought suitable brothers there. Through them he cultivated and developed the place for many years. After this, the men of Schaffhausen and Tuoto’s heirs began to claim the place, asserting that it rightfully belonged to both of them, and thus they have been a great hindrance to its growth down to the present.

§ XXV. On King Henry

At the same time there was a great schism in the Church because of the excommunication of King Henry and of his intruder Wibert, some supporting the latter and others the Church. Consequently, some bishops were driven from their own sees and wandered in exile. Among them was Diemo, archbishop of Salzburg [Note: [Col. 0348D] Our local records also show that this Thiemo was an exile with Gebehard. From them we learn that a charter of Uto, abbot of Saint Blaise, concerning the foundation of the monastery of Ochsenhausen was drawn up in 1100 with the advice of Archbishop Thiemo of Salzburg and Bishop Gebehard of Constance; see the cited *History of the Black Forest*, vol. III, p. 39.].

After being an exile for many days, he stayed with Bishop Gebehard of Constance at the monastery of Domus Petri. Later, while traveling to Jerusalem, he was captured by pagans on the journey itself, brought to the city of Chorazin, and handed over to custody. Finally, he was crowned with martyrdom.

§ XXVI.

King Henry therefore appointed the abbot of the monastery of Saint Gall [Note: [Col. 0348D] This was Udalric III, son of Margrave Marquard of Carinthia. In 1086 Henry IV appointed him, his kinsman, to the see of Aquileia. For more on him, see Burchard, *On the Affairs of Saint Gall*, chapter 4.] patriarch at Aquileia and permitted him to exercise both powers, because he always supported Henry’s errors with all his strength. Ordained by Wibert, Udalric exercised tyranny against the Catholics.

For this reason he also urged the king to expel the venerable Gebehard, Bishop of Constance, and appoint another in his place, because Gebehard had never been willing in any way to associate with Henry or any of his supporters. At that time Gebehard was the apostolic legate and vicar in the German regions.

The aforementioned Udalric, after maintaining a long conspiracy with the king, finally offered him one of his monks, named Arnold, descended from Sanctomonte, promising that if the king granted him the bishopric, he himself would install Arnold without difficulty. When the king had granted his request, Udalric returned home, gathered a large military force, and brought Arnold to Constance. But when the citizens rushed to arms and resisted with determined courage, they withdrew without accomplishing anything [Note: [Col. 0348D] On this matter, see Bucelinus, *Chronology of Constance*, under the year 1087, and Manlius, *Chronicle*.].

§ XXVII.

Likewise, Heinricus, Arnold’s brother and advocate, came with a multitude of his men and exercised tyranny in the monastery of Saint Gregory. For they seized the brothers’ provisions with reckless hands, tested their swords on the brothers’ animals, and [Col. 0348C] committed many shameful acts.

Amid these varied and manifold conflicts, Bishop Gebehard built a fortress for himself at the head of the Rhine River, in the very waters of the stream, so that he could remain safe there. Finally, both his brother, Duke Bertold, and nearly all the others were corrupted by bribes and became hateful to him; there was no one who would do him good, except for one Theodoric, whom he found faithful in all his tribulations.

§ XXVIII.

Accordingly, giving way before their treachery, he withdrew and exercised throughout the kingdom, with great glory although in exile, the office of the apostolic lord. Then, as though unbridled, they brought Arnold with great uproar and installed him in the chair of the Church of Constance on the Purification of Saint Mary, in the year 1103 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

This war, prolonged for nearly twelve years, had now reached its complete evil. After Arnold obtained the bishopric, he immediately sent word and earnestly requested that the community of Domus Petri remain quietly and peacefully in its monastery and serve the Lord, promising that he would cause them no trouble whatsoever. He then went to Rome and received consecration from Wibert [Note: [Col. 0349D] According to *Gallia Christiana* and Manlius, Arnold had already been ordained by the antipope Clement III, who died in 1100.].

§ XXIX.

But Abbot Theodoric was not permitted to enjoy any peace after the departure of Bishop Gebehard, because he loved him as his own soul. In that same year, 1103, he left his monastery, distributed and entrusted his monks and bearded brothers among various monasteries, and took with him twelve whom he had chosen. He led them to Bavaria, to the monastery called Wezzinisbrunnin [Note: [Col. 0349D] Wessobrunn, a famous Benedictine monastery in Upper Bavaria and the diocese of Augsburg, over which Adalbero was abbot from 1065 to 1110.]. The venerable Abbot Adalbero received him and his companions honorably and treated them with affection for several months.

§ XXX.

Afterward, a most noble and religious man named Fridericus took them from there and entrusted to them a cell that he had begun on his own estate, on a high mountain called Castellum [Note: [Col. 0349D] A formerly magnificent monastery of the Benedictine order in the Upper Palatinate, founded by the aforementioned Count Fridericus of Castelberg, who is said to have died in this very year, 1103. His son was Count Otto of Hirsberg, or Hebberg, or Habsperg, in 1105. See Bruschius, *On the Monastery of Castellum*, p. 120.], [Col. 0349C] and he supported and honored them with every kindness.

Finally, this hero of blessed memory, named Fridericus, had a son named Otto, a man of the highest nobility and distinction. Together with his father and with the other nobles of that region—his kinsmen, relatives, and friends—he honored the venerable Theodoric and his brothers with the greatest respect and enriched the place with great wealth. As a result, Theodoric soon gathered many brothers around him and established monastic life there with the greatest propriety.

§ XXXI.

After Theodoric had departed from Domus Petri, those who remained there at that time appointed a certain Wernher, born at Epfindorf, as their abbot. [Col. 0349D] Forgetting the regular discipline they had learned, they began to act more laxly.

Arnold, the intruding bishop, also began granting its benefices to his own men, [Col. 0350A] something that no bishop had ever been permitted to do. After Wernher and his supporters, and Arnold with his supporters, had reduced the monastery’s possessions to the utmost poverty and destitution, Wernher abandoned the name of abbot and went to Theodoric in Bavaria. He submitted himself to him, and Theodoric received him kindly and restored to him the altar’s ministry, against the will of Bishop Gebehard. But the horn of the sinner did not remain long [Note: [Col. 0350D] See below, § 36.].

§ XXXII. On King Henry V

Finally, in the year 1105, Henry, son of King Henry III (IV), withdrew from his excommunicated father. With the princes’ consent, he seized the kingdom against his father. From this arose the greatest opportunity for quarrels. For his father Henry, unable to recall his son to himself, gathered an army and harassed all his supporters with the greatest plundering and burning, though he never gave them the opportunity for battle.

§ XXXIII.

After Henry had obtained the kingdom, he immediately expelled Arnold and restored Gebehard to his bishopric with the greatest honor. He chose Abbot Theodoric as his confessor, restored him to his monastery, and sent him thirty marks of silver. With this money the abbot repaired the monastery’s scattered and ruined affairs suitably and effectively.

§ XXXIV.

Afterward, the elder Henry and the younger Henry held a general assembly at Mainz. There the father handed over to his son the royal scepter and crown, together with the other royal insignia. He then prostrated himself on the ground before Gebehard, as the legate of the Apostolic See, and, weeping bitterly, asked to be absolved from excommunication.

Gebehard refused to do this because he feared that, if he happened to absolve him, the kingdom might again pass to him, and “the latter error become worse than the first” [Note: [Col. 0350D] See the *Annals of Hildesheim* under the year 1103 and the *Life of Henry IV* in Urstisius, p. 389. There the name of the legate is not given, but here it is shown to have been Gebehard.].

Nevertheless, since the elder Henry died at Speyer not long afterward, his son, having obtained permission from Pope Paschal, secured ecclesiastical burial for him on account of the satisfaction he had performed publicly before clergy and people without shame, lying prostrate [Note: [Col. 0350D] Conrad of Ursperg, under the year 1111.].

§ XXXV.

Thus, after the venerable Theodoric had founded the monastery of Castellum, begun to build its basilica, and gathered a community of brothers, he appointed the venerable Altmann [Note: [Col. 0350D] He is called Otto by others. An ancient Castellum record reads: “Altmann, the first abbot of this monastery, undertook the governance of this place in 1103,” though it says nothing there about Theodoric.] as their abbot, and he himself returned with his companions to Domus Petri.

§ XXXVI.

[Col. 0350D]

After this, the elder Count Hartmann of Dillingen [Note: [Col. 0350D] Father of Udalric I, Bishop of Constance. See above, Book I, § 8, and the preliminary dissertation, § 21.] asked him to bring monks to the mountain called Nernistheim [Col. 0351A] [Note: [Col. 0351D] Now Neresheim, a Benedictine monastery in Swabia. See Bruschius, p. 337, and below, § 39. P. Khaman says nothing about it in *Augsburg Hierarchy*.], where he had established regular canons, and to institute monastic life there.

Theodoric consented to this request and brought suitable men: Bernold, whom he appointed prior; Gebino, my maternal uncle; his own deputy, Wernher [Note: [Col. 0351D] That is, the abbot of Petershausen, elected in his absence, § 31.]; and others sufficient for that place.

To speak once and for all about the aforementioned Wernher: while he was directing the work at that place, acting freely in whatever he wished, and being honored by everyone beyond his deserts, he departed when he had grown old, laid aside the monastic habit, and assumed a secular one. While he was building a tower for someone, he was overtaken by death and perished.

§ XXXVII.

In the year 1110 [Note: [Col. 0351D] Rather, in the following year, 1111. See the Saxon annalist.] King Henry V, with a great army, went in the greatest glory to Rome so that the pope might make him emperor. But when the pope demanded back from him the investitures—which kings had until then freely granted according to their will—so that the election might be free, Henry became angry. He reduced Pope Paschal to captivity, insulted the cardinals, and inflicted limitless plundering and slaughter upon the Romans. The Romans indeed made war against him, but the victorious king carried out indescribable massacres.

§ XXXVIII.

Meanwhile, the Bishop of Constance, Gebehard, of reverend memory, departed from this world [Note: [Col. 0351D] Manlius correctly assigns the death of Gebehard III to the year 1110, on 12 November.]. While the king held the apostolic lord in custody [Note: [Col. 0351D] Namely, from 12 February to 8 April 1111.], a messenger arrived and announced to the king the death of Bishop Gebehard. He brought him the pastoral staff and ring. The king immediately gave these to Udalric, son of Count Hartmann [Note: [Col. 0351D] See above, Book I, § 8. Although others incorrectly name his father as Hugobald, who is called by Bruschius and Lazius Udalric’s brother, Bruschius likewise calls Udalric the son of Hartmann, p. 337.], Count of Dillingen, and designated him bishop for the people of Constance.

Afterward the apostolic lord and the king were reconciled to one another, and the king, consecrated emperor by him, departed. Udalric, however, found the pope especially hostile to him, because while the pope was being held captive he had received investiture from the king. He was never able to obtain consecration while the pope lived; consequently, for the eight years during which Paschal survived, he held the bishopric without consecration.

§ XXXIX.

When the cell of Nernistheim [Note: [Col. 0352D] See immediately above, § 36. Moreover, this does not agree with Bruschius’s catalogue, which lists neither Sigiboto nor Wernharius among the abbots of Neresheim; nor does Franciscus Petri in *Ecclesiastical Swabia*. Perhaps neither remained there, or they were never blessed as abbots.] had reached the point of being suitable for an abbot, Abbot Theodoric brought from Hirsau an old man named Sigiboto, [Col. 0351D] and appointed him abbot.

After he had presided for some time without consecration [Col. 0352A] and could no longer endure the burden, he left the place and returned to his own monastery. Therefore, when Theodoric was asked again, he appointed as abbot Wernharius of Alshusin, whose eyesight was dim, a veteran monk of his own. He too presided for some time without consecration.

§ XL.

It happened that at a certain time Udalric, the elected Bishop of Constance, was compelled by grave necessity to acquire money. At that very time Abbot Theodoric had sold an estate called Totirnhusin [Note: [Col. 0352D] Perhaps Dotternhausen in the chapter of Ebingen.] for ten marks, because he could not redeem it from those to whom Lambert of Birhtilingin had previously granted it as a benefice, although Lambert had transferred it to the monastery.

When this opportunity arose, the abbot gave eight marks to the elected Udalric for a certain island called Rotse [Note: [Col. 0352D] Now Rottsee, a filial parish of Kißlegg in the chapter of Isny and the district of Nibelgau. On this place and on Blessed Ratperonius, its founder, see below, Book V, § 6.]. Long ago, a certain religious and God-fearing monk named Ratperonius had built a great basilica there, and God had glorified his tomb with frequent signs of miracles.

The blessed Ratperonius himself had received that place as property from the nobility then flourishing at Arnanch [Note: [Col. 0352D] Arnach in the chapter of Isny and the aforementioned district.], out of devotion, and had transferred it to the Church of Constance in the hope that he might thereby be elevated. That hope, however, had been frustrated. After the venerable Theodoric had purchased it, a privilege was evidently drawn up concerning it in the following form.

§ XLI.

Let it be known to all how Lambert of Birthilingin, [Col. 0352C] a nobleman, gave to the monastery of Pope Saint Gregory, called Petershausen, two estates that belonged to him by hereditary right from his parents—one at Geilinouwa and the other at Totirnhus—for the service of the brothers who serve God there day and night, without any opposition, into the hand of Heinricus [Note: [Col. 0352D] Count of Sanctomonte, as he is called shortly below.] the advocate of that monastery, before suitable witnesses.

But since Lambert could not redeem one of these, namely Totirnhus, from those to whom he had granted it as a benefice, after taking counsel, Abbot Theodoric of that monastery sold the aforesaid estate called Totirnhusa for ten marks. Taking advantage of the opportunity, he gave eight marks from that very price for an island in the district of Nibelgau called Rotse, which belonged to the Church of Constance.

The bishop of that Church, Udalric, having received the aforementioned price—that is, eight [Col. 0353A] marks—transferred the same island, with its oratory and everything belonging to it, namely fields, meadows and waters, woods, things already acquired and things still to be acquired, to the monastery of Pope Saint Gregory, called Petershausen, for the use of the brothers of that monastery. The advocate Heinricus of Sanctomonte exerted himself in the matter and both conveyed and received the property.

The aforementioned bishop transferred the island, with all its appurtenances, from the legal possession of his church into the legal possession of the monastery by a legitimate conveyance, and confirmed that conveyance before the canons of the Church of Constance and other suitable witnesses.

§ XLII.

361 During these times [Note: [Col. 0353D] These events belong to the year 1112. See Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book V, chapters 14–15.] Adalbert, the elected archbishop of Mainz, was rebelling against the king. It was then commonly reported that, at his counsel and with his assistance, he had committed all those evils that he had perpetrated at Rome; but now he was trying to deprive him of the kingdom, supposedly in revenge for the apostolic pope, but more truly out of ambition than justice. The emperor captured him, put him in prison, and afflicted him most harshly for many days. Finally, at the petition of the people of Mainz, he was released and reconciled with the emperor; but soon afterward he again sent forth a spark that set the whole kingdom ablaze. For he himself and Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, had spread an anathema against the emperor because he had reduced the apostolic pope to captivity, and within a short time they turned the whole kingdom so completely against him that he could no longer remain in Germany; instead, he entrusted supreme authority to Frederick, duke of the Swabians and his sister’s son, and withdrew himself into Italy [Col. 0353C].

§ XLIII

At that time, when an aged monk named Amilhard was departing from this world at the monastery of Domus Petri, as Abbot Theoderic himself openly related in the chapter, voices of angels singing and demons wailing were heard.

§ XLIV

In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1116 [Note: [Col. 0353D] From this it is clear that Bucelinus was mistaken when, in his *Constance Chronology* [Col. 0354D], he wrote that Abbot Theoderic had already died in 1111], Udalric, the elected bishop of Constance, overcome by excessive weariness because of the prolonged delay in his ordination, sent Abbot Theoderic to Rome after persuading him with many prayers. He hoped that Theoderic would obtain permission for his consecration from the apostolic pope, on account of the familiarity he had long enjoyed with that pope and of the many benefits he had conferred upon the pope’s envoys [Col. 0353D].

Accordingly, he went to Rome and petitioned Pope Paschal on Udalric’s behalf, but achieved nothing. On this journey my uncle Gebino was with him. He sent him a second time for the same reason; but on the first journey he had provided adequately both for himself and for the place, whereas on the second he scarcely greeted his brothers and left them entangled in many debts. Thus, throughout that entire summer, he wandered through Italy, sometimes going to the pope and sometimes to the emperor. But when he delayed there for a longer time, Udalric followed him and remained with the emperor [Col. 0354A], whom the pope and the others abhorred as an excommunicate.

§ XLV

Therefore, when Abbot Theoderic and his companions, through imprudence, exposed themselves at Rome to the unusual heat of summer, they began to die around the Kalends of August. Seeing that danger threatened them, those who still survived withdrew from Rome and went to Sutri. There, having all fallen ill together, they kept dying, until they left him alone in sickness. Whoever wishes may consider what anguish and grief he then endured, what bitter death he drank down, when he saw that none of his companions remained and that he, deprived both of his possessions and of his companions, was going to die alone in a foreign land.

From the very beginning of his conversion [Col. 0354B], he had always avoided the companionship of women as though it were a plague. No man had ever been able—not merely to touch his naked body, but even to see it—because he was truly modest and most chaste. Yet he then came to such misery that he had to be content with the service of little women, who spread his bedding, laid him down, lifted him up, bathed him, and performed the other services he required.

§ XLVI

Thus, after a fitting repentance, he passed from the valley of tears to the joys of the citizens above, being translated, as we believe, to the heavens on the fourth day before the Nones of August. He was honorably buried beside a certain oratory in that same city, and afterward was transferred into the sanctuary of that oratory and placed in a stone sarcophagus on the western side, opposite the altar [Col. 0354C]. We do not know the day of death of the others who made the journey with him: namely, the priest Sigifrid, Opertus the bearded man, and the three laymen Eberhard, Reginbold, and Gozobald.

§ XLVII

The bishop of the city of Piacenza announced his death in a letter of the following kind:

> “A., by the grace of God bishop of the Church of Piacenza, sends fraternal love in Christ to the canons and to all the faithful of the holy Church of Constance.
>
> “We give thanks to the Lord, examiner of hearts and kidneys, because, happily incorporated into the womb of Mother Church, nobly begotten, gratefully nourished by her milk, strengthened by her solid bread, you have grown into manly vigor; and through this you have fully learned to rejoice with those who rejoice, to weep with those who weep, and to maintain a fitting moderation in prosperity and adversity. Therefore, concerning the death of our confrater, namely the abbot of Petrishusen, a man beloved by God, I say, let not your heart be troubled, but rather rejoice, for he has happily departed, exchanging uncertainties for certainties and temporal things for eternal ones; and because he multiplied the talents entrusted to him, he entered joyfully, as a faithful and prudent steward, into the joy of his lord. He should truly be believed to have entered the land of the living, because we know and testify that he completed his departure through us in pure confession and fitting repentance [Col. 0355A]. For this reason we commend him earnestly to your prayers and to those of the whole Church.
>
> “Furthermore, we assure you that our confrater, but your elected bishop, Lord Udalric [Note: [Col. 0355D] The elected bishop of Constance, who was then staying in Italy with the emperor], is in good health, and that we, together with all our fellow bishops, have unanimously undertaken in Christ to prosecute his cause and that of his Church. Pray for us. The death of our aforementioned confrater the abbot occurred on the fourth day before the Nones of August.”

§ XLVIII

When this letter had therefore been brought to Constance, the canons unanimously went to the monastery, entered the brothers’ chapter, and read it aloud to the entire community. An intolerable mourning arose among all, and they grieved deeply, even those who had received little good from him. [Col. 0355B] The emperor ordered the things he had left behind to be returned in full to Udalric; but Udalric spent them and gave nothing to the brothers, and thereafter always remained ungrateful to that monastery.

§ XLIX

The venerable Abbot Theoderic was ordained in the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1086. In the one hundred and third year after the monastery was founded, he governed it for thirty years [Col. 0356A], and thus rested in peace in a good old age in the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1116, the one hundred and thirty-third year after the monastery was founded. He left behind a library nobly increased; for he ordered the books he had acquired to be catalogued [lacuna].

§ L

364 The same Father was tall in stature and of excellent bodily form, with lowered eyebrows and venerable white hair. His voice was subdued because of his abstinence. He was devoted to prayers and tears, beloved by the good and terrifying to the vicious, saying that a master ought to be like a lion in the chapter, like a father in the community, and like a mother at table.

He himself was also a most diligent guardian of monastic discipline and custom, urging his subjects toward them as well. He was thoroughly learned in letters. He mortified his body with frequent fasts and often scourged himself with rods, especially in the secret silence of night. He performed no divine office publicly, neither by singing nor by reading; and although he himself was unable to perform it, he took delight in seeing others carry it out most diligently and decently, performing the divine work with harmonious song. He was so moved by it that he was often brought to tears. He entirely forbade men to sing in a thin voice [Col. 0356B].

**THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS**

[Col. 0355]

§ I. On the election of Bertolf as abbot

[Col. 0355B]

When the death of the venerable Father Theoderic had become widely known, the canons of Constance assembled and came to the monastery of Domus Petri. They entered the brothers’ chapter, and, after the letters concerning both the abbot’s death and the exhortation of Udalric, the elected bishop—which urged the brothers to choose an abbot—had been read, the canons supposed that the election would take place according to their judgment; they also urged that it be carried out immediately.

The elders then replied modestly and humbly that the matter could not be conducted so hastily, but that the brothers ought to deliberate among themselves, with prolonged counsel and prayers to God, and carefully consider whom they should appoint, since they would entrust to him their souls and bodies, the monastery’s possessions, and the place itself. They said that no one ought to take part in this election unless he also wished to submit to the one elected.

At that time Cuono, the venerable abbot of Altorf [Note: [Col. 0355D] Cuno was the fifth abbot of Altorfensis ad Vineas], happened to be present; he had always been a friend of that monastery. When the canons insisted that they ought to participate in the election, the entire congregation began together to oppose them with one voice, and made them leave. Then, after consulting among themselves, they elected the venerable old man Bertolf, who had long held the office of prior in that same monastery; no outsider at all took part in this election.

For Wernher [Col. 0356B], who had been appointed abbot of Neresheim [Note: [Col. 0355D] See above, book III, § 39], happened to be present and had occupied the principal seat. Bertolf was ordained by Wito, bishop of Chur, in the year 1116 [Note: [Col. 0355D] Udalric had not yet been confirmed as bishop by the pope].

§ II

Then, in the following year, Pope Paschal died and Gelasius succeeded him [Note: [Col. 0356D] Since Gelasius was first elected in 1118, Udalric’s ordination could not have taken place earlier]. At that time Udalric was ordained bishop by the archbishop of Milan, and thereafter became a friend of the Romans.

When the emperor learned of Paschal’s death, he hastened to Rome, hoping that the election of the pope would pass through his hands. But Gelasius, already ordained, heard of the emperor’s unexpected arrival and fled during the night; he was unwilling either to see or to await him in any way. When the emperor could not recall him, he appointed another for himself, named Burdinus [Note: [Col. 0356D] He was Maurice Burdinus, archbishop of Braga in Spain, called Gregory VIII, who held his see at Sutri; the Saxon Annalist later writes that, after his capture, he was confined in the monastery of La Cava to perform penance, under the year 1121], and called him Gregory. But Gelasius excommunicated both of them. By the emperor’s power Burdinus obtained Rome, while Gelasius [lacuna]

§ III

[Col. 0356D] Earlier, though still in that same year of the Lord’s incarnation, 1117, on the third day before the Nones of January, around the third watch of the night, and again on that very day at about the eleventh hour, a great earthquake occurred far and wide throughout the world, so that many churches and certain cities collapsed from the immense shaking [lacuna].

§ IV

[Col. 0357A]

At about this time a certain noble matron named Azala gave her estate to the monastery of Saint Gregory the Pope, which she herself possessed near the village called Pfruwanga [Note: [Col. 0357D] See above, book II, § 18], and she remained in that same monastery in a religious habit until the end of her life. Abbot Bertolf, however, scarcely managed to redeem this estate from her daughters and sisters, and only at the cost of a great deal of money.

§ V

[Note: [Col. 0357D] Although this account was placed in the margin, it seemed to us worth retaining because of the information it provides; no further record survives of this noble family in the Linzgau.] There was a certain nobleman in the Linzgau, named Cuono. His was the village called Pfruwanga, left to him in its entirety by his parents by hereditary right. He fathered two sons, one named Meguizo and the other Cuono.

After their father’s death, they divided the aforementioned village of Pfruwanga between themselves. Later, one of them, Meguizo, gave his portion to the Church of Constance on the condition that, as long as he lived, and afterward his heirs, they would possess without contradiction both the church’s investiture and the advocacy.

His brother Cuono took a wife and fathered two sons by her, one named Wezil and the other Gebino. After his father’s death, Wezil added to the church at Pfruwanga, from his own property, a chapel, which he caused to be dedicated in honor of Saint Nazarius the martyr. From his own servants he gave one man there as a dowry, named Gisilmar, giving him a freeborn woman named Azala as wife; all their descendants, as can be seen today, belong to that same chapel [Col. 0357C].

His brother Gebino likewise gave his estate at Ringginwilare [Note: [Col. 0357D] See above, book II, § 18] to the monastery of Saint Gregory the Pope, called Petrishusen, and supplied the brothers then living there with many other goods. He remained there until his death.

Wezil, of whom we spoke above, the brother of Gebino, took a wife who bore him a son named Cuono. Bishop Ruomald, however, had granted as a benefice to Heinric, advocate of Sanctomonte, the estate that the aforementioned Meguizo had offered to the Church of Constance; Heinric himself granted it to Benno of Speichin [Note: [Col. 0357D] This seems to refer to the now-unknown noble family of Spaichingen in the county of Hohenberg, which Gerbert discusses frequently in his *History of the Black Forest*].

This Benno was the first to begin litigation with Cuono over the advocacy at Pfruwanga, which all Cuono’s ancestors had held without any contradiction. The dispute continued until, in the time of Gebhard III, bishop of Constance of that name, the case was brought before a synod for judgment.

When the complaint concerning this matter had been brought forward, and the bishop asked the synod for a decision while different men offered different opinions, Count Luitold of Achalm [Note: [Col. 0357D] This Liuthold founded the monastery of Zwiefalten with his brother Cuono and was buried there after his death in 1098. See the history of that foundation in P. Hess, *Monumenta Guelfica*, p. 165 ff., and Berthold of Constance, *Chronicle*, under the year 1099] was finally questioned about what he thought concerning the case, since he was the elder and steadfast in what was right and true.

He replied that it seemed entirely just to him that, since the Church appeared to possess that estate through the parents of those whose property it was, the privilege of advocacy or investiture should in no way be taken away from them. The synod likewise concluded that day with this decision.

Thus Cuono himself, the man of whom we are speaking, retained the advocacy and investiture, took a wife, and fathered a son named Conrad and five daughters. To one of them, named Azala, he gave everything he possessed at Pfruwanga; her advocate was her brother Conrad, who had lived at Frikkinga [Note: [Col. 0358D] Frickingen, in the chapter and county of the Linzgau; from there perhaps came Burchard and Albert of Frichingen, mentioned in charters of 1142 and 1185 in Herrgott].

§ VI

[Col. 0358B]

After this, Heinric [Note: [Col. 0358D] Namely, of Hirzisegga, perhaps the son of Heremann, mentioned above in book II, §§ 17 and 21], a most noble and prudent man, as he approached the end of his life, gave half of a small estate near Elinchofin [Note: [Col. 0358D] Perhaps Ellhofen, in the chapter of Stiefenhofen]. His wife Rihinza, when dying, gave the other half, on the condition that on the anniversary of both their deaths the brothers should be served bread, wine, and fish from it.

§ VII

When Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz, heard of Heinric’s death, he sent a letter in which he ordered Bishop Udalric to cast Heinric’s body out of the cemetery, or else that divine worship in the monastery should cease as long as he lay there.

For while Emperor Heinric was in Italy, and Frederick [Col. 0358C], duke of the Swabians, was devastating the Church of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0358D] The Saxon Annalist relates this Mainz war under the year 1117] because of the rebellion by which Adalbert, archbishop of that Church, was rebelling against the emperor, that same Heinric of Hirzisegga had aided the duke. For this reason the archbishop wished to have him expelled from the cemetery.

Udalric himself, however, had buried him with his own hands and, during the funeral rites, had borne great witness to his repentance. Nevertheless, on that Thursday of Holy Week [Col. 0358D], he prohibited the Work of God from being performed in the church. When the brothers tearfully begged him, for the sake of the soul of Abbot Theoderic, who had died in his service, to allow singing at least during the Easter festivals, he swore by Theoderic’s soul and by all souls that he would not permit it. He sealed the prohibition so strictly that he allowed no one to offer even private prayers in the church or in the chapels attached to it [Col. 0358D].

Only with difficulty did he grant, after being entreated, that the divine offices could be celebrated at Saint Mary’s beside the infirmary. This occurred in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1121. First Waltherus, and afterward Wisericus, monks of that place, went to the archbishop with letters of supplication; at last, moved by compassion, he granted them permission to serve God and allow the dead man to rest.

§ VIII

That year the emperor came to Reichenau, celebrated the feast of Saint Mark there, and then he and the queen, the daughter of the king of the English, came to Constance [Note: [Col. 0359D] Matilda, daughter of Henry I, king of England]. Yet almost none of the clergy remained there, because the bishop had departed and had forbidden the others to remain, since the emperor had already been condemned by Pope Calixtus.

The emperor was not angered by this, nor did he visit the monastery of Domus Petri; neither he nor any of his people caused it any trouble.

§ IX

[Col. 0359B]

Then the aforementioned Azala, worthy of good remembrance, again confirmed before the leading men the estate at Pfruwanga to the monastery, as the privilege written below demonstrates:

> “Let it be known to all the faithful of Christ, both those present and those to come, that a certain religious woman named Azala transferred, with the assistance of her advocate Berthold, a certain estate to the monastery of Saint Gregory the Pope, situated on the bank of the Rhine and then governed by Abbot Berthold. She appeared to possess it without contradiction in the Linzgau, in the county of Count Hartmann [Note: [Col. 0359D] Three counts of the Linzgau are mentioned in the charters of this chronicle: Otto, in Swigger’s charter of 1058 concerning the village of Ouveltingen, which Lunig and others, misled by him, incorrectly call Suiltingen above, book II, § 12; Hartmann, mentioned here under the year 1121; and Heinric, in Witigo’s charter concerning Frichingen in 1135, below, book IV, § 27. We count the first among the counts of Chur in Rhaetia, who may also have been of Bregenz; Hartmann may have been of Dillingen and Kyburg, concerning whom see *Disquisitions*, §§ 21–22. Heinric, however, is called below in book V, § 11, of Neiligenberg or Sanctomonte], namely, half of the village called Pfruwanga, together with another small estate belonging to it, called Taverna [Col. 0359C], and with all things belonging to it: namely, courtyards, buildings, male and female servants, cultivated and uncultivated lands, fields, meadows, open country, pastures, woods, waters, fisheries, mills, roads and trackless ways, exits and entrances, things acquired and to be acquired, and every other implement that can still be stated or named. She lawfully transferred all of these, from her right into their right, to the same monastery built in honor of Saint Gregory, and to the monks serving God there under the rule of Saint Benedict.
>
> “This transfer was made at Constance in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1121, in the fourteenth indiction, in April, on the twenty-ninth day of that month, that is, the third day before the Kalends of May, on a Friday, while the emperor Heinric the Younger, son of Heinric the Elder, was reigning. He too was at Constance at that time together with the queen, and these things were carried out in his presence [Col. 0359D], before many witnesses. At that time Calixtus, also called Guido, held the Roman Church, and Udalric held the Church of Constance.”

§ X

In the year 1122 Wito, bishop of Chur, died [Note: [Col. 0359D] In the necrology he is recorded under 18 May: “Wido, bishop of Chur: he was kind to us”] at the monastery of Domus Petri. He had always shown great favor and friendship toward that monastery and had provided many benefits to the brothers.

When he died there, Berthold and his brothers clothed him in the monastery’s vestments, as is customary for bishops, enclosed him in a *Tunna* [German: *Tonne*, “barrel”], and brought him to Chur with great honor, though with great difficulty.

His successor Conrad [Note: [Col. 0359D] The cited necrology also records him under 1 March: “The burial of Conrad, bishop of Chur: he was kind to us”] gave the monastery a silver chalice, which the abbot gilded, and a purple cope. He honored both the abbot and the brothers who were present with individual gifts. Among them he especially rewarded Conrad, then a chaplain and later abbot, giving him a *Zendath* [Note: [Col. 0360D] *Zendath*, *cendal*, *centatum*: a silk cloth], from which Conrad made a cope, as well as a pound of silver. To this he and the other brothers added further contributions, and they most beautifully adorned the arm of Saint Philip the Apostle with gold, silver, precious stones, and pearls [lacuna].

§ XI

At that time Wernher the Elder, who had been appointed abbot of Neresheim [Note: [Col. 0360D] See above, book III, § 39], enticed by Bishop Udalric’s promises, left that place and returned to Domus Petri. When Abbot Berthold refused to appoint another in his place, the bishop brought Heinric from the monastery of Zwiefalten [Note: [Col. 0360D] P. Sulger describes the mission of Henry of Berrieden at greater length under the year 1118 in his *Zwiefalten Annals*, part I, p. 63. See Bucelinus, *Constance Chronology*, under that year] and made him abbot there. Thus the care of that place passed away from Domus Petri, though it continued to be held for many years afterward.

When Bishop Udalric provided Wernher none of the things he had promised, Wernher withdrew to the monastery of Erla [Note: [Col. 0360D] This monastery seems to be none other than Erlach on Lake Biel in Bernese territory, to which, toward the end of the eleventh century, a colony of monks was brought from Saint Blasien with Abbot Eckehard. See Gerbert, *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, p. 248], and remained there for many days [lacuna]. Later he enclosed himself in a certain oratory consecrated in the name of Saint Peter and remained in God’s service until the end of his life. He was buried in that same place after his death, and it is said that healings are divinely granted there. Since we have not learned this through reliable report, we refrain from saying more about it.

§ XII

During these times the cell of Wagenhausen [Note: [Col. 0360D] See above, book III, § 24, and below, § 30. Folchnandus is called its second abbot in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 932, while the Uto mentioned here is entirely omitted] was under the care and governance of our monastery. But, obstructed by the dispute of the people of Schaffhausen, it made little progress down to the present day [Col. 0360D].

At that time a certain elderly priest named Folchnandus was sent there and presided over it. I too was then there under him, and we had as allies both the people of Schaffhausen and those of Stein am Rhein, who likewise disputed that the place belonged to them, had often previously devastated it, and were still devastating it.

But since at that time divine and human affairs there were being conducted in fairly orderly fashion, Bishop Udalric, believing that he would quickly accomplish something important, dismissed us and made a certain Uto abbot there, assisting him as far as he could. But he presided only for a short time, as our narrative may perhaps show in its proper place.

§ XIII

In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1126 there was a severe famine, so that many people, overcome by want, perished. In the basilica of Saint Gregory there was a principal panel attached to the altar on its western side [Col. 0361B]. It had been beautifully covered with gold and silver and was opened only on the greatest feast days.

When scarcity grew severe, Abbot Bertolf ordered it to be broken up. It was found to contain one talent and a quarter of a *ferto* of gold [Note: [Col. 0361D] A *ferto* is a type of money, or one quarter of a mark], and five of silver [Col. 0361A]; all of this gold and silver was of the purest and finest quality.

In the middle section of the panel, a beautiful image of Saint Mary, Mother of God, was raised in gold, with the figure of a dove upon her breast. In silver, across the width of the panel, were exquisitely formed images of the apostles and other saints.

§ XIV

In addition, an estate near Bozze [Note: [Col. 0361D] Boos, in the chapter of Saulgau] was pledged to a certain Bernhard for twelve pounds of silver by a written agreement [Col. 0361C]. Later, during another famine, Abbot Conrad sold it to Rupert of Otoldiswanc [Note: [Col. 0361D] Perhaps Otterschwang, in the same chapter], who still possesses it.

§ XV

In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1127, when Abbot Bertolf was already weighed down by old age and had also become so difficult in his conduct that he neither made provision for the necessities of the place himself nor allowed others to do so, and everything seemed already to be approaching collapse, some of the elders began to deal secretly with Bishop Udalric. They asked him to persuade Bertolf to resign the abbacy and allow another to be appointed in his place, so that he might rest in retirement for the remainder of his life; for he was excessively stout.

Since the bishop was eloquent and cunning, he persuaded Bertolf, although Bertolf resisted for a long time. On the appointed day Bishop Udalric arrived, together with Udalric, abbot of Zwiefalten [Note: [Col. 0361D] He presided over the monastery of Zwiefalten from 1095 to 1136, according to *Gallia Christiana*, vol. V, p. 1054. He is discussed by P. Sulger in the *Zwiefalten Annals*, vol. I, p. 28 ff.]. After prolonged deliberation they came to the chapter and announced the matter to the assembled community.

When Bertolf willingly agreed to live as a private person, some said that he should settle the matter there; others said that he ought to go to the altar and resign there. The bishop said: “It is not necessary. Let him return the staff of governance to me.”

Then everyone protested, saying that this had no connection with him whatsoever. Bertolf therefore went to the altar and laid the staff upon it, saying: “Behold, what by the grace of God and of you I have possessed, I lay down; and I release all of you from obedience to me.” Having said this, he returned to his bed and first chose Conrad the chaplain.

§ XVI

372 Then the community returned again to the chapter. The bishop withdrew, and the entire congregation elected Conrad in a free election. Conrad himself had also withdrawn, because until then he had lived there as a guest. After the election had been completed, he was sought and found; crying out and resisting fiercely, he was brought there by force and, after being overcome only with difficulty, was placed upon the abbatial seat.

§ XVII

Four months later Bishop Udalric, at the cell of Saint Mary in the Breisgau [Note: [Col. 0361D] The cell of Saint Mary, commonly called Sankt Märgen, is a collegiate foundation of regular canons in the Black Forest. [Col. 0362D] See Gerbert, *History of this Forest*, vol. I, p. 477, and Peter of Swabia, *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 233], whose habit he had also adorned, was struck down by a malignant disease and died a painful death, his eyes being violently forced from his head. He was a man very well suited to the episcopal office, had his disposition not been so fiercely harsh.

At Constance he established canons at Saint Udalric [Note: [Col. 0362D] This is another collegiate foundation of canons outside Constance, called Kreuzlingen. Its foundation charter, dated 1125, is given in the cited *History*, vol. III, p. 54]. His body was brought to Constance and honorably buried in the choir of the basilica of Saint Mary.

§ XVIII

Thus, when the venerable Abbot Bertolf [Note: [Col. 0362D] In the necrology, under 25 September, he is said to have presided for ten years after Theoderic; from this we learn the year of Conrad’s election, namely 1127] had first resigned his authority, he was cared for diligently for some time; afterward he was treated with great negligence. A few years later he himself became almost deranged and behaved childishly [lacuna]. At the end of his life he was scarcely granted enough awareness to ask for and receive viaticum.

Nevertheless, after his death, through the brothers’ kindness, he was clothed in priestly vestments, as is customary for abbots, and was honorably buried at the head of the abbots’ tombs, although Abbot Conrad was absent.

§ XIX

Let anyone who wishes carefully consider the remarkable matter I am about to relate. For during nearly seventy years, from the time of Abbot Adalbert down to Bertolf, none of those who were abbots at Domus Petri departed from this world without disgrace; each of them either died abroad or perished after being struck by some infirmity.

Adalbert therefore died a sudden death at Buochowa. Siggo, his back having been broken, died in the second year of his ordination. Arnold, Meginrad, and Liutold were deposed. Theoderic died abroad. Bertolf, after being deposed and becoming deranged, died [lacuna].

Who could believe that this happened without the strict judgment of God? [lacuna]

§ XX

Accordingly, at the very beginning of his promotion, Abbot Conrad began to construct new dwellings for himself and his successors. Laboring over the work for many years, he finally completed it with distinction.

At that time Udalric, the second bishop of that name [Note: [Col. 0363D] Baron of Castel, formerly a monk of Saint Blasien, *History of the Black Forest*, vol. I, p. 370. Gebhard III had built the castle that he demolished. Rudolf, count of Bregenz, was Udalric’s son; concerning them see above, book III, §§ 17–23. See Bucelinus, *Constance Chronology*, under the year 1132], destroyed his own fortification, called Castellum, out of fear of Count Rudolf of Bregenz. His predecessor Udalric had built it with much labor and expense. He granted Abbot Conrad the ceiling panels of two chapels, and Conrad had one attached to his own chapel and the other to the chapel of Saint John the Baptist [Col. 0363B]; for he had built two chapels, one above the other.

§ XXI

In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1129, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, the upper chapel that Abbot Conrad had built was dedicated in honor of Saint Martin, Saint Oswald the martyr, and the other saints whose relics are contained there [lacuna]. It was dedicated by Udalric, the second bishop.

§ XXII

In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1134, in the twelfth indiction, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, the lower chapel was dedicated by the venerable Udalric, the second bishop, in honor of Saint Faith, Saint Mary Magdalene, and the other saints whose relics are contained there [Col. 0363C] [lacuna].

§ XXIII

In the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1129, in the seventh indiction, my uncle Gebino renovated the chapel of Saint John the Baptist. He added to it an oratory of Saint James the Apostle, which had previously possessed its own altar; he demolished that altar and usefully made the two oratories into one. From Abbot Conrad he obtained ceiling panels bearing a painted representation of Saint John the Baptist and hung them there.

Udalric, the second bishop, dedicated it on the ninth day before the Kalends of September in honor of Saint John the Baptist, John the Evangelist, James his brother, Philip, and Nicholas. These are its patrons [lacuna].

§ XXIV

[Col. 0363D] That same Gebino had long before renovated the cloister, constructing new columns with their bases on two sides out of squared stone.

He had a silver chalice made and decorated it with gold and jewels in beautiful workmanship. But when the goldsmith was supposed to make the paten and wished to set many stones in it, the little towers and wormlike ornaments could in no way be securely fastened to the body of the paten as a whole, and each time he found some defect in what had been begun. Thus the work was interrupted for a long time [lacuna].

§ XXV

[Col. 0364A]

During these times an estate near Bozze was sold for seventeen marks; likewise, Eilingen [Note: [Col. 0364D] Perhaps Ailingen, in the chapter of Thuringen] was given for forty marks.

§ XXVI

A certain priest named Witigo, born at Alospach [Note: [Col. 0364D] Allenspach, in the chapter of Reichenau], had for a long time been chaplain to the archbishop of Trier and to the archbishop of Cologne. He sent nearly forty marks of tested silver to Domus Petri for the purchase of fields, which he would possess during his lifetime and leave to the monastery after his death.

But all the silver was spent, and nothing was purchased with it. When he therefore came to see what had been done, the abbot and his brothers, not knowing what else to do, showed him the monastery’s property [Col. 0364B] at Frichingen. A small portion of it had recently been enlarged with some of the money that had been taken for Eilingin. They gave it to him in exchange for the money that had been spent.

He gratefully accepted it and, with the abbot’s consent and command, had the following written agreement drawn up concerning it.

§ XXVII
Know to all, present and future, how I, Witigo, priest by the grace of God, through divine providence inspiring me, acquired an allodial estate near the village of Frichingen, in the district of Linzgau, in the county of Count Henry [Note: [Col. 0364D] Count Henry of Linzgau is mentioned in the year 1135, below, Book V, § 11, concerning Sanctomonte.], paying twenty-two marks for it. While, as I believe, I still enjoyed sound judgment, I petitioned Abbot Conrad and the brothers of the monastery of Petershausen; and they granted me, as a rightful benefice, [Col. 0364C] the farmstead which that monastery possesses near the same village. In return, I transferred to them twenty other marks of silver for the same benefice, on this condition: that, for as long as I live, I may possess as a benefice both parts of the aforesaid estate—the newly purchased part and the part previously held—without any opposition, and may apply its produce to my own uses, wherever I may be; and that I may entrust the same farmstead to whichever one of the brothers of that monastery I choose, so that he may faithfully preserve for me everything he acquires there.

When I have departed this life, I wish the same monastery to possess the allodial estate in perpetuity, on this condition: that thereafter every year, on the anniversary of my death, the brothers together receive from it a charitable provision—namely, three malters of spelt grain for making fine flour, of which one measure is to be made specifically for the abbot; three urns of wine, one-half for the abbot and two and a half for the brothers; and twelve shillings for purchasing fish. I also wish twelve poor people to be fed on that day, and that each poor person be given bread, a cup of wine, and a serving of food.

Likewise, on the anniversary of my father Opertus, which falls on the fourth day before the Ides of March [12 March], I wish one malter of fine flour and two urns of wine to be given generally to the entire congregation. In the same way, from the same [Col. 0365A] property, I wish this to be done on the anniversary of my mother Pechilda, which falls on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September [18 August].

But so that all these provisions may be preserved inviolate, exactly as they have been written down, I adjure all who, in the succession of time, shall be in the same monastery, by the Rewarder of all the faithful and by all the power that serves God either in heaven or on earth, that no one at all—whether abbot or anyone else—dare violate these provisions; or, if anyone should do so, which God forbid, let him be condemned to the company of Judas the betrayer on the day of the final just judgment.

Done and confirmed in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1135, on the feast of Pope Saint Gregory, before all the brothers and the witnesses Henry, Hermann, Eberhard, Luitfrid, Arnold, Burchard, Adelbert, and many others.—The death of the same Witigo: the Nones of October [7 October].

§ XXVIII.

[Col. 0365B]

Gisilfrid of Turingen [Note: [Col. 0365D] This was doubtless once a noble family in the district of Linzgau, where Turingen, Jettenhausen, and Fischbach were situated.] also came with great devotion and, before the entire congregation, offered his only son, named Rupert, to God and Saint Gregory, with many tears. He also offered all the estates which he possessed by right of ownership in the land of the Swabians, both at Turingen and at Jettenhausen [Note: [Col. 0365D] Today Jettenhausen, in the district of Thuringen.]. Thus he transferred everything in full to the monastery, to be possessed in perpetuity for the service of the brothers serving God there, except for the portion belonging to his brother Gerald.

He also bought a vineyard near Allenspach for twenty-two marks and established, by the firmest agreement, in the presence and with the consent of the abbot and the entire congregation, that once each week, forever, on one day a Mass should be sung for all his deceased relatives, and that on that day wine from the aforesaid vineyard should be served generally to the monks. Whenever the Mass was sung, it was to be announced by a single familiar signal.

And so that the vineyard could be cultivated without expense to the monastery, when at that same time a certain matron named Truitlint wished to be converted and to offer her field near Fischbach [Note: [Col. 0365D] Fischbach, in the district of Linzgau], and the abbot refused to accept her, Gisilfrid gave the abbot ten talents so that he would accept the woman together with her field and permit the same property [Col. 0366A] to be used for cultivating the aforesaid vineyard. All these things were done in the presence of suitable witnesses, with the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as witnesses, and Philip, Gregory, and Gebehard.

§ XXIX.

Afterward, when certain quarrels arose between the abbot and the same Gisilfrid, he took his son—who had already been made a monk—out of the monastery and alienated the estates he had given, namely Turingen and Jettenhausen. He himself, however, usually remained in the monastery in the habit of the lay brothers, and died not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0365D] He is recorded in the Necrology on 6 May], and was buried at the monastery. After his father’s death, his son took up arms and unjustly took possession of the inheritance.

§ XXX.

[Col. 0366B]

At the same time, when Utto, abbot of Wagenhausen [Note: [Col. 0365D] See above, § 12], had fallen into disrepute, he was deposed; and Gebino was brought by Bishop Ulrich from the monastery of the House of Saint Peter and was appointed abbot of that place. After governing it suitably for several years, he was also entrusted with a new cell called Wischina [Note: [Col. 0365D] Fischingen, “pond” or “island,” the monastery of Saint Mary in Thurgau, whose brief history is given in Gallia Christiana, vol. V, p. 1027. There is no mention of Gebino there; instead, Waltrammus is placed ninth among the abbots and is said to have restored the monastery in 1138. [Col. 0366D] Perhaps this means that monastic life was initiated there by him, since the Hirsau customs were introduced from the House of Saint Peter through Gebino; for this monastery had already been founded long before.], and through him it was initiated into monastic life.

377 § XXXI.

After some time, since he could not endure the labor, he abandoned it. At the request of Bishop Ulrich, Abbot Conrad again appointed Waltrammus abbot of that place in his stead. Waltrammus began to construct the church there from its foundations and acquired many ornaments and furnishings for the church.

§ XXXII.

[Col. 0366C]

After this, Abbot Conrad brought in a certain monk named Aaron, a priest from Camberch and highly skilled in the art of music. Aaron made for him organs of the most elegant tone and installed them on the south side of the same basilica. He had previously made an instrument of the same kind for the Church of Constance, at the expense of Herimannus, then vicedominus and custodian of the church.

## BOOK FIVE. ON THE TRANSLATION OF THE BLESSED GEBEHARD, BISHOP

[Col. 0365]

§ I.

[Col. 0365D]

… Since the body of the blessed confessor of Christ, Gebehard, once bishop of Constance and founder of the monastery called the House of Saint Peter, had lain beneath the earth in the manner of the dead for approximately one hundred and forty-two years [Note: [Col. 0366D] Since Saint Gebehard II died around the year 996, the one hundred and forty-second year denotes the year of Christ 1137; nevertheless, this first translation is elsewhere dated 152 years after the monastery was founded (in 983), and thus to the year 1134. Here, however, only the first translation of Saint Gebehard—that is, the raising of his body from the earth—is being discussed; it seems that his cult began from this point without a formal canonization. See above, Book I, § 46.], and faithful God, who does not [Col. 0366D] forget, nevertheless frequently glorified that same place of his tomb with miracles; since the basilica itself, both because of its age and because of the weakness of its foundations, was already threatening imminent collapse everywhere through the splitting of its cracks, the venerable Abbot Conrad, encouraged by Hugh, a canon of the Church of Constance, undertook to renew it ……

§ II.

[Col. 0367A]

Therefore, in the year 1134 from the Virgin’s childbirth, but 152 from the foundation of the monastery, in the twelfth indiction, Abbot Conrad summoned the venerable Bishop Ulrich of the Church of Constance, the second of that name, opened the tomb of the blessed Bishop Gebehard, and found the treasure of his body, more precious than every pearl … still wrapped in sacred vestments. For the greater part they had rotted away, but they clung to the bones because no hand had touched them. When they began to be touched by hand, however, they immediately fell apart, except for the sole and upper part of the chasuble, which had been made from a saffron-colored pallium. Thus, a portion of these vestments remained intact.

In the 152nd year from the foundation of the monastery, Bishop Ulrich arrived, together with seven abbots invited by Conrad, the abbot of the oft-mentioned monastery [Note: [Col. 0367D] We understand this to mean the abbots of neighboring monasteries]. A considerable crowd of clergy, monks, and other faithful was also present. With immense joy and rejoicing, with hymns and praises, they honorably transferred the bones and ashes of the blessed confessor of Christ and bishop Gebehard from the place of his former burial, placed them in a sarcophagus, processed around the monastery, and afterward buried them with great honor in a new tomb.

On that same day—that is, the sixth day before the Kalends of September [27 August], which is his birthday, in the twelfth indiction—the altar situated above the tomb itself was consecrated …… On the following day they consecrated the basilica itself ……

This was done in the time of Pope Innocent II and the Emperor Augustus Lothair II, in the tenth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0367D] Lothair II was elected on 30 August 1125 and first crowned emperor in 1133; therefore, the years of his empire here must be understood as years of his reign.], in the twelfth indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September [28 August], successfully and gloriously.

§ III.

In those days a serious illness was spreading through the congregation itself, from which, I confess, I was miraculously delivered through the merits of the blessed Gebehard …… After this, Abbot Conrad made a sufficiently magnificent bell, and Heribert, the church custodian, made a second; I too made one small bell …… Then he built a bell tower over the church, since previously the bells hung on four columns beside the church.

§ IV.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1136, in the fourteenth indiction, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December [16 November], the altar of Saint Peter the Apostle was consecrated for the second time by the venerable Bishop Conrad of Chur [Col. 0367D] [Note: [Col. 0367D] Perhaps because by then Bishop Ulrich had already left his see and withdrawn to Saint Blaise.].

§ V.

379 It happened that the priest Henry, who administered the oratory of Saint Mary at Rotsee, departed from this world. Immediately Abbot Conrad sent there the monk Adelbert, a thoroughly suitable man, in the hope that through him divine service might in some measure increase in that place. When he died a few years later, another Adelbert, younger, was sent there with the same purpose as his predecessor.

As we said much earlier [Note: [Col. 0367D] Book III, § 40], the venerable Ratperonius was the first to inhabit this place and built the basilica. We consider it worthwhile to insert some account of his deeds into this work, lest the virtues of so great a man be entirely consigned to oblivion, since among people today scarcely any memory of them remains.

### Life of the Blessed Ratperonius

§ VI.

The man of God Ratperonius was born, as is said, of noble and religious parents from Thuringia [Note: [Col. 0367D] In a later marginal hand: Count of Rappenberg, also Landgrave. Elsewhere it is useless to seek information about this Ratperonius; our author writes about his birth solely from tradition, and he is not mentioned anywhere in the Life of Saint Ulrich.]. His entire lineage is believed to have been adorned and brought to completion in him like a golden clasp.

Having therefore left his homeland, he crossed into Alemannia and joined the most holy bishop Ulrich of Augsburg. Under his direction he lived for a long time according to the regular way of life, since that same bishop then governed the monastery of Kempten [Note: [Col. 0368D] From 941 to 962; the monastery had been devastated by the invading Hungarians in 940. See Gallia Christiana, vol. V, p. 993; Brusch, p. 105.].

Since he was closely attached to that holy bishop and was instructed by him in every good work, it happened that one day they traveled together and came to places adjoining the Red Pond. After they had rested for some time in a certain meadow following bodily refreshment, the bishop awoke after his rest and foretold to the blessed Ratperonius through the Spirit that nearby there was a place which would have to be cultivated through his labor, and where he would also await the day of judgment.

When the man of God Ratperonius [Col. 0368C] received this oracle, he immediately and resolutely devoted himself to this task and began to negotiate shrewdly with the nobles of those regions, asking whether they would grant him the place designated for the work. When he was despised by them, he pronounced a curse against them; and for this reason it is believed that their descendants were wiped out, as it is written: “The seed of the wicked shall perish.”

§ VII.

Therefore, so that the almighty Lord might fulfill the prophecy which, through the mouth of his servant Ulrich, he had deigned to foretell to his servant Ratperonius, he finally inspired a certain nobleman named Berngar to agree to his undertaking and desire. From his estates Berngar gave him [Col. 0368D] the place now called the Red Pond (Rotsee), then barren but now, in terms of the character of the region, fertile and pleasant.

In this place, it is said, a certain most savage robber formerly lived, who practiced the most atrocious brigandage throughout the surrounding area …… The blessed Ratperonius, after the aforesaid Berngar of Arnach [Note: [Col. 0369D] Now Arnach, in the district of Isny, not far from Rotsee] had handed the place over to him, began to build a basilica there. He undertook this immense work with infinite labor, since he possessed nothing with which to begin it. Nevertheless, through God’s assistance …… he founded the basilica on a magnificent scale and brought it to completion.

§ VIII.

The same man of God suffered many persecutions and many calamities from the neighboring clergy, to such an extent that they even incited Warmannus, then bishop of Constance [Note: [Col. 0369D] From 1026 to 1034. The other authors report nothing about Warmannus’s death on the journey to Rome. The chronology of the years mentioned can scarcely be reconciled unless we say that Ratperonius lived to an extremely advanced age. For if he was already a disciple of Saint Ulrich in at least 962, then in the time of Bishop Eberhard, around 1035, he must have been at least one hundred years old.], against him; Warmannus inflicted many injuries upon him and finally drove him from the place ……

It happened, however, that after expelling the man of God, Bishop Warmannus set out for Rome and, on that very journey, died with all who accompanied him [Col. 0369B]. His brother Eberhard succeeded him in the episcopate and was at all times exceedingly kind and merciful toward the blessed Ratperonius.

The man of God, previously expelled from Rotsee, had moved to another place and built an oratory there for himself. From there he was kindly recalled by the bishop to his former place, and thereafter devoted himself there to God’s service. The same bishop also dedicated the basilica which the man of God had built in honor of the Mother of God, and assisted him in every way he could. The man of God entrusted that same place to the Church of Constance, because he hoped that through it he could advance more effectively in God’s service.

There was a very small grove near the oratory, from which they could obtain a little of the wood they needed. When certain wicked men were destroying it against his will and, although he repeatedly asked them, refused entirely to stop, he prayed the Lord to cause the waters there to overflow, so that people would no longer burden themselves with such plunder. In a wondrous manner, therefore, water immediately began to rise there to a great depth, cover the wood, and form the beautiful pond seen today; and from this the same place came to be called Rotsee ……

Thus, after many struggles and labors, the blessed Ratperonius, filled with the Holy Spirit, departed to the Lord on the seventh day before the Kalends of August [26 July]. His body lies honorably buried in the basilica he built, where to this day he does not cease to bestow many benefits ……

§ IX.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, Pope Innocent held a council at Rome of unheard-of magnitude [Note: [Col. 0369D] This was the Second Lateran Council, at which the canon cited here was issued as canon 18, concerning incendiaries. Labbé, Councils, vol. X, p. 1007.]. Eight hundred bishops and a thousand abbots with clergy and innumerable laypeople attended this council, as they said. Among many useful decrees, it was decided that the burning of houses was not to take place; this was also carefully observed for several years.

Abbot Conrad was present at this synod as well, and on his return brought back two small pallia, from which he made two copes.

§ X.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1142, Hugh, provost of Constance [Note: [Col. 0369D] This provost should be inserted in Gallia Christiana, vol. V, p. 928.], gave five talents and bought a small estate at Altheim [Note: [Col. 0370D] Perhaps in the district and county of Linzgau]. The good-memory Gisilla had previously given this estate to the monastery. After the aforesaid Hugh had bought it from Abbot Conrad in the presence of the brothers and many others, he returned it and handed it over again to the monastery, on the condition that every year, on the anniversary of his death, which falls on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May [17 April], provision should be made from that estate for the entire congregation, as far as possible.

§ XI.

382 In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1143, the priest Gerungus gave the monastery, through the hand of his advocate Henry, into the hand of our advocate Conrad of Sanctomonte, two small estates: one at Schuwindorf [Note: [Col. 0370D] Perhaps Schyggendorf and Wangen in the district and county of Linzgau], the other at Wangen in the district of Linzgau, under the county of Henry of Sanctomonte [Note: [Col. 0370D] At this time the counts were simultaneously counts of Heiligenberg and of Linzgau; perhaps some of the preceding persons also belonged to them]. He gave them without any opposition, by lawful transfer and before many suitable witnesses.

Gerungus himself came to the monastery, fell ill there, and was treated kindly until his death. In the same year Gundelo of Constance gave his estate at Gerboldiswilare [Col. 0370C] [Note: [Col. 0370D] Gebhartschweiler, in the same district] and at the same time offered his daughter.

§ XII.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1146, a great famine oppressed peoples far and wide. Driven by want, certain persons therefore came from Triboltingen [Note: [Col. 0370D] Tribeltingen, in the district of Frauenfeld, or Thurgau] and Tegernweiler to the monastery and transferred themselves and their small possessions there. Some of them, however, were entirely unable to make this transfer secure, because the properties were tributary to the Island monastery.

§ XIII.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1147, Abbot Conrad renovated parts of the church. He also renewed and enlarged the chapel of Saint Ulrich and adorned it with the finest paintings. Hermann, bishop of the Church of Constance, dedicated it on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January [21 December] ……

§ XIV.

It happened, in the time of King Conrad [Note: [Col. 0370D] Other contemporary writers discuss this holy expedition extensively, especially Otto of Saint Blaise, chapter 2 and elsewhere, and Otto of Freising, On the Deeds of Emperor Frederick, Book I, chapter 44 and following], that Pope Eugenius sent letters to Louis, king of the Franks. Bernard, abbot of the monastery called Clairvaux, and others also traveled through Gaul and preached that all—both great and small—who wished to obey God’s will should proceed armed to defeat the pagans, especially against a certain bloodthirsty tyrant who had invaded the city of Edessa, formerly called Rages, [Col. 0371A] and had either killed or taken captive all the Christians whom he found there, and had plundered, polluted, and overthrown the sacred things of God.

When this report had spread everywhere, a great movement arose throughout the land, so that Conrad, king of the Romans, and Louis, king of the Franks, together with many dukes, counts, and other nobles, and with an infinite multitude of people from different regions, offered themselves to the Lord. Very many from the monasteries also offered themselves, and at that time prepared themselves and their possessions with the greatest zeal, devoted minds, and complete readiness.

They therefore proceeded armed—an exceedingly vast army—through Pannonia and the Bulgarian forest, and with a great multitude of ships along the Danube, carrying weapons and every necessity. When they arrived in Greece, they were honorably received by the Greek emperor and, under his leadership, were conducted into an immense wilderness, believing that they would come to the lands of the nations.

One day, when they were setting up camp in a certain place where a valley lay between them, and, after pitching their tents, were resting in exhaustion, suddenly, in the middle of the night, a tremendous flood came. The violent torrent carried out to sea whatever it found in the valley [Col. 0371C]. This first misfortune afterward became an omen of various disasters. For while at first they proceeded humbly and peacefully in the fear of God, everything turned out favorably for them. But afterward, when they were lifted up in pride and began to devote themselves to plunder, they were consumed by various calamities.

As they traveled through the desert and found no food, many died of hunger. Others, weakened by starvation, were killed by the pagans or taken captive and perished in captivity. Some, however, were crowned with glorious martyrdom.

When King Conrad saw that he could accomplish nothing according to his will, he returned to Constantinople to the Greek emperor. From there he was sent by ship across the sea to Jerusalem. The king’s brother, Otto, bishop of Freising [Col. 0371D], had already withdrawn from the army that followed the king and wished to cross to Jerusalem by the royal road, together with about thirty thousand armed men from the army. The army of the pagans then attacked them and killed almost all of them.

§ XV.

King Louis of the Franks also proceeded with his wife and with much pomp, separated from the others, together with his army, until he reached the city of Antioch. There he was honorably received by the city’s prince. After he had rested there for several days, as the story goes, the prince of the city violated his wife; [Col. 0372A] the king himself barely escaped with a few companions, and reached King Conrad, who was then staying at Acre. Conrad received him kindly and afterward reconciled him with his wife when she returned to him.

§ XVI.

After this, King Conrad set out for Jerusalem with a large army and was received with the greatest courtesy by the king and clergy of that city. He immediately proclaimed his expedition with the two kings and their armies against Damascus. When they were besieging it and the city was already on the point of being captured, the soldiers of God, corrupted by money from those inside, withdrew the army and departed without accomplishing anything.

[Col. 0372B]

During this expedition, some who had set out from our place have still not returned. Many Christians who had been carried away captive by the pagans were ransomed by Armenians [sic] for a price and permitted to return to their homeland.

§ XVII.

Conrad, duke of Zähringen [Note: [Col. 0371D] Concerning this expedition against the Slavic Obotrites and Lutici, see the Chronicle of Monte Sereno and Albert of Stade under the year 1147], therefore declared that he would go with the countless others who had found the journey we have described too arduous, so that they too might proceed through Saxony against those pagans who dwell beyond the river called the Elbe [Albis, Elb].

When they reached that region, they found the land impassable, extremely wet, and full of marshes. The inhabitants of the land did not live together but were scattered, so that they could not easily be found. The Christian army, wearied by its ignorance of the terrain, therefore returned without achieving any result.

§ XVIII.

At the same time, when Waltrammus [Note: [Col. 0371D] See above, Book IV, § 31], abbot at Fischingen, had accomplished many good works, he lost his sight. He returned to our monastery, recovered his sight through medicine, and thereafter remained in the congregation in a good manner of life. Finally, he died a blessed death.

§ XIX.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1156, Abbot Gebino, detained by a prolonged illness at Wagenhausen [Note: [Col. 0372D] Above, Book IV, § 30] … when he was already about to die, summoned his household, wished them forgiveness, and asked them to do the same for him ……

§ XX.

[Col. 0372D]

385 In the year 1159, Burchard of Husen died and left to the monastery the estate which he possessed at Birihttlingen [Note: [Col. 0372D] Perhaps Bichtlingen, in the district of Mösskirch. In the Necrology, on 20 March, the estate is called Birthilingen].

§ XXI.

In the year 1159, the estate which the monastery had in the village called Heiggau [Note: [Col. 0372D] Haidgau, in the district of Wurzach] was sold for sixty talents ……

In the same year, the estate which the monastery of Saint George in the Black Forest possessed in the village called Mimmenhausen was put up for sale.
