Since our monastery also possessed an estate in that village, which the good-memory Gerold had once given to it together with himself and his other estates—namely, Rüti, Efrichweiler, and Neuwirren—it therefore strove with all its strength to acquire this property as well.

For this reason, the panel which had been placed on the main altar of Saint Gregory on the eastern side, facing the choir, and which was most beautifully covered with gold and gems, was stripped of its gold …… With this gold, taken from the aforesaid panel, the estate at Mimmenhausen which the monastery of Saint George had possessed there was purchased. In addition, the estate which we had at Assenheim [Note: [Col. 0373D] Assenheim, in the district of Villingen], once given by Duke Bertholf of Zähringen, brother of Bishop Gebehard III, was given in exchange for it [Col. 0373B], for lodging forcibly taken at our monastery.

§ XXII. The Burning of the Monastery

When they had already been freed from every debt in an extraordinary manner, though at great cost, and both the site and the monastery had been cultivated and maintained exceedingly well, what is written came to pass: “Before destruction the heart is exalted” (Proverbs 14:12).

There was a small building adjoining the infirmary, in which there was a fireplace; beside the fireplace, on both sides, was bedding on which the brothers slept …… There, the monastery boys, carelessly lighting a fire, caused the flames to seize the bedding placed nearby. In an instant the fire spread throughout the entire monastery; it consumed the basilica of Saint Gregory and all the monastery buildings at once …… [Note: [Col. 0373D] This fire and the restoration of the monastery are discussed in the account of the dedication of the new basilica at Petershausen [Col. 0374D], in Gerbert, History of the Black Forest, vol. III, p. 118.]

The sacristy and the repository of books, together with what was inside them, were scarcely saved [Col. 0373C]. It was a sight of misery. The dormitories of both the monks and the external brothers were consumed, and many were pitiably stripped naked. The dwelling of the sisters, although untouched by the flames, was nevertheless immediately completely dismantled, and the sisters themselves were scattered in every direction. Some of the monks, too, were sent to whatever monasteries could receive them.

This occurred in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1159, the 177th year from the original foundation of the monastery, in the seventh indiction, on the second day of the month of June—that is, the fourth day before the Nones of June [2 June], Tuesday of the most sacred week of Pentecost ……

§ XXIII.

After almost everything that had been built or collected, whether in ancient or recent times, had been destroyed, Abbot Conrad and Prior Hermann arose and girded themselves manfully for the restoration of the things mentioned above. The remaining brothers also helped them: some joyfully carrying burdens, others traveling through the regions with the relics of the saints and asking both rich and poor for assistance toward restoring the monastery consumed by fire.

From these contributions they began to build, first of all, the abbot’s residence; two chapels, one above the other—the upper one in honor of Saint Martin and Saint Oswald, the lower one in honor of Saint Mary Magdalene and Saint Faith, virgin and martyr. The dedication of Saint Faith continued to be held as before, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December [22 November], because that altar was found intact and divine offices were celebrated there [Col. 0374B].

§ XXIV.

They also built two refectories, one above the other, as well as a kitchen, a cellar, a winepress, a warming room, an infirmary, and the chapel of Saint Mary; they also built a chapter house and a dormitory.

For these buildings they burned lime at great expense near Tettingen in the forest. They also felled a great quantity of large beams and other timber in the forest near Bregenz and brought it to us across the broad lake by more than fifty oarsmen. Other monasteries also sent gifts of their own good will: the monks of Hirsau sent a good pallium and a cartload of wine; from the cell of Saint Peter [Col. 0374C] [Note: [Col. 0374D] In the Black Forest] one chalice; the monks of Zwiefalten one chasuble, an alb, and a stole; and others other small gifts. May all these be acceptable to God.

387 In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1161, in the ninth indiction, on the sixth day before the Ides of December [8 December], the chapel of Saint Mary beside the infirmary was dedicated by the venerable Hermann, bishop of Constance, with Abbot Conrad officiating ……

On the same day, the same Bishop Hermann dedicated the chapel of Saint Martin and deposited there the relics which had previously been there. From that day onward they celebrated the divine offices in the aforesaid chapel of Saint Mary. All the gold remaining after the purchase of the estate at Mimmenhausen was spent on these buildings.

## BOOK SIX BEGINS

[Col. 0373]

§ I.

[Col. 0373D]

…… Earlier, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1160, Hermann, bishop of Constance, dedicated the chapel of Saint John the Baptist in the cemetery, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January [26 December] ……

§ II. The Restoration of the Church

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1162, in the tenth indiction, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June [16 May], while Emperor Frederick was reigning and Bishop Hermann presided over the Church of Constance, under Abbot Conrad, on the vigil of the Ascension of the Lord, the first foundation of the new structure of the church of Pope Gregory was laid in the place of Saint Gebehard, the first founder of that same church. The threshold of the door opening toward the cloister was also set on the western side, in the third year after the same monastery had been burned.

At that time the Roman Church lacked a certain ruler, because two men were usurping it for themselves: Alexander and Victor. The emperor favored Victor, while the eastern churches favored Alexander [Note: [Col. 0375C] See Radevicus, On the Deeds of Emperor Frederick, Book II, chapter 50 and following].

§ III.

At the same time, Emperor Frederick had besieged the city of Milan, and its citizens had already been compelled to surrender by the great force of famine. Therefore, terrified by the destruction of this city, since it was the most powerful of all the cities of Italy, all the cities that had previously resisted brought immense sums of money to the emperor to gain his favor.

From these sums, and from others which he had acquired earlier and later under various conditions, he decided that tithes should be given as alms to monasteries throughout both Italy and Germany. For this reason he also sent five marks to us at that time. Thereafter, little by little, day by day, the basilica of Saint Gregory was restored through construction, under a certain Wezilo of Constance, a craftsman formerly among the clergy.

At the same time, the small estate at Liutprehtisruti [Note: [Col. 0375C] Lipperatsreuthe, in the district of Linzgau; it seems that a noble family took its name from this place] was redeemed for six talents. Ruodiger had given it through the hand of his son Egilward and of his lord Conrad, advocate of Sanctomonte.

§ IV.

In the same year, that is, 1162, Emperor Frederick, returning from the destruction of the city of Milan, held a conference at the city called Tulln [Note: [Col. 0375D] According to Otto of Freising, Book II, chapter 26, Emperor Frederick returned to Germany from the Italian expedition through Trent and Bavaria, so Tulln must be sought in those regions. It seems to be Tulln, or Tulna, a town of Lower Austria, where Otto II also held an assembly in 983. According to the Chronicle of Ursperg and the Chronicle of Weingarten (Hess, Monuments of the Guelphs, p. 49), the conference at Constance was held around the feast of Saint Clement, 23 November. There the divorce of Henry the Lion, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, from Clementia, daughter of Conrad, duke of Zähringen, took place because of their blood relationship (Guelphic Origins, vol. III, p. 182).], then another at Ulm, and a third at Constance. At that time he again gave us five pounds of silver.

Henry, duke of Saxony, also gave us another five pounds; he was likewise at that time separated from his wife. In the same year, Henry of Neuwirren gave us the small estate which he possessed at Mose ……

§ V.

…… Abbot Conrad had removed his brother from Friesberg [Note: [Col. 0375D] This apparently indicates the Cistercian monastery of Friensperg, or Aurora, in the territory of Bern (Gallia Christiana, vol. V, p. 938). The name of this brother of Abbot Conrad cannot, however, be determined from the cited Gallia Christiana [Col. 0376C], since no abbots bearing that name are found in either of the monasteries mentioned around this time]. He had first changed his habit there. Because of this and other offenses, he was expelled from the priory. Later, after becoming abbot at Fischingen, he soon departed from there as well, wandered through many monasteries in Bavaria, and was finally appointed abbot at Bregenz ……

§ VI.

Before Conrad became abbot, he wrote Ambrose’s *Hexameron* in his own hand and covered the arm of Saint Philip the Apostle with gold and silver. After he became abbot, he carried out many splendid works, which fire nevertheless consumed. Thereafter he persisted as much as he could in restoring the buildings and other equipment. He also acquired some small estates at Niuheim from tributary freemen, from whose revenues he arranged that both his own anniversary and that of his predecessor, Abbot Theoderic, his nephew [Note: [Col. 0376C] This kinship is not otherwise attested. [Col. 0376D] As we saw above, Book III, § 4, Theoderic’s father was Count Cuno; it is uncertain to which family he belonged, although Bucelinus, in *Chronologia Constantiense* under the year 1111, assigns him to the Kyburg family. Hesso is named as the father of Abbot Conrad in the Necrology for 21 April.], should be celebrated. For his own anniversary, which falls on . . . [Note: Since the day of death is omitted here, we conjectured above, in the preface, that the author died before Conrad. The day to be supplied here is IV Kalends of July [28 June], as appears immediately below and in the Necrology of Petershausen.] [Col. 0376B] he decreed that ten solidi should be spent, but three solidi on that of his nephew. In his time and with his assistance, churches were renewed and dedicated, and chapels were built at Eychstettin and at Epfindorf, also at Obirwangin and at Miminhusin, and likewise at Neuheim and at Rinhart. He also made two censers of orichalcum, several books, and, finally, a small building for storing books.

§ VII.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1164, in the month of June, Abbot Conrad began to fall ill. Since neither medicine nor any treatment applied to him could help, and since he had begun, though unwillingly, to despair of recovery, he gave us a rather fine stole [Col. 0376C] and redeemed a jeweled and gilded chalice that he had formerly sold. He also summoned the bishop, with whom he had been intimate, and several other excellent men; with them, I believe, he discussed his situation carefully. He died in the thirty-seventh year of his ordination, on IV Kalends of July [28 June], and on that very day was honorably buried beside the entrance of the basilica in the cloister . . . [Note: The catalogue of abbots in Brusch must consequently be corrected, since it makes Gebhard abbot as early as 1059.]

# THE SEVENTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0375]

§ I.

[Col. 0375C]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1164, on a Sunday, namely 14 Kalends of June [19 May] [Note: This date is erroneous: neither did 18 June fall on a Sunday in that year, nor had Conrad yet died. It therefore seems that III Nones [5] of July should be supplied; this was the only Sunday between Conrad’s death and 11 July, when Gebehard was ordained.], the brothers assembled together [Col. 0376C] and, by a free election, with no outsider present, elected Gebehard, a suitable and irreproachable man, and canonically and regularly established him as their abbot [Col. 0377A] with great freedom. Bishop Heremannus also ordained him with the greatest honor on the Translation of Saint Benedict, while all the canons of the church of Constance, together with a large crowd, attended and expressed their approval with complete eagerness. Thus great joy, praise, and celebration took place on that day over such agreement among the brothers, because at that time great disputes were occurring among many people in other monasteries. For that reason they greatly congratulated us, since absolutely no one among us, neither greater nor lesser, differed from the others.

§ II.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1163, Rudolph, our monk and priest, at his own request contributed a little money, collected from the offerings of the faithful, for the work of the monastery [Col. 0377B]. He also decorated with gold, silver, and precious stones the arm of one soldier from the Theban Legion of martyrs, companions of Saint Mauritius. Heremannus the elder of Hirzisegge presented this arm to our monastery [Note: See Book II, § 17.]. He himself had acquired it from a certain provost known to him at the place of Agaunum, when he passed through that place while traveling from Italy. At that time the same Rudolph also redeemed a fine chalice, which Abbot Conrad had sold some time before.

In the year 1164 Abbot Conrad improved the wheel of Saint Gregory, and the priest Otto restored the arm of Saint Philip the Apostle where it had been broken.

§ III.

[Col. 0377C] Nor will I remain silent about the memory of our beloved Abbot Conrad; rather, I shall commit certain things concerning his diligence to memory. He was skilled in the arts of meter and music, possessed an excellent intellect, a calm voice, and an agreeable manner of conversation; he had venerable gray hair and was modest in conduct and speech. He had built many splendid things that fire had consumed.

§ IV.

At that time Count Rudolph of Rammisberch [Note: Count Rudolph of Ramesberg subscribed as a witness in two diplomas of the Emperor Conrad III, dated 1141 and 1142, in Herrgott, vol. II, pp. 166 and 168; likewise in another diploma of Frederick I, dated 1155, and elsewhere. In Crusius, part III, book V, chapter 5, under the year 1359, another Rudolph of Ramsberg is still recorded.] bought from Conrad of Sanctum Mons a castle called Rinegge, which that man had held as a benefice from the Church of Constance. When he inhabited and occupied this same castle, he learned that the monastery of Saint Gregory, called Petershausen, [Col. 0377D] possessed nearby a holding that would be very useful to him. He began therefore to negotiate with Abbot Conrad so that this possession, called Rinisgimunde, might be granted to him for money until the end of his life, so that he could raise livestock there and obtain fodder and pasture from it; after his death, the monastery would recover in its entirety, without any opposition, both the holding itself and everything then found there. By persistent demands and repeated promises he pressed the matter until he persuaded the aforesaid abbot and the brothers to consent. He promised to give ten talents, some part of which he paid while retaining the rest, and he brought the holding adjoining his own at Rinisgimunde under his control. Concerning all these matters he therefore had the following charter written and confirmed it with his seal.

> In the name of the Holy Trinity, namely, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
>
> I, Rudolph, Count of Rammisberch, make known to all who wish to know, both present and future, how I, by the favor of divine providence, began to negotiate with Abbot Conrad and the brothers of the same monastery of Saint Gregory the Pope, which is called Petershausen [Col. 0378B], so that they might grant me such an estate as that monastery appeared to possess in the place called Rinisgimunde. Since this holding is near and useful to me for feeding livestock, and since my men were unable to avoid causing them harm, it seemed better to me that I, Rudolph, should give Abbot Conrad of Petershausen and the brothers of the same monastery ten talents, and that they should grant me the aforesaid estate at Rinisgimunde.
>
> The condition was that, for the remembrance and confirmation of this agreement, they should record and celebrate the anniversary of my mother Adelheid with their brethren at its appointed time; and that every year, for as long as I lived, I should have wine served to the brothers from my own resources on that day [Col. 0378C], as a payment and memorial of the present agreement.
>
> After my death, none of my heirs whatsoever shall have any power over this holding or over anything then found in it, whether livestock or other furnishings or property of any kind. Rather, the abbot then presiding over the monastery of Petershausen and the brothers of that place shall possess the whole of it in its entirety, without any opposition, for the salvation of my soul, my mother’s soul, and the souls of all my relatives.
>
> I, Rudolph, ordered this testament to be written for the specific reason that none of my heirs should dare, after my death, to violate this act of mine or trouble the aforesaid brothers in this estate. Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1163, while Frederick was reigning as emperor, Herimannus was bishop of Constance, and Conrad was abbot. And I, Gebehard, priest, wrote this charter in the first year of Gebehard’s abbacy.
>
> The witnesses to this transaction are my wife Elisabeth and my brother Arnold; Rudolph of Gutingin [Note: Gutingen was formerly a castle in Thurgau, from which a noble family took its name. From this family Heinrich the elder, a nobleman of Gutingen, issued a charter in 1257 (Herrgott, no. 414). In the Necrology, on 10 May, Diethalmus of Gittingen occurs, doubtless belonging to the same family.]; Count Adilbertus [Note: Perhaps this is Count Adelbertus of Winterthur and Kyburg, concerning whom see Book I, § 8.]; Rupert of Turingin; Adilbertus, priest of Tale; Diemo of Bregenz [Col. 0379A]; Arnold of Criessa; Bertoldus of Lustinowa [Note: Lustinova or Lustenova, formerly a royal estate in the district of Ringowe near the Rhine, is mentioned in a charter of 891 in Herrgott, no. 95.]; and many others.

§ V.

There was in the city of Constance a certain matron named Mathilda, who had with us a son named Heinrich, a well-educated priest, but alas, one who had been ill for far too long. For love of this son Heinrich, she therefore paid us forty talents in various ways, on the condition that her son Heinrich should receive the usufruct of the estate called Ouwingin, so that from it he might have the necessities he could not obtain from the common provisions, and, as assistance during his illness [Note: Read *infirmatus*, “having been weakened,” or *tempore infirmitatis*, “during his illness.”] [Col. 0379B] should unquestionably have these without diminution for as long as he remained in this life.

All these arrangements were confirmed by a very firm agreement [Col. 0379B] in the presence of Abbot Gebehard and the brothers of the same monastery, with this provision and confirmation: when the two of them died, their anniversaries were to be commemorated and celebrated at the proper time with the Office for the Dead, and on that day the brothers, or the entire community, were to be supplied generously and fully from the same estate [Col. 0380A].

Mathilda herself, however, after a few days, on III Ides of April [11 April] of that same year [Note: Since these acts took place in April in the presence of Gebehard, they must be assigned to the year 1165. In April 1164 he was not yet abbot.], departed this life and again gave us five pounds of silver, asking to be buried among us. This was done with great honor. These things were enacted in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1164, while Frederick was reigning as emperor, Herimannus was presiding as bishop of the Church of Constance, and Gebehard was abbot. Prosperously. Amen.

§ VI.

In the year 1170 many calamities overwhelmed the monastery of Saint Gregory, about which I am weary of saying anything further. For Abbot Gebehard was deposed [Note: This cannot be reconciled with a charter of Herimannus, bishop of Constance, dated 1183 ( *Historia Nigrae Silvae*, vol. III, p. 108), where a dispute is said to have existed between Theopertus, abbot of Saint Blasien, and Gebehard, abbot of Petershausen. Theopertus, however, first became abbot in 1174. Thus either Gebehard had not yet been deposed in 1170, or he was later restored.], and this place was grievously oppressed and plundered.

[Col. 0380B] In the year 1173 the foundations of the church of Saint Gregory were laid on the eastern side. In the year 1202 the bishop of Würzburg was killed [Note: Namely, Conrad I.].

In the year 1203 Philip [Note: Namely, the Swabian, elected Caesar.] marched with an army against the Landgrave. Amen.

[Col. 0379] THE PETERSHAUSEN CHRONICLE ENDS.

[Col. 0379]

# HERMANN THE LAME, MONK OF REICHENAU, ON THE MEASUREMENT OF THE ASTROLABE

(Printed in R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. III, part II, p. 94, from a manuscript of the illustrious monastery of Saint Peter at Salzburg, of the Order of Saint Benedict, recovered by the Reverend and illustrious Father Placidus Bökn, ascetic of that place.)

## NOTICE BY R. P. BERNARD PEZ

. . . As for Hermann’s present books *On the Measurement and Usefulness of the Astrolabe*, which we are now publishing for the first time from a six-hundred-year-old parchment manuscript of Saint Peter’s library, these are the very works that won him such esteem that many people considered him to have been the author of the astrolabe itself. Among those who held this view, as Possevinus testifies in *Apparatus sacer*, vol. I, p. 737, were Durandus, *On Divine Offices*, book IV, chapter 22, and Antonius Demochares, *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*, vol. IV, chapter 15.

For the rest, the arrangement and division of Hermann’s short books on the astrolabe are somewhat confused in the Saint Peter manuscript, owing, as we believe, to the copyist. He seems to have regarded the two later short books *On the Usefulness of the Astrolabe* as the second and third books of one continuous and complete work. This is sufficiently demonstrated by the title of the first book, although Hermann has only one single book *On the Measurement of the Astrolabe*.

Nor should Trithemius be trusted in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 321, where he says that Hermann wrote three books *On the Construction of the Astrolabe* and then another book *On the Usefulness of the Astrolabe*, of which the first three begin, “In measuring, therefore, . . .,” while the single later book begins, “Whoever [undertakes] astronomical . . . .” Anyone who examines our edition will see how poorly these statements fit together.

Therefore, to avoid all further confusion in the writings of Hermann on the astrolabe, understand the matter as follows. First Hermann published one book *On the Measurement of the Astrolabe*, which Trithemius titled *On the Construction of the Astrolabe* [Col. 0381], and which is printed here, together with its preface, from column 381 through column 390. It is clearly not earlier than some other book of the same kind and order, as is evident from the words with which Hermann concludes it:

> The various and numerous uses possessed by all the measurements described above must be made known elsewhere to the reader of the little book *Astrolapsus*, and to anyone exercising his intellect in the use of such things.

Second, Hermann wrote two books *On the Uses of the Astrolabe*, which Trithemius lists under that same title in the place cited, although he says that there is only one; we shall not dispute the matter with so learned a man. Certainly, from the words of Hermann himself in the book *On the Measurement of the Astrolabe*, just quoted, one can scarcely draw any other conclusion. He sends his reader not to “short books” but to the “short book *Astrolapsus*,” that is, *On the Uses of the Astrolabe*.

Nor would we have established any other division had the Saint Peter manuscript not suggested it to us. Since what follows chapter 21 had no connection whatsoever with what precedes it, yet everything was written by the same hand in the manuscript and joined together, we did not think ourselves at liberty to present it without the title of a new book, whether it belonged to Hermann or to someone else. Perhaps others will judge the matter better when more handwritten copies of Hermann’s work fall into their hands.

In an obscure and perplexing matter, we thought we should follow what was plainer and clearer. For Hermann’s words present a considerable obstacle. At the end of the book *On the Measurement of the Astrolabe*, he may have intended to compose only one short book, *Astrolapsus*; later, however, as the material increased or for other reasons, he may have enlarged it with a second book, as frequently happens to authors. Perhaps the epilogue of this second short book would have taught us something more certain, had it not, we do not know by what accident, been torn from the manuscript.

# HERMANN’S PREFACE TO THE BOOK ON THE MEASUREMENT OF THE ASTROLABE

[Col. 0381]

[Col. 0381A] Hermann, the vilest refuse of Christ’s poor and a follower of philosophy slower than a little donkey—or rather than a slug—sends perpetual greetings in the Lord to his beloved B.

Since I was often asked by many friends to try to write more clearly and fully about the measurement of the astrolabe, which among our people is found confused and therefore obscure and in many places mutilated, I had until now avoided doing so, partly through ignorance and partly because of the wretched sluggish idleness so familiar to me. At last, driven especially by your insistence, and as far as my inertness and laziness allowed, I set aside my customary [text uncertain: *mendacium fabrorum*] and hesitantly applied my idle hand to the work. I was concerned not with wit or elegant composition of words [Col. 0382A], but with explaining a complicated subject.

If in this matter the unlearned boldness of an obedient servant has committed any fault, may the kindly charity of the friends who gave the command be indulgent, and may it attribute the whole offense rather to their own zeal, which did not hesitate to lay so heavy a burden upon weak shoulders.

You, then, my dear friend, however others may receive these writings of mine, accept with gratitude, as befits a friend, the simple measurement of the aforesaid instrument, however it has been described. If I later learn that some matter concerning its construction troubles you, I shall gladly endeavor, insofar as leisure permits, to investigate it with you to the best of my ability.

# THE FIRST BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0381]

## CHAPTER I. How the equinoctial circle and the circles of the solstitial colures are to be found on the astrolabe

[Col. 0381B]

In measuring Ptolemy’s exceedingly subtle invention, the *Walzachora*, that is, the plane sphere, which we call the astrolabe, we must first find three circles. The middle one, which is the celestial equinoctial—for it extends through Libra and Aries—has the function and name of the equinoctial. Its size should be adjusted according to the size of the plate, at one’s discretion, so that it does not become excessively cumbersome. Carefully draw it around center *a*, divide it into four equal parts at points *b*, *c*, *d*, and *e*, and let *b* be the eastern point on the left; *c*, opposite it on the right, the western point; *d*, below, the northern point; and *e*, above, the meridian.

[Col. 0381C] Then, placing a straightedge, draw through points *b-a-c* a straight line from one end of the plate to the other, that is, from east to west. Likewise draw another line through *d-a-e*, that is, from north to south. The Arabs call these lines, which divide the circle into four parts, *Alcotan*; we call them colures.

With these lines in place, divide each quadrant of the circle into 90 equal parts, and from these take 24 on either side of *c*, toward *d* and toward *e*. To make this easier, divide each quadrant into three, so that each third contains 30 parts; then divide the two thirds adjoining *c* into five equal sections, understanding each group of five parts to contain 16 of the 90 parts.

Of these five sections, separate four on each side around *c*, and mark the upper point *f* and the lower point *g*. Thus you will know that between *c* and *f*, and likewise between *c* and *g*, there are 24 of the 90 parts enclosed.

Next place the straightedge on points *e* and *f*, or, if you prefer, on *d* and *g*. Observe where the line drawn from east to west through *b-a-c* touches the circle outside it, and mark that place with *h*. Fix the legs of the compass at *a* and *h*, and with center *a* and radius *h* draw the broader circle of the winter solstice. Likewise place the straightedge on points *e* and *g*, or *d* and *f*, and wherever it touches the aforesaid line, mark the point *i*. Then, fixing the compass at *a* and *i*, draw with center *a* the smaller circle of the summer solstice.

## CHAPTER II. On the *almucantarath*

Once these circles have been found, determine how many degrees constitute the altitude of whichever climate you wish to establish: namely, 15 for the first climate, 23 for the second, 30 for the third, 36 for the fourth, 41 for the fifth, 45 for the sixth, and 48 for the seventh.

Separate that many parts out of 90 from *c* toward *e*, and likewise the same number from the opposite point *b* toward *d*. For example, if you wish to measure our climate, that is, the seventh, take 48 of the 90 parts from *c* toward *e*, namely the upper 24 parts by which you found the circles, doubled, and mark the endpoint *k*. Likewise separate 48 parts from *b* toward *d* and mark the endpoint *l*, so that the complete half-circle from *a-k* to *d-l* is found.

Next divide the semicircle from *a-k* through *e* and *b* to *d-l*, as far as *l*, into six, and divide each sixth likewise into six by marked points. When this has been done, you will have 36 intervals from *k* to *l*, each containing five parts of the 360 parts of the entire circle.

Then place the straightedge on points *c* and *k*. Observe where it touches the meridian line *d-a-e*, extended far beyond the circles on another plate above which the *Walzachora* being measured is placed, and mark that point *m* [Col. 0383B]. Without moving the straightedge from point *c*, place it successively on each of the points you made from *k* to *l*. At each position mark the aforesaid line *d-a-e* where it is touched by the straightedge, until, when the straightedge is placed on points *c* and *l*, you make the thirty-sixth mark, namely *n*.

When this is done, divide the portion of the line between *m* and *n* into two with a compass. Fix the center at the midpoint and draw a semicircle, which the Arabs call the *Almucantarath*, curving it between the three circles through *b-n-c*. Likewise divide in two the portion of the line between the mark nearest *m* and the mark nearest *n*, and, fixing the center at its midpoint [Col. 0383C], curve another semicircle in the same way. In the same manner, after finding the midpoint of the portion of the line between the third mark from *m* and the third mark from *n*, curve a third semicircle.

Proceeding in order through each mark of the same line, advancing inward from both sides and dividing in two the space between the corresponding marks, draw with the compass alternately partial and complete circles, until, upon reaching the middle of the marks, you have completed eighteen small *Almucantarath* circles. Thus, from *n*, that is, from the first *almucantarath*, to the center of the middle circle, 90 degrees are counted, with five degrees counted in each interval of the *campilograms* [technical term uncertain].

From *n* itself to the middle center *a*, however, you find in each climate as many degrees as the altitude of the climate being measured contains: for example, in the seventh, whose model I have now set out, 48 degrees.

You will find 15 degrees in the first climate as follows: divide the quadrant into three parts, and divide one third into two. Each of the two resulting parts then contains 15 degrees.

In the second climate you will find 24 as follows: divide the quadrants into three parts; then divide one third on the *almagrip* [technical term] into five, each part containing six degrees. Remove the half-sized fifth part of the *almagrip*, namely six degrees, and 24 will remain.

In the third climate you will find 30 as follows: divide the quadrant, namely 90 degrees from *c*, into three, and each part will be 30.

In the fourth climate you will find 36 as follows: again divide the quadrant, namely 90 degrees [Col. 0384A], into three, and each part will be 30. Then divide two parts, namely 60, into five, so that each part is 12; remove two parts, namely 24, and 36 will remain.

In the fifth climate you will find 40 as follows: divide the same quadrant into three, and then divide two parts, namely 60, into six, so that each part is ten. Remove two parts, namely 20, and 40 will remain.

Finally, in the sixth climate you will find 45 as follows: divide the same quadrant in half, and each part will be 45, since twice 45 makes 90. The seventh climate has already been described above.

## CHAPTER III. On finding the hour lines

[Col. 0384B] When the *Almucantarath* campilograms have been completed in this way, the space of the three circles first mentioned that remains below the first *almucantarath*, namely on the side of *d*, the northern side, must be distributed equally for the twelve hours as follows.

Beginning at the *almucantarath* itself on the side of *c*, divide the space of each of the three circles up to the line *d-a-e* equally into the six ante meridian hours. Likewise, measuring six intervals in each circle from the line *d-a-e* to the *almucantarath* on the side of *b*, assign them to the post meridian hours.

Then take a compass and fix one leg at such a place that the other can touch the three points marking the limit of the first hour in each of the circles. By rotating the compass, curve the final line of the first hour between the three circles [Col. 0384C]. Proceed in the same way for each hour, now contracting and now expanding the compass and fixing it at different places as the position of the points requires; thus draw the final lines of the individual hours.

In this way, each hour will produce intervals that are narrower toward the inner circle and broader toward the outer circle, with the northern line *d-a-e* marking their middle. Mark the seven climate tables with such measurements and diagrams, in fourfold sets [the text appears corrupt: *quaternas 7 scilicet*].

## CHAPTER IV. Description of the *Alhancabuth*

Next the *volvellum*, or “web,” which the Arabs call the *Alhancabuth*, perforated by repeated punching, is to be measured as follows.

First draw on its somewhat thicker plate—thicker than the other underlying wheels, of which there are three—three circles of the same size as those above, namely the equinoctial, winter-solstitial, and summer-solstitial circles. Divide these in the same manner with straight lines, the colures, into four equal parts as above.

Divide in two one colure, directed from north toward south, from the point where the smallest summer circle cuts it at its end to the point where, on the opposite side, it joins the largest winter circle. Fix the center at the midpoint and describe the zodiacal circle, in which the whole effectiveness of this art consists, so that the smallest circle, containing the entire area beneath it, joins it on one side, while on the opposite side the largest circle is joined to it along its diameter [Col. 0385A]. The middle circle should intersect it on both sides, together with the other colure, at the individual points; and it should be divided by the line of that colure into two hemispheres, though not equally. Give it also, at your discretion, a suitable width in which the names of the twelve signs and of certain stars can be written.

The spaces and positions of the twelve signs are determined as follows.

## CHAPTER V. On finding the spaces of the signs

Divide the third and largest of the circles into twelve, dividing each quadrant into three. Then place a straightedge from the center of the three circles to each of the twelve divisions, and cut the zodiacal circle you have made wherever it is touched by the straightedge. In this way form twelve spaces in it, unequal in size, and arrange the six signs, from Aries to Libra, in the six spaces of the smaller hemisphere, against the order of the heavens—that is, from right to left.

In the larger hemisphere likewise make an equal number of spaces and place in them the same number of signs, from Libra to Aries. Thus from the equinoctial circle to the summer circle extend Aries, Taurus, and Gemini; from there Cancer, Leo, and Virgo bend back toward the equinoctial circle. From there Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius descend toward the winter circle; and from there Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces rise again toward the equinoctial circle.

At the boundary between Sagittarius and Capricorn a certain little projection appears, called in Arabic *Almeri*, that is, “the calculator.”

[Col. 0385C] To distinguish the portions or degrees of the signs on the sloping side of the same zodiac, divide the aforesaid twelve parts of the largest circle into six, and divide each individual part likewise. Then place the straightedge, as above, at each of these divisions and at the center of the three circles, marking the zodiacal circle wherever it is touched by the straightedge. You will thereby make six intervals in each of the twelve signs, seventy-two in the entire zodiac, each containing five of the 360 degrees of the whole circle.

## CHAPTER VI. On the positioning of the stars

[Col. 0386A]

When the zodiac has been completed in this way, the astronomers teach that the sharp little pegs scattered and fixed at specific places in the *Alhancabuth*, whose points represent certain very bright stars, are to be positioned as follows.

Whenever you wish to place a star on it, first look on the page written below to see opposite which degree of whichever of the twelve signs that star should be placed. Then place the straightedge at that same degree and at the center of the three circles, and direct it through the middle line of the same peg or star.

Afterward, beginning at the degree where the largest circle is touched by the straightedge, count again on that largest circle as many degrees in both directions as you see assigned to the same star on the corresponding page [Col. 0386B]. Where that number ends on either side, place the straightedge on the opposite side; wherever the star’s line is touched by the straightedge, cut off the point of its projection there.

For example, Alramech is fixed in the constellation of Boötes at the twenty-fourth degree of Libra. Draw a line through it by placing the straightedge at the center of the three circles. From that degree, count 65 degrees in both directions on the largest circle. Where that number ends, place the straightedge, and let the point of Alramech be assigned to the corresponding endpoint.

In the same manner, according to the numbers assigned to each star on that page, place after Alramech on the zodiac itself Elfeca the white, Althahir, Delfin, and Zalferaz.

On the small circle drawn around the center for this purpose according to convenience, arrange Benenaz, Wega, Alrif, Algol, Albazoch, Egregez, and Alrucuba.

On the equinoctial part of the circle, from the region of Taurus to Virgo, likewise left for this purpose, place Aldebaram, Algenze, Algomeiza, Aldiraan, and Calladarazeda.

On the largest winter circle, which is likewise left for this purpose at the outermost edges of the *volvellum* from Aquarius to Sagittarius, place Denebalgedi, Benebcaitox, Patancaitox, Rigel, Alhabor, Alhurab, Alchimech, and Calbalagrah. Although these are not so useful, since they are in the south and immersed near the horizon, place them as the page written below instructs.

[Col. 0387A] Once the *Alhancabuth* has been measured in this way, have the entire thing carefully perforated and polished wherever it is open, leaving intact the zodiac and the parts of the other circles I have mentioned, together with their stars, as well as a certain straightedge drawn through Pisces and Virgo along another colure. This straightedge should be capable of holding these elements together with the middle circle of the center, thereby providing solidity to the parts left behind.

When it is placed over a climate and revolved around the axis called the *Alchitob*, all the outlines of that climate will appear through the openings, and the risings, settings, and exaltations of the signs and stars, together with the calculation of the hours, will be clearly revealed, as experience and use of its risings [manuscript: *ortis*] plainly confirms to those who wish to know.

## CHAPTER VII. On the division of the boss

[Col. 0387B]

When this has been completed, divide the boss, which must surround the mother *Walzachora* itself and enclose all the tables of the climates, as well as the *Alhancabuth* placed upon it, first into four equal parts, so that it corresponds to the aforesaid colures.

Then divide each quarter into three, and each of these into six, so that the entire circumference of the boss contains 72 equal intervals distinguished by straight lines. Divide each of these intervals internally, where the projecting *Almeri* on the *Alhancabuth* reaches it, into further groups of five degrees, so that the revolving *Almeri* can calculate the lengths of days and hours.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the division of the signs, months, and days

[Col. 0387C]

What remains is to measure the rear surface of the *Walzachora*, which is to be marked with all the degrees and signs of the zodiac and with the months and days of the year.

Divide its outer circles into four equal parts with straight lines drawn through the center, and distinguish them by the same measurement as the boss described above: each quadrant is first divided into three and those parts into six, making 18 intervals, while the entire circumference is divided into 72. Divide each of these into five degrees, which together make 360.

The next interval of the circles beneath these is to be divided into three signs in each quadrant and marked with their names. Beginning at the western line, that is, on the right, and proceeding to the upper southern point, from which the circle is suspended by a plumb line, arrange, against the order of the heavens, Aries, Taurus, and Gemini. From there to the eastern line, that is, the left, place Cancer, Leo, and Virgo. From there to the lowest northern point place Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius. From there return to the western line with Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. Assign to each sign six times five, that is, 30, of the aforesaid 360 degrees of the whole circle.

The next interval of the circles beneath this is to be distributed among the twelve months, beginning approximately at the middle of the signs to which they belong, and marked with their names.

Beneath this, divide another interval [Col. 0388A] into the days of the year—360, or rather with five additional days. You can do this more easily as follows: set aside an eighteenth part of one quadrant of the circle. Excepting this, divide the entire remaining circumference into twelve, and divide each twelfth into six parts. When you add the quadrant portion that you had set aside, you will find seventy-three intervals in the whole circle [OCR/contextually uncertain; likely “seventy-three” as printed], and, dividing each of them into five, you will have a circle divided into 365 days.

Beginning at the autumnal equinox, which modern authorities believe should be assigned to the first degree of Aries, that is, 15 Kalends of April [18 March], assign the fourteen days following the equinox—that is, following the western line at which you began Aries—to the month of March. Then assign 30 days to April, 31 to May, 30 to June, 31 to July, 31 to August, 30 to September [Col. 0388B], 31 to October, 30 to November, 31 to December, 31 to January, 28 to February, and 17 to March up to the aforesaid line of the vernal equinox. In this way you will complete the entire circuit of the current year, with two lines dividing the circles into four parts—namely, four quarters of the year—intersecting two equinoxes and an equal number of solstices.

What remains beneath this, the circle nearest the center, divide in each month in such a way that you mark off groups of five days—or, what seems more convenient on account of the weeks, groups of seven—by lines, leaving any days of the month that still remain unmarked. When this has been completed, you will be pleased that the entire measurement of this instrument pertaining to astronomical and, specifically, horological study has been finished. But you should not hesitate to write a few words concerning the measurement of the quadrant, which is situated within the circle of days between the western and northern lines, toward the middle of Aquarius, and is exceedingly useful for geometrical measurements.

## CHAPTER IX. On the square

Divide the fourth part of the aforesaid circle of days between the aforementioned western and northern letters into two. Then, after making a point at the middle, likewise divide another quarter between the western and southern [letters], and another between the northern and eastern [letters], separating the halves with points b and c. Next, placing the rule on points a and b, direct a straight line from the western line toward a. Likewise, placing the rule on a and c, draw another line from the northern [line] to a. Thus you have a right-angled, equilateral square, one angle of which is at a, the opposite one at the center along the diagonal; the remaining two are bounded by the western and northern lines.

Divide the two sides that form the angle at a, giving them whatever width you wish, into twelve equal parts; and, enclosing two of these inwardly, divide them into six parts, so that, as the *Alhidada* passes over them—that is, a certain rule pierced with two upright sights along a straight line—it may be possible to see which part of the side of the square is being indicated. What advantages, and how great, all the measurements described above possess should be explained elsewhere to anyone who reads the little book *Astrolapsus* and exercises his intellect in the use of such things.

[Col. 0389]
