# BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER I. On the uses of the astrolabe

[Col. 0389B]

Whoever strives, through diligent investigation of the truth, to probe more deeply the expertise of astronomical study and the higher knowledge of the geometrical measurements of the celestial spheres, and endeavors industriously to distinguish the most certain methods of all horologia belonging to the various climates, together with everything else pertaining to these matters, should seek out and learn this *walzacora*—that is, Ptolemy’s plane sphere, or astrolabe—with skillful inquiry; and, once investigated, should entrust it firmly to tenacious memory, so that, after learning all the circles and embossed divisions written and engraved upon it, he may retain each of them by name. For if, through careful examination of these things, he embraces their whole meaning, [Col. 0389C] and, as a diligent student, uses them with the celebrated constancy of his attention, he will derive from this the greatest advantage and a subtle depth in astronomical and geometrical studies.

[Col. 0390B] Through it he will discover, according to the circuit of spherical rotation, the precise risings and settings of all the heavenly bodies at each hour; which decan and which degree of each sign emerges at rising or sinks at setting; the movements of the heavenly bodies through all the regions of the sky; the positions of the signs; the degrees of the sun; its daily or monthly altitude; and how many stadia of the terrestrial sphere it traverses. Likewise, he will discover the signs and altitudes of the fixed stars, and, in addition, the most exact hours of nights and days, whether natural or artificial, with their increases and decreases.

How necessary this knowledge is for divine services, how useful for practice, and how useful for exposing and invalidating the false and deceptive horologia of certain people, a prudent mind can understand and an imprudent one can learn. He will also learn the beginnings of the months, changes in horologia and climates, and many other things useful for understanding Ptolemy’s canons—things which it would be superfluous to introduce here, since they will be disclosed more appropriately in what follows [Col. 0391A]. Hence the reader will be not so much delighted as astonished. Let him therefore investigate with every effort the names that follow and the others written below, and, once investigated, retain them most firmly in the little chest of his heart; then the way to discover the matters described above will be clear, without any uncertainty.

Having thus given these preliminary indications, and not frightened away by laziness, I shall speak briefly—so as not to offend by writing too much—about its circles, arranged according to an architectural or mechanical method, and about their names, so that I may fulfill my promises more promptly.

## CHAPTER II. Description of the circles

The *walzachora* is a tablet shaped according to the roundness of the sky. Each of its two surfaces is divided by lines extending from the very center through the diameter, at equal intervals and into four parts; these lines are the *colures*. Drawn from both the eastern and the northern vertex in different directions, they divide the zodiac into four parts, so that one passes through Aries and Libra, and the other through Cancer and Capricorn. The center itself, where these lines intersect, is designated by the letter a.

The left-hand line, marked b, is called *Almarech*—that is, the eastern line, from the rising of the stars and of the day. The right-hand line, where c is located, is called *Almagrip*—that is, the western line, from the setting of the stars and of the day. This is the line drawn from east to west, which is also indicated by the sun’s ray at its first rising, or by the shadow of the gnomon.

The upper line, marked d, is called *Walzazene*—that is, the meridian line—because, when the sun ascends and touches it, it produces midday after six measured hours, and, descending, begins to turn toward setting. The lower line, where e is located, is called *Cathezenuel*—that is, the line of equality or the sphere’s bisecting line. It is the line extending from south to north, which the sun’s ray, or the shadow of the gnomon at the summer solstice, indicates at the summer tropic.

On the front surface of this [instrument] three circles of the divided zodiac are inscribed. One of them, placed in the middle according to the equinoctial arrangement, marks without deviation the course of Aries and Libra. It is also called the equinoctial circle, because there the spans of daylight and night are measured in equal compensation. It is also called the ecliptic, for when the sun and moon come together there, it is necessary that one or the other of them undergo an eclipse.

[Col. 0391D] Of the two terminal circles, one is seen as the lower circle revolving near the boundary of the center. In accordance with the observed natural arrangement, the nearer it is to the center, the more contracted it is in its revolution. This circle is called the summer tropic of Cancer. At the outermost hours of the tablet, the circle of Capricorn—that is, the winter tropic—is inscribed with a more widely extended revolution. Their inscriptions, placed in the likeness of the celestial sphere, enclose the breadth of the zodiacal circle and set a boundary for the courses of the sun and the other planets.

Between these outermost circles, in the northern region, *hototaltasab*—that is, the short hour-lines—is arranged by an artificial method, with equal divisions of intervals, so that, drawn out from the narrower interior, they become progressively broader as they run through the breadth toward the outside [Col. 0392A]. The middle one is the diagonal line of midday. Together with this line, its two sides, doubled and each containing six divisions, establish the limit of the twelve hours; each is marked with an impressed name. These names are Arabic and are inscribed below in the form of the [hour] table. The line on the right carefully marks the ante meridian hours, while the one on the left marks the post meridian hours, and, when the horoscope is applied with an attentive gaze, it demonstrates them.

XII. *Ethesiafer.* XI. *Aldimata.* X. [Col. 0392B] *Alhansira.* IX. *Ethezea.* VIII. *Ethemima.* VII. *Escebea.* [Col. 0392A] I. hour. *Elewiul.* II. *Athenia.* III. [Col. 0392B] *Atheziza.* IV. *Arrabea.* V. *Alcamiza.* VI. *Escendelisza.*

In the upper half of the region they have also skillfully fashioned semicircles and complete little circles, which they call *Omucantarath*, that is, the sun’s progressions. Through frequent circling and repeated curvature, some more extended and others more contracted, they form a crown in a precise and necessary arrangement. The effectiveness of this instrument largely depends upon them.

Within their intervals, the degrees of the sun’s daily and monthly ascent and descent are measured, doubled on both sides, up to 90. Thus, in this *walzacora* there are fifteen little circles, each divided into six parts, by which the number 90 is completed—that is, a quadrant of the entire circle. These little circles, however, together with their numerical values, are increased or diminished according to changes in the horologia and according to the position of places and climates; this will become clearer elsewhere.

At the outer edges of the tablet, a boss projecting through rotation is fixed with firm solidity. They call it *Alnogiza*. Extending upward, it receives and encloses the projecting tablets of the other climates. To accommodate these, its front is pierced by a small hole into which the pointed heads of the tablets are inserted. This hole corresponds to the meridian rule. Its thickness does not rise higher than the capacity of the tablets.

Next, through the perforated projecting side-vertex, hanging circles are introduced, or rather linked together. When they are attached, the instrument is raised whenever the sun’s ray is to be perceived. Its upper polished surface is divided into square parts equal to 360 parts, by intervals divided into five; these, if distinguished by careful partition, serve multiple purposes. Above all, from the pattern impressed upon them, the natural hours of nights and days are known with complete certainty, together with their increases and decreases, as will be explained more suitably below.

Other tablets are also engraved on these circles, for whatever climates they may be intended, although the *almucantarath* themselves vary slightly according to changes in places and climates. A definite account of this variation will be given in its proper place. Above these tablets rests the *Alhancabuth*—that is, the revolving disk—which is turned by hand to demonstrate the rotation of the celestial sphere and to indicate the hours.

For, through its rotations and the degrees of the sun, together with the corresponding horoscopes marked at fixed places along the divisions of the zodiacal circle, the clearest properties of the hours become evident, and the contractions and increases of nights and days are demonstrated. It is engraved with a hollowed mechanism according to the intervals of the circles mentioned above and the positions of the fixed stars, by which the hours of the night are recognized.

There are, in fact, three circles on it. The innermost is divided by a diameter into two semicircles; through linear division, each of these is divided into six, and thus the number twelve is assigned to the six signs of each half of the zodiac. When it is placed above the others and moved by rotation, you will see it mark Aries and Libra by running through the middle circle, and Cancer and Capricorn by running through the terminal circles.

It is also naturally arranged so that it rises in the northern part but sinks in the southern part toward the boundary of the lower regions. The narrower hemisphere, beginning with Aries, although contracted by the shortening of its intervals, nevertheless ascends by widening through the spring signs and is marked at its summit, at Cancer, by the solstitial line. From there, by the same revolution, it contracts the days as it passes through the summer signs and ends at Libra, the equinoctial point.

Beginning with Libra, the larger hemisphere, depressed through its expanded revolution, contracts the autumn days and reaches the solstice of Capricorn. From there it is brought back by the wintry revolution to the sign of Aries. On the sides of this circle [in the margin: “or on the little squares”], the parts of the signs are carefully distinguished by division. Each sign is divided into intervals of five; these, assigned six to each fivefold division, give the number thirty, and thus, proceeding in order, they complete the number of the zodiac.

They have also fashioned sharp little teeth on it, which, placed at fixed locations, mark the fixed stars through which we recognize the hours of the night; these stars are also inscribed with their proper Arabic names. On the circumference, or on the projecting face of the circumference, there is a tooth placed above Capricorn and extending toward the boss. By calculating, it distinguishes the total number of hours from the number placed on the face of the boss. It is called *almeri*, that is, “the calculator.” The *halbancabuth*, placed above it, covers the winding of the tablet.

Now the stylus is turned from the front surface just described to the rear, on which information about the signs and months is provided. On the inner circles, the proper days are carefully inscribed for each month. The signs belonging to each of these months are placed above them by linear division. On the outer edges of the tablet, the parts of the zodiac are marked by quadrants [Col. 0394A], with their proper intervals, or by signs distributed through intervals divided into five and then into six. All this can be grasped more easily by sight than by words.

There is also the *Alhidada*—that is, the pivot—which we may call the ray. Extended like a rule, it is placed over the tablet. At its ends are two upright sights, which have corresponding pairs of holes, either for receiving the ray of the sun and of the fixed stars or for the science of geometrical measurements. When it is turned by touch, its back-and-forth movement shows the sun’s altitude to an attentive observer.

There is also the *Alchitob*—that is, the rounded bar—which is inserted into the perforated center of the *Walzacora* to fasten the tablets of the climates. At its perforated top another wedge is inserted transversely, together with part of the *Alhancabuth*; they call this *Alferaz*, that is, “the horse,” because it is shaped like a horse.

So that I might make the matter clearer, I have explained its circles briefly, except for one quadrangle, about which I shall speak more fully in its proper place. But this object is complicated by concealed interconnections, and cannot be unraveled for everyone’s understanding, except by those who have practical experience in these matters. If anyone has understood little from what has been written or will be written, let him test the object itself, and without doubt he will find that everything has been stated carefully. Having thus set out these preliminary matters, I shall, while fulfilling my undertaking, explain how we practice with it, beginning with the artificial hours of day and night.

## CHAPTER III. On determining the sign and degree of the sun

[Col. 0394C]

If you wish to know with complete certainty the natural or artificial hours of day and night, you must first know in which sign the sun is and in which decan or degree of that sign. Although you can learn this by various methods of calculation, nevertheless, after acquiring great skill from this figure, you will recognize it completely. I consider it appropriate to set it out here, since the place and subject require it and since it is presented in Arabic.

This figure has, on one side, the names of the months written above it; on the other side, the days of the months expressed numerically; and in the middle, on the surface of the entire zodiacal circle, the signs with their degrees. If you wish to learn through it the sign and degree of the sun on any given day, look on both sides for the current month and the current day of that month [Col. 0394D], and enter by the two lines from opposite sides until the angular *proselis* [Note: An old gloss says: “that is, meeting, as though leaping together with and corresponding to it.”]. Then look at the number you find there above on the same line, together with the sign: that is the degree of the sun you seek.

If you wish to learn it in another way, add 15 to however many days of the current month have elapsed. Having collected this total, begin counting from the first degree of the sign belonging to that month, using intervals divided into five; when the count comes to an end, the degree reached is the degree of the sun you seek. For example, once twenty days of April have passed, add 15, and the total will be 35 [Col. 0395A]. Now begin counting with this number from the first degree of Aries, which belongs to April, and in counting you will arrive at the fifth degree of Taurus. For after assigning thirty to Aries, five remain for Taurus. You will therefore say: on the twentieth day of April the sun is in the fifth degree of Taurus.

You will learn this through the astrolabe as follows. On its rear surface, look at the days of the months and the divisions of the signs. Place the *Alhidada* over the current day, the day on which you are, and whichever degree the outer tip of the *Alhidada* indicates [Col. 0396A] is the degree of the sun that you seek. Thus, if you place the *Alhidada* over the twentieth day of April, its tip marks the fifth degree of Taurus. Mark that degree on the *Alhancabuth*, in its proper place on the other side.

Here it should be noted that the progress of your calculation in these matters proceeds according to the sun’s revolution against the world, as though from right to left. For the Chaldaean method proceeds in this way, whether in calculation or in writing.

[Col. 0395]

## CHAPTER IV. On finding the sun’s *nadir*

[Col. 0395B]

Once the degree of the sun has been found and marked on the *Alhancabuth*, you must find the *nadir*—*Ascemath*, that is, the sun’s opposite—which we may call the horoscope, because it indicates the hours when observed. The horoscope is formed by the diameter of the sphere in the sixth sign: the sun occupies the same proportion of the sixth sign as the degree of its own sign, that is, from the sun’s degree to the 180th part, which is the diameter of the hemisphere, according to the natural rule that necessarily completes the circuit by equal correspondence.

You will find the *nadir* through the astrolabe as follows.

[Col. 0396B] Place the degree of the sun already marked on the *Alhancabuth* over the first *Almucantarath*, or over the eastern line, and observe which sign and which degree lies beneath the final *Almucantarath* or the western line. That is the sun’s *nadir*.

You can also find both things—the degree of the sun and its opposite—simultaneously by means of the *Alhidada*, observing the tips on either side of it, as is clear to anyone who investigates carefully. For just as the day rises together with the degree of the sun, so the night rises together with the sun’s *nadir*. Moreover, the risings of day and night take place through the diameter of the hemisphere [of the zodiac]. For the day is closed by the 180 parts of the hemisphere, with five degrees assigned to each hour.

There is, in fact, the same and equal rotation of rising and setting bodies across the horizon of the celestial sphere, as can be demonstrated by the astrolabe. Once these things have been found, carefully apply the impressed notation of day and night. When these are managed attentively, everything else will easily become clear.

## CHAPTER V. On determining the sun’s altitude and the other hours of the day

Next, if you wish to know the exact hours of the day, you must determine the sun’s altitude, which in Arabic they call *Erufamazeat*, for whatever hour you wish. By the sun’s altitude we mean its course, by which, from its first rising, it gradually proceeds—as though by degrees—receding from the earth through the world’s momentum and ascending into the higher spaces of the sky, or descending toward the lower regions [Col. 0397B].

For while its upper edge has barely emerged from the horizon, if you apply the astrolabe, you will see that, with the *Alhidada* resting on the eastern line, the sun’s ray inevitably passes through both of its holes. From there it ascends to visit the higher regions until it reaches the meridian line; descending, it sets along the same line of its rising.

You will find the sun’s altitude at any hour by proceeding with your investigation as follows. Take the astrolabe and stand facing the sun attentively, so that your left shoulder is turned toward the sun. Let the astrolabe hang from your hand, with its rear surface facing you and your right hand turned toward you. Turn the *Alhidada*, with its face directed toward the sun, repeatedly back and forth until the sun’s ray passes normally through both holes [Col. 0397C].

When you see this, keeping your bodily and mental attention fixed carefully upon it, mark by a reliable notation the number counted from the eastern line in intervals divided into five, the number indicated by the tip of the *Alhidada* among the ten divisions. Whatever the number is, that is the entire altitude of the sun.

Having carefully observed and committed this to memory, turn the front surface of the astrolabe toward you and find the same number, which you discovered as the sun’s altitude, among the intervals divided into six parts, as follows. Assign six to each interval, beginning with the first *Almucantarath*, until you find the number you received—on the eastern side if it is before midday, and on the western side if it is after midday.

Once this has been found, place the degree of the sun marked on the *Alhancabuth* over the sun’s altitude. Then look in the lower region for the sun’s *nadir*, above which the hour is situated. That is the present hour you seek. In the same way test the truth for any of the hours of the day, whether in summer or winter, without any uncertain hesitation.

This appears exceedingly useful for celebrating the office of the daytime hours, and all things proceed more acceptably and fittingly when, with the highest reverence, the divine services are performed at the proper hours under the rule of the just Judge, who in no respect wishes to be deceived by the obscuring veil of temporal change.

## CHAPTER VI. On the altitude of the stars and the hours of the night

Once these matters have been acquired through care, and the daytime offices have been completed at the most exact hours [Col. 0398A], you, as a vigilant observer of the hours, must immediately investigate the altitudes of the fixed stars, which indicate the nocturnal hours. For just as the hours of the day are found through the sun’s altitude, so the hours of the night are drawn from the fixed stars.

At this point the subject and method require that we say something about what these stars are, where they are, how many there are, and about their configurations or names. But since brevity is being pursued here, lest the purpose be driven away by too great a digression, this will be explained more appropriately and more fully in what follows [see below, ch. 17].

Seek the altitude of any star as follows: raise the astrolabe and turn the *Alhidada* so that it is properly aligned, until you can observe any of the fixed stars then visible and marked on the astrolabe through both holes with the assured sight of one eye [Col. 0398B]. Once it has been seen, match the altitude indicated by the *Alhidada* with that same altitude among the *Almucantarath*, on the side on which you received the star. Place the head of that star over this altitude in the *Almucantarath*, and observe which hour the degree of the sun indicates, for that is the hour you seek. But observe this rule: learn the hours of the day through the sun’s *nadir*, and the hours of the night through the degrees of the sun.

## CHAPTER VII. On the division of the hours among the four regions

There are four regions of the world. One of them, the northern region, never receives the sun into itself in our parts [Col. 0398C]. Therefore the twelve hours are distributed among the other three—the eastern, southern, and western—which admit the sun, four to each. For three times four produces twelve.

The eastern region is assigned hours 1, 2, 3, and 4; the southern, 5, 6, 7, and 8; the western, 9, 10, 11, and 12. Of these hours, two are always under one number or measurement, except for the sixth and twelfth. For just as the sixth hour, because of the sun’s highest ascent, cannot be equal to the others in number or measurement, so neither can the twelfth, because of its lowest descent. The sixth is placed at the summit; the fifth is measured with the seventh, the fourth with the eighth, the third with the ninth, the second with the tenth, and the first with the eleventh. The twelfth remains, placed at sunset.

[Col. 0398D]

## CHAPTER VIII. On equinoctial and unequal hours

[Col. 0399A]

Having thus far arranged the artificial hours, I shall next speak of equinoctial and unequal hours. First I shall explain how the 360 parts are divided by equinoctial and unequal hours, which the Arabs call *Muzzewine*, that is, “equal,” and *Ezemenie*, that is, “unequal.”

If you wish to know how many *Muzzewine* hours there are in the entire zodiacal circle—that is, in its 360 parts—divide half of that number, 180, by the twelve equinoctial hours, assigning fifteen parts to each hour, that is, three intervals divided into five. You will unquestionably find twelve equinoctial hours in that hemisphere. If you do the same in the other hemisphere, you will mark the same number [Col. 0399B]. For fifteen times twenty-four is 360. Thus, when the entire sphere has revolved once, twenty-four hours are found in day and night.

If you wish to know how many *Ezemenie*—that is, unequal hours—are made in the same number, assign nineteen parts to each, and you will undoubtedly find nineteen unequal hours in the whole circle. An equinoctial hour has fifteen parts because, when fifteen is multiplied by twenty-four, the result is 360. For as many hours are found in 360 parts as there are hours in the natural day.

The hours are called equinoctial because they are equal on only two days of the year, namely those on which the sun is in the first part of Aries and Libra. At all other times they are called unequal, because of the mutual alternation of shortening and lengthening. This alternating change always varies within the parts of one sign, that is, within thirty parts [Col. 0399C]. For the shortest *Ezemenia* hour decreases to no fewer than eleven parts, while the longest increases to no more than nineteen parts. Hence nineteen parts are assigned to it, although through increase or decrease it returns to the parts of an equinoctial hour, that is, to fifteen.

## CHAPTER IX. On the parts of the unequal hours of the day

If you wish to know the parts of the unequal hours of the day, place the sun’s *nadir* over the first line of any hour. Once this has been done, observe carefully and assign the part indicated by *Almeri* among the 360 parts. Then move the *nadir* to the last line of that same hour; however many parts *Almeri* has counted within its boundaries [Col. 0399D], that many are the parts of the unequal hours of the day.

## CHAPTER X. On the parts of the unequal hours of the day

If you wish to know the parts of the hours of the night, do with the degree of the sun as you did with the *nadir*: place the degree over the first line of any hour and mark the position indicated by *Almeri*. Then, after rotating it to the last [line], however many degrees *Almeri* marks as the sun’s degree proceeds, that many are the parts you seek.

But take care to learn the parts of the daytime hours through the *nadir*, and those of the nighttime hours through the degree of the sun. If, after determining the parts of the daytime hours, you wish to know how many remain for the night, subtract those same parts from 30; whatever remains [Col. 0400A] is the number of parts of the nighttime hours. Conversely, after subtracting the parts of the nighttime hours from 30, the daytime parts remain, because, as stated, their alternating change of shortening and lengthening occurs within thirty.

## CHAPTER XI. On investigating the extent of the circle of the day

When you wish to know how many equinoctial hours there are in the day or night, or how many more equinoctial hours the night or day contains, you must first investigate the extent of the circle of day and night. By the circle of the day I mean the amount the sun traverses each day, in 360 parts, from first rising to setting as the sphere turns; by the circle of the night I mean what remains.

You will find it as follows. Place the degree of the sun over the first *Almucantarath* on the side of *Almarech*, and carefully mark the position of *Almeri*. Once it has been marked, transfer that degree to the last *Almucantarath* on the side of *Almagrip*, mark the position of *Almeri* again, and the arc from the first position to the second position of *Almeri* is the circle you seek.

## CHAPTER XII. On the extent of the circle of the night

The same method is used to find the circle of the night, through the sun’s *nadir*. Just as the circle of the day is obtained through the degree of the sun, so the circle of the night is unquestionably obtained through the *nadir*, whenever desired. Once the circle of the day has been found, whatever remains of the 360 parts is the circle of the night.

## CHAPTER XIII. How many equinoctial hours there are

[Col. 0400C]

When you wish to know how many equinoctial hours there are in the day, divide its extent, from the first position to the second, by the parts of the equinoctial hours, that is, by 15—the equivalent of three intervals divided into five—assigning fifteen parts to each hour as far as you can. However many hours you find by calculating the parts in this way are the equinoctial hours of the day. In the same way you will determine the shortenings and lengthenings of days and nights.

By the same division you will examine the extent of the night and find the nighttime hours. This is clear to anyone who investigates carefully. For after the hours of the day have been removed from the 360 parts, the hours of the night necessarily remain. These hours, as stated above [Col. 0400D], are always unequal except on the two equinoctial days, when they return to equal parity. Many authors discuss their alternation and their mutual increases and decreases quite clearly. Therefore I shall pass over them here. If anyone strives to investigate this more perfectly, let him consult Ptolemy’s *Canons*, where he will be able to drink more abundantly from the source of all these matters.

## CHAPTER XIV. On perceiving the approach of dawn

If you wish to know how near dawn is, take the altitude of any star written on the astrolabe, place the head of that star over the received altitude in whichever region you choose, and observe where the sun’s *nadir* is. If it is above the eighteenth *Almucantarath* on the side of *Almagrip*, behold: dawn.

## CHAPTER XV. On perceiving the rising and setting of each sign at any given time

At any hour of the day, if you wish to know which sign, which part [of a sign], or which star is rising or setting, take the sun’s altitude and place the degree of the sun over it, in whichever region it may be. Once this has been done, observe which sign, which part of that sign, or which star lies above the first *Almucantarath*: that is what is rising. Whatever lies above the last *Almucantarath* is what is setting, which is the seventh from the east.

Whatever indicates the meridian line is the midheaven above the earth; whatever indicates the northern line occupies the midheaven below the earth [Col. 0401B]. By proceeding in this manner you will recognize the positions and movements of the heavenly bodies without ambiguity.

You may make the same determination at night. Take the altitude of any star written on the astrolabe, place the head of that star over its altitude, and observe the lines of the regions. They themselves indicate what you seek.

## CHAPTER XVI. In which sign the stars are situated

When you wish to know in which sign any of the hour-stars is situated, place the head of the star whose sign you seek over the meridian line. Whatever sign lies above it is where that star is situated. For the star occupies whatever line it indicates.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the names of the stars in Latin and Arabic

[Col. 0401C]

This place and subject require me to fulfill my promise: namely, to speak about the stars of the hours, how many they are, where they are, and their names and configurations.

In the Great Bear’s Plough, which is formed in this manner, there is one star of the hours, called in Arabic *Benenaz*—the first in the Plough—and it is represented on the astrolabe. After it comes *Almarech*, that is, such a bright star as the Bear-warden. Following this is the crown, formed in this manner, in whose middle is a brighter star, which they call *Mirmur* or *Elfeca*. There is also, in the Lyre, another brighter star formed in this manner, which they call *Alwagakha*.

After this comes *Archeitus*, or *Alrif*, or [in this form], and it is in the Swan. In the Charioteer there are two brighter stars: *Menreb*, *Alroech*—that is, “shoulder”—and *Rigel*, that is, “foot,” [or in this form]. Pegasus is [formed] in this manner; it contains one star of this kind, which they call *Alferaz*. The Arrow is [formed] in this manner, and in its middle is one star which they call *Alhadib*. In the middle lower part of the Swan is one which they call *Alceir*.

In Taurus there is one brighter star of this kind, which they call *Aldebaram*. In Gemini there are two: *Alhaioch Algeuze*, that is, “shoulder,” and *Rigel*, that is, “foot.” In Leo there are two, *Aldiranai*, that is, “forehead.” The one is smaller and lower, while *Calbalaceda*, that is, “heart,” is higher and bright. In Scorpio is *Calbalagraf*, that is, “the heart of Scorpio.” In Aquarius there is one which they call *Benebalgedi*.

[Col. 0402A] In the tail of Capricorn is the Dolphin, which is represented on the astrolabe in this manner. There are also *Denehcaitoz* and *Panta*, that is, “tail” and “belly” of a certain animal; these are either rarely or never seen in our climates, and are [represented] in this manner. There are *Vigel* and *Alhabor*. But why should I speak of these, since they are scarcely visible to us? There is *Algomeiza Aldirnam*, about which different opinions are held; for that reason I pass over it as doubtful.

Besides these there are two—*Ganamalgurab*, *Albazal*, or *Alhimech*—in the Centaur. The Chaldaeans use them extensively for distinguishing the hours, but they are seen by us very rarely, and when they are seen they appear for only two or three hours. There are many other stars used for distinguishing the hours, which I shall now pass over in silence, since we have no need of them [Col. 0402B] if we know the stars described above well.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the description of the climates and the discovery of their latitude
Here the method—both highly useful and very necessary—must be given; if you lack it, you will by no means attain knowledge of the hours. For one must know how the climates change, or in which climate you are. For just as, because of the earth’s position, noon does not occur at the same moment everywhere, so the same sundials cannot be used everywhere. Sundials must be changed according to the earth’s position and the divisions of the climates. Ptolemy and Eratosthenes discuss these changes sufficiently clearly. Marcianus, moreover, treats not only the changes of the climates but also the noon, altitude, or equinoctial hours of each region sufficiently fully. It is not useless to record his knowledge—and its Arabic counterpart.

You can learn the divisions of the climates and the changes of the sundials in the following way. When you are seeking to determine in which climate you are, or which sundial you should use in each place, in the month of March, when the sun is in the first degree of Aries, or in September, when the sun is in the first degree of Libra—for then the days of those months are equal—observe everywhere what the sun’s altitude is at noon, how much it falls short of 90, and what number is obtained as the amount by which it falls short of 90. That number is the entire altitude of the climate in which you are. Then observe in which table the same number—the number lacking from the complete 90—is written. For beneath the Almucantaraths the noons are written according to the latitude [Col. 0402D] of the climates; whichever number, or whichever table, contains it is the climate in which you are, and its noon and the table itself containing the number belong to that same climate.

The climates’ altitudes are found by means of 8. For when 8 is added to 15, the result is 23, which is the altitude of the second climate. From that point onward, continually subtracting units of eight according to the number of the tables, and adding what remains from eight to the latitude, you will find the latitudes in order. Thus, between the second and third climates, subtract one from 8, leaving 7; between the third and fourth, subtract one, and so on.

The latitude of the first climate is 15 degrees and 20 minutes, and its longest day is 13 equinoctial hours.

The latitude of the second climate is 23 degrees and 15 minutes, [Col. 0403A] and its longest day is 13 hours and 30 minutes [OCR corrected], which is half an hour.

The latitude of the third climate is 30 degrees and 22 minutes, and its longest day is 14 hours.

The latitude of the fourth climate is 36 degrees and 9 minutes, and its longest day is 14 hours and half an hour, that is, 30 minutes.

The latitude of the fifth climate is 41 degrees and 66 minutes, and its longest day is 15 hours and half an hour, that is, 30 minutes.

The latitude of the sixth climate is 45 degrees and 51 minutes, and its longest day is 15 hours.

The latitude of the seventh climate is 48 degrees and 32 minutes, and its longest day is 16 hours.

## CHAPTER XIX. How the globe is divided into seven climates, and where their beginnings and ends are

[Col. 0403B]

The beginning of the first climate is on the eastern side, at the Ocean, where the mouths of the river Ganges are. It runs through India and Asia and all their boundaries, on the side of the east wind, as far as the island of Taprobane, which is in the Indian Ocean, including the ten cities of that island and many others. Thus, extending eastward as far as the Red Sea toward the south, it includes, namely, Antiochia armata, Piternnata, [Pitinnata or Pitanen] or Bithynia, and Persia; some cities of Assyria; Alexandria of Persia; the Persian Sea; the land of Arabia; and as far as Egypt, the land of Ethiopia, the river Nile, and the island of Meropis [or Merois]. One climate is also called Merois [Col. 0403C] after it. Then, in the regions of Africa, it runs southward through the Garamantes, the river Geon, and Mount Astrixi, and through the sandy deserts and the remaining regions, and through the Mauri Matibienses; thus it extends westward as far as the Ocean, where it ends.

The beginning of the second climate is at the Ocean on the eastern side, from the island of Costra. It passes through Parthia and its boundaries and through certain parts of Persia, toward the north as far as Mount Sinai, and toward the south through the great deserts of Sodom and Gomorrah, Alexandria in Egypt, the peoples of Libya, and part of Lower Egypt. It then extends through Tripolitania as far as Mauretania.

The beginning of the third climate is in the east, at the Ocean, from Mount Timavus. It runs through Antioch and all its boundaries, crosses the river Phison, and encompasses Aracusis and Albania, as well as part of Mesopotamia and Gatogoras. Hence it is itself now called Damascus. It crosses the Dead Sea and part of Cyrenaic Libya, and thus, through the various boundaries of the regions—whose enumeration would be lengthy—it extends as far as the Ocean of the West, where it ends [codex: “extended,” feminine].

The beginning of the fourth climate, however, is in the east. At its head it occupies, partly together with the fifth climate, Scythia; it crosses the Caucasus and divides. It shares part of Mesopotamia with the third climate and Cappadocia with the fifth; it crosses the river Jordan and Galilee; it occupies part of Jerusalem and all its boundaries. Thus, extending westward, it shares Cyrene with the third climate, encompasses Leptis Magna and part of Numidia, Tingitania, and the remaining boundaries as far as the Ocean, where it ends.

The fifth begins in the east at the Caspian Sea and occupies part of Scythia. It shares Armenia with the sixth climate, crosses the Ceraunian Mountains, shares Galilee with the fourth, and encompasses Samaria and Mount Carmel. It reaches as far as the Mediterranean Sea and the island of Sardinia, Carthage, and part of Numidia. It then extends through Tingitania and through the islands of the Mediterranean Sea as far as the Ocean of the West, where it ends.

The sixth begins in the east at the Caspian Sea and shares Armenia. It encompasses all of first Macedonia with all its boundaries and the islands of the Great Sea; it crosses [Col. 0404B] the Mediterranean Sea and shares Arcadia with the seventh. Toward the south it occupies Salernum, Naples, Romania, and the other Rome; it extends through Italy and Germany; it shares Greater Gaul with the seventh; and, extending through all the regions toward the west, it claims the whole of Spain for itself, ending at the very shore of the Ocean.

The seventh begins at the eastern Ocean. First, toward the north, it includes the Albani; then Thrace and the plains of Smyrna; it crosses the Pontic and Aegean Seas. There it contains lofty Constantinople and parts of Greece; toward the south, part of Arcadia and all Thessaly; toward the north, Dacia and the barbarian peoples; and part of Greater Gaul, Britain, Scotland, and the land of the English, [Col. 0404C] as well as the Gauls. Thus extending westward as far as the basilica of Saint James the Apostle, it ends there in the Western Ocean. Concerning the islands called the Cyclades, it is uncertain to which climate they should be assigned. A diligent investigator of the *walzacora*—if he has been on the islands themselves—will remove this uncertainty; the matter is left for anyone to judge. These distributions and latitudes of the climates are made according to Arabic authorities.

## CHAPTER XX. How to know whether it is before or after noon

When you wish to know whether it is before or after noon, take the sun’s altitude on the back of the astrolabe and see whether the sun is ascending or descending along the 90 divisions. If it is ascending, it is before noon; if it is descending, it is after midday.

## CHAPTER XXI. Finding the hours on the back of the astrolabe

[Col. 0404D]

When you wish to know the hours on the back of the astrolabe, first determine how far the sun ought to ascend on the day on which you wish to ascertain the hours. Divide that ascent, or the sun’s altitude, from the first degree of sunrise to the last into six parts, and divide those parts among the signs. When the sun has reached those signs on the *alhidada*, you will thereby know the exact hours up to six. After six, return by descending toward sunset. But you, reader, if you wish to attend carefully, can yourself make various sundials with the aforesaid *walzacora*, that is, the plane sphere.

## CHAPTER I. Demonstration of constructing a portable horological instrument with a reversible shadow-maker

[Col. 0405A]

A certain simple and small horological instrument for travelers is constructed in the form of a smooth, evenly thick staff or cylinder. It is suspended from a crosspiece affixed orthogonally at its top and has a rotatable shadow-maker (*sciotherus*). As it turns, its shadow reaches and indicates the exact hours on lines marked around its side for each of the twelve signs or months. At your command, dearest brother Werinher, I shall try to describe its measurements clearly, as far as I have been able to determine them by the method of the astrolabe.

First, then, I divide its circumference into six intervals by drawing lines from top to bottom. On these six signs, in which the days increase—Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces, Aries, Taurus, and Gemini—I write their names. Then, turning back, I fill the remaining signs of the decreasing days in the same way, matching them in quantity with days of equal length: Cancer with Gemini, Leo with Taurus, Virgo with Aries, Libra with Pisces, Scorpio with Aquarius, and Sagittarius with Capricorn.

Next, because the individual months begin at the middle of each sign, I divide each of the aforesaid six intervals of the signs into two, again by drawing lines as before. Thus, with twelve intervals made around the whole circumference, I assign the first interval—which contains the end of Sagittarius and the beginning of Capricorn—to December, in whose middle the winter solstice occurs. I assign the next two intervals to January and its counterpart, November. The fourth and fifth belong to February and October; the sixth and seventh to March and September, in the middle of which the two equinoxes occur and Aries and Libra begin. Next come the eighth and ninth, for April and August; the tenth and eleventh contain May and July. The twelfth, which remains and contains the end of Gemini and the beginning of Cancer, receives June, with the summer solstice at its middle.

[Col. 0406B]

After the twelve intervals have been distributed in this way among the signs and months, you must determine the lines marking the ends of the individual hours of the day according to the sun’s daily or monthly ascent and descent. But, to spare you the painstaking labor of inquiry here, I shall briefly describe in the following diagram how many degrees the sun ascends at the end of each hour at the beginning of each sign or month in our climate, insofar as I can understand it through experience with the astrolabe.

[Col. 0405]

[Col. 0405C]

With these preliminaries established, on a flat board I carefully draw a quarter of a circle from a fixed center *a*, and divide its arc—that is, its curved line—into three parts, each third into six, and each of those into five, so that, like the quadrant of the astrolabe, it is divided into 90 degrees. Having done this, from the center itself, *a*, where the *coraustus* and the *cathetus*—that is, the overlying and downward-hanging line—meet to form a right angle, I mark off from the *coraustus* as much as the length of the *sciotherus*, or gnomon, that I wish to assign according to the size of the instrument. From that mark I draw downward a perpendicular line, equally distant from the *cathetus*, of a length corresponding to the size of the suspended instrument.

[Col. 0405D]

Next, I place a ruler on the aforesaid center or angle *a* and on the first degree of the 90 that I had marked on the arc of the quadrant on the *coraustus* side. Wherever the ruler touches the perpendicular line I have just mentioned, I make a mark. Then, descending downward in order through each successive degree, I place the ruler, without moving it from the original angle *a*, and mark that line at each position wherever the ruler touches it, continuing up to degree 66, at which the sun’s greatest ascent in our climate is found.

Taking this perpendicular line, marked in this way with 66 degrees, as the downward length of the instrument from the *sciotherus*, I consult the prescribed diagram at the beginnings of each sign and month to see how many degrees the sun ascends at the end of each hour. I then measure downward along the instrument from the *sciotherus* the same amount of space that the number of those degrees occupies on this line from the *coraustus*. On the line where I had established the beginning of that sign or month, I make this the endpoint of the corresponding hour. For example: at the beginning of Capricorn, the sun ascends 18 degrees at the end of the sixth hour. Therefore, whatever space is contained on the often-mentioned line from the *coraustus* to the end of the eighteenth degree, I establish that same space on the line where Capricorn begins, up to the endpoint of the sixth hour. In this way, finding the definite endpoint of each hour at the beginnings of all the signs and months, I mark them with dots. Then, at the end of each hour, I draw oblique lines from dot to dot, moving downward as the increases and decreases of the days require, and thereby complete the measurement of this entire sundial. So that these things may appear more clearly, let us draw here the quarter of the circle divided into 90 degrees in the manner described above, together with the perpendicular line hanging in place of this sundial and marked, as I said, with 66 degrees, [Col. 0407B] so that by the respective spaces and number of degrees prescribed in the preceding diagram we may measure the intervals of the hours for each sign and month.

*(Thus the manuscript presents the figure.)*

[Col. 0407C]

Having measured the instrument of this sundial in this manner, suspend it in the sun’s rays, turning the *sciotherus* toward the line of the current month and sign. Whatever hour the tip of the gnomon’s shadow touches, do not doubt that that hour is present.

If, moreover, on this sundial you wish to add a thirteenth interval to the twelve intervals of the signs and months mentioned above, and distinguish it by the measurement I shall describe, you will easily be able to determine the height of any upright body standing on a level surface by means of its shadow. For when the shadow of any upright body on level ground forms a right triangle, and when, likewise, on this instrument the *sciotherus* has a triangular shadow corresponding to the shadow cast by it, the shaded plane will undoubtedly have the same relationship to any body that casts a shadow.

Therefore, in the thirteenth interval I mentioned, carefully distinguish and mark the following portions of the *sciotherus*: 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, a half, a two-thirds portion (*bisse*), its three-quarters (*dodrans*), its two-thirds (*dextans*), and its entire length, as well as any multiple of a particular portion—double, or eight times that portion—or any other proportions. Then, by turning the *sciotherus* to those dimensions and allowing the sunlight to cast its shadow upon them, the proportion between the *sciotherus* and its shadow will immediately be apparent.

For if the shadow reaches the sixth part of the *sciotherus*, the shaded plane will be six times the height of the object casting the shadow. If it reaches the fourth part, the plane will be four times the height; if the third, three times; if half, twice; if it reaches the entire length of the *sciotherus*, the plane will be equal to it. If it reaches twice its length, the plane will be twice the height; if three times its length, one-third [the source’s proportional wording is uncertain]; and similarly in the other cases.

## CHAPTER II. On the magnitude of the circumference of the entire globe

Although the authority of Ambrosius Theodosius makes the circumference of the entire globe worthy of note, since the basis of his authority has been almost entirely left aside, it is proposed here for those who wish to know it. What modern people judge impossible, the ancients, guided by wisdom, affirm to be very easy; and what seems incapable of being investigated by the bodily senses is held to have been examined, through the acumen of reason, more clearly than light.

Having taken the horoscope under the brightness of a starry night, and having observed the pole through both apertures of the *mediclinum*, and noted the number of degrees at which the *mediclinum* stood, the measurer of the cosmos proceeded in a straight line northward from the south for as long as necessary. Then, on the brightness of another night, having seen the same pole standing where it had stood before through both apertures of the *mediclinum*, he found that the *mediclinum* stood higher by one degree.

After [Col. 0408C] this, guided by reason, he measured the distance of the journey and, having noted its amount as 700 stadia or 87 miles, declared it. Then, since the astrolabe has 360 degrees, the circumference of the terrestrial globe was found to contain that many stadia or miles. For, multiplying the distance corresponding to one degree by the remaining degrees, the result of that multiplication is proved to be contained in the entire circuit of the world.

## CHAPTER III. Eratosthenes’ view on the same subject

The philosopher and exceptionally astute geometer Eratosthenes ingeniously determined, through the change in the shadows of a gnomon on the earth according to the divisions of the zodiac, that the circumference of the entire terrestrial globe contains 252 stadia, that is, 31,000 miles [the numeral is corrupt in the source]. Assigning to each of the 360 parts of the zodiac 700 stadia, that is, 87½ miles, you can, according to the rule of the circle and the thickness or diameter of its geometrical figure, comprehend the earth’s diameter as follows. (See chapter 93 of Gerbert’s *Geometry*.)

Subtract one twenty-second from the earth’s circumference; that is, from 252 stadia subtract 21,454½ and one twenty-second of a stadion. There remain 230 [numeral corrupt] stadia, together with half and twenty-one parts of one stadion. One third of these—that is, 80,081½ stadia and six twenty-seconds of one terrestrial stadion—will contain the diameter or thickness of the terrestrial globe, according to the aforesaid circumference, with no uncertainty remaining. This is sufficiently clear to anyone who calculates it carefully, although Macrobius, in his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*, says that the same diameter is only 80 stadia, or not much more.

## CHAPTER IV. The same matter in other words

On the authority of the philosopher Eratosthenes, the circumference of the terrestrial globe is proved to be 252 stadia, or 31,000 miles [the numeral is corrupt]. The Sun traverses one twenty-fourth of this—namely, 10½ stadia, or 1,312 miles—in one hour. But since a fifteenth part of an hour is the ascent or descent of the Sun through one of the 360 degrees, division of the aforementioned terrestrial circumference by 360 will clearly show that the Sun traverses 700 stadia, or 87½ miles.

According to the geometrical rule of the circle, the diameter of the earth is proved to amount to 80,181½ stadia, or 9,922 miles and 111/160 of a mile [the numerals are corrupt], although Macrobius admits that the same diameter is 80 stadia, or not much more.

## CHAPTER V. On dividing a quadrant so that you can find the exact hours of the day

Divide the quadrant of the circle at the top into 90, in intervals divided by five. Then measure the runner that moves below as follows. With the center of the quadrant turned toward you, on the left side subtract 24 from the 90. With the runner held firmly in its concavity, and the ruler remaining fixed at the center and at the twenty-fourth degree, draw a line. On the right side, subtract 19 from the 90; with the ruler remaining at the center and at the nineteenth degree, draw a line through the runner and cut it off at both ends. This is the length of the runner.

Next, draw a circle below the circle according to preference, with two other circles drawn between them. Divide these by six and mark the twelve hours on them. Then, with the ruler remaining at the center, draw a line directly through the boundary between hours 3 and 4 and between 10 and 11, and through the forty-fifth degree. This line is called the equinoctial line. Then divide the runner on this equinoctial line into five parts on the left. Divide each of the three parts nearest the equinoctial line into four, and the remaining two into nine. Do the same on the right side and mark those small intervals.

The division of the months is to be made as follows. On the right side, assign the two remaining intervals as follows: six to January, five to February, six to March, six to April, and six to May; four to June before the solstice, in the upper circle. In the lower circle, assign two portions after the solstice to June; six to July, six to August, six to September, six to October, six to November, and four to December before the solstice, in the lower circle. After the solstice, assign the two remaining portions in the upper circle of the months to December. Then, as I said above, six belong to January. With the pole turned toward you, divide the final line on the left side, from the pole itself to the outermost circle, into 30.

Next, divide the innermost circle on the right side, from the first point to the end of the sixth hour, into 30. Thus, from point to point, draw the lines called [Col. 0410A] *Almucantaraths*. According to this description, the upper part of the quadrant is to be drawn. *(Thus the manuscript presents the figure.)*

[Col. 0410B]

To find the hour with the quadrant that has the runner, place the runner’s equinoctial line—the line distinguishing March and September—over the number on the boss whose degrees indicate the altitude of the climate in which you are. For example, if you are in our climate, that is, the seventh climate, place the aforesaid line over 48, beginning the count from the bottom upward. Having positioned the runner in this way, draw a perpendicular over the present day for which you are seeking the hour, and observe which line of the *Almucantaraths*, proceeding from the left, touches the lower part of the runner. Having noted it, draw a perpendicular to the head of that same line, on the other side, toward the fins. Wherever the perpendicular touches it, make a point in the wax of the perpendicular; or, if the perpendicular, as is customary among some people, has a small runner, move that runner to the place where the aforesaid line touches the perpendicular.

Having found the point in this way and marked it in the wax around the circle of the perpendicular, determine where the calculation requires the sun’s altitude to be. To find this altitude, raise the quadrant, oppose its left shoulder to the sun, and turn it this way and that until the sun passes straight through both apertures of the fins. The degree that the perpendicular then touches on the boss will clearly show you how far the sun has already ascended or descended. With the perpendicular lying on that same degree, observe which line of the *Almucantaraths* touches the region above. Place on this line the point made in the wax on the perpendicular—or the circle of the perpendicular—wherever it can touch it, and observe over which hour the perpendicular lies. That is the hour which your labor [codex: “how great the labor”] seeks.

## CHAPTER VI. Measuring the height of anything standing on a plane by its own shadow, with the square of the astrolabe

*(From Gerbert’s* Geometry, *chapter 21.)*

If you wish to find, by its shadow, the height of a tree, column, tower, or anything of that kind standing upright on level ground, suspend the astrolabe and direct the sun’s ray straight through both apertures of the *alhidada*. Observe on which part of the side of the quadrant—divided into 12 parts—the line of the *alhidada* stands. Whatever proportion the number of parts visible on the *alhidada* bears to 12, that is, to the entire side of the square, the height you wish to find will undoubtedly bear to the shadow it casts on the ground.

For example, if two parts appear, and 12 has a sixfold proportion to them, the shadow likewise will be six times the height. If three appear, the proportion will be quadruple; if four, triple; if five, double and two-fifths; if six, double; if seven, it will be in the ratio 12:7 (a super-five-partient ratio of sevenths); if eight, sesquialteral; if nine, sesquitertial; if ten, sesquiquintal; if eleven, sesqui-undecimal; if all 12, the height and shadow will be equal.

Indeed, whatever proportion the *alhidada* forms as a triangle within the square, a triangle of that same proportion will immediately be formed by the shadow of any upright body on the ground. In that triangle, the shaded ground is the base; the upright height is the perpendicular; and the sun’s ray, which bounds the shadow transversely, is understood to take the place of the hypotenuse.

## CHAPTER VII. Another method of measuring the height of things

*(Taken from chapter 82 of Gerbert’s* Geometry*.)*

There is another method of determining height, as follows. Raise a right triangle whose perpendicular is 6 feet, whose base is 8, and whose hypotenuse is 10, so that its base rests on the ground and its perpendicular is raised toward the object whose height is to be measured. Draw the hypotenuse from the top of the perpendicular to the top of the base.

If, while lying on the ground, you place your eye directly at the point where the base joins the hypotenuse, then move yourself this way and that, keeping your eye always aligned, until the top of the perpendicular appears to you to be level with the top of the object whose height you seek, mark the place where you were holding your eye. From that mark measure the distance to the foot of the object, divide this distance by four, and subtract one quarter; take the remaining three quarters as the height you were seeking. This method of determining height is entirely reliable, provided that the ground over which the perpendicular is moved is neither mountainous nor hollowed out, but level.

## CHAPTER VIII. How the circles of the *asmut* are to be drawn

[Col. 0411D]

After the *Almucantaraths*, which are to be drawn, comes the *Assumuth*, or direction, because by means of these one learns in which direction of the world a given region lies. First find the center of the region by taking the region’s latitude from point *e* toward *b* and making a mark. On this mark place the ruler and point *c*; wherever it cuts the diameter from *e* to *d* will be the center of the region, which you will mark with point *o*.

Afterward take the same latitude from point *c* toward *d*. On it place the ruler and point *c*, and make a mark where the ruler touches the diameter *e–d*, extended over the wooden board; write *i e*. Then draw a circumference passing through points *o* and *p*, with its center midway between the two. One part of it, from *a* to *b* through *o*, will be visible; the other, from *a* to *c* through *p*, will be hidden, because the part from *a* to *b* through *o* will be marked with the lines of the *Assumuth*; the other part will be erased after the *Assumuths* have been made.

Once this has been done, divide the same circle into two halves by drawing a diameter lengthwise across the wooden board on both sides of the circle. On this diameter you will find the centers of the *Assumuths*. Divide the part of the circle extending from *a* to *b* through *o* into nine, and likewise the part from *o* to *c* into nine. Do the same with the other lower parts, although they are larger than the upper ones. Since these divisions comprise the entire circle, each will contain ten degrees.

After marking these divisions, place the ruler over point *o* and the second division—that is, over the first degree—and wherever it cuts the diameter, make the first center of the *Assumuth* far out on the wooden board. Through this center draw a circumference passing from the circle of the hemisphere through point *o* as far as the circle of Capricorn, and then make another *Assumuth*. At its division—that is, at the tenth degree—having found the center, make another *Assumuth* pass through the same point *o*. Know that when you make an *Assumuth* at 10, they will come out at 10; and when at 10 [the source is corrupt], they will come out at 5 [the numeral is uncertain]. When you have completed one half of the circle, return to the other, and thus complete all the *Assumuths*.

After the hour lines, place the head of Cancer over *Almucantarath i.g.* in the west and mark the location of the head of Cancer in the part of the hours. Do the same with the heads of Aries and Capricorn, and mark the heads opposite them in the aforesaid hours. Through these three marks draw the line of eastern twilight. Do the same on the opposite side for western twilight.

The rest is lacking.

[Col. 0413]

# THE MUSICAL WORKS OF HERMANNUS CONTRACTUS, MONK OF REICHENAU

*(In D. Gerbert,* Ecclesiastical Writers on Music, *vol. II, p. 124.)*

## Notice

Joannes Trithemius, in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1005 and in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, no. 321, immediately places, in his recension of Hermann’s works, one book *On Music* and one book *On the Monochord*. The anonymous writer of Melk, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 91, passes over these works in silence, although he testifies that Hermann was subtler in music than almost all modern writers and that he published many musical compositions and sufficiently authoritative chants concerning the saints. It is therefore clear that, just as he excelled in composing verse for sacred song, he also excelled in both theoretical and practical music.

In general, Honorius of Autun, book IV of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 12, testifies that Hermann wrote certain works and composed melodious song. I have found various verses, which I append at the end, scattered in manuscripts under his name. As for the books listed by Trithemius, I searched for them in vain in the libraries of Italy, Gaul, and Germany. At last, while manuscripts were being transferred from the Vienna Civic Library to the Imperial Library, I found one whose beginning Trithemius gives in the cited passage of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. While I was then working in Vienna, I eagerly copied it and publish it here.

# THE MUSIC OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN HERMANN

[Col. 0413]

[Col. 0413A]

In considering the construction of the monochord, the first theoretical point that presents itself is that its entire extent is contained within the quadruple, that is, the double diapason. Each of these is produced by the combination of the sesquialteral and sesquitertial proportions, that is, the diapente and diatessaron.

The reason why it does not extend beyond the quadruple or contract below the sesquitertial is this: since the diapente and diatessaron together produce one diapason; since the diapason consists of five tones and two semitones; since the diapente consists of three tones and a semitone; and since the diatessaron consists of two tones and a semitone; and since the diapason is doubled, there will henceforth be no consonances that extend beyond the quadruple or contract below the sesquitertial. Only the tone, which joins these proportions—the difference between the sesquialteral and sesquitertial—remains.

Thus, in each of the two diapasons there are altogether seven voices entirely distinct from one another, for none of them agrees perfectly with another except with its octave. The upper diapason, because it is sung in the grave voices, is plainly marked with larger letters; the lower one, because of its high pitch, is marked with the same letters but with acute forms. Here one must understand that new voices are not born again and again, but that, once born, they are repeated or renewed in the manner of the seven days of the week.

It should not seem surprising that there are no more than seven distinct voices. In defining things, diversity is required only so far as things cease to appear distinct. To give a few examples: grammar is reduced to eight varieties, the *Isagoge* to five, and the Categories to ten; likewise with other disciplines. So too, in the elementary monochord, the quadruple containment, fixed by the established measurement of proportions, is capable of seven distinct voices and always returns the same mode in the eighth place—not only with the same power of sound but also with the same character. Although modes recur in other places as well, they are nevertheless different in the arrangement of the letters, just as they are different in sound.

Among these matters, it will also be worthwhile to consider why the quadruple proportion suits the completeness of music more than any other proportion. At the outset, for anyone who looks carefully, it becomes clear that the generation of the quadruple emerges immediately from the first roots of all numbers, that is, from one and two. For one compared with two produces the double and therefore the diapason. Two multiplied by itself generates four; when one is compared with four, it restores the quadruple, which is the double diapason.

Within these terms, therefore—one and four—the numbers two and three are naturally included. Through their superparticular proportions they constitute the diapente and diatessaron. For two compared with three produces the diapente, and three compared with four produces the diatessaron. One compared with three also establishes, in triple proportion, the diapason combined with the diapente.

Since the difference between the diapente and diatessaron is the tone, and since the tone, although excluded from the consonances, nevertheless joins the consonances, let us see whether its proportion also lies hidden in these seeds, having been produced by the Pythagorean hammers.

At this point a certain wonder first arises concerning the nature of the tone. The tone itself does not require consonances; rather, the consonances established by it seem, because of the spaciousness—or something like the vastness—of their intervals, to have the sesquialteral proportion. How this is so will become apparent after we have taught how to find the individual voices. For now, meanwhile, let all its measurable parts prepare and bring themselves together so that they may correct it and fill its gap. Thus the diapason presents two parts, the diapente three, and the diatessaron four. When two, three, and four are collected into one, they make nine, and therefore produce the tone in the sesquioctave proportion.

It is therefore clear and evident that music has rightly claimed for itself this dignity from the primary position of unity: the primordial nature of numbers created it through the most excellent proportions. This, I say, is the thing which, beginning from the primary position of unity, so that it could not waver, ended in the square of four. Four is the first number resting on two halves; it binds together the conflict of the elements and tempers the diversity of times. It is also supremely necessary for music, so that music may not be considered in any respect contrary or discordant to a human being, who exists from four elements.

It may still seem remarkable that, just as in every seed the entire future form of the body is present all at once, so in the original seed of the consonances mentioned above the numbers discovered in the weights of the hammers are also concealed. We shall strike them out as though from flint to produce fire in this way: first let the multiplier, that is, two, multiply four, while three multiplies itself. Once this has been done, 6, 8, 9, and 12 are found.

These numbers, emerging like a tender shoot, are in a marvelous way greater in quantity than their own seed, but more contracted in their proportions. For in the seed—as in the whole—all the proportions of music are found together: double, triple, quadruple, sesquialteral, sesquitertial, and sesquioctave. These are also found wonderfully in the number six, but the later numbers will equal them only when multiplied by two.

Whoever does not wish to perform that multiplication will have these numbers: 6, 8, 9, 12, 16, 18, and 24—the complete structure, that is, of the consonances.

Having dealt with these matters in a barren manner of consideration, let us see what the seven different voices, joined to one another, produce. First, let us resolve something that might trouble anyone of simple understanding: why, when twice seven yields fourteen, there are nevertheless fifteen voices. This is evidently a matter of number alone, not of variety; for whether you count twice seven upward or downward, a fifteenth remains, which, because it is the octave of the *mese*, is equal to it both in power and in notation. The same thing may also be anticipated in the simple diapason. For when seven unequal voices have been counted, an eighth remains, which has the same sound and notation as the first.

Let us now carry through what we began. Thus, in the quadruple—that is, twice the diapason, twice seven—the same aggregate of fifteen voices, preserving its proportion, is again resolved into four-chords in the likeness of its elemental parent. Once generated, these four-chords, by the arrangement of the four primary strings, continue to follow one another until every mode can be shaped by the proper species of all the consonances and can receive a lawful terminus both of arsis and of thesis. The names of these four-chords are *grave*, *final*, *higher*, and *excellent*. Since, in the number of their strings, their continuous succession, and their modal arrangement, they represent only a fourfold grouping, they display their own nobility like sons born in the likeness of their parents’ faces. It must nevertheless be observed that, in place of repetition, there are four, while by natural principle there are two: for grave and higher are of one nature, as are final and excellent.

What others call *grave*, we call *first* or *principal* because of the manifold force and power of its effect. As far as the name of primacy is concerned, when it is measured toward the right, it contains the first step of the quadruple; but, as far as the name of four-chord is concerned, when it is measured toward the left, it also embraces the step of the first division, and by itself has the greater force as the fourth. The first is empty, the second is the diapason, the third the diapente, and the fourth the diatessaron—that is, the source of all four-chords and modes—just as the third wonderfully draws forth the source of all five-chords. For one of these naturally generates all the species of the diatessaron, and the other all the species of the diapente.

From this it is also gathered that naturally there are no more than four modes. The fourth step of the quadruple, as has been said, included them first, although each of them has been divided into two by the counsel of the elders, so that graves may agree with graves and acute voices with acute voices. Hence it also came about that the four which exist in nature are counted as eight.

The arrangement of these four-chords is therefore as follows: since there are three intervals between the voices of a four-chord, the first and third spaces are occupied by a tone and the middle space by a semitone. Thus the two outer intervals are tones, while the middle semitone is the distance between two modes.

It must also be known that, although there are seven different voices in one diapason, they form only two four-chords. Since the number seven plainly possesses one midpoint, it is necessary that the two four-chords be contained by that single midpoint. The Greeks call this *synaphēn* (συναφην), which we may call “conjunction”: the upper four-chord’s fourth, or highest, voice is accordingly the lower four-chord’s first, or lowest, voice. By lot of arrangement, this principle of the midpoint was assigned to be carried out only by the letter D.

In this matter a certain author of the *Enchiridion of Music* made a considerable mistake. Separating the two seven-voice four-chords by two midpoints contrary to nature, he doubled the mode of the midpoint, which is impossible; and thus, instead of the natural arrangement of two continuous tones, he brought about a continuous tritone. In this way, having disturbed the monochord’s entire structure and its regular order, he destroyed it and confused both the harmonic theory according to the ancient and modern authorities and that according to the authority of nature itself. As will be evident to all who read that little work, its description contains no arrangement of species required either by usage or by the constancy of nature, no disposition of modes, no sound or complete operation of the principal strings, and no orderly sequence in the recognition of the modes. For no string in the same arrangement is found to be the same in the octave—although that this must be so is confirmed both by the unanimous assertion of everyone and by the invincible truth of nature.

Since, in order to signify equal pitch, every diapason must end on the same letter on which it begins, what sort of description is this? When you have sung A, according to him G—that is, the tetrardus—answers in the eighth place; when you have sung B—that is, the deuterus—A, the protus, occurs in the eighth place. To put the matter briefly, whatever string you begin, upward or downward, you find its counterpart not in the octave, where it ought to be, but rather in the ninth position. We have therefore criticized this here because the occasion presented itself, lest a simple reader, seeing one arrangement here and another elsewhere, should be left uncertain about everything.

It must further be understood in the investigation of the four-chords that, although they possess many functions in common, they have in this matter private and proper functions. The first and fourth, opposed to each other at the extremities, respectively contain the lowest descent and the highest ascent of the melody; of the two middle strings, one contains the end of the chant and the other, with one exception, the beginnings of all the differences. Here it should not be passed over that, just as a disciple is not above his teacher, so no difference of the subjugal modes is either above the teacher or alongside him, but always occupies a lower place. Every authentic protus places its deuterus difference in the fifth place from the final; every subjugal mode places its difference below, on the second or third string.

The question also arises why, when there are only four four-chords, both the subjugal and the authentic modes possess three. This is easily resolved by considering the principle of their progression. Since every authentic mode, beginning from its own final, passes through the higher strings by its own species of diapason to its own excellent string, and every subjugal mode ascends from its grave through the finals to its higher strings, it is necessary that the two extremes be counted once, but the two middle strings, because they are traversable in two ways, be counted twice.

From this it is also gathered that the graves and higher strings contain the subjugal modes, while the finals and excellents contain the authentic modes. The extremities of the subjugal modes are therefore the graves and higher strings, with the finals as their middle strings; the extremities of the authentic modes are the finals and excellents, with the higher strings as their middle strings. We have already stated, and shall state further, what the functions of the principal, final, higher, and excellent strings are.

Meanwhile, we must not grow weary as though we were sluggish, but must examine the difference between the four-chords that are made in two ways on the monochord. Those counted toward the right—and about which we have already said something—may be called constitutive of the modes. As stated, they have a tone at the extremities and a semitone in the middle, twice *synaphē* at D, and twice *diezeugmenon* between G and a. Those counted toward the left belong to the principle of measurement. They have, after two tones, a semitone; that is, at the end they contain twice *synaphē* at E and twice *diezeugmenon* between a and b, whereas the former exclude it between a and b. The former exclude the tones between g and a, while the latter include them there. The former are counted as tone, semitone, tone; the latter as tone, tone, semitone. The former pass from graves to acute voices; the latter from acute voices to graves.

Whether they begin from a grave or an acute voice, the former maintain the same arrangement for themselves. The latter, however, take a different arrangement: from the acute voices they proceed by tone, tone, and semitone, but from the graves, conversely, by semitone, tone, and tone. Since the names of these measuring four-chords have been given by many, we shall refrain from stating them.

It is enough, then, that we have said this about the uniform or modal four-chords, which may perhaps have opened a path for more diligent investigators toward greater matters. Let us now carefully inquire how, from what we called the principal of all four-chords—that is, the diatessaron—the order and character of its species arise.
