For greater clarity, let us mark the voices of two four-chords—that is, of the four modes set out twice—with their proper letters according to their ordered arrangement. One voice in the middle is counted twice because of the principle of the midpoint mentioned above, but is not measured twice.

These, then, are the graves or principals: A, B, C, D. These are the finals: D, E, F, G. The first species of the diatessaron therefore necessarily consists of A–D, comprising tone, semitone, tone, enclosed by its proper letters. The second consists of B–E, comprising semitone, tone, tone, bounded on either side by its proper letters. The third consists of C–F, comprising tone, tone, semitone, secured on both sides by its own letters. The fourth is D–G. In its first position, but fourth in constitution and power, it regularly determines the distinctions of the seven voices by its proper letters in this way:

- The first species of the diatessaron consists of the first grave and the first final, A–D.
- The second consists of the second grave and the second final, B–E.
- The third consists of the third grave and the third final, C–F.
- The fourth consists of the fourth grave and the fourth final, D–G.

Do you see, please, how the generation of the principal four-chord produces all the species of the diatessaron enclosed by their proper letters, with nothing lacking and nothing in excess? In this description it must be noted that the principality or property of the species is contained in their beginning and end; the intervening voices serve them in accordance with their relationship.

The fact that there are two different letters at the extremities of the species should not seem surprising. Since none of the voices mentioned above agrees with another—although the same position and therefore the same mode returns in the fourth place—it nevertheless does not represent an equal voice and therefore does not represent the same letter. Equality both of voice and of letter is reserved for the diapason alone, as will become clear later.

Thus, according to the number of the seven voices, the first voice agrees with the fourth, the second with the fifth, the third with the sixth, and the fourth with the seventh. But according to the return of the modes in the fourth or fifth place, the first agrees with the first, the second with the second, the third with the third, and the fourth with the fourth—according to position, I say, not according to voice.

It must also be known that there is, as it were, a species of the diatessaron, F–b, and it is found; but because it has no place among lawful constitutions, it is rejected. Nor are the two sides of it sharpened or flattened against each other. From this the error of someone who establishes an interval from the same elements is also refuted.

We may also marvel at the power and force of nature in the constitution of these species. For if we transpose them into the following four-chord, which the third—and therefore diapentic—step of the quadruple discovers, the first will be D–G according to an inverted principle. Although D may be first because of its common relation, G, seventh in number and fourth modally, can never be first.

The second, beginning from E, which is the deuterus, ends at a, which is the protus. The third, if nature is considered, does not exist there. The fourth, beginning from G, which is the tetrardus, ends at c, which is the tritus.

But since this confusion arises when the elements are counted in order, one may judge how greatly he erred who, looking only at the forms and not at the causes of natural constitutions, defined D–G as the first, E–a as the second, and G–c as the third, while correctly placing only the first of the remainder, namely a–d—yet contradicting himself, since he had previously placed D–G as the first. This happens both to him and to all musicians because, in the position of the first, no consideration is given to the fourth.

These matters being so, it must be understood that if anyone attempts to do in the second diapason what has been described, he will see that no new generation of the diatessaron arises, but that the one already described is repeated. What was done among the graves or principals can be effected among the higher strings, which are of the same nature.

Thus it is gathered that there are four firsts: A, D, a, d; four seconds: B, E, b, e; four thirds: C, F, c, f; and four fourths: D, G, d, g.

Since, as has often been said, the fourth step of the quadruple, capable of containing four voices, generates the order of the four modes and the four species of the diatessaron, let us also examine the species of the diapente, to see whether they too, arising naturally from their own source—that is, the third step of the quadruple—and proceeding in orderly sequence, refuse to be arranged among the graves, just as the species of the diatessaron are arranged among the finals.

First it must be known that, just as the species of the diatessaron are made through the graves and finals, so the species of the diapente are made through the finals and higher strings.

The first is D–a, consisting of tone, semitone, tone, tone, and enclosed on both sides by its proper letters. The second is E–b, consisting of semitone, tone, tone, tone, and resting on its letters on either side. The third is F–c, consisting of tone, tone, tone, semitone, and secured on both sides by its proper letters. The fourth is G–d, consisting of tone, tone, semitone, tone, and, by its proper letters, terminating both itself and either four-chord.

To make these clearer, let us repeat them in other words:

- The first, D–a, consists of the first final and the first higher string.
- The second, E–b, consists of the second final and the second higher string.
- The third, F–c, consists of the third final and the third higher string.
- The fourth, G–d, consists of the fourth final and the fourth higher string.

If these are in turn transposed to the graves, the first that appears is A–E. I speak of it as having the natural arrangement of tones and semitones, but it does not consist of the first voices of the two four-chords, nor does it begin and end in the same mode. Rather, on one side it ends with the first of the graves and on the other with the second of the finals; therefore on one side with its proper mode and on the other with a foreign one, namely the deuterus.

The second is B–F, which will subsequently be shown not to be a species of the diapente. The third is C–G, if it can be called a third: where the first deviates, the second is altogether absent. Nor does it itself consist of the two third voices of the two four-chords, but on one side of the third of the graves and on the other of the fourth of the finals, and therefore of unlike modes, namely the tritus and tetrardus.

Only the fourth appears as perfect, namely D–A, except that it is assigned not to the fourth but to the first order.

Do you not therefore observe that, in turn, both the diatessaron among the finals and the species of the diapente among the graves are being demanded by force? Accordingly, what the constitution rejects can, by form alone, if the Greek Γ is added, also be made *synemmenon*, so that the arrangement is as follows:

- The first: Γ, A, B, C, D.
- The second: A, B, C, D, E.
- The third: B, C, D, E, F.
- The fourth: C, D, E, F, G.

Now let us also examine the species of the diapason. It was stated above that two divisions of seven voices produce four four-chords. According to the uniform succession of the modes, all four are equal; but according to the arrangement of the species of the diapente and diatessaron, the first corresponds to the third and the second to the fourth.

Since the higher strings of the graves are the octaves of the finals, it is therefore necessary that the four species of the diapason, begun from the graves, end in the higher strings, and that the same species, repeated from the finals, end in the excellent strings.

The first is A–a, consisting of the first grave and the first higher string. The second is B– , consisting of the second grave and the second higher string. The third is C–c, consisting of the third grave and the third higher string. The fourth is D–d, consisting of the fourth grave and the fourth higher string.

Likewise, because of the common relation mentioned above:

- The first is D–d, consisting of the first final and the first excellent string.
- The second is E–e, consisting of the second final and the second excellent string.
- The third is F–f, consisting of the third final and the third excellent string.
- The fourth is G–g, consisting of the fourth final and the fourth excellent string.

What, please, could be more pleasing or more certain than that none of all the species of the diapason, diapente, and diatessaron should deviate from its order, but that all the first species should be contained in the first letters of the four-chords, the seconds in the second, the thirds in the third, and the fourths in the fourth?

One voice still remains, but why this is so will become clear later. For now, let us examine the modes.

A mode is a measured arrangement of many voices, fitted together by suitable intervals into one body, within each diapason. There are four modes in nature; but, as stated above, because of the distinctiveness of acuteness and gravity, they are subdivided into four. Thus there are eight altogether: four authentic modes, that is, authoritative modes, and four plagal modes, that is, lateral or subjugal modes.

Among the ancients the authentic modes are called Dorius, Phrygius, Lydius, and Mixolydius; the subjugal modes are called Hypodorius, Hypophrygius, Hypolydius, and Hypomixolydius.

The authentic modes, because they are enclosed by finals and excellents, receive these names according to the position of the letters: D, E, F, G, d, e, f, g. The subjugal modes, because they are connected with the graves and higher strings, derive their names from these letters: A, B, C, D, a, , c, d.

The authentic modes are also called, according to their order, protus, deuterus, tritus, and tetrardus. But this is according to their position on the monochord, not according to their dignity. For each of them is authentic—that is, an authority or teacher. The protus is a tone from the deuterus, while it is itself a semitone from the tritus, which in turn is a tone from the tetrardus.

Let us now bring to an end in a concise account what has been drawn out at length up to this point: let us shape each mode by its principal letters and also by the proper species of all the consonances, so that the protus may receive every first, the deuterus every second, the tritus every third, and the tetrardus every fourth, leaving nothing idle and nothing superfluous.

The protus and its subjugal, because they are first, necessarily require everything that is first: the first letters in all the four-chords, namely A, D, a, d; the first species of the diapason, namely A, a, D, d; the first species of the diapente, namely D, a; and the first species of the diatessaron, namely A, D.

This general arrangement is now specially subdivided for each according to its own character. Of the four letters mentioned above, the authentic claims three for itself, namely D, a, d. Its diapason is D–d, in one of which it ascends as high as the law permits and in the other ends; in the middle one, a, it sings the *saeculorum. Amen*. It has the diapente D–a and the diatessaron a–d in the higher strings. How these species are constituted must be sought above.

The subjugal is similarly formed from three letters, A, D, a. Its diapason is A–a, that is, the highest and lowest. D, however, its middle string, brings it to an end together with the teacher; with him it also shares the diapente. It takes the diatessaron in the graves, exactly as the teacher does.

Just as, then, the protus is shaped by its principal letters alone, so all the others are shaped according to order.

The deuterus and its subjugal, because they are second, necessarily require everything that is second: the second letters in all the four-chords, namely B, E, b, e; the second species of the diapason, namely B, b, E, e; the second species of the diapente, namely E, b; and the second species of the diatessaron, namely B, E.

This general arrangement is specially subdivided for each in the following way. Of the four letters mentioned above, the authentic claims three, namely E, b, e, and its diapason is E–e, that is, its highest and lowest; b is its middle string for the *saeculorum. Amen*, but because of the imperfection of the semitone it transfers it to c. It has the diapente E–b and the diatessaron b–e in the higher strings.

Its subjugal is likewise formed from three letters, namely B, E, b. Its diapason is B–b, that is, its highest and lowest; E, its middle string, brings it to an end together with the teacher, with whom it also shares the diapente, while it possesses the diatessaron among the graves.

The tritus and its subjugal, because they are third, necessarily demand everything that is third: the third letters in all the four-chords, namely C, F, c, f; the third species of the diapason, namely C, c, F, f; the third species of the diapente, namely F, c; and the third species of the diatessaron, namely C, F.

This general arrangement is subdivided for each in the following way. Of the four letters mentioned above, the authentic dominates three, namely F, c, f. Its diapason is F–f, that is, its highest and lowest; c, its middle string, performs the *saeculorum. Amen*. It has the diapente F–c and the diatessaron c–f in the higher strings.

The subjugal is likewise constituted from three letters, namely C, F, c. Its diapason is C–c, that is, its highest and lowest; F, its middle string, brings it to an end together with the teacher, with whom it also shares the diapente, while it takes the diatessaron among the graves.

The tetrardus and its subjugal, because they are fourth, necessarily require everything that is fourth: the fourth letters in all the four-chords, namely D, G, d, g; the fourth species of the diapason, namely D, and G, g; the fourth species of the diapente, namely G, d; and also the fourth species of the diatessaron, namely D, G.

This general arrangement is subdivided for them as follows. The authentic takes three of the four letters mentioned above, namely G, d, g. Its diapason is G–g, that is, its highest and lowest; D, its middle string, contains the *saeculorum. Amen*. It has the diapente G–d and the diatessaron d–g in the higher strings.

Its subjugal is likewise arranged from three letters, namely D, G, d. Its diapason is D–d, that is, its highest and lowest. G, its middle string, brings it to an end together with the teacher, with whom it also shares the diapente, while it places the diatessaron among the graves.

Behold: all the letters have been dealt with in order and have been completed together with the modes.

As stated above, one voice remains, namely the superacute a. Its relation according to measurement is this: in it the first step of the quadruple ends, just as the second ends in the middle a. According to the distribution of the letters, since every mode receives one voice above the diapason by permission, the tetrardus, which is nearest to it, will also rightly possess that voice, namely a, by permission.

Ptolemy, failing to consider this principle and also failing to perceive the aforementioned doubling of D—which, placed at the midpoint and at the conjunction of the four-chords, ought to shape both the tetrardus subjugal and the protus—reckoned four authentic modes and three subjugal modes, because according to him the tetrardus lacked a subjugal. Since a remained over after all had been compared with one another, he arranged the eighth tone by the a that is the *mese* and by the aforementioned a, which is the *nete hyperbolaeon*, and in this he made several errors.

For after properly arranging three subjugal modes, he removed the fourth from the fourth place; then, placing it after all the finals, he set the disciple above the teacher and therefore called it Hypomixolydius, although the others rightly retained names derived from subjection. Finally, in what is most absurd, since his arrangement extends from a to a, he arrived at no position other than the Hypodorian, which has already been discussed. For there is no other position from the *mese* to the *nete hyperbolaeon* than that from the *proslambanomenos* to the *mese*; and therefore, by the law of nature itself, it is Hypodorian at both ends.

For a is the diapason, that is, its highest and lowest voice; D is its middle, and can be the final of no mode other than the protus and its subjugal. Likewise, E and F, which belong to the deuterus and tritus, will not be middle strings between A and a, and therefore will not be finals either.

What then? Since it is the disciple of the tetrardus, perhaps it ends on the teacher’s letter, namely G, and takes it as its middle—and therefore as its final. But G is not the middle between A and a; therefore it is not a final either.

Furthermore, every subjugal ascends from its own grave to its own final by its proper species of the diatessaron, and from the final it ascends by the same species of the diapente by which the teacher ascends. Therefore, if G is to be the middle or final between A and a, it must have a diatessaron below itself and a diapente above itself. But G has twice the diatessaron below and a tone above; it is therefore not a subjugal.

Let us proceed, then: suppose it is a fifth authentic mode from A to a. But every authentic mode has some middle among the letters a, b, c, d, and between A and a the middle is D. Yet this has been shown to belong to the protus and its subjugal. Therefore this is not some new mode, but the Hypodorian is repeated.

Let this be said to the Ptolemaic mode: because you wished to be above the teacher, you have lost both your own right and that of the teacher. Let the eighth tone for you be from D to d, with G as its middle.

It is therefore pleasing to repeat all the modal arrangements and make them clearer in the briefest possible statement:

- Hypodorius is arranged from A to a; its middle and final is D.
- Hypophrygius is constituted from B to b; its middle and final is E.
- Hypolidius is constructed from c to c; its middle and final is F.
- Hypomixolidius is ordered from D to d; its middle and final is G.

Here it must be noted that every subjugal mode takes its middle in the fourth place, while every authentic mode, as will be shown later, takes its middle in the fifth place. This is not surprising. The fourth step of the quadruple, from which the subjugal modes arise, contains four voices, whereas the third step, from which the authentic modes proceed, contains five.

Since each of the four graves has received its octave among the four higher strings, to serve as its middle or final, the four subjugal modes, weighted, provided with middles, and raised through the graves, finals, and higher strings, have rightly completed their arrangement.

Here one must carefully observe that if the fourth subjugal did not follow its companions in the fourth place, G alone among the middle strings would be deprived of half of the midpoint. Having examined these matters not unprofitably, let us now do something similar with the authentic modes.

- Dorius is arranged from D to d; its middle and beginning is a.
- Phrygius is constructed from E to e; its middle is b, but it does not begin in b.
- Lidius is ordered from F to f; its middle and beginning is c.
- Mixolidius is set to melody from G to g; its middle and beginning is D.

Just as the subjugal modes, equipped above with their proper principal strings and letters at the beginning, middle, and end, occupied the first three four-chords—the grave, final, and higher—and left the excellent aside, so the authentic modes, established by their proper principal strings and letters, possess the next three—the final, higher, and excellent—and leave the grave aside.

It must be noted that, although all have an extremity, only two four-chords possess a middle; these are the final and the higher.

It must also be understood with the greatest care that the authentic modes are not called authentic, as some think, because, occupying the three highest four-chords, they can rise by acuteness. For if attention is paid to the voice in this matter, they may also be found among the graves. Rather, they are so called because in the middle, which possesses primacy, they have the primordial arrangement of the modes together with the first letters, while at the extremities they have the second arrangement or repetition of the modes together with those letters.

The first letters are A, B, C, D; the second are d, e, f, g. The subjugal modes are called so because in the principal position of their middle they receive the second letters, namely D, E, F, G, while at the extremities they receive the first letters, namely A, B, C, D.

If someone more subtly objected that, since the arrangement of the four-chords or modes is similar, it is not especially important which letters any four-chord receives, we too admit this, provided that the two diapasons are marked by corresponding letters.

Since, as stated, two divisions of seven voices produce four four-chords, each voice in the first two has its own diapason—which is its octave or equal-pitch counterpart—and in the following two requires the same by the same permission. Therefore, whether the two diapasons are marked by the letters mentioned above or by others, this cannot harm the preceding principle. Whatever letters are proposed as the first will come to the middles in the authentic modes and to the extremities in the subjugal modes; those proposed as the second will come to the middles in the subjugal modes and to the extremities in the authentic modes.

Let it therefore be proposed that the first letters are H, I, K, L, and the second L, M, N, O. Let us arrange these in the four four-chords.

Do you see, please, that the change of letters alters nothing in the foregoing account of the authentic and subjugal modes? Those regarded as first retain the middle of the authentic modes, and those regarded as second retain the middle of the subjugal modes.

From all this it is also concluded that those who, making no distinction among voices or four-chords, place almost everywhere the same signs in the fifth positions have erred, since it is unquestionably true that no sound agrees perfectly with its fifth.

It is also worth considering why, when there are four modal four-chords and one rises higher after the graves, only the third is called “higher,” when there is still another above it, namely the excellent higher four-chord.

It must therefore be understood that this is so both according to position and according to dignity, as the comparative name itself shows. Since there are two middle four-chords, the final and the higher, the higher rises above the final both in dignity and in position.

There is no need to speak about position. Concerning dignity, from which it especially received its name, this must be said: it alone among the middle four-chords received by lot the primordial arrangement of the modes together with the first letters. Hence the authentic modes receive their primacy from it, just as the subjugal modes receive their dignity from the following middle, which obtained the second arrangement of the modes together with the second letters.

The excellent received its name not from greater dignity but from the most acute quality of the voice, as its positive name also shows. Since the final is equal to it both in position and in letters, one may ask why the ends of chants have been assigned to the final rather than to the excellent.

The answer is that intensification precedes relaxation, and the progress of every work seeks intensification, while its end seeks relaxation. Hence, after the intensification of the excellent strings, chants require an end or relaxation among the lower strings; for this reason they are also called finals.

At this point one may ask why the authentic modes, ascending through three four-chords and descending through the same, come to rest, whereas the subjugal modes, likewise ascending through three, do not descend through three but stop halfway, that is, at the finals.

The answer is as follows. It is fitting that the two principal functions—the *saeculorum. Amen* and the endings—be held in the principal position of the two middle four-chords, so that just as the *saeculorum. Amen* is held once in the primary middle, all the endings may likewise be possessed together in the secondary middle.

Since it is our purpose to collect into this little work, as into a single bundle, whatever suitable investigation suggests for clarifying the manifold obscurities of the monochord, we do not wish to leave unexplained why both the Hypomixolydius and the Dorius take their arrangement between D and d.

It may seem surprising how two different modes can be produced in one and the same region. The matter is resolved in this way. Since fourteen voices are produced by four four-chords, it is necessary, according to the nature of an even number, that they have two middles, which also produce the aforementioned *diezeuxis*. These are G and A. One of them terminates the middles or finals of the subjugal modes; the other begins the middles of the authentic modes.

Therefore the one which, in the fourth place, terminates the subjugal modes according to their middles belongs properly to the tetrardus and to its subjugal, since they are fourth—that is, G. The one which begins the authentic modes according to their middles belongs properly to the protus alone—that is, A.

These two middles therefore produce, within one diapason, the two different modes under discussion in the following way. The protus, arranged from D to d, has A as its middle and D as its final. By repeatedly returning in its cola, commas, and ending to these proper letters, and by recognizing in its singing its proper species of the diatessaron and diapente, namely A–D and D–a, it will be utterly unlike the Hypomixolydius.

Similarly, because of the repeatedly mentioned midpoint of the seven voices—which, just as it joins two four-chords, also receives the arrangement of two modes—the Hypomixolydius, arranged from D to d, has G as its middle. Returning to it repeatedly through cola and commas, whether by intensification or relaxation, and frequently employing its proper species of the diatessaron and diapente, namely D–G and G–d, it becomes utterly opposed to the protus.

Having learned these things, it is not unworthy to know also the indifferent arrangements of the modes. In this description, what these eight specifically receive, the four generally receive in the following manner:

- Protus is arranged from A to D; its middle is D and a.
- Deuterus is constructed from B to e; its middles are E and b.
- Tritus is ordered from C to f; its middles are F and c.
- Tetrardus is set to melody from D to g; its middles are G and d.

To make all the preceding matters clearer, let us lay out the arrangement of all the modes individually in the following way:

Now what I postponed saying at this point becomes more apparent: why they are called “middles.” They are called so because each mode, enclosed within its own diapason, receives one middle. In the subjugal modes this middle receives the diatessaron from the graves and the diapente from the acute voices; in the authentic modes it receives the diatessaron from the acute voices and the diapente from the graves.

Since seven different voices produce eight modes altogether different from one another, it can be gathered that seven, multiplied by itself—that is, seven times seven—produces forty-nine distinctions of voices in different positions, as follows:

A, B, C, D, E, F, G, a, B, C, D, E, F, G, a, C, D, E, F, G, a, c, D, E, F, G, a, c, d, [Col. 0427B] E, F, G, a, c, d, e, F, G, a, b, c, d, e, f, G, a, b, c, d, e, f, g.

[Col. 0427A] In the preceding figure, arranged with the greatest care, it is clear even to those of lesser understanding with which kinds of diapason, diapente, and diatessaron every mode consists; that the authentic modes include the finals and the highest notes, while the plagal modes include the graves and the upper notes; that the authentic modes depress, mediate, and raise the finals and upper notes, while the plagal modes do the same with the graves, finals, and upper notes; that the plagals have first the diatessaron and then the diapente, whereas the authentics have first the diapente and afterward the diatessaron; that, according to the rule, there is no transition for the authentics into the graves, nor likewise for the plagals into the highest notes; that the authentic modes communicate with the plagals through the diapente in the finals, while the plagals communicate with the authentics through the diatessaron in the upper notes; that the diapente is found in the graves, and the diatessaron in the finals, only in forms that are not legitimate according to the established arrangement; that three different species constitute the diatessaron, four the diapente, and eight the diapason, on account of the qualities of the eight [Col. 0428B] modes; that the eighth species is found within one and the same diapason by which the protus is arranged, but is distinguished by a different median note and also by different species of diapente and [Col. 0429A] diatessaron—as was explained more fully above; that D alone among all the strings is two-formed (biformis). This is because it is the fourth of the graves and the first of the finals; because, inasmuch as the fourth represents the fourth species of diatessaron in the position of the first, the acute d is likewise the fourth of the upper notes and the first of the highest notes; because, as the first, it once again closes the first species of diatessaron and diapente while beginning the other; because, as the fourth, it once again represents the fourth species of diatessaron; because, as the first, it carries the protus upward according to the rule by the highest ascent; and because, as the fourth, it begins both the fourth plagal together with the protus and the fourth authentic, the tetrardus, through the *saeculorum Amen* (“Amen through the ages”). To put it more clearly: in the name of the first and [Col. 0429B] fourth, the first authentic and the fourth of the plagals are depressed from here by the lowest descent, with the protus still having its special ending on it; from there they are raised by the highest ascent, with the tetrardus still specially singing its *saeculorum Amen* (“Amen through the ages”) on it. These matters have been briefly recapitulated so that, once presented to the reader’s eyes at a single glance, they may be grasped by a readier and more lasting memory.

We ought to know, moreover, that the whole purpose of musical theory is directed toward acquiring the knowledge by which chant may be composed rationally, judged according to rule, and sung suitably. Whoever possesses the ability for all three of these may rightly at last be called a musician. Yet one should not be regarded as insignificant who, though unable to compose, knows how to judge competently. [Col. 0429C] As for the third activity—that is, the zeal for singing, or rather for howling—the blind crowd of singers is entirely occupied with it, yielding to no rational account and accepting no one’s judgment. They also constantly repeat, not as a proverb but as though it had been imposed by law, the word *neuma* as if it meant *nemo* (“no one”), although in Greek speech *neuma* is said as *noeumane*, that is, “ascending breath.” [Col. 0430A] Breath has two parts, namely *arsis* and *thesis*, that is, elevation and depression. But *neuma* is named from the better of these, namely elevation, so that we may be reminded that, in the sweetness of chant, it is produced by the breath driving the sound from lower to higher notes, so that we may raise the heart from earthly things to heavenly ones. Otherwise, he sings in vain whose mind does not agree with his voice. Either, then, these people are mistaken, or “divine wisdom—which, because all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in it,” also wished the inspired knowledge of this art to be sung wisely to itself. But how do those sing wisely who know nothing of the matters mentioned above, who confuse one mode with another by exchanging them, and who praise only loudness of sound? In this respect, however, they are inferior and more ignorant than an ass, which, by a just judgment, both brays much more loudly [Col. 0430B] and never changes its bray into a bellow or any other voice. O the insane wretchedness of human beings! No one tolerates a fault in grammar, which is established by convention; but in music, which is entirely natural, almost no one corrects faults—in fact, they even defend them.

Up to this point I have lingered over these matters more tediously than was proper, since they cause me both annoyance and shame. Now I address you who take delight in this study: I exhort and advise you to grasp what has already been said and what will be said hereafter through practice both of the hand and of the voice. Above all, make the recognition of the modes your concern, since almost the whole purpose of music is occupied with them. For this purpose it will be of great benefit if someone impresses upon his memory the proper species of each diapente and diatessaron through use both of the monochord and of the living voice. For no one who merely hears a mode will be able to declare with certainty which mode it is unless he has been long and diligently exercised in what has already been said and what will be said hereafter. Thus, sing the species of the diatessaron upward and downward:

[Col. 0429]

[Col. 0429D] Do you see how all begin in regular and unconfused order from their own graves or principals, are raised at their own finals, and are then depressed again to the place where they began? Among them a certain twofold character may be observed, because it is both the highest note of the first and the lowest of the fourth. The first and the fourth are also alike in position, though not in function; they differ in that the first is first intensified and afterward relaxed, while the fourth is first relaxed and afterward intensified. You will easily sing these species even with one voice if you begin them through the customary melody of *saeculorum Amen* and end them with the first definition. Although these definitions are sung fully and perfectly at the finals and at the upper notes, the final neumes in each tetrachord do not differ from their own mode.

[Col. 0430D] As was said much earlier, F–[uncertain note] seems almost to be a species of diatessaron; but since the reason why it is not was not stated there, it seems appropriate to state it here. First, we say simply that, although the different species of diatessaron are arranged through the graves and finals, none of them consists in the arrangement of a tritone. Again, since every species of diatessaron consists of two tones and a semitone, F–[uncertain note], because conversely it is contained continuously by a tritone, is not counted as a diatessaron. Further, all species of diatessaron and diapente are completed by the comparison of two tetrachords: the diatessaron from the graves and finals, and the diapente from the finals and upper notes.

Therefore, if I wish to call D–G the first species of diatessaron because it is not formed from two tetrachords, I am wrong. It will necessarily be the fourth, consisting of the fourth grave and the fourth final. If I say that I called it first formally, not according to the established arrangement, remember this most firmly. If I define E–a as the second species, I am in error. Although it is formed from two tetrachords, it does not follow the proper order: E is the second of the finals, whereas a is the first of the upper notes, and the first does not correspond with the second either in position or in mode. It remains, therefore, that E–a is formally the second species.

Likewise, if I call F–[uncertain note]—the matter under discussion—the third species, I am corrected, because, although it is formed from two tetrachords, F, the third of the finals, does not agree with the second mode either by the nature of its position or by that of its mode; and because it is contained by a tritone, which contains no other species, it must be regarded as neither a constitutive nor a formal species. It remains, therefore, that in this place the third [Col. 0431B] species is formed formally through F and through *b synemmenon*, although by an extraordinary arrangement.

In the same way, G, the fourth of the finals, is not joined with c, the third of the upper notes, so as to form the fourth species of diatessaron. For if its regular position is examined—that is, tone–semitone—it will rather be the third species of diatessaron. Therefore, in this place too, the fourth species is formally taken through G–c, with a semitone interposed, by means of *synemmenon*. It is therefore clear that, according to the established arrangement, the species of diatessaron are rightly removed from the finals and upper notes, because if they were naturally present there, no species would be lacking. For if I remove *synemmenon*, which is not regular, I simultaneously sing there both the third species with the fourth, both naturally and formally. But this, as was said much earlier, is not surprising; for the third step of the first measurement, because it includes five notes, operates in these places more as a pentachord than as a tetrachord.

[Col. 0432A] There is still a subtler reason why F–[uncertain note] is not considered a diatessaron. It may be considered as follows. I intensify D–G, a diatessaron; and I can relax the diapente G–e, because the diatessaron and diapente differ by a tone. Again, I intensify E–a, a diatessaron; and I can relax the diapente a–D, because the difference between the sesquialter and sesquiter­tian ratios corresponds. Again, I intensify E–[uncertain note], a diapente; but I cannot relax the diatessaron [uncertain note]–F, because a semitone will never be the difference between the sesquialter and sesquiter­tian ratios.

This most beautiful solution is set apart from the foregoing statements solely by privilege and is undeservedly called “golden.” It should also be known that Boethius, following the most ancient musicians, defines three different species of diatessaron, but does not arrange them at all in their natural order, because he does not draw them from their proper source. Anyone diligent in comparing our words with his will be able to see this clearly. But concerning the first species, according to him, there is no mention at all in its formal sense. Hence it also happened that, because the proper character of this species was unknown, the mode called hypomixolydian, of which it is itself the species, was likewise given an incongruous arrangement. Since we have fully resolved this matter above, we do not repeat it here.

You, therefore, so long as you are my student, impress upon your memory, as I told you above, the species already mentioned for recognizing the modes, both by moving along the strings and by the living voice. In this way you will relieve the weariness either of your hand or of your voice by applying the arguments proposed in the foregoing discussion, and you will rejoice in a double pleasure: both the sweetness of musical performance and the variety of alternating [Col. 0432C] discussions.

Once you have perfectly learned the notes of the diatessaron, sing the species of the diapente upward and downward as follows:

[Col. 0431]

[Col. 0431C] Do you not, if you carefully consider what has been said, see that the species of diapente also begin in natural order from their own finals, [Col. 0431D] are raised to their own upper notes, and return by an unhindered step to their starting point? If you sing them, as I said above, with the customary differences and definitions, you will acquire pleasant recognitions of the modes.

Just as was stated above, in the proper arrangement of the diapente there are two notes, namely F–[uncertain note], which, although they enclose four notes, are nevertheless excluded from the species of diatessaron. Likewise, in the places properly belonging to the diatessaron—that is, among the graves and finals, and among the upper and highest notes—there are two notes, namely B and F, which, although they include five notes, are nevertheless excluded from all the species of diapente. Consider the reason as follows. Every regular diapente consists of three tones and a semitone; but this anomalous species is completed by two tones [Col. 0432C] and an equal number of semitones. These two joined semitones do not make a whole tone, and thus, for the completion of the diapente, a comma together with a semitone will be lacking. Therefore, because it is held by such an imperfection, it does not deserve to be counted among the species of diapente.

Furthermore, among the four different species of diapente that are naturally constructed by comparison of the finals and upper notes, there is none that contains two tones and an equal number of semitones. Therefore what is not found at the source is judged to have been discovered outside it, in hypocrisy, and is rejected.

A subtler explanation could also be offered from this point, proceeding as follows. I can intensify the diapente A–E and relax the diatessaron E–B, because the difference corresponds. Again, I can intensify the diatessaron B–E, but I cannot relax the diapente B–F, because the semitone prevents the difference from being complete. I can relax the diatessaron F–C, but I cannot relax the diapente F–B for the same [Col. 0433A] reason.

The same must be said concerning F–[uncertain note]. I can intensify the diapente F–c and relax the diatessaron c–G. Again, I can intensify the diapente F–c, but I cannot intensify the diatessaron F–[uncertain note], because a semitone will not constitute the difference. Again, I can intensify F–b, but I cannot relax the diapente b–E, because the difference will not be achieved through a semitone. I can relax the diapente [uncertain note]–E, but I cannot relax the diatessaron b–F, because a semitone does not produce the difference between the sesquialter and sesquiter­tian ratios.

F differs from B in this respect: F, from itself as a middle note, can extend a diapente upward and a diatessaron downward; B alone among all the notes, from itself as a middle note, neither extends a diapente upward nor a diatessaron downward. Hence B is called ignoble by some, and it does not even receive the *saeculorum Amen* (“Amen through the ages”) of the deuterus in its proper order.

Boethius, however, seems to fall into inconsistency in defining the species of diapente. Although he says that there are four varieties of them, he relaxes those same four from the square note to low B. Since he does not find all the natural notes in those places, he places F–B last, although it has been proved that, because of the deficiency of its difference, it is not to be counted among the species of diapente. Later, as though he had forgotten himself, while discussing which species are contained in immovable notes [Note: [Col. 0433D] In the margin, in another ancient hand: “He calls those species immovable which are naturally constitutive in themselves.”], he passes over the anomalous F–B, which he had previously placed last, and finally marks four natural species of diapente by intensifying from E to e. Yet he does not show which species is to be assigned to which mode, or in what order or place. Since this matter, having often been stated by us above, is already very well known, it need not be recalled further. Let us therefore proceed onward and consider what else is useful for recognizing the modes.

Thus, once the species of diapente and diatessaron have been practiced individually, as stated above, both with the voice and on the string, a still greater recognition of the modes follows. It consists in learning to recite, upward and downward, the complete order and character of each mode by joining pairs of species—first with first, second with second, third with third, and fourth with fourth—namely, the diapente followed by the diatessaron in the authentic modes, and the diatessaron followed by the diapente in the plagal modes, as follows:

[Col. 0433]

[Col. 0433C] Is it not evident that the foregoing species of diatessaron and diapente, drawn from the purest source, have been arranged in the correct order? For when joined together, as the preceding figure shows, they begin, mediate, raise, and end all the octochords—that is, the diapason of each mode—from their proper letters.

Just as two lesser symphonies are enclosed at their proper points by two unequal but nevertheless proper letters, so conversely the greatest symphony, namely the diapason, is enclosed at both ends by two equal notes, because of the nature of unisonance; it is mediated or divided by one different but nevertheless equally proper note.

As was said much earlier, it should not seem surprising that each diatessaron, together with the diapente corresponding to it, ought to be joined in the middle by its proper letters; nevertheless, since there is not yet unisonance there among the notes that enclose the diapason, they will necessarily be different. Hence those who place the same signs almost everywhere in the fifth places, as though perfect concord existed there, are far removed from the truth.

They also fall into this error: contrary to the common agreement of all musicians, indeed contrary to the laws of nature itself, the same signs appear in the ninth region rather than the eighth; and thus, in a most absurd manner, the characters alone, and not the notes, possess equality. Therefore those who linger over the construction of such an arrangement ought to consider that, where the operation of the principal strings has been scattered, the constitution of the species disturbed, and the order of the modes broken apart, with almost no truth and scarcely any certainty remaining, they should know that they will accomplish nothing true or certain in practice. To make this clearer, let us place the same arrangement before our eyes.

[Note: [Col. 0434] Double-click the ornament icon that follows to view the structure of the figure whose contents are keyed below.]

A, tone. B, semitone. C, tone. D, tone. [Col. 0434D] A, tone. B, semitone. C, tone. D, tone. A, tone. B, semitone. C, tone. D, tone. A, tone. B, semitone. C, tone. D, tone. A, tone. B, semitone.

[Note: [Col. 0433D] Concerning this arrangement, more has been said in Hucbald’s *Musica*, part I, p. 152 and following pages, although there is some discrepancy there in the notes and signs. The first there are the highest notes, but with X in place of N; the second are the upper notes, but with / in place of [uncertain sign]; the third are the finals, but with / in place of N; the fourth are the graves, but with N in place of X.]

[Col. 0435A] If anyone should be so studious as to attempt to exemplify through this arrangement everything said from the beginning of this little work and everything that will be said hereafter, he will undoubtedly discover into how great an error the same description would entangle him. Leaving to those who wish to do so the opportunity for this undertaking, we omit it in order to moderate the readers’ weariness and the length of the work.

As we began, let us still examine one rule for recognizing the modes. It was indeed excavated by earlier authorities as a rough mass, but was not completely freed from rust; let us render it bright and pure, as will be evident to the diligent. Although this recognition is compressed into a brief form, it is nevertheless broad and celebrated in its distinction, because what is especially beautiful in it is constructed among the proper and legitimate seats of the modes.

[Col. 0435B] Its reasoning is as follows. Take whichever tetrachord you wish—for example, that of the graves—and add a tone at each end. You then have the boundaries of the modes, which become the seats of the modes.

There are four modes and an equal number of types of notes. The first type of notes is lowered by a tone and raised according to the first species of diapente. It is recognized in this antiphon: “The prophets proclaimed”; and in “At your coming,” and similar pieces, which do not exceed six strings. This mode is recognized in the principal strings of the protus: A, D, a, d.

The second type, lowered by a ditone and raised according to the second species of diatessaron, existing in the principal strings of the deuterus—B, E, [uncertain note], e—is displayed by this antiphon: “This is glory,” and by similar pieces, whether authentic or plagal, which do not exceed six strings.

The third type [Col. 0435C] is lowered according to the third species of diatessaron and raised by a ditone, as the principal strings of the tritus—C, F, c, f—show. Its indication is found in this antiphon: “A little while, and you will not see me,” and in similar pieces.

We assign the fourth type, raised by a tone and lowered according to the fourth species of diapente, to the tetrardus, because its principal strings—D, G, d, g—constitute it. It can be recognized in these antiphons: “If you truly are brothers,” and “Many will come,” and in similar pieces.

What has been stated, constructed from six notes, demonstrates both the perfection of the number six and of the greatest interval, which consists of that number of notes.

These statements have been made according to our own speculation. The earlier authorities, however, energetic in excavating these matters but sluggish in clearing them, failed to attend to the often-mentioned twofold character of D; by removing the recognition of the fourth mode from the fourth place, they went wrong. They did not consider that the modes are converted into one another: the protus, lowered by a tone, is raised according to the first species of diapente; the tetrardus, on the other hand, opposed to it in the fourth place, is raised by a tone and lowered according to the fourth species of diapente; the deuterus, lowered by a ditone, is lowered according to the second species of diapente; while the tritus, conversely, raised by a ditone, is lowered according to the third species of diatessaron.

Here it should also be noted that [Col. 0436A] the extremes—that is, the protus and tetrardus—are varied by a tone and their proper species of diapente, while the middle modes—that is, the deuterus and tritus—are varied by a ditone and their proper species of diatessaron.

Thus, with one wound in this error healed, let us seek out the other, sick with three wounds, and humbly restore it to health. Those of whom we are speaking, ignorant of the fact that what has been stated is most perfectly contained in six notes, extracted three modes in regular fashion through A, B, and C. Since, according to them, the fourth would then be missing, they took seven notes as well and, repeating the order of the aforesaid modes according to an equal rule through D, E, and F, finally raised the fourth mode through G alone, lowered by a tone and raised by two tones and a semitone.

In doing so they committed the error already described: they did not convert that mode against its opposite, the protus, in the manner stated. Next, by raising it beyond measure, they exceeded the legitimate boundary of six notes, which begins at C and extends to a. Finally, they completed that same raising by no proper species.

It is therefore clear that this recognition of the modes can be perfectly achieved in any tetrachord with a tone added at either end. If you choose the tetrachord of the graves, the fourth mode under discussion will be for you on D, because D is common to the protus and tetrardus. If you take the final tetrachord, the protus will conversely be on D and the tetrardus on G, without the aforesaid rule ever wavering. The same may be observed in the upper and highest notes.

It is therefore clear that the earlier musicians did not direct this rule toward the recognition of the modes, but simply counted seven modes through the seven distinctions of the notes. Hence some, being unaware of the twofold character of D, entirely omitted the eighth mode; some placed it above the master; some established it together with the master. No one who understands the matter can fail to know that all these alternatives are equally absurd.

For if the fourth authentic has no plagal, why do the preceding three have one? If it does have one, but is unjustly placed above its head, it has been sufficiently shown above that it has no place there both by the right of subordination and by the reasoning of the arrangement. If, according to some, it will usurp for itself a path belonging to the master, that will be ridiculous, because, with one median note—namely d—existing between G and g, the simple species of diatessaron and diapente succeeding one another will not produce the twofold character in the manner in which, between D and d, two median notes, G and a, together with species of diatessaron and diapente that do not exist simply, most appropriately open the bosom of the twofold character to two modes. But enough has now been said about these matters.

It will also contribute somewhat to the recognition of the modes if someone observes all the differences of all the modes together, with their places counted, as follows:

[Col. 0437]

[Col. 0437A] If anyone is so dull-witted that he cannot make sufficient progress from reading what precedes, let him fix his eyes on the present figure, place his finger upon it, and without labor mark out the whole difference and agreement of the modes, as well as the properties and order of all the species; in accordance with his ability, he will acquire sufficient knowledge of this art.

It also helps greatly in understanding the quality of the modes if you constantly rehearse the customary definitions, the verses of the definitions, and the many lengthy chants of each mode, especially the more extended ones. Such are, in the hypodorian: the antiphons “The chief priests gathered” and “With the maker.” In the hypophrygian: “Entirely beautiful,” and “The holy one showed,” marked “Gamm.”, and similar pieces. In the hypolydian: “Adorn the bridal chamber,” “Give thanks to the Lord,” the responsory “Today for us,” and similar pieces. In the hypomixolydian: “Six days before,” “When the King of glory,” “Christ, who reigns,” and similar pieces.

In the Dorian, which is the first authentic: “Hail, full of grace,” “Today they have been fulfilled,” “Your nativity,” “A certain man,” “Two men,” and similar pieces. In the Phrygian: “The Lord has sworn,” marked “Gr.”, “I will exalt you,” the antiphon “Look upon me,” and similar pieces. In the Lydian: the offertory “He sanctified,” with its verses, and many similar pieces. In the mixolydian: “When the people had heard,” “The angel sat,” and similar pieces.

I have said this because, when the voice dwells for a longer time on an extended chant, knowledge of the quality of the mode is formed more fully in the mind.

It should also be known that, by becoming thoroughly accustomed to these matters, to those mentioned earlier, and to those still to be mentioned, one will be able to recognize any mode upon hearing it and will also be able to produce a melody according to rule. Yet one will not be able to find a name that expressly designates the character of each mode, just as in the appearance of a person one may say that this man is dressed in a white tunic and that one in a black tunic; just as in the artificial representations of an ox, horse, wolf, dog, ass, sheep, and crow we customarily give proper names to their sounds—lowing, neighing, howling, barking, braying, bleating, and croaking; and just as we distinguish the sun’s appearance by its clear ray in spring, its burning ray in summer, its whitish ray in autumn, and its pale ray in winter.

If I say protus, deuterus, tritus, and tetrardus, I have named their orders according to the arrangement of the monochord, not their characters according to the quality of the melody. Likewise, if I call them Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, and mixolydian, I have applied the names according to which people were more attracted to or accustomed to one nation or another, not according to the character of the melody.

Similarly, if, in general accordance with natural reasoning, I call the hypodorian sweet, the hypophrygian restrained or grave, the hypolydian lamenting, the hypomixolydian cheerful or exultant, the Dorian grave or noble, the Phrygian excited or dancing, the Lydian voluptuous, and the mixolydian chattering, I have designated something more in these names than in the others; yet I have not found specific names that express the force of this sweetness, restraint, lamentation, cheerfulness, and the other natural effects. O the wondrous profundity of music in this matter, which, though somewhat open to understanding, can be indicated only by certain superficial names!

Perhaps I seem verbose to the tedious, who think that they know everything without instruction. But let them, I ask, [Col. 0438C] pay attention: these matters are not being thrust upon philosophers as trivialities, [Col. 0439A] but are being offered as milk-like nourishment to simple people—that is, to people like me—so that they may be strengthened for greater things.

If they should at some time, laying aside their raised eyebrows, devote leisure to reading these matters, they will see that I have labored in the arrangement of the monochord out of goodwill, in order to clarify what was obscure in the statements of the ancients, repeat what had been omitted, and correct what was open to criticism. Just as someone who possesses gold or silver, provided it is in a chest, does not care very much in which part it lies, so I too, provided that whatever I am able to examine is found in this little work, do not care greatly, as some do, about the diligence of the order.

Therefore, since I have now spoken at length about the modes, let whatever else the mind may suggest still be added. Every mode—that is, something undivided—consists of all the elements, namely, of the four principal strings of its own character and of its species. Thus the protus consists of the first of the graves, the first of the finals, the first of the upper notes, and the first of the highest notes; of the first species of diatessaron, which extends from A to D; of the first species of diapente, which extends from D to a; of the first species of diapason, which extends from low A to high a; and of the first species of that consonance which is a diapason with a diatessaron, from low A to acute d. The same applies to the other strings and species of the modes.

All the authentic modes, beginning from the finals, ascend to the highest notes and are divided at the upper notes; all the plagal modes, beginning from the graves, end at the upper notes and are mediated at the finals. Consequently, the finals and upper notes are common to both groups.

The following material is found in the same Vienna codex, [Col. 0439C] immediately after Hermann. Here, however, we present it from various other codices—especially the Ottoburian, the Saint-Blaise, and the Leipzig manuscripts—with their own annotations, so that those skilled in the subject may also acquire practical knowledge of this music.

## I. Explanation of the letters and signs occurring below

[Note: [Col. 0439D] Hermann thought that the letters explained here—namely e, s, t, ts, tt, d, Δ or δ, δs, and δt—placed above the syllables, could usefully be substituted for the ancient, freely varying musical notations, at a time when the lines and clefs that we use today, invented by Guido of Arezzo, had not yet become widespread. The principle of their arrangement is given here. The signs inserted between them determined their quantity: a comma placed after a letter indicated a long note, while a point indicated a short one. Hence it is said here that notes with points are relaxed, whereas those without points are intensified; this will become clearer from what follows.]

[Note: [Col. 0439C] In Migne, the letters in square brackets are printed above the words after which they appear here.]

E (e) [e.] makes [e. t,] unison notes [e, e, t. t,] equal [e, s.]. S [,] marks [S, s. ts, t, t,] the distance [t, t, ts, s, t,] of a semitone [te, tt.]. T [t] sounds [t, t.] the difference [t, t, et, t. t,] of a tone [t, ts.]. S [,] together with [ts. Ts,] T [,] establishes [e, ts. s, ts. t,] a semiditone [ts, ts. ts, t.]. TT (tt), doubled [tt. tt, t, ts.], designates [e, tt. tt,] a ditone [d, tt, s t.]. D [,] (d) indicates [d, d dt d] the diatessaron [dt. t. s. d,] symphony [d. t, δ]. Δ (δ), delta, distinguishes [δ, s, tδ. e.] the diapente [δ, e, t, s. t.] consonance [t. t, s. d,]. Δ (δ), together with [ds,] S [,], teaches [δs. e.] two limmata [δs] with a tritone [d, t, t, d, t.]. Δ [ts] (δ) [δt.]elta together with [t te.] T [Col. 0440A] determines [s, s, t, t,] four tones [e,] with [t. t, s.] a limma [t. t.]—the greatest [δt, t, t.] interval, namely [s, t. ts, s.] in [s,] our chants [ts, t. s, e] of phthongoi [e g,] (“sounds” or “notes”) [s, t, t,]—[δt. t, d, t,]. But [s, t. t, e,] these [δ,] notes [s.] with [t, δ.] points [d,] distinguish [ts, t,] relaxed [t, s, t,] differences [t. t,] of the foregoing [t, s,] notes; without [t, t, ts,] points, they distinguish intensified [e, δt.] differences [t, d, t, δt, e.] of notes [t, t t.] already set forth [s, t. ts, s.].

## II. Hermann’s verses for distinguishing chant

[Note: [Col. 0440A] In Migne, the letters in square brackets are printed above the words after which they appear here.]

Hermann brought forth these verses and notes,

So that they might reveal examples of notes familiar to everyone.

[Col. 0440B] Three times three are the intervals of joined sounds,

For now a little voice makes phthongoi in unison equal;

Now it distinguishes a limma, nearly like a similar sound;

Now a tone gives distinctions to a related note;

And also the limma and tone, joined together continuously;

And often two tones likewise continued one after another;

And often, moderating the sweet-sounding diatessaron, it regulates melodies;

And frequently, sweetly soothing the ears, the diapente;

Sometimes two tones together with a limma make three;

And sometimes a limma joined with four tones makes four.

If you know how to distinguish these things simultaneously by voice and by notes,

You can soon compose any distinct chant from them,

Distinguishing, without a precentor, either the thesis or the arsis.

The following material is appended immediately to the preceding passages in the twelfth-century Saint-Blaise codex; elsewhere it has also been read by me.

There are three times three modes from which every chant is woven, namely: unison, semitone, tone, semiditone, ditone, diatessaron, diapente, semitone with diapente, tone with diapente, and, in addition, sound and diapason. If anyone delights in it, let him recognize that this is its manner. Since the whole of harmony is formed from so few clausulae, it is most useful to commit them deeply to memory and not to rest from this kind of study until, once the intervals of the notes have been recognized, one can very easily grasp knowledge of the whole of harmony.

[Col. 0441] To make these matters clearer, we append below Hermann’s preceding verses with the notes called chorale notes, taken from the Leipzig codex. We again place above them the letters and signs already set out above, so that the entire artifice of the ancient musicians may become evident to the eye through mutual comparison.

[Note: [Col. 0441] Double-click the ornament icon that follows to view the musical notation, whose text is keyed below.]

[Note: [Col. 0441] In Migne, the letters in square brackets appear above the words after which they are printed here.]

[Col. 0441] Thrice three are the intervals of conjoined sounds. Now the voice makes equal the unison *phthongoi*; now the *limma* distinguishes a nearly similar melody; now the tone gives distinctions to a related voice. Moreover, the semitone and tone are continuously conjoined, and often two tones follow one another alike; often, sweetly moderating melodies, the diatessaron; and frequently the diapente, pleasantly soothing the ears. At times three tones are joined with two semitones, and at other times a semitone with four tones. If you know how to distinguish these together by voice and notes, you can soon compose from them any distinct chant, distinguishing *thesis* without a precentor, or *arsis*.

[Col. 0441] In the same Leipzig manuscript and in the manuscript of Saint Peter, the same material follows with musical notes, though without letters written above them; we have already given it above from the San Blas manuscript.

[Note: [Col. 0441] Double-click on the ornament icon that follows to view the musical notation, the text of which is keyed below.]

[Col. 0441] Three times three are the modes by which every melody is woven: namely, unison, semitone, tone, semiditone, ditone, diatessaron, diapente, semitone with diapente, tone with diapente, and, in addition to these, the sound of the diapason. If anyone delights in it, let him recognize this as its mode. And since the whole harmony is formed from so few clauses, it is most useful to entrust them deeply to memory, and not to rest from studies of this kind until, once the intervals of the voices have been recognized, one can very easily comprehend knowledge of the whole harmony.

[Col. 0443]

## The Sequence of Hermannus Contractus on the Blessed Virgin Mary

[Note: [Col. 0443B] This song of Hermannus, which was sung both at the Assumption and on all festivals of the Blessed Virgin, although distinguished by the praise of the ancients and extremely common in ecclesiastical books, cannot, in my judgment, by any means carry off the palm. The longer spans of its stanzas are foreign to the character of sequences and disturb the minds of readers; the obscure and confused arrangement of its words and sentences is displeasing. The monk of Salzburg made a German song from it: “I greet you gladly, star of the sea, hope of all Christendom, who leads us to God” (*Ich gruss dich gerne meressterne aller christenheit, zu got uns beleit*; Hoffmann, *D. K. S.*, p. 143), as did Sebastian Brant: “Hail, through-radiant star of the sea,” and so forth (*Ave durchleuchte Stern des meres*, etc.; Wackernagel, p. 124).

1. Isaiah 42:6: “And I have given you as a covenant of the people, as a light of the nations.” *Ad.* Mary is written with five letters, in which the five mysteries of the Blessed Virgin are signified. By the letter M is understood “mediatrix,” mediator; the second is A, by which “auxiliatrix,” helper, is understood. The third letter is R, by which “reparatrix,” restorer, is understood; the fourth is I, by which “illuminatrix,” enlightener, is understood; the fifth is A, that is, “adjutrix,” assistant.

2. *M.* II: “gate of heaven,” a phrase taken from the hymn *Ave, maris stella* (“Hail, star of the sea”), which Hermann imitates in the first two clauses. On the unopened gate, see Wackernagel, p. 61. Ezekiel’s gate: “It was never opened; through it the glorious King went out and entered” (*Diu nie wart ûf getàn, dur die der künec hêrlîche wart ûz und in gelân*).

3. *M.* 14: “lightning.” Song of Songs 6:9: “Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?”

4. Mary had faith in Gabriel’s message. Gregory, moreover, teaches in his account of the Lord’s Passion that all the apostles almost lost their faith, while Mary remained steadfast in faith and awaited the Lord’s resurrection as something absolutely certain. *M.* 14. *Ad Torr.* “they desired.”

5. *Ad.* Sin arose in the tree that stood in paradise, the tree of our first parents; correspondingly, Mary restored the tree of life when she brought forth the Savior of the world. More correctly, however, the tree of life should be referred to Mary herself, with Sebastian Brant, who sings thus in German: “You, tree of life, moistened and illumined by dew from heaven; Gabriel proclaimed the spirit of the rich almond” (*Dich, holtz des Leben, auss thau vom hymmel umbgeben hat gefeuchtet, erleuchtet der geyst der feyst mandell verkündet Gabriel*).

“With the Spirit dripping dew.” The Church loves the image taken from Gideon’s fleece, miraculously wet with dew, Judges 6:36 and following. It is very frequently used in German poems. Wackernagel, p. 101: “Clear Mary, you are truly well figured by the fleece which Gideon received from God as a sign for fighting gloriously” (*Maria klar du pist fürwar figurlich woll pedeutenn / Das kitzfell fron, das Gideon / Von got siglich zu streiten / Betzaichnet wart*).

That Christ the infant is often called an almond may be clear to you from Numbers 17:8: “Moses returned and found that Aaron’s staff had blossomed in the house of Levi; and when the buds swelled, flowers burst forth, which, as their leaves spread, were transformed into almonds.” The staff is a type of Mary, the almond of Christ. Finally, hear the poets of our own nation. Wackernagel, p. 56: “Within the earth Aaron laid a rod, which bore almonds” (*Inin erde leite Aaron eine gerte din gebar mandalon*). Nuzze: “Thus noble: You have borne the sweet staff for our benefit, sweet Mother, without a man’s counsel, Saint Mary” (*Die suezze hast du fure brath / Muoter âne mannes rât, Sancta Maria*, p. 634). “Tonight Lord Aaron’s rod blossomed, from it grew almond fruit—this was the good maiden,” and so forth (*hinaht het blügt herr Aarons rut, da us ihr mandels fruthe wut—dis ist gesin die magct gut*, etc.).

6. Thus Isaiah says in his prophecy against Moab (16:1): “Send forth the Lamb, Lord, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.” Setting aside this prophetic expression, interpreters have labored wonderfully hard and devised many empty explanations.

7. Isaiah 27:1: “On that day the Lord will visit with his hard, great, and strong sword Leviathan, the serpent-bar, and Leviathan, the winding serpent, and he will kill the sea-monster that is in the sea.” Mary bore the Redeemer and, by the same act, struck down the devil. From this arose the custom by which, in pictures or images, the conquered and crushed serpent is triumphantly trampled beneath the Virgin’s feet.

8. *M.* 10: “who are.” *Ad.* “in what manner you are.” *M.* 14. *Ad Torr.* We refer back to “they desired.” “The remnants of the nations”: Sebastian Brant, “those who come from the heathen” (*die von Heyden komme synt*). To understand this clause fully, recall to memory the canon of the Mass. For every priest, after recalling Christ’s Passion in the celebration of Mass, also commemorates the Blessed Virgin and says: “In communion with, and venerating the memory, above all, of the ever-glorious Virgin Mary.”

9. *Ad.* Abraham. Sebastian Brant: “From you proceeds the true bread of heaven, which formerly came from heaven to the true Abraham; the great wonder that it signified may we poor people today behold as its unveiling” (*Von dir aussgat / Des ware hymmelbrot, / Das vor ee dem waren sam / Abrahe vom hymmel kam, / Die gross wunder nam: was das bedeut / Mögen heut wir armen leut / Schawen schon al deckung an*).

It is part of Catholic devotion that Christians, before receiving the sacrament, approach in prayer both the angels, martyrs, saints, and holy women—however many there are—and especially the most blessed Virgin, praying that, strengthened by the intercession of the saints, they may receive worthily the food of angels, the Lord’s body, especially at the hour of death. Compare Wackernagel, p. 103: “Obtain, Virgin, before my end, when I grow old and gray, that the holy and worthy sacrament may become food for me” (*Erbirb, iunckfraw, vor meinem endt / so ich wird alt und greyse / Das heilig wirdig sacrament / Werd mir zu ainer speise*).

11. But elsewhere: “as flame.” *M.* II: “the pure.” Just as Moses approached barefoot when he came to the figure and image of the divine being, so we too ought to approach him barefoot—that is, detached from worldly cares and pleasures—whom we now see not in a figure but incarnate.

14. *Md. Ad. Nb.* “the pure.”

(Apud Daniel, *Thesaurus hymnologicus*, vol. III, p. 30.)

[Col. 0443A]

1. Hail, glorious star of the sea, Mary, divinely arisen as a light for the nations.

2. Rejoice, gate of God, which is not opened; you lead into the world the light of truth itself, the Sun of justice clothed in flesh.

3. Virgin, glory of the world, Queen of heaven, chosen like the sun, beautiful as the moon’s radiance: acknowledge all who love you.

4. You, full of faith, destined to become the gracious branch of Jesse’s stock, the fathers and prophets of old had long desired.

5. Gabriel marked you as the tree of life, destined, with the holy Spirit dripping dew, to bring forth the almond of the divine flower.

6. You brought the Lamb, the ruler and lord of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness of Moab to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.

[Col. 0443B]

7. Striking down raging Leviathan, both the winding serpent and the serpent-bar, you freed the world from its destructive crime.

8. Therefore we, the remnants of the nations, under the worshipful remembrance of you, call to the altar, for mystical sacrifice, the wondrous Lamb of propitiation whom you bore, reigning eternally in heaven.

[Col. 0444A]

9. Therefore the true manna is now granted to true Israelites, true sons of Abraham, who once admired in Moses what the type represented; the veil has now been removed, and it can be seen. Pray, Virgin, that we may be made worthy of that bread of heaven.

10. Grant that we may taste with sincere faith the sweet fountain that the rock foreshadowed in the wilderness, that our loins may be girded after being washed in the sea, and that we may behold the bronze serpent on the cross.

11. Grant that, having become loosened from the animal hide, barefoot, pure in lips and heart, we may draw near to the holy fire and the Father’s Word which you, virgin mother, carried like the bush carried the flame.

12. Hear us, for the Son honors you, denying you nothing.

13. Save us, Jesus, on whose behalf the Virgin Mother prays to you.

[Col. 0444B]

14. Grant that we may behold the fountain of goodness; grant eyes of pure mind to fix upon you.

15. Once it has been drunk, may the mind be able to understand the taste of the wisdom of life,

16. To adorn the Christian faith with works, and, after a blessed end to its dwelling in this world, to pass over to you, author of the world.

[Col. 0445]

## The Poem of Hermannus Contractus on the Contest between the Sheep and the Flax

(Edélestand Du Méril, *Poésies latines populaires*, Paris, 1850, p. 379)

[Col. 0445A]

At the season when a plant of the fields is usually called flax,

When the old woman already promises herself uncertain webs,

Standing beside the flax set out in the neighboring field, I marveled;

While the knotty crop held my heart and eyes,

A new thought seized my lingering mind,

And because it seemed worthy of the stylus, I set it down.

A sheep—from the flock (the flock was present), moving a little apart—

Enters and tramples this down with her foot.

After running about, she now lies upon the sufficiently crushed plants;

The grassy earth gives pleasant refreshment;

And, lying there, recalling the food she has taken in order to chew it again,

She sends to her mouth by another route what returns from it.

The plant—for who would believe it? Great pain almost gives speech

Even to the mute—does not remain silent any longer.

### FLAX

[Col. 0445B]

“Of all the common plants you see,” it said,

“Why have I been preferred for these uses,

So that you might heap filth from your stinking fleece upon me,

Rather than trample me with your foot and defile me with your mouth?”

### SHEEP

“But,” she said, “why should the others be spared?

Because they are food either for humans or for livestock?

But since the earth produces you for no use at all,

If you had sense, you would rejoice that you are useful even for these purposes.”

### FLAX

You have shown plainly that you are part of a brutish animal.

Meanwhile, relieve me of this fleece,

With which, whether you wish it or not, you will soon lie stripped,

Disgracefully bound before the feet of your mistress.

[Col. 0445C]

Meanwhile the old woman will run through all your wool with her shears,

Nor will she leave untouched even the filthy fleece of your tail.

Then, with your body naked, your mange will lie exposed in the open;

Do not continue speaking further.

[Col. 0446A]

### SHEEP

If you had sound judgment, you would ask to be consumed willingly,

Either underfoot or, better, buried beneath dung.

You live in order to perish, and labor not to exist;

You are born only for punishment and harm!

Who could say into how many punishments you will be dragged,

Torn completely from the ground by women’s hands?

So that you may indeed perish, dissolved in water and rotting,

You will first endure the dark, mutilated pits;

After a long time you will pass from water into heat,

So that you may be reduced while dry by a slight labor.

Having been beaten, you will utterly exhaust the various strong arms

Of country people, and, crushed, the little mallets.

When you have already lost whatever strength you previously possessed,

You will go, surrendered to women’s mockery.

[Col. 0446B]

Stretched upon wood, which serves this purpose,

You will be struck with swords made of wood.

Oh, how often you will pass through a comb constructed from a thousand points!

How often, as you pass by, will you groan!

Such terrible teeth will tear your entrails;

A violent hand will drag you a thousand times.

When nothing remains in you that can be seized,

You will then endure this new punishment.

Pitch smeared upon a cloth will bind your solid bristles,

With evenly arranged spikes on the outside.

As they probe your marrow, deeply, deeply,

They will consume everything, if anything remains.

Now, a green plant, you swell vainly with pride;

Then, crushed in so many ways, you will be nothing but fluff.

A plaything of the winds, a light weight snatched into the air,

[Col. 0446C]

Do not continue speaking further.

### FLAX

Yet you yourself proclaim our honor too sparingly,

If you properly distinguish everything you say.

[Col. 0447A]

For human labor, skillful and prepared for profit,

Considers what it works so hard for to be far from worthless.

Grain, threshed in a thousand ways, is transferred to the granaries

Once it has been stripped of its chaff by repeated threshings.

Wines do not enter the storerooms, nor nourish kings beforehand,

Until they have been freed from their grapes.

Repeated pounding prepares what its own stone adorns in temples;

In this way hewn timbers take their forms.

Force, pressure, crosses, tortures, dangers, and deaths

Purify souls so that they may earn their rewards.

The commonwealth of the world seeks the support of flax;

The public cause demands it, and public care cultivates it.
