They ask for me in common and labor for me in common;

Each person prepares me for his own services.

Flax is the one useful thing that the Creator,

After the elements, gave to worldly affairs!

But since you say that I am dissolved and rotted beneath water,

Turn your own eyes upon yourself, so that you may be silent.

A hide drawn from a filthy corpse, itself filthy,

Is dragged onto a roof, long scorched by the sun,

And at the same time turns completely black in cooked poison;

Hardened, it enters baths worthy of it.

Thus a foul mixture of bran and water is a bath for you;

You rot there, more worthless in a worthless vessel.

The man who immersed you will repeatedly stir you with a stick;

He twists his nose and turns his head away from you.

For such a great stench spreads everywhere

That even the masters themselves often flee the house!

Why should I be silent about the rest, since much remains?

Do not continue speaking further.

[Col. 0447C]

### SHEEP

When you magnify yourself and boast grandly of yourself,

If I remain silent, I may perhaps be considered inferior.

Two great necessities suffice for human life:

Clothing that drives away the cold, and food that removes hunger.

For human affairs there is absolutely no second hope:

Take away either of these two gifts.

The sheep supplies both: it repels the cold with wool

And draws forth foods rich in nectar from its udder.

That freshly drawn liquid, while still warm,

Fills all the veins with welcome sweetness.

When it grows cold, if you wish to mix in ground meal,

You will swear in amazement that Jupiter’s nectar is present.

You will turn it into a solid if you touch it with a remedy,

And it is sweet by this very process by which it is sour.

Pressed upon wood through dense curds,

It takes a smooth shape from the mold.

[Col. 0447D]

If you eat it soft, complete pleasure will not be lacking;

If you wish to preserve it, you can do so for many seasons.

There is a place where, served whole with no small quantity of wine,

Cooked in its own juice, it nourishes its masters.

There is a race that makes dishes for itself from this mixed with bacon;

It eats raw foods, itself more raw than they.

Flanders, skillfully weighing my thousand powers,

Makes my milk travel in a thousand forms.

Forming this rich milk into elongated butter,

It makes not only food but also an antidote.

Filling its jars with the milk’s ripened juice,

It uses what remains in baskets and bowls as sauce.

[Col. 0448A]

What benefits, and how many, does the sheep bring to the world?

Even Flanders could not enumerate them all if it wished.

### FLAX

As you say, clothing and food are the greatest necessities

Of human affairs; we do not deny that truth.

But without you the world would have clothing, and without you milk,

Removing cold and hunger without yours.

By a foolish robbery you wish to transfer to yourself

What you seek to remove from all the others;

And while you praise yourself—or rather labor to praise yourself—

Your praise is excessively hateful to many.

Who could count how much the generous hand of the Lord

Provides for nourishment, giving everything to humankind?

How many animals provide skins for clothing?

Their number, I think, is immense—or innumerable.

[Col. 0448B]

You too will be a witness, if only you confess the truth,

That your own use is more worthy of our assistance.

Many have never found you useful as food;

They also shun milk, whether pressed or liquid.

When your hide or other woolen clothing exists,

It is rejected as cheap, or because it appears coarse.

Thus a person often lacks sheep and could always do without it,

But no one is ever found naked of linen.

Finally, so pleasant and so delightful a gift

A person carries with him continually.

He carries it carefully, with the greatest solicitude;

He draws it close and applies it inwardly.

He applies it inwardly, binds it to his naked limbs,

As though saying, “I love what is thus joined to me.”

If snow or rain, or turbulent air, descends,

[Col. 0448C]

Cautiously he assigns our sheep to serve him.

He hands you over to the winds and exposes you to the raging blasts;

Snow drenches you, and hail beats you as well.

Thus whenever untimely heat arrives,

You yourself are forced to endure the aerial flames.

Meanwhile the soft and precious linen garment

Lies safely within, protected from cold and sun.

Roofs cover people, bark covers the hearts of trees;

Shelters serve their kernels, and the sheep serves me.

Great glory to you! Rejoice that you have earned this,

That nature has prepared you to serve my purposes.

### SHEEP

You speak on your own behalf, and your glory needs words;

What is lacking in service, you repair with eloquence.

But in vain you diminish, or rather labor to diminish,

So common a good that it defies enumeration.

If many animals provide skins for clothing,

Few, I ask, provide wool; indeed, none do so more readily.

The usefulness that wool confers is evident to all;

Yet I shall mention a few things, so as not to remain entirely silent.

Wool pleases by itself; by itself it becomes black and white;

By itself it spontaneously assumes many forms.

Simple wool is pleasing: add foreign colors,

And it displays Assyrian and Tyrian dyes.

For the renowned Seres do not possess so many varieties in their famous fleece,

Nor does our material equal the saffron of Corycus.

As much as blood, sun, or flame reddens anything,

So red, Briton, does my gleaming garment make you.

Indeed it is a hard, thin, smooth garment without fluff,

[Col. 0449A]

Soft to the touch and no less pleasing to the sight [sic].

Gaul, which the ancients once called “Long-haired,”

Adds manifold variety to its fleeces.

A people of varied mind desires garments of varied appearance,

Showing by the mobility of its clothing that its character is changeable.

Here one garment bears a thousand different stripes,

So that, just as one stripe is unlike another, one stripe may be like the rest.

Here the remaining body is covered with whitish fleece;

One sleeve is green, but another is red.

Here, while it splits its cloak into two tails,

It is rustic unless one of these is of a different color.

But when this people buys coverings of many colors,

Each person chooses one according to his own taste,

This province nevertheless makes an excellent cloth

That is green, gray, or almost blue.

[Col. 0449B]

Flanders, you send these garments for lords to wear,

Some with curled fluff, others gently compacted.

You, German, do not know how to dye my fleeces;

Yet your hand is no less industrious.

You work the fine wool skillfully beneath your thumb

And transform it into the delicate pleasures of craftsmanship.

You, Rhine, dye light garments with beautiful blackness,

And send them to virgins and sacred orders.

Swabia supplies reddish cloth from undyed fleece;

With these it covers kings’ skins and these it places upon nobles.

There is a color made from red, green, and white,

Which you properly call yellow.

This appearance, naturally born in the cloth as a spontaneous color,

You, Danube, prepare for kings as tunics to be loved.

This noble garment is penetrable by no rain;

[Col. 0449C]

No greater gift than this does the German possess.

As the rainbow shines, distinguished by varied colors,

So, my wool, you paint so many garments in so many ways.

The sheep brings these and still more benefits,

Which a human being can admire but cannot count.

### FLAX

I do not entirely see what reason requires

That the sheep be praised by counting its varieties of color.

The sky has its own splendor, the field its own greenness;

What snow makes white will be its beauty.

Thus different colors have their own praise in their form;

If there were no sheep, would there be no color at all?

There is one appearance belonging to flax, but it is not an accidental external feature:

It is simple and pleasing by itself.

With the world as witness, this appearance suits flax,

And wherever the earth extends, our form is pleasing.

A white, solemn, and precious linen garment,

Suitable for joy and ignorant of sadness;

We not only clothe and gladden mortal humanity,

But also provide varied delights.

With flowers woven into it and other delicate patterns,

We offer linen cloths for wiping hands.

White tablecloths, laid beneath the world’s gifts,

Are the adornment and support of royal banquets;

If someone by chance places woolen cloths beneath the food,

Offended minds will reject the dishes.

[Col. 0450A]

Linen gently inserted among the feathers

Adorns and warms the cushions it produces.

Thus flax, spread out above, gives shining linen cloths

And, with proud elegance, surrounds softly built beds.

Add to these ornaments that curl outward

With their own fleece, and you can make them resemble snow.

Rich hangings depend there, crowning the bed;

Here you can count living forms of beauty.

Who could equal the wealth of kings

To a tent whose beautiful columns support it?

Who could unfold my cloths, my rounded gifts,

Whose name and form are derived from a pavilion?

Armies rest in ordered camps;

From here the free horse roams about.

You know how pleasing a sight from afar

Are linen palaces spread across grassy fields.

People sheltered in these houses are harmed neither by storm nor heat;

They provide protection and sweet refreshment.

Public utility, the delight of war and peace,

Signify a greater spiritual dignity.

A woman uses flax for the adornment of her head,

To say nothing of what it does for the rest of her limbs.

Why do you boastfully claim that your fleeces become garments?

If I order it, there will be nothing further of you.

If pieces of cloth lie divided, scattered in fragments,

How do they come together when they make a garment?

The needle passes through the cloth, carrying my small gift, the thread,

And draws it through with its pierced eye.

By this means my grace binds the joined pieces,

So that they become a garment and acquire a proper form.

Whenever a slight tear damages you, you return

[Col. 0450C]

Supplicating and once again needing our work.

Then you lie humbled, then sober, then daring nothing,

Lying in pieces and asking for our gifts.

Flax is the adornment of things and has the fairest glory;

Who could count how many benefits it brings?

### SHEEP

Many things can be said with greater noise than substance;

I see that, if you could, you would make yourself great.

Do not claim common praises as yours alone, I beg;

If you have sense, allow us to share in them as well.

Because you cling more closely among all garments,

You magnify yourself and think yourself more valuable.

But in this too a greater glory falls to us:

The sheep clings to the naked limbs of the saints.

[Col. 0450D]

To those who flee the world and touch heavenly things in hope,

Whom a free mind joins to the highest Lord,

To those whom the blessed right hand of God has already enrolled

Among the nobles of heaven and its unfailing honors.

For such men, therefore, the innermost garment is woolen;

For this is fitting for their pious purpose.

Here they shun flax and bind wool to their bodies,

Which they would not do if they did not know it useful to them.

You said, if I remember correctly, that the air is harmed

By the stench of our corrupted hide.

To say nothing of clothing, consider also the other benefits

That this hide possesses for various uses.

Let him whose skill is sought as fit for sacred ministries assign this its due value.

If the words that are read were not written in books,

[Col. 0451A]

The sacred order of the holy Church would perish.

How would they discover the order in which all are commanded:

At the font when born, and at the tomb when dying?

There would no longer be a bishop, nor would a pope sit in Rome;

The synod would be dissolved, along with the ranks of the Church.

Moreover, whatever pleasing ingenuity has left behind,

Whatever Egypt gave, whatever the Assyrian teaches;

Finally, all deeds from the first father,

Whatever existed before chaos, whether serious or comic;

What Phoebus taught the Muses, and the Muses taught the poets;

What reason moves the stars, and what moves the poles;

What things the wicked must fear, and what the blessed may hope for;

What the God who presides over all things himself may be—

The sheep knows all this; through sheep the world teaches it;

The sheep itself knows the mysteries of God the Father.

[Col. 0451B]

The vilest part of our whole body, our entrails,

Provides a sweet use for human pleasures.

It makes hearts resound with a certain divine sweetness,

When fastened to the lyre, psaltery, and cithara.

This sound drives away cares and softens anger;

It relieves anxious hearts and dispels all weariness.

The hostile force flees and abandons the hearts it possessed,

When a well-trained hand awakens these sounds.

Orpheus, Amphion, Phoebus with the Muses, and Arion,

As they strike the strings, carry their names to the stars.

And let no one think that this service is beneath the saints:

The one who cast down Goliath was its lover.

The sacred page says that there are twenty-four elders,

Holding citharas and bowls before God’s throne [the supplied text reads *thronum* and notes *Dei*].

[Col. 0451C]

Consider what the sheep is, whose lowest part is received into heaven,

Gladdening holy souls.

### FLAX

There is no need for words; no one can fail to know

What sort of melody comes from the bleating of sheep itself.

When they return after feeding, they seek with trembling cries

The offspring they are nursing; how pleasing that sound is!

What a writer sometimes prepares for himself from sheep’s hide

Is indeed a kind of glory, but an easy one.

This glory belongs more justly to calves; this glory belongs more justly to kids;

The skin of goats is better suited to such studies.

Finally, suppose that the race of sheep had never been created:

Could the world not possess these uses?

I think what you boast is truly worthy of ridicule:

“The sheep clings to the limbs of the saints.”

It is indeed true—but what, I ask, do you consider becoming

If you torture the very bodies themselves?

To restrain the flesh, they fatigue the flesh through hardships;

Among hardships, the sheep sufficiently deserves a place.

Whatever painful things they bear, they seek things harsher still:

Ashes for food, stones for rest.

Will anyone therefore rightly think that ashes should be preferred

To beds, or stones to grain?

You touch upon the mysteries of the Church and pass over earthly things;

You boast of heavenly citharas with the fathers;

And, repeating ancient figures in your praises,

You recall the strong young man’s plectrum in his hand.

[Col. 0452A]

How many praises the sacred books bring to flax

You perhaps do not know, or, I think, you conceal.

In the books of Moses—which the whole canon accepts—

You have indeed read that many mystical things were performed.

God himself demands flax for many uses;

Yet it is pleasant to recall a few briefly.

What house, distinguished by its size or the excellence of its beauty,

Can contain the unbounded God?

And yet, when dictating the construction of dwelling places for himself,

He especially seeks flax for this work.

He requires ten curtains for this purpose;

For from them the house of the covenant is made.

He commands Moses to weave them from twisted byssus,

Which is a soft and excellent kind of flax.

That man, filled with God, together with the venerable leader of the assembly,

[Col. 0452B]

Earned God’s favor through such a dwelling.

The ark of the covenant is clothed in twisted byssus;

Blessed is the care of so sacred a ministry!

When the high priest goes to the altar for divine service,

He shines in significant garments.

First, a garment tightly enclosing the arms with sleeves

Is called the *poderis*; it extends down to the feet.

There is also another, a more worthy, ankle-length garment;

An airy color wholly illuminates it.

It has no sleeves; from its edges hang

Golden apples, suitably intermingled with bells.

The *Abaneth*, conspicuous with flowers and various gems,

Binds these garments with its smooth belt.

Then the *Ephod*, covering the shoulders and reaching to the loins,

Bears gems inscribed with names in two groups of six.

[Col. 0452C]

The Greek calls it *logion*, and the Hebrew also calls it *essen*;

The fifth garment, smaller in extent, is more worthy in significance.

This garment displays twelve gems, distinguished by their forms and names,

Upon the high priest’s breast,

In four rows; each row contains three.

It gives titles to as many fathers as it numbers stones.

Then the tiara adorns the head, though not all of it,

As though you were looking at half of a divided sphere.

Nor are coverings lacking for the shameful thighs,

When the proper hour for sacred ministries returns.

For the sacred plate contributes nothing to our purpose,

Though it hangs upon the forehead and bears the name of the Lord.

But the Lord’s command requires all the other garments

That we have listed here to be made of byssus.

Nevertheless, so that the sheep might not be wholly deprived of this service,

Moses also seeks it for this work.

He prepares a covering from the reddened fleece of sheep;

It is pleasing for keeping away dirt and rain.

So that I may not suspect this is merely invented,

Recite continually what you read in Moses.

### SHEEP

I truly know many things in the books of Moses;

The sheep has devoted more attention to the books than flax has.

For either you do not know, or, if you admit that you know,

You suppress the remaining things blindly through envy.

Through Moses, when giving the people the ritual of sacrifice,

God himself chooses what he wishes in these matters.

When he commands in the Law that guilt be cleansed by a gift,

He does not seek flax at all for this work.

[Col. 0453A]

Rather, at solemn or ordinary times,

He wishes our kind to be appeased through sacred rites.

“If you wish the Lord to be reconciled to the people,” he says,

“You shall slaughter two wool-bearing animals from the flock.”

The washed entrails of one of them you shall burn for me;

From it a sweet odor rises in smoke to the Lord.

The poured-out blood of the other washes the sacred altars;

It cleanses the priests and the priests’ garments.

This sprinkling also consecrates the high priest’s ear;

It consecrates the right foot and hand.

We consecrate that hand which consecrates the rest;

The right hand of the highest priest consecrates everything.

The sheep’s tail is ordered to be set apart for sacred use;

Its fat is part of the net-like covering of the liver.

The synagogue continually purges guilt through us,

[Col. 0453B]

Redeeming itself daily with twin lambs.

Why should I recall all the sacred rites spread throughout the world,

Which bear as many sacraments as they contain words?

The house of Jacob, heavily oppressed under a harsh ruler,

Worn out by evils, directs its groaning to the Lord.

He raises his signs and powerful hand against the king,

So that he may open a path for the holy people.

The tyrant’s hard mind, incapable of being softened,

Remains unmoved and earns ten mighty plagues.

The thirst of the Nile could not be relieved at all,

For as many rivers as there were, they were blood.

The frog, the second plague, enters the people’s tables,

The king’s beds, and his food, everywhere as a companion.

Then the gnat rose into the air from stirred-up mud;

The troublesome fly was exceedingly persistent in its bites.

[Col. 0453C]

The fourth plague fills everything with more grievous flies;

That species is usually a pest to dogs.

The land, once rich in herds and flocks,

Remained barren throughout all its fields under grievous disaster.

All Egypt, swollen with sudden ulcers,

Suffered the same thing and sought the physician’s help.

The seventh: a hard hand, thunder mixed with hail;

The storm, killing human beings, destroys the beasts.

The locusts consume what remains of the crops and trees;

They ravage the fields battered by hail.

For three days, suffering Stygian darkness, a man does not see

The limbs that he bears before him.

Throughout all the firstborn of humans and animals,

Egypt lost its tenth plague.

From the king’s throne to the man confined in the shadows,

[Col. 0453D]

This sword reached every captive mourner.

So that such a common plague might not envelop everything,

God himself dictates what his people should do.

“A memorable pledge for you, Hebrew, and for your descendants,” he says:

“A male lamb shall be kept, lest you perish.”

Offer this to me reverently, roasted in the fire;

Consume it swiftly with an eager tooth.

You shall not be ungirded when you devour my sacraments,

Nor barefoot, nor without a staff.

Take care that not even a small part of these sacred things remains.

If, nevertheless, any part remains, burn it in the fire.

Nor cast the blood about recklessly as though it were common;

Your salvation rests wholly in this blood.

With this gore sprinkle the doorposts and both thresholds;

[Col. 0454A]

Everything else that the right hand strikes it will pass over.

Whenever the annual festival day returns,

It will commemorate this for the people through an everlasting covenant.

If you penetrate the sacred mysteries of this holy cause,

You do not receive these things without a repentant heart.

The end of exile, the cause of the desired rest—

The Lamb was the pledge of the promised homeland.

That the sea was opened to the saved people when Pharaoh was killed,

That it performed a twofold service of obedience;

That by day it earned a cloud, by night fire,

And the bread of heaven and conversation with God—

The Lamb was the cause.

But since at last there is no worthy hearer,

We refrain from saying more.

Considering what the sheep is and honoring the sheep reverently,

Correct, in my judgment, your foolish proposal.

[Col. 0454B]

### FLAX

An enemy is not usually admitted as judge in a case,

Nor does this dispute depend upon your decision.

There is certainly no lack of due reverence for the ancient law,

Nor does piety go astray in those utterances.

Yet it was nevertheless a shadow; apart from moral matters,

You should know that whatever that ancient Law commands signifies something else.

We reject legal shadows and figures

And turn toward the light of the holy Church.

Let its common practice judge between us,

The practice established by the celebrated leaders of the faith.

That flax surrounds the sacred altars with garments

I neither magnify nor consider worthless.

Finally, the most discarded part of purified flax

Keeps watch in pious service at sacred places.

[Col. 0454C]

In shifts divided according to the hours, what the sun performs by day,

Flax performs by night.

This brightness, produced by human hands, gives light to temples;

You know better what it does within.

When the bishop, about to perform the sacred rites, takes up the sacred garments,

What place is there for wool in his vestments?

I pass over the garments that custom names from their whiteness

And that properly cover the sacred shoulders.

On both hands, at the solemn time of worship,

His garments shine white, made of flax.

He also carries upon his sacred, curling head a mitre,

So that he may not lack flax even in this part of his dress—

A mitre made of flax, immersed in baptism,
The human being receives the pledge of life upon his head;

Linen supplements baptism and the prescribed offerings,
and opens the sacred entrance into the Church.

Whenever beloved souls are presented in white garments,
it will be a favorable omen.

What else but sorrows, anxieties, or various labors
does a woolen garment signify to me?

The dwellers of heaven are said to appear on earth in white,
whenever they come bringing joyful messages.

Let your glory in this matter also not be lacking: a certain angel
is always in black garments.

Throughout the many months of the uninterrupted year,
the people called by Christ celebrate festivals;
but then especially fervent devotion burns with care
when a special mention of joy is made.

Then, most strictly, eternal law forbids
a sheep’s garment from profaning the sacred choirs.

Then too, when divine linen shines everywhere,
the sheep is driven farther away from the holy places.

Then also, you wool-bearing order of which you boast,
your wool-bearing order that delights in this garment,
is accustomed to conceal it beneath linen worn over it;
by disguising the ill-omened garments, it denies them.

If any unwary person presumes to join the sacred assembly
in the rough garments of a sheep,
the sacred congregation immediately drives him from his station,
as though his mind had been wounded by a grievous omen.

They do not permit the angelic garments, shining with festive whiteness,
to be profaned by a sheep’s garment.

This is no jest, nor does any secular law command it;
holy custom has established it in the Church.

What this act advises or proclaims—
even the mind of ordinary understanding grasps.

There is no place for evil things among the good,
or for the profane among the sacred;
sorrowful and joyful things cannot exist together.

Now, unless it is to seek pardon, do not pour out words before me,
so that, as a suppliant, you may deserve to obtain mercy for yourself.

Do not be ashamed to be defeated under such a judge:
we conquer by the judgment of the holy Church.

---

Here the sheep, having shown by its silence that it had been wounded by reproach,
blushed, and at last replied as follows.

## SHEEP

Nor do we shrink from accepting as judge
one whose Lamb is spouse, father, and lord.

When the bishop, about to celebrate the sacred rites,
puts on the sacred vestments,
his sheep is more worthy in its garments.

The holy churches which common usage calls mothers,
whether because of the merit of their life or the age of their faith,
Rome raises to greater honor by the gift of the pallium,
granting it through the apostolic authority.

This distinguished emblem displays the fullness of consecrated adornment
and rises above the remaining vestments:
simple on the right, double on the left,
hanging from the shoulders, it bears mystical gifts.

Throughout the many months of the uninterrupted year,
the people called by Christ celebrate festivals;
but then especially fervent devotion burns with care
when a special mention of joy is made.

Then each person diligently reveals the joys of his devoted mind
through his own service.

Nothing so bears witness to the joy of the sacred festival
as a church resplendent with festive decorations.

Then precious hangings rise, adorned with their figures,
and hold gazes captivated by themselves.

Then Spanish tapestries, laboriously woven with their wool,
display red patterns on one side and green on the other.

Then the station of the sacred rite, and the very seats of the clergy,
covered by my gift, delight the eyes.

Anyone instructed by the splendor of our prepared furnishings
will recognize that the day is being celebrated.

Your beloved servant, O Christ, writes for the seven churches,
to be proclaimed throughout the whole world, mystical things.

The Church receives these divine oracles, full of holy figures,
with the care they require.

Yet nothing there does devotion embrace so greatly
as the praises of the Lamb celebrated there.

“The book which I saw set there was filled, within and without,
with the greatest mysteries,” he says.
Yet no one was found worthy to break the seals of the closed book
and reveal what words it contained.

As I wept that such great mysteries of the world’s knowledge
were being denied, a single voice said to me:
‘The one whom the imperfection of the flesh prevents from undertaking
the gifts of merit can undertake them if he is free from all deceit.’

Then there appeared something resembling a slaughtered lamb,
with seven eyes and an equal number of horns.

But beautiful in number and most beautiful in merits,
an order of twenty-four elders stands before him.

Four living creatures also stand before him,
celebrating him with devout diligence:
a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle.

When the book, denied to heaven and earth, was sought,
the right hand of the Great One seated upon the throne
offered it to him.

With silent devotion, the people of God
can no longer contain their joy at so great a gift.

They prostrate their bodies and pour out their mouths in praise;
sound proceeds from harps and fragrance from bowls.

They say: “The Lamb is worthy to undertake this task;
by dying, the Lamb has restored us to God.”

O truly great thing for you, fierce lion:
through the Lamb a nation, a language, a tribe, and a holy people have been won.

The whole court of that exalted army
agrees with these worthy voices.

Every heavenly order, subject to no number,
sings praises to you, O Lamb, with a single mind.

They multiply their voices, and the highest courts resound;
this blessed labor knows no weariness.

Glory, majesty, honor, and divine power
are owed to your merits, O slain Lamb.

The earth is yours, O Lamb, and the abyss serves subject to you;
you rule the heavens, O Lamb, and the chaos below.

Let all these things and whatever is within them belong to you;
receive such rewards for your freely given death.

Gather what this statement conveys in a few words,
and even now, with the Lamb as judge, yield to heaven.

If you count linen as a part of the remaining things,
it is rightly subject to the Lamb, who makes everything that exists.

So that you may not be led further astray by the ambiguity of the word,
this Lamb is God; this is what our gracious faith maintains.

If you desire pardon, I will be your guide;
only correct your grandiloquent tongue with sound counsel.

All our intercessions can win favor for you;
often a sheep has reconciled God to the wretched.

---

Here linen first stood amazed and kept silence;
then, recovering its composure, it replied as follows.

## LINEN

Certain faith commends to us the words of John,
the disciple to whom flesh was entrusted above the others.

Yet anyone who believes that a sheep’s offspring exists in heaven
is foolish and does not understand John.

It would truly be ridiculous if you grasped the words
of the holy prophet with the understanding and tender heart of a child.

Has God prepared the heavenly kingdoms and everlasting glory
for birds, cattle, and wild beasts?

Among living beings endowed with reason alone,
these attain the heavenly dwelling and receive this rest.

The vision sent frogs down from heaven to Peter;
do you therefore count these among the inhabitants of heaven?

There is a reason why he represented himself as a lamb,
although he himself did not become a sheep made of wool.

It was the prophet’s right to see a symbolic form;
that is appropriate to figurative language.

If glory of such a kind is owed to a sheep because of its office,
and a worm will have the same glory because of its name,
then by the name of a serpent, and often by the name of a lion,
we likewise signify him—yet he is neither of these.

But linen is not without a devout reverence for the divine:
a true reality produces it, not an ancient shadow.

Since such great mysteries have been reported concerning our subject,
I wish briefly to recall them,
except insofar as they transcend us.

Meanwhile, O Christ, suggest to the heart or lips
of the one who is wise what he should say, and what this also signifies.

The true sacrifice to God the Father was God’s Son;
on the tree he restored to him what had perished through the tree.

He directed before the Creator a pleasing fragrance,
the smoke freely offered by such a victim.

Christ was the sacrifice, yet Christ himself performed the offering;
it was wrought by the Lord: hearts are astonished at these names.

Offered once, he paid every offense,
whether drawn upon a person by his own fault or by the fault of his race.

This death, having outwitted the deceived enemy,
does not cease to outwit him, daily carrying away spoils.

That power now often causes souls,
absorbed by countless deaths, to rise again.

Grace has now wiped away these sins,
as though they belonged to the past,
among the peoples of the Church not yet born.

This faith frees all the elect:
those whom the world first possessed and those whom it will possess at the end.

That blood, poured out once for the purposes of redemption,
is poured out again and again in the holy Church.

What the wicked nation did then under the guidance of unbelief
has been transformed for the better through the work of devotion.

This cup distributes the gifts of that liquid
which was poured out by the lance that pierced him.

By the same saving act by which he concealed the whole God in a body,
he now conceals this sacrament from human eyes.

Human beings would recoil from flesh with raw blood
and would refuse to consume the flesh of their kindred.

Yet believe profoundly that, with the order of things changed from its origin,
these elements have become new creatures.

If this were not something else, no one would consume it—
neither the evil person for punishment nor the good person for pardon.

It would not nourish souls if it were merely bodily bread,
nor would it wipe evil from the repentant mind.

It would not give strength to a human being,
nor take strength from the enemy,
nor subject the flesh to the commands of the mind.

O how secure, how freed from the law of the flesh,
how unlike themselves are human beings at this feast!

This food carries intoxicated hearts toward heavenly things
by a devout desire, if it is consumed as it ought to be.

Why are you surprised, human being?
God is present in a true body;
from the source by which he first redeems,
from that same source he now nourishes.

Yet in these words the wisdom of the flesh laughs
and wishes to subject divine things to its own rules [sic].

They say: “What reason is there? What order is discerned in these things?”

They are unwilling (or, perhaps, willing) to silence the laws of God with their mouths,
and while they touch the mountain which they cannot climb beyond:

[lacuna]

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 1054. SAINT LEO IX, ROMAN PONTIFF

## PROLEGOMENA

## THE LIFE OF SAINT LEO, BY WIBERTUS, HIS CONTEMPORARY

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, Sixth Century, Part II, p. 49.)*

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

### 1

Besides the authors who wrote the deeds of the supreme pontiffs, several also published separate Lives of blessed Leo IX.

Wibertus, his archdeacon in the bishopric of Toul, first published a single book concerning what Leo had done before he was elevated to the apostolic see, leaving it to the Romans—as he himself says in the prologue—to transmit to posterity what the Roman pope had accomplished.

Later, however, he changed his mind and added a second book to the first, in which he explains at greater length what the blessed man accomplished until his death.

An anonymous author, himself an eyewitness, composed an account of that same death. In it he relates accurately and in detail how the blessed pontiff, when near death, prepared himself throughout the entire three-day period to meet it; he then adds several miracles said to have occurred immediately after his death.

Ferdinand Ughellus published this account from a very ancient manuscript of the Beneventan Church, written in Lombard script, in *Italia sacra*, volume VIII, where he discusses the bishops of Benevento.

Moreover, in a manuscript of the archmonastery of Saint Remigius at Reims, we found a collection by another anonymous author of miracles appended to the Life of the blessed pontiff written by Wibertus. It relates numerous miracles performed at his tomb shortly after his death.

Godefridus Henschenius stitched together the works of these two anonymous authors, along with other miracles copied from various manuscripts, into a single collection, and published them on April 19 in the Bollandists’ volume, together with the Life written by Wibertus.

In addition, Bruno, bishop of Segni, composed a Life of blessed Leo, which was printed among Bruno’s other works.

To omit the many authors who, when occasion arose, wrote about some of the deeds of this holy man, Anselmus, a monk of Saint Remigius at Reims, published a little book under the title *The Itinerary of Pope Leo IX*. In it he reports what the blessed pontiff accomplished in various places in Germany and Gaul in 1049, especially at Reims, where he dedicated the church of the archmonastery of Saint Remigius and held a general council there.

Finally, Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, who later became supreme pontiff under the name Victor III, related several deeds and miracles of this same holy man in Book III of his *Dialogues*.

Of all these authors, however, it seemed sufficient for us to publish here Wibertus’s two books, together with the anonymous work which we have just mentioned from Ughellus’s *Italia sacra*.

Those who desire the rest should consult Bollandus for April 19. Nevertheless, if anything worthy of notice should occur in other authors that could help illuminate the acts of the blessed pontiff, we shall not fail to report it when appropriate, either in notes to the text of the Life or in these preliminary observations.

### 2

The great care with which the blessed pontiff governed the Church entrusted to him by God is demonstrated, besides the treatise he composed against the Greeks—which Wibertus praises—by the many letters he wrote to various bishops of the Christian world.

Some of these were addressed to the Africans, to support the condition of that once-famous Church, which groaned under the tyranny of the barbarians.

Others were sent to the Gauls, Germans, and Italians for the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline.

Several were addressed to the patriarch of Antioch, to confirm him in obedience to the apostolic see.

Others went to the emperor Constantine Monomachus, in order to strengthen his mind in the true faith.

Finally, to omit the other letters he issued as circumstances required in response to various pressing affairs, he wrote more than once to Michael Cerularius, patriarch of Constantinople, exhorting him to promote peace between the Greeks and Latins.

When Michael refused to cease the calumnies he spewed against the Roman Church, Leo ultimately expelled him from his see through his legates, whom he sent to Constantinople for that purpose. The emperor wished Leo’s sentence to be carried out and ordered Michael himself to be deported into exile.

The most devout pontiff labored no less to eradicate simoniacal priests and priests living with wives.

On this occasion he issued a celebrated decree praised by Peter Damian in a letter to Cunibertus, bishop of Turin, included as Book XVIII of the new edition of his works. It provided that any condemned women found within the walls of Rome prostituted to priests should thereafter and henceforth be assigned as slaves to the Lateran palace.

Both vices were treated in many councils under Leo and his successors, as can be seen in collections of the councils, where the letters of the blessed pontiff that we have just mentioned are also published.

### 3

Blessed Leo removed from ecclesiastical communion Berengarius, archdeacon of Angers, who rose up against the real presence of the body of Christ the Lord in the Eucharist.

These controversies provided the occasion for convening and publishing various synods and formulas of confession of faith, by which the integrity of the Catholic faith might be preserved intact; but we shall discuss these elsewhere.

Here it is enough to observe how great was the vigilance of our pontiff both in matters concerning the establishment of ecclesiastical discipline and in those concerning the defense of the true faith.

It is therefore not surprising that Victor III asserted in Leo’s praise that he had renewed all ecclesiastical institutions, and that, from the moment he assumed the pontificate, the world seemed to see a new light arise.

Yet the testimony of so great a pontiff is too illustrious for us not to reproduce it here in full. These, then, are Victor’s words, which he places before certain miracles performed by blessed Leo in Book III of the *Dialogues*:

> “Leo, of whom we are now speaking, was in every respect an apostolic man, born of royal stock, endowed with wisdom, distinguished by religion, and thoroughly instructed in all ecclesiastical learning. As it is written, he began to invoke the name of the Lord. I also saw him and was privileged to enjoy his friendship; often, when he celebrated Mass in church, I stood with him at the divine altar dressed in sacred vestments, and read the Gospel to him.
>
> “Through him all ecclesiastical studies were renewed and restored, and a new light seemed to arise for the world. Often summoning a priestly council, he removed priests, deacons, and other clergy who had not been regularly ordained, and appointed in their places men able to minister worthily for the worship of the true and supreme God.
>
> “Daily, through himself and his disciples sent everywhere, he showed the peoples the way of the Lord, preaching it in writing and speech. Always walking by an apostolic life, he also imitated the apostolic men in miracles. I had the opportunity to hear many more things about him,” and so forth.

In these few words Victor completes the summary of his praise of blessed Leo, who is likewise said to have illumined all Gaul in the testament of Odalricus, provost of the Church of Reims.

There Leo is remembered as having spoken at the council of Reims against the corrupt morals of ecclesiastics with such force of eloquence that many, terrified by his words, considered abandoning even benefices they had obtained lawfully.

Odalricus, who had attended that council, acknowledges that he was among them.

Leo of Marsica, in Book II, chapter 88 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, testifies that, as long as the blessed pontiff remained in Rome, he customarily went three nights each week from the Lateran church to Saint Peter’s, in private clothing and barefoot, accompanied by two or three clerics, singing psalms and praying.

Peter Damian relates in Booklet 47, chapters 3 and 4, the story of a certain holy woman, blessed Leo’s aunt, who drove away the devil by the sign of the cross. He states that he heard the story from Adelaide the empress, who had heard it from the mouth of blessed Pope Leo IX.

But enough of this.

### 4

Some doubt whether blessed Leo ever made a monastic profession. Certainly, besides Benedictine writers, many outsiders also assign him to our order. Trithemius explicitly affirms the same in the *Hirsau Chronicle* under the year 1048, where he writes:

> “Bruno, bishop of Toul … was the son of the count of Egisheim, and a monk of our order.”

The Bollandists, however, who say in their preliminary observation that they wish so great a pontiff could be counted among the students of the Benedictine Order, later state in their notes to chapter 5 of the Life written by Wibertus that, in their view, Wibertus’s words can easily be understood to show that Leo should by no means be assigned to the Benedictines, since Wibertus says:

> “Moreover, those who read what follows will surely cease to wonder that he was restored to health through Saint Benedict rather than through any other saint, once, as the wheel of the narrative turns, they can perceive from a few words how greatly he burned with zeal of devoted love for the instruction and correction of monks.”

Yet these words are not opposed to a monastic profession, which could very well have combined with that holy pontiff’s devotion to monastic affairs.

Certainly, most of the blessed pontiff’s deeds favor our position.

For scarcely ever did he lodge outside our monasteries during his journeys, which he undertook frequently. When he stayed in monasteries, especially the principal ones, he attended the chapter and ate in the refectory with the other monks.

Thus, after the dedication of the basilica of the archmonastery of Saint Remigius at Reims and the dissolution of the council, he came to the chapter, asked the brothers for fellowship, and received it.

At Monte Cassino, on a Saturday, he came at the brothers’ command and washed the feet of twelve monks; they in turn washed his. Afterwards he also entered the refectory and shared a common meal with the others, as Leo relates in Book II, chapter 85 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*.

I omit the monks of our order whom he brought out of monasteries for embassies and other more important affairs, or whom he raised to episcopal sees.

Finally, when he was near death, he summoned Richerius, abbot of Monte Cassino, so that, on returning to Rome, he might have him as his companion on the journey.

But why seek evidence of this matter elsewhere, when the blessed pontiff himself, near death, explicitly said that he had been a monk? “The cell,” he says, “in which I lived as a monk …,” according to the anonymous author in the account of his death, which we shall present after his Life, no. 4.

It is therefore not surprising that he said injuries inflicted upon monks had been inflicted upon himself, as he states in a letter to Stephen, lord of Châteauneuf, which he wrote while he was still bishop of Toul.

It is found in Perardus’s collection of Burgundian charters. In a charter there concerning the cell of Bertinacourt, he speaks as follows:

> “When divine clemency first raised me to the honor of the pontificate, I immediately began to aspire to the restoration of my Church and to the religious life of the monastic order: wherever it existed, to increase it; wherever it had perished, to recover it as far as I could.”

### 5

If we wish now to speak of the benefits with which the blessed pontiff enriched our monasteries, they were almost countless.

He permitted the abbot of Monte Cassino the use of sandals, the dalmatic, and gloves.

He subjected the Saxon monastery within the city of Rome to the Cassinese monks, confirmed the monastery of Terracina to them, granted them a free ship in the Roman harbor, and provided many other benefits in their favor, which are related by Leo of Marsica in Book II.

He restored the monastery of Subiaco, which had been almost destroyed by an invader, to its former condition.

In Gaul he confirmed the privileges of Corbie, Saint Remigius of Reims, Cluny, Saint Arnulf of Metz, La Chaise-Dieu, and other monasteries, and defended their possessions.

He carefully restored the monasteries of his own diocese to the practice of the Rule of Saint Benedict, with the assistance of blessed Abbot William, then famous.

There is scarcely a province in the Christian world in which he did not dedicate a church of our order and fortify it with privileges.

At the monastery of Hirsau, which had lain destroyed for forty-eight years, he ordered monks to be restored under threat of anathema, as Trithemius explains at greater length in the chronicle of that place.

The Magdeburg chronicler also wrote about the same matter; we possess his manuscript. Under the year 1048 he likewise records, among other deeds of Leo, the raising from the tomb of the body of Saint Richardis the empress, in the convent of virgins at Andlau in Alsace, which she herself had founded.

The same pontiff released Edward, king of the English, from his vow to travel to Rome, provided that he donated the money he would have spent on the journey to some monastery, either one to be newly founded or one to be restored.

His letter on this matter is found in Spelmannus, volume I of the *Councils of England*, and in Labbeus, volume IX of the *General Councils*.

### 6

It is not surprising that the blessed pontiff was so favorably disposed toward our order, since he received this inclination from his parents almost as a hereditary right.

For they consecrated to God under the monastic habit not only their possessions but themselves as servants.

Wibertus states both facts explicitly in chapter 1, although he does not specify where this took place.

At the monastery of Altorf, which the same author says was founded by the parents of blessed Leo, there is an ancient oratory dedicated to Saint Gregory. In it those same parents of the blessed pontiff, the founders of the place, are said to be buried.

In the necrology which we saw there, the following entry appears under September 4:

> “The count Eberhard, who rests in the high choir; likewise the lady Bertha, countess, his wife; likewise Count Hugh, a monk of this place, who rests before the altar of Saint Gregory in the chapel; likewise Count Hugh, brother of the aforesaid Hugh, who rests in this monastery. These were the founders of the monastery.”

The monks of that place possess a bull, whose copy we saw, by which the blessed pontiff confirms all the goods donated to the monastery by his parents, on the condition that it continue under the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Concerning his mother Helvide, John of Bayon writes in the *History of the Monastery of Moyenmoutier* that, when war broke out between the emperor Henry and Theodoric, bishop of Metz, she fortified the castles belonging to her and withdrew to the monastery of Moyenmoutier.

There, while devoting herself to pious works, she uncovered the bodies of Saint Lazarus the king and his daughter Aza, which ninety-five years earlier had been hidden in the ruins of the basilica of Saint Peter because of the Pannonian people who had invaded Gaul.

The same author has more to say about Saint Leo, which we shall mention in its proper places when appropriate.

We owe our knowledge of this writer to the most reverend Father Lord Hyacinth Alliot, abbot of the monastery of Moyenmoutier in the congregation of Saint Vanne.

He not only sent us a copy of this author’s *History*, as well as every other ancient document and writing he was able to obtain in Lorraine, Alsace, and the neighboring monasteries of Germany, but also spares neither care nor labor, nor even expense, in assisting the elucidation of the acts of our saints and the composition of Benedictine annals.

From him we also learned some things about the monasteries which Wibertus says were built by the parents of blessed Leo.

Four in particular are listed: Hesse, Saint Cyriacus, Lure, and Woffenheim.

Richerius also mentions them in Book II, chapter 14 of the *Chronicle of Senones*, in these words:

> “In the year 1002,” he says, “the birth of blessed Bruno … whose parents built the monastery of Hesse for nuns near Sarrebourg. They also built another monastery called Altorf, of the Order of Saint Benedict, situated in Alsace; a third, called Lure; and a fourth for nuns, in honor of the holy cross, also in Alsace, called Woffenheim.
>
> “They endowed these monasteries with their own possessions so generously that their communities could be maintained in great abundance.”

The same author, in Book IV, chapter 21, omitting the monastery of Lure, writes that the other three were built and endowed by the father of Pope Leo.

The monastery of Lure had in fact been built almost four hundred years earlier by Saint Deicolus, at the beginning of the seventh century.

But the parents of the blessed pontiff, and his grandparents—as Wibertus puts it—may have contributed something toward its restoration at the end of the tenth century. At that time, as the author of the Life of Saint Deicolus reports, the monastery of Lure, which had been devastated, was restored by Count Hugh, later a monk, and his sons.

An imperial decree of Otto the Great survives concerning this matter, in favor of Baldramnus, who was appointed abbot there.

The monastery of Lure still exists today, commonly called Lure, in the diocese of Besançon. It has one abbot jointly with the monastery of Murbach, though that abbot enjoys two votes among the princes at imperial diets.

After the peace concluded between the Empire and France in 1697, however, all the territories situated on this side of the Rhine were to belong to the French dominion; thus both monasteries are now situated under French rule.

Hesse still retains its ancient name, commonly Hesse, about one league from Sarrebourg, a town of Lorraine at the foot of the Vosges Mountains.

This place was reduced to what is called a simple priory and united to the Cistercian abbey of Haute-Seille.

The monastery of Altorf, which Wibertus calls Saint Cyriacus, still exists and belongs to the Benedictine order. It lies not far from Molsheim, a notable city of Alsace.

Bucelinus discusses it in *Sacred Germany*.

Finally, the convent of Woffenheim, after various fortunes, was reduced to a cell and now lies almost completely ruined.

Only its ruins survive: the walls of its church and other buildings, still roofless, can be seen not far from the town of Egarsheim.

The convent for women at Woffenheim stood about one mile from it, and four or five miles from Colmar, the seat of the supreme senate of Alsace.

This is the very monastery of the handmaids of God, Saint Cross, whose advocacy was disputed by Hugh and Gerard, the nephews of blessed Leo, in the time of Gregory VII.

This is clear from Gregory’s fourteenth letter of Book II, addressed to Warner, bishop of Strasbourg, and Burchard, bishop of Basel. There the same pontiff testifies that this

> “monastery of Saint Cross, founded in the land of his inheritance by Pope Leo of blessed memory and built from his own resources, was transferred by him into the ownership of the holy Roman Church, over which he piously and holily presided.”

It was issued on October 19, in the thirteenth indiction.

Besides these foundations, Louis, the grandfather of the blessed pontiff, is said—if we believe John of Bayon—to have built a cell for the monks of the monastery of Maurmunster, in honor of Saint Quirinus, not far from the castle of Dagsburg.

That castle, they say, was the principal seat of Hugh, the father of blessed Leo.

There is also another nearby cell under the title of Saint Leo, whose ruins remain in the old castle. The castle, together with the county of Dagsburg itself, came into the possession of the counts of Leiningen, adherents of the Lutheran sect.

Richerius explains in Book IV, chapter 21 of the *Chronicle of Senones* how this county passed from the family of blessed Leo to outsiders.

That castle, once extremely strong, still retains its former name, Dasbourg, or, as the common people say, Dabo. Situated on a crag of the Vosges Mountains toward Alsace, to which it belongs, it was destroyed in 1678 by order of the king of France, together with the small town subject to it and the neighboring territory.

But let us return now to blessed Leo.

### 7

There seems to be no difficulty concerning the final year of Leo’s life. Everyone agrees that he went to heaven in 1054, except Wibertus alone, who assigned the following year.

The Bollandists believe that this entered Wibertus’s text through a copyist’s error. It is indeed plausible that the mistake arose because the election of Victor II, his successor, did not take place until nearly a full year after Leo’s death.

Nevertheless, this is how not only the printed editions but also two manuscript codices of the Remigian Library at Reims, which we consulted, read.

Whatever the case may be, we judge the agreement of all the other writers, including contemporaries, preferable to Wibertus’s single testimony.

Leo began to be venerated immediately after his death, not only in Rome, where his sacred body shone with daily miracles, but also at Benevento, where a church was built in his honor and his feast was celebrated.

Bruno gives the same testimony concerning his own church at Segni.

His name appears in the calendar of the manuscript breviary of the monastery of Monte Cassino, written under Abbot Oderisius, and in the first of the Capuan calendars recorded by the monk Michael in the *Sanctuary*.

We do not doubt that it appears similarly in other places, where, as in the Roman Martyrology, his feast is celebrated on April 19.

His feast is not commemorated only at Rome or in Italy; his memory is also celebrated in other regions, especially in the diocese of Toul, where it is observed with a double rite, and among our monks of Saint Remigius with a semidouble rite.

The same is done in the diocese of Basel, by order of John of Schönau, its bishop.

There is no doubt that the same is observed in various places in Gaul, Germany, and Belgium, which Leo visited during his lifetime and consecrated and fortified by his presence, his pontifical blessing, and various privileges.

Moreover, if he was enrolled among the citizens of heaven because of the holiness of his life, he also gained a place among ecclesiastical writers because of his learning.

Nothing concerning his works needs to be noted beyond what others have already observed.

Sigebertus, after listing his works, compares him with Gregory the Great because of the works he composed in honor of the saints, in chapter 149, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Aubertus Miraeus, in his notes on this passage of Sigebertus, adds that, besides his various letters—which are found in editions of the councils and in the *Annals* of Baronius—homilies and sermons of the same holy pontiff were published at Leuven in 1565 and at Cologne in 1618. Cardinal Bellarmine noted the same.

Finally, Wibertus demonstrates Leo’s extraordinary devotion to learning, presenting it almost as something marvelous, in Book II, chapter 14: although he was more than fifty years old, he pursued his studies with such zeal that he learned to read the divine Scriptures in the Greek language.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0465]

[Col. 0465C] When Bishop Herimann entered upon the way of all flesh [Note: [Col. 0465] Bishop Henimannus of Toul departed this life in the year 1026], the venerable Bruno succeeded him, a man wonderfully endowed by the Lord with the distinction of noble birth and the excellence of his character. Although he appears almost last in the catalogue of episcopal succession, he nevertheless shone forth first by the privilege of the supreme pontificate. Like Lucifer, last in the heavenly ranks but nearer to the sun, he emerged after a long succession of predecessors and, through his priesthood, illumined the city of Toul—indeed, the whole Christian world—and, dispelling the darkness of error, displayed the true Sun near him through the liveliness of his radiance.

He suffered no disadvantage from being born later, for he had been divinely appointed to a time fixed before the ages. For the immutable God, before whom all things done and to be done stand together, so orders the alternations of mutable things that, in the order of events, He perceives nothing as either too late or out of due sequence. Indeed, to say nothing meanwhile of other matters, the redemption most necessary to the human race was shown to have been presented at the end of the ages; and Paul, who labored more than all, was called from heaven after all the other apostles—hence he is also found to have called himself “an untimely birth.”

But, lest we linger here too long, let the pen return to its undertaking, so that what was not merely heard but witnessed concerning so great a prelate may be transcribed for the edification of many. His own kindness, indeed, deigned to allow my smallness to remain continually in his more intimate company. Through no merit of my own, this enabled me to recognize personally many things worthy of imitation in him; several others I learned from the reports of truthful and serious people. Some of these I touch upon only very briefly; others I knowingly pass over, lest I be either more verbose than is proper or be accused of a flatterer’s encomium—or, since he is still alive, lest I incur the rebuke of Solomon’s proverb: “Do not praise a man during his lifetime” (Ecclesiasticus 11:30).

And since our purpose is to praise in him the gifts of God that deserve praise in a human being, we do not praise the man, but Him by whom and through whom every person coming into this world is illumined, so that he may think, speak, or do what is good. Do we, then, claim that so great a prelate lived or lives in this wretched life—which is wholly a time of testing—without ever sinning, when not even an infant of a single day can do so? But those who take pains to proclaim, for the benefit of others, the divine virtues impressed upon some human being should not wish to expose the person’s sins, already covered by God, to his reproach.

This is why the Israelites, at God’s command, carried away from Egypt gold and silver fashioned into vessels, while they left behind everything made into idols. Accordingly, let our account now begin from his origin; and we shall consider ourselves to have succeeded greatly if, by whatever style, we transmit to posterity at least some of what he laudably accomplished in the episcopate of Toul. It will belong to the wise—and especially to the Romans—if they faithfully and gratefully transmit in the page of the Catholic Church what the Roman pope himself accomplished.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0467]

## I. Bruno’s parents and lineage

The reverend Bruno preserved the noble line of both his parents to such a degree that, from his great-grandfathers and earlier ancestors, insofar as any could come within our knowledge, some had held the reins of a kingdom or empire, while others had borne honors immediately next to those of kings and emperors.

He was born in the territory of beloved Alsace [Note: [Col. 0467D] A very well-known province on the banks of the Rhine, in which it is quite clear from what we have said in the preliminary observations that Bruno’s parents possessed many estates], to his father Hugh and his mother Heilewide. Their religious devotion was accustomed to open the mouths of many in praise of God. His father was a Teuton by nation, a cousin of Emperor Conrad [Note: [Col. 0467D] Hugh is called Conrad’s cousin because Adelais, Conrad’s mother, and Hugh, Bruno’s father, were descended from two brothers: Eberard, Adelais’s father, and Hugh, the grandfather of our Bruno. John Bayon calls his grandfather Louis, count of Dasporch; this cannot be understood of his paternal grandfather], and highly eloquent both in his native language and in Latin. His mother too was Latin and equally skilled in both languages.

Their fathers and grandfathers, from their earliest youth, had courageously subdued, beyond measure, those who resisted them by arms and spirit, defending themselves and their respective causes. But in old age, casting aside all pride of lineage and worldly luxury, they put on the humility and poverty of Christ: they gave their patrimonies to churches and built monasteries on their own estates and from their own resources. Thus, in the end, having perfectly followed Christ, they also denied themselves; setting aside altogether the foolish wisdom of the world, they submitted with complete contrition of heart to the wise foolishness of God and to the monastic habit, and finally departed with a laudable end in every respect.

Among the many gifts they distributed here and there to divine churches, they founded two monasteries from their own estates [Note: [Col. 0468D] We have discussed these monasteries at length in the preliminary observations]: Hissam, in honor of blessed Martin the bishop, and another monastery dedicated to the veneration of Saint Cyriacus the martyr. They also greatly enlarged the Lutrense monastery with their patrimonial goods.

Imitating their devotion, Count Hugh, a distinguished man, and his most devout wife—the parents, of course, of the aforesaid Lord Bruno—built a monastery suitable for a secluded life at Wofeinheim, near their noble castle called Eginiskeim [Note: [Col. 0468D] It is situated in Upper Alsace, not far from the city of Colmar. Furthermore, the blessed bishop had decreed that whoever among his descendants was the eldest and lived in this castle should hold the monastery’s advocacy, as we learn from Letter 14 of Book II of Pope Gregory VII], from the tithes of their estates. To this day a community of nuns remains there, for the veneration and glory of the nourishing and most victorious Cross.

## II. He is born in the year 1011

These two parents, finally, displayed such a great and honorable manner of life before everyone that even ecclesiastical persons holding various ranks, from bishops to laypeople, discovered in them something worthy of imitation. To say nothing now of their many forms of watchfulness toward God, they tested under the judgment of cold water whether they had rendered a full accounting of their possessions.

When Almighty God had decided to appoint from them a prelate for His Church, He deigned to reveal to the pregnant mother what sort and how great a child she was carrying in her womb. One night, a man in religious dress appeared to her in a vision and informed her that she had conceived a male child who would become great before God; he ordered that the child be named Bruno.

On the eleventh day before the Kalends of July—that is, 21 June—in the year 1002 from the incarnation of the Word of God, in the fifteenth indiction, when he was brought forth into this light, his entire little body was found, astonishingly, to be marked (*charaxatum*) [MS 1: “carved”], as though with the stigmata of little crosses. His mother, shaken by the novelty of this event and made more certain by the promise of the earlier vision, departed from her custom and allowed no one but herself to sustain him with the nourishment of milk.

When he had been weaned at the proper time, she entrusted him, at the age of five, to Bertold, bishop of the holy Church of Toul, to be liberally educated and instructed in literary studies. This Bertold, an extraordinary follower of innate goodness, ennobled the city of Toul beyond his predecessors by making it illustrious with the sons of nobles; greatly increased its treasures and dignity in various forms; adorned it with very many buildings; filled it with persons devoted to literary study; and restored the discipline of monasteries both within and without.

## III. His education. The encomium of Adalbero, bishop of Metz

This suitable man therefore gladly received the child, had him instructed in letters, and trained him in every form of honorable conduct appropriate to free-born boys. As his body grew day by day, so too grew the noble disposition of his mind, which commended him to everyone above his other companions. For, as the most learned Father Jerome testifies:

> “Soft wax, easy to shape, was formed by a certain natural pliability divinely bestowed; even if the hand of the external craftsman were to cease.”

Thus, with heavenly grace going before and following after, he drew everyone’s goodwill to himself, because they saw in him no arrogance arising from royal descent, wealth, beauty, or excellence of intellect—the qualities through which worldly people commonly swell beyond measure and soon deflate.

He was affable toward everyone, even the lowliest; cheerful both in appearance and in speech; and most obedient not only to his elders and equals, but also to those younger than himself. His companions, although they were somewhat older than he, included two of his kinsmen named Adalbero. The first of these was taken from this world by a premature death, the son of Duke Theodoric [Note: [Col. 0469D] Adalbero, son of Frederick, ascended the see of Metz in 1047 and died in 1072]. The other, the brother of Duke Hezilo and son of the eminent prince Frederick, was appointed under the schoolmaster as master of his little nephew Bruno, because at that time he was considered learned.

Later, chosen to the episcopate of the city of Metz by the will of clergy and people more than by his own, this man shone forth in his age as one especially worthy of praise. From his earliest years, eager to please God alone, he attempted to crucify his flesh with its vices beyond what his age and health permitted. He burned so fervently with the fire of divinity that, from the very beginnings of his Christian training, he was thought to be most perfect.

To say nothing for the present of his abundant chastity, his dove-like innocence, his serpent-like prudence, his disciplined severity, and his mature gravity in a tender character, he afflicted himself with fasts and vigils to such a degree that the words of blessed Job may be applied even in their historical sense:

> “My bone clung to my skin, my flesh having been consumed” (Job 19:20).

## IV. Bruno devotes himself to study together with him

Closely joined, then, by an inseparable affection to such a companion, the distinguished boy Bruno applied himself to the school of letters, and the two rejoiced together in their liberal education. Although noble groups of boys also attended them, these two surpassed all their companions both in capacity for the liberal studies and in excellence of character.

As is first appropriate for beginners, once they had completed the trivium of the arts, they became distinguished not only in prose and verse, but also skillfully resolved—or diligently dispelled—legal controversies grasped with a sharp and lively eye of the mind. Finally, by following the quadrivium with natural ability, they gained a taste of it and proved quite capable in it as well, as what follows will indicate in part.

While the boys mentioned above were thus being educated together, Bruno’s mother was informed in a dream of her son’s future advancement. She seemed to see herself entering, from the side of the episcopal chamber, the venerable basilica of the most blessed protomartyr Stephen [Note: [Col. 0469D] The cathedral church of Toul, dedicated to Saint Stephen]. The bishop Gerard, of holy memory and glorified by miracles in life and after death, met her, and, removing from his own neck the orarium—commonly called a stole—he placed it upon her sleeve.

This, as may be inferred, foretold that her son would be appointed from heaven not so much as the successor to Gerard’s see as the successor to his good way of life. For although the reverend Bruno is reckoned the fifth after Lord Gerard [Note: [Col. 0470D] We discussed him in the appendix to the preceding century], he appears to have been chosen by Gerard alone, and not by any of his successors, because, with God’s favor, he imitated Gerard more than they did.

But because the pious dispensation of Almighty God customarily mingles scourges and temptations with His gifts—as we know happened to blessed Job, the apostle Paul, and nearly all the elect—it seems necessary to relate how Bruno was endangered at the beginning of his adolescence and, when heavenly medicine soon came, was saved.

## V. He is wounded by a toad; after suffering severely, he is healed by Saint Benedict

Once he had gained a neck somewhat freer than usual from the schoolboy’s yoke, he often visited his parents’ residence, delighted not only by natural affection but also by their religious way of life and by the very free arrangement of his household among soldiers and servants.

One summer, while he was staying with them as usual at the noble castle called Eginisheim, he fell asleep on a certain Saturday night in a most pleasant chamber. The poisonous frog called a toad, or *rubeta*, climbed onto the right side of his face. It fastened one of its forefeet to his cheek, the other beneath his lip, one of its hind feet behind his ear, and the other beneath his chin, and began to suck and constrict him savagely.

Awakened by the pain, he discovered the horrible animal resting upon his face as a deadly burden. Stunned by so great and unfamiliar a danger, he quickly tore himself from the bed. Unable to endure the excessive torment, he struck the poisonous creature behind his ear with a blow of his palm and knocked it back onto the same bed, fearing that, if he tried to seize and remove it by hand from the middle of his face, it would burrow in more deeply.

Then the wicked creature, although its fall upon the bed produced a crushing sound, nevertheless did not delay, before his very eyes, to climb back onto the pillow at the head of the bed, for the entire interior of the chamber was then illuminated by moonlight. Immediately a crowd of servants, summoned by the sudden cry of their beloved master, came running and brought a lamp with them; but, when they entered, the pestilential animal had disappeared without a trace.

The servants searched everywhere with the greatest care, but although all the furnishings of the chamber were overturned and examined, it was not found at all. Whether the creature was real or imaginary, however, it left behind real wounds and real pain.

As a result, his entire face, throat, and chest became swollen, and he was so weakened that recovery of health seemed almost hopeless. For two full months both his parents [Col. 0470D] and all their household were miserably overwhelmed by this calamity. They expected only his funeral to be carried out, and awaited that mournful procession of burial with continual sighs and tears.

But the merciful Jesus, accustomed to come to the aid of desperate circumstances, suddenly consoled his parents with his complete recovery and remembered, according to His purpose, the restoration of His Church through him. For when he had been unable to rise from his bed unaided for two months, and, as the severity of his illness increased, had remained without speech for eight days, he finally opened his eyes one day and, lying on his back as he was, saw while awake what seemed to be a luminous ladder rising by itself from his very bed. Passing the window at his feet, it extended all the way to heaven.

Down this ladder descended an old man of extraordinary radiance and venerable whiteness of hair, dressed in monastic habit; in his right hand he carried a conspicuous cross on a long staff. When he reached the sick man, he held the ladder with his left hand, while with his right he first applied the cross to Bruno’s mouth, then marked the places of the swelling with it, and drew out from behind his ear the cooked and putrefied mass of all the poison. Immediately he returned by the way he had come, leaving the sick man feeling better.

At once Bruno spoke to his cleric Adalbero, who alone at that time was sitting beside his bed, and through him the long-standing cries throughout his father’s house were stilled by the desired news. Several days later, after the entire poison had been expelled through the ruptured skin of the pustule behind his right ear, he emerged healthy and unharmed, to the greatest astonishment and joy of everyone.

As he is accustomed to recount to his closest companions in admonitory conversations even to this day the unmistakable mercy of God recognized in his own case, he declares that during the aforesaid ecstasy he immediately recognized, as clearly as daylight, the most blessed Father of monks, Benedict, by the character of his face and dress. He recalls that figure’s bodily appearance as though he still had it before the eyes of his flesh.

Those who read what follows will certainly cease to wonder that he was restored to health through Saint Benedict rather than through any other saint, when, as the wheel of the narrative turns, they are able to perceive from a few details how intensely he burned with zealous love for the formation and correction of monks.

## VI. He obeys Herimann, bishop of Toul. He sympathizes with the afflicted monks of Saint Aper. He lives at the emperor’s court. He decides to prefer a poorer bishopric to richer ones

When Lord Bertold, his educator, died, Bruno did not refuse to obey his successor Herimann as well, as though he constantly had before the eyes of his mind the saying of blessed Pope Gregory:

> “Let no one dare to be first who has not learned to be subject, lest he command obedience from those beneath him which he has not known how to render to those above him.”

At that time he sympathized with those suffering adversity, especially the monks of the venerable monastery of the venerable man Aper, against whom the shameless tongues of flatterers and envious people were excessively provoking the mind of the aforesaid bishop. Sometimes Bruno set himself as a wall before them, as far as he could; sometimes, when they wept, he did the only thing he could do—he wept with them.

Through his authority and diligence, the canonical discipline and provision within the enclosure of the most blessed deacon and protomartyr Stephen remained completely intact under Herimann, in the condition in which he had received it from capable earlier bishops.

But since “everything has its time,” according to the dispensation of the Timeless Creator of time, who leads His own to their destiny through certain others, it happened that the distinguished young man was assigned by his parents and relatives to his kinsman, the glorious Emperor Conrad, to be educated at his court and to serve in the basilica.

Before many days had passed there, he gained perfectly the goodwill of all the courtiers, since the herald of his character and prudence, and the distinction of his lineage and appearance, made him agreeable. Since several other Brunos were also called by that name there, he alone deserved to be called “Good Bruno.”

By increasing this distinction day by day, he claimed it for himself without arousing the envy of his companions: he adapted himself to his juniors through a certain reasonable condescension, and in every respect suited himself to his elders with generous dignity.

Moreover, he was loved by the Emperor and Empress with such unique and familial affection that he was gladly admitted even to their most secret counsels. His opinion was reverently and graciously awaited and, once expressed, was accepted without hesitation.

Since they deliberated daily and continually sought to raise him to the greatest possible honor—or, to speak plainly, to bestow upon him a bishopric made exceedingly wealthy with temporal resources—he, already warned by the irreproachable and golden style of the lord Gregory, began to regard this with grave suspicion. He feared that it might be charged against him by God, as though a gift had drawn him away from the service from which no bodily fatigue and no destruction of personal property could recall certain of his associates, because of the hope of a little advancement.

Thus, since he could neither leave the Emperor’s side nor willingly serve in such a manner, he resolved in his heart, with God alone as witness and knower, that if, with God’s good pleasure, he were invited to govern even the poorest Church, he would approach that office more eagerly than if royal majesty, through some carnal affection, drove him toward the dignity and wealth of the highest power.

This is all the more remarkable in the lightness of youth, since it is rarely found even in the gravity of old age. But it now seems necessary to say how this man, eager to be humbled for God, was gradually and wonderfully exalted by Him, as the prophet testifies in the Book of Kings:

> “Those who honor me I will honor; but those who despise me shall be held of no account” (1 Samuel 2:30).

## VII. He leads soldiers into Lombardy
