In the twenty-third year of his life, when he had entered the second week of adolescence, and when the year 1025 from the incarnation of the incarnate Word of God the Father was passing, the distinguished Bruno went to Lombardy—and especially against Milan, then in rebellion—on behalf of his bishop Herimann, in the expedition of the aforesaid Emperor Conrad, bearing the insignia of the diaconate.

For his bishop, weighed down by years and illness, had entrusted to Bruno, with the approval both of the bishop and of the Emperor, the auxiliary troops coming from Toul, to lead and arrange them, while preserving in every respect the sacramental character proper to his rank.

In the organization of that secular military force, he suddenly appeared so shrewd and provident that one would have thought he had previously been trained exclusively in such affairs. He measured out camps for his men, arranged stations and watches, and administered supplies and pay at suitable places and times. He distributed sober but sufficient prepared meals to each of his men. He took care to assign them to offices appropriate to each one, so that both nobles and common soldiers had to concern themselves only with their own duties.

His vigilance was protection to his own men, ruin to the enemy, and worthy praise to himself. Thus, by rendering “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s,” in accordance with the command of his apostle that “every soul must be subject to the higher powers, since there is no power except from Him,” he deserved to pass swiftly through another’s office to his own.

And because he had served faithfully and wisely in outward matters, he was fully rewarded in inward things, so that, set over many, he might cling more loftily to his Creator and show deeper compassion toward his neighbor.

## VIII. He becomes bishop of Toul

Finally, as the year 1026 from the humanity of the Son of God approached, Bishop Herimann of Toul was taken from the dwelling of the flesh while staying at Cologne during Lent on one of his estates.

At once, deprived of their protector, the clergy and people, united in concordant vote and common judgment, demanded with unanimous and repeated voices Bruno, whom they had long desired and loved. Impatient of any further delay, they sent the Emperor letters of entreaty and protest concerning this entirely unanimous election.

In brief, their argument was as follows. After offering the reverence due in an opening salutation, they set forth the deeply lamentable tragedy of their misfortune. They said that they were attacked and disturbed on every side by almost daily plundering and conflicts, since they were situated at the boundaries of three kingdoms—namely, at the borders of the Emperor’s realm—where they suffered more fiercely from enemies because greater stretches of land kept them at a distance from his presence.

Furthermore, their city was continually claimed by the kings of the Franks through many and varied schemes. If the Emperor would deign to prevent this loss to the commonwealth, this distress to himself, and this affliction of his people, he should designate for them a pastor of the greatest nobility and wisdom, whose vigor and diligence could drive back the fury of their hostile enemies.

He would not have to search far for such a man, since Bruno, chosen by the unanimous agreement of clergy and people, was his kinsman and held in the affection of God and good men. They knew him very well, since he was their own fosterling, educated among them and by them in the knowledge of the liberal arts, living among them without complaint, and regularly advanced through each ecclesiastical grade to the order of the diaconate.

Not only the townspeople with their suburbs, but all the neighboring peoples and the bishops of the surrounding province, desired him. Therefore, either he should grant them this man with God’s good pleasure, or no one at all, since they had at hand the decree of blessed Pope Celestine (Letter 2):

> “Let each person receive the fruit of his service in the Church in which he has passed his life through every office. Let him not intrude upon another’s stipend, nor dare to claim for himself the reward owed to another. Let clergy have the freedom to resist if they see themselves being overburdened; and, when they recognize that something is being thrust upon them from the side, let them not be afraid to reject it. If they are not to receive the reward they deserve, they should at least have the freedom to judge the one who is to rule them.”

And they had the celebrated saying of Lord Leo, the distinguished teacher:

> “Let no one be ordained against the will and without the request of the people, lest a city either despise or hate a bishop it did not desire, and become less religious than it ought because it was not permitted to have what it wanted.”

Even if earthly power could inflict violence upon them contrary to such evident and canonical authority, it could never succeed in turning their goodwill away from this man whom they had chosen.

Finally, then, the Emperor’s serenity would be moved by their unanimous and heartfelt prayer, and in this matter the welfare of God’s Church would receive greater consideration than the worldly concern by which his kinship was striving to exalt him still more highly.

Meanwhile, special letters were also sent to Lord Bruno. The clergy, abbots, all the religious communities, and the entire people of the diocese of Toul sought in them to plead their desire and cause in these terms: having been deprived of their shepherd, they had unanimously chosen him alone for themselves, and, for fear and love of the Almighty, they demanded him from the Emperor. They begged that Bruno should not disturb them in this matter under any circumstances and should not recoil from their poverty, of which he had long been well aware.

They adjured him by Him who, although rich, became poor for us. He should not regard it as an insult, or as any arrogance—an arrogance they had not yet detected in him—that people so lowly and insignificant preferred for themselves a person of such renown and nobility, and begrudged him to cities greater and more suited to his merits. They did this for the sake of Him who humbled Himself for us even unto death.

They should be permitted to enjoy the fruit of their labor and, in return, to be nourished by the one whom they had nourished, because, according to the Apostle, “the laboring farmer ought first to partake of his fruits” (1 Corinthians 9:10). It would be fitting, therefore, that the Church which had deserved to educate such a man should also deserve to have such a man as its pastor after being deprived of one. He could even say, in accordance with the measure of that special good divinely granted to mortals:

> “I know my own, and my own know me” (John 10:14).

They were not unaware that the piety of the earthly prince intended to promote him to greater things, on account of their kinship and the agreeable companionship he had enjoyed with him. Therefore, if the Emperor thought that the people crying out behind him ought to be heard, they would thereafter knock continually at the generosity of the heavenly Emperor in prayer, so that He might heap heavenly and earthly honor upon Bruno.

But if the Emperor thought them worthy of contempt because Bruno was worldly-mindedly yearning for the summit of a more eminent dignity, divine justice, the avenger of their contempt, would intervene in such a way that Bruno would never ascend either to the honor he sought or to any other.

## IX. The Emperor resists the election because of the bishopric’s poverty. Bruno obtains his consent

After Lord Notbert—then a monk of praiseworthy life, formerly a canon of the holy protomartyr Stephen—and Liethard, still a canon, had received letters of this sort, they were designated by the clergy and people as the energetic and tireless executors of so great and important a cause. Both the Emperor and Lord Bruno, who was especially dear to him, were consequently affected by a great and varied tumult of cares.

The Emperor was glad that the affection he possessed for the venerable Bruno—genuine and brotherly, founded both upon their kinship and upon his recognition of Bruno’s energy—was commended and confirmed by the praise and testimony of many. Nevertheless, he was greatly saddened because he felt that his desire to raise Bruno to a higher temporal dignity was being thwarted.

He feared offending God if he resisted the unanimous vote of His Church; he grieved if he failed to reward so eminent a person according to his merits. Why linger over the details? Caught in this great wavering of mind, he tried through envoys sent from his side to turn the aforesaid Lord Bruno away from his intention by every device: at one moment recalling the frequent conflicts and devastations of that Church and exaggerating its poverty beyond measure; at another pointing out that, situated at the farthest borders of his empire, the city was judged worthy of an imperial lodging either never or only very rarely; and at another saying that he could not bear, with equanimity, to be separated by so great a distance from this nephew of his, so dear to him in every respect.

Bruno should spare himself, then, and look after his own advantage and peace as much as after the will and distress of the Emperor, who loved him from the depths of his heart. Rather, he should turn a deaf ear to those who valued their own need or consolation more highly than his welfare and honor—especially since the Emperor had earnestly planned for him a dignity worthy of his lineage and merit.

But “there are many plans in a man’s heart, but the Lord’s purpose will stand,” as Solomon says (Proverbs 19:21). The letters sent to the reverend Bruno by the people of the Church affected his submissive heart quite differently. Through their unanimous and humble invitation, he felt himself being invited to humility by the very teacher of humility, who refused to become king of men and willingly went to the cross. [Note: [Col. 0475] From the following words, taken from chapter 7 of the Benedictine Rule, Saint Leo’s monastic profession appears to be indicated.]

Nor was he forgetful of his earlier resolve, by which he preferred to serve Christ continually in complete humility, lowliness, and extremity rather than to be raised temporally, with some corruption of an untainted conscience—that is, by any form of venality. From the words of blessed Gregory he had learned that venality was threefold: through money, through service, and through favor.

Recognizing that ecclesiastical dignities were gravely confused and undermined by these three attendants of ambitious venality, and that it was not easy to find anyone free from one or another of them, he believed that nothing would be safer for him than to assent to the popular election drawing him toward humility or adversity, and to resist the imperial urging that drove him toward greatness or prosperity.

It is indeed praiseworthy for anyone to reject prosperity for God’s sake; but it is much more praiseworthy voluntarily to offer oneself to adversity. Thus Moses, called by God to leadership, excused himself and asked that another be sent in his place, saying:

> “I beg you, Lord, send whom you will send” (Exodus 4:13).

Isaiah, although not specifically designated, thrust himself forward willingly for the shame of nakedness and manifold suffering, crying:

> “Here am I; send me” (Isaiah 6:8).

Inflamed, then, by these and other incentives to virtue, and filled with the oil of divine grace, Bruno scattered the flame of his upright intention all the more eagerly the more fiercely he was driven by the blasts of carnal affection. The dissuasive breeze coming from Caesar and his court had the effect of increasing and nurturing, rather than calming or extinguishing, the fire of the divine sacrifice upon the altar of his devoted mind.

Accordingly, he gladly embraced the saying of blessed Peter:

> “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that He may exalt you at the time of His visitation” (1 Peter 5:6).

Breaking every bond of delay, he presented to the still-dissuading Emperor the letters sent to him by the clergy and people, his naturally—and, so to speak, virginally—modest face suffused with blushes. When the illustrious prince had been informed of the contents of the letters, he was moved to tears; and, by his abundant weeping, he openly revealed outwardly how highly he esteemed Bruno inwardly.

At last, after a brief silence, he released his tongue in these words:

> “My decision concerning your honor, my sweetest nephew, long deliberated, I see being opposed—indeed, overcome—by a heavenly decision. I am compelled to support it by yielding, as I ought, since I cannot continue to resist without harm to both of us and to many others. May the piety of the Almighty now assist you in this matter; He knows better what is expedient for both of us and for everyone.
>
> “I now willingly accept what cannot be avoided. You, however, content with the grace of God, by which alone you are believed to have been chosen to govern that Church and by no form of venality, must not win the affection of either my wife or any other mortal to your side. Otherwise, from you, the blemish of this simoniacal plague may spread among all the sheep entrusted to you.
>
> “Without doubt, He who began the good work in you will soon bring it to completion. Cast your thoughts upon His free generosity, and He Himself will nourish you, according to the truthful promise of His divine declaration.
>
> “As for the comfort of our counsel and assistance, whatever its extent, do not in any way doubt it. For, above all those of your order, I shall always be concerned for the success of your affairs. You are commended to us both by your tireless labor in faithful service to us and by the mutual affection of ancestral kinship.
>
> “Only strive to serve the Almighty faithfully, and endeavor to increase the noble character of good conduct that has been in you from the cradle.”

Strengthened by these and other words of royal sweetness, the venerable Bruno willingly submitted himself to the burdensome charge, trusting in the Lord alone, for he knew that he was not being called to the joys of prosperity but to endure the perils of arduous labors.

## X. He departs from Italy and escapes the ambushes of the Lombards

Having therefore obtained [Col. 0477A] the gift of the papal dignity, he left behind no small number of members of the imperial court in sorrow. They had always relied upon his salutary counsels, and he had diligently advanced their causes as an energetic advocate. Although they congratulated him on the honor bestowed upon him, they nonetheless grieved that they were deprived of the exceedingly sweet comfort of his companionship and conversation.

After receiving permission from the imperial authority to depart, new reports of adversity were brought to him as he was preparing for the journey: namely, that unless he took precautions, he would suffer an ambush at the hands of the Lombards of Patria, who at that time were still rebelling against the emperor with proud hearts. For in those days the royal army was attacking Orba, [Note: [Col. 0477D] Bollandus thinks that Ortam should be read, since a town of that name exists in that region beside the lake also called Orta.] a town of the Milanese, because treacherous men were hiding there—apostates who, in their faithlessness, refused submission to the emperor. His friends therefore warned him to avoid their ambush by taking a detour, asserting that it would be more advantageous to choose any other route, however much longer, than to fall heedlessly into their hands for the sake of shortening the journey.

But he, free from fear, in accordance with the saying of Solomon, “The just man is confident as a lion and will be without terror” (Proverbs 28:1), “fortified beforehand with the shield of faith, adorned with the breastplate of righteousness and the helmet of the hope of salvation,” spoke thus to those who discouraged him from the direct route:

“Let us entrust the whole care of our salvation to the hands of the Almighty, for no one can harm the one whom divine protection wills to defend. But if he has ordained that he cleanse me by the fire of tribulation from the dross of sins, I do not refuse to submit myself to the will of the gracious Craftsman, so that he may shape me. For neither should ‘the thing formed say to the one who formed it, Why have you made me thus?’” Let us proceed along the royal road without turning aside, and whatever the heavenly Judge has foreseen for us, let us endure with willing hearts.”

Having thus wisely encouraged his companions with this exhortation, he continued the journey he had begun, now confident in heavenly aid. Yet because he was a vessel of humility dedicated to God, lest he be marked by the brand of pride if he altogether refused to follow the advice of his friends, he partly complied with their wishes: he went ahead of the group of travelers with only a few companions, separating himself from them by one day’s journey.

Meanwhile, ambushes of the Lombards were concealed in nearly all the hidden places along the routes where they expected that he would spend the night in order to refresh his body. In particular, at the city of Iporcium [Note: [Col. 0477D] Eporedia, distinguished by an episcopal see and the title of a margraviate, in Piedmont.], treacherous preparations of this kind were made. But he, as has been said, accompanied by only a few—no more than five—entered the middle of that same city while the sun’s heat was already burning beneath the sun’s axis. By God’s gracious favor, he passed through all the city’s public crowds so securely that no one obstructed his way even by addressing him, nor did any necessity arise for him to address anyone else.

When the sun’s sphere was already shining upon the waves of Ocean, his companions, left behind, entered the city in his tracks. Immediately the ambushers rushed out from all their hiding places, and the companions were violently seized as though they were dogs’ prey long sought. Bruno alone was sought in every face, but the one whom Christ had rescued—Bruno alone—was nowhere to be found among them. Throughout the entire night they investigated whether he had gone ahead or was still to come, but no true account revealed what he had done. Suspicion arose that he had passed through some time earlier, and mounted couriers were sent swiftly to pursue him.

But the beloved bishop had already reached the furthest boundaries of Italy and had entered the place called Camera [Note: [Col. 0477D] A town in the Maurienne valley, commonly called La Chambre.], where divine protection freed him through a marvelous plan. His few companions, exhausted by the long journey, had decided to remain there and recover their strength. But he, prescient in mind, went alone through the gates of Camera, content with a single companion, intending to await the others while they were refreshed by a brief rest.

When he had gone about two bowshots beyond them, suddenly the aforementioned pursuers arrived at a breathless run. They found his weary companions already reclining, seized them, and quickly led them back by the road they had come to Iporcium, hoping that they had found the prey they had long sought. God, however, wished in a kind of joyful miracle to mock them.

Thus, by this plan, divine power deprived the wicked of their prey by frustrating their own hope and freed his faithful servant from their fury. Soon afterward, with the help of his kinswoman, the niece of Rudolf, king of the Jura, and the wife of his brother, the most energetic and distinguished knight Gerard [Note: [Col. 0477D] John of Bayon calls him Count of Ekeimsheim and says that he was killed in a certain conflict against Reginbald. Beyond doubt he was the father of the two nephews of blessed Leo mentioned in the already cited letter of Gregory VII, Book II, Letter 14.], it also restored all his possessions to him intact.

## XI. He arrives at Toul and undertakes the reform of the monasteries

With favorable progress, therefore, he continued the journey he had begun. In every city he passed, he was received with enthusiastic acclaim; by his own citizens, who stood eagerly astonished in their longing for him, he was favorably awaited. Finally, on the Sunday of the Ascension, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, [Note: [Col. 0478D] Bollandus believes that “the tenth day before the Kalends of June” should be read, since, he says, Easter had fallen on 10 April, with the second lunar cycle, the twenty-seventh solar cycle, and Sunday Letter B.] he was received amid the immeasurable joy of all and, in the presence of all the leading men of Belgic Gaul, was elected and acclaimed and pontifically enthroned by his cousin, Lord Theodoric, [Note: [Col. 0478D] He died in 1046. Sigibert calls him the brother of Saint Cunegund, the wife of blessed Emperor Henry.] bishop of the Mediomatrici.

Knowing that in the house of God he ought to be a lamp placed not beneath a hiding bushel but upon a shining lampstand, he immediately applied himself with vigilant care to bringing forth the fire of divine religion with which he had always burned. By word and example he ardently kindled those subject to him in zeal for heavenly virtue.

Just as, according to a secular proverb, fire burns more intensely the more it is covered, so the fervor of heavenly love, long enclosed within him, began to blaze forth—like a fire that, from his excellent natural disposition since infancy, had habitually grown hot through the inspiration of Christ.

He therefore directed his wise efforts above all toward promoting monastic religion, which, apart from the monastery of Saint Aprus, Christ’s confessor, had unfortunately grown cold throughout his entire diocese for a long time. At the very beginning of his election he deposed the superiors of the monasteries of Medianum [Note: [Col. 0479D] The monastery of Medianum, commonly called Moyenmoutier, in the Vosges, and the monastery of Saint Mansuetus in the suburb of Toul; both still exist under the congregation of Saint Vanne, as does the third monastery, that of blessed Aprus, in another suburb of Toul, Saint-Èvre, which is also discussed here.] and Saint Mansuetus, who, neglecting the care of the souls entrusted to them, thought themselves appointed solely to govern external matters. He entrusted them to the venerable lord Guidricus, then provost of the aforementioned monastery of blessed Aprus. Through his administration and diligent effort, the monastic order fervently revived in those places, as it remains plainly evident today. [Col. 0479B]

## XII. His ordination is delayed; he is ordained

When victorious King Conrad heard the fame of his praiseworthy deeds spreading abroad, he burned from day to day with ever greater affection of devoted love toward him, foreseeing that he was a faithful vessel suited to reforming the standard of sacred religion and strengthening the Roman commonwealth, which was already declining.

Since pressing circumstances had caused him to postpone until the following Easter the imperial blessing that was to be given him at Rome by the apostolic lord, he likewise ordered the episcopal ordination of this man—bound to him by the ties of perfect affection—to be delayed, so that both might receive together in one basilica the consecration of the office destined for them by the Vicar of the heavenly Key-bearer.

But Bruno, predestined and beloved of God, [Col. 0479C] guardian of true humility and most faithful observer of the commands of the Lord’s authority, learned that this earthly honor bestowed upon him by the emperor was being gnawed at by the tooth of envy, and that the archbishop of Trier was attempting, by producing some privilege of his own, to obstruct the king’s will. Our Bruno therefore immediately approached the king with earnest entreaty, asking him to desist from such an attempt. He preferred to be deprived of the honor of this blessing rather than remain involved in a dispute of opposition against anyone.

Only with difficulty and after great exertion did he persuade the emperor to abandon that intention. Then, with his sweet permission, he returned to Belgic Gaul and humbly requested the pontifical blessing from Poppo, archbishop of Trier [Note: [Col. 0479D] Poppo administered the church of Trier from 1015 until 1047, when he died.]. They mutually fixed a time for this holy ordination to take place.

They therefore went to Trier and sought to follow the customary order of consecration. There, however, a stubborn difficulty in the question prolonged and entangled the entire proceedings, so that, after all the labor had proved fruitless, the aforementioned gracious Father returned home.

For the aforesaid archbishop promulgated a certain privilege containing the following excessive and impossible law, which no one could observe: each of his suffragans whom he was to ordain had first to promise, under witness of the divine presence, that in every matter requiring action he would take him as his counselor, and, with every exception removed, would presume, like a servant, neither to do nor to will anything outside his command.

Faithful Bruno, remembering the divine Scripture—that an unfaithful and foolish promise is displeasing to God—absolutely refused to become the guarantor of this unsuitable arrangement, lest through the impossibility of fulfilling it he incur the offense of lying.

For a long time the dispute of this kind continued on both sides, and it happened that our aforementioned father returned from Trier with the matter unresolved. When the emperor Conrad, of blessed memory, learned this, he summoned both men in haste to his palace at Worms. Relying upon his authority, the archbishop was finally overcome by the demonstration of what was just, and he withdrew the excessive oath of profession that he had unjustly demanded. He required only that Bruno promise to use his authority as counselor in conducting ecclesiastical affairs.

After this promise had been accepted, the holy ordination took place on the fifth day before the Ides of September, amid the greatest rejoicing of all. From that time onward the two men remained unshakably firm in perfect friendship.

We have recounted this so explicitly in order to make clear what kind of humility this man possessed and, to avoid the stain of falsehood, how cautious he was insofar as is possible for a human being.

## XIII. He appoints Abbot Guidricus over the monasteries; his gentleness of character; his skill in music; his patience

Returning, therefore, to his own see, he was received with the joyful celebration of all. Since his devotion to the holy and glorious Aprus was especially great, he appointed the aforementioned Guidricus, a man of religious life and conduct, over that monastery under the title of abbot, at the will and request of Lord Guillelmus, [Note: [Col. 0479D] This is blessed William of Dijon, whose Life we published under the year 1031. He arranged for Widricus to be appointed in his place.] the venerable father of that place at the time. His holy reputation was renowned across the sea throughout every region of the world.

With the support of this bishop, the aforesaid Father Guidricus labored greatly to increase the beauty of his monastery. He began to equip it from its foundations when it was already almost collapsing, and the same bishop, in his generosity, contributed thirty pounds toward its completion.

He also appointed him abbot over the previously named monasteries of Medianum and Saint Mansuetus, to which he granted several churches in order to increase the state of sacred religion within them.

Moreover, at the monastery of Portus Suavis [Note: [Col. 0480D] A monastery near Mirecourt, in Upper or Vosgian Lorraine, now converted into a collegiate church or abbey of noble secular canonesses of the Benedictine order, commonly called Poncé. John of Bayon writes that nuns were established there by Saint Leo in 1047.], begun by his predecessor from episcopal revenues but embellished to perfection by Bruno through his own painstaking labor and expenditure, he established a devout congregation of holy women. He appointed as mother of that community a woman of noble birth and praiseworthy life named Berrenna [Note: [Col. 0481D] Bollandus gives Berzenna. The aforementioned John of Bayon calls her Berhenna.]. Through her diligent care the fervor of divine service flourished and grew there, and, with the help of divine grace, it will continue to grow and flourish for generations to come.

There was also in him a marvelous and honorable elegance of character, so that, together with the splendid bodily beauty that the munificence of the Almighty had bestowed upon him above all men of that time, whatever he did pleased everyone’s mind, and whatever he said delighted all hearts with the deepest affection of love.

In him serpent-like cleverness was joined to such dove-like simplicity that, in the judgment of the prudent men of this age, he seemed superior to all in prudence, while those wise in divine matters greatly honored him for the innocence of his pure mind.

He abounded in such generous charity that, distributing almost everything indiscriminately into the wealth of others, he often found himself in need. Above all and beyond all else he labored in the virtue of almsgiving. No day passed, whatever worldly obstacle might arise, without his personally serving the crowd of the poor every morning and, following the example of the Lord, washing their feet and giving them sufficient food.

He overflowed marvelously with devotion of a contrite heart and the compunction of tearful sighs. He presented nothing of sacred prayer and no act of divine worship before the heavenly countenance without immediately watering his face and breast with a stream of tears. He continually sacrificed himself as such a burnt offering in the presence of the divine majesty, knowing with complete certainty that “a contrite spirit is a sacrifice pleasing to God.”

The wisdom of divine and human arts shone most abundantly in him, especially his knowledge of the delightful art of music. In this he could not merely be compared with ancient authors; in the honeyed sweetness of his music he even surpassed some of them. Composing responsories in honor of the glorious martyr Cyriacus, [Note: [Col. 0481D] Saint Cyriacus is the patron of the monastery of Altorf; Saint Hidulfus of the monastery of Medianum; and Saint Odilia of the monastery bearing her name, or Hohenburg, on the lofty mountain from which nearly the whole region of Alsace beyond the Rhine toward the Black Forest can be seen. The old oratory at the monastery of Altorf is dedicated to Saint Gregory; the parents of blessed Leo are said to have been buried there. John of Bayon records that the responsories mentioned here were composed in 1044 by Humbert, later a cardinal but at that time a monk of Medianum, where the old oratory of Saint Gregory was also located.] and of Saint Hidulfus, archbishop of Trier, as well as of blessed Odilia the virgin and Gregory, the venerable apostle and teacher of the English, he magnified the praises of divine service with marvelous distinction.

The gift of humility and patience also shone so brightly in him that, if he happened to rebuke one of his subjects for some fault, and the man, moved by impatience—as often happens, responded with many bitter insults and reproaches against the accusing bishop, Bruno would answer the verbal injuries not with blows but with compassionate tears.

## XIV. He suffers the attacks of the envious; he falls ill; he is healed by Saint Blaise

Seeing from these and other good deeds that he was becoming renowned, the adversary of the human race [Col. 0482A] attempted by every means to oppose his holy religion. Although he could not make Bruno deviate entirely from the straight path, he nevertheless strove through his agents to deter him from his holy purpose by the arrows of temptations and adversities.

For certain leading men of the country, seeing him shine with the light of wisdom and surpass everyone else in arranging the counsels of the kingdom before the imperial majesty, were envious of him. Since they could not plot against him among the courtiers, all of whom he had bound to himself by extraordinary affection, they contrived against him among outsiders the artful devices of cunning.

Thus they incited Odo, count of the neighboring French borderland, [Note: [Col. 0482D] This is the man called Odo of Champagne, son of Count Odo and Berta, sister of Rudolf the Negligent, king of the Burgundians, who died without children. While he was seeking the kingdom of Burgundy against Conrad, he was killed by Gozelo near Bar. He was buried at the Great Monastery near Tours beside his father, the restorer of that place.] against the blessed bishop and labored, through many assaults of adversity, to shake him from the stability of his loyalty to the emperor.

One might have seen faith in Bruno, alone against the frauds of many, [Col. 0482B] fighting bravely; enduring with marvelous patience the many arrows of his enemies with equanimity; grieving with heartfelt compassion over the losses suffered by his subjects; and readily forgiving the enemies themselves with affectionate charity.

There is no need to recount what wars he endured, or the devastations, plunderings, and burnings inflicted upon the Church entrusted to him, since the grace of the Almighty soon deigned to bring an end to all his rivals rooted in wickedness and, through a pious consolation granted in a vision, wished to restore his faithful servant.

While he was still being oppressed by the anguish of adversity, one night, exhausted by the labor of many cares and tearfully reflecting upon the misery of the people subject to him as though it were attributable to his own sins, he fell asleep. In a dream he saw someone with an angelic countenance presenting him with a sphere brighter than the splendor of the sun. It seemed to contain within itself the entire structure of the world, and within it two men of splendid appearance were shown to him in particular.

When he wished to learn their names, a voice of this kind reached his ears: “Know that these are Mary Magdalene and Galienus the bishop; in the future you will rejoice to enjoy their companionship.”

As he joyfully received the same sphere and wished to place it in his lap with his hands, he awoke from sleep, having been given foreknowledge of the future. It is not surprising that he is said to be the companion of blessed Mary, since a comparable affection of love toward God and the continual flow of tears like streams of water made him a participant in her merits.

[Col. 0482D] Although it is still unknown to us who this Galienus was, there is nevertheless no doubt that he was a man of great merit, since the divine voice placed him on an equal footing with a man of such praise.

This vision was followed by an effective consolation of divine grace: the aforementioned Count Odo was disgracefully delivered to death by Gozelo, the warlike leader of our country, and peace was restored through this blessed bishop—not only to the kingdom of Lotharingia but also to the neighboring provinces, through the favor of Christ’s assistance.

For through Bruno’s intervening wisdom, embassy, and counsel, the kingdom of Austrasia was joined to and strengthened by the Roman Empire. Rudolf, king of the Jura and Burgundy, had long held it from its origin. The same bishop was also sent as a direct envoy to establish peace between the aforementioned Conrad, ruler of the Romans, and Robert, king of France.

France bears witness to how honorably he fulfilled that embassy. It still reports almost as something new how greatly his wisdom shone forth in him, what humility he possessed, and finally what effectiveness he displayed in all his undertakings; how distinguished he was in the bearing of mind and body, and how appropriate in delivering the words of his embassy. Everyone received him as a father with extraordinary love, and all revered him as a saint with the highest veneration.

He therefore established peace and concord between the two kingdoms with such firmness that, for as long as the princes previously mentioned lived, and afterward through their succeeding sons, the two Henrys, [Note: [Col. 0483D] Namely, Henry I, king of France, son of Robert, and Henry II—or III—called “the Black,” the emperor who succeeded his father, Conrad II, called “the Salian,” in 1039.] no one, however fraudulent his skill, was able to sow discord between the two realms.

But the envious enemy of the human race, seeing that through his agents he could not divert Bruno’s devotion from the straight path, rose against him personally by divine permission and weighed him down with an excessive bodily illness that continued for an entire year.

The whole grieving multitude of the people was present, despairing of his recovery. A company of physicians was also present, increasing his suffering with words of hopelessness. Tears watered every face, and hope of life had already failed him.

Then, warned by divine inspiration, he ordered that he be carried at night before the altar of Saint Blaise, trusting that through the saint’s worthy merits he would be freed as quickly as possible from his present distress.

There, carried into ecstasy—I do not say into sleep, which had entirely fled from him—he saw what appeared to be Saint Blaise proceeding from the altar, visiting him and compassionately asking about the nature of his illness. With all his sickly inner organs laid open, as though the saint himself could see them, Blaise washed them with a merciful hand and revived them with medicine. After restoring everything to its proper place, he returned by the way he had come.

When he recovered from the ecstasy, he rose healthy from his bed, summoned those standing around him, and joyfully disclosed the vision he had seen. Then, just as the aforementioned martyr had commanded, he sang with those present in a voice of jubilation the responsory, “Who is a great God like our God?” (Psalm 76:14). After completing the nocturnal offices, he returned home cheerfully on his own feet.

## XV. The piety of Bruno’s mother; her illness; her request to be buried without adornment; her death

But since my pen hastens to write of greater matters, it seems appropriate briefly to relate something worthy of remembrance about his mother. It is not easy to express in words how serene her devotion was, how generous her almsgiving remained to the very last measure, how persistent she was in divine prayers, vigils, and fasts, and how patient her penance was in the mortification of the flesh. The end itself, in which all praise is securely proclaimed, made these things plainly manifest.

For the abundance of excessive fluid had caused the size of her body to grow to such a degree that she could scarcely be carried in a wagon wherever necessity required. Because this bodily heaviness seemed intolerable to her, she repeatedly implored the grace of Christ with abundant tears: just as the womb of a single mother had brought her forth into the world, so might the arms of a single woman be able to commit her to an earthly grave.

The Dawn from on high heard her voice. Through the prolonged wasting of illness [Col. 0484B] she was so reduced at the end that, almost all the moisture of the flesh having dried up, she seemed to consist only of bones held together by skin and sinews.

When she therefore came to the final boundary of life, she had distributed everything that she herself, apart from her husband’s revenues, had accumulated from her own resources by spending daily on the needs of the poor. Strengthened by holy anointing and participation in the life-giving Communion, she lay for a long time lifeless and without any vital breath, while the entire household wailed together with crowds of poor widows and orphans.

Suddenly recovering her breath, she ordered the confused cries of the mourners to cease and commanded everyone to leave the house. She retained only Regelwida [Bollandus gives Regilinda, abbess of the monastery of the Holy Cross. [Col. 0484C]] together with her own husband.

When they asked her through tears what she meant, she said:

“Do not mourn me as though I were dying, for now the most merciful Mother of God, Mary, has come to me. She consoled me with the sweetest kindness and promised that I would live eternally with her and happily reign with her in everlasting glory. I therefore humbly ask one thing of you, my most beloved husband: do not take with displeasure the words of my request that I am about to speak.”

When he, ignorant of what was to come, gladly promised that he would fulfill whatever she might command of her own free will, she said:

“I ask that, just as I came naked from the womb of my mother, so the womb of the earth may receive me naked in the grave; and whatever adornment you had prepared for my burial, strive faithfully to distribute for the use of the poor.”

Although unwilling, the aforesaid husband consented to her request. With the greatest readiness of spirit, he stripped her as she had ordered and committed her to burial in the manner she had prescribed.

I have related these matters so carefully so that it may be evident to those now living and to those yet to come how great was this woman’s faith and devotion, and how ardent she was in generosity toward the poor.

But it seems fitting to cast anchor here in our voyage, so that, taking a little breath and restoring our equipment, we may be able to cross the sea we have begun to traverse with renewed strength.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0483]

## 1. Bruno visits Rome every year; he heals his traveling companions from an epidemic; he sees Saint Peter in a dream; another vision

With the help of Christ’s favor, we shall continue the work we have undertaken and show how the blessed man attained apostolic dignity and what happened to him there—or rather, what the Lord wished to accomplish through him and in his time. It seems appropriate first to set out the preceding circumstances relevant to this matter and to make known how heavenly grace revealed its coming to him.

He possessed the greatest devotion to revisit each year the first shepherd, the Key-bearer of heaven, and to implore his assistance with humble prayer for the sheep entrusted to him by God.

At one time, therefore, he undertook his customary journey accompanied by a company of clerics as well as laymen, numbering more than five hundred. Because of his merits, affability, and holiness, they followed him in an inseparable company. A dreadful plague arising from the corrupted Italian air crept over them all, so that none infected by this disease had any hope of postponing death until the following day.

But the man of God, exceedingly grieved by the affliction of the crowd accompanying him, found a swift remedy, with divine grace going before him. With his own hand he dipped relics of the saints that he carried with him into wine, especially those of Saint Aprus, to whom he commended himself with particular devotion. Whoever tasted even a little of this drink immediately recovered, whatever illness had seized him, provided only that he was able to taste that liquid.

Almost every day throughout the journey he himself offered the sacrifice of the divine sacrament. During the solemn celebration of Mass he exhorted the people standing by to correct their morals and practice penance. He encouraged them all by pious admonitions to seek heavenly things and freed them through holy prayers from the moment of imminent death.

Throughout the night, therefore, the company of his companions and of the inhabitants of the region whose need required it kept vigil at his lodging with lights. In the morning, through the merits of the saints and with his intercession granted, they carried away complete health.

When these events had been rapidly spread throughout every part of Roman Italy, the man of God was honored with the greatest veneration, and affection for him was deeply implanted in everyone’s heart.

It was his constant custom, when he was about to surrender his limbs to nighttime rest, to commend himself attentively to the relics of the saints, to release his mind from worldly cares, and to relax it in holy contemplation, receiving in that meditation the sleep necessary for the body.

While he was asleep one night in this pious state of mind, he was brought in a vision to the principal church of the city of the Wangiones [Note: [Col. 0485D] The city of the Wangiones, or Worms, a very famous episcopal city under the metropolitan church of Mainz.]. There he contemplated what appeared to be an infinite multitude of men dressed in white, most of whom seemed to be priests. Among them he recognized one who had once been familiar to him, the archdeacon Bezelinus, who had died during Bruno’s Roman journey.

When Bruno asked him what such a great multitude was, he heard that all these men had completed their earthly life in the service of the prince of the apostles. As he wondered inwardly about this, blessed Peter, the Key-bearer of heaven, appeared and said that this multitude was about to participate in holy Communion from Peter’s hands.

The same blessed Peter, together with Stephen the protomartyr, led them, pontifically vested, to the altar of the aforesaid church with ineffable musical melody [editorial reading: “whom . . . appointed”]. When the sacred offices had been completed, they all received the life-giving gift from Peter’s hands.

It also seemed to him that after the sacred Communion Saint Peter presented him with five golden chalices; to the one who followed him he gave three; and to the third he gave one chalice. [Note: [Col. 0485D] The author later interprets this vision as referring to the years during which Bruno and his two immediate successors were to hold the papacy. [Col. 0486D]]

He reported these things to his close companions and wondered what they might signify for him. What their outcome was will be related in its proper place below.

At another time, likewise during the rest of sleep, it seemed to him that a certain misshapen old woman was assaulting him insistently and asking to join herself to him in a familiar but nevertheless sincere conversation. She appeared to have such a horrible face, torn clothing, and shaggy, shamefully disordered hair that he could scarcely recognize anything human in her.

Struck with great terror by her deformity, he very much wanted to avoid her, but she pressed upon him all the more insistently. Overcome by her importunity, the man of God traced the sign of the cross upon her face. She fell to the ground as though dead, but then rose again in extraordinary beauty.

Awakened by terror at this vision, he rose for the nocturnal vigils. Then, once again, while wondering at what had happened, he returned his limbs to sleep. In a dream it seemed to him that the venerable Abbot Odilo was present, and he asked him to reveal what the vision signified.

Odilo, exceedingly joyful, answered him with this oracle:

“Blessed are you, and you have freed her soul from death.”

That these events were not fabricated is proved by the reliable testimony of venerable men—namely, Lord Walter, dean of the monastery of the Leuci, and his intimate fellow-priest Warneherus. They assert that they heard Bruno relate these things with tears and were greatly astonished at what they signified.

Nor does it seem incredible that such things were shown to him beforehand by the supreme divinity, since his frequent nighttime sighs in bed, the repeated beating of his breast, and the bed often found soaked with tears by truthful chamberlains demonstrate that he was worthy of a divine vision.

No one who has read the nearly similar dream of the great Constantine concerning the restoration of the city of Byzantium can doubt what the vision of the aforementioned woman signified. [Note: [Col. 0486D] Sozomen relates this vision of Constantine the Great in Book II, chapter 3, of his Ecclesiastical History.] For it is certain that ecclesiastical beauty—or rather, the Christian religion—had horribly withered throughout various parts of the world, and that through him, with Christ’s assistance, it was restored to its former honor.

## II. The pope is elected at Worms. In the guise of a pilgrim he makes for Rome. He restrains Flavius’s exuberance. He arrives at Rome. He is canonically elected pope.

Meanwhile, in the city of the Wangiones, before the presence of the glorious Henry II, Roman Emperor, a considerable assembly of bishops and other nobles took place. Among them this bishop, worthy of Christ, was summoned, since nothing of importance was arranged within the imperial court without his counsel. Suddenly, while he suspected nothing of the kind, he was chosen by everyone to undertake the burden of apostolic honor.

For a very long time he refused this burden, urged on by humility; but when he was compelled more and more insistently, he requested three days for deliberation. During that time, devoting himself to fasting and prayer, he remained entirely without food or drink. When he was again pressed to complete the act of obedience, he freely made his confession before everyone, attempting, as it were, by the enormity of certain of his sins, to alter the common election. Who could relate the flood of his tears, which he poured forth in a public confession, when he even moved the feelings of everyone present to excessive weeping? Hence these pious words resounded unanimously from the mouths of all: “God forbid that the son of such tears should perish.”

Seeing, therefore, that he could in no way escape the imperial command and the common desire of all, he was compelled to accept the office imposed upon him, in the presence of the Roman legates, on the condition that he should hear that the common consent of all the clergy and Roman people was beyond doubt. Thus he returned to his own see, that is, to the see of the Leucori, and there, with the greatest devotion, celebrated the Lord’s Nativity in the presence of four bishops: namely, Hugo of Cisa, an Italian city, legate of the Romans;

> **[Note: [Col. 0487D]]** So the Remigianus codex and other manuscripts cited by the Bollandists read. The printed editions have *Pisa*, as does John of Bayon in his *History of the Monastery of Moyenmoutier*; but Hugo was not then in charge of the Church of Pisa. Nevertheless, it has not been possible to find any episcopal city called Cisa on maps of Italy. Perhaps *Assisia* should be read; for at that time Hugo, bishop of that same city, was living. In 1050 he transferred the body of Saint Rufinus, as Ughellus notes in *Italia sacra*, vol. I, col. 224.

Everard, archbishop of Trier, Adalbero of Metz, and Theodoric [ed., Theodorus], bishop of Verdun.

Then, with humility as his guide, and contrary to the custom of all the apostolic men, he assumed the garb of a pilgrim

> **[Note: [Col. 0488D]]** From this passage the opinion of those who assert that Leo assumed the pilgrim’s habit at Cluny, on Hildebrand’s advice, is plainly disproved. Hildebrand, they say, reproached him for having worn the purple before he had been received at Rome. The first author of this fiction seems to have been Otto of Freising. See the *Life* written by Bruno of Segni.

and set out on the journey to Rome, devoting himself tirelessly to sacred prayers and divine contemplation, and applying himself with extraordinary concern not so much for the affairs entrusted to him as for the care of souls.

While he was absorbed in this meditation near the city of Augsburg, he merited divine consolation: in a revelation he heard an angelic voice sing out a harmonious melody, sweetly blending in accord:

> “The Lord says: I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction; you will call upon me, and I will hear you, and I will bring back your captivity from all places.” [Col. 0487D]

Strengthened by this pious consolation and now made more certain of heavenly assistance, he undertook to complete the journey he had begun. As befitted a person of such merit, an innumerable multitude coming from every direction accompanied him. Among them a handmaid of God, devoted to the religious life, attached herself to him and, by divine command, admonished him in these words:

“Just as soon as you have set your first steps within the doors of the church of the Prince of the Apostles, do not forget to use these divine words: ‘Peace to this house’ (Matthew 10:12), ‘and to all who dwell in it.’”

He received this command of the Lord humbly and fulfilled it devoutly.

He therefore arrived with so great a company at the river Tero,

> **[Note: [Col. 0488D]]** The Tevere, a river which, flowing from the Apennine mountain, descends into the Tiber.

which had so greatly swollen beyond its proper channel that it forced the entire people there to remain for seven days. The man of God, saddened by the distress of the people, who had long been waiting with him, invoked heavenly aid and began the blessing of a church of Saint John built nearby. But before the sacred rite of the consecration that had been begun could be completed, the river was so calmed, its waters subsiding, that it immediately offered a safe crossing to everyone who passed over. The entire crowd present affirmed that this had occurred through the merits of the blessed man.

Strengthened, therefore, by the consolation of the Almighty, he approached Rome, and the whole city prepared to go out to meet him with hymns and musical singing. But he himself walked on foot after the long journey, with bare soles, directing his mind more toward devotion of spirit than toward the delight of praise. Who could report the feelings of his contrite heart in devoted prayer—or, indeed, the continuous streams of tears flowing like rivulets—when such things are penetrable to no one’s thought, much less expressible in words?

After he had for a very long time sacrificed himself in this way to Christ upon the altar of his heart, as a “living, holy sacrifice, pleasing to God,” he began, before the clergy and people standing by, to deliver the divine exhortation with which he was richly supplied. In a brief address he announced the imperial election concerning him for so arduous an office; he demanded that they disclose their will, whatever it might be toward him; he declared that the election of the clergy and people, by canonical authority, took precedence over the arrangement made by others; he affirmed that he would gladly return to his homeland unless his election were made with the common approval of all; and he showed that he had come under compulsion to undertake so great a burden. When he saw the unanimous acclamation of everyone, he resumed his exhortation concerning the correction of life and humbly sought the prayers and absolution of all.

Accordingly, by the favor of divine grace and with everyone applauding, he was consecrated and enthroned in the apostolic chair on the day before the Ides of February, at the beginning of the Lord’s Lenten season. But who could briefly explain how greatly the fervor of his devotion to the service of the Almighty grew, or with what energetic diligence he strove to order ecclesiastical affairs, when almost the whole world would scarcely suffice to recount it?

I do not, however, think it should be hidden under the key of silence how great an indulgence divine mercy granted through his worthy prayers to his brother Hugo. For some time before his election to the apostolate, Hugo had already died; and while this blessed man was making his way to Rome for the aforementioned ordination, he had arrived at Populeium,

> **[Note: [Col. 0489D]]** It is uncertain whether *Populonium* or *Forum Popilii* should be understood by this name, for both cities lay equally on the route to Rome.

where the aforementioned brother appeared in a vision to a cleric of good repute and earnestly begged him to seek his intercession with the apostolic lord.

The cleric saw the aforesaid Hugo seated in a place filled with indescribable beauty, rejoicing with many others on a curule chair, but with his feet hanging down to the ground because there was no footstool beneath them. When the cleric inquired about the condition of his situation, Hugo replied that everything was well with him except that he was laboriously hanging down toward the lowest place, with feet that were not firmly supported. He also asked the cleric to entreat his brother, this blessed man who was going to Rome for consecration, to remember him when he entered the doors of the church of the Prince of the Apostles, saying that through his prayers divine mercy would grant him pardon.

The cleric reported this vision to the holy pontiff and encouraged him to entreat the grace of Christ for the salvation of his brother. Later, Hugo appeared in a vision to the same apostolic lord and joyfully gave him countless thanks, because through his merits heavenly clemency had released him from all his labors.

## III. He assumes the name of Leo. He is wonderfully enriched. His fame spreads everywhere.

This man, supremely devoted to God, imitated the conduct and life of the Great Leo, whose name he had also received; indeed, insofar as he could, he followed the Lion of the tribe of Judah. He became an example of right living to everyone. He shone forth as “a burning and shining lamp,” not under a bushel but upon a lampstand; and, like true salt of the earth, he poured the seasoning of heavenly wisdom into the minds of all.

Although Christ adorned his crown with the jewels of every virtue, these qualities nevertheless shone in him more brightly than the rest: mercy and patience; speed in granting pardon to those who had offended; extraordinary compassion, so that he wept with those confessing their own crimes; and such indiscriminate generosity in almsgiving that he gave everything away, even to the point of personal need.

But since the divine testing of adversity usually overtakes all who devote themselves earnestly to God’s service—testing that reveals the fervor with which the affection of each person’s mind is directed toward God—this venerable father, while staying at Rome at the beginning of his arrival, was struck by considerable distress and sorrow.

For when he arrived there, he found none of the funds required for pontifical expenses. Everything had already been consumed for household purposes; indeed, all that he had brought with him had been distributed in alms. The full purses carried by all his companions had run dry. There was no hope of assistance except to sell their own clothes for very little and, by some hidden stratagem, to take the most kindly father back to his homeland by flight.

The blessed man resisted this counsel and wisely urged them to trust in divine consolation; nevertheless, in compassionate affection, he deeply shared their distress. When the day approached on which all his companions had decided secretly to depart, behold, envoys of the nobles of the province of Benevento arrived, bringing gifts appropriate to apostolic dignity and humbly asking to obtain his blessing and assistance.

The bishop, worthy of God, received them as befitted his honor and strengthened them with a sacred blessing. He was not so much delighted by the offering of gifts as he was moved to return thanks to God for the devotion of the faithful. Then he turned to those who had recently been distrustful because of their excessive anxiety and immediately rebuked them with charitable admonition, urging them never again to despair or lose confidence in God’s mercy.

From that time the fame of the blessed man spread among the peoples and even to the ends of the world; his reputation traveled among every nation. The glory of Christ was proclaimed everywhere in his wondrous servant, and the name of Pope Leo echoed with unanimous voice throughout every part of the earth.

Nor is it surprising that rational creatures should resound with his praise, since even irrational animals—wonderful to relate—formed a human voice in proclaiming his name. For, as trustworthy narrators report, near Benevento a rooster frequently repeated his name; and, just when it was about to utter its natural call, it astonished everyone by sounding out, “Pope Leo.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0489D]]** On account of this rooster, some writers, apparently, recorded that wherever the blessed pontiff passed, roosters immediately cried out in a human voice, “Pope Leo.” See Richer, *Chronicle of Sens*, book II, chapter 14. [Col. 0490D]

## IV. A dog speaks. Leo gives what is offered to him to the poor. He convenes councils. He comes to Cologne.

### Then to Reims, where he consecrates the church of Saint Remigius. He celebrates a council.

It is also said that in those times, in the territory of Apulia, there was a dog accustomed to call out “My God” in human words while barking. It is not incredible that a brute animal in that region invoked God’s mercy in some fashion, since it is certain that the Christian religion there had almost entirely perished and that the inhabitants of that land were subject to foreign power,

> **[Note: [Col. 0490D]]** Namely, to the Normans, who at that time held Apulia.

so that at least an irrational beast might rouse them by its voice to invoke heavenly assistance.

Thus, when the fame of his exceptional praise had been spread everywhere, it inspired more people than usual to visit the threshold of the supreme Prince of the Apostles. All were refreshed by his consolation and strengthened by his blessing. If impossibility prevented some from enjoying his presence, they sent him gifts in faith, expecting to receive from him the gifts of apostolic blessing.

He also had this practice, along with his other good works: if anything was offered to his feet in the apostolic manner, he allowed nothing to be spent for his own use or that of his household, but distributed everything to the needs of the poor.

Among the many who sought to visit him, the king of Denmark sent him a parrot as a gift. Divine grace appeared in it through an astonishing power. Although certain birds learn to form human words through the instruction of hunger, this one, it is said, without being compelled by anyone, repeated throughout the entire journey while it was being carried to the lord pope, “I am going to the pope.” As soon as it was presented to him, it cried out in a sweet voice, “Pope Leo,” without anyone teaching it.

Whenever this venerable shepherd, wearied by the ordering of external affairs, withdrew into a private chamber, or whenever some sadness oppressed his mind, afflicted by excessive cares, the bird frequently provided relief from his distress. Repeating “Pope Leo” clearly and distinctly, it aroused strength of mind in him.

No one should regard it as blameworthy that this righteous man used the song of this bird for his consolation, since we read that blessed Augustine, inconsolably lamenting the death of his mother, employed musical melody to relieve his grief, and that Saint Antony at a fixed time allowed a little entertainment to relieve the severity of monastic discipline.

How much diligence he applied to preserving Catholic law he demonstrated at the first Roman council,

> **[Note: [Col. 0491D]]** Peter Damian discusses the decrees of this synod in his letter, or treatise, to Henry, archbishop of Ravenna.

which he held with many bishops seated in council. There he confirmed by living voice the statutes of the four principal synods and affirmed that the decrees of all his predecessor pontiffs were to be observed. He also condemned the Simoniac heresy, which had already invaded some regions of the world, and at the same council deposed certain bishops whom that heresy had stained with the blemish of its wickedness.

What happened at this council should not be passed over in silence, since Christ deigned by his grace to strengthen Leo’s authority there. A bishop of Sutri,

> **[Note: [Col. 0491D]]** Ferdinand Ughellus calls him Kilinus in volume I of *Italia Sacra*, where he discusses the bishops of Sutri.

accused of the same offense, wished to clear himself unjustly by producing false witnesses. But when he was about to swear the oath, he was suddenly struck by divine power; and, carried away in the hands of others, he was removed from human affairs not long afterward. All who heard this were seized by immense fear, lest human shame should induce anyone in his presence to render a false judgment.

He also restored to the churches the tithes that all Christians were to pay, although there was no mention of them in Apulia or in certain other regions of the world. He prohibited, under anathema, the sale of altars; but he decreed that the portions of the tithes belonging to the bishop should either be retained by each bishop or given to whomever he wished, while the portion belonging to the altar should be freely granted to the church’s own pastor.

He dissolved the incestuous marriages of blood relatives, which were being contracted indiscriminately in many parts of the world, and separated many nobles bound by this shameful tie. He also labored to renew many other chapters of the canons, which we refrain from reciting here lest they cause weariness.

Applying himself intensely to these holy endeavors, he revisited his ancient homeland and was received at Cologne by the most noble and reverend archbishop of the entire people, Herimann. At his request, the lord pope granted this privilege to the see of the Church of Cologne: that at the altar of Saint Peter seven cardinal priests should celebrate the divine office daily in sandals.

He also gave Herimann the office of chancellor of the holy Roman see, granting it to him and his successors, together with the church of Saint John before the Latin Gate.

From there he was invited by Herimar, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, to consecrate a church rebuilt in Saint Remigius’s honor.

> **[Note: [Col. 0492D]]** We presented the history of this dedication above, under the year 1049, when it took place.

There it is not easy to express how great a multitude came from the ends of the earth—Spaniards, Britons, Franks, Scots, and English—to visit his presence. A considerable gathering of bishops was also present, among whom came the venerable archbishop of the Chrysopolitans [i.e., Besançon], Hugo, beloved of God and human beings, distinguished above all by pleasing eloquence and affability. No predecessor or successor of his can be compared with him in restoring the property of his church; in him the wondrous power of Christ was then made manifest.

For the glorious apostolic, having held a council of bishops there, deposed certain men infected with the Simoniac heresy from offices they had unjustly assumed. Among them was Hugo, bishop of Langres, who, having been denounced by many terrible accusations, was summoned to give an account.

He chose the aforementioned archbishop of the Chrysopolitans, as the most eloquent of men, as his advocate and spokesman. Thus compelled by the apostolic lord, Hugo undertook to plead his case, but suddenly became speechless before the presence of everyone, so that it might plainly be revealed that God did not wish the tongue of so great a pontiff to be polluted by false excuses for genuine crimes.

Therefore Hugo of Langres, terrified by this miracle, fled by night, fearing the council’s judgment. On the following day the same bishop was sought at the synod and found not to be present. After the sentence was read, he was summoned a third time [Rem. adds: “and excommunicated”].

Then the bishop of Besançon rose and disclosed before everyone how he too had attempted to defend the accused man but had become speechless. When the lord pope heard this, he attributed the miracle to the merits of blessed Remigius. Rising with everyone who was present, he gave thanks to God and then, with great psalmody, rendered thanks to the holy lord Remigius.

Later, however, the aforementioned bishop of Langres, admonished by divine prompting, returned to the lord pope. With abundant tears he publicly confessed his crimes, voluntarily undertook penance, and went to Rome barefoot. From that same pious shepherd he merited absolution. On his return, worn down by excessive fasting and bodily mortification, he ended his present life in steadfast goodness.

> **[Note: [Col. 0493D]]** He died in the monastery of Saint Vitonus of Verdun, which was governed by his brother Walerannus. Much about him is related above in the *Life of blessed Richard*, abbot of that place. He wrote a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* against Berengar, which was published by our Acherius.

## V. The Council of Mainz. Leo frees a demoniac at Reichenau.

Returning from there through the city of Metz, at the request of the venerable abbot Guarinus he consecrated there the basilica of the holy pontiff Arnulf. At the request of the lord Sigifrid,

> **[Note: [Col. 0493D]]** This passage shows that Sammarthani must be corrected, since he does not list Sigifrid among the abbots of Gorze. We discussed the monastery of Gorze, founded by Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, in honor of Saint Gorgonius, whose body he had obtained from the pope, in the preceding century, where we presented the *Life* of Saint John, abbot of that place.

the abbot of Gorze, he composed a sweet melody for the nocturnal responsories in honor of the glorious martyr Gorgonius.

From there he held a general council at Mainz. At it Sibicho, bishop of Speyer,

> **[Note: [Col. 0493D]]** Others call him Sigebotho. He succeeded Reginobald in 1039 and administered the Church of Speyer for eleven years. [Col. 0494D]

accused of a criminal offense, wished to clear himself by the terrifying sacrament of the Lord’s Body. But, as the story goes, his jaw remained twisted by paralysis for as long as he continued in this present life.

I have wished to record this briefly so that those who hear it may know how terrible it is to approach such a judgment even with a confident conscience, since Holy Scripture says: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31).

Finally, the lord pope dedicated a church at Reichenau

> **[Note: [Col. 0494D]]** A once-famous monastery, commonly called Richenow, now inhabited by only a few monks because the abbot’s table has been united to the bishopric of Constance.

in honor of the life-giving cross. There divine mercy wonderfully displayed its grace in its own servant. For during the sacred rites of Mass, a demoniac was brought there, bound in chains. He could scarcely be restrained by the crowd, and, possessed by an alien violence, he uttered dreadful shrieks, cries, and groans, overpowering the harmonious hymnody of the entire clergy with his terrible voice.

Therefore, as Christ’s servant was about to begin the sacred Canon, unable to endure such disturbance, since he was directing his entire mind toward God, he made the sign of the cross from a distance and commanded silence with his hand. The demon immediately became silent, and the man, released from his bonds, returned safely to his own home, to everyone’s astonishment.

## VI. He returns to Rome. He restores a broken cup. He goes to Apulia. He heals a bedridden woman. The Council of Siponto. He returns to Rome.

Returning, then, to Rome, he gladdened the people, who were saddened by his long absence. There heavenly grace made his wondrous merit known to everyone.

For the aforementioned Herimar, abbot of the monastery of Saint Remigius, bishop of Reims, had offered him, as a remembrance of himself, a cup made of precious *mazer* wood,

> **[Note: [Col. 0494D]]** The Bollandists have *marmoris* (“marble”), from a manuscript codex, as they say; but not only the printed editions, but also the manuscript codex of Saint Remigius, read *mazeriis*, by which name some precious kind of wood seems to be indicated. For Bruno of Segni says that this cup was wooden, and Desiderius of Monte Cassino, or Victor III, calls the vessel a wooden drinking cup. On such cups, see Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under the word *Mazerini*.

which the holy man had decided to keep for his own use out of affection for the giver. But on one occasion, when a servant was about to give him a drink, he found it accidentally broken into many pieces.

The elect of the Lord ordered its fragments to be brought to him wherever they were, and, suspecting nothing of what was to happen, arranged them all in their proper places as though playfully. Then, with joy, he said to those standing by: “The majesty of the Almighty is able to restore these broken pieces to their former wholeness.”

At these words the pieces were immediately joined together, so that a sign of the break, resembling the finest hair, appeared all around as a memorial of the event. But, still more wonderfully, none of the liquid placed inside leaked out.

A suitable witness to this event is the venerable Hugo, the aforementioned archbishop of the Chrysopolitans, who testifies with tears that he was present and rejoices that, in a pious theft, he carried the vessel away from the holy man.

Always mindful of the office entrusted to him by God, as a “faithful and prudent servant dispensing the measure of wheat in due season,” he undertook a journey through the regions of Apulia to restore the Christian religion, which there appeared almost to have perished. Above all, he strove to establish peace between the inhabitants of the region and the Normans, whom the princes of the kingdom had once received as allies against foreign peoples but whom they then endured unwillingly as savage tyrants and devastators of their homeland.

Zealously intent upon this holy work, he came to Benevento. After remaining there for some time, he gave life-giving assistance, preceded by divine grace, to a certain bedridden woman.

> **[Note: [Col. 0494D]]** This is what a woman is called when she lies continually in bed; for *κλίνη* means “bed.”

For nearly fifteen years she had been worn down by prolonged illness and could not leave her own bed unless carried by the hands of others; all her limbs had been weakened by the disease of paralysis. Through a revelation she was shown to drink water in which the blessed shepherd had washed his sacred hands after celebrating Mass, and to recover her health without delay.

After obtaining this water and drinking it with faithful hope, she went safely on the following day to the sacred rites of Mass, intending to give thanks to God and the holy pontiff.

Thus the venerable bishop, burning with zeal for the holy religion, held a council at Siponto and deposed two men from the office of archbishop. They had assumed the sacred ministry for payment, and one, through the fault of arrogance, sought to surpass the other.

From there he retraced his steps and returned to Rome. There, instructed by a heavenly revelation, he decreed that Gerard, formerly bishop of his own see—that is, of the Leucori—should be numbered among the saints. In the same year he returned to his homeland and transferred the saint’s holy remains with the greatest glory.

All these matters are clearly written in Gerard’s *Life* and miracles.

> **[Note: [Col. 0495D]]** The Bollandists present this *Life* on April 23. We discussed Saint Gerard in the preceding century, p. 891, where his canonization bull is found, p. 894.

## VII. A bishop who opposed him is punished. The bishop of Ravenna is punished as well.

This man of God had a considerable struggle against those who seized the possessions of the holy Roman see, especially against the bishop of Ravenna, who was filled with the spirit of obstinacy and rebellion. Certain palace officials supported him, envying the glory of the apostolic lord.

Their leader in fomenting discord was Nizo, bishop of Freising,

> **[Note: [Col. 0495D]]** Sirmond’s edition has *Vizo*. Walter calls him Nicerus in his *Catalogue of the Bishops of Freising*. [Col. 0496D]

against whom divine power deigned to display a terrible vengeance of this kind. Sent to Italy on imperial business, he came to Ravenna and began, in favor of the Ravennate, to utter disparaging words against this blessed man. Among them, drawing his finger beneath his throat, he burst into this blasphemous statement:

“May this throat be cut by the sword unless I have him deposed from the dignity of the apostolate.”

No sooner had he said this than, at that very moment, intolerable pain seized his throat. Unrepentant, he died on the third day.

The archbishop of Ravenna, because of his incorrigible presumption, was excommunicated by the holy pope. Therefore, summoned to Augsburg by imperial command, he was compelled to seek absolution after returning the things he had unjustly seized.

Although he lay prostrate at the feet of the saint with an unrepentant heart, and although the entire assembly of bishops present pleaded for his absolution, the blessed man said:

“According to his devotion, may the Almighty grant him absolution from all his crimes.”

When the man rose, he still smiled mockingly, his pride swelling within him. Then the venerable shepherd, dissolved in tears, secretly said to those standing around:

“Alas! This wretched man is dead.”

Immediately he was struck by illness, and, scarcely carried back to his homeland, was swiftly deprived both of the life and the honor with which he had been swollen.

VIII. Leo frees a demoniac woman. He appoints Udo of Toul as his successor. He attempts to reconcile the Hungarians with the emperor. He foresaw future evils. [Col. 0495D] The Council of Mantua. The dead visit holy places.---

While the magnificent pastor was revisiting the Roman See and was about to celebrate the offering of the divine sacrament at Saint Lawrence during the solemn rites of Easter, they brought before him, amid the sacred ceremonies of Mass, a certain woman who, possessed by a demon, had lost her reason. Seeing her rage incessantly, and unable to endure the uproar of those standing around her and dragging her along bound, [Col. 0496A] he raised the banner of the cross against her and ordered everyone to stand far away. But immediately the unclean invader abandoned her, and she returned home sound and unharmed, with her reason restored.

Concerned first for the salvation of the souls specially entrusted to him, while he was in Rome he chose the venerable primicerius Udo as his successor in the holy See of Toul, and sent a personal envoy to the imperial majesty to have him appointed in his place.

[Note: [Col. 0496D] The edition mistakenly has Odo. In fact, Udo is the form found repeatedly in several documents. Previously he had been librarian and chancellor of the Roman Church, as is evident from the bull of Saint Leo in favor of Saint Mansuetus.]

Indeed, because of his honorable conduct, his fervor for holy religion, and the pious devotion and purpose of his intentions, he judged him worthy of this office; and, embracing him with fatherly affection, he habitually called him his own son. He also hoped that, through Udo’s prudence—in which he abounded richly in divine and human affairs—whatever he had accomplished less fully in the enlargement of his original see might be brought to completion.
