This is now being fulfilled for the greater part, with Christ’s favor, and, as we truly believe, his holy devotion toward the Lord will increase day by day.

But his praises must now be set aside, since every praise may be sung more securely at the end. He also possessed no small zeal for strengthening the commonwealth. Therefore he had approached the princes of Hungary, who had recently dissented from the Roman Empire, through numerous envoys, urging them not to refuse to pay the emperor the customary tribute owed from ancient times. They had agreed to this, provided that pardon for their past offenses were granted them.

Consequently, compelled by holy compassion, he was obliged to return for the third time to his ancient homeland and, out of pity for the accused who had taken up war against the Empire, to seek the imperial ears with persuasive prayers. But because, through the faction of certain courtiers who envied the successful actions of the holy man, the emperor’s ears were closed to the prayers of the apostolic lord, the Roman commonwealth lost the subjection of the Hungarian kingdom, and even now grieves to see the neighboring land devastated by plunder and fire.

While he remained there for some time, laboring anxiously for the peace of the kingdom, divine predestination wished to reveal to him in a dream what his future would portend. For he seemed to himself to be standing in a high place, receiving his companions as they fled to him from danger; and, after enclosing them beneath a rain-cloak, called a *cappa*, he saw that his garments were stained with their blood. By this vision he was assured that sorrow was approaching for himself and his companions, and he prepared himself to endure the coming trial, like wheat to be stored in the Lord’s threshing floor.

Accordingly, returning to Italy, he arranged for a council to be held at Mantua. A faction of certain bishops who feared the severity of his just judgment disrupted it. For the households supporting their crimes suddenly stirred up a riot against the household of the apostolic lord, which was standing securely before the basilica where the public council was being held. Thus the holy man was compelled to rise from the midst of the assembly and proceed before the door to calm the uproar.

Those hateful to God did not respect his presence; indeed, becoming ever more obstinate in wickedness, they attempted to stab before his eyes those who, disarmed, were fleeing to him for refuge, and to drive them away from the doors of the church so that they could not be protected there. Arrows and stones flew around the ears and face of the same holy man, and wounded some who sought to defend themselves with his garment.

The disturbance was brought to an end only with great difficulty, and it forced the council to abandon the strict proceedings it had begun before they were completed. But on the following day, all the instigators of this sedition, who were to be condemned after severe examination, were released by the most merciful father through an indulgence of mercy, lest he appear to exercise the harshness of vengeance against them as the motive of his judgment.

Nor does it seem right to consign to the late seal of oblivion the memorable event reported to have occurred at Narni in his time, to the glory of God. All the inhabitants of that city, from the least to the greatest, are said to have been eyewitnesses of the event.

For two years before this venerable pope celebrated the Lord’s Nativity there, it happened one summer day that an infinite multitude passed beside those same walls. Terrified by it, the entire population climbed the walls, as though to take up a defense for the city. The crowd filled an immeasurable expanse of land, as far as human sight could comprehend, and moved swiftly toward the east.

They all appeared in garments of extraordinary whiteness; their faces and the grayness of their heads made them venerable, and they were beautiful in an almost identical form and appearance. This astonishing sight left all who watched from the city walls stupefied, and the multitude did not cease passing from early morning until the ninth hour. As the sun declined, that wondrous crowd gradually began to thin.

One of those watching from the wall, more confident than the others, dared to go outside. Standing nearby in fear, he watched to see whether he could recognize any of them. Then, among the last, he saw someone who had once been familiar to him: a citizen of that city, a man of good reputation and devout mind, who had not long before completed the course of his present life.

Calling him by name and summoning him to himself with a solemn adjuration, he asked him to reveal what such a great multitude might be. The other replied:

“Although you are unworthy to know the divine mysteries, nevertheless know that we are sinful souls, still not deserving to possess the joys of the heavenly kingdom. In place of penance, we continually travel around holy places, and now, coming from the Great Monastery of Saint Martin, we are journeying to the monastery of the blessed Mother of God Mary at Farfa.”

[Note: [Col. 0497D] The Great Monastery is situated near Tours, as everyone knows. Farfa is a celebrated monastery in the Sabine diocese in Umbria.]

After saying this, he disappeared, leaving the other overcome with immense terror. The man then lay sick in bed for an entire year and personally reported these same things to the apostolic lord.

[Col. 0498A]

IX. The heresy of the Fermenters. Leo writes against it. Nicetas Pectoratus recants. Michael, bishop of Constantinople, is excommunicated.---

At that time the heresy of the Fermenters arose. It slanders the holy Roman See, and indeed the entire Latin and Western Church, for offering to God the life-giving sacrifice with unleavened bread. The bishops Michael of Constantinople and Leo of Acrida also published this accusation in writing, persistently breathing out poisonous fumes against the holy and apostolic faith.

This accusation, composed in the Greek language and sent to John, bishop of Trani, as an insult to all Latins, was presented at Trani to Brother Humbert, bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida. Through Humbert’s efforts it was translated into Latin and [Col. 0498B] conveyed to Lord Pope Leo IX.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Michael, surnamed Cerularius, to whom the blessed pontiff wrote an outstanding letter, or rather a book. He was the parent of the Greek schism and was expelled from his see in the year 1058.]

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Humbert is commonly said by John of Bayon, in his History of that place, to have been a monk of Moyenmoutier; it is said that his parents offered him to the monastery there in the year 1015. The books by this same Humbert against the Greeks were published by Baronius in the appendix to volume XI of the *Annals*. Leo’s letters, however, may be found in Labbe, volume IX of the *Councils*.]

Accordingly, the glorious apostolic lord composed a very lucid treatise against the aforementioned presumptions and their excessive vanities, endeavoring to lead them back to the way of truth. But afterward he condemned them, since they remained uncorrected, with an ecclesiastical anathema.

The aforementioned Brother Humbert also published a response, in the form of a dialogue, against their rotten writings. He had written it himself in Latin during the time of his legation at Constantinople, and, at the command of the religious and orthodox emperor Constantine Monomachus, it was published in Greek under the names “The Constantinopolitan” and “The Roman,” in the year of the Lord 1054.

Lord Frederick, then chancellor and later, chosen by God, apostolic lord of the Roman See,

[Note: [Col. 0498D] He is called Stephen X; his eulogy is given below, in the section concerning the holy men of Monte Cassino.]

also replied vehemently to certain objections raised by Nicetas, a Constantinopolitan monk, also called Pectoratus, against the Latin Church. He had entitled his treatise: *On Unleavened Bread, on the Sabbath, and on the Marriages of Priests*. This vehement reply was translated from Latin and recited publicly before the aforementioned emperor. After a disputation held at the Studion monastery in the city of Constantinople, Nicetas was compelled to condemn and burn his own writings.

Indeed, the glorious apostolic lord had sent to Constantinople envoys of the holy Roman See: namely, the aforementioned Humbert; Peter, archbishop of the Amalfitans; and Frederick, then a deacon and chancellor. Nicetas, wishing to receive a complete resolution of his propositions, once more voluntarily anathematized everything he had said, done, or attempted against the first and apostolic See. He was thereby received by them into communion and became their close friend.

But Michael, bishop of Constantinople, avoided their presence and conversation and persisted in his folly. The aforementioned envoys of the apostolic lord therefore went to the church of Hagia Sophia. Complaining about his obstinacy, they placed the document of excommunication upon the principal altar at the third hour on Saturday, before the eyes of the clergy and people present, while the clergy were prepared according to custom for Mass.

They then immediately departed and even shook the dust from their feet as a testimony against them, according to the saying of the Gospel (Luke 9:5), proclaiming: “Let God see and judge” (Exodus 5:21).

Afterward they organized the churches of the Latins within Constantinople itself and anathematized all who thereafter received communion from the hand of a Greek who disparaged the Roman sacrifice. Having obtained the orthodox emperor’s permission, they returned cheerfully, carrying gifts from the emperor to Saint Peter and to themselves, and bearing the emperor’s kiss of peace.

The emperor, angered against Michael because he had refused to come to a council in the emperor’s presence and in the presence of the apostolic lord’s envoys, and indeed had incited the populace to revolt against him, deprived Michael’s friends and relatives of their honors and expelled them from the palace. Against Michael himself he maintained a grave anger until the end.

X. The expedition against the Normans. The savagery of the Normans.---

Meanwhile the most pious pastor, concerned for the sheep entrusted to him by God and compassionately grieving over the unheard-of affliction of the people of Apulia, gathered a considerable retinue and once again set out toward Benevento, striving by every means to moderate the savage violence of the Normans.

It is not our task to recount in tearful words everything that happened to him on this journey, since he himself reported the whole matter in a brief letter to the emperor of Constantinople.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] This may be found among the other letters of this blessed pontiff, in volume IX of the general councils.]

For, among other things, he says:

“With that concern with which I ought to watch over all the Churches, seeing the undisciplined and alien people of the Normans rising against the Church of God with cruel and unheard-of fury and more-than-pagan impiety; slaughtering Christians indiscriminately; afflicting some with new and terrible tortures until their souls failed; sparing neither infant nor old man nor the weakness of women out of any regard for humanity; making no distinction between sacred and profane; plundering, burning, and utterly destroying the basilicas of the saints—I repeatedly rebuked their wickedness, admonished, entreated, preached, insisted in season and out of season, and announced the terror of divine and human vengeance.

“But because, as the Wise Man says, ‘No one can correct one whom God has rejected’ (Ecclesiastes 7:14), and, ‘A fool is not corrected by words’ (Proverbs 18:2), their malice remained so obstinate and hardened that day by day they added worse things to the worst.

[Col. 0499D]

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Peter Damian criticizes this in his letter to Bishop Firmius, asserting that Gregory the Great did not act in this way. Baronius, in his account of the year 1053, which you should read, refutes Peter’s opinion with many arguments.]

“Therefore, since I desired not merely to expend external goods for the liberation of Christ’s sheep but even most eagerly wished to expend myself, it seemed to me that nothing would be so effective for restraining their stubbornness as drawing human defense from every source. I heard from the Apostle that rulers do not bear the sword without cause, but are God’s ministers, avengers in wrath against everyone who does evil; and that rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to evil (Romans 13:3–4); and that kings and rulers are sent by God for the punishment of evildoers (1 Peter 2:14).

“Therefore, supported by such a retinue as the brevity of time and the pressing need allowed, I judged it necessary to seek the conversation and counsel of the glorious commander and most faithful master Argyrius, your servant—not because I desired the destruction or death of any Norman or any other person, but so that at least by human fear those who have no fear of divine judgments might come to their senses.

“Meanwhile, as we attempted to break their obstinacy by salutary admonition, while they on the contrary falsely promised complete submission, they suddenly attacked our retinue. Yet even now they grieve over their victory more than they rejoice in it. For, as your piety took care to write for our consolation, because of this presumption they expect an even greater indignation to come upon them shortly, after the diminution of their troop that they have experienced.

“We too, confident that divine help will be present and human help will not be lacking, will not abandon this purpose of liberating Christendom, nor will we give rest to our days (Psalm 131:5), except when rest has come to the holy Church in peril.”

Thus far the apostolic lord.

XI. The pope passes unharmed through the midst of the enemies. He takes care of the funerals of the slain.---

Accordingly, the very wicked people of the Normans, after massacring the household of the most gentle pope, though not without great loss to their own men, attacked the town called Civitatula, where the blessed man, unaware [Col. 0500C] of what had happened, was awaiting his delayed retinue.

When he saw the enemies approaching and understood what had happened to his men, he set out toward Benevento with the remnant of the clergy who were with him. While all the enemies stood astonished, he passed through their midst without fear, like a confident lion.

Recognizing such astonishing courage, they changed their minds and turned to serve him. Kissing his footprints, they begged from him the pardon they did not deserve. The holy man, saying little as the occasion required, took care, with their assistance, to arrange honorable funerals for the slain, burying them in a nearby church that had long ago been destroyed.

Because they had been willing to undergo a devoted death for the faith of Christ and the liberation of the afflicted people, he showed through numerous revelations that by divine grace they were rejoicing eternally in the heavenly kingdom. They themselves also appeared to Christ’s faithful in various ways, saying that they should not be mourned with funeral lamentation, but rather that they had been joined with the holy martyrs in heavenly glory.

At the same place, a basilica was rebuilt over them by their very slayers with beautiful workmanship, and a congregation of servants of God was gathered there. Through them the almighty power of God performs many notable miracles.

The fiercest people of the Normans, terrified by these events, laid aside their cruelty. From that time onward they treated the peoples among whom they lived more amicably, as fellow countrymen, and faithfully served the venerable pope in complete submission for as long as he lived.

XII. His pious exercises. He learns Sacred Scripture in Greek.---

The outstanding pastor came to Benevento. Even the Normans, without being ordered, accompanied him ceremonially along the entire route. He remained there for a considerable part of the year, exercising himself in holy virtues: patience, vigils, fasts, and prayers.

Indeed, he avoided every softness of the bed. Taking a hair shirt for his body and lying upon a mat spread on the ground, with a stone placed beneath his head, he allowed himself a little sleep during the night hours. He spent the rest of the night reciting the entire Psalter and innumerably genuflecting.

Repeating the same Psalter each day, together with the offering of the divine sacrifice, he indefatigably completed the course of his manifold prayers. Another remarkable thing about him was that, although he was more than fifty years old, he was so ardent in his study that he learned to read the divine Scriptures in the Greek language.

And because he overflowed with the entrails of piety and mercy beyond what can be believed, an innumerable multitude of poor continually hastened to his generosity, and he supplied them with what they needed, without distinction.

XIII. He places a leper in his own bed. He frees a demoniac woman.---

While he was engaged in these pious activities, one evening, when all his household had withdrawn to sleep for the night, he himself was walking through the empty space of his palace with a boy, carrying a lamp before him. He saw, lying in a corner, a leper wrapped in torn rags and covered with sores, wasted by foul and livid decay. Crushed by excessive illness, the man could not move his feet and could scarcely utter words from his exhausted body.

The venerable father spoke with him familiarly for a long time while kneeling before him. Then he carried him on his shoulders, wrapped in his own garments, and brought him to the bed that had been prepared for him according to pontifical custom. After carefully closing the doors from within and putting the servant to sleep, he himself devoted himself to his customary psalmody in a nearby oratory.

After a long while he returned, intending as usual to lie down on the ground, but he did not find the leper whom he had placed upon the constructed bed. He asked the awakened boy where the poor man had gone. Astonished, the boy went around every corner of the house and carefully tested the entrances of the doors. Finding everything locked, he returned in the greatest amazement.

After this, the apostolic lord, stupefied, gave his weary limbs over to sleep. Seeing—I do not know what divine thing—in a dream, he commanded the boy the next morning, with fearful astonishment, not to reveal in any way, as long as he lived, what had happened.

I believe that in his dream Christ appeared to him clothed in his garments, as he had appeared to the blessed Bishop Martin; or that he saw, like the monk Martyrius,

[Note: [Col. 0501] The blessed Gregory discusses him in Homily 39 on the Gospels. Bollandus gives his life under 23 January.]

the leper rising from his arms and ascending to heaven. And, out of humility, so that the poison of pride might not creep into him through human praise, he wished this miracle to remain hidden. Nevertheless, it was not without cause that he ordered this deed to be concealed under so grave a warning.

Again, one day, while he was there alone with a single cleric and engaged in sacred psalmody, a certain peasant arrived, bringing with him his insane daughter. He repeatedly cried out in anguish that she was tormented by a very wicked demon, and with tears begged that she be freed through the holy man’s merits.

The compassionate father resisted his pleas for a long time and ordered him to implore, with a humble vow, the intercession of the saints, whose innumerable relics are kept there. But the peasant, stubborn in his purpose—or rather firmly established in steadfast faith—said that he would not leave until, through the holy man’s blessing, he obtained divine assistance.

Thus the holy man, overcome by the peasant’s persistence, blessed a grain of salt found nearby and cast it into the girl’s mouth while invoking the divine name. Immediately the demon was expelled together with a discharge of purulent blood, and the joyful father returned home with his daughter restored to health.

Many more astonishing things could be related about this holy man. But the eager reader—or the skeptical listener—must be allowed to proceed; therefore, briefly recalling his passage from this life, let us bring the work we have begun to an end.

XIV. He falls ill at Benevento. He comes to Rome. He is taken to Saint Peter’s oratory. He is fortified with holy oil and the Eucharist. He dies. He is buried.---

Having completed the course of the good struggle, he burned each day with an ever greater desire for heavenly blessedness. As though saying with Paul, “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14), he renounced the cares of this life so completely that, while still in the body, he seemed to practice the blessed purity of angelic conduct.

He also devoted himself, as usual, more frequently to the celebration of the incorrupt sacraments for the repose of the dead. Although this work had been his principal labor throughout the entire period of his residence, he applied himself to it with more fervent zeal and a greater abundance of prayers as the day of his death approached.

And because divine providence works the salvation of those who serve it both by indulgence and by chastisement, it scourged him so greatly with salutary affliction, for the increase of his virtue, that he lost all desire for food. The pain of the disease that was creeping upon him forced him to continue the fasts he had once undertaken voluntarily, with only a drink of water providing support for his weakened body.

Meanwhile, a full year having passed, the anniversary of his ordination was approaching. Each year on that day he devoted himself to Christ in pious prayers with his customary devotion. Although the increasing distress of his illness was already weakening his exhausted body for divine works, nevertheless, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, by whom the entire course of his life was directed, he celebrated the solemn rites of Mass on that day with the honor of his apostolic dignity and filled the Beneventans, among whom he was then staying, with the joyful delight of gracious affability.

This was his final service in the divine sacraments, as though he were bidding farewell to the life-giving mysteries, to which he had always shown himself worthy.

Assured that the end of his calling was near, he had himself carried to Rome in a litter. During this journey, divinity reconciled him not only with his own people but also with those who had recently been his enemies. A great number of Normans—the very men whom we have mentioned as having long been at odds with this man—vied with one another to serve him with the most sincere devotion of their hearts.

It was fitting that the strongest defender of the Christian religion, as he was about to enter the palace of his King Christ, should be escorted in a noble triumph of victory, preceded by the tamed multitude of enemies whom he had already subjected.

After remaining for a short time in the Lateran palace, he awaited what the most merciful disposition of the inner Judge would decree concerning him. Blessed Peter, not forgetting the long labor by which this memorable man had cooperated with him in governing the fold of the Church, decided to unite him more closely to himself, since he was destined to share the magnificent honor and glory that, through the preceding grace of the supreme Shepherd, he had bestowed upon the Roman Church.

By divine revelation, therefore, he was taught that the dissolution of his flesh would occur nowhere else than in an oratory near the places of blessed Peter. Immediately, rejoicing over such a vision and understanding that he was being called through the mercy of divine regard, he was carried again in a litter and entered the oratory of blessed Peter.

There, with tears continually flowing from the depths of his heart, he extended his pure mind and hands toward God and invoked the Lord’s clemency for a very long time in secret prayers.

Then he was carried to the nearby episcopal residence, where a great crowd of the faithful gathered to visit him, drawn by the deepest love for him. Considering their pious concern, he decided that he should no longer be detained in the prison of the flesh, since crowds of bishops, abbots, and other faithful had assembled, and that, in their presence, he should be anointed with the sacred oil.

After this act he was gladdened and completely fortified by communion in the Lord’s body and blood. In the German language, as those who were present testified, he then spoke to God in this prayer:

“Merciful Lord, Redeemer of all, our only salvation: if, in the judgment of your majesty, it is expedient that I should still serve the common welfare of your peoples, I ask that I may deserve, through the swift medicine of your visitation, to escape the affliction of this illness now pressing upon me. But if your divine providence determines otherwise, I beseech you, Lord, that I may be permitted as soon as possible to leave the dwelling of this body.”

When his prayer was finished, he looked upon those standing around him and thanked each one for the service shown to him. Arranging his weary limbs for rest, he declared that he felt the pain more bearably than usual.

The multitude of the faithful around him believed that he would soon lay aside the remains of his flesh, and with sighs and sobs they performed the funeral rites appropriate to a departing soul. The blessed man silenced their voices and said:

“Defer what is now being done until the third hour of tomorrow, awaiting what the omnipotence of God may will concerning me.”

Accordingly, on the following day, at the third hour, a large gathering of the faithful was present with more watchful affection. Around the ninth hour they escorted his spirit, released from the flesh and making its way toward heaven, with the most devoted commendation.

The entire Roman populace assembled in abundance, and his funeral rites were celebrated with the greatest honor. As he himself had arranged, he was buried beside the altar of the blessed pontiff Gregory, before the doors of the church. And rightly he stands joined in the glory of his burial to the man whom he faithfully imitated in divine religion and the restoration of the holy Church.

Someone expressed his life and holiness in this brief couplet:

> Victorious Rome grieves, widowed of Leo the Ninth,  
> From among the many, she will not [al., will scarcely] have another father such as he.

This magnificent man was released from the labors of this life at the age of fifty, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1055,

[Note: [Col. 0503] All authorities without exception assign the death of Saint Leo to the year 1054; after his death the See remained vacant for nearly an entire year.]

in the twenty-eighth year of his episcopate at Toul and the sixth of his apostolate. He had indeed sat in Rome for five years, two months, and nine days, fulfilling the vision concerning the revelation of the cups that we related above.

For the five cups given to him by blessed Peter signified the five-year span of his life; the remaining three signified the three-year period of his successor Victor; and the next one signified the course of one year in the apostolate of Frederick, of blessed memory.

But since many further things remain to be said concerning the miracles divinely wrought at his tomb, we leave their recording to the Romans, among whom these events are displayed daily. Our task is to beseech his merits with devout prayers, so that, now placed in heavenly glory, he may deign to open for us the entrails of pity and mercy with which he abounded during his earthly life. Thus, through his holy intercession and the bonds of our sins broken, may we deserve to share in heavenly glory, by the favor of him who works wonders in his saints, to whom praise and thanksgiving are also sung forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0505]

## On the Death of Saint Leo IX, Pope

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of Saint Benedict, sixth century, part II, from a very ancient manuscript of the Beneventan library, written in Lombard script.)*

[Col. 0505A]

### I. The Author’s Date

In the year 1054 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, the seventh indiction according to the Arnican reckoning, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, let us rejoice in the deposition of our blessed father Pope Leo IX, while Henry, son of the emperor Conrad, was reigning as emperor at Rome.

For the praise and glory of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and of Pope Leo, we, every priest and deacon and all the Catholics of the Roman Church, undertake to make known this labor of the struggle that we saw with our own eyes.

We often saw him during his life distributing many alms to guests, the poor, citizens, and pilgrims, so that he gave a very large portion of the Church’s treasures and of everything he was able to possess to widows, orphans, and those who feared God.

For this reason the treachery of the Romans stirred up murmuring and wars against him. But so that the Lord might raise up this man as an impregnable wall of his Church against the deranged heretics, many people had been instructed by him in the studies of letters.

This beneficent Leo gently encouraged the humble; this man broke the necks of the proud; this man supplied necessary sustenance to those who disparaged his life; he preached virginity and defended chaste marriages. Wherever he went, by the examples of all—including pagans—he turned people’s zeal toward himself.

Of the many things concerning this holy man, however, let us bring forward only a few, especially those that occurred as his death approached.

### II. Leo, Sick, Exhorts the Clergy. He Foresees His Death Approaching.

After many labors and hardships, after the dangerous wars, terrors, and ambushes that he had undertaken for the sheep entrusted to him against the persecutors of Mother Church, in the fifth year of his pontificate, when he was held by a serious illness, he summoned to himself bishops from various dioceses and various men of the ecclesiastical order and said to them:

“Brother fellow bishops, sons of Mother Church, and inmost members of my body, to whom the Lord has entrusted the governance of his Church and given the power of binding and loosing: the Lord’s flock has been committed to you.

“Therefore I earnestly beg you, remembering the evangelical saying, ‘Keep watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come’ (Matthew 25:13), and knowing that the lender himself will not forgo his talent once it has been multiplied: watch diligently over his flock, and defend your sheep manfully from the attacks of wolves.

“What excuse, then, dearest brothers, will the one who has carelessly lost the Lord’s sheep be able to offer—the sheep that the Lord himself deigned to place upon his shoulders?

“Watch, therefore, I beg you, and show whose stewards you are. I also commend myself to your brotherhood, me whom the Lord made, though unworthy, the vicar of blessed Peter in his Church. For the time of my dissolution is near. The Lord has deigned to call me from this life.

“Last night, in a vision, I saw the heavenly homeland. When I was overcome with awe, among other things there were shown to me those brothers who were killed in the regions of Apulia for the Church of Christ, crowned among the martyrs. They said to me with one voice: ‘Come and remain with us; through you we have received this blessedness.’

“Then from another side a voice thundered, saying: ‘Not now, but within three days you will join this company. This is your place, and your seat is prepared.’

“While the citizens of heaven were saying these and similar things, the holy vision withdrew. Therefore, brothers, I beg you to bear with me for three days, and know without doubt that you will not see me afterward.”

After saying this, he ordered everyone to depart and attend to their own needs, for night was near. Having received permission, some left. Others, however, in whom a more fervent love dwelt, remained with him throughout that night. They afterward reported to the others that he had remained prostrate on the ground in prayer throughout the entire night.

### III. He Is Carried into the Church. He Prays to God. He Sets Forth Human Misery. He Declares That He Had Been a Monk.

When morning came, and everyone had assembled, the venerable man ordered that the sarcophagus which he had prepared for himself—and he himself as well—be carried into the church of blessed Peter and placed there. When the Romans saw this, supposing that he was dead, they went to the Lateran palace so that, according to their usual custom, they might plunder all his possessions; but the merits of the saint were so great that no one was permitted to enter.

Meanwhile, the venerable man, desiring now to be released and to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23), did not cease offering all who were present words bringing salvation and filled with every sweetness. Since we are hastening on to other matters in order to relate the miracles, we refrain from discussing these words one by one.

When he had finished speaking, he looked toward the sign of salvation and, with prayers poured forth more abundantly than before, granted absolution to all who were present and dismissed their offenses, provided that they took care to observe the instructions he had previously given. Having done this, he again looked up to heaven and poured out this prayer:

> “Lord Jesus Christ,” he said, “who alone are the good shepherd and to whom every creature is subject, you said: ‘Seek and you shall find; ask and you shall receive’ (Matthew 7:7). Mercifully hear me, your servant, on behalf of your Church, over which you willed me, unworthy as I am, to preside in the place of your apostle Peter. To you, Lord, I commend her. Defend her with the unconquerable wall of your protection, and drive away from her every schism and every faithlessness of heretics, so that they may faithfully serve you, the true God. Guard and protect her from all the plots of her enemies, and do not disdain her, for whom you poured out your most precious blood. If I have separated from her too harshly any whom I bound or excommunicated for the sake of your faith, merciful Lord, I beg you to absolve them.”

When he had completed the prayer, a fragrance of such sweetness began to issue from the altar of blessed Peter that it seemed to surpass all perfumes. After an interval of one hour had passed, he ordered bread and wine to be brought to him. When they had been offered, he gave thanks and blessed them; and, having eaten as much as he could receive in three mouthfuls, he distributed the remainder to the others as a blessing.

After this he proceeded to the tomb which he had ordered to be carried into the church. Looking at it with tears, he said:

> “See, my brothers, how worthless, fragile, and transitory human glory is. See, I say, and let each one of you who shines with the honors of this fragile world always keep me as an example before his eyes. Consider how changeable is the condition of the human lot. I, who was raised from almost nothing to the summit of human glory, am now about to be reduced again almost to nothing. The cell in which I lived as a monk I have long since seen transformed into spacious palaces; now I must return once more to the narrow confines of this sarcophagus. Look, I say, how, after splendid garments, I shall be covered with spiders’ webs and already be destined to become food for worms. Today I am flesh and blood with you; tomorrow I shall be changed into ashes.”

Then, turning toward the stone of the tomb, he uttered these words in a most sorrowful voice:

> “May you be blessed among stones. May he bless you who made you from nothing and willed you to be the guardian of my earth and body. I beg you, be my most faithful rock, so that, just as Christ established his Church upon the apostolic rock, so it may be granted to me to have you as the faithful guardian of my bones until the day of judgment; so that on that day, when the strict Judge comes, you may return me and yourself to your Creator.”

As he said these things, the entire crowd standing there broke into lamentation. He said to them:

> “It is enough, my brothers, that you have remained with me until this point today. Go now, each one of you, to your own affairs, and come to me tomorrow morning, so that you may see what is to happen.”

And so it was done. He himself spent the entire night prostrate in prayer, remaining awake.

### IV. He Is Visited by Saints Peter and Paul. He Dies.

As the hour of dawn approached and the stars were already falling from the sky, those who were present, wearied by the exertion required for such a matter and overcome by sleeplessness, gave their limbs a little rest. Though they were neither truly awake nor entirely asleep, two men in white garments appeared to them, speaking with him and writing something.

When those who were present carefully investigated who these men were who, at such an hour, were troubling their lord, it was shown to them in the very vision that they were the apostles Peter and Paul.

Meanwhile the sun appeared over the earth, and the delightful vision was received into heaven. When morning had come and everyone had assembled, the venerable man, awaiting his final day, again ordered himself to be carried into the church of blessed Peter. When this had been done, he prostrated himself before the altar and prayed privately for a long time with tears.

After completing his prayer, he returned to his bed and did not cease, as far as he was able, to admonish the people. But because the final hour was now approaching, he summoned the bishops to him, made his confession, and, signing himself with the sign of the cross, strengthened himself with the heavenly sacraments.

After this, asking for silence so that he might obtain a little sleep, he inclined his head on the bed and rested for about half an hour. In that very peaceful sleep, his most holy soul was released from the body. In attendance upon him, the bell of blessed Peter began to sound of its own accord, without anyone compelling it.

### V. He Frees a Demoniac.

On the second day after his death, a certain woman possessed by a demon was brought from distant regions to the thresholds of blessed Peter and Paul. As she was being led to the tomb of blessed Leo, the demon cried out through her mouth, among other things:

> “O Leo, O Leo, why are you dragging me away from my dwelling with fiery chains?”

Then one of the bishops standing nearby said to him:

> “I adjure you by the true and eternal God and Judge to tell me whether Leo, of whom you speak, truly possesses a holy place among the saints.”

The demon, greatly distressed by this oath and unable to lie, replied unwillingly:

> “Truly he has been crowned among the saints and possesses a holy and venerable place. Through him I am to be driven out, before your eyes, from this dwelling which I have possessed for nine years and two months.”

When he had said this, one of the women standing nearby, bolder than the rest—as is customary among women, given to talkativeness—burst out laughing and said something like this in mockery:

> “Whenever Leo drives the demons out of this body, I shall be queen; and, what is more, I shall restore to life those whom he himself caused to be killed.”

Wonderful is the power of God! She had scarcely spoken these words when, after the other woman had been released, the demon began to torment her cruelly. Thus it happened that the woman who had come supplicantly to the holy man’s body recovered her health and returned safely to her own home; while the woman who had dared to utter mocking words suffered the punishment she deserved and, by God’s just judgment, carried away the evil of the other woman who had already been freed.

From that time Leo’s name became renowned, and immense fear seized everyone. But who could recount all the miracles of blessed Leo? Whoever undertakes this task will perish before he exhausts the material. Nevertheless, I do not think that this one thing, which I am about to relate, should be withheld from the many.

### VI. Another Woman.

After these events, the people, continuing to await the miracles of Leo to which they had now grown accustomed, saw accomplished without delay in deed what they awaited with devoted minds. For at approximately the same hour, the demon began to cry out through the mouth of the woman already mentioned and to say:

> “Alas! Alas! Leo, why are you driving me out of this dwelling again? Do I not possess it because you gave it to me? Why do you change your mind so quickly? It is most shameful to change so quickly the decision that you made not long ago.”

Then one of the bishops adjured him and said:

> “How do you know, wicked one, that today you are to be recalled from this woman and driven out?”

The demon replied:

> “At the hour when yesterday he loosed a mute man’s tongue, he went to Benevento with Marcus [Note: Marcus, bishop of Lucera, is honored on June 14, and Marcianus, bishop of the see of Frigento, on July 14. Both sees are under the metropolitan church of Benevento.], and Marcianus, bishop of the see of Frigento; and, setting out for Apulia with them accompanying him, he arrived at the place where he had already fought against his enemies. Now he is hurrying here so that he may drive me out from here.”

Then the bishop, leaving nothing unexamined, continued:

> “By what sign, then, can their arrival be detected?”

The demon answered:

> “By the lamp which you see hanging before the altar.”

After saying this, he fell silent.

When approximately two hours had passed, a marvelous fragrance spread throughout the entire church of blessed Peter. Then, while everyone watched, the lamp mentioned above began to rise higher than usual on its own, and three lights appeared burning within it. After this, the demon began for a short time to torment the woman with lamentations; but, when Leo arrived as he had foretold, turning his fury back upon himself, he disappeared completely.

### VII. A Church Is Built in His Honor at Benevento.

The fame of the miracles of the most blessed Leo having spread far and wide, a church began to be built at Benevento in his honor, so that the citizens of Benevento, who had seen him alive while he was held prisoner by the Normans, might now venerate him dead and enjoying the expanses of heaven.

Meanwhile it happened that a certain Nicolaus from the castle of Molliniana and Berardus from the place called Carrara—one of them having lost his right arm, with his hamstrings and sinews contracted, while the other suffered chills and fever progressing to dysentery—had themselves carried to the aforementioned church being built at Benevento. Immediately, in everyone’s judgment, they recovered their health, which had been regarded as hopeless.

A certain peasant from the town of Ordonum used to celebrate the feast of blessed Leo each year with a vow. It happened that, because of the excessive burden of the labors he was undertaking in the fields, he had not gone to church on Sunday, when the feasts are announced to the people. The feast day of Saint Leo, however, was on the following Thursday, a fact unknown to the peasant.

He therefore rose very early, took with him a little boy who was his only son, and, as soon as he had brought an axe and a hoe to his field, he set his son down beside the bundle. He himself began anxiously to dig. From the other side, a wolf, with open mouth, seized his little son and fled.

Seeing this from a distance, the father began to run after the wolf, shouting:

> “O Saint Leo, my patron, help me now in my present need and restore my only son to me!”

He had scarcely spoken when, behold, the wolf released the boy so unharmed that not even the slightest trace of the wolf’s teeth appeared on his clothing at the place where the wolf had seized him.

The peasant returned to the town and recounted all these things. Realizing that that very day was the annual commemoration of blessed Leo, he bound himself by a new vow to observe it solemnly every year. Thus the name of Leo became famous not only at Benevento but throughout the whole coast of Apulia.

God so ordered it that, in those same places where, a few years earlier, his army and that of the Church had been defeated and he himself had been held captive, the very people who had stood against him in battle later honored his memory as suppliants and reverent worshipers, and showed themselves increasingly faithful toward the holy Church, to the praise and glory of almighty God, whose name is blessed throughout all ages. Amen.

---

## Commentary on Saint Leo IX, Roman Pontiff

*(In Bollandist, Acts of the Saints, April, volume II, April 19.)*

### § I. Various Written Acts; Sacred Veneration; Relics

#### 1.

The eleventh century of Christ was illumined by the teaching and holiness of Pope Leo IX. Before the Roman pontificate he was Bruno, bishop of Toul under the metropolitan church of Trier in Belgica Prima, born of the most noble Dagsburg family in Alsace.

Wibertus, his archdeacon among the people of Toul, wrote his deeds in two books. In his prologue he declares that he is transcribing “for the edification of many what he had not so much heard about such a great prelate as seen,” since “his own kindness had deigned to allow him to attend him more familiarly and continually.”

The author intends these words to refer to the events of Leo’s youth before the Roman pontificate and to his actions as bishop of Toul, which are indicated in the first book. He wrote them while Leo was still alive in the Roman pontificate, intending to leave to the Romans what the Roman pope would later accomplish. Changing his plan, however, he subsequently presented those matters in the second book.

Jacobus Sirmondus was the first to publish this Life from manuscripts, in Paris in 1615. We publish it here, expanded and corrected in many places, from two manuscript codices: one received from the imperial monastery of Saint Maximin near Trier, the other sent from elsewhere, perhaps from the library of the monastery of Saint-Hubert in the Ardennes, where we know that it exists.

Molanus, in his Notes on Usuard’s Martyrology, indicates that “at Gerardsberg, in the church of Saint Adrian, there is his Life, by a contemporary author, in two books.”

#### 2.

Another writer, and indeed an eyewitness, accurately described how Saint Leo prepared himself during the final three days for his blessed death. He also adds renowned and truly wondrous miracles that occurred at his tomb in Rome during more than seventy weeks after his death.

We give these materials as we transcribed them at Florence in 1661 from the codex of the most illustrious Senator Carlo Strozzi, marked number 690, folio 201; its title added that they had been taken from a manuscript Collection of Offices.

There were, however, more miracles in the Hubertine manuscript, formerly sent to us by Dom Romualdus Hancart, prior of that monastery. We publish them from that source and supplement the conclusion with several items from the aforesaid manuscript.

Ferdinand Ughellus, in volume VIII of *Sacred Italy*, in his account of the archbishops of Benevento, page 129, published from a Beneventan codex written in Lombard script the same account of the events of the three days preceding Leo’s death and some of the miracles. His version is more concise and is expanded here and there in different wording; the obliging reader may find it there.

From that same volume of Ughellus, however, we give what it contains concerning the church of Saint Leo erected at Benevento after his death and concerning several miracles performed there. We append more of these from the Strozzi codex mentioned above. We also had a brief compendium extracted from some of this material transcribed at Rome, made by Petrus Calo; we omit it.

#### 3.

Saint Leo counted Hildebrand among his familiars and trusted friends; Hildebrand was later called “Supreme Pontiff and Gregory VII.” He governed the Church from 1073 until 1085; he died on May 25 and is entered in the Roman Martyrology on that day.

From this holy pontiff, Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino and later Pope Victor III, received some materials which he published in Book 3 of his *Dialogues*.

Saint Bruno of Asti, bishop of Segni, also composed a Life of Saint Leo IX, printed among his other works at Venice in 1651. We omit it here so that the volume may not grow excessively, since it appears to contain only a few excerpts from the Acts or materials received from Saint Gregory VII; we mention these in the Notes.

“Anselm, a monk of Rheims” (as Sigebert indicates in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 153) “wrote an itinerary of Pope Leo IX from Rome into Gaul, chiefly to make known with what authority he celebrated a synod at Rheims and in other cities; with what justice and subtlety he examined ecclesiastical cases; with what discretion he corrected sinners; and how the power of God cooperated with him.”

All these matters have been published in the volumes of the Councils under the title of the Council held at Rheims in 1049. We insert some of them and omit the rest, since they can be read there. We do not list other chronicles or treatises that mention him; we refer to some of them in their proper places.

#### 4.

Sacred veneration began with the pious death of Saint Leo, because of the many miracles that soon occurred. Among them are counted a lamp kindled by divine fire at his tomb on the sixth day after his death, and a candle taken from his tomb which twice kindled itself spontaneously in the following month.

He was soon venerated not only at Rome but also at Benevento, where a church began to be constructed in his honor and his annual feast was publicly proclaimed and devoutly celebrated. Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni, testifies that his feast was celebrated in the Church of Segni.

His memory is also recorded in ancient Martyrologies. One of these is Usuard’s, enlarged at Rheims, from which Molanus published his own. At the end, in an ancient script, the following was added under April 19:

> “On the same day, at the Church of Saint Peter in Rome, the burial of Lord Leo IX, Pope, who dedicated the Church of Blessed Remigius.”

The first part of this eulogy is entered in the manuscript Martyrology of Ado at the monastery of Saint Lawrence in Liège.

The Brussels manuscript of Saint Gudula contains the following:

> “On the same day, Saint Leo IX, Pope and Confessor, who, first bishop of Toul, was promoted to the papacy by Emperor Henry; afterward, having become conscious of this, he resigned; and, having been duly elected a second time, was buried in the Church of Saint Peter after a praiseworthy life, shining with miracles.”

His memory is likewise celebrated in the Roman manuscript of the Duke of Altemps and in the *Florialium of the Saints*, as well as by Bellinus, printed at Paris in 1521, by Maurolycus, Galesinius, Molanus, Saussayus, and Canisius; and with them in the present Roman Martyrology, in these words:

> “At Rome, Saint Leo IX, Pope, distinguished for the renown of his virtues and miracles.”

Constantinus Ghinius also includes him in the *Nativity Days of Holy Canons*. Wion, Dorganius, Bucelinus, and Menardus count him among Benedictine monks.

Menardus, however, wonders in Book I of his *Observations* “that no mention is made of Saint Leo’s monastic life in his Life,” and excuses this on the grounds that “this could have been omitted, as many other things were, which concern the life of this pontiff and can nevertheless be found in other historians.” He does not indicate which historians.

Arnoldus Wion cites Trithemius in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* and the Spanish Benedictine monk Brother Francisco Yvanez in the *Epitome of Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*. Their authority, however, is uncertain, because the Acts, which Wibertus accurately records before Leo’s episcopate, suggest otherwise.

Meanwhile, we wish him to the Benedictine Order, so that at least they may honor him as an exceptional benefactor, as the monks of Saint Remigius at Rheims rightly honor him—indeed with an office of twelve lessons.

The people of Toul celebrate his feast throughout the entire diocese with a solemn office under the rite of a double feast; we possess their Breviary, printed in 1535.

The Romans likewise celebrate his feast on this day in the Basilica of Saint Peter in the Vatican with a double office, prescribing the *Gloria* and the *Credo* in the Mass, because they still possess his sacred body.

#### 5.

He was formerly “buried, as he himself had arranged, beside the altar of blessed Pope Gregory before the doors of the church,” as Wibertus records at the end of the Life.

A Roman canon of the same basilica, who lived in the preceding century, states the following in his description of the Vatican basilica:

> “Pope Leo IX rests inside the Church of Blessed Peter, in a marble pillar near the Ravenna Gate. We have many great miracles connected with him. He established the privilege of the canons of Blessed Peter concerning the confirmation of their churches.”

Lucius Saccus, in his historical description of the city of Suessa—which lies between Capua and Gaeta in Campania—reports in chapter 7 that “the body of Pope Leo IX was found under Paul V in 1608 without one arm, which is preserved at Suessa; and that at that time a letter was displayed in the Congregation of Cardinals, showing that by an ancient and certain tradition the said arm was preserved at Sinuessa.”

Masinus, in *Bologna Surveyed*, also reports that some relics of this Leo are at Bologna in the church of Saint Stephen.

It was said that the sacred bodies of four Roman pontiffs named Leo were displayed on August 1, 1580, and again on May 25, 1608. This is mentioned on April 11, in the Life of Saint Leo the Great, page 21.

### § II. Chronology. Acts of the First Year of the Roman Pontificate. Several Controversies Decided.

#### 6.

Saint Leo was born on June 21, 1002. At the age of five he was entrusted for instruction to Berthold, bishop of Toul, and afterward to the latter’s successor, Herimannus.

He was then transferred to the court of Emperor Conrad and made a deacon. In 1025 he led a contingent of soldiers from Toul into Lombardy. The following year, 1026, while absent, he was elected bishop of Toul. Returning from Italy, he came to Toul on the Feast of the Ascension of Christ and was consecrated on September 9.

These facts are certain and beyond dispute from the Acts themselves.

While he was governing the bishopric of Toul in holiness, the Roman pontiffs were John XIX and then Benedict IX. After Benedict was expelled from the Apostolic See and the schism of Sylvester III was settled, Gregory VI became pope in 1044.

After all three of these men had been deposed, Clement II, previously bishop of Bamberg, was elected in 1046. When Clement died the following year, 1047, Benedict IX occupied the see again. Against him Damasus II was elected, previously bishop of Brixen, and was consecrated in 1048 on July 17. But after occupying the see for twenty-three days, he died, as is believed, from poison.

After him, still in that same year, our bishop of Toul—then called Bruno—was designated at the assembly of Worms. After celebrating the Nativity of Christ at Toul, he set out on December 27 through Germany. At Augsburg he “heard a harmonious melody resounding in an angelic voice.”

Hastening his journey thereafter, he was forced by flooding to remain with his company for seven days. Nevertheless, in that winter season he reached Rome, perhaps toward the end of January or the beginning of February 1049, if, as Anselm says in the *Itinerary*, “he was invested with the insignia of pontifical dignity at the Lord’s Hypapante,” that is, at the feast of the Purification of the Mother of God. He was then solemnly “enthroned on February 12, the first Sunday of Lent,” as Wibertus records in his Acts.

#### 7.

A certain controversy arises here with Otto of Freising and those who followed him. They claim that “Saint Leo, destined for the See of Blessed Peter, having assumed the papal purple, traveled by way of the Gauls; that at Cluny he was rebuked by Hildebrand, laid aside the purple, assumed the garb of a pilgrim, and came to Rome with Hildebrand.”

Otto of Freising was a full century younger and died in 1158. We should therefore give greater credence to Wibertus, an eyewitness, who states that Leo “at Toul, having assumed the garb of a pilgrim, undertook the journey to Rome and was refreshed at Augsburg by an angelic melody.” Nor was there an intervening period that could be assigned to a journey to Cluny.

Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni, writes that Hildebrand was present at Worms at the very designation of Saint Leo to the supreme pontificate:

> “In those days,” he says, “there was there a certain Roman monk named Hildebrand, a young man of noble character, distinguished intellect, and holy religion. The blessed bishop summoned him to himself and asked him to return to Rome together with him . . . And when the bishop came to Rome, he brought the aforesaid monk with him, serving Blessed Peter greatly in this very matter, because he was bringing back with him a man by whose counsel and wisdom the Roman Church was someday to be governed and directed. For this is Pope Gregory VII,” and so forth.

Paul of Bernried, a contemporary author, wrote the Life of this holy pontiff. In it he relates that Hildebrand “spent some time at the court of Emperor Henry.” He then adds that Pope Leo IX “honored from his heart and embraced the prudence and holiness of this admirable man, following his counsel in everything; and that their concord bore much fruit in the Lord’s field by uprooting thorns. Meanwhile, the pope ordained him subdeacon and appointed him over the monastery of Saint Paul, which had been disastrously desolated.”

Later, “the spiritual farmer, namely Saint Pope Leo, observing and greatly admiring the abundant fruit of this branch, because it remained in Christ and Christ in it, enlarged Christ’s dwelling in him by conferring the Levitical order; and, so that he might bear more fruit for the Roman Church, appointed him archdeacon.”

So it is written there.

From all these facts we conclude that Saint Leo was not at Cluny on that journey, nor did he bring Hildebrand from there; rather, he brought him from the imperial court. Nor was it at Hildebrand’s urging that, after laying aside the purple at Cluny, he assumed the garb of a pilgrim; he had adopted that garb at the beginning of the journey.

Hildebrand initially hesitated when Leo invited him, objecting “that he would seize the Roman Church not according to canonical institution but through secular and royal power.” Leo, however, being by nature simple and exceedingly gentle, patiently satisfied him by giving an explanation of everything, as Hildebrand had wished.

So says Bruno.

#### 8.

A second controversy is drawn from the *Cassinese Chronicle* of Leo Marsicanus, bishop of Ostia, who died in 1115. He writes in Book 2, chapter 81, that “Pope Saint Leo went to Mount Gargano for the sake of prayer in the same year in which he was ordained.”

In fact, as will be shown below, this occurred the following year. It appears that the author began counting the years from Easter and likewise began Saint Leo’s first year at that point; on this basis he subsequently assigned each event accurately to its proper year, as we shall show below.

As Anselm teaches in his *Itinerary*, however, Leo completed “the fasts of Lent at Rome and celebrated the solemn rites following the resurrection of the Lord.”

Furthermore, Hermannus Contractus, who was a monk of the monastery at Reichenau in the same year in which Saint Leo died—that is, 1054—writes as follows:

> “He was ordained during Lent and took the name Leo IX. At the following Easter he consecrated Udalricus, administrator of the monastery of Reichenau, who had come to Rome, with the abbatial blessing; and by his authority he confirmed and renewed the privileges of that monastery, anciently granted by the Apostolic See, in the second Indiction, on March 26,”

that is, the day before Palm Sunday.

Therefore he did not celebrate the feast of Palm Sunday that year at Monte Cassino, as was inferred from Leo Marsicanus; rather, as will be said below, he celebrated it the following year.

#### 9.

“That same pope,” says Hermannus Contractus, “held a synod with the bishops of Italy at Rome in the week after the White Sunday,” that is, after the Sunday *in Albis*.

As Wibertus explains below, it was held against the Simoniacs. Leo deposed such bishops, prescribed the use of tithes, and dissolved incestuous marriages.

Blessed Peter Damian also gives various details concerning this synod in a letter to Henry, bishop of Ravenna, cited by Baronius and in the volumes of the Councils.

Then, according to the same Hermannus, “that same pope convened another synod at Pavia during the week of Pentecost, and from there, by way of Mount Jovis, crossed into the transalpine regions with a number of Romans.”

First, as Anselm writes in the *Itinerary*, he “visited the emperor, who was staying in the Saxon region.” The two of them “arrived at Cologne in the Agrippina district on the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul.”

There Saint Leo granted various privileges to Archbishop Herimannus. He also promised Herimarus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Remigius at Rheims, whom he encountered there, “that he would come to Rheims on the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel and celebrate the sacred rites of the Mass in the Church of Blessed Mary; that he would devote the feast of the glorious Father Remigius to the elevation of his precious body and the following day to the consecration of the basilica; and that he would assign the remaining three days to the celebration of synods.”

Afterward, when the pope departed from Cologne, he came to Toul on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. From there he ordered the bishops and abbots of the surrounding regions, by letters bearing his authority, to meet him on the appointed day in order to celebrate a synod in the basilica of the aforementioned Apostle of the Franks . . .

#### 10.

“Finally, Lord Pope, having departed from the city of the Leuci, undertook the journey toward the city of Rheims. On the eve of Saint Michael he arrived at the estate of Curmola; on the following day he reached Saint Remigius, accompanied by three archbishops—namely, those of Trier, Lyon, and Besançon—and by other distinguished men. Among them were John, bishop of Porto, and Peter, deacon of the Roman Church and prefect of the city itself.

“In the atrium of the basilica a most fitting procession was arranged. Three bishops—namely, those of Senlis, Angers, and Nevers—preceded it in widely separated ranks, carrying the Gospel book, blessed water, and vessels containing the fragrance of spices.

“Thus they received the arriving pope with worthy music. After completing his prayer, he gladdened those present with the Apostolic blessing, and from there he was escorted to the city walls.

“There the clergy of Rheims, proceeding to meet him with their archbishop and other bishops, accompanied him as far as the Church of Saint Mary. There, wearing the priestly insignia, he proceeded to celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass.

“On the following day he returned to Saint Remigius, intending to celebrate on the next day the approaching solemnity of so great a Father. On that day, around the third hour, wearing the priestly mitre, he proceeded to the tomb of the glorious Father Remigius with thuribles and crosses. Four archbishops accompanied him—those of Rheims, Trier, Lyon, and Besançon—along with certain others, the abbot of the place, and the venerable Father Hugh, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, together with many members of his order.

“With them, after a litany had been performed . . . he moved the saint’s bier a short distance from its place. When it had been suitably prepared, he devoutly and tearfully lifted it, placing his shoulders beneath it, together with the archbishops and abbots mentioned above . . .

“After it had been placed in the Church of the Holy Mother of God upon the altar of the Holy Cross, the archbishop of Besançon celebrated the solemn rites of the Mass for the feast of that glorious Father.”

#### 11.

“When the course of the day had passed, night followed. In the morning, Lord Pope summoned the bishops and, within the hidden interior of the monastery being dedicated, assigned to each one the consecration of a particular altar. The pontiff himself celebrated the solemn rites of the Mass for the feast of the dedication.

“After the Gospel had been read, he ascended the pulpit and delivered a sermon of exhortation to the people standing around him, preaching many useful things concerning the sanctification of that church. He ordered that the day be celebrated throughout the boundaries of the bishopric of Rheims . . .

“He also decreed that at the altar which he had consecrated in honor of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the martyrs Clement and Christopher, and the glorious confessor Remigius, the sacrosanct mysteries should no longer be celebrated indiscriminately by just anyone, as had previously been the case; rather, according to the custom of the Roman Church, only seven more distinguished priests should be appointed to this office.

“Then, having completed the divine Offices, he sanctified the people with the Apostolic blessing and dismissed them.

“On the following day, which was October 3, twenty bishops assembled in the basilica mentioned above, together with nearly fifty abbots and very many others of the ecclesiastical order . . .

“When they had taken their seats, Peter, a deacon of the holy Roman Church, rose and explained the matters to be discussed in the synod: many unlawful practices, namely, the Simoniac heresy; ecclesiastical ministries and altars held by laymen; wicked customs by which payments were received from them in church atria; incestuous marriages, and those who abandoned their legitimate wives and became involved in adulterous remarriages; monks and clerics abandoning their holy purpose and habit; clerics devoted to worldly military service; the seizure of property and unjust exactions from the poor; the vice of sodomy; and certain heresies that had arisen in those same regions.”

Thus far from the *Itinerary* written by Anselm, or from the Council of Rheims, has been excerpted. The remainder may be read there. Matters concerning the elevation of Saint Remigius’s body and the dedication of the church will be elucidated under October 1. Wibertus treats below of the Simoniacs who were then deposed.

#### 12.

Wibertus relates in the Acts that, after departing from Rheims, Leo went to Metz, consecrated the basilica of Saint Arnulf, composed responsories for Saint Gorgonius the Martyr, and afterward held a council at Mainz.

Adam of Bremen, Book 3 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 31, calls it “a general synod held under the presidency of the Apostolic Lord and Emperor Henry, with the bishops Bardo of Mainz, Eberhard of Trier, Hermann of Cologne, Adalbert of Hamburg, Engelhard of Magdeburg, and the other priests of the provinces.”

At that council a certain bishop of Speyer, named Sibicho, against whom the crime of adultery had been alleged, was cleared by the test of the Sacrament. Many other measures were also enacted there for the benefit of the Church, above all the Simoniac heresy and the shameful marriages of priests, which were perpetually condemned by the synod’s own written act.

Hermannus Contractus states that “the synod consisted of forty bishops.”

From there Saint Leo “went into Alamannia and celebrated the feast of Saint Clement and the Sunday before Advent, November 26, at Reichenau.” Wibertus adds that there he “dedicated a church in honor of the life-giving Cross and, during the solemn rites of the Mass, freed a demoniac.”

From there, according to Hermannus, “passing through Augsburg and Bavaria, he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Verona.”

### § III. Deeds in the Years 1050 and 1051
### 13

In the year of Christ 1050, having returned to Rome, he restored the broken cup; he proceeded to Apulia and cured a bedridden man at Benevento; and at the Council of Sipontum, near Mount Garganus, he deposed two archbishops. Wibertus sets these events out in his *Acts*. To this account, as we said above, should be referred what Leo of Ostia writes in Book 2, chapter 81, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*. His words are these:

> “The holy Pontiff Leo, in the very year in which he was ordained, went for the sake of prayer to Mount Garganus, in the diocese of Sipontum. Returning from there, he came to this monastery with great devotion on the very feast of Palm Sunday; and, received most reverently by the Brothers, he solemnly celebrated Mass that day. Eating with the Brothers in the refectory, he came after dinner to the chapter house. There, giving the Brothers the greatest thanks for their most honorable reception of him and promising that he would always exalt the monastery to the extent of his strength, he departed.
>
> “On the following day he solemnly dedicated the church of St. Maurice, constructed by that same Abbot near the island called Limara, and the church of the Holy Savior in the territory of Atina, and then returned to Rome. The Abbot, having gone to him, honorably obtained from him a privilege according to the custom of his holy predecessors. In it the same holy Pontiff, by Apostolic authority, granted, as a mark of honor for this holy place, the use of sandals, the dalmatic, and gloves on the principal feasts, both to that Abbot and to all those who should thereafter be regularly promoted in this monastery.
>
> “At the same time that Apostolic Pontiff also handed over to the said Abbot the monastery of Holy Jerusalem, called Sessorianum, situated within the city of Rome, together with all its rights. He then issued him a privilege, reserving to himself only the consecration of the Abbot—although the Abbot of Monte Cassino was to elect him.”

This Abbot of Monte Cassino was Richerius, a Bavarian by nation. It is said that he had previously been Abbot among the people of Liège, was dear to Emperor Conrad, and came to Cassino in his company; having been elected Abbot in the emperor’s presence in the year 1038, he died in the year 1055, on 11 December.

### 14

Having therefore returned to Rome, “Lord Pope Leo,” says Hermannus Contractus, “again convened a synod at Rome after Easter.” There, according to Wibertus, he “determined that Gerard, formerly Bishop of his own see—that is, of the Leuci,” or Toul, “should be enrolled among the Saints.”

Second, as Blessed Lanfranc, who took part in that Council, writes in chapter 5 of his *Commentary against Berengar on the Body and Blood of the Lord*, while “Leo presided over the Synod, and there sat with him no small multitude of Bishops, Abbots, and religious persons of various Orders from various regions … a sentence of condemnation was issued against Berengar, depriving him of communion with the holy Church, which he had endeavored to deprive of communion with the holy Body of the Lord.”

Then, when “Blessed Lanfranc had set forth his faith, it pleased everyone and displeased no one.”

Third, as Baronius observes from the written *Chronicle of Andrea Dandolo* under this year, “Pope Leo decreed the pallium for Dominicus, the Venetian Patriarch”—rather, the Patriarch of Grado—and granted him the privilege that a cross should be carried before him. He approved the Patriarchal See and wrote to the Bishops of the province of Venice and of Istria that they should obey and honor him as their Primate.

Ughellus, however, in volume 5 of *Sacred Italy*, writes that all these things were done at the Council of Vercelli, held in the same year, and says that the said Dominicus, Patriarch, took part in it.

### 15

In the Strozzian manuscript mentioned above it is said:

> “Saint Pope Leo, pious and gentle, reached Venice for the sake of prayer, to St. Mark the Apostle and Evangelist.”

For, according to Hermannus Contractus, after the Council held at Rome, “proceeding beyond Rome, he subjected certain local princes and cities by oath both to himself and to the Emperor, and excommunicated the Beneventans, who were still in rebellion …”

“In that same autumn Lord Pope convened a Synod at Vercelli and suspended Hunfridus, Archbishop, from office on account of a certain dispute between the Church of Ravenna and the Roman Church.”

Leo himself, in a letter to the princes of Britain, writes that “a Council would take place on the Kalends of September”; and he indicates that “in that same month of September a Synod was celebrated at Vercelli with the Pontiff presiding.” Lanfranc, mentioned above, took part in it. Guitmundus, Archbishop of Aversa, likewise confirms this in Book 1 of *On the Truth of the Eucharist*:

> “When these matters”—Berengar and those adhering to him—“began to be heard, Catholic men were deeply disturbed and could not endure it; and, with the most blessed Pope Leo of revered memory presiding in person, they convened a Council at Vercelli. There, in the hearing of all who had gathered from various parts of the world, John Scotus’s book on the Eucharist was read and condemned; Berengar’s statement was presented and condemned; and the faith of the holy Church was heard and confirmed by the unanimous judgment of all.”

Saint Leo never departed from this judgment in any of his Councils, whether those at which he was personally present or those which he arranged to be convened through his legates in various provinces.

### 16

After these events, says Hermannus Contractus, he “visited Gaul and his own bishopric, the city of the Leuci.” As Wibertus reports, he “transferred the holy remains of Gerard, Bishop of Toul, with the greatest reverence.” We shall illustrate the life of this holy Bishop on 23 April.

At that time Saint Leo brought with him from the monastery of Saint Mansuetus among the people of Toul “Humbertus,” says Lanfranc in chapter 2, “a religious man, perseveringly distinguished by Christian faith and most holy works, highly learned in divine and secular letters.” He ordained him Archbishop “to preach the word of God to the Sicilians,” and afterward the holy Roman Church made him its Bishop and Cardinal.

In the diocese of Toul there is Mount Romaricus in the Vosges, not far from the bank of the Moselle, where Saint Romaricus built a convent for women under the rule of Saint Columbanus. There, says the same Lanfranc in Letter 13,

> “Saint Leo, Supreme Pontiff of the Roman See, dedicated the church of Romaricus in his presence, and completed, without the chasuble, everything which the order required to be done before Mass.”

Joannes Ruerus, in Part 1, Book 4, chapter 12, of *The Antiquities of the Vosges*, asserts that Pope Leo IX, after making Odo Primicerius of the Church of Toul, “enrolled Romaricus, Amatus, and Adelphus in the Catalogue of the Holy Confessors with every honor, solemnity, and reverence.”

In the time of Louis the Pious, their bodies had formerly been raised and transferred to an altar, and afterward deposited in the place indicated by an apparition of Saint Romaricus. These matters will be discussed more fully on their feast days: Saint Adelphus on 11 September, Saint Amatus on 13 September, and Saint Romaricus on 8 December.

At the same time he also “dedicated the church of Saint Arnulf at Metz,” as the *Chronicle of Sens*, Book 2, chapter 18, records.

### 17

Since Saint Leo remained in the transalpine and German territories until February of the following year, many of the events which Joannes Trithemius touches upon under the year 1050 in his *Chronicle of Hirsau* appear to belong here. He writes:

> “This most sacred Pope Leo IX did much good in Germany. In various places he personally consecrated churches, chapels, and altars without number; and what many little pontiffs today are ashamed to do, although they are bound to do it by reason of their office, the Supreme Pontiff did not disdain to do, though he was not bound by obligation.”

Trithemius gives an extensive account under that year of Saint Leo’s visit to Count Adelbert of Calw, Advocate of the monastery of Hirsau, when the body of Saint Aurelius, Bishop of Armenia, was sought out by order of that Pope. The body had formerly been brought there from Rome when the monastery was being built and had been hidden underground during the Norman persecution; it was found in an underground chamber.

Moreover, because the abbey of Hirsau had been vacant since the year 1002, Saint Leo ordered the Count to restore the monks and return everything taken from the monastery. These matters may be examined more fully in the life of Saint Aurelius, either on 25 May, the day of his death, or on 25 August, when his body had formerly been deposited there, or on another day assigned to his cult. Afterward Saint Leo IX was honored as a second Patron of that monastery on account of the illustrious benefits he had bestowed.

### 18

A certain assembly was subsequently held at Augsburg, to which the aforementioned Hunfridus, Archbishop, was summoned. In the presence of the Emperor and other Pontiffs, he was absolved by Pope Leo, who had suspended him from office. Hermannus Contractus indicates that this occurred on 2 February, the feast of the Purification itself, adding that they “departed from one another in charity, and that the Pope returned to Rome.” There, during the solemn celebration of Mass on Easter Day, he freed a demoniac.

“After Easter he convened a Synod at Rome, where, among other matters, he excommunicated Gregory, Bishop of Vercelli, in his absence and without his knowledge, on account of adultery committed with a certain widow who had been betrothed to his uncle, and on account of continual perjury. Yet when Gregory came to Rome not long afterward and promised satisfaction, he restored him to his former office.” Thus Hermannus.

It is believed that the regulations which Peter Damian cites in his letter to Cuntbertus, Bishop of Turin, inserted in *Opusculum* 18, dissertation 2, chapter 7, were established at that time:

> “In a fully plenary Synod, Pope Leo of holy memory decreed that whatever condemned women were found within the walls of Rome prostituted to priests should from that time forward be assigned as slave women to the Lateran palace.”

Also, while he was “situated at Rome,” he chose Odo Primicerius as his successor in the Holy See of the Leuci, as Wibertus writes in the *Acts*.

### 19

The events which Leo of Ostia relates in Book 2, chapter 84, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* belong to this year. His words are:

> “In the following year the aforesaid Pontiff came again to the monastery and solemnly celebrated Mass on the next day and on the day after that, the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul.
