Since that day was a Saturday, he entered at the Brothers’ request and washed the feet of twelve monks; and he himself, in turn, having been washed by them, entered the refectory to drink together with them.”

Here we have the feast of Saints Peter and Paul falling on a Saturday, which occurred in this year, 1051, with Dominical Letter F; this confirms what we stated above.

“From there he proceeded to Benevento and, with kindness, released the city from the excommunication imposed by his predecessor.” Rather, Hermannus Contractus says that in the preceding year he “excommunicated the Beneventans who were still in rebellion.”

It appears that on the same journey he proceeded “to the monastery of Subiaco. Finding the monastery without a superior, he was saddened; and, having held a Council, he appointed Humbertus, brought from France, to that monastery. He summoned the monks of Subiaco to him, examined their documentary records, marked them as extremely false, and had a large part of them burned in his presence. By pontifical command he therefore confirmed the monastery of Subiaco and the whole abbey.”

Baronius reports these matters from the ancient chronicle of that monastery under this year, number 6. The same Pope, by an Apostolic letter dated “the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, in the third year of his Pontificate, Indiction IV,” and sent to John, Archbishop of Salerno, confirmed the metropolitan rights of that same church.

### 20

In this same year Saint Edward, King of England, having made peace with Earl Godwin and intending, in fulfillment of a vow, to travel to Rome, consulted Saint Leo the Pontiff because the nobles of his kingdom were resisting him. The Pontiff released him from his vow and imposed other pious works, in these words:

> “We command you, in the name of holy obedience and penance, to distribute among the poor the expenses which you had prepared for that journey; and either to establish a new monastery of monks in honor of Saint Peter, Prince of the Apostles, or to repair and enlarge an old one; and to provide the Brothers with an adequate supply of food from your revenues. Thus, while they continually praise God there, glory may be increased for the Saints and forgiveness granted to you.”

The rest may be read in our published life of Saint Edward, 5 January, chapters 2 and 3.

## IV. Events of the years 1052 and 1053. His blessed death in 1054

### 21

In the year of Christ 1052, the fourth of his Pontificate, Saint Leo again undertook various journeys. Leo of Ostia appears first to indicate one of them in the chapter cited above:

> “In the following year, coming likewise to Capua, he proceeded again to Benevento, and from there to Salerno; then, in order to drive out the Normans, he went to the Emperor to request military aid.”

Wibertus in the *Acts* suggests another purpose for his subsequent journey toward Germany: namely, to reconcile Emperor Henry and Andrew, King of Hungary, who were at odds. Sigebertus writes under this year:

> “The King of the Hungarians disagreed with the Emperor. To reconcile them, Pope Leo came to the Emperor, but, because friends interfered and aggravated the discord, this proved fruitless.”

Meanwhile Saint Leo accomplished many things on this journey. For “at Regensburg, on 7 October, in the fourth year of his Pontificate,” he issued a diploma concerning the body of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, which was present there. The diploma was addressed to the King of the Franks and to the other prelates and subjects of that kingdom.

This is a difficult controversy, debated by many, especially by those who maintain that this Dionysius the Areopagite is the same man who became the Apostle of the Parisians and was crowned with martyrdom there together with Saints Eleutherius and Rusticus. Others assert that Dionysius the Areopagite was crowned with martyrdom at Athens on 3 October, whereas Dionysius, Bishop of Paris, was killed at Paris nearly two hundred years later, on 9 October, together with Saints Eleutherius and Rusticus; and that his body is there in the monastery of Saint Dionysius. To that place Pope Innocent III also sent, in the year 1215, the body of Saint Dionysius, Bishop of Corinth, as we said in his life on 13 April.

The remaining details may be gathered from Saint Leo’s letter and will require further examination on 3 and 11 October.

### 22

From Wigulejus Hundius alone, Book 1 of *The Salzburg Metropolitan Church*, under Gebhard III, Bishop of Regensburg, we report the following:

> “Under him Leo IX, Supreme Pontiff, summoned by Andrew, King of Hungary, to establish peace with Emperor Henry III, came to Regensburg. He enrolled Saint Wolfgang among the blessed, and likewise Saint Erhard. He also saw, touched, and confirmed by an Apostolic diploma the bones of Blessed Dionysius—concerning which there had long been doubt as to whether they were kept in the church of Saint Emmeram. The diploma is preserved there; and, in the presence of Emperor Henry, Gebhard, Bishop of Regensburg, and many other Bishops and Cardinals, indeed also with envoys of the Parisians present, he approved and confirmed it.
>
> “He likewise consecrated the church of Saint Emmeram, recently devastated by fire, together with its western crypt; he ordered the ceiling of the same church to be made at his own expense; and he also consecrated in that city the chapel of Simon and Jude Thaddeus, adjoining the chapter house above the vault.”

Contradus of Monte-Puellarum, in chapter 2 of the life of Saint Erhard which we published, confirms that “Leo IX transferred the body of Blessed Erhard in the time of Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1052.”

Saint Emmeram is celebrated on 22 September, and Saint Wolfgang on 31 October; both were Bishops of Regensburg.

Hundius continues:

> “When Pope Leo was traveling from Regensburg to Nuremberg, the Counts of Schwarzenburg met him and asked him to dedicate a certain chapel in honor of the Holy Cross, which today is called Prugdorf. The Holy Father, seeing the chapel from a distance, consecrated it.
>
> “When the importunate petitioners thought that they were being mocked by this distant consecration and insisted that he consecrate the chapel in person, the Most Blessed Father said: ‘Go, and unless you find all the signs of a consecrated church, I will come and consecrate your little building in person.’
>
> “When they found everything intact, however, they gave thanks to God and were satisfied. Records of this event still exist today.”

Thus far Wigulejus Hundius. Andreas Bruner embellished all these matters in the second part of his *Annals of Bavaria* in his more elegant style.

### 23

Leo of Ostia, in the place cited above, asserts that “a transfer was then made between the Apostolic Pontiff and the Emperor concerning Benevento and the bishopric of Bamberg.” Hermannus Contractus sets out the matter more fully in these words:

> “The Emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Worms with the Lord Pope and many Bishops and Princes. There, when the Pope, as he had begun long before, demanded from the Emperor the abbey of Fulda and certain other places and monasteries which are said to have been given to Saint Peter in ancient times, he obtained them. Finally, in exchange for the Cisalpine territories, the Emperor handed over to him most of the things belonging to his own jurisdiction in the regions beyond Rome.”

He adds the matters which we reported above from Leo of Ostia:

> “Since the same Pope had complained at length of the violence and injuries of the Normans, who against his will held the possessions of Saint Peter by force, the Emperor also assigned him auxiliaries to drive them out from those territories … The Lord Pope, intending to remove their wicked and inextricable crimes from those regions and to free the inhabitants from them, departed from the Emperor with the greatest affection as he returned to Rome.”

The year 1053 had by then begun. Many Germans followed him, some at the command of their lords, others attracted by the hope of profit; many were also wicked and insolent men, expelled from their homeland for various offenses. He received all of them kindly and gratefully, both out of his customary mercy and because it appeared that he needed their services for the war that was imminent.

Passing through Alemannia, he celebrated the Purification of Saint Mary at Augsburg; he celebrated Quinquagesima at Mantua; and, after a disturbance arose there among some of his men and several were killed, he reached Rome during Lent.

These are the events recorded there. In that year, 1053, Quinquagesima Sunday fell on 21 February. Wibertus writes in the *Acts* that Leo had determined to hold a Council at Mantua, but that it was disrupted by the faction of certain persons.

Hippolytus Donesmundi, in Book 2, page 203, of his *History of Mantua*, describes Leo’s arrival as though he had come to adore in person the sacred blood of Christ preserved there. He says that, after unsuccessfully attempting to obtain permission to carry it away to Rome, he praised the zeal of the people, who turned to sedition in order to retain it; and that he dedicated the new church of Saint Andrew, although it was not yet fully completed. Except for a small portion of the precious treasure—which he brought to Rome for the church of Saint John Lateran—he deposited the remainder, together with the body of Saint Longinus the Martyr, in a place prepared for that purpose.

We discussed the body of Saint Longinus, found at Mantua together with the sacred blood of Christ, on 15 March, in the *Acts of the Two Longini*, section 3.

### 24

Hermannus Contractus affirms that another Synod was held at Rome after Easter, but he does not indicate what matter it concerned. Certainly it was not, as it is printed in the volumes of the Councils, the canonization of Saint Gerard, Bishop of Toul, which took place in the year 1050; nor was it the primacy of the Patriarch of Grado, which, as we showed above from Baronius and Ughellus, took place in the same year, either at Rome or at Vercelli.

We would rather suppose that it was convened because of the heresy of the Fermentarians, which Wibertus says arose at that time, and against which he asserts that Saint Leo wrote a very lucid treatise. This is the first letter in the volumes of the Councils, divided into forty-one chapters.

He also sent to Constantinople as legates of the Holy Roman See Humbertus, then Bishop of Silva Candida; Frederick, later Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and at that time Chancellor; and Peter, Bishop of Amalfi.

Afterward he came from Rome to Cassino, where he restored and established the monastery of Saint Stephen, situated above Terracina, as Leo of Ostia records at greater length in chapter 87.

### 25

Afterward “Pope Leo raised an army against the Normans,” in the words of Hermannus Contractus.

> “When they sought peace and promised him submission and service, saying that they wished, by his favor and grace, to retain the possessions which they had previously invaded and usurped unjustly, the Pope refused. He demanded the return of the possessions of Saint Peter which they had seized wrongfully and ordered them to withdraw from the place they had improperly occupied.
>
> “But because they greatly outnumbered the others, they rejected what was proposed to them as an unjust demand and declared that they would meet him in battle, defend with arms the homeland acquired by arms, or die.
>
> “Thus, engaging in a fierce battle on 18 June, they were almost defeated in the first line by the Germans. But, bringing up reserve forces, they surrounded our men from ambush. The Italians quickly turned their backs, while most of the Germans fell, though not without inflicting losses, by the hidden judgment of God.
>
> “Whether this was because a spiritual rather than a carnal battle over perishable things was more fitting for so great a Priest; or because he was leading with him many wicked men, who had flocked to him for impunity in their crimes or for greedy profit, to fight against equally wicked men; or because divine justice was punishing our men for other reasons known to it—however that may be, the enemies gained a victory excessively bloody for them.
>
> “The Lord Pope himself was besieged in a certain fortress by them. When the fortification was already on the point of being stormed and necessity compelled him, he restored to them the communion which had previously been forbidden. They then received him and escorted him honorably to Benevento. He was detained there for some time and was not permitted to return”—namely, by the Beneventans.

According to Leo of Ostia:

> “Hunfridus, Count of the Normans, approached the Pontiff and, receiving him and all his people under his protection, brought him to Benevento. He promised that whenever the Pope decided to go to Rome, he himself would escort him as far as Capua.
>
> “The Pope entered Benevento in June, on the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, and remained there until 12 March. Having fallen ill there, he summoned the aforesaid Count, who escorted him as far as Capua. He remained there twelve days; then, at last, having summoned the Abbot of Monte Cassino, his companion on the journey, he returned to Rome. There he rested a few days later. At his tomb God performed many signs at that time.”

This is Leo of Ostia’s account. Hermannus Contractus, who survived Saint Leo by only a few months, adds at the end of his *Chronicle* that “he was renowned for miracles.”

### 26

Desiderius, Abbot of Monte Cassino and Cardinal of the title of the Holy Cross, later created Supreme Pontiff in the year 1086 and called Victor III, gives this testimony concerning him:

> “Leo was in every respect an Apostolic man, born of royal stock, endowed with wisdom, distinguished by religion, and thoroughly instructed in every form of ecclesiastical learning. He was one who—as it is written [Genesis 4:26]—began to call upon the name of the Lord. I also saw him and was permitted to enjoy his intimacy. Often, when he celebrated Mass in the church, I stood with him at the divine altar clothed in the sacred vestments, and I read the Gospel to him.
>
> “From him all ecclesiastical studies were renewed and restored, and a new light appeared to rise upon the world. He often summoned a priestly council and removed Priests, Deacons, and other Clerics who had not been regularly ordained, appointing in their places men capable of ministering worthily to the worship of the true and supreme God.
>
> “Every day, through himself and through his disciples sent everywhere, he showed the peoples the way of the Lord by writings and words. Always walking in the Apostolic way, he also imitated the Apostolic men in miracles.”

These are Desiderius’s words, from which we shall relate certain miracles below.

We conclude this preliminary Commentary with the words of Leo of Ostia:

> “This holy Pontiff, among the innumerable marks of his goodness, for as long as he remained in Rome went every week, three days each week, from the Lateran church to Saint Peter’s, at night, singing psalms and praying, wearing ordinary clothing and barefoot, accompanied by two or three Clerics.”

# THE HISTORY OF THE DEATH AND MIRACLES OF SAINT LEO IX

Collected from the Strozzian, Hubertine, and Beneventan manuscripts.

## Prologue

### 1

In the year 1054 of our Lord Jesus Christ, Indiction VII, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, let us rejoice in the deposition of our blessed Father Leo, Pope IX, while Henry the Emperor, son of Emperor Conrad, was reigning at Rome.

> **Note:** The Strozzian manuscript adds several details, namely: “With Monomachus as Emperor of the whole world, and with Dominicus Contarenus reigning as Duke of Venice and Dalmatia, and likewise with Dominicus as Patriarch in the city of the church of Grado, Leo, the blessed Pope, pious and gentle, came, to the praise of Venice, for the sake of prayer to Saint Mark the Apostle and Evangelist, and was received there.”
>
> The dates agree. The aforementioned Contarenus governed from the year 1041 until the year 1069. Saint Leo mentions Dominicus, Patriarch of Grado, in his letter to the Bishops of Venice and Istria; he wished them to be subject to him as their Primate.

For the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ and for the memory of Blessed Leo the Pope, we undertake to make known this labor of the contest which we, all the priests and deacons and all the Catholics of the Holy Roman Church, saw with our own eyes.

We often saw in his life great generosity, as he distributed alms to poor citizens and pilgrims, so that he gave a very large portion of all the treasures of the Church and of everything he was able to possess to widows, orphans, and those who feared God.

Therefore the treachery of the Romans raised murmuring and wars against him. For, so that the Lord might raise up this man as an impregnable wall of his Church against deranged heretics, many had been instructed by him in the study of letters.

This beneficent Bishop Leo gently encouraged the humble; he restrained the necks of the proud; he supplied necessary food to those who disparaged his life; he preached virginity; he defended chaste marriages; he praised with great approval the glorious contests of virtue; he accused Clerics of falling and monks of depravity; and, when circumstances required it, he also mingled examples from the Gentiles with a most pleasing variety.

Yet this was not his desire, but, so to speak, the result of the gravest necessity: namely, to demonstrate the things which had been foretold before the ages by the holy prophets in the languages and writings of the Greeks, Latins, and other peoples. He explained and adorned everything fully, and in every kind of disputation he always proceeded with the same consistency.

When we truly speak of that man’s Catholic knowledge, sound doctrine remains firm in the stability of faith wherever he lived.

> **Note:** In the Beneventan manuscript, with many omissions, the Prologue concludes as follows: “Let us bring forward a few things from the many deeds of this holy man, especially those which occurred as his death approached.”

For we have selected these few passages from his Life; we leave the greater number to the expertise of scholars. Concerning the miracles which we saw, we shall give a faithful account.

## Chapter One  
### Saint Leo’s final deeds and admonitions; his most devout death

### 2

On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, when his body was severely worn down by a grave illness, on the Lord’s Day, the fifteenth day after Easter, he summoned all the Bishops and Clerics to him and addressed them as follows:

> **Note:** Easter was celebrated on 3 April.

> “Listen, my brothers and fellow Bishops: the Lord has called me from this life.”

> **Note:** These matters are set out more fully in the Beneventan manuscript, but almost entirely paraphrastically.

> “
>
> “Remember the evangelical saying: ‘Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come’ [Matthew 25:13].
>
> I ask you, dearest ones, to look upon me and consider how quickly the flowers of this world wither. For I am wretched, having unworthily received the honor of the Apostle Peter, and now, as far as the parts of my body are concerned, I have been reduced almost to nothing.
>
> “This present world is so darkened for me that it is as though I already lived in the darkest house. For last night, in a vision, I saw the world to which I am going; and I seem already not to inhabit this age, but rather that which I foresaw in the vision. Because of this I am exceedingly fearful and afraid.
>
> “I saw many things which I was terrified to see. Yet I rejoiced in our Brothers who were slaughtered in Apulia while fighting for God. I saw them among the number of the Martyrs, their garments shining like gold; all of them held palm branches in their hands, filled with unfading flowers. In a loud voice they called me, saying: ‘Come, remain with us, because through you we possess this glory.’
>
> “Then, from the other side, in reply to one voice, I heard another: ‘By no means; but on the third day he will be in our company, for this is his place, and his seat among us has been happily prepared.’
>
> “If you do not believe my vision, test what I have said. If I remain in this world for more than three days, let this vision be judged empty and vain; but if I depart on the day announced, you must keep everything I say.
>
> “Now let each of you go to your places and come to me at daybreak.”

While many withdrew to their homes according to his command, certain persons remained with him throughout the night. They are said—and the testimony is remarkably confirmed—to have observed that, despite being afflicted by such a massive illness, he spent that entire night awake and, prostrate on the ground, remained in prayer for the flock entrusted to him.

> **Note:** Saint Bruno of Segni gives these and the following words in almost the same language.

### 3

When morning came, and all the Clergy and the entire Roman people had arrived, he ordered them to carry him to his marble tomb in the church. This having been done, he ordered the bed on which he was lying to be brought into the church.

When the Romans saw his tomb being carried to the church, they rushed together toward the Lateran palace to strip it, as was their custom. But such was the merit and power of the Most Blessed Leo that not one of them could proceed or enter the palace. When they saw this, they all returned confused and terrified, with great shame.

Meanwhile, when the most blessed Pontiff had ordered his bed to be carried inside Saint Peter’s church, he summoned all the faithful who were present and commanded them to sit down and listen attentively to his instructions. When they had sat in complete silence, he said:

> “Brothers and fellow servants of our Lord Jesus Christ, remember the commandments of God and walk in good works while you still have light.
>
> “I command that no one dare purchase a villa, vineyard, or piece of land, or any property belonging to the administration of the Holy Church, and retain it for his own use by right of possession. Whoever dares to do this will undoubtedly incur the wrath of the eternal Judge.
>
> “I also command that the practice of swearing be erased from your hearts. For you are known to have committed many perjuries, which I forgave you for God’s sake, although you have fallen into the same sins again.
>
> “Moreover, I charge all of you not to have intercourse with your female relatives.
>
> “I further command that no one offer any impediment to those who come from almost every region to pray to God and to his Apostle for their own salvation and that of all Christians.
>
> “I also command that from all the crops of the earth which God has given you, and from your animals, you give him the first fruits. Unless you do these things, you will not be able to be saved.”

> **Note:** The following material was omitted in the manuscript by a scribe who was hurrying onward to other matters.

### 4

After saying these and similar things to the people, he called all the bishops and clergy to his side. Making a true confession with them, he turned toward the east, and, leaning on his little bed, gazed upon the holy Cross; then, covered with tears, he prayed for a very long time. And releasing from their sins those who had been bound by him canonically, he absolved them—indeed, all the others as well:

“If you preserve what I have commanded you,” he said, “may forgiveness for your former evils be granted to you.” Saying this, he again looked toward heaven and prayed:

“Lord Jesus Christ, Good Shepherd, who yesterday [Note: Thus these things occurred on the day before his death, 18 April; for in this year, 1054, 17 April was celebrated as the Second Sunday after Easter, whose Gospel is this one from John 10.] through your Gospel deigned to say: ‘I am the good shepherd, who lays down my life for my sheep’—[Col. 0528B] you, merciful Shepherd, descended from heaven; you overshadowed blessed Mary with the Holy Spirit; and you wondrously dwelt in her womb alone, whom the whole world cannot contain. For us sinners you assumed the form of a servant, and you chose twelve Apostles, to whom you granted the particular authority to bind and loose. You made the Apostle Peter the foundation of the Church, saying to him: ‘Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven’ (Matthew 16:19).

“You, Lord, said: ‘Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you’ (Matthew 7:7). Therefore I beseech your clemency and ask that, in your accustomed mercy, you deign to grant my petition to me, whom you willed, though unworthy, to sit upon his most holy chair.

“For I ask that you guard your holy Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world; grant it peace; protect and defend it from visible and invisible enemies; and drive away from it every depravity and faithlessness of heretics. I also implore your clemency to grant absolution from all sins to your faithful brothers, our brothers, who shed their blood in defense of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, and to command that you associate them with those who laid down their lives for your name, so that all the faithful may know that you are the faithful rewarder of all good things.

“I also implore your clemency, immense God, to break all the depravity of unbelievers and heretics, so that they may recognize that you, Jesus Christ, are the true God. I also beseech your goodness to deign to absolve the bonds and sins of all who have been anathematized or excommunicated, and make them truly turn to your [Col. 0528D] truth, so that they may know that I acted not from hostility but to confirm the truth of the faith, and that your most merciful blessing may be shown upon them.

“Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your Apostles: ‘Into whatever house or city you enter, say: Peace to this house’ (Luke 9:4), I ask your goodness to grant peace and concord to every city or province through which I have walked, to those who received me for the sake of your peace and blessing and rendered obedience to me in your name. For you said: ‘Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me’ (Matthew 10:40).

“Lord, who, not because of my merits but through your goodness, established me as the Vicar of your Apostle Peter and gave me the power of binding and loosing, deign to bless the male and female servants [Col. 0529B] of the whole province through which I have walked. May those whom I saw with my eyes and blessed bodily be filled spiritually; deign to absolve them from all sins; and make the preaching that I delivered to them fruitful in them. Command the faithlessness of the Jews and heretics to repent, and deign to convert them to you throughout the whole world and make them fulfill your will.

“Grant to all the provinces and cities through which your servant has walked an abundance of grain, wine, and oil, so that they may know that I have walked in your name, just as you commanded the Apostles: ‘Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature’ (Matthew 16:14). I have indeed walked according to your command; I taught, pleaded, and rebuked. You know that all these things were done faithfully. But because you are a merciful Father, deign to turn all your adversaries toward your goodness, so that they may know you as the true God, who are blessed forever and ever.”

Then all who were there answered, “Amen.”

### 5

At that hour such a great fragrance proceeded from the altar of the holy Apostle Peter and filled the entire church that no one among human beings would have thought it anything other than the pleasant fragrance of Paradise.

After this had occurred, he ordered a golden cup, full of bread and wine, to be brought to him. When it had been brought, he ate from it as much as he could take into his mouth [Note: [Col. 0529D] The Beneventan manuscript says: “as much as he could receive into his mouth in three times.”], and ordered it to be given to the bishops present. They likewise ate from it and gave it to all who were standing there.

When this had been done, he raised his eyes toward heaven and prayed privately for approximately an hour. Then, raising his voice, he said softly:

“Great God, Redeemer of the human race, who through your Apostles Peter and Paul commanded Simon’s faithlessness to fall from on high [the supplied text has *de alto* with *cadere* supplied editorially] when your name was invoked: just as you deigned to hear them, so deign to hear me, your servant, and convert Theophylact, Gregory, and Peter, who have strengthened the Simoniacal heresy throughout almost the whole world. Make them recognize the way of truth, so that they may abandon their error and return to you, most gentle Lord.

“For you promised, saying: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live’ (Ezekiel 33:11). Recall them from error, you who converted Paul the persecutor; convert them so that they may know you, the true God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.”

And all those standing around answered, “Amen.”

Again he said to those around him: “Go, children, each of you to your own home, and return to me tomorrow at the first hour of the day.”

Immediately he rose from the little bed on which he had been lying and went to the tomb prepared for him. Leaning over it, he said with tears:

“See, brothers, from such great riches and honors what a small and most vile little dwelling we await. For I, who until now have been filled with such riches and adorned with dignities, await only this marble that you see.”

And raising his hand, he marked it with the sign of the holy Cross:

“Blessed are you among stones, who have been deemed worthy to be joined with me, not by my dignity but by God’s mercy. Receive me with joy, and at the time of recompense present me to the bed of resurrection. For I believe that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and in my flesh I shall see God my Savior.”

And he said this weeping [Note: [Col. 0529D] The same source says: “As he said this, the entire crowd standing there turned to lamentation” [Col. 0530D].]

### 6

Returning to his little bed, he blessed everyone who was there. Some returned to their homes; others remained with him and later reported to us that they had heard him continuing in great prayers throughout the whole night. They had also heard him praying publicly:

“Lord God Sabaoth, look upon me, your servant, and hear my prayer. Through your grace, deign to hear all who truly pray to you. Grant that your preaching may not be empty for all who hear it, but show your truth in us. Wherever your name is invoked through me, your servant, deign to hear those who call upon you, whatever tribulation they may cry out from.

“And if any of the faithful should wish to commemorate my anniversary, whether through churches or through the distribution of alms, deign, Lord, to repay them a hundredfold, and after this age grant them eternal life. I ask this not because of my dignity but because of your goodness; for you said: ‘Ask, and you will receive’ (Matthew 7:7).

“I ask continually that I may be heard by you, so that you may grant grace to the faithful. I knock, so that you may open your doors to me. I do not ask according to my merit but according to your goodness; I do not knock according to my justice but according to your great mercy. I do not ask that my name be exalted, for I am not worthy of such gifts, but that you may deign to exalt the Apostolic See for your name’s sake, Lord, who are blessed forever and ever. Amen.”

### 7

On the following night, certain devout men saw a vision not unlike this one: two men clothed in brilliantly white garments standing before the little bed of the aforementioned Pontiff, holding a document in their hands, speaking with him and writing. They recognized them as truly the Apostles of Christ, Peter and Paul [Note: [Col. 0530D] The same source says: “In the vision itself this was shown to them.”].

When they saw this, they rose from sleep, and the bells began to be rung at the hour of matins. When day had dawned, all the bishops, priests, and deacons, together with the entire clergy and Roman people, having assembled in the church of blessed Peter, he rose from his little bed, supported on either side by two of his attendants, and went to the sacred altar of blessed Peter itself.

There, after prostrating himself on the ground in tears, he prayed for approximately an hour. Returning to his little bed, he ordered silence and admonished the people in a brief address. Then he fortified his body with the sign of Christ’s glorious Cross, called the bishops, made confession, and ordered one of the bishops to sing Mass for him. Receiving the Body and Blood of Christ from him, he said:

“Listen, for the Lord’s sake; keep silence. Perhaps I may be able to get a little sleep.”

And when he had inclined his head upon the bed, he rested for about half an hour. During that rest he fell asleep in peace.

Then one of the bishops rose and touched him, thinking that he was alive. When he realized that he was dead, he announced to all the other bishops who were present that they should pray earnestly to the Lord.

I am about to tell of wonders that the Lord deigned to accomplish through his saints. At the hour when the distinguished Bishop entrusted his soul to Christ, without any attendant striking it, the bell of Saint Peter began to sound of its own accord.

At that same hour, a certain man named Albert and five others from the city of Todi testified that they had seen what appeared to be a roadway adorned with shining coverings and glittering with countless lamps, along which his soul was being led to heaven by angels [Note: [Col. 0531D] Desiderius of Monte Cassino says: “From this unstable light he departed to Christ, who is the true and eternal light, amid the rejoicing citizens of heaven, borne upon angelic hands” [Col. 0532D].]

Thus such stillness prevailed throughout the whole city of Rome at his death that not even a breeze stirred the leaves of the trees slightly.

The most blessed Pope Leo died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May [April 19], on a Wednesday, and was buried in peace. Truly, by his goodness, God made Leo a pious man.

But lest the delay of time overtake me, I shall proceed to what I am going to relate. We have briefly removed these details from the many events of his life; now let us faithfully describe the miracles that the Lord deigned to display through him after his passing.

## CHAPTER II. Miracles after his death up to the Vigil of the Ascension

### 8

On the day after his death, a certain woman from the regions of Tuscany came to the church of the blessed Apostle. When she began to climb the steps, a demon began to torment her and to cry out through her mouth:

“O Saint Leo, why do you drag me bound in fiery chains? I have never harmed you.”

When she had been brought to his tomb, those standing around began to rebuke the demon, saying:

“Tell us, accursed one, how you came here, or from where you acquired such power over Christians to torment them.”

The demon replied:

“I and those who are with me have been sent to overthrow a human soul and to test it until we make it fulfill our commands. When it consents to obey us and serve us, we enter its body as if it were our own house, and we secretly inhabit it for a long time.”

Then some of the priests said:

“Tell us, wicked one: when you secretly inhabit a human body, how do you first harm that person?”

The demon replied:

“First we begin to send into that person sleepiness, sluggishness, and hunger. While he rests in sleep and idleness, we gain the greatest profit. When we have subjected his entire body to our power, it happens that he goes to church and mingles among good and Catholic men. Unable to endure their spiritual eloquence, we begin, stirred to anger, to tear his body, because we can no longer remain hidden.”

Then one of the bishops standing there said:

“I adjure you by him who lives forever and ever to tell us whether Leo, the servant of God and Pope, enjoys any authority among the saints.”

But the demon, with a groan and sigh, said:

“O evil man, why did you name that adversary and deceiver of our whole province? Through him so many people have been overthrown and separated from our fellowship. He also drives us out daily, binds us with chains, and expels us from our dwellings. Thus, wandering, unstable, and for sale, we travel through desolate and barren places and never find rest anywhere.”

The bishop said:

“You do not answer what I asked; instead, you seem to be setting down other matters.”

The demon replied:

“Leo, your Pope and Lord, is truly among the saints, among whom he holds a great triumph. He does not cease persecuting us daily, so that he may destroy our name. Through him I too am to be driven from this house today.”

As he said this, a certain woman among the others, with a treacherous mind, replied [Note: [Col. 0532D] Bruno of Segni and Peter Calo contain much of this material]:

“At the hour when Pope Leo drives out the demons, I shall be queen; and all whom he caused to be killed by the sword I shall immediately bring back to life.”

Scarcely had she finished these words when she suddenly began to be cruelly tormented by the demon. But the woman who had come from the regions of Tuscany was freed from the demon at that very hour.

Then all the people who were present began to be terrified with fear, crying out together:

“Saint Leo, spare us, for we have acted unjustly.”

### 9

At that hour two crippled men came to his tomb. Their knees were knotted and twisted, and their heels touched their buttocks. After coming there, they returned healed, bearing no sign of their former infirmity.

That same day, at the evening hour, a certain mute and deaf man came who had a withered left side and was wholly marked by some kind of apparition. When he had been carried to the sacred tomb, he was released from the bonds that held his body.

Then everyone began to honor God, the author of salvation, with uninterrupted praises, because he worked such great wonders through his holy Pontiff Leo. The Romans, seeing such powers, ran eagerly with candles and offerings, rejoicing and exulting.

### 10

On another day a certain man came from France whose body was compressed by an iron belt, so that a great amount of pus ran down onto the ground all around his body. When those present saw this, they covered their nostrils because of their excessive fear and the stench, beseeching the Lord to deign to assist the wretched man through the merits of Saint Leo.

A marvelous thing occurred: immediately the iron cracked, and, after a great discharge of pus, the man was restored completely to health. At this, everyone rejoiced and began to praise God and his servant, the holy Pontiff, together.

### 11

At that hour the demon, speaking through the mouth of the woman who had earlier said, “At the hour when Pope Leo drives out the demons, I shall be queen, and those whom he caused to be killed by the sword I shall bring back to life,” began to cry out:

“Alas! Alas! Why do we enter and then are forced to leave in torments? We have harmed you nothing, Leo. Why do you not allow us to rest even for one hour?”

The bishops who were present then said:

“Accursed one, return to the place from which you came, and leave her.”

He replied:

“I cannot return to the place from which I came, because she has been sealed. Yesterday I left my own house and received this woman in exchange.”

The bishop said:

“Why, then, are you leaving her of your own accord?”

He replied:

“Because yesterday Leo gave her to me to possess, on account of the blasphemies she spoke against him. Yet he is changeable, and his words are not true: yesterday he gave her to us, and today he will drive us out of this dwelling.”

Then the bishop said:

“From where do you know that he will drive you out today?”

The demon replied:

“Did you see yesterday, when he released the mute woman’s tongue? At that very hour he went with Mark, Bishop of Apulia, and Marcian, Bishop of the Church of Frequentina [Note: [Col. 0533D] These two saints are greatly venerated at Benevento: Saint Mark, Bishop of Lucera and patron of Bovino in Apulia, celebrated on June 14; and Saint Marcian, Bishop of Frigento, celebrated on July 14. Both were under the metropolitan see of Benevento.] [Note: Frequentum, commonly Frigento, a most ancient city of the Hirpini in the Further Principate, is twelve Roman miles from Benevento.].”

The bishop said:

“For what reason did they go?”

The demon replied:

“I do not know, but I know that they are in Apulia, where the Normans fought a battle against the saints.”

The bishop said:

“Are those who were killed there truly holy Germans?”

The demon replied:

“Thirty-five of them have been sanctified. Through them signs and wonders are performed in that place, because they came voluntarily and preferred to fight faithfully for justice. All the others who died there at that time are in Paradise, but because they came unwillingly, they are not counted among those others.

“Those thirty-five also came of their own will and gladly surrendered themselves to death for the sake of the God whom they worshiped; and through them many evils increase among us.”

The bishop said:

“Did those saints come to Rome?”

The demon replied:

“Truly, he said, they will come today with Pope Leo.”

Some of the priests who were present said:

“How shall we know when they come here? Or when shall we be able to recognize them?”

The demon replied:

“They are already near Rome. When they arrive, I shall no longer be able to remain here. Other brothers of mine are also here; when they come, all of us will flee with me. But look at the lamp before his image, and you will recognize the sign of their arrival.”

Then, just as the demon had said, around the fourth hour a great fragrance arose throughout the whole church. When they looked at the lamp, they saw it rise almost to the roof of the church, and with it three lamps also appeared to be burning.

At that very hour the demon began to howl like a wolf, and after tormenting the woman briefly, came out of her. Then those standing around began to praise God and blessed Leo, his servant [Note: [Col. 0533D] The following miracles are recorded more carefully in the Hubertine manuscript; for that reason we take them chiefly from it, comparing them with the Strozzian manuscript.].

### 12

On the third day after the burial of blessed Pope Leo IX, two miracles occurred at his tomb. Two men who had long lain crippled before the doors of the Prince of the Apostles went away upright through the merit of blessed Pope Leo. Nearly the whole city knew this, since it had previously seen them crippled.

A certain woman who had been ill and crippled for sixteen years, lying on a pallet, was carried to his tomb. Because she believed faithfully, she returned from there healed and upright; this too was known to the citizens.

Another woman from the Lateran, named Stephana, the wife of a certain Peter, who had a demon, came to his tomb. There, vomiting blood and rolling about, she expelled three black coals from her mouth. With them the demon also departed, and, having recovered her senses, she returned praising God.

### 13

During the Greater Litany, a lamp at his tomb was kindled by divine fire. This did not happen only once, but twice and three times; and the entire Roman multitude that streamed to the church of blessed Peter that day saw it.

In the district of Merulana [Note: [Col. 0533D] Fourteen districts of the City are named today, commonly called *rioni*. But these were either differently divided then than they are now, or each was subdivided into several parts, of which this may have been, or may still be, one. For just as the district of the Colosseum—the Amphitheater, which can be sought nowhere but Rome—is named below, although it is not one of the said fourteen but belongs to the district of the Mountains, so we persuade ourselves that the other places named here are also districts of the City. We leave their elucidation to Roman citizens, since the diligence of chorographers cannot extend to such minutiae. The Church of Saint Matthew, numbered twenty-two in the district of the Mountains, is called Saint Matthew in Merulana.], a certain woman named Rogata, who had had a demon from infancy, heard of the miracles and came to the tomb. There, lying down, she expelled unclean spirits in this fashion: first a three-headed mouse; second, a little frog; third, a lizard; fourth, a frog; fifth, a hornet [Note: [Col. 0534D] This seems to be used for a larger scarab beetle.]. After a great discharge of blood, she was restored to health, as many witnesses proved not only by hearing but also by seeing.

A certain woman named Stephania, living across the Tiber and tormented by a demon for a long time, heard the fame of the blessed Body and came. She vomited two coals together with much blood. After this had happened, she was restored to health, and all who stood by saw her return freed and in possession of her mind.

In the district of Arenula [Note: [Col. 0535D] The Strozzian manuscript reads “Ternula.”], a certain man named John lived. His nerves were contracted, and he had had a withered hand from his mother’s womb. Coming to the tomb of the blessed man, he carried it back extended and strong.

### 14

A certain man who came from distant regions, bound with iron as a penance, stood before the tomb. While he remained there for a long time, devoted to prayer and weeping over his sins, by the gift of divine mercy the iron cracked at its strongest point.

Likewise, a certain religious woman bound with iron approached the little tomb. In the same manner she was freed from the iron and, blessing the Lord who is wondrous in his saints, returned unharmed to her own home.

In one day two young men were restored to health. One had a twisted mouth turned toward his right ear, and a withered hand together with his entire side. His mother, named Maria, the wife of John Orbitanus, brought him on her shoulders in tears. But, made doubly joyful by the miracle, she returned rejoicing with her son; this man is known to all who live near Saint Angelo.

The other had been deprived from infancy of the use of both hands. Restored to health, he lives by the labor of his hands.

### 15

In the presence of many people, a certain mute man named Guido, born at Casamala, recovered his speech.

A certain boy named Peter recovered the use of his right hand.

A boy from the district of the Colosseum had a withered right hand, together with his entire side and foot. His mother, named Stephania, brought him weeping to the tomb itself; and he was restored to health in the presence and sight of many people.

A certain man named Benedict, a *phlebotomator* [Note: [Col. 0535D] Greek *phlebotomía*, “bloodletting,” hence *phlebotomare* in Bede and others, meaning “to cut a vein”; also *phlebotomatus*, *phlebotomator*, and so forth.], living in the district of the Seven Ways and covered with ulcers, heard of the miracles and came to the tomb. There, through the merit of the blessed Pontiff, he was made well, so that not even a scar appeared on his flesh.

A certain man named Majus, from Palliano [Note: [Col. 0535D] This is a small town of the Roman territory or Campagna.], living across the Tiber and tormented by a demon for fifteen years, heard the fame of the blessed man and came to his tomb. He vomited two little worms [Note: [Col. 0535D] Here *blactulae* seems to mean worms, as a diminutive of *blatta*], together with much blood, and the demon departed with them.

A certain young man named Franco, who had been blind, recovered his sight. He was the nephew of the doorkeeper of Saint Mary of the Rocky Mount.

A certain young man from the city of Tibur, named John, son of John, mute from his mother’s womb, recovered his speech in the presence of many people.

### 16

A certain man named Benedict, living in the Campus Martius, had a son named Gratian [Col. 0536A] who had a withered left foot. Through the merit of blessed Leo he was restored to health and returned joyfully with his father.

A certain man named Peter, son of Nuccius the phlebotomator and an inhabitant of that same district, mute from his mother’s womb, recovered his speech in the presence of many people.

A certain woman from Fallari [Note: [Col. 0535D] A not insignificant town in the territory of Orvieto. The aforementioned city of Falerii was formerly an episcopal city near the city of Civita Castellana, and is now subject to its bishop [Col. 0536D].], tormented by a demon, came to the tomb and was freed there.

A certain woman from Acquapendente, who had a withered hand, heard of the miracles and came to the place; she recovered the use of her hand.

A certain man born in the regions of Tuscany, who had a withered hand, was restored to health through the merit of blessed Leo.

A certain woman named Maria, living in the fort of Cornazzano, who had a withered left hand, came to the tomb and was healed there.

Another woman, named Beatrix, from the regions of Apulia, who had a withered right hand, was likewise restored to health.

A certain young man there recovered his sight through the merits of blessed Leo.

A certain woman named Ermengarda, widow of Peter the weaver from the village of Castro [Note: [Col. 0536D] In the Sabine territory there is a place called Vico di Sarrento; its proximity to the city of Rome makes it preferable to the other places bearing the same name.], who had a withered left hand, recovered the use of it through the merit of Pope blessed Leo, in the presence of many people.

## CHAPTER III. Miracles performed from the Vigil of the Ascension until beyond the Octave of Pentecost

### 17

On the Vigil of the Lord’s Ascension, three women were healed through the intercession of the most blessed Pope Leo: one recovered the use of her hand, another her hearing, and another her sight.

During the night vigil of the Lord’s Ascension, a certain woman named Berta, servant of Peter the craftsman, who is called “of Udo,” living in the district of Campitello [Col. 0536C] [Note: [Col. 0536D] This is one of the fourteen named districts, and the first among them. It derives its name from the Capitol, which it includes; the name has been corrupted in the form commonly used, *Campidoglio*, for *Capitolio*.], who had a demon, was freed there.

During the same night vigil, a certain woman whose name we do not know recovered the use of both hands, which she had kept contracted.

After this, a remarkable miracle occurred there. A certain John of Civita, living in the district of the Campus Martius, took into his hand a candle lit from the tomb of that most blessed Pope Leo and extinguished it. While he held it securely extinguished, he suddenly saw it alight. Thinking that he had not extinguished it properly, he extinguished it again. But who can investigate the miracles of God? It again lit itself in his hand.

This candle was also preserved as a testimony.

### 18

On the day of the Lord’s Ascension, a girl named Amata [Note: [Col. 0536D] The Strozzian manuscript reads “Amriata.”], born to a father named Engelbert, was healed. They were from the region of Campania, from Rocca di Risa. She had been so crippled that she had never walked on her feet.

Another girl, named Maria, daughter of Cica, who lived in the district of Arenula, recovered her sight; she had not seen for fifteen years.

A boy born to a peasant father, from the city of Orte, was so crippled that he had no control over one side of his body. But the Lord healed him through the merit of the most holy Pontiff. Having recovered the use of his side, he made a vow to him with his rejoicing father and returned unharmed.

It was nearly the middle of the night when he wonderfully healed two blind men. One was called Pipo, the other Adelbert. They were from the city of Lama [Note: [Col. 0537D] Perhaps Larino, a city of Capitanata in the kingdom of Naples; elsewhere in the same Capitanata is Torre della Lama.].

He also healed a certain man named Randifus, son of Berard, Count of Marsica, who had been struck by a lance and so contracted that he could not place one foot on the ground. But, at God’s command, he departed healed through the merit of the blessed Pontiff.

A certain girl had been so completely crippled in her hands and feet that she could never walk or bring her hand to her mouth. Through the merit of blessed Leo she recovered the use of her limbs and departed healed.

### 19

On the day after the Lord’s Ascension, two women who were tormented by an unclean spirit were restored to their former health through the merit of the holy man.

A certain woman, servant of Amantius the Deacon, went to wash the quilt-covering—an extraordinary and unheard-of miracle—which properly belonged to the bed of blessed Pope Leo. While wringing water from it, she held it between her legs, and the middle part of her body became numb, as if she had paralysis. But another affliction came upon this evil: for she appeared to be covered with ulcers on that same part of her body.

She came to the tomb of blessed Leo and departed healed.

### 20

A certain girl named Rogata, daughter of Maria, came on the seventh day, when the month of May was beginning, on the fourteenth day of that same month, to his venerable tomb, carrying a contracted left arm. Through his holy intercession she obtained the benefit of health. She was from a place called Stabla [Note: [Col. 0537D] I believe this to be what is commonly called Castellammare di Stabia, a town of the Papal territory on the Bay of Naples.].

A certain man from the city of Florence came blind to the tomb of that most blessed Leo, together with his servants. With divine grace accompanying him, he recovered his sight; and, because of the great joy he received from this, he granted those same servants their freedom.

A certain Roman named Adelbert was cutting back his vineyard with an iron tool when he happened not to shrink from speaking disgracefully about the apostolic lord Leo. But this crime did not pass without punishment: for an evil spirit suddenly entered his body and began to torment him severely. This happened while Leo was still alive.

But, by divine grace, after Leo’s death Adelbert came to his tomb and was healed through Leo’s merit.

### 21

A certain man named Grimoald, from Saint Benedict of Monte Cassino, came to the tomb of the blessed Pontiff on the Sunday called Rose Easter [Note: [Col. 0537D] Thus the Italians call Pentecost. The authors of the *Vocabolario della Crusca* explain the name by saying that roses generally bloom around that time.]. He was so mute through illness that no one could understand his speech. But, by God’s gracious favor, he recovered clear speech through the merit of blessed Leo.

A certain boy from Verona, crippled in both feet, was healed there through God’s accompanying grace and the merit of the blessed man, and returned with his parents.

A certain woman from Acquapendente was freed from a demon on that same night called Rose Easter.

A certain boy named Petrunculus, from Siena, came to the tomb with his parents. He was crippled in both feet and hands. When, at the request of the Sienese who had brought him for the reward of his soul [Note: [Col. 0537D] More clearly below, no. 36: “for the benefit of his soul.”], I raised him upright at the tomb of the blessed Pontiff, he suddenly recovered the use of his limbs before my eyes and in the presence of the entire people [Col. 0538B].

A certain priest named Franco, from the town of Cora [Note: [Col. 0538D] Commonly Cori, a town of the Roman Campagna.], had been tormented for five years. When he was brought to the tomb of the same most holy man on the Sunday called Rose Easter, he immediately vomited out the demon with blood and fell dead upon the ground.

When all the people wished to carry him away because they saw that he was lifeless, by God’s gracious favor he returned to life, healed through the merit of blessed Leo. All the people who were present gave thanks to the Lord and the saint.

### 22

A certain man named Benedict brought his daughter, named Bona, to the tomb of the blessed Pontiff so that she might recover her health. Her two hands were contracted. But, by God’s gracious favor, she recovered the joys of health through the merit of the blessed Pontiff.

In the Marsican village of Monte [Note: [Col. 0538D] Today two places called Marsico are known on the borders of the nearer and farther Principate, one old and one new. I believe the old one is intended here, since the chorographers of the kingdom of Naples place the new one on a river.], there was a woman from the city of Spoleto who had been blind for a long time. While she sought the tomb of the blessed man for the sake of prayer, in the Sabine bishopric, before she reached the place where his body rests, she received her sight through the merit of the holy Pontiff and joyfully completed the journey she had begun.

A certain five-year-old boy from the aforementioned city, deprived from birth of walking and speech, was brought to the Saint’s tomb with the help of his parents. Through his merit he recovered both walking and speech at the same time.

Likewise, another boy from the same territory, seven years old, had been deprived of the use of his feet for three years. But when he approached the tomb of the Bishop, he was suddenly raised upright through his merit.

A certain boy named Leo [Note: [Col. 0538D] The Hubertine manuscript reads “a certain poor man”; that manuscript ends here, so the remainder comes only from the Strozzian manuscript.], from Monte Cassino, came on that same Sunday so lame that he could in no way walk without two supporting crutches. But through the merit of the blessed Pontiff he returned carrying the health of his limbs with him, without a guide and after throwing away his crutches.

A certain boy whose two feet had been contracted was wondrously stretched out before the people. Immediately, although he had never walked, he began to run toward the shrine of Saint Peter. The innumerable multitude who were present gave immense praises to the Lord God and Saint Leo.

### 23.

On the thirty-second day after the burial of the same Pontiff [Note: This would have been the very eve of Pentecost, and this miracle ought to have preceded some of the foregoing material], a certain mute man from the Castellan episcopate, from a parish of that same episcopate called Graciolum, came to the tomb of the aforesaid Pontiff. There, in the presence of his own bishop and of many who knew him, he recovered the power of speech; the consecrating bishop, who knew him well, is a witness to this event.

[Note: In the year 1033, Benedict, Bishop of Fallariana and Castellana, subscribed a privilege of Benedict IX [Col. 0539D] (for these sees were united and remained so, the designation of the former see, already deserted by that time, having been abolished). Later Ughelli, in volume I of *Italia sacra*, lists three bishops of the city of Castellana, all named Peter, although no reasonable basis for distinguishing them is apparent. For the first, who is found subscribing the Roman Council in 1059, by the initial letter P of his name, and the last, whose final recorded memory extends to the year 1183, comprise only twenty-four years, which could easily have been filled by one and the same man. Indeed, even if this was the same man as the one indicated here, an episcopate of thirty-two years would not be incredible.]

A certain old monk from Monte Cassino, named John, was mute, deaf, blind, and afflicted by paralysis of his right hand. He bore these ailments in his body for nine years. But when he learned that the miracles of our most holy Confessor, Pope Leo, were being proclaimed daily, he made a vow to him in his heart: if the blessed Pope should save him through his prayers, he would come to his tomb with lights. After he had said this, he was suddenly visited by divine grace and recovered the former health of his body. Thus he appeared healthy, as though he had never suffered these infirmities. When he saw himself restored, he fulfilled the vow that he had made to the Lord and to the most holy Confessor, came to his tomb, and rendered him praise. Together with all the people who were present there, he joyfully proclaimed how God, through His Confessor, had deigned to restore his former health.

A certain man named Peter, from the city of Gaeta, brought his little son John, whose left side, together with his hand, had been withered for seven years, to the fame of the most holy Leo, coming with the boy to obtain healing. When the son kissed the tomb and the father wept, the boy, visited by divine grace, recovered his former health and joyfully returned home with his father.

### 24.

An old woman named Maria Marsicana, from the village of Alvo, had been tormented by a demon for thirty years. But on the Monday immediately following Pentecost, at the ninth hour of the day, she vomited out the demon in the form of a fly. Another woman, named Berta, from the territory of Saint Benedict, on the same day and at the same hour, likewise vomited out a demon with a foul discharge. Thanks be to God and to the most holy Pontiff, who restored her to health.

### 25.

A certain little boy who had been blind for a long time received his sight at the ninth hour on the octave of Pentecost. His father was called Arnulfus, and he was from the territory of Saint Benedict.

A certain man named Lodoicus, from the territory of Forcone, came to the tomb of the most blessed Confessor with his son, who was crippled at the knees. While they were sitting beside the tomb, with the father praying and weeping, our most holy Pope suddenly bestowed upon them the gifts of healing. Thus the boy, who had never been able to walk without sticks, threw them aside and, before all the people who were present, began to go firmly and run from the altar of Saint Peter. Together with his father, he offered praise to the one who had healed him through the merits of Blessed Leo.

On the same day a certain woman, who had long been grievously tormented by a demon, arrived. When she kissed the tomb, the ancient enemy immediately abandoned the dwelling of her body through a vomiting of blood, and she recovered her health. She was from the territory called Camerino [Note: This is an episcopal city in the March of Ancona].

A certain girl named Laeta, whose left hand had been paralyzed, reached the tomb with her mother, by God’s accompanying grace. When she touched the Saint, she suddenly recovered, sound, the hand that she had lost through paralysis.

### 26.

There was a certain woman in the city of Rome who bought and sold pepper and incense. When a simple man from the regions of Croatia came, he bought incense from this woman to carry to the tomb of Blessed Pope Leo. Having been poisoned by the woman’s spells, he paid a denarius, and it seemed to him that he had received a great quantity; in fact, he had received nothing.

When he proceeded to the tomb, he rose from prostrating himself in prayer and put his hand into the pouch to take out the incense. He found that it contained nothing. Then he began to cry out in a loud voice, saying:

“O Saint Leo, you wished to remain among the Roman heretics! If I return to my own house, I shall speak the greatest blasphemies against you unless I am avenged upon that wicked and unjust woman for her sorcery.”

That same day, while the woman was in the portico conducting her evil business, she put her hand into her pouch to sell pepper and found it full of little snakes. She withdrew her hand, wounded by them. Recognizing her guilt, she ran to the tomb of Blessed Leo and openly confessed her deeds before all the people.

When all who were present saw that the woman’s hand was entirely wounded by the snakes, they were struck with great fear and amazement. The woman, unable to endure the pains, cried out in a loud voice:

“Saint Leo, most blessed Pope, forgive me, a wicked woman, and free me from the torments of these snakes by which I am cruelly tortured!”

Then the man who had bought the incense from her, seeing this, began to say:

“You are worthy, most blessed Leo, of great honors, since you protect those who come to you and restrain the deeds of the wicked. I rejoice in the power of your triumph. Please do not become angry with me, unworthy as I am, because I spoke wickedly against you. Have mercy on me.”

The woman, however, did not cease crying out:

“Saint Leo, help me! Have mercy, and free me from these torments that I suffer. For I promise that never again will I practice the evil business I have conducted.”

While she said these things with tears, and the others who were present, together with that simple man, prayed for her, divine clemency came to her aid and freed the woman from the plague. Having fully recovered her health, she gave the man three times what she had previously taken from him. All who saw and heard this blessed God and Saint Leo, His servant.

## Miracles Performed at Benevento

Partly published by Ferdinand Ughelli from the Beneventan Manuscript among the bishops of Benevento, and partly received from the Strozzian Manuscript.

### Ughelli’s Preliminary Notice

### 27.

It must not be passed over that, while Walderic was bishop [Note: According to Ughelli, Valderic was consecrated bishop by Saint Pope Leo at the beginning of July in the year 1053. He adds that a notable bull was then granted to him for the confirmation of the churches subject to him], Pope Leo IX, the Supreme Pontiff, departed for heaven. After his death, when he had become renowned for many miracles, the people of Benevento built within the city walls a church in the name of that most holy man, who had deserved so well of them and of their city [Note: Some, following Baronius, write that the Emperor Henry II offered Benevento to Pope Leo IX, so that in this way the annual payment customarily made by the Church of Bamberg to the Roman Church might be compensated. Thus Ughelli in his preface on the metropolitan church of Benevento; we have also treated this matter here in the *Prolegomena*, no. 23]. They began to honor it every year with solemn ceremony and display. They also caused several of the miracles performed in the Beneventan region through his merits to be committed to writing.

When our Coelestinus found these accounts written in Lombard script in a very ancient codex in the Beneventan library, he transcribed them faithfully and sent them to me, so that we might present them here to readers for the increase of piety. We gladly did so, since they contain certain matters omitted by others who committed the life of the most holy Pontiff to writing. The author is anonymous and a contemporary of Leo.

## History of the Miracles

### 28.

When the widely disseminated fame of the miracles of the blessed Leo had spread, a church began to be built at Benevento in his honor, so that the citizens of Benevento, who had seen him alive while he was detained in prison by the Normans, might venerate him now dead and enjoying the heavenly expanses.

Meanwhile it happened that a certain Nicholas from the Castle of Molliniana and Berardus from the place called Carrara—one of them having lost his right arm, with his hamstrings and tendons contracted, and the other suffering chills and fever progressing to dysentery—had themselves carried to the aforesaid church, which was being built at Benevento. Immediately, by everyone’s judgment, they recovered the health that had been despaired of [Note: This double miracle is also related in the Strozzian Manuscript [Col. 0542C]. The first place is called Marca there, the second Carre. These locations seem to be sought near Benevento; otherwise, Carrara and Modigliana belong to the duke of Tuscany].

### 29.

A certain peasant from the town of Ordonum [Note: Perhaps Ortana, of which there are two: one by the sea, in the nearer Abruzzo; the other in the farther Abruzzo, called Marsorum], who annually celebrated the feast of Blessed Leo as a vow, happened, because of the excessive burden of the labor he was performing in the fields, not to go to church on Sunday, when the festivals are announced to the people.

The feast day of Saint Leo, however, was on the following Thursday [Note: Perhaps in the year 1061, with Dominical Letter G; thus this final miracle would have occurred after the others that are about to be added from the Strozzian Manuscript]. The peasant did not know this. Rising very early, he took with him a little boy, his only son, as well as an axe and a digging rake. As soon as he reached his field, he sent the boy to look after the baggage, while he anxiously began to dig.

From the other side, a wolf, with its mouth open, seized his little son and took flight. Seeing this from a distance, the father began to run after the wolf, crying:

“O Saint Leo, my patron, help me now in this present moment and restore to me my only son!”

He had scarcely spoken when, behold, the wolf released the boy so unharmed that not even a trace of the wolf’s teeth could be seen on his clothing where the wolf had seized him.

The peasant returned to the town and recounted all these things. Realizing that this was the anniversary commemorating Blessed Leo, he bound himself by a new vow to observe it solemnly every year.

Thus the name of Leo became renowned not only at Benevento but along the entire coast of Apulia. God so ordained it that, in those same places where, a few years earlier, after his army and that of the Church had been defeated, he himself had been held captive, the very people who had stood against him in battle later, as the fame of his miracles spread, cultivated his memory as suppliants and reverent worshipers, and showed themselves increasingly faithful toward the holy Church—to the praise and glory of almighty God, whose name is thus blessed throughout all ages. Amen.

[Note: Up to this point, from the Beneventan Manuscript; now from the aforementioned Strozzian Manuscript.]

### 30.

These are the miracles that God wished to perform through the blessed Leo, His servant, at Benevento.

A certain man named John, from a castle called Serra [Note: There are also two places called Serra in Capitanata, one surnamed Capriola and the other della Castagna. The latter is about forty Roman miles from Benevento, the former about thirty], was afflicted with pain in the head from some cause. Specifically, while he was threshing barley in a threshing floor, a single grain of that crop flew into his eye, covering it with darkness so that he could not see the light. The power of God and of Saint Pope Leo first healed him at Benevento, restoring his sight.

[Note: Here the miracles related above concerning Nicholas and Berardus, or Bernardus, who were healed, had been inserted.]

Likewise, a certain little boy whose arm had been paralyzed up to the shoulder, with the tendons stiffened, for seven years, came to the church being built at Benevento in honor of Blessed Pope Leo and, through the mercy of God and the prayers of Leo himself, recovered his former health.

Another John, from a region of a certain city called Vico [Note: Perhaps Vito; for geographical maps mark, between Troia and Benevento, the town of Saint Vito. They also mark Vico, but at four times the distance, toward the sea and the outermost boundaries of Capitanata], suffered paralysis and lost the use of his tongue, arms, and other limbs for three years. He could not walk in any way except by crawling along the ground with the aid of little stools. Yet in that same church he recovered his former health.

Again, another John, from a castle called Celone [Note: Could this be Celano, by Lake Fucino, which now bears that name in the farther Abruzzo?], struck his mother contrary to God’s law. By divine vengeance he lost four toes and two fingers through the bite of a crab, and the tendons of his legs also contracted, so that he could not stand upright but walked with bent knees toward Benevento. He was healed on the way.

### 31.

Likewise, a certain woman named Uzancia of Benevento, of a certain cleric named Balzanus [relationship unspecified in the text], happened perhaps by chance to fall from her bed. As a result of the fall, her leg became so paralyzed that she could not walk at all and lay sick in bed for three years. At last, when she invoked the aid of Blessed Leo, she was immediately restored to [health] [Col. 0543C]. At once she went to the aforesaid place, where the church was being built in his honor, and gave thanks to God and to Blessed Leo.

A girl of a noble woman had lain sick in bed for one year and could neither walk nor leave her bed unless supported by the arms of her attendants. When his blood was found and carried with hymns and praises into the church of the episcopal see, she was brought there and prostrated before the altar of the holy Mother of God; immediately she rose and walked.

[Note: We read nowhere else of the discovery of this blood. Perhaps it had been preserved at Benevento by someone after a bloodletting and had subsequently been forgotten.]

A certain boy named Dominicus, from the castle of Vicari [Note: Elsewhere called Biccaro, near Troia, about eighteen Roman miles from Benevento], possessed by a demon, came to Benevento, led by his mother. The demon had deprived him of the use of his tongue, so that he would not speak unless beaten very severely, and then only two or three words at most. Through the merit of Blessed Leo he was restored so completely that he spoke correctly and fluently.

### 32.

From the territory of the city called Saint Agatha [Note: Besides the two towns of this name in farther and nearer Calabria, there is a third in Capitanata, not far from Lesina and near the sea. It is much less distant from Benevento than those two, although still no less than forty Roman miles away], which borders on Benevento, it is related that a young man named Nicholas, while cultivating vineyards with his father and brother after the month of May had passed, suddenly fell to the ground, having lost the use of his tongue and all his other limbs.

His father and brother, deeply grieved by this event, began to weep. Then they found a donkey, placed him upon it, and led him home. On the following day, having adopted better counsel, they placed him again on a bed and brought him to Benevento, to the church mentioned above. There, through the merits of Blessed Leo, he was restored to perfect health. Thus he who had come mute and had been carried on the shoulders of others returned home—speaking of God’s mighty works, healthy and joyful, walking swiftly on his own feet—to the castle from which he had come, called Torrelicosi [Note: The geographical maps simply call it Torre; it is very near the town just mentioned, on the seashore itself].

A woman from the region of the city of Murrone [Note: Commonly Morrone, across the Apennines in the county of Molise], who had been tormented by several demons, heard reports of the miracles of Blessed Leo and conceived a hope—which was not disappointed—that if she came to the aforesaid basilica, she would be healed of the demon. She did so. While she was standing [before the altar], the demon that had been accustomed to deceive her flew away from her shoulders like a raven and never again tormented her. By the favor of God’s grace and the intercession of Blessed Leo, she was freed from the demon.

### 33.

A certain man, originally from a city called Confinia [Note: Nicolaus Samson, in the alphabetical table of the places of Italy, calls it the castle of Confidiani, in the Kingdom of Naples], heard the fame of Leo’s signs and came to Benevento with others from the same place. Through the intercession of Saint Pope Leo, he obtained the health he had lost.

A certain man [crippled in the arm], after spending six days in the aforesaid church, was overcome by sleep. But a crowd of people forced him to flee and remain awake. Having stayed awake, he rose and felt that divine aid had been granted to him. For he began to stretch out the arm that, with its tendons contracted, he had kept bound to his neck; he moved it this way and that and performed with it, easily, the tasks he had been accustomed to perform. When those present saw this, they blessed almighty God and Saint Leo.

Again, one young man and two girls obtained healing there on the feast of Blessed Augustine. One of the girls was from the city of Monopoli, the other from the city of Frequentina [Note: We discussed Frequentina above, at no. 11, section c. Monopoli is also an episcopal city between Bari and Brindisi, on the Adriatic Sea].

The young man and the girl who came from Frequentina had lost the sight of their eyes for five years. But through God’s merciful generosity and the intercession of Blessed Leo, both began to see on the same day, as well as they ever had. The girl from Monopoli, who had entirely lost the use of one side of her body, likewise recovered her health through the merits of Saint Pope Leo.

The whole city of Benevento gathered to witness this spectacle and was a witness to these three miracles, while it resounded with hymns of praise to God and thanksgivings in loud voices.

### 34.

A certain woman from the territory of Benevento had an only daughter who, from infancy, had been deprived of the use of her hands and feet. With all her tendons contracted, she could neither walk nor perform any task with her hands. When the mother heard reports of the miracles that Christ, through His servant, the most holy Leo, had deigned to perform in the aforesaid church, she placed her daughter upon a little donkey and had her carried there.

After she had remained lying there for six days, while many others were restored to health and she herself obtained no benefit, she said to her mother:

“Mother, since our sins outweigh the merits of the Saint, let us leave here quickly. We are unworthy to obtain healing from him.”

Her mother immediately placed her upon the little donkey, and they began to make their way home.

Truly, the merciful Lord never rejects those who ask Him, and He glorifies His Saints in every manner. For when they had gone about five stadia from the church, and the mother had paused briefly, she wished the donkey on which she was sitting to pause. The support holding her arm and hand fell to the ground. Immediately, forgetting her infirmity, she threw herself to the ground like a healthy man after her staff, in order to pick it up again and remount the donkey.

But when her feet touched the ground, she felt the power of Christ come upon her so greatly that, when her mother arrived, she found her entirely healthy, standing beside the donkey on unhindered feet and with her whole body upright, praising the heavenly Healer in a clear voice.

They immediately returned to the church of Saint Pope Leo, from which they had departed, and openly proclaimed the power of the Lord to those who met them. There they gave thanks and praise to Christ and to Saint Leo, while the people marveled and praised the grace, glory, and power of Christ Himself.
