For, as He wills, He glorifies His Saints everywhere, so that they may always deserve to receive the praises of human beings and, with Him, be glorified without end in heaven among the angels. Amen.

## Two Miracles

Described by Desiderius, abbot of Cassino and later Pope Victor III.

### 35.

After the death of the most blessed Pontiff Leo, many great miracles became manifest through him, by the Lord’s granting, at his tomb and in other places. Omitting the rest, I shall relate only two for the sake of edification, just as they were reported to us by truthful men.

Pope Victor [Note: This is Victor II, elected after the See had been vacant for nearly an entire year, on 13 April 1055; he died on 28 July 1057. The miracles related above, however, were performed while the See was vacant, when Victor was absent: he was then Bishop Gebhard of Eichstätt in Germany], who had succeeded him in the priestly governance, did not believe the reports of his miracles—that the Lord worked such things through him.

But because, as the Apostle says, “Tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers” (1 Cor. XIII), almighty God wished to teach him by experience what he stubbornly refused to believe when told by many.

### 36.

A certain Bishop of Chur, whose name has slipped from memory [Note: Namely, Diethmar, who was made bishop among the Rhaetians in the German Alps in 1040 and died in 1070, having presided, according to Bruschius, laudably and most usefully for thirty years. See also Guillimannus, book IV *On the Affairs of the Swiss*, chapter 2, and others], came from Germany with the aforementioned Pontiff Victor and remained in Rome in his service.

This bishop had a boy who had been mute from his mother’s womb. He fed and clothed the boy for the sake of his own soul’s reward and was accustomed to take him with him wherever he went. In the boy’s empty mouth there seemed to be not even the slightest indication of a tongue.

The bishop, like the Pope, also maintained an incredulous attitude toward the miracles at Blessed Leo’s tomb. When one day he had already received permission and decided to return to the seat of his bishopric, he entered the church of the blessed Apostle Peter for the sake of prayer. After commending himself earnestly to Saint Peter, together with his attendants, he mounted his horse and hastily left the City by the road leading to his homeland, forgetting the boy in the same church.

When he had gone a considerable distance from the City, he suddenly remembered that he had left the mute boy in Saint Peter’s church. He immediately stopped and sent back some of his servants to bring the boy.

When they had left the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, they saw the boy standing before the tomb of Saint Leo and speaking with those who were standing around it. As they marveled and asked how this had happened, the boy said:

“After my master left me in this church and departed, I came here to the tomb of Saint Leo, in case almighty God might deign, through his merits, to restore to me the faculty of which I was deprived. I have not been cheated of the wish I sought in my heart. As soon as I had lain prostrate for a little while, weeping, before his venerable memory, I immediately rose with my voice restored and speaking, as you yourselves see.”

From that day onward—and this is even more marvelous—the tongue that had been missing began gradually to grow in his mouth, so that within a few days he fully recovered a tongue and uttered words without impediment.

[Note: Saint Bruno also relates this same miracle, having received it from the Bishop of Porto.]

Finally, those who had been sent arranged to lead the boy to the bishop. The one whom the bishop had left behind silent, with Blessed Leo’s merits assisting him, they brought back speaking.

The bishop therefore returned and approached the Roman Pontiff, showing him what almighty God had deigned to perform through Blessed Leo. From that time they themselves began to proclaim his venerable merits to everyone—those whom, when others had previously recounted them, they had refused to hear.

### 37.

The illustrious man Maximus, a citizen of the city of Rome, recently told me what I am about to relate concerning the same venerable Bishop.

There was a certain soldier named Bernardus, of the most wicked disposition, who displayed himself as opposed to the Apostolic See in every way he could. But in the war fought against the neighboring inhabitants around Rome, who had conspired with Cadalaus, Bishop of Parma [Note: Cadalaus was elected Antipope against Alexander II in the year 1061, as we stated on 2 February, in section 3, concerning the Life of Blessed Peter Damian, § 5], who was then attempting to invade the Apostolic See, Bernardus was pierced and killed among the soldiers defending the Roman Church, by the just judgment of God.

After hearing the fame of the miracles that almighty God displayed through the merits of Blessed Leo for faithful peoples, he not only refused to believe them but also ridiculed and blasphemed them with his sacrilegious mouth.

One day, when he appeared in a gathering of the people and conversation arose among them about the signs and powers of Blessed Leo, he began to laugh, saying:

“If he is a Saint, as you say, let him contract one of my fingers.”

Those standing by restrained him from speaking such things about a holy man. The gathering then broke up, and he departed.

Then, as it happened, a dog that was following him attacked a pig it found in the street. To prevent the pig from being torn apart, Bernardus ran up quickly and tried to seize the dog by putting out his hand. But the pig, opening its mouth, bit his finger. From that day for the rest of his life he had the finger contracted and could not extend it in any way.

Thus it came about that the man who had dared to ridicule God’s servant was himself regarded by everyone as an object of derision because of his contracted finger.

Let this suffice concerning that great Father, Blessed Leo, since we are hastening to relate the deeds of others.

## Notice Concerning Saint Leo from *Gallia Christiana*

*(Volume XIII, p. 985.)*

Hugh, the father of Bruno, was a cousin of the Emperor Conrad, surnamed Salicus. Bruno’s mother was Heilewidis, or Helvidis, no less noble. They were alike in piety and devoted their very considerable patrimony, following the example of their ancestors, to founding monasteries and assisting the needy.

From their estates they established three religious houses: Hissé, in honor of Saint Martin, near Sarrebourg, for nuns; another for men, under the title of Saint Cyriacus the Martyr, at Altorf; and another for girls, under the title of the Holy Cross, namely Woffenheim in Alsace, near their castle of Engesheim. For the benefit of this foundation, Bruno himself, after being raised to the summit of the pontificate, granted it a bull.

The foundation of the Priory of Saint Quirinus in Alsace is attributed to Bruno’s brother or sister; John of Bayon holds that it was founded by Louis, Bruno’s maternal grandfather.

The monastery of Lutry in the diocese of Besançon owes the greatest debt to this noble family, as is read in the Life of Bruno, written under the name of Pope Leo IX by Vipertus, who speaks as follows:

“The father of Bruno, a German by nation and a cousin of the Emperor Conrad; their fathers and grandfathers, casting aside all pride of lineage, assumed the monastic habit with complete contrition of heart and departed with a praiseworthy end in all things . . . They also enlarged the monastery of Sutrensis with their patrimonies.”

Bruno was born in a castle of Alsace called Engesheim, his entire body marked with the signs of the cross, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July in the year 1002.

When he reached the age of five, his pious mother Helvidis, who had nursed him herself, entrusted him to Bertold, Bishop of Toul, to be educated and instructed in letters. At that school he had two relatives as fellow students, older than he, both named Adalbero. One, the son of Duke Theoderic, died prematurely; the other, the brother of Duke Hezelon, became the teacher of his young kinsman Bruno.

When both had distinguished themselves in the humanities and philosophy, they devoted themselves to the study of jurisprudence.

One night, while Bruno was sleeping in the castle of Engesheim among his parents, whom he had gone to visit, a poisonous frog settled upon his face and poured its venom into his blood. The illness increased so severely that no hope of recovery remained.

By chance, while Bruno was awake during the night, he believed that he saw Saint Benedict carrying a cross in his hand; with it the Saint dispelled the poison. From that time he is believed to have embraced the monastic life in the suburban monastery of Saint Aper.

Indeed, when he was close to death, he is said to have spoken these words about himself:

“For a long time now I have seen the cell in which I lived as a monk transformed into spacious palaces.”

Vipertus, alluding in Bruno’s Life to chapter 7 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, says:

“Not forgetful of his former purpose, by which he preferred continually to serve Christ, content with complete humility, lowliness, and extremity.”

It also happens that Bruno himself, in a charter concerning the restoration of the monastery of Saint Aper, says:

“In this monastery I placed our community before my episcopate; after I had become bishop, I enlarged it as far as I was able.”

After Bertold had been taken from the living, Bruno remained at Toul with Herimannus, his successor, rendering him the same service he had rendered to his predecessor and taking care that the common and canonical life established in the cloister of Saint Stephen should flourish.

From there his parents sent him to the court. He won the favor of the Emperor Conrad, whom he accompanied into Italy to subjugate Milan, which had rebelled. He brought with him the forces that the Church of Toul was required to supply to the emperor for military campaigns.

He accepted this responsibility at the request of Bishop Herimannus, who was burdened by illness, and duly completed it.

Meanwhile, Herimannus died in the year 1026, on the Kalends of April, and Bruno, who was absent, was appointed in his place by clergy and people. They sent letters through Notbertus the monk and Liethardus the canon to King Conrad, who was then in Italy, and to Bruno himself, who was in the king’s retinue, earnestly requesting that Bruno be given to them as their bishop—a man of exceptionally noble birth and vigor, capable of protecting the people of Toul from the frequent attacks of their neighbors. Conrad initially resisted their petition, since he had destined Bruno for higher honors. But Bruno, preferring a Church impoverished in resources to a wealthier one, consented to the election and persuaded the king himself [Col. 0549C] to yield to the wishes of the people of Toul. He also brought it about that Bruno would be consecrated not by the Roman pontiff, as the king desired, but by his own metropolitan.

Accordingly, Bruno soon returned from Italy to his homeland in Lorraine, not without danger from those who lay in wait for him, and proceeded to Toul. There, on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, he was received with the greatest joy by everyone and installed in the episcopal see by his cousin Theodoric, bishop of Metz. But when he was about to be ordained by Poppo, metropolitan of Trier, and Poppo demanded that he do nothing in the episcopate without his advice, Bruno refused to comply. For this reason his consecration was postponed until the following year. In that year Conrad returned from Italy and summoned both men to Worms, binding the one to be ordained only to the condition that in ecclesiastical affairs—especially those of greater importance—he would follow the advice of the metropolitan. Under these terms Bruno was ordained on 9 September, amid the greatest rejoicing of all.

After his consecration he immediately turned his attention to restoring monastic religion, which had greatly declined in all the monasteries of his diocese except that of Saint Aper—especially in the monasteries of Saint Mansuetus and Médiano, where the abbots, neglecting the care of the souls entrusted to them, thought that they had been placed there solely to exercise external dominion. At the very beginning of his election he removed these men from office and entrusted both monasteries to the venerable Widricus, who held the office of provost at Saint Aper.

He also appointed Widricus abbot of the monastery of Saint Aper, at the request of William, abbot of Dijon and reformer of that same community, whose holy reputation was then famous beyond the sea throughout every region of the world. For the restoration of the declining monastery, he miraculously provided the same Widricus with a subsidy of thirty pounds. In 1033 he obtained from Emperor Conrad a privilege in favor of this monastery.

At a plenary synod held on 13 October 1036, he granted the churches of Solini-Mont and Wolferci-Curte, at the request of the aforementioned Widricus, to the monks of Saint Benignus of Dijon. In the same year he gave Saint Mansuetus the church of Gossani-Curte and the altar of Bertiliacum, which Canon Stephen had left when he departed to take up the monastic life among the Cluniacs. The following year he granted to Doddo, abbot of Saint Mansuetus, the church of the village of Paterniacum on the River Meuse.

Moreover, at Portus Suavis, in the nunnery begun by his predecessor Herimannus, he completed the buildings and established there a devout community of nuns. Over them he placed an abbess of noble birth and praiseworthy life named Berzenna. Through her constant care, it is said, the fervor of divine service there increased greatly.

Around this time he gave judgment in favor of the widow Raingardis. He combined remarkable stature with such courtesy and prudence that he won the reverence and esteem of everyone. He is especially praised for his immense generosity toward the poor, and also for his piety and faith, which were so living that he never offered the sacrifice without first shedding an abundance of tears. Skilled in the art of music, he adorned with melody the praises of many saints composed in verse by Cardinal Humbertus [Col. 0550C].

Because of his efficiency in handling affairs, Emperor Conrad sent him as envoy to Robert, king of France, and he established a firm and lasting peace between them. He repelled Odo, count of Champagne, who had approached to besiege the city of Toul, and compelled him to abandon the siege, with King Conrad’s assistance. The kingdom of Austrasia remained in Conrad’s possession; it had previously been held by Rudolph III, king of Transjurane Burgundy, and the count of Champagne was attempting to invade it.

Not long afterward Bruno is said to have fallen into a deadly illness. Through the merits of Saint Basil, whose altar he asked to be carried to, he recovered so completely that the man who had been borne there with another’s help returned home from the altar briskly under his own power. At approximately the same time he lost his pious mother Helvidis, who died in holiness [Col. 0550D]. As death approached, she earnestly asked her husband, in the presence of Regelwide, abbess of Woffenheim, to see that she was buried without any pomp and not to hesitate to distribute to the poor whatever ornament he might otherwise wish to spend on her burial.

It was Bruno’s custom to visit the thresholds of the apostles every year. Once, perhaps, while he was undertaking this pilgrimage with a retinue of five hundred men, the entire company was struck by plague. The holy bishop cured them with wine into which he had immersed sacred relics.

He approved the foundation, in the year 1043, of a monastery which Golterus of Daguliacum founded on his own estate with the consent of his wife Adila [Col. 0551A]. He is said to have dedicated the monastery of Hoenburg in honor of Blessed Mary in the year 1045.

Bruno had now held the bishopric of Toul for twenty-two years when, by the unanimous voice of the prelates and nobles at the assembly held at Worms by Emperor Henry III, he was elected supreme pontiff after the death of Damasus II. He did not wish to accept the election unless the Roman clergy and people approved it.

The election therefore took place in the year 1048, shortly before the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, which Bruno celebrated in his Church of Toul. Then, having assumed the garb of a pilgrim, he set out for Rome on the third day after the feast, accompanied by many prelates. In Rome, his election having been approved, he was placed in the apostolic chair on the first Sunday of Lent, the day before the Ides of February 1049, and was called Leo IX.

During the first two years of his pontificate he retained the name and title of bishop of Toul. In the same year he undertook a journey into Gaul and held a council at Pavia during the octave of Pentecost. Afterward he went to Saxony to meet the emperor. From there the two proceeded to Cologne, where they celebrated the feast of Saints Peter and Paul the Apostles.

Leo did not hesitate to visit his beloved Church of Toul, where he celebrated the solemnity of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. Then, at the request of Herimannus, abbot of Saint Remigius at Reims, he went to Reims on 29 September, the feast of Saint Michael. There he transferred the body of Saint Remigius, dedicated the church, and began a council on 3 October [Col. 0551C].

Returning to Rome, at a synod held in May 1050 he enrolled Gerard, bishop of Toul, among the saints [Col. 0552A] and ordered his feast to be celebrated on 24 April. Indeed, on returning once more to Toul, he raised Gerard’s body from the earth in October of the same year.

The following year, while he was staying in Rome, he handed over to Udo the primicerius the bishopric of Toul, which he had retained until then, and granted a bull confirming its possessions and privileges.

In 1052 he returned to Germany to establish peace between Emperor Henry and Andrew, king of Hungary. Since Andrew resisted every settlement, Leo subjected him to ecclesiastical censures. Before leaving Germany, he obtained from the emperor a powerful army to defeat the Normans. With these forces he crossed the Alps and reached Rome during Lent in 1053.

When the camps on both sides had advanced into Apulia [Col. 0552B], a fierce battle was fought by both sides on 24 June, but the Normans were victorious. Leo withdrew from the battle to a fortress, which was soon fiercely besieged, and he was captured. After the sacred Communion which Leo had taken away was restored to the Normans, he was led unharmed by Hunfridus, duke of the Normans, to Benevento on 24 July. He was detained there for some time, until Easter of the following year, when he was permitted to go to Rome. There he peacefully ended his life on 19 April, renowned for miracles performed before and after his death.

He died at the age of fifty, in the sixth year of his pontificate, and was buried by the altar of Saint Gregory in the Vatican basilica. Wibertus, archdeacon of Toul and his companion, wrote two books about the deeds accomplished by him; the Bollandists published them in volume II of the April collection, under 19 April [Col. 0552C].

[Col. 0551]

## ANOTHER NOTICE

*(In Mansi, Expanded Collection of the Councils, vol. XIX, col. 633.)*

[Col. 0551C] Leo, commonly called Leo IX, was created pope, to the immense benefit of the whole Catholic Church, from the count of Dagsburg, Bruno by name, bishop of Toul among the Leuci, on the Ides of February [Col. 0551D], in the year 1019, during the time of Emperor Henry [H.; reading uncertain]. The cardinals, through a legation, asked the emperor, in his name, to elect and present someone suitable who could expel Benedict, already called the Third, who was violently invading the apostolic see.

The emperor chose Bruno, descended from a noble family of the Franks and bishop of Toul, and sent him away clothed in the papal purple, so that he might present himself before the assembly of cardinals to be elected.

“When he was traveling through Gaul,” says Otto of Freising, “it happened that he came to Cluny, where the aforementioned Hildebrand was then administering, as they say, the obedience of the priory. Hildebrand approached Leo and, filled with zeal for God, firmly reproached him for what he had begun, saying that it was unlawful for the supreme pontiff to enter violently into the governance of the whole Church through the hand of a layman. But if Leo wished to entrust himself to Hildebrand’s counsels, he promised to bring about both that the imperial majesty would not be embittered against him and that the freedom of the Church would be restored in the election. Persuaded by this warning, Leo laid aside the purple, assumed the garb of a pilgrim, and set out, taking Hildebrand with him. When they had come as far as the City, Bruno, on Hildebrand’s advice, was elected supreme pontiff by clergy and people.”

Thus Leo, just as divine revelation had shown him five years earlier through prophecies and visions, was lawfully elected the excellent pontiff of the Roman Church. He was highly distinguished for his merits and, because of the angelic life he led, most worthy of the company of angels.

Sigebertus reports this memorable event concerning him: as Leo was journeying from Gaul toward Rome, he heard the voices of angels singing, “The Lord says: I am thinking thoughts of peace and not of affliction” (Jeremiah 29).

I therefore believe that, as soon as he had received his papal consecration at Rome, he hurried without delay to Sipontum in Apulia, to visit the church of Saint Michael situated on Mount Garganus and to gain the intercession of the holy angels with God—a pilgrimage that was exceedingly famous in that age [Col. 0553A].

Returning from this pilgrimage, he entered the monastery of Monte Cassino. After celebrating Mass there, he gave thanks for the honors shown him and enriched both the monastery and its abbot with many privileges.

He proved such a great lover of the Church of Toul that he did not wish to abandon the former title of the bishopric of Toul. He spent his patrimony on the construction of the monastery of the Holy Cross and enriched it with very ample revenues.

After settling the affairs of the Church in Italy, he came to Germany [Col. 0553B] and, holding several councils there, reformed it with regard to morals. When he traveled from Gaul into Italy, he brought with him from Lorraine Humbertus, a man outstanding in every virtue and branch of learning, and ordained him archbishop to preach the word of God to the Sicilians. Humbertus later became a cardinal of the holy Roman Church.

From the abbot of the monastery of Saint Remigius in Gaul he had received a wooden cup offered for the purpose of blessing, which he greatly treasured out of love for so great a pontiff. When it accidentally fell from the hand of the servant carrying it and was broken, the pontiff was deeply saddened. He ordered the fragments to be brought to him, and, after a prayer had been said, one part was joined to the other.

He caused a certain priest, who, after corrupting the chancellor of the apostolic see with money, had tried secretly to obtain letters of absolution, to become insane after returning the gifts to him with an apostolic imprecation.

“Whenever he remained in Rome,” says Leo of Ostia, “three days every week, at night, in ordinary clothing and barefoot, he went from the Lateran church to Saint Peter, singing psalms and praying with two or three clerics.”

The tenth part of the offerings which his predecessors had been accustomed to divert to their own use, Leo assigned to the needs of the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles.

He compelled Sueno, king of the Danes, surnamed the Great and lord of three kingdoms, to dismiss the wife whom he had married, his cousin.

Summoned from Rome to settle the disputes between the emperor and Andrew of Hungary, Leo came to Germany; but, deceived by the king of Hungary, he accomplished nothing.

He requested and obtained the emperor’s assistance against the Normans. When he fought the Normans in an unfortunate battle, the entire army was put to flight: some of the German soldiers were killed and others captured. Indeed, the pontiff himself fell into the hands and power of the Normans, not without grief and repentance on the part of the victorious Normans. Thus it happened that, although he had been defeated, they treated him in every respect as a victor, out of reverence for the apostolic dignity, and released him and all his companions, as he had requested, [Col. 0554B] escorting them honorably to whatever safe place he wished.

Peter Damian, in a letter to Bishop Firminus, wrote against Leo for waging war and involving himself with military forces; he reproached and mocked him on this account, as though he had done something evil and unsuitable to the ecclesiastical order. But since the whole Church thinks otherwise about this matter, one must pardon the grieving hermit, who, in criticizing German and Gallic bishops clothed in breastplates and helmets, let his style become too unrestrained and, as frequently happens under such emotions, exceeded the limits of legitimate criticism.

Peter, patriarch of Antioch, being learned in matters of the Catholic faith, as soon as he was made patriarch, according to ancestral custom, sought communion with the Catholic and apostolic Church by sending Leo a letter together with a profession of faith; and, as is clear from Leo’s reply, he obtained it.

After receiving and refuting the impious letter of Michael, patriarch of Constantinople, Leo sent a legation to Constantinople to Emperor Constantine Monomachus, both to establish peace between Latins and Greeks and to prepare for war against the Normans. The legation consisted of Humbertus, bishop of Silva Candida, Fridericus, archdeacon and chancellor, both cardinals, and Peter, bishop of Amalfi. A brief and concise account of what they did at Constantinople is found in Baronius.

Before they returned from the legation, Leo fell ill at Benevento in the company of Gunfridus, a Norman who had once been his enemy. He was taken to Rome and there piously and holily fell asleep in the Lord on 18 April, after occupying the see for five years, two months, and eight days. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, beside the tomb of Saint Gregory, and became renowned for very celebrated miracles. The bishopric remained vacant for eleven months and twenty-four days.

[Col. 0555]

## ON THE GREEK SCHISM RAISED AGAINST THE ROMAN CHURCH BY MICHAEL CERULARIUS

### And on Their Objections to the Latins

*(Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, Sixth Century, Part II, Preface, p. III.)*

[Col. 0555A] Almost two hundred years had passed since the Photian schism when, before its scar had been properly healed, another schism no less pernicious and, to the present day, incurable arose.

After the death of Alexius, patriarch of Constantinople, which occurred in February of the year 1044, Michael, surnamed Cerularius, was appointed in his place. According to John Curopalates, Michael had previously been driven into exile by John, the emperor Michael’s brother, because he had aspired to tyranny.

Thus, a neophyte raised to the patriarchal dignity, after attempting to diminish the prerogatives of the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch, finally turned against the Roman pontiff and the entire Latin Church—ostensibly to restore communion with the Roman pontiff and the Latin Church, but in reality to seek and fabricate grounds for reviling both.

At that time Leo IX presided over the Roman Church. He had succeeded Damasus II in the year 1049, when the Greeks in Apulia had rebelled against the emperor.

On this occasion Cerularius wrote a letter to Pope Leo, with, as he himself claimed, great humility, “both so that Leo might agree with the Greeks and remove the scandals that were being circulated about the Latins concerning the orthodox faith, and so that he might make Leo well disposed toward him, in order through him to obtain Frankish assistance for the emperor against the rebellious Greeks” [Note: [Col. 0555D] Cerularius, letter to Peter of Antioch].

At the same time Peter, the new patriarch of the Church of Antioch—which, like the Church of Alexandria, had always retained a certain communion with the Latins—sent a letter to Pope Leo together with a profession of the Catholic faith [Col. 0555C]. Leo praised and confirmed his elevation.

Cerularius could not tolerate this moderation of Peter of Antioch and strongly disapproved of his commemorating the Roman pontiff in the sacred diptychs. Moreover, with Leo of Acrida, archbishop of the Bulgarians, and Nicetas Pectoratus as his associates, he harassed Pope Leo and the Latin Church in various writings.

Peter of Antioch replied to Cerularius’s letter with the moderation for which he was distinguished and treated some of Cerularius’s objections to the Latins as unworthy of attention [Note: [Col. 0555D] Cotelerius, vol. II of the Monuments, pp. 145 ff.]:

“Some things, indeed,” he says, “appeared detestable, such as the addition of the phrase Filioque to the holy Creed; others were curable; and still others deserved to be passed over in silence. But whenever there is no danger concerning God or the faith, one must always incline toward peace [Col. 0555D] and the love of the brethren [Col. 0556A]. In the East, too, many practices are tolerated which, after much labor and study, could not be eradicated.

“If we cannot prevail over even those who live under our authority, how shall we be able to recall that proud and stiff-necked people from their customs? In any event, one should not readily lend one’s ears to empty slanders, nor rashly place faith in suspicions.”

Finally, he concludes the letter as follows:

“And this I exhort your divine Beatitude to accept: lest, while we demand everything, we lose everything.”

This letter was written after the death of Pope Leo, which occurred in 1054. Peter advises that a letter be written to Leo’s successor, so that he might either deny or excuse the accusations.

### 2

Pope Leo, intending to apply an immediate remedy to the urgent evil [Col. 0556B], had sent envoys with letters to Emperor Constantine Monomachus: namely, Cardinal and Bishop Humbertus, Peter, archbishop of Amalfi, and Fridericus, chancellor of the holy Roman Church. After first visiting the monastery of Monte Cassino in order to commend the success of their legation to God, they proceeded to the imperial city.

The emperor received them kindly and honorably. Cerularius, however, was struck with an anathema by the envoys, since he remained obstinate in error.

Humbertus had first been a monk of the monastery of Médiano in the diocese of Toul. From there he went to Rome with Bruno, the elected pontiff, who made him cardinal and bishop of Silva Candida, or Saint Rufina. He played the leading role in this affair and, both orally and in surviving writings, alone refuted Cerularius’s objections and errors, and brought Nicetas Pectoratus to repentance.

Peter, archbishop of Amalfi, is unjustly blamed by Cerularius, as though he had been expelled from his see for crimes. Peter Damian calls him “a man of pious memory” [Note: [Col. 0556D] Peter Damian, beginning of Opusculum XXXIV]. Thus Damian rebukes the foul impostor Bennon, who tries to defame Peter on account of bad practices—as Bennon himself foolishly claims—in order to cast a stain upon his disciple Gregory VII.

The third of the envoys, Fridericus, was the brother of Godfrey, duke of Tuscany, and a relative of Pope Leo and Emperor Henry. He later became a monk and abbot of Monte Cassino, then a cardinal, and finally, for a brief period, supreme pontiff under the name Stephen X.

[Col. 0556D] 3. The principal objections which Cerularius made against the Latins were partly the same as, and partly different from, those which Photius had already raised in the ninth century. Cerularius summarizes them in his letter to Peter of Antioch:

“Namely, that the Latins had added the phrase Filioque to the Creed; that they use unleavened bread in the sacrifice; that on Wednesday they eat meat, on Friday cheese and eggs, and that on Saturday they fast; that they eat strangled animals and polluted food; that monks use swine’s fat and that their sick eat meat; further, that the Latins prohibit the marriages of priests; that at Mass, at the time of Communion, one of the ministers eats the unleavened bread and greets the others; that bishops wear rings on their hands as bridegrooms; moreover, that they perform baptism with a single immersion; and finally, that they all shave their beards.”

It would be tedious to set out point by point what Humbertus answered. One point alone may be noted: he denies that the Latins had, up to that time, eaten strangled animals or blood [Col. 0557B].

Peter of Antioch refutes the objections themselves more closely in many respects in a letter to Cerularius [Note: [Col. 0557D] Cotelerius, as above, p. 149], and excuses the Latins both for shaving their beards and for bishops’ wearing rings.

“But as for the Latins’ eating polluted food, and their monks’ eating pork and swine’s fat,” he says, “you will also find, if you investigate the matter, that some among us do the same.” He proves this by the testimony of Basil the Great and by the example of Saint Pachomius, who, he says, fed pigs in his holy monastery with crumbs and table scraps:

“After slaughtering them, he provided the meat as food for guests, but served the entrails and the extremities of the feet and head to elderly monks and the sick. Truly,” he says, “an excellent and pleasant dish—to eat lentils and beans cooked with swine’s fat because of the lack of good oil!”

Nevertheless, from this objection of Cerularius against monks—that the sick ate meat by permission of the rule of Saint Benedict—the holy Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, perhaps took the occasion to prohibit the eating of meat among his followers, even the sick. Yet Guigo’s statutes make no explicit mention of that abstinence in chapter 38, where the purchase of fish is permitted solely for the sick.

But in the first part of the compilation of the ancient statutes, made in the thirteenth century, the eating of meat—which the Order renounced—is permitted to none of the sick, not even lepers, in chapter 44. The venerable Stephen, founder of the Order of Grandmont, likewise expressly forbids this abstinence to his disciples in chapter 57 of his rule [Col. 0557D].

As for the accusation made by certain Greeks against the Latins, as though they diminished the honor paid to sacred relics and images, Peter of Antioch proves it false [Note: [Col. 0557D] Ibid., p. 158 ff.], both from the worship which the Romans offer to the relics of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and “from what we see: Frankish pilgrims entering our wholly venerable churches and showing every honor and reverence to the sacred images.”

“Therefore,” he adds, addressing Cerularius, “I ask, implore, and entreat you, embracing your sacred feet in spirit, that your divine Beatitude, relaxing its insistence on what is overly exacting, accommodate itself to circumstances [Col. 0558A]. For it is to be feared that, while wishing to mend a tear, it may make a worse one; and while striving to raise up what has fallen, it may cause a greater fall. Would that all the Greeks had always kept this moderation in mind, or at least possessed it now!”

### 4

Meanwhile Pope Leo died. When the news was received, the envoys prepared to return to Rome. The emperor dismissed them loaded with gifts and supplied them with no small offerings to be presented to blessed Peter. At their further request, he established an annual payment to the monastery of Monte Cassino—namely, two pounds of gold [Note: [Col. 0558D] Ibid., book III, chapter 8].

On their return, however, Trasimundus, count of Chieti, intercepted and robbed them. Fridericus the chancellor nevertheless suffered suspicion before Henry, king of Germany, as though he had returned stuffed with money and gifts. The king disliked him because his brother Godfrey had rebelled against him.

Struck by this slander, Fridericus approached Richerius, abbot of Monte Cassino, who was then in Rome, and asked to be admitted as a monk. Richerius readily agreed. He sent Fridericus ahead to Monte Cassino with his companions and followed a few days later with the messengers whom King Henry had sent to the princes. In their presence Fridericus cast aside the precious garment he had been wearing and put on the habit of sacred religion.

He later became abbot, then cardinal under Victor II, and finally, after Victor’s death, pope under the name Stephen X, in the year 1058.

As soon as he assumed the pontificate, he had nothing more at heart than to restore the Greeks to communion with the Church. Therefore [Col. 0558C] he resolved to send a legation to the East, to the city of Constantinople, appointing Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, to the task and associating with him two colleagues: Cardinal Stephen and Mainardus, later bishop of Silva Candida. He instructed them to return as soon as possible [Note: [Col. 0558D] [ [Col. 0558D] This note appears at the foot of column 558, but the callout number (117) has not been printed in the text.] Chronicle of Monte Cassino, book II, chapter 89.]

But before this legation could achieve its purpose, the pontiff’s death soon intervened. An attempt was subsequently made to restore the Greeks to communion with the Church, but until now—with great sorrow—this has produced little or almost no fruit.

### 5

It should be observed in passing that Leo IX, in his letter to Cerularius, reproaches the Church of Constantinople for its frivolity in ordaining eunuchs as bishops. He says that it was reported that, in place of one of them, a woman had been ordained [Col. 0558D]. Leo certainly would not have reproached Cerularius with this if the story of Pope Joan had already been in circulation; he would have foreseen that Cerularius could easily turn the accusation against Leo himself and therefore against the Roman Church.

But among learned people this tale now smells so badly that modesty forbids saying more about it, although certain heterodox writers continue to defend it in order to feed their followers with a ridiculous fiction.

I will add only this, which no one has so far noted: in an old poem about the Roman pontiffs, which ends with Eugene III, there is no mention of the fabled Joan, nor is there any in the poem of Frodoardus. After Valentinus, the still-unpublished anonymous poet writes:

> Gregory the Fourth, and Sergius, and Leo the Fourth  
> Were called pontiffs; after them we read of Benedict.  
>   
> Hence, Nicholas, your Rome rejoices in your adornment.

From this it is understood that the tale had not yet been invented in the middle of the twelfth century. Most people attribute it to Martin of Troppau, although nothing similar is found in some copies of his work, such as one belonging to the most distinguished abbot Francis de Campis.

It must nevertheless be admitted that the tale was already in circulation at that time—that is, toward the end of the thirteenth century—and that it is found in John of Ypres.

## THE MINOR WORKS OF POPE LEO IX

[Col. 0559]

### A LITTLE BOOK ON THE CONFLICT BETWEEN VICES AND VIRTUES

It appears at the end of the edition of the works of Saint Leo the Great published at Venice in 1553.

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE

*(Literary History of France, vol. VII, article “Saint Leo IX,” p. 470.)*

[Col. 0559B] Several bibliographers—Bellarmine (*Scriptores*, p. 279; Labbe, *Scriptores*, vol. II, p. 18; Sigebert, *Scriptores*, chapter 149, note; Cave, p. 524)—attribute to Leo IX several homilies or sermons printed, according to them, after those of Saint Leo the Great in the editions of Louvain 1565, Cologne 1568 and 1598, and Antwerp 1583.

But they specify nothing in particular and give us no further information about them. Since I had been unable to unearth any of these editions, I was fortunate enough to find another, printed at Cologne in 1548. At the end of this edition there is printed, under the name of Saint Leo the pope, a treatise *On the Conflict between Vices and Virtues*. Peter Canisius, its editor, testifies that it is found in very ancient manuscripts among the writings of the great Saint Leo; but at the same time he admits that it is not by this pope [Col. 0559C]. The only proof he offers is the difference in style.

To this proof, which is obvious, he could have added another that is conclusive: at the end the author of the treatise refers the person to whom he is writing to the Rule of Saint Benedict, which he highly praises as containing all the instruction necessary for leading a Christian life.

Three reasons persuade us that this treatise—which may perhaps be the same work as the homilies or sermons mentioned by the cited bibliographers—belongs to our holy pope:

1. It bears the name of Leo in the ancient manuscripts and is not a work of Saint Leo the Great.

2. The praise of the Rule of Saint Benedict found in it is entirely appropriate to Leo IX, who had professed that rule.

3. Finally, its style, which is clipped, easy, and flowing, retains the characteristics of our learned pontiff.

There is only one substantial difficulty that can be raised against our view: the author, speaking of the city of Milan, identifies it as the place where he was writing. But this may also be understood as referring to the place where the person to whom the writing is addressed was staying. If it truly belongs to our holy pope, he may have composed it during his imprisonment at Benevento. The author indicates that he was extremely occupied and that he had to take time from his sleep in order to find the opportunity to write it [Col. 0560C].

This treatise is divided into twenty-five chapters. In each one the author introduces a vice and the opposing virtue, which fight against one another. It begins with pride and humility and ends with love of the present world and desire for future blessings. Its principal substance is drawn from Holy Scripture, and the editor valued it so highly that he called it a golden book.

## ON THE CONFLICT BETWEEN VICES AND VIRTUES

[Col. 0559C] The apostolic voice cries out throughout the world, dearest brother, and tells those stationed in the battle line of faith not to grow sluggish through complacency:

> “All who wish to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (1 Timothy 3).

And behold, Christendom is now religious and faithful in its rulers. For those who live godly lives in Christ Jesus there are no chains, beatings, scourges, prisons, racks, crosses, or any of the various kinds of torture.

How, then, can what was uttered through the Apostle be true—that all who live godly lives should suffer persecution? Or perhaps no one wishes to live a godly life in Christ Jesus in a time of peace, and therefore these things are absent? Who, even in folly, would say this?

In the Apostle’s statement, therefore, we must understand not the persecution of certain individuals in particular, but the general persecution of all. Indeed, there are many within the bosom of Mother Church who, living godly lives in Christ, are subjected to insults and provoked by abuse, affronts, and mockery. Yet this is not that general persecution which the Apostle described as suffered by all who live godly lives, since there are certain religious persons whom no wicked person would dare disparage to their face.

[Col. 0561B] But another kind of persecution must be understood, one more savage and more harmful, which is not inflicted by any material severity but is generated by the opposition of vices. For when pride fights against humility, vainglory against the fear of God, hypocrisy against true religion, contempt against submission, envy against brotherly rejoicing, hatred against love, slander against the freedom of just correction, anger against patience, insolence against gentleness, arrogance against making satisfaction, worldly life against spiritual joy, sluggishness or indolence against the exercise of virtue, dissolute wandering against firm stability, despair against confidence in hope, greed against contempt of the world, hardness of heart against mercy, fraud and theft against innocence, deceit and lying against truth, gluttony of the belly against moderation in food, foolish merriment against measured sorrow, loquacity against discreet silence, impurity and lust against bodily chastity, spiritual fornication against purity of heart, and the appetite for the present age against love of the heavenly homeland—when these array themselves against one another, what else is being done than that a cruel persecution of those living piously rages against the serried ranks of the virtues? O how hard, how bitter is the conflict with pride! It cast angels from heaven and expelled human beings from paradise; its army and the weapons of its warfare are the vices that we have briefly touched upon. But let us see how the camps of heaven and hell engage in battle, and how the arms of Christ and the counsels of the devil contend.

**PRIDE SAYS:**

Certainly you are better than many—indeed, than almost everyone—in speech, knowledge, wealth, honors, and all the various gifts, whether carnal or spiritual, that are available. Therefore despise everyone and regard yourself as superior to them all.

**TRUE HUMILITY RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. I.** “Remember that you are dust and ashes” (Gen. III), “that you are rottenness and a worm” (Job XXV); and even if you are something, unless you humble yourself in proportion to your greatness, you altogether fail to understand what you are. Are you higher than the first angel? Are you more splendid on earth than Lucifer in heaven (Isa. XIV)? He fell from such great eminence through pride; are you, in your pride, climbing from the depths to such a height? You remain subject, so long as you live here, to the condition concerning which a certain wise man says: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. IX).

How deeply do we suppose that the clay of which you are made is wrapped in the darkness of earthly pride, if in heaven the star that rose at dawn could lose the orbs of its own light? Hear, then, rather, the light of truth saying: “He who follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII). Elsewhere he taught in what way he should be followed, saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI). Hear, swelling pride; hear again the teacher of humility saying: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV and XVIII). And this: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble, the peaceful, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI.)

Hear also what the Apostle says about him who invites you to pursue these things: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. II). If, therefore, divine majesty lowers itself with such great humility, human weakness ought not to be proud of anything.

**VAINGLORY SAYS:**

Come, display to everyone the good that you are able to do; show them the good deed you are performing, so that everyone may call you good, so that all may proclaim you holy and venerable, so that you may be recognized as chosen by God, so that no one may despise or look down upon you, but that everyone may render you the honor that is your due.

**THE FEAR OF THE LORD RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. II.** If you do anything good, do it not for passing honors but for eternal ones. Conceal what you do as far as you are able. If you are not wholly able to do so, let the desire to conceal it be present in your heart, and there will be no rashness of display; nor will it be a crime ever to reveal what you always wish to keep hidden.

Thus you will seem to fulfill two sayings of the Redeemer that appear almost contrary to one another. It is said: “When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing; but let your alms be in secret, and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. VI). And: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Luke II).

Take great care lest this saying apply to you, the saying addressed to hypocrites: “They do all their works so that they may be praised by human beings” (Matt. XXIII). “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Luke X). Pay attention to yourself in all that you do, lest, driven by exaltation, you hear, together with those who gloried in the signs of miracles: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke X).

[Col. 0563A] **THE SIMULATION OF TRUE RELIGION SAYS:**

Since you do nothing good in secret, lest you be hated once everyone knows you, pretend outwardly to be what inwardly you do not desire to be.

**TRUE RELIGION RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. III.** Rather, strive to be what you are not. For to show people that you are what you are not—what else is that but condemnation? Remember, therefore, what is said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside you are full of rapine and uncleanness. Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside the cup and the dish, so that what is outside may also become clean” (Matt. XXIII).

And again, this saying, repeated insistently: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to people, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and of every impurity” (Matt. XXIII). Thus you too appear outwardly righteous to people, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity. There is also this written concerning such people: “They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII).

**DISOBEDIENCE SAYS:**

Who are you to obey those who are worse and to serve those who are inferior? It was more fitting that you command than they, since they cannot equal you in intelligence or industry. Therefore obey the Lord’s command instead, and do not concern yourself with anyone else.

**BLESSED SUBMISSION RESPONDS:**

[Col. 0563C] **CHAP. IV.** If the Lord’s command must be obeyed, it is necessary to submit to human authority. For he himself says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke XVIII). “That is so,” you say, “but only if the one who commands is such a person through whom God commands.” Yet the Apostle says the contrary: “There is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been established by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists what God has appointed” (Rom. XIII).

What those who command ought to be like is not for subjects to debate. Indeed, to the first shepherds of the Church the Lord says: “You know that the kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. But it shall not be so among you” (Luke XXII). Rather, “whoever wishes to be greater among you shall be the servant of all” (Mark X). Likewise, “the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve” (Matt. XX).

But because he foresaw that not all such persons would be, the one who subjected himself to all, assuming the persons of all in his disciples, gave this warning: “The scribes and Pharisees have taken their seat on the chair of Moses. Therefore do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not act according to their deeds; for they bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on people’s shoulders, while they themselves are unwilling to move them with a finger” (Matt. XXIII).

**ENVY SAYS:**

In what respect are you less than this person or that? Why, then, should you not be their equal or even their superior? How much are you capable of doing that they are not? Therefore they ought not to be superior—or even equal—to you.

[Col. 0564A] **THE JOY OF THE BROTHERS RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. V.** If you surpass others in virtues, you preserve yourself more safely in the lowest place than in the highest. For a fall is always worse from a height. But if, as you claim, some are superior or equal to you, what harm or injury does that do you? Take great care lest, while you envy the place of eminence, you imitate the one of whom it is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world, and those who belong to his party imitate him” (Wis. II).

**HATRED SAYS:**

Far be it from you to love one whom you find opposed to you in everything; one who disparages you, insults you, provokes you with injuries, reproaches you for your sins, and hastens to surpass you in words, deeds, and honors. For unless he envied you, he would never put himself so far above you.

[Col. 0564B] **TRUE CHARITY RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. VI.** If these things that you recount are to be hated in a human being, does it follow that God’s image in that human being is not to be loved? Christ, who loved his enemies while hanging on the cross, warned us before the torment of the cross, saying: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Luke VI).

Thus Solomon and the Apostle also say: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink” (Rom. XII); “for by doing this you will heap burning coals upon his head” (Prov. XXV). To this saying the same Apostle adds from his own teaching: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Rom. XII).

In contrast, John says concerning those known to hate their brothers: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (I John III). And again: “Whoever hates his brother walks in darkness and is in darkness even now, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (I John II).

“But,” you say, “it is enough for me that I love those who love me.” The Lord replies: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this?” (Matt. V; Luke VI.) What can you offer in objection to this? Certainly, “whoever hates his brother remains in death, while whoever loves remains in God, and God in him” (I John III, IV).

Therefore vomit out all the bitterness of gall, and take up, by whatever means you can, the sweetness of charity. Nothing is sweeter than it; nothing is more blessed. “God,” John says, “is love” (I John IV). And the distinguished preacher says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V). Thus it is not without reason that brotherly charity is said to cover the crimes of sins, as it is written: “Charity covers all offenses” (I Pet. IV).

**SLANDER SAYS:**

Who can endure, or cover in silence, how many wrongs this person or that commits, except perhaps one who consents to them?

[Col. 0565A] **THE FREEDOM OF JUST CORRECTION RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. VII.** The evils of one’s neighbor are neither to be concealed in silence nor approved; but one’s neighbor should be reproved to his face with brotherly charity, and not secretly slandered. If someone objects, “For this reason I do not wish to rebuke my brother before his eyes: lest, exasperated by correction, he make no progress but instead take offense at the correction,” divine Scripture replies—and, in turn, declares that the greater offense is committed—saying: “When you sat and spoke against your brother, you placed a stumbling block against the son of your mother” (Ps. XLIX).

The one who understands that he is being slandered is more offended than the one who endures a rebuke. And because the faults of those who offend must sometimes be concealed for a time so that they may be corrected at a more suitable moment, the passage continues: “You did these things, and I was silent.” But lest slanderers applaud themselves because of this measured silence—those who always prefer to disparage secretly and never come forward into open rebuke—the passage adds: “You thought wickedly that I would be like you.” As if it said: “It is wicked to think that I should appear like a slanderer because, by remaining silent for a time, I await a suitable opportunity for correction.”

Therefore it immediately continues: “I will rebuke you and set you before your face.” This is as if it said: “Not secretly, as is your custom, but openly, as is mine, I will rebuke the sinner, awaiting a suitable time for correction, and I will set his offenses before his face.”

“But,” you say, “I do not hate him; I love him, and for that reason I judge and rebuke him in secret.” And I reply: “Rather, you hate him for this very reason: you slander him instead of correcting him.”

How detestable the slander of one’s neighbor is, the divine utterances testify in many places. Hence there is this saying: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Ps. C). And this: “The one who slanders his brother will be uprooted” (James IV). And also the saying of the Apostle Paul: “See that you do not bite and devour one another” (Gal. V).

**ANGER SAYS:**

What is done against you cannot be endured with equanimity. To tolerate these things patiently is sinful. Even if you do not resist them with great exasperation, they will thereafter accumulate against you without measure.

**PATIENCE RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. VIII.** If the passion of the Redeemer is recalled to mind, nothing is so hard that it cannot be endured with an even spirit. “For Christ,” as Peter says, “suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow in his footsteps” (I Pet. II). He himself said: “If they have called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more the members of his household?” (Matt. X.) And elsewhere: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John XV).

But how great are the things we suffer in comparison with his sufferings? He endured insults, mockery, abuse, blows, spittle, scourging, a crown of thorns, and the cross; while we wretched people, to our shame, are wearied by a single speech and cast down by a single word. And what shall we do about the saying: “If we do not suffer with him, neither shall we reign with him”? (II Tim.)

Therefore the goads of anger must be blunted, and its condemnation feared. For “whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. V).

Where the remedy is found is clear from what follows: “If you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. V). This is as if it said: “Do not pour out even a silent prayer in your heart unless you first bring the offended person to gentleness by making satisfaction.”

Our gift is our prayer, and our altar is our heart. Whoever diligently does this whenever anger has arisen between two people will by no means incur the condemnation mentioned above. But there are many who do not forgive the sins of those who ask them for pardon. Against such people comes the Lord’s saying: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins” (Matt. VI).

“But,” you say, “he commits many offenses and frequently wrongs me.” To this I do not reply; the Lord does. For when Peter said to him, “How often will my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” he answered him: “I do not say to you, up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matt. XVIII).

How many people are slow to release their own injuries but quick to forgive those against God; and so it sometimes happens that, under the pretext of avenging the Lord’s injuries, angry people avenge their own. What should also be said about those who, blinded by fury, rush as far as uttering words of cursing, except what the Apostle says: “Neither will those who curse inherit the kingdom of God”? (I Cor. VI.)

James, detesting and amplifying this vice, says: “No human being can tame the tongue; it is an restless evil, full of deadly poison. With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse human beings, who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, this ought not to be so. Does a spring pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening?” (James III.) For this reason it is also said elsewhere: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII).

**INSOLENCE SAYS:**

Should gentle words be offered to fools, to senseless people, and to brute animals? Should not the harshest words instead be directed at them, as befits such people when they do wrong?

**GENTLENESS RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. IX.** In these matters you must follow not your own persuasion but the Apostle’s instruction. Concerning this very subject he admonishes his beloved disciple, saying: “Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all purity” (I Tim. I and V).

And again: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, a patient teacher, correcting with modesty those who resist.” And again: “Reprove, exhort, rebuke, with all patience and teaching” (II Tim. IV).

This evil of insolence harms subjects even more than rulers. For it often happens that they disdain correction offered gently and with the sweetness of charity, and launch arrows of contempt in response to words of humility. Hence it is written: “Whoever rebukes a scoffer brings injury upon himself.” In contrast, it is said of the person who advances through rebuke: “Rebuke a wise person, and he will love you” (Prov. IX).

**ARROGANCE SAYS:**

You have God in heaven as your witness; do not concern yourself with what people on earth suspect about you.

[Col. 0567B] **HUMBLE SATISFACTION RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. X.** One must not give occasion for slander or grounds for suspicion and whispering. But if there are things that need correction, they must be made known; or, if they are absent, they must at least be denied with a humble declaration. For the Apostle also warns us “not to give the devil any occasion for reproach” (I Cor. VIII).

He likewise condemned those who, while professing to judge the Christian faith, reclined at idols to eat and, although they considered the idol itself nothing, consumed what had been sacrificed as though the food were harmless; nevertheless, by this action they drew the weak consciences of their brothers toward the abominable rites of idols.

**SORROW SAYS:**

What do you have to rejoice about, when you bear such great evils from your neighbors? Consider with what sorrow all those who are stirred by such a great bitterness of gall against you must be regarded.

[Col. 0567C] **SPIRITUAL JOY RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. XI.** I know that sorrow is twofold—indeed, I know that there are two kinds of sorrow: one that produces salvation, and another that produces ruin; one that draws a person to repentance, and another that leads to despair. You are recognized as possessing one of them, but certainly the one that produces death.

Therefore one must not be saddened by the things you recommend, but rather rejoice in what you do not yet understand, because the giver of everlasting joy has said: “When people persecute you and say every evil thing against you falsely for my sake, rejoice and exult on that day; for behold, your reward is in heaven” (Matt. V).

Remember what the apostles of our religion did: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been deemed worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus.” Therefore there should be no place for sorrow where such great joy follows.

**SLOTH OR INDOLENCE SAYS:**

If you persist in reading with continual application, you will bring darkness upon your eyes. If you pour out tears without ceasing, you will lose your very eyes. If, by prolonging vigils, you pay the appointed measure of psalms, you will acquire madness of the head. If you wear yourself out by daily labor, when will you rise for spiritual work?

**THE EXERCISE OF VIRTUE RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. XII.** Why do you set before yourself such long stretches of time in which to endure these things? Do you know whether you will live tomorrow? Indeed, whether you will live even one hour in this life? Or has it escaped your mind that the Savior says in the Gospel: “Watch, because you do not know the day or the hour” (Matt. XXV)?

Therefore shake off the body’s sluggishness, and always remember that the kingdom of heaven is seized not by the lukewarm, the soft, or the idle, but by the violent, who use force to take it (Matt. II).

**DISORDERLY WANDERING SAYS:**

If you believe that God is everywhere, why do you guard one particular place in which so many things are perpetrated, instead of moving on to other places?

**FIRM STABILITY RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. XIII.** If it is as you claim, that you confess God to be everywhere, then this place that you desire to flee must not be abandoned, because God is in it as well. But you say: “I seek a better place; I find a better one.” I reply: Do you find one better—or even one like the one that you know the devil and human beings have lost?

Remember, therefore, that the first angel fell from heaven (Isa. XIV), and that the first human being was expelled from paradise (Gen. III) and came to the misery of this age. Consider that Lot, tested amid the practice of evils, was righteous among the Sodomites; but when he was sluggish in security on the mountain, he became drunk and sinned with his daughters (Gen. XIX).

This pursuit of wandering also produces another form of the same evil: while withdrawing certain people who persevere in one place from spiritual things, it strives either to entangle them in earthly business or to occupy them with matters that are otherwise useful, acting contrary to the Apostle’s words: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II). And again: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things” (I Thess. V).

**DESPAIR SAYS:**

Consider what and how much you have committed: what grave crimes, what countless offenses—and you have scarcely changed your life for the better or profitably corrected your way of living. For behold, as you see, you remain bound by an evil habit. You try to rise, but weighed down by the burdens of sins, you fall back again. What, then, is to be done, when certain condemnation threatens on account of the past, while no amendment comes to the aid of the present, except that the pleasures of temporal things should not be abandoned when the delights of the future age cannot be attained?

**CONFIDENCE IN HOPE RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. XIV.** If the matter concerns crimes and offenses, behold David, guilty at once of adultery and murder, described as rescued from the jaws of hell by the Lord’s mercy. Behold Manasseh, the most impious, most impure, foulest, most seductive, and most criminal of all sinners, returning through repentance from death to life. Behold Mary Magdalene, defiled by countless filthinesses of fornication, running anxiously to the fountain of cleansing, watering the Lord’s feet with tears, wiping them with her hair, kissing and licking them, and anointing them with perfume, and thereby deserving to be washed clean. Behold Peter, bound by the chains of his denial, loosening the knots of his faithlessness with the bitterest tears. Behold the robber, guilty of sedition and the shedding of his brothers’ blood, passing from the cross to paradise in the space of a single hour and with one confession. Behold Saul, persecuting the Church, killing many for the name of Christ and, so to speak, staining himself entirely with the blood of martyrs, becoming an Apostle and being transformed into a vessel of election.

Since so many and such great examples proceed from this source, let evil conversations give no place to despair, especially since it is also written: “Whenever a sinner turns and groans, he will be saved” (Ezek. XVIII). And again: “I do not desire the death of the wicked, says the Lord” (Ezek. XXXIII).

As for a way of life that has not yet been changed for the better, what else can I answer except that each person should do today what he did not do yesterday, while he is still permitted to live? Let him not defer from day to day, but always resisting his evil habit according to the strength given from above, let him say morning and evening: “Behold, now I have begun; this is the transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI).

**GREED SAYS:**

Certainly there is no guilt in desiring to possess certain things, because you do not seek to multiply them, but fear to put them to use; and what another holds badly, you yourself would spend better.

**CONTEMPT OF THE WORLD RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. XV.** These things are not procured without danger or offense even among worldly people, because the more each person begins to possess, the more he desires to possess. Thus it comes about that he has no limit in his desire, while he hastens to serve the countless cares of this age. As Scripture says: “The greedy person is not filled with money” (Eccles. V).

Paul indicates how detestable this vice is when he says: “And greed, which is the service of idols” (Eph. V). Explaining how harmful it is, he says: “Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and into the devil’s snare and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction” (I Tim. VI). A certain wise man declares how detestable it is when he says: “Nothing is more wicked than a greedy person” (Eccles. X).

James again makes clear how harmful it is, saying: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted; your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you, and it will devour your flesh like fire” (James V).

Nor did our Redeemer wish to pass over the evil of greed without showing how harmful it is. For he says: “It is difficult for those who have money to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Luke XVIII). And again: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.).

If, then, the activity of greed is so dangerous for worldly people, how much more dangerous is it for those who have already ceased to be worldly in dress and way of life, who have devoted everything that they are to the Lord? To them especially apply the Redeemer’s words, by which the disease of avarice may be destroyed: “Do not be anxious about what you will eat, or what you will drink, or what you will wear. For the nations seek all these things. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. VI).

O how blessed, how secure, how worthy of embrace is this saying! No one in this life is so secure as the one who desires to possess nothing except Christ. For he is shown to possess, under this promise, all that is necessary, just as Paul, though exceedingly rich, said as a poor man: “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (II Cor. VI). Certainly he means not superfluous things, but only what is necessary, as he himself confirms by saying: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (I Tim. VI).

But perhaps you say: “For this reason holy and religious men ought to possess more, so that Christ’s poor may receive more abundantly from them than from ordinary people.” I agree—but this applies to superiors, not to subjects. Subjects are especially warned by the example of Lot’s wife, who, as she was leaving Sodom, looked back behind her, was turned into a pillar of salt, and breathed out her spirit (Gen. XIX).

Christ therefore warns against such a thing, saying: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX). Hence Peter says: “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them” (II Pet. II). For the true proverb will happen to them: “The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (Prov. XVI).

This disease of avarice is never restrained more effectively than when the day of death is remembered without forgetfulness, and when one considers what kind of person he will shortly be in the tomb. This remained fixed in the memory of the one who said: “A human being is rottenness, and the son of man a worm” (Job XXIII). It had not departed from the one who said: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. VII).

What good, I ask, will preserved riches do then? Hear what is said: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there” (Job I). Hear also: “We brought nothing into this world, and neither can we take anything away” (I Tim. VI).

**HARDNESS OF HEART SAYS:**

If you give what you possess to the needy, from where will you feed your subjects without money?

**MERCY RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. XVI.** If you follow the Apostles’ measure in this matter, you will be able to accomplish both. For the same Apostle says to the Corinthians (II Cor. VIII): “If the will is ready, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. For it is not that there should be relief for others and affliction for us, but that, by equality, at the present time your abundance should supply their want, so that their abundance may also supply your want, and there may be equality, as it is written: ‘The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little’” (Exod. XVI).

A certain righteous man likewise admonishes his beloved child, saying: “If you have abundance, give generously; but if you have little, share even that” (Tob. IV). The incarnate Truth also says: “Whatever is left over, give as alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke XI).

Hear also what is written: “Judgment without mercy will befall the one who has not shown mercy” (James II). In contrast, the prophet admonishes, saying: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. LVIII).

Remember what happened to the rich man clothed in purple. He was not condemned because he had taken what belonged to another, but because he had not given what was his to the needy poor; and when he was in hell, he could not obtain what he had refused here in small measure (Luke XVI).

Consider also what the judge of heaven will say to those placed on the left: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and the other things that are terrifyingly enumerated there (Matt. XVIII).

The terms “theft” and “fraud,” although they have distinct modes of expression, nevertheless say the same thing.

**THEFT SAYS:**

If you do not take what belongs to another, you cannot be rich or even adequately supplied from what is your own.

[Col. 0571C] **FRAUD SAYS:**

If you deliver intact everything that your superior entrusted to you for safekeeping, and do not consider even a little of it worth reserving, from where will you provide for your own needs or please your friends and fellow soldiers?

**INNOCENCE RESPONDS TO BOTH:**

**CHAP. XVII.** It is better to be poor and lacking, and to please no one by what is given, than to harm anyone through theft or fraud. For whoever unjustly seizes what belongs to another, in whatever manner, closes the way to the kingdom of heaven against himself.

Hence the distinguished preacher once rebuked such conduct, saying: “It is altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why not rather suffer injustice? Why not rather endure fraud? Instead, you do injustice and defraud” (I Cor. VI). And he says to these brothers: “Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God?” (ibid.) Among other things he adds: “Neither thieves nor the greedy will possess the kingdom of God” (ibid.).

Deceit and lying also say the same thing. Deceit is carried out through ingenuity, while lying is carried out through a simple word.

**DECEIT THEREFORE SAYS:**

To offer one example: when you seek to mock someone by refusing to give, why do you delay by entangling him in requests? “I do not have anything that I can give.” In his heart he conceals what he has, either to preserve it for himself or, if he wishes, to give it to someone else.

**LYING ADDS:**

“I absolutely do not have what you are asking for”—not through artful ingenuity, as in deceit, but by a simple word of denial one ought to deceive the person.

**TRUTH RESPONDS TO BOTH:**

**CHAP. XVIII.** God can never be deceived. But you deceive yourself rather than God, because, however one lies, “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I); “and the portion of those whose mouths lie will be in the lake of fire burning with sulfur” (Apoc. XXI).

**GLUTTONY OF THE BELLY SAYS:**

God created everything clean for eating; and one who refuses to be filled with food—what else is he doing but contradicting a gift that has been granted?

**MODERATION IN FOOD RESPONDS:**

**CHAP. XIX.** One part of what you say is true. In order that human beings might not die of hunger, God created everything clean for eating. But to prevent them from exceeding the measure of eating, he commanded abstinence.

Among its other evils, Sodom perished especially through the satiety of bread, as the Lord testifies when, through the prophet, he speaks of Jerusalem: “This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: fullness of bread.” Therefore, just as a sick person approaches medicine, so everyone should approach food, seeking no pleasure in it but attending to necessity.

Hence the incarnate Truth says through the Gospel: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke XXI). In contrast, the Apostle says of the Jews’ insatiable greed: “Many walk, of whom I often told you, and now tell you even with tears, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ, whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things” (Phil. III).

And again: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both one and the other” (I Cor. VI).
