That person fully overcomes this vice who, in taking food, not only maintains moderation—that is, eats while always remaining hungry—but also, except in the case of bodily illness and the reception of guests, despises dishes that are more elaborate and more delectable at once.

**FOOLISH MERRIMENT SAYS:**

Why do you hide the joy of your heart within? Come out into public rejoicing. Say something outwardly that will make either you or your neighbors laugh. Make them happy with your happiness.

## MODERATE SORROW REPLIES:

### CHAPTER XX

Why is there such great joy in you? Have you already conquered the devil? Have you already escaped the punishments of hell? Have you already come from exile into your homeland? Have you already gained assurance concerning your election? Or has what the Lord says perhaps fallen into oblivion: “The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful; yet your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John 16)? Or has what he says elsewhere likewise slipped from memory: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep” (Luke 6)? And what is said through Solomon: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning will take possession of the end of joy” (Proverbs 14). Conversely, through the Gospel it is said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5). Again, through Solomon it is said: “A person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred; but all things are reserved uncertain for the future” [Col. 0573A] (Ecclesiasticus 9). Restrain, therefore, your empty joy, because you have not yet escaped punitive distress. Is not someone judged insane who, shut up in the darkness of a prison, attempts to rejoice?

## GARRULOUSNESS SAYS:

He will not be held guilty who speaks many things, provided that they are good; but the one who is proved to speak at least a few things, provided that they are evil.

## DISCREET SILENCE REPLIES:

### CHAPTER XXI

What you say is true. But while many good things seem to be spoken, it often happens that speech, beginning with good things, turns toward something perverse, as Holy Scripture itself declares: “For in much speaking sin will not be absent” (Proverbs 10). Perhaps criminal words are intermingled among countless others; [Col. 0573B] but can useless and idle words be avoided—words for which an account will have to be rendered in the future (Matthew 12)? A measure must therefore be maintained in speaking, and sometimes even useful words must be restrained, just as the blessed Psalmist is read to have done. He says: “I was humbled, and I was silent even from good things” (Psalm 38).

## IMPURITY SAYS:

It is no great crime to be defiled, whether by intercourse between man and woman or by one’s own hands or those of another.

## INTEGRITY OF THE FLESH REPLIES:

### CHAPTER XXII

The Apostle does not speak thus. What, then, does he say? “Nor will the impure,” he says, “possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

## LUST SAYS:

Why do you not now indulge yourself in your pleasure, since you do not know what will follow you? You ought not to waste the time granted to you in desires, because you do not know how quickly it will pass. For if God had not wished human beings to unite in the pleasure of intercourse, he would not have made male and female at the very beginning of the human race (Genesis 2).

## UNVIOLATED CHASTITY REPLIES:

### CHAPTER XXIII

I do not wish you to be ignorant of what you will receive after this life. For if you have lived chastely and devoutly, you will rejoice without end. But if you have lived impiously and luxuriously, you will be subjected to eternal fires. For that very reason you ought to live more chastely, since you say that you do not know how quickly the time granted to you will pass.

As for your professing that at the beginning of the human race God created male and female for this purpose, that they should unite in mutual embraces, you perhaps speak entirely truly; but the permission to marry is granted to some—that is, to those who have by no means professed virginity or widowly chastity. To others it is not granted, namely, to those who have decided to be virgins or continent. Fornication, however, is permitted to no one with impunity.

Do you not pay attention, or do you think it should be disregarded, when the Apostle says to the lustful: “Flee fornication, brothers. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but whoever fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Corinthians 6)? And if you consider this insignificant, hear what you will later lament and bewail forever: “Neither adulterers,” he says, “nor fornicators, nor those who lie with males, will possess the kingdom of God” (ibid.). [Col. 0574A] O how brief is the hour of intercourse, by which future life is lost! What benefit, I ask, does it bring to the body, or what profit does it provide, when it so quickly leads the soul to Tartarus?

## SPIRITUAL FORNICATION SAYS:

Are you doing anything that should be condemned, if someone consents to lust in his heart but does not proceed to the act of lustful desire?

## PURITY OF HEART REPLIES:

### CHAPTER XXIV

He certainly sins who does not guard the chastity of his soul. Therefore the author of purity says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5). In opposition to this, it is said through blessed Job: “I made a covenant with my eyes, so that I would not even think about a virgin” (Job 31). “For what portion would God have from above, and what inheritance from the heights would the Almighty have?”

For unless the thought of wicked consent were displeasing to our Creator, it would by no means have been said through Isaiah: “Take away the evil of your thoughts from my eyes.” Nor would he have said in the Gospel to the Pharisees: “Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts?” (Matthew 9). Nor would the Apostle Paul have said: “Their thoughts accusing or even defending one another, on the day when the Lord will judge the hidden things of human beings, according to my Gospel” (Romans 2).

## LOVE OF THE PRESENT AGE SAYS:

What can be more beautiful, more honorable, more lovely, or more delightful than what we see each day in the present [Col. 0574C] life? O how wondrous is the chamber of heaven: the pleasant air, the light of the sun, the waxing and waning of the moon, the variety and courses of the stars.

How pleasing is the earth: the flowers of the groves, the sweetness of fruits, the delights of meadows and streams, the luxuriant stalks of the crops, the leaves of vineyards and the branches full of clusters [botris], the shade of forests and the green palms, the running of horses and dogs, the leaps of deer and goats, the flights of hawks, the feathers and necks of peacocks, doves, and turtledoves, the painted walls and ceilings of houses, the ringing songs of organs and all musical instruments [resonis], the lovely appearance of women, their eyebrows and hair, eyes and cheeks, [Col. 0574D] throat and lips, nose and hands, and the gold applied externally, with necklaces adorned with gems—and whatever else the senses do not now recall.

## LOVE OF THE HEAVENLY HOMELAND REPLIES:

### CHAPTER XXV

If the things beneath heaven delight you so greatly, if the prison is so beautiful, what must the city and the home be like? If such are the things that strangers cultivate, what must those be that sons possess? If mortals and wretched people are rewarded in this life in such a manner, how richly must immortals and blessed people be endowed in that life?

Therefore let love of the present age depart—an age in which no one is born without dying—and let love of the future age take its place, an age in which everyone is brought to life so as not thereafter to die; where no trouble disturbs, no adversity agitates, and no necessity constrains, but everlasting joy reigns. [Col. 0575A]

But you ask what is there, unless such and so great a blessedness endures. It cannot be stated otherwise than that whatever is good is there, and whatever is evil is never there. “What,” you ask, “is good?” Why do you ask me? It has been defined by the prophet and the Apostle: “The things that eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (Isaiah 64 and 1 Corinthians 2).

Toward this happiness David, surrounded by the many riches of the world, yearned when he said: “What remains for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Psalm 72). Though abounding in many dishes of royal banquets, he said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” [Col. 0575B] (Psalm 16); and again: “My soul thirsted for the living Lord. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41); and again: “For my sojourn has been prolonged” (Psalm 119). Hence Paul also said: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1). But much better—

Having thus traversed these matters, although I have omitted many things, nevertheless, as it seems to me, I have shown you the camp of our enemy, the fornicator, with which he never ceases to attack those who live devoutly in Christ Jesus. Yet not content with these things, he turns to other devices: he often foretells true things to some in dreams, so that eventually he may draw them into falsehood; he awakens sleepers before the proper hour or time, so that during the time intended for wakefulness he may plunge them into the worst sleep; and when they are singing psalms [Col. 0575C] and praying, he disturbs them with hisses, screeches, various barks, and discordant voices, even throwing stones or excrement, so that, withdrawing them by any means from spiritual work, he may render them ineffective.

But you, man of God, attend to what I say with vigilant care, and give credence to what I am about to recount—things even more astonishing. I recently learned what I am saying from the report of someone. A certain religious man, living in monastic habit, was in our own time afflicted by an unheard-of temptation from the ancient enemy, so that the same evil spirit repeatedly befouled pieces of his clothing, even when they had been removed from him, with an unclean filth.

This filth was so horrible, foul, and harmful that the part of the clothing it touched was thereafter fit for no use, even if it had been washed. When I was asked why almighty God had given such power over him to the cunning serpent, I replied that it was so the uncleanness of his heart might be displayed outwardly: he would never have done this to his exterior clothing unless he had utterly corrupted his interior, either through unbelief and blasphemy or, certainly, through empty and vain glory. For an abscess within flows outward through the clothing.

Although I myself, being far away, did not see the man, nevertheless I truly foresaw these things in him, as I believe. And if this is not so, is the event nevertheless thought to have happened without cause? It may also have happened so that this filth might preserve purity of heart in him, lest the crafty enemy stain it with the mark of vain glory, just as Paul received a thorn in the flesh lest he become conceited because of the greatness of his revelations [Col. 0576A] (2 Corinthians 12).

Let it therefore be whichever of these explanations you choose; or, if none of them is correct, will the final explanation, if I propose it, nevertheless not be true? It is entirely true, it is true that I say: that filth is not harmful to the soul externally if the soul itself strives to preserve purity of heart within.

Meanwhile, as you yourself took care to point out, I hear that some among us say that no one can be perfect in the homeland of his birth, taking as their argument what the Lord said: “No prophet is accepted in his own homeland” (Luke 4). First, they must be refuted by the reasoning of truth, and only then must it be shown how the statement that was uttered is to be understood.

[Col. 0576B] Let those who say these things listen patiently, because, by failing prudently to consider the meaning of Sacred Scripture, they almost despise all the saints. For if matters are as they assert, then all those Romans who have been converted and live among Romans; all Greeks among Greeks; all Italians among Italians; all Gauls among Gauls; all Iberians among Iberians; all Germans among Germans; all Aquitanians among Aquitanians; all Britons among Britons; and all English among English who live religiously will be imperfect.

Behold, Paul and Antony, from the Thebaids, were perfect among the Thebaids. Behold, Hilarion, from the Palestinians, was perfect among the Palestinians. Behold, Macarius, from the Egyptians, was perfect among the Egyptians. Behold, the city of Oxyrhynchus was entirely perfect through its own citizens. Behold, to come to our neighbors, Protasius and Gervasius, remaining in this very city of Milan and in their own home, and practicing the monastic life for ten years, were so perfect that they became martyrs. Or will our province alone perhaps be excluded from this rule, so that it has monks not from its own people but only from foreigners?

One must strive rather to live according to the rule of the perfect wherever one may be, without turning aside from the path of perfection through the allurements of parents, relatives, or kinsmen. In this way, certainly, according to the Savior’s sentence (Luke 14), one will be able to renounce father and mother, brothers, sisters, wives, children, houses, fields, and everything one possesses.

I say this not to deny the highest praise to those successors who pass from kingdom to kingdom and from the public world to the desert, but to show that even those who flee their homeland more in their affections than with their footsteps are happy and perfect. I therefore beseech those who deny that this can happen among us to consider with vigilant care why the Lord did not say, “No prophet is perfect in his own homeland” (Luke 4), but said “accepted”—which must mean nothing other than “received.”

He wished this to be understood both of the ancient prophets and of himself, who was not accepted among the unbelieving Jews but rather despised, as Stephen said to them: “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute, those who foretold the coming of the Just One, whose murderers and betrayers you have now become?” [Col. 0577A] Who, however, does not see how great the rashness and presumption would be of anyone assuming the name of prophet for himself?

You, therefore, rebuke such people with charitable affection, and always strive to live according to the rule of the Fathers, especially that of the holy confessor Benedict. Do not depart from it, add anything to it, or take anything away. For it contains everything sufficient, and nowhere is it lacking. Its words and commands [Col. 0578A] lead its followers to the palaces of heaven.

Behold, dearest brother, amid my other occupations I dictated and wrote this discourse for you during the night hours, although in an unpolished style. Since I recognized that it exceeded the form of a letter, I preferred to call it a little book, *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*. If you find anything in it conducive to edification, you ought to have it read and pass it on to others.

[Col. 0577]

# THE SPEECH OF SAINT LEO IX, ROMAN PONTIFF, TO COUNT ADELBERT

Concerning the restoration of the monastery of Hirsau. (Year 1049.)

(From Baronius, *Annals*, volume XI, page 184, under the year 1049.)

## EDITORIAL NOTICE

Trithemius must be corrected for placing in the *Chronicle of the Monastery of Hirsau* the arrival of Saint Leo in Germany and the council held by him at Mainz not in this year (1049) but in the following year. He also describes as follows what then took place concerning the restoration of that monastery between the pontiff himself and his sister’s son, Count Adelbert.

## [SPEECH TO COUNT ADELBERT]

[Col. 0577B] In the year 1050 [1049] from the Lord’s Nativity, in the third indiction [second], Saint Pope Leo IX, having departed from Rome with many cardinals in order to settle the affairs and condition of the churches and restore peace to Gaul, came to Germany.

At that time Count Adelbert of Calw was advocate of the monastery of Hirsau, but a patron of its desolation. He not only scorned restoring what had been impiously taken from Saint Aurelius by his great-grandfathers, but, believing that he possessed everything by a just title, thought of nothing less than repairing the monastery.

It happened, therefore, in the year mentioned above—which was the forty-eighth year of the monastery’s desolation and, as we have said, the fiftieth year after the thousandth year of the Lord—that the same most holy Pope Leo, related by blood to the aforesaid count, departed from Rome and, having crossed Italy, directed his journey through the lands of the Suebi toward Mainz.

When the aforesaid Count Adelbert learned that his uncle, the pontiff of the holy Roman and universal Church, would be passing through his lands, he hurried to meet him and, by his most humble entreaties, prevailed upon him not to disdain entering his nephew’s lodging. The pope, moved both by the devotion of his petitioner and by their blood relationship, consented and entered the count’s castle. Received with great courtesy, he sowed the word of saving instruction, as was his custom, and strove with the utmost zeal to raise the minds of his enemies to love of the heavenly homeland.

[Col. 0578B] One day, for the sake of recreation, the pontiff embraced the count with his right arm and went out from the castle not far away, to the summit of a neighboring mountain. While they were conversing there, he said:

“How suitable, my son, this place seems to me: surrounded on every side by mountains, made useful by an abundance of water, and rendered peaceful by solitude. Here a monastery of servants of God ought to be built, so that, continually offering praises to our Creator, they might devoutly intercede for the salvation of many.”

The count replied: “Most blessed Father, there is nearby a church built by my ancestors in honor of a certain Saint Aurelius, whose body is also said to be buried there. It was formerly constructed as a dwelling for monks, together with the other necessary buildings. After monks had served almighty God there religiously for not a few years, they eventually grew miserably slack in regular discipline and would not heed the admonitions of their superiors; therefore my ancestors expelled them from that place as a scandal to the people.”

[Col. 0578C] After hearing this, the most holy pontiff went personally to the place and examined the books that remained, wishing to learn the truth of its history. Among the others there was an elderly cleric named Berthold, who had formerly seen monks serving God in that place. He disclosed the whole matter to the pontiff as it had happened, including [Col. 0579A] how Count Adelbert’s grandfather had stripped the monastery of all its goods and, after expelling the monks, had installed a few clerics there.

When Saint Leo had learned these things, he groaned; but, wisely concealing the pain of his heart, he asked the same cleric where the body of the holy Aurelius was. The cleric said that he had heard from his elders that, at the time when the Northmen ravaged Gaul, the sacred relics of Saint Aurelius had been hidden beneath the earth by an abbot of that place and had remained unknown to everyone up to that day.

The holy pope then summoned workmen and began digging the earth in various parts of the church, carefully searching for the hidden treasure. But after the craftsmen had labored long in vain and found absolutely nothing, everyone present began to despair of finding the saint’s body.

[Col. 0579B] Then, while the holy pontiff lay prostrate in prayer and encouraged the craftsmen not to despair, one of them—more skilled than the others in his craft—who had recently arrived with his sons from the lord of the Venetians and had bestowed much benefit on this place through his labors, carefully examined each location. At last, from the rebound of the hammers, he detected that the ground beneath was hollow.

Following his advice, the workmen began digging at that spot. Eventually, after removing the earth with great difficulty, they found a fairly well-formed underground chamber, in which a sarcophagus appeared, externally arranged with considerable ornament.

[Col. 0579C] When the most holy pope saw it, he was filled with great joy and ordered everyone to bend their knees in prayer and praise God for the desired discovery of his confessor. When the prayer was complete, Saint Leo approached more closely and ordered the tomb to be opened. When it was opened, an exceedingly sweet fragrance exhaled, refreshing all who were present with its wondrous sweetness.

They found the most sacred bones of Christ’s most holy confessor Aurelius wrapped in silken cloths, beautifully arranged in the proper order in the form of a body. At his head was a lead tablet containing the following:

**THE BODY OF SAINT AURELIUS, BISHOP, DEPOSITED IN THE TIME OF KING ARNULF, WHEN HERDERADUS WAS ABBOT, ON THE EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF SEPTEMBER.** [Col. 0579D]

When the holy pope had read this inscription aloud before everyone, he groaned, saying: “Woe to those who have desolated the place sanctified by the merits and presence of so great a prelate!”

He closed the sarcophagus, lest the saint’s relics be removed in any way, and returned with his attendants to the count’s castle.

The next day, when Saint Pope Leo saw that the time was suitable for carrying out his purpose, he summoned the often-mentioned Count Adelbert and his wife Wiltrude, a most devout woman, into the presence of his cardinals, excluding the others, and said to his nephew:

[Col. 0580A] “Yesterday, dear nephew, we saw the sacred relics of Christ’s confessor deprived of their due honor, and the place itself—once properly dedicated by your ancestors to almighty God and sacred monastic religion, for the love of the heavenly homeland, and inhabited for many years by Peter, a servant of God—laid waste.

“Your ancestors, your grandfather and father, driven by the worst and most cruel avarice, desolated it of the abbot’s possessions and goods. And what is more wicked than every crime, after expelling the monks they changed the workshop of holy virtues into a den of every vice by introducing secular clerics of the most dissolute life.

“You too, clinging to the evil footsteps of your ancestors, as we have been taught by trustworthy testimony, not only possess without fear of God those things which they, polluted by sacrilege, unjustly took from the monastery of the servants of God, but, utterly forgetful of your salvation, you seized everything they had left untouched through their own restraint [Col. 0580B]. You have made God and Saint Aurelius—and indeed all the citizens of the heavenly homeland—your adversaries by provoking them.

“For it must not be considered a small sin when something is committed against God and his saints, since even among human beings the unjust usurpation of property belonging to another is judged a very grave crime.

“Behold, together with your ancestors you have violated an agreement. You first corrupted—or rather destroyed—the holy testament of your forebears, and what they offered to almighty God with simple and holy devotion for the remedy of their souls, you, inflamed by impious cruelty and cruel avarice, did not fear to strip from God and his saints.

“You have become an enemy and adversary not only of God and his saints but also of yourself, and you have been declared an enemy of your own lineage. As a cruel prelate, you have bound by a most serious crime the very offspring destined to be generated from your seed. So long as it is polluted, even unknowingly, by sacrilegious inheritance, it will either perish, failing within a few generations, or become wretched in this life, to be tormented after death by eternal punishments according to its deserts.

“What hope of attaining eternal happiness can there be for you, my son, when through such an evident crime and sacrilege you have made almighty God, together with all his saints, your enemy and adversary? Believe us: it is wholly dangerous and damnable for you to have God opposed to you. Although he may now appear patiently to endure injuries done to him, since he is a just avenger and judge, do not doubt that after death he will avenge this patience with eternal punishments.

[Col. 0580D] “We, for our part, who are concerned with the salvation of you and your family, both by reason of our pastoral office—by which, although unworthy, we are officially debtors to the salvation of all—and also by reason of our blood relationship, since you, born of our sister, are intimately connected with us, will not allow you and yours to perish eternally, insofar as it lies within us.

“Therefore, by the authority of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, whose representatives we are on earth, we admonish and require you, and under threat of eternal damnation, by the strict judgment of God, we call you to account. Under the bond of anathema, and strictly commanding you by apostolic authority, we order you to restore the aforesaid place to its former condition.

“You must expel the clerics, whom by apostolic authority we now decree deprived of every benefice and residence in this place. You must establish monks and an abbot according to the rule of the holy Father Benedict, just as they are said to have been there from the beginning. You must restore without delay each and every thing taken by your ancestors, by yourself, or by anyone else. And if anything more is required to accomplish this, you must faithfully and without any resistance provide it lawfully from your own substance, for the love of eternal life.

[Col. 0581B] “By the authority of almighty God, we earnestly enjoin upon you and your wife, beloved by us, that these things be completed and brought to fulfillment there as quickly as possible, for the remission of your sins.

“If, however—which God forbid—you neglect this and are found to be a despiser of our commands, know that you will incur the indignation of almighty God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of all Christ’s elect. Bound by the bond of anathema through apostolic authority, you will be subject to the judgment of divine examination and punished without end with the impious in the gravest torments of Gehenna.” [Col. 0582A]

Struck by the pontiff’s speech, the count fell at his knees and, publicly confessing with tears that he had sinned grievously, promised to do everything he was ordered to the best of his ability. Asking the pontiff for pardon and absolution for his offenses, he heard him say:

“If you complete what, in response to our commands, you promise to do, we will grant you not only pardon for your offenses together with absolution [Col. 0582B], but we also promise you many rewards of eternal happiness, stored up for you in heaven.”

[Col. 0581]

# RECORD OF BRUNO, BISHOP OF TOUL, LATER POPE LEO IX

Concerning the restoration of the monastery of Saint Aprus. (Around the year 1030.)

(From Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, book VI, page 602, from the autograph.)

[Col. 0581C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, the creator and governor of all things that subsist eternally, I, Bruno, by the grace of God bishop of Toul, address the present clergy and people, and all the sons of this church, both those now living and those who will succeed them.

It is known to many how, in the time of Lord Bertold, bishop of this see, God visited the place of Saint Aprus, which had been deprived of all religious observance, through Lord Abbot William. The same Bishop Bertold, having scarcely prevailed upon him by entreaties, brought him from the regions of Burgundy and regularly appointed him over the brothers there.

But because monastic life, when it is not understood, appears almost contrary, when, with the situation changed, people saw and heard unfamiliar things concerning the order of monks, and the familiarity of the brothers—which had previously been open and easy, common to everyone everywhere—was forbidden to the curious, complaints against the place began to arise for these and other reasons.

Together with defamatory reproach, scandal arose, as a certain wise man says: “Every sudden change of circumstances does not occur without some disturbance of minds.” Thus it happened that, because of the murmuring, slandering, blaspheming, and accusing of neighbors, the place endured adversity for a long time—adversity provoked in some not so much by malice as by an ignorance that was less culpable.

After peace had been restored [lacuna], with the bishop residing in his see, those who had formerly been hostile began [lacuna], after coming to their senses, to investigate the matter and to venerate and love what they had believed to be invented [uncertain OCR: i…ventam], spreading everywhere the reputation of its good odor.

[Col. 0582C] Hence it happened that many of them, seeking fellowship, obtained it, while many others even became monks. And as the devotion of the faithful increased, the aforementioned place began to be raised up through the generosity of its donors.

For whoever offered himself to the fellowship of the brothers freely gave perishable things, so that through participation with those serving God he might merit things that endure. Therefore they undertook to make an eternal memorial from their expenditures, so that the alms of such people might be conspicuous in the sight of the faithful, present and future, and might in this age be a memorial of blessing before God, with perpetual reward.

Accordingly, they determined to erect as a dwelling the ancient monastery of Saint Aprus, which was collapsing from age and had formerly been burned once and twice, renewing it from its very foundations. And so that it might be known for which benefactors it was being built, they recorded below both their names and their expenditures individually, leaving to posterity a pious remembrance of themselves to be recalled continually with devotion.

From this point onward we beseech the bishops who succeed us in this see not to become harsh oppressors, forgetting their fatherly duty by estimating the resources of the place according to the size of its structure. And so that they may know how just this petition of ours is, let them deign to read the charter that Bishop Gauzlinus made and confirmed for the aforesaid place together with a royal decree.

Before becoming bishop I entered into fellowship with that place; after assuming the episcopate, I enlarged its possessions as far as I could, and I obtained from the faithful devotion of the brothers that a continual remembrance of me might be maintained there at every hour of the day [Col. 0583A], throughout all the days of my life.

These are the names of the almsgivers, together with their alms.

Lord Emperor Conrad: fifteen pounds and four ounces of gold. Lady Empress: three pounds and two ounces of gold. Lord Bishop of Metz: two pounds. Count Leitfridus: six and a half pounds. Countess Alberada: one pound, an excellent curtain seventy-two cubits long, and four hundred measures of grain. Duchess Matilda: one and a half pounds. Henry the Advocate: five pounds. Filista, his wife: five pounds. Hugh of Briscia: three pounds. [Col. 0583B] Widricus the Fat: five pounds. Henry of Fau: five pounds. Henry of Tussiacum: five pounds. Hildeburg of Bar: five pounds. Oda of Saint Martin: four and a half ounces of gold. Mainfredus: five pounds. Emma: six pounds. Walderada: five pounds. Mainherus of Calmis: five pounds. Lambert the canon: five pounds. Ingobertus: five pounds. Lord Abbot Richard: one pound. Lord Abbot Norbert: one pound. [Col. 0584A] Lord Abbot Sigifred: one pound. Lord Abbot Poppo: four pounds. Lord Abbot Erlinus: one and a half pounds. Lord Abbot Herbert: two pounds. Lord Azechinus: one and a half pounds and five solidi.

### Alms of the Converts

Lord Herbert the chief cantor: five pounds. Lord Herbert the archdeacon: eighteen pounds and a purple cloak. Lord Gozelinus: five pounds. Lord Girbertus: twelve pounds. Lord Albert: six pounds. Lord Theoderic: seven pounds. Lord Goisfridus: one and a half pounds. Lord Harwardus: one pound and one cloak. Lord Tendo: vineyards yielding ten cartloads of wine. Count Oddo: ten pounds.

Nor do they receive with less gratitude what our citizens and suburban dwellers did for them in cart-hauling: with all their strength, spontaneous effort, and ready willingness, they transported enormous rocks and stones for the walls [Col. 0584B], and with their own hands cleared away the ruins of the old walls of the entire monastery and carried them away on their shoulders, when the unhappy misfortune of burnings, plunderings, and devastations had not yet befallen them.

And because the present charter cannot contain their names individually, may the hall of the heavenly kingdom contain them for what they built for God and Saint Aprus in this mortal life.

Moreover, it is worthy to count here those whose goodwill was far greater than their ability to give could have been: those who contributed five, ten, or fifteen solidi, or twelve or six coins, or more or less.

[Col. 0583]

# DIPLOMAS OF SAINT LEO IX, GIVEN WHILE HE WAS STILL BISHOP OF TOUL

## I. Bruno, Bishop of Toul, Confirms the Possessions of the Abbey of Saint Aprus. (Year 1034.)

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, Documents, I, 413.]

[Col. 0583C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, creator and governor of all things that eternally subsist, Bruno, humble bishop of the holy Church of Toul.

By the grace of the divine dispensation, it happens whenever the mind of any person is inspired to will what is good—especially that person who is seen to possess more than others in this world—when he takes care that, through the things of earthly dominion, God’s clemency may be made favorable to him. Yet upon us, the shepherds of the Church, a pious solicitude is imposed, so that the Lord’s flock established under our care may be fed by our provision and strengthened under temporal administration with the twofold substance of life. Therefore we wish it to be clearly known to all the members of our Church, over which by God’s authority we preside, both to those present and to those who will follow long afterward, that when we came to the place of Saint Aprus and piously considered the provision of food for the monks, we believed that it would greatly benefit us at the severity of the future judgment if we increased what pertains to the sustenance of the brothers serving God there; so that by this our memorial might be established more securely in that place, and the prayer of God’s servants for the attainment of our salvation might never cease.

Moved, therefore, by this consideration and stirred by paternal solicitude, we have, with the counsel of our faithful, by synodal decree firmly granted to them the altars of the churches which in our own times they appear to have newly acquired from free men or from any neighboring persons, with this stability and condition: that, when the vicars whom we entrust solely with the care of souls by their election die, they are in no way compelled to redeem those same altars, but shall merely provide, by their own election as stated, suitable vicars who will receive the care of souls from our hand.

The altars that we have granted to them are these: namely, the altar of the church in the village called Vallis-Curia; the altar of the church in the village called Saint-Germain-d’Archais; the altar of the church at Saponaria; the altar of the church at Mollenis-Villa; and the altar of the church at Claregio.

They also possessed half of the church at Tantonis-Villa, which Rainard, a man of venerable memory, formerly a count and later made a monk in the monastery mentioned above, had transferred to the heavenly treasures, together with all the patrimony he had possessed there, while he was still alive. The other half belonged to the prebend of the canonical brothers of this see. Since the altar could not be divided under the law stated above, we granted both portions by a common donation, so that by this act of piety the brothers might continually be reminded of how earnestly they ought to beseech almighty God on our behalf in their good will.

Finally, we ask, beseeching and entreating the paternal benevolence of our successors, that this offering of our generosity be held firm and valid, just as they themselves too will establish their decrees and preserve them perpetually inviolate; knowing beyond doubt that they will be rewarded according to their good will, just as, for their rashness, they will be more severely punished by the Author of the world for whatever has been established for the salvation of souls.

So that this concession of our grant may be held more securely in future times and preserved perpetually unharmed, we caused it to be confirmed by the hand of all our faithful, and by the authority of our office we decree that it shall endure through successive ages.

[Col. 0585C] I, Bruno, unworthy bishop, have subscribed with my own hand.

Sign of Gibuin, primicerius. Sign of Dudo, primicerius of Verdun. Sign of Ulderic, archdeacon. Sign of Ebydric, archdeacon. Likewise, sign of Udelric, archdeacon. Sign of Lambert, archdeacon. Sign of Benzelin, archdeacon. Sign of Gebero, archdeacon. Sign of Lanzelin, archdeacon.

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1034, indiction II, in the tenth year of Lord Conrad’s kingship, the ninth of his empire, and the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Bruno, with Rainard the younger as count.

[Col. 0585D] I, Harduin, priest and monk, wrote this at the command of Lord Abbot Vidricus.

Enacted at Toul in a plenary synod.

## II. Bruno, bishop of the Church of Toul, consecrates the oratory of Bertiniaca curtis. (Year 1036.)

[Perard, *Collection of Various Pieces Serving the History of Burgundy*, p. 185.]

In the name of almighty God, in the name of the Triune, by the power of the One: BRUNO, humble bishop of the Leuci, by God’s gift, what he is.

Let the diligence of Christ’s faithful, both of the future and of the present time, know that once, while we were making our customary pastoral visitation through the parish of our episcopal office, it happened that we lodged at the cell of Bertiniaca with the faithful. Thus the lord abbot of Dijon, named Halinard, whose cell it was, and likewise our lord abbot Vuidricus, from the monastery of Saint Aprus—both praiseworthy in their manner of life—came together for our sake.

That place had been constructed quite suitably for the service of God, but had not yet been fortified with the blessing of dedication; and, what pleased us more, it was inhabited in disciplined fashion by religious monks. Accordingly, the aforesaid abbots asked us to dedicate it as an oratory, since it was a church of our diocese and jurisdiction. By granting their request, we fulfilled what belonged to our office.

After all the matters about which we had been consulted had been arranged, we remained there in consultation with the faithful, so that we might support by some donation Saint Benignus, the martyr of Christ in whose honor we consecrated that place, in order that by this means a memorial of us, both living and dead, might be established there.

After we had long deliberated on these matters, and no substantial gift that could be given had been proposed, it was suggested to us that the altars of two churches belonging to that saint were dependent upon our authority, and that it lay within our power and will to grant them.

But since clear matters are often obstructed by a certain mist of doubt, we feared that a sudden and unexamined donation, once introduced, might in the future give rise to some evil, and that it might at some time become a source of scandal. Since, however, we were attempting to do this with the protection of the law and the balance of equity, we postponed the matter until we could return to our see, after setting a period for deliberation.

Finally, on a subsequent day, we ordered a council of our clergy to be summoned. The petition of the aforesaid abbots was read before it. It was reported that, according to all who were present at the council, this could neither be completed nor stabilized without wills or written instruments, marked with the signatures of both parties.

With their approval, and at the insistence of Lord Abbot Vuidricus more urgently than the others, we gave two altars to Saint Benignus—namely, those of Solvis-Mont and Volferei-Curtis—on the condition that the monastic way of life should be regularly observed there. If this should not happen, however, since, alas, the powerful of this age are not what they once were, and if perhaps the bishop of Sens should seize that monastery for his own uses through the zeal of greed, or if, after the regular monks had been driven out, worldly pomp should enter that monastery in their place, then these altars, granted to that Church without any dispute and without apostrophic quibbling, shall return to our authority.

And because memory is the treasury of all things, so that our successors may not be obstructed by any deceptive confusion, but so that this agreement may be plainly revealed to them without concealment, we caused these written instruments to be recorded in both parts with signatures, so that, by the confirmation of true testimony, there might be a suitable means of defense both for those who hold them and for those who wish to remove them.

Sign of Bruno the bishop, confirming this document with his own hand; sign of Lord Abbot Halinard; [Col. 0587A] sign of Gregory, prior of the aforesaid cell; sign of Vuidricus, abbot; sign of Hunaldus, abbot; sign of Gibuin, primicerius; sign of Walter, dean; sign of Odelbric, archdeacon; sign of Lietard, archdeacon; sign of Gelizo, archdeacon; sign of Herbert, archdeacon; sign of Vuidricus, archdeacon; sign of Lambert, archdeacon; sign of Stephen, archdeacon; sign of Rudolf, archdeacon; sign of Beselin, archdeacon; sign of Rainard, count of the same city; sign of Hugh, brother of the lord bishop; sign of Milo; sign of Bruchard; sign of Stephen; sign of Boso; sign of Henry the advocate; sign of his son Sigifrid.

Therefore, since, according to the Apostle, “we must see to it how cautiously we walk, because the days are evil,” we do not remit this census from these altars, but reserve it to be paid to us and to our successors as a firm vesting payment. Whenever they become vacant through the death of their vicars, they shall freely have the power, without regard to the bishop or archdeacon, to appoint others and to sell those altars to them.

These things were enacted at Toul, in a plenary synod held on the eighth day before the Ides of October, on the thirteenth day of the lunar month, with epact I, concurrent IV, in a leap year, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1036, indiction V; in the thirteenth year of Conrad’s reign and the tenth of his empire.

I, Dizilin, chancellor, unworthy levite of the house of Saint Stephen, wrote this and publicly read it again.

## III. Bruno, bishop of Toul, confirms the foundation of the priory of Daguliacum (Deuilly). (Year 1044.)

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, I, Documents, p. 417.]

[Col. 0587C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, Bruno, bishop. We are admonished by the precept of divine law that, while doing good, we should not grow weary, but, increasing the places of the saints from day to day, should advance, with Christ’s favor, in the generosity of almsgiving according to our strength.

Therefore let the whole assembly of believers know that Walter of Daguliacum, with the counsel and consent of his wife Adila, built on an ancient estate belonging to him a certain small monastery suitable for the monastic order. For the salvation of himself, his predecessors, and his successors, he gave it in perpetual possession, subject to the monastery of Saint Aprus situated in the suburb of the city of Leuci; and he assigned to that same place, to be held perpetually for the support of the brothers serving God there, certain churches belonging to his inheritance. As a testimony confirming his donation, he caused this charter to be written and strengthened in our presence with apostolic authority.

Among the Franks, namely at Maireium (between Frain and Maré), two manses as the endowment of the church of the aforesaid monastery, with lands, meadows, and the serfs Durand, his wife Gisla, and their sons.

The church of Lord Valerius (Domvallier), with five and a half solidi from the fisc, and five modii of oats, together with the chapel of Sirei-Curtis (Sérécourt), and the serfs Thihero and Durand with their mother.

The church of Malisei-Curtis (Morizécourt, formerly Malsécourt), [Col. 0588A] with twelve denarii from the fisc, and the serfs Grimald, his wife and their sons, and Robert.

Half of the church of Lord Peter (Dampierre, now La Petite-Martigny), with one mansus, land, and meadow.

Half of the church of Aureliani-Mansions (Oreilmaison).

The church of Totelenei-Curtis (Tolaincourt), with twelve denarii from the fisc and one receipt-payment, and with the serfs Joselin and Haimon, together with their brothers, sisters, wives, and children, and Humbert with his children.

The church of Seivilla, with one receipt-payment and twelve denarii from the fisc.

The church of Madon’s village, with five solidi from the fisc and the same number of modii of oats, together with the chapel of Morlenicurtis (Morlaincourt), three annual receipt-payments, and the serf Rainfred with his wife and children, [Col. 0588B] lands and meadows.

Half of the church of Ciricis-Curtis (Xircourt), with one receipt-payment and twelve denarii.

The church of Saint-Hilary-of-the-Mount (Hilairmont), with one receipt-payment and twelve denarii, together with the whole estate—woods, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, male and female serfs.

Three parts of the church of Faucaudi-Curtis (Foucaucourt), with two receipt-payments and the same number of solidi, and with half of the alms and offerings, together with the entire estate—woods, vineyards, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, male and female serfs.

A third part of Radalli-Villa, with one receipt-payment and six denarii, together with the serf Rainer and his mansus.

The church of Monasteriolum (Le Mouserot), with one receipt-payment and six denarii, and with the serf Rudolf, his wife and children, and a mansus.

The church of Frasnello (Frenel), with the serfs Jospert and Angelrada, and Bernard with half of his children.

Half of the church of Roverium (Rouvre-en-Saintois), and of the other half a sixth part, with two receipt-payments and fifteen denarii, and with the serfs Folbert, his wife and children, and a mansus.

The church of Masnillum (Mainil), with the serf Baldwin, his wife and children, with two receipt-payments and twelve denarii.

Of the church of Saint Hilary, half, with the two chapels of Mannonis-Curtis (Manoncour) and Girandi-Curtis (Girancour), and the serf Theobald with his wife and children, and the territorial ban of that church, with three receipt-payments and fifteen denarii, and with a third part of the alms and offerings.

The field adjoining the monastery, as far as the wood called Banosus; and beyond the wood, another field extending to the stream; and another field there with its attached wood, which the priest Erembert gave for the remedy of his soul.

A mill toward the west, with two adjoining meadows.

A field given by Romold the steward, situated beside our corvée-land.

A mansus at Mannonis-Curtis, given by the priest Everard, with the land and meadow adjoining it there, and a vineyard given by the priest Erembert.

At Martiniacum (Martigny), a meadow sufficient for three carts, given for the remedy of Albric.

The allod of Rosolium (Ronceux), with male and female serfs, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, waters, and the fishing rights belonging to his portion, together with Albert, his wife and children.

Also a meadow at Gimiriacum sufficient for twelve carts [Col. 0589A] of hay.

Estates at Bonfagit (Bonfay) and Danvilla; he granted the monks and the men subject to them the use of the wood adjoining his castle, in the manner in which his own serfs used it.

He also granted the serfs of that cell who lived there the use of the other woods, pastures, and waters on all his estates, so that they might use them without any service obligation, as his own serfs did.

From the market adjoining his castle he also granted them the tenth denarius—that is, from the toll, from judicial revenues, or from every other income.

One of the ovens subject to the ban.

Widricus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Aprus, also contributed many ornaments to the aforesaid cell, and at Vallerias a vineyard producing five carts of wine, called the Enclosure of Lambert, in the district of Toul.

He also granted that, if a serf of Saint Aprus took a wife from among the female serfs of this cell, he might retain her without any opposition; and likewise, if a female serf of this cell took a serf of Saint Aprus in marriage, a stable common community should be established.

Walter retained the advocacy of the aforesaid place for himself and his wife Adila, and after them for whichever of their heirs should be the eldest. He established that none of his heirs who held this advocacy should be permitted to give it to anyone as a benefice, but should possess it himself in his own lordship; after them it was to pass to his son Odelric, and after him whichever nearer heir lawfully possessed the castle of Daguliacum was to hold the same advocacy.

He established as the total annual service to be given to himself and his heirs in memory of the advocacy, beyond which nothing further was to be demanded, two solidi in the coinage of that district, on the feast of Saint Mary of the Candles. From the judicial revenues of complaints which the provost of that place could settle personally, he granted the advocate nothing. But if a monk were unable to overcome someone’s contumacy and called upon the advocate for assistance, then the advocate should receive three denarii, provided that he first caused two parts to be given to the monk. Everything else he left to be arranged at the disposition of the abbot of the monastery of Saint Aprus.

I, Bruno, unworthy bishop by the grace of God, on account of the good intention of the faithful man, dedicated to God and blessed Mary the church built there. I removed it from subjection to the church of Lord Valerius, together with all its appurtenances, subjected everything contained within the churchyard [Col. 0589D] to the authority of the monks, and by apostolic authority forbade anyone—whether bishop or any other person—to demand justice in that place for any act of violence committed within the churchyard, unless the monks should bring a complaint through their vicar or some wicked persons should rebel.

In that church three altars were constructed and blessed by us. By the privilege of apostolic authority, with the bond of perpetual anathema, we granted the church this liberty: henceforth no one should presume to violate it, seal it, or celebrate divine offices at its altars except with the permission or command of the monks.

Those who live outside, in the castle or suburb, we decreed to be parishioners of that church and in all things subject to its vicar and the monks.

Moreover, because of the good affection that I have held toward that place and toward Saint Aprus, [Col. 0590A] as an addition to the alms I granted that place four altars with their revenues, namely: the altar of Totileni-Curtis; the altar of Medonis-Villa (Médonville); the altar of Faucaudis-Curtis; and the altar of the church of Saint Hilary.

They were granted on the condition that thereafter, when the vicars died, they should not be redeemed according to the custom of the other churches, but that suitable vicars should be chosen by the person presiding over the monastery, and that the care of souls alone should be entrusted to them by the bishop.

So that these agreements of ours might be established more firmly, we decreed that every year, on the Purification of Saint Mary, the provost of that cell should pay twelve denarii of the same value to the altar of Saint Stephen of the see of Leuci, in memory of its subjection.

If any of our successors in the course of time should wish to weaken or violate this alms, or to oppose our devotion contrary to justice, let him be bound by pastoral authority and also by anathema, and be compelled to return to what is right.

So that this grant of ours might be held more firmly and securely, we caused this charter to be read in our presence in a plenary synod and gave it to be strengthened by the witnesses subscribed below, with the praise and consent of all our clerics. And we separated from the communion of the holy Church by perpetual anathema all who should rebel against this sanction of ours, unless they should repent and make worthy satisfaction to God through penance.

*(What follows appears to differ somewhat from what precedes in ink and script.)*

[Col. 0590C] This prebendary arrangement also, by the authority mentioned above, we took care to establish in complete peace between the monks and the chaplain, with the counsel of the lord himself who had built the cell, and we caused it to be written below for the memory of posterity: five modii of wheat with rye, peas, or beans; five modii of spelt; five annonae (grain-rations); private Masses; the first Mass at the body of the deceased; purses; weddings; women’s purifications; burial of the white-clad [i.e. baptized]; confessions; the feast of the holy souls; without a candle at the five annual festivals; one denarius each; and at those festivals, a meal with the brothers, with alms for the deceased in whatever amount he gave while alive. To the monks, however, whose church it is, we granted all the rest; and we condemned under perpetual anathema all who should oppose this arrangement.

Sign of Gebiso, primicerius and chancellor. Sign of Stephen, archdeacon. Sign of Robert, archdeacon. Sign of Widricus, archdeacon. Sign of Rainard, count. Sign of Conrad, count.

In the nineteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Bruno, with Rainard the younger as count of the city; and with Ricuin the younger as count of the district of Sezanne, where the cell itself is situated.

I, Lambert, levite, wrote and subscribed this at the request of Lord Gebiso, primicerius and chancellor.

[Col. 0591A] *(What follows is in the original ink and by the same hand as the beginning of the diploma.)*

I, Bruno, unworthy bishop of the Leuci by the grace of God, have subscribed and affixed my sign.

Sign of Hugh of Cisa, a city of the Italians. Sign of Herberard, archbishop of Trier.  
[Note: He did not become archbishop until 1047.]

Sign of Adalbero, bishop of Metz. Sign of Theodoric, bishop of Verdun.  
[Note: He likewise did not become bishop until 1047.]

Sign of Hugh, archbishop of Chrysopolis. Sign of Widricus, abbot of Saint Aprus. Sign of Herbert, primicerius. Sign of Herbert, archdeacon. [Col. 0592A] Sign of Walter, count. Sign of Rainard, count. Sign of Odelric, count. Sign of another Odelric, count. Sign of Henry the advocate. Sign of Gombert. Sign of Norbert. Sign of Reimbald.

These things were given in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1043, indiction II, epact XIV, concurrent VI, while Henry II was reigning as Augustus of the Romans.

# [Letters and Decrees]

[Col. 0591]

# Letters and Papal Decrees of Saint Leo IX, Roman Pontiff

## [Genuine]

### I. Bull of Pope Leo IX confirming to Berard I, abbot of Farfa, and to his monastery all goods, rights, and privileges. (Year 1049.)

[Muratori, *Italian Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, II, 585.]

[Col. 0591B]

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ BERARD, abbot of the monastery situated at Farfa, and to your successors, perpetual greeting in the Lord.

When pious petitions are repeatedly brought to our ears, it is fitting for us to grant our assent and not resist such desires, so that sacred places may prosper and increase in our times and, God forbid, suffer no diminution.

Therefore, since you asked us that, from our generosity and by our gift, we should grant your religious community a confirmation of your monastery and of the honor which it now possesses and shall possess forever—namely, the estate called Massa, in which the church of Saint Valentine is situated; three ounces from the estate of Mucianus; the estate of Paternus, in which the church of Saint John is situated; the estate of Carbonianus; the estate of Septinianus; the estate of Pipilianus; the estate of Agellus; the estate of Mutella; the estate of Lorinianus; the estate of Urbana; the estate of Bucciniano; the estate of Albucianus; and other estates with houses, vineyards, olive groves, and tenant farmers—

we confirm to you and to your successors the aforesaid estates, ounces, and churches, with their houses, vineyards, meadows, woods, willow groves, watermills, and all their appurtenances, tenant farmers, and households, and generally everything belonging to them in its entirety, just as they were first and are now possessed by your monastery, whether in the county of Sabina, or in that of Narni, or in the county of Rieti, or of Forcona, Ascoli, Fermo, Apruzzo, and Penne, [Col. 0592B] also in the Roman and Tuscan counties, together with all the adjacent lands and dependencies of that monastery.

We grant you these to hold in their entirety, both what you now justly possess and what in the future, by the Lord’s generosity, you and your successors may be able to acquire, just as they were confirmed to the same venerable monastery through the privileges of blessed Adrian, formerly pope, and of Paul, and are to remain so.

We also grant that from the tolls of merchants, bridges, and tithes, to be given for the stipends of the monks and for the poor, beginning with the present second indiction, your religious community and the abbots who succeed you in your monastery may perpetually receive their due from all these revenues, as well as the offerings of the dead.

By apostolic censure, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, under divine adjurations and the prohibitions of anathema, we establish that none of our successors who are pontiffs, nor any other person, great or small, shall ever be permitted in any way to remove or alienate from your power and jurisdiction, or from that of your successors and your monastery, the aforesaid places, or whatever places your monastery may hereafter acquire with God’s help, according to the provisions stated above.

If any person, great or small, should presume by rash attempt to act against this privilege of ours, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and condemned with all the impious to eternal fire and punishment.

But may whoever, with pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from the most merciful Lord our God, forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Peter, scriniarius of the sacred palace, in the month and second indiction.

[Col. 0593A] Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Leo IX, indiction II.

### II. Bull of Pope Leo IX by which he removes the monastery of Saint Mary of Vallis-Pons at Perugia from the bishops of Perugia. (Year 1049.)

[Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, VI, 333.]

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to JOHN, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Vallis-Pons, and to your successors who shall be abbots, perpetual greeting in the Lord.

Since, with the Lord’s assent and not through our merits, we have attained the position in which the care of all the Churches looks to us, we ought to be especially solicitous concerning those Churches which are entrusted directly to our hands.

Therefore, at your petition, dearest son John, abbot, we have inclined our ears and have decided to fulfill it: namely, that we should confirm and strengthen for your monastery, and for you and your successors as abbots, all movable and immovable goods which in any manner now belong or shall forever belong to you and your monastery for its use; and that we should do likewise concerning tithes and first fruits, and concerning clerics whom it may happen to be necessary to ordain; and that you should provide no *fodrum*—a fiscal levy—to anyone on any condition except the pope, to whom you properly belong, as is contained in the mandate of blessed memory, our predecessor, Lord Pope Clement.

Therefore, through the tenor of this mandate of ours, we confirm and strengthen for your monastery, as we have said, and for you and your successors as abbots, whatever your monastery now possesses or shall possess forever, whether movable or immovable, however it may have come into its possession or may come into it.

We also establish that you may receive the tithes and first fruits from these goods according to customary practice, and that it shall be permitted for you and your successors to present your clerics for ordination to whichever bishop you wish.

Moreover, we prohibit anyone from exacting the *fodrum* from you, except the pope alone.

We also wish to make you free and secure from every alienation. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we annul and abolish those mandates which the unjust pontiffs Benedict and Gregory granted to Andrew, [Col. 0593D] bishop of Perugia, concerning your monastery.

For this confirmation, establishment, and abolition, we decree by apostolic censure, under the extinction threatened by divine judgment, that none of our successors who are pontiffs, nor any other person, great or small, and especially the bishop of Perugia, should ever presume to act against this mandate of ours.

If anyone should attempt it, let him be bound by the chain of anathema by the Lord God and not be released from it except by worthy satisfaction.

But let whoever proves to be the guardian and inviolator of this mandate of ours be blessed by the Lord God, because he has chosen to preserve it unshaken.

Farewell.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic [Col. 0594B] see, in the first year of Lord Pope Leo IX, indiction II.

### III. Privilege of Saint Leo IX for the Church of Trier. [Note: The present confirmation of the primacy of Trier deserves all the more attention because, notwithstanding the opposition of others, it seems to have been enacted in a contentious proceeding, and not by the Roman pontiff alone but by a synod in which Italians alone did not participate. Hildebrand, certainly raised in the Church of Cologne, did not wish his mother church to be humbled by the elevation of the see of Trier. What efforts he made to obstruct this synodal confirmation, later, after being made Roman pontiff under the name Gregory VII, he records in these words to Anno, archbishop of Cologne, in the year 1074, Letter 79, Book I of the *Register*: “Because of the memory of the discipline in which, during the time of our predecessor, we were raised in the Church of Cologne, we have shown it a special affection beyond the other Western Churches; and, as the sons of the Roman Church still testify, in the time of blessed Pope Leo we resisted with all our strength on behalf of the honor of your Church the grant made to the bishop of Trier, which the same blessed Leo bore with difficulty.” If Hildebrand’s opposition did no harm to the primacy confirmed by Leo, his faithful account of what happened is nevertheless useful here, preserved as it is in the letters of Gregory VII, since it also shows from this that the rights of the primacy of Trier extended over the archdiocese of Cologne, as over part of Belgic Gaul.] (Year 1049.)

[Hontheim, *History of Trier*, Diplomatic Documents, I, 386.]

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved Eberhard, archbishop of Trier, and to your successors, greeting in the Lord.

The eternal plan of the divine dispensation, by which he decreed that all things should be distributed through the ages, is changed by no mutability of things and varied by no diversity of times.

Thus it came about that the immutable order of this eternal dispensation promoted our mediocrity from the humility of the bishopric of Toul to apostolic eminence—not indeed through any merit demanded by us, but by a freely given gift.

For this reason your fraternity, dearest brother, accompanied us through the life of our charity and remained with us for some time at Rome.

Meanwhile, since we wished in every way to restore to each person his own right and justice, whether it had been entirely removed or somewhat altered, you brought us the privileges of your affection. They asserted that the primacy of Belgic Gaul had been granted in the manner set out below to your predecessors by our apostolic see, because at the beginning of the faith your Church of Trier was the first in those regions to receive the rudiments of Christianity through the eminent teachers Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus, whom blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, instructed, ordained after instructing them, and sent there to preach.

Those privileges also mention that more ancient privileges had been consumed by fire. These had been authentically granted from the beginning concerning the same matter to the aforesaid saints and to their successors—namely, the most worthy men Agritius, Maximinus, Paulinus, and Severus.

Pope John XIII, Benedict VI, and likewise another Benedict VII had also piously granted such privileges to Theodoric, archbishop of Trier, and to Egbert, likewise archbishop of Trier, in the times of Otto I and Otto II.

After considering and carefully weighing these matters, we judged it fitting, with the counsel and consent of all the clergy and people of Rome, to confirm that same primacy as it had been established and to strengthen it with our apostolic letters.

[Col. 0595B] When, on the Sunday of the Passion, in the church of Saint Peter, we ourselves, standing above in the ambo, revealed this in the presence of the entire clergy and people and caused the same privileges to be read, for love of the disciples of Saint Peter whom we have preferred—Eucharius, Valerius, and Maternus—all acclaimed that the primacy itself was rightly owed to you and to your successors, since you sit in the chair of the disciples of Saint Peter.

Therefore, with all praising and approving, as an investiture of this primacy we marked your head with the Roman mitre, which you and your successors shall always use according to Roman custom in ecclesiastical offices, and you shall always remember that you are disciples of the Roman see.

We nevertheless established this more fully and firmly in our synod, which we celebrated under God’s presidency around the seventeenth day after Easter, with the bishops, archbishops, and the other orders giving their consent.

The condition was, however, that every year you and your successors should send your legates once to us and to our successors, through whom we might send back instructions concerning the business of our interests to be conducted in those regions; and that every third year you yourselves should come to Rome for a visit, as dearest brothers come to their firstborn brother, unless unavoidable necessity should intervene.

Therefore, granting your desires, according to the tenor of the aforesaid privileges, by this privilege of our apostolic authority we decree and confirm this primacy to you and to your successors in the following manner: you shall have the first place after the apostolic legate sent to Gaul and Germany, and so forth.

And if no envoy of the Roman Church is present, you shall sit after the emperor or king, together with whatever other provisions are recounted in their proper places in the privileges granted to Theodoric.

I, Halmardus, unworthy archbishop of the Church of Lyons, sitting in the aforesaid synod, preserving the force of the ancient constitutions and the authority of the Church of Lyons, praised this decree and, strengthening it with my own hand, subscribed it.

[Note: The authority of the Church of Lyons is preserved. By this reservation concerning Lyons, the provisions stated above concerning the primacy of Trier throughout the Gauls and its rights are clearly confirmed. Halmardus feared for the special privileges of his own Church, not for the primacy; this primacy Pope Gregory VII finally granted in 1079 to Gebuin, archbishop of Lyons, namely over the four provinces of Lyons, Rouen, Tours, and Sens.]

I, John, bishop of Porto, sitting in the aforesaid synod, confirmed and subscribed.

I, Cadalus, bishop, subscribed.

I, Benedictus, bishop of the Church of Tusculum, subscribed.

I, Gerhardus, bishop of Florence, subscribed.

I, Crescentius, bishop of Santa Rufina—not by merit but by grace—subscribed below.

I, Hugo, bishop of Assisi, subscribed.

I, Wido, bishop of Asti, subscribed.

I, Wido, bishop of Volturno, subscribed.

I, Cunibertus, bishop of Turin, subscribed.

I, Henricus, bishop of Spoleto, subscribed.

Given on the Ides of April, through the hands of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction II.

### IV. Pope Leo to Cawallon, abbot of Redon. (Year 1049.)

[Morice, *Mémoires pour servir à l’histoire de Bretagne*, I, 396.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved in Christ Catwallon, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Saviour, built in the place called Redon, situated in Brittany, and to his successors who shall be regularly appointed there, forever.

The care of the office entrusted to us compels us to exercise concern for all the Churches and, with the balance of equity, to assist all those placed in need, insofar as, with God’s gift, we are able. Yet we ought especially to assist and provide for those venerable places which are known to belong to the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church and which pay it an annual census, with the highest attention, for the honor due to the supreme and apostolic see, whose members they are.

Therefore, in accordance with your petition, we grant, concede, and confirm by this decree of our authority the following privileges to the aforesaid monastery, over which you are known to preside and which is known to belong to the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church, from which an annual census of three gold denarii is paid to the Roman Church. We decree that no king or emperor, no person endowed with any dignity, may diminish or take away, under any pretext or occasion whatsoever, anything that has already been donated from its own right to that venerable place by any persons—just as is established concerning Bella Island, which Geoffrey, duke of the Bretons, bestowed upon the aforesaid monastery from his own right, and which Alan, his son, later granted and, as you assert and those who are with you testify, firmly confirmed in perpetuity.

This we also confirm by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and by our own authority, and we grant that you and your successors may possess that island itself in perpetuity and without disturbance. [Something is missing.] Nor shall anyone dare, under the appearance of any cause or pretext, to diminish or take away anything that has been or may in the future, by God’s mercy, be granted there. Rather, we wish that everything offered there or that may happen to be offered there, both by you and by your successors, be possessed forever and without disturbance, and that it serve in every way the uses for which it was granted, namely their support.

But if any king, priest, cleric, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him know that he has rendered himself guilty before the divine judgment because of the iniquity he has committed. And unless he comes to his senses and makes suitable correction, let him be separated from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe this page of our constitution, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at the Lateran, on the Ides of April.

### V. Saint Leo IX asserts to Eberhard, archbishop of Trier, that the cell of the Four Crowned Martyrs was formerly granted to the archbishops of Trier by Benedict VII. (Year 1049.)

[See above under Benedict VIII and the *Gesta Treverorum*, edited by Wyttembach and Muller, I, 150.]

### VI. Saint Leo IX confirms the freedom and privileges of the monastery of Saint-Saviour at Septimo. (Year 1049.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, III, 68.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Peter, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Saviour at Septimo, and to his successors as abbots, perpetual blessing and salvation in the Lord.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to assist with benevolent compassion those who are endowed with devout religion and to grant appropriate support to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, moved by your prayers, by the text of this our ordinance we confirm and strengthen for you the monastery itself of Saint-Saviour, with all its movable and immovable goods, and with all things that move themselves, whatever may justly and legally belong to it.

We further decree that the monastery itself be secure from every injury and free from the interference of the bishop; that the ordinations of priests and of the other grades be conferred in that monastery by any Catholic bishop; that alms both of the living and of the dead be given to the same monastery without the bishop’s accusation or challenge; and that you receive the tithe from the monastery’s possessions. Whoever asks to be buried at the monastery shall be buried by the monks.

Moreover, except by the Apostolic See, the abbot shall not be judged or summoned to a synod, just as he receives consecration from no other. We establish by apostolic censure that none of our pontifical successors, no margrave, duke, count, bishop, or any other person, great or small, dare act against this our ordinance. Whoever does so shall be struck by the bond of anathema. But whoever is its guardian and observer shall obtain blessing from the Lord God.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, through the hands of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction II.

### VII. Saint Leo IX attests that John, made bishop of Porto from the see of Tusculum, was sanctioned by the synod held in the Church of Saint-Saviour. He confirms the privileges of the Church of Porto.

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, I, 120.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved brother in Christ and fellow bishop John, bishop of the Church of Porto, and to his successors forever, greeting in the Lord.

Both reason and kindness require us to grant the wishes of those who petition, since what it is reasonable to provide should certainly not be denied in kindness. Therefore, because you transferred from the see of Tusculum to the same see of Porto, we considered it appropriate first to examine this matter in synod, whether it had been done justly or unjustly. We did so while sitting in synod and in the Church of the Saviour.

When the matter had been carefully examined—how it had happened that you passed from one episcopate to another—it was found that this had been done both out of necessity and for the sake of usefulness, and it was judged that it could be done. What the necessity and the usefulness were has been expressed plainly enough. The necessity was that the Roman Church had already been deprived of the sons whom she herself had nourished, of whom you were the surviving remnant. The appropriate usefulness lay either in matters concerning that Church, which were known to you better than to others; or in giving counsel; or even in mediation between the Roman Church and the emperors, whose mediator you had often been.

Moved, therefore, by this consideration, we resolved to satisfy your petition—namely, to confirm the episcopate of Porto to you and your successors—because we gladly do so.

First, therefore, we confirm the episcopate itself of the Church of Porto, which appears to be situated outside the aforesaid city of Porto and is called Saint Hippolytus, with its vineyards, gardens, enclosed vineyards, and olive groves surrounding the same church; likewise, the enclosure of one vineyard situated wholly at Cardetum; at Finilia, two enclosures with vineyards and lands; and at Basi, all these properties being situated on the larger island.

Also, the Church of Saint Mary and another Church of Saint Lawrence, with cells, gardens, vineyards, and five enclosures: one at the Church of Saints Gregory and Theodore, another at the Church of Saint Vitus, as bounded by the wall, the river Tiber, and the surrounding boundaries; a third on the riverbank; a fourth beside Saint Mary as far as Trajan; and a fifth beside Saint Lawrence as far as Trajan.

Also, the vineyard enclosure at the place called Scarajo; another parcel situated within the enclosure; one parcel of vineyard in the land of Cucuzuba; and another at Montone. Likewise, the entire estate called Baccanum, with its appurtenance called Criptula, in which there are ancient cisterns situated beside the same city of Porto, as follows:

It begins on the first side at a tree called a tamarisk and runs toward a small column that appears to stand in the field, two miles distant from the same city; then it proceeds by a straight route along the Via Salaria as far as the fishermen’s hut; then it returns to the sea through Buccina and follows the seashore around to Saint Nympha and as far as the mouth of the Micina, with the places called Vincera as far as the bathhouses and the place called Trajan’s Port.

Also, another smaller castle in its entirety, with all its appurtenances; and in the city of Constantiniana everything known to be held there, together with the Church of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, with its crypts, where the animals belonging to that church appear to remain; then as far as Saint Mary, which is situated in an arch with a crypt; and the house called the Bath of Venus; and as far as the public road within the same castle; and the reed-bed of this city.

Also, the monastery of Saint Agnes, with its saltworks and vineyards, which appears to have a passageway. Furthermore, the entire estate called Polmus, with houses, vineyards, lands, pastures, extending as far as the ancient oven belonging to the aforesaid episcopate.
