In the same estate there appears to be an ancient tomb, on the Via Portuensis, approximately ten miles from the city of Rome.

Likewise, the entire larger island, with gardens, vineyards, or lands at the place called Scarajo—which was formerly Trajan’s harbor—adjoining the same estate of Baccanum, with everything belonging to it. Likewise, the estate called Judaeorum and the estate called Gualdus, with all their appurtenances, situated beside the aforesaid city; and the entire Salt Line, extending in a single line.

Also, at Baccanum, at Genestula, and in the nine lines, all the salt lines known to belong to your episcopate; and the entire estate called Greater Gualdus, with the Church of Saint Aurea and its tomb, and the land of Semitaritia, which is called Planura, in which cisterns appear to exist, situated between the river and the boundary called Arcione.

We also confirm to you in its entirety the estate called Galeria, in which there is the Church of Saint Mary, with halls or dining rooms and various chambers, together with all its buildings known to be contained within it; with all its borders, boundaries, and limits; lands, farmsteads, woods, and marshes; with the bridge and the stream itself called Galeria as far as the river; with places suitable for making a watermill; and with everything generally and completely cultivated and improved, as stated above.

It is situated in the field called Meruli, on the Via Portuensis, approximately twelve miles from the city of Rome. Its boundaries begin at the entire estate on the first side, at the meadows of Caracus, which are called Meruli; then continue as far as the mountain formerly held by John of Mincia and his heirs, and the heirs of Stephen the Nomenclator; then beyond the road through the farmstead formerly held by John of Sergius; then cross another cart-road and arrive at the farmstead held by the heirs of Franco of Trastevere, as marked by marble boundary stones.

Then the boundary runs through the farmstead of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian; crosses an ancient ditch that in spring carries water into the stream of Galeria; ascends along that stream to the mill in the wood; turns along the cart-road to the middle valley of the mountain called Zunili; and continues as far as Staffili, which stands at Lintistinum, and as far as the head of the valley of Stabla.

Then, through the ditch of that valley, it proceeds from the foot of the Salt Line, enclosing the entire field as far as the small field called Viscoli and the Galiarda fishpond, enclosing that small field, which consists of thirty lines. It continues beside the lines where the monasteries of Miranda stand, as far as the larger pond; follows the bank of the pond as far as Burdunaria; runs from the foot of the line as far as Baccanum and the land of the aforesaid episcopate; and follows the boundary called Arcione as far as the stream called Galeria, and the Marsh of Ricorde, as far as the first boundary of the meadows of Caracus.

Within these boundaries, the places and names are as follows: Saint Caesarius, Palmis, Sorbilanum, Old Clusa, Greater Marsh, Medianum, Rusty Mountain, the Mountain of Zumilis, Canaparvis Mountain, Celsa, Limes, Major, the Accursed Little Pond, Tiocli, Gagliarda Fishpond, Olivastrum, and the Little Foreigners’ Pond, with all their appurtenances.

We also confirm to you in perpetuity four complete principal ounces of the entire larger pond of Porto, with all its fishing, revenue, and station, and with everything belonging to those four ounces, just as it was granted to the aforesaid Church of Porto by our predecessors.

Furthermore, we grant and confirm to you and your successors the entire tower called the White Tower, with houses, vineyards, gardens, lands, fields, meadows, pastures and woods, marshes and streams, cultivated and uncultivated places, empty and occupied places, and everything generally and completely belonging to that tower, as its boundaries indicate: on the first side, the stream called Galeria; on the second side, the river Tiber; on the third side, Pulverinula; and on the fourth side, the boundary called Arcione.

We also grant to the people who from time to time will dwell within the tower that they shall be subject to no authority or jurisdiction and shall serve no one or perform military service except the bishop who shall be in the aforesaid episcopate.

We also confirm to you and your successors forever all the movable and immovable property and resources of those people who die without an heir and intestate in the aforesaid city of Porto, whether in Trastevere, on the island of Lycaonia, or wherever they appear to belong to the jurisdiction of your episcopate. We establish the Church of Porto itself as their legitimate heir, so that the bishop of that Church may have the power to arrange everything according to his will, provided that the goods do not perish, so that they may benefit the dead forever.

Moreover, from the right of our sacred Lateran palace, which belongs to our public authority, we grant and confirm to you and your successors forever the castaldus of Porto, or whatever until now our castaldiones have held from the entire city of Porto, whether from its gates or ships, and likewise from the whole of Burdunaria, or whatever, inside or outside, belonged to that office everywhere. We grant all this to you and your successors to possess forever.

Thus it shall be in your power to appoint there as castaldus or agent whatever person you wish; and whatever he acquires from that office shall be rendered to you and your successors. Provided, however, that, if it pleases our count or the count of our successors, he shall swear fealty to him concerning what belongs to our palace.

The counts who are in office at any time, whether appointed by us or by our successors, shall in no way dare to appoint or establish another castaldus or agent except those whom you or your successors appoint or establish. If they do so, or violently take away anything from the aforesaid office of castaldus, or attempt to violate or oppose what has been handed over by us to you and your successors, each one shall pay four pounds of gold—half to our palace and half to your episcopate—and whatever has been appointed by them as castaldus shall be void. If he remains obstinate thereafter, let him remain excommunicated until he satisfies you.

Likewise, we grant and confirm to you and your successors forever, from the city of Porto, fishermen and two curiales, whoever among them you may wish to choose forever, so that thereafter they shall make no payment or service and shall not be compelled to appear at court by any person. To you and your successors we entrust this power.

We also confirm to you and your successors in perpetuity one entire farmstead called Genesianum, also called Mallianum, with the small island situated beyond the stream at that place, with everything belonging to it, situated on the Via Portuensis beside Mallianum and belonging to the monastery of Saint Pancratius.

We also confirm to you and your successors forever the entire island called Lycaonia, where there is the Church of Saint John the Baptist and Saint Adalbert. Concerning this island you lodged a complaint in the synod that we held in the Church of the Saviour, because Crescentius, bishop of the Church of Santa Rufina, was claiming that same church for his episcopate.

When both parties stood before our presence and that of the entire synod, it was agreed that, if you had a document concerning the matter, you should produce it for examination and reading. Immediately you brought forward the privilege that our predecessor Benedict VIII had issued for your predecessor Benedict, the bishop who was called of Pontius, concerning the entirety of the episcopate.

When it had been read, that church was found expressly named there—the church which, as you stated in your complaint, your predecessor himself had dedicated in the time of the emperor Otto III, by whom it had been built in honor of Saint Adalbert, who in his own time suffered martyrdom for the name of Christ.

But that bishop asked us to grant him an adjournment until a fixed date, so that he might bring before you the justice which he said he possessed. Since the synod was ending on that day, we granted it. When the date arrived, you came to us humbly and alone, whereas he, relying on a great multitude of men, disdained to come to us.

Nevertheless, while we were sitting with our judges, we sent a legate to him so that he might come to us. He said that he would come only with his redeemed helpers. Having said this, he withdrew with his entire multitude.

Disregarding his contumacy, we then sent our archdeacon Hugh to his house, on the advice of the judges, so that he would come to us on the following day, as a bishop who was to give an account to another bishop.

When we sat in the same way on the next day awaiting him, he did not come. Instead, he sent certain letters bearing a request for pardon. Since he gave no reason why he should be awaited any longer, and with all the judges approving, Brother Alinardus, archbishop of Lyons, pronounced a canonical and definitive sentence: the first concerning the punishment of the contumacious; the second concerning the churches that are within the boundaries of the episcopate and the manner in which they belong to it.

After this sentence had been pronounced by us and approved by all, it was confirmed. Therefore, by this our privilege, we grant and confirm that same church to you and your successors, and we perpetually prohibit both that bishop and his successors from bringing any complaint concerning that church. It is situated on the aforesaid island, with its farmsteads and oratories within those farmsteads, and with everything generally and completely belonging to them, including their gardens and watermills.

It lies within this city of Rome, extending from one end, where the river divides, as far as the other end of the island, where it joins together.

In the same manner, we grant and confirm to you and your successors forever all episcopal ordinations that must be carried out throughout Trastevere, whether of priests, deacons, deaconesses, or subdeacons, and the consecration of churches or altars—unless, perhaps, cardinals, deacons, subdeacons, or acolytes of the sacred Lateran palace are to be appointed.

We grant the power of ordaining, blessing, and consecrating all these persons to you and your successors, or to whatever bishops you invite for this purpose.

And so that your parish may not be invaded by any bishop, we take care by this our privilege to set out and confirm its boundaries to your Church.

The first boundary begins at the broken bridge, where the water is said to pass through the wall of the city of Trastevere, then through the Septimian Gate and the Gate of Saint Pancratius; along the paved road of that gate as far as the marble bridge over the Anio; and along that paved road to the tribunal.

From there it turns through the marshes as far as the sea; then along the sea for two miles beyond the lighthouse as far as the greater mouth; from there along the greater river as far as Rome, at the broken bridge beside the Marmorata; through the Bridge of Saint Mary as far as the Bridge of the Jews; across the middle of the river; and straight to the middle of the broken bridge, where we began at the water. This is the first boundary, excluding the Catholic churches of Trastevere: Saint Mary in Trastevere, Saint Chrysogonus, and Saint Cecilia, as well as the monastery of Saint Pancratius and the monasteries of Saints Cosmas and Damian. Nevertheless, whatever must be done by bishops in the aforesaid churches, we grant to the bishops of Porto, when invited by those churches.

Likewise, within the aforesaid episcopate, we grant and confirm the parish church of Saint Mary and Saint Apollinaris at Mola Rupta; the parish church of Saint Stephen at Pansi; the parish church of Saint Mary at Apuniana; and all the small or large churches of whatever name that are or may be within the aforesaid boundaries, except those situated in Trastevere that we have already mentioned.

Meanwhile, we decree and order, just as our predecessors ordered, that in the river which flows beside the city of Porto no one dare establish mills or a bridge in any manner without your order or that of your successor bishops, according to the ancient custom. When mills or a bridge have been established or built either by you or by others to whom you have entrusted the work, those mills or that bridge shall be administered at your discretion.

If a bridge is built, no one shall dare cross from here to there, or from there to here, with a loaded wagon carrying provisions or wine.

Again, we decree and order that no priest or cleric of any order from the entire episcopate dare compel anyone to appear at court, force anyone to settle disputes, or exact any service from them, except the bishops of Porto, in whose parish they are.

But if any presumptuous person—whether duke, count, viscount, chamberlain, a person sent by our apostolic see, or any other authority—should exercise dominion over that city of Porto, whatever his rank, and should wish to take away or diminish from the jurisdiction, power, and authority of the aforesaid episcopate any of the aforesaid immovable properties, the aforementioned castaldus, the two fishermen, the two curiales, or all the aforesaid clerics; or should attempt to violate the parish; or should recall to public service the people living in the aforesaid tower, or those dwelling wherever the property of the episcopate is situated, let him know that he shall pay to that episcopate twenty pounds of pure gold and shall moreover be subject to anathema.

Establishing this by apostolic censure, under invocation of the divine judgment and prohibition by anathema, we decree that none of our pontifical successors, nor any other person, great or small, shall ever dare to oppose, transgress in any respect, or diminish anything of what we have established for the praise of God and for the stability and increase of the aforesaid episcopate.

Just as we have established or granted above, so let everything remain forever, throughout everlasting and perpetual times, without any diminution.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should presume with reckless boldness to act against this our privilege or break it in any respect, and should fail to allow what we established above to remain firm, and should offend in any matter, let him know that, unless he repents, by the authority of almighty God, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us, who exercise his office, he is bound by the bond of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, and destined to be burned in eternal fire with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, with the devil and all his pomp.

But whoever, with devout regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this our privilege may deserve to obtain from the just Judge, the Lord our God, blessings, grace, and eternal life, forever and ever. Amen. Farewell.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, through the hands of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction II.

I, Eberhard, archbishop of Trier, although unworthy, was present and subscribed.

I, Alinardus, archbishop of Lyons, praising this decree, subscribed with my own hand.

I, W., bishop, subscribed.

I, Cunibertus, bishop of Turin, wrote.

I, Cadalus, bishop of Parma, wrote.

I, Oppizo, bishop of Pisa, wrote.

“We therefore decree that no person at all be permitted…” etc. “If, therefore, anything…” etc. “But to all…” etc. Amen.

### VIII. Privilege of Saint Leo IX for Richerius, abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino. (Year 1049.)

[Tosti, *Storia della badia di Monte Casino*, I, 255.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our dearest son in Christ, Richerius, lord and religious abbot of the most sacred monastery of the blessed Benedict, confessor of Christ, situated on the mountain called Cassino, and to his venerable congregation, perpetual greeting in the Lord.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to assist with benevolent compassion those who are endowed with devout religion and to grant appropriate support to the desires of petitioners.

Therefore, since you asked us that we should fortify by our privilege, and through us and our successors forever, according to the custom of our predecessors, the monastery of Saint Benedict situated on Mount Cassino—whose abbatial consecration we recently received through the gift of the most pious emperors Henry and Conrad—and withdraw it from the power of all archbishops and bishops, and defend, grant, and confirm its properties under the prohibition of anathema, we, moved by your prayers, grant and confirm to you and your successors the aforesaid monastery, to be consecrated forever by us and our successors without any intervening Simoniacal wickedness, together with all its churches, monasteries, cells, castles, cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards, watermills, gardens, meadows, woods, appurtenances, and adjoining properties, wherever or however they are known to belong to the rights of that monastery … [lacuna in the source].

Moreover, we prohibit any bishop of any church from exercising any jurisdiction whatsoever in the aforesaid monastery, apart from the Apostolic See, so that no bishop may presume in any way to celebrate the solemn offices of Mass there unless he has been invited by the abbot of that monastery.

After your death, no one shall appoint an abbot there except one whom the common agreement and will of the brothers from that congregation has elected; and the elected man shall come freely and without payment to us or our successors to be consecrated. But if he comes from elsewhere—which cannot be said of you, since you have come from our monastery and to be consecrated by us—or if he prefers to be consecrated by another archbishop or bishop, then both the consecrated man and the consecrator shall be anathema.

We promulgate, etc. [lacuna in the source].

Farewell.

### IX. Saint Leo IX subjects the monastery of Holy Cross at Rome to Richerius, abbot of Cassino, and to his successors. (Year 1049.)

[Gattula, *Historia Casinensis*, 252.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Richerius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict, situated on Mount Cassino, and to your successors, perpetual greeting in the Lord.

We are impelled by the care of the oversight entrusted to us, and are moved by the ardor of Christian religion and zeal for the advancement of divine worship, to consider the stability of venerable places and the security of those who serve God, so that, through this pious labor, souls dedicated to Christ—who have resolved to serve him during the days of their lives—may persevere undisturbed. Moreover, let those things remain firm to the end that Christians have undertaken in praise of God.

Since, therefore, it is clear that the monastery of Jerusalem, also called Holy Cross, had for some time lacked a community of monks of God appropriate to such a place, and had been handed over with no provident superior or monks dwelling there, we were moved by compassion for so great a sacrilege and compelled by grief. By apostolic authority we have therefore provided that the same monastery be joined to the monastery entrusted to you, so that, both in the present second indiction and forever, it may be governed by you and your successors, together with everything belonging to it in its entirety, and be ruled in the fear of God; and so that, joined to your monastery, it may remain united with it, so that in that venerable place you may offer praises to our Lord God.

We establish that you are to render no account concerning it or anything belonging to it except to God alone and to our authority. The construction or repair of the building and the provision of lamps shall likewise unquestionably be carried out through your diligent care.

Therefore, let no delay arise in offering praises to God or in preparing the lamps; hasten to perform these duties with devoted sincerity, lest fear of the future judgment shake you because of the fault of careless negligence. Rather, strive to labor so that divine mercy may be pleased by your effort and so that what has been decreed by us after just deliberation may remain unshaken in future and perpetual times.

Nevertheless, the consecration of the abbot of that place, chosen by you according to God, shall always be awaited from our apostolic see, under whose jurisdiction it exists.

The number of monks who serve God there shall always be as large as the capacity of the place can sustain, but no more than twelve; they too shall have food and clothing according to the capacity of the place, so that there may never be any negligence in divine service. For we have made this an instrument and an increase for that church, so that its poverty may be supplied from the abundance of your monastery, and so that eternal reward may be granted both to us and to you and your successors.

### X. Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions and privileges of the canons of the Church of Verona. (Year 1049.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, V, 761.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved sons in Christ, Toton, archpriest; Amelricus, archdeacon; and Arduino, provost; and to all the canons of the Church of Saint Verona, both present and future, perpetual greeting in the Lord.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with devout religion through benevolent compassion, and to grant suitable assistance to the wishes of petitioners. Therefore, in the name of almighty God the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and all the other saints whose names are written in the book of life; and also by the authority of the holy canons, we command all patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, dukes, marquises, counts, and all persons, great and small, that no one be permitted to injure, dispossess, disturb, or withdraw the investiture of your persons, or your estates and benefices, or any of your rightful possessions and investitures of the benefices of the aforesaid canonry, which you have held until now. [Col. 0606D]

Likewise, we command that none of you, by any device, seek from your bishop the benefices which you have been accustomed to invest, or receive their investiture from his hands. Likewise, we command concerning all the property of your canonry, both its estates and its castles or villages, hospices, cultivated holdings, uncultivated holdings, leasehold properties, tithes, male and female servants, lands, vineyards, meadows, willow-groves, mountains, and plains, both within the city and outside the city, which have been or shall be bestowed upon you by the faithful, [Col. 0607A] that no person, great or small, interfere in them; but that it be permitted for you to hold them peacefully, just as until now you have held them through the generosity of my pontifical predecessors, or of emperors and kings, namely according to the order contained in the pages of your charters.

And let no archpriest or archdeacon be placed over you from any other church, nor let anyone from the clergy be appointed to your association without the election of all the brothers. I say this because I hope that your church will never lack clerics who are suitable for these honors. But if the archpriest or archdeacon should attempt to give any of the aforesaid church properties without the will and approval of the brothers, we altogether forbid it, lest scandal arise in the Church. [Col. 0607B]

But if—God forbid—the archpriest and archdeacon should die at the same time, let the provost be permitted to enjoy their offices and investitures until an archpriest or archdeacon has been appointed. For if any written invention should be found, composed by anyone for the destruction of the rightful order, or of your inheritance, or of the things mentioned above, we command that it be utterly destroyed and never appear again.

But if—God forbid—anyone should attempt to act against this written declaration of our authority, or should offend you in the matters mentioned above, and should not make amends within a year, may his attempt become void, and may the earth swallow him alive as it swallowed Dathan and Abiram in the rebellion of Korah; may the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian come upon him; may the curse pronounced on Mount Ebal and the anathema *maranatha* come upon him; and may all those plagues and curses with which God struck Pharaoh and Egypt, and which are written in the five books of Moses, come upon him. May he be joined to Judas the betrayer and, together with Ananias and Sapphira, suffer eternal punishment, and be subject to the judgment of us and of our successors. [Col. 0607C]

Issued on the Nones of May, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo, indiction II.

## XI. Saint Leo IX confirms the privileges of the monastery of Cluny, at the request of Abbot Hugh. (Year 1049.)

[Cluniac Bibliotheca, p. 1824.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in Christ, Hugh, abbot of our monastery of Cluny, founded in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and to your successors in the abbacy, perpetual salvation in the Lord. [Col. 0607D]

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with devout religion through benevolent compassion, and to grant suitable assistance to the wishes of petitioners. For from the Creator of all things, God, we shall gain the chief reward of profit if, in our time, venerable places are either brought into a better condition or strengthened so that they may never be diminished in any respect.

Therefore, moved by your prayers, dearest son, we confirm and strengthen for our monastery of Cluny, which by God’s authority you appear to govern, through this privilege of our apostolic authority, just as our predecessors did in their privileges, whatever property and resources it now possesses and shall possess forever; so that nothing may ever be mutilated from them by any human recklessness, but that everything, with God preserving it, may remain intact for the use and support of the brothers now serving there and those who shall serve throughout the ages. In the protection of this apostolic safeguard, we also grant to the place itself the ancient liberty conceded to it by our predecessors—not establishing something new, but confirming what is old.

Namely, let no mortal, whether emperor, king, duke, marquis, archbishop, bishop, or any other human authority, presume to exercise any power in any respect over that monastery of Cluny. [Col. 0608A] Nor, after your body has been released from life, may anyone dare to appoint and install another there; but it shall always remain within the judgment and election of the brothers to choose and set over themselves as abbot any member of their congregation whom they wish, according to God and according to the rule of Saint Benedict. His consecration shall not be sought from a designated bishop, but from whichever person the congregation itself prefers; it shall not be purchased for any price, but received freely.

We likewise command and confirm the same concerning all ordinations to ecclesiastical orders and the consecrations of altars or churches: it shall be permitted for you and your successors to request these freely from whichever bishop you wish, and no one shall dare to oppose you. [Col. 0608B]

We have decided to grant this prerogative, conceded to your monastery by our predecessors and rightly confirmed by us, for this reason: just as until now it has existed under the sole law and authority of the apostolic see, so henceforth it shall always remain so, and shall look to no other authority, so that, placed beneath the shelter of apostolic protection, it may always grow and continually increase, fearing neither the tyranny of wicked men nor any human power. Thus the daily services of God may be carried out there devoutly and peacefully, as is customary, and those who perform them may not be troubled, harassed, or disturbed in any way by anyone. This prerogative also includes the free reception of chrism from whatever bishop you wish.

All these things, as we have stated above, just as we found them decreed by our predecessors, so we have decided to establish and confirm them also. By apostolic censure, under the solemn warning of divine judgment, we decree that no person, great or small, endowed with spiritual or secular dignity, or deprived of every dignity, should ever attempt to act against this privilege of our apostolic authority or infringe it in any respect. Whoever, with rash daring and impious presumption, acts against God and Saint Peter, against his own soul, let him know that he is then +only pierced by the goad of our apostolic curse, pierced through by the weapon of our apostolic excommunication, and transfixed by the sword of our apostolic anathema; nor shall he be restored to his former state of salvation by any worthy satisfaction. [Col. 0608C]

But whoever observes this and approves that our privilege remain inviolate shall obtain from God, the giver of all good things, blessing, grace, and every good both in the present age and in the future. [Col. 0608D]

Given on the fourth Ides of June, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction II.

## XII. Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Fulda. (Year 1049.)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, 359.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Echbert, pious [Col. 0609B] and religious abbot of the venerable monastery of the Savior of our Lord Jesus Christ and Saint Boniface, situated in the place called Bochonia, beside the bank of the river called the Fulda, and through you to that venerable monastery and to your successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with devout religion through benevolent compassion, and to grant assent with eager devotion to those who make just and religious requests. For from the Creator of all things, God, we shall doubtless earn the chief reward of profit if venerable places, suitably ordered, are without doubt brought into a better condition.

Therefore, because you have asked us, we have decided by our apostolic command perpetually to grant anew and reconfirm to you and your successors the aforesaid monastery of the Savior of our Lord Jesus Christ and Saint Boniface, situated in the place called Bochonia beside the bank of the river called the Fulda, together with all its movable and immovable property, which it now possesses and, with God’s help, shall possess in the future. [Col. 0609C]

We also grant and donate to you, dearest and most beloved son, and perpetually to your successors in the abbacy, out of our great love and the excessive affection which we have for you and desire henceforth to have, the monastery of the apostle Saint Andrew called Exaiulum, situated at Rome beside the church of holy Mary, ever-Virgin and Mother of God, called *ad Praesepe*, together with all its dwellings, heated rooms, cells, wine stores, and kitchen; with vineyards, gardens, and various kinds of fruit trees; with its estate and well; with an entrance through the principal gate from the public road; and with everything generally belonging to that monastery, situated both within and outside the city, which is rightly and properly recognized as belonging to it. [Col. 0609D]

We prohibit every priest of any church from exercising any authority or jurisdiction over this monastery of yours at Fulda, apart from our apostolic see, and especially the bishop in whose diocese it appears to have been built; thus, unless he has been invited by the abbot of that monastery, he shall not presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there.

We confirm and strengthen in perpetuity for your monastery, without opposition from any person, the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful, according to the privileges of our predecessors. [Col. 0610A] We also decree that no person, great or small, may inflict any force or controversy upon that monastery concerning its property and dependents. By our apostolic authority we also forbid any woman ever to presume to enter there, and we forbid anyone ever to hold a court there or in any of its other places, or to compel its slaves or tenants to any service, except one to whom the abbot has granted permission for the sake of his necessary needs.

The brothers shall also have the power, whenever necessary, to choose an abbot for themselves from among their number according to the rule of Saint Benedict, without opposition from any person.

Furthermore, after deliberation, we decree that at suitable times information be given to our ecclesiastical care concerning the manner in which monastic religion is directed in the regular habit and devoted, in fitting concord, to ecclesiastical discipline, lest—God forbid—under the pretext of this privilege the mind and conduct of your rectitude be in any way turned aside from the norm of justice. [Col. 0610B]

We also grant you—whom we know to be a well-educated and eloquent man—the right to preach the word of God by the authority of the apostle Saint Peter and of us, his unworthy vicar. We further grant, by our apostolic authority, that both you and your successors may hold, before the other abbots of Gaul or Germany, the first place of sitting in every place and assembly.

By the license of our apostolic authority we also grant to you and your successors the use of the dalmatic and sandals during the solemnities of Mass, according to what is contained in the privileges of our predecessors. [Col. 0610C] The abbot, however, shall receive his blessing only from our apostolic see, from which he ought to be blessed. And if he is accused of any crime, he shall await judgment only from that same apostolic see.

We have also deemed it worthy to add this general provision: whatever is known to have been granted to your monastery of Fulda by the authority of any of our predecessors, kings, and emperors, shall also be confirmed and strengthened by our apostolic authority through this privilege of ours. By apostolic censure, under the solemn warning of divine judgment, we decree that none of our successors, Roman pontiffs, kings, dukes, marquises, counts, archbishops, or persons of any rank or condition, ever dare attempt anything against this privilege of ours. [Col. 0610D]

If anyone should presume to do so, let him know that he is indissolubly bound by the bond of our anathema until worthy satisfaction. But whoever guards himself with devout regard and observes that it not be infringed in any respect, may deserve to obtain from God, the giver of all good things, the grace of blessing and absolution from his sins, so that he may rejoice in the heavenly dwelling.

(Signature of the papal symbol.) Fare well.

Given by the hand of Peter, deacon and librarian of the holy Roman and apostolic see, in the month of June, in the first year of the lord Leo IX, indiction II.

## XIII. Saint Leo IX confirms the privileges granted by his predecessor Clement VI to the Church of Nivelles. (Year 1048.)

[Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, I, 661.]

[Col. 0611A]

Leo, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of Christ, apostolic blessing.

Let both those who come after and those who are now living know that Richela, abbess of Nivelles, together with Godscalc, provost of the same place, presented to me a certain decree of the lord Pope Clement, who preceded me in the apostolic see, and requested that it be confirmed by the attestation of our authority. That decree reads as follows.

Near the frontier where the Lotharingians join the Franks, [Col. 0611B] there is situated a certain abbey, namely Nivelles, of Saint Gertrude the virgin. It is rich in resources of land, but has been most miserably devastated by the fury of an untamed people.

The emperor Henry took pious compassion on this oppression, and, moved by compassion, came vigorously to its aid, restoring to the service of the virgin the aforesaid borough or village, together with all its equipment, its market, toll, mint, fortifications, exchange-houses, and mills; with cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, woods, and pastures; with the entire household residing there; and with the inheritance of all those dwelling in it.

Let there be no count or advocate except one whom the abbess has chosen; nor may he demand a court [Col. 0611C] or any judgment unless summoned by the abbess or provost. The emperor confirmed and sealed this primacy, defined by the counsel of the kingdom, through an imperial decree.

Therefore, compassion for that Church, which was its due, moved us, and imperial affection urged us that what he confirmed by decree should also be confirmed by this privilege of ours. In this matter, by our apostolic authority, we intend that no other priest dare celebrate Mass at that altar, except the bishops alone and the weekly priests alone who are appointed there for the time being.

Therefore, whoever should be guilty of such great destruction, and should presume unjustly to violate this liberty of the Church, or should seize for himself any of the other possessions of the Church assigned for the use of the nuns, or should alter their provision by turning it to worse use, or should in any way inflict damage [Col. 0611D] and not repent by making satisfaction, shall incur apostolic curse and excommunication.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, by the hand of Peter, deacon and librarian of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Leo IX, indiction II.

## XIV. Diploma granted by Pope Leo IX to Abbot Theoderic.—He confirms the privileges of kings and emperors and the right to elect an abbot. (Year 1049.)

[Martène, *Amplissima collectio*, II, 67.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Theoderic, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Peter and Saint Remaclus, situated at Stavelot, and to his successors forever. [Col. 0612A]

The summit of the highest apostolic dignity is recognized to shine forth in the love of divine providence when it strives more earnestly to offer the contest of its labor in acquiring the praises of God. For this reason, the proper care of apostolic pastoral solicitude compels us to proclaim abundantly and to confirm by the censure of apostolic institution whatever is recognized as pertaining to the establishment of pious places.

Therefore, because you have asked us, brother, to fortify with the privilege of our authority the monasteries built by the venerable Father Remaclus—that is, Stavelot and Malmedy, situated in the Ardennes forest—in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles; and because your request has appeared just to us, we grant and strengthen our assent to you by the constitution of this privilege, by apostolic authority, according to the decrees of kings and emperors read out in our presence.

We therefore decree as ratified whatever was given by the first founder of these places, namely Sigebert, king of the Franks: Germigny in the pagus of Reims; two mills beneath one roof on the Semois; a vineyard with its vine-dresser at Bethere; the tolls belonging to the port of Vetraria on the rivers Taunaco and Itta; and the port called Sellis and Vogatium on the river Loire, which he handed over to the holy Remaclus while he was still alive.

With the same firmness we strengthen the acts and ordinances of the kings Clovis, Dagobert, Childeric, and Theoderic, who confirmed these things by their decrees and added many others; and likewise those of the emperors Charles, Louis, Lothair, and the three Ottos, as well as the emperors Henry I, II, and III, who were founders and protectors of these places. Whatever is contained in their decrees concerning the boundaries and immunity of the land of Liège, we judge to be stable. [Col. 0612B]

We also confirm the exchanges made concerning Lukesengeis and Astelebrunna, as well as whatever Christian people have bestowed and donated to these monasteries for the salvation of their souls: from Frederick, count of Ferrières, Canses; from Frederick, duke of Sprimont, an allod with its church; and whatever possession has remained theirs from the beginning of the construction of these places until the present, or is to be granted to them in the future. We decree and confirm that all these things remain secure with firm stability and perpetual right. [Col. 0612C]

Let them have no advocate except one or two appointed by him, each of whom is to receive the ban of advocacy from the emperor. According to the aforesaid decrees of the emperors, let none of them presume to hold courts in the villages or possessions that appear to belong to these monasteries, to have manses or precarial holdings, to demand compensations or fines, to take provision horses, or to inflict violence on anyone without the abbot’s permission and consent. Nor may any person, whatever his dignity or order, ever receive that abbey as a benefice or in exchange.

If anyone—God forbid—should attempt to weaken any of these provisions, by the authority of blessed Peter and our own we strike him with eternal anathema. [Col. 0612D]

Furthermore, as the emperors themselves have determined, we decree that when an abbot dies, the monks from both monasteries joining together in one or the other shall have the entirely free choice of electing an abbot, without pretense, without exclusion of any person, and without regard to money, according to the rule of Saint Benedict.

Nevertheless, a consideration shall prevail, with the assent of the monks of Malmedy: because Saint Remaclus, founder of both monasteries and formerly bishop and shepherd of Tongeren, preferred to choose for himself a place of burial in one of them, namely Stavelot, they shall have the first opportunity of election, provided that a man of better merits and greater worth is found among them. But if a better man is found not there but at Malmedy, he is to be placed over both places and admitted from there rather than taken from outside. [Col. 0613A]

But if anyone—something we do not desire—should presume with wicked daring to oppose what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monasteries, or to transgress these provisions in any respect, we exclude him from the thresholds of holy Mother Church and assign him to be burned in everlasting fires together with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, and with the devil and his angels.

But whoever, with devout regard, proves to be an observer and guardian of this apostolic constitution of ours, which concerns the worship of God, may obtain in manifold measure from our merciful God the grace and mercy of blessing and may deserve to become a participant in eternal life. [Col. 0613B]

Given at Mainz on the third day before the Nones of September, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy [Col. 0613C] apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction III.

## XV. Saint Leo IX, at the request of Milo, abbot of the monastery of Saint Bercharius at Der, grants liberty to a church in the village of Villa. (Year 1049.)

[Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, IV, 737, from the chartulary of Der.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

I, Leo, by the mercy of God the most humble pope, wish all the faithful of this holy see of Toul to know how Milo, abbot from the monastery of Saint Bercharius, came into my presence, asking that I grant and establish liberty for a certain altar of his church, for the love of God, whose service he intended to arrange there. That church is on the river Blaise, in a village called Villa, where he had decided to establish monks to serve God. [Col. 0613D]

When he presented this matter to my sons and to those of this Church of God, clergy and laity alike, they judged that I should grant his request, so that the abbot himself, the congregation, and their successors might always pray to the Lord for my smallness—or for my successors. Accepting their counsel, we granted complete liberty to the aforesaid church, so that the monks dwelling there might perpetually possess, without any purchase, the altar dedicated to Saint Maurice in his honor.

For this reason, the chaplain who has care of the souls at Villa shall provide the synod and council and pay the census; but when another succeeds him, one presented by the monks shall hold the place without any servitude. Therefore, if anyone should presume in any way to transgress what we have granted to the aforesaid little place, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema. But whoever grants them any benefaction shall obtain manifold rewards from our most merciful Lord Jesus Christ and deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Therefore, so that this work of our piety may always remain inviolate, I have judged that it should be strengthened by my own hand and by those of the lords, bishops, clergy, and laity who were present.

I, Leo, bishop of the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of Toul, have confirmed this.

[Col. 0614B]

Sign of Halinard, archbishop of Lyon.

Sign of Evrard, archbishop of Trier; John, bishop of Porto; Albero, bishop of Metz; Wido, primicerius of Toul; Stephen, archdeacon; Albero, archdeacon; Rudolf, archdeacon; Lambert, archdeacon; Widric, archdeacon; Ulric, archdeacon; Walter, dean; Warner, dean; Durannus, priest; Albero; Rotbert; Milo, abbot of Der; Albert, prior; Hingon; Wandalger.

I, Peter, deacon of the holy Roman Church, librarian and chancellor, have subscribed.

I, John, subdeacon of the schola cantorum, have subscribed.

## XVI. Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions and privileges of the convent of Saint Mary at Port-Suavis, begun and completed by Berthold, formerly bishop of Toul. (Year 1409.)

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, I, Proofs, col. 432.]

[Col. 0614C]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the orthodox governors of the holy Roman Church, and to all present and future cultivators of true religion and true faith.

We clearly recognize and hold as an established rule that, for all endeavors of good action and all spiritual increases of the soul, a crown and reward are prepared for us by God in heaven. Therefore, just as places deprived of holy religion must be diligently corrected and [Col. 0614D] recalled to a state of rectitude by vigilant care, so monasteries in which good works have begun must be solidified and fostered by us, especially since divine providence has entrusted us with the guardianship of souls and the governance of churches, commanding us to feed his sheep with life-giving nourishment, confirming what has been well begun and carefully cultivating what flourishes.

While considering these matters, when at the beginning of our ordination I had by God’s gift been elected bishop of Toul, it came to my attention through the diligence of my concern that my predecessor, the venerable lord Berthold, had begun to construct, from the resources of his episcopal prebend, a convent in the village called Port-Suavis, but, taken away before its completion, had been unable to carry the good work through to its end. [Col. 0615A]

Seeing his holy intention, and desiring to gain some small share in the reward of his devotion, I diligently strove, with Christ’s favor, to complete the work he had begun. I gathered there a community of nuns who would serve God, and consecrated the place in honor of the glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy virgin Menna, whose body rests there.

After I had been summoned by God’s dispensation to the burden of the apostolate of the holy Roman see, it happened that I revisited the regions of Gaul to strengthen the holy religion of God. While I was staying at the seat of the holy Church of Toul, which I still retained under the arrangement of our authority, the abbess Berenna of that convent came into our presence, asking that the possessions bestowed upon it by us or by other persons devoted to God be strengthened by our apostolic authority. [Col. 0615B]

Recognizing her request as useful, we confirmed for that place, by the authority of Saint Peter, all the things we had previously assigned to it: namely, twenty-two and a half manses in the same village of Port-Suavis, with the ban and jurisdiction, and whatever we possess there in woods and meadows, watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands; also three mills in that village; and the church of Saint Maurice with the chapel of Saint Andrew, for which no census or service is owed to anyone.

The church of Babainvilla (Bainville), with the chapel of Xuilleyo (Xuilly), and the chapel of Mazeriis (Maisières); half of the church of Saviniacum (Sepvigny), and half of the chapel of Sampiniacum (Champougny); half of the church of Morlain-curte (Morlaincourt), and the chapel of Lagniacum [Col. 0615C] (Lagny); at Faveriis (Favières), half of the church and half a mansus of allodial land with male and female servants.

We also grant that the altars of the aforesaid churches may be possessed perpetually in future times without redemption by any payment. A third part of the land of Cauleyum (Chauloy), with half the ban; four vineyards at Domnum-Germanum (Dom-Germain), and the dean’s wine; at Straflede-villare, one mansus; at Grandis-Frasnus (Fresnel-la-Grande), half a mansus.

We also confirm for that place the possessions which the aforesaid abbess acquired after the construction of the convent through her diligent labor. At Humberticurtis (Humbercourt or Ambercourt), three quartarii and half a mill, which the knight Dado gave to that monastery. At Bactris, half a mansus, and the wood at Valdonis-curtis (Vaulioncourt), which Mamsedis, wife of Windricus, gave; at Bossevini-frontum, three quartarii with wood and meadows, which Odilla, wife of Elbo, gave; between Domnum-Martinum (Dom-Martin) and Morli-curte, a mansus which Vindistoldis, wife of Birallus of Vendopera, gave; at Domnum-Martinum, above the water, one and a half quartarii of ploughland, and three parts of half the church; half of the church of Puteoli (Puisieux) and its altar; and a quartarius of the allod at Puteoli, which Radulf gave for his wife. [Col. 0615D]

Furthermore, we decree that an abbess be placed over that convent who is able to govern and benefit it according to the rule of Saint Benedict. Whenever any abbess departs this life, a worthy abbess shall be chosen by them, with the approval of the bishop. But if a worthy election cannot be made among them, a suitable abbess shall be sought from some other congregation. [Col. 0616A]

Therefore, with the assent of the entire assembly of the faithful present, we prohibit and command, and under invocation of the divine name we solemnly declare, that each bishop of that see—namely, our successors—never presume to take away or diminish anything from the aforesaid resources of the handmaids of God which we have granted to them by testament, nor dare at any time to disorganize or unjustly disturb that congregation. But whenever he wishes to visit them for a charitable and pious purpose, let him come; and if anything among them needs to be ordered or corrected, let him strive to order or correct it mercifully and according to God. [Col. 0616B]

Nevertheless, if anyone, persuaded by wicked greed, should attempt to infringe or violate this arrangement established by us, let him incur the anger of almighty God and pay irreversibly the penalty of eternal damnation. Let him have no share with God in the reward of the just, but let him share with the prince of darkness and undergo the judgment of divine vengeance, transfixed by the anathema of perpetual curse.

But whoever proves to be, with devout regard, a guardian and observer of this privilege of ours shall obtain grace from the Lord God and become a participant in eternal glory.

In the circle of this bull is written: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord.” [Col. 0616C] And in the middle of the circle: “Pope Leo.” Afterwards, a large B. L. as the subscription.

Given on the Kalends of October, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, in the second year [Note: [Col. 0615D] Read: first year.] of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction III, with lead seal and cord on parchment.

## XVII. Saint Leo IX orders the day of the dedication of the church of Saint Remigius (1 October) to be celebrated throughout the boundaries of the bishopric of Reims. (Year 1049.)

[Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, sixth century, part II, p. 726.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Catholic brothers and sons established throughout the entire kingdom of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing. [Col. 0616D]

We believe it has become known to your charity that, after our consecration—that is, the consecration by which God’s goodness willed our humility to preside over the holy Roman Church—we visited Germany and Gaul. Coming to the city of Reims, with the greatest vow and fullest devotion, and with God’s assent and through the supporting merits of that most holy man, we dedicated the church of blessed Remigius with great glory, as we had desired long before.

After the consecration of the church, while celebrating a synod there, we confirmed by decree, with the counsel of our fellow bishops and also with the assent and approval of the clergy and people, whose countless multitude had gathered for the celebration of such devotion, many things necessary for the benefit of the Christian religion. [Col. 0617A] We ordered all these matters, arranged in chapters, to be preserved among the canons, and afterward took care to confirm the same things in every synod that we held.

And since we know blessed Remigius to be the preacher and apostle of the Frankish people, we ought, insofar as we can, to venerate and honor him whom the Lord glorified on earth and in heaven—especially since the love of him always burns more fervently in our breast because, transferring with our own hands the most precious body of that holy man, we placed it in the site prepared for it and adorned with a work of marvelous beauty. [Col. 0617B]

Therefore we wish to admonish your affection that, just as you perceive us rejoicing in his services, so you too, for love of us and especially out of the duty of filial honor, should celebrate his solemnity, which is on the Kalends of October. For although he is not an apostle to others, he is one to you; for you are the first fruits of his apostolate in the Lord.

Therefore, render this honor to your father and apostle, so that, according to the Lord’s promise, you may deserve to live long upon the earth and, through the prayers of that same Father, to possess the happiness of eternal blessedness.

Farewell.

## XVIII. Saint Leo IX adorns the monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims with privileges in synod. (Year 1049.)

[Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, sixth century, part II, p. 726.]

[Col. 0617C]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Herimaro, abbot, and to the entire congregation of the monks of Saint Remigius, perpetual salvation.

Not unmindful and not ungrateful for the divine goodness, which by its grace exalted my humility to the apostolic see of the holy Roman Church, I have resolved—lest my negligence bring danger upon me and ruin upon the churches—to order, govern, and correct in accordance with Catholic principles the churches subject to our apostolate, and also to make them immune and free by apostolic authority, if the benevolent favor of the Holy Spirit should grant me assent.

Therefore, after visiting, with zeal kindled by charity, certain churches, and correcting them as far as I was able, with divine mercy going before me, I came to this church of blessed Remigius in order to dedicate it and also to deal with and settle ecclesiastical matters. I trusted that I would be aided by his most holy merits in obtaining God’s mercy, if I should do anything worthy and memorable for his honor and glory.

Accordingly, after this church had been dedicated, it pleased us to leave here suitable and praiseworthy memorials of our authority and visitation. Therefore we deliberate and, in the presence of this holy synod, promulgate, establish, and confirm that this church shall possess this privilege of our authority above the other churches of France, so that no person of the ecclesiastical order, great or small, may presume to celebrate Mass at this altar which we have consecrated, except the archbishop of Reims, the abbot of this place, or anyone to whom he grants permission. The same permission is granted to the canons of the church of Reims twice a year—namely, at Easter and at the Rogations—provided that seven legitimate priests deputed for this office are appointed, men distinguished by learning and commended by gravity of conduct and integrity of life.

Moreover, because this church has suffered grave and manifold injuries to its possessions from wicked usurpers, we prohibit, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, anyone henceforth from imposing heavy and unjust customary dues upon the villages of blessed Remigius which it possesses or shall possess, or upon persons dwelling within or outside those villages. Whatever has hitherto been unjustly imposed, we forbid, by that same holy and inviolable authority, to be imposed any further. In all things, however, this provision shall be preserved: the customary dues which were justly established for it in ancient times shall remain valid and inviolate.

We also confirm by our authority that Wido, archbishop of Reims, donated to blessed Remigius, through our intervention, the share which he held in the market held on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, on the condition that no one should forcibly take from anyone at that market goods worth five denarii, and that no one except the abbot of this place, or someone whom he orders, should take anything there.

No one shall strike, hinder, or forcibly take anything from those who come to the same market—which we establish and promulgate as being held on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November—either on their way there or on their return.

We establish, under invocation of the divine judgment, that whoever presumes to violate this privilege of the holy Roman see shall incur eternal damnation.

Under the same invocation, at our request and with the voluntary consent of the aforesaid archbishop, the payment which the archbishop of Reims used to receive from the church on the feast of Saint Remigius has been remitted.

Given on the third day before the Nones of October, through the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction III.

## XIX. Bull of Leo IX granted to Gedulf, treasurer of the Church of Stavelot, by which he confirms all the possessions granted as the endowment of the altar, together with other privileges of the treasurer of Stavelot. (Year 1049.)

[Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 69.]

**Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gedulf, treasurer of the church of Stavelot, and to all his successors: apostolic blessing.**

The vigilance proper to pastoral care urges us, with personal concern, to attend with every effort to the interests of the churches of God, and to provide with cheerful and generous spirit whatever may contribute to the peace of the brethren and the security of their possessions.

Since, therefore, brother Gendulf, sacristan of the church of Stavelot, a man known to us and accepted into our familiarity, approached our providence, asking that we add the support of our authority’s decree to the office which he serves, we, moved both by the equity of justice and by the brother’s earnest petition, establish by the edict of this present document that all possessions known to belong to the endowment of the altar of the aforesaid church shall remain inviolate.

We further command that, just as the same brother, together with his predecessors, has hitherto received without opposition the payments due from those who pay wine or a larger number of denarii to the altar as a head-tax, so henceforth he and his successors shall possess them with unshakable firmness. That is, whatever is paid under secular law for the killing of a man, for the shedding of blood, or for unequal marriages shall come to the treasurer of the church without any resistance.

Nor shall the abbots or any of the provosts be permitted to grant as a fief either this tax or the payments arising from the matters mentioned above and other matters, or in any other way to diminish or alienate any part of them from the sacristans. Whoever presumes to do so shall be irrevocably bound by the bond of anathema, by the authority of blessed Peter and of ourselves.

Because this is absolutely necessary for that church on account of the extent of its possessions, we confirm it by an immovable decree under the authority of blessed Peter: since blessed Remaclus, the first founder of both places, left the bishopric of Tongeren with its episcopal insignia and became the first abbot over those same places, firm and free power of binding and loosing shall remain with all the abbots of those places, and they shall be able to exclude invaders of their possessions from the Christian community and to restore them again to holy communion.

Given at Reims on the third day before the Nones of December.

[Note: For “the third day before the Nones of December,” one should read “the third day before the Nones of October”; nor are the remaining chronological indications free from errors. Jaffé.], through the hands of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy and apostolic see, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1049, in the second year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction IV.

## XX. Privilege of Saint Leo IX concerning the immunity of the priory of Saint Marculf, or the church of Corbiniacum, dependent upon the monastery of Saint Remigius. (Year 1049.)

[Marlot, *History of the Metropolitan Church of Reims*, II, 108.]

It is fitting that our apostolate should take care, on behalf of all the churches of God, that they suffer no loss of their possessions, but rather that their goods be increased and enlarged for the better.

Therefore, since your affection as a brother requested that we fortify by a privilege of the holy apostolic see the monastery ennobled by the body of blessed Marculf and situated in the bishopric of Laon, so that, for the praise of almighty God and the honor of that same Marculf, it might not be violated in anything by the greed or presumption of any person, but rather might be increased and grow—because of the intervention of your affection we confirm and strengthen, by this privilege of our authority, all the possessions of that monastery, and so forth.

Given on the third day before the Nones of October, through the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction III.

## XXI. Saint Leo IX confirms the privileges of the abbey of Saint-Denis. (Year 1049.)

[Doublet, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, p. 461.]

**Leo, servant of the servants of God and bishop of the Roman Church, to kings and dukes, princes and rulers, and to those who now are and those who shall come in future times.**

Since it is fitting for us to grant our assent to just petitions and vigilantly to serve the interests of the holy Church, we undoubtedly hope to please our God by compelling ecclesiastical possessions and constitutions, established by the holy Fathers, to remain as they were established, and by strengthening them through our authority so that thereafter they may not be corrupted with impunity by the wicked.

Therefore we make known to those present and to those to come—namely, to all kings and dukes, princes and rulers, and to all the faithful of the apostolic see—that the venerable abbot Hugh and a monk of the monastery of the blessed martyr Dionysius, where that saint rests bodily, implored our goodwill with prayers, asking that we deign to strengthen by our authority the privileges granted to that monastery by Lord Dagobert, king of the Franks and founder of that place, as well as the confirmations of all their immunities granted by Clovis, his son, and by all their royal successors, by whoever promulgated and bestowed his authority upon that monastery of the blessed martyr Dionysius.

They also asked us to confirm the privilege which Lord Landeric, venerable bishop of the city of Paris, issued with the consent of his canons and likewise of the bishops of that region, concerning the freedom and release of clerics in all their orders. By that privilege he released from his authority and that of all his successors all those serving the churches within the defined boundaries of the circumscribed area, according to the limits which he himself had determined, and handed them over to the abbot and monk-brothers of the aforesaid monastery to govern and administer.

They further sought confirmation of the holy decrees of the privileges of our holy predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Zachary, Stephen, Leo, Adrian, and Nicholas, confirmed by holy and apostolic authority, as well as of the privilege of Lord Aeneas, bishop of the city of Paris, and of the bishops of that province, concerning the confirmation of the aforesaid place, made in the time of King Charles. Finally, they asked that we, laying our hand upon all these matters, deign to strengthen them also by our authority.

Therefore, providing for that church, for the protection of the abbot presiding there, and for the present and future brethren who appear to serve God in that venerable monastery, we, by the authority of blessed Peter the apostle, whose unworthy vicars we are, and by the privilege of this document, strengthen the decrees of the aforesaid kings, of our predecessors, and of the venerable bishops of that same province.

We adjure, by Christ-given authority, all kings and our successors not to permit forever the place of Saint Dionysius, martyr of Christ, fortified by their authorities and privileges, to be violated in any way, either by themselves or by their subordinates.

We therefore decree and promulgate that no bishop of the city of Paris, for any reason or under any pretext, may deny the abbot or brothers of the aforesaid place justice concerning their parishioners when a complaint has been brought before him regarding wrongs committed by them.

If he does so, then, just as Lord Stephen, our predecessor, granted them by a special privilege the power to choose one of their own number and to have him as bishop, so we too, by our own special privilege, grant them the power, in place of our name, to strike such persons with anathema and to release them after satisfaction has been made. We have seen this established and confirmed in the privilege of the aforementioned Aeneas, bishop of Paris, issued with the consent of his canons while King Charles was presiding at the royal synod at Soissons, and granting it with the assent of those present concerning his parishioners. The violators of this constitution were to be struck by the sword of anathema by the metropolitans of that province—namely, Hincmar of Reims, Wanelon of Sens, Wenilo of Rouen, Rodulf of Bourges, Herard of Tours, and Frotarius of Bordeaux—as well as by their suffragans, who are more fully listed in the same privilege.

We also command that none of the bishops from whom they may request these things presume to deny them oil, chrism, tablets, blessings, or ordinations at the times appointed, whenever the abbot, brothers, or their successors request them. If any bishop of the city of Paris should deny them these things, or at any time attempt to summon another who has supplied them, we altogether forbid and prohibit it.

We further order that, concerning the affairs and responses of their church, they may freely appeal to and approach the hearing of ourselves and our successors, and that meanwhile no one may attempt to condemn them or seize their property. This was previously established for them by our predecessors.

If anyone of whatever power, or any person of whatever order or age, should dare in any way to violate this privilege of our authority or that of our predecessors, let him be condemned by perpetual anathema, bound by the power granted by God to blessed Peter and to us. May those who preserve it, however, enjoy perpetual blessing.

Given on the third day before the Nones of October, through the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction III.

## XXII. At the synod of Mainz, attended by forty bishops and by Emperor Henry, Saint Leo IX condemns the heresy of simony; rejects Bertald, usurper of the church of Besançon; establishes Hugh as archbishop; and grants him the use of the cross and pallium.

[Theiner, *Critical Investigations*, p. 203.] (Year 1049.)

**Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the holy Church, present and future.**

Giving thanks to God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who raised our insignificance—supported by no merits—to the summit of the apostolic see, and who permitted us, through synodal decrees, to cut away from the body of the sacred Christian community, of which he himself is the head, whatever was unsuitable and even harmful, we make known by this document of our command some of the things which we carried out at the synod of Mainz. At that synod the most prudent majesty of our son, Henry II, Roman emperor, sat with us, together with the revered holiness of many of our brothers and fellow bishops, as well as abbots, in the presence of a considerable multitude of honorable clerics and religious laymen.

After the heresy of simony had been condemned and eradicated from its roots, various matters arose concerning divine offices and sacred orders. Then a certain man named Bertald appeared before the assembly and declared himself to be archbishop of Besançon. He said that he wished to bring a complaint on this matter, because he had been consecrated many years earlier but had not been received, and because another was occupying his see by usurpation.

After making this declaration, he asked for a legal advocate. With the synod’s approval and our assent, he obtained our brother Lermoennus, archbishop of Cologne, as advocate. Taking up his case, Lermoennus began by addressing King Rudolf of Burgundy, to whom Bertald had been serving and rendering an unlawful subjection. At that time it happened that Archbishop Hector of Besançon was released from the bonds of the body, and his chair remained vacant.

By the favor of the king, Bertald, at the direction of his advocate, declared that he had received the investiture of that archbishopric; that, at the king’s command, he had been consecrated by the suffragan bishops; and that he had sat in the episcopal see and performed ordinations. But, he said, a certain Count William had opposed him concerning the bishopric; Bertald was later expelled by Walter, predecessor of Hugh, archbishop of that same see, who was also present at our synod, and against whom he brought his complaint concerning his see.

He further said that, after his expulsion, he had received the pallium from the Roman pontiff together with a privilege, and confirmation of the dignity he had assumed. We ordered Archbishop Hugh himself to answer this complaint. With our indulgence, he accepted Archbishop Albert of Bremen as his legal advocate.

Through Albert’s statement he began to repel the charges as follows: neither Hugh himself nor his predecessor had taken away from Bertald the see which he claimed, because Bertald had never ascended to the see, had never performed any episcopal act there, and had not been elected by the clergy or people, nor received by them. Rather, he had been rejected in every way, because he had given a large sum of money to the king in order to become bishop, and because he had acted contrary to the law of the place, which had always retained the right to elect its own bishop.

Hugh recalled that, while serving in the same church as cantor, after the death of his predecessor, he had been elected by the clergy and people and had even been taken away against his will. Although he had already completed eighteen years in the episcopate, Bertald had never again brought any accusation against him at any synod, although Hugh had attended many synods. Nor had anyone anywhere spoken a word against him on this matter, since he had peacefully assumed the pastoral office and had continued peacefully to administer it.

The synod then asked Bertald whether he could prove by clear witnesses anything that he had alleged—namely, that he had sat in the see and performed ordinations there, and also that he had been elected by the sons of the Church, as the canons prescribe.

Why say more? He asked for time to deliberate, and we granted it. When he returned, and was unable to prove what he had alleged, we asked the holy synod what should be decreed concerning the matter.

Thus, by unanimous consent and common deliberation, after the judgments of the holy canons had been brought forward, the holy synod decreed that Bertald, who had not been elected by the sons of the Church, had not been received, had not been regarded as pastor, but had always been rejected and repulsed, could not and ought not to have been imposed upon unwilling persons. Therefore he must cease forever from such a complaint.

Archbishop Hugh, however, who had been sought and elected by the clergy and people and had peacefully possessed the see for so long, was never again to be disturbed by any accusation from Bertald, but was to possess that bishopric in perpetual peace, because he was the pastor who entered through the door, whereas the one who entered by another way was a thief and robber.

Our authority and that of the apostolic see confirmed this judgment as just and canonically issued, with the approval of our most beloved son, the aforesaid Augustus, and of all the clergy and people present.

The entire synod also determined that the same Archbishop Hugh ought to be protected by our apostolic safeguard. We therefore imposed the anathema of our authority, so that thereafter Bertald might never bring any accusation either against the archbishop himself or against his church of Besançon. We did this, and the synod responded with its own voice: “Let it be done, let it be done.”

Therefore we judged it fitting, both to preserve the memory of this matter for future times and to provide an example for posterity, that everything should be written down as promised.

These matters having been settled, we also grant and confirm to the same Archbishop Hugh, together with his episcopal office, the archiepiscopal insignia by this document—namely, the cross and pallium, and whatever his predecessors are known to have deserved from our predecessors. Thus, since he excels in the praiseworthy dignity of his merits, both in the strength of his learning and in the uprightness of his conduct, he may also excel in the beauty of his adornments, in the full dignity of an archiepiscopal elevation. May he always remember to cultivate inner beauty amid outward splendor, so that, made a model for the Lord’s flock, he may offer his people an example of good works, possessing the virtue of the pontificate together with its name, making himself a bridge and conveying the people of God across himself to Him.

To make everything that is read here more certain, we have also strengthened this document with our own handwritten subscription, and ordered it to be confirmed by the imperial hand and by the personal subscriptions of our fellow bishops who were present there, to the praise of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Henry, by the grace of God, second Roman emperor, Augustus.

John, bishop of Porto. Here are two Romans. Bardo, archbishop of Mainz. Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt. Albert, bishop of Strasbourg. Ruod, bishop of Paderborn. Sibico, bishop of Speyer. Gebhard, bishop of Eichstätt. Arnulf, bishop of Worms. Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg. Theoderic, bishop of Constance. Herimann of the Castle of Felicity, bishop. Herimann, archbishop of Cologne. Benno, bishop of Utrecht. Bruno, bishop of Minden. Alberic, bishop of Osnabrück. Robert, bishop of Minden? [*Munigardevordensis*]. Tetuinus, bishop of Liège. Hugh, archbishop of Chur. Theoderic, bishop of Basel. Hebreard, archbishop of Trier. Adalbero, bishop of Metz. Hescelo, bishop of Strasbourg. Henry, bishop of Augsburg. Ascelin, bishop of Bamberg.

Stephen, bishop of the Ancient City. Ascelin, bishop of Hildesheim. Baldwin, archbishop of Salzburg. Gebhard, bishop of Regensburg. Nizo, bishop of Freising. Two bishops of the Leuticians. Theodoric, bishop of Verdun. Hunfred, bishop of Magdeburg. Bruno, bishop of Verden? [*Smannensis*]. Wunald, bishop of Merseburg. Tancoard, bishop of Brandenburg. Ebbo, bishop of Naumburg. Albert, archbishop of Bremen. Walo, bishop of the Danes at Oldenburg? [*Iburgensis*]. Tetuinus, bishop of Concordia, from Aquileia.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, through the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo, indiction III.

## XXIII. Saint Leo IX, at the request of Emperor Henry, undertakes to protect the monastery of Lorsch and confirms its possessions. (Year 1049.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XIX, 691.]

**Leo IX, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved lord Udalricus, religious abbot of the venerable church of Lorsch, and through you to your successors in that same venerable monastery forever.**

Since those things which are known to pertain to reasonable desires ought to be granted, the authority of our apostolate should by no means refuse, in the granting of privileges, to strengthen the pious devotion of those who build holy places.

Therefore, since the excellence of our spiritual son, Lord H., the most devout emperor Augustus, requested that the monastery of N.—which is certainly known to have been built by the most devout emperors Charles the Great and his son Louis, and by their successors, and where the venerable abbot N. now appears to preside over regular discipline—be adorned in every way by a privilege of the holy Roman and apostolic see, so that it be subjected to the jurisdiction and authority of no one, we, favoring the pious desires of our spiritual son, decree by this apostolic authority of ours that the aforesaid monastery, with everything belonging to it, shall remain now and until the end of the age under the protection of the holy Roman and apostolic Mother Church.
