We therefore decree, under invocation of the divine judgment and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and under the prohibition of our humility, that no one holding any rank, or belonging to any order or ministry, presume to trouble himself with the affairs of that monastery, or in any way to take away or alienate its property or possessions, or disturb the monks serving God there, or attempt to inflict upon them any malice or harmful injury. We firmly establish that it shall remain, with stable security and jurisdiction, under the protection of our holy Roman Mother Church.

We add, moreover, that after the death of the abbot no one shall appoint an abbot there except one whom the consensus and common will of the brothers living there according to the rule shall have elected from their own congregation. No bishop shall demand any payment or gift for the consecration of the abbot who is then in office. If he is unwilling to ordain him without payment, let the abbot be ordained either by our Roman Mother Church or by any venerable bishop acting by our authority.

Indeed, promulgating this, and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before God and his terrible future judgment, we establish by the constitution of this apostolic privilege that all things granted by our predecessors and successors, whether movable or immovable, as well as possessions bestowed by kings and princes or by any of Christ’s faithful, or which may hereafter be bestowed, shall remain with unshaken stability under the right and ownership of the holy martyr Nazarius throughout perpetual times.

As stated, no person, great or small, shall have the right to seize or take away anything belonging to that monastery, so that what we have justly decreed to be subject to the jurisdiction and protection of the Church may remain secure and peaceful for the praise of God, well endowed and to be endowed still more abundantly.

If anyone, which we do not desire, should presume by wicked daring to transgress what has been established for the honor of the Lord God and our Savior, for the stability of that monastery and the peace of the monks, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema and assigned with the devil and all the impious to the most terrible punishment of fire.

But may whoever, from pious consideration, proves to be their guardian and observer deserve to obtain from the most merciful Lord our God the grace of every blessing, absolution and forgiveness of all his sins, and the blessedness of heavenly life with the saints and elect, throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, through the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo. Indiction III.

## XXIV. Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions and privileges of the nunnery of Saint Maurus at Verdun. (Year 1049.)

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, I, Proofs, p. 424.]

**Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother Theoderic, bishop of the church of Verdun, and to his successors forever.**

If we grant assent to the petitions of God’s devoted faithful—namely, if we wish to strengthen by the authority of our apostolic privilege the possessions of the holy churches entrusted to their administration, by which the Lord’s flock ought to be sustained with the double nourishment of refreshment—we have no doubt that this will greatly benefit the condition of the universal holy Church. Indeed, we believe that we shall be richly rewarded by the very fountain of divine mercy.

Therefore, let all Catholics and all who please God know that, with the consent of the aforesaid most beloved bishop Theoderic and through the pious intervention of Ave, abbess, I have confirmed by the protection of apostolic authority the place situated in the suburb of Verdun beside the stream called the Scancia, built in honor of Saint John the Baptist and Saint John the Evangelist, where the bodies of Saints Maurus, Salvinus, and Arator are venerated by the inhabitants of that city.

Bishop Heimo renewed and furnished this place because of the convenience of its water, so that the nuns whom he established there under monastic rule might be able to possess all their customary necessities within the boundaries of the place itself. I have confirmed it so that whatever the same bishop and other faithful of God had piously bestowed there might not thereafter be violated by any enemy of the holy Church.

The possessions belonging to that church which we establish as confirmed are shown by the description of this present document, namely:

The estate at Calvus-Mons, with everything belonging to it; the estate of Marseium, and whatever appears to belong to it; Hatton’s Masnile, Caslon-Villa, Vilegium, with vineyards and the household of Amalgis; the estate of Adase, with everything belonging to it; likewise Gundricus-Curtis; at Labria, nine manses with their household; Berlei-Curtis; at Briodorum, eight manses with a mill and its appurtenances.

At Molengeia-Curtis, seven manses with a mill; below Liège, at the place called Saint Remigius, seven manses with a church. At Samongeia, seven and a half manses. At Grimaldus-Curtis, eleven manses with a mill. Below Verdun, Novavilla, nine and a half manses. At Tullida, nine and a half manses.

Peter’s Villa in the Ardennes, and the estate called Nervia, twenty manses with their household. At Parperia, tithes with all demesne holdings. At Tranculfivilla, one church. At Sampiniacum, one. At Saint Julian, one. One at Mandres. One at Villa. At Caslon, one with a chapel. At Imbeia, one. At Trogium, one. At Ranserias, one. At Malameia, one. At Prodagio, one. At Arberti-Villa, one and a quarter with a fishery. At Saint Peter, one. At Lovus-Mons, one; at Orna, one; at Bras, one; at Unffi-Villa, one. At Romanas, one. At Pilon, one.

The chapel of Saint Lambert in the city, and Saint Medard, adjacent to the abbey church itself. At Saint Hilary, a fishery with one mansus. At Samongeia, one fishery. The toll in the city. Within the walls, manses yielding two pounds. Two mills below the new bridge.

At Floracum on the river Aira, nine manses. Countess Auda bestowed these upon the same church, in which she is also buried. At Saint John, twelve manses with a church above the Cosantia, and the estate which he acquired.

At Lovomons and Brabant, a church in honor of the Holy Cross, which Bishop Heimo enlarged with possessions acquired from every direction. Canons were established there to serve the divine offices as weekly ministers in the aforesaid monastery, and they are to receive no canonry except from the abbess.

The names of these possessions are as follows: at Romanas, four and a half manses, with the ban; at Asena, the ban, with a wood; at Villa, one mansus with a mill; at the Cross, an allod with a wood; at Caston-Curtis, half a mansus; at Alde-Villa, an allod; beside the city, three at Cumminas; at Aldebert’s Gate, one; at Doda-Valley, one; at Dormar-Valley, one; at Elna, seven quarter-units, and within the walls two vineyards; at Ronnei-Villa, two manses and three quarter-units; in the city, manses which pay nine solidi, and one oven; at Nova-Villa, one and a half manses.

All these things contained in our foregoing description, both urban and rural—buildings, vineyards, meadows, woods, cultivated and uncultivated fields, bondservants of either sex, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries, churches, and chapels—we grant and confirm in perpetuity to you and to your successors as bishops, just as they legally and canonically belong to this monastery.

Furthermore, concerning the altars of the churches situated in your bishopric, just as you have granted them to those churches, no one shall be permitted to introduce another person except one whom the abbess, with the advice of her sisters, has appointed.

We grant to the sisters the free power to elect an abbess according to the fear of God and the decrees of the canons. But if a dispute should arise, it shall belong to the bishop, as a good shepherd, to provide that church with a suitable person, either from his own diocese or from another.

If anyone, which we do not desire, should attempt by reckless daring to act against this privilege of ours, let him know that he is bound by the anathema of almighty God, of the prince of the apostles Peter, and of ourselves, so that he may be excluded from the kingdom of God, become the companion of the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ in hell, and remain subject to excommunication until, coming to repentance, he makes satisfaction and suitable correction.

But may whoever, from pious consideration, proves to be the guardian and observer of this apostolic privilege of ours deserve to obtain from the Lord our God the grace of blessing and the joy of the heavenly kingdom throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of November, through the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction III.

## XXV. Privilege of Saint Leo IX by which all the possessions of the canons of the church of Verdun are confirmed. (Year 1049.)

[Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, Supplement, p. 99, from the original document of the church of Verdun.]

**Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rotmiro, first among the clergy of the principal church of Saint Mary at Verdun, and to Warmundus, dean, and through them to the other canons, present and future: perpetual salvation in the Lord.**
Our office is to have compassion on sufferings and calamities and to offer whatever assistance we are able; for if piety is not found in us, from whom the example of piety ought to proceed, it is uncertain where it ought to be found. Thus, as we were returning from the synod of Rheims, [Col. 0628C] it happened that we lodged at Verdun and did not rejoice but rather wept. For we beheld the city’s cruel destruction, of a kind that no human being could fail to lament. Indeed, after the savagery of tyrants had entered the city, it utterly destroyed it through terrible fires; and that fire did not spare even the church of Saint Mary, but, raging everywhere and in every place, consumed it. As a result of this unexpected conflagration, even the documents of your prebends were destroyed, so that none remained.

Therefore, prostrate at our feet amid tears, you all asked that a privilege of our apostolic authority be made for you concerning those same prebends, uses, and stipends, granted to you from ancient times. [Col. 0628D] Accordingly, yielding to your petitions, by this privilege of our apostolic sanction we confirm and strengthen, for you and your successors in perpetuity, those same prebends established by the faithful under the right of that most blessed Mother of God, for the daily services of the divine offices.

You also asked that the names of those prebends be inserted into this privilege, since much of the privilege of our predecessors has remained with you, where they may be found. They are as follows, together with their banns and centenae:

Lemnia, with the church at Oschera, two manses, and all its appurtenances; the church at Domnus-Agericus, with its lands; Nuvilleniacum, with the church, mill, and all its appurtenances; the court of Usio at Pusio, five and a half manses, with bann and woodland; Superiacum-minor, with the church, woodlands, and all its appurtenances; Bella-villa, with bann, centena, mills, and Malbert’s Mount; at Ex., half a mansus, with mill and meadow; Mons, with bann, centena, church, mills, and all its appurtenances; Agericus-villa, with bann and centena; Berthinea-villa, Porario, Pictavilla; Profundo-rivo, with churches, mills, and all its appurtenances; Monaldi-villa, with bann, centena, church, and all its appurtenances; at Monaldi-villa, one mansus; between Haldi-court and Villare, four manses; at Maroa, two manses; at Apletium, one mill; at Grossumrubrum, half a church.

Between Erpeia-court and Soli, seven manses with bann and centena; at Gislahadi-villa, two manses with bann, centena, and mill; at Erasnidum, one church; at Alnidum, one; at Domnus-Eligium, one; Udesvillare, one mansus; half a mill at Ramisvachum, one mansus, with bann, centena, and other lands, vineyards, and woodlands; Laumerengie, with church and all its appurtenances; Aquae-ductus, with church, woodlands, and all its appurtenances; Stadonis (Eston)-villa, with woodlands and all its appurtenances; Miseriacum, with church, mill, Sumomonte, and Losoni-court; Arenceium, with woodland and meadow; Frumisiacum, with Warch and church, and all its appurtenances; Domnus-Lupus, with church and mills; at Sasleium, one mansus; at Todenna, four parts of a church, with lands, woodland, and meadow; at Wamma, one quarter of a church, with three quartarii of land and meadow; at Milleium, seven quartarii of land, with woodland and meadow; at Salmoreium, half a church; Lineium, with church and half a mill; Fontane, with church and mill; Harald’s Mount, with church and all its appurtenances; Wandersaltis, with church and all its appurtenances; Merla, with church, mill, and all its appurtenances; Superiacum-major and Subterior-villa, with church, mills, and all their appurtenances; Consauradum, with church, mills, and all its appurtenances; at Braibannum, seven quartarii of land, with vineyard and woodland; Moslavilla, with church, mill, and all its appurtenances; Flabasium [Col. 0629D] with church; Haudimons, with woodlands; at Junchereium, one mansus, with bann and centena; Ansellisartum, with church and all its appurtenances; Post-villare, with church, mill, and all its appurtenances; Moreium, with church and all its appurtenances; at Areium, whatever is held there, with harbor and fishery; Beslaric, with two churches; at Haudi-court, three manses; at Balareias, one mansus; half the woodland of Saint Martin; and the prebends of the brothers, the rights of patronage, and the altars of our churches; a mill on the Braceolus in the middle of the city; Junchereium before the castle of Ramerudis; at Ars, four manses with one quartarius, woodland, bann, centena, vineyards, and mill.

All these possessions Dado, bishop of the Church of Verdun, of pious memory, gave to the brothers to hold, with the common counsel of Count Haganon and his other faithful men, on this condition: that any man or woman from the whole bishopric of Verdun, whatever benefice or law he or she belonged to, who wished to remain in that jurisdiction should belong perpetually to the brothers and pay from his or her own head one modius of wine. But if sons or daughters born of them wished to return to other jurisdictions, they should always pay, when pursued by the steward of that jurisdiction, the amount of the previously mentioned census. And so that this might stand more firmly forever, they asked that the same conditional law be confirmed for them by our privilege, just as the aforesaid bishop had taken care to establish it when he made the grant.

All these things, noted above in sequence, we not only confirm [Col. 0630B] and strengthen for you, but also whatever may henceforth be contributed to you and your successors by Christian faithful people. We establish, by apostolic censure and under threat of divine judgment, that no human person—great or small, of whatever dignity or order, of whatever sex or age—shall attempt to act against this privilege of ours. Whoever dares to do so shall be struck by the sword of our anathema until worthy satisfaction has been made; but whoever observes it, unharmed and unshaken in every respect, shall merit the grace of divine blessing and become a participant in eternal life.

Pope Leo. “The glory of the Lord fills the earth.” Farewell in good health.

[Col. 0630C] + Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of Pope Leo IX, indiction III.

A leaden bull is attached, bearing this inscription: “OF POPE LEO.”

## XXVI. Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions of the Old Monastery of Saint Mary of Verdun, consecrated by him. (Year 1049.)

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, I, Proofs, p. 423.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Theodoric, brother and bishop of Verdun, and to his successors forever.

[Col. 0630D] If we grant assent to the devout petitions of God’s faithful—namely, if by the authority of our apostolic privilege we confirm the properties of the holy churches entrusted to their care, from which the Lord’s flock ought to be sustained by the nourishment of a twofold refreshment—we have no doubt that this will benefit the order of the universal Church; indeed, we believe that we shall be rewarded by the very fountain of divine mercy.

Therefore, let the whole company of Catholics and those who please God know that, with the consent of the aforementioned most beloved bishop Theodoric and through the intervention of Ermenfred, archdeacon of Verdun, I confirm this place, anciently called the Old Monastery, which Ermenfred himself completely renewed and, indeed, which I myself devoutly dedicated and consecrated in honor of Saint Mary Magdalene, lest whatever Bishop Heymo, together with his other successors, and the aforesaid Bishop Theodoric contributed should thereafter be violently taken away by any enemy of the holy Church, and so forth.

[Col. 0631A] But if anyone should become an invader of the aforesaid possessions through rash audacity—which may it not happen!—let him know that he is bound by the chain of our anathema and will be tormented in the fire of infernal Gehenna with Judas the traitor, unless, coming to his senses, he repents of his evil deeds and corrects what he has committed through fitting satisfaction.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo.

## XXVII. Saint Leo IX undertakes the protection of the church of Saints Simon and Jude at Goslar, granted to him by Emperor Henry at the synod of Mainz, confirms its possessions, and grants the emperor the right of advocacy and the power to appoint provosts. (Year 1049.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 725.]

[Col. 0631B]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of Christ.

The vow of a holy purpose is fulfilled not only through divine accomplishment but is also assisted by human support. Let it therefore be known to all the sons of the holy Church, present and future, that our most beloved son, the second august Emperor Henry, founded from the ground a certain church in honor of the holy Mother of God, our Lady, the Virgin Mary, and of the blessed apostles Simon and Jude, situated at a place called Goslar, where brothers live under a canonical rule. He appointed over them a certain priest named Rumald.

For the remedy of his own soul and that of his wife, the Augusta, our daughter Agnes, and also for the salvation of his parents Conrad and Gisila, of blessed memory, he granted it wholly to Saint Peter and his apostolic see, with pious affection and pious intention, by a document signed with his own hand and delivered through us, the unworthy vicar of that same prince of the apostles, when we were with him at Mainz and were holding a synod there. Thus the church, placed under apostolic jurisdiction, might remain forever free and undisturbed from every right and dominion, from every injury and [Col. 0631D] molestation, retaining its integrity in all the properties and resources that it now possesses at the aforesaid place of Goslar, at Egeln and Ihereselib, at Scemmenstete, at Gerstete, and at Valentro situated beside the Rhine, and in other places and villages, as well as whatever it will possess in perpetuity, whether movable or immovable.

Receiving this gift from the hands of our aforesaid son the Augustus, by this privilege of our apostolic authority we have decreed that the church of Saint Mary and of the holy apostles Simon and Jude should receive and be granted the full apostolic force of protection, so that, remaining forever intact in its property and possessions, it might fear no loss or damage from an emperor, a king, or any public or private person.

Nevertheless, we have judged it fitting to leave the advocacy of this sacred place to our most beloved son the Augustus and to his successors, on this condition: that they shall always have the power to appoint provosts according to God, but shall not give any part of these goods to anyone as private property or grant it as a benefice. If any of them should attempt to act contrary to our prohibition, we order that the provost and the canons who are there at the time be free thereafter to look entirely to the Roman Church, fearing nothing from imperial or royal authority.

The bishop in whose diocese the monastery of this church has been built shall have no right or power in it except ecclesiastical governance and episcopal authority according to the canonical institutions. Therefore, by apostolic censure and under threat of divine judgment, we establish that no imperial or royal power, ecclesiastical or secular, nor any human person, great or small, of whatever sex or age, shall attempt to act against this privilege of our apostolic confirmation. Whoever—man, woman, or any other person—does so shall remain wounded by the injury of our apostolic anathema until worthy satisfaction has been made. But whoever guards himself from what is prohibited here and observes faithfully everything written here shall have our full blessing and receive everlasting salvation from God.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo, indiction III.

## XXVIII. Bull of Saint Leo IX for Saint Deodatus in the Vosges. Returning from the Council of Mainz, he grants various privileges to the canons of Saint Deodatus. (Year 1049.)

[Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 169.]

[Col. 0632C]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to you, Saint Deodatus, and through you to all those serving you, whoever at the time may serve you in your church in the valley called Galilee: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

Because, by the will of divine favor and not as our merits demanded, we have moved from the see of Toul to the first of all sees, namely the apostolic see, we must be all things to all people and do good to everyone, but especially to those places which the faithful of Christ have built for the worship of God and the divine offices.

Therefore, when we were returning from the synod of Mainz, which we had arranged to celebrate for the welfare of the German and Gallican Churches, and when it happened that we came to your church, Saint Deodatus, situated in the Vosges valley called Galilee, moved by our love for you, while the bishopric of Toul was still vacant, we judged it worthy to grant a benefice to your servants who may be there at the time: namely, the censuses and offerings that the people gathering there may give to the altar for the remedy of their souls, whether as a royal gift or through the offerings of other faithful people. Whether these consist of sacred books, gifts, and ecclesiastical ornaments, or of those things which the servants of God may henceforth add there through their own labor, let the brothers henceforth possess those offerings in common.

Whenever the prelate of that Church is called by God, let a provost be substituted whom the congregation shall unanimously elect from its own number. For the blessing of altars or the initiation of sacred orders, let them seek whichever bishop they wish; and let no church presume to separate or take anything away from them. No one shall be permitted to enter the enclosure of that monastery except at the invitation or with the permission of the entire congregation.

If any bishop, commonly requested by them, should come for their benefit, then, as soon as he has completed his ministry according to the will of the congregation and has taken his meal, let him depart without demanding any gift, so that the brothers may rejoice for a long time in the peace they have received, with the Lord’s help, and may pray to God more quietly for the welfare of the Catholic Church.

But if they commit some transgression of their rule and refuse to be rebuked by their own shepherd, and if the prelate, who is also their bishop, is unable by himself to calm the congregation’s uprising, then let him summon to that monastery others who serve under the same rule, so that they may strive to suppress the scandal by a regular judgment.

We strengthen and confirm the granting of this arrangement by these present letters, as well as the other goods, movable and immovable, wherever located, which your church, Saint Deodatus, now has and possesses and may possess forever, whether acquired through Christian faithful people, great or small, of either sex and of any age. [Col. 0633C] No one shall be permitted in any way to take away or diminish anything from those goods, present or future.

We establish, by apostolic censure and under threat of divine judgment, that no human person, great or small, shall attempt to oppose this apostolic grant and confirmation of ours. Whoever dares to do so shall remain subject to the perils of our anathema until worthy satisfaction has been made. But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this grant and confirmation of ours shall be blessed by the recompensor of all good things and shall merit attaining eternal life.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic [Col. 0633D] see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction III.

## XXIX. Bull of Saint Leo IX to Mathilda, abbess of the monastery of Saints Fabian and Felicitas, confirming the privileges of that monastery, whose church he had consecrated after the body of Saint Richarda had been transferred there. (Year 1049.)

[Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 170, from the notes of the monastery of Stivaig.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ, Mathilda, abbess of the venerable monastery of Saint Fabian and Saint Felicitas, called Helionis, situated in the district of Alsace, and to your successors, abbesses, perpetual salvation in the Lord.

[Col. 0634A] Divine mercy grants fulfillment to illustrious vows. Accordingly, as we were returning from the synod that we held at Mainz, it happened that we came through your monastery and blessed and dedicated to God the church that you had recently built but had not yet fully completed. At your request, we also transferred there the body of blessed Richarda, the first builder of that venerable place, which she had bestowed, together with her husband, the august Emperor Charles, by a deed of donation.

Therefore, yielding to your intercessions, following the example of our predecessors and for the security of future times as well as the stability of that place, we grant and confirm to you the same monastery by this privilege of our apostolic authority, together with all its property and resources, which it now appears to possess and which, with the Lord’s help, it may henceforth acquire by any means, whether from kings or from people of whatever dignity or order.

Moreover, in the new church’s high altar, consecrated by us, we prohibit any priest from celebrating Mass except one whom you and your successors shall wish.

As we have already said, we grant and confirm the monastery itself to you intact, on this condition: that throughout all the days of your life it shall remain entirely under your authority and governance, to be arranged as seems right to you according to God. But when, by divine calling, you have departed from this present light to the Lord, we establish that an abbess shall be made from the congregation itself, whom the unanimity of the aforesaid monastery of the servants of God shall elect in harmony, without contradiction or obstacle from any person, provided that she pays annually to us and our successors three linen cloths suitable for pontifical use.

If this payment is not made for two or three years, let only the outstanding amount be paid; and let nothing further be demanded from your successors in any manner.

Therefore, by the present decree we command that no emperor, king, or person of whatever dignity or order dare, under any pretext or occasion, disturb or in any way molest the aforesaid monastery—which the previously mentioned most glorious Empress Richarda, for love of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and for the sake of the everlasting reward of her soul, together with her most beloved husband, Charles, the most serene august Emperor, offered to the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by a deed of donation—or transfer it to his own right or to that of another.

Nor shall anyone at any time presume to create any opposition or invasion concerning its people or resources. Rather, let the aforesaid servants of God be permitted to live peacefully with their own abbess in the service of almighty God, and to dwell safely under the protection of the holy apostolic Church, which by God’s authority we serve, and to remain there secure.

But if anyone—which may it not happen, and we do not believe it will—should attempt to act or proceed against this apostolic privilege of ours, let him remain bound by the chain of perpetual anathema and condemned to everlasting vengeance with Judas the traitor, unless he repents. [Col. 0635A] But whoever proves to be its true guardian and observer shall merit obtaining the grace of blessing and mercy from the Lord our God.

## XXX. Saint Leo IX subjects the nunnery of the Holy Cross at Woffenheim, founded by his father Hugh and his mother Heliwigd, to the apostolic see and adorns it with privileges. (Year 1049.)

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, I, Proofs, p. 425.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

O holy and wondrous cross, + on which Jesus Christ our Lord hung! Overcome by love, indeed bound by obligation, I, endowed with the right of lawful succession, transfer to our apostolic see—and decree that it be transferred perpetually for defense against all who oppose or attempt to oppose it—the church of my father Hugh and my mother Hfilwilgdis, and of both my brothers, namely Gerard and Hugh, now deceased, and mindful of myself, still living and, although most unworthy, seated on the apostolic see. This church was founded by those same parents of mine, dedicated through their efforts, and assigned to me by hereditary right.

Thus no person of any kind shall arrogate to himself any right or exercise of power in that place or in the places attached to it. Rather, it shall always remain peacefully and freely granted to its complete liberty, free from every human right and every assault, and subject to no one except our apostolic see.

But if the bishop in whose diocese it lies wishes to perform the consecrations of its altars or nuns without payment, let him do so. Otherwise, let the abbess have the churches and her nuns blessed by whatever bishop she wishes, on the condition that, neither on account of this liberty nor on account of anything else, may a king, emperor, bishop, archbishop, or person of any other dignity or condition exercise any dominion in that place or over its property, or hold any advocacy there.

Rather, the advocacy itself shall remain, as I have now entrusted it to my nephew Henry, who holds the castle of Hegensheim, with him throughout his life. For this advocacy he shall receive nothing more than what he is justly entitled to receive from the stewardship called Orbeis, on the condition, however, that one suitable villein shall always remain with his benefice, who shall guard the tithes of the village’s church and the church itself for your venerable place, holy and life-giving cross +. He too shall be free from every advocate’s authority, so that he may safely perform his service.

After my nephew Henry has closed his final day, the advocacy shall belong to the oldest among the possessors of the aforesaid castle, if there should be several; and then it shall be in the choice of the abbess of your place, often-mentioned most glorious cross +, and of your congregation, whom they wish to appoint for themselves. He shall be entitled to no greater payment for the advocacy than what has been stated and established for Henry.

But if no heir should survive, then let them turn not elsewhere but to the lineage of our family, and from it let them receive as advocate whichever of their relatives they wish, the nearest to them, so that the advocacy may always remain in our family.

Furthermore, whether under this Henry, my nephew, or under any future advocates, if the monastery itself should increase in property, whoever the advocate may be, apart from the profit of the stewardship of the aforesaid village, shall dare to claim for himself no more benefit from that increase than a twelfth part.

Thus, if there are fewer than twelve manses, the advocate shall wait until the number twelve is completed; then he shall receive such a mansus as the abbess gives him, either in that place or elsewhere, of equal value. The same shall apply if there are more than twelve: whatever remains toward the number twelve, whether in villages, lands, or vineyards, he shall meanwhile wait until the number is completed.

But if he should presume to seize more than has been established for him from all the monastery’s property, movable or immovable, and, after being admonished, should not return within twelve weeks either that same property or other property of equal value to the venerable place, the most sacred cross +, then the abbess may appeal to our see and lodge a complaint with the Roman pope concerning the injustices inflicted by the advocate upon her monastery.

If the advocate corrects his fault according to the pope’s judgment, which has justly inclined the matter, let the advocacy remain with him. But if he refuses, the abbess and her congregation may acquire for themselves another advocate from our family, choosing the nearest relative who can be found to be more suitable.

Concerning the election of an abbess after the death of Kuentza, whom we ourselves blessed, we establish the following: it shall be in the discretion of the sisters themselves whom they wish to elect from among them and place over themselves according to God, if a suitable woman can be found among them. Otherwise, let them seek elsewhere and choose whichever better woman they are able to find.

We grant the blessing of the abbess and the gift of office to no one other than our apostolic see; and at the consecration of the abbess, if there has been any negligence concerning the payment mentioned below, let the matter be strictly determined.

Therefore, in return for this grant of liberty, O cross +, brighter than the sun itself and more precious than all created things, granted to the apostle Peter and to your monastery for the salvation of my soul and of my parents, who sleep there in Christ our Lord, an annual payment is established, to be paid at the appointed time by the abbess of that place to our apostolic see: namely, a golden rose weighing two Roman ounces, either made in the customary manner or an equal amount for making one during Lent. It is to be sent eight days before it is customarily carried by us and our successors on the preceding Fourth Sunday, that is, on the Sunday when the Introit “My eyes are always toward the Lord” is sung.

I have decreed that this should always serve as a memorial of this liberty, because at that time the victory of our Lord Jesus Christ is celebrated—he who suffered upon you, O most sacred cross +, then feared, but now sought and honored.

Let there also be no forgetting in Rome of your monastery, situated in my patrimony and endowed by me with complete liberty, as stated above—Rome, where every religion claims its head, and where I, though unworthy, have taken up the office of the apostolate.

Therefore, so that the decree of our ordinance may remain firm and unshaken, by the censure of our apostolic authority we establish that no one ever dare go beyond what is written here, and that no impious violator should ever presume, through tyrannical audacity, to seize or arrogate to himself anything from the property of that church—whether my parents or I have given it to the church, or any Christian person may give it there in the future.

Whoever attempts this shall incur the obligation of our apostolic anathema until worthy satisfaction has been made, and shall receive from you, O fearful cross +, a curse. But whoever, through wiser counsel, keeps himself from this rashness shall be worthy of the abundance of our blessing and shall not lack the grace of almighty God.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo, indiction III.

## XXXI. Saint Leo IX strengthens the goods and rights of the monastery of Altorf in Lower Alsace, founded by his parents, and records that he himself dedicated its altar of Saint Stephen. (Year 1049.)

[Grandidier, *History of Alsace*, I, 255, and Schoepflin, *Alsatia diplomatica*, I, 164, according to Jaffé.—“Sacred devotion.”]

[Col. 0637C]

## XXXII. Saint Leo IX confirms the foundation and advocacy of the monastery of the Holy Cross at Werdea. (Year 1049.)

[Cocquelines, *Expanded Collection of Bulls*, I, 366.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gunderarda, beloved daughter in Christ, recently appointed and consecrated by us as abbess of the monastery of the Holy Cross founded by your father Manegold, and to the abbesses who shall succeed you forever: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

The labor of sacred devotion, because it is always aided by divine favor, always reaches its desired conclusion. Therefore, daughter, your father’s great devotion to God has produced a praiseworthy fruit, together with a portion of the holy and life-giving cross, on which our Lord Jesus Christ, our salvation, hung, decently adorned with gold and gems, then given as a gift by the autokrator of Constantinople named Romanus.

When Emperor Conrad had sent him to Romanus to give his daughter in marriage to Romanus’s son, he founded a church upon rock, because he did not build upon sand, so that when winds pressed against it, rivers came, and rains descended, what he had built would [not] collapse but, firmly founded, would endure forever.

**2.** In order to fulfill to God the vow of its construction, according to the one who said, “Make vows and render them to the Lord your God, all you who are around him and bring gifts,” when we were returning from the synod of Mainz toward Rome, he invited us to come to that temple of God. We dedicated it with due honor on the third day before the Nones of December, and he finally gave and offered it willingly to the right of the Holy Roman Church and to the most blessed apostle Peter. He also asked us to make his daughter, whom he had already consecrated to God in monastic conduct and habit, abbess of that place.

With God as our guide, we did so, observing in you, insofar as is possible for a human being, fear of God, contrition of heart, humility of mind, gravity of conduct, and an old age already displayed in youthful limbs. We established that the same place should perpetually be a monastery of the servants of God, where you, for yourself and your sisters, might offer to God the firstfruits of religion, the merits of chastity, [Col. 0638B] and every form of goodness.

**3.** Your father made this offering of the same place to our apostolic see under the following condition: that, while he lived, he should hold its advocacy; and likewise, after his death, the son whom he now has should hold it. If that son should have an heir, he too shall be advocate. But if neither Manegold nor his little son should leave a surviving son, then the abbess and the congregation may choose an advocate for themselves according to God, though he must be requested from the apostolic see.

**4.** The law governing all advocates after Manegold shall be this: if any of them does not administer the office of advocacy properly, the abbess and the congregation may complain about him to the pope. If, after being summoned by him, he satisfies the monastery, let him retain his advocacy. But if he delays coming, or if he comes and does not give satisfaction, then the abbess and the congregation may, with the pope’s consent, choose for themselves an advocate who is according to God.

After your death, an abbess shall be elected from that congregation, the best available, if a suitable one is found; and she shall receive from the pope the gift and consecration of the abbacy. Otherwise, a suitable woman shall be chosen from another congregation and likewise receive the gift and consecration from the pope.

**5.** We further decree that no one shall dare to celebrate Mass at the high altar, which we ourselves consecrated, except a bishop or abbot, and the three weekly priests appointed for this office and their successors. The bishop in whose parish the place lies shall likewise dare to claim nothing for himself there except the ordination of clerics and nuns, provided that he performs it without payment. Otherwise, they shall seek ordination from whatever other bishop they wish.

**6.** In order that the place itself might pay its annual pension to the pope during Lent, Manegold himself established that the pension should be an *anabolagium*, that is, a *fanon*, a stole with gold, a maniple, and a belt.

But because the place itself was founded for the sake of the portion of the holy and life-giving Cross mentioned above, we wish, desire, and decree that it remain there forever and be taken away by no one. By apostolic censure and under threat of divine judgment, we establish that no emperor, no king, no bishop, no power, and no person, great or small, shall dare to remove that portion of the life-giving wood from the monastery in any way, or to act against anything written above.

Nor shall anyone diminish in any manner—by theft, seizure, or any form of alienation—the goods of that monastery which it now possesses and will possess forever. Whoever presumes to do so shall be accursed until he has made worthy satisfaction. But whoever, with pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours shall receive blessing from the Lord God and become a participant in eternal life. +.

Given on the third day before the Nones of December, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the first year of Pope Leo IX.

[Note: [Col. 0639D] Gretserus, at the end of the notes appended to this bull, asserts that the enclosed cross was surrounded by a double circle. On its circumference was read: “The mercy of the Lord fills the earth.” Within the circle: “Leo P.” I believe that the rest has been worn away by age. Thus I think the inscription should be restored as “Leo PP. IX,” as I have seen it written on other seals.]

## XXXIII. Letter of Saint Leo IX to Edward, king of the English, concerning the monastery of Exeter (Year 1049.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 221.]

[Col. 0639B]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Edward, king of the English: most beloved greetings with apostolic blessing.

If you are in good health and prospering, we render no small thanks to the Lord Jesus Christ for it, and we desire this: that you may possess the reins of the kingdom so splendidly that you may remain in the eternal dwelling places. And because we have heard that you are diligent and religious toward the churches of God and ecclesiastical men, we rejoice greatly; and we admonish and kindly ask you to strive to persevere in the work of God in such a way that you may be able to please God, the King of kings, and remain with him in the heavenly kingdom.

It is therefore known to our piety that Bishop Leofric holds the episcopal see without a city; at this we marvel greatly—not at him alone, but also at all those bishops who do such things. When we sent our legate to you, speaking about the others, we now command and ask you concerning our aforementioned brother Leofric that, for the love of the Lord and of us, you provide assistance so that he may be able to transfer the episcopal see from the little village of Cridion to the city of Exeter. Strive to perform these and other good works in such a way that you may acquire an eternal kingdom from Christ the Lord. Farewell, dearest one, always in the Lord.

### XXXIV. Bull of Saint Leo IX for the abbey of Etelsus (1050)

*[Gallia Christiana*, VI, Instruments, 106.]

[Col. 0639D]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son G., venerable abbot of the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary called Etelsus, and through you to all succeeding abbots forever.

Whenever things are requested from us that unquestionably accord with reason, it is fitting that we grant them with a willing mind and provide appropriate assistance to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, since you requested from us that we strengthen the aforesaid monastery by a document of apostolic authority, confirm all its possessions so that they may remain there inviolate under perpetual right, and reinforce them by the page of our privilege without the yoke or jurisdiction of any person whatsoever, we, moved by your prayers, establish and decree through this privilege of our authority that you and all your successors, the abbots, may possess in great security and quiet all urban or rural places—that is, estates, manses, halls, castles, farmsteads, vineyards, lands, and various properties, cultivated or uncultivated, with male and female tenants, male and female slaves—which have been granted to the same monastery by any Christians, or which appear, through any documents, to belong to that pious place.

[Col. 0640A–B] This includes the monastery of Saint Paul of Vallon, Saint Mary of Urbion, and the land called Coplata, as well as whatever may be found anywhere that is owed by right to the same holy place. By apostolic authority we forbid anyone—man or woman—from contradicting this, and decree that this most glorious place shall always possess these things, so that no archbishop, bishop, duke, margrave, count, viscount, or any person, great or small, henceforth or in the future, may have permission to sell or appraise that monastery, nor dare to invade or molest any of the aforesaid possessions that appear to belong to it … [lacuna] … may willingly provide consecration.

The abbots who are to be consecrated in that place shall likewise be chosen from the same community by common agreement, and shall not be sought from elsewhere except on account of a lack of suitable persons.

[Col. 0640C] If disagreement should arise among them concerning the election, let the person whom the greater number, and the greater holiness, has chosen become abbot. But if any bishop should demand a payment for consecration and refuse to consecrate, the elected abbot may approach any neighboring bishop he wishes and receive consecration freely.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we decree that from now on no archbishop or bishop may excommunicate the monastery itself, the abbot who has served there, any member of the community, or anyone belonging to the monastery, or bind them with the bond of anathema; nor may anyone place under interdict any altar of that place or any church belonging to it. If anyone should presume to do so, he shall himself be bound by our excommunication, while the said monastery, with its abbot and all its possessions, shall remain absolved by apostolic authority from the excommunication imposed upon it.

We establish, under apostolic censure, invoking the divine judgment and prohibiting anathema, that no future supreme pontiff, nor any other person, great or small, shall ever be permitted to act against or usurp this our apostolic privilege. If anyone, however, should act with reckless presumption, etc.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of April, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy Apostolic See, in the second year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction 4.

[Note: [Col. 0641D] The callout number for this note is printed in the text as (128). The legal indiction is 3. Jaffé.]

### XXXV. Saint Leo IX approves the privileges granted by his predecessors to the monastery of Corbie (1050)

*[D’Achery, Spicilegium*, III, 349.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Fulco, abbot of the monastery of Corbie, situated in the district of Amiens, perpetual salvation in the Lord.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to assist with benevolent compassion those endowed with pious religion and to provide appropriate support for the desires of those who ask. Therefore, because you requested that, following the examples of our predecessors, we fortify your monastery and its goods, both present and future, by the privilege of our apostolic authority, and also confirm the prerogative granted to that monastery by the bishops of Amiens, the archbishops of Reims, and the apostolic men who were our predecessors, we, inclined by your prayers, confirm and strengthen through this censure of our apostolic authority whatever is found in the privileges of our predecessors Benedict, Nicholas, and Christopher.

Thus, let your aforesaid monastery possess free dominion over its goods, and whatever has been offered to the same monastery in gold, silver, fields, servants, or any other things shall remain under the disposition and free power of you, your successor abbots, and the brothers. The bishop of Amiens shall not be permitted to take or demand any portion of these things, nor to exercise authority over the abbot, the brothers, or the monastery itself, whether over the cells of that monastery—namely Busco, Braczo, Taneta, Naurdi, Uscia, and Thenis—or over its clerics, laymen, servants, and all possessions belonging to the same monastery and its cells, as we know was granted long ago to that monastery and commended by the bishops of Amiens, the archbishops of Reims, and all the other bishops of Gaul.

[Col. 0641D] We prohibit any bishop of Amiens from ever having authority—whether personally or through his steward, archpriest, or archdeacon—to come to your monastery or its cells, unless perhaps he has been summoned by the abbot of the monastery out of necessity or affection. Even then, he shall not dare to cause disturbance or harassment in the churches subject to the monastery or among the clerics of those churches, nor establish a new custom for the abbot or brothers by arranging anything against their will. Nevertheless, he shall not delay the ordinations of monks or canons requested by the abbot with the brothers.

[Col. 0642A] The same applies to the consecration of altars and basilicas, both in the monastery itself and in its possessions. He shall also provide chrism and consecrated oil each year, without demanding any gift for it.

We further establish that throughout the provinces of Gaul and Germany no one, whether lay or clerical, may exercise any personal will in the churches, fields, or among the servants, apart from the will of the abbot and brothers—not even if he is a king, duke, margrave, archbishop, or bishop.

We decree further that the brothers shall elect an abbot among themselves according to God’s will, and that no prince may dare to do this; nor may the abbot, once elected, be deposed unless he is found guilty of a credible offense. He must instead be examined and judged canonically.

[Col. 0642B] If anyone violates this decree of ours, let the bishop of Amiens admonish him to make satisfaction. If he does not obey, let the archbishop of Reims do so as well. If he will not heed him either, let the brothers of the monastery appeal to the Roman See, and let the Roman pontiff not delay anathematizing the violator with his own mouth.

Finally, because you, dearest son, have come so devoutly to the Apostolic See, it has pleased our munificence to grant you the use of the dalmatic and sandals, on the condition that you do not neglect to send a messenger to the Apostolic See every year and report what is appropriate concerning your monastery, so that we may assist you if necessary.

[Col. 0642C] We establish by apostolic censure that no mortal—whether king, count, archbishop, bishop, or any other person, great or small—shall ever attempt to act against this privilege of ours. Whoever does so shall remain bound by the bond of anathema until he has made due satisfaction. Whoever keeps it inviolate shall be blessed by the Lord God and made a participant in eternal life. Amen.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, and chancellor of the holy Apostolic See, in the second year of Pope Leo IX, indiction 4.

[Note: [Col. 0642D] Legally, 3. Jaffé.]

### XXXVI. Privilege of Saint Leo IX for the monastery of Vézelay

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gaufrid, abbot of the monastery of Vézelay, which was founded in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and in veneration of his mother and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of blessed Mary Magdalene, and to his successors forever.

Since you requested from the Roman See, which by God’s authority we serve, that the privileges granted to your church by our predecessors be confirmed, we considered it fitting to fulfill your request. Accordingly, we grant, confirm, and strengthen by decree of the privilege of our apostolic authority the aforesaid monastery, founded in the district of Aval and within the borders of Burgundy and endowed with the resources of certain members of the holy Church … [lacuna]

[Col. 0643A] We grant and confirm it so that no king, no prelate, and no person endowed with any rank whatsoever may disturb the monastery itself, diminish or take away the things offered there by the aforementioned founders or by other faithful people, or those that may happen to be offered in the future, under any pretext or occasion, or apply them to his own uses. Rather, we wish and command that they be possessed without disturbance for the support of the monastery and the uses of the abbots and monks serving God there under the rule of Saint Father Benedict.

The condition is that none of our successors, pontiffs of this holy See, which by God’s authority we serve, shall ever or anywhere in future times permit any of these possessions to be granted as a benefice to anyone, exchanged, or conceded under any form of rent. Instead, accepting only the rent assigned in the founders’ deed of transfer by which they made the Roman Church, through this monastery, their holy heir—namely, one pound of silver each year—our successors shall strive, through paternal assistance and pastoral vigilance, to protect the monastery diligently against all who attack it.

We further establish that, when the abbot of the aforesaid monastery dies, no one else shall be appointed there through any trickery or underhanded maneuver, except the person whom the consensus of the monks has chosen according to the fear of God and the institution of the Rule of Saint Benedict, and whom the pontiff of this Apostolic See has judged should be appointed, or whose appointment he has approved at the monks’ request.

[Col. 0643C] We add this provision to the present chapter in order to exclude avarice: no king, no bishop or priest, and no faithful person whatsoever, either personally or through an intermediary, may dare to receive anything under any pretext as a gift in connection with the appointment of the abbot, clerics, or priests, the distribution of chrism, the consecration of a basilica, or any matters belonging to the monastery. Nor may the same abbot presume to give anything for his appointment, lest on this occasion the offerings made by the faithful to the pious place be consumed.

Nor may the bishop of that city or parish celebrate public Masses there unless invited by the abbot of the monastery; nor may he announce stations in the same monastery, lest the repose of the servants of God be disturbed in any way by a popular gathering; nor may he presume to demand provisions or lodging dues from it.

We do not merely permit the reception of the faithful and religious men, and the charity that the Apostle commands to be shown to all, insofar as the place and its resources allow; we also recommend it. Yet the size of the community must be kept in such proportion that neither an excessive number brings poverty nor too few inhabitants bring desolation upon the place.

[Col. 0644A] We also confirm by our authority the privilege granted to the same monastery by our predecessor, Pope Nicholas of pious memory, except that he assigned it under the name of “handmaids of God”—women who, because of the frequent assaults of the world, can no longer appropriately remain there. For the sake of more suitable usefulness, we decree instead that they should fittingly live under the monastic habit.

If any king, bishop, priest, abbot, judge, count, or secular person should attempt to act against this document of our institution, let him, struck by apostolic anathema, lose the dignity of his power or office, recognize himself guilty before the divine judgment, and, unless he mourns the wrongs he has committed, be excluded from the most sacred body of our Lord Jesus Christ and subjected to the eternal examination of stern retribution.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve what is just toward this place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the stern Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Peter, deacon and librarian of the holy Apostolic See, in the second year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction 3.

### XXXVII. Saint Leo IX commands William, count of Nevers, under penalty of excommunication, to restore what he took from the monastery of Saint Bercharius at Dervy (1050)

*[Mabillon, Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, IV, 327.]

[Col. 0644C]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, apostolic blessing to William, count of Nevers.

We command and order you to do what is right before God, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, Saint Bercharius, and the monks residing there, concerning their estates, as we have already commanded you and as you agreed with their abbot. If you do not do this, and after four complaints have been made a fifth complaint concerning the matter reaches me, you will certainly be excommunicated. Farewell.

Given on the Kalends of May, by the hand of Peter, librarian of the holy Apostolic See, in the second year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction 3, to the abbot of Saint Bercharius, whom he had blessed as abbot in his Lateran chapel on that same day and to whom he had given his own name, Bruno.

[Note: [Col. 0643D] We learn from Bruno’s own letters that he had previously been called Wandelgerus. In those letters he made an agreement with Count Rodulf concerning a certain wood situated near the village of Losa. He relinquished to the men of Dervy the portion held by the count, as did his sons Walter and Simon and his other heirs, on the condition that every Monday of every week a Mass should be celebrated for the salvation of himself and his heirs, and that one poor person should perpetually receive food and a provision at the same monastery.]

### XXXVIII. Saint Leo IX, in a synod of fifty-five bishops, enrolls Gerard, formerly bishop of Toul, among the saints and orders that he be venerated on April 23 (1050)

*[Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, V, 894.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, greetings and apostolic blessing in Christ to all the sons of the Catholic Church.

The power of divine action is wondrous in all things, but especially in his saints, whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, and whom he also called and sanctified (Romans 8:29–30) before the ages came into being, before they themselves existed.

Since the Lord himself says in the Gospel, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17), he unquestionably demonstrates this daily when he says that those whom he has called are to be sanctified, and that those whom he has predestined are called solely through the goodness of gratuitous mercy, not through any merit of the human race, since by nature we are all children of wrath and children of hell.

Why we have begun to say these things we shall immediately make clear. Just as no one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but places it on a lampstand so that it may give light to all who are in the house (Matthew 5:15), so our Lord Jesus Christ acts by glorifying through miracles in the world those whom he causes to live and rejoice with him in heaven. Since they have become children of God by adoption, grace preceding them makes it clear that they are heirs of the kingdom that God promised to those who love him.

A little before us in the episcopate of Toul—whence, by the will of the Almighty, who arranges all things according to his own judgment, and not through any advancement of our merits, we were transferred to the Apostolic See—there was a bishop named Gerard. Having received from the heavenly master of the household the two talents of understanding and action, he strove so to fulfill in deed the divine law, which he understood profoundly, that he became worthy to receive from God that desirable greeting:

“Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:21).

For he distributed his Lord’s talents in such a way, and won souls by preaching words of salvation, that he returned the money doubled to his Lord and heaped up eternal benefits for himself.

He girded his loins by preserving chastity; he carried lamps in his hands by offering others examples of good works. He awaited the Lord returning from the wedding of the holy Church, not sleeping but keeping watch at the first, second, and third watches, longing anxiously for his appearance, according to what he sang daily:

“As a deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you” (Psalm 41:2);

and again:

“My soul thirsts for you; how greatly my flesh longs for you!” (Psalm 62:2).

Because he always sighed for God in his heart, accompanied by his strength and leading an angelic life, receiving Christ daily at his table in the poor, devoting himself daily to pious deeds, and neither teaching nor doing anything except what was holy and pleasing to God, he shone forth through many miraculous wonders that bore witness to his holiness. For this reason many witnesses still exist.

After the death of his flesh, while living in spirit with Christ our Lord and glorifying him, he often performed and still often performs miracles, curing various diseases and infirmities.

Although his venerable body had, as we have said, shone with many miracles up to the present, and although he had been numbered among the saints by divine judgment, he had not yet received human confirmation in the catalogue of the saints. The merciful clemency of God left this task for us, his servants, to undertake when we had ascended to the Apostolic summit.

While we were residing at Rome in synod in the church of the Savior with many of our fellow bishops, around the sixth day before the Nones of May, Udo, provost of Toul, reported to us that on that very night the lord Gerard himself had appeared in a vision to a certain venerable monk named Albizo, who was attending the synod. Udo had compelled him with earnest prayers to beseech the Lord to show him what standing the lord Gerard possessed before God, since he shone with so many rays of miracles.

It seemed to Albizo that Gerard was standing before him—someone whom he had never seen bodily and whose name he had never heard—and saying that he himself was Gerard, for whom Albizo had resolved to pray to God.

Rejoicing, Albizo began earnestly to ask whether Gerard was numbered among the saints before God. With a joyful face, Gerard replied that he was unquestionably with God, and that those who are honored in heaven before God by the hosts of angels ought rightly and justly to be honored on earth by human beings.

We ourselves proclaimed this vision in the synod, explaining the venerable life of the lord Gerard, his remarkable conduct, the multitude of his miracles, and the abundance of divine power manifested through his body. Then we asked the holy synod whether he ought to be venerated as a saint and henceforth called a saint.

[Col. 0646C] To this question the archbishops and bishops, abbots, clergy, and laymen—of both groups there was a great multitude—shouted with virtually one voice that the lord Gerard was a holy man, numbered by God among the saints, and to be numbered and venerated by human beings among the saints. While living in the flesh, the miracles testified that he was a holy man; and after being stripped of the flesh, his place in heavenly blessedness makes known to the world each day what kind of man he had been through those same miracles.

Therefore, with the holy synod assenting and praising the decision, we decreed that from this time onward he should be regarded and venerated as a saint on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, both at Toul, like Saint Mansuetus and Saint Aper, and throughout the world, like the other saints. We ourselves desire to transfer the venerable body of this saint and place it with due honor and in a worthy site upon its own altar, for the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, who became human for us so that he might not only free us from sins but also grant us the reward of eternal blessedness and a dwelling in heaven, where he lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Names of the bishops and abbots who were present at the synod in Rome:

Joannes, archbishop of Porto; Joannes, bishop of Siena; Vido, bishop of Volterra; Crescentius, bishop of Silva Candida; Joannes, bishop of Velletri; Joannes, bishop of Ostia; Joannes, bishop of Sabina; ### XXXIX. Privilege of Leo IX for the church of Karroff (1050)

*[Labbe, New Library of Manuscripts*, II, 757.]

[Col. 0648A]

To Hugh, religious abbot of the monastery of Saint Savior at Karroff, he confirms the possessions of the monastery, which he enumerates.

Likewise, he confirms those possessions located in the district of Auvergne or in its vicinity which had formerly been taken away from the same place and in the present time restored to it by William, prince of the Auvergnats, and by his sons: namely, the castle of Saint Yvo, whatever belonged to it, the church of Cadilocus, the church of Molangia, the church of Nobiliacus, the church of Chrosogilus, the village of Perusia, the church of Gaudiniacus, and everything belonging to these churches.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of May, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, [Col. 0648B] and chancellor of the Holy Apostolic See, in the second year of Pope Leo IX, indiction 3.

### XL. Letter of Saint Leo IX to the princes of Brittany—He pronounces judgment in favor of the church of Tours against Dol, and excommunicates those who resist, the Simoniacs, and those ordained by them (1050)

*[Martenne, Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 869.]

Leo, by the grace of God pope of the Holy Apostolic See, to E. [Note: [Col. 0647D] Read C., namely Conan, of this name] prince of the Bretons, to Count Alanus [Note: [Col. 0647D] It seems that this should read Alanus, namely the son of Duke Hoel, who later also became duke of Brittany, in the second year of 1084, and who held the duchy of Brittany in the time of Pope Leo.] and to the other princes of Brittany who wish to live according to God: life and salvation.

In the writings of the ancients we find that all the bishops of your country ought to be subject to the archbishop of Tours. Concerning this matter, complaints were made in the times of Pope Nicholas and of John and Leo, as well as of others whose names it would take too long to insert. Among them, Pope Nicholas sent a letter to King Solomon of the Bretons, in which he commanded that all the bishops of his country should be subject to the church of Tours. Other apostolic men likewise excommunicated them for this reason by apostolic authority.

A complaint of this kind also came to us at the council of Reims. We immediately ordered that your archbishop, together with his subjects, should appear before the Roman council, not only to render an account concerning this matter, but also concerning the fact that he was proved to be a Simoniac and an outlaw with his suffragans, seeking the things of the world rather than the things of Jesus Christ. We also ordered the legates of the archbishop of Tours to be present.

The legates of Tours appeared; your bishops withdrew with their head. We were therefore in no way able to establish that your prelate ought to be archbishop, especially since an archbishop cannot exist without a city as his see and without the archiepiscopal pallium.

We excommunicate all those about whom we have spoken, by the authority of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and of Saint Peter and ourselves—not only because of this presumption by which they disdain to be subject to the church of Tours, but also because they are polluted by the Simoniacal heresy and appear to contaminate those whom they have ordained. They are to be treated in such a way that they neither perform nor hear the divine office, nor confer a blessing. Those ordained by them shall likewise be struck by the same sentence.

To you, dearest son, we command that you withdraw, together with all the faithful, from their assemblies. Then admonish them to obey our commands and abandon the Simoniacal heresy and live according to God.

We also exhort you by apostolic authority to establish peace throughout the kingdom entrusted to you, love justice, and rule your subjects piously. For it is disgraceful that, although you are regarded as one of the greatest princes of Gaul, you should be enslaved to natural vices.

If I hear that you are living according to God and providing a good example to your subjects, you will receive the blessing of Saint Peter and of ourselves. But if you act otherwise and join yourself to the excommunicated, you shall be excommunicated by our authority like them.

If, however, your archbishop and his suffragans wish reasonably to defend themselves concerning the complaint raised by the bishop of Tours and concerning the Simoniacal heresy, let them appear at the council of Vercelli, which will be held on the Kalends of September; and, if God permits, we shall be there to hear their cases. Farewell.

### XLI. Bull of Saint Leo IX confirming all the rights of the monastery of Saint Mary at Gradus in the diocese of Arezzo (1050)

*[Muratori, Italian Antiquities*, V, 1019.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Albizo, a religious man: eternal salvation in the Lord God of all.

Having attained a more eminent rank among our brothers and fellow servants beneath the profound and incomprehensible abyss of the judgments of the Godhead, we ought all the more intently, with fear and trembling, unceasingly to work for our own salvation, by condescending to and advising them, the more certainly we know … [lacuna] … that we shall render an account of our disposition and action to him whose every way is deservedly believed and seen to be mercy and truth in the whole governance of the world.

Wherefore, … [lacuna] … we are debtors to the wise and the foolish, and are compelled by the admonitions of the Teacher of the Gentiles … [lacuna] … to render to all. If we must by no means deny these things to any outsiders, nor in … [lacuna] … how much more [must we render them] to those of the household of faith within, especially when what is required of us is something that is in no way doubted to be most pleasing to the Almighty?

[Col. 0649D] Therefore, dearest son, since you have most humbly … [lacuna] … approached the Apostolic See, mistress of all, and urgently requested of us by a most welcome prayer that by the command of our authority we protect from the rapacity of anyone and the attacks of wicked men the monastery of the most blessed Virgin Mary, mother of the Lord and Mother of God, situated in the diocese of Arezzo, we do not in any way … [lacuna] … your wholly just petition. Rather, we desire in every respect to assist it, and have judged that special protection should not be denied to your religious devotion, since we owe [it] to all and … [lacuna]

For we rejoice with you in the Lord that you have attempted to rebuild and somewhat restore there a primitive and once most renowned church, long neglected and entirely abandoned because of sins, through contributions not only from your own patrimony or benefice but also from your brothers, relatives, and other religious people, so that a monastic order might serve God there perpetually.

Since our founder also ennobled and honored this church among countless other things through the miracle of the broken and restored chalice, and through the martyrdom of the glorious blessed bishop Donatus, we too honor it gladly by a command of our Apostolic See.

Subject to the due subjection that the bishop of Arezzo is accustomed by right to exercise over the aforesaid place, we confirm perpetually by the tenor of this command and establish by decree whatever the same monastery presently appears to possess in movable or immovable property, whether through your donation or that of anyone else, and whatever pious people may add or donate there in the future.

No one shall presume to steal, defraud, alienate, or diminish … [lacuna] … by any device the aforesaid things acquired there up to the present and, by God’s favor, to be acquired … [lacuna] … and preserved for the benefit of the monks serving God there, whom we permit under no other ecclesiastical order ever to be disturbed, in accordance with the statutes of the holy Council of Chalcedon, which decrees the matter as follows:

“Once monasteries have been dedicated to God, they shall remain monasteries forever with the consent of the bishops, and the possessions belonging to them shall be reserved for the monasteries,” etc.

If anyone should presume in any way to oppose this present decree, promulgated by us for God and according to God, and should additionally attempt to claim for himself or transfer to others any offerings assigned to the aforesaid place, let him know by apostolic authority that, as a sacrilegious person and a rebel against God, he will be punished with strict anathema until perhaps he repents.

But whoever observes it fully and devoutly, and does not consent to sacrilegious persons but rather resists them to the best of his ability and knowledge, may deserve an abundance of heavenly blessing and the reward of everlasting salvation. Amen.

Farewell in good health.

[Col. 0650D] Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, by the hand of Peter, deacon, librarian, in the second year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction 3.

### XLII. Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Saviour, situated on Mount Amiata. (Year 1050.)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, III, 626.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Theuzo, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Saviour, situated in the county of Chiusi, in the territory of Mount Amiata, and to your successors: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

Since whatever the faithful ask reasonably and appropriately ought always to be granted, out of devotion to our pious founder it is fitting that we in no way deny our generosity when granting privileges. Therefore, because your affection has humbly begged from our apostolate that the aforesaid monastery of Saint Saviour, established in the above-named county and territory, be adorned with the privileges of the Apostolic See, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church—which, by the Lord’s authority, we preside over—it may not be subjected to the right or jurisdiction of any other Church, we therefore willingly grant through this authority of ours what you ask, in accordance with your pious desires.

And so we forbid any priest of any Church, apart from the pontiff of the Apostolic See, to exercise any jurisdiction, power, or authority whatsoever in the aforesaid monastery; thus, unless he has been invited by the abbot of that monastery, he shall not presume to celebrate the solemn offices of Mass there at all. Finally, by this apostolic authority of ours, we establish that no person, great or small, shall presume to inflict any disturbance upon that venerable monastery, whether against the servants of God, the attendants, the male or female servants, the free persons, or any of the things belonging to it—namely, houses and possessions—or in any way cause them harm.

Likewise, we grant and confirm to that holy monastery the first fruits and tithes from its people, whether from those holding by charter (*praeceptales*), and permission to celebrate holy baptism freely, both in the church of Saint Benedict and in that of Saint Mary, just as this was granted to it by the kings through a charter, or whatever appears to be contained therein; and if anything was granted to that monastery by our holy predecessors, the pontiffs Stephen, Hadrian, John, Formosus, or by other predecessor pontiffs, we grant and confirm all of it to you and your successors in its entirety by apostolic authority. They may also freely receive chrism and holy oil from whatever church they wish or are able to approach.

By apostolic censure we establish and command that no duke, margrave, count, viscount, *castaldus*, or any other great or small person shall dare to exercise jurisdiction in any place belonging to that monastery, to judge there, or to hold any court, unless invited by the abbot of the monastery itself.

By this apostolic authority we likewise command and sanction that neither a bishop nor anyone else of the clerical order shall in any way presume to take away or alienate the churches, parishes, cells, estates, or any places or possessions of the aforesaid monastery; nor shall anyone dare to inflict any dispute, injury, or other loss upon the monastery in its goods, possessions, utensils, or ornaments.

All these things mentioned above—namely, tithes, first fruits, and offerings—shall belong to the often-mentioned monastery, as shall baptism, chrism, and oil. To you, our beloved son Theuzo, abbot, and to your successors, we confirm and grant them perpetually from this present fourth indiction through this charter of our privilege, by apostolic authority and according to the aforesaid arrangement.

Finally, we establish that when the said abbot has departed from this world, neither king, duke, margrave, bishop, count, nor any other person shall presume to appoint an abbot there.
