Since you have asked us, dearest son, to grant, confirm, and strengthen for you and your successors, by the page of our privilege, the monastery dedicated in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of the Lord, and situated on the island of Gorgona—which island, as is read in the privileges of Saint Peter, belongs under the jurisdiction and authority of our holy mother, the Roman Church—therefore, inclined by your prayers, we grant, confirm, and strengthen for you and your successors forever, by the page of this privilege, that monastery together with the aforesaid island, so that they may always be habitations of monks and not become a den of robbers, as the house of prayer formerly was.

Let no abbot be appointed in that monastery for money, but let the one who, according to the rule of Saint Benedict and with the counsel of the brothers, is found to be the better man in that monastery be appointed. Whatever religious and God-fearing men have granted or shall grant in perpetuity for the use and support of the monks serving God there, whether on this side of the sea or the other, we confirm and strengthen for you and your successors in perpetuity by this command and confirmation of ours.

We establish by apostolic judgment that no emperor, king, duke, marquis, count, viscount, castaldus, bishop, or any person of whatever order or dignity, great or small, dare attempt to act against this page of our command, grant, and confirmation. Whoever proves a violator of this privilege shall be bound by the bond of anathema and excommunication and, unless he repents, shall be handed over with Judas, the betrayer of Christ, to eternal damnation. Whoever observes it, however, shall be blessed by almighty God and filled with spiritual joys. We also establish that the abbot of this monastery shall receive the blessing of consecration from the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 0678B]

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, through the hand of Frederick, deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord Herimann, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the third year of Lord Pope Leo IX, indiction 4.

### LXI. Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions of the monastery of Subiaco. (Year 1051.)

[Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, IV, 1062.]

… Therefore, holy and venerable Father, we confirm to you what is yours with every care, every devotion … and may your worthy sister, the virgin Scholastica, have salvation in the pious and devout observance of what is yours, and possess all these things with you forever.

With fraternal charity and special reverence, we confirm and strengthen for you, by the privilege of the holy Roman see, whatever has been granted to you by Christ’s faithful, whatever you possess, and whatever you shall possess in the future, under the protection of the supreme Judge and by the authority of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles.

First, the dark cave, for a time the lowly resting-place of your body for Christ—[lacuna]—to you, regular in deed and name, [lacuna], O Father of great discernment, Saint Benedict: just as you specially chose a solitary retreat for yourself as a solitary, so also we decree that it be possessed specially by you alone. Thus we wish everything to be held by you and by your sister in fraternal communion, etc.

Given on the second day before the Kalends of November, through the hand of Frederick, deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church and apostolic see, acting in place of Lord Herimann, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne.

### LXII. Bull of Saint Leo IX confirming the privileges and rights of the monastery of Farfa.

[Muratori, *Italian Historical Writers*, II, ii, 583.] (Year 1051.)

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable Church of the holy virgin Mother, blessed Mary, situated at Farfa, and through it to Berard, abbot, and to his successors who lawfully enter, forever.

[Col. 0679A]

“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Warned by fear of him and due reverence, we gladly offer, with pious devotion, honor to the glorious and chaste Son and likewise to the glorious and chaste Mother; and we desire to provide necessary and regular support to her servants, so that while they serve well with our assistance, we may share in the reward and receive benefit in body and soul.

Among these matters, because we purely desire—and indeed most earnestly wish—to serve the living God by the benefit of our will, we want holy Farfa Church, just as it is renowned among other churches for the fame of its name, to be more gloriously exalted through our humility by the things necessary to it. We do not possess silver and gold; but what we have we gladly return to him who freely bestowed it on us, our Lord and Lord of the angels, and to our Lady: namely, a humble heart, good will, and devoted service, as is fitting, according to the capacity of our weakness.

Churches have always had their goods confirmed, and they are still confirmed, by the apostolic privileges of the supreme see. By God’s gift, the Queen of spirits and human beings, the Mother of humility, our gracious, gentle, and good Lady Mary, will not refuse humbly to receive this privilege from us. Receive, therefore, holy Virgin, holy Parent, together with your Son, your goods—not given to you by us, but secured for you by our privilege. Hold what you hold; with the blessing of your Son, possess what you possess. You are blessed among all women: let no one take away what is yours; let no one ever be permitted to offend you in your goods. And in her stead, to you, Berard, beloved son in Christ and faithful abbot of this monastery, we grant this written sacred document to observe, so that you may preserve both the document of the Church and every good entrusted to you.

Therefore, by holy apostolic authority, we confirm and strengthen everything that the Church possesses in the aforesaid place, just as it now possesses it and has possessed it from the beginning, both within and beyond it. Namely, whatever it appears to possess in the territory of Sabina: the Church of Saint Benedict; the estate of Saint Gethulius; the castle of Tribuco; the Podium of the sons of Palumba; and the entire bed of the Farfa. All these, with all their appurtenances, in their entirety.

The Church of Saint Michael at Tancia, with its woodland and all its appurtenances; the castle of Bucciniano; and the entire Rocca, with the estate granted to that monastery by Pope Benedict; the Castle of Fara. Again, all these together with all their appurtenances and dependencies.

The land of Ortella; in the city of Orte, the Church of Saint Theodore in its entirety. At Viterbo, the Church of Saint Mary in its entirety. At Tuscania, the cell of Saint Mary beside the Minio River, with its woodland, and with Mount Gosberti itself, as well as the bank of Aduella and the port of Marino.

In the county of Narni, the monastery of Saint Michael and the Church of Saint Antimus in their entirety. In the county of Perugia, the cell of Saint Mary at Diruta, and those of Saint Apollinaris, Saint Blaise, and Saint Muntanus, with their churches, castles, villages, and all their appurtenances and dependencies. Near the city of Tivoli, the Church of Saint Adrian in its entirety. At Collina, the Church of Saint Andrew with all its appurtenances.

In the city of Rome, the Church of Saint Mary and that of the Holy Savior, with their crypts and walls, and the Campus Agonalis in its entirety. In the county of Assisi, the cell of Saint Benedict in its entirety. In the county of Fermo, the cell of Saint Mary at Clenti; the nuns’ monastery called Saint Savior; the Church of Saint Benedict at Ripa; and the cell of Saint Victoria, with all their appurtenances and dependencies.

In the county of Ascoli, the cells: one of the Holy Savior beside the Asso River, and the other of Saint Mary at Offida, in its entirety. In the county of Chieti, the cell of Saint Stephen in its entirety. In the county of Senigallia, the estate of Luzano. In the county of Camerino, the estate of Sala Bona. In the county of Osimo, the estate of Monte Paulisco in its entirety.

Therefore, we decree that this greater and principal Church of the holy Mother and Virgin of God, Mary, at Farfa, together with all the aforesaid possessions and also its other greater cells and their lesser churches, with castles, villages, and towns, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures and vineyards, woods, waters and watercourses, fisheries and fishing rights, sea ports and shores, and every appurtenance of whatever extent or kind, together with everything it holds from the Roman see by apostolic privileges or from emperors and kings by charters, shall remain undisturbed and peaceful against all.

Whatever has been granted to it by any of Christ’s faithful, or is granted in the future, if it seeks the regard of divine mercy, let no one invade, diminish, or take away. For if anyone knowingly offends the pious Mother of the Lord, he can in no way possess the good will of her only-begotten Son—indeed, the firstborn of our Savior.

Let this Church hold its tithes and the offerings for the dead in peace. No bishop shall ordain monks or priests of this monastery or of its cells, unless the abbot has invited him, or, if the abbot is absent, the community has done so at his command; for this is provided in the privilege of Pope Paul of blessed memory: no bishop shall hold a synod here, nor compel the priests of this abbey to go elsewhere, since we do not wish to violate what this place obtained from him by privilege.

The abbot shall seek the consecrations of churches from any suitably religious bishop and shall also receive the chrism. For the election of a suitable abbot, there shall be common agreement according to the rule of Saint Benedict, and the request of the brothers shall be fulfilled.

It is written in the canons: “Invaders of churches shall be excommunicated without delay.” For this reason, and so that every invasion may cease throughout the Church, especially in places which blessed Mary holds dedicated to herself, let anyone who takes away what is hers fear incurring anathema. Great indeed is the excommunication: the indignation of the Son of the Virgin Mother.

Mary, exalted above the choirs of angels, may exalt him who preserves her goods. For reverence toward his Lady, may Peter, prince of the apostles, always enrich him with apostolic blessing, with the grace of the Father of the Virgin and of the Virgin Mother of God Almighty consenting to this. Farewell.

Given on the third day before the Ides of December, through the hand of Frederick, deacon and librarian of the holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord Herimann, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the third year of Lord Pope Leo IX, indiction 5.

### LXIII. Bull of Saint Leo IX by which he grants Stephen, bishop of Anician (Le Puy), and his successors the use of the pallium, on condition that they be ordained by the Roman pontiff. (Year 1051.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, II, 227.]

Leo, servant of the servants of God, to Stephen, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Anician (Le Puy), perpetual salvation in the Lord.

If shepherds of sheep endure frost day and night for the protection of their flock, etc.

We grant the pallium to your fraternity for the celebration of solemn Masses, out of due reverence for blessed and glorious Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God. In this Church of Anician (Le Puy), which is also called Vellave or Podium of Saint Mary, her memory is honored, loved, and venerated more specially and more deeply than in the other churches dedicated to her, by all who dwell throughout the surrounding regions of Gaul.

This holy, pious, and illustrious dignity of the Virgin Mary must be exalted by all with the highest honor and multiplied glory, more closely and more blessedly through us, so that we may have her intercession favorably directed to her only-begotten Son, true and kind in his great mercy, etc. For we shall find no one more deserving of appeasing the Judge’s anger than she who merited to be the mother of that same Redeemer and Judge.

We grant you, brother, permission to use the pallium at her most humble Nativity and Epiphany; at the memorial Supper of the Lord himself; at his most holy Resurrection and glorious Ascension; at the solemnity of Pentecost; on the feasts of the apostles Peter and Paul, and likewise of the apostle Andrew; at all the solemnities of your pious intercessor, our gentle Lady and yours, blessed Mary; and at the dedication of your church.

This is on the condition that, just as, while the privileges of your Church remain in force, the ordination of the bishops of this see belongs to the Roman pontiff, so also the bishop to be ordained for this place must enter through an election by us—namely, through the election of the clergy and people of this city—etc.

### LXIV. Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Peter of Perugia. (Year 1052.)

[Margarini, *Casinian Bullary*, II, 84.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Church of the blessed apostle Peter situated outside, indeed beside, the city of Perugia, in the place called Caprarius, and through it to Bonizo, abbot, and to his successors who lawfully enter, forever.

[Col. 0682A]

Since the universal holy Mother Church has been especially gathered together, instructed, and enlarged through the glorious princes of the earth—namely Peter, fisher of men, and Paul, teacher of the nations, above all her other co-workers—it is fitting that everything found to belong specially to her jurisdiction and authority should be confirmed and retained.

1. Therefore, to increase continually the honor of the aforesaid monastery and never diminish it, we grant this privilege of apostolic protection, so that it may hold what it possesses: namely, its cells and churches, its estates and parishes; also its lands and farmsteads, specifically the parish churches of Saint Constantius, Saint Rufinus, and Saint Martin; the Church of Saint Mary at Agellione with its appurtenances; the estate of Casale and the estate of Saint Justin; half of the Church of Saint Mary situated beside the Tiber River, with its appurtenance; the estate of Petroniano; the Church of Saint Mary at Petiniano; the Church of Saint Clement; and half of the Church of Saint Donatus at Civitella; as well as the land of Hugh, nephew of Berno, at Monte Nero.

Furthermore, we confirm to the same monastery in perpetuity the estates situated in the county of Perugia: one called Pusulo and the other called Casalini, with their churches, houses, vineyards, fields, gardens, cultivated and uncultivated mountains, and all their appurtenances.

2. We also grant you permission to ordain all your clerics, both those living in the monastery and those residing outside it on its possessions, through any suitable and canonically appointed bishop whom you choose, and to receive the chrism in your parishes, provided that you cannot easily and freely obtain or secure ordinations or chrism from the bishop in whose diocese the aforesaid monastery is situated; and the same applies to the consecration of churches.

3. No bishop shall dare to excommunicate or condemn anyone belonging to the same monastery if, in his case, he seeks the protection and judgment of us and of the holy apostolic see.

4. The abbey shall perpetually be a gift of the Roman pontiff, and the abbot himself and the abbot’s consecration shall likewise belong to him forever.

[Col. 0682D]

5. With every excuse removed except a canonical one, the abbot shall come to the synod whenever he is summoned by the supreme pontiff.

6. The offerings made to the same monastery, both for the living and for the dead, shall be seized by none of the bishops, but shall wholly benefit the monastery’s needs and those of the brothers.

7. The tithes of the same monastery shall, according to the canons, be given at the monastery gate for the reception of guests and pilgrims.

8. Moreover, no one shall prohibit anyone from being buried there.

9. The bishop shall in no way fail to celebrate public Masses and stations there at the appointed times, namely on the second day of Easter and on the solemn feasts of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. But he shall take no offerings from there against the will of the abbot and the brothers.

10. We establish that, whenever the abbot of the same monastery dies, no abbot shall be chosen there by outsiders if the community is able to choose a suitable brother from among itself for this office; the choice shall be made by common and regular counsel, without payment, and the elected man shall be consecrated by the Roman pontiff.

11. We also command that all harmful charters of your monastery’s Church shall be entirely void and empty.

12. Furthermore, by our apostolic authority, we establish and confirm that no emperor, king, bishop, duke, marquis, count, viscount, castaldus, or any other person, great or small, shall dare to expel or disturb you, the aforesaid abbot, or your canonically entering successors, from the aforesaid monastery or from any of its movable or immovable goods and properties. Whoever presumes to do so shall know that he is anathematized by the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and ourselves.

13. Whoever honors this Church and, taking nothing away from it, gives something of his own for the redemption of his soul shall obtain the grace of blessing from the Lord God and, through the key-bearing prince of heaven, deserve to be led into the gates of the heavenly kingdom.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of March, through the hand of Frederick, deacon, librarian and [Col. 0683C] chancellor of the holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord Herimann, archchancellor and bishop of Cologne, in the fourth year of Lord Pope Leo IX, indiction 5.

### LXV. Bull of Pope Leo by which he confirms various rights and possessions of the monastery of Saint Mary of Pomposa. (Year 1052.)

[Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, V, 337.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Church of the glorious and perpetual Virgin Mother, blessed Mary, situated on the island of Pomposa, and through it to Mainard, beloved son in the Lord Jesus Christ, venerable abbot, and to your successors who lawfully enter, forever.

[Col. 0683D] The Queen of heaven, Mother of God, exalted above the choirs of angels, ought, insofar as our diligence is able, to be raised by our devout veneration—namely, by increasing the benefice in places dedicated to her name, so that her special servants may more conveniently render her service. Therefore, venerable son, whom we see faithfully . . . [lacuna] . . . the monks serving her in the aforesaid monastery, we wish to place in charge with our assistance, so that you yourself may live morally, as is fitting, giving due counsel, and confirming for you by this privilege of holy apostolic authority the goods which your church either holds from elsewhere, or chiefly from the Roman See, or may acquire in perpetuity.

Therefore, since you ask us to grant from our generosity and gift to your religious community the entire estate called Materaria; the entire estate called Mauseuli; the entire holding called Casale Pubblico; the estate called Nepoti; the estate called Caputbovis; the land and vineyard, just as you now possess and hold them by right of the blessed apostle Peter; and also the bank of the river Alemon on both sides, beside the estate called Prata, the bank itself extending from Bigaziolo to the field of Bedullus; and the land and vineyard beside the walls of the city of Ravenna, with the tower called Branca, in its entirety, from Pusterula Augusta to the Taurentine Gate; and one entire garden at the place called Ponte Calciato, in . . . [lacuna] . . . of Saint Andrew, bounded on two sides by the right of that saint and on the other two by the public road; and the lake called Sanctus, with all its properties and appurtenances, together with its parish church, chapels, and titles, bearing the names of Saint Mary, Saint Martin, Saint Peter, and Saint Venantius; with the fishery called Tidini, the Archpriest’s Ditch, and the fishery called Falce; with the place called Monticello Laci Sicco; with the banks of the rivers Po and Gaurus on both sides as far as the sea, and from the place called Concha Agathae on one side as far as the sea; with the entire place called Masinzatica, within the boundaries of the whole place and territory of the estate called Lacus Sanctus: on one side, the Ditch of the Mill of Volta Latercli, descending into the small stream, and from the river Tribba as far as Ellia, and through the marsh as far as the middle of Curba, and beyond Curba as far as the Po, and beyond the Po as far as the bishopric of the Holy Church of Comacchio, and from there as far as the river called Cesi; on another side, Curlo, descending into Concha Agatulae and through it into the Gaurus; on the third side, the marsh extending between the stream of Anzelus and Masenzaticum as far as Monticelli, and Vedetosa flowing into the Po; on the fourth side, Vaculino, Arzere Malo, and the road of Vincareto extending toward Laterculum.

Moreover, we would grant you the entire fishery called Volana, with the Rivo Badarino and Greater Gavelona belonging to that fishery, together with the small harbors on both sides, which likewise belong to it, just as formerly they extended into the sea. We ought to grant all the aforesaid places, with all their entirety and appurtenances, insofar as they appear to belong to the holy Roman Church, over which by God’s authority we preside and which we serve, to you for possession by written decree.

Moved by your prayers, we perpetually grant and concede to you and your successors, leading the regular life and to the monks living religiously, all the aforesaid places, and whatever you now possess and hold, with all their entirety and appurtenances, as written above; and, moreover, by our gift and benevolence, if from now on in the future you are able to acquire anything belonging to the holy Roman Church in your vicinity throughout the Exarchate of Ravenna, we grant you and your successors the permission of ourselves and of our successors canonically entering office to have and to hold it in perpetuity.

Thus, however, each year, without resistance, you and your successors shall pay three silver solidi, by way of rent, to the officials of our holy Roman Church. Furthermore, out of love for that undefiled Mother of God, and for you, beloved son in the Lord, by the authority which Christ our Lord granted to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to the rulers of his Church, we establish and ordain that neither this place nor the properties belonging to it shall ever be subjected to any person except apostolic protection and royal authority.

No mortal person, apart from the height of imperial power, shall presume to exercise any ordinance, jurisdiction, or power in the aforesaid monastery, or in its courts, castles, parishes, cells, villages, or in all its movable and immovable properties, nor over its male or female servants, or even over the stewards residing upon the land of the same monastery; nor shall anyone impede the monks’ way of life, inflict trouble upon them, hold a district court or judicial hearing in any of its places, invade or alienate the monastery’s properties in any manner, or dare to demand fodrum, provisions, or any public obligations.

We irrevocably withdraw the monastery’s properties from the power both of archbishops and of all mortals, except the . . . [lacuna] . . . of royal majesty, and declare them free, with the authority of the apostolic See preserved there, and with the hearing of the First See invoked if necessary. In acquiring the goods of Saint Peter, however, this condition shall be observed: first, their nature and extent shall be reported to us or to our successors; then, once permission, a decree, and counsel have been received from the Roman See, they shall be accepted from you with a just rent added. In this way the ownership of the lands and waters will remain with Saint Peter, while you will henceforth enjoy their beneficial use.

Therefore, unless he repents and comes to fitting satisfaction, let the violator of this sacred privilege be condemned by apostolic anathema. But may the glorious intercession of our lady, blessed Mary, bring joy to its protector.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, through the hands of Frederick, [Col. 0685D] librarian and chancellor of the holy Roman See, acting in place of Lord Hermann, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Leo IX, in the fifth indiction.

### LXVI. The letter of Saint Leo to all the bishops throughout Italy—That no one should give all his possessions to a monastery, but at least half of them to the Church to which he belongs. (1052)

[Mansi, XIX, 670.]

Leo, bishop, to all the bishops in Christ throughout Italy.

It has been reported to our ears that certain men are acting perversely, attempting to overturn and divide the unity of the Church: namely, abbots and monks who do not labor from zeal for charity but from zeal for rapacity, and who teach and do not cease to seduce secular men whom they can ensnare, so that they may hand over their goods and possessions, whether during life or at death [Perhaps *in* is redundant, H.], to their monasteries, and leave nothing of their property to the churches to which they appear to be subject and from which they have received, or receive, baptism, penance, the Eucharist, and the nourishment of life with milk.

Observing this pattern of discord, we wish to prohibit it in every way; and, so that it may not happen again, we entirely forbid it. For we consider that it is not good that those who formerly were sharers in sufferings, according to the Apostle, should be excluded from sharing in consolations (2 Cor. 1:7); and because “the laborer is worthy of his wages.”

Therefore, we command and order that whoever henceforth wishes to enter religious life in a monastery, whether during life or at death, shall leave half of all the goods and possessions which he has decided to dispose of for the salvation of his soul to the church to which he is recognized as belonging. Only then shall he have permission to go to and convert himself to the monastery as he wishes. Whoever, however, becomes a contradictor and violator of this decree shall be subject to the sword of anathema.

### LXVII. The bull of Saint Leo IX for the monastery of Casa Dei among the Auvergnats. (1052)

[Baluz., *Works of Blessed Servatus Lupus of Ferrières*, p. 527.]

[Col. 0686C]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the church of the blessed martyrs Vitalis and Agricola, which is called Casa Dei, and through it to the abbot named Robert and his successors canonically entering there, in perpetuity.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to provide the shields of protection against the blows of all adversaries to all who wish to live piously in Christ, so that whoever takes upon himself the yoke of Christ may recognize and experience, through the aid and protection of the supreme See, even in temporal matters, that which the true and only Bridegroom of the holy Church declares to those who accept his yoke, making it gentle, saying: “My yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30).

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we grant and bestow upon the aforesaid church the grace of a privilege by which it may defend itself against the calumny of all who unjustly attack it, so that whatever has been bestowed there by Bishop Rencon, or has already been or shall be bestowed by any of Christ’s faithful, may remain forever secure under apostolic protection. Thus those serving there, dwelling in peace and safety, may cling all the more devotedly to Christ’s discipleship insofar as, protected by this apostolic document, they have been kept apart from the world’s furious assault.

Therefore, acting in the place of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles—whose vicars we are, although unworthy—we command that no emperor, king, duke, marquis, count, or viscount, nor anyone endowed with ecclesiastical authority, namely an archbishop, bishop, or any vicedominus, dare invade the aforesaid church or plunder its goods, which it now justly possesses or may at any time possess.

Whoever violates this privilege of sanction by reckless boldness shall, unless he repents, suffer the bond of anathema forever. But may its protector possess the rewards of happiness in eternal joys.

Given at Ginon, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, through the hands of Frederick the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord Hermann, chancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Leo IX, in the fifth indiction.

### LXVIII. Saint Leo IX confirms the privileges of the metropolitan church of Cologne and grants to Archbishop Hermann and his successors the title of chancellor of the holy Roman Church and cardinal of Saint John at the Latin Gate; in the church of Cologne he also creates seven cardinal priests and an equal number of deacons and subdeacons. From the *History of Cologne*. (1052)

[Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*, II, 1181.]

[Col. 0687B]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hermann, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, and to his successors canonically entering there, perpetual greeting.

We give thanks to God and to our Lord Jesus Christ, who, without any preceding merits of ours, caused us to ascend to the summit of apostolic dignity and to undertake concern for all the Churches, offering the assent of piety to their rulers.

Since you requested that the privileges granted to your church by our predecessors be confirmed by the Roman See, it seemed to us honorable and necessary for the Church to consent to your petition.

Especially since this church has been consecrated under the name of the prince of the apostles, the most blessed Peter, like its mother, over which by divine clemency we preside: as the daughter imitates its mother in name, so may it also imitate her, in some measure, in dignity, and be protected beneath the wings of her defense.

Therefore, moved by your devotion, as by that of all Christ’s faithful, and by our own and apostolic authority, we confirm to you everything that is written in the privileges of our fathers, the apostolic men: namely, the cross and pallium to be carried at its proper time and in its proper place, and also the emblem of the ceremonial horse which our Romans call the *Naccus*.

We also confirm to you, by this page of our decree, the chancellery of the holy apostolic See and the church of Saint John the Evangelist before the Latin Gate, so that Peter may have you as chancellor and John may provide you lodging.

We also grant and perpetually bestow that seven suitable cardinal priests, clothed in dalmatics, shall reverently minister at the principal altar of your mother church, dedicated to the honor of the Virgin, and at another altar there dedicated to the prince of the apostles, blessed Peter. We also grant and establish that they shall use sandals together with an equal number of deacons [Col. 0688A] and subdeacons prudently chosen for this ministry.

Furthermore, we confirm with the shield of apostolic protection the authority and honor which the Church has hitherto possessed, both among others and from its own members: if a synod should at any time be assembled within your diocese, either in the presence of the archbishop of this First See or of a legate sent from his side, its ruler shall hold the first place after him and shall be first in declaring the authority of the sacred canons. Yet, just as he is first in this commendable dignity, so also let him excel first in moral excellence and uprightness of life, so that the one whose words he proclaims may be imitated in his example.

We strengthen by the protection of apostolic power the royal consecration to be carried out within the boundaries of his diocese [Col. 0688B]; and by this page of our decree we also sanction for the sons of the Church the election of the archbishop, according to canonical authority.

As for the goods which it has held until now or may justly acquire forever, we praise and strengthen them by this apostolic protection: namely, the monasteries and churches situated in Cologne; the monastery of Saint Heribert with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Mary within the city; and the church of Saint Gereon with all its appurtenances. We also confirm to you by apostolic authority the other sacred places, both within and around the city, the city’s mints, the toll, and every civil right, under the authority of the archbishop.

[Col. 0688C] The abbeys in various places, villages, districts, and castles, with all their appurtenances, male and female servants, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters, meadows, fields, woods, and forests.

Moreover, we strengthen the church’s estates which you yourself gave, namely the monastery of Brauweiler and the castle called Zonneburg, with all their appurtenances. Just as we subject you to none of your fellow archbishops, so we decree that you shall be governed by no primate, without prejudice to what is due to us in you, as in the other archbishops, by the authority of apostolic subjection.

By apostolic censure we establish that no emperor, king, duke, marquis, count, viscount, and, moreover, [Col. 0688D] no archbishop, bishop, provost, or any person, great or small, of whatever order or dignity, dare act against this page of our decree and confirmation.

If anyone—which we do not wish—should attempt with reckless boldness to act against this written instrument of our apostolic authority, piously published by us, let him be bound by the chains of anathema and excluded from the kingdom of God until he repents. But may whoever becomes its pious guardian and observer, out of reverent devotion, deserve to obtain from our most merciful Lord the grace of blessing and the joys of the heavenly kingdom.

Given on the Nones of May, through the hands of Frederick the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord Hermann, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne. [Col. 0689A] In the year of our Lord 1052, the fourth year of Pope Leo IX, in the fifth indiction.

### LXIX. The bull of Saint Leo IX for the monastery of Altorf. 1052

[*Gallia Christiana*, V, 473.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Jugitbert, abbot of the church of Saint Cyriacus, situated in Alsace, in the place called Altorf, and to his successors, and through him to the monks who will perpetually serve there, perpetual salvation in the Lord.

Since it is fitting for apostolic authority to protect venerable places by its own guardianship, so that those serving God may always remain quiet and free from those who unjustly attack them . . . [lacuna]. Therefore, we have judged it most just that, by our page of sanction, the aforesaid church, built by our forebears, should remain perpetually fortified and be inviolably dedicated to the monastic order at all times.

Therefore, by the authority through which we act in the place of Saint Peter, we confirm and strengthen by the power of our apostolic privilege whatever has been or shall be granted there by our parents to the aforesaid church, so that no one may diminish anything from it or take anything away, but everything may always remain entirely intact for the monks serving God there.

We have also decreed that this be confirmed: whenever the abbot of that place dies, the monks of the same monastery shall have the power to elect an abbot who will rule over them lawfully and justly, according to the institution of the most blessed Benedict. We command that they choose one from among themselves if they are able to find someone suitable; otherwise, they shall accept the better man whom they can find elsewhere and bring the chosen man to the bishop for consecration. If the bishop refuses to comply with the brothers’ just petition or attempts to do anything simoniacal against him, they shall have the power, by apostolic authority, to approach our presence.

Furthermore, we decree that no person, great or small, of whatever condition or fortified by whatever protection of power, dare demand anything from the aforesaid church or monastery, unless the abbot of the said place has voluntarily offered it.

Therefore, by apostolic censure we decree and irrevocably confirm that no emperor, king, duke, [Col. 0689D] marquis, count, or viscount, no advocate, no archbishop or bishop, and, moreover, no person of either sex or any age, dare attempt to act against this confirmation and constitution of our apostolic authority. Nor shall the abbot appointed there unjustly dare to sell or distribute the monastery’s goods.

Whoever does so shall remain struck by our apostolic anathema until he makes worthy satisfaction. But whoever guards and observes this confirmation and constitution shall be enriched by our blessing and become a participant in eternal life.

Given on the Nones of May, through the hands of Frederick the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, acting in place of [Col. 0690A] Lord Hermann, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Leo IX, in the fifth indiction, and in the year of the Lord 1052.

### LXX. The privilege of Saint Leo IX for the monastery of Monte Cassino. (1052)

[Gattula, *History of Cassino*, 117.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Richerius, abbot of the monastery of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Benedict, which was built on the mountain called Cassino in the territory of Benevento, and to all your successors canonically entering there according to the statutes of the aforesaid confessor Benedict, in perpetuity.

Since it is fitting for apostolic authority always to provide those serving God with the just, most equitable, and unfailing defenses of all protection, so that they may possess what they hold without any just disturbance and may recover what has been unjustly taken from them, therefore, when we were passing through Campania and were staying at San Germano, situated below the aforesaid mountain, with many of our brothers—namely, archbishops and bishops, as well as other faithful of Saint Peter and of ourselves—the aforesaid Richerius, abbot of the monastery written above, together with his brothers, one of whom is called Firmus, complained that the Church and monastery of the most holy Benedict had been deprived and stripped of the church and monastery of Saint Stephen situated beside the city of Terracina, which the aforesaid and most worthy man Benedict had built while still alive.

Finally, they brought forward the account of his life written by the most blessed Pope Gregory. There it was found, upon investigation, that when this same saint had been asked by someone to build a monastery on his estate, he appointed an abbot and a provost, who was to be second to him, to construct the monastery. He announced the day on which he would be present, so that he could show them individually where they were to build the places, workshops, and facilities necessary for the monks’ residence and for the arrival and reception of guests.

When the night before the promised day arrived, the most holy man of God, Benedict, appeared in a dream to both of the aforementioned men, namely the chosen abbot and his provost, and showed them each place, as he had promised. They reported to one another individually what they had seen, in mutual discussion; nevertheless, not trusting that vision, they awaited his bodily presence.

When they did not see him come on the appointed day, they returned sadly, complaining that they had waited for the servant of God and that he had not arrived according to his promise. When he demonstrated to them that he had certainly fulfilled what he had promised, since he had appeared to each of them separately in the same manner and had shown both the same places, suitable for each purpose, he therefore ordered them to complete the work as they had learned from the vision. And so it was done.

Therefore, after examining all these matters most carefully with our brothers and recognizing them to be true, we judged and decreed it most fitting to restore to the aforesaid and chosen monastery of the most holy confessor Benedict, and to confirm by apostolic authority, the church of Saint Stephen situated beside Terracina, which, as has been said, had been dedicated to monastic religion from its beginning. Thus, that which was founded under his direction might always be ruled and protected by his authority.

Accordingly, to you, Abbot Richerius, and to all your successors who justly enter the monastery situated on Monte Cassino, built by the most blessed Father Benedict, and to the monastery and church of the aforesaid and repeatedly mentioned Benedict, we restore, grant, and strengthen the aforesaid church and monastery of Saint Stephen, with all their appurtenances.

Therefore, by the highest apostolic censure, we establish that no one at any time may invade or secretly seize the aforesaid church, or harm or diminish it in any respect, contrary to justice, among the things belonging to it, or claim for himself what has been unjustly taken from it; nor may anyone tear it away from or alienate it from the monastery of the holy and most blessed Benedict situated on Monte Cassino; nor may anyone, contrary to equity and justice, seize, invade, divert, or in any manner claim anything that has already justly been granted to it, even if it appears now to be possessed by others, or anything still to be granted to you.

No emperor, king, duke, marquis, count, or viscount, no archbishop or bishop, nor any person of whatever order, condition, or sex, supported by whatever protection of power, shall dare to act against this privilege of our sanction.

Whoever, therefore, acts against this decree and privilege of most just moderation—which, by apostolic authority, with the consent of almighty God, we have made, confirmed, and strengthened for the monastery of the most worthy servant of God Benedict and for all abbots duly appointed there—and remains rebellious, shall, unless he repents, suffer forever the avenging punishments of perpetual anathema.

But may the protector, having been heard through the prayers and merits of the most blessed Benedict, father and distinguished leader of the monks, deserve to be absolved from every guilt and attain the grace of blessing and eternal life.

Given through the hands of Frederick the deacon, chancellor and librarian of the holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord Hermann, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Leo IX, in the fifth indiction.

### LXXI. Saint Leo IX announces to Bishop John and to all those residing at Terracina that he has restored the church and monastery of Saint Stephen to the monastery of Cassino. (1052)

[Gattula, *History of Cassino*, 118.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to John, bishop, and to all those residing at Terracina or within its borders who are faithful to Saint Peter and to us, greeting with apostolic blessing.

Let your devotion know that we have restored and confirmed the church and monastery of Saint Stephen, situated near Terracina, [Col. 0692A] to the monastery of Saint Benedict, situated on Monte Cassino, with all the appurtenances that justly belong to it.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we command that no one dare violate the privilege which we have made and strengthened for that monastery, if he does not wish to incur the penalty of anathema. Rather, whoever unjustly holds anything belonging to it shall restore it justly, so that he may have the blessing and not lose my good will.

### LXXII. Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Sophia of Benevento. (1052)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XIX, 687.]

[Col. 0692B] Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Sicenolphus, our beloved son in Christ and abbot of the venerable monastery of Sophia, gracious and coeternal with the Lord Father, built within Benevento at the place called Urbs Vetus, and to your successors canonically promoted in the same monastery after you, in perpetuity.

We have been placed at the summit of the priesthood for this purpose: to uproot, to destroy, and to build and plant in his name. As the duty of our office requires, we have judged it best, during our days, insofar as heavenly grace permits, to cut away with the ecclesiastical sickle whatever unlawful things meet us, and everywhere to provide lawful things with the opportunity to bear fruit.

Therefore, after the great calamity of the people of Benevento, [Col. 0692C] which they justly endured because of the injury and pride of the Roman pontiffs and imperial lords, and after their miserable and grievous satisfaction, we confirm in full to you, the aforesaid Sicenolphus, whom we appointed in place of that deposed and wicked Gregory, improperly called abbot and no longer to be called so, according to the terms of your petition, the aforesaid abbey of Saint Sophia, with its churches, courts, villages, farms, vineyards, lands, male and female servants, and all its movable and immovable goods justly belonging to it—both those which it has been able to acquire until now and those which thereafter it may obtain through the generosity, donation, or grant of any religious persons—and absolutely whatever has been granted to it and confirmed by the decrees or charters of pious emperors or princes.

Moreover, by the authority of the apostolic Roman See, we grant and confirm to you and your successors forever, in full, all offerings of the living and the dead which from now on and thereafter shall be given to that monastery or to the churches subject to it by any persons.

Let the monks of that congregation also have permission to elect an abbot for themselves, if they find someone suitable for this office there; otherwise, let them choose for themselves a worthy ruler from wherever they can. And let the often-mentioned monastery forever remain free and exempt under the protection or jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church, from every subjection and yoke of the monastery of Cassino, so that no voice of accusers concerning this matter shall be admitted, but shall be deemed wholly frivolous and invalid.

Let the settlement of that controversy, publicly and manifestly made by the religious princes Jandolphus and Pandolphus, and by their magnates and dukes, remain valid, at the time when first Malepotus and then John, abbots of Cassino, undertook a lawsuit over these matters against Ursus and Gregory, rulers of the abbey of Saint Sophia.

Therefore, let it always retain and possess the liberty granted and confirmed to it hitherto by the privileges of our predecessors and the decrees of emperors, so that henceforth no emperor, king, duke, prince, or marquis, nor any person of whatever dignity, dare act against this authority of ours or against the terms of the privileges, or presume in any manner or by any device to usurp, diminish, or alienate anything from the goods of the same abbey granted by us or by anyone else, lest he fall under the judgment of strict anathema.

Furthermore, since monasteries often suffer burdens from certain bishops, while we neither wish nor ought to prejudice anyone, we finally grant you by this authority of ours that, if you are unable to obtain ecclesiastical ordinations freely and canonically from the bishop in whose diocese you reside, you may have permission to obtain them justly from any bishop you choose, for yourself and your people.

Let no one at any time presume by any device to infringe or annul the statutes of this privilege of ours, lest he incur the condemnation promulgated from the beginning by the holy Fathers against sacrilegious persons. For whoever reverently observes these things out of pious regard for the Divinity, we trust [Col. 0693C] that he will have the blessing of the Holy Trinity and will obtain a share with those who kept the Lord’s commandments and transferred earthly patrimonies to heavenly treasures.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, through the hands of Frederick the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord Hermann, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Leo, in the fifth indiction.

### LXXIII. Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Ascoli at the request of Bishop Bernard. (1052)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, I, 449.]

[Col. 0693D] Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Berard II, bishop of the Church and episcopate of the holy Mother of God, the virgin Mary, and of the most blessed martyr of Christ, Emigdius, situated in the county of Ascoli within the city, and to all his successors canonically entering there, in perpetuity.

Because by the divine generosity of grace the Church has been wholly entrusted to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to govern, administer, and defend from every assault of the wicked—so that the Church whose doctrine feeds her may also be fortified by his protection—it is fitting that we, who exercise the office of the apostolate in his place, extend the hands of just protection to each Church, so that what benefits them as a support for their defense may free us from the debt that we owe to all.

Therefore, at the request of the above-mentioned Bernard, bishop of the holy Church of Ascoli, we grant the protection of apostolic authority, and through it to the aforesaid bishop and to all his successors canonically enthroned there, whose church is dedicated to the honor of God’s mother and ever-virgin Mary. We do not confer this protection as a matter of lesser generosity, but as an obstacle to aggression and a shield of complete protection, so that the church dedicated to the name of the supreme omnipotent King of martyrs may also be protected by the written word and defended by the sword of his supreme soldier, his son.

Therefore, acting with apostolic authority, we confirm and strengthen for you everything that was justly brought to that church, so that from now on no one may dare to strip it of anything, molest it, or inflict any disturbance upon it. Namely: the entire city of Ascoli, together with its own portion of the monastery of Saint Angelus, built within that city; and the monastery of Saint Mary, situated on the holy mountain, together with everything justly belonging to it, or that may hereafter legally come to belong to it by the lawful gift of anyone.

The castle called Trione, with the monastery of Saint Lawrence and all its appurtenances; the estate of Massa with the Pojo of the Bright Valley; the estate of Monte; the estate of Pazano, as it is recorded and read in the charter of Mainard, son of Sigolf. The castles called Sculcula, Matrice, and Spinetula; the estates of Ilica, Cariano, Core, Belenterio, Flaminiano, Api, Tarracina, Bapino, Vuasto Promarese, Saxa, Salli, Patareo, and Villa Magna; and everything belonging to the aforesaid bishopric, both within the above-mentioned castles and estates.

The estate of Montariolo within the city of Spoleto; the estate of Paterno in the place called Ponte; the estate of Primocasu; Gualdo of Languine; Nursiacasa; and the estate within the place where the city once stood; the estate of Sala in the same Nursia; Gualdo of Fesso; the estate of Savelli; likewise, in the county of Ascoli, in the place called Aqua, the castle of Luco; the tower of Fotiano; the Pojo of Quintodecimo; the estate of Mazzano with its saltworks; the castle of Murro; the castle of Fundanianum; Mount Purus with its forests and woods; the Pojo called Clamatorium; Plage with the castle of Lusianum; Villamagna with its Pojo and castle; Cicilianum; Mount Calvus; Bajuanum; the castle of Gualdo; the estate of Agelli; the castle of Ligunianum; the estate of Pupilliana; the estate of Saint Stephen; the estate of Paterno; and the castle of Spelunca with the estate of Valeriano itself; the estate of Bofiano; Mount Andrew; the Pojo called Silvistus, which lies before the castle of Gusianum; and also the castle of Spinetulo with its estate called Francisca; the estate of Fassiana; the estate of Prostitula; the Pojo of Valenterius; the castle of Ottavo; the Pojo of Gaminaldus; the estate of Cervinaria; the estate of Chrisiana; the estate of Vivarium; the estate of Saint Felix; the Pojo of Pignole; the estate of Saint Martin; the castle of Corato with the Pojo of Helicetus and Cisimula; the estate of Popillano; the estate of Lauretiana; the estate of Maltiniana; the castle of Castelli in Frondaria; the estate of Porile; the estate of Diana; the estate of Quarto; the castle of Post-montes; the estate of Capitinnula; the estate of Paternion, with the Pojo of Avignon; the castle of Callonnata with its estates; the estate of CInianus with its castle; the estate of Casule; and the castle of Vina.

All the things named above, with their individual parishes and churches and their endowments, with male and female servants, little estates [the text reads *vi lulis*, probably an OCR corruption], tenant holdings, dependents, and colonists; with alpine pastures and mountains, woods, meadows, pastures, vineyards, olive groves, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters, mills, fishponds, fisheries, saltworks, and watercourses; likewise with herds and the forest pastures of horses, and with everything else justly belonging to them—we confirm in their entirety and strengthen by apostolic authority.

We also grant to you, according to the canonical institution of the holy Fathers, the tithes, first fruits, and all offerings of the faithful, living and dead, that justly and canonically belong to the same bishopric.

Moreover, by establishing this we decree that no bishop, supported by the authority or power of anyone, may dare, without the leave of the aforesaid bishop, to make any ordinances or constitutions there, to arrange judicial proceedings, or to constrain or harass clerics or priests through any kind of synod.

Therefore, by apostolic authority—which must be observed by everyone and in every matter—we establish and, under anathema, bind all to observe that no emperor or king, no duke, margrave, count, viscount, castaldus, or any public exactor, nor any person whatsoever, of whatever order, dignity, or religious status, may dare to oppose or in any way violate this pragmatic sanction of privilege. Whoever attempts this shall perish, struck by divine anathema from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, because he did not fear offending the Mother of God and those who serve her, and considered it nothing that God should observe this. But the protector, supported by blessing, shall obtain eternal life from almighty God.

Given on the Kalends of July, by the hand of Frederick, deacon, librarian of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, acting in place of Lord Herimann, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the fifth indiction, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Leo IX, pope. Done at Benevento, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### LXXIV. Saint Leo IX grants Liuthbald, archbishop of Mainz, the use of the pallium and the *cuphia*, and permission to ride “upon the *nattum*.” (Year 1052.)

[Gudenus, *Codex diplomaticus*, I, 17.]

**Note on *cuphia*:** This is the same as a mitre, or head covering, which surrounded the entire head. (Du Fresne, *Glossarium*, vol. V, part III, p. 1233, new edition.)

**Note on *nattum*:** *Nattum*, or more properly *nactum*, is an ornament of a ceremonial horse, also called by some *nacuum*. For on a festival or procession the whole horse was spread with a covering, and this was counted among the distinguished privileges if a bishop was granted the ability to sit and proceed in the Palm Sunday procession and on the Monday after Easter upon a horse covered with a *udo* or *nacta*. No one was permitted to do this without a special concession. (The same, under “Equus,” vol. III, p. 119; supplement, vol. II, p. 134, under “Nactum.”)

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Liuthbald, archbishop of Mainz, our beloved son and spiritual brother.

If shepherds of sheep are content to endure the sun and frost, day and night, for the protection of their flock, and with ever-watchful eyes look around lest any of the sheep perish by wandering or be seized and torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, with how much labor and care ought we to remain vigilant, who are called shepherds of souls? Let us pay attention, and let us not cease to perform the office entrusted to us for the protection of the Lord’s sheep, lest on the day of strict judgment the guilt of negligence, arising from our laziness, torture us before the supreme Shepherd, since at present we are judged superior to others in honor and reverence.

We grant your fraternity the pallium, according to custom, for celebrating the solemnities of Mass. You know that we permit you to use it only as your predecessors and earlier forebears used it, with the privileges of your Church otherwise remaining in their proper condition: namely, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, at the Epiphany, at the Lord’s Supper, on Holy Saturday, on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, at the Lord’s Ascension, on the holy day of Pentecost, on the festivals of Saint Mary, on the birthdays of the apostles, at the festival of Saint Martin, and at those of Saints Alban, Sergius and Bacchus, Aureus and Justina; at the ordination of bishops and clerics, on your birthday, and at the dedication of the church.

And because we love you as a son, we charitably grant you these two days that your predecessors did not possess: namely, the octave of the Lord and the festival of All Saints. In addition, we permit you the *cuphia*, grant you permission to ride upon the *nattum*, and give you permission to have the cross carried before you. If anything should occur in your church or in those of your suffragans that requires apostolic judgment or the presence of an apostolic legate, and such necessity presses that you cannot reasonably wait, we judge that you may settle the matter in our place by apostolic authority.

Since the honor of these dignities must be preserved by the modest vigor of your conduct, we urge you to make all the ornaments of your character correspond to them, so that, with God as author, you may rightly be distinguished in both respects. Thus let your life be a rule for your sons. If any crookedness has been introduced into them, let them be straightened by it; let them observe in it what they should imitate; let them continually improve by examining themselves in it, so that, after God, whatever good they live may appear to be yours. Therefore let neither prosperity, by which temporal things flatter them, lift their hearts up, nor adversity cast them down; whatever it may be, let it be overcome by the virtue of patience.

Let hatred find no place with you, and let no indiscriminate favor find one. Let them recognize the distinction between good and evil. Let no evil accusation make an innocent person guilty in your presence. Let favor not excuse the guilty; do not show yourself lenient toward offenders, lest what you have failed to avenge you permit to be committed.

Let there be in you both the sweetness of a good shepherd and the discernment of a severe judge. Restrain anger by judgment, and use disciplinary correction in such a way that you strike faults while not withdrawing your affection from the persons whom you correct. Show yourself merciful in all your actions, and let there be no acceptance of persons with you. Do not accept anyone’s face against justice, and do not despise anyone seeking what is just. Let the guardianship of equity excel in you, so that, by God’s mercy and assent, you may be able to prove yourself such as sacred Scripture describes when it says: “It is necessary that a bishop be blameless” (1 Timothy 3:2).

But you will be able to use all these things beneficially if you possess charity, which is the mother of virtues. Behold, dearest brother: among many other things, these are the duties of the priesthood; these are the duties of the pallium. If you carefully observe them, you possess inwardly what you have shown outwardly that you received.

May the Holy Trinity strengthen your fraternity by the protection of its grace, and direct us in the way of its fear, so that after the bitterness of this life we may deserve to reach the unending joy of eternal happiness, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man”—most clearly and certainly promised to all who love God.

Given by the hand of Frederick, archdeacon, librarian and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church and Apostolic See, acting in place of Lord Herimann, archbishop of Cologne and archchancellor. On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1052, in the sixth indiction, in the fourth year of Lord Leo IX, pope.

### LXXV. Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Bamberg after the dispute between Bishops Hartwig of Bamberg and Adalbero of Würzburg was settled at Bamberg in the presence of Emperor Henry. (Year 1052.)

[Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores*, IV, 802.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hartwig, bishop of Bamberg, and to those who shall canonically succeed him in the episcopal see, forever: eternal salvation in the Lord.

When, required by the pastoral care of the whole holy Church of God entrusted to us by divine providence, we had come into those parts of Germany adjoining eastern Francia, at the request of our beloved son Henry, second emperor and third king, and of our aforesaid beloved brother Hartwig, bishop, we came to Bamberg. On the day of the birth of blessed Luke the Evangelist, during the solemnities of Mass, while we were speaking the word of God to the people, in the presence of our aforesaid dearest son Henry and many bishops, with laymen and various secular authorities also standing by, the privileges of our predecessors were reread, by which that place had been founded and strengthened by the authority of the Roman Apostolic See.

There too was reread the document and confirmation of Henry, bishop of Würzburg, by which he had confirmed the aforesaid Church of Bamberg with an episcopal ban and episcopal boundary, having received an agreed exchange. It was executed as follows:

When Henry, first in the empire and second in the kingdom, inflamed by the love of divine fire, desired to increase the service of God by establishing and ordering a bishopric from the estates that by God’s grace had come into his possession by hereditary right, he began earnestly to request that Henry, the venerable administrator of the Church of Würzburg, transfer from his own right to the king’s right, for the accomplishment of this purpose, the aforesaid place called Bamberg together with the district called Ratenzgowe, which seemed to belong to the status of his diocese.

Since the causes appeared just and reasonable, the administrator, yielding to the petitions of that invincible king, and with the counsel and consent of his clergy, soldiers, and the whole people, handed over the aforesaid place with the aforesaid district to the king’s authority, after excepting three parish churches with their appurtenances, whose names are Wachenrode, Lonerstat, and Mulihusen, and after removing every subsequent objection.

Of the other district called Volcfelt, in which the aforesaid place is situated, he granted the same king that portion extending from Bamberg to the river Uraha, from Uraha to the river Ratenzam, and then along the course of that river to the Main, and from there to the stream Wichibach; then to the head of that stream, and from there by the quickest and nearest route to Uraha. And so that this transfer might remain firm and unshaken, the aforesaid Bishop Henry himself confirmed and subscribed it with his canons.

After this document had been reread, and since, in accordance with everyone’s wish, we ought always to favor just works, we desired to strengthen that venerable place by apostolic authority. The bishop of that place, Hartwig, then made a formal complaint that his see had been invaded by the clerics of Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg, through reckless presumption.

Since both bishops were present, and the case stood between them, we wished to examine it there. We therefore gave Bishop Adalbero, by whom the injury had been inflicted, the opportunity either to refute the accusation if he could, or to satisfy justice. Then, after taking counsel with all his clerics and laymen who were present, he returned to the ambo, excused himself with satisfaction for the injury inflicted, and renounced, from that time forward, everything belonging to the ban, episcopal jurisdiction, and authority of the bishop of Bamberg, except those cases concerning the goods of the two bishoprics that the bishops themselves could legally settle between them.

But we, just as we always rejoice in the advancement of the faithful and ought to promote just works, strengthened the same place of Bamberg by apostolic authority, as it had been strengthened by our predecessors, there by our living voice. We now also mark that same confirmation in writing, so that no one may ever dare to steal, remove, or exchange that place and all the things there transferred to God and Saint Peter by Henry of blessed memory, second king and first emperor, or anything that may lawfully be acquired in the future or has been justly acquired: estates, servants, gold, silver, vestments, vessels, ornaments, or other utensils—unless for the benefit of the same church.

Rather, the bishop of that place, or those who shall forever succeed him, shall possess these things in secure tranquility and shall have free power to order, arrange, or even increase all the goods and properties of that place; but they shall have no power or authority to squander or disorder them.

Moreover, by our authority we decree that within the boundaries and possessions of the same church there shall be no assault by tyrants or by any other wicked persons, whether in Bamberg itself, or in castles, villages, male or female servants, tributaries, tithes, forests, woods, hunts, fisheries, mills, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated or uncultivated lands, or anything that now belongs there or may justly be acquired in the future. All these things, strengthened by the privilege of our apostolic authority, shall remain in secure peace.

No count or judge shall dare to hold or conduct any assembly or exercise any jurisdiction there, except what the bishop of that place shall determine by concession of the glorious Emperor Henry II or of his successors. No person placed in any dignity, great or small, shall violently intrude.

Let that bishopric be free, subject only to Roman protection, so that the bishop may more freely and pleasantly devote himself, together with his clerics, to the service of God, and may constantly remember Henry I, emperor and venerable founder of that place; ourselves, namely Leo IX, pope; our successors; our beloved son Henry II, emperor; and all to whom they are indebted.

Nevertheless, let the same bishop be subject and obedient to his metropolitan, the bishop of Mainz, only in canonical matters.

Therefore, after deliberating, decreeing, and strengthening all the matters stated above, we judged it pleasing to add to that holy place a distinguished ecclesiastical honor by our apostolic authority, moved by love and reverence for Clement, our predecessor of pious memory, whom God, by a wonderful order of providence, graciously summoned from the leadership of this place to the summit of the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church, and even more wonderfully brought his dead body back from Rome’s neighboring regions.

We wished this church, as we believe, to be made like a new church adorned with so great a patron, while the Roman Church might remain content and sufficient, adorned by Fathers of the past and the future. Moreover, out of love and desire for the brothers who received us upon their ecclesiastical revenues and daily provisions, we grant permission to wear mitres to one brother acting in our stead, on the condition that the bishop select the more worthy and honorable priests and deacons, distinguished by good morals, mature age, or even by the offices of that place.

They may wear them on these days: the Nativity of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ; the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; the day of his glorious Resurrection; holy Pentecost; the day of Saint George; the day of Saints Peter and Paul; the Assumption of the most blessed Mary; the day of Saint Dionysius, out of reverence for our aforesaid predecessor, Lord Clement, pope, whose anniversary is then celebrated by those same brothers; and the anniversary of Emperor Henry, venerable founder of that place.

We grant this dignity only to those who specifically keep vigil or serve at the tomb of our aforesaid predecessor. We decree, however, that they must be content with these days and that no one may rashly usurp the privilege beyond them, lest the honor proper to the Apostolic See be cheapened.

We decree, confirm, and strengthen by our apostolic authority that all the foregoing shall be observed and preserved forever. Whoever, God forbid, becomes a reckless transgressor of this privilege shall be cursed with the eternal curse of God, the most blessed Mary, the blessed Peter and Paul, all the saints, and ourselves, and shall be bound by the chains of perpetual anathema, unless he repents and makes canonical satisfaction through worthy reparation.

But whoever observes this privilege with a devout heart may deserve to become a participant in the eternal kingdom, enriched by the blessing of almighty God, gracious Mary, and the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given by the hand of Frederick, deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1052, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Leo IX, pope.

### LXXVI. Saint Leo IX sends the pallium to Hartwig, bishop of Bamberg, at the request of Emperor Henry, for use three times a year. (Year 1053.)

[Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores*, IV, 801.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hartwig, venerable bishop of the Church of Bamberg: perpetual salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ.

If shepherds of sheep are content to endure the sun and frost, day and night, for the protection of their flock, and with ever-watchful eyes look around lest any of the sheep perish by wandering or be seized and torn apart by the bites of wild beasts, with how much labor and care ought we to remain vigilant, who are called shepherds of souls? Let us pay attention, and let us not cease to perform the office entrusted to us for the protection of the Lord’s sheep, lest on the day of divine judgment the guilt of negligence, arising from our laziness, torture us before the supreme Shepherd, since at present we are judged superior to others in honor and reverence.

Therefore, for celebrating the solemnities of Mass, we send the pallium to your fraternity. It had never previously been granted to your predecessors, but we now grant it to you first, at the request of our beloved son Emperor Henry, out of reverence for your predecessor, Lord Clement, pope of pious memory, and in memory of Emperor Henry I, the most gracious founder of the aforesaid church.

Without prejudice to the authority of the lady metropolitan Church of Mainz, we permit you to use it three times a year: on the day of the holy Resurrection, on the birthdays of the apostles Peter and Paul, and at the solemnity of Saint Dionysius, since the anniversary of the aforesaid Lord Clement, pope, is then celebrated. By apostolic authority we decree that this day shall be celebrated throughout the entire bishopric.

Since the honor of this garment must be preserved by the modest vigor of your conduct, we urge you to make the ornaments of your character correspond to it, so that, with God as author, you may rightly be distinguished in both respects. Thus let your life be a rule for your sons. If any crookedness has been introduced into them, let it be straightened by it; let them observe in it what they should imitate; let them continually improve by examining themselves in it, so that, after God, whatever good they live may appear to be yours. Therefore let neither prosperity, by which temporal things flatter them, lift your heart up, nor adversity cast it down; whatever it may be, let it be overcome by the virtue of patience.

Let hatred find no place with you, and let no indiscriminate favor find one. Show yourself merciful to the poor insofar as virtue permits. Let your defense assist the oppressed, and let measured firmness oppose their oppressors. Do not accept anyone’s face against justice, and do not despise anyone seeking what is just. Let the guardianship of equity excel in you, so that neither a rich man’s power may persuade you to hear anything contrary to reason, nor a poor man’s humility about himself cause him to despair before you. Thus, by God’s mercy, you may prove yourself such as sacred Scripture commands when it says: “It is necessary that a bishop be blameless” (1 Timothy 3:2).

But you will be able to use all these things beneficially if you possess charity as your teacher. Whoever follows it never strays from the right path. Behold, dearest brother: among many other things, these are the duties of the priesthood; these are the duties of the pallium. If you carefully observe them, you will possess inwardly what you have shown outwardly that you received.

May the Holy Trinity surround your fraternity with the protection of its grace, and direct us in the way of its journey, so that after the bitterness of this life we may together deserve to reach eternal sweetness.

Given on the third day before the Nones of January, in the fourth year of Lord Leo IX, pope, in the sixth indiction.

### LXXVII. Saint Leo IX confirms the privileges of the Church of Hamburg and grants Archbishop Adalbert the use of the pallium and mitre. (Year 1053.)

[Lappenberg, *Hamburg Documents*, I, 74.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved brother Adalbert, venerable archbishop of the Church of Hamburg, and to you and your successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those flourishing in devout religion with benevolent compassion and to grant the wishes of petitioners with eager devotion. For by this, above all, a reward of gain is without doubt earned from the Lord, creator of all, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have been brought by us to a better condition.

Therefore, since you asked us to confirm in its entirety the archbishopric of the Church of Hamburg for you and your successors, just as it was decreed by our predecessors, namely Nicholas, Agapitus, and Benedict, bishops of this Apostolic See, we yield to your petitions. By apostolic authority we grant and confirm it, together with everything generally and specifically belonging to that archbishopric: namely, everything that your predecessors acquired by their labors, or that the faithful among Christians have given or are giving there out of love for the eternal homeland.

We include also those who in our time have been converted to the faith of Christ through the protecting grace of God: namely, the bishops among all the peoples of the Swedes or Danes, the Norwegians, the Icelanders, the Scridefinns, the Greenlanders, and all the northern nations; likewise those in the Slavic regions extending from the river Peene to the river Eider, so that they may remain under the authority of you and your successors, archbishops of the Church of Hamburg. Whatever, with divine grace favoring the strenuous labors of you and your successors, you have been or shall be able to acquire from the error of unbelief—whether people or places—for the Christian religion, we decree that you and your successors shall hold perpetually.

Moreover, we decree and sanction that no archbishop, whether the archbishop of Cologne or anyone else, may claim any authority for himself within your diocese. Indeed, we urge them and all worshipers of the true religion to provide you and your successors with assistance and support in every matter, so that, in return for the grace of this benefit, they may deserve to receive a full reward from the Lord. For we do not doubt that everything shown to benefit the Church and not to oppose divine commands must be carried out and provided by the authority of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

By this decree we further decree, in accordance with the sanction of Pope Nicholas of good memory, Pope Benedict, and Pope Agapitus, that those dioceses—namely Hamburg and Bremen—are and are to be called not two but one.

We strike with the sword of anathema everyone who opposes or contradicts this, or in any way plots against our devout endeavors, and we condemn them, as guilty of perpetual vengeance, to the lot of the devil, so that, in the manner of our predecessors, we may protect the apostolic summit and the cause of God, cherishing them with pious regard, from hostile forces on every side.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we command and urge the bishops of the Churches of Halberstadt, Hildesheim, Paderborn, Minden, and Verden, while preserving in every respect the due subjection owed to their archbishops, to provide you and your successors with as much support as they can in every matter for the pursuit of the salvation of souls. They must nevertheless remain subject to your archbishopric and that of your successors, both those already acquired for the Lord and those yet to be acquired.

And because we have decreed that you are to exercise the legation of the Apostolic See and our authority among the peoples mentioned above, just as the most blessed Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, was formerly established as German legate by the privilege of our most reverend predecessors Gregory II, Gregory III, and Zachary of the holy Roman and Apostolic See, we decree that you and your successors shall be enlarged not only with ancient honors but also, according to the increase of your merits, with new ones—provided that, following the example of the aforesaid martyr Boniface, you are always ready to obey us and our successors in the Apostolic See with an oath and due submission.

Therefore, according to the tenor written above, we grant to you, and through you to your successors forever, permission to ordain bishops within your diocese or province, or indeed throughout the provinces of the peoples mentioned above, wherever, with divine grace preceding and following, you may be able to bring them into Christ’s sheepfold either yourselves or through your messengers.
