We also grant you the use of the pallium, as it is known to have been granted to you by our predecessors: namely, at the Nativity and octave of the Lord; at the Epiphany; at the Purification of holy Mary; on Palm Sunday; at the Lord’s Supper; on the holy day of Easter; at the Lord’s Ascension; on the day of Pentecost; at the festival of Saint John the Baptist; on the birthdays of all the apostles; at the Assumption, Nativity, and Annunciation of holy Mary; at the festivals of the blessed martyrs Laurence and Maurice; at the festival of the blessed archangel Michael; at the feast of All Saints and of blessed Martin, bishop; at the festivals of the saints whose bodies rest within that archbishopric; at the consecration of bishops and churches; and on the day of your ordination.

We also grant you permission to have the cross carried before you. In addition, we grant permission to ride upon the *nactum* on solemn days and in suitable places, a privilege that Pope Clement of good memory granted you through the intervention of our beloved son Emperor Henry.

And because we know your devotion, which desires to evangelize the peoples, from our own generosity we add to your aforesaid honor permission to use the pallium also on Holy Saturday of Easter, at the Invention of the Holy Cross, and at the festival of Stephen the protomartyr; and permission for your head to be adorned with a mitre, the insignia of the Romans.

If anyone attempts to oppose this privilege of our authority or recklessly violate it in any way, let him be anathema. But whoever devoutly observes it shall obtain grace and blessing.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of January, by the hand of Frederick, deacon, librarian and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord Herimann, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the fourth year of Lord Leo IX, pope, in the sixth indiction.

Farewell.

### LXXVIII. Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions and liberty of the Church of Olivolo and of Bishop Dominic. (Year 1053.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, V, 1217.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Church of Olivolo, and through it to Dominic, bishop, and to his successors who shall be canonically promoted, forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to grant places flourishing in devout religion the assistance of suitable defense and to aid them with benevolent compassion, so that a reward may come to us from the Lord when they have been brought or confirmed in a better condition through our efforts.

Therefore, under apostolic and canonical authority, we confirm to the aforesaid Church of Olivolo, and to the aforesaid Bishop Dominic and his legitimate successors forever, everything that it has so far justly acquired and may likewise justly acquire hereafter, so that no emperor, duke, count, or any other person, greater or lesser, may presume to alienate or usurp anything from it.

By the privilege of apostolic authority we also prohibit any patriarch, fellow-provincial bishop, or any other bishop from daring, within that diocese and without the consent of its bishop, to perform confirmations, consecrations of churches, clerics, or nuns, excommunications, absolutions, or any synod other than a provincial one. Nor may anyone presume to judge the clerics of that church, whether ordained by him or by anyone else, or to defend them against that bishop when he wishes to treat them canonically.

If anyone becomes a bold violator of this privilege, let him remain under anathema from God, Saint Peter, and us until he repents. But whoever obediently observes it out of regard for piety, let him share in blessing and eternal life. Amen.

Given on the third day before the Ides of March, by the hand of Frederick, deacon, librarian and chancellor of the Holy Apostolic See, acting in place of Lord Herimann, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the fifth year of Lord Leo IX, pope, in the sixth indiction.

### LXXIX. Saint Leo IX enumerates the churches subject to the monastery of Saint Martin, together with their estates and rights, and confirms them to the canons of Saint Peter. (Year 1053.)

[*Vatican Bullarium*, I, 22.]

In the name of the Lord, amen. This is a copy, or transcript, of a certain apostolic letter of Leo IX, pope, of holy memory, bearing his genuine leaden bull, suspended by a hempen cord, sealed according to the custom of the Roman Curia, neither damaged, erased, nor canceled, nor suspect in any part, but entirely free from every defect and suspicion. Its wording is in every respect as follows.

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to JOHN, archpriest of the venerable church of the blessed apostle Peter, and to the canons of that same church, now appointed and to be appointed in the monastery of Saint Martin, so that in the choir of blessed Peter they may sing the divine offices day and night forever.

[Note: [Col. 0703D] Saint Leo IV speaks of the monastery of Saint Martin, which was formerly the dwelling of those serving in the choir of the Vatican church. This distinguished monastery perished during the construction of the new basilica of Saint Peter. Formerly, as the *Liber Pontificalis* records in its account of Saint Leo IV and in other passages, it adjoined that Vatican basilica; or, as Mollius and Romanus say, it was situated behind Saint Peter, that is, behind the apse at the entrance of the church of Saint [Col. 0705B] Peter. Alpharan’s ground plan should be consulted; its letter *a* clearly shows that this monastery once stood where we now see an altar marked by the name Veronica. Shaken by extreme age, it was almost entirely restored from its foundations by Lord Leo III; and, after approximately fifty years, when it was again falling into disrepair, it was repaired by another Leo, Leo IV.

We pass over the many benefits bestowed upon this very ancient monastery, which Stephen II mentions in his letter to Frebradus and which are recorded by the Roman pontiffs in the *Liber Pontificalis* and by other authors. Yet the account written by the venerable Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, book IV, chapter 18, must not be passed over in silence. He speaks of the venerable John, chief cantor of the church of Saint Peter and abbot of the monastery of blessed Martin. When Biscop, the abbot, also known by the name Benedict, asked Pope Saint Agatho that John teach in his monastery the annual cycle of singing as it was performed at Saint Peter’s in Rome, John, having gone to England at Agatho’s command, fulfilled the wishes of that same Biscop. He also took part in the Synod of Hertfeld and likewise confirmed the decrees of the Catholic faith.

More noteworthy still is the fact that Saint Leo IV, before he was enrolled among the cardinal priests of the Holy Roman Church, lived the monastic life in the monastery under discussion, as his biographer Anastasius the Librarian, Peter Mallius, and others attest.]

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through benevolent compassion, and to grant with cheerful devotion the assent requested by their hearts. For by this means we shall especially earn a reward before God, the creator of all things, if venerable places, suitably ordered, are without doubt brought to a better state.

Accordingly, because you asked us to confirm what has been granted to you and confirmed by privileges by the most holy Pope Leo IV and by certain Roman pontiffs, out of love for almighty God, for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, for Aurea, defender of Rome, and for blessed Martin the confessor, whose church is situated behind the apse, at the entrance [Col. 0705B] of that church—

[Note: By “that church” I understand the Vatican basilica. Its western-facing door, marked beside Alpharan’s plan as no. 13, not only provided access to the old basilica of Saint Peter but also led directly to the monastery of Saint Martin and its church.]

—beside the barred enclosure—

[Note: We can gather the meaning of the word *ferrata* from Peter Mallius, who, in chapter 13 of his *Sacred History*, reports that the body of Saint Sixtus, pope and martyr, was buried beside the barred enclosure near the body of blessed Peter, where there is still an arch of mosaic, and so forth. The same is reported by the *Liber Pontificalis*, where we read that Pope Paschal I built an altar to blessed Sixtus in Saint Peter’s basilica, before the entrance leading to the body of Saint Peter, in the barred place.]

—inclined by your prayers, we confirm by the privilege of this present document what you have justly requested, on the model of our predecessor Leo IV, the emperor Charles, and the other Roman pontiffs, John X and John XIX—

[Note: We diligently sought the diplomas of these pontiffs, but found them nowhere.]

—establishing that whatever possessions and whatever goods justly belong to the same venerable monastery, and whatever in future, with the Lord’s approval, it may be able to acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought it right to specify the following by their proper names: namely, the church of Our Lord and Savior—

[Note: In our own age the extremely ancient walls of this church still stand; they delimit the palace of the Sacred Inquisition facing the gate of the light cavalry, commonly called *dei Cavalleggeri*. The ancients called this church by various names: Saint Savior of the *Terrione*, of the Bones, and of *Magella*. Numerous monuments of considerable antiquity testify that it was built by Charlemagne for the burial of pilgrims. Among these, a celebrated privilege of that same Charles, brought to public light by Franciscus Maria Turrigius from the Vatican basilica’s archives in his book *On the Vatican Crypts*, holds a distinguished place. We shall have to discuss its authenticity when we address the diplomas of emperors and kings.

An inventory of the churches, hospitals, and monasteries subject to the Vatican basilica, compiled around the year 1300 by Cardinal Giovanni Gaetano, contains much concerning the church of Saint Savior, which we are now discussing. “Also,” it says, “the church of Saint Savior of the *Terione*, belonging to the said most holy basilica of the chief Apostle of the city, is subject to it; this church was built by the emperor Charlemagne for the burial of all those from beyond the Alps,” and so forth. The continuation may be seen in the work of the aforementioned Turrigius, pp. 525–526 of the second edition, where a fairly lengthy fragment of the inventory is reproduced.]

—which is called the School of the Franks—

[Note: A college of twelve clerics, called *Scholastici*, gave this sacred building chiefly the name “School of the Franks.” Charlemagne, as stated in his privilege, assigned them to the church of Saint Savior, selecting some from Francia and some from Aquitaine and Gaul, together with three priests, so that they might care for brothers arriving in Rome as pilgrims and, if any happened to die in that city, bury them in the aforesaid church according to Christian rites.]

—together with its possessions, rights of use, and revenues, which the emperor Charles donated to the church of Saint Savior and confirmed by privilege, and which Leo IV granted by privilege; and the payments which they established should annually be sent from the regions beyond the Alps and received through the hands of the administrators, we grant to the same monastery in perpetuity, for the benefit of those who serve God with willing spirit in blessed Peter. This church is situated beside the wall of the city of Nobia, which is called Leonine, above the *Terrione*, and was established for the burial of all people coming to Rome from every part of the world, for whatever reason, just as Leo IV granted it to the said church of Saint Savior.

But if the pilgrims and newcomers are from beyond the Alps—rich or poor, noble or ignoble—and happen to die in this blessed city of Rome or in its vicinity, all of them, from Alba—

[Note: By Alba, of course, is meant Albano, a very ancient city among the towns of ancient Latium; see Cluverius, *Italian Antiquities*, book III, chapter 40, vol. II, p. 900.]

—to Sutrium, shall be buried in the aforesaid *Euteria Salvatoris*, noble and ignoble, rich and poor, newcomers and pilgrims, or wherever you order if necessity compels it. No one shall presume to conceal any of them or his property, or to retain it against your will, except for the English coming from England. If they fall ill and die in the School of Saxia—

[Note: This place stretches not far from Saint Peter’s basilica as far as the Tiber. In very ancient monuments it is called the village of the Saxons and the School of the Saxons. Baronius mentions it under the year 804, and the note in the Roman Martyrology for 10 November states that, after the Saxons had repeatedly rebelled against Charlemagne and had finally been compelled to leave their homeland, many of them were sent to Rome to be instructed in the Christian faith and ecclesiastical discipline and were given the place under discussion, near the Vatican basilica, as a residence; for this reason it was called Saxia.

This opinion of Baronius does not entirely please us if it cannot be reconciled with what follows. For the Saxons mentioned in the present diploma are certainly not inhabitants of Germany and ancient Saxony, but islanders—Anglo-Britons, transmarine peoples, and Anglo-Saxons—called by that name after, as the Venerable Bede reports in his *History of the English*, they occupied a large part of England in the fifth century of the Church and ruled it for several centuries.

Indeed, many writers on English affairs report that King Ine of the West Saxons in Britain, after renouncing his kingdom, went to Rome and, with the approval of Pope Gregory II, founded a house where the leaders and nobles of his people, especially clerics, might be instructed in Roman rites, and built a church for the use of ordinary pilgrims who came to the thresholds of the apostles out of devotion; he assigned a foundation to both, namely a portion of the coin called Saint Peter’s penny. Here, then, according to Peter Saulnier, *Dissertation on the Chapter of the Sacred Order of the Holy Spirit*, chapter 11, arguments 10 and 11, no. 2, is the origin of the School of the Saxons.

In the twelfth century of the Church, however, another tradition prevailed: the School of the Anglo-Saxons was said to have been first established by Offa, king of the Mercians, or Middle English, who had come to Rome during the pontificate of Hadrian I. This is attested by William of Malmesbury, famous in that same twelfth century, in book II, chapter 2 of *On the Deeds of the Kings of England*. Pope Alexander II, in a letter to William, king of England, published by Labbe, vol. XII of the *Councils*, cols. 80 ff., speaks of the annual payment made by the English to the apostolic see; one part of it was conveyed to the Roman pontiff and the other to the church of Saint Mary called the School of the English, for the use of the brothers.]

—let them be buried there, according to the leases which the priests and hosts, called *Scholentes*, of that School of Saxia received from the church of Saint Savior, concerning the church with fireplaces—

[Note: *Camminata* appears to designate a kind of building in which there is a fireplace. This interpretation is favored, apart from Du Cange in his *Glossary*, by Giovanni Maria Crescimbeni in his *History of the Basilica of Saint Mary in Cosmedin*, book IV, chapter 1, although others hold a different opinion. The word also has this meaning in the Etruscan idiom, as may be seen in Boccaccio, whose words are quoted by the aforementioned Crescimbeni.]

—and the School of Saxia, together with all its appurtenances; and also concerning the burial of the English who fall ill and die in that School. But if they fall ill outside it, wherever they die, let them be buried in the church of Saint Savior according to its own right.

The emperor and Pope Leo did not take away what the church of the Savior had possessed; rather, out of favor they gave it much and granted it by privileges. Therefore we grant that payments be made twice a year in the monastery of Saint Martin by the priests of Saint Mary, and that the leases be held by both parties.

The Frisians, too, who fall ill outside the School of the Frisians, which is called the church of Saint Michael—

[Note: There we are told that a church of Saints Michael and Magnus stood near the palace called Nero’s. Soldiers who fell in battle against the Saracens at Rome during the pontificate of Leo IV are said to have been buried there. Hence Leo is said to have founded a church there under the name of Saint Michael.

Not long afterward, when three soldiers from Frisia had found the body of Saint Magnus in Campania, they unsuccessfully attempted to carry it to their homeland. Therefore, warned by divine intervention, they brought it to Rome and deposited it in the aforesaid church of Saint Michael. At the same time they decreed that three hundred marks of silver should be given annually to that church, so that the souls of the faithful resting there might be aided by devout prayers to God and pilgrims from the German people of Frisia, who flocked to the threshold of the prince of the apostles, might be received hospitably.

This history is related by Franciscus Maria Turrigius in a separate work printed on the subject, and by a marble tablet visible in the church of Saint Michael, inscribed in a character certainly not recent. Whatever judgment should ultimately be made concerning its authority cannot be examined here.

If we affirm that Pope Leo IV was the founder of the sacred building, the stonecutter was certainly mistaken when he wrote on the marble tablet that the relics of Saint Magnus had been transferred to the city under the emperor Charlemagne and placed in the crypt over which the church of Saint Michael had already been built. For this reason Baronius, under the year 851 in volume X of his annals and in the note for 8 May in the Roman Martyrology, believes that *Ludovicus*, the son of Lothair and king of Italy, should be read in place of *Carolus*.]

—shall be buried in the church of Saint Savior, according to the terms of the lease which the priests of Saint Michael received from the priests of the Savior.

We also except all Latin pilgrims and newcomers, however many die in the Leonine city or outside it within three miles. We grant that they be buried in the church of Saint Justin, which is called the School of the Lombards—

[Note: Turrigius, in his book *On the Vatican Crypts*, p. 112, states that this was established in the place now called the Campo Santo, beside Saint Peter’s basilica. Severanus, pp. 98 and 394, even confuses it with the church of Saint Mary of the Conception, also formerly in the Campo Santo, belonging to the German nation. Martinellus places it on the Rock of the Holy Spirit and says that it was destroyed when the vineyards of the Caesius and Vercellus families were constructed.

In any event, Leo IV donated to the canons of Saint Peter the church of Saint Justin, situated on Mount Saxorum, which he had built for the burial of all Latin pilgrims. These are the words of the Roman canon, title 11. In that text, however, the aforementioned Martinellus believes that *Saccorum* should be read as *Saxonum*. An old document, mentioned by Turrigius in the cited place, refers to the rector of the church of Saint Justin in the portico of Saint Peter.]

—and, according to the terms of the lease, secured by the same provisions among the Latins as the church of the Savior among the other nations. All other pilgrims and newcomers who have died in the Leonine city and within three miles around it, including those from beyond the Alps, from Alba to Sutrium, as stated above, shall be buried in the aforesaid church.

No one shall conceal a sick person so that he dies intestate, but he shall hasten to notify the priests of that church, or your representative, before the sick person loses his mind. If he dies, let no one conceal him or his property, but let him promptly proceed to disclose them to the priests.

Likewise, no one shall dare maliciously or secretly to remove a sick person from another’s house, or persuade him to leave the house or the city, lest, deceived, he be stripped of his property and abandoned on the road, die miserably, and be devoured by dogs or wolves. Rather, with your consent and judgment, let such persons be moved to places where they may be served more suitably, and let their goods be faithfully administered for the support and preservation of their bodies, lest through negligence they themselves perish and their property be squandered.

But if a sick person is in such good health that he can return to his homeland, he shall be permitted to go, after receiving all his property back, with your provision and oversight. Nothing shall thereafter be retained as a price for permission to leave, even if it had been promised; nothing shall be accepted.

And according to the lease which the church of Saint Savior made with all the people of the Leonine city concerning the lodging of *Oratores*—

[Note: That is, pilgrims visiting the thresholds of the apostles for the sake of prayer and piety. The word *Orator* is used in this sense by Nicholas II in his decree of 1059 and at the Roman council of 1078, as may be seen in Du Cange’s *Glossary*. A single passage from the canon of Peter Mallius, quoted by Severanus in book *On the Seven Churches of the City*, p. 172, sufficiently confirms the point: “Many,” he says, “come here from different parts of the world as *Oratores*, out of reverence for the same apostle, so many indeed that often we can scarcely approach the altar.”]

—and the sale of necessities, just as they granted to the monastery of Saint Martin and the church of the Savior, in the presence of Leo IV, as compensation for the benefit of the lease, what they had received, which we grant and confirm: whoever among the inhabitants of the Leonine city, and outside it within one mile, dies without a son or daughter born of a lawful marriage, all movable and immovable property which he then possesses shall pass in the said monastery for the benefit of the brothers—

[Note: That is, the canons. See Molanus, *Treatise on Canons*.]

—and no one shall dare to leave anything of his goods to anyone except the expenses for his burial and whatever he may owe to another.

Likewise, if any of the servants or innkeepers, of whatever condition, dies without an heir, all his goods shall pass to your jurisdiction. If he has an heir, he shall be buried as a newcomer in the aforesaid cemeteries of Saint Savior and Saint Justin. [Col. 0710A]

The inhabitants are men and women, whoever lives in his own houses or in houses which he holds not for one day or one year, but through long-established use under written leases.

We also grant and confirm one estate called *Palatiolum*—

[Note: Berthold, a priest of Constance, famous in the eleventh century of the Christian era, mentions this. Speaking of Henry IV entering the Leonine city, he says, in Baronius under the year 1083, no. 2: “Near Saint Peter he raised a certain hill, called *Palatiolum*, into a fortress, and stationed many soldiers there to attack the Romans.” This hill or little mountain called *Palatiolum* by Berthold is, if we are not mistaken, the one now occupied by the church of Saints Michael and Magnus and the urban garden of the Barberini family.

Not far from here stood the sacred building of blessed Mary called *in Palazzola* or *in Palatiolo*, which will be discussed below. I believe that the estate called *Palatiolum* took its name from Nero’s palace, which the *Liber Pontificalis*, in its account of Saint Peter, and the Roman canon, title 16, place at the Vatican; an old marble inscription preserved in that same church, as stated above, locates it near the church of Saint Michael.

Although Nero, as Suetonius says, extended his house from the Palatine to the Esquiline, it is nevertheless not implausible that the same emperor had another building in the Vatican, near the Circus and his gardens, which was later called Nero’s palace by the ignorant populace.]

—and two *Burgura*, one called the Frisians’ and the other the Saxons’, with their boundaries and limits and all their appurtenances, together with the church of Saint Zeno—

[Note: According to Jacopo Grimaldi, this was leveled to the ground when the palace of the Sacred Inquisition was built.]

—and the church of Saint Nicholas—

[Note: It was not far from the church of Saints Michael and Magnus, as may reasonably be gathered from the wording of the diploma itself.]

—and the church of Saint Michael—

[Note: This formerly stood on Mount Saint Michael near the vineyards of the Caesius family, as Martinellus and others report from Grimaldi. It was called Saint Mary *in Palazola* or *in Palatiolo*. The diplomas of the Roman pontiffs Innocent III, Gregory IX, Clement VI, and others, to be produced below, mention it very frequently, and the Roman canon, title 11, records that it was donated by Saint Leo IV to the canons.

I believe that the temple under discussion was itself designated by the biographer of that same Saint Leo in these words, preserved by Anastasius: “in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which that most blessed pontiff Leo IV newly built from its foundations above the village of the Saxons, and presented with vestments,” and so forth. On the village of the Saxons, see note H, p. 23.]

—which is called the School of the Frisians, and the church of Saint Mary, virgin and Mother of God, which is called the School of the Saxons—

[Note: Now called the Holy Spirit in Saxia.]

—in this church, however, the appointment of the archpriest shall be made with our counsel; that of the other priests and of the *Scholentes* shall be made by you, entirely free from venality.

And whatever they appear to contain within the boundaries set down below:

Among the adjoining properties, beginning on the first side at the river, from the place called Spellari, and proceeding along the wall of the Leonine city as far as the gate called that of the Saxons—

[Note: One of the gates of the Leonine city. The biographer of Leo IV, accurately describing the dedication of that city by the holy pontiff, calls it the postern of the Saxons. “Third,” he says, “he sang a prayer over another postern, which faces the School of the Saxons; and because of their name it is called the postern of the Saxons.”]

—then along the road toward *Formale* on the right hand, and ascending through *Formale* itself until it directly faces the third tower, which is the property of the aforesaid monastery; then proceeding along the wall to the brow of the hill, and from there along the descending path to the road beside the place belonging to the monastery of Saint Stephen Major—

[Note: We shall speak of this monastery below, in connection with the second bull of Saint Leo IX, issued on the Kalends of April in the fifth year of his pontificate.]

—and from there to the *Fossatum* and the garden of the Savior, then as far as the *Fossatum*—

[Col. 0711A]

—which carries water through the wall of the Leonine city.

On the second side, the land of Saints John and Paul—

[Note: The monastery of Saints John and Paul is discussed below in connection with the second document of Saint Leo IX.]

—and the garden of Saint Mary in the Oratory—

[Note: Although the *Liber Pontificalis*, in its account of Leo III, mentions the sacred building of Saint Mary of the Oratory in the monastery of Saint Michael, there was nevertheless in the Vatican basilica a famous chapel dedicated under the title Saint Mary in the Oratory. Paul I, as the writer of his life reports in Anastasius, caused it to be erected and adorned with mosaic work and various metals. The Roman canon, title 13, contains further information, and Alpharan’s plan, *Ichonographia*, no. 17, carefully indicates its location.]

—and the road which goes toward the *Agulia*—

[Note: That is, the obelisk in the Vatican Circus of Gaius and Nero, transferred by Sixtus V from the place where it lay behind the sanctuary of Saint Peter’s basilica into the Vatican area and erected there.]

On the third side, the road which comes from the *Agulia*, which is called the Tomb of Julius Caesar—

[Note: The populace believed, but wrongly, that the Tomb of Julius Caesar was the bronze globe placed at the summit of the aforementioned obelisk, because it was thought to contain the ashes of that emperor. Antonio Cicarelli, in his life of Sixtus V, testifies that Domenico Fontana found the globe entirely solid after it had been melted down and detected no joint in it; consequently, nothing could have been inserted into it by any means. See the book *On the Marvels of the City*, published by Bernard de Montfaucon in his *Italian Diary*.]

—and goes through the portico—

[Note: There was one portico belonging to the Vatican basilica and another which led from the mausoleum of Hadrian—that is, the Castel Sant’Angelo—to the basilica itself. The latter was called the greater portico. Although the Goths had already approached the mausoleum of Hadrian, it concealed them from the view of the Romans, as Procopius relates in book I, chapter 22 of *The Gothic War*, and protected the Romans from their weapons.

Pope Hadrian I, as his acts preserved by Anastasius report, repaired a portico of extraordinary size, laying more than twelve thousand blocks of tufa in the riverbed for its foundations, raising it from the ground to the top of the roof, and restoring it as far as the steps of blessed Peter.]

—of Saint Peter, as far as the great arch which stands at the head of the portico—

[Note: That the head of the portico stood near the mausoleum of Hadrian is proved both by what Turrigius records in his *Vatican Crypts*, pp. 514–515, and by other evidence which we shall soon present.]

—and thence as far as the river Tiber, except for three houses belonging to the School of Singers: two in the portico and another beside your larger house, which has a garden behind it reaching to the road descending from Saint George—

[Note: Our Maphæus Vegius mentions the church of Saint George, which stood behind Saint Peter, in book II of *On Ancient Matters*, concerning Saint Peter’s basilica, preserved among the Bollandists, vol. VII, June, p. 71. This sacred building stood at the foot of the slope of the Pertusa Gate. Its remains, as Grimaldi says in his manuscript work on the Veronica, p. 33, were visible in his day in the houses near the palace of the Armellini family, in the Street of the Stonecutters of the Fabric of Saint Peter.]

—and as far as the *Fossatum* of the *Terrione*. It lies beside the road which comes from the land of Saints John and Paul and reaches the road leading into the portico.

On the fourth side, the aforesaid river Tiber and the place called Spellari.

We likewise grant and confirm in their entirety the estates called Greater Taliano and another called Lesser Taliano; the estate of Fasciola, the estate of Casanillo, the estate of Casapindola, the estate of Rotula, the estate of Cucumelli, and the estate of Protellaris, all adjoining one another, together with various estates and their names, fields, meadows, pastures, and woods, with houses and vineyards, and with everything generally and wholly belonging to those same estates, situated on the Claudian Road—

[Note: This road proceeds from the Via Cassia through Galeria and Bracciano, as may be seen in no. 98 of the topographical map of the Roman Campagna prepared by Francesco Eschinardus. Ovid and Frontinus, among others, mention the Claudian Road; the latter writes in book I of *On Aqueducts* that the Alsietine water was collected by the Claudian Road.]

—outside the Gate of Saint Peter—

[Note: “Outside the Gate of Saint Peter,” and so forth. William of Malmesbury, called of Somerset and famous in the twelfth century of the Church, enumerating the gates of the city in book IV, chapter 2 of *On the Deeds of the Kings of England*, among the English historical writers, p. 135, Frankfurt edition of 1601, says: “The first,” he writes, “is the Cornelian Gate, now called the Gate of Saint Peter, and the Cornelian Road. Beside it stands the church of blessed Peter, in which his body lies, adorned with gold, silver, and stones.”

The testimony of William just quoted is indeed splendid, as is also another testimony which may be drawn from the diploma of Saint Leo IV cited above; yet it does not sufficiently indicate the location of the Gate of Saint Peter. In the eighth and ninth centuries of the Church, the gate called Saint Peter’s Gate stood at the head of the portico. This is clear from the *Liber Pontificalis*, where we read that Pope Hadrian I established three deaconries, one of them dedicated in honor of the Mother of God, situated outside the Gate of blessed Peter the apostle, at the head of the portico—that is, near the mausoleum of Hadrian, as we stated above in note C.

This is conclusively demonstrated by the booklet *Description of the Regions of the City*, believed to have been written in the eighth century and first published by Mabillon in volume IV of the *Analecta*. There its anonymous author calls the gate under discussion the Gate of Saint Peter at Hadrian’s, namely beside the mausoleum of Hadrian, commonly called Castel Sant’Angelo.]

—approximately four or five miles from the city of Rome, among adjoining properties.

On the first side, beginning at the Greater Quarry, proceeding directly along the paved road which runs between the aforementioned estates and the farmstead called *Pratanella*, belonging to the monastery of Saint Stephen Major, and leading as far as the stream which flows from the bridge of Sofflari.

On the second side, the same stream, which divides the said estates from the farmstead called *Menori*, belonging to the monastery of Saint Stephen Major.

On the third side, the farmstead of *Suberete*, belonging to Saint Lawrence of the Palatine—

[Note: In the diploma above, Saint Leo IV calls it the monastery of Saint Lawrence of the Palatine. Some may perhaps judge it to be identical with the monastery called by Anastasius, in his accounts of Leo III, Gregory IV, and Benedict III, the monastery of Saint Lawrence in the Palatine or *Pallacini*, which, according to our Grimaldi, formerly stood at Saint Catherine’s, commonly called *dei Funari*.

But, unless I am mistaken, the additional designation “of Saint Peter,” used both by Leo IV and by Leo IX, rather clearly suggests that the monastery of Saint Lawrence of the Palatine stood not far from the Vatican basilica of Saint Peter. This conjecture may be confirmed by the diploma of Sergius III to Hildebrand, bishop of Silva Candida, where the supreme pontiff, in order to identify the monastery of Saint Stephen situated near the Vatican basilica and distinguish it from others of the same name, appropriately called it “the monastery of Saint Stephen, which is called Major by Saint Peter,” as may be read in Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, vol. I, col. 107.

A similar manner of speaking leads to a similar inference. Whether any trace of the monastery of Saint Lawrence of the Palatine by Saint Peter still exists in the Vatican, however, I do not dare to determine. Perhaps the place not far distant called *Palatiolum*, discussed above, gave its Palatine designation to the church of Saint Lawrence formerly in the Fish Market, now Saint Lorenzino in the Borgo.]

On the fourth side, the aqueduct called *Sabbatina*—

[Note: Thus the ancients called the channel of the Trajan water, or Bracciano water.]

—which meets the Cornelian Road—

[Note: The Cornelian Road must be located between the Aurelian and Triumphal Roads. We gather this with some clarity from two ancient inscriptions reported by Gruterus on folios 457 and 465. One mentions Gaius Sallius Arisiaenetus, curator of the Aurelian, Cornelian, and Triumphal roads; the other is the monument of Gaius Popillius, curator of the old and new Aurelian, Cornelian, and Triumphal roads.

The Roman maps of Agerius should be consulted, both the one appended by Fabretti to the end of Dissertation 2 of his book *On Aqueducts* and the one published on a much larger scale by Domenico de Rossi. From these it is perfectly clear that the Cornelian Road rises from the fork of the new Aurelian Road, at the tavern called *del Pidocchio*, toward the vineyard of Carpinea, two miles from the city, beside the channel of the Trajan or Sabbatine water, also called the Bracciano water. It then turns right toward the Triumphal Road and runs toward the Caeretan territory. Thus writes the distinguished prelate Francesco Bianchini, volume II of Anastasius Bibliothecarius’s new Roman edition, p. 143.]

—which leads to the basilica of Saints Rufina and Secunda—

[Note: Proceeding from the estate called *Porcoreccina*, one comes, according to the aforementioned Eschinardus, p. 186, upon the ruined church of Saint Rufina on the left of the road, which William of Malmesbury mentions when he says in book IV, chapter 2 of *On the Deeds of the Kings of England*: “On the same road, the Cornelian, there is another church in which the holy virgins Rufina and Secunda rest.”]

—and the farmstead called *Casagurdi*, belonging to the same monastery of Saint Stephen; then leading through the valley as far as the Baths, and ascending directly through another valley which divides the aforesaid estates from the hill of Saint Stephen, and proceeding straight into the valley of Cannara, and reaching the aforesaid paved road, or *Cava*, which is the first boundary.

We also grant in its entirety one estate called *Cletandris* [or *Cleandris*], together with the church of Saint Agatha the martyr—

[Note: Concerning this church, the *Liber Pontificalis* records: “This Pope Symmachus built the basilica of Saint Agatha the martyr on the Aurelian Road, in the estate of Lardarius.” Consult the biographer of Saint Leo IV preserved by Anastasius, and the privilege of Charlemagne in Turrigius, p. 506.]

—situated on Pine Hill.

Furthermore, the Lardarian house—

[Note: See the preceding note. From Giovanni Severano, book *On the Seven Churches of the City*, p. 90, we understand that it stood not far from the estate of Saint Pius V, commonly called *Casaletto*.]

—two miles from the city of Rome, and the estate of Attalianus, with houses, vineyards, and lands, as it appears to have been delimited, with baths, crypts, and tombs situated outside [Col. 0714A] the Gate of blessed Peter the apostle, on the Aurelian Road.

We likewise grant the church of Saint Anatolia—

[Note: A diploma of Innocent III given to the canons of Saint Peter at Rome on the Ides of October 1205 teaches that the church of Saint Anatolia was situated in the old city of Portus. After the time of Saint Leo IV, this name was given to ancient Centumcellae, or the port of Centumcellae. Consult the acts of this pontiff in Anastasius and consider what our Holstenius argues from them in Cluverius’s *Italian Antiquities*, p. 482, line 2.]

—with houses, vineyards, and lands on the island, and crypts, ruined walls, and a fishery beside it, with side-buildings—

[Note: *Manica* sometimes designates a type of building which, according to Du Cange in his *Glossary*, forms something like the side of another building.]

—and twenty paces below Trajan—

[Note: The Port of Trajan, whatever Niger and Ortelius may think, was at Centumcellae, where Civita Vecchia now stands; the notable harbor there was restored by Paul V and Urban VIII upon the remains of Trajan’s port. Thus Holstenius in the note cited above.]

—so that a small boat may freely go to the *mastices* and return, together with everything generally and wholly belonging to it.

We also confirm the church of Saint Benedict—

[Note: In the judgment of Jacopo Grimaldi, according to the manuscript book of instruments, p. 156 verso, this stood where the guardhouse of the light cavalry now is. The author flourished under Paul V. Floriano Martinelli records another church of Saint Benedict in the Vatican and wishes it to be identical with the church of Saint Catherine, which was leveled under Alexander VII.

It is certain from several papal diplomas that an ancient convent of Benedictine nuns once stood beside Saint Peter’s basilica. This will be explained below.]

—situated beside the wall of our Leonine city, with fireplaces, and with the garden behind it, and beyond the fireplaces land with houses, and with all their appurtenances, just as the roads extend: one beside the wall and the other beside the portico, as far as the *Meta*—

[Note: The Roman canon, title 48, describes it as follows: “In the *Naumachia*, beside the church of Saint Mary in Traspadina, formerly near the Castel Sant’Angelo, there is the tomb of Romulus, which is called the *Meta*. It was covered with marvelous stone slabs, from which the steps of Saint Peter were completed.

“A twenty-foot Tiburtine pavement with a sewer and its flower garden surrounded it. The terebinth of Nero also stood around it, as high as the round building itself, with two stories, like a fortress; their lips were covered with stone slabs to carry away rainwater. Beside this building blessed Peter the apostle was crucified.”

The stone building, therefore, not far from the mausoleum of Hadrian, was called the *Meta*. Alexander VI demolished it to open the Alexandrine Road, named after him and now called the New Borgo, as Francesco Albertini, who flourished under Pope Julius II, recorded in his short work *On the Marvels of the New and Ancient City of Rome*, in the chapter on obelisks and *metae*, as did many others. As for the form of the *Meta*, learned men examine it.
in the bronze doors of the Vatican basilica, magnificently constructed by Eugenius IV. It is called the Memorial of Romulus.] We likewise grant the church of Saint Mary of the Staff-Bearers [Col. 0714B] [Note: [Col. 0714D] So called, as Turrigius finds plausible (*De Cryptis Vaticanis*, p. 548), from the travelers’ staffs that came near this sacred building; or, as Martinellus thinks, from the staffs carried by the singers devoted to celebrating the divine praises beside the altar of Saint Peter, as Mallius relates [Col. 0715D]. Our canon Benedictus, no. 67, in discussing the Roman Order and the solemn procession customarily held on Saint Mark’s day, says: “Coming,” he says, “to Saint Lawrence in the greater portico, where the simple litany begins to be sung all the way to the bier, before Saint Mary of the Staff-Bearers at the end of the curtain,” etc.—that is, the area or square of the Vatican.] with heated chambers, houses, and workshops [Note: [Col. 0714D] *Argusteriis*, and so forth. I think that *argasterium* in this place means the same as *ergasterium*, namely, a workshop where some work is carried out. Consult Du Cange, under “Arbasterium” and “Ergasterium.”], [Col. 0715A] and all its appurtenances, bounded as follows: on the first side, a lane from the curtain to the portico; on the second, a road through the portico; on the third, the road that exits through the Arch; on the fourth, a paved road as far as the curtain.

And because Martin is said to rejoice piously, let those who dwell in his monastery rejoice, so that they may always devote themselves more diligently to the service of almighty God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; let no hour delay them. And because Martin is piously said to weep, let those also weep who show themselves unworthy of so great a gift, who seek worldly things rather than the things of God. But those who live piously in Christ we reward.

Therefore, by apostolic censure, we decree that none of our successors in the pontificate, no emperor, no bishop, no other authority, and no human person presume to act in any way against this privilege of our confirmation and grant [Col. 0715B]. And if anyone should wish to despise all the things written above, which have been confirmed for their nourishment and support so that they may serve God without murmuring and which have been granted to them in the aforesaid monastery, and should refuse to preserve them under their authority and administration, let him know that he shall pay twelve pounds of the purest gold to our sacred Lateran palace; moreover, let him be bound by the chain of anathema, be burned with the impious and wicked in everlasting fire, and suffer torment in hell with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever, moved by pious concern, proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours, may he deserve to obtain from our Lord Jesus Christ the grace of blessing and everlasting joys.

[Col. 0715C] Written by the hand of Albinus, scriniarius of the sacred palace, in the fifth year of Lord Leo IX the pope, in the sixth indiction, in the month of March, on the twentieth day.

Issued on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, through the hands of Frederick, deacon of the holy Roman Church, librarian and chancellor, acting in place of Lord Herimannus, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Leo IX, in the sixth indiction.

[Note: [Col. 0715]

The foregoing acts, documents, transcripts, publications, and readings were carried out in every respect before the reverend father in Christ, Lord James, by the grace of God bishop of Capri, sitting in judgment at Rome near the church of Saint Tryphon. Having found this present transcript, written, read, published, copied, and read aloud, to agree with the original public privilege, he interposed his episcopal authority and issued a decree; and he wished and decreed that in all things and through all things, both in court and outside it, full faith should be accorded to it as to the aforesaid original public privilege. He further ordered that this transcript should henceforth enjoy full probative force wherever it might be used in legal proceedings, commanding that his seal be attached to it as evidence and for greater strength and firmness, in the presence of the discreet men, Lords Paul de Colonna and Angelo of Rome, brothers of the Order of Hermits of Saint Augustine; Lord Peter Lelli Mangialicerda, beneficiary of the said basilica; and also Master Peter Berti Calzectarius of the district of Parione, [Col. 0716A] and learned men; likewise in the presence of the discreet men John son of Andrew, John son of Thomas, and Anthony son of Francis, the public notaries undersigned, specially summoned and requested for this publication of the decree and interposition of authority, in the year of the Nativity of the Lord 1362, while the apostolic see was vacant after the death of Lord Pope Innocent VI, in the first indiction, on the eighth day of the month of November.

I, John son of Andrew of Cangniano, notary by the grace of God and by imperial authority, saw and read the aforesaid public privilege before the said Lord Bishop sitting in judgment, as stated above; and together with John son of Thomas, Anthony son of Francis, and Paul son of Sabas, the public notaries undersigned below, I read it aloud. Since I found the original public privilege to agree with this present transcript, with nothing added, omitted, or altered that changed the substance of the matter or varied its meaning, [Col. 0716B] I therefore subscribed my name by order of the aforesaid Lord Bishop and, having been requested, affixed my customary sign.

And I, John son of Thomas I . . . of Rome, notary by the grace of God and by imperial authority, saw and read the aforesaid public privilege before the said Lord Bishop sitting in judgment, as stated above; and together with the aforesaid John son of Andrew of Cangniano, Anthony son of Francis, and Paul son of Sabas, the undersigned public notaries, I read it aloud. Since I found the original public privilege to agree with the aforesaid present transcript, with nothing added, omitted, or altered that changed the substance of the matter or varied its meaning, I therefore subscribed my name by order of the aforesaid Lord Bishop and, having been requested, affixed my customary sign.

And I, Anthony son of Francis Picard, notary by imperial authority, saw and read the aforesaid public privilege before the said Lord Bishop sitting in judgment, [Col. 0716B] as stated above; and together with the aforesaid John son of Andrew and John son of Thomas, and with Paul son of Sabas, the undersigned public notaries, I read it aloud. Since I found the original public privilege to agree with the aforesaid present transcript, with nothing added, omitted, or altered that changed the substance of the matter or varied its meaning, I therefore subscribed my name by order of the aforesaid Lord Bishop and, having been requested, affixed my customary sign.

And I, Paul son of Sabas, a Roman citizen and scriniarius, public notary by the grace of God and by the authority of the sacred prefecture, transcribed, copied, and made a transcript of the aforesaid public privilege in every respect, exactly as I saw and found it contained word for word in the said original privilege, with nothing added, omitted, or altered that changed its substance or varied its meaning, except perhaps a letter or syllable inserted by mistake. I read aloud and faithfully listened to this transcript, before the aforesaid reverend father in Christ, Lord James, the aforementioned bishop, sitting in judgment as stated above, in the presence of the learned men named above and several other witnesses specially summoned and requested for the foregoing matters, and also in the presence of John son of Andrew of Cangniano, John son of Thomas I . . . ., and Anthony son of Francis Picard, the public notaries written above, specially summoned and requested for this publication, decree, and interposition of authority, as stated above, while they saw, read, and listened to the transcript being read together with the aforesaid original privilege. Therefore, by order of the aforesaid Lord Bishop, I reduced the transcript and copy to this public form with my own hand and, having been requested, marked it with my seal.]

**LXXX. Saint Leo IX lists the possessions, rights, and churches of the monastery of Saint Stephen Major and confirms them to the canons of Saint Peter. (Year 1053.)**

*[Vatican Bullarium, 29.]*

[Col. 0717A]

In the name of the Lord, amen. This is a copy or transcript of a certain papal privilege of blessed memory, Lord Pope Leo, its genuine lead bull, with its silk threads, neither damaged, scraped, erased, nor suspect in any part, but free from every defect and suspicion. Its text, word for word and in every respect, is as follows.

**LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to JOHN, archpriest of the venerable church of Blessed Peter the Apostle, and to the canons of that church, presently appointed and to be appointed in the monastery of Saint Stephen Major, [Col. 0717B] in perpetuity.**

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through kindly compassion, and to grant the desires of petitioners with willing devotion. For by this we chiefly earn a reward of gain before the Lord, the Creator of all, if venerable places established for sacred purposes are undoubtedly brought into a better condition. Therefore, because you asked us to confirm what was granted to you and confirmed by privileges by the most holy Pope Paschal I [Note: [Col. 0717B] If this pontiff’s diploma has not entirely disappeared, it lies hidden so thoroughly that, although long sought, no one has yet been able to find it.], by Leo IV, and by certain Roman pontiffs, for love of almighty God, Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and Saint Stephen the protomartyr, we, inclining to your prayers, confirm by this present privilege what you have justly requested, following the example of our predecessors, Paschal, John X, and John IX, Roman pontiffs. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods rightly belong to the same venerable monastery of Saint Stephen Major [Note: [Col. 0717B] It is established that the monastery of Saint Stephen Cata Galla Patricia near the Vatican basilica of Saint Peter existed from the most remote times, as is clearly shown by the biographer of Saint Leo III and by other ancient records. Who first built it is uncertain: some attribute the work to Saint Leo I; others to Galla Placidia, daughter of the elder Theodosius; and others to a most pious woman of the same name, namely Galla, daughter of the consul Symmachus. That it received its name from Galla Patricia, who either built it at her own expense or on her own lands, enriched it with her property, or ultimately had it near her own residence, is a matter touched by no controversy. For the Greek word *kata* signifies “in,” “at,” “near,” “against,” and so forth. The splendid monastery had partly fallen into ruin under Pope Leo III, who, as Anastasius records, “making an effort from its foundations and at the same time laying a firm foundation together with the oratory,” raised it to a better condition, and entrusted its governance to a man endowed with every virtue, who was later elected Roman pontiff under the name Paschal I. From this we confidently conclude that the monastery of Saint Stephen Cata Galla Patricia must be regarded as identical with the monastery of Saint Stephen Major, whose governance Leo IX explicitly states in this diploma to have belonged to the aforementioned Paschal I. [Col. 0717D] Consult Alpharani, *Tabula Ichnographica*, plate I, letter b; Ciampini, *De sacris aedificiis*, chapter 4, pp. 93 ff.; and our Vegius in Janning, p. 80, vol. VII, June, of the Bollandists. From these you will learn more concerning the monastery of Saint Stephen Major, especially its location: namely, at the church which, from the Abyssinians who inhabit the place, is called Saint Stephen in Egypt, commonly *de Mori* (“of the Moors”), and which still exists beyond the Vatican church of Saint Peter, recently restored but displaying the greatest antiquity. The doors and upper threshold of the church itself demonstrate this sufficiently. See Turrigius, *De crypta Vaticana*, p. 328, second edition.], and whatever in the future, with the Lord’s consent, they may acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and inviolate for you. Among these we have judged it appropriate to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of Saint Peregrine [Note: [Col. 0717D] The church of Saint Peregrine stands beyond the Pontifical-Vatican Palace, near the city gate called Angelica. The *Liber Pontificalis* supplies us with three testimonies by which we may briefly illuminate the sacred building and hospice mentioned in this diploma. The first two are drawn from the deeds of Leo III. The first appears in section 408 of the latest Roman edition of Joseph Maria Salvioni: “In the oratory of Saint Peregrine, which is situated in the hospice of the Lord at the Naumachia, he made baskets of silver,” and so forth. The second is as follows: “This illustrious prelate, Leo III, divinely inspired, newly built from the foundations a hospice for Blessed Peter the Apostle in the place called Naumachia [some manuscripts read *Nummentia*], adorned it there with various buildings, and newly built a church in honor of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.” This should, unless I am mistaken, be understood as meaning that the pontiff Leo established such a church and hospice to provide for the convenience and welfare of pilgrims traveling to the threshold of Saint Peter. The third testimony from the *Liber Pontificalis*, which we promised, is found in the Life of Paschal I: “Because of the love he bore for his predecessor, Lord Leo III, Paschal I enriched the hospice of Saint Peregrine situated at Saint Peter the Apostle, in the place called Naumachia, which the same Leo had built.” Romanus, title II, and Vegius, book II, chapter 3, no. 61, report that the church of Saint Peregrine, with its appurtenances, was given by Saint Leo IV to the canons of Saint Peter. Therefore, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, the Dedication of Saint Peregrine is noted in the Roman Church according to the ancient usage of the canons of the Vatican basilica; these ancient ritual booklets were published through the care of the venerable Cardinal Thomasius. Anyone can readily understand that the offerings made to this sacred building were not insignificant from the constitution of Innocent III, issued on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the eighth year of his pontificate, and to be presented below.], together with its hospice and the vacant property adjoining it; and Dalmachia [Note: [Col. 0718D] From the diploma of Benedict IX for the bishops of Silva Candida, published by Ughelli in *Italia Sacra*, volume I, we learn clearly that Dalmachia was a fortress in the territory of Nepi. But the word *Naumachia*, as we have just seen, was changed into *Nummentia*; and into *Almachia*, according to Ferdinand Carlo in Severano, *De septem Urbis ecclesiis*, p. 286, through corruption in the Latin language or the carelessness of copyists. It is therefore possible to conjecture that it likewise degenerated into *Dalmachia*, and consequently that in the constitution of Saint Leo IX under discussion the name Dalmachia is equivalent to Naumachia. Compare the testimonies cited from the *Liber Pontificalis*, in which the church and hospice of Saint Peregrine located at Naumachia are discussed.] as far as Centumcellae; and the stream that descends through the valley of Arnecto and flows into Dalmachia, or Gajano [Note: [Col. 0718D] Publius Victor, or another author, after listing the neighborhoods of the Transtiberine region, immediately adds Gajiunium. The same little book, which Panvinius published in a certainly fuller but interpolated form, has, instead of Gajano, the neighborhood of Gajanara. By the name Gajano, Panciroli understands the obelisk of Gaius, which once gave distinction to his circus in the Vatican and now rises in the area of Saint Peter.], and the land of Sgirante on the road beside the wall [Col. 0719A], together with all its possessions and appurtenances.

We also grant and confirm the estate with Terrione, with its lake and everything belonging to it in its entirety, and the estate of Casagurdi situated on the Cornelian Way [Note: [Col. 0719D] Compare the preceding constitutions of Saint Leo IX, from the *Vatican Bullarium*], which leads to the basilica of Saints Rufina and Secunda [Note: [Col. 0719D] We discussed this in the preceding diploma of Saint Leo IX, in the same collection], and beside the Sabbatine aqueduct [Note: [Col. 0719D] We mentioned this above in the immediately preceding bull of Leo IX, in the same collection].

We also grant the estate called Sueretu [Note: [Col. 0719D] John Gaetan, deacon of Saint Theodore, gave the lands of the vineyards of Suveretus and its entire appurtenance to the Vatican basilica, as recorded in a fragment of a manuscript at Turrigius, *De crypta Vaticana*, p. 161, edition of 1639.] belonging to Saint Lawrence in Palatio, from Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 0719D] Consult the preceding diploma of Leo IX, in the same collection], and the estate called Zaga . . .; the estate of Bialum; and the estate called Brecti, together with everything belonging to each of them in its entirety.

We grant and confirm the estate called Saint Cassianus; the estate called Menore; and the estate called Scuppla Ancilla Dei [Note: [Col. 0719D] Benedict IX, in his privilege for the bishops of Silva Candida, mentions a forest called Magna, with everything belonging to it: on one side the stream of Galera, and on the other the mountain called Stupha Ancilla Dei. Likewise, the bull of John XIX issued to Peter, bishop of Silva Candida, in the same *Bullarium*, reads Huppla Ancilla Dei.]; and the estate called Palombarolum, all adjoining one another as far as the stone called Strata, with its boundaries and appendages, and with everything generally and entirely belonging to them; all of these are the property of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Stephen Major, situated on the Clodian Way [Note: [Col. 0720D] Concerning this, see the preceding diploma of Leo IX], at approximately the fourth or fifth milestone.

We also grant the estate called Casa Mala, just as it is contained within its boundaries. These are its ancient boundaries: on the first side is P . . . a; on the second, the estate of Menore and Palombarolum; on two sides, the forest of your monastery.

Likewise, we confirm the estate called Peritanella, situated on the Cornelian Way at the Sofflari bridge, beside Talianum, Menore, and the land of the title of Saint Angelus.

We also grant and confirm the estate of Camelianum, Olibula Agellum, Pinus Camaranus, Lauretum [Note: [Col. 0720D] We read in the Librarian concerning this pontiff of the Domusculta Lauretum, newly established by Saint Zachary; the diploma mentioned by the often-cited constitution of Benedict IX for the bishops of Silva Candida frequently records Lauresium.], and all those contained within the boundaries written below: on the first side, the territory of Buccege, property of the monastery of Saint Martin; on the second, the estate of Celisanum, property of the monastery of Saint Sabas, and land belonging to the monastery of Saint Stephen Major; on the third, the stream called Galero; on the fourth, the stream called Arrone, situated in the territory of Galeria.

Likewise, in the said monastery we grant the other estates called Galdo, Mansae Palumbae, Valle de Paulo, Ortianum, Spinableta, and Barbulanum, situated beside the estate of Celsanum.

We also grant the estate of Actitianum and the estate of Villarustica from the domain of the valley of Preyta.

[Col. 0720A] Thus we grant and confirm other estates in that territory of Galeria: the estate called . . . . ., within the boundaries written below, together with its churches and appurtenances. On the first side is the stone called Strata, and the estate of Octavianum as far as the aqueduct called Artiones; then to the estate of Toroni. On the second side the monastery of Saint Sabas and the land of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Stephen extend; on the third, the estate called Decimum and Farotianum; on the fourth, the estate of Actilianum and Villarustica from the domain of the valley of Praeyta as far as the stream called Galera.

We likewise grant the estate called Cosarianum and the estate of Agolli, in which are the island of Agolli, Sulianum, Calcitani, and Margaritarum, situated on the other side of Strata.

Likewise, we grant and confirm the estate of Octavianum [Col. 0720B] and the estate of Cesanum with all its territory, except the estate of Trani with its crypts, dwellings, and households; and the estate of Pisinianum with the mountain of Saint Angelus.

We grant the estate of Clodiana with the place of Paparanum, extending as far as the estate itself extends, to Sora with the lake of Baccana and all its appurtenances.

And we confirm the church of Saint Alexander which is at Baccana, and the estates of Visanum and Perpinianum.

And we confirm the estate of Germanellum, situated on the Flaminian Way in the territory of Nepi, at approximately the twenty-second milestone.

Likewise, we grant and confirm the estates called Tracquata, Cornelianum, and Vivariolum, situated at Macoranum beside Capracorum [Note: [Col. 0720D]

Concerning this we shall speak shortly in the next diploma. For the present, accept the inscription reported by our Suaresius in his dissertation *On Holes in Stones*, and so forth:

“THIS TOWER AND PAGINEUMA WERE MADE BY THE MILITIA OF CAPRACORUM IN THE TIME OF LORD LEO IV, POPE. I, AGATHO C . . .”]

and beside the stream of Gralli, and near the court of Macoranum.

We also grant [Col. 0720C] the estate called Balneolas Faticlas, otherwise Monte Lupis, above Saint Alexander at Baccana, and the estate called Fisa with the village of Saint Alexander.

Moreover, we grant and confirm the island of Martana [Note: [Col. 0720D] See Cluverius, *Italia antiqua*, book II, p. 559], together with the churches of Saint Stephen and Saint Valentine, its houses, households, fisheries, and everything belonging to it, for the use and support of the monks residing in the monastery of Saint Stephen. This is just as our predecessor Paschal, who had been rector of that monastery [Note: [Col. 0720D] Anastasius the Librarian says this in his account of Leo III, as we stated above], gave this patrimony of his own for the support of the monks of Saint Stephen Major who serve in the choir of Blessed Peter, and under an anathema forbade [Col. 0721A] anyone to trouble them by ecclesiastical or private authority; rather, they were always to appoint an abbot in that monastery of Saint Stephen of the Island. That same pontiff Paschal called the monastery of the Island Saint Stephen after the monastery of Saint Stephen Major, to which it belongs.

We grant and confirm the church of Saint Mary called “in the Tower” [Note: [Col. 0721C] It is mentioned in the preceding constitution of John XIX, from the *Vatican Bullarium*], which the aforesaid Paschal granted to the said monastery by privilege, together with books and vestments, silver crosses and censers, houses and cells adjoining it, with the *paradise* [Note: [Col. 0721C] By this name our predecessors customarily called the atria of churches, and especially they designated the splendid portico of the old Vatican basilica [Col. 0721D], concerning which Paul the Deacon, book V, chapter 31, says: “Pope Domnio of the Roman Church magnificently paved with white marble stones the place called Paradise before the basilica of Blessed Peter.” The biographer of the same Lord Domnio likewise agrees, saying in Anastasius the Librarian: “He paved with great marbles the upper atrium of Blessed Peter the Apostle, which is called Paradise and which is before the church in a four-sided portico.” See Saint Paulinus of Nola, Letter 13 in the new edition, formerly 37, which mentions the atrium of the Vatican basilica and the doors of that atrium.], and porticoes as far as the silver gate; so that you may close and open the doors that are before the silver gate [Note: [Col. 0721D] This was the principal gate of the Vatican basilica, facing east, which Saint Paulinus calls “royal” in his letter to Pammachius. Honorius I, as the *Liber Pontificalis* reports, “clad the royal doors at the entrance of the church [of Saint Peter], the larger ones called the middle doors, with silver, weighing 975 pounds.” Saint Leo IV did the same after the Saracens stripped them of their silver, as the biographer of that pontiff records in Anastasius in these words: “That distinguished and outstanding prelate, after completing countless works of the highest splendor in the basilica of Blessed Peter, the key-bearer of heaven, raised up the doors which the Saracen race had destroyed and stripped of silver, adorned them with many shining silver panels carved with saving histories, and restored them to a more beautiful form than they had previously possessed,” and so forth. Consult the Roman Canon, title 44.], together with everything contained within them, including the sewer and the greater and lesser steps [Col. 0721B], as far as the street called Cortina.

All these things we grant to the said monastery, together with all its possessions and appurtenances. Let two priests also be appointed there from the community of the aforesaid monastery, who shall render the service of praise to the Lord day and night and minister what is necessary to the people.

Moreover, we grant the church of Saint Justin, built for the burial of all Latins, so that all pilgrims and foreigners, rich and poor, noble and ignoble, whoever dies in this Leonine city or within three miles outside it, shall be buried in the church of Saint Justin [Note: [Col. 0722D] We discussed this in the preceding constitutions of Saint Leo IX. We are pleased to append here another record of this sacred building: namely, in the year of the Lord 1279, the priest Apollinarius, rector of the church of Saint Justin in the Leonine city, acquired for that church and in its name, by right of exchange, a vineyard situated outside the Pertusium Gate in the place called Breccetum. This is established by an old instrument in the secret apostolic Vatican archive, in the book attributed to the chamberlain Cencio, p. 416, reverse, columns 3 and 4. The Roman Ordo of the same celebrated Cencio also contributes evidence: in chapter 18, where it discusses the manner of giving the presbytery for incense, the church of Saint Justin is given six denarii. See Mabillon, vol. XII, *Museum Italicum*.]

Let no one conceal a sick person or hide a dead person, but let him hasten to notify the priest or your procurator; and let no one conceal that person’s goods, but let him promptly return them to you. Let no one persuade a sick person to leave the house or the city.

But we grant that all these things shall remain unshaken for perpetual times for you and your successors, who willingly and courageously serve God and Blessed Peter honorably day and night; you will recognize them by their fruits.

Therefore, by apostolic censure we decree that none of our pontifical successors, no emperor, no bishop, no other authority, and no human person shall presume to act against this privilege of our confirmation and concession [Col. 0722A]. And if anyone should wish to diminish all the matters written above, which have been confirmed for their food and support so that they may serve God without murmuring and which have been granted in the said monastery, and should refuse to preserve them under their authority and administration, let him know that he must pay twelve pounds of the purest gold to our sacred Lateran palace; moreover, let him be bound by the chain of anathema, be burned with the impious and wicked in eternal fire, and be tormented in hell with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever, out of pious regard, proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours, may he deserve to obtain from our Lord Jesus Christ the grace of blessing and everlasting joys.

Written by the hand of Albinus, scriniarius of the sacred palace, [Col. 0722B] in the fifth year of Lord Leo IX the pope, in the sixth indiction, in the month of March, on the twenty-fourth day.

Issued on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, through the hand of Frederick, deacon of the holy Roman Church, librarian and chancellor, acting in place of Lord Herimannus, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne. In the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Leo IX, in the sixth indiction.

The foregoing acts, documents, transcripts, publications, and readings were carried out in every respect before the most reverend father and lord in Christ, Lord Anibald, by divine mercy bishop of Tusculum, cardinal of the holy Roman Church and legate of the apostolic see, sitting in judgment at Rome in the papal palace near Saint Peter. Having found this present transcript, written, read, published, copied, and read aloud, he interposed his authority and that of his office and issued a decree; and he wished and decreed [Col. 0722C] that everywhere, in court and outside it, full faith should be accorded to it as to the original privilege, ordering that his seal be affixed there for greater strength and firmness, in the presence of the venerable men, Lords Stephen Palosius, canon of Saint Mary Major, and Poni of Perugia, and Francis de Baroncellis, scribe of the sacred senate of the City, and Master Peter Bartholomew, John Gentilis, notary of Rome, and several other notaries and learned witnesses specially summoned and requested for the foregoing matters. Also present were myself, Walter, and Paul of Saint Victoria, and Matthew of Spoleto, the notaries undersigned, specially summoned and requested for all the aforesaid matters, in the year of the Lord 1350, in the Jubilee, on the fifth day of the month of June, in the third indiction, in the ninth year of the pontificate of the most holy father and lord, our lord Clement VI, pope by divine providence.

And I, Matthew Salvi, a cleric of Spoleto, public notary by apostolic and imperial authority, saw and read the aforesaid apostolic letters before the aforesaid lord legate sitting in judgment; and together with Paul son of Francis, written above, and Walter D. Frederick of Claramonte, written below, public notaries, I read them aloud. Since I found the said apostolic letters to agree with the said present transcript, with nothing added or omitted that altered the substance of the matter or varied its meaning, I therefore subscribed my name by order of the aforesaid Lord Legate and, having been requested, affixed my customary sign.

And I, Walter, son of Lord Francis of Claramonte, a cleric of the diocese of Fermo, public notary by apostolic authority [Col. 0723B], wrote, transcribed, and copied the aforesaid apostolic letters in every respect, exactly as I saw and found them contained in the letters themselves word for word, with nothing added, omitted, or altered that changed their substance or varied their meaning, except perhaps a letter or syllable inserted by mistake. I read aloud and faithfully listened to this transcript before the aforesaid Lord Legate sitting in judgment as stated above, in the presence of the witnesses named above and very many other notaries, and also of Paul son of Francis and Matthew of Spoleto, the aforesaid public notaries specially summoned and requested for this publication and for the decree and interposition of authority, as stated above, while they read, saw, and listened to the transcript being read together with the aforesaid apostolic letters. By order of the said Lord Legate, and at the request of the venerable men, the lords prior, canons, and chapter of the most holy basilica of the prince of the apostles in the City, who were present there, I therefore reduced this transcript and copy to this public form [Col. 0723C] with my own hand and, having been requested, marked it with my customary sign.

**LXXXI. Saint Leo IX enumerates and confirms the possessions, churches, and rights of those serving the Vatican church of Saint Peter. (Year 1053.)**

*[Vatican Bullarium, p. 33.]*

In the name of the Lord, amen. This is a copy or [Col. 0724A] transcript of a certain papal privilege of blessed memory, Lord Pope Leo IX, its genuine lead bull, with its silk threads, neither damaged, scraped, erased, nor suspect in any part, but free from every defect and suspicion. Its text, word for word and in every respect, is as follows.

**LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to JOHN, archpriest of the church of Blessed Peter, and to the servants of that church, perpetual greeting in the Lord.**
It is fitting for apostolic governance, out of pious concern, to come to the aid of those endowed with religious devotion through benevolent compassion, and to grant the requests of petitioners with eager devotion. For in this way we earn above all the reward of profit from the Lord, Creator of all things, if venerable holy places, ordered toward improvement, are without doubt brought into a better condition.

Therefore, inclined to your petitions [Col. 0724B], by the privilege of this present document we confirm the most sacred churches of Saints John and Paul [Note: [Col. 0723C] This sacred building is called the monastery of Saints John and Paul in the constitutions of John XIX and Benedict IX; that it was built near the Basilica of Saint Peter by Saint Leo the Great is clearly attested in the *Liber Pontificalis*, in the Life of that same Saint Leo. At present no remains of the monastery survive by which it might be determined what its former boundaries or neighboring properties were. Nevertheless, it is believed to have stood in the place now occupied by the left-hand side of the Vatican Basilica, furnished with the altars of Saint Michael the Archangel and Saint Erasmus, as may be seen in the ground plan published by Alpharanus, table I, letter h.], of Saint Martin, of Saint Stephen Major [Note: [Col. 0723D] Consult the diploma of Lord Leo IX cited above.], and of Saint Stephen Minor [Note: [Col. 0723D] Two diplomas have been published: one of Innocent III, on the Ides of October, in the eighth year of his pontificate; the other of Gregory IX, dated 22 June in the second year of his pontificate. There the following is placed under the canons of Saint Peter: “The hospice of the Hungarians at the church of Saint Stephen Minor.” This provides a fairly clear indication of the location of this church or monastery of Saint Stephen Minor. Since the hospice of the Hungarians was built beside the Basilica of Saint Peter to the south, and the church of Saint Stephen Minor still stands there, its façade bears an inscription—not written yesterday or the day before yesterday—of this kind: “Church of the Hospital of Saint Stephen, King of the Hungarians.” We must therefore locate the church of Saint Stephen Minor here. We have shown in the annotation to the highly praised diploma of Innocent III that King Stephen of Hungary contributed greatly to it from his own munificence. Who first built it is uncertain; nevertheless, its antiquity is very remote. Janning, vol. VII, June. Bollandus, in *Commentary on the Ancient Basilica of Saint Peter*, no. 408, thinks that the monastery of Saint Stephen Minor is the same as the monastery of Saint Stephen *cata Barbara Patricia*, concerning which the biographer of Adrian I in Anastasius writes: “This most blessed prelate, moved by divine inspiration, established in the monastery of Saint Stephen *cata Barbara Patricia*, situated near Blessed Peter the Apostle, a community of monks, appointing there a suitable person as abbot. He decreed that they should offer continual praises in the church of Blessed Peter, just as in the other three monasteries, namely those of Saints John and Paul, Saint Martin, and Saint Stephen Major, so that two monks might sing praises to our God at the side of that church; for that monastery had been left in great idleness, neglect, and dishonor, and no divine office was celebrated there with due worship.”], assigned for your use, following the example of our predecessors Sergius II [Note: [Col. 0724D] The constitution of Sergius II on this matter has either entirely perished or is hidden somewhere.] and Leo IV, Roman pontiffs.

We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods justly belong to these venerable places, and whatever in the future, with the Lord’s approval, they may acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.
