Among these we have judged that the following should be stated in their proper names: the estate of Luternum, with the church of Saints Paul and [Col. 0724C] John, together with its lands and farmsteads, situated in the territory of Caere, near the estate of Praecoriola [or Praetoriola], approximately thirty miles from the city of Rome; the church of Saint Andrew, with all its appurtenances, situated in the same estate of Luternum; the estate of Sessanum Major and Sessanum Minor [Note: [Col. 0724D] We conclude from the bull of Adrian IV, issued on the fourth day before the Ides of February in the Christian year 1158, that these estates were situated in the territory of Caere, near the fortress of Luternum, thirty miles from the city of Rome.], with the church of Saint Stephen, together with its lands, vineyards, woods, and all its appurtenances; the fortress of Capracorum [Col. 0725A] [Note: [Col. 0725D] Adrian I, as the Roman Canon relates, title 12, and as Vegius says, book IV, no. 114, in the June volume VII of the Bollandists, generously gave the canons of Saint Peter—or, as Vegius says, the monastery of Saint Stephen—the fortress of Capracorum. Situated in the territory of Veii, it had come to Adrian himself by paternal inheritance. See Anastasius the Librarian on this pontiff, as well as Turrigio, *On the Vatican Crypt*, p. 401 and following, edition of 1639.] with its lands, vineyards, estates, farmsteads, mountains, hills, tracts, plains, mills, and millstream, together with the church of Saint John called “of La Tregia” [Note: [Col. 0725D] A manuscript book that lists the churches subject to the Vatican Basilica, preserved in Turrigio at the place cited immediately above, has the following at folio 402: “Diocese of Nepi: the church of Saint John, directly beside the fortress of Capracorum, or Caprarola, with all its appurtenances, situated in the territory of Veii, at the place called Treja or Trequati; it is to pay annually to the said Vatican Basilica three pounds of white wax, according to the long rental register of the year 1535.” Let the author be trusted that Capracorum and Caprarola are here regarded as one and the same place; others distinguish them.] together with its cells, lands, vineyards, and everything belonging to that same church, situated in the territory of Veii [Note: [Col. 0726D] In this territory stood the most ancient city of Veii, which, as our Holstenius skillfully demonstrates on page 55 of Cluverus’s *Ancient Italy*, must certainly be placed on a steep hill near the island and the village of the Farnese, although others think otherwise. In fact, Anastasius the Librarian, in his account of Adrian I, and Cencius Camerarius, when speaking of Adrian II, place the fortress of Capracorum in the territory of Veii and report that it was fifteen miles distant from Rome.], approximately twenty-seven miles from the city of Rome.

Moreover, the estate called Agellum, situated in the aforementioned territory of Veii. We also grant and confirm to you the estate and valley called Frictilli, with its gardens [the reading *ortuis* is uncertain], mills, and all its appurtenances, situated in the territory of Sutri, beside the city of Sutri itself. Finally, the mill of Cava, situated in the same territory of Sutri.

Furthermore, we grant and confirm to you [Col. 0725B] the church of Saint Sylvester, situated in the aforesaid city of Sutri, with its houses, cells, lands, vineyards, and everything belonging to that same church. Likewise, we confirm to you three houses situated in the forum of Sutri. At the same time, we grant and confirm to you permission to build churches on your estates.

Also, so that in the vicinity [Note: [Col. 0726D] We have supplied the word *vicinia* from another copy in the archive of our basilica, in the transcribed document, letter B, folio 66; the exemplar from which the present constitution of Leo IX was produced is damaged at this point.] . . . there may not exist an abbey or community of religious men . . . which could in any way be greatly disturbed by this. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecrations of churches, and the ordinations of the clergy serving in your churches from the diocesan bishops, provided that they are Catholic and willing to provide these services freely. Otherwise, approach whichever Catholic prelate you prefer, provided that he remains in the favor of the Apostolic See and grants what is requested.

Moreover, by apostolic censure we decree that none of our pontifical successors, no emperor, no other authority, no bishop, and no human person shall presume to act against this charter of our confirmation and grant. Rather, each shall endeavor to preserve all the aforesaid matters, in the administration and ordering of the aforesaid church, for the support of those for whom they were granted. If anyone does so, let him pay six pounds of the purest gold to our sacred Lateran palace and, in addition, be bound by the chain of anathema.

But whoever, moved by pious concern, proves to be the guardian and observer of this confirmation and grant, may he deserve to obtain from our Lord Jesus Christ the grace of blessing and eternal life throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0726A] Given on the Kalends of April, by the hand of Frederick the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord Herman, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the fifth year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction VII.

All the foregoing matters were enacted, written, transcribed, published, and heard in the presence of the most reverend father and lord in Christ, Lord Anibald, by divine mercy bishop of Tusculum, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See, sitting in judgment at Rome in the papal palace near Saint Peter. After seeing, reading, publishing, copying, and hearing the present transcription, he interposed the authority of himself and his office and issued a decree; he wished and decreed that everywhere, in court and outside it, full faith should be given to it just as to the original privilege. He ordered that his seal be attached there [Col. 0726B] for greater strength and firmness, in the presence of the venerable men Lords Stephen Palosius, canon of Saint Mary Major, and Poni of Perugia, chaplain of the said lord legate; Francis de Baroncellis, scribe of the sacred senate of the City; Master Peter Bartholomew, son of John Gentilis, notary of the City; and many other notaries and learned witnesses summoned and specially requested for the foregoing matters; and also in the presence of me, Gualterius, and of Paul of Saint Victoria and Matthew of Spoleto, the notaries written below, specially summoned and requested for all the foregoing matters, in the ninth year of our most holy father and lord, Lord Clement, by divine providence Pope VI.

And I, Matthew Salvi, a cleric of Spoleto, public notary by apostolic and imperial authority, saw and read the aforesaid apostolic letters before the said lord legate, sitting in judgment, and together with Paul Francis, written above, and Gualterius son of Frederick of Claramonte, the public notaries written below, I heard them read [Col. 0726C]. Since I found that the said apostolic letters agreed with the present transcription, with nothing added or omitted that altered the substance of the matter or changed its meaning, therefore, by order of the aforesaid lord legate, I subscribed my name and, having been requested, affixed my customary sign.

And I, Gualterius, cleric of Lord Frederick of Claramonte, of the diocese of Fermo, public notary by apostolic authority, wrote, transcribed, and copied the aforesaid apostolic letters in every respect, exactly as I saw and found them contained in the apostolic letters themselves, word for word, with nothing added, omitted, or changed that altered the substance or changed the meaning, except perhaps a letter or syllable through error. I also heard this transcription read faithfully, before the aforesaid lord legate sitting in judgment as above, and in the presence of the aforesaid witnesses and very many other notaries, as well as Paul Francis and Matthew of Spoleto, the public notaries mentioned above, who had been specially summoned and requested for this publication and for the interposition [Col. 0726D] of the decree and authority mentioned above. Having been summoned and requested, I read and heard it read together with the aforesaid apostolic letters [Col. 0727A], and by order of the said lord legate, and at the request of the venerable lords, the prior of the canons and the chapter of the most sacred Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles in the City, who were present there, I myself reduced this transcription and copy into this public form and, having been requested, signed it with my customary sign.

## LXXXII. Saint Leo IX orders the bishops of Venetia and Istria to render obedience to the patriarch of Grado, whose primacy, granted by the Apostolic See, he had confirmed in synod. (Year 1053.)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 657.]*

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops of Venetia and Istria, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Let your most beloved fraternity in Christ know that in this present sixth indiction our most beloved brother Dominic of Grado, or rather patriarch of New Aquileia, came to our synod held at Rome and tearfully lodged a complaint before it concerning his own Church and that of Forum Julii, a matter which we believe you are not unaware of. After his privileges, granted to him by the Holy Roman and Apostolic See, had finally been reread, the judgment of the entire holy synod determined the following: New Aquileia was to be regarded perpetually as the head and metropolis of all Venetia and Istria, in accordance with the most evident privileges of our predecessors. The bishop of Forum Julii, however, was to be content only with the boundaries of the Lombards [Col. 0727C], according to the privilege of Gregory II and the revision of Gregory III.

We granted him this much, moreover, as a great concession beyond what the canons allow, because, although we had already summoned him four times, he neither came nor offered an excuse, whereas the patriarch of Grado—that is, of New Aquileia—had attended our synod five times, even without being summoned.

Therefore, admonishing you, we command and order you, on behalf of God, Saint Peter, and ourselves, to be obedient in all things to the aforesaid patriarch of Grado and his successors, according to the canonical laws, as you ought to be to your primate and patriarch, and as our predecessors have perpetually confirmed with respect to his predecessors. If anything belonging by right to him is contained in your cities or parishes and ought properly to be subject to his rule, let none of you presume to oppose him.

But if any of you appears to have a just complaint against him, let him either present his case before you, his brothers and fellow provincials, and settle it peacefully with him if he can; or let both parties come into our presence for examination, while in the meantime his patriarchal reverence and property remain secure in every respect. If you act otherwise, canonical sentence will keep watch over you.

## LXXXIII. Letter of Saint Leo IX to Thomas, bishop of Africa. He shows that the archbishop of Carthage is the primate of all Africa; that the bishop of Gummi cannot, without his consent, consecrate bishops or summon a provincial council; and that only the Roman pontiff can depose bishops and convoke general councils. (Year 1053.)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 657.]*

[Col. 0728A]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Thomas, his most beloved brother and fellow bishop, greeting.

When we recall from the authority of the venerable canons that two hundred and five bishops attended the Council of Carthage, and now hear from your fraternity that scarcely five bishops remain throughout Africa—indeed, a third part of this corruptible world—we grieve with all the inward feelings of our heart over so great a diminution among you. But when we learn that the very remnants of Christianity are being torn apart and scattered by internal and mutual dissension, and that they are puffed up against one another by zeal and rivalry for primacy, nothing first comes to mind for us to say except that of the holy prophet Amos: “Spare, Lord, spare, I beseech you: who will raise up Jacob, for he is small?” (Amos VII).

Although we grieve greatly over such a grave decline in religion, we nevertheless rejoice greatly because you seek and await the judgment of the Holy Roman Church, your mother, concerning your questions. You think it best that, like streams bursting forth from one source and dispersing in different directions along their courses, you should return to the first spring of that source, so that from there you may recover the path of direction from which you received the beginning of the whole Christian religion.

Know, therefore, beyond doubt, that after the Roman pontiff the first archbishop and greatest metropolitan of all Africa is the bishop of Carthage. Whoever he may be, the bishop of Gummi has no authority to consecrate or depose bishops, or to summon a provincial council, without the consent of the archbishop of Carthage, whatever his dignity or power may be, except in matters belonging to his own parish. In other matters he shall act, like the other African bishops, with the counsel of the archbishop of Carthage.

For this reason our most beloved brothers and fellow bishops Peter and John rightly judge concerning the dignity of the Church of Carthage, and do not agree with the error of the Church of Gummi.

But I do not want this to be hidden from you: a universal council ought not to be held, nor bishops condemned or deposed, without the judgment of the Roman pontiff. For although you may examine certain bishops, you may not, without consulting the Roman pontiff, deliver a definitive sentence, as has been said. If you seek this provision in the holy canons, you can find it there.

For although the Lord said generally to all the apostles, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XVIII), nevertheless it was not without cause that he said specially and by name to Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XVI). And in another place: “Strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII). This is because the greater and more difficult cases of all the Churches are to be decided by the successors of Blessed Peter through the holy and principal See of Blessed Peter.

Since we have also decided to respond to the questions of our brothers and fellow bishops Peter and John, we wish that the holy and undivided Trinity may always preserve your holy fraternity, constantly watchful for the interests of the holy Catholic Church and devotedly praying for us, dearest brother.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fifth year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction VII.

## LXXXIV. Saint Leo IX praises the bishops Peter and John because, at his command, they held a council concerning ecclesiastical affairs and defended the rights of the archbishop of Carthage against the bishop of Gummi. (Year 1053.)

*[Mansi, same volume, 658.]*

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brothers in Christ, the bishops PETER and JOHN, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We grieve exceedingly that the glory of the African Churches has been so trampled by the nations that now scarcely five bishops can be found where formerly two hundred and five were accustomed to be counted in plenary councils; and that a few little sheep, destined for daily slaughter, remain there where once an innumerable flock of the Lord rejoiced in profound peace under numerous rams.

But attributing these things to our sins and praising the justice of the Creator, let us fear and earnestly seek his mercy, so that he may at last deign to look upon his servants.

As for what you wrote to us—that you had implored the Lord while giving thanks for the condition of the Holy Roman Church and for our safety—know that we give thanks to your fraternity and always pray for your consolation. Indeed, brothers, this is pleasing to our Lord Jesus Christ: that the head should care for and watch over all the members, while the members continually seek and desire the salvation of their head.

You acted well in holding, at our command, a council concerning ecclesiastical affairs; you ought also to do this every year, at least once. Moreover, you rightly defended the dignity of the Church of Carthage against the bishop of Gummi, because without doubt, after the Roman pontiff, the first archbishop and greatest metropolitan of all Africa is the bishop of Carthage. Nor can he lose, on account of any bishop in all Africa, the privilege once received from the Holy Roman and Apostolic See; rather, he shall retain it until the end of the age and as long as the name of our Lord Jesus Christ is invoked there, whether Carthage lies deserted or someday rises again in glory.

This is plainly demonstrated by the council of the blessed martyr Cyprian, by the synods of Aurelius, by all the African councils, and—what is greater still—by the decrees of our venerable predecessors, the Roman bishops. Whoever he may be, the bishop of Gummi has no authority to consecrate or depose bishops, or to summon a provincial council, without the consent of the archbishop of Carthage, whatever his dignity or power may be.

The bishop of Gummi shall attend only to matters belonging to his own parish; in other matters he shall act, like the other African bishops, with the counsel of the archbishop of Carthage, who alone in Africa customarily possesses the pallium from the Apostolic See.

Therefore he also retains the principal and ancient right of consecrating bishops, as may be understood from the words of Aurelius at the Council of Carthage (Council of Carthage III), chapter thirty-nine, where he says: “In the Church to which your holiness has deigned to come, we frequently, and almost every Sunday, have bishops to be ordained,” and so forth.

But do not let this be hidden from you: a universal council ought not to be held, nor bishops condemned or deposed, without the knowledge [or judgment] of the Roman pontiff. For although you may examine certain bishops, you may not, without consulting the Roman pontiff, deliver a definitive sentence, as has been said.

If you seek this provision in the holy canons, you can find it there: namely, that the greater and more difficult cases of all the Churches are to be decided by the successors of Blessed Peter through the holy and principal See of Blessed Peter, since it is said to him by divine authority: “Strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII), and “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew XVI), and so forth.

Now, since you ask our judgment concerning archbishops and metropolitans, the statements of our venerable predecessors plainly demonstrate it, namely those of Clement, Anacletus, Anicetus, and others, where it is read:

“The order of priests is divided into two parts, and no more than two orders have been conferred upon us, namely those of bishops and presbyters; nor did the apostles teach otherwise. The order of bishops, however, is one, although some are placed above others, either because they hold the chief and more renowned cities according to secular power or laws, or because the holy Fathers have granted them some privilege of dignity on account of the reverence due to holiness.

“For just as every worldly power is distinguished by these ranks of dignity from one another—that is, first Augustus or the emperor, then Caesars, then kings, dukes and counts, and tribunes—so ecclesiastical dignity is found ordered by the holy Fathers. Blessed Clement says (Epistle 1, vol. I, p. 91):

“‘In those cities in which, among the pagans, their chief flamens and chief teachers of the law once held office, primates or patriarchs were appointed, who were to judge rightly the cases and greater affairs of the others, and who were to preside not over one province but over several. Then, where the pagans had archflamens, archbishops were established among Christians to preside over individual provinces. Where there was a metropolis—which means a mother-city—there were metropolitans, since they were to preside over three or four cities within a province as the greater and mother city over the others. These are sometimes called only metropolitans, but sometimes archbishops, if there are no others greater in that province. Where there were only smaller cities with flamens or counts, bishops were appointed. Finally, the tribunes of the plebs may reasonably be understood as presbyters or the other clergy of lower rank.’

“By divine and human privilege, the Roman pontiff has been placed above all these.”

[Col. 0731A] But the primates of Africa must be understood differently, because in each of its provinces primates were anciently appointed not according to the power of any city but according to the time of their ordination. Nevertheless, one stood above all of them, namely the archbishop of Carthage, who may also appropriately be called metropolitan because Carthage is the metropolis of all Africa, as we mentioned above.

Thus it is read in the Council of Carthage, chapter twenty-six: “The bishop of the first see shall not be called prince of priests, or high priest, or by anything of this kind, but only bishop of the first see.”

May the holy and undivided Trinity always preserve your holy fraternity, continually watchful for the interests of the holy Church of God and devotedly praying for us, dearest brothers.

## LXXXV. Saint Leo IX grants a ship for the use of the monastery of Cassino, together with its captain and crew, free and exempt from every toll and payment. (Year 1053.)

*[Margarini, Cassino Bullary II, 85.]*

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the church or monastery built on Monte Cassino of the most illustrious confessor of Christ, Benedict, and through it to Richerius the abbot and all his successors canonically entering there, in perpetuity.

Moved by consideration of divine mercy and prompted by the prayers of our beloved Richerius for the growth of that church, we have judged it fitting, out of love for the most holy Benedict, already mentioned and often to be mentioned, to bestow and grant forever to the same monastery, for the use of the brothers living there and serving God, something from the possessions of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

Thus the most noble flock and fruitful offspring of so great a father—Benedict, to be blessed by every mouth—may enter the harbor of salvation unto eternal life, raised up by the assistance and munificence of Peter, the heavenly supreme key-bearer, and filled with them.

Considering that they have withdrawn from secular business and, at Christ’s command and following the example of their pious father, have abandoned whatever they possessed in any manner, we have granted, with grateful and benevolent intention, that their ship, loaded with certain merchandise and assigned, together with its cargo, for the use of the abbot and all the brothers, shall be free [Col. 0731D], together with its captain and sailors, from every obligation of payment for as long as the aforesaid place remains established in the same religious condition in which it now exists.

One ship of that monastery, carrying what is necessary for the use of the brothers, as we have said, shall be free, together with its captain and sailors, from every condition of payment. It shall pay no toll on anything it brings, and no one shall presume to exact anything from it.

But if anyone, of whatever condition, power, or dignity, should rashly oppose or violate this donation and grant of ours, let him be struck perpetually with anathema and deprived of eternal blessing until he comes to his senses.

But whoever, as a lover of his own salvation, proves to be the guardian of the apostolic gift and offering or decree, may, through the intercession of the most holy Benedict, having attained the harbor of salvation, obtain from Almighty God mercy and blessing forever.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, by the hand of Frederick the deacon, librarian of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, acting in place of Lord Herman, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the fifth year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction VI.

## LXXXVI. Saint Leo IX grants the pallium to Uldaric, archbishop of Benevento, and confirms his privileges. (Year 1053.)

*[Ughelli, Sacred Italy VIII, 78.]*

. . . Considering the Beneventan Church, we restore to its jurisdiction and ownership and permanently subject and hand over to it the following: namely, the church of Saint Michael situated on Mount Gargano, and the very fortress where the aforesaid sacred and venerable church is situated; the church of Siponto with all the rights legally belonging to it; Luceria, Asculum, Bovinum, Larinum, Trivento, Saint Agatha, Avellino, Quintodecimo, Ariano, Vulturara, Telesia, Alife, Sessula, Lesina, and Termoli; and likewise the two abbeys, Saint Peter of Duddi and Saint John situated beside the Golden Gate, with their respective properties, rights, parishes, or dioceses. We except nothing, but have granted and irrevocably confirmed everything, in accordance with their lawful rights, to this frequently mentioned Beneventan church, dedicated in honor of Mary, the holy Mother of God, where the most precious body of the most blessed apostle Bartholomew rests, without prejudice to the authority of the Holy Roman and Apostolic See.

We also grant to your fraternity the use of the pallium for celebrating the solemn Masses, namely on the feasts of the Nativity of the Lord and his Epiphany, and also on the Lord’s Supper, on the Sunday of the holy Resurrection, on the Ascension of Christ into heaven, and on the Sunday of Holy Pentecost; on the birthdays of the apostles and of the most blessed Forerunner of Christ, John the Baptist; on the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary; on the day of the holy apostle Bartholomew; on the Nativity of the most holy Mother of God, Mary; at the consecrations of bishops; on the day of the consecration of the church; and on your birthday, just as our predecessors instituted and granted it to your predecessors.

In the secretarium, however, your fraternity shall be clothed with the pallium . . . . . . . . . . .

We also grant you this: throughout each place subject to the jurisdiction of the archbishopric of Benevento, wherever episcopal sees are held according to ancient lawful institution, you may canonically establish and consecrate bishops. Whatever has been instituted otherwise than is proper and than the sacred canons command, you shall eradicate and correct; namely, whatever, through the exigencies of sin, has been established against the rights of the canons and the institutions of the holy Fathers. For certain men, utterly corrupt in mind, do not fear to usurp what belongs properly to bishops, subjecting clergy enrolled in the sacred order to their own jurisdiction and withdrawing them from the judgment of bishops [Col. 0733A]. This we utterly detest and forbid under perpetual anathema.

But whatever belongs to ecclesiastical and episcopal office within the entire archbishopric of Benevento shall, as determined above, be governed and ordered by your sound judgment.

Therefore, everything that justly and lawfully belongs or may in the future belong to the aforesaid archbishop—whether monasteries, fortresses, cities, or estates, with their churches, villages, vineyards, woods, and everything justly belonging to them—we hand over, confer, and establish forever for you and for your fraternity and the church entrusted to you.

Therefore, by apostolic censure we decree, and under the solemn appeal of divine judgment and the prohibition of the strongest anathema we declare, that none of our successors, nor any person of whatever dignity or power, shall ever dare by any rash attempt to inflict force upon the aforesaid Beneventan church, or . . . . . . diminish, lessen, withdraw, invade, or alienate in any way or by any device anything belonging to the aforesaid archbishopric. Rather, just as the matters above have been specified, so shall they remain permanently undisturbed.

Thus the holy Beneventan church, dedicated in honor of the holy and ever-virgin Mother of God, Mary, raised by our predecessors to the honor of an archbishopric, and enriched with the most precious bodies of the saints—namely, of the apostle Bartholomew, the martyr Januarius, and Barbatus, confessor of that see—shall remain forever inviolate and endowed with apostolic privileges as the seat of most glorious prelates and of the others [Col. 0733C].

But if anyone, which we do not wish, should presume by criminal audacity to violate or diminish these provisions, which we have established and suitably decreed for the praise of God and for the stability and firmness of the Beneventan church, or should in any way establish something else to the detriment of the aforesaid archbishopric, may what he has attempted be annulled, and may he perish eternally, struck by divine anathema, unless perhaps he comes to his senses.

But may the guardian of this apostolic privilege of ours, filled with apostolic blessing, rejoice forever with all the saints within the walls of paradise.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of July, by the hand of Frederick the deacon, librarian of the Holy Roman Church and vice-chancellor, acting as vicegerent for Lord Herman, archchancellor [Col. 0733D] and archbishop of Cologne, in the fifth year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction VI.

## LXXXVII. Bull of Saint Leo IX by which he confirms to the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Bari the church of Saint Nicholas, granted to it by Nicholas, bishop of Bari. (Year 1053.)

*[Muratori, Italian Antiquities VI, 213.]*

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the church and monastery of the Holy and Undivided Trinity built within the city of Bari, and through it to Mark, our beloved son and abbot, and to all his successors canonically entering there, in perpetuity.

[Col. 0734A] We gladly assent to all just petitions, since requests that are just and pious are always known to be pleasing and acceptable to God. Therefore, seeing the right of the church entrusted to you concerning the church of Saint Nicholas—which Nicholas, the aforementioned bishop of the said city, offered to the aforesaid church of the Holy Trinity as a voluntary gift and confirmed in perpetuity—we have been entirely pleased, and our decretal ordinance has decreed that it shall remain perpetually valid by apostolic authority.

And just as the aforesaid church of Saint Nicholas was firmly and irrevocably bound by the aforementioned Nicholas, the bishop named above, to the church of the Holy Trinity, together with all its benefice, garden, and orchard, and with its access and exit, under penalty of anathema—so that neither he himself nor anyone of whatever condition, dignity, [Col. 0734B] or power might in any way or by any device withdraw or alienate the aforesaid church of Saint Nicholas, together with everything granted along with it, from the aforesaid church or monastery of Saint Nicholas—so we entirely confirm, decree, and strengthen it.

Therefore, whoever attempts to oppose the ordinance of this privilege of ours shall remain under the penalty of anathema until he repents. But whoever preserves it, filled with apostolic blessing, shall obtain everlasting salvation from the holy and undivided Trinity.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of September, by the hand of Frederick, deacon, librarian and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of Lord Hermann, archchancellor and archbishop of Cologne, in the fifth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Leo IX, in the sixth indiction [the printed text reads *secta*].

(Lead seal.)

LXXXVIII. Saint Leo IX confirms Dominicus, formerly a monk whom he himself made bishop of Valva. (Year 1053.)

[Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, I, 1361.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Dominicus, bishop of the Church of Valva, and to all your successors canonically promoted in that same Church, forever.

Although we are commanded, while we have time, to do good by the Lord—especially to those who belong to the household of faith—we nevertheless have concern for all the Churches of Christ, in keeping with the stewardship entrusted to us. Thus we must watch over those who are far away, lest we be absent in any way from those who are near.

Accordingly, dearest brother and fellow bishop Dominicus, whom we have promoted from the discipline of the monastery to the care of the episcopate, we rejoice at your petition, and we recognize that in the Holy Roman Church you have faithfully and continually served our predecessors and us. Yet we extend the protection of an apostolic privilege over the Church of Valva, which by the Lord’s authority you govern, although, through the sins of its people, it has been excessively desolated and destroyed by the wickedness of secular men and of sinners who seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ—protecting it against the assaults and schemes of sacrilegious persons.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, through this privilege of our constitution, we grant [Col. 0735A] and confirm to you and, as stated, to your successors in perpetuity the episcopate of Valva in all its integrity and with all its dependencies, as it is defined by its ancient and rightful boundaries: namely, from the ditch of Luparellus to the little gates or pillars, and from the fork of Gorza to Stasilus between the mountains; from there, from the castle of Furca to the Serra of Cannatina, and from the Serra of Sigella to the Serra of Mount Christ; thence from Mount Ceneracici to the cross; thence from the valley of Araldus to the rocky height of Celici; and from the land of Cantu to the fork of Mizula; then from the oak of Cerurcus, and the field of Olomeus, and from Canite to the little pillar of Campo Mezzo, where the River Sangro emerges; and it proceeds to the ditch of Luparellus, already mentioned.

We also principally confirm to you, for the episcopal see, the Church of Saint Pelinus with all its rightful dependencies, and likewise the Church of Saint Pamphilus with the other churches and chapels known to be situated within the aforesaid boundaries, together with all their dependencies. Thus you shall arrange and administer the tithes and offerings of both the living and the dead, according to the authority of the canons, as shall seem appropriate to you and as befits a bishop.

Do not permit the causes and affairs of clerics to pass to secular men and their courts; rather, you and your successors shall hear and canonically determine them yourselves. And because it is known that, through the negligence and wickedness of evil men, the written records or privileges of our predecessors—and any other instruments by which the possessions and goods of that episcopate were confirmed and retained—have been lost or taken away, we decree through this privilege of our authority that this shall harm the aforesaid Church in no way. Instead, in accordance with what the Emperor Otto also commanded by a decree to Grimuald, bishop of that Church, wherever the necessity and justice of that episcopate require it, an inquiry shall be conducted under oath, by truthful men, both rich and of modest means, whom the same bishop shall name, whatever person’s power that justice may be in; and what belongs to the said Church shall be restored to it.

Moreover, under the threat of a strict anathema, we decree that whoever knows of possessions or goods that rightfully belong to the aforesaid episcopate, yet are held after being alienated by wicked men, must disclose them to the bishop or his representatives, lest by consenting to and concealing the wrongs of others he become sacrilegious before the Lord. All documents made to the detriment of the Church, or taken from that Church and retained by invaders, shall by apostolic authority be null and void.

Therefore, by the authority of the Holy Roman and Apostolic See, whose jurisdiction that episcopate is specifically known to be, and under threat of a strict anathema, we forbid any person, great or small, of whatever condition or dignity, to presume to harass, disturb, or dispossess him—without investigation—from any movable or immovable property that he now possesses or may hereafter justly acquire and possess. [Col. 0736A]

But if anyone, an enemy of God and of his own soul, should not fear to become, in any way or by any device, a rash transgressor of this apostolic privilege, and should presume to claim for himself anything that we confirm or invalidate here, contrary to the judgment of our authority promulgated here, let him know that he is irrevocably consigned by a perpetual sentence of anathema to hell with the devil and his angels, unless, while he lives, he should duly make satisfaction to the Lord and His Church.

But whoever, out of regard for divine mercy and reverence for holy obedience, proves a faithful guardian of this privilege shall merit blessing here and, in the future, the reward of everlasting blessedness among the assemblies of God’s elect. Amen.

Given at Benevento on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of Frederick, deacon and librarian, and chancellor of the Holy Apostolic See, acting in place of Lord Hermann, archbishop of Cologne and archchancellor, in the fifth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Leo IX, in the sixth indiction.

LXXXIX. Letter of Saint Leo IX to Henry, king of the Franks. Fragment. (Year 1054.)

[Duchesne, *History of the Frankish Writers*, IV, 145, from Ivo’s *Decree*, part IX, chapter 8.]

Your father Robert, with the praise and counsel of the bishops of your kingdom, took Berta, the mother of Count Odo, as his wife. Because she was related to him by blood, he and she were excommunicated by our predecessor together with the bishops who had attended the hearing. Later they came to the Apostolic See with an act of satisfaction, received penance, and returned to their own land.

XC. Saint Leo IX grants to the Vatican church of Saint Peter a tenth part of the offerings. (Year 1054.)

[*Vatican Bullary*, I, 35.]

In the name of the Lord, amen. This is a copy, or transcript, of a certain papal privilege of blessed memory, Lord Pope Leo IX, bearing his genuine lead seal suspended on silk cords; it has not been damaged, scraped, erased, or cancelled, nor is any part of it suspect, but it is free from every defect and suspicion. Its text, word for word and in every respect, is as follows.

Blessed Peter the Apostle, I, Leo, bishop, your servant and the servant of all God’s servants, offer you a small portion of your gifts. I have judged it fitting, worthy, and just, considering the concerns with which I am surrounded, to take it away and offer it to you as though it were mine, although it is yours. For whatever there is that belongs to our rights, [Note: That the gifts which great princes and the rest of the faithful multitude offered in the Vatican, in the church of Saint Peter, chiefly belonged to the Roman prelates and were counted among the rights of the Apostolic See is clearly demonstrated not only by this diploma of Leo IX, but also by the bulls of Eugenius III, Innocent III, and other supreme pontiffs, which will be presented below. The reason for this custom, unless we are mistaken, is that the glorious confession of blessed Peter was understood by our ancestors to represent the Roman Church. We have therefore thought it necessary to give the reader this advance notice, lest he wonder why papal diplomas were needed for the Vatican basilica and those serving it to receive lawfully some portion of the offerings made in that very church.]

although it is little in comparison with what our predecessors possessed, nevertheless, however small it may be, I have judged it worthy to share with you. For behold, from the offerings of the faithful that are presented to you upon your altar, beneath which your sacred and venerable body rests, and also at the confession of that altar, we humbly and with complete prostration of heart offer, give, grant, strengthen, and confirm to you a tenth part—although the whole is yours—for the construction and repair of your sacred church: its buildings, walls, paintings, beams, roofs, tiles, and also the continual maintenance of its lamps, oil and wax, glass lamps, and *cicindelae* [Note: That is, glass lamps. This is clearly established by the *Life of Saint Caesarius of Arles*, where we read: “One of the chamberlains, while he was tending a *cicindela*, let it fall from his hands onto a stone; it was neither overturned nor broken nor extinguished.” Consult Du Cange’s *Glossary*, and the *Index of Exotic Words* appended to the *Rule Codex* of Luke Holstenius.]

and incense, together with all the other utensils that pertain to the use, need, and adornment of the entire church.

We wish this tenth part always to be the tenth day, so that the offering owed to you may be separated from the other offerings and suffer no error through confusion. In addition, if any vessels, ornaments, or ecclesiastical vestments should be offered upon your sacred and venerable altar for the worship of God, necessary for the divine offices and mysteries, we assign all of them to your church, where they shall remain perpetually for use, serving God and you there now and hereafter.

We also believe that the following offering should be added: whatever the faithful offer at your altar and at that confession during the vigil of your Nativity and on the day itself of your Nativity, blessed Peter the Apostle, shall be wholly your special possession, for lamps and for the other various needs pertaining to the celebration of your solemnities.

Nor have we thought it should be omitted that, whenever tributes from whatever kingdoms and lands are offered to your altar, or placed at the feet of the Apostolic See, or paid in any way to your Apostolic See, over which, by God’s authority, we preside, a tenth part of them shall always be owed to you, blessed Peter the Apostle, for the restoration of your church and for the other matters mentioned above. [Note: No one who has even briefly examined the ancient records of the Roman Church will deny that the offerings formerly made in the Vatican basilica were numerous and especially wealthy. To pursue the matter here would be superfluous, for examples occur everywhere in Anastasius the librarian; and the learned men Justus Fontanini and Petrus Morettus have noted many matters relevant to this institution—the former in his brief work *On the Votive Silver Dish*, the latter in his *Work on the Portions of Priests*, part I, section 4.]

But so that all these provisions may be observed inviolate both by our successors who will sit upon your see, blessed Peter the Apostle, until the end of the world, and by all people, great and small, rich and poor, of middling rank, of either sex and every age, we establish them by the apostolic censure which, though unworthy, we exercise in your place, under solemn appeal to divine judgment and the imposition of a terrible anathema.

Thus, whoever attempts to act against this gift of our humility, faithfully and purely bestowed upon you from what is yours, blessed Peter the Apostle, and does not preserve it undefiled, shall not only be separated from the communion of the faithful in this temporal life, but shall also be condemned in that eternal life to everlasting punishments and the torments of hell.

Conversely, whoever proves a devoted guardian and careful observer of our offering shall be increased by divine blessings; here, through you, blessed Peter the Apostle, may he be released from the bonds of sins, and there, through you, may he be admitted within the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore, so that this privilege of our devotion might be believed more truly and held more securely, we have strengthened it with our subscription and ordered that, once strengthened, it be indicated by our seal [Note: An impression of the lead seal hanging from the diploma issued by Leo IX for the monastery of Fulda; it is reproduced accurately by Friedrich Schannat in the new edition of the *Roman Bullary*, p. 383.], for the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. Before whom, blessed Peter the Apostle, always remember us and all the sheep whom He entrusted to you to feed as His own, and whom through us, in His mercy, He feeds and will continue to feed through others throughout the ages of ages.

+ I, Leo, bishop, your servant, blessed Peter the Apostle, have personally strengthened the gift that I made to you from what is yours.

All the foregoing was enacted, written, transcribed, published, and heard in the presence of the most reverend father and lord in Christ, Lord Anibaldus, by divine mercy bishop of Tusculum, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and legate *a latere* of the Apostolic See, seated in judgment at Rome in the papal palace near Saint Peter. He placed the authority of himself and his office upon this present transcript, after it had been read, published, copied, and heard; he wished and decreed that it should everywhere, in court and outside it, be given full credence, just as the original privilege, and ordered that his seal be attached to it for greater strength and security.

This was done in the presence of the reverend men, Lords Francis, abbot of the monastery of Saint Bartholomew of Camporegio in the diocese of Gubbio, doctor of decrees and chancellor; Robert of Piacenza, doctor of law and auditor; John Thomas of Ceccano, canon of Paris and nephew; and the chaplains of the aforesaid lord legate; as well as many other notaries and learned witnesses, summoned and specially requested for the matters stated above; and in the presence of me, Walter, and Paul of Saint Victoria, and Matthew of Spoleto, public notaries, specially summoned and requested for this publication, hearing, and the interposition of the decree and authority. In the year of the Lord 1350, the Jubilee Year, in the eighth year of the pontificate of our most holy lord Pope Clement VI, in the third indiction, on the tenth day of May. [Col. 0738D]

And I, Matthew Salvi, a cleric of Spoleto and public notary by apostolic and imperial authority, saw and read the aforesaid apostolic letters before the aforementioned lord legate, seated in judgment, and heard them together with this present transcript, subscribed jointly with Paul son of Francis and Walter, cleric of Lord Frederick of Clermont, the public notaries written below. Since I found that they corresponded with the present transcript, with nothing added or omitted that altered the substance of the matter or changed its meaning, I therefore, by order of the aforesaid lord legate, subscribed my name and, being requested, affixed my customary sign.

And I, Walter, cleric of Lord Frederick of Clermont, of the diocese of Fermo, public notary by apostolic authority, wrote, transcribed, and copied the aforesaid apostolic letters in every respect, exactly as I saw and found them contained in the apostolic letters themselves, word for word, without adding, omitting, or changing anything that altered the substance or changed the meaning, except perhaps a letter or syllable through error.

I also read and faithfully heard this transcript, by order of the aforesaid most reverend father and lord, Lord Anibaldus, cardinal of the Apostolic See and legate, seated in judgment as stated above, in the presence of the aforesaid learned witnesses—the lord chancellor, auditor, nephew, and chaplains of the said lord legate—and of many other notaries and learned witnesses, as well as Paul son of Francis and Matthew of Spoleto, the aforesaid public notaries, specially summoned and requested for this publication and for the interposition of the decree and authority, as stated above, while they were reading, seeing, and hearing it, together with the aforesaid apostolic letters.

By order of the aforesaid lord cardinal legate, and at the request of the venerable men—the prior and canons of the chapter of the Most Holy Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles in the City, who were present there—I reduced this transcript and copy into this public form with my own hand and, being requested, marked it with my customary sign.

XCI. Saint Leo IX orders W[ibert], bishop of Modena, to attend the consecration by the bishop of Mantua of the church of Blessed Simeon (Padilironensis). (Year 1054.)

[Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, sixth century, part II, p. 168.]

[Col. 0739C]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to W[ibert], bishop of Modena.

God is wondrous in His saints, glorious and gentle, of great mercy and exceedingly patient toward wickedness. As we have learned from the trustworthy report of many faithful people, He has rewarded a hundredfold the merit and labor of His holy confessor Simeon. Honor should be shown to the most reverend abbot, Saint Benedict, together with his companion Simeon, a monk, hermit, and deacon.

The bishop of Mantua will consecrate a new church there. We wish you to show it honor; specifically, we wish you to be present at this consecration and at the elevation of this body, and for an altar to be consecrated in his honor—him whom God has glorified with the highest dignity of virtues.

XCII. Saint Leo teaches the clergy and people of Auximum that those who follow that “perverse and altogether execrable custom of certain peoples—namely, that when their bishop has died, they hostilely break into and seize the bishop’s house, plunder his possessions, burn the houses on his estates, and, with a ferocity more savage than that of beasts, cut down his vines and orchards”—are to be anathematized. (Year 1054.)

[See among the works of Blessed Peter Damian, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLIV, col. 347.]

XCIII. Saint Leo praises highly Peter Damian’s book, the *Gomorrhianus*, “against the fourfold pollution of carnal contagion.” (Year 1054.)

[Col. 0740A]

[See Peter Damian, *Works*, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLV, col. 159.]

XCIV. Saint Leo IX adorns with privileges the hermitage of Peter Damian “called Ocri, situated in the territory of Saxena.” (Year 1054.)

[See *Patrologia*, vol. CXLV, p. 15.]

XCV. Saint Leo IX grants Berard, abbot of Farfa, permission to summon whichever bishop he wishes to consecrate the Farfa church. (Year 1053.)

[Muratori, *Writers of Italian Affairs*, II, II, 620.]

[Col. 0740B]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to Berard, abbot of Saint Mary of Farfa.

We do not refuse to fulfill your just petitions. Therefore, by our authority, you may seek whichever bishop you wish, from whatever place you choose, to consecrate your church for you. Take care, however, that he is not a Simonist.

XCVI. Bull of Saint Leo IX for the nunnery of Saint Lawrence in Alsace. (Year 1054.)

[Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, IV, 736.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the church situated in the place called Hesse, dedicated in honor of Mary, the holy Mother of God, and in memory of the saints Martin the Confessor and Lawrence the glorious levite and martyr, roasted in purifying fire; and through it to Seberga [probably Gerberga], our niece, the abbess, and after her to the female servants of God who will succeed there, forever.

Martin, poor and lowly here, gently urges us to serve him and his own lovingly, so that we may enter heaven rich. Lawrence, roasted like a fish, as he himself says, earned a sweet glory; and he likewise wishes us to serve him and his Lord Jesus Christ through many labors, so that we may be made worthy workers for His reward.

Admonished by the gentle mildness of the one and the sprinkled impetus of the other, we freely grant, as we customarily and ought to do, a confirmation of our privilege to this church as well, out of due veneration for the saints and from heartfelt devotion to the memory of our parents resting there in Christ.

For the martyr shelters our paternal cousins, the counts Mathiridus and Gerhard of blessed memory, and his wife Cunisa, a devoted servant of God, as well as our brother Hugh, the sweet comfort of our heart during his life. And because his gentle confessor has claimed for himself the bodies of whichever saints belong to him, he will not withdraw or estrange himself, at their prayers’ demand, from obtaining forgiveness of souls before God, so that those under whose protection they lived may, through his gracious guardianship, merit eternal joys.

We also confirm to that place the goods which the persons named above, or other relatives of ours, have bestowed upon it, and whatever any faithful person has already granted there or will grant in perpetuity. And so that all may know how much honor we have always desired for this place, at the just prayers of Lady Matilda and her son Henry, formerly our nephew, we ourselves dedicated three altars in that church.

Because one of these has been established more prominently and at a higher level than the others, we have also decreed that it be glorified with a more distinguished special honor: no one may celebrate Mass there except an archbishop, the bishop of that diocese, or suitable weekly officiants of that church. If any other person should arrive for prayer or some other business, he may not presume to approach that altar to perform the solemn rites of Mass without the consent and permission of the abbess or of the other holy women.

The dedication shall also be celebrated by all the inhabitants of that place on the seventh day before the Kalends of December.

So that this church might receive credible testimony from everyone concerning its goods, we had the names of the estates and properties which it now freely possesses faithfully written below. They are these:

In the city of Metz, three small estates; the entire church of Albertorf with its dependent holdings, and half of the same village; Landeldingen, given by Beselmo; at Nunhirchen, a holding with a fishpond, given by Trusing; at Volteringen, a forest given by Bezolin; and the entire church of Steinsilide with its dependent holdings and in complete possession.

Volfresingen belongs to the court of the hospice and to receiving people, and at Halbessurt, a mill and one holding; at Terolnesheim, a vineyard producing only two cartloads of wine per year.

To the abbey itself, as to the other properties mentioned above, also belong a quarter of the church at Sitterfdorff, and a third of the toll at Sarburg; the entire church of Monheim with its dependent holdings and in complete possession, and a quarter of that village; half of the village called Meingeringem, together with its church, dependent holdings, and a third of the tithe.

The priest of that church pays the abbess thirty coins each year at the Nativity of the Lord as offerings of blessing.

The entire church of Berthingen with its dependent holdings and in complete possession; and half of the village of the same church, Igolingen, with its dependent holdings and village, given in full through the hands of Matilda, beloved wife of our brother Hugh mentioned above, and her son Henry; the coinage at Hesse with the entire profit of the market; a quarter of the church of Tesselingen with its dependent holdings and in complete possession; and the entire church of Belnoylre with its dependent holdings and in complete possession.

Five solidi are paid annually from this church. The entire church of Malscheidt with its dependent holdings and everything pertaining to Christian worship; five solidi are also paid annually from this church. The entire church of Elbersmytre with its dependent holdings and in complete possession; five solidi will also be paid annually from this church. The entire church of Bettelingen with its dependent holdings, the whole village, and complete possession; two solidi will also be paid annually from it.

At Rodesheim, three parts of the tithe of the lower church, and the church itself with its dependent holdings and everything there pertaining to Christian worship.

From Dreheim, six cartloads of wine are given annually to the nuns’ cellar, and ten solidi are paid there on the feast of Saint Martin, apart from the other benefices established there.

At the villages of Bosseringen, Schalhembach, Olba, and Richenhofem there are meadows, fields, and substantial estates.

Regarding the church’s household and its Catholic faith and honorable religious life, our father Hugh, the rightful advocate and heir of these same goods, established this agreement: that they should have free permission to join one another in lawful marriage according to their condition, so that, if numerous offspring should be born from that union, they should be divided equally between the church and the heir.

But if only one male or female dependent should be born from it, the church shall have that child as a special mark of its reverence.

We too confirm this and establish that it shall remain so perpetually. We also strengthen by this page of our ordinance all things belonging to that church, stable and firm and in no way to be violated. No emperor, king, duke, margrave, count, viscount, advocate, heir, archbishop, bishop, person of ecclesiastical rank or worldly condition, great or small, may presume to violate, diminish, or invade any of these things.

If anyone should presume to do so, the church shall have free permission to appeal to the Apostolic authority. Therefore, may pious Martin not defend the violator of this ordinance unless he repents; may Lawrence, wounded by him, rise against him in anger; may he be displeasing to all his companions and suffer divine anathema. But may divine grace surround the preserver, and may apostolic blessing preserve and protect him. [Col. 0742C]

XCVII. Saint Leo IX confirms the foundation of the abbey of Saint John the Baptist of Florines for Benedictine monks in the diocese of Liège, recently established by Gerard, lord of Florines and later bishop of Cambrai. (Year 1054.)

[Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*, IV, 4.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Church of Saint John the Baptist, and through it to Goniso, abbot, and [Col. 0742D] his successors at the place called Florines, greetings and apostolic blessing.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to provide wisely in all matters for ecclesiastical honor. Therefore, Goniso, abbot, beloved son in Christ, in whom monastic religion fully possesses its proper honor—a quality that has greatly pleased me—we grant, at your most earnest request, a firm privilege concerning the goods of your church, so that, through the mutual goodwill of the petitioner and the donor, it may obtain salvation and glory for your soul and ours before the Lord.

With paternal kindness we have given a favorable assent to the just petitions of the venerable Gerard, bishop of Cambrai [Note: See the foundation of Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, confirmed by a diploma of Saint Emperor Henry in the year 1012, at the beginning of *Patrologia*, vol. CXL.], so that, since he built and endowed the aforesaid church at his own expense and from his own property together with his brother Godefrid, he might receive this favor from us.

We have willingly assented, I say, both for him and for you, dearest brother. Although your age and externally venerable gray hair commend you to others, your inner morality and unshakable faith have made you pleasing to me. In this petition of yours we have also remembered your brother, Lord Wazo, the most watchful shepherd of the Church of Tongeren, who throughout his life was always a standard of equity, Catholic religion, and canonical integrity.

Therefore, we ordered this page of our ordinance to be made, establishing by apostolic censure that no one may ever dare, with rash audacity, to violate or diminish any of the things granted or to be granted to the aforesaid monastery by any of the faithful, lest, by offending the Lord’s forerunner and Baptist—than whom no one greater has arisen among those born of women—the unwary offender incur the anger of almighty God.

Given … [lacuna]

XCVIII. Letter or brief of Saint Leo IX concerning the cemetery of the priory of Saint Orientius, of the Cluniac order. (Year 1054.)

[*Cluniac Bullary*, 13.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Raymond, archbishop of Auch, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The cry of the monks living at Saint Orientius, in the suburb of the city, has reached our ears concerning the injury you are attempting to inflict upon their place regarding the cemetery, contrary to ancient custom. For we are not better than our fathers.

Therefore, under the authority of God, Saint Peter, and ourselves, we command and instruct you not to trouble or molest the aforesaid monastery in any way through new laws or unheard-of customs, either concerning the cemetery or concerning any other matters belonging to that place.

Accordingly, by canonical and apostolic authority, we decree that no church may go beyond the boundaries established by the Fathers. We therefore wish to admonish and command you not to claim unjustly for yourselves what you have not possessed until now, either within the city or outside it. In particular, just as the cemetery existed in the time of your predecessors, so let it remain forever in the future.

XCIX. Saint Leo IX confirms the foundation of the renowned abbey of Saint Mary at Saintes. (Year 1054.)

[*Gallican Christiania*, II, Documents, 481.]

By the ordering of God, who governs all things, I, Leo, pope of the Roman See.

I wish it to be known to all worshipers of the Catholic Church that Goffrid, count of Anjou, and Agnes, countess, have requested that the place of Saint Mary of Saintes—a nunnery which they devoutly founded for nuns living there under the rule of blessed Benedict—be confirmed and authorized by our authority and strengthened under the protection of our governance.

Granting assent to their petition, we confirm it and receive this place, established under such a constitution, under our protection by a liberal right, as they requested. Therefore, we charitably admonish all the faithful of God not to permit so great a work, the service of God and of those devoted to God, to be disturbed or destroyed.

If anyone should presume to plot against this divine work, attacking and devastating what has been granted or is to be granted, let him incur the anger of eternal damnation; let him not escape the accusation of the holy Mother of God and of all the saints; and let him feel our anathema, insofar as it has been entrusted to us by God’s judgment and granted through apostolic authority, so that the enemy of God may be handed over to destruction and suffer eternal loss. [Col. 0744B]

To ensure that this written charter might possess firmer force, we have had it marked with the impression of our seal.

C. Letter of Saint Leo IX to Michael, patriarch of Constantinople, against his unheard-of presumptions and excessive vanities, and those of Leo, bishop of Acrida [Note: See below, in the appendix, the letter of Michael Cerularius and Leo of Acrida.]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Michael of Constantinople and Leo of Acrida, bishops.

# I. “Peace on earth to men of good will” (Luke 2)

This kind of opening was taught us by that saying of the Lord: “Into whatever house or city you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house’; and if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you” (Luke 10). For God has called us to peace (1 Cor. 7)—he who is our peace, who made both one, and, coming, proclaimed peace to those who were far off and to those who were near (Eph. 2). Among other things he said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5).

Admiring their feet, the God-speaking Isaiah proclaims: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace!” (Isa. 52; Rom. 10). To this the great Paul, bearing witness, exhorts his disciples: “Pursue peace with all, and holiness, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12). And: “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, be at peace with all men” (Rom. 12). And again: “Keep peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you” (2 Cor. 13).

Nor was it without reason that the Lord himself said to his disciples, indeed to all Christians: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John 14). From this it can be understood with what sincere and unanimous affection, and with what bond of an indissoluble covenant, it ought to be preserved: for he commended it to his co-heirs and fellow-partakers as an inheritance and perpetual right, and left it under his testament, soon to be signed with his own blood and confirmed by his holy death—as though he were saying:

“My brothers and co-heirs, from our patrimony I leave you a portion, namely temporal peace. If you present it to me whole and undefiled at the end, I will add to you my portion, namely everlasting peace.”

Nor content with this, he who is equal to the Father and lesser than the Father, praying to the Father for this very thing, as he was about to return to his own Father and our Father, from whom he had never departed, said: “Father, those whom you have given me, I will that they be one, just as we also are one, and that they be perfected into one” (John 17).

# II

But “woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. 18)! For although almost every page of divine Scripture invites us together to the good of unity and peace, so that we may be one heart and one soul in him who makes those who are of one mind dwell in his house, which is the Catholic Church, nevertheless there have been, and still are, wretched men who seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2), in every respect worse than the soldiers who crucified the Lord of glory.

Those soldiers spared his corruptible tunic because it was seamless and woven from above throughout, saying: “Let us not tear it” (John 19), admiring, with a certain reverence, both the diligence of its weaver and the elegance of the workmanship. These men, however, impiously and sacrilegiously lay murderous hands upon his incorruptible charity, by which he united the Church so as to present her to himself as a glorious garment without spot or wrinkle; they sharpen boastful and deceitful tongues to pierce her. They attach no value to the ineffable and singular artistry by which she was joined and woven together with the Wisdom coeternal with God the Father, and not stitched together by human ingenuity or by the syllogisms and arguments of philosophers: “For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Cor. 1).

He did not gather fishermen through rhetoricians and sophists; rather, through fishermen and simple men he caught sophists and orators, because, as the outstanding Paul says: “The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power” (1 Cor. 4).

# III

Let the impious heresy blush and be confounded, shamelessly yearning for the cutting and division of an indivisible and undivided unity, although not only the nature of that unity but even the conjecture of human wisdom cries out and resists.

Let the faithless ravens, kites, vultures, and whatever birds feed on tearing or on the death of others depart. Let the dove alone return to the ark and, remaining upon the head of the Lord Jesus, unite, suffuse, and fill his whole body, which is the Church. Let her form one dove from people of diverse professions and nations and from all languages, as though from different members, to whom her Head, who is Christ himself, says: “My dove is one, my perfect one, my undefiled one” (Song 5).

For she who is always called one, and is one, is never divided or cut apart; she who is always perfect—that is, complete—is never diminished or emptied; she who is always undefiled is never corrupted or stained. For although many sometimes withdraw from her in such a way that they do not return, her unity is not thereby torn apart, nor her perfection diminished, nor her virginity violated.

Indeed, the raven-like members return for the purpose of being reincorporated into their own body, from which they had seemed for a time to be separated, while that one, most completely intact dove remains—the dove into which they falsely boasted that they had been incorporated and united.

And she who groaned under the dangers posed by false brothers, once their departure had been revealed, freely declares through the mouth of the blessed apostle John: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2).

Those who used to press upon the dove’s breast like diseased humors and continually provoke nausea are shown—having departed or been driven out at the prompting of some addition or occasion, or rather discharged—to relieve her and, by their departure, restore her to a state of good health.

All who depart intending to return cannot be torn or cut away from her at all. And if they seem for a time to be torn away or cut off, because “God knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2), through whose predestination they are within without error—even those who are thought to be outside and to be in error—“no one snatches from his hand those whom we had already supposed completely snatched away.”

# IV

But woe to the pride and arrogance [ignorance] of men who, having become members and forerunners of Antichrist—who is king over all the sons of pride—do not cease scattering the pestilence of weeds among the wheat and, as far as lies in them, trampling down the harvest for which a heavenly granary is being prepared.

Concerning that perilous time the beloved virgin of the Lord, John, wished to instruct us: “Little children,” he says, “it is the last hour; and as you have heard that Antichrist is coming, so now many Antichrists have arisen” (1 John 2). This last hour, begun at the first coming of the Savior, is to extend until his second coming. Who could say how many Antichrists it has already had or exposed?

Concerning them also the teacher of the nations, the wonderful Paul, says to the Ephesians in the Acts of the Apostles: “I know that after my departure fierce wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock; and from among your own selves men will arise speaking perverse things, to draw the disciples after them” (Acts 20).

But, O Lord Jesus, ever-watchful Shepherd and Lion from the tribe of Judah, who, according to the Psalmist, walks upon the asp and basilisk and tramples the lion and dragon (Ps. 90), look mercifully now, at the end of the ages, upon the sheep of your pasture, wearied until now by various snares and the fury of innumerable wolves. Rebuke the beasts of the reed (Ps. 67), which rage and gnash their teeth against the humility of your Church, supported and protected by a reed-bed—that is, by worldly power, outwardly shining but inwardly empty.

There, as the divine voice says to blessed Job, “not only do all the beasts of the field play” (Job 40)—that is, the whole multitude of evil spirits rages according to its own desire—but Behemoth, their prince, sleeps there beneath the shade, in the secret place of the reed and in watery places, when he rests secure, without any disturbance or opposition, in the hearts of the proud and the wanton.

But the Catholic Church, holding fast to your promises, O Lord, rejoices daily that the saying of Wisdom is fulfilled in her teachers: “The righteous shall shine, and like sparks they shall run through the reed-bed” (Wis. 3), and they shall burn the reeds shaken by the wind.

Then the beasts of the reed will perish together, among whom is the assembly of bulls (Ps. 67)—that is, the gathering of heresiarchs who, under stiff-necked leadership, drag after them heifers, namely the wanton souls of peoples—so that those who have been tested by silver may be embossed—that is, may appear, stand out, or be revealed as perfect in divine utterances and steadfast in faith.

Silver signifies the divine utterances, as the same Psalmist attests: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11). By “exclusion,” silver or gold is raised, elevated, and pressed upward by a certain technique, so that it suddenly appears sprinkled and marked with a pleasing representation of various flowers or images, whereas previously it lay low and flat.

The great Paul expresses the whole matter more briefly and clearly: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11).

But, malignant heresy, do not flatter yourself on this account because you have heard from the Apostle, “There must be heresies.” For in the holy Gospel our Lord says: “It is necessary that scandals come; nevertheless, woe to the one through whom the scandal comes!” (Matt. 18.) Indeed, straw is not placed in the goldsmith’s furnace without purpose, since gold is not purified unless the straw is burned.

# V

Although almost every page of sacred Scripture thunders against the shameless madness of heretics with these and many similar testimonies, we are utterly astonished and lament with tears of charity that the priests of the Church have fallen so deeply asleep that those who ought to be God’s helpers do not shrink from becoming followers of men whose memory they see to have perished with a crash and whose cities they see destroyed.

From this arises all that which, at last, we pour forth with unspeakable contrition and with groaning of heart and body. In it all the inward parts of the Catholic mother are shaken; in it all the senses of Christians are dulled; in it ecclesiastical discipline and the strength of the holy canons are confounded and trampled down.

For you, our dearest brother and, as we must still call you, brother and bishop in Christ, O Constantinopolitan, and you, Leo of Acrida, are said to have openly condemned the Apostolic and Latin Church with novel presumption and incredible audacity, without having heard or convicted her—chiefly because she dares to celebrate the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion with unleavened bread.

Behold your heedless criticism; behold your ill-founded boasting, when you set your mouth in heaven while your tongue passes through the earth, and attempt by human arguments and conjectures to pierce and overturn the ancient faith.

Behold, unless you repent as quickly as possible, you will be incorporated and numbered—God forbid!—among that tail of the dragon which dragged down a third of the stars of heaven and cast them upon the earth.

Behold: now, after a thousand and nearly twenty years from the Passion of our Savior, the Roman Church is beginning through you to learn how the memory of that Passion ought to be recalled—as though the presence, conversation, and longstanding instruction of the one by whom he glorified God had contributed nothing to her, or as though the precious death of that venerable old man had contributed nothing, to whom Christ, the Son of the living God, said especially: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16).

# VI

Do you not therefore consider how shameless it is to say that the Father who is in heaven concealed from Peter, the prince of the apostles, the worship or rite of visible sacrifice, although through the dispensation of his Only-Begotten Son he deemed it worthy to reveal fully, through himself, that ineffable mystery of the invisible divinity of this same Son?

And to him—not through an angel or a prophet, but with his own mouth—the Lord of angels and prophets makes this promise in what follows: “And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (ibid.). Yet you strive to remove Christ Jesus from the head of that man, although no one can establish any other foundation for the universal Church besides him (1 Cor. 3).

That most devoted Peter demonstrated this not only while living but also while dying, when, with profound humility and appropriate symbolism, he requested to be crucified with his head turned downward. Surely, by divine inspiration, he prefigured himself as the first and square stone fitted, joined, and connected into the foundation, which is Christ Jesus. As one placed upon the cornerstone, he would bear the entire weight of the ecclesiastical structure with incorruptible firmness and, by the support of his own head, would raise to heaven, with an unbending neck, all the members of Christ’s body, growing through suitable and natural joints until the consummation of the age, as far as the feet.

# VII

Thus the holy Church, built upon the rock—that is, Christ—and upon Peter, or Cephas, son of John, who was formerly called Simon, could in no way be overcome by the gates of hell, namely by the arguments of heretics, which lead the foolish into destruction.

The Truth itself, through whom all things that are true are true, promises this: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16).

The Son himself testifies that he obtained the fulfillment of this promise through his prayers to the Father, saying to the Father: “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and you, when you have returned, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22).

Would anyone, then, be so mad as to dare consider the prayer of him whose willing is able to accomplish anything empty in any respect? Have not the inventions of all heretics been rejected, convicted, and defeated from the seat of the prince of the apostles—namely, the Roman Church—both through Peter himself and through his successors? And have not the hearts of the brethren been confirmed in Peter’s faith, which until now has neither failed nor will fail to the end?

# VIII

We pass over, by naming them individually, the more than ninety heresies that arose in the East, or among the Greeks themselves, at different times and from different errors, to corrupt the virginity of the Catholic Church, their mother.

It seems appropriate to say, in part, how many plagues the Constantinopolitan Church has raised through its prelates—plagues which the Roman and Apostolic See bravely fought, crushed, and suffocated.

Behold Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, invader of the see of Constantinople and standard-bearer of the accursed Arius.

The fourth was Macedonius, the heresiarch: the strangler of his predecessor, blessed Paul; blasphemer of the Holy Spirit; torturer and persecutor of Christians even unto death; and a second Julian, marking Catholics with a sign on their foreheads. He and his followers perpetrated these and other evils throughout all the cities of the East, and especially at Constantinople, while the regions of the West remained unmoved by this storm, as your historian Socrates testifies (Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 2).
