The fifth was Eudoxius, the Arian invader of the see and ordainer of the heretic Eunomius. He said that the Father was ἀσεβῆ, “impious,” because he worships no one, and the Son εὐσεβῆ, “pious,” because he worships the Father.

The sixth was Demophilus, himself an Arian.

The ninth was Maximus, a Cynic and Apollinarian.

The tenth was Nectarius, a holy man, ordained by the holy First Council of Constantinople. Concerning him, when the holy Fathers wrote to Pope Damasus and his fellow bishops, they said: “We have drawn the new Church of the city of Constantinople, so to speak, from the mouth of the lion, suffocated by heretical blasphemies”—as your historian Theodoret testifies (Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 9).

But that aged and poisonous basilisk was not thereby entirely suffocated, because his successor John Chrysostom was deposed twice by the ungrateful Church and died in exile. The Western bishops—that is, the Latins—not enduring his deposition, were separated from communion with the Easterners.

His successor Arsacius attacked the Johannites with military force, that is, the followers of blessed John.

The fifteenth in the catalogue was Nestorius, the heresiarch, who, full of the spirit of the devil, vomited forth among the other blasphemies of his perversity this poison:

“Let no one call Mary Mother of God; for Mary was a human being, and it is altogether impossible for God to be generated from a human being.”

He also falsely asserted two persons in God Christ.

Then, the seventeenth was Flavian, a blessed prelate later crowned with martyrdom because he condemned the abbot Eutyches, who asserted one substance or nature in Christ. For this reason the Council of Chalcedon was held under the most blessed Pope Leo and the most Christian Emperor Marcian, with six hundred and thirty bishops.

What shall we say of Acacius, the accuser and restorer of Peter, bishop of Alexandria, through whom very many murders occurred, except that the most holy Pope Gelasius condemned them both forever, together with John, the successor and defender of Acacius? (In the volume On the Bond of Anathema, letters 9 and 11.)

After them, Anthimus, the Eutychian heretic, was deposed in Constantinople itself by the present Pope Agapetus (Agapetus, letters 4 and 5).

As for Eutychius, because he taught that the human body would become impalpable at the resurrection, subtler than wind and air, he was so refuted by blessed Gregory, then a deacon, that in the presence of the Emperor Tiberius, of pious memory, the books containing his doctrine were committed to a deserved fire.

# IX

John also succeeded him. Although the whole world could not contain his pride, a narrow patch of earth nevertheless confined it after not much time.

He was the first to usurp for himself a new title of excessive vanity, when he decreed that he ought to be called and written “ecumenical patriarch,” that is, “universal.”

For this presumption he was struck with a deserved excommunication by the blessed pontiffs Pelagius and Gregory.

The stain of this contagion, together with its curse, still clings to you, so that even now you do not fear either to call or to write yourselves “ecumenical patriarchs.”

Certainly, this title was offered by the holy Fathers at the Council of Chalcedon, out of reverence for the holy Roman and Apostolic See, to our most holy predecessor, Pope Leo, that illustrious teacher, and to his successors. Yet it is established that neither he nor any of his successors has ever accepted it.

And to whom after Christ Jesus could this title have been more fittingly applied than to the successors of Peter? But the revered pontiffs imitated humility, observing that the prince of the apostles himself is nowhere called the universal apostle, and utterly rejected the proud designation by which it seemed that equal dignity was being withdrawn from all the bishops throughout the world when it was arrogated wholly to one—as though each of them were saying in word and deed what their master and first to be crucified said: “I am not worthy to raise my head, but to turn my face toward the earth.”

Let your fraternity therefore see how great a perversity swells within you: you persist in usurping, with such obstinate defiance, for more than four hundred years now since the blessed Pope Gregory and beyond, a superstitious title that was neither offered to you by anyone nor granted, but rather denied and forbidden, under threat of anathema, by the Apostolic and First See and by the holy and orthodox Fathers.

And consider how, following the example of our Lord Jesus Christ and his followers, you are ready to lay down your lives for your brothers, when for so long you have refused even to set aside an empty title—one that by its insolence scandalizes the unity of the entire Church.

What effect has that confession of the glorious Apostle, so often proclaimed in your ears, had upon your minds? He says: “Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (1 Cor. 11.) You not only do not burn because of the scandal of others, but by your scandal you burn the Church of God every day.

# X

But, to return to the rest of your predecessors, what is to be said of Pyrrhus, bishop—or rather heresiarch—follower of Macarius of Antioch? When he came to Rome, he anathematized in writing everything that he and his predecessors had held against the Catholic faith and the Apostolic See.

But, returning to his vomit as quickly as possible, he was condemned by Pope Theodore. His successor Paul, because he did not repent when warned and rebuked by the same Roman pontiff, defined that our Lord Jesus Christ, whom he regarded as some insensible image or phantom, possessed neither one nor two wills or operations; and he overturned the altar of the Latins and of the legates of the Roman Church, something no heretic before him had dared to do.

To destroy the rage with which he raged against Catholics, the most holy Pope Martin, having gathered one hundred and five bishops, condemned Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul, bishops of Constantinople.

In this madness you are by no means inferior even now to that Paul of yours: you condemn with anathema the Supreme and Apostolic See and all its most faithful observers of its institution. You are blinded by such heedless and shameless arrogance that you do not notice what you are doing, who is doing it, or against whom.

You are in fact injuring the one against whom neither you nor any mortal is permitted to pronounce judgment, since the blessed and apostolic pontiff Sylvester divinely decreed, and his spiritual son Constantine, the most religious Augustus, approved and subscribed together with the entire Council of Nicaea, that the Supreme See is to be judged by no one.

That privilege was preserved for it inviolate and unshaken: the same emperor, on the fourth day after his baptism, devoutly conferred it upon the Roman pontiff—namely, that throughout the whole world the priests should regard him as their head, just as all judges regard the king as their head.

All the later universal councils embraced their judgment, always reverenced by the whole world and truly promulgated by divine inspiration: the First Council of Constantinople, with the consent of the pious Augustus and the devout elder Theodosius; the First Council of Ephesus, under the younger Theodosius, son of Arcadius; the Council of Chalcedon, under the rule of Marcian, of divine memory; and the Third Council of Constantinople, at the request and with the consent of the younger Constantine.

With unanimous will and with concordant word and writing, they confirmed that the holy Roman and Apostolic See, after the Lord Jesus, is the head of all the Churches of God, and that this must be believed, confessed, and written by all venerators of the Council of Nicaea. A strict anathema against those who despise even one iota of its decrees was established by the five councils named above and by all the subsequent synods of the holy Fathers.

# XI

Thus, according to the Wise Man, “a stone thrown does not go up to heaven” (Ecclus. 27), and “a curse uttered without cause returns upon its author” (Prov. 26). Thus, according to the proverb of the common people, whoever tries to spit above his own head soon has the spittle fall back upon his face.

Thus, because we have not returned curse for curse but, with the Psalmist, have long placed a guard upon our mouth while the sinner stood against us (Ps. 38), through your swelling pride you have incurred—we grieve to say it—an anathema from all the Fathers of all the venerable councils, because you injured the Supreme See, against which no human being is permitted to pronounce judgment.

You will be bound by it indissolubly if, by retaining an impenitent heart over so great a presumption, you are not released from it by his vicars to whom Christ, the Son of the living God, especially said: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16).

If we compare ancient things with new, that diviner Balaam was in this respect more cautious than you. Revering God, he could not be bent by either the promises or the threats of the king of Moab to curse the children of Israel: “How can I curse one whom God has not cursed? Or how can I detest one whom the Lord does not detest?” (Num. 23.)

But neither love of God and neighbor, nor reverence for the divine canons, nor the prohibition of your orthodox rulers, as they are called, restrains you from publicly cursing and detesting the chosen race, the royal priesthood, and the holy nation (1 Pet. 2).

# XII

Although this was truly said by the prince of the apostles, Peter, to all the Churches of Christ, which together form one Catholic Church throughout the world, it is more truly applied to the one over which he himself properly presides, since he deserved to obtain the governance of the heavenly kingdom. The Lord Jesus Christ said to him: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16), together with the privilege of the supreme priesthood in the special power of binding and loosing.

But, as Solomon testifies, “The heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord; wherever he wills, he will turn it” (Prov. 21). The most prudent prince of the earthly monarchy, Constantine, deeply reverencing such a pinnacle of heavenly dignity in blessed Peter and in his vicars, adorned through blessed Sylvester not only all the pontiffs who would succeed that apostle in the Roman See until the end of the world with imperial power and dignity, but also with imperial insignia and attendants.

He judged it utterly unworthy that those whom divine majesty had placed over the heavenly realm should be subject to an earthly empire. Compared with that heavenly dignity, this earthly realm is nothing but vanity of vanities, by which human beings, forgetting the Lord their Creator, swell with pride and soon subside.

Nevertheless, the imperial majesty accomplished all that it could when, in complete devotion, it returned to God in his ministers whatever it had received from the Lord. For, as the venerable Paul teaches: “There is no power except from God; and whatever powers exist have been ordained by God” (Rom. 13).

We are instructed by the prince of the apostles himself not to resist these powers in the proper administration of the earthly kingdom: “Be subject for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of those who do good, for such is the will of God” (1 Pet. 2). And shortly afterward: “Fear God; honor the king” (ibid.).

Likewise, through his fellow apostle Paul: “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities. For whoever resists authority resists what God has appointed; and those who resist acquire condemnation for themselves” (Rom. 13).

Hence Wisdom thunders in Proverbs, saying: “Through me kings reign, and princes decree what is just” (Prov. 8).

The often-mentioned Augustus Constantine also perceived this with the liveliness of his discerning soul, and wrote thus to his religious mother Helena, among other things:

“He who governs the ages and arranges the resources of the whole world, by which we are nourished and sustained, gives life to those things that breathe through himself, but through the hearts of rulers dictates his laws to the ages.”

# XIII

By these and very many other testimonies, you ought already to have been satisfied concerning the earthly and heavenly empire, indeed concerning the royal priesthood of the holy Roman and Apostolic See, especially concerning its special disposition in heaven—if in any way you wish to be, or to be called, Christians, and if you are not openly attacking the truth of the Gospel, which God forbid!

Whoever does not awaken at its thunder is not asleep but entirely dead, and it is already futile for human beings to cry out to him.

But lest some scruple of doubt still remain among you concerning its earthly dominion, and lest you lightly suspect that the holy Roman See wishes to claim and defend its unshakable honor through foolish and old-womanish tales, we shall bring forward a few passages from the privilege placed by the hand of that same Constantine, with a golden cross, above the venerable body of the heavenly key-bearer. Through these passages truth may be established and vanity confounded, so that all the members of the Catholic mother may know that we belong to the discipline of that Peter who says of himself in his Epistle:

“For we did not follow cleverly devised fables when we made known to you the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, but became eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2 Pet. 1).

And we wish to impress these things upon you not merely through some report but through what we have learned by sight and touch.

Or, admonished by these things, recognize that the same glorious prince, in the privilege already mentioned, after a clear and perfect confession of the Christian faith and an explicit commendation of his baptism, proclaimed the special dignity of the holy Roman Church, saying:

“We have judged it useful, together with all our satraps and the entire senate, as well as the nobles and all the people subject to the empire of Roman glory, that, just as blessed Peter appears to have been appointed on earth as the vicar of the Son of God, so also the pontiffs of that prince of the apostles, in his place, should possess the authority of a principate granted by us and by our empire, greater than the gentleness of our earthly imperial serenity appears to possess. We choose for ourselves that same prince of the apostles, or his vicars, as firm patrons before God.

“And just as our power is earthly and imperial, so we decree that his most holy Roman Church be reverently honored, and that the most sacred seat of blessed Peter be gloriously exalted above our empire and earthly throne, granting it power, dignity of glory, vigor, and imperial honor.

“And we decree and establish that it hold the principate both over the four sees—Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, and Constantinople—and over all the Churches of God throughout the entire world; and that the pontiff who at that time is the pre-eminent ruler of that most holy Roman Church should also be first among all the priests of the world, and that whatever must be arranged for the worship of God or for the stability of the faith of Christians should be governed by his judgment.

“For it is just that holy law hold the principate as its head where our Savior, the institutor of the holy laws, commanded blessed Peter the apostle to possess his chair; where, bearing the punishment of the cross, he drank the cup of blessed death and appeared as the imitator of his Master and Lord; and where the nations should bow their necks in confession of Christ’s name, where blessed Paul the apostle, their teacher, was crowned with martyrdom for Christ with his neck extended.

“And there, until the end, they should seek the teacher where the bodies of the holy teachers rest; and there, bending forward and prostrate upon the ground, they should serve the heavenly King, God and our Savior Jesus Christ, where the proud earthly king served under imperial authority.”

After briefly recalling his zeal and devotion in constructing certain basilicas of the saints, and the magnificence with which imperial donations had richly endowed them, he says:

“We grant to those holy apostles, our most blessed lords Peter and Paul, and through them also to blessed Sylvester, our father, supreme pontiff and universal pope of the city of Rome, and to all his successors, the pontiffs who will sit in the see of blessed Peter until the end of the world, and at the present time we hand over to them our imperial palace of the Lateran, which is preferred and pre-eminent among all palaces throughout the world.

“Next, the diadem, namely the crown of our head, together with the phrygium, and also the shoulder-cloth, that is, the strap customarily worn around an emperor’s neck; likewise the purple cloak, the scarlet tunic, and all the imperial garments; as well as the dignity of the imperial commanders of the cavalry.

“We also confer upon him the imperial scepters, together with all the standards and banners, the various imperial ornaments, and the entire procession of the imperial majesty and the glory of our power.

“We decree that the most reverend clerics of various orders serving that most holy Roman Church should possess that pinnacle of singular power and pre-eminence with which our most ample senate appears to be adorned: that is, that they should be made patricians and consuls, and we proclaim them adorned with the other imperial dignities as well.

“And just as the imperial army is adorned with distinction, so we decree that the clergy of the holy Roman Church be adorned. And just as imperial power is adorned with various offices—namely, chamberlains, doorkeepers, and all the guards—so we wish the holy Roman Church to be honored.

“And so that pontifical splendor may shine forth most fully, we also decree that the clerics of the same holy Roman Church ride horses adorned with mappulae and linen coverings, that is, with the whitest color.

“And just as our senate uses footwear with udones, that is, footwear embellished with white linen, so also let the clerics use them; and thus let heavenly things, just as earthly things, be adorned to the praise of God.

“Above all, however, granting permission, we concede to our most holy father Sylvester, bishop and pope of the city of Rome, and to all the most blessed pontiffs who shall come after him in succession and in perpetual times, the right, for the honor and glory of Christ our God, in that great Catholic and Apostolic Church of God, by our edict, to ordain as clerics whomever he may choose by his own calm judgment and to number them among the religious clergy, without anyone from among them presuming to act arrogantly.”

Source/review notes: One proposed correction was removed because the draft’s wording is substantively adequate; no unresolved coverage issue remains.

### XIV

“We have therefore decreed this also: that our same venerable Father, Silvester, supreme pontiff, and all pontiffs succeeding him, must use a diadem—that is, a crown—which we have granted him from our own head, made of the purest gold and precious gems, and must wear it on their heads to the praise of God and in honor of blessed Peter. But the most blessed pope did not permit himself to use that crown of gold over the clerical crown which he wears to the glory of blessed Peter. Instead, with our own hands we placed upon his most sacred head the *phrygium*, shining with a white brilliance and signifying the Lord’s splendid resurrection; and, holding the bridle of his horse, we performed for him, in reverence for blessed Peter, the office of *strator* [horse-leader]. We establish that all his successors are individually to use this *phrygium* in processions, in imitation of our empire.

“Therefore, so that the pontifical summit may not be diminished but may be adorned even more than the dignity, glory, and power of an earthly empire, behold: we transfer and leave to the aforementioned most blessed pontiff and our Father Silvester, universal pope, both our palace, as stated above, and the city of Rome, and all the provinces, places, and cities of Italy and the western regions. By this imperial decree and pragmatic ordinance, we determine that he and his pontiff-successors shall have firm authority and dominion, under imperial sanction, to administer them; and we grant them to remain under the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church.

“Accordingly, we have judged it fitting that our empire and royal power be transferred and moved to the eastern regions; that a city be built in the finest place in the province of Byzantium in our name; and that our empire be established there. For where the principate of the priests and the head of the Christian religion has been established by the heavenly Emperor, it is not right that an earthly emperor should exercise authority there.

“All these things, which we have established and confirmed through this imperial sacred decree and through our other imperial decrees, we determine shall remain unimpaired and unshaken until the end of the world.”

Then, after an oath before the living God and his awesome judgment, and after invoking eternal condemnation upon anyone who should violate or despise this privilege of his, the same venerable Constantine continued:

“Having strengthened the document of this imperial decree with our own hands, we placed it upon the revered body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. There, pledging to that same apostle of God that we would preserve everything inviolate and leave orders to our successors, the emperors, that they preserve it, we deliver it—with the assent of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ—to our Father Silvester, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and through him to all his pontiff-successors, to possess happily and perpetually.”

### XV

Supported, then, by so many such testimonies and by very many others, truth does not blush but shameless vanity is refuted. Yet on this matter we have a testimony greater than Constantine’s. For, as blessed John the Evangelist says, Constantine “is of the earth and speaks of the earth” (John 3). We scarcely accept testimony from a human being, being content with the testimony of him who came from heaven and is above all, and who says:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16).

In the catalogue of the apostles, Peter—called by the Lord Jesus Christ himself “Cephas,” that is, “Peter” [Rock]—was placed first, like a hinge. To him specially and by name, not only before his Passion but also at the very moment of his Passion, immediately after he had entrusted generally to the disciples the wondrous mystery of his body and blood, the Shepherd of shepherds commended both the sheep that were to be scattered when he was struck down and those that were to be gathered, to one fold and one shepherd, until the end of the age. He said:

“Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has desired you, to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And you, when once you have returned, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22).

The angel also invited him by name, through the women who had come to see the glory of their risen Master, when he said:

“Tell his disciples and Peter that he has risen, and behold, he will go before you into Galilee. There you will see him” (Matthew 20).

On the very day of his resurrection, the compassionate and truthful Master also appeared to him, as the venerable evangelist Luke instructs us, saying:

“The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon” (Luke 24).

That this manifestation was made first to Peter alone and afterward to him together with the other fellow disciples is declared by his glorious co-apostle Paul, who writes to the Corinthians:

“Christ rose on the third day according to the Scriptures, and he was seen by Cephas, and afterward by the eleven” (1 Corinthians 15).

### XVI

When the glory of his assumption was already imminent, while the Lord was dining with his seven disciples, he asked Peter three times about his love for him. When Peter had confessed it three times, he commanded him three times to feed his lambs and sheep. He signified to him by the future extension of his hands and the girding of himself with what death he would glorify God.

Immediately afterward, following the Lord’s ascension, Peter rose in the midst of the hundred and twenty brethren. Expounding the profound meanings of the most holy Psalmist, he filled out the apostolic number by his authority, adding Matthias by lot; he judged it wrong that the number should remain eleven.

When the Holy Spirit had likewise been sent to them in different languages, some were astonished in wonder, while others, with the blindness of old, mocked and said that they were full of new wine. Peter instructed the ignorant and overthrew the unbelieving with a single testimony from the holy Joel (Joel 2). Then, boldly reproaching them for their wicked conspiracy against the Lord and his Christ—in which they had condemned and killed the author of life by the most shameful death—he established by the clearest prophecies of blessed David Christ’s holy resurrection, glorious ascension, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, now accomplished by him.

Thus, when the Jews were pierced with remorse, he, first among the apostles, imposed repentance upon those guilty of Christ’s blood, and immediately baptized three thousand of them (Acts 2).

### XVII

He alone, as the learned-speaking evangelist Luke testifies, while those who had been scattered because of the persecution that arose under Stephen went about the cities, speaking the word of life to no one except Jews, was praying in the upper room when he fell into an ecstatic state. He saw a sheet, filled with all the four-footed animals of the earth, reptiles, and birds of the sky, being lowered from heaven by its four corners. A heavenly voice said to him three times:

“Rise, Peter; kill and eat.”

Three times he replied:

“Because nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.”

And three times the heavenly voice answered:

“What God has cleansed, you must not call common” (Acts 10).

By this he was sufficiently instructed that the Gentiles, formerly considered unclean, were to be gathered from the four parts of the world into the unity of faith. Once their consciences had been cleansed by faith and their former uncleanness—whose service they had offered through their members—had been killed, they were to be incorporated with delight into Christ, as three messengers invited Peter in the mystery of the Trinity.

Attacking that enormous boar from the forest of the Gentiles, the centurion Cornelius, Peter killed and ate him when he had cleansed him with water and the Spirit and brought him into the Church. When Cornelius’s household and friends had been gathered together, while Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word. They were speaking in tongues and magnifying God (ibid.). Nowhere is it read that this was granted to any Jews, not even to the apostles themselves: that they should receive such fullness of the Paraclete before baptism.

Is it not therefore clearer than daylight that Peter was the first to draw Jews and Gentiles into the building of Christ’s Church, and, like two walls coming from opposite directions, to join them through Christ, the cornerstone, with an indissoluble bond of love?

Later, seeing that the harvest was plentiful and the laborers few, he sent Paul and Barnabas from Antioch as preachers to all nations. While they diligently devoted themselves to this office, he gave them the right hand of fellowship, so that they would serve among the Gentiles, while he served among the circumcised, as is clearly shown in the Epistle to the Galatians (Galatians 2).

Yet, although the burden had been divided among them, he did not withdraw from the vocation and care of the Gentiles that he had begun—a vocation whose effect, after Asia and from Illyricum, all Europe and Africa, and especially Rome, the capital and mistress of the world’s nations, recognize.

For when certain false apostles had disturbed the hearts of the brethren, saying that they ought to be circumcised according to the law of Moses, and Paul and Barnabas had gone to Jerusalem to consult about this question, Peter alone, by his authority, removed the burden of circumcision and the yoke of the old law from the disciples’ necks. He judged the grace of the Gospel sufficient for the full salvation of believers, saying:

“Why do you wish to impose upon the disciples’ necks a heavy yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we believe that we shall be saved, just as they also are. For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you” (Acts 15).

Strengthened by this reply, Paul, the Doctor of the Gentiles, declares to the Galatians:

“If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Galatians 5).

### XVIII

But this too must no less be observed about Peter: the shadow of his body brought the remedy of desired health to the sick. It is established that this was granted to none of the saints before him. Nor did the Holy of Holies, through whom Peter was able to do whatever good he was able to do, ever grant such a gift to anyone from his own most holy body. Rather, he specially reserved this privilege for his Peter, as a great sign of the present and future Church: namely, because Peter was to be the principal ruler of both, and was to prefigure in himself the state of both.

Thus, by the hidden power of these sacraments of visible and passing things, as illnesses of souls are healed on earth by his shadow, he may display to us in heaven that solid form of truth and blessedness, still invisible to us, like a solid body.

The Apostle briefly demonstrates the difference between these states:

“Now we see through a mirror in an enigma; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Corinthians 13).

Agreeing with him, his fellow apostle John says:

“Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

That the present Church is saved by faith and hope, Paul expresses as follows:

“Without faith it is impossible to please God. Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11).

In another place he says:

“We have been saved by hope; but hope that is seen is not hope. For what does a person hope for if he sees it?” (Romans 8).

Thus, by believing and hoping now, and patiently awaiting what we do not see, we are freed from sins through faith and hope, and we see that “the just shall live by faith.” In the future we shall see and possess complete blessedness in reality, and shall be satisfied by love alone, without weariness, when his glory appears.

### XIX

Yet your insolence, making light of such things, does not fear shutting Christ’s special sheep out of, and forbidding them, the sheepfolds in which they had for a time rested to the praise of God. He never ceases to invite them and lead them into the pastures of eternal life.

When he was already placed at the final suffering of the cross, he looked upon these sheep—alone among all the others in sharing his suffering—and, laying down his life for them, commended his blessed spirit to the Lord with thanksgiving and the most devout prayer at the moment of its release, saying:

“I give you thanks, good Shepherd, because the sheep whom you entrusted to me suffer with me. I ask, therefore, that they may share your grace with me forever.”

Will any enemy, through the little keys of errors or the snares of sophistries, prevail in bolting or obstructing the gates of life against those whom so great a friend, by his authority, merits, and prayer, unlocks and opens—he with whom the gates of hell cannot prevail, who is all-powerful in heaven and on earth through the final desire of his soul and the will of his lips? Will he be defrauded by the Lord, to whom he was going? Far be it!

### XX

Therefore recover now from such great madness. Cease mocking true Catholic Latins—the more familiar disciples of the great Peter and the more devoted followers of his teaching and institution—by calling them “unleavened,” or denying them churches, or inflicting tortures upon them, as you have begun to do, if you wish now and always to have peace and a portion with Peter.

The Doctor of the Gentiles, who was indebted to the wise and the foolish, snatched up to the third heaven and into paradise, commends Peter’s teaching and tradition in the Epistle to the Romans in every respect, saying:

“First, I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Romans 1).

Taking occasion from this chapter, blessed and Catholic doctor Augustine, most distinguished in the Latin language, and our Chrysostom, says:

“This faith which the Romans possess is that very same faith, and not another, which is proclaimed and believed throughout the whole world. It is preached not only on earth but also in heaven, because Jesus reconciled through his blood not only earthly and infernal things but also heavenly things” (Colossians 1).

And this is what it means for faith to be preached throughout the whole world: through it the whole world is made subject to God.

But hear what Paul says next:

“I desire to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift for strengthening you” (Romans 1).

Lest anyone think that he wished to add anything to Peter’s institution or take anything away from it, he explained what he meant by “strengthening you”:

“That is, that we may be mutually consoled in you through the faith that is in one another, yours and mine” (ibid.).

At the end of the Epistle, warning them to avoid false brethren who departed from the teaching they had received, he says:

“I ask you, brethren, to watch those who cause dissensions and scandals contrary to the teaching which you have learned, and avoid them. For such persons do not serve Christ our Lord but their own belly; and by smooth speech and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent. Your obedience has been proclaimed everywhere. I rejoice, therefore, in you” (Romans 16).

### XXI

Behold: throughout the whole Epistle, the great Paul is not found correcting the faith of the Latins or reproving their faults. Rather, he congratulated them on their faith and manner of life and admonished them to persevere. This is unlike the Greeks, against whom he inveighed most fiercely from beginning to end of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, not merely on account of reprehensible conduct but also because of the swift shipwreck of their faith.

This is certainly clear in a few words, where he says:

“God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord. But I appeal to you, brethren, through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you; but that you be perfected in the same understanding and in the same knowledge.

“For it has been reported to me about you, my brethren, by those of Chloe’s household, that there are contentions among you. Now I say this because each of you says: ‘I indeed belong to Paul,’ ‘I to Apollos,’ ‘I to Cephas,’ ‘I to Christ.’ Is Christ divided?” (1 Corinthians 1).

And when he had marked them as arrogant because of false and worldly wisdom, he added:

“Already you are filled; already you have become rich; you reign without us—and would that you did reign, so that we also might reign with you!” (1 Corinthians 4).

Threatening their arrogance with the rod, he said:

“It is heard that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as does not occur even among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst” (1 Corinthians 5).

After completing these admonitions, he warned them to feast with him, not in the old leaven, which corrupts the whole lump, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (ibid.).

### XXII

Since these and similar apostolic and patristic sayings clearly prove the sincere obedience of the Latins and condemn the corrupt insolence of many Greeks, there are still many more matters favorable to our side on this subject. If it were permitted to bring them forward, they would not merely exceed the limits of an epistle but could even burden bookcases.

Omitting these matters, therefore, we charitably admonish you not to be absent from yourselves, but to place yourselves before yourselves; carefully consider the ways of your predecessors and your own; do not flatter us out of private affection; and, while searching for a speck in your brothers’ eyes, do not fail to see the beam in your own.

Recall that infamous synod which your heresiarchs wished to be called the Seventh. Through their conspiracy, the revered images of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the saints were either given to the flames or plunged into water, while the paintings were erased from the walls of the basilicas.

[Note: This was the Constantinopolitan synod under Constantine Copronymus.]

Although the authority of the Roman pontiffs always resisted these actions, the freedom of the most holy pope Nicholas is especially worthy of praise everywhere. Through his legates, both on behalf of the sacred images and concerning the deposition of the blessed bishop Ignatius and the substitution of the neophyte Photius, he closed the church of Hagia Sophia until the Apostolic See’s decrees were obeyed.

### XXIII

But far be it from us to wish to believe what public rumor does not hesitate to assert happened to the Church of Constantinople: that, by indiscriminately promoting eunuchs, contrary to the first canon of the holy Council of Nicaea, it once elevated a woman to the seat of its pontiffs.

Although the enormity and horror of this abominable crime, and brotherly affection, do not permit us to believe it, nevertheless, considering your neglect of the censure of the holy canons—for you still indiscriminately and solemnly promote eunuchs and those diminished in some part of the body not only to the clergy but even to the pontificate—we think that it could have happened.

But why say more? You have already overflowed with so many and such great schismatics and heretics openly attacking the Catholic and Apostolic Church and striving to tear it apart that the Latin, or Western, Church may rightly complain about you, speaking in the voice of the bride in the Song of Songs:

“The sons of my mother have fought against me” (Song of Songs 1).

And truly: is the Roman and Apostolic See—which through the Gospel gave birth to the Latin Church in the West—not the mother of the Church of Constantinople in the East? Through her glorious son Constantine and through noble and learned Romans, she undertook to restore it not only in morals but also in its walls.

If you deny this, why are Latin praises recited to your emperor and Latin readings recited in the Greek Church? Surely this is out of reverence for that mother who, already harassed and attacked by all the cruelties of the pagans and by the tortures of various sufferings, and refined like gold in the excessive fires of persecutors, brought forth a cherished daughter—namely, the Church of Constantinople.

### XXIV

Certainly, the tenth persecution of Christians, begun by Nero, had already completely cooled; the whole conflagration of worldly madness had already been extinguished; Rome, mature and long-established, victorious and crowned in divine worship, was already triumphing in profound peace; an innumerable army of martyrs of both sexes and every age, nourished on our unleavened bread, had already shattered every assault of idolatry; it already held the world, and the prince of the world himself, beneath its feet.

Not only the bishops of our institution but also their ministers—among them Laurence and Vincent—while the whole world marveled, had mocked the torments and torturers themselves when these failed.

Now the pampered daughter sits secure in her chamber, dissolved in luxury, wantonness, and prolonged leisure. She has never properly advanced onto the field of those who strive, while her devout mother labors and fights on her behalf. Yet she is not ashamed or afraid to claim primacy, to disparage her mother’s already honored old age, or to consider with even some human regard her body worn out by labors and years, and her wrinkled and weakened limbs, once strong and stretched out for divine battles.

She shows no reverence for her mother’s venerable gray hairs, but with childish frivolity, after innumerable triumphs, provokes her to renewed wars against herself. Having deprived her of the solid food of the mature, she shamelessly tries to draw her back to the milk of carnal things and to drip it into her mouth—against the order of nature—from the very breasts of her puberty, so often broken in Egypt, as was said above.

### XXV

And would that it were at least true milk! But, alas, it is not milk with which the tender infancy of the faithful may gradually be nourished until it reaches solid food. It is what Solomon warns must be avoided when he says:

“My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Proverbs 1).

And:

“Woe to him who gives his friend milk and leads him along an evil way” (Proverbs 16).

Nor is it the water of which whoever drinks will never thirst again, because it will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life, and rivers of living water will flow from his belly (John 7). Rather, it is stolen water from wells which the Philistines, loving mud rather than water, filled with earth (Genesis 26); or from broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2); or from the rivers of Egypt and Babylon, by which the belly is stretched and, burdened, is not filled but emptied and swells (Numbers 5), so that, like a dropsical person, one thirsts all the more disastrously the more one drinks.

Concerning these waters the Lord complains through Jeremiah against certain people, saying:

“They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns—broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 2).

And later:

“Why do you wish to go on the road to Egypt, to drink turbid water? Or what do you seek on the roads of Assyria, to drink the water of the river?” (ibid.)

To prevent us from thirsting for these waters, he likewise says:

“Keep your throat from thirst” (ibid.).

Thus Solomon, showing which waters we ought to desire and which we ought to avoid, says:

“Drink water from your own cistern and streams from your own well. Let your springs flow outward, and distribute your waters in the streets. Keep them for yourself alone, and let strangers not share in them. May your vein be blessed” (Proverbs 5).

Later, he introduces heretical vanity, colored and depicted in a visible form under the appearance of a foolish woman, saying:

“A foolish and clamorous woman, full of enticements and knowing nothing at all, sits at the doors of her house upon a chair in the high place of the city, to call to those passing by on the road and proceeding on their way: ‘Whoever is simple, let him turn in to me.’ And she says to the senseless: ‘Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant.’ But he does not know that giants are there, and that her guests are in the depths of hell” (Proverbs 9).

### XXVI

So that the daughter may not share in them amid the flames of Tartarus, which she would in turn continually feed with her own marrow, let her now remember the groans of her devout mother, and how many and how great dangers she has seen in her womb until now, whether on her account or on account of her sisters.

By God’s grace, let such a daughter learn, at least after being admonished, to become the kind of daughter who strives to raise and support a mother who has deserved well of her—even though the mother is aged, bent by constant labor, and trembling—by giving her a hand and offering her shoulder, rather than pushing her toward ruin, depressing, disturbing, or afflicting her.

With devout affection and humble heart, let her continually consider what Solomon says:

“A foolish person despises his mother” (Proverbs 15);

and again:

“Do not despise your mother when she grows old” (Proverbs 23).

Otherwise, if—God forbid—she wishes to remain stubborn and refuses to spare and obey her devout mother, who still conceals her daughter’s haughtiness and arrogance and patiently awaits satisfaction, she will discover in her little old mother youthful arms extended in defense of the traditions of the fathers, the agility proper to a young woman, and the effective steadfastness of a maiden.

And, according to Solomon, “the stubborn person shall eat the fruits of his way and be filled with his own counsels” (Proverbs 1), because, as the same author testifies:

“The father’s blessing strengthens the houses of his children, but the mother’s curse uproots their foundations” (Ecclesiasticus 3);

and again:

“How evil in reputation is the person who forsakes his father; and accursed by God is the one who provokes his mother” (ibid.).

And:

“Whoever afflicts his father and drives away his mother is shameful and unhappy” (Proverbs 19).

Whoever strives to please his father takes care not to offend her, just as one of the wise men of the world also says:

“Do not offend your mother while wishing to be good to your parent.”

### XXVII

From these and very many other assertions it is clear what even contempt for a carnal mother deserves. What, then, shall be said about the insult and reproach directed against a spiritual mother?

The former conceived and gave birth to us in iniquities unto death; the latter, after our sins had been forgiven, regenerated us unto life. Just as their merit differs, so also the reward differs according as they are honored or [and, or] disgraced. To one who honors his carnal mother, longevity upon the earth of the dying and the stability of a house destined to fall are promised; but to one who provokes her, the foundations of earthly things are uprooted.

Those who venerate the spiritual mother will see length of days in God’s right hand (Psalm 90) and will dwell without end in the land of the living. Those who scorn her, however, will be crushed by double contrition, and, as with a double garment, will be clothed in their shame (Psalm 108), and their root will be torn from the land of the living (Psalm 52).

Indeed, if affection for a carnal mother prevents us from reverence for the spiritual mother, it must be completely abandoned and cut away from us, as Moses says of the tribe of Levi in Deuteronomy:

“He who said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to his brothers, ‘I do not recognize them,’ and did not know his own children—these kept your covenant, your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 33).

To those who do this, the Lord Jesus promised a hundredfold in this life and eternal life in the future (Matthew 19).

### XXVIII

But behold, the daughter ought no longer to appear ungrateful, since her mother has deemed her worthy of honor above the others. Although the Church of Constantinople possesses no divine or human privilege making it more honorable or distinguished than the other Churches, and although Antioch and Alexandria retain their rights of dignity among the others because of their reverence for the prince of the apostles, nevertheless her devout mother—namely, the Roman Church—not wishing her beloved daughter to be entirely deprived of the dowry of honor, arranged through our blessed predecessors at several synods that, while preserving the ancient dignity of the principal and apostolic sees, the bishop of Constantinople should be honored as bishop of a royal city.

This was so even though the religious Augustus Justinian had wished to establish by human laws that, after the Roman pope, the bishop of the Church of Constantinople should sit in precedence.

Certainly Constantinople attained this through no other excellence of merits than that the Roman Church, out of love for the venerable Constantine—who honored and exalted herself as far as he could—distinguished his city with this privilege of honor by purely human benevolence, in accordance with the prophet’s saying to Eli:

“I will glorify those who glorify me; but those who despise me shall be held of no account” (1 Samuel 2).

### XXIX

Or, if she retains or thinks she possesses some other privilege of dignity, you rebels against light and truth, standard-bearers of shadow and vanity, bring it forward.

For we address you who, as the Lord says of the Pharisees, have taken away the key of knowledge (Luke 11), who shut the kingdom of heaven before human beings, neither entering yourselves nor permitting others to enter (Matthew 23). Rather, you forbid entry while seeking to spit upon the venerable face of your mother, while pursuing her with insults and curses, and while striving to separate her lambs from her—even through anathema and scourges—so that they may neither recognize nor follow their mother’s voice.

For, as it is reported, you closed all the basilicas of the Latins in your territory and took monasteries from the monks and abbots until they lived according to your institutions.

Behold, in this respect, how much more discerning, moderate, and merciful the Roman Church is than you! For although many monasteries or churches of the Greeks are found within and outside Rome, none of them has yet been disturbed or forbidden to follow the tradition of its fathers or its own custom. Rather, it is urged and admonished to observe it.

She does not possess the animosity of an impious heresy, which always rejoices in division and says through the murderess harlot:

“Let it be neither mine nor yours; divide it” (3 Kings 18).

Rather, with the piety of a true mother, she entreats Solomon:

“I beg you, Lord, give this infant the living child, and do not kill him” (ibid.).

For she knows that differing customs according to place and time do not harm the salvation of believers, when one faith, working through love whatever good it can, commends everyone to the one God.

### XXX

Although, in accordance with the duty of your rank and position, you ought to have known and preached this, so that you might deserve to receive grace from the good shepherd for the sheep gathered together, rather than condemnation for those scattered, you have incurred the Apostle’s saying to the Hebrews:

“Although by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need to be taught what are the elementary principles of the words of God” (Hebrews 5).

“For you have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Romans 10).

Had you grasped this knowledge, you ought to have reached the summit of the episcopate from lay life not by a leap but by canonical stages—or rather, with a level step—lest the Apostle’s words concerning a bishop stand against you:

“Not a recent convert, lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Timothy 3).

For when an unlearned person usurps the teacher’s place, it is necessary either that he learn what he is to teach, or that, as a blind shepherd or a mute dog unable to bark (Isaiah 56), he remain harmful to himself and to those subject to him; or else, ashamed to learn and remain silent, he presumptuously teach what is even more harmful.

It rarely happens that someone placed at the summit can learn humility when he has not ceased to be proud in the lowest places.

To this is added the fact that anyone who has a white film over the eye is forbidden the priesthood. Whoever is blinded by the arrogance of justice or wisdom has a white film over his eye.

### XXXI

But far be it from us to think that religious and orthodox princes, and a most Christian city devoted to God, should consider you worthy of being heard in this error of yours. Rather, by the terror of their power they ought to compel you toward the good of unity.

Let them remember that in ancient times the bishops of Constantinople suffered so greatly from the disease of pride, which was most familiar to them, that an edict of the emperors Theodosius, Arcadius, and Honorius forbade anyone from the Church of Constantinople to hope for the pontificate after the death of Bishop Sisinnius. Instead, they were always to seek a pontiff from elsewhere, because they were devoted to empty glory and arrogant beyond measure, as the historians relate.

They also report that seventy-six Eastern bishops, avoiding the Council of Sardica, held at Philippopolis in Thrace an assembly to be condemned. They adulterated the holy and undefiled faith of the Council of Nicaea and confirmed their error by common subscription. But three hundred Westerners, embracing the sound judgment of the holy Fathers, strengthened it by their unanimity.

All this is said so that, once the conduct of earlier times is known, no one may recklessly believe what is presented in the present.

### XXXII

For the faith of the Roman Church, built through Peter upon the rock, has neither failed until now nor will it fail throughout the ages, since Christ its Lord prays for it, as he testifies at the very time of his Passion:

“I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, when once you have returned, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22).

By these words he demonstrated that the faith of the brethren would be endangered by various forms of failure, but that it would be anchored and confirmed upon the foundation of the universal Church through Peter’s unshaken and unfailing faith, like the support of a firm anchor.

No one denies this except one who openly attacks these very words of the Truth. For just as the entire door is governed by its hinge, so the welfare of the entire Church is arranged through Peter and his successors.

And just as a hinge, remaining immovable, guides the door as it opens and closes, so Peter and his successors possess free judgment concerning the whole Church, since no one ought to dislodge their position: the highest See is judged by no one.

For this reason their clerics are called cardinals, adhering especially closely to that hinge by which all other things are moved.

### XXXIII

Therefore, holding most firmly to Peter’s venerable institution, universally acknowledged throughout the world, [Col. 0765C] and to the faith of his fellow apostle and teacher of the nations, Paul, inscribed in the clearest script, we proclaim freely from the apostolic see to everyone what that same Paul said to the Galatians: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what was preached to you, let him be accursed. As I said before, and now I say again: if anyone preaches to you anything contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. I).

Nor will we be silent merely because we are said not to be what we ought to be, or what Peter is. Indeed, we ought to act thus if we were commending ourselves to anyone. But since, as the Apostle says, “we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as servants of his servants through Jesus” (II Cor. IV), it matters little to us whether we are judged by you [Col. 0765D] or by a human tribunal, “for the one who judges us is the Lord” (I Cor. IV). “For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends” (II Cor. X).

And, rejecting rash judgment, he says elsewhere: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master; and he will stand, for God is able to make him stand” (Rom. XIV).

### XXXIV

Indeed, although you swell with pride to the greatest degree and think excessively highly of yourselves, we do not believe that you would dare to say that you are what you ought to be, or what Alexander, John Chrysostom, or Flavian was. Nor did the Antiochene dare to profess himself such as Peter himself was, nor the Alexandrian claim himself equal to Mark or Athanasius, since they would have been [Col. 0766A] punished without reprieve by their own people.

Therefore, although pride urges you toward this, fear nevertheless restrains you. Yet, despite this, no one’s reproach prevents you from diligently demanding milk and wool from the sheep; nor do you fear that it may be said that you are not equal to those great predecessors of yours. Why is this, except that all priests, although unequal in merit, are nevertheless equal in office? What is owed on account of office cannot be denied on account of merit. Otherwise the priesthood would not endure if it became greater or lesser, or varied according to the diversity of human merits; there would be nearly as many priesthoods as there are people.

### XXXV

Therefore, brothers—would that we did not say this to our condemnation—we are like Peter and we are not like Peter: we are the same [Col. 0766B] in office, but not the same in merit. And whenever we demand milk and wool from the sheep of God—that is, payment and honor—no mention is made there of our merit; rather, the recompense due to our office is sought.

Thus, although we do not possess Peter’s merit, we carry out Peter’s office; and we demand the honors due to our office, as the Apostle says: “As long as I am a minister, I will honor my ministry” (Rom. II). And, warning Christ’s sheep to pay what is owed to each person, he says: “Render to all what is due; honor to whom honor is due” (Rom. XIII). This is not because it is good for those who receive it, but because it is evil for those who do not render it.

Thus also our most blessed predecessor Gregory says: “Let no one despise us on account of ourselves in Peter’s place, because from his chair, over which, by God’s authority, we preside, whatever we may be, our office claims the rights due to it.” [Col. 0766C]”

What we say often tends to happen: a powerful person in this world may have a despised servant. Yet when through him he gives some command to his own people or to strangers, the person of the servant sent is not despised, because reverence for the master who sent him is preserved in the heart. Shall a servant, then, deny to whatever fellow servants he may have at least what the Lord granted to the Pharisees and scribes sitting in Moses’ chair? “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ chair,” he says. “Therefore, whatever they tell you, observe and do” (Matt. XXIII).

Thus, the fact that we live badly is ours; but the fact that we speak good things belongs to the chair, on whose account [Col. 0766D] we are obliged to preach what is right. Hence that most experienced Paul says: “Whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is being proclaimed, and in this I rejoice, and I will continue to rejoice” (Phil. II). Behold, the Apostle considers such people so necessary that he rejoices over them. Who, then, are you to turn their negligence into an injury against the apostolic chair?

What are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord. By resisting his ordinance, you acquire condemnation for yourselves, since our power, like every power, comes from no one other than him. It must be understood that false justice produces disdain, whereas true justice produces compassion. You are deprived of this compassion by insulting rather than sympathizing with another’s calamity.

Perhaps you cannot approve [Col. 0767A] what you presume to bring forward or allege against us; indeed, it is clear that you cannot approve it. But let it be so. Behold, our judge is in heaven, and our witness is on high (Job XVI).

### XXXVI

As for the man, men, think of him whatever you wish. Yet conscience gives us one answer: we earnestly desire the salvation and exaltation of all the Churches of God.

But we cannot tolerate anyone seizing anything whatsoever out of pride and arrogating it to himself against our apostolic see and its laws. Whoever tries to nullify or diminish the authority or privileges of the Roman Church is plotting not the overthrow and destruction of one Church, but of all Christendom. By whose compassion or support [Col. 0767B] will daughters oppressed by anyone else continue to breathe, once that one mother has been suffocated? Whose refuge will they invoke? To whom will they flee? For she received Athanasius and all Catholics; she cherished and defended them, and restored those driven from their own sees.

### XXXVII

Therefore, desiring all of you with us in the inmost heart of Jesus Christ, we admonish you not to inflate yourselves against one another by seeking the false name of knowledge, justice, or glory; not to let ashes and earth grow dangerously proud; and not to let an abominable and wretched man, “drinking iniquity like water” (Job XV), follow outward things and cast away his inward self during his life.

Let us be one body and one spirit, just as we were called in one hope of our calling (Eph. IV). The very structure of the body [Col. 0767C] and its members should teach us how and how greatly the unity of the Church must be valued. For it is itself the body of Christ, as the Apostle says: “You are the body of Christ and members, each of another” (I Cor. XII).

And just as in one body there are many members, yet all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another (Rom. XII). If the ear or the hand says, “I am not an eye; I am not part of the body,” is it therefore not part of the body? If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? (I Cor. XII)—and the other senses?

But now God has arranged the members of the body as he wished, each suited to its own office. A member that is not content with its own office, but desires to seize another’s, disturbs the entire order of the body. Suppose sight tried to distinguish voices, hearing colors, [Col. 0767D] taste odors, smell hard or soft things, and touch flavors: would they not all suffer in vain?

Thus the adornments or garments of individual members are not suitable or appropriate for every member; each requires what belongs to it and rejects what is alien. The foot refuses a crown, helmet, or cap, and the head does not apply sandals or foot-coverings to its own use. So too, although the dignity and great usefulness of the hands may fashion the splendid crown of imperial power, the hands do not adapt or place it upon themselves, but upon the head, content with their own bracelets, armlets, and rings.

The same occurs in the other members. There is such a discordant concord among them that each absolutely refuses to assign its own function to another; yet each rejoices equally in the good of one member, just as all grieve together at its evil. They perform their functions not only for themselves, but rather for their mutual benefit.

Hence the same Apostle continues: [Col. 0768A] “If one member is glorified, all the members rejoice together” (I Cor. XIII). What folly it is not to imitate what we are, and not to consider what we have received for maintaining this transitory life for a time, so that we may endure forever.

### XXXVIII

Since, above all, the pestilential mother Pride and her most savage daughters—namely envy and vainglory—are everywhere, with obstinate rage, striving to disembowel and tear apart Christ’s body, let us not become desirous of vainglory, provoking and envying one another (Gal. V), lest, God forbid, the Apostle’s saying come upon us: “If you bite [Col. 0768B] and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (ibid.).

And likewise the saying of James: “If you have bitter jealousy and rivalry in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but earthly, unspiritual, demonic. But the wisdom from above is first chaste, then peaceable, modest, open to persuasion, loving the good, without dissimulation” (Jas. III).

Distinguish these two kinds of wisdom, so strongly opposed to each other, with vigilant minds. And if Peter, uniquely the figure of our supreme Head and his vicar, and his successors on earth, retain a special dignity over the earthly and heavenly kingdom, [Col. 0768C] do not envy or disparage the summit of the Roman Church. Through charity you are all able to attain it, and yourselves to reign in us.

Otherwise you will hear what was said above: “Already you are full; already you have become rich; you have begun to reign without us—and would that you did reign, so that we might reign with you!” (I Cor. IV).

### XXXIX

Behold, we regard your glory as our own. Why do you strive to abolish what has been granted to us by divine and human authority? Does not the hand or foot regard the honor or dishonor of its head as its own? It does not grieve, but rather rejoices, when the body, endowed with one sense—that is, touch alone—has a head placed above it that possesses all the senses, since the head makes them serve and watch over the interests of the body subject to it.

The head, judging all the senses, is judged by no sense, since it is entirely sufficient by its own judgment, as the Apostle [Col. 0768D] says: “The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (I Cor. I).

If you do not perceive within yourselves what has been said above about the harmony of our body, you are not in the body, nor do you live in the body. And if you are not in Christ’s body, which is the Church, you do not live from it either. Consider, then, where and what you are. You have been cut off; you are rotting; and, like a branch cut from the vine, you have been cast outside and are withering, so that you may be thrown into the fire and burn—which may divine mercy keep far from you.

### XL

But since we now seem to have exceeded the proper limits of a letter, we have considered it fitting to reply in another opening to your calumny, which you did not hesitate to direct to our brothers and fellow bishops in Apulia, to disparage our unleavened bread and promote your leavened bread. [Col. 0769A]

Along with this letter, we are sending some writings of our venerable Fathers that contradict your quibbles concerning these matters; then, as God inspires us, our own replies, so that your arrows may be repeatedly blunted and driven back, and strike the one you do not wish them to strike.

For if you are not ashamed or afraid of your loquacity, we ought to fear our silence even more than we ought to be ashamed of it, since the souls of many depend upon us. If false brothers accuse while we remain silent, those souls are bound to perish.

### XLI

Meanwhile, we reply to you with paternal tenderness and brotherly affection on these matters. We believe that we have sufficiently held back, lest we fall into Solomon’s saying: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, [Col. 0769B] lest you become like him” (Prov. XXVI).

But if you do not repent, you will experience what he immediately adds: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself” (ibid.). And the Apostle’s command: “Avoid a heretical person after one or two admonitions, knowing that such a person is perverted and sinful, being self-condemned” (Tit. III).

And, avoiding the typological prohibition of the ancient law, we will not henceforth boil a kid in its mother’s milk; rather, we will vigorously rub its rash and scabies with biting vinegar and much salt. For what cannot be touched and healed with a gentle hand must be cut away with pain, as the Lord warns, saying: “If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. And if your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out [Col. 0769C]” (Matt. XVIII).

But may God’s mercy precede these words of ours and spare both us and you, so that henceforth it may not be necessary to occupy ourselves with questions and quarrels over words, but that we may console one another in our pilgrimage through this world from the divine pages, and exhort one another peacefully, as the Psalmist sings: “Great peace have those who love your law, O Lord, and there is no stumbling block for them” (Ps. CXVIII).

That charity and the unity of the brothers are themselves the law of God is shown by the Gospel’s saying: “This is my commandment, that you love one another” (John XIII).

May he who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (I Tim. II) grant that we preserve this charity sincerely here, and in the future behold without end the one who is God. [Col. 0769D] Amen.

### CI. Letter of Saint Leo to Peter, Bishop of Antioch

He congratulates him on his devotion toward the apostolic see. He confirms his ordination, provided that he was promoted according to the canons. He urges him to defend the dignity of his Church. He approves the faith written to him by Peter as identical with that held by the Roman Church, and sends him the principal articles of that faith. (Year 1054.)

*[Mansi, Concilia XIX, 660.]*

**Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop Peter.**

We greatly rejoice in the Lord over your most holy fraternity, and, as is fitting, we render manifold thanks to him who is the true peace and charity [Col. 0770A] of his own, because at last, through you, dearest brother, the zeal of the holy Church of Antioch appears to have blossomed again, and to perceive what ought to be perceived.

For by this all will know that we are Christ’s disciples—we who were first called Christians in that great Antioch itself—if we have love for one another (John XII), and if we all say the same thing, with no divisions among us, and are perfect in the same understanding and in the same knowledge (I Cor. I).

For God, who is one, does not dwell in divisions of mind, but only in unity and a pure heart; he makes those of one mind dwell in a house. Otherwise the house will be rebellious, no longer worthy to be called the Church of God, but rather the synagogue of the evil one.

Moreover, just as it is disastrous when unity is absent among the good, so it is ruinous when it is present among the wicked. You, viewing this from the watchtower [Col. 0770B] of that holy Church over which you appear to have been divinely appointed as watchman, have prudently considered your promotion to the episcopal dignity—which, as you assert, was accomplished by the election of clergy and people—and have taken care to announce and explain your faith to the apostolic and first see, over which, by God’s authority, we preside, unworthy though we are, according to the pious and most necessary practice of ancient custom.

In this action, let your affection know that we have been greatly refreshed and rejoiced in the Lord, because you did not delay doing what was especially necessary for yourself and for the Church over which you preside temporarily.

Indeed, by consulting our apostolic see from your apostolic see, we understand that you do not wish to deviate from the concordant decree of the Lord and of all the holy Fathers, by which the holy Roman and apostolic see is inviolably placed as head over [Col. 0770C] all the Churches throughout the world, and to which the greater and more difficult cases of all the Churches are referred for decision.

Thus all venerable councils teach; thus human laws promulgate; thus the Holy of holies himself, King of kings and Lord of lords, confirms it: so that the principal dignity and venerable summit of all ecclesiastical discipline may shine forth and excel there where Peter, the summit and hinge of the apostles, awaits the blessed resurrection of his flesh on the last day.

He alone is the one for whom the Lord and Savior declares that he prayed, so that his faith would not fail, saying: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat; but [Col. 0770D] I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII).

That venerable and effective prayer obtained that Peter’s faith has not failed until now, nor is it believed that it will fail on his throne throughout the ages of ages. Rather, it will strengthen the hearts of the brothers, who will be shaken by various trials of faith, just as it has not ceased to strengthen them until now.

Because of this excellence, Antioch holds the third rank after the Roman Church. We urge you most earnestly to defend it—not for the sake of your own glory, but for the ancient honor of the see over which you preside for a time. Let no pomp or arrogance deter you from this purpose; steadfastly defend the honor that all the councils of the holy Fathers left to the Church of Antioch.

For this purpose, if necessary, the greatest mother—the Roman and first see—will [Col. 0771A] never and nowhere fail so beloved a daughter, indeed, her partner. We say all this because we have heard that certain people are attempting to diminish the ancient dignity of the Church of Antioch.

As for your request that we compassionately address the causes of division in the universal Church, we confess that, through the mercy of the Lord, we still hold most firmly to the bond of holy unity. We do not see that we have suffered schismatic harm anywhere, since the integrity of concord and the fullness of ecclesiastical discipline govern us continually.

Each of us is owed honor, and each person’s rights are preserved. No one is arrogantly permitted to transgress the boundaries established by our fathers. Rather, let your fraternity look carefully [Col. 0771B] to ensure that no root of bitterness and dissension—God forbid!—grows up in your regions, through which many may be defiled and which may need to be uprooted from the field of the Catholic Church by the sharp sickle of the holy canons.

My humility, exalted at the summit of the apostolic throne so that it may approve what is approved and condemn what is condemned, gladly approves, praises, and confirms the episcopal promotion of your most holy fraternity. It earnestly entreats the common Lord that what you are now said to be with human lips, you may prove to be before his eyes.

You should know, however, that we approve your promotion only if you did not obtain it as a neophyte, a curial official, or a bigamist, or through money, or in any other manner contrary to the sacred canons—God forbid!

As for your faith, which you set forth in your own writing to the supreme [Col. 0771C] and apostolic see, we declare it sound, Catholic, and orthodox in every respect. We embrace it as truly one and salutary, and, rejoicing greatly in the Lord over your affection, we profess with devoted heart and ready speech that it is our own faith.

For I firmly believe that the holy Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is one almighty God, and that the entire Godhead in the Trinity is of one essence and substance, coeternal and co-omnipotent, of one will, power, and majesty; the Creator of all creatures, from whom all things exist, through whom all things exist, and in whom all things exist, those in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible.

I also believe that each individual person in the holy Trinity is one true, complete, and perfect God.

I further believe that the Son of God the Father himself, the Word of God, was eternally begotten before all ages from the Father, consubstantial, co-omnipotent, and in every respect coequal with the Father in divinity; that he was born in time from the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-Virgin, with a rational soul; that he has two births, one eternal from the Father and the other temporal from his mother; that he has two wills and operations; that he is true God and true man, proper and perfect in each nature; that he suffered neither mixture nor division; that he is neither adopted nor merely apparent; and that he is the one and only God, the Son of God, in two natures but in the singularity of one person.

He is impassible and immortal in his divinity, but in his humanity [Col. 0772A] he suffered for us and for our salvation with a true suffering of the flesh, was buried, and rose from the dead on the third day with a true resurrection of the flesh. To confirm this, after his resurrection he ate with his disciples—not from any need for food, but solely by will and power. On the fortieth day he ascended into heaven with the flesh in which he had risen and with his soul, and sits at the right hand of the Father. On the tenth day thereafter he sent the Holy Spirit. From there, just as he ascended, he will come to judge the living and the dead and repay each according to his works.

I also believe that the Holy Spirit is full, perfect, and true God, proceeding from the Father and the Son, coequal, coessential, and co-omnipotent, in every respect coeternal with the Father and the Son, and that he spoke through the prophets.

[Col. 0772B] I believe and confess this holy and undivided Trinity not as three gods, but as one almighty, eternal, invisible, and immutable God in three persons and one nature or essence. I truly proclaim the Father unbegotten, the Son only-begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son.

I believe that the holy Catholic and apostolic Church is one true Church, in which there is one baptism and true remission of all sins.

I also believe in the true resurrection of this same flesh which I now bear, and in eternal life.

I also believe that the God and almighty Lord is the one author of the New and Old Testaments, of the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles; that God predestined only good things, but foreknew [Col. 0772C] both good and evil. I believe and profess that God’s grace precedes and follows the human person, yet in such a way that I do not deny free will to rational creatures.

I believe and proclaim that the soul is not a part of God, but was created from nothing, and that, without baptism, it is subject to original sin.

Moreover, I anathematize every heresy that exalts itself against the holy Catholic Church, and likewise anyone who believes or venerates as authoritative any writings other than those which the Catholic Church receives.

I entirely receive the four councils and venerate them as the four Gospels (Gregory, Letter 24, Book I), because, through the four regions of the world, the universal Church stands founded upon them as upon a four-sided stone. [Col. 0772D]

The first is the Council of Nicaea, of three hundred and eighteen Fathers, under the blessed Roman pope Sylvester and the great Emperor Constantine, presided over by the Roman priests Victor and Vincentius.

The second is the First Council of Constantinople, of one hundred and fifty Fathers, under Pope Damasus and the elder Theodosius.

The third is the First Council of Ephesus, of two hundred Fathers, under Pope Celestine and the younger Theodosius.

The fourth is the Council of Chalcedon, of six hundred and thirty Fathers, under the blessed Pope Leo and the Emperor Marcian.
