In the same way I receive and venerate the remaining three councils: the Second Council of Constantinople, under Pope Vigilius and the Emperor Justinian; then the Third Council of Constantinople against the Monothelites, under Pope Agatho and Constantine, the grandson [Col. 0773A] of Heraclius; and finally the Second Council of Nicaea, under Pope Adrian and Constantine, the son of Irene, concerning the reverend images of the Lord Jesus Christ and of the saints.

Whatever the seven holy and universal councils mentioned above judged and praised, I judge and praise; and whoever they anathematized, I anathematize.

The holy Roman and apostolic see believes this faith in its heart for righteousness and confesses it with its mouth for salvation (Rom. X). By the Lord’s gift it strives to live according to it and, if necessary, is prepared to die for its defense. We recognize that this faith is perfect in you also, dearest brother, and we admonish you to live with us according to it, knowing with certainty that “faith without works is dead” (Jas. II).

With the entire fraternity [Col. 0773B] or college of the holy Roman and apostolic see, we greet your holy fraternity and the entire college subject to you in the Lord. We earnestly ask that you continually pray to almighty God for our twofold salvation, reverend and longed-for brother.

### CII. Letter of Saint Leo to Michael, Patriarch of Constantinople

He congratulates him because he was striving to reconcile the Greeks with the Latins. He reproves him both for attempting to subject the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch to his authority and for arrogating to himself the title of universal patriarch; he also reproves him for condemning the Roman Church, which celebrates the holy Eucharist with unleavened bread. He proves that Christ consecrated with unleavened bread. (Year 1054.)

*[Mansi XIX, 663.]*

[Col. 0773C]

**Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Michael, archbishop of Constantinople.**

The writings of your honored fraternity have finally reached us. In them you strive to exhort people to the good of concord and unity, which is most necessary and must be embraced by all Christ’s faithful, so that, after excessively long and harmful disagreements, the daughter may rejoice in reconciliation with her own mother.

We wish to listen all the more readily to you as you provoke and admonish us toward this, the more attentively we recognize that this alone is the proper and distinctive virtue of the devout and holy. For the other virtues may be common to the good and the wicked, as the Lord demonstrates: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII).

And Paul declares: “Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. XII).

Therefore we rejoice greatly with your fraternity in the Lord, because by your diligence you have anticipated our greatest desire. Indeed, if you had been slow to carry it out through any chill of charity, our own diligence ought to have preceded yours.

For, in accordance with the Apostle mentioned above, we greatly desire, “if it is possible, to live at peace with all people” (Rom. XII). How much more, then, with you, whom we see able to become a highly useful and necessary minister of the Church of God, provided that you do not strive to transgress the boundaries established by our fathers? [Col. 0774A]

And since Christian perfection consists in being peaceful even with those who are enemies of peace, in hope of correction and not in agreement with wickedness, we ought to remove all occasions of scandal from our midst with all the greater care, the more firmly we desire to retain the friends of peace. [Col. 0773D]

For a long time, rumor has brought many intolerable reports concerning your fraternity to our ears. We have left them unexamined until now, partly because they seemed incredible and partly because no opportunity was granted us to investigate such matters.

In particular, you are said to be a neophyte and not to have advanced step by step to the episcopal dignity. Both the Apostle (I Tim. III) and the venerable canons teach that this must by no means be done.

Then, driven by new ambition, [Col. 0774B] you are attempting to deprive the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch of the ancient privileges of their dignity and to subject them to your rule, against every divine and human law. How dangerous this attempt is for you is clear to everyone of sound mind.

For, lifted up by vainglory and worldly pomp, you are striving to alter the ancient plan of the divine will concerning the establishment of the pillars [Col. 0774C] of his Church [Here something is missing: perhaps “to change,” or something similar], as though you intended to prejudice him through deceitful riches who, although truly and uniquely rich, became poor for us (II Cor. VIII) and chose for his temporal birth a little town and a shelter in a cave (Luke II), not some royal palace.

Whoever recoils from his examples belongs to the lot of him who then through himself and now through his satellites dares to say: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV).

But “my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways, says the Lord” (Isa. LV), who scatters the proud in his wrath, looks upon every arrogant person and humbles him, and rises so that no human being may prevail, before whom there is no God.

So that pride might not imagine that, because of its height, it was joined to God, the Psalmist says: “The exalted Lord recognizes from afar” (Ps. CXXXVII). Hence he himself testifies: “What is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God” (Luke XVI).

What could be more sacrilegious, detestable, and lamentable than that usurpation by which you proclaim yourself universal patriarch everywhere, both in writing and in speech, when every friend of God has hitherto shuddered at being honored with such a title?

And after Christ, who could properly be distinguished by this title except the one to whom the divine voice says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI), and so forth?

Nevertheless, because he is not found to have been called the universal apostle, although he was appointed prince of the apostles, none of his successors ever consented to be called by so monstrous a title, even though the holy Council of Chalcedon decreed this for our predecessor Leo the Great and his successors.

They clearly understood that he is not the friend of the bridegroom who wishes to be loved in the bridegroom’s place, but rather a bridal attendant and procurer of Antichrist, who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped. [Col. 0774D]

Behold that John of yours, whose insane invention you continue to inherit, who, according to the Psalmist, still calls his lands after his own names through you, [Col. 0775A] although when he died he did not take everything with him, nor did glory descend with him into hell, because, when he was in honor, he did not understand (Ps. XLIII).

He was anathematized for this insolence by the most blessed pontiffs Pelagius and Gregory (Pelagius II, Letter I; Gregory, Book VI, Letter IV, and Book VII, Letter XXX), and by their successors. He died unreformed in his obstinacy, and for four hundred and forty years his followers have not ceased to plunge headlong after his contumacy.

What did pride profit them? What did the boast of riches contribute? “Everything passed away like a shadow” (Wis. V). Finally, what does it profit a person to gain the whole world but suffer the loss of his soul? [Col. 0775B] (Matt. XVI.)

And how can you lay down your lives for your brothers when you disdain to abandon an empty name that scandalizes the whole Church? Repent, then, we beg you, of this madness, lest you too—God forbid!—become the companion of him of whom it is said: “He sees every proud person, and he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job XLI).

Who would not be astonished at this: after so many holy and orthodox Fathers, after one thousand and twenty years from the Savior’s Passion, you have emerged as a new calumniator of the Latin Church, anathematizing all who participated in the sacraments from unleavened bread and stirring up public persecution?

Your presumption was brought to us both by report and by the text of the letters sent under your name to the Apulians. These letters [Col. 0775C] attempt to assert by force that the bread with which the Lord entrusted the mystery of his body to his apostles at the Supper was leavened.

That this is entirely false is very easily detected from both Testaments. For Christ, who had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, fulfilled the old Passover according to the command of the Law with unleavened bread and wine; and immediately, with unleavened bread and wine, he gave the new Passover to his disciples, as Luke plainly relates.

For throughout those eight days no leavened bread appeared anywhere in the territory of Israel, and anyone with whom it was found perished from his people (Exod. XII). If it had appeared at the Supper of the Lord Jesus, or if he or his disciples had tasted it in any manner, they would justly have perished as transgressors [Col. 0775D] of the Law. Nor would the Lord himself have said to his adversaries: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John VIII).

There would have been no need to seek false witnesses in order to destroy him, since he would justly have been destroyed on this one account. But he “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (II Pet. II). What he commanded his disciples to do, he clearly recalled through the Apostle, in whom he was speaking, saying: “Let us celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (II Cor. XIII).

Finally, “a little leaven leavens the whole lump” (I Cor. V). Wherever there is corruption, there is without doubt deterioration of nature and the introduction of some vice.

Moreover, our Pascha is called new for this reason: the former was prescribed to the Israelites in memory of their departure from Egypt [Col. 0776A], whereas this one is for Christians in memory of the Lord’s Passion, by which he passed from this world to the Father. But since you will be instructed more fully, both about these matters and about the others concerning which you accuse us, by our messengers through other writings of ours that they carry, it is enough to have touched on them briefly here. Let your fraternity, at least after this admonition, learn to speak cautiously and humbly, lest the Lord should at some time say to you also: “The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Matt. XII).

You have indeed written to us that, if one Roman Church through us bore your name, all the churches throughout the world would through you bear our name. What sort of monstrosity is this, dearest brother? Does the Roman Church, the head and mother of the churches, have no members and daughters? And how can it be called head or mother? For we believe—and therefore speak and constantly profess—that the Roman Church is so far from being alone or, as you suppose, one only, that whatever nation throughout the world proudly dissents from it is no longer to be called or regarded as any church at all, but as nothing whatever—indeed, as a gathering of heretics, a conventicle of schismatics, and a synagogue of Satan.

You seem to utter what holy Elijah then presumed concerning himself: “I alone am left” (III Kings XIX). But hear what he heard from the Lord: “I have left to myself seven thousand men” (III Kings XVIII). Cease, cease now, venerable brother, from these superstitions, lest Solomon’s saying be applied to you: “There are those who pretend to be rich, possessing nothing” (Prov. XIII). This is plainly most like the devil’s arrogance. Thinking that the kingdoms of the world, made by the Creator of all, were his own, he said to him: “All these things I will give you” (Matt. IV).

Therefore let us now return to our senses, and let such pernicious scandals be removed from our midst; then, according to the Psalmist, “the Lord will speak peace to his people, and to his saints, and to those who turn back to the heart” (Ps. XXXIV). For we cannot have any peace with the stubborn who remain in their error, lest we share in the works of the wicked; nor do we find that the Lord Christ ever did such things anywhere. Even at his birth the angels announced peace only to people of good will. He also indicates that the eye causing scandal must be plucked out, and the hand or foot causing scandal must be cut off [Col. 0776D].

Let heresies and schisms therefore cease; then, for those who love the law of God, there will no longer be scandal but abundant peace. Whoever boasts of the Christian name, let him cease to curse and assail the holy and apostolic Roman Church; for he honors the master of a household in vain who dishonors his wife. And in vain does he magnify the head and face of the mistress of a household who, while attacking her least children, tramples them as though they were her toes.

Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: “How evil in reputation is one who flees from his father; and he is accursed by God who provokes his mother” (Eccles. III). And in Proverbs: “The eye that mocks its father and despises its mother, let the ravens of the valleys pluck it out, and the sons of the eagle devour it” (Prov. XXX).

Nevertheless, we trust [Col. 0777A] through divine goodness that you will either be found innocent of these things or corrected, or that, at any rate, after being admonished, you will quickly correct yourself. When this has been accomplished, our peace will not return to us but will rest upon you, as upon a son of peace; and genuine charity will reign between us, proceeding from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (I Tim. I). You will not need to supplicate us, but to command. In addition, collaborate, as you have begun, so that the two greatest kingdoms may be joined together in the desired peace.

May the Holy Trinity preserve your honorable fraternity, which prays for us, forever.

Given in the month of January, in the year 1054, indiction VII.

### CIII. Letter of Saint Leo to Constantine Monomachus

He praises him for seeking to reconcile peace between Latins and Greeks. He urges him to defend the Roman Church. He complains of the arrogance of Michael of Constantinople and commends the legates. (Year 1054.)

[Mansi, XIX, 667.]

[Col. 0777B]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the glorious and religious emperor of New Rome, Constantine Monomachus, beloved son, greeting.

How great the thanks we ought continually to render to the holy and undivided Trinity, creator and governor of all, for his ineffable gift by which he works all things in all (I Cor. XII), we can also discern from your devotion and religious diligence, most glorious son and most serene emperor. He has shown you to our times as such a man and, in his gratuitous goodness, has provided for us through you; by your faithful aid we trust that the condition of the holy and Catholic Church will be restored and the commonwealth of the earthly empire improved.

For after exceedingly long and destructive dissensions, you are becoming the first proclaimer, bearer, and eagerly desired enforcer of peace and concord. With the most humble Paul, that chosen vessel, you seem to say: “We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us; we beseech you on Christ’s behalf, be reconciled” (II Cor. V)—to him “who is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II).

Indeed, as the offspring of a religious and excellent character, you do not forget the groans of your mother. You do not regard her as contemptible because she has grown old, but rather consider her worthy of reverence; and with a heart full of charity you intend to return to her, so that you may become dearer and closer to the one God and Father of all, the more kind and humble you are toward that principal mother. For your wisdom is not unaware of what is written in Ecclesiasticus: “A father’s blessing strengthens the houses of sons; but a mother’s curse uproots their foundations” (Eccles. III). And this: “Do not abandon the law of your mother; bind it continually upon your heart” (Prov. I).

These proverbs take care to commend to us the mother who generates and instructs us for eternal life, rather than the one who gives birth to us for death and loves and instructs us carnally. Unless the former succeeds her, to regenerate and nourish us, the latter undoubtedly consigns her children to the second death.

Moreover, this Catholic mother and incorrupt virgin, although she has occupied the whole earth and the boundaries of the world and filled them with her members, nevertheless raises and presents one head for all to revere and regard [Col. 0778A]. Whoever dishonors it counts himself among her members in vain. Your imperial majesty entirely knows what this is: namely, the one whom Christ’s voice placed above and wished to preside over all, and whom the succeeding piety of the Church and the universal agreement of the holy Fathers have continually celebrated to this day.

You too intend to honor his venerable face, not ungrateful toward her who fittingly adorned your head with the diadem of earthly rule, made you both feared and loved by the peoples, and anointed you with the chrism of adoption so that you might reign forever. For that ancient and now veteran Rome herself nurtured, advanced, and set above all mortals the first most noble and religious Constantine, whose lineage you glory in and whose power you magnify, and whose famous city, named from him, she produced for temporal rule; nor did she cease her benefactions until she crowned him with the glory of the eternal kingdom [Col. 0778B].

Therefore, while magnifying your excellence with manifold thanksgiving, most glorious son, we are filled with the greater joy at your devotion and recognition, the more numerous the souls that depend upon your government and rely upon your example. And for that reason we do not cease to pray to the common Lord, through whom kings reign and princes decree what is just (Prov. VIII), that he may preserve you long-lived in his good pleasure and fulfill your desire with good things.

Moreover, I myself, however unworthy a vicar of the apostolic see, striving according to the measure of my humility and ability to discharge the office of administration entrusted to me, in accordance with Paul’s divine utterance—“Woe is me if I do not evangelize; for necessity lies upon me” (I Cor. IX)—am about to render an account to the eternal and strict Judge for the governance of one Church, [that is, from] the merit of all the churches [Col. 0778C].

With that concern, therefore, with which I must watch over all the churches, seeing an undisciplined and alien people rise everywhere against the churches of God with incredible and unheard-of fury and with impiety worse than pagan, slaughter Christians, afflict some with new and horrible tortures even to the point of death, spare neither infant nor old person nor female weakness out of any regard for humanity, recognize no distinction between sacred and profane, and plunder, burn, and raze to the ground the basilicas of the saints [Col. 0778D], I have very often rebuked, entreated, preached against, and pressed its perversity, in season and out of season; I have announced the terror of divine and human vengeance.

But because the Wise Man says, “No one can correct one whom God has rejected, and a fool is not corrected” (Eccles. VII), its wickedness remained so hardened and obstinate that day by day it added worse things to the worst. Therefore, desiring not only to expend external goods for the liberation of Christ’s sheep but also very eagerly wishing to expend myself, it seemed to me, as a testimony to their wickedness or, if that should be expedient, for the suppression of their obstinacy, that human defense should be drawn from every quarter. I heard from the Apostle that rulers do not bear the sword without cause, but are God’s ministers, avengers for wrath against everyone who does evil; and that rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to evil (Rom. XIII); and that kings and commanders are sent by God for the punishment of wrongdoers [Col. 0779A].

Supported, therefore, by such an escort as the shortness of time and the impending necessity permitted, I judged that I ought to seek a meeting and counsel with your most faithful servant, the glorious duke and master Argyros—not because I desired the destruction or death of any Nortmann or of any other person, or was plotting death, but so that at least those who have no fear of divine judgments might come to their senses through human fear.

Meanwhile, while we attempted to break their obstinacy by salutary admonition and they, on the other hand, falsely promised every submission, they suddenly attacked our escort. Yet they now grieve over their victory more than they rejoice in it. For, as your piety took care to write for our consolation, because of this presumption of theirs they expect a greater indignation to descend upon them shortly, in addition to what they have already experienced—the diminution of their band [Col. 0779B].

We too, believing that divine assistance will be present to us and that human help will not be lacking, shall not abandon this purpose of liberating Christendom, nor shall we give rest to our days except with the rest of the holy Church in peril. For acquiring and securing this we have, through divine goodness, the greatest comfort and protection in our dearest and most illustrious son, the emperor Henry. We await from day to day his promised and imminent arrival, since he is hastening to our aid with an imperial army and expedition [Col. 0779C].

For this purpose heavenly grace has also inspired your serenity, so that, with you two on either side, as though with two arms driving the hostile people away from the Church of Christ and scattering them far off, the honor of afflicted Christendom may now be restored and the condition of the commonwealth reestablished.

And because, while iniquity abounded and charity grew cold, the holy Roman Church and apostolic see had for far too long been besieged by hirelings rather than shepherds—men who sought their own things, not the things of Jesus Christ—and had until now lain miserably devastated, divine counsel willed that my humility should assume the burden of so great a chair. Although the weakness of my shoulders is greatly weighed down and oppressed by it, I have no small measure of holy hope, since on either side such sons, distinguished in religion and power, stand beside me [Col. 0779D].

Therefore, most devoted son and most serene emperor, deign to collaborate with us for the restoration of your mother, the holy Church, and for the recovery of her privileges of dignity and reverence, as well as her patrimonies in the regions under your authority, as you will be able clearly to learn from the writings and deeds of our venerable predecessors—or of yours.

You, therefore, great successor of the great Constantine, made so by blood, name, and empire, we exhort to become also an imitator of his devotion toward the apostolic see. Whatever that remarkable man bestowed upon, confirmed for, and defended on behalf of that see after Christ, do you, in accordance with the etymology of your name, steadfastly help to recover, retain, and defend [Col. 0780A]. Thus, fighting in a singular way on God’s behalf, you will be called by the name by which you have long been called among human beings.

Our most glorious son Henry is striving to accomplish all this in his own regions. All these things will come to us and to you more happily and abundantly when, as soon as possible, with the grace of God going before, with the blessed leaders of the apostles interceding, and with me, however unworthy a vicar of theirs, mediating and securing it, the firmest treaty of peace and friendship between you both has been established.

Furthermore, our confrater, Archbishop Michael, sent us letters exhorting us to concord and unity. We must receive one who admonishes us toward so desirable and necessary a good with the greater devotion and eagerness, the more clearly we consider that no one can be counted among Christ’s disciples who disdains to submit to fraternal peace, since the Lord says to his own: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII); and the great Paul declares: “Pursue peace with all and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebr. XII).

But let your glory know that many and intolerable matters concerning his presumptions have long since reached our ears. In particular, inflamed by open persecution against the Latin Church, he did not fear to anathematize all who handle the sacraments with unleavened bread; and, attempting to deprive the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch of their ancient dignity, he seeks in a new ambition to subject them to himself contrary to law and justice; as for the many other things he is said to usurp, you will be able to learn them carefully from our messengers [Col. 0780C].

If in these matters he should be obstinate—which God forbid—he will in no way be able to retain our peace, for undoubtedly it will return to us, as the Lord says, if he refuses to be a son of peace (Luke X). Hence the Apostle also says: “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. XII).

Indeed, he honors the master of a household in vain who dishonors his wife. And in vain does he magnify the head and face of the mistress of a household who attacks even the least of her children, trampling them as though they were her toes. Against such a person the wisdom of God thunders in Ecclesiasticus: “How evil in reputation is one who flees from his father, and he is accursed by God who provokes his mother” (Eccles. III).

Nevertheless, we trust that, with God’s grace going before, he will be found innocent of these matters, or corrected, or will quickly come to his senses after being admonished; and that he will prove to be not what he is said to be, but what we piously desire and hope him to be.

For this reason we commend to your glory in every respect the sons presently with you, our messengers of the holy Roman and apostolic see, so that, as is fitting, they may be received generously, treated reverently, kindly, and honorably, heard reasonably and patiently, and sent back to us as soon as possible, lest they regret having undertaken so great a labor in vain and we be ashamed of having sent them.

As for the bishop from Amalfi, let no suspicion arise in you, for he is entirely Roman and, having withdrawn from the Amalfitans, has lived familiarly with us now for almost a full year.

May the blessed God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation (I Cor. I), deign to bless your excellence with every spiritual blessing and fill you with every joy and peace, so that in the present age you may rule happily for many years, and in the future may enjoy blessedly, without end, the kingdom of heaven with the King of kings and Lord of lords. You are honorable and desirable to us in Christ, son and glorious Augustus. Amen.

### CIV. Saint Leo confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Salvator and Saint Mary of Nienburg, at the request of Abbot Albuin, “for the love of God and at the request of his faithful Richerius, abbot of Monte Cassino, and through the intervention of Abbot Egbert of Fulda.” (Year 1054.)

[Knaut, *Grundliche Furstellung*, p. 17, according to Jaffé, *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*, p. 379. — Incipit: “If grants are always to be made.”]

[Col. 0781B]

### CV. Saint Leo grants to Albuin, abbot of Saint Mary of Nienburg, and to his successors, “at the request of Richerius, abbot of Monte Cassino” (cf. Leo’s *Chronicle of the Monastery of Monte Cassino*, p. 686), that they may use dalmatics and sandals in administering sacred rites. (The year 1054 should be read instead of 1048, as shown by the sixth year of the pontificate and indiction VII.)

[Beckmann, *History of the Principality of Anhalt*, according to Jaffé, *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*, p. 379. — Incipit: “If shepherds of sheep.”]

### CV bis. Saint Leo IX writes concerning the chastity of clerics against the letter of Nicetas, abbot of the monastery of Studium. Fragments.

[Mansi, *Councils*, XIX, 696.]

[Col. 0781C]

The Fathers count Book I of Clement, the *Itinerary of the Apostle Peter*, and the *Canons of the Apostles* among the apocrypha, excepting fifty chapters, which they decreed should be added to the orthodox books.

[Col. 0782A]

Among us no one is admitted even to the rank of subdeacon unless he professes perpetual continence, even from his own wife; nor is anyone permitted to take a wife after attaining that rank.

Leo IX, in the letter mentioned above.

He proceeds systematically and explicitly concerning what the Holy Roman Church also does regarding the ranks of clerics. If clerics—doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, and acolytes—are found outside the [usual] garb and habit of a monk and do not wish to profess continence, it permits them to marry a virgin with priestly blessing, but not a repudiated widow. Whoever does so may thereafter neither be promoted to the subdiaconate nor, if a layman has taken a non-virgin as wife or is a bigamist, be admitted to the clergy.

If anyone from the aforementioned orders wishes to ascend to the subdiaconate, he cannot do so without his wife’s consent, so that their carnal marriage may thereafter become a spiritual union, with no one compelling them. Nor is the wife afterward permitted to be joined carnally to the same husband, nor may she marry anyone else during his life or after his death [Col. 0782B].

The same, in the same place.

We absolutely confess that it is not permissible for a bishop, priest, deacon, or subdeacon to cast away his own wife from his care for the sake of religion—that is, so that he may provide her with food and clothing—but not so that he may lie with her carnally according to custom. Thus we read that the holy apostles acted, the blessed Apostle Paul saying: “Do we not have the right to lead about a sister as a wife, as the brothers of the Lord [and] Cephas?” [Col. 0782C]

See, foolish man, that he did not say, “Do we not have the right to embrace a sister as a wife,” but “to lead her about”—namely, so that she might be supported by them from the reward of preaching, while nevertheless thereafter no carnal marriage would continue between them.

## Spurious

[Col. 0781]

### CVI. Bull of Saint Leo IX in which he declares that he dedicated the church of Saint Arnulf and conferred many privileges upon the abbot and brothers of the same monastery. (Year 1049.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, XIII, 394, from the archive of Saint Arnulf.]

[Col. 0781D]

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greeting and apostolic blessing to the church specially dedicated by us in honor of the blessed John the Evangelist and Saint Arnulf, confessor of Christ, and through it to the venerable Abbot Warinus, his successors, and the monks serving God there.

Although we must always care for all the churches of God, we ought nevertheless to look after those upon whom, by the cooperation of divine mercy, we lay the hand of holy blessing with more attentive care and more watchful diligence in every respect.

Therefore we do not wish the diligence of Christ’s faithful, both present and future, to be unaware of how, solemnly invited to that city by our venerable confrater Adalbero, bishop of Metz, we consecrated to Christ, among the other things which by divine favor we brought there for correction, the monastery of Saint Arnulf, confessor of Christ, on the fifth day before the Ides of October [Col. 0782C].

Desiring therefore to add one dignity to this dignity, we do not withhold from the aforementioned church the privilege of our authority [Col. 0782D]. We therefore will and decree by the sacred authority of the first see that the same church, and the most sacred table of the Lord itself dedicated by us in his honor, shall inviolably possess this privilege: apart from bishops and abbots, the seven priests of the same monastery, and three canons from the house of Saint Stephen—the first-ranking priest, the dean, and the first chorepiscopus—no one shall ever presume to celebrate Mass at the principal altar, except another religious person who approaches it reverently at the request and with the consent of the abbot or brothers.

We also decree that no archbishop or bishop, so long as that altar remains inviolate, shall rashly lay his hand upon it, or presume on any pretext to shut out or prohibit there the most sacred mystery of our redemption. But if homicide or anything of that kind should occur there—which God forbid—because sins demanded it, we judge that it must be examined and determined by the prelate of the Roman see or by those whom he appoints [Col. 0783A].

We have also decreed that an annual market shall be held there each year on the anniversary of its dedication, with the assent of our dearest son, Lord Henry, third king and second emperor. We likewise command with no lesser authority that all should always celebrate that dedication there festively.

With fatherly affection, we establish and grant to you, Abbot Warinus, and to your successors in perpetuity, that on the holy day of its dedication and on the other principal feasts you may use sandals and the dalmatic in the celebration of Mass. We admonish your fraternity that, as this honor is increased, so the love of the Most High may increase in you [Col. 0783B].

For the culmination and furtherance of monastic religion we add that the churches, villages, and possessions which the most serene sons of the Roman Church, the kings and emperors—namely Charles the Great, Louis the Pious, Arnulf, Hendebold, Otto, and Conrad—bestowed upon this place with pious devotion, or which they confirmed by the authority of their privilege after being given by other Christian faithful, shall perpetually serve the uses of the abbot and the brothers serving the Lord there, and shall always remain whole and undisturbed for their provision, without any contradiction.

These are: Mareolas; Arx; Jussiacum, with its church and tithe; Floriacum and Flaviniacum; Nugaredum [Col. 0783C]; and Vigiacum; also thirty manses, with their church and tithe, in the village or estate called Rumeliacum; moreover Maurivilla and the village of Deivillare; Tiliacum; and Caminetum and Buxeria, which Queen Hildegard, together with its church and tithe, woods and vineyards, waters and watercourses, and mills already built—or mills to be transported and constructed by the brothers’ stewards wherever, within the ban of that estate, she might wish along the Salian River—frequently bestowed upon the aforementioned place.

Also Pomeriolum, with which and through which we have often endowed the aforesaid monastery in ecclesiastical fashion. Likewise the castle of Laium, which Countess Eva had assigned for the provision of the brothers, together with the wood called Heis and all the utility or produce of that wood, as well as the bridge and fishing rights around the River Murt [Col. 0783D].

Also Bivera, given to the same place by Countess Assidelinde but confirmed by the authority of the most glorious Emperor Conrad; and likewise the village of Navis beside the Moselle River, given and strengthened by King Dagobert; and whatever belongs to the aforesaid monastery in the lower regions within the bishopric of Cologne.

All these things we assign and confirm forever to the provision of the church of the brothers by this apostolic decree.

Furthermore, the church—or rather, the little abbey—of Saint Felix adjacent to that place, where the blessed Clement, the first pastor of the same church of Metz, rests bodily. The aforementioned venerable Bishop Adalbero related that his predecessor, another man named Adalbero, had given it to Saint Arnulf in exchange for the estate called Rumeliacum, and demonstrated it by the testimony of the estate [*curtis*] [Col. 0784A].

This abbey, with its houses, fields, woods, and vineyards, and with all its appurtenances, we confirm to the monastery of Saint Arnulf by the authority of the blessed Peter and of us, his unworthy vicar, at the request of the aforementioned Bishop Adalbero and Abbot Warinus, on the following condition: the aforesaid abbot, or the brothers and their successors, shall hold and possess it perpetually under their care; and no one shall thereafter presume in any way to receive or carry a pastoral staff there.

Rather, the abbot of Saint Arnulf shall always order and arrange through his own or other religious brothers whatever must be ordered there—always taking care and keeping this in mind: just as he and his brothers desire to be somewhat relieved by it in their own needs, so they must never cease to honor and frequent that place through their constant service [Col. 0784B].

Therefore, this abbey, with all things justly and legally belonging to it, and also the villages, churches, and possessions mentioned above, we assign and confirm in such a manner to the monastery of Saint Arnulf and to the brothers serving God there that no emperor or king, no archbishop or bishop, no duke, no count or viscount, nor any person, great or small, may dare to inflict any injustice or violence upon them in these goods, or presume to place any advocate over them unless the abbot or brothers, according to the circumstances of the times or the diversity of places, should request one to be appointed [Col. 0784C].

But just as kings and emperors, bishops, and other faithful people have bestowed these goods there with pious devotion, so may they remain safe and undisturbed for their various uses.

Whoever, fearing for the present and taking precautions for the future, strives to preserve this sacred document of our confirmation, may always be fortified by our apostolic blessing through the grace of almighty God. But whoever presumes to violate or infringe it in any respect, struck by the bond of divine anathema, may find the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, with all the saints, opposed to him—although what he has done shall be void and shall not remain valid. The abbot and brothers of that place shall instead seek judgment and justice concerning it from the most serene sons of the Roman Church, namely the kings and emperors [Col. 0784D].

If they should make little progress in this, may they always possess from us this honor and singular privilege: just as they rejoice in the same monastery because of the benefit of our consecration, so may they forever be fortified by the aid of apostolic protection from the Roman see against every adversity.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of October, through the hands of Udo, chancellor and librarian of the holy apostolic see, and of the first-ranking priest of Toul, in the first year of the lord Pope Leo IX, indiction II, and in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1049.

Eberhard, archbishop of Trier, subscribed.

[Col. 0785A] Saint Hugo, archbishop of Chrysopolis.

Saint Adalbero, bishop of Metz.

Saint Udo, bishop of Toul.

Saint Alinard, bishop of Lyon.

Saint Humbert, cardinal and bishop of Silva Candida.

Saint Theoderic, bishop of Verdun.

Saint John, etc.

### CVII. [Note: [Col. 0785D] A privilege granted by Pope Leo IX to the monastery of Saint Grata is extant in volume IV of *Italia Sacra*, but it is uncertain at which year’s council it was issued. For Leo did not celebrate only one council at Rome. Therefore, the date 1049 assigned by Ughelli is mere conjecture. The privilege itself perhaps ought to be called a complete forgery, since it mentions Emperor Conrad as present at that council, although he had died a full ten years before Leo’s pontificate. Ughelli suspects that the name Conrad entered through a scribal error [Col. 0786D]. If that is so, and confidence can be placed in the privilege, it must certainly be admitted that it was issued at some council of which no other record has come down to us. For the four Roman synods of Pope Leo IX that survive were all held immediately after Easter; therefore the privilege dated the sixth day before the Ides of June can be assigned to none of them. Whatever its character, I present it here.]

Saint Leo IX confirms the possessions and privileges of the nunnery of Saint Grata at the request of Emperor Conrad. (Year 1049.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, volume XIX, col. 727.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

[Col. 0785B] I, Leo, servant of the servants of God, together with the most reverend archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other faithful of the holy Catholic Church sitting in the sacred synod, as well as judges and teachers of the law, with our spiritual son Lord Emperor Conrad present, have granted, at the interceding prayers of Ambrose, bishop of Pergamo [that is, Bergamo], and also Olderic, bishop of Brescia, and at the request of the aforementioned emperor and likewise of the aforementioned most reverend bishops, who entreated us and the holy synod, to the monastery of Saint Grata, by the generosity of ourselves and the entire holy synod, the estate and castle, dependencies, and all that Adelaide, mother of Saint Grata, who built this monastery from her own property, established as belonging to it by imperial constitutions or decrees, all things pertaining to the same monastery having been confirmed with many rights.

We establish that elections of the abbess in the ordering of the sisters shall endure, and that everything shall remain in the power of the abbess without any diminution. We establish in perpetuity that these things shall remain inviolate from kings or pontiffs, patriarchs, archbishops, metropolitans, bishops, the abbess, any of you, and the clergy.

We grant them to the holy mother church of Bergamo, where Lord Bishop Ambrose appears to have been appointed beforehand, by our synodal and concordant generosity, together with everything it is spiritually bound to do—namely, concerning the consecration of the abbess or nuns—and they shall interfere in no matter [f. “in no matter,” Hardouin], neither in the castle and estate of Saranica [Col. 0785C], nor in the other castles and villages, fields, vineyards, houses, and mills, whether in the city of Bergamo or outside it throughout the entire county, together with all things and everything belonging to the monastery of Saint Grata from the aforementioned bishop, which we grant with religious right.

Therefore, if any bishop, as an invader, should plot anything against this apostolic and synodal authority and grant, or resist what we have stated above, whatever his rank, order, office, dignity, or lineage, let him know that he will incur the anger of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of all the saints and of us and our predecessors [f. “will have incurred,” Hardouin], and will be eternally condemned by the bond of anathema and remain in the excommunication of the universal Church and the entire Christian people [f. “will incur,” Hardouin] [Col. 0786A].

Moreover, unless he turns back from evil, let him be punished by irrevocable exile or struck with the ultimate penalties, and let his goods be confiscated. But whoever proves in all things a guardian and observer through pious regard may deserve to possess the grace of blessing and eternal life with all the saints forever and ever. Amen. Let it be done, let it be done.

The following were present at these proceedings: archbishops, bishops, abbots, Roman judges, and judges from neighboring and distant cities. Lord Emperor Conrad was present, together with Bishops Ambrose and Olderic, etc. At their urging were present N., bishop of Palestrina; George, bishop of Porto; Deodatus, bishop of Holstia [printed *Holstiensis*]; Martianus, bishop of Narni; Benedict, bishop of Tivoli; Bernard, bishop of Castro; John, bishop of Petrosino; Gregory, bishop of Orte; George, bishop of Tivoli; Valentinus, bishop of Manoto [printed *Manotensis*]; Theodorus, bishop of Mileto; Savinus, abbot of Planeta; and Lord, abbot of Altinum—all the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and many other cardinals. Thus they took part in the proceedings.

Gregory, cardinal of Saint Peter ad Vincula; Benedict, of Saint Cecilia; Andrew, priest and patriarch of the Lateran; Julian, priest of the Lateran; Faustinus, priest of Saint Peter; Marcus, priest [Col. 0786C] of Saint Peter the Apostle. All these cardinals took part in the proceedings.

Faustinus, head of the senate and consul, and judge of the palace; Julian of Ferna Muana, a Roman; Paul of the palace temple; and many others.

Given and confirmed successfully on the fourth day before the Ides of June in the Lateran patriarchate of the Lord Savior. Amen, amen.

The notary’s subscription, with the sign omitted.

I, Stephen, notary, was present, and at the command of Lord Leo, supreme pontiff, I wrote and delivered all the foregoing.

### CVIII. Letter of Saint Leo IX to Leodegarius, bishop of the holy Church of Vienne. (Between the years 1048 and 1054.)

[Bosco, *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, p. 68.]

[Col. 0786D]

Leo, bishop of the holy Roman Church, to the venerable confrater Leodegarius, archbishop of Vienne, and through you to your Church, forever.

The privileges of your Church, which Pope Sylvester I and his successors—namely, our predecessors—granted, and which we have established: the estates [Col. 0787A], goods, and fortifications that the Roman emperors and the kings of the Franks and of Burgundy have given to your Church, we order, by the authority of God, Saint Peter, and ourselves, to remain secure. Likewise, we order the bishops of Gaul’s seven provinces that, just as they themselves or their predecessors obeyed your predecessors by the authority of the holy Roman Church, so also they are to obey you. For it is fitting, at the command of blessed Peter through Clement, that each nation should recognize, through its bishops, who among them is first.

Given by the hand of Peter, chancellor of the sacred Lateran palace, on the fifth day before the Ides of May.

### CIX. Diploma of Saint Leo IX by which he grants John, abbot of Saint Justina of Padua, the use of pontifical ornaments. (1048–1054)

[In R. P. Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, VI, 244.]

#### [Col. 0787B]

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to JOHN, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Justina: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

By virtue of the primacy of the apostolic see, over which, by God’s authority, we preside, we are permitted to honor with certain priestly insignia above others those religious priests of Christ whom we see distinguished beyond others by every moral excellence, just as we embrace them above others with a certain familiar affection. We may likewise securely strengthen them, together with the property of the churches they govern, through the protection and defense of our apostolic authority, so that others may be more fervently encouraged toward religion, holiness, complete moral integrity, and also toward the due submission, reverence, devotion, and most ardent love owed to the holy Roman Church and the pontiff of the supreme see.

Therefore, dearest brother and venerable abbot John, because we observe that you abound in religion, holiness, humility, and every virtue, and that you burn with the most devoted submission and service to the holy Roman Church and to us, we grant you the use of sandals and a dalmatic in the celebration of Mass, and likewise that you be adorned with the mitre and gloves both at Mass and at solemn processions, so that through the prayers and merits of that blessed virgin and martyr whose body rests in the monastery entrusted to you—and in whose honor and love we grant you the foregoing—we may be able to receive assistance.

Moreover, we receive under the protection and defense of the apostolic see everything belonging to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Justina, whether justly acquired or still to be acquired, without prejudice, of course, to the rights of your mother Church of Padua.

Therefore, let no archbishop, bishop, duke, marquis, count, viscount, or any person, great or small, thereafter presume to inflict any violence upon the property of the aforesaid monastery. If anyone should presume to violate the privilege of this apostolic sanction of ours, and does not quickly repent and, after being admonished, correct his evil deeds by making worthy satisfaction, let him be excluded from communion with the holy Church and subjected to perpetual curse. But let whoever proves to be an observer of it be filled with the abundance of apostolic blessing.

Given at Padua by the hand of Bernard, deputy for Peter the chancellor, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1053, indiction VI, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Leo IX, on the fourth day before the Nones of August. Done successfully. Amen.

### CX. Saint Leo IX grants privileges to the monastery of Bèze. (1052)

[D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, II, 425.]

#### [Col. 0788B]

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to OLGERIUS, abbot of the monastery of Bèze, and to your successors: perpetual salvation in the Lord.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid, with benevolent compassion, of those who abound in devout religion, and to grant appropriate assistance to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, yielding to your prayers, dearest son, we have decided, following the custom of our predecessors, by this privilege of our apostolic protection, to grant your monastery of Bèze a worthy liberty on account of the persecutions threatening it and the countless misfortunes that arise: namely, that no person or power, whether ecclesiastical or secular, may dare to usurp dominion or authority over it, except the bishop of Langres, who is to protect it justly and canonically.

This provision is made, however, on the condition that neither he nor his ministers may exchange or give away the lands or benefices of the monastery, nor remove its vessels, ornaments, or books, or plunder them on any pretext. Whatever the aforesaid place possesses or holds, or may acquire, let it possess and hold in perpetuity by our apostolic confirmation, regardless of whose diocese it may be in.

We also forbid, by our authority, anyone to dare to inflict violence upon the aforesaid monastery or to reduce it to subjection to any other monastery. Robbers, whatever their order or dignity, who have seized or removed property belonging to the aforesaid monastery—whether people, lands, or any other possessions by which those serving God there must be supported and live—we bind with the bond of Saint Peter until they make suitable satisfaction.

We also prohibit anyone from attacking another person or taking away his property within one league of the monastery. By apostolic censure we decree that no person, great or small, may attempt to act against this privilege of ours. If anyone does so, he shall be subject to apostolic anathema until he makes worthy satisfaction. But whoever observes it shall be increased by the grace of our blessing and made a participant in eternal life.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of October, by the hand of Peter the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in indiction V, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1052, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Leo IX.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE SPURIOUS DIPLOMA ABOUT THE BODY OF SAINT DENIS

[In Mabillon, *Annales Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, book XL, no. 21, vol. IV, p. 533.]

#### [Col. 0789]

On that journey through Germany, Pope Leo went to Regensburg and raised from its tomb the body of Saint Wolfgang, bishop of that city, as is recorded in the Saxon Annals for that year. Taking advantage of this occasion, the monks of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, producing I know not what documents, induced the pontiff similarly to transfer a certain body recently discovered in their church while it was being restored, which they claimed was that of Saint Denis, the first bishop of Paris.

A bull of Pope Leo concerning this matter is circulated, addressed “to the most illustrious son, the renowned king of the Franks, and to the venerable brothers, archbishops and bishops, and beloved abbots, priors, provosts, and deans, and to all subjects and prelates of that kingdom.” In this bull the pontiff is made to say that he had been invited by Emperor Henry to visit the regions of Germany and had gone to Regensburg when summoned there to transfer the venerable body of blessed Wolfgang, bishop of that city.

After this had been completed, the envoys of the king of the Franks allegedly induced the pontiff to settle the long-disputed quarrel between the Franks and the aforesaid city over possession of the body of the most blessed Denis the Areopagite. The Franks asserted that it remained in their possession; the people of Regensburg, on the other hand, maintained that it had been transferred by Emperor Arnulf to the church of Saint Emmeram, where it had been preserved up to that time. The venerable abbot Reginward and his brothers, together with the entire city of Regensburg, asserted this claim.

After hearing them, the pontiff is said to have carefully examined the coffers, reliquaries, and chests in which the sacred relics were said to have been enclosed, as well as the labels and inscriptions that the people of Regensburg produced for their case, together with imperial and papal documents, very ancient paintings and sculptures expressing signs of the truth. He then allegedly discovered with unquestionable certainty that the venerable bones of the aforesaid martyr were contained in the monastery of blessed Emmeram, except for a portion of the right hand.

He is also said to have ordered the miracles and portents that he carefully had recorded to bear witness to this; and for that reason he strictly commanded that the solemnity of the transfer be celebrated thereafter every year both by the brothers of that monastery and throughout the city.

The Franks, moreover, were supposedly told not to grieve so greatly that the body of Saint Denis had been taken from them, since they still retained Rusticus and Eleutherius, his companions in preaching and suffering. Nor should they take it hard if, even in death, he now deigned to visit the Germans, having glorified the Gauls during his life through preaching, signs, and martyrdom. The treasure the Franks had lost was indeed precious, but they ought to consider the dignity of the one who had taken it: the man who had inclined an imperial crown in order to steal these relics.

Given and enacted at Regensburg by the hand of Frederick the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, in the year of the Lord 1052, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Leo, indiction V [VI], on the Nones of October.

This is the substance of the circulated diploma, whose spurious character is suggested even by a reading of its composition—that is, by its style, which is entirely foreign to the papal letters of Leo and the other Romans. Moreover, that fictitious diploma contains many false statements.

First, it is false that the dispute had been debated for a very long time, as it says. Before that time there is no mention of this controversy among earlier writers. It is false that Leo had been equipped for investigating it with both imperial and papal letters—“the German word”—of his predecessors. For who ever produced these imperial and papal letters? Finally, it is false that this was done by Emperor Arnulf, as we have shown elsewhere.

### [Note: The tale of the removal of the body of Saint Denis]

(Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, book XXXIX, no. 28.)—During the time of Ebalus, abbot of Saint Denis, they say that the body of Saint Denis was secretly taken away by a certain Gislebert [888] and transported to Regensburg, to the basilica of Saint Emmeram.

As evidence of this event, the people of Emmeram produce two stones, on one of which is written:

**UNDER EBALUS, ABBOT, GISLEBERT STOLE IT**

and on the other:

**HE STOLE IT ON THE FIFTH DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF JUNE.  
HE CAME HERE ON THE DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF DECEMBER,  
IN THE TIME OF TUTO, BISHOP.**

Later writers tell the story as follows. Gislebert, a German, thought he would do Emperor Arnulf a favor if he could steal and present to him the body of Saint Denis, bishop and martyr. For this purpose he pretended to take refuge in the monastery of Saint Denis as though he were guilty of a crime, in order to escape punishment under the protection of the holy place. While staying in this asylum, he therefore had easy access to the sacred tomb.

Having arranged everything for the theft, he prepared a lavish banquet for the abbot and the monks. When all had fallen asleep after the meal, he opened the entrance to the tomb, opened the reliquary, took away the sacred relics, and brought them to Arnulf. The latter ordered them to be carried five months later to the basilica of Saint Emmeram, where they were presented together with a splendid Gospel book and a portable altar that he used to carry about in the army.

The Gospel book and the altar are indeed still kept there, but they were given to Saint Emmeram much later and on another occasion. As for the body of Saint Denis, they say that it was hidden in an unknown place.

They add that this theft occurred while Ebalus was abbot of Saint Denis, whereas the body was brought to Regensburg while Tuto was bishop; and that before Leo IX it was proved to be truly the body of Denis, the first bishop and martyr of Paris, and confirmed by a papal diploma.

Yet to refute this little tale we need no other authorities than German ones—namely, Witichind, Ditmar, and Arnulf, a monk of Saint Emmeram—all of whom wrote toward the end of the tenth century.

Witichind, a monk of Corvey, states in the first book of his *Annals* that Henry, king of Germany, after crossing the Rhine, began to invade the kingdom of Lothair. Envoys of Charles, king of the Franks, surnamed the Simple, who was then being held in prison, came to meet him and declared that, surrounded as he was by enemies, nothing could happen more pleasantly to him than to hear of Henry’s glorious successes. They then offered him, as a pledge of the alliance, the hand of the precious martyr Denis, enclosed in gold and gems.

Ditmar, bishop of Merseburg, says that this was done so that Charles might win the aid of King Henry for himself. Conrad, abbot of Ursperg, and Sigebert agree with these authorities.

Since this arm was removed from the body of Saint Denis during the reign of King Henry, who ruled twenty years after Arnulf, it follows that the sacred body was still being preserved at that time among the people of Saint Denis. For it is not plausible that this arm had been granted to the underage Charles, who had not yet been declared king, before that time.

But the strongest, although negative, evidence is this: Arnulf, a former count who became a monk of Saint Emmeram and was writing around the year 1000, specifically records the benefactions of Emperor Arnulf to Saint Emmeram. He mentions the estates given by the emperor and the splendid Gospel book presented as a gift, but makes no mention whatsoever of the body of Saint Denis.

Finally, when the people of Regensburg began publicly to proclaim their fictitious possession, Henry, king of the Franks, ordered the reliquary of Saint Denis to be opened in the presence of a large assembly of bishops and nobles, and demonstrated to their eyes that the sacred relics of blessed Denis were still inside it. The anniversary of this event is customarily celebrated each year under the title of the Discovery of Saint Denis.

I pass over the fact that the terms *Alemanni* and *Alemannia*, which occur in such documents to designate the Bavarians and Bavaria, reflect the usage of a later period. And what sort of words are these said to be Pope Leo’s to Henry, king of the Franks, by which he tries to console him for this removal? What sort of pontifical speech is it, approving Arnulf’s theft? But I am dwelling too long on these trifles.

Nevertheless, I would not categorically deny that, while Pope Leo was staying at Regensburg, a question concerning the body of Saint Denis was debated—for the Saxon Annals also report this—and that a certain body was then discovered in the church of Saint Emmeram. The people of Regensburg, producing I know not what documents, asserted that it was the body of that same Saint Denis, and Leo may perhaps have been persuaded of this.

For this reason King Henry, in order to refute that opinion, ordered a large assembly of bishops, abbots, and nobles to be summoned in the monastery of Saint Denis by Hugh the abbot, and ordered the reliquary of Saint Denis to be opened.

### CXI. Diploma of Saint Leo IX concerning the body of Saint Denis. (1048–1064)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 674.]

#### [Col. 0791A]

In the name of our Savior Jesus Christ. Amen.

LEO, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most illustrious son, the renowned king of the Franks, and to the venerable brothers, archbishops and bishops, and to the beloved sons in Christ, abbots, priors, provosts, and deans, and to all subjects and prelates of that kingdom: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Almighty God, who is rightly proclaimed by the Prophet to be wondrous in his saints, disposes all things with the marvelous profundity of his inscrutable counsel. When the human mind is not sufficient to contemplate these things and, failing through its own weakness, is compelled to be carried away into a kind of ecstasy and astonishment, we ourselves recently experienced this. We are compelled to proclaim it to you, beloved in Christ, and to the whole community of the faithful, so that we may likewise admire the works of God.

For when, at the insistence of the most serene Emperor Henry, we had been summoned to visit the regions of Germany, and especially the city called Regensburg, or Ratispona, in order to transfer the venerable body of blessed Wolfgang, bishop of that city, and had accomplished this with the reverence and devotion appropriate to it, your envoys, dearest son in Christ, king of the Franks, acting on your behalf and on behalf of all your people, earnestly asked us to settle, after investigating the truth, the dispute that had long been debated between you and the aforesaid city concerning the most sacred bones of the most blessed Denis the Areopagite.

You said that the same bones were in your possession; but the citizens and inhabitants of that city maintained, on the contrary, that they had been transferred by the invincible former emperor Arnulf to the church of the blessed martyr Emmeram and had thereafter remained there.

That church, situated there, is known to be free and exempt from the subjection and jurisdiction of all others, and to belong immediately, by right and ownership, to blessed Peter and the apostolic see, through the donation of the most excellent Roman emperor Charlemagne and of his successors, whether in the empire or in the kingdom. The venerable abbot Reginward and the brothers of that church, together with the entire community of Regensburg, also pressed us most urgently to make this determination.

We therefore yielded to the prayers of both parties, unwilling that the hearts of the faithful should remain any longer clouded by the uncertainty of this doubt. In the presence and sight of our brothers and of many bishops and prelates, we carefully read through the writings of Augustus Arnulf and the order of events. Not content with this, we examined with diligent scrutiny, as far as the eye could determine, the coffers, reliquaries, and chests in which the sacred relics were said to have been stored, together with their labels and inscriptions, omitting nothing relevant to the investigation of certainty.

Sufficiently supplied with the imperial and papal letters of our predecessors, and also with the many wall paintings and very ancient sculptures expressing signs and marks of the truth, we discovered with unquestionable certainty that the venerable bones of the aforesaid teacher and martyr were contained intact in the monastery of blessed Emmeram, except for one single and very small portion of the right hand.

Indeed, lest the human testimonies already mentioned should prove insufficient, divine miracles and portents were also not lacking; they entirely dispelled every doubt. We likewise ordered them to be carefully recorded and sent to you through your messengers and envoys, and also preserved perpetually in the aforesaid church, so that knowledge of what occurred might be transmitted to posterity and all further grounds for litigation might completely cease.

Moreover, we strictly command and decree that the venerable solemnity of this transfer be celebrated every year, both by the brothers of that church and by all the people of the aforesaid city, with complete delight and joy, and that the entire region of the Germans rejoice at the arrival of so great a Father and patron, not showing itself ungrateful.

But you, beloved sons in Christ—the king of the Franks and your faithful people—although you may seem to have just cause for envy of the German people, so that you think you have good reason to grieve over the joy of the Alemanni, nevertheless, considering the will both of almighty God and of his invincible martyr, whom you lament as having been taken away, finally admit the consolation of reconciliation.

Consider more attentively that he has not been taken from you, since he left with you his most beloved companions in his preaching and passion, Rusticus and Eleutherius, as a pledge and assurance of his continuing love and protection. Nor should you grieve if, even in death, he has deigned to visit the Germans—he who preached to you while still alive and, among you, by fighting the good fight, completing his course, and keeping the faith (1 Tim. 4), achieved the triumph of his most victorious passion, accomplishing among you the signs of his apostleship both in life and in death.

Why, then, do you not permit Alemannia to shelter his bones, for its consolation and protection, when Athens permitted you to receive him alive, to hear him, and to send him to heaven, so that he might win you for Christ?

Another reason for consolation will also be added: namely, the authority and eminence of the one who took him away. We admit that you have lost a precious treasure, but consider the dignity of the thief. Rejoice together in the glory of your Father and apostle, who, after enriching you with the treasure of his merits and teaching, has at least in his relics and repositories of his remains a thief of his body who is as devoted as he is distinguished—better than gold and topaz—one whose worth caused even an imperial crown to bow in order to remove his most holy bones.

Neither imperial majesty nor royal highness felt shame at bearing in Arnulf the mark or name of a pious thief, provided that he might sanctify and enrich himself by the resources of the blessed body through fraud, theft, or sacrilege—he who was accustomed to condemn thieves and sacrilegious persons. Provided that he might enjoy the precious body of Macarius Denis, he did not then disdain to become himself both a thief and a sacrilegious person.

Moreover, faith and devotion have completely removed every doubt through this consideration: he did not seek to choose a burial place for himself in Rome, in any metropolis, or in any city or fortress of the kingdom, but in the place where he both knows and rejoices that he buried his own Denis, hoping that he would be defended by his protection and raised again with the blessed on the last day.

Therefore, in the presence of these matters, we earnestly admonish your devotion and exhort you in the Lord, strictly commanding that, content in piety with Rusticus and Eleutherius, you should not deceive yourselves and others, but recognize and confess that the bones of the most blessed Denis shine forth in the city of Regensburg, at the church of the blessed martyr Emmeram.

Given and enacted at Regensburg by the hand of Frederick the deacon, librarian and chancellor of the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church, in the year of the Lord 1052, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Leo IX, indiction [F. sixth, HARD.] fifth, on the Nones of October.

# APPENDIX TO THE LETTERS OF SAINT LEO IX

### I. Letter of Michael Cerularius, patriarch of Constantinople, and Leo, archbishop of Acrida among the Bulgarians, to John, bishop of Trani in Apulia

[In Baronius, *Annales*, vol. XI, under the year 1053, p. 210.]

#### [Note]

Michael, surnamed Cerularius, together with Leo of Acrida, archbishop of the Bulgarians, wrote a letter attacking all Latins, against the holy Roman and apostolic see, indeed against the entire Western Church. They sent it to John, bishop of Trani in Apulia, so that it might be circulated among all the Latins. In the manuscript it bears this title:

“Calumny of the bishops Michael of Constantinople and Leo of Acrida, stubbornly exhaling the pestilential fumes of various heresies against the holy Roman and apostolic see, indeed against the entire Latin and Western Church.”

This calumny, composed in Greek and directed to John, bishop of Trani, as an attack upon all the Latins, was presented at Trani to Brother Humbert, bishop of Silva Candida and cardinal of the holy Roman Church. Through his efforts it was translated into Latin and brought to Lord Leo IX. It is inserted here for the caution and information of many, not for any particular benefit, and has been faithfully preserved for all who wish to know it. Their letter itself runs as follows:

#### [Col. 0793C]

MICHAEL, universal patriarch of New Rome, and LEO, archbishop of Acrida, metropolis of the Bulgarians, to the beloved brother JOHN, bishop of Trani.

The great love of God and the pleasing compassion of harmony have moved us to write to your holiness, and through you to all the chief priests, priests, monks, and peoples of the Franks, and to the most reverend pope himself, and to remind you concerning unleavened bread and Sabbaths, which you observe in an improper mystical manner and in which you share with the Jews.

For the Jews themselves were commanded by Moses to observe unleavened bread and Sabbaths; but Christ is our Passover. In order not to be found an adversary of the law, he was also circumcised and first celebrated the legal Passover. After departing from that observance, he established our new Passover. This is clear in the Gospel according to Matthew.

Speaking of the mystical supper, the evangelist also says: “On the first day of unleavened bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying to him: Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover? He said: Go into the city to a certain man and say to him: My time is near; I will keep the Passover with you and my disciples” (Matt. 26).

A little later: “When evening came, he reclined with the Twelve, and while they were eating he said: Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me. And a little later, when Judas said, ‘Surely it is not I, Rabbi?’ he said to him, ‘You have said it’” (ibid.).

Thus far, O men of God, everything belongs to the legal Passover. Then the evangelist added what belongs to the mystical and Christian Passover, saying: “While they were eating, Jesus took bread, broke it, and gave it to his disciples and said: Take and eat; this is my body, which will be given for you. And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: Drink from it, all of you; this is my blood of the new covenant” (ibid.).

By saying “new,” he showed how the things belonging to the Old Covenant had ceased. Observe how, under the New Covenant, he called bread his body: as something life-giving and full of spirit, and as a manifestation of warmth. You call it *bread*; we call it *artos*. *Artos* is interpreted as “raised up” and “carried upward,” possessing warmth and elevation through leaven and salt. Unleavened bread, however, differs in nothing from a lifeless stone, or from brick clay consumed downward into earth, or from dry mud. Moses commanded wretched Jews to eat it once a year together with bitter things.

Because unleavened bread is a symbol of evil suffering and tribulation, it is significant; whereas our Passover is entirely joy and gladness, and through joy it raises us from the ground to heaven, just as leaven, through its own warmth, raises bread, which is filled with every sweetness. Unleavened bread, having neither salt nor leaven, is dry mud.

Have you not heard Jesus say to his disciples, “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5), and that “the kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until it was all leavened” (Luke 13)? By “woman” he means the holy Church; by the three measures filled, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, of whom muddy unleavened bread has no share.

David also says of Christ: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). Before Moses and Abraham, Melchizedek, recognizing the Lord of heaven and earth and of the other creatures, rose and offered him bread and wine.

Therefore the divine Apostle says: “If perfection had been through the Levitical priesthood” (Heb. 7), Christ would not be called a priest “according to the order of Melchizedek.” And since the priesthood has been transferred, it is necessary that the law also be transferred (ibid.), the law that established the observance of unleavened bread for the Jews.

The same great Paul, speaking of these matters in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, says: “Brothers, I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and giving thanks, broke it and said: Take and eat; this is my body, which will be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me. Likewise concerning the cup: This is the cup of the new covenant in my blood; do this, whenever you drink, in remembrance of me. For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you will proclaim the death of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11).

But unleavened bread neither contains the remembrance of the Lord nor proclaims his death, like the Mosaic unleavened bread, established by the law fourteen hundred years ago and cursed and abandoned through the New Covenant, that is, through the holy Gospel and through Christ.

But how do you observe Sabbaths in a Jewish manner during Lent? Have you not heard the Gospel saying that, as the disciples passed through the fields on the Sabbaths, they began to make their way, plucking ears of grain and eating them? The Jews said to Christ: “Do you see what they are doing on the Sabbaths?” He said: “Yes.” Do you not know what David did when he himself and those with him were hungry—how he entered the temple and ate the bread of the Presence? And so forth.

“And because the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2). They also said: “This man is not from God, for he does not observe the Sabbath” (John 9). Again, when Christ was speaking on the Sabbath, and concerning the man who had the withered hand (Matt. 12), and likewise concerning the man who had a demonic spirit and was cleansed on the Sabbath, while the Jews murmured and said many things, Christ said: “Hypocrites, does not each one of you untie his donkey from the manger, or his ox, and lead it to water?” (Luke 13). The same applies to the paralytic whom he healed.

Therefore those who observe Sabbaths together with unleavened bread are neither Jews nor Christians, but are like the leopard, as the great Basil says, whose hair is neither black nor altogether white.

But how do such people also eat strangled animals, in which the blood remains? Or do you not know that the blood of every animal is its soul, and that whoever eats blood eats its soul? (Gen. 9.) For this reason they are not entirely Gentiles either; those people kill animals or eat them after striking them.

Again, during Lent you do not sing *Alleluia*, but only once at Easter. It is interpreted as: “The Lord has come; praise him, sing a hymn, and bless him.” Therefore, according to this, you sing neither “Lord of the Lord” nor “Blessed is he who comes.” This *Alleluia* itself is a Hebrew expression.

Why do you not see and understand such a great deception, nor correct the peoples and yourselves, as those who will be judged by God on account of these things? Do you not abandon what is said—that Peter, Benedict, Paul, and the others taught these things? You have deceived yourselves and the people in these matters.

What I have written is what Peter, Paul, the other apostles, and Christ taught, and what the holy and catholic Church accepted and religiously observes. You too, once corrected, should observe these things. Cast away unleavened bread and the observance of Sabbaths to the wretched Jews; likewise, cast away strangled animals to the barbarian nations, so that we may become pure in the right and undefiled faith and may be one flock of Christ, the one shepherd.

Having been purely inebriated with the divine blood of Christ on the cross, we praise in purity the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, abandoning all the things of the Mosaic law to the godless Jews who observe it, who, like blind men seeking Christ, have lost the light and remain perpetually in shadow like fools.

These things, man of God, you yourself have often recognized and taught together with the people; once corrected, you also wrote to many who held a similar custom. For the salvation of your soul, send this to the chief priests and priests, and adjure them to correct themselves and the people of God in these matters, so that you may receive God’s reward for them. If you do this, I propose, in a second letter, to write you things greater and more perfect than these, as a true manifestation and firm foundation of the faith of the souls for which Christ gave his life.

#### [Note]

Thus far the letter of Michael Cerularius and Leo of Acrida, as you saw from its title. Moreover, when this letter of Michael and Acrida had been sent to Apulia and had been received at Trani by Humbert, cardinal bishop of Silva Candida of the holy Roman Church, he translated it into Latin and brought it to Pope Leo himself.

This is what the written manuscript says, in which all these things are recorded: “After Pope Leo had read it, he wrote that lengthy letter to the same Michael and Leo of Acrida, which is placed first among the letters of Leo himself in their printed collection.”

From the chronological note attached to that letter it is also learned in what year it was written: it says that one thousand and nearly twenty years had elapsed from Christ’s Passion to the time when the letter was being written. By saying “nearly twenty,” it clearly indicates that one thousand and twenty years had not yet elapsed. For at the beginning of the following year he says in a letter sent to the same Michael in January that one thousand and twenty years had already elapsed.
