It has been stated above, in its proper place, that the Roman Church customarily began counting the years from Christ’s Passion with Christ’s thirty-fourth year.

### II. Letter of John I, abbot of Fécamp, to Saint Leo IX

After praising the supreme pontiff, he complains about the violence inflicted upon him by the Italians.

[Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 207, from the Bigot manuscript.]

#### [Col. 0797B]

To the supreme pontiff of the apostolic see, LEO, sanctified by the grace of God as Peter’s representative: JOHN, the least of the brothers and the last in the number of abbots, sends primacy in the heavenly court amid the festal glory of the apostolic senate.

Let the Roman world rejoice, adorned with the mitre of so great a prelate, who gleams like a purple Lucifer among the stars, shining with a devotion both pious and unprecedented, to drive the mists of manifold error from the bosom of Mother Church. Indeed, what shepherd has arisen in the Roman Church after those golden ages in which Leo and Gregory shone forth—lights of spiritual teaching purer than glass—so diligent and watchful as you, most holy of prelates, who feed the Lord’s flock upon the living mountains of pasture?

For, to make my words credible, who would not marvel and burst forth into a jubilation of praise at the unheard-of foresight of a vigilant shepherd in our age? You are not content to care for one people in your own seat in the city of Rome, or merely to irrigate fertile Italy with the rain of heavenly teaching; rather, you travel around and inspect the Churches beyond the Alps with synodal scrutiny. If anything uncultivated or distorted from the rule of uprightness has been introduced, you immediately seize it with ecclesiastical censure and amend and correct it by the rule of justice.

Hail, Father, wondrous pope. Hail, exceptional prelate of prelates. Hail, I say, that pillar of fire which once went before the Israelite people, and which, leading the way along an unhindered path through the vast wilderness of this world, conducts God’s holy people to the heavenly Jerusalem, the true promised land.

Therefore, let our mouth be filled with praise and our tongue with exultation. Glory to God in the highest: “The Orient from on high has visited us.”

But, O condition of mortals! How little is trustworthy, and how little is wholly blessed, in this unstable age! Behold, revered pontiff, while I tune the melodies of my tongue to your praises, rejoicing that peace has been restored throughout the lands through the gracious foresight of your administration, pain strikes me from the side and interrupts the instruments of joy with a shrill lament.

I speak secretly into the pontiff’s ear about the violation of ecclesiastical peace which was inflicted upon me by those to whom you sent your faithful messenger, who was carrying out the legation of Peter himself, prince of the apostles—not by foreign nations, but by Roman citizens themselves, and, secondly, by the most powerful inhabitants of the suburbs of Richefburh and Aquaependente. These men, certainly, despising the apostolic peace established by your sanction, attacked me, despoiled me, and lamentably dishonored me before all pious people, although I vainly displayed the instructions of your legation and invoked the protection of apostolic authority in my defense.

Moreover, the Italians’ hatred of the Northmen has burned and grown so fiercely that throughout almost all the suburbs of Italy scarcely any Northman is ever permitted to travel safely, even when he is traveling out of religious devotion, without being assaulted, dragged away, stripped, slapped, bound in chains, and often even breathing out his sorrowful spirit after being worn down by the foulness of a long imprisonment.

Let this therefore be known to you, most humane Father of the Christian people: unless Roman piety abolishes this undisciplined barbarism by apostolic prohibition, and avenges it—especially when it is directed against your own special legate—in such a way that the whole world hears and trembles, the authority of Roman majesty will be greatly diminished, nor will that warlike nation of the Northmen remain so ready and devoted to your fidelity.

It also concerns your reputation, man of complete generosity and glory, to restore with a lavish hand what we have lost. For behold, as you ordered, our messenger has arrived at the Easter term, with letters and a firm guarantee concerning the matters omitted. I repeat these matters not only on my own behalf, but also on behalf of those whose devotion I grieve for, who had entrusted these things to the Holy Trinity under the testimony of my fidelity.

Having proceeded thus far, I cannot fail to report what I hear being circulated under an evil interpretation about my apostolic lord, whom I embrace with special devotion and whom I wish to be secure before God and men.

The tale of mockery concerns Count Tedbald and the foolish duke R. of Burgundy, who confuse right and wrong as transgressors of pontifical decrees; having rejected the marriages of legitimate beds, they wallow in dishonorable chambers defiled by consanguinity.

Hence the people hiss; hence every crooked-minded man insults me—me, I say, who contend for your honor and wipe this stain of collusion from your integrity. And, to confound me still further and convict me by an unhappy victory of bringing your authority into ridicule, they bring forward and point to my face the fact that Tedbald also came into your presence, and that nothing worthy of this offense was done; indeed, as though strengthened by your authority, he claims for himself the wolfish sheep—called that false Agnes—and, while her husband is alive, takes her in execrable fornication through the unlawful divorce of his lawful wife.

Concerning this, therefore, let the most prudent prelate himself, I beg, weigh what the matter requires for its correction, lest the work and effort of his ecclesiastical sanction be annulled and rendered void.

[Col. 0799]

## III. Letter of Saint Peter Damian to Saint Leo IX

(See among the letters of Saint Peter Damian, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLIV, col. 208.)

## In the Year of the Lord 1057: Pope Victor II

[Col. 0799]

## Historical Notice

(Ciacconius, *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*)

[Col. 0799C]

In the name of God and of our blessed Savior Jesus Christ. Amen.

After the death of Pope Leo IX, Eberard, bishop of Eichstätt, a prudent, learned, and wealthy man, was elected. He was German by nation, from the province of Swabia, descended from the Counts of Calw, born in the castle of Hisprug, and related by close blood to the emperor. His father was Arduigus and his mother Vitzela, both very noble parents. Although he was young in age, he was so prudent in learning, wisdom, and seriousness of character that he could be compared with old men.

He had been elected bishop of Eichstätt in the year 1052 with the consent of that clergy, and possessed such great authority among all the leading men of the empire that Emperor Henry especially relied upon his counsel. Henry took it hard to lose so great a man and so faithful a friend.

Hildebrand therefore brought him to Rome, although unwilling, after a year had passed since Leo’s death. He was received with joy and the acclamation of the entire people and, in the Vatican basilica of Saint Peter, through the ministry of the cardinal bishops, received the insignia of the Roman pontificate under the name Victor II, on Thursday of Holy Week, the Ides of April, in the year of the Lord 1055, through Maynard, archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church. He governed that Church with the highest praise for two years, three months, and sixteen days, under the emperors Henry III Augustus and his son Henry IV.

He recovered several cities, fortresses, and towns that the Roman Church had lost in earlier centuries. Following the footsteps of his predecessor Leo, he continued to strengthen the present condition of the Church. For this reason he suddenly summoned an assembly at Florence and invited Emperor Henry to it as well. There, since Victor himself was an extremely severe censor and reformer of the clergy, when the emperor arrived near Pentecost in the year 1056 and attended the council, Victor condemned and removed from their bishoprics many bishops affected by the stain of simony and convicted of fornication. He admonished the clergy concerning the chief duty of their office and imposed the penalties of ecclesiastical laws upon transgressors.

At the same time, Victor sent Hildebrand as his legate to France and charged him with a grave inquiry against the Simoniacs and Nicolaitans. After he had condemned six bishops who were manifestly guilty of these crimes, he overcame the archbishop of Embrun, who was accused of simony but shamelessly denied it, although Hildebrand could not convict him by witnesses, through a stratagem.

Peter Damian recorded from memory how the archbishop related this to him. For, in the presence of many people, Hildebrand said:

“Come now. Since you claim to be innocent of this crime, pronounce the *Gloria Patri et Filio et Spiritui Sancto* as a declaration for the expiation of your offense.”

Then the bishop, thinking that by saying this he would escape the entire judgment of a more serious danger, began to recite it. He said, “Glory to the Father and to the Son,” but, although he tried repeatedly, he could not get out, “and to the Holy Spirit.” It was believed that, because in the trafficking of holy things the Holy Spirit is especially offended, he could not say that he was a participant in his guilt. Afterward, once he had confessed his sin, he pronounced the words without any hesitation.

When Pope Victor learned that, after Leo’s death, Berengar had returned to the same madness and heard that many people in France were being led into error by him, he went there and held an assembly at Tours. There he refuted Berengar’s opinion, already detested for the third time.

This Berengar was a native of Tours and archdeacon of Angers. He was the first to raise a heresy against the divine Eucharist, a heresy which, though condemned so many times, was restored, strengthened, and propagated even in our own age by Zwingli, Oecolampadius, and Calvin. Berengar was given the option of defending his opinion. Since he did not dare undertake its defense, he confessed before everyone the common faith of the Church.

From Tours, Victor was invited by Emperor Henry into Saxony and, received with an admirable gathering of all the princes, celebrated the Nativity of the Virgin with him at Goslar.

Not long afterward, however, Henry was seized by a severe illness and died on the third day before the Nones of October, in the year of the Lord 1056, near Föllde in Saxony, at the age of thirty-nine. Victor had his body taken to Speyer and, in his presence, honorably buried in the church of the Blessed Virgin that Henry himself had built, beside his father’s tomb. His son Henry IV assumed and held the titles of the empire for nearly fifty years.

Meanwhile, after Victor had arranged affairs of the Church beyond the Alps as circumstances then permitted, and after celebrating the solemn Nativity at Regensburg with the young king who had been established there, he returned to Italy at the beginning of Lent and stopped at Florence, where he spent almost the remainder of his life.

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1057, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, Pope Victor II died at Florence in Tuscany. His body was buried in the cathedral church of Saint Reparata at Florence.

[Col. 0802C] The see was vacant for four days.

[Col. 0801]

## Second Notice

(From Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, XIX, 833.)

[Col. 0801C]

Victor, whose name was Gebehard and who governed the Church of Eichstätt with great benefit, was requested from the emperor by order of the Roman clergy through Hildebrand, subdeacon of the Roman Church. He was brought to Rome and, with the consent of the entire clergy and people, elected pontiff in the year of the Lord 1055, during the reign of Emperor Henry III, and solemnly consecrated on the day of the Lord’s Supper.

They requested that he be presented to them by the emperor because, as Leo of Ostia says, no person suitable for so great an office could be found in the Roman Church.

To correct the corrupt practices of the Gallican Church and to investigate the cases of certain bishops, he sent Hildebrand, cardinal subdeacon of the Roman Church, who later became pope under the name Gregory VII, as a legate *a latere* into Gaul. At Lyons [Note: In Gaul, indeed, in the region of Lyons; but the precise place is uncertain.] he summoned a council and miraculously compelled a bishop accused of simony to confess his own offense. When ordered to recite the hymn of glorification, the bishop was completely unable to pronounce in it the words “and to the Holy Spirit.”

In the first year of his pontificate, he suffered a horrible act of treachery when a certain subdeacon—dreadful even to say—put poison into the sacred chalice in order to kill him. But God prevented the pontiff from drinking it by a double miracle and exposed the author of so great a sacrilege.

Lambert describes the event as follows:

“The subdeacon put poison into the chalice for Pope Victor. When Victor himself wished to lift it after the consecration but could not, he knelt with the people in prayer before the Lord, intending to inquire into the cause of the event. Immediately the poisoner was seized by a demon. Thus, when the cause had been revealed, the lord pope ordered the chalice containing the Lord’s blood to be enclosed in an altar and preserved there forever as a relic. Then he knelt in prayer with the people again for as long as it took for the subdeacon to be freed from the demon.”

This is the account of Lambert of Aschaffenburg, together with that of several others.

Summoned from Rome by Emperor Henry, Victor went to Germany in the second year of his pontificate, in the year 1056 of Christ the Redeemer. There he found Henry suffering from a grave illness and already at the point of death.

This undoubtedly occurred through the singular grace of God. For shortly afterward, after Henry had confessed his sins before the pontiff, restored what he had taken away, asked forgiveness from those present, and presented to Pope Victor his son Henry—still five years old, then made king by the electors who were present and entrusted to the Roman Church—he surrendered his soul to God as a great divine favor, having reigned in the empire for eighteen years.

Agnes, the Augusta, began to raise the boy religiously; but when he had passed beyond adolescence, he was taken away from his mother and became an enemy of the Roman Church, through whose favor, by means of Victor the Roman, he had obtained the kingdom of Germany.

In the following year, after returning from Germany to the City, Victor excommunicated Count Trasimund of Teano, who had despoiled legates returning from Constantinople.

During Victor’s pontificate, to the great benefit of the entire German Church, Saint Anno was placed in the chair of Cologne as archbishop. Because he freely reproved Emperor Henry, who was gravely harassing him, Anno foretold Henry’s future death.

Pope Victor died at Florence in the year of Christ 1057, on 28 July, after sitting for two years, three months, and fifteen days. He was buried in the same place where he had died. According to Lambert, the episcopate was vacant for five days, from 28 July until 2 August.

[Col. 0803]

## Diplomatic Notice

(Jaffé, *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*, p. 379.)

[Col. 0803B]

On the seal which, according to Gattula’s testimony, displays Victor’s bull impressed on lead, the following saying is contained:

**“You left the ship for me; take up the key.”**

The subscriptions of the bishops and cardinals of the Roman See, which had been added only very rarely to the bulls of earlier pontiffs, began to be added more frequently under Victor II. His documents contain the following:

Boniface, bishop of Albano. Humbert, called cardinal and bishop of the Holy Church of Silva Candida. Hildebrand, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church. Frederick, cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus.

The bulls were written by the hand of Gregory, notary and scriniarius of the Holy Roman Church. Issued by the hand of Hildebrand, cardinal subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church; Hildebrand, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of Herman, archchancellor of the Apostolic See (no. 7), chancellor and librarian of the Holy Apostolic See; Herman, archbishop of Cologne (5); Frederick, chancellor of the Holy Roman Church; Aribo, deacon, acting in place of Anno, archchancellor of the Holy Roman Church and archbishop of Cologne; Aribo, deacon.

[Col. 0803]

# Letters and Pontifical Charters of Pope Victor II

## I. Privilege of Pope Victor II for Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, confirming all monasteries, possessions, and rights granted to the monastery of Cluny

(Year 1055.)

[*Cluniac Bullary*, p. 13.]

[Col. 0803C]

Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Hugh, abbot of the monastery called Cluny, consecrated in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and situated in the county of Mâcon, and through you to all your successors, the abbots, forever.

The desire that is shown to endure through the stability of religious superiors and holy places ought, with God as its author, to be fulfilled without any delay. Whenever our assent and the protection of our customary apostolic authority are requested for the benefit of such places, it is fitting for us willingly to assist them out of kindness and to make the arrangement firm for complete security, so that, through this, the supreme reward may also be inscribed for us by the Creator of all things, God, in the heavenly citadels.

Therefore, because you asked us to fortify the aforesaid monastery with the series of apostolic authority, to confirm by perpetual right all that belongs to it so that it might remain there inviolate, and to establish it securely by the text of our privilege without the yoke or dominion of any person whatsoever, we have inclined to your prayers.

By this privilege of our authority, therefore, we establish and decree that all the estates and monasteries belonging to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny which have been granted to that place by faithful Christian kings, bishops, dukes, or princes, and acquired by your predecessors the abbots—namely Berno, Odo, Aymard, and your predecessors of blessed memory, Saints Majolus and Odilo—or whatever else appears to belong to the same place, you shall possess peacefully and with complete security, without anyone’s opposition, and through you all your successors forever.

This includes the monastery of Cluny itself, founded by the once most powerful duke William in the county of Mâcon, together with all the property situated around that place and in other regions belonging to it.

In the county of Mâcon: the cell dedicated in honor of Saint Martin, together with the church situated nearby and dedicated in honor of Saint John; the estates called Covinias, with the church; the estate of Solestriacum, with the church; Escutiola, with the church; Galliniacum, with the church; Rufiacum, with the church; Masilia, with the church; Clairmanum; the estate of Barjeserena; the estate of Curtilia; Petroniacum; Arpasiocum; Darboniacum; Besurniacum, with the church of Saint Columba; Vitreziam; the estate of Burguli; the church of Saint Lawrence; Castrum; Lurdonum; Blanuscum; the estate called Cotta; also the monastery called Catus Locus, with everything belonging to it; the church of Saint Victor, with everything that appears to pertain to it; also the cell dedicated in honor of Saint Victor, with all its appurtenances; and the churches and lands situated near it, for which the church of Saint Gengulf was once given.

Also Eguiranda, with the church of the apostle Saint Andrew and with the other churches and all its appurtenances; likewise all the churches and lands, or everything that the aforesaid place appears to possess in the said county.

In the county of Chalon: the cell of Beaumont, built in honor of Saint Mary, with everything that appears to pertain to it; also the estate called Juliacum, with the churches and lands formerly granted to that place by Bishop Manasses; and all the churches and lands, and whatever the aforesaid place appears to possess in the said county; the church of Saint Gengulf, with its appurtenances and dependencies.

In the bishopric of Autun: the cell of Ojadellis, built in honor of the holy Mother of God, with all its appurtenances; also the churches and lands which the cleric Teotard granted to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny.

We also confirm and strengthen by our apostolic authority the agreement made by Lord Walter, bishop of the Church of Autun, concerning the monastery called Magabrense, which belonged to his church, together with everything belonging to it: Marciniacum, with all its dependencies, just as your brother Gauffred gave it to Saint Peter and to you; the church of Varennes, as Artaldus gave it, with all its dependencies; and all the churches, lands, and whatever the aforesaid place of Cluny appears to possess in the said bishopric.

In the territory of Dijon: the estate of Gluriacum, with all its dependencies; the cell of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian; and the monastery of Saint Marcellus, with all its dependencies, in the suburb of Chalon.

In the county of Auvergne: the monastery of Silviniacum, where your predecessors Saints Majolus and Odilo rest, with everything belonging to it; also the cell called Firmitas, with everything belonging to the same place; the cell called Scuriolas; the church dedicated in honor of Saint Sulpicius in the estate called Langiacum; the small cell called ad Boscum, consecrated in honor of Saint Peter; and the estate called Frigidus Mons.

Also the monastery called Rivis, consecrated in honor of the holy Mother of God, with the estate of Lipsiacum and all its appurtenances; the church called Marengum, with the other lands given to that monastery by Eustorgius, a most noble man; and the small cell situated nearby in the same county, consecrated in honor of the holy Mother of God, which is called ad Montes.

Also the monastery of Celcignanum, with its churches, estates, and lands—namely Carniacum, Burnunculum, Abolniacum, Ginniacum, and Cardonetum—and with all the churches and lands belonging to that monastery of Celcignanum; also the cell situated in the same county where Saint Florus rests, which the cleric Eustorgius gave to the aforesaid place, together with everything belonging to it.

Also the residences in the town of Brioude belonging to the aforesaid place; and the monastery called Volta, consecrated in honor of the holy cross, just as your predecessor Odilo built it on his parents’ estate, with all its dependencies; the cell of Reiliacum, with the estate and everything belonging to it; and the cell consecrated in honor of Saint Mary, called ad Pentem.

Also all the churches and lands, or whatever the aforesaid place of Cluny appears to possess in the said county.

In the bishopric of Nevers: the cell called Saint Reverianus, with all its dependencies; also the church called Superciacum, which Frotimund gave, with all its dependencies.

In the bishopric of Viviers: the cell of Mizoscum, with everything pertaining to it; the cell of Mount Rumpon; the cell ad Fontes; and the cell of Rioms, with everything that the aforesaid place of Cluny appears to possess in the said bishopric.

In the bishopric of Uzès: the monastery dedicated in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Saturninus, situated on the bank of the Rhône, with the castle of Colonellas and the estate of Tulleta, together with everything belonging to it on both sides of the river.

In the bishopric of Troyes: the cell built in honor of Saint Amandus.

In the bishopric of Orange: the cell at Podium Odolenus; and the monastery built in honor of Saint Pantaleon, with everything belonging to it.

In the bishopric of Gap: the cell built in honor of Saint Andrew, granted to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny by the cleric Rigaud, with all its appurtenances; also the small monastery of Ganagobie and the estate of Valentiola, and everything that the aforesaid place of Cluny appears to hold and ought to possess—namely, whatever property is covered by its donation and description—and also the estate and castle of Sarrians, together with everything it possesses in the land called Provence.

In the bishopric of Valence: whatever the place of Cluny appears to possess in the estate called Ales and in Montélimar; the monastery of Saint Marcellus called ad Salcetum, with all its appurtenances and dependencies; and everything that the same place appears to possess in that bishopric.

In the bishopric of Vienne: the monastery called Taderniacum, with the cell called Causella, the estate called Bracost, and the estate called Insula, together with all the churches, estates, and lands which the aforesaid place appears to possess in the named bishopric.

In the bishopric of Lyons: the cell of Blessed Mary called Taluzatis; the cell of Poliacum; the small cell of Arthedunum; and the cell of Amberta, with the churches, estates, and lands belonging to it.

Also the cell of Saviniacum; the estate of Ambariacum; the church of Saint Andreolus; the church called Oratorium; the estate of Romans; the cell of Cavariacum; the small cell of Luviniacum; and the estate of Tusciacum.

Also all the churches, estates, and lands which Wichard, at his death, granted to the same place of Cluny, with everything that the aforesaid place appears to hold in the said bishopric.

The monastery of Peterniacum, built by Empress Adelaide Augusta and granted to the same monastery of Cluny by King Conrad and his son King Rudolf through royal charters, with everything that it appears to possess in Burgundy and with everything that the Augusti emperors Otto gave to that monastery in Alsace.

We also grant the monastery called Romanum, with everything belonging to it, to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny, and to you and your successors, to possess forever.

We also confirm and strengthen by our apostolic authority the agreement made by Lord Hugh, bishop of the Church of Geneva, with the approval and consent of King Rudolf and Lady Adelaide the empress, concerning the church of the martyr Saint Victor, together with everything belonging to it.

All the places and monasteries written above, with their cells, churches, estates, villages, small villages, male and female slaves, woods, vineyards, fields, meadows, waters and watercourses, and all cultivated and uncultivated lands belonging to the aforesaid possessions, we grant by the authority of this privilege of ours to that place of Cluny, to you, and to your successors, to hold and possess forever.

No duke, bishop, prince, or any person, great or small, shall dare to harass or disturb you concerning any of all the aforesaid property and tithes that appear to belong to it there.

Moreover, under proclamation of divine judgment, solemn adjuration, confirmation, and the prohibition of anathema, we decree and strengthen this privilege: no bishop or any priest shall presume to come to that venerable monastery to perform any ordination, consecration of a church, ordination of priests or deacons, or celebration of Masses, unless he has been invited by the abbot of that place. Rather, the monks of that place shall be permitted to receive whatever grade of ordination they wish, wherever it pleases you and your successors.

The abbots who are to be consecrated shall be elected from that congregation itself by common agreement with the counsel of the brothers, and, for their consecration, they shall summon whichever bishop they wish.

Whatever lands you now hold, and whatever you and your successors may acquire, we grant you to possess forever.

If anyone, however, should attempt, through reckless audacity—which we do not believe will happen—to act or proceed against the terms of this apostolic confirmation of ours, let him know that he is bound by the chain of the anathema of our lord Peter, prince of the apostles, and that he is to be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most dreadful pomp, together with Judas, betrayer of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and submerged in the abyss and Tartarean chaos, where he will perish with the impious.

But whoever proves to be the guardian and observer of this privilege of ours shall obtain from the Lord the grace of blessing and eternal life.

Farewell.

Given on the third day before the Ides of June, by the hand of Hildebrand, cardinal subdeacon of the Holy Apostolic See, in the first year of our lord Pope Victor II, in the ninth indiction.

## II. Victor II undertakes the protection of the canons of Ferrara and confirms their possessions

(Year 1055.)

(Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, II, 533.)

[Col. 0808C]

Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gerard, archpriest, and Leo, archdeacon, and the other canons of the Holy Church of Ferrara, and to their successors, forever.

If we satisfy the just petitions of God’s servants, we undoubtedly observe the apostolic precepts. Therefore, inclined by your prayers, dearest sons, we confirm and strengthen for you and for your successors, the canons, whatever you have justly acquired or may acquire through a charter of concession and confirmation, so that you may remain quiet and secure from every injury.

Inclined, as we have said, by your desire and petition, we receive you and your successors under the protection of our apostolic defense. We also receive and confirm all the property which that canonical body justly has or will have: namely, the estate called Quartisana; the holding across the Po; the place called Cuculi; Caput Redae; Baniolo; Wartiaticum; the holding of Pecorile; and the other possessions belonging to the aforesaid church for the use of the canons—estates, lands, vineyards, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated fields, waters and watercourses, fisheries, hunting rights, mills, male and female slaves, *aldiones* and *aldianae*, and all movable and immovable property that can be stated and named.

This includes whatever they hold, possess, or have, whether from the portion of the church or from their own property and the inheritance of their parents, or acquired in any other way through the protection of charters.

It is likewise provided that no one shall presume to injure the inhabitants residing on the lands of the canons—the male or female tenants—or dare to distrain or molest them concerning any of their possessions without the will and consent of the prelate of that church.

We have also deigned to strengthen the charter of confirmation and to receive under our protection twelve men of that city, who are to transport the canons by boat wherever their use requires, without any payment.

Consenting to their worthy petitions, as far as we justly and legally can, we confirm and strengthen all the matters written above, so that they may hold and possess them quietly and peacefully, with every person’s opposition removed.

Therefore, prescribing and ordering, we command that no duke, margrave, archbishop, bishop, count, viscount, or any person, great or small, molest them concerning any of all the aforesaid property, whether ecclesiastical or their own; disturb them in court; or distrain their male or female tenants, or compel them to pay any public levy.

Whoever does so with reckless audacity, unless he makes amends within forty days, shall be bound by the chain of anathema and excluded from the thresholds of Holy Church until he has made worthy satisfaction.

But whoever proves to be the guardian of this sanction of ours shall have the blessing and grace of almighty God, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us, and shall receive an eternal reward in the future.

Amen, amen.

Place of the seal.

Farewell.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, in the year 1055, by the hand of Hildebrand, cardinal subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, in the first year of Pope Victor II, in the eighth indiction.

## III. Privilege of Pope Victor II for the Church of Bologna

(Year 1055.)

(Savioli, *Bolognese Annals*, I, II, Appendix, p. 92.)

Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Peter, archpriest, and the other canons living according to the rule of the holy Church of Bologna, and to their successors forever.

If we satisfy the just petitions of God’s servants, we undoubtedly observe the apostolic precepts. Therefore, inclined by the prayers of Adelfred, bishop of that Church, and by yours, dearest sons, we confirm and strengthen for you and your successors, who live according to canonical law, whatever you have justly acquired or may acquire from him or from others through a charter of concession and confirmation, so that you may remain quiet and secure from every injury.

Inclined, as we have said, by the desire and request of the aforesaid bishop and also by your petition, we receive you and your successors under the protection of our apostolic defense. We likewise receive and confirm all the property which that canonical body of Saint Peter has or will have, namely:

the house situated beside the same church, held perpetually by canonical right; another ancient house for the poor; another house of hospitality; the church of Saint John the Baptist situated beside the house of your lord bishop; all the tithes of the parish of Saint Mary called in Buida, as they appear to have been granted to you by the aforesaid Adelfred; the church of Saint Mary called in Monte Palensi, with its offerings and all its dependencies; half of all the tithes of the entire parish of Saint Peter called Inbarbarorum; and all the olive groves of the Church of Bologna that are in the territory of Garda.

Moreover, whatever you now possess by right of the same holy Church of Bononia, or whatever you or your successors may justly acquire, together with the entire demesne of the same canonical institution—that is, all movable and immovable property that can rightly be described and named—we confirm and establish all these things by the command of the apostolic see’s confirmation and protection. This is also on the condition that no one presume to wrong the male or female tenants residing upon the land of those canons, nor dare to distrain or harass them with respect to any of their possessions. We command that they be able to hold and possess all the things written above quietly and peacefully, with the opposition of all persons removed.

Therefore, we desire and order that no duke, margrave, archbishop, bishop, count, viscount, or any great or humble person compel them to suffer harassment or disturbance in court concerning any of the aforesaid properties, whether ecclesiastical or otherwise, or compel their tenants to submit to distraint or to pay any public levy. Whoever rashly does this, unless he makes amends within forty days, shall be bound by the chain of anathema and excluded from the thresholds of Holy Church until he has made worthy satisfaction. But whoever proves to be the guardian of this our decree shall receive the blessing and grace of almighty God, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of us, and may he receive eternal recompense in the future. [The final verb is incomplete in the supplied text: *…ciat*.]

Issued [lacuna], on the Kalends of July, through the hand of Hildebrand, cardinal subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, in the first year of Pope Victor II, indiction eight.

## IV. Victor II confirms a decree forbidding the possessions of the monastery of Moliana to be invaded. (Year 1055.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, V, 514.]

### Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

Having examined the decree of our most beloved son Henry, by the grace of God august emperor of the Romans, issued for the defense and security of the monastery of Saint Mary, holy and perpetual virgin, situated in the place called Muliana, for the remedy of his soul, at the intervention of his empress, namely his most beloved wife Agnes, and also for the advancement of his most dear son Henry IV, king—we give, grant, and confirm that same decree by our apostolic authority, just as it was issued and confirmed by his imperial power.

Because of the duty owed to the supreme and apostolic see, over which by God’s grace, not through our own merits, we preside, we must care for all the Churches. For from this we obtain from God the greatest reward of gain: if venerable places ordered for the worship of God are brought by us into a better condition. Therefore we wish it to be known to all who desire to live devoutly in Christ how we decree and confirm, by the authority of Saint Peter and of ourselves, that all the properties which Roso, bishop of Treviso, transferred to the aforesaid monastery shall there remain valid and permanently established.

Furthermore, we establish for the said monastery that, with the disturbance of all wicked persons removed, it shall inviolably retain the properties which it now legally holds or which it may hereafter justly and legally acquire: namely, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, fisheries, mills, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and every use that may at any time arise from these things.

In addition, we command and order that no archbishop, bishop, duke, margrave, count, viscount, or any great or humble person presume to violate the written rights of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, concerning what it now possesses or may legally acquire in the future, or to disturb it in any way without a legal judgment. But if anyone should presume, with rash audacity, to act against this privilege of our apostolic authority, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema through the power of almighty God and the apostolic authority of blessed Peter the apostle, and alienated from the kingdom of God, unless he repents and comes to worthy satisfaction. But may whoever proves its observant guardian deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from the most merciful Lord our God.

Issued on the fourth day before the Nones of October, through the hand of Hildebrand, cardinal subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, in the first year of our lord Pope Victor II, indiction eight.

[Note: [Col. 0811D] Read “indiction nine,” according to Jaffé.]

## V. Victor II grants Adalbert, archbishop of Hamburg, the use of the pallium and mitre, and confirms the privileges of his Church. (Year 1055.)

[Lappenberg, *Hamburg. Urkund.*, I, 77.]

### Victor II, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our beloved fellow-bishop Adalbert, venerable archbishop of the Church of Hamburg, and to your successors forever.

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with devout religion through kindly compassion, and to grant with eager devotion the assent requested by their hearts. For by this we unquestionably earn the greatest reward from the Creator, the Lord of all, when venerable places, suitably ordered, are brought by us into a better condition.

Therefore, since you asked us to confirm in full the entire archbishopric of the Church of Hamburg for you and your successors, just as it was decreed by our predecessors, namely Nicholas and Agapetus, Benedict and Leo, bishops of this nurturing apostolic see, we, yielding to your prayers, grant and confirm by apostolic authority everything generally and specifically belonging to the aforesaid archbishopric of yours. This includes everything that your predecessors acquired through their labors, or that the faithful worshipers of Christ have given or are giving there out of love for the eternal homeland.

Together with these, we include those who in our time have been converted to the faith of Christ through the prompting and protection of God’s grace—namely, the bishops among all the peoples of the Swedes or Danes, Norwegians, Icelanders, Scridefinns, Greenlanders, and all the northern nations, as well as in those regions of the Slavs extending from the River Peene to the River Eider. We decree that all these shall remain under the authority of you and your successors, the archbishops of the Church of Hamburg. Whatever, with divine favor, can be acquired by you from the error of unbelief—whether persons or places—for the Christian religion, we likewise decree that you and your successors shall hold perpetually and retain inviolably.

Moreover, we decree that no archbishop, whether the archbishop of Cologne or anyone else, may claim any authority for himself within your diocese. We also permit your head to be adorned with the mitre, which is the insignia of the Romans. But if anyone attempts to oppose this privilege of our authority or rashly violate it in any respect, let him be anathema. Whoever observes it, however, shall obtain grace and blessing from the Lord Jesus Christ.

Issued on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, through the hand of Frederick, chancellor of the holy Roman Church, in the first year of the lord Pope Victor II, indiction eight.

## VI. Victor II takes the canons of the Church of Pisa under his protection and confirms their possessions. (Year 1055.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, III, 359.]

### Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most beloved sons in Christ, the canons of Saint Mary, holy Mother of God and perpetual virgin, and to your successors forever.

A favorable assent is owed to just and reasonable petitions. Whatever takes nothing away from divine religion, but in the future contributes greatly to human welfare, ought indeed to be granted and sought. Therefore we wish it to be known to all Christ’s faithful, present and future, how the brothers of the Pisan Church, belonging to the canonical community of Saint Mary, holy Mother of God, as we have said, approached our clemency, humbly entreating our fatherhood that we receive them, together with the goods rightfully belonging to the aforesaid canonical community, under the protection of the apostolic defense by issuing them our privilege.

Yielding to their petition through the benevolence of the apostolic see, over which by God’s authority, though unworthy, we preside, we receive those same brothers under our protection. By issuing this privilege, we grant and confirm, by the authority of God and holy Peter, all these possessions—both tithes and estates—which the same aforesaid canonical community now holds by right or may justly acquire in the future.

Furthermore, desiring quiet peace and security for the aforesaid canonical community and its possessions, we establish and confirm by that same authority of God, holy Peter, and ourselves that no person, great or small, dare or presume to inflict any force, damage, or harassment upon it, to trouble it, or to usurp any of its goods for himself without a legal or canonical judgment.

If anyone—which we do not wish—should presume to violate this privilege of our grant and confirmation, and, forgetful of our command, inflict damage or harassment upon them, or usurp anything for himself from the possessions of the aforesaid canonical community, unless he repents and makes worthy satisfaction for his wrongdoing, let him be bound by the chain of anathema. But whoever proves its guardian and observer, let him be filled with apostolic blessing and obtain mercy in the Lord God. Amen.

Around the rim of the lead seal these words are engraved:

“Of Victor II, holy Roman and universal pope. Jesus Christ, Peter, Paul. In the year 1055, first year of the pontificate.”

## VII. Victor II confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Ascoli at the request of Bishop Bernardo. (Year 1055.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, I, 449.]

### Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Berardo, second bishop of the Church and bishopric of Saint Mary, holy Mother of God and virgin, and of the most blessed martyr of Christ Emigdius, situated within the city in the county of Ascoli, and to all his canonical successors entering there, forever.

Since, by the generous gift of divine grace, the whole Church has been entrusted to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to govern, administer, and defend from every attack of wicked persons, so that the Church whose doctrine nourishes it may be fortified by his protection, it is fitting that we, who exercise the apostolic office in his place, extend the hand of rightful protection to each Church. Thus what advances their support and defense may release us from the debt we owe to all.

Accordingly, at the request of the aforesaid lord Bernardo, bishop of the holy Church of Ascoli, granting the protection of apostolic authority, we confer upon the aforesaid bishop and all his successors canonically enthroned there—[namely, the Church] dedicated to the honor of Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin—not a privilege of lesser generosity but a barrier and shield of complete protection. Thus the church dedicated to the name of the supreme almighty King of martyrs may also be protected by a written instrument and defended by the sword of his Son, the supreme warrior.

Therefore, providing by apostolic authority for each individual possession, we confirm and strengthen for you whatever has justly been brought to the same church, so that no one may thereafter dare to strip it of anything or harass it, or inflict any disturbance upon it. These possessions are: the entire city of Ascoli, together with its portion of the monastery of Saint Angelus, which has been built in that city; and the monastery of Saint Mary, situated on the holy mountain, with everything justly belonging to it or which may hereafter legally belong to it through the rightful donation of anyone.

Also, the castle called Trione, with the monastery of Saint Laurence and all its dependencies; the estate of Massa, with the Pojo of the Lucida Valley; the estate of Monte; the estate of Pazano, as it is recorded and read in the charter of Maynard, son of Sigolf; the castles called Sculcula, Matrice, and Spinetula; the estate of Ilica; the estate of Cariano; the estate of Core; the estate of Belenterio; the estate of Flaminiano; the estate of Api; the estate of Tarracina; the estate of Bapino; the estate of Vuasto Pomarese; the estate of Saxa; the estate of Salli; the estate of Patarco; the estate of Villamagna; and everything belonging to the aforesaid bishopric, both within the aforementioned castles and elsewhere: the estate of Montariolo within the city of Spoleto; the estate of Paterno in the place called Ponte; the estate of Primo-casu; Gualdo of Laguine; a house in Norcia; and an estate within the place where the city formerly stood; the estate of Sala in the same Norcia; Guallum of Fesso; and the estate of Savelli.

Likewise, in the county of Ascoli, in the place called Aqua, the castle of Luco; the tower of Fotiano; the Pojo of Quintodecimo; the estate of Mazzanna, with its saltworks; the castle of Murro; the castle of Fundanianum; Mount Purus, with its parks and woods, together with the Pojo called Clamatorium; Plage, with the castle of Lusianum; Villamagna, with its Pojo and castle; Cicilianum; Mount Calvus; Bajanum; the castle of Gualdo; the estate of Agelli; the castle of Ligunianum; the estate of Pupilliana; the estate of Saint Stephen; the estate of Paterno; and the castle of Spelunca, with the estate of Valeriano itself; the estate of Bofiano; Mount Andrew; the Pojo Silvistum, which lies before the castle of Gusianum; as well as the castle of Spinetulum with its estate called Francisca; the estate of Fassiana; the estate of Prostitula; the Pojo of Valenterius; the castle of Ottavo; the Pojo of Gaminaldus; the estate of Cervinaria; the estate of Chrisiana; the estate of Vivarium; the estate of Saint Felix; the Pojo of Pignola; the estate of Saint Martin; the castle of Corato, with the Pojo of Helicetus and of Cisimula; the estate of Popiliano; the estate of Lauretiana; the estate of Maltiniana; the castle of Castelli; in Frundaria, the estate of Porile; the estate of Diana; the estate of Quarto; the castle of Postmontes; the estate of Capitinula; the estate of Paternion, with the Pojo of Avignon; the castle of Callonnata with its estates; the estate of Ciniano with its castle; the estate of Casula; and the castle of Vina.

We confirm and strengthen in full, by apostolic authority, all the things named above, together with the parishes and individual churches and their endowments, with male and female slaves, small villages, farms, dependent holdings, and individual tenants; with alpine lands and mountains, woods, meadows, pastures, vineyards, olive groves, cultivated and uncultivated lands, waters, mills, fishponds, fisheries, saltworks, and watercourses; as well as herds of cattle, horse pastures, and everything else justly belonging to them.

We also grant you, in accordance with the canonical institution of the holy Fathers, the tithes, first fruits, and all offerings of the faithful, living and dead, that justly and canonically belong to the same bishopric.

We further establish and decree that no bishop, supported by the authority or power of anyone, dare without permission make any arrangements there contrary to the ordinances or constitutions of the aforesaid bishop, or establish judgments, or distrain or harass clerics or priests by any kind of synod.

Therefore, establishing by apostolic authority—a rule to be observed by everyone and in every respect—we decree and bind under anathema that no emperor or king, no duke or margrave, count, viscount, castellan, or any public official or collector, nor any person whatever, of whatever order, rank, or religious status, dare oppose or in any way violate this pragmatic sanction of privilege. Whoever attempts this shall perish, struck by divine anathema from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, because he did not fear offending the Mother of God and those who serve her, and considered it nothing that God should behold this. But may the protector, supported by blessing, obtain eternal life from almighty God.

“Of Victor II, bishop of the first see and universal pope.”

JESUS CHRIST. PETER. PAUL.

Issued on the fourth day before the Nones of January, through the hand of Hildebrand, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, acting in place of Hermandus, archchancellor of the apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Victor II, indiction eight. Issued at Rome, prosperously, in the name of God. Amen.

## VIII. Victor II confirms the rights and privileges of the abbey of Andlau. (Year 1055–57.)

[Wurdtwein, *Nova Subsidia diplomatica*, vol. VI, p. 223, from the Salic parchment book of the abbey of Andlau, fol. 1, and from the autograph bull of Pope Martin V, year 1426.]

### Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in Christ, Mehtild, religious abbess of the venerable monastery of Saint Fabian and Saint Felicitas, called Helgonis, situated in the district of Helizaze, and to your successors as abbesses, perpetual salvation in the Lord.

The effects of fitting and just petitions ought, through divine mercy, to be granted. Therefore, yielding to your intercessions, following the examples of our predecessors, for the security of future times and the stability of your institution, we grant and confirm to you, through this privilege of our apostolic authority, the same monastery with all its possessions and resources, which it now appears justly to possess and which thereafter, with the Lord’s help, it may receive either from kings or from persons of whatever rank or order.

Indeed, we forbid any priest to celebrate Mass at the major altar of the new church except one whom you and your successors shall choose, just as this was confirmed to you by our predecessor Leo. The monastery itself, as we have already stated, we grant and confirm in its entirety, on the condition that throughout all the days of your life it belong wholly under our authority or governance, to be disposed of as you see fit according to God.

When, however, by divine calling you have departed from this present light to the Lord, we establish that an abbess shall be appointed from the very congregation whom the unanimous community of the monastery’s servants of God shall concordantly elect, without the opposition or obstruction of any person. In return, you and your successors shall provide annually three linen cloths suitable for episcopal use.

If this payment is not made within two or three years, we wish the entire census owed for those years to be paid in the fourth year alone, and nothing more is to be demanded from your successors in any manner.

Therefore, by this present decree we order that no emperor, king, or person of whatever rank or order dare, under any pretext or occasion, disturb or in any way molest the aforesaid monastery—which the most glorious empress Richarda, for love of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and for the eternal reward of her soul, together with our most beloved son Charles, most serene august emperor, offered to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, by a deed of donation—or transfer it to his own right or that of another. Nor shall anyone at any time presume to make any opposition or invasion concerning its people or resources.

Let the aforesaid servants of God therefore be permitted to live quietly with their own abbess in the service of almighty God, and to remain securely under the protection of the holy apostolic Church, which by God’s authority we serve. But if anyone—which God forbid and which we do not believe will happen—should rashly attempt to act or cause anyone to act against this apostolic privilege of ours, let him remain bound by the chain of perpetual anathema and condemned to everlasting punishment unless he repents. Whoever proves its guardian and observer, however, may deserve to receive blessing, grace, and mercy from the Lord God, so that he may rejoice in the heavenly seat.

## IX. Victor II’s privilege for the liberty of the monastery of Ely. (Year 1055–57.)

[*Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 94.]

### Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Edward, most beloved son, king of the English, and to all the princes of the kingdom, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We briefly renew, for your pious petition, and strengthen with perpetual stability—or rather, loudly proclaim as strengthened—the privilege concerning the monastery of Ely, originally written by the authority of the apostolic and Roman Church and repeatedly authenticated by the testimony of many, which the glorious Fathers of Holy Church established with devout affection and generous hand.

Therefore we command and by apostolic right prescribe that the church be free, together with everything contained there, adjoining it, or to be added to it: cells, lands, fields, pastures, marshes, woods, hunting rights, waters, fisheries, liberties, due services, tithes, rents, head taxes, laws, customs, hearings of cases, corrections, and compensations, whether ecclesiastical or secular. This includes absolutely everything that can be recalled in the writings or testaments of that place, or by the testimony of good men, namely whatever kings or any of the faithful have bestowed or granted to the saints in that monastery.

No one, under any pretext, judgment, or authority, shall presume to remove, diminish, or squander any of these things, nor shall any bishop or minister of any order intrude upon them. But if anyone, moved by a spirit of wickedness, should wish to violate the liberty of that place, despise or reject our privilege, let him be condemned by God and all his saints, excommunicated by us insofar as permitted, and separated from the fellowship of all the faithful, unless he repents.

## X. Victor II’s bull confirming to Rolando, bishop of Ferrara, and to his Church, all its rights and privileges. (Year 1055.)

[Muratori, *Antichità Italiane*, VI, 223.]

### Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

Let it be known to all Christ’s faithful and our own, present and future, how we have confirmed, by a privilege of our authority, to Rolando, bishop of the Church of Ferrara, and to his successors, all the movable and immovable possessions of that Church, just as the Church itself now justly holds them or may in the future justly and legally acquire them, so that it may recover what it has lost and possess more securely what it holds.

We declare to everyone that whatever Gregory, more a destroyer than a ruler of that Church, composed in charters or superscriptions, or caused to be written, shall have no force forever. We also confirm that the parishes, monasteries, chapels, estates, villages, riverbanks, castles, marshes, fisheries, woods, and everything that the aforesaid Church justly held in the time of its predecessors, or ought to hold, shall be possessed permanently. We annul and destroy by our authority any harmful document or agreement that his predecessors had contracted through kinship, family connection, or evil intent.

We confirm to Rolando, bishop of the aforesaid Church, and to his successors, the entire jurisdiction over all their castellans, slaves, and all those residing on their land, both clerics and laypeople, just as the Church of Ferrara itself now appears justly to hold it.

In the same manner we confirm to them the parish of Saint Stephen situated at Vicoventia, with the Church of Saint Leo and all its dependencies—namely Vicoventia, Corrigia, Vicovaria, and half of the Castle of Rupina—and the monasteries of Saints Bartholomew, Laurence, and Vincent, with the village called Monasteriolo, and the Church of Saint Leo near the Aventine village, together with everything justly acquired and everything to be justly acquired thereafter. Thus the clerics and monks of that bishopric shall remain under the governance, consecration, and jurisdiction of their bishops, and no one among them shall turn to any other tribunal except the judgments of his own bishop.

Furthermore, we confirm to the aforesaid Church those lands which were assigned to it by oaths in the time of its predecessor, in For[lacuna], in the parish of Saint Stephen in Galigo, in the parish of Saint Donatus, in that of Saint George, and in that of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, together with these villages, whose names are Quartixiana, Caput de Reda, and Contrapadum, and the estate called Carali, so that no one may inflict harassment upon it without a legal judgment.

In addition, we confirm to him twelve men of that city, who shall transport him and his successors by boat without payment, wherever the usage of his predecessors required.

If, therefore, any duke, margrave, archbishop, bishop, count, viscount, or any great or humble person should presume to act against this privilege of ours or attempt to violate it, unless he makes amends and comes to worthy satisfaction, let him be bound by the chain of anathema and separated from the boundaries of Holy Church. But whoever proves the guardian and observer of this our command shall obtain apostolic blessing and mercy from the Lord God.

## XI. Victor II commends Bruno, abbot of Dervent, to Count Theobald. (Year 1055–57.)

[Mabillon, *Annales Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, IV, 557.]

### Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Count Theobald, apostolic blessing.

Trusting that your Excellency has always shown itself devoted to the support of its friends, we strive to commend to you the causes of those whom you love. The affection owed to good sons also urges us diligently to advance their interests and to help them insofar as reason permits.

Therefore we greet you and ask that our son Bruno, abbot of the monastery of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of Saint Bercharius the martyr, may always find you such as he has hitherto known you, and may obtain the support of your Excellency wherever it is necessary and find great consolation in you. So that he may not unjustly be subjected to any affliction or burden, may your Magnificence arrange this.

We have learned from the report of our aforesaid son how much concern you show for monasteries, for religious and irreligious monks alike; how much glory almighty God has granted you among men on this account, so that more religious monasteries may endure under your protection. May the merciful God, from whom all good things proceed, multiply this for you until the day of recompense.

He also related to us, in the presence of the testimony of many, now weeping, now rejoicing, how greatly the magnificence of your piety has benefited the monastery over which he presides: by beseeching and reproving the brothers, by restoring to it villages and churches with mills and various possessions, and by rebuilding bridges belonging to the same monastery. Many rejoice in these bridges, especially those who inhabit the islands of the sea, namely the Scots and the English; and he told how unjust men reproach you in order that you may desist.

Accordingly, while returning abundant thanks, we ask you willingly to hear whatever is urged upon you by those distinguished for good works, to act devoutly, and to keep it in memory. For if you listen to those who speak on God’s behalf, the Almighty will likewise hear those who pray on your behalf.

For this reason almighty God brings good men to the governance of peoples, so that through them he may bestow the gifts of his power upon all those over whom they have been set. Do what belongs to God, and God will do what belongs to you.

May almighty God protect and guard you, your sons, and your entire household by his protection from every adversity, and grant you both prosperity in the present life and the joy of the future one.

## XII. Victor II’s bull for the monastery of Vendôme. (Year 1055–57.)

[Gallia Christiana, vol. VIII, Instruments, p. 418.]

### Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Geoffrey, venerable count of Anjou, and to Agnes, his wife, countess, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Moved by the very apostolic office, we recognize that we ought to assist every petition that proceeds from a pure and just desire. For the more intensely anyone else raises the eyes of his mind toward contemplation of the divine vision, the more diligently ought we to encourage and exalt his intention, so that his good desire may attain to Him who is the fruit and reward of good works.

But because you, dearest sons, have resolved to ask and petition with humble devotion from the authority of the Roman See, over which by God’s will we preside, that by apostolic power we should confirm and make free from all human persons—except the pontiff of the First See alone—the monastery of the Holy Trinity situated near the fortress of Vendôme, which you have newly founded from your own goods and offered in alod and patrimony to blessed Peter and his successors, we have judged it worthy to grant your petitions and fulfill your desire in all respects.

Therefore we confirm it, and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul we specially strengthen that monastery, so that no person of any dignity or order may stand between the pontiff of the First and Apostolic See and the venerable abbot of the place of Vendôme. If it should happen that a legate of the Roman Church visits the aforesaid place of blessed Peter, he shall be received there with all charity, and, insofar as the resources of the place permit, the brothers shall supply him with what is necessary for the body. He himself, however, shall not presume to correct anything in that place on his own authority, nor, on the pretext of his legation, molest the rector of the place or the brothers. But if he sees anything requiring correction, he may report it by letter to the pope, in whose sole power the entire governance and correction of that monastery rests.

The abbot, who is known to be an alodial holder of the Roman Church, shall neither come nor be summoned to a council unless it has been convened by the supreme pontiff of the Apostolic See himself. Rather, he shall diligently visit his mother, the Roman Church, either personally or through his messenger, and there each year pay a census of twelve solidi of his own coinage, to provide lights before the venerable body of the most blessed Peter.

Furthermore, we decree that, when the abbot of that congregation dies, his successor shall be chosen from the same congregation, if someone worthy of the prelacy is found there. But if none should be found among them—which God forbid—the monks shall choose an abbot for themselves from Cluny, or from the Major Monastery, or from wherever they can find someone better, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. In choosing their shepherd, however, they shall make use of the counsel of three abbots whom they can find to be the most religious in the neighboring places.

The elected abbot shall receive his consecration from the bishop of Chartres, without any subjection or exaction, so that he is not wearied by immediately coming to Rome, provided that this bishop has canonically received the episcopate and has not shown himself hostile or suspect toward the place of blessed Peter. Otherwise, let him have recourse to us or to our successors and receive from the See of blessed Peter, to which the right belongs, both the staff and consecration.

Once the abbot has been ordained, both the abbots and the monks of that place shall take care to inform the pope by letter how and in what manner the ordination was carried out, so that he may either correct what needs correcting or, if the election or ordination was made according to our decree, rejoice in it with good will.

We also command that the count of Anjou shall at all times be the helper and defender of the monastery of Vendôme, for the honor of the Apostolic See. He himself, however, or any of his successors, shall impose no exaction or customary due upon the monastery or its possessions, nor presume to claim anything in them, except the protection alone which he is permitted to provide for the honor of the Apostolic See and for the salvation of his soul.

We further add that both in the place of Vendôme and in the church of Saint Saviour beside the walls of Angers, no person except the Roman pontiff alone may exercise any power or lordship, excommunicate, or impose an interdict. Even if the region of Chartres or Angers should be excommunicated for whatever offenses, those who have been excommunicated shall nevertheless not be received by the monks.

We confirm by our authority everything that has been offered there by you or by other persons up to the present day, so that it may remain perpetually with that place, without diminution or any revocation. If anyone wishes to bring a lawsuit or disturbance against that place concerning any possessions, the abbot or brothers shall in no way answer him before consulting the Roman pontiff, because whatever is decided or alienated without the judgment of us or our successors shall be invalid.

The possessions belonging to the aforesaid monastery and offered to blessed Peter as patrimony upon his altar by Count Geoffrey of Anjou and Agnes, his wife, the countess, are set down here for the knowledge of those to come.

In the county of Vendôme: the church of Saint Nicholas of Ferraria; the church of Prunet, with all its customary dues; half of the church of Saint Mary at Villa Episcopi; the church of Saint Stephen at the pond; and the four churches which Theodoric, bishop of Chartres, gave to the monastery of Vendôme out of love for God and at the request of Count Geoffrey—namely, the church of Saint Beatus, the church of Saint John of Châteaudun, the church of Baigneaux, the church of Villarebla, and the church of Anscheric.

In the bishopric of Le Mans: the church of Saint John the Baptist of Villa Dei, and the villa itself with its lands and woods, vicariate, and all customary dues; the land of Pinis and the land there beside half of the church of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Michael of Hulseto, and the land with its pond and mills, woods, vicariate, and all customary dues; half of the church of Torcy.

In the bishopric of Angers: the church of Saint Saturninus and the entire estate, together with the wood called Latez and the land of the wood, if the wood should be cleared.

At the fortress of Craon: the church of Saint Clement and its entire parish; the churches of the village of Meduanilis; the church of Saint John upon the Loire, with nineteen arpents of vineyards and two mills; the church of Saint Peter of Maziac and the entire estate; the church of Saint Medard of Caviriac.

In the bishopric of Poitiers: the church of Olonne.

In the bishopric of Saintes: the church of Saint George and the third part of that island, with all customary dues.

In the fortress of Oleron: the church of Blessed Mary; the church of Puy-Rebellis; the church of Blosmeriaco; the church of Saint Saturninus; and the land of Saint Anianus with its saltworks, fisheries, and all customary dues.

In the forest of Wastina: all the pannage from the monastery’s own pigs belonging to all the monks of the Holy Trinity; half the pannage of other men; and the honey and wax of that forest for the monastery’s lights. Also, all the Vendôme monks and all their people shall have the right to take trees for all their uses on lands belonging to the monastery, without the permission of the foresters.

If the abbot of the aforesaid place and the count of Vendôme should have a dispute with one another, or if any of their men should have a complaint against the other, judgment shall not be rendered in the count’s court or in any other court, but the complaint shall be settled in the abbot’s court, in accordance with the dignity of the place. This shall nevertheless be done so that, for love of the Most High Trinity, in whose name and honor the monastery itself was built, no one may demand or grant half of the forfeiture.

But if anyone knowingly violates this our decree, or withdraws anything from the possessions written above belonging to the monastery of Vendôme, let him be condemned by the curse of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; let him be confounded and perish—the place having been built in His honor and name. Moreover, let him incur the wrath of the Mother of God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of all the saints; by our apostolic authority let him be excommunicated and bound by the bond of anathema, so that he may never see the kingdom of God, but may be condemned forever with the devil and Judas the traitor and all the impious, and remain in darkness and the shadow of death and in sulphurous fire, in that Tartarean cold where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 8:12), unless he makes worthy satisfaction and repairs what he has taken from that place.

But whoever proves himself a keeper and violator-free guardian of this our apostolic confirmation and protection, let him be blessed with every blessing, so that he may have a share in the kingdom of God with the saints and elect, and rejoice in everlasting joy in that light and splendor of the heavens where all goodness is, forever and ever. Amen.

Brief sign of Victor, bishop of the First See and universal pope.

### XIII. Bull of Pope Victor II for the Church of Saints Simon and Jude (1057)

[Heineccius, *Goslarian Antiquities*, book I, p. 63.]

**Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of Christ.**

The vow of a holy purpose is fulfilled not only through divine action but is also assisted by human support. Let it therefore be known to all the sons of Holy Church, present and future, that our dearest son, the emperor Augustus Henry II, constructed from the foundations a certain church in honor of the holy virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of the blessed apostles Simon and Jude. It is situated in the place called Goslar, where brothers live under the canonical rule, and over whom he placed his chancellor Gunther.

For the remedy of his own soul and that of his wife, the Augusta and our daughter Agnes, and also for the salvation of his parents Conrad and Gisela, of blessed memory, with pious affection and pious intention he wholly granted it to blessed Peter and his Apostolic See by a document signed with his own hand, through our hands—that is, through the hands of us, the unworthy vicar of that same prince of the apostles—so that the church itself, placed under apostolic law, might remain forever free and undisturbed from every right and dominion, from every injury and molestation, retaining its integrity in all the possessions and resources that it now has in the aforesaid place of Goslar, in Egeln, Jeresleben, Adesleben, Summensteten, Slansteten, Valentro, Aldendorf, Dingelstetein, Borestorff, Ogtkersleve, Balbria, Walchesleve, and Herlingerode, as well as in other places and villages, and in whatever it shall possess forever, whether movable or immovable.

Having received this gift from the hands of our aforesaid dearest son, Augustus, we have decreed through this privilege of our apostolic authority to contribute and grant to that church of Saint Mary and of the holy apostles Simon and Jude every apostolic protection and strength, so that, remaining intact in its possessions and properties, it may fear no loss or diminution throughout the ages from an emperor, king, or any public or private person.

Nevertheless, we have judged it fitting to leave to our same dearest son Augustus and to his successors the advocacy of that holy place, on this condition: that they shall always have the power to appoint there, according to God, provosts; but they shall not give any of its goods for their own use or grant them as a benefice. If any of them should attempt to act contrary to our prohibition, we order that the provost and canons who shall then be serving there be free thereafter to look to the Roman Church in every way, so that they fear nothing from imperial or royal authority.

The bishop in whose diocese the monastery of this church has been built shall have no right or power in it except ecclesiastical governance and episcopal authority according to canonical institutions.

Therefore, by apostolic censure and under invocation of the divine judgment, we decree that no imperial or royal power, ecclesiastical or secular, nor any human person, great or small, of whatever sex or age, attempt to act against this privilege of our apostolic confirmation [the word *apostolicae* is absent]. Whoever, man or woman, should do so—which God forbid!—shall remain wounded by the penalty of our apostolic anathema until worthy satisfaction has been made.

But whoever has guarded himself from these prohibitions and observed everything written here without violation shall receive from us a full blessing and from God everlasting salvation.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of January, through the hands of Aribo, acting in place of Anno, archchancellor of the Roman Church and archbishop of Cologne, in the second year of Lord Pope Victor II, indiction 10.

[Note: A lead seal of unusual character is attached to this charter. One side displays Rome with the inscription:

**AUREA ROMA**  
“Golden Rome.”

Around it, in a circle, are the words:

**+ VICTORIS PAPAE II**  
“Of Pope Victor II.”

The other side depicts a mitred pope extending a key from heaven with his hand, together with the inscription:

**TU PRO ME NAVEM LIQUISTI, SUSCIPE CLAVEM.**  
“You left the ship for me; receive the key.”]

### XIV. Privilege of Victor II for the Monastery of Fulda (1057)

[Dronke, *Diplomatic Code of Fulda*, no. 364.]

**Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Echbert, pious and religious abbot of the monastery of Our Lord Jesus Christ the Saviour and of Saint Boniface, situated in the place called Bochonia beside the bank of the river called Fulda, and through you to that venerable monastery and its successors, forever.**

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those endowed with pious religion through benevolent compassion and to grant those who ask justly and religiously a favorable response with eager devotion. For by this we undoubtedly earn the chief reward of gain from God, the creator of all, if venerable places, suitably ordered, are plainly brought to a better condition.

Therefore, because you have petitioned us, we have resolved by our apostolic command perpetually to grant back and reconfirm to you and your successors the aforesaid monastery of Our Lord Jesus Christ the Saviour and of Saint Boniface, situated in the place called Bochonia beside the bank of the river called Fulda, with all its movable and immovable possessions, which it now has and, with God’s help, shall have in the future.

We also grant and give to you, dearest and most beloved son, and perpetually to your successors, the abbots, out of the great love and excessive affection that we have for you and desire henceforth to have, the monastery of the apostle Saint Andrew, called Exaiulum, situated in Rome beside the church of Saint Mary, the ever-virgin Mother of God, called *Ad Praesepe*. It includes all its dwellings, heated rooms, wine cellars, and kitchen, together with vineyards, gardens, and various kinds of fruit trees; its estate and well; its entrance through the principal gate from the public road; and everything generally belonging to that monastery, situated both within and outside the city, which is rightly and properly recognized as belonging to it.

We forbid every priest of any church to exercise any jurisdiction or authority over your monastery of Fulda, except our Apostolic See, and especially the bishop in whose diocese it appears to have been built. Thus, unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, he shall not presume to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass there.

We confirm and strengthen, with perpetual firmness and without opposition from any person, for your monastery itself, according to the privileges of our predecessors, the gifts, offerings, and tithes of the faithful.

We also decree that no person, great or small, may inflict any force or controversy upon that monastery concerning its possessions or dependents. By our apostolic authority we also prohibit any woman from ever presuming to enter there; no one shall ever hold a court there or in any of its other places; and no one shall compel its slaves or tenants to any service, except one to whom the abbot has given his consent for the useful fulfillment of his needs.

The brothers shall also have the power, whenever necessary, to choose an abbot from among themselves according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, without contradiction from any person.

Furthermore, after deliberation, we decree that at appropriate times it shall be reported to our ecclesiastical concern how monastic religion is being directed in regular discipline and entrusted to fitting ecclesiastical concord, lest, God forbid, under the pretext of this privilege, the mind and conduct of your uprightness be in any way turned aside from the norm of justice.

We also grant you, dearest son—whom we know to be a well-educated and eloquent man—the authority to preach the word of God, by the authority of Saint Peter the apostle of God and of us, his unworthy vicar. We further grant that both you and your successors shall, by our apostolic authority, have the primacy of sitting before the other abbots of Gaul or Germany in every place and assembly.
