The abbot shall receive his blessing only from our Apostolic See, from which he ought to be blessed. If he is accused of any crime, he shall await judgment solely from that same Apostolic See.

We also grant and confirm the use of the dalmatic and sandals, according to what was granted to you by our predecessors.

Therefore we have judged it fitting to add this general provision: whatever is known to have been granted to your monastery of Fulda by the authority of any of our predecessors, kings or emperors, shall also be confirmed and strengthened by our apostolic authority through this privilege of ours. By apostolic censure and under invocation of the divine judgment, we decree that none of our future pontiffs of Rome, kings, dukes, margraves, counts, archbishops, bishops, or persons of any dignity or condition shall ever dare to attempt anything against this privilege.

If anyone presumes to do so, let him know that he is indissolubly bound by the bond of our anathema until worthy satisfaction has been made. But whoever guards himself with pious care and observes that this privilege not be violated in any respect, may deserve to obtain from God, the giver of all good things, the grace of blessing and absolution from his sins, so that he may glory in the heavenly court.

(S. p. s.) B. V.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of February, through the hands of Aribo, acting in place of Anno, archchancellor of the holy Roman and Apostolic See and archbishop of Cologne, in the second year of Pope Victor II, indiction 10.

### XV. Privilege of Victor II for the Church of Trier (1057)

[Gunther, *Rhenish-Moselle Diplomatic Code*, p. 134.]

**Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to you, beloved brother and archbishop of the holy Church of Trier, and to your successors, forever.**

Just and pleasing petitions to the Lord deserve an affectionate response. For what is at present so just and so pleasing to God as that due authority, reverence, and usefulness should be claimed and preserved for venerable and pious places, to the praise and glory of his name?

Therefore we rejoice greatly, dearest and reverend brother and fellow bishop Eberhard, that according to your request you have been temporarily entrusted with the care of confirming and perpetually retaining the right of the holy Church of Trier. In accordance with your petition and the privileges of our predecessors—namely Pope John XIII, Pope Benedict VII, and Leo IX of blessed memory—by the authority of this privilege of ours we decree and confirm to you and to your successors after you the primacy of Belgic Gaul, in this manner:

Whenever a priest, deacon, subdeacon, or any ordinary legate is sent from our principal and Apostolic See for the sake of ecclesiastical benefit or to conduct a synod in Gaul or Germany, you and your successors shall occupy the first place among the other bishops after that apostolic legate. If no envoy of the Roman Church is present, you shall likewise have the primacy, after the emperor or king, of sitting, giving judgment, and canonically promulgating synodal decisions, as those deservedly constituted vicars of our Apostolic See in those regions.

Nor is it fitting that the prelate of that Church should at any time not be regarded as superior to the others, since its honor in those regions was originally established under the prince of the apostles himself.

And since we know that the archbishop of that Church, blessed Eucharius, was ordained by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, just as was blessed Apollinaris of the city of Ravenna, it has pleased us to permit you, our brother Eberhard, archbishop of the holy Church of Trier, and all your successors after you, that just as, through the ordination, blessing, and direction of the one blessed apostle Peter, preachers of the Gospel of Christ from other cities were made equal in preaching to the nations, so also, in celebrating the solemn rites of Mass, they may be equal in rank, in riding with the *naccus* through the stations, and in every honor.

Let a cross be carried before you, as before the archbishop of Ravenna. Let your cardinal priests, when you, our brother, celebrate Mass, use dalmatics, and let the deacons, together with the priests, use sandals.

You and your successors shall also use the Roman mitre in ecclesiastical offices as a mark of primacy, according to Roman custom, and shall always remember yourselves to be disciples of the Roman See. This shall be on the condition that you and your successors send your legates to us and our successors once each year—unless, of course, a canonical summons should come to you from the Apostolic See for this purpose—through whom we may send you instructions concerning matters to be undertaken for our interests in those regions. Moreover, every third year, except when such a canonical summons has occurred, you yourselves shall come to Rome for the sake of visitation, unless prevented by unavoidable cause.

In the same way we decree that all who live in your parishes, whether they receive ordination or promotion to any ecclesiastical rank from you, must canonically please, obey, and rightly submit to that mother Church and its archbishop. For the decree of blessed Pope Clement appears to have taken precautions concerning this matter:

“If all the priests, deacons, and other clerics do not obey the bishops, and if all princes, both of higher and lower rank, together with the rest of the peoples, tribes, and tongues, do not obey, they shall be excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church of God. For the Lord says: ‘Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.’”

Among all these matters, everything that appears to belong to the aforesaid Church of Trier, inside and outside the city—that is, churches with all the possessions belonging to them, and monasteries of both monks and virgins, which belong or ought to belong to it by the commands or documents of kings or emperors or by the authority of their founders, and whatever that same Church possesses or ought to possess for any rightful reason—we grant in general and in particular to that Church, because we have found this recorded in the privileges of our predecessors.

We reconfirm all these things to you, our brother and fellow bishop, and to your successors, for the perpetual gift and authority of the holy Church of Trier, through this series of our apostolic command, to remain valid from the present tenth indiction until the end of the age.

If anyone should presume to act against this in any way, or attempt in any respect to violate what has been decreed by us justly and canonically, let him know that by the authority of almighty God, of the aforesaid most blessed prince of the apostles, and of all the saints, and thereafter by our authority, he is to be condemned and anathematized and assigned to eternal punishment with all the impious.

But whoever faithfully strives to observe, guard, and fulfill this privilege of ours may effectively deserve from the Lord God to obtain the grace of blessing and the fullness of mercy in the heavenly camp among the number of the elect.

Written by the hand of Gregory, notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of April, in the indiction stated above, on the twenty-fifth day.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, through the hands of Arebo, deacon, acting in place of Anno, archchancellor of the holy Roman and Apostolic See and archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, in the third year of Lord Pope Victor II, indiction 10, in the month of April, on the twenty-fifth day.

### XVI. Letter of Pope Victor II enlarging the privileges of the Church of Silva Candida for Bishop Humbert (1057)

[Mansi XIX, 835.]

**Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop Humbert, and through him to the Church of the holy virgins and martyrs Rufina and Secunda, which is called Silva Candida, forever.**

It is recognized as belonging to our office that, from the summit of the supreme Apostolic See over which by God’s will we preside, we should care for the whole community of Churches as for our other members.

If, in pious and necessary concern, we ought to extend our service even to those who are far away and do not ask for it, we ought with even greater reason to prolong it to those who are near and demand it. For, while we have the opportunity, we must do good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith (Galatians 6:10), according to the teaching of the holy apostle Paul. As he himself bears witness, whoever does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8).

For, like visible fire, invisible charity seizes what is nearest to it in small spaces [possibly: “in limited intervals”], and from there gradually extends itself to what is farther away.

Therefore, in accordance with your petition, our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Humbert, [lacuna] and in consideration of what you have hitherto continually offered to our predecessor Lord Leo and to the holy Roman and Apostolic See, even beyond your strength and resources, by the sanction of this privilege we decree, grant, and confirm to you, and through you and on your account forever, for the venerable Church of the holy virgins and martyrs Rufina and Secunda, called Silva Candida, in the estate called Boscus, whatever gold, silver, vestments, wax, or any other things whatsoever shall have been cast down, placed, or offered upon the greater altar of Saint Peter, or at his venerable confession, or offered to it and to its successors, from the beginning of Matins on the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper until Compline has been completed, and likewise on Holy Saturday from the third hour throughout that entire day and thereafter until after Mass has been completed on the following day.

Whatever offerings, of whatever kind or amount, the aforesaid altar and its confession have deserved and retained, or now retain, through the privileges of the venerable Sergius and many of our predecessors, let the said church of Saints Rufina and Secunda also retain them, for the perpetual reward of our soul and for the remembrance of our name and service in the holy Roman Church. To these offerings we add, grant, and confirm through this privilege of ours, as stated above, those made from the beginning of Matins on the Thursday of the Lord’s Supper until after Compline, with the concession and confirmation of all the offerings that, through the privileges of our predecessors, it has hitherto received and possessed—namely, those on Palm Sunday, the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, Holy Saturday, and Easter Sunday—entirely preserved, reserved, and confirmed to it forever by this privilege of ours.

For we do not add this provision in such a way as to diminish in any respect the gift of our predecessors. In this concession and confirmation we believe that we have done nothing novel, but have followed the example of our most reverend predecessors and, according to apostolic instruction, supplied through praiseworthy generosity the poverty of a neighboring and especially a daughter Church from the abundance of the holy Roman Church.

By venerable apostolic censure, under invocation of the divine judgment and with the imposition of anathema, we forbid that any of our future pontiffs, any administrator of public affairs, or any other person, however great or small, ever dare or presume to compel anything contrary to this privilege of our gift, or otherwise alienate, take away, or diminish anything from it. Rather, let it remain firm and stable forever, as it has been granted and confirmed.

If anyone, which we do not desire, should presume by reckless daring to violate in any respect this statute of our Apostolic See, or should in any way become his accomplice, by the authority of the holy and undivided Trinity and of the prince of the apostles Peter, whose office, though unworthy, we exercise by divine favor, let him be bound by the bond of anathema and separated from the kingdom of God, and, unless he repents and makes satisfaction, be indissolubly joined to the devil and his angels.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves himself an observer and defender of this concession and confirmation may, by the power of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and through the prayers of the holy virgins and martyrs of Christ, Rufina and Secunda, deserve to receive entry into the heavenly kingdom, grace and glory from the just Judge, the Lord our God, and eternal life, forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hands of Gregory, notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of May, indiction 10. Farewell.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of May, through the hands of Aribo, deacon, in the third year of Lord Pope Victor II, indiction 10.

“We decree, therefore, that no human being whatsoever shall be permitted,” etc. “If, therefore, anything in the future,” etc. “But to all,” etc.

### XVII. Privilege of Victor II for the Monastery of Saint Bertin (1057)

[Guérard, *Collection of Cartularies, Abbey of Saint-Bertin*, vol. III, p. 180.]

**Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Bovo, religious abbot, and to all his successors, who are to be regularly promoted in the monastery of Sithiu, forever.**

It is fitting for apostolic governance that, just as by the dignity and authority of Peter, prince of the apostles, we surpass all others through a singular privilege, so we should have concern for all the Churches of God and provide timely assistance to each of the faithful and to pious places.

Therefore, inclined by your prayers, dearest and religious abbot Bovo, by this judgment of our authority we confirm and strengthen for you and your successors, who are to be regularly promoted, the monastery of Sithiu forever. It is situated in the bishopric of Thérouanne in honor of Saint Peter and all the apostles, where also the illustrious confessor of Christ Bertin, the first founder and abbot of that place, rests bodily with the blessed confessors Folquin and Sylvin.

We likewise confirm to you and your successors forever, as stated, everything rightly belonging to that monastery: both what has hitherto been bestowed there through the devotion of Christ’s faithful and what shall thereafter rightly be bestowed—fields, plains, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries, villages, churches, counties, dependents, vineyards, orchards, and all its movable and immovable, cultivated and uncultivated possessions.

Thus, whatever you have arranged or shall arrange there according to the fear of God for the benefit of that monastery, you shall have free power to do in all respects. The immunity or liberty which blessed Audomar, bishop of Thérouanne, granted and confirmed to the aforesaid blessed Bertin and to that monastery in his own written charter shall remain entirely safe for you and perpetually confirmed by this privilege of ours.

According to what was previously granted by Pope Gregory to the illustrious abbot, when the abbot of that monastery dies, no bishop shall, under any pretext, interfere in recording, inspecting, or pursuing the church’s possessions, whether those already sought or those to be sought.

The congregation as a whole, or, if it is small, that part of the congregation which offers the sounder counsel, shall appoint as abbot for that monastery not someone else, but the person whom it proposes by common agreement, according to the fear of God, as worthy in character and suitable for monastic discipline.

We entirely prohibit public processions from being held there by the bishop, lest popular gatherings provide any occasion for crowds in the retreats of the servants of God and, as a result, draw simpler souls into scandal, which God forbid.

Nor shall the bishop make frequent entries, unless, in accordance with the statement of Pope Nicholas, he comes when summoned by the abbot of the monastery or by the brothers for a matter of necessity or as an act of affection. Thus neither the brothers nor the abbot shall suffer any disturbance through his importunity or the unrest caused by his attendants; all power of causing injury having been wholly removed from him, he shall never at any time be a burden to you.

Therefore, by the censure of the Apostolic See, under invocation of the divine judgment and with the imposition of anathema, we decree and prohibit that any bishop, or cleric of whatever order, or any administrator of public affairs, or any other person whatsoever, however great or small, should dare or presume to act against this privilege of ours, [Col. 0831A] or to alienate, remove, diminish, or violate anything from it. Rather, let it remain perpetually firm and stable, as it has been granted and confirmed by us. Let the abbot or brothers of that monastery be permitted to appeal to the Apostolic See against the injury of any persons, if they should disdain to provide satisfaction to the aforesaid monastery and its rulers through the bishop of Thérouanne or the archbishop of Reims.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should presume, with reckless audacity, to violate or break in any respect this statute of ours of the Apostolic See, or should oppose it in anything, then, by the authority of the holy and indivisible Trinity and of the prince of the apostles, Peter, whose office, though unworthy, we nevertheless hold, let him be bound by the chain of [Col. 0831B] anathema, separated from the kingdom of God, and, unless he repents and makes satisfaction, inseparably joined to the devil and his angels.

But whoever, with pious regard, observes it and proves to be a defender of this confirmation and grant, may, by the power of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the holy confessors Audomar and Bertin, deserve to receive entry into the heavenly kingdom, grace and glory from the just Judge, the Lord our God, and eternal life, forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Gregory the notary, in the year 1057 from the Lord’s nativity.

I, Humbert, called bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida, was present and subscribed with my own hand. [Col. 0831C]

I, Benedict, called bishop of the holy Church of Bellitrensis, have acknowledged this and subscribed with my own hand.

I, Boniface, called bishop of the holy Church of Albano, have acknowledged this and subscribed with my own hand.

I, Peter, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church, have acknowledged this and subscribed with my own hand.

I, Hildebrand, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church, have acknowledged this and subscribed with my own hand.

I, Frederick, deacon, have subscribed.

Given on the third day before the Ides of May, by the hand of Aribo, deacon, in the third year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Victor, in the month of May, in the tenth indiction, on the thirteenth day.

## XVIII. Bull of Victor II for the monastery of Monte Cassino

*(Year 1055–1057.)*

[Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, IV, 744.]

[Col. 0831D]

Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Frederick, beloved son, abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy Father Benedict, called Monte Cassino, and to all his successors who are canonically promoted there to its governance, forever.

If the good of our pastoral solicitude ought to look after and benefit even strangers and those far away, much more ought it to do so for those who are members of our household and near to us. Visible charity must indeed be directed toward them in the second degree after God, so that through them, like a visible flame, it may gradually spread to all who are more remote. [Col. 0832A] Therefore, since we are about to extend the hands of due consolation and defense to pious places venerable for divine religion, we do not doubt that preference must be given to that place which is known to be the principal training-ground of the monastic rule, which is adjacent to the holy Roman and apostolic See, which the eminent Roman citizens—the fathers Benedict, Maurus, and Placid, together with certain others—founded, which Roman pontiffs nevertheless rebuilt by their authority after it had been destroyed by pagan peoples, and which they rightly preferred to other monasteries through the privileges of the Apostolic See and effectively fortified against the suspected injuries of all persons.

As we succeed to their sacred authority in time and place, so we rely, as is fitting, upon their example. Through the tenor of this decretal document of ours, therefore, we praise and confirm to you, our dearest [Col. 0832B] son and abbot Frederick, the election to govern the aforesaid monastery that was transferred to you by the sounder judgment of all the brothers in the presence of our representative, after Peter the monk had been elected through the conspiracy of certain wicked men.

Accordingly, in keeping with the privileges of those same predecessors of ours and with custom, we grant to you, whom we have consecrated as abbot, the monastery of the holy Father Benedict situated at Monte Cassino, together with the entire abbey belonging to that monastery, completely and with its cells, castles, estates, and all its appurtenances. By our authority we decree that this grant applies both within the territories of the Beneventans, Apulians, and Calabrians, and within the territories of the Marsicans and the Marches, as well as wherever, near or far, anything has hitherto rightfully belonged to you, or whatever it may thereafter rightfully acquire anywhere. [Col. 0832C]

Moreover, we gladly remit to your monastery’s own ship any tax or other due that the officials of our sacred palace exact from ships putting in at the Roman port. Whenever you come to Rome in the service of the holy Roman Church, you shall have lodging at Holy Jerusalem in the Sessorian Palace. When the abbot dies, an abbot shall be appointed there by your or your successors’ election and consecrated by the Roman pontiff.

We preserve for you and your successors the privilege that our immediate predecessor, Saint Leo, confirmed to Abbot Richerius, both concerning your ship and concerning the church itself, which had been destroyed so that it might in this way be rebuilt.

We also grant to you and to the place, for the honor of so venerable a monastery and out of affection for you, the use of sandals [Col. 0832D] and the dalmatic—although you have received them from the Apostolic See by virtue of your cardinalate—henceforth only on principal feasts, according to the privilege that our aforesaid predecessor granted to your aforesaid predecessor.

Furthermore, we confirm to you and your successors, in every assembly of bishops and princes, a seat superior to that of all abbots, and in councils and judgments the first vote among men of your order, out of reverence for so great a place, which has deserved to preserve alive and dead the first and supreme legislator of monastic law, and which has caused his legislation, in writing, speech, and example, to shine throughout the world like the sun for those seeking the communal monastic way of life.

When the abbot dies, [Col. 0833A] the community itself shall elect an abbot from among its members according to the sounder judgment of the wiser and senior brothers, and shall present him to the pontiff of the Apostolic See for confirmation and consecration. No abbot shall be appointed there otherwise, nor shall anyone from elsewhere be introduced, unless perhaps they have no one among themselves suitable for so great a governance and therefore, after sounder deliberation, choose an outsider for themselves.

Moreover, apart from the supreme prelate of the Apostolic See, we prohibit by this authority of ours that any bishop or priest of any Church presume to exercise any jurisdiction over the aforesaid monastery or its cells. Thus, unless invited by the abbot, he may not even dare to celebrate the solemn offices of Mass there. Rather, with every oppression by ecclesiastical or secular persons removed and driven away, let it remain, as it has hitherto remained, from this present tenth indiction onward, perpetually quiet and free, for the service and glory of God, under the protection and jurisdiction of the holy Roman and apostolic See, together with all its possessions. Of these, although in summary and general terms all belong to it, we have set down here only the following by name and in particular:

The cells of Albaneta and Ciconia; the cell of Saint Gregory at Aquino; those of Saint Nazarius, Saint Benedict at Clia, Saint Benedict on the Island, Saint Sylvester, Saint Urban, Saint Paul, Saint Michael in the Valley of Light, Saint Michael, Saint Mary in the White Lands, Saint Lucy at Fractas, Saint Michael at Canucio, Saint Stephen at Terracina, Saint Scholastica at Gaeta, Saint Mary at Berula, Saint Nicholas at Pica, Saint Maurice at Limata, Saint Peter at Esculeto, Saint Benedict at Sessa, and Saint Benedict at Teano, with its cells; Saint Benedict at Capua, with its cells and the surrounding lands; likewise in Apulia, Saint Benedict at Martia; Saint Liberator at Teti, with its sixty cells, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and all its appurtenances; Saint Scholastica at Pinna; Saint Mary at Murena; Saint Martin at Salinis; Saint Nicholas at Esculo; the cell of Saint Justa; Saint Benedict at Tronto; Saint Benedict at Trinio; Saint Mary at Casales Planos; Saint Eustatius, which Alferius of Pantasia gave; Saint Benedict at Alarino; Saint Benedict at Pectinari; likewise Saint Mary at Casales Planos; the Holy Trinity at Termoli; Saint Benedict at Ascoli; Saint Focatis at Alesino, with its inlets and fishery; Saint Eustatius at Arcu; Saint Michael at Barreio, with cells, castles, and many lands; Saint Mary at Barretano; Saint George at Luca near Posterula Virivuala, which Henry and Roland, brothers seeking the habit of holy conduct, conferred upon Saint Benedict and for which, because of the novelty of the act, we issued a privilege at your request; Saint Valentine at Comino; Saint Savior there; Saint Benedict at Venafro; Saint Mary there; Saint Nazarius likewise; the estate of Saint Felix; Saint Benedict at Cesamo; and Saint Bartholomew at Miniano.

The castles are these: first, at the foot of Mount Saint Savior, Saint Germani; Saint Peter; Pignatari; Plumbarola; Saint Stephen; Saint George; Saint Apollinaris; Cold Valley; Saint Andrew; Bantra Comitalis; [Col. 0834A] Bantra Monacisca; Junctura; Saint Michael; Turudum; Saint Victor; Saint Peter at Clia; Cervara; Round Valley; Saint Elias; Saraciniscum; Conca; Capriata; Francilone; Saint John; and Lesser Saint Benedict; Saint John at Capua.

Some of these were once monasteries, but, after being destroyed by the Saracens, were subsequently made into castles as necessary for the defense of the homeland. In addition: Lastinianum and three other castles—Mount Albrici, Muccla, and Saint Quiricus—with a harbor for ten ships. Two of these Count Transmundus, son of Acto, conferred upon blessed Benedict at Monte Cassino by legal donation and with documentary safeguards. The third, the castle of Frisa, the wife of the aforesaid Transmundus likewise surrendered for the sake of her soul, just as her husband had done. After his wife’s death, however, the aforesaid count did not fear to seize it, [Col. 0834B] but at the Lateran, in the chapel of Saint Lawrence, in the presence of Humbert, bishop of Silva Candida, and with you also, our son Frederick, not yet elected to the governance, he was admonished by us during the confession of his offenses and voluntarily renounced it on the fourth Sunday after Easter.

Therefore, having established and confirmed by apostolic censure, under the imposition of a strict anathema and invocation of the divine judgment, all these things and everything that now rightfully belongs to the aforesaid monastery or shall rightfully belong to it in the future, under the protection and Roman liberty, we perpetually forbid all persons, present and future, whether of whatever order, dignity, condition, or office, and every person, however great or small, to inflict any violence upon, or bring any accusation against, any things or persons rightfully belonging to the aforesaid monastery, or to trouble them. [Col. 0834C]

If anyone—which we do not wish—should attempt with reckless audacity to infringe in any respect this decretal document of our privilege, let him know that he will be bound by the chains of eternal curse and will pay perpetual penalties with the devil and his angels, unless he should first repent and make satisfaction. But whoever, out of regard for piety, proves to be a devout observer of it shall, through the intercession of the holy Father Benedict and his perfect followers and companions, become a participant in everlasting blessing and a blessed possessor of paradise. Amen.

[Col. 0834D] + Humbert, called cardinal-bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida, reread this as acknowledged and subscribed.

+ Heldibrand, cardinal subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, consented by giving approval and subscribed.

## XIX. Privilege granted by Victor II to Winimannus, archbishop of Embrun

[Note: [Col. 0833D] Under Pope Victor II, Labbe mentions a certain Roman council reconstructed from the letters of Pope Stephen IX, but scarcely touches upon anything except its name and the indication that the bishopric of the Marsicans had been joined together, although his predecessors had once divided it into two. I do not know whether I have encountered, under more favorable auspices, the bull of Victor II by which Pope Victor, who consecrated Winimannus after his election in his own province, confirmed by an expedited bull all the rights of his bishopric to Winimannus, archbishop of Embrun. I judge, moreover, that this bull was issued at the Roman council of 1057. The evidence for this is provided by the names of several Italian bishops, appended to that pontiff’s letter and brought forth from the Embrun cartulary by the latest authors of *Gallia Christiana*, volume III, page 178, appendix. The year attached to this document agrees with the council, as does the stated indiction. The month differs: here it is July, whereas the council met in April. The discrepancy is easily reconciled, however, for that document of *Gallia Christiana* joins, in the same sequence of writing as the papal bull, the decree of the clergy of Embrun, by which they acknowledge and accept their bishop, already consecrated by Pope Victor, as well as the papal bull obtained from him. The date—the third day before the Nones of July, in the third year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Victor II, in the tenth indiction—belongs to this decree, not to the bull. Then follow the names of the Italian bishops who were present and confirmed these writings, namely, the bull; for it is not plausible that these Italian bishops confirmed by their authority the decree of the people of Embrun, by which they accepted Winimannus, already consecrated by the pontiff. Thus I conceive the whole matter as follows: Elected by the clergy of Embrun, Winimannus went to Rome, where he was consecrated by the pontiff and attended the council. At the council he obtained the bull from the pontiff, and the council fathers strengthened it with their subscriptions. He was then restored to his people and presented those letters, together with the other documents of his consecration, to the clergy, who accepted all these things in a new decree.] (Year 1057.)

[Mansi XIX, 858.]

Victor, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop Winimannus, and through him to the holy Church of Embrun and to its successors who are canonically promoted, forever.

The Lord of the universe established the summit of the holy Roman and apostolic See over nations and kingdoms in Peter, the prince of his apostles, so that, in his name, it might uproot, destroy, plant, and build (Jer. 1:10). Since his holy Church, spread throughout the whole world, will remain subject to the mutability of temporal existence, it will alternate, like the moon in its monthly phases, through the varied and continual changes of its failings and advances, so that within it there may always be found something that the diligent gardener ought to uproot or plant, and something that the wise architect (1 Cor. 3:10) ought to destroy or build. [Col. 0835B]

Therefore, although by no merit of our own but solely by the divine will we have been raised above others to the watchtower of the holy and universal Church and observe its varied fortunes, among its other dangers we have perceived that the Church of Embrun—first through the invasion and occupation of the Saracens, and second through the reception and possession of fugitives and undisciplined persons; then through the long oppression of its pastors, or rather of its hirelings; and, worse still, through the heresy of simony and the mutual slaughter of those raging against one another—has been miserably overthrown and corrupted. Once wonderfully elevated and flourishing in religion and resources, it now lies desolate and fallen in every respect. Deeply sympathizing with its complete desolation and decline, we appointed and consecrated you, dearest brother and fellow bishop Winimannus, as archbishop and ruler of that Church, on account of the merit of your life and the instruction of your wisdom, according to the election of the clergy and people, and also at the request of religious princes and the recommendation of venerable primates of the surrounding provinces. [Col. 0835C]

Their unanimous judgment was that, if any restoration were to be sought for the Church of Embrun, a preacher and pontiff should be requested from that mother—the Roman Church—which had formerly sent blessed Marcellinus, its preacher and bishop, there.

Accordingly, as your devotion requested a privilege of our apostolic authority for the strengthening of your archbishopric, in a raw and undisciplined church scarcely retaining even its bare name and already displaying its ruins, and as we bend to your prayers, by this decretal document of ours, in the tenth indiction of the present year, we grant and confirm to you the diocese of Embrun in its entirety, together with the principal basilica of Our Lady, Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, which is the archiepiscopal see, and with all its ancient and rightful appurtenances: baptismal churches, chapels, monasteries, cemeteries, possessions, villages, castles, pastures, fields, vineyards, woods, waters and watercourses, fisheries, houses, slaves, tenants, livestock, and absolutely all its movable, immovable, and self-moving property rightfully belonging to it—both what it now peacefully and legally possesses and what it may thereafter acquire through the gifts of the faithful, restitution, purchase, or any other lawful means. [Col. 0836B]

We also confirm to you the tithes, firstfruits, and offerings of all the churches throughout your diocese, from both the living and the dead, the judgments concerning clerics, and all ecclesiastical offices, so that they may depend upon your disposition according to canonical ordinance. Likewise, we confirm the consecration of your suffragans, their due subjection, reverence, and obedience, as well as the authority to summon them to council and to hold council, according to every right that suffragans canonically owe their metropolitans, while in all things preserving, as is proper, the authority of the holy Roman and apostolic See.

Furthermore, by the tenor of this privilege of ours, we grant and confirm to you the use of the sacred pallium according to the ancient custom of your predecessors, who were accustomed to use it on the solemnities listed below, in accordance with the privileges granted to them in ancient times by our predecessors: on the holy day of Easter; on the day of the Lord’s Ascension; on the holy day of Pentecost; on the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ; on the Epiphany of the Lord; on Maundy Thursday; on the Assumption of blessed Mary ever-virgin; on the feasts of all the apostles; on the feast of All Saints; on the feast of Saint Marcellinus, archbishop of the aforesaid city of Embrun; at the dedication of the principal basilica of blessed Mary ever-virgin; at the consecration of bishops; at the ordination of priests and deacons; on the Saturdays of the fasts of the four seasons; and at the consecration of new and principal basilicas.

[Col. 0837A] Moreover, to supplement apostolic beneficence and as an insignia of the archbishop, we grant and decree, by the privilege of apostolic authority, that the banner of the Lord’s cross be carried before you wherever you possess rights in your parish and in the parishes of your suffragans.

We wish you to use the sacred pallium in such a way that you carefully and vigilantly consider what is required of your fraternity. Its use signifies, among other things, that you crucify your flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. 5:24), that, with the Apostle Paul, you bear the marks of Jesus Christ in your body (Gal. 6:17), and that you always carry his mortification upon your breast and shoulders (2 Cor. 4:16)—not as a sign of your own ostentation or singular excellence, but to display, for remembrance and imitation by the sheep entrusted to you, the venerable sign of our Savior, who in ineffable compassion carried the hundredth sheep back upon his shoulders. [Col. 0837B]

Finally, since all the matters written above have been granted and confirmed to your affection by the authority of the Apostolic See through this privilege of ours, by that same apostolic authority we prohibit anyone from rashly opposing or contradicting them.

If anyone—which we do not wish—should presume with wicked audacity to oppose or resist this decree of ours in any respect, whether he is an ecclesiastic, cleric, or layman, slave or free, a great or small person, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema and, unless he should first repent, destined for the punishments of eternal Gehenna with the devil, his most savage ministers, and Judas the traitor.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves in all things to be an observer of this apostolic constitution of ours shall receive the grace of blessing in manifold measure from our most merciful Lord and become a possessor of eternal life. Amen.

The city of Embrun, a metropolitan city. The city of Digne. The city of the Solingenses [variant: Solinenses]. The city of the Rigomagenses. [Col. 0838A] The city of the Samasienses, or Saniciccium. The city of Glannatina. The city of the Semelenentes, that is, the Nicentians. The city of Veciencium [variant: Vensiontium]. The city of Antipolis, that is, Grassensis.

By the ancient authority of our holy predecessors, we, the clergy and people of Embrun, elect, praise, and confirm Winimannus as archbishop in the archiepiscopal see of Embrun, at the command of the supreme pontiff and universal pope Victor, with William, Bertrand, and Geoffrey, as well as Count Pontius of Die, confirming it. Thus, let him preside over and govern all the churches of the aforesaid city, as it is written in the privilege that the lord Pope Victor, his consecrator, granted to him by Roman authority, together with the tithes [Col. 0838B] and firstfruits, as is fitting for an archbishop to hold and administer.

But if anyone should violate this decree, unless he comes to make satisfaction, let him know that he is condemned and anathematized. Let it be done, let it be done. Amen.

Given . . . on the third day before the Nones of July, by the hand of Arabolus, deacon, in the third year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Victor II, in the tenth indiction.

Frederick, cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus.

Ludovicus, bishop of Nocera.

Ermannus John, bishop of Siena.

Gregory Guido, bishop of Egubium; together with the bishop of Pistoia, all these were present, as was Humbert, called cardinal-bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida.

Arnold, bishop of Arezzo.

Gerald, bishop of Florence.

The bishop of Castello.

Litgrinus, bishop of Populonia.

The bishop of Vercelli.

Cimibert, [Col. 0838C] bishop of Turin.

The bishop of Velletri, the bishop of Fiesole, and the bishop of Pisa confirmed the foregoing writings.

Thanks be to God. Amen.

## XX. Letter of Saint Peter Damian, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, to Pope Victor II

*(See in Saint Peter Damian, under the year 1702, Works, volume I, letter 5.)*

### Around the year of the Lord 1057: Berengar, viscount of Narbonne

## Complaint of Berengar against Guifred, archbishop of Narbonne

Presented at the council held at Toulouse under Raimbald, archbishop of Arles, and Pontius, archbishop of Aix, legates of Pope Victor II, in the year of Christ 1056.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] I see that there is no unanimous opinion concerning the time when this complaint was presented, for some think that it occurred in 1056, specifically at the council held at Narbonne. They were misled, I believe, by the authority of certain proceedings from that year, mentioned by Catel on pages 582 and 781, which nevertheless testify that serious controversies then existed between the archbishop and the viscount. But many considerations cause me to think otherwise. This complaint was brought before the legates of the supreme pontiff, in the presence of Raimbald, archbishop of Arles, and, as I believe, while Pope Victor was still alive. We know that the legates of that same Victor—Raimbald, archbishop of Arles, and Pontius, archbishop of Aix—held a synod in the city of Toulouse in 1056, which Guifred, archbishop of Narbonne, attended. Moreover, this complaint was made at a synod attended by the bishops of Lodève and Elne. Now it is established from the acts of the council that Rostagnus, bishop of Lodève, and Arnald, bishop of Elne, attended the Toulouse council of 1056. Finally, if these proceedings took place after Victor’s death, why does Berengar mention only Victor’s anathema against Guifred, whom the testimony of Gregory VII shows to have been excommunicated by many Roman pontiffs? That would undoubtedly have served to increase hostility and could have brought powerful support to Berengar’s case. But evidently Guifred had not yet been excommunicated by any Roman pontiff other than Victor. Baluze.]

*(In Mansi, Councils, volume XIX, column 830, from Baluze, Council of Narbonne.)*

[Col. 0837D] To this holy gathering of vicars of God—namely, the legates of the supreme Roman pontiff, who holds the place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and the archbishops, bishops, [Col. 0839A] and abbots acting in his stead, who are gathered in this holy synod and deliberate according to the Catholic faith—this not inconsiderable complaint is presented, that it may be read and heard, judged, and determined. But, so that it may be judged more fully, let it begin from the beginning:

I, Berengar, proconsul of the city of Narbonne, make this complaint openly before all of you, concerning the great grievance I have against my metropolitan, your brother. The archbishopric of Narbonne belonged to one of my uncles, Ermengaud the archbishop. In his days that bishopric was one of the finest existing from Rome to the borders of Spain, richly endowed with villages and castles and enriched with estates and allodial lands. Its church was full of books, adorned with golden panels, chests, and crosses, and gleamed with golden crowns and precious stones. The voices of many canons were heard there at the appointed hours; prayers were offered; and the increase of every good work was carried on there. The castles, villages, estates, and possessions of that church were not enjoyed by laymen but were held by those serving God within it.

That church had formerly been built by the pious king Charles, who had it consecrated in honor of Saints Justus and Pastor, and had it splendidly endowed with castles, villages, lands, and vineyards, as is handed down in the sayings of the elders and as is read in the royal charters of that Church.

After the death of the aforesaid archbishop of blessed memory, Guifred, count of Cerdanya, came to Narbonne. I was already married to one of his female relatives. He sought both my parents and me concerning the aforesaid archbishopric, for the benefit of his aforementioned son, our bishop, who was not yet more than ten years old, and promised, on his behalf, to give a great gift—between the count of Rodez and my father, one hundred thousand solidi. But my father and mother would not consent to him. I, however, led by love of such kinship and deceived by the pretended friendship, separated myself on this matter from the company of my parents; and, if they would not agree with me, I resolved to kill them.

For my father, seeing me agitated and so hostile toward him, yielded to my will and to the petitions of the aforesaid Geoffrey. After receiving one hundred thousand solidi between himself and the count of Rodez, he gave the price of the bishopric with the aforesaid son of his, our bishop. He, swearing an oath and calling God to witness, declared that his word and his faith toward us were firm: if he became our bishop, as he did and remains, neither any of us nor any of our people would suffer harm, nor would there be harm to the bishopric itself.

While he sat in the episcopal chair and increased in age and honor, I trusted that he would be my guide, my arms and shield against the weapons of all enemies; that he would remember my wife’s kinship and the importance of the position into which I had helped place him; and that, as he had promised me, he would help me retain and possess my honor. Then he rose up like a devil, proudly and suddenly, provoked me to anger, and built castles against me. He came against me with a huge army, waged cruel war upon me, and nearly a thousand men were killed on both sides because of it.

Then he took away from God and those serving him the castles, villages, estates, and possessions that belonged to the domain of the aforesaid church, as well as the revenues and possessions of the canons and everything held in common, and gave them to the devil and those serving him. Thus he turned everything else over to lay jurisdiction, so that all who possess these things now hold them as if they were hereditary allods.

Meanwhile, it happened that Eriballus, bishop of Urgell, died. The aforesaid archbishop acquired that bishopric for the benefit of his brother William [Note: [Col. 0840C] His brother William. This occurred around the year 1041 of Christ. For Heribald, bishop of Urgell, was still alive in the year 1040, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, as is clear from the cartulary of the Church of Urgell. William, bishop of Urgell, Heribald’s successor, attended the council of Narbonne in 1043, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April. Perhaps, therefore, this took place in 1042 or at the beginning of 1043, since Berengar immediately says that Guifred, the archbishop, convened a considerable council at Narbonne not long after he had installed William in the see of Urgell, and that Raimbald, archbishop of Arles, attended this council. Moreover, the acts of the council preserved in the archive of the monastery of Cuxa show that Raimbald attended the council of Narbonne mentioned shortly afterward. Unless we interpret this as the council held in the same city of Narbonne by Guifred on the Kalends of August of that year, which Raimbald also attended, as is demonstrated by ancient documents not yet published.] and promised to give one hundred thousand solidi for him.

I would have been quite pleased with this if it had not been to my detriment. Once so great a gift had been fixed for that bishopric, the aforesaid archbishop, enemy of God and man, returned to his see and entered his Church, and removed all the treasures that had been gathered there since its foundation. He stripped the golden and silver panels and shutters, the crosses, and the reliquary chests. He also sent the golden and silver patens of the chalices, from which the holy [Col. 0841A] sacrifices were received, to Jewish goldsmiths to be destroyed, and sold them in Spain to pay for that bishopric. Of the books that were there in various kinds, he left none of the better ones. He so wickedly dissipated his church that even its clergy are lacking; those who remain there are poor and beggars, and no handsome object is seen in it. There are no cloaks, no military capes, no cyclades, no dalmatics, no *cureballi*, and no Wood of the Lord. All these things, of which many had been gathered there since its foundation, he dissipated and gave away for his brother’s bishopric.

Moreover, what is worse and dishonorable, he placed himself under the protection of the countess of Urgell. For this reason he fell into great hatred not only with me but also with all the nobles of our homeland.

After this had occurred, he assembled a considerable council near the aforesaid city of Narbonne, of many bishops of his diocese, among whom was this Raimbald, archbishop of Arles. In their presence and in the presence of all of us, he laid aside all military arms and all worldly soldiery, and, by excommunicating them, placed both himself and all the bishops of his diocese under anathema if from that day forward they should take up arms.

Not long afterward, however, he took up arms like a soldier—not with a sword-belt around his loins but with iron—and fought against me. If I wished to recount one by one how many were killed, how many wounded, how many mutilated, and how many churches were burned and relics consumed, perhaps it would weary you, and the day would run out before my supply of words.

[Col. 0841C] Then the bishops came into my territory and, together with me and the same archbishop, firmly established that the inviolable Peace of God should be maintained throughout all my land, and that the most severe justice should be inflicted upon violators of it.

Accordingly, the same archbishop and I made this agreement: of everything that was restored because of the breaking of that truce, one half would belong to the aforesaid church and the other half to me, for the administration of justice. I agreed, however, to assign my half to the administration of that church. But he used it not for its administration but for its destruction, since he took it from the church and assigned it to soldiers as pay, rather than as ten thousand solidi.

After this grant had been given to God and firmly confirmed, the first people to break it in our homeland were his soldiers. Coming out from his castle, they killed one of my soldiers under the Peace of God. I detained those murderers but could obtain no justice from him.

Then Peter Raimund, count of Béziers, violated the church of Saint Mary under the Peace of God—the monastery of the chosen place, where a miraculous Wood of the Lord is kept—and dragged out from there two soldiers who were humble and innocent. One of them, who was my kinsman, he hanged on the wood and killed by a cruel death, as though he were a thief.

Therefore, the same archbishop proved such a supporter that he protected those sacrilegious men and murderers when they placed themselves under his authority; he became their advocate, and I was unable to find any justice in him.

[Col. 0842A] Moreover, he never kept the many oaths that he had sworn to me with his hands upon the holy altars, but broke them all. At last, however, he performed a good deed, one quite pleasing to God and to the entire people of Narbonne. We would have forgotten all these evils if he had come to us for good. For the bodies of the saints Justus and Pastor—which the aforementioned King Charles, bringing them from Spain, had lost on the way, and which he had wished to place in the church built in their honor, bodies greatly desired by us and by our fathers—the same archbishop, having discovered and seized them, carried them with honor to his own church and honorably deposited them there. For this reason he was praised and loved not only by me but also by his own citizens.

Not long afterward, however, when he was in dispute with his archdeacon, he wished to remove the bodies of the aforesaid saints from their church. I begged him not to do this, and I wished to give him hostages for ten thousand solidi, so that, if any man or woman should do him any violence concerning the bodies of those saints, or concerning any gift offered or presented to them, I would, in good faith and without pretense, assist that bishop against whoever did this. But that same archdeacon wished to make satisfaction to him before the judgment of the bishop of Arelate. He refused; but the archbishop took away the bodies of such great saints from that see and dishonorably placed them in a certain village church.

There he built his cathedra; there he established his order; there he held his synods; there he carried away the books, crosses, and Lord’s Wood; there he installed the clerics of the principal see whom he found to be the best. Thus, choosing a member, he left the head like a hut. Moreover, he deprived all the nobles of our country, and the entire populace—who were accustomed to come to the city and to his see, and who were accustomed to bring and present their penitential offerings at his see, as well as to contribute many aids toward the work of his church—of these practices. He gave those offerings to his soldiers as military pay, and left his church deserted and without a head.

Meanwhile, that same archbishop held a hearing with me and compelled me to satisfy him according to his pleasure. He gave me his word and the pledge that I could require from him as the best: that he would return to his see and restore the holy bodies there. He lied to me; but, as he testified to me, he did not wish to do it, and he deceived me concerning his word and his pledge.

Then, when my wife saw him, she asked him to restore the holy bodies and to return to his own church, and to accept our rightful claim in full measure. He would not listen to her; rather, he declared to her that he would carry those holy bodies to Altitona [reading uncertain], into a foreign land, and that they would never be recovered by us. Hearing this, and fearing that he might suddenly do what he had sworn to do while I was absent and unaware, she went to the aforesaid village church, which had not yet been consecrated, removed the holy bodies from there, and restored them to his see, where she honorably reinterred them.

Then my wife, prostrating herself before him, asked him to accept her rightful claim; [Col. 0843A] he refused. As soon as I learned of this, I went to the aforesaid archbishop and wished to affirm before him my rightful claim—and that of my wife and all my people—in the judgment of the bishops of his diocese and of the bishop of Arelate, for ten thousand solidi. He refused.

Then I appealed in the judgment of the apostolic legate and of this holy synod; he rejected this as well. Finally, I called upon Saint Peter and the judgment of the apostolic lord, asking to go before him and to affirm my rightful claim to the archbishop in his presence. He treated this with the utmost contempt. Instead, he cruelly and unjustly excommunicated me, my wife, my children, and all our land, so severely that no one there was baptized, [Note: [Col. 0843B] “No one there was baptized.” This was harsh and extremely inhuman, and wholly contrary to ecclesiastical regulations, which, during a period of interdict, preserve a place for humane provisions by permitting the baptism of infants, the penance of the dying, the viaticum at the hour of death, the burial of clerics, the poor, pilgrims, and infants of two years and younger, nuptial blessings, and the purification of women, although the rules vary in different regions. In general, however, it may be affirmed that during an interdict the baptism of infants and likewise the penance of the dying were permitted. See [Col. 0844B] the chapter *Inquisitioni tuae*, *On the Sentence of Excommunication*, Baluze.] nor was Communion administered, nor was anyone buried.

But for the fear of God, we would have paid little attention to his excommunication, since we know him, so stained by so many crimes, to have been anathematized by Pope Victor together with 120 bishops. [Note: [Col. 0844B] “Anathematized.” Namely, in the Council of Florence, which had been held by Pope Victor II in the preceding year. This passage states that 120 bishops took part in that council. Gregory VII appears to have had this excommunication of Guifred of Narbonne in mind when he enacted the following at the Roman council in 1078: “We also renew the excommunication made by our predecessors against Guifred, archbishop of Narbonne, and remove him from episcopal office without any hope of restoration.” [Col. 0844C] The same.] He is a Simoniac who sold all his orders; he compelled all the bishops—not to mention those of other lands, but all whom he ordained in my territory—to redeem them down to the last farthing. If you do not believe this, ask the bishop of Lodeve and the bishop of Elne, and let them testify to you concerning these matters, [Col. 0844A] for they were ordained by him. He also refused to consecrate the churches of my land until he had retained the payment due for them.

Recently, two of my soldiers returning from the vigil of Saint Salvator at Aniane on the day of Epiphany were captured and imprisoned at his command and with his support. He protects those who captured them and gives them military pay. Therefore I, the aforementioned Berengarius, make this complaint to you and to the Lord God, and I seek justice. Unless I obtain it, I shall pay little heed to his excommunication, shall observe no truce at all in my land, and shall no longer appeal to the judgment of the apostolic lord.

I, Berengarius, have made the complaint set out above to the legates of the supreme pontiff and to all bishops and abbots, because I was attempting to present it at the synod of Arelate. But since this achieved nothing, I have therefore gladly taken care to send it to the apostolic lord. I beg him, by God and Saint Peter, to absolve me from this excommunication and to satisfy my prelate on my behalf, since I do not hesitate to go willingly to Rome to make satisfaction; but he, unless bound, will never go there of his own accord.

## In the Year of the Lord 1057. Theuzo, Hermit and Monk of Saint Mary of Florence

[Col. 0843]

## Historical Notice

(*Camaldulian Annals*, vol. II, p. 163.)

[Col. 0843D] Theuzo the hermit and monk of Saint Mary of Florence must be distinguished from another famous and blessed Theuzon, a disciple of Saint John Gualbert, who lived at the same time. On him, consult the Vallombrosan authors.

He also appears to be different from Theuzo the monk and unworthy priest who subscribes, after Peter—second of that name, abbot of Saint Mary of Florence—to a charter restoring a certain hospital near Puccinelli (*Chronicle of the Abbots of Florence*, p. 254). For Theuzo the hermit was probably not a priest: according to Damian’s testimony, he received the divine sacraments only once during the entire year, and then not from the priests of his own monastery but from priests sought elsewhere.

Finally, he is different from Theuzon the monk, through whose intervention the emperors Otto II in 1002 and Henry in 1020 received the Pratalia monastery under their protection.

Theuzo the hermit is thought to be the author of the *Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict the Father*, which he dedicated to Bishop Odelricus. The Brescian bishop of that name was living in 1027 and died in 1048. Another Odelricus, bishop of Fermo, subscribed to the Roman council of 1059, to which Damian also sent a letter around the year 1061.

Nevertheless, the author of that *Commentary* may have been another monk Theuzo, likewise of the Florentine abbey, or some other monk of the same name. Indeed, we would wager that the author of this *Commentary* should be sought among the Milanese [Col. 0845A] monks.

We have gone through the entire work, and nowhere does the author reveal himself by any indication except in chapter 14, where, while asking how vigils should be performed on the anniversaries of saints, he gives the example of the Church of Milan, where the bodies of Saint Ambrose and Saints Gervasius and Protasius are kept and venerated.

In chapter 61, speaking of foreign monks and giving as an example the formal letters that abbots ought to write to bishops, he has these words:

“To the venerable lord N., bishop, adorned with a life devoted to Christ, nearer to heaven than to earth: the venerable N., abbot of the Milanese monastery, [sends] tokens of perpetual happiness and fellowship in the assembly of angels.”

Apart from the copy of Theuzon’s Commentary preserved in the Florentine abbey under number 58, which Mabillon says was written in the sixteenth century, our monks of Saint Matthew of Murano preserve another exceptionally fine parchment copy, written in the fourteenth or fifteenth century. From it we also publish his dedicatory letter to Odelricus, which is prefixed to the *Commentary*, or rather to the collection drawn from the sayings of the earlier Fathers.

[Col. 0845]

## Prologue to the Exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict, Our Holy Father and Abbot, Written by Theuzon the Monk

(*Camaldulian Annals*, vol. II, Appendix, p. 156, from a thirteenth-century manuscript of the monastery of Saint Matthew of Murano in Venice.)

## The Exposition of the Rule of Blessed Benedict the Abbot Begins

[Col. 0845B] To the venerable lord Odelricus, bishop, overflowing with the prerogative of true love, Theuzo the sinner offers the provisions of perpetual happiness and the rewards of unfailing fidelity.

Although, my venerable Father, the sayings of the Rule of blessed Father Benedict appear in most respects to be open and clear, nevertheless, among those who are less attentive—or, as I might say, unwilling either to imitate or to know them—they are not easily made plain, as their deeds demonstrate. If they would ask even lightly for entrance, they would immediately find the door open to them, so that they could penetrate to the interior. For the key of that same door, hanging there continually, would not withdraw itself from the hand of one willing to open it.

Whoever has once been worthy to enter would no longer remain ungrateful amid the troubles of fleeting and earthly things. But because, as blessed Gregory says, “we do not wish to taste the sweetness prepared for us within; wretchedly, we love our hunger outside,” I have therefore briefly and concisely drawn together this little work from the sayings of the earlier Fathers. It is not entirely composed by me, but gathered from the labors of others, lest anyone perhaps wish to adopt for himself the evil of an excuse, claiming that he could not grasp the bare text of the Rule.

Finally, arranging that same text by dividing it into sections at suitable points, I marked it beforehand with commas, so that whatever one seeks in it might more easily be found. I have therefore taken care to offer this collection for examination by your fatherhood, so that, if it should perhaps be brought into the hands of detractors, they may find nothing there to gnaw with a dog’s tooth, but rather something that may remove them from their unhappy obstinacy. Farewell.

## In the Year of the Lord 1058. Odo, Monk of Fosses

[Col. 0845]

## Historical Notice

(Fabricius, *Library of Middle and Late Latin*, vol. IV, p. 158.)

[Col. 0845D] Odo, monk of Fosses, wrote in the year 1058 the *Life of Lord Burchard, Count of Melun*, who enjoyed the favor of Hugh Capet and his son Robert and died in the year 1012. It appears in the supplement to the *Antiquities of Paris* by Brolius, or Jacques du Breul, a Benedictine, Paris, 1614, quarto; in volume IV of André du Chesne’s *Writers on the Affairs of the Franks*, p. 115; and, in French, translated by Sebastian Roulliard, in his *History of the City of Melun*, Paris, 1628, quarto.

Under this writer’s name, Montfaucon’s *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum*, p. 1278, lists a *Life of Saint Maurus*, written in verse and prose, which he says exists in some French library—though he does not indicate which. The authors of the *Literary History of France*, vol. VII, p. 494, judge that the prose *Life of Saint Maurus* is not different from the one that had appeared long before Odo, although it may perhaps have been revised by this same Odo. They consider that the other, written in verse, can readily be attributed to this Odo himself.

They further note, following Mabillon, *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, vol. II, p. 596, that the Responsories in honor of Saint Barolinus, the first abbot of Fosses, which were formerly sung by those monks in the office of that saint’s feast, are owed to the pen of the same Odo.

[Col. 0847]

## Life of Lord Burchard, Venerable Count, Who Flourished under Kings Hugh Capet and His Son Robert, by Odo, Monk of Fosses

(In Duchesne, *Writers on the Affairs of the Franks*, vol. IV, p. 115, from the edition of Jacques Brolius, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in the *Supplement to the Antiquities of Paris*.)

## The Prologue Begins

[Col. 0847B] We judge it worthy and most just to hand down to the memory of posterity the deeds of religious men, the lives of those who faithfully pleased God. For as the ages of the human race pass away, the things done by the faithful are handed over to oblivion unless it happens that someone commits to parchment the honorable deeds they performed while alive.

Thus, encouraged by the examples of the earlier Fathers, who left us many accounts of the deeds of their own time—and especially by blessed Gregory, the apostolic bishop of the city of Rome, who discusses the deeds of many saints both in his *Dialogues* and in his *Homilies—I have endeavored to write something for the brothers of the Church of Fosses: how the venerable Count Burchard and his son, namely Bishop Ragenaldus, moved by the Holy Spirit, raised that place to honor and possessions, and afterward, as their end approached, in the religious habit.

For although many of their good deeds have been erased from memory in our own age, I have nevertheless undertaken to run through in writing the few that can still be seen and that I learned from those born before us, so that they might be recalled for their perpetual remembrance.

But since, according to the Lord’s saying, “when iniquity abounds and charity grows cold, all who wish to live piously suffer persecution,” and since the aforesaid place has fallen into the extremity of misery, before it collapses completely into ruin I am compelled to leave my native soil, where I was brought up as a child in the manner pleasing to Christ.

Driven by very many afflictions, struck and put to flight by the arrows of persecution, I desire to visit foreign lands, not knowing, as the Apostle says of himself, what will happen to me. Nor, in doing this, do I fear that I am acting outside the Lord’s command, for he orders his faithful to flee from city to city so that they may escape the rage of their persecutors.

Nevertheless, I ask the generosity of his holy mercy that he may deign continually to protect me, rescued from the assaults of visible and invisible enemies, whom he redeemed with the precious blood of his holy blood.

Before, therefore, I undertake the labor of this journey or change of place, I have taken pains to leave this writing with the aforesaid Church of Fosses, so that the brothers, who show me devotion and holy love, may remember the sinner Odo when, taught by an unlearned man, they receive the words of this reading, and so that through their holy prayers I may deserve, after the death of the flesh, to attain the prize of eternal happiness. Amen.

[Col. 0847] The Prologue Ends.

## The Life Begins

[Col. 0847D] Illustrious Burchard, born of noble stock, was begotten anew through holy baptism and nobly trained in the Catholic religion through the discipline of military service. While he was passing through the years of childhood, his parents presented him to the royal court, according to the custom of the Frankish nobles. Rich in Christian works, he acquired every advantage of prudence and honor.

In the court of the glorious Hugh, king of the Franks, he was instructed in every discipline, both heavenly and military. When, by the providence of the Lord’s grace—which foresaw him as a future faithful soldier—he reached the years of adolescence and youth, the king embraced him with great affection, so much so that he seemed to surpass all his contemporaries.

He was loved by everyone, and all the nobles of the Franks accorded him the greatest honor. The illustrious king also honored him, enriched him with gold and silver, fortresses and many possessions, and made him his most faithful counselor.

It happened in those same times, by God’s judgment, that a certain count of the fortress of Corbeil, named Haymo, went to Rome to pray at the thresholds of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and there, during that same journey, met the end of this life. When he had died, both the king and the other leading men of the Franks advised Burchard, a recruit of vigorous youth, to take the aforesaid count’s wife in marriage.

He, whom the necessity of youth and human nature already compelled to do such things, willingly obeyed the royal commands. Thus, by royal gift, the wife of the aforesaid Count Haymo, named Elisabeth, herself born of noble parentage, was given to him. They were joined in the marriage bed so that, in accordance with the Lord’s command, they might afterward rejoice in their most delightful offspring.

In the chamber of that union King Hugh gave his faithful soldier the fortress of Melun, the aforesaid Corbeil, and the county of the city of Paris; and in this way he became a royal count. Having received temporal honor, he governed the household entrusted to him according to the Lord’s will. For he was a faithful defender of the churches held under the authority of the Frankish kingdom, a giver of alms, a comforter of the afflicted, and a most merciful supporter of monks, clerics, widows, and virgins serving God in monasteries.

Since he strove to please the Lord by these and many other virtues, although he was devoted to secular military service and entangled in all the affairs of the world, his mind, faithfully devoted to the King of kings, could not remain hidden from the world. For it was not fitting that a lamp placed beneath a bushel should remain concealed in darkness for long; rather, it should be placed upon a lampstand, so that the light of the brightly burning lamp might shine openly for all who entered through the threshold of the holy Church.

In the time of the aforesaid king of the Franks, Hugh, the church of the monastery of Fosses, which had once been nobly elevated by the ancient kings, was more confused than the others and deprived of every kind of human assistance. This had happened partly through the lack of justice and partly through the negligence of its rulers.

In those same days a certain nobleman, Magenardus, nobly born according to the honor of this fleeting age, governed that church. He did not act according to the command of Father Benedict; being greatly devoted to the world, he neglected the welfare of souls and bodies. For he delighted in hunting dogs and beasts and in the flight of birds.

Whenever he wished to go somewhere, he would lay aside his monastic garments and adorn himself with coverings of precious furs, while placing an excellent cap or headdress—*calamaneum*, or, alternatively, *calamantium*—upon his humble head. All his subjects likewise pursued these practices as far as they could.

Lest anyone find it strange that the inhabitants of that place behaved in this way, this custom was followed by all the monks of that kingdom. While these and many other things were being done, a certain monk named Adicus took the matter seriously and silently pondered how this might be prohibited in God’s sanctuary.

Without anyone’s knowledge, including the abbot’s, he approached the religious count, disclosed to him the whole desire of his heart, and begged him with every prayer to restore that place, mindful of his own soul, to its former condition. The aforementioned count, reflecting on these matters in his mind, promised that he would grant his request.

Approaching the king’s presence, he began to speak with humble mind and voice:

“Although, glorious king of the Franks, your royal Majesty has made me richer than the rest of your court in fortresses and many earthly honors, I still ask one thing of your kindness. I beg you above all my other petitions not to refuse this request.”

The king replied:

“What is this, dearest one, that could be denied you in our kingdom?”

The venerable count answered:

“The matter I ask does not appear very great or especially lavish, but small. I beg that your exalted Majesty deign to grant me, who serve you obediently, the church of the monastery of Fosses, which is subject to royal authority and appears to belong to your treasury.”

The king said to him:

“Since it is clear to everyone that the abbey has always been royal in the time of our predecessors, how can it be separated from our royal power? For if this is done by us, perhaps after the death of your body it will be subverted by the wickedness of your heirs or successors. Then we shall be blamed and shall suffer harm to our souls, when there is no place for justice and the brothers living there suffer immeasurable loss.”

The count replied:

“Since I cannot now obtain it as a perpetual gift, at least let this be granted: that, for the sake of reform and restoration, and also for the salvation of our souls, I may be deemed worthy to receive this gift that I request. I take great delight in undertaking the reform of so precious a place, and, supported by your assistance, in raising it through many honors and possessions—if life should accompany me by God’s favor—and restoring it to its former condition.

“Through that place’s distribution of alms, with God’s assent, I also hope to obtain the salvation of my soul and the lessening of my crimes and sins. And after the course of this fleeting age, I wish the fragile members of my body to be buried there.”

The king, seeing that what this great man requested was in accordance with God’s will, entrusted the place to his care for the purpose of reform and benefaction, as he had promised, so that he might serve as its faithful supporter and defender against wicked enemies and invaders of its lands. Receiving this with joyful gladness of heart, the count gave thanks and praise to God and to the mortal king.

In those days the fame of the venerable Maiolus, abbot of Cluny, was renowned throughout all Gaul. Having received the king’s permission, the count went to that holy man. Maiolus received him reverently, as was fitting, and the count prostrated himself on the ground. Maiolus then sought to learn the reason for his coming to him from so distant a homeland.

The count replied:

“It must not be thought that I have undertaken the labor of so long a journey and come to you for some frivolous reason. Humbly I ask you to receive the words of my petition, lest, fatigued by so long a journey and having come to so distant a land, I be found to have repented.

“Recently I received from Lord Hugh, king of the Franks, the church of Fosses for the purpose of reform. I ask that it be reformed and elevated by your support, so that the institution of Saint Benedict may be religiously observed there. I have sought the assistance of no one except yours, since I have learned that you please God.”

Father Maiolus, astonished, replied:

“Since many monasteries are found in your kingdom, why do you not obtain from them what you request from us? It is very laborious for us to visit foreign and unknown regions, to leave our own, and to seek yours. This should therefore be sought from your neighbors rather than from us, who are distant and unknown.”

When the count heard this, he became very sad and sorrowful, fearing that he had undertaken such a great journey in vain. Again and again he prostrated himself at the holy man’s feet, asking that his heartfelt desire be received.

Saint Maiolus, overcome by the many prayers of the venerable count, took with him the more perfect brothers of his monastery and traveled with the count as far as Paris. When they reached the harbor of a small village on the River Marne, near the monastery of Fosses, the count ordered the abbot and the entire community to come to meet him across the river.

They, unaware of what was to come, cheerfully obeyed the count’s commands. When they had all assembled, he ordered that those who wished to remain in the monastery with Abbot Maiolus and obey him in all things should have free permission to return. Those who did not wish to do so were to go wherever they pleased.

They became exceedingly sad, being deprived of all human assistance, and preferred to follow the paths desired by their own hearts rather than return to the church with the abbot or with monks unknown to them. None of them was permitted to take away anything they had with them, except the garments they were wearing.

Abbot Magenardus, who, as we have said, was of noble birth—for he was descended from Ansoaldus, the wealthy man of the city of Paris—was sent to the monastery of Saint Maurus, called Glannafolium, so that he might serve as shepherd of the brothers living there. He remained in that place as long as he lived. When he died, his body was buried in the church before the face of the crucified Lord.

Saint Maiolus, therefore, taking possession of the aforesaid place with his monks, began to observe strictly the discipline of the regular order, so that nothing at all might be omitted from what the Rule of Saint Benedict commanded.

When everything within and without had been carried out according to the Rule, and all things had been carefully corrected as far as possible, he approached Hugh, king of the Franks, and asked him to increase and augment the food allowance for the servants of God living under Maiolus’s authority.

The king kindly received his request and, urged on by Count Burchard, granted to the church of Fosses the village called Mansiones, with its churches and all its appurtenances, situated in the Paris region between the Seine and the Marne, just as it appeared to be held by him under royal right.

The grant was made secure by a charter bearing a monogram, and the seal of royal majesty was placed upon it by Ragenaldus the chancellor, the count’s son, later bishop of Paris, in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 988, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July. It was preserved perpetually in the same monastery. For this reason, the anniversary of that king’s death, the ninth day before the Kalends of November, is celebrated solemnly in that monastery to this day.

After these things had been accomplished, Saint Father Maiolus hastened to return to his own place. Entrusting the monastery to a certain religious man named Teutoni, whom he had brought with him from Cluny along with the others, he himself returned from where he had come.

After a considerable time, while the holy man Maiolus continued to delay his return to Gaul, the illustrious King Hugh died.
