When his son Robert, of pious memory, had assumed the kingdom, that king, on the advice and urging of the count, gave Teutoni the gift of the abbey and ordered him to be appointed abbot.

When this reached the ears of the Cluniacs, they became very sad, because they wished to reduce that place to a cell dependent upon themselves. Once the aforesaid man had been appointed to the honor of governance, he strove with great zeal to administer the burden entrusted to him with balanced moderation and to raise the church committed to him to the highest honor.

The walls of that building, which had been constructed in antiquity, had been consumed by excessive age. Seeing this and desiring to restore it by improving it, that same Father demolished the entire building to its foundations and, with God’s help, constructed another of greater size and more excellent dignity.

Afterward he ordered two precious bells to be made for the honor of the Lord, placing his own name on one of them. This worthy abbot performed these and many other good works for God in that place.

The venerable count, being very concerned for the salvation of his soul and urged on by the Holy Spirit, gave to the church he loved, to holy Mary the Mother of the Lord, to her apostles Peter and Paul, and also to the venerable confessor Maurus, possessions from his own property that seemed precious to him.

Countess Elisabeth, joined to him in marriage, together with their son Ragenaldus, who had already become bishop of the city of Paris, approved this deed and shared in his desire. Approaching the king’s presence, the count asked him to approve this according to royal custom and to order a charter of his authority to be made and strengthened with his seal, so that in future times the aforesaid monastery might enjoy those same possessions and his memory might always be preserved in prayers.

Urged by the king’s clemency—by his mother Adelaide and his wife, Queen Bertha—the king most willingly assented to what such a great man requested.

The aforementioned Count Burchard therefore gave these possessions from his own property to the church of Fosses: namely, the village called Nobiliacus, situated in the diocese of Paris on the River Marne, with its advocacy and vicariate, its church and altar, and everything belonging to it.

Likewise, in the same district, in the county of the fortress of Corbeil, in the village called Licias, he gave the holding of Algardis, with everything belonging to it.

In the district of the Gâtinais, in the county of Nemours and in the diocese of the city of Sens, he gave his own property called Seia, with its advocacy and vicariate, its church, and everything belonging to it.

In the county of Melun he also gave the allod called Curciacus, with its advocacy and vicariate and everything belonging to it.

When many of the Franks saw and heard of this holy devotional purpose, they too contributed many things from their own possessions to that same place. Among them was Joscelinus, viscount of the fortress of Melun, who asked the devout count to grant to God and his saints the church situated in the village called Nosiacus Siccus, which he held as the count’s benefice. The count, filled with joy, gladly granted this as well.

That viscount himself, laying aside the military belt for Christ, afterward became a monk in the same monastery and, worthily completing the course of his life, died there on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April.

Concerning all these matters, the illustrious King Robert ordered a charter of his authority to be made, made the grant to Abbot Teutoni and the other monks, and confirmed it for the aforesaid church by a decree of his generosity. Through it he ordered and commanded that, until the end of the world, the monks of that place should hold and fully possess all these things, and that no king, no bishop, no count, and no mortal power should presume to dispose of those possessions, determine anything concerning them under its own authority, or transfer them elsewhere.

Rather, they were to remain in the monks’ right with perpetual security, so that they might arrange and use them for the benefit of the place in whatever way they chose.

So that the decree of that command and confirmation might retain an inviolable strength throughout all the ages, the king confirmed it with his own hand according to royal custom and ordered it to be marked with the impression of his ring. The chancellor Rogerius faithfully carried this out; afterward, by God’s permission, he was elevated to the honor of the episcopate in the city of Beauvais.

These things were enacted in the city of Paris in the year of the Incarnation of the Word 998, in the tenth year of King Robert, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May.

There was also in those days a certain distinguished knight, greatly exalted in worldly power and wealth and faithful to the venerable count, named Ermenfredus, who desired faithfully to please God. Terrified by fear of eternal punishment and religiously inspired by the example of the man just mentioned, he told him that he greatly loved the place entrusted to him and wished to bestow some of his own possessions upon it. He therefore begged him to give to the church of Fosses the estate which he held from him as a benefice, called Licias (Lices), and likewise, of his own free will, to grant the property belonging to his possession called Jureum (Jury). The count, who desired that all the knights of France should perform similar deeds, freely granted him permission to give whatever pleased his mind.

Accordingly, he came with his wife, named Ermensendis, to the place he loved above all others and disclosed the secret of his heart to the religious abbot Teuto and the other brothers. Giving thanks to God, they received the aforesaid husband and wife into their prayers; thus they became familiars of God’s servants and received the place of their burial after the dissolution of their bodies. They therefore gave there the property mentioned above, Jureum, situated on the river Seine, a mile and a half from the fortress of Corboil, together with the church, the vicarage, and the right of advocacy, with everything belonging to it.

[Col. 0854A] In the same way they made a donation of the aforementioned estate called Licias, situated in the aforesaid district, a mile and a half from the fortress. They held it as a benefice from Count Burchard and from his son Rainald, illustrious in pontifical dignity. With their consent and will they made this gift for the reward of eternal life and for the absolution of their own souls, and of the soul of Gelo, whose successors they were, as well as of their parents, together with the advocacy, the authority of the vicars, and everything pertaining to it.

They placed the gift of these possessions upon the altar of Saint Mary and Saint Peter the Apostle, on the understanding that they should receive from them an annual payment of a specified amount; but after both had departed this life, the monks should possess them perpetually. After this they approached the presence of the king and begged him to strengthen these gifts by the authority of his charter and to deign to secure them with the impression of his ring. He, at the urging of his mother Adelaidis and his wife Bertha, carried out what they had requested.

Once the charter had been written, and the royal monogram made by the king’s own hand, Franco, then chancellor and later bishop of Paris, affixed the royal image. This was done in the aforesaid city in the year of Christ’s incarnation 1000, in the twelfth indiction, and happily in the twelfth year of the reign of the illustrious King Robert.

Having related these matters, let us turn our pen back to our Burchard. The very hostile Count Odo, at the instigation of the enemy of the human race, was exceedingly hostile to this venerable count and envied his good deeds, because he saw that Burchard was preferred to him at the king’s court, honored, and loved by everyone. For this reason, through a certain deception and betrayal, he stole from him the castle of Milidunum. When Burchard learned of this, with the king’s assistance he gathered the army of the Franks and surrounded it with many thousands of soldiers. Seeing that he could not remain there safely or retain the castle under his own authority, Odo secretly departed and fled with his men. Burchard, however, entered and recovered his own castle. Galterius, through whose treachery this great crime had been perpetrated, was hanged with his wife on the hill overlooking it.

[Col. 0854D] At another time, with the enemy of peace and light urging them on, these two counts declared war against one another at a place in the same district called Milidunensis. When they had arrived there and battle was being fiercely prepared by both sides, the aforesaid knight Ermenfredus, subject at that time only to the authority of the king, humbly submitted himself with his men to the king’s power. For it was not, nor is it, the custom of the Franks to enter any war without the presence or command of their own lord.

Burchard therefore humbled himself greatly before God, asking that victory be granted him against the proud enemy who rigidly raised the neck of both body and heart. They came together to fight in the field of the little village called Orceiacus (Orsay). While they were contending in battle line, by God’s judgment Odo’s army, fighting among itself, was overthrown in a great slaughter. Burchard, trusting confidently in the Lord, rushed upon the enemy; many thousands were killed, and victory was granted him from heaven.

When Odo saw his army greatly diminished and many of his men lying slain across the plain, and realized that he could by no means emerge victorious that day, he was shaken by intense fear and became utterly confounded. He feared that he could not escape from there, but secretly sought the aid of flight with all speed. Thus the count faithful to God, victorious and praising the Lord with his men, returned joyfully to his own possessions.

At last the religious abbot Teuto, continually devoted to fasts, prayers, and nights spent in vigil, faithfully desired always to please God. Since he could not, as he wished, maintain the arduous life in the place entrusted to him, on account of the care of pastoral oversight, [Col. 0855C] he chose the district of the city of Reims as his dwelling. There was indeed a small estate there which the glorious King Charles the Bald had given to the church of Fosses and to Abbot Godofredus as a refuge because of the persecution of the Normans; in it the body of Saint Maurus had also been reverently preserved for many years.

The aforesaid abbot therefore lived there for a long time, leading an arduous life for Christ. Wishing to go there and remain there, he sent the pastoral staff to the brothers through a servant of his office named Valterus, whom he himself had raised in the fear of the Lord, instructing them to choose for themselves a worthy pastor according to Christ’s will.

When the monks heard this, they were greatly astonished and became very sad. [Col. 0855D] They immediately took care to inform the chief count and his son Rainald, bishop of Paris. They in turn brought all these matters to the king’s ears.

The venerable father Teuto, while remaining for many days in the village just mentioned, led a solitary life in fasts, prayers, and every display of good works, as far as was possible for a mortal man, with God coming to his aid. Later, wishing to visit the place entrusted to him and the brothers he had left behind, he reached as far as Nogent (Nogent-sur-Marne), near the monastery. There he stopped, sent word to the brothers that he was present, and announced that he wished to come to them.

When many heard this, they prevented the fulfillment of his devout desire, saying that they had already received an abbot in his place and that he ought not to be received, because he had entirely abandoned the care of souls. When this was announced to the servant of God, he became very sorrowful, not knowing what to do or where to turn.

At last, reflecting in his heart, and strengthened by the Lord, who does not abandon those who hope in him, he found wholesome counsel. He suddenly returned to Cluny, the place of his monastery. There he outlived two abbots who were appointed after him in the place entrusted to him, and remained in the holy way of life with which he had begun. Neither of them was able to live long, because, by the judgment of the Lord, they held authority over the government for no more than five years. When the term that cannot be extended had been completed, he happily died there on the Ides of September.

[Col. 0856B] At his tomb, as we have heard reported, many sick people afterward received health.

Having related these matters, let us turn our pen to what has been omitted. When the king heard that Father Teuto had abandoned the place and the brothers in this manner, he began carefully to deliberate with the venerable men, namely Burchard and Bishop Rainald, how they might arrange that place according to the Lord’s will.

Advised by their prudent industry, they ordered Theobald, son of Count Haimo and brother of that bishop, to come to them. He was already presiding over the monastery of Cormaric. The king gave him the abbey and appointed him father of the monks, because he too belonged to the Cluniac community and had been instructed by the teaching of the holy Father Maiolus.

Although exalted in the nobility of this world, the count bestowed many good things not only upon the place of which we are speaking but also upon many monasteries throughout the kingdom of the Franks. Among these, he took care to enrich by his own gifts the monastery of Saint Peter of Milidunum, which Siguinus, archbishop of Sens, had begun to build.

[Col. 0856C] He also possessed numerous castles in other districts, of which he retained under his own authority Vendocinum (Vendôme), Lavarzinum (Lavardin), and Montemaureum (Montoir), apart from others whose names are unknown to me and which many knights held from him as benefices in return for service and loyalty.

Finally, he established a decree that any one of his faithful men who wished to give some portion of the lands belonging to his castles to the church of Fosses should have free permission to give whatever he desired, without the command of his successors. Some observed this decree and afterward bestowed many gifts upon us.

He had given a certain provost of his, named Bado, and his two heirs a benefice on the condition that during their lifetimes they should pay its census to the monastery, namely seventy-two coins; but after they had departed this life, the monks should possess the land perpetually.

When the aforesaid man died, his son named Alrannus, who had been the first heir and whose name was contained in the charter, went to Odo, who later presided over the place. Having received a payment, he placed the same little charter upon the altar of Saint Mary and handed over to the abbot and monks everything written in it.

[Col. 0857A] These possessions are not large but very small, situated in the district of Paris, not far from the castle of Corboil but within the circuit of that castle. They include, in the village called Licias, a little village called Burgunnaria because Burgundians lived there, where there is woodland together with arable land.

Likewise, near the mill-fortress called Tolvia, there is half an aripennus of land, for building if necessary. In the same place there is also a small amount of land belonging to Saint Stephen. The rest is situated opposite the castle of Saint Exuperius, in both the younger and the older Corboil, and at Ateias, Sosiacum, and Sintrium.

Anyone who wishes to know all these details will be able to find them clearly in the charter, or in the testament of King Robert, which was made in the year of the incarnate Word 1028, in the twelfth year of his reign.

[Col. 0857B] At that time, while the kingdom of the Franks was being governed in the best peace by the glorious King Robert and the Church of God was filled with peaceful concord, that same kingdom was suddenly disturbed by malignant adversity. It happened that a certain man of this world, wealthy in vainglorious nobility, called Arnulfus and distinguished by the office of count, rose up against Lord Robert, burned with fire everything that appeared subject to his authority, and inflicted every evil he was able to bring upon all.

As this discord prevailed and the devil’s fury led the way, he came to the monastery of Saint Walaricus, burned everything he could with fire, and subjected the very body of the confessor of Christ to his own authority.

[Col. 0857C] The monks, therefore, filled with great sorrow and deprived of so great a patron, hastened to the king of the Franks and asked him to deign to come to their aid. Unable to present himself to them in person, he earnestly begged Lord Burchard to help them in his place and to arrange, as far as he could, for the holy body to be restored to them.

The venerable Count Burchard came there, trusting in his heart in the grace of God. He approached the count of Flanders, conveyed the king’s words, and begged him earnestly to restore, by the will and mercy of God, the limbs of the confessor of Christ which he had taken through wicked greed, restoring them to their own place.

The count consented to his request, made peace with the king and the Franks, and what so great a count had been asked to do was swiftly accomplished.

When they reached the river called the Somme and wished to cross it, they suddenly saw that the sea had flooded the land and was denying a way to the holy body, to Count Burchard, and to the others who were with him.

[Col. 0857D] Then the count, who was carrying the holy body, said in the hearing of all who were present and who knew God with their whole minds:

“Lord Jesus Christ, if it is the will of your mercy that the body of this holy man of yours be restored to its own monastery, command that, by the graciousness of your goodness, this sea-river be divided for us, and do not disdain, by the graciousness of your kindness, to open the way of this journey to us, so that this people, serving your name, may be able to offer gifts of praise to the glory of your praise and to the honor of this holy servant of yours with devoted heart and joyful exultation.”

[Col. 0858A] At this voice of the servant of God, and moved by the prayers of his saint, the Lord was entreated. Suddenly the watery sea was divided in such a way that the bearers of the holy body and the whole people, praising and blessing the Lord God with the greatest devotion of praise, crossed that danger of the sea on dry feet, without any peril from the waters.

By this deed the Lord deigned to repeat the miracle which he had deigned to perform through his servant Moses, when the children of Israel were fleeing, in the midst of the sea. Wishing also to return that monastery enriched with many possessions of its estates, he bestowed many gifts within and without it as a perpetual memorial of himself.

For this reason his anniversary is solemnly celebrated there, as though he were physically present. They even declare in their testament that, if it were possible for his body to be kept among them—and this cannot happen, since we do not believe it would please God’s will—his venerable body would nevertheless be placed beside the body of Saint Walaricus, so that the one whom he strove to honor on earth might, together with him, be honored by Christ in heaven and on earth.

But, leaving these matters aside, let us turn our discourse back to our Burchard and, with the Lord’s help, let our pen relate how he entered the sacred order and afterward came to Christ, making it clear by our account and reasoning to all mortals who are ignorant of these things.

[Col. 0858C] In the days of the aforesaid abbot, the invincible knight and God-devoted Count Burchard fell into the weakness of illness. But since every son whom God mercifully receives is chastised, he desired to be found watchful and wished to be a vigilant guardian of his soul.

Immediately he rejected secular knighthood, desired the monastic life, and longed for the heavenly kingdom with the whole vision of his mind. Fearing that he could not escape the danger of death, he took gold and silver, cloaks, and many monastic ornaments, and in the place he himself had built and established requested and received monastic clothing.

There was immense mourning among all the nobles of the Franks, among monks, clerics, widows, and every order of both sexes and all ages, because their patron was abandoning those whom he had been accustomed to strengthen with kindly counsel and sweetest speech.

[Col. 0858D] All the knights grieved, and all the poor lamented, because the consoler of the wretched, the helper of the afflicted, and the hope and refuge of all the knights was being withdrawn from their sight, and they were losing the support of their entire salvation and consolation.

The monks, however, servants of Christ, although saddened by his illness, nevertheless rejoiced, because so distinguished a knight, shining with comital honor, was abandoning everything according to the Lord’s command and receiving his easy yoke and light burden with devoted mind.

Among his other ornaments, many vessels of gold and silver, bronze and wood, as well as precious candelabra, were brought. All these, as was fitting, were assigned to the service of the holy church and altar.

Among them were two precious vessels for pouring or receiving water in the hands of a priest. One of these we call a *manipulus*, because it is carried by hand. It bears an inscription stating that it belonged to King Abagarus for drawing blood. The king himself is also depicted upon it, together with the man who is bleeding him and another servant attending him, all made of precious, pure gold. It is said that no vessel so precious and beautiful is to be found in this country.

[Col. 0859A] Nor was there lacking a copy of the book of the holy Gospel, excellently written in letters of gold and beautifully worked with engraved gold, silver, and ivory.

A golden sword with a golden belt, from which this great monastery is said to have been begun, was loosened from his waist and brought as his gift. He also brought with him a very precious vessel made of the stone called beryl, from which water was poured into the holy chalice, and a place where knights customarily train, excellently fashioned from crystal.

He also gave an immeasurable number of male and female servants. What more can be said? No one clothed in this mortal flesh could fully enumerate all his gifts.

Although so glorious a count had been distinguished in the world by countless honors, he left none of his heirs, friends, or retainers as much as he gave—apart from the castles—to God and his saints in the place he loved above all others, for the salvation of his soul.

[Col. 0859C] Clothed religiously in the sacred habit, he lay ill for many days in a house prepared for him beside the church. Later, when the merciful Lord was appeased by the prayers continually poured out for him by his servants, he began to recover and to go out with the other brothers.

When restored to health, he diligently sought to please the Lord. He continually gave him thanks and blessed him with humble mind, because the Lord had granted him the grace of his holy mercy even in this order.

The service of Holy Church, which those converted from the world are required to offer to God according to the custom of the monks, this most noble man performed with humble devotion.

When the brothers said to him, “Why does so noble a man, exalted by secular dignity and already broken by the labor of old age, deign to afflict himself by humbling himself?” he replied:

[Col. 0859D] “If, when I was exalted in military honor, surrounded, as you say, by a troop of soldiers, and shining with the dignity of a count, I carried a candle in my hand before a mortal king who required a lamp, how much more ought I now to serve the immortal Emperor and reverently carry before him burning candelabra in my hands, together with the practice of humility?”

By saying and doing this, he offered to all who saw and heard him a great example of humility.

Thus approved by God and tested like precious gold in the fire, he was again seized by the distress of illness and brought to his final extremity. Strengthened by receiving the sacred body and blood of Christ, he gave his blessed spirit back to the Lord on the fourth day before the Kalends of March.

When he had died, the bishop immediately arrived with a number of clerics, and the abbot likewise with a company of monks. Funeral rites were performed for the body, commending his holy soul to God.

Suddenly a cry arose throughout the city, the castles, the villages, and the streets. Knights, rich and poor, old and young, widows and virgins all came running, mourning and wailing, filled with grief and misery.

Fosses was filled with mourning, groaning, and every kind of sorrow, having lost the patron and advocate whom it had deserved to possess as its most faithful defender and helper. It declared that it would never again find one of such a kind, whose nobility would enrich it and whose aid would protect it so faithfully, but that it would lie open to the bites of the wicked, be plundered by the invasion of enemies, and be surrounded by the malice of all adversaries. That this later came to pass is clear today to everyone living throughout the world.

[Col. 0860B] The bodily remains of so noble a man were therefore buried before the face of our Redeemer, in the building where the brothers gathered for chapter at morning and evening.

The ancient fathers took care to adorn his mausoleum with verses such as these, so that his perpetual memorial might remain forever inviolate:

> This great man once lived while he possessed a body,  
> > Burchard by name, known throughout the regions of the world.  
> > Exalted in merits, modest in words and deeds,  
> > Generous to the poor, everywhere kind to widows.  
> > Behold, his body rests in this tomb;  
> > March shows that he departed on the fourth day before the Kalends.

That tablet of his tomb had been excellently fashioned and decorated by our predecessors. A gilded cross bearing the letters α and ω had been placed above his breast, and we ourselves saw it with our own eyes in the time of our childhood. All these things, however, were afterward entirely destroyed, as is evident today.

The venerable Countess Elisabet, his wife, also took care, according to the nature of her sex, to enrich that place with great gifts. Having departed from the world, she lies buried there. Her day of death is observed on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February.

Her burial monument is also adorned with these verses:

> It pleased the Lord to join these two together while alive,  
> > And thus he willed that they should be joined together in one burial place.  
> > Whoever reads this, recite the verses of a psalm,  
> > So that their spirits may be able to ascend the realms of heaven.

It is enough to have recounted these matters from the many deeds of the count. There are, in fact, countless records of his good works which, compelled by weariness, we leave aside, because our mind hastens to undertake other matters.

[Col. 0860D] Therefore, brothers, we must diligently ensure that we serve before the eyes of the Creator for this man and for the other benefactors whose alms they contributed to this place for the redemption of their sins, in such a way that—God avert it from us—they do not result in eternal condemnation.

For we must know that, with God’s help, we pass through the course of this present life by means of the alms of good men. We must therefore store in our hearts what the Lord, terrifyingly reproaching sinners through the prophet, cries out, saying: “They have eaten the sins of my people” (Hos. 4:8).

The anniversaries of these spouses must likewise be solemnly celebrated by the servants of God on the days mentioned above, so that what they may have loved this place above all others and wished their bodies to be buried there may benefit their souls, and so that they may deserve to be raised by Christ the Lord on the day of judgment.

To this very day—that is, up to the present year, which is the year 1058 of the incarnate Word and the twenty-eighth year of the reign of Henry, king of the Franks—the same observance has been devoutly carried out in this church. It must humbly be acknowledged that it should also be done in the future.

The rulers of the place and its ministers must also take the greatest care that, just as we have said it should be done in the church, so too a meal of choice foods and spices should be solemnly prepared for their spirits, because, as the common saying goes, labor appears empty when it provides no nourishment.

[Col. 0861B] And lest this seem to anyone futile or worthy of contempt, it was established with the favor and consent of Abbot Giraldus and the whole congregation that, for Count Burchard, who bestowed such great benefits upon this church that anyone can learn of them from the account given here, the steward of Nobiliacum should carefully perform the duty; for Elisabeth, the steward of Cruciacum; for Bishop Rainald, the steward of Seia; for King Hugh, the steward of Mansiones; and for Ermenfredus and his wife, the stewards of Licias and Jureum. For the abbots of this congregation, the steward and treasurer of this place should diligently fulfill it, without incurring any negligence.

Whoever afterward attempted to despise or destroy this decree would be condemned perpetually under the anathema of excommunication.

[Col. 0862A] In the preface of this work I had proposed, after these matters, to discuss something about Bishop Rainald, so that his memory might become known to posterity. But since a man’s life is not in his own power, and since many difficulties press upon me, I am now unwilling to complete this until the time of the desired peace and tranquility arrives.

Nevertheless, let us always give thanks, in prosperity and adversity alike, to Jesus Christ and to the holy Paraclete, who lives and remains one God indivisibly throughout all ages. Amen.

**Here ends the Life of Lord Burchard, the Venerable Count.**

**In the year of the Lord 1058. Anselm, canon of Liège.**

**Anselm’s History of the Bishops of Liège.**

(See *Patrologia*, vol. 139, under Heriger of Liège, at the year 1008. Although Anselm is fifty years younger than Heriger, we have wished not to separate him from Heriger because of the close connection between the two works.)

**In the year of the Lord 1058. Drogo, bishop of Beauvais.**

**Historical Notice.**

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. IV, p. 708.)

[Col. 0861C] Drogo occurs as early as 1035, when, with King Henry’s permission, he founded the monastery of Saint Symphorianus not far from the city. In the following year he established two other monasteries: namely Flaviacum, for men, and an oratory for virgins, now distinguished by the name of Saint Paul. According to Luvetius, [Col. 0862C] vol. I, p. 50, he also founded, about the year 1037, the collegiate church of Saint Lawrence; and in the same year another collegiate church of Saint Bartholomew was founded by the knight Hailo, King Henry confirming the foundation. Moreover, on his advice monks were restored with an abbot at Britolium; and he himself gave his canons the churches of [Col. 0863A] Haudivillari, Exulium, and Saint Eusebia; and to the monks of Saint Lucian other churches, together with the county and vicariate of Warlosi. A charter for this matter is found in Luvetius, vol. II, p. 190. In 1047 he subscribed King Henry I’s judicial decision on behalf of the monastery of Saint Medard at Soissons against Robert of Coudic; and in the following year he was present at the council of Senlis for the donation of Chancellor Baldwin in favor of the monks of Saint Praejectus at Quintinopolis. In 1049, summoned by Pope Leo IX [Col. 0864A] to the Council of Reims, he neither attended nor sent an excuse; but, remaining in the king’s company, he went to war. For this reason he was excommunicated along with the archbishop of Sens, the bishop of Amiens, and the abbot of Saint Medard. Yet we infer that shortly afterward he was released from excommunication, for he continued to govern his church and peacefully closed his final day in it. He is said to have died in 1058.

**Letter of Drogo to W., his fellow bishop.**

(In Baluze, *Capitularia*, vol. II, col. 1549.)

Consulted, apparently, by Bishop Wido of Senlis concerning what should be done about certain men who had violently beaten a priest, he replies, among other things, from the *Capitularies*, and adduces in support of his judgment chapter 98 of book VI, “On priests, Levites, and monks who have been killed or disabled.”

[Col. 0863B] To his brother and fellow bishop W., D., bishop of Beauvais, greeting.

If the matter stands as your faithful man has related it to you, you have not so much excommunicated those sacrilegious men as declared them to be excommunicated. For even if a human tongue is silent, divine authority nevertheless immediately anathematizes them once the crime has been committed. We gather this from the words of the Lord speaking thus to his disciples: “He who despises you despises me. He who touches you touches the pupil of my eye.” For these men have not merely touched the members of Christ and the pupil of the Lord’s eye, but, as I hear, have severely beaten them. Therefore they were immediately deprived of communion by divine judgment.

Where a perishable matter is at issue, delays in such summonses may perhaps be granted in some cases. But when such a grave and enormous sacrilege is committed, in which the true temple of God, not made by hands, is violated, at that very moment the perpetrator of this iniquity becomes not only liable to excommunication, but also to some great punishment which may even surpass Gehenna. You therefore rightly excommunicated without delay those who did not fear to stretch out their hands against God’s saints.

[Col. 0863C] But if it is asked how they ought to be punished or corrected, it would be fitting that, weighed down with a millstone, they be drowned in the depths of the sea: they who, by inflicting scandal upon Christ’s servants, have afflicted them with blows and insults. The secular laws in the *Capitularies* also command that persons of this kind be punished either by a capital sentence, or transported into exile, or have their outstretched hands cut off at once, or, after laying aside military arms, be confined in a monastery under perpetual penance.

But for the present, and in accordance with secular custom, you should act more leniently: first, let the excommunication be atoned for to you; then, if capital goods have been taken, let them be restored threefold according to the law. Likewise, each blow and seizure should be compensated threefold according to the law. Afterward require of them thirty pounds, which are customarily given for violation of the church precinct. For God’s minister is far more precious than the court of the temple or its walls. Moreover, a suitable penance of either seven or five years should be imposed upon them, so that they may be corrected and others may have fear.

This is an excerpt from book VI of the *Capitularies*, chapter 98: “If anyone disables a priest, Levite, or monk, let him make compensation according to the enactments of the preceding chapters which were added to Salic law; and in addition let him pay our ban, that is, sixty solidi, to us; let him relinquish his arms and serve God in a monastery for the days of his life under rigorous penance, never thereafter to engage in the world or in secular military service, nor to take a wife.”

[Col. 0864C] It is related that, in the time of King Louis, father of Lothair, the following took place. When a certain man, stirred by anger, had inflicted the gravest injuries upon a priest and had not feared finally to tear him with many blows, both men were brought before the royal tribunal. After carefully examining the case, and wishing to teach that every reverence must be shown to Christ’s ministers, the king addressed all those standing around him as follows: “All worship of our religion is celebrated through the offices of priests; therefore the worship due to divine reverence must in every way be rendered to them—not because their merit of life always demands it, but so that in them Christ may be seen to be obeyed by us. Therefore I decree that this man, who in such unrestrained fury has been brought against God’s priest, be bound to the trunk of a tree, [Col. 0864D] stripped of every protection of clothing.” When, therefore, in accordance with the king’s sentence, he had been seized, stripped, and bound naked outside to a tree, it is reported that so vast and grievous a swarm of flies suddenly arrived there that, before the king, returning, had travelled a mile [lacuna], his entire body was reported to have been eaten.

**Ancient Litanies of the Church of Beauvais.**

(In Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Luc. edition, p. 283.)

[Col. 0865A] Christ conquers. Thrice. Christ reigns. Thrice. Christ commands. Thrice. Hear us, O Christ. R/. Life to John, supreme pontiff and universal pope. Thrice. Saviour of the world, help him. Holy Mary, help him. Saint Michael, help him. Saint Gabriel, help him. Saint Raphael, help him. Hear us, O Christ. Salvation and life to Rotger, bishop of this Church, and to all the flock entrusted to him. Redeemer of the world, help him. [Col. 0865B] Saint Peter, help him. Saint Paul, help him. Saint Andrew, help him. Saint Simon, help him. Hear us, O Christ. Life and victory to Robert, most serene, God-crowned, great, and peaceable king. Saviour of the world, help him. Saint Stephen, help him. Saint Denis, help him. Saint Lucian, help him. Saint Justus, help him. Hear us, O Christ. Salvation and life to Queen Constance. Redeemer of the world, help her. Saint Felicity, help her. [Col. 0865C] Saint Perpetua, help her. Saint Agatha, help her. Saint Agnes, help her. Hear us, O Christ. Life and victory to all judges and to the whole army of Christians. Saviour of the world, help them. Saint Sylvester, help them. Saint Gregory, help them. Saint Leo, help them. Saint Ambrose, help them.

[Col. 0866A] Christ conquers, Christ reigns, Christ commands. Christ, King of kings, conquers. Christ, our mercy, conquers. Christ, our deliverance and redemption, conquers. Christ, our most unconquerable arms, conquers. Christ, our impregnable wall, conquers. Christ, our defense and exultation, conquers. Christ, our protection and victory, conquers. To him alone be dominion, glory, and power through the immortal ages of ages. Amen. To him be honor, praise, and jubilation through the infinite ages of ages. Amen. To him alone be might, strength, and victory through all ages of ages. Amen. Christ, hear us. Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. [Col. 0866B] Lord, have mercy. Let us spend this day joyfully. Thrice. May God preserve Lord John, the apostolic pope. Thrice. Saviour of the world, help him. Saint John, help him. Saint James, help him. Saint Philip, help him. May God preserve Lord Bishop Rotger. Thrice. Redeemer of the world, help him. Saint Martin, help him. Saint Remigius, help him. Saint Medard, help him. May God preserve Lord King Robert. Thrice. Saviour of the world, help him. Saint Cornelius, help him. [Col. 0866C] Saint Lawrence, help him. Saint Vincent, help him. Happily. Thrice. Happily. Thrice. Happily. Thrice. May they have good times. Thrice. May they have good times. Thrice. Many years. Amen. Go; the dismissal is made. Thanks be to God.

# In the Year of Our Lord 1058. Pope Stephen X

[Col. 0865]

## Historical Notice

*(Ciaconio, Lives of the Roman Pontiffs.)*

[Col. 0865D] In the name of the blessed God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Amen.

[Col. 0866D] Our most holy lord Stephen IX, a Lotharingian, previously called Frederick, born of the most noble house of the dukes of Lotharingia, son of Duke Gothelon and brother of the great Duke Godfrey IV, descended from the royal stock of the Franks and by nation a Gaul, was instructed in the liberal arts from childhood and devoted to ecclesiastical service. For he was first made a regular canon of Saint Lambert in Lotharingia. Soon afterward he was created cardinal deacon by the blessed Pope Leo IX and chancellor of the Apostolic See. He was sent as a legate *a latere* to Constantinople together with Humbert, cardinal bishop of Silva Candida, and refuted the errors of the Greeks. Then, having returned to Rome, after the death of Pope Leo IX he went to the monastery of Monte Cassino, where, having assumed the habit of the religion of Saint Benedict—which he had always loved from childhood—he spent some time living there.

Yet scarcely two years after his entrance, he was unanimously designated the thirty-sixth abbot of Cassino, in place of the deceased Abbot Robert, who had received him. For his consecration, as was customary, he went to the Roman pontiff Victor II, who was then residing at Florence. Accompanied by eight monks, he was not only consecrated abbot of Cassino but also ordained cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. As he departed from Victor to return to his monastery at Cassino, when he had reached Rome, the death of Pope Victor II was immediately announced.

When this news reached Rome, the Romans at once held an assembly to provide a successor to the pontiff. Some thought that Hildebrand, who was with Victor, should be awaited; others held that no delay should be introduced into the election. Finally, all with one accord approached Frederick himself, the cardinal who had shortly before returned from Tuscany. They forcibly led him from his lodging to the basilica of Saint Peter ad Vincula, and, having elected him pontiff, called him Stephen by name. It was the fourth day before the Nones of August, the day on which the Church celebrates the memory of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr. From there, amid universal applause, they conducted him to the Lateran. The following day, a Sunday, when all the cardinals together with the clergy and Roman people had gathered to him, they consecrated him in the Vatican with great ceremony. He sat during the reign of the emperor Henry IV for seven months and twenty-eight days.

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1057, on the third day before the Nones of August, the day after his election, Pope Stephen X was consecrated bishop and pontiff at Rome in the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles, and received the insignia of his coronation from Mainardus, archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church.

After beginning his pontificate, Stephen immediately sent Hildebrand as legate to Agnes Augusta, the mother of Henry IV, to inform her of what had been done. He then turned to pursuing the reform of the Church that had been initiated. For a great struggle remained with Henry himself, her son, who, corrupted by his advisers, had begun selling churches—not to those who deserved it most through learning and excellence of life, but to those who offered the greatest reward and the most money—in an open traffic in sacred things. Thus, having remained four months in Rome, he devoted them all to these deliberations and plans. He did not hesitate to accuse Henry of the heresy of simony and to condemn his action by a severe decree; he also prohibited, through new constitutions, clerical incontinence and the marriages of blood relatives.

Stephen X convened a synod at the Lateran. At that synod the Church of Milan, which, in the proud arrogance of its self-importance, had withdrawn from the Roman Church nearly two hundred years earlier, chiefly through Hildebrand’s efforts, finally began once more to obey the Roman Church as the true mother and teacher of all Churches. Thereafter it honored her in the manner in which legitimate daughters customarily honor a most devoted mother.

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1058, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, Pope Stephen X died at Florence. His body was buried there in the cathedral church of Saint Reparata.

The see was vacant for twenty-eight days.

[Col. 0867]

## Another Notice

*(In Mansi, Councils, vol. X.)*

[Col. 0867D] Stephen, previously called Frederick, formerly abbot of Cassino and cardinal priest, was unwillingly made pontiff by the common consent of the entire clergy. He was the ninth pope of that name, in the year of Christ the Redeemer 1057, during the reign of Henry IV. Having held numerous councils in Rome against concubinage and many other vices of the clergy, he reformed the conduct of the Church. He drew Peter Damian from his hermitage and created him cardinal bishop of Ostia.

He sent a legation eastward to unite the Church of Constantinople, divided by schism, with Catholic and apostolic communion. The legation was carried out by Cardinal Stephen, Mainardus, bishop of Silva Candida, and Desiderius, designated abbot of Cassino. Having given them written instructions concerning the matters to be handled, he ordered them to prepare their return as soon as they could.

He issued a decree concerning the election of the future pontiff, which Leo of Ostia describes in these words:

> “After this, having assembled the bishops and clergy within the church, together with the Roman people, he established under an exceedingly strict prohibition that, if he should happen to die before Hildebrand, then subdeacon of the Roman Church, returned from the empress, to whom he was being sent by common agreement on certain affairs of state, no one at all should dare to elect a pope. Instead, the Apostolic See was to remain vacant and untouched until his return, and only then was it to be ordered by his counsel.”

He went to Florence to visit Saint John Gualbert, renowned above all for his reputation for holiness, but there fell ill. A few days after becoming sick, he died on the fourth day before the Kalends of April in the year 1058.

“In the meantime,” says Leo of Ostia, “Gregory, count of the Lateran and Tusculum, having learned of the death of the Roman pontiff and having joined himself to Gerard of Galese [or Galera; Benedict X, a false pope and schismatic] and several Roman nobles, invaded the church by night with bands of armed men. They installed John, bishop of Velletri, later known as Mincius, as pope, imposing on him the name Benedict. When Peter Damian, a very religious man whom Pope Stephen had at that time drawn from his hermitage and made bishop in the Church of Ostia, learned of this, he began, together with the cardinals, to resist, protest, and pronounce an anathema. Nevertheless, all these men, struck with fear, fled to various places.”

How the schismatic was expelled from the see will be related below in the Life of Nicholas II.

[Col. 0869]

## Diplomatic Notice

*(Jaffé, Regesta of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 381.)*

[Col. 0869B] In his bulls, Stephen X used this phrase: “He himself is our peace” *(n. 2, 5).*

His bulls were written by the hand of Gregory, notary and archivist *(nn. 2, 3, 4, 6, 7).*

[Col. 0870B] They were dated by the hand of Humbert, bishop of the Holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the Holy Roman and Apostolic See *(nn. 2, 3, 4, 5, 7).*

[Col. 0869]

# Letters and Privileges of Pope Stephen X

## I

[Note: [Col. 0869D] This letter, together with four letters of Nicholas and sixteen of Alexander II written to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims, was published from the library of Papirius Masson. In the Lives of Stephen, Nicholas, and Alexander II, Papirius had written “Willelmus, archbishop of Reims,” instead of Gervasius. I previously followed him incorrectly; in this edition I believe that Gervasius should be written in place of Willelmus. For in the time of these pontiffs, it is recorded that not some Willelmus but Guido and Gervasius I presided over the Church of Reims, as can be seen in the catalogue of the bishops of Reims preserved by Flodoard. This is not the other Gervasius whom Ivo mentions in Letter 206 and the continuator of Sigebert mentions under the year 1114. He lived in the time of Paschal II, to whom he wrote a letter that the said Papirius includes in the Life of Paschal II. — Severus Binius.]

Letter of Stephen X to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims.—He promises assistance to one acting courageously for religion; postpones the case of the archbishop of Bourges to another time; and summons him to the city for a synod together with his suffragans. (Year 1057.)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 862.]*

[Col. 0869C]

**Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gervasius, archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We do not doubt that, as you have written to us, you rejoice at our promotion. We both wish and desire that sincere friendship between us may also endure forever. Moreover, if you preserve with complete integrity the obedience and fidelity that you promise us—as you ought and as befits you—you are doing what you know very well must be done: you are reverencing in us not only us but the principal and common mother.

Concerning the holding of a council at Reims, what else can be said except that the lord Victor, of blessed memory, was snatched from this life by God’s judgment, and that you, as was agreed between us, did not write back whether the king’s consent had been obtained in this matter? As for the archbishop of Bourges, because our beloved son Hildebrand, who is especially well informed about his case, is absent, we answer only this: when he returns and you come to us with him, we shall have your counsel both on this matter and on other ecclesiastical affairs.

Do not lose heart or be broken if you suffer adversaries for your fidelity to the Holy Roman Church, indeed for the defense of the sacred canons. Know, according to the Apostle, that you have been placed in this position (1 Thess. 3). For our assistance and counsel will not be lacking during our pontificate to you who are contending for justice, although I seem to have been raised to it without any merit of my own. And, in accordance with your prayer, we shall pray the Lord Jesus that you may never fall away from your good purpose.

Furthermore, since we intend to celebrate a synod at Rome on the fifteenth day after Holy Easter, we wish—and by apostolic authority command—that your Fraternity attend together with its suffragans, unless prevented by unavoidable necessity.

## II

Bull of Stephen X by which he confirms the immunity of the secular clergy from the judgments and burdens imposed by secular authorities. (Year 1058.)

*[Muratori, Italian Antiquities V, 973.]*

[Col. 0871A]

**Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved sons in Christ, all the priests, levites, and persons of every sacred order residing at Lucca, or belonging to all the parishes, clergy, acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, and suburban presbyters of the bishopric of Lucca, and to all their successors forever.**

If it is proper for us to observe toward the order of faithful laymen the lawful custom and decrees of piety, much more must we observe and confirm what equity requires concerning the ranks of the clergy who faithfully minister and serve the Church of God. Therefore, at the intervention of our most beloved fellow bishop Anselm, bishop of Lucca, and likewise of Benedict, bishop of Belletrino, and Boniface, bishop of Albano, and Lord Humbert, bishop of the see of Saint Rufina, as well as Peter, bishop of Lavicanum, together with John, bishop of Porto, and also Lord Hildebrand, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, and our other faithful servants, by this document of our command we establish and confirm—as the authority of the sacred canons demonstrates and human laws prescribe, and as appears also to have been granted and confirmed to them by the emperor Otto Augustus and the other emperors by written command—that henceforth they shall not be dragged by any person, great or small, before secular courts for any controversy whatsoever, nor be examined or restrained before secular judges, except by their own bishop.

No one shall dare to make any invasion in their houses or presume to inflict harm upon them; and no tribute, tax, rent, or extraordinary levy shall be imposed upon or demanded from these priests and all the sacred orders by any person whatsoever. Nor shall anyone dare to interfere, without lawful judgment, with any of their household goods, with male or female slaves, with their dependents, or with all their peasants, nor with their movable or immovable property, fields, cultivated lands, vineyards, olive groves, woods, grazing meadows, or all their inheritances, whether acquired or otherwise, nor with their goods or anything that is seen justly and lawfully to belong to them.

Moreover, by this our apostolic privilege we grant to all priests, levites, and persons of every sacred order of the aforesaid bishopric that their advocate may swear, alone and without opposition, as is done in the Holy Roman Church. Let them be permitted to live quietly and peacefully according to their ecclesiastical ranks, to serve God, and to remain under the protection of this our privilege.

Thus shall we assist them, so that no duke, margrave, count, viscount, gastald, court official, collector, dean, *vocemissarius*, or any other person may dare to prohibit or constrain what has been established and confirmed by us. If anyone—for we do not believe this will happen—should oppose this our apostolic privilege with rash audacity, let him know that, unless he repents and makes good the damage he has caused, by the authority of Almighty God, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of ourselves, he is bound by the chain of anathema, excluded from the kingdom of God, and joined to Judas the betrayer. Moreover, let him be liable to pay ten pounds of the finest gold, half to our sacred palace and half to those who have suffered the injury.

Whoever, however, out of regard for this our apostolic decree proves its guardian and observer, may deserve to obtain from the Lord our God the grace of apostolic blessing and eternal life throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

Written by the hand of Gregory, notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of October and in the eleventh indiction.

Given at Rome by the hand of Humbert, bishop of the Holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the Holy Roman and Apostolic See, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Stephen IX, pope, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh indiction.

## III

Confirmation by Stephen X of the grants and other concessions of the sacred monastery of Saint Peter of Perugia. (Year 1057.)

*[Coquelines, Most Extensive Collection of the Bulls of the Roman Pontiffs I, 396.]*

[Col. 0872C]

**Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable monastery of blessed Peter the apostle, situated outside, or rather beside, the city of Perugia, in the place called Caprarius, and through it to Bonizo, its abbot, and to his successors who shall be lawfully and regularly promoted there, forever.**

Since the universal holy mother Church has been especially united, instructed, and enriched through the glorious princes of the earth—namely, Peter, the fisher of men, and Paul, the teacher of the nations—it is fitting that everything special found to belong to their jurisdiction and power should be confirmed and retained. Therefore, for the continual increase, never the diminution, of the honor of the monastery mentioned above, we grant this privilege of apostolic protection, so that it may retain what it possesses: namely, its cells and churches, its estates and parishes, its lands and farmsteads; specifically, the parish of Saint Constantius, Saint Rufinus, and Saint Martin; the church of Saint Martin at Agellione with its appurtenances; the estate of Casale; the estate of Saint Justin; the estate of Petronianus; the church of Saint Andrew of Aliano with its appurtenance; the church of Saint Mary at Pitiniano; the church of Saint Clement; half of Saint Donatus at Civitella; and the land of Hugh, nephew of Berno of Montenigro.

Moreover, we confirm to the same monastery forever three estates situated in the county of Perugia: one called Pusulo, another Filontio, and the third called Casalini, together with all their churches, houses, vineyards, fields, gardens, cultivated and uncultivated mountains, and all their appurtenances.

We also grant you permission to ordain all your clerics—both those living in the monastery and those residing outside on your possessions—through any suitable and canonically appointed bishop whom you choose, and to receive chrism in your parishes, provided that you have been unable to obtain or receive ordinations and chrism canonically and freely from the bishop in whose diocese your aforesaid monastery is situated. The same shall apply to the ordination of churches. No bishop shall dare to excommunicate or condemn anyone belonging to the same monastery if, in his case, he seeks the protection and judgment of ourselves and of the Holy Apostolic See.

The gift of the abbacy by the Roman pontiff, the abbot himself, and the consecration of the abbot shall remain in perpetuity. Whenever he is summoned to a synod by the supreme pontiff, he shall come without any excuse except a canonical one.

Furthermore, offerings given to the same monastery, both for the living and for the dead, shall be seized by none of the bishops, but shall be devoted in their entirety to the monastery’s benefit and the needs of the brothers. The tithes of the same monastery shall be allotted to the reception of guests and pilgrims at the monastery gate.

No one—not the emperor, king, margrave, or any other person—shall be permitted to demand from that monastery or from anything belonging to it the service commonly called *fodrum*, except our Apostolic See alone. Moreover, no one shall forbid the burial of the dead there.

If the bishop wishes to celebrate public Masses and stations there, he shall do so at the appointed times, namely on the Monday of Easter and on the solemn feasts of the births of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. But neither he nor any of his clergy shall take away any offerings from there against the will of the abbot and the brothers.

We establish that, whenever the abbot of the same monastery dies, no one shall be elected abbot there from among other persons, provided that they are able to choose a suitable brother from the congregation for this task—namely, by common and regular counsel, without payment, and to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff.

We further order that all charters harmful to the church of your monastery shall be entirely void and empty. In addition, by our apostolic authority we establish and confirm that no emperor, king, bishop, duke, margrave, count, viscount, castald, or any other person, great or small, shall dare to harass, dispossess, or disturb the aforesaid abbot and his canonically entering successors concerning the said monastery or any of its movable or immovable goods and properties.

Whoever presumes to do so shall know that, by the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of ourselves, he is condemned by anathema. Moreover, he shall be liable to pay twelve pounds of gold, half to our sacred palace and half to the monastery itself.

Whoever honors this church and, taking nothing away from it, gives something of his own to it for the redemption of his soul, may obtain the grace of blessing from the Lord God and deserve to be brought by the key-bearing prince into the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

Written by the hand of Gregory, notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of November and in the eleventh indiction.

Given at Rome on the fourth day before the Nones of November by the hand of Humbert, bishop of the Holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the Holy Roman and Apostolic See, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Stephen IX, pope, in the eleventh indiction.

## IV

Stephen X confirms the property of the canons of Arezzo at the request of Bishop Arnaldo. (Year 105.)

*[Ughelli, Sacred Italy I, 416.]*

[Col. 0874B]

**Stephen, servant of the servants of God.**

It is fitting for apostolic authority to assist those endowed with pious religion through benevolent compassion, and to grant the requests of those who ask with eager affection. Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of the Holy Church of God, both present and future, and to our own people, that we, at the intervention of Arnaldo, bishop of Arezzo, following the footsteps of our predecessor Victor, of most blessed memory, confirm and strengthen by our apostolic authority everything that has been justly given and lawfully bestowed upon the canons of the Church of Arezzo, whether by kings, by the prelates of the Church of Arezzo, or by any of the faithful of the Holy Church of God as a grant for the redemption of their souls.

If anyone thereafter wishes to confer any of his own property upon the same chapter of Blessed Donatus, bishop and martyr of Arezzo, whether in the county of Castello or in any other place, let him have, supported by our authority, the permission to give and to make a gift to Blessed Donatus for the use and expense of the canon brothers serving in the same chapter of Blessed Donatus, without prohibition by any person, great or small. Let that gift or donation remain forever free from every fiscal exaction.

Whoever proves to be a violator of this confirmation or donation of ours shall, excommunicated by our apostolic authority, be struck by the dart of perpetual anathema.

Written by the hand of Gregory, notary and chamberlain of the Holy Apostolic See, in the month of November, on the nineteenth day, in the second indiction.

Given at Rome on the tenth day before the Kalends of December by the hand of Humbert, the aforesaid bishop of the [Holy Church of] Silva Candida and librarian of the Holy Roman and Apostolic See, in the year 1057, by God’s favor, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Stephen IX, in the second indiction.

## V

Stephen X confirms, at the request of Bishop Pandulf, the boundaries and possessions of the bishopric of the Marsi, restored to its former condition by Victor II. (Year 1057.)

*[Ughelli, Sacred Italy I, 889.]*

[Col. 0875A]

**Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop Pandulf, and to all the bishops who shall canonically succeed in the Holy Church of the Marsi, forever.**

The more prominent we appear to be on the watchtower of the Holy and universal Church, which is still journeying as a pilgrim, the more vigorously we ought to respond to its vicissitudes. For just as the moon wanes and waxes in its monthly course, so the Church militant, subject to temporal conditions, continually suffers great declines and advances amid the disputes of worldly people. Just as it is necessary for us to sympathize with its decline or diminution, so without doubt it is fitting for us to rejoice in its progress or fullness.

Therefore, because the one Church of the Marsi had been miserably torn apart by an internal and long-standing evil, by more than civil discord among secular people, and divided by the man called Pope Theophylact into two bishoprics contrary to the canons of the holy Fathers—and afterward, with permission rather than consent, through necessity rather than advantage, had been left by our most holy predecessor Leo just as he found it—and because under our predecessor Victor, of blessed memory, it had, by the judgment of a general council, through divine grace been reunited within the bosom of the Constantinian basilica on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth indiction, that division of one diocese into two parts having been annulled and renounced and the diocese restored to the unity of its ancient condition, and because it was decreed forever, as was just, that the diocese should be one and belong to one bishop—therefore, with the intervention of the entire holy synod, Bishop Acto, who at that time unjustly occupied part of the diocese of the Marsi, having been transferred to the city of Chieti, by the decretal document of this privilege we henceforth grant and decree to you, most blessed brother and fellow bishop Pandulf, and to your successors forever, in accordance with what was synodally judged for you as stated above, the firm bishopric of the Marsi in all its integrity and appurtenances, among the properties specifically assigned to the Church of Saint Sabina of the ancient city of the Marsi, as an episcopal see.

We likewise grant the other churches of the entire diocese of the Marsi with their appurtenances, tithes, and offerings, both for the living and for the dead, according to the decrees of the sacred canons; likewise, the church of Our Lady, Saint Mary, the holy Virgin and Mother of God, at Carsoli, with its tithes and offerings, indeed with all the churches and properties adjoining it and justly belonging to you, both in the fortresses of Tuphus and Scallelli, as well as at [text uncertain], at Alto di Santa Maria, at Civitella, and at Pamperano as far as Capistrello and throughout the valley of Nerfacenda.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we decree that, whenever it is expedient, you may perform there the ordinations of clerics and the consecration of altars, and in the monasteries that are under your jurisdiction, as the sacred canons determine. You may also carry out without anyone’s opposition everything else that belongs to a bishop, namely within the proper boundaries of the entire parish of the Marsi, both that part which you formerly held and the other part which bishops had unjustly invaded from you.

Thus, supported by the authority of the Apostolic See, establishing indissolubly this privilege of power and confirmation, and invoking also the judgment of God, we forbid under threat of anathema that any successor of our pontiffs, any administrator of public affairs, or any other person, however great or small, should ever dare or presume to act against this privilege of our confirmation, or to alienate, remove, or diminish anything from it. Rather, it shall remain firm and stable forever, just as it has been granted and confirmed by us.

If anyone—which we do not desire—should presume by rash audacity to alienate or violate in any respect this statute of our Apostolic See, and should oppose it, let him, by the authority of the undivided Holy Trinity and of the prince of the apostles, be consigned to the bond of anathema, separated from the kingdom of God, and indissolubly joined to the devil and his angels, unless perhaps he repents.

Whoever, however, proves to be a respectful observer and defender of this concession and confirmation may, through the power of the holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary, of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, through the prayers of blessed Sabina the martyr and of all the saints, and through the multitude of the heavenly angels, deserve to receive glory and eternal life from the just Judge, our Lord Jesus Christ, throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

Written by the hand of the notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Apostolic See in the month of December, in the second indiction.

Given at Monte Cassino on the fifth day before the Ides of December by the hand of Humbert, bishop of the Holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the Holy Roman and Apostolic See, in the first year of Lord Pope Stephen IX, in the second indiction.

## VI

Constitution of Pope Stephen X for the monastery of Saint Prosper of Reggio. (Year 1057.)

*[Margarini, Cassinese Bulls II, 90.]*

**Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved and most reverend son Landulf, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Prosper, confessor of Christ, situated below the city of Reggio, and through him to all his successors who shall be regularly promoted there, forever.**

Just as we desire to be ruled, defended, and governed by the one from whom we come, so we do not doubt that, according to what is known to have been entrusted to us, the entire Christian world expects this from each of the stewards of the Churches of God, insofar as it is expedient for each. Therefore we ought to devote ourselves to this work with vigilance proportionate to the attention we give to the fact that, with God’s permission, the savagery of evildoers has at this time become fierce against the shepherds of the Lord’s sheep, with no one resisting.

### 1

Therefore, moved and instructed by your just and salutary petition, dearest son Landulf, abbot, for your benefit and that of your successors, by this document of our apostolic constitution we confirm and strengthen for the venerable monastery of Saint Prosper, bishop, that the election or ordination of the abbot of that monastery shall be carried out entirely according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

### 2

And because commands issued by the emperor Henry, of most blessed memory, and by his son Conrad, as well as by certain other kings, and a decree issued by Alberic, bishop of the aforesaid holy Church of Reggio, exist not only concerning the election of the abbots themselves but also concerning all things justly acquired by that monastery or to be acquired in the future, in accordance with the tenor of those documents and, what is more important, according to the standard of truth and justice, by this privilege of our authority we specifically grant and decree to the venerable monastery of Saint Prosper—which we receive under the protection of Saint Peter and ourselves—the estate of the aforesaid church of Saint Prosper situated in the city of Reggio, with its cemetery, and nine *jugera* of land with the chapel of Saint Nazarius, which the abbot who was then in office received by a properly executed exchange from the provost of the church of Saint Prosper situated within the fortress of the aforesaid city.

We also grant the whole territory of Corticella that was given to the monastery in that place by the bishops of the locality; twelve *mansi* at Fossolo; four at Palude; four at Campaniola; three at Quingente; one at Gurgo; one at Fossedunde; five at Baniolo; the chapel of Saint Mustiola with its appurtenances; one *mansus* at Old Crustulo; one in the village of Desbergato; one at Magno Casale, with the chapel of Saint Sylvester and the demesne of that same village of Magno Casale; three *mansi* at Reggio and the demesne of Reggio; the Braid of Reggio and all the land of the aforesaid monastery situated around that city; three *mansi* at Rodano; four at Lovari; one at Banio; one at the estate of Rodano; three at Marmirolo; one at Aliano; one at Bibiano; one at Piano; one at Mulazzano; one at Planzo; one in the fortress of Oleriano; and the estate of Nasseto with Lamma Fraularia, the field and the stream of Nasseto, which are known to have been given by the most pious king Charles to the Church of Reggio in writing, according to the boundaries designated there.

Also the land given by Roland, son of Eribert; at Mutilena, four *mansi* with a chapel and a certain part of the castle; at Albinea, four *mansi* and the chapel of Saint Mary at Pisignano, with the adjoining olive grove; at Vergnano, two *mansi*; and eight *mansi* given by Ardicio, son of Atto, son of Gandulf; the chapel of Saint Damian at Medola, which was given by Hubert; a vineyard with seven hills; the chapel of Saint Peter at Convanello with all its appurtenances; at Spetiano, one *mansus*; at Saint Florian, one; one on Mount Baranzone; a certain portion of the chapel of Saint Martin at Revere; four portions at Revere; two at the church of Saint Mary; one at Saint Florentin; one at Saint Lawrence; two *mansi* at Bibianello; and whatever it justly possesses within the kingdom of Italy, or, if it does not possess it, ought justly to possess.

Thus, both what we have listed above and whatever thereafter has been justly acquired through the devotion of any of the faithful, we decree by apostolic authority that the aforesaid monastery, which we perpetually receive under the protection of blessed Peter, shall possess forever without disturbance by anyone.

### 3

Also, out of reverence for the holy confessor and especially for the Lord, by the present authority we grant by apostolic privilege to you, dearest son Giselbert, abbot, and to your successors, and to those whom you or the brothers of the aforesaid monastery appoint to the priestly office, and we confirm by the charity which is God, through the power of the Holy Spirit and by the authority of blessed Peter, key-bearer of heaven, that when peoples from every direction come throughout the ages seeking the intercession of the most holy confessor, or when the inhabitants of that land come to the same church, you may, for the honor of God and of the most blessed confessor Prosper, devoutly celebrate solemn and public Masses over his sacred relics.

You may suitably nourish them with the bread of God’s word, and, strengthened by the merits of the aforementioned lord and great patron, the most blessed Prosper, and by our present authority, you may receive their devout confessions and grant them consolation for the expiation of their sins, supplying them with the assistance of your prayers and those of others, as well as of sermons, vigils, fasts, and almsgiving.

### 4

We also command that no bishop of the same city—not even any primate or metropolitan, nor any ecclesiastical or secular person, great or small—dare alter anything that we have specified above. Nor may anyone exercise any authority against your monastery, celebrate Mass there on any pretext, perform any ordination there, however insignificant, without the will of the abbot and the brothers, pronounce excommunication against them, or establish any office or burial of the dead, unless he wishes to be eternally condemned and struck by perpetual anathema.

### 5

If at any time anyone should appear who wishes to act against these provisions, let whatever he has presumed to attempt be considered void by the authority of blessed Peter, as we have stated above; and neither you nor your successors shall obey him.

### 6.

Moreover, concerning the election or ordination of an abbot—which is of the greatest importance for the salvation of the coenobites—we repeat this at the end, so that it may cling all the more firmly to the minds of those now living and of future generations, the more frequently it is impressed upon them for its particular and singular usefulness. Therefore, if anyone should presume, by any device whatsoever, to have a successor appointed to him through bribery or human favor, or should act in the election or ordination of an abbot otherwise than our most blessed Father Benedict established, let that election or ordination, by the authority of the holy Roman and apostolic see, be considered wholly invalid; and let its authors or intermediaries, unless they repent, be eternally condemned with the anathema *Maranatha*.

### 7.

Therefore, whoever rashly presumes to attempt to violate this privilege, let him know that he has been condemned by a strict anathema, unless, repenting, he should make worthy satisfaction.

### 8.

But whoever proves to be a faithful guardian shall be filled with divine blessings and, by the authority of the prince of the apostles, shall be absolved from all the bonds of his sins. Amen.

Written by the hand of Gregory, notary of the holy Roman and apostolic see, in the month of December, in the eleventh indiction.

[Col. 0879B] Given at the fortress of Cassino, by the hand of Humbert, bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the holy Roman Church.

## VII. Letter of Pope Stephen X to the Brothers of the Monastery of Cluny

*(Year 1058.)*

*[Bullar. Cluniac., 15.]*

Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to his most beloved sons, the monks of the monastery of Cluny.

Although, on account of the dignity of our see, we are debtors to all, nevertheless we have a special affection of charity for you, who, placed beneath the shelter of the holy and apostolic [Col. 0879C] see, have received from it the solace of protection and have offered the comfort of prayers. This you must always do, so that under its protection you may grow and produce fruit. We have charitably retained our most beloved son with us until the synod. But to you, just as we blessed you at the beginning, we bless you now; and, on God’s behalf and on behalf of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we absolve both the living and the dead.

## VIII. Privilege of Pope Stephen X by which he Confirms All the Monasteries, Properties, Rights, and Privileges Previously Granted to the Monastery of Cluny

*(Year 1058.)*

*[Bullar. Cluniac., 15.]*

Stephen, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend son Hugh, abbot of the venerable monastery which is called Cluny from the valley of Cluny, consecrated in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and situated in the county of Mâcon, and through you to all your successors, the abbots who shall regularly be appointed there, forever.

By God’s authority we stand as eminent watchmen in the watchtower of the holy and universal Church, in order that we may watch with greater care over the salvation and peace of all. Since we have obtained this office through the special privilege of the apostolic see, if we must tirelessly provide for everyone, how much more must we do so for those whom we know to pursue, under apostolic discipline, a stricter observance of the commandments of God, after the pattern of the primitive Church—those among whom all things are not merely held in common, but who also have one heart and one soul. Among their number the monastery of Cluny is by no means reckoned inferior. From the very beginning of its foundation until now it has sent forth, far and wide, the most brilliant radiance of holy conduct, so that, by practice and teaching, it has been and remains a model of holiness and a mirror for the monasteries of Gaul, Germany, Italy, and plainly for all monasteries of the Latin tongue.

Therefore, devoted with all our heart, as is fitting, to so praiseworthy a school of monastic philosophy and so well-ordered a battle line of the heavenly camps, in accordance with the tenor of your petition, dearest son and Abbot Hugh, by the authority of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, upon whose patronage the aforesaid monastery of Cluny rests, and through the inviolable strength of this our decretal page, we establish and confirm to you the monastery of Cluny—and through you to all your successors, as stated above, forever—all the places and monasteries lawfully belonging to that monastery of Cluny, whether granted to that place by any of Christ’s faithful, kings, bishops, dukes, or princes, or acquired by your predecessors, the abbots Berno, Odo, Eymard, Maiolus of blessed memory, and Saint Odilo, both movable and immovable property, as well as things that move themselves, so that you may possess them securely, peacefully, and without anyone’s opposition. Among these we have listed the following by name:
