First, the monastery of Cluny itself, founded by the once most powerful Duke William in the county of Mâcon, together with all the properties situated around it and in other regions that lawfully belong to it: in the county of Mâcon, a cell dedicated in honor of Saint Martin; also the church nearby dedicated in honor of Saint John; and the estates Cavinias, with a church; Solestriacum, an estate with a church; Escutiolas, with a church; Galliniacum, with a church; Rufiacum, with a church; Massilias, with a church; Clairmannum; Barjeseranum, an estate; Curtilias, an estate; Petronniacum; Arpajacum; Darboniacum; Besurniacum; the Church of Saint Columba; Vitreria, an estate in the Burgundian region; the Church of Saint Lawrence; the fortress of Lurdonum; Blanuscum; an estate called Cotta; also the monastery called Carus-Locus, with everything belonging to it; the cell called Regniacum, with everything belonging to it; the Church of Saint Victor, with all its appurtenances; and the churches and lands beside it, for which the Church of Saint Gengulf was formerly given; also the estate of Equiranda, with the Church of Saint Andrew the Apostle, together with the other churches and all its appurtenances; and all the churches and lands, or whatever the aforesaid place is shown to possess in the aforementioned county.

In the county of Chalon: the cell of Bellomonte, dedicated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, with everything belonging to it; also the Church of Campilocus, with all its appurtenances; likewise the estate called Juliacum, with the churches and lands formerly granted to that place by Bishop Manasses; and all the churches, lands, and whatever the aforesaid place is shown to possess in the said county; the Church of Saint Gengulf, with its appurtenances; the cell of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian; and the monastery of Saint Marcellus, with all its appurtenances.

In the diocese of Autun: the monastery in Aurea Vallis, called Parendus, consecrated in honor of Saint John the Baptist; also the cell of Oiadella, with all its appurtenances; and the estates, churches, and lands which the cleric Theotard gave to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny.

We also confirm and strengthen by our apostolic authority the agreement made by Lord Walter, bishop of the Church of Autun, concerning the monastery called Magabrense, belonging to his church, with everything belonging to it; and all the churches, lands, and whatever the aforesaid place of Cluny appears to possess in the said diocese.

In the territory of Dijon: the estate of Giuracum, with all its appurtenances.

In the county of Auxerre: a cell dedicated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, in the fortress of Dunziacum.

In the county of Auvergne: the monastery of Silviniacum, where Saint Maiolus and Saint Odilo rest, with everything belonging to that place; and the cell called Firmitas, with everything belonging to it; the cell called Scuriolas; also a church dedicated in honor of Saint Sulpicius in an estate called Langiacum; and the little cell called ad Boscum, consecrated in honor of Saint Peter; also the estate called Frigidus Mons; and the monastery called Rivis, consecrated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, with the estate of Lussiacum and all its appurtenances; the church called Marengum, together with the other lands given to that monastery by Eustorgius, a most noble man; also the nearby little cell consecrated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, called ad Montes; and the monastery of Celsinianum, with its cells, churches, estates, and lands—namely Carniacum, Burnunculum, Abolniacum, Ginniacum, and Cardonetum—and with all the churches and lands belonging to that monastery; also the cell where Saint Florus rests, which the cleric Eustorgius gave to the aforesaid place, with everything belonging to it; also residences in the town of Brioude; and the monastery called Volta, consecrated in honor of the Holy Cross, just as Saint Odilo, your predecessor, built it on his parents’ estate, with all its appurtenances; also the cell of Relliacum, with the estate and everything belonging to it; also the cell consecrated in honor of Saint Martina, called Ad Pontem; and all the churches and lands, and whatever Cluny appears to possess in the aforesaid county.

In the diocese of Nevers: the cell called Saint Reverianus, with all its appurtenances; also the church called Luperciacum, which Frotmund gave, with all its appurtenances.

In the county of Poitiers: the cell of Saint John in an estate called Mongon.

In the diocese of Saintes: the abbey of Saint John, which is called Engiriacum. We also grant you the abbey of Maillezais and confirm it by apostolic authority. In the abbey of Saint Cyprian, which is at Poitiers, we grant you what your predecessors possessed there.

In the diocese of Cahors: we confirm and commend to you by our apostolic authority the abbey of Saint Peter of Moissac, so that you may possess it in peace.

In the diocese of Viviers: the cell of Mizoscum, with everything pertaining to it; the cell of Rumpono Monte; the cell ad Fontes; and the cell of Riom, with everything that the aforesaid place of Cluny appears to possess in the said county or diocese.

In the diocese of Uzès: the monastery dedicated in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Saturninus, situated on the bank of the Rhône, with the fortress, the little cells, and the estate of Tulleta, together with everything belonging to it on both sides of the river.

In the diocese of Troyes: a cell consecrated in honor of Saint Amandus.

In the diocese of Orange: the cell at Podium Odoienum; and the monastery built in honor of Saint Pantaleon, with everything belonging to it.

In the diocese of Gap: the cell built in honor of Saint Andrew, granted to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny by the cleric Rigaud, with all its appurtenances; also the little monastery of Ganagobie; the estate of Valentiola; and everything that the aforesaid place of Cluny appears to possess, and for which it has a deed of donation and description, as well as the estate and fortress of Sarrianum, and everything it possesses in the land called Provence.

In the diocese of Valence: whatever the place of Cluny appears to possess in the estate called Ales; and on Mount Zion, the monastery of Saint Marcellus called ad Salcetum, with all its appurtenances; and everything that the same place appears to possess in that diocese.

In the diocese of Vienne: the monastery called Taderniacum, with the cell called Causella, the estate called Brocost, and the estate called Insula; also the cell in the fortress of Candiacum, with all the churches, estates, and lands that the said place appears to possess in that diocese.

In the diocese of Lyon: the monastery called Amberta; also the cell called Saluzatis; the cell of Polliacum; the little cell of Arthedunum; also the cell of Saviniacum and the estate of Ambariacum; the Church of Saint Andreolus; the church called ad Oratorium; the estate of Romanis; the cell of Cavariacum; the little cell of Luiniacum; the estate of Tusciacum; and all the estates and lands which Wichard, at his death, granted to that place of Cluny, together with everything the aforesaid place appears to possess in the said diocese; also the cell called Burgum, which Count Ansedus gave to God and Saint Peter for its brothers, with the approval of Burchard and Odo; also the cell consecrated in honor of Saint George and given to the aforesaid place of Cluny by Ainard, which is beside the fortress called Domena; and the cell called Portus, consecrated in honor of Saint Stephen, situated in the diocese of Besançon.

In the diocese of Toul: the cell called Ramengas.

We grant you the abbey of Vézelay, where Saint Mary Magdalene rests, to possess.

As for the monastery of Paternacum, granted to that place of Cluny by royal charters, with everything it appears to possess in Burgundy, and what the August emperors Otto granted to that monastery in Alsace, and the monastery called Romanum, with everything belonging to it, we grant that the aforesaid monastery of Cluny may possess them forever.

We also confirm and strengthen by our apostolic authority the agreement made by Lord Hugh, bishop of the Church of Geneva, concerning the Church of Saint Victor the Martyr, with everything belonging to it, with the approval and consent of King Rudolf and Lady Adelaide, the empress.

We grant you the abbey of Saux, with the consent and permission of our lord Henry, the August emperor, just as your predecessors possessed it.

And by the authority of our apostolic privilege, we grant to the aforesaid place of Cluny, and to you and your successors, all the aforesaid places and monasteries, with their cells, churches, estates, villages, little villages, male and female serfs, woods, vineyards, fields, meadows, waters and watercourses, and all cultivated and uncultivated lands belonging to the aforesaid jurisdictions, to be held and possessed forever, so that no duke, bishop, prince, or any person, great or small, may dare to trouble or disturb you concerning any of all the aforesaid properties and tithes that appear to belong there.

Moreover, under the testimony of divine judgment and the imposition of a strict anathema, we establish and decree that no bishop or any priest may presume to come to or enter this venerable monastery for any ordination, or for the consecration of an oratory or altar, or of priests or deacons, or for the celebration of Masses, unless he has been invited by the abbot of that place. Rather, let the monks of that place be permitted to receive whatever grade of ordination they wish, wherever and from whomever you and your successors may approve. Let the abbots also be elected from that congregation collectively, with the counsel of the God-fearing brothers, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict; and, for their consecration, let the brothers themselves summon whichever bishop they wish.

Nor may any bishop or archbishop in any way dare to excommunicate or judge that place or its monks. Rather, always remaining under the protection and immunity of the Roman see and subject solely to the judgment of the Roman pontiff, let them serve almighty God in security and peace.

They may also receive from whatever bishop they choose chrism, holy oil, and oil for the sick, ready for the consecrations to be carried out in that place.

We also grant and confirm by apostolic authority that you and that venerable place may, whenever and for as long as you wish, strike your own coinage or currency, just as we have learned was granted and confirmed to you by the privileges of our venerable predecessors.

Finally, through this privilege of our apostolic authority, we strengthen for you and your successors whatever you have hitherto possessed and acquired, and whatever you may thereafter legally and justly acquire by any means, forever.

But if anyone, with rash audacity and impious presumption against God and his holy apostles and against his own soul, should [the text is materially defective here]—pierced by the goad of our apostolic curse, stabbed by the weapon of our apostolic excommunication, and transfixed by the sword of our apostolic anathema—let him be restored to his former salvation only through worthy satisfaction.

Whoever, however, observes himself from this offense and approves that this privilege of ours remain inviolate, may he obtain blessing, grace, and every good thing from God, the giver of all good things, both in the present age and in the age to come.

Written by the hand of Gregory, notary and archivist of the sacred Lateran palace, in the month of March, in the eleventh indiction.

Given at Rome, in the Lateran palace, on the second day before the Nones of March, by the hand of Humbert, bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the holy Roman and apostolic see, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Stephen the Ninth, in the eleventh indiction.

## Around the Year of Our Lord 1059. Gozechinus the Schoolmaster

[Col. 0885]

### Notice Concerning Gozechinus the Schoolmaster and the Following Little Work

*(In Galland, Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. XIV, Prolegomena, p. VIII.)*

Gozechinus, a German by nationality, once taught letters at Liège. There he had among his pupils a certain Walcher, especially dear to him, to whom he writes the lengthy letter that we present from Mabillon’s *Analecta*. Mabillon himself suspects that Walcher was none other than Walter the Burgundian, about whom Adelmann writes in the *Rhythmus*. Walcher complained that Gozechinus had changed his chair and abandoned Liège; Gozechinus responds to him, but especially to his adversaries, by writing an apology for his action. After this he also proceeds to lament at greater length the evils of his time, which had arisen chiefly from depraved morals and the heresy of Berengar. He endeavors above all to show that someone may abandon those from whom he expects little or no advantage. He reveals himself to be a man not unlearned in letters, considering the conditions of that age. The letter was written shortly after the death of the Emperor Henry and of Archbishop Luitbold, who died in the year 1059.

[Col. 0885]

## Letter of Gozechinus the Schoolmaster to Walcher, Likewise a Schoolmaster and Formerly His Pupil

*(In Galland, Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. XIV, p. 230.)*

After an apology for having abandoned his teaching position at the chair of Liège and withdrawn to Mainz, he laments the evils of his time, arising especially from Berengar’s perverse doctrine.

[Col. 0885A] **I.** To his like-minded brother and son Walcher, brother Gozechinus wishes that he may happily co-exist in him who is Being itself.

When I recall the many acts of kindness that you have often displayed to me at my request, I both hold and return manifold thanks to you, dearest one—not only for the sweet, pleasant, and delightful remembrance of former times, but also for the cheerful presentation of this new gift. For you sent me the book I had requested, plainly the work of your fingers, in which you clearly show how highly you regard me and that you do not count as insignificant what you know I desire.

This book renews all the gifts of affection that you formerly bestowed upon me, as though, bringing them all back together with itself, it presented them to me anew. Therefore, when at last I saw the book that I had long awaited from you, when I received it into my hands, I recognized in it your fingers—or rather, you yourself—and I burned wholly with a new love for you, as though I had not previously known and loved you.

My spirit truly triumphs because I myself once guided your unformed fingers in writing, and because I struck your poorly shaped letters and other faults of that kind which tender youth commits upon your back, so that, thinking I was removing from our little tree an unnecessary shoot and an excess of leaves, I might afterward rejoice in its growth and fruit. For who plants a vineyard and does not receive some of its fruit? I have often reaped the sweet fruit of my labor in those whom God caused to grow after I had planted and watered them. Yet from none of them has such abundance flowed to me that the richer harvest of good fruit I always see smiling upon me from you.

**II.** Oh, that I had nurtured all the followers of both our schools as such people! Would that I could find among them even one such staff for my old age! But alas! In accordance with the divine oracle that the prophet utters in complaint, today one must nourish and raise children, while they—apart from very few—despise the one who raises them.

Let those who are of this kind beware lest, for their contempt of a father who gives good instruction, they be deprived by the Father of fathers of the testament of eternal inheritance.

**III.** But you, my dearest, do what you have begun: increase toward what is greater and better the good things you received from me, and never cease from your innumerable kindness toward me, for which you may receive an eternal inheritance from him who placed me over you.

In this you are doing nothing new or unusual if you show yourself so kind toward me. Even when you still wept beneath the schoolmaster’s rod, you served me with the same goodwill. Whereas fear alone was enough to extract from you, as from the others, whatever I wanted, you displayed this more than the rest through voluntary kindness, as could be expected in such a living creature. You depended entirely upon the nod of my mouth and would not permit any of my words to fall to the ground.

Since, while you were still a boy, I began to love you for this reason and also for certain other signs of virtue that even then stood out in you, as you grew older it came about that day by day I formed a more honorable hope concerning you. I observed your industrious power in penetrating obscure readings, your discernment and vigilance, and the sharpness of your lively intelligence in pursuing subtle subjects. Thus, while the other hearers of our catechetical instruction could not match the teacher’s words either in speech or in writing, you seemed to pour the whole teacher into yourself.

For this reason I used to glory with your brother and with the other friends with whom it was appropriate to do so, thinking that something special was being added to the little garden in which I planted: namely, that among adults you were a wise boy.

**IV.** But when, as an adult, I rejoiced to have you constantly with me because of your good morals and upright life, what was dearer or more lovable to me than you? Could anyone or anything intervene that would cause you to be less valued by me?

The constant presence of many things and people usually brings satiety. But your association with me, at home and abroad, brought you more deeply into my heart, so that each day you were regarded as dearer and newer. And rightly so. For you showed yourself so united with me in everything that you not only rejoiced in my success, but, whenever adversity shook our affairs, you endured it much more bitterly and with much greater indignation than I, whose concern it was.

Even then you showed how powerful you were in counsel: sometimes eagerly agreeing with our advances, sometimes bravely resisting our disadvantages, you often restored our affairs to a better state.

Whenever external business prevented me from taking leisure, you performed the duties of the absent teacher amid the discussions of our assistants in such a way that whenever something arose, whether confusedly entangled in reading or disputation, or in theological or sophistical matters, you yourself skillfully untied the tangled knots and satisfied every uncertainty according to our desire.

**V.** Since these things and many others of the same kind are so, can I, I ask, consign your probity, industry, kindness, and the other duties of a good and prudent life to oblivion, and not love you even if I wished not to? Just as formerly, when you were a boy, I embraced your outstanding natural gifts, so now I embrace with all my heart the mature ripeness of your aged youth.

Nothing grieves me more than that, deprived of the fruit of your sweetness, I seem to live in a kind of desert solitude. Not because I lack very frequent companions and dearest associates, but because among them there is no one—or hardly anyone—upon whom I may rest my head, and indeed my spirit, so gently.

Therefore, if it were lawful and reason permitted it, I would continually assail the ears of divine mercy with prayers, in case our voices might be admitted into the sanctuary of hearing, so that at last he might establish us in a place where we could still enjoy, as before, the kindness of you and of the others with whom I grew up or whom I nurtured, a kindness whose pleasant enjoyment I experienced when the opportunity was available, and where I might glory in your company as in former times.

**VI.** For although the golden head of the kingdom—namely, noble Mainz—sprinkles me generously with the honeyed streams of its abundance, with which it flows forth on every side, and places my curule chair in no lowly position within the splendidest crown of its sacred senate, nevertheless, if I may say so with its permission, that corner smiles upon me above all others which Mother Liège, strong and knotty with the power of virtue, displays to her natives as delightful and pleasant.

For, as you know, on its western side it rises gently, not beneath the sloping sides of hills subjected to it, and, situated softly between the two bends of the public mountain—which, upon a ridge not excessively bold, bears four flocks of the regular life—this city, I say, gathers, cherishes, and nourishes her children beneath her wings, just as a hen does her chicks. She forms and instructs them in everything civil and conducive to good morals, and allows nothing to be lacking that can either govern abundance or moderate want.

The two-horned Meuse also glides and washes toward the defense of the place and the reinforcement of its abundance, a river not unjustly preferred to the rivers of our Belgium. It flows generously, rich in fish not only for the citizens but also for the natives of the land, suitable for the varied transport of merchandise, and useful for every kind of convenience.

Except that—if you will pardon me for playing satirically, though without meter—whenever it is summoned into the banquet of the gods with its cloud-bearing river brothers, with King Aeolus and his winds, within Juno’s palace, and, exhausted by long labors, returns intoxicated after Aeolus has poured out his drink more abundantly than usual, bringing snow or rain, then, having gathered together the river waters that flow into it, as though it had assembled an army, it rages throughout the surrounding region in a flood of swirling water. It tramples and ravages whatever lies in its path; it prevents and punishes the nocturnal thefts of fishermen, of which it has often complained that they escaped them with impunity; and it washes away and lays flat the crops that greedy farmers had sown in the green meadows of the bank, violating with a bold furrow the place where it wished to rest at midday.

It too, indignant that we had settled too near the courts of its watery palace and that our servants often disturbed it, enters our homes not as a suppliant. Having expelled everyone and asked no permission, it lodges there by force. And because we pray more frequently and familiarly to the hostile divinity, it excludes our household god, tortured, from the hearth; and, washing away and extinguishing every remnant of the divinity it hates—even ash and cinder—at last, when our patience is scarcely satisfied, and because we cannot resist it, it returns, finally appeased, to its channel, leaving its traces all too bare, and withdraws into its own palace.

Our suburbs also have, on every side, sweet-smelling gardens of vegetables and groves of trees glowing with lovely red. Turning its arms toward regions more suited to vineyards than ours, it has put the finishing touch upon them by pruning the highest shoots of the vines and scattering a few branches.

Our Liège, richly endowed with these and many other advantages, nevertheless possesses things much more important than these and far surpassing them. In short, itself the flower of threefold Gaul and another Athens, it flourishes nobly in the study of the liberal disciplines and—what is more excellent than these—prospers wonderfully in the observance of divine religion. So much so that, if I may say so without offending the churches, as far as the study of letters is concerned, you need seek nothing from Plato’s Academy; while as far as religious worship is concerned, you need desire nothing from Leo’s Rome.

**VII.** From there, therefore, scattering the good fragrance of Christ in every direction, it attracts and receives a very great multitude flocking together to it. No one has yet attached himself to it without making progress toward what is better, unless he has himself been excessively asleep.

Since our Liège is of such a character, whoever disparages it, whoever does not love what is known about it—if I may speak crudely—let him have the hatred of God.

This is why, dearest one, I rush there with continual prayers; and although I live elsewhere, in spirit I dwell there with you.

**VIII.** But perhaps you accuse me of fickleness, as though I were seeking a place in which to live well—or rather to take my ease and glory, which is certainly the behavior of a vain mind. You rebuke me sharply because, as though moved by desire, I praise so greatly the location, pleasantness, abundance, and wisdom of our Liège, to which I once preferred the glory of Mainz and gave a letter of repudiation; and because I am carried along by such instability of spirit that, when situated at Liège, I sigh for Mainz, while, planted at Mainz, I return in spirit to Liège.

You also summon Flaccus to your defense, so that the sore which you seem to cut may be rubbed with satirical salt all the more harshly:

> “They change their sky, not their mind, who cross the sea.”

Likewise:

> “The fault lies in the mind, which never escapes itself.”

I know, dearest one, that you are plotting nothing hostile against me, nor have I therefore set you against me in resistance. But I know those dogs who, always ready with a secret bite, gnaw at another’s life by criticizing it, while rolling their own lives, wrapped in disgrace, in the mud of their vices.

I set these men against myself when they disparage me behind my back under your identity, as though resisting me face to face. Under your name—of you, concerning whom I suspect nothing hostile—I prepare to answer them, so that, once the clever abuse of the quibblers has burst apart, whatever the bow of envy has ever shot at me concerning these matters may be dissolved, and whatever the serpent’s hiss of hatred has more bitterly mocked in me may be weakened.

There is, however, one word—and one word for everything—which you must always remember throughout all the little gardens of this volume: whatever has been said in this seeming conflict with elegance, wit, and affection, apply to yourself; but whatever has been sprinkled in harshness, bitterness, and biting sarcasm, attribute to the opposing party of detractors.

**IX.** I see, brother—I see whoever you are whom I have set against myself under the guise of a friend, whom I have made speak in opposition under the stage-setting of an imagined advocate. I see, I say, that you attack me with a two-edged sword and engage me with a double weapon: with one, prepared to accuse me of the fickleness of a light-minded spirit; with the other, stirred to stab my persistence in vices.

It must therefore be examined more attentively, since you use against me the subtle scales of the critics, what answer it is appropriate to make to each of the objections.

You accuse me, then, of the fickleness of a vain spirit, as though, drifting here and there, I desired to take my ease and glory because I have praised our Liège so highly and said that I was happy to live there with my dependents. You seem to regard this as an injustice and as something unworthy of a fair and good man; rather, you contend that I polish our advantages with the sidelong eye of envy and poison them with the cynical bite of detraction.

Do you really charge it to fickleness if someone gathers the principles of a better life from different places and times, as though from varied studies of letters and experience of the disciplines, and packs away the clarified honey of knowledge? Do you consider it vanity to wish to advance toward what is better?

Are not health-giving waters and herbs sought from different places—things which by their own power can heal whatever is diseased? Are there not twelve hours in the day? Is it not arranged in an orderly fashion what must be done in the morning, in the hours before noon, in the afternoon hours, and in the evening?

But now, alas, the morning, in which there was joy, has passed, and the evening, in which weeping will remain, has arrived. The Lord has now made rivers into a desert and springs of water into thirst, fertile land into saltiness, and so forth.

And what is to be done for the rest in this cesspit of affairs, where morals and times so greatly resist all the studies and disciplines that have flowed down to us from the Fathers?

Is one therefore, as you foolishly suppose, to desist from good things and devote oneself to fairs, so that, forgetting what is fitting and what is not, we become the vicious crew of the Ithacan Ulysses’ oarsmen?

Is it not rather necessary that anyone who will truly become a man, while always avoiding what is worse, should pursue that by which he may always become better than himself?

Indeed, these things are so far from being the behavior of a vain spirit that they are rather the behavior of a spirit which vigilantly keeps watch in the morning at the doors of the gate of wisdom. To think or say this of a brother is the work of malignant envy and hatred.

### X [Cols. 0891A–0891B]

But when, pressing me with a hostile weapon, you say, “What have I to do with Leogius?”—as though I once insolently abandoned him and branded him with a disgraceful epithet, and, preferring the glory of Mainz, regarded him as worthless refuse—you have certainly strayed too far from the path of truth, or rather, you have fallen wholly away from truth.

Tell me, I ask: you who bark like a wolf beneath a sheep’s fleece, which of two is preferred—the one who asks, or the one who is asked? Why do you hesitate to answer? Do you suppose that I have set a snare for you? So you are silent? You concede plainly enough that the one whom it is clear the other asked for is preferred.

Say, then, did I inflict an epithet—that is, an insult—upon Legia, when she chose that a man richer than herself should petition her on my behalf? Or was Legia exalted when, whether invited or commanded by the foremost men of that golden age, I came to Mainz? Did I reject Legia as a mother? Did I insolently despise her, whom, clasped as a mother in the embraces of affection, I never abandoned? Certainly not, as you croak. I did not give her a bill of repudiation, but the adornment of a triumphal dance; not the mark of disgrace, but a crown of honor. This was when her heart poured forth through my mouth a good word; when I placed in the treasuries of this abundance what I had received in the treasuries of her wisdom.

Nor will you ever escape this point, even if you were another Proteus, until, overcome by the truth, you admit that a change of place does no harm when it is made with due regard to circumstances, provided that nothing is changed in the good purpose; and that a wise person ought to measure every manner of life according to place and time, rather than, in the manner of frivolous Diogenes, hold everything in common.

### XI [Cols. 0891B–0891C]

As for the fact that you use your Flaccus against me as a mark of vice—whether that passage is poetic or philosophical—it sufficiently constructs the argument of its author in support of what he undertook to establish, though it is not as necessary for his proposed conclusion as he presented it. For those who travel across the sea can change their soul as well as their climate: for example, if some ignorant and foolish person should go or sail to Athens and, there sprinkled with the salt of learning, exchange folly for wisdom.

The passage that follows, where he is silent about changing place or climate and rebukes the soul, is more relevant to the argument: place neither helps nor harms a good life, except according to the definite rationale of such changes. Indeed, the soul that never escapes from the condition in which it lies amid corruption and the mire of vices, and does not flee back to itself by the narrow path of moral discipline, so as to become what it can be in the school of virtues, deserves severe blame.

But it is not now our leisure or task to pursue more elaborately what may be extracted from these arguments. For the moment, if you please, let us leave this to those whose whole bent and whole method consist in spending all their leisure and effort in disputing with shameless chatter and sophistical quibbles, whether in learning or in speaking.

### XII [Cols. 0891D–0892A]

We have, however, arguments older than these that bear upon the question and prove that neither one’s fatherland nor any particular place contributes or takes anything away from a wise person’s living well; rather, virtue itself is everywhere sufficient for a good and blessed life.

Thus Teucer, forbidden by his father to return, when his father rejected him from Salamis, was asked by his companions—who were sighing for their homeland—where he wished to live. “Everyone’s fatherland,” he replied, “is wherever he is well.”

I do not see what sharper statement could be made concerning the manner of life under discussion, if “being well” is understood in its proper sense.

Socrates, likewise, when asked what citizenship he acknowledged, replied that he was a citizen of the world—that is, not an inhabitant and citizen of one particular place, but of the whole world. By this saying he indicated that, wherever he might be, he would remain the same, changing nothing in his purpose of virtue, and that he shared a common citizenship of life with all who used reason throughout the world.

The most distinguished philosophers also, as we read in the monuments of antiquity—Xenocrates, Crantor, Chrysippus, Aristotle, Carneades, Panaetius, and countless others—chose no fixed place of residence for living well. Once they had set out to investigate wisdom, which flees throughout the whole world, they never returned home.

Such is the life of the perfect and consummate wise person: wherever circumstances may carry him, no place turns him aside from the gravity of constancy or the strictness of his purpose—not even the bull of Phalaris or the executioner’s blade. For him the whole world is one place in which to live well and happily.

But why all this? Clearly, so that the accuser may be refuted and may see that either remaining in a place or changing it does no harm to the wise person, whose purpose is to be the same everywhere in the constancy of virtue.

### XIII [Cols. 0892B–0892C]

But what have these foreign examples to do with us? The apostles, whom the one who made the world chose out of the world, were first instructed under the heavenly Teacher in the school of truth, by hearing his living voice. Then, sent forth like rays of the true Sun to illuminate, and scattered like the salt of the earth to cleanse and season, they claimed for themselves neither a homeland nor a place, neither a field nor a house, nor anything belonging to the world.

Instead, for the salvation of souls they first expended the hardest labor of preaching, amid cold, hunger, and empty dangers; then, following the example of the Teacher, they laid down their lives for their brothers, in a love greater than which no one has.

All that blessed posterity which descended from this spiritual generation of the Fathers—the people of God’s possession, adopted through the covenant of Christ’s blood into the dignity of Israel and succeeding, by the Lord’s choice, to become an elect race and a royal priesthood—all these, I say, entered the same way of life, though under varying distinctions of rank and office. Since they were in a foreign land, they labored not for what was their own but for what belonged to others; since they had no enduring city here, they sought the one that was to come.

Therefore, happily transferred into the true promised land of the children of Israel by him who, ascending, led captivity captive, they became there fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household.

### XIV [Cols. 0892D–0893C]

Nor should you think that I, overwhelmed either by the blindness of ignorance or the darkness of forgetfulness, am passing over the ordered ranks of the Christian army, or arrogantly inflicting injury upon them with the insolence of a wandering freedom. These ranks, evidently, seem to keep watch for those entering the new Jerusalem, protecting both themselves and the weaker members of the Church with the armor of God; and they are forbidden to change, by migration, the rule of regular life or the station of military watchfulness.

For we know that the divine decrees of the Fathers have provided that no one should migrate elsewhere except for a sound reason, and that no one should entice away another church’s cleric. Nevertheless, we also know that it has freely been permitted that, if a church in various functions of rank and office is insufficiently supplied, it should not be denied what it requests from another church where such an abundance exists.

By ranks I mean, for example, if one church asks another to provide an ordained bishop or presbyter. By offices I mean, for example, if it asks that a regular superior or a teacher of letters be appointed for it.

We also know that within these same flocks of spiritual life there are some for whom the blessed leisure of contemplative sweetness lies open, while others are charged with the evangelical work of active administration in winning souls. Some have become the wheels, some the bars, and some the bearers who carry the ark of the New Testament until they establish it in eternal life, to the praise and glory of almighty God.

This is the distinction of ranks and offices, and the splendor of the good works accomplished in them, which the prophet saw in the adornment of the queen: she stands at the right hand of the royal Bridegroom in a golden garment, shining amid manifold variety.

The same prophet contemplated this distinction in an allegory when, amazed at the Lord’s wondrous name throughout the earth because his majesty had been exalted above the heavens, he marveled at the son of man, made a little lower than the angels and, because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor in the presence of the Father. “You have subjected all things beneath his feet,” he says: “sheep, oxen, the beasts of the field, the birds of the air, and the fish of the sea.”

O blessed man who saw such things! Blessed also is the Church of the saints, concerning which, to which, and within which he foresaw such things!

There he saw beneath Christ’s feet the gentle birds of heaven distinguished from those that devour the gentler birds in the air with the hooked beak of avarice and the curved talon of rapacity; and also from those that swim in the waters for the purpose of plunging into the depths of desire and feeding the gaping maw of avarice by the predatory capture of wretched fish.

From these, I say, those gentle birds of heaven are distinguished—those clothed in the variegated feathers of good works, possessing also the wings of virtues and the double wings of charity, flying like doves to their windows.

There too are the stars of heaven that Abraham received in the promise: “I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea.” These stars shine in heaven with the brightest purity of life, radiant in the Church’s words and glowing in its examples.

### XV [Cols. 0893D–0894B]

But what have we to do with birds? What have we to do with the stars of heaven? We are wretched fish of the sea; we are the sand of the sea, crushed by the waves of the world like sand; we are carried about like wandering fish by the surges of worldly uncertainty.

What comparison is there between us and the pious birds of heaven? What comparison between us and the shining stars? Certainly the comparison is that of nothing with something—if, indeed, such a comparison can be called a comparison.

Would that we might rest in some spiritual hollow, far from storms! Would that we might hide beneath some concealed part of a living rock, where the winds of fortune could not exert their strength or make us their plaything!

I would choose and desire Legia for myself as this hollow of rest and hiding place in a living rock, were it not that you rub my frivolity with so harsh a salt from your Flaccus.

I would choose, I say, Legia, the nurse of studies, certainly a fountain of refined intellects and a place fruitful in divine wisdom—a city marked out by the finger of God with manifold grace, and one that, by God’s gift, has always produced men like itself.

But what have I said? As though it needed my praise and did not already stand out sufficiently by itself! It does not need to be shaded by anyone’s praise or painted by anyone’s speech into an imaginary likeness of a blessed city, because it is truly a living city and a blessed place, alive through the institutions and laws of divine religion.

Since, then, the narrow head of our mother and nurse shines whiter than snow with the revered cradles of ancient wisdom; since she wears upon her worn brow a splendid diadem of divine religion; since she also gleams in golden-covered robes of illustrious deeds and is wholly desirable, clothed on every side with the varied adornments of virtues—would you be of sound mind if you advised me not to seek the shelter of her wings? That would amount to urging me to hate her.

Is it so that you alone may possess her and alone enjoy the common advantages and joys? But may this be far from your modesty and integrity; may my soul, which has known you for so long, never believe this of you.

Indeed, I am so far from hating her that, even if she forbade it, I would nevertheless be directed toward her with the greatest intensity.

### XVI [Cols. 0894B–0894D]

I do not say this as though the fertile settlement that I inhabit did not offer me the entrails of a father and the breasts of a mother. Rather, I am playing with you, or expressing what I would wish, if God’s grace allowed it without prejudice to honor.

Nor should you count it as a vice in me that among distinguished men, when circumstances demanded it, such a thing is known not to have been unusual. Antiquity is full of examples, and the novelty of the modern age is full of them as well, showing how many illustrious men changed their places for a sound reason; how they avoided not the places themselves but whatever in them was harmful to their morals; or how, in order to benefit many people’s salvation, they migrated elsewhere.

Abraham and his patriarchal sons would not have changed places so often, nor dug so many wells in search of living water, if they had found in one place all the goods suited to their life.

Jacob too, no less a prophet than a patriarch, would never have gone down with his seventy souls—seventy being a mystical number—to Egypt, first into its abundance and afterward into slavery, unless he had been fleeing a dog-like famine.

Joseph too, twice sold by his envious brothers, changed places to good effect and, in a time of distress, benefited many by preserving their lives. This man, first instructed by the rod of temptation and refined to purity in the furnace of tribulations, grew into the ruler of Egypt from the very condition in which he had subjected his patient back to burdens and his obedient hands to servitude in the basket.

### XVII [Cols. 0894D–0895A]

I could bring forward countless examples of this kind, if I thought that these, offered as correction to you, would suffice.

Let your Flaccus, then, together with his climate and soul, be answered more chastely from these examples than his own copiousness suggests, so that henceforth he may not attack anyone’s purpose so recklessly.

Take your Flaccus, therefore, together with his climate, from your hands, and take up my Psalter. If you do not wish to do so, love and keep him alone, without a rival. Yet the invincible light of reason seems sufficiently to have proved above that, wherever you are, there is a place for living well, provided that your spirit does not fail you; even a horse is healthful [the transmitted reading *equus* is uncertain].

### XVIII [Cols. 0895A–0895B]

Nevertheless, though one may seek a place for living well by wandering and leisure, the rule of reason expels headless vipers from the sanctuary of the wise; yet it matters greatly with whom you associate.

Do you not remember what divine oracle was spoken to the suffering prophet? “Son of man,” it says, “you dwell among unbelievers and perverse people, and you live with scorpions.”

Are you unaware of the characteristic malice of scorpions? They do not bite with their teeth, infect with their tongues, or poison with their mouths; they harm only with their tails.

The Psalmist marked such scorpions when he said: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I pursued.” Likewise: “Those who speak peace with their neighbor,” and so forth. How greatly he himself and all holy men have always detested such people, he makes clear by adding: “Give them according to their works,” and the other words that follow.

### XIX [Cols. 0895B–0895D]

Here again, pressing me obstinately, you add: “Does that same oracle command the same prophet to change place or spirit by fleeing, rather than to resist perverse people and neutralize the venom of the scorpions even unto blood?”

Did not that same prophet endure bonds, hunger, a muddy pit, and many other things of that kind, which the perversity of the malicious has always inflicted upon the pious from the beginning?

Certainly, brother, it is so. Yet it is always beyond the strength even of men of exceptional virtue to remain perpetually on active duty, never to release the spirit to the sweetness of divine contemplation; to be continually struck by tumultuous assaults and never to be cherished by the repose of inward sweetness.

Now again you arm yourself with the saying of that ancient Musonius as with a hostile weapon, saying, “To relax the spirit is to lose it”; and you fortify yourself with the shield of our Christian theologian:

> “There are never wars or dangers lacking for the good.”

To this I reply: To dissolve the spirit into delights and pleasures, and, setting aside those things that work for and protect the soul’s salvation, to release it into earthly desires—this truly is to lose it.

But if the spirit, as far as a human being has leisure, takes a holiday from secular tumult; if, rising to the heights, it passes beyond the clouds of cares, the winds and rains of slanderous tongues, and the storms and whirlwinds of false brothers; and if, released from the strict severity of military discipline, it wholly dissolves into that most peaceful and luminous repose of divine contemplation—then it is not truly lost, but rather preserved, or, more importantly, seems at last to live.

As for what our theologian says, that a Christian must always be fighting, I have nothing from which I would dare or be able to dissent. Nevertheless, while preserving the constancy of virtue, we may say that there is more than enough labor if, while wars and seditions cease outwardly among false brothers, our efforts inwardly contend with all their strength against the temptations of the ancient enemy, until, having overcome and defeated these by the armor of God, we receive, through Christ’s gift, the rest of perpetual peace.

### XX [Cols. 0896A–0896D]

Still more obstinately pressing the matter, you say that Augustine, Ambrose, Athanasius, and countless other Fathers of renowned reputation always labored in the camps of the Christian army with both kinds of warfare: outwardly against the apostles and disciples of Satan, and inwardly against spiritual wickedness, fighting bravely to the crown of victory.

I agree, brother, with what you argue both truly and carefully. Yet you do not seem to me entirely correct in confining the whole Church of the elect to this one kind of warfare.

For if you gather the annals from calendars and chronicles—or, indeed, from the authentic monuments of Scripture concerning those who served God—you will certainly find that God was pleased by both theoretical and practical virtues, that is, by both the contemplative and the active.

To touch briefly upon a few examples in support of the faith, consider under the shadow of the Law Joshua, Gideon, David, and the crown of the Maccabees; then Moses and Aaron, Elijah and Elisha, and the choir of the prophets.

In sum, note what Paul says about these same ancient Fathers: “The saints,” he says, “through faith conquered kingdoms,” and so forth, down to “they went about in *melotes* [sheepskins], wandering in deserts.” Finally, after listing them all, he concludes: “And all these, having been approved by the testimony of faith, were found faithful.”

If you apply careful consideration to these and similar examples, you will certainly see that the patriarchs were most energetically occupied with practical affairs, while the prophets enjoyed serene leisure in contemplative repose.

How otherwise could the former defend the salvation of their people with strong hands, or the latter behold blessed visions with the tranquil eye of the mind?

I do not say this as though there were not many in each order who pursued both purposes; nevertheless, this general distinction is assigned to the two orders.

When the night of the Old Testament had passed—during whose firmament the Fathers mentioned above shone like brilliant stars—and the day that the Lord made had dawned, with Christ Jesus, the Sun of Justice, risen, observe Bar-Jonah Peter and Paul, the vessel of election, standing in the battle line until the crown of martyrdom.

John, however, the theologian of angelic virginity, and Luke, fellow servant of the Gospel, followed another course. The former first fought bravely against the beast Domitian and other antichrists; then, when the fury of those beasts had been calmed, he devoted himself to the leisure of theology, dipping the pen of the Gospel into the very mystery of divinity, and grew old in peace.

Luke, meanwhile, first labored throughout the world with the peripatetic Paul and the other heralds of the Gospel; then, withdrawing into the leisure of theology and weaving the sacred history of the incarnate Word, he fell asleep in peace with a blessed end.

Next observe the Augustines and Ambroses whom you mentioned: as you rightly assert, they remained happily in the battle line under both forms of warfare.

Conversely, consider Paul, Antony, and countless others crucified with Christ, who lived almost entirely at leisure from the outward storm; with the grace of Christ assisting them, they also cast behind them the struggles of inward warfare and now reign with him as though in heaven, the one who said: “Our citizenship is in heaven.”

### XXI [Col. 0897A]

Nor were only theologians illuminated by the brilliance of evangelical light. Many earlier philosophers and heroes, wrapped in pagan darkness before the Sun of Justice had risen, exercised their lives with the greatest diligence in their own conception of what was honorable and useful, through both active and contemplative virtues, which they attained partly by nature’s gift and partly through study of the liberal disciplines.

Some of them, bound to military service or having completed public administrations, established a lasting and celebrated name for themselves—so it was thought—by acting seriously at home and abroad and fighting bravely by land and sea.

Others, either granted noble leisure after labors honorably completed, or withdrawing into the leisure they had chosen because of their hatred of worldly affairs, served both themselves and the commonwealth by writing or disputing.

### XXII [Col. 0897B]

And if, argumentative as you are, you continue to resist what has already been said with still greater combativeness, Truth itself will come to our aid, surrounded by supporting sentences, and will not cease to defend its own cause.

To make our assertion more truthful and more firmly attested, it will bring forward for the defense of the faith persons drawn from the counsel of both Testaments: from one, Rachel and Leah; from the other, Martha and Mary.

But why all this? Clearly, so that you may plainly understand, as was stated above, that God has always been pleased with his elect through both contemplative and active virtues, and that neither side has ever prejudiced the other.

For just as God accepts what is laboriously accomplished in active practice, so what is contemplatively observed in sabbath rest at its proper time is not excluded from his good pleasure.

### XXIII [Cols. 0897C–0897D]

Good heavens, brother, how knotty you are, how mushroom-headed, and how completely you cover yourself!

I had already thought that you had stopped, and that, pressed either by the authority of the speaker or, rather, by the weight of his words, you had surrendered to truth.

And behold, again you sound the trumpet; again you make a din for arms; again, under the pretext of defense, you attack the spirit that so greatly embraces leisure and repose. You threaten to drag into the light, from the lair it cherishes and with its skin stripped away, the laziness and dullness that cloak themselves in the mantle of theory.

You return to the prophet mentioned above, saying that he applied himself all the more earnestly and fiercely to correcting the perverse and neutralizing the venom of the scorpions in proportion as he saw them more furiously roused to resist and tear him apart.

You also add Flaccus’s spur to the one who lingers—the spur by which he, adorned with the satirical commentary of his Damasippus, attacks idleness, saying:

> “You seek to appease envy after abandoning virtue.”

### XXIV [Col. 0897D]

You propose, wretched man—or at least seem to propose—despising that most powerful consolation of constancy which the vessel of election and the most steadfast mind revealed under the hand of the primitive persecution against the elect, saying:

> “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution.”

And:

> “No one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully.”

You also offer the combatant the shield of divine protection, with which the Lord, strengthening his servant against bitter enemies in the prophet, says:

> “Do not fear their faces, for I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord.”

### XXV [Cols. 0898A–0898D]

I admit, dearest brother, that what you bring forward from the coarse wit of the satirist Damasippus is true, where poetic fiction contains a philosophical argument; and what you produce from the divine oracle is also true, where the truth of the argument appears clearly, without the cloud of fiction.

They are true, I say, and entirely suitable, but not entirely effective for persuasion when the spirit, with irrevocable resolve, chooses a different purpose.

You learned from Cicero’s teaching the duty and end of an orator: the duty is to speak suitably for persuasion; the end is to persuade by speech.

You therefore fulfill one of these excellently, since you speak suitably for persuasion; but not the other, because, when you are unable to persuade by speech, you fall short of the end.

You know that the duty is valued, if it does not attain its end—that is, its effect—as much as sowing is valued when it never reaches harvest.

Therefore, by speaking appropriately about labor, you perform your duty correctly; but because you cannot persuade one who chooses rest and leisure, as stated above, you fall short of the end.

Who today would not prefer leisure to business, when, if labor falls fruitlessly, or if you cease working, it is worth the same? Who would not refrain from labor where, even when the agreed-upon denarius is withheld, the one who labors receives the least while the one who rests receives the most—provided, of course, that he uses leisure well?

Who, unless out of his mind, would continue sowing upon thorns in such a season, where the bad soil, bristling with the thistles of innate perversity, rejects the life-giving hand of the cultivator and refuses to receive the good seed of the word?

Blessed indeed is the earth in which the word of God is sown through the word of a human being, which, watered and drenched by the heavenly clouds of its teachers, yields a hundredfold harvest for the storehouses of the Lord its God.

Conversely, that iron land fittingly has a bronze sky: having received the seed without being made fruitful by a germinating shoot, whatever thorns and weeds it produces is, at harvest time, bound into bundles and thrown into the eternal fire.

Finally, the householder rightly becomes angry with the cultivators of such land and such a vineyard when it does not respond, and through the prophet threatens them, saying:

> “It shall not be pruned, nor dug; and I will command the clouds not to rain upon it.”

By this word, he separates those whom, according to the purpose of predestination, he foresaw as destined for condemnation from those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.

Hence also, as I think, the Lawgiver and Lord of the prophets speaks in his Gospel, upon which the whole Law and the prophets depend:

> “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine.”

By this saying he separated those who were to be condemned from those who were to be saved, lest the pious labor of the one who preaches be poured out uselessly upon the deaf.

### XXVI [Cols. 0898D–0899C]

At last, dearest brother, you admit, as I think, that at such a time I desired leisure for myself, for you, and for all the pious—not without reason and not idly. For business neither corresponds to what is honorable or useful, nor, certainly—which is more important than either—to salvation.

Therefore, overcome, as I think, by the truth and led on by the allurements of repose, you yield to our settlement. If you are wise, do not henceforth insinuate a complaint against leisure’s defender as its enemy.

So that you may fully understand what is chiefly at issue in this volume: I seek leisure that is desirable for me, since I have served long, long beyond the limit of legitimate release and have completed the term of my service.

For you, however, though you are still vigorous and green, and for all the pious, I seek the same thing because I fear—or at least see—that by laboring you are uselessly turning the wheel of your birth.

Why uselessly? This has been expressed sufficiently above; to repeat it in a chastened disputation would be superfluous.

You also know that, by command of the Law, Levites are ordered to minister from the age of twenty-five years and upward, but from the age of fifty—which is both the Jubilee and a number especially celebrated for mystical sacraments—to be custodians of the vessels.

According to the laws of military sanctions, recruits are enrolled for service at an earlier age; nevertheless, they too have the same limit of legitimate release.

The chair of scholarly teaching likewise has, in accordance with the limit of military discipline, a door into the auditorium of catechesis, but it is completed much earlier at the conclusion of the necessary term of service.

Since no labor under the sun is more difficult or more exhausting to the strength of its workers, the wise have fixed its period at seven years, unless thereafter the person in charge presides by authority rather than by labor.

Thus all these limits have been passed: you, dearest brother, have passed them in part; I passed them entirely long ago. Yet we still groan beneath the burden, still sweat at the same labor, and no grace of earned honor has yet smiled upon us that might compensate us equally for so great a toil.

There is scarcely anyone, except a very few, who revisits that work; there is no one who reflects upon it again.

The liberal disciplines are relegated behind mimes and actors and seem almost to beg through taverns. They philosophize about that money beyond [lacuna]; mammon rules over kings and tetrarchs alike.

In sum, savage avarice possesses all the rewards of virtue, and in the kingdom of money ambition sets the price of its merchandise.

What may we believe will happen to us insignificant people when the stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street?

What service of dignity, or guardianship of spiritual vessels, can be hoped for or desired when everywhere we see not vessels of mercy prepared for glory, but vessels of wrath fitted for destruction—from vessels of drinking bowls to every kind of musical vessel?

### XXVII [Cols. 0899D–0900A]

From the same poisoned root of avarice, therefore, and from this pestilential seed of weeds, there has arisen—and daily grows worse—the ruinous loss of morals and discipline.

The result is that in no administration of regular office is it permitted to use the customary severity or rod of our ancestors. If, with the rod of correction, you restrain a hand caught in the crooked windings of vice, immediately, in the case of the greater offenders, either a multitude of their like arrives as their champion, or money as their defender; in the case of the lesser, either premature freedom or flight with feet already in motion intervenes as their liberator.

It would be better to remain silent about the greater offenders, for truth produces hatred.

But those who ought still to be instructed under the schoolmaster’s rod, because they have surrendered their hands to laziness, dullness, and their god, their belly, refuse to be trained in the seriousness of moral discipline. They are carried about like light straw by every wind of doctrine and, in accordance with the same Apostle, do not endure sound teaching but heap up teachers for themselves according to their desires, having itching ears; they serve vain and pestilential novelties of words and questions.

Those who ought still to be formed as naked and soft clay on the wheel of discipline, by the craftsman’s skilled thumb and vigorous turning, into vessels of glory, recoil from there by fleeing outward and are deformed into vessels of dishonor.

Even if they gather some scrap of extreme or merely loquacious knowledge through the schools of learning, they wander about like vagrants, roaming without satisfaction.

Since they have little or no concern for morals, they return to their own people, shaking the yoke of fear from their untamed necks and breaking the bridle of discipline. By living ruinously they destroy themselves, by corrupting others with the leaven of malice, and hurl their whole selves headlong into destruction.

### XXVIII [Col. 0900B]

Some, having become false teachers of a certain instruction of their own, because they know no fixed manger and cannot return to their own—since they possess none—run here and there through villages, rural districts, and cities.

They teach new readings of the Psalter, Paul, and the Apocalypse. They draw after themselves a youth eager for novelty, a follower of frivolity, and a fugitive from discipline, down the slopes of pleasure.

They confuse and utterly ruin the reverence owed to discipline, submission to obedience, observance of religion, and finally every duty of regular life, through the most depraved corruption of morals.

### XXIX [Col. 0900C]

And lest you perhaps think that I am directing the weapons of a disparaging tongue against such people and weaving an envious attack upon the new—or rather, the better—teachers, do not believe my words entirely; believe your own eyes and ears.

See, if you please, what theologians emerge from the academy at Tours in sound doctrine and salutary discipline, over which that apostle of Satan, Berengar, presides.

See, I say, what pestilential—or rather, deadly—scorpions and basilisks burst from the caverns of the Babylon of our entire age: men drunk with the must of their heresiarch and smeared with poison, introducing sacrilegious novelties of questions concerning sacred matters, useful for nothing except the subversion of their hearers.

Their speech spreads like cancer, because knowledge that puffs up does not build up but subverts.

### XXX [Cols. 0900D–0901B]

These men take up sacred matters—namely, the heavenly sacraments—which the holy Fathers, whenever their discussion dared to rise toward them, approached with reverence and as was fitting, recognizing that they surpassed not only speech but also human reason. When necessary, possessing the key of David and exercising subtle discretion in opening and closing, they explained these matters catholically to the extent sufficient for the sobriety of the wise.

Of these matters and sacraments, I say, these men forge new and foreign interpretations contrary to the faith.

They contend that the very heavenly sacraments consecrated upon the altar are a shadow rather than the truth—a statement from which the tongue recoils and the ear shudders—and that they are subject, according to nature’s necessity, to the belly and the privy. Yet the Lord of nature, by his omnipotence, made this sacrament in the covenant of human reconciliation and gave it as spiritual food to the Christian soul, so that it might live forever.

These men eat the same paschal lamb—the one who ineffably transformed the same sacraments into himself and established and consecrated them for us—raw or cooked in water, not roasted by fire. What remains of it, and always will remain—for no mortal, however learned, has ever been able, or ever will be able, in this life to penetrate the mystery of the incarnate Word with complete understanding—they do not burn with fire.

Seizing the imprudent simplicity of their more straightforward brothers, and especially the inquisitive frivolity of wandering renegades, by a new kind of teaching seduction, they first present the very surface of Scripture as though it showed a level road to the seven-pillared house of wisdom, and point out a straight path, as though to the harbor of salvation.

Then, having caught them in the nets of sophistical disputation and blunted them with the sharpness of carnal knowledge, they lead them through the deceptive windings of necessary argument.

Until, beautifully equipped for destruction by the foreign novelty of questions alien to salvation, they plunge them together with themselves into the pit of ruin.

### XXXI

Since such men fail to notice that matters pertaining to God must not be discussed according to human or worldly judgment, and that honey, once enough has been found, should not be eaten to the point of nausea, they rely on their own wisdom and probe too deeply into the depths of majesty. Overwhelmed by glory, they are hurled into the depths of error. While, with the rashness of carnal wisdom, they attempt to fix the bleary eyes of the animal man—who does not perceive the things of God—upon the true Sun, they are struck by the rays of that inaccessible light and cast into the outer darkness of error.

While these men do not fear to subject the divine mysteries of the sacraments—always worthy of reverence and never attainable by human judgment or reason—to impious disputation, they deserve to define nothing worthy of a sound hearing. While they wish to confine the limits of nature, and by human reason seek to conclude what surpasses the understanding of every rational creature, they truly stumble against the stone of offense and the rock of scandal. For from the pious and nourishing breasts of doctrine they strive to draw out, instead of milk, butter or blood.

May Christ Jesus root this deadly pestilence of doctrine out of his Church before a little leaven corrupts the whole mass.

### XXXII

Since, then, the whole Church is everywhere being leavened by this poisonous and manifold leaven of malice and wickedness, and almost nowhere is an unleavened portion of sincerity and truth preserved intact; and since there is scarcely anyone who either works against these things by adhering to the true principles of a good life, or rewards one who does so with the recompense due to his life; and since for this reason the small number of those who still labor, overcome by weariness, refrain from their work—who would not prefer leisure to business? Who would not prefer rest and silence to useless labor and shouting at the deaf?

“I set a guard over my mouth,” he says, “when the sinner stood against me; I was silent, and was humbled, and kept silence from good things.” And Jeremiah teaches what should be done by those who are thus humbled and silent concerning the good, saying: “He shall sit alone and keep silence, because he has lifted himself above himself.”

[Col. 0902A]

### XXXIII

All these things Herimannus of Reims, Drogo of Paris, Huoremannus of Speyer, Meinbardus of Bamberg, and many other distinguished men of exceptional authority wisely despised. Having cut off their occupations and renounced their labors, they bade farewell to their studies and, following wise counsel, withdrew into the leisure of theology.

But what was I to do? Why should I not henceforth choose the same purpose of life? I did so gladly and willingly. For even if the general complaint—or the general cause—of all devout men did not urge me to it, the course of my own life and the outcome of my affairs would sufficiently advise me to make the same choice.

The course of life, by the continuous friction of labor, exhausts and wears out whatever bodily strength remains, and scatters premature snow upon the head. It therefore threatens me with an early death unless I withdraw in due season into rest and leisure.

As for the outcome of my affairs, although an abundance of things greatly to be desired flows in profusion, there is nevertheless a scarcity of what is most desirable: namely, those things which I had formerly heard of from the golden age of our ancestors and which, in the happier days of our own memory, I myself saw with my own eyes—sincere faith and complete truth; preserving the Lord’s commandment toward one another; placing nothing before justice and equity; relaxing nothing of the seriousness of discipline and religion; admitting nothing that was not for the public benefit and honor; and all the other things of that kind which can build up minds in the gilded trellises of human nature and store desirable treasures in earthen vessels.

These are the things that, in the better days of our memory, I rejoiced seriously to see and to share. But now, since they have almost entirely disappeared, I mourn not so much my own misery as the common misery.

### XXXIV

Let me pass over still more ancient times, and therefore better ones, and speak of those which we ourselves partly saw and partly learned from faithful reports of recent events. From the days of Lord Notger, bishop of our city, and of the foremost bishops who flourished in the Church at the same time as he, down to these two lustrums which have now slipped into misery, “Mercy and truth met one another; justice and peace kissed one another.”

But now truth has been removed from the earth, and justice has withdrawn into heaven, and, by a sudden assault of fortune and a monstrous disordering of affairs, everything has been overturned and perverted—indeed, to put it briefly, everything has become the opposite of what was described above. Thus, if anyone amid these storms of the world wishes to govern himself and what has been entrusted to him by the same clear reason and along the same path of the commandments, as though guided by heavenly stars, he is struck by the very violence of the turmoil and compelled to abandon what he began.

How horrible and monstrous this is, no one can easily explain. We read that the noble gold of the former age gradually degenerated into silver and other metals of lesser value, little by little and at intervals over time, and did not so suddenly lose the appearance of its own color. Now, however, as has been said, by a monstrous and unheard-of disturbance of affairs, everything has been overturned from its proper state as though in a moment. There is scarcely anyone who preserves the lawful requirements of his own rank or office. That desirable gold of our time has been reduced by a sudden catastrophe—not, as before, at intervals over time, nor into silver or other metals of however great a value, but entirely into straw and hay, or at least into ashes and cinders.

To gather briefly into a concluding summary all that I lamented above in answering your objections: after God had kindled, far too late, the two brightest lights of the Church, and had hidden them far too soon in the refuge of his face from the disturbance of men—I mean the emperor Henry II and Liutbold, primate of the see of Mainz, in whom the golden age reached its end with the greatest splendor of its beauty—after, I say, these two brightest lights had been taken from these shadows into the true light, from which they had also shone here upon the world, as we pray and desire, whatever of divine religion, whatever of equity and justice, whatever of liberal studies, whatever of liberal discipline flourished everywhere, just as at that time the Church flourished with varied adornment of virtues and with the manifold growth of the liberal arts, was buried together with them—or rather, was received into heaven.

So little of these things has remained on earth that what does remain is scarcely more than the traces of an empty shadow.

### XXXV

For, first of all, those who occupy positions of government and leadership among the people of God seek almost everything that is their own, without regard for the God who sees and without fear of a man who corrects, rather than what belongs to the community and to others. “There is no fear of God before their eyes”; therefore, “destruction and misery are in their ways.”

And how will those who, as he says, “devour my people as though they were eating bread” recognize the way of peace? Since there is no one to demand an account of this, no one to rebuke it, the pursuits of factions have prevailed in place of the study of the divine Scriptures; glory and the boasting of empty arrogance have prevailed in place of the seriousness and modesty of religion. While they eagerly strive to outstrip one another in wealth and honors, they do not fear to serve profane hatreds and quarrels with profane minds, and they take no account of anything, even though they exercise tyranny rather than rule. To what end—or rather, to what destruction—must such things come?

When this majesty and such power sits upon the tribunal to examine the deeds of its subjects, and to remove the speck from another’s eye while neglecting the beam in its own, avarice, standing in the midst as its companion, cries out its complaints. It sweats out its cases and laments that right and wrong, sacred and profane, are being treated alike. It implores the mercy of judges, the authority of laws, and divine and human rights. Unless the accused is punished with whatever has been charged in the moneybags of that wealthy man who has brought the case, it complains that the whole judicial order will be thrown into confusion.

When all have been struck with terror by this thunder, avarice itself inclines an ear to both sides as they whisper; it fits each party with a purchasable tongue; it turns a grim eye upon both; it stretches out a grasping hand to each promising party. The person whom a moment ago it accused for possessing what it coveted, it now excuses for giving what it sought. When the case has been pleaded, it sits in the midst of violence, rapacity, and its other curial associates, reads from its own book what is just, and, with the same sworn laws agreeing with it, pronounces judgment against the defendant according to the law of money. The defendant is kept bound until the god Mammon releases him.

The same man whom a moment ago the Caecilian law is sufficient to crucify as a Labeo, the monetary law now presents with the curule chair as a Cato. In every assembly, the authority of the laws proposes this, and the supreme body of judgments agrees to it: that whoever cannot pay from his immense wealth should pay what is equivalent from his measured means; and if he has no means from which payment can be made, let him be crucified without mercy.

### XXXVI

This is why, when at the fairs we see the holy Gospel, and those who sell doves and chairs for money in the Church, with the tables of the money-changers not far from them—for today nothing is received without payment and nothing is given without payment—we all devote ourselves more attentively to the marketplace than to the choir, more cautiously to usury than to the Scriptures, more earnestly to commerce than to religion, and more to filling capacious money-pouches than to pursuing liberal studies.

We gape so eagerly after worldly desires, and are so occupied with accumulating riches, that we seem to think we deserve to purchase eternal life at such a price, while entirely setting aside the things that evangelical truth, apostolic instruction, and the authority of the holy Fathers have established as ecclesiastical discipline.

Why is this? Because you are worth as much as you possess. For, as the man whom you know says:

> Virtue, fame, honor, and divine and human beauty  
> Obey the riches that someone has amassed; he will be  
> Renowned, brave, just, wise, even a king,  
> And whatever he wishes.

Since this horrible forest of thorns grows from avarice, which is the root of every evil, it is easy—indeed, horrible—to see what fruit this thorn-brake bears.

This is why, while we linger over the pursuits of acquisition and outstrip one another in obtaining honors, rather than surpassing one another in honor; with the ancient face of divine religion changed, and the ancestral discipline of moral instruction reduced almost to a fable; we envy brother, and by biting one another we diminish one another’s reputation. Accusing one another, we stir up civil wars and pierce our brothers’ hearts with the sharp darts of words. We turn deceit over in our hearts, display pretense on our faces, and bring forth fraud in our words. In every respect, contrary to the commandments of God, we regard all his commandments as worthless in comparison with money.

Finally, we are all shaken by fickleness and instability of character like a reed by the winds, so that what yesterday you pursued with intense or even excessive zeal, you do not remember at all today.

And what do we hope will come of these things? Surely this: that the Lord will make a whip from little cords and drive all such people out of the temple.

That triple scourge of punishment which the Lord threatens through the prophet against the sinful people is also greatly to be feared, when he says: “Behold, I will bring upon them the sword, famine, and pestilence, and I will scatter them into every wind.”

We see certain branches and heralds of this scourge gradually rising from the earth: the Lord is little by little breaking the staff of bread and the gladness of wine, while among Christians we hear of wars and rebellions being waged, and of frequent incursions by pagans against Christians. From this we may infer what remains, unless God is appeased by our correction: it will not be long delayed.

### XXXVII

Go now, brother, act against leisure and rest, and call lazy and sluggish anyone who desires them at this time. Would that, with the rewards of labor despaired of, we might attain that desired and salutary rest, to be followed not by labor but by glory in the senate of the heavenly court!

If you know anything better, brother, impart it candidly; if not, follow this course with me.
