But if the noble strength of your great-hearted courage still refuses to accept these things, and is not reluctant to undertake anything arduous, seek another Ferentarius for yourself rather than me, because at this time you will not have me as your companion in the battle. Or seek another Martius to whom you may entrust this task, but grant him better results from good beginnings than you grant that Roman.

As for me, although bound in that prison—both savage and long-lasting—I shall console my exhausted strength with as much rest as I can. I hope that at last I shall be heard, and, uttering the sighs of a long-desired release, shall, if not honorably discharged, at least released, hand over my sorrowful realm to someone.

I place nothing in my own vow or leave anything to my own will; I entrust myself wholly, as his clay, to my potter. Let him shape me upon the wheel of the secular order according to what pleases him. However his power turns me, I shall add nothing except that solemn word of obedience: “Your will be done.”

### XXXVIII

It is clear, brother, how far we have strayed and how far we have diverted our course from the straight line of the right path, since you led me away unwittingly and drew me, drunk with the sweetness of your affection, into the byways of words.

Take care, brother—take careful care—that while we heedlessly follow certain stars of the Scriptures, we are not driven upon reefs and sandbanks and meet a Charybdean shipwreck. Take care, I say—even if it is less pleasing—that what is said be no more than is permitted, because the blow of a scourge produces a bruise, and the scourge of the tongue breaks bones.

Therefore, let the discourse now return to the place from which it departed, and return to you, from whom its first stream flowed forth. Since it began in charity, let it end in charity. May charity never fail, but, sown and increased here, may it anticipate the true fullness of itself in eternal life.

Enough has already been said above about your integrity, seriousness, modesty, constancy, and the other exercises of a good life. But about your affection, goodwill, and the other duties of humanity, it will never be possible to say enough, either here or there.

This alone I wish for you: that you may always advance toward what is better and greater, until you aspire to that fullness of increase in which you need fear no loss.

Since you preserve this desirable treasure in an earthen vessel, I do not consider it idle to remind you to employ the vigilant care of constant guardianship. You will do this if you keep all the gates of your city and all the windows of this earthen house secured under the bolt and seal of humility; if you fortify all the exits and entrances of this earthen vessel with the barriers of the virtues, so that neither an exit is open to those kept inside nor an entrance to those lying in wait outside.

For if, through the lightness of self-exaltation, the things which the industrious hand of diligent labor had carefully gathered within should flow outward, the wind of pride will immediately scatter and dissipate them to the destruction of its own vanity, so that they will either be difficult or never again to gather. But if wicked enemies rush in through an entrance left open from outside, they will violently plunder what you have achieved within through immense labor, leaving you, once conquered, nothing but hell.

Therefore, whatever grace has been divinely bestowed upon you, whatever divine gift has been gathered in the treasury of your conscience, let it be attributed neither to me, who plant and water, nor to you, who make the earth bear fruit abundantly. Let everything be referred to the Father of lights, from whom every good and perfect gift comes.

### XXXIX

I could indeed applaud the gift of your perfection more abundantly and fully, but the seriousness of modesty does not permit this because of the notoriety of flattery.

As for the book that you wrote for me, and for which you gave me the occasion by writing it—a book in which you impressed upon my mind your fingers, eyes, and spirit, the inclination of your neck, the labor of your head, indeed your whole self—I find nothing among my external possessions with which I can repay you equally or return a fitting recompense for your abundant kindness.

But first I ask that it be repaid to you by him from whom you received these things and all the good things you possess, so that, in exchange for this goodwill, your name may be written in the book of life in golden letters of good works.

Then our perpetual devotion toward you will not sleep, if an opportunity should gradually appear for rewarding you in a modest manner from our limited resources, insofar as it may contribute to the honor of us both.

### XL

Now, at last, with the things that had to be said brought to an end as circumstances permitted, let the pen circumcise itself entirely with the new scribe’s knife—not in the Judaic manner but in the scholastic manner—and prepare itself to receive, greet, and entertain you, not as broadly as possible but as lavishly as it can. For you, whom I hold embraced inwardly in the bowels of Jesus Christ, I shall not release outwardly until you have been richly received.

Know that you are indebted for this banquet, since you presented yourself to us as a festive guest and fellow-seated participant at our feast.

I greet you with a few, although I am among many: either there are few natives of the colony that I serve who know with how great a gift of virtues your industrious mind is adorned, or there are few good assessors of affairs who form sound judgments about things. If those who know many good things and hate them knew you and judged you according to your merits, they would surely love you.

I greet you with those of our fellow workers who, trained for good fruit, have risen from our academy and have claimed for themselves the chair of teaching in truly distinguished places.

I greet you with our beginners, who are still laboring in the school arena: a most noble flower of good disposition, which, at the command of our mouth, meditates its fruit even beneath the rod. Even if you were to read their names written for you, you would nevertheless lack acquaintance with them, since you do not know their faces.

Yet by this very remark I convict myself, for if you measure someone’s acquaintance by his face, you do not know yourself either, since you have never seen your own face.

Above all, I greet you with that genuine charity with which I nourished you in the cradles of discipline with the elementary milk of learning and led you onward to the solid food of more perfect doctrine, so that henceforth you may be my fellow soldier in the battle line and my fellow settler in labor, my fellow citizen of the heavenly city and co-heir of the eternal inheritance.

Having been greeted, greet in my name my brothers—not those whom flesh and blood joined to me in a single kinship, but those whom water and the Spirit regenerated with me into a single adoption—so that, as co-heirs of Christ in the kingdom of God the Father, we may receive by the testament of his blood our share of eternal blessedness.

I greet, then, the fathers, lords, brothers, and friends: fathers by the care of governance, lords by the dignity of preeminence, brothers in God, and friends in charity. Greet each one of them, I say, according as you know him to be united with me or with you.

May my greeting reach all of you, so that, with the help of him in whom we believe, we may together be participants in eternal life. Amen.

**In the year of the Lord 1059. John, Bishop of Sabina.**

[Col. 0907]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, I, 159.)

[Col. 0907B] John succeeded John and was elected cardinal-bishop of Sabina by Leo IX. He took part in the Roman council under Nicholas II in the year 1059. Under Alexander II he departed this life.

An anonymous author of the Vatican manuscript concerning the destruction of the monastery of Farfa, in the third year of Leo IX, recounts the unworthy deed of this John, bishop of Sabina, against the monastery of Farfa, and the divine vengeance inflicted upon him:

> “In the time of Pope Leo, John, bishop of Sabina, who was lying in wait against the monastery of Farfa on account of tithes and offerings for the dead, especially on account of the church of Saint Angelo at Tancia—for he had formerly made an unjust agreement concerning it with Lord Hugh the abbot, who held and possessed that same church of Saint Angelo as the property of this monastery—we call it an agreement for this reason: in the time of Lord Adrian I’s pontificate, Duke Hildebrand granted it to this monastery by his charter.
>
> “The aforesaid Abbot Hugh knew none of these things, being a foreigner, and received the aforementioned agreement from the bishop without knowing the facts. Thereupon the aforesaid bishop rose up and went armed to the same church of Saint Angelo. He removed and destroyed its altar, and took away its relics and carried them off with him. As he was returning from there to the episcopal residence, the sky having suddenly become perfectly clear, a great storm of rain, hail, and lightning arose.
>
> “When he saw this, the bishop withdrew from the road to a place called the Area and stayed there for a while with the relics. A great miracle then occurred: at the very place where the relics remained, not a drop of rain or hail fell. When the storm had ceased, he returned to the episcopal residence in great fear.
>
> “The next day, when Lord Bernard, abbot of Orte, heard of this, he chose a certain bishop who happened at that time to be lodging in this monastery, from the regions beyond the Alps, and, gathering the men of the abbey and faithful soldiers, took great pains to rebuild the altar with great honor, placing precious and distinguished relics there.
>
> “The aforesaid bishop then grieved greatly for the Church of Sabina because he had destroyed the altar and carried away the relics. That very night he was struck down, and, with one entire side of his body becoming numb, he remained afflicted until he died.
>
> “Afterward, fearful and trembling at this, and grieving greatly over the restoration that our lord abbot had undertaken, the bishop went to the same place. He removed the new relics that he found there and honorably reburied the earlier ones. Of the new relics he built and consecrated a small altar in his episcopal residence. Finally, he made the following complaint in synod against our lord abbot.”

[Col. 0909]

## COMPLAINT OF JOHN, BISHOP OF SABINA, AGAINST THE MONKS OF FARFA AT THE ROMAN SYNOD OF 1051

(Mansi, *Concilia*, XIX, 797, from the *Chronicon Farfense*, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, III.II, 581.)

[Col. 0909A] “Let the Lord hear, and let the most equitable ruler of the whole kingdom [lacuna], or the bishop of the chief see, hear; and let this entire holy synod hear and perceive the just complaint that I make against the abbot of Farfa, from whom I have suffered and continue to suffer many injuries.

“There is a certain church in honor of Saint Michael the archangel, situated on a mountain called Tancia, namely within my episcopate. It belongs to the jurisdiction of my bishopric, and its altar is believed to have been founded and dedicated by the most blessed Silvester, bishop of this venerable see. That abbot did not fear, with reckless audacity, to add a wall to it and to have Masses sung by his monks over the violated consecration of so great a consecrator, without any bishop either doing or commanding this.

“As for that church, the church of Saint Mary, of which he himself is abbot, holds one half through some donor unknown to me; my episcopate possesses the other half. But between Abbot Hugh and me an agreement concerning these halves was made as follows: during Lent and in the month of May, my official was always to sit there with his official; at other times, only his official was to sit there, from whom I was to receive three gifts each year.

“And if that abbot, or any successor of his, should ever sell to anyone, give away, grant as a benefice, or in any other way transfer his half of that church, then it would pass into the ownership of me and my successors. And if I or any of my successors should do anything of that sort with the half of that church belonging to my episcopate, then that half would pass into the ownership of the abbot.

“And behold, that lord abbot has fallen short in all these matters: he neither treated my official as he ought, nor sent the promised gifts, but gave his half to two female servants of God.

“One day the aforesaid church burned down. After the fire, he brought the bishop of Siponto and, against my will and without my knowledge, had it consecrated.

“When he learned that one day I would be going to a certain place to fulfill the command of my lord, he prepared an ambush against me, of such a kind that, if he could, he would kill me, or, if he could not, burn down the house in which I would be lying at night. Peter the monk, called ‘of Lawrence,’ was the author of this wicked plot, together with Datus son of Ubertus, Teuzo son of Berizo, Albertinus Adulterinus, Barocco, Peter Castellanus, Raino son of Crescentius, Follia, John Ferrarius, Rainaldus son of the priest Guido, and Azolinus.

“Finally, he cut down the forest belonging to one of my archpriests because he discovered that man to be my loyal supporter; it was worth no less than one hundred pounds.

“He seized one of my servants, and because the man said that he belonged to me, he took away his horse and all his clothing.

“Moreover, he claims all the tithes belonging to me, as well as my share of the goods of the dead, wherever it is applicable, but especially at Buccinianum and Vulpianum.

“Oppressed by these and other adversities from that abbot, I bring my complaint against him and ask for your mercy, so that you do not permit my Church—or rather, both yours and mine—to be burdened by such great adversities and harassed by such great troubles. Rather, once freed from the disturbances caused by so great a disturber, may we render the greatest thanks to God and to you.”

[Note: [Col. 0909C] After these matters had been recited, the advocate of the lord abbot asked that, with the holy synod’s permission, the lord pope grant time for investigating and answering more accurately and carefully each of the charges that the bishop of Sabina had proclaimed. This was then granted with benevolent generosity.

“Present there were more truthful and peaceable friends of both parties, who, investigating the matters canonically, reported to the lord pope that he should judge according to law or the sacred canons, lest both parties suffer the gravest harm—specifically, because of the violation and destruction of the altar and its relics, which the same bishop of Sabina had presumed to remove, and because of the plundering and burnings subsequently carried out by the army of the lord abbot’s soldiers.

“For the ownership of the church was found in every respect to have belonged to our monastery from an earlier and prior acquisition and authentic declaration. The supreme prelate, discerning this with greater certainty, caused the dispute to be settled as best he could and issued to this monastery a remarkable privilege confirming, in his pious authority, its completely free possession of all acquisitions belonging to the monastery.

“Finally, after a long time, in our own days, we saw and heard a certain Roman bishop named Peter—already very old, who lived in Rome at Saint Vincent’s, near the holy church of blessed Peter the apostle—reporting and bearing most certain witness that all the matters mentioned above had been examined and settled in his presence, and that the privilege had been issued in this form. (The privilege follows.)]

**In the year of the Lord 1061. Humbert, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, bishop of Silva Candida.**

[Col. 0911]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(From J.-G. Eggs, *Purpura docta, or The Deeds, Legations, etc., of the Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church*, compiled from Ciaconius, Andrea Victorello, Augustinus Oldoinus, and others; vol. I, p. 15.)

[Col. 0911A] Humbert, whom the authors do not distinguish by any surname, originated in Burgundy. A professed member of the Order of Saint Benedict, he lived in the monastery of Saint Mansuetus, the first bishop of Toul, situated in the suburbs of Toul; he was a man exceptionally learned in Greek and Latin.

When Saint Leo IX, bishop of the same city of Toul, was setting out for Rome, he chose Humbert as his traveling companion in the year of salvation 1049. A few months later, Humbert was sent to Sicily to proclaim the word of God to its peoples and, while energetically carrying out the office of archbishop of that region, was soon appointed by the same Leo cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Silva Candida.

Lanfrancus, the learned and devout archbishop of Canterbury of that age, summed up the virtues of Cardinal Humbert in an outstanding eulogy in his book against Berengar the arch-heresiarch, published on the Eucharist. He states:

> “Humbert was a religious man, adorned with Christian faith and most holy works, and thoroughly cultivated in knowledge of the divine and secular letters, as all testify who either knew him from personal experience or learned of him from others who had experienced him. Saint Leo did not bring him to Rome from Burgundy, as some have wrongly written, but from Lotharingia, and ordained him archbishop to preach the word of God to the Sicilians. Later he appointed him cardinal prelate of the Holy Roman Church. Once placed in that position, he lived and taught in such a way that no report, not even the slightest, of sinister suspicion concerning his faith or doctrine ever arose. Almost the whole Latin world bears witness to this, for, on account of the excellence of the apostolic see, whose councils and deliberations he always attended and presided over, it could not fail to know him.”

The same Lanfrancus, addressing Berengar in the same book, says:

> “The venerable Humbert, whom you name a Burgundian as though reproaching him—as if God could not have faithful servants in Burgundy—did nothing other than present the Scripture itself, as the synod commanded, from hand to hand.”

Many other encomia of him by other authors are found throughout the sources.

In the year of the Lord 1053, when Pope Leo learned that the monastic discipline of the monastery at Subiaco had shamefully collapsed through the negligence and indolence of Abbot Otho, he went there with Humbert to confront the evil. After removing Otho, who was responsible for the lax observance, he placed Humbert in charge. Through his vigilance and the example of his most approved life, Humbert restored and raised the discipline—which had almost been extinguished and was lying on the ground—to its former dignity. In defending it, he afterward endured many labors following Leo’s departure.

While Humbert was spending several days at Trani in Apulia on business, he was given a copy of a letter written in the Greek language by Michael Cerularius, patriarch of Constantinople, and Leo of Acrida, archbishop of the Bulgarians, to John, bishop of Trani. He translated it into Latin and submitted it to Pope Leo for examination.

The letter bore this title, full of arrogance:

> “Michael, universal patriarch of New Rome.”

Its contents consisted chiefly of three accusations—or rather insults. First, that the Latin Church imitated the Jews in a superstitious fashion in blessing unleavened bread; second, that it followed the custom of barbarians who ate strangled animals; third, that it sang the *Alleluia* only during the Easter season.

After reading all these calumnies, Pope Leo gave a full reply in an extensive letter addressed to Michael and Leo. This letter is listed first among the letters of Leo IX.

In the year 1054, by order of Pope Leo, Humbert served as legate to Constantinople together with Frederick, the Lotharingian cardinal, and Peter, archbishop of Amalfi. They were sent to Constantine Monomachus IX, emperor and husband of the empress Zoe, and to Michael Cerularius, patriarch, to reconcile the Greek Church with the Latin Church and to seek assistance against the tyranny of the Normans.

The emperor received these legates of the apostolic see with fitting obedience and honor, kissing each of them according to the custom of the people as a sign of friendship.

Humbert, the chief of the legates, committed to writing for Pope Leo what had been accomplished on the embassy. Among other things, he noted that the monk Nicetas, called *Pectoratus*, in the presence of the emperor himself, the legates, and the nobles, had commended with much verbal bitterness a certain booklet composed against the Latin Church with Attic envy and arrogance. It contained chiefly three sections: *On Unleavened Bread*, *On the Sabbath*, and *On Priests’ Marriages*.

Since the booklet contained nothing solid or sound beyond insults and errors, the orthodox Augustus, at the urging of the legates, ordered it to be burned.

When these matters had been settled and Humbert and his colleagues were preparing to depart for Rome, Michael, the impious, fraudulent, and cunning patriarch, deeply disturbed by the burning of the booklet, approached the emperor. He intended to arrange for the legates to be detained, so that, under some pretext of convening a public assembly, they might be brought into the church of Hagia Sophia and attacked with stones by the people, being exposed to ridicule contrary to the law of nations—indeed, contrary to natural and divine law.

But the most prudent emperor detected Michael’s wicked intention and foresaw the scandal that would arise from it; he absolutely refused to consent to the impious request. Rather, after presenting the legates with royal gifts and wishing them prosperity, he urged them to set out on their journey under God’s guidance.

Meanwhile, Michael, bearing with the greatest difficulty the frustration of his schemes, turned to constructing new ambushes. He sent a letter to Peter, patriarch of Antioch, fulminating with an unrestrained pen against Humbert and his companions and ordering Peter to seize them as contemptuous enemies of the Greek religion and strip them of their gifts.

But Peter, recognizing the innocence of the legates, disregarded Michael’s insulting commands, received them with the humanity that was fitting, and, adding new gifts to theirs, dismissed them with honor.

In the year 1055 they hastened to Rome and found Victor II, who had succeeded the deceased Leo, seated at the helm of the Church. A few months later, Humbert was sent to the monastery of Cassino because of the bitter disputes that had arisen among the monks concerning the intruded abbot Peter.

Humbert nevertheless easily settled these disputes when Peter voluntarily relinquished the prelacy and Frederick, the Lotharingian cardinal, was substituted in his place by the suffrage of the monks.

After the death of Victor II, he took part, with his vote, in the elections of three pontiffs—Stephen X, Nicholas II, and Alexander II—under whose rule he exercised for several years the very important offices of librarian and chancellor with extraordinary distinction and ability.[Col. 0914A] In the year of salvation 1059, at the command of Nicholas II and the Lateran synod, he composed the formula of faith which Berengar, the heretic then pretending to repent, was to pronounce before two hundred and thirty bishops and prelates at the council. But when, after the synod had ended, Berengar, like an unclean dog, had returned to his vomit, he poured out a wagonload of insults, both in speech and in writing, against Humbert and against the Roman Church, as the already-cited Lanfranc, a vigorous defender of the Church and of Humbert, bears witness.

When Frederick of Lorraine had been raised to the pontificate under the name Stephen X—or, as Baronius and others prefer, when Alexander II of that name was seated in the chair of Peter[Col. 0914B]—Humbert was sent as legate to England. There, after a council had been summoned in the presence of the entire English clergy on the sixth day before the Ides of April in the year 1072, he settled with such great skill the very serious dispute that had arisen between the Churches of Canterbury and York concerning primacy that Thomas, archbishop of the Church of York, convinced by his arguments and reasoning, accepted as valid the primacy adjudged to Canterbury, issuing this public profession:

> “It is altogether fitting that every Christian should be subject to Christian laws. Therefore I, Thomas, already ordained metropolitan archbishop of the Church of York, having heard and understood the arguments, make to you, Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, and to your successors, an unconditional profession of canonical obedience; and I promise that I shall observe whatever you, or they, may justly and canonically enjoin upon me.”[Col. 0914C]

Having returned to Rome after settling the dispute between the English prelates, full of days and merits, he received the sacraments of the Church and was translated to the heavenly realms on the third day before the Nones of May, in the year 1064 from the Virgin’s birth. He was buried in the Constantinian basilica, by order of the supreme pontiff, near the bodies of the holy virgins and martyrs Matern(a) and Secundina.

[Col. 0913]

## ANOTHER NOTICE

*(FABRIC. Biblioth. med. et inf. Lat., IV, 306.)*

[Col. 0913D] Humbert, formerly a monk of the Benedictine order at the monastery of Saint Mansuetus in Moyenmoutier, in the diocese of Toul, was made cardinal from the year 1049 and bishop of Silva Candida. In 1051 he was sent as a legate by Leo IX to the emperor of Constantinople, Constantine Monomachus; afterward, in 1057, he was sent by Victor II to settle disputes in the monastery of Monte Cassino. On this matter see Leo of Ostia, Book II of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, chapter 88.

Besides his learned writings against the Greeks—Michael Cerularius, Leo of Acrida, and Nicetas Pectoratus—which were published by Baronius under the year 1054 and in the appendix to volume XI of the *Annals*, by Canisius in volume VI of the *Lectiones antiquae* (volume III of Basnage’s new edition, p. 277), and in the *Bibliothecae Patrum*, volume XI, Cologne, and volume XVIII, Lyons, p. 389, 405, 415, Edmund Martène most recently published his three books against the Simoniacs from the Laurentian Library, in volume V of the *Anecdota*, pp. 633–844. In the third book, the final eight chapters are missing. *Spinosulus*, which he touches upon on p. 647, does not seem to be a proper name, but rather an insult directed at the more thorny subtleties of his adversary. The same Humbert is reported to have prescribed for Berengar the abjuration made at the Roman council of 1059, which begins, “I, Berengar,” and is also inserted in Gratian’s *Decree*, Distinction 2, *On Consecration*, chapter 42.

[Col. 0915]

## HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE

*(Histoire littéraire de la France, volume VII, p. 527.)*

[Col. 0915A] Humbert, whom others call Hubert[Note: [Col. 0915C] He is indeed called Ubert in the *Life of Saint John Gualbert*, written in the twelfth century; and a large number of modern writers give him the same name, spelling it with an H. But Blessed Lanfranc, his contemporary, and Sigebert, who wrote shortly afterward, always call him Humbert.], one of the most learned men of his time, is the first well-known Frenchman to have been raised to the dignity of cardinal. (LANF. *in Ber.*, chapters 2, 4, 8, 16.) He was born in Burgundy[Note: [Col. 0915D] The opinion that supposes Humbert to have been born in Burgundy rather than Lorraine is based, on the one hand, on the fact that Berengar, who had no reason to identify one country rather than another, always calls him the Burgundian. (MAB. *act.*, volume IX, p. 274, note 22.) Moreover, Blessed Lanfranc (LANF., same work, chapter 2), undertaking to defend this illustrious cardinal against the insults directed at him by Berengar, merely says that it was not from Burgundy but from Lorraine that Pope Saint Leo brought him to Rome—which is true. He then adds that even if Humbert had been Burgundian, Berengar was wrong to use that as grounds for insulting him, because the Spirit of God blows where it pleases; that is, every country has its learned and worthy people. This neither denies that Humbert was Burgundian nor proves that he was Lorrainer. In any case, since Burgundy and Lorraine border one another, it is easy to attribute to one what belongs to the other.] at the beginning of this century, or, at the very latest, at the end of the preceding century. Those who make him a Lorrainer have taken the place of his education for the place of his birth. (CAL., *Hist. de Lor.*, volume IV, part II, p. 66.) In 1015 his otherwise unknown parents placed him at Moyenmoutier, where he undertook the monastic profession. Speaking of him (SIG. *scri.*, chapter 150), Sigebert calls him a monk of Toul because the abbey lies within that diocese. From this it has happened that most modern writers, misunderstanding this author, have made Humbert a monk of Saint-Mansuy, another abbey in the city of Toul itself. (UGH., volume I, p. 126; *Rom. Pont. vit.*, volume I, p. 795; LAB. *scri.*, volume I, p. 484; PAP. *bib. de B.*, volume I, p. 322.)

(CAL., same work, p. 66, 69; LANF., same work, chapter 2; TRIT. *scri.*, chapter 332.) Immediately after entering the cloister, Humbert, although still very young, devoted himself seriously to study. He neglected none of the literary disciplines then in use, and with a fine intellect made great progress in them. The more knowledge he acquired, the more he wished to acquire. As early as 1028 he was regarded as possessing a substantial body of learning. Later, however, he advanced much further under the abbots Nortbert and Lambert, who took care to direct his studies. (MAB. *act.*, volume IX, p. 76, note 9.) He devoted particular attention to Greek, which was not very common at that time, and learned it sufficiently to be able to translate writings in that language. At that time the diocese of Toul offered special assistance for studying it with success. (CAL., same work, part I, pp. 146, 147, chapter 52.) Some time earlier, Bishop Saint Gerard had given refuge there to entire communities of Greeks who had come seeking asylum.

Some modern writers even claim that Humbert also knew Hebrew; but they offer no proof other than their own authority. (*Rom. Pont. vit.*, same work; FRIZ. *Gall. pur.*, p. 89.) By these means he acquired, during his lifetime and after his death, a reputation as a man highly versed both in the divine sciences and in secular letters: “pre-eminently learned in knowledge of divine and secular literature.” Blessed Lanfranc (LANF., same work) paid him this testimony shortly after his death, on the authority of all who had known him personally and of those to whom they had made him known. What Lanfranc says of Humbert’s steadfast virtue and piety, recognized by everyone, is even more impressive.

(CAL., same work, part II, p. 69.) So brilliant a light could not remain forever hidden in the darkness of the cloister. Richer, the chronicler of Senones, asserted that Humbert had been abbot of Moyenmoutier (RICH., *chr.*, Book II, chapter 18), but there is no longer any doubt that he was mistaken on this point. Providence had other designs for Humbert and destined him for greater things. (CAL., same work, pp. 69, 70.) Pope Leo IX, who had known him when he was still merely bishop of Toul, wanted him near his own person; in this, Baronius remarks (BAR., under 1049, no. 28), Leo earned great merit for himself and rendered the Church a notable service. Humbert might perhaps have been of no use to him in Lorraine, whereas he served him advantageously at Rome. (MAB., *ann.*, Book LIX, no. 61.) After the council that this pontiff held at Reims in October 1049, he traveled through Lorraine and took the monk Humbert with him.

Baronius says that Leo installed him as abbot of Subiaco, commonly called Subiago, and offers as proof a fragment of the chronicle of that monastery, in which the abbot in question is indeed called Humbert and described as having come from France, *ductum ex Francia*, “brought from France.” (BAR., under 1051, no. 6.) Nevertheless, this Humbert is truly different from our cardinal, as is evident from the features of his history contained in the same chronicle; Dom Mabillon asserts this without hesitation. (MAB., same work, Book 60, no. 2.) He nevertheless deserves to be known for the care he took to restore his monastery, whose library he did not fail to furnish with good books, and for the Christian patience with which he endured the hardships and afflictions that beset his administration. In his person we have a meritorious pupil, otherwise unknown, whom our schools supplied to Italy, among the many others they gave her in the same century.

(LANF., same work; MAB. same work, Book 59, nos. 72, 75, volume IV, appendix, p. 739, I; RICH. *chr.*, same work; CAL. same work, p. 70.) The man who is the subject of this article was ordained archbishop of all Sicily by Pope Leo immediately after their arrival in Rome. He held this dignity before the council held there in April or May 1050, since he describes himself as such in the subscription to the bull of canonization issued there on behalf of Saint Gerard, bishop of Toul. The pope’s purpose in conferring it upon him was that he should go and preach the faith to the Saracens who ruled the island. Ughelli claims that Humbert carried out this praiseworthy plan and that it met with success. (UGH., same work.) But a much older author (CAL., same work) informs us that, since Humbert could not enter Sicily because of the incursions of the Normans who held Apulia and Calabria,[Note: [Col. 0917D] Barthius was extremely careless (BARTH. *adv.*, Book 46, chapter 6) in making our cardinal bishop of Senlis. It is clear that he confused him with Humbert, bishop of that church at the end of the eleventh century and during the first years of the following one.] (UGH., same work, pp. 104, 106, 126), Leo IX made him cardinal-bishop of Blanche-Selve, or Santa Rufina, ten miles from Rome on the Via Aurelia. This diocese continued until Pope Callixtus II united it with that of Porto because of its small number of inhabitants.

(Same work, p. 126; RICH. *chr.*, same work; CAL., same work; PEZ., same work, volume III, part II, p. 587.) This promotion took place in 1051, and Pope Leo found in Humbert a faithful counsellor, a zealous collaborator, and an inseparable companion on his journeys. In the same year the new cardinal[Col. 0917C] accompanied him to Lorraine, where the supreme pontiff went to raise from the earth the body of Saint Gerard, one of his predecessors in the see of Toul. (CAL., same work.) There Humbert had an opportunity to show that he was not ignorant of history and that he had read the works of Saint Augustine with profit.

While Halinard, archbishop of Lyon, was conversing with the pope, the discussion turned to the discovery of the relics of Saint Stephen, the first martyr. Since this prelate regarded the story as at least doubtful, Humbert proved its truth by means of a book by the holy doctor, which he had expressly caused to be brought from Moyenmoutier, since apparently it was not available at Toul. Our cardinal followed the pope on his devotional pilgrimages and other journeys during the remainder of that year and the following one, undertaken both for the good of the Church and for the interests of the empire.

(MAB., *Act.*, same work, p. 76, note 9.) In 1053, while he was at Trani, John, bishop of that place, showed him a letter addressed to him on behalf of Michael Cerularius, patriarch of Constantinople, and Leo, bishop of Acrida and metropolitan of Bulgaria. In it they loaded the Latin Church with reproaches concerning the matters discussed elsewhere. Humbert read the document, which was in Greek, translated it into Latin, and brought it to Pope Leo, who answered it as has been related in its proper place.

(CASS. *Chr.*, Book II, chapter 88; SIG., under 1054.) This peace-loving pontiff, wishing to restore unity between the Latin and Greek Churches, decided to send three legates to Constantinople. For this purpose he chose Humbert; Frederick, archdeacon and chancellor of the Roman Church; and Peter, archbishop of Amalfi. Before departing, the legates went to Monte Cassino to commend themselves to the brothers’ prayers.

[Note: [Col. 0917D] (BAR. under 1054, no. 1, same work; *Rom. Pont. vit.*, volume I, p. 796.) Baronius and most other modern writers place the legates’ departure in 1051, relying on the text of Leo of Ostia. But the expression *eodem anno*, “in the same year,” in chapter 88 of Book II refers not to the death of Pope Saint Leo, which occurred in 1054, but to the year 1053, which the author explicitly identifies in chapter 87 of the same book. Father Labbe is even less accurate in placing this legation as early as 1051. (LAB., same work.)]

Then, having set out toward the end of 1053, they arrived safely at Constantinople. They were received[Col. 0918B] with great honors by the emperor Constantine Monomachus, who lodged them for several days in his palace. During their stay in that great city, Humbert, who was the soul of the legation, directed its entire course. He himself worked to refute the letter of Patriarch Michael and the bishop of Acrida, although Pope Leo had already done so. He opposed it with a fairly long work, which will be discussed below, and wrote another in response to the work of Nicetas Pectoratus, a monk of Stoudios, which contained the same reproaches as the earlier letter.

The first writing of our cardinal was unsuccessful, but the second had a happy effect. When Nicetas read it, he was moved by Humbert’s arguments, opened his eyes to the truth, and renounced the schism. (Conc., volume II, p. 991.) Accordingly, when the legates went to the monastery of Stoudios on Saint John the Baptist’s day, 24 June 1054, Nicetas anathematized the writing published under his name against the Holy See and the entire Latin Church. He even allowed the emperor, who was present at this recantation, to burn his book in the sight of everyone. To demonstrate that his conversion was sincere, he went the very next day to the legates’ lodging, and, after receiving further explanations from them concerning his difficulties, renewed his recantation of the preceding day. The legates, for their part, received him into their communion, and he became their particular friend.

(Ibid.; SIG., same work.) The patriarch Michael, on the other hand,[Col. 0918D] unwilling either to speak with them or even to see them, led them to go to the Church of Hagia Sophia on Saturday, 16 July, at the hour of terce, when the clergy had prepared for Mass. There, having complained of the patriarch’s obstinacy, they placed an excommunication upon the high altar in the presence of all those attending. (Conc., same work, p. 992.) Then, leaving immediately, they shook the dust from their feet[Col. 0919A] according to the Gospel, so that it might serve as a testimony against them, crying: “Let God see it and judge.”

(Ibid.; CASS. *chr.*, same work.) Meanwhile, news of Pope Leo’s death, which the legates had received, led them to think of returning. They therefore went to take leave of the emperor, who gave them the kiss of peace and loaded them with gifts, both for themselves and for Saint Peter. After this they departed very satisfied on the eighteenth of the same month. (Conc., same work; SIG., same work.) Two days after their departure, Patriarch Michael had them recalled on a specious pretext, intending to make them fall into a trap he had prepared for them. But the emperor enabled them to avoid it, and they reached Rome without serious difficulty.

(Hist. de l’Acad. des insc., volume I, part I, p. 276.)[Col. 0919B] Among the curious antiquities in the king’s cabinet is a beautiful agate which, after having remained for a very long time in the treasury of the Abbey of Saint-Evre at Toul, was presented to King Louis XIV toward the end of 1684. Formerly, according to the tradition of that monastery, it was regarded as one of the gifts that Cardinal Humbert had brought from Constantinople. At that time people believed they could discern in it Saint John the Evangelist, carried off by an eagle and crowned by an angel. It has since been recognized, however, as a purely pagan antiquity, perhaps the apotheosis of Germanicus.

(PEZ., same work.) What Humbert had been beside Pope Leo IX, he continued to be beside Victor II, his successor. Having accompanied him on a journey to Regensburg in Bavaria, Othlon, the bishop of that place, had an opportunity to know this great cardinal, and regarded that as a genuine distinction. On the same occasion it was observed that Humbert was so troubled by the corruption of the morals of his age, especially the corruption prevailing in princes’ courts, that he could not refrain from openly lamenting it.

(CASS. *Chr.*, same work, chapter 94.) Pope Victor, indignant that the monks of Monte Cassino had elected an abbot without informing him, and that the election had supposedly not been conducted according to the rules, sent our cardinal there to investigate what had happened and to administer justice. This was at Pentecost in the year 1057. (Chapter 95.) Humbert ran some risks on this mission. The abbey’s serfs,[Col. 0919D] stirred up by four monks without the knowledge of the others, and imagining that the visitors had come to depose their abbot, threatened serious consequences. But the newly elected abbot, acting prudently, calmed the disturbance and voluntarily renounced his election. Our cardinal took part in the subsequent election of the monk Frederick, formerly his colleague in the legation to Constantinople and later pope, as has been seen. After this ceremony, which took place on the Friday in the octave of Pentecost, (chapter 96) he accompanied the new abbot to Tuscany, where the pope was then staying and where Frederick received the abbatial blessing. Humbert praised to the pontiff the good discipline observed at Monte Cassino and issued the bull that the pope granted to Frederick to confirm his election. From this it is clear that our cardinal was at that time performing the functions of chancellor and librarian of the Roman Church.

(Chapter 97.) At Victor II’s death, Frederick himself—whose advice the Romans wished to follow in choosing his successor—first named Cardinal Humbert to them, and then four others, as the men most capable of occupying the Holy See. But the votes united in favor of Frederick himself, who took the name Stephen IX (Conc., same work, p. 1090) and retained Humbert in the offices of librarian and chancellor. In this dual capacity Humbert subscribed the privilege of that pope in favor of the church of Marsi.

[Col. 0920B] (CASS. *chr.*, same work, chapter 101.) Always assiduous at the side of the new pope, Humbert was present at his death, which occurred at Florence after a pontificate of very brief duration. Having learned that an election had immediately been held at Rome in violation of every rule—an election that caused the schism mentioned above—and that his fellow cardinals who had opposed it had been forced to hide, he withdrew to Benevento. From there he was asked to go to Monte Cassino, where he spent Easter of the year 1058. (Book III, chapters 7, 10.) There he presided over the election of Abbot Desiderius, who later became pope under the name Victor III. Humbert was already bound to him by friendship and had formerly introduced him advantageously to Leo IX, thereby securing for him the pope’s esteem and goodwill.

[Col. 0920C] When peace was restored to the Church through the canonical election of Nicholas II, which took place at the very end of the same year, Humbert attached himself to the legitimate pope and enjoyed with him the same influence he had held under his three predecessors. He and Cardinal Boniface, bishop of Albano, were, in the words of Saint Peter Damian (PETR. DAM., Book I, letter 7), like the eyes of that pope. (Conc., same work, p. 1094.) During Nicholas’s pontificate Humbert continued to perform the offices of librarian and chancellor of the Roman Church, as is shown by the privilege that Nicholas granted, only a few days after his election, to the monastery of Saint Felicity near Florence. (Pp. 1105–1107.) He attended the councils that the same pope held at Rome and Benevento, and doubtless also those at Sutri and Melfi.

(LANF., same work, chapter 2.) At the Roman council of 1059, where the famous Berengar acknowledged his errors, Humbert was charged with drafting the profession of faith that Berengar had agreed to subscribe as proof of the sincerity of his return to the Church’s common belief. This unfortunate scholastic later had the misfortune to protest against that profession and to use it as an occasion to heap atrocious insults upon our illustrious cardinal. Humbert was no longer alive at that time. But in Blessed Lanfranc he found a powerful apologist who knew how to turn back upon Berengar the blows with which he had sought to pierce his innocent adversary.

(CAVE, p. 527, 2; *Rom. Pont. vit.*, volume I, p. 797; OLD. *Ath. Rom.*, p. 349; CAL., same work, p. 71, chapter 55.) Authors are greatly divided concerning the date of this great man’s death. Some defer it indefinitely until after the year 1064, while others extend it as far as 1073. John of Bayon, a fourteenth-century writer, places it instead as early as May 1061 and adds that Pope Nicholas himself took care to bury our cardinal with appropriate honors in Constantine’s basilica at the Lateran, near the bodies of Saint Rufina and Saint Secunda—or rather, as Ughelli states (same work, p. 127), of the holy virgins and martyrs Materna and Secondina. What is certain concerning the date of his death is that it cannot be placed later than 1063. We have proof of this in the writings of Saint Peter Damian (*opusc.* 9, chapter 7). This celebrated writer, citing the testimony of Cardinal Mainard when fewer than three years had yet passed since the death of Pope Nicholas II—and therefore after July 1063, or during the first months of the following year, 1064—already described Mainard as bishop of Blanche-Selve, where he had succeeded Humbert. This agrees with Ughelli’s opinion (UGH., same work), which places Humbert’s death before 7 May 1063. The day he assigns him is the same day assigned by John of Bayon. (CAL., same work.)

All posterity has shown extreme respect for Humbert’s memory. Saint Peter Damian (PETR. DAM., same work, 19, chapter 4), who had lived with him and could therefore speak about him with authority, reporting certain events on the basis of his testimony, calls him “a man of the highest authority,” *summae auctoritatis vir*, whose words bore every mark of truth. Blessed Lanfranc (LANF., same work) gives him, in a few words, praise as grand in expression as it is true in meaning. After exalting his learning, orthodoxy, and perseverance in the practice of every Christian virtue, he calls the entire Latin Church to witness what he asserts; Lanfranc adds that the Church knew Humbert well because he had always attended, and sometimes even presided over, its assemblies and councils. (MAB. *act.*, volume IX, p. 274, note 22.) “Humbert’s memory,” says Bishop Atto, the historian of Saint John Gualbert, who wrote somewhat less than a century after Lanfranc, “is still celebrated at Rome and continues in our own day through a multitude of good works.”

By giving Humbert two separate entries in his *Apparatus* (POSS. *App.*, volume I, pp. 773, 776)—one in which he makes him a monk of Toul and then a cardinal, and the other in which he presents him as legate at Constantinople—Possevin appears to have made two different persons of him.

We have lingered somewhat over the history of this great man because, until now, no one had taken the trouble to collect in sequence and present from a single perspective the material that could show him as he truly was.

[Col. 0922A] ## HIS WRITINGS

According to Lanfranc’s testimony (LANF. *in Ber.*, chapter 2), Humbert’s learning was very extensive. Nevertheless, he did not employ it to write a great deal, limiting himself to doing so on occasions when the needs of the Church required it. In this he imitated the Fathers of the early centuries, who took up the pen only in the same cases of necessity. The following works by him have been preserved:

1. A reply to the letter of Michael Cerularius, patriarch of Constantinople, and Leo, bishop of Acrida and metropolitan of Bulgaria—the same letter that had been addressed to John, bishop of Trani in Apulia, and that Humbert had translated into Latin before his legation[Col. 0922B] to Constantinople (HUMB. *in Gr.*, pp. 283–307).

At first it is not clear what motive or reason induced our cardinal to write again against this letter, which Pope Saint Leo IX had already refuted, as has been seen, and whose refutation by that pontiff Humbert himself and the other legates were carrying with them. But two things may have occurred, either of which would have been sufficient to lead him to undertake this new work. Since he began it in Constantinople, he may have learned, being on the scene, either that the authors of the letter were making verbal replies to Saint Leo’s writing, or that they complained that he had not answered them point by point. Therefore, in replying to it in turn, Humbert followed the latter method.

After a brief and well-composed preface, he reports the text of the letter article by article and then answers each one, imitating in this what Saint Augustine had already done when refuting the writings of Julian of Eclanum. To distinguish the text of his reply from that of the letter, Humbert took care to put obeli beside the latter and asterisks beside his own. Later, instead of these distinguishing marks, the word “Constantinopolitan” was placed at the head of the letter’s text and “Roman” at the head of Humbert’s text. Thus arranged, the writing forms a kind of dialogue between these two persons. It was already so arranged in Sigebert’s time, who presents it to us under this title (SIG. *scri.*, chapter 150).

Humbert knew enough Greek to translate it, but he did not possess the language sufficiently to write in it. (Chapter 150, 151; *conc.*, volume X, pp. 991, 992.) He therefore wrote in Latin; afterward the emperor had his reply translated into Greek by a certain Paul and his son Smaragdus, and ordered that it be preserved in the city archives.

We shall not stop to provide an extract from this work of Humbert. Abbé Fleury has already done so with his customary adequacy (FLEU. *H. E.*, Book LX, no. 6), and from what he says one may obtain a proper overview of the entire work. We shall merely observe that the matters with which it deals[Col. 0923A] are neither grave nor particularly important. It is concerned with rebutting the reproaches—or “calumnies,” as they are called—that the schismatic Greeks directed against the Latin Church: using unleavened bread in the sacrifice of the altar, fasting on Saturday, eating blood and strangled meats, and finally interrupting the singing of the *Alleluia* during Lent. In his reply Humbert handled these matters with as much advantage and intelligence as a learned man could display.

Nevertheless, able theologians (Perp. *de la F.*, volume I, Book II, chapter 6) reproach him for attributing to the Greeks certain consequences that he draws from their writings, as though they were doctrines that the Greeks had explicitly maintained. He sometimes proceeds in the same way in the following work. Cardinal Bona (BON. *not. auc.*, p. 23), for his part, judges that Humbert, through excessive zeal in defending the rites of the Latins, sometimes descends into minutiae.

2. (HUMB. *in Nic.*, pp. 314, 324.) A refutation of the writing of Nicetas, surnamed Stethatos by the Greeks and Pectoratus by the Latins. He was a monk of Stoudios, a famous monastery in Constantinople itself, who, having come to the support of Patriarch Michael and Bishop Leo, made the same reproaches against the Latin Church as they did and further defended, against Latin usage, the marriage of priests. For this reason Humbert believed himself authorized to accuse the Greeks of the heresy of the Nicolaitans (Conc., same work, p. 1096), a designation that Pope Nicholas II later applied to married clerics in one of his letters.

[Col. 0923C] Since Nicetas’ writing was in a somewhat lively style bristling with barbs, Humbert replied in the same tone and even surpassed him. For the rest, his reply displays considerable learning and even a critical sense, which was then very rare. It contains a good many details concerning the rites of the Latin Church of that period, especially regarding the Mass and fasting. It also contains proofs of the real presence of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist. But the most favorable idea one can give of this reply is that God used it to convert Nicetas, who consequently retracted his errors and anathematized his own writing, as related above.

[Col. 0923D] 3. (HUMB. *com.*, pp. 325, 326.) A short account of what took place in Constantinople during the legates’ stay, but only from 24 June 1054 until 20 July of the following month, the day of their second departure. For, as has been seen, after departing on the eighteenth, they were recalled two days later and immediately sent away again in order to avoid the trap that Patriarch Michael had laid for them. The account also includes several events that occurred afterward.

(Pp. 326–328.) Following this account comes the act of excommunication that they had placed upon the altar of Hagia Sophia on 16 July. First, in a few words, they praise the orthodoxy and religion of the emperor, the great men of the empire, and the wise citizens of Constantinople. Then, turning to Michael—improperly called patriarch, they say—and to his followers, they compare them with nearly all the ancient heretics: the Valentinians, Arians, and Donatists, and attempt to support this comparison. Consequently, the legates pronounce anathema against them unless they convert. It is principally in this act that Humbert imputes to the Greeks consequences drawn from their doctrine or conduct as though these had been formal dogmas. It is addressed to all the children of the Catholic Church and bears the names of Humbert and the two other legates.

(LAMB. *Bib.*, book III, p. 160.) This act is found translated into Greek and embedded in one of the accounts that Michael Cerularius composed on his own side concerning what had taken place in this great affair. The manuscript containing both is in the Emperor’s library. There are two different accounts by this patriarch on the subject: the first is contained in two letters addressed to Peter of Antioch and printed among M. Cotelier’s *Monuments of the Greek Church* (*Eccl. Gr. Mon.*, vol. II, pp. 135–145, 162–168). The other account is properly nothing more than the decree that this patriarch opposed to the legates’ excommunication—a decree written in a historical style and published in Greek and Latin by Leo Allatius (*ALLAT. De lib. gr.*, pp. 161–181). It is in this decree that the act in question is embedded, having first been faithfully translated into Greek from the Latin original (*HUMB. com.*, p. 326; *Sig. an. 1054*). It is nevertheless certain that Cerularius had initially falsified it, intending thereby to incite the people against the legates; he was convicted of this by the faithful copy that they sent to the emperor. Apparently he feared exposing himself to the same disgrace thereafter. For this reason he inserted it into his own writing in its original form.

We have four editions of the three or four writings of Cardinal Humbert that have just been discussed.

In 1604 Baronius and Canisius published them independently of one another (*BAR. An.*, vol. XI, appendix, pp. 995–1014; *CANIS.*, vol. VI, pp. 111–197), without consultation: the former in the appendix to the eleventh volume of his *Annals*, from a Vatican manuscript; the latter in the sixth volume of his *Lectiones antiquae*, from a manuscript in the library of the Elector of Bavaria. The entire difference between these two editions is that Baronius did not provide the continuous text of the letter of Michael Cerularius and Leo of Acrida (*BAR. An.* 1054, nos. 19–20), and transferred into the body of his work the brief account of what occurred at Constantinople, together with the act of excommunication that follows it. In Canisius’s edition, by contrast, these two pieces appear immediately after the others; and the collection begins with the letter that Humbert refutes in his first work. In both editions, the writing of the monk Nicetas was likewise placed at the beginning of the second work. From Canisius’s edition the collection passed into the various *Libraries of the Fathers* (*Bib. PP.*, vol. XVIII, pp. 389–416), where the name of the diocese of Bishop John, to whom the letter of Michael and Leo is addressed, could easily have been corrected. It is there given as *Cannensi* instead of *Tranensi*. The finest, as well as the most accurate, of the four editions is the one published by M. Basnage when he renewed Canisius’s collection, reprinted at Antwerp in 1725 (*CANIS. B.*, vol. III, part I, pp. 277–328). The brief account together with the act of excommunication is also found in the general collection of the councils (*Conc.*, vol. IX, pp. 991–993).

[Col. 0925B] Gesner records a separate edition of the writing against Nicetas, produced at Cologne in 1521 (*GESN. Bib. univ.*, p. 361-1). But since he is mistaken in giving this writing the title *Dialogue*, which belongs to the refutation of the letter of the patriarch Michael and Bishop Leo, he may very well also have been mistaken in reporting this edition, which is unknown to the other bibliographers.

**4.** Humbert has another writing, much longer than all the preceding ones taken together. It is a treatise against the simoniacs, who were so numerous in his century and against whom all the popes of his time issued so many repeated decrees. The work is divided into three books, and each book into several chapters, often quite long. As many as fifty-three are counted in the third book; but the last nine are missing, as appears from the table at the beginning of the book, where they are listed. Dom Mabillon had taken this treatise from a manuscript in the Laurentian Library of the Grand Duke of Tuscany, which seemed to him contemporary with the author and might well have been Humbert’s autograph (*MAB., It. Ital.*, p. 168; *MART., Anec.*, vol. V, p. 631). It was from Mabillon’s copy that Dom Martène first presented it to the public in the fifth volume of his *Anecdotes* (*MART.*, ibid., pp. 629, 844).

The first book of the Treatise, and several passages of the subsequent books, are in dialogue form, sometimes between the Corrupter and the Censor, sometimes in the form of objections and answers (*CAL., Hist. de Lor.*, vol. IV, part II, p. 72). John of Bayon, author of the Chronicle of Moyenmoutier, who counts only two books in this treatise, says that Humbert composed it during his stay in Florence. We have seen that he did in fact spend some time in that city, following Popes Victor II and Stephen IX. It was precisely at that time that he began the work. We have proof of this in the work itself (*HUMB., in Sim.*, book III, chap. 7). Praising the Emperor Henry the Black for his zeal in combating simony, he praises him as already dead, which occurred in 1056. Speaking, by contrast, very harshly of Henry I, King of France, because he favored it, he supposes him still alive; and it is known that Henry died only in 1061. This, considered together with the events of the author’s life, shows that he completed his work in 1057, or before March of the following year, when he left Florence to withdraw to Benevento, and from there to Monte Cassino.

(L. I, chaps. 7, 8.) Humbert undertook it to refute a certain writer named Spinosule, who had published a work in favor of ordinations performed by simony or by simoniacs. As far as one can judge from the passages Humbert quotes from him, Spinosule seems to have defended these ordinations not merely as valid but also as lawful: *ut puta quibus nihil desit in nulla gratia* (“as though they lacked nothing in any grace”) (chap. 7). Humbert undertakes to demonstrate the contrary on both points, so that the principal aim of his work is to establish that such ordinations are at once null and illicit.

To achieve this, the author lays down various principles, supporting them with the authority of Scripture, the Fathers, and the councils, and draws from them consequences favorable to his purpose (L. I, chap. 11; L. II, chaps. 11, 21; L. I, chap. 3; L. II, chaps. 34, 41). He establishes that heretics are worse than Jews and pagans, but that among all heretics none surpasses the simoniacs; that they believe the Holy Spirit to be not only lesser than the Father and the Son, and consequently subject to both, but also inferior and subject to themselves, as though he were a saleable thing (L. I, chap. 12); and that those ordained by heretics become their accomplices and are consequently subject to public penance. From this it follows that they cannot be ordained, since the canons forbid the ordination of public penitents.

(C. 19.) Humbert raises certain objections against himself—or rather reports those that were made to him. The strongest consists in saying that the canons prescribe that those who have been ordained through simony be deposed; from this it follows that they had received the grace and honor of ordination, since deposition is merely the deprivation of an honor received. To this he replies by citing the second canon of the Council of Chalcedon against simoniacs, which states that the grace of ordination cannot be sold. He further adds that it is clear from several passages of Scripture that the Holy Spirit can neither be sold nor bought (L. III, chap. 33). Returning elsewhere to the same objection, he maintains that the deposition of simoniacs is not the deprivation of an honor they had received, but an open refutation of their alleged promotion.

(L. I, chap. 21.) He further objects that it is at least true that simoniacs unjustly receive the Holy Spirit and the grace of ordination, and that, having received it unjustly, they confer it in the same manner upon those whom they ordain. Humbert replies that the Holy Spirit, being eternal justice, can never be acquired unjustly. It is evident from this that our author here confuses the grace of ordination with the essence of ordination. He was not, moreover, the only person in his time to regard simoniacal ordinations as null. We have seen that Pope Nicholas II established the same thing in one of his decrees (*BAL. Misc.*, vol. VII, p. 68, chap. 9); and perhaps he was influenced in this by Humbert’s work.

This work, for all that, is highly suited to inspire a salutary horror of simony, to make all its pernicious consequences felt, and to show the great evils that it had already caused in the Church. It is also written with an air of piety that moves the reader, and with a certain elegance that was not then common. It contains eloquence and great learning. The author does sometimes cite false documents, such as the decretals attributed to the earliest popes. It appears that he had read especially much of the poetry of Saint Prosper and had an exceptional appreciation for it.

**5.** Richer, chronicler of Senones (*Chron.*, book II, chap. 18), and John of Bayon (*CALM.*, ibid., p. 69), attribute to Humbert hymns and other pieces for the offices of various saints, specifically Saint Cyriacus, martyr; Saint Gregory, pope; Saint Hidulf; Saint Deodatus; Saint Columbanus; and Saint Othilia, virgin. They add that, after composing them, Humbert sent them to Brunon, Bishop of Toul, later pope under the name Leo IX, so that he might set them to music, or to plainchant. But Wibert, historian of this pope, who lived in his time, explicitly attributes these pieces to Leo both in substance and in musical notation (*MAB., Aet.*, vol. IX, p. 64, no. 13).

[Col. 0928A] **6.** Ciaconius (*Rom. Pont. Vit.*, vol. I, p. 797), Oldoini (*Ath. Rom.*, p. 349), and several others also attribute to Humbert a collection of various histories, which they do not otherwise specify. Vassebourg gives it the title *History of Humbert, Cardinal of Sicily*; and the learned Dom Calmet informs us that it concerns the history of the abbots of Moyenmoutier. But we have shown in its proper place that this work belongs to Valcande, a monk of that monastery who flourished before Humbert.

**7.** The authors already cited, and others after them, also wish to credit our cardinal with a commentary on the Rule of Saint Augustine. Here, however, they confuse Humbert, Bishop of Blanche-Selve, with Humbert, the fifth master general of the Order of Saint Dominic, who is the true author of this commentary.

[Col. 0928B] **8.** Finally, Oldoini attributes to Cardinal Humbert a writing in defense of the perpetual virginity of the Blessed Virgin, against those who attacked it. This, however, he does not prove, and it is established nowhere else. Yet one cannot deny him the translation of the letter of the patriarch Michael and Bishop Leo to John of Trani, as it is read at the head of the reply he made to it, since the historian of Pope Saint Leo IX attributes it to him (*MAB., Act.*, vol. IX, p. 76, no. 9). It was also stated above that Humbert drew up the profession of faith that Berengar signed in 1059.

[Col. 0927]

# ANOTHER NOTICE FROM GALLAND

(*Biblioth. vet. Patr.*, Prolegomena to vol. XIV.)

## On Humbert, Bishop of Silva Candida, and Nicetas Pectoratus

[Col. 0927C] Humbert was a monk of the Tullian monastery, of the Order of Saint Benedict. He came from Lorraine to Rome with Leo IX in the year 1049. He was soon made a cardinal and placed in charge of the monastery of Subiaco. He was learned in Greek; for this reason, in 1053, he translated into Latin the letters of Leo of Acrida and Michael Cerularius to John of Trani. After he had been designated Bishop of Silva Candida, he was sent the following year, 1054, as legate to Constantinople to suppress the schism. Having accomplished nothing, he returned to Rome. In 1059, under Pope Nicholas, he is said to have composed Berengar’s formula of abjuration, and finally to have died after the year 1064. While he was in Constantinople, at the request of Constantine Monomachus, he wrote a disputation between a Roman and a Constantinopolitan. And when Nicetas Pectoratus, a disciple of the younger Symeon and a monk in the Studion monastery, had published an infamous pamphlet against the Latins, which you will find below, Humbert vigorously refuted it. This occurred before the eleventh year of Monomachus. For in that year, when Humbert and the other legates came to the Studion monastery on the very feast day of Saint John the Baptist, Pectoratus anathematized that infamous pamphlet of his; he did the same again on the following day. Thereupon he was received by them into communion and became their intimate friend. Whether he persevered is doubtful; the praises bestowed on him by the Greeks give rise to suspicion. We have also appended to the preceding writings a commentary on what the apocrisiarii did against Michael and the others, taken from the Canisian-Basnage collection. These writings concern especially the unleavened bread, the celibacy of priests, and the observance of the Sabbath during Lent.

[Col. 0929]

# HUMBERT OF SILVA CANDIDA AGAINST THE CALUMNIES OF THE GREEKS

(*GALLAND, Biblioth. vet. Patr.*, XIV, 192.)

## [ARGUMENT]

The calumny of the bishops Michael of Constantinople and Leo of Acrida, who obstinately breathe forth the pestilential fumes of various heresies against the holy Roman Church and the apostolic see—indeed, against the entire Latin and Western Church. This calumny, composed in Greek and addressed to John, Bishop of Cannae [read: of Trani; Michael addressed his letter to the Bishop of Trani, who, because he favored the Greeks and was more inclined toward them, was deposed by Nicholas II at the Synod of Apulia, as Peter Damian testifies], as an insult to all Latins, was brought to Trani and presented to Brother Humbert, Bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida. Through his efforts it was translated into Latin and delivered to Lord Leo IX. It has also been faithfully preserved here for the caution and information of many, not for any practical benefit, but so that all who wish to know may have access to it.

[Col. 0929A] **MICHAEL**, universal patriarch of New Rome, and **LEO**, archbishop of Acrida, metropolis of the Bulgarians, to their beloved brother **JOHN**, Bishop of Cannae.

### I

The great love of God and the joyful compassion of our hearts have moved us to write to your holiness, and through you to all the chief priests and priests of the Franks, and to the monks and peoples, and to the most reverend pope himself, and to speak of the unleavened bread and Sabbaths that you improperly observe in a mystical sense, and of your communion with Jews. For the Jews themselves were commanded by Moses to observe unleavened bread and Sabbaths; but Christ is our Passover. In order that he might not be found an adversary of the Law, he was circumcised and first celebrated the legal Passover. Then, when he departed from it, he instituted our new Passover. This is clear [Col. 0929B] in the Gospel according to Matthew. Speaking of the mystical supper, the evangelist says:

> “Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying to him: ‘Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’ He said: ‘Go into the city to a certain man and say to him: “My time is near; I am keeping the Passover with you and my disciples.”’”

And a little later:

> “When evening had come, he was reclining at table with the Twelve. And while they were eating, he said: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me.’”

And a little later, when Judas said, “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” he said to him, “You have said so.”

Up to this point, O men of God, everything belongs to the legal Passover. Then he added the things that are mystical and ours; for the evangelist says:

> “While they were eating, Jesus took bread, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which will be delivered for you.’ And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: ‘Drink from it, all of you; this is my blood of the New Testament.’”

By saying “new,” he showed how the things belonging to the Old Testament had come to an end. See how, under the New Testament, he called the bread his body. You call it *bread*; we call it **ἄρτον** (*arton*). *Artos* is interpreted as “raised” and “carried upward” from leaven and salt, possessing warmth and elevation. Unleavened loaves, however, differ in no respect from lifeless stone and are comparable to brick-clay joined to the earth below and to dry mud. Moses commanded the wretched Jews to eat them with bitter herbs once a year, because they are symbols of evil suffering and tribulation. But our Passover is entirely joy and gladness, and because of its joy it raises us from the ground to heaven, just as leaven, by its own warmth, raises bread—a bread filled with every sweetness. Unleavened bread, having neither salt nor leaven, is dry mud.

Or have you not heard Jesus saying to his disciples, “You are the salt of the earth”? And that “the kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until it was all leavened”? He calls the woman the holy Church. The three measures, filled in three ways, signify the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, of whom the muddy unleavened loaves have no share whatsoever.

David also says of Christ: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” Before Abraham and Moses, acknowledging God as the God of heaven and earth and of all other creatures, Melchizedek rose and offered him bread and wine. Therefore the divine Apostle says:

> “For if perfection had been through the Levitical priesthood, Christ would not have been called a priest according to the order of Melchizedek” (Heb. 7:11).

And because “when the priesthood is changed, there is necessarily a change of the law” (ibid., 12), this is the law that established the observance of muddy unleavened bread for the Jews.

[Col. 0931A] ### II

The same great Paul, speaking of these matters in his First Epistle to the Corinthians, says:

> “Brothers, I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which will be delivered for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also concerning the cup: ‘This cup is the New Testament in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.’ For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup in remembrance of me, you will proclaim the Lord’s death” (1 Cor. 11:23–26).

The unleavened loaves also commemorate God, but they do not proclaim his death, like the Mosaic loaves established by the Law fourteen hundred years ago, and cursed and abandoned through the New Testament—that is, through the holy Gospel and through Christ.

[Col. 0931B] ### III

But how do you observe Sabbaths in a Jewish manner during Lent? Or have you not heard the evangelist saying that, as the disciples were passing through the grainfields on the Sabbaths, they began to make their way by plucking ears of grain and eating them? The Jews said to Christ: “See what these men are doing on the Sabbaths?” He said: “Yes. Or do you not know what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him—how he entered the temple and ate the bread of the Presence,” and so forth? And because “the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” They also said, “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” [Col. 0931C] (Mark 2:23ff.; Luke 6:1ff.).

Again, when Christ was speaking on the Sabbath, and when the man who had a withered hand was cleansed, and likewise the man who had a demonic spirit was cleansed on the Sabbath, while the Jews murmured and said similar things, Christ said:

> “Hypocrites! Does not each one of you untie his ox or donkey from the manger and lead it away to water?” (Luke 13:15).

He said the same concerning the paralytic whom he healed. Therefore those who observe Sabbaths together with unleavened bread are neither Jews nor Christians, but resemble a leopard, as the great Basil says, whose hair is neither wholly black nor wholly white.

[Col. 0932A] ### IV

But how do such people also eat strangled animals, in which the blood remains? Do you not know that the blood of every animal is its life, and that whoever eats blood eats its life? Therefore, on this account, they are not wholly pagans either. For pagans kill or eat animals after striking them.

### V

Moreover, during Lent you do not chant *Alleluia*, but only once at Easter. This is interpreted as “The Lord has come: praise him, sing a hymn, and bless him.” Therefore, on this account, you do not chant either “Lord, Lord,” or “Blessed is he who comes.” This word *Alleluia* is also spoken in Hebrew.

### VI

Why do you neither see nor understand such an enormous deception, nor correct the peoples and yourselves, as those who must be judged by God on account of these things? Do you not abandon what is said—that Peter, and Benedict, and Paul, and the others taught this? You deceive yourselves and the people in these matters. What I have written is what Peter, Paul, the other apostles, and Christ taught, and what the holy Catholic Church has received and religiously observes. You too, once corrected, must observe these things. Cast away unleavened bread and the observance of Sabbaths to the wretched Jews, and likewise strangled animals to the barbarian peoples, so that we may become pure in the right and undefiled faith, and one flock under the one shepherd, Christ.

Having been filled with divine blood at his cross, we praise in purity and without impurity the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We abandon all the practices of the Mosaic Law to the godless Jews, who, like blind men seeking Christ, have lost the light and remain forever in the shadow, like fools.

These things, O man of God, you yourself have often acknowledged and taught together with the people, and, once corrected, you have written to many who held similar customs. To secure the salvation of your soul, send this to the chief priests and priests, and adjure them to correct themselves and God’s people in these matters, so that you may have God’s reward for them. And if you do this, I propose, in a second writing, to write to you things greater and more perfect than these, as a true exposition of the faith and a strengthening of the souls for whom Christ laid down his life.

# THE TEXT OF THE AFOREMENTIONED SLANDERERS EXPLAINED

[Col. 0931]

## [ARGUMENT]

Here begins the response of Brother Humbert, called Bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida, written by him in Latin in the form of a dialogue during the time of his apocrisiariate at Constantinople. At the command of the devout and orthodox emperor Constantine Monomachus, it was published in Greek under the names of the Constantinopolitan and Roman, in the year of the Lord 1054.

[Col. 0931D] ### I. THE ROMAN

With the grace of the holy and undivided Trinity shining before us, in whose hand we and our words are held, we now undertake a reply to your letters and quibbles, so that it may be clear that we have been instructed in the discipline of that supreme Peter who said:

> “Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with gentleness and fear, keeping a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who malign your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame.”

The Lord figuratively indicated this through Moses, when he commanded that the poles by which the ark was to be carried should always remain in its rings and never be removed from them, lest there be any delay whenever it was necessary to lift the ark. The ark signifies the holy Church; its rings, divine Scripture; and its poles, the overseers of the Church, who should always be occupied with sacred Scripture, lest they shamefully wish to learn only at the moment when they are already required to resolve everyone’s questions for the exaltation of the holy Church. Accordingly, since we are about to examine your calumny point by point, we do not hesitate to begin from its very opening.

Moreover, so that your words may be distinguished more clearly from ours, yours are marked beforehand with obeli, while ours are marked with asterisks. But let us now see what sort of preface your calumny has, by which you labored to make your hearer favorably disposed, saying:

### II. THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN
