The great love of God and the joyful compassion of our hearts moved us to write to your holiness, and through you to all the chief priests, and to the priests of the Franks, and to the monks and peoples, and to the most reverend pope himself; and to speak of the unleavened bread and Sabbaths that you improperly observe in a mystical sense, and of your communion with Jews. For the Jews themselves were commanded by Moses to observe unleavened bread and Sabbaths.

### III. THE ROMAN

From this preface of yours, as you profess, we would believe that you seek the salvation of the entire Latin or Western Church solely out of the great love of God—if we knew that you did not neglect yourselves and your own people. But since you neglect both yourselves and those entrusted to you, keeping among yourselves and in your company the impious Jacobites, indeed the Theopaschites, or other plagues of heretics, and neither avoiding their companionship, their conversations, or their meals, nor refusing to pray together with them, how can we even suspect that you have been moved by any love of God or neighbor to sympathize with our perdition, as you suppose?

And why have you so hardened the ears of your hearts against the commandment of the glorious Paul that you do not heed him when he says:

> “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second admonition” (Titus 3:10).

Paul himself, knowing that the faithful have no part with the unfaithful, avoided Irenaeus and Philetus. He also commanded Timothy to avoid Alexander the coppersmith. Why do you likewise fail to heed blessed John, who solemnly declares to the faithful:

> “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, and do not say ‘Hail’ to him. For whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works” (2 John 10–11).

But you, as though everything clean were unclean to you, closing your eyes against yourselves and your own people, proclaim the holy Roman Church and the entire Western Church polluted by heresy and Judaism, and avoid it as though it were some abomination. From this blind and hitherto unheard-of audacity you have advanced to the point of surpassing the presumption of all the heretics whom we have so far been able to identify. Although individual heresies have each afflicted certain members of the Church with their inventions, none has yet erupted into such madness as to presume to impose its opinion upon the first and apostolic see, together with the imposition of an anathema.

Review, if you please, the volumes of all the heresies from the beginning of Christianity down to our own times, and you will see whether any of them has dared to do such a thing. When you find none, then at least come to your senses, lest—God forbid!—you remain the nearest precursors of that Antichrist who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped.

Standing upon the mountain of his arrogance, and judging from his lofty brow that everything beneath you lies prostrate, you say that the compassion of your hearts has moved you to write to all the priests of the Franks and to the most reverend pope. But not only the Roman and Frankish priests, but the entire Latin Church, cries out from the mountain of the house of the Lord, contradicting you:

> “I trust in the Lord. How can you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Psalm 10:2).

Yet the one whom you called the most reverend pope you ought to have revered, not detested.

### IV

As for your shameless calumny that we share with the Jews by observing unleavened bread and the Sabbath typologically, we believe that long-standing madness has so utterly destroyed your understanding that you neither consider your own deed nor your own statement. Therefore we advise you to return to your senses and attend to what Moses commands in Exodus concerning unleavened bread:

> “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, toward evening, you shall eat unleavened bread, until the twenty-first day of the same month toward evening. For seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened, that person shall perish from the assembly of Israel, whether resident alien or native of the land. You shall eat nothing leavened; in all your dwellings you shall eat unleavened bread” (Exod. 12:18–20).

Likewise, earlier:

> “For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day there shall be no leaven in your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened, that person shall perish from Israel, from the first day through the seventh day. The first day shall be holy and solemn, and the seventh day shall be venerated with the same solemnity. You shall do no work on them, except what is required for eating, and you shall observe the unleavened bread” (ibid., 15–17).

Likewise, in what follows, namely in chapter thirteen of the same book of Exodus:

> “You shall eat unleavened bread for seven days, and on the seventh day there shall be a solemnity of the Lord. You shall eat unleavened bread. For seven days no leaven shall appear with you, nor in all your borders” (Exod. 13:6–7).

Likewise:

> “You shall observe the solemnity of unleavened bread: for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time of the harvest of the new grain” (Exod. 34:18).

And in Leviticus:

> “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month toward evening, it is the Lord’s Passover; and on the fifteenth day of this month is the solemnity of the Lord’s unleavened bread. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. The first day shall be especially solemn and holy for you; you shall do no servile work on it, but shall offer a sacrifice by fire for seven days. The seventh day, however, shall be more celebrated and holier, and no servile work shall be done on it” (Lev. 23:5–8).

And in Numbers:

> “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, it is the Lord’s Passover, and on the fifteenth day is the solemnity. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. The first of these days shall be venerable and holy; you shall do no servile work on it, and you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven year-old lambs without blemish, with the offerings for each of them and fine flour mixed with oil—three-tenths for each bull, two-tenths for the ram, and one-tenth for each lamb, that is, for the seven lambs—and one goat as a sin offering, to make atonement for you” (Num. 28:16–22).

And in Deuteronomy:

> “Observe the month of new grain and the first of spring, so that you may keep the Passover to the Lord your God, because in this month the Lord your God brought you out of Egypt by night. You shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God from sheep and cattle, in the place that the Lord your God will choose, so that his name may dwell there. You shall not eat leavened bread with it; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, the bread of affliction, because you came out of Egypt in fear, so that you may remember the day of your departure from Egypt all the days of your life. No leaven shall appear within all your borders for seven days, and none of the flesh that was sacrificed in the evening on the first day shall remain until morning” (Deut. 16:1–4).

### V

All these things, if the legislator of the old law judged that they were to be observed in this manner by carnal Jews in a carnal sense, are plainly altogether foreign to us according to their carnal observance. For during those seven days leavened bread is found, appears, and is eaten every day throughout all our boundaries and territories and in our houses. Nor do we observe those seven days with unleavened bread in any way differently from the other days of the whole year. Nor among us does the soul of anyone—whether immigrant or native—who eats leavened bread during the aforesaid days perish from our assembly.

Nor, like them, do we take on the tenth day of the first month a year-old male lamb from the flocks and keep it until the fourteenth; nor do we sacrifice it at evening and mark our doorposts with its blood; nor do we eat its flesh roasted by fire at night, hurriedly, girded and shod, holding staffs in our hands, with unleavened bread and wild lettuces.

Moreover, on these days we do not offer incense or a burnt offering to the Lord every day—two young bulls from the herd, one ram, seven unblemished year-old lambs, with the offerings for each and fine flour mixed with oil—nor one goat for sin, so that atonement may be made for us.

In what, then, do we share with the Jews? And in what do we keep the feast of unleavened bread? Or perhaps it is because we hold the same days as solemn and free from work, and observe them from the fourteenth moon until the twenty-first? And why do you observe the same things, unless they signify one thing for us and another for them? For to them these things were given [Col. 0935D]

[Note: [Col. 0935D] Here something is evidently missing that would fully and reasonably supply the sense, referring back to the opposition marked in the preceding clause by “one thing for us” and “another thing for them.” It may therefore reasonably be supposed that the author originally wrote the beginning of this phrase in the following words, or in words scarcely different: “For these things were given to them to be observed in memory of their departure from Egypt; but to us in memory of …” EDIT.]

in memory of our spiritual departure from this world, so that we may be free to contemplate and see that he is the God who called us from darkness into his marvelous light, making us rise again and sit with him in the heavenly places; and so that, like the lunar sphere, we may begin to turn the light of our heart—that is, our understanding—away from earthly things and toward heavenly things. Thus, by thinking upon and seeking the things above, we may live again for God and die to the world.

So, too, everything that above we denied that we observe carnally, with the Lord’s approval we both observe spiritually and earnestly desire to observe in every respect. We undoubtedly believe that whatever was written was written for our instruction, as blessed Paul declares:

> “All these things happened to them in figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Cor. X, 11).

### VI

Now let us come to the observance of the Sabbath. Concerning it, this is prescribed in Exodus:

> “Remember that you sanctify the Sabbath day. Six days you shall labor, and shall do all your work. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. You shall do no work, neither you, nor your son, nor your daughter, nor your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your beast, nor the sojourner who is within your gates. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth and the sea, and all that is in them, and he rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the Sabbath day and sanctified it” (Exod. XX, 8–11).

Likewise, in the same book:

> “Six days you shall labor; on the seventh day you shall cease from plowing and reaping” (Exod. XXXIV, 21).

In this observance of the Sabbath, then, where and how do we share with the Jews? On the Sabbath they are idle and keep the day free from work; they neither plow nor reap, and do no work as usual, but hold a feast and banquet, while their male and female servants, oxen, and beasts rest.

We, however, observe none of these things, but do every kind of work, just as on the preceding five days, and fast just as we fast on the Friday immediately before it.

But if you do not Judaize, tell us why you share with the Jews in a similar observance of the Sabbath. They certainly celebrate the Sabbath, and you celebrate it; they feast, and they always break their fast on the Sabbath. In their Lent they break their fast every Sabbath except one, and in your Lent you break your fast every Sabbath except one.

For them there is a twofold reason for celebrating the Sabbath: first, the commandment of Moses; and second, because they rejoiced on this day over the death of the Lord, whom they did not believe would rise again, while the disciples were mourning.

Therefore, because you celebrate the Sabbath with the Jews and Sunday with us, you seem in this observance to imitate the sect of the Nazarenes, who receive Christianity in such a way that they do not abandon Judaism.

The Latin Church, however, sharing in the grief of the Lord who suffered and was buried, rejoices with him as he rises on Sunday, when the Jews were overcome by excessive sorrow and the guards of the tomb attempted to conceal the truth with money.

Therefore, since we retain the apostolic tradition concerning the Sabbath even to the present day and desire to retain it to the end, we have thought it appropriate to set down here what our ancient and venerable Fathers thought and confirmed concerning this matter. Among them the most blessed Pope Sylvester, the spiritual father of the great Emperor Constantine Augustus, said, among other things:

> “If every Sunday is to be honored in the joy of Christians because of the resurrection, then every Sabbath is to be devoted to execration because of the burial. For all the Lord’s disciples spent the Sabbath in weeping, sighing for the buried Lord, while joy was present among the rejoicing Jews. But while the apostles were fasting, sorrow prevailed. Let us therefore sorrow with those who sorrow over the Lord’s burial, if we wish to rejoice with those same people over the Lord’s resurrection. For it is not lawful for us to observe, in the Jewish manner, the destruction of foods and the ceremonies of the Jews.”

When Saint Sylvester had said these and similar things, certain Easterners were displeased with this tradition of the apostolic see and preferred instead to celebrate the Sabbath with the Jews.

Agreeing with this opinion, Saint Pope Innocent says:

> “The clearest reasoning demonstrates that one must fast on the Sabbath. For if we celebrate Sunday out of reverence for the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ—not only at Easter, but also every week by repeating an image of that day—and if we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s passion, we must not omit the Sabbath, which appears to lie between the sorrow and joy of that time. It is certain that the apostles were in grief on those two days and hid themselves because of fear of the Jews. It is also beyond doubt that they fasted for those two days to such an extent that the tradition of the Church holds that the sacraments were not celebrated at all during them. This pattern must certainly be maintained every week; therefore the commemoration of that day must always be observed.”

If you think that one should fast only once, on a single Sabbath, then Sunday and Friday too should certainly be celebrated only once, at Easter. But if the image of Sunday and Friday must be renewed every week, it is madness to observe the custom of two days while omitting the Sabbath, since it has the same cause as Friday—namely, the day on which the Lord suffered and was also among the dead, so that, rising on the third day, he might restore joy after the preceding two-day sorrow.

We do not, therefore, deny that one should fast on Friday; rather, we say that this should be done on the Sabbath, because both days imposed sorrow upon the apostles and upon those who followed Christ. They, gladdened on Sunday, not only wished it to be the most festive day, but also judged that it should be observed every week.

Let us now examine the rest of your statements.

### VII. THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN

Christ is our Passover. In order that he might not be found opposed to the law, he was circumcised and at first celebrated the legal Passover; then, when that had passed away, he instituted our new Passover.

### VIII. THE ROMAN

You should understand that we grant that Christ is your Passover if you assert that he is also our Passover—indeed, the Passover of the whole Catholic Church.

But if, God forbid, you stubbornly contradict this, we shall listen to our Lord Jesus Christ himself warning his followers concerning false Christs and false prophets:

> “If anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ or, ‘There,’ do not go out, nor follow them” (Luke XVII, 23).

As for your statement that the Lord Jesus, after celebrating the old Passover, handed over the new Passover to his disciples for celebration—what wise person denies it?

But who would ever dare to maintain that our Lord Jesus Christ was circumcised and celebrated the old Passover so that he would not be found opposed to God according to the law, unless he were an obvious heretic?

In this matter you seem perversely to agree with the Marcionites and Manichaeans that one God gave the old law and another the new; or, to speak more openly, you wish to introduce a bad God and a good God. To prevent this good God of light from being found opposed to that evil one—that is, the God of darkness—he was circumcised and celebrated the old Passover. As though avoiding the anger of that tyrant, imagining him stronger, he pretended for a time to observe his law.

Far be such a poisonous doctrine from the ears and hearts of the faithful: that anyone should even suspect that the omnipotent and utterly simple Truth, who is Christ our God, ever pretended anything, or that the author of the old law is someone other than the author of the new. For the Truth itself declares:

> “Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have not come to abolish, but to fulfill” (Matt. V, 17).

And the Psalmist says:

> “For the lawgiver himself will give a blessing” (Ps. LXXXIII, 8).

Then you added:

### IX. THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN

This too is clear, as the Evangelist says in the Gospel according to Matthew, speaking of the mystical supper:

> “On the first day of unleavened bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, ‘Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’ He said, ‘Go into the city to a certain man and say to him: My time is near; I will keep the Passover with you and my disciples’” (Matt. XXVI, 17–18).

And shortly afterward:

> “When evening came, he was reclining with his twelve disciples. And while they were eating, he said, ‘Amen I say to you, one of you will betray me’” (ibid., 20–21).

And shortly afterward, when Judas said, “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” (ibid., 25), he said to him, “You have said it” (ibid.).

Up to this point everything belongs to the legal Passover of the God-man. Then the Evangelist added what is mystical and ours, saying:

> “While they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying, ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which will be given for you.’ And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying, ‘Drink from it, all of you; this is my blood of the New Testament’” (Matt. XXVI, 26; Luke XXII, 17–20).

By saying “New,” he showed that the things belonging to the Old Testament had ceased.

### X. THE ROMAN

We believe all these things—not from you, but as written by truthful Evangelists and consistently proclaimed by all orthodox Fathers. We proclaim that our Lord Jesus Christ completed the old Passover on the evening of the fourteenth moon and immediately began the new one.

Therefore, let us examine what follows.

### XI. THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN

Observe how he called bread his body under the New Testament, as something life-giving and full of spirit, and as a manifestation of heat. You call it *bread*; we call it **ἄρτος** (*artos*). Now *artos* is interpreted as “raised up” and “carried upward” by leaven and salt, possessing heat and elevation.

But unleavened bread differs in no respect from a lifeless stone and from clay joined downward to the earth, comparable to dry mud, which Moses once ordained that wretched people should eat with bitter things under the divine law, since these are significant symbols of evil suffering and tribulation.

### XII. THE ROMAN

In this argument of yours we approve only this: that the Lord Jesus called the blessed and broken bread his body under the New Testament, in remembrance of himself; that every such bread gives life and vivifies the world, being full of the spirit and heat of the living God; and that you call it **ἄρτος**, while we call it bread.

But we vehemently detest and anathematize the rest, as smelling and sounding of heretical vanity and presumption.

For who would dare to assert that any bread, apart from the mystery mentioned above, is full of spirit and animate, unless he were a disciple of Manichaeus? For in their madness, being truly filled with insanity, they shamelessly assert that bread and wine, wood, stone, clothing, and other such things possess a soul.

You should also know that your attempt to defeat us by denying that unleavened bread is bread, through the etymology of its name, **ἄρτος**, is utterly vain and childish. Experts in languages assign different etymologies to one name, according to human convention rather than the nature of things.

And throughout all the Scriptures we find bread called by the same name without distinction, whether it is unleavened or leavened. We shall begin to demonstrate this here.

### XIII

First of all, behold the manna: in the law, the prophets, and the Psalms, as well as in the evangelical and apostolic writings, it is called bread—that is, **ἄρτος**.

Thus in the Psalm:

> **ἄρτον οὐρανοῦ ἔδοκεν αὐτοῖς, ἄρτον ἀγγέλων ἔφαγεν ἄνθρωπος**

That is, in Latin: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels.”

And in the Gospel:

> **Κύριε, ἀεὶ δὸς ὑμῖν τὸν ἄρτον τοῦτον**

“Lord, always give us this bread.”

And in Exodus:

> **Οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἄρτος, ὃν ἔδωκεν ὑμῖν Κύριος**

“This is the bread which the Lord has given you.”

If, then, the manna—which was white and small like coriander seed, and as though ground with a pestle in the likeness of frost, and whose taste was like fine flour with honey—is called bread, or **ἄρτος**, by divine authority, although it had no resemblance or true taste of bread, we do not see how the name “bread” can be taken away from unleavened bread, which by nature, form, and taste is entirely bread and is called bread.

This is especially so since the angels are said to have eaten at Abraham’s and Lot’s houses hearth-baked loaves—**ἄρτους ὑποτέφρους**, “loaves baked under the ashes”—and since an angel is read to have brought such bread to Elijah in the desert.

But why say more? In the law and in the Gospel we find **τοὺς ἄρτους προθέσεως**, that is, “the loaves of the Presence,” which no one with any knowledge of the Mosaic law doubts were unleavened.

It is said:

> “Every offering that is offered to the Lord shall be made without leaven; neither leaven nor honey shall be burned in the sacrifice of the Lord” (Lev. II, 11).

And in Deuteronomy Moses called unleavened bread **ἄρτον ταπεινώσεως**, that is, “the bread of affliction.”

The word of the Lord addressed to Ezekiel also says:

> “And you, son of man, take for yourself wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt, and put them in one vessel, and make yourself loaves” (Ezek. IV, 9).

Behold, both here and in what follows they are called loaves, although no mention of leaven is made—so much so that one of them is called hearth-baked and barley bread.

Nevertheless, to say something from your own authorities, listen to what John the monk Damascene says in praise of the Mother of God:

[Note: [Col. 0939D] The passage is plainly corrupt.]

> **Ἐπεὶ αὖτε τῶν βροτῶν οὐσία διὰ σοῦ ὁμιλήσασα θείῳ πυρὶ ὡς ἔγκυμα**  
> [Note: [Col. 0939D] **ἄζυμα**.]  
> **πανάγνε παρθένε, ἐξ οὖ ὤπτης θεοτόκον ἀληθινὸν διαφυλάξαντα.**

“O all-holy Virgin, since again the substance of mortals, having through you communed with divine fire as [**ἄζυμα**, ‘unleavened bread’], … from whom the baker (?) [is said to be] preserving the true Mother of God.” The Greek is materially corrupt; the translation preserves all surviving words without supplying a conjectural sense.

Moreover, we want you to say whether the bread of which Solomon says, “Bread of deceit is sweet to a man” (Prov. XX, 17), and, “Stolen bread is sweeter” (Prov. IX, 17)—namely, the bread promised by the foolish woman—is leavened or unleavened.

Here too and there too it is called not unleavened bread but **ἄρτος**.

And because your entire argument attempts to draw us to believe, merely because Matthew says **λαβὼν ὁ Ἰησοῦς τὸν ἄρτον**, that is, “Jesus took bread” (Matt. XXVI, 26), that the Lord gave his disciples leavened rather than unleavened bread in remembrance of his passion, you should know that your position is quite weak if you have nothing else to support your side.

For every proposition that proceeds from opinion is doubtful; but what proceeds from knowledge is entirely certain and established. Therefore, if you have no stronger position, you will not claim our agreement on the basis of this one ambiguous expression. For, as we have shown at length above, unleavened bread, just like leavened bread, is called **ἄρτος**.

Moreover, Matthew, who wrote his Gospel in Hebrew, did not say, as the Greek does, **λαβὼν ὁ Ἰησοῦς τὸν ἄρτον**, but, as a Hebrew speaking to Hebrews:

> **Lachah Jesus lechem**—“Jesus took bread.”

You should know that in Hebrew *lechem* also denotes unleavened bread in Deuteronomy, where it is written:

> **lechem oni**, that is, “bread of affliction.”

And the loaves of the Presence are called **lechem pavini** [Note: **Panim**].

Thus in the Psalm manna is likewise called **lechem albicini** [Note: **Abirim**]:

> **achal is**, which is interpreted, “man ate the bread of angels.”

### XIV

Consider wisely, then, how your etymology from the name **ἄρτος** has been weakened by such abundant examples from the three principal languages, and take care not to prefer your leavened bread to our unleavened bread.

For if you do not obstinately resist manifest truth, and if you do not openly attack the Old and New Testaments, you must agree and profess with us that the bread which the Lord Jesus distributed at the supper to the first founders of his Church, in remembrance of his passion, was unleavened.

For, as has been sufficiently demonstrated above, during the seven days of Passover leavened bread was neither found nor seen in any of the houses or territories of Israel. Whoever was found to have it would perish from the assembly of the Israelites without delay, by just punishment, as a transgressor of the divine law.

If we believe the words of the Truth, who says, “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17), then we must also believe and proclaim that the Lord Jesus did not pass over even one iota or one stroke of the law, and that, entirely free from every transgression, he could say to his plotters:

> “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John VIII, 46).

Otherwise he did not bear the sins of many, nor pray for transgressors so that they might not perish; nor did he suffer for us, but was justly punished for his own transgression—especially since he would not only himself have been found to be a transgressor of the law when leavened bread was found with him at that time, but would also have made many disciples liable to death by feeding them leavened bread.

See where this argument of yours leads. For if it is said that anyone used leavened bread during the feast of unleavened bread, then the one who did not sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found is truly asserted to have died in his sin.

Moreover, you provide the Jews with great grounds for rejoicing in the Lord’s death, remaining in their error, and emptying our faith, if, boasting in the Christian name, they should charge Christ with what no Jew dared to charge him, either then or now, unless perhaps instructed by your teaching.

Although the chief priests and the whole council had sought false testimony against Jesus in order to put him to death, and had found none even in his words, none of them brought forward anything like what you allege. If such a charge had been made, it alone would have sufficed to destroy him.

They would no longer have said to Pilate, when he told them, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law” (John XVIII, 31), “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death” (ibid.), since they themselves would have killed one who had shared in leavened bread.

Indeed, the whole accusation against Jesus can easily be observed from Pilate’s question and the Jews’ answer, according to the Gospels of Matthew and Mark. When Pilate asked, “What evil has he done?” (Matt. XXVII, 23), they cried out, “Let him be crucified!” (ibid.).

According to Luke, the whole crowd that handed Jesus over to Pilate said:

> “We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding the payment of tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king” (Luke XXIII, 2).

A little later Pilate said to them:

> “I find no cause in this man” (ibid., 4).

And they said:

> “He stirs up the people throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee and reaching even here” (ibid., 5).

Then, after some further words, Pilate said to them:

> “You brought me this man as one who was turning the people away, and behold, I, having examined him in your presence, find no cause of death in this man regarding the charges you bring against him; neither has Herod. I will therefore chastise him and release him” (ibid., 14–16).

But they demanded that he be crucified.

John, however, reports that Pilate said to the Jews:

> “What accusation do you bring against this man?” (John XVIII, 29).

They replied:

> “If he were not a malefactor, we would not have handed him over to you” (ibid., 30).

And afterward, when Pilate said to them:

> “Take him yourselves and crucify him” (John XIX, 6),

they answered:

> “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (ibid., 7).

Would not this one lie of yours have been sufficient, among so many unjust witnesses rising against the Lord and lying in support of their injustice, if they had at least known this one fact? Would they not have pressed Pilate and said:

> “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he ate leavened bread at Passover”?

Or at least:

> “Because leavened bread appeared in his possession”?

Perhaps you will say that he did this secretly. Far from it! For he said to the high priest who questioned him, not only concerning his deeds but also concerning his words:

> “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews assemble, and I have said nothing in secret. Why do you question me? Ask those who heard what I said” (John XVIII, 20–21).

Could the master of the house in which he celebrated the Passover have been unaware of a violation of the holy law, when he was plainly an outstanding observer of ancestral traditions?

And if this too could have escaped him, or if he himself consented, could it have escaped Judas, an accomplice of the wicked Jews, who, according to the Psalmist, was “his like-minded guide and acquaintance” (Ps. LIV, 14), and especially since Judas was the treasurer?

The Lord himself pointed him out to the beloved John, saying:

> “It is he to whom I shall give the dipped bread” (John XIII, 26).

And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Simon Iscariot.

Behold, here he twice used the word **ἄρτον**, which you accept as meaning only leavened bread. If this is so, what prevented the wretched Judas, once that leavened bread had been pointed out, from openly betraying the blood of his teacher, just as he intended to betray him secretly?

Or why, in despair, did he need to say, “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. XXVII, 4), when by betraying a transgressor of the law he would have turned the Lord’s wrath away from himself and the people and earned favor?

To touch briefly on the divine law concerning this matter, consider what is said more fully in Deuteronomy:

> “If any prophet, or your brother, your son or daughter, your wife, or the friend whom you love as your own life, wishes secretly to persuade you to turn away from the observances of the law, do not consent to him or listen to him; nor let your eye spare him so as to pity or conceal him. Instead, immediately expose him to the people and kill him, so that the Lord may turn away from the anger of his wrath, have mercy on you, and multiply you, as he swore to your fathers” (Deut. XIII, 6–8, 17).

### XV

Here, lest anything seem to have been left undone, we also confront the ridiculous opinion of your people. Finding no cord from the holy Scriptures with which to draw the boat of their assertion to a shore of stability, they are dragged, as they drift, into the sea of divine omnipotence.

When we ask how the Lord Jesus could have had leavened bread at the supper, since it was not found anywhere in the territories of Israel, they answer:

“If he is believed to be omnipotent, he could suddenly have produced leavened bread from anywhere; or certainly he could have fermented the unleavened bread itself by blessing it.”

Everyone understands how frivolous this is. For in whatever way leavened bread might have appeared in his possession during the feast itself, he would have become a transgressor of the law, plainly deserving punishment, since he had handled leavened bread in contempt of the holy law.

But even if it had happened in some way, one of the Evangelists would have narrated so great a miracle, no less than the miracle in which water is said to have been changed into wine.

And although they describe the deeds and words at the supper so carefully that they even seem to recount certain details that might appear less necessary—such as the dispute among the disciples about precedence, or the Lord’s own command to sell one’s tunic and buy a sword—how could they have passed over in such obstinate silence the beginning of so necessary a sacrament, and, so to speak, the total metamorphosis that you imagine?

It certainly should not have been carelessly omitted, since it is the foundation of the whole Church and will preserve the condition of Christianity until Christ’s second coming. Through it we remain in Christ, and he in us.

Therefore, because you have been distressed by the difficulty of your assertion, you labor to prejudice us by appealing to Christ’s omnipotence. But we answer you faithfully and firmly:

Although the Lord Jesus has done and does whatever he wishes, he could not do this, just as at one time he could not make bread from stones.

If it is asked why, the brief answer is: because he did not wish to. But how is it known that he did not wish to? Because he could neither transgress nor did he transgress the law, which he came not to abolish but to fulfill.

You must therefore choose one of two alternatives. Either, rejecting leavened bread during the feast of unleavened bread, he fulfilled the law; or, having taken leavened bread, he abolished the law, for whose fulfillment he is found—God forbid!—to have claimed that he came.

Concerning the omnipotent Son of the omnipotent God, the Gospel of John says:

> “The Son can do nothing of himself” (Matt. V, 19).

According to Mark also, in his own homeland he could not perform many miracles.

### XVI

Here, omitting none of your evasions, we address the following argument. Since you realize that, according to the law and the Gospel, your leavened bread is rightly rejected, you attempt to assert that the Lord did not celebrate the Passover with the Jews on the fourteenth moon of the first month, but before the legal removal of leavened bread.

You endeavor to prove this from the Gospel of John, who says:

> “They themselves did not enter the praetorium, so that they would not be defiled, but that they might eat the Passover” (John XVIII, 28).

Consider at least from this with what absurdity you speak, since you once again do not hesitate to pronounce Christ a transgressor of the law. For it is said:

> “When the hour had come, he reclined at table” (Luke XXII, 14).

Although the law permits the Passover to be celebrated twice, it nevertheless expressly commands that the fourteenth moon be observed in every respect: the fourteenth moon of the first month for the clean, and the fourteenth moon of the second month for the unclean. Whoever presumed otherwise would perish from the midst of his people.

If it is asked why John called the fifteenth moon—the second day after Passover—“Passover,” when he seems to have needed to say, “They did not enter the praetorium so that they would not be defiled, but that they might eat unleavened bread,” of which that day itself was the first, you should know that the Evangelists use “Passover” and “unleavened bread” interchangeably.

Although the Lord said to his disciples, “You know that after two days the Passover will take place” (Matt. XXVI, 2), Matthew, mentioning the very day on whose evening the Passover took place, says:

> “On the first day of unleavened bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, ‘Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’” (ibid., 17).

Agreeing with him, Mark says:

> “It was Passover and unleavened bread after two days” (Mark XIV, 1).

And shortly afterward:

> “On the first day of unleavened bread, when they sacrificed the Passover” (ibid., 12).

If “Passover” and “unleavened bread” are not used interchangeably—so that at one time Passover means the feast of unleavened bread, and at another the feast of unleavened bread is understood as Passover—how can the statement stand:

> “It was Passover and unleavened bread after two days”? (ibid., 1).

According to your opinion, it ought to have been written:

> “It was Passover after two days, and unleavened bread after two days.”

But blessed Luke, dissolving every such controversy, says:

> “The day of unleavened bread was approaching, which is called Passover” (Luke XXII, 1).

And because the seven following days of unleavened bread were also called “Passover” by extension, along with the day that was properly called Passover, he makes unmistakably clear which day he specifically means when he says:

> “The day of unleavened bread came, on which it was necessary for the Passover to be sacrificed” (ibid., 7).

This plainly took place on the fourteenth moon at evening, when the lamb was killed. The Evangelist also testifies that this lamb was called Passover, since he says that the Passover itself was to be killed.

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles he relates that Herod arrested Peter and sent him to prison, intending to bring him out to the people after Passover. What he means by “Passover” he immediately explains by adding:

> “Now it was during the days of unleavened bread” (Acts XII, 3).

Nor is this surprising. For even in Exodus 3, when the Lord commands three feasts, he passes over the word “Passover” and orders only that the feast of unleavened bread be observed—a feast that cannot be observed without also observing Passover.

John, moreover, shows how he wished his statement to be understood:

> “So that they would not be defiled, but that they might eat the Passover” (John XVIII, 28).

A little later he says:

> “It was the preparation of Passover, about the sixth hour” (John XIX, 14).

“Preparation of Passover” means the preparation for Passover, when the celebration of the great Sabbath day was already being prepared or was imminent. Among the Jews this day was considered more solemn than the other paschal days. Out of reverence for it they feared being polluted by the presence or entry of a Gentile into the praetorium; moreover, they took precautions lest the bodies remain on the cross during the Sabbath.

There is no contradiction in calling the feast of unleavened bread “Passover,” since Passover itself was eaten with unleavened bread. Nor, throughout that entire day, as it is written, did leavened bread appear in those territories until the evening of the eighth day, which they held as the most solemn.

### XVII

Moreover, the consecutive eight days of these three feasts were treated as one day, just as the Lord says concerning the days of the Feast of Booths:

> “You go up to this feast; I am not going up to this feast” (John VII, 8).

Yet afterward he is said to have gone up when the feast was already halfway through and to have stood and cried out on the last day of the great feast:

> “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (ibid., 37).

### XVIII

Behold, in resisting your opinions we have perhaps been more verbose than necessary. But we must not be criticized for this, since we wished to eliminate a matter more necessary than anything else for the human race.

If the Lord Jesus could have transgressed the law, our faith would be empty, and our preaching empty as well; for it could then be taught that Adam’s sin harmed the human race, but Christ’s death accomplished nothing.

Now let us examine what follows. After you had interpreted **ἄρτον** in your empty declamations, as shown above, as “raised up and carried upward by leaven and salt, possessing heat and elevation,” you abominated unleavened bread in dreadful blindness and said:

### XIX. THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN

But unleavened bread differs in no respect from a lifeless stone and from clay joined downward to the earth, and is comparable to mud.

XX. **ROMANUS.** Alas! alas! alas! Lord God! Behold, we see the prophecy of the prince of the apostles fulfilled in our own times. “From among you,” he says, “there will be false teachers who will introduce destructive sects, and deny the Lord who redeemed them. Bringing swift destruction upon themselves, many will follow their debaucheries; because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed, and in greed they will trade upon you with fabricated words. Their condemnation has not ceased from ancient times, and their destruction does not sleep” (II Peter 2:1–3). In agreement with this sentence, the teacher of the Gentiles says to Timothy: “Know that in the last days perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, boastful, proud, blasphemers” (II Timothy 3:1–2), and so forth. A little later he says: “Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth—people corrupted in mind, rejected with regard to the faith. But they will not advance further, for their folly will be manifest to all, as theirs also was” (ibid., 8–9).

Thus, shamelessly disparaging unleavened bread, you do not fear to inflict unheard-of insults even upon that life-giving mystery of our redemption. Nor is it surprising that your mind grows dark in heavenly secrets, when on earthly matters it wanders so perversely that it believes unleavened bread—which sight, touch, taste, and daily use alike prove to be bread—to be a stone or dry brick clay. And, oh, how worthy a punishment for your error your madness would receive if, after you had been shut away and deprived of every comfort of human nourishment, someone were to set before you a stone or dry brick clay instead of unleavened bread! There, without doubt, in your extreme danger you would learn very clearly how greatly a stone or brick differs from unleavened bread, and that a wall is strengthened by stones or bricks, but the human heart by unleavened bread. Although these things sustain human life temporarily, no one dares deny that they are without a soul, just as leavened bread is—unless he is a mad Manichaean. Yet in the mystery of Christ’s body it unquestionably becomes life-giving food forever.

But while you strive to disparage the apostolic see concerning unleavened bread, you reveal yourselves to be teeming with the decay of an ancient heresy, by asserting that leavened loaves contain a soul, even apart from any mystery of the Lord’s passion.

XXI. As for your accusation that unleavened bread is joined below to the earth, we do not deny that such things are commonly prepared on stones or clay—not, as you say, joined to the earth. But these pass into the ordinary uses of human beings and other animals; they do not approach Christ’s great table. Only that bread which the deacons with the subdeacons, or the priests themselves, clad in sacred vestments, mix amid the melody of psalms and prepare on iron, then bring forth from the sacristy, is admitted there.

Indeed, as the apostolic Acts indicate, deacons were appointed especially for this work, when Peter said: “It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables” (Acts 6:2). But you, just as you reproach us for doing so, prepare your leavened bread neither on stone nor clay nor any kind of metal. Therefore you either prepare it in water, or manna comes down from heaven for you, which you possess for human and divine uses.

XXII. But let us come to the rest of your frivolous arguments. Moses is not found to have said that unleavened bread symbolized an evil passion and tribulation, but rather *lechem oni*, that is, “bread of affliction”—not because it naturally contains anything afflictive, but because it recalls to the Hebrews that, compelled to leave Egypt, they carried on their shoulders the flour they had mixed before it was leavened. As we have sufficiently explained above, these matters do not concern us according to the observance of a carnal rite. Let us therefore examine what follows.

XXIII. **CONSTANTINOPOLITANUS.** Our Passover is entirely joy and gladness, and because of its joy it lifts us from the earth to heaven, just as leaven, because of its own heat, raises bread; and that bread is filled with every sweetness. But unleavened bread, having neither salt nor leaven, is dry clay.

Have you not heard Jesus saying to his disciples: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13)? And: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened” (Matthew 13:33)? By “woman” he calls the holy Church; by “three measures,” that is, three filled *modii*, he means the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, of whom muddy unleavened bread is in no way a participant.

XXIV. **ROMANUS.** We wish to celebrate with you a Passover that is wholly glad and full of joy, in the land, certainly, of the living, because this has been granted to human beings in the land of the dying, where there is both lament over past scandals and fear of those to come. Therefore, if you desire afterward to rejoice continually in the Passover, do not meanwhile remain without fear in this state of mind. Rather, as the Psalmist exhorts: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Psalm 2:11). Earnestly ask with the apostles that your joy may be complete.

What you also assert—that Passover lifts you from the earth to heaven through joy—must indeed be put into practice. For if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on things above, not on things upon the earth. Otherwise your soul is not lifted toward God, but against God.

XXV. Since you compare your joy to leaven, which raises bread by its heat, we now wonder what kind of joy it is, because we scarcely find leaven used in a good sense, nor is leavened bread, apart from consecration, in any way more pleasant than unleavened bread; indeed, most people consider unleavened loaves healthier and more flavorful. But what your proposition amounts to is disclosed by this conclusion of yours.

XXVI. **CONSTANTINOPOLITANUS.** Unleavened bread, having neither salt nor leaven, is dry clay.

XXVII. **ROMANUS.** You assail unleavened bread with such repeated insults that you almost inflict injury upon all visible and invisible natures. For if, as you define it, whatever has neither salt nor leaven is dry clay, then blessed spirits and the souls of the righteous, or even the four elements themselves from which all visible things exist, are clay, since they have neither salt nor leaven.

Nor was it enough for you to spew forth such sacrilege unless you also produced the Lord as a witness to your opinion, as though, merely to commend and prepare your leavened bread, he had said to his disciples: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13), and “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven” (Matthew 13:33).

Therefore, since you are pleased to understand literally words that are spirit and life, be pleased also to add some vine branches and mustard to your leavened bread. For the same Lord says to his disciples: “You are the branches” (John 15:5), and: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed” (Matthew 13:31)—which, of course, supplies the heat that your entire calumny praises so highly in leaven.

Know, nevertheless, that your exposition of the hidden leaven is contrary to catholic doctrine. If that woman signifies the Church, and the three measures the holy Trinity, where, when, and for what purpose does the Church hide leaven in the blessed Trinity? Or could anyone ever have contributed, or ever contribute, any increase to the supreme and immutable good, God?

You would therefore have expounded this parable more suitably if you had said that the kingdom of heaven signifies the holy Church; that the leaven signifies apostolic teaching; and that the three measures signify the three sons of Noah, for whom, after the Flood, flour was measured—that is, the mass of the entire human race. In this mass the woman, that is, Wisdom, coeternal with God the Father and made from a woman, hid apostolic teaching like leaven, and united the kingdom of heaven—that is, the present Church—from diverse nations.

XXVIII. Since, after your repeated disparagements of unleavened bread, your insolence has now burst forth to the point of openly and irreverently attacking the terrible and life-giving sacraments of our redemption themselves, crying out that unleavened bread is muddy and in no way a participant in the holy Trinity, we are compelled henceforth to answer you fools according to your folly, lest you appear wise to yourselves.

Know with absolute certainty that your boasting is dung and a worm. Today you are exalted, and tomorrow you will not be found. According to the Psalmist, you will be crushed like dust before the face of the wind and wiped away like brick clay; according to the proverb of the Wise One, you will be fit to be pelted with ox dung and trampled like dung in the road, just like your heretical predecessors and forerunners of Antichrist.

For as it is said in the book of blessed Job: “From the time God placed humanity upon the earth, it has been known that the praise of the wicked is brief and the joy of the hypocrite lasts but a moment” (Job 20:5). Since you think yourselves wise when you disparage the teachings of others, we shall repay you in kind with what will bite your shamelessness, so that it may withdraw [it or you] from insulting the revered sacraments.

XXIX. Therefore, with the reverence due to the body of our Lord Jesus Christ preserved, let us inquire whether, among leavened and unleavened bread prepared for human tables, leavened bread is more sincere and purer than common unleavened bread. First, let us reconsider leavened bread, so that, having carefully examined its source, we may form a true judgment concerning its purity.

A stream must necessarily follow the quality and nature of its spring. We therefore wish to discover the origin of leaven just as we discover the origin of every human being in earth, the mother of all things. For if we call one human being the origin of another, that will already be offspring, not origin; likewise, leaven cannot be the origin of leaven.

According to common opinion, leaven originates when either the foam of must, or the dregs of a certain rustic drink called *cervisia*—“beer”—among the Gauls, or indeed the broth of boiled barley or chickpeas, or corrupted fig-milk or animal milk, is put into mixed flour.

Since foam, dregs, boiled legumes, and the corrupted milk of figs or animals are counted among filthy things by human beings, it is clear that leaven is not entirely free from filth. Whatever dough leaven is put into must be corrupted, as the most wise Paul says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole mass” (Galatians 5:9). Wherever corruption is mentioned in divine or human writings, there too some deterioration or defect of substance is shown to have occurred.

Therefore, if corruption can never be understood in a good sense, there is no doubt that unleavened bread is cleaner than leavened bread, since it admits no corruption from leaven and is made only from clean flour and pure water. If leaven is neglected in dough for some time, it corrupts it with such sourness that it is no longer useful for human purposes.

Moreover, leavened bread becomes moldy after a short time, whereas this happens very rarely to unleavened bread, which is full and solid, not swollen and cavernous like leavened bread. Although the latter is for the most part unequal to our praises, it is entirely equal to your morals. Corrupted by old leaven, it is discovered to be sour, cavernous, and swollen; and you likewise, corrupted by human opinion, appear sour in your loquacity and cavernous in your craftiness. Empty of divine knowledge, you proceed inflated with human knowledge, according to the apostolic saying: “Knowledge puffs up” (I Corinthians 8:1).

The Apostle also testifies there that the aforementioned vices are present in such a person, saying to Timothy: “If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the teaching that accords with piety, he is conceited, knowing nothing, but diseased with disputes and quarrels over words, from which arise envy, strife, blasphemies, evil suspicions, and conflicts among people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth” (I Timothy 6:3–5).

That leaven is placed in an evil sense in divine and human writings, as we have said, the Lord testifies in the Gospel: “Beware,” he says, “of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy” (Luke 12:1). And Paul says: “Purge out the old leaven” (I Corinthians 5:7). A little later: “Let us feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness” (ibid., 8).

In secular writings also, the satirist, rebuking the effeminacy and corrupt morals of the Romans, says:

> What did he learn? Only this: leaven, and how the wild fig, once it has been born within, comes out when the liver bursts?  
> > (Persius, *Satire* 1.24.)

XXX. If you search all the Scriptures, you will never and nowhere find leaven used in a good sense except in one passage of the Gospel, where the Lord compares the kingdom of heaven to leaven, signifying apostolic teaching.

But if you review all the Scriptures, you will never and nowhere find unleavened bread used in a contrary sense; rather, it signifies either sincerity or truth, as the Apostle says: “Let us feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (I Corinthians 5:8).

Therefore, let your duplicity, content with its leavened bread, cease trying to wrest unleavened bread from Roman and Latin simplicity. Otherwise, if it persists, let *anathema maranatha* fall upon it together with its leavened bread, and let it hear the prophet reproaching it: “Go to Bethel and transgress, and sacrifice praise from leavened bread” (Amos 4:5).

XXXI. Now let it be seen which of the Churches imitates the character of the Lord’s body with greater diligence and more subtle symbolism.

The Roman and Western Church offers unleavened bread prepared by the ministers of the sacred altar in the sacristy. It is made from a grain of wheat and clear water, prepared by fire, signifying that in the one person of the mediator between God and human beings, the God-man Jesus Christ, it believes and venerates three perfect substances: human flesh, a rational soul, and the Word of God, who is God.

The grain is likened to the flesh, which the omnipotent Divinity animated, formed solely from the Virgin’s flesh—like a grain from mother earth—by heavenly power alone and without any male mixture. Into it he infused a purer substance, namely the soul, like clear and noble water. From the beginning of his virginal conception the Word of God duly assumed these two substances, and, through the heat of his divinity as through fire, fashioned and consolidated them for himself.

Thus prepared, the unleavened bread, through the faithful invocation of the whole Trinity, becomes the true and unique body of Christ—not, as the Theopaschites wish, the body of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. You too seem to hold this view when you say that unleavened bread is not a participant in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; but understand, if you please, that leavened bread is a participant in them.

If you do not wish to be condemned with the Theopaschites on account of this perverse opinion, do not grant to the holy and impassible Trinity, in the very commemoration of the Lord’s passion, any participation or communion beyond consecration or cooperation alone. For in that visible sacrament the death of the Son of God’s humanity alone is commemorated, as the Apostle says: “Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (I Corinthians 11:26).

The Lord Jesus himself, distributing bread to his disciples in the special privilege of commemorating himself, said: “This is my body, which will be delivered for you” (ibid., 24). “My body,” I say, which, strengthened by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, the very Wisdom of God the Father eternally built for himself as a temple, over forty-six days, in and from the womb of the untouched Virgin. This body, soon to be dissolved into death for you and for many through the passion of the cross, the omnipotent Trinity will raise after three days, not permitting its Holy One to see corruption.

“My body,” I say—this is the body of the Son of God and the Son of Man, who goes as it is written of him. Therefore, as we said above, the whole blessed Trinity cooperates in the consecration of the Eucharist, but only Christ’s death is proclaimed in its breaking and use.

XXXII. Let us now consider what discipline and caution you observe regarding so great a mystery. At times you obtain leavened bread prepared by any man or woman for a price, to such an extent that sometimes you transfer bread bought from public merchants’ shops to the Lord’s table. You cannot deny that it has been handled by the unwashed and filthy hands of just anyone.

According to our account, it is composed of five substances: leaven, flour, salt, water, and fire. If you have corresponding meanings for all these in the simple and sincere flesh of the Savior, give them to us. It is only fair that you provide an explanation of leaven to us, just as we provide one concerning unleavened bread to you.

Lest it happen—God forbid!—that the perversity of the Manichaeans, in order to support its error, assert that these five substances are taken into the Christian sacrifice because of the five caves of darkness that they deceitfully imagine for themselves, give also a clear reason for that cutting by which you lift with iron a little crown from the bread for the holy sacrifice, when an unblemished host would seem more suitably to signify the immaculate body of the Lord, and the wholeness of the bread the wholeness of the Church, which becomes Christ’s body through participation in his completely whole body.

How this ought to be done Paul teaches the Corinthians: “The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the Lord? Because we, though many, are one bread and one body, all who partake of one bread and one cup” (I Corinthians 10:17).

Thus the Lord is read to have taken bread, blessed it, and broken it; he is not read to have cut it either before or afterward. Furthermore, what answer do you give for your custom of taking the holy bread of eternal life, crushed into the chalice and consumed with a spoon? For the Lord himself did not crush bread in the wine-cup and give it to the apostles, saying, “Take and eat it with a spoon, for this is my body.” Rather, as the holy Roman Church observes to this day, he blessed the bread whole and distributed it broken into individual portions, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body” (Matthew 26:26). After the meal he offered them the cup, saying: “Drink from it, all of you” (ibid., 27).

XXXIII. The holy Church of Zion, namely the first Church, has faithfully retained this institution, reverenced by angels and human beings, down to the present day, just as it received it from the apostles. Indeed, certain bishops of Jerusalem, in letters they sent, indicated how much their practice differs from that of the Greeks. For they left this written:

> From the holy city of Jerusalem itself, which is also called holy Hierosolyma, the Christian faith went forth. In this same holy Zion and holy Resurrection, the first Church is named and truly established. In that holy and venerable place the divine and immaculate offering of our Lord Jesus Christ is fulfilled, as is fitting, according to due order.

And I think they do well there in placing only whole and holy offerings upon the sacred patens, and in not having, as the Greeks do, an iron lance with which to cut the offering, that is, the *proscomide*, in the form of a cross.

Moreover, in the aforementioned holy Churches, when they elevate the holy anaphora—that is, the offering—with the holy paten itself, the offerings are genuine and appropriate, thin, and made from fine flour. They know no iron lance except that which opened the side of our Lord Jesus Christ. Nor do they have a spoon with which to administer Communion, as in the Greek Church, because they do not mix the holy Communion in the chalice in this way; rather, they give Communion to the people through the bread alone.

Thus, in both the great and the small Churches, all the Christians of that province possess this custom handed down to them by the holy apostles. The Greeks, living among them, follow it in some places, while elsewhere they follow whatever they received from their own people.

Furthermore, if anything remains of the holy and venerable Eucharist in the churches of Jerusalem, they neither burn it nor throw it into a pit. Instead, they place it in a clean container and the following day give it to the people in Communion, because they communicate daily there, since Christians from different provinces gather there who, because of their faith and their great love for the Son of God, desire to receive Communion there. For that place itself is more venerable and holier than all places throughout the earth. There is the holy and honorable tomb of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the holy place of Calvary.

To bury or place the holy Eucharist in the earth, as some are said to do, or to put it into a flask, or to pour it out, is great negligence and shows no fear of God. For the faith of Christians consists in these undefiled and divine mysteries, according to what Christ said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood will live forever” (John 6:55, 59).

But enough of this, especially since you yourselves can gather these matters more precisely from the substance of the letter that we have rendered from Greek into Latin for this purpose. There it is made clearer than daylight that the holy Church of Jerusalem anciently observed the same rite of the divine sacrifice which the holy Roman Church has not ceased to observe to this day.

We too place upon the sacred altars thin, whole, and sound offerings prepared from fine flour; after consecration we break them and communicate the people from them. Then, finally, we drink from the chalice pure and liquid blood, since we find that the Lord offered dipped bread to none of the disciples except Judas the betrayer, thereby signifying that he would betray him. In the same way, we also store what remains of the Lord’s offering.

XXXIV. Since it has been sufficiently established from the authority of the New and Old Testaments that our Lord Jesus Christ commended the commemoration of his passion to his disciples in unleavened bread at the very meal, just as the holy Roman and Latin Church is known to commemorate it today, you ought to say whose institution you defend so obstinately in leavened bread.

Whoever or whatever he may have been, according to blessed Job, compared with God, who is justice and wisdom itself, will not be wise. Nor could anyone have commended the most holy mystery of faith more suitably or truly than the one who offered himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a pleasing fragrance, the immaculate Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. Compared with him, that other institution is imperfect, and its ignorance is the greatest ignorance. Therefore, let us sift through the rest of your statements.

XXXV. **CONSTANTINOPOLITANUS.** David said of him: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4). Before Abraham and Moses, recognizing God as the God of heaven, earth, and the other creatures, he rose and offered him bread and wine.

Therefore the divine Apostle says: “If perfection had been through the Levitical priesthood, Christ would not be called a priest according to the order of Melchizedek; and since the priesthood is changed, it is necessary that the law also be changed” (Hebrews 7:11). That muddy law established that the Jews should observe unleavened bread.

The same great Paul, speaking of these matters in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, says: “Brothers, I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which will be delivered for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup: ‘This cup is the new testament in my blood. Do this, whenever you drink it, in remembrance of me.’ For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord” (I Corinthians 11:23–26).

XXXVI. **ROMANUS.** As long as you faithfully followed the footsteps of eloquent Paul, you ran entirely without reproach. But as soon as you tried to run ahead, you fell miserably. It was not enough for you to go astray; in addition, you preferred to drag behind you, resisting, the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, rather than escape your error by retracing his footsteps.

Moreover, you inflict an unheard-of injustice upon him when, attacking him with his own words, you declare unleavened bread to be muddy, although he himself and every catholic Christian assert it to be a sign of sincerity and truth.

Then, in defending your etymology of bread against us, you labor to make the Apostle your accomplice, as though, when he follows the truthful Evangelists and says, “He took bread” (Matthew 26:26; Mark 14:22; Luke 22:19), he had intended to affirm nothing but leavened bread. If this could be so, the preaching and labor of so great an Apostle would be empty. Christ’s death would be nullified, because he would no longer have delivered himself for us, but would have died justly as a transgressor of the law.

How frivolous your etymology is has already been shown sufficiently and abundantly. Let us now see where you are attempting to drag so great an Apostle by the ropes of your assertion.

XXXVII. **CONSTANTINOPOLITANUS.** Unleavened bread has neither a commemoration nor does it announce death, as the Mosaic law established fourteen hundred years ago; and through the New Testament—that is, through the holy Gospel and through Christ—it was cursed and abandoned.

XXXVIII. **ROMANUS.** O sacrilegious boldness! O poisonous and mad loquacity of the Manichaeans! O impiety that must be driven far from the strength and hearts of all! Have you dragged the Apostle into such an abyss of treachery that you have hurled him headlong there with you?

Behold the pestilential egg that you have been laboring to produce for so long: suddenly you have brought it forth. Whoever eats from it will die, as the prophet Isaiah says: “And what has been warmed will burst forth into a basilisk” (Isaiah 59:5).

Behold: clearly, you conceived pain, gave birth to iniquity, and, lying against the truth itself and all the divine pages, shamelessly bark that the Son of God cursed the law and the unleavened bread that he had established.

But O holy, O good, O venerable law, with all your commandments and observances! Whoever has cursed, curses, or will curse you and yours even to the least letter—let that person be accursed!

Could our Lord have been, or ought he to have been, so ungrateful as to overwhelm with any curse so faithful and devoted a herald and steadfast witness of his, one who never ceased proclaiming his glory with his whole purpose, by signs, commandments, sacrifices, ceremonies, and words?

And where did you learn that the Lord cursed the law and unleavened bread? Perhaps you will say: where he gave the new Passover to his disciples, or where he rose from the dead. But, as was clearly shown above, on that very occasion he instituted the new Passover with blessed and broken bread; and on the day of his resurrection itself, when two disciples invited him into the village of Emmaus, he took bread, blessed it, and immediately:

> “They recognized him in the breaking of the bread”  
> > —Greek: **ἐγνώσθη αὐτοῖς ἐν τῇ κλάσει τοῦ ἄρτου**  
> > (Luke 24:13, 30–31, 35).

It is entirely clear that this bread was unleavened, since until the octave of Passover no leavened bread appeared anywhere throughout the borders of Israel.

Indeed, that he himself, having been made under the law, had the testimony of the law, he says to the Jews: “Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life; and they are the ones that testify about me” (John 5:39). And again: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me” (ibid., 46).

Thus elsewhere he declares that he did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17). Whoever abolishes even the least commandment of it would be least in the kingdom of heaven—that is, in the present Church—not to mention entering in any manner that future kingdom in which the doer and teacher of the law would be called great.

On the day of his resurrection itself, to the two disciples mentioned above, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted the Scriptures that concerned him. Then, when the eleven were gathered, he said: “It was necessary that everything written about me in the law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms be fulfilled; and that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations” (Luke 24:44, 46–47).

In brief, the Savior made known that the humility of his incarnation and passion, the glory of his resurrection, and the calling of all nations and their salvation through baptism had been foreshadowed in the Old Testament and manifested in the New. Thus the Gospel ought rightly to be called nothing other than an exposition of the law.

That law, as the bearer and nurse of Christ and the Church—that is, of bridegroom and bride, head and body—being the lamp preceding evangelical grace and truth in the fullness of time, revealed openly what it had long hidden in the secret chamber. Then suddenly the one “more beautiful in form than the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3) shone forth in splendor to every creature, when through the holy apostles, to whom he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, he sent throughout the whole earth and to the ends of the world the mystery hidden throughout all former ages.

Therefore, should that womb be cursed which, made pregnant by the Spirit of God, from the beginning brought forth all the mysteries of Christ and the Church, and at the end of the ages gave birth to the Gospel itself, to be preached everywhere?

The Old Testament makes it possible for the virgin birth to be preached with open face through the New Testament, for the resurrection from the dead to be believed, and for the restoration of the human race through wood, water, and the Spirit. Otherwise, if the Old Testament were erased, the New would vanish and be considered a fable; nor could it be retained without its own distinguishing character, since a wall cannot stand without a foundation.

The Lord himself established this by his deeds and words, and inspired his apostles and preachers to secure the course of his narrative with the anchor of the Old Testament. The first teacher of the Church declares its authority more certain than the voice he heard spoken over the transfigured Lord. Therefore it must be believed most firmly and professed most freely that whoever contradicts the Old Testament is also an opponent of the New, which the holy Ezekiel saw existing within the Old like a wheel within a wheel (Ezekiel 1:16; 10:10).

### XXXIX. [Cols. 0955C–0956B]

Furthermore, the Old Testament is, as it were, the foundation or underpinning, while the New Testament constitutes its building or upper part. The latter must necessarily fail or collapse if the underpinning on which it rested fails or collapses; while the foundation remains, the structures resting upon it are often changed, but when it perishes or falls, they likewise cannot fail to perish or fall.

The Lord, author of both Testaments, wishing this to be understood, could by his omnipotent will have filled six empty jars at the wedding with wine suddenly created from nothing. Yet, for the sake of a certain mystery, he preferred that the same jars first be filled to the brim with water by the servants of the feast, and that afterward, by his mere command, the marvelous wine be made. In this prudent deed of our Redeemer, we say that the water changed not its substance but its qualities—that is, its taste, color, and whatever else belongs to this kind—so that we may understand that the Lord himself did not empty the Old Testament, with which he had filled the six ages of the world through the ministry of the earlier fathers, but renewed it; nor did he diminish anything in it by rejecting it, but, by approving it, displayed what was contained and hidden within it.

In some matters, apart from the mere change of times or variety of circumstances, the Law and the Gospel proclaim the same things in harmony. For example, the Law foretells: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers” (Deut. XVIII, 15; Acts VII, 27). And: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII, 14). The Gospel proclaims: “A great prophet has arisen among us” (Luke VII, 16). And: “The virgin conceived and bore a son” (Luke II, 7).

In some matters, while the time and subject remain the same, they recall words of piety and impiety. Thus: “My God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII, 46; Mark XV, 34). And: “He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him, let him save him, since he wants him” (Ps. XI, 9).

Moreover, if such water seems tasteless to anyone, let him know that this happens not through any defect of the water but through the excessive dullness of his palate. For the natural man does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God. The law of God is foolishness to him; he does not know how to fill the belly of his mind with it for health, but distends it ruinously. The spiritual person, however, who judges and discerns all things, faithfully sings with our steward Paul: “We know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully” (I Tim. I, 8). And: “We know that the law is spiritual” (Rom. VII, 14).

If the law is spiritual, then the ministry of the Spirit is examined spiritually, while the ministry of death is investigated carnally. Although the law by its nature is life, through human fault it becomes death, as the same Apostle says: “What shall we say, then? Is the law sin? Certainly not! But I did not recognize sin except through the law” (ibid., 7). And shortly afterward: “Therefore the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. Did then what is good become death to me? Certainly not! But sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good” (ibid., 12–13). And again: “I discover, therefore, a law wishing to do me good, while evil lies close to me” (ibid., 21).

Finally, if you have listened wisely to what we have set forth above, cease your insults against the Law, which the Apostle declares to be holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good. Otherwise you will seem, like a madman, to be burying under stones the physician who points out diseases and wishes to cure them.

### XL. [Cols. 0956C–0957B]

Moreover, you should know that the numerous marriages of the fathers, marriages within their own tribe, the carnal sacrifices, the ceremonies of circumcision and various purifications, and the distinctions among foods were temporarily either permitted or commanded to carnal people. This was so that the yoke—or the license—of such commandments might restrain them, lest they fall into idolatry or other crimes; while, through the spiritual meaning of the good things promised in them, it continually lifted them up, so that they might behold from afar the things that were to come and greet them devoutly.

Although, in accordance with their place and time, they seemed excessively devoted to such observances, so that by this condescension they might gradually draw the brutish multitudes through signs toward realities, what they understood by these things is clear from the words of blessed David: “If you had desired sacrifice, I would indeed have given it; you will not delight in burnt offerings. The sacrifice to God is a spirit troubled” (Ps. L, 18). Hence he says again: “In me are your vows, O God” (Ps. LV, 12).

Assuming David’s person, he bears witness to the carnal people, saying: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High” (Ps. XLIX, 13–14).

Had not the water of the Law changed its color and taste for this man and the other fathers, appearing pale and tasteless to carnal people? For those things were cold to them which burned so fiercely in the others that even then the disciples of Jesus could say: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV, 32.)

The letter of the Law, given through Moses, was killing the carnal; its spirit, brought about through grace and truth by Jesus Christ, gave life to the spiritual. Thus the former, contracted as though by the cold of temporal death, grew pale at the very source from which the latter, invigorated as though by the warmth of eternal life, blushed; and with Paul they freely proclaim: “The fullness of the Law is love” (Rom. XIII, 10). Truth declared that the whole Law hangs upon the two commandments of love.

If God is love, then unquestionably whoever attempts to remove anything from the Law of Moses opposes God, since God himself testifies that the whole Law hangs upon love. This twofold love, covered over by carnal and earthly ceremonies, like a two-pronged hook fitted with worms or flying feathers and lowered from heaven into the sea of human captivity, pierced with its invisible point human beings wandering empty of heavenly things, having been lured by visible objects; and, once pierced, it drew them back into the bosom of angelic freedom. They say to God in the Song of Songs: “Draw me after you” (Song I, 3). And: “I am wounded by love” (Song IV, 9).
