Thus, while the human being clings to God and is near to another human being, by a most fitting line and, as it were, a golden chain of the divine commandments, both are drawn back together toward paradise.

### XLI. [Cols. 0957B–0957C]

Furthermore, with what earnestness Euphration, bishop of the Rhodians, defended the Old Law against the Severian heretics is clear from his words quoted below. Among other things he said:

“The foundations of a splendid house are laid around filthy places, so that the upper parts may suffer no insult from dung. The upper parts of the house, therefore, are raised with gilded ceilings, painted walls, and varied marblework; but the lower parts, being close to the earthly moisture, also receive all the refuse from above.

“What, then, shall we do now? If we remove the lower parts, the upper parts collapse. Yet, if the lower parts had to be destroyed, no one else could do this except the Son of God. Let us see, therefore, whether he himself destroyed what we say remains. ‘Do you think,’ he says, ‘that I came to abolish the Law or the prophets? I did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it’” (Matt. V, 17).

You, therefore, at least, called back from your attacks upon the most sacred Law by these and other words of your own teacher, cease, lest you be anathematized with the Severians by him and by all Catholics.

### XLII. [Cols. 0957D–0960A]

But lest you still take excessive pleasure in your opinions, although you possess nothing, let us examine more carefully the Apostle’s statement, which above you attempted violently to draw to your support. He says:

“If perfection was through the Levitical priesthood—for under it the people received the Law—what further need was there for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not to be called according to the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that a transfer of the Law also take place” (Heb. VII, 11–12).

As was shown above, in these words you understand “consummation” to mean nothing other than consumption—that is, abolition and an end, not an end that perfects, but one that destroys. The same Apostle teaches that this is quite otherwise when he says: “Christ is the end of the Law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4).

Therefore, since “I have finished bread” is said in one sense and “I have finished a cloth” in another, we must understand Christ as the end of the Law in the sense of bringing it to completion, not consuming it; perfecting it, not annihilating it; completing it, not emptying it.

This End, promised from the beginning of the world and manifested at the end, became the evening and final sacrifice while he hung upon the cross for us. Knowing that all things had already been completed, “so that the Scripture might be fulfilled,” he said: “I thirst” (John XIX, 28). When he had received vinegar, he said: “It is completed” (ibid., 30). And, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.

There the Evangelist certainly does not say, “so that it might be consumed,” but “so that the Scripture might be completed.” Nor does the Lord himself say, “It has been consumed,” but “It has been completed.” At the voice of the dying man the veil of the temple was torn even to the bottom, signifying, according to the Apostle, that for those approaching Christ the veil that had until then been placed over the reading of the Old Testament was removed.

This completion did not come through the Levitical priesthood, because, as the Apostle testifies, it “brought nothing to perfection.” Lest you take from these words of the Apostle an opportunity for further slander, observe that he did not say, “The Law did nothing good,” but “It perfected nothing.”

For, as the same Apostle says, it had ordinances of worship, an earthly sanctuary, a tabernacle made by hand, and high priests of the good things at hand, who, entering the holy of holies once a year through another’s blood, sanctified the defiled for the purification of the flesh. From them gifts and sacrifices were offered, which could not perfect the worshiper according to conscience, being imposed only in matters of foods and drinks and various baptisms and carnal ordinances, until the time of correction.

But Christ, appearing as high priest of the future goods, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle not made by hand—that is, not of this creation—and not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, entered once for all into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption. When, through the Holy Spirit, he offered himself unblemished to God, he cleansed our conscience from dead works so that we might serve the living God.

Indeed, according to the Law, many became priests because death prevented them from remaining. But this man, because he remains forever, possesses an eternal priesthood. He alone, through his own blood offered once, completed eternal redemption; the others, continually imitating it through another’s blood, represented it imperfectly.

When this redemption arrived, the entire course of sacrifices and carnal ceremonies rightly came to rest. We no longer need many sacrifices, because in one sacrifice we have found eternal redemption. It was begun through the Levitical priesthood and is established as perfected through the high priesthood of the Lord Jesus. He is called a priest not according to Aaron but according to the order of Melchizedek because he established for his faithful that bread and wine should be offered and received in the truth of his flesh and blood.

His generation is ineffable: from the Father, without a mother; from the Mother, without a father; having neither beginning of days nor end. He alone is the true King of righteousness and peace.

Because Melchizedek is more fittingly likened to him than Aaron—not only because of the one sacrifice and genealogy but also because of the name—Christ is called a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, not according to Aaron.

That Melchizedek, finally, neither offered his own body and blood to the Divinity in bread and wine, nor was he without parents or beginning and end, nor was he substantially the King of righteousness and peace. Rather, whatever Scripture either kept silent about or said concerning that man signifies all these things more clearly in our Melchizedek. That man, like Aaron, was his shadow, not the reality.

When the priesthood is transferred to him, it is necessary that a transfer of the Law also take place: from the letter that kills to the Spirit that gives life; from oldness to newness; from imperfection to perfection; from slavery to freedom and adoption as the sons of God; from the Jews to the Gentiles, to whom the Apostle says: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. VIII, 15).

The Law has therefore been altered through its transfer, not made into another law; modified, not changed; increased by the arrival of grace, not emptied by its departure. As the Lord says to his own: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 20).

Did he say, “Unless you reject or altogether abandon the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven”? No. Rather, because their righteousness consisted only in refraining from evil deeds, the Lord willed that the righteousness of his own should abound beyond it, so that they would strive not only to cut off evil from their actions but also from their thoughts.

For according to the Law it was good for them not to kill and not to commit adultery; for these, however, through grace, it was something greater and perfect not to become angry and not to lust. Thus the Law cut off the branches of wickedness, while grace also tore out its roots.

And just as at the resurrection this same body of our humiliation, and not another, will be restored, so the Law itself, reformed through the Gospel, is proclaimed throughout the whole world. In this reformation, although the beauty of nature is greatly increased, its integrity is in no way removed. Just as with a grain, the animal body that was sown will rise as a spiritual body, and what was sown in weakness will rise in power.

By this reformation heaven and earth also will pass away, but they will not perish; they will be transferred, not removed. Nor should we be shaken from our understanding or terrified if the natural human sense recoils from some mysteries of the Law, since it has likewise recoiled from certain mysteries of the holy Gospel—to such an extent that, when the Lord said, “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI, 54), even the greater part of his disciples departed from him, saying: “This is a hard saying. Who can hear it?” (ibid., 61.)

Moreover, the New Testament is called “new” because what it promises is unquestionably eternal, just as the punishment of the wicked is eternal. As for its recitation or inscription, however, the Gospel itself will pass away entirely on the last day, when no Scripture will thereafter be necessary.

### XLIII. [Cols. 0960A–0961D]

Furthermore, if it were relevant to the matter, we could show that not merely fourteen hundred years, as you wrote, but more than fifteen hundred years elapsed from the institution of unleavened bread through Moses to Christ’s Passion. But since our intention is to approve the Roman rite of sacrifice, we leave it to the chronographers to refute your opinion concerning the number of years stated above.

Therefore, if unleavened bread, as you attempt to assert, was cursed, rejected, and abandoned through Christ and his Gospel, and if it ought no longer to be offered in the Lord’s sacrifice because it was established by Moses for the Jews, know that leavened bread was likewise established by Moses for the Jews.

As Leviticus says: “This is the law of the peace offering: he shall offer loaves of leavened bread with the sacrifice of thanksgiving, which is offered for peace” (Lev. VII, 11, 13). The same Moses says in the same book: “At Pentecost you shall offer him loaves of firstfruits made from two-tenths of fine flour, fermented, which you shall bake as firstfruits for the Lord; and you shall offer with the loaves seven lambs” (Lev. XXIII, 17).

Salt also, which you proclaim so emphatically together with leaven, was established for the Jews by Moses in Leviticus as follows: “Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt; nor shall you remove the salt of the covenant of the Lord your God from your sacrifice. In every offering you shall offer salt” (Lev. II, 13).

Consequently, if unleavened bread ought not to be offered by us because it is Mosaic, neither ought leavened bread or salt to be offered by you, since they are equally Mosaic.

And because, hearing from the Apostle, “The old things have passed away; behold, new things have come to be” (II Cor. V, 17), you foolishly think that all the mysteries of the Old Testament have been rejected, utterly destroyed, and reduced to nothing, you must now consider toward what difficulties this opinion of yours is hastening.

For if the old things passed away not by advancing but by failing, whence do you have a temple, altar, sacrifice, lampstand, and the other vessels and ornaments of holy ministry, or priestly garments? Whence do you have dedications, Pentecost, and Passover or Lent? Whence do you have high priests, priests, Levites, and the other ecclesiastical ranks in their order? Whence do you have firstfruits and tithes? Finally, whence do you have love of God and neighbor, and the other commandments of the Decalogue?

Therefore, according to you, if the new things were made so that the old were wholly abandoned and cursed by Christ, then all the things we have mentioned, and many others we have left unmentioned, must undoubtedly be cast away from his Church, and things contrary to the old must now become new. Let God and neighbor be hated; let father and mother be dishonored; let human beings be killed; let everyone commit adultery, steal, rage, lie, lust, and violate marriage; let there be no marriages at all. Let every person approach the nearest member of his own blood and anyone related to him by affinity.

To sum up, let no one eat, drink, or sleep. Let everything the Old Testament displayed and practiced, both in divine worship and in human use, be abandoned, and you will see that you will be neither beasts, much less human beings; indeed, you will pass from being something to being nothing.

We, rather, listening with the catholic ear to the great Apostle who says, “Therefore, if anyone is a new creation, the old things have passed away; behold, new things have come to be” (II Cor. V, 17), believe with the heart and confess with the mouth that the old things have become new by passing from the old man to the new man, Jesus Christ. The same Apostle immediately took care to explain this when he continued: “But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ” (ibid., 18).

By his singular newness all things heavenly and earthly are renewed, since whatever that former people had received from heaven for the worship of God or for its own benefit, he transferred to the new people.

The latter is called “new” because it has been transferred from shadow to truth, from signs to realities, from fear to love, from slavery to freedom and adoption as sons of God, and from the sons of wrath to the sons of grace—from flesh to spirit. Hence the Apostle says: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. VIII, 9).

And how were those to whom he gave instruction in his letters not in the flesh, unless in the sense in which he himself says: “Although walking in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh” (II Cor. X, 3)? Again he says: “None of you lives for himself, and none dies for himself” (Rom. XIV, 7). And: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 20).

Thus for us, and for all who strive to walk in the newness of the Spirit, all things have become new: temples, altars, priests, sacrifices, lampstands, censers, food and drink, and everything that carnal Israel retained both in its furnishings and in its commandments. All these things are old and not old at the same time, like the eagle, which, while naturally being renewed, gains youth and sheds old age, but not its substance.

In the same way we proclaim that the unleavened bread of Christians is very different from the unleavened bread of carnal Jews. The latter were invited to observe and grasp the shadow of truth by promise alone and by desire for earthly happiness: long life, abundance of crops, succession of children, destruction of enemies, and the like.

We, however, rightly venerating and retaining the body of truth from unleavened bread and in unleavened bread, already taste in mouth and heart how gracious the Lord is. We ask and seek from him this one thing: that we may remain in him and he in us forever.

Indeed, if you wish to change unleavened bread into leavened, change wine into some other liquid. For, like unleavened bread, wine is what Christ used to bring the old Passover to an end and begin the new. If you accept wine, why do you reject unleavened bread?

### XLIV. [Cols. 0961D–0962B]

That Christ’s Passion and death are more suitably proclaimed through unleavened bread than through leavened is demonstrated by the fact that the Lord himself entrusted the remembrance of him to his disciples in unleavened bread; and by the fact that in the Law it is called “the bread of affliction,” so that through it we may be admonished to afflict our souls and likewise offer to God a spirit troubled, a heart contrite and humbled (Ps. L, 19), recalling the Apostle’s words: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. II, 12). And: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (II Tim. II, 12).

Furthermore, Paul briefly gathers together the things that were imposed upon the carnal Jews through the Law until the time of correction, saying: “Gifts and sacrifices are offered which cannot perfect the worshiper according to conscience, being imposed only in matters of foods and drinks and various baptisms and carnal ordinances” (Heb. IX, 10).

The carnal sacrifices and various purifications in the Law—among which circumcision was the chief, together with the other carnal ordinances, such as distinctions among foods, the feast of Tabernacles, not plowing with an ox and an ass together, not sowing a field with different kinds of seed, and similar practices—which conferred no holiness upon consciences except through the devotion of obedience and the admonition of spiritual purity, were given until the time appointed by the Father, when, through his Son made under the Law, he redeemed those who were under the Law.

Escaping these carnal ordinances, the same Apostle says: “Whatever things were gain to me, these I have considered loss because of Christ; indeed, I consider all things loss, and even refuse, so that I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the Law, but that which is through faith in Jesus Christ” (Phil. III, 7–8).

He also declares this to the Colossians, saying: “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast day, a new moon, or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of future things” (Col. II, 16).

Let it suffice that we have thus far defended the Law of Moses and the unleavened bread of Christ’s Eucharist. Let us now examine what remains of your arguments.

### XLV. THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN. [Cols. 0962B–0962D]

But how do you observe the Sabbaths in Lent in a Judaizing manner? Or have you not heard the Gospel say that, as the disciples passed through on the Sabbaths, they began to make their way, plucking ears of grain and eating them? The Jews said to Christ: “See what they are doing on the Sabbaths!” He answered: “Yes. Do you not know what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him—how he entered the temple and ate the bread of the Presence?” (Matt. XII, 1–4; Mark II, 23–26), and so forth. “And because the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark II, 27).

They also said: “How can this man be from God, since he does not keep the Sabbaths?” (ibid.) Again, when Christ spoke on the Sabbath to the man who had a withered hand, and likewise to the man who had the spirit of a demon and was cleansed on the Sabbath, while the Jews murmured and said similar things, Christ said: “Hypocrites! Does not each one of you untie his ox or ass from the manger and lead it to water on the Sabbath?” (Luke XIII, 15). He said the same concerning the paralytic whom he made well.

Therefore those who keep the Sabbaths together with unleavened bread are neither Jews nor Christians, but “are like a leopard,” as the great Basil says, “whose hairs are neither altogether black nor white.”

### XLVI. THE ROMAN. [Cols. 0962D–0963B]

That we do not observe the Sabbaths in a Judaizing manner, either within or outside Lent, has been sufficiently shown above. But if you do not Judaize, why at least do you not spare Lent? Take care lest, keeping holiday and feasting with the Jews, you dissolve Christ’s fast on the Sabbath.

Therefore the Gospel testimonies you have cited wholly contradict you, while they support us. For we, like the disciples of Jesus, not only travel on the Sabbath and pluck ears of grain, but also fish, perform whatever work is necessary, and eat at the appropriate hour.

You, however, although you read that the disciples ate ears of grain as they passed by, strive from first light until evening to prolong drunkenness with various delicacies and much unmixed wine.

Nor is this surprising, since here too, having forgotten your own etymology, from the word ἄρτος [artos, “bread”] you said that David ate the bread of the Presence—that is, τοὺς ἄρτους τῆς προθέσεως [tous artous tēs protheseōs, “the loaves of the Presence”]—which you cannot deny were unleavened, if any knowledge of the ancient Law remains among you.

Furthermore, because the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark II, 27), it is not honored among us by a banquet or leisure as though it were a lord; rather, it is burdened with fasting and labor, like a devoted servant occupied with the Lord’s burial.

Immediately afterward, when the day arrives that the Lord made especially his own, we solemnly rejoice and celebrate, because on it Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over him.

Nor, for the sake of observing the Sabbath, do we fear being charged with hypocrisy by Christ, since on it we offer to God and to physicians not merely a withered hand but the whole body to be healed. Nor do we merely untie the ox and ass from the manger and lead them to water; we also plow.

But you, wishing to be teachers of the Law and understanding neither what you say nor the matters about which you make assertions, concluded your argument as follows.

### XLVII. THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN. [Col. 0963C]

Therefore those who keep the Sabbaths together with unleavened bread are neither Jews nor Christians, but “are like a leopard,” as the great Basil says, “whose hairs are neither black nor white.”

### XLVIII. THE ROMAN. [Cols. 0963C–0964A]

O marvelous philosophy of the Greeks! O Pelasgian art! O Athenian and Academic discernment! Whence has come upon you such stupor and sudden dizziness? Truly your tongue has been divinely bound with a threefold cord.

For the Greeks seek wisdom, which the simple preaching of the Christian faith has made foolish, as the Lord promised: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent. Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age? Has God not made foolish the wisdom of this age?” (I Cor. I, 20.)

Filled with this foolishness, you have defined nothing according to the divine Scriptures, and you show that the great Basil, according to human standards, defined nothing either.

For it is utterly false that those who keep Sabbaths and unleavened bread are neither Jews nor Christians. Those who keep Sabbaths and unleavened bread carnally are most truly Jews.

But the other statement also falls into endless uncertainty, and it will in no way follow that only a leopard is meant, whose hairs are neither white nor black, since besides the leopard there are countless animals whose hairs are neither white nor black.

O excellent investigators of divine discourse! O teachable disciples of the great Basil, from whose splendid fountain you have managed to draw nothing but mud! All around you that heavenly stream of eternal milk and honey was resounding, calling the Roman and Western Church its mistress and begging it to come to the aid of the ruin of the East.

Now, while gratuitously attempting to overthrow the Latin Church, you arm yourselves against us with a sentence of Basil that is found to be far more senseless than the ridiculous prophecy of Tiresias:

“Whatever I say, either it will be, or it will not.”

Indeed, what happened to you is expressed by the satirist’s proverb:

> The mountains labor; a ridiculous mouse will be born.  
> (Horace, *The Art of Poetry*, 139.)

Would that you had remained silent, so that you might have been thought wise, as Wisdom says: “A fool, if he keeps silent, will be considered wise.” But now your foolishness is known to everyone.

Let us examine what follows.

### XLIX. THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN. [Col. 0964B]

But how do such people also eat strangled animals in which blood remains? Or do you not know that the blood of every animal is its soul, and that whoever eats blood will eat its soul? Accordingly, they are not even wholly Gentiles, since those people kill animals, or eat them after striking them.

### L. THE ROMAN. [Cols. 0964B–0965A]

Why do you bring against us a command from the Law which, according to you, was cursed and abandoned through Christ? Are you alone permitted to do whatever you please, so that now you humbly flee to the protection of the Law, and now arrogantly recoil from it as though it had been anathematized?

Is it not the ancient Law, and not the Gospel, that forbids the eating of every strangled animal and everything seized by a beast? “For the soul of every animal is in its blood” (Lev. XVII, 11).

This command clearly belongs among those things that were given temporarily to the carnal people for some kind of purity or carnal righteousness, not for any holiness of mind. It concerns food; hence the Apostle says: “Let no one judge you in food” (Col. II, 16).

It is as though he were saying openly: Let no one distinguish you, as Jews, from those among whom you live by differences in food and in the other matters that the same Apostle added.

That here he used “to judge” in the sense of “to distinguish” is clear in the Epistle to the Romans, where, speaking of the different fasting practices of certain people, he says: “One judges one day to be above another; another judges every day alike” (Rom. XIV, 5).

Therefore, as the same Apostle says: “One believes that he may eat everything” (ibid., 2). Let the one who does not eat certain things, observing the custom of his homeland and province and the precepts of his ancestors, not judge the one who eats.

Who are you to judge another’s servant, who, with sound faith and a pure conscience, eats whatever he received from his ancestors as food? For, as the Lord says: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person” (Matt. XV, 11).

And according to the Apostle: “All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, and their mind and conscience are defiled” (Titus I, 15).

Addressing this to the Romans, he says: “I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean through him, except for the one who considers something unclean; for him it is unclean” (Rom. XIV, 14).

And shortly afterward: “The one who distinguishes, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith; but everything that is not from faith is sin” (ibid., 23).

Although all things are clean, nevertheless, according to the same Apostle: “It is evil for a person to eat through giving offense” (ibid., 20), when a brother of little faith and still weak in faith believes something to be unclean and therefore not to be eaten.

We ought to accommodate him by abstaining from such foods, so that we may win him for the Lord, lest he begin to abominate the Christian religion because of some food, and the brother for whom Christ died be lost through our food.

### LI. [Cols. 0965A–0966A]

Although, therefore, we have permission from the Lord and the Apostles to eat everything that harms neither our own salvation nor that of our brother, nevertheless, held until now by the customs of our provinces and the precepts of our ancestors, we avoid eating certain things—not because they are evil or unclean, but because they are in some way unsuitable for us or because, through long habit already turned into nature, they cause us disgust.

Is it not said that the dragon was given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia? And do not some nations eat things that others utterly abominate? Why is this, unless each nation, being sufficient in its own judgment, has adopted some things for itself and rejected others?

Thus we too, without guilt, consume in antidotes many things that we do not doubt were taken from serpents and other animals that we abominate.

What medicine of whatever kind is to a sick person, food of whatever kind is to one perishing from hunger. And just as a sick person is not to be abominated when artificially restored by the blood and carcass of certain reptiles, so neither is one wasting from hunger to be condemned if he naturally sustains his miserable limbs with blood and strangled meat. He can even say literally with blessed Job: “Things which my soul formerly refused to touch are now, in my distress, my food” (Job VI, 7).

For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving, since it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.

Do you not even count Christ’s pilgrims, needy and poor, among the Gentiles, to whom nothing is clean, because at times they retain from God the gift of the present life through whatever food they can obtain?

Why do you not instead open your sealed chests of money and storehouses overflowing from one place to another, and scatter their contents among the poor, so that your righteousness may remain forever and they may no longer be forced to take up unfamiliar food?

But now, enriched and exalted by usury and the oppression of the wretched, you reproach a needy person if he is sustained by something that you, fattened and gorged, abominate. You do not consider that the Lord desires mercy rather than sacrifice.

At the beginning of the human race after the Flood, he removed certain things as though they were unclean, although he had made all things very good. Yet it is the vice of rational creatures that is abominable to God, not that of irrational creatures. Human will also sometimes claims certain things for itself and sometimes relinquishes them.

Thus the Romans, only a few years before Constantine the Great, claimed for themselves the eating of pork through the emperor Aurelian. The Greeks, even to this day, reject bear meat.

And certainly, if you consult human judgment concerning these matters, the pig will prove more unclean than reptiles, filth, and the rest of its food.

But whether we or you eat what we have received from our ancestors or retain by custom, let us observe it in such a way that the one who does not eat does not despise the one who eats, and the one who eats does not judge the one who does not eat.

### LII

Consider, nevertheless, to what great folly your writing and wisdom have sunk: although it ought to seek from human beings the end of God’s commandments—that is, love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith—it thinks that the sole question to investigate is whether they have ever eaten bear meat. Although you do not admit the eating of it, you ought not to count it as a crime in those who do admit it, since evangelical and apostolic authority has established that everything is to be eaten by them. [Col. 0966B]

### LIII

Nor do those who defend “what has been strangled” and blood against you say this without qualification. For, carefully retaining the ancient custom or tradition of our forefathers, we too abhor such things—so much so that, among us, even when the person who has eaten it survives without immediate danger to life, severe penance is sometimes imposed for eating blood, or any animal killed by suffocation, or anything suffocated by water or by any other human negligence. This is especially because we regard the ancient customs and traditions of our forefathers, provided they are not contrary to the faith, as apostolic laws.

But concerning the other creatures that die through bird-catching, dogs, or hunters’ snares, we follow the Apostle’s command: “Whatever is sold in the market, eat, asking no questions for the sake of conscience” (1 Cor. X, 25). “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.” He also granted this when you are invited to a feast of the gentiles, saying: “If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience” (ibid., 27). The Lord also, providing food as a reward for his preachers, said to them: “Remain in the house of those who receive you, eating and drinking what they have” (Luke X, 7).

Behold, the Lord did not say, “Eat certain things that they have,” but indiscriminately, “what they have.” Therefore, any knowledgeable person who simply eats and drinks whatever comes to the market or whatever is set before him is in no way to be blamed, unless he thereby contracts some impurity in his conscience. For it is not what enters the mouth but what comes out of the mouth that defiles a person (Matt. XV, 11). No food is blameworthy; only an immoderate appetite is.

Yet, so that a brother weak in faith may not be scandalized—one who thinks that something is common or unclean—if someone says, “This was strangled,” or “This is carrion,” it should not be eaten, as the Apostle says concerning food sacrificed to idols: “If anyone says, ‘This was sacrificed to idols,’ do not eat it, for the sake of the one who disclosed it and for the sake of conscience. I mean not your own conscience, but that of the other” (1 Cor. X, 28–29).

Indeed, many things we observe through custom or the tradition of our forefathers, so that we shrink completely from doing otherwise—for example, eating with unwashed hands. Although, according to the judgment of Truth, this does not defile a person, nevertheless a person commonly shudders as though at something unclean when he sees someone eating with unwashed hands. [Col. 0966C–0967A]

### LIV

But perhaps you will say: “It was handed down by the Apostles to the gentiles, not only in the Old Testament but also in the New, that they should abstain from blood and from what has been strangled.”

We do not deny this. Nevertheless, we know that, according to place and time, the Apostles observed certain carnal commandments of the old law while darkness and light still mingled, as in the twilight of morning, and drew the eyes of those who looked now this way, now that. Thus the Apostles, while dwelling in Judaea, sometimes, awakened by the brightness of the Gospel, withdrew from the shadow of the law; at other times, sluggish through necessity or custom, they fell back into it. Finally, they associated Matthias with themselves by lot, and they regularly attended the Temple for the sake of prayer, where the blood of animals was still being offered.

Peter himself, the foremost of the Apostles, sometimes ate with gentiles and sometimes, fearing them, withdrew from them. His fellow Apostle Paul, although he said to the Galatians, “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V, 2), nevertheless circumcised his beloved disciple because of the false brothers who had slipped in, and, purified together with others, presented the sacrifice of the law in the Temple.

But once they had been driven out of Judaea’s narrow confines and had gained the wide expanse of the gentiles, they immediately—as though openly freed from the chains of servitude—did not cease turning away from the law’s carnal ceremonies all whom they drew toward spiritual grace. This is undoubtedly understood from Paul’s preceding and following words, where he declares:

“The Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are branded, who forbid marriage and command abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer” (1 Tim. IV, 1–5). [Col. 0967B–0967C]

Behold, so great an Apostle, caught up to the third heaven and into Paradise itself, proclaims that “all things are clean to the clean” and that nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, because it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer. And who are you, who, giving heed to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speak lies in hypocrisy, sending writings to the Latin peoples so that they may abandon God’s commandments and the weightier matters of the law—judgment, mercy, and faith—and follow your traditions and opinions, as though until now they had had no preachers or fathers, and as though they needed to be taught by you what the first elements of God’s utterances are? [Col. 0967D]

### LV

Indeed, among other things, you attempt to instruct people ignorant of everything about what they should eat and how it should be prepared, and you assert that they are neither gentiles nor Jews unless they obey. For, as you say, “gentiles kill, or eat after beating the animals”—as though Latins were accustomed to eat animals alive or whole.

Have you perhaps been appointed chief cooks for all nations? And if, by chance, a person weakened by hunger lacks food, but a bird or an egg is available and no knife is at hand, would it be better for him to perish from hunger than to kill and eat it by whatever means he could?

Thus, because we do not wish to be led astray by various and foreign doctrines, “we know and are confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing is common through him, except to the one who considers something to be common; to that person it is common,” as Paul says (Rom. XIV, 14). Moreover, “it is best to establish the heart by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those who walk in them.” But now let us proceed to the remaining matters. [Col. 0968A–0968B]

### LVI. THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN

Indeed, you do not sing Alleluia during Lent, but only once at Easter. This is interpreted as: “The Lord has come; praise him, sing a hymn, and bless him.” Therefore, according to this, you sing neither “Praise [him]” nor “Blessed is he who comes.” And this word Alleluia itself is said in Hebrew.

### LVII. THE ROMAN

We know that Alleluia is a Hebrew word and is translated into Latin as “Praise God.” But that it is also interpreted as “The Lord has come” or “Blessed is he who comes,” we do not know, nor have we heard it from anyone but you until now.

Furthermore, we do not sing Alleluia only at Easter, as you slanderously claim, but at all seasons of the entire year, except for the nine weeks during which we have received from our fathers the practice of discontinuing it—namely, the weeks in which we ought to apply ourselves more diligently to washing away the negligences of the other seasons.

For just as once the people in the wilderness, intending to punish within themselves the sin of idolatry, and the Ninevites, undertaking repentance at Jonah’s preaching, laid aside all their adornment and pleasures and put on sackcloth and ashes, and cried out to the Lord not with strange, elaborate, or sweet-sounding words and melodies, but in their own speech and with uncomposed or bitter lamentations, so our venerable fathers have been accustomed to act.

Therefore, laying aside the ornaments and pleasures of an affluent language during Lent, we put upon ourselves the very poor garment of our language and, having become fools for Christ, judge that we know nothing except Christ crucified. Keeping his strict judgment before our eyes, bound and burdened by sins, like unlearned people we scarcely dare to entreat God even in our own idiom.

For from the Book of the Wise One we have learned that “praise is not becoming in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV, 9). Yet at that time we continually sing a hymn to the Lord, and we sing “Blessed is he who comes,” and invite every creature day and night to praise him, saying “Praise the Lord”—but, as we have said, only in our native tongue.

At that time we also discontinue another angelic hymn, namely, “Glory to God in the highest.” In fact, these two alone are the hymns found to have been sung by angels in the New Testament: Alleluia and “Glory to God in the highest.” [Col. 0968C–0969A]

We discontinue both during Septuagesima because, expelled through the sin of the old human being from the fellowship of angelic rejoicing into the Babylon of this wretched life, we sit and weep beside its rivers while remembering that Zion in which a hymn is due to God, saying to our adversaries: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. CXXXVI, 4).

For the old human being can sing only an old song, not a new one, until, after this laborious life signified by Lent, he is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.

Nevertheless, during Lent we do not discontinue “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth,” although it is an angelic hymn sung in the New Testament and previously spoken in the Old Testament. It offers to God the perfect faith of the fathers in humility, while exalting none of their merit in good works.

So we too, during this Lent of our pilgrimage, knowing that we walk by faith and not by sight, presume before God by faith alone, saying in humble confession: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth.” Of him, distrusting our works, we proclaim with the Psalmist: “Do not enter into judgment with your servants, for in your sight no living person will be justified” (Ps. CXLII, 2). [Col. 0969B]

### LVIII

When we discontinue “Alleluia” for nine weeks, we not improperly understand by the nine weeks the nine orders of angels. Their tenth order, having fallen through pride, diminished the angelic number and disturbed its happiness. Mourning their diminishment and fearing an equal ruin for themselves, they were hindered from perfect praise of the Creator.

To provide for their restoration and consolation, the almighty Creator first formed the human being from the mud of the earth, so that through the multiplication of his race he might repair the losses of the heavenly homeland and complete the joys of the angels.

At this hope the angelic choir rejoiced for a little while; but soon it was troubled by the fall of the human being himself. Thus the harmony of the nine orders remained incomplete in the praise of the Creator until, when Christ rose, that first-created human being who had fallen rose again.

There the angelic host rejoiced at the increase of its fellowship and at the better hope, and the whole host rose together into a new “Alleluia,” remaining devoted in it. [Col. 0969C–0969D]

We imitate it according to our limited capacity. From Septuagesima, when the fall of the first-created human being is recited in the Church, we discontinue “Alleluia” for nine weeks—namely, until Easter, when Christ, rising from the dead, turns our sadness into joy and restores “Alleluia.”

Even if the Latin Church did not at some time sing it, you ought not to reproach it, since it was sounding the Lord’s praise in its own language. Now we marvel at the nature of your pride, which barks that Latins do not belong to God if they do not perform both the hymn and the prescribed office in Hebrew or Greek, even though the Latin language itself chiefly confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

Indeed, together with Hebrew and Greek, Latin completed the inscription of the crucified Lord; and, though it was the last, it became first, defending for itself by sword and faith the earthly and heavenly power until the coming of the evil Antichrist and the gracious Jesus Christ.

Having resisted your slanders for a long time, let us now briefly address the intention of your epilogue. [Col. 0969D–0970A]

### LIX. THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN

Why do you not see, understand, or correct the peoples concerning the great deception of such things, as those who must be judged by God? Do you not abandon what is said—that Peter, Benedict, Paul, and the others taught this? In these matters you deceive yourselves and the people.

What I have written is what Peter, Paul, the other Apostles, and Christ taught, and what the holy and catholic Church has accepted and religiously preserves. You too, once corrected, should preserve it.

### LX. THE ROMAN

As has been sufficiently shown above, these words would proceed more appropriately with the order and roles reversed—namely, if we called you deceived, deceivers, and persons soon to be judged by the Lord.

For, wishing to be teachers while understanding neither what you say nor the matters about which you make assertions, you corrupt the pure teaching of the holy Apostles and Catholics through human presumption, utterly deceiving yourselves and others in these matters.

What we have now written to you Christ taught, as did his Apostles; and the holy and catholic Church, receiving it from them and from the holy Fathers, has religiously observed it until now. You too, once corrected, should observe it, if you do not wish to be anathema by Christ.

Moreover, Benedict, the distinguished Father of monks, is in no respect to be disparaged by you. Outstanding in faith, teaching, and life, he never turned aside from the straight path either to the right or to the left; he did not transgress the boundaries established by the Fathers; he did not concern himself with defining the leopard, but handed on to cenobites a rule full of discretion.

Although in it he assigned the eating of meat to the weak and undergarments to those on a journey, far be it from him to have thought that these two things were worse than fornication. Yet some of your people defend fornication so fiercely that they neither blush nor fear to profess publicly that fornicating is the same as eating and being refreshed by any fruit!

Thus they venerate the fornicating Sarabaites, but utterly detest cenobites who use undergarments and eat meat in necessity.

But what does the Prophet say? “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil!” (Isa. V, 20). Did blessed Paul, the chosen vessel, ever define anywhere: “Those who use neither meat nor undergarments shall possess the kingdom of God”?

Yet in many places he emphatically insists, saying: “Do not be deceived: neither adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. VI, 10). Again: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. XIII, 4). And: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Cor. VI, 18). [Col. 0970B–0970D]

### LXI. THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN

But cast unleavened bread and Sabbath observances to the wretched Jews. Likewise, cast what has been strangled to the barbarian peoples, so that all of us may become pure in an undefiled and upright faith, one flock of Christ, one shepherd.

Intoxicated by whose divine blood on the cross, we pure people praise the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit purely, abandoning to the godless Jews the whole of the Mosaic law and the things observed by him. Like blind people seeking Christ, they have lost the light and remain in the shadow like fools forever. [Col. 0971A]

### LXII. THE ROMAN

We have shown above at length that we do not observe Sabbaths or unleavened bread in a Jewish manner, nor eat what has been strangled in a gentile manner, but principally retain the apostolic and catholic faith.

We do not arrogantly reject the one flock, but humbly flee to the one fold of the one supreme Good Shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep. He continually feeds with his flesh and gives his blood to drink to those sheep which, recognizing and following his voice rather than that of strangers, may praise the holy and undivided Trinity in heart, mouth, and deed.

Therefore, above all things we grieve that the old novelties of words have not yet been torn from your lungs. Of these it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Athenians devoted themselves to nothing else except saying or hearing something new” (Acts XVII, 21).

But now, avoiding profane novelties of speech, cast off the old skin as quickly as possible, lest—God forbid—the Bridegroom’s voice say to you: “If you do not know yourself, go out and depart after the tracks of the flocks, and feed your kids” (Song I, 7)—namely, those whom the shepherd himself separates at the end from the lot of the humble sheep, because, wanton and insolent, they do not cease here to exalt themselves by the force of pride. [Col. 0971B–0971C]

### LXIII

Furthermore, if we abandon the whole Mosaic law to the Jews, no decency or holiness will remain for us, as you can gather from what was said above. Let only the carnal commandments and the holy secular observance be left to them, in which, while following the shadow, they seek what they might discover and are exiled from the light.

Your Sabbath too is numbered among that shadow, as the Apostle says: “Let no one judge you concerning food or drink, or in respect of a festival, a new moon, or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come” (Col. II, 16).

Moreover, just as the Jews are without God, so are all heretics. But, so that nothing may be lacking, let us attend to what follows. [Col. 0971C–0971D]

### LXIV. THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN

You yourself have often acknowledged and taught these things of this kind to the people, and, once corrected, have written to many who held a similar custom. And so that you may have salvation for your soul, send to princes of the priests and to priests, and adjure them to correct themselves and the people through these matters, so that they may receive a reward even in these things.

And if you do this, I propose, in a second writing, to write to you matters greater and more perfect than these, with a true exposition of the faith and a strengthening of souls, for whom Christ laid down his life. [Col. 0971D–0972A]

### LXV. THE ROMAN

O men of understanding, consider this and beware of the crafty insinuation of heretics, who deceive the hearts of the innocent through blessings and pleasant words.

Behold, addressing John, bishop of Trani, in particular, to whom you wrote such things, you strive to grease his head with the oil of a sinner, saying: “You yourself, having often acknowledged these things of this kind with the people, taught them, and, once corrected, wrote to many who held a similar custom.”

But we say to you, on the contrary, through Solomon: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I, 11). For the bishop mentioned above was never corrected by you for teaching such things to the people or for writing them to anyone.

If he had done so, he would have been corrected by us. Why, then, would he have presumed to do such things after being reproved—but not corrected—by you?

Whatever he may be in his conduct, he has nevertheless until now remained sound in orthodox faith, according to the capacity of his understanding. Therefore, yielding to none of your whisperings, he has not yet been persuaded to send any of your nonsense to any priest, with his assistants, as a correction for them and the people.

Not only would he receive no reward for this, but he would also incur danger to his office. Yet, if he obeys you in your trivialities, you promise him another reward: namely, that you will write to him a second time about matters greater and more perfect than these, with a true exposition of the faith and a strengthening of souls, for whom Christ laid down his life. [Col. 0972A–0972B]

In these promises you plainly retain the ancient rite of heretics, whose speech spreads like cancer and promises the curious the height of perfect knowledge, so as to drag them into the abyss of utter folly.

Demonstrating their vanity through Solomon, the Wisdom of God says specifically:

“The foolish and clamorous woman, full of enticements and knowing nothing at all, sits at the doors of her house, on a lofty place in the city, to call out to passersby who go along their way: ‘Whoever is simple, let him turn in to me.’ And to the senseless she says: ‘Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant.’ But he does not know that giants are there, and that her guests are in the depths of hell” (Prov. IX, 13–18). [Col. 0972C]

Here, precisely here, is an effective portrait of you: you promise matters greater and more perfect for the manifestation of faith and the strengthening of souls, inviting the simple and senseless to the sweetness of stolen water and the pleasantness of hidden bread.

Truly, it is entirely stolen water when you rebaptize Latins who have been baptized catholically—something no Catholic has yet presumed to do, namely, to rebaptize those baptized by the heretics themselves in the name of the holy Trinity.

Truly, you invite people to some hidden bread when you trample under profane feet the life-giving and awe-inspiring sacraments of the body and blood of Jesus Christ. [Col. 0972D]

### LXVI

Are these the “greater and more perfect” things—that so large an offering should be placed on the altar that it cannot be consumed by the ministers or the people, and therefore must be buried or thrown into a well prepared for that purpose?

Are these also the “greater and more perfect” things—that a newly married man, still relaxed by recent sexual pleasure and wholly enervated, should minister at Christ’s altars, and should immediately transfer his hands, sanctified by Christ’s immaculate body, to the embraces of a woman?

Are these the more perfect things—that communion should be denied to Christian women endangered in childbirth or during menstruation? Or that baptism should be forbidden to pagans? Or that regeneration through water and the Holy Spirit should be withheld from dying infants before eight days have passed?

In this matter you slaughter daily an innumerable population of little ones, more cruel than Herod, not only in body but also in soul, and you consign them to eternal fire.

Is it also from this that you fasten the image of a dying human being to the image of the crucified Christ, so that some Antichrist sits upon Christ’s cross, displaying himself as worthy of worship as though he were God?

Is it also from this that it is worse for monks to wear undergarments and eat meat than to fornicate?

Is that why you close the churches of the Latins and send writings throughout the world, in order to drag the entire Christian people toward these “greater and more perfect” things?

These are not a manifestation of true faith, but an invention of the devil. They are not a strengthening but a destruction of souls. For all these errors and others, which it would take too long to set down in writing, unless you repent and make worthy satisfaction, you will be under irrevocable anathema here and in the future, from God and from all Catholics, for whom Christ laid down his life. [Col. 0973A–0974A]

**THE RESPONSE ENDS.** [Col. 0973]

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOKLET OF A CERTAIN NICETAS, PRIEST AND MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF STUDIOS, PUBLISHED AGAINST THE LATINS AND FOUND BY THE REPRESENTATIVES OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE AT CONSTANTINOPLE

### I

Nicetas, priest and monk of the monastery of Studios, who am surnamed Pectoratus, to the Romans concerning unleavened bread, Sabbath fasts, and the marriages of priests.

Love of neighbor is good, O Romans, wisest and most noble of all peoples. For from the habit of love toward one’s neighbor, humility also abounds toward the one who possesses it. This abundant love makes a person love everything and endure everything, as the divine Apostle says, and never become puffed up against his neighbor, nor seek what belongs only to himself, nor harbor jealousy, contention, or rivalry against him.

For all these things persecute love and humility and cause a person to walk not according to God but according to human desire. Paul also rebukes this, saying: “When there is jealousy, contention, and discord among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?” (1 Cor. III, 3).

For this reason I ask your charity to humble yourselves for the sake of God’s commandment and to hear us, unworthy and least though we are. [Col. 0973B–0973C]

### II

When we inquire of those who travel here from various Roman provinces concerning unleavened bread, what shall we say about them to you in Christ’s love? Those who still partake of unleavened bread are under the shadow of the law and eat at the table of the Hebrews, not at the rational and living table of God—the supersubstantial table for us who have believed, just as above we were taught to ask for supersubstantial bread.

For what is “supersubstantial” except that which is consubstantial with us? There is no other bread consubstantial with us except the body of Christ, which is like us according to the flesh of his humanity.

But if the substance of our mass, with which the Word clothed himself, is animate, then you do not eat bread substantial to us, because you partake of unleavened bread. For unleavened things are inanimate, as the very nature of things shows and teaches more clearly.

When a little leaven is mixed into flour and mingled with it, it makes the whole into one thing through the leaven’s life-giving power; it warms it and makes it both active and alive. But this never happened, nor will it ever happen, in the unleavened leaven of the Pharisees, from which the Word warns us to flee.

For we have become participants in the divine nature, and daily partake of it, since we have fellowship with Christ, as Peter, the foremost, says: “May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord” (1 Pet. I, 2). And shortly afterward: “That through these you may become participants in the divine nature” (2 Pet. I, 4), not in the unleavened leaven of those who have slain God.

Whoever possesses reason—would he ever call the divine nature the unleavened and dead leaven of the Jews, which you offer to God in sacrifice, eating it as a figure of the Lord’s true and living flesh?

How will you have unity with Christ, the living God, while eating what has been called dead and unleavened leaven, belonging to the law and its shadow rather than to the New Testament?

For if you say this too, the matter is not so. The beloved disciple of Christ says: “If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth. But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from every sin” (1 John I, 6–7).

Therefore, whoever eats unleavened bread walks in the darkness of the law. And how will he [not] have fellowship with Christ, who is in the light of his New Testament and grace?

For those who walk in the light of grace eat the bread that is the body of Christ and drink his undefiled blood. Thus they have fellowship with one another and with Christ, cleansed, as has been said, from every defilement.

But unleavened bread is not bread. It is neither compounded nor complete in itself; it is deficient and only partially complete, lacking the fullness of leaven. Bread, however, is compounded, complete in itself, and entirely full, like that which possesses the whole fullness within itself. [Col. 0974A–0975B]

### III

Observe and pay attention: in unleavened bread there is no living power; it is dead. But in bread—that is, in the body of Christ—there are three things that live and grant life to those who eat them worthily: Spirit, water, and blood.

John himself, who reclined upon Christ’s breast at the supper, also bears witness to this in these words: “There are three that bear witness: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three are one” (1 John V, 8), namely, in the body of Christ.

This was also made clear at the time of the Lord’s crucifixion, when water and blood flowed from his undefiled side: when his flesh was struck by the spear, the Holy Spirit, the giver of life, remained in his deified flesh.

When we eat this flesh in the bread, which has been changed through the Spirit and made the body of Christ, we live in him, as though eating living and deified flesh.

Likewise, when we drink his living and exceedingly warm blood together with the water flowing from his undefiled side, we are cleansed from every offense and filled with the fervent Spirit.

For, as you see, we drink a warm cup, as though from the Lord’s side, because from living flesh, warm with the Spirit of Christ, exceedingly warm blood and water flowed out for us.

This cannot happen in those who eat unleavened bread. [Col. 0975B–0975C]

### IV

But if you eat dead leaven, O most wise men, as the argument has shown, why do you boast, saying: “We do not, as you do, mix flour with salt, leaven, and water and thus make our offering of unleavened bread; rather, we prepare our unleavened bread with water alone, flour, and fire, and in these three we make our offering pure”?

We therefore ask you: for what purpose do you take these three—water, flour, and fire—and whose image do you think they are?

The flesh of the Lord? But the beloved disciple of Christ does not say, “There are three that bear witness: water, flour, and fire.” What does he say? “The Spirit, the water, and the blood, and these three are one” (ibid.), namely, in the body of Christ, as has been said.

When we eat it, we are united to Christ, who for our sake became incarnate and was sacrificed; incorporated into him, we become like his flesh, as it is written.

But if you apply this to the uncreated and incorporeal nature of the holy Trinity, you fall into the heresy of those who assert that God suffered, who say that the Word suffered together with the flesh and that the very divinity itself endured suffering.

For the Trinity was not incarnate as a whole—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—so that these three, water, flour, and fire, might be seen in it, and so that you might make unleavened bread in its image and offer a sacrifice.

Rather, one of the Trinity, the Son and Word of God, became incarnate, becoming human from the most pure flesh of the holy Virgin. Fulfilling everything ordained for him, he was crucified in the flesh, while his divinity did not suffer.

Therefore, crucified in the flesh, he gave us his flesh to eat through bread, which we declare to be alive in the Holy Spirit: “Take and eat; this is my body, which is broken for you, for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. XXVI, 26–28). [Col. 0975D–0976B]

### V

What, then, is the meaning of this for you, our brothers in Christ, and for the law that is accursed in Christ—that you still eat its unleavened leaven?

We are a new creation in Christ; the old things have passed away. Hear Paul saying: “Behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. V, 17).

But if you decide that eating these things is right, why are you not also circumcised? Christ was circumcised. Why are you not also purified? Paul did this as well. And why do you not likewise observe all the other ancient practices, just as those who practice the things of the law do—through whom the name of God is blasphemed among the gentiles, as it is written?

“Your boasting is not good” (1 Cor. V, 6). And, to speak Paul’s words to you: “Do you not know,” he says, “that a little leaven corrupts the whole mass?” (ibid.). And in the end it becomes bread, not unleavened bread.

But what is the Apostle speaking about here in his letter to the Corinthians? Is it, as you think, about the celebration that you observe in unleavened bread? Certainly not.

The Corinthians despised the fact that someone had taken his stepmother and boasted in their ancient customs and false knowledge. Wishing to convert them and remove them from their old wickedness, Paul used this comparison—of leaven, I mean, and of the mass—to show them that one evil, like a small offense, will cause great injury throughout the whole body of the Church.

Therefore he adds: “And you have not mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst?” (1 Cor. V, 2).

This iniquity, he says, can pass into all your cities; and, just as a little leaven leavens the whole mass, so all may be seized and leavened, producing one mass of greater iniquity.

“Purge out,” he says, “the old leaven” (ibid., 7), of sin. Remove this person from your midst, so that you may become a new dough for Christ, as you were baptized—that is, either unleavened or pure, having been put to death to the world and to the desires of the flesh.

For this is our Passover: Christ was sacrificed in order to rescue us from iniquity and death. Therefore he says: “Let us celebrate, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (ibid., 8)—that is, with a pure life and the faith by which we believe in God and become his truthful worshipers.

Thus Gregory the Theologian understood this word.

O most wise men, understand the things belonging to the Apostle’s mind, and do not interpret it, as you have done, as concerning the festival and participation in unleavened bread.

For if Paul had instructed the Corinthians concerning unleavened bread and its celebration, and had commanded them to feast on unleavened bread, he would not, together with the eleven, have promulgated and imposed upon the entire Church of the faithful, under penalty of excommunication, in the seventieth canon, that no one should accept such a practice from the Jews:

“If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all from the ranks of the clergy fasts with the Hebrews, or feasts with them, and accepts gifts from their festivals, such as unleavened bread or anything of that kind, let him be deposed. If he is a layman, let him be excluded.” [Col. 0976B–0977B]

## CONTINUATION OF NICETAS’S TREATISE AGAINST THE LATINS

[Cols. 0977C–0984B]

### VI

[Cols. 0977C–0977D]

But if you say, “We do not receive it from the Hebrews, but customarily make it at home,” why is this so? Whether you receive it from them or make it at home, it is unleavened bread. And on this account you will incur the heavier punishment, because you abandon what Christ and his Apostles commanded you to do, acting like those who are under the bondage of the Law, as the Jews do, sitting in the shadow and darkness of the Law, and in no way believing Paul when he says:

> “Brothers, let each person remain in the condition in which he was called” (I Cor. 7:20, 24).

For you will find nowhere at all in divine Scripture that Christ or his Apostles called it unleavened bread when the mystery of the New Testament was administered by him. For Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says:

> “You ought to discern the cup of blessing which we bless: is it not participation in the blood of Christ? The bread which we break: is it not participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one bread” (I Cor. 10:16).

And again:

> “For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread”—not unleavened bread—“and, giving thanks, broke it and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which will be broken for you. Do this in remembrance of me’” (I Cor. 11:23–24).

He did not say “bread” only once, but repeatedly. Nor did he alone say this: the other Apostles did so as well. Matthew, for example, says:

> “While they were dining and eating, Jesus took bread” (Matt. 26:26).

You see that here too he says “bread”:

> “And, giving thanks, he broke it and gave it to his disciples and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body’” (ibid.).

Mark says the same, as do the others; nowhere do they mention unleavened bread.

### VII

[Cols. 0978A]

It was necessary for Christ to suffer on the day of the legal Passover, on which the Hebrews also sacrificed the lamb. For the Passover had to be carried out by the slayers of God on Friday, on which, according to the first month, the fourteenth lunar day finally occurred, in the year that amounted to 1534 years. The solar cycle was 18 and 5. Before the appointed Passover had yet arrived, he anticipated giving his own Passover to the disciples, reclining at supper toward the evening of the fifth day. After he had supped, he took bread, broke it, and entrusted to the Apostles the mystery of the New Testament on the fifth night, on which he was betrayed by Judas, as it is written.

But what does the Apostle Luke say?

> “He took bread and, giving thanks, broke it” (Luke 24:30).

Behold, Luke too says that Christ took bread, not unleavened bread. For it was not yet Friday. It was the thirteenth lunar day on that Thursday, and there was neither unleavened bread nor yet the offering of fermented bread.

### VIII

[Cols. 0978B–0978C]

Unleavened bread had been prescribed in the Law for the fifteenth lunar day, so that on the fourteenth day, toward evening, the lamb would be sacrificed; and the Law called the Passover the fourteenth day of the first month, while it called the fifteenth day the first day of unleavened bread and the Sabbath.

Alas for the ignorance of the unlearned! There was no unleavened bread on Thursday, since the moon was at its thirteenth day, not its fourteenth. The making of unleavened bread had been ordained for the fifteenth lunar day, just as the lamb had been commanded to be sacrificed toward evening on the fourteenth day. According to that ordinance Christ was sacrificed, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.

But if Christ was sacrificed and crucified on the fourteenth lunar day, Friday, while the Sabbath was the feast of unleavened bread, when did he eat unleavened bread? Did he also transmit to the Apostles that they should do this in the New Testament? How can you say that you received from the Apostles the practice of making unleavened bread after the resurrection from the dead? Do you not see that the facts plainly convict you, since it was not unleavened bread at the time when Christ entrusted the mysteries of the New Testament to the Apostles?

### IX

[Cols. 0978D–0979A]

I shall demonstrate this to you from the legislation of Moses. For he says:

> “These are the feasts of the Lord, the holy convocations, which you shall proclaim at their appointed times. In the first month, on the fifteenth day of this month, is the feast of unleavened bread of the Lord; and on the fourteenth day of the month, between the evenings, is the Passover of the Lord; and on the fifteenth day of this month is the feast of unleavened bread for the Lord. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread” (Lev. 23:4–6).

From the legislation of Moses, therefore, you have learned that it was not unleavened bread when, after supper toward the end of Thursday, Christ transmitted the mystery of the New Testament through the breaking of bread. He did this before the feast of unleavened bread, when it was the thirteenth day of the month. According to the legislation of Moses, the fifteenth day of the month was the feast of unleavened bread.

Christ was crucified on Friday, according to the fourteenth day of the month, when the Jews were to sacrifice the lamb. On the Sabbath, according to the fifteenth day of the month, when it was the feast of unleavened bread, he lay buried in the tomb.

Since unleavened bread was not present before the feast of unleavened bread, and since the Jews ate unleavened bread for only seven days, as Moses instituted—beginning their feast on the fifteenth day of the first month—where was the unleavened bread when Christ ate supper with his disciples? If, as you say, the Apostles received unleavened bread from the Lord and in turn transmitted it to you as a figure of Christ’s body in the mystery of the New Testament, although neither the breaking of bread took place according to Moses’ ordinance nor was there unleavened bread at that time, where did it come from?

How can we forget the legislation of Moses? He transmitted to you the practice for seven days only. But you trample Moses’ ordinances throughout the entire year. Christ did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it (Matt. 5:17).

### X

[Cols. 0979B–0979C]

You are indeed strongly resisting the truth, brothers. If the Apostles transmitted to you that you should eat unleavened bread, how did your most holy Pope Agatho, who was a predecessor when the Sixth Council was held under the emperor Constantine, and the holy Gregory, bishop of Agrigentum, fail to abstain from it, when the holy Fathers of that council established a law against unleavened bread, decreeing that no believer should do this?

To demonstrate their legislation against unleavened bread, I add to my argument their canon, which reads in its eleventh chapter:

> “No one in the sacerdotal order, nor any layman, shall eat the unleavened bread found among the Jews, or live with them, or invite them in sickness, or receive medicine from them, or bathe with them. If anyone undertakes to do this, if he is a cleric, let him be deposed; but if he is a layman, let him be excommunicated.”

Whoever prepares and eats unleavened bread, even if he has not received it from the Jews but has imitated them in this, is understood to be a Jew and is outside the Law—just as one who circumcises himself, or is circumcised by Jews, thereby shares their knowledge and transgresses the canons and ordinances of the Apostles and the holy Fathers, making everything void, as our argument has demonstrated.

But concerning unleavened bread we have sufficiently demonstrated to you from all divine Scripture that it is forbidden.

### XI

[Cols. 0979D–0980A]

Come now: after we have demonstrated the other matters to you, it has suddenly occurred to you to raise the question of fasting on Saturdays, because you taunt us. Where did you obtain the practice of fasting on Saturdays, and from which holy Scripture? From the Apostles? Certainly not.

The leaders of the Apostles, in the fifth book of the *Constitutions*, entitled *Concerning Martyrs*, according to Clement, command this:

> “The Lord commanded us to fast on Wednesday and Friday: one because of the betrayal, the other because of the Passion. He did not command us to fast on the Sabbath, because it is not proper to do so, except on that one Sabbath on which the Creator of all lay beneath the earth.”

Accordingly, near the end of the same book, he again says:

> “We declare that every Sabbath and every Sunday is to be celebrated. On these days one ought to rejoice and not mourn.”

In the seventh book of those constitutions, in chapter 24, they say:

> “We celebrate the Sabbath and the Sunday, because the former is a memorial of the divine work, while the latter is a memorial of the resurrection. Only one Sabbath in the whole year is to be observed for the Lord’s burial, on which one ought to fast. For when Christ lay in the tomb, the disciples had greater sorrow for him than joy at the memory of the divine work.”

Nevertheless, these provisions were not merely established mystically by Pope Clement; knowing that fasting on Saturdays incurred great condemnation, they bind the Church with a firm excommunication on this matter. For he says in the sixty-fourth canon:

> “If anyone is found fasting on Sunday, or on Saturday, except for that one Sabbath, let him be deposed; but if he is a layman, let him be excommunicated.”

### XII

[Cols. 0980B–0980C]

Following this, the Fathers who assembled at the Sixth Council promulgated the matter in harmony with it, with Pope Agatho presiding at Rome and Gregory, bishop of Agrigentum, present with them:

> “Since we have learned that those in the city of Rome fast on the Saturdays of the fasts of holy Lent, contrary to the ecclesiastical observance transmitted to them, it has pleased the holy council to preserve immovable the canon of the Roman Church, which says: ‘If any cleric is found fasting …’”—and so forth, as it is written below.

Thus, as you see, the Church of the faithful is bound by the Apostolic constitutions and canonical decrees, together with Pope Agatho at Rome. From where and from whom did you receive the contrary practice of fasting on Saturdays?

Moreover, where did you become accustomed to celebrating the complete Mass throughout every day of the fasting seasons, whether on Saturday or Sunday? From which teacher did you receive this? From the Apostles? Not at all. For the Apostles established a canon that says:

> “If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, reader, or cantor does not fast the holy Forty Days and Wednesday and Friday, let him be deposed, unless bodily illness prevents him.”

Since, therefore, we ministers begin and complete the ministry of the holy Mass near the third hour of the day, at which time it was also decreed that the sacrifice should be offered, how do you observe the fast until the ninth hour of the day, thus dissolving these provisions at the time of the ministry of the Mass? Certainly not. But if this is impossible, you will be punished by a curse.

### XIII

[Cols. 0980D]

The Fathers who were at the council of Gangra speak as follows in chapter 19:

> “If anyone, exalted by continence without bodily necessity, dissolves the fasts established in common and observed by the Church, presuming to possess perfect understanding, let him be anathema.”

Likewise the Fathers who were at the council of Laodicea, according to canon 50, said:

> “It is not proper to celebrate the birthdays of martyrs during Lent, but to commemorate the saints on Saturdays and Sundays.”

And according to canon 48 they likewise say:

> “It is not fitting to offer bread during Lent except on Saturday and Sunday alone.”

### XIV

[Cols. 0981A–0981B]

The Fathers who assembled at the Sixth Ecumenical Council similarly decree, according to canon 52, with the most holy Pope Agatho saying:

> “On all the days of the holy Lenten fasts, except Saturday and Sunday and the holy day of the Annunciation, the Mass is to be celebrated from the presanctified offerings.”

Accordingly, on Saturday and Sunday, near the third hour of the day, at which time the Holy Spirit also descended upon the disciples, we offer sacrifice and sanctify the gifts themselves, from which we preserve what is sufficient for the entire week.

On the other days of the week, at about the ninth hour of the day, we conclude the entire service at the completion of Compline. We priests, together with the deacons, make our entrance carrying only the censer. After the reading of the Prophets, we recite the appointed prayers of the great Basil, transfer the gifts to the altar of presentation, and pray with them.

In addition, reciting the prayer transmitted to us by the Lord, we elevate the presanctified bread and give the presanctified holy things to the holy. United by communion in the bread and cup of the mysteries of Christ, and thus giving thanks to God, we leave them and dismiss them from the assembly. We ourselves then take the common meal of leaves and vegetables, and hot water for those who wish it.

There are also others who persevere throughout the entire week with communion and blessing alone.

But you, by offering the complete service during Lent on every day, although it is proper for it to be offered around the third hour of the day, transgress the canons of the Church. In this also you fall under the curse of the Fathers, as has been said.

### XV

[Cols. 0981C–0982A]

Who was it who taught you to forbid and dissolve the marriages of priests? Which teacher of the Church transmitted this depravity to you?

If a man has not married, he will receive the laying-on of hands. Thus he who has been ordained unmarried proceeds lawfully to marriage. Do you act according to the canons when you forbid such marriages?

But if the man ordained as a priest had previously had a wife and continued in chastity and a virtuous life, you dissolve his marriage and transgress. I shall demonstrate this to you from the command of the Apostolic canons.

In the sixth book of Clement’s *Constitutions*, which he composed, the Apostles say in chapter 17:
