> “We say that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has one wife may be ordained, whether his wife is living or dead. After the laying-on of hands they may not marry, nor, if they already have wives, take second wives; the wives they had when they came to ordination must suffice.”

In the fifth book of the holy canons it says in chapter 2:

> “A bishop, presbyter, or deacon must not put away his wife under the pretext of religion. If he puts her away, let him be excommunicated; if he persists, let him be deposed.”

In canon 40 they plainly say:

> “The property of the bishop belongs to him.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Let not the bishop’s own property, under pretext of ecclesiastical property, pass to his wife, children, or relatives, lest under pretext of them he divert what belongs to the Church.”

And then:

> “There are indeed those who forbid priests their lawful wives.”

The leaders of the Apostles did not interpret the ecclesiastical canons in this way. But if you say that the Apostles called the woman “the Church,” then your statement will appear faithless and empty, since the sacred canons of those Apostles, which we cited above, decree that bishops and presbyters are not to put away their wives under the pretext of religion, lest the bishops’ possessions fall from their authority because of their children and wives.

### XVI

[Cols. 0982B–0982C]

But if anyone should speak of the holy and universal council—which, as we have said very often, had the most holy Pope Agatho of Rome presiding—the council of 170 Fathers under the emperor Constantine, grandson of Heraclius and father of Justinian: how did the holy Agatho not oppose the holy council when it decreed against these impious practices that you still maintain?

If you had received these traditions from the Apostles, he would perhaps have opposed the council and would not have accepted what it promulgated among us. Since the Pope was yours and knew those traditions to be adulterated and foreign to the Apostolic teaching, he therefore promulgated, together with the Fathers of the holy Sixth Council, concerning the marriages of priests just as concerning unleavened bread, Saturday fasts, and the mysteries of the holy Mass. In chapter 13 he says:

> “Since we have learned that in the Roman Church it has been handed down as a canonical rule that those judged worthy of the laying-on of hands for the diaconate or presbyterate must declare that they will no longer live with their wives, we, following the ancient canon of apostolic diligence and order, will that the lawful unions of holy men shall henceforth remain valid, in no way dissolving their union with their wives or depriving them of one another at the fitting time.”

And shortly afterward:

> “If anyone is found worthy of the laying-on of hands as a deacon, subdeacon, or presbyter, he is in no way to be forbidden to ascend to such a rank while lawfully living with his wife; nor at the time of ordination is he to be required to make a declaration, because of his own wife, in accordance with a rule of separation.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore, if anyone dares, contrary to the Apostolic ordinances, to deprive any of the sacred presbyters or deacons of union with lawful women, let him be excommunicated. Likewise, if any presbyter or deacon casts away his foster-sister under the pretext of religion, let him be separated; if he persists, let him be deposed.”

### XVII

[Cols. 0982D–0983B]

From where, then, and from whom did these dreadful infirmities come upon you, O most wise men of the Romans and noblest of all the other nations?

I suppose that certain Jews who came to believe in the time of the Apostles, found to be desiring empty profits and lovers of money, wishing to draw many of the faithful away from the Gospel—that is, from the preaching of faith—corrupted them by their earlier teachings. Through this, both Christianity and Judaism were corrupted.

John spoke of such people:

> “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (I John 2:19),

speaking of those associated with Simon, Deman, Nicolaus, and Cleobius.

The other leaders of the Church, in the seventh book of the *Institutions*, chapter 16, stated the matter more clearly:

> “For we know,” he says, “that those who wrote books about Simon, Cleobius, and Judas in the name of Christ and his disciples circulate them for the deception of you and of those who love Christ and us, his servants.”

In former times some also wrote apocryphal books of Moses, Enoch, and Adam, of Isaiah and David, of Elijah, and of the three patriarchs—books that introduced corruptions and were enemies of the truth.

The Apostle Paul, as I suppose, foreseeing these things and knowing that such deceivers would arise among you, weaving a snare for you, writes to the Philippians:

> “Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the mutilation” (Phil. 3:2).

And again to Timothy:

> “In the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their own conscience seared, forbidding marriage and abstinence from foods which God created” (I Tim. 4:1–3).

And what follows. For this reason he also commanded Titus:

> “Rebuke them sharply,” he says, “so that they may be sound in the faith, not attending to Jewish fables and commandments of men who subvert the truth” (Titus 1:14).

### XVIII

[Cols. 0984A]

For this reason we have investigated these matters with the greatest care, brothers, so that you may never again accept as true the lies that have been stated and refuted—namely, unleavened bread, Saturday fasts, the marriages of priests, and offerings during fasts.

Knowing now that the first of these matters is contradicted by every Scripture inspired by God, flee from practicing such things. You are the Church of God and the ever-shining eye of the whole world. Thus, united with us, your fellow brothers—whom you have torn apart by the matters already mentioned, although you are the body of Christ—let us, with unveiled face, contemplate the glory of the Lord in harmony and unity with the orthodox faith, and let us be transformed into his image by a living demonstration, to his everlasting glory, according to the Spirit of the Lord. For he is the head of our Church, which is his body, and in him, as in one body, we are all joined together.

### XIX

[Cols. 0984B]

This is what we have to say to you Romans. If, since you are human beings, we can bring you back with us to belief through what we have said, and if by teaching you we have refuted you from divine Scripture, then—thanks be to God—you will know how rightly to believe in the Holy Spirit and to follow the argument already set forth from the Scriptures.

But if you hold otherwise, provide us with testimonies consistent with divine Scripture. I wish you to be well disposed in these matters, so that you may rest upon seats of understanding, and so that we, knowing how to obey the ineffable reasoning of the Spirit, may teach you all that we have written to you.

We greet you in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom, with the Fathers and the Holy Spirit, belong glory and power, now and always, and forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0983] End of the little book of Nicetas, presbyter and monk of the monastery of Studium, against the Latins.

[Col. 0983]

## HERE BEGINS THE RESPONSE, OR CONTRADICTION, TO THE SAME LITTLE BOOK, BY BROTHER HUMBERT, BISHOP OF SILVA CANDIDA

### I

[Cols. 0983C–0985A]

If you had carefully considered the fourth chapter of the holy Council of Chalcedon, content with monastic quiet, fasting, and prayers in your monastery, you would never have meddled in ecclesiastical affairs or caused disturbance. Therefore, by the unanimous decree of 630 Fathers, you have been suspended from communion, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed through you.

For it is fitting that each profession restrain itself within the measure of its own state and rank, lest it disturb the entire order of ecclesiastical doctrine by seeking, dissatisfied with its own office, to seize another’s.

But woe to you, Sarabaita, who, having undergone no examination in coenobitic discipline, driven by your own will and pleasure, have howled horribly against the holy Roman and Apostolic Church and the councils of all the holy Fathers. You are more foolish than an ass: with a lion’s forehead, you have attempted to break through an adamantine wall!

In this effort you are not the victor over error, but defeated by error; not a presbyter, but an ancient of evil days and a cursed child of a hundred years. You should be called Epicurus rather than a monk. Nor should you be believed to dwell in the monastery of Studium, but in an amphitheater or brothel.

You are truly called *pectoratus*—“the chest-bearing one”—because you crawl with the ancient serpent across your breast. As one of the Fathers said:

> “Whoever wishes enters and unties the ass.”

For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matt. 12:34).

Moreover, more detestable than every poison, you steeped lips bearing a deadly cup in the honey of charity and the good fragrance of humility. From these virtues mentioned above you presented a pleasing preface, so that the sweetness first tasted might cause the gall of dragons and the remaining poison to be swallowed without hesitation.

But woe to him who gives his friend a turbulent drink! For this reason we considered it necessary to strain it through a finer cloth, so that the manner of its composition and its power might to some extent be detected and thereafter avoided, since it enters gently but at the end will bite like a serpent and spread poison like a basilisk.

### II

[Cols. 0985B]

Behold, in the very threshold of your livid work you proposed three matters: unleavened bread, the Sabbath, and the marriages of priests. From these you spewed forth such a quantity of such enormities that, in perverting divine statements, you seem no inferior to the depraved and rabid dogs Julian and Porphyry.

Finally, you have twisted backward, as far as you could, the ladder of divine speech raised toward heaven, turning it toward hell, so that you would not ascend with the angels to the Catholics but descend with the apostates to the heretics.

That is why, detracting from the sacrifice of the holy Roman and Apostolic See, you most falsely declared that we eat at the table of the Jews. This is sufficiently demonstrated in our preceding account, where we wished to oppose the inventions of your accomplices—namely Michael of Constantinople and Leo of Acrida. There is no need for us to repeat the same things so often. A single flame can suffice for collected tinder, gathered straw, and accumulated tares. Therefore we have decided merely to set alight, lightly, those matters which you alone seem to have piled up more extensively than they did.

### III

[Cols. 0985C–0985D]

Accordingly, what you said—that “consubstantial” and “supersubstantial” mean the same thing—is entirely futile. For although the Lord Jesus is consubstantial with us in his humanity, so too the breads of a human table, though consubstantial with one another, are nevertheless inferior to the supersubstantial bread of the divine table.

And, O liar against God and open adversary of the holy Gospel, where and when did the Truth, the Son of the truthful Father, say:

> “Beware of the unleavened ferment of the Pharisees” (Mark 8:15)?

Can unleavened bread in any way be called “ferment” when it is called unleavened precisely because it is without ferment? And wherever ferment is present, must it not either produce fermentation or remain ferment?

Since fermented bread does not exist without ferment, and ferment can never exist without it, how did you dare even to dream of fermented unleavened bread?

Although by saying such things you have woven spiders’ webs, you may entangle flies, gnats, or wandering worms in them; but you will not entangle simple pillars or sheep who recognize the voice of their creator.

### IV

[Cols. 0986A]

Then, O perverse perverter, you attempted to pervert the statement of the Apostle John:

> “If we say that we have fellowship with him while we walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth” (I John 1:6).

You used this testimony of his more wickedly than an adulterer uses the eye or a thief the sword—things that are good in themselves. They attempt to injure some; you seek to destroy everyone.

Thus you conclude:

> “Whoever eats unleavened bread walks in the darkness of the Law.”

But that same John, explaining your intention, demonstrates it more clearly than daylight when he adds:

> “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness” (I John 2:9).

Here it is perfectly clear that you received your statement not from the holy Apostle but from an apostate angel: “Whoever eats unleavened bread walks in the darkness of the Law.” For that entire epistle mentions neither fermented nor unleavened bread, but only charity.

### V

[Cols. 0986B]

After this, with no lesser sacrilege, you abused another testimony of the same Apostle:

> “There are three who bear witness on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three are one” (I John 5:7).

You perversely attempt to transfer to the bread of Christ’s table what he intended to indicate concerning his baptism. In baptism there are indeed these three, and they produce one baptism. The Spirit sanctifies, the water washes, and the blood redeems. If any one of these is absent, there is no baptism, as the venerable Father Augustine says:

> “Take away the water: there is no baptism; take away the word: there is no baptism. But the word comes to the element, and it becomes a sacrament.”

But you, wicked chest-bearer, by wickedly interpreting and corrupting the statement of the one reclining on Jesus’ breast, said: “And these three are in one,” namely, in the body of Christ. His beloved disciple neither perceived nor wrote this, but wrote:

> “These three are one” (I John 5:7–8),

according to the preceding sense concerning baptism.

### VI

[Cols. 0986C–0986D]

These matters are small and almost nothing compared with the blasphemy that follows, in which you strive to assert that at the time of the Lord’s Passion and crucifixion, when blood and water came out from his side, the holy and life-giving Spirit remained in his deified flesh.

If this is established, he was not dead. If he was not dead, he did not rise. If he did not rise, our faith and preaching are empty, because neither shall we rise. As the Apostle says:

> “If I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what advantage is it to me if the dead do not rise?” (I Cor. 15:32).

Why, then, do we suffer so much every day? Let us eat and drink—indeed, let us live like beasts, for tomorrow we shall die like beasts. If our hope in Christ is only for this life, we are more pitiable than all human beings. But may this be far from the whole human race!

For the same illustrious Evangelist, who saw this very thing with his own eyes, testifies that Christ’s flesh was truly lifeless on the cross, saying:

> “And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit” (John 19:30).

Mark and Luke, moreover, say that he expired (Mark 15:39; Luke 23:46). Therefore in the Creed we confess that he died and was buried. Otherwise he should not have been buried if he was not dead.

Be silent, dog! Wicked dog, bite your tongue! Christ truly died for our sins and rose from the dead for our justification (Rom. 4:25), the firstfruits of those who sleep (I Cor. 15:20).

### VII

[Cols. 0987A–0987D]

Behold the pestilential doctrine, behold the diabolical suggestion, of which you have become the standard-bearer, as you attempt to defend the opinions and inventions of your associates against apostolic tradition and manifest truth, saying that hot water and blood came forth from Christ’s living and warm body, and that therefore the Greeks rightly mix boiling water with his blood.

The whole matter is quite otherwise. For the truthful Evangelists unanimously relate that our Lord died on the cross at the ninth hour, and that in the evening Joseph asked for him, took him down from the wood, and buried him. When he gave up his spirit, the veil of the Temple and the rocks were torn, the earth was shaken, the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints rose.

In that great disturbance, and in what was virtually the shipwreck of the whole creation, not only was the Lord’s side not opened by a lance, but even those who had previously insulted him and had gathered for the spectacle, when they saw the earthquake and what was happening, returned beating their breasts. The centurion himself, to whom he had been handed over for punishment, said:

> “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. 27:54).

But when the turmoil of the world had subsided and some security had returned, since it was already evening, the Pharisees asked Pilate that the legs of those crucified might be broken and that they might be taken down because of the solemn Sabbath day. Joseph then also asked Pilate to take away the body of Jesus.

Pilate, however, wondered whether he had already died. After summoning the centurion, and learning that Jesus was already dead, he gave the body to Joseph. The soldiers, at Pilate’s command, broke the legs of the first criminal and of the other. But when they came to Jesus, seeing that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. One of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out, from which the Church was formed, just as Eve was formed from the rib of the sleeping Adam.

If, then, he died at the ninth hour and, in the evening, when he was already to be taken down from the cross, was struck with a lance, that blood was not naturally warm, since the whole body was already dead and cold. But if it was warm in some way, why did the Gospel remain silent about so great a miracle and mystery?

We wish you, new fellow-initiates in the mysteries, to tell us whether only the blood, or only the water, or both together were warm. If only the blood, why do you heat the water? If only the water, why do you heat Christ’s blood with it? If both together, why are both not heated together? And by whose sight or touch could it be discerned that either of these two, bursting forth together from a single wound, was warm or cold?

Moreover, if that water was warm, why is the water of baptism not also warmed, especially since it prefigured baptism, just as the blood prefigured redemption?

We also wish to know with what intention you called Christ’s rib immaculate. If you meant its holiness and innocence, very well; but if you meant that it was impenetrable to iron, very badly, because from a true wound he poured out true, not phantom, blood for us. And it came not from a rib, as you write, but from his side, because bone ordinarily does not emit blood, nor was any bone broken from the Lord’s body.

### VIII

[Cols. 0988A]

Moreover, that the bread is and is also called unleavened bread; that we do not err with the Theopaschites in the holy oblation; that we eat not the unleavened bread of the old Law but the bread of sincerity and truth; and that the old things have passed away and new things have come to be—this is sufficiently demonstrated in another letter of ours.

### IX

[Cols. 0988A–0988B]

But you, accursed man—and accursed be the word of your mouth—called the holy Law accursed, like Severianus. Nor is this surprising, since, while desiring beyond measure to praise your bread, you excessively disparaged it, saying:

> “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump, and finally the bread becomes not unleavened.”

Thanks be to God that unleavened bread is not made from a lump corrupted by leaven, like your bread. For corruption is never and nowhere understood as something good, because wherever there is corruption, there is also deterioration of substance.

Moreover, when you explained the saying of blessed Paul—which, after so many orthodox Fathers, we do not wish to have explained to us by heretics—you unwillingly praised unleavened bread, saying: “As you have been baptized, that is, unleavened and pure.”

If, then, according to your confession, the baptized are unleavened, what are the unbaptized except leavened—that is, corrupted?

### X

[Cols. 0988C]

Tell us, however, where and how Paul, together with the eleven Apostles, promulgated those canons with excommunication, the seventieth chapter of which you bring against us, altogether ignorant of what you are saying:

> “If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all among the clergy fasts with the Hebrews, or feasts with them, and accepts any of their festival gifts, such as unleavened bread or anything of that kind, let him be deposed; but a layman shall be excommunicated.”

Even if this chapter had been produced from authentic books, it would in no way touch us, because we neither fast with the Hebrews nor feast with them nor accept any of their festival gifts.

But what you, madman, add—“Whether you receive it from them or make it at home, it is unleavened bread”—we hurl back at you, saying:

> “Whether you feast with the Hebrews on the Sabbath or at home, it is a feast.”

Indeed, this would more properly be directed against you, because on the Sabbath you retain nothing other than the solemnity of the Jews, whereas in unleavened bread we retain and embrace an entirely different mystery.

For if we ask the Jews what they celebrate on the Sabbath, they will answer:

> “The Lord’s rest.”

If we ask the Greeks, they will say the same and nothing else. Therefore they are under the bondage of the Law, sitting in its shadow and darkness.

### XI

Then, after your empty barking about the word “bread,” you brought before us a reckoning of the years from the beginning of the world to Christ’s Passion, when, according to you, the solar cycle was eighteen and the lunar cycle five [Col. 0988D]. You did this so that by means of this fiction at least you might escape with your leaven—as though, according to your calculation, the thirteenth moon should have occurred at the Lord’s Supper, when the Hebrew people had not yet discarded the leaven.

But leaving such matters to chronographers and calculators—especially since Greeks, Latins, and Hebrews have different systems for reckoning times—we say only this: Christ dissolved not one jot or tittle of the old law. Thus, on the evening of the fourteenth moon, on the fifth day of the week, he celebrated the Passover; and immediately, that same night, he was seized, and was crucified on the fifteenth moon, that is, on the sixth day of the week, which was specifically called the first day of Unleavened Bread.

Indeed, throughout the entire preceding day also, that is, the fourteenth moon [Col. 0989A], no leavened thing appeared anywhere within all the borders of Israel. For the lamb too was eaten with unleavened bread. If, according to your assertion, Christ celebrated the Passover on the thirteenth moon with leavened bread, he was guilty on two counts and deservedly punished according to the law: because he celebrated the Passover at a time not appointed for it, and because he did so with leavened bread. Consequently, his death would profit us nothing, since he died not for our sins but for his own—namely, because he was a transgressor of the holy law. But we have discussed these matters at length elsewhere.

### XII

Then, if, as you assert, the Jews eat leavened bread throughout the whole year except for the seven days, who should more properly be reproved: the one who imitates them in eating unleavened bread for the shortest period, or the one who does so throughout the whole year with leavened bread? [Col. 0989B] Yet far be it from us to imitate their carnal rite in anything!

### XIII

But since you are being led through a labyrinthine error—now entering by the route by which you should exit, now leaving by the route by which you entered—and are once again treading the same path, you say:

“If it was handed down to you by the apostles that you should eat unleavened bread, how did your pope Agatho, predecessor of the holy Sixth Council, establish a law against the making of unleavened bread, together with Gregory, bishop of the Agrigentines, and the other Fathers?”

Listen, fool and empty talker: it was handed down to us not merely by the apostles, but by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, that we should not eat unleavened bread from the Jewish Passover, but receive it from the Christian Pascha.

### XIV

Nor are we bound by the matter you brought against us from chapter 11 [Col. 0989C] of the Sixth Council, saying:

“No one constituted in priestly order, nor any layman, shall eat the unleavened bread found among the Jews, or dwell with them, or summon them when ill, or receive medicine from them, or bathe with them in the baths. If anyone does these things, then, if he is a cleric, let him be deposed; but if he is a layman, let him be excluded.”

Which one of us, I ask, eats the unleavened bread that is found among the Jews? Although we observe the other provisions of this chapter, we observe this one above all concerning unleavened bread.

### XV

But what will you say? Did not Basil the Great receive medicine many times from Joseph the Jew? Yet you, expounding the chapter as the devil does the psalm, added:

“Therefore, whoever makes and eats unleavened bread, even if he has not received it from the Jews, is nevertheless an imitator of the Jews, just as is the one who is circumcised.”

“Lord, you will destroy all those who speak falsehood!” (Psalm 5:3.)

Is every Christian absolutely forbidden ever and anywhere to eat unleavened bread, just as he is forbidden ever to be circumcised? Why is this so? Because by these acts they imitate the Jews? We grant that circumcision belonged exclusively to the Jews; nevertheless, unleavened bread belongs to all nations, and you maliciously reject it altogether not only from the divine table but from the human table as well.

But what will you do, O leavened one? The Jews, as you asserted above, ate leavened bread throughout the year except for seven days, and sometimes offered it. Will you also take this away from human beings?

[Col. 0990A]

### XVI

Let us now see whether you are not Sabbatarians, whom the Fathers of the holy Fifth Council mention. Rebuking us because we fast on Saturdays, you say:

“One must fast continually on the fourth and sixth days of the week: the one because of tradition, the other because of the Lord’s Passion; but on Saturday, never except on one.”

You try to establish this from apocryphal books and canons, which the holy Fathers unanimously rejected. For Clement’s book—that is, the *Itinerary of the Apostle Peter*—and the Apostolic Canons are numbered among the apocrypha, except for fifty chapters which they decreed should be added to the orthodox rules. Therefore, rejecting every apocryphal work, we disdain listening to their fictitious traditions, because they are not like the law of the Lord.

Accordingly, setting these matters aside, see in another letter what the blessed and ancient Roman pontiffs, Silvester and Innocent, thought about the Sabbath; the opinion of Agatho, although he was most holy, is in no way to be preferred to theirs. Yet far be it from us to suppose that Agatho ever held an opinion contrary to them!

Nevertheless, here too, as in other matters, you are mistaken when you say that he presided over that council, whereas only his legates presided over it. It has seemed appropriate to insert its proceedings here in summary.

### XVII

In the time of Constantine, son of the emperor Constantine, in the seventeenth year of his reign, Pope Agatho, at the request of the most devout rulers Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius, sent his legates to the imperial city. Among them was John, then a deacon of the Roman Church and much later a bishop, sent to bring about the union of the holy Churches of God.

They were received with great kindness by the most reverend defender of the Catholic faith, Constantine. They were instructed to set aside philosophical disputation and to inquire into the true faith through peaceful conversation; and all the books of the ancient Fathers that they requested were supplied to them from the library of Constantinople.

One hundred and fifty bishops were also present, with Gregory, bishop of the imperial city, and Macarius of Antioch presiding. Those who asserted that there was one will and one operation in Christ were convicted of having falsified the statements of the Catholic Fathers in many places.

When the conflict had ended, at that very moment so many spiderwebs fell into the midst of the people that everyone was amazed. By this it was signified that the filth of heretical perversity had been driven away.

Gregory was corrected, whereas Macarius, together with his followers and his predecessors—Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter—was anathematized; and in his place Theophanius, an abbot and bishop from Cilicia, was installed.

Such grace accompanied the legates of Catholic peace that John, bishop of Porto, who was one of them, celebrated the public Mass in Latin on the Sunday within the octave of Easter in the church of Saint Sophia before the emperor and the bishop of that city.

At that time Damian, bishop of the Church of Ticinus, under the name Mansuetus, bishop of the Church of Saint Michael, composed a very useful letter of orthodox faith, which carried considerable weight at the aforesaid council.

### XVIII

The right and true faith is this: just as there are two natures in our Lord Jesus Christ, namely, divine and human, so too we must believe that there are two wills or operations.

Do you wish to hear what belongs to his divinity? “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Do you wish to hear what belongs to his humanity? “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

Observe him sleeping in the boat according to his humanity. Observe his divinity when the Evangelist says: “Then he arose and commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm” (Matthew 8:26).

### XIX

This is the Sixth Ecumenical Council, held at Constantinople and written in the Greek language, during the pontificate of Pope Agatho, with the most devout emperor Constantine conducting and presiding over it within his palace, while the legates of the apostolic see and 150 bishops were likewise seated [Col. 0991B]. They all condemned the heresy.

Then the most devout emperor Constantine asked them what practice the Roman Church followed concerning the sacrifice of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. They replied:

“In the Lord’s chalice, wine alone must not be offered, but wine mixed with water. For if wine alone is offered, Christ’s blood begins to exist without us. And if pure water is offered, the people alone begin to exist without Christ. When the two are mixed together—that is, wine and water—then the spiritual sacrament is perfected.

“The offering that is offered as the sacrifice of the altar must have no mixture or corruption of leaven, just as the blessed Virgin Mary conceived and gave birth to Christ without any corruption. Hence the custom has arisen in the Church that the sacrifice of the altar is celebrated not on silk or dyed cloth, but on earthly linen, just as the Lord’s body was buried in a clean shroud. Thus the clean offering must also be free from leaven, according to what we read in the pontifical proceedings that was established by the blessed Silvester.”

Then the most devout emperor Constantine approved this tradition of the apostolic see. Behold: the faith and tradition of the apostolic see pleased this emperor and all the holy Fathers and orthodox emperors of this and the six other councils in every respect. And who are you, that it displeases you?

But we want you to say whether it seems appropriate to you that you fast every fourth and sixth day of the week because of tradition and Christ’s Passion, and, because of his burial, on no Saturday except one. Since, then, you celebrate the Resurrection every Sunday and fast every fourth and sixth day because of tradition and the Cross, why do you not also fast every Saturday because of the burial, since in celebrating the Sabbath you follow no reasoning except that of the Jews—namely, because God rested on it?

God certainly was not wearied: by his word he created whatever he wished. Rather, by this he prefigured our rest. If, then, one Saturday in the entire year must be observed as a fast because of Christ’s burial, one Wednesday in the entire year must likewise be fasted because of his tradition, and one Friday because of his Passion. One Sunday also must be celebrated because of his Resurrection.

### XX

It is not surprising that you attribute your delirious statements to Pope Agatho and the holy Fathers of the Sixth Council [Col. 0992A], when you attribute fabrications even to the Lord Jesus himself and to his apostles.

Therefore, since we know that the Sixth Council was convened to destroy the heresy of the Greek Monothelites, not to impose new regulations upon the Romans, we utterly reject the chapters that you bring against us under its authority. The first and apostolic see never accepted them and has not observed them to this day; either they are nonexistent or, as you pleased, they have been corrupted.

You corrupted the statements of John Chrysostom, Gregory the Theologian, and other orthodox Fathers and produced them at that same Sixth Council. For from the First Council of Nicaea to this Sixth Council, more than three hundred years are said to have elapsed. How, then, is there no mention in Nicaea or in the other four ecumenical councils of matters so necessary?

Did Greeks and Latins remain ignorant until the Sixth Council of the proper order of the Mass and of fasts, and did they err in such matters for more than six hundred years after Christ’s Passion? Or perhaps the Greeks knew these things while the Romans did not?

But from the Roman missal books, received from ancient times throughout the whole Western Church, it is clearly understood what practice of fasting and the Mass they followed under the most revered pontiffs: Silvester, the author of the Nicene Council; Gelasius, condemner of your Acacius; and especially Gregory the Dialogist, co-godfather of the emperor Maurice.

In Gregory’s missal books, every day of Lent has the complete office of a distinct Mass, and, except for Sunday, no day of it releases the fast that has been undertaken. If Pope Agatho had attempted in any way to remove this tradition from the Romans, they would not have listened to him. For although he himself was a great man, he was inferior to those predecessors of his in both time and knowledge and authority.

Consequently, the chapter in which you claim that he promulgated that any cleric who fasted on more than one Saturday should be deposed should rather be said to belong to the Nazarenes than to the apostles, to Cerinthus and Ebion rather than to the Sixth Council and Pope Agatho.

The Apostle Paul’s letter openly contradicts this chapter, where he says: “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast day, a new moon, or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come.”

Therefore the Romans, obeying their own author and teacher of the nations in faith and truth, assign neither feast nor rest to any Saturday, nor to the new moon, because these are plainly Jewish observances and, in any case, shadows of things to come.

### XXI

Moreover, where we received the practice of celebrating a complete Mass on every day of fasting, we have taken care to show above. Nor do we fear the chapter that you call apostolic concerning those who do not fast during Lent, on the fourth day and also on the sixth day of the week. Except in the case of the gravest illness, we all diligently fast on the days of Lent, to such an extent that sometimes we make even ten-year-old children fast with us.

Nor do we interrupt our Lenten abstinence on Saturdays, just as our Lord did not interrupt it during the forty days of his fast. We would not interrupt it even on Sunday, as neither did he, unless the judgment of all the Catholic Fathers from the beginning—together with an anathema—had forbidden this because of the joy of his Resurrection.

Following them, the holy Fathers of the Council of Gangra said:

“If anyone, without discerning the Lord’s Day, fasts as though in contempt of it, let him be anathema.”

Here, as all authentic books attest, they certainly do not contradict fasting on Saturday, but fasting on Sunday.

### XXII

But, O perfidious Stercoranist, who think that the Lenten and ecclesiastical fasts are dissolved by faithful participation in the body and blood of the Lord, believing altogether that heavenly food is discharged into the privy through the foul and filthy excretion of the belly, you plainly share the sentiments of Arius.

He fell into a dark pit for his other blasphemies against the Son of God—and also for this one—and, with his entrails spilled out, remained empty and hollow in his belly [Col. 0993B].

Where, then, is the Savior who, giving his disciples the bread blessed and broken by himself, said: “Take and eat; this is my body” (Matthew 26:26)? Elsewhere he says what he was giving in it: “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52); and: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:56).

How is it true food? Because “whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:55). And what is eternal life? Clearly, Christ Jesus, as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Therefore, whoever eats the bread of God eats the flesh of Christ God. Whoever eats his flesh eats Christ; whoever eats Christ undoubtedly eats eternal life.

Therefore, O pestilential procurer of the ancient serpent, who by your cunning try to corrupt the understanding of Christ’s bride, which is the Church, so that she may be cut off from love of so great and such a bridegroom, do you believe that we, eating incorruptible life, corrupt the integrity of our fasts as though by some corruptible food?

### XXIII

We shudder to say this, but your shameless wickedness compels us. You try to send Christ—or rather, life itself—down through digestion into the latrine like foul dung.

Where, then, is what he said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57)? Since life is not possessed without this nourishment, Life itself, which is Christ, solemnly declares as though by an oath:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

Did he say here: “If you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will dissolve the fast”? If only we were nourished every hour by this sacrament alone, not for our condemnation! But because we are burdened with corruptible bodies and the great misery of our conscience, and are unable even to bear our own good, the holy Fathers fixed definite hours for receiving so great a sacrament.

So that it might not become cheap in the eyes of the carnal, and so that some bodily appetite might murmur while receiving spiritual food, we taste it with the utmost restraint, desiring only to see how sweet the Lord is, whose bread does not produce disgust, just as manna did not.

There is no doubt that, however small the portion, the faithful eat the whole of life—that is, Christ—whereas the unfaithful eat death—that is, their own judgment—for they become guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.

Moreover, whenever Mass is celebrated by us daily, whether at the third hour, the ninth hour, or any other hour, it is celebrated only as a complete Mass. No part of its offering is reserved so that an incomplete Mass may be celebrated over the course of five days.

For we do not read that the holy apostles reserved anything from that first mystery of Christ’s body and blood distributed during the Supper itself; nor do their acts indicate that they ever did or commanded such a thing.

Indeed, as Luke relates: “The faithful persevered in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread” (Acts 2:42). He shows shortly afterward how and on which days this fellowship took place, saying: “Every day they persevered with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, they took their food” (Acts 2:46).

Behold, the truthful Evangelist testifies that under the apostles the faithful prayed and broke bread every day. And who are you, who say that a complete Mass should be celebrated on only two days of the week, and an incomplete one on the other five?

Certainly, in this breaking and sharing of bread, we must understand nothing other than a complete action of the Mass, just as we read that the Lord himself handed on to his disciples not an incomplete but a complete commemoration: in bread blessed by him, then immediately broken and distributed.

For he did not merely bless it and reserve it to be broken on the following day; nor did he merely break it and put it away. Rather, once broken, he immediately distributed it.

Hence the blessed martyr and pope Alexander, fifth after the Apostle Peter, who inserted the Lord’s Passion into the canon of the Mass, did not say, “Whenever you do this,” but: “These things, as often as you do them—that is, bless, break, and distribute them—you shall do in remembrance of me.” For any one of these three performed without the others—blessing without distribution, or breaking without blessing and distribution—does not represent a complete remembrance of Christ, just as distribution is ineffective without blessing and breaking.

That we celebrate a complete Mass every day and at whatever hour of the day, rather than only at the third hour, is authorized by the words of the Lord himself according to the blessed Paul:

“Do this whenever you receive it in remembrance of me” (1 Corinthians 11:25).

Immediately afterward the same Apostle added: “Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:26). And for how long? “Until he comes” (ibid.), namely, to judge the living and the dead.

Do you think he said anywhere, “Do this at the third hour in remembrance of me”? Certainly not. He excluded no hour or time, but said: “Whenever.”

Nor did Paul, taking account of any fasts or some fixed cycle of years, say: “Whenever, after so many years, you eat this bread and drink this cup at the ninth hour, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death.” He said simply: “Whenever,” and: “Until he comes.”

### XXIV

Nor are we unaware that the holy Fathers customarily celebrated Masses on Sunday and on the chief solemnities at the third hour, because the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the disciples at the third hour. They handed this practice down to posterity so that that single action of the Mass might be marked by a double privilege: namely, Christ’s Resurrection and the coming of the Paraclete; and so that, because of the joy of the feast, the restraints of fasting might be relaxed for everyone.

Nevertheless, the reason for Sunday and for solemnities is one thing, and the reason for fasts another. Therefore, if a complete Mass is celebrated at the ninth hour or in the evening on days of fasting, no fault is incurred by this. For the Lord instituted the first and complete administration of so great a sacrament for his disciples at the evening Supper; and at the ninth hour, giving up his spirit, he completed the evening sacrifice on the Cross with outstretched hands and after offering prayer to the Father.

Therefore, although the third and ninth hours are more suitable for the celebration of Mass for the reasons mentioned above, whenever Mass is celebrated at other hours because of travel or some necessary circumstance, it is celebrated in remembrance of Christ; and the integrity of the fast is not thereby violated.

For this reason the blessed Pope Telesphorus, seventh after Peter, holding this view, also instituted that Masses should be celebrated at night on the Nativity of the Lord; nor did he fear that any breaking of the fast would thereby occur before the third hour and the daytime Mass, as you perversely suppose.

But tell us, if you can, why Saturday and the other weekdays outside Sunday ought to have a Mass at the third hour, since the Holy Spirit is not read to have descended upon them.

Accordingly, supported by divine authority, as has been shown above, we neither break our fast when Mass is celebrated at whatever hour of the day, nor do we break it on any feast of the martyrs, nor even on the Annunciation of the Virgin Mary. Therefore, we are not struck by the anathema of any ecumenical council.

Other gatherings of holy Fathers, although they may have been able to discuss the usefulness and practice of their own Churches, nevertheless did not establish any traditions for the universal Church.

Concerning Pope Agatho also, we know absolutely that he neither presided over the Sixth Council himself nor subscribed to any of its chapters except those promulgated against the heresy of the Monothelites.

You must consider where you obtained the things you put forward, since the Roman Church has hitherto known nothing of such matters. Nor can it be believed that, after so many years, a Roman pontiff promulgated for the Greeks any regulations concerning the Mass.

Furthermore, we do not care to learn your practice, because we recognize in it the least caution and the greatest negligence: when breaking and receiving the holy bread, you do not take care of the crumbs that fall here and there.

This also tends to happen when you disgracefully scrub the holy plates with palm leaves and pig bristles. Many of you also place Christ’s body so irreverently that you fill the pyxes with it and, lest it fall out or overflow, press it down with your hand.

You sometimes consume the remains of the offering like ordinary bread, even to the point of disgust. And if you cannot consume them, you bury them or throw them into a well.

If, as you say, you elevate on the following day bread that was offered and consecrated long before, you appear to offer one offering twice.

And why have you not attended to the letter of Pope Clement, whose traditions, as you think, you defend against us, and what he is thought to have promulgated there?

“Certainly,” he says, “let them offer as many holocausts on the altar as should suffice for the people. But if any remain, let them not be reserved for the following day; rather, let them be consumed with the fear and trembling, care and diligence, of the clerics.”

As for your assertion that you pass immediately from holy Communion to ordinary food, the same Clement is found to have thought otherwise in the aforesaid letter. Concerning those who have consumed the remains of the sacrifice, he added:

“Those who consume the remains of the Lord’s body left in the sacristy shall not immediately proceed to eat ordinary food, lest they think that foods which are discharged through the belly into the privy should be mixed with the holy portion.

“If the Lord’s portion is eaten in the sacristy in the morning, let the ministers who have consumed it fast until the sixth hour. And if it is eaten at the third or fourth hour, let them fast until evening.”

These words clearly show not only that Mass may be celebrated at the third hour, but also in the morning at the fourth hour; and that the fast is not broken by the sacrifice, since it says that those who have consumed it should fast until the sixth hour or evening. Otherwise, how could they fast if they had broken the fast by the sacrifice?

Then, while preaching to us about the abstinence of a very few, you remain silent about the gluttony of many, who offer little or none of the Lenten fast to God, since they do not fear or blush to gorge themselves from early morning until evening.

Some even bring legumes and other foods to church and eat them there, paying no attention to Paul, who says: “Let the hungry person eat at home” (1 Corinthians 11:34); and: “Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing?” (1 Corinthians 11:22.)

As for us, knowing nothing of the one-week Lent that you attribute to Saint Theodore, we strive diligently to observe only the Lent of our Lord Jesus Christ for forty days. We cannot tolerate anyone’s violating it in any way, except in the case of serious illness.

Nor is anyone among us permitted, as among you, to eat any fruit or vegetables during the days of fasting after a single meal.

### XXV

Considering, then, that you defend adulteries rather than the marriages of priests, we judge that the nefarious deacon Nicholas, the originator of this heresy, has risen from the underworld.

Your Epiphanius wrote of him as follows:

“The fourth heresy, that of the Nicolaitans, was devised by Nicolaus, one of the seven deacons ordained by the apostles. When he was reproached for jealousy concerning his most beautiful wife, he began to teach that wives might be used indiscriminately, not only by laymen but also by those who exercised the office of the priesthood.

“Saint John, the Evangelist and Apostle, condemned these people and ordered that anyone who had shared conversation with them should, for that very reason, be deprived of communion. He taught, reasonably, that from the beginning of the world chastity had been especially pleasing to God.

“Then, in himself, Christ the Son of God dedicated the glory of chastity, since, possessing a virgin mother and remaining himself a virgin, he did not permit any of his disciples to use even a legitimate marital union. He said: ‘If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me’ (Matthew 16:24).

“Thus the same Lord Jesus, commanding the Apostle John in the Apocalypse to write to the angel of Ephesus, said among other things: ‘You have this in your favor: you hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate’ (Revelation 2:6).

“Likewise he says to the angel of Pergamum: ‘I have a few things against you, because you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and to commit fornication; so you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans’ (ibid. 2:14–15).”

### XXVI

These things would indeed have been sufficient, O Nicolaitan Nicetas, to refute your error. But since you appear to press us with canons issued under the name of the apostles, we have decided to explain your chapters to you, although until now we have counted most of them among the apocrypha, so that it may plainly be understood that you cannot defend your absurdities either by apocryphal or by authentic writings.

Above all, however, we prove that you lied against truth itself in saying that our men are first ordained and afterward take wives. For among us no one is admitted even to the rank of subdeacon unless he professes perpetual continence, including continence from his own wife. Nor is anyone ever permitted to take a wife after receiving that rank.

But you, wishing to turn the Church of God into a synagogue of Satan and a brothel of Balaam and Jezebel, say with Nicholas:

“We say that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has one wife may be ordained, whether his wife is living or dead. Nor is it permitted to them, after the laying on of hands, to remain unmarried, or thereafter to marry; nor, if they marry, to embrace other wives. Rather, those whom they have when they come to ordination should suffice for them.”

O abominable Cynic, how were you not ashamed to spew out such wickedness? Therefore, is no one permitted to be without a wife after the laying on of hands? If this is so, the Apostle John himself, Paul, Barnabas, and every celibate man in an ecclesiastical rank are undoubtedly guilty.

It is therefore necessary that a future bishop, presbyter, deacon, and subdeacon first obtain a wife who must suffice for carnal embraces? Is one wife not sufficient for laymen, unless perhaps for the disciples of the wicked Muhammad, whose stuff you entirely are?

And since you are a presbyter, you too ought not to be without a wife, according to your own assertions.

### XXVII

But let us now examine the chapters by which you think the adulteries of priests, rather than their marriages, can be defended.

“A bishop, presbyter, or deacon,” you say, “shall not put away his wife under the pretext of religion. But if he puts her away, let him be excluded; and if he persists, let him be deposed.”

We fully acknowledge that a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or subdeacon may not put away his own wife from his care on religious grounds—that is, so that he may provide her food and clothing—not so that he may lie with her carnally according to custom.

Thus we read that the holy apostles acted. The blessed Paul says: “Do we not have the right to lead about a sister as a wife, as do the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?” (1 Corinthians 9:5.)

Observe, foolish man, that he did not say, “Do we not have the right to embrace a sister as a wife,” but “to lead her about”—namely, so that she might be supported by them from the wages of preaching, while thereafter there would nevertheless be no carnal marriage between them.

Moreover, why would any married layman hesitate to ascend to ecclesiastical orders, when the one wife without whom he ought not to be can suffice for his carnal embraces?

And why do you, who put forward Clement’s chapters so insistently, not heed the letter of his that we mentioned above? For there it says:

“To three ranks the sacraments of the divine mysteries have been entrusted: presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons.”

And a little later:

“Let ministers of the altar be chosen for the Lord’s services who knew wives before ordination, provided that they are willing thereafter always to remain continent. But if, after ordination, it should happen that a minister enters the bed of his own wife, let him not tread the thresholds of the sacristy, nor become a bearer of the sacrifice, nor touch the altar, nor receive holocausts or offerings from those who present them, nor approach the portion of the Lord’s body.

“Let him carry water to the priests’ hands and close the outer doors; let him perform only the lesser offices. He shall not, however, bring the pitcher to the altar.”

### XXVIII

Moreover, the wholly venerable and authentic Council of Nicaea says the following concerning its acts, that is, concerning women introduced into clerics’ households:

“The holy council absolutely forbids, and permits neither a bishop, nor a presbyter, nor a deacon, nor any cleric whatsoever, to have an unrelated woman living with him, unless she happens to be his mother, sister, or aunt. For in these persons and those similar to them every suspicion is avoided. Whoever acts otherwise will endanger his ecclesiastical rank.”

### XXIX

The blessed Pope Innocent, writing more fully on this matter to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, says:

“You have asked what should be observed concerning those whose sons have revealed that they are or were incontinent while placed in the ministry of the diaconate or in another office. Concerning these matters, the discipline of the divine laws and the clear instructions of the man of blessed memory, Bishop Siricius, have been transmitted: those who are incontinent while placed in such offices must be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor and must not be admitted to undertake a ministry that can be fulfilled only through continence.”

The same pope, writing to Bishop Victricius, says:

“Moreover, the Church must preserve in every way what is worthy, chaste, and honorable: priests and Levites must not have intercourse with their wives, because they are occupied with the necessities of their daily ministry.

“For it is written: ‘Be holy, because I am holy, says the Lord your God’ (Leviticus 11:44).

“In ancient times they did not leave the temple during the year of their service, as we read concerning Zechariah, nor did they touch their homes at all. Marital relations had been permitted to them for the succession of offspring, because no one from another tribe had been allowed to approach the priesthood for the sake of Aaron’s descendants.

“How much more must these priests or Levites preserve chastity from the day of their ordination, since their priesthood or ministry is without succession and no day passes on which they are free either from the divine sacrifices or from the ministry of baptism?

“For if Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying: ‘Abstain for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer’ (1 Corinthians 7:5)—and he certainly gave this command to laymen—how much more must priests, whose constant duty is both to pray and to offer sacrifice, always abstain from such intercourse?

“If one has been defiled by carnal desire, how can he believe that he can be heard, when it has been said: ‘Everything is clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean’ (Titus 1:15)?

“But perhaps he thinks this is permitted because it is written: ‘The husband of one wife’ (1 Timothy 3:2). He did not say this on account of continuing in desire to beget children, but on account of future continence.

“For he did not exclude those who were physically intact, since he said: ‘I wish that all were as I myself am’ (1 Corinthians 7:7). And he declares more openly: ‘Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are no longer in the flesh, but in the spirit’ (Romans 8:8–9).

“He spoke of one who has a son, not of one who is begetting.”

### XXX

The venerable Pope Siricius likewise says:

“We do not permit any women in the houses of clerics except those whom the Council of Nicaea permitted to live with them solely on account of necessary family relationships.”

### XXXI

Then Saint Pope Leo, the remarkable teacher and author of the holy Council of Chalcedon, cutting off all ambiguity in this matter, says:

> “The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and presbyters. While they were still laymen, they could lawfully marry wives and beget children. But once they reached the aforementioned ranks, what had been lawful for them ceased to be lawful. Therefore, so that a carnal marriage may become a spiritual one, they ought not to dismiss their wives, but to have them as though they did not have them: thus the affection of marriage remains intact, while the acts of marriage cease.”

Behold these men, made key-bearers of the kingdom of heaven with Peter and through Peter, so shatter all the little keys of the gates of hell that no heresy of the Nicolaitans now remains.

### XXXII

But lest you say that something has been left undone, we shall proceed point by point and openly explain what the Roman Church does concerning the clerical ranks. It permits only clerics who are doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, and acolytes—if they are found outside a monk’s vow and habit and do not wish to profess continence—to marry a virgin, with a priestly blessing; but not a widow or a divorced woman. For this reason alone, thereafter they will neither be able to advance to the subdiaconate, nor will a layman who has taken a non-virgin as his wife, or a bigamist, be admitted to the clergy.

If any man of the aforementioned orders desires to ascend to the subdiaconate, he cannot do so without his wife’s consent, so that thereafter the carnal marriage may become a spiritual one; no one compels them to this. Nor is the wife thereafter permitted to unite carnally with that same husband, or to marry anyone else during his lifetime or after his death; otherwise she is to be anathematized. Likewise, a deacon, subdeacon, presbyter, or bishop who takes back his own wife or marries another is to be deposed, in accordance with what the orthodox Fathers decreed at the Council of Neocaesarea.

### XXXIII

[Col. 1000B] Through such traditions, therefore, the holy Roman Church and apostolic see has until now shone throughout the whole world. It has never submitted to Jewish fables or apocryphal writings, but, founded through the first apostles upon that supreme cornerstone, Christ Jesus, it has yielded to no heresies. Nor has it forbidden laymen to marry, but only ministers of the sacred altar and monks who profess apostolic perfection.

### XXXIV

Yet that Church which Arius corrupted and Macedonius prostituted, which gave birth to those broods of vipers—Nestorius, Eutyches, the Monothelites, the Theopaschites, and the remaining plagues of heretics—has still been unable to tear itself away from the embraces of the heresiarch Nicolas. Indeed, when men are to be ordained for the ministry of the sacred altar, it asks whether they have wives. Those who answer that they do not have wives are compelled first to marry and only then to receive the imposition of hands, so that, as new husbands, entirely relaxed and enervated by the recent pleasure of the flesh, and thinking during the sacred sacrifices about how they may please their wives, they may handle and distribute Christ’s immaculate body to the people, and immediately thereafter return their consecrated hands to handling women’s limbs. Thus it is “as the people, so the priest,” and finally the people become like their wicked priests.

### XXXV

Therefore spare yourselves now, and do not heed spirits of error and doctrines of demons, so that, together with us, you may rejoice here and in the future in the true peace, which is Christ.

But you, most wretched Nicetas, until you recover your senses, be anathema, cut off from the entire Church of Christ, together with all who obey you in such perverse doctrine. For, wishing to be a teacher of the divine law, you do not understand either what you say or the matters about which you make assertions; and, being yourself foolish, you appear wiser to yourself than seven men who speak parables. But at least learn to be silent sometime, since you have never learned to speak.

[Col. 0999] The response of Brother Humbert, bishop, against the blasphemies of Nicetas ends here.

[Col. 1001]

## A Brief and Concise Account of What the Legates of the Holy Roman and Apostolic See Did in the Imperial City, and How Michael and His Followers Were Anathematized

[Col. 1001A] **I.** In the eleventh year of the reign of Constantine Monomachus, in the seventh indiction, on the very day of the nativity of blessed John the Baptist, when the legates of the Lord Pope Leo IX arrived at the Studite monastery within the city of Constantinople—namely Humbert, cardinal-bishop of Silva Candida, and Peter, archbishop of the Amalfitans, together with Frederick, deacon and chancellor—Nicetas the monk, also called Pectoratus, in the presence of the aforesaid emperor and his nobles, at the insistence of those Roman envoys, anathematized a certain document published under his name against the apostolic see and the whole Latin Church, entitled *On Unleavened Bread, on the Sabbath, and on the Marriages of Priests*.

Moreover, he anathematized all who denied that the holy Roman Church was the first of all Churches, and all who presumed to criticize its faith, which had always been orthodox, in any respect. Immediately afterward, in the sight of everyone and at the urging of those same Roman envoys, the same orthodox emperor ordered the aforesaid document to be burned. Thus they departed.

**II.** On the following day, Nicetas left the city and voluntarily went to the envoys in the palace of Pege. After receiving from them a complete answer to his propositions, he again of his own accord anathematized everything said, done, or attempted against the first apostolic see. He was then received by them into communion and became their intimate friend.

Furthermore, the statements and writings of those same envoys against the various slanders of the Greeks, and especially against the writings of Michael, bishop of Constantinople, and Leo, metropolitan bishop of Acrida, as well as those of the aforementioned monk Nicetas, were translated into Greek by order of the emperor and preserved in that same city thereafter.

**III.** Finally, when Michael avoided their presence and conversation and persisted in his folly, the aforementioned envoys went to the Church of Hagia Sophia on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August. Having complained about his obstinacy, and with the clergy already prepared according to custom for Mass at the third hour of the Sabbath day, they placed the document of excommunication upon the principal altar in the sight of the clergy and people present.

They then immediately departed, even shaking the dust from their feet against them as a testimony, proclaiming the saying of the Gospel: “Let God see and judge.”

After this, they organized the churches of the Latins within Constantinople itself and pronounced an anathema upon all who thereafter communicated from the hand of a Greek who censured the Roman sacrifice. Having received the orthodox emperor’s permission with the kiss of peace, and having accepted imperial gifts for Saint Peter and themselves, they joyfully began their return on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

But Michael made repeated and urgent pleas, promising that he would then finally engage with them. The emperor, compelled by Michael’s insistence, recalled them by letters from Solebria on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August. They hurried back on that same day and arrived at the palace of Pege.

When the aforementioned heresiarch Michael learned that they had returned, he attempted to bring them into the Church of Hagia Sophia for a council on the following day, intending that the people there should overwhelm them after the document—which he had completely falsified in translating it—had been displayed.

The prudent emperor, anticipating this, refused to allow any council to be held unless he himself were present. [Note: [Col. 1001D] Michael gives the contrary account; for he asserts that the envoys always refused a council and were excommunicated by the emperor’s command [Col. 1002D]. See Michael’s letter in Coteler., *Monum. Ecclesiae Gr.*, vol. II.] When Michael opposed this in every way, Augustus ordered the envoys to set out immediately. This was done.

But the deranged Michael, angered that his plots were not succeeding, stirred up a tremendous revolt of the populace against the emperor, as though the emperor’s will had cooperated with the envoys. Consequently, the emperor was compelled to hand over to Michael the Latin interpreters, Paul and his son Smaragdus, after they had been beaten and tonsured; thus the tumult subsided.

Afterward, however, the emperor sent his own men after the Roman envoys and received from the city of the Russians the authentic copy of the excommunication that had been sent to him. He displayed it to the citizens and finally discovered and proved that Michael had falsified the envoys’ document.

Accordingly, he was enraged, expelled Michael’s friends and relatives from the palace after stripping them of their honors, and continued to harbor severe anger against Michael himself.

Finally, the text of the document of excommunication is as follows:

> “Humbert, by the grace of God cardinal-bishop of the holy Roman Church; Peter, archbishop of the Amalfitans; Frederick, deacon and chancellor, to all the sons of the Catholic Church.
>
> “The holy Roman first and apostolic see, to which, as to its head, the care of all the Churches pertains in a special way, has deigned, for the sake of ecclesiastical peace and advantage, to make us its legates to this imperial city, so that, according to what is written, we might descend and see whether the outcry that continually rises from so great a city to its ears has been fulfilled in deed, or, if not, that it might know this.
>
> “Therefore, let the glorious emperors, the clergy, senate, and people of this city of Constantinople, and the whole Catholic Church, know above all that here we have perceived one very great good, over which we rejoice exceedingly in the Lord, and one very great evil, over which we grieve miserably.
>
> “For as regards the slanders against the empire and its distinguished citizens, this city is wise, most Christian, and orthodox. But as regards Michael, abusively called patriarch, and the supporters of his folly, an excessive abundance of tares of heresies is sown daily in its midst.
>
> “For, like the Simonians, they sell the gift of God; like the Valesians, they castrate their guests and promote them not only to the clergy but even to the episcopate; like the Arians, they rebaptize those who have been baptized in the name of the holy Trinity, especially Latins; like the Donatists, they assert that, except for the Church of the Greeks, the Church of Christ, the true sacrifice, and baptism have perished throughout the whole world; like the Nicolaitans, they permit and defend carnal marriages for ministers of the sacred altar; like the Severians, they call the law of Moses accursed; like the Pneumatomachi, or Theumachi, they have cut out from the Creed the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son; like the Manichaeans, among other things, they declare that everything fermented is animate; like the Nazarenes, they observe the carnal purity of the Jews so strictly that they forbid infants who are dying to be baptized before the eighth day after birth, and forbid women who are menstruating or endangered in childbirth to receive communion, or, if they are pagans, to be baptized. They also refuse communion to those who grow the hair of their heads and beards, to those who cut their hair, and to those who shave their beards according to the institution of the Roman Church.
>
> “For these errors and many other deeds of his, Michael, admonished by letters from our lord Pope Leo, refused to repent. Moreover, when we, his envoys, wished reasonably to restrain him because of such great evils, he denied us his presence and conversation, and forbade the churches to celebrate Mass, just as earlier he had closed the churches of the Latins and had everywhere persecuted them in word and deed, calling them ‘unleavened ones.’ To such an extent did he proceed that, in his sons, he anathematized the apostolic see, against which he still writes that he is the ecumenical patriarch.
>
> “Therefore, since we cannot endure the unheard-of insult and injury inflicted upon the holy first apostolic see, and since we perceive that the Catholic faith is being undermined in many ways, by the authority of the holy and indivisible Trinity and of the apostolic see, whose legation we bear, and of all the orthodox Fathers from the seven councils and of the whole Catholic Church, we subscribe to the anathema that our most reverend pope likewise pronounced against Michael and his followers unless they should repent.
>
> “Michael, abusively called patriarch, a neophyte who assumed the monastic habit solely through human fear, now also notorious for the worst crimes; and with him Leo, called bishop of Acrida, and Constantine, Michael’s sacristan, who profanely trampled the sacrifice of the Latins with his feet; and all their followers in the errors and presumptions mentioned above—let them be anathema, Maranatha, together with the Simonians, Valesians, Arians, Donatists, Nicolaitans, Severians, Pneumatomachi, Manichaeans, and Nazarenes, and with all heretics, indeed with the devil and his angels, unless they should perhaps repent. Amen, amen, amen.”

Another excommunication was pronounced there, in the presence of the emperor and his nobles, aloud:

> “Whoever stubbornly contradicts the holy faith of the Roman and apostolic see and its sacrifice, let him be anathema, Maranatha, and let him not be regarded as a Catholic Christian, but as a *prozymite* heretic [that is, one who refuses to use unleavened bread in the sacrifice]. Let it be done, let it be done, let it be done.”

[Col. 1005]

# Three Books of Humbert, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Against the Simoniacs

*(In D. Martène, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, vol. V, p. 629, from the Laurentian Library.)*

## Preliminary Admonition

After the prince of the apostles pierced simony, together with its own father Simon Magus, with a spiritual dart, not even the name of so horrible a monster ought to be heard among Christians. Yet its wickedness is such that, although nothing is more harmful to the Church than this evil, nothing is more frequent within it; indeed, since it seems to have been born with the Church itself, it appears that it will perish only when the Church perishes.

Although it has prevailed at all times and has never been restrained by the preaching or writings of any holy teachers, by the censures of bishops, or by the decrees of councils, nevertheless in the eleventh century that monstrous plague spread so widely that one might say it had infected nearly the whole world.

Then the supreme pontiffs, by apostolic authority—Pope Leo IX, Gregory VII, and Urban II—rose up against it; Peter Damian and Cardinal Humbert opposed it in their writings; and Peter Igneus and John Gualbert opposed it by their deeds and miracles, all of them members of our order, and their labor was certainly not in vain.

To say something about Cardinal Humbert, whose three books against the Simoniacs we publish here: he was born in Lorraine. While still a boy and wearing the monastic habit, he was entrusted to Abbot Hardulf at the monastery of Moyenmoutier in the diocese of Toul. He had scarcely reached adolescence when he attained the whole perfection of the religious life.

After being trained in the liberal arts, he was soon instructed in every branch of knowledge. Since he combined learning with piety and was especially skilled in music, he so won the friendship and favor of Bruno, the most holy bishop of Toul, who delighted in these qualities, that when Bruno became supreme pontiff as Leo IX, he brought Humbert with him into Italy and used his assistance in the Church’s most important and difficult affairs.

“For,” says Cardinal Baronius under the year 1049, “the Roman Church owed much to Leo, who at this opportune moment placed so great a man, perhaps otherwise remaining idle in Lorraine, upon the stage of the world to labor for the whole Catholic Church.”

As soon as Leo reached Rome, he made Humbert archbishop of Sicily. Not long afterward he created him cardinal and bishop of Silva Candida, and had in him a champion against the enemies of the Church. He also sent him as legate to Constantinople to restrain the schism of the Greeks. There Humbert debated with them concerning unleavened and leavened bread. At the emperor Constantine Monomachus’s command, Caesar Baronius published the debate in writing from a Vatican manuscript, together with Humbert’s response to the objections of Nicetas Pectoratus.

Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, commends Cardinal Humbert in the following terms in his *Commentary Against Berengar*:

> “All who knew Humbert by their own experience, or learned of him from others who had experienced him, testify that he was a religious man, most steadfastly adorned with Christian faith and holy works, and especially learned in the knowledge of divine and secular literature. Saint Leo brought him to Rome, not from Burgundy but from Lorraine, and ordained him archbishop to preach the word of God to the Sicilians. Later the holy Roman Church appointed him its cardinal bishop. In that position he lived and taught in such a way that no report even of a sinister suspicion concerning his faith or teaching ever arose. Nearly the whole Latin world bears witness to this, for, because of the excellence of the apostolic see, whose councils and counsels he always attended and directed, it could not fail to know him.”

This testimony of Lanfranc is supported by Trithemius, Bellarmine, and other later writers.

Besides the works of Humbert already mentioned, and others published by the learned Henry Canisius in the sixth volume of his *Antiquae Lectiones*, Humbert composed three books against the Simoniacs, in which he mentions his legation to Constantinople.

A certain Spinosulus, who approved the ordinations of Simoniacs—which Humbert, on the contrary, attacked—seems to have provided the occasion for writing these books. At least, we infer this from the following words of Humbert, Book I, chapter 7:

> “Thus, even against his will, this Spinosulus is already known, as the disputation proceeds, to be revealing the beginning, progress, and end of his perverse intention; and, like a hedgehog caught in a snare, he is compelled, as water approaches, to unfold his head, feet, and tail. For it is clear that he stubbornly defends those ordained by heretics, and especially by Simoniacs, because, as is abundantly shown above, once an order has been received in the Catholic Church, it is not repeated. He also struggles with various but empty arguments to establish that those ordained by Simoniacs, as it is said, ought to be regarded and retained in the Catholic clergy without penance or the imposition of hands, as though they lacked nothing in any grace. But we have proved above by sufficient testimonies of the holy Fathers that the Simoniacs are heretics worse than the worst Arians,” and so forth.

Who this Spinosulus was, whom Humbert attacks by name as the sole opponent in these books, I have not yet been able to discover.

We infer the time when Humbert produced this work from Book III, chapter 7, where he first attacks Henry, king of the Franks, because he favored the Simoniacs more than was proper and, despite being admonished by the revered pontiffs Leo and Victor, was unwilling to be corrected.

From this you will conclude that Humbert wrote before the year 1060, in which King Henry died, and after the pontificates of Leo and Victor, the supreme pontiffs whose successor was Stephen X in the year 1057.

Mabillon recovered these books from the Laurentian Library and our Renatus Massuet, heir to his labors and successor in his studies, entrusted them to me for publication while he was occupied with greater matters. The manuscript from which they were copied was written during the author’s lifetime, so that it may even be regarded as an autograph; in every other respect it is of excellent quality.

# The Preface of Humbert, Cardinal Bishop of the Holy Roman Church, in His Response Against the Simoniacs Begins Here

[Col. 1007]

[Col. 1007A] Lest he appear wise to himself, we are compelled to answer a fool who, having erased the title from the front of his work—or rather the title from his barking—and suppressed his name, shamelessly attempts to persuade us that the precious must not be separated from the worthless, and that the holy and the profane, the clean and the unclean, do not differ.

Since the divine law makes some distinction even between leprosy and leprosy, this prodigious evasive sophist and demonic reasoner, like another Jovinianus and a revived Stoic, contends that one and the same grace exists and operates in Catholics and heretics, and that it makes no difference whether the administration of Christ’s sacraments takes place or is possessed outside or within the Catholic Church, since he believes that the fullness of the Holy Spirit operates indifferently and equally within and outside it, and that nothing can be conferred upon those who return to the Catholic Church or taken away from those who depart from it.
