Whatever this most vehement reasoner may be, he is nevertheless proved to be an enemy of God, even if in certain matters he appears to defend Him, because, according to the Apostle, he has “the appearance of godliness, but denies its power” (II Tim. III, 5), considering godliness to be a source of gain (I Tim. VI, 5).

Although he sometimes offers certain things correctly, he sins by failing to divide what is right correctly. He is Cain, to be struck by the curse and sentence and cast from the face of the earth—that is, from the Catholic Church—since, to the destruction of himself and of many of Christ’s simple ones, he twists and corrupts the holy Scriptures and the correct judgments of the holy Fathers, shortening some passages and lengthening others by presenting them as his own.

Finally, having forcefully bent his bow, he prepared his arrows in his quiver “to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. X, 3). Worse still, lifted up and blinded by the arrogance of his knowledge or whatever continence he may possess, he has, as it is thought, zeal for God, “but not according to knowledge” (Rom. X, 2), and supposes that he is rendering service to God (John XVI, 2) if, like a cancer, he spreads through pestilential words, infects and corrupts, and cuts away from the chastity that is in Christ the understanding of his simple brethren.

Indeed, having abandoned the fountain of living water, he has dug cisterns for himself, “broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. II, 13). He does not care to draw living water from the wells that Isaac’s servants dug (Gen. XXVI, 15–22), but instead to carry mud into them.

And like that garrulous and wandering woman of Proverbs, impatient of quiet, foolish and loud, full of seductions, knowing nothing at all and unable to keep her feet still in her house, utterly lacking the true bread, now lying in wait outside, now in the streets, now beside the corners, she sits at the doorway of her house upon a seat in the high place of the city, to call out to passersby and travelers on their way:

> “Whoever is simple, let him turn in to me.”

And she says to the senseless:

> “Stolen waters are sweeter, and hidden bread is more pleasant.”

But they do not know that giants are there, and that her guests are in the depths of hell (Prov. VII, 10–12; IX, 13–18).

From the shrine—or rather the mire—of this prostitute, from her stubborn shamelessness and shameless stubbornness, there is nothing by which we may more suitably and cautiously frighten and recall our simple ones than these denunciations or reproaches of Jeremiah, who was sanctified in the womb:

> “What have you to do on the road to Assyria, to drink the water of the river? What have you to do on the road to Egypt, to drink the turbid water?” (Jer. II, 18.)

And we may use these admonitions of the blessed Paul, the vessel of election:

> “You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (I Cor. X, 20–21).

And again:

> “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, as God says: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord, and do not touch what is unclean; and I will receive you, and I will be a father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty’” (II Cor. VI, 14–18).

> “Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God” (II Cor. VII, 1).

In these words of the Apostle we are plainly warned to separate marriage and carnal intercourse from unbelievers; much more, then, must spiritual union be separated from them, and what is unclean must not be touched, so that we may present ourselves to our God as a glorious Church, “without spot or wrinkle or any such thing” (Eph. V, 27), so that He Himself may dwell in us and receive us, bringing our sanctification to completion.

When you hear “unbelievers,” understand not only pagans but also heretics, whom blessed Jerome and the entire chorus of holy teachers declare to be worse than pagans, because among pagans there is still hope of faith, whereas among heretics there is already the battle of discord.

A heretic is one who dissents from the Catholic faith, believing and defending what ought not to be believed, whether concerning God or His creatures. Yet a person is not immediately to be regarded as a heretic whenever he holds some opinion against the faith; rather, he becomes one when he obstinately and irrationally defends his opinions or judgments.

Therefore he must immediately be avoided, as the same Apostle says:

> “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second admonition, knowing that such a one is perverted and sins, being self-condemned” (Tit. III, 10–11).

If a heretic is to be condemned and cast away with such abhorrence and such sudden severity, what does his defender deserve? For one who defends the error of others is much more worthy of condemnation and notice than they are, because he not only errs himself but also prepares and confirms stumbling blocks of error for others.

Therefore, because he is a teacher of error, such a man is rightly called not merely a heretic but also a heresiarch, since he is first in error.

Let the obstinate defenders of the Simoniacs, disciples or followers of Simon Magus—the first heretic after grace had been revealed—see among the faithful by what rank or under what name they ought to be regarded.

But now, kindly Spirit, come and join Yourself to our voice. Bring reproof and, if possible, correction to the man who speaks a word against the madness of simony and blasphemes You. Through me, Your mute beast of burden, speak from heaven in a human voice according to Your omnipotence, and restrain the folly of the false prophets who, wishing to be teachers of the law, understand neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions (I Tim. I, 7).

Defend, O God most free of all, and Lord in every way coequal and coeternal with God the Father and the Son, Your unique freedom from sacrilegious merchants, from the money-loving heirs of Simon the Samaritan, lest, contrary to the sentence pronounced by the great Simon Peter at the very beginnings of Christianity, Your little ones and simple people be led into so destructive an error that they should in some measure believe—or, as is thought more tolerable, suppose—that You, the supreme and incomparable gift of God, can be possessed for money, which is a crime even to say, as though You were a purchased slave, a beast for sale, or a servile bondman.

And what will become of that freedom of ours by which we already presume through You and glory in the hope of the freedom of the children of God, as the Apostle proclaims:

> “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (II Cor. III, 17).

And:

> “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. VIII, 14).

What will become of it if You Yourself have been handed over as a slave to money-changers and servants of Mammon? And do You, O dove, offer Yourself to be torn apart by kites, whether from necessity or by Your own will?

If You descend or pour Yourself into creatures to be sanctified at the command of such wicked servants and worst merchants, it must be said either that You are violently compelled to do so by fear of such masters, as though the instruments and documents of Your purchase had been offended, or that, having become fully united and of one mind with wicked masters, You are sweetly drawn by love and a kind of reverence for money. In that case grace is no longer grace, because it is not received freely.

If You are compelled by fear, Your omnipotence and freedom perish, because You no longer breathe where and when You will. But if You are drawn by love, then blessed are no longer the poor in spirit; rather, they are wretched, since You are discovered to be a stubborn follower of money, which You falsely command to be despised and scattered without any future recompense.

But far be it from us even lightly to suspect such a thing of You, O Spirit of inviolable and irreproachable truth, whom God gave us as the pledge of faith and hope: that, bound by the pledge of money to the Simoniacs, You should be proclaimed not Lord of lords but, three degrees lower—or even a thousand degrees lower—the slave of the worst servants of a worse lord, namely Mammon.

Therefore let us now refute with opposing words the statements of those who blaspheme You and presume to claim for themselves a priesthood not owed to them. Let Your fire go before us and consume the rash; and finally, when their alien fire has been scattered here and there, let the bronze censers—sanctified, as it were, by the deaths of sinners—be hammered into plates and fastened to the Lord’s altar, so that from their utterances, vocal indeed but obscure, the Lord’s pure words, like silver and gold, may become more recognizable and more clearly and evidently known by comparison with them.

“For there must be heresies,” says the Apostle, “so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (I Cor. XI, 19).

# The Chapters of the Book of Humbert, Cardinal Bishop of the Holy Roman Church, in His Response Against the Simoniacs Begin Here

[Col. 1009]

[Col. 1009D]

**I.** An attack against the corrupter, convicting him of falsehood.

**II.** Concerning the pseudo-bishops whom the decretal chapter of Pope Leo marks out.

**III.** That the Simoniacs are worse than the Arians and than Simon, their own teacher.

**IV.** The anger of the Holy Spirit against Simon; a comparison of him and his followers, and what they receive.

**V.** That the chapter of Saint Leo is to be understood not of heretics but of Catholics.

[Col. 1010D]

**VI.** Concerning pseudo-bishops and their ordinations.

**VII.** Concerning the chapter of Saint Gregory forbidding reordination; where he also concedes that the Simoniacs are at least to be equated with the Arians.

**VIII.** Concerning the canons of the apostles and a second imposition of hands.

**IX.** How the baptism of heretics is permitted, and what “permission” means.

[Col. 1011A]

**X.** Concerning the imperfection of the baptism of heretics according to the judgment of the holy Fathers.

**XI.** Where the judgments of the holy Fathers are brought forth, showing in what circumstances heretics are to be avoided.

**XII.** Concerning the ordinations of heretics, according to blessed Innocent.

**XIII.** Further on the same subject, according to blessed Gregory.

**XIV.** A recapitulation of the preceding judgments of blessed Gregory against false reasoners.

**XV.** Concerning proper and improper expressions, and the vanity of the Simoniacs.

**XVI.** The judgment of Saint Ambrose concerning the ordinations of Simoniacs.

[Col. 1012A]

**XVII.** A recapitulation of the preceding matter. Then the judgment of blessed Augustine.

**XVIII.** The judgments of the holy Fathers concerning those who traffic in ecclesiastical dignity.

**XIX.** A refutation of those who say that the Simoniacs possess grace from which they may be deposed.

**XX.** That the Simoniacs are without faith, and that they deprive those who consent to them of faith.

**XXI.** A refutation of those who say that the Holy Spirit can rightly be possessed and given by one who received Him unjustly.

The chapters of the first book against the Simoniacs end here.

# The First Booklet Against Heretics, Especially the Simoniacs, in the Form of a Dialogue Between the Corrupter and the Reprover, Published by Humbert, Cardinal Bishop of the Holy Roman Church, Begins Here

[Col. 1011]

## Chapter One

[Col. 1011B]

**REPROVER.** At the very threshold of his controversy, having prefixed several chapters in defense of himself and his associates, arranged like traps or snares set out to entangle the unwary, the subverted subverter and seduced seducer finally emerges violently from the tunnels of his ambush and suddenly bursts into these arguments in order to choke those who have been caught:

**CORRUPTER.**

> “After rereading these chapters, O lovers of justice, you have heard more clearly that an ordination performed by pseudo-bishops could remain valid.”

**REPROVER.** It is characteristic of sorcerers to smear the rim of a deadly cup with a little honey, so that the sweetness tasted beforehand may make whatever lethal substance remains be swallowed without hesitation.

This is what this slanderer is accused of doing when, having begun to lay out the snares of his chapters—which he had corrupted by begging them from every direction and placing them before the doors of his argument—he begins:

**CORRUPTER.**

> “From this point onward follow splendid testimonies by which it is shown that the ordination of Pope Formosus was valid and legitimate.”

**REPROVER.** To secure the greatest favor for this little statement of his and make it appear venerable to everyone because of the authority of the first and greatest synod, he falsely gave it the heading “from the Council of Nicaea.”

What presumption he displays becomes clear in what follows: he polluted the doorway of his narrative with a lie, or rather with sacrilege. For that first chapter, or that verse, is found neither in the whole of Nicaea nor in any council held afterward. Nor is anything discussed or demonstrated at Nicaea or in any later council concerning whether the ordination of Pope Formosus should be regarded as valid or invalid, since even to suspect such a matter slightly would be considered the height of folly.

For between the Council of Nicaea and Pope Formosus there are more than five hundred years, just as between the great Constantine and the Emperor Arnulf, with whose assistance Formosus succeeded in retaining the Roman pontificate. Moreover, Arnulf is counted as the sixth or seventh emperor after Charlemagne.

If he thought that chapter ought to be given the heading “from the Council of Nicaea” because some of the chapters he appended came from that council, let him be informed—or recognize—that he appended nothing from it except the single chapter concerning the Cathari.

Thus it is evident how great a slanderer he is: defeated by error, he nevertheless labors shamelessly to appear victorious by lying even against that venerable council, the greatest and best known throughout the world.

But let his statements now be sifted and distinguished.

## Chapter Two
Having prefaced this with a chapter of Pope Leo, the blessed and great teacher, he attempts to bolster his error from it, as though there he had been speaking of some Simoniacs or at least of other heretics, and not rather of Catholics—if any whom the ignorance, presumption, or necessity of the Church’s leaders causes, or has at some time caused, to be consecrated not according to the strictness of the canons. For it could and can happen that one, or two, or all three of these qualifications are lacking in those consecrated: that they were neither elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by the provincial bishops with the metropolitan’s judgment. Nevertheless, they are not without consecration, because it was performed without monetary sale, although on account of the three qualifications mentioned above it wavers and strays, unstable and uncertain.

Otherwise, if there were no episcopal consecration in them, there would be no ordination of them at all, even though they might ordain clerics in churches belonging to their proper bishops, according to the customary judgment of those presiding there, so to speak. For no church, nor any judgment of those presiding over it, could or ever can enable someone to give another what he himself is proved in no way to possess: to administer to others, by his prayer and action, a valid consecration that he himself could in no way receive or possess.

Would not the ordination of a Catholic layman be considered more commendable in this respect than that of any heretical bishop, [Col. 1013A] if merely by the judgment of bishops presiding over churches he could give what he does not possess? For our layman, if necessity requires it, baptizes for the remission of sins through the Holy Spirit; whereas no heretic whatsoever, even if he is called a bishop, ever grants this to anyone. The blessed Leo himself professes this in another of his Decretals, declaring that even baptism given by heretics in the name of the Holy Trinity possesses only the form of baptism, without the power of sanctification:

> “Those who have received baptism from heretics, if they had not previously been baptized, are to be confirmed by the invocation of the Holy Spirit alone through the imposition of hands, because they have received only the form of baptism, without the power of sanctification.”

And, as you know, we proclaim that this rule must be observed in all churches: that a washing once begun must not be violated by repetition, since the Apostle says, “One God, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5). Its cleansing must not be rashly repeated; rather, as we have said, only the sanctification of the Holy Spirit is to be invoked, so that from Catholic priests they may obtain what no one receives from heretics: sanctification, cleansing from sins, and renewal from the old condition. [Col. 1013B]

It is therefore clear from these words of the most blessed Leo that the baptism of heretics possesses only the form or appearance of true baptism, and provides washing or cleansing merely to the bodies, not also to the souls, because it is given and received without the power of sanctification or the sanctification of the Holy Spirit—something that no one receives or obtains from heretics.

But if the baptism of the Lord Jesus, according to the testimony of the Baptist, is in the Holy Spirit, and was made and accomplished so that the remission of all sins might proceed from it and our old person be renewed, it is evident that the baptism of heretics, since it is without the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, effects no remission of sin and no renewal of the old person, but only visible washing. Catholics certainly did not agree to refrain from repeating it because of any holiness or reverence belonging to it. Rather, prudently avoiding the scandal of a contentious and foolish multitude, and seeking by every means to bring more people back to Christ, they allowed their washing—imperfect, certainly, in its better aspect—to remain valid. Yet they did so on the condition that from Catholic priests, through the imposition of hands and invocation of the Holy Spirit, they receive the sanctification, cleansing from sins, and renewal from their former state that they had previously possessed not at all. [Col. 1013C]

And so that we may perceive more clearly how imperfect they are judged or considered even after this reception, the universal canon has also established that no such person may be promoted into the Catholic clergy. If someone is thought to exist in the clergy among the heretics, he is to be content with lay communion—except for the Cathari, whom the holy Council of Nicaea alone permits, when found among their clergy, to remain in the Catholic clergy, though not without the imposition of hands. These Cathari, although greatly and remarkably sound in conscience, have not deviated in any respect from the confession of the Catholic faith and the unity of the apostolic Church, except in the sole matter of avoiding the communion of criminals. Nevertheless, the fathers continually admonish them to produce fruits worthy of repentance and to seek and await pardon alone. [Col. 1013D]

## CHAPTER III

If, then, the Cathari were counted heretics for this minor error—or rather for this excessively severe and insufficiently discerning judgment of theirs—although they disagree in no other respect from the truth of the Catholic faith, and if they could not be admitted to the Catholic clergy without the imposition of hands, can the ordination, or—as it is called—the consecration, of greater and worse heretics be regarded as valid, when returning Cathari cannot obtain or retain it for themselves without the imposition of hands?

To put it more explicitly: will ordinations and consecrations presumed by Simoniacs be received into the Catholic Church without any examination or reconsideration, when the Seventh and Universal Council, in the letter of Patriarch Tarasius to Pope Adrian, unequivocally defined them to be worse than the Arians? [Col. 1014A]

The Arians, although they err above all in asserting that the Son is less than the Father and a creature, and likewise that the Holy Spirit is less than the Father and the Son and a creature, nevertheless, when making both assertions, contend that neither of them is subject to any creature whatsoever, but only to the Lord the Father, the Creator of all things visible and invisible.

The Simoniacs, however, not content with so great a sacrilege as that of the Arians, believe the almighty Holy Spirit to be not only less than the Father and the Son, or subject only to the Father and the Son, but even inferior to themselves and subject to themselves, like any saleable and worthless slave. They believe that he must obey their wills and words, whether he wishes it or not; that, drawn by the cords of money or bound, as it were, by their golden chains, he must administer the fullness of his sanctification and grace through their sacrilegious offices and accursed consecrations, and cooperate with their sale or activity. [Col. 1014B]

To judge this for a moment, it is an intolerable and perhaps unforgivable blasphemy, because it is to sin against the Holy Spirit, or at least to speak a word against him. It was on this sole account that Simon, the first author and standard-bearer of their sect, from whom they are also called Simoniacs, was condemned irrecoverably.

Simon might in some way have been excused by the novelty of the religion or by ignorance under so evident a manifestation of the Holy Spirit—by which, either delighted or astonished, like someone still inexperienced in baptism and a novice in knowledge of the faith, he suddenly, as a vigorous disciple impatient of delay, judged that so immeasurable a gift of knowledge ought to be sought and received from effective teachers even at the cost of a great sum of money. But he proved inexcusable before the blessed Apostles Peter and John. [Col. 1014C]

The most gentle Peter—“Bar-Jonah,” that is, son of the dove, most simple and innocent—without reserving any gentleness, without first offering the moderate rebuke customary toward novices, without requiring satisfaction, without awaiting correction, and without giving any admonition that he should henceforth beware of attempting such a thing, burned against that wretched man with such zeal and thundered with such severity that, without observing the order of judgment, he first pronounced an irrevocable sentence and struck the guilty man with an anathema, saying:

> “May your money perish with you” (Acts 8:20).

Then he added the reason for so great and sudden a condemnation:

> “Because you thought that the gift of God could be obtained with money” (ibid.).

Immediately denying him any share in spiritual grace according to his estimation, he says:

> “You have neither part nor lot in this matter” (ibid., 21),

that is, in this gift.

Finally, execrating and vehemently rebuking his wickedness and perversity of heart, he says:

> “For your heart is not right before God; for I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity” (ibid., 21, 23).

And when he summoned him to repentance, he made the possibility of pardon uncertain and doubtful because of so great a blasphemy, saying:

> “Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours and pray to the Lord, if perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you” (ibid., 22).

In this final sentence of blessed Peter against Simon, it is the thought of his heart alone that is rebuked, just as in the first sentence only his estimation is condemned. [Col. 1015A]

## CHAPTER IV

It is therefore clearer than daylight to all that Peter, a man of excessive patience and rustic simplicity, did not pronounce so sudden and so severe a sentence under his own impulse or from human passion and agitation. Rather, the Holy Spirit himself, dwelling in Peter as in his temple, could not endure so great an injury, blasphemy, and insult; he was utterly indignant—no one can resist his wrath—and, as it is read metaphorically in Genesis, being “touched with grief of heart within” (Genesis 6:6), he defended and avenged the liberty of his grace through the venerable Peter, anticipating by a detestable and terrible judgment the future punishment of the Magus’s avarice and of the shameless, self-seeking presumption of his followers, since it was thought that the Spirit could be reduced to servitude by money.

That madman, terrified by such thunder and lightning of words, sought through the apostles’ intercession to have so great an indignation of God removed from him, saying:

> “Pray to the Lord for me, that none of the things you have said may come upon me” (Acts 8:24).

Yet he earned no answer from them concerning this, either then or afterward, so that later generations might learn what an enormous precipice he had fallen into, when not even the holy Apostles presumed to extend to him the hand of their intercession. They judged it more just to leave him, cut off from their communion, to the irrevocable wrath of the Lord, because they recognized his offense as inexpiable.

If, as Chrysostom says, “the fall of those who came before ought to be a warning to those who follow,” we ought to consider what the same teacher adds: “If we fall into it frequently, those who fell first deserve pardon more than we who fell second.”

Where, then, I ask, will the Simoniacs at last awaken—together with their closest chamberlains and faithful attendants? Let them see into what ruin their first author has fallen and into what precipice he has descended; let them recognize, even if late, where they lie. They have dared to believe that through money they can become priests, or be made into anything else belonging to the ecclesiastical order, or obtain such things for themselves, or confer them on anyone, freely or for a price. Yet it is clear that they could in no way obtain these things through money, since the prince of the Apostles himself protested to their prince Simon:

> “You have neither part nor lot in this matter” (Acts 8:21). [Col. 1015B]

In this presumption, the Magus’s error is more pardonable: he merely judged that the Lord’s gift could be obtained with money, whereas these men boast and trust—and even say—that they have nevertheless acquired it through money and possess it, and can give it to anyone.

For if they did not believe that they could be made bishops through money, they would preach this with us and cease usurping an office that is not theirs. Rather than communicate to others any ordination or consecration of episcopal ministry, they would communicate the condemnation of their own perdition. But if they believe that they can be made bishops through money, they are manifestly heretics, worse than the man who first merely judged or thought this.

If they do not believe it, why do they presume to exercise another’s office? Why do they not recognize that they do not possess for themselves what they cannot grant to others in the ministry?

In this too they are manifestly heretics and despair; or at least, in hope, they add daily accursed blasphemies to their first blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. They are worse than their master, who, after his rejection, neither believed that he had received or possessed the Lord’s gift—namely, the Holy Spirit—nor laid hands on anyone for this purpose, although he had sought from the Apostles only the power by which he could lay hands on anyone and that person might receive the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1016C]

That man was wicked because he offered money for this purpose; these men are worse because they not only offer money but also obstinately confer the gift.

He was wicked because, before half a year had passed since his conversion, he fell once into this sacrilege; how much worse are these men, who, having received the faith of Christ from the womb of their carnal mother, desire from childhood to old age to think of and do nothing else?

That criminal was wicked because, when rebuked and admonished, he did not recover through repentance; these men are far more criminal because, having become incorrigible and impenitent, and pierced by no rebuke or admonition, they do not abandon the alien office or position they have presumed for themselves, nor withdraw themselves into continual repentance, lest perhaps they may at some time be forgiven for having destroyed many along with themselves and infected Christ’s Church with the contagion of their condemnation. [Col. 1016D]

That wicked man was so because, scarcely a second year after the Lord’s Passion had begun, he undertook such a crime, deterred by no example of anyone condemned for it; but these men are much more wicked because, after a thousand or more years have passed since the Magus’s condemnation and rejection, they have been made, as it were, bolder by the examples of innumerable condemned men. They do not cease to undertake so great a crime, and by persevering in that guilt to transgress even more than their master, against the manifest sentence of Truth, who is Christ, believing, teaching, and doing that they have not received the Holy Spirit freely or that they can give him freely, while Truth herself protests:

> “Freely you have received, freely give” (Matthew 10:8).

It is therefore evident that those who do not seek to receive the Spirit of truth freely do not receive him at all. What, then, do they receive? Surely the spirit of falsehood, which without doubt they give whenever they lay hands on anyone, whether freely or not freely. For they cannot give anything other than what they have received, since “figs are not gathered from thorns, nor grapes from a bramble bush.”

In the end, grace, unless it is received freely, is not grace and cannot rightly be called so. The Simoniacs, however, do not freely receive what they receive. Therefore they do not receive the grace that operates especially in ecclesiastical orders. If they do not receive it, neither do they possess it; if they do not possess it, they can neither freely nor non-freely give to anyone what they do not have.

What, then, do they give? Obviously, what they possess. And what do they possess? Surely the spirit of falsehood. How do we prove this? Because, if the Spirit of truth is received freely—as Truth herself, from whom he proceeds, testifies—then what is not received freely is without doubt proved to be the spirit of falsehood. [Col. 1017A]

## CHAPTER V

Let us now return to the discussion of the chapter proposed, and demonstrate that when blessed Leo mentions pseudo-bishops there, he establishes those rules not against Simoniacs or any other heretics, but against certain Catholics.

It has already been sufficiently demonstrated above that he was not speaking there of Simoniacs or of other heretics. Now it must be demonstrated that he was speaking of pseudo-bishops who were nevertheless Catholics.

Anyone consecrated as a bishop according to the decrees of the holy canons must first be elected by the clergy, then sought by the people, and finally consecrated by the neighboring bishops with the judgment of the metropolitan. Otherwise he cannot be called or considered a genuine and established bishop, unless he has a definite clergy and people over whom he presides and has been consecrated by his neighboring bishops with the authority of the metropolitan, to whom, by apostolic delegation, the care of that province belongs.

He must be called and considered neither genuine, nor established, nor true, but a pseudo-bishop; nor may he be counted among bishops planted or created canonically. For since a bishop is called an overseer or superintendent, over what clergy or what people does such a man preside, when he has had no election by any clergy or people over whom he might preside, and moreover lacks the authority of the metropolitan and neighboring bishops?

What follows in the chapter under discussion—“Therefore, since the question of an improperly received honor often arises, who could doubt that what is taught not to have been conferred must by no means be granted to these men?”—is to be understood in this way: the episcopal honor, namely consecration, was indeed received, but improperly—not because it was obtained through money or from Simoniacs, for in that case no consecration could precede or be regarded as having been obtained, as is sufficiently shown above, but because it was received without clergy and people and without the authority of the metropolitan.

Accordingly, there is no doubt that bishops of this sort are unworthy to be granted what is taught not to have been conferred upon them when they were consecrated: namely, a definite parish of their own and the authority to ordain their own clergy. Or, as is read concerning priests ordained without the names of titles in the African Council, they are to minister or ordain nowhere, to the injury of those who ordained such men noncanonically.

Yet in the same chapter he took care to show where, among whom, through whom, and in what manner the ordination of such men could stand. If clerics were ordained by these pseudo-bishops in churches belonging to their proper bishops, and their ordination was carried out according to the customary judgment of those presiding over them, it may be regarded as valid, so that they may remain in those churches.

Otherwise, the ordination must be considered void, since it is founded neither in a place nor supported by authority. It is therefore clear that if they ordained the clerics of bishops who possessed their own churches, with the judgment and consent of those bishops, the ordination could be regarded as valid, so that the clerics ordained by them might remain in the churches of their own bishops, because these pseudo-bishops do not possess churches of their own to which they could assign those whom they ordain.

Thus their consecration is rendered stable by the authority of the other bishops and founded in a place—namely, in the churches belonging to those bishops. [Col. 1018B]

## CHAPTER VI

Therefore, lest anyone perversely argue that pseudo-bishops of this sort can never make ordinations valid, just as Simoniacs or any other heretics cannot; or, conversely, that Simoniacs or any other heretics can make valid ordinations, just as these men can; and lest anyone claim that these and those must be treated in the same way because these are called pseudo-bishops just as those are—that is, false bishops—let anyone who is concerned observe that “false” is not always said in one uniform sense. Sometimes it is said partially, sometimes wholly. This is very easily demonstrated by an everyday example.

A coin is called false, yet it is perceived differently by the vigilant and by those who are asleep. It deceives the former in its impression, or in its material, or at least in its weight; the latter, however, in every respect, because it neither was, nor is, nor will be—it is false in its entirety and nothing.

Although human contrivance deprives the former coin, to a greater or lesser extent, of its proper quality, it nevertheless leaves it something, little or much. The other, through diabolical deception, is fashioned empty of all genuineness and attributes nothing to it except deception alone.

Rightly, then, the pseudo-bishop who belongs to the Catholics is compared to a false coin—one which human workmanship, although imperfect in some respects, nevertheless forms perfectly in others. On the other hand, the pseudo-bishop who belongs to the heretics is likewise rightly compared to a false coin—one which diabolical workmanship fashions as wholly nonexistent, though perfect in illusion alone. [Col. 1018C]

Our coin, although false, will nevertheless have some value, however great its falsity may be. For if it is rejected on account of its weight, it will be approved on account of its material and its impression; or, if not by two of these together, it will nevertheless be approved in some way by one of the three.

So too our pseudo-bishop, however little justice he possesses in himself, is nevertheless approved before God and sane-minded human beings either on account of the sincerity of his faith or life, or on account of his consecration alone, even though he is rejected because of the election of those who snore.

But a false coin, however perfect it may appear, is nothing and has no value or significance in any part of its existence. To believe that it is, was, or will be a coin is a pernicious lie.

So too the pseudo-bishop of the heretics, however great his continence or holiness may seem—if he ought to be called holy—is counted as nothing before God and before people of vigilant heart, because whatever is without faith is sin. To believe him to be a bishop is not merely sin but also monstrous sacrilege.

To confirm our assertion, I would like to insert into this little work a remembrance of certain men who were neither elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by neighboring bishops with the judgment of the metropolitan, and yet were found in Christ’s Church to possess, through consecration alone, such authority, holiness, and usefulness that no one except a sacrilegious person would presume to call them pseudo-bishops in any respect.

First, let us recall the most blessed Apostles, the founders and princes of the universal Church—unless we should rightly judge that laws and natural conditions must necessarily be silent where the Lawgiver and Lord of nature has bestowed blessing, grace, and glory. [Col. 1019B]

Passing over, therefore, with the reverence owed to them and to such ordinations, and also passing over the bishops with whom those blessed Apostles themselves, following the example of their Lord and teacher, illuminated Asia, Europe, and Africa—especially Peter, who caused his Italy and all the Gauls to run after Christ through preachers ordained by him in this manner—we think that only two of their successors, ordained in this way after the sacred canons had already been promulgated, need be mentioned, as is recorded in the Tripartite History.

“Perigenes was ordained bishop in Petra, and because the citizens refused to receive him, the bishop of the Roman city ordered him to be enthroned in Corinth, the metropolis, after its bishop had died, and he presided over that church as long as he lived.

“Likewise Sisinnius, the bishop of Constantinople, consecrated Proclus at Cyzicus. Before Proclus departed for Cyzicus, however, the citizens, proceeding ahead, ordained Dalmatius the monk as their bishop. Proclus therefore remained without his own church, although he flourished greatly in the teaching of the churches of Constantinople; later he was enthroned in the see of Constantinople.”

It is therefore evident that neither of them had been elected by clergy or people; it is also clear that they had not been received by them.

The same History, making mention above of the Second Universal Council, namely the Council of Constantinople, says:

> “The Fathers again confirmed the Nicene faith and established patriarchs, assigning provinces so that the bishops of each diocese would not go to foreign churches.” [Col. 1020A]

This practice was initially carried out indiscriminately because of the time of persecution. Thus, concerning those ordained in this manner, another synod proposed the following rule:

> “If a bishop ordained for a parish does not proceed to the parish for which he was ordained—not through his own fault, but either because the people rejected him or because of some other cause not arising from necessity—he is to share only in the honor and ministry, and is not to be involved in the affairs of the church in which he celebrates the church’s assembly; rather, he is to await what the synod of the province determines by its judgment.”

From this, then, it may be understood that our Catholic predecessors, both formerly and later, obtained valid consecration without those three qualifications. Heretics, however, and specifically Simoniacs, obtained no valid consecration at all, either then or later, even if those three qualifications were present—namely, election by the clergy, the people’s request, and the metropolitan’s judgment—because no purity or grace can adhere to unbelievers until their hearts have been cleansed by faith.

In saying this, nevertheless, we venerate the ordination of our holy fathers, made necessary by the circumstances of the time and supported by their very great authority, in such a way that we bear complete witness, both for ourselves and for our descendants, that the ecclesiastical rules are to be observed. Necessity and their freedom excuse the ancients; the moderns, however, are accused solely by their own will and rashness. [Col. 1020B]

## CHAPTER VII

**CORRUPTOR.** You have also heard that, just as no one ought to be baptized again, so no one can be consecrated again in the same order. [Col. 1020C]

**CORREPTOR.** Who says or thinks that anyone can be consecrated again in the same order? Far be it from us to think so!

Among the other things we have received from the holy Fathers concerning this matter, we have also accepted with due veneration the chapter proposed from the blessed Pope Gregory. For, as he himself testifies there, the man who dared to do such a thing was rightly judged: namely, because he first deposed Probus, who had fallen from office, and subjected him to penance; after the penance had been completed, he consecrated him again in the same order, as though he had never been a priest.

This certainly was and is not to be done in any way. But if someone was unjustly deposed and afterward found innocent, then, as the Council of Toledo established, the bishop is given his staff and ring, the priest his planeta and stole, and so, through the remaining orders, each receives whatever was taken from him when he was deposed.

If someone is found guilty of a lesser offense, a private penance is imposed as satisfaction, but they are not deposed; rather, the order they possess is preserved for them in every respect. This is evidently what the blessed Gregory himself understood at the end of the present chapter, although that crafty and impure man is shown to have removed it because he clearly perceived that it opposed his quibbles:

> “If someone perhaps falls from the priesthood through a minor fault, penance ought to be imposed, and yet the order should be preserved.”

For someone justly deposed for criminal offenses is either never, or only with difficulty, found to have been lawfully restored. If he was unjustly deposed, he is restored, as was stated above from the Council of Toledo; but someone justly deposed is nowhere and never lawfully restored.

A person found guilty of less serious offenses is not deposed; rather, while his order is reserved to him, he is suspended from it for a time.

Who, then, is accused of being consecrated again by Catholics? For, apart from clerics of irreproachable life, the only other clerics found in the Catholic Church fall into the three kinds mentioned above. They will either have been justly deposed, unjustly deposed, or not deposed at all. And if there are any more who have been found guilty of lesser offenses, they are undoubtedly outside the Catholic Church. They are heretics, whether called bishops, priests, deacons, or clerics of any other rank.

Thus, even against his will, this little “thorny one” [Note: Fabricius says: “It does not seem to be a proper name for a person, but rather an insult applied to the opponent’s more thorny volumes.” —Editors of the Patrologia.] is now seen, as the argument proceeds, to reveal the beginning, development, and end of his perverse intention; like a hedgehog caught in water, he is compelled to unfold his head, feet, and tail.

For it is clear that he stubbornly defends those ordained by heretics, and especially by Simoniacs, because, as is abundantly shown above, an order once received in the Catholic Church is not repeated. He also labors, with various but vain arguments, to establish that those ordained by Simoniacs ought to be regarded and remain in the Catholic clergy without penance and without the imposition of hands, as though they lacked nothing in any grace. [Col. 1021B]

We, however, have sufficiently proved above through the testimonies of the holy Fathers that Simoniacs are heretics worse than the worst Arians.

And if there is still doubt whether Simoniacs are to be regarded as heretics, let the books of the Catholic Fathers on various heresies be consulted—those of Saints Epiphanius, Philastrius, Augustine, and the others who attempted to write on the subject. In all of them Simoniacs are found, and Simoniacs are placed first in the Catalogue of Heresies. Their author, Simon, deserved condemnation as a manifest heretic because he judged or thought that the Holy Spirit could be bought with money and bestowed on whomever he wished.

Let the Simoniacs consider what they deserve, since they most certainly believe that they can or could be made bishops through the intervention of money and bestow ecclesiastical consecrations or ordinations upon anyone. If they did not believe that they could do this, they would restrain themselves from so great a presumption.

From this judgment of theirs, if Simon is clearly proclaimed worse than the worst Arians because he sought to subject the Holy Spirit to himself, then, since his Simoniacs believe so great a wickedness altogether, who will they be worse than? For in the Catalogue of Heresies they are not recognized as worse than the Arians.

It is therefore evident that the Simoniacs are prior to the other heretics both in time and in error. Yet, lest they complain that we are burdening them beyond measure, we finally concede that they are equal to the Arians, although we have shown Simon, their author, to be more perverse than the Arians—and therefore these disciples of his are proved more perverse still. [Col. 1021D]

Once this equality has been shaken, the Simoniacs will necessarily have to expect from Catholics, against themselves, a judgment equal to that passed on the Arians, their equals.

Let them therefore now be attacked and overwhelmed not by our weapons, but by the darts and judgments of the most ancient and wholly Catholic and orthodox Fathers. Then, according to Solomon’s praises, let those who imagine themselves rich grow ashamed, even late, that they possess nothing but extreme poverty (Proverbs 11:22); or, in accordance with the testimony of God and his Father, let them see that when all the men of wealth awaken from their sleep, nothing is found in their hands—that is, in their ordinations (Psalm 75:6).

First, however, let the sum of their calumny be fastened here; then let it be pierced by the evident thunderbolts of the Fathers.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 1022B]

**CORRUPTOR.** Therefore, above, in the canons of the Apostles, which Saint Isidore confirms should be received:

> “If any bishop, priest, or deacon receives a second imposition of hands from anyone, let both he himself and the one who attempts to ordain him be deposed. For it is impossible that those who have been baptized or ordained by such men should be either faithful or clerics.”

**CORRECTOR.** When he says “above,” it is clear that he joins the preceding chapter of Saint Gregory to the supposed chapter of the Apostles for the purpose of asserting that the ordination of Catholics and heretics differs in nothing. He attempts to transfer generally to the heretical side what Saint Gregory expressly declares concerning the ordination of Catholics, as though the Apostles had forbidden those ordained by heretics—as he claims—to receive a second imposition of hands from Catholics.

From the canons of the Apostles, therefore, we know that only the first fifty chapters ought to be received—not so much on the authority of blessed Isidore as on that of the most holy Pope Clement and many of his successors; the following ones are reckoned among the apocrypha.

[Note: [Col. 1022D] Gelasius admits only the fifty canons, the following ones being listed among the apocrypha: canon *Sancta*, distinction 15.] Yet, as can be proved from authentic and ancient copies, the present chapter is plainly found here to have been defrauded and deprived of its proper sense and integrity near its end, with an alien fabrication added to it under the appearance of truth. For in the older and more reliable canons it is found thus:

> “If anyone has received a second imposition of hands, let him himself be deposed, and likewise the one who has attempted to reordain him, unless perhaps he proves that the man was ordained by heretics.” [Col. 1022D]

The most wicked tavern-keeper, having removed the wine of Sorek, mixed in water from a ruined cistern to serve to those whom he had deceived, saying that those baptized or ordained by such men could be neither faithful nor clerics. This is found neither in this canon of the holy Apostles nor in any canon of the Catholic Fathers. By this fraudulent presumption of his, or by the novelty of his profane wording, it becomes clearer than daylight how much he ought to be received or heard in his preceding or subsequent argument.

For he openly attacks, and insofar as he can strives to annul and abolish, the holy Council of Nicaea, which also contains the chapter that that madman thought would later be brought forward against us in his own defense. In that chapter the Cathari—that is, heretics nearer to the Catholic faith—are judged, whenever they come to the Catholic Church, to receive an imposition of hands and thus to remain in the Catholic clergy.

Nor should one suppose that the holy Fathers established this concerning the lay Novatians, who had received no imposition of hands for attaining the clerical orders, but concerning their clerics, upon whom the leaders of their sect had laid hands so that they might be promoted to some ministry of the altar. When these men come to the Catholic Church and Catholic priests lay hands upon them, are they not known to receive a second imposition of hands? They receive it from Catholics precisely because they are proved to have been ordained by heretics, as the second ancient reading of the aforesaid apostolic canon says. This corrupt editor did not fear to suppress that reading and is consequently found to have inflicted public injuries even upon the holy Council of Nicaea.

Let us also consider his conclusion, in which he declares that those baptized or ordained by such men can be neither faithful nor clerics. If this is so, leaving other matters aside for the moment, it follows that when the heretical Novatians pass over to the Catholic Church, they flee, as it were, from the face of a lion, only to have a bear meet them, since through the imposition of the Catholic priest’s hands this is inflicted upon them to their destruction: henceforth neither they themselves nor those baptized or ordained by them can be regarded as faithful or clerics. In that case it would have been more tolerable for them to remain as they were than to come to the Catholic Church and there receive an imposition of hands after the one they had received from their own people. For they are shown to be crushed by a double crushing, since their baptism or clerical status is proclaimed to be now worth nothing.

But far be it from us even lightly to think this! Otherwise the Council of Nicaea would be convicted of having not cut off error but propagated it; and the holy Fathers, following its authority, would have made all the heretics who passed over to the Catholic Church worse both here and in the future by laying hands upon them.

Therefore, if that calumniator is not blind in both respects, he can now clearly recognize that neither lay heretics are to be received into communion nor heretical clerics into the Catholic clergy without an imposition of hands by a Catholic priest after the imposition they are known to have received from their own people. If they are laymen, they are confirmed in the faith through the imposition of hands and anointing with chrism; if they are clerics, they nevertheless remain through the imposition of hands in the order which they had hitherto appeared to possess.

Hence it is clear that a second imposition of hands is authentic and entirely necessary, provided that it is performed by Catholics after heretics, not after Catholics. Yet this imposition of hands, if carefully considered, is properly called neither “second” nor “another,” but rather one imposition—the former one and this one. For blessed Pope Innocent declares that the imposition of hands by all heretics is corrupt, whereas that of Catholics is sound.

[Col. 1024A] If, then, the imposition of hands by heretics is corrupt, while that of Catholics is sound, it is clear that the corrupt imposition is abusively called “second” through a wholly empty resemblance, since the two have no enumeration in common, either substantially or accidentally. For if the one abusively called “second” were likewise corrupt or more corrupt, it would be called second not abusively but truly. But now, since the former is corrupt and the latter sound, it is evident that two things wholly contrary and dissimilar to one another ought not to be called first and second, but that each should be called one: that one, one; and this one, one.

The same must be understood of ordinations, or, as the detractors insist, reordinations. If a heretic lays hands upon someone after a heretic, the reordination is corrupt or more corrupt and therefore is not an ordination but a single purification. If a Catholic presumes to repeat it after a Catholic, as is supposed, he indisputably confuses what is sound with what is corrupt. He should therefore not be said to have reordained, but to have led or drawn himself and the other from what was sound into what was corrupt.

For this reason, in accordance with the apostolic chapter cited above, both must be judged—that is, both must be deposed—because, by thinking that a Catholic ordination could be repeated, they incurred equal danger. Since these things are so, the rule of the Fathers stated above is thought to be necessary in no respect for Simonians alone, as though either they should not be reckoned heretics, or at least were the sort to whom nothing spiritual could be conferred by the Catholic Church—being people for whom the fullness of the Holy Spirit serves or submits at their will, whether they wish to bestow it freely or not freely.

**CHAPTER IX.**

[Col. 1024C]

But since Catholics cry out against heretics while both profess themselves Catholics and call one another heretics, so that in the tangible darkness of this plague-stricken Egypt of our time it cannot easily be discerned whose spirit belongs to whom, let us set aside all these matters concerning which it may presently be doubtful who should be regarded as Catholic or heretic. Let our pen be directed only against two men from antiquity whom no one doubts to have been notorious and certain heretics from the beginning, condemned by the holy Fathers with unanimous judgment.

The holy Apostle exposed and condemned the first; the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, revered throughout the world, exposed and condemned the second, as did all who were or are thereafter of the Catholic faith. We name Simon Magus with his Simonians, and Arius of Alexandria, the presbyter, with his Arians. Although the former is regarded by the holy Fathers as worse, nevertheless, since we have already conceded that both are equal in heresy, let us brandish and hurl against the pliable shield and armor of the faithless and revived Simon the darts of the holy Fathers by which the elaborate armor of mad Arius—now nowhere to be seen—was attacked and overcome.

First, by producing the testimonies and rules of the Catholic Fathers, let it be shown how highly they regarded the baptism of the Arians and other heretics, or what they believed it to be. Thus, in the canons of the holy Fathers the Apostles, which our present opponent above said ought to be received on the authority of Saint Isidore—and which we say ought rather to be received on the authority of blessed Pope Clement and many of his successors—these two chapters are certainly found:

**(Canon 47.)** “We command that a bishop or presbyter who accepts the baptism of heretics be condemned. For what agreement is there between Christ and Belial, or what share does a believer have with an unbeliever?” (2 Corinthians 6:15.)

Another of the same kind follows:

**(Canon 48.)** “If a bishop or presbyter presumes to rebaptize one who has received baptism according to the truth, or fails to baptize one polluted by impious heretics, let him be deposed, as one who mocks the cross of the Lord and utterly fails to distinguish true priests from false priests.” [Col. 1025B]

Because this rule, owing to its considerable strictness, offended and scandalized many people, it was removed by the successors of the Apostles and surrounded with a certain moderation. They permitted baptism—that is, immersion in water—to remain valid under the invocation of the Trinity, and decreed that it was in no way to be repeated if it was established that it had been performed in the name of that same holy Trinity.

Blessed Leo also used precisely this word of permission when he said: “We permit the baptism of heretics to be valid.” The glorious martyr and bishop Cyprian’s view concerning the baptism of heretics can likewise be clearly known from his council. For with his fellow bishops he decreed the same thing against it as did the apostolic canons cited above. [Col. 1025C] But the later rule prevailed because it recalled more people, removed the disputes of those who followed, and restrained the contentiousness of the unlearned crowd.

Now, although something that is permitted is lawful, it is not for that reason considered wholly good. Blessed John Chrysostom, discussing at greater length the precise meaning of this word in his exposition of Matthew, says:

> “Moses saw that the Jews, because of their carnal pleasure, were devoted to the practice of sacrifices. If he had commanded them to withdraw from sacrifices, he would not have been obeyed, because an old affliction is not cured by a momentary medicine. He ordered them to sacrifice, but no longer to demons, as in Egypt, rather to the living God. He permitted half the evil lest he lose the whole good. For this reason he also permitted them to give a bill of divorce, because he judged it better for marriage to be dissolved by the permission of the law than for hatred to compel murder.
>
> “He permitted them to do evil lest they do worse things. Thus, by permitting this, he did not display God’s justice to them, but removed the guilt of sin along with the sin, so that, because they were acting as though according to the law, their sin might not appear to them to be sin. For example, if someone has a servant who steals and gets drunk, and the master considers that, if he ordered him to avoid both at once, he would accomplish nothing, he orders him to drink as much as he wishes, but to drink publicly, so that little by little he may learn to obey commands.
>
> “Thus divorce was also permitted: evil indeed, but nevertheless lawful. For this reason the Apostles also commanded men, because of human lack of self-control, to enter upon second marriages. To take a second wife, according to the Apostle’s command, is lawful; but according to the rule of truth, it is truly fornication. Yet when it is publicly and lawfully committed with God’s permission, it becomes respectable fornication. Therefore the Lord rightly said that Moses permitted this, but did not command it. For to command is one thing, and to permit another. What we command, we want; what we permit, we command unwillingly, because we cannot completely restrain the evil wills of human beings.”

Thus far Chrysostom. The effective testimony of this distinguished man is supported by many great authorities and teachers, and also by the proverb now worn smooth through use: “God permits what he does not will to be done.”

**CHAPTER X.**

[Col. 1026B]

But in what follows it will appear more clearly how imperfect the baptism of heretics is. Blessed Pope Siricius replied as follows to the bishop of Tarragona, who had inquired about baptism:

> “At the very beginning of your letter you indicated that many baptized by the impious Arians are hastening to the Catholic faith, and that some of our brothers wish to baptize those same people again. This is not permitted, since the Apostle forbids it, the canons contradict it, and, after the Council of Ariminum was annulled, the general decrees sent to the provinces by my predecessor of venerable memory, Liberius, prohibited it.
>
> “We join these people, together with the Novatians and other heretics, to the Catholic assembly by the sole invocation of the sevenfold Spirit and by the imposition of the bishop’s hand, as has been established in the synod. The whole East and West also observe this. You too must henceforth in no way deviate from this path, if you do not wish to be separated from our synodal fellowship by judgment of the council.”

In this decretal chapter it is finally intimated openly that Catholics, from the time of the Apostles until Pope Liberius, retained not one uniform rule but a twofold rule concerning the reception of those coming from the heretics. After the Council of Ariminum had been annulled, Liberius was the first to prohibit by a general decree that those baptized by Arians should be rebaptized by Catholics; instead, they were to be joined to the Catholic assembly through the imposition of a bishop’s hands.

But how imperfect those baptized by heretics are considered within the Catholic Church, blessed Pope Innocent clearly demonstrates by producing the ancient and authentic rule of the holy Roman Church:

**(INNOCENT, Letter 22, no. 4.)** “It is the law of our Church that to those coming from heretics who were nevertheless baptized there, communion is granted through the imposition of hands only as laymen, and that none of them is to be appointed, even to the least clerical honor.”

From this rule it is clear what the holy Fathers think of those baptized by heretics: they do not consent to their promotion not merely to any rank of the sacred altar, but even to the simple honor of the clergy, with the exception of the Cathari, as stated above.

What the distinguished teacher of the faith, Leo, thought about the baptism of heretics, although it has already been set forth at length above, we have not hesitated to insert here again his chapter on the subject:

**(LEO, Letter 129 to Nicetas, chapter 7.)** “Those who received baptism from heretics without having previously been baptized are to be confirmed through the invocation of the Holy Spirit by the imposition of hands, because they received only the form of baptism without the power of sanctification. We proclaim that this rule, as you know, is to be observed in all Churches: the washing once begun must not be violated by any repetition, since the Apostle says: ‘One God, one faith, one baptism’ (Ephesians 4:5). Its cleansing must not be violated by repetition; rather, as we have said, only the sanctification of the Holy Spirit is to be invoked, so that what no one receives from heretics may be obtained from Catholic priests.”

Hence the same teacher says above:

**(LEO, Letter 2 to Rusticus, chapter 18.)** “There are some who do not know whether they have been baptized, but acknowledge that they do not know of what faith those who baptized them were. Therefore, since they received the form of baptism in some manner, they are not to be baptized, but, through the imposition of hands and the invocation of the power of the Holy Spirit—which they could not receive from heretics—they are to be joined to the Catholics.”

Blessed Eusebius, who governed the Roman Church before Melchiades and Sylvester, likewise instructed the Gallican bishops concerning the reception of heretics:

> “Since you have indicated what ought to be done with converted heretics, know that we receive those who have been baptized in the faith of the holy Trinity through the imposition of hands.”

Likewise, as stated above, to the bishops of Campania and Tuscany:

**(Letter 3.)** “We command that all heretics who are converted to the grace of God and have been baptized as believers in the name of the holy Trinity be reconciled through the imposition of hands, in accordance with the rule of the Roman Church.”

The sacrament of the imposition of hands is to be held in great reverence. It cannot be performed by others except the highest priests; nor is it read or known to have been performed in apostolic times by anyone other than the Apostles themselves. Nor can it ever be performed or ought to be performed by anyone except those who occupy their place, as has already been said. If it is presumed otherwise, it is to be regarded as invalid and void and is never to be reckoned among the ecclesiastical sacraments.

Hence, as stated above, from the Council of Arles, whose author is said to have been blessed Pope Sylvester:

**(Council of Arles, canon 8.)** “If anyone comes to the Church from heresy, let them question him concerning the Creed; and if they see that he has been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, let hands be laid upon him, so that he may receive the Holy Spirit.”

By these and many other testimonies of this kind from the holy Fathers, we are plainly instructed how highly the founders and preachers of the Catholic faith regarded the baptism of heretics, and also their imposition of hands—neither of which was performed without chrism. For those who come from them to the Catholic Church receive from Catholic bishops the imposition of hands with the invocation of the Holy Spirit and are anointed with sacred chrism, as though they had hitherto possessed none of these things.

**CHAPTER XI.**

[Col. 1028A]

Moreover, having now produced other rules of the holy Fathers, we shall strive to show how highly they esteemed—or rather, decreed—that heretics should be regarded in every action and manner of life. They judged them worse than pagans and Jews, as we learn more clearly than daylight from the exposition of blessed John Chrysostom on Matthew. He says:

> “When the King sees someone in the Church of Christ not clothed in the wedding garment—that is, in the true faith—he orders his ministers, that is, the evil spirits of deception, to act. For he repays evil through evil spirits, such as the spirit of error which God sent to deceive Ahab, as it is written in the Third Book of Kings, or such as the working of error which God will send them who did not receive the love of God, so that they may believe the lie.” [Col. 1028B]

And shortly afterward:

> “They seize him by his very works and by his very counsels and cast them into the outer darkness—that is, into the error of the Gentiles, Jews, or heretics. Perhaps the darkness of the Gentiles is near; that of the Jews is farther outside; but the darkness of the heretics is worse and farther outside, because the Gentiles reject the truth which they have not heard, the Jews reject the truth which they have not believed, but the heretics reject the truth which they have heard and learned. Among those very heretical darknesses, some are near the light of truth, while others are farther from the truth and therefore blacker; still others are farther away and therefore more oppressive and more exterior—that is, involved in the most perverse heresies.”

From this judgment of Chrysostom, heretics are convicted of being worse than pagans and Jews, although among the heretics themselves some are nearer to the truth—that is, to the Catholic faith—and others farther away.

In what matters heretics are to be avoided by Catholics and held at a distance like pagans or Jews, we are taught both by many writings of the holy Fathers and by the following chapters of Catholic councils.

From the Council of Laodicea, canon 6:

> “Heretics who remain in heresy are not to be granted entry into the house of God.”

Likewise, from the same council, canon 9:

> “Catholics are not to go to the cemeteries or places called martyria of heretics for the sake of prayer or to seek healing. Those who do go, if they are faithful, are to be made non-communicants and subjected to penance for a certain period of time. But those who repent and confess that they have erred ought to be received.”

Likewise, from the same council, canon 10:

> “Those who belong to the Church must not indiscriminately join their own children in marriage to the children of heretics.”

In agreement with this chapter, the Council of Carthage decreed (chapters 26, 16, and 17) that the children of clerics were not to be joined in marriage to pagans, heretics, or schismatics, and that bishops or any clerics were to contribute nothing through gifts of their property to those who are not Catholic Christians, even if they are relatives.

Likewise, from the Council of Laodicea, canon 40:

> “It is not proper to mix in banquets with everyone, or to give sons or daughters in marriage, but rather to receive them, provided that they profess that they will become Christians and Catholics.”

[Col. 1029A] Likewise, from the same council, canon 42:

> “It is not proper to receive the blessings or *eulogies* of heretics, since these are curses rather than blessings.”

Likewise, from the same council, canon 46:

> “It is not proper to pray with heretics or schismatics.”

Likewise, from the same council, canon 47:

> “It is not proper to receive from Jews or heretics the festival gifts that are sent.”

Hence, as stated above, in the apostolic canon:

> “A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has prayed with heretics is to be deprived of communion only. But if he has urged them to act or pray as clerics, let him be condemned.”

Hence, from the decrees of Pope Fabian:

[Note: [Col. 1029] These letters of Fabian, like the preceding letters of Eusebius and the following letters of Popes Dionysius and Gaius, are spurious and were attributed to them by Pseudo-Isidore.]

> “All who do not teach sound doctrine or do not hold the sound faith cannot rightly accuse anyone who believes rightly, because they are marked with infamy and have been cut off from the bosom of Mother Church by the public sword until their right conversion and return. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we establish and decree with all the sons of that same apostolic and universal Church that all who are suspect in the Catholic faith are not to be admitted as accusers of those who believe rightly, because all who are suspect must always be removed and not received. Their accusation is therefore rightly rejected, since they are suspect in the sound faith, and they are not to be believed at all.”

Likewise, from the decrees of blessed Pope Dionysius and martyr:

**(DIONYSIUS, Letter 2 to Bishop Severus.)** “Do not allow the charges which you say are being brought against bishops by others to be made in any way except by those who themselves bring the charges, provided that they appear worthy and irreproachable and demonstrate by public acts that they are free from every suspicion and hostility and lead an irreproachable life and faith. For no one can be believed concerning another’s crime if he has confessed something about himself; his profession concerning every matter is dangerous and must not be admitted.”

Also, from the decrees of Pope Gaius to Bishop Felix:

> “First of all, know that pagans and heretics cannot accuse Christians or bring a voice of defamation against them.”

By these and similar decrees and judgments of the Catholic Fathers it is clearly recognized that heretics are forbidden entry into the house of God and are removed from every form of communion with Catholics: prayer, banquets, nuptials or marriages, gifts of property or inheritances. They are not granted permission to accuse Catholics or testify against them. Catholics are also altogether forbidden to enter their cemeteries for the sake of prayer or to receive their *eulogies* or festival gifts.

Therefore no one doubts that heretics are to be rejected by Catholics in every respect, or indeed treated more severely than Jews or pagans, because in the latter there is still hope of faith, as stated above, whereas in the former there is already the struggle arising from discord.

**CHAPTER XII.**

Let us now also consider what the holy Fathers thought about the orders—or rather, the ordinations—of heretics.

From the letter of blessed Pope Innocent to the bishops of Macedonia:

**(INNOCENT, Letter 22, no. 3.)** “We have come to the third question, which because of its difficulty requires a longer discussion. We say that those ordained by heretics have a wounded head through that imposition of hands; and where a wound has been inflicted, medicine must be applied so that health may be restored. But the health that follows a wound cannot be without a scar; and where the remedy of penance is necessary, the honor of ordination cannot have a place.

“For as it is written: ‘Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean’ (Numbers 19:22), how can that be granted to him which purity and cleanness customarily receive? On the contrary, it is asserted that one who has lost honor cannot give honor, nor has that man received anything, because there was nothing in the giver which he could receive. Certainly it is true that he could not give what he did not possess. He gave the condemnation which he had through a corrupt imposition of hands. And I cannot see how one who has become a partner of the condemned can be found worthy to receive honor.”

Let those who have been ordained by Simonians finally awaken. Let them, suddenly disturbed and confounded by such thunder and such lightning from so distinguished a pontiff among distinguished pontiffs, at least belatedly recognize what they received from their ordainers—or, if they can or dare, rationally teach us that Simonians neither are nor ought to be called heretics.

For those ordained by heretics are taught to have a wounded head through that imposition of hands, because: “Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean.” It is therefore established that every heretic is unclean. Whatever he touches undoubtedly becomes unclean, according to the Lord’s saying in the law of Moses.

An unclean heretic could not and cannot bestow what cleanness and purity customarily receive, since it is clear that his heart has not been cleansed by sincere faith. To one to whom no cleanness or purity could be imparted, what else can whatever he touches impart except the uncleanness which alone he possesses? It therefore remains that the one touched by the unclean man is nothing other than unclean, because through the corrupt imposition of his hands he gives the condemnation which he possesses.

For one who does not have honor cannot give honor. Where there is nothing in the giver, there is nothing that anyone, however much he may wish it, can receive. Thus the recipient receives the condemnation possessed by the one who gives him a corrupt rather than sound imposition of hands. Someone ordained in this way, as it is supposed, and thereby made a partner of the condemned—that is, of a heretic—is declared by so great a pontiff to be irrecoverable in respect of honor. For he judges the wound—which has certainly been inflicted upon that man’s head—to require the medicine of penance.

Even if health follows, the scar is not wholly removed, because after penance no one is to be admitted to ecclesiastical honor. It is therefore clear that those proved to have been ordained by heretics are rejected for two reasons: because they have become their partners and because they are penitents. Let them therefore consider what a fall they have suffered, since even the medicine itself—that is, penance—prevents them from aspiring to ecclesiastical honor.

But lest they merely hunt for words while neglecting the meaning and think they have something to hold on to in the statement of the aforesaid chapter that one who has lost honor cannot give honor, and that one who has become a partner of the condemned—as though this had been said of someone who once possessed honor and later lost it, or who was once regularly ordained and later condemned—let them recognize from the other divine Scriptures that it is not to be understood in this way.

Rather, he lost honor because he sought to receive it disorderly and was condemned precisely where he did not fear to become a heretic. By receiving it, as it were, he lost it; or certainly he was condemned because he earned the inability ever thereafter to receive ecclesiastical honor, according to what the Psalmist says: “You cast them down when they were being lifted up” (Psalm 72:18). For he does not say, “You cast them down after they had been lifted up,” but “when they were being lifted up.”

**CHAPTER XIII.**

Blessed Gregory, speaking in the *Moralia* about the ostrich, from which God had taken wisdom and to which he had not given understanding, says:

> “Although to deprive is one thing and not to give another, he nevertheless repeated the former by adding ‘he did not give’ to what he had previously said, ‘he deprived.’ It is as though he were saying: What I said—‘he deprived’—does not mean that he unjustly took away wisdom, but that he justly did not give it. Thus the Lord is also described as having hardened Pharaoh’s heart—not because he himself imparted hardness, but because, in accordance with Pharaoh’s merits, he did not soften it with any awareness of fear infused from above.”

From the words of this same blessed Gregory, let it now be shown whether a Simonian is to be regarded or called a heretic.

From his letter to Brunichild, queen of the Franks:

> “Nor do we pass over this matter, but detest it as altogether execrable and most serious: that sacred orders are there conferred through the Simoniacal heresy, which first arose against the Church and was condemned at its origin by a strict curse. Thus the dignity of the priest is brought into contempt, and holy honor becomes a crime.
>
> “Reverence perishes and discipline is removed, because the man who ought to correct faults commits them, and through wicked ambition the honor of the venerable priest is brought into corrupt judgment. For who would again venerate what is sold? Or who would not consider worthless what he has bought?
>
> “Therefore I am greatly saddened and grieve for that land, because, while they disdain to possess as a divine gift the Holy Spirit whom Almighty God deigns to bestow upon human beings through the imposition of hands, they obtain him through rewards. I do not think that the priesthood will long endure there.
