For where the gifts of heavenly grace are judged to be for sale, it is not life that is sought for the service of God; rather, money is worshiped against God.”

Likewise, to Theodoric and Theudebert, kings of the Franks:

> “It is reported that the Simoniacal heresy—which first arose against the Church of God through a diabolical planting and was struck and condemned at its very origin by the zeal of apostolic vengeance—dominates within the boundaries of your kingdom.
>
> “Since faith together with life is to be chosen in priests, if life is absent, faith has no merit, as blessed James bears witness when he says: ‘Faith without works is dead’ (James 2:20). What works can a priest possess who is convicted of obtaining the honor of so great a sacrament through payment?
>
> “As a result, those who seek the sacred orders do not strive to correct their lives or reform their conduct, but to gather the wealth with which sacred honor is purchased. Hence the innocent and poor are also excluded and scornfully driven away from the sacred orders. And while the innocence of the poor is displeasing, there is no doubt that payment commends crimes there, because where gold is pleasing, vice is pleasing also.
>
> “Thus a deadly wound is inflicted not only upon the soul of the ordainer and the ordained, but also upon the kingdom of Your Excellency, which is weighed down by the guilt of bishops whose intercessions ought rather to have helped it. For if one is believed worthy of the priesthood who is supported not by the merits of his conduct but by the abundance of his payments, it follows that gravity contributes nothing to ecclesiastical honor, industry defends nothing, and the profane love of gold obtains everything.
>
> “And while vice is rewarded with honor, the man who perhaps ought to have been punished is brought into the place of the avenger; hence priests are shown not to advance but rather to lead the way in vice. When the shepherd is wounded, who will apply medicine for the healing of the sheep? Or when will he protect the people with the shield of prayer who exposes himself to be struck by the darts of the enemy? Or what fruit will he produce from himself when his root has been infected by the plague of corruption?
>
> “A greater calamity, therefore, must be feared in those places where such intercessors are brought into positions of rule—men who provoke God’s anger against themselves more than they ought to have appeased it on behalf of the peoples.”

Also, to Bishop Siagrius of Autun:

> “A report long circulating among us has made it widely known that, in the regions of Gaul, sacred orders are conferred through the Simoniac heresy; and we are afflicted with intense sorrow if money has any place in ecclesiastical offices, and what is sacred is made secular. Whoever therefore strives to obtain this by the payment of a price desires not to be a priest, but merely to be called one vainly. What, indeed, is being done by this except that there is no testing of conduct, no concern for morals, no examination of life, but only he is judged worthy who has been able to provide the price? If this is weighed by the scales of true judgment, then, while someone wickedly hastens to seize the place of humility for empty distinction, by that very fact the one who seeks the honor is more unworthy.
>
> “Just as the man who, when invited, refuses, and when sought out, withdraws, ought to be brought near to the sacred altars, so the one who eagerly seeks the office or thrusts himself forward importunately must unquestionably be rejected. For he who thus strives to climb to higher things—what is he doing except diminishing as he grows, and descending inwardly into the depths while ascending outwardly?
>
> “Therefore, dearest brother, let sincerity prevail in the ordination of priests; let consent be straightforward and free from venality. Let a pure election be preferred, so that the one advanced to the highest priesthood may be believed to have been raised not by the support of those who sell their votes, but by the judgment of God. For since it is an altogether grave crime either to purchase or to sell the gift of God for a price, the authority of the Gospel bears witness [Matthew 21:12]: When our Lord and Redeemer entered the Temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves.
>
> “What else is it to sell doves except to receive a price for the laying on of hands and to sell the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God grants to human beings? The fact that such men’s priesthood falls before God’s eyes was plainly signified by the overturning of the seats. Yet the perversity of wickedness still exerts its strength. For it compels those whom it deceives to sell, so that they may buy; and, since it does not heed what is commanded by the divine voice, ‘You received without payment; give without payment’ [Matthew 10:8], it acts so that the condition of one and the same crime—namely, that of buyer and seller—may increase and become doubled.
>
> “And since it is clear that this heresy first crept in with a pestilential root and was condemned with apostolic detestation at its very origin, why is it not guarded against? Why is it not considered that the blessing is turned into a curse for the man who is promoted in order to become a heretic?
>
> “Often, therefore, the enemy of souls, when he cannot insinuate himself into things that are plainly wicked, cleverly tries to overthrow them by casting over them the appearance of piety. He perhaps persuades people that something ought to be received from those who possess it, so that it may be distributed to those who do not, provided that by this means he may pour out deadly poisons concealed beneath the shadow of almsgiving. For neither would the hunter deceive a wild animal, nor the bird-catcher a bird, nor the fisherman a fish, if the first openly set the snare before the animal, or the second did not have the hook hidden beneath bait.
>
> “The cunning of the enemy must therefore be altogether feared and avoided, lest those whom he cannot overthrow by open temptation he may slaughter with a concealed weapon. Nor is it to be considered almsgiving if what is received from illicit things is distributed to the poor, because he who accepts something wickedly with the intention of distributing it as though for a good purpose is burdened rather than helped. The almsgiving pleasing to our Redeemer is that which is not gathered from illicit acts and wrongdoing, but is expended from permitted and honestly acquired resources.
>
> “Hence it is also certain that, even if monasteries, hospices, or something else are built, this does not benefit the reward; for when the perverse purchaser of honor takes the place of the seller and establishes others in his own likeness through the payment of a benefit, by arranging many things wickedly he destroys more than the man who received money from him for the ordination can build.
>
> “Therefore, lest we strive to accept anything with sin under the pretext of almsgiving, Holy Scripture openly prohibits us, saying: ‘The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable to the Lord, offered as they are from crime’ [Proverbs 21:27]. For whatever is offered in God’s sacrifice from crime does not appease the wrath of the Almighty, but provokes it. Hence it is written again: ‘Honor the Lord from your righteous labors’ [Proverbs 3:9]. Therefore, he who takes wrongly in order to give as though rightly undoubtedly does not honor the Lord.
>
> “This is also said through Solomon: ‘He who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is as though he were slaughtering a son in his father’s sight’ [Ecclesiasticus 34:24]. Let us consider how great the father’s grief would be if his son were sacrificed in his presence; and from this we shall easily understand how greatly almighty God is angered when a sacrifice is offered to him from robbery. Therefore, dearest brother, we must turn away most carefully from committing the sins of the Simoniac heresy under the pretext of almsgiving. For it is one thing to give alms on account of sins, and another to commit sins on account of alms.”

And shortly afterward, the same writer to the same person, as above:

> “Lest perhaps anyone should still wish to defend himself by appealing to a wicked custom, let your fraternity’s discernment restrain such men with the bridle of reason and not permit them to fall into unlawful practices, because whatever deserves punishment must be brought forward not for imitation, but rather as an example of correction.” [Column 1034B]

And a little later:

> “With regard, therefore, to the matters stated above, we wish your fraternity, by God’s authority, to convene a synod. Through the mediation of our most reverend brother Bishop Aregius and our dearest son Cyriacus the abbot, let everything contrary to the holy canons, as we have said, be strictly condemned there with the imposition of anathema: namely, that no one presume to give any payment in order to obtain ecclesiastical orders, or to receive one for orders already given; that no one from the lay state suddenly dare to reach a position of sacred governance; and that no women other than those permitted by the sacred canons live with priests.” [Column 1034C]

Also, the same writer to Bishop Victorius:

> “Whoever, in considering his office, is not seen to burn intensely with zeal to correct the crime of the Simoniac and Neophyte heresies must not doubt that he shares in the portion of the one from whom this peculiar outrage first took its origin.”

From the decrees of the same writer, as above:

> “Following the ancient rule of the Fathers, I establish that nothing is ever to be received for ordinations—neither for the giving of the pallium, nor for the delivery of documents, nor for that designation which a new pretense, born of ambition, has invented, namely, *pastellus*. For since the pontiff lays his hand upon the bishop being ordained, while the minister reads the Gospel, and the notary writes the letter of his confirmation, just as it is not proper for the pontiff to sell the hand he lays upon him, so the minister or notary ought not to sell, in his ordination, either his voice or his pen. I therefore entirely prohibit the man being ordained from giving anything for the ordination, the use of the pallium, documents, or *pastelli*. If anyone should presume to demand or request some payment from these aforementioned matters, under whatever name he may call it, he will be subject to guilt at the strict judgment of almighty God.” [Column 1034D]

Also, to Bishop Virgil of Arles:

> “From certain reports I have learned that, in the regions of Gaul or Germany, no one reaches sacred orders without the payment of a benefit. If this is so, I say with tears and proclaim with groaning that, when the priestly order has fallen inwardly, it will not be able to stand long outwardly either. For we know from the Gospel what our Redeemer himself did: he entered the Temple and overturned the seats of those selling doves [Matthew 21:12].
>
> “To sell doves is to receive a temporal benefit from the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God, consubstantial with himself, grants to human beings through the laying on of hands. From this evil, as I said, it is already indicated what follows: for those who presumed to sell doves in the Temple suffered the fall of their seats under God’s judgment.
>
> “This error is propagated among their subordinates with increase. For the very man who is brought to sacred honor, already corrupted at the root of his advancement, is more ready to sell to others what he bought. Where is what is written: ‘You received without payment; give without payment’ [Matthew 10:8]? And since the Simoniac heresy first arose against the holy Church, why is it not considered, why is it not seen, that when someone ordains and promotes a man for a price, he causes him to become a heretic?” [Column 1035B]

The same to John, Bishop of Corinth, as above:

> “Because the holy universal Church utterly condemns this most wicked depravity, we exhort your fraternity to restrain, by every means within its care and diligence, so detestable and monstrous a sin from all the places subject to it. For if we should perceive anything of this kind happening hereafter, we shall correct it no longer by words, but by canonical punishment, and we shall begin to form another judgment of you, one that is not fitting.
>
> “Your fraternity knows that previously the pallium was not given unless a payment had been made. Since this was inappropriate, after a council held before the body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we strictly prohibited the receipt of anything for this or for other ordinations. Therefore you must neither consent nor permit anyone to be brought to sacred orders through payment, favor, or the supplication of certain persons. For the sin is grave, as we have said, and we will not tolerate its remaining without correction.” [Column 1035C]

## CHAPTER XIV

From these many and repeated statements of so distinguished a teacher it is clearly established that the venality of sacred orders is a heresy, called Simoniac, the first of all, and condemned at its very origin with apostolic detestation and strict malediction, as having first spread its pestilential root against the holy Church. Consequently, all priestly reverence and conduct, inwardly and outwardly, are corrupted, and a sacred honor is held in criminal fashion. For no one considers worthy of reverence what is sold; rather, whatever is bought is considered altogether worthless.

Finally, when the gifts of heavenly grace are judged to be for sale, money is worshiped in opposition to God, so that now, in wretched humanity, not the true and ancient God but a false and recent one holds dominion—namely, the most wicked mammon, who presides over such money. There is no doubt that the innocence of the poor is displeasing wherever reward is approved as commending crimes, because where gold is pleasing, vice is pleasing also. [Column 1036A]

Thus it is proclaimed that a lethal wound is inflicted not only upon the soul of the ordainer and the ordained, but also that those who ought to have been helped through the intercession of bishops are weighed down by guilt. The same teacher further asserts that, if the man to whom an abundance of money gives support is believed worthy of the priesthood, it follows that integrity can defend nothing for itself in ecclesiastical honor, but that the profane love of gold obtains everything. Thus vices deserving punishment are rewarded with honor, while the man who ought to be corrected usurps the place of the corrector.

He declares, indeed, that such priests do not advance but rather perish, since their root is infected with a grievous disease. He likewise asserts that greater calamity is to be feared in those places where such intercessors are placed in authority—men who provoke God’s anger against themselves more than they ought to have appeased him on behalf of the peoples.

Next, he testifies that he is afflicted with intense sorrow if money has any place in ecclesiastical offices, because what is sacred immediately becomes secular. For he asserts that anyone who strives to obtain what is sacred for a price is not a priest, but merely wishes vainly to be called one. Finally, after much by which he condemns them, he asserts that the blessing is turned into a curse for them, and that they are promoted for the sole purpose of becoming heretics. Their every action, even if it appears to have some importance, is nevertheless judged before God to be nothing.

But because from these and certain statements of blessed Gregory some people presume to derive grounds by which they impudently and stubbornly defend their erroneous opinion, even to the point of dogmatizing that the Holy Spirit is both sold and purchased, we must press the matter so that at last they may repent of having thought or said this. They say:

“Behold what blessed Gregory thought about this; the wording of his letter to the leading men of the Franks clearly shows it.”

> “We altogether execrate and detest as most abominable and most serious the fact that sacred orders are conferred in your regions through the Simoniac heresy.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore I am deeply saddened, and I grieve for that land, because, while they disdain to possess as a divine gift the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God deigns to bestow upon all through the laying on of hands, they obtain him through rewards.” [Column 1036C]

From this proposition of the words of so great a pontiff, those foolish men draw the grounds of their treacherous argument. As it is said through the Wise Man, “From the face of a word in travail” [Ecclesiasticus 19:11], they say:

“Here blessed Gregory plainly testifies that the Holy Spirit is sold and conferred for money, and that, through the laying on of hands purchased for a price, the Holy Spirit is nevertheless received and given. Indeed, he professes that sacred orders are conferred through the Simoniac heresy, and that people obtain the Holy Spirit through rewards.”

Alas, wretched men—indeed, wretched beyond measure—who, more criminal than the soldiers who crucified the Power of God and the Wisdom of God, are not afraid to lay violent hands upon that seamless tunic and to cut pieces from it for themselves; and, what is even more serious, they think that the whole garment has fallen to their share. [Column 1037A]

For although the entire passage of so great a teacher ought to have been examined, these men seize for themselves that fragment of the sentence in which sacred orders are said to be conferred, and reject what he inserts there: “through the Simoniac heresy.” If they had considered with a simple eye of understanding what heresy is, and especially what the Simoniac heresy is, they would never have thought that sacred orders—that is, holy orders—are conferred through the Simoniac heresy, but rather that ... [lacuna] ... that is, execrable orders, and therefore not orders but errors.

They also cut away the statement that “people obtain the Holy Spirit through rewards,” and do not attend to what he inserts there: “whom almighty God deigns to grant to all through the laying on of hands, they disdain to possess as a divine gift.” If they had perceived this, they would never have thought that any human beings could obtain the Holy Spirit through the laying on of anyone’s hands, at any price whatsoever, since they disdain to possess him as a divine gift. [Column 1037B]

For how can the man who scorns to possess the gift of almighty God as his gift obtain it, while moreover striving to attack and seize it by producing money? He is miserably foolish who thinks that any force can be brought to bear upon almighty God so that he will grant his grace to someone who disdains to receive it as a gift from him.

Moreover, those who, in defending the blasphemy once conceived, intensify it further add the following:

“In another place also, the glorious Gregory, explaining the words of the Gospel, says among other things:

> ‘I speak to you priests with mourning, because we know that some of you perform ordinations for prices, sell spiritual grace, and pile up temporal profits from the sins of others, with the cost of sin.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “The dove is sold because the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received from heaven, is offered for a price.” [Column 1037C]

If in these words of blessed Gregory they accept his statement that some sell spiritual grace, why do they disregard what he adds: that they heap up temporal profits from the sins of others, with sin? And how can spiritual grace be sold and bought there where one person’s iniquity—namely, the buyer’s—accumulates temporal profit for another, namely the seller, with sin?

For what spiritual grace can be given and received where iniquity is shown to operate in both parties, since, as the beloved John asserts, “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin is iniquity” [1 John 3:4]? Far be it—far be it—that the Holy Spirit should in any way be judged a mediator in such shameful and wicked transactions, where iniquity accompanies and rules on both sides!

Therefore the dove is not sold and is not bought; rather, it is thought or appears to be sold or bought by sacrilegious and foolish men whenever their wicked laying on of hands is offered for a price. Yet through that laying on of hands, whenever it is performed by those to whom the matter belongs, the Holy Spirit is received from heaven. He does not, by his grace, deem worthy in any respect the laying on of hands of such traders as we have described, but, by a sentence of condemnation alone, he equally abhors what is received in this manner.

## CHAPTER XV  
### On Proper and Improper Expressions, and the Vanity of the Simoniacs

[Column 1038A]

If they had heard these and similar statements of the orthodox Fathers with a devout ear and had piously pondered them in a catholic heart, they would at last proclaim with us that the Holy Spirit can neither be sold nor bought. But, neglecting or disguising their own condemnation, they accept the holy Fathers when they speak improperly and according to common usage, while rejecting them when they explain themselves properly and according to rule.

Blessed Gregory speaks according to common usage, or improperly, when he says that sacred orders are conferred by such men; but he explains properly and according to rule what he means by those orders when he adds “through the Simoniac heresy,” and that no spiritual grace intervenes where a malignant heresy has become the mediator. [Column 1038B]

Likewise, he speaks according to common usage when he says that people obtain the Holy Spirit through rewards, but he explains himself according to rule as to what he means when he adds: “whom they disdain to possess as a divine gift.” For who can possess the Holy Spirit—namely, God’s gift—without God? God is not one thing and his gift, the Holy Spirit, another, although the latter is rightly said to be, and is, another.

This mode of expression is so common in divine and human writings, and even in our everyday conversations, that ancient grammarians customarily designated it by a proper figure called *catachresis*. They explain the force of this term in the following way:

> “Catachresis is the use of an inappropriate name, as when one says ‘fishpond’ (*piscina*) even though it contains no fish.”

This figure therefore occurs when a thing lacking its own name makes use of another. It is consequently clear that in this manner our holy Fathers rightly used names belonging to other things on the basis of some similarity, whenever their proper names—which are in any case few and sometimes less suitable for the narrative—happened not to be available.

Thus, among many others, blessed Pope Innocent says that certain men were ordained by heretics, while immediately asserting that they obtained nothing from that ordination except condemnation. If he had spoken properly and said that they were condemned by heretics, he would have been thought to say that some Catholics had been deposed or excommunicated by heretics.

Indeed, blessed Gregory himself shows at the end of his account with what intention he said that sacred orders were conferred by such men, or that spiritual grace was sold or bought, and the other expressions of this kind. There he declares that the blessing is turned into a curse for them, and that they are promoted in order to become heretics. Whoever did not burn intensely with zeal to correct this, in consideration of his office, would surely know without hesitation that he would share in the portion of the author of this heresy.

By nearly the same mode of expression it is said every day that someone sells God when he sells justice, although it is clear that neither can be sold, but that both are offended for a price. The seller grants nothing except falsehood, and the buyer receives nothing except that same falsehood, for which both incur an equal condemnation.

And yet, although both are truly guilty and both are condemned by their own conscience as witness, one of them is abusively called the judge and the other the acquitted party, although he is rather bound. [Column 1039A]

Likewise, among heretics they are said to have bishops, priests, clergy of the remaining orders, churches, ordinations, consecrations, sacrifices, and all the other sacraments—but only in name and appearance, not in any power or reality belonging to those things.

Nor is this surprising, since nearly all the names of our sacraments are also found among the pagans; nevertheless, no one but a madman thinks that anything but sacrilege, and not holiness or truth, is present in them. For “whatever is without faith is sin” [Romans 14:23].

Therefore, once a name has been misused, no one who has been deceived by improper expressions should depart from the proper and inward truth of the sacraments, so as to believe or proclaim that he or anyone else can receive, freely or otherwise, from anyone whatever he seeks. He neither receives nor possesses what he seeks.

For however eagerly you devote yourself to or linger over a fishpond, hoping to catch from it fish which, because it has not received them, it does not possess, neither its name nor the similarity of the thing provides you with anything except vain labor, whether you demand this freely or for a price.

It remains, therefore, that Simoniac priests, together with the other heretics, may appropriately be likened, in comparison with priests who are what they are by the grace of God [1 Corinthians 15:10], to little statues and images of gold and silver. As the Psalmist sings:

> “They have mouths, but they will not speak;  
> they have eyes, but they will not see;  
> they have ears, but they will not hear;  
> they have noses, but they will not smell;  
> nor is there spirit in their mouth.  
> They have hands, but they will not touch;  
> they have feet, but they will not walk;  
> they do not cry out in their throat” [Psalm 113:5–7].

For faith did not devise them, but perfidy.

Thus, although they bear the same names and reproduce some likeness of true limbs as far as hearing or sight is concerned, they retain no truth within themselves. Their mouth offers nothing except the empty name of a true mouth and some small likeness—yet a vain one—since in material, construction, and operation it is altogether dissimilar. It lacks bones, joints, nerves, veins, blood, flesh, skin, life, and motion, as well as the functions of tasting, blowing, spitting, or clearing the throat. Understand the same concerning the other limbs, by which they can benefit neither themselves nor anyone else, nor perform any functions.

Simoniac priests, therefore, in the likeness of images, usurp nothing but the empty name of Catholic priests and the semblance of their external worship. Because avarice, which is the service of idols [Ephesians 5:5], has acted as mediator, they have been made of gold and silver, and, like golden or silver images, have received their form from idolatry.

Since everything about them is painted over and counterfeit, it is plainly evident that what are called sacraments among them are not to be esteemed at all. Therefore the bishop who makes such men—even if he had previously been regarded as Catholic—when payment is added to him, himself becomes a little statue. Likewise, those who place their hope of salvation in such men and revere their vanity become images, or rather idolaters, in accordance with the Psalmist’s imprecation:

> “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” [Psalm 113:8].

And again:

> “Let all who worship carved images be put to shame, those who glory in their idols” [Psalm 96:7].

Do not those who proclaim that valid consecrations are performed by Simoniacs glory in their idols? They must therefore be put to shame, because what is demonstrably not received cannot be conferred upon anyone by a price.

And because everyone becomes what he worships, the worshiper of an image becomes an image, just as the worshiper of God becomes like God—by grace, however, not by nature—as the Psalmist says: “I said, You are gods” [Psalm 82:6].

Hence the most avaricious men, worshiping money as a foreign god, consider it omnipotent, as the pagans consider their various gods omnipotent, to such an extent that it can prevail over the Holy Spirit. Trying to measure the immeasurable majesty, they themselves grow pale at the sight of a coin and perform right and wrong alike at its command. They altogether believe that what cannot fail to please them must please God as well.

The satirist also rebukes their madness in these words:

> “Souls bent toward earthly things and empty of heavenly matters:
>
> What does it benefit us to bring our ways into the temples,
>
> and to derive good things for the gods from this criminal guilt?”

But even if a pagan, abusing reason, believed idols to be omnipotent gods and the authors of every good, nevertheless, as a rational creature, he was led by reason to believe that those whom he considered supremely good could not consequently approve vicious human dispositions or passions. For supreme virtue must necessarily be free from every vice.

Do you think they are Christians who make the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift is and descends [James 1:17], so imperfect that they believe they can reconcile themselves to him with the money they love above all things and obtain his greatest gift—and that God cannot fail to approve the transaction that pleases them so greatly?

## CHAPTER XVI  
### The Judgment of Saint Ambrose concerning the Ordinations of Simoniacs

Let us now add certain statements of the great Ambrose, by which the Simoniacs are shown, because they are avaricious, to be usurers as well, and therefore, according to what is written, cursed above all others [Ecclesiasticus 10:9]. For every avaricious man is a usurer, and every usurer is avaricious.

Blessed Ambrose, speaking about the life and ordination of bishops, says among other things:

> “Although the length of this little book already constrains us, and time urges us to bring this work to its conclusion, concern arising from fraternal love holds us back—especially concern for those priests who, dulled by the torpor of their minds, disgrace priestly honor. They are known to have prodigiously produced this new rule and this storm, following the judgment of Gehazi and Simon, and to have bought the grace of the holy episcopate with money.
>
> “They do not fear that, when buying priestly honor with money, they have been condemned together with Simon by blessed Peter the Apostle, as he says: ‘May your money be with you unto perdition, because you thought that the gift of the Holy Spirit could be purchased with money’ [Acts 8:20].
>
> “They should also believe that they received leprosy from their holy Elisha together with Gehazi, since they think they purchased the priestly rank with money. When we have said these things to them, it ought to have been enough that by their purchase they possess their own leprosy.
>
> “For just as, when the head is corrupted by more powerful diseases, the rest of the body must necessarily be fatally drenched by the overflow of the disease above, so those who appear to be the head of the Church corrupt the fraternal body with a pestilential disease, so that nothing in the entire structure of the body can escape uninjured from the deadly poison of negligent priests’ depravity.
>
> “Thus you see scattered throughout the Church men whom not merit but money has advanced to the episcopal order, and a foolish and uneducated people who have taken such a priest for themselves. If you wish to ask them honestly who appointed them priests, they will immediately reply and say:
>
> “‘I was recently ordained bishop by the archbishop, and I gave him a hundred solidi so that I might deserve to obtain episcopal grace. If I had not given them, I would not be a bishop today. Therefore it is better for me to bring gold into the treasury than to lose so great a priesthood. I gave gold and purchased the episcopate. Yet, if I live, I do not doubt that I shall soon recover those solidi.’
>
> “Behold, I have received back in my treasury the gold that I gave, and I have received the episcopate for nothing. This is precisely what grieves me: the archbishop made the bishop in a carnal manner. For the sake of money he specifically ordained him leprous.
>
> “‘May your money be with you unto perdition,’ he says, ‘because you purchased the gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit for a price,’ and you carried out a wretched transaction to the destruction of souls.
>
> “Ignorant and uneducated people shout at their ordinations and say, ‘You are worthy, and you are just’; but the wretched conscience says, ‘You are unworthy and unjust.’
>
> “A bishop of this kind proclaims to the people, saying, ‘Peace be with you.’ To carnal eyes he appears to be a great bishop, but to divine eyes he is seen to be a great leper. Through money he acquired an illicit order, and before the Lord he lost the inner man. The flesh received dignity, and the soul lost honor. The flesh, which was a servant, became mistress of the soul; the soul, which was mistress, became the servant of the flesh. The flesh rules the peoples, and the soul serves the demon. He purchased priesthood for the flesh and prepared ruin for the soul.
>
> “‘What does it profit such a man if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a man give for his soul?’ [Matthew 16:26]
>
> “What he gave when he was ordained bishop was gold; what he lost was his soul. When he ordained another, what he received was money; what he gave was leprosy.

> “‘These are the transactions of the wicked, carried out for their destruction. Yet I ask our brother and fellow bishop—for I too am a bishop, and I am speaking with a bishop. Tell me, brother bishop, when you gave the money, what did you receive?’
>
> “He replies: ‘I received episcopal grace.’
>
> “Therefore I ask you: Why is this grace called by such a name?
>
> “He answers: ‘Why do you ask? As I understand it, it is called grace because it is given freely.’
>
> “Therefore, if grace is given freely and cannot be valued in gold, why did you purchase grace with money?
>
> “He replies: ‘It would not have been given to me if it had not been bought with money, nor would I have been ordained bishop if I had not given money.’
>
> “Therefore, as is clear from your answers, you did not receive grace when you were ordained, because you did not obtain it freely. And so, brother, if you did not receive grace, how could you become a bishop? For the Lord also says to the disciples: ‘You received without payment; give without payment’ [Matthew 10:8].
>
> “Why, then, did you judge that freely given grace could be possessed for a price? For, as I see, by giving gold you lost it, and you did not acquire holy grace.
>
> “Still, I ask my brother once more, so that we may not seem to have omitted any truthful tests of the matter. Who gives episcopal grace, brother—God or man?
>
> “You will undoubtedly answer: God. Yet God gives it through human beings. A man lays on hands; God grants grace. A priest lays on a suppliant right hand; God blesses with his powerful right hand. A bishop initiates the order; God bestows the dignity.
>
> “O justice! O equity! If money is given to a man who performs nothing more in the ordination except the service entrusted to him, why is everything denied to God, who grants you the order itself? Does it seem just to you that the servant is honored, while the Lord suffers injury; that the priest unjustly receives money, while God suffers injury at the hands of man?
>
> “But since God expects nothing from you for the order granted, why does the priest shamelessly expect money from you? The Lord wished to grant freely to man, while the rapacious bishop freely demands money from man. God, certainly in his kindness, gave freely to man; and the unworthy priest robbed him without cause.
>
> “‘What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?’ [1 Corinthians 4:7]
>
> “Behold into what evils the divine order has rolled; behold into what disgrace the priests have fallen who deserved to hear from the Judge of the world: ‘You are the light of the world’ [Matthew 5:14].
>
> “Behold to whom the nations are subjected, to whom it was said by the Lord: ‘You are the salt of the earth’ [ibid., 5:13].
>
> “Therefore, if the bishop is the light of the Church and is ordained by the Lord so that, through the radiant eloquence of his preaching, he may illumine the darkness of ignorance in consciences, why is he himself held bound by tangible darkness?
>
> “And not only does he rightly perish when he acts wickedly himself; he also rightly destroys others along with him. For if you deserved to possess the flavor of salt so that you might season the hearts of the foolish, why did you offer yourself, made tasteless by such a vice, to be trampled under the unclean feet of swine, so that you can season neither yourself nor others?” etc.

Again, blessed Ambrose (Book VI on Luke IV), explaining the Gospel passage, “There were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian” (Luke 4:27), says after some intervening remarks:

“Learn also the rules of virtue appropriate to the matter. The one who refuses rewards will prove his faith. Learn from the instruction both of these words and of these deeds what you should follow. You have the Lord’s command and the prophet’s example: receive freely, give freely, and do not sell the ministry, but offer it. For God’s grace is not assessed at a price, nor is profit sought in the sacraments, but rather the priest’s service.

“Yet it is not enough if you yourself seek profit; the hands of your household must also be restrained. Nor is this alone required, that you preserve yourself alone chaste and undefiled. For the Apostle did not say merely ‘yourself,’ but ‘keep yourself chaste’ (1 Timothy 5:22). What is sought, therefore, is not only your own purity from such trafficking, but also that of your household. ‘For a priest must be blameless, set well over his own household, having children submissive with all purity. But if anyone does not know how to preside over his own household, how will he take care of the Church of God?’ (1 Timothy 3:2–5.)

“Therefore instruct your household, exhort it, and guard it. Has a servant deceived you?—for I do not exclude any human condition—then, having been exposed by the prophetic example, let him be rejected. The leprosy quickly follows shameful payment, and money wickedly acquired stains both body and soul. ‘You have received,’ he says, ‘the money, and with it you shall possess fields, vineyards, olive groves, and flocks; but the leprosy of Naaman shall also cling to you and to your seed forever’ (2 Kings 5:27).

“Do you see that, because of the deed of the author, the heir’s succession is condemned? The guilt of the sold mystery is inexpiable, and vengeance for heavenly grace passes to descendants. Indeed, the Moabites and others shall not enter the Church of God until the third and fourth generation—that is, to interpret the matter more simply, until the succession of many generations has erased the guilt of their authors.

“But although those who sinned against God through the error of idolatry appear to have been punished to the fourth generation, certainly the sentence seems harsher by which Gehazi, because of his desire to possess, is condemned by prophetic authority forever—especially since our Lord Jesus Christ, through the washing of regeneration, has granted forgiveness of sins to all.”

## CHAPTER XVII  
### Recapitulation of the foregoing; then the opinion of blessed Augustine

Behold: from the assertions of so great and prudent a man, we are taught in many ways that episcopal grace cannot be received for a price, but only leprosy. Yet someone dares to object and mutter that from such lepers—namely, Simonians—some grace of the sacred orders, which they do not possess, can be given either to themselves or to anyone else, rather than only that which they have received and possess: leprosy.

And since this most distinguished teacher plainly declares that the guilt of the sold ministry is inexpiable and that vengeance for heavenly grace passes to descendants, so that Gehazi’s example clings forever to the seller and his seed, what weight can be assigned to the statements that contradict this from the opposite direction: “The soul that sins shall itself die, and the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezekiel 18:20), especially since the Lord says of himself: “I will repay the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation” (Exodus 20:5)?

Nevertheless, both statements are true, because both belong to the Lord; but they must be suitably understood according to the character of the persons and the sins, in light of their circumstances. For one uniform sentence must not be applied to all blasphemers, since blasphemy itself is not uniform, as Truth itself testifies: “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings; but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven” (Matthew 12:31).

Is it not evident that concerning this blasphemy against the Spirit, the prophet, the Apostle, and the teacher are shown to have dictated the same and uniform sentence as the Lord himself? The prophet says: “The leprosy of Naaman the Syrian shall cling to you and to your seed forever” (2 Kings 5:27); the Apostle says: “Your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts 8:20). And shortly afterward: “Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord, if perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you” (ibid., 22).

Following these authorities, the teacher says: “The guilt of the sold mystery is inexpiable.”

Blessed Augustine also says, in the passage cited above from his exposition of the holy Gospel according to John:

“That Simon wanted to buy the Holy Spirit because he wanted to sell the Holy Spirit, and he thought that the Apostles were merchants such as the Lord drove from the temple with a whip. For he himself was such a man, and he wanted to buy what he would sell. He belonged to those who sold doves; for the Spirit appeared in the form of a dove. Who, then, are the ones who sell the dove, brothers? Those who say, ‘We give the Holy Spirit.’ Why do they say this, and at what price do they sell him? They receive the price of their honor, the price of temporal seats, so that they themselves may appear to sell doves. Let them beware of the whip made from cords. The dove is not for sale; it is given freely, because it is called grace.”

The same author says in the same exposition cited above (Augustine, Tractate 6 on John 2:18):

“We read in the Acts of the Apostles that many believed in Samaria through the preaching of Philip (Acts 8:12). He is understood to have been either one of the Apostles or one of the deacons, since we read that seven deacons were ordained there, among whom Philip’s name also appears (Acts 6:5). Through Philip’s preaching, therefore, the Samaritans believed, and Samaria began to abound in believers.

“There was there this Simon Magus. Through his magical practices he had driven the people mad, so that they thought him to be the power of God. Yet, moved by the signs performed by Philip, he himself also believed. But what sort of belief he had, the events that followed later demonstrated. Simon too was baptized.

“The Apostles who were in Jerusalem heard this; Peter and John were sent to them. They found many who had been baptized, and because none of them had yet received the Holy Spirit—as he then descended to manifest the sign of the Gentiles who would believe, so that they would speak in tongues when the Holy Spirit descended upon them—they laid hands on them, praying for them, and they received the Holy Spirit.

“That Simon, who was not a dove in the Church but a raven, because he sought what was his own and not what belonged to Jesus Christ, and who therefore had loved power more than righteousness among Christians, saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the Apostles’ hands—not because they themselves gave him, but because he was given while they prayed. He said to the Apostles: ‘What do you want me to give you in money, so that through the laying on of my hands the Holy Spirit may be given?’

“And Peter said to him: ‘Your money be with you unto perdition, because you thought that the gift of God could be purchased with money’ (Acts 8:18–20).

“To whom does he say, ‘Your money be with you unto perdition’? Certainly to one who had been baptized. He already had baptism, but he did not cling to the dove’s inward parts. Hear that he did not cling to them, and observe the very words of the Apostle Peter. For it follows: ‘You have neither part nor lot in this faith, for I see that you are in the gall of bitterness’ (ibid., 21–23). The dove has no gall; Simon had it. Therefore he was separated from the dove’s inward parts. What benefit did baptism provide him?”

In these words of the most eloquent and keen-sighted teacher, those who impudently and impiously attempt to assert that the dove, or spiritual grace, can be sold must necessarily observe the statement: “The dove is not for sale; it is given freely, because it is called grace”; and likewise the statement that “Simon saw the Holy Spirit given through the laying on of the Apostles’ hands, not because they themselves gave him, but because he was given while they prayed.”

God grants his Holy Spirit to human beings, but through the prayer and invocation of those who are known to have received the ordination of this ministry or office freely from Catholics, even if they are regarded as having an evil way of life in the eyes of human beings. In this faith or ministry, however, heretics have neither part nor lot, because they are made not ministers of Christ but of Satan through a price. Nor is the Holy Spirit given through their prayer or invocation, because their ministry—even if they appear to have a righteous way of life—is not recognized by God. Therefore their prayer becomes sin (Psalm 118:7), in accordance with what the Psalmist is known to have prophetically uttered in imprecation concerning another most wicked merchant.

For, as blessed Paul the Apostle says to the Corinthians:

“Such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light. It is therefore no great thing if his ministers also disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness; their end will be according to their works” (2 Corinthians 11:13–15).

Thus, just as Satan, disguised as an angel of light, cannot fail to be an angel of darkness—more perverse in proportion to his greater presumption—so also his ministers, disguised as ministers of righteousness, cannot fail to be ministers of unrighteousness. They are more detestable in proportion to their greater audacity: they falsely claim to be what they neither are nor can become.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### Concerning those who traffic in ecclesiastical dignity: the opinions of the holy Fathers

Again, from the Apostolic Canons, chapter 30:

“If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon has obtained this dignity through money, let him and the one who ordained him be deposed, and let him be entirely cut off from communion, as Simon Magus was by Peter.”

Again, from the same canons, chapter 31:

“If any bishop, using secular powers, obtains a church through them, let him be deposed, and let all who communicate with him be expelled.”

Those who purchase powers for themselves with a price, even if those powers are ecclesiastical, undoubtedly become secular, contrary to this canon, as blessed Gregory says:

“If money has a place in ecclesiastical offices, what is sacred becomes secular.”

Again, from the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 2:

“If any bishop has performed an ordination for money and reduced to a price the grace that cannot be sold, and has ordained for money a presbyter or deacon, or anyone among those numbered in the clergy, or has promoted for money a steward or defender, or anyone subject to the rule, for the advantage of the most shameful profit, he whose guilt has been proved by testimony to this effect shall be subjected to the danger of losing his own rank.

“And let the one who was ordained or promoted through this transaction gain nothing from that ordination or promotion, but let him be excluded from the dignity or office that he purchased with money.

“If anyone has acted as mediator in such shameful and wicked payments or receipts, then, if he is a cleric, let him fall from his own rank; but if he is a layman or monk, let him be anathematized.”

Again, from the examples of Pope Hormisdas (Letter 25):

“Those known to have purchased sacramental dignity for a price, though unworthy of it by their merits, must, once convicted, be excluded, because the condemnation of Simon, which sacred Scripture testifies to, entangles seller and buyer alike.

“We therefore join this to what immediately precedes, lest the blessing through the laying on of hands, which is believed to be from God, be purchased for a price, since Simon, wishing to buy the Holy Spirit for a price, was struck by the Apostle’s detestation.”

Again, from the Exposition of Remigius:

“The Lord, to show that all sellers and buyers of heavenly grace must be expelled from association with the holy Church, therefore began by driving sellers and buyers from the temple and overturning the seats of those who sold doves, to teach that the priesthood of such traders is destroyed.

“For although some are not physically excluded from association with the holy Church, nevertheless they have been spiritually rejected by God and deprived of their proper honor.”

## CHAPTER XIX  
### The rejection of those who say that Simonians possess grace from which they may be deposed

Since it is thought that the arguments above have sufficiently answered those who weigh words while neglecting their meaning—arguments based on certain expressions used figuratively and improperly in the chapters mentioned above, according to the trope of catachresis, such as “has obtained a dignity for a price,” “has performed an ordination,” and similar expressions—let us now address what they vainly attempt to bring against us.

They say:

### Objection

“Behold, those ordained for money are commanded to be deposed. Therefore it is clear that they obtained spiritual grace and were promoted to the rank of honor from which they are commanded to be deposed. For the disposition of an honor possessed is its loss or deprivation.”

### Rejection

It has already been shown that a place may be called a pool even when it has no fish, by the same trope. If they do not wish to be obstinate, they can quickly recognize that deposition may likewise properly be spoken of where there has been no promotion or possession of an honorable rank, unless this is established superficially from some similarity—especially since the chapter of the Council of Chalcedon plainly supports our position. At its beginning it reads (Council of Chalcedon, canon 2):

“If any bishop has performed an ordination for money and reduced to a price the grace that cannot be sold,” and so forth.

Therefore, having been brought back to their senses by the harmonious and unanimous thunder of six hundred and thirty holy bishops, let those transgressors learn that grace cannot be sold. For those holy Fathers are read to have professed themselves defenders of this synod even unto blood.

Finally, although in an unusual manner, we speak in a proper sense if we call such deposition a revelation, just as the Lord Jesus is proclaimed by Simeon to have been appointed for the fall and resurrection of many (Luke 2:34). For in falling, each person rises again: he abandons evil and girds himself for good.

Since it is therefore clear from many testimonies of divine authority that the Holy Spirit cannot be sold, let those foul and misty arguments—or rather, phantoms containing no truth but wholly vanity—with which they argue such things now fade away, as smoke fades away (Psalm 67:3).

### Objection

“If the one who receives a price for the laying on of hands does not give the Holy Spirit to the one whom he consecrates for a price, then surely neither did the former sell the Holy Spirit nor did the latter purchase him. Yet priesthood is neither given nor received without the giving of the Holy Spirit. It is therefore evident that the one who obtains priesthood through the laying on of hands is not a priest. It follows that he need not be deposed from that order which he never obtained. The canons promulgated by the holy Fathers, therefore, which decree that such persons be deposed, are cited in vain.”

### Rejection

By such a sophistical and confused syllogism, perversity—having openly dared to resist the Holy Spirit, because it perversely believes that he is sold and bought wherever the names of seller and buyer are heard—concludes ironically that the person need not be deposed from an order which he never obtained, or, if he obtains it, must not be deposed. Thus it would cancel the chapter of the holy Fathers promulgated against Simonians.

That fantastic syllogism threatens with its horns: whichever side you press, you are immediately pressed by the other. For if you concede that they must be deposed, you necessarily concede that they obtained a dignity from which they are to be deposed. If you concede that they obtained a dignity, it will follow that the Holy Spirit was also sold and bought by them. If that is established, you will necessarily also have to confess that the Holy Spirit is possessed, given, and received by them; and consequently you will have to confess that ordinations or consecrations performed by Simonians, who are certainly heretics, whether freely or for a price, are entirely valid and lack nothing in comparison with those performed by Catholics.

But if you deny that they obtained a dignity, you must necessarily maintain that they cannot be deposed from a dignity which they never obtained. If you do not concede that they must be deposed, you will necessarily judge that the decrees of the holy Fathers—which decree that sellers and buyers of grace be deposed—were issued in vain.

It will therefore remain either that, once the deposition of Simonians is conceded, the other conclusions mentioned above, which plainly seem absurd to concede, must also be conceded, and thus those chapters of the holy Fathers will be approved; or else, once their deposition is denied, those chapters will be rejected.

Yet although it has been shown at greater length above that the Holy Spirit can neither be sold nor bought, without whom priesthood cannot be acquired or possessed, nor any consecration performed, and that such presumptuous persons must therefore be deposed from that disguise or appearance which, as ministers of righteousness, they unjustly usurp and arrogate to themselves, nevertheless let it be conceded that a material object of commerce must necessarily exist between seller and buyer, since neither the one can rightly be called a seller nor the other a buyer otherwise.

But that object cannot be the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit is called and truly is grace. Grace, however, unless it is received and given freely, is neither grace nor truly called grace. For if grace is sold and bought, it is rightly concluded that it is no longer grace. It is therefore established that the Holy Spirit—or, certainly, grace—is not the object of buying and selling.

Accordingly, another object must be sought. So that we may not weary ourselves by seeking everywhere for too long, or perhaps go astray, let us attend to blessed Ambrose, who points it out to us:

“What he gave,” he says, “when he was ordained bishop, was gold; what he lost was his soul.”

From this outstanding man’s judgment we learn without ambiguity that the object of this wicked commerce is rightly and truly called the destruction and damnation of souls, and leprosy alone. It is destruction according to the chief of the Apostles, damnation according to blessed Innocent, and leprosy according to Ambrose himself.

Therefore, wherever destruction or damnation is identified, the author and ruler of such destruction or damnation—the devil—necessarily cooperates and presides; no less does that unclean spirit preside wherever leprosy is given. For the one who is the author of a thing can indeed preside over and rule it.

But those over whom the spirit of destruction, damnation, and uncleanness presides are cut off from the saving Spirit of our Lord Jesus, who is the author of all purity. For what fellowship has Christ with Belial?

Those, therefore, who possess destruction and uncleanness, and whom destruction and uncleanness in turn possess—what can be given or received from them except the destruction or uncleanness that alone they have acquired?

Since it is therefore necessarily concluded that destruction and leprosy are sold and bought, it remains that such traders are improperly called priests and clerics, but properly called destroyed men and lepers. Their wicked laying on of hands gives what evil alone it acquired and grants no good, because through such trading it acquired no good.

For what is worshiped unjustly is never rightly bestowed. Thus it destroys and defiles others along with itself; it does not sanctify or cleanse, as Scripture clearly cries out:

“Whatever the unclean person touches shall become unclean” (Numbers 19:22).

“Likewise, the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from deceit, and he will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding, and he will be reproved by the iniquity that overtakes him” (Wisdom 1:5).

He is called the Spirit of discipline because he makes disciplined those whom he breathes upon, and through them distributes the gifts of his graces to each person for discipline, as he wills. But he thrusts the undisciplined far from himself—or rather, because they are deceitful, he flees from them.

And who is proved to be more deceitful than the one who, against Catholic discipline—whose special administrator the Holy Spirit is believed to be—pretends to be what he neither is nor can in any way be, namely, a bishop or a cleric of some other order through the payment of money?

## CHAPTER XX  
### That Simonians are without faith and deprive those who consent to them of faith

Other hypocrites are less harmful through association with these men, because they scarcely harm anyone except themselves. These men, however, kill Christians in whole crowds along with themselves: while their leprosy remains active, they make others participants in the condemnation or destruction that has been sold or bought under the pretext of ordaining or sanctifying them.

These dissemblers and tricksters, more than others, provoke rather than appease God’s anger, because, being sold and selling others, they daily sell Christ’s sheep and oxen—that is, the simple and the clever, or rather the weak and the strong. And to whom do they sell them, unless, as blessed Augustine says, to the devil?

When the deceived believe that priests can be made for a price and that the Holy Spirit can be sold and bought, the firstborn possession of their hearts—that is, faith—is shown to be corrupted. Once faith is corrupted, whatever good may have been in them must necessarily be corrupted to such an extent that it becomes altogether nothing, because the soul’s one virginity is an incorrupt faith.

The Apostle feared that this faith would be corrupted by false apostles, and therefore said to the Corinthians:

“I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy. For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ Jesus” (2 Corinthians 11:2–3).

This faith the same Apostle, according to the grace given to him, laid among them as a wise architect’s “foundation”; and, as he continues, “No one can lay any foundation other than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11).

Moreover, Christ Jesus dwells in hearts strengthened by the Holy Spirit, as he himself indicates to the Ephesians:

“I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Ephesians 3:14–17).

If, therefore, according to that most excellent fellow-initiate (*symmysta*)—who was caught up even to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2), or into paradise itself—the faith of Christianity is the foundation, and Christ Jesus is the foundation, it follows that faith is Christ, who, dwelling in us strengthened through the Spirit of God the Father, governs us.

From this it is undoubtedly clear what must be thought of a person who has an evil opinion of the Holy Spirit among Christians. For it is established that he has neither the Son nor the Father. As Catholic teaching proclaims, the works of the Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are inseparable; and whenever the visitation of any one of the three is absent from anyone, the other two must necessarily also be absent.

Whoever, therefore, believes that the Holy Spirit can be acquired not only by faith but also with money does not have God the Father, before whom the devout Apostle bent his knees so that the Ephesians might be strengthened through that same Spirit. He does not have the Son either, besides whom no other foundation of Christianity can be laid, because, lest we fail beneath the weight of so great a foundation, we are supported and strengthened by the Holy Spirit.

It follows, then, that the one who does not have the Holy Spirit, upon whom the foundation that is Christ Jesus rests, does not have the foundation itself. If he does not have the foundation, he does not have Christ. If he does not have Christ, he does not have faith, through which Christ may dwell in his heart.

Thus it follows that whoever does not have faith is an unbeliever. Since he does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ. To whom, then, does he belong? Certainly to the one who was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him; for he is a liar and the father of lying (John 8:44). Whoever does not gather with Christ scatters (Matthew 12:30); and because he is not with him, he is against him.

Hence it is clear that Simonians have strayed from the faith through greed—or rather, have apostatized—and have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith, as the Apostle says to Timothy:

“The root of all evils is greed; by desiring it, some have strayed from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” (1 Timothy 6:10).

Such people are plainly to be called and regarded as erring, apostate, or shipwrecked in faith—not as bishops or clerics.

For if merchants of earthly and temporal wages sometimes stray from the faith through greed, when by careless and contrived swearing and perjury they take up the name of their God and their own souls in vain, in order to scrape together some small profit, how far do we think those have strayed from the faith who not only hold their own souls for sale but also attempt to sell the Holy Spirit, who is God and Lord?

They have truly strayed from the whole way of faith. The Spirit abhors their condemned trafficking from the beginning and flees far from them. When he flees, the foundation that is Christ Jesus cannot remain with them, because the Spirit himself withdraws, whose task it is to support and strengthen.

Thus it happens that, while the greediest of mortals compete to buy and sell what cannot be compared with anything, they make evil spirits more eager outwardly to destroy not only the walls of their good works but also inwardly to tear down faith itself, that is, the foundation. They exhort one another, as though toward complete destruction, saying what the Psalmist conveys in lament:

“Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundation” (Psalm 136:7).

When the foundation—that is, Christ, who always rests upon the Holy Spirit—is torn from human hearts, it is certain that such a house is left deserted and utterly destroyed by God and becomes a den of thieves (Matthew 21:13), who immediately claim it for their own mockery.

Thus a person is now called Christian only by an empty name, with nothing of faith—that is, of Christ—remaining in him at all. Consequently he is shown to be without God and worse than a pagan, because he is at once an unbeliever and an apostate. A pagan, although an unbeliever, cannot rightly be called or regarded as an apostate from Christian faith or conduct, which he never possessed.

As was said above, the Holy Spirit also removes himself from such people’s thoughts, because they are without understanding. What thoughts are more without understanding than those which suppose that the Holy Spirit can be sold and bought? For it is less harmful to think irrationally about a creature than about the Creator.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### The rejection of those who say that the Holy Spirit can be possessed and justly given by one who unjustly received him

If the Holy Spirit withdraws from those who suppose that he can be sold, much more does he withdraw from those who not only suppose this but believe it so strongly that, to the destruction of many, they proclaim it in word and writing:

### Objection

“It is clear,” they say, “that the grace of the Holy Spirit is both sold and purchased. Therefore, whoever unjustly acquired the Holy Spirit unjustly possessed him; the one to whom he unjustly granted him he condemned along with himself; but the one to whom he gave him justly may justly possess him, if that person is righteous, since the good person rightly received good from the wicked.”

### Rejection

What understanding, or what element of reason, can be found in such a judgment?

O God and Lord, Holy Spirit, who are eternal righteousness! According to the faithlessness of these preachers—or rather, these lost men—you can be unjustly acquired, unjustly possessed, and unjustly granted! And where is justice to be sought if justice can be unjustly acquired and possessed?

Wretched and insane men, who think of you as though you were some animal acquired by theft and possessed by a thief, and knowingly purchased in this way! Let them first become like horse and mule, which have no understanding (Psalm 31:9), because human beings, when they were in honor, did not understand; they were compared with senseless beasts and became like them (Psalm 48:13).

Although they were created rational animals by God, nevertheless, because they abuse reason, they do not understand that justice and injustice cannot be joined, nor can virtue coexist or agree with vice.

As blessed Jude the Apostle says:

“Whatever they do not understand, they blaspheme; and whatever they know instinctively, like irrational animals, in these things they are corrupted” (Jude 10).

Therefore, when the Holy Spirit has been driven away and removed from such thoughts, as was said above, they are seized—that is, wholly carried off—by the iniquity that overtakes them, namely, by the evil spirit. He is so wicked that he is himself iniquity, as the glorious Paul declares:

“The mystery of iniquity is already at work”; and shortly afterward: “Then the lawless one will be revealed” (2 Thessalonians 2:7–8).

He is so murderous that he is himself death; so lost and destructive that he is also destruction itself.

Having been wholly seized by this iniquity, they no longer, as utterly natural people, perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14). For they are foolishness to them, and they cannot understand them because they are examined spiritually.

But, as the same Apostle adds:

“The spiritual person judges all things, but is judged by no one. For ‘who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?’ But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Corinthians 2:15–16).

For, as he states shortly beforehand:

“God has revealed these things to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. For who among human beings knows what belongs to a human being except the human spirit that is in him? So also no one knows what belongs to God except the Spirit of God.

“Now we have received not the spirit of the world but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God. We speak of these things not in words taught by human wisdom but in the Spirit’s teaching, comparing spiritual things with spiritual” (ibid., 10–13).

Among the Apostle’s words, we must especially consider this statement: “We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God.”

The world, as blessed John writes, lies in the evil one; the spirit of the world is the evil spirit, whom the Lord in the Gospel calls the ruler of the world, as in the statements:

“The ruler of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31);

“The ruler of this world has been judged” (John 16:11);

“The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

It is plainly evident that those who know what has been given to them by God have not received this spirit. The knowledge of these things is produced in them by the Spirit who is from God. They are said to have received him for this purpose: that they may know what has been given to them by God.

The proof, therefore, that they have received the Spirit who is from God is their recognition of the things granted by him. We show that we retain this knowledge perfectly because we profess—and defend, according to our limited ability—that a gift is given as a gift, that is, received and given freely, according to evangelical and apostolic tradition, comparing spiritual things with spiritual.

From the opposite side it follows that those have received the spirit of the world who, against evangelical and apostolic discipline, believe, think, profess, and, as far as they can, attempt to defend that God’s gift can be possessed for money, comparing spiritual things with carnal things.

If they would recall what this spirit of the world is, and where it is, and what he has already suffered, they would seek, with great contrition of heart, to be rescued from the power of darkness and, while it is still permitted, to be transferred into the kingdom of the Son of the Father’s glory.

For he is the ruler of the world, the ruler of those darknesses—that is, of unbelieving human beings—in whom, as sons of unbelief, the ancient serpent himself reigns and works. He is the devil and Satan, already judged, condemned, and cast out—not outside the structure of heaven and earth, but outside the hearts of the faithful, whom Christ has made a kingdom and priests for God and his Father.

If the spirit of the world has already been judged and cast out, it is clear that the world over which he rules has also been judged and cast out with him, and is no longer in the world which God loved and, having redeemed it by the blood of his Son, cleansed by the washing of water in the word, so that God himself might be their God.

For what share has the faithful person with the unbeliever?

Therefore, whoever has an evil opinion of the Holy Spirit should consider what blessed Pope Damasus says in a letter to Paulinus, patriarch of Antioch, among other things:

“If anyone thinks rightly concerning the Father and the Son, but does not hold a right belief concerning the Holy Spirit, he is a heretic.”

All heretics who hold an evil opinion concerning the Son of God or the Holy Spirit are found in the faithlessness of the Jews and the Gentiles.

Thus, when the Jews said, “We were not born of fornication”—meaning idolatry—“we have one Father, God,” the Lord Jesus replied:

“If God were your Father, you would certainly love me. For I proceeded from God and came; I did not come of my own accord, but he sent me. You are from your father the devil” (John 8:41–44).

Likewise, when Simon Magus desired to purchase the Holy Spirit, Peter said to him:

“You have neither part nor lot in this faith” (Acts 8:21).

But lest this continued rejection, although entirely necessary, if prolonged, press and attack the deserter so severely that our fellow soldier, exhausted, should perish, the writer’s intention ought to provide the delicate reader with an opportunity to breathe. Let this, at last, be the end of this first little book.

## The First Book Ends

THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 1055]

CHAPTER ONE. What the blessed apostle Peter and his fellow apostles thought about heretics.

[Col. 1055B]

I have undertaken, as far as my small talent allows, to defend against obstinate detractors the judgment of Simon Peter, the most devout prince of the apostles, concerning the most impious Simon Magus—a judgment uttered in zeal for that dove of which he was the son. I have considered no beginning more suitable than the words of that same man, whose outstanding faith neither failed nor ever will fail. The concordant judgments of his fellow apostles may be added like subscriptions.

For, speaking at greater length in his second letter about him and such faithless apostates, he says:

“There were false prophets among the people, just as there will also be false teachers among you. They will introduce destructive sects, denying the Lord who bought them, and bringing upon themselves swift destruction. Many will follow their debaucheries, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. In their greed they will exploit you with fabricated words. Their condemnation has not been idle for a long time, and their destruction does not sleep (II Peter 2:1–3).”

And shortly afterward:

“These men, like irrational animals, naturally destined for capture and destruction, blaspheming what they do not understand, will perish in their corruption, receiving the reward of unrighteousness … They entice unstable souls; their hearts are trained in greed; they are children of a curse. Abandoning the straight way, they have gone astray, following the way of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved the reward of wickedness. But he received a rebuke for his madness: a speechless beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s folly.

“These are waterless springs and mists driven by storms, for whom the gloom of darkness has been reserved. For, speaking arrogant words of vanity, they entice with the desires of the flesh those who have barely escaped from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves of corruption; for whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.

“For if, after escaping the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled and overcome by them, their final condition has become worse than the first. It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What has happened to them accords with the true proverb (Prov. 28:12): ‘A dog returns to its own vomit, and a washed sow to wallowing in the mud’ (II Peter 2:22).”

The apostle Jude likewise warns us about such men, saying:

“Certain men have slipped in—men long ago designated for this judgment, ungodly men who pervert the grace of our God into debauchery and deny the only Sovereign and our Lord Jesus Christ (Jude 4).”

And shortly afterward:

“Woe to them, for they have gone in the way of Cain, have poured themselves out in the error of Balaam for a reward, and have perished in Korah’s rebellion. These are blemishes at their feasts, feasting with you without fear, feeding themselves; waterless clouds carried about by winds; autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the storm of darkness has been reserved forever.

“Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied concerning them, saying: ‘Behold, the Lord has come with his holy myriads to execute judgment against all and to convict all the ungodly concerning all the works of their ungodliness by which they acted impiously, and concerning all the harsh things that sinful and ungodly men have spoken against him.’

“These are grumblers and complainers, walking according to their desires; their mouths speak arrogance, and they show partiality for the sake of gain. But you, beloved, remember the words foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ. They told you that in the last time there would be mockers walking according to their own desires in ungodliness. These are the ones who separate themselves, sensual, not having the Spirit.

“But you, beloved, build yourselves up in your most holy true faith, praying in the Holy Spirit. Keep yourselves in the love of God, awaiting the mercy of our God Jesus Christ for eternal life. And indeed rebuke some, making distinctions; save others by snatching them from the fire; and on others have mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh (Jude 11–23).”

John also—whether the evangelist, as is believed, or the presbyter of the Church of Ephesus—writing to a holy woman, says:

“This is the commandment of God: that, just as you heard from the beginning, you should walk in it. For many deceivers have gone out into the world, those who do not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. This is the deceiver and the Antichrist. Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose what you have accomplished, but may receive a full reward. Everyone who turns away and does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God; whoever remains in the teaching has both the Son and the Father. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house, and do not say ‘Greetings’ to him. For whoever says ‘Greetings’ to him shares in his evil works (II John 6–10).”

From this point, Paul—least among the apostles in his calling but greatest in preaching and works—warns the Galatians, who had been bewitched by false apostles, saying:

“I am astonished that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you in the grace of Christ to another gospel—which is not another, except that there are some who trouble you and wish to pervert the gospel of Christ. But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed. As I said before, and now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed (Gal. 1:6–9).”

The same apostle says to the Philippians:

“Let all of us who are mature think this way; and if you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you. Nevertheless, let us continue in the direction we have reached, thinking the same thing and remaining within the same rule. Become imitators of me, brothers, and observe those who walk in this way, just as you have us as an example (Phil. 3:15–17).”
