The same apostle says to the Colossians:

“I say this so that no one may deceive you with subtle arguments (Col. 2:4).”

And shortly afterward:

“See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ (ibid., 8).”

The same apostle says to the Thessalonians:

“If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, take note of that person and do not associate with him, so that he may be put to shame. Yet do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother (II Thess. 3:14–15).”

The same apostle says to Timothy:

“The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. Some, having departed from these things, have turned aside to empty talk, wishing to be teachers of the law, understanding neither what they say nor the things about which they make assertions (I Tim. 1:5–7).”

And shortly afterward, to the same man:

“The Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving attention to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are seared (I Tim. 4:1).”

And again, to the same man:

“If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine that accords with piety, he is conceited and understands nothing, but is diseased with controversies and disputes about words. From these arise envy, quarrels, blasphemies, evil suspicions, and conflicts among people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose that piety is a means of gain.

“Piety with contentment is indeed great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and there is no doubt that we can take nothing out of it. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation, the devil’s snare, and many foolish and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. The root of all evils is greed; by desiring it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pains (I Tim. 6:3–10).”

The same apostle says to the same man:

“Do not quarrel about words; it is useful for nothing except the ruin of those who hear. Take pains to present yourself approved before God, a worker who cannot be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth. Avoid profane and empty talk, for it advances greatly toward ungodliness, and their speech spreads like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have fallen away from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already occurred, and they overthrow the faith of some.

“But the firm foundation of God stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his,’ and ‘Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.’ In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; some for honor, some for dishonor. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.

“Flee youthful desires. Pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart. Avoid foolish and undisciplined controversies, knowing that they generate quarrels. The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward everyone, teachable, patient, correcting opponents with modesty, in the hope that God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to knowledge of the truth, and that they may recover from the devil’s snares, by whom they are held captive for his will (II Tim. 2:14–26).”

Know this, however: in the last days perilous times will come. People will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, without self-control, savage, without kindness, treacherous, reckless, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having the appearance of piety but denying its power. Avoid such people.

For among them are those who enter houses and take captive weak women burdened with sins and led by various desires, always learning but never arriving at knowledge of the truth. Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses (Exod. 7:11), so these also resist the truth—people corrupted in mind and disqualified with regard to the faith. But they will not progress further, for their folly will be evident to all, as theirs also was (II Tim. 3:1–9).”

And shortly afterward:

“For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but, according to their own desires, they will heap up teachers for themselves, itching in their ears; they will turn away their hearing from the truth and turn instead to myths (II Tim. 4:3–4).”

And again, to the same man:

“Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; the Lord will repay him according to his works (ibid., 14).”

Likewise, to Titus:

“There are many disobedient people, empty talkers, and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision, whom it is necessary to silence. They overthrow entire households, teaching things that ought not to be taught for the sake of disgraceful gain. One of their own prophets said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.’ This testimony is true. For this reason rebuke them sharply, so that they may be sound in faith and not pay attention to Jewish myths or commandments of people who turn away from the truth (Titus 1:10–13).”

And shortly afterward, to the same man:

“Avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, quarrels, and disputes about the law, for they are useless and futile. After one or two warnings, avoid a heretical person, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment (Titus 3:9–11).”

CHAPTER TWO. On piety and impiety, and on the presumption of Cain and Balaam.

[Col. 1059C]

Let no one consider it superfluous that we have extracted these passages at length from the apostolic writings and inserted them here in continuous sequence. For, although they expose other heresies as well, they chiefly mark out that heresy which pursues disgraceful gain and considers piety a means of profit.

Here, however, piety is not to be understood in the sense in which it is commonly understood and improperly called mercy, but in the sense of what is called in Greek *eusebeia* (εὐσέβεια), that is, “good worship,” or rather *theosebeia* (θεοσέβεια), that is, “worship of God.” According to this, a worshiper of God—or a worshiper of what is good—is called pious: namely, one devoted and reverent toward God in right faith. Conversely, impious is anyone who, ignorant of the true God—whether unbelieving or distrustful—is promiscuously prostituted to spirits of error and serves their wishes.

Faith is the doorkeeper of piety, without which one neither pleases God, nor appeases God, nor worships him. Therefore, attentive to this term, all of us who are faithful rightly and beneficially confess that we are sinners while we are absent from the Lord (II Cor. 5:6), but we shrink from and avoid calling ourselves impious in every respect.

Accordingly, every impious person is indeed also a sinner, but not every sinner is also impious, because every faithful person, so long as he lives here, is not without sin, though he is without impiety—that is, without unbelief. An unbeliever, however, is neither without sin nor without impiety. Such are the impious Jews and pagans, concerning whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged, just as the ruler of this world has already been judged (John 3:18).”

Therefore, according to the Psalmist: “The impious shall not rise in the judgment (Ps. 1:5).”

If, then, according to the Apostle, those who consider piety—namely, the worship of God—to be a means of gain are deprived of the truth, how much more are the Simonians, who consider piety so much a means of gain that they put all the offices of piety itself—that is, the orders of divine worship—up for sale for the sake of profit? They even confidently believe that the author of piety itself, the Holy Spirit—the gift of God, which operates principally in ecclesiastical orders or sacraments—can be possessed by money.

Nor should it be passed over carelessly that in the writings of the holy apostles themselves, where present and future heresies are reproved, innumerable guilty persons from before the law and under the law are mentioned without their names, while Cain, Balaam, and Korah are named, and Jannes and Jambres are brought forward typologically as examples.

Jude of James presents the first three in order, saying: “Woe to them, for they have gone in the way of Cain, have poured themselves out in the error of Balaam for a reward, and have perished in Korah’s rebellion (Jude 11).”

The blessed Peter recalls the middle one in this way: “They followed the way of Balaam son of Bosor (I Peter 2:15).”

The blessed Paul exposes the last two as follows: “Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth (II Tim. 3:8).”

Accordingly, if the matter is examined carefully, presumption, greed, and obstinacy are found to be reproved in these five men. These three are indeed the seeds of all heresies, their means of increase and support.

Cain’s presumption, among other things, consisted in this: according to the statement of the blessed apostle John, he was “from the evil one” (I John 3:12), and, although his works were evil, because of envy toward his most holy brother, whose works were righteous, he presumptuously claimed for himself the priestly office by offering sacrifice to God (Gen. 4:8).

Before the law, devotion alone conferred this prerogative of priesthood upon the fathers, so that, like priests under the law, they might sacrifice on altars to the Lord and offer victims, as did Noah, Melchizedek, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and blessed Job.

Greed also took such possession of Cain that he was the first to strive to reduce to his own private possession what was a common and public good for all, by presuming to cross its appointed spaces and boundaries. As a grim and tireless digger, he worked upon it so intensely that whatever came to him from it he anxiously stored within it, until at last, with greed scarcely yielding, he lifted from the earth and offered only a sheaf out of envy for his brother.

Truly, this was the wretched and astonishing greed of a faithless man: although at that time there were only two other men—his father and his brother—the whole world, together with all its parts, seemed small and cramped to him.

Finally, obstinacy bound him to itself beyond escape, since he refused to heed even the Lord when the Lord restrained and warned him against sin and the premeditated murder of his brother. Genesis reports that the Lord said to Cain:

“Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, will you not receive? But if you do evil, sin will immediately be present at the door; its desire will be under you, and you will rule over it (Gen. 4:6).”

Or, according to another translation:

“If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be quiet.”

Balaam is marked by this presumption because, although he was a diviner and an idolater, he believed himself to be a prophet and blessed the one whom he blessed and accursed the one whom he cursed; and, as though he were a priest of God, he built altars.

His greed is also clearly recognized both from the Book of Numbers and from the epistle of the blessed apostle Peter. There Peter foretells that false teachers will come out of the Church, “enticing unstable souls, having hearts trained in greed, children of a curse; abandoning the straight way, they have gone astray, following the way of Balaam son of Bosor, who loved the reward of wickedness” (II Peter 2:15; Num. 22:23).

His fellow apostle Jude of James agrees with this and pronounces woe upon those “who have poured themselves out in the error of Balaam for a reward” (Jude 11).

Balaam’s obstinacy is especially proved by the fact that, although rebuked and warned four times by the Lord, he by no means changed his mind from the curse [lacuna] destruction of Israel. For, as the sacred history relates, while he was still at home the Lord warned him twice:

“Do not go with these men, and do not curse the people, because they are blessed (Num. 22:12).”

Later he commanded him:

“If these men have come to call you, rise and go with them, but only do what I shall command you (ibid., 20).”

When Balaam was already on the road, an angel appeared to him after the rebukes delivered by the donkey and threatened him as follows:

“I have come to oppose you, because your way is perverse and contrary to me (ibid., 33).”

Yet, allowing him to proceed, the angel said:

“Go with these men, but take care that you speak nothing other than what I command you (ibid., 35).”

But that impious man, enslaved to savage greed, secretly prepared snares of destruction for them, by which he openly desired to make himself like one destined for death.

CHAPTER THREE. On the sin of Korah and his supporters, and their punishment.

In Korah’s rebellion itself, presumption and greed appear to be the same thing. For by seeking a priesthood not owed to him, he presumed; and by presuming, he sought it.

Moreover, as blessed Gregory says, greed concerns not only money but also exalted position. It is rightly called greed when eminence is sought beyond measure. For if the seizure of honor did not belong to greed, Paul would never have said of the only-begotten Son: “He did not consider it robbery to be equal with God (Phil. 2:6).”

The devil therefore drew our forefather into pride by arousing in him greed for exalted status.

Korah’s obstinacy is likewise shown by the fact that he did not return to his senses either through rebuke or through warning. Finally, as the history relates, when Korah was angrily and shamelessly quarreling with Moses and reproaching him, the meekest of men answered him:

“Tomorrow the Lord will make known who belong to him; he will draw the holy ones to himself, and those whom he chooses will approach him. Do this, then: let each one take his censer—you, Korah, and your whole assembly—and tomorrow, having taken fire, place incense upon it before the Lord. Whoever he chooses will be holy. You have gone too far, sons of Levi.”

Again he said to Korah:

“Listen, sons of Levi. Is it too little for you that God has separated you from the whole people and joined you to himself, so that you might serve him in the worship of the tabernacle and stand before the assembly of the people to minister to them? He has therefore brought you and all your brothers, the sons of Levi, near to himself, so that you might also claim the priesthood, and that your entire company should stand against the Lord (Num. 16:5–11).”

When Moses learned through messengers of the insolent contradiction of Dathan and Abiram, he became very angry and said to the Lord:

“Do not regard their sacrifices. You know that I have not taken so much as a donkey from them, nor have I harmed any one of them.”

Then he said to Korah:

“You and your entire assembly, stand apart before the Lord, you and Aaron, tomorrow separately. Let each one take his censer and place incense upon it, offering before the Lord 250 censers; Aaron also shall hold his censer.”

When they had done this, while Moses and Aaron stood there and the whole assembly was gathered against them at the entrance of the tent of meeting, the glory of the Lord appeared to everyone. The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying:

“Separate yourselves from the midst of this assembly, so that I may suddenly destroy them.”

They fell on their faces and said:

“O strongest God, God of the spirits of all flesh, shall your anger rage against everyone when one person has sinned?”

And the Lord said to Moses:

“Command the whole people to separate themselves from the tents of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram.”

Moses rose and went to Dathan and Abiram, and, with the elders of Israel following him, he said to the crowd:

“Withdraw from the tents of these impious men, and do not touch anything belonging to them, lest you become entangled in their sins.”

When they had withdrawn all around from their tents, Dathan and Abiram came out and stood at the entrance of their tents with their wives and children and their entire company.

Moses said:

“By this you shall know that the Lord has sent me to do all these things that you see, and that I have not brought them forth from my own heart. If these men die the usual death of human beings, and if they are visited by the plague by which others are commonly visited, the Lord has not sent me. But if the Lord does something new—if the earth opens its mouth and swallows them and everything belonging to them, and they descend alive into the underworld—you shall know that they have blasphemed the Lord.”

As soon as he had finished speaking, the earth split beneath their feet. It opened its mouth and swallowed them with their tents and all their possessions; they descended alive into the underworld, covered by the earth, and perished from the midst of the assembly.

All Israel, however, who stood around them, fled at the cries of those who were perishing, saying:

“Lest perhaps the earth swallow us also.”

Fire likewise came out from the Lord and killed the 250 men who were offering incense (ibid., 15–35).”

From this judgment of divine severity, even at the level of the historical account—which we have judged should be inserted almost in its entirety into this little work—we can infer what those deserve or what they will suffer who presumptuously claim for themselves, in a worldly manner, the priesthood of Christian grace, if those who attempted to seize the priesthood of the Mosaic law contumaciously were punished with such severity.

Just as the difference between those two priesthoods is greatest in their sacraments, so the difference between the ministers of each must also be greatest—namely, as great as the distance ordinarily is between a servant and the person of an emperor.

The Mosaic priesthood, occupied with bodily sacrifices and presenting the blood of goats, bulls, and certain other animals—by which, according to the Apostle, it was impossible for sins to be taken away—bore only a shadow of the good things to come. The Christian priesthood, however, occupied with spiritual offerings, daily pours out the blood of Jesus Christ, the spotless and undefiled Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, for the remission of sins, through the manifest truth of present and future good things.

This also must be noted: Korah did not seek the priesthood for himself with money, but because of the proximity of his rank and his kinship with Aaron. They belonged to the same tribe, although not to the same family, and he trusted that he too belonged to the Lord, as is plainly shown by his words:

“Let it be enough for you that the whole multitude is holy and that the Lord is among them. Why do you raise yourselves above the people of the Lord? (Num. 16:3).”

It must be noted no less carefully how Dathan and Abiram descended alive into the underworld in a dreadful and pitiable manner, with all their households and all their possessions, although they had not sought the priesthood for themselves—for they were not from the tribe of Levi—but had merely supported the presumptuous men.

Yet the supporters and defenders were punished more severely than the presumptuous men themselves. For it is more grievous to be swallowed alive by the earth, together with one’s possessions and even one’s innocent little children, than for those who sinned to be burned by fire alone.

Let laymen and clerics who do not fear to sponsor wicked and undisciplined people take note of this, especially those who, by their power, favor, or payment, press forward the unworthy for promotion to sacred orders.

Let them also observe that the people were forbidden to touch anything belonging to Dathan and Abiram, lest they become entangled in their sins. Yet Korah’s possessions did not perish entirely, since even their censers were beaten into plates and, by God’s command, applied to the altar.

As the history relates in what follows, a great miracle also occurred: although Korah perished, his sons did not perish. Let the defenders and supporters of the wicked finally recognize how much worse the supporters are than the wicked themselves.

For just as the first to commit the crime—Dathan and Abiram—were first swallowed by the earth, afterward fire seized Korah and his accomplices and consumed them.

Above all, let the Simonians take note—those who, after innumerable anathemas, presumptuously assail the Holy Spirit with money in their ambition for ecclesiastical rank, and who believe that he can overcome them or be overcome by them—how much more wicked they are than Korah, who, before any anathema had been uttered, attempted to seize the priesthood of the Jewish synagogue without money offered or promised, relying only on kinship or confidence in his own holiness.

Furthermore, let the supporters and obstinate defenders of Simonians or of any undisciplined people consider what they ought to fear from evangelical truth, if Dathan and Abiram suffered such destruction under the shadow of the law.

For the warning of the Gospel is more severe than that of the law: under the law only an evil deed is punished, whereas under the Gospel even the thought is punished.

Certainly, Dathan, Abiram, and Korah are believed to have been crushed by a double destruction, bodily and spiritual, as Jude, the brother of James, testifies.

CHAPTER FOUR. On the rabble that follows presumptuous men, and on the difference between true and false priesthood.

Jesus, while saving the people from the land of Egypt, secondly destroyed those who did not believe. But let us now consider what the same history adds:

> “On the following day the whole assembly of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying: ‘You have killed the people of the Lord.’ And when sedition arose and the tumult increased, Moses and Aaron fled to the tabernacle of the covenant. After they had entered it, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the Lord appeared. Then the Lord said to Moses: ‘Withdraw from the midst of this multitude; even now I will destroy them.’ And while they lay prostrate on the ground, Moses said to Aaron: ‘Take the censer, draw fire from the altar, and put incense upon it; go quickly to the people, that you may pray for them. For wrath has gone forth from the Lord, and the plague is raging.’ When Aaron had done this and had run into the midst of the assembly, which the fire was already ravaging, he offered the incense. Standing between the dead and the living, he pleaded for the people, and the plague ceased. Those who were struck numbered fourteen thousand seven hundred, besides those who perished in the rebellion of Korah” (Num. XVI, 41–49).

This event clearly demonstrates that even the mob which follows the wicked is grievously struck down by divine indignation, when it laments those same wicked men whom the people of God falsely believed and said had been killed. Nor is this surprising, for, as Solomon says, “He who is the companion of fools will become like them.” He teaches that their company must be avoided in these words:

> “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them. If they say: ‘Come with us; cast in your lot with us; let there be one purse for us all’—for their feet run to evil—do not emulate wicked men, nor desire to be with them, because their lips speak deceit. Do not mingle with slanderers, for suddenly their destruction will arise, and who knows the ruin of both? Do not give your honor to strangers, nor your years to the cruel, lest strangers be filled with your strength, your labors be in another’s house, and you groan at the end, when you have consumed your flesh and your body, and say: ‘Why did I hate discipline, and why did my heart not acquiesce in correction? Why did I not hear the voice of those teaching me, nor incline my ear to my instructors?’ (Prov. I, V, XXIV.) I was almost involved in every evil in the midst of the Church and the synagogue.”

We have gathered these sayings from Proverbs at greater length because the brutish multitude of human beings—dull, sluggish, and inclined to evil—despises learning the doctrine of truth. It desires only to imitate the wicked deeds of its elders or rulers and strives to excuse itself by its ignorance, to which it willingly subjects itself, as Paul says: “Whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Cor. XIV, 38).

Therefore, let the Christian people cast ignorance away from themselves, since it is the mother of vices. Let them learn who is a shepherd, who is a hireling, and who is a thief and robber. Let them follow and listen to the shepherd in every respect; let them listen to the hireling only and meanwhile endure him; but let them neither listen to nor endure the thief and robber, because they come only to steal, slaughter, and destroy.

And alas, how lamentably corrupted is the condition of our humanity! Hardly ever, even when wearied by daily meditations and continual admonitions, does it recognize what it ought to desire or avoid, whereas all other animals, from the very beginning of their existence, instinctively desire what is suitable for them and avoid what is harmful—or, as turtledoves [avoid] kites and such creatures, namely hawks and birds of their kind.

The history set before us also unmistakably shows how greatly those who take honor for themselves differ from those who are called by God. Korah and his accomplices, by offering incense and prayers to the Lord, benefited no one, but harmed themselves in every respect; and immediately they deserved to be consumed by fire. Aaron, however, alone offered incense and prayed for those who were perishing. Standing between the dead and the living like an unconquerable and impenetrable wall, he himself remained unharmed by so great a fire and turned it away from the survivors.

Thus the offering and prayer of one legitimate priest appeased the indignation of the Godhead, which two hundred and fifty presumptuous men had provoked against themselves and others. Let the Simoniacs and their defenders hear this, if they have ears to hear, and at last cease by their prayers and sacrifices to kindle the wrath of God unquenchably against themselves and against the people.

## CHAPTER V. On Jannes and Jambres, whom the Simoniacs surpass in wickedness

There remain Jannes and Jambres, whose presumption and avarice are evident. Since they were sorcerers, they presumed, out of a twofold avarice, to imitate divine signs, either so that the people might esteem them equal or superior to Moses and magnify them, or at least so that they might be loaded with royal gifts.

Their stubborn deceit was not restrained by the naked truth or by the very great power of Moses’ signs, until the opportunity for deceiving openly failed them before everyone. Since they did not wish to use reason to distinguish good from evil, the signs rather than the words admonished and rebuked them as unbelievers. Thus admonition and rebuke were applied to them simultaneously: when the rods of Moses swallowed their rods, and when the water turned into blood and the frogs that had been brought forth returned, through Moses alone, to what they had been, whereas the sorcerers themselves could only add those plagues to themselves and others, not remove them.

When, moreover, during the third plague they lost even the ability to deceive and cause harm, they said: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII, 19). It is therefore clear that the Holy Spirit, whose operation in Moses they were resisting, then rendered their magical illusions void; and afterward, in the third plague—which was already the sixth, because of their obstinacy—he also disfigured and condemned them, together with their animals, by ulcers and swelling blisters, so that they could no longer stand before Moses.

The Lord himself indicates in the Gospel that the finger of God is the Holy Spirit, saying: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke XI, 20). Another Evangelist explains this by saying: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God.”

From this, heretics should consider whom they resemble, and should beware of comparing their own secrets—or, as they presumptuously call them, their sacraments—with the sacraments of Catholics, upon which the finger of God operates. Otherwise, because of their irrational obstinacy, they may be struck irrecoverably by the Holy Spirit, whom they do not fear stubbornly to resist, like irrational beasts.

Let them also consider that those sorcerers could not, by any of their invocations or curses, remove or lessen the disasters affecting themselves and others; rather, they increased them. Having finally confessed the finger of God, let them begin humbly, by declining ecclesiastical orders, to fear for themselves and their own people, rather than arrogantly usurping those orders and multiplying destruction.

If they do not make this effort, let them know without doubt that they are worse than Jannes and Jambres. Those men, when they perceived the finger of God opposing them, yielded and confessed it, although, remaining unrepentant, they did not merit forgiveness. These others, however, possess nothing but obstinacy, and are therefore so much worse as those men were lesser in their crime: the former were magicians of Pharaoh, a mortal man, whereas these are, under the name of religion, procurers of the ancient serpent.

Therefore, terrified by the example of Cain, Balaam, and Korah, of whom we spoke above, and by the example of these magicians of whom we are speaking, all who desire to rejoice forever in the peace of the Catholic Church should beware of presumption, flee avarice, and avoid obstinacy, always keeping before their eyes the saying of blessed Paul:

> “Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. XV, 4).

And again:

> “All these things happened to them as a figure. They were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. X, 11).

## CHAPTER VI. In which Christians are warned to avoid the overthrowing deceit of heretics, whose evil and punishment are shown here

And now, priests, kings of the earth, and all peoples, understand! Be instructed, princes and all judges of the earth; young men and maidens, old men together with the young: take hold of discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way.

Love justice. Remember who gave you the pledge of the Spirit, and do not grieve that same Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

> “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own?” (1 Cor. VI, 19).

> “You are the temple of the living God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you. If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. III, 16–17).

> “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are. You were bought at a great price” (1 Cor. VI, 20).

Do not sell yourselves again to the devil for the smallest coin; until you repay it, you will vainly hope to escape from the prison of the strict Judge. Do not make the house of God the Father a house of commerce, nor the house of prayer a den of thieves.

Think well of the Lord in goodness. Presume upon him for beginning, doing, and completing what is good. Seek him in simplicity of heart, not in any duplicity; for you cannot serve or cling both to God and to Mammon.

Since the Holy Spirit is simplicity itself and makes people simple, and since he seeks that he be sought by the simple, he fittingly appeared and remained upon the simplest of birds, above the most simple Lord Jesus. Content with simple food, this bird longs for no prey; rather, it cautiously avoids deceitful kites and other birds of prey.

> “The simplicity of the righteous shall guide them, but the deceit of the wicked shall destroy them” (Prov. XI, 3).

Accordingly, the righteous, living by faith, whether they simply lay hands on someone in accordance with their office or do anything else in the name of the Lord, have all things work together for their good.

The wicked, by contrast, because they insatiably long to overthrow one another, whatever they do is sin, since it exists without faith. For where there is deceit, there is fraud; and where there is fraud, there are also faithlessness and a curse, as the prophet declares:

> “Cursed is he who performs the work of the Lord deceitfully” (Jer. XLVIII, 10).

Let that deceit of the Simoniacs, among other things, be considered by which they overthrow one another through buying and selling. The buyer, by giving the price, deceives the seller, defrauding him of God’s grace so that the seller may not possess it; or, by accepting the price, he nevertheless deceives the buyer, defrauding him of God’s grace so that he may not receive it.

Because each defrauds the other of God’s grace by this deceit, the blessing by which they subsequently condemn others is removed far from them. Whoever their laying on of hands contaminates, whether freely or for a price, is thereby ruined; and thus the deceit of the wicked destroys them, leaving them neither root nor shoot of spiritual grace.

How dangerous even the business of secular matters is for lay people is shown by this saying of the Wise Man:

> “Two kinds of things have appeared difficult and dangerous to me: it is difficult for a merchant to strip himself of negligence, and a tavernkeeper will not be justified from the sins of his lips. Because of poverty many have sinned, and he who seeks to become rich turns his eye away, as a stake is driven into the middle of a joint between stones. So, amid selling and buying, sin is constricted” (Ecclus. XXVI, 28; XXVII, 1–2).

If buying and selling are so difficult and dangerous for lay people in their ordinary and private interests, who can describe how difficult and dangerous they are for clerics in ecclesiastical ordinations?

Certainly, the sale of your own property is permitted to you, because, according to blessed Augustine, things that are lawfully bought are not unlawfully sold. The Lord himself said to a certain young man: “Go, sell everything that you have” (Matt. XIX, 21). Elsewhere, when he said to Judas the betrayer, “What you do, do quickly” (John XIII, 27), some of the disciples thought that he had told him, as usual: “Buy for us what is necessary for the feast.”

And yet, although the sale of one’s possessions is lawful and very necessary for many mortals, it scarcely fails to implant sin; Scripture asserts that sin is fixed and constricted between seller and buyer like a stake between the joints of stones.

How great a crime, then, do we suppose is incurred by those who presume, through an unlawful and destructive sale, to dispose of another’s property against the opposition of its owner? They are plainly violent men and robbers, of whom the Apostle says:

> “Robbers, he says, shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. VI, 10).

Among such people, if they are able, let them rightly consider how great a robbery they presume to commit—those who wickedly seek to conduct business concerning God himself, the Lord of all visible and invisible things. They do not hesitate to sell and buy, to the destruction of many souls, the grace that he commands to be given freely because it was freely received.

In this they are not only robbers and sacrilegious persons, but also murderers, perjurers, apostates, and heretics. The various and innumerable torments of the lower hell would scarcely suffice for their just punishment. Not content with the crimes already mentioned, they blaspheme the Holy Spirit, whom they preach and believe to cooperate so fully with their sacrilege, robbery, and other wickedness that whatever these lepers and accursed persons touch with mouth or hand is sacrificed and blessed according to their desire.

## CHAPTER VII. On the condemnation of those who falsely seek the Lord, under the example of Ananias and Sapphira

Therefore, all who are sons of God, since you are led by the Spirit of God, seek that same Spirit of God in simplicity of heart, for he is found by those who do not tempt him.

He is simple—or rather, he is simplicity itself—and the duplicity of hypocrites and schemers is wholly abhorrent to him, according to what is written:

> “Hypocrites and schemers provoke the wrath of God” (Job XXXVI, 13).

Wherever there is hypocrisy or cunning, there too is fraud; and wherever there is fraud, there too the divinity is tempted. Through that temptation the wrath of God is provoked, as the words and deed of the chief of the apostles demonstrate in the Acts of the Apostles, where we read:

> “A certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira his wife, sold a field and, with his wife’s knowledge, defrauded the price of the field; bringing a part of it, he laid it at the apostles’ feet. Peter said to him: ‘Ananias, why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to defraud the price of the field? While it remained, did it not remain yours? And when it was sold, was it not in your power? Why have you put this matter in your heart? You have not lied to men but to God.’ When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and expired. Great fear came upon all who heard it. The young men arose, removed him, carried him out, and buried him.

> “After an interval of about three hours, his wife entered, not knowing what had happened. Peter said to her: ‘Tell me, did you sell the field for so much?’ She said: ‘Yes, for so much.’ Peter then said to her: ‘Why have you agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.’ Immediately she fell at his feet and expired. The young men entered, found her dead, carried her out, and buried her beside her husband. Great fear came upon the whole Church and upon all who heard these things” (Acts V, 1–11).

These events undoubtedly testify that the one who defrauds and lies not to men but to God—that is, to the Holy Spirit—is shown to have tempted the Spirit of God. This wretched man is punished by sudden death; Sapphira soon afterward suffers the same fate, although at that moment she was ignorant of the killing but had previously been aware of the fraud.

In them the saying is also fulfilled literally: “Those who do and those who consent are punished with the same penalty”; and: “Those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. I, 32).

Blessed Peter identifies this consent as a conspiracy when he says: “Why have you agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord?” For the Holy Spirit, by the outpouring of his grace, had inspired this charity in the primitive Church: that the multitude of believers should have one heart and one soul, and that none of them should call anything that he possessed his own, but that all things should be common to them (Acts IV, 32).

No one who had once put his hand to such a plow was permitted to look back; otherwise he was not fit for the kingdom of God (Luke IX, 62). Whoever willingly becomes a defrauder of his former superior thereby utterly apostatizes.

Hence, according to the saying of the Wise Man:

> “Whoever passes from righteousness to sin, God has prepared him for the sword” (Ecclus. XXVI, 27),

that is, so that, excluded from his paradise, he may be left to join the devil and his angels.

Moreover, even if someone, withdrawing from a higher vocation, turns to something good but inferior, it is clear that the good itself is no longer good but sin. For example, if women who have professed virginal or widowed continence turn to marriage, which is indeed good, they incur condemnation according to the Apostle, because they have made their first faith void.

Hence Moses also says in Deuteronomy:

> “When you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay in fulfilling it, because the Lord your God will require it of you; and if you delay, he will charge it to you as sin. If you are unwilling to promise, you will be without sin. But what once has gone forth from your lips you shall observe, and you shall do as you promised the Lord your God, speaking of your own free will and with your own mouth” (Deut. XXII, 21).

Therefore, the Holy Spirit did not permit fraud to be inflicted, even for a moment, upon his institution—namely, the common life. As soon as the wretched Ananias entered and placed part of the price at the apostles’ feet, he was rebuked and expired. He was not permitted to share, even for a moment, with the saints whom he had defrauded, neither alive nor dead; nor was his wife, who was conscious of the fraud.

Certainly, as far as human judgment is concerned, this punishment appears excessively severe: a man still very inexperienced or a novice in that monastic way of life, of whom it is not recorded that he had previously received any prohibition concerning this matter, is condemned with his wife in so sudden and horrifying an end. Moreover, they had not taken what belonged to another, but, as Arator says:

> “A thief of his own wealth through fraud.”

Yet because of the common-life commitment, what had been his was no longer his, since it belonged also to those who neither presumed to claim anything as their own nor called anything their own. Thus he became not only a defrauder but also a sacrilegious thief, because what had previously been in his power to retain or sell had begun, through his vow and profession, to be sacred. And because he stole something sacred from what was sacred, defrauding the saints of his property, he became subject by right to a harsher punishment than if he had stolen something non-sacred from what was sacred, or something sacred from what was non-sacred.

Those who profess the common life must carefully consider this, lest after the prohibitions they defraud one another, even of the last portion of their former possessions, and lest they suffer in their souls, together with all who presume to commit any fraud or robbery against the Church, the condemnation of true sacrilege which Ananias and Sapphira endured bodily—suffering it all the more grievously in proportion as the soul is better than the body.

They should also consider that every thought, word, and deed of those people in the fraud and after the fraud, even if it appears good to human beings, is nevertheless held by the Holy Spirit to be a lie and a temptation. Peter said to Ananias:

> “Why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to defraud the price of the field? Why have you put this matter in your heart? You have not lied to men but to God.”

Here it is clearly shown that by placing the fraud in his heart he lied to God. Shortly afterward he said to his wife:

> “Why have you agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord?”

[Note: [Col. 1069D] Here Humbert indicates that Ananias and Sapphira were condemned only to bodily death, a view taught with him by the most authoritative holy Fathers: Origen, *Tractate 8 on Matthew*; Augustine, Book III *Against Parmenian* [Col. 1070D] and Sermon 148; Cassian, *Conference* 6; Saint Benedict, *Rule*, chapter 57; and others. Humbert himself teaches the same explicitly below, Book III, chapter 27.]

## CHAPTER VIII. That one must not only make a vow to the Lord but also fulfill it

But lest someone of little faith say to himself, “If what is vowed is demanded so strictly, I must henceforth beware of making such a vow,” let him hear the Psalmist, speaking in the Holy Spirit, admonish him thus (Ps. LXXV, 12): “Make vows.”

And lest you think that making the vow alone is sufficient, he immediately adds: “And fulfill them.” And as though you were asking to whom the vow should be made and fulfilled, he replies: “To the Lord your God.”

And lest perhaps you think that you or others who offer outward gifts—for example, oil, wax, incense, fasting, and many things of this kind—are exempt, he adds:

> “All who around him offer gifts.”

It is as if he were saying: “I do not condemn your offering outward things to the Lord, but I warn you to offer yourselves also—your soul and body—as a living, holy, pleasing sacrifice to God. Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed in the newness of your mind, so that you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and pleasing and perfect.”

Lest you neglect the vow, he emphasizes to whom you have vowed by saying: “To the Terrible One.” Do you wonder who this Terrible One is? He adds: “To him who takes away the spirit of princes.” Still striving to reveal to mortals the character of one truly ineffable, he concludes:

> “To the Terrible One before all the kings of the earth.”

Therefore, since it is supremely unworthy that we should be ungrateful to our Lord Jesus Christ, who has done and suffered such great things for us and in us, let us vow and fulfill to him everything that we have, live by, and are.

Otherwise, it is better not to make a vow than, after making it, not to fulfill it, since Moses also shows that it is sin if we delay in fulfilling a vow. If it is sin to delay in fulfilling it, how much more is it sin not to fulfill it?

If we vow something to a fellow human being and do not fulfill it, we will perceive him as hostile to us, insofar as he is able, as though we had defrauded him of his own property. But if, after undertaking to fulfill a vow to God, we fail, we turn back to Satan, becoming like a dog returning to its vomit and a washed sow returning to wallowing in the mud (2 Pet. II, 22).

Thus, after it has been sufficiently established by many arguments how greatly fraud must be avoided, let the Simoniacs—around whom almost the whole of this tragedy is woven—come to their senses and, once admonished, recognize what fraud they commit.

If Ananias, marked by fraud, theft, sacrilege, lying, conspiracy, and the temptation of the Spirit of God, was punished by sudden death for merely retaining a little of the price of his small field because he was anxious about the future, let these men, if they are capable of it, estimate how great a theft, sacrilege, lie, conspiracy, and temptation of the Spirit of God burden them, and what punishment they deserve.

They seek to defraud the Holy Spirit of one another and to set him before themselves as both mediator and object of the price, so that, hunting after another’s property and another’s wealth, they may complete their conspiracy—by which they have agreed to tempt the Holy Spirit himself.

Yet because he is not found by those who tempt him, every thought, word, and deed of theirs is undoubtedly regarded by the Holy Spirit as a lie, even if it appears to human beings to display some sign of truth.

## CHAPTER IX. That the Holy Spirit appears to the faithful but remains hidden from the faithless, who do not seek him

[Col. 1071D]

The death of Ananias and Sapphira cries out that a lie against the Holy Spirit acquires condemnation for itself and for its accomplices, but no sanctification for anyone whatsoever.

Moreover, if God appears to those who have faith in him, it is certainly clear that the Holy Spirit does not appear to the Simoniacs, who attack him through faithlessness and lying. For where there is lying, there is faithlessness.

Therefore, the Lord, who appears to the faithful, hides himself from the faithless. He appears to Catholic faith, in which and through which he dwells in our hearts; but to faithless heresy, which he utterly abhors, he is present nowhere and never except as one who is angry and avenging.

Thus it is clear that he is not found by them, since they tempt him by defrauding and lying—by those, that is, who do not have faith in him. Warning against the unbelief of the Jews, the Apostle says:

> “Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him and perished by serpents” (1 Cor. X, 9).

The Psalmist also says of them:

> “They tempted God in their hearts, asking for food for their souls” (Ps. LXXVII, 18),

saying, as the history reports: “Is God among us or not?”

Consider also the saying of Wisdom: “The wicked will seek me and will not find me.” If “in this age” is understood, it must be taken according to what precedes, as though it said: “The wicked will tempt me, but they will not find me favoring them according to their desire.” Otherwise, who has sought the Lord and not found him?

> “For his mercy endures forever” (Ps. CVI, 1),

and:

> “Whoever seeks finds” (Matt. VII, 8).

But if “in the future” is understood, then he will be sought and will not be found, because, while he can now be found, he is not sought. Hence the prophet, admonishing us to seek the Lord truly, says:

> “If you seek, seek” (Isa. XXI, 12).

Whoever falsely seeks God will never find him. The Psalmist says:

> “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. CIV, 4).

Yet because it is altogether true that whoever seeks finds, let us grant that the Simoniacs seek eagerly, though not falsely, and that they undoubtedly find what they seek.

But what do they seek? The Psalm rebukingly declares:

> “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek a lie?” (Ps. IV, 3.)

And what do they find? The father of lies, namely the devil, who, as the Lord attests, did not stand in the truth because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from what is his own, because he is a liar and its father.

Hence the Wise Man also says:

> “The wicked always seeks quarrels” (Prov. XVII, 11).

A cruel angel is sent against him, the author of discord.

If, then, someone finds what he seeks, and if the one who seeks a lie or a quarrel finds the father of lies or the author of discord, what do the Simoniac sellers and buyers seek? Undoubtedly, earthly profit—or, to state it briefly and plainly, money alone.

But what do they find? The temptation and snare of the devil, because, while attacking the grace of God, they wish to become rich.

And whose devil is it? Mammon’s, who presides over earthly profits and money.

And for what purpose do they find him? So that he may be their lord and they his servants, according to the saying: “The lover of money is Mammon’s servant.”

## CHAPTER X. On the difference between the transgressions of those who transgress upon the foundation of Christ and of those who are without his foundation

Although even among Catholics a person who rejects money is considered a rare bird, there is nevertheless a great difference between those who rightly seek it only for necessary use and those who seek it even for excess. The traders under discussion ought not in any respect to liken themselves to our own, who prefer to conduct temporal affairs rather than to make the homeland of God saleable, trusting that nothing will be lacking to those who fear him.

Even if they sometimes go too far in business concerning earthly things, they can certainly appease the Lord quickly through almsgiving and other good works, because they preserve the foundation of Catholic faith intact in their minds. By virtue of that foundation they are saved, though as through fire, even if they have built upon it wood, hay, or straw (1 Cor. III, 12). This is believed concerning all sinners who retain that foundation, provided that in this life they produce fruits worthy of repentance.

But what will the purchased slaves of Mammon do—those who are the leaders and standard-bearers of his insane wickedness, who not only hold their own souls for sale but also strive to sell the Creator and Sanctifier of those souls?

Where will those most deceitful kites flee from the face of the very dove whom they think can be sold, when they have deprived themselves through faith of the foundation that is Christ Jesus, upon whom, as upon a firm rock, he builds his Church?

They cannot be helped by almsgiving or other good works, which, once the foundation itself has been removed, do not exist in them. Rather, whatever produces salvation for others is counted as sin against them.

Nor is this surprising, since in their ecclesiastical offices they seek neither their own salvation nor anyone else’s. Their wicked presumption is proved by the fact that money alone rules them and money alone operates in their actions. Money is requested, sought, knocked upon, proposed, adored, invoked, given, received, held, and possessed.

If it is removed from the midst of them, or if, while it is demanded, it is denied, it is undoubtedly clear that God is neither requested, sought, knocked upon, proposed, adored, invoked, given, received, held, nor possessed.

Conversely, money itself requests; money knocks; the buyer proposes it, adores it, invokes it, gives it; through it he receives, through it he has what he has, and through it he possesses what he possesses.

But what do they give and receive? Outward whitewashing and inward blackness—ruin, condemnation, a curse, sacrilege, lying, and apostasy. They give and receive these things among themselves, and hold and possess them.

Rather, they are possessed by as many demons as there are ways in which, by conducting their wicked business, they deceive and are deceived. In particular, they are possessed by wicked Mammon, whose greatest usurers they are, and to whose service their every intention and action is devoted.

Neither of them—the seller or the buyer—sets God before his eyes. Rather, he puts God himself up for sale to the one to whom he proposes the sum.

Thus, by placing God second, they set before themselves a new god instead of the first and the last, the Ancient of Days, whose kingdom is without end. By abandoning their own Lord, they worship another’s, while the Psalmist contradicts them:

> “Israel, if you will hear me, there shall be no new god among you, nor shall you worship a foreign god” (Ps. LXXX, 10).

But because they did not obey, he adds:

> “And I let them go according to the desires of their hearts” (ibid., 13).

And shortly afterward:

> “The enemies of the Lord lied to him” (ibid., 16).

Of them it is gathered elsewhere:

> “Yet they planned to drive away my price” (Ps. LXI, 5),

that is, to drive my God away from me.

He adds what they reached through this thought:

> “With their mouth they blessed, but with their heart they cursed” (ibid.).

If those who planned to drive God away from the holy man already curse in their hearts, although they bless with their mouths, what do you think those others do who labor not only by thought but also by word and deed to drive the Lord away from themselves and from others?

Whatever the blessing of their mouths may be, it becomes an unspeakable curse before God, who weighs human words and deeds solely according to the intention of the heart. He does not consider what good they say, but what they intend by saying it.

To discern this belongs to God alone, as the Apostle openly proclaims:

> “The word of God is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, penetrating to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. No creature is invisible in his sight; all things are naked and open to his eyes, to whom our word is directed” (Hebr. IV, 12–13).

## CHAPTER XI. That heretics must be avoided, following the example of vipers and the evil tree
But lest anyone think himself exempt from guilt if he neglected to beware of such men, as though he were unable to penetrate their hearts, the Lord himself, in the Gospel, while warning that one must beware of false prophets, immediately added the indication by which they may be recognized, saying: “You will know them by their fruits (Matt. 7:16).” [Col. 1074C] Hence, when the avarice of certain men is plainly seen to rage so fiercely that they do not hesitate to put the Holy Spirit up for sale, it is clear that they are false prophets, because, like the hidden shoot of a profane tree, the taste of its poisonous fruit reveals what sort of tree it is.

Thus, the things that proceed from the mouth come forth from the heart; and therefore, if they are evil in the heart, they cannot be good in the mouth, even if they appear to be so. For these are the things that defile a person. In the mouth of one whose blessing does not sound for God but for money, it is reckoned a copious curse and no blessing at all. Such men, as the Apostle says, “through sweet words and blessings deceive the hearts of the innocent (Rom. 16:18).” Behold what sort of blessings these are—blessings that deceive the innocent! And what does “they deceive” properly mean? They lead them aside. From where, and to where? From God to the devil. For if they led them from the devil to God, they would deceive them beneficially. [Col. 1074D]

Truly, “the evil man brings evil things out of the evil treasure of his heart (Luke 6:45).” For what else can he bring out from it except what he has stored up? Against such men the Lord inveighs, saying: “Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil? Either make [make] the tree bad and its fruit bad (Matt. 12:33–34).”

In these words of Truth they are shown to be worse than bad trees, because bad trees display to human beings in their fruit the same character they possess at their roots; but these men, although evil in their hearts, nevertheless presume to present good things in their mouths, at least in words. [Col. 1075A]

And how appropriately are pagans represented by bad trees, which indeed live but do not perceive: they display in their mouths the unbelief in idolatry that they possess in their hearts. By “broods of vipers,” however—creatures that live and perceive but do not discern—are represented unbelieving and perverse heretics, who retain unbelief in their conduct as well, but sometimes show in their speech that they too perceive something right. Because they do not discern this, they are worse and more harmful both to themselves and to many others than pagans, who perceive nothing of the Christian faith—just as vipers are more harmful than a bad tree, to the extent that poisons differ from a bitter or harmful fruit.

Vipers, moreover, if they are not attacked or injured, attack other animals of their own accord and harm them by nature. A bad tree, however, attacks no one with its fruit, nor does it harm anyone if it is not attacked. [Col. 1075B] Since, then, vipers—said to prefigure heretics—and bad trees—said to prefigure pagans—differ so greatly, who can doubt that pagans are more tolerable to Catholics than heretics?

Pagans, unless you provoke them, do not provoke you; and when provoked, if they prevail, they inflict damage upon external possessions and insults, while they scarcely ever inflict death upon the body. Heretics, on the other hand, under the assumed appearance of Christian understanding, attack you of their own accord even when you remain quiet and silent; and, stubbornly seeking only the death of the soul, they regard the destruction of external possessions and the death of the body as nothing, although, when they prevail, they sometimes inflict these things also upon those who steadfastly resist them. [Col. 1075C]

In this conduct they are altogether like the devil, who, thirsting only for the death of souls, does not care—as Blessed Gregory teaches—to take away earthly things, but to strike charity in us, whose foundation is faith. Pagans, when provoked, resemble beasts in their savagery: beasts that tear the clothing of those who provoke them and sometimes rage against them even to the death of the flesh. Pagans were therefore more tolerable to the good, and heretics more intolerable, in proportion as beasts are found to be inferior in cruelty to demons: the cruelty of beasts is natural, whereas in heretics it is vice.

## CHAPTER XII. That heretics must be avoided more than vipers; and concerning their nature and its typological meaning

[Col. 1075D] Therefore, if we shudder at vipers which, driven by the laws of nature, incur no guilt through their savagery, how much more must heretics be abhorred, who, impelled solely by the breath of demons, irreverently commit whatever vices and crimes exist anywhere?

It is not unfitting to understand them as the Chaldeans who take captives—that is, as something like demons—because, although they are human by nature, by their vice they are demons, since they take captive faithful peoples. They must be guarded against all the more carefully because, being the most wicked of beasts, they harm not only with their teeth but, more grievously, also destroy countless crowds of human beings with their tongue. Other beasts generally attack what is placed before them only with their teeth, horns, or feet; and they are less to be feared in proportion as what they seek is external and as their savagery is more openly displayed. [Col. 1076A]

Concerning these things the Psalmist says: “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, their tongue a sharp sword (Ps. 56:5).” Blessed Job shows how greatly that tongue prevails by enchantment, saying: “He will kill with the tongue of the viper (Job 20:16).”

The nature of the viper is so abhorrent to human beings that, although it is not known to them by any personal experience, it is scarcely heard, when it happens to be recounted, without a disturbance—perhaps “horror”—of mind. For, as the natural philosophers assert, when a female viper is about to conceive, she approaches her mate with open mouth; and he, driven by insane love, inserts his head into her mouth. She, being still more insane, bites it off and swallows it. After this has been accomplished through the death of her mate, she immediately conceives; and when the time of mature birth has arrived, the wretched mother is killed by her offspring as they hasten toward the light, because nature has denied her the common processes of conception and childbirth. [Col. 1076B]

Thus the worst of beasts perish: the male while mating, the female while giving birth. The male perishes by the female, and the female by her offspring, who themselves will not long afterward perish under the law governing their parents.

If this is examined typologically—for “nothing happens on earth without cause (Job 5:6)”—it plainly corresponds to a soul stirred by its evil desires and by the flesh, and thereby desirous of committing fornication away from God, its lawful Spouse. Its mate, like a viper’s mate, comes to it: the devil, who, being first both in rational nature and in apostasy, like an adulterer inserts into the mouth of that desire his head—that is, his suggestion or persuasion. The wretched soul, excessively delighted by it, takes it from him and hides it in its secret places. [Col. 1076C]

From this she immediately conceives and gradually and little by little forms and nourishes within herself the seeds of depravity. When these have matured, because they do not find, through the mind’s excessive application, natural and suitable channels or outlets for their efforts—for neither the nature of the soul nor that of an angel is such that it produces works of vice—they kill their wretched mother, that is, the soul. For when they perceive that her nature obstructs their birth, they become so violent that, having gnawed through her vital organs and ribs—that is, her immortality and strength—they achieve their effect amid the complete destruction of their mother and burst forth.

Thus, “when sin has been completed, it gives birth to death (Jas. 1:15).” And: “The soul that sins, it itself shall die (Ezek. 18:4).” [Col. 1076D] But the soul dies in giving birth, while its seducer—the devil—dies in mating with it, that is, in offering evil persuasion. For the devil’s head is his persuasion; and if it is received, it becomes the seedbed and beginning of every sin.

And lest anyone think that he can suggest evil without dying, let him understand that the devil himself—the spiritual viper—dies as many times as he suggests evil to human beings. Since he was created immortal, although he always lives, he nevertheless always dies: both through his own sin, which he incurred in the beginning, and through the evil suggestion by which he continually desires souls to perish.

He dies, therefore, without interruption, and yet he does not die, since he is never entirely deprived of life itself. Nevertheless, he is relentlessly afflicted by torments that are multiplied and renewed. His life grants him only this: that, although he is always dying, he may never at some point die completely and thus be freed from the punishments that continually increase for him. [Col. 1077A]

For he himself “was a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44).” He first killed the original human being, and afterward as many as he could and can. Certainly, he did not approach the first-created man armed with iron, poison, or any other instrument of death. He sowed an evil word and killed him.

Therefore, let no one who persuades others to evil doubt that he is a murderer. And lest he think that, after killing another, he himself still lives, let him heed the Apostle John saying: “You know that every murderer does not have abiding life in himself (1 John 3:15).” And lest we evade the matter or twist his judgment at will, he prefaced this by saying: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer (ibid.).” [Col. 1077B] But Christ says: “You are all brothers (Matt. 23:8).” Without doubt, the one who knowingly suggests evil to them hates them.

Thus he is held guilty of a murder all the greater, the more closely he imitates the first murderer, the devil, in this respect, and the more important the soul is than the body. Yet the same Apostle omitted no kind of murder when he said: “You know that every murderer, and so forth (1 John 3:15).”

## CHAPTER XIII. How vipers correspond to the Simoniacs

What we have typologically referred concerning the nature of vipers to the devil can indeed be referred to all his members, but it more particularly corresponds to the leading ones, namely heretics, as though they were his secondary members. [Col. 1077C] For just as no spirits intervene between God and the seraphim, so no human beings intervene between the devil and heretics.

But since we are not equal even to naming so many monsters, let us see how these things correspond specifically to the Simoniacs, with whom the present discussion is concerned.

Any person professing Christianity, if he is seized by an unhealthy movement of his soul’s natural faculty—that is, of the naturally and commendably concupiscible, or appetitive, faculty—by ambition for honor, is first deprived of the love of God. Then, having become ambitious, he no longer waits for the Lord to glorify him as one who glorifies the Lord. Therefore, unable to endure repose or delay, he eagerly and indiscriminately searches for someone equal to his desire. [Col. 1077D]

When he happens to find such a person, he breathes into him, with open mouth, the vast flame of his breast, revealing by anxious disclosure what he has hitherto kept stored in his heart and with his heart. “For where your treasure is, there your heart is also (Matt. 6:21).”

Thus that wretched man, like another adulterer after the devil, sees the money and, as though another person’s avarice—once hidden but now revealed to him—were before him, madly in love with money, surrenders his own head to it. [Col. 1078A] There, forgetful of the enemy of his life and of eternal death, he plunges his faith—or the reason that he had received from the Lord as his principal member—into the other man’s unbelief and irrationality, in an act both faithless and irrational.

But once deprived of his head in this way, he dies; yet the remaining viper does not possess the head of its mate for its own benefit or anyone else’s, except for destruction alone. For the ambitious person does indeed destroy his accomplice by offering him the desired money and taking away his faith, his principal possession; yet he does not possess the faith that has been taken away, either for himself or for anyone else, but only the unbelief that, drunk with the devil’s poison, he has swallowed as the seedbed of his own destruction and that of others.

For faith cannot become unbelief; rather, as soon as unbelief approaches, faith departs, as though it had no communion with it. And just as the viper’s mate, when he offers his head to be severed, is no longer a head either for himself or for his monstrous spouse, but becomes death to him and a seedbed of death to her, so these abominable Simoniacs, when they bring spiritual grace forward for sale and purchase, are abandoned by grace in the seller; yet grace does not enter the buyer. Instead, the wrath of God horribly overtakes both. [Col. 1078B]

Thus they kill one another with their tongues, like vipers, because one by demanding and the other by offering grace for sale, they perish after becoming heretics. Since they are poisoned, only poisoned offspring are born from them, as a certain Sage testifies:

> Children of abominations become children of sinners,  
> and those who dwell beside the houses of the impious.  
> The inheritance of sinners’ children will perish,  
> and continual disgrace will accompany their offspring.  
> Children are sought from an impious father,  
> because through him they are held in disgrace.  
> Woe to you, impious men, who have abandoned the law of the Most High Lord;  
> and if you are born, you will be born under a curse,  
> and if you die, your portion will be under a curse.  
> All things that are from the earth will return to the earth;  
> so the impious pass from curse into destruction (Eccli. 41:8, 13).

And elsewhere: [Col. 1078C]

> The children of adulterers will reach their end,  
> and offspring from an unlawful bed will be exterminated.  
> Even if they live long, they will be counted as nothing,  
> and their final old age will be without honor.  
> And if they die sooner, they will have no hope,  
> nor a response on the day of recognition.  
> For the end of an unrighteous nation is dreadful (Wis. 3:16, 19).

The Lord also, through the prophet, rejecting a false priesthood, says: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not serve as priest for me (Hos. 4:6).”

The knowledge of God is, for example, to give freely the grace of God that one has received freely. For he himself knows what he says, as it is written in Deuteronomy. Because the Simoniacs reject this knowledge and refuse to grant it access to themselves, they say to the Lord God by their deeds, even if not by their words: “Depart from us; we do not want to know your ways (Job 21:14).” [Col. 1078D]

Therefore, rightly rejected by God, so that they may not serve him as priests, whatever priestly office they presume to exercise in outward appearance, they exercise only for themselves and not for God or his people—unless, indeed, they exercise it for God because they exercise it for his people.

“Their bread is turned in their bellies into the gall of asps within (Job 20:14),” because they turn the drink of life into a cup of poison for themselves and die from what they appear to be nourished for life by. Having fallen into the error of heresy, they suffer this fate: just as from the gall of asps, so these wretched men die from their own bread. [Col. 1079A]

They find death in their sacrifice, because in the sacraments of life—or in the words of life—they seek life not at all. And it must be noted that such bread is now called not the bread of God but “his bread,” that is, the heretic’s bread, in the book of blessed Job (Job 20:14).

## CHAPTER XIV. That the subverters of Christ’s sacraments and words are of one kind, and that they neither ask of him nor obtain from him

Following the sense of blessed Gregory in this verse, where he referred the words of Scripture to heretics who pervert sacred utterances, we have not inappropriately transferred them to those who pervert the altar’s sacraments, because the word of God and the bread of God are likewise of equal—indeed, identical—dignity and coeternity. [Col. 1079B]

For, according to Isaiah, the word of our God “will stand forever (Isa. 40:8)”; and in the Gospel the Word, coeternal with God the Father, says: “My words will not pass away (Mark 13:31).” Blessed Peter likewise says to him: “You have the words of eternal life (John 6:69).”

In the same way, the bread of God—as the Word himself teaches in the Gospel, indeed, as the bread that came down from heaven—gives life to the world: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever (ibid., 51–52).”

From this, then, the equality and coeternity of the Word of God and his bread become evident, because just as the former grants eternal life through the holy Scriptures, so the latter grants it through the sacraments. Nor is this surprising, since our one and the same Lord Jesus Christ is both the Word of God in the holy Scriptures and the bread of God in the sacraments. [Col. 1079C]

It follows, therefore, that we must avoid the overturners of the divine utterances with an equal abhorrence to that with which we avoid the overturners of the heavenly sacraments.

Even if such men ask the heavenly Father, as it is supposed, for bread, they are nevertheless given a stone; if for a fish, a serpent; if for an egg, a scorpion (Matt. 7:9–10). For, as the Psalmist prophetically invokes, the Lord gives them according to their works; and according to the wickedness of their devices, according to the works of their hands he repays them; he gives them their recompense. “Because they have not understood the works of the Lord, and in the works of their hands you will destroy them and will not build them up (Ps. 27:4–5).” [Col. 1079D]

Nor is this surprising. They do not ask the heavenly Father for what is heavenly, and therefore obtain nothing heavenly from him. Rather, by the just permission and judgment of God the Father himself, they receive from the devil—or evil sons from their worst father—in place of the bread of charity or the sacrament, a stone of hardness; in place of the fish, a serpent of unbelief; and in place of the egg, a scorpion of despair.

For this evil father can bestow no heavenly benefit upon his children, since earthly fathers, even when evil, refuse to give their children anything except good gifts, insofar as this present age is concerned, when they ask them: if he asks for bread, he gives bread; if for a fish, a fish; if for an egg, an egg.

In this matter it is clear that those to whom harmful things are given asked for harmful things themselves. They asked nothing from the Father of lights, from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes (Jas. 1:17), nor did they ask in the name of Jesus. [Col. 1080A] Otherwise Christ himself would be contradicted when he promises: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you (John 16:23).” And: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you (John 14:13).”

It is therefore clear that these heretics are given what they ask from the one whom they ask. And whom do they ask? Their father and lord, Mammon. And what do they ask for? Bread. What bread? Certainly, the bread that usually tastes sweet to them, as Solomon says: “The bread of lying is sweet to a man (Prov. 20:17).” And lest anyone doubt that this is a stone, he added: “Afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel (ibid.).”

Do you see here that, in place of the bread of charity, a stone of hardness is given, through whose evil merit unbelief is given to those asking for faith, like a serpent in place of a fish? For where the bread of lying is eaten and the wine of iniquity is drunk, there is no doubt that unbelief alone holds dominion. [Col. 1080B]

Thus, when they have been possessed by so poisonous a serpent, if they ask for the egg of hope, they deserve the scorpion of utter despair. In them is fulfilled what the Sage says: “When the impious comes into the depths of evils, he despises (Prov. 18:3).”

These three principal evils, opposed to the three aforementioned principal virtues of the soul, proceed from avarice alone. Concerning its most evil offspring, someone composed this couplet:

> The miser is always needy; for nothing is more wicked than he;  
> the miser always loves lies, thefts, and robberies.

He incurs such want and misery because, asking faithlessly for bread, he deserved a stone. Thus, having lost the heart of flesh in which the spirit of piety and mercy might rest, he finds a stony heart, insensibly hardened against every work of charity and humanity. [Col. 1080C]

The Lord neither gives this heart to a person nor makes it; rather, by justly abandoning him, he permits it to be made. When the person has submitted himself to voluntary hardness, the Lord does not soften him by his inspiration but leaves him hardened—and still further hardened—by spiritual wickedness.

If it were truly requested, the spirit of charity would be graciously bestowed, and through its warmth the coldness of avarice would be dissolved. For if, as the Lord says, fathers, “although evil, know how to give good gifts to their children, how much more will the Father from heaven give the good Spirit to those who ask him! (Luke 11:13),” this makes it understood that, if evil fathers are generous in response to the requests and wishes of their children, the supremely good Father is much more, and incomparably more, generous toward children who ask him—just as good and evil are incomparable. [Col. 1080D]

It is therefore clear that no heretics, and especially no Simoniacs, receive the good Spirit because they do not ask the heavenly Father for the good Spirit. And what do they ask, and from whom? A wicked spirit, from their wicked father, the author and inventor of every evil.

But an objection is raised: Do such people not appear to invoke the heavenly Father and to ask for the good Spirit for themselves or for others? To them the apostolic response is given: “How will they invoke one in whom they have not believed? (Rom. 10:14).” And lest it be said that they truly and catholicly believe in God, the text continues: “How will they believe him whom they have not heard? (ibid.).”

Setting aside the daily excesses of human frailty and sudden desire, how do they believe him when, after long deliberation and planning, they have fallen into the crime of this heresy and persist in it, while they do not heed him who says: “You have received freely; give freely”? [Col. 1081A]

It is therefore clear that they do not believe in him. They do not heed the one who, in his sacraments, decrees and establishes inviolable and perpetual privileges.

## CHAPTER XV. How certain people do not heed the Lord in some respects but heed him in others

But lest anyone suppose that this gives him an occasion to turn a charge of slander against us, asserting that we too do not believe in God because we often fail to heed him when he forbids sins and crimes and invites us to virtue, let him know that just as there is a very great diversity among the divine commandments, so there is a very great diversity among those who observe them. [Col. 1081B]

There are some divine commandments which, if someone transgresses them piously, he obtains not only no guilt but even a great reward.
