Such was that glorious transgressor Paul, who, although he had received from the Lord—as had his fellow Apostles—the command that one who proclaims the Gospel should live by the Gospel (1 Cor. 9:14), made use of none of this but lived by the labor of his own hands, so as not to give any occasion for the Gospel of Christ (Acts 20:34).

There are also certain commandments from which one deviates significantly if they are observed continuously and never interrupted according to circumstances—for example, the instructions concerning not taking or taking a purse, a bag, or other provisions, according to whether the time is one of peace or persecution. For the one who had first said, “Do not carry a purse or a bag (Luke 10:4),” later says the same: “Now let the one who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag (Luke 22:36).” [Col. 1081C]

When such commandments of the Lord are interrupted with discernment, the one who interrupts them in this way is undoubtedly blessed. There are also other commandments whose excessive subtlety troubles even the perfect, such as “You shall not covet (Exod. 20:17),” and the severe prohibition not only of insulting but even of idle words (Matt. 12:36). When they transgress these, their faith is not wounded, but the holiness of their conduct is impaired. Nevertheless, by not following their covetous desires and by severely judging themselves also on account of their words, they may recover and improve themselves, especially when in heart, mouth, and deed they daily say to their Father God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors (Matt. 6:12).” [Col. 1081D]

There are still other commandments which, although they invite the less perfect to perfection, nevertheless weigh upon their free choice with an obligation, such as: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have (Matt. 19:21).” And: “Let the one who can grasp it grasp it (ibid., 12).”

These four kinds of divine commandments apply to the spiritual and genuinely Catholic. Although they do not heed every commandment of God in such a way as to carry it out, their sound faith is nevertheless illuminated by their right works.

A fifth kind remains. It instructs the faithful who are nevertheless carnal and inexperienced, and restrains them from shameful acts and crimes. Such are the Decalogue and other commandments of this sort, for example: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart (Deut. 6:5)”; and: “Honor your father and mother; you shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery (Deut. 5:16–18).” [Col. 1082A]

If such people turn away from evil but do not do good, they are indeed faithful, but their faith is idle. If, however, they do not turn away from evil but moreover destroy themselves through criminal sins, then their faith is counted as a dead tree, though not uprooted from the root. It nevertheless lives in some fashion through the hope by which they hope for forgiveness, through God from whom they hope for that forgiveness, and through the small amount by which they love their neighbor.

Finally, as the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for (Heb. 11:1).” It is therefore evident that faith is the substance of hope. And where there is hope, there is also love, because one must love the good things that one hopes for.

Accordingly, the statement of blessed Gregory is established: “Each person hopes and loves in proportion to how much he believes.” [Col. 1082B]

Hope is properly said to concern good things so exclusively that grammarians regard it as a fault—called in Greek *acyrologia*, and in Latin an improper expression—whenever it is found used otherwise, as in the poet’s line:

> Hence, if I was able to hope for so great a pain.

Accordingly, they explain it thus: he said “to hope” instead of “to fear.” Preserving the proper meaning of the word, another poet says:

> May the one who fears be permitted to hope.

Therefore, although faith concerns both good and evil things, hope concerns only good things. For we believe both the good things that God promises and the evils that he threatens; nevertheless, we hope only for the good things, while we fear only the evil. [Col. 1082C]

Thus, although blessed James says: “You believe that God is one; you do well. The demons also believe, and they tremble (Jas. 2:19),” the belief of wicked human beings nevertheless differs from that of demons in this respect: wicked human beings believe and hope, whereas demons believe but do not hope; rather, they despair, and therefore tremble. But if perverse human beings believe yet do not hope, they differ in no respect from the belief of demons.

It must be understood, however, that just as it is evil for human beings to sin through despair, so it is evil to hope excessively: to postpone repentance from day to day, to add sins to sins, and to weave from them, as it were, a long rope by which they may at the end be bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness. [Col. 1082D]

As long as such people neither despair nor defend their sins, we do not by a final judgment condemn them from the paradise of the Catholic Church, although at times we remove them from our communion for a while as a remedy. It is therefore clear that they are still counted among the faithful. Although criminal, they are not properly called impious, because “the impious”—that is, the unbeliever—“when he comes into the depths of evils, despises (Prov. 15:3).”

Thus these people too have not heeded the Lord when he forbids crimes, yet they believe him, as has been clearly shown above. The same must be said of those who sometimes fall in like manner from the highest summit of virtue to the depths of vice.

## CHAPTER XVI. Where it is shown that heretics, unlike criminals, do not heed God within the Church

[Col. 1083A]

Lest the aforementioned heretics attack us with these weapons of ours as though we were unwary, asserting that they too believe in God, after the example of those whom we have recalled, although they do not heed him when he commands, “You have received freely; give freely,” let them know that our case is fundamentally different from theirs.

Our people sometimes appear not to heed certain commandments of Christ because they pass beyond them eagerly for the sake of their highest perfection; or because, terrified by weakness of mind, they do not approach them; or because, occasionally led on by human frailty, they pass them by carelessly; or because, overcome by diabolical temptation, they fall into them and then return from them. [Col. 1083B]

The first of these are not only to be praised and imitated but also to be called blessed. The middle group is to be praised but also pitied. The last group is likewise to be pitied and corrected; yet, according to the time and the circumstances, if they allow themselves to be admonished and corrected, they must be patiently tolerated and awaited.

Although by the perpetration of an evil deed they have apostatized from God, they are nevertheless still with him and stand for him through the profession of faith that they retain in heart and mouth. For they depart from God by their deeds, though not by faith, while they believe and say that he is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works (Ps. 145:15), even when they neglect to establish that faith itself by their deeds.

To believing, they heed Christ the Lord when he says: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent (John 6:29)”; and: “You believe in God; believe also in me (John 14:1).” [Col. 1083C] But they do not heed him when he commands them to act: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you (Matt. 5:44)”; and: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth (Matt. 6:19),” along with very many commandments like these.

Of those who live—or are green—with respect to faith, but die—or become dry—with respect to conduct, the prophetic saying is appropriately spoken: “One part was drenched, and the part upon which it did not rain dried up (Amos 4:7).”

They are therefore green with the sap of the faith that they received by hearing it for belief and retain; and they are dry through neglect of the good work that they heard but do not retain for action. [Col. 1083D]

With respect to faith, the Lord’s statement by which he rebuked the unbelieving Jews does not fully apply to them: “If I speak the truth, why do you not believe me? Whoever is from God hears the words of God. Therefore you do not hear, because you are not from God (John 8:46).”

For all carnal people within the Church believe that Christ speaks the truth, and they hear his words, even if they do not hear them for their own advancement. Hence they are from God insofar as they hear the words of God, and they are not from God insofar as they do not heed them.

Heretics, however, hear neither God nor his words in either respect. Whether they have not lost faith or have lost it, they not only do no good, but even if they appear to do something, it is all sin, since it is without faith. Otherwise, if they are not without the Catholic faith, which alone is faith, they are not heretics. [Col. 1084A]

But, for the present, setting aside other cases, the Simoniacs have been called and regarded as heretics from the very beginnings of Christianity. Therefore they are without faith. If they are without faith, they can have no hope, because faith is the substance of hope. If they have no hope, neither do they have charity, because one cannot love what one neither hopes for nor believes in, as was sufficiently established a little earlier.

From this it may be inferred that heretics and pagans are inferior to demons in unbelief, because demons believe that there is one God and tremble, whereas heretics and pagans do not possess even this small degree of belief.

Yet in this respect they are superior to demons: pagans can be saved through baptism, and heretics perhaps through repentance.

Nevertheless, if the definition of faith is carefully considered, faith—or belief—is not properly said to exist in demons, but only abusively. For if faith, as the Apostle defines it, “is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen (Heb. 11:1),” it is clear that demons neither have faith nor believe in the God whom, created by him in evangelical dignity, they knew before their fall and were accustomed to contemplate face to face. [Col. 1084B]

Accordingly, they do not believe that God exists; they cannot say what the fool said in his heart: “There is no God,” because, from having seen him previously, they know that he exists. For what does one hope for that one sees?

It is therefore clear that demons do not have faith. Otherwise, if they truly had faith, they would not lack hope and charity; and consequently they would no longer be demons.

Therefore the devil’s hope, of which the Lord says to blessed Job, “His hope will fail him (Job 40:28),” is not true hope but a certain security by which he or his followers vainly flatter themselves concerning the mercy of God, while they do not fear the strictness of his justice. [Col. 1084C]

They would certainly fear it if their hope arose from faith, because faith believes in God both insofar as he is to be feared and insofar as he is to be loved. Thus faith, retaining fear within itself, shares with hope the love of the most righteous Judge and the most merciful Father, so that it hopes only by loving what faith also believes ought to be loved.

Thus neither the devil nor the impious possess faith and hope, although they are abusively said to possess them, just as blessed Gregory asserts that unbelievers have faith when they believe that they were born from those whom they call their parents, although they did not see their conception or birth, along with many similar matters of human life and conduct. [Col. 1084D]

Concerning these matters that most learned Father himself says: “Unbelievers have faith—but would that it were in God!”

## CHAPTER XVII. The difference between worldly merchants and those who are called Simoniacs
But, these points having been prefixed—not altogether without purpose—let us investigate how ecclesiastics, who do not give freely what ought to be given freely in ecclesiastical sacraments, are said to lose faith altogether, and more than any Christian, cleric or layman, even if the latter, for the sake of earthly gain, defraud their brothers in business (I Thess. 4:6), or sell too dearly what they bought cheaply, or indeed received for free. First, let us consider what intention or motive is continually common to traders of both kinds, and then what is peculiar to each.

To put it briefly, this intention appears common to both in their business: each seeks to become temporally rich through temporal goods. Hence both are alike, although unequally according to the difference of their offices, struck by the Wise Man’s saying: “He who seeks to become rich will not be innocent” (Prov. 28:20). For, according to their common intention, both incur a common loss of innocence, although, because of the difference in their orders, one does so more and the other less.

It is also common to both, for the sake of business, to offer goods for sale, set their price, sell them, and desire a buyer. If nothing else intervened in these actions, there would be either no fault or very little. For it cannot be counted as a fault if, because of common necessity, goods are offered for sale, priced, sold, and bought, since what is lawfully bought is not unlawfully sold. Defrauding a brother is also at times common to them: whenever one of them conducts business, he both defrauds and is defrauded; the other does so sometimes, but not always. Although the Lord is avenging toward both in this deception, he is not more severe toward one than the other, according to the character of the deception and its cause.

Likewise, selling cheaply what was acquired dearly is sometimes common to both. One of them, whenever he sells something he had acquired at a high price, disposes of it cheaply; the other does so sometimes, but not habitually. Yet the former, by always selling cheaply what is expensive, sins outrageously; the latter, however, by doing so, prepares for himself good merit and grace with God and with human beings.

We have now stated what is common to both; let us also state what is peculiar to each. For bishops and the rest of the clergy, whose office it is to administer the divine sacraments, the distinctive and singular duty is to offer or display only a heavenly commodity; for laymen and the other practitioners of secular business, only an earthly and secular one. It is also the duty of the former always to offer, price, and sell what is not theirs, against the wishes of its owner; the latter, what is theirs alone, with no one objecting. Similarly, the former always sell cheaply what is not theirs; the latter scarcely ever dispose of their own cheaply.

Nevertheless, it belongs to the former to give away what they received freely, but not freely; to the latter, to give away what they did not receive freely, but not freely. For if the matter is carefully considered, no person ever obtains anything beneficial from another person freely. Either he receives what he receives for service, or for human favor or goodwill, or in recompense for a service rendered by hand. And if he receives from another person for God alone, he receives it even less freely, because that person himself received from God in order to be able to give to another, and by giving stores up merit with God, who alone is truly God and Lord because, according to the Psalmist, he has no need of our goods (Ps. 15:2).

From this complete and solitary fullness, the distinguished Prosper, following the understanding of the most learned Father Augustine, explains the matter first in prose and then in verse:

> God commands nothing that benefits himself, but him to whom he gives the command. Therefore he is truly Lord who does not need the servant, and by whom the servant is in need.

## EPIGRAM: Its source and origin, above

God does not command anything for his own benefit,

Nor does the true Lord need the service of a servant.

He who serves is increased by his commands,

And whoever neglects the command becomes less.

For God almighty, holding all power at once,

Loses nothing of his own and acquires nothing perishable.

He has never lacked what he possesses, giving whatever

Will benefit the recipient, and taking only what he has given.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How the carnal members of the Church are not without faith, after the manner of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh

[Col. 1086B] But, to return to the traders under discussion, it belongs to the former to believe and possess God himself, the Lord, namely the Holy Spirit, as a commodity for sale; whereas the latter, if they reach the depths of avarice’s wickedness, possess their own souls as commodities for sale, yet do not believe that they can sell or give them to any human being.

Let us therefore retrace with a lively mind the common and particular lines of these traders that we have noted above, distinguishing them one by one, so that we may see which of them sins more, or which approaches more closely to the Scylla or Charybdis of faithlessness. First, let us consider the points on which practitioners of secular business commonly offend.

Clearly, they offend in seeking to become rich through temporal means. But who is found to be pious and not desirous of becoming rich beyond what is just? Certainly, such a bird is exceedingly rare. They also offend in this: out of zeal for profit they defraud their brothers in business, selling cheap goods to them at a higher price, or taking expensive goods away from them cheaply.

For some of them there remains that highest summit of avarice at which they also possess their souls as commodities for sale: by pursuing various crimes and sins for the sake of gain, they kill their souls. Although their souls die through these acts, faith is not wholly torn away from them. For they do not attack or reject sound faith; rather, even though it is dead in their hearts, they strive to defend it with heart and mouth.

They are aptly signified by the sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh. Armed, they cross the Jordan before their brothers, acquire the promised land for them by the power of their arm and by the sword, and subject it to them. Yet they seek no other lot for themselves, but return to dwell in their own land, which they had left behind beyond the Jordan.

Nevertheless, they build an altar for themselves over the Jordan itself as a testimony that the Lord himself is God, lest afterward the sons of the other tribes should say to their sons: “You have no share in the Lord, because the Jordan has been placed between us and you” (Josh. 22:25–27).

So too, all those who are secular and yet faithful within the holy Church, whenever, while Catholics preserve baptism in faith and works, a contest over the faith is imposed by heretics or pagans, immediately run to their brothers to fight for the faith, armed with the judgments of the holy Fathers and sometimes supported by secular power. They do not leave before, having strongly defeated the enemy, they obtain for their brothers the desired peace.

But they quickly return to their own land beyond the Jordan. Although for a time they support Catholics through their zeal for the Catholic faith—which they profess—after crossing the Jordan, that is, after receiving the sacrament of baptism, they transgress the faith of baptism with regard to their works, and pass it by in peace, though they bravely defend it in war. Seeking only things that pass away and are transitory, they do not care that any other inheritance be provided for them with their brothers except the profession and defense of the same faith.

They confirm this as though by the testimony of an altar established by them beside the Jordan in the promised land. Whenever Catholic and spiritual men rebuke and detest their carnal manner of life so severely as to deny them a share in God, they return to the confession of the Catholic faith that they and their fathers professed and built above the font of holy baptism, like an altar above the Jordan, in order to claim for themselves fellowship with the saints. By this means they claim a share in God: they faithfully retain the creed in heart and mouth and, whenever called upon, energetically defend it according to their strength.

Thus the altar that had previously been thought and called sacrilegious, as though it had been built for holocausts and sacrifices contrary to the divine commands, is afterward approved for a reasonable cause and called a testimony of faith and Christian fellowship [Col. 1087C] between the carnal and the spiritual: that the Lord of the spiritual, who is Lord through faith and works, is also, through faith, the God of the carnal.

For the examination of this matter Phinehas is not without reason sent as an envoy. The Lord established for him the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because it is the priest’s duty to investigate carefully lest anyone, having abandoned God and his one faith—as though he had despised the one altar—presume upon an unlawful priesthood for himself, choose another altar for sacrifices to his faithlessness, and establish the worship of demons.

This is indeed what they do: they stray from the faith and usurp the outward form of ecclesiastical sacraments, just as, many years later, the children of Israel, having abandoned the Lord through the impious Jeroboam, established altars with golden calves and priests for demons against the Lord’s altar and priesthood.

But this will be discussed more fully elsewhere. For now, let this one point be observed: as long as the children of Israel presumed to have an altar besides the one altar and another priesthood, they maintained peace among themselves under the worship—that is, the faith—of the one God. But as soon as they presumed to do so, they immediately attacked one another in continual war. Judah could not reconcile with Israel, nor did it dare to establish friendship, while the Lord opposed it and rebuked King Jehoshaphat for this attempt in these words: “You join yourself in friendship with those who hate the Lord, and you offer help to the impious; therefore you deserved the wrath of the Lord, and so forth” (2 Chron. 19:2).

Moreover, it is shown without doubt from the *Moralia* of blessed Gregory how many and what kinds of people live badly within the Church and are rightly called faithful. For he says in Book XXXIII:

> Behemoth devours some who are placed under the name of Christianity, because he causes them to stumble through an error of faith itself. He does not avoid others who are upright in faith, but inclines them to the practice of wickedness. He does not wish to bend others, as much as he wishes, into the practice of impurity; but inwardly he twists them within themselves in the zeal of their intention, so that, while they divide their minds from charity, whatever they do outwardly is not right.
>
> They therefore hold faith, but do not hold the life of faith, because they either openly do unlawful things, or the things they do are perverse because of their perverse heart, even if they appear holy. For some are faithful by confession, but not by their manner of life. Hence the Voice of Truth says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21). Again he says: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46).
>
> And shortly afterward: “Let no one trust that faith can suffice without works, since we know what is written: ‘Faith without works is idle’” (Jas. 2:20, 26). Let no one think that he has wholly escaped Behemoth’s bite through the confession of faith alone, because he has indeed swallowed the river, but still thirsts for the Jordan; and the Jordan flows in his mouth as often as any Christian falls into iniquity.
>
> We have indeed already been in his mouth, faith lifting us up; but we must take great care lest we slip through this slippery conduct. If caution in walking is neglected, it is useless to hold the right path by believing, because the life of faith benefits us for the heavenly homeland but does not lead those who offend there.

## CHAPTER XIX. How the Simoniacs are invaded by Satan after the example of Judas, who undertook the betrayal of the Lord

After it has been shown, on the occasion of secular traders and by abundant and evident authority, how far our carnal people—even with their dead faith—are separated from heretics, for whom not even dead faith remains but none at all, as though it had been torn up by the roots and emptied out, we must now show in order the points on which the sellers of ecclesiastical ministry offend.

They offend, plainly, when they too seek to become rich through temporal means. But they offend all the more than other traders by how much eternal heavenly things are more valuable than temporal earthly things—or, to put it more briefly and clearly, by how much the God who created all things is preferred to the most worthless creatures.

Whenever they seek to become rich by trading in his sacraments, they undoubtedly prepare, like another Judas, to betray God himself, who is essentially present and cooperates in those very sacraments, to the faithless. Therefore those whom the same intention makes equal to the wicked and cruel Judas must be bound by the same fault and enveloped in an equal condemnation.

Certainly the devil, who stands at Judas’s right hand, entered the heart of that thief—not an ordinary thief, but a sacrilegious one—to seduce him, merely because he was contemplating the betrayal, as the Gospel of John testifies: “And supper being ended, when the devil had already put into the heart of Judas Simon Iscariot that he should betray him” (John 13:2), and so forth.

Luke shows most plainly what the wretched Judas gained from this entry of the devil:

> Satan entered into Judas, who was surnamed Iscariot, one of the twelve. And he went and spoke with the chief priests and magistrates about how he might betray him to them. And they rejoiced, and agreed to give him money. And he promised. And he sought an opportunity to betray him without the crowds (Luke 22:3–6).

In these most truthful words of the truthful evangelists it is openly suggested how great a guilt the worst traitor incurred from conceiving that betrayal. Although long before the betrayal itself he had been a sacrilegious thief, when he secretly carried away from the purse the Lord’s money—which he carried in his ministry and which was intended to benefit the poor, he is nevertheless not said to have had the devil enter into him until the devil was sent into his heart so that he might betray the Master. If he deserved such a inhabitant merely through the desire to betray, what do we suppose he deserved through the deed itself?

Finally, it must be understood that, just as goodness has its stages, by which it gradually advances as it ascends, so wickedness has its own, by which it continually declines as it descends into worse things. This is not surprising, since the suggestion of good is the seed of God, while the suggestion of evil is likewise the seed of the devil.

And just as the seed of God, cast upon good soil according to the parable of the evangelical farmer, first sends forth the shoot, then produces the blade, then the ear, and afterward the full grain in the ear—which is immediately cut down with the sickle and separated from the chaff and stored in the heavenly granary (Matt. 13; Mark 4; Luke 8)—so the seed of the devil strives to grow in bad soil through its stages of increase, in order soon to reach its own place, namely everlasting fire. For no one suddenly becomes utterly evil, just as no one suddenly becomes perfect in goodness.

Thus the seed of the devil’s darnel, cast into the heart of the wicked Judas, first secretly germinated as the plan of betrayal. Then it openly burst forth as the blade of a deadly plot, when, by departing and speaking to the Jews, he communicated through his words, like luxuriant leaves providing shade for his wickedness, with another evil seed in order to kill the principal and unique grain of wheat.

When they rejoiced over this and bargained with him for money, and he promised them what they requested, he put forth something like an ear, which continued to grow while he sought an opportunity to hand him over (Matt. 26:15–16). He displayed the full darnel when he completed the betrayal with the sign of a kiss (ibid., 49). At last the sickle came upon him when he hanged himself and burst apart in the middle, and from there went to be placed in his own place (Acts 1:18).

The Simoniacs, who became his closer followers, descend through no lesser avarice to the point of attempting to betray the Holy Spirit. With this entry of the devil, he violently enters their hearts after breaking through the doors of faith—namely, fear and love. Until then he had stood outside them, tripping them up when they were enticed by other evils of avarice, but he had not removed whatever faith in God they possessed from their hearts.

But as soon as they think it permissible to think wickedly about God and to attempt wicked things, they do not fear even in secret and lose faith altogether. Thus, when Christ departs—Christ who had previously dwelt in their hearts through faith—the devil, the guest of faithlessness, takes his place and invades them.

Then, having conceived the secret pus of such great wickedness, they carefully seek those into whom they may pour it. When they have found them, they whisper such words to them: “What do you wish to give us, and we will hand over the Holy Spirit to you?” Was this not the voice that belonged to Judas, and that for only one day? Yet in these men it is almost continuous and daily.

Would that these kites, according to Isaiah, gathered one to another in their Babylon, whispered this unspeakable voice softly and quietly to one another, rather than shouting it insolently and loudly! But what is worse, the practice of this commerce has grown to such an extent that now, as though by authority and rule, the Holy Spirit in his sacraments is openly offered for sale to everyone, openly priced, his price openly demanded, openly—so it is believed—sold, and openly bought.

In this matter they are more criminal than the most criminal Judas, who attempted a betrayal that no one ought to attempt, whether openly or secretly. If, among his other offenses, he grievously offended the Lord God even by leaving him—who is beyond estimation—to be valued at the discretion of the Jews, and by treating the incomparable One as so little worth that he handed him over to the profane for a number of denarii, where will these men go from the Spirit of God and from his presence? Where will those flee who now, according to their own judgment or that of others, customarily put a price on the Holy Spirit, and make so little of him that—shameful and painful to say—they do not hesitate to sell him not only for a small sum of money but for a dog, a pig, a hawk, and other things of any kind, even for such little gifts?

It is a guilt beyond estimation to wish to dispose of the Creator of heaven and earth in exchange for any merchandise, however great or valuable. Therefore, as was said above, they perpetrate an intolerable crime whenever they attempt to sell cheaply what is precious and dear above all things.

For what is dearer and more precious than God? The Wise Man commends his incomparable excellence under the name of wisdom, saying:

> I considered nothing to be of value in comparison with her; nor did I compare any precious stone with her, because all gold, in comparison with her, is a little sand, and silver in her sight will be reckoned as clay, because her light is unquenchable. For she is an infinite treasure to human beings (Wis. 7:8–14).

And shortly afterward:

> For in her is a spirit of understanding, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, mobile, eloquent, undefiled, and so forth (ibid., 22).

Blessed Job likewise says of her:

> Human beings do not know her price. Gold of Ophir will not be given for her, nor will silver be weighed in exchange for her. She cannot be compared with dyed colors, nor with the most precious sardonyx or sapphire. Gold is not equal to her, nor glass, nor shall vessels of gold be exchanged for her. High and eminent things will not be remembered in comparison with her. But wisdom is drawn from hidden places. The topaz of Ethiopia is not equal to her, nor can the purest dye be compared with her (Job 28:13–19).

Shortly afterward, briefly explaining what wisdom is, he says to humanity on God’s behalf:

> Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom itself, and to depart from evil is understanding (Job 28:28).

Hence blessed Jerome, in his exposition of Zechariah, says:

> The Savior, seeing his price—that is, the price of his majesty—in the thirty pieces of silver, and seeing himself betrayed for so cheap a payment, says ironically: “A noble price at which I was valued by them” (Zech. 11:13).

This must be read with the irony of one saying:

> “This is how much my people, and the poor of the flock who were once mine and chosen by me as sons, judged that I should be bought and sold!”

## CHAPTER XX. How many curses the Simoniacs share with Judas, and how they sell the whole Church

Just so, these heretics, seeking through the ambition of their unspeakable commerce to break the bonds of Christian law and cast off from themselves the yoke of apostolic discipline, are mocked and derided by him who dwells in heaven (Ps. 2:3–4). When they impudently trade, they find nothing in their hands from God (Ps. 75:6) except what Judas and the Jews found in theirs: perpetual curse and condemnation.

For, after the example of Judas, their sons become orphans (Ps. 108:9), and their wife a widow, because the blood of Christ remains upon them and upon their children for vengeance (Matt. 27:25). Their sons plainly become orphans from the moment of conception and birth, because they are without God the Father; and their wife—that is, their people—becomes a widow, because she is without her lawful husband, Christ.

Thus it is evident that they die while generating heretics, whose wife remains a widow and whose sons remain orphans. Indeed, they die utterly to God when they do not fear to sell the grace of his sacraments by perversely ordaining others, so that the children of both are born as nothing but orphans, because they are immediately deprived of the eternal Father when they are initiated through the sacraments said to exist among heretics.

For both groups, as an accumulation of their condemnation, there is added the fact that the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, who is the remission of sins, will be required from their generation, just as the blood of Christ, which was shed for the remission of sins, was required from the insane Judas and the faithless Jews.

That faithless usurer, Mammon, searches out all their substance in exchange for the coin lent to their faithlessness, and strangers seize their labors—those whose voices Christ’s sheep do not recognize.

And what more need be said, since the psalm from which we have briefly extracted these matters pursues such people at greater length? If the faithful reader examines it with Christian understanding, he will immediately observe, under the title of Judas the traitor, how many, what kinds, and how great are the curses and punishments owed to the Simoniacs. For that psalm’s prophetic imprecation, directed against the seller of Christ and his buyers, cannot be applied more aptly to any heretics than to those who make the Holy Spirit a commodity for sale in the grace of all his sacraments.

To mention some of these specifically: they sell catechism, baptism, and the seal of perfected Christianity—that is, from the first nourishment of consecrated salt all the way to confirmation by the bishop, which is the seventh of the sacraments of regeneration, according to the sevenfold Spirit, for the remission of all sins.

They sell these whenever they ordain for a price bishops, presbyters, and others whose offices serve the grace of regeneration in the Catholic Church. Likewise, in the case of deacons, whatever belongs sacramentally to deacons; in the case of subdeacons, whatever belongs to subdeacons; in the case of acolytes, whatever belongs to acolytes; in the case of exorcists, whatever belongs to exorcists; in the case of lectors, whatever belongs to lectors; in the case of doorkeepers, whatever belongs to doorkeepers; among clerics, whatever belongs to clerics; among stewards, whatever belongs to stewards; in churches, whatever belongs to churches; in monasteries, whatever belongs in monasteries; and likewise with all the rest.

In this way, leaving no order of the Christian religion free from sale, they omit nothing in the whole world of Christianity that they do not sell. Not the corner of any small possession, not a little field, not a tiny hut, not even the smallest obol—not even present offerings of the faithful in the Church, but also future ones—are found to have been sold before they were given.

Thus those who are called Christians sell, as far as they can, the entire world of Christians—the world that “God so loved that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16) as its redemption. And to whom do they sell it except the devil? And for what purpose is it sold to him? So that they may again belong to him and do evil according to his will, and so that the sacraments of Christianity may profit them nothing, because, having been received freely, they are neither given nor administered freely.

Even if they appear to do good deeds, they are no longer good, because they are credited to the one to whom servants are bound by the ill-considered written contract of their masters. These masters, as though girded with the vessels of the good shepherd, deceitfully draw back to the malignant lion those whom they obstinately withdraw from the kindly Lamb.

[Note: [Col. 1091D]

In the manuscript codex the following is written in the margin:

“According to Jerome, we ought to understand the shepherd’s distinctive vessels as his insignia and attire: the staff, the bag, the pipe, and the whistle. Judas sells Christ; the Simoniacs sell the Holy Spirit a thousand times.”]

For this reason they must be mourned inconsolably, because they perish through their own injury or ignorance, while they either neglect or do not know how to avoid the wickedness of so many and such wolves.

If the fury of these people is compared with Judas’s fury, his will be found tolerable in many ways. For he, driven by sudden madness, sold once the Master whom he saw as mortal and did not doubt was capable of suffering. These men, however, inflamed by prolonged deliberation, sell a thousand times the Holy Spirit, whom they profess with their mouths to be immortal and incapable of suffering.

Although he disturbed a few disciples for a brief time, he did not also take Christ, even after Christ had been killed, away from them. These men, however, both continually disturb the universal Church and expel Christ’s grace from countless peoples of Christ.

He, by betraying one person, destroyed himself and a few accomplices, yet, unwillingly and unknowingly, served the salvation of the whole world. These men, while countless people betray the one Spirit, destroy themselves and their supporters; as they rage toward the ruin of the whole world, they resist the salvation of all the faithful and can at some time benefit neither themselves nor anyone else, except perhaps by repenting.

He sold only the Master, without the possessions of himself and his associates. These men sell not only the Paraclete Spirit, but also everything that belongs to him and everything belonging to their own people everywhere, down to the smallest coin.

He presumed to seek no mediator or witness except himself. These men very often not only take and appoint themselves and their household as mediators and witnesses of their business, but also outsiders.

He, led to repentance, returned the thirty pieces of silver even to those who did not want them. These men, unrepentant, not only do not return whatever price they have received, but would like to have received more.

Indeed, lest they be thought inferior in any respect to the lost Judas and his accomplices—although they are shown to be superior to them in so many crimes—they too rejoice when they have put a price on the Holy Spirit, just as those men rejoiced when they put a price on Christ. And just as Judas sought an opportunity for betrayal, so these men seek opportunities for their commerce.

## CHAPTER XXI. How no almsgiving of any kind benefits the Simoniacs

Like an extremely avaricious trader, anxiously waiting and breathlessly longing for the annual market, so these men await the ordinations to be held at their appointed time, either to redeem the goods they have pledged in hope of such a price, to fill an empty purse, or to pour more into one that is already full.

From this money—which they love so much that they do not fear to sell the Holy Spirit—they will receive no fruit even if they spend it on the poor and on holy places. Judas likewise received no benefit from the money by which the field for the burial of foreigners was bought; it brought no reward for the souls of either the seller of Christ or his buyers. Indeed, the profane Judas would not have received even a worthless tomb there, nor would he have lain there unburied.

If we consider that the chief priests, believing that the money of the betrayal had been returned to them, simultaneously declared that it was not lawful to put it into the treasury—that is, to deposit it with the coins of the holy temple—because it was the price of blood (Matt. 27:5–8), shall we not regard these men as much more criminal than the Jews, since they sometimes think that the price of the Paraclete may be deposited with the offerings that the devotion of Christians has brought or brings to the churches of God?

These sacrilegious men customarily add to the possessions and treasuries of the churches of God, out of so sacrilegious a price and with a certain vain hope of redeeming their souls, sometimes estates, sometimes cloaks, sometimes books, sometimes various and superfluous objects of distinction and equipment belonging to ecclesiastical ministry.

By doing this they acquire for themselves not only no reward but a very great increase of condemnation, since by contact with their unclean offering they pollute the sanctuary and everything belonging to it, just as the Lord declares through Moses: “Whatever an unclean person touches will be unclean” (Num. 19:22).

To prevent this, the same Moses forbids it in Deuteronomy:

> “You shall not offer the wages of a prostitute or the price of a dog in the house of the Lord your God, whatever it is that you have vowed, because both are an abomination before the Lord your God” (Deut. 23:18).

By this command of the divine law, an offering acquired through vice is rejected, because the Lord hates robbery in a burnt offering. He rightly disdains the wages of a prostitute, which the profane prostitute obtains from the corruption of her own and another’s flesh by fornicating with the profane. How much more does he disdain the price that the Simoniac obtains by fornicating against the Christian faith through the prostitution of his own soul and of many others?

He likewise abhors the price of a dog—not because the nature of any animal is abominable to him, but because he abhors an offering that someone has earned from vicious people by flattering and favoring the vices of others, like a mute dog. Or certainly, the price of a dog before God is whatever a person offers after repentance when he has returned to the vomit of sin.

Either way it is an abomination before God, whether you vow to offer him the price of your fornication or of your flattery, however great and precious that price may be.

How, then, will God be appeased by the price at which the virginity of countless souls—that is, uncorrupted faith—is prostituted, or by the price at which obstinacy or impenitence is administered to the wicked, whenever “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul and the unjust person is blessed” (Ps. 10:3)?

And if they acquire possessions, households, and other things useful only for secular human life for themselves, their relatives, and their friends, as another Gehazi did, they will nevertheless receive no benefit from them, because the leprosy of the Simoniacal curse will cling perpetually to them and their offspring, so that their children will be driven about, beg, and be expelled from their dwellings (Ps. 108:10).

Whether, therefore, they spend those prices spiritually or materially, it is clear that they labor altogether in vain, because no one who takes unjustly ever gives anything to anyone justly or fruitfully.

Thus these men defraud one another through their commerce and take from one another what they possessed. The seller, by demanding the money, steals from the buyer both faith and money at once. The buyer, by handing it over to the seller, likewise steals faith and the grace of the Holy Spirit.

In a strange and wretched way, therefore, neither possesses what he has stolen from the other. Instead, each loses what he previously possessed and receives from the other only the condemnation that he did not previously possess.

What if both are wretched? More wretched, nevertheless, is the one who lost both his money and his faith and the spiritual grace that he demanded in exchange for the price he paid: he took it away from the other but did not receive it for himself; rather, in place of a blessing he incurred a curse.

Thus, just as one who takes another’s life indeed takes it from that person but does not thereby possess two lives—for he loses his own as well—so these men take faith and grace from one another, but neither possesses either of them. Moreover, they horribly fall into the hands of the living God (Heb. 10:31), where completed sin generates death for them (Jas. 1:15).

Therefore they are immediately handed over by divine judgment to the devil, who first entered their hearts to invade them, so that he may possess them forever in his own peace. Thus Satan enters them again, like another Judas, after the dipped morsel (John 13:27), when he claims as his own the traitors to their faith, convicted through mutual fraud.

For the dipped bread signified a mind infected by the traitor’s fraud. Finally, what is dipped is not always washed clean; sometimes it is polluted.

## CHAPTER XXII. What the foxes of Simony do or suffer
Therefore, since these fraudulent and shifting men consider it worthless that the Lord should be their portion and they themselves the Lord’s portion, like little foxes, lest they be destroyed like the vineyard of Sodom, they seize even the flourishing vineyard of Christ [Col. 1095B] and become portions of those foxes that have their dens in them. Since they allow themselves to be possessed by these foxes according to the character or distinction of their exceedingly wicked power, Isaiah thus prophesies concerning Idumea under the names and representations of various harmful birds, trees, plants, and unclean beasts:

> “The pelican will possess it, and the hedgehog; the ibis and the raven will dwell in it” (Isa. XXXIV, 11).

And shortly afterward:

> “Thorns and nettles will spring up in its houses, and the buckthorn in its fortifications. It will be a den of dragons and a pasture of ostriches; demons will encounter onocentaurs, and the hairy one will cry out to the other. There the lamia will lie down and find rest; there the hedgehog will have a den and nourish its young, and will dig around and cherish them in its shade [Col. 1095C]. There the kites will gather, one to another” (Isa. XIII, 5).

Thus these little foxes, whose portions and participants they have become, are possessed by, and possess, foxes of such a kind and so devious. Because of their duplicity, they are multiplied and divided among the manifold wickedness of demons—and are still to be divided more abundantly—and they themselves divide them in many ways, while the very things by which they are to be possessed divide among themselves those who are to possess them in turn. Concerning such creatures Wisdom once said:

> “Foxes inhabit souls that remember wickedness, and beasts lie in a turbulent heart.”

But Christ’s little sheep are blessed because of their simplicity; their Lord is their God, who is wholly the one and splendid portion of their inheritance [Col. 1095D]. He himself will restore this inheritance to them (Ps. XV, 5), wholly present in each one, while each one is wholly present in the whole of him, so that all may be perfected into one (John XVII, 23), and God may be one in all and all things in all (I Cor. XV, 28). Thus truly they will be his people, and he himself, their God, will be with them as their God (Zech. VIII, 8).

Because the aforementioned little foxes recoil from their single simplicity, they inhabit the deserts of dragons and ostriches, deprived of the splendid and populous inheritance of one fold and one shepherd. Since they sometimes occupy the office of pastoral care or the mind of divine contemplation, and, by presumptuously taking upon themselves both the governance of the Church and the study of Holy Scripture, dissipate both through wicked action and interpretation, Jeremiah rightly complains in his Lamentations:

> “Our heart has become sorrowful in grief; our eyes have been darkened because of Mount Zion, for it has perished; foxes have walked upon it” (Lam. V, 17–18).

Although Mount Zion sometimes perishes on account of such interpreters, we nevertheless have some consolation in the fact that they are said not to have dwelt or stood there, but merely to have walked upon it. For in the Catholic Church or in canonical Scripture, the episcopate or ministry of heretics can never rest or stand for any length of time. Since they do not speak truth in their hearts, since they practice deceit with their tongues, and since they accept gifts against the innocent, they cannot dwell in God’s tabernacle or rest upon his holy mountain (Ps. XIV, 1–3). Likewise, because they take up their souls in vain and swear deceitfully against their neighbor [Col. 1096B], they cannot prevail to stand in his holy place. And when it is said that they will not stand, this refers to the place into which such men do not even ascend. The Psalmist declares what kind of person ascends, saying:

> “He who is innocent in his hands and pure in heart,” and so forth (Ps. XXIII, 3–4).

Hence it is clear that these very crafty and predatory foxes did not even walk upon the mountain of Catholic Zion, which they could not ascend. Yet, according to the estimation of the believing populace, who imagine that such men rule God’s Church or investigate its teaching, they are said to have walked upon it, while the Lord says through the prophet:

> “They themselves have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not acknowledge them” (Hos. VIII, 4).

And elsewhere:

> “All its princes will be nothing” (Isa. XXXIV, 12).

Accordingly, that mighty Samson typologically captured these three hundred foxes; and, as the History [Col. 1096C] relates, he tied their tails together, fastened torches between them, kindled them with fire, and released them so that they ran here and there. They immediately went into the fields of the Philistines. When these were set alight, both the harvested grain that had been gathered and the standing crops in the burned stubble were consumed, so extensively that the flame also destroyed the vineyards and olive groves. No one who believes Paul’s Gospel doubts that this event happened as a figure for them and was written for our instruction.

For our Lord Jesus Christ, the mightiest and most zealous of all, unwilling that the wife whom he had taken from the Gentiles should be married to anyone else, seized, in his cunning, as foxes, those who were wise to do evil but did not know how to do good, in order to avenge such a great injury against himself. These three hundred in number represent only those heresies that boast in the Christian name—such as the Simonians, Sabellians, Arians, and the rest—excluding the heresies of the Jews and pagans, for whom Christ crucified is either a stumbling-block or folly.

## CHAPTER XXIII. An allegory concerning the foxes captured by Samson

That the number three hundred signifies the universality of Christians marked with the cross of Christ is shown by the letter *Tau*, which, formed in the shape of a cross, expresses that very number. Concerning it, the man clothed in linen is told in Ezekiel:

> “Mark a Tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve” (Ezek. IX, 4).

And, so that the destroyers may not touch them, it is added:

> “Upon whomever you see a Tau, do not kill him” (Ezek. IX, 6).

This mark was also present with Gideon, when, instructed by a divine oracle, he struck down the Midianites with three hundred men. This prefigured our Gideon, who, circling the heavens, remained wholly in the Virgin’s womb. With three hundred men armed with trumpets of spiritual preaching, jars of bodily frailty, and lamps of divine miracles, he conquered the world and conquers those whom he taught to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow him.

Their Sun—that is, Samson—afterward, since there is no one who can hide from his heat and radiance, hunted and separated from the fold of his Church, upon which he poured the rays of justice, the deceitful and unclean foxes of the heresies. In appearance they possessed piety, but not its power: three hundred of them, which he tied together tail to tail [Col. 1097B]. By this he taught that, although their faces and mouths are directed toward different things, they nevertheless conceal and retain one common end of error in their hind parts, as though joined by a single knot of treachery.

Although each heresy, like a tower of its Babylon, seeks in its pride to exalt itself against God, and although, confused by God through the diversity of their tongues, they think and speak differently about the Christian religion and openly attack one another, they nevertheless secretly agree at the end in one knot of impiety. There they are discovered to be attempting nothing other than to overthrow the faith through treachery and seize Christ’s flock for themselves.

In their midst—that is, in the joining of their tails—our Samson placed torches. By this he set their wicked harmony ablaze, a harmony joined at the end, and stirred them up against one another through mutual and internal hatreds and the zeal of envy [Col. 1097C]. Hence, while each tries to drag the other behind it or tear itself away from the other, they all serve one another with stubborn minds.

> “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. XLVIII, 22).

He kindled these torches when, through the sentence of his Catholic Church, he openly inflamed their hatreds to their own destruction and that of many others with an irrevocable anathema, like the fire of his wrath, which would burn to the deepest regions of hell. Thus, released, wandering, and fugitive, they run here and there, because, when God’s anger quickly blazes forth, they have perished from the right way (Ps. II, 12–13).

Finally, when they entered the land of the Philistines, they burned with them all the provisions of that adulterous and foreign people. For clearly those who consent to the adultery of Christ’s wife lose whatever good they possessed, consumed by the fire of his just judgment, which the heresies carry at their end, as though in their tails.

Thus the Philistines are interpreted as “falling by the mouth” or “by a cup,” whether by their own or by another’s. For whether foreigners—that is, pagans—or their foolish neighbors, badly living Christians, fall by another’s mouth whenever they believe the doctrines of heretics, which are certainly doctrines of demons. Such were the wretched Goths, some of whom passed from paganism and others from the Catholic faith to the Arian heresy through the emperor Valens and Eudoxius of Constantinople.

They also fall by their own mouth when they protect and exalt heretics through their own favor. Nor is it without reason that the destruction of their grain, vineyards, and olive groves is specifically reported, although some other things perished with them. Why is this, unless to make known that heretics and their supporters have lost the true sacrifice and sanctification? In the grain and vineyards, the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, from which it is prepared for the life of the faithful people, is not inappropriately understood. In the olive groves, the oil of sacred anointing is understood. When these have been emptied among them, the only thing remaining to them from all the ecclesiastical sacraments is the water of baptism—which alone they can give, and give only for destruction, as has been sufficiently demonstrated above.

Our Samson, Christ, is therefore said to have done or to do these great evils—not because he commanded such things, but because he justly permitted them to occur. Paul likewise warns the Philippians to beware of these foxes, who walk about and, whether from opportunity or envy, preach the Crucified One in such a way that they seek to empty his cross of its meaning. He says:

> “Be imitators of me, and observe those who walk in this way, as you have us for an example. For many walk—of whom I often told you, and now say even while weeping—that they are enemies of the cross of Christ” (Phil. III, 17–18).

Showing that the fire of their destruction is present in their tails, he adds:

> “Their end is destruction” (ibid., 19).

Furthermore, as naturalists assert, a hungry fox throws itself into a filthy place and pretends to be dead; thus it suddenly seizes and kills birds foolish enough to trust it. Heretics are known sometimes to do the same. Hungry for earthly profit or popular favor, they pretend, through a certain continence, to be dead to this world, and they strangle with their treachery souls that are indeed flying but are still carnal, having been made careless of dangers; and they incorporate the devil with themselves.

Herod was one of these. He pretended that he wished to see Jesus because of his miracles, while he was seeking to kill him. Hence the Lord himself, when this was reported to him, replied:

> “Go and tell that fox” (Luke XIII, 32).

This is clearly shown in the Passion, where Jesus is said to have been mocked and despised by Herod and by his entire army (Luke XXIII, 11).

## CHAPTER XXIV. A comparison between the actions of Judas and those of the Simonians

Let us now consider the end of the betrayal and of Christ’s betrayer, and by comparing Judas’s action and deserts, weigh those of the betrayers of the Holy Spirit.

Judas, the worst of merchants, said to his accomplices:

> “Whomever I kiss, he is the one; seize him and lead him away carefully” (Matt. XXVI, 48).

The Simonians say likewise to their own accomplices:

> “Whomever among you we lay hands upon while praying, the Holy Spirit immediately comes upon him. He must receive him and hold him for the free exercise of ecclesiastical office.”

In this presumption they become much worse than Judas. Judas did not think that the Lord, once betrayed, would remain in his possession, and he warned that he should be led away not rashly but carefully. These men, however, betray the Holy Spirit in such a way that they either believe he remains with them, or command, on the authority of their office, that the grace betrayed to others be handled according to their pleasure.

Judas, while greeting and kissing, pretended with his mouth, nod, and gesture to possess the peace and love that he did not have in his heart, and handed over the Lord Jesus for a price. These men, while supplicating, praying, laying hands upon others, and so forth—doing outwardly what belongs properly to legitimate priests—hand over the Holy Spirit for a price, as is supposed.

What response could the Holy Spirit more appropriately make to their words and external reverence than Christ made to Judas?

> “Judas, are you handing over the Spirit of the Father and of the Son with a kiss?”—as though he were saying ironically: “Do you suppose that I have been granted to you in such a way that you may hand me over, even falsely, and sell me to whomever you wish? But woe to him through whom the Holy Spirit will be handed over for a price. It would have been better for him if he had not been born.”

This Simoniac is not improperly called Judas, whose name means “confession.” Just as Judas, confessing with his mouth and saying “Rabbi,” betrayed the Teacher, so this man, confessing and invoking the Holy Trinity with his mouth, barters away the Holy Spirit, whom he names as God and Lord.

Yet God in no way cooperates with such heretical attempts. Rather, the evil spirit cooperates—the spirit concerning which it is said to Christ’s betrayers:

> “This is your hour, and the power of darkness” (Luke XXII, 53).

Nor can these men thereafter possess the Holy Spirit for others or for themselves, even if they once possessed him, just as neither the Jews nor Judas possessed Christ, although Judas had possessed him previously.

But why is it said that they can no longer possess him, when they can no longer even invoke him? The detestable end of Judas signified this. After betraying Christ, he hurried to the noose and died by a punishment worthy of his crime, his throat being knotted and completely constricted—the throat that had dared to open or lend its passages to the deadly voice of betrayal. After the true words of his evil plot, and after the false words of his still worse supplication, he could invoke God neither truly nor falsely.

His arteries are rightly constricted, so that they can no longer emit the breath of life, since they rashly produced a voice that dared to sell the Redeemer of the world. Hence:

> “Having been hanged, he burst open in the middle, and all his entrails were poured out” (Acts I, 18).

Nor did he deserve to have the common and natural departure of the spirit that other human beings have, since he conspired against the common Lord of nature. Thus, hated by heaven and earth and loathed by every creature, he perished between the two: the earth refused to receive his most foul and fetid corpse, while the air refused to receive his most impious and polluted spirit.

Therefore, in these first fruits of their kind, let the Simonians learn what they are, what kind of people they are, and what they deserve. And if first fruits are crushed with a double crushing, how great will be the heaps of them, and how often will they be crushed?

Do they not see that after the very voice of betrayal they cannot invoke the Lord, because their throats are constricted by the inextricable noose of treachery? For how will they call upon one in whom they have not believed? Perhaps, still obstinate with an iron neck and shameless with a brazen forehead, they stubbornly insist that they believe in God with Catholic understanding, although they sell the Holy Spirit.

Let them therefore search out, in every way they can, all the hiding places of their first author in the selling of the Lord God, and produce him if anywhere they find that he believed in Jesus after Satan entered his heart to betray him. If he had believed in him in any way, he would certainly never have attempted such a thing [Col. 1100A]. For he would have recognized that the Lord cannot be sold and that no one can resist his will and power.

But the wretched man recognized in him only what belonged to the human nature and what he saw. Nor is it surprising that he did not fully understand even what he saw, since perhaps, corrupted by Pharisaic leaven, he attributed the Savior’s miracles to the prince of demons. For if he had recognized him, he would certainly have believed; no one believes what he in no way recognizes, although through believing he may deserve to recognize it more perfectly, as the Apostle says:

> “Now I know in part; then I shall know even as I am known” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

And elsewhere:

> “Knowing God”—that is, through faith—“you have been known by him” (I Cor. VIII, 3).

But who would doubt this concerning the carnal and mortal Judas, when the same Apostle asserts that none of the rulers of this age—even though they are of a subtler and immortal nature, such as the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places—knew the incarnate Wisdom of God the Father?

> “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 8).

## CHAPTER XXV. That Judas repented without faith, and that those who consented with the chief priests were deprived of faith

Lest they perhaps suppose that Judas believed because he is said to have repented and returned the price, they should understand that repentance is used improperly in that passage. Properly speaking, it was “the sorrow of the world” that produces death, not that repentance which, as the Apostle says, “is according to God and produces repentance leading to lasting salvation” (II Cor. VII, 10).

In fact, repentance is not praiseworthy without hope, and its substance is faith. Since Judas’s repentance was without hope, it is clear that he had no faith. Accordingly, seeing himself condemned and driven by worldly sorrow, he preferred in despair to cut his throat rather than in hope humbly to offer worthy fruits of repentance. If he had done the latter, his error would not have harmed him.

But the faithless man who had first blasphemed the Son of God, whom he had believed could be sold, finally blasphemed the Holy Spirit, whom he believed could not grant him pardon for so great a sin.

That he believed Christ Jesus to be not God but merely a man, although a just one, is shown by his confession:

> “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matt. XXVII, 4).

Immediately the worst buyers replied:

> “What is that to us? You see to it” (ibid.).

As though they were saying: “What does your sin concern us, since we merely bought the one whom you sold? You see what you have done; for we, having rightly received and now holding the one who was bought and handed over, will not release him.”

Do not the Simonians use this reply every day whenever their sacrilegious ordination is rejected?

> “What does the crime of the Simoniac heresy have to do with us? Let those who sold and handed over spiritual grace to us see what they have done. What we once received we retain, and we will not relinquish our office.”

Lest they think themselves exempt from the fate of those men, although they are supposedly much more tolerable because they received the grace of ecclesiastical orders freely from buyers of grace, let them consider that the chief priests were unable to give Jesus, whom they had bought, to the crowds whose favor they had secured. Instead, in accordance with what they had persuaded the crowds to do, they obtained from the judge Barabbas, a rebellious robber and murderer.

Thus that wretched people, persuaded and deceived by the Pharisees, deserved to become Pharisaic—that is, divided from God the Father and Teacher—and to become the son of their father or teacher, so that thereafter it would be their brother, since they were from the devil as father or from his instruction. This is what Barabbas, or Barrabbas, means.

By this act the people suffered such a loss of their former faith that those who shortly before had come to meet the Lord with palms, had spread their garments and branches of trees on his way, and had cried out, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! King of Israel! Hosanna in the highest!” suddenly began to cry out for Barabbas.

Whenever the judge—for example, as though they were foolish—tried to bring them to their senses and correct them from their error, he accomplished nothing. Rather, the tumult increased, their voices grew stronger, and they wanted nothing except to cast Jesus away from themselves and demand Barabbas, saying:

> “Not this man, but Barabbas” (John XVIII, 40);
>
> “Take this man away, and release Barabbas to us” (Luke XXIII, 18);
>
> “Take him away, take him away! Crucify him, crucify him!” (John XIX, 15);
>
> “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25);

and other things like these.

By this conspiracy and sentence they handed themselves and their descendants over to the devil. Very few believed afterward in comparison with those who did not believe, and they did not take care to withdraw themselves and their descendants from eternal death.

Thus, together with the most shameful and bitter death of the soul, they also suffered the death of the body, as through Vespasian and Titus, and through Aelius Hadrian.

Concerning this people we must also consider that all who were saved from them deserved to be perfectly reconciled to God not merely through baptism—which undoubtedly grants remission of all sins—but also only after they had first labored to appease him through repentance. Thus, when they were pierced with compunction at the evident outpouring of the Holy Spirit and at Peter’s preaching, it was said to them:

> “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts II, 38).

Nor could ignorance excuse them from repentance, although Peter himself subsequently bore witness concerning that ignorance, saying:

> “And now, brothers, I know that you acted through ignorance, as did your rulers. Repent therefore and be converted, so that your sins may be blotted out.”

He shows in what, especially, their sins consisted by saying earlier:

> “The God of our fathers glorified his Son Jesus, whom you indeed handed over and denied before Pilate, when he had judged that he should be released. But you denied the Holy and Just One and asked for a murderer to be granted to you; you killed the Author of life” (ibid., 13, 15).

If those who did not believe, or who doubted, that Christ was God and handed him over to the judge to be killed as though he were merely a man, are said to have denied Christ, can there be doubt that those deny the Holy Spirit who claim that they fully believe him to be God and Lord, yet sell him for gold? And how much more tolerable would this denial be if it were done for the sake of a human being!—as much more tolerable as a human being is more valuable than a stone.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That even those ordained freely by the Simonians receive nothing but condemnation, and that they cause idols to be worshiped instead of Christ

From this they should infer what they have received, persuaded by such merchants of the Holy Spirit and ordained in this way without payment. They would in no way accept the laying on of hands unless they had been persuaded that these men were priests of the Lord.

Let them also consider with what great repentance they must be chastised, since even the Jews were not excused from repentance before baptism, although they acted in ignorance. Certainly, as far as human judgment is concerned, ignorance ought to have excused them. But it did not, because, as the Apostle says:

> “He who is ignorant will be ignored” (I Cor. XIV, 38).

And how many and how great are the bands of simple and rustic people who, while seeking the truth, have been led astray in ignorance by heretics! We believe that they perished justly, though we cannot fully understand how this was just. Truly:

> “He who touches pitch will be defiled by it, and he who associates with the proud will put on pride” (Ecclus. XIII, 1).

“If a man is wicked toward himself, to whom will he be good?”

Let them learn, or at least be warned, that all who are thieves and robbers come only “to slaughter and destroy” (John X, 10). From their bloodstained hands these people received not only no sanctification but a great deal of contamination, so that their once faithful soul, full of judgment, became a prostitute. In the place where justice previously rested, there is now a murderer, whose silver has become dross and whose wine has been mixed with water (Isa. I, 22).

And why is this? Because all its princes are faithless companions of thieves. Persuaded by them, ignorant of the simplicity of the Catholic faith and unwary, they receive in place of Christ that rebellious robber who said in his heart:

> “I will set my seat in the north; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 14),

and that murderer who existed from the beginning.

Thus those who had until then been ready praisers and devoted receivers of the Lord become his wicked blasphemers and importunate petitioners for a robber. Their intention seeks only that robber, even when their voice pretends to address God.

Whom, I ask, do they address except Mammon? He would not utter or even murmur a word, nor lift a hand, either for God or for his neighbor, unless he received or hoped for money.

But the benevolent Spirit of wisdom did not free the blasphemer from his lips. For although God is the witness of his kidneys, the true searcher of his heart, and the hearer of his tongue, he did not free the accursed heretic from his cursed lips. For to such a man speaking well means nothing other than condemning and cursing himself by his own voice.

The Spirit of the Lord hears the tongue that blesses, since he fills the world and contains all things. Yet, because he possesses knowledge of the voice, while the searcher of kidneys and heart knows what a person intends, he does not consider what someone says but what he intends by saying it.

The Holy Spirit himself, scorning such words and outward devotions, protests through Isaiah:

> “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you. And when you multiply your prayer, I will not hear. Your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I, 15).

Are not the companions of thieves and robbers themselves thieves and robbers? Solomon says:

> “A companion of fools becomes like them” (Prov. XIII, 20);
>
> “Whoever shares with a thief hates his own soul” (Prov. XXIX, 24).

Thieves and robbers are men of blood and deceit. Whoever participates with them must therefore be bloodstained and fraudulent.

Since his hands are full of blood, and since he shares in the fellowship of the robbers allied with him, his prayer is rejected by the spotless majesty. As the Wise Man says:

> “He who turns his ear away so as not to hear the law—his prayer is accursed” (Prov. XXVIII, 9).

If this happens to those who do not obey the law commanding that the Lord be honored from one’s own native substance (Prov. III, 9), what will happen to those who impiously sell another person’s almsgiving entrusted to them, which they received freely in order to give freely?

Their prayer or blessing is not merely unheard or unaccepted; it is turned into sin and into a curse, because:

> “There is no truth in their mouth; their heart is empty” (Ps. V, 10).
>
> “Their throat is an open grave; they acted deceitfully with their tongues; the poison of asps is under their lips. Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes. Will all those who practice iniquity not understand, who devour my people as though eating bread? They have not called upon the Lord” (Ps. XIII, 3–4).

Who devour God’s people more than those who carry all the sacraments of the Christian religion as goods for sale and deny them to God’s people unless the people buy them back from them at a price?

But woe to the wretched person who is afflicted by such a double loss: through his commerce he loses his external goods, and he does not receive the internal ones. Rather, he incurs condemnation, because he is rejected from the body of Christ like corrupted bread, adorned by heretics, and so incorporated into them that he is consumed with the companions of the one who is not.

While foolish people try carelessly to flee from the lion who prowls around roaring and seeking someone to devour, they encounter him in visible form—namely, the cunning heresy that presents a certain appearance of humanity, as though of reason. Thus it bestially tears apart their innermost liver—that is, their right intention—and secretly hands them over to the lion whom they had foolishly thought they had escaped, to be devoured.

Since it is further said of such devourers:

> “They have not called upon God” (Ps. LII, 6),

we must ask whom they do call upon, since they sometimes offer lengthy prayers and are heard invoking God and seen to do so by human beings.

Blessed Jerome, characteristically concise, removes this difficulty for us when he explains these words of Zechariah:

> “And it shall be in that day, says the Lord of hosts, that I will destroy the names of the idols from the earth, and they will no longer be remembered; and I will remove the prophets and the unclean spirit from the earth” (Zech. XIII, 2).

Just as idols are made by the hand of a craftsman, so the perverse doctrine of heretics turns whatever it has fashioned into an idol and causes the Antichrist to be worshiped in place of Christ.

Even if they sometimes curse the devil in words, they certainly curse themselves, as is confirmed by the saying of the Wise Man:

> “When the impious curses the devil, he himself curses his own soul” (Ecclus. XXI, 30).

No one can deny that these things are so unless he is an obvious heretic. Therefore, let those who have in any way been appointed and substituted by robbers to bless and pray—even freely—consider what they have acquired for themselves or for others through communion with those whose participants they have become and to whom they voluntarily subscribed, since they not only believed their act to be valid but also preached it.

They are murderers, plainly like those to whom they consent. They kill the inner person in themselves and in others, so that their outer person lives in vain, soon to undergo eternal punishment. For wherever the soul finally perishes, the body will follow afterward.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The judgment of Saint Augustine by which all heretics are convicted of denying that Jesus Christ came in the flesh

[Col. 1104C]

Lest anyone accuse us of composing a new taunt against heretics from our own imagination rather than from the divine books, and lest anyone suppose that they are not altogether without faith or that they do not deny the Lord God, let him observe the venerable Catholic teacher Augustine, who thunders these words in his *Epistle of Blessed John the Apostle* (Augustine, *Tractates on the Epistle of John*, 2.4):

> “All heretics, all schismatics, have gone out from us—that is, they have gone out from the Church—but they would not have gone out if they had been of us before they went out.”

And a little later:

> “Certainly all who go out from the Church and are severed from the unity of the Church are Antichrists; no one doubts this. For he himself designated them: ‘They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us’ (I John II, 19).
