They also give spirit to his image, commending it by imitating him through the lie of their preaching and defense, insofar as they can. Among the other signs they fabricate, they also make fire descend from heaven to earth whenever, in the manner of the apostles, they lay hands on someone and presume that he receives the grace and consecration of the Holy Spirit.

But they seem to perform this on the earth that they call their Church, and in the sight of human beings—that is, of carnal people. Or, in another sense, they bring fire down from heaven upon the earth when their impiety prospers in worldly terms, so greatly that even the elect, in whom God dwells as in heaven, are shaken with astonishment and cast the fire of human zeal against the Church, while, being less upright in heart, they behold the peace and abundance of heretics and grow jealous of them.

## CHAPTER XLI. The Savagery of This Beast, and the Mark of Christ and of Antichrist

But this beast, which at first, as though domesticated, fawned through signs in order to deceive, at the end frightens everyone like an untamed wild animal by its roar and ravaging, so that no one may now oppose its savagery out of fear of death.

This can be clearly understood from the single heresy of the Simonians. In earlier times it appeared so mild that its wickedness could scarcely be detected. Now, however, it has broken out into such ferocity that, just as once in the time of the Arians, people of our own time are also reported to have been publicly beaten, stripped of their possessions, exiled, and killed by Simonians merely because they admonished them to come to their senses with charitable and gentle words.

Thus this beast, which first brought forth a head apparently mild and lamb-like, gradually tightens its tail like a cedar, so that now it spares no age, no sex, no condition, no profession, no rank, and no authority. From the greatest to the least, it leads peoples in organized masses into battle against the Lamb and his army.

It sends many ahead of itself, but drags innumerable others behind it, so that, along with those who set their minds on earthly things, it also drags down to earth by the dragon’s tail those who seemed to shine spiritually in the Church like stars in heaven—when that tail, as it were, has become its follower.

Thus the fire that came forth from the ambitious and thorny bramble not only burned the barren forests—which, rejected by the olive, vine, and fig tree, had chosen it as their king—but also devoured the cedars of Lebanon themselves.

To complete its wickedness, it marks the right hands and foreheads of all who consent to it with the mark of Antichrist. Whoever does not have this mark will be unable to sell or buy.

Perhaps it may be asked what this mark is. It is surely faithlessness, which is properly called impiety. For just as Catholic faith, which is also called piety, is the mark of Christ, so heretical faithlessness is recognized as the mark of Antichrist.

And just as Catholics bear the mark of Christ on their right hand and forehead, so likewise do heretics bear the mark of Antichrist. With our right hand we carry the stigmata of Christ’s cross, which we bring forth with a slight movement of that right hand, for ourselves and for others, whenever it is appropriate. We also bear it impressed upon our foreheads by saving chrism. We are not ashamed of it; rather, we glory in it so that, with the Apostle, we may profess: “I bear the marks of Jesus Christ in my body” (Gal. 6:17). And, with Jerome: “I bear the banner of the cross on my forehead.”

How fittingly it is marked on the forehead, which is the chief and more honorable part of the head and the seat of modesty, as though on the lintel of our outer person. This warns us that the cross of Christ must be impressed upon the principal part of our inner person, which is reason, as an eternal memorial and protection. We must so share in his suffering that we may reign with him, and consider it the highest glory to suffer disgrace for his name. We must be ashamed of nothing for his sake except sin.

Likewise, the mark of the cross is present on our right hand, which holds primacy among the limbs after the head, and which, laboriously imitating the arts and administering the body’s various useful functions for itself and for others, reminds us that in every action we must attend to the deeds and words of Christ crucified. The Apostle says: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God the Father through him” (Col. 3:17).

When we have done this, nothing left-handed but everything right-handed will be what we have done, and our left hand will not know what our right hand of good works is doing (Matt. 6:3).

## CHAPTER XLII. The Merchants of Christ and of Antichrist

Since, above all, God recognizes us through faith, faith is certainly the mark by which we are marked. It is detected on our right hand and forehead whenever we seek to conduct profitable and peaceful business in the kingdom of our king.

For if we consider carefully, no one, whether good or evil, can live even one hour in this world without conducting business. Hence Christ, when he was about to go into a distant region under the guise of a certain nobleman, said to his servants: “Conduct business until I come” (Luke 19:13).

Hence also it is said of the holy Church in Proverbs: “She is like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from far away. She made linen and sold it, and delivered a belt to the Canaanite” (Prov. 31:14, 24).

Christ and his people are merchants; Antichrist and his people are merchants. Why does the Lord, through Ezekiel, speak under the guise of the king of Tyre, saying: “You were a protecting cherub, and I placed you on God’s holy mountain; you walked in the midst of fiery stones. You were perfect in your ways from the day of your trading; your innermost parts were filled with iniquity” (Ezek. 28:14–15)? And shortly afterward: “By the multitude of your iniquities and the iniquities of your trading, you polluted your sanctification” (ibid., 18).

He also said of that one: “You were filled and greatly glorified in your trading in the heart of the sea; your rowers brought you into many waters” (Ezek. 27:25–26).

It is therefore evident that human life here is not lived except through trading. But the faithful, under the mark of Christ, sell perishable goods and buy eternal ones. The faithless, under the mark of Antichrist, also sell perishable goods and buy eternal evils.

The former give their temporal life and receive eternal life; the latter give their temporal life and receive eternal death. The former sell themselves and all that belongs to them, and receive them back a hundredfold with the full interest of eternal life. The latter sell themselves and all that belongs to them, and afterward find none of it except the accumulated interest of eternal death. No one serving as a soldier for God will become entangled in their business (2 Tim. 2:4).

Faithlessness, or impiety, is the general mark of all of them—pagans, Jews, and heretics, as alien children and liars to God. But what is it that some of these impious people bear the mark of the cross on their right hand and forehead? Will they therefore, by this mark, be counted among the merchants of Christ? Are they not thieves and robbers?

Whose cross, then, do they bear as the mark of their faithlessness? Without doubt, it is the cross of that blasphemous and shameless robber who, through the crucified Son of God—namely, the robber—insulted the Lord who was crucified with him.

But why do these robbers display the mark of the cross in such a way that they invoke the name of Christ? It is not surprising, because they do this to the disgrace and detriment of our Christ, and to the glory and advantage of their robber.

For the companion and fellow disciple of those people, although he said to God, “If you are the Son of God, save yourself and us” (Luke 23:39), was insulting and disparaging Christ’s omnipotence and providing his enemies with material for mockery. While that insolent man, drunk on the dragon’s gall, reproached Christ for the punishment of the cross and for being the equal of robbers, he felt neither his present nor his future shame arising from Christ’s shame.

But when his former companion rebuked him (ibid., 40), and did not hesitate to believe in his heart and confess with his mouth that Christ was King and Lord, even as he died on the cross, he changed the mark of the robber to whom he had been joined into the mark of Christ. Under the latter mark, from the punishment of a robber, he deserved the triumph of a martyr.

Thus, whatever heretics appear to do or possess as something right or especially distinguished is entirely the business of Antichrist. This is accomplished through the recognition of his mark—namely, faithlessness—made effective on their right hand and forehead, even though they themselves, together with the Jews, call their own Antichrist “Christ.”

## CHAPTER XLIII. By What Mark the Simonians Are Recognized as Being of Antichrist

Just as Arians are recognized as belonging to Antichrist by this mark: that they preach the Son as lesser than the Father, and the Holy Spirit as lesser than both; so the Simonians are likewise recognized as belonging to Antichrist by this mark: that they supposedly sell and buy the Holy Spirit, or believe and say that he can be sold and bought.

They do not merely conduct business secretly under Antichrist, like other heretics; they also openly and in worldly fashion offer the Holy Spirit for sale as a cheap slave, and bargain for and accept a worldly price in exchange for him.

No one can sell or buy him unless marked with the mark of Antichrist—that is, with faithlessness—on the right hand and forehead, namely, in the principal part of his thought and action, so that he may continually enrich Antichrist through his business.

Therefore the prophet, lamenting Judah, says: “Her enemies have become her leaders; her enemies have grown rich, because the Lord has spoken against her” (Lam. 1:5). Another Psalmist, rebuking the idol, says: “A foolish heart will worship it, and it will not save his soul; nor will he say, ‘Perhaps there is a lie in my right hand’” (Isa. 44:20).

But this business is not completed unless both parties—the seller and the buyer—are found to bear the mark of Antichrist. Peter did not possess it and therefore could not sell, although Simon Magus, marked with that sign, wished to buy.

Here one should observe from how great a weakness this heresy has reached such great strength. At first it found no seller; then, after a long time, it found a seller, but one who sought payment from the buyer alone and no one else. From that point the seller is no longer ashamed to demand from the buyer, by every means, not only his own money and that of his associates, but also ecclesiastical funds.

Alas for me! I learned from those who perpetrate this dreadful crime that, after the precious marble of the walls and the decorative inlays of basilicas had been sold for this business, even the tiles were torn from their roofs under the pressure and command of the seller, so that the sum of the promised price might be paid to him by the wretched buyer, who was already lamenting such an action too late.

Let anyone who can say what heresy has ever plotted such desolation against the churches of God as this one. Yet the wise are said to preach that one should deal more gently with the Simonians than with others, and that the severity of the canons should be moderated toward them more than toward the Novatians, toward whom the Catholic Church showed itself more merciful and lenient.

Let the wolves, thieves, and robbers be spared—if they have ever spared, or do spare, the sheep, or if, when they seize or steal them, they do not slaughter and destroy them. Let them be permitted to grow and beget children with impunity; but let it be considered whether this is beneficial to the little flock of lambs.

Let the kid be cooked in its mother’s milk, even though the Lord forbids it (Exod. 23:19); but let care be taken lest a goat thus be made subject to an irrevocable curse.

Let surgical instruments be withheld from diseased sheep, and let biting salt, vinegar, and live sulfur be withheld from their scabby ribs; but let it be seen that the dreadful contagion does not gradually spread through everything.

Let sacrilegious people also be spared, although no laws spare them; but let care be taken lest this piety toward them become impiety toward God and his own people, and lest holy places, if anything remains to them, lose it.

Let Cain the fratricide be spared, if he too, after being admonished, ceased from fratricide. Let murderers be spared, if they have not sinned unto death. Let robbers be spared, if they have not merely ceased robbing but have also properly restored what they robbed and still retain by force.

## CHAPTER XLIV. How Guilty the Simonians Are of Crimes against the Church, and Concerning the Number of the Name of Christ

Oh, how many fratricides and murderers, and how great their number, are the Simonians found to be, above all other heretics! Apart from the common people, they daily kill so many companies of God’s household—namely, clerics, monks, and nuns—with monstrous sacrilege.

By selling and giving away their stipends to secular people, they deprive them of their support; they kill their bodies through intolerable hunger and want of every necessity; and they likewise compel their souls to commit the sins by which they die.

For when those who ought to lead a celibate and spiritual life perceive that none of their stipend has been left to them for their support, they are forced to flee for refuge to the assistance of secular people. In trying to relieve their bodies, they are necessarily compelled to subject their souls.

Oh, how many poor people, widows, and orphans—who should have been nourished by ecclesiastical assistance—have they killed! Oh, how many holy places have they destroyed, where they perpetually sold or gave to secular people the portion of tithes and offerings owed to the poor and to the churches!

It is therefore now necessary that whoever wishes to serve Christ must serve at his own expense, contrary to the privilege of Christian soldiery.

Hence no one dares compel clerics, monks, or nuns to a regular way of life, or summon them with a free and open face, except according to the will of each one of them.

Here, then, let us briefly indicate something about the number of the beast’s name. Just as the name of our Christ, who is Jesus, when considered in Greek letters, expresses 888, so the name of Antichrist expresses 666. This number is found in many Greek words when considered in Greek, among them *Teitan*, written among us as *Titan*. Its plural is *Titanes*, understood as “giants,” who, according to ancient fables, once attempted to attack and conquer the inhabitants of heaven.

It is also found in the name of the sun, which is said formerly to have rejected its companions; hence the sun is still called *Titan*. He is also called *Apollon* in Greek, that is, “Destroyer,” because by his heat he destroys all the sap of growing plants by boiling it away.

By this name the Apocalypse calls the king of the abyss, who, as it adds there, has in Latin the name “Destroyer” (*Exterminans*) (Apoc. 9:21, as cited); its Greek derivative, *ἀπολλύειν* (*apollyein*), signifies destruction. If you consider it, you will likewise find 666.

Whether, then, you call Antichrist a giant or destruction, it makes no difference. He is a giant because he opposes God and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped (2 Thess. 2:4); and he is destruction because he is the man of sin and the son of destruction (John 17:12). Although he promises salvation to everyone, he does not save himself, as the Psalmist cries: “A king is not saved by great power, nor is a giant saved by the abundance of his strength” (Ps. 33:16).

Before him that giant also fights, girded backward, as it were, before a power opposed to him. Concerning this the Psalmist also testifies: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 19:5).

Blessed Ambrose, accompanying this passage, says: “He proceeds from his bridal chamber, the royal hall of the twin modesty; a giant, vigorous in substance, so that he may run his course.”

By his grace, just as we are saved by seeing, so the former fathers deserved to be saved by hoping. The Apostle Peter says: “We believe that we shall be saved through the grace of Jesus Christ, just as they also were” (Acts 15:11).

They set him before themselves under the name of future salvation in the number eight, as Noah, the eighth person, in the ark, and Abraham in the circumcision of Isaac on the eighth day. We too retain him in the same number under the name of salvation both displayed and to be displayed.

Through his resurrection, which took place on the eighth day, and through the coming of his Spirit on the first day of the eighth week from that resurrection, we believe that through the number eight Jesus now raises us in our souls and will raise us in our bodies on the last day.

He is not signified without reason by the number that contains both six and seven. Thus, in the likeness of the Creator of the world, it demonstrates that after the perfection of good works, as after the number six, we shall have the seventh—the rest of souls—and at last shall receive the eighth—the resurrection of bodies.

## CHAPTER XLV. Concerning the Number of the Name of Antichrist

Hence Antichrist, so that he may be believed to be nothing less than the devil, and being exceedingly skilled at deception, attempts insofar as he can to turn the mystery of Jesus Christ, through signs and numbers, toward himself. He also misuses Christ’s names, so that he too may be called Messiah or Christ, Giant or Strong One, although in truth he is the son of destruction, who comes to destroy everything that the Lord Jesus, according to his name, came to seek and save, because it had perished.

To insult Christ and disguise his own darkness, he wishes to be called Titan or Apollo, like the sun, so that he may be thought to be that principal Sun whom Malachi foretold: “For you who fear my name, the Sun of justice will rise” (Mal. 4:2).

Yet he is entirely a slave of pitch-black and sulfurous Gehenna, rebellious against the unchanging Sun, destroying all the greenness and growth of faith.

He is to be secretly conceived and born from an abominable incest, and at his very conception is to be seized by the prince of darkness, adopted and held as his son, so that by his power and lying signs our first hope—the birth from the Virgin, namely the most holy Mary—may be nullified, and this one may be called and regarded as a *manzer*—a bastard—in place of the Son of Man, who is nevertheless far superior and more powerful than he.

He will fabricate all these things and many more like them, so that through pride he may overturn the humility of our King, through impiety his piety, through cruelty his clemency, and through falsehood his truth. Through these deceptions, in which there will be some resemblance to truth, he will more easily subject the unwary to himself.

For this reason he will work in vain to make the number of his name equal to the number of the name of Jesus Christ, because he does not approach it. Although he appropriates the number six, he lacks the seven and the eight.

From this it is clear to the prudent that Antichrist and his followers can attain only the perfection of evil works. They cannot reach either the seventh, the rest of souls, or the eighth, the resurrection of bodies, except in the second death, because beyond the six of their visible and temporal activity they take no care to store up any reward for the future.

We have discussed these matters about the signs, the mark, and the number of Antichrist’s name at perhaps excessive length, but necessarily, so that no one ignorant of his snares and hidden iniquity may suppose that at the end of the world he will raise the dead to life, or burn a visible mark upon people’s right hands and foreheads, or inscribe them with the number of his name, and boast in vain that he will accept such things without any torture of his body if he should then be alive—when perhaps he will already have voluntarily subjected himself to all of them.

Alas, how many and how great are those who have not seen the times of Antichrist and yet are in his body! The more numerous and powerful he enfolds within himself, the more cunningly he conceals his wickedness from them.

For poison is drunk more eagerly than noble wine; it is judged not only from a precious cup but also by its color.

## CHAPTER XLVI. How Satan Constructs a Profane Trinity against the Divine Trinity

[Col. 1134C]

Therefore the ancient dragon, always greedy and skilled at fabricating things, among all the many and great attempts and imitations that he has been shown above to undertake, also strives by every means to accomplish this: just as there are three who bear witness to the truth in heaven and three on earth (1 John 5:7–8), so he too, in opposition, transforms three who bear witness to his falsehood in this murky air—which he is still permitted to occupy—and three on earth.

His pride has burst forth to such an extent that he now seeks to become like the Most High, while nevertheless exalting himself above everything that is called or worshiped (2 Thess. 2:4).

Thus, rebelling against God and opposing his blessed and undivided Trinity, he establishes his own abomination over against it: himself, namely, and his Antichrist, and the false prophet of both. In this way he himself, the father of lies, resists the Father of truth; Antichrist resists Christ, or falsehood resists truth; and the false prophet, as the conspiracy of the liar and the lie, resists the Spirit of truth and truth itself.

Likewise, in opposition to the three who bear witness to the truth on earth, these three spew from their mouths three unclean spirits in the form of frogs. These spirits pollute, invade, and sell those whom water washes, the Spirit imbues, and the blood of Christ redeems.

These unclean spirits are aptly compared to frogs, which avoid clear, flowing waters and desire muddy pools. In these pools they croak with shameless and discordant chatter, multiply their offspring, and raise them.

In them you will find no place where you may set your feet to walk and rest, but only where you may be polluted and swallowed up. Nothing is produced there except mists, stench, sharp sedges, marsh reeds and rushes, venomous serpents, deadly worms, and barren trees.

Such is the multitude of the reprobate which, like stagnant and bitter water, turns land that was formerly dry and habitable by human beings into foul and impassable marshes. In these marshes nothing is now found that is not destined for unquenchable fire.

Nothing is heard there except the foolish and contentious talk of carnal and loquacious people, defending their drunkenness and disturbing the sobriety of spiritual and silent people through their shamelessness. Such are the poets and philosophers of the pagans, the fabulists of the Jews, and the heretics, who, like muddy frogs in slimy marshes, irrationally and obstinately declaim their dirges.

These three authors rule over them and inspire their songs: Satan among the pagans, Antichrist among the Jews, and the false prophet among the heretics.

Through these three, the devil attempts to hunt, snare, and fish for three sects from the whole human race: through himself, like Behemoth, the pagans; through Antichrist, like a bird, the Jews; and through the false prophet, like Leviathan, Christians.

All who are captured from among them are dragged back, like senseless people, to forbidden waters, because they are deceived either by worldly wisdom, temporal prosperity, or the Christian name.

The third group is more harmful because, unlike the others, it professes two waters—wisdom and baptism.

This is also suggested by the fact that, from that time onward, the dragon and the first beast appear in the Apocalypse to be at leisure. The dragon and the beast now rest secure because the pagans have been possessed by the devil from the beginning and the Jews have been seized by Antichrist, and the false prophet alone does not doubt that he can prevail in deceiving and subjugating Christians.

Babylon, built by these three unclean spirits from people of the three professions, is given by the Lord—as the prophet says—to that hedgehog, who did not stand in the truth, and to the pools of waters, that is, to assemblies of profane crowds, whose minds are possessed by mists of error and whose bodies are possessed by every kind of stench of lust (Isa. 14:23).

In them nothing is produced except unrestrained anger, empty pomp, hypocrisy and snares, dullness, and sterile and insolent verbosity. Among these are “the two daughters of the leech, saying, ‘Give, give’” (Prov. 30:15).

Avarice is the most savage leech, which will not release the skin until it is full of blood. Its two daughters are greed and rapacity. Although these cling to all carnal people, they do so more vigorously and openly among the Simonians.

For they do not cease to say to one another, “Give, give.” For example, the greedy buyer says to the seller: “Give me invisible grace”; and the rapacious seller likewise says to the buyer: “Give me visible money.” Or the buyer says: “Give me the Holy Spirit”; while the seller, in return, says: “Give me a sound coin.”

Hence it is clear that they are inhabitants of the marshes of Babylon, who can contribute nothing without a bite, without a wound, without blood. Unless they first vomit out, by drinking some error, the poison of the avarice innate in them, they know only how to invite pestilence.

## CHAPTER XLVII. That Heretics Gain Nothing, Either for Faith or for Salvation, Even If They Sing the Catholic Creed in Loud Voices

Let the Simonians now go on and loudly confess that Jesus came in the flesh—the one whose body they are not satisfied merely to torment and tear apart, but whose death feeds them.

When corrected and convicted, they obstinately and shamelessly, as is their custom, recite the Catholic Creed. With all, as it is said, nine instruments of the human voice, let them shout and proclaim that they believe in Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who for us human beings and for our salvation descended from heaven, was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and was made human, and so forth.

Let them cry out as well, if they can and wish, with an iron or bronze voice, and let their chests breathe out a hundred sounds by which they profess “that they believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, who together with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified, who spoke through the prophets; and in one holy Catholic and apostolic Church,” and so forth.

Do they not deny that he came in the flesh when they inflict upon the body of Christ, which is his Church, the wounds described above? Do they not deny that the Holy Spirit is Lord, worthy to be worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son, and that he spoke through the prophets, when they inflict upon him the blasphemies and injuries described above?

And what the Novatians are said to deny must be proclaimed to be what the Simonians confess.

Although the Novatians are heard singing our Creed in clear and loud voices and subscribing to it, they are nevertheless convicted of denying that Jesus Christ came in the flesh—not because they wound his healthy members, but because they despair that wounded members can be healed by the Church of God.

How, then, are the Simonians to be listened to when they sometimes cry out that they believe Jesus came in the flesh, or that the Holy Spirit is to be worshiped with the Father and the Son, since they not only fail to heal Christ’s wounded members but also wound the healthy ones to the point of death?

Yet, so that the Novatian heresy may be shown to be more tolerable in comparison with the Simonians, we have thought it appropriate to insert here, from the *Tripartite History*, who and from where their error arose.

“After the definition of faith had been written and subscribed by the Council of Nicaea,” it says, “the emperor asked Acesius, bishop of the religion of the Novatians, ‘Whether he too agreed with the faith and with the definition concerning the celebration of Easter.’”

But he replied: “The synod has defined nothing new, O emperor. For long ago, and from the times of the apostles, I myself received both the rule of faith and the time of the Easter celebration.”

Then, when the emperor asked again, “Why, then, do you separate yourself from communion?” he repeated what had happened during the persecution under Decius and brought forward the strictness of a most severe rule, because “those who sin after baptism ought not to be made worthy of communion with the saints for the sin which the divine Scriptures declare to be unto death; rather, they should indeed be invited to repentance, but they should await the hope of remission not from priests but from God alone, who has the power to forgive sins.”

But enough of this.

Desiring now to provide both for the reader’s breathing space and for the writer’s refreshment, we have judged it necessary to set here a second boundary for this little work.

[Col. 1137] THE SECOND BOOK ENDS.

THE CHAPTERS OF THE THIRD BOOK BEGIN.

[Col. 1137A] I. Against those who say that they purchased not consecration but the property of the Church. II. Proof that possession is of no benefit without its privilege. III. On the zeal of holy kings for divine worship, and on reward, sin, and the vengeance inflicted upon peoples. XVII. On the merits of Israel and Judah as types of heretics [Col. 1137D] and Catholics. XVIII. On the difference between the priesthood of Catholics and that of heretics, and on the first beginnings of the Simoniacs. XIX. How even the priests under the law avoided communion with the impious, and how they purified what had been contaminated by them. XX. On the danger of priests and the undisciplined ambition of the clerics of our time. XXI. On Italy’s chief evil, and on a certain vain bishop, and on the office of priests, rulers, and peoples. XXII. On the novel silence of priests, or the loquacity of flatterers. [Col. 1138A] XXIII. On the danger of priests who keep silent wrongly and of those who speak wrongly, and on the indivisible unity of the Godhead and of its members. XXIV. On the model of the indivisible Trinity in all creatures. [Col. 1138B] XXV. That sanctification is indivisible from the things which it sanctifies, and how they are sanctified. XXVI. On the punishment of those who divide, and that they do not receive the Holy Spirit unless they are followers of the apostles’ faith. XXVII. On the grace of the Holy Spirit after the Resurrection, and the vengeance inflicted upon Ananias. XXVIII. How much the same Spirit has done and continues to do in the Church until the end of the age. XXIX. The opinion of Saint Augustine concerning the power of the soul, his retraction concerning it, and what sort of men are promoted by laymen, together with their metropolitans. XXX. On criminal Catholics who have been promoted, or who have fallen afterward, and on their ministry and deposition. XXXIII. That Catholics promote no one on account of crime, whereas the Simoniacs promote everyone solely on account of crime. [Col. 1138D] XXXVIII. In what matters hirelings are to be heard, and in what matters they are not to be heeded. XXXIX. On those who knowingly and unknowingly deserve evil, and Paschasius’s judgment concerning their ministry. XL. On Simoniac thieves, and how they enter the sheepfold. XLI. How the Simoniacs imitate the thieves of the world, and what their voice is, which the sheep do not hear. XLII. With what vigilance the sheep ought to resist thieves once they have entered the sheepfold. XLIII. By examples it is shown that heretics were not tolerated even for an hour by the ancient Catholics, whereas hirelings were tolerated. [Col. 1139A] XLV. That Saint Gregory, while still a deacon, avoided Eutychius, and that Saint Jerome asserts that one should not await a public judgment against such men. XLVI. The chapters are ended.

THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 1139]

CHAPTER I. Against those who say that they purchased not consecration but the property of the Church.

[Col. 1139B]

Just as nothing in the nature of things is more solid and preferable than rounded and open truth, so nothing is emptier and worse than angular and hidden falsehood. For truth possesses such clarity and efficacy that, like the true light, it not only strikes the eyes of all but also shines in darkness. Conversely, falsehood possesses such obscurity and weakness that it neither grasps nor perceives the truth by which it is comprehended and pierced.

The author of truth himself, the Truth, wished to show in the Gospel that human beings incur this condition by a just judgment, saying:

> “This is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil. Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved. But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be manifested, because they have been accomplished in God” (John 3:19–21).

It is as though he said: A physician came into the world and found every person sick. Some, preferring to remain sick rather than appear sick by approaching the physician, made falsehood their way. Others, preferring to appear sick rather than remain sick, made truth their way by approaching the physician. Thus, whether the former or the latter, all were equally sick. But the works of the former were evil, because in their pride they resisted the physician and denied their sickness. The works of the latter, however, were good, because in humility they yielded to the physician and confessed their sickness.

This judgment is plainly also apparent in the Simoniacs and in those ordained through their hands, as one part of them wisely accepts the judgments pronounced by the holy Fathers against the Simoniacs, humbly revealing their guilt and asking for the appropriate remedy, while another part foolishly resists, arrogantly defending its fault and insisting that it has no need of a remedy. Nor is this surprising, since without doubt they belong to that generation which, according to Solomon, appears clean in its own eyes but is not considered washed from its filth (Prov. 30:12).

When this generation perceives that its falsehood is overcome and refuted by truth, it does not cease to cover it with clouds, and it endeavors to invalidate God’s command on account of its own invention. Those whom the Truth refutes in the Gospel belonged, in any case, to this same generation, when he says:

> “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who say: ‘Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound by his oath.’ Blind men, which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold? And whoever swears by the altar, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gift that is upon it is bound by his oath. Blind men, which is greater, the gift or the altar that sanctifies the gift?” (Matt. 23:16–19).

They are rightly called blind and hypocrites, because they oppose the divine law, which bears witness:

> “Whoever touches the temple and the altar shall be sanctified” (Exod. 29:37),

and they shamelessly seek to persuade people that the sanctifying element is nothing, and that only the things sanctified ought to be valued and considered.

The present-day Simoniacs, their followers, when they are reproved for trafficking in sanctification—or in the Holy Spirit, the sanctifier of human beings—take refuge in another corner of their falsehood and from there disgorge these useless clouds of excuses. Far be it that a hireling should contend that he purchased ecclesiastical consecration rather than ecclesiastical property alone, as though, treading the Pharisees’ path in reverse, he maintained that only the sanctifier ought to be honored, while the things sanctified are nothing.

Since in the preceding discussion we labored with all our strength to defend the sanctifier against them, let us now, guided by that same Holy Spirit, undertake to defend the things sanctified.

First, let us examine what sort of thing is the argument by which some of the aforementioned traffickers try to disguise and defend themselves, or rather to establish and confirm their heresy: they claim that they purchased for money not the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit but only the visible property of the churches, because they happened to receive consecration from the metropolitan free of charge.

They would not make this claim if they possessed even a spark of prudence or the slightest sense of shame. But because they neither understand nor blush, they sew together, like our first parents, from the leaves of the fig tree cursed by the Lord, short and fluttering aprons for “excuses in sins” (Ps. 140:4), and put them over their shameful parts as they are to be cast out from God’s paradise under the ban.

Since this cloak of their falsehood is short, it cannot cover both parts at once: if they try to cover their head with it, they immediately uncover their feet; if they cover their feet, they uncover their head at the same time. Their action or intention is exposed either at the beginning or at the end.

If they wished to purchase only the patrimony or revenues of the Church, why do they immediately after the sale and purchase invade the episcopal see and its authority, even though they have not been consecrated? Why do they leap from a lower grade to a higher one? Why do they pronounce episcopal judgments and counsels over offenders? By what right do they demand the consecration that is to be given to those canonically elected to the episcopate, unless it is because they cling to the ecclesiastical property that they previously purchased and do not trust that anyone will occupy the church above them?

If they purchase ecclesiastical resources only so that they may use them, why, not content with their use, do they additionally and shamelessly demand the blessing which, they say, they did not purchase?

Perhaps—though I do not think so—they will boldly say that when they bought the ecclesiastical estates, they did not know that they were for that reason also to be consecrated, but thought that they would possess what they had bought as laymen. Let them therefore show everyone that they did not know this at the time, and let them cease demanding episcopal grace, which, when they gave money for ecclesiastical property, they neither considered nor demanded.

And although they sacrilegiously possess only what they purchased, let them not presume to claim from it the justice due to bishops. Rather, like laymen, let them pay whatever is owed to bishops, not only from the revenues but also from the estates themselves. Let others receive consecration, episcopal authority, and the care of souls, which are plainly spiritual things and belong to invisible grace.

But they recognize what they certainly knew before they began trafficking: that the property of the churches belongs to bishops, and that they cannot retain it in any other way except under the episcopal habit and name. Therefore they demand the consecration which they previously bought along with the other goods of the churches, as though it were lawfully owed to them.

When a layman buys fields or lakes, does he not likewise buy whatever will freely come to him from them? Does he not also buy the cultivation by which he exercises possession?

CHAPTER II. Proof that possession is of no benefit without its privilege.

[Col. 1141D]

For if he does not purchase the cultivation itself—or rather, the permission to possess and cultivate—what benefit does the purchased possession provide him? He appears to have wished to waste his money and, in addition, to have purchased harsh injuries to himself and his own people, [lacuna], whenever he presumes to exercise the cultivation that he did not purchase along with the field.

From this it is entirely clear that no powerful person—or indeed no human being—purchases anything in comparable transactions except what is apparent. For example, someone purchases numerous cities, provinces, and kingdoms. What has he purchased in them except the permission to possess and rule?

Let us come down to smaller things. Someone purchases a horse. What does he purchase in it except the permission to possess it, ride it, and do with it whatever he wishes? Otherwise, what does anyone purchase? It is therefore clear that nothing is purchased except the permission to use or the use of the things that are sold.

Accordingly, let the Simoniac thieves stop whitewashing the gallows of their own condemnation. Rather, since they are parricides and fratricides, let them cease uselessly whitewashing the sack in which they are to be sewn up and punished, and let them at last, however late, learn that they purchased not ecclesiastical possessions but only the permission to possess them.

This permission is the episcopal blessing, as though it were the privilege of possession. Certainly, if an edict were issued somewhere requiring the following rule to be observed—that nothing there could be possessed by anyone without the subscription of the royal hand—what could one of these men be said to have purchased by right except the royal subscription, whether he obtained it freely or not freely? For without that permission the possession would not pass into his legal right, although it had been purchased.

Thus permission—whether free or purchased—transfers ownership of a possession to another person more fundamentally than an estate granted or purchased transfers permission. In this way episcopal dignity claims possession for itself rather than possession claiming episcopal dignity.

Yet the episcopal office is such that without those to whom its functions must be applied or entrusted, it is not an office at all—as if someone were said to have permission to cultivate a field but had no field to cultivate. Is not that permission superfluous and void?

By the same example, a bishop, who is called an overseer, will be no bishop if he lacks those over whom he is to preside. And what more need be said? Whatever is inseparably contained in anything cannot be sold or purchased separately from it.

Episcopal dignity contains things consecrated to God; it is also contained by them—or rather, in them—for they themselves have been consecrated by God. It is as though any subject contained its accidents in such a way that it too were more fundamentally contained by them.

Therefore, just as in all visible things, whenever they are sold, not only their visible matter is sold but also their substantial properties and accidents—which are themselves visible, although neither can be sold without the other—so too in things consecrated to God, in which the consecration, or sanctification, is sold even more than the things themselves. This sanctification is the grace of the Holy Spirit, invisible in itself, although the things themselves are also sold.

Finally, for example, whoever purchases a tree purchases its form more than its matter: its height, thickness, and, in brief, its quantity and quality, which are invisible in themselves, rather than the matter subjected to the senses through those forms. The same is true of one who purchases a horse, or a field, or anything of this kind.

CHAPTER III. On the decree of the Council of Chalcedon against the persons mentioned above.

The followers of Simon Magus have now been detected and refuted in many ways. Let them lay aside the frivolous tricks by which, while covering their natural masks and true faces, they mock and deceive anyone they can with impunity. Let them either come to their senses or perish alone, learning that God mocks those who mock.

Although we have sought to refute them by the preceding arguments of human knowledge, we nevertheless have at hand the divine judgments of the holy Fathers. These alone are sufficient to close their mouths and halt their evasions.

The holy and universal Council of Chalcedon (canon 2), by unanimous agreement, issued the same judgment concerning an *oikonomos*—that is, a steward promoted through money—as concerning a bishop or priest and the other ministers of the clerical order: the promoter is to be deposed, and the person promoted is to be excluded from the administration that he purchased with money; and the intermediaries in so shameful and wicked a giving and receiving, if they are clerics, are to be deposed. If they are laymen or monks, they are to be anathematized.

Do you think, Simoniac—do you understand—that your cloak has been stripped from you by a heavenly breath, and that you have been left naked beneath the winter lightning from above? Do you feel yourself pierced by the beam-like weapons of six hundred and thirty Fathers, and do you understand how much less you have by purchasing ecclesiastical administration or stewardship than those who purchased consecration itself?

Behold: the steward sought to administer ecclesiastical property, not to be consecrated for a price—for a steward is not consecrated—and yet, if he is promoted for money, he incurs the same condemnation as a bishop or priest promoted for money.

Why is this so, unless it is because the Holy Spirit operates not only in the greatest but also in the smallest offices of ecclesiastical administration? The faithful steward had learned this by experience, when he said:

> “Let a man regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Here, moreover, what is sought among stewards is [lacuna]: that one be found faithful” (1 Cor. 4:1–2).

Finally, wishing the Corinthians not to be ignorant concerning spiritual matters, he says:

> “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of activities, but the same God who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:4–6).

Immediately afterward, in accordance with what he had seen when he was caught up into the third heaven—the orders of the nine heavenly ranks—he likewise enumerated nine distributions of grace in this kingdom of heaven of ours, that is, in the present Church, and added:

> “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11).

Consider that the Apostle, who had first comprehended spiritual graces under the number three, soon expands them into the number nine. He signifies that, in imitation of the blessed Trinity, only three varieties of people are found in the Church of this age: teachers, continent persons, and married persons.

Nevertheless, if these three are considered according to the diversity of their offices, as though according to persons, nine varieties of people are plainly found in this Church, after the pattern of the heavenly army, as the venerable Father Dionysius the Areopagite carefully and sufficiently attests in his writings *On the Celestial Hierarchy*.

CHAPTER IV. On the sanctification that sanctifies ecclesiastical property, followed by testimonies of the holy Fathers.

[Col. 1144A]

It is therefore not surprising that a steward of any ecclesiastical property, however insignificant, who has been promoted through money is condemned by the ecclesiastical regulations together with his promoters and intermediaries, even if he is not consecrated, as though he had been consecrated.

For whatever serves the sanctuary and altar and is assigned to their uses must necessarily be holy. If these things are holy, as they truly are, they must possess holiness and sanctification within themselves, because they are holy. Holiness, however, or sanctification, neither is nor can be without the Holy Spirit; indeed, it is the Holy Spirit himself.

Just as anyone who is wise or chaste must possess wisdom or chastity within himself because he is wise or chaste, so it is clear that sanctification or holiness—that is, the Holy Spirit—is present in sanctified or holy things and persons.

Therefore, whoever sells or buys an ecclesiastical stipend or benefice unquestionably sells or buys the Holy Spirit—not in the sense that the Holy Spirit himself is possessed in the thing sold or purchased, or together with it, but in the sense that he is offended by the thing he had sanctified, departs from it, and leaves it open to be polluted by an unclean spirit.

This agrees with what is said through Malachi:

> “Judah has profaned the sanctification of the Lord, which he loved” (Mal. 2:11).

For sanctification itself cannot be polluted. Rather, by metonymy, what contains something is said to be polluted in place of what is contained. Here, the thing that sanctification had previously sanctified is polluted in the manner just described.

That one should not pray for such persons as long as they have not repented, Saint Jerome plainly shows in his commentary on this same prophet:

> “Since they have done this, the prophet’s word is directed against them, and they are drawn back from sin by curses. He did not say, ‘May the Lord curse the one who has done this,’ but ‘whoever shall do it,’ extending the curse into the future so that sinners may be summoned to repentance. ‘Teacher,’ he says, ‘and disciple—whether he is a priest or a Levite—shall be struck by one curse. And as for the one who offers a gift to the Lord of hosts,’ the implied meaning is: ‘May the Lord destroy the one who wishes to offer a gift at the altar for such men,’ whose sole remedy is not to do what they have done.”

In this learned man’s severe and exact judgment, observe what those deserve who pollute things sanctified to God by conducting business with them. Through their traffic, what is sacred becomes secular, as blessed Gregory teaches.

Because they steal sacred things—that is, they commit theft—they are rightly called sacrilegious. They steal sanctification by removing or seizing the things that it sanctified, taking it away with such fraud that, like an unwary man who has suffered theft, they pretend to have become rich through ecclesiastical possession while now possessing none of it.

Such sacrilegious people are certainly to be avoided.

[Note: This letter of Pope Pius I, as also the following letters of Urban, Lucius, and Stephen, was forged by Isidore Mercator.]

Pope Pius, pontiff of the apostolic see, thus denounces them, saying (Epistle 2):

> “Every insult must be removed from all usurpations of that sort, lest estates dedicated to the heavenly mysteries be harassed by certain persons who invade them. But if anyone should presume to do so, let him be considered a sacrilegious person and judged as a sacrilegious person. We have heard that those who do this persecute and defame clerics and priests of the Lord, adding evil to evil and becoming worse, because they do not understand that the Church of God consists in its priests and grows into the temple of God. And just as one who ravages the Church of God, strips and invades its estates and offerings, becomes sacrilegious, so one who persecutes its priests is guilty of sacrilege and is judged sacrilegious.”

And blessed Pope Urban says (Epistle 2):

> “Ecclesiastical property is called the offerings of the faithful because it is offered to the Lord. Therefore it must not be converted to any uses other than ecclesiastical ones, or to the common life of Christian brothers who wish to live together, or to the support of the needy, because these are the vows of the faithful and the prices of sins, handed over to the Lord for the fulfillment of the work mentioned above. But if anyone—God forbid!—acts otherwise, let him beware lest he receive the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira and become guilty of sacrilege, like those who defrauded the price of the property mentioned above.”

And shortly afterward:

> “These things, brothers, must be greatly avoided and feared, because the property of the Church must be faithfully distributed, with the greatest fear, not as private possessions but as common things offered to the Lord, and not for uses other than those mentioned above. Otherwise those who remove them from the place where they were entrusted will incur the guilt of sacrilege and become *anathema maranatha*—accursed, ‘the Lord has come’—and, if not in body, as Ananias and Sapphira did when they fell dead, then in the soul, which is more important than the body, they will be separated from the fellowship of the faithful, fall, and sink into the depths of the abyss.

> “If anyone does this, then, after the severity of the deserved vengeance that is rightly to be inflicted upon sacrilegious persons, he is condemned to perpetual infamy and handed over to prison, or thrust into perpetual exile and deportation. For, according to the Apostle, such a person must be handed over to Satan, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord (1 Cor. 5:5).”

Blessed Pope Lucius likewise says (Epistle 6):

> “The property of your churches and the offerings of the faithful, which you indicate are being harassed by certain invaders and taken away from you and your churches, is unquestionably a very great sin, as Scripture bears witness, saying: ‘Whoever takes anything from his father or mother and says, “This is not a sin,” is a partner of a murderer.’ Our father, therefore, is without doubt God, who created us, and our mother is the Church, which spiritually gave us birth in baptism. Thus whoever takes away, defrauds, or seizes the money of Christ and of the Church will be regarded as a murderer in the sight of the just Judge.

> “Hence it is written: ‘Whoever seizes his neighbor’s money commits iniquity.’ Whoever takes away the money or property of the Church commits sacrilege. Thus Judas, who defrauded the money intended for the uses of the Church—that is, for the poor whom the Church ought to feed—became, by the Savior’s command—he in whose place bishops stand—not only a thief but also a sacrilegious person.

> “Concerning such men, that is, those who seize, defraud, or take away the resources of the Church, the Lord issues a threatening word through the Prophet to all, saying: ‘O God, who is like you? Do not be silent or restrained, O God. For behold, your enemies have made a sound, and those who hate you have raised their heads,’ and so forth to the end of the psalm (Ps. 82:2).

> “The decrees of the prophets, the apostles, and all the Catholic Fathers who succeeded them forbid such things and judge such presumptions to be sacrileges. Following their examples, by apostolic authority we repel all such presumptuous persons, robbers of the Church, and alienators for the sake of their own pleasures, from the thresholds of the holy mother Church, together with you; we anathematize and condemn them, and judge them to be sacrilegious.

> “And not only them, but also all who consent to them, because not only those who do such things are judged guilty, but also those who consent to those who do them (Rom. 1:32). The same punishment seizes both the perpetrators and those who consent.”

Of these persons blessed Pope Stephen and martyr likewise says:

> “We declare those persons infamous who are marked with infamy for some fault, that is, those who reject the norm of Christian law and despise ecclesiastical decrees. Likewise, thieves, sacrilegious persons, and all those entangled in capital crimes,” and so forth.

The same author, in the passage cited above, says:

> “Whatever is unjustly done concerning the sacred things of God and concerning bishops will be regarded as sacrilege, because they are sacred and may not be violated by anyone.”

Again:

> “Although laymen may be religious, no authority to dispose of anything from ecclesiastical resources is ever recorded as having been granted to them.”

CHAPTER V. How the Simoniacs attack the Church of God through their traffic, and how nearly all laymen and clerics continually seek to conduct business from the Church.

These decretal judgments of blessed pontiffs and martyrs, signed with their blood, make it clearer than the sun that invaders and devastators of ecclesiastical property are infamous, thieves, sacrilegious persons, even murderers, excommunicated, and to be handed over to perpetual imprisonment or exile.

Let the hypocrites go, then, and shamelessly insist that they purchased not ecclesiastical consecration but the property of the Church. And lest they still try to disguise themselves by claiming that they did not rush upon, invade, or harass ecclesiastical property, let them learn that they do—or have done—all these things when, through the price they pay, they break through the immunity and privileges of such property, privileges confirmed by the holy Fathers, and presume—or have presumed—to claim for themselves the use of what is owed to ecclesiastical persons and to the poor.

For just as robbers rush into other people’s houses with weapons, and thieves with ladders or any kind of contrivance, and seize for themselves by force or fraud what belongs to another’s legal right, so these men attack and conquer the churches of God with their money, as though with weapons and machines, and claim for themselves what was owed to the ecclesiastical household.

If some criminal were to invade another man’s bride, together with all her possessions, after giving or promising money to her most unjust and avaricious guardian, would he not truly be said to have attacked and conquered both that money and all the bride’s possessions, and would he not rightly be convicted? The guilt of this presumption is punished by the sacred canons with excommunication lasting until death—both for the ravisher and the guardian, and for all their supporters—and by secular laws with blood or perpetual exile.

From this punishment one can understand how despised the bride of Christ is considered, since no one who grieves over her injuries is found; no one defends her chastity when it has been prostituted, sold, and handed over to sacrilegious ravishers; no one even rescues her from them and restores her to the Bridegroom, whether violated or not.

And is Jesus thought destined to endure this forever—Jesus whom now no ecclesiastical or lay person deigns to look upon or hear as he complains of the rape of his bride? Yet when his complaint is rejected by judges and patrons, however abject he may be, he often avenges the rape of his bride by every means available, even by the most dreadful flames.

What, I ask, remains for the bride of Christ except, wasting away under an intolerable and incurable calamity, to console herself, if she can, with that desperate saying:

> “My father sold me; the king purchased me. To whom shall I complain? Who among them will do me justice?”

For from whom will she now be redeemed, when she is sold by the very people to whose protection, after God, she had been entrusted?

From the highest rank of the Church to the lowest, no one ceases to conduct business for himself with ecclesiastical property. Emperors, kings, princes, judges, and all who possess any power in the world practice this above all and seek it—those who ought to defend ecclesiastical property by ecclesiastical right and with the spiritual sword, and those who ought to do so with the material sword.

They do not consider how criminal and detestable before God and human beings they become when they squander what they undertook to protect for Christ’s poor. If the guardian of any orphan sold the little patrimony entrusted to him for safekeeping for his own profit, or gave it away according to his pleasure, or knowingly and deliberately transferred the guardianship entrusted to him to some spendthrift who would destroy the substance left to the orphan, would he not be regarded and judged by everyone as abominable and murderous?

How abominable, then, and guilty of how many murders must we think those persons are who, according to their pleasure, squander the patrimony of the churches whose guardians they have been appointed by him to whom the poor man has been entrusted (Ps. 10:14), who is also the father of orphans and judge of widows (Ps. 67:6)?

Thus it is that the kings and princes of the world, appointed as protectors and defenders of God’s churches, abandon the office entrusted to them from above. They carry the sword which, as ministers of God and judges, they are supposed to display in anger against every wrongdoer, but with which they procure either never, or scarcely ever, the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good (1 Pet. 2:14).

Would that they grew so cold or lukewarm toward this office of theirs that they did not grow hot or burn with eagerness to command what belongs to another!

Having abandoned the military task by which they ought to protect the state and their homeland from external attacks, and likewise having abandoned the judicial authority of their laws, whose force and terror oblige them to restrain violators of divine and human justice from internal and daily offenses, they transfer all their power, all their terror, and all their zeal to attacking and wholly claiming for themselves the ecclesiastical property over which they had been appointed guardians.

Not content with their own court, they enter the ecclesiastical court, preside over it, and rule the synod. Terrible through earthly power, they make everything proceed and be determined according to their nod and judgment.

They take precedence over primates and metropolitans in the election of bishops. Those primates and metropolitans ought merely to confirm, in accordance with God, the consent and desire of the clergy, the people, and every order of the city, as blessed Pope Celestine teaches (Epistle 2):

> “Let foreigners and outsiders who have served in their own churches, and those who were previously unknown, not be placed over those who have deserved well of the testimony of their fellow citizens. Let no bishop be given against the will of the people. The consent and desire of the clergy, the people, and the order must be sought.

> “Only then should someone be chosen from another church if, among the clerics of the city in which the bishop is to be ordained, no worthy person can be found—which we do not believe can happen. First, the local candidates must be rejected before someone from another church is deservedly preferred.

> “Let each person enjoy the fruit of his service in the Church in which he has spent his life through all the offices. Let no one seize another’s stipend in a foreign church, nor let one person otherwise dare to claim another’s deserved reward. Let the clerics have the freedom to resist if they see themselves being oppressed, and let them not fear to reject what they recognize as extraordinary. For they ought to have either the reward due to them or a free judgment concerning the person who is to govern them.”

Agreeing with him, blessed Pope Leo, pope and teacher, says:

> “No reason permits those to be counted among the bishops who were neither elected by the clerics, nor sought by the peoples, nor consecrated by the bishops of the province together with the judgment of the metropolitan,” and so forth.

CHAPTER VI. On staffs and rings given through the hands of secular authorities.

When these venerable supreme pontiffs, esteemed throughout the world, had decreed all this under the direction of the Holy Spirit—namely, that the election of a cleric should take place with the metropolitan’s judgment, while the consent of the prince was sought, and the approval of the people and clergy was confirmed—everything is done in an inverted order, in violation of the holy canons and in trampling upon the whole Christian religion; the first become last, and the last first. For secular power is first in electing and confirming, and the consent of the order, the people, and the clergy follows it, whether it wishes this or not; finally comes the metropolitan’s judgment. [Col. 1149A] Hence those promoted in this manner, as is declared above, are not to be counted among the bishops, because their appointment hangs downward from its head: what ought to have been done last was done first, and by those to whom it belonged not at all.

For what does it concern lay persons to distribute the ecclesiastical sacraments and the pontifical or pastoral grace—namely, the curved staffs and rings by which the whole episcopal consecration is chiefly completed, carried out, and supported? Indeed, in the curved staffs—hooked and bent above for drawing and inviting, but pointed and armed below for driving back and striking—the pastoral care entrusted to them is signified. Their very construction admonishes future pastors that they should be upright and straightforward, yet gently lower and bend the lofty and rigid [Col. 1149B] summit of their action or contemplation, so as to imitate and draw the flock of God to themselves. Even so, they must always attend to themselves also and never turn the gaze of their mind away from consideration of themselves. Their end indicates that they are to terrify the undisciplined by stern rebuke and, if they prove obstinate, drive them from the Church by a final sentence. The Apostle briefly expresses all this as follows: “We exhort you: reprove the restless, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, and be patient toward all” (1 Thess. 5:14).

Moreover, the ring indicates the seal of heavenly secrets, warning preachers, with the Apostle, to designate [or: “make known”; the reading *disignent* is uncertain] the hidden wisdom of God and to speak among the mature (1 Cor. 2:6–7); they should withhold it, as though sealed, [Col. 1149C] from the imperfect, who still need not solid food but only milk (Heb. 5:12). Or else the ring signifies that, as friends of the Bridegroom, they should continually present and commend the one faith of his bride, which is the Church.

Whoever, therefore, initiates someone with these two objects undoubtedly claims for himself, by this presumption, the whole of pastoral authority. For after this investiture, what free judgment can the clergy, the people, the order, or the metropolitan who is to consecrate such men still exercise over these rulers, once they have already been appointed, except to connive? Thus, having first been invested, the violent intruder invades the clergy, the people, and the order in order to rule them before he is known, sought, or accepted by them. Thus he approaches the metropolitan, not to be judged by him but to judge him; for he [Col. 1149D] no longer seeks or receives the metropolitan’s judgment, but merely demands and extorts the service which alone has been left to him in prayer and anointing.

What benefit is it now to return to him the staff and ring that he carries? Is it because they were given by a lay person? Yet baptism given by a layman is not repeated; rather, if the recipient survives, what is lacking is supplied by a priest through prayer and anointing. Without these, unless the person survives, he undoubtedly enters the kingdom of heaven, just as no one does so without the washing of water. Hence it is clear that the whole episcopal office is given to them in the ring and staff. Without the imitation and episcopal authority represented by these, they cannot exercise it, [Col. 1150A] although it is evident that the holy apostles received this without visible anointing, solely through the assignment of pastoral care, which is visibly shown and conferred by the ring and staff.

I ask, then, why is what has been received returned, unless either ecclesiastical property is once more sold under the appearance of such a command or gift, or the earlier sale is ratified by the metropolitan and his suffragans subscribing to it, or at least the presumption of lay ordination is concealed beneath the color and some sort of veil of clerical discipline? If this has not happened and does not happen, let anyone accuse me here of lying. But what is more serious is that this is not merely remembered and proclaimed as something done in earlier times; it is also seen and known to be customary in our own. Did not the princes of this world first sell, and do they not still sell, ecclesiastical property under the false name of investiture, and then sell it to the metropolitan under the terms of consecration?

## CHAPTER VII. On the age of the Ottos, the zeal of Emperor Henry, and the wickedness of the king of the Franks

[Col. 1150B]

To say nothing further of earlier centuries, the memory of many people still retains the madness of this reciprocal sale, which spread throughout Germany, Gaul, and all Italy from the time of the Ottos up to the emperor of august and blessed memory, Henry, son of Conrad. During his own days, he somewhat removed so great a sacrilege both from himself and from the ecclesiastical persons of the empire entrusted to him, although it pressed upon him greatly and he desired to remove it altogether. Prevented from fulfilling this excellent desire of his heart by an untimely death, he was, as is believed, [Col. 1150C] transferred to the kingdom of eternal life either for this intention alone or, as it were, for the purity of his eye, since he was also praised for many other good qualities.

His contemporary and namesake, the destroyer of western Francia and tyrant against God, acts in the opposite manner. Like the son of perdition and the Antichrist, he opposes Christ, whose grace he attacks and does not cease to assail throughout all the regions under his rule. By this merit of his he is thought to be the tail of the dragon whom he follows, the dragon that has dragged and continues to drag, has cast and continues to cast, innumerable and glorious stars of heaven—that is, the churches of the Franks—into a dark earth covered by the shadow of death.

May the Holy Spirit, against whom he sins without interruption more than Simon Magus did, either quickly bring him to remorse and correction or quickly remove him from the midst by striking him down, lest he continue too long to inflict upon that same Holy Spirit so many blasphemies and injuries, to the increase of his own [Col. 1150D] condemnation and the destruction of holy Christianity. God permitted him to reign on account of the sins of the people, so that through him those who were reckoned Christians in name only might be dragged completely into the devil’s lot.

That lost man, the destroyer, openly and obstinately resists Christ to this day like another Julian. Although he has been admonished and rebuked many times concerning such apostasy by the pontiffs of the apostolic see, the lords Leo and Victor, of reverend memory, he grows worse each day and, rebellious against God and his priests, scorns putting an end to his wickedness. He is also harmful to the land which he occupies like a barren tree. His imitators, equals, and accomplices with this profane money dare to approach and frequent the thresholds of Simon [Col. 1151A] Peter, believing that they can please him with money acquired against his judgment, following the example of Simon Magus. They do not fear that, together with him, the Prince of the Apostles may say to them: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts 8:20).

Their money, whatever its amount, is now made unclean whenever simoniacal money comes near it and touches it. But let us return to the subject.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the fourfold sale among the Latins, and on the devotion of the great Constantine toward the clergy

Ecclesiastical property is therefore sold everywhere and in scattered places: first by princes and their associates, then by metropolitans and their associates. Neither sale, of course, takes place without intermediaries. [Col. 1151B] How much more tolerable would the selling be if, at least following the example of the Eastern and transmarine Church, it were carried out only by the metropolitans and their associates, since it would then be sold only twice rather than four times.

Although the churches of the Constantinopolitan Empire are harassed by errors of many kinds, they are nevertheless known to be entirely free of this particular abuse. Indeed, as I established by hearing and sight, and further learned from the mouth of the emperor Constantine Monomachus, of orthodox memory, while I was stationed in that royal city as a representative of the apostolic see, neither the emperor himself nor any layman presumes to make any disposition concerning churches, ecclesiastical ordinations, or ecclesiastical properties. Rather, once these matters have been left, everything is left to be arranged by the metropolitans and ecclesiastical persons. [Col. 1151C] This has been so from the time of the great and first Constantine, who issued a memorable judgment on these matters, revered by all Catholics.

For when he presided over the holy synod assembled at Nicaea and saw that the complaint of certain persons had been brought before him, he said: “You can be judged by no one, because you are reserved for the judgment of God alone. For you have been called gods; therefore you cannot be judged by human beings. Go, and settle your cases among yourselves, because it is not fitting that we should judge gods.”

For this reason the holy synod itself promulgated the following: [Col. 1151D] “It is an ancient custom that the bishop of the city of Rome should hold the primacy and govern the suburban districts and the whole province through his care. The bishop of Alexandria, likewise, shall have care of all those who are in Egypt. Similarly, the proper privileges of the metropolitan churches shall be preserved both around Antioch and in the other provinces.”

Moreover, we think that what is found inserted in the decrees of the Roman pontiffs concerning ecclesiastical property and business should also be inserted here. It is as follows.

No one who reads the divine Scriptures is unaware that, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, when the disciples were gathered together with the multitude of believers, among whom there was one heart and one soul (Acts 4:32), they sold their estates and possessions, brought the proceeds, and distribution was made to each according to his need (Acts 2:45). The apostles foresaw that the future Church would be among the Gentiles, especially because the Lord had foretold to them: [Col. 1152A] “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel” (Mark 16:15). Or, because they knew that they would be driven out of Judaea and scattered among the Gentiles, and that the Church would be gathered from an unformed people, they acquired no estates in Judaea, but only money for the support of the needy.

But when the Church grew amid the storms and adversities of the world, it reached such a point that not only the Gentiles but also the Roman princes, who held the monarchy of nearly the whole world, hastened to the faith of Christ and the sacraments of baptism. Among them, the deeply religious man Constantine the First, having openly embraced the faith of truth, granted permission to all who lived under his rule throughout the world not only to become Christians but also to build churches, and he established that estates should be granted for this purpose.

[Col. 1152B] Finally, that same prince instituted immense gifts and the construction of the church of the first see of blessed Peter, the Prince of the Apostles. He went so far as to abandon the imperial seat over which the Roman princes had presided and to grant it for the benefit of blessed Peter and his bishops.

From that time onward, religious men consecrated to the Lord not only the possessions and estates they had owned but also themselves, building basilicas on their own lands in honor of the holy martyrs throughout cities and monasteries, where communities of those serving the Lord might assemble. Finally, kings, governors, and magistrates not only granted this permission but also gave from their own resources throughout all the kingdoms of the earth, so that the needy [Col. 1152C] who possessed nothing in the world might be fed, churches might be built and restored, and the provisions necessary for the servants and ministers who rightly served God and his Church might be supplied without want.

By receiving these things, they could, according to the Apostle’s instructions, offer prayers, petitions, supplications, and thanksgivings for all people, for kings, and for all who are in high positions, so that they might lead a quiet and peaceful life. The same teacher of the Gentiles declares that this is good and acceptable before God (1 Tim. 2:1–3). He was the one upon whom the care of all the churches rested (2 Cor. 11:28), and who appointed bishops through the Holy Spirit to govern the Church of God (Acts 20:28). To them he says: [Col. 1152D] “Tend the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion but willingly according to God, and not for shameful gain but eagerly” (1 Pet. 5:2). “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business” (2 Tim. 2:4).

What secular business is, the holy canons make clear and prohibit in the following terms:

“Since it is evident that certain men who appear to have been chosen into the clergy for the sake of shameful profits become leaseholders of other people’s possessions and undertake secular business under their care, making light of the ministry of God while running about the houses of secular people and, on account of greed, assuming responsibility for patrimonies, the aforesaid synod has decreed that henceforth no cleric shall lease possessions or involve himself in secular business, except on behalf of wards, orphans, and widows, or if perhaps the bishop of the city should order him to care for ecclesiastical property.” Here it is plainly evident that some businesses are secular and others ecclesiastical.

[Col. 1153A] Was Moses not in the world when he repeatedly entered and left the tabernacle? Within, he was carried away into contemplation; outside, he was pressed by the affairs of the weak. Within, he contemplated the mysteries of God; outside, he bore the burdens of the carnal (Exod. 34:34–35). Priests ought to enact his figure in the Church, so that when they go out to conduct business for the needs of their subjects, they may return inwardly to themselves through contemplation of the commandments.

So did Paul, who was joined to heavenly secrets and yet, through the compassion of condescension, examined the bedchamber of the carnal. [Col. 1153B] So did Jacob, who saw angels ascending and descending (Gen. 28:12), since the rulers of the Church not only seek God through contemplation but also descend in compassion toward his members. While priests imitate the deeds of these men, they both guard themselves and bear the burdens of their subjects. They appear to be such as the same outstanding Paul commands: those who use this world as though they did not use it, those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice, and those who buy as though they did not possess (1 Cor. 7:30–31).

## CHAPTER IX. On the distinction between clerics and laymen, and on the zeal of blessed Gregory in such matters
