From these considerations we are likewise taught that, just as clerics are forbidden to presume upon secular business, so laymen are forbidden to presume upon ecclesiastical matters. And just as clerics are separated from laymen, so laymen are removed from clerics, from the right of mutual accusation and testimony. [Col. 1153C] Just as clerics are distinguished from laymen by dress and profession, so they must also be distinguished in conduct and manner of life, so that neither may seize for himself the office or hereditary lot of the other. Each must observe the boundaries established by the holy Fathers and orthodox princes.

For just as clerics and laymen must be separated and recognized by their places and offices even within the walls of basilicas, so they must be separated and recognized outside them by their business. Therefore laymen should arrange and administer only their own affairs—that is, secular affairs—while clerics should arrange and administer only their own affairs—that is, ecclesiastical affairs.

Each has rules prescribed for this purpose, both by the holy pope and martyr Stephen and by the other pontiffs and councils of the holy Fathers, as well as by Catholic princes. This is sufficiently demonstrated in the Deeds of blessed Gregory, where we read:

[Col. 1153D] “No layman shall administer any ministry of the sacred Lateran palace or any ecclesiastical patrimony. Rather, men of the clergy shall undertake all the functions belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction, while laymen are assigned only military service with weapons or the continual care of lands.”

For this reason some of the nobles first began to have themselves tonsured under the pretext of religion. Emperor Maurice prudently countered their evasion. Through a law issued by Longinus the Strator, he ordered that whoever was entangled in administrative offices should not be permitted to enter ecclesiastical office. Gregory greatly praised this law, saying: [Col. 1154A] “He who, while wearing secular dress, hastens to ecclesiastical offices does not wish to abandon the world but to change it.”

This blessed pontiff also appointed industrious men of his Church as administrators of patrimonies in various provinces, for the protection of sacred religion and the vigorous governance of the affairs of the poor. Among them were Cyprian the Deacon, administrator of the Sicilian patrimony; Pantaleon the notary, administrator of the Syracusan patrimony; and the others named there, down to Candidus the priest, of the Gallican [patrimony].

For this reason he also wrote to Januarius of Cagliari, among other things, as follows:

“It has been reported to us that you have entrusted the care of your patrimony to certain laymen. Henceforth your Fraternity must take care that the property of the Church is not entrusted to secular men, or to those who do not live under your [Col. 1154B] rule, but to approved clerics from your own office. If any wrongdoing should be found in them, you will be able to correct in your subjects whatever illicit conduct has occurred. Their own manner of life, moreover, ought to suit their office more than excuse them.”

Writing also to the Emperor Maurice concerning priests, he says among other things:

“May our Lord not be quick to become angry with priests because of earthly power; rather, with excellent consideration, because of him whose servants they are, let him rule them in such a way that he also pays them the reverence that is due. For in the divine utterances priests are sometimes called gods and sometimes angels, and so forth, down to ‘they served at the stones.’” [The concluding wording is fragmentary in the supplied text.]

[Col. 1154C] It is also shown by other statements of that same pontiff that the ordinations of bishops were carried out with his judgment and consent. This appears unmistakably from two letters in which, writing to the people and clergy, he orders as follows:

“Since, by God’s authority, the apostolic see is acknowledged to be set above all the churches, so among its many concerns it is especially solicitous where our decision is awaited for the consecration of a bishop. Therefore, after Laurence, bishop of the Church of Milan, had died, … down to ‘may he not diminish.’”

But several years later, when Constantius, having served his distinguished pontificate, had fallen asleep in the Lord, the clergy and people of Milan chose the deacon Deusdedit, but were frightened by King Agilulf into choosing the man whom the barbarian of the Lombards wished. They sent their decree to Gregory and requested his counsel. He replied to them, among other things:

[Col. 1154D] “Let what you report as having been written to you by Agilulf not disturb your affection, … down to ‘was ordained.’”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, in the matter of ordaining, … down to ‘be consecrated.’”

## CHAPTER X. How much freer the Greek Church is from lay power than the Latin Church

Thus, as has been said, these statutes of the holy Fathers and religious princes concerning ecclesiastical persons and property have until now been inviolably observed in the transmarine empire, and such matters have been left to the metropolitans alone, or to the other bishops, for arrangement.

Accordingly, every ecclesiastical administration is arranged solely according to their judgment, whether they wish to entrust it to any cleric freely or for payment. [Col. 1155A] Nor is it customary for it to be sold except by the metropolitans or bishops and their associates. Although such sale is heretical and utterly detestable even when it occurs only once, it is nevertheless more tolerable for those churches of God than for ours, which, as has been shown above, are continually sold four times.

For the arrogance and greed of the princes of our age and empire cannot endure being confined within fixed limits. Having transgressed divine and human laws—which are silent amid arms—they presume to possess everything, including ecclesiastical property, so that no cleric can live in or derive a livelihood from it without giving or selling something to them.

The result is that those who ought to be freer than all human beings—for God himself is their portion and inheritance, and they in turn are God’s lot—become more contemptible than everyone else. [Col. 1155B] For however lowly a layman’s servant or hired laborer may be, he is compelled to serve no one except the person to whom he belongs and is subject only to him, while remaining free from others with regard to his own affairs. Likewise, the possession of any ordinary or wealthy layman is subject only to the lord to whom it belongs; it is neither invaded nor sold by any prince.

Only the clerics and the Church are exposed to the calumny, violence, power, and plunder of everyone, to such an extent that if laymen happen to bestow anything upon the churches of God for the redemption of their souls, it immediately becomes an object of calumny and sale, although it had previously been peaceably possessed by those very donors.

And by whom are these things most forcibly claimed and sold, if not by those who profess to be the advocates or defenders of the churches of God? [Col. 1155C] By the emperors themselves, by the princes themselves, and by their satellites. Under the name and pretext of defense, they presume to claim for themselves, alienate, or sell not only the churches but also everything belonging to them, whether property, persons, or offices.

Let them therefore, when corrected, consider how much less they revere God than they revere human beings subject to them, whose possessions they fear and take care not to invade. They think that they must yield to the human beings beneath them, while they do not consider that they must yield to God above them. They fear and blush before men whose earthly or civil rights they preserve, while they neither revere nor blush before God, to whom they reserve neither earthly right nor heavenly law.

[Col. 1155D] Although they do not hesitate to make themselves sacrilegious toward God, whose inheritance they claim for themselves, they desire to be called and regarded by human beings as religious and Catholic princes, when in truth they are enemies of God, against whom they conspire with one accord in order to possess his sanctuary as an inheritance.

Therefore, according to what the Psalmist prophetically invokes, they must be made like Horeb, Zob, Zebee, and Salmana, who were princes of foreigners and enemies of the Israelites (Ps. 82:12). Let the princes of our time, who follow their wickedness, see where they have been brought.

Indeed, as is clearly evident from the preceding statements of blessed Gregory, the ambition of the treacherous Simon has already brought them to the point that their rule now weighs more intolerably upon the Catholic churches than did the former tyranny of the Lombards.

[Col. 1156A] For although the Lombards were then barbarians and Arians—and although their king Agilulf was exceedingly hostile to Roman liberty and dignity—neither they nor Agilulf attempted to resist the Roman pontiff when he appointed the metropolitan of the Church of Milan according to the ancient and canonical privileges of his apostolic see. The king’s consent and the desire of his people did not prejudice the matter, nor did they extort from the apostolic prelate his judgment concerning the election of metropolitans, even though by the power of arms and the cruelty of their barbarism they devastated and terrified the whole Italian land and, what is even more serious, persecuted every Catholic in their Arian madness.

[Col. 1156B] Indeed, he preserved this privilege not only in Italy, which was then overrun by barbarians and Arians, but also in Germany and throughout Gaul, as is clearly proclaimed in his deeds and sayings.

## CHAPTER XI. How and by whom the churches were deprived of their privileges

This solid and special canonical authority was reserved to the Roman pontiffs in all metropolitan churches, and likewise to all metropolitans in their suffragan churches, as anyone who searches the Deeds of blessed Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, will find.

Neither King Pippin nor his son, the great Charles, the first emperor of the Franks, attempted to violate this canon. Nor did any of their great-grandsons or heirs of the kingdom and empire do so, down to the time of the Ottos.

[Col. 1156C] When these men began to grow and advance toward imperial power, the strength of the Roman pontiffs began to diminish and fail, to such an extent that, through their cowardice and ignorance and through the arrogance of inexperienced princes, the whole ecclesiastical office and jurisdiction was gradually snatched and extorted from their hands. They struggled to retain scarcely the empty name of their former dignity, not the dignity itself.

Thus, when the head of the clerical order had been weakened and cast down, secular power soon usurped the whole body for itself, to be subjected to its will, with impunity. At first it did not seize all ecclesiastical things at once and together, but separately and little by little, as is customary with other forms of wickedness.

[Col. 1156D] First it favored those greedy for ecclesiastical dignities or possessions by entreaties, then by threats, and afterward by words of concession. Seeing in all this that no one opposed it—not one who would move a feather, open his mouth, or even squeak—it proceeded to greater things. Finally, under the name of investiture, it began first to give tablets or present whatever sort of rods it could, then staffs to laymen, and at last to ecclesiastics.

This greatest of crimes has now become so established that it alone is believed to be canonical, while no one knows or attends to what ecclesiastical discipline is. I certainly remember seeing some men invested by secular princes with pastoral staffs and rings for bishoprics and abbeys, while their metropolitans and primates, although present, were neither consulted nor bold enough to utter a protest.

[Col. 1157A] When these men were discovered amid such adultery of wives and slaughter of sons, the Mosaic curse befell them as a consequence of their negligence and transgression: “You shall take a wife, and another man shall sleep with her before your eyes” (Deut. 28:30). As blessed Jerome testifies in his Commentary on the Prophet Zechariah, nothing more cruel or more miserable can be found than that, through fear of their own death, men should not dare to defend either the safety of their children or the chastity of their wives.

The prophet Amos also speaks in threatening terms to Amaziah, the impious priest: “Your wife shall fornicate in the city, your sons and daughters shall fall by the sword, and your land shall be measured out by a measuring line” (Amos 7:17).

[Col. 1157B] The priest’s wife is unquestionably violated by others whenever the Church is administered or ordered by laymen to whom this does not belong. Its land, too, is measured out by a line whenever ecclesiastical property is alienated from the lot of the Lord’s priesthood and transferred to the lot and dominion of laymen.

If these men were defenders of the Church and not plunderers or invaders, they would surely not neglect to defend it against whatever fault or negligence belonged to the priests, nor would they claim its jurisdiction for themselves. For, as blessed Gregory teaches, the deed of an individual must not be turned into harm for the Church. Rather, the individual must be punished in such a way that ecclesiastical property remains entirely unharmed.

The Church has its own laws and its own judges, by whom, with the counsel of religious and wise men, the faults of its superiors and ministers may be rebuked or corrected. [Col. 1157C] If ecclesiastics disregard these matters or pay no attention to them, then secular princes and faithful laymen must necessarily persevere in the defense and recovery that they owe to their mother, the Church. They must approach and admonish such men at opportune and inopportune times, lest by silence and concealment they favor the destroyers of the churches of God and the undisciplined; rather, they should rise together with them to restore the Church’s canons.

If they do not take care to resist the wicked even after admonition, let lay power at last do what degenerate sons of a free and beloved mother do when they discover that her chastity has been seized by adulterers: without delay they gird themselves to avenge her, even if their father, after being admonished, neglects to avenge so intolerable a wrong.

[Col. 1157D] Good sons, guarding against a stain upon their family and no small disgrace upon their name, do not cease to avenge the injuries done to their mother even when their father fails to act. But if, after rescuing her from the adulterers, they did not restore her to her lawful marriage and instead prostituted their mother’s chastity to their own lust, would they not be worse and more detestable than any adulterers? Would it not have been more tolerable not to have defended her from others than to seize and appropriate her for themselves after defending her?

I ask Christian princes and laymen to consider this with Christian piety and finally to recognize how much more disgraceful they are if they defend their spiritual mother in such a way that they do not restore her to her father but prostitute her solely to themselves. And to which father? To him, certainly, to whom no earthly father—not merely one who should be preferred, but indeed no father at all—is comparable, according to the saying: [Col. 1158A] “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37). For even if we have fathers who oppose us in the spiritual way, we must hate and flee from them.

## CHAPTER XII. On the presumption of women and the dignity of consecrated things

But why do we complain only about laymen, when laywomen themselves—women who are not permitted to speak in the Church (1 Cor. 14:34) or to exercise authority over a man (1 Tim. 2:12)—not only entrust ecclesiastical property to laymen for administration but even invest clerics with pastoral staffs and rings for bishoprics and abbeys, choosing and commending those whom favor, secular service, or temporal payment wins over to them?

[Col. 1158B] They too exercise authority over every ecclesiastical council and judgment. At their nod, even when they are absent, some are appointed, others deposed, while others, although guilty, are either passed over or defended. Through this most perverse abuse, as the impious Porphyry slanders it, our senate consists of women. Moreover, priestly insignia are given by them, and ecclesiastics are not permitted to assume for themselves what they receive except from their gift. Yet these objects ought not to be touched not only by women but by no male except a cleric, as blessed Stephen, pope and martyr, declares:

“The ecclesiastical garments by which God is served must be both sacred and honorable. No one should use them for any purpose other than ecclesiastical and God-worthy offices, [Col. 1158C], nor should they be touched or carried by anyone except men consecrated to God, lest the divine vengeance that struck Belshazzar come upon those who transgress and presume upon such things, and cause them to fall into the depths.”

From the decree of so great a pontiff, it necessarily follows that laymen and laywomen must take care not to profane ecclesiastical garments by their touch, and not to presume upon greater things when lesser ones are forbidden them.

For those who are not permitted to receive the key of the doorkeeper, with which he locks and unlocks the doors of the holy temple, or the cord of the bell, with which he signals the appointed hours of God’s work, are much less permitted to touch the bishop’s staff and ring. By these the bishop is chiefly marked out, and he consecrates not only the doorkeepers but the remaining ecclesiastical orders, the temple itself with all its furnishings, and the altar [Col. 1158D] with all its implements, to almighty God.

Likewise, those who are not permitted to touch the belt or small cloth of the subdeacon who carries the offerings to the altar are much less permitted to touch the bishop’s ring, by which he is marked when he assists at the altar, sanctifies and sacrifices the Lamb of God, consecrates the chrism of the Holy Spirit, or blesses the people of God.

It is no wonder that we revere Christ’s truth in the New Testament so greatly, since in the Old Testament the Lord decreed that its shadow should be revered and honored in the following manner. In the Book of Numbers he says through Moses:

“The tablets of the tabernacle, its bars, its columns, their bases, and everything pertaining to such worship shall be under the custody of the Levites; likewise the columns of the court with their bases all around, and the tent-pegs with their cords. [Col. 1159A] Moses and Aaron with his sons shall camp before the tabernacle of the covenant, that is, on the eastern side, having charge of the sanctuary in the midst of the children of Israel. Whoever else approaches shall die” (Num. 3:36–38).

He then shows elsewhere in the same book with how much reverence the vessels of the altar are to be treated, saying:

“They shall cover the fire receptacles, forks, three-pronged forks, hooks, shovels, and all the vessels of the altar together with a covering of violet skins, and they shall insert the carrying poles. When Aaron and his sons have wrapped up the sanctuary and all its vessels during the breaking of camp, then the sons of Kohath shall enter to carry the wrapped objects, but they shall not touch the vessels of the sanctuary, lest they die” (Num. 4:14–15).

Warning again against this danger, he says to Moses and Aaron:

> “Do not destroy the people of Kohath from among the Levites; but do this for them, so that they may live and not die when they touch the holy of holies. Aaron and his sons shall enter, and they themselves shall arrange the duties of each person and assign what each one ought to carry. Let no others, out of curiosity, see what is in the sanctuary before it is wrapped; otherwise they will die” (Num. 4:18–19).

The Levite Uzzah later incurred this penalty when he attempted to support the Lord’s ark as it tilted—something only the priests were permitted to touch. From this, let those who handle and carry, out of sheer presumption, the garments and vessels of ecclesiastical ministry consider what they deserve, if those who, moved only by curiosity, merely looked upon such things, or, compelled by sudden necessity, attempted to support them, were struck down from heaven.

And certainly the Levites were consecrated men whom such a severe punishment restrained. How great a severity, then, do we suppose it employed to deter laymen from these things? But lest anyone perhaps think that these matters had to be guarded only by the people under the Law, and not by us under grace, let him hear the Apostle saying:

> “Whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. 15:4).

Let him also hear blessed Pope Stephen, who earlier decreed things similar to these; and let him hear our Lord in the Gospel, impressing upon his own the perfection of a greater righteousness, to whom he first said:

> “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20).

Indeed, the Law punishes neither anger, nor mockery, nor verbal abuse against a brother with death, but only actual homicide. The Gospel, however, also punishes its source and seed—namely, anger and open abuse—and with a death all the more grievous because the soul is better than the body. The fear of that bodily death, which alone they experienced as servants, restrained them from transgression; whereas we, as free persons, ought to practice righteousness solely out of love for the eternal Father.

If, then, as it were, we cast aside his discipline and resist its restraining rule by an undisciplined will, we shall not only be disinherited but also suffer perpetual punishment through the death of the soul—a death which, though we believe it threatens us, we have despised to avoid. Nevertheless, in this too we differ from them: since we are like free persons, the opportunity for satisfaction is reserved for us; whereas for them, as servants, temporal punishment by death was applied without delay—a punishment that was undoubtedly regarded as the shadow of eternal death.

Therefore, as the Apostle says, having been called into freedom (Gal. 5:13), let us not abuse our freedom; let us not delay returning to our Father; and let us not, through despair or excessive hope, put it off from day to day, because just as the one who despairs is cursed, so also is the one who sins in hope.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the dignity of the priesthood under the Old Law, and on the presumption and punishment of the kings of Judah and Israel

Let them also consider that, although the twelve tribes of Israel then had an equal number of princes—including Nahshon of the tribe of Judah, from whom the scepter and ruler was not to be taken until the King of kings, Christ (Gen. 49:10)—none of them except Moses himself presumed to appoint from among his fellow tribesmen a high priest, priests, and Levites, or to establish and arrange all the ceremonies of that time.

For Moses himself, in the place of the supreme high priest and greatest leader, clothed his brother Aaron and Aaron’s sons, priests of a lower rank, with priestly vestments, consecrated them, and anointed them. He also erected both tabernacles and dedicated them, together with all their utensils, altars, and vessels, by anointing them and sprinkling them with water and hyssop. With that same water he sanctified the sprinkled people:

> “When every commandment of the Law had been read by Moses to all the people,” says the Apostle to the Hebrews, “he took the blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: ‘This is the blood of the covenant that God has commanded for you.’ He likewise sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels of ministry with blood. Almost everything is cleansed by blood according to the Law, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission” (Heb. 9:19–22).

Then, after his brother Aaron had died, Moses clothed Aaron’s son Eleazar with his father’s garments on the mountain, so that he might exercise the high priesthood in Aaron’s place (Num. 20:27–29).

Is it found anywhere that the princes or peoples of the other tribes designated or appointed high priests and the remaining ministers of the tabernacle or the Lord’s temple, or presumed to claim anything of their lot and right? They themselves, independently and among themselves, conducted their appointments and affairs as seemed best to them. The entire Levitical tribe was subject only to its own high priests for arrangement and governance, with no prince or member of the people opposing them; rather, everyone depended upon their command and will, both in offerings and in the remaining observances. Whoever did not obey them was to perish from the midst of his people.

It is clear that this lawful right was inviolably rendered to the tribe of Levi by the others until the wicked king Jeroboam, who by his schism divided the kingdom and the priesthood. He established other altars and other priests for idols; their priests were made not in the Mosaic manner but in the simoniacal manner. For, as the history testifies, whoever wished filled his own hand and became a priest of those who are not gods.

Judah and Benjamin, together with part of the tribe of Levi, retained the priesthood assigned to their lot for some time, although they occasionally deviated from it. Hence the temple and altar were sometimes profaned by the wickedness of certain priests and kings, and sometimes cleansed by the devotion of their successors. In the kingdom’s original unity and its later schism, the concord of Catholics and the discord of heretics were most clearly prefigured: the fewness of Catholics in the Jerusalemite Jews, and the multitude of heretics in the Beth-avenite Israelites.

Among these matters it must likewise be considered that those who retained only a false priesthood for themselves, together with the Mosaic Law—which they read in vain—and David’s psalms—which they sang to demons and not to God—first incurred irrevocable and perpetual captivity. Those, however, who retained the priesthood instituted by God, although falling and rising again, incurred only a captivity of seventy years, and that long after the former. From it they returned, as though improved and renewed, with the Law and the psalms, with their priests and prophets, and also with the sacred vessels and the gifts of many gentile rulers, in order to rebuild the temple and the holy city.

To the former, like a wife stubbornly practicing prostitution, the Lord once gave a bill of divorce, so that she might now satisfy her lusts without regard for marital jealousy. To the latter, like wanton and dissolute sons, he applied paternal scourges so that they might repent, in accordance with what he says through Zechariah:

> “I have been jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and with great indignation I have been jealous for her. Thus says the Lord of hosts: I have returned to Zion and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, and Jerusalem shall be called the City of Truth, the Mountain of the Lord of hosts, the Holy Mountain” (Zech. 8:2–3).

This can be plainly inferred from many other things, and then from this one fact: although Jeroboam presumed to take the priesthood of the ten tribes over which he ruled, standing upon the altar at Bethel and casting incense (3 Kings 13:1), he escaped without being struck by any visible plague.

But when Uzziah, king of Judah, attempted the same thing—although he was indiscreetly ardent in his zeal for God—he was struck with leprosy even before he could approach the altar of incense with the censer, which alone he had already seized (2 Chron. 26:19).

> “He,” as blessed Jerome asserts according to the History, “was a just man and did what was right in the sight of the Lord: he built the temple, constructed an aqueduct, offered vessels, and on account of this merit overcame his adversaries, which is the greatest indication of piety. He had many prophets in his kingdom. As long as Zechariah the priest, surnamed ‘Understanding,’ lived, Uzziah pleased God and entered his sanctuary with every reverence. But after Zechariah died, wishing to offer gifts himself, he invaded the priestly order—not so much piously as audaciously. When the Levites and the other priests protested, ‘Are you not Uzziah, the king, and not a priest?’ he would not listen, and immediately he was struck with leprosy on the forehead. That part of the body the priest protected with a golden plate. For this reason it is established that an earthquake arose in the temple of God, which the prophet Zechariah and the title of Amos also mention. He therefore remained a leper until the day of his death and lived in a separate house, while his son held the kingdom. While that leper lived and, in practical terms, was disrupting the priesthood, Isaiah could not see the vision of God. As long as he held the kingdom in Judea, the prophet did not lift his eyes to heaven; the heavenly things were not opened to him; the Lord Sabaoth did not appear to him; nor was the thrice-holy name heard in the ministry of faith. But when he died, all these things revealed themselves in an open light.”

And shortly afterward:

> “As long as Uzziah lives, Isaiah, you do not understand that you are wretched; you are not pierced with remorse, nor are you moved. But when he died, then you perceived that you had unclean lips; then you recognized yourself as unworthy of the vision of God. Isaiah was just, but because he had sinned only in speech, he therefore had only unclean lips—so far as I believe, because he had not rebuked Uzziah when he burst into the temple, nor denounced the impious man with a free voice after the example of Elijah.”

## CHAPTER XIV. On Saul’s presumption and punishment

Saul, too, as we read, was an excellent and good man, and there was no one better among the children of Israel (1 Kings 9:2); he was also little in his own eyes. Yet was he not rejected for usurping the priesthood, losing forever the kingdom that the Lord had prepared for him, and finally killing himself?

Nevertheless, we do not hesitate to recall here, according to the History, how great the necessity was under which he usurped it:

> “The Philistines gathered to fight against Israel: thirty thousand chariots and six thousand horsemen, and the remaining common people as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They went up and encamped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven. When the men of Israel saw that they were in a difficult position—for the people were distressed—they hid themselves in caves and hiding places, and also among the rocks” (1 Kings 13:5), and so forth, up to: “Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death” (1 Kings 15:35).

In this sentence of the Godhead, so strict against both kings, Christian rulers should observe that neither devotion nor necessity was excused, so that either of them might escape divine punishment for presuming upon the priesthood.

Uzziah lost the health and purity of his body, as well as his kingdom. Saul, however, was handed over to an evil spirit, lost the Holy Spirit, and lost the kingdom, the life of his soul, and the life of his body. He killed himself and brought about the ruin of his entire household.

Certainly neither of them presumed to take for himself the breastpiece, the holy robe, the golden plate, or any other priestly vestment, except that the former offered a burnt offering, while the latter seized a censer in order to burn incense.

It should also be noted how much more excusable and tolerable is what necessity compels than what the will presumes. Although Saul, compelled by necessity, offered a burnt offering, he did not so provoke the Lord or the prophet that he was entirely abandoned by them. Later, the Lord glorified him in many triumphs, and the prophet visited him many times, greeted him, and, speaking the Lord’s command, ordered him to go and destroy Amalek.

But when he presumed to do this by his own will, the good spirit of the Lord immediately departed from him, and an evil spirit from the Lord began to torment him. Afterward he had no victory, nor did he see Samuel.

## CHAPTER XV. How many scourges weigh upon rulers together with their peoples because of presuming upon priestly office

Christian rulers must necessarily attend to this and cease now to presume anything of priestly office for themselves, lest they put on not merely a simple but also a double garment of confusion.

For God, the Lord of vengeance, the strong and jealous God of vengeance, does not usually leave such a great crime unpunished. He either avenges it in the present age, or in the future, or certainly in both.

Therefore let them consider the external wars, internal rebellions, nation rising against nation, kingdom against kingdom, great earthquakes in various places, terrors from heaven and storms, pestilences and famines, which continually disturb Christians. Above all these things, let them consider that they have laid hands upon God’s apostles and ministers; and, chastised by so many scourges, let them finally recognize this, lest perhaps even after the scourges they incur eternal death.

Let them also consider that, although kings arise in the land of the Franks from a hereditary line, which king is remembered as having reigned through his sons, or even to the fourth generation, for a hundred years or more? The Ottos, who above all the kings before them presumed upon priestly office, scarcely reached the third generation. After them, the first Henry reached none. Anyone who investigates will be able to find that the same thing has occurred in other kingdoms and principalities.

Yet, with astonishing blindness, rulers of this kind imagine that they are rendering service to God if, from money or estates acquired in such a manner, they establish new churches or other pious places. Not only does this benefit them nothing; it also harms them greatly, as is sufficiently shown above from the words of blessed Gregory.

Indeed, what benefit is it to rulers to destroy a thousand churches and build one, after the example of those rulers whom we mentioned earlier? From the spoils of many churches, and especially of the provinces of wretched Italy, they built two bishoprics, so that they might at least be approved by human judgment, although they are condemned by divine judgment. And, as though they had done something great, they transferred them in name only to the jurisdiction of the apostolic see, while nevertheless retaining all dominion over them for themselves and their successors.

Without doubt, whether these men or any imitators of them deceive others or are themselves deceived, if they believe that the Prince of the Apostles can now be pleased by such offerings or money, contrary to his sentence against Simon Magus—as though he had repented of his earlier judgment.

Why do they not understand that it is not their task to create the churches of God, but to defend those already created? For this purpose they receive the sword from Christ’s priests; for this purpose they are anointed: that they may fight in defense of the churches of God and fight wherever there is need—not that they may establish churches, or sanctify or presume upon them or anything belonging to them.

If sheepfolds for rational sheep are to be built somewhere, let secular rulers be devoted and vigorous assistants to their shepherds, so that these structures may be built not from the milk and wool of others, but only from those of the people concerned:

> “For whoever,” says the Wise Man, “builds his house at another’s expense is like one who gathers stones in winter” (Eccl. 21:9).

Certainly, how highly is this regarded by God and by sound-minded people? Suppose someone, solely for the sake of almsgiving, were to strip a rich or moderately prosperous person, or kill anyone in order to clothe the naked or give life to the dying. How much more praiseworthy would he be if he neglected the wretched rather than showed them pity in such a manner?

Therefore, let those powerful in secular affairs, lest they suffer powerful torments (Wis. 6:7), beware, among the other ecclesiastical sacraments, of conferring ecclesiastical rings and staffs upon anyone, knowing that this belongs not to their office but to priests.

For priests themselves, as household servants, according to the evangelical parable, at the command of the master of the house bring forth the first robe for the returning prodigal son—that is, they catechize him. They clothe him—that is, they baptize him. They place upon his feet the shoes of imitation of the earlier fathers. Much more do they place in his hand the ring of preaching or ecclesiastical administration.

If it does not belong to secular rulers to baptize and preach, still less does it belong to them to give the ring, by which the preaching and teaching authority of the Church’s rulers is especially signified.

It also belongs to priests to bring and kill the fattened calf—that is, to prepare the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood for his household to feast upon.

If secular rulers wish to provide for the reward of their souls through the defense and administration of ecclesiastical persons and resources, let them support the preservation of dwellings and expenses through priests exercising priestly functions. Wherever the ecclesiastical order is found intact, let them follow the example of the most holy king David, who strove to arrange the priesthood in the priestly courses, through appropriate and due offices, so that it might remain intact for the Lord. From the spoils of the Lord’s enemies and from resources belonging to him, he supplied and prepared expenses for his son Solomon to build the temple for the Lord, as the conclusion of the First Book of Chronicles shows more explicitly.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the zeal of holy kings for divine worship and its reward, and on the vengeance upon peoples

[Col. 1164D]

Wherever the ecclesiastical order and divine worship have been diminished or abolished, let rulers gird themselves with the zeal and method of King Josiah, in order to recover and avenge them. Let them approach their priests with pious devotion and humble pleas and admonitions, even if the priests are unafraid to neglect their own office, following the example of Hezekiah.

For this is reported of him in the Second Book of Chronicles:

> “In the first year and first month of his reign, Hezekiah opened the doors of the house of the Lord and restored them. He brought in the priests and Levites, gathered them in the eastern square, and said to them: ‘Hear me, Levites, and sanctify yourselves. Cleanse the house of the Lord, the God of your fathers, and remove every impurity from the sanctuary. Our fathers sinned and did evil in the sight of our God, abandoning him. They turned their faces away from the tabernacle of the Lord and turned their backs. They closed the doors that were in the portico, extinguished the lamps, did not burn incense, and did not offer burnt offerings in the sanctuary to the Lord God of Israel. Therefore the wrath of the Lord was stirred against Judah and Israel, and he delivered them to turmoil, destruction, and hissing, as you yourselves see with your eyes. Behold, our fathers fell by the sword; our sons, daughters, and wives were led away captive because of this crime. Now, therefore, it is my will that we enter into a covenant with the Lord God of Israel, so that he may turn away from us the fury of his anger. My sons, do not be negligent. The Lord has chosen you to stand before him, minister to him, worship him, and burn incense’” (2 Chron. 29:3–11).

The devotion of this king will not be satisfied with correcting only his subjects; it will also admonish outsiders, as is added there shortly afterward:

> “The couriers went with letters by the command of the king and his princes throughout Israel and Judah, preaching according to what the king had commanded: ‘Children of Israel, return to the Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and he will return to the remnant that has escaped the hand of the king of Assyria. Do not be like your fathers and brothers who departed from the Lord God of their fathers, and he delivered them to destruction, as you yourselves see. Do not harden your necks as your fathers did. Give your hands to the Lord and come to his sanctuary, which he has sanctified forever. Serve the Lord God of your fathers, and the fury of his wrath will turn away from you. For if you return to the Lord, your brothers and sons will find mercy before their masters who led them captive, and they will return to this land. For the Lord your God is merciful and compassionate, and he will not turn his face away from you if you return to him’” (2 Chron. 30:6–9).

What more need be said? For those who wish to rule well and happily, the deeds and salutary words of this king contribute to the salvation of himself and his people. His industry pleased God so greatly that, by one prayer, he slew one hundred and eighty-five thousand of his enemies and obtained fifteen additional years of life for himself when he was about to die, although “men of blood and deceit do not halve their days” (Ps. 55:23).

Finally, through his piety and righteousness David acquired for himself, in his offspring, a throne of the kingdom forever. Neither Jeroboam nor any of his successors, except Jehu, reached the third generation on account of their impiety and injustice; rather, among the descendants of some of them not even one “who urinates against the wall” was left.

Let the counselors and attendants of rulers pay attention to this; let their peoples pay attention as well. Let them not think themselves free from participation in their rulers’ presumption, but let them know that, above all, they are participants in—and indeed authors of—their guilt.

After all, although a hawk may try, it cannot prey without wings and feathers. Thus, when the one ruler abandons his duty, an innumerable multitude of the people is often prostrated and scourged, because he could accomplish nothing of this kind without their favor or support.

For, fearing or loving a human being more than God, they not only favor masters who do evil but also take boldness from their wickedness and grow proud and rise up against those whom they can. If they unanimously resisted and protested against those attempting evil—as they sometimes do for their own disadvantages or advantages, or for money received or promised to them by certain persons—they would very easily recall their rulers and superiors from evil.

After all, if the crowd had not supported the chief priests by the importunity of its shouting, Pilate would have released the Lord Jesus, and those rulers would not have fulfilled their will by seizing the Lord.

But even if, out of necessity, the powerless and worthless common people follow the will of rulers, let them beware lest that very necessity become for them both a will and a freedom to do evil. If they ought to restrain themselves from harming any human being, how much more ought they to restrain themselves from presuming upon ecclesiastical possessions, remembering:

> “If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased toward him; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?”

Let them also remember that peoples are punished more numerously, even when their rulers sometimes escape temporal punishment: either because the peoples themselves are more numerous and the rulers fewer, or because the presumption and wickedness of rulers proceed chiefly from the peoples themselves as from their roots.

This is why Pharaoh perished with his entire people. Likewise, seventy men of Beth-shemesh, together with fifty of the people, perished because they had looked upon the Lord’s ark. And while David, who had ordered the census of the people, escaped, seventy thousand men were struck down by the angel over three days.

It should be noted that, when rulers offended more particularly in a divine matter, they perished together with their people; but when they sinned in a human matter, the rulers escaped while the people were struck down.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the merits of Israel and Judah as types of heretics and Catholics

Since we have taken some care to deter and at the same time encourage the rulers and peoples of our own time through the examples of the rulers and peoples of Israel, it remains for anyone who wishes to discern how highly the prayer and action of the two peoples—Israel and Judah—were regarded by God and his true Israelites to read the prophets, especially Hosea and Amos. Let him also read King Abijah of Judah, proclaiming, in the place and voice of the Catholics, against Jeroboam and his heretics, who were certainly his, words such as these:

> “Hear, Jeroboam and all Israel: do you not know that the Lord Jesus, the God of Israel, gave the kingdom over Israel to David forever, to him and to his sons, by a covenant of salt?” (2 Chron. 13:4–5.)

And shortly afterward:

> “Now you say that you can resist the kingdom of God, which he possesses over the sons of David. You have a great multitude of people and golden calves, which Jeroboam made for you as gods. You have expelled the priests of the Lord, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and made priests for yourselves, like all the peoples of the lands. Whoever comes and fills his hand with a bull, calves, and seven rams becomes a priest of those who are not gods. But our Lord is God, and we have not abandoned him; the priests who minister to the Lord are sons of Aaron, and the Levites are in their proper order. They also offer burnt offerings to the Lord every day, morning and evening, and incense prepared according to the commands of the Law. The loaves are set out upon the purest table, and among us there is a golden lampstand and its lamps, to be lighted in the evening. We keep the commands of the Lord our God, whom you have abandoned. Therefore God is the leader in our army, and his priests are with us, sounding the trumpets and raising the cry against you. Children of Israel, do not fight against the Lord God of your fathers, for this will not benefit you” (2 Chron. 13:8–12).

If anyone carefully considers in the Israelite people, separated from Judah, the type of the priesthood of heretics, he will understand with the greatest clarity what their doctrines and ordinations produce.

For thus it is read in the Fourth Book of Kings:

> “Israel was carried away from its land into Assyria until this day. The king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and settled them in the cities of Samaria in place of the children of Israel. They possessed Samaria and lived in its cities. When they had begun to live there, they did not fear the Lord, and the Lord sent lions among them, which killed them. It was reported to the king of Assyria, and they said: ‘The nations that you transferred and settled in the cities of Samaria do not know the ordinances of the God of the land; therefore he sent lions among them, and behold, they are killing them because they do not know the religious practice of the God of the land.’ The king of Assyria commanded: ‘Take there one of the priests whom you brought away captive from there; let him go and live with them and teach them the ordinances of the God of the land.’ So one of the priests who had been led away captive from Samaria came and lived at Bethel, and taught them how they should worship the Lord. Each nation made its own god, and they placed them in the shrines on the high places that the Samaritans had made, each nation in its own cities where it lived. Nevertheless, they also worshiped the Lord. Though they worshiped the Lord, they served their own gods as well, according to the custom of the nations from which they had been transferred to Samaria. To this day they follow their former practice. They do not fear the Lord, nor do they keep his ceremonies, judgments, Law, or commandment that the Lord had given to the children of Israel. These nations therefore feared the Lord, but nevertheless served their idols; their children and grandchildren, as their fathers did, continue to act in this way to the present day” (4 Kings 17:23–41).

This deed plainly reveals that the heretics whose type these people are both fear God and do not fear him; worship him and do not worship him.

Although they boast that they possess and observe the Law of Moses and worship and fear God, even to this day the Jews do not associate with the Samaritans. The Lord showed in the Gospel to the Samaritan woman what the religion of both groups was like, saying:

> “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22).

And when their teachers, the Sadducees, attempted to abolish the resurrection of the dead, he said:

> “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God” (Matt. 22:29).

After refuting them by adducing the example of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, he added:

> “Therefore you are greatly mistaken” (Mark 12:27).

How far they had gone astray, and how far the Pharisees had advanced beyond them, the Book of Acts makes clear:

> “The Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit; but the Pharisees confess both” (Acts 23:8).

Hence the Sadducees are also said by them to have a demon.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the difference between the priesthood of Catholics and that of heretics, and on the first fruits of the Simonians

Furthermore, it can be inferred how greatly Catholic priests, even when living badly, differ from heretics. As the Babylonian captivity approached, the fire of the altar, hidden in a well by priests who worshiped God, was discovered by Nehemiah after seventy years to have remained alive even beneath and in the water, with the wood and the sacrifice laid upon it.

Restored to the altar according to the Law for burnt offerings, and continually rekindled through the work of devout priests, it did not fail from the days of Cyrus, king of the Persians, until the reign of Antiochus. Antiochus was undoubtedly a type of Antichrist, whose prophets are understood to be heretics. Among these, as among the first and greatest in both Testaments, are the Simonians.

This is demonstrated not only by other Scriptures but also by the deeds recorded in the Books of the Maccabees. For Antiochus, the type of Antichrist, was the first to sell the Jewish priesthood to Jason, who represented the type of Simon Magus.

The account is given there as follows:

> “After the death of Seleucus, when Antiochus, who was called the Illustrious, had assumed the kingdom, Jason, the brother of Onias, aspired to the high priesthood. He approached the king, promising him three hundred and sixty talents of gold, and eighty talents from other revenues. In addition to these, he promised another one hundred and fifty if authority were granted to him to establish a gymnasium and an ephebeion, and to register those in Jerusalem as Antiochians. When the king consented and he had obtained the leadership, he immediately began transferring his fellow citizens to the gentile way of life” (2 Macc. 4:7–10).

And shortly afterward:

> “This was not the beginning but a certain increase and advance of gentile and foreign conduct, because of the impious and non-priest Jason’s wicked and unheard-of crime, so that the priests were no longer devoted to the duties of the altar” (ibid., 4:13–14).

Do you see how the Jewish priesthood itself was so destroyed by the Simoniac heresy that, because of the crime of selling and purchasing it, it was transferred toward the increase of gentile practice? This clearly demonstrates that the Simoniac heresy is the seedbed and propagation not of Christianity but of paganism.

For a Simoniac can neither accomplish nor wish anything else except to transfer his fellow citizens—who are, of course, Christians—to the gentile way of life. This is plainly established to be a wicked and unheard-of crime. Hence that same Jason is condemned as not a priest but an impious man, a name by which he is specifically shown to be a pagan.

At the same time, consider that in this first conspiracy of the Simonians—namely, Antiochus, Jason, and Menelaus, who was born of the tribe of Benjamin and had extorted the high priesthood from the aforementioned Jason by money—eighty thousand Jews were killed in Jerusalem, while forty-two thousand, having been bound, were sold no less (2 Macc. 5:14).

At that time, too, Antiochus, with Menelaus as his guide, entered the temple as Antichrist with Simoniac leaders—this temple, which with its sacraments signified the Catholic Church—and seized its altar, the golden lampstand of light and all its vessels, the table of the bread of the Presence, libation vessels, golden bowls, golden mortars, the veil, crowns, and the golden ornament that hung on the front of the temple. He shattered everything, then ordered the temple to be polluted and called the temple of Olympian Jupiter (2 Macc. 6:2).

He took the silver and gold, the precious vessels, and the hidden treasures that he found; and after removing everything, he departed for his own land.

Each of those ornaments of that temple prefigured the sacraments of the Church, as the numerous writings of orthodox fathers testify. Among them, the golden ornament that was on the front of the temple plainly signified the title of faith, by which we know that God exists and by which entry is made to God.

[Col. 1169C] These things, indeed, having been shattered and taken captive by heretics under the Antichrist, are prefigured in the shattering and captivity of that golden ornament. When it had been taken captive, the Lord drove away his tabernacle, where he had dwelt among human beings; he delivered their strength into captivity, and their beauty into the hands of the enemy; he shut up his people by the sword and rejected his inheritance. Fire devoured their young men, and their maidens were not mourned. Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows were not lamented (Ps. 77:60–64). Why was this? Because, as Jeremiah lamented, “the Lord rejected his tabernacle and cursed his sanctuary” (Lam. 2:7).

Hence even the temple itself was no longer called [Col. 1169D] the Lord’s, but that of Olympian Jupiter, to show that whatever visible sacraments of the Lord had formerly been in it had passed to the prince of this air. But Jason, the author of so great a crime, expelled from the priesthood by Menelaus, fled from city to city, hated by all. As a deserter from the laws, accursed, an enemy of his country and fellow citizens—and one who had driven many from their homeland—he perished abroad. He who had cast many away unburied was himself cast away unmourned and unburied, enjoying neither a foreign burial nor a share in his ancestral tomb.

His supplanter Menelaus, after the slaughter of the most holy priest Onias and many other saints, was himself supplanted by his brother Lysimachus, who not long afterward was killed beside the temple treasury in a secular uprising. Scripture identifies him as sacrilegious [Col. 1170A] not only because he obtained the priesthood with money, but also because he secretly carried away the sacred vessels and furnishings of the sanctuary. No one doubts that this crime belongs especially to the Simoniacs. For they do not merely attempt to purchase the priesthood; they also seize and steal whatever may remain for the churches of God.

Nor did the seller escape unpunished. Struck by an incurable and invisible affliction, consumed by worms, and filled with a stench intolerable both to his army and to himself, he died a miserable death abroad in the mountains—as though he were a type of him whom the Lord Jesus, according to Daniel’s prophecy, kills on the holy mountain by the breath of his mouth.

## CHAPTER XIX. How the priests themselves under the Law avoided communion with the impious and purified what had been defiled by them

[Col. 1170B]

If the false prophets and false Christs of the Simoniacs thus perished even under the shadow of the Law of Moses, how do we suppose such people perish now under the truth of the Gospel of Jesus Christ? Those who wish may learn from the Books of the Maccabees how Mathathias, his sons, and certain others avoided communion with them, at what peril to their bodies and loss of their possessions. Indeed, many thousands of people of both sexes—not only in the cities but also in the mountains and deserts—were then crowned with glorious martyrdom for the Law of God, which they zealously defended.

Moved by this zeal, the priest Mathathias and his five sons likewise left everything they had in the city and fled [Col. 1170C] to the mountains, withdrawing into a deserted place. There they lived among the wild beasts in the mountains and remained there, eating grass for food, so that they might not share in the defilement. In what respect, then, did these men avoid communion with heretics less than our holy Fathers have done in Christianity, though they were still in Judaism?

Let us also consider that, as long as the Jewish priesthood flourished, no temple utensil or sum of money could be seized or taken captive, being guarded by angelic sentinels, although Heliodorus attempted this with obstinate purpose under the high priest Onias. It is evident that this was accomplished then without any punishment because of the priesthood’s having been sold, or because it had been attempted by one not of his own tribe [lacuna].

Nor should we consider less carefully, in the legitimate conduct of the priests of that time, with what zeal and in what manner [Col. 1170D] Catholics must purify what they find contaminated by heretics. For we are taught there as follows:

“Judas chose priests without blemish, who were devoted to the Law of God. They purified the holy places and carried the stones of defilement to an unclean place. He deliberated about the altar of burnt offerings, which had been profaned, and what he should do with it. A good plan occurred to them: to destroy it, lest it become a reproach to them, because the nations had defiled it. They demolished it and placed the stones on the mountain of the temple, in a suitable place, until a prophet should come and give an answer concerning them.

“When the temple had been purified, they took whole stones according to the Law and built a new altar according to the former one; they rebuilt the holy places and the inner rooms of the house and the temple, and sanctified the courts. They made new sacred vessels, brought in the lampstand, the altar of incense, and the table into the temple; they placed incense upon the altar and lit the lamps that were upon the lampstand, and they shone in the temple. They placed the loaves of the Presence upon the table, hung the curtains, and, having completed everything, they rose before dawn. Taking fire from stones that had been kindled, they offered sacrifice according to the Law upon the new altar of burnt offerings that they had made” (1 Macc. 4:42–56).

[Col. 1171A] After these things had been done, they prostrated themselves on the ground and prayed to the Lord that they might never again fall into such evils, but that, if at any time they should sin, he would correct them more gently and not deliver them into the hands of blasphemous or barbarous nations.

On the day when the temple had been polluted by foreigners, its purification took place on the same day, the twenty-fifth of the new month Casleu; and they celebrated with joy for eight days, after the manner of the Feast of Booths. By common command and decree they resolved that the entire Jewish people should celebrate this every year for eight days (2 Macc. 10:4, 8).

“They adorned the front of the temple with golden crowns and shields, dedicated the gates and the side-chambers, and put doors upon them; and there was exceedingly great joy among the people. The reproach of the nations was turned away” (1 Macc. 4:57–58). The truth of the Gospel, walking straight onward, engraves these lines of the legal shadow almost in the same manner, while Catholic Fathers, according to the circumstances and time of their own age, purify churches contaminated by heretics. It will be our task to demonstrate this elsewhere with clearer examples [Col. 1171C].

Meanwhile, let us also consider that before the first captivity, under priests who were living badly, neither the Lord’s altar nor its utensils nor its fire were entirely renewed; rather, they were purified from the filth of idolatry and other contaminations by the hands of legitimate priests, with water alone for purification. That matters were handled differently after the captivity, because of the sale of the priesthood, has been shown above: even the stones of the formerly holy altar were removed from there, and a new fire was kindled from burning stones (2 Macc. 10:3). From the priesthood of Aaron until the perfidious Jason, fire had not failed from the altar of burnt offerings, nor had any king built upon it the abominable idol of desolation [Col. 1171D].

This third reconciliation of the altar and temple, carried out by several legitimate priests—including Zacharias, the father of the forerunner of Christ—was consecrated even during the reign of Herod. It remained so until, when our Lord Jesus Christ was already preaching, Annas and Caiaphas, through their ambition and money, made the priesthood not only venal but also annual.

Through the business of these men and their like, the house of prayer had become “a den of thieves” (Matt. 21:13), as the Lord protested. Shortly afterward, exalted upon the cross as though upon a pontifical throne, he condemned them and deposed them irrecoverably. When the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom (Matt. 27:51), he laid bare all their [Col. 1172A] sacraments and transferred their priesthood, with all its ceremonies and the Law, spiritually to himself and to his coheirs, as to the tribe of Judah, which confessed his name, rejecting those who denied him by crying out: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15).

Finally, whatever priestly office was afterward presumed and performed there, both by those men and by their kind and followers, was the worship of the devil, not of God, in accordance with what the blessed pope and teacher Leo asserts: “The angelic powers also protesting and saying: ‘Let us depart from these seats.’”

Thus, once the continual sacrifice had been taken away, abomination and desolation remain there until the end, according to what the blessed Jerome says when discussing the three and four crimes of certain nations:

“The prophet Amos announces to the nations addressed in his book that the wrath of God will come upon them for the reasons he mentions. Since he says in what follows, ‘For three transgressions, and for four, I will not revoke it,’ he indicates that God can grant forgiveness for the third offense; but when the same sins are committed for the fourth time, he declares that God will grant neither repentance nor forgiveness. For by the likeness of the fire that he foretold would be sent against the aforesaid nations, he intended to demonstrate the severe and irrevocable wrath and punishment of God” [Col. 1172B].

By the testimony of so great a man, may the Simoniacs awaken and learn how much less they themselves are to be forgiven, since they commit the same crimes not merely three or four times but even a hundred or a thousand times, continually trafficking in the grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1172C].

Although these offenses must be severely punished in the buyers, they must be punished much more severely in the sellers. For it sometimes happens that a buyer sins only once by purchasing, while afterward refusing to sell again to anyone what he is thought to have acquired. But what grace remains for the seller, or what wrath does not threaten him, who makes a practice of nothing but selling?

But lest this be thought to have been said only of other crimes and not of the Simoniac heresy, let us attend to what the same prophet says about Israel, whose ambition, as a type of the heretics, produced a divided kingdom. Then the former business of those men, by which they wickedly sell, and the other by which they more wickedly purchase for themselves the tongues of those who rebuke them, as though they were prophets, will be seen more clearly than the sun.

For he says:

“Thus says the Lord: ‘For three crimes of Israel, and for four, I will not revoke it, because he sold the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of sandals; and they reclined upon pledged garments beside every altar, and drank the wine of the condemned in the house of their God’” (Amos 2:4, 8). “And I raised up prophets from your sons and Nazirites from your young men; you gave the Nazirites wine to drink and commanded the prophets, saying: ‘Do not prophesy’” (ibid., 11–12).

## CHAPTER XX. On the danger of priests and the undisciplined ambition of our time

But woe, woe to us priests and clerics, because we ourselves provide the laity with the boldness and the sword to presume upon and invade ecclesiastical possessions—things they would neither presume upon nor invade unless either our negligence or our favor encouraged them to do so [Col. 1173A].

Indeed, although we are the dogs of the heavenly householder, we not only fail to drive away the rapacious from his flock and folds by free and continual barking or by a sharp bite; rather, mute, with the tongues of our entreaties ruined or the teeth of our rebukes restrained, utterly abased in voice and tail like sluggish dogs, we invite them to plunder by shameless and blind flattery.

We take no care to avoid incurring the displeasure of our Lord through either fear or love, nor do we remember that, like a destructive dog, we are rushing headlong into the ravenous Charybdis and will be overwhelmed by the final punishments. But what is even more grievous, we become terrifying to the Lord’s household and gentle toward its robbers.

Moreover, such stupor besets us [Col. 1173B] that we believe what belongs to us belongs to the laity. Hence certain of us, driven by blind ambition—the chief evil with which we struggle in Italy—setting aside ecclesiastical superiors, whose sole concern this is, break into palaces in rivalry, neither requested nor summoned; shamelessly approach secular powers; and, by attaching themselves and rendering service to princes and their households, spend the revenues and resources of their patrimonies, so that, eventually, they may hunt down some ecclesiastical dignity after enduring prolonged, immense, and continual hardships, which they bear day and night with utterly insane patience: exile, hunger, cold, and excessive vigils.

In this respect they must certainly be considered more detestable than the ambitious Catiline, who did not refuse to become a parricide of his country out of ambition for the consulship [Col. 1173C]. If Catiline was called and regarded as a parricide because, driven by desire for an earthly dignity, he disturbed and confused an earthly and pagan kingdom, attempting to rule even at the cost of destroying the city in which he had been born when he perceived that the senators opposed his ambition, what are we to call and regard those who, through their ambition, confuse and destroy the heavenly Christian kingdom—the Church, their mother—while Christ himself, the King of kings, and the council of all venerable Fathers, past and present, oppose them?

Who would hesitate to call those men Simoniacs beyond measure, since they spend not only money but also themselves in such transactions? For those who buy what they seek all at once, in one place and for themselves, are more tolerable than those who buy piecemeal and repeatedly, wandering and rushing from place to place throughout the days of their lives [Col. 1173D].

Having finally obtained from secular persons, through no merit of their own but solely through service or human favor, a dignity that they ought to have obtained through the Church had they served well in their own churches, they enter upon the labors of others with tyrannical fury.

Of such men the Church—that is, the clergy and people of whatever city—may complain and lament with the Lord, saying: “They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. 8:4).

By saying this, however, we do not accuse those who, because of their outstanding character and public usefulness, remain and serve in the earthly palace at the invitation and request of princes, and with the permission or command of their own superiors; nor those who, when churches are deprived of their superiors and have no one among their own people able to succeed profitably, are sought out and undertake governance [Col. 1174A]. Such men cannot be said to have invaded the labors of others, but rather to have come to the aid of brothers failing in their labor.

What is more praiseworthy, they charitably devote their advancement—owed to the Church in which they served and whose stipends they received—to churches in danger, without considering the dignity that, as veterans, was due to them in their own church or homeland. Such men are all the more worthy of reverence because they seek not their own interests but Christ’s.

All those who, for this reason, thrust themselves forward importunately and shamelessly do injury to these good men—and indeed resist the will of the Almighty, in whose dominion all things are placed. So great is the multitude of these undisciplined wanderers, both noble and learned and, no less, ignoble and uneducated, that, with churches and monasteries emptied and lying vacant, palaces and secular houses can scarcely contain the swarms of clerics [Col. 1174B].

Among them are some who pursue ecclesiastical honors not so much through clerical office as through medicine, buffoonery, or the art of a parasite. I would be lying if Italy had not produced many such men, whom no merit of character or learning advanced, but either buffoonery, deceitful flattery, or—something considered more excusable—medicine alone.

Although no Christian ought to communicate with such men, who truly wander about acephalous, without letters or permission from their own superiors, ecclesiastical governance is nevertheless entrusted to them. Once they have obtained it, they not only confuse and dissipate it like undisciplined and foolish men, but also pollute it, like lustful men, with manifold fornication and filth.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Italy’s chief evil, a certain vain bishop, and the duty of priests, princes, and peoples

Since certain provinces are defiled by such ordinations, Italy is especially so. This kind of sewer commonly flows into it, and not only forces those who desire to sail toward the kingdom of heaven to fall ill from its stench, but also sinks them beneath its weight [Col. 1174D].

Such men are exceedingly slow to hear what is good and still slower to live well, while they are quick to speak and highly practiced in flattery. By crafty deceit they deceive the guileless ears of princes, who by nature judge others favorably, and corrupt their upright endeavors.

For, skilled in inflating themselves and now pretending, then concealing, whatever they please—the carnal wisdom that, as God’s enemy, cannot be subjected to his Law—they employ plausible arguments and fragments of the sayings of Christ and the holy Fathers to persuade. Thus, at one moment festive with theatrical frivolity, at another severe with philosophical gravity, at another witty with secular refinement, and at another importunate with monetary generosity, like a second wicked and multiform Proteus, these fickle men, violent according to their own will, and—what is more grievous—blasphemous, twist [Col. 1175A] whatever had been established among God and human beings as useful and honorable for the holy Church.

Admiring persons for the sake of profit, among their other ravings and tricks by which they ensnare the unwary as though by a new kind of bird-catching, they magnify worldly power—and especially imperial and royal power—beyond measure before the open and greedy ears of princes, while diminishing ecclesiastical dignity.

And because everything under the sun alternates, sometimes advancing and sometimes declining, they measure the merit and power of priestly dignity according to the external advancement or decline of the ecclesiastical cause. Thus at one time they place secular powers above it, like the sun above the moon; at another they set one sun against another; and at another—which happens most rarely—they subordinate it, in the sole name of sonship, like a son to a father [Col. 1175B].

This fabrication of impure and shameless flattery has prevailed in our time to such an extent that, for the confusion of the holy Church and his own destruction, the aforesaid bishop was accustomed to win popular favor by saying something like this among his other flatteries: “The Roman pope is the father, the emperor is the son, and I, who move between these two, am the Holy Spirit.”

What Catholic could endure such blasphemy—not to declaim it, but even patiently to hear it? Yet this blind flatterer, taking extraordinary pleasure in the effect of his flattery and striving to be esteemed by human beings above what he was or appeared to be, is shown to have incurred the blasphemies of two heresies. By his presumption he established ranks within the Holy Trinity, like Arius; and, like Manes, he professed himself to be the Holy Spirit [Col. 1175C].

Through this sacrilege and many others, hated by God and his faithful, he perished abroad like another Jason, wandering and exiled.

Therefore, whoever among princes seeks to prepare happiness for himself here and blessedness in the future should beware of yielding to such men. For “a king who willingly listens to words of falsehood will have all his ministers wicked.”

Nor should the priests of Christ, and matters pertaining to them, have any other position than that held by Maximus Constantine and his orthodox imperial successors, as is shown in part above in this work.

Therefore, whoever wishes to compare priestly and royal dignity irreproachably and usefully should say that, in the present Church, the priesthood is likened to the soul and the kingdom to the body, because they love and need one another and mutually require and provide their respective services.

Just as the soul takes precedence over and commands the body, so priestly dignity takes precedence over royal dignity, as the heavenly over the earthly. Thus all things are neither reversed nor disordered: the priesthood, like the soul, should give prior instruction concerning what must be done; then the kingdom, like the head, should preside over all the members of its body and excel insofar as expedient.

For this is how kings ought to follow ecclesiastical authorities; so also the laity ought to follow their kings for the benefit of the Church and the homeland. Thus the people should be taught by the one authority and governed by the other; neither authority ought thoughtlessly to follow the people [Col. 1176A].

The authority of the holy Fathers impresses this upon priests as follows:

“The people must be taught, not followed; and if they do not know what is permitted and what is not permitted, we must admonish them, not give our assent to them.”

Concerning kings and the princes of the world he says:

“Sometimes the princes of the world hold within the Church the heights of the power they have acquired, so that through that same power they may strengthen ecclesiastical discipline. Otherwise, powers within the Church would not be necessary, except so that what a priest cannot accomplish through the word of teaching, authority may command through the terror of discipline.

“Often the heavenly kingdom advances through an earthly kingdom, so that those who, placed within the Church, act against the faith and discipline of the Church may be crushed by the severity of princes, and so that the authority of rulers may impose upon the necks of the proud the discipline that the Church’s usefulness or human kindness cannot enforce [Col. 1176B].

“Let the princes of the world recognize that they must give an account for the Church, whose protection they have received from Christ. For whether the peace and discipline of the Church are increased through faithful princes or dissolved, he will demand an account from them who entrusted the holy Church to their power.”

## CHAPTER XXII. On the harmful silence of priests and the loquacity of flatterers

Since no Christian dares contradict these things, woe to us priests, because we are silent, because we are men of polluted lips! If the most holy Isaiah incurred pollution of the lips because he did not freely rebuke, like Elijah, a king who had once attempted the priestly office, and, according to the judgment of blessed Jerome, could not be perfectly cleansed from that pollution until he was cruelly cut apart and died, when, I ask, will our lips be cleansed, since we continually fail to rebuke princes who presume upon ecclesiastical matters and instead praise them?

And do we dare to call upon or name the Lord with such lips? What benefit is there in saying every day, “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. 119:2), and, “Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Ps. 50:17)?

Are not those lips wicked which do not reprove wickedness, or which do not defend wickedness? If all Christians must pray to be delivered from such lips, how much more must priests do so, since they must devote themselves to prayer and preaching not only for themselves but also for everyone, lest, when they multiply their prayers, God, offended by their polluted lips, should find them of no avail [Col. 1176D].

As blessed Jerome explains concerning Malachi, “the law of truth” in the priest’s mouth is the teaching of the peoples. In the priest it must not be corrupted by any falsehood, but must proceed wholly from the fountain of truth, so that he may have peace himself and make others peaceful, show partiality toward no person in judgment, and turn many away from iniquity by correcting others.

“The lips of the priest shall guard knowledge” (Mal. 2:7). He did not say “shall proclaim,” but “shall guard,” so that he may speak at the proper time. “And they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7) [Col. 1177A].

He has also been appointed a watchman by the Lord over the house of Israel. From whose mouth will instruction and reproof be required, if he does not announce to the righteous that he must not sin and to the wicked that he must convert? The blood of both will be required from the hand of his tongue.

If lips are struck by such a punishment merely for the silence of iniquity, by what punishment, do you suppose, will deceitful lips be struck—lips that not only conceal the iniquity they are commanded to rebuke, but also labor by lying to present it as righteousness?
