Hence: “Woe to you who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter. Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight; who justify the wicked for gifts and take away the justice of the righteous from him” (Isa. 5:20, 23) [Col. 1177B].

For, as Solomon says, “Whoever says to the wicked, ‘You are righteous,’ will be cursed by the peoples, and tribes will detest him.”

The prophet, declaring that such men must be avoided, says:

“My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your steps. The Lord stands to judge, and he stands to judge the peoples. The Lord will enter into judgment with the elders of his people and its princes. For you have devoured my vineyard, and the spoil of the poor is in your house” (Isa. 3:12–14).

This most wicked vice of flattery must be attacked with all the more courage because we understand it to be more harmful than almost all other vices. It destroys priestly authority itself, royal power and moderation themselves; it confuses right and wrong, so that what is owed to God and to human beings is not rendered [Col. 1177C].

A flattering person is a sweet-talking enemy, perjured toward princes, to whom he is unfaithful against his oath when he either persuades them to do evil or extols their deeds with wicked favor, so that, remaining impenitent, they may store up a way for themselves in the future. He is most harmful to peoples, whom he does not permit either to be wise or to recover their senses; he is hated by God, against whom he acts as the devil’s effective assistant, laboring to draw people away from good and incite them to evil.

Hence the venerable Prosper, outstanding in both prose and verse, says of such men:

> The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins;
>
> They delight in doing what incurs no fear of a rebuker,
>
> But even hears a praiser praised.
>
> The tongue of the flatterer piles up the sinner’s vice
>
> And elegantly binds the one delighted by his crime.
>
> Let there be no breath of healing hope for the fallen,
>
> While pernicious honor flatters the guilty.
>
> Rather let the free voice of a friendly corrector be heard,
>
> And let it not allow blind poisons to creep into books.
>
> Nor let the sick person, trusting a physician’s deceitful words,
>
> Love the harmful wounds of the praised disease.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the danger of priests who are silent in the wrong way and speak in the wrong way, and on the indivisible unity of divinity and of those who belong to it

Let these things, and many others of the same kind, be heard patiently. Finally, if the ministers of Christ, and especially priests, care to avoid their own destruction and that of others, let them beware—whether through human fear or human favor—of remaining silent not only about evil but also about good. Otherwise they will die if, whether entering the tabernacle of God or departing from it, they do not produce a sound [Col. 1178A].

Likewise, let the parasites and ventriloquists who are ministers of the devil, especially erring clerics, cease trying to please their superiors or inferiors by favoring the wicked and slandering the good. Let the former presume to speak; let the latter learn to be silent. Otherwise “the Lord will dry up the tongue of the Egyptian sea” (Isa. 11:15), and “those who call the seducers blessed will themselves be led astray, and those who are called blessed will be cast down” (Isa. 9:16).

The Psalmist declares their wickedness and punishment in the psalm against transgressors, saying:

“They have spoken vanity, each one to his neighbor; they have spoken with deceitful lips in heart and mouth. May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things. They have said: ‘We shall magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is our lord?’” (Ps. 11:3–5) [Col. 1178B].

Therefore, just as he is accursed who withholds his sword from blood, so woe to him who makes his friend drunk and leads him along a bad path! Hence, as the prophet admonishes, “the tongue of the stammerers shall speak swiftly and plainly” (Isa. 32:4); and let the heart of the foolish understand knowledge, and let those who mutilate learn the law. Otherwise, God forbid, by remaining silent and consenting to that division—which cannot be applied to God—and by persisting in and favoring it through flattery, the former and the latter may alike be divided from God as schismatics and heretics.

Without a doubt, schism or heresy consists in attempting to divide God and those who belong to him from one another. Blessed Paul testifies this to the Corinthians as follows:

“I beseech you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no schisms among you. Be perfected in the same mind and in the same knowledge. For it has been reported to me concerning you, my brothers, by those of Chloe, that there are contentions among you. I mean this: each one of you says, ‘I am of Paul,’ ‘I am of Apollos,’ ‘I am of Cephas,’ ‘I am of Christ.’ Is Christ divided?” (1 Cor. 1:10–13.)

The implied answer is: By no means [Col. 1178C].

Otherwise, God forbid, that prayer of his would be fruitless—the prayer he poured out to God the Father as he went to his passion, when, among other things, he asked especially that his own might be one in him, saying:

“I have given them your word, and the world has hated them, because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.

“Just as you sent me into the world, I also sent them into the world; and for them I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in the truth. I do not ask for these alone, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I am in you, so that they too may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me.

“And I have given them the glory that you gave me, so that they may be one, just as we are one. I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected in one” (John 17:14–23).

Do you see, blasphemous divider, that the indivisible things of Christ cannot be divided? Christ and his ministers are indivisible. And what is even more astonishing, mere human beings are indivisible from God the Father, who alone is God, through Christ, who is God and human, as he himself says: “I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected in one” (John 17:14–23) [Col. 1179A].

Yet this wondrous and desirable unity is owed by nature to Christ, as the Only-Begotten; to the human being, as adopted, it is granted by grace alone. Finally, so that Christ Jesus might appear as the uniquely faithful mediator uniting God and humanity, he united human nature and sanctification to his divine nature and holiness, by which he was suitably related to God. He was born holy and without sin, so that, on the one hand, he might correspond to the human being conceived in sins and provide for him, and, on the other, might aid him in such a way as also to restore the sanctification that had been lost.

This sanctification, divinely bestowed upon the son of earth and taken away from the devil’s power, is bestowed upon the Son of the Virgin Mary. Through it the same true human being was predestined to be the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification. Concerning this Spirit of sanctification, the Son of God and human being himself, asking it for his own, says: “Sanctify them in the truth”—that is, in me, who am the truth—“so that they too may be sanctified in me” (ibid. 17) [Col. 1179B].

From this it is truly gathered that divine things are joined to human things through sanctification alone. Therefore, if the ministers and servants of Christ become one with Christ in God because they have been sanctified in him, it is clear that whatever belongs to Christ’s ministers is one with them in Christ, because it has been sanctified in them for Christ.

If the property of a bodily servant is united to the servant’s master through the servant who belongs to him, how much more is everything that belongs to Christ united and yielded to Christ—especially since these people possess nothing except what he himself, from his gifts, gives back to them, and since the Lord himself is also the portion of their inheritance, while they themselves are his inheritance [Col. 1179C].

## CHAPTER XXIV. On examples of the indivisible Trinity in all creatures

But, alas, detestable people attempt to divide this union and to divide what is indivisible from what is indivisible and from the one by whom it is divided, even though sanctification so contains it within itself that it is itself contained by sanctification.

Indeed, like bleary-eyed people suffering from a muddy film over their eyes, or drenched from excessive drinking, they think that the sun, the moon, or any lamp is not merely doubled for them but multiplied. Thus the excellent Prudentius, refuting the Marcionites who imagined two gods, namely the good and the evil, says:

> No one has seen two suns except under a glaucomatous film.

Therefore, if they can, let them consider how alienated from God are those who labor to divide things that are indivisible. Finally, God himself commends his indivisible Trinity through unity, and grants and preserves this pattern of his unchangeable and invisible nature not only in invisible and mutable things, but also in his visible works. For God marked all things that he made in his one Wisdom with the Trinity by which they subsist, giving everything measure, number, and weight (Wis. 11:21). These three exist simultaneously and inseparably in all creatures, and none of them can be found either earlier or later than the other two, or sensibly separable from them. For whether you consider measure, number, or weight in any bodily natures, you will perceive through the bodily senses that all three arise, exist, grow, diminish, and even perish together and inseparably in them. You will likewise understand this in corporeal creatures if you pay attention. They have a measure by which they are also bounded, the weight of merits, and the number of differing affections. Indeed, just as the diversity of limbs or parts gives bodies their number, so the diversity of effects gives created spirits theirs. Thus, as the venerable Prosper says, the appearance of works proclaims the craftsman, who fashions forms, places, times, and movements in things according to their measures, numbers, and weights. Although he inserts these three equally into all creatures, they nevertheless produce a certain unity and are held together by unity, so that, in accordance with their mode, they are expanded through their trinity and likewise constrained through their unity. Thus they have, and do not have, number, after the likeness of their author, who is called both the supreme Three and the One. Moreover, just as this blessed and incorruptible Trinity is rightly called and held to be one God, so that incorruptible trinity in each individual creature is called and held to be either one spirit or one body.

From all these considerations we are taught in many ways that God, both in himself and in all his works, commends and loves above all things the monad, and especially detests and hates whatever rises away from himself. For the Monad, by the benefit of its indivisible nature, brings even what is divided back to the indivisible through union, and joins it to the indivisible. The Dyad, however, through the evil of its own defect, seeks even to divide what is indivisible. The former, as inviolable and peaceable, knows only how to draw things back from what is divided, diverse, and private, and to unite them to its present, indivisible good common to all. The latter, on the contrary, as violated, violating, and schismatic, attempts to burst and cut away nothing except from what is indivisible, alike, and common in the good.

Without doubt, this latter, voluntarily withdrawing from that unchangeable and indivisible Monad, first sought for itself a place in the sides of the north, a private and solitary seat; then it divided humanity from God. It also, in its customary manner, spoke through the prostitute: “Neither for me nor for you, but let it be divided” (3 Kings 3:26). In the Gospel, speaking through another person, it likewise desires to persuade the eternal Monad to division, saying: “Tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me” (Luke 12:13). The blessed Monad, protesting against this, proclaimed the impassibility of its nature in these words: “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?” (Luke 12:14).

And if you consider all the works of divinity, you will find that they subsist entirely through the monad but perish through the dyad. Just as the monad is their principle of subsistence, so the dyad is the beginning of their cessation. For as long as the diversity and multiplicity of limbs or parts are held together by union, or are joined to their whole, the thing subsists. But once it approaches the dyad, it begins to cease and perish. Moses too intimates this. Although he records that God saw the works of each individual day and that they were good, when speaking of the second day he remained silent, signifying that something does not appear good to God when, departing from his unchangeable unity, it begins to enter into and fall under the mutability of plurality.

## CHAPTER XXV. That sanctification is indivisible from the things it sanctifies, and how they are sanctified

Since, then, it is clear from these and many other testimonies of Holy Scripture that the Lord God takes the greatest pleasure in the universal and common good throughout the whole of his creation, and, conversely, is displeased by what is particular and private, what knowledge—or rather, what audacity—do those possess who proclaim that anything sanctified to God may, without impunity or sacrilege, be divided from the very sanctification by which it is joined to God?

The old law, which is a type of the new, shows in many ways how such things are sanctified. Some are sanctified by obligation, such as the firstborn, firstfruits, and tithes, which are required as pure things sanctified to the Lord before they come into being; some by offering, such as the breast, the shoulder, livestock, or whatever is sanctified to the Lord when it is rightly offered; and some by vow, namely whatever is voluntarily vowed. For they are known to be sanctified to the Lord from the very moment of the vow.

These matters are briefly gathered together in Leviticus, where it is prescribed:

“No one may sanctify or vow the firstborn that belongs to God, whether it is an ox or a sheep; they are the Lord’s. But if it is an unclean animal, the one who offered it shall redeem it according to his valuation and shall add a fifth part to its price. If he does not wish to redeem it, it shall be sold to another for whatever value has been assigned to it.

“Everything consecrated to the Lord, whether it is a human being, an animal, or a field, shall neither be sold nor redeemed. Whatever has once been consecrated shall be most holy to the Lord.

“All the tithes of the land, whether of grain or of the fruit of trees, belong to the Lord and are sanctified to him. If anyone wishes to redeem his tithes, he shall add a fifth part to all those tithes. Of ox, sheep, and goat, whatever passes under the shepherd’s rod, every tenth one that passes shall be sanctified to the Lord. It shall not be selected, whether good or bad, nor shall one be exchanged for another. If anyone exchanges it, both the thing exchanged and its replacement shall be sanctified to the Lord, and it shall not be redeemed” (Lev. 27:26–33).

If you investigate carefully, you will find that the tabernacle and all its utensils, anointed with the oil of sanctification, were called the Holy of Holies; whereas the other things outside, which belonged to it or to its ministers, were called merely holy. Hence it is understood that these holy things received their sanctification from the communion by which, through the devotion of the faithful, they were joined to the Holy of Holies.

From that communion they borrowed and possessed such great sanctification that, according to the degree of distinction, some were owed only to the priests in the sanctuary, some also to the males of their lineage, and some even to their entire acquired or household family, while all foreigners, as well as a priest’s resident alien and hired servant, and also lepers and unclean persons, were excluded. If, among these sanctified things, a soul that transgressed the ceremonies sinned through error, it offered for its offense an unblemished ram from the flocks, which could be bought for two shekels according to the sanctuary weight; it restored the damage it had caused, placed a fifth part on top of it, and handed it over to the priest, and thus the offense was forgiven.

If anyone ate of the sanctified things through ignorance, he added a fifth part to what he had eaten and gave it to the priest in the sanctuary, lest he profane the sanctified things of the children of Israel that they offer to the Lord, and lest those who ate the sanctified things bear the iniquity of their offense. “I,” says the Lord, “who sanctify them” (Lev. 21:23).

From this it is clearly proved that the Lord sanctifies his tabernacle and its ministers in such a way that whatever belongs to them remains sanctified. Therefore, if anyone, through error or ignorance, presumed to take even the smallest amount for himself, he had to restore it with an increase, lest he perish from the midst of his people. But if he did so through pride, he could in no way escape the sentence of dreadful death. In this way the Lord, the sanctifier of all things, sometimes gently admonishing and sometimes harshly warning, establishes that his sanctification is inseparable from those whom, or that which, he sanctifies.

Who are these people who speak iniquity against the Most High, asserting that sanctified things may be purchased or received as gifts without their sanctification? They ought surely to have been instructed even by visible things, which plainly cannot be sold or given away without their measures, numbers, and weights—the qualities that God once and simultaneously implanted in them. If this has been conceded to those things whose use and service he leaves and permits even to his enemies, namely, so that they may not be possessed without their qualities, how much more is it conceded to those things which, for the sole expenses of his holy Church and his holy ministers, he has set apart through his sanctification not only from his enemies but also from his lay friends?

Without doubt, that lament of Christ may aptly be directed against such schismatics: “They divided my garments among themselves” (Ps. 21:29). For do these people, like profane soldiers, in exchange for the reward of the mockeries and injuries that they obstinately inflict upon Christ in order to please his enemies and turn his enemies away from him, not continually divide his garments whenever they presume to seize and divide among themselves the goods devoted to him alone by the devotion of the faithful and sanctified for the sustenance and clothing of his members who still suffer need here—not for any sanctification of themselves, but only for their own curse and everlasting damnation?

Moreover, they feed him with gall and give him vinegar to drink, because, withholding the nourishment due to his poor, they fill their lives with unbearable bitterness through hunger and thirst. Even when they sometimes appear to distribute something of their own to them, it is like a scarlet cloak, which, as is thought, is applied to the less honorable members of Christ. For they do not preserve his dignity by this, but their own, when they relieve the misery of the wretched for the sole purpose of avoiding the appearance of inhumanity—or, at any rate, of avoiding the shame of being accused of not blushing at their importunity.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the punishment of those who divide, and that they do not receive the Holy Spirit unless they follow the faith of the apostles

Since these things are so, “what a human being has joined, let no human being separate,” because anyone who does this will act perniciously, as the Lord himself teaches in the Gospel when questioned about the divorce of married couples (Mark 10:9). For just as two people who existed separately before marriage are, after marriage, no longer two but one flesh, according to the Lord’s testimony—or just as a rational soul and flesh constitute one human being—so the clerical order and ecclesiastical possession are one sanctification of the Lord. Whoever divides it in a worldly manner produces nothing but spiritual destruction, as though, by committing adultery, he dissolved a marriage and killed the man. By doing this, it is necessary that he invalidate two while dividing one: namely, God and the husband, if he divides a wife; or God and the inner human being, if he divides the outer.

Thus you sin against God and his servants when you separate their sanctified possession from its sanctification. Here you do something more dangerous than in adultery, because there you scandalize one person, whereas here you scandalize many thousands. If anyone scandalizes one of God’s little ones, he must be drowned in the depths of the sea with a millstone hung around his neck (Matt. 18:6); what, we may ask, does the person deserve who, through his ambition and invasion, scandalizes so many of God’s little ones together with their superiors?

By this scandal he dissolves the marriage of Christ and the Church through his adultery, homicide, and sacrilege, when through his wicked zeal he expels from the Church the pledge of the divine marriage—namely, the Holy Spirit, by whom it was sanctified, given life, and adorned. Just as he fills the whole world and contains all things as Creator, so he fills and contains the Church and everything belonging to it as Sanctifier, so that they may not merely subsist but also be holy.

This sanctification is invited to sanctify whatever the faithful contribute to the holy Church by good will, devotion, and prayer. They obey the Lord’s commands by raising earthly patrimonies from the earth to the heavenly treasures and transferring them through the hands of the poor in spirit, to whom the kingdom of heaven belongs and whose advocate and consoler is the Holy Spirit—from whom all sanctification comes, or rather, who is sanctification itself.

Through him the whole body of the Church is sanctified and governed. He, as Christ’s vicar, protects his disciples and all the faithful everywhere in place of Christ’s bodily presence. The Son asked the Father to give this other Paraclete to his own, so that he might remain with them forever. The world, lying in wickedness—namely, heretics, Jews, unbelievers, and pagans—cannot receive this Spirit of truth, which is Christ. Otherwise, if the world composed of such people can receive the Spirit of truth while remaining in unbelief, either there is no Church or, if there is, the Truth is proved a liar when it asserts that the Holy Spirit cannot be received outside it.

For if heretics and the other unbelievers can receive the Spirit of truth, it follows that Catholics either do not receive him or differ in no respect from heretics—in fact, that Catholics themselves are heretics. But may such unbelief be far from Christian minds! The inviolable Truth confirmed the judgment of its promise with an inviolable subscription, immediately adding: “Because it neither sees him nor knows him” (John 14:17).

Since receiving anything is more than merely seeing or knowing it, it is clear that the lying world does not receive the Spirit of truth, of whom it is proclaimed that it neither sees nor knows him. Therefore, whoever does not deserve even what is least may well be doubted to deserve what is greatest. Is someone who is judged unworthy even of the last spark worthy to receive the whole flame?

But the same Truth, assuring his own concerning the Spirit, added: “But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you” (John 14:17). From this it is proved that the Holy Spirit is known by Christ’s disciples and remains with them and in them forever.

If some slanderer attempts to assert that Christ promised the Holy Spirit only to those who at that time adhered to him, let him hear the words: “so that he may remain with you forever” (ibid. 16:11). And lest he still evade the matter, let him recall what we adopted slightly earlier as an example, where Christ, asking the Father to sanctify his disciples, says: “I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one” (John 17:20).

Moreover, sanctification is neither given nor possessed without the Holy Spirit. It is therefore clear that the apostles and their successors recognize, receive, and have the Holy Spirit abiding with them and in them, because they believe in their hearts and confess with their mouths the apostolic faith.

Therefore, leaving aside the other plagues for the moment, let the Simonians prove that, by following the apostolic faith and teaching, they sell and purchase the Holy Spirit. If they can prove this, it should be granted to them without controversy that they may receive and possess the Holy Spirit, and obtain or give him to whomever they wish, either freely or for a price. But if they cannot prove it—as indeed they cannot—especially since they know, and cannot deny, from the very pillars of the primitive Church and of the whole Church, Peter, prince of the apostles, and John, the Lord’s beloved apostle and evangelist, that their founder was irrecoverably crushed for merely judging such a nefarious transaction, let them recognize that they belong to that world which cannot receive the Spirit of truth, and, coming to their senses, hasten to become part of that world which Christ chose from among their world.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the grace of the Holy Spirit in the disciples after the resurrection, and the punishment of Ananias

The Father indeed sent this Paraclete in the name of his Son, so that he himself might teach the faithful all things and remind them of everything that the same Son had said to them. Because this Spirit proceeds from the Father, the Truth sent his Spirit to his own so that he might bear witness through them concerning him. He would neither have been sent by the Son to them nor have come if the Son himself had not departed from this world. This was especially beneficial for them, lest they remain carnal if they cared to know Christ only according to the flesh.

When he came, he convicted the unclean world concerning the sin of unbelief, concerning the righteousness of Christ’s own, and concerning the judgment of the devil who had been cast out. This Spirit of truth, coming also, teaches Christ’s disciples all truth, so that, having been made spiritual through him, they may learn many things that Christ had to tell them but that, because they were still carnal, they could not bear. He does not speak on his own authority; whatever he hears, he speaks, and he announces to them the things that are to come. He glorifies the Son, who had not been given before the Son’s passion, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.

This is that living water to whose drinking the same Son invites those who thirst. He is also the Spirit of truth who, as a faithful advocate, speaks through the disciples before kings and governors, so that it is unnecessary for them to plan beforehand how they should answer; in that hour they are given what they should say. For it is not they who speak, but the Holy Spirit.

He made the apostles witnesses of Christ in Jerusalem, and from there in every direction, even to the ends of the earth. He also visibly inflamed them and, by the grace of his sevenfold gift, bestowed upon them all languages. In the apostles, who were uneducated and without literary training, he stood against the chief priests and the magistrates of the Jews, so that, when forbidden to speak, they answered steadfastly: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5:29); and, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves. For we cannot refrain from speaking about what we have heard and seen” (Acts 4:19–20). When they had been beaten, they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been found worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus.

When they prayed, he moved the place in which they were gathered and filled them so that they might speak the word of God with confidence. He performed many signs and wonders through the hands of the apostles. He made the multitude of believers one heart and one soul.

He killed, by Peter’s word, those who defrauded the money owed to the coenobites:

[Note: That is, those living in common, as the first Christians did; according to the book of the Acts of the Apostles, everything was held in common among them.]

“Ananias, why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to human beings but to God” (Acts 5:3–4). “And surely you have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord” (ibid. 5:9).

Here it is openly proclaimed that the money by which those coenobites were temporarily sustained, so that no needy person was found among them, belonged not to human beings but to the Holy Spirit. They are accused of lying to him and immediately perish because they attempted to alienate that same Holy Spirit from the money that, through their vow, he had sanctified to himself for the support of his coenobites. They fraudulently sought to retain secretly for themselves something peculiar and to purchase, with part of it, the food and clothing of Christ’s poor, while openly displaying another part.

He condemned Simon Magus forever through the mouth of Simon Peter, because Simon Magus judged that the Spirit’s grace could be sold and bought. In this irrevocable sentence we must consider how much more pardonable was Ananias’s offense in defrauding transitory money than the wicked Magus’s offense in merely judging that a fraudulent transaction involving eternal grace could be conducted.

Thus Ananias, who tempted the Holy Spirit by defrauding an external and visible thing that he had sanctified, was punished only by the death of the outer human being; whereas Simon, who contemplated fraud against an interior and invisible grace, was struck by the death of the inner human being. Although each sinned against the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, in proportion to their offenses, Ananias, punished by temporal death, is thought to have escaped eternal death; whereas Simon, condemned to perpetual death, postponed temporal death, because his blasphemy against the Holy Spirit was to be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come.

Ananias was not permitted to live in the flesh even for a moment, so that that death might be an unseen remedy for him and an obvious example for the living. Simon, however, dead in soul, was permitted to live for some time in this world, to increase his future torments and to exercise the good, although, crushed and destined to be crushed, he was to be removed from the midst of humanity.

In their punishment it is necessary to observe this: as Blessed Prosper says, “Nothing is more unfortunate than the happiness of sinners, because impunity is nourished for punishment, and an evil will is strengthened like an inner enemy. What is neither punished nor cut away by a temporal scourge is reserved for eternal punishment.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How much this same Spirit has done and continues to do in the Church until the end of the age

Furthermore, after the display of the heavenly linen, the almighty Spirit told the apostle Peter that Cornelius’s messengers were present and directed him to baptize the Gentiles. Through his outpouring and the inspiration of all languages, he cleansed their firstfruits even before baptism.

This Spirit removed from the Gentiles the circumcision and the burden of Jewish ceremonies, when Peter said: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts 15:28). This Spirit of Jesus did not permit the apostles to go to Bithynia or to evangelize in Asia. He commanded Paul and Barnabas to be set apart for the work of the Gospel. He warned that same Paul to cross into Macedonia, and afterward foretold that he would be bound with Jewish chains and handed over to the Romans.

The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God and heirs, and co-heirs with Christ. Through him, who searches all things, God revealed to his own even the depths of God—things that eye has not seen and that have not entered the human heart. Through Paul he gives advice to virgins, and likewise to married women and widows.

We have him as Christ’s pledge, crying in our hearts, “Abba, Father.” In him we have been sealed for the day of redemption. Whoever does not have him does not belong to Christ.

Finally, “the Spirit,” as the same Apostle testifies, “helps our weakness. For we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself pleads for us with unspeakable groanings; and he who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he pleads for the saints according to God” (Rom. 8:26–27; the printed citation reads “Rom. XXVI, 27”).

The apostles received him from Christ’s mouth after the resurrection, so that they might forgive and retain human sins. And why say more? He taught the laws and ceremonies of catechism, scrutinies, baptism itself, the Masses, and the canonical hours to be celebrated. He instituted the holy chrism. He established the various ranks and offices of clerics and ministers in the Church. He distinguished people of different professions not only by their dwellings and food but also by their clothing. He appointed rulers over each profession, rank by rank, to be brought together into unity.

He dictated whatever pertains to the service of divinity or is honestly and usefully expedient for human conduct. He foreordained all the Church’s sacraments that have existed, exist, and will exist. He joins together the Church’s paradise with the roses of martyrs and the lilies of confessors.

Finally, he imbued, carried forward, and guided the pens and minds of the evangelists and apostles and of all the orthodox, so that wherever his impulse went, they too might walk, following him. He is the Spirit of life in the wheels—that is, in the canonical Scriptures—so that they may move with the living creatures when they run, stand with them when they stand, and rise from the earth with them when they are lifted up, because their words are spirit and life.

He gives them life in such a way that he also gives life to human beings through them. Without him, the letter of Scripture not only profits nothing but even kills, like the flesh of Christ understood in a carnal manner.

He also promulgated, for the correction and discipline of God’s churches, both generally and specifically, the decrees of apostolic men and the canons of the holy Fathers issued in various councils. Blessed Pope Damasus bears witness to this when he writes to Aurelius, archbishop of Carthage:

[Note: All learned authorities agree that this letter of Damasus to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, is spurious and forged.]

“Those who voluntarily violate the canons are judged severely by the holy Fathers and condemned by the Holy Spirit, by whose inspiration and gift they were dictated. For those who, against these same canons, not compelled by necessity but willingly—as has been stated—act insolently, presume to speak, or voluntarily consent to those wishing to act, seem not improperly to blaspheme the Holy Spirit. Such presumption is plainly one form of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, since, as has already been said, it acts against him by whose effort and grace those holy canons were produced.

“Diabolical wickedness commonly deceives many subtly, and very often mocks the imprudence of some under the appearance of piety, persuading them that harmful things are beneficial. Therefore, the authority of the sacred canons, which were formed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, must be known faithfully and handled diligently, lest in any way—God forbid—we transgress the statutes of the holy Fathers without unavoidable necessity. Rather, walking most faithfully by means of them, may we, with those who composed them under divine inspiration, deserve, with the Lord’s help, to possess the glory of reward and the full measure of labor through their merits, and so forth.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. The judgment of Saint Augustine concerning the power of the soul, its application here, and the character of those promoted by laymen and of their metropolitans

If there is still doubt whether the sanctification of this Spirit sanctifies and governs the whole body of the Church, or if it is asked how he does so, let it be understood that this is ineffable and beyond human capacity. Therefore it must be believed and understood piously, lest, if it is impiously investigated, offense be given.

Nevertheless, insofar as this is granted to a creature, the soul can proclaim the Spirit to be such a great craftsman that, from even a small conception formed by the mind, a person may conjecture something about his ineffable diffusion and thereby attain some degree of ability to think, however faintly, about the incomprehensible power of the Savior.

For, as blessed Augustine says in writing to Saint Jerome:

“The soul is extended throughout the whole body that it animates, not by local diffusion but by a certain vital intention. For it is wholly present simultaneously in all its parts; it is neither smaller in the smaller parts nor greater in the larger, but more intensely present in one place and less intensely in another, while it is wholly present in all and wholly present in each.

“Otherwise, although it senses what exists in the body as a whole, it would not sense it as a whole. For when something living in the flesh is touched at a tiny point, although that place is not merely the whole body but scarcely even appears to be part of the body, nevertheless the whole soul is not unaware of it. Nor does what is sensed travel through all the parts of the body; it is sensed only where it occurs.

“How, then, does what does not happen throughout the whole immediately reach the whole, unless the whole is also present where it happens, without abandoning the rest by being wholly present there? For those other parts also live in its presence, although nothing of this kind has happened there. If such a thing happened in both places, and both happened simultaneously, the whole soul would likewise be unaware of neither. Therefore it could not be wholly present simultaneously in all and in each of the body’s parts if it were diffused through them in the manner in which we see bodies diffused through spaces: their smaller parts occupying smaller spaces and their larger parts occupying larger ones.”

Both the judgment of so great a teacher and daily experience establish that the soul acts in this way.

Therefore, what faithful person could still doubt that the Holy Spirit, in a manner far more ineffable through his sanctification, fills the whole Church, sanctifying each thing joined and owing allegiance to it according to the quality of its ministers and possessions?

The clerical order is the preeminent part of the Church, like the pupil of the eye in the head, concerning which the Lord says: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zech. 2:8). There is also the lay power, strong and extended for obeying and defending the Church, like the breast and arms. Then there is the common people, like the lower or extremal limbs, equally subject and indispensable to ecclesiastical and secular powers.

The Church’s possessions may aptly be understood as the hair of the head, and worldly resources as the nails or the hair of the rest of the body. Whoever indiscriminately or violently removes these from the outer human being must gravely offend the inner human being because of the injury of dishonor or presumption.

There is no doubt that the Holy Spirit does this: throughout the whole Church he operates all things in all things, far more excellently than the soul, distributing to each as he wills and announcing to the disciples many things that they could not bear before Christ’s passion.

Therefore, just as, when the soul departs, foul odors and worms immediately seize the body and dissolve it into dust amid the greatest loathing and rejection of human beings, so ecclesiastical possessions, when their sanctification departs from them, are immediately abandoned to the power of demons and perish amid the utter curse of God and the holy Fathers.

Therefore, in accordance with what the Lord says in the Gospel to the man demanding a division of the inheritance, “See and beware of all greed” (Luke 12:15), you who are divided and divide others—recognize, even if late, that indivisible things cannot be divided, and no longer give heed to those who divide, if you wish to care for your own souls and for theirs.

Indeed, by following visible things and scorning invisible ones, you temporarily grasp the reed of empty honor, while after a little while you do not look toward either the hall of supreme blessedness or [lacuna] of ultimate misery.

If the greater part of you reflected on such things with a Christian mind, the Church would by no means be continually afflicted by so great an evil. But, alas! having obtained ecclesiastical dignity from lay dignities, although by canonical authority they ought, together with their instigators and supporters, to be deprived not only of communion at the altar but also of entry into the church, they gain first place in it, the administration of the sacraments, and the government and ordering of Christ and of all things—though they are forbidden even to touch its thresholds. They are, that is, perjurers toward princes, with whom, in so great a presumption, unbelievers either concur or persist; sacrilegious thieves and robbers toward God, from whom they steal and violently plunder his holy things; moreover, murderers toward Christ’s poor, whose patrimonies and monies they defraud and claim for their own uses; excommunicated from God and all his saints, past, present, and future, whose discipline they destroy and [uncertain reading: conciliant], while taking no care to scandalize and offend them.

These men must truly no longer be regarded as merely undisciplined Christians within the Church, but as heretics truly blaspheming the Holy Spirit, since they insolently and willingly transgress laws written and subscribed by the finger of God. Their primates and metropolitans undoubtedly share in their sins when they lay hands on such men without canonical examination, despite the Apostle’s protest in the Epistle to Timothy. What the Church itself visibly suffers at times because of such princes, priests, and their supporters is plainly indicated by the prophet Micah: “Hear this, princes of the house of Jacob and judges of the house of Israel, who abhor judgment and pervert everything that is right; who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity. Its princes judged for gifts, its priests taught for payment, and its prophets divined for money; yet they rested upon the Lord, saying, ‘Is not the Lord in our midst? Evils will not come upon us.’ Therefore, because of you Zion shall be plowed like a field, Jerusalem shall become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the temple a wooded height” (Mic. 3:9).

## CHAPTER XXX. Recapitulation concerning the deposition of heretics and Ezekiel’s judgment upon them.

[Col. 1190B] Since by the Lord’s gift I have now for the most part either driven back, struck aside, or at least blunted the darts hurled by the adversaries against the Catholics, I nevertheless think that, at the end of this book, I must blunt that dart steeped in excessive poison by which the ecclesiastical rule is stubbornly attacked: namely, that if, according to this rule, it follows that heretics are to be deposed, it must also follow, according to their assertion, that those same persons have obtained ecclesiastical grace, from whose elevation they must be deposed. Therefore, here too, I patiently ask the weighers of words for the moment: from what degree of divine grace are those deposed for whom the Psalmist thus prays: “Scatter them in your strength, and depose them, my protector, O Lord” (Ps. 58:12). And furthermore, from what ecclesiastical rank are those deposed for whom the Catholic Church prays on the day of the Lord’s Passion:

“Almighty and everlasting God, who saves all and wills no one to perish, look upon the souls deceived by the devil’s fraud, so that, every heretical depravity having been deposed, the hearts of those who err may recover their senses and return to the unity of your truth.”

Behold, here the Catholic Church asks that heretical depravity be removed from souls deceived by the devil’s fraud. The Psalmist above likewise prays that his enemies be deposed. In this deposition, surely, we can understand no deposition from any excellence of grace or dignity that they previously possessed, except the presumption of heretical falsehood, which they obstinately arrogate to themselves under the appearance of Catholic truth. Thus, when Simonians or any heretics are ordered to be deposed, they are not ordered to be deposed from any grace of ecclesiastical ordination that they have hitherto possessed; rather, they are to be removed from the outward appearance of ecclesiastical ranks, which they abuse through imposture to their own destruction and the deception of the Christian people.

To them the fable of the ass dressed in a lion’s hide can be applied most aptly. Having assumed—or, more properly, feigned—the strength of a lion, he terrified the timid sheep throughout the countryside, although from those garments or spoils he could acquire for himself or anyone else nothing at all of leonine strength except empty terror. When a peasant stripped the lion’s hide from him, he took away from the ass none of the lion’s power that he had received or possessed from that hide; he removed only the presumption that he had acquired from that hypocrisy. Thus, when the peasant saw the ass stripped, he is said to have addressed him:

“Perhaps by imitating a roar you deceive the ignorant;

But to me, who once [knew you], you will always be an ass.”

There is also another matter requested in that prayer: namely, that heretics and schismatics may return to the unity of divine truth. In the preface to that prayer we are likewise admonished to pray for them, so that God and our Lord may deign to recall them from all their errors to the holy Catholic and apostolic mother Church. Hence it is clearer than daylight that they are not in the unity of the Catholic and apostolic Church, to which the universal Church prays that they may be recalled and return.

Therefore, either Simonians or heretics are not heretics and are in the Church, or else they are heretics and are outside the Church. Now, if they are in the Church, they are Catholics and can receive the Holy Spirit; and thus they must no longer be regarded or called heretics. But if they are outside the Church, they are certainly either heretics or pagans, and therefore cannot receive the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit cannot be received outside the Church. The Lord himself testified to this above. His sentence was undoubtedly followed by all the orthodox, and by the distinguished Prosper, who says:

“Just as one must consider what and to whom one vows, so also one must consider where one vows: for outside the Catholic Church there is no place of true sacrifice.”

Explaining this also in verse, he adds:

“Let him who renders pious vows to the thundering Lord know

That there is one place for divine worship,

Which the true Church provides throughout the whole world,

And without which there is no merit of righteousness.”

In these words it is plainly proclaimed that they are convicted of possessing neither the true Church, nor the true sacrifice, nor the place of true sacrifice, nor divine worship, just as the other heretics do not possess them. What, then, do they possess in common? Only falsehood and demonic worship.

But let it be granted, they say, that among them there are sacrifice, priesthood, and the other sacraments and insignia of Catholics. And, oh, how many things are said which are proved to contain absolutely nothing of the realities indicated by their names! Although this has been abundantly demonstrated above, it may also be demonstrated from the words of the prophet Ezekiel, where he speaks of those who prophesy from their own heart: “Woe to the foolish prophets,” and so forth, up to: “and you shall know that I am the Lord” (Ezek. 13:3).

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the proper meanings of the expressions appended in the words of the aforesaid prophet and of blessed Gregory

We inserted the prophet’s words there in sequence for this reason: even if everything else were lacking, these alone would suffice for the refutation of heretics, and especially for the objections of the Simonians. Passing over, then, the other parts of the prophecy already cited, let us touch briefly upon what alone is useful for the present work: namely, that the wall built by the people is plastered by the prophets without straw.

For in certain provinces, especially in the East, bricks are made in such a way that straw is mixed with mud, by which the muddy material is bound together, so that heat does not afterward dissolve what moisture had glued together. Hence the straw itself is there called *temperatura*—“tempering”—because it tempers the dissoluble mud so that it does not come apart.

The people therefore build themselves into a wall while striving to become the Church of Christ. But because it is plastered by false prophets, that is, by heretics, with the visible mud of the sacraments without the tempering of invisible grace, it is destined to fall. That wall is consequently called not a wall, and the plaster not plaster, and the prophets not prophets, and the souls made alive not living, and the slain not dying.

There too the punishment is proclaimed of those who grieve the heart of the righteous, whom God has not grieved, and strengthen the hands of the wicked so that he does not turn back from his evil way and live (Ezek. 13:22).

That the reality of the visible sacraments found among heretics who bear the name of Christianity is not merely loss but also refuse may be shown from the words of the Apostle to the Philippians. There he declares how highly he formerly valued the sacrifices and ceremonies observed among heretics of Judaism after Christ’s Passion, and how highly he values them now, saying:

“As to the righteousness that is in the law, I lived without reproach. But whatever things were gains to me, these I have considered losses for Christ. Indeed, I consider everything to be loss because of the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord, for whom I have suffered the loss of all things and regard them as refuse, so that I may gain Christ” (Phil. 3:6).

The Lord also, rejecting the Jewish priesthood through Malachi, says:

“Behold, I will cast the arm away from you and scatter upon your faces the refuse of your feasts, and it will carry you away with it” (Mal. 2:3).

Blessed Jerome, explaining this, adds:

“Because he is speaking to the priests, he says: ‘I will cast upon your faces those things which you consider most holy in the law, and which were granted to you by God from the sacrifices as the reward of your virtues.’ For the priests received from the sacrifices the shoulder, that is, the arm, and the breast, and the tongue, and the stomach, and the things described in Leviticus. He declares that, because of their sins, he will cast all these away and throw them into the faces of the priests, so that those who offer such things may be such as those things offered are. And, he says, ‘it will carry you away with it’—that is, the refuse of your feasts—so that their stinking faces may be disfigured by the foul mixture of refuse.”

Moreover, from the words of blessed Gregory, whose improper expressions the defenders of the Simonians accept as proper ones, it is shown how many things are spoken improperly. For in his homily on the Gospel of the Epiphany he says:

“All the elements testified that their Creator had come. To speak of them in human usage: heaven recognized this man as God, because it immediately sent a star. The sea recognized him, because it offered itself to be trodden under his feet. The earth recognized him, because it trembled when he died. The sun recognized him, because it hid the rays of its light. The rocks and walls recognized him, because they were split at the time of his death. Hell recognized him, because it restored the dead whom it held. And yet the hearts of the unbelieving Jews scarcely recognize as God him whom all the insensible elements recognized as God; they refuse to be split open for repentance, though they are harder than rocks, and they deny that they should confess him whom the elements, as we have said, proclaim to be God either by signs or by their splitting.”

Therefore the Simonians and their obstinate defenders must necessarily admit that blessed Gregory spoke improperly here. Otherwise, if they maintain that he spoke properly, they must necessarily profess that he was a Manichaean, who believed and taught that insensible things possessed not only a living soul but also sensation.

If they fear to profess this, they must finally admit with us that neither the heavens, nor the sea, nor the earth, nor the sun, nor the rocks, nor the walls, nor hell recognized or proclaimed their Creator, nor did all those things do in his service what is said to have been done; rather, through a sudden and unusual alteration or disturbance of themselves, they made him known and proclaimed by human beings *κατὰ τρόπον μετωνυμίαν*—“by way of metonymy”—whereby what is done is customarily indicated by the thing through which it is done, as when a man is called “dust” and the sky “air.”

By this same trope, God is said to have recognized something when he causes it to be recognized by human beings. In the same way blessed Gregory admits that spiritual grace, or the dove, is sold when it is thought to be sold. For, as he himself says, speaking according to human usage, just as he preached that insensible things sensed, so he also preached that things incapable of being sold were sold.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Catholic criminals who are promoted or later fall, and on their ministry and deposition

Thus, by these and many other arguments, it is established that the Simonians obtained no ecclesiastical dignity, although their defenders shamelessly strive to persuade people that the honor received by them continues unless the bishop of the Roman and apostolic see, or their metropolitan bishops of the same province, depose them synodally.

For how can something continue in them that was in no way received? But when they add that this must also be considered with regard to all crimes—so that, if a priest commits adultery, he is to be deposed—they should know that this must be understood and handled in a very different way.

Indeed, heretics differ so greatly from Catholics that however criminal a Catholic may be, he is more acceptable to God and more tolerable to human beings than however just a heretic may be, if a heretic may be called just. Therefore, whatever good a criminal Catholic does or possesses is undoubtedly good by the merit of faith, without which it does not exist. But whatever good a heretic, even if regarded as just, appears to do or possess is undoubtedly evil by the desert of his faithlessness, since whatever he does with that faithlessness is sin. This has been demonstrated above by so many testimonies that nothing further need be said about it here.

For sometimes the dignity of the priesthood is granted to unworthy persons when the crimes or sins of human frailty are unknown, concealed, or overlooked. Through their promotion, the necessity or usefulness of their neighbors in the Catholic Church is provisionally served, or their wishes are accommodated.

Because these men belong to the Catholic faith, one must believe that, when they are promoted by Catholics, the Holy Spirit whom they possess is conferred upon them—if not for their own salvation, nevertheless for the accomplishment of the salvation of others. The Holy Spirit is therefore present with them when they minister, and absent when they transgress. He is present in the ministry, which recognizes what has been entrusted to their faith by the faithful; he is absent from their iniquity, which he does not recognize. He deigns to be present in his sacraments when they serve him, and disdains to be present in the perversity of their conduct when they resist him.

Thus, however slight the faith of their hearts may be, the Holy Spirit, invited by the ministry of their mouths and hands, is poured into the things being sanctified for the salvation of his own people; but, offended by the wickedness of their crimes, he is stirred up for the condemnation of the wicked. Since they are both ministers and criminals, he accepts their ministry, despises and punishes their crimes: present with them as ministers, absent from them as criminals.

To them can aptly be applied that saying of the prophet addressed to the Lord: “You are near their mouth, but far from their reins” (Jer. 12:2).

For the Holy Spirit, presiding in the hearts of such ministers over the faith whose author he is, asks according to God’s will for the saints and obtains whatever is expedient for them according to God’s will. This is indeed said metonymically: he is said to act because he causes something to be asked and obtained, although he himself is asked together with the Father and the Son, and also gives through the ministry of criminals—but criminals who have been installed by Catholics for the purpose of serving, at the proper time and place, the necessity or usefulness of Catholics.

Although many evils accuse such ministers, certain good things nevertheless excuse them: namely, faith, which according to its measure is capable of hope and charity; then necessity and usefulness; also the devotion or petition of the Church; and finally, gratuitous ordination by those who received it gratuitously.

If they lack the innocence of life required by canonical discipline, they nevertheless possess obedience—or at least promotion to ecclesiastical ministry without any venality, according to the rule given by the Lord Jesus Christ himself. By this rule the matter is strengthened on one side, even if weakened on the other. If that rule of the Lord were absent, no one, however otherwise innocent, could give or receive any grace.

It is therefore clear that by this rule alone even the wicked are directed toward something good when they consent to it, while without it even those who are not slightly upright are corrupted when they dissent from it.

Consequently, in ministers promoted in the manner described, or who have fallen into some crime after their promotion, the honor they received continues as long as the Church either does not know their faults, conceals them, or tolerates them for the usefulness of others in the hope of their repentance.

As long as their deposition is postponed for any reason by those whose responsibility it is, they are permitted to fulfill the office of which they are now unworthy; and everything they do in the meantime, through the ministry previously entrusted to them or afterward permitted to them, is regarded as holy. Although this benefits them toward punishment, it nevertheless benefits others toward life.

Such men are truly deposed when they are deposed, because, even if not deservedly, they are nevertheless known to have possessed true promotion by virtue of their office. Nor are all those canonically promoted by them before their deposition deposed or condemned along with them, nor are the things they administer Catholicly invalidated with them.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On persons of every sort promoted by Simonians, and the refutation of the adversaries’ objection

[Col. 1195A]

But it is not so with the wicked Simonians—not so. Their deposition is not the deprivation of an honor possessed, but the uncovering or refutation of a promotion that was feigned or merely presumed.

Although there are many things that accuse them, there is nothing that excuses them. For in their supposed ordination, the necessity or usefulness of the Church is not served, nor is devotion or petition accommodated; only the avarice of both parties is provided for. Catholic faith and apostolic doctrine are not considered, but heretical faithlessness and Simonian ambition; not any innocence of life, but money alone.

Therefore they strive to sell and buy what can be given and received only gratuitously. Whose interests, then, are served in such ordinations, except the avarice of two men? For the first does not extend his hand or open his mouth, either for God or for his neighbor, before the other has extended his hand to his purse or opened his mouth in a promise.

With what confidence can it be asserted that people who are however just can receive any grace gratuitously from such men, when it is recognized that nothing of Christian faith, but everything of demonic faithlessness, has cooperated or cooperates in them?

Even if they sometimes appear to promote certain people gratuitously, it is clear that they do not do so without payment. They seek either the service of those persons or merely worldly favor from others. If those two things are openly absent, it may nevertheless be inferred that, in the supposedly gratuitous promotion of noble or religious persons, they secretly seek to snatch their favor or authority for themselves, so that those already promoted by them may be more secure in their own promotion, those to be promoted more ready to buy, and they themselves bolder to sell.

Thus either the present transaction is carried out by them, or a past transaction is confirmed through the present one, or certainly a future one is invited.

Although the hands of ecclesiastics must be kept clear of every kind of gift, above all they must be kept clear of money, which was expressly rejected by the Apostle Peter and condemned in Simon Magus himself.

Moreover, it does not seem absurd to meet here also another argument of the empty talkers. They say:

**OBJECTION.** The laws of the emperors decree that if anyone does this or that, he is to be punished with death. Now it happens that some layman commits that crime for which, under the enacted law, he ought to be put to death. While the judge whose responsibility it is postpones carrying this out, whether through mercy or negligence, does he not in the meantime remain alive? Does he not continue to bear the head that he justly ought to lose? And finally, if he later begets a son, will the son be guilty of the blood-crime of his father? Certainly not. For the one who committed the crime alone will bear the sentence of punishment.

**REFUTATION.** This argument is shown to work for us, not against us—for the *cephali*, that is, the “headed,” not for the *acephali*, the “headless.” For it was demonstrated a little above that those gratuitously promoted by Catholics, although they may be found criminal either before or after their promotion, are not without a head; and likewise that those promoted by them before their deposition do not perish on their account.

Therefore it is clear that the preceding argument provides no defense for the headless or for their sons, because they neither have nor have had a head—that is, an ecclesiastical office—from which they could be deprived. For a law is shown to be superfluous when it decrees that someone be deprived of what he does not possess.

It is like saying: “If a beheaded man does this or that, let him be deprived of his head.” Every heretic is indeed beheaded, cut off by his heresy from Christ, the head of the Church; and so are all who afterward appear to be promoted by them. Hence the dead are born from the dead, and consequently no one receives from them anything except something dead. What can be taken away from them in their deposition has been sufficiently demonstrated above: no one receives from them anything but a corpse-like thing (*morticinum*).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Arguments from secular laws against those who promote or are promoted as Simonians

[Col. 1196B]

Thus, by their own judgment, the action of these defenders is shown to have been weakened. For they are not dealing with the person whom they undertook to defend, but against him. While they strive to prove that the headless can have and carry a head, or can lawfully beget people who have been beheaded, they conceived a superfluous argument from the headless—that they bear and beget a head before they are beheaded—and, after a long labor, cast it out as an aborted offspring from the womb of their iniquity.

Therefore, having dismissed this truly frivolous argument, let arguments be taken from related and similar cases.

Suppose there is a certain man who, after bribing a judge with money, obtains another person’s estates through that judge’s favor and unjust sentence. If afterward a just judge, having discovered the matter, expels him from there, and the property rightfully passes to its former owner or to his heirs, does the lawful possessor preserve the lots that the usurper gave or sold to certain people, or the titles, offices, and rights that he conferred there, rather than removing them from the property for the sake of his own and his heirs’ interests?

If, out of reverence or favor toward the usurper, he fails to do this, as though the usurper had rightfully arranged something there, by his negligence he weakens and alienates his own right and confirms and restores it to his adversary.

By this argument concerning unjust acquisition and just loss or just recovery, it can be shown what the Simonians sell, what is bought, what is conferred by those promoted by them, gratuitously or otherwise, and what is usefully arranged and carried out by them or for others in property belonging to someone else.

For although the usurper, with the unjust judge bearing witness on his behalf, claims that he received, possessed, and gave or sold his right to others, or that it was afterward unjustly taken away from him, it nevertheless remains clear that neither he nor anyone through him acquired in such estates anything except injustice and their own loss.

When both the perpetrators and their supporters are expelled from them and punished by the penalties of the laws and by multiplied restitution for the things they presumed to possess, they are deprived not of a justice that they never had, but only of the injustice they incurred.

Finally, the judge, stripped through penance of the crime of perjury and falsehood, is deposed; the usurpers likewise are cleansed of the leprosy of falsehood and robbery. Otherwise, what is contracted temporally here will be repaid eternally, down to the last farthing. For “a false witness will not go unpunished” (Prov. 19:5). And no one long rejoices who wins through an unjust judge.

Furthermore, if someone is discovered to have stolen any property, will he not, as Solomon testifies, restore it fourfold and hand over all the substance of his house? But if someone knowingly purchases stolen property, he both loses the price he paid and is nevertheless held liable for the thief’s wrongdoing and punishment. Whoever purchases it unknowingly also loses the price paid and restores the purchased merchandise without the thief’s mark.

If, however, by oath he proves to those accusing him that, when he bought it, he did not know that it had been taken by theft, he is cleared; otherwise, if he either attempts to retain it by force or delays in excusing himself concerning the theft, he will bear the thief’s wrongdoing, together with the mark and punishment.

This must necessarily be suffered by one who has received stolen property from a thief even gratuitously.

From this it may be gathered that, if no one escapes infamy, loss, and punishment after acquiring anything stolen from a thief whenever it is found in his possession, much more will this apply to those who, knowingly or unknowingly, acquire from Simonian thieves, by payment or gift, the dove of God that appears to have been stolen—and all the more so because divine things are greater and more precious than human things.

Therefore either let it be proved that the Simonians, like the other heretics, are not thieves and robbers, or let it be conceded that nothing received or obtainable from them can be obtained without infamy, loss, and punishment—things that certainly cannot be avoided without legal satisfaction.

If it is still less established whether the Simonians are thieves and robbers, let it be carefully considered and faithfully believed that, if they are heretics, they are undoubtedly thieves and robbers; but if they are Catholics, they will be either shepherds or hirelings.

But so that we may not linger longer over this ambiguity, let the supreme good Shepherd himself be heard as he specifically resolves the matter. In his discourse, as though by an index, he points out separately shepherds, hirelings, thieves, robbers, sheep, and wolves.

Indicating the shepherds, he says:

“He who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep; to him the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out; and when he has brought out his own sheep, he goes before them” (John 10:2); “and the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (ibid., 11).

Then, showing the hirelings, he says:

“The hireling, and he who is not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, and leaves the sheep and flees. The hireling flees because he is a hireling, and he has no concern for the sheep” (ibid., 12).

Then, indicating thieves and robbers, he says:

“Amen, I say to you: he who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (ibid., 1). And all who came”—understood: not through the door—“were thieves and robbers” (ibid., 8). “The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy” (ibid., 10).

Specifically designating the sheep, he says:

“The sheep follow their shepherd because they know his voice; but they do not follow a stranger; rather, they flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers” (ibid., 4), “nor do they listen to thieves and robbers” (ibid., 8).

Finally, expressing the wolves, he says:

“The wolf seizes and scatters the sheep” (ibid., 12).

## CHAPTER XXXV. Restatement of the Lord’s teaching concerning good shepherds and hirelings

Although the Lord’s words are sufficient for a complete recognition of the good and the evil, we nevertheless think they should be briefly reiterated for the sake of certain slower minds.

First, concerning the good shepherds, we indicate only this: they are members of the supreme Shepherd himself, in whom alone, as in one head, all the perfected are united through him, beneath him and with him—one shepherd of one fold.

These men, whether they are bishops or the other rulers and ministers of the Church, like sons and household servants of the great master of the household, pasture his sheep not for themselves but for him. They do not seek their own profits but his, being content with simple food and clothing, which the master of the household provides for them from the milk and wool of their sheep.

They exact tithes, first fruits, and the offerings of the faithful, together with the reverence due to rightful submission, only so that they may be sufficient to feed the sheep and not fail midway along the road through [hunger] and nakedness.

They go before the sheep, know them, and are known by them. They provide the sheep with healthy and life-giving pastures, and at the proper time they now console and now threaten them. They diligently guard the fat and strong sheep, and carefully devote themselves to healing, restoring, and strengthening the sick, weak, and broken.

With staffs and powerful cries they drive wolves away from the sheep, setting their vigilance against the powers of the air or of the earth for their defense, lest either the devil, by spiritual temptation, or any worldly robber, by bodily persecution, seize and scatter them.

Therefore, in resisting such enemies, they sometimes steadfastly undergo grave dangers and cheerfully lay down the life of their own bodies for the sheep’s devoted souls. By this sign above all they are recognized as good shepherds: they do not flee when they see the wolf coming.

Such men enter the sheepfold through the door, Christ. They are freely chosen and promoted to this ministry, and freely and sincerely proclaim Christ by their words and conduct.

They do not receive temporal stipends from the sheep because they preach, but so that they may be able to preach—not so that they may grow rich or splendid in temporal things, but so that they may provide for their temporal necessity for the perpetual salvation of Christ’s sheep.

Nothing hinders them in their homeland because they accepted provisions on the journey, since they did not seek to fill temporal purses for themselves from the sheep, but to live temporally among their brothers in Christ, using here the provisions due to them so that there they may enjoy full rewards.

We have spoken of the very few who are chosen; let us speak of the many called to pastoral ministry.

First, let us speak of the name “hireling.” *Mercenarius* is a compound name derived from *merces* (“payment”) and *annus* (“year”), because, hired for an annual wage, he manages the business or feeds the sheep of the person who hired him.

Although he feeds them, he is nevertheless declared by the Lord not to be a shepherd, because the sheep are not his own. He does not seek their salvation and growth as though they belonged to him, but seeks his wage from them as from someone else’s property.

The coming of the wolf reveals this, because as soon as the hireling sees him, the wolf drives him to flee. He would not flee if the sheep were his or if he himself were a shepherd. But because he is a hireling, he flees; for he has no concern for the sheep, whose life and good health he does not seek, but only the wage he hopes to gain for feeding them.

Since the wage concerns him, not the sheep, he does not rescue them or defend them from the dangers threatening them at any risk to himself. He preserves only the wage agreed upon, for whose sake he was feeding the sheep.

Just as he did not seek their safety before the agreed wage, so he does not seek it after the wage has been paid. If they perish altogether, even while they are being fed, he does not care, provided that he himself does not lack his wage.

He is nevertheless necessary to the master of the household, leading his sheep to pasture and bringing them back, but useless for driving away wolves.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the hirelings’ wage and their promotion

All those who, sitting under the name of shepherd upon the pastoral chair, rule Christ’s Church while seeking only their own things and not Christ’s are undoubtedly such men.

And what are their own things? The first couches at banquets, the chief seats in the synagogues, greetings in the choir, and being called Rabbi by men.

Then there are the wool and milk of the sheep—that is, all the revenues of the faithful peoples—which they convert to their own use and profit. They demand these so violently, out of a desire for luxury and avarice, that sometimes they draw and extort from the sheep not only milk and wool but even blood, compelling the poor by tyrannical domination to return what they do not possess.

They do not oppose the wolves with any defensive weapons for the sake of the sheep. Nor do they utter a sound if they sense that they themselves may be harmed by wolves, or if they fear that, because of the sheep’s ill health, they may for a time be deprived of wool or milk, while the sheep refuse to be healed.

They are not blamed, however, because they justly accept things not entrusted to them, but because they love and seek only the gift and use of these things, not their fruit, and feed the sheep solely for their sake. These things are so owed to shepherds that failure to render them becomes evil, even if receiving them is not good when they alone are exacted.

Because they proclaim Christ through Catholic preaching, they do enter through the door into the sheepfold of the sheep, to the sheep whom they will lead out and bring back. But because they are servants and not sons, they do not remain in the house forever.

They must not be said to have descended from elsewhere, or to feed the sheep—that is, the Church—outside the Church, nor to have come in order to steal, slaughter, and destroy. Rather, they were invited by others for this sole purpose: to guard and feed the sheep in expectation of receiving their wage.

Because they do this more out of love for temporal wages than for eternal ones, they are not shepherds but hirelings. They are not content, as household members of the master of the house, with food and clothing, but demand annual wages with which to fill their private purses, lest, if they are ever removed from the care of sheep who are not theirs, they remain empty-handed.

To such men, because they receive on the way everything they seek from the sheep, it will be said in the homeland: “Amen, I say to you, you have received your reward” (Matt. 6:2).

These men are certainly not among the few who are saved, because they do not now strive to enter by the narrow [way], but belong to the many who afterward seek to enter and will not be able.

For when, as Luke testifies, the master of the household enters and shuts the door, and they begin to stand outside and knock at the door, saying, “Lord, open to us,” he will answer them: “I do not know where you are from.” Then they will begin to say: “We ate and drank before you, and you taught in our streets” (Luke 13:25); or, as Matthew says: “In your name we prophesied, and in your name we cast out demons, and in your name we performed many mighty works.” And then he will declare to them: “I never knew you. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Matt. 7:22).

Nevertheless, as long as these hirelings are permitted to preside over the faithful, they are necessary, because on account of their wage they dispense and preach the ecclesiastical sacraments and the Catholic faith.

Therefore their evil life is tolerated, and the office by which the necessities of the people are provided is honored.
