Since common necessity, not private greed, was the intermediary that led people to consent to their promotion, there is no doubt that many faithful people, attending to their salvation as the circumstances of the time required, received what the Lord promises to grant when two agree, saying:

“If two of you agree on earth about anything whatsoever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father” (Matt. 18:19).

Therefore, when necessity commands, their present or past conduct is not investigated; rather, provision is made only for the ministry and preaching of the Christian faith in such men.

Even their conduct of whatever sort after promotion is sometimes tolerated by the Church, unless perhaps they depart from the faith. For just as secular hirelings are not examined on the basis of faults by which they harm only themselves, but according to the care and usefulness by which they can benefit the sheep, so too with the Church’s hirelings.

And just as secular hirelings, if discovered to have been thieves, are not taken on, or, if taken on, are cast out when they begin to steal, so too these men: if they are known to have been infected with heresy before their promotion, they are not admitted; if after it, they are cast out.

And just as secular hirelings are sought out and invited to any ministry in the hope of a worldly wage, so these are sought out and invited in the hope of an ecclesiastical stipend.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the fact that Catholics promote no one on account of crime, whereas Simonians promote everyone on account of crime

[Col. 1200D]

Nor, moreover, do these men give or allow any payment to their ordainers for this; rather, they themselves receive it, like the hired servants of the world, who, unless they are assured of the wage agreed upon, will bind themselves to no service. Otherwise they are accused of plotting theft from another’s property, since under the pretext of benefiting others they hunt down the payments offered and seize them for themselves. Therefore, whether the one group or the other is meant, they are necessarily sought out and enlisted for the benefit of others—not as a needless favor and not for a price. Hence, whether they are considered guilty or innocent, they must necessarily be placed over the governance of others without payment.

No one is unaware that this is not done among the Simonians: for them, whether the candidates are guilty [Col. 1201A] or innocent, it is neither necessity nor the devotion of the people but money alone that recommends them. For they are not accustomed, nor can they truly, say to those whom they are promoting: “Come forward to be promoted, because you are necessary or pleasing to the Church”; rather, they say: “Because you have given, or are going to give, us one hundred solidi, or whatever amount.” Has it ever yet been heard that any Catholic, however wicked, said to someone being promoted: “Come forward to be promoted because you have committed adultery, perjury, and similar offenses”? Certainly not! What, then? “You are necessary for the ministry and pleasing to the Church.” Nor does the person being promoted say: “Give me an ecclesiastical rank because I am a fornicator or sacrilegious,” but rather: “Because I wish to offer my service to the Church of God, so that through it I may deserve the stipend due to me.”

Finally, just as the prince of demons, as is written, promotes and crowns his satellites for his deception, by which they hurl good people into crimes, so the Simonians promote their accomplices. Their shamelessness is so great that they openly proclaim their guilt to everyone, saying to the seller: “We gave you the payment; give us the rank we sought, or return the payment you received.”

It is therefore established, according to the judgment of blessed Gregory, that among the Simonians vices are rewarded—namely, avarice, the root of all evils, and heretical faithlessness. These are more serious than fornication or adultery, insofar as it is more grievous for someone to sin against God than against his own body or against another man. It is surely from these Simonians that “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked is blessed” (Ps. X, 3). May it never be that anything of this kind is done by Catholics of any sort, [Col. 1201C] even when guilty men are promoted by them!

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. In what matters hired servants are to be heard, and in what matters not

From this point let the sheep learn from the Shepherd himself in what matters they ought also to listen to hired servants. Concerning them he says in the Gospel: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses. Therefore, whatever things they shall say to you, observe and do” (Matt. XXIII, 2). Behold how much obedience the supremely good Shepherd wishes to be shown to wicked hired servants, so that the people may not merely preserve their words in mind but also fulfill them in action.

Immediately afterward he adds the matter in which they are not to be heeded: “Do not act according to their works” (ibid., 3). Why this, Lord? Did you not command your people to observe and do everything they say? He adds: “For they say and do not do” (ibid.). It is as though he were saying: “Pay attention because they speak, but do not pay attention because they do not do what they say.”

Here he briefly warned that the teaching of their mouths and the ministry they received from God for the salvation of others were to be honored and accepted, while their carnal works, which they possess from the Evil One for their own destruction alone, were to be avoided. Let the sheep therefore not act according to the works of the hired servants, lest, just as those men say and do not do, the sheep likewise hear from them and fail to act, because they observe them saying and not doing.

The Lord reveals with what intention their works are performed when he says: “They do all their works so that they may be seen by men” (Matt. XXIII, 5). In this statement he shows in summary that they seek nothing from their preaching or ministry except to become known and pleasing to men. Then he explains what works of theirs he means:

“They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on men’s shoulders, but with their finger they do not wish to move them. For they enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their fringes. They love the first places at banquets and the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men” (ibid., 4–7).

By these words of our Redeemer they are not reproved because they impose the burdens of God’s commandments upon men—for this is recognized as their duty—but because they impose unbearable burdens and do not lighten them by even the smallest of their own actions. Nor are they reproved because they have phylacteries and fringes, but because they enlarge the former and magnify the latter; nor because they recline or sit first, as teachers, or are greeted or called Rabbi, but because they love these things alone. Yet although the ministers of Christ may be such that in the ministry of Christ which they administer they seek nothing belonging to Christ but only what belongs to the world, Christ nevertheless wills that what is his be faithfully rendered to them: that is, that they be heard and honored and rewarded with the tithes and offerings of the faithful.

If they are so wicked in the sight of men, what sort of people do you think they are in the sight of God? Yet God tolerates them, whether secretly or openly wicked or falsely good, and does not defraud them of the payment they seek. Because they are ministers of Christ, though they do not preside well, they are to be regarded as worthy of simple honor—that is, of present honor. For those presbyters who preside well, as the Apostle says, “are worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and doctrine” [Col. 1202C] (1 Tim. V, 17).

For Scripture says: “You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain” (ibid., 18); and: “The laborer is worthy of his wage” (Luke X, 7). If it is asked what the Apostle’s judgment is concerning hired servants, his Epistle to the Philippians shows it as follows:

“Some indeed preach Christ because of envy and contention, but some also because of good will; some out of charity, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the Gospel. But some announce Christ out of contention, not sincerely, supposing that they can stir up affliction for my bonds. For what does it matter? Provided that in every way, whether by occasion or in truth, Christ is announced, in this I rejoice, and I shall also rejoice. For I know that this will turn out for my salvation” (Phil. I, 15).

From the judgment of so great a teacher we are instructed how necessary hired servants are. Concerning those who preach Christ insincerely he rejoices in such a way that, whether Christ is preached out of envy or by occasion, so great an Apostle declares that he rejoices and will rejoice, provided that Christ is announced.

And who is unaware of how great a crime envy is? Yet if Christ is preached through envy, as through contention and disparagement of the good, the Apostle rejoices. Again, how great is the imperfection of seizing an opportunity for preaching merely for the sake of bodily advantage? Nevertheless, the Apostle still rejoices in preaching of this sort.

Therefore, bad works must not be adopted on account of good preaching and ministry, nor must the good things of holy preaching and ministry be despised on account of bad works. Hence, if a cluster of grapes hangs from a hedge and is gathered, the thorn of the hedge must nevertheless be avoided.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On those promoted knowingly or unknowingly despite their wickedness, and on the judgment of Paschasius concerning their ministry

In order that the Lord might show that such men would exist in his Church until the end of the age, and that the teachers of the Church would sometimes have to overlook them so that they might either be promoted or serve, he wished the sacrilegious thief Judas to be promoted to the apostolic rank, although from the beginning he knew what was in the man.

Likewise, the holy apostles, chosen from so many thousands of holy coenobites, unknowingly promoted Nicolas, a pig from Epicurus’ herd, to the diaconate—so it may be said. In these two men it was clearly prefigured that, when persons are promoted in the Church, some are known and others unknown; yet their office is either approved in their own case or meanwhile tolerated for the sake of others.

Whatever they temporarily perform in the divine sacraments through the office entrusted to them is wholly holy, as was the case with Judas before the agreement to betray, and with Nicolas before the invention of his abominable sect. This is also confirmed from Paschasius’ little book *On the Body of the Lord*, where we read: “Although the priest is guilty, etc., [it is] the gift of his bounty.”

Concerning the judgment of the aforesaid man, lest a charge of slander perhaps be brought against us because it is said here at the end that the Holy Spirit is given through the ministry of guilty men, although they themselves do not possess him, let attention be paid to what he inserted at the beginning, where he speaks hypothetically as follows:

“This mystery is in no way diminished by any unworthy person, provided that the consecration is performed according to the institution of apostolic succession; for it is fulfilled not by him but through his office, through the grace which the supreme Pontiff—the Truth himself—promised.”

Hence it is clear that they possess the Holy Spirit through the ministry which they received through the institution of apostolic succession, and yet do not possess him for themselves. They possess good things for ministering to others, but do not possess them for turning away evil from themselves. They also possess what is needed for believing rightly, but not for living rightly, as has been sufficiently demonstrated above. And the ministry of heretics is not Christ’s, for it has not been received through the institution of apostolic succession.

## CHAPTER XL. On the thieves of the Simonians, and how they enter the sheepfold

Since it has been said about hired servants within the Church, let us also speak about thieves outside the Church. Their greatest and first sign is that they do not enter through the door but climb in by another way. Because of this transgression and presumption, thieves and robbers are so designated by the Lord that the oath prefixed to the statement is also read for this reason:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: he who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber” (John X, 1).

If he had said this even without an oath, who except a liar and Antichrist would refuse to believe the Truth himself, Christ speaking? But he took care to affirm it with an oath because he wished it to be heard more attentively and retained more firmly.

According to the literal sense, therefore, the proverb of the Truth is true, and it is no less true according to the intention of the speaker. Among men, thieves and robbers are those who do not enter the sheepfold through the door but climb in by another way; and before God, no less, thieves and robbers are those who do not enter the Church through Christ, who, as he teaches, is the door of the Church, but climb in by another way.

These are undoubtedly all heretics, Jews, and pagans. For all alike do not enter the Church through Christ, whom they deny to have come in the flesh. If it is asked how all heretics deny that Christ came in the flesh, when some of them confess that he came in the flesh, let the judgment of Saint Augustine in the third book of this work be read there.

Now let us see how they climb in by another way. The Arians, for example, climb in by another way, since they distinguish the Trinity of persons in such a way that they also divide the unity of the divine substance. The Sabellians climb in by another way, since they preach the unity of the divine substance in such a way that they also confuse the Trinity of persons.

It would be lengthy, and beyond the powers of our intellect, to review individually the plagues of the remaining heresies. Therefore, leaving the others aside, let us show how the Simonians—whom our dagger attacks more particularly—climb in by another way.

They too, certainly, despising Christ the door and his doorkeeper, the Holy Spirit, climb in by another way. With their money, as though with ladders and siege engines, they attack the Lord’s wall—that is, the unanimous agreement and solidity of the people of God—in order to storm it; they either crawl over it or break in by subduing it or, at any rate, by forcing their way through.

For they do not respect the law of the door, which says: “Freely you have received, freely give” (Matt. X, 8), nor do they await the favor of the doorkeeper. Driven by a headlong desire for precedence, they cross over, undermine, or break through the wall, and the worst of thieves and robbers invade the sheepfold.

They cross over the wall of God’s sheepfold when, abusing secular powers, they prevail temporarily in dominating the sheep. They undermine it when they extract ecclesiastical persons who adhere to the foundation of the Church and draw them over to themselves. They break it when they separate ordinary and lay persons from the charity of Christ and join them to themselves.

They also tear apart the roof when they strip the Church’s superiors of the integrity of their office. Whether, then, they invade the sheepfold by crawling over, undermining, or breaking in, it is evident that they climb in by another way rather than through the door.

Finally, they either storm secular powers through payment, or ecclesiastical persons of lower rank, or their superiors, or certainly laymen of moderate influence. For these four orders are set against the lesser peoples, as against weaker sheep, for their protection: the secular authorities are a wall against visible attacks, and the ecclesiastical authorities a roof against invisible ones.

It is therefore established that the Simonians, the robbers, in order to prevail in slaughtering and destroying the sheep, have gained access within through those who were appointed as defenders from without. Nor do those defenders themselves escape without vengeance: like roof tiles or stones removed from a building, they now lie neglected and useless outside Christ’s building, upon the face of the earth. The walls and roof themselves also seem dangerously to remain or survive after the doorkeeper has been driven away and the sheep extinguished, left to desolation and ruin, and even to wild beasts and unclean birds.

## CHAPTER XLI. How the Simonians imitate the thieves of the world, and what their voice is, which the sheep do not hear

Let us now consider how closely the robbery of the Simonians corresponds to what is sometimes done by the thieves of the world. Having entered the sheepfold by force, they first attack the doorkeeper and immediately strangle or bind him, so that they may more safely drive away and destroy the sheep for themselves.

Daily experience makes clear that this crime is committed by the Simonians, and all the more wickedly because divine things are more valuable than human things. They themselves strive first to extinguish the Holy Spirit in the people—or to enslave him, bound and delivered into their power—so that they may freely devour and destroy the people.

Do they not seem to drag him along as though he were bound when they trust that they can sell his grace as a captive to whomever they wish? Do they not neglect him as though he had been extinguished by them when, through their faithlessness, they extinguish him in the sheep whom he was giving life?

The Holy Spirit is said to be extinguished when faith—which is certainly a gift and over which he presides—is extinguished in each person by the intrusion of faithlessness. Hence the Apostle also gives this warning: “Do not extinguish the Spirit; do not despise prophecies” (1 Thess. V, 19–20).

These thieves plainly extinguish the Holy Spirit in the sheep when, offended by their fellowship or consent in impiety, they compel him to withdraw and flee from them. Once he has been extinguished, they now despise all prophecies, that is, the holy Scriptures. For with what reverence will they now receive the judgments of others, when they so stubbornly trample upon the decree of that great Prophet and Lord of the prophets himself, who, subscribing to the institution of his sacraments, says: “Freely you have received, freely give” (Matt. X, 8)?

Although such men seem to be within the Church—since thieves too, when they steal, seem to be inside the sheepfold—they would certainly be condemned less severely if they stole outside. Do Jews and pagans not sometimes appear within the material walls of churches? Yet as they enter, so they depart; indeed, inside they are worse because of their presumption, their violation of the sacraments, and the contamination of others.

“For what fellowship has the faithful with the unfaithful?” (2 Cor. VI, 15). Yet while they appear to be inside, are they considered Christians? So, without doubt, the Simonians, while they appear to be within the Church, are then all the more to be rejected and regarded as thieves.

They are to be believed not to be thieves and robbers only when it has been proved that they entered the sheepfold through the door and did not climb in by another way. Otherwise, without exception—even the heretics—all who came by some route other than the door are, as the Lord testifies, thieves and robbers.

Lest they perhaps be thought useful in some respect, as hired servants are, it is added: “The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy” (John X, 10). Where, then, are those who preach to the good that the good they received from wicked Simonians not only does no harm but even does good, when the Lord protests that thieves come only to steal, slaughter, and destroy?

Therefore, those who possess only these things and come only for these purposes—what good can they give to anyone, however good, unless they first change themselves through repentance and receive the good which they are able to give to others?

Not only their deed, not to mention it, but even their very voice is so deadly that, if the sheep hear it, they cannot fail to die. For when they hear it, they cease to be Christ’s sheep, since he himself testifies that the sheep did not hear them.

It is therefore evident that such sheep are no longer those of the good Shepherd, since they have heard thieves. What are they, then? They have been seized, slaughtered, and destroyed by thieves, and therefore are now nothing other than the victims of robbers. The wretched sheep would not succumb to these evils if they had not heard their voices.

Although thieves sometimes prevail in breaking in upon the sheep, they cannot steal, slaughter, or destroy them unless the sheep first listen to them. Nor do the thieves accomplish what they attempt so long as the sheep do not lend them their hearing.

What harm, then, could the Simonians inflict upon Catholics if, warned beforehand by their good Shepherd Christ, they refused to listen to them as shepherds and to give such thieves their favor and consent?

For this reason, the multiplication and boldness of thieves and robbers arise chiefly from the wretched patience of the sheep, who perish by the just judgment of God because, warned and instructed by two signs as by two witnesses, they have either neglected or despised the need to beware of thieves.

The good Shepherd set before his sheep two signs by which they could recognize thieves, so that, if one should occur without their knowledge or consent, they might avoid the other. The first sign of thieves and robbers is presented in their entrance into the sheepfold: it is not through the door but by another way.

The second is presented in the voice unfamiliar to the sheep. We must briefly impress upon them what this voice is, since enough has been said about the perverse entrance.

For example, the voice of the Arians is to assert that the Son is less than the Father, while the Son himself protests: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30). Likewise, the voice of the Simonians is to possess the Holy Spirit for sale, while Christ, whose Spirit he is, protests: “Freely you have received, freely give” (Matt. X, 8).

If Christ’s sheep recognize and know this voice of Christ, they must follow their Shepherd and not the thief, who is undoubtedly a stranger. The sheep do not follow him but flee from him because they do not know the voice of strangers, “whose mouth speaks vanity and whose right hand is the right hand of iniquity” (Ps. CXLIII, 8).

Therefore, let no one flatter himself; let no one, as an excuse for his sins, fit fig leaves to his shameful parts. Whoever hears the voice of the Simonians saying:

“I do not give you baptism; I do not give you the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ; I do not give you the Holy Spirit; I do not give you any ecclesiastical rank; I do not consecrate churches or perform any other administration of the divine sacraments unless you give me a payment”—

is certainly not a sheep of Christ. Against Christ’s voice he hears and recognizes the voice of strangers.

He therefore now follows a stranger rather than Christ, by whom he is no longer recognized, even if he is heard crying, “Lord, Lord,” to him whose voice he has ceased to recognize. If he had retained Christ’s voice, he would flee as quickly as possible from the stranger uttering a voice unknown to him.

## CHAPTER XLII. With what vigilance the sheep ought to resist thieves who have entered the sheepfold

Therefore, if the sheep cannot prevent the Simoniacal thieves from breaking into the sheepfold, let them at least resist those who have entered in the one way that is possible: let them neither wish nor be compelled to listen to such men as though they were shepherds whom they should follow, or even as though they were hired servants whom they should hear. Rather, as has been said, let them do what alone they can do: flee from them, avoiding their fellowship, offices, and assembled workshops fashioned from the blood of the sheep whom they slaughter and destroy.

Besieged or oppressed by whatever human terrors, or by danger to their bodies or possessions, Christ’s sheep should strive above all to escape injury to their souls, lest they be swallowed alive by the robbers. Let them not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul, but rather him who can destroy both body and soul in the Gehenna of unquenchable fire (Mark IX, 44).

Let them consider that, if all those who at the end of the world, amid the greatest failure of Christian faith, follow Antichrist will be without excuse—deceived not only by great signs and wonders but also compelled by tortures of every kind of persecution—then much more without excuse are those who now, when the Christian name enjoys the greatest glory, follow thieves and robbers, deceived by blandishments and terrors.

For just as it was foretold to the former that false prophets and false Christs would arise, so it was foretold to the latter that thieves and robbers would come and enter the sheepfold. The Lord thus warned his own through the apostles:

“See that no one seduce you. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and they will seduce many. Then if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ or ‘There,’ do not believe; do not go out, nor follow them. Behold, I have foretold it to you. Therefore, if they say to you, ‘Behold, he is in the desert,’ do not go out; ‘Behold, he is in the inner rooms,’ do not believe. For behold, the kingdom of God is within you. Therefore, see; behold, I have foretold everything” (Matt. XIV, 4).

It is as though he were saying: “It is in your power to be deceived or not to be deceived, and therefore you will be without excuse if you neglect or despise guarding yourselves, because I have foretold everything to you.”

For he showed beforehand where the kingdom of God is: in the Catholic Church, that is, within you who preserve and retain the apostolic faith and teaching in heart and mouth. Hence, where these things are shipwrecked or corrupted, Christ—and his kingdom—must not be believed to be present there, even if the place is called and appears to be a desert or an inner room.

O how many hermits, during the time of the Arians, said that Christ was in their desert, while, infected with the Arian plague, they had Antichrist among them! O how many and how great were those thought to be churchmen who clashed and cried out that Christ was in their inner rooms, while nevertheless they concealed Antichrist among themselves!

Such was Eusebius of Caesarea, the most ardent defender of Arius, as blessed Jerome declares: “Such was Didymus, and Eutyches, and very many others both from the cities and from the solitudes.”

What has therefore been said about the aforesaid heresy should be understood as said also about the others.

If anyone considers the Lord’s foregoing words, he will find that thieves and robbers are expressed by John through more evident passages than the false prophets and false Christs are by the other evangelists, although those whom the latter call false prophets or false Christs John calls thieves and robbers.

The other evangelists gave no identifying mark of them except that they would give great signs and wonders—something that not only leads the unwary away from error but also leads the cautious into error. John, however, indicated them to everyone, as though with a finger, by their entrance and their voice, so that no one could thereafter excuse himself on the grounds of ignorance of his own destruction if he had not feared to hear and follow thieves marked out for him.

Finally, if the sheep are at some point deprived of free judgment concerning the one who is to rule them, they can nevertheless refuse to hear the voice of strangers, and can refrain from following the stranger and instead flee from him.

Even if they see someone marked out by the appearance of a true shepherd, they should not dare to hear and follow him before learning from his entrance and his voice whether he is a shepherd or a thief. With Joshua son of Nun, they should say to him with laudable curiosity: “Are you one of us or one of our adversaries?” (Josh. IX, 13).

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the difference between hired servants and thieves, and that heretics are not to be tolerated by Catholics like Catholics who live badly

From what has preceded it is now sufficiently clear how far thieves and robbers differ from hired servants. Hired servants are to be heard in everything they say, since the Lord commands concerning them: “Observe and do all things whatever they shall say to you” (Luke XVII, 10). Thieves and robbers, however, are not even permitted to be heard, because as soon as they are heard, the hearers perish.

Hired servants are such that the Apostle also rejoices in their preaching; thieves and robbers, however, are such that the same Apostle, weeping, calls them corrupters of God’s word and enemies of Christ’s cross.

Although hired servants seek what is theirs rather than what is Christ’s, they nevertheless do not seek for themselves anything other than what is owed and commanded to be rendered to those who feed Christ’s sheep—namely, due tithes and reverence. In seeking these they do not sin, because they seek to render to God what belongs to God.

They sin by seeking these things for themselves alone, because they say that these alone are theirs. Yet while they feed God’s pasture-sheep for a time on account of these things, they also render to God what belongs to God in this respect.

For blessed Jerome explains in his commentary on Malachi that tithes and the other offerings of the faithful are owed and rendered to the Lord alone, and that they have been divinely assigned for the temporal support of his ministers of whatever kind:

“Who, I ask, among you, O priests, closes the door and kindles my altar for nothing? For there is no one among you, down to the very last of the ministers—not merely a priest and the others, but not even a doorkeeper or the one who places the fire beneath the altar to burn the holocausts—who does not receive from me payment for his labor.”

He says this while signifying the tithes of all the crops offered by the peoples. When robbers demand these, they are certainly not seeking what is theirs. For no stipend is owed to them for a divine ministry of which they are entirely devoid; only the gallows or the ultimate punishment is owed to them for their robbery.

Yet, alas, they very often receive not only what they find assigned to Christ’s ministers but also what is forbidden, since they come and are able to do nothing other than steal, slaughter, and destroy.

Who in his right mind considers such thieves and robbers tolerable for Catholics, when the Lord judges that they are to be fled from in such a way that he testifies that those who hear them are not sheep?

And with what face does anyone preach that their ministry should be tolerated and accepted until they are deposed synodally, and that everything performed in the sheepfold through their ministry in the meantime is good and holy, when their ministry consists solely in stealing, slaughtering, and destroying?

If it is good and holy to steal, slaughter, and destroy Christ’s sheep, then let thieves and robbers be endured, since they know and can do nothing else, as the Lord protests. If anyone dares to contradict him, asserting that thieves and robbers know or can do anything else good, let him dare also to debate and contend in judgment with the Lord, and, if he can, accuse him of lying.

If no Christian dares to do this, it must be conceded that such thieves and robbers do nothing but evil to themselves and to others.

Why, then, are the Simonians thought to be deposed synodally many times and almost every day, when from the beginning they were once and irrevocably deposed by the chief apostles, just as afterward other heretics were deposed by orthodox and Catholic Fathers at the very moment of their arising?

Whenever a bad tree is uprooted completely, its branches are believed uselessly to live, or to be going to live, unless they too are uprooted, since they are counted as uprooted in the uprooting of their mother. In the same way, the deposition of any heretic, as a cutting off, need not be sought in each individual person, as in each individual branch, if the author of the heresy has been completely uprooted as the root of the bad tree.

It is certain that this does not happen with Catholics who live badly. Their root—the Catholic Church—is never uprooted, even when some of its branches are cut off because of their barrenness or disorder. As long as they are borne by their mother tree, they are either improved or serve for the shade of men or the rest of birds.

So also wicked ministers of the good Catholic Church, although they live badly for themselves, until their deposition is postponed, either happen to be improved or meanwhile confer some benefit upon others.

From these considerations it can be observed that the deposition of Catholics who live badly is often postponed for a time and according to circumstances, and sometimes carried out; but the deposition of heretics is postponed neither for a time nor according to circumstances, but is carried out as soon as they become known.

Therefore, concerning Christ’s ministers who live badly, the Catholic people ought to await the judgment of Catholics in synod and not cast them out until the decision of their fellow ministers or teachers casts them out, in accordance with Solomon’s teaching: “Let your eyes see what is right, and let your eyelids go before your steps” (Prov. IV, 25).

It commonly happens that what seems intolerable to the imperfect seems tolerable to the perfect, and, conversely, what seems tolerable to the imperfect is regarded as intolerable by the perfect. To prevent the Church from being deceived or scandalized by this ambiguity, the matter must be awaited patiently and wisely until a synodal judgment discerns and determines it.

Anyone who thinks that this judgment should be awaited in the case of heretics as well, after councils have once been held concerning them, I do not know whether he could truly be called a Catholic. For whoever considers any heresy tolerable in the Church has undoubtedly suffered shipwreck of, or fallen away from, the Catholic faith.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Examples demonstrating that the ancient Catholics did not tolerate heretics even for an hour, while they tolerated hired servants

At the time of the Arians or of other heretics, if any heretic was appointed bishop anywhere among Catholics, did Catholics tolerate his ministry or regard it as holy until he was deposed synodally?

That this was never tolerated by Catholics is clear from many histories, and especially from the *Tripartite History*, which recounts that boys purified a toy ball by fire because it had accidentally rolled beneath the feet of the little donkey on which the heretical bishop of that city was then riding.

The Catholics are also said to have so detested the man’s baths that they refused to wash there not only with him but even without him, until they had first purified the places themselves with fresh water.

Lest anyone think that this zeal of the Catholics—good and proposed for imitation by all Catholics—was demonstrated during a time of peace and some temporary Christian power, let it be known that this occurred during the reign of Arian emperors and princes. Because of it, the city itself was given over to the sword, and the greater part of its citizens were slaughtered.

Whoever wishes to know more precisely with what eagerness they hastened to death in confession of the Catholic faith, and how the executioners first grew weary of slaughtering before the devoted citizens ceased offering and thrusting themselves before those who killed them, should reread the aforesaid history.

There he will find that Catholics suffered from the heretics not only these things but also very many other insults, beatings, dangers, and losses.

After such evils, who could adequately enumerate with what steadfastness the Catholic Church in Africa resisted the Vandals, more savage than every beast, compelled to live for a long time under countless and carefully devised punishments and scarcely permitted to die at last?

Therefore, woe to the prosperity of the Catholics of our time, under which the Christian faith is withdrawn and extorted without any, or scarcely with any, loss of itself and its possessions under most Christian princes—whereas our predecessors were unable to withdraw or extort it even amid indescribable adversities and under sacrilegious tyrants!

How long heretics are to be endured, or how they are to be deposed, the Lord first established when he made it known that they were not to be heard by the sheep but fled from; and afterward Paul, the spokesman of God, confirmed this by deeds and words.

Although he tolerates hired servants who are contentious, stubborn, avaricious, greedy, and envious in such a way that he even declares that he rejoices and will rejoice in their preaching, he indicates that thieves and robbers—heretical men—are to be avoided after one and a second admonition.

He clearly shows that he did this when he handed Alexander, Hymenaeus, and Philetus, who said that the resurrection had already taken place, over to Satan, so that they might learn not to blaspheme.

Blessed Augustine, too, in his exposition of the Gospel of John, asserting that hired servants are in some respect necessary and useful, although blameworthy in many respects, says by way of concession:

“Let the Lord’s sheepfold have superiors, sons, and hired servants. The superiors who are sons are shepherds. But superiors who seek their own things, not those of Jesus Christ, are hired servants.”

The same man says later:

“You already know, in the name of the Lord, who the good shepherd is, and how the good shepherds are his members, and therefore there is one good shepherd. You know who is the hired servant to be endured; who the wolf, thieves, and robbers are, whom one must beware of; what the sheep are; what the door is through which both the sheep and the shepherd enter; and how the doorkeeper is to be understood. You also know when someone has not entered through the door: he is a thief and a robber, and he comes only to steal, kill, and destroy” (John X, 10).

Behold, although so great a teacher said that the hired servant was to be endured, and that the Church should have hired servants as superiors, is he ever found to have said anywhere that thieves and robbers should be endured, and that the Church should have them as superiors?

Whoever thinks that he has not found sufficient satisfaction here should examine more carefully his exposition, where he will find the hired servants, thieves, robbers, and the rest clearly identified.

On the fact that Saint Gregory, while still a deacon, avoided Eutychius, and that Saint Jerome asserts that a public judgment should not be awaited in their case.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF HUMBERt

[Col. 1211]

## FRAGMENT OF A DISPUTATION AGAINST THE GREEKS

(From Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, p. 815, from a manuscript of Fleury.)

### PRELIMINARY NOTICE

The following fragment of a disputation against the Greeks was supplied to us by a Fleury codex written by hand approximately six hundred years ago. We have not yet been able to discover who its author was, since both the beginning and the end of the disputation are missing from the manuscript. Nevertheless, we can establish something with certainty about the period in which he lived or wrote.

He did not compose his work before the time of Michael Cerularius, patriarch of Constantinople, who revived the schism against the Latins, which had been dormant, and did so with no little fury. Nor did he write it before Leo of Acrida, bishop, or Nicetas, abbot of Studium, the most bitter enemies of the Latins, whose names he objects to the Greeks having inscribed in the sacred diptychs. Yet two considerations persuade me that he published his work before the end of the eleventh century.

The first I derive from the antiquity of the Fleury codex, whose script appears to approach an age of six hundred years. The second is that the author plainly accuses the Greeks of offering the consecrated Eucharist dipped to communicants, contrary to the custom of the Latin Church. “But,” he says, “we receive the body separately and the blood separately, and we know that dipped bread was given to no one except Judas the traitor.”

Although, according to the decree of the Council of Tours reported by Burchard, book V, chapter 9, “the sacred offering ought to be dipped in the blood of Christ, so that the priest may truthfully say to the sick person, ‘May the body and blood of the Lord benefit you,’” this decree was nevertheless weakened by canon 1 of the Third Council of Braga, which forbade “offering the Eucharist soaked in wine as the completion of communion.”

This prohibition had the force of law among the Latins until the twelfth century. At the beginning of that century the Eucharist began to be given generally dipped, as we learn from the letter of Ernulf, bishop of Rochester, to Lambert, where he attempts to defend this rite, as he says, “introduced by a new custom,” with many arguments. Ivo of Chartres also supports it in his treatise *On the Divine Offices*.

It is therefore clear that the disputation against the Greeks, of which we present this fragment, was written during the period when Michael Cerularius stirred up the schism in the Church—a schism which Nicetas Pectoratus tried with all his strength to defend—that is, approximately between the years 1050 and 1100. At that time Cardinal Humbert and Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, two lights of our order, vigorously refuted the Greeks’ inventions in their writings. Nor do I doubt that others also undertook the same task; would that we possessed their labors! But, so that they may not perish altogether, let us at least present this fragment.

## FRAGMENT OF A DISPUTATION AGAINST THE GREEKS

[Col. 1213]

[Col. 1213A] You will say that you are ignorant of their faith. Does your ignorance prejudice the orthodox Fathers? Does it not rather condemn you for the fault of negligence? If you maintain that the holy Fathers did not possess that faith, and assert that their books have been falsified, you are in no way to be accepted on this point either, since you cannot prove such excuses by any assertions.

For at no council is such sacrilege charged against our people, whereas the Sixth Council testifies that your people committed it. But let us come to the matter itself and see how you sin even against Holy Scripture and against the Catholic faith itself.

Since the Holy Spirit is fully and perfectly God, and in every respect equal to the Father and the Son, the expressions that he is called “the Spirit of the Father,” and that the Father gives, sends, or pours him forth—or whatever similar expression is read—signify no servitude or inferiority. For the Father is neither his God nor his Lord, because he is not greater than him. There is no greater or lesser in God. For whoever is lesser is not perfect God; and whoever is not perfect is not God at all, because God is perfect.

The Holy Spirit is God because he is from God. Nothing is from God except what is God. He is therefore the Spirit of the Father solely because he is from the Father; for if he were not from him, he could in no way be his Spirit. And just as the Son has his essence from the Father by being born, so the Spirit has his essence by proceeding. For “procession” signifies the essence of the Holy Spirit. In his simple nature nothing is other than what it is.

Therefore, whether the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father, or to be sent by the Father, given by the Father, poured forth by the Father, or to be the Spirit of the Father, all these expressions are one and signify one thing: the essence of the Spirit, since in a simple nature nothing is diverse.

That he is the Spirit of the Father is his essence. That he proceeds from the Father, is given, sent, or poured forth by the Father is his essence; and he has nothing from the Father except what he is. Whatever he is, he is God; nor does he have another nature, as the Son does, in which he might possess something other than what is God. The Spirit is of the Father as God, proceeds as God, is given as God, is sent as God, and is poured forth as God, because he is wholly God.

He is one with the Father because he is from the Father. He is consubstantial with him; he proceeds from him, is sent by him, given by him, and poured forth by him, because he is from him, and there is nothing in him except what he is.

Likewise, when he is called the Spirit of the Son, and is said to be given, sent, poured forth, breathed, exhaled, brought forth, to go forth from him, and to receive from him what he announces, this indicates the same procession—that is, the same pure essence.

The Spirit is not the Spirit of the Son in one way and of the Father in another. Nor does the Son give, send, pour forth, or breathe him in a manner different from the Father. Nor does he proceed from the Father in a way different from that in which he is brought forth and goes forth from the Son. Nor does he receive from the Son what he announces in a way different from that in which he receives it from the Father.

The simple nature of the Godhead does not have different essences, nor does it possess anything from the Father or the Son except what it is. There is no accident in God. What he is, he always is.

Just as the Father always begets and the Son is always begotten, and neither the Father nor the Son is anything that is not always present, so the Holy Spirit always proceeds, is always sent, always given, always poured forth, always breathed, always brought forth, always breathed into, always goes forth, always receives what he announces, and is always the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

And just as the Son’s being begotten, born, sent in the form of God, proceeding from the mouth of the Most High, and going forth from the Father all signify his one essence, which he has from the Father, so everything that is said of the Holy Spirit demonstrates one and the same essence, which he has from the Father and the Son. For the various expressions do not signify different things in him, in whom there is nothing except what he is.

Thus, whether one speaks of procession, mission, or anything else that he has from the Father and the Son, it signifies the one pure, simple, identical, and only essence that he has from the Father and the Son. If it signifies something different, then either the simple nature will have different essences, or there will be something in God besides what he is—neither of which the Catholic faith accepts.

Again, since the Holy Spirit is one with the Father and consubstantial with him because he is from him, that is, proceeds from him, the same Spirit would not be consubstantial with the Son as he is with the Father, nor one with the Son as with the Father, because he is neither from him nor proceeds from him. The Catholic faith does not accept this, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one not in different ways, but in one undivided manner.

Again, if the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, how does he proceed through him, as the Seventh Council states? For what is it to proceed through a house, if not to proceed from the house? Or how does the Spirit go forth from the Son if he does not proceed from him? What is “to go forth” except “to proceed”? Or how is he breathed, breathed into, poured forth, or brought forth by him, if he does not proceed from him?

Is the Spirit of the Father one thing and the Spirit of the Son another, so that he is the Spirit of one by proceeding from him, but not at all the Spirit of the other? How does he not proceed who is breathed, sent, given, poured forth, brought forth, breathed into, who is his Spirit, who goes forth from him and receives from him what he announces?

For what can God receive from God except what he is? Is God needy and diminished in some respect, so that a more powerful God must supply his need? Or did he assume the form of a servant in which he might receive what he does not have? If you think so, you think wrongly; you think against God, you think against the faith.

Finally, if the things said of the Holy Spirit signify not his essence, which he has from the Father and the Son, but something on account of which you regard him as lesser than the Father and the Son, then you join the Macedonian Pneumatomachians.

We accuse you of detracting from God’s sacrifice and sharpening your tongues like serpents against the Lord (Ps. 63:4), so that some among you, holding the highest ecclesiastical rank, have pronounced an anathema against the body of Christ, thrown it to the ground with many insults, and trampled with unclean feet upon the blood of our redemption.

This horrifying crime ought to have terrified the devil himself. The Jews sinned less when they laid impious hands upon Jesus, drove him on, and crucified him through the soldiers. They acted in ignorance; for if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8). But you have both seen and hated him and, according to the prophet, hated the Lord without cause.

But let the body of the Lord, which was unleavened when it was bread, be punished—what did his blood deserve that it should be poured out and trampled upon, though your authority has not yet issued a sentence of condemnation against it?

But perhaps you did not consent to this. Why, then, do you commemorate Michael the patriarch during the solemn celebration of the Mass? Why have you not erased Leo of Acrida, bishop, and Nicetas, abbot of Studium, from the sacred diptychs? Why do you still not communicate in our sacrifice with the Lord’s blood?

Perhaps the blood is polluted by contact with the body. For it is written: “Whatever touches what is unclean becomes unclean” (Lev. 11:26). But we receive the body separately and the blood separately, and we know that dipped bread was given to no one except Judas the traitor.

Consider also what absurdity follows from your opinion concerning Christ’s body. If you believe that the Lord’s body is made from unleavened bread, why is it not received? Why is it not adored as the Lord’s body? Why is it forbidden to make it? Why is it attacked with insults? Why is it called imperfect and lifeless? Why is it expelled from the churches together with those who offer it? Why is leaven preferred to it? Why do you suspend its worshipers from communion? Why do you call us “Azymites”?

Did Christ have two bodies—one perfect and the other imperfect, one living and the other lifeless, one unleavened and the other leavened, one signifying and the other signified? Who would dare think such things about Christ’s body except one who neither reveres nor believes in Christ, one who openly blasphemes, one who knowingly and deliberately attacks Christ?

If you deny that unleavened bread becomes Christ’s body, why do you call it imperfect? For Christ’s body is not imperfect if it is in no way his body. Why, finally, do you regard us as Christians? Why do you not condemn us as idolaters? For it is an idol if unleavened bread is adored as God.

Why do you not publicly refute this most impious heresy? Why do you not anathematize the Romans in the Church along with the other heretics? There is no middle position: either it is Christ’s body and must be adored by all, or it is not his body and must be despised as an idol.

But on what basis do you prove that it does not become his body, when none of the teachers holds this opinion and no council contradicts it? Why do you despise ecclesiastical canons and traditions? Why do you add to the decrees of councils something they do not contain concerning Christ’s body? What have unleavened bread or leaven to do with Christ’s body? Is it merely bread, so that it may be either unleavened or leavened? Why do you not rather leave undiscussed what you do not know? Why do you rashly affirm what you do not understand?

At least consider that you may not be both accusers and judges in the same case, that judgment is not legally rendered before proof, and permit others to judge in your case. Do not condemn the Lord’s body before judgment.

### That they assert that Christ celebrated Passover with leavened bread

We accuse you of maintaining that the Lord celebrated Passover before the fourteenth day of the moon, or violated the law on the fourteenth day by eating leavened bread. Thus you make him a transgressor of the law and assert that he abolished the law before it had been fulfilled.

Yet the Gospel records the first day of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover, and Christ affirmed that he had come not to abolish the law but to fulfill it. He certainly would not have done so if, before the law was fulfilled, he had abolished it by eating leavened bread.

It follows that the Lord committed sin and that deceit was found in his mouth, and that, as a transgressor of the law, he perished—according to his own judgment.

### That they call leavened bread living

We accuse you of asserting that leavened bread is living. Neither the Old nor the New Testament agrees with this opinion. Nor has any natural philosopher invented this new animal—or rather this new monstrosity—except the Manichaeans. The holy Church long ago condemned this astonishing opinion among the heresies of the Manichaeans.

### That they maintain that the soul of the bread gives life to Christ’s body

[Col. 1216C] We accuse you of maintaining that the soul of the bread gives life to Christ’s body. Does Christ have two souls, one human and the other belonging to the bread? Or, just as the bread is changed into Christ’s flesh, is the soul of the bread changed into Christ’s soul? Or does Christ dismiss his own soul and admit the soul of the bread?

If the bread lacks a soul, will Christ’s body not be living? Why do you not observe that, before you offer it, it is killed, pierced with a lance, and cut off from the whole portion that is to be consecrated; and that, already mutilated and lifeless, it is carried to the altar?

For the soul cannot be divided, so that divided portions might retain corresponding divisions of the soul. But suppose that, because of the leaven, the portions too possess a soul. What will happen when the bread has been emptied and the leaven has entirely ceased to have a soul? Will its soul remain even then, and will the Lord’s body be given life?

For the entire altar bread is changed into Christ’s flesh, and nothing of the bread’s nature remains except its outward appearance. Why do you not consider that the Lord broke what he gave and called it his body, and that the disciples ate what they received? Is the soul called a body? Is it broken? Is it eaten? What Gospel handed down this faith? Which apostle taught this giving of life to the Lord’s body?

This is an Origenist, not a Catholic, understanding: that the souls of some pass into the bodies of others and, according to the quality of their merit, receive either better or worse bodies.

### That they strike Christ’s body with a lance

[Col. 1217A] We accuse you of striking Christ’s body with a lance. Christ did not do this, nor did he in any way instruct his disciples to do it in remembrance of him. “Take,” he said, “and eat”; he did not say, “Kill it” or “strike it with a lance.”

Christ neither killed himself nor ordered his disciples to kill him. Soldiers, not apostles, killed the Lord; soldiers, not apostles, pierced his side with a lance.

The Lord was not living in the manner of your leaven when his side was pierced; he was dead, lest, when the legs of the thieves were broken, a bone of him should be broken. And although your lance does not, as you boast, reach the killing of Christ, it strikes not Christ’s body but only bread. For what you pierce is not yet flesh but pure bread; and you kill the living leaven before it can give life to Christ.

### That they bury Christ’s body in the earth

[Col. 1217B] We accuse you of burying the Lord’s body in the earth and compelling Scripture to witness corruption. The Lord commanded that his body be eaten, not buried; and the disciples ate it, they did not bury it.

But you, not following the apostles, cast it into a pit of corruption and compel the Holy Spirit, who said through the prophet, “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10), to lie, since, insofar as you can, you make him see corruption.

### That they consume it with hot water

[Col. 1217C] We accuse you of consuming the Lord’s body with ordinary food, that is, with hot water. Christ did not institute this, nor was there hot water in the sacrament of the blood. Christ changed wine, not water, into blood, and he offered nothing else in the cup but the fruit of the vine.

You, however, cannot abstain at the divine table from what you customarily take at an ordinary meal, and you assign to religion what you possess as an excuse for your sins.

### That they say that blood flowed warm from Christ’s side

[Col. 1218A] We accuse you of saying, contrary to nature and the Gospel, that blood flowed warm from Christ’s side. Scripture says that he had already died, already expired, already been dead when his body was wounded and his side pierced with a lance.

Does nature allow his dead body to remain warm when life was no longer in it and its vital heat had already departed? Perhaps the Lord’s body possessed this privilege. On what basis do you prove it? Where do you read it? What Scripture teaches it? Which Gospel contains it?

Either prove from Scripture what you produce, or attribute it to your customary presumption, since Scripture does not contain it.

### That they deny baptism to children before the seventh day

[Col. 1218B] We accuse you of denying baptism before the seventh day to a newly born child. The Lord did not establish a fixed day for baptism, nor did he place the seventh day before the first day. Rather, simply and without deceit, he sent his disciples to baptize and said: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16).

Can the Lord save one baptized on the seventh day but not one baptized on the first? God is almighty, and he has done everything he wished; there is no one who can resist his will. Or can he do what he can, but does not wish to do it, even though he wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth?

Where “all” is said, no one is excluded—not even an infant whose life has lasted a single day upon the earth. Christ saves every human being; why do you exclude this human being? Christ casts no one out; why do you drive this person farther away from Christ? Christ alone baptizes; why do you forbid the water? Christ alone forgives sins; why do you retain sins?

If external filth offends your eyes, do you think that Christ too is offended? If your touch recoils from the uncleanness of the flesh, do you think that Christ too recoils? He who bore the weaknesses of the flesh for us supports the weak person rather than casting him down. He who washes away the stains of the soul that we have contracted through guilt mercifully bears the stains of the body imposed upon us by necessity.

For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses. Yet you surpass all murderers beyond comparison, since you snatch those who are perishing from the hand of the Savior, do not allow the dying to enter into life, and plunge them into hell while Christ’s death cries out against you.

# A DISSERTATION ON THE EUCHARISTIC BREAD, UNLEAVENED AND LEAVENED, BY THE LORD JEAN MABILLON, PRIEST AND MONK OF THE ORDER OF SAINT BENEDICT, OF THE CONGREGATION OF SAINT MAUR, TO THE MOST EMINENT CARDINAL BONA

(*Vet. Analect.*, new edition, p. 522.)

## TO THE MOST EMINENT CHURCHMAN, JEAN BONA, PRIEST-CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, FROM FR. JEAN MABILLON, MONK OF SAINT BENEDICT

[Col. 1219A] Your modesty, most eminent churchman, has brought me to the point that, if I do not offer you this little book of mine, I shall incur the fault of ingratitude; but if I do offer it, I shall incur that of imprudence.

For since this little book was conceived at your suggestion and command, formed with you supplying and outlining the material, and finally brought to light through your efforts, it is unworthy that it should appear under another name when it acknowledges you as its principal author.

Yet your Eminence prescribed the manner in which the subject of unleavened bread was to be treated in such a way that I should sincerely set forth not what you yourself think, but what I should understand from the truth of the matter. Consequently, I am forced to depart somewhat from your opinion, despite my reverence for you; and I rightly fear that the book will be the less acceptable to you the less it approaches your judgment.

I would indeed have good reason to fear this if you belonged to the class of people who approve only what they themselves think. But your greatness of mind and fairness are so great, most eminent cardinal, that, while in your own writings you devote yourself solely to truth, in the writings of others you chiefly value a sincere desire to seek the truth. The person who departs from your opinion out of love of truth will deserve more from you than one who subscribes to your view through the compliance of deceitful flattery.

[Col. 1220A] Accordingly, while laboring on this little work, I took special care to compose it not so much in imitation of your opinion as in imitation of your spirit. I judged that your dignity and character would shine more brightly if you kindly received even those who think against you than if everyone applauded you ambitiously.

Throughout this discussion, however, I have said nothing merely from a desire to contradict, nor asserted anything with the obstinacy of definition. Whatever it may amount to, I have completed it with the intention of obeying you and consecrating my little labor to you, so that, if at some time, when leisure permits, you should wish to treat the same subject again with renewed attention, you may have before you this memorial of my service.

Nothing could happen to me more happily or honorably than to contribute something of value in support of your studies, by which you wonderfully illuminate the Catholic Church and the republic of letters.

These are the reasons for my purpose and work, most eminent sir. If you approve them, I hope that this little gift also will not be displeasing to Your Eminence—which I most earnestly desire.

Farewell, and live forever.

Paris, in the suburban monastery of Saint-Germain, 10 October 1673.

## TO THE READER

[Col. 1219]

[Col. 1219B] I wish to say a few words to you here, diligent reader.

Twenty-two years ago, James Sirmond, of illustrious memory, a priest of the Society of Jesus, composed a *Disquisition on Unleavened Bread*. In that book he argued that the use of unleavened bread had prevailed among the Latins for approximately eight hundred years.

Almost the same opinion was adopted two years ago by the most eminent Cardinal Jean Bona in book I, chapter 23, of his *Liturgical Matters*. At that time I too, while sending to the press the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, which concern the third century of that order, collected several observations against Sirmond’s opinion in my preface.

After reading them, the most eminent cardinal did not hesitate to explain to me, in a letter, what he thought of the arguments I had presented; he also replied to them with exceptional graciousness. In addition, by sending me the little work of Ildefonsus, bishop of Hispalis, which I had previously investigated, he used his authority with me to have me explain the entire question of unleavened bread in a new commentary.

You have his notable letter on this subject, placed at the beginning of this work, both as an ornament and as a source of instruction. My dissertation follows it. At its conclusion I have appended the work of the aforementioned bishop Ildefonsus, written eight hundred years ago, on the Eucharistic bread; since it has never previously been published, it will serve as evidence.

This is the entire structure of the work. Continue, reader, and farewell.

# LETTER OF THE MOST EMINENT CARDINAL BONA TO THE AUTHOR OF THE DISSERTATION

[Col. 1221]

[Col. 1221A] MOST REVEREND FATHER,

When I noticed that some people had been displeased by what I had written about unleavened and leavened bread in book I, chapter 23, of my *Liturgical Matters*, I had resolved to treat this subject more carefully and to explain my opinion more clearly and distinctly. But since new affairs arise daily—affairs that I can neither postpone nor neglect—I am compelled to withdraw from my plan and leave the task of adorning this subject to you, who have written about it at length and learnedly in the preface to the third century of the Benedictine order and who, as I learned from your letters, intend to take up the same matter again in the prolegomena to the fourth century.

Through your varied learning you will cause truth to emerge and shine forth from the ruins of antiquity, and you will bind me more closely to you if you kindly correct my errors. My constant desire has always been to know and recognize the truth. I shall never be ashamed, if something foreign to the truth should happen to slip from my pen through carelessness, to erase and correct it.

To comply with your request, I shall briefly indicate the method by which I thought this inquiry ought to proceed.

First, my intention was to distinguish what is certain from what is uncertain, and the dogmas of faith from the rites of the Church. It is certain that Christ the Redeemer ate unleavened bread at the Last Supper and instituted the Eucharist in it. This must be upheld against the schismatic Greeks and also against certain Latins.

Yet from this act of Christ it is not permissible to infer that the Eucharist must be made exclusively from unleavened bread. For if this were necessary, the Church would never have permitted the use of leavened bread.

It is likewise certain that both unleavened and leavened bread are truly bread, and that consecration is valid in either. Finally, it is certain that it is more fitting to follow Christ’s example and consecrate in unleavened bread.

Whether the Latin Church ever used leavened bread, however, is a matter of fact belonging to history and to ritual—a ritual subject to change and innovation—not to the faith, which always remains firm and unchanging.

This must be proved as indisputable against those who turn a matter indifferent by its nature into a dogma of faith. Algerus treats the matter very well in book II, chapter 10, *On the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of the Lord*:

“Whether Christ’s body ought to be made from unleavened or leavened bread is the subject of a great dispute between the Latins and the Greeks, although it is not contrary to the Christian faith whether unleavened or leavened bread is offered—both because either is bread and also because, although Christ made his body from unleavened bread, perhaps he did so not because the thing being accomplished required it, but because the supper at which it was accomplished did not require another kind of bread. Nevertheless, he did not forbid leavened bread.”

With this established as a foundation, we must investigate what kind of bread the apostles and their successors used in the sacrifice for several centuries: unleavened, leavened, or both indiscriminately.

I myself have thought, not implausibly, that they used both without distinction—either leavened bread, because it was more common and readily available, or unleavened bread, which could easily be prepared from finer flour and immediately baked beneath ashes or in small ovens.

Indeed, during the persecutions, when they celebrated secretly in prisons, private houses, crypts, or underground caves, they had to use whatever bread happened to be available at the time.

I collected many arguments for the use of leavened bread; nevertheless, as I stated after the preface, I never denied the use of unleavened bread. I said that the apostles consecrated whatever kind of bread they found in the homes of the faithful, whether unleavened or leavened.

In your preface, however, you bring forward many arguments for unleavened bread. I shall briefly indicate what I think of them—not from a desire to contradict, but from a desire to discover the truth.

**No. 65.** You argue from Christ’s action, but, as I said above, this argument proves too much.

**No. 66.** You produce Isidore as a witness; in discussing the composition of Eucharistic bread, he makes no mention of leaven. Isidore, however, copied that opinion from Cyprian’s Letter 63 to Caecilius, and nothing certain can be concluded from it.

For it does not exclude leaven. Perhaps the word “joined” is to be understood in the passage where he says that the Lord’s body cannot consist of meal alone or water alone: “unless both have been united and joined together and solidified by the structure of one bread.” What joins, unites, and solidifies is leaven.

Isidore’s letter to Redemptus is unquestionably spurious, as you yourself acknowledge. You cite the authority of the Council of Toledo in support of unleavened bread, whereas I used it in support of leavened bread. It is not for me to judge which of us has better understood the mind of those Fathers.

[Col. 1222C] **No. 67.** You present the testimony of Ildefonsus of Toledo from the report of the distinguished gentleman Emeric Bigot. But you yourself will pronounce what should be thought of it once you have read it. I am sending you the complete treatise from a Vatican manuscript, which Holstenius praised, accurately transcribed.

**No. 68.** The testimonies of Bede and Paschasius do not prove the universal use of unleavened bread, nor does Rabanus Maurus establish it. They do nevertheless show that, if not everywhere, at least in some Western churches, the use of unleavened bread was in force in the time of Photius.

He speaks clearly, and the suspicion of interpolation is removed, since you assert that the oldest manuscript codices agree with the printed editions. Yet he proves too much when he says that the bread ought to be unleavened.

**No. 69.** From the offerings presented impressed with an iron stamp, you infer that they were without leaven. This too is of considerable importance for proving that unleavened breads were in use in the West during the ninth century. But whether this custom prevailed everywhere is not clear.

**No. 70.** You use Leo IX as a witness asserting the perpetual use of unleavened bread in the Roman Church. I, however, interpreted the most holy pontiff in such a way that he should be understood as speaking not of ritual but of doctrine.

He declaims against heretics and treats of the faith of Peter, which will never fail. He then attacks the Greeks, who said that unleavened bread was not true bread and that Christ had consecrated in leavened bread, having celebrated the Last Supper before the day of Unleavened Bread.

Thus, if Leo’s words are carefully considered, they seem to me to concern not a rite that admits change but the dogmas of faith.

Humbert, Abbot Rupert, and the other witnesses testify to the customs of their own times. It is not implausible that they believed a custom to have been perpetual when it was in use during their own lifetimes.

You know, however, what credence should be given to those who testify that a custom existed continuously from the time of Christ down to their own age, while producing no witness who lived in the preceding centuries. Certainly, legal scholars completely reject testimonies of this kind.

[Col. 1223A] **No. 71.** You weaken Sirmond’s first argument in favor of leaven by appealing to the ancient custom of the faithful, who offered bread—bread evidently intended to be consecrated for the communion of the priest and the faithful.

Although anything left over was customarily distributed to the poor, the offerers’ first intention nevertheless concerned the sacrifice. I asserted, after Sirmond, that this bread was ordinary and customary bread, and normally leavened, of the kind found in people’s homes. I cited Ambrose as a witness; speaking of the bread to be consecrated, he calls it “customary.”

I now add Justin Martyr, who, toward the end of his Second Apology, speaking of the sacrifice of the Mass, says: “For we do not receive it as common bread and common drink”; or, as another translator renders it, “as ordinary bread and an ordinary cup.”

Similarly, Irenaeus says in book IV, chapter 34: “It is no longer common bread, but the Eucharist.”

I am convinced that by the terms “customary,” “common,” and “ordinary” bread, leavened bread is meant. I know that both kinds of bread were in use among the Romans and other peoples.

For Cornelius Celsus, book II, chapter 24, lists bread without leaven among the things suitable for the stomach; in chapter 25 he says that leavened bread is harmful to the stomach; and he mentions both kinds in chapter 28.

Nevertheless, it is clear that leavened bread was the common and, so to speak, daily bread. Pliny praises it above all others in book XXII, in its final chapter. Galen, discussing bread in book I, chapter 2, of *On the Faculties of Foods*, teaches that bread without leaven is suitable for no one.

Ambrose likewise takes this for granted in Sermon 21, where he explains the parable of the leaven.

If, therefore, the faithful offered ordinary bread, and if this bread was leavened, this provides a substantial argument for proving the use of leaven in the sacrifice.

Num. 72: You say that it is not established whether the Latins or the Greeks differed regarding the material of the bread. This is certainly most true [Col. 1223C], and from it arises the darkness in which we are enveloped, since we do not know whether, at the beginning, all the Churches followed one custom, or used either kind of bread indifferently, or employed only unleavened or only leavened bread as a fixed rule; nor do we know who first changed the ancient practice, at what time and on what occasion, when the Greeks began obstinately to adhere to leavened bread and the Latins to unleavened bread; whether the practices of the various Churches were different, as formerly they were in the celebration of Passover; why, for a thousand years, no controversy arose between Greeks and Latins over this difference of bread; why Photius, the father of the Greek schism, who brought against the Latins accusations both much lesser and even false, remained silent on this matter, which was afterward debated between the parties with such intensity; and why, among the Eastern peoples, only the Armenians and Maronites use unleavened bread, and when and on what occasion they began to do so. All these uncertainties would have to be investigated and resolved with the greatest care.

The older scholastics readily extricate themselves from the difficulty of this question by asserting that both the Greek and Latin Churches, from the beginning and thereafter, consecrated with unleavened bread until the Ebionite heresy arose. The Ebionites taught that the law of Moses was to be observed together with the Gospel and that unleavened bread had necessarily to be consecrated. In abhorrence of them, the orthodox Church everywhere throughout the world employed leavened bread. After that heresy had been extinguished, the Easterners retained leavened bread, while the Westerners returned to their former practice of using unleavened bread. But I have shown in my *Liturgics* that no credence should be given to this account.

I related in the same work that the Armenians adopted unleavened bread when they separated from the Greeks, and that at that same time they decreed that wine should not be mixed with water. The historians of those peoples consistently affirm the same thing, and several Armenian bishops and priests whom I questioned, together with some of our own men who are skilled in their rites and language, confirmed that this is the ancient tradition of that Church. Therefore, among the errors that the Armenians abjured when they returned to the orthodox faith, the following is found in an old formula [Col. 1224A] published by D. Cotelerius in his most learned notes on Book V of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, p. 237:

> “If anyone does not put leaven and salt into the bread of the offering, nor water with the wine into the holy chalice, let him be anathema.”

It is plausible that the Maronites adopted the use of unleavened bread when, after abjuring heresy, they were converted to the Catholic faith. William, archbishop of Tyre, writes that this happened in his own time and in his presence, in Book XXII of his *History*, chapter 8. They themselves, however, deny this and produce very ancient writers who assert that that people had always adhered to the Roman Church.

Recently I saw a book *On the Explanation of the Liturgy*, translated from Syriac into Latin by D. Faustus of Mount Lebanon, nephew of Abraham Ecchellensis, and attributed to St. Maron. They say that Maron lived in the fifth or sixth century. In its sixteenth chapter the following is read:

> “Regarding what you asked—whether it is fitting to offer with unleavened or leavened bread—we answer that we have no dominical or apostolic command which orders the one or forbids the other. Therefore some consecrate with the one and others with the other, according to the custom they have retained. For those who offer with leaven accuse us, together with the Westerners and Armenians, saying that unleavened bread is not bread.”

Then, from Scripture, it proves that unleavened bread truly is bread and that Christ consecrated with unleavened bread. Yet this book appears to have been written after the Greek schism had arisen and after the disturbances over unleavened bread had been stirred up; I leave its examination to your learning.

Num. 73: You resolve another argument, namely, the objection that the Ebionites were marked out because they used unleavened bread contrary to the custom of others. You cite the authority of Epiphanius to prove the use of unleavened bread in the time of the Ebionites, as though they offered the sacrifice with unleavened bread in imitation of the Church. But, subject to your judgment and that of other learned men, I have understood Epiphanius’s words differently; and, unless I am mistaken, Epiphanius himself explains himself in *Heresy* 46, saying that Tatian instituted certain mysteries in imitation of the holy Church, but employed nothing in them except water. There you see that the imitation of the Church refers not to the thing offered but to the offering itself.
