Num. 74: You show that nothing certain can be inferred from Photius’s silence, which I too acknowledge, both because of the reasons and conjectures you have brought forward and because of what Leo Allatius noted at the beginning of Exercise 28 against Creygton, for the Council of Florence. Nevertheless, I should like to know why, nearly two centuries after Photius’s death, such a fierce controversy arose over unleavened bread. I should also like you to clarify what I brought forward in support of the use of leavened bread from the decrees of Melchiades, Siricius, and Innocent, the Roman pontiffs. Nothing could be more welcome to me than to be corrected and improved by friends.

So that I may omit nothing that could bear upon the present question, I mention that there exists at Milan a manuscript and unpublished *Chronicle* attributed to St. Datius, bishop of Milan, in which the following words are read:

> “Saint Ambrose reverently imitated the Greek Church in many offices; he also blessed their sacrifice—that is, leavened bread—together with our unleavened bread on the most celebrated festivals, especially on the Lord’s resurrection.”

But many have already observed that this *Chronicle* is spurious and belongs to a later age. Nor is the testimony of Simeon of Thessalonica of any importance, since he is both later and schismatic. In his book *On the Temple and the Mass*, in Goar’s *Euchologion*, p. 214, he says:

> “Saint Gregory, that author of the *Dialogues*, testifies that the sacrifice is offered with leavened bread.”

Similarly, the heterodox writer Fehlavus, p. 366 of his commentary on Christopher Angelus’s *On the State of the Greek Church*, asserts that Apollinaris was the first inventor of unleavened bread. But this is a fable of the Greek schismatics who wrote against the Latins: they say that a certain disciple of Apollinaris, named Leucius or Felix, migrated to Rome and, by feigning holiness of life, was raised to the supreme pontificate and introduced unleavened bread among the Latins.

An anonymous writer whom I saw in the Barberini Library among the Greek manuscripts, no. 75, also says that when Charlemagne went to Rome in the time of Leo III, he had as companions on the journey several monks infected with the errors of Arius and Apollinaris. After entering the City, they corrupted the people by teaching that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father alone but also from the Son, and that the sacrifice ought to be offered with unleavened bread, so that unleavened bread originated in France.

So says this writer. Other accounts agree with him in the work cited by Leo Allatius, pp. 571 and following, where he also recounts the aforementioned little story of Felix from a certain Simeon of Jerusalem. I omit the other inventions of the more recent Greeks, lest I waste time uselessly on trifles.

I have written these things to arouse your study and diligence, as it is written: “Give a wise man an opportunity, and wisdom will be added to him” (Prov. 9:9). For the rest, I pray God to reveal to us the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom, and to grant us to think the same thing toward one another according to Jesus Christ, so that, as the Apostle exhorts us, “Having purged out the old leaven, let us feast with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5:8).

Rome, 14 March 1673.

# Dissertation on Eucharistic Bread, Unleavened and Leavened

[Col. 1225]

## Occasion and Argument of the Dissertation

[Col. 1225B]

When, in publishing the *Acts of Our Saints*, I came upon certain passages favoring the use of unleavened bread in the Latin Church, I thought it appropriate, in accordance with my custom, to illuminate them with some observations and, having assembled the arguments that almost presented themselves, to show that this usage is more ancient than Jacobus Sirmundus, a man of outstanding learning, had believed.

All scholars are familiar with the opinion of that distinguished man in his separate *Inquiry into Unleavened Bread*: namely, that leavened bread was used in the Latin Church for many centuries in the Mass, and that unleavened bread had not yet been adopted at the time of the Photian schism, but only during the interval between the schism of Photius, the false patriarch of Constantinople, during the pontificate of Pope Nicholas I, and the second schism of Michael Cerularius, likewise patriarch, under Pope Leo IX—that is, during the period extending from A.D. 867 to 1054 [Col. 1225C].

I, however, along with many others, and especially persuaded by the authority of Rabanus, had become convinced that unleavened bread had prevailed in sacred matters before the Photian schism. Nor did Sirmundus’s arguments seem so effective that they compelled us to admit that leavened bread had ever been used among the Latins.

Therefore, since Sirmundus had wished that those who did not agree with his opinion concerning the more recent use of unleavened bread should at least be prompted to investigate the matter thoroughly, I devoted myself to this very task, as far as the ability of my weakness, the brevity of my observations, and the difficulty and obscurity of the subject permitted [Col. 1225D].

For although it seemed presumptuous for so insignificant a man to contend against Sirmundus, I recalled what Sirmundus himself had offered in his own defense in chapter 5 of the *Inquiry*. There, intending to give an opinion about the leaven of Melchiades and Siricius different from that of Baronius, he was not afraid that he might appear to have acted contrary to Baronius’s intention and desire, since Baronius had invited everyone precisely for this purpose, that they might freely bring forward what they had found. Sirmundus did not think that anyone who remembered Baronius’s singular modesty would be displeased to depart from his opinion, since Baronius was accustomed to hear the opinions of others without resentment and, if he recognized anything better than his own, to embrace it willingly. I was persuaded of this concerning Sirmundus’s mind, modesty, and sincere love of truth, and this was likewise my defense of what I had done.

When I was first preparing to commit my observations to the press, I was informed at the same time that the eminent Cardinal Bona, whose virtue, learning, and scholarship are known to all, was treating the same subject in his work *On Liturgical Matters* and was departing somewhat from Sirmundus’s proposal. As soon as that outstanding work reached my hands, I read it with great pleasure, especially the passage on unleavened bread, in which the entire matter is explained no less sincerely than learnedly [Col. 1226C].

The substance of that passage is that, from the time of the apostles down to the Photian schism, the Latin Church used both leavened and unleavened bread indiscriminately, and that unleavened bread was not received everywhere among the Latins by a common and general law before the beginning of the tenth century. In this matter the distinguished author moderated Sirmundus’s opinion: Sirmundus appears not to have admitted the use of unleavened bread before Photius’s division, but only the use of leavened bread, whereas the eminent cardinal acknowledges that both were used indiscriminately according to the convenience of time and place.

This opinion disturbed certain minds in the City [Col. 1226D], astonished—as it seemed to them—by the novelty, or rather, let me say, the indignity of the matter, as though it were impious to depart even briefly from the common opinion of recent writers, who defend the perpetual use of unleavened bread in the Latin Church no less than if it were a Catholic dogma.

The most modest cardinal sought to restrain the growing murmur of complaints by publishing an admonition on the subject [Col. 1227A], in which he attempted to demonstrate the basis of his assertion to those who thought otherwise. When this did not fully succeed according to his wishes, he intended to revisit the subject and explain his opinion more clearly. He would soon have done so, had not a multitude of affairs distracted him while he was engaged in the matter.

But when he learned that I was considering the same plan, he sent me the literary materials he possessed for this purpose and encouraged me to undertake the task—that is, to explain what I believed to be in accordance with the truth of the matter, which was his constant desire. I could not refuse my work to an exhorter of such dignity, especially since it was necessary for me to set out matters which some people were interpreting otherwise than they should have, because I had expressed them either too obscurely or too briefly in my observations.

[Col. 1227B]

There are two points that I intended to establish in my observations. The first was that the use of unleavened bread in sacred matters had prevailed among the Latins before the Photian schism; this I undertook to prove explicitly against Sirmundus. The second was that the arguments proposed by Sirmundus did not conclusively prove that leavened bread had at some time been used by the Latins.

I did not, however, undertake to demonstrate this latter point as though I considered it certain and manifest that leavened bread had always been absent from Latin worship. My entire argument aimed only to prove that what Sirmundus presented as certain was not certain. In a word, I thought that I should defend this second point not so much by affirming it as by denying the certainty claimed by the opposing side and overturning its foundations.

[Col. 1227C]

I said nothing about the middle position of the eminent cardinal or about the new arguments he brought forward in favor of Sirmundus’s opinion, partly because my observations were already about to be submitted to the press when his work *On Liturgical Matters* was brought to this city, and partly because my opinion was closer to that of the eminent cardinal. For he does not deny that unleavened bread was sometimes used before Photius’s time, indeed from the very age of the apostles; he says, however, that this was done without distinction, not by a common law, but according to the circumstances of places and times.

But since I must now undertake to treat this entire question anew according to my limited ability, I shall endeavor to do so historically rather than polemically—not because I think that I can resolve and settle a difficult controversy of such magnitude, but so that I may contribute to the common stock whatever small observations concerning the ancients I have been able to make that may help illuminate it. And so that the whole matter may be treated more clearly and accurately, I shall attempt to explain it in the following chapters.

[Col. 1227D]

## Table of Chapters

I. That Christ the Lord instituted the Eucharist with unleavened bread.  
II. That Christ’s example does not impose the necessity of consecrating with unleavened bread.  
III. Whether the Greeks used leaven at the beginning of the Church.  
IV. What kind of bread the other Christian communities use.  
V. Various opinions concerning the Latins’ use of unleavened bread.  
VI. Certain testimonies of doubtful credibility in support of the Latins’ use of unleavened bread are examined.  
VII. Certain conjectures and arguments are proposed in support of the ancient use of unleavened bread among the Latins.  
VIII. Other proofs from the form and conditions of the hosts. Two canons are explained here: one of the Second Council of Tours, the other of the Sixteenth Council of Toledo.  
IX. That this custom prevailed by general usage among the Latins before the division of Photius.  
X. The arguments for the use of leaven among the Latins are examined.  
XI. Epilogue and conclusion of the foregoing.

# Chapter One

## That Christ the Lord Instituted the Eucharist with Unleavened Bread

[Col. 1228B]

It is certain that our Savior, at the final Passover which he celebrated as death approached, instituted in the evening of Thursday the venerable sacrament of his body and blood. Later Latins and Greeks dispute whether he used unleavened bread for this purpose, the Latins preferring unleavened bread and the Greeks leavened bread. The resolution of this controversy depends upon another question: namely, whether Christ celebrated the legal Passover in that year—that is, whether he ate the lamb together with unleavened bread and the other paschal foods at the time and in the place prescribed by the law.

There is no doubt concerning the place: Christ celebrated his last Passover at Jerusalem [Col. 1228C], as the law required. Concerning the time and the eating of the lamb, however, there is a serious controversy, not only between Greeks and Latins but also among members of the same community, between the ancients and the moderns. Both matters must be treated separately, and first the foundations of the opposing parties must be set out.

Those who maintain that Christ celebrated the legal Passover before his death derive their authority from the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Matthew testifies that the paschal meal was prepared by the disciples on the first day of unleavened bread; Mark, on the first day of unleavened bread, when they sacrificed the Passover; and Luke, when the day of unleavened bread was approaching, on which it was necessary for the Passover to be sacrificed.

Others, whether those who think that Christ anticipated the legal Passover [Col. 1228D], those who deny that he ate the lamb, or those who remove both the lamb and the unleavened bread and the other foods of that kind from Christ’s final supper, rely chiefly on the twofold testimony of the evangelist John.

The first passage is in chapter 13, verse 1, where he writes that the supper took place before the feast of Passover—or, as it is read in the Persian version, two days before Passover. The second testimony is in chapter 18, verse 28, where he says that the Jews, after Christ had been seized and brought to Caiaphas, did not enter the praetorium, so that they would not be defiled, but might eat the Passover. This is an argument that they ate the lamb on the following evening, since the sacrifice and eating of the lamb was properly called Passover.

To this is added a passage from the same Gospel [Col. 1229A], chapter 19, verse 14, where Christ is said to have been crucified on the day that was the Preparation of Passover, on which the Jews were preparing what was necessary for eating the lamb on the following evening. These are, for the most part, the arguments that have led both ancient and modern Latins and Greeks to divergent opinions. Let us now consult the older tradition of the Greeks, and afterward that of the Latins.

First of all, the letter of Polycrates, metropolitan of the Churches of Asia, deserves consideration. Toward the end of the second century, when a dispute had arisen between the Asians and the other Churches throughout the world concerning the day on which Passover should be celebrated, he wrote a letter in his own name and that of the other bishops of Asia to Pope Victor I. Eusebius Pamphilus reports a fragment of it in Book V, chapter 24, of his *Ecclesiastical History* [Col. 1229B].

All the Churches of Asia believed that the feast of Passover should be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the moon, whatever day of the week it happened to be, the day on which the Jews had been commanded to sacrifice the lamb. The other Churches throughout the world, however, celebrated it only on the day of the Lord’s resurrection. Polycrates defended his own custom as having been handed down to him by his ancestors, citing as authorities the apostle Philip, the evangelist John, Polycarp, and seven bishops related to him. He says that all of them celebrated Passover “when the Jewish people removed the leaven” (*hótan ho laòs érnye tēn zýmēn*), indicating that this custom had descended in an unbroken stream from Christ’s example.

The exceptionally learned Henri Valesius restored this passage in this form, whereas the Greek text had previously read *ērtue*, “he prepared,” entirely contrary to Polycrates’ meaning and to Rufinus’s interpretation, who rendered the Greek word with a verb meaning “to remove.” This single testimony could suffice to prove that Christ completed the legal Passover on the first day of unleavened bread toward evening and to explain the meaning of the evangelist John, on whose authority the tradition of the Asians, received from the very source, chiefly rested.

Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea, likewise proves the custom of the Asians in his *Paschal Canon*. He shows that they rightly celebrate Passover each year according to John’s example whenever the fourteenth lunar day occurs and the lamb is sacrificed among the Jews, refusing to submit to the authority of certain persons—that is, the successors of Peter and Paul, the Roman pontiffs—who taught all the Churches in which they had planted the spiritual seeds of the Gospel to celebrate the solemnity of the Lord’s resurrection only on Sunday [Col. 1229D].

There appears to be no reason why the Asians would have been so eager to retain their custom unless they had received from their ancestors that Christ himself had completed the Passover prescribed by the law on the very fourteenth day of the moon.

Origen holds the same opinion in Treatise 35 on Matthew, where, at the beginning of the treatise, he relates that Christ was seized by the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon. Accordingly, he considered it established that Christ celebrated Passover on that same moon, since Christ’s paschal supper was followed immediately by his seizure. Hence, later in the treatise, he says that Christ celebrated his final Passover according to Jewish custom [Col. 1230A]. In his *Commentaries on the Gospel of John*, he says that the Jews committed a criminal deed during the very Passover by killing Jesus.

Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, is also to be added. In his letter to the emperor Theodosius concerning the holy Passover, he writes:

> “Moreover, our Savior was handed over on the fourteenth day of the moon, that is, on the fifth day after the Sabbath; he was crucified on the fifteenth and rose on the third day, that is, on the seventeenth day of the moon, which on that occasion fell on the Lord’s day, as we also learn from the indications of the Gospels.”

Theodoret teaches the same in Question 24 on Exodus, asserting that Christ was handed over toward the end of the fourteenth day of the moon, when the Passover was being sacrificed.

John Chrysostom, in several passages, especially Homilies 81, 82, and 83 on Matthew [Col. 1230B], proves that Christ completed the Passover according to the legal rite, whereas the Jews, or at least the Jewish leaders, postponed it contrary to the prescription of the law so that they might fulfill their intention of killing Christ. Gregory the Protosyncellus collected the arguments for this from Chrysostom in his *Apology against the Letter of Mark of Ephesus*. Arcudius did likewise in Book III, chapter 4, of *On the Eucharist*, and in the following chapter he resolves the objections drawn from the same Chrysostom.

Certainly, Photius admits in chapter 116 of his *Bibliotheca* that Chrysostom held the opinion that Christ observed the legal Passover at the Last Supper.

To all these witnesses must be added two patriarchs of Alexandria, the first of whom is Cyril. He proves that Christ instituted the Eucharist after the eating of the lamb in these words:

> “Our Lord Jesus Christ joined together on one day the Jewish lamb and the true manna, when he blessed the bread and wine, saying: ‘This is my body and my blood.’”

The other is Proterius, Cyril’s successor. When questioned by the emperor Marcian about the manner of celebrating Passover, he replied that Christ the Lord ate the typical Passover with his disciples in the upper room on Thursday, the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month, and shortly afterward was betrayed by Judas.

The opinion of these Alexandrian patriarchs—Theophilus, Cyril, and Proterius—has all the greater weight in this matter because the ancient Fathers entrusted the entire responsibility for determining the date of the paschal feast each year to the bishop of Alexandria. Pope Leo I reports this in his letter to Marcian:

> “Since among the Egyptians there was believed to have been handed down from ancient times a knowledge of this calculation, by which the day on which the aforesaid solemnity would occur each year was reported to the apostolic see, so that the judgment of this writing might generally reach the more distant Churches.”

By this knowledge they could easily determine on what day the paschal feast had fallen in the year in which Christ celebrated his final Passover.

From these considerations we may reasonably conclude, with Photius in chapter 116 of the *Bibliotheca*, that it was not only the opinion of John Chrysostom but also that of the Church, at least the Greek Church, that Christ completed the *nomikon*, or legal, Passover before he instituted the mystical supper of the Eucharist. Victor of Antioch also reports this in his commentary on Mark, chapter 14.

[Col. 1231A]

I find three or four ancients who dissent from this ancient Greek tradition: Epiphanius, John Philoponus, and two anonymous writers. Epiphanius thinks that Christ did indeed use the legal foods at the Last Supper, but anticipated the time established by the law. Philoponus and both anonymous writers, however, deny that Christ completed the legal Passover.

In *Heresy* 30, no. 22, Epiphanius argues against the Ebionites, who believed that one should abstain from eating meat. He refutes them on the ground that the Lord ate the Passover of the Jews at the Last Supper—that is, the lamb and unleavened loaves. But in *Heresy* 51, when arguing against the Alogoi, he says in no. 26 that Christ suffered on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, since they had anticipated one evening—that is, the middle of the night of the fourteenth day of the moon [Col. 1231B]:

> “They therefore ate the Passover two days before it was to be eaten, that is, on the evening of the third day, whereas it ought to have been eaten on the evening of the fifth.”

Thus they celebrated the paschal meal two days before the legal day, namely on Tuesday evening, whereas it ought to have been celebrated on Thursday evening. For Thursday fell on the fourteenth day of the moon.

Nor should you suppose that Epiphanius means that the Jews anticipated the legal Passover by two days. It is clear from what follows that he is speaking of Christ and his disciples, where he asserts that Christ was seized on that same Tuesday evening, during the eleventh night of the moon, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.

Epiphanius’s opinion seems to rest on the authority of the evangelist John, who says that Christ instituted the supper before the day of the feast of Passover [Col. 1231C]. By these words he appears to have understood “two days before Passover,” as the Persian version renders it.

John Philoponus, a man of the sixth century, adopted another opinion in his *Disputation on Passover*, which Balthasar Corderius first published at Vienna in Austria together with his seven books on the *Hexaemeron*. This Greek author, a member of the Eutychian sect but otherwise a learned man, argues that the mystical supper of the Lord took place on the thirteenth day of the moon, the day before the legal Passover, and that Christ did not then eat the lamb or unleavened bread with his disciples. He attempts to prove this by many arguments.

Two anonymous writers agree with this opinion [Col. 1231D]. Photius discusses them in chapters 115 and 116 of his *Bibliotheca*. The first, arguing against the Quartodecimans, asserts that Christ did not eat the legal Passover on Thursday—for that had not been appointed as the day on which he should eat it, but the following day—nor did he eat the lamb, unleavened bread, or anything else that those who observe the legal Passover follow according to the custom and rite of their ancestors. Thus he maintains that Christ ate only a private, though mystical, supper and, from it, gave bread and the cup to his disciples.

The uncertain author praised by Photius in chapter 116 tends in the same direction. He writes that Christ celebrated the legal Passover in other years of his coming, but not in the year in which he was betrayed. Photius then adds that this deserves consideration because Chrysostom—and indeed the Church—taught that our Savior completed the Passover prescribed by the law before instituting the Eucharist [Col. 1232A].

From this a question arose in my mind: whether this anonymous author is different from the author of the *Disputation on Passover* published by Corderius under the name of John Philoponus in Greek and Latin, in which exactly the same opinion is found; and also whether Philoponus should truly be regarded as the author of that disputation, since Photius, who praises him in chapters 21, 43, 55, 75, 215, and 240 of his *Bibliotheca* and discusses his work on the *Hexaemeron* and other writings, nowhere mentions the aforementioned disputation.

It is also strange that Corderius, who read and noticed these things, offered no reason for attributing that work to Philoponus. Later, however, I discovered that this disputation really is Philoponus’s. Near its end he mentions his work on the *Hexaemeron*, which Photius confirms to be his genuine production [Col. 1232B]. Nevertheless, it remains very plausible to me that the later anonymous writer’s book on Passover, praised by Photius, is precisely Philoponus’s disputation, whose author Photius did not know.

Whatever the truth may be, neither Epiphanius’s authority nor that of John Philoponus and the two anonymous writers ought to prejudice the common tradition of the older Greeks, whose testimonies I have cited above. Epiphanius does not deny—indeed, he explicitly affirms—that Christ used the legal foods at the Last Supper, namely the flesh of the lamb and unleavened bread, although he thought that Christ anticipated the Passover by two days.

[Col. 1232C]

Still less should we accept the opinion of the more recent Greeks who, from the time of the schism created by Michael Cerularius, became violently hostile to the Latins and denounced the use of unleavened bread by every lawful and unlawful means.

Some of them, led by Nicetas Pectoratus, maintain that Christ celebrated the supper not on the fourteenth day of the moon, when leaven had to be removed, but on the thirteenth, with leavened bread. Others, as Humbert reports in his response to the letter of Michael Cerularius, when we asked them where the Lord Jesus could have obtained leavened bread at the supper, since it was not to be found throughout all the territory of Israel, replied:

> “If he is believed to be omnipotent, he could suddenly have produced leavened bread from anywhere; or, certainly, by blessing it, he could have made the unleavened bread itself leavened.”

But this is a marvelous escape devised by delirious schismatics who, unable to give an account of their accusations, flee—as Cotta says in Cicero—to God as to an altar. This is enough concerning the Greeks.

As for the Latins, almost unanimously all the ancients agree that Christ instituted the Eucharist with unleavened bread on the fourteenth day of the moon.

First there is Ambrose, bishop of Milan, who writes in his letter on the feast of Passover to the bishops established in Aemilia:

> “He, therefore, who spoke the law, afterward coming through the Virgin in the last times, completed the fullness of the law, because he came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it; and he celebrated Passover during the week in which the fourteenth day of the moon fell, on Thursday. Finally, on that very day, as the preceding events teach, he ate Passover with his disciples; on the following day, that is, Friday, he was crucified—that is, on the fifteenth day of the moon.”

Augustine agrees with Ambrose in Letter 86 to Casulanus. There, explaining the fast of Wednesday and Friday, he explicitly proves that the Jews began their plan to seize Christ on Wednesday. Then, after an intervening day, “on the evening of which the Lord ate Passover with his disciples, which was the end of the day we call Thursday,” Christ was betrayed on that night “which already belonged to Friday.” He then adds:

> “This day,” namely Friday, “was the first of the unleavened days, beginning at evening. But the evangelist Matthew says that Thursday was the first day of unleavened bread, because its evening was to be followed by the paschal supper, at which unleavened bread and the sacrificial lamb began to be eaten. From this it is inferred,” he says, “that it was Wednesday when the Lord said: ‘You know that after two days the Passover will take place’” (Matt. 26:2).

From these words it is clear that Augustine held the opinion that Christ celebrated Passover on that evening when “the unleavened bread and the eating of the lamb began,” and that he ate the Passover with his disciples according to the legal custom before instituting the Eucharist.

The authority of Jerome is equally clear. In Book IV of his *Commentary on Matthew*, on chapter 26, verse 17, he says:

> “The first day of unleavened bread is the fourteenth day of the first month, when the lamb is sacrificed, the moon is completely full, and the leaven is removed.”

And on verse 26:

> “After the typical Passover had been fulfilled, and he had eaten the flesh of the lamb with the apostles, he takes bread, which strengthens the human heart, and passes over to the sacrament of the true Passover, so that, just as Melchizedek, the priest of the Most High God, had offered bread and wine as a prefiguration of it, he too might represent the truth of his body and blood.”

I add to these Junilius Africanus, a sixth-century bishop, who in his *Commentary on Genesis* testifies that Christ the Lord, “after eating the typical lamb, announced that the mysteries of his body and blood were to be celebrated for us.” I pass over the testimonies of Rabanus and other authors of the Middle Ages who held the same opinion.

[Col. 1233D]

Although these things are established among the older Fathers, the more recent Latin writers should not be disregarded. They devoted great diligence to explaining this question but were divided into various opinions.

Some of them, including Paul of Bruges, Jansenius, bishop of Ghent, Maldonatus, Zegerus, and several others, maintain that Christ celebrated Passover on one day and the Jews on another, although both used the legal foods. These writers themselves are divided into two groups. Some assert that Christ anticipated the legal time; others say that he celebrated Passover on the appointed day, while the Jews transferred it to the following day.

They assign the following reason for this transfer: among the Jews there was an established rule that, in order to avoid certain inconveniences arising from successive solemnities, Passover should never be celebrated on the second, fourth, or sixth day of the week. In the year in which Christ suffered, however, the legal Passover fell on Friday and was therefore transferred by the Jews to the following day because of the concurrence of the Sabbath.

Others deny that Christ celebrated his final Passover according to the legal custom, and deny that he consumed unleavened bread or any other foods of that kind belonging to the paschal feast. Marcus Antonius de Dominis defends this opinion in Book V, chapter 6, beginning at no. 258, of *On the Christian Republic*. He says that Christ ate an ordinary supper with his disciples on the day before the vigil of Passover, that is, on the thirteenth day of the moon, and that he instituted the Eucharist with ordinary, or leavened, bread.

[Col. 1234B]

Among these opinions Hugo Grotius takes a middle course in his commentary on chapter 26 of Matthew. Although he approves the aforesaid Jewish custom of transferring Passover, he nevertheless denies that there is any certain argument proving that the feast of unleavened bread, or Passover, fell on Friday in the year in which Christ died.

Indeed, even if this had happened, he says that the rule was so just that neither Christ would have departed from it nor would the disciples have asked him about preparing the Passover before the day fixed by that regulation. Therefore Grotius himself thinks that Christ anticipated the Passover—not the full and solemn *thysimon*, which was celebrated by the slaughter of the lamb and the other rites prescribed by the law, and which it was unlawful to perform outside the appointed place and time [Col. 1234C], but the *mnēmoneutikon*, or commemorative Passover, which consisted only in eating unleavened loaves and wild lettuces, such as the Jews celebrate even now.

The task of passing judgment on these various opinions of more recent Latin writers does not belong here. To dispose of the matter briefly, two points in this controversy seem certain to me.

First, Christ celebrated not a partial but a complete and solemn Passover, whether he anticipated it or the Jews postponed it. For when the disciples asked the Lord about preparing the Passover, and he sent them to prepare it, he excluded none of the things prescribed by the law. Moreover, when sending them to the host at whose lodging they were to prepare the supper, he suggested that they should say these words to the host on his behalf:

[Col. 1234D] “With you I celebrate the Passover with my disciples” (Matthew 26:18).

He plainly understood this in the sense in which the common people and the host himself would understand it. Furthermore, when he himself had entered the upper room, with everything prepared according to custom, he said that he had earnestly desired to eat “this Passover” with his disciples before suffering death. “This Passover,” he said—that is, the Passover which he saw prepared by the disciples—not so that he might stop with it, but so that he might replace the shadow with the reality. This, I say, seems certain and established to me, whether Christ anticipated the Passover or the Jews postponed it. For that Christ celebrated it on the same day on which all the Jews celebrated it appears contrary to the testimony of John.

[Col. 1235A] The second point is this: whether Christ kept the legal Passover or omitted it, whether he used unleavened bread at the Last Supper or abstained from it, the ancients—that is, the earliest Fathers of the Church—were nevertheless persuaded that Christ celebrated that Passover with unleavened bread and instituted the Eucharist after eating the lamb. This belief may have led the Church’s earliest leaders, when establishing the form of ecclesiastical discipline, to introduce the practice of celebrating the Eucharist with bread free from leaven, since they believed that leaven had been absent from the Lord’s Supper.

## CHAPTER II. Christ’s example does not impose the obligation of consecrating with unleavened bread

[Col. 1235B] Although both the will and the example of Christ instituting the Eucharist have the force of law, certain things must nevertheless be excepted which he observed because of the time or the persons among whom he lived. Religion and the nature of the sacrament forbid us to omit the fact that he used wheat bread, wine mixed with water, and certain words. But the fact that he did this once, and indeed at Passover, after the legal supper, and with unleavened bread, he either intended to leave as an open question or did not intend to be taken as an example at all.

Thus, without dishonoring the Lord’s example, the Church established—and “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit”—as Augustine teaches in Letter 118 to Januarius, “that, in honor of so great a mystery, the Lord’s body [Col. 1235C] should enter the Christian’s mouth before any other food.” For although “the Savior,” as the same holy teacher adds shortly afterward, “wishing to impress the greatness of that mystery more forcefully, wanted this final act to be fixed in the hearts and memory of the disciples from whom he was about to depart for his passion, he nevertheless did not prescribe the order in which it was thereafter to be received, so that he might preserve this place for the apostles, through whom he was going to organize the Churches. For if he had instructed them that it was always to be received after other foods, I believe no one would have altered that practice.” Nevertheless, as Augustine observed in the same place, “a certain reasonable consideration has pleased us: that on one fixed day each year, the day on which the Lord gave that supper, as though for a more solemn commemoration, the body and blood [Col. 1235D] of the Lord may be offered and received after food.”

The same thing happened, more or less, with unleavened bread. Because Christ used unleavened bread when instituting the Eucharist, the Latin Church observed that practice—not because his example imposed an obligation, but for a “more solemn commemoration” of the Lord’s example. But because Christ had preferred unleavened bread to leavened only on account of the occasion of the Passover feast, the Greeks judged that they were not bound in this respect by Christ’s example, and that the freedom of the new law should not be subjected to a Jewish rite. Both practices are legitimate, and both are supported by a plausible rationale, although the former seems preferable, both because of Christ’s example and because of its suitability to the mystery.

[Col. 1236A] Indeed, the practice of each Church has always been approved by prudent men belonging to the other society, even after the schism initiated by Michael Cerularius, who was the first to bring the Latins to trial on this matter. Cardinal Humbert, although in keeping with his temperament he was accustomed to answer the Greeks rather harshly, nevertheless acknowledges, in his response to Michael Cerularius, that reverence for the Lord’s body remains unimpaired “in leavened and in unleavened bread.” Hence Pope Gregory VII writes in Book VIII, Letter 1:

“We, defending our unleavened bread with an unassailable argument according to the Lord, do not condemn their leavened bread either.”

When Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, was asked by Waleram of Nuemberg what he thought of the Greeks’ leaven, he replied as follows:

[Col. 1236B] “Concerning the sacrifice, in which the Greeks do not agree with us, many reasonable Catholics think that what they do is not contrary to the Catholic faith. For whether one who sacrifices uses unleavened or leavened bread, he sacrifices bread . . . For unleavened and leavened bread do not differ substantially, as some think.”

And below:

“After we passed from the old figure to the new truth, and ate Christ’s unleavened flesh, that old figure is not necessary for us in the bread from which we make that flesh. Nevertheless, it is perfectly clear that it is better to sacrifice with unleavened than with leavened bread, both because it is much more suitable, purer, and more carefully prepared, and because the Lord did this.”

With no less sincerity, Guibert, abbot of Nogent, indirectly defends the Greeks’ practice of celebrating the Eucharist with leavened bread in Book I, chapter 2, of *On the Deeds of the Franks*:

[Col. 1236C] “When the Lord was bringing the ancient ceremonies to an end, after he had eaten the lamb with unleavened bread, he gave the sacrament of his body from that same bread, because no other bread was available and, according to the law which he was fulfilling, another could not then be introduced. The use of unleavened bread, which was then imposed by necessity, does not seem to them to belong to the institution of the mystery. Just as the dipping of the morsel was not for the performance of the sacrament but for the disclosure of Judas’s betrayal.”

This is the opinion of all theologians, both recent and ancient; to it may be added the Council of Florence, whose authority approved the Greek practice.

The more prudent and moderate Greeks likewise held this attitude toward the Latins’ unleavened bread. Theophylact, in his address to the deacon Nicholas, a fragment of which survives in Book V of *Eastern Law*, severely reproves the untimely zeal of his countrymen who reproached the Latins for various rites differing from Greek practices, including the use of unleavened bread. Demetrius Chomatenus, bishop of the Bulgarians, followed him in this. The Greek Theotianus, in a letter to priests living in the mountains, says that it is superfluous to argue whether the sacred mysteries are celebrated with unleavened or leavened bread.

[Col. 1236D] But above all, the moderation of Barlaam, bishop of Hierace, seems worthy of praise. In a letter to the Greeks on the union of the two Churches, after approving the use of both kinds of bread [Col. 1237A], he adds:

“I consider the Latins much more prudent in this respect, because they do not in the least reproach those who use a leavened offering, but venerate it in the same way.”

Finally, to omit many others, Gregory the Protosyncellus considers the sacrifice ἀδιάφορον—that is, indifferent—whether it is celebrated with unleavened or leavened bread, in his *Apology against the Letter of Mark of Ephesus*.

From these statements it may be understood that the controversy over unleavened and leavened sacrificial bread is a question of historical fact: the Church may have used either kind according to the circumstances of time and place. Each society should therefore preserve its own custom, and no quarrels on this subject should be stirred up between those who use different kinds of bread.

[Col. 1237B] For this reason I cannot tolerate the excessive zeal of those who consider it impious to doubt whether the Latin Church has used any bread other than unleavened bread, as though it had been bound to unleavened bread by a necessary law from the beginning, or as though the use of unleavened bread belonged to the dogmas of the faith. What more sacred ordinance could there have been than the one established by the apostles under the direction of the Holy Spirit: that Christians should abstain from blood and from what had been strangled? Yet that law, which prevailed in the Church for many centuries, eventually ceased to be observed. Why could the same thing not have happened with the use of unleavened bread? And if it could have happened, why may one not raise the question?

## CHAPTER III. Whether the Greeks used leaven from the beginning of the Church

[Col. 1237C] Although Bede, in Book IV, chapter 1, of his *History*, says that the Greeks were accustomed “to mingle things contrary to the faith,” Glaber Radulfus, in Book V, chapter 1, praises them on the ground that among them “the ecclesiastical order has always flourished with the greatest caution.” And although they may have been inclined to introduce new teachings, it is certainly evident that they have always been extremely tenacious of their rites.

We must therefore first inquire whether they maintained from the origin of the Church the use of leaven—which they had tried, beginning in the eleventh century, to impose on the Latin Church with such great exertion, or whether, having once accepted unleavened bread, they later admitted leavened bread. Let us consider both the various opinions of the authors and the matter itself.

[Col. 1237D] Pope Innocent III, in Book IV, chapter 4, of *On the Mass*, believes that after the Greeks “divided the Lord’s seamless tunic, so as to introduce the scandal of perpetual division, they rashly changed the rite of the sacrifice,” namely, by using leavened bread instead of unleavened. James of Vitry, in chapter 38 of his *Western History*, expresses essentially the same opinion in nearly the same words: the Greeks, after separating from the Latins, abandoned the use of unleavened bread “so that they would not appear to imitate the Church of Rome.” Neither author explains which schism they mean—whether the Photian schism or the one brought about by Michael Cerularius. Most recent Latin writers have embraced this opinion.

[Col. 1238A] Among the Greeks, Barlaam, bishop of Hierace at the beginning of the fourteenth century, in his letter to the Greeks on the union of the two Churches, believes that the use of leaven prevailed among the Greeks from the beginning, just as the use of unleavened bread did among the Latins:

“Because,” he says, “the apostles, while handing down the same mysteries, made no distinction between leavened and unleavened bread, the Eastern Church immediately adopted leavened bread, while the Western Church adopted unleavened bread, because it bears the image of purity, sincerity, and truth.”

This is also the opinion of Gregory the Protosyncellus in his response to the *Letter of Mark of Ephesus*, where he says that the Greeks used leaven from the beginning and always retained that custom.

By contrast, Cortesius Brana Mazaracenus, professor of Greek literature at the public university of Naples [Col. 1238B], teaches in his treatise *On the Agreement of the Greek and Latin Masses*, following Soto in his commentary on the fourth book of the *Sentences*, that at the beginning both Churches celebrated the most holy Eucharist with unleavened bread. Later, on account of the heresy of the Ebionites, who wanted the legal observances to be maintained, they abandoned unleavened bread. After that heresy had been extinguished, the Latin Church returned to unleavened bread, while the Greek Church continued to use leaven.

After presenting the various opinions of the authors, we must observe that from the very beginning of the Christian religion the Eastern Church possessed rites different from those of the Western Church. Evidence for this includes both the controversy over Easter, which raged between the Asians and Pope Victor, and the letter of Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, a fragment of which Eusebius Pamphilius cites in Book V, chapter 24, of his *History*.

[Col. 1238C] In that letter Irenaeus writes that “the blessed Polycarp came to Rome in the time of Pope Anicetus, and that there was a brief controversy between them concerning Easter and certain other matters; then they immediately embraced one another with the kiss of peace, communicated with one another, and Anicetus granted Polycarp the honor of performing the consecration in the Church.”

Although Irenaeus does not state what those other matters were on which Anicetus and Polycarp disagreed, there is nevertheless room for conjecture that one of them may have been a difference in the Eucharistic bread, since the two Churches used different kinds.

[Col. 1238D] This conjecture is supported by Origen’s authority in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 16, verse 16. Discussing the leaven of the Pharisees, he says that “leaven” is used not only for doctrine but also for other things in both the Old and the New Testament. Then he adds:

Οὕτω δὲ μήποτε ζύμη οὐ προσφέρεται ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον

“Is leaven, then, perhaps not also offered upon the altar?”

Although it is not entirely certain whether he is speaking rather of the New Testament than of the Old, in which leavened loaves were sometimes offered according to chapters 7 and 27 of Leviticus, he seems more likely to be understood as referring to the New Testament because he uses a present-tense verb. It also helps the argument that in Treatise 35 on Matthew he addresses certain uninstructed people who might have thought that, following Christ’s example, Easter should be celebrated in the Jewish manner and the day of unleavened bread observed.

[Col. 1239A] He replies that all these things must now be practiced not in their literal reality but in a spiritual sense. Although this may appear to have been said about the whole observance of the Passover rite, it seems also to extend to the removal of the use of unleavened bread. The same must be said of John Chrysostom, whose homily on Judas’s betrayal contains similar words.

Another testimony for the ancient use of leaven among the Greeks may be drawn from the manuscript *Chronicle of Datius*, bishop of Milan, who lived in the middle of the sixth century. In this Chronicle Saint Ambrose is said to have “venerably imitated the Greek Church in very many rites,” and to have “blessed their sacrifice, namely, the leavened bread, together with our unleavened bread at the most celebrated festivals, especially at the Lord’s resurrection.”

If the use of leavened bread was established among the Greeks in Ambrose’s time, it is reasonable to believe that this custom descended from the original Greek Church. But since some doubt the authority of this Chronicle and consider it spurious and of a later age, more will have to be said about it below. For the present I note that even if this Chronicle belongs to a more recent author, everything recorded in it should not therefore be rejected, especially individual facts which that author—whoever he may have been—could have learned only from older records.

[Col. 1239C] But John Philoponus offers a clear testimony concerning the Greeks’ leaven in his discussion of Easter. As I have already said, the author there tries to prove that Christ did not celebrate the legal Passover at the Last Supper, and did not eat the lamb or unleavened bread; he also argues that the Eucharist was made not from unleavened bread but from leavened bread.

For when he raises the objection of those who said that Christ gave the Eucharist to his disciples on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover was sacrificed and the lamb was eaten together with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, he replies that they are refuted above all by this very point:

Οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐν τῷ δείπνῳ, γέγονε τοιοῦτον, ὡς ἠδη εἶπον, οὐδὲ ἄζυμον ἄρτον ἀντίτυπον τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος τοῖς ἐαυτοῦ μαθηταῖς ἔδωκεν ὁ Χριστὸς . Ἐγενετο γὰρ ἂν καὶ μέχρι, νῦν . Εῖ δὲ ἦν πρώτη τῶν ἀζύμων ἐκείνη, ἀδυνατον ἦν ζυμοτὴν ἄρτον αὐτοῖς εὑρεθῆναι

That is:

“For none of these things occurred at the supper, as I have already said, nor did Christ give his disciples unleavened bread as the counterpart of his own body. For this would still be happening even now. But if that day had been the first day of Unleavened Bread, it would have been impossible for leavened bread to be found for them.”

[Col. 1239D] From these words of Philoponus it is clear that in his time the Greeks used not unleavened but leavened bread in the sacred rite, since he says that if Christ had offered the Eucharist to his disciples in unleavened bread, this would still be done in the Church. But since the matter was otherwise, Philoponus concludes that Christ did not conduct the supper according to the legal observance with unleavened bread.

It is also sufficiently evident that Philoponus believed that the Greek Church had never used any bread other than that which was then customary, namely, leavened bread. For if he had acknowledged that the unleavened bread had at some point been changed into leavened bread, his argument would accomplish nothing.

[Col. 1240A] Therefore, already in the time of Philoponus—that is, toward the end of the sixth century, for he wrote under the emperor Justin II—the use of leaven had prevailed among the Greeks from before all living memory.

This explains why, when the Latins, after the schism of Michael Cerularius had arisen, argued that unleavened bread could rightly be preferred to leavened, they nevertheless nowhere, as far as I remember, accused the Greeks of having introduced an innovation, as though they had once received unleavened bread and later introduced leavened bread. This proves that the Latins were persuaded that the Greeks’ leaven had prevailed from the earliest times.

Finally, Cardinal Humbert, in his response to Nicetas, plainly suggests that at the time of the Sixth Council—that is, toward the end of the seventh century, when it was held in the year 680—the Greeks used bread different from that of the Latins, and that the legates of the Roman See had commended their own custom of using unleavened bread to Emperor Constantine.

Other conjectures may be added. Photius, in Letter 64, acknowledges a difference and diversity among the Churches “in the mystical sacrifices” (ἐν ταῖς μυστικαῖς θυσίαις); this may also be understood of the Eucharistic bread, since Saint Nikon, less than a century after Photius, reproved the Armenians for using unleavened bread contrary to the custom of the Greeks.

Furthermore, before the Photian schism the Greeks used bread prepared in the same manner as today—thick and whole—and employed exactly the same instruments and rites in the sacred liturgy. The principal instruments are the λόγχη, or lance; the δίσκος, or diskos; and the ἀστήρ, or star, which John Chrysostom mentions in his Liturgy and Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, in his *Contemplation*.

[Col. 1240C] Since they removed from the whole and dense loaf a small crown with the lance as an offering, I infer that the loaves they used at that time were thick and swollen, like those used for ordinary purposes—that is, leavened.

These conjectures, however, are less compelling than the arguments drawn from the testimonies of the authors cited above. Philoponus’s authority alone seems sufficient to prove that leaven had been accepted among the Greeks from the beginning of the Church, or at least near the beginning, and that its use continued into the seventh century. From that period onward, it is clear that it was never interrupted.

Nevertheless, a passage in Saint Justin’s *Dialogue with Trypho* appears to contradict this. There the offering of fine flour for those cleansed from leprosy, which was unleavened, is said to have been “a figure of the Eucharistic bread”:

τύπος ἦν τοῦ ἄρτου τῆς εὐχαριστίας

“It was a type of the Eucharistic bread.”

But it is not necessary that a figure correspond in every respect to the thing figured.

## CHAPTER IV. What kind of bread the other Christian societies use

The Muscovites and Ruthenians, as in other rites of the Greeks, use leavened bread. Alexander Gwagninus, in his *Description of Muscovy*, observes that women of advanced age, especially widows left by priests, prepare among the Ruthenians the sacrificial bread, which they call “proskura.”

[Col. 1241A] The Nestorians, so called from Nestorius, whose errors they follow, likewise “prepare it from leavened bread according to the divine custom of the Greeks,” as James of Vitry testifies in chapter 78 of his *Eastern History*. The same is true of those who live in the land of Prester John, who are also Nestorians. Cassander notes that they make a large or small loaf according to the size of the nation, since everyone receives Communion; and according to its size it is half a finger thick, or a whole finger thick, or even thicker than a thumb.

The Syrians, who live in Syria and are likewise entangled in Greek errors, celebrate the sacraments with leavened bread, according to James of Vitry in chapter 75 of the same History.

[Col. 1241B] By contrast, the Maronites and Armenians, or Jacobites, use unleavened bread; the Armenians mix no water into the chalice.

It may be useful to note here that the Armenians fell into the heresy of the Eutychians under the emperor Theodosius, as the letters of Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, and of Dionysius Exiguus, who translated Proclus’s letter into Latin, teach us. From that time they seem to have used unleavened bread and wine alone in the sacred rite, as the Armenians themselves report.

Certainly, because they used wine alone and rejected water, they were condemned by the bishops who composed the canons published at Trullo after the Sixth Council. This is clear from canon 32, in which they are severely reproved for offering “wine alone” (οἶνον μόνον) on the sacred table. Although that passage makes no mention of unleavened bread, it nevertheless seems certain that they were already using it.

The first to accuse them of using unleavened bread was Saint Nikon, himself an Armenian by nationality, who flourished in the middle of the tenth century. Among the various errors for which he censures them is this: “that in the mystical bread they use unleavened bread, and that they do not pour water into the holy chalice.”

[Col. 1241C] From this it is understood that the Fathers of Trullo regarded the use of unleavened bread among matters indifferent, since they did not object to it in the case of the Armenians.

For this reason, the formula of the confession of faith which the Greeks required from Armenians returning to the Greek Church—as it was published by the most learned John-Baptist Cotelier—appears to have been composed after the schism of Michael Cerularius. Among the various anathemas pronounced by those who were repenting, we read the following:

Εἴ τις οὐ βάλλει εἰς τὴν προσφορὰν ζύμην καὶ ἅλας, οὐδὲ ἅγιον ποτήριον (read: οὐδὲ ὕδωρ εἰς ἅγιον ποτήριον) μετὰ τοῦ οἴνου, ἀνάθεμα

That is:

“The printed text reads, ‘If anyone does not put leaven and salt into the offering, nor a holy chalice with the wine, let him be anathema’; read instead: ‘If anyone does not put leaven and salt into the offering, nor water with the wine into the holy chalice, let him be anathema.’”

[Col. 1241D] This formula, I say, in which the Seventh Council is mentioned, seems to have been composed after the schism of Michael Cerularius. From that time the Greeks began to curse the Latins with terrible imprecations because of their use of unleavened bread.

In this formula, when it says that Armenians returning to the faith of the “orthodox Romans” were accustomed to issue the formula of “Renunciation,” the term “Romans” should be understood to mean those belonging to the Greek communion. They were so called by the inhabitants of New Rome, which is the capital of the Eastern Empire. Theorianus likewise calls the Greeks “Romans” in his *Dialogue against the Armenians*, although it was published after the schism, as do many others.

[Col. 1242A] Finally, the use of unleavened bread is not peculiar to the Armenians on account of their Eutychian sect, since John Philoponus, who was himself an Eutychian, approves the use of leaven in the sacred rite, as we saw above.

Besides these, the Mozarabs—or Goths living in Spain, who were called Mozarabs because they were later mixed with the Arab Saracens—also used unleavened bread from ancient times, as I shall demonstrate more fully below. The inhabitants of Jerusalem likewise used it, as Cardinal Humbert proves in his response to Michael Cerularius.

## CHAPTER V. Various opinions concerning the Latins’ unleavened bread

It is remarkable how varied the opinions are concerning the use of unleavened bread [Col. 1242B] in the Latin Church. I find five classes of authors who disagree among themselves on this matter. The first consists of certain Greeks; the second, of those Latins who lived during or shortly after the time of the schism brought about by Michael Cerularius; the third, of the older and more recent scholastics, who do not all agree with one another; the fourth, of Martinus Polonus, Platina, and John Calvin; the fifth, of James Sirmond, whose view the eminent Cardinal Bona somewhat moderated, as has already been sufficiently explained.

Some Greeks, whom Allatius mentions in Exercise 28 on the Council of Florence, adopted the opinion that unleavened bread was introduced into the Latin Church during the reign of Charlemagne. Among them was Demetrius Chomatenus, archbishop of the Bulgarians. Observing that the Latins had established no canon in favor of admitting unleavened bread [Col. 1242C], he thought that its use had not prevailed in the Latin Church until after the Photian schism. This is precisely Sirmond’s opinion.

But it is worth observing that none of the Greeks who wrote against the Latins at the beginning of the schism of Michael Cerularius ever attributed a recent use of unleavened bread to the Latin Church. That idea occurred only to more recent Greeks.

The Latins, on the other hand, who responded during the height of that schism to the Greeks’ reproaches against unleavened bread, either assume or prove that its use had prevailed among them from the beginning of the Church; so far as I know, no Greek objected.

Above all, Pope Leo IX teaches two things in his letter to Michael Cerularius concerning unleavened bread: that Christ used it when instituting the Eucharist, and that the Latins, following his example, had maintained this practice from the beginning.

[Col. 1242D] The pontiff presses the second point as follows, addressing Michael:

“Who would not be astonished that, after so many holy and orthodox Fathers, for one thousand and twenty years from the Savior’s passion, a new accuser of the Latin Church has arisen—anathematizing everyone and stirring up public persecution against those who partake of unleavened bread?”

From this I conclude that Leo believed that the use of unleavened bread had existed in the Latin Church for one thousand years from the Savior’s passion—that is, from the founding of the Church up to his own time.

For when Leo complains that, “after [Col. 1243A] one thousand and twenty years from the Savior’s passion,” no one except Michael had been found who dared to reproach the Latins for using unleavened bread, it follows that they had used it throughout that entire period—or at least that Leo was persuaded of this. Otherwise his argument against Michael would have no force. Nor could that practice have provided an occasion for slander if it had not yet existed.

That this was Leo’s meaning, and that he was speaking not about legal obligation but about historical fact, is evident from Letter 1 to the same Michael. There he writes that all the martyrs who had existed among the Latins from the founding of the Church had been nourished with unleavened bread—that is, with the Eucharist consecrated in unleavened bread—and shortly beforehand he suggests that this Latin custom descended from the institution of Saint Peter:

[Col. 1243B] “Therefore,” he says, “recover now from so great a madness, and cease mocking truly Catholic Latins, the familiar disciples of the greatest Peter and the more devoted followers of his institution, by calling them ‘unleavened-bread people.’”

The same was the opinion of Cardinal Humbert, who says in his response to Michael that the Roman Church had not ceased to use unleavened bread up to his own time, and in his response to Nicetas that this was a tradition of the apostolic see.

Algerus agrees in Book II, chapter 3, asserting that the whole Church except the Greek Church celebrated with unleavened bread by the tradition of the principal Church leaders, Peter and Paul. So too does Hugo the Tuscan, or Eterianus, who says in Book II, chapter 17, of *On Heresies* that the Latin Church had always offered unleavened bread; and Rupert, in [Col. 1243C] Book II, chapter 22, of *On the Divine Offices*, who believes that the Roman Church had never used leaven in the sacrifice.

At the beginning of the thirteenth century Pope Innocent III was a defender of the same tradition. Discussing the Latins’ unleavened bread, he defends its perpetual use in Book IV, chapter 4, of *On the Mass*:

“From the blessed apostles Peter and Paul themselves, whom the Roman Church possessed alive and guards now that they are dead, it received this rite of sacrifice, which it has preserved to the present with inviolable worship.”

The age of the scholastics followed immediately after Innocent. Their opinion concerning the Latins’ unleavened bread was that its use began at the origin of the nascent Church; later [Col. 1243D], when the heresy of the Ebionites arose, teaching that the legal observances ought to be maintained, it was commanded that leavened bread be admitted and unleavened bread rejected; then, when the heresy ended, the Latins returned to unleavened bread.

Some say that Pope Leo was the author of this command; others say that he was not its author but its witness; still others say that he was neither witness nor author.

The first of these is John Duns Scotus, in Book IV, distinction 11, question 5:

“Under Pope Leo,” he says, “there was a heresy that maintained the law together with the Gospel. And then, so that the Latins would not appear to be observing the law of the Jews, it was commanded that the sacrament be made with leavened bread. But later, when the faith returned and prevailed, the Latins used unleavened bread as before.”

Richard holds the same opinion in his commentary on the same passage.

[Col. 1244A] In the second group is Alexander of Hales, in Book IV, question 32, member 3, at the final objection; Bonaventure, who followed him and uses the same words; and Saint Thomas, in his fuller commentary on Book IV, distinction 11, question 2, article 2. These authors produce Pope Leo as a witness, saying that when the heresy of the Ebionites threatened, the holy Fathers commanded that the sacrifice be made temporarily with leavened bread.

Finally, Durandus, in Book IV, distinction 11, question 4, in the body of the question, says that the apostles maintained the use of unleavened bread in the primitive Church, and that the Roman Church received this practice from them. Later, as the heresy of the Ebionites increased—those who said that the legal observances must be maintained together with the Gospel—the holy Fathers, so that they would not appear to agree with them, wanted the sacrament to be made temporarily with [Col. 1244B] leavened bread. When the heresy ceased, the Roman Church returned to its former practice, while the Greeks did not wish to return.

Such were the opinions of the older scholastics; most recent writers adhere to them, one or another according to his own school. John Gerson, in his *Treatise on Communion*, holds that Latin priests once celebrated the Eucharist with leavened bread, but he does not state when or for what reason.

Certain more recent historians took another path—namely, Martinus Polonus and Platina, followed by John Calvin. The first of these, under the year 132, when discussing Pope Alexander, writes:

“He also established that water should be mixed with wine . . . and that the offering should be made from unleavened bread and in a small quantity [Col. 1244C], saying: ‘The more excellent this offering is, the rarer it is.’”

I do not know whether Barlaam, bishop of Hierace, who was nearly Martin’s contemporary, drew from the same source; he reports the same thing in his letter on the union of the two Churches.

Platina says that Alexander established this “so that the heretics called Ebionites would be deprived of an opportunity to slander.”

Calvin, in Book IV of his *Institutes*, writes:

“They tell us that before the time of Alexander, bishop of Rome, the bread was leavened and ordinary; he was the first to take pleasure in unleavened bread. I do not see why he did so, unless it was to draw the eyes of the people into admiration by the novelty of the spectacle rather than to instruct their minds in sound religion.”

Radulfus of Tongeren, in *On the Observance of the Canons*, chapter 23, agrees with the same opinion.

[Col. 1244D] It was useful at least to report these sharply conflicting opinions, so that everyone may understand how intricate the controversy over unleavened bread is and how many winding paths surround it. It is equally important to recognize how necessary it is to extract the truth not from the common stream of false traditions or from spurious authors, but from the best monuments of antiquity.

Those who have not followed this path have fallen into gross and conspicuous errors. In the age of the older scholastics, certain writings or decrees of Leo and Alexander were circulating—certainly spurious, but not yet known to be false. Influenced by them, the earlier authors adopted various opinions concerning unleavened bread.

Perhaps those who said that, because of the Ebionite heresy, it had been decreed that the use of unleavened bread should cease [Col. 1245A] were also led to this view by the authority of Saint Epiphanius. For when they read in Epiphanius that the Ebionites were censured for the error of offering the mysteries with unleavened bread and water alone, they thought that on this account the Church had rejected or suspended the use of unleavened bread.

And because they were persuaded that the Latin custom of using unleavened bread descended from Christ’s example, they finally devised this way of resolving the difficulty: they said that the Church had rejected or suspended unleavened bread because of the Ebionites, and that after the heresy ceased it was restored. But more about Epiphanius later.

## CHAPTER VI. Certain testimonies of doubtful reliability in favor of the Latins’ unleavened bread are examined

[Col. 1245B] In every controversy, just as it is useful to separate truth from falsehood, so it is useful to distinguish what is certain from what is uncertain and doubtful. For this reason, in order to accommodate the less expert, who approach such matters untrained and unprepared, I have decided to deal separately here with several testimonies, either false or doubtful, which may be produced in favor of unleavened bread. Otherwise, if I silently passed them over, the unwary might either place excessive confidence in doubtful evidence or, misled by false evidence, fall into error.

Among the doubtful testimonies, the first that appears is the Chronicle preserved under the name of Datius, bishop of Milan, in the library of that same Church. In this Chronicle the following is said about Saint Ambrose:

“Saint Ambrose venerably imitated the Greek Church in very many rites. He also blessed their sacrifice, namely, the leavened bread, together with our unleavened bread at the most celebrated festivals, especially at the Lord’s resurrection.”

[Col. 1245C] If the authority of this Chronicle were established, we would have a clear testimony proving that in Ambrose’s time the Latin Church consecrated with unleavened bread.

But some learned men believe that this Chronicle is later than Datius, the bishop who governed the Milanese Church under Pope Vigilius—that is, before the middle of the sixth century. I diligently investigated the reason why this Chronicle was attributed to Datius, both by writing letters to friends and by requesting a copy of it from the Milanese Library, so that by reading the Chronicle I might discover the truth of the matter.

But I have been unable to learn anything else about it beyond what I shall soon present, nor [Col. 1245D] have I yet received the requested copy. Consequently, I cannot pronounce with certainty on the authority of this Chronicle.

What first of all makes this work suspect is what Antonius Possevinus reports about this *Chronicle*, “[Col. 1246A] in which, he says, there is written that the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* was sung extemporaneously and alternately by Saints Ambrose and Augustine immediately after the latter’s baptism, and that from then onward it began to be frequently sung by the whole Church.” This may seem to some suspicious, not to say false, and invented by some more recent author. Yet in a manuscript book of Psalms which Charlemagne sent to Pope Adrian, whose autograph is preserved in the Imperial Library, this hymn appears with the following title: “The hymn which Saint Ambrose and Saint Augustine composed together.” However uncertain this may be, it nevertheless shows that the belief concerning the authors of this hymn is not especially new or recent, but was accepted either in Datius’s own time or shortly afterward.

Our Menardus, in his notes on the *Book of the Sacraments*, where he discusses this hymn, is moved by two arguments to withdraw this *Chronicle* from Datius: first, that Augustine’s conversion is reported in the *Chronicle* differently from the way it is related by Possidius and by Augustine himself; and second, that the *Chronicle* is found cited by no author. As to the first point, even contemporaneous authors not infrequently differ in their account of one and the same [Col. 1246B] event. The second is refuted by the fact that this *Chronicle* appears to be cited under Datius’s name both by Paul the Deacon in book XVI of the *Miscellaneous History* and by the commonly circulated Anastasius in his *Deeds of the Pontiffs*, under Pope Silverius, where a great famine is said to have raged during that pontificate “according to the report of Datius, bishop of Milan.” If this matter is found in the aforementioned *Chronicle*, it must be admitted either that Datius was its author, or at least that its author was someone earlier than Paul the Deacon—that is, earlier than the eighth century—and that he held the belief that the use of unleavened bread had prevailed among the Latins in Ambrose’s age.

Finally, even if this *Chronicle* belongs to a later period, everything it contains should not therefore be rejected, both because its author, whoever he may have been, could have taken it from ancient records, and because what it says there about unleavened bread seems to derive weight from the Ambrosian Mass. For in this Mass, which is concerned with the offering of bread, the following title precedes the prayer in Pamelius’s text: “Offering of unleavened bread with the paten.” Moreover, Walafrid Strabo recognizes Saint Ambrose as the author of this Mass, which is called Ambrosian, and says in chapter 22 of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*: “Ambrose, bishop of Milan, ordered the Mass as well as the arrangement of the other offices of his church, and of those of the other Ligurians; these are still observed today in the Church of Milan.” Nor can it readily be said that the aforementioned title was inserted by later writers unless this is proved by suitable arguments. [Col. 1246C]

Among the spurious testimonies for unleavened bread must be counted a fragment of a letter under the name of Pope Gregory, partly cited by Saint Thomas Aquinas in the third part of the *Summa*, but more fully in his *Catena* on Matthew, in these words:

“Gregory, in the *Register*. It is customary to trouble some people that in the Church some offer unleavened breads, while others offer leavened ones. For the Roman Church offers unleavened breads because the Lord received flesh without any admixture. Other Churches, however, offer leaven, because the Word of the Father clothed itself with flesh and is true God and true man. For leaven is mixed with flour. Nevertheless, when we receive either unleavened or leavened bread, we become one body of our Lord and Savior.” [Col. 1246D]

These words are found neither in the *Register* of Pope Gregory I nor in that of Gregory VII. There is indeed a letter of Gregory I, surnamed the Great—namely, letter 64 of book VII, in the second indiction—in which the most holy pontiff discusses various rites of both the Greek and Roman Churches; but there is not even a word about unleavened bread. Consequently, we can establish nothing certain from the fragment mentioned above. [Col. 1247A]

Another argument of the same kind is supplied by a certain letter of Isidore, bishop of Seville, to Redemptus the archdeacon, in which these words are read:

“You have informed us that you are troubled by a scruple: the Eastern Church of Christ customarily prepares the sacrament of the most holy body from leavened bread, while the Western Church does so from unleavened bread, and the Easterners do not hesitate to criticize the Latins on this matter.” [Col. 1247B]

The author then attempts to approve the custom of the Roman Church and to answer the objections of the Greeks. Yet this letter rightly appears suspect, not to say spurious. For although Isidore, bishop of Seville, did have an archdeacon named Redemptus, nevertheless, in this letter, as also in the preceding one, there are many things that persuade us it is an invention of a later age. To pass over other considerations, there was no controversy between the Easterners and Westerners concerning unleavened bread before the eleventh century, as is established above all by the testimony of Pope Leo IX, who declares that Michael Cerularius was the first slanderer of the Latins on account of unleavened bread, arising 1,020 years after Christ’s Passion. [Col. 1247C]

Among the doubtful arguments for unleavened bread must also be listed what Cardinal Humbert reports in his response to Nicetas Pectoratus from certain acts of the Sixth Synod. In these acts it was said that, after the synod had concluded, the apostolic legates were asked by the Emperor Constantine what practice the Roman Church followed concerning the sacrifice of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that they replied, among other things:

“The offering which is presented as a sacrifice on the altar must have no admixture or corruption of leaven, but must be pure, in accordance with what we read as having been established in the *Deeds of the Pontiffs.”*

Humbert then adds: “At that time this apostolic tradition pleased the most devout Emperor Constantine.” [Col. 1247D]

This testimony would indeed be strong evidence for proving the ancient use of unleavened bread among the Latins before the Sixth Synod, if the authenticity of these acts were established. But the acts appear suspect, both because no mention of this matter is found in the commonly circulated acts of the Sixth Synod and because the *Deeds of the Pontiffs* contain no statement that Pope Sylvester established anything concerning unleavened bread, but only that he prescribed that the cloth should be linen.

Nevertheless, the monk Hilarion seems to lend these acts some authority in his discourse *On the Mystical Bread of the Greeks and the Unleavened Bread of the Latins*, when he says that, after the synod had ended, the legates, in order to give thanks to God, celebrated the sacred rite in the church of Hagia Sophia according to the Latin prescription, with all the Greeks praising the Latin manner of sacrifice. He says in Greek:

> Ἐν τῷ νάῳ τῆς Ἁγίας Σοφίας τῷ Θέῷ χαρίζμένους ἑορτάσαι Λατινικῶς, ἐπαινοῦντων ὅλων τῶν Ἑλλήνων τρόπον τὸν θυσίας Λατινικῆς.

That is: “In the temple of Hagia Sophia, celebrating in the Latin manner in thanksgiving to God, while all the Greeks praised the manner of the Latin sacrifice.” [Col. 1248A]

Hilarion may perhaps have taken this from the commonly circulated Anastasius, who says the following under Pope Agatho:

“Such great divine grace was granted by Almighty God to the envoys of the apostolic see that, for the joy of the people and of the holy council then present in the imperial city, John, bishop of Porto, celebrated public Mass in Latin on the Sunday of the octave of Easter in the church of Holy Sophia before the emperor and the patriarch, so that on that day all might unanimously acclaim in Latin words the praises and victories of the most devout emperors.”

From these words we understand that the Mass was celebrated by the legates according to the Latin rite; but it does not follow from them that it was celebrated with unleavened bread. This concludes the discussion of doubtful and false arguments. [Col. 1248B]

## CHAPTER VII

### Conjectures and Some Arguments for the Ancient Use of Unleavened Bread among the Latins

First of all, one must consider the silence of the Latin Fathers who lived before the time of Photius. They teach that the Eucharist was instituted at the beginning of the evening of the Unleavened Bread and therefore with unleavened bread.
