Since they say that Christ’s action must be followed in the celebration of this sacrament, and since, when a change has occurred in certain rites, they inquire into the reasons for that change, nevertheless they raise no question concerning a change from unleavened to leavened bread. [Col. 1248C]

Thus several of the earlier Fathers carefully investigate why the Eucharist is received by those who are fasting, since it was received by the apostles after they had eaten supper; but no one asks why the Church, abandoning unleavened bread, preferred leavened bread. Surely, if this had occurred, they all seem unlikely to have passed it over, since leaven is more closely related to the sacrament itself than either the fasting or the having eaten of the recipient.

You may say that it was already clear to the ancient Fathers that Christ used unleavened bread for the Eucharist only because of the occasion and the custom of the people, and that therefore, even if they used leavened bread, they did not think it necessary to inquire into the reason for a change whose cause was evident to everyone.

I reply that Christ also mixed water into the chalice only because of the occasion and Jewish custom. For, as James of Vitry observes in chapter 38 of the *History of the West*, “No one in those regions uses pure wine.” [Col. 1248D] Yet the ancient Fathers—especially Cyprian in his letter to Caecilius—defend with such religious seriousness the admixture of water in the chalice on the basis of the Savior’s example that they regarded those who acted otherwise as heretics. If, therefore, those ancient Fathers were convinced—as is certainly clear from their writings—that Christ used unleavened bread in instituting the Eucharist, I do not see why, if the Church had then done otherwise, no one would either have asked about or explained the reason for it.

A related argument is that those same Fathers, who flourished in the earliest centuries of the Church, when they discuss the sacrificial bread and describe its composition, nowhere mention leaven. Among them Cyprian, in his letter to Caecilius, and after him Isidore, bishop of Seville, in book I, chapter 18, of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, speak as follows:

“Thus the chalice of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be water alone or wine alone, unless the two are mixed together; in the same way, the body of the Lord cannot be meal alone or water alone, unless the two have been united and joined together and solidified by the structure of one bread.” [Col. 1249A]

Amalarius repeats the same words, apart from Isidore, in book III, chapter 19, of *Ecclesiastical Offices*. Since Cyprian is here discussing the composition of the Eucharistic bread and distinctly explaining its parts, he would not have omitted leaven if unleavened bread had not been in use in his time. [Col. 1249B]

But, you object, he sufficiently expresses leaven when he says that the body of the Lord cannot be meal alone or water alone “unless the two have been united and joined together and solidified by the structure of one bread.” For that which joins, unites, and solidifies is leaven.

Augustine, however, counters this response in sermon 83 *On Various Matters*. Explaining the sacrament of the Lord’s table to the newly baptized and applying each element to moral conduct, he not only makes no mention of leaven but also teaches that the joining and union of the grains or flour occur through water alone, in these words:

“He commends to you, in this bread, the love of unity in a certain way. Was that bread made from a single grain? Were there not many grains of wheat? But before they came to form bread, they were separate; through water they were joined together, and after a certain crushing. For unless the wheat is ground and moistened with water, it does not reach the form called bread. So you too, before the humiliation of fasting, were as though ground by the sacrament of exorcism. Baptism and water followed; you were, as it were, moistened, so that you might come to the form of bread. But bread is not yet present without fire. What the fire signifies is the chrism.” [Col. 1249C]

Augustine carefully distinguishes each element in these and other words: the crushing of the grains, their moistening and joining by water alone, and their baking. His profound silence concerning leaven sufficiently suggests that it was not in use at that time. Add that the holy doctor uses the word “moistened,” which evidently signifies dough joined together with water without the admixture of leaven, as I shall demonstrate below. [Col. 1249D]

Other Fathers likewise speak about the composition of the Eucharistic bread, among them Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, in *Treatise 2 on Easter*, the Venerable Bede in his commentary on Luke, chapter XXII, and others, without making any mention of leaven.

Moreover, among the ancients there is no law, decree, or trace of a law or decree concerning the adoption of unleavened bread in the Church, the abandonment of leaven, or the transfer from the mixed use of unleavened and leavened bread to the common practice of unleavened bread. This would certainly be surprising if a change in the Eucharistic bread had ever occurred in the Latin Church. For since the holy Fathers were so careful about matters relating to the most august sacrament of the Eucharist; since they established so many decrees concerning fixed and movable altars, sacred vessels, the linens used in the sacrifice, and the pious and reverent celebration, distribution, reception, and preservation of the Eucharist; and since they decreed by so many statutes that the admixture of water in the chalice was to be retained, it would certainly be astonishing if the Latins had at some point rejected leaven and admitted unleavened bread, doing so by common consent without a law, with no one objecting or recording the matter. [Col. 1250A]

It is useful here to recall what I observed above concerning the Ambrosian Mass, in which “the offering of unleavened bread with the paten is prescribed.” Pamelius read these words in the manuscript he used for his edition of that Mass, which is traditionally attributed to the ancient Ambrose. I would not readily believe that the mention of unleavened bread was added by later writers, for they could have had no reason to doubt whether unleavened bread should be offered. [Col. 1250B]

Furthermore, the arguments that will be brought forward below to establish the common use of unleavened bread before the Photian schism apply here as well. For those authors who approve unleavened bread show that it was used from time immemorial.

## CHAPTER VIII

### Other Proofs from the Form and Characteristics of the Hosts, Including an Explanation of Two Canons: One of the Second Council of Tours and the Other of the Sixteenth Council of Toledo

That the offerings or hosts were small and thin in the ninth century, much as we use them today, is clear both from the fact that they are called *rotulae* by Iso, a monk of Saint Gall, and from the fact that they were made within engraved irons. I conclude that they were small and thin long before that time both from the Sixteenth Council of Toledo and from certain figures that have survived on ancient coins. [Col. 1250C]

Claudius Boterovius, a man who rendered distinguished service to literary scholarship, presents three such figures in his collection of ancient Frankish coins. All belong to Charibert, king of the Franks, who began to reign in the year 561 and reigned for six years. The first figure appears on page 247, where a handled chalice is depicted, projecting into the two horns of a crescent. Between these horns appears a small circle, which Boterovius took to represent a host; around the circle is the inscription “Gavaletano,” the place where the coin was struck. On the other side is the king’s image without an inscription. [Col. 1250D]

Two others appear on page 252. The first is entirely similar to the preceding one; the second displays three circles, which Boterovius likewise thinks are hosts, with the same inscription and the same royal image, but without any designation of the name.

Boterovius attributes these coins to King Charibert for two reasons. First, several other coins which he presents bear on one side a handled chalice with a cross above it and the name of the place where the coin was struck—namely, Banniaciacum. This place is likewise expressed on the three coins already mentioned by only the first three letters, together with the word “Gavaletano.” On the other side, they represent the king’s image with the inscription “Charibertus rex.” [Col. 1251A]

His second argument is that, during Charibert’s reign and under his authority, the Second Council of Tours was held in the year 566. At that council the Fathers established in canon 3 “that the body of the Lord should be placed on the altar not in an imaginary arrangement, but under the sign of the cross.” From this passage the scholar of antiquities concludes that Charibert approved the royal coins being marked with a handled chalice and hosts, in memory of this statute enacted under his supervision, in the same manner by which Boterovius intends to prove that the Eucharist was preserved in handled chalices from that time onward. [Col. 1251B]

If all these points are certain, we have a probable argument that the offerings in the sixth century were thin and small, much as they are today, and consequently unleavened.

But, to state what I think about the matter, I am first convinced that chalices were anciently made with handles, as Boterovius proves by many arguments, both from the commonly circulated Anastasius in the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs* and from other sources. This custom may perhaps have arisen because the chalice which Christ our Lord used at the Last Supper is said to have had handles, according to Adamnan, the monk of Iona, in book I, chapter 8, of *On the Holy Places*. I shall quote the passage here for the benefit of students:

“Between that basilica of Golgotha and the Martyrium there is also an exedra, in which is the Lord’s chalice. He himself blessed it and, with his own hand, gave it to the apostles at the supper on the day before he suffered, while they reclined at table. It is a silver chalice holding the measure of a Gallic sextarius, and it has two small handles attached on opposite sides.” [Col. 1251C]

Adamnan reported this nearly a thousand years ago from the account of Arculf, a Gallic bishop who had seen that chalice.

Second, I am convinced that the coins presented by Boterovius truly belong to King Charibert, since several others of the same kind appear to be stamped with his name.

Third, I likewise regard it as established that those coins really represent handled chalices, especially since most of them have the sign of the cross above them, and one even has Christ’s monogram attached.

Fourth, I am also convinced that the third canon of the Council of Tours must be interpreted as referring to the preservation of the Eucharist. [Col. 1251D]

Yet I am not equally certain that the very small circles placed above the handled chalices are actual offerings. This is not because it seems altogether implausible to me, but because the artist’s lack of skill does not make the matter entirely clear to the eye. I do not wish to give arguments more weight than they themselves possess.

Some may also doubt whether the Eucharist was ever preserved in chalices. It was usually placed either in a small tower or in a silver dove. We do indeed read in Gregory, bishop of Tours, book I, chapter 47, of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, that a crystal chalice which had been broken was restored through a deacon’s prayer and, at the bishop’s command, hung above the altar, with the memory of this event celebrated each year in an annual festival. But whether the Eucharist was preserved in it is unclear. [Col. 1252A]

A clearer passage occurs in the *Deeds of Pope Gregory III*, where the author says that he gave “one silver chalice which hangs in the apse of the oratory”; this appears to have been intended for no other use than the consecration of the most holy Eucharist.

### Explanation of Canon 3 of the Second Council of Tours

Since the discussion has reached this point, it is useful to make several observations concerning the interpretation of the third canon of the Council of Tours, which prescribes “that the body of the Lord should be placed on the altar, not in an imaginary arrangement, but under the sign of the cross.” [Col. 1252B]

This canon has long troubled learned men and led them in various directions. To say something about it, we must note that in certain manuscripts the prepositions “in” and “under” are absent. We must also note that an “imaginary arrangement” means the arrangement commonly assigned to sacred images. In this sense Anastasius speaks of “imaginary painting” in his translation of the Second Council of Nicaea.

There are now three different interpretations of this canon. The first is that of Severinus Binius, who says that the decree forbids “placing the body of the Lord among the sacred images customarily set upon the altar, and instead orders it to be placed beneath the cross itself, which is customarily placed in the center of the altar.”

The second is that of Jacques Sirmond, in chapter 4 of his *Investigation of Unleavened Bread*. He believes that the canon means nothing other than “that the bread to be consecrated as the body of the Lord should not be formed according to each person’s individual preference, but should be shaped with an impressed cross.”

The third is that of a very learned man who believes that this canon concerns arranging the offering together with the chalice during the sacrifice, opposite the cross placed in the middle of the altar, rather than to the right or left opposite the images. [Col. 1252C]

But, to state my mind frankly, the canon cannot, in my view, be explained either as concerning the composition of the Eucharistic bread or as concerning the position which the offering ought to occupy during the sacrifice. For, unless I am mistaken, among the ancients the word “Eucharist” is nowhere used except for the consecrated host. Moreover, in ancient times the offering was not customarily arranged during the sacrifice in a straight line opposite the cross, but on the left side of the chalice—or rather, the chalice was “on the right side of the offering, as though about to receive the blood of the Lord, which we believe flowed from his side,” as the Micrologus writes from the *Roman Order*, together with John, bishop of Avranches.

I therefore consider the first interpretation preferable, though certain difficulties remain for me, and I shall attempt to discuss them here. [Col. 1252D]

Two difficulties complicate this interpretation of the canon. The first concerns where images were located in churches at that time; the second concerns by what rite the Eucharist was placed “on the altar under the sign of the cross.”

As to the first, I would believe that sacred images were not placed on altars throughout the first ten centuries of the Church. Pope Leo IV attests this in a homily in these words:

“Let nothing be placed upon the altar except reliquary chests and relics, or perhaps the four Gospels, and a small box containing the Lord’s body for the viaticum of the sick; let everything else be stored in a clean place.”

Rather, bishop of Verona, repeats the same words in a synodal address to his priests. Yet Venantius Fortunatus proves that flowers too were placed “upon the altar” in book VIII, poem 8. A cross also used to hang above the altar, as Gregory of Tours and others testify. [Col. 1253A]

Although the chests containing the relics of saints could be regarded as taking the place of images, it is nevertheless certain that sacred relics, and therefore the reliquaries themselves, were scarcely placed upon the altar before the ninth century, as I demonstrated elsewhere in the preface to the second Benedictine century. From this it is clear that images had no place on altars at the time when the Council of Tours was held.

“Where, then?” you ask. Certainly in baptisteries, in the *secretaria* or sacristies, as we call them, in porticoes, and on the walls and ceilings of churches. Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, teaches in letter 12 to Severus that images were placed in the baptistery. The statue of Christ our Lord, which had been erected by the woman freed from the flow of blood, was mutilated by pagans; the faithful brought it into the *diaconicum* or sacristy of the basilica and gave it appropriate care and reverence.

Philostorgius is a witness in book VII of his *History* to sacred images painted or affixed in porticoes and on ceilings. The same is attested by Paulinus in the letter just mentioned. The Venerable Bede likewise testifies in book I of *The Life of Biscop, His Abbot*, where he says that Biscop brought from Rome “paintings of holy images, which he had prepared to adorn the church of the blessed apostle Peter: namely, an image of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, together with the twelve apostles. With these he encircled the central vault of the same church by means of a wooden structure extending from wall to wall.” [Col. 1253B]

If the reliquaries, as we call them, are considered to have taken the place of images, they were at that time stored beneath or inside the altar itself. I presented evidence for this in the preface to the second Benedictine century. Therefore, to return to the meaning of the canon, when the Fathers forbid the Eucharist to be placed “in an imaginary arrangement,” their intention seems to be that it should not be preserved together with sacred images in baptisteries, sacristies, or even beneath the altar, as was customary in certain places. This is the negative part of the aforementioned canon. [Col. 1253C]

That the Eucharist was sometimes preserved in sacristies can be inferred from Gregory, bishop of Tours, in book I, chapter 86, of *The Glory of the Martyrs*. He says that a certain impure deacon, when the time of the sacrifice approached, “took the tower in which the ministry of the Lord’s body was kept” and carried it “to the door”—that is, to the entrance from the sacristy into the interior basilica, or to the place where access to the altar was provided. “When he had entered the church in order to place it upon the altar, it slipped from his hand and was carried through the air.” [Col. 1253D]

From what place could he be said to have carried “the ministry of the Lord’s body” except from the sacristy? This place was contained in an exedra attached to the outer part of the basilica, which some called the *destina*, on the right side of the altar, as Paulinus testifies in the aforementioned letter to Severus. There he speaks of “two sacristies beside the apse”—the place of the altar—located on either side, and reports verses indicating “the functions of each.” On the right were these:

> This is the venerable storehouse where the nourishing solemnity  
> of the sacred ministry is stored and from which it is brought forth.

[Col. 1254A]

On the left were the sacred books, with another couplet.

Nevertheless, it may reasonably be doubted whether in these passages “the ministry of the Lord’s body” should be understood as the Eucharist, since it may rather refer to the sacred furnishings assigned to the sacrifice. The same may be said of the “tower” of Felix, bishop of Bourges, which Fortunatus praises in book III, poem 23. [Col. 1254B]

The reason for doubt is drawn from Gregory himself, in book II, chapter 8, of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, whose title is: “On the destruction of those who carried away the ministry of the basilica.” There he understands by “ministry” “the paten and the pitcher, which is called an *anax*,” and writes that these were stolen by certain wicked robbers. [Col. 1254C]

Fortunatus’s verses about a golden chalice can also be properly explained in this way, for he sings as follows in his poem about the tower of Bishop Felix:

> How fittingly they are joined together, so that golden gifts may bear the great pearl of the Lamb’s consecrated body.  
> Let Solomon’s vessels yield to chrysolites and metals;  
> art itself and faith make it more pleasing.

Finally, in a manuscript *Book of the Sacraments* preserved in the Library of Saint Thierry near Reims, the *chrismal*—which we call the corporal—is called “the bearer of the ministry of Christ’s body” in the prayer by which it is blessed for sacred use. [Col. 1254D]

From these considerations, as I have already said, it may be doubted whether Paulinus, Gregory, and Fortunatus are speaking of the Eucharist in the passages mentioned. Nevertheless, there are ancient writers who explain Gregory’s passage as referring to the Eucharist. Among them is Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, in book II, chapter 32, of his *Collations*, where he discusses that infamous deacon mentioned by Gregory, “who, while carrying a chest with the Lord’s body, let it slip from his hands, and it returned through the air to the altar.”

Moreover, the Eucharist was preserved in the *chrismal*, which is described above as “the bearer of the ministry of Christ’s body,” as I infer from book V, chapter 1, of Rodulfus Glaber. Speaking there of the *chrismal*, “which some call the corporal,” he says that it provides many remedies “if the faith of those who ask demands them. For,” he says, “when it has often been lifted against fires, it has either extinguished and restrained them, driven them back, or turned them aside in another direction.” [Col. 1255A]

He then relates an event that occurred in the monastery of Rougemont “in the time of the venerable Abbot William,” namely, at the beginning of the eleventh century. When “a fire was ravaging the parts surrounding the monastery,” the brothers of that place “took the *chrismal*, set upon a pole,” and raised it “against the flames of the fire, which were blazing directly before them. Immediately,” he says, “the fire turned back upon itself and was unable to seize anything beyond what it had already consumed.”

He then adds what is relevant to our subject:

> Yet that Lord’s bread, carried by the blowing air, slipped from the pole and flew more or less two miles, as far as a village called Tivalgas. There it came down and settled upon the house of a certain man. Pursued from there, it was graciously brought back to the monastery.

From this it is clear that in that *chrismal*, or corporal—which, according to Udalric in book II, chapter 30, of the *Customs of Cluny*, “always lies at the left horn of the altar, so that it may be at hand in case of the danger of fire”—the Eucharist was kept at least in some places. [Col. 1255B]

Therefore, nothing prevents us from understanding by “the ministry of the Lord’s body” the furnishings and sacred vessels in which the Eucharist too was preserved, whether in the sacristy, in the baptistery, or upon the altar “under the title of the cross.”

Another reading of this canon must not be overlooked. In place of “in an imaginary arrangement,” some manuscripts read “in a cupboard, or in an imaginary arrangement.” I believe that “cupboard” was added as a gloss, not to designate our more recent tabernacles, but to explain “imaginary arrangement.” For images were customarily hung and painted on the walls adjacent to the altars, and in certain places cupboards were located there, on the Gospel side or toward the north, in which the most holy sacrament was stored. [Col. 1255C]

This custom still continues in certain churches—for example, in Rome in the church of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme; in certain Gallican churches, such as the parish church of Saint John the Baptist at Parona; until ten years ago in the basilica of Fursano; and in many Belgian churches. The Council of Tours appears to have abolished this practice by decreeing that the Eucharist should be placed upon the altar “under the title of the cross.”

This is the other difficulty that must now be examined: how, precisely, the frequently mentioned canon prescribes that “the Eucharist be placed on the altar under the title of the cross.” The title of the cross signifies the cross itself that used to hang above the altar, as Gregory, already cited, testifies in book II, chapter 43, of *The Miracles of Saint Julian*: “Above the very altar,” he says, “hung a cross of pure gold, made with elegant workmanship.” [Col. 1255D]

But where and in what manner the cross hung above the altar remains obscure. It is therefore worthwhile to know that among the ancients it was customary for *ciboria*, or small towers, to be erected above the holy altars. They rested on at least four columns, which were joined together at the center by transverse beams and supported a cross corresponding to the middle of the altar. From this cross the sacred Eucharist hung, enclosed in small silver or gold vessels or doves, and sometimes also in little stones. This is certainly the arrangement which the Council of Tours seems to prescribe. [Col. 1256A]

The council’s intention is not contradicted by a practice still observed in certain churches, where from the upright shaft of a cross fixed high above the altar an arm extends toward the middle of the altar, projecting and curving downward; from it the divine Eucharist hangs in a small vessel.

These are the thoughts that have occurred to me for understanding the aforementioned canon. I do not know whether what has been said, occasioned by the hosts represented on ancient coins, will be of any use to students.

### Explanation of Canon 6 of the Sixteenth Council of Toledo

Another argument for the ancient use of unleavened bread among the Latins is drawn from the fact that the ancient Fathers of the Latin Church used bread deliberately prepared, whiter than ordinary bread, round and thin, neither thick nor dense. All these characteristics together suit unleavened bread better than leavened bread, which is usually swollen and dense. [Col. 1256B]

Moreover, the sixth canon of the Sixteenth Council of Toledo requires all these characteristics of Eucharistic bread. The Fathers there rebuke certain priests who used bread “prepared for their own meals” in the sacrifice and decree that, according to ancient custom, “only whole and clean bread, carefully prepared, and not anything large, but only a small offering,” should be offered.

If, therefore, I can prove that this canon must be understood not of leavened bread, as Jacques Sirmond thought, but of unleavened bread, everyone will concede that in the seventh century, at the end of which the council was held, the bishops of Spain were convinced that the Latin Church had never admitted any bread other than unleavened bread for sacred use. [Col. 1256C]

Let us now see whether this canon can be explained as referring to any bread other than unleavened bread. It is useful first to set out the entire text:

“It has been brought to the attention of our assembly that in certain parts of Spain some priests do not offer upon the Lord’s table in sacrifice clean breads carefully prepared, but take from bread prepared for their ordinary use a crust, cut it into a round shape, and offer it upon the altar with wine and water as a sacred offering. This practice is in no way found to have been carried out in the history of sacred authority. Therefore our unanimous assembly has decided that bread is not to be presented for sanctification on the Lord’s altar by the priestly blessing in any other form than whole and clean bread, carefully prepared; and not anything large, but only a small offering, according to the custom maintained by the Church.” [Col. 1256D]

All the presumptions seem to require that this canon be explained as referring to unleavened bread. First, the ancient Mozarabs, or Goths, living in Spain among the Arabs—and the same must be said of the earlier Gothic inhabitants of that kingdom—had long used unleavened bread in the sacrifice. Second, a hundred years after the Council of Toledo they agreed with the other Latins in using unleavened bread, as I shall demonstrate later. Third, the work of Bishop Ildefonsus establishes that the same practice was still in force among the Spaniards in the year 845. [Col. 1257A]

But the very words of the council favor this interpretation no less. In the first place, as is clear, the Eucharistic bread had to be different from that which had been prepared for the uses of the common table—different, I say, from ordinary bread. By what reasoning, then, does Sirmond infer from Ambrose’s calling Eucharistic bread “ordinary” that it was leavened? By the same reasoning I infer that the Fathers of Toledo judged sacred bread to have to be different from ordinary bread, that is, from leavened bread. Sirmond’s words deserve examination. After citing Ambrose’s testimony from Book IV, chapter 4, of *On the Sacraments*, where it is said, “You perhaps say: My bread is ordinary, etc.,” he adds: “Certainly, one who calls bread ordinary and used at daily meals does not in the least mean unleavened bread.” Therefore, according to Sirmond’s reasoning, when the Fathers of Toledo exclude and remove from the sacrifice bread that is ordinary and used at daily meals, they unquestionably mean unleavened bread.

Nor can this argument be turned against me, since I maintain that in that passage of Ambrose “ordinary bread” is not being used to mean leavened bread. For if it were clear that the passage concerned two kinds of material bread, one ordinary and the other less common, I would readily grant that ordinary bread is being contrasted with unleavened bread. But here ordinary bread is contrasted not with less ordinary bread, but with consecrated bread, that is, with the body of Christ; and consequently the comparison does not hold in my interpretation. It does, however, hold in Sirmond’s interpretation of this passage, and in mine when applied to the canon of the Council of Toledo, since in both places ordinary bread is conceded to be contrasted with unleavened bread.

Second, the Fathers of Toledo accuse those Spanish priests of offering “not clean loaves,” and then prescribe that “bright bread” be offered. “Clean bread,” insofar as it is opposed to ordinary bread, can mean nothing other than bread free from leaven, which is both an effect and a symbol of corruption. Cardinal Humbert rightly applies this point in his reply to Michael Cerularius:

“According to common opinion, leaven originates when either the froth of must or the lees of a certain rustic drink—which among the Gauls is called beer—or else the juice of boiled barley or chickpeas, or spoiled sap of the fig tree or milk of livestock, is added to kneaded flour. Since froth, lees, boiled legumes, and spoiled fig sap or animal milk are counted among filthy things by human beings, it is evident that leaven is not entirely free from filth. Moreover, any dough into which leaven is introduced must be corrupted, as the most wise Paul says: ‘A little leaven corrupts the whole lump’ (Gal. 5:9).”

Alger likewise pursues this point in Book II, chapter 10, of *On the Sacrament*. Since, therefore, the Fathers of Toledo require for the sacrifice bread that is “clean and bright”—which in this passage may perhaps amount to the same thing—they wish it to be free from all filth and from the leaven of corruption.

If, however, you think that “bright bread” in this passage means white bread as compared with ordinary bread, I do not object, for this too is more suitable to unleavened than to leavened bread. Udalric, in Book III, chapter 13, of the *Customs of Cluny*, speaking of the preparation of hosts according to the custom of his monastery, says:

“They knead them with cold water, because by this means the hosts become whiter; but this practice cannot be observed with leavened bread, for the preparation of which hot water is necessary.”

Bede mentions such bright bread in Book II, chapter 5, of his *History*. For the three idolatrous sons of Sebert, the Christian king of the East Saxons, seeing the bishop Mellitus give the Eucharist to the people after the solemn celebration of Mass in the church, said to him, puffed up with barbarian arrogance: “Why do you not also give us the bright bread which you used to give our father Saba?” Here they call it “bright bread” because, beyond the usual custom, it was white. My argument, however, does not depend on this point, as though I wished to prove that this name everywhere meant unleavened bread. Certainly, I read of leavened bread being designated by this term in the *Annals of Fulda* under the year 870. Nevertheless, since the Fathers of Toledo contrast “bright” bread with ordinary bread, they must be understood to mean unleavened bread, which is much whiter than leavened or ordinary bread.

Third, the Fathers prescribe that the sacrificial bread be “carefully prepared.” Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, says in *Capitularies*, article 5:

“The loaves which you offer to God as a sacrifice must be made either by you yourselves or by your children in your presence, cleanly and carefully.”

With what reverence bread for sacrificial use was prepared among the monks of Cluny, Udalric explains in Book III, chapter 13. The “grain selected kernel by kernel” was brought to the mill with great reverence by a monk dressed in white, and was ground. Then the flour, sifted with the same ritual, was kneaded “with cold water.” Afterwards a lay brother held the implement in which the hosts were to be baked, with his hands covered by gloves.

Long before the monks of Cluny, hosts were formed “with the praise of psalmody” among the monks of Andaginum, that is, of the monastery of Saint Hubert in the Ardennes, as is read in chapter 8 of *The Miracles of Saint Hubert, Bishop of Tongeren*. There it is said that in the year 841 the monks “offered to Count Odo, as he reclined at table, loaves formed by their own hands with the praise of psalmody.” These were *eulogiae*, or blessed hosts, which were provided each day in the refectory to monks who had not communicated, before the common food, as is evident both from the petition which the monks of Fulda presented to Charlemagne, in which they call the reception of the *eulogiae* “the communion of broken bread,” and from the Synod of Aachen of 817 and from Udalric in Book II, chapter 30. For at that time the *eulogiae*, or blessed bread, were made from the same bread as the material of the sacrifice, namely, from the remaining unconsecrated hosts, which all the monks offered at Mass.

Loaves of this kind, or *obliae*, were also often made for ordinary use, as Udalric testifies in Book I, chapter 40, where he says:

“At Quinquagesima there are customarily placed on the table those things which are made from an extremely thin kneading of flour in an engraved iron, and which, he says, the people of the Roman tongue call *nebulae*, while our people call them *oblatae*.”

The monk Burchard likewise bears witness to this in his book *On the Affairs of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, speaking of Abbot Nortpert, who “ordered wine and *oblatae* to be served at midday during Easter week.”

Einhard’s letter 52 seems to refer to such *oblatae*. In it he instructs his steward and his other faithful servants “to have *eulogiae* prepared according to custom, as one normally does for the Lord’s service, both for the service of Lord Louis and of N., his wife.”” From this it is clear that such *obliae* were formed in the same way as the bread prepared for the Lord’s sacrificial use. Consequently, in Einhard’s time—he lived under Charlemagne and his son Louis—hosts made within an engraved iron and unleavened were in use.

To return, then, to the point from which I digressed: long before the monks of Cluny, hosts were carefully prepared—that is, with certain pious rites—not only among monks but also among clerics, as the already-cited Bishop Theodulf prescribes, assigning this care to priests or to their children and attendants.

Humbert proves that the same practice existed in his own time in his letter to Michael Cerularius, in these words:

“The Roman and Western Church offers in the sacristy, through the ministers of the sacred altar”—that is, as he says elsewhere, “through deacons with subdeacons and the priests themselves, clothed in sacred vestments”—“unleavened bread prepared from a grain of wheat and clear water.”

Yet this care did not belong so exclusively to priests and sacred ministers that pious or devout matrons, whom they called nuns, did not sometimes undertake this duty themselves, even at a time when the hosts are known to have been unleavened. For in Book II, chapter last, of *The Miracles of Saint Wandregesilus the Abbot*, we read of a certain nun, or devout woman, who had been healed through the merits of the holy man in the year 891. She “had formed the *oblatae* which she was to offer to the Lord on the following day”; then she approached the fire and “seized the iron with which the *oblatae* were to be impressed and baked” (the author of that period calls this iron an *oblatorium*).

With the same religious devotion, Saint Radegund, queen in the sixth century—as is also evident in the case of a certain Roman matron in the *Life of Gregory the Great*—after she had become “a nun, following the custom of Saint Germanus during Lent,” ground grain with her own hand and thereafter “making offerings with her own hands, distributed them continually to venerable places,” as Venantius Fortunatus testifies in her *Life*. This Germanus was the bishop of Paris, who therefore did not refuse such labor either, namely, grinding grain in order to prepare bread for the sacrifice.

From these examples it is clear how great was the religious care which the ancient Latins devoted to preparing Eucharistic bread. It was not so among the Greeks, whom Humbert reproaches for their negligence in this matter in the aforesaid letter, as follows:

“Sometimes you obtain leavened bread for a price from any man or woman, to such an extent that you occasionally transfer to the Lord’s table bread purchased from the public shops of merchants, which you cannot deny has been handled with unwashed and filthy hands.”

Hence it follows that it is especially characteristic of unleavened bread that it be “carefully prepared.”

But lest anyone say that nearly the same religious care could readily be observed in preparing leavened bread, and that this is what the Fathers of Toledo required, there is a fourth point to be noted in their decree: they wish “an entire loaf, yet not anything large, but only a small offering,” to be offered.

By these words they plainly designate small and thin offerings, such as are customarily made in engraved irons. Nor is it without significance that they require “an entire loaf,” yet not anything large, but only a small offering. For they thereby make clear that their intention was not for that small and thin offering to be cut from a thick loaf, but that it should itself be an entire loaf; and this plainly cannot apply to leavened bread. Bread made with leaven is not ordinarily prepared so thin and slight, but thick and dense; otherwise leaven would be used in vain, since it is mixed in only to inflate and knead the dough.

Certainly, Humbert proves in his reply to Michael that, because the people of Jerusalem offered only “entire, thin, and sound offerings,” not ones cut with a small knife from a solid loaf in the Greek manner, they were unleavened.

Finally, the Council of Coyaca, held in the year 1088, defines unleavened bread in chapter 3 in no other words than these: “Let the host be sound and whole, of wheat.” Everyone can see that the definition of the Fathers of Toledo designates unleavened bread much more precisely through all the conditions I have explained above: bread different from that which “has been prepared for the uses” of the common table; bread that is clean and bright, carefully prepared; bread, I say, that is entire, yet not anything large, but only a small offering.

This description is far more exact for designating unleavened bread than that of the Council of Coyaca, although it is clear that the decree of that council signifies unleavened bread, since the council was held after the schism of Michael Cerularius.

And yet Sirmond applies this canon of the Council of Toledo—which I have shown to correspond so strikingly to unleavened bread—to leavened bread, in these words:

“What, then, is it that the bishops of this council criticize in these priests? Is it that they did not consecrate unleavened bread? By no means. Yet this ought above all to have been reproved if unleavened bread was required, because the loaves prepared for their own uses, which they offered, were not unleavened but leavened. By what charge, then, are they reproved? Because the loaves which they used were neither bright nor carefully prepared for that purpose, as custom required. Moreover, since the title shows that this council was held in the year 731, that is, in the year of Christ 693, who cannot see from this that the Latin Church abstained from unleavened bread at least until that time?”

This is Sirmond’s chief argument. If it proves what he intends, I shall by the same reasoning prove that at the beginning of the twelfth century the Latins too, at least in Gaul, abstained from unleavened bread.

I draw this argument from letter 44 of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, to the bishop of Angers. In it he writes that he is sending back to the aforesaid bishop the priest who carried the letter and who, “when he had not found bread prepared for this purpose in order to minister at the sacred altars, had offered the sacrifice from ordinary bread. In this matter,” Hildebert says, “although custom rather than faith is under attack, we nevertheless recognize some fault in it, judging that the scandal to the church ought to be punished more severely than the offense.”

What, to use Sirmond’s own words, is it that Hildebert reproves in this priest? Is it that he had not consecrated unleavened bread? By no means. By what charge, then, does he reprove him? Namely, that he had offered the sacrifice not “from bread prepared for this purpose,” but “from ordinary bread”—in the same way that the Fathers of Toledo reproved the Spanish priests for making an offering not from “loaves carefully prepared, bright and clean,” but from “loaves prepared for their own uses.”

Sirmond must therefore concede either that the canon of the Council of Toledo is to be interpreted as referring to unleavened bread, just as Hildebert’s letter is, or, if he continues to explain the aforesaid canon as referring to leavened bread, logic requires him also to admit that Hildebert’s letter must be understood as referring to leaven. Since neither Sirmond himself nor anyone else can admit this, and since the words of the Council of Toledo do not establish that leavened bread was then in use, but rather point to unleavened bread, I have said enough concerning the Toledo canon.

Finally, the bread assigned to the sacrifice, which had to be entire, was made in the shape of a crown—not a piece cut off in the form of a little wreath, as among the Greeks, but as an entire offering, which was round. When this circumstance is compared with all the others mentioned above, it almost sets before our eyes the form of our more recent offerings.

Gregory the Great, speaking of sacrificial bread, calls them “crowns of offerings” in Book IV, chapter 55, of the *Dialogues*.

Iso, a monk of Saint Gall, likewise writes in Book I, chapter 3, of *The Miracles of Saint Othmar*, speaking of the elevation of that saint’s body, which took place in the year 844, one hundred and five years after his death:

“Under the head and around the breast of the man of God, certain little round loaves of bread, commonly called *oblatae*, were found by the same bishop so untouched and free from every kind of corruption that, without losing their color or appearance in any part whatsoever, they seemed to the eyes of those who looked at them to have been made within the space of that very week. By what order, or at what time, they had reached that place is unknown to us, but manifest to God. Yet this we all know for certain: no mortal had opened his tomb for thirty-five years before the present bishop, relying on the authority of his office, ordered the brothers of the same congregation to do so. The same bishop, nevertheless, reverently taking them up, placed them upon the sacred body and, after wrapping the body with the greatest care, honorably entrusted it to a bier.”

I have quoted this passage at greater length both because it is notable for the present subject and because it gives me an opportunity to observe what Iso seems not to have known: namely, that it was sometimes the custom for offerings to be placed in the tomb together with the body of a deceased priest, along with other objects and priestly vestments.

I infer this from an anonymous contemporary writer in Book IV of *The Life of Saint Cuthbert, Bishop of Lindisfarne*. The anonymous author’s words in Book IV are these:

“Brought by sailors to our island, after his entire body had been washed, his head wrapped in a cloth, offerings placed upon his holy breast, and clothed in priestly garments, with his shoes prepared to go forth to meet Christ, his body cared for in a waxed shroud, possessing a soul rejoicing with Christ, incorruptible in body, resting and as though sleeping in a stone tomb, they honorably deposited him in the basilica.”

Amalarius wrongly attributes these words, here quoted, to the Venerable Bede. They especially illuminate the passage cited above.

Furthermore, when Iso speaks of another translation of Saint Othmar, carried out three years later, he writes of the same offerings in Book II, chapter 1:

“He marvels that those offerings, which in the preceding account we reported as having been found in his tomb, continued until then incorrupt and entirely undamaged; and he placed some of them, wrapped up, likewise upon the sacred body, while he stored others in a small reliquary and ordered them to be preserved for future times as a testimony to his holiness.”

From these two passages of Iso, as also from Gregory the Great and from canon 6 of the aforementioned Council of Toledo, we understand that thin and round offerings, in the manner of “little round loaves,” were in use a thousand years ago. Perhaps, therefore, the ancient commentator on the Roman Order, quoted by Cassander, inveighs somewhat too severely and without sufficient consideration against the form of the extremely thin offerings which in his own time had been reduced to the likeness of coins. In contempt he calls them “the little trifles of money-changers’ offerings,” declaring them, because of their thinness, “unworthy of the name of bread” and greatly different from the ancient custom of the Church.

I should certainly believe that the ancient offerings were not as thin as our more recent ones, but somewhat thicker, like the *nebulae* which Udalric says were customarily made for ordinary use. Nevertheless, they were baked in an engraved iron just as ours are, as I shall explain more fully in the preface to the little work of Eldefonsus.

Whatever the case may be, from what I have argued throughout this chapter it follows, if I am not mistaken, with some clarity that unleavened bread was in use in the Latin Church a thousand years ago; that this was the conviction of the Fathers of Toledo; and that no contrary practice ever existed anywhere among the Latins.

“But,” you object, “these are conjectures.” I deny that they are mere conjectures. In my judgment, the Fathers of the Council of Toledo could not have placed unleavened bread more plainly before our eyes than by describing it in the manner I explained above.

Let the arguments I have presented indeed be mere conjectures. What more than conjectures are brought forward in favor of leavened bread? And yet, even if the conjectures are equal on both sides, they are far more advantageous to the case of unleavened bread. Its ancient use is certain, and its beginning cannot be shown to have occurred after the founding of the Church. To prove the antiquity of a customary practice, it is enough to refute the arguments proposed against it. But to prove the use of leaven among the Latins, conjectures are not enough; true, clear, and necessary arguments must be produced.

Finally, if what I have said so far is not sufficient to prove what I intend, I hope that the evidence I shall bring forward in the following chapter will establish it.

## CHAPTER IX. That this custom prevailed generally among the Latins before the schism of Photius

To demonstrate the general use of unleavened bread among the Latins, no one will demand that we review each individual Latin church. I think it enough either to prove this even for any single region or to bring forward arguments that demonstrate it universally. I shall attempt to settle the matter in this chapter by both methods.

First, the authority of Alcuin is of the greatest importance for proving that, in his own time, the use of unleavened bread had been accepted from time beyond human memory throughout the Church—not only in the island of Britain, where he was born, and in Gaul, where he lived, but also in the Roman, indeed the universal, Church.

The passage occurs in letter 69 of the Chesne edition. Alcuin, who is known to have died at the beginning of the ninth century, reproves certain Spaniards who thought that salt ought to be mixed “into the sacrifice,” that is, into the material of the Eucharistic bread.

“This custom,” he says, “is observed neither by the universal Church nor by the authority of Rome.”

He then enumerates individually the things that may be used in the sacrifice:

“There are three things,” he says, “which are to be offered in the sacrifice: bread, water, and wine.”

What kind of bread?

“The bread,” he says, “which is consecrated into the body of Christ must be most pure, without leaven or any other contamination.”

But leavened bread is not without leaven or other contamination, nor is it “most pure,” for leaven is an effect and symbol of corruption, as I have already said.

Of what, then, must this bread consist?

“Let the bread which is consecrated into the body of Christ,” he says, “be made from water and flour.”

I have already cited several passages of the Fathers that convey the same point. But there is this difference between them and Alcuin: those Fathers speak of Eucharistic bread in order to shape the conduct of the faithful, whereas Alcuin here acts against those who corrupted sacred bread by mixing foreign substances into the material of the sacrifice. It was therefore his task to set out precisely the method and ingredients by which bread was to be made.

Since, then, he says that bread consists of only two ingredients, namely “water” and “flour,” and removes from it “all leaven and every other contamination,” we must admit that at that time it was free from leaven.

You will say that leaven is a kind of bread and is sufficiently expressed by the names “water” and “flour,” of which it certainly consists.

I concede that leaven consists of flour; but it also consists of a foreign substance of the kind proper to leaven, namely, as Humbert says, either the froth of must, or the lees of beer, or spoiled milk. Alcuin would have had to mention these forms if they had then been in use.

Moreover, if that bread had then consisted of any of these substances, it could not have been called “most pure, without leaven or any other contamination,” as Alcuin requires.

Finally, it is characteristic of unleavened bread that it is free from salt, whereas bread assigned to the sacrifice is leavened and made with salt. Michael Cerularius says in his letter against the Latins:

“Unleavened offerings possess neither salt nor leaven.”

Humbert and all the Latins likewise acknowledge this in the letter to Nicetas Pectoratus.

But Greek leavened bread, according to Humbert in his reply to Michael, and as the Greeks themselves admit, “participates in five substances: leaven, flour, salt, water, and fire.”

Indeed, the Greeks require the mixing of salt into Eucharistic bread with such severity that they subject those who do otherwise to curses. This is evident both from the formula of renunciation which the Armenians profess when they return to communion with the Greeks and from Isaac the Catholic in his invective against the Armenians.

I would not doubt that those Spaniards whom Alcuin reproves received the notion of mixing salt from the Greeks. The same must be said of those priests who offered loaves prepared for their own uses, whom the Fathers of Toledo reproved.

To make it still clearer that Alcuin there requires unleavened bread, it must also be shown that the Spaniards were using unleavened bread at that time.

For what reason, then, does Alcuin reprove them? Namely, because some of them were putting salt into the unleavened bread itself.

“But,” you ask, “by what evidence is the use of unleavened bread among the Spaniards established before the Photian schism?”

Certainly by the testimony of Eldefonsus, a Spanish bishop, who in the year 845, speaking of the weight and inscription of the Eucharistic bread from a divine revelation—as he presents it—admits that it was unleavened and baked within an iron.

This little book, which I had mentioned in my *Observations* at the suggestion of the distinguished Emeric Bigot, was copied from a manuscript in the Vatican library and sent to me by the most eminent Cardinal Bona, who omitted nothing that might shed light on the antiquity of unleavened bread in the Latin Church.

In a copy that appears to be five hundred years old, the little book bears this title:

“Revelation shown to the venerable Spanish bishop Eldefonsus in the Holy Spirit, in the seventh month.”

It then begins:

“In the year 845 of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, this disk—that is, an *angulus* (‘corner/angle’) measuring three fingers—was thus formed round in the manner of unleavened bread.”

And near the end:

“In one iron, although a large one, five hosts can be formed at the same time, in such a way that the middle one is larger.”

Although this author introduces revelations concerning a matter that does not require them, he nevertheless belongs to the period indicated by the title, as I shall later explain in the preface to the edition of his little work, which I have thought appropriate to append to this book.

His entire revelation is directed not toward defining that the bread ought to be unleavened or that it ought to be baked within an iron, but toward prescribing with greater authority the weight, inscriptions, and number of hosts that were to be offered on each feast.

It is therefore clear from this author that in the ninth century unleavened bread was customary among the Spaniards and was baked within an iron. From this it is also evident that in the letter just cited Alcuin is speaking of unleavened bread, from which he orders salt to be removed, and that this was then the custom of the Roman and universal Church.

And certainly the Mozarabs—that is, the Spaniards and Africans living among the Arabs, as must also be said of the earlier Goths living in Spain—although they had distinctive rites, nevertheless “made the sacrament of the altar from unleavened bread, just as the other Latins did,” as James of Vitry reports in chapter 81 of his *History of the West*, where he says that this rite continued among them until that time.

Although this author lived only in the thirteenth century, his authority on this matter should not be dismissed, especially since it is supported by the testimony of Eldefonsus and by other evidence.

Since the Spanish Mozarabs were always so attached to their rites that, when in the eleventh century Pope Gregory VII acted through legates, with the support of King Alfonso, to compel them to change their ecclesiastical office to the Gallican or Roman one, they did not consent unless the matter was settled by a duel—as Rodrigo of Toledo testifies—it is reasonable to believe that this use of unleavened bread descended from the founders of the Mozarabic rite and that it had prevailed among the Goths before the arrival of the Arabs or Moors in Spain. Hence the rite was also called Gothic.

The published books present Isidore, bishop of Seville, as the author of these rites, and almost all more recent Spanish writers affirm this. Guitmund supports them in Book III against Berengar:

“In a certain Spanish Missal which they say Saint Isidore dictated, etc.”

Long before Guitmund, Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, in a letter to Albinus or Alcuin, attributed to blessed Isidore a certain prayer customarily sung at the vigil of Easter.

Yet in the earlier part of the same work Elipandus acknowledges the holy Fathers of Toledo as the authors of the Mozarabic Masses. Who those Fathers of Toledo were is explained by the Spanish bishops—or perhaps by Elipandus himself—in the little book which the Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt refuted, in these words:

“Likewise, our predecessors Eugenius, Hildefonsus, and Julianus, bishops of the see of Toledo, said the following in their teachings in the Mass of the Lord’s Supper,” and so forth.

From this it is understood that there was not one but several founders of these rites and offices, and that Isidore in fact enlarged them.

Moreover, if the metropolitan church of Braga observed the same rites as Toledo, these rites were not all, but most of them, derived from the Roman Church. They were the rites which Profuturus, bishop of Braga, had prescribed for his church, as is attested by the First Council of Braga, held in the year 563, in canon 4:

“It was likewise decided that Masses should be celebrated by all in the same order which Profuturus, formerly bishop of this metropolitan church, received in writing from the authority of the apostolic see.”

I have said this incidentally about the rite of the Mozarabs, whom I have thus far shown to have used unleavened bread before the ninth century.

The same is also clear concerning the island of Britain, both from the letter of Alcuin already cited, in which he says that this custom belonged to the universal Church in his time, and from the little book *On the Miracles of Saint Wandregesilus*, chapter last, which I discussed above.

There we read of a certain woman “from across the sea,” that is, an Englishwoman, who, after being healed by Saint Wandregesilus, asked her fellow nuns on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord “to form the offerings which she was to offer to the Lord on the following day, and to bake them at the fire which she did not dare approach,” but could not obtain her request. She then approached the fire and, seizing the iron with which the offerings were to be impressed and baked, immediately the sinews of her right hand contracted; and she held the *oblatorium* which she had voluntarily taken up, against her will, by the force of the divine power.

This occurred in the year 891.

From this it is clear that the offerings were then baked inside an *oblatorium*, or engraved implement—this is what Udalric calls it in Book III, chapter 13—and consequently were free from leaven. For leaven is never used in loaves formed in this manner.

Indeed, this custom was common not only in Gaul, where the event took place, but also in the regions across the sea, that is, in England, from which the woman had recently come.

Egbert, bishop of York in the eighth century and Alcuin’s teacher, seems to be speaking of unleavened bread in chapter 98 of his *Excerpts*, where he praises and approves a canon which he calls that of the saints, in these words:

“Let the priests of God carefully ensure that the bread, wine, and water, without which Masses can in no way be celebrated, are pure and clean.”

I think that “pure bread” here means unleavened bread.

Certainly, the authors of the canons composed under King Edgar in the year 967—at which time the use of unleavened bread was flourishing—explain unleavened bread by no other term in canon 39:

“We also teach that a priest should never be so reckless as to celebrate Mass unless he has everything pertaining to the Eucharist, namely, a pure offering, pure wine, and pure water.”

This concludes the evidence concerning England.

The same tradition, at least for Germany, is confirmed by Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz and a disciple of Alcuin, who died two years before Photius was intruded, that is, in the year 846.

For in Book I, chapter 31, of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, he declares that the sacrificial bread ought to be unleavened. After citing the passage from Leviticus which commands that the bread of the ancient sacrifice be without leaven, and after citing the example of Christ, who used such bread at the Supper, he concludes:

“Therefore, unleavened bread and wine mixed with water ought to be sanctified as the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ.”

This is how Rabanus reads in both the printed and manuscript books, as is confirmed by two copies in the library of the Most Christian King, one nearly six hundred years old and the other eight hundred.

No clearer testimony for the present controversy can be produced. There are two elements in the testimony just cited: reasoning and authority. By reasoning, Rabanus seems to prove the necessity of unleavened bread; his authority, however, bears witness to the rite of his own time. I do not concern myself with Rabanus’s reasoning. One authority is enough for me, and from it it is clearly established what kind of bread was used for the sacrifice at that time, namely, unleavened bread.

Nor can it be said that Rabanus’s testimony applies only to Germany, where the use of unleavened bread was accepted at that time. In the preface to this work Rabanus promises that he will treat “the office of the Mass according to the custom of the Roman Church.”

And in Book I, chapter 33, after recounting all the rites of the sacred service, he adds the following after discussing the use of unleavened bread:

“The Roman Church therefore maintains this order, handed down by the apostles and apostolic men, and throughout nearly the whole of the West all the churches preserve the same tradition.”

From this I think it is clear that in the year 819, when this work was composed, unleavened bread was in use not only in Germany but also “in the Roman Church and throughout nearly the whole of the West,” and that it was not a recent invention, but a practice believed to have been handed down “from the apostles and apostolic men.”

[Col. 1267C] Now, concerning the use of unleavened bread adopted before the ninth century, the matter is established with respect to Spain, England, Germany, and the Roman Church in particular, and generally with respect to almost the whole of the West. It remains for me to prove it also by particular arguments concerning Gaul, although what I reported above both from Alcuin and from the case of the English woman settled in Gaul is sufficient to establish it.

Paschasius Ratbertus, abbot of Corbie and a contemporary of Rabanus, supplies me with one argument. In his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 20, he explains the parts of the sacrifice and applies them to the formation of moral conduct in these words:

> “This mixing, then, made from many grains, produces one body—namely, a body of sincerity and truth—provided that we are unleavened, that is, without the leaven of malice and wickedness, so that we may worthily receive the bread mixed from this water … Therefore, O man, preserve the mixing of grace; for although you are wheat, unless by the teaching and power of the Holy Spirit you have been thoroughly ground into flour for this unity and mixing, and then mixed with grace and baked by the fire of charity, you will not be able to be strengthened into the solidity of faith.”

Here it should first be noted that the Eucharistic bread is called a “mixing” and “bread mixed with water.” Next, when the ingredients of this bread are enumerated, only flour, water, and baking are mentioned, with leaven excluded. Indeed, the terms “mixing” (*conspersio*) and “mixed” (*conspersum*) signify a mass of flour without leaven.

Haimo, bishop of Halberstadt, is a witness to this in his commentary on chapter 5 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians [Col. 1268A], where he writes that the Israelites, when they departed from Egypt, did not bring away “leavened flour, but only flour mixed with water.” John of Genoa likewise writes in the *Catholicon*: “A mixing is flour joined together by water without leaven.” Finally, before both of these, Gregory, bishop of Tours, writes in book 1 of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 16:

> “The woman, having mixed flour on the Lord’s Day, formed a loaf, which she covered with separated embers and hot ash to bake.”

This was a kind of unleavened cake such as Michael Cerularius falsely reproached the Latins for using in the sacrifice.

Amalarius will close the series. In book 3 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 24, after citing Cyprian’s statement, “so that in the sacrifice of the Mass we too may do what the Lord did” [Col. 1268B], he adds:

> “Although he had concluded this concerning the mixture of wine and water, we can understand it as fulfilled with respect to the whole institution of the Lord, in which his command and the observance of the apostles are contained.”

Amalarius undoubtedly understood this not of the time when the supper took place, nor of the meal preceding the institution of the Eucharist, nor finally of the eating of the lamb, but of the sacrificial bread. He judged that bread of the same kind as that which Christ had used at the supper ought to be employed—that is, unleavened.

The arguments I have brought forward throughout this chapter to prove the general use of unleavened bread among the Latins seem to me to possess every mark of truth. They are drawn from authors worthy of belief, being learned men of the same period; and they appear clear, evident, and sufficient to establish what I intend. If it is granted that these arguments prove the general use of unleavened bread among the Latins before the Photian Schism, it must also be granted that this practice was then believed to be necessary and to have originated with the apostles or apostolic men, and consequently to have been received before the memory of all people of that time.

Moreover, if this was the conviction of the Fathers of Toledo at the end of the seventh century, it must be acknowledged that this custom had passed down to those times either from the apostles themselves or from a period close to the apostles, unless arguments are produced to the contrary that clearly and necessarily establish that the use of leaven had at some time prevailed in the Latin Church.

# CHAPTER X. Arguments for the Use of Leaven among the Latins Examined

[Col. 1268D]

The first argument is drawn from the fact that among the Latins the Eucharist was consecrated in the earliest centuries of the Church, and also in later centuries, from the offerings of the people. For it may seem certain that the people offered not unleavened loaves but ordinary and customary bread—that is, bread normally prepared with leaven.

But what prevents the faithful from having made and offered unleavened bread in accordance with the Church’s prescription and the instruction of custom? That this was indeed done in later centuries, when the use of unleavened bread certainly prevailed, is proved by the example of the English woman mentioned above. She wished to bake unleavened offerings in a marked or stamped baking-iron, “which she was to offer to the Lord on the following day.”

The women of Armorica, when about to receive Communion, still each offer their own unleavened offering, as Sirmond testifies. The same practice was carried out daily by the Cluniacs, according to Ulrich, book 2, chapter 30. The greater Church of Milan still represents that ancient custom of offering in solemn worship. It retains rites notable not only for their antiquity but also for their religious splendor.

In that Church, men and women alike, of advanced age—called *Velones* and *Veglonissae*—appointed by the archbishop customarily offer the material of the sacrifice in the following manner. When the time of the offering approaches [Col. 1269A], two *Veglones*, followed by others who take their places, come forward dressed in the ancient fashion, carrying three hosts and a small vessel of wine. Entering the choir, they offer these to the priest celebrating the mysteries.

Two *Veglonissae* do the same, likewise dressed in the old apparel of matrons, accompanied by others and standing outside the choir screen. There the celebrating priest receives the same offering from them—or certainly the archpriest, if the bishop himself is performing the sacred rites.

These ten men and ten matrons represent the entire city and perform the office that formerly belonged to the whole people, as is recorded in the Ambrosian Ceremonial, which Cardinal Frederic Borromeo, archbishop of Milan, took care to arrange from the ancient rites of that Church.

Now the hosts which the Milanese offer according to this ancient rite are free from leaven [Col. 1269C]. Why, then, would it not have been equally easy and straightforward for the ancient Christians to offer unleavened bread, whether they themselves had prepared it or had received it prepared by others? Certainly, long before the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, the sacrificial bread had to be “prepared with care,” that is, with certain pious rites and ceremonies. Why, then, could unleavened bread not have been made if the custom and practice of the Church required it, when we see that in our own age this is properly done by hired laborers?

Nor is there any obstacle in Cyprian’s rebuke, in his book *On Works and Almsgiving*, of the wealthy woman who had not offered a sacrifice, that is, a host. He reproaches her severely in these words:

> “You are wealthy and rich, and you believe that you celebrate the Lord’s service, although you come to the Lord’s service without a sacrifice; although you take a portion of the sacrifice which a poor person has offered.”

This, I say, presents no difficulty. Either it should be understood of the offering made for the meal established after the reception of the Eucharist—the meals called *agapae*—or, if it concerns the Eucharistic bread, it supports bread carefully prepared, or unleavened bread, more than ordinary and leavened bread.

For if ordinary and customary bread had been used in the sacred rite, it is scarcely conceivable that anyone would have presumed to approach the Lord’s table without bringing an offering of his own. It was easy and obvious either to take an entire ordinary loaf—which is never lacking in the houses of the wealthy—or at least a piece of one and bring it as an offering.

But since the Eucharistic bread had to be prepared with certain religious rites [Col. 1270A] and care, it could easily happen that the rich, through negligence in preparing such bread, sometimes had none to offer and received Communion from bread offered by the poor.

The same answer applies to the passage of the unknown author in the sermon numbered 215 among the Augustinian sermons, where he says:

> “Offer the offerings which are to be consecrated on the altar. A capable person ought to be ashamed if he has received Communion from another’s offering.”

For this reason it should be observed that entire forms of hosts—such as those impressed in a marked iron mold for five or six hosts—were often offered by individual members of the faithful. These were not always consecrated individually for individual communicants; sometimes entire forms were consecrated for the number of communicants.

I seem to gather this both from the Roman Order, from Cardinal Humbert, and from the established practice in the consecration of bishops, priests, and virgins. In the Roman Order, the archdeacon is instructed, after receiving the offerings which the faithful had presented, to “place as many upon the altar as can suffice for the people.”

Then, after the consecration, when the time for Communion approaches, “the acolytes prepare the folds of the bags for the archdeacon, in which to place the offerings,” and afterward “break them,” so that each person may receive his portion from the entire forms of the hosts. They are broken in bags so that crumbs or particles might not fall during the breaking onto the ground or into some less suitable place.

Humbert explicitly declares the same thing in his *Response to Michael*:

> “We too place upon the holy altars thin offerings made from fine flour, whole and sound, and after they have been broken following the consecration, we receive Communion together with the people.”

Finally, in the consecration of bishops, priests, and virgins, one consecrated form of an offering was provided for the person for several days: for a bishop and a priest, for forty days, as is evident concerning bishops from the Roman Order and concerning priests from the second letter of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, to Einard; or certainly for a priest for eight days, according to the Roman Order.

The same was done for a newly consecrated virgin, as is read in the manuscript Pontifical of our Remigian Library at Rheims, in these words:

> “Let the parents offer the virgin to the bishop together with an offering, and let him receive her hand, wrapped, upon the altar cloth … After they have received Communion, let them reserve part of that Communion until the eighth day, and then let them receive Communion.”

Perhaps the reading should be “for eight days.” For priests cut off daily a particle from the reserved offering, from which they received Communion, as Fulbert testifies in the letter already mentioned. In the manuscript copies this letter is addressed to Einard; in the printed editions it is incorrectly addressed to Finard.

“What, then,” you ask, “was done with the other offerings which were not consecrated, if they offered individual forms, one of which sufficed for several people?”

The author of the book *On the Roman Order* replies that, “when the archdeacon brings the offerings on a paten, none of which have been sacrificed, he should take from them as much as seems sufficient and return the rest to the archdeacon, who entrusts them to the church custodian for safekeeping” [Col. 1271A].

Afterward they were used whenever Mass had to be celebrated without anyone offering, which happened especially on ordinary weekdays; or they were blessed into *eulogiae*. The latter practice was carried out daily among the monks.

Certainly, the Council of Mâcon, celebrated in the year 585, chapter 4, requires offerings to be made by men and women not every day but only on Sundays. Finally, at least in the time of Hincmar, not everyone offered, but only the heads of each household, as will be seen below from Hincmar.

You may object that the ministers of the Church, widows, the poor, and the needy—whom they called *matricularii*—were fed from the remaining offerings, and therefore that the bread offered must have been ordinary bread prepared with leaven.

[Col. 1271B]

To this I reply that anciently two offerings were made in the Church: one before Mass, or before the Gospel, and the other after the Gospel had been read, at the offertory, as we call it.

In the first, the faithful offered bread, wine, wax, and anything else as support for the priests, widows, poor, and needy; in the second, bread and wine for consecration.

Hincmar of Rheims admirably clarifies this passage in chapter 16 of his first capitulary:

> “Whoever wishes to offer a candle, whether specifically or generally, should bring it to the altar either before Mass or during Mass, before the Gospel is read. For the offering, however, let him offer only one offering and the offertory for himself and all his relations and household. If he wishes to offer more wine, in a small bottle or a vessel, or more offerings, let him give them either before Mass or after Mass to the priest or his minister, so that the people may receive *eulogiae* in almsgiving and by his blessing, or so that the priest may have some support.”

Moreover, the Council of Nantes expressly distinguishes the ordinary bread customarily offered by the faithful from the offerings to be consecrated, when it decrees in chapter 9:

> “Let the priest have suitably cut portions in a clean vessel, either from the offerings which are offered by the people and remain after the consecration, or from the loaves which the faithful offer to the Church, or indeed from his own supply, so that after the solemnities of the Mass those who were not prepared to receive Communion may receive *eulogiae* from them every Sunday and on feast days.”

There was therefore one bread offered for consecration [Col. 1271D], and another “for the Church,” that is, for feeding the ministers of the Church. From either of these *eulogiae* were made; this is the bread now called blessed bread.

Read the first capitulary of Hincmar, article 7, in this way, as well as the *Customs of Cluny*, book 2, chapter 30, where it is prescribed:

> “On ordinary days, unconsecrated hosts are to be brought into the refectory, so that they may be distributed to those who did not receive Communion that day.”

These were the very hosts which had also been offered at the solemn Mass by those who were not going to receive Communion. Although everyone offered every day, it was customary on weekdays to consecrate only three hosts for those receiving Communion, alternately from each choir, and five on Sundays.

Another objection is drawn from Epiphanius, heresy 30, where he notes that the Ebionites celebrated the mysteries “through unleavened bread” (*δι’ ἀζύμων*).

At first sight this objection once seemed to me extremely powerful; but it does not seem so to one who reads the entire passage. Epiphanius’s words are:

> “They supposedly celebrate the mysteries in imitation of the saints who are in the Church, from year to year, through unleavened bread; but the other part of the mystery through water alone” (*Μυστήρια δὲ δῆθεν τέλουσι κατὰ μίμησιν τῶν ἁγίων ἐν τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ ἀπὸ ἐνιαυτοῦ εἰς ἐνιαυτόν δι’ ἀζύμων, καὶ τὸ ἄλλο μέρος τοῦ μυστηρίου δι’ ὕδατος μόνου*).

From these words one might reasonably argue as follows: Epiphanius seems to show that the Ebionites, in offering sacrifice once a year with unleavened bread, imitated at least the Latin Church. In this passage he reproaches them only because they used water alone for the other part of the sacrifice. Therefore, at that time the Church made the sacrifice from unleavened bread.

Certainly, this interpretation does no violence to Epiphanius’s words; indeed, it seems consistent with his meaning, since he praises their practice on account of their imitation of the Church. One may reasonably maintain that this imitation consisted in offering unleavened bread.

It should also be added that Epiphanius usually attacks nearly all the errors he enumerates. He refutes the Encratites, who used water alone in the sacred rite; yet nowhere does he criticize the use of unleavened bread. And who would suppose that Epiphanius condemned the Ebionites for using unleavened bread in the most sacred mystery, which he acknowledges was instituted by the Lord Christ with unleavened bread, as was established above?
