One difficulty arises here: Epiphanius himself, in heresy 46, while enumerating the errors of Tatian, says that Tatian instituted certain mysteries “in imitation of the holy Church” (*κατὰ μίμησιν τῆς ἁγίας Ἐκκλησίας*), but used nothing in them except water. Here it is clear that the imitation of the Church concerns not the thing offered but the offering itself. The same must therefore be said concerning the earlier testimony.

This argument does indeed correctly establish that nothing certain can be proved from that earlier passage of Epiphanius in favor of the use of unleavened bread. I deliberately did not cite it above, where I was discussing the leaven of the Greeks. Yet it does not follow that Epiphanius understood the imitation of the Church in both cases to concern the offering itself rather than the thing offered.

For he may have recognized a more explicit imitation in the Ebionites than in Tatian. Besides, even if he does not relate the use of unleavened bread to imitation of the Church, it still cannot be certainly inferred that he counted that practice among the errors—especially since, as I have already said, Epiphanius acknowledges that Christ originally instituted the Eucharist with unleavened bread.

Suppose that the Greeks at that time used leavened bread in the sacred rite, while the Latins used unleavened bread. Epiphanius certainly would not have related the use of unleavened bread to imitation of the universal Church if the Greek Church had used leavened bread. Yet neither would he have condemned the use of unleavened bread as an error, since he did not disapprove of it among the Latins.

Furthermore, if he reproaches the Ebionites because they used unleavened bread, he did so because they used it with the intention of teaching that the legal observances ought to be maintained together with the Gospel. In a word, if that earlier passage contributes nothing to the case for unleavened bread, it certainly favors leavened bread no more; it leaves the matter undecided, and the issue must therefore be settled by other arguments.

Finally, to bring the matter to a brief conclusion: having established that the Greeks and the Churches adhering to them used leaven, while the Latins used unleavened bread from the beginning, and having admitted that Epiphanius reproached the Ebionites because they used unleavened bread in sacred rites, I reply that Epiphanius reproached them not because he thought that no Church could use unleavened bread, but because the Ebionites, although they belonged to the Greek communion, used it contrary to the custom of their community.

By the same reasoning, if someone following the Latin practice were to prefer leaven to unleavened bread in the sacred rite, the Latins would reproach him—not because the Latin Church rejects the leaven of the Greeks, but because it is unlawful for Latins to violate the Latin custom in sacred matters. This response can also be applied to the Armenians, whom Saint Nicon reproached in the tenth century for using unleavened bread for the same reason.

The third argument in favor of leavened bread is drawn from book 4 of Ambrose’s *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4:

> “Perhaps you say: ‘My bread is ordinary.’ But this bread is bread before the sacramental words; when the consecration has been added, from bread it becomes the flesh of Christ.”

From this Sirmond argues:

> “Clearly, when he says ‘ordinary bread,’ bread used at tables and for daily meals, he certainly does not mean unleavened bread.”

But neither does he mean leavened bread. Ambrose calls it ordinary bread not insofar as it is unleavened, but insofar as it is opposed to consecrated bread, that is, to the body of Christ, as the very order of the words makes clear.

Moreover, unleavened bread can also be called common or ordinary, since it is made from the same material as leavened bread. Rupert, abbot of Deutz, certainly speaks in almost the same way as Ambrose above concerning the unleavened bread which Christ consecrated at the Last Supper. In book 3 of *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, chapter 21, he writes:

> “He took common bread; but by blessing it he changed it into something altogether different from what it had been.”

Here Rupert calls the bread which Christ used at the Last Supper common bread; yet, in Rupert’s judgment, it was undoubtedly unleavened.

I have already shown above that the fourth argument, drawn from canon 6 of the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, not only contributes nothing in favor of the use of leaven but supports unleavened bread most strongly.

The fifth argument is supplied by the decrees of the Roman pontiffs Melchiades, Siricius, and Innocent.

Concerning Melchiades, the following is read in his *Life*:

> “He arranged that consecrated offerings should be sent throughout the Churches from the consecration of the bishop; this is called the ferment.”

Concerning Siricius:

> “He established that no priest should celebrate Mass throughout the week unless he received the consecrated offering sent by the bishop of the place; this is called the ferment.”

Finally, Innocent writes to Decentius in letter 5:

> “You have wished to consult us unnecessarily about the ferment which we send on Sunday through the titular churches, since all our churches are situated within the city. Their priests cannot meet with us on that day because of the people entrusted to them; therefore they receive from us, through the acolytes, the ferment which has been sent, so that especially on that day they may not consider themselves separated from our communion. I do not think this should be done through the parishes, because the sacraments do not have to be carried far, nor do we send them through different cemeteries to priests stationed there; and their priests possess the right and permission to consecrate them.”

There are various opinions concerning this ferment: some deny that it was the Eucharist, while others affirm it. I agree with Baronius, who denies that it was the Eucharist and holds that it was merely *eulogiae* sent by the pontiff as a sign of mutual communion.

For this ferment is called both “consecrated bread” and “the sacrament,” and only priests are said to possess the right and permission to consecrate it. Finally, it is called “consecrated bread,” a name by which the Eucharist is called by Justin in his *First Apology*, by Irenaeus cited by Eusebius in book 5, chapter 24, and in book 5 of *Against Heresies*, chapter 2, and by Clement of Alexandria in the first *Stromate*, page 117, as the distinguished scholar Henri Valois noted in his annotations on Eusebius.

That the Eucharist was formerly sent as a sign of ecclesiastical communion is witnessed by Justin in his *First Apology* and by Eusebius in book 5, chapter 24, although canon 14 of the Council of Laodicea forbade this from being done during the Easter festivals.

No one should be troubled by the statement that the Eucharist was transmitted through an acolyte, since Eusebius reports that it was sent through a boy to the aged Serapion, in book 6, chapter 44.

The pontiff sent the Eucharist to the titular churches of the City for two reasons: as a sign of authority and as a sign of ecclesiastical communion. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, commands that the Eucharist be considered valid when it is under the bishop’s authority or when the bishop himself has granted permission for it.

Leo the Great, in his letter to the bishops of Gaul and Germany, says that when a bishop is present it is not lawful to consecrate the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood except by his command.

Thus, to testify that he granted the priests of the titular churches of the city of Rome the power to consecrate the Eucharist, the pontiff himself sent them the Eucharist, which was also a symbol of mutual union. This is said to have been established by Melchiades and Siricius and explained by Innocent.

Later, *eulogiae*, or unconsecrated offerings, were sent in place of the Eucharist. Thus, in the *Life of Pope John III*, it is recorded that he established “that offerings, vessels, or lamps should be supplied from the Lateran to the cemeteries on every Sunday.” In the *Life of Gregory III* we read “that offerings from the patriarchium should be carried by the bearer of offerings for the celebration of Masses”—offerings, I say, of bread and wine, such as Gregory II ordered to be sent daily to the Church of Saint Paul.

Yet even if the pontiff sent the Eucharist to the titular churches of the City [Col. 1275A], the priests undoubtedly consecrated another Eucharist themselves. For they celebrated Masses, and the Eucharist was sent by the pontiff so that they might be permitted to do so; moreover, the priest and the people received Communion from both offerings: from the one consecrated by the pontiff and from the one consecrated by the priests themselves.

The newly ordained priests did something similar. They were nourished for forty days by the Eucharist received from the bishop’s hand on the day of their ordination; yet they could celebrate Mass daily and receive at the same time the Eucharist consecrated by themselves, as Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, testifies in his second letter to Einard.

But to return to the ferment of Melchiades and the other pontiffs: we must inquire why the Eucharist was called by this name. Although the passage seemed to support the use of leaven, which he wished to assert, Sirmond explains the name in this way: it was not called ferment because it consisted of leavened bread, but because, whatever kind of bread it was made from, it served the Churches to which it was sent in place of leaven and acted as their bond of union, like leaven in the dough with which it is mixed.

Indeed, if the words quoted from the *Lives* of Melchiades and Siricius are carefully considered, the Eucharist seems so far from being called ferment because it consisted of leaven that the name appears instead to be an additional designation derived from elsewhere rather than from the substance of the thing itself.

Concerning Melchiades we read:

> “He arranged that consecrated offerings should be sent throughout the Churches from the consecration of the bishop; this is called the ferment.”

In Siricius:

> “This is called the ferment.”

When I read the words “this is called the ferment,” the thought immediately occurred to me that this was an extrinsic term, not derived from the substance of the thing itself. I am therefore convinced that nothing certain can be established from this passage in favor of leaven.

“But,” you object, “if the bread was unleavened, why was it called by the contrary name, ferment?”

The answer is not easy when one is required to explain why each thing has received its particular name. Sirmond offered one highly plausible explanation. I myself think that the Eucharist was also called by this term so that, under an obscure name, so great a mystery might be concealed from the profane.

For in those times it was customary among the Fathers to express the Eucharist only in obscure language. This is well known from Augustine, throughout his works, from Theodoret in the *Dialogue of Eranistes*, and from others.

I therefore think that Melchiades, Siricius, and Innocent designated the Eucharist by the additional name “ferment,” so that they would not appear to disclose the sacred matter to the pagans.

It may also be added that Caesarius the Greek interprets the parable of the ferment as referring to the Eucharist, not in a literal but in a moral sense. In his *Dialogue* he writes:

> “If you wish to hear the words understood in another way, let the ferment be understood as the venerable and divine body of God, which he formed in the womb of the holy virgin Mary to clothe himself with it, woven without seed and united both to soul and body.”

What if, for this or a similar reason, the pontiffs mentioned above gave the Eucharist the name “ferment,” without regard to its material, but with reference in a moral sense to the body of Christ?

I would also add that Nicetas Pectoratus calls the unleavened bread of the Latins “unleavened ferment” (*ἀζύμην ζύμην*), unless he appears to have said this reproachfully and mockingly.

The sixth argument in favor of leaven is drawn from the silence of Photius. Since he gathered every opportunity for accusing the Latins in all matters in which they differed from Greek customs and rites, yet never reproached them for using unleavened bread, he would not seem to have omitted this objection if that practice had then prevailed.

Certainly, the more recent Greeks who provoked the dispute with the Roman Church during the pontificate of Pope Leo IX did not omit it. This is offered as evidence that the use of unleavened bread began among the Latins during the interval between the two schisms.

[Col. 1276B]

To this I reply that Photius did not reproach the Latins for using unleavened bread because John Chrysostom had taught that this custom arose from Christ’s example, and because Photius was convinced that in his own time even the Greek Church followed it, as he himself admits in chapter 116 of the *Bibliotheca*, as I reported above.

Moreover, Photius did not reproach the Latins for failing to sing the *Alleluia* during Lent, nor did he criticize Western monks because, with the permission of the rule of Saint Benedict, they ate meat when ill, or because they wore breeches while traveling. All these things were objected to the Latins by the Greeks in the time of Leo IX.

Finally, Photius omitted many other matters of this kind in which the Latins then differed from the Greeks. Such was the tonsure of the head—although he made a petty objection concerning the shaving of the chin—the laying on of hands in confirmation, the prohibition against baptizing on Epiphany, and other matters of the sort which Photius prudently passed over in silence.

In any event, Photius’s silence has no force whatever against the certain and necessary arguments by which I have shown that the general use of unleavened bread prevailed among the Latins before Photius.

The final argument is drawn from the fact that before the age of Photius no law concerning the use of unleavened bread is recorded. Sirmond presses this argument, together with Demetrius Chomatenus, archbishop of Bulgaria, in his responses to the bishop of Dyrrachium, in chapter 3 of the *Disquisition*.

But if this argument proved anything, it would certainly prove that unleavened bread was not used in sacred matters even after the Photian Schism. For, unless I am mistaken, no decree concerning the rejection of leaven or the adoption of unleavened bread, no constitution, and no canon is found after that time and before the schism of Michael Cerularius; yet in Michael’s time the use of unleavened bread prevailed universally in the Latin Church.

Since no law concerning this matter exists either before or after Photius and before the age of Michael, it must be said that this custom was received from the very beginning of the Latin Church.

It would certainly have been easy for the Greeks to reproach the Latins for the novelty of this practice if it had become established only after the Photian Schism. Nor would Pope Leo and the other Latins have proceeded with such brazen confidence—or such shameful ignorance—as to claim that the custom had come down from the time of the apostles, if it had been so recent.

# CHAPTER XI. Epilogue and Conclusion of the Foregoing

Thus far I have set forth, in my spare hours and according to my ability, whatever I have been able to observe concerning the ancient use of unleavened bread among the Latins. I have attached myself obstinately to no opinion, but have been moved solely by the desire to recognize and demonstrate the truth.

If I have accomplished anything, I wish to attribute it all to Supreme Truth. If anything slipped from my pen carelessly, or if I have imposed something false or doubtful as true, I wish it to be refuted.

I could indeed have gone further if I had indulged conjecture more freely; but since I began to pursue the matter historically, it seemed better to place a limit on inventions of that kind [Col. 1277B]. It remains for me to gather in a brief statement what I explained more expansively and at scattered points above.

I have proved that the Eucharist was instituted by the Lord Christ with unleavened bread. Yet it does not follow from his action and example that there is a necessity of consecrating with unleavened bread.

Thus the Greeks could have used leavened bread and the Latins unleavened bread from the beginning of the Church, and indeed they did so, without danger to Christian fellowship. “For diversity of observance does not offend us where the unity of faith is not divided,” as Fulbert says in his second letter.

I have said nothing about the apostles, because all antiquity is silent about what they did in this matter, unless one excepts the testimonies of Pope Leo IX and his followers, who derive the Latin custom from the example of the apostles Peter and Paul.

They pronounce nothing concerning the other apostles, whom one cannot easily prove to have been certainly committed to any particular kind of bread in the sacred rite. In the preceding letter of the most eminent Cardinal Bona you have conjectures on this matter that are highly probable, and to which nothing seems necessary to be added.

From the time of the apostles ecclesiastical discipline began to be established. Its principal founders among the Latins seem, not without reason, to have prescribed the use of unleavened bread.

To sanction this discipline, the canons which we call apostolic were composed. The third of these decrees:

> “Nothing else is to be offered in the sacrifice except what the Lord appointed.”

These words can also be explained, not without foundation, as referring to the use of unleavened bread, since the more ancient Fathers were persuaded that Christ offered unleavened bread at the Supper.

You may object that it seems probable that during the persecutions which, as people say, raged in those earliest centuries, the faithful used leavened bread in sacred matters because it was more readily available.

That is certainly not at all unlikely. Yet unleavened bread is not so difficult to prepare that it could not have been made without danger of revealing those responsible, or that the diligence and piety of the Christians of that time would have been beyond its reach.

Pope Leo IX certainly testifies that our martyrs—that is, the martyrs of the Latin Church—were nourished with unleavened bread.

Many other things far more difficult were being done or prepared at that time: the rites of public penance, the Church’s immense treasury, golden and silver vessels for sacred use, and many other things of the same kind.

Finally, even in our own times, Latin Catholics who are forced to hide among infidels or heretics are nevertheless not deterred in the least from preparing unleavened bread for sacred use.

These considerations concerning the earliest times seem more probable and credible. They are not supported by any certain and necessary argument, but only by conjectures, and I have thought it right to stop there until firmer evidence becomes available.

There is indeed a passage supporting the use of unleavened bread by the Latins in the *Sermon on the Lord’s Supper* by the author of the book *On the Cardinal Works of Christ*, a work published under Cyprian’s name. But this author is more recent: he is Ernaldus, as certain arguments establish, abbot of Bonneval in the territory of Chartres, a contemporary and friend of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and later than Cyprian by a full nine hundred years.

The evidence concerning the fourth and subsequent centuries is more firmly established. Yet the matters I set forth above concerning the universal use of unleavened bread among the Latins before the ninth century appear certain and clear.

Since this custom is believed to have become established before the memory of all the people of that age, it must be acknowledged that it was received either from the very beginnings of the Latin Church or from a period close to them.

The arguments brought forward in favor of the leaven of the Latins, although they carry great weight with me because of the dignity and authority of the eminent men who support that opinion, do not seem so necessary that they compel us to admit it. Nor are they certainly stronger than the arguments that can be offered by defenders of the contrary opinion.

Therefore, concerning those earliest centuries, much obscurity remains, and this may provide grounds for doubt. But, with the permission of those who think otherwise, it does not seem to me a sufficient reason for asserting the use of leaven among the Latins.

## In the Year of Our Lord 1061–1062. Adelmannus, Bishop of Brescia

# HISTORICAL NOTICE CONCERNING ADELMANNUS
*(Histoire littéraire de la France, vol. VII, p. 542.)*

[Col. 1279A] Adelmann, whom others incorrectly call Adelin, is unknown to us both in regard to his family and the precise place of his birth. A writer of this century, who published at Leipzig in 1710 a work entitled *Illustrious Germans*, wishes to do his homeland the honor of having given birth to our prelate (*Journal des savants*, 1739, p. 657); but his opinion is unsupported by solid evidence, being based only on the fact that Sigebert calls him Almanne rather than Adelmann (SIG. *Scrip.*, c. 153), in which it is entirely natural to recognize a copyist’s error. Moreover, when Adelmann himself speaks of the Teutonic countries—that is, Germany—he regards them as a foreign land in relation to himself (ADEL. *ad Ber.*, p. 438).

[Col. 1279B] The first appearance he makes in the world is at the school of Chartres, where he studied under the celebrated Fulbert and where his fellow students included Hildier, Sigon, Berengar, Lambert, Engelbert, and several other learned men (ibid., MAB. *Analect.*, p. 482). Adelmann was one of those beloved pupils whom the venerable Socrates—as he calls his teacher Fulbert—would take with him in the evening into a little garden near a city chapel, in order to give them private instruction in addition to the public lessons he gave them at other hours. There he earnestly exhorted them, with tears and the transports of holy fervor, always to follow the highway, carefully walking in the footsteps of the Fathers and never departing from them.

[Col. 1279C] Adelmann was so deeply impressed by the happiness of having received such instruction that long afterward he spoke of it only with the most lively sentiments of gratitude (MAB. ibid.). Let us hear him explain it himself for a moment:

> O memorable pontiff, glory of the city of Chartres,
>
> When I first endeavor to speak of you, Father Fulbert,
>
> Speech flees, my heart melts, and my tears begin anew.
>
> Many things deserving lamentation I remember one by one,
>
> Since I was often your companion, clinging to the old man’s side,
>
> Drinking with my ear from the golden fountain of your honey-flowing mouth.

Elsewhere we have seen with what praises he extols the doctrine of this excellent teacher and his admirable manner of teaching. All this moved him to offer God continual thanksgiving for granting him the advantage of spending some time beside such a teacher; and, he says, with far greater reason than Plato had for thanking nature that she had caused him to be born a human being rather than a beast in the time of Socrates (ADEL. ibid.).

But if he felt such tender attachment to Fulbert, Fulbert felt no less toward him. Adelmann was already a subdeacon when he went to Fulbert’s school. It seems that this occurred toward the final years of the episcopate of Durand, bishop of Liège (FULB. ep. 57; MAB. *Act.*, vol. IX, pref., no. 8). When Réginard succeeded him in 1024, he wrote to Fulbert [Col. 1280B] to ask for his subdeacon back, describing him as a wandering sheep; from this we learn that Adelmann was a diocesan [Note: [Col. 1279C] Although at that time a diocesan of Liège, Adelmann could have been born elsewhere. Valère André (*Bib. Belg.*, [Col. 1280C] p. 5) asserts that he was French by language and birth.] of Réginard. Fulbert (ibid.) replied with his customary politeness that he truly praised Réginard’s pastoral concern, but at the same time asked him not to regard his brother Adelmann, who was feeding at Chartres in good pastures, as a sheep outside the flock; that he ought to remain calm concerning him, since by God’s grace this sheep was feeding profitably and was diligent in avoiding the wolves’ deceitful snares; that he should cease calling a soldier a fugitive who was carefully preparing to fight both within and without the entire army of errors and [Col. 1280C] vices; and that, in any case, Adelmann would soon return to Liège. Fulbert nevertheless asked Réginard to send him back to Chartres with a formal letter of dismissal, so that it might serve as a pledge of their mutual union.

Here one sees with what zeal, sagacity, and fruitfulness Adelmann devoted himself to study. One sees the great hopes he already inspired at that time and how well he took steps to sustain them. Finally, one sees the desire that Fulbert, who was well able to recognize merit, had conceived to attach him to his Church.

[Col. 1281A] But Providence ordered otherwise. Bishop Réginard exercised his right and kept Adelmann near him. Continuing his studies according to the plan on which he had begun them, Adelmann acquired every kind of distinguished knowledge: “A man most learned in every variety of the Scriptures” (SIG. *Scrip.*, c. 153; TRIT. *Scrip.*, c. 320; *Chr. hir.*, vol. I, p. 167). He became not only a grammarian—that is, skilled in literature—but also a philosopher, above all one of the most famous dialecticians of his time, and a good theologian. The little that remains of his writings is sufficient to support this praise.

The school of Liège was then headed by the learned Wazo. Before becoming a bishop, Wazo had withdrawn to the court of Emperor Conrad, and Adelmann was chosen [Col. 1281B] to fill the office of scholasticus (MAB. *Analect.*, ibid., p. 422). This school, already famous in the time of Bishop Notger, acquired a new reputation under these two learned directors. The influx of students was great, but we do not know in detail those whom Adelmann formed in the learning and morals that were the subjects of his lessons. It is highly probable that Francon, one of his successors, and several other learned men who brought distinction to the city of Liège toward the end of this century, were among them. Lambert is expressly counted among them; he later became abbot of Saint-Laurent and left various writings of his own (TRIT. *Chr. hir.*, vol. I, p. 180). William, who later became abbot of Saint-Arnoul at Metz and of [Col. 1281C] Saint-Remi at Reims and who left several writings, also enjoyed the same advantage (MAB. ibid., p. 273; *Analect.*, l. LXIII, no. 89). When Adelmann learned that William had withdrawn into the cloister, he wrote to rebuke him—not, apparently, from any lack of esteem for his purpose, but in the hope that he would have been more useful to the Church had he remained among the clergy. His letter elicited a reply that did not inspire him to adopt the same decision, although his disciple offered him many reasons for doing so (*Analect.*, ibid.).

After teaching publicly at Liège for several years, Adelmann left his school and withdrew to Germany as though into a kind of exile. He does not tell us why; but it is reasonable to suppose that it was for the same reason that later led the scholasticus Gozechin, his successor, to take the same course (MAB. *Annal.*, vol. IV, pp. 382–390). He had already been away from Liège for some time when he learned that the errors of Berengar of Tours—one of his fellow students at the school of Chartres—concerning the mystery of the Eucharist were causing a stir in Germany as elsewhere. Adelmann was struck equally by surprise and grief, but charity caused him to suspend judgment. He immediately resolved to write to Berengar himself, in order to learn the truth with certainty. He nevertheless judged it more appropriate to involve Paulinus, primicerius of the Church of Metz, their mutual friend, who was less distant from Tours. He therefore [Col. 1282A] asked him to write to Berengar and afterward inform him of the facts. Adelmann waited in vain for two full years for Paulinus’s reply. At the end of that period, having found a favorable opportunity, he wrote to Berengar himself the excellent letter that will be discussed: a tender and illuminating letter, as courteous as it was powerful in argument, and consequently capable of making a salutary impression upon a less hardened heart and a less prejudiced mind. But it had no other effect than to display, on the one hand, Adelmann’s Christian tenderness, ardent zeal, and profound learning, and, on the other, to reveal Berengar’s ingratitude, insensibility, evil disposition, and obstinacy in his errors.

From Germany our scholasticus proceeded to Lombardy, [Col. 1282B] either to seek another place of retreat or because some authority summoned him there. Since the Church of Brescia was then vacant, he was elected bishop (UGH. vol. IV, pp. 738–739). According to the common opinion, this occurred in 1048. But if proper attention is paid to the details just set out from Adelmann himself, it will be agreed that his episcopate began no earlier than 1050. Let us recall these details in two words. At least two years had passed since Adelmann had heard the rumors circulating everywhere about Berengar’s errors when he wrote to him. The terms he uses in his letter, calling him his holy brother, show indeed that it preceded the councils of Rome and Vercelli, at which Berengar’s errors were condemned; this is confirmed by Adelmann’s silence concerning these public events. On the other hand, the two years that had elapsed since these same errors began to make a stir in the world do not permit the letter to be dated earlier than the end of 1049 or the beginning of the following year; and it must not be forgotten that it was written from Germany. It is therefore certain that its author could not have occupied the see of Brescia as bishop earlier than 1050.

Those who were best placed to inform us about the events of his episcopate tell us nothing about them (UGH. ibid.). But one may reasonably presume that a bishop who had received the education described above, who had distinguished himself in the office of scholasticus, and who had given such brilliant proofs of his zeal and charity for the salvation of a friend, governed the diocese entrusted to him fruitfully. It is known in particular that Pope Nicholas II ordered him, in accordance with the decrees of the councils, to depose priests and deacons living in concubinage. From this and from what has been said above, it is easy to judge how much weight should be given to the authority of Rubeus, who places Adelmann’s death as early as 1046. It is marked in the catalogs of his Church under the year 1057. But that too is an error; it cannot be placed earlier than 1062 or the following year. Ughelli had proof of this in the handwritten acts of the pontificate of Nicholas II, which establish that our learned bishop lived beyond 1061. He was buried in the church of Saints Faustinus and Jovita, from which his body was transferred in 1612, together with those of three of his predecessors, to a more honorable place, as the following inscription attests:

> Until they put on immortality,
>
> The remains of Apsidius, Peter Rampertus, and Adelmann,
>
> Bishops of Brescia,
>
> The grateful Cassinese congregation
>
> Deposited here.
>
> 1612

Sigebert and nearly all the bibliographers who followed him have not forgotten Adelmann in their catalogs of authors. He rightly deserves [Col. 1283B] to have a place there, although what remains of his writings today amounts to little if one considers the size of the volume, though not if one pays attention to their contents.

**1.** The letter to Berengar is, in every respect, one of the finest pieces of literature of that period. We have already stated the occasion and time at which it was written. All that remains is to give an accurate account of it. Yet anything that could be said about it would still fall short of what it actually is. One would have to read it oneself to know its full worth. It may be said without exaggeration that charity conceived it, theology, in concert with philosophy, elaborated it, and eloquence [Col. 1283C] wrote it.

One perceives in it an ingenious author who, in order to convince the mind more effectively, first tries to win the heart. To achieve this, Adelmann recalls to Berengar the tender feelings he had always held for him and adds the memory of that paternal affection with which the venerable Fulbert honored them both—an affection which, he says, far from having suffered any weakening since Fulbert left them to go to heaven, has only become more perfect and ought to make present to them the salutary instructions he gave them when, exhorting them always to follow the highway, he earnestly urged them to remain inviolably attached to the doctrine of the Fathers.

[Col. 1283D] After this introduction, Adelmann speaks to him of the distressing rumors circulating everywhere against him and tells him that he refused to believe them before learning the truth from Berengar himself. If they were well founded, he implores him, by the mercy of God and by the memory of their common teacher—which ought to be so dear to them—to hold fast to Catholic unity and not disturb the peace of the Church, for which so many thousands of martyrs had fought so triumphantly against idolatry and the powers of Satan, and which the holy doctors had defended against the attacks of heretics in writings from which rivers of salutary eloquence flowed, so that whenever another heretic arose, he was immediately pierced by a thousand arrows. “Where are now,” Adelmann continues, “the Manichaeans and the Arians?” Their memory is accursed. By contrast, the memory of Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and the others who struck them down becomes more glorious from day to day, and they are spoken of only with praise.

Here our author anticipates an objection that might have been made to him: how could it have happened that the Fathers of the Church, who were human beings, did not err and did not lead others into error, when it is certain that the greatest philosophers of paganism fell into error? Adelmann replies that, because they were humble of heart and poor in spirit, the heavenly Father revealed to them what he had hidden from the wise and prudent (Matthew 11:25); and because they had attached themselves to him who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6), they were made participants in these divine attributes.

He then proceeds to establish the Church’s common belief concerning the mystery of the Eucharist, and he does so as a skilled theologian. First he employs this very simple and at the same time decisive argument: Jesus Christ had promised to give us a bread that would be his own flesh; this he accomplished when he instituted the Eucharist. To this argument, drawn from Jesus Christ’s promise, he adds one derived from his omnipotence. He who said, “Let there be light,” and light was made—and made from nothing—says equally of the bread, “This is [Col. 1284C] my body.” For, Adelmann continues, proving the point by several authorities, it is Jesus Christ who consecrates, just as it is Jesus Christ who baptizes, whatever minister performs the act. He strengthens these arguments with an admirable thought. The intercession, he says, of Jesus Christ at the right hand of the Father on behalf of the faithful, of which Saint Paul speaks, is not made by words but by the power of the Eucharist, in which Jesus Christ offers himself and renews the mystery of his Passion.

From this our author turns to the favorite objection of sacramentarians of every period: that one sees nothing of the change supposedly made in the Eucharist, since the things appear the same as they were [Col. 1284D] before consecration. He replies that if the change made in the sacraments were visible, and if they appeared outwardly as they are in themselves, faith—which according to the Apostle is the full conviction of things not seen and which gives life to the righteous—would here have no object and would be inactive, or even reduced to nothing. This sacrament of life, he continues, speaking specifically of the Eucharist, is hidden with all its power and efficacy beneath sensible appearances, just as the soul is hidden in the body it animates. “O carnal man,” Adelmann eloquently exclaims, “who does not understand the things that belong to God!” In baptism, where a real change occurs, since the recipient becomes what he was not, do the things not appear the same as they were before? The one who is baptized does not become white from being black, nor learned from being ignorant before his regeneration.

The author next undertakes to show that the human mind, however penetrating it may be, cannot attain the sublimity of our mysteries. But what remains of his writing unfortunately ends with the argument he makes concerning what occurs in baptism and with its application to the mystery of the Eucharist. It is evident from the plan Adelmann had formed that he intended to carry his work much further; and perhaps what remains of it is only the smallest part. This is what nearly all the editors seem to have understood, since they took care to indicate at the end that several things appear to be missing. It is, after all, very surprising that the work could not be recovered in its entirety, since it still existed in that form in Trithemius’s time, who describes it as an extremely lengthy work, *valde prolixe* (TRIT. *CHR. HIR.*, vol. I, p. 167)—something that cannot be said of the portion that has come down to us. The complete scarcity of manuscripts of this same work might lead one to suspect that human malice had suppressed them. The last two centuries and our own have produced countless men who were uncomfortable with Adelmann’s doctrine. This is easy to judge from the manner in which Calvin treated him—a manner unworthy of a Christian and of any honorable man. This supposed reformer, seeing his false principles overturned by those of our author and having nothing reasonable to answer, employs against him the crudest insults, calling him ignorant, a boor, and a sophist who speaks only to deceive [Note: [Col. 1285D] “When the heresiarch Calvin felt himself held fast by the bonds of his arguments and despaired of finding a more honorable escape, he turned to insults, calling Adelmann ignorant, barbarous, and a sophist.” UGHELLI, *in episc. Brixiens.*, vol. IV, p. 540.]—the ordinary recourse of nearly all those who undertake to defend a desperate cause.

Berengar, who was precisely in the same situation, paid no attention to the affection of his friend Adelmann, who sought only to recall him from his deviations. He answered his writing with another full of presumption and arrogance, in which he obstinately persisted in defending his errors (SIG. *Script.*, c. 154). We possess, in some [Col. 1285D] fragments of this wretched reply, enough to justify the judgment passed upon it here by the historian Sigebert (MART. *Anec.*, vol. IV, pp. 109–113).

What remains of Adelmann’s writing against him was printed together with treatises by Paschasius Radbertus, Lanfranc, and others on the same subject, all in a single octavo volume published at Louvain by Martin Rotaire and Pierre Phalesius in 1551. This edition, regarded as the first, was prepared through the efforts of Jean Coster. Ten years later, in 1561, Jean Ulimmier, prior of the Canons Regular of Saint-Martin of Louvain, had our author’s writing reprinted together with the preceding works and several others. The edition is in the same format, but better produced, and was again distributed at Louvain by Jérôme Vellaus. Around the same time, Jean Garet, another canon regular, incorporated into his treatise on the real presence (GAR. *de Euch.*, pp. 67–68) nearly everything that we possess of Adelmann’s work. Du Boullay did the same in the first volume of his *History of the University of Paris* (EGAS. BUL., vol. I, pp. 411–413).

In 1575, Margarin de la Bigne once again published all that remains of it in the first volume of his *Bibliotheca Patrum*, pp. 487–492. From that collection Adelmann’s writing [Col. 1286B] passed into all the others bearing the same title (*Bib. PP.*, vol. XVIII, pp. 438–440). Finally, M. Galcardi, a canon of the cathedral of Brescia, who published under the patronage and direction of the learned Cardinal Quirini a new edition of the works of Saint Philastrius and Saint Gaudentius, added Adelmann’s little work to it (*Journal des savants*, 1739, p. 650). This collection, in a single folio volume, came from the press of Jean-Marie Aizzardi, printer at Brescia, in 1739.

**2.** Sigebert (ibid., c. 153), after giving an account of this little work by our prelate, adds that he wrote another letter on the same subject to Paul—or rather Paulinus—the primicerius of the Church of Metz, so that he might work to bring Berengar, their common friend, back from his error. Adelmann himself mentions this letter, which has not come down to us and which no one since Sigebert testifies to having seen. M. Cave (p. 523), misunderstanding the meaning of the bibliographer whom he cites, asserted that this letter was also intended to try to change Paulinus’s view of the Eucharist. People naturally like to increase the number of those who think as they do, often without troubling much over whether this is really so, as self-love would have them wish. Apparently for this reason, this English writer counted Paulinus among the sacramentarians. But apart from the fact that Sigebert’s text implies the contrary, Adelmann says nothing of the sort; he merely complains [Col. 1286D] of the primicerius’s negligence in informing him, as he had requested, of the truth concerning the rumors circulating against Berengar. The favorable impression given of the preceding work should make us regret the loss of this one.

Trithemius (*Script.*, c. 320), who does not mention these rhythms, adds generally, in speaking of their author, that Adelmann had composed several other works, both in prose and in verse, besides his letter to Berengar. But either they remain hidden in libraries or they are irretrievably lost. It seems [Col. 1287A] that they had not all been lost even in Trithemius’s time, who suggests (*Chr. Hir.*, vol. I, p. 180) that he had read one of these writings in which Adelmann gave great praise to Lambert, one of his disciples, a monk of Saint-Laurent of Liège, who later became its abbot. It is true that a Lambert is mentioned in the alphabetic rhythms, but he was a teacher who had taught in Paris and who was no longer alive when Adelmann praised him, whereas Lambert of Saint-Laurent outlived Adelmann. Thus the writing designated by Trithemius is different from the rhythms.

**3.** Adelmann also composed alphabetical rhythms (MAB. *Analect.*, p. 382), that is, cadenced and rhymed prose, in which each stanza of three verses begins with a letter of the alphabet, from A through Z inclusive. He composed them while serving as scholasticus at Liège, as is apparent from the conclusion. [Col. 1287B] He had two principal aims in them: first, he gives a highly favorable portrait of his master, the venerable Fulbert, vividly extolling his doctrine and manner of teaching; second, he provides posterity with an account of the greatest men of letters who had been trained in his day at the schools of Chartres and Liège. Although the piece bears the defects of its age, it is nevertheless ingenious and has other beauties as well. It is difficult to understand how the author could have said so much in so few words.

Having unearthed it in a manuscript from Gembloux, Dom Mabillon was the first to publish it. He accompanied it with several remarks of his own that clarify various passages. But the Sigon [Col. 1287C] mentioned in it is not the celebrated abbot of Saint-Florent at Saumur of that name, as the learned editor maintains. He is another Sigon, who attended to the funeral of Bishop Saint Fulbert and was successively scholasticus and cantor of the Church of Chartres, quite distinct from Abbot Sigon.

Some forty years later, Dom Martène and Dom Durand came upon the same Gembloux manuscript, in which these rhythms are mixed, without order, with various fragments concerning the council held at Rome in 1078 under Gregory VII—fragments drawn for the most part from [Col. 1288A] Berengar’s writings—and published them anew together with those fragments (MART. ibid., pp. 113–114). In this edition, in accordance with the manuscript, there appears at the head of the rhythms a brief notice from the author to Berengar. Adelmann tells him that this piece, which he had composed some years earlier, while he was still at Liège, on the death of several of his friends, most of them known to Berengar, had come into his hands, and that he had thought he ought to send it to him. It is evident from this that Adelmann had enclosed it with his fine letter to Berengar himself; and the place occupied by these rhythms in the second edition in question shows that Berengar had mixed them among his papers. This is further apparent from the impertinent reply he made to them, [Col. 1288B] which reveals at once his bad taste and his bizarre temper. This reply is printed at the foot of the rhythms in these words: *Berengar replied: “A ridiculous mouse is born.”*

Finally, Abbé Galeardi republished these same rhythms (*Journal des savants*, ibid., p. 657) after the little work by the same author already discussed. This last edition was made from that of Dom Mabillon, and his notes were not separated from it.

**4.** Trithemius, who says nothing of these rhythms, adds generally to what he says of their author that Adelmann composed several other writings, both in prose and verse, besides his letter to Berengar. But they are either still hidden in libraries or irretrievably lost. It seems [Col. 1288C] that not all of them had yet been lost in Trithemius’s own time, for he implies (*Chr. Hir.*, vol. I, p. 180) that he had read one of these writings, in which Adelmann bestowed great praise on Lambert, one of his disciples, a monk of Saint-Laurent at Liège, who afterward became its abbot. A Lambert is indeed mentioned in the alphabetical rhythms, but this one was a teacher who had taught at Paris and was no longer alive when Adelmann praised him, whereas Lambert of Saint-Laurent outlived Adelmann. Thus the writing identified by Trithemius is different from the rhythms.

[Col. 1289]

**ADELMANN, ONCE SCHOLASTICUS OF LIÈGE AND BISHOP OF BRESCIA, LETTER TO BERENGAR ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE EUCHARIST.**

(*Bibliotheca Patrum*, XVIII, 438.)

[Col. 1289A] To his beloved brother in Christ, the scholasticus **BERENGAR**, Adelmann sends greetings in the Lord.

I called you my foster-brother because of that most delightful companionship which I enjoyed with you when you were a youth and I myself somewhat older, at the school of Chartres, under that venerable Socrates of ours [Note: [Col. 1289C] It appears that he is speaking of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, from what follows shortly afterward: “By the most sweet memory of Fulbert,” he says, “may you love Catholic peace,” etc.], whose fellowship we may rightly boast of more than Plato boasted, giving thanks to nature that in the days of his Socrates she had caused him to be born a human being rather than a beast. For we experienced the holier life and the more salutary teaching of a Catholic and most Christian man, and now we ought to hope that we are aided by his prayers before God. For we must not suppose that he has lost the memory in which he almost always carried us as though in a mother’s womb, or that the charity of Christ, by which he embraced us as sons, has been extinguished in him. Rather, without doubt, remembering us and loving us more fully than when he journeyed as a pilgrim in this body of death, he invites us to himself through vows and silent prayers. He appeals to those secret conversations we so often had with him in the evening in the little garden beside the chapel of that city which, by God’s will, our senator now possesses; and he implores us, through the tears that sometimes burst forth in the midst of his speech and flowed out under the force of his overflowing holy ardor, to hasten there with every effort, walking directly along the royal road and clinging with the utmost care to the footsteps of the holy Fathers, so that we may leap into no byway at all and onto no new and deceptive path, lest we fall into snares and stumbling blocks; [Col. 1289C] for as the Psalmist says: “Beside the path they placed a stumbling block for me” (Psalm 139). For what is beside the path is outside the path. But what does he say about the way? “Great peace have those who love your law, and there is no stumbling block for them” (Psalm 118). And what is the law of the Lord except the way of the Lord? As it is sung in another psalm: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (ibid.). Therefore, in the way there is peace; outside the way, a stumbling block. Those incur this stumbling block who, straying through heresies and schisms, sever Catholic peace by impious disputes. [Col. 1290A] We nevertheless observe them marked out in this way in Psalm 13: “Destruction and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known.” Behold the stumbling block—or rather, the stumbling blocks: destruction and eternal misery—which confront those paths of heretics who refuse to know the way of Catholic peace. May the Lord turn such paths away from you, holy brother, and direct your feet toward his testimonies; and may he show to be liars those who strive to stain your reputation with so foul a blemish, spreading it everywhere so that they have filled not only Latin ears but also Teutonic ears, among which I have long been a sojourner, with the claim that you have separated yourself from the unity of holy Mother Church and appear to hold a different view from that of the Catholic faith concerning the body and blood of the Lord, which is offered daily upon the holy altar throughout the whole earth. That is, to use their own words about you, that it is not the true body of Christ and not the true blood, but some figure and likeness!

Having heard this two years ago, I resolved to approach your Fraternity by letter and determined that the matter should be ascertained more certainly from yourself. Knowing, moreover, that your familiar associate, Lord Paulinus, the primicerius of Metz, was closer to you and somewhat nearer to you than I, I entrusted him with carrying out this business, both at my request and on the strength of his own promise. But he—indeed, I cannot praise him in this matter—whether neglecting one or both of us, has left me in suspense up to the present.

But divine grace, which never neglects us, unexpectedly offered me something better than I had hoped. I had hoped to find a man practiced in travel and not unfamiliar with the region and language of the Franks; and behold, this brother G. stood at my side, greeting me in your name. I was astonished with joy, and yet I could not place complete confidence in so sudden an event, because the brother brought no written sign from you—as is customary among friends so far separated and so long unseen. This, however, he readily excused on many quite persuasive grounds.

Whether, then, he was acting truthfully or otherwise, I did not doubt that he had been prepared for me by the Lord. I therefore did not wish to conceal any longer that I myself, in mind and spirit—my spirit clothed with the present letter as with wings—should fly across so many expanses of land, beseeching you, by the mercy of God and by the sweetest memory of Fulbert, to love the catholic peace and not disturb the commonwealth of the Christian city, well ordered by our forebears. For that peace many thousands of martyrs, fighting bravely against idolatry and the kingdom of the devil, triumphed; and afterward the holy teachers extinguished the civil wars stirred up by heretics with the rivers of their saving eloquence. Thus they fortified it on every side, so that now no new enemy can arise who, attempting anything against it, will not immediately be overwhelmed by a thousand darts raining down from above.

Therefore “all were confounded and failed.” For where are the Manichaeans? Where are the Arians? Where has that whole faction of most depraved citizens vanished? Their memory, too, has rotted away. But Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and many other suppressors of such beasts live on with praise and grow daily more splendidly.

It is good, brother, for us little ones to hide beneath the titles of these leaders, whose authority among ecclesiastical hearers is so strong and so credible, preeminent in the splendor of holy virtues and the heavenly light of wisdom, that it would now be the height of madness to oppose them in anything concerning either the reason of faith or the order of right living.

Why? Were they not human beings, capable of being deceived by others and of deceiving others themselves? For truthful Scripture says: “Every man is a liar” (Psalm XI). How, then, did they reach such a summit that whatever they thought and committed to memory concerning the divine mysteries must now be regarded as established?

Indeed, certain great and noble pagan philosophers are found to have held many false opinions, which we rightly despise—not only concerning God the Creator, but also concerning this world and the things in it. For what could be affirmed more absurdly than that the heavens and all the stars stand still, while the earth is carried around at the center in rapid rotation; and that those who think the heavenly bodies move are deceived, just as sailors are deceived, to whom towers and trees seem to recede together with the shores? Who could tolerate hearing, besides, that the sun is not hot or that snow is black?

There are among them many other equally monstrous things, which it would be tedious and frivolous to pursue. Concerning them our Teacher says: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Romans I). The Lord did not choose these men, who, puffed up by the spirit of pride, “vanished in their thoughts.”

But our Fathers, humble in heart and poor in spirit, for whom the Savior glorifies the Father in these words—“I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew XI)—are truthful because they shared in and adhered to him who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

From him also they learned inwardly what they taught outwardly concerning this sacrament of which we are speaking. For they heard him proclaiming about himself in the Gospel:

“I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever; and the bread that I shall give is my flesh, for the life of the world” (John VI).

He says, “I shall give”; he does not say, “I have given.” When, then, did he begin to give it? When, on the day before he suffered, he took bread and, raising his eyes to heaven, gave thanks, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body.” Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: “Take and drink from it, all of you. This is the cup of my blood, which will be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins” (Matthew XXVI.

Who does not believe that this is so, unless he either does not believe Christ or does not believe that Christ himself said it? But the unbelieving have nothing to do with us.

That Christ said it is proved not merely by two or three witnesses, “on whose testimony every word stands,” but by four most approved and most trustworthy witnesses: two, namely, from the circumcision, and two from the uncircumcision, so that each people might employ its own legitimate authorities, whether for salvation or for judgment.

He certainly spoke—he who spoke and they came to be. For he who in the beginning said, “Let there be light,” and light came to be from nothing (Genesis I), could he not, by saying of the bread, “This is my body,” bring it about that it became so? And he who by silent power changed water into wine—if anything more efficacious ought indeed to be said of God—could he not, with the same power sounding forth vocally, transfer the wine itself into his blood?

If someone should say to himself that this could be done by that one man who was also God, but was impossible for others who are not such, we agree with him, provided that we confess that Christ himself works through human ministry. For while he was still mortal and among human beings, he had said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). And when he had become immortal and was about to ascend bodily into heaven, he said: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII).

Because he was constituted from two different natures—one circumscribed, the other uncircumscribed—through the circumscribed nature he moved from place to place; through the uncircumscribed nature, however, by which he is wholly everywhere without being confined to any place, he remained with them. Yet he did not separate the Son of God from the Son of Man.

Indeed, even before the Son of Man actually ascended into heaven, he was there with the Son of God, as he himself attests when he says: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III). If, then, he was there through the unity of person, although he had not yet ascended there according to the distinct property of his nature, then, because of that same unity, when he ascended into heaven he remained with human beings on earth.

For who else was saying, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX). Nor should it be thought that an angel appeared to him in place of Christ, since Saul himself, later made Paul, says: “Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me” (I Corinthians XV). And elsewhere: “Have I not seen the Lord Jesus Christ?” (I Corinthians IX).

Either Saul, still an unbeliever, was carried up into heaven so that Christ might speak to him there; or Christ himself descended from heaven—which ought to happen only once, at the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, “when all who are in the tombs, hearing the voice of the Son of God” (John V), will come forth.

He himself, therefore, always remaining with human beings, both baptizes human beings through human beings and consecrates whatever is consecrated through human beings. For in the Gospel we have both statements: that Jesus baptized, and that he himself did not baptize, but his disciples did.

He baptizes, certainly, because when the body is immersed in water with certain solemn words, he gives life to the dead soul by remitting sins, just as he says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (ibid.). This can be understood only of the resurrection of souls.

A human being also baptizes, through whose hands and tongue that work is administered; but he baptizes most fully and principally who supplies all its power and efficacy. Hence it was said to John the Baptist: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes” (John I).

Otherwise there would not be one baptism; rather, according to the merit of the baptizer, one baptism would be more worthy and another less worthy, and the one baptized by a holier person would be better baptized. But far be this from us! Whoever baptizes in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—whether worthy or unworthy, holy or sinful, catholic or heretical—it makes no difference; for their ministry alone is involved, and it is not by them but through them, if we wish to speak correctly, that one is baptized.

Christ, therefore, baptizes through the hand and mouth of the priest; Christ, through the hand and mouth of the priest, creates his body and blood.

[Note: [Col. 1293] Understand “creates” properly, that is, “makes,” for transubstantiation has something resembling creation. See St. Thomas, III, part, question 85, article 8.]

“Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (I Corinthians XIII.) The Apostle said this not by arrogantly exalting himself, but by teaching truthfully: Christ speaks in his ministers what they are heard to speak, and works what they are seen to do. For this reason Christ is a priest forever, because it is he who baptizes and who offers sacrifice.

For what he once did passibly through himself, he performs daily impassibly through those to whom he gave power to become children of God. Nor, I think, can what the Apostle says of him—“who is at the right hand of the Father and who also intercedes for us” (Romans VIII)—be better understood than as meaning that this intercession takes place not by uttering words, but by commending his obedience and humanity to God the Father through remembrance of his Passion.

He also left this most certain pledge of himself to his beloved disciples in the institution of the same sacrament, when he was already struggling at the point of his Passion and, with foreknowing spirit, was soon to tremble at the pains of the flesh to come. “Do this,” he said, “in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII)—in remembrance, I say, of my love toward you, for whom I lay down my life, and of my obedience before the Father, because “just as the Father gave me a commandment, so I do” (John XIV).

If anyone is troubled by why this sacrament is not visibly changed into the appearance of flesh and blood, let him consider what the Apostle says: “We walk by faith, and not by sight. Now faith is”—he himself defined it—“the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews XI). For if the sacraments displayed outwardly what they are inwardly, faith, by which “the just person lives,” would not merely be idle but would not exist at all. “For who hopes for what he sees?” (Hebrews X.)

Therefore, so that faith may be exercised by believing what does not appear, the life-giving sacrament lies hidden bravely beneath bodily appearance, just as the soul lies hidden in the body.

Finally, the water of baptism is seen by the eyes of those who look upon it, whatever its kind, and the baptized person appears to be nothing other than what he was before. Through the bath of regeneration he does not become white from black, or a grammarian from an unlettered person.

“O sensual person,” who does not perceive the things that are of God! O flesh drunk more by carnal fantasies than by wine, how long will you be so unhappily deceived by these things? For this error is not like the denial of the salvation of souls, nor like the illusions of dreams, nor like the images reflected from water and mirrors; in those cases one is deceived without danger, whereas here one errs with irrecoverable loss unless one comes to one’s senses.

Awake, therefore, and cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans VII.) And apostolic consolation will answer you: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid.).

And although we believe it true that a human being is freed not only from the distress of spiritual struggle—which he calls “death” in this passage—but not even from the misery of errors, except by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, we shall nevertheless understand it better if we carefully examine the composition and power of human nature, which consists entirely, to be sure, in bodily sensation and the understanding of the mind, and briefly indicate what is accomplished through both together and what through either separately.

There are many things that we do through bodily sensation alone, such as hearing and seeing; many that sensation commonly administers together with the understanding, such as reading and writing; but very many to which sensation has absolutely no access, such as the rational principles of numbers, the proportions of sounds, and altogether the notions of incorporeal things. All these any intellect can perceive, provided that it is pure and also refined through use.

Nor am I unaware of that first faculty which precedes these two powers, but it seems irrelevant to our present purpose, and care must be taken not to make a longer digression than necessary.

For, with divine grace assisting us, we are attempting to show that no human faculty—which itself is plainly also a divine gift—is nevertheless sufficient, however far it may extend, to comprehend the height of the sacraments by which we are initiated and perfected for the eternal salvation that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Let us therefore set baptism itself before us and see what sensation and what reason apprehend there.

When asked, touch declares that there is some liquid; sight, if it happens to be in a vessel, is uncertain what sort of liquid it is; but taste, called in as a third witness, unhesitatingly discovers that it is water. Beyond this, if I am not mistaken, sensation does not promise to perform its office in the matter.

Reason, however, penetrates far and wide into the interior and clearly perceives its insensible nature: that it is mobile and dull, substantially moist, naturally cold, and capable of being converted into air or earth—and whatever else, known or unknown to us, can be investigated concerning the nature of waters.

But how the soul is regenerated through water and the Spirit, and remission of sins is granted—just as bodily sensation was taught a little earlier that it cannot rise to the excellence of reason, so surely reason is perhaps even less able to aspire to this inscrutable mystery. Nevertheless, we firmly hold and confess most truly that an incorporeal soul is reborn through corporeal water and restored to the condition in which Adam was before he transgressed.

[Note: [Col. 1295C] This applies only to the essence of justifying grace, not to the other excellent qualities of its blessed condition. [Col. 1296C]]

We also know God himself, whose enigma surpasses every intellect, not merely to exist—as unbelievers admit—but to be one and the same, uncircumscribed in three persons, wholly everywhere without being confined to any place. Yet we do not possess this knowledge through sensation or reason as something comprehended.

It appears that much is missing.

[Col. 1295]

## ADELMANNUS, FROM A SCHOLASTIC OF LIÈGE, BISHOP OF BRESCIA: ALPHABETICAL RHYTHMS ON THE ILLUSTRIOUS MEN OF HIS TIME

(Apud Mabillon, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 382.)

[Col. 1295B]

With the grace of the harmonic art inspiring me,

I recount illustrious men, lights of letters,

Whom a mind wounded by recent grief remembers.

Death, raging with savage ferocity,

Fierce against scholars like a roaring lion,

Everywhere inflicted slaughter more dreadful than pestilential air.

Memorable bishop, glory of the city of Chartres,

Father Fulbert, when I first try to speak of you,

Speech flees, my heart melts, and my tears break open anew.

Many things worthy of lament I remember individually,

Since I often clung as a fellow-guest to the old man’s side,

Drinking with my ear from the golden fountain of his honey-sweet mouth.

Alas! With what dignity of moral discipline,

With what gravity of subject and sweetness of words,

He unfolded the secrets of deeper knowledge!

[Col. 1295C]

Under your fostering care the studies of Gaul flourished;

You cultivated divine and human teachings,

Never allowing virtue to be darkened by sloth.

As a deep whirlpool divides into smaller channels,

And as a great fire sends forth many rays from itself,

So you propagated many eminent men through diverse places.

Hildierus, whom we were accustomed to call “the Little One,”

Because he was small in body, but in truth of penetrating mind,

First among the others and fellow-worker with the bishop.

He reproduced his teacher in face, voice, and manners,

Joining the art of Hippocrates with the discourses of Socrates,

[Col. 1296B]

And he was no less devoted to the Pythagorean lyre.

Our Sigo, full of charity and grace,

Offering much comfort by mouth and hand to visitors,

Reigned as a singular master of instrumental music.

Lambert occupied Paris, Engelbert Orléans,

In the leisure of paid lessons,

Seeking no small profit from the youth of the Franks.

I deem Rainaldus of Tours, a fellow citizen of Martin’s city,

Though not equally sober, also worthy of remembrance:

Ready with his tongue, generous with his pen, and a capable grammarian.

Nor shall I deprive you, Girard-Gilbert, of your dirge.

Returning to the yellow Loire from the Jordan and Jerusalem,

You were slain beside the Meuse beneath the walls of Verdun.

[Col. 1296C]

Oh, and you too were destroyed by the dreadful faction of your rivals,

After you had been sent through Europe with burning zeal,

Ransacking many schools, Walter of Burgundy.

Alas! If only you had never returned to the borders of the Allobroges,

With what authority you would now adorn Latium,

Teaching whatever you had brought back from the gardens of the Hesperides.

Who, sacred hero, would ever have mourned you enough?

[Note: [Col. 1296C] Fulbert.]

Whose workshop produced these men and many others,

Each of whom displayed before him what he had gained from your instruction.

Raginbaldus of Cologne, a man powerful in intellect,

Tempering barbarian ears with Latin eloquence,

Known from the ocean all the way to the Roman citadels.

He is buried in our city, Liège, a long-time guest,

Liège, once the nurse of great arts,

Under Watto and under the very man whose are these rhythms.

Muse, recount for me three citizens from among the many:

That man who died far away from us of fevers beyond the Alps—

The arts mourn him, the cities mourn him with their leading men.

I would scarcely have lamented his loss, had Odulphus survived,

The man of Alestum, as great as he was in ancient knowledge

[the reading *uter is* is uncertain],

As are those whom he instructed, who flourish strongly today.

Warine, you had been denied by a harsh bishop

Xerampeline ornaments with a few acres;

But, having fled to Metz,

You acquired many possessions there and were buried,

In subterranean chambers and in the bosom of your ancient parent.

May those who sleep there, to be awakened on the final morning of the world,

Enjoy eternal peace with you, Christ, in your favor.

With great zeal his heart inflamed for the funeral of his dear ones,

Adelmannus lamented these things on the shore at Nemetum,

Himself also keeping watch over his own there each day.

## NOTE

[Col. 1297]

At my request the religious man Michael Delmerius, librarian of the same monastery, transcribed these rhythms from a manuscript codex of Gembloux; he also generously devoted his services to me in many other matters.

No learned person is unaware who Adelmannus, the author of these verses, was. He is that very man who was Berengar’s fellow student under Fulbert, bishop of Chartres: a grammarian and, from a cleric of Liège, bishop of Brescia, as Sigebert testifies in chapter 153 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. There he is called ALMANNUS and is said to have written two letters *On the Truth of the Body of the Lord in the Eucharist*, one to Berengar and the other to Paulinus, primicerius of Metz.

In the Gembloux copy, these words precede the rhythms:

“I also send you some rhythmic verses arranged according to the order of the alphabet. A few years ago, while I was still at Liège, I found them composed as I mournfully reviewed certain friends of mine, several of whom you yourself knew; I have recently edited and published them.”

These words are Adelmannus’s, sending these verses to Berengar, concerning whom the following is read at the end of the rhythms:

“BERENGARUS REPLIED: The ridiculous mouse is born.”

Berengar was accustomed to call Adelmannus ironically *Aulus-Mannus*, as is added in the same place. Many things in these verses would deserve comment, but I shall note only what presents itself to me.

Under the letter K, Sigo is praised, namely the abbot of the monastery of Saint Florentius at Saumur on the Loire, a man most distinguished in his time. His contemporary was Rainaldus, archclaviger or custodian of the church of Saint Martin of Tours, who is mentioned here under the letter M.

The stanza beginning with the letter N appears corrupt in its first verse:

“Nor shall I deprive you, Girard-Gilbert, of your dirge.”

It seems that one should read:

“Nor shall I deprive you, Girard the Bald, of your dirge.”

Under the letter S, Watto is discussed. Liège, the nurse of great arts, is said to have flourished under him and under the very man whose are these rhythms. From this we learn that Adelmannus was the scholasticus, or director of the schools, in the city of Liège—namely, after Watto, who is called Wazo by Anselm, a canon of Liège. His words in book 84 of *On the Bishops of Liège* are:

“He”—namely Wazo—“first served as chaplain under Bishop Notger; afterward he was appointed by the same man as master of the schools.”

The Liège Chronicle, in Labbe’s *Bibliotheca nova*, volume I, says:

“In the year 1041 Hithardus died, and Walto succeeded him; his death is assigned to the year 1048.”

Here one sees that Watto is no different from Wazo, as he is read in Anselm, who writes Nithardus instead of Hithardus. Therefore, as I stated above, Adelmannus was director of the schools of Liège—something that, unless I am mistaken, no one has hitherto observed.

Under the letter X, Warine is discussed. He appears to have been a cleric of Liège, then a monk in the monastery of Gorze, and finally abbot in the Metz monastery of Saint Arnulf, as is evident from Warine’s own letter.

The harsh bishop who is here said to have denied Warine xerampeline ornaments with a few acres was Durandus, bishop of Liège; his name is written between the lines in the manuscript codex. Therefore this Warine had asked Durandus, bishop of Liège, to give him a few acres together with some dignity in the church of Liège, or some other office whose insignia was a xerampeline garment.

When the harsh bishop had denied these things to Warine, Warine, angered, secretly fled to the city of Metz, where he acquired many possessions together with the abbacy of Saint Arnulf.

The Gembloux codex interprets *xerampeline ornaments* as follows:

“Xerampeline garments are called old and thoroughly dried garments, having the color of vine leaves; and the term is used here for any old garments.”

This interpretation teaches us that here one should read *xerampeline ornaments*. The word is Greek and composed of two elements: ξηρός (*xēros*), meaning “dry,” and ἄμπελος (*ampelos*), meaning “vine.” Thus *xerampeline ornaments* are called garments of the dry vine-leaf, imitating the color called the color of the dried rose, as learned men have observed in their notes on Juvenal.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1061: POPE NICHOLAS II

[Col. 1299]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Ciaconius, *On the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 312.)

[Col. 1299A]

While the antipope Benedict occupied the Roman see, Hildebrand, returning from Germany and approaching Siena in Tuscany—since the pontifical election could not safely be held at Rome, ecclesiastical liberty having been oppressed by Benedict’s satellites—summoned by letter to himself all the cardinals and Roman nobles who shared his position.

With their votes, Gerard the Burgundian, surnamed the Allobrogian, bishop of Florence, was proclaimed supreme pontiff in the year of the Lord 1058, on account of his virtue and excellence of character, after the adulterous Benedict had been rejected; he took the name Nicholas II.

After the election, he set out toward Rome with Hildebrand, the cardinals, clergy, and Roman nobles, together with an armed force, but halted at Sutri. There, with the bishops of Tuscany, Lombardy, and Campania assembled, and with the princes of the imperial court and other leading nobles of Italy present, he held a synod.

In it the apostate Benedict was deposed and banished permanently to Velletri; Nicholas himself was again confirmed in the apostolic see. He later proceeded to Rome with the forces of Duke Gothefrid toward the end of December [Col. 1299B], expelled Benedict and his entire faction from the pontificate and the city, and was received with the greatest honor by the Romans, clergy, and people at the basilica of Saint Peter and by the cardinal bishops on Sunday, the third day before the Nones of January, at the beginning of the year of the Lord 1059.

Under the emperor Henry IV Augustus, he held the apostolic see for two years, six months, and one day. He branded Benedict and his supporters with anathema. Not long afterward, on the ninth day before the Kalends of February, through the intervention of certain cardinals, he absolved Benedict when he approached him stripped of his pontifical vestments and humbly seeking pardon for his past actions. He ordered him to remain deprived of the priesthood at the church of Saint Mary Major, where, shortly afterward, on the fifth day before the Ides of April, exhausted by grief of mind, he died and was buried.

Meanwhile, Duke Gothefrid, by whose arms Nicholas had brought the city under his authority after Benedict’s expulsion, departed for Tuscany. When the Roman nobles, in whose power the city lay, harassed him because of Benedict’s defection, he went into Picenum and remained at Auximum with Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, until affairs at Rome had been settled by Hildebrand.

When the pontiff returned to that city for the Easter festivities, he made Hildebrand archdeacon of the Roman see in place of Mantius, as a reward for the successful management of the affair. At his urging, after Easter he summoned a general council at the Lateran. Among other matters, he enacted a law that is found in Gratian under Distinction XXII, most salutary for the Roman Church. Its substance is as follows:

“If anyone is placed in the see of Peter through money, human favor, or the tumult of the people or the army, without the harmonious and canonical election of the cardinals and clergy, let him be called not apostolic but apostatic. Let the cardinals, clergy, and religious be permitted to anathematize him as a robber, expel him from the apostolic see by any human assistance, and, wherever it cannot be done in the city, assemble Catholics for this purpose.”

So Gratian. He decreed this in order to forestall schisms that might arise in the future, taking the occasion from the rebellion of Benedict.

At the same synod, Berengar of Tours, dean of Saint Maurice of Angers and arch-heretic, was condemned a second time and recalled from his error. His recantation, which appears in the *Decrees*, Distinction II, *On Consecration*, and begins “I, Berengar,” was issued by Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida.

In it Berengar publicly confessed that in the sacrament of the Eucharist the true body and blood of Christ are present, not merely as a sign or figure, as he had previously taught.
