Against this error, at the insistence and urging of Pope Nicholas, Alberic, a monk of Monte Cassino and, formerly abbot of Condon, archbishop of Canterbury, cardinal deacon, a most learned man in speech and writing, and Lanfranc, the most learned man of his age, disputed, the latter having published an elegant book.

Afterward a great host of learned men refuted this pestilential heresy. The principal among them were Adelmannus the grammarian, formerly a cleric of Liège and later bishop of Brescia, once a student of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, and a fellow student of that arch-heretic; Guitmundus, formerly a monk of the monastery of the Cross of Saint Leufredus and bishop of Aversa; Hildebertus, first bishop of Le Mans and afterward archbishop of Tours; and Algerus the German, formerly a scholasticus and later a monk of Corbie in Saxony.

In our own age the unfortunate Zwingli revived this doctrine, and now suffers the deserved penalties of his crime.

Nicholas II, weary of the war that the Normans were constantly waging against the Church and harassed by the Roman nobles, then first decided to make peace with the Normans under specified conditions and with mutual assistance. He attempted this voluntarily through legates, so that, aided by their resources and protection, he might restrain the Roman nobles who opposed him and recover the towns of the Church that they had occupied.

Robert Guiscard, who at that time held both Sicilies, having learned the pontiff’s wishes, eagerly embraced the conditions of peace. He wished thereby to stabilize his rule through alliances with princes and legitimate titles and to extinguish the enduring hatred that the Roman pontiffs had until then held against his people.

The pontiff summoned him to Apulia, and the conditions were these: that the Normans should be released from the anathema; that their prince, Robert Guiscard, should acknowledge and accept, by beneficiary right, everything he possessed in Italy from the Roman Church, paying an annual rent of twelve denarii for each yoke of oxen; that the Roman pontiff should protect the entire people and its rights; and that, in turn, the Norman princes should swear to preserve faith with the Roman pontiffs and defend their territory.

They were to receive from the pontiffs, through acceptance of the banner, the principality, their insignia, titles, and rights; and they were to restore what they had taken from the Roman see, especially Troy and Benevento.

When these matters had been completed, the pontiff received Robert Guiscard and the Normans into the grace and communion of the apostolic see. He made Robert, now a tributary of the Church, duke of Campania, Calabria [Col. 1301A] and Apulia, and count of Sicily.

These things were done in the year of Christ 1060, at the place where Aquila is now built, between Amiternum and Forcone, and were confirmed in the council assembled at Melfi.

After these agreements had been made, the pontiff, in order to recover the ecclesiastical territory, returned to Rome with a large part of Robert’s army, according to the terms of the treaty. He received the Praenestines, Tusculans, Tiburtines, and Nomentans, rebels against the Roman Church, into submission. Crossing the Tiber, he plundered Galeria and the other towns of Count Gerard.

He captured all the castles as far as Sutri and made the ecclesiastical territory completely secure.

He sent Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, as legate to Milan, which was suffering from civil wars. After quelling the sedition, Peter returned to Rome for the synod that the pontiff had called as his fourth.

Many bishops from throughout Italy attended it. Several decrees were issued there against simoniacs and incontinent priests.

Shortly afterward Nicholas, a man most approved in every aspect of life, went to Florence. There, on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the year of the Lord 1061, having rendered the greatest service to the Roman Church, he peacefully died and was buried in the cathedral church.

The see then remained vacant for two months and twenty-six days because of the schism that followed.

[Col. 1301]

# LETTERS AND DIPLOMAS OF POPE NICHOLAS II

## I. Pope Nicholas II confirms the possessions and property of the monastery of Saint Peter of Perugia. (Year 1059.)

[Margarini, *Bullarium Casinense* II, 92, from the archive of the monastery of Saint Peter of Perugia, in the privilege chest, no. 10.]

[Col. 1301B]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable monastery of Blessed Peter the Apostle, situated outside—or rather beside—the city of Perugia, in the place called Caprarius, and through it to Bonizo, its abbot, and to his successors who are to be duly and regularly promoted there in perpetuity.

Since the universal holy mother Church has been especially united, founded [Col. 1302B], and enlarged through the glorious princes of the apostles—namely Peter, the fisher of men, and Paul, the teacher of the nations—more than through her other co-workers, it is fitting that everything found to belong specifically to their jurisdiction and power should be confirmed and maintained. Therefore, to increase perpetually, and never diminish, the honor of the aforesaid monastery, through this privilege of apostolic protection we grant that it may peacefully and quietly hold and possess what it has hitherto held and possessed, and now holds and possesses: namely, its cells and churches, its estates and parishes, as well as its lands and farmsteads—specifically the parish of Saint Constantius, Saint Rufinus, and Saint Martin; the church of Saint Mary in Agellione, with its appurtenances; the estate of Casale and the estate of Saint Justin; the estate of Petronianus; the church of Saint Andrew of Aliano, with its appurtenance; the church of Saint Mary in Petithianus; the church of Saint Clement; and half of the church of Saint Donatus [Col. 1303A] in Civitella; as well as the land of Hugh, nephew of Berno of Montenigro.

Moreover, we confirm in perpetuity to the same monastery three estates situated in the county of Perugia: one called Pusulo, another Filomio, and the third called Casalini, with their churches, houses, vineyards, fields, gardens, mountains, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and all their appurtenances; likewise the monastery of Saint Angelus in the county of Arisate, in the place called Tolliano and Lunisano, with its cells and chapels and all that belongs to it. Whatever the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter may henceforth acquire in any manner recognized by divine or human law, we likewise confirm by the force of this apostolic privilege.

We also grant you permission, concerning all the clerics—both those residing in the monastery and those living outside it on its possessions—to have them ordained by any suitable and canonically appointed bishop whom you choose, and to receive chrism in your parishes. But if you cannot canonically and freely obtain or secure ordinations and chrism from the bishop in whose diocese the aforesaid monastery is situated, and likewise concerning churches to be consecrated, then no bishop shall dare excommunicate or condemn anyone belonging to the same monastery if, in his case, he seeks the protection and judgment of us and of the holy apostolic see.

The Roman pontiff’s gift to the abbey, the abbot himself, and the abbot’s consecration shall remain in perpetuity. And, with every excuse removed except a canonical one, whenever he has been summoned by the supreme pontiff, he shall come to the synod.

Moreover, offerings presented to the same monastery for the living as well as for the dead shall be seized by none of the bishops, but shall in their entirety serve the needs of the monastery and the necessities of the brothers. The tithes of the same monastery shall be devoted to receiving guests and pilgrims at the monastery gate. Nor shall anyone—emperor, king, marquis, or any other person—be permitted to demand from the monastery or from its possessions the service and what is commonly called *foderum*, except our apostolic see alone.

Furthermore, no one shall in any way prohibit the burial of the dead there. The bishop, however, shall not dare celebrate public Masses or hold a station there [Col. 1303D] unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery, lest, as blessed Gregory says, any opportunity be offered for popular gatherings in the retreats of God’s servants, and lest the frequent entrance of women should generally—God forbid!—draw the simpler souls into scandal.

If, at the invitation or with the consent of the abbot, the bishop wishes to celebrate public Masses there, he shall do so only on these days: the second day of Easter and the feasts of the Nativity of the blessed Peter and Paul. But neither he nor any of his clerics shall take away any offerings from there against the will of the abbot and the brothers.

We also decree that, when the abbot of this monastery dies, neither the bishop nor any of his clerics shall involve himself in listing or inspecting the property already acquired or to be acquired by the same monastery [Col. 1304A]. The congregation as a whole shall request for the same monastery not another abbot, but one whom it has unanimously judged worthy in conduct and suitable for monastic discipline—if it has such a man from among its own members, or, if it chooses one from another congregation—and he shall be consecrated by the Roman pontiff without any venality.

We also decree that all charters contrary or harmful to the same monastery shall be wholly void and empty. Furthermore, by our apostolic authority we establish and confirm that no emperor, king, bishop, duke, marquis, count, viscount, gastald, or any other person, great or small, shall dare molest, divert, or disturb you, the aforesaid abbot, or your canonically succeeding successors, concerning the said monastery or any of its movable, immovable, or self-moving goods and properties [Col. 1304B].

Therefore, if anyone rashly attempts or presumes to act against the decree of this apostolic privilege, let him know that, by the authority of the holy and undivided Trinity, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and of us, he will be subject to the anathema of perpetual curse until, coming to his senses, he has made satisfaction. Moreover, he shall pay twelve pounds of gold: half to our sacred palace and half to the monastery itself.

But whoever willingly observes this privilege out of pious devotion, and does not defraud the aforesaid monastery of any of its rights or goods, or whoever, reverencing it, contributes something of his own for God’s sake, may obtain from the Lord God the grace of blessing [Col. 1304C] and may deserve to be led by the prince who bears the keys into the gates of the heavenly kingdom.

Written by the hand of Octavian, scrivener and notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of February and the twelfth indiction. Farewell.

Given at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1059, through the hands of Humbert, called bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the holy Roman and apostolic see, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Nicholas II, the twelfth indiction.

## II. Bull of Nicholas II, supreme pontiff, by which he confirms to the monastery of Saint Vincent at Vulturnum, and to John IV, its abbot, all its goods and rights. (Year 1059.)

[MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores* I, II, 5, 4.]

[Col. 1304D]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son John, abbot of the venerable monastery of Christ’s martyr Vincent, built above the very source of the river Vulturnus, and through him to all his successors who are regularly promoted to its governance, forever.

Although we ought to extend our solicitude and the protection of the apostolic see to all, nevertheless we should bestow more abundantly whatever piety and usefulness we can upon holy places, and especially upon those distinguished by monastic religion, so that through the pious provision made for cenobites we may, by God’s mercy, earn a full reward with them and on their behalf in the future.

Therefore, graciously assenting to your petitions, dearest son and abbot John, by this decretal document of apostolic authority, according to what our predecessors are known to have done for your predecessors, we grant and confirm to you and to your successors who shall regularly succeed you forever the aforesaid monastery of Saint Vincent the martyr, situated above the source of the Vulturnus in the territory of Benevento in the region of Samnium, with all its appurtenances and cells—namely, the monastery of Saint Peter the Apostle situated beside the river Sabbatus; also the monastery of Saint Adeodatus within Benevento; the church of Saint Stephen; and the cell of Saint Mary in the place called Sano, and so forth.

We grant you and your successors permission to invite whichever bishop you wish to consecrate altars and ordain clerics in any rank [Col. 1305B]. We also forbid any bishop to dare summon the abbot or a monk from the same monastery to his synod or excommunicate him.

We also command, while granting you this privilege, that if a cleric of any church comes to enter the religious life, you receive him according to monastic discipline [lacuna]. You shall acquire chrism and holy oil from a bishop acceptable to you, and so forth. But if anyone—which we do not desire—[lacuna].

Written by the hands of Octavian, scrivener and notary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of March and the twelfth indiction. Farewell.

Given at Spoleto on the sixth day before the Nones of March, in the year of Jesus Christ 1059, through the hands of Humbert, bishop of the holy Church of Silva [Col. 1305C] Candida, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Nicholas II, the twelfth indiction.

## III. Pope Nicholas II confirms all the goods and privileges granted by Pope Leo IX to the monastery of Cassino. (Year 1059.)

[COCQUELINES, *Bullar.*, I, 401, from the register of Peter the Deacon, no. 18, fol. 17 verso.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Desiderius, abbot of the venerable monastery of the blessed Father Benedict, called Monte Cassino, and to all his successors who shall regularly be promoted to its governance there, forever.

[Col. 1305D]

If the good of our pastoral solicitude ought to look after and benefit even outsiders and those far away, much more should it do so for those who are our own and near to us. For toward them, after the Lord, invisible charity must be directed in the second degree, so that through them, as through a kind of visible flame, it may gradually extend to all who are farther away.

Therefore, as we extend the hands of due consolation and protection to holy places venerable for their divine religion, we do not doubt that we should prefer above the others that place which is known to be the principal training-ground of the monastic rule and is adjacent to the holy Roman and apostolic see; that place which the Roman citizens—namely the distinguished fathers Benedict, Maurus, and Placid, together with certain others—founded; and which, after being destroyed by pagan peoples, the Roman pontiffs nevertheless rebuilt by their authority [Col. 1306A], and rightly preferred to other monasteries through the privileges of the apostolic see, fortifying it effectively against the suspicious attacks of all.

As we succeed those pontiffs in sacred authority, just as we succeed them in time and place, so we rely, as is proper, upon their example. Through the tenor of this decretal document, therefore, we grant to you, dearest son Desiderius, whom we have consecrated abbot, according to the privileges of our predecessors and custom, the monastery of the blessed Father Benedict situated on the mountain of the fortress of Cassino, and the entire abbey of that monastery, intact, with its cells, castles, estates, and all its appurtenances. We confirm it by our authority both within the borders of the Beneventans, Apulians, and Calabrians, and within the borders of the Marsians and the Marches, wherever, near or far, anything has hitherto rightfully belonged to it, or whatever it may henceforth rightfully acquire anywhere.

In addition, we willingly release to you and your monastery whatever duty or other payment our officials of the sacred palace exact from ships arriving at the Roman port. Whenever you come to Rome in the service of the holy Roman Church, you shall have lodging in the palace of the Lateran [text: *sancta Jerusalem palatii Susurriani*]. When the abbot there dies, an abbot shall be appointed by your election or that of your successors, to be consecrated by the Roman pontiff. The privilege shall remain with you and your successors, both concerning what Leo, our holy predecessor, confirmed to Abbot Richerius from your ship and concerning what he confirmed from the church itself after its destruction, so that it might be rebuilt [Col. 1306C].

Although you have received the use of sandals and the dalmatic from the apostolic see by right of your cardinalate, we nevertheless grant them henceforth to you and to the place, but only on the principal feasts, for the honor of so venerable a monastery and out of affection for you, according to what our aforesaid predecessor granted to you.

Moreover, we confirm to you and to your successors the higher seat among all abbots at every assembly of bishops and princes, and in councils and judgments the precedence in sentence over men of your order, out of reverence for so great a place, which has deserved to retain, living and dead, the first and supreme legislator of the monastic law, and which, by pursuing the way of cenobitic life through the writing, word, and example of that legislator, has displayed it throughout the world, bright as the sun [Col. 1306D].

When the abbot dies, the congregation itself shall choose an abbot according to the soundest counsel of the wise and elder brothers, and present him to the pontiff of the apostolic see for confirmation and consecration. No other person shall be appointed abbot there, nor shall anyone from elsewhere be introduced, unless perhaps they have no one among themselves suitable for so great a governance and therefore, after sounder deliberation, choose an outsider.

Furthermore, apart from the supreme prelate of the apostolic see, we forbid by this authority any bishop or priest of any church to presume to claim any jurisdiction for himself in the aforesaid monastery or its cells. Unless invited by the abbot, he shall not dare celebrate the solemnities of Mass there [Col. 1307A]. With every oppression by ecclesiastical or secular persons removed and driven away, the monastery shall remain, as it has hitherto remained, from this present twelfth indiction and forever, quiet and free, for the service and glory of God, under the protection and right of the holy Roman and apostolic see, with all its possessions.

Of all these things, which in summary and general terms belong to the aforesaid monastery, we have here set out only the following by name and in detail:

First, the monastery of the Lord Savior situated at the foot of the mountain itself; also the monastery of Saint Mary, Mother and Virgin of God, called Plumbarola; likewise the castle of Saint Peter at the foot of the mountain, formerly called the fortress of Cassino; and the castle of Saint Angelus; the castle called Piniatario [Col. 1307B], and Junctura; the castle of Saint George, Saint Apollinaris, Saint Ambrose, and Saint Andrew; the castle called Vallisfrigida; the castle called Bantra, and Saint Peter in Hia; Saint Victor, Toroculum, Cervaru, Saint Elias, Vallemrotundam, and Rocca de Bontra, with all their appurtenances; the castle called Sarasiniscum and the castle of Saint Stephen; the cell of Saint Mary in Albaneta; Saint Nicholas in Ciconia; Saint Benedict in Clia; Saint Angelus in Vallelucis; and the cell of Saint Michael.

In the county of Aquino: the cell of Saint Gregory, Saint Maurice, and Saint Nicholas in Pica; Saint Angelus in Cannuccio; Saint Mary in Barole; and Saint Peter in Ascleto. Likewise, in Lucca, the cell of Saint George near Posterula; Wiriwala, which the brothers Henry and Roland, seeking the habit of holy life, gave to Saint Benedict [Col. 1307C]; the cell of Saint Benedict and Saint Scholastica in Gaeta; Saint Stephen in Terracina; Saint Lucy and Saint Peter in Curuli; Saint Sylvester and Saint Lucy in Arpino; Saint Benedict on the hill of Insula; Saint Germanus in Sora; the estate of Saint Urban in Comino; the cell of Saint Paul there, and those of Saint Nazarius, Saint Valentine, and the Savior; the cell of Saint Benedict in Venafro; Saint Nazarius and Saint Mary in Sala; the smaller estate of Saint Benedict there; the castle called Capriata, that of Francilo, and that of Saint John; the estate of Saint Felix; the castle called Conca; the cell of Saint Benedict in Cesama; Saint Benedict in Teano; Saint Benedict in Suessa; and the cell of Saint Benedict in Capua, with the Gualdo of Ligure itself [Col. 1307D] and all its appurtenances; the cell of Saint John of the handmaids of God in the same city; Saint Mary in Calvi; Saint Mary in Cingoli; Saint Adjutor in Alife; Saint Cecilia in Naples; the Church of the Holy Cross in Amalfi; the cell of Saint Benedict in Salerno; the cell of Saint Sophia within the city of Benevento; the cell of Saint Benedict in Ascoli; the cell of Saint Benedict in Trani; and Saint Benedict in Bari.

The cell of Saint Mary of the handmaids of God in the city of Cosenza; the cell of Saint Benedict in Pectinaro; Saint Mary in Banse; Saint Benedict in Alarino; the cell of Saint Eustasius, which Adelpherius Pantasia offered to Saint Benedict; the cell of Saint Mary in Murone; Saint Eustasius in Petra Abundanti; Saint Mary in Batratano; Saint Mary in Casmeta beside the river Trinius; Saint Benedict in Ripa Ursa, with all its [Col. 1308A] appurtenances; also the castle called Lastinianum and three other castles—Mount Alberic, Mucela, and Saint Quiricus—with a harbor for ten ships. These two [apparently, the first two of the three castles] Count Trasemundus, son of Alton, gave to blessed Benedict on Monte Cassino by lawful donation and documentary records; the third castle, Frisam, the wife of the aforesaid Trasemundus offered to Saint Benedict for her soul, with her husband’s consent.

Saint Justa there; the cell of Saint Focatus in Alarino; Saint George in Termoli; the cell of the Savior in the Marches, with forty cells; the Savior in Tabe; Saint Scholastica in Pinne; Saint Martin in Salina; Saint Nicholas in Apruzzo; Saint Angelus in Maranno, with all the cells of the seven holy brothers; Saint Lawrence and Saint Benedict in Tronto [Col. 1308B]; Saint Apollinaris in Fermo; Saint Benedict in Tisino; Saint Mary in Arboscola; the cell of Saint Benedict in Marli and that of Saint Cosmas; the cell of Saint Angelus in Valleregia, with its castles and all its appurtenances; also the castles in the county of Ascoli, namely Octavus, and those beyond Mount Cinianus—Trivilianus and Cavino—which Roland offered to the aforesaid monastery together with his nephews; the cell of Saint James in the Tremiti, with the islands themselves; and, in Comino, the castle called Vicalbo, with all its appurtenances.

All these things, therefore, and everything that now rightfully belongs to the aforesaid monastery and that shall rightfully belong to it in the future, having been established and confirmed by this privilege under the protection and Roman liberty, for the perpetual peace of the servants of God, both present [Col. 1308C] and future, we prohibit by apostolic censure, under the imposition of a strict anathema and by the testimony of divine judgment, all persons, present and future—whatever their rank, dignity, condition, or office, and every person, great or small—from inflicting any violence upon, making any false claim against, or burdening any goods or persons rightfully belonging to the aforesaid monastery.

Moreover, since the monastic course, according to the precept of the rule of the blessed Father Benedict, is fixed for the summer and winter seasons, by apostolic authority we grant the brothers permission to ring the signal in the same monastery and its cells, both for the daytime and nighttime hours, whenever they wish.

The brothers of the monastery and its cells may also receive, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, any cleric of any order and from any bishopric, together with his possessions, to live there and receive the monastic habit, without the prohibition of any bishop. The monastery’s subjects shall likewise be permitted to judge both monks and holy women, without the prohibition or contradiction of any secular or ecclesiastical power.

And because we desire to prevent the wicked avarice and wrongdoing of both present and future persons, by this apostolic authority we likewise prohibit the disturbances called *levae*, or plunderings, from being carried out in any way upon the death or election of any abbot [Col. 1309A] or rector.

Furthermore, you may receive sacred chrism, ecclesiastical orders, and the consecration of altars from any canonically promoted bishop; celebrate the rite of Christian initiation in your churches through your clerics; and properly sing the angelic hymn on Sundays and feast days during the solemnities of Mass.

No bishop shall presume to come into the said monastery, or to excommunicate a priest in the churches subject to it, or summon him to a synod, or excommunicate the abbot and the monks who may then be there.

Moreover, wishing to provide for monastic religion, which is widely corrupted because of the pressure of sins, we have decided to appoint you alone, for the days of your life, as our vicar for the correction of all monasteries and monks from the river Piscaria, where it flows into the sea—that is, throughout Campania, the Principate, Apulia, and Calabria [Col. 1309B]. You shall have a chapter over them and, in our place, correct the undisciplined with the assistance of the bishops to whom the monasteries themselves belong. What needs correction you shall, if able, amend according to the Lord, or report to the pontiff of the apostolic see, for the everlasting reward of your soul and for the reform and preservation of monastic religion, as well as for the dignity of your cardinalate and the honor of the most holy Benedict. This is granted so that the monastic order in those regions may be corrected through you, its religious and most prudent successor.

If anyone—which we do not desire—attempts by rash audacity to violate in any respect the decretal document of this privilege [Col. 1309C], let him know that he is bound by the chains of perpetual curse and will suffer everlasting punishments with the devil and his angels, unless he first comes to his senses and makes satisfaction.

But whoever proves to be a devoted observer out of regard for piety may, through the intercession of the blessed Father Benedict and his perfect followers and companions, become a participant in everlasting blessing and a blessed possessor of paradise. Amen.

Written by the hand of Octavian, notary and scrivener of the holy Roman Church and apostolic see, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Nicholas II, the twelfth indiction.

Given at Osimo on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the year of Jesus [Col. 1309D] Christ 1059, through the hand of Humbert, bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see.

## IV. Pope Nicholas II confirms the establishment of the chapter of the Blessed Virgin Mary of the Steps at Cologne, a college of twenty canons founded by Saint Anno, archbishop of Cologne, and endowed with many estates by Blessed Richeza.

[Note: Blessed Richeza, also called Ritza, niece of Saint Anno, archbishop of Cologne, and wife of Mieszko, king of Poland, was the mother of Blessed Casimir, who, having been a Cluniac monk and deacon, became king of Poland by the pope’s dispensation. She died in 1057 and was buried in the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary of the Steps at Cologne. She is commemorated on 20 March.]

(Year 1059.)

[MIRAEUS, *Opera diplomatica*, IV, 3.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Anno [Col. 1310A], archbishop of Cologne, perpetual greeting in the Lord.

It is the duty of our pontifical apostolate, with universal vigilance, to provide beneficially for all ecclesiastical affairs; nevertheless, we should devote the greatest solicitude, with pious devotion, to the interests of religious places. Although we owe this generally to all, we always desire to show, in a special way, the assent of preferential affection toward the reverence due to your fraternity.

Accordingly, since every just petition deserves an easy assent, the promptness of your benevolence has elicited the affection of our charity. Therefore, in accordance with the love expressed in your petition, we receive under the protection of the apostolic see the church of Blessed Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, situated within the walls of the city of Cologne in the place called “at the Steps.” Your pious devotion built it and enriched it, for the honor of almighty God and the perpetual reward of your soul, with possessions and goods within and outside it [Col. 1310B].

By apostolic authority we likewise confirm to the same church whatever your devout religious purpose has thus far contributed through the fervor of divine zeal—namely, Blisenna, Wissa, Unckelo, Heigenbach, Elinke, and Flamnersheimb—and whatever your predecessor, Archbishop Hermann, acquired from the possessions of others for the construction of the same church. We also confirm what, through your industry and that of Richeza and her co-heirs, was acquired at Meckenichem, Cloteno, Demunderedo, and Assela, as well as the tithe in Saxony that had been Henry’s fief [Col. 1310C], and whatever in the future your charity, or any of the faithful, may lawfully acquire in any manner recognized by divine or human law.

Therefore, by the decretal document of this privilege, we establish that no person, great or small, of any dignity, rank, or order, shall ever dare or presume to disturb or molest that church or those religiously serving it in any way, or, with rash audacity, investigate its movable or immovable possessions. For it is fitting that those who are continually exercised in the service of Christ alone should be protected by the salutary defense of our unfailing oversight.

Therefore, by the authority of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [Col. 1310D], and of the blessed princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, with joyful heart assenting to your holy devotion, dearest brother, we establish and command, under the imposition of perpetual anathema and the observance of divine judgment, that your statutes and these statutes of ours, established for the perpetual increase of the aforesaid church, remain inviolate.

If anyone—which we do not desire—becomes a violator of the decretal document of this privilege through rash audacity, and presumes to corrupt its decrees by obstinate rebellion against the holy apostolic see, let him know that he will be condemned by the anathema of perpetual curse and burned in the fire of everlasting punishment with the devil and his followers [Col. 1311A], unless perhaps he repents and makes worthy satisfaction to God and to the aforesaid church.

But whoever proves to be its preserver with pious devotion shall, through the prayers of the blessed princes of the apostles, obtain forgiveness of all his sins and, together with all observers of the divine law, deserve the glory of eternal blessedness.

Written by the hand of Octavian, keeper of the sacred archive and notary of the holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of May, the twelfth indiction, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1058, through the hands of Humbert, bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Nicholas II, the twelfth indiction [Col. 1311B].

## V. Nicholas II confirms the possessions of the Church of Penne at the request of Bishop John. (Year 1059.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, I, 1116.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother John, bishop of Penne, and through you to the church of Saint Mary and of Christ’s glorious martyr and Levite Maximus, and to your successors forever.

It is our duty to provide for all ecclesiastical interests and readily to grant just desires and petitions. Therefore, because you asked us, dearest brother, to confirm forever, by the document of our privilege, to your church, to you, and to your successors, everything that rightfully and lawfully belongs to the aforesaid church [Col. 1311C], gladly assenting to your petition, by the decree of this constitution and the edict of the apostolic see we grant and confirm to you forever, as stated above, whatever you presently possess in the episcopal estate of the aforementioned church of Blessed Mary and of Christ’s glorious martyr and Levite Maximus, and whatever you may lawfully acquire in the future by any manner recognized by divine or human law.

Specifically, we confirm the episcopal estate itself, with all its goods and possessions and appurtenances, movable, immovable, and self-moving, with castles, villages, and territories, churches with first fruits and tithes, and everything that the pious devotion of the faithful has contributed there in sacred offerings, both for the salvation of the living and for that of the dead [Col. 1311D].

By this inviolable constitution of this holy apostolic see, over which, with God’s approval, we are known to preside, we establish that no emperor, marquis, count, viscount, or any other person, great or small, of whatever dignity or order, shall presume, contrary to this privilege, to strip the said episcopal estate, or you, dearest son, or your successors forever, of its goods, disturb you, or establish or order anything there contrary to the sacred canons.

If anyone does not permit it to possess what has been granted by our apostolic authority, and the grants [lacuna] to belong to it, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema from the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and by the authority of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; and that, together with the devil and Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, he will be burned in the punishment of fire [Col. 1312A]. Moreover, let him know that he shall pay ten pounds of gold: half to our sacred palace and half to the aforesaid episcopal estate.

But whoever proves to be a pious observer in all things, preserving the constitution of this privilege or showing regard for the worship of God, shall receive the grace of blessing from the most merciful Lord God, share in eternal life, and enjoy mercy forever and ever.

Given at Rome on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1059, through the hands of Humbert, bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Nicholas II, the twelfth indiction [Col. 1312B].

## VI. Nicholas II confirms the possessions and boundaries of the Church of Chieti (Theate) at the request of Bishop Acto. (Year 1059.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VI, 676.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Acto, bishop of the holy Church of Chieti (Theate), and to all your successors who shall be canonically promoted in the same Church, forever.

Source preparation: Supplied local source with restored foreign-script passages; translated as part of this section.

Although we are commanded, while we have the opportunity, to do what is good, especially toward those who belong to the household of faith, we therefore owe our solicitude [Col. 1312C] to all the Churches of Christ, in accordance with the stewardship entrusted to us; thus we must watch over those who are far away in such a way that we are not in any respect absent from those who are near. Therefore, at your petition, dearest brother and fellow bishop Acto, whom we rejoice was promoted from the bishopric of Marsica to that of Teate by our lord Victor, of revered memory, and whom we know has faithfully and continually served our predecessors and us in the care of the holy Roman Church, we confirm the bishopric of Teate with all its integrity and appurtenances, as it is delimited by its ancient and just boundaries: namely, from Staffilo between the mountains, and the mountain itself of Ursa, and as it proceeds toward Coya, and sets its boundary at the water, beneath the earth as far as Aquasonula, and as it proceeds as far as the mountain of Teste, and goes across the mountain of Vina, and as it proceeds as far as Mount Clavi, and as it proceeds by that river of Trinio [Col. 1312D] as far as the shores of the sea, and along the sea as far as Piscaria, and returns to the former boundary, which is Staffilo itself.

Therefore, establishing by apostolic authority, we confirm to you, to your successors, and also to your Church, the city of Teate, the castle of Tribullianum, the estate of Cisterna, and the estate of Patroncello; likewise the castle of Genestrale with the parish of Saint Michael; Mount Filardus with the chapel of the Holy Trinity; the parish of Saint Martin of Turri; and part of Aterno with the parishes of Saints Langutianus and Domitianus; and part of Portus; and the castle of Saint John with its chapel; likewise the castle of the parish of Saint Hilary with that parish; and the castle of Villamagna with the parish of Saint Michael; [Col. 1313A] also the parish of Saint Mary of Caramancio; the castle of Luco; likewise the castle of Petra; and the parish of Saint John of Albateco; the castle of Pulveri with its chapel; also the parish of Saint Stephen in Baxamo; and the parish of Buvlanico; and the parish of Saint Martin of the land of Don Tresidius; and Mount Perge with Saint Angelo and the sites of the mills; and the parish of Juliano; and the parish of Saint Cecilia; and the parish of Piro Coartio; and the parish of Oucule; likewise the parish of Saint Mary in Bari; and the parish of Saint Mary in Domo; and the parish of Attissa; and the monastery of Saint Maurus; and the parish of Saint Nicholas of Mount Oderisius; and Mount Acutus; and, at the fork and beyond Piscaria, the lands belonging to that bishopric.

All these possessions, and many others belonging to the aforesaid bishopric that are not listed here, we confirm—[Col. 1313B] namely, parishes, chapels, castles, and estates, with all their appurtenances and tithes, the offerings of the faithful, living and dead, and also firstfruits, together with all gifts canonically belonging to the bishopric. But if anyone—God forbid—should presume, with rash audacity, to violate, diminish, or retain any of all that we have stated, whether emperor, margrave, count, or any layperson, or any bishop, abbot, monk, or priest, against your Church or against your will and that of your successors, we establish by apostolic authority, under threat of divine judgment, that no person of whatever great or small dignity or order, as stated above, [Col. 1313C] shall ever dare to disturb or harass you or your successors concerning the aforesaid goods of your Church or anything justly belonging to it; nor shall any archbishop or bishop dare to establish or undertake anything in your diocese without the permission of you and your successors. With all opposition removed, let the Church remain perpetually undisturbed with its rights.

Whoever, however, should presume to violate or transgress in any respect what has been promulgated by us with pious regard, as we have said, shall incur the wrath of almighty God, perish pierced by our anathema, and groan condemned with the devil. Moreover, let him know that he must pay one hundred pounds of gold, half to our sacred palace and half to the aforesaid bishop himself. But whoever proves [Col. 1313D] in all things a devout observer, preserving the provisions of this privilege of ours, which are directed toward the worship of God, may he receive the grace of blessing from the most merciful Lord God and deserve to be a participant in eternal life forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Crescentius, notary and scriniary of the holy Roman Church, in the month of May, on the second day, in the twelfth indiction. The place + of the sign of the lord pope.

Given at Rome on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1059, by the hand of Humbert, bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the first year of the pontificate of the lord pope Nicholas II, in the twelfth indiction.

## VII. (In the year 1059)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XIX, 873.]

Nicholas II’s Letter to the Bishops of Gaul, Aquitaine, and Gascony. It contains several decrees promulgated in the Roman synod of 1059.

[Col. 1314A]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all archbishops, bishops, abbots, clerics, and faithful laypeople, both great and small, dwelling in Christ throughout all Gaul, indeed also among the Aquitanians and Gascons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1059, in the first year of our pontificate and the twelfth indiction, while celebrating a holy synod in the city of Rome, in the basilica of Saint Saviour called the Constantinian, [Col. 1314B] we canonically arranged, with God’s favour, for the common good matters concerning the condition of the holy Church, with the participation of the holy Fathers—namely, 113 bishops, not counting the abbots, religious clerics, and laypeople. Among other matters, concerning the heresy of the Nicolaitans—that is, married priests, deacons, and all those established in the clergy—the following was established and confirmed by the whole council:

> “Whoever among priests, deacons, and subdeacons, after the decree concerning the chastity of the clergy issued by our predecessor, the most holy pope Leo, of blessed memory, has publicly taken a concubine or has not dismissed one whom he had taken, we command and absolutely forbid, on behalf of almighty God and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, to sing Mass, to proclaim the Gospel, [Col. 1314C] to read the Epistle at Mass, to remain in the presbytery for the divine offices with those who have obeyed the aforesaid constitution, or to receive a portion from the Church, until, God granting it, a judgment concerning this matter proceeds from us.
>
> “And commanding, we establish that those of the aforesaid orders who, obeying the decree of that same predecessor of ours, have observed these requirements shall, beside the churches in which they were ordained, eat and sleep together, as religious clerics ought to do. And exhorting, we admonish them to strive with the utmost zeal to attain the apostolic—that is, common—life, so that, having attained perfection, they may deserve to be enrolled in the heavenly homeland with those who are enriched by a hundredfold fruit.”

Concerning those clerics who cast off the tonsure and [Col. 1314D] withdraw from the clergy, whom we rightly call apostate Julianists, we establish that, unless they return to the clerical profession, they are to be deprived of all Christian communion.

Concerning monks who do not keep their way of life, we decreed that, until they return to their profession and remain regularly in the monastery, they are to remain deprived of communion.

Those who have plundered pilgrims or worshippers of any saint, whether clerics, monks, women, or unarmed poor people, or have seized their goods, or have met them with evil intent, shall also be struck by the bond of anathema unless they make worthy amends.

Concerning the boundaries of cemeteries, just as they were established in ancient times by the [Col. 1315A] holy Fathers, we establish the following: a major church is to have sixty paces around it, but chapels or smaller churches thirty. Whoever attempts to violate their boundary, or removes from it a person or that person’s goods, unless he is a public robber, shall be excommunicated until he makes satisfaction and restores what he has taken.”

The aforesaid holy synod therefore judged that these and other matters of this kind, whatever is contained in the sacred canons, must be observed as authoritative.

## VIII. Nicholas II records for all bishops, and for the entire clergy and people, the decrees of the Roman synod *(In the year 1059)*

[Note: [Col. 1315D] The callout number for this note is printed in the text as (2).] The council was held in April, in the third week after Easter, as is gathered from Pope Nicholas II’s letter to the archbishop of Reims. From his letter to the bishops of Gaul, however, it is said to have been celebrated by the holy Fathers—namely, 113 bishops, not counting abbots, religious clerics, and laypeople. Nicholas repeats this at the beginning of the acts of this council: “in the Roman synod recently celebrated before 113 bishops.” Yet in the Vatican manuscript presented below, among the subscriptions of this council, no more than sixty-three bishops are found subscribed. Hence perhaps “63” should be read instead of “113 bishops” in the cited passages of Nicholas; for this sign, L, is frequently copied in place of C, and conversely. [Col. 1316D] In this council, Wido, archbishop of Milan, accused by Ariald and Landulf Cotta of the stain of simony, was defended by Oddo or Atto, bishop of Novara, together with the bishops of Asti and Turin, according to Ughelli, volume IV, *On the Bishops of Novara*, no. 48. He further asserts that Wido, archbishop of Milan, attended this council and subscribed first, as appears from the acts preserved in the Vatican. Yet in the acts presented below, the first to subscribe was V., archbishop of Bomegrad and patriarch, not the archbishop of Milan, who nowhere appears subscribed, nor does the bishop of Asti.

[Mansi, *Councils*, XIX, 897.]

[Col. 1315B]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all Catholic bishops, and to the entire clergy and people: most affectionate greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since through the vigilance of universal government we owe constant solicitude to all, and since we also provide for your salvation, we take care to notify you of what was canonically established in the Roman synod recently celebrated, with us, although unworthy, presiding before 113 bishops, because we desire you to be its executors for your salvation; and by apostolic authority we command and enjoin it.

I. First, with God as witness, it was established that the election of the Roman pontiff should lie in the power of the cardinal bishops, so that if anyone is enthroned in the apostolic see [Col. 1315C] without their prior harmonious and canonical election, and thereafter without the consent of the succeeding orders of religious persons, clerics, and laypeople, he is to be regarded not as pope or apostolic, but as an apostate.

II. When the Roman pontiff, or the bishop of any city, dies, no one is to presume to seize his possessions; they are to be preserved intact for his successors.

III. No one is to hear the Mass of a priest whom he knows certainly to have a concubine or a woman introduced into his household. Therefore the holy synod itself established this chapter under excommunication, saying:

> “Whoever among priests, deacons, and subdeacons, [Col. 1315D] after the decree concerning the chastity of the clergy issued by our predecessor, the most holy pope Leo, of blessed memory, has publicly taken a concubine or has not dismissed one whom he had taken, we command and absolutely forbid, on behalf of almighty God [Col. 1316A] and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, to sing Mass, to read either the Gospel or the Epistle at Mass, to remain in the presbytery for the divine offices with those who have obeyed the aforesaid constitution, or to receive a portion from the Church, until, God granting it, a judgment concerning this matter proceeds from us.”

IV. And commanding, we establish that those of the aforesaid orders who, obeying that predecessor of ours, have observed chastity shall, beside the churches in which they were ordained, eat and sleep together, as religious clerics ought to do; and whatever comes to them from the churches, they shall hold in common. And exhorting, we admonish them to strive with the utmost zeal to attain the apostolic—that is, common—life. [Col. 1316B]

V. Next, that tithes and firstfruits, or the offerings of the living and the dead, be faithfully rendered by laypeople to the churches of God, and that they be under the disposition of the bishops. Those who retain them are to be separated from communion with the holy Church.

VI. No cleric or priest is to obtain a church through laypeople, either without payment or for a price.

VII. No one is to assume the monastic habit with the hope or promise of becoming an abbot.

VIII. No priest is to hold two churches at the same time.

IX. No one is to be ordained [Col. 1316C] or promoted to any ecclesiastical office through the heresy of simony.

X. Laypeople are not to judge clerics of any order.

XI. No one is to marry a wife from among his own blood relations up to the seventh generation, or until the relationship can be recognized.

XII. A layman who has both a wife and a concubine is not to communicate with the Church.

XIII. No layman is suddenly to be promoted to any ecclesiastical rank unless, after changing his secular habit, he has been tested by a long period of conduct among clerics.

Therefore observe these and the other statutes [Col. 1316D] of the holy Fathers faithfully and with Christian reverence, if you wish to enjoy the peace, communion, and blessing of the holy Roman Church and apostolic see.

## IX. Nicholas II communicates the decrees of the synod to all the bishops suffragan to the Church of Amalfi, and to the entire clergy and people

*(In the year 1059)*

[Mansi, *Councils*, XIX, 907.]

[Col. 1317A]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops suffragan to the Church of Amalfi, and to the entire clergy and people: most affectionate greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since through the vigilance of universal government we owe constant solicitude to all, and since, out of the special love owed to your most beloved brother and our fellow archbishop, your archbishop, we particularly provide for your salvation, we take care to notify you of what was canonically established in the Roman synod recently celebrated before 113 [Col. 1317B] bishops, with us, although unworthy, presiding, because we desire you to be its executors for your salvation; and by apostolic authority we command and enjoin it.

First, with God as witness, it was established that if anyone is enthroned in the apostolic see without the harmonious and canonical election and blessing of the cardinal bishops, and thereafter without the consent of the succeeding orders of religious clerics, he is not to be regarded as pope or apostolic.

And when the Roman pontiff, or the bishop of any city, dies, no one is to presume to seize his possessions; they are to be preserved intact for his successors.

[Col. 1317C]

No one is to hear the Mass of a priest whom he knows certainly to have a concubine or an introduced woman. Therefore the first synod itself established this chapter under excommunication, saying:

> “Whoever among priests, deacons, or subdeacons, after the decree concerning the chastity of the clergy issued by our predecessor, Pope Leo, of blessed memory, has taken a concubine or has not dismissed one whom he had taken, we command and absolutely forbid, on behalf of almighty God and by the authority of the blessed apostles, princes Peter and Paul, to sing Mass, or to read the Epistle or the Gospel at Mass, or to remain in the presbytery for the divine offices with those who have obeyed the aforesaid constitution, or to receive a portion from the Church, [Col. 1318A] until, the Lord granting it, a judgment concerning this matter proceeds from us.”

And commanding, we establish that those of the aforesaid orders who, obeying that predecessor of ours, have observed chastity shall, beside the churches in which they were ordained, eat and sleep together, as religious clerics ought to do, and shall hold in common whatever is assigned to them by the churches.

And exhorting, we admonish them to strive with the utmost zeal to attain the apostolic—that is, common—life, so that, having attained perfection, they may deserve to be enrolled in the heavenly homeland with those who are enriched by a hundredfold.

Finally, that tithes and firstfruits, or whatever offerings of the living and the dead, be faithfully rendered by laypeople to the churches of God [Col. 1318B] and be under the disposition of the bishops, to be distributed according to the canons; those who retain them are to be separated from the bosom of the holy Church.

No cleric or priest is to obtain a church through laypeople, either without payment or for a price.

No one is to assume the monastic habit with the hope or promise of becoming an abbot.

No one is to be ordained, or promoted to any ecclesiastical office, through the heresy of simony.

Laypeople are not to judge clerics of any order, nor expel them from churches.

No one is to marry a wife from among his own blood relations [Col. 1318C] until after the seventh generation, or until the relationship can be recognized.

A layman who has both a wife and a concubine is not to communicate with the Church.

No layman is suddenly to be promoted to any ecclesiastical rank unless, after first changing his secular habit, he has been tested by a long period of conduct among clerics.

Therefore observe these and the other statutes of the holy Fathers faithfully and with Christian reverence, and especially those which your archbishop commanded you in the synod that he held among you in the first year of his ordination, if you wish to enjoy the peace, communion, and blessing of the holy Roman Church and apostolic see.

74. Placidus, bishop of Veroli. Gregory of Vercelli. All confirmed. The number of bishops who attended this most holy [Col. 1322C] synod was 123.

## John Dominic Mansi’s note and conjectures on the foregoing subscriptions

[Col. 1321C]

No one will understand how valuable this catalogue produced by Martène is unless he has undertaken a careful comparison of it with the Vatican catalogue, the Ughellian catalogue, and various documents of that age. So that readers may accomplish this more easily and derive abundant benefit from it for correcting, extending, and illustrating the succession of the bishops of so many distinguished Italian sees, let them regard this work and these conjectures of mine as having been produced for that purpose.

Peter of Laricanus: [read: Labicanus]. This bishop is missing from Martène’s catalogue; he must be supplied from the Vatican, and he agrees with documents of his age in Ughelli, volume X, p. 119 of the new edition.

Guido, archbishop, certainly of Milan, whom I discussed in the Preface. He is not actually absent from the Vatican; but a corrupt reading has so badly distorted him that he can scarcely be recognized. For the reading “V., archbishop of Bomegrad and patriarch” must be restored as follows: “Wido, archbishop, patriarch of Grado.”

Alfanus of Salerno: thus the corrupted reading of the Vatican must be corrected, for the documents of his age in Ughelli call him Alfanus.

Alard, bishop and abbot. He appears subscribed to the charter of the consecration of the church of Farfa in the year 1060, in Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, volume V, p. 1039, where he is called Aylardus.

John, bishop of Terracina. He is absent from the Vatican, unless perhaps he is the same bishop who appears there under the false name of John of Fermo. For the records of Fermo admitted no bishop of that name at that time.

Atto, bishop of Teate. In the Vatican he is incorrectly called bishop of Rieti. For Ughelli, who had seen no other reading than the Vatican one, [Col. 1322C] is forced by it to give Rieti a bishop Atto, although he would have preferred Jocundus, supplied by the records of Rieti. Conversely, the records of Teate announce Atto.

John of Parma is perhaps John of Pennensis, who obtained a privilege from Pope Nicholas in this year; it should be read in Ughelli under the bishops of Penne.

Godefried, bishop of Perugia. This agrees well with Ughelli, and he is absent from the Vatican catalogue.

Godefried, bishop of Atella. Ughelli was prevented by the corrupted Vatican reading from properly including this bishop in the succession of the bishops of Atella; for the Vatican has “Avellinensis.” What see is this?

William of Numana, now called Humanus; for that city was called Humana in the Middle Ages. A document in Ughelli under the Aprutine bishops shows that a certain William held that see at that time.

[Col. 1322D]

Erasmus of Fiesole. The Vatican reads “Transmundus.” But Ughelli cites a document of the year 1067 in which Transmundus’s inauguration is mentioned as taking place in that same year, 1067. How, then, could Transmundus have subscribed to this council in 1059? Erasmus is therefore rightly recorded, and must be inserted into the records of Fiesole before Transmundus, since he is missing there.

Rofred of Ateste [read: Asti], since a bishop of Asti attended is clear from Arnulf, whom we discussed in the Preface. The Asti records in Ughelli have a great gap here, so that they can conveniently admit this bishop. The Vatican incorrectly has “Nofred of Siena,” since both the records of Ughelli and the present catalogue show that John presided over Siena at that time.

Marius of Fondi. The Vatican has “Martinus.” Which reading is better?

[Col. 1323A]

Guido, bishop of Volturno [read: Volterra], for a bishop of that name was active at Volterra at that time, according to Ughelli. Conversely, Peter of Volturno, who is added immediately afterward, was invested with the episcopal insignia of Volturno.

Adulfus, bishop of Fertranus [read: Feltre]. The name of the see is absent in the Vatican. The records of Feltre have a gap to be filled by this bishop.

Peter of the Aprutine territory. The documents of Ughelli agree. What is the Vatican’s “P., bishop of Atri”?

Anselm of Lucca. Excellent; in the Vatican he is incorrectly called bishop of Luni. This is supported by a document of the year 1058 in Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, volume V, p. 974. Therefore Anselm of Luni must be removed from Ughelli, as he arose from a corrupted reading.

Theotius of Senigallia. Saint Peter Damian mentions him, according to Ughelli. Therefore the Vatican incorrectly calls him Visodonius.

Arduin of Todi. The Vatican has “Martinus.” Which reading is better?

[Col. 1323B]

Arduin of Fano. The records of Fano also offer him in Ughelli.

Gerard of Teate. I would prefer “of Rieti,” as in the Vatican, since neighboring bishops are listed here.

Benedict of Simphronia. So too does Ughelli. What is the Vatican’s “B., bishop of Siponto”?

Gislebert of Tuscania. I do not know where Ughelli read the name of this bishop among the Fathers of this synod, since these subscriptions from the Florentine manuscript had not yet been published in his time. Nevertheless, he asserts that this Gislebert attended the synod—and rightly so, as we learn from this source.

Achinus of Assisi is known from this one document alone and is unknown to Ughelli.

Ingo of Bagnoregio. The Vatican has “Isidore.” From this one document Ughelli gave “Gibertus.” Which reading should we follow?

Tegrunus of Populonia. The Vatican has “Regino.” But Tegrinus is known in the records of Ughelli, although we must place his beginning two years earlier, in 1061, than Ughelli does, since this subscription requires it.

Deodatus, bishop of Corbinum—namely, of Mount Corbinum in Apulia, which later lost its name when its bishopric was united with Volturno. From this single document we learn that this union had not yet taken place in 1059.

Arechis, bishop of Alife. In the Vatican catalogue this name has merged with the word “bishop,” producing the monstrosity “archbishop of Alife.” Yet you do not find the name even in Ughelli.

Gunibert, bishop of Paulinia. The Vatican has “Cumebert, bishop of Maurienne.” The reading is corrupted everywhere; he is Cunibert of Turin, whom I discussed in the Preface.

Opizo of Bobbio. Is he perhaps the “Luiso of Bobbio” known to Ughelli under the bishops of Bobbio?

Benzo of Alba. This bishop is known from the panegyric of the emperor Henry III, written by him and frequently cited by me in this work. He was unknown to Ughelli.

[Col. 1323D]

William of Pompilia. Is he William of Pompilia or Forum Pompilii? Ughelli indeed establishes an Honestus as bishop of that Church at that time, and asserts that he read the same man subscribed among the Fathers of this Roman council in the Vatican manuscript. But the Roman manuscript, represented by Labbe, has no such thing and contains nothing concerning Honestus of Pompilia. Ughelli produces one document concerning Honestus from the year 1037 and another from 1062; in the latter, however, Vecchiazanus in the new edition of Ughelli printed not Honestus but Gualfonius, which comes somewhat closer to William.

Gregory of Vercelli. This prelate is known to Ughelli. I omit the remaining subscriptions, since they require no explanations or corrections.

## X. Nicholas II commands Gervase, archbishop of Reims, to remove [Guilbert], bishop of Beauvais, who was consecrated against Gervase’s will, from administering his office until he comes to the synod

*(In the year 1059)*

[Duchesne, *History of France, Writers*, IV, 199.]

[Col. 1324A]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gervase, venerable archbishop of Reims: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have heard from the report of many that the bishop of Beauvais was consecrated contrary to the provisions of the canons, without you and without your consent, and, what is worse, was raised to the episcopate. Therefore gird yourself, and supported by this authority of ours, forbid him, on behalf of almighty God and by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, every episcopal function until he comes before us to be examined at the Roman synod in the third week after Easter. [Col. 1324B]

But if it is openly established that he gave money, forbid all the clerics and laypeople of Beauvais, under excommunication and by the authority of the aforesaid apostle Peter, to obey him before our aforesaid judgment. For he was not promoted in order to be a bishop, as blessed Gregory says, but in order to become a wolf, an invader of the holy Church, and a detestable heretic.

Likewise forbid your suffragan, the bishop of Senlis, every episcopal function, by the authority of the blessed apostle Peter, until he comes to the aforesaid synod and makes worthy satisfaction to us and to you, if he knew that the man had given money and did not have your consent to bless an heir of the curse.

## XI. Nicholas II confirms to the monastery of Saint Peter of Perugia the tithes of the castles of Arno, Civitella, and Pilonico

*(In the year 1059)*

[Margarini, *Casinense Bullary*, II, 94, from the archive of the monastery of Saint Peter of Perugia, privilege chest no. 9.]

[Col. 1324C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Nicholas, by the assent of divine clemency, pontiff of the holy Roman and apostolic Church, in the first year of his pontificate, in the most sacred see of the blessed apostle Peter, in the thirteenth indiction.

[Source ends here.]

[Col. 1324D] We ought not to be found ungrateful toward the devotion or goodwill of those who faithfully and diligently obey the holy Roman and apostolic see during the days of our priesthood; rather, we must strive to grant them whatever the mercy of Almighty God inspires us to grant, for the praise and glory of his name and for the increase of our consolation. We are indeed urged to this by the words of the Lord: “He who is faithful in little will also be faithful in much,” and, “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound.” Therefore, considering your diligence and goodwill, dearest son and abbot Bonizo, which have hitherto been ready and generous toward the service of Saint Peter and of our faithful, and considering that you continually burden yourself beyond the resources of the monastery entrusted to you with service to the holy Roman Church, it pleased us, with the counsel and [Col. 1325A] intervention of our faithful, to add something to your monastery, so that you may be able to serve us and our successors more generously and freely.

Since your monastery therefore belongs especially to Saint Peter, whose name it also bears, we gladly grant it what we are presently able to grant, and, as it were, transfer it from our hand into our hand nevertheless, by adding to your monastery certain possessions of our apostolic see that are known to belong to that same see: namely, from the three castles and their villages, with their appurtenances, established in the estate of Saint Peter—that is, Arni, Civitella, and Pilonico—the entire tithe from fields, vineyards, woods, vegetables, livestock, and all animals that pass under the shepherd’s staff; or, as blessed Augustine admonishes, tithes from military service, trade, and craftsmanship, and the first fruits of all crops.

All these things, in their entirety, we grant perpetually to the monastery entrusted to you, and through it to you, dearest son Bonizo, and to your successors who shall regularly be promoted there; and by this document of our apostolic authority we confirm them for the honor of God and of the blessed apostle Peter, for the advancement of the monastic order, and for the devotion and reception of the faithful of the aforesaid apostle and of the other poor of Christ. If anyone, however—which we do not desire—should presume with rash audacity to violate in any respect this concession of our apostolic authority, let him know that he will incur the guilt of strict excommunication for his sacrilege, together with the lost Judas; moreover, as one guilty under human law, let him pay a fine of ten pounds of gold [Col. 1325C], half to our sacred Lateran palace and half to the aforesaid monastery of blessed Peter. Whoever devoutly observes it, however, shall obtain remission of his sins and blessing from the Lord through the intercession of the holy apostles.

Amen.

I, Nicholas, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Roman and apostolic see, have granted and subscribed.

I, Peter, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.

I, Humbert, called bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida, have consented and subscribed.

I, Hildebrand, a certain archdeacon of the holy Roman Church, have consented and subscribed.

I, Aimo, notary of this concession, have acknowledged [Col. 1325D] and subscribed.

In the year of the Lord 1059, on the second day before the Ides of October.

### XII. Bull of Nicholas II for the church of Saint Andrew of Empoli. (Year 1059.)

[LAMI, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Florentinae* IV, p. 104.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Martin, rector of the parish church of Saint Andrew situated at Empoli, and to his successors who shall live there together perpetually.

Although, by the favor of the Lord, we preside over the universality of the apostolic see and must constantly provide diligent care for all the churches, nevertheless we take pains to devote to the Florentine Church, specially entrusted to our episcopal governance, the appropriate care required, with such ardent love that it may remain in perpetual religion and enjoy stable security [Col. 1326A]. Although, with Christ assisting, very many parishes have been advanced through our zeal and our work to the point that around them a common society of clerics, gathered together, may live in holy purpose in fellowship and everlasting perseverance, for this reason they unanimously petitioned our mercy by common agreement, asking that the things which we ourselves had granted from our resources, or which the faithful had contributed in sincere devotion as the price of their sins, be confirmed by our authority.

We, bending to their need, assent to their religious petitions. Indeed, the more clearly we know that the wicked continually devise plots against the good, the more ought we—even though there is no reason for fear while we live—to oppose shields of defense on every side, lest [Col. 1326B] they prevail. Thus the good, following the religious path, may rejoice in the gift bestowed and, according to the Psalmist’s prophecy, go from strength to strength, always advancing toward better things; while those on the opposing side, seeking lower things, may wither and waste away in their obstinacy when they see the progress of their superiors.

Following canonical authority, therefore, what we once granted to the aforesaid parishes when we exercised the simple office of a bishop, we now grant with a firmer and more powerful apostolic privilege; we confirm, establish, and perpetually sanction it for you upon an unshakable foundation. We grant to your parish the first fruits; the fourth part of the tithes both to you and to the other clerics living canonically with you [Col. 1326C]; half of the bequests of the dead; all clothing; all burials; and, finally, all offerings in their entirety. We also grant all estates, whether donated by us, granted by our predecessors, or justly acquired or to be acquired in any manner by any of the faithful.

By the authority of our privilege, we also make you free and exempt from every secular and worldly condition, so long as you strive to persevere in holy conduct, so that you may not be compelled, under any sworn authority, to submit to public courts, except before the Florentine bishop himself. He, for his part, must provide you with suitable protection according to his means, setting aside excessive exaction, and may not compel you to pay him by right more than what you pay us in our time [Col. 1326D].

Therefore, whoever proves a pious keeper and an upright defender of this our command and promulgation shall have the grace of Almighty God, the blessing of the princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, and our own blessing. But whoever attempts to violate it with rash audacity, whether bishop or any person, great or small, shall know himself excommunicated and anathematized by the authority of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, unless what he has done wrong is corrected by suitable restitution. So that all this may remain fully effective for you, we have ordered that this document be marked with our seal and fortified by our subscription, and so forth.

Given at Florence on the third day before the Ides of December, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1058, by the hand of Humbert [Col. 1327A], bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Nicholas II, in the thirteenth indiction.

### XIII. Privilege of Nicholas II for the monastery of Saint Martin of Autun. (Year 1059.)

[BULLIOT, *Historical Essay on Saint Martin of Autun*, vol. II, p. 30.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, Gregory, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin of Autun, and to the entire monastery of that congregation, perpetually.

Whenever people desire us to grant those things which properly belong to a gift for the soul, it is fitting that we willingly grant them [Col. 1327B] and provide appropriate assistance to the desires of those who ask. Therefore, since you have requested from us a privilege of the apostolic see for the monastery of Saint Martin, situated in the suburb of the city of Autun, over which you are known to preside worthily—a monastery which was restored and rebuilt by the most devout emperor Charles Augustus, for love of the Almighty and in reverence for that most blessed confessor Martin, for the remission of his sins and the reward of eternal life—we have, bending to your petitions, graciously assented and fortified the aforesaid monastery, in which you have been appointed to divine service, with the protection and privilege of the apostolic see.

We will, grant, and decree that the same monastery shall be bound to answer to no one except the apostolic Church alone, and shall be free and exempt from every other jurisdiction and subjection. No emperor, no king, no bishop, no person endowed with any rank whatsoever, shall ever be permitted to diminish, remove, or apply to his own uses any movable or immovable property that has hitherto been granted to the same monastery by charters of the aforementioned most devout emperor Charles, or by other emperors or kings, or by any other persons whatsoever, or that shall in the future lawfully be donated from their own possessions by anyone, under any pretext or appearance of cause [the manuscript or print has *munere*; perhaps *minuere*, “to diminish”]. All that has been offered there, or may happen to be offered, from the present thirteenth indiction onward [Col. 1327C] shall, without disturbance, be possessed for the support of the aforesaid monastery and for the uses of the abbots and monks who serve God there under the rule of Father Benedict.

This is on the following condition: no bishop of the said city, nor any count, shall dare to lay claim to or, by any usurpation, annex anything to the aforesaid monastery and all the possessions belonging to it. Rather, let the servants of God dwelling there be permitted to serve Christ freely and peacefully, without the harassment of anyone.

We further establish and will that, when the abbot of the same monastery dies, the person whom the brothers elect by common consent shall be given and appointed as abbot; or the person whom the Roman pontiff provides to be ordained; or the person whom the monks of that place consent to have ordained subject to them.

We also append the following clause to the present chapter [Col. 1328A], so that we may exclude avarice: no king, bishop, or priest shall dare, either personally or through an agent, to receive anything from any of the faithful under any form as a reward for the appointment of the same abbot, clerics, or priests, or for the distribution of chrism, or the consecration of the basilica, or for any matters whatsoever belonging to the same monastery; nor shall the same abbot give anything for his appointment.

Nor shall the bishop of that city celebrate public Masses there unless invited by the abbot of the monastery; nor shall he announce or conduct assemblies or visitations in the same monastery, lest the quiet of God’s servants be disturbed in any way by a popular gathering. Nor shall he presume to demand provisions, lodging dues, or services.

We do not merely refuse to allow the reception of the faithful and of religious persons, and the charity which the Apostle commands to be shown to all, according to the capacity of the place and its resources; rather, we urge that these be practiced there.

If any bishop, priest, abbot, judge, count, or secular person attempts to act against this document of our institution, struck by apostolic anathema, let him lose the dignity of his power or rank and know himself guilty before the divine judgment. Unless he mourns what has been wrongly done, let him be separated from the most sacred body of God and our Lord Jesus Christ and subjected to the strict vengeance of the eternal judgment.

But for all who preserve the rights of that place, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ; let them receive here the profit and fruit of good action [Col. 1328C], and let them find rewards of eternal peace with the strict Judge.

Amen.

Given at Florence on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1059, by the hand of Humbert, bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Nicholas II, in the eighth indiction.

### XIV. Privilege granted by Nicholas II to the monastery of Saint Felicity. (Year 1060.)

[MANSI, *Councils* XIX, 870.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Teiberga, abbess of the monastery of Saint Felicity situated near [Col. 1328D] Florence, and to her successors, who shall remain in the holy purpose, perpetually.

Since the condescension of Almighty God, by his freely given gift and without any worthy preceding work, has deemed it fitting to raise our humility to this point, so that through us it might administer unfailing light to the Church redeemed throughout the world by his own blood, we rightly consider it our duty, with his assistance—of whom we presume to speak—to distribute to each person, according to our own abilities, the talent entrusted to us, lest, when his majesty appears, we be found to return like an unprofitable servant without having acquired any gain.

We hope by divine mercy to attain this if we take care, with serene affection, to supply such assistance as we can to his members who, through faith, still on earth aspire through faith to heavenly things [Col. 1329A]. Thus, indeed, we win heavenly help for our weakness; and, while our intention remains pure within the dwelling of our heart, we obtain the honorable favor of human beings. Although we are debtors to all nations whose light is the faith, we also devote special care, in a spirit of goodwill, to those of our own household, following the Teacher of the nations, who commands that good work be done toward all, especially toward those who belong to the household of faith.

Therefore, the monastery of Saint Felicity, with all the possessions belonging to it—which, because of the negligence of certain of our predecessors, our episcopal administration, while it was still simple, took care to rebuild completely by assembling a college of many noble nuns—we now, in accordance with the power of the apostolic see which we serve, strengthen with enduring stability, having dedicated it through our hands; we confirm it and, so that it may flourish in perpetual religious observance, entrust it to the protection of Almighty God, with the assault of the wicked kept at a distance.

To it also, as seems fitting to us, because through the negligence of the Florentine bishops its estates were wickedly dispersed and through the rashness of certain sacrilegious persons invaded, we grant and establish by apostolic authority the holdings and estates offered to this venerable place in pious devotion, and those to be offered, wherever they are shown by truthful report to have been assigned to its name and invested, or to be invested, in its right through religious care.

Moreover, we make the same monastery free and exempt from every secular and worldly [Col. 1329C] condition or constraint, so that no person, great or small, may by any device evade or by any fraud steal or diminish the estates restored and firmly established by us, nor certain tithing revenues granted by us, nor finally demand a tax or due subjection. Rather, let this venerable place remain secured in its holy purpose by our protection and be subject to no one except the Florentine bishop.
