The Florentine bishop, mindful of our devotion and of his own weakness, while observing the standard of justice and showing the same nuns appropriate honor according to the command of the Teacher of the nations, shall demand from them by right nothing beyond a gentle lordship.

If, however—which we do not believe—someone of rash mind attempts cruelly to break this apostolic sanction and, by harming the institution according to its circumstances, to invalidate our establishment, then, unless he repents when admonished and makes worthy correction, let him be struck by the sword of anathema from Almighty God. Let vengeance hurled from heaven overtake him in this present flesh, and let God slay him by the breath of his mouth when he comes to judge the world.

But whoever proves a pious keeper of our confirmation may at the second coming deserve to hear that honey-sweet voice: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25).

Furthermore, so that this document may establish its credibility for those who read it, we have taken care to fortify it both with our own hand’s subscription and with the impression of the apostolic seal.

+ Seal of Pope Nicholas.

[Col. 1330A] I, Boniface, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.

I, John, bishop of Porto, have subscribed.

I, Peter, bishop of Lavanica, have subscribed.

I, Bruno, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.

I, Peter, sinful monk, have subscribed.

Given at Florence on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1059, by the hands of Humbert, bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Nicholas II, in the thirteenth indiction.

### XV. Privilege of Pope Nicholas II for the church of Saint Michael and Saint Eusebius of Poio. (Year 1060.)

[LAMI, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Florentinae* II, 946.]

[Col. 1330B]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in the Lord Peter, rector of the Church of Saint Michael and Saint Eusebius situated in the place called Poio, and to his successors who shall be canonically ordained there, and to all who shall live there together perpetually.

Since the condescension of Almighty God, by his freely given gift, has deemed it fitting to raise our humility to this point, so that through us it might administer unfailing light to the Church spread throughout the world, we consider it entirely reasonable to provide continually, by appropriate provision, the special governance of the Florentine Church entrusted to our care. Thus we shall be able to imitate the salutary instruction of the Teacher of the nations, who commands us, according to our abilities, to perform good work for all, especially for those of the household of faith [Col. 1330C], particularly when, according to our abilities, we provide worthy services for places dedicated to divine worship, so that tireless praise may be celebrated in them throughout all ages.

But since stone walls were not built for the purpose of offering worthy praises to God, it plainly seems appropriate, for the perfection of the divine work, to arrange the diligent attendance of clerics around venerable places. Unless they are materially supported by earthly stipends, they can scarcely be fit for divine worship, since the Creator of the world himself, according to the human substance united to him, deigned to endure [Col. 1330D] thirst and hunger.

Therefore, for the glory of him through whom we live and have our being, we caused the basilica of the most precious archangel Michael and of Eusebius—renovated in beautiful form through our encouragement and at the expense of the citizens of Florence—to be consecrated, with an assembled company of bishops, by the hands of the bishops of Perugia and Roselle.

We judged it extremely unworthy, in our apostolic diligence—which is especially bound to pursue what is honorable and to assist all who suffer injury with pious concern—to leave it bare and without an endowment. Therefore, strengthened by the urging of the assisting brothers and also by our own decision, in the presence of the Florentine people, for the sins of the bishops of that city, for the sake of our own devotion, and finally for the salvation of the entire people, we offered apostolic investitures of the estates and all their possessions, at least those which we could provide for the present, after the altars had been consecrated [Col. 1331A].

Receive, therefore, most holy Michael and Eusebius, the voluntary gift of Pope Nicholas, long devoted to you; and from now and forever undertake, without any dispute, the singular and complete lordship of your possessions through me, so that in the hall dedicated to your name a religious clergy may resound with songs of praise to Almighty God.

Let your estates be designated by the following names: the entire circuit adjoining the Church, in its entirety; also the harbor and the glassworks; likewise the demesne lands and the vineyard held by the sons of John, son of Bonizo; and the vineyard held by Aczo, priest of Cresci, together with the willow grove held by the sons of Morando. All these things [Col. 1331B] are held as the property of this church; also a piece of land situated at the head of the bridge of the stream of Saint Andrew, and a *mantum* at Rusciano.

We have mentioned all these things only in outline, lest anyone doubt that this church possesses much more extensive estates.

Moreover, we absolve and free the same venerable place and order it to remain so by apostolic sanction. No person, great or small, shall be permitted to dishonor the clerics canonically gathered there and harass them by legal summons, or demand from them a due tax, or on any pretext invade, remove, or diminish the possessions granted or to be granted to them by us or by any of the faithful. Let the aforesaid place be exempt from every payment [Col. 1331C], under the protection of Saint Michael and Saint Eusebius, and subject to no lordship except that of the Florentine bishop.

If anyone, therefore—which we do not believe—with sacrilegious mind attempts to violate what we justly established in the presence of Humbert, cardinal of Silva Candida, and Hildebrand, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church, as well as the bishops of Perugia, Roselle, and Furconium, let him be compelled to pay one hundred pounds of gold to the aforesaid basilica, half to the Florentine bishop and half to the clerics residing in the same church. Let all those curses which holy Moses wrote in Deuteronomy descend upon him, unless, after being admonished, he makes satisfaction; and let God slay him by the breath of his mouth, like Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive.

Furthermore, so that [Col. 1331D] this document may establish full credibility for those present and for posterity, we have fortified it with our own hand’s subscription and with the impression of the apostolic seal.

I, Boniface, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.

I, Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Gabii, have subscribed.

I, Bruno, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.

I, Stephen, servant of the apostolic see, priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed.

I, John, bishop of Porto, have subscribed.

I, Peter, sinful monk, have subscribed.

I, Desiderius, priest of the holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed.

Given at Florence on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1060, by the hands of Humbert, bishop of the holy [Col. 1332A] Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Nicholas II, in the thirteenth indiction.

### XVI. Nicholas II confirms the possessions and privileges of the church of Saint Andrew of Musciano. (Year 1060.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra* III, 63.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in the Lord John, prior and worthy head of the Church of Saint Andrew of Musciano, and to his confraternity living canonically, and to their successors who shall remain there canonically, perpetually.

Since the condescension of Almighty God, by his freely given gift, has deemed it fitting to raise our humility to this point [Col. 1332B], so that through us it might administer unfailing light to the Church spread throughout the world, we consider it entirely reasonable to provide continually, by appropriate provision, the special governance of the Florentine Church entrusted to our care. Thus we shall be able to imitate the salutary instruction of the Teacher of the nations, who commands that good work ought to be done for all, especially for those of the household of faith, particularly when, according to our abilities, we provide worthy services for places dedicated to divine worship, so that tireless praise may be celebrated in them throughout all ages.

Since stone walls were not built for the purpose of offering praises to the Lord, it plainly seems an excellent thing, for the perfection of the divine work, to arrange the diligent attendance of clerics around venerable places. Unless they are materially supported by suitable earthly stipends, they can scarcely assist at divine worship [Col. 1332C], since the Creator of the world himself, according to the human substance united to him, deigned to endure thirst and hunger, for the glory of him through whom we exist and live and by whose mercy we are governed.

Strengthened by the great urging of the assisting brothers, by the most worthy request of the priest John, venerable head of the Church of Saint Andrew of Musciano, and also by our own decision, in the presence of the faithful of our court and of the patrons of the same church—namely John called Corbacchione, son of Rusticus; Hugh, son of Ubertus; Sichelmus called Morellus, son of Anselm; Rolandino; and Anselm, distinguished sons of Hildebrand [Col. 1332D], son of Leo; and Signorello and Bonomo, distinguished sons of Rodulfus, son of that same Hildebrand—who earnestly implored our devotion on account of their sins, and finally for the future governance of the same church and also for the salvation of the entire people, we offered an apostolic investiture, so that we might grant the church, by privilege and charter, the tithe of their estates and all their property, at least what we could provide for the present, and so that it might be observed inviolate and perpetually in the future.

Receive, holy Lord, almighty and eternal Father, together with your Son and the Holy Spirit, and also with your blessed apostle Andrew, the voluntary gift of Pope Nicholas, long devoted to you; and henceforth and forever undertake, without any dispute, the singular and complete lordship of the possessions of that church through me [Col. 1333A], so that in the hall dedicated to your name a religious clergy may render songs of praise to you, almighty Lord.

Now, therefore, by apostolic privilege we grant, confirm, establish, and perpetually sanction upon an unshakable foundation, in the aforesaid church and canonry of the most blessed apostle Andrew, all the tithes in their entirety from the possessions of the aforementioned men: namely John called Corbacchione; Hugh, son of Ubertus; Morellus, son of Anselm; Rolandino; and Anselm, distinguished sons of Hildebrand, son of Leo; and Signorello and Bonomo, distinguished sons of Rodulfus, himself the son of that same Hildebrand—that is, from all the possessions which the aforesaid men possess, or which others possess through them, or which they may acquire in the future, throughout the entire territory of the parish of Saint Julian situated at Settimo, of the parish of Saint Martin situated at Brozzi, of the parish of Saint Vincent situated at the Pesa, throughout the entire valley of Greve, at Villa Nova, throughout the entire chapel of Saint Paul, and at Casignano, excepting the estates of Cuilatico, whose tithes they must pay to the Florentine canonry.

Moreover, by this same privilege and charter, we firmly grant to the same church all the tithes of those possessions which once belonged to Benzo, son of Petronius of Radda, situated at Godosola, Villa Nova, Saint Paul, Carignano, and other places and under other names throughout the entire parish of the aforesaid church.

In addition, we grant to the same canonry all the tithes of the newly cultivated lands in the woods of the aforementioned men, wherever they are now or shall in the future be worked, and of all other woods whatsoever that are now or shall in the future be worked throughout the entire territory of that church [Col. 1333C].

Likewise, we perpetually and without end grant to the same church all the first fruits of its people; all voluntary offerings, in their entirety, of the living and the dead; all bequests; and free burial for its entire people, especially for its patrons and for all who dwell or shall dwell within the diocese of the aforesaid church.

In short, we grant all estates justly acquired or to be acquired in any manner from any of the faithful.

We also grant and establish perpetually to the canons of the same church the free right to elect their own pastor, to arrange the entire administration of that house, and to present the clerics to their own bishop for ordination [Col. 1333D].

We grant all these things to the clerics canonically remaining in that hall, because formerly, when we exercised the simple office of a bishop, we established and granted them to the aforementioned priest John, its head, and to his confraternity and their successors.

Moreover, we absolve and free the same venerable place and order by apostolic sanction that it remain so. No person, great or small, cleric or lay, shall be permitted to dishonor the clerics canonically dwelling there and harass them by legal summons, or demand from them a due tax or any form of subjection, or on any pretext invade, remove, or diminish the possessions granted or to be granted to them by us or by any of the faithful [Col. 1334A].

Let the aforesaid venerable place remain under the protection of Almighty God, of us, and of our successors, and be subject to no lordship except that of the Florentine bishop. Let that bishop, treating them kindly and honorably and setting aside every excessive exaction, always encourage them.

If anyone, therefore—which we do not believe—with sacrilegious mind attempts to violate what we justly established in the presence of Bishop Humbert, cardinal of Silva Candida; Hildebrand, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church; the bishops of Perugia and Roselle; and Rozo, archpriest of the holy Florentine Church, let him be compelled to pay ten pounds of gold to the aforesaid basilica, half to the Florentine bishop and half to the clerics residing in the same church. Let all those curses which holy Moses described in Deuteronomy descend upon him, unless, after being admonished, he makes satisfaction; and let God slay him by the breath of his mouth, like Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive. Moreover, if he is a cleric, let him be deprived of the office of his order.

Furthermore, so that [Col. 1334B] this document may establish full credibility for those present and for posterity, we have fortified it with the subscription of our own apostolic hand.

I, Nicholas, servant of the servants of God, have subscribed to this document of privilege.

I, Hildebrand, archdeacon of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed.

I, Gerard, bishop of the holy Church of Roselle, was present and subscribed.

I, Rozo, archpriest of the holy Florentine Church.

[Col. 1334C] Given there on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February by the hand of Humbert, bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida, cardinal and librarian of the apostolic see, in the year of the Lord 1059, and in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Nicholas II, in the twelfth indiction. On that same day, in the aforesaid church, by order of the same lord Pope, the bishop Humbert consecrated two altars: one in honor of blessed Mary ever-Virgin and of the holy virgins Prisca and Margaret, and the other in honor of Saint Blaise and of the saints Fabian and Sebastian.

### XVII. Bull of Pope Nicholas II concerning the consecration of the basilica of Saint Lawrence of Florence, subscribed by Saint Peter Damian. (Year 1060.)

[MITTARELLI, *Camaldulian Annals* II, Appendix 164.]

[Col. 1334D]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Giso, rector of the church of Saint Lawrence situated beside the walls of the city of Florence, and to your successors who shall be canonically ordained there, and also to all who shall live there together perpetually.

Since the gracious favor of the Almighty has deigned, by his gratuitous gift, to raise our humility to this office, so that through us he may administer unfailing light to the Church spread throughout the world, we consider it entirely reasonable to provide continually, by special governance, suitable provision for the Florentine Church entrusted to our care. Thus we shall be able to imitate the wholesome instruction of the Doctor of the Gentiles, when, according to our means, we provide worthy services for places dedicated to divine worship—he who commands that good works be imparted to all, especially to those who belong to the household of faith—so that unceasing praise may be celebrated in them throughout all ages.

But because stone walls were not constructed for this purpose, that they might offer fitting praises to God, it plainly seems appropriate, for the completion of the divine work, to arrange for the clergy to attend diligently upon the venerable places. Unless they are supported temporarily by earthly stipends, they can scarcely be adequate for divine worship, since the very Creator of the world, according to the human nature united to him, deigned to endure thirst and hunger.

Therefore, for the glory of him through whom we live and exist, we have, with a gathering of bishops, dedicated with our own hands the basilica of the most precious martyr of Christ, Laurence, which was restored in beautiful form through our exhortation and at the expense of the citizens of Florence. We judged it wholly unworthy to leave it bare and without an endowment, in accordance with the apostolic firmness whose particular duty it is, by striving after what is honorable, to assist all who suffer injury with pious concern.

At the urging of the brothers assisting us, and strengthened also by our own counsel, in the presence of the Florentine people, for the sins of the prelates of that city, and also on account of your devotion, indeed for the salvation of the entire people, we have offered to the altar consecrated by us the apostolic investiture of estates and all their possessions, insofar as we have been able, at least for the present.

Receive, therefore, most holy Laurence, the voluntary gift of Pope Nicholas, long devoted to you; and henceforth and forever undertake the singular and complete dominion of your possessions through me, without any dispute, so that in the hall dedicated to your name the devout clergy may resound songs of praise to almighty God.

Let your estates be designated by the following names: the entire circuit adjoining the church, in its entirety; likewise the demesne which borders the royal field and is surrounded on the west, south, north, and east by a public road. Moreover, beside the river Munio there is a large estate belonging to this church. Finally, we declare that two other estates, one situated at Carditulo and the other at Junkero, which are held by the nephews of Teuzo the cleric, are retained specifically for the administration of the aforesaid Church.

The Mount of Saint Laurence, which on one side borders the land of Saint John, on another that of Saint Romulus, and on a third that of Saint Mary, is granted by right to your Church. Likewise, the estate situated on Mount Hugo is assigned to the jurisdiction of the said church. We have mentioned all these only in outline.

Nevertheless, lest anyone doubt that this church possesses estates much more extensive, we further release it and order by apostolic sanction that this venerable place remain free. No person, great or small, may dishonor the clergy canonically assembled there, harass them by litigation, demand a due tribute from them, or on any pretext invade, remove, or diminish anything granted or to be granted to you by us or by any of the faithful. Let the aforesaid place be exempt from every payment, under the protection of Saint Laurence, and subject to no dominion except that of the bishop of Florence.

If anyone, which we do not believe, should attempt with a sacrilegious mind to violate what was justly established in the presence of Bishop Humbert, cardinal of Silva Candida, and Hildebrand, archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, as well as the bishops of Perugia, Roselle, and Furconium, let him be compelled to pay one hundred pounds of gold to the aforesaid basilica: half to the bishop of Florence and half to the clergy residing in that Church. Unless, after being admonished, he makes satisfaction, may the curses of the Almighty descend upon him, which holy Moses recorded in Deuteronomy; and may God destroy him by the breath of his mouth, like Dathan and Abiron, whom the earth swallowed alive.

Moreover, so that this document may establish full confidence for those present and for posterity, we have fortified it both with the subscription of our own hand and with the impression of the apostolic seal.

**CONFIRM THIS, O GOD, WHICH YOU HAVE WORKED IN US.**

I, Bruno, bishop of Palestrina, have signed.  
I, Peter, the monk called “the Sinner,” have signed.  
I, Peter, bishop of Labicum, have signed.  
I, Boniface, bishop of Albano, have signed.  
I, Desiderius, cardinal priest of the Roman Church, have signed.

Given at Florence on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1060, through the hands of Humbert, bishop of the Holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the first year of the lord Pope Nicholas II, indiction XIII.

## XVIII. Bull of Pope Nicholas II for the canons of Pisaurum. (Year 1060.)

[OLIVIERI, *Memorie per la storia della Chiesa Pesarese nel secolo XIII*. Pesaro, 1779, quarto.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, Urso, venerable provost, and the other canons of the Church of Pisaurum, and to their successors who will dwell there forever.

We fulfill the duty of the oversight entrusted to us if we provide suitable protections for pious and venerable places against the assaults of secular persons. Therefore, since we desire you to advance and persevere in the purpose of canonical life, we receive, in accordance with the tenor of your petition, the aforesaid canonical community, yourselves, and all your possessions under the protection of our defense. Whatever it now appears to possess justly and lawfully, whether in writing or without writing, or whatever it may hereafter acquire in any manner known to human and divine law, we confirm forever through this document of our privilege.

That is: the demesne house beside the Church within the city, and whatever is yours around it; the Church of Saint Clement with all its appurtenances; the estate which Constantine, formerly son of Constantine, assigned to the aforesaid canonical community; and everything which the said canonical community is known to possess or will henceforth justly and lawfully acquire in any manner, whether churches, houses, lands, vineyards, tithes, first fruits, or offerings of the living and the dead, which you ought to have from your mother Church itself or from anywhere else. We confirm all these things forever to you and your successors, who, as stated above, will continue to live there, and we strengthen them by this document of our constitution.

Therefore, by apostolic authority we decree that no person of any ecclesiastical or secular order or dignity, great or small, shall dare to dispossess the aforesaid canonical community, or you or your successors, of their possessions or despoil them in any way, without the sanction of a canonical or local judgment.

If anyone, therefore, should presume with rash audacity to violate the edict of this statute of ours—[lacuna]—and, when admonished according to ecclesiastical custom, should disdain to amend his conduct, let him know that he is to be bound by the bond of anathema and compelled to pay ten pounds of gold—[lacuna]—half to the aforesaid canonical community and half to our sacred Lateran palace. But whoever faithfully observes these provisions out of reverence for the apostolic see shall, through the prayers of the saints, become a possessor of the heavenly kingdom.

Farewell.

**CONFIRM THIS, O GOD, WHICH YOU HAVE WORKED IN US.**

Given at Fano on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in the year from the [lacuna] of the Word 1060, through the hands of Humbert, bishop of the Holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Nicholas II, indiction [Col. 1337C] XIII.

## XIX. Nicholas II confirms the foundation of the abbey of Saint Peter in the town of Ager, and grants certain privileges for its freedom. (Year 1060.)

[COCQUELINES, I, 404.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the clerics living and destined to live canonically in the church constructed in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, in the fortress of Ager: greeting and blessing forever.

Since we must keep diligent watch over the care of the Churches of God entrusted to us, it seems worthy and most honorable to us that we should not cease to assist, defend, support, and enlarge all the Churches of God. Therefore, receiving the Church of Saint Peter, situated in the aforesaid fortress, under the protection and ownership of Saint Peter, we wish in every way to ensure that it remain, supported by the protection of us and of our successors.

We know that it was recently freed by divine power from the authority of the pagans and the error of paganism through our dearest Arnold, a most noble and religious man, adversary and conqueror of the enemies of God, the Hagarenes. We receive it, offered to God and to Saint Peter by him, by his wife Arsendi, for the redemption of their souls, and by Guillelmo, [one] of their sons, as a reward for eternal recompense; and by apostolic authority we have granted it to the ownership of Saint Peter and our own.

We order that it possess, with inviolable force, whatever we can canonically and justly give you in ecclesiastical and worldly matters. No bishop, or any messenger of his, or any other person may demand from the clerics serving there any service, revenue, or subjection concerning anything which it now possesses or will possess. No bishop may prohibit divine worship in the aforesaid church, excommunicate any of the clerics dwelling there, disturb the performance of their office, separate or exclude from it in any way those who come to him for conversion or penance, those who come to hear the divine office, or those who intend to remain there, or otherwise harm them, so that, with every disturbance removed, those living canonically may not be impeded in anything—unless, God forbid, they should do something against their bishop contrary to canonical regulations, for which they ought to suffer this.

We also will and firmly command, by the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul, that the aforesaid church quietly possess and hold forever all churches, cells, and estates belonging to it, both those it now has and those it will acquire; and that in none of its churches may divine worship be prohibited or anyone excommunicated contrary to the commands of the canons, unless the clerics are at fault.

Establishing this by apostolic censure, we decree that no person, great or small, shall presume to demand or receive any census from the same church and all that belongs to it, except the Roman Church, which shall receive a census of ten gold solidi every five years.

Arnold, that most prudent man, together with his wife, son, and descendants, shall receive fitting subjection and honor because, with God’s help, he freed that land from the power and error of the Hagarenes. They shall also have the right to appoint an abbot in the aforesaid church according to their will, provided that he is suitable, competent, and fit for the service of God, and that he is canonically chosen by Arnold together with the clerics of the Church of Saint Peter.

The abbot of the aforesaid church may in no way sell or alienate any estates or castles to the detriment of the church.

If anyone should rashly violate this privilege of ours and, when canonically admonished, disdain to amend his conduct, let him know that he is bound by perpetual bonds of anathema and, in addition, condemned to a penalty of one hundred pounds of gold, half to our sacred palace and half to the aforesaid church.

But whoever strives to be its faithful guardian out of pious devotion, and gives anything of his own to the aforesaid church or renders it assistance, shall, through the prayers of the apostles Peter and Paul, obtain from almighty God forgiveness for all his sins and the glory of eternal blessedness.

Written by the hand of Octavian, scrivener and notary of the sacred palace, in the month of April and indiction XIII.

Given at Rome on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year from the Incarnation of Jesus Christ 1060, in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Nicholas.

I, Bruno, bishop of Palestrina.

[Col. 1339A] I, Arnold, bishop of Arezzo.

I, Cumbertus, prelate of Turin.

I, Anselm, by the mercy of God bishop of Lucca, have acknowledged this.

I, Dodo, by the will of God bishop of Roselle, have acknowledged this.

I, Anselm, by the grace of God bishop of Castro.

I, Godefrid, bishop of Perugia.

I, John, archpriest, have signed. The archpriest of Lucca; Saint Peter’s John; Albert, archpriest, have signed.

Given at Rome on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year from the Incarnation of Jesus Christ 1060, through the hands of Humbert, of the Holy Roman Church and librarian of the apostolic see, and bishop of the Holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Nicholas II, [Col. 1339B] indiction XIII.

## XX. Bull of Nicholas II confirming the rights and possessions of the monastery of Saint Thomas of Aposella, where Pope Clement II died. (Year 1060.)

[MITTARELLI, *Annal. Camald.* II, Appendix, 173, from the original document in the archive of Saint Mary of Porto at Ravenna.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Peter, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Thomas the Apostle, situated in the county of Pisaurum beside the river Aposella, and to his successors who will be regularly appointed there forever.

Such is the authority of the apostolic see that firmness is sought from it in all things, and nothing is considered stable unless it has been confirmed by its strength. Since we preside over it and, though unworthy, exercise the office of blessed Peter, we ought with every diligence to direct and assist those who serve God and are filled with divine fear, so that, supported by our protection, they may serve God without any impediment and remain more freely in his service.

Therefore, at the intercession of our brother Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, and of Peter, abbot of the same monastery, together with his spiritual monks living according to the rule, we have decreed to confirm and strengthen for the Church of Saint Thomas the Apostle and its present and future rectors both the movable and immovable possessions which it now has or will possess forever, so that the monastery of the aforesaid Church may remain in complete security and quiet, and God may be served there.

Moved by the prayers, as we have said, of the religious monks, we strengthen, confirm, and establish these things for you and your successors in the same monastery, over which you now preside and over which they must preside forever. Moreover, we make it quiet and secure from every attack and injury by men, so that no one may dare to inflict any harassment or injury upon the same monastery.

By apostolic censure we decree that no emperor, king, duke, marquis, count, viscount, nor any archbishop or bishop—especially the bishop of the diocese of Pisaurum, whoever he may now be or may hereafter become—nor the citizens of that place, nor any other person, great or small, shall presume to inflict any loss or harm upon the aforesaid monastery of Saint Thomas or upon any of its possessions, whether those it now has or those it will possess forever.

Furthermore, we grant and confirm to the aforesaid monastery all the land, together with its chapels and appurtenances, which the lord Pope Clement, who died there, offered to the aforesaid monastery forever for the remedy of his soul and the restoration of the Church. It lies in the county of Pisaurum within these boundaries: on the first side, the stream Reanus; on the second side, the bank of Pizele, as it runs to the Rock of Acero and reaches the public road leading to Lavacelli; on the third side, the stream which seasonally runs above the fortress of Liciole; and on the fourth side, the river Aposella, which runs as far as your monastery itself, together with Mount Calvello, the Gelata valley, and the fortress of Liciole, with everything enclosed within these boundaries: lands, fields, houses, vineyards, trees, fruit-bearing and fruitless, and everything generally and universally belonging to the aforesaid land.

Moreover, we confirm forever to the same monastery the tower within the city of Pisaurum called Castellione, with its appurtenances inside and outside, as far as the gate called Fanestra.

Therefore, by this our decree we annul, and wish and command always to be considered annulled, those grants which the sons of Ungar possessed concerning that land, so that they may have no value or validity. Through this decree we grant the land forever to you and your successors, from us, for the remedy of the soul of that Pope Clement and of our own.

This is done, however, on the condition that you pay annually from it one gold bezant to the appointed officials of the Holy Roman Church at the proper time.

If anyone should rashly violate this privilege of ours and, when canonically admonished, disdain to amend his conduct, let him know that he is bound by the bonds of perpetual anathema and, in addition, condemned to a penalty of fifty pounds of gold, half to our sacred Lateran palace and half to the aforesaid monastery.

But whoever strives to preserve these provisions out of pious devotion shall, through the prayers of the apostles Peter and Paul, obtain from almighty God forgiveness for all his sins and the glory of eternal blessedness.

Written by the hand of John, scrivener of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of April and indiction XIII.

I, Peter, bishop of Gabii, have signed.

I, Bruno, bishop of Palestrina, have signed.

I, John, bishop of Porto, have signed.

I, Peter, the monk called “the Sinner,” and bishop, have signed.

I, Stephen, called a monk and priest of the title of Saint Grisogonus, have signed.

Given at Rome on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord Jesus 1060, through the hands of Humbert, bishop of the Holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Nicholas II, indiction XIII.

## XXI. Privilege of Pope Nicholas II for the monastery of nuns of Saint Julia of Brescia. (Year 1060.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullar. Casin.* II, 95, from the archive of the monasteries of Saints Saviour and Julia of Brescia.]

[Col. 1341A]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest daughter in the Lord, Otta, abbess of the monastery of the Lord Saviour and of Saint Julia, virgin and martyr, called the New, situated in the city of Brescia, and to your successors, both present and future.

Since whatever is reasonably and suitably requested by the faithful ought always to be granted, out of devotion to our gracious Creator we must in no way deny our generosity when privileges are being bestowed.

Therefore, because your affection humbly petitioned our apostolic dignity that the aforesaid monastery of the Lord Saviour, as well as that of Saint Julia, virgin and martyr, constructed within the city of Brescia by the most pious Queen Ansa, should be adorned with the privileges of the apostolic see, so that the monastery of the Lord Saviour, subjected by the aforesaid most pious Queen Ansa always under royal right and authority, might never be subjected to the dominion of any other jurisdiction, power, or administration, we willingly grant your pious desires and what you have requested through this authority of our privilege.

Therefore we prohibit any priest or any other person from exercising in the aforesaid monastery or in its appurtenances any jurisdiction, power, authority, or administration other than the supreme authority and disposition of royal power. Thus no priest may presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there in any way unless he has been invited by the abbess of that monastery.

Finally, by this apostolic authority we establish that no person, great or small, shall presume to inflict any harm upon the same venerable monastery, whether upon the women servants of God, the households of either sex, or the free persons residing upon the land of the same monastery, or upon any of its possessions and properties, whether houses or any movable or immovable goods.

Likewise, we grant and confirm to the same venerable monastery the jurisdiction over servants and free persons, and the tithes and first fruits of all your labors belonging to the basilicas and cells constructed on the lands of the same monastery, just as they are held to have been granted and strengthened there by the aforesaid Queen Ansa from the most pious King Desiderius and from his royal and imperial successors, and by our predecessors, the pontiffs of the Holy Roman Church.

Moreover, we confirm to the same venerable place certain estates: Sermione, Cervaniga, Nuvolaria, Berciagum, Macho, Vico, Guarsenagum, Barbada, Alsianum, Monticello, Novum, Calato, Ciconiaria, Miliaria, and Sormida, with all their appurtenances; and also all the other estates, villages, castles, cells, and churches established on the lands of the same monastery, and everything belonging to that monastery.

Whatever else, by God’s gift, you may lawfully and canonically acquire in the future shall remain secure and inviolate for you, your successors, and the same monastery.

We also grant that the abbess appointed at any time in that monastery shall have the power to build castles and churches wherever she wishes on the lands belonging to the aforesaid monastery.

Chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or basilicas, the ordination of abbesses or nuns, or of clerics who are to be advanced to holy orders, and whatever pertains to the sacred ministry, when requested from any Catholic prelates, shall be granted freely and without any reproach, just as Anselperga, the first abbess of the same monastery, obtained from Paul, pontiff of the apostolic see of blessed memory, on account of the weakness of the female sex.

Finally, establishing this by apostolic censure, we command that no bishop, duke, marquis, count, viscount, gastald, or any person, great or small, presume to exercise jurisdiction in any places of that monastery, to hold court or conduct any hearing without the permission of the abbess, to alienate or invade the ecclesiastical or secular possessions of the monastery in any way, or to inflict any harm there. Nor may anyone dare to demand from them fodrum, lodging-tax, river toll, prepared provisions, or any public services.

Wherever the abbess wishes to establish a market or build in the places of the monastery, no one may presume to oppose her. We also grant the fisheries belonging to the aforesaid monastery to that monastery, and by apostolic authority we command that no one dare invade them or interfere with them.

All these provisions mentioned above we confirm, grant, and strengthen by apostolic authority, according to the aforesaid terms, to you, Otta, abbess and daughter in the Lord, and to your successors, beginning with the present indiction XIII, through this document of our privilege.

But if any rash person, which we do not wish, should attempt to act against this privilege of ours and fail to allow it to remain as it was granted and strengthened by our apostolic authority, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. He shall likewise be burned with the devil and Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the punishment of eternal fire. In addition, let him know that he must pay thirty pounds of gold, half to our sacred palace and half to the aforesaid monastery.

But whoever proves in all things to be an observer out of pious regard, preserving the provisions of this privilege of ours that pertain to the worship of God, shall receive the grace of blessing from the most merciful Lord God and be deemed worthy to share in eternal life forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1343A] Written by the hand of Octavian, scrivener and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day of the month of May, indiction XIII.

Given at Rome on the third day before the Nones of May, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1070, through the hands of Humbert, bishop of the Holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Nicholas II, indiction XIII.

## XXII. Privilege of Pope Nicholas II for the royal monastery of Saints Saviour and Julia of Brescia. (Year 1060.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullar. Casinens.*, vol. II, p. 96, from the archive of the monastery of Saint Julia of Brescia.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest daughter in the Lord, Ermengard, abbess of the monastery of our Lord Saviour and of Saint Julia, virgin and martyr, called the New, founded within the city of Brescia by the most pious Queen Ansa; namely, to you and to your successors in office, forever.

Since whatever is reasonably and suitably requested by the faithful ought always to be granted, out of devotion to our gracious Creator we must in no way deny our generosity when privileges are bestowed.

Therefore, because your pious affection humbly petitioned our apostolate that the aforesaid monastery of our Lord Jesus Christ the Saviour, as well as that of the most blessed virgin and martyr Julia, constructed within the city of Brescia by the aforementioned Queen Ansa, should be adorned with the privileges of the apostolic see, so that the said monastery, subjected by its foundress always under royal right and authority, might never be subjected to the dominion of any other jurisdiction, power, or administration, we willingly grant your pious desires and what you have requested through this authority of our privilege.

Therefore we prohibit any priest or any other person from exercising in the aforesaid monastery any jurisdiction, power, authority, or administration other than the supreme authority and disposition of royal power. Thus no priest may presume to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there in any way unless he has been invited by the abbess of the often-mentioned monastery.

Finally, by this apostolic authority we establish that no person, great or small, shall presume to inflict any harm upon the same venerable monastery, whether upon the women servants of God, the households of either sex, or the free persons residing upon the lands of the same monastery, or upon any of its movable or immovable possessions.

Likewise, we grant and confirm to the same venerable monastery jurisdiction over servants and free persons, and the tithes and first fruits of all those who labor for the basilicas or cells lawfully and justly belonging to the same monastery, just as they are held to have been granted and strengthened there by the decree of the aforementioned Queen Ansa and of her royal and imperial successors, and by our predecessors, the pontiffs of the Holy Roman Church.

Moreover, we confirm to the same venerable monastery certain estates long possessed and endowed by the often-mentioned monastery: namely Sermione, Cervaniga, Nuvolaria, Berciagum, Barbada, Alfianum, Calvato, Ciconiaria, Millarina, and Sormida; likewise Gosenagum Novum and Monticello, with all the basilicas belonging to the same monastery: one at Sermione, one at Nuvolaria, two at Berciagum, one at Barbada, one at Alfianum, one at Ciconaria, and one at Millarina. Also, the other estates, villages, castles, basilicas, and everything belonging to the same monastery that can be said or named.

Chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or basilicas, the ordination of abbesses, monks, or other clerics who are to be advanced to holy orders, and whatever pertains to the sacred mystery, when requested from any Catholic prelates, shall be granted freely and without reproach, just as Anselperga, the first abbess of the same monastery, obtained from Paul, pontiff of the apostolic see of blessed memory, on account of the weakness of the female sex.

When the abbess of the aforesaid place dies, no one shall be placed there through any stratagem of concealment or by force, except one whom the sisters, by common consent or the sounder part of the community, elect according to the fear of God and the rule of Saint Benedict.

We also grant that the abbess appointed at any time in that monastery shall have the power to build churches, establish a market, and construct castles wherever she wishes on the lands belonging to the aforesaid monastery.

Finally, establishing this by apostolic censure, we command that no bishop, duke, marquis, count, viscount, gastald, or any person, great or small, presume to exercise jurisdiction in any places of that monastery, to judge, or to hold any hearing without the permission of the abbess; nor may anyone alienate the ecclesiastical or secular possessions of the monastery in any way, inflict harm there, or dare to demand or exact fodrum, lodging-tax, river toll, prepared provisions, or any public services.

All these provisions mentioned above we confirm, grant, and strengthen by apostolic authority, according to the aforesaid terms, to you, Ermengard, daughter in the Lord, and to your successors in office, beginning with the present third indiction, through this document of our privilege. Strive always to possess the fear of God and every virtue in your hearts, so that you may always be considered more worthy of this grace; and the freer you are from secular disturbances, the more eagerly may you strive to please God with every virtue of mind and soul.

But if any archbishop, bishop, emperor, king, prince, duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person should rashly attempt, which we do not wish, to act against this privilege of ours and fail to allow it to remain as it was granted and strengthened by our apostolic authority, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose office we, though unworthy, exercise. He shall likewise be burned with the devil and Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, in eternal fire.

But whoever proves in all things to be an observer out of pious regard, preserving the provisions of this privilege of ours that pertain to the worship of God, shall receive the grace of blessing from the most merciful Lord God and be deemed worthy to share in eternal life forever and ever. Amen.

Written by the hand of Octavian, scrivener and notary of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Ides of May, in the aforementioned indiction XIII.

Given at Rome on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1060, through the hands of Humbert, bishop of the Holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Nicholas II, in the indiction stated above.

## XXIII. The consecration of the altars of the basilica of Farfa by Nicholas II, Roman pontiff, and the confirmation by the same pontiff of the freedom of that monastery. (Year 1060.)

[MURATORI, *Antiq. Ital.* V, 1039.]

In the name of the Lord, Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

Out of reverence for the holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin, and our Lady Mary, after, with God’s favor, we had honorably completed the renewal of the consecration of this Church of Farfa, wishing henceforth by divine authority—namely, that of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and of blessed Mary ever-Virgin, blessed Michael the archangel, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and all the saints venerated in heaven and on earth—to restrain and destroy the invasions, plunderings, and thefts from the property of this monastery committed by wicked men of whatever dignity or rank, we excommunicate and anathematize, and expel from the thresholds of holy Mother Church, those who have violently carried away, or henceforth carry away, from this monastery of Saint Mary pigs, oxen, or sheep, or any other animals, or footwear or clothing, or books, or crops, wheat, wine, or bread, or various utensils; or who have stolen such things, or henceforth presume to do so, or continue to receive them for a longer time or outside [the monastery]. [Col. 1345C]

Therefore, let them receive the curse of the abyss lying below, and the heavenly curse, and the earthly curse. Let them receive the present curse in the weakening of their bodies. Let them be cursed with the accursed in perdition and the torment of their souls; scourged with the ungrateful; perish with the proud; tormented with the blasphemers; tortured in hell. Let them be accursed with those who blaspheme the name of the Lord; let them be accursed with the despairing; let them be accursed in the east and in the west; let them be accursed in the south and the north; let them be accursed by day and by night; [Col. 1345D] accursed within and without; accursed on the right and on the left. Let them be accursed in the house and in the field; accursed standing and sitting, walking and remaining in place; accursed drinking and eating; accursed waking and sleeping. May the sun grow dark for them while it is still midday, and may they be attacked by the devil and his angels. May their souls be tortured with pains, and may their lamp be extinguished for ever and ever. Amen—unless they come to satisfaction and suitable reparation. [Col. 1346A]

### XXIV. Letter of Nicholas II to R. . . ., count of Rouergue

He urges him to be a defender of churches and the poor, and to restore to the monastery of Verdun certain possessions that he unjustly retains.

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to R., beloved son and count of Rouergue, greetings and apostolic blessing. [Col. 1346B]

Having learned the purpose of your mind, and that for the sake of the kingdom of God and his justice you have wished to renounce the temporal eminence of secular occupations, we confidently declare to you that, in accordance with what we enjoined upon you when we spoke face to face, you should set yourself forward as a defender of the Churches of God and of the poor. By securing justice for them, you may stand acquitted before God, since you do not carry the sword without cause.

And because it is our duty to admonish you whenever we learn that you are neglecting something that ought not to be neglected, we admonish and command you, praying and at the same time ordering by apostolic authority, to restore to the monastery of Saint Peter situated at Verdun—which the venerable man Waleran, your kinsman, governs as abbot—the estates that it is known to possess within the territory of your property. [Col. 1346C] Otherwise—God forbid!—by retaining them longer, to the perdition of your soul, you will incur the excommunication invoked by our predecessors against their invaders.

Nor do we wish you to say that these were taken from the servants of God by your parents or by your wife’s parents, because the just Lord repays the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation. For, as antiquity, conscious of the truth, bears witness, Saint Amantius, your particular patron, handed them over for the use of the servants of Saint Peter.

### XXV. Letter of Nicholas II to the clergy of Sisteron, in which he commends Bishop Gerard and prescribes certain matters for him

(About the year 1060.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, vol. XI, p. 494.]

[Col. 1346D]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy, order, and people residing in the city of Sisteron, greetings and apostolic blessing, if they obey.

[Note: Certain supreme pontiffs had added these words to the address of their letters; but after giving the salutation, Nicholas II was the first to use “apostolic blessing” consistently and uniformly. (*Literary History*, vol. VII, p. 521).]

Since it is our duty to care for the universal Church, we ought to strive to benefit everyone everywhere. Therefore, for your salvation, we have appointed as your priest our brother and fellow bishop Gerard, elected by religious men living in the regions of Gaul—namely, by our venerable brother Hugh of Cluny, who was acting in those regions in our place; by the archbishop of Arles; the bishop of Avignon; the bishop of Chalon; the bishop of Apt; the bishop of Vaison; the bishop of Digne; and the bishop of Die. [Col. 1347A] With these men as witnesses, we have no doubts concerning his life.

We have instructed him never to presume to perform ordinations for one who has not taken a virgin as his wife, nor for an illiterate man, nor for anyone physically impaired in any part of his body, nor for anyone from among the penitent, or subject to a cure [parish charge], or liable to any other condition, and marked as such, to approach the sacred orders; but if he should happen to discover persons of this kind, he must not dare to promote them.

He must in no circumstances receive Africans who everywhere put themselves forward for ecclesiastical orders, because some of them have been found to be Manichaeans and some to have been rebaptized.

He must not strive to diminish the ministries or adornment of the Church, or anything else belonging to its patrimony, but to increase them. [Col. 1347B]

As for the Church’s income or the offerings of the faithful, he must make four portions: one he should retain for himself; a second he should distribute to the clergy in proportion to their diligent performance of their offices; a third to the poor and pilgrims; and the fourth he should understand to be reserved for ecclesiastical buildings. For these matters he will have to render an account at the divine judgment.

He should also know that the ordinations of priests and deacons are to be celebrated only during the fasts of the fourth, seventh, or tenth months, and also at the beginning of Lent and on the middle evening of Saturday. The sacraments of holy baptism, moreover, should be administered only on the feast of Easter and Pentecost; except that those who are pressed by the danger of death, lest they perish eternally, must be aided by such remedies. [Col. 1347C]

Now, therefore, it is fitting that he who observes the commands of our see should obey with devoted minds, so that the body of the Church may become irreproachable and pleasing through Jesus Christ, etc.

[Note: Gerard, or Gerard II, was elected bishop of Sisteron at the great Council of Avignon by Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny and legate of Pope Nicholas II. Sent by the council to Nicholas, he was consecrated by him as bishop of Sisteron. Furnished with this bull or letter, the pope directed him to his see. Treated indignantly by the people of Sisteron, he went to Forcalquier, where he was honorably received. This Council of Avignon is omitted from collections of councils. Honoratus Bouche observes that its acts were formerly preserved in the archive of Forcalquier but are now missing. The date of this council cannot be later than the year 1061, when Nicholas II died, since it was held during his pontificate. (*New Christian Gaul*, vol. I, col. 483.)] [Col. 1348D]

### XXVI. Letter of Nicholas II to Gervase, archbishop of Reims

(1059–1061.)

[DUCHESNE, *Writers of the History of the Franks*, IV, 198.]

[Col. 1347D]

Nicholas, servant of the servants of God, to Gervase, venerable archbishop, greetings with apostolic blessing.

Although certain unfavorable reports concerning your brotherhood, and matters that could not be dismissed without investigation, have reached the apostolic see—namely, that you favored those who had invaded it and that you had set aside pontifical acts—nevertheless, because a person of no slight standing has defended you by testimony, and because you are instead praised for your fidelity to Saint Peter, we pass over these matters and desire that the testimony concerning you prove true.

You, for your part, must strive with every effort to live in such a way that your enemies have no means by which they can grieve us concerning you. [Col. 1348A] For you know how kindly the common mother, the holy Roman Church, has treated you, and how great is her confidence in you, so that through your diligence you might come to the aid of the Church of the Franks, which has almost fallen.

Therefore, act as the apostolic see has hoped you would. Rebuke, entreat, and admonish your glorious king, lest he be led astray by the counsel of the worst men, who think that through our disagreement they can evade apostolic censure. Let him beware of resisting the sacred canons—and indeed blessed Peter—and of stirring against himself us, who wish to love him as the pupil of our eye.

For it is astonishing enough that the bishop of Mâcon should, on behalf of some fool—as he is—whom he wished to have ordained, wish to offend God and Saint Peter and to make light of our affection and sincere love toward him. [Col. 1348B] Does some member of Antichrist suppose that the grace of blessed Peter cannot benefit him more than the treacherous loyalty of all the impious?

Let the glorious king act against us as he pleases, since we are always prepared to pray to God for him and for his army. As for Duke Gotfrid, let no one frighten you when it is necessary for you to come to Rome, for he will not merely fail to obstruct you but will also faithfully render you service.

Our dearest brothers, the cardinal bishops, salute you, as does the humility of our son Hildebrand.

### XXVII. Nicholas II urges Anna, queen of Gaul, to encourage the king to govern according to the principles of piety and justice and to preserve the condition of the Church

(1059–1061.)

[Col. 1348C]

[The author of this letter is Peter Damian. See his letters, *Works*, vol. I, p. 124.]

### XXVIII. Nicholas II commands Gervase, archbishop of Reims, to repair the injuries inflicted upon the Church of Verdun

(1059–1061.)

[DUCHESNE, *Writers of the History of the Franks*, IV, 199.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gervase, archbishop of the Church of Reims, greetings and apostolic blessing. [Col. 1348D]

Since it has been entrusted to us and handed over by the authority of blessed Peter—upon whom the foundation of the universal Church has been established—to correct errors and to strive so that the members joined to our head may not be discordant, we paternal­ly command you, as one who is, so to speak, among the members of ourselves and of the holy Roman Church, that, through you, whom we hope to be enclosed in the bosom of your mother, namely the universal Church, you henceforth permit no injury to be inflicted upon the Church of Verdun, which has been entrusted to us together with our brothers, either by you or by your men. [Col. 1349A]

As for the loss and injury that both you and your men have recently inflicted upon the brothers of that same Church, we admonishingly order you, with every pretext removed, to make complete restitution, both for the sake of the holy Roman Church and out of love for us. This concerns the plunder from Postviller, which came under your authority, and from Mecla, which Engobrandus pillaged: the plunder consisted of 264 animals, the number written below.

As for the canonical clerics of that same Church, command that they be released from captivity without any delay, so that, for having diligently carried out this matter and the matters mentioned above, you may deserve to possess both the favor of the prince of the apostles and ours.

### XXIX. Letter of Nicholas II to Gervase, archbishop of Reims

(1059–1061.)

[DUCHESNE, *Writers of the History of the Franks*, IV, 199.]

[Col. 1349B]

Nicholas, servant of the servants of God, to Gervase, venerable archbishop, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since, through the report of our son G., we have learned that you persist in fidelity to blessed Peter and reverently rise to meet his authority in all things, we embrace you with paternal affection as a most beloved son and, in embracing you, love you with the whole affection of our mind.

Indeed, so long as you show yourself a faithful son, our fatherhood will never be lacking to you; rather, it will support you with due affection, and our authority will ceaselessly protect you. [Col. 1349C]

Concerning what you sent us through our son about the bishop of Senlis, because it is canonical, we grant it to you together with that same son of ours. For we do not wish to oppose justice, for which, if necessary, we consider it gain to die.

As for our coming to Francia, we presently write to you no certainty. When our son comes to you, he himself will inform you both about this and about all other matters.

We also command and order you to make peace with our dearest son the duke, so that your men may be able to come to us safely and we may be able to hear them. For we do not wish two sons so dear to us to remain in discord.

### XXX. Letter of Nicholas II to Lanfranc

(1059–1061.)

[THEINERUS, *Critical Investigations*, p. 206.]

[Col. 1349D]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his brother Lanfranc, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Dearest brother, I would gladly see your much-desired presence and would gladly be refreshed by your counsel in our ecclesiastical concerns; for we have heard that you are highly useful in Roman and apostolic service.

But since this perhaps cannot now happen so easily, we wish your present station to be fruitful for us and for the Roman mother Church, so that from the fruit of your station the desirable fruit of your coming may also be recognized.

Therefore, we are sending to your charity these sons of our affection, chaplains of the emperor and our own, to be instructed by you in the arts of dialectic and rhetoric. [Col. 1350A] Just as, thanks be to God, we have heard that you are outstanding in this twofold field, so we may see them, together with you, as outstanding—whether in Rome as soon as you can come, or perhaps when I soon come to you.

But if, as we have heard, the divine page keeps you from such study, then on behalf of Saint Peter and ourselves we command you, and in true obedience we charge you, to instruct those whom we are now sending to your affection; and we leave them to your charity to be assisted in every way.

As for your count, our friend, whom we have heard, thanks be to God, readily submits to your counsels, guard him in such a way that here and in Christ he may be able to prosper. [Col. 1350B] For I have good hopes concerning him, whose counsel and way of life I hear that he shares with you.

If you can bear fruit among the clergy and among that rough people, so that you may finally deserve to hear concerning the talent entrusted to you: “Well done, good servant,” amen.

### XXXI. Bull of Pope Nicholas II to Grimald John the priest and others

(1061.)

[SPERANDIO, *Sacred Sabina*, p. 272.]

[Col. 1350C]

John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Grimald John the priest, Benedict the judge, Martin son of Sabinus, Riccho de Raynerio, John de Abizza, Martin de Joanne, Peter de Urso, Leo de Lupo, Peter de Hendo, Homo de Martino, and to their sons and heirs, and to whatever associates they may appoint as advocates in the matter written below, for all time.

Since it is our office to watch over the interests of all the Churches of God, it is nevertheless fitting that we diligently concern ourselves with the welfare of the Roman and apostolic see, over which, by God’s authorization, we preside.

Therefore, since we have acquired for Saint Peter in perpetual right the castle called Roccha de Antiquo from Grimald, son of Benedict, and Teobald, together with all its appendages and dependencies, by this charter of our privilege we grant and confirm it to you, to those associates, and to these and other advocates appointed by you in the same matter, as well as to your sons and heirs; and we strengthen it forever in the following manner and form:

With its appendages, after rebuilding the houses, you shall summon there as many inhabitants as you can from among your own people. House by house and household by household, each of you shall annually pay, according to the extent of his ability, as a rent at Easter, the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, to blessed Peter, to us, and to our successors: the greater men twelve denarii; those of the lower rank, *retrogradu* [uncertain printed reading], eight denarii; the third [rank], six denarii; and the fourth, two denarii. [Col. 1350D]

You shall also provide the fodrum and faithfully observe the court obligations owed to us, our successors, and our messengers in the territory of Sabina on account of these possessions.

We also establish and decree by apostolic authority that you shall remain tranquil under the protection and defense of the apostolic see and secure from every molestation and attack; and that henceforth you shall be subject to no emperor, duke, marquis, or count, but only to the Roman and apostolic see and its messengers.

If any person, great or small, presumes to act against this charter of privilege, let that person know that he is bound by the bond of anathema. Moreover, if any of us, or of our successors, or any one of you, or of your heirs, successors, or associates, fails to observe all these acts and statutes, let that person know that he must pay one pound of fine gold for each house or household. [Col. 1351A]

But whoever strives to be an observant person out of pious devotion may obtain from almighty God, through the prayers of the princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, forgiveness for all his sins and the glory of eternal reward.

Written by the hand of Octavian, scrivener and notary of the sacred palace, in the month of April, in the fourteenth indiction.

Given at Rome on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 1061 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, by the hand of Humbert, bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the apostolic see, in the third year of Lord Nicholas, in the fourteenth indiction. [Col. 1351B]

### XXXII. Bull of Pope Nicholas II for the monastery of Saint-Denis

(1061.)

[DOUBLET, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, p. 464.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all kings, bishops, and princes, present and future, now and in times to come.

It is fitting that apostolic dignity lend an ear to appropriate petitions, so that venerable places, if they have been exalted by our authority, may now and in the future remain valid and entirely unshaken. [Col. 1351C]

Therefore, let the unity of all present and future kings, bishops, and all the faithful of the apostolic see know that the brothers of the venerable monastery of Christ’s martyr Dionysius, where the Lord himself rests bodily, have implored our benevolence, asking that we issue for them a privilege of apostolic dignity concerning a certain small abbey belonging to the aforesaid place.

This small abbey is in the county of Alsace, situated in the Vosges forest, and is called Lebroha. Abbot Fulrad founded it from his own property, through the munificence of the lord Charles, the most invincible emperor, and gave it to his most glorious patron, namely Lord Dionysius. [Col. 1351D]

Considering and recognizing that their petition is just, we promulgate and decree by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that the aforesaid small abbey, supported by apostolic confirmation, shall remain forever inviolate and devoted to the place of Saint Dionysius.

We also establish by the authority of blessed Peter that no king, no bishop, no abbot, nor anyone endowed with any dignity whatsoever, dare disturb that place in any way—not in its villages, not in its serfs, not in its gold, not in its silver, not in its clothing, nor in any other possessions—as is fully contained in the privileges of our predecessors, namely Lords Stephen, Leo, and another Nicholas, and also in the charters of the aforesaid Charles the Great, Henry, and the other emperors and kings. [Col. 1352A]

We therefore decree that the things contained in the charter of this decree and ordinance of ours shall be preserved forever, both by you and by all who shall succeed you in the rank and place in which you now stand, by the authority and honor of the holy Roman Church and by the privilege of the apostolic see.

But if any person, great or small, presumes with rash daring to act against this apostolic decree of ours, let that person know that he is bound by the bond of anathema, wholly alien from the kingdom of God, and condemned, together with all the impious, to the punishment of eternal fire.

But whoever proves an observer of this decree may deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from the most benevolent Lord Jesus Christ.

Farewell.

[Col. 1352B] Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Humbert, chancellor of the holy apostolic see, in the Lateran basilica, in the third year of Lord Nicholas II, pope, in the twelfth indiction.

### XXXIII. Privilege of Pope Nicholas II for the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme

(1061.)

[LAUNOI, *Works*, III, 354.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Oderic, religious abbot of the venerable monastery of Vendôme, and to all his successors who shall regularly be advanced there, forever.

A fitting and ready assent is owed to just petitions that look to the peace of the servants of God. [Col. 1352C] Therefore, concerning the monastery of the holy and undivided Trinity situated near the castle of Vendôme—which we know was offered to blessed Peter and to the Roman Church as freehold and patrimony by its founders, namely Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and Agnes, his most noble countess-wife—we decree by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, in accordance both with the wish of the founders of that place and with the desire of your holiness, dearest son Abbot Oderic, as follows:

No person whatsoever shall stand between the pontiff of the apostolic see and the abbot of that venerable place.

We also establish that, when the abbot dies, his successor shall be elected from the same congregation, provided that someone worthy of such a government is found. [Col. 1352D] But if no worthy person is found among them—God forbid!—the monks shall arrange to elect for themselves, according to God, a father from Cluny, or from a greater monastery, or from wherever they can best obtain one; yet not without the counsel of three abbots whom they can find to be the most religious in neighboring places.

The elected abbot shall not immediately be compelled to come to Rome, but may receive consecration from whichever Catholic bishop he wishes. The monks shall take care to inform the pope by letter how the election or ordination was carried out, so that he may either correct what needs correcting, if necessary, or, if the election or consecration was made according to God and our decree, rejoice with fitting goodwill and confirm it himself.

We also order that the abbot himself, who is known to be a freeholder of the Roman Church, shall not be summoned to a council by that bishop or by any representative of the apostolic see, nor be compelled to attend; but he himself, or his legate, shall strive to visit the Roman Church. [Col. 1353A]

As for the annual census of twelve solidi in the coinage of his own region, established by the founders of the place, we wish it to be paid to blessed Peter for perpetual remembrance and acknowledgment.

If, however, a legate of the Roman Church should wish to visit the aforesaid place of blessed Peter, let him be received there with every courtesy, and let the brothers diligently provide him with whatever is necessary for the body, according to the ability of the place.

But he himself shall not presume to correct anything in that place on his own, or to harass the rector of the place or the brothers on the pretext of his legation. If he sees anything that ought to be corrected, he may report it to the pope by letter. [Col. 1353B]

We also confirm that the place of Saint Saviour, built near the walls of the city of Angers, shall always remain under the monastery of Vendôme, and that no rector or provost shall ever be appointed there except by the will of the abbot of Vendôme.

Relying also upon the confidence of apostolic authority, we prohibit anyone ever from exercising power or domination, or from excommunicating or imposing an interdict, in the monastery of Vendôme or in the aforesaid church of Saint Saviour, except the pope alone—even if the region of Chartres or Angers has been excommunicated or placed under interdict. Nevertheless, they must not receive excommunicated persons.

We confirm and strengthen by our authority everything that has been offered to that place by the founders themselves or by other persons up to this day, so that it may remain forever, without diminution or any withdrawal, in the right of that same place. [Col. 1353C]

If anyone wishes to bring a case against the aforesaid place of blessed Peter concerning any possessions, the abbot or brothers shall not answer him before consulting the Roman pontiff, because anything decided or diminished without the judgment of us or our successors shall be void.

These are the possessions known to belong to the aforesaid monastery:

In the county of Vendôme: the Church of Ferraria and the estate of Prunet; also the churches that Theoderic, bishop of Chartres, gave to the monastery of Vendôme; the Church of Saint Beatus; the Church of Saint John of Châteaudun; the Church of Balneola; the Church of Valle Rebla; the Church of Autheni.

In the bishopric of Le Mans: the Church of Saint John of Villa Dei, and the villa itself with all its customary dues; the Church of Saint Michael of Hullet, with its mills and woods and all its customary dues.

In the forest of Gastines: all the pannage from the monastery’s own pigs; half the pannage from other people’s animals; and the honey and wax of that forest. Also, all the Vendôme monks and all their people may take timber for every use of theirs on the monastery’s lands without the foresters’ permission. [Col. 1353D]

In the bishopric of Angers: the Church of Saint Saviour near Angers; the Church of Saint John upon the Loire, with nineteen arpents of vineyards and two mills; the Church of Saint Saturninus and the whole parish; the forest called Later and the forest land, if the forest should be cleared; at the castle of Craon, the parish church of Saint Clement.

A dispute concerning this arose between the men of Vendôme and the monks of Saint-Albini in our presence, and by judgment of the apostolic see it was adjudicated to the monastery of Vendôme.

Also, the church of the borough of Méduanil, and the entire borough with all its integrity; the entire Church of blessed Peter of Maziac.

In the county of Poitiers: the Church of Olona and the Church of blessed Martin of Avalia. [Col. 1354A]

In the county of Scone, on Oleron: the Church of Saint George and one-third part of the church of the island, with all its customary dues.

At the castle of Oleron: the parish church of Saint Mary; the Church of Rodii Rebelli; the Church of Blasneriac; the Church of Saint Saturninus; the land of Saint Saturninus; and the land of Saint Anianus, with its saltworks, fisheries, and all its dependencies.

If the abbot of the aforesaid place has a complaint against the count of Vendôme, or against any of his men, whatever honor that man may possess, the complaint shall be settled in the court of the monastery of Vendôme, for the dignity and veneration of the place; nor shall anyone seek or grant, in the court of that monastery itself, half of any forfeiture. [Col. 1354B]

Furthermore, we wish it to be known to the faithful of the holy Church of God, and to be attached to this confirmation of ours, that Theoderic, bishop of Chartres, in whose diocese the aforesaid monastery of Vendôme is known to be situated, sent his letter to the presence of Pope Clement, asking him to strengthen that monastery by his authority in such a way that none of his successors after him would be permitted to take away or diminish the possessions of that place, excommunicate or interdict it, exercise power or domination there, or dare to disturb the rector of the place or the brothers in any way. Pope Clement graciously consented to this, and we have judged it worthy to consent to it by our authority as well. [Col. 1354C]

If anyone becomes a violator of this command of ours, unless he repents and also makes satisfaction to the Church, let him know that by apostolic authority he has been struck with perpetual anathema, separated from the body of the aforesaid Church, and handed over to the devil together with the impious.

But whoever is a preserver of and obedient to this confirmation of ours and to apostolic authority, may he enjoy the blessing and grace of almighty God. May he remain humble amid prosperity and secure amid adversity, so that, protected by divine mercy, he may enter the heavenly kingdoms through blessed Peter and rejoice eternally with Christ. [Col. 1354D]

Written by the hand of Octavian, scrivener and notary of the sacred palace, in the month of April, in the fourth indiction.

Given at Rome on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, by the hand of Humbert, cardinal bishop of the holy Church of Silva Candida and librarian of the sacred palace, in the year 1061 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the third year of the pontificate of Pope Nicholas II. [Col. 1355A]

### XXXIV. Bull of Nicholas II confirming the privileges of the chapter of the canons of Soana

(1061.)

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities*, V, 253.]

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Vitalis, provost of the holy Church of Soana, dedicated in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to your successors who shall be regularly advanced and remain in the holy undertaking, forever.
