Since the dignity of the Almighty, by his gratuitous gift and without foreseeing any meritorious work, has deigned to raise our humility to this position, so that through us we might administer an unfailing light throughout the world to the Church redeemed by his own blood, we rightly judge that, with his cooperation—for we presume to speak of him—we should distribute to each person, according to our abilities, the talent entrusted to us, lest, when his majesty appears, God forbid, we seem to return without profit acquired, like an unprofitable servant.

We hope indeed by divine mercy to attain this, if we take care, with serene affection, to supply whatever support we can to his members who, through faith, still aspire to heavenly things on earth. For thus, truly thus, we both secure heavenly assistance for our weakness and, while our intention remains pure within the lodging of our heart, obtain the honorable favor of men. Although we are debtors to all peoples who shine with the light of faith, we devote greater care, out of goodwill, to the cathedral churches that serve diligently, perform the divine offices reverently every day, and live canonically within them, than to the other clergy subject to them.

Accordingly, we receive under the protection of Saint Peter, and under our defense and that of our successors, the canonica of Saint Peter in the city of Suana, once built with pious devotion by Rainerius, bishop of that same holy Church, and afterwards enlarged by John, his successor, with the intervention of Anselm, their successor, the venerable bishop who now, by God’s arrangement, governs the aforesaid Church. We receive it with everything it rightfully possesses and will possess in the future, without prejudice to the authority and reverence due to the aforesaid Bishop Anselm.

This is not, however, so that he may have the right to cancel what we confirm by apostolic authority, nor that any of his successors may canonically sell the aforesaid possessions, alienate or encumber them by any agreement, or justly inflict any violence upon any cleric ordained in the aforesaid canonica.

But so that what was canonically granted by the previously named bishops of that holy Church, and what we confirm by this page of our privilege, may be understood more clearly, we specify it by name:

the parish situated at Pitilianum, with its lands, tithes, revenues, and offerings;

your estate situated at Palmula, with all its appurtenances and revenues;

all the tithes of your lands in every place wherever they are [Col. 1356A];

the lands which Osso gave to it for the sake of his soul;

the lands which Guidolfus offered to it at Baranello and Oliano;

the lands which Gotifredus donated to it on this side of the river Calisina;

the lands which Anselm, son of Rainerius, handed over to it at Calonicum;

the lands which Bonizo contributed to it at Supanum;

the land which Evrardus the notary presented to it;

the land which the bishops granted to it beside that same city;

the church of Saint Martin situated at Coronzano, with all its appurtenances and revenues;

the church of Saint George situated at Pertitium, with everything belonging to it;

three mansi, namely those of Corbulo the cleric, Dominicus the priest, and Sigizo, likewise a priest, formerly custodian of the parish situated in the city;

all tithes without exception, except those which the bishops formerly granted as benefices to certain soldiers [Col. 1356B];

half of all the offerings and alms offered and to be offered to the aforesaid parish;

and also half of all the lands which Giso, the father of Bishop John, possessed and gave to the aforesaid Church and its canons together with a house in the city—namely, the church of Saint Mary situated at Lapegi, two mansi at Ilci, and a vineyard and land in the plain of Suana.

All these things, and whatever has been offered by the faithful to the oft-mentioned canonica or shall henceforth be offered, we grant and confirm to you, beloved son Vitalis, to your successors, and to the clerics ordained or to be ordained in it who remain in the holy purpose.

No bishop, emperor, king, duke, margrave, viscount, castaldus, or any great or small person whatsoever shall ever dare to take or remove these things from you, disturb you, or inflict trouble upon you. Rather, you shall be permitted to live in peace and serve God.

If anyone, however, should attempt with rash boldness to violate this apostolic decree, unless, after being admonished, he comes to his senses and makes amends, let him be struck by the sword of anathema; let him perish in the present flesh; and when God comes to judge, let him be slain by the breath of his mouth.

But whoever proves himself a pious guardian may merit Saint Peter’s blessing and ours, and eternal recompense from the Lord Jesus Christ.

Given by the hand of Humbert, cardinal-bishop of the Church of Holy Silva Candida, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May [Col. 1356D], in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1061, the third year of the pontificate of Pope Nicholas II, indiction XIV.

### XXXV. Nicholas II confirms the possessions and privileges of the Church of Dorchester. (Year 1061.)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 875.]*

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Wilwinus, venerable bishop of Dorchester, and to his successors who shall be canonically promoted there, forever.

Since the care of watching over all the Churches of God and pious places presses upon us with great concern, lest they suffer any loss through necessity but receive the resources of their proper benefit, it is therefore fitting that we provide, with complete integrity of mind, for these venerable places, so that what belongs to them may remain secure.

Therefore, because you, dearest son, requested from us, together with the envoys of King Edward and the letters of our friend, that by the page of our privilege we should perpetually confirm to your Church, to you, and also to your successors everything that lawfully and legally belongs to the aforesaid Church, gladly assenting to your petition, by the decree of this our constitution and by the liberal edict of the Apostolic See we grant and confirm to you, as written above, and to your successors canonically promoted there, forever, everything belonging to the aforesaid Church—both what it presently possesses or has possessed, and especially the parish of Lindsey and the church of Stow with Newerka and its appurtenances, which Alfric, archbishop of York, unjustly invaded, as we have learned from the statements of our envoys and from the testimony and writings of our predecessors—and also whatever the aforesaid Church may acquire in the future in any manner according to divine and human law.

This includes the aforesaid Church with all its goods and possessions and their appurtenances, movable and immovable and self-moving: namely, castles, houses, villages, territories, churches, first fruits, and tithes, together with everything that the pious devotion of the faithful has bestowed or shall bestow upon it by offerings for the salvation of the living and also of the dead [Col. 1357C].

By the authority of this Apostolic See, over which by God’s authorization we preside, and by the inviolable constitution of our edict, we decree that neither king, archbishop, duke, margrave, count, nor viscount, nor any other person, whether great or small, of whatever dignity or order, shall presume, contrary to this our privilege, to strip the aforesaid Church, or you, dearest brother, or your successors forever, of its goods; to disturb you; or to establish or ordain anything there contrary to the holy canons.

Rather, just as the aforesaid Church has held all the things we have mentioned, better and more securely, from the beginning of its foundation, so shall you and your successors hold and possess them under the protection of this constitution and apostolic sanction.

If anyone, therefore—which we do not wish—should attempt to act against this our privilege and fail to allow it to remain as it has been commanded and strengthened by apostolic authority, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema and has a share with Judas the betrayer and with Dathan and Abiron, unless he should repent and make worthy satisfaction.

But whoever, with pious regard, proves himself observant in all things, preserving the provisions of this privilege of ours, which looks toward the worship of God, may obtain the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord God and deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of May by the hand of Bernard, bishop of the Holy Church of Palestrina, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1051 [Col. 1358A], the third year of the pontificate of Pope Nicholas II, indiction XIV.

### XXXVI. Letter of Nicholas II to Edward, king of the English. He praises his devotion to Saint Peter and confirms the privileges and possessions of the monastery of Saint Peter of Westminster. (Year 1061.)

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 1054.]*

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most glorious, most pious, and wholly honorable spiritual son Edward, king of the English: complete visitation, honey-sweet greeting, and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to Almighty God, who has adorned and distinguished your most prudent excellence in every respect toward blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; who has granted you affection toward us; and who has made you assent in all things to apostolic censures.

We therefore send letters to your nobility, and through them grant you fellowship with the holy apostles and with us. We pray the mercy of him who is Lord of all and alone King over all, that he himself may make you a participant in all our good works, if any are found before God, and establish us as brothers and companions in his love forevermore. May he also assign you no smaller share of our service in his kingdom than we desire to come to ourselves.

Henceforth, without doubt, we shall pray for you continually, that God himself may subject to you the enemies and adversaries who may wish to rise against you, and may confirm you upon your father’s throne and in your hereditary possession.

May blessed Peter always be your guardian and helper in every tribulation. For it is evident that the kings of the English, because of the reverence and devotion they have shown to blessed Peter, have flourished in glory and honor and have obtained famous triumphs through his patronage.

By the merits of that blessed apostle, may Almighty God bring your desire and will to effect, confirm for you the authority of your father’s kingdom, grant you an increase of peace, and, after the course of the present life, lead you to the dominion of eternal and abiding glory.

Therefore we renew, confirm, and enlarge your privileges: namely, that you be absolved from that vow which you feared, and from all your other sins and iniquities, by the authority of him who, although unworthy, willed me to preside over his holy Church.

Moreover, regarding that place which you undertook to establish and improve under the name of holy penance—for, as is reported, it first received its consecration long ago from blessed Peter, whose unworthy vicars we are, and because it is an ancient royal seat—we grant, permit, and most firmly confirm, by the authority of God, of the holy apostles, of this Roman See, and of ourselves, that it shall henceforth and forever be a place of royal establishment and consecration, a repository of royal insignia, and the perpetual dwelling of monks.

These monks shall be subject to no person whatsoever except the king, and shall have the power, according to the rule of Saint Benedict, to elect suitable abbots from among themselves in succession. No outsider shall be introduced by force, except one whom the concordant community has chosen beforehand.

We also absolve that place from every service and domination of the bishop, so that no bishop may enter it to ordain anyone or command anything, except at the request and with the consent of the abbot and monks.

That place shall likewise have a free precinct—that is, an enclosure and cemetery for the dead around it—without episcopal or any other oversight or exaction. Whatever, by our authority, can contribute to the liberty and exaltation of that place for the honor of God, we grant with joyful and most willing disposition.

As for the possessions which ancient kings, or any other men, and you and your barons have bestowed upon that place, and the charters made concerning them, we strengthen by divine authority and by ours, and decree that they shall be valid and secure.

Those who violate, invade, diminish, disperse, or sell them we condemn, together with Judas the betrayer, to eternal cursing, so that they may have no part in the blessed resurrection. Let them know that they will be judged by blessed Peter the apostle when he sits with his fellow apostles judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

To you and your successors, the kings, we entrust the advocacy and protection of that place and of all the churches of England, so that, in our stead, with the counsel of the bishops and abbots, you may establish everywhere what is just, knowing that through this [or: for this] you will receive a reward from him whose kingdom and dominion shall neither cease nor diminish forever.

Farewell.

### XXXVII. Privilege of Pope Nicholas II for Aldred, archbishop of York. (Fragment. Year 1061.)

*[Stubbs, Acts of the Pontiffs of York, in Twysden, Historical English Writers, London, 1652, fol. I, 1701.]*

Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop Aldred, archbishop of York: a privilege and greeting of apostolic blessing, and through him to his Church and to his successors who shall be canonically promoted, forever.

[Col. 1359D] Since the hidden dispensation of divinity, etc.

### XXXVIII. Decrees of Pope Nicholas II.

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 875.]*

In the first year of King Philip. These are the precepts of Pope Nicholas, found in various places among the sacred canons, which the Roman Church especially asserts that it observes.

**I.** First, that the peace and kingdoms of the Lord, discovered and praised by the faithful Christians, should be firmly maintained just as they are found in Scripture; but those who violate them should be struck with anathema.

**II.** That no bishop or priest should knowingly communicate with another person’s excommunicate or with his own. If he does so, let him know that the danger of his rank threatens him.

**III.** That married priests should either dismiss their wives and not live with them without legitimate testimony, or lose the Church together with their orders.

**IV.** That priests, deacons, subdeacons, and all who are canons should not have wives. If they marry, they are to be deposed and separated from the fellowship of the canons.

**V.** That churches and altars should neither be sold nor bought. Those who henceforth sell or buy them shall be subject to anathema.

**VI.** That bishops and clerics should not bear arms, devote themselves to hunting or bird-catching, or play with board games or dice.

**VII.** That bishops should not sell canonicae or ecclesiastical offices, and that neither they nor their clerics should demand anything for the consecration of churches or the ordination of clerics.

**VIII.** That churches consecrated for a price by Simoniacs should be consecrated again.

**IX.** That priests and all those knowingly ordained by Simoniacs from the time of Pope Nicholas until now, and henceforth, should know that they have not been ordained, and that such ordinations should not be performed thereafter.

**X.** That markets should not be held on Sundays, except annual fairs and matters pertaining to food.

**XI.** We certainly know that churches do not at all belong to laymen. But wherever they cannot be wholly taken away from them, we at least entirely forbid laymen to receive the offerings of Masses and altars.

**XII.** We entirely forbid exactions to be made concerning cemeteries, burials, and baptisteries.

**XIII.** If anyone has or thereafter takes a wife within the seventh degree of consanguinity, his bishop shall canonically compel him to dismiss her. If he refuses to obey, let him be excommunicated.

**XIV.** That no abbot should sell his obediences, nor any monk buy obediences. If they presume to do so, let both lose their order and office, because they are acting in a Simoniacal manner. Monks must not have private property at all.

**XV.** Abbots, priests, and ministers may not alienate or encumber anything belonging to ecclesiastical property or sacred ministry without the permission and subscription of their community. Whoever presumes to do so shall be degraded, with communion granted; and whatever has been rashly presumed and alienated shall be restored by order of his bishop.

### XXXIX. Letter of Gervasius, archbishop of Reims, to Pope Nicholas II.—He gives thanks for the kindness shown to his envoys. He expresses grief at the death of King Henry and declares that he will receive the pontiff with due honor if he comes to Gaul.

*[Mansi, Councils XIX, 874.]*

To the most excellent Father of fathers and bishop of bishops, Nicholas, Gervasius, called bishop, offers faithful service together with the prayers of my insignificance.

First I give thanks to divine mercy, and also to your moderation, excellent Father, because the report of my accusers did not prevail so far with you that the truthful defense of our envoys was not admitted, nor did apostolic judgment deny mercy to me, against whom, to the astonishment of many, it had raged so fiercely.

I likewise give thanks to your humility [perhaps: humanity; Hurd.], which, with a kindness as great as befitted the ruler and shepherd of the holy Roman Church, received our envoys when they were well, visited them when they were ill, and buried them when they died.

Although you extended these consolations of visitation and burial to only one who became ill and died in your presence, in that one you nevertheless visited the others and buried the others. It is not I, who am nothing, but the whole Church of Reims that bears witness to his good conduct.

When I heard of his death and of the deaths of the others, almost all of whom have died, I was affected by incredible sadness, and I can never cease hating the man whose pride caused them to be sent. For if I had sent an envoy such as I believed him to be, these men would neither have been sent nor perhaps have died. Your prudence recognizes this very well.

Moreover, a much heavier sadness afflicts me because of the death of the lord king, a matter also not hidden from your prudence. For you know how unrestrained and untamed our people are, and I fear that the division of our kingdom will become its desolation.

To avert this, I implore your counsel and help, which, as father of all, you cannot deny to any kingdom, especially since our country must always acknowledge to you what the best men have judged it owed.

While the lord king was alive, I sufficiently indicated, as I think, to your fatherhood what attitude I held toward your coming into our Gaul, although I have been defamed as unwilling to allow it. And now, God as my witness, I am of the same mind: I not only desire but thirst for your arrival, so that I may receive your authority, when you come, with as much joy and honor as is fitting for the vicar of Peter to receive, and may prove myself in every respect a co-worker with apostolic judgment.

Let my adversaries call me as faithless and rebellious toward your authority as they please. I profess my submission to you; and whoever denies it to you, whatever his order may be, shall not be able to share communion with me.

That obedience also rebukes my adversaries which they preserve toward you without regard for your suspension and interdict, not without great loss to our Churches and to us. That suspension also hindered my service toward you. If there were at least some hope that the rest could be restored, so far as recovery is possible, I would rise from so great a sorrow as from a deep sleep, in order to restore it.

For I am minded—and I do not despair that it will happen—to receive your apostolate one day with joy and reverence, and to show you as much honor as plainly suits your person and office. I do not believe that in our times there has been, or will be, anyone in your See whom I would desire to honor more abundantly.

For you honored us so greatly by your prudence and holiness that Rome chose from our kingdom one whom it appointed as head for itself and for the world. We, too, honor you with as great an honor as our Lord Jesus Christ bestowed upon Peter when he raised him to the primacy of the Church.

May Almighty God preserve your holiness for a very long time for the benefit of the holy Church, and keep it from your prudence that anyone’s thoughtless speech should take away your favor from me, or my service and fidelity from you.

### XL. Letters of Saint Peter Damian to Nicholas II.

[Col. 1362C]

*(See Patrologia, vol. CXLIV, col. 210.)*

## APPENDIX

[Col. 1361]

### A LETTER UNDER THE FALSE NAME OF ULRIC TO POPE NICHOLAS II

*(D. Martene, Amplissima Collectio I, 449.)*

### Notice

This letter may have come from the same source as the one which we published for the same purpose in volume I, page 230, of our *Thesaurus of Anecdotes*. We believed its author to be Guenricus, a schoolmaster of Trier, a most shameless man.

We give it here in order to demonstrate how corrupt the morals of priests had become in that age, and how well Pope Gregory VII served the Church when, with almost incredible labor, he abolished the marriages—or rather concubinage—of priests.

[Col. 1361D] This is the reply of Saint Ulrich, bishop, in which he responds to Pope Nicholas, who was treating the continence of clerics not justly but impiously, not canonically but indiscriminately.

To Nicholas, lord and Father, ever-watchful guardian of the Holy Roman Church, U., a bishop in name alone, offers love as a son and fear as a servant.

When I found your decrees concerning the continence of clerics, recently transmitted, to be alien to discretion, fear disturbed me together with sadness. [Note: This decree appears in chapter 3 of the Roman council of 113 bishops held under Pope Nicholas II in 1039, and renews a similar enactment issued by Pope Leo IX.]

Fear, indeed, because it is said: “The pastor’s sentence, whether just or unjust, is to be feared.” For I feared for weak hearers of Scripture, who scarcely obey even a just sentence: lest, freely trampling upon an unjust one, they should bind themselves to a burdensome, indeed unbearable, transgression of the pastor’s command.

But sadness, or compassion, arose lest the members should in any way be deprived of their head while it suffered from so grave an illness. For what is more serious, what is more worthy of the compassion of the whole Church, than for you, pontiff of the highest See, to whom the judgment of the whole Church belongs, to deviate even slightly from holy discretion?

You have indeed deviated from it significantly, since you wished to compel by imperious violence those clerics whom you ought to have admonished to abstain from marriage.

Is this not rightly judged violence by the common judgment of all wise men, when someone is compelled to carry out private decrees contrary to evangelical institution and the instruction of the Holy Spirit?

Since, therefore, many examples from the Old Testament are available that befit the holy discretion which, as you know, is required, I ask that it not be burdensome to your fatherhood for a few of the many to be inserted in this letter.

In the old law, the Lord established marriage for the priest; nor is it read that he later forbade it to him.

But the same Lord speaks in the Gospel: “There are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, but not all can accept this saying. Let him who can accept it accept it.”

Therefore the Apostle also says: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice.”

Considering that, according to the foregoing, not all are able to accept this counsel, and seeing many supporters of the same counsel wishing to please men rather than God through a false appearance of continence, and observing them commit more serious crimes—namely, assaulting the wives of others and not shrinking from the embraces of males and beasts—he said, lest the condition of the Church be shaken as they grew strong through the spread of this disease: “Let each man have his own wife.”

The same hypocrites falsely claim that this applies specifically to laymen. Yet although they may be established in any very holy order, they do not hesitate to abuse the wives of others and—what we say with horror—rage in the crimes mentioned above.

These men plainly have not understood Scripture correctly. Because they pressed its breast too harshly, they drank blood instead of milk.

For the apostolic statement, “Let each man have his own wife,” excludes no one except one who has professed continence or who has made a commitment before the Lord to continue in virginity.

Nevertheless, it befits your vigor, revered Father, to compel by obligation every person who has made a vow of continence to you, whether by word or by hand, and afterwards wishes to apostatize, either to carry out his vow or to depose him from every order by canonical authority.

And so that you may be strong enough to accomplish this manfully, you will have me and all the men of my order as energetic helpers.

But so that you may know that those ignorant of this vow must not be compelled at all, hear the Apostle saying to Timothy: “The bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife.”

Lest anyone turn this statement toward the Church alone, he added: “If anyone does not know how to preside over his own household, how will he take care of the Church of God?”

Likewise, he says, “deacons must be husbands of one wife, managing their children and their own households well.”

I know that you have adequately taught that this wife must be blessed by a priest, according to the decree of Pope Saint Sylvester.

Agreeing with these and similar statements of Holy Scripture, the writer of the canonical rules says: “Let a cleric be chaste, or at least let him be bound by the bond of one marriage.”

From all these things it is truthfully gathered that a bishop and a deacon are marked as blameworthy if they divide themselves among many women.

And if they reject one woman under the pretext of religion, this canonical sentence condemns both bishop and deacon, without distinction of rank.

A bishop or priest, however, should not reject his own wife under the pretext of religion. If he rejects her, let him be excommunicated; if he persists, let him be deposed.

Saint Augustine, who was not ignorant of holy discretion, also says: “There is no crime that ought not to be admitted in order to avoid a worse one.”

Moreover, we read in the second book of the *Tripartite Ecclesiastical History* that when the Council of Nicaea wished to enact these same decrees—namely, that bishops, priests, and deacons should, after consecration, either abstain entirely even from their own wives or lay down their rank—Paphnutius rose in their midst.

He was one of those martyrs whom the emperor Maximinus condemned after their right eyes had been torn out and the sinews of their left legs cut.

He objected, confessed the honorableness of marriage and chastity, and said that intercourse with one’s own wife was [lawful]. He persuaded the council not to establish such a law, declaring that it would furnish a serious occasion of fornication either to the men themselves or to their wives.

Paphnutius explained these things, although he himself had no experience of marriage, and the council praised his judgment. It enacted nothing on this matter but left it to each person’s will rather than necessity.

There are, however, some who enlist Saint Gregory as an ally of their sect. I laugh at their recklessness and grieve over their ignorance.

They do not know that the dangerous decree of this heresy, made by Saint Gregory, was later cleansed by him through the fitting fruit of repentance [Col. 1363D: *A fable.*].

For on one occasion, when he had placed fish in his fishpond and saw that more than a thousand infant heads had been taken from it, he was immediately moved to profound repentance. He confessed that the decree he had made concerning abstinence had caused such slaughter and cleansed it, as I have said, through the fitting fruit of repentance.

Having utterly condemned his own decree, he praised the apostolic saying: “It is better to marry than to burn,” adding on his own part: “It is better to marry than to provide an occasion of death.”

If those men had read with me perhaps this outcome of the matter, they would not have judged so rashly, at least fearing the Lord’s command: “Do not judge,” and so forth.

Therefore let your holiness cease compelling those whom you ought only to admonish, lest, God forbid, you be found contrary to both the Old and the New Testament through a private command.

For, as Saint Augustine says to Donatus: “The only thing we fear in your justice is that you may judge something worthy of coercion not from consideration of Christian gentleness but on account of harshness. Through Christ himself we beg you not to do this. Sins must be restrained in such a way that those who repent of sin may remain.”

We also wish you to remember what Augustine says: “Let nothing be done from a desire to harm, but let everything be done from charity that seeks counsel; let nothing be done savagely, nothing inhumanely.”

Again, concerning the same matter: “In the fear of Christ, in the name of Christ, I exhort you: those of you who do not possess temporal goods, do not desire to possess them; those who possess them, do not presume upon them. I do not say that you are condemned because you possess these things, but that you are condemned if you presume upon them. If you consider yourselves great because of these things, if through outstanding vanity you forget the common condition of the human race.”

He draws this cup of discretion from that fountain of apostolic preaching where it is said: “Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release.”

There it is also added: “Let those who have wives be as though they had none, and those who use this world as though they did not use it.”

He also says of a widow: “Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.”

To marry in God means attempting nothing in entering marriage that the Lord forbids.

The prophet Jeremiah also says: “Do not trust in lying words, saying, ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this.’”

Jerome says of this: “I declare that this properly applies to those virgins who boast of chastity and, with shameless face, proclaim their purity, while their conscience is otherwise and they do not know the Apostle’s definition of virginity: that she be holy in body and spirit. For what does chastity profit a mind that has been defiled, if it does not possess the other virtues described by prophetic speech?”

Since we see that you possess these virtues to some extent, and since we know that, although discretion has been neglected in this matter, it has nevertheless been honorably preserved in the other institutions of your life, we do not doubt that you will quickly correct this depraved intention.

Therefore, although we condemn or judge this exceedingly serious negligence with less severity than we might, we do condemn and judge it.

For although, according to the terminology established by usage, a bishop is higher than a priest, Augustine is nevertheless lower than Jerome. Yet correction must not be rejected or despised even when it comes from anyone inferior, especially when the person being corrected is found to be striving both against truth and in favor of men.

For, as Saint Augustine says to Boniface, we ought not to treat the disputations of just anyone, even Catholic and celebrated men, or the canonical Scriptures themselves, as though we were not permitted, while preserving the honor due to them, to disapprove and reject something in their writings if we happen to find that they have understood it otherwise than the truth holds—whether the matter has been understood by others through divine assistance or by us.

What, then, could be found more contrary to truth than this? For Truth itself, speaking of continence, plainly says of all people, except those who have professed continence: “Let him who can accept it accept it.”

These men, I do not know from what provocation, say instead: “Let him who cannot accept it be struck with anathema.”

What, moreover, could be more foolishly done for the sake of men? What could bind one more tightly to divine malediction than when some of them—whether bishops or archdeacons—are so headlong in lust that they do not shrink from adultery, incest, or, shamefully, the most disgraceful embraces of males, yet say that the chaste marriages of clerics stink?

They do not ask clerics to be continent out of true compassion for justice, but, out of disdain for false justice, command them to abstain as though they were slaves.

To persuade them to this command—or rather, not to call it counsel—they add such a foolish suggestion that they say it is more honorable to be secretly entangled than to be openly joined to one woman in the conscience of men.

They certainly would not say this if they were from him, or in him, who says through the prophet: “Woe to you, Pharisees, who do everything for the sake of men.”

And through the Psalmist: “Those who please men are confounded, because God has despised them.”

These men are perverse: they ought first to persuade us to be ashamed of being sinners in the sight of him before whose sight all things are naked and open, rather than to be men in the sight of men.

Although, therefore, by reason of their depravity they deserve no merciful counsel, we nevertheless, mindful of divine humanity, offer them through the compassion of charity a counsel of authority that is never empty of mercy.

For we say: “First remove, hypocrite, the beam from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.”

We also ask them to consider what the Lord says concerning the prostitute: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her”—as though he were saying: If the law commands it, if Moses commands it, I too command it. But I choose suitable ministers of the law, and you consider whom you are bringing forward.

Consider, I beg you, what you are, for Scripture says: “If you have examined yourself, you will never slander anyone.”

It was also reported to us concerning certain of them that they swell with such self-exaltation that they dare to tear apart with beatings, without reason, the Lord’s flock, for which good shepherds would not hesitate to lay down their lives. Saint Gregory, lamenting their savagery most bitterly, says: “What will become of the sheep when shepherds become wolves?” But who is overcome? Is it not the one who rages? Who will judge the persecutors, except the one who likewise offered his back to the whips? What [lacuna] is this, however? Let them hear [lacuna] lest the Church be brought only scandal as its fruit, and lest the clergy suffer contempt from the bishops themselves or from their unbelieving associates. Nor would I hesitate to call those men unbelievers of whom the Apostle Paul said to Timothy: “For in the last days some will depart from the faith, attending to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, and having their conscience seared, forbidding marriage” [Col. 1366B]. This, if you look closely, is the whole bundle of their tares, the whole greenery of their tares: while clerics are compelled to abandon the lawful companionship of one wife, overcome—God forbid!—by Pharisaic fury, fornicators and adulterers, and the most disgraceful ministers of other depraved practices are made their associates. Like blind guides blindly plotting, they introduce this heresy into the Church of God, so that what the Psalmist, knowing their error in advance, invokes against them may be fulfilled: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see”; and: “Always bend their backs.” Since, then, no one is unaware that if, by the judgment of your decree, you had discerned this as a future pestilence with the clear-sightedness of vigilant discretion, you would never have consented to the wicked suggestions of anyone, we counsel you, in faithful obedience owed to you, to awaken even now and drive so great a scandal from the Church. after you have, in accordance with the discipline of our discernment, uprooted the Pharisaic doctrine from the Church, lest the Lord’s sole [lacuna]—a holy nation and royal priesthood—be any longer abused by adulterous husbands and be torn away from her bridegroom, namely Christ, by an irreparable divorce, since no one will see our Lord reigning throughout all the ages of ages without chastity—not only in the bloom of virginity but also in the married state. Amen.

# In the Year of the Lord 1065. Hugh II, Bishop of the Church of Nevers

## Historical Notice

*(From Gallia Christiana, new edition, vol. XII, p. 633.)*

[Col. 1365D] Hugh, son of Hugh, viscount of Nevers, and Elisabeth, and brother of Hugh the viscount, Leo, and Reginald, as well as uncle of Hugh the dean and later bishop of Nevers, was made bishop of Nevers from a canonry of Auxerre in the year 1013. In July, in the twentieth year of King Robert, he granted to the Cluniac monks of Vallis Aurae the land of Saint-Cyr, situated in the county of Auxerre and called Vivenz. He subscribed the charter by which Bishop Helmoin of Autun donated the cell of Saint George of Colches to Flavigny in the thirtieth year. [Col. 1366D] In the thirty-second year he granted Albuin the land in the village of Saint-Benignus, as his predecessor Gausbert had once granted it to Adelard. Following the example of his predecessors Herimann and Natrann, he also gave his church the abbey consecrated in honor of Saint Troesius the Confessor, and the church of Saint Francoveus in the county of Nevers, with its two altars—one of which had been established by a charter made by his predecessor Roclenus—so that the canons might live in common. This was in the eleventh year of his ordination. He granted two altars to the canons in December, in the thirty-third year of King Robert [Col. 1367A]. He subscribed the foundation charter of the church of Saint Denis at Vergy in 1032, in the fifteenth indiction and the second year of King Henry. He also subscribed the charter by which Bishop Helmuin of Autun restored the monastery of Corbigny to Flavigny in 1034. He attended the Council of Bourges in 1040 and subscribed the donation made by Archbishop Aymo to the monastery of Saint Sulpicius. In 1041 he subscribed the donation made to the chapter by Itherius. He subscribed the charter of Hugh, archbishop of Mainz, for the canons of Saint Paul, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April 1044. In the fifteenth year of the following reign of King Henry, he granted to the canons the provostship which Provost Hugh had administered corruptly and had relinquished into the bishop’s hands; in compensation they gave him the church of Saint Troesius, a transaction confirmed by Leo IX at the Synod of Vercelli in 1050.

He entrusted the abbey of Saint Savior to Odilo, abbot of Cluny, to reform it in 1045, on the eighth day before the Ides of November. In 1047 he took part in the dedication of Saint Mary of Saintes. He attended the Synods of Sens and Troyes in 1048 and subscribed the charter [Col. 1367B] of King Henry for the cell of Saint Aigulf of Provins, united that year to the monastery of Saint Peter of Troyes. He attended the Council of Reims in 1049, where he confessed that a very large sum of money had been given by his parents for the bishopric without his knowledge, and that, after obtaining it, he had committed certain acts contrary to ecclesiastical religion [lacuna] and therefore wished to relinquish the episcopal office rather than ruin his soul by retaining it. After saying this, he placed his pastoral staff at the feet of the apostolic pope. The latter, moved by the devotion of so great a man, restored the episcopal office to him through the ministry of another staff, after Hugh had sworn that the money had been given without his consent.

After the council Hugh followed Leo, attended the Roman synod [Col. 1368A] in 1050, and shortly afterward the Council of Vercelli. At his request King Henry granted Blessed Robert, founder of La Chaise-Dieu, permission for that monastery to become an abbey in 1052. He is mentioned in a charter of the same king concerning the restoration of the abbey of Saint Victor, in the twenty-second year of the king’s reign, on the Kalends of May. He attended the sacred assembly of King Philip on the tenth day before the Kalends of June 1050 and, in that same year, the Roman council, where he and other bishops were commissioned to investigate the case of the monks of Vendôme and Saint-Aubin. His letters on this matter had been read at the Synod of Bordeaux in 1068.

Hugh, bishop of Nevers, subscribed the charter by which Isembard, bishop of Orléans, granted a prebend in his church to the Cluniacs around that time; he is described there as abbot and canon of the church of Orléans. The church of Saint Stephen, founded by Saint Columbanus for nuns in the suburb of Nevers, had by then been reduced partly by age, partly by fire, and partly by other necessities to such a state that scarcely any walls remained. Hugh granted it in 1063 to the canons who followed the rule of Blessed Sylvester, Roman pope. His nephew Hugh, a cleric and dean, held half of it from Count William [Col. 1368B]. This donation was confirmed at the Council of Chalon in 1064, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, during the octave of Blessed Lawrence, which Hugh attended; it was read on the following feast of the Nativity of Blessed Mary in the church of Saint Stephen.

Finally, Hugh subscribed, in 1065, in the fifth year of King Philip, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, the charter by which Gauzbert, a knight of the county of Watrin, donated a church called Kadelat to the monks of Fleury. In that same year, returning from Rome, where he had attended two councils, he died on the journey in the fifty-fourth year of his episcopate and was honorably buried in the abbey of Parody. He is commemorated on the Nones of May in the martyrology of Auxerre.

[Col. 1367]

## Letter of Hugh, Bishop of Nevers, to Bartholomew, Archbishop of Tours

### Concerning the Cell of Crédon, Asserted for the Monks of Vendôme at the Roman Council under Pope Nicholas

*(Mansi, Councils, vol. XIX, col. 901.)*

[Col. 1367C] To Blessed Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours; E., bishop of Angers; and Count Geoffrey: Hugh, bishop of Nevers, wishes each of you the gift of perpetual happiness.

Last year, while we were at Rome in the holy synod, a questionable complaint concerning a certain church of Saint Clement at Crédon came to the ears of Pope N. The brothers of the church of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme and the monks of Saint-Aubin presented their claims to us in turn. The pope, being occupied with many matters, ordered the issue to be investigated separately by the bishops of Metz and Troyes, and by myself, the bishop of Nevers, as well as by the bishops of Le Mans, Arezzo, and Limoges [Col. 1368C], so that it might be determined to whom the aforesaid church should be granted according to law. After hearing both groups of monks, we reported the same matter to the pope. In the full synod he adjudicated the aforesaid church to the monastery of the Holy Trinity, because we judged that no one can relinquish to a church a fief which he holds from someone else, nor to anyone except through the permission of the person from whom it derives. Farewell.

# In the Year of the Lord 1065. Bovo, Abbot of Saint-Bertin

[Col. 1367]

## Historical Notice

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis, vol. I, p. 267.)*

Bovo, a Gallo-Belgian, was abbot of the Benedictine monastery of Sithiu among the Morini around the year 1060. His account, composed in 1052, of the discovery and elevation of the body of Saint Bertin, abbot, which had been concealed out of fear of the Northmen, was published by Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century III, p. 153.

[Col. 1369]

# In the Year of the Lord 1065. Frolland, Bishop of Senlis

[Col. 1369]

## Historical Notice Concerning Frolland

*(Literary History of France, VIII, 17.)*

Frolland is not known to us before his episcopate. He was raised to it in 1043 (Gallia Christiana vetus, vol. XXXI, p. 1017) to govern the Church of Senlis after the death of Guy, surnamed “the Good.” It is therefore by mistake that some suppose the forty-ninth letter of Fulbert of Chartres to have been addressed to him, since Fulbert had died as early as April 1029. Accordingly, the name of the bishop of Senlis to whom the letter is written is designated by an R, meaning Rodulf, Guy’s predecessor.

Frolland was one of the bishops who made up the celebrated Council of Reims in 1049 (Councils, vol. IX, p. 1036), presided over by Pope Leo IX. Four years later, around 1053, he was present at the assembly of Saint-Denis near Paris, where the discovery and verification took place of the relics of the saint of that name, which the monks of Saint-Emmeram boasted that they possessed. In 1059 he also attended the coronation of Prince Philip, son of King Henry I. It is agreed that our prelate had died before 1074, when Yves II occupied the episcopal see of Senlis (Gallia Christiana, same place; Mabillon, *Acta*, vol. IX, preliminary document no. 22). But it appears doubtful that he lived beyond 1071. Let it not be forgotten that his episcopate had begun at least by 1043.

It is unknown whether Frolland left any other writings besides a letter to the famous Berengar of Tours, which has been preserved for us (Spicilegium II, 509) and deserves to be known. It is well written for its time and entirely filled with expressions of esteem and affection for Berengar. Frolland, although he was a bishop, calls him there not only his brother but also his very dear lord, and names him before himself in the address of the letter, contrary to the practice of other bishops writing to their inferiors. The great confidence he shows in Berengar’s prayers demonstrates that he regarded him as a man of rare piety. This is why he ardently wished to enjoy his presence while suffering from the double illness with which he was then afflicted. It is clear from what he says to him near the end of the letter that it was written at the time when Berengar was seeking protectors everywhere at the court of King Henry, in order to regain the good graces of that prince, who was angry with him. There is, moreover, considerable likelihood either that our prelate did not yet know Berengar’s true views, or that, if he did know them, he showed him such esteem and friendship only in order to bring him back to the common belief of the faithful.

Dom d’Achery, having brought this letter out of obscurity, published it in the second volume of his *Spicilegium*. A few years later, M. du Boulay thought it appropriate to reprint it among the monuments of his history of the University of Paris (E. du Boulay, vol. I, pp. 421–422). Oudin later included it in his history of Berengar (Oudin, *Scriptores*, vol. II, pp. 629–630).

[Col. 1369]

## Letter of Frolland to Berengar

*(In Achery, *Spicilegium* II.)*

[Col. 1369A] To the lord and brother Berengar, Frolland, bishop of Senlis, his servant, wishes, insofar as a faithful man may, the joys of future happiness.

Detained by illness in both respects, I cannot come here to you as I had planned and told you I would [Col. 1370A]. But, I ask you, pray for me—and pray more earnestly—that I may be freed from the illness which is killing my soul. I do not know whether in this present age I shall be able to see you again, my very dear lord. But strive that I may deserve to see you in the next life in tranquillity.

Yet if God preserves my life and health for so long that an opportunity arises for me to come to you, I shall never fail to fulfill my long-conceived desire for you by approaching you. For I would not dare to ask you to come to our region, even during this Lent, for the sake of prayer. But if I should be surrounded by such misfortune that neither I can come here nor you come to me, and if death should overtake me, I entrust my soul to you. Send messages of supplication on its behalf to the heavenly court; entreat the princes of the archangels and apostles, and the other centurions of that court who attend upon so great a King in closest familiarity, asking them to deign to suggest to him that he command my sinful soul to be freed from the prison of death [Col. 1372A]. Indeed, strengthened by the gift of prayer, approach the most merciful and kind King yourself, as you are accustomed to do for others, on my behalf also; and confidently beseech him yourself to deign to spare me.

Greet in my name Lord Abbot R. and the other lords and brothers whom your affection has won for me, and ask them to remember me in their prayers. Send me word of whatever you wish. Let your fraternity know that I have firmly secured for you the favor of my lord the king. Farewell; although you need no reminder to remember me, pay heed to doing so.

# Around the Year of the Lord 1065. Widric, Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Ghislain in Hainaut

[Col. 1371]

## Historical Notice

Widric, or Guidric, was abbot of Saint Ghislain in Hainaut around the year 1065. His letter to Emperor Henry [Note: [Col. 1371A] specifically Henry III, surnamed “the Black,” who died in 1056, not Henry IV, who was not proclaimed Augustus until 1084, by which time Widric had already been dead for several years [Col. 1372A]] survives. It was written against Baldwin, count of Hainaut, who had grievously harassed the monastery of Saint Ghislain.

[Col. 1371]

## Letter of Widric, Abbot, to Emperor Henry III, Surnamed “the Black”

*(Edited by Dom Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. V, p. 26.)*

[Col. 1371B] To the glorious lord, Roman emperor, Caesar Augustus, H. W., abbot of the monastery of Cell, together with the flock entrusted to him, wishes happy triumph and reign with Christ.

Supreme prince of those who came before us, to whom God entrusted the reins of the kingdom so that you might seek judgment for the poor and examine the cause of the oppressed: to you we direct the cry of our miseries and of the tyrannical oppression we endure; from you we implore relief for our groans.

Count Baldwin, in whose destructive county our church was formerly founded by royal munificence in honor of the prince of the apostles and our holy father Ghislain, and called a royal alms, now scarcely survives. For three years and more he has so devastated, crushed, and plundered us [Col. 1371C] that we have no hope of continuing to exist unless you, glorious emperor, whose fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers founded us and established us as free under royal law, extend the hand of your defense and offer the shield of your protection [Col. 1372B].

Let your piety not judge that we complain without cause. The miracles which the Lord often works through our patron, Saint Ghislain—when, because of the robberies and acts of violence committed against us, his sacred body is presented to Baldwin in order to cool his fury—do not turn the tyrant back from his criminal undertaking. The decrees of the imperial lords do not restrain him; majesties impressed with seals do not deter him; nor do the warnings of good men, the correction imposed by Christian authority, or the various expenditures of our solidi, pounds, and marks.

As the culmination of all this, how often he lingers in the villages, manors, and possessions granted to us through the generosity of kings, dukes, bishops, and other faithful servants of God for love of God and Saints Peter and Ghislain, and confirmed by imperial liberty; he lies there, holds conversations, and finally, as he leaves, plunders, devastates, and pillages everything [Col. 1372C].

While he was staying for five days at Hornut, Durnum, and Buxutum—places granted by royal liberality and confirmed by royal law—on the fifth day, which at that time was marked by the commemoration of the Passion of Saint Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist, he carried away whatever booty he found [Col. 1373A]. When we placed the body of our holy father before him and appealed to the fear of God and royal liberty, some of his men inflicted such severe beatings on those of ours who were supporting the sacred body that the shrine was stained with the blood of the wounded.

Alas! How many servants and faithful dependants of our church he has handed over as captives to his kidnappers and how much of their property he has seized! Alas! How many spoils—not only from our households but from our own wealth, worth two hundred pounds or more—he has taken from us! We are afraid to say how he disposed of all these things, lest we offend royal ears.

Even in the present year, seeking by every means to calm his rapacious fury, we gave ten marks of silver from our poverty on behalf of ourselves and our people, as though they were pledges of peace and tranquillity. Once he had received them, he immediately attacked one of our villages, called Villare, and, plundering the booty throughout the entire village within the church precinct, departed [Col. 1373B].

After the recent celebration of the feast of Saint John the Baptist, he seized in another village, called Erchana, booty worth one hundred solidi and more from the servants and maidservants of our church, and in addition took from one of our monks the horse which he used for our necessities [Col. 1374A].

Now, supreme Caesar, glorious king and lord, since the honor of a king loves judgment and, as the Apostle testifies, you do not bear the sword without cause, open the ears of your piety to our cry for the soul of our lord, your father of blessed memory, whose royal majesty granted us our freedom. Vigorously extend the right hand of justice; following the example of the evangelical king who avenged the death of the widow’s son, avenge us against our adversary, lest Holy Mother Church, crying out and left unavenged, accuse you when judgment comes.

May the mercy of the King of kings and Lord of lords, in whose hand are the hearts and times of kings, order and arrange your imperial rule so that it may make your enemies peaceful and subject, and multiply and protect the faithful and your friends. Farewell, glory of the empire.

# In the Year of the Lord 1065. Franco, Scholastic of Liège

[Col. 1373]

## Specimen from Franco’s Work on the Squaring of the Circle

*(Mai, *Classical Authors*, III, 346.)*

### [Note]

We said that Bertius seems wrongly to attribute to Boethius the work on the squaring of the circle, which is Franco’s. We now wish to present a specimen from this unpublished work, which is divided into six books, while first giving, as before, an account of the man and the work from Sigebert. Thus Sigebert says, chapter 164:

“Franco, scholastic of Liège, distinguished in religion and in both branches of literary knowledge, made known to posterity how much he was worth by his writing. Let secular lovers of knowledge assess his learning from the book which he wrote to Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, *On the Squaring of the Circle*. Concerning this subject Aristotle says: ‘The squaring of the circle is knowable, but it is not yet a science.’ For that knowable achievement, let secular philosophers esteem him, or even place him above others. We praise him because he devoted himself to Holy Scripture and wrote several works, including one book on the method of computation, along with other writings held by others.”

Trithemius tells the same story about Franco in chapter 346 and adds that he flourished under Emperor Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1060. The same Trithemius notes that Franco’s patron was Hermann II, whom we know to have held the see of Cologne from 1036 to 1055. It is therefore sufficiently clear that Franco’s work was composed within that period.

Here, then, are part of the prologue to the first book, the beginning of the work itself, and almost the entire prologue to the third book. I have selected these passages as a specimen because they contain several items of historical information.

## The Prologue to the First Book of Lord Franco on the Squaring of the Circle Begins

[Col. 1373C] Since you, my father, ornament of prelates and crown of all the clergy throughout the world, have never been forgetful of any honorable quality, and since you freely confirmed your generosity toward me, from that very time onward I have been unable to pass an hour without wondering by what service I ought to earn so great a favor [Col. 1374C].

For there was no money: no hollow hoof of a proud warhorse, no Minervan price for an elaborate and artfully worked garment, no work of molten metal embossed with marvelous figures, no sight of a foreign stone in its manifold and varied colors [Col. 1375A]. Even if I possessed an abundance of such things, I would never have dared allow it to enter my mind to offer trifling gifts of them to such nobility and dignity.

For when such objects are distributed among the common people through the generosity of princes, they relieve want and necessity; but when the goodwill of the princes themselves is purchased by offering them such things, their avarice is unquestionably reproached by a kind of hidden inscription. Gifts could not buy them off if they were not delighted by the gifts themselves because of that monster, avarice—which is precisely what happens—and so on.

Thus I was led by this path to publish a little book on the squaring of the circle, with inexperience offering the greatest resistance, but devotion driving me on toward rash attempts. Since, therefore, this work has been published [Col. 1376A] with you inviting us to study by your benefactions, it cannot be anyone else’s work but yours. Accordingly, be assured that all its diligence—whether it ought to be rejected altogether, corrected in part, or advanced in its entirety—is of the greatest concern to you.

For you have many Tuckuses and Varuses, men who are by no means accustomed to envy the studies of others. To their fidelity and charity you will entrust our labor, so that they may not only cut away what is superfluous but also, with your approval, apply correction to its errors. Thus let them purify this work through their editorial labor, so that it may not be unworthy of being consecrated to your name, as to a divinity.

## The First Book of Lord Franco on the Squaring of the Circle Begins

[Col. 1375B] The squaring of the circle is so deeply hidden among the secret natures of things that today no one would even doubt the possibility of its method, unless Aristotle—whom they also report to have discovered it—had inserted a mention of it in his *Categories*. Its science, they say, remained unquestioned down to Boethius; but when he was removed, the whole of it perished at the same time, apart from the mere doubt which is so great and so extensive that all the learned men of Italy, Gaul, and Germany have failed before it.

Indeed, our Adelbold, Wazo—the greatest of teachers—Gerbert himself, the restorer of learning [Col. 1376B], and many others diligently investigated this problem. If they had attained the result, would the whole matter have remained hidden from those who followed them, some of whom are still alive? Gerbert’s geometrical little book is certainly available [Note: [Col. 1375C] We have read the geometrical writings of Gerbert and Adelbold in Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. III, part II, p. 6 and pp. 82 ff. Adelbold’s little work on the squaring of the circle is in my manuscript collection. Finally, information about Wazo—or Wason—who was Franco’s contemporary, is available in Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina mediae et infimae aetatis*, vol. VI, Padua edition, with Mansi’s additions [Col. 1376C].], along with other writings of his; and, if I am not mistaken, he would never have omitted these matters if his diligence concerning this science had produced a result.

We therefore wish to promise nothing except study and labor. The first of these will sweat over the question that also greatly wearied our predecessors, namely the comparison of angles, and so on.

## Prologue to the Third Book

[Col. 1375C] If you were a prelate whose own praises delighted and nourished your mind, no eloquence would suffice for what could be proclaimed about you yourself, about your grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and all your ancestors—not only the most illustrious princes of the Romans but also those of the Greeks: about their nobility, dignity, glory, power, resources, the greatness of their affairs, their splendid deeds, virtue, wisdom, and merits.

Virgil, wishing to magnify Augustus through his ancestors, composed the *Aeneid* in twelve books. How many more books would be needed if someone wished to gather the deeds of the first, second, and third of the Ottos? The first received the kingdom from his father Henry but left the empire to his son; the father was the first to reign among the Germans, and the son the first to rule as emperor among them [Col. 1376C]. And to whom but these men does Germany owe the fact that Italy, together with the entire world, pays tribute to it? Through whom else did our emperors become successors to the Roman scepter?

I wish you would tell me, O Maro, what such a contribution your Aeneas—that pious, great, goddess-born man of yours—made to your Latium. Recognize, Augustus, how far beneath your lineage he stands when compared with the pious and illustrious Octavians. But suppose that Aeneas really was such a man—what does that matter to you? You scarcely reach Aeneas as a descendant one thousand generations removed. Do you therefore suppose that the descendant of the Octavians, if he had a Virgil such as yours to exalt him by praising his ancestors, would not overshadow your reputation with how great a glory? And so on.

# In the Year of the Lord 1067. Blessed Maurilius, Archbishop of Rouen

[Col. 1375]

## Life of Blessed Maurilius

*(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, century VI, part II, p. 222.)*

[Col. 1375D] 1. In this present age the most devout bishop Maurilius [Col. 1376D] illumined the Church of Rouen, the metropolitan see of Second Lyonnaise; the most distinguished writers of his age celebrated his praises. No one, however, so far as I know, committed his life to writing [Col. 1377A]. The authority of Trithemius does not contradict this, for in the new Saint-Gall edition of the *Chronicle of Hirsau* he reports that the deeds of Blessed Maurilius were written down under the year 1064. By these words that author may have intended nothing more than the various eulogies of our Maurilius which occur here and there in the writers of that period.

This conjecture is supported by Trithemius himself in another edition of the same *Chronicle*, where, after making a distinguished mention of Maurilius, he adds these words: “Of whose holy way of life lofty proclamations of praise are reported.” And in book four of *On Illustrious Men of Our Order*, chapter 120: “Maurilius … concerning whom many good things are related.” But it would be pointless to discuss the matter at greater length, since the *Life* of Maurilius, if it ever existed, is now entirely unknown [Col. 1377B]. We shall therefore, following our customary practice, compose a brief eulogy of him from the various authors who have written about him, as the occasion permits.

2. No one would deny that Maurilius was born at Reims if Orderic Vitalis had been consistent with himself. But since, in book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, he said from Maurilius’s epitaph that the holy bishop was born at Reims, while elsewhere, in book V, he wrote that the same man was of Mainz ancestry, later authors adopted various positions. Our own Menard took a middle course in his notes on the Benedictine Martyrology: he admitted that Maurilius was born at Reims but from parents of Mainz. Many thereafter adopted this method of resolving the dispute.

For my part, I have nothing to say about Maurilius’s parents, since no documents are available on the matter [Col. 1377C], except that William of Poitiers and an anonymous monk of Saint-Ouen at Rouen—Maurilius’s contemporary and the author of the *Deeds of the Archbishops of Rouen*, edited from the autograph in volume II of the *Analecta*—assert that he excelled in nobility of lineage. In a brief summary of Maurilius’s life, this anonymous author explicitly states that Maurilius arose from a noble family in the district of Reims. I certainly think that his birth at Reims cannot be denied, since it is expressed in clear words in the epitaph placed upon his tomb.

That epitaph was not composed by an unknown man or long after the blessed bishop’s death, but by an eminent man, a canon of the Church of Rouen, so that it might be placed over Maurilius’s body, as Orderic Vitalis himself attests [Col. 1377D]. Moreover, in book V Orderic may have said that Maurilius was of Mainz ancestry because his companion Gerbert was born at Mainz, as is clear from Gerbert’s epitaph; or perhaps because Maurilius himself lived for some time in the province of Mainz. In this way the same author calls John, abbot of Fécamp—who is certainly known from the *Life of Blessed William* to have been Italian—a compatriot of our Maurilius, because Maurilius himself had also spent some time in Italy and served there as an abbot.

3. Not only have more recent historians written that Maurilius was educated among the clergy of the Church of Reims [Col. 1378A], but the same is attested by our anonymous author mentioned above. From him we also learn that, after devoting himself diligently to the study of philosophy at Liège, Maurilius obtained the position of scholastic of the Church of Halberstadt.

But none of these things could hold the attention of Maurilius, who aspired to more perfect gifts. Accordingly, he withdrew to the monastery of Fécamp, which, as it seems to me, was then governed by Blessed William. After spending many years there, he obtained permission to leave and went to Italy, where he led an anchoritic life with his companion Gerbert, who later became abbot of Saint-Wandrille.

William of Poitiers, a contemporary author, extols their holy way of life in those regions in magnificent language in his book *On the Deeds of William the Duke*, later king of England, where he says:

“Both of these men, in the very flower of youth, contemplating divinity and the blessedness which divinity bestows, escaped the impediments of temporal affairs through the naked profession of their faith, with an acuteness of mind far keener than Plato’s. They despised the gymnasia of worldly philosophy, which they had loved through intense devotion; the sweet smile of their native soil; their family connections, distinguished by wealth and nobility; and the hope of advancement to lofty positions.

“Thus freed and unencumbered by a victorious spirit, now under the yoke of monasteries, now in the struggle of the desert, they contended with labors rivaling those of the Maccabees. In exchange for limitless generosity and peace, they embraced every extremity and sought no position of authority in the exile of this passing world.”

[Col. 1378C] 4. Such great virtue in Maurilius could not remain hidden under a bushel for long. Therefore, so that he might also be useful to others, he was placed in charge of a monastery in that same region. In this position, as the same William asserts, he shone forth as outstanding above the other abbots.

Orderic Vitalis writes in book V that the monastery governed by Maurilius was situated in the city of Florence. Our anonymous author, however, gives its name and also praises Margrave Boniface, through whose agency Maurilius assumed the dignity of abbot. He says: “When the abbot of the Florentine church, which was built in honor of Blessed Mary [lacuna], died, Margrave Boniface chose him,” and so on.

The monastery of Saint Mary, commonly called La Badia, still remains famous near Florence, attached to our order under the Cassinese congregation and situated not far from the metropolitan church. Ughelli discusses it in volume II of *Sacred Italy*, as does Lubin in his *Account of the Abbeys of Italy*.

At the time Maurilius was placed in charge of it, however, the monks of that place had become so morally corrupt that, unable to endure the fervor of the holy man’s discipline, they are said to have attempted to kill him with poison. This was the reason Maurilius returned to Gaul, as Orderic relates:

“In the city of Florence he ruled a monastic house by right of abbacy, and, hated by transgressors because of the rigor of discipline, he discovered poison that had been mixed into his drink. Therefore, following the most holy Father and teacher Benedict, he abandoned the incorrigible and came to Neustria with Gerbert, a wise and religious monk. In the time of John, his compatriot and abbot, he came to Fécamp and there chose for himself a permanent dwelling for the worship of the supreme and undivided Trinity.”

The anonymous author relates substantially the same account.

5. In those times the Church of Rouen was governed by Archbishop Malgerius, uncle of Duke William. Because of various crimes, he was deposed at the Council of Lisieux in 1055. Nor was there any lengthy deliberation about appointing a successor. Maurilius, with the agreement both of all the bishops of the province and of the apostolic legate presiding over the council, as well as of the duke himself, was elevated to this dignity. William of Poitiers speaks of the matter in the passage already cited:

The prince—namely, Duke William—observing that admonitions were no longer sufficient in a matter of such great importance, lest by tolerating it any longer he provoke against himself the anger of the heavenly Judge, deposed his uncle in the presence of the holy synod, while the apostolic legate and all the bishops of Normandy gave sentence according to the authority of the canons, by unanimous consent. But he provided Maurilius for the vacant see . . . most worthy of the supreme archiepiscopate because of his noble birth, his person, his virtues, and his learning.

William of Jumièges agrees in book VII, chapter 24 of his *History of the Normans*, where he writes that, by decree of the synod, the metropolitan see was entrusted to Maurilius, a monk of Fécamp, distinguished by many virtues. Orderic, in book V, observes that he was appointed to this dignity by ecclesiastical election. Finally, William himself, when near death, recalled the election of Maurilius while reviewing, in Orderic’s book VII, all the good things he had rightly done for the benefit of his peoples:

“I deposed by papal decree the insolent prelate who was devoted neither to God nor faithful to me from the episcopal see, and in his place I installed Maurilius, the venerable monk whom God had sent me from the city of Florence in Italy.”

Maurilius ascended the throne of Rouen in 1055, as may be inferred from the Council of Lisieux mentioned above. The same date is given in the *Chronicle of Rouen*, in Labbe’s first volume of the *New Library*, and in the *Chronicle of Caen*, in Quercetanus’s *History of the Normans*. There appears to be no disagreement among the authors on this point; they all likewise agree that he was elevated to this dignity from the status of a monk of Fécamp.

6. But before proceeding further with the account of Maurilius’s deeds, we should present a summary of his life from the frequently cited anonymous author of the monastery of Saint-Ouen, in the *Deeds of the Archbishops of Rouen*, printed in volume II of the *Analecta*, p. 439. It reads as follows:

After Malgerius had been deposed, Duke William chose a certain monk named Maurilius. Born of noble lineage in the district of Reims and educated in the church of that same city, he was thereafter instructed in every branch of the liberal arts in the Church of Liège. He became scholasticus of the Church of Halberstadt, a place regarded as exceedingly wealthy in Saxony, where he lived honorably for many years.

Later, inflamed by love of the heavenly homeland and scorning all things of the world, he sought the monastic life. Thus, entering the monastery of Fécamp, he became a monk there, where he lived holily for a long time and offered the others an example of sanctity.

Finally, burning with the fire of divine love and choosing a harsher life, he obtained permission from the abbot who presided over the church and set out for Italy. As a cultivator of the desert, leading a solitary life, he lived by the work of his hands.

When, therefore, the abbot of the Florentine church built in honor of the blessed Mary ever-virgin had died, Marquis Boniface, a noble and most powerful man, chose him. And so, although unwilling, he was overcome by the admonitions of good men and was ordained abbot of that place. There he governed his subjects holily and according to the Rule, as far as he was able, for a long time.

But because the life of the just is a loss to the wicked, the monks who had lived without discipline in the time of his predecessor, unwilling to endure the strictness of the Rule of Father Benedict by which he had bound them to regular observance, and resisting him in every good work, plotted the destruction of his life.

Since he labored over this for many years and saw no progress in them whatsoever, he looked to his own salvation, abandoned the abbey, and returned to his own place, namely Fécamp. There he lived holily until he was enthroned in the episcopate.

Here he completed the church begun by Archbishop Robert. In the presence of William, Duke of the Normans and later King of the English, together with all his suffragans, he solemnly celebrated a council in the Church of Rouen concerning the preservation of chastity and the vigorous restoration of the other institutions of the holy Fathers, which had been negligently set aside through the carelessness of pastors.

After the church had been completed, he dedicated it in the presence of William, Duke of the Normans, in the year 1063 of the Lord’s Incarnation, while Henry, the most noble king of the Franks, was reigning. The diocesan bishops were also present: Odo of Bayeux, John of Avranches, Hugh of Lisieux, William of Évreux, Ivo of Sées, Geoffrey of Coutances, and the other venerable abbots. Pope Victor II likewise presided over the apostolic see.

He also accomplished many good works for the restoration of Christian law and ecclesiastical religion. Persisting in fasts, prayers, and almsgiving until his final day, he gave his soul back to God on the fifth day before the Ides of August [9 August].

After the death of the venerable bishop Maurilius, the aforementioned William, etc.

The anonymous author relates the *Deeds of John*, who succeeded the blessed man. We, however, shall continue the eulogy of Maurilius from other authors, as we had begun.

7. Having thus become the first bishop of all Normandy, Maurilius had nothing more at heart than to erase the disgrace of his predecessor and repair the losses inflicted upon the Church through his negligence. For this reason, in the first year of his pontificate he summoned a council, which was held at Rouen. All the bishops of the province attended. At it, as Bochellus writes—and our anonymous author says the same—discussion was held concerning chastity and the observance of the other institutions of the Fathers, which had been neglected through the carelessness of pastors.

Dadraeus mentions a second council held there in the first year of Pope Stephen IX, that is, in 1057 or the following year. More famous was the synod, or rather assembly, of Caen, which was attended not only by the bishops and abbots but also by the leading men of the whole province, summoned by order of Duke William in 1061, so that public security and the common ecclesiastical and secular welfare might be provided for by common counsel.

Sacred relics were also brought there from various churches at the duke’s command, so that greater religious solemnity might be added to the assembly and the decrees enacted in the presence of the province’s patron saints might be observed by everyone with greater reverence. The people of Rouen brought the bodies of Saints Romanus and Ouen; others brought other relics of the saints.

Furthermore, the prince granted that a truce should be given every week, from the evening of Wednesday until Monday of the following week. This truce was called the Truce of God (*Trevia Dei*). To make the decree more secure, the bishops pronounced an anathema against those guilty of violating the peace.

Among many other provisions, most of which the injury of time has erased, it was decreed that abbots and other prelates should not wander here and there to the public detriment. It was also decreed that every evening, at the ringing of a signal, everyone should be summoned to pour forth prayers to God and warned, with the doors of their houses closed, that further wandering about was forbidden.

8. No less celebrated was the council held at Rouen for the dedication of the major church, which Maurilius himself had completed. Orderic Vitalis speaks of it in book V:

In the year 1063 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second indiction, Archbishop Maurilius dedicated in the city of Rouen, with immense rejoicing and in the month of October, the metropolitan basilica which Robert had begun, in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God.

The anonymous author cited above likewise records the dedication of the Church of Rouen in the year 1063. Certainly our Pommeraye places the Council of Rouen in that very year. He thinks that the council should be identified with what William of Jumièges and Orderic relate in book III concerning Osbern, who was placed in charge of the monastery of Jumièges after Abbot Robert’s departure and was given a pastoral staff by Archbishop Maurilius.

But Robert, abbot of Jumièges, had fled on account of the disputes that had arisen between William and the nobles of Normandy. Orderic explains these disputes more fully under the year 1063. All this seems more than sufficient to prove that the dedication of the Church of Rouen should be assigned to the year 1063, although the second indiction assigned by Orderic in the passage cited above seems to indicate the following year.

Since, however, we learn from the martyrology of that church that the dedication took place on 1 October, perhaps Orderic began the indiction in September, as some people customarily did. For the same author writes elsewhere, namely in book IV, that the dedication of the Church of Rouen took place in 1063, in the first indiction.
