9. The same Orderic, in book V, further testifies that on the occasion of this dedication Maurilius transferred into the sacred church the bodies of the dukes Rollo and William, called Longsword. He buried Rollo first, namely near the southern side, and William beside the northern door, and inscribed their epitaphs above them in golden letters.

Orderic reports these epitaphs, which some believe to have been composed by Maurilius. It will be enough to present here a few of the verses that concern the history of our order. From them we learn that William was so inclined toward the monastic life that he would have embraced it in the monastery of Jumièges, if Abbot Martin had permitted him to do so.

> He beautifully restored the monastery of Jumièges  
> And resolved there to bear the monk’s yoke.  
> Fervently he observed the rule of unconquered Benedict,  
> To whom, filled with the love of God, he sought to submit.

> Abbot Martin delayed this; divine power,  
> Through savage arms, preferred that he should die.

The monk William of Jumièges has more to say about this William and his desire to embrace the monastic way of life, but there is no room to reproduce it here.

10. Another celebrated synod of the bishops of Normandy was held in 1067 on the occasion of another dedication, namely that of the Church of Saint Mary at Jumièges. Maurilius, together with his suffragans and in the presence of William, then already king of England, solemnly and devoutly performed the dedication on the Kalends of July [1 July], as testified by William, monk of Jumièges, in book VII, chapter 37; Orderic Vitalis in book IV; and others. The memory of this dedication is celebrated in the Benedictine martyrology on the Kalends of July itself.

In the preceding year, however, these same bishops, together with the leading men of the province, had been summoned by the duke and assembled at Lillebonne to discuss the English expedition. Since such an assembly should rather be called a provincial parliament than a council, we shall say no more about it. For in these conferences of the nobles, secular affairs were chiefly discussed, and at that time matters of any importance were scarcely handled without the counsel of the bishops.

11. From so frequent a celebration of councils, one may gather that Maurilius vigorously fulfilled the duties of a most watchful pastor. The writers of his age may rightly be accused of negligence because they did not transmit to posterity the decrees enacted in these synods.

Certainly, we can infer the magnitude of this loss from the profession of faith concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist that has come down to us. Catholic truth is explained in it so clearly and precisely that no avenue of escape is left to heretics.

We therefore present it in full, copied by our Pommeraye from an old pontifical of the Church of Rouen, where it appears among other professions of faith in the order of a council to be celebrated. From that time it became customary for this profession of faith to be required of every bishop being consecrated in the province of Normandy. It reads as follows:

It is also necessary, dearest brothers, that your faith concerning the body and blood of the Lord, which, when Maurilius of venerable memory presided over this holy see, you defined by common agreement against the most filthy utterances of Berengarius and his successors, should be recited again.

With heart we believe and with mouth we confess that the bread placed upon the Lord’s table is merely bread before the consecration; but that in the consecration itself, by the ineffable power of the Godhead, the nature and substance of the bread are changed into the nature and substance of flesh. This is not the flesh of anyone else, but that which was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, which also, for us and for our salvation, was scourged, hung upon the wood, lay in the tomb, rose from the dead on the third day, and sits at the right hand of God the Father.

Likewise, the wine mixed with water and offered in the chalice for sanctification is truly and essentially changed into that blood which, through the wound in the Lord’s side, flowed forth happily for the redemption of the world by the soldier’s lance.

But we anathematize those who think proudly and heretically against this holy and apostolic faith and chatter with impious recklessness.

This profession of faith, which appears to have been decreed at the council held in 1063, was issued by Maurilius against the errors of Berengarius, so that no one from the flock entrusted to him might entangle himself in the snares of the heresiarch. Berengarius had indeed attempted to infect the Normans with his heresy, as is evident from what is recorded concerning the assembly of Brionne in the work of Durand of Troarn, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*.

12. How great Maurilius’s zeal for divine matters was can be understood from the letter prefixed to the book *On the Divine Offices* by John, bishop of Avranches, which he dedicated to Maurilius. We present it here in full, as it was published together with the book itself by certain canons of the Church of Rouen from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint-Sauveur:

To the truly holy Lord Maurilius, worthy of honor for his merits, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Rouen, John of Avranches, least of all the bishops in merit, offers the gift of complete obedience in body and spirit.

Because I have learned, through the very frequent discussions held with me on this subject, that the holiness of your fatherly dignity, always concerned for the advancement of ecclesiastical dignity, is afflicted by its decline through grievous error; and because your ardent desire to restore it is increased by the fact that the weakness of illness has taken away your strength for this task, my littleness has desired to support your most holy wish—not inflamed by any arrogance, but moved by pious compassion—so that what is corrupted by the negligence of careless pastors might be restored through the vigilance of your holy religion.

Therefore, trusting in your authority, I have undertaken the judgments of the holy Fathers, examined the practices and customs of various churches, and considered what pertains to the offices of divine worship and what they mystically contain. From these things I have composed a kind of compilation, which, still hidden from everyone else, I submit to the examination of your discernment, so that you may inspect this little work and, in inspecting it, apply that diligence by which you may show us that you are truly the man whom you fittingly display in fatherhood and teaching.

It is your concern, therefore, that if there are matters deserving approval, you should willingly assent to them with fatherly affection; but if the contrary is the case, you should correct them with the judgment of a vigilant teacher.

If your authority judges the work useful and sound, then, after we have seen it flow from the metropolitan see, we shall strive, following the statutes of the canons, to offer it to our people as nourishment.

13. Maurilius also cultivated sacred places. Besides the metropolitan church, which, as we have said, he completed and solemnly consecrated, Count Robert of Eu testifies in the foundation charter of Saint Michael of Vauport that the monastery was founded by him chiefly on the advice of Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen.

The same bishop subscribed the charter of Count Robert of Évreux for the monastery of Saint-Sauveur at Évreux, belonging to the nuns of our order, which was founded by that same count while Maurilius was seated in the episcopate.

Our brethren of the monastery of Dives also maintain that the church of their monastery—namely, Saint Mary above Dives—was consecrated by the same blessed bishop. Orderic Vitalis appears to suggest this in book IV.

The same bishop granted the monks of Saint Peter of Chartres immunity from the toll at Andely, which belonged to his jurisdiction, as is evident from his charter published by the Sammarthani.

14. He was no less concerned that pious men suited to sacred ministry should be placed over churches. They assert that Walkelin was appointed to the see of Winchester by King William of England through Maurilius’s efforts. William of Malmesbury testifies that such a man was not unworthy of the recommendation of so great a man. In book III he says of him:

Walkelin . . . whose good works, surpassing his reputation, will drive old age into oblivion as long as the episcopal see of Winchester endures, etc.

He also delayed for a time Theoderic, abbot of Jumièges, whose eulogy we gave above under the year 1058, when the latter was considering resigning the governance of the monastery.

When that pious abbot, because of disturbances that had arisen in his monastery, returned his pastoral staff to Duke William, the duke entrusted Maurilius with investigating the cause of the scandal. Thus, in 1056, as Orderic relates in book III, Maurilius, Hugh, bishop of Lisieux, Ansfrid, abbot of Prêaux, Lanfranc, prior of Bec, and other distinguished men came to Jumièges.

After the solemnity of the Apostles Peter and Paul had been celebrated there, they heard and carefully examined the sources of the dissensions. They ordered Abbot Theoderic to remain in charge and, in an extended address, admonished Robert, the prior of the place, who was stirring up turmoil in the monastery, to obey his father.

But that peace did not last long. Scarcely a year had passed when new disputes arose again. Therefore Theoderic, truly a son of peace, laid down the burden of governance before the saddened bishops, as the cited author says in book VI, before Maurilius of Rouen and Hugh of Lisieux.

15. The monastic order also owes Anselm to Maurilius. When Anselm’s mind was wavering over what manner of life he should follow, he consulted Lanfranc, then prior of Bec, about what ought to be done. Lanfranc, says Eadmer at the beginning of book I of *The Life of Anselm*, delayed giving an opinion and advised that the matter should rather be referred to the judgment of the venerable Maurilius, bishop of Rouen.

Anselm agreed. Together they went to Rouen and approached the archbishop. When Anselm had explained to him the anxieties of his mind, Eadmer says:

Without delay, the monastic order was praised above all others, and its way of life was preferred to every other.

Hearing and approving this, Anselm set aside all other options, abandoned the world, and became a monk of Bec in the twenty-seventh year of his age.

Later, when he had been elected prior of the monastery, Maurilius turned him away from resigning the care of his brothers, as Eadmer likewise relates:

But when Anselm was wearied by the various affairs of different people and his mind was sometimes disturbed from its tranquility by them, he came to Rouen to seek counsel concerning these matters from the aforementioned archbishop of the Church of Rouen, Maurilius of venerable memory.

When he explained to the bishop the reason for his arrival and, in the course of his words, wept most bitterly over the tranquillity of his former state, he began earnestly to beg that he might be relieved of the burden of the prelacy, which he confessed to be unbearable.

But he, as a man of great sanctity, said:

“My dearest son, do not seek what you are seeking, nor, concerned only for yourself, wish to withdraw from supporting others. For I truly tell you that I have heard of many and seen many who, because they desired their own peace, refused through pastoral care to watch over the welfare of their neighbors; walking always through negligence, they advanced from bad to worse.

“Therefore, lest the same thing happen to you—God forbid!—I command you under holy obedience to retain the prelacy that you now possess and not to abandon it in any way unless your abbot orders you to do so. And if at any time you are called to a greater office, do not refuse to accept it. For I know that you will not remain long in the position you now hold; before long you will be advanced to a higher degree of prelacy.”

When he heard this, Anselm said:

“Woe is me, miserable man! I fail under the burden I bear; and if a heavier burden is imposed, I dare not reject it.”

The bishop repeated his command and, as before, ordered him not to transgress it.

16. Thus, full of merits and years, Bishop Maurilius departed this life in 1067. On this point all ancient and modern historians agree, except for a single Fécamp chronicler, in volume I of Labbe’s *New Library*, where the blessed man’s death is mistakenly assigned to the following year.

William of Jumièges writes that in 1067, on the fifth day before the Ides of August [9 August], Maurilius departed free and rejoicing, already destined to live with his King Christ. Orderic Vitalis says in book V that he flourished for twelve years during the pontificates of Popes Victor, Stephen, Nicholas, and Alexander, and summarizes his brief eulogy in these two verses:

> Bishop Maurilius, filled with the light of learning,  
> Shone forth in exceptional conduct and noble deeds.

In book IV, under the year 1067, he treats the death of the same holy man somewhat more fully and reports the epitaph placed upon his tomb:

In the twelfth year of his episcopate he took to his bed. After completing everything that belongs to a devout servant of God, he departed to God, whom he had served for a long time, on the fifth day before the Ides of August.

His body was carried into the episcopal church, which he himself had dedicated to holy Mary, Mother of God, five years earlier, in the first indiction, and was honorably buried before the crucifix.

His epitaph was composed by Richard, son of Herluin, a canon of that same church, and was written above him in letters of gold on bronze plates:

> Citizens of the human world, do not refuse a tear  
> For your bishop, the monk Maurilius.  
> Reims gave him birth; Liège, nurse of learning,  
> Made him drink from its threefold philosophical spring.  
> For you he brought this church, once begun, to perfection,  
> And with great joy celebrated its dedication.  
> While the sober Christian people keeps vigil for you, Laurence,  
> He passes on and celebrates festive crowns in heaven.

17. Among other proofs that Maurilius did not abandon the practices of monastic life even as archbishop is the fact that his name is scarcely ever found among contemporary authors without mention of his monastic profession.

This is evident from the epitaph we have quoted here, as well as from the many other testimonies of William of Jumièges and Orderic Vitalis that we have cited throughout this eulogy.

The *Chronicle of Caen* reads:

In 1067 Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen, died, a monk of Fécamp.

The *Chronicle of Rouen*, in Labbe’s first volume of the *New Library*, has the same words. And William the Conqueror, when near death, as we observed above from Orderic, congratulates himself on having secured Maurilius, the venerable monk, as archbishop of the Church of Rouen.

18. We must not omit here a remarkable event which, according to William of Malmesbury in book III of *The Deeds of the Kings of England*, occurred shortly before Maurilius’s death.

Our Hugh Menardus also copied it from a manuscript of Saint-Victor in Paris in the appendix to his observations on the Benedictine martyrology. Pommeraye published it in French in his *History of the Archbishops of Rouen*, from another manuscript, namely one from the library of the cathedral Church of Rouen. But we shall reproduce it in William’s words, since he is the more ancient author.

It reads as follows:

Maurilius, a monk of Fécamp, succeeded Malgerius. He was praised for many virtues, but especially for abstinence. After living a good and holy life, when he had reached the end at God’s call, he lost the breath of life and lay dead for nearly half a day.

But when preparations were already being made to carry him into the church, he regained his soul and filled those standing around him with tearful joy. He strengthened them in their astonishment with these words:

“Listen attentively, receiving the final words of your pastor. I was released by natural death, but I have been brought back so that I might tell you what I saw. I shall not remain much longer, for it is pleasing to me to sleep in the Lord.

“The guides of my spirit were composed in face and clothing with every elegance. The gentleness of their words corresponded to the brightness of their garments, so that I desired nothing except the service of such men.

“Thus, rejoicing in their gentle flatteries, I went, as it truly seemed to me, toward the East. A paradisiacal seat was promised to me, which I was soon to enter. In an instant we had passed through Europe and, entering Asia, came to Jerusalem. After worshiping there among the saints, we proceeded to the Jordan. The inhabitants of the nearer bank, mingling with the companions of my guides, formed a joyful assembly.

“I was hastening to cross, eager to see what lay beyond. Then my companions said that God had commanded that I first be terrified by the sight of demons, so that the venial sins which I had not cleansed through confession might be purged by fear of dreadful forms.

“At once there appeared on the other side such a host of demons brandishing sharp spears and breathing fire that the field seemed iron and the air fiery. I was so affected by their horror that, even if the earth had opened and heaven had been revealed, I would not have thought myself safe in either place of refuge.

“Thus, while I was fearful and uncertain where to go, I suddenly recovered my breath, as though saying this: ‘Unless you neglect it, I would provide for your salvation.’”

He spoke, and with the word he almost breathed out his spirit.

His body, which had then been buried in the ground in the Church of Saint Mary, was, as they say, by a divine miracle raised three feet above the earth.

19. Since Maurilius’s death was so precious in the sight of God, it is not surprising that later generations recognized his sanctity. They did not hesitate to honor him with the title of saint or blessed.

Orderic calls Maurilius “holy” in book III. Milo, in chapter 5 of the *Life of Saint Lanfranc*, a contemporary of Maurilius, writes that the Church of Rouen had been deprived of “the holy and venerable archbishop Maurilius.”

In the Hirsaugiensis Chronicle of Trithemius, in the Saint Gall edition, under the year 1064, he is called a man of most holy conduct who, because of his learning and the merit of his life, was substituted for Archbishop Malgerius. Trithemius then writes of him:

He is held famous for virtues and miracles, and his deeds have been written down.

In the older edition:

Saint Maurilius, archbishop and formerly a monk of the monastery of Fécamp in our order . . . a man adorned with the beauty of many virtues, an outstanding cultivator of charity and abstinence, whose holy conduct is celebrated with lofty praises.

He repeats nearly the same account in book IV of *On Illustrious Men of Our Order*, chapter 120.

Hence his name is found inscribed in various Gallican and monastic martyrologies on 9 August, the day of his death. Others, however, on account of another Maurilius, commemorate him on 13 September; on that very day he is also commemorated by Ferrarius.

Bucelinus celebrates him on both days, and even on 26 February mentions Maurilius, a monk of Fécamp, as though he were someone other than the archbishop; he attributes to him the vision that we quoted above from William of Malmesbury. Bollandus also mentions him on this occasion among those passed over on 26 February.

The brothers Sammarthani and our Pommeraye in their accounts of the archbishops of Rouen, Marlotus in the metropolitan church of Reims, and many other authors everywhere have celebrated this same holy bishop with abundant praise. It would be unnecessary to list them individually.

20. Nevertheless, blessed Maurilius has not yet obtained any public office in the diocese of Rouen, although his tomb—commonly called the tomb of Saint Maurilius—has always been venerated by the people of Rouen, especially by the clergy of the metropolitan church. From ancient tradition it was also customary to incense it solemnly on appointed days.

But in 1480, when the canons of Rouen granted Cardinal William of Estouteville, then archbishop, permission to construct his own tomb there, a stone coffin was discovered when the ground was dug up. Besides the bones of the blessed man, it contained pieces of wood from the cross and several relics of sacred vestments.

The cardinal’s tomb was nevertheless placed there, and in 1483 his heart was buried in it. But the heretics of the Calvinist sect violated all these things in 1562, and thereafter no memory remained either of the blessed man’s relics or of his tomb.

[Col. 1387]

## Letter of Maurilius, Archbishop of Rouen, and John, Abbot of Fécamp, to the Bishop of Évreux

They complain that, without consulting the abbot, he had punished a monk for violating the truce.

*(Marten, Anecdota, vol. I, p. 206.)*

To the most reverend bishop M., of the holy mother Church of Évreux, Maurilius, humble archbishop of the Church of Rouen, and John, servant of the monks of Fécamp, offer rightly and divide more rightly.

[Col. 1389]

We have heard that your fraternity condemned a certain monk to banishment because he was discovered to have violated the Truce of God. We praise you for having acted rightly, but we judge that you examined the matter incautiously.

For the institution of Saint Benedict is prescribed for the judgment of no one. Therefore, dearest brother, we are commanded to offer rightly and to divide more rightly. Let us therefore follow the golden virtue, namely discretion, which is called the mother of all virtues.

When the care of souls is entrusted to an abbot by a bishop, the pastoral care of the sheep of Christ committed to him is entrusted to him in every respect. Unless the bishop is invited by the abbot for some matter whatsoever, the bishop is held to have no jurisdiction in the monastery. But if anyone should attempt to resist what we have said, we set before him the Rule of Saint Benedict.

[Col. 1389]

## Maurilius’s Profession of Faith concerning the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of Christ

It appears above, in no. 11 of the *Life of Blessed Maurilius*.

[Col. 1389]

## Epitaphs of Rollo and William Longsword, Dukes of Normandy, by Maurilius, Archbishop

*(Orderic Vitalis, Ecclesiastical History, book V, in Duchesne, Norman Writers, p. 567.)*

### I. Epitaph of Rollo

[Col. 1389A]

> Rollo, Duke of the Normans, the terror of his enemies and the weapon of his people,  
> Is enclosed beneath this inscription in the tomb.  
> His valor advanced his ancestors so greatly that  
> Neither grandfather, father, nor great-grandfather served him.  
> He defeated in battle the Danish king leading  
> Brave men and many cohorts.  
> Frisians, Walerans, Halbacenses, and Hainautians—  
> Rollo drove them all together into flight.  
> He forced the Frisians, conquered through many wounds,  
> To swear allegiance to him and pay tribute.  
> He captured Bayeux and twice overcame Paris;  
> No one was more formidable to the Frankish battle-lines.  
> For thirty years he filled the fields of Gaul  
> With the slaughter of the Gauls, waging war against sluggish Charles.  
> After many massacres, plunderings, burnings, and killings,  
> He entered into a useful treaty with the eager Franks.  
> As a suppliant, he deserved to be washed in Frankish baptism;  
> Thus all the guilt of the former man perished.  
> As he had once been a wolf, so afterward he became a lamb among the gentle;  
> May peace soothe him, thus transformed, before God.

### II. Epitaph of William Longsword

> No one oppressed those whom William defended;  
> Whoever he wished to harm lacked assistance.  
> His hand was feared by kings and dukes;  
> The warrior Emperor Henry feared him.  
> For twenty-five years he ruled the Normans,  
> Ready in the duties of soldier and commander.  
> He beautifully restored the monastery of Jumièges,  
> And resolved there to bear the monk’s yoke.  
> Fervently he observed the rule of unconquered Benedict,  
> To whom, filled with the love of God, he sought to submit.  
> Abbot Martin delayed this; divine power  
> Preferred that he should die through savage arms.  
> For, caught unarmed in the plots of Count Arnulf,  
> He fell. May he possess the heavenly God. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 1067: Raimbald, Archbishop of the Church of Arles

[Col. 1389]

## Historical Notice

*(From the old edition of the* Gallia Christiana, *vol. I, p. 553.)*
[Col. 1389C] When Pontius entered the monastery of Saint Victor at Marseilles, that holy congregation provided him with a successor, namely Raimbald, a pupil of Saint Isarnus, abbot. He was born of noble stock in Provence. His father was Boniface, lord of Relliana, and his mother Vandelnusia, as the charters of Saint Victor teach us. [Col. 1390C] His brothers were Boniface, Fulco, Boso, and Atanulfus. He was related to Guillelm and Fulco, viscounts of Marseilles. Having made great progress under the discipline of Saint Isarnus, abbot, he was judged worthy of the see of Arles, to which he was elected in 1031, in the fourteenth indiction, in August; [Col. 1391A] shortly afterward he took his seat at the Council of Narbonne. In his pontificate, however, mindful of his former institution, whenever he subscribed his name he was accustomed to add not only the title of archbishop but also that of monk.

Without doubt he thereby showed favor to the monastery of Saint Victor. For in 1035, indiction III, he gave it the share that he possessed in the castle of Auriol. He also placed in the hands of Abbot Isarnus, under whose instruction he had learned the monastic life, the church of Saint Genesius, or Saint Honoratus, retaining for the altar of Saint Stephen or Saint Trophimus a rent of one pound of incense, payable on the feast of Saint Trophimus. It is worth observing that the name and title of Saint Trophimus was not added to the name of Saint Stephen in the church of Arles before the pontificate of Pontius in 1029, as may be seen in his charter; Raimbald followed his example. [Col. 1391B] In 1037 he subscribed the letters of Gauffred and Bertrand, counts of Provence, on behalf of the monastery of Cluny, according to the same charters. In 1040, on the Ides of October, he was present at the dedication of the basilica of Saint Victor of Marseilles, performed through the agency of Pope Benedict IX. In that same year, in the eighth indiction, he settled a dispute between the people of Marseilles and the monks of Montmajour, in the presence of Counts Gauffred and Bertrannus and of Guillelm and Fulco, viscounts of Marseilles. In that very year he subscribed the charter of Amelius, bishop of Senez, for Saint Victor. From then on he is frequently mentioned in the charters of Saint Victor, so that it would seem superfluous to review them individually, especially since more noteworthy matters remain.

About the year 1050, Pontius, archbishop of Aix, promised submission and reverence to Raimbald, according to the precepts of the canons [Col. 1391C] and the institutions of the Fathers. Honoratus Bouche likewise testifies that Bertrand of Fréjus, Angelricus of Riez, and Benedict of Avignon made the same promise, and he praises the sacramentary of Arles, so called because it contains sacraments of this kind. He is listed among the Fathers of the Council of Barcelona in 1054. In 1056—if Baluzius and Labbeus conjecture correctly—on the day before the Nones of September, he held, together with Leodegarius of Vienne and the legates of Narbonne, a council of twenty-two bishops at Saint-Gilles. Yet it seems almost certain that it was held earlier, even from the list of the bishops of Lodève alone. It is established that this synod took place on the day before the Nones of September, and the Council of Toulouse on the Ides of the same month, in 1056. At the Narbonese council [Col. 1391D] at Saint-Gilles, Bernard, bishop of Lodève, was present, and at the Council of Toulouse, Rostagnus. If these synods were held in the same year, only nine days elapsed between them. But how could there have been, in so brief a time, two bishops of Lodève who attended them? Certainly, after Bernard’s death, an election could not have taken place until permission had been granted by the metropolitan. The bishops of the province would have had to be summoned for the consecration of the new bishop. Was a period of nine days sufficient for all this? At the aforesaid Council of Toulouse [Col. 1392A] our Raimbald was appointed president by the pope, as vicar of the Holy See. In 1060 he presided over the Council of Avignon.

Not content with doing good in his own diocese, he founded in the diocese of Fréjus a church for clerics whom, having established them under a regular rule, he ordered always to remain subject to the Roman Church, as he writes to Pope Alexander II. Consequently, this cannot have been done before 1061, the year in which Alexander’s pontificate began. Alexander welcomed Raimbald’s proposal and therefore took the Church of Barjols under the protection of the Roman Church; as a sign of subjection, he imposed an annual rent of a gold denarius. The same archbishop led the canons of the major church [Col. 1392B] to adopt the institution of regular canons. To them Guillelm, viscount of Marseilles, donated extensive estates and possessions in the Crau; this arrangement was later renewed by Archbishop Aycard, as appears from a charter preserved in the archive of Arles.

Finally, in 1065 he blessed the church of Saint Peter at Correns [variant: Saint Mary of Correno], where a monastery had been built, and on the day of its consecration granted an absolution from penance to all who would provide benefactions to that church. From the fact that the anniversary of that day was formerly celebrated with great festivity, it is clear from a charter of the monastery of Montmajour that there was a jubilee at Correns. He subscribed the letters of Almodis, countess of Rouergue, Nîmes, and elsewhere, by which she subjected the monastery of Saint-Gilles to the abbot of Cluny; dated 1066, the eighth day before the Kalends of January. In the subscription Raimbald [Col. 1392C] likewise calls himself archbishop of Arles and vicar of the Roman Church. That he lived on until 1067 is proved by a letter of a certain Jerome, which the distinguished Antoninus de Ruffi extracted from the great cartulary of Saint Victor and sent to us, as is his customary kindness.

Nevertheless, Ruffius maintains that Raimbald had already yielded the see to Aycard in 1060; in that year, he says, Aycard subscribed a certain charter which Ruffius himself read. On the other hand, it is regarded as certain that Raimbald, well before his death, laid down his pastoral burden and once again embraced monastic life in the monastery of Saint Victor. To state our own view, it seems clear to us that Raimbald lived [Col. 1392D] until 1067. Before his death he indeed returned to the monastic state, but we do not dare determine when. At the election of Bernard II as abbot of Saint Victor in 1065, when subscribing his name, he calls himself both archbishop and monk. Throughout that period there is either no mention of Aycard, his successor, or only rare mention of him. The day of Raimbald’s deposition is recorded as 13 March in the Necrology of the Canons of La Canourgue.

[Col. 1393]

## Raimbald’s Charters

### I. Privilege for the Monastery of Saint Victor (1035)

*[Christian Gaul, old edition, vol. I, Instruments, p. 95.]*

[Col. 1393A]

Since it is evident that Almighty God, with ineffable providence and according to his will, created all things, it is also evident that he gave the earth to humanity for possession, together with the things existing in it or derived from it. Therefore I, Raimbald, raised by the grace of God to the honor of the episcopate of the see of Arles, greatly considering my enormous sin, as well as the examination that will take place at the future judgment of sinners, and terrified by the immeasurable flames of Gehenna, etc., remembering these things, fearing the terror of the Judge, and embracing the mercy of the Redeemer, have determined that the land under my authority and jurisdiction be given to Almighty God and to the monastery of Saint Victor the Martyr, founded not far from the walls of Marseilles, and to the abbots and monks, present and future, serving God there, to be held perpetually.

Specifically, from the castle called Auriol, I give my entire share, which I possess there either personally or through another on my behalf, except for the allod already given in the village and castle, and throughout the whole territory, in cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards and meadows, pastures and woods, scrublands and thickets, together with all the mills belonging to my share of the allod and fief, except for two manses, which I gave to Aldoardus and Pontius. Thus, in every respect and in all things, from the aforesaid castle and all its dependencies belonging to what may be called my freehold, I give all these things perpetually to Saint Victor, [Col. 1393C] from fear of my sins and likewise from love of eternal rewards. To that venerable place and holy community of brothers I hand them over to possess, hold, and retain, for the remission of all the sins of my soul and of my parents.

If any of our relatives or brothers, or anyone whatsoever, should wish to annul this gift, may he be unable to accomplish it; instead, let him pay as a penalty ten pounds of gold, and in this way incur the eternal punishments of Almighty God, suffer them forever, and be thrust into hell. Thereafter, may this gift remain perpetual and firm forever.

This donation was made in the year 1035 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third indiction.

I, Raimbald, ordered this charter to be made with my heirs and requested that it be confirmed. At my request my brother Boniface confirmed it, followed by these others: Guillelm, viscount of Marseilles, together with his sons, Lord Pontius the bishop, Aycard, Fulco, Stephen, and Bertrand, confirmed it. Autrannus confirmed. Pontius of Lambesc confirmed. Guiquiramus confirmed. Fulco confirmed. Majolus confirmed. Noe confirmed. Rainaldus confirmed. Arenulfus confirmed. Boniface confirmed. Faraldus confirmed. Guisla confirmed. Her son Pontius Milo confirmed. Pontius [Col. 1394A] Autricus confirmed. Rostagnus Willamurus confirmed. Bonporus confirmed.

### II. Absolution from Penance Granted at the Consecration of the Endowed Church of Saint Mary of Correns (1065)

*[Apud Acherium, Spicilegium, vol. VI, p. 441.]*

Raimbald, servant of the servants of God, by apostolic authority, sends health to all, both clergy and laity, and grants assistance to penitents. At the blessing and consecration of the church of the Holy Trinity, Saint Mary, Saint John, and Saint Peter at Correns, we grant the following absolution: whoever enters this church to give a benefaction may rejoice that he has obtained every benefit; and [Col. 1394B] the penitent who comes to it at its consecration may receive such a remedy for himself. We remit to him a third part of his penance, restore him to the church until the beginning of the year, and grant him peace; he is also to have his hair cut. If death should occur during the year, or even after the year has passed, he shall remain absolved on our behalf; and if it occurs in another year, annually or even after the year has passed, he shall remain within that absolution.

We received this absolution from Saint Peter, to whom, as nearly the whole Catholic world acknowledges, power was conferred from heaven: the one who frees whomever he wishes from … bonds, binds whom he wishes in heaven and on earth, forgives whom he wishes, and destroys whom he wishes. Therefore, with our permission, whoever does good to this place shall receive such a blessing [Col. 1394C] as we have stated above.

Whoever goes to this church shall travel safely from all his enemies; and whoever causes him any impediment shall know that he is excommunicated and anathematized. If, therefore—which we do not desire—anyone should attempt, with reckless boldness, to act against this our command and should commit an offense in the village commonly called Correno, then, if he does not come to make amends within forty days, let him know that he is accursed with all the curses contained in the New and Old Testament, etc.

### III. Charter for Saint Victor Confirmed by Raimbald, Archbishop of Arles (1069)

*[Christian Gaul, ibid., p. 555.]*

[Col. 1394D]

I, Jerome Rainois, formerly son of …, and my wife Mirmanda, in the presence of Lord Raimbald, archbishop of the city of Arles, give to Saint Victor the houses which we appear to possess in the aforesaid city, beside the Church of Saint Genesius and above the bank of the Rhône River, in the year 1067. I, Jerome, my wife, and my brother Boso confirmed this donation. Lord Archbishop Raimbald confirmed it. Hugo [Col. 1395A] of Balé confirmed it. Volveradus and his brother Amelius confirmed it. Fulco, the archbishop’s brother, confirmed it.

### IV. Sermon and Confirmation of the Holy Fathers Concerning the Holy Truce of God (1041)

*[Edited by Dom Martene, Thesaurus Anecdotorum I, 161, from the Talveran manuscript.]*

In the name of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, Raimbald, archbishop of Arles, together with Benedict, bishop of Avignon, and Nitardus, bishop of Nice, and also the venerable abbot Lord Odilo, together with all the bishops and abbots and the entire clergy dwelling throughout Gaul, to all archbishops, bishops, priests, and the entire clergy residing throughout Italy: grace and peace to you from God the almighty Father, who is, who was, and who is to come.

[Note: [Col. 1395D] Hugo, abbot of Flavigny, expressly asserts in his Chronicle that the truce was first established in 1041 under the authority of Saint Odilo, and that it was confirmed not only by human authority but also by divine terrors.]

We ask and beseech you, all who fear God, believe in him, and have been redeemed by his blood, to take care and make provision for the salvation of your souls and bodies, and to follow the footsteps of God, having peace with one another, so that you may deserve to possess with him perpetual peace and tranquility.

Receive, therefore, and hold fast that peace and the Truce of God which we too, through the divine inspiration of mercy, have now received as sent to us from heaven and firmly hold. It has been established and arranged as follows: from the evening hour of Wednesday, among all Christians, friends and enemies, neighbors and strangers, there shall be firm peace and stable truce until Monday, that is, until sunrise on the second day of the week, so that during these four days and nights they may at every hour be secure and, freed from all fear of enemies and strengthened in the tranquility of peace and of this truce, may do whatever is necessary.

Whoever observes and firmly keeps this peace and Truce of God shall be absolved by God the almighty Father, by his Son Jesus Christ, and by the Holy Spirit; by Saint Mary with the choirs of virgins; by Saint Michael with the choirs of angels; and by Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, with all the saints and all the faithful, now and always and for ever and ever.

But those who have accepted the promised truce and knowingly wish to violate it [Col. 1395D] shall be excommunicated by God the almighty Father, by his Son Jesus Christ, and by the Holy Spirit. They shall be excommunicated, accursed, and detested by all the saints of God, here and forever; they shall be condemned like Dathan and Abiron and like Judas, who betrayed the Lord; and, unless they come to make amends as established, they shall be plunged into the depths of hell like Pharaoh in the midst of the sea.

If anyone commits homicide during the days of the Truce of God, he shall be made an exile and expelled from his own country; he shall travel to Jerusalem and suffer prolonged exile there. But if he breaks the aforesaid peace and Truce of God in any other matter, he shall be examined according to the decrees of secular laws and compelled to pay according to the measure of his offenses; and according to the rules of the holy canons he shall be sentenced to double penance. We consider this fitting so that, if we should presume to violate in any respect the promise made there, we may be condemned twice over, by worldly and spiritual judgment.

For we believe that this matter was inspired in us from heaven by God’s assistance, since, as we believe, no good was being done among us when it was sent by God to his people. The Lord’s appointed day was not being celebrated, but every kind of servile work was performed on it. Therefore we promised and vowed to God the four-day period mentioned above: Thursday because of the Ascension, Friday because of Christ’s Passion, Saturday in veneration of his burial, and [Col. 1396B] Sunday so that the Resurrection might be celebrated inviolably. On Sunday no rural labor whatsoever was to be performed, and an enemy was not to fear an enemy, according to the authority granted by God and handed down by the apostles.

We bless and absolve all who love this peace and Truce of God, as stated above. But those who oppose it we excommunicate, curse, and anathematize, and expel from the thresholds of holy Mother Church.

When anyone happens to take vengeance upon those who have dared to violate this charter and the Truce of God, let those who exact vengeance be held liable for no offense; rather, as defenders of God’s cause, let them depart from and return to all Christians blessed.

But if anything is taken during the remaining days and encountered during the days of the truce, it shall in no way be retained, lest an opportunity appear to have been given to the enemy. Furthermore, we ask you, brothers, that on whatever day the aforesaid peace and truce has been established among you, you devoutly commemorate that day in the name of the Holy Trinity.

Expel all robbers from your region, abominate them, curse them, and excommunicate them in the name of all the saints written above. Offer your tithes and firstfruits from your labors to God. Carry your goods to the churches for the salvation of the living and the dead, so that God may free you from all evils in this life and, after this life, lead you to the kingdom of heaven. He lives and reigns as God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. [Col. 1396D] Amen.

### V. Charter of Raimbald by Which He Gives the Church of Saint Genesius and Saint Honoratus to the Monks of Saint Victor

*[Christian Gaul, new edition I, 95, from the cartulary of Saint Caesarius.]*

Having attained, by the incomprehensible disposition of Almighty God, the pontifical height of this holy see of Arles, I began thereafter to turn many thoughts concerning that same administration over in my mind, etc. Therefore, one day, reflecting at length on a religious place built in honor of Saint Genesius or Saint Honoratus, situated outside the walls of our city [Col. 1397A], I considered how a place once devoted to the spiritual service of monks in ancient times had been converted to the service of secular possession. I resolved with myself to give that place to the monastery of Saint Victor of Marseilles, where Abbot Isarnus might establish monks for the service of Christ.

Therefore I, Raimbald, raised by the grace of God to the honor of the episcopate, give, donate, and cede in perpetual right to Isarnus, abbot of Saint Victor of Marseilles, the church of Saint Genesius with all the churches subject to it, all the other things which it now appears to possess, and whatever it may be able to acquire in the future, whether from the property it already holds or from anything acquired elsewhere, except for those lay fiefs and whatever the laymen have ceded to the abbot of the community from those fiefs of theirs. With the counsel of my fellow bishops and of my successors [Col. 1398A], and with the consent of all the princes or counts of the province, namely Josefredus and Bertrand, as well as the canons of our see of Arles and Pontius, bishop of Marseilles, together with the brothers, we hand over and donate the whole to him.

The arrangement is that the monks or the abbot shall pay each year to the altar of Saint Stephen or Saint Trophimus one pound of incense on the feast of Saint Trophimus. For this very act, which we have carried out at God’s inspiration, is likewise commanded by the authority of the sacred canons and the law: that a monastery be built from the property of a bishopric.

## In the Year of the Lord 1067. Gervasius, Archbishop of Reims

[Col. 1397]

### Historical Notice

*[From Christian Gaul, new edition, vol. X.]*

[Col. 1397B] This prelate, whom almost everyone praises, was violently and maliciously attacked with curses by William, abbot of Metz, who even called him a tyrant. Yet that abbot is said to have been a man devoted to God and of most holy life. Still, if credence is to be given to the history of Blessed Theoderic, abbot of Andage, it must not be denied that although he was shrewd and energetic in every matter and worthy of the episcopate, by nature and character he was more savage, harsh, and brutal than was fitting.

He was born in 1007, or perhaps 1008, on the Nones of February, at Château-du-Loir, to Hamelin or Aymo, lord of Château-du-Loir, and Hildegard or Hildeburg of Bellême, sister of Avesgaud, bishop of Le Mans. He succeeded his maternal uncle Avesgaud in the episcopate in 1036. But scarcely [Col. 1397C] had he ascended the episcopal throne, says Marlot, when Herbert, surnamed Bacchus, who had long been hostile to Avesgaud, laid an ambush for him and, with unheard-of tyranny, excluded him from entering the city of Le Mans for two years.

Subsequently, Geoffrey of Anjou, to whom Gervasius had promised the bishopric for as long as he lived, and who had again been harassed by Herbert’s wickedness, changed from friend into enemy. Believing himself deceived, he besieged Château-du-Loir; then, under the pretext of arranging peace, he lured Gervasius into a private conference, treacherously seized him, and held him captive in chains for seven years, as can be gathered from the acts of the Council of Reims under Leo IX. There Geoffrey was placed under anathema and ordered to set Gervasius free. Yet Gervasius did not obtain his freedom [Col. 1397D] until he had first surrendered, even against his will, Château-du-Loir, which had come to him by hereditary right [Col. 1398B].

Rescued from his long and wearisome imprisonment, Gervasius withdrew to Normandy, where Duke William received him courteously and heaped upon him gold, silver, honors, and many estates. As his fame spread throughout Gaul, the king, wishing to attract so distinguished a prelate and bind him to himself by favors, first appointed him to his council. Then, when Archbishop Gindon yielded to fate, he eagerly secured for him the see of Reims, which Gervasius obtained with the consent of clergy and people on the Ides of October 1055.

Four years later, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, on Pentecost itself, he anointed Philip I, while the king’s father Henry was present, attended by twenty-four bishops and legates of Pope Nicholas V. An old charter sets out what happened; we have arranged to transcribe it from volume II of *The Liberties of the Gallican Church* among the instruments. Taking advantage of this occasion, Gervasius claimed for himself the primacy of all Gaul, the power to consecrate the kings of the Franks, and the office of supreme chancellor, which his predecessors had held.

Apart from that charter, which is supported by very numerous others, and apart from Alberic of the Three Fountains, the Chronicle of Reims, and the appendix to the Chronicle of Mouzon, it is established that Gervasius began to sit in 1055. If this seems to conflict with certain other instruments, it is necessary to conclude that an error entered their chronological notices through the fault of scribes or copyists. Below you will see what we shall say on this matter concerning the Abbey of Saint-Denis [Col. 1398D] of Reims.

There survive numerous letters of Pope Stephen X to Gervasius, inviting him to act courageously on behalf of religion and promising that the assistance of the Apostolic See would not be lacking. After expressing his desire for a lasting friendship with him, Stephen urges him to attend the Roman synod. There are also letters of Nicholas II ordering the bishop of Beauvais, promoted—as was believed—through simony, to be suspended from office together with the bishop of Senlis, likewise accused of that crime. There are also letters of Alexander II urging Gervasius, in investigating the case of an abbess unjustly expelled from a monastery of Laon, to assist Bishop Elinand according to the terms of the apostolic commission; forbidding him also to consecrate Josselin, bishop of Soissons, who had been convicted of simony; ordering that the bishop of Beauvais be corrected and that the bishop of Amiens be compelled to make satisfaction for the injury inflicted on the abbey of Corbie; and finally commanding that the body of Saint Memmius, improperly transferred from his church [Col. 1399B] by the bishop of Châlons, be returned to its own basilica under threat of ecclesiastical censures.

Two letters written by Gervasius are also read: one in 1060 to Nicholas II, after the foundation—or rather restoration—of the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs in Paris, to which he subscribed, and after the death of King Henry I; the other in 1061 to Alexander II. In them he openly demonstrates his obedience to the Roman See. He also wrote about the miracles of Saint Melanius, bishop of Rennes. Finally, he is said to have composed the Life of Saint Donatian, archbishop of Reims.

He earned his greatest praise, however, by being counted among the founders of the church of Château-du-Loir [Col. 1399C] in the diocese of Le Mans and by completely restoring three churches in his metropolitan city.

First, he repaired at his own expense, in 1060, the basilica of Saint Nicaise, whose extensive ruins everywhere, and whose disfigured elegance and beauty within and without, he could not behold without tears. Then, in 1064, he founded twelve canons in the church of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris, with the assistance of the monks of Saint-Remi, to whom it belonged. Finally, at Saint-Denis he both renovated the basilica and introduced regular canons in 1067.

He had appointed Guido bishop of Beauvais in 1063 or 1064, and in 1065 had confirmed with his own charter the instruments of Baldwin, count of Flanders, and Philip I, king of France, concerning the restoration of the monastery of Hasnon.

[Col. 1399D] He died on IV Non. Kal. in 1067, after giving, at the point of death, while receiving the sacred viaticum, an outstanding proof of his faith. It is worthwhile to report this in the very words recorded in a manuscript of the Church of Reims written by Odelricus, the provost, who witnessed the event:

“Before the twelfth year of the episcopate of Lord Gervasius had ended, but while it would have ended on the Ides of October if he had lived, on the third day before the Kalends of July, the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, toward evening, the aforesaid Lord Gervasius, archbishop, was overcome by the illness from which he died six days later. He summoned to himself the brothers and canons who could then be found. When they had been called and were present, he opened his profession of faith and made his confession as a true Catholic; afterward he received communion from the sacrifice of the Lord’s altar. He also enjoined and requested us to bear witness before God that he truly believed it to be the body and blood.”

After this, as the same parchment records, he was admonished to make satisfaction to the Church of Reims for the losses he had inflicted upon it. He gave a pledge to Provost Odolricus and promised that, if he survived, he would make full restitution. He made the same promise [Col. 1400B] to Herimarus, abbot of Saint-Remi.

The same manuscript says that Gervasius bestowed many ornaments upon the Church of Reims, all of which are listed. In addition, it says that he gave the brothers of the Church of Reims, for the celebration of his anniversary, four well-equipped mills at Deux-Ponts on the Vesle, etc.

In the old Necrology contained in the same manuscript, it is stated that Lord Gervasius, archbishop, died on the fourth day before the Nones of July. He gave to Saint Mary the mills beyond the bridge, so that whatever proceeded from them might be divided among the canons on his anniversary. This date agrees with what we have just reported about his death; from it, it is clear that Marlot is mistaken in saying that he died in April.

The place of his burial can still be visited, says the same Marlot, beneath a black stone in the choir of the major church near the eagle, on which this brief epitaph is inscribed:

### Gervasius, Archbishop

A man of exceptional virtue and, among those who flourished in Gaul in that century, by far the most renowned; diligent, generous, wise, and deserving of praise of every kind. For when the kingdom was in turmoil, he administered affairs of the greatest importance worthily as supreme chancellor and took care that schism and the stain of simony should not infect the Church of Gaul.

His generosity shone forth especially in the restoration of the monasteries of Saint-Denis and Saint-Nicaise, whose assistance he experienced immediately after his death; his learning in the composition of the Life of Saint Donatian, according to Colvenerius; and his piety in the constant and timely obedience he rendered to the Holy Apostolic See.

The Chronicle of Fleury calls him “a most vigorous man”; Guibert of Nogent, after the author of the Life of Saint Melanius of Rennes, calls him “a most famous archbishop”; the cartulary of Saint-Denis of Paris calls him, in comparison with Nogent, second to no one in the kingdom in wisdom and integrity; the Chronicle of Saint-Nicaise calls him “a Catholic man, eloquent in speech, distinguished in justice, humble in merit, and severe toward vices.” The Reims Breviary condenses all these statements into fewer words.

[Col. 1399]

## Letters of Gervasius to the Roman Pontiffs Nicholas II and Alexander II

See above under Nicholas II and below under Alexander II.

[Col. 1401]

## Charters of Gervasius

### I. Charter Establishing or Restoring Twelve Canons in the Church of Saints Timothy and Apollinaris (1064)

*[Acts of the Ecclesiastical Province of Reims, II, 75.]*

[Col. 1401A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Gervasius, archbishop of Reims by the grace of God, to the faithful of the holy Church, both present and future.

If we diligently attend to the welfare and dignity of the church entrusted to us by God; if we preserve inviolate whatever has been established within it for divine worship through the prudent vigilance of our predecessors; and if we strive to restore whatever through negligence or various misfortunes has perished from these arrangements [addition: E.P.], we believe that, by our decree as stewards, we shall bring forth manifold profit from the talent entrusted to us and shall hear the “Well done” of the most certain reward.

Therefore, considering that the church of Saint Timothy the Martyr, situated in the town of this holy see over which, by God’s authority, we preside, once flourished in the number of its clerics and the dignity of its worship, but had partly through adverse circumstances and partly through neglect been reduced to the title of a single priest, and that for this reason Archbishop Adalbero had granted it to the monastery of Saint-Remi for possession, so that the needs of hospitality might be supplied from its revenues, we took care, through the work of pious diligence, to restore it to its former state of dignity.

Accordingly, notifying Abbot Herimarus of this, we instructed him to bring this purpose of our will [Col. 1401C] to fulfillment. He was to make the church of Saint Timothy, with its revenues, a stipendiary church of God and restore the provision for hospitality from other possessions of Saint-Remi in his monastery, for the clerics who would serve there.

He willingly obeyed our ordinance and, under the privilege of our authority, assembled twelve canons in the same place. He established for them a canonical prebend so that they might regularly devote themselves there to divine service.

To make this constitution more effective, we also decreed that the altar of that church should perpetually belong to them as an increase to their stipend. As long as canons remain there, we forbid any successor of ours, under divine authority, to take it away from them.

Furthermore, we wish them to be exempt from every exaction by archdeacons and archpriests, placed solely under the dominion of Saint-Remi, yet under our authority and the subjection of the abbot, just as are the monks of Saint-Remi. And just as the abbot has assumed from us the care of their souls, so in the same way he shall receive from us the care of the souls of these clerics; he shall entrust that care personally to the dean whom he appoints as their faithful guardian. He, [Col. 1402A] the abbot, shall provide them with the necessities of food and, if he finds anything blameworthy in their conduct, shall strive to correct it, so that he may safely render an account of them to God on the day of judgment.

We forbid under anathema that anyone presume to overturn or in any way violate this decree of our ordinance. We commend it to the memory of posterity in a charter witnessed by the bishops, abbots, leading members of our clergy, and all the other faithful who were present.

The meal which the canons of Saint Mary’s Church of Reims used to receive on the feast of the holy martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris, for the love of God and of us, they have unanimously granted in perpetuity to Abbot Herimarus and the aforesaid clerics, so that they may be their brothers and commemorate them in their prayers. We threaten, under the invocation of the divine majesty, that no one in future dare overturn the generosity of this donation, with the bishops present with us and the whole clergy.

+ Sign of Lord Gervasius, archbishop. + Sign of Elinandus, bishop of Laon. + Sign of Adelardus, bishop of Soissons. + Sign of Frotlandus, bishop of Senlis. + Sign of Guido, bishop of Beauvais. + Sign of Odo, archdeacon. + Sign of Herimarus, abbot of Saint-Remi.

Done publicly at Reims in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1064, in the second indiction, during the reign of King Philip, in his fifth year, on the Ides of [Col. 1402C] June.

### II. For the Foundation of the Abbey of Saint-Denis of Reims (1067)

*[Acts of the Province of Reims, II, 79.]*

I wish it to be known to those present and not unknown to posterity that I, Gervasius, prelate of this holy see of Reims, after restoring other churches which, through age and negligence, had appeared abandoned and deserted from ancient times, undertook to renew the church of Saint-Denis, which had already almost been wiped out.

I had often pitied and grieved over it as I passed by, once richly endowed but, with wickedness bearing down upon it, reduced to the deepest poverty. At last, having applied diligence, I did not delay the work of restoration in execution and construction, with God’s grace present: rebuilding what had been destroyed and constructing from the foundations what had not been founded.

Because it belonged to the table of the canons of my lady, Saint Mary, the Mother of God, I received it from those same sons of mine, with everyone’s consent, under a rent of six solidi, to be given perpetual freedom. This custom was retained: their servants, both household and common, were to be delivered there for burial without any exaction of payment, as they had previously been accustomed to do. If, in the course of time, the church itself should by some misfortune fall back through renewed calamity into the condition from which it had first been rescued, it shall be subjected to their authority as before, unless this happens through their fault or deliberate action.

The church, therefore, having been completely restored at my expense and through my labor, together with various buildings adapted to the needs of the brothers, I grant the canons dwelling there for the honor of Saint Mary and for the commemoration of my anniversary, for the use of the canons; and just as we formerly decreed that its tithe should belong to this church, so now also we decree it, as we establish without distinction concerning all my possessions. So that the decree of this constitution of ours may remain ratified and inviolate for all time, we confirm it by the present writing of our authority and seal it with the impression of our seal.

Done at Reims, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1067, Indiction V, in the seventh year of King Philip’s reign, in the twelfth year of my episcopate.

Odolric the chancellor wrote and subscribed this.

## In the Year of the Lord 1067. Leodegarius, Archbishop of the Church of Vienne.

[Col. 1403]

## Historical Notice

*(From Gallia Christiana, old edition, vol. I, p. 799.)*

Leodegarius is mentioned in a diploma of Ermengard, wife of Rudolph, king of Burgundy, in the year 1037, together with Pontius of Valence, Artaldus of Grenoble, and other bishops. He wrote a work on the life, character, origin, and deeds of his predecessors the archbishops, as is read in a manuscript chronicle. He subscribed the testament of Hugh, archbishop of Besançon, in 1044, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April; Pope Leo IX also sent him a letter. He died on the day before the Ides of June. From this it is evident that those are mistaken who introduce another Leodegarius bearing the same name.

[Col. 1403]

## Charters of Leodegarius

### I. He grants the church of Saint Ferreolus to Saint Victor in a full synod.  
*(Year 1036.)*

[Martene, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 404.]

[Col. 1403B]

It is plainly evident to all that the first man was created by God and placed in paradise so that, if he did not wish to sin, he would have no necessity of sinning. But because he was led astray by the devil’s envy and cast by God into this sorrowful exile, nature subsequently made all human beings born from him equal. Yet God, who is the highest good and himself knows the future, did not afterward cease, throughout the passage of many years, to govern his dear human creature, placing one person over others: first patriarchs and prophets, then kings, and finally priests. He wished to do this so that, if anyone did not wish to avoid sins through love of him, that person might at least be restrained by fear of another.

There are therefore many things that he commanded through Moses and entrusted to Aaron, the first priest. Finally, he conferred upon the blessed apostle Peter, the chief of the apostles, the power of binding and loosing; and from him down to us, although unworthy, he has allowed this power to remain.

Therefore I, Leodegarius, archbishop of the holy mother Church of Vienne, servant of all God’s faithful, moved by the example and love of my predecessors and desiring to adorn our church, which once flourished most gloriously, propose and desire to serve the most blessed lord and martyr Ferreolus, the tribune of our city. His church, or monastery, which they call Grinensium, once contained a community of forty monks.

But we, whom God has brought into these unhappy times, shall at least fulfill what we can, even if not to the same extent. We therefore return to him—to Saint Ferreolus—and to his former monastery whatever of his inheritance we held in our own possession; and wherever anything else from his inheritance may be found, we return it all entirely. Those who hold such property, if they are willing to return it, we associate with this act of almsgiving.

Furthermore, our faithful Bladinus returns everything that he held from us as a benefice from Ferreolus’s inheritance, and in addition gives from his own hereditary property. We do this, therefore, with the counsel of our faithful, with the entire clergy and people of our church joining in praise, and also with the assent of the illustrious queen Ermengard, wife of King Rudolph, now a widow.

We therefore place at that very site servants of God from the monastery of Saint Victor, the most glorious martyr of Marseilles, and permanently give that place, with everything belonging to it, to Saint Victor and to the venerable man Lord Isarnus, abbot, with the counsel and consent of Lord Odilo, abbot of Cluny, and of all the brothers of his congregation.

This charitable donation was made in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1036, Indiction IV, epact I, in the eighth year of Conrad, emperor of the Romans.

[Col. 1405B]

We therefore beseech, by the authority of almighty God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and by our own authority we prohibit and excommunicate, that none of our successors, whether bishops of this church of ours or any other person, be able or dare in any way to break or disturb this charitable donation. If anyone should do so, let him be subject to all the curses of God; separated from the Church of God on the day of judgment, let him be buried condemned in hell. Moreover, let this donation of ours remain firm and stable, supported by stipulation.

I, Nuspa the monk, acting in place of the lord chancellor, wrote this at the dictation and command of Lord Archbishop Leodegarius, in the sixth year of his ordination, on the third day before the Nones of November, on the tenth day of the moon, on Wednesday.

[Col. 1405C]

This was enacted publicly in the synod of Vienne, in the presence of Lord Leodegarius the archbishop, the canons of his church, and nearly five hundred faithful abbots, monks, and other clerics of various ranks. With complete devotion they acclaimed and praised all that is inserted here; and likewise, should any secular or ecclesiastical person ever attempt in any way to disturb this gift—which God forbid—they excommunicated and anathematized, by divine invocation and the authority of all the saints and heavenly powers, those who at any time and in any manner might attempt to disturb this gift. Amen.

I, Leodegarius, archbishop, confirm this with my own hand.

[Col. 1405D]

### II. Charter of Leodegarius, archbishop of Vienne, by which he grants the church of Saint Symphorian to the monastery of Saint Ferreolus.  
*(Year 1037.)*

[Martene, cited above, col. 404.]

[Col. 1406B]

… When the most orderly arrangement of almighty God … of the holy canons … so that ecclesiastical property acquired by persons of whatever order, from whatever source, even if possessed by us … with whatever benefit, however great, in buildings, possessions, and resources, as soon as they have rightly been claimed by the heirs of the church to which they legally belong, should be returned in its entirety without any opposition; while those unwilling to return them ought to be separated from the fellowship of the holy Church of God.

I, Leodegarius, archbishop of the Christians of the holy mother Church of Vienne, servant of all God’s faithful, wish it to be known to the sons of our church, present and future, that, moved by divine love and by the desire to rebuild the venerable places of the monastery of Saint Ferreolus situated on both sides of the Rhône River, with the consent of the entire clergy and people, and with the assent of the venerable abbot Isarnus, servant of God, I have summoned from the monastery of Marseilles men to serve God in the aforesaid places, and have resolved, with every intention and desire, to restore in full whatever belonged by right to those places, insofar as I am able.

Therefore, I now restore, cede, and convey in its entirety to the same monastery the church of Saint Symphorian, situated on the northern side of the city of Vienne, which by the testimony of the faithful, by authority, and by the judgment of God is shown to have belonged to the domain of the monastery of Saint Ferreolus; and I give it to the monks serving God who remain there, namely with its parish, first-fruits, cemetery, and, in addition, its tithe, every toll, forced labor, and every service …

[Col. 1407A]

… the other church itself on the bank of the Rhône, or … which is clearly excellent, situated at the head of that church, and everything else whatever that appears to belong to the same place, with fields, vineyards, meadows, gardens, mills, fruit-bearing and non-fruit-bearing trees, waters and watercourses, as the boundaries are known and are written here.

On the east, the land of Saint Mauritius, at the boundaries called Suspuli;

[Note: That is, the cathedral church dedicated to Saint Mauritius.]

on the west, royal land; on the south, the land of Saint Severus; on the north, the land of the castle called Saxol; and from the villages of Masin and Macen, the parish and everything belonging to the parish, with the entire tithe, first-fruits, and cemetery.

Moreover, I return one mansus called Adamaredas, situated above the church of Saint Desiderius, with its fields, vineyards, and absolutely everything belonging to that mansus.

[Col. 1407B]

If anyone should attempt to disturb this donation or restoration, let that person, whatever his rank or dignity, be subject to all the curses of God, and let him be excluded from the fellowship of the faithful, while this donation remains forever unshaken.

This donation was made in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1037, Indiction V, in the ninth year of Conrad, emperor of the Romans.

I, Nuspa the monk, acting in place of the lord chancellor, wrote this at the command of Lord Leodegarius, archbishop, in the seventh year of his ordination, on the first day of the station at Saint Ferreolus before the Nativity of the Lord.

Lord Leodegarius, archbishop, confirmed it.

### III. Concerning the Debased Coinage of Vienne  
*(Year 1043.)*

[In Acherius, *Spicilegium*, old edition, vol. XII, p. 284, from the cartulary of Vienne, supplied by D. d’Herouval.]

Notice concerning the coinage of Vienne, made between Leodegarius, archbishop of Vienne, and Adelaide, marchioness, with her sons.

For a long time the coinage itself remained sound in weight and measure, in tens. Recently, however, during the time of Odo, her husband the marquis, thieves and counterfeiters in the town called Aquabella debased, corrupted, and falsified it, without the said marquis’s knowledge. As soon as he heard the complaint of the aforesaid archbishop of Vienne, he ordered that this should happen no more. Nor did it happen while he was alive.

After his death, however, other thieves arose, followed the earlier ones, and again falsified it, until the aforesaid Archbishop Leodegarius came to Italy to the aforementioned Lady Adelaide, the marchioness. As soon as she likewise heard of it, she ordered that it should happen no more.

Nevertheless, so that this might be known to all, the money-changer who had been excommunicated by Lord Pope Leo, struck by paralysis and with all his limbs disabled, ended his impious life by a death he deserved.

Now, without the knowledge of the aforementioned Lady Adelaide, marchioness, others have arisen, and the aforesaid evils continue. But through the mediation of Lord Adraldus, abbot of Bremet, and Artaldus, provost of our church, the aforesaid wrongs are relinquished. Lady Adelaide, marchioness, together with her sons Peter, Amadeus, and Odo, promises to God and Saint Mauritius, into the hand of Lord Leodegarius, archbishop of Vienne, that throughout the whole extent of her authority the coinage of Vienne shall no longer be falsified or produced, and that no false coin made at Vienne shall be accepted.

She did this, together with her associates, for the love of God and Saint Mauritius; she was honored by his benefaction, and did it for the soul of her lord Odo, the marquis, and for her own salvation and that of her sons, who approve and confirm this: namely Peter, the firstborn, Amadeus, and Odo.

Lord Adraldus, abbot of Bremet, approves this, as does Artaldus, provost of the Church of Vienne, together with his other faithful, whose names are these.

[Col. 1408C]

Given by the hand of Boso, acting in place of the lord chancellor and chief secretary, on the second day before the Kalends of December, on the sixteenth day of the moon, on Wednesday, under Henry II, king—not yet emperor—the son of the Caesar and emperor and son-in-law of this lady marchioness.

Received by the hand of Lord Archbishop Leodegarius.

## In the Year of the Lord 1068. Stephanus, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.

[Col. 1407]

## Historical Notice

*(From J. G. Eggs, *Purpura docta, seu Res gestae S. R. E. cardinalium*, drawn from Ciaconius, Andrea Victorello, Augustinus Oldoinus, and others, book I, chapter 15.)*

Stephen, a Gaul by nationality and, for his time, a man of very great learning, was raised to the purple by Saint Leo IX and deserved to be numbered among the cardinal priests of the Holy Roman Church. Before receiving the purple, he is said to have lived a solitary life under Abbot Odilo in the monastery of Cluny, founded by Bennus on the river Gournam and endowed by William, duke of Aquitaine and count of Auvergne.

Stephen X, successor of Saint Leo, had appointed him as legate to Constantinople, together with Desiderius and Maynard, learned Cassinese monks, to extinguish the schism of the Greek Church. He had already set out with his companions when the pope’s death occurred and was announced; abandoning the legation, he returned home.

Not long afterward, however, he served as legate in Gaul by order of Pope Nicholas II, as Goffridus of Vendôme records. Continuing this mission under Alexander II, he struck with anathema Goffridus Barbatus, count of Anjou, who had been denounced before the Holy See for numerous crimes and did not repent.

He was then sent by the sacred college of cardinals to Germany, to Henry the king, son of Henry III, surnamed the Black, emperor, while Henry was still a young and beardless man. Although Stephen brought apostolic letters, Henry did not hear him. For five days he remained outside the royal doors, not without injury to the Apostolic See, because the king’s ministers, who hated Frenchmen, barred his way.

The purpose of the legation was twofold. First, that King Henry should aid the Roman Church, which was being extremely harassed by the tyranny of the Normans, and should restrain the insolence of the Lombard bishops, who, contrary to the provisions of the sacred canons, had elected Cadalus—a layman of compromised reputation—as bishop of Parma. Second, that by royal authority he should abolish the infamous decree of the pseudo-synod by which Nicholas II, the Roman pontiff, after his death, had been condemned by synodal judgment and everything done by him declared void.

The mission having failed, Stephen returned to Rome, and not long afterward, namely in the year 1068, surrendered to fate. He attended the assemblies of Nicholas II at Siena and of Alexander II at Rome.

Because of his outstanding learning, Cardinal Peter Damian rightly called him “the glory and defender of the Roman Church.” Concerning him he also says in a certain letter:

> No one who knew the man doubts that Cardinal Stephen was adorned with the pious flowers of virtues, holy deeds, and the rays of learning.

Alphanus, bishop of Salerno, Stephen’s contemporary, commended him after his death in this epitaph:

> Stephen, what sort of priest you were, and how great,  
> In Peter’s church, Gaul knows together with Latium.  
> Nobility, gravity, integrity, and sharpness of mind,  
> And great strength of spirit were yours.  
> Although the sun was destined to remain for five days,  
> You were enclosed in this urn. May Christ grant you rest. Amen.

He is remembered by Blessed Peter Damian in his letters; by Alphanus, bishop of Salerno; by Ciaconius in his *Life*; and by Augustinus Oldoinus in his additions to Ciaconius.

[Col. 1409]

## Council of Tours

In this council many matters concerning ecclesiastical discipline were established by Stephen, cardinal and apostolic legate, and ten bishops, in the year of Christ 1060, Indiction XIII, on the Kalends of March.

*(Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 925.)*

## Titles of the Chapters

[Col. 1409A]

I. That no one may give or receive a benefice for money or through any other agreement contrary to the canons.

II. That clerics should oppose a bishop who confers a benefice contrary to the aforesaid rule.

III. That no bishop may sell, give away, or alienate what belongs to the Church.

IV. That no one may accept a church from a layman without the consent of the bishop, nor accept one for sale.

V. That no one may accept a clerical office except in the churches of a single city.

VI. Concerning bishops, priests, deacons, and subdeacons who, while held in carnal intercourse with a woman, have not ceased from office.

VII. That a cleric serving as a soldier loses his benefice.

VIII. Concerning laymen who possess, sell, or give away the Church’s offerings, burial rights, or a third part of the tithes.

IX. That incestuous persons, adulterers, and those who dismiss their own wife and take another are excommunicated.

X. That a deserter from monastic religion is excommunicated; likewise an abbot who does not receive him when penitent.

## Preface

From the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the year 1060, Indiction XIII, on the Kalends of March, on the thirteenth day of the moon, on Wednesday, with Stephen, cardinal priest of the Catholic city of Rome and vicar of the Apostolic See, presiding, the holy synod assembled at Tours, the metropolis of Gaul, by command of our lord, the most blessed supreme pontiff and universal pope Nicholas.

With the most holy Gospels set before them and fervent prayers first offered to God, the synod carefully reconsidered the matters in which the condition of the churches throughout almost the whole world, and especially in Gaul, seemed to be wavering and collapsing; and it defined, with fitting concern, those matters which it seemed appropriate to append briefly below.

## Chapters

### I

By the authority of the Holy Spirit, as we believe, the judgment pronounced against simoniacs at the Council of Chalcedon shall be observed by all in the following manner:

Whoever thereafter attempts, by money, by any improper secular agreement, or in any manner contrary to canonical discipline, to give or receive a bishopric, abbacy, archdeaconate, archpresbyterate, or any ecclesiastical dignity; or any rank, ministry, or benefice that the authority of the holy Fathers has decreed may be held only by clerics, in any way contrary to the canons—the giver shall fall from his own rank and dignity, while the receiver shall lose the ministry or benefice unlawfully usurped, never to recover it.

### II
