If any bishop or other prelate should wish to arrange or grant any ecclesiastical ministry, or even the prebend called canonical, contrary to the rule established above, the clerics shall be entirely free to oppose him and to appeal to the judgment of neighboring bishops or, if necessary, even to the Apostolic See itself.

### III

Likewise, no bishop or prelate shall henceforth presume, contrary to the canons, to sell or give to anyone any new benefice from property belonging to the rights of the Church.

Whoever has previously presumed to alienate anything belonging to the Church, under the name of a benefice or in any other manner—if he still survives, let him either restore to the Church what he wrongly removed or be punished by canonical judgment.

### IV

Henceforth no one shall presume to accept a large or small church from laymen in any manner without the consent of the bishop in whose parish it is situated; nor shall anyone accept it from a cleric, monk, or layman as a sale for any price. If anyone does so, both the seller and the buyer shall forfeit it.

### V

We also confirm that from now on no one may accept any clerical office except in the churches of a single city. Whoever violates this shall be struck by canonical punishment.

### VI

Furthermore, if any bishop, priest, deacon, or subdeacon, after learning of the prohibition of our lord Pope Nicholas, has continued in the ministry and altar benefice while held in carnal intercourse with any woman; or if thereafter, knowing the aforesaid prohibition of the Apostolic See, he does not immediately abandon either the woman or the ministry of the Church together with its benefice, let him know that no possibility of restoration to his former rank has been reserved for him.

### VII

All clerics who henceforth serve under arms shall lose both their benefice and their fellowship with the clergy.

### VIII

Any layman who thereafter presumes to possess, sell, or give to anyone under the name of a benefice anything belonging to the Church’s offerings or alms—whether burial rights or even a third part of the tithes—shall be struck by the sword of anathema.

### IX

Whoever takes or has taken in marriage a woman related to him by blood; or one whom his kinsman had previously known; or whose female relative he has carnally taken in marriage; or who, after learning of the relationship, has not immediately dismissed her or does not dismiss her upon learning it; or who has abducted or shall abduct another man’s wife; or who, dismissing his own wife without episcopal judgment, has taken or shall take another—until he devotes himself fruitfully to penance, let him recognize that he is excluded and alienated from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and from the thresholds of the Church, and that he has been cut off in every respect like a putrid member from a healthy body by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

### X

Whoever is found to have deserted the monastic life shall be excluded from the kingdom of God and from the fellowship of Christians, like an apostate, and shall remain alienated until he comes to his senses and performs fitting penance.

Likewise, anyone who refuses to receive such persons when they are fittingly penitent, after being admonished a third time, shall, if he does not comply, be suspended from communion with the brothers—whether he is an abbot or an abbess—until he complies.

I, Stephen, called cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church, presiding over the synod in the place of my lord Pope Nicholas, have subscribed to these constitutions canonically promulgated by us, giving them the assent of my humble person.

Afterward ten archbishops and bishops subscribed.

[Col. 1411]

## Letter of Cardinal Stephen to John, Bishop of Dol

That he should attend the Roman synod of Nicholas II after Easter, or the synod to be held by Stephen himself at Tours before mid-Lent.

[Note: Sent before the synod described above.]

[Col. 1411D]

Stephen, cardinal of Peter, chief of the apostles, and of the holy Roman Church, advises J——, called archbishop of the Church of Dol, to repent and return to the way of salvation and correction.

My lord, the supreme pontiff and universal pope Nicholas, although you are rebellious and turned away from salutary admonitions, nevertheless judged you by no means unworthy of the paternal and customary mercy of the Roman Church. He therefore sent a legation—if indeed it reached you—and summoned you to the synod that would be held at Rome after Easter according to ancient custom, still granting you an opportunity to repent.

But after letters had been sent to you, following the foresight of his counsel and the necessity created by circumstances and events, he dispatched me to these regions. Entrusting his authority to me, he charged me, with God’s help, to correct whatever I could in the Gallican Church through councils and other labors.

Accordingly, I have summoned a synod at Tours on the Sunday before mid-Lent. In accordance with my lord’s concern, and relieving your modesty of expense and labor, I call you to it by the authority of Saint Peter and his vicar entrusted to me; and I guarantee you safety from any danger that might befall you from the ruler of that city.

But if you do not wish to come either to us or to my lord within the dates specified, you will experience without mercy the vengeance of ecclesiastical discipline.

I am also sending a copy of the letter by which my lord entrusted this authority to me.

[Col. 1413]

## At the Council of Bordeaux

Stephen, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, upholds the cell of Saint Clement of Credon for the monks of Vendôme.

*(Edited by Dom Martene, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. IV, col. 635, from the cartulary of Vendôme.)*

[Col. 1413B]

Although the complaint of the monks of Saint-Albans against the monks of Vendôme concerning the church of Credon, which they seemed to believe they rightly possessed, had often been examined and had always been shown by legal judgment to be unjust and to have arisen from the root of envy, they nevertheless persist, with their customary insolence, in provoking them with words and in disturbing them again concerning matters already settled.

Their first calumny concerning the aforesaid church was brought before Count Geoffrey, in the hearing of Lord Eusebius, bishop of Angers, Lord W., namely Wlgrinus, then abbot of Saint Sergius and later bishop of Le Mans, Lord A., abbot of Saint Vincent of the same city, and many other reputable men.

When the count asked them to produce letters or witnesses concerning the donation which they asserted had been made to them by the old Suardus, and which his father, Count Fulk, and he himself had authorized, they replied that they had never possessed letters concerning it. They said, however, that they could inquire whether they might have witnesses among the men of that time, if they were granted sufficient opportunity.

Count Geoffrey therefore allowed them a full year and ordered them to bring their witnesses confidently and without any fear, from wherever they could find them—even if they were among his enemies.

When they were unable to do this—for they could not find anywhere witnesses whom they had never possessed—they temporarily abandoned the complaint and remained silent for ten years and more, throughout the remainder of Count Geoffrey’s life.

Immediately after his death, however, thinking that they had found a suitable opportunity for making their complaint, they again began to devise new measures and attempted, through the agency of Count Geoffrey the Younger, successor of the other Geoffrey, to obtain new judges against the monks of Vendôme. They even bribed certain powerful men whom they rashly believed would be especially useful to them in this matter, against right and law, so that they might accomplish by gifts, in one way or another, what they had been unable to achieve by just reasoning.

But when, by God’s providence, their hope was frustrated in this matter as well, they devised further schemes to obtain what they desired. They sent to Rome as an envoy G., one of their monks, to present their complaint concerning this matter to the lord pope.

But things turned out very differently from what they had hoped, because the stricter the standard of justice is held there, the less avarice, the contriver of injustice, finds that it can corrupt.

Finally, Abbot O., who had gone to Rome on the business of his monastery, stood with the others at the council then assembled before Pope Nicholas. He gave the accuser a fitting reply concerning the gift of the church made to the monastery of Vendôme and concerning the judgment later publicly determined at Angers by the aforementioned Count Geoffrey and the other men named above.

By the common decree of the lord pope and the bishops who were present, it was established that the aforesaid church of Saint Clement of the castle of Credon unquestionably belonged by lawful right to the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Vendôme.

Thus, although they had often been convicted by so many judgments, so manifest and established with such authority, they were still heedless of innocence and utterly failed to remember the many injuries they had inflicted upon the monks of Vendôme, their brothers in Christ, willingly or unwillingly. Again they attempted to renew the proceedings and to bring in other judges in foreign regions, as though traveling into another country could extinguish the truth established by a proper examination.

After a long interval, when a certain Stephen, called cardinal of blessed Peter, was exercising in Gaul the legation of Alexander, the Roman bishop and pope, he was staying in Anjou at the castle of Saumur. Once again, the monks of Saint-Albin brought to his ears a complaint against the monks of Vendôme concerning the church of Credon, as though they were beginning the matter anew.

He did not promise to answer them there immediately, but promised that at the city of Bordeaux, where he was also going to hold a council, he would answer them and carefully examine the case, after first notifying the monks of Vendôme and summoning them there.

[Note: Stephen the legate held a council at Bordeaux in the year 1068; this passage appears to refer to it.]

When they had assembled at the council on the Kalends of April, and the monks of Saint-Albin had made their complaint before all who were present, one of the brothers of Vendôme who had come for this purpose, named Vitalis, replied that the case had already been publicly settled long before at a Roman synod under Pope Nicholas of venerable memory.

Several bishops from Gaul who had traveled to the council had heard it—namely Hugh of Nevers, Walter of Meaux, Hugh of Troyes, and Wlgrinus of Le Mans. Three of these—Hugh, Wlgrinus, and the other Hugh—while they were still alive, and when the monks of Saint-Albin had repeated the aforesaid calumny, sent their letters to B., archbishop of Tours, and E., bishop of Angers, as testimony on behalf of the monks of Vendôme. They declared that they had seen and heard that the complaint had been weighed in a just examination and settled before Pope Nicholas in a general council.

When Cardinal Stephen heard this, after the bishops’ letters had first been read, he replied that it was neither proper nor in any way permissible for something once justly decided by the Roman pontiff to be examined again differently by anyone else.

He left them only this option: if they refused to believe the monk and the letters of the bishops, which offered corroborating testimony, they should approach the bishops themselves and learn directly from their own living voices whether the matter was so, before the following feast of Saint Peter, which is celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of July.

[Col. 1416A]

If they learned that the matter was indeed as the bishops’ letters declared, they were not to presume thereafter to disturb the monks of Vendôme any further concerning it. Otherwise, both parties were to go to Rome in the following year to have the judgment of this complaint discussed in a council.

This sentence, delivered reasonably and justly, was attested by the bishops, abbots, and other devout men of the ecclesiastical order who were present, whose names are subscribed:

Goscelinus, archbishop of Bordeaux; Goderannus, bishop of Saintes; Guillelmus, bishop of Angoulême; Isembertus, bishop of Poitiers; Ragomundus, bishop of Valence; Quiriacus, bishop of Nantes; Mengisus, bishop of Venasque; Iterius, bishop of Limoges; and Guillelmus, bishop of Agen.

## In the Year of the Lord 1089. Leo, Bishop of Atina.

[Col. 1415]

## Historical Notice

*(From Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. VI, col. 426.)*

Leo, a man of outstanding learning and of exceptional knowledge of divine matters, was ordained bishop of the Church of Atina by Adenulfus, archbishop of Capua, in the year 1044. He presided with distinction for twenty-eight years and died in the year 1072.

In his time, says the Atina Chronicle repeatedly, the church of Saint Mary was built in the temple of Saturn. In his time also the body of Christ’s martyr Mark was discovered, having lain hidden in the episcopal residence of Atina beneath a smaller altar, which Leo afterward dedicated in honor of Saint Bartholomew beside the bodies of Saints Nicander and Marcian.

The year of Christ was 1046, on the Kalends of August, when Leo found and transferred the sacred relics of the holy martyr. He himself, that distinguished prelate, wrote the account of this event; below you have a copy from a manuscript written in Lombard letters in the library of Monte Cassino.

Other works written by Leo are reported as evidence of his talent, though few survive. Several sermons on the blessed martyr Mark, his predecessor, exist in a manuscript in my possession. So that age may not consume them, as it consumes other things, I shall not hesitate to transcribe them here, in order to assert the praise of so great a martyr. Peter the deacon of Monte Cassino also composed several sermons in his honor; so far as I know, they have not yet been printed and lie hidden in the celebrated library of Monte Cassino.

[Col. 1415]

## The Discovery or Translation of the Body of the Most Blessed Mark, Martyr and Bishop, Written by Lord Leo, Bishop of Atina

[Col. 1415B]

Dearest brothers, let us humbly ask for the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that, filled with its sweetness, we may speak appropriately about the discovery of the body of the most blessed Mark.

Therefore, the most blessed Mark was bishop of Atina during the reign of the Emperor Domitian. In his time, at the command of the proconsul Maximus, he was fastened by nails driven into his head and finally struck on the neck with a sword; thus he gloriously won the palm of martyrdom and was happily buried on the outskirts of the aforesaid city. The Christians who were then present, with great zeal, built a basilica in his honor. After a long period, however—as its ancient walls show—it was devastated by wicked men and reduced to the ground.

Since it remained in this condition for a long time, the peasants began to keep their beasts, horses, and asses there during the night. But the almighty Lord wondrously [Col. 1417A] avenged the injury done to His beloved servant Mark. It happened that travelers passed that way and, not knowing that the venerable body of the most holy Mark rested there beside the tomb, wished to place their horses in that very spot. A certain religious woman opposed them with loud cries, saying:

“Do not, brothers, do not lodge in this holy place, lest something evil happen to you. For we have often seen God’s mighty works performed in this most holy place.”

But they treated these words as worthless, stayed there that night, and, when morning came, began their journey while mocking her words. Before they had gone far, however, as though struck by an arrow, they immediately began to repent of what they had done: one of their horses collapsed dead upon the ground, while the other perished on the road before it had completed its course. Thus the almighty Lord [Col. 1417B] avenged the injury done to His beloved martyr Mark.

At another time, as certain faithful people have reported to me, some Calabrians came late to the aforesaid place with asses laden with merchandise and sought lodging for the night. A venerable woman said to them:

“Do not, dearest ones, put your asses in this place, because it is a holy place. For if you dare to do so, you will not be able to leave here without suffering loss.”

They, intoxicated by their own madness, said to her:

“Then we too are dead if we cannot guard our asses!”

When night had fully fallen, they settled down, placing their asses among themselves. Although they had acted boldly, they were nevertheless afraid that wolves or robbers might carry them off, and so they set a futile watch—ignorant of the Scripture that says: “What the wicked man fears will come upon him.”

After they had fallen asleep and become like the dead, a wolf came from the opposite direction, entered among them, seized one of the asses, and killed it. A similar miracle comes to mind, reported to me by the same people who recounted the earlier events. One day, likewise at that same place, at sunset, a certain man came with his ass and, seeking lodging, turned aside there. Although the aforesaid woman tried to prevent him from lodging there, he immediately settled down with his ass, tied the ass’s foot together with his own, and then lay down on the ground to rest.

Some robbers passed by and found him sleeping as though dead. Inciting one another to evil, [Col. 1417D] they immediately cut the rope and took away his ass. He awoke from sleep at once, discovered his loss, and departed sadly from the place. From that time the people mentioned above began to fear the place and reverently ceased to injure it.

Therefore, after taking counsel, the citizens endeavored to restore the same church. They summoned the bishop who was then present and had an altar dedicated there in honor of the most blessed apostle Bartholomew, not knowing that the body of the venerable martyr Mark rested there. In my judgment, the church had previously been blessed in his honor.

Accordingly, during the reign of the most pious Emperor Conrad, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1044, by the favor of divine grace, a certain bishop who had been appointed there was concerned to restore the churches of his bishopric that had been laid waste by wicked and evil men. While he was visiting them from place to place, he eventually reached the episcopal residence of the most ancient city of Atina. Entering the aforesaid church, which stands in the suburb of that city, and inspecting it, he found before the holy altar a heap of stones that had formed a pile from the broken walls. It was highly displeasing both to his own eyes and to those of others.

Then he summoned a certain priest, assigned the place to him, and ordered him:

“Take this place, my son, and clean it carefully.”

The priest took charge of the place assigned to him and devoutly began to clear it. As he dug around the altar, he found a stone inscription which, although broken, revealed the name of the martyr Mark. When the bishop saw it, [Col. 1418B] he cried out:

“O great martyr, show us, though we are unworthy, your holy relics!”

Then, turning aside, he began to entreat the Lord with his whole heart and the deepest devotion, saying:

“I beseech You, Lord, I beseech You to deign to show us sinners the tomb of Your beloved martyr Mark. For I hope and faithfully believe that the body of the martyr Mark rests here, whose name this inscription makes known to us.”

When these things had been done, he immediately returned to his own quarters and spent that night sleepless, consumed by the most ardent desire. When morning came, he seemed, as though by divine command, to order two priests to go and dig before the altar until he himself should descend there. He was in no small doubt, since many human bodies lay there, and he could not remove from himself the bitterness of uncertainty. Therefore he began to assail the Lord with prayers, asking Him to deign to show him what he was devoutly seeking.

The priests proceeded to the right side of the altar of Saint Bartholomew and began to dig. The bishop followed them and found them laboring in vain. Seeing this, he took the spade and began to dig with his own hand. When he had grown weary from the work, he handed it back to them. As they continued digging, they reached the tomb in which the body of the holy martyr Mark rested. Filled with immense fervor, they cried out:

“Rise, gracious Father; behold, what you are seeking is here!”

He immediately rose from the place, prostrated himself upon the ground, and praised the almighty Lord in these words:

“Exalted thanks to You, O King who governs the offices of the world, who, whenever You will, bring to completion without delay whatever You desire.”

Rejoicing and exulting greatly over the patron granted to him, he gathered the holy relics. Yet he was not so joyful over the whole body as he remained sorrowful over the head, because it was not there. It was already Saturday, about the eleventh hour, and although he forbade anyone to disclose the matter, the whole city was suddenly filled with the news.

He began carefully to wash the holy relics with his own hands and place them in a casket. That same night he ordered the appointed clergy to remain awake throughout the night in hymns and spiritual songs, so that in the morning they might carry them with praise and glory to the episcopal residence of that city.

The priest who had first found the inscribed stone, whom we mentioned above, was at that time gravely afflicted by illness, so that he despaired of his life. When he heard what had happened, he immediately sent to the bishop, asking him to deign to send him some of the water with which he had washed the sacred relics, so that he might deserve to receive healing from it.

When morning came, the bishop rose and urged the people to descend with him and transfer the most holy body to the aforesaid church with every mark of honor. He was dressed in sacred vestments, together with the ministers who were with him, carrying censers and candles, and accompanied by the entire ecclesiastical apparatus. Men and women, boys and girls, carrying lit candles and chanting the litany, proceeded to the place. Having lifted the body from there and placed it on a bier, they reached [Col. 1419B] the city while singing the Lord’s praise.

Before he entered the episcopal residence, that priest whom we mentioned above as almost dead came out unharmed, carrying lit candles, to meet the holy body, praising and blessing the Creator of all. The bishop, offering immense thanks to the Lord God, the Redeemer of all, entered the episcopal residence of that most ancient city and placed the venerable body in the shrine of the Mother of God, awaiting the almighty God’s revelation of the place in which He wished the venerated relics to be reburied.

On the very day when the body of Saint Mark was lifted, it happened that a certain religious woman passed by. As she was trying to continue farther on, she heard of what had happened and turned aside to the place. When she had prostrated herself face down to adore the holy tomb, she looked around and saw a small portion of the relics lying in the middle. She secretly picked it up and, rejoicing with great joy, wished to carry it away with her. But when she was not far from the church, before she reached the ford of the river, such great fear seized her that she could turn neither backward nor forward.

Remembering the relic of the holy martyr, she immediately removed the silken veil that covered her head, wrapped the sacred relic in it, and returned it to the body. At once, as though released from bonds, she continued the journey she had begun.

Afterward the bishop began to hesitate greatly about what he should do with the body, where he should place it, and whether he should build it a house of its own. While he was considering these matters, the Lord’s beloved Mark appeared in a dream to a certain religious woman and said:

“Go and tell the bishop to consider carefully and clearly understand our honor. For the house from which he has now taken our body was wonderfully built for the sake of our honor. Therefore I seek a house of my own. If he neglects to build it, let him know that he will be exposed to danger this year.”

When he heard this, the bishop was terrified and had no doubt about the vision, since the very fearful woman who had seen it affirmed it under a dreadful oath. After consulting with his people, he immediately began laying the foundations at the place where the saint had appeared to her, in order to complete the work.

But he completed it sooner than he expected, not without divine prompting. For if God had granted him the means, as he had desired, perhaps today the head would not be joined to the limbs. How the head of the most glorious martyr Mark was found must not be passed over in silence.

One night, as a veteran priest was sleeping—as he himself has related ever since—a voice came to him saying:

“Rise, and do not sleep.”

Awakened, he thought that he was being called by his companion who was staying with him in that place. When he asked, “Why?” and no one answered him, he went back to sleep. Before he was fully asleep, however, he again heard a voice saying to him:

“Do not be so lazy. Rise and seek the treasure in the corner of this basilica.”

The priest was astonished and began to reflect within himself about the vision. But before he could rise from his bed, a similar third voice was heard, ordering him to get up at once and no longer doubt the vision.

Then the priest became joyful, thinking that he would certainly find money. He hurriedly rose, took a tool suitable for cutting thorn bushes, and, as though guided by divine providence, reached the place. He cut away the thorns that covered it and found, in the very corner, a small chest-shaped coffin. He immediately opened it and discovered inside the head of the most glorious martyr Mark, together with the nails with which the impious had tortured him.

Although he had not found what he had expected, he nevertheless rejoiced with great joy and went happily to the bishop, recounting everything he had seen. The bishop was filled with such great joy that, if he had found ten thousand talents of gold, he would not have been happier than he was over this head of the holy martyr.

Although the vision had not more certainly declared the name of this athlete of the Lord, the bishop nevertheless affirmed that this was the head of the most holy martyr, preserved by God’s providence so that the body would not be buried without its head.

When the year had been completed, the church built in his honor was finished, and the head was joined to the body. With the utmost reverence, it was solemnly dedicated on the third day before the Nones of October. He also composed a stone inscription like the earlier one and placed it beside the site. It read:

> Here rests in his body the great martyr Mark,
>
> whom Leo, by God’s grant, has buried here,
>
> bishop of Atina; this stone shall also be his witness.

The body had been found on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1046. At that time there was immense drought over the land, so that many among the people believed that the end of the world had come, since fires and a great darkness had seized the entire earth. The grasses of the fields had failed, and everything green was burning.

In the midst of this danger the Lord’s beloved Mark appeared to a certain religious woman, with a radiant face, a tall and handsome body, and white hair and beard. He said to her:

“Rise and tell the bishop: Why does he keep our body so long above the earth? Behold, my house is already prepared; what is delaying him? Does he not see that the people are in danger because of the drought? Let him know for certain that if my body is returned to the earth, the Lord, in His goodness, will immediately water the whole land.”

When morning came, the woman rose and reported what she had seen. The bishop began to wonder what he should do. He had decided to dedicate the basilica on the very day [Col. 1421A] on which the body had been found. The people had indeed pressed upon him in earnest, saying:

“We no longer wish to trust you if you intend to delay these benefits that God has promised us.”

The religious woman, however, affirmed under oath:

“Keep me in custody and return the holy body to burial. If you do not have rain on the third day, cut off my head without delay.”

Overcome both by the woman’s assertions and by the people’s reproaches, on Wednesday he himself fasted with some of the people. When evening came, with only those who knew the place present, he secretly buried the body and announced to all the people the day of the consecration.

That day passed, and, as the woman had promised, on the following day the almighty [Col. 1421B] God granted such abundant rain for the honor of His beloved martyr that the entire land was suddenly filled with water. The whole city rejoiced at this, because without delay it received what it had desired.

We have omitted a great and astonishing miracle that the almighty God deigned to perform on that same day, while the bishop was still handling the holy relics with his hands. A certain young man who had a withered hand came forward and pressed into the midst of the surrounding crowd. Seeing that the bishop was offering the sick water with which the sacred relics had been washed, so that they might drink it, he too began to ask with full faith and devout mind that the bishop deign to give him some for the healing of his condition.

The bishop immediately took a small vessel, blessed it, and offered it to him to drink. But as soon as it was brought to his mouth, by the favor of divine grace his hand was instantly restored, and he removed the vessel from his own lips after drinking. When they saw such a great miracle, everyone began in amazement to glorify the omnipotence of the Savior, who in these last days had deigned to perform such miracles for the strengthening of the faithful’s minds.

What the merciful Lord has deigned to perform in this city in the present year at the venerable relics of that saint must not be passed over in silence. A certain smith’s daughter was driven mad by the ancient enemy, so that she did not recognize either the place where she was standing or even her own mother.

As soon as her mother learned of this, she hurried with her from the field where she had sent the oxen to pasture and ran to the episcopal residence. She informed the bishop who was present. When he learned that the girl had been so pitifully changed through the envy of the ancient enemy, he said to her:

“O woman, I do not know what I can do for you. Yet, as one who has received mercy, I offer you counsel for recovering your daughter’s health. Take her, then, and immediately cast her down in faith in our Savior Jesus Christ before the sacred tomb of His glorious martyr. For I trust and confidently believe that, through his holy aid and by his interceding support, your daughter will be healed of this affliction.”

As soon as the woman heard this, strengthened by his declaration, she took hold of her daughter’s hand, led her into the church with full faith and devout confidence, and threw her down before the sacred tomb while tearfully imploring the Lord.

It was then the third hour of the day. She remained in prayer until nearly the fifth hour, and a sacrifice was offered to God on the girl’s behalf. By the Lord’s help she became well, and she and her mother—who had come to the episcopal residence in deep anguish and sorrow—returned home with joy and gladness.

Finally, while this miracle was being written down for the praise of our Lord Jesus Christ and the proclamation of His beloved martyr Mark, and while a soul filled with wonder marveled at these acts of power, a monk of the monastery of Saint Benedict, of blessed memory, devoutly took the recorded miracle into his hands. He entreated the prayer of this most holy martyr, asking him to deign to help him and remove the pain in his head, by which he was often tormented.

Placing his stylus on either side of his head upon the bed, he raised himself reverently and prayed:

“Come, revered martyr, help me as I pray, and for your honor remove the pain from my head.”

As he was saying this with the deepest devotion, by the Lord’s gracious generosity the headache immediately departed from him. He promptly returned to us rejoicing and recounted how great a mercy God had shown him through the merits of His beloved servant. Prostrating himself upon the ground and raising his hands toward heaven, he began with great exultation to praise the Lord and His martyr.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us rejoice, and let us delight with all our strength. Let us exult and rejoice in the Lord, for whose love this most glorious martyr Mark endured the punishment of death. Let us glory not so much in miracles as in his most sweet protection, in which we place the hope and confidence of our devotion. Without doubt, through his holy intercession, we shall rejoice, protected here from great dangers and delivered from them in the future.

As for signs and wonders, one ought not always to marvel at them, since not only saints but also sinners can perform them in the Lord’s name. Thus in the Gospel they will say on the day of judgment:

“Lord, did we not cast out demons in Your name and perform many signs?”

To them the Lord will say:

“Depart from me, workers of iniquity, because I do not know you.”

Indeed, blessed Gregory also reports in his sacred teaching that signs have been given to unbelievers. Therefore, if signs are granted to unbelievers, why do we faithful marvel at signs and miracles and not rather trust in holiness? For where signs are lacking, the helps of holiness are present.

Therefore, dearest ones, prostrate before the Lord with complete confidence and the full devotion of our minds, let us ask forgiveness from Him through this holy martyr, so that we may deserve to obtain it through his sacred merits. For if with our whole heart and faithful mind we ask for what we seek for our salvation, the Lord says:

“If you ask anything of the Father in my name, it will be given to you.”

Let us therefore seek help from Him who is powerful, and let Him who glorifies His holy name and His martyrs forever continually deliver us from impending dangers through their merits. For we know and believe without doubt that if anyone strikes Him with prayers without a lukewarm mind, whatever he asks for his salvation he will undoubtedly obtain, as He Himself has deigned to promise His faithful. For He says:

“If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move; and if you do not waver in faith, whatever you ask, you will undoubtedly obtain.”

There are indeed some who ask with lukewarm faith, and therefore do not deserve to receive what they seek. There are others who ask with such ardent faith as though they had Him present and were speaking mouth to mouth. These, therefore, deserve to be heard and obtain the fulfillment of their prayer.

I exhort you, therefore, dearest ones, to implore the help of this holy martyr Mark, to rejoice with us in his protection, and to deserve to have his companionship in heaven, since here on earth we continually raise proclamations of holiness to him. May our Lord Jesus Christ assist us in this—He who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1423]

## The Solemn Donation of Lord Leo, Bishop of Atina, Made to the Canons and Clergy of the Church of Atina

*(In Ughelli, Italia sacra, vol. VI, p. 432.)*

[Col. 1423B] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

In the year 1056 from His Incarnation, in the month of July, in the ninth indiction, while the supreme and universal pontiff, Lord Pope Victor, was residing in the city of Rome, and the most pious Emperor Lord Conrad was reigning, and Lord Adenulf, archbishop, was governing the Church of Capua:

We, Leo, by the dispensation of divine grace bishop of the Church of Atina, looking with the upright eye of judgment upon those things that pertain to the advantage of the Church, and desiring that the ecclesiastical order may live justly and piously in the house of the Lord, have resolved and established in our mind that the clergy of Atina should come together freely and willingly at the church of Saint Mary and unanimously render divine service to the Lord.

This decision of our will was pleasing, and He from whom every good proceeds granted and bestowed it through His mercy, since He who gives good will also provides the pious effect of action.

Therefore, having summoned all the clergy, together with the most illustrious Lord Count Lando and our advocate Bernard, and likewise with all the people of the city, we discussed our decision and took care to disclose aloud to them all the purpose conceived in our mind, so that nothing might be done in the house of the Lord without worthy counsel, since it is written: “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not regret it.”

When the matter had finally been disclosed, it seemed worthy and just to everyone that clergy who wandered about in various places and were always occupied with secular cares and anxieties could not properly devote themselves to divine service. Therefore, after taking counsel, certain of them, neither unwilling nor compelled, freely and sincerely devoted themselves to the service of the Church: namely, the priests Theoto, Angelus, John, Almundus, Albert, John, Leo, Benedict, Peter, and John; Benedict the archdeacon; Gregory and Mark, primicerii; Dominic and Atinus.

[Col. 1424B] All these, presenting reasonable service to the Lord, so that they might walk in the house of the Lord in concord, humbly offered themselves, together with all their possessions, to the altar of the holy Mother of God.

When these things had been done, the aforesaid count, together with all the people attached to him and with the clergy mentioned above, addressed humble prayers to us. They earnestly begged that we should confirm both those who had already joined themselves to the embrace of the Church and those who in the future would follow in their footsteps. Attending to their prayers with a gracious and merciful regard, we judged that they should be heard.

Therefore, after taking and deliberating counsel, we grant and donate to that church of the holy Mother of God, and to all its canons, both those present and those who will follow, the churches of Saint Lawrence, Saint Marcian, Saint Blaise, Saint Sylvester, [Col. 1424C] Saint Peter, and Saint Stephen, and all the churches that may be built within the boundaries of the city of Atina, together with their tithes, first fruits, and offerings of the living and the dead.

Moreover, in honor of the holy Mother of God and out of reverence for the body of the most blessed martyr Mark, bishop of this city, we grant to you and to your successors the appointments and canonical ordinances of all your churches.

We further grant you that whenever we or our successors are absent, you shall possess the fullness of authority in the exercise of our power, so that by episcopal right you may hold judgment over the clergy in your chapter and judge canonically all criminal matters, namely, the dissolution or joining of marriages and cases of oppression.

And so that the instrument of this document may be preserved forever firm and inviolate by our successors just as by us, we bind ourselves and our descendants to pay one hundred pounds of gold to the court; and it shall likewise be preserved inviolably in the same manner and with the same force.

But if anyone should attempt by any means and with reckless daring to violate or remove the decree of this constitution, we bind him perpetually with the chain of anathema, on the part of almighty God, blessed Mary ever-virgin, blessed Michael the archangel, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, all the apostles, blessed Mark the martyr, and all the saints, so that on the day of judgment he may not rise to be crowned on the right hand, but may receive his place with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord, and with Dathan and Abiram, whom the earth swallowed alive. Amen; so be it, so be it.

[Col. 1426A] I, Benedict the notary, wrote this at the command of the aforesaid venerable bishop.

Done successfully at Atina.

I, Leo, bishop by the grace of God, wrote this.  
I, Lando, count by the grace of God.  
I, Peter, son of Adon, judge.  
Peter, son of John Sergius, judge.  
I, Jubone, am witness.

[Col. 1425]

## Sermon of Lord Leo on the Passion of Blessed Mark

*(Ughelli, as above, col. 433.)*

[Col. 1425B] Dearest brothers, let the faithful people throughout the whole world, taking up the drum of harmony, return to the bosom of Mother Church and sing praises to the magnificent King concerning the passion of the most blessed pontiff Mark.

Today the most holy bishop Mark, a disciple of the apostle Peter, crowned before the Lord, has arrived. Today, crowned and adorned with heavenly insignia, he stands in the presence of Him who says:

“Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, you shall have authority over many.”

Today, I say, he deserved to hear these words. Today, for Christ, he was fastened to his head with two nails. Today, he received the prize of everlasting victory. Today, he was placed beneath the heavenly altar. Today, rejoicing with those who suffered for Christ, he sings a new song to God. Today, he left his body to be buried in the city of Atina. Today [Col. 1425C] he illumines the Catholic Church throughout Campania.

His most excellent glory was so preeminent that by his passion he illumined not only the Church of Atina but also all Campania. This most blessed martyr and pontiff glorified Jesus Christ our Lord by his passion, since for His name he was pierced in the head with two nails.

By his passion and by the dignity of his episcopal office he illumined the Church: as the blessed apostle Peter had entrusted it to him, he kindled some to the worship of the true God by words, others by the punishment inflicted on his body, and others by signs of miracles. For who, remaining in the bosom of holy Mother Church, would not willingly receive nails in the head with Mark for Christ, so that he might deserve to be rewarded with him forever by Christ the Lord?

Of him and of other martyrs the prophet David had foretold:

“Burn my kidneys and my heart.”

Therefore, through the faith of this most excellent martyr, the Church of Christ spread throughout the world is driven toward the goal of martyrdom, summoned to preaching, and instructed for battle.

Let the minds of the faithful, then, grow fervent today. Rejoicing with the Church’s mighty champion, let them offer Christ songs and honey-sweet words of praise. For who would not be astonished at such a monstrous passion? Who would not marvel at the savage cruelty of the torturer?

The most holy preacher of the Trinity is seized; the magnificent bishop is fettered with iron chains, delivered to prison, subjected to punishments, proscribed, condemned, and finally pierced in the head with exceedingly sharp nails. See, brothers, see the mystery of Mark; see such great endurance; see such great patience. Consider with what fervor he was burning, since, while fearlessly announcing the word of life to his persecutors, he did not fear receiving sharp nails in his head for Christ’s name.

The most holy martyr burned with desire for eternal life, and therefore willingly endured the cruel points of the nails. Hence Paul says:

“The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts of God” (Hebrews 4:12).

Blessed Mark, therefore, was subjected to the punishment of nails, but he burned more powerfully with the fire of the Holy Spirit. While the martyr’s mind was set ablaze with love of the faith, the wicked torturer was all the more driven to kill him, together with savage executioners.

He cries out more quickly, cries out more insistently:

“O wicked soldiers, you who bear an effeminate spirit by sparing the most criminal Mark!”

The city of Atina resounds with praise of Christ. Let new punishments be prepared; let the sword be sharpened; let the bishop and teacher of the Christians be handed over to death [Col. 1426D] and his body be left to be devoured by wolves and dogs.

O savage sentence of the torturer! Alas, alas! Wicked phalanx, why do you rage in vain against Christ’s martyr? Behold, I say, the exalted power of the Thunderer is present, and the magnificent mercy of God will be present to free the most blessed Mark from your hands.

His head is pierced, but the firmest constancy of his heart did not withdraw from the love of the Almighty. His body suffers punishments, but he acquires the salvation of eternal life.

O happy steadfastness! O inexpressible hope! While it did not fear enduring the torments of nails, it deserved to arrive crowned before the mercy of almighty God.

Crowned, I say, blessed Mark came before the Lord, and soon he was placed by the Lord Jesus Christ among the ranks of the saints. This is the most blessed martyr; this is the most worthy bishop; this is the disciple of the prince of the apostles; this is the magnificent preacher and witness of Jesus Christ [Col. 1428A] our Lord.

But since today we celebrate his venerable feast, let us earnestly ask him, as our patron, to intercede continually for us with the Lord. For it is fitting that we who had him on earth as a preacher and teacher of truth should deserve to have him likewise as our helper in heaven. May Christ Jesus, the eternal King of all kings, grant this—He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1427]

## Sermon of Lord Leo on the Octave of Saint Mark, Bishop and Martyr

[Col. 1427B] Today, beloved ones, we celebrate the eighth day of the most holy martyr and pontiff Mark. On it he trampled the devil who persecuted him, conquered the world that flattered him, and crushed beneath his feet the emperor who raged against him.

You heard, when his passion was read, with how great glory and honors he shone in this world, how he became a hearer of the prince of the apostles, and how he departed to the heavenly kingdoms. It is therefore right that the solemnity of the holy martyr and bishop should be celebrated through the eighth day: he preserved the seven times, that is, the seven laws from the world through the seven days by which human life is signified, while keeping hidden in his heart the eighth day, which belongs to the resurrection and judgment, and he did not fear dying for the faith of Christ.

That each faithful person ought to give seven parts and also eight, Solomon declares, saying:

“Give portions to seven and also to eight.”

For, brothers, three days are declared in the holy Church: before the law, under the law, and under grace. Seven are also declared through the seven laws from the world. But now, as the Lord grants, let us proclaim to your brotherhood how the aforesaid number is to be understood, how it is to be applied to each person, and what it mystically signifies.

### On the First Day

In the first number we understand God the almighty Father. In the second, Jesus Christ His Son, our Lord. In the third, the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son. These three are one: one in divinity and three in persons.

The day is God the Father; the day is the Son; the day is the Holy Spirit. The Day of the Day, the Son, is from the Father. He is also the sun of righteousness. Of this day the prophet says:

“For those who fear God, the sun of righteousness will rise.”

Therefore, if the Father and the Son are day, and day is light, it is plainly evident that the Holy Spirit is true illumination, enlightening the hearts and minds of the faithful.

By the first day we are to understand one God, one faith, and one baptism. Similarly, by the first day we can understand the period from Adam to Noah, the infancy of every human being, correction, and the preaching to the ignorant.

### On the Second Day

In the second number we must understand the law and grace, fear and repentance; straight feet, according to the words, “The upright love you”; and the appearance of amber, that is, the incarnation of the Son of God. We must also understand body and soul, the active and contemplative life, the practical and theoretical modes, the historical and allegorical senses, doing and teaching, and the childhood of each person; and, in accordance with the Lord’s command, refreshing the hungry.

The period from Noah to Abraham is the rebuke of sinners. Through the law human beings are restrained from sin; through grace sinners are pardoned; through fear mercy is sought; through repentance forgiveness is granted to sinners; through the feet one runs along the way of God’s commandments; through the amber the incarnation of the Son of God is revealed.

### On the Third Day
In the ternary number we understand the mystery of the Trinity, and the three strings on a lyre, praising God through the craftsman’s hand, as well as the three days from the origin of the world, as I have already said, until the consummation of the age. For the Father, the unbegotten, the Son, the only-begotten, and the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, are a journey of three days: the Father in the voice, the Son in human nature, and the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove and of fire. For in the Book of Ezekiel God shows him three words written down: lamentations, a song, and woe; by lamentation repentance is signified, by song the joy of eternal blessedness, and by woe the punishments of eternal damnation. There are also three things for which each believer goes to the Church: to receive baptism and judgment, and to receive the body and blood. In the life-giving sacrifice three colors are indeed seen: beauty of form, whiteness, and redness. Hence David says of its appearance: “Fairer in form than the sons of men”; in the whiteness, the virginal flesh; in the redness, the mystery of the Lord’s Passion. From this life-giving sacrifice the priest then makes three portions: he places the first on the paten, the second in the chalice, and takes the third himself. The first portion, which is placed on the paten, signifies the Incarnation of the Son of God; the second, which is placed in the chalice, the incorruptible body that lay hidden in the tomb; the third, which the priest receives, signifies Christ’s resurrection.

## On the fourth day

In the quaternary number we understand the figure of the four living creatures, the four wheels, and the four rings of the ark; and the four principal virtues, namely prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance; or the four regions of the world; or man, created from the four elements; and the four rivers flowing from one paradise. In the fourth place also is written what God said: “Let there be light, and there was light.” In the fourth place of human life, likewise, youth is situated, as is the period from Moses to the transmigration to Babylon.

## On the fifth day

In the number five we understand the five books of Moses, and the period from the transmigration to Babylon until David; or the five bodily senses, namely sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Likewise, in this number are described the five wounds of Christ’s body hanging on the cross, and the five keys of wisdom, as well as the five barley loaves with which the Lord satisfied five thousand men.

## On the sixth day

In the senary number we should understand the visitation of the sick, as well as human old age, persevering service under the Gospel, and the period from the transmigration to Babylon until Christ. Likewise, in the senary number God created and ordered all things; on the sixth day he made man, and at that age he came to redeem the world. At the sixth hour, too, Christ offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father for our salvation. At the wedding that took place in Cana of Galilee, six water jars were set there. The first jar is from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to Moses; the fourth, from Moses to David; the fifth, from David to the transmigration to Babylon; the sixth, from the transmigration to Babylon until Christ. Each held two measures, that is, the Old and the New Testament.

## On the seventh day

Through the number seven we understand the holy apostles, of whom the Lord says: “You are the light of the world.” We also find seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and fear of the Lord. In the holy Church each believer likewise receives seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: the nourishment of salt, entrance into the church, spittle, the oil of anointing, Christ’s baptism, the chrism of priests, and the chrism of bishops.

We also read of seven seals in John’s Apocalypse. The first seal is the announcement of the Incarnation of the Son of God; the second, baptism; the third, the Passion; the fourth, the resurrection; the fifth, the ascension; the sixth, judgment; the seventh, the recompense of merits. There are also seven beatitudes: the kingdom of heaven, possession of the land of the living, consolation, fellowship in righteousness, mercy, the vision of God, and adoption as children of God.

## On the eighth day

In the octonary number we understand Holy Scripture, love of God and neighbor, the life of those who contemplate, the universal resurrection, or the decrepit old age of human beings. The eighth day for each person is the end of the present life and the beginning of the future life. The eighth day was signified by the cataclysm that occurred under Noah, in which eight souls were saved. In Ecclesiastes Solomon says: “Give a portion to seven and also to eight.” For seven and eight make fifteen, and there are fifteen Songs of Ascents, which the children of Israel used to sing when they gathered at the temple.

Christ is the first, seventh, and eighth day: the first, because none existed before him; the seventh, because in him the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit came to rest; the eighth, because he is eternal and everlasting. The Lord also expounded eight beatitudes to his disciples on the mountain; this most holy martyr and beneficent bishop retained and increased them in himself. Therefore, let us now earnestly beseech this martyr and bishop, Mark, to pour out prayers for us, unworthy as we are, to almighty God, so that, with the help of him who lives and reigns forever and ever, we may deserve to have in heaven as our companion the one who stands on earth as our father, protector, and defender. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 1072. Avesgot, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of the Couture at Le Mans

[Col. 1431]

## Historical Notice

*Literary History of France*, vol. VIII, p. 76.

Avesgaud, or Avesgot, was abbot of the Couture, in one of the suburbs of the city of Le Mans. He must not be confused, as a famous author confused him [Mabillon, *Annales*, book LXI, no. 41], with another Avesgaud, abbot of Saint-Vincent in the same city, who in 1039 attended the coronation of King Philip. The man who is the subject of this article was at that time still only a simple monk, and was not raised to the dignity of abbot until after 1061. This appears from a letter that he wrote around that time. Not only does he give himself no other title than that of monk, but he gives no title at all to Saint Anselm, to whom the letter is addressed and who became prior of Bec the following year; this proves that the letter was written earlier. Although Avesgaud was different from the abbot of Saint-Vincent of the same name, he may nevertheless have belonged to the same house, that of Bellesme, from which came a third Avesgaud, who died bishop of Le Mans in 1036. He in fact speaks of his family as powerful in the region of Maine. He governed the monastery of the Couture as abbot until the end of 1079, and had Johel as his successor from the end of that year or the beginning of the following one.

Avesgaud did not write badly, as can be seen from his letter to Saint Anselm, which Baluze rescued from obscurity. It is the only product of his pen that has come down to us. The author’s purpose was to persuade Anselm to take charge for a time of the education of one of his nephews. But it had no other effect than to elicit the beautiful reply that forms the sixteenth letter of the first book of Anselm’s letters. In it Anselm responds, with equal modesty and ingenuity, to a verse of Persius that Avesgaud had quoted to him. After all, it is astonishing that Bec, which had opened a public school for the young, should on this occasion have refused a young pupil of good birth. But the astonishment ceases when one reflects that the matter concerned the rudiments of grammar, which Anselm could not provide in the way the boy’s parents desired, because he was occupied in teaching the higher sciences.

[Col. 1431]

## Letter of Abbot Avesgot to Saint Anselm, later Archbishop of Canterbury

(Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. II, p. 174.)

[Col. 1431A] Avesgot, monk of the monastery of Saint Peter of the Couture, to Anselm, greetings.

Until now we have been friends and intimates only in speech, but we have never tested one another in action, if action were necessary. For a long time I have wished that you would command me to do something, and then you would see how much you can rely on me. Believe me: either through me or through my parents, I would gladly obey your command. But since you neglect to do this, I ask this gift of you first. I have a certain nephew of mine, already a young man, whom I cherish above all else; and, if you could bear it, I desire him to remain with you, so that he may be educated in grammar under your instruction. I could send him to other teachers, but I would have greater confidence in you than in any living man. I should feel entirely secure if he stayed in the place where you are.

Why does the fame of Lanfranc and Guimundus fly throughout the world more than yours? Why do you hide your lamp for so long under a bushel? Do you not remember the poet who says:

> Your knowledge is nothing unless another knows that you possess it.

I have no doubt that you will grant my request. But I earnestly beg you to tell me what service I should offer your abbot and the congregation subject to him, so that they may permit what I have described to take place for at least three or four months, if they do not wish it to continue longer. Therefore, if my words are received by you as I desire, send me the time at which I may find you; and, if I remain safe and well, I shall go there. Farewell, dearest friend.

[Note: Anselm’s reply is found among his works, book I, letter 16.]

## In the Years of the Lord 1066 and 1076. Saints Ariald the Deacon and Herlembald, Martyrs

[Col. 1433]

## Acts of the Holy Martyrs Ariald and Herlembald: On the Ancient Veneration of Their Tombs, with the Writers of Their Acts and Struggles, and Their Companion, the Priest Luitprand

(In Bollandus, *Acta Sanctorum*, June, vol. V, 27th day, p. 280.)

[Col. 1433A] 1. When Joannes Petrus Puricellus, archpriest of the collegiate church of Saint Lawrence in Milan, had published in 1645 the monuments of the Ambrosian basilica and monastery there, arranged chronologically, in which the acts of the saints named above are treated at some length, he published two years later a work specifically about them, divided into four books. The first contains “Testimonies collected in support of their sanctity,” most of which are historical accounts, arranged by date from the eleventh to the seventeenth century in thirty chapters; their principal witnesses will be indicated in their proper places.

Among these, the chief relevance here belongs to the “Catalogue of the Archbishops of Milan,” compiled in 1310. Under the name of Guido, the seventy-second archbishop, it records the following: “At this time Blessed Ariald, martyr and Levite, suffered, namely in the year 1066. He lies in the nave of the church of Saint Dionysius. Also Blessed Heribald, a soldier, who persecuted the mistresses and sons of priests.” This testimony is based on the monuments of both men, which long survived, and on the epitaphs carved when they were erected, to be produced below.

The next place after that catalogue belongs to the “Ambrosian Calendar,” prefixed in 1381 to a parchment codex containing the Epistles to be read at Mass throughout the year. Under 28 June it has: “Saint Ariald, Levite and martyr. He lies at Saint Dionysius.” There is also Puricellus’s own book, written exactly one hundred years after that codex, “On the indulgences granted to the churches of Milan, and on the bodies of the saints resting in that city and its diocese.” On folio 16 verso it says: “At Saint Dionysius: Saint Dionysius, Saint Arioldus, Saint Aurilius,” elsewhere written “Arialdus” and “Aurelius.”

[Col. 1434A] 2. But although “Saint Herlembald” is omitted there, elsewhere he is also listed as a saint without “Ariald,” namely on a very ancient panel of the collegiate church of Saint Babylas, made of boards joined together, in the chapel that is to the left of the principal chapel. There “Saint Ambrose occupies the central position, dressed in archiepiscopal vestments, holding a threateningly raised scourge in his right hand and a banner in his left. On the banner are painted the persons of the Most Holy Trinity, differing neither in form nor in age from one another.

“To Ambrose’s right sits an armed holy soldier, bearing upon his breast, on the right side, the coat of arms of the noble Cotta family—namely a white Cotta—and identified by these letters as Saint Arembaldus. In his left hand he carries a martyr’s palm, and in his right a white banner marked with an inserted red cross. The other figure seated on the left likewise carries a similar banner and palm, and is called Saint Julian.”

But who this latter figure is I have so far been unable to determine. His appearance certainly indicates someone other than the Saint Julian of that name, the deacon who is honored with his brother Saint Julius, priest of Novara, on 31 January.

3. The second book of the aforementioned work contains “The Life of Saint Ariald,” which Constantine Caietanus communicated to Puricellus from an old codex. It was written not by the priest Syrus—whose letter stands at the end of the work and to whom Baronius wrongly attributed the Life under the year 1066—but by “Blessed Andrew,” first a disciple of Saint Ariald until his death, then a Vallombrosan monk and abbot of Saint Fidelis of Strumi. I attempted to collect some accounts of him on 10 March.

The aforementioned Syrus did write something immediately after the murder had taken place, “with his companion Herimbertus,” as Andrew himself says in a letter to him; but what he wrote has not been found. Since Syrus had omitted much, Andrew wrote a fuller and more accurate account at the command of his abbot Rudolf, in the tenth year after the saint’s death—counting incompletely, as I shall show elsewhere, that is, in the year 1075. At that time Herlembald had recently died, crowned with a similar martyr’s laurel. Andrew stated, in chapter 44, that he was leaving Herlembald’s passion “to another volume and another writer”; this has compelled us to collect his acts from the histories or annals of contemporary authors, though almost all were hostile. Puricellus promised to publish them, but death overtook him and left the long-deferred work still desired.

4. The first of these authors is a certain Arnulf, who comprised the history of his country in four books. From the second book onward he professed to write what he himself had learned by sight concerning events since the election of Archbishop Aribert in 1019; and he continued doing so until 1077.

Then comes Landulf, who, in relation to another Landulf named below, must be called “the Elder.” He was writing around the year 1080. In the matters for which we praise Ariald and Herlembald—and which he twists in order to provoke hatred against both—the substance of his account deserves greater belief precisely because he wrote with a more hostile mind, even though he was manifestly “a liar when he asserted that both Ariald and Pope Alexander II had repented and grieved over everything they had previously done against the Nicolaitans and Simoniacal clergy of Milan; and when he also invented three miracles that God performed in favor of the cause stubbornly defended by married priests, a cause that the Roman Catholic Church condemned so many times.”

Thus Puricellus writes in his preface to book I, rightly rebuking Tristanus Chalchus, Carlo Sigonio, and Giuseppe Ripamonti, historians of Milan in more recent times, because, in explaining the disturbances that agitated the Milanese Church as the eleventh century advanced beyond its midpoint—and because of which these publicly recognized saints lost their lives, consecrated by the Roman pontiffs with the title of martyrdom—they preferred to follow schismatic authors and blame the saints themselves rather than follow “Landulf the Younger,” who was writing around 1515 what he had learned from his uncle, the venerable Liprand, who had been mutilated in the nose and ears for the same cause.

5. Here we give the first Life of Saint Ariald from Puricellus’s edition, and with it we assign his death to the year 1066, specifically to the very day on which Andrew says Ariald suffered, “the fifth day before the Kalends of July.” Since that day, however, was occupied by the celebration of the octave of Saint John the Baptist, it was transferred in the aforementioned Calendar to the fourth day before the Kalends.

Nor does Puricellus’s number 67 persuade us to change the date: it says that, after the saint had been carried away captive, “before the third hour of the day, while the vigil of Saint Peter was being celebrated, it was announced throughout Milan.” For since Lake Maggiore, to which the saint was taken and in which he was killed that same day, lies fifty or more thousand paces from Milan, and since he was captured not far from that place, within an interval of only a few hours, it was sufficiently remarkable that the treachery by which he fell into the hands of his enemies resounded in the city the following morning, even though there was still no certainty about his death or the manner of it.

The author first reached the place on the 29th, after proceeding there on foot throughout the day and night. Then the criminal priest met him and said: “From the third day a joyful voice”—that is, a voice full of joy—“has sounded in our place: Ariald, the adversary of the clergy, is held bound in a boat on the shore of the lake”; and on that same day he described the murder as having been completed.

Here I do not read “externa” with Puricellus, as though it might mean “yesterday,” but “ex terna,” or “ex tertia die,” that is, “the day before yesterday,” then the fifth day before the Kalends of July.

Since nothing definite is known about the day of Saint Herlembald’s death, which occurred—as I think I shall sufficiently prove—in 1075, not 1076, shortly after Dominica in albis, then celebrated on 12 April, I thought it fitting not to separate in the history those whose deeds in life, monuments after death, and cult had been joined together. Instead, I have appended to Ariald’s Life the remaining events up to Herlembald’s murder.

6. Since the aforementioned priest Luitprand, also called Liprand and Leoprand, had shared the final ordeal with him, and died on 6 January 1513, in old age and in a good confession, at the monastery of Saint James of Pontida, though he had not yet been numbered among the saints, I decided to add, as an appendix to the history of the two saints, the surviving accounts about him that are entirely remarkable and directly relevant to the same subject.

If Puricellus had found any evidence of a cult of him among the monks of Pontida, among whom he died and was buried, he would undoubtedly have examined it with care. Nevertheless, considering what Luitprand’s nephew reports about miracles performed by him both while alive and after death, and especially about the courage of his soul, divinely inspired, in voluntarily submitting to the ordeal by fire, I can scarcely doubt that they counted him among their blessed. I also suspect that the monks of Pontida honored the bones of the deceased, but that, after the monastery was at some time destroyed or burned by war or other disasters, the memory of his tomb perished, together with whatever might have enabled him to be called without scruple “blessed,” indeed “saint,” if it were established that the bones mentioned at Pavia among other relics were his.

This opinion of the Pontidans’ affection toward Luitprand is confirmed for me by the memory of the cult bestowed by the Vallombrosan monks upon Saint Peter, whom they call “the Fiery,” after the event in which he underwent a similar ordeal by fire at Florence in 1063—that is, thirty-eight years before Luitprand underwent his. For his monks have long honorably enshrined Peter’s relics on an altar shared with several blessed men of the same profession, and they have now also obtained from the Sacred Congregation of Rites permission to celebrate his feast with an Office on 8 February.

7. Andrea Alciati, a most celebrated jurist who flourished in 1530, is said to have indicated, in one of his *Antiquaria*, cited by N. Fontana from manuscripts and quoted by Puricellus on page 15, “the tomb of Ariald from the Alciati family,” and to have added: “The historian Arnulf of Milan described his sermons, disputations, death, and miracles.”

But since this Arnulf, as we have seen, was extremely hostile to Ariald, it is not likely that he wished to write a separate Life of the saint apart from his History, as described above, even though he was corrected at the end and reconciled with the Church. For even then he could not be dissuaded from believing that the saints just mentioned had acted for a good cause, but with insufficient judgment and discretion, and therefore were not to be praised for dying in such a manner.

Whatever the case, the Life that Puricellus makes the third book cannot be his. We shall frequently use it in our notes. Besides strongly approving the acts of the saints everywhere, it reveals that its author wrote after the year 1100, when, speaking of the “church of Rozone,” he adds: “which is now called the Church of the Holy Sepulchre,” a name it first acquired at that time.

Puricellus gathers much more on this matter in the preface to book III, and judges that the work is by Landulf, called “of Saint Paul,” whom we shall call “the Younger.” After carefully reading the Life written by Andrew—and Arnulf could scarcely have read it, much less have written such contrary things earlier without later retracting them more distinctly—Landulf reduced it to an abridgment, arranging and supplementing certain matters somewhat more skillfully from the same knowledge, while also writing his own Annals, which we shall chiefly follow in the appendix.

8. The same Alciati either wrote or began to write another Life of Saint Ariald. Its beginning survives, and Puricellus makes it chapter 12 of book I. Here he had it from Matteo Valerio, prior of the Carthusian monastery at Pavia, and saw a fragment of exactly the same kind in the museum of Aloysius ab Ecclesia, formerly Urban’s secretary. The reader will also find this fragment inserted among our notes.

The reader will likewise find there certain material by Peter Azarius, evidently a military man, who in 1456 was employed in reforming the army and then brought his work of Milanese Annals, preserved in manuscript by the aforementioned Carthusian prior, down to the year 1402, when he was already very old.

For the remaining authors, whose passages and testimonies fill Puricellus’s book I, concerning the shared history of Saints Ariald and Herlembald—whom some call Arembald, Herenbald, and Heribald—see Puricellus himself. See also his fourth book, which claims to provide the Life of Herlembald alone but in fact contains the history of the entire schism that tore the Church apart in the eleventh century, when Cadalus and Guibert were raised as antipopes by Henry, a rebel against the Church, King Henry IV of that name and Emperor III.

[Col. 1437]

## The Life of Saint Ariald, by Blessed Andrew the Vallombrosan, disciple of the saint

## Preface

[Col. 1437C]

1. You commanded me, venerable Father Rudolf, to describe the passion of the blessed martyr Ariald. Although I have attempted to do so—for I speak truthfully, not merely out of humility, as many learned men are accustomed to do—I attribute whatever is suitable in it, even in the composition of the words themselves, not to my own wisdom, which is so small that it is almost nothing, but solely to the grace of God, to the merits of the saint himself, and to your prayer.

Let whoever reads it know that I have said absolutely nothing except what I learned from reliable men: namely, from the marquis, his faithful brother, or from Bonovisinus, his most faithful servant, who served him from the cradle onward. Indeed, there can be as many witnesses to these things as there are men in that place who, possessing mature age and sound judgment, remain alive.

2. Throughout this little book, however, let my name be concealed. I am such a person that it is more fitting for me to be unknown than known, and the saying of Isaiah rightly applies to me: “Close,” he says, “your door, and hide yourself behind it, until the Lord’s wrath has passed” (Isaiah 26:20). But let your name be displayed on its front, since, whether you wish it or not, Christ has placed you upon a lampstand so that you may give light to all. Thus, if the one who wrote it is unknown, the person for whom it was written will not be unknown.

Moreover, since this work contains many things in words and deeds useful for edification, I ask you to assign it for reading to the twelve monasteries over which the heavenly Judge has set you, so that, when they hear what others in our time said and endured in defense of the truth, they too may be inflamed to say such things and, if necessary, to suffer similar things for the same truth.

## Chapter One. Ariald’s Birth, Education, and First Sermon against the Incestuous Clergy

[Col. 1438D] 3. Although the world is already so old that its setting seems now very near, since no mortal knows when it will end, I wish to commit to writing and make known for the instruction of posterity the steadfastness of the new saints, comparable to that of the ancients, and the savagery of the treacherous men who persecuted them to death in our times—indeed, before our very eyes.

4. In a certain village called Cutiacum, situated between Milan and Como, twenty miles from the greater city and five from the lesser one, as common opinion reports, there lived a certain Bezo with his wife Beza. They were noble by birth, but nobler in character.

[Note: Landulf the Younger says: “In Cuzago, near Canturium,” commonly “Cantu,” which is marked on maps; this place is not. Alciati calls it “Cucciacum,” “under the jurisdiction of Canturium,” three times nearer Como than Milan, between the rivers Lambro and Mura.]

[Note: “From noble parents of Alzate,” by which name there is a village six miles beyond Novara. Others make it the family name and render it in Latin as “Alciati.” But the aforementioned Alciati, in the fragment of the Life, adhering to Andrew’s words, preferred to omit this—perhaps because he did not dare to claim Saint Ariald as a kinsman? Later, however, he did so in his *Antiquarium*, cited in no. 7 of the preliminary commentary, saying that Ariald belonged to the “Alciati family.” Yet perhaps these words belong to Fontana; and it is necessary that he was not especially noble, since Landulf the Elder says that he “foresaw that Landulf, the senior canon, would attach himself to him as being the more high-born,” because he himself “was humbly born.” I do not think that writer would have wished to lie in this matter, although he is sometimes by no means truthful when he deals with the cause of the clergy, which he defends against the saint.

“Marchio,” who is called the saint’s brother in the prologue, I therefore think was his baptismal name, not a title derived from rank, as was the case with another man whom we read of in Puricellus, page 237, from Arnulf, as having been hurled from a high rock.

Diamans Marinonus, in the manuscript *On the Origins of the City and the Families of Milan*, preserved in Puricellus, book I, chapter 12, derives the name from Alcathous, son of the Aeolian king and suitor of Hippodamia, or from Alcaeus, grandfather of Hercules. I believe the most learned Alciati would have regarded these as ridiculous if he could have read them. Yet he is said—though I do not know where or how—to “establish that Alciati was of royal stock.” In Italian, *Alzatus* means “raised up”; hence *inalzare* means “to raise.” I think this is sufficient for the true etymology of the name, despite the fables attached to it.]

We are instructed by many accounts of the saints to dwell briefly on the praise of these parents, and we all know that the praise of a lofty building will be freer when the solidity of its foundation is clearly established. They so detested the cause of the reprobate, which is greed, that, although they possessed an excessive abundance of servants and horses, none of their servants dared to bring even a handful stolen or violently taken from another’s field for the horses in their presence.

They also so abhorred pride, which is the devil’s cause, that, although they could freely dominate their neighbors in every way and could be compelled by none of them if they were unwilling, they voluntarily submitted to every just agreement with them as though they were among the least of those neighbors.

5. But since it is little for anyone merely not to do wrong unless he exercises himself in good works, they devoted themselves to the needs of the poor and sick. No one among their neighbors lay ill in bed whom Beza, worthy of remembrance, did not visit, and whom she did not support from her own resources if he needed such assistance.

Moreover, through the benefits that she diligently bestowed on other orphans and needy people, her life was so pleasing to God and to human beings that the poor themselves would say to one another: “If she dies, surely it will no longer be worthwhile for us to live.”

I myself saw this practice of holy active life, maintained over many years through the labor of the venerable Beza and her children after her husband had died, together with many other things suitable for edification. I omit them because I desire to proceed quickly to the matters for whose sake I undertook this work.

6.
