One night, while this woman was sleeping, and while her husband—by whom she was then carrying a son—was still alive, a marvelous light shone down upon her in a vision, like the brilliance of the midday sun. Its radiance, driving away all darkness from her, filled the entire house in which she lay.

When morning came, she marveled at the extraordinary vision she had experienced and disclosed it to the elderly matrons. They immediately told her that she was carrying in her womb a male child who would attain great merit.

When she had given birth to him at the appointed time, they called him Ariald, made him a cleric, and diligently entrusted him to the schools until no local teachers capable of instructing him remained.

Whenever he returned from them in due course, as is customary for students—and as he had often learned from his aforementioned mother—if the girls of the household, more carefully and brightly adorned than usual, presented themselves before his face, he would drive them away from his sight, saying: “This is Satan’s snare.”

Finally, in various lands, he devoted himself without interruption to scholastic studies until he possessed excellent knowledge both of the liberal arts and of divine letters, and had also reached mature age.

[Note: Alciati says: “First he devoted himself to all the liberal studies, in which, given the times, he made considerable progress. For in that period, through the constant turmoil of wars and the wrath of God, good letters had perished, and there were no schools throughout Italy. Therefore he went to Gaul, to the academy at Paris, and, having remained there for a long time, acquired a great reputation.”

Likewise Landulf the Younger, in the *Ambrosian Monuments*, page 530, says that Ulric, the Milanese vice-lord, and Anselm of Pusterla went to “Laon I”—that is, Laon in Gaul—“to hear the distinguished master Anselm of Laon,” and that they were pleased to take Landulf himself with them.

“And,” Alciati says of Saint Ariald, “they report that he advanced so far in the profession of divine matters, which they call theology, that he left all his fellow students behind. But he despised dialectic, which he called a kind of surface of learning, more than he was ignorant of it.”

Landulf the Elder, hostile to Ariald, accuses the saint before Puricellus of ingratitude, saying on page 179 that, “having been nourished by Bishop Guido with many delights and heaped with many honors, while devoting himself to literary study, he became a most severe interpreter of divine law, exercising harsh judgments only against the clergy.”]

[Col. 1441A] 7. At that time the ecclesiastical order was so led astray by innumerable errors that scarcely anyone could be found who could truly be found in his proper place. Some, roaming here and there with dogs and hawks, devoted their service to slippery hunting; others were tavernkeepers, worthless stewards, or impious usurers. Almost all led their lives disgracefully with public wives or prostitutes, and all sought what was their own, not what was Christ’s.

For—something that cannot and should not be said or heard without groaning—all were so entangled in the Simoniacal heresy that from the least to the greatest no order or rank could be held unless it was bought in the same way that livestock is bought.

And, what was worse, at that time no one appeared who would resist such great perversity. But although they were ravenous wolves, they were thought to be true shepherds.

8. Clearly, to expose and correct their perversity, Ariald was sent by God to Milan, where this wickedness was more widespread because the city itself was more populous than the others. He was well instructed in the divine laws, as we have said. When he entered the city [Note: [Col. 1441D] “At Varisium, where he was staying,” Ariald began his preaching; both Landulfs say this, and Syrus does not deny it, below, no. 84. “Varisium” lies between Angera and Como, nearly forty Roman miles from Milan. In our own time it is a celebrated religious site because of the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion represented on the nearby mountain; it is about ten miles or somewhat more from Cantù. Alciatus does not say that the saint lived there, but that he “withdrew there for a time because he still considered himself unequal to the faction of wicked priests.” Both Landulfs say that Ariald was then “one of the decuman canons.” [Col. 1442D] Puricellus teaches in the *Ambrosian Monuments* that these are now called “titular canons”; elsewhere they are called “lesser canons” or “vicars,” distinguished from the “greater” or “ordinary” canons. In the Mazarine dissertations, p. 444, Puricellus likewise teaches that these “decumans,” numbering one hundred, were “distributed among eleven collegiate churches and ten other chapels.” Thus Ariald himself, swearing by the words of St Peter Damian, begins: “I, Ariald, called the Deacon of the chapel of the archbishop of Milan”; here “St Ariald” should be understood as one who goes before the others by his example.], almost the entire population flocking to hear him, he began to speak as follows:

“My beloved, at the beginning of our discourse I wish to tell you what I know you know, so that little by little I may lead you on to those things that you do not know and that are greatly necessary for you to know. I truly believe that you know that the human race was blind until the coming of Christ our Lord—not in the eyes of the body [Col. 1441C], but in the eyes of the heart. It was blind because it regarded what was false as true, saying to stone, wood, and metal: ‘You are my God.’

“Because of this blindness, or rather this misery, the supreme and eternal Light, through which all things were made and in which all things subsist, had such compassion that, instead of sending an angel to remove it from human hearts, it descended from heaven in person, assumed flesh, and, in order to drive it completely from human hearts, willingly went even to the death of the cross. During the days of his earthly life he chose from the world as many men as he had foreseen before the ages would suffice to illumine the whole universe. Having expelled all the darkness of falsehood from their hearts, he illumined them with eternal light, sent them throughout the entire world, and commanded them to carry everywhere the light they had received; thus he returned to the Father from whom he had come.

9. “This supreme, eternal, and living Light left on earth two means by which all who were to be illumined might be illumined and might remain radiant until the end of the age—both those who were still to be illumined and those who had already been illumined. Do you wish to know what these things were? The Word of God, namely, and the life of teachers.

“Concerning the Word of God, that it is light, hear not my testimony but that of the Psalmist: ‘The commandment of the Lord is radiant, enlightening the eyes’ (Psalm 18:9); and again: ‘Your word is a lamp for my feet’ (Psalm 118:105). Concerning the life of teachers, that it ought to be light, Truth itself openly declares in her own words: ‘You are the light of the world’ (Matthew 5:14), and immediately adds: ‘So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven’ (ibid., [Col. 1442B] 16).

“From these two things, therefore, the same Lord placed one before them and the other before you. Those to whom he gave knowledge of Scripture and whom he chose for his service he established so that they might always live in the light of his radiant Word; and he ordained that their life should be your reading, you who do not know letters. But while the enemy of the human race lay in wait, and while our negligence and sin worked alongside him, they, by turning backward, lost their light, and you lost yours.

10. “Nevertheless, so that the same enemy might deceive you more securely, he who took the truth of fellowship away from them promised them the likeness of holiness in their outward appearance. I say this with grief, not to your disgrace but for your caution. Have you not returned to the same blindness from which Christ mercifully descended from heaven to free mankind? As we have said, the human race before his coming was blind because it accepted falsehood as truth. Whoever now does something similar, does he not incur the same guilt?

“For just as those deceived people believed stones and pieces of wood to be gods, so you regard your priests as genuine, although it is plainly evident that they are false. How can we know this? Do you wish to know how? We are in darkness; to recognize this plainly, let us go to the light. To what light? To the Word of God, namely. Behold, Christ says: ‘Whoever serves me must follow me’ (John 12:26). This plainly means: no one serves me except the one who follows me.

“I know that you know the life of your priests. Hear where Christ goes and what he says, and then you will more fully recognize whether these men are his ministers or rather his adversaries. Behold, Christ cries out: ‘Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble [Col. 1443A] in heart’ (Matthew 11:29). And again he says of himself: ‘The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head’ (Luke 9:58). And again: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 5:3).

11. “But, as you see, your priests are considered happier when they can become richer in earthly possessions, loftier in building towers and upper rooms, more honored, and more splendid in soft and luxurious clothing. And, as you observe, they openly take wives like laymen; they pursue fornication like criminal laymen, and for committing this abominable deed they are all the more powerful because they are less burdened by earthly labor—living, of course, from the gift of God.

“Christ, on the contrary, seeks and desires such purity in his ministers [Col. 1443B] that he condemns the sin of fornication not only in deed but also in the heart, saying: ‘Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart’ (Matthew 5:28).

“Return, my beloved, to your hearts; return, and learn to accept what is true and reject what is false. I have tried to bring the guilty back to their light, but I have been unable. I came here in order to bring you back to yours, and I will either accomplish this or, for your salvation, I am prepared to surrender my soul to the sword.”

While the man of God was saying these and many other things of the same kind, almost the entire populace became so inflamed by his words that, condemning those whom it had previously revered as ministers of Christ, it proclaimed them enemies of God and deceivers of souls.

## CHAPTER II. Ariald, having gained Landulf as his companion, goes to Rome, and both are harassed by the injuries of the wicked.

[Col. 1443C]

12. While these events were taking place, a certain cleric named Landulf rose from the middle of the crowd [Note: [Col. 1443D] Landulf the Younger calls him “Landulf of Cotta, an ordinary Levite of the Milanese Church.” Alciatus assigns the first meeting of the two men to Varese and gives the following fuller account:

“Landulf, a man of great reputation in the city, an ordinary member of the principal church and extremely eloquent in sermons, greatly beloved by the people, was then flourishing there. Ariald had been joined to him by an old friendship. Accordingly, when he met him, he complained at length about Guido [the archbishop], and still more about the excessive license of the sacred order, as well as about the need of the people and everyone to become better. Landulf promised that he would not abandon the cause and that he would dare to act once he had learned that the matter could succeed according to their wishes.

“In the meantime Ariald himself preached through the streets and meeting places, seeking to gather to himself those priests who were separated from urban refinement [or, perhaps, urban uncleanness?] and therefore retained their ancient integrity; then he would do in the city what he had undertaken in the countryside. After this conversation Ariald began at Varese to deliver his celebrated speeches against the corruption of the priests, attacking their morals with great severity, restrained by no fear, and setting everything forth on behalf of truth. Landulf did the same, but more sparingly, and only when an opportunity presented itself.”], a man eminent in the city both by rank and by birth, exceptionally powerful in voice and speech, and asked for silence. When this was granted, he uttered the following joyful words:

“‘I give thanks before you to almighty God, who now permits me to hear what has caused my heart to burn for countless years. For long ago, although I knew and grieved over these things, I remained silent because I had no one with whom to discuss them. But now, dearest lord Ariald, because God has given you to me as his gift, know that I have been bestowed by him upon you; and henceforth, whatever you say or do concerning this matter, I shall say and do also. Just as you have professed that you are ready to lay down your soul for the salvation of the brethren, so I now assure you without hesitation that I am prepared to lay down mine.’

“When the already faithful people heard this, it rejoiced and grew in the praise of God; the opposing party, wasting away, faltered. But God’s servant Ariald, raising his eyes and hands upward, rendered immense and fitting thanks to the Giver of all good things.

13. Finally, another layman rose, named Nazarius, a moneyer by profession, whose life, although he was married, was highly praised by everyone. He asked for silence. When it had been granted, he gave the following reply before them all:

“‘Lord Ariald, what you say is true and useful; not only the wise can recognize this, but even the dull-witted. Who is so foolish that he cannot clearly perceive that the life of those whom I invite into my house to bless it, whom I refresh as far as I can, and to whom afterward I offer a gift while kissing their hands—the men from whom I receive everything sacred, for which I hope for eternal life—ought to be far different from mine? Yet, as we all plainly see, their life is not only no cleaner, but visibly dirtier than mine.

“‘Know, however, that this crime has taken such root among us and grown so old that it will scarcely be uprooted, or only with great labor. But now, because the Giver of all good things has bestowed upon me such abundant possessions as can sufficiently provide both for me and for you, I beg you, by that same almighty Lord, to deign to enter my house and enjoy all my goods as I do, so that through your continual exhortation both I and this entire people may be freed from this error and confirmed in all truth.

“‘Take care not to look to the high blood from which you have sprung or to the great resources at your disposal, lest, disregarding the oath by which I adjured you, you should appear to seek not the things of God but your own.’”

14. When the man of God heard this, and considered both the seriousness of the adjuration and the man’s excellent reputation, he trampled underfoot all earthly considerations that might have resisted him, willingly entered the house of the man who had justly invited him, and for a long time faithfully accepted from him the work of Martha. What Peter did in Cornelius and his friends, Ariald did in Nazarius and his neighbors.

In these men the two shrubs that the Lord promised through the prophet to place together in the desert—namely, the vine and the elm [Col. 1444D] (Isaiah 41:19)—were then doubtless represented: one would intoxicate minds, while the other would support the one that intoxicated them.

Finally, when Ariald and Landulf had exhorted the people [Note: [Col. 1444D] Landulf the Elder, in Puricellus, p. 179, blames Landulf, Ariald’s companion, “because, having attained no ecclesiastical rank, he had usurped for himself, contrary to the custom of the Church, the office of preaching and imposed a heavy yoke upon the necks of the saints.” Among the other things he daily impressed upon the ears of the people, he preached one day as follows:

“‘Dearest elders, I can no longer keep within me the speech conceived in my heart. Do not, my lords, do not despise the words of a young and inexperienced man; for God often reveals to the lesser what he denies to the greater. Tell me: Do you believe in the triune and one God?’ They all replied, ‘We believe.’ And he added: ‘Fortify your foreheads with the sign of the cross.’ And it was done.

“‘After this he said: “I rejoice with you in your devotion, yet I grieve with you over the great destruction that threatens. For many years now the Savior has not been recognized in this city. It has long been since you have gone astray, since you have no traces of truth. Instead of light you grope in darkness; you have all become blind, because your guides are blind. But can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit?” (Luke 6:39).’

“For fornications abound in many forms. That Simoniac heresy also exists among priests, Levites, and the other ministers of sacred things. Since they are Nicolaitans and Simonians, they rightly ought to be rejected. Therefore, if you hope for salvation from the Savior, henceforth beware of them entirely, venerating none of their offices . . . . . I too have committed many acts deserving punishment; but, worse still, by communicating until now with the unworthy I have offended the King of heaven. Now, with God propitious, I repent and intend to guard against such things in the future.

“‘Therefore, my beloved, be imitators of me, and walk as you have us for an example’ (Philippians 3:17).”

That writer attributes this speech to Landulf through his excessive partiality for the clergy, though he himself is everywhere more unjust toward Landulf and Ariald. He charges the latter as though he had said not only that the “sacrifices of the Nicolaitans and Simonians were the same as if they were dogs’ dung, and their basilicas the stalls of beasts” (which indeed might be said insofar as such sacrifices, although true and valid so far as the sacrament performed by such persons is concerned, nevertheless defile those who communicate with them, because it is unlawful to communicate with notorious heretics and excommunicates); but also as though he had added that “now that they have been rejected, all their goods should be confiscated, and everyone should have the power to plunder everything in the city or outside it.” It must be beyond doubt that this was attributed to the pious zealot through sheer slander or extravagant exaggeration, since the people did nothing of the kind; on the contrary, the faithful suffered such abuses from their adversaries and went no further than preparing to repel force with force, as will appear from what follows.], through faithful and constant instruction, the shameful fornications of the clerics and their detestable marriages were pursued and abolished by that same people within a short time, so that no one remained who was not compelled either to abandon such utter wickedness or not to approach the altar [Note: [Col. 1445C] Alciatus—whose remaining fragment is useful to append here—then continues with the slanders that followed and with what the archbishop Guido, or Wido, did amid these events:

“There were some who thought that Landulf, ambitious for Wido’s favor and dignity, had agreed with Ariald. But certainly no innocence has ever avoided envy and slander. Accordingly, certain wicked men, believing that a great reward would be paid to them for their denunciation, accused both men before Wido, heaped accusations upon them, and cried out that the majesty of the supreme priest had been insulted and that the occasion for new seditions had been sought.

“Wido did not then dare to take action against them, because he knew that both enjoyed the highest reputation among the people. Therefore he summoned them to his chamber, received them courteously, and mingled threats with entreaties while defending his own cause and that of the priests.

“‘It is not fitting,’ he said, ‘for a priest to speak evil of a priest; for in this way they would stab themselves with their own weapons. It is better even to endure things undeserved than to bring about some rash dissension. Nor is it right to condemn one’s brother, whose salvation Christ God redeemed.

“‘Anyone who is prepared to speak against another must first cleanse himself of every stain, unless he believes that one who is himself sick can properly heal others. Would anyone listen to an armed soldier, lacking courage, discussing peace? Or would anyone prefer that Greek saying as wise? “Why,” it says, “do you not first reconcile yourself with your wife and children, and only then call us to peace by your example?” First the beam must be removed from your own eye, so that you may draw the splinter from another’s without reproach.

“‘Open and public correction displays not correction but hatred and censure. You wish to condemn someone and rebuke him before the people; first you must place before your eyes whether you have ever suffered from a similar fault or, when you were once caught in it, refrained from it. If you were ever liable to that offense, you should consider that you are human and of such a condition that you could have been caught by that sin.

“‘If, while you served that fault, you appealed for freedom, let the memory of our common weakness come to you. Do not rebuke the man publicly; admonish him privately, so that he too may take care to recover his senses in imitation of you.’

“When Wido had said these things calmly, he brought his speech to an end by declaring that priests were permitted to take wives, and by threatening that he would punish them if they dared to say anything contrary.”

He seems to indicate that Landulf himself had previously lived as a concubinary within the clergy, or at least had been married before receiving the tonsure, and that for this reason he had separated from his wife and children—perhaps with the wife’s consent, but nevertheless with a cause that seemed suitable for accusing the man, as though he had separated from her because of domestic disputes.

Alciatus continues:

“Then Ariald and Landulf said: ‘It makes no difference by what kind of death or at what time we perish; for those who fight for truth are glad to die. We have fixed this conviction in our minds: as perpetual enemies of crimes, while life remains we shall preach daily against criminals. For what burden of preaching should we undertake if we are compelled to conceal the truth and betray the cause of all Christians?

“‘Indeed, if these priests of yours were sinning secretly, none of us would have approved of punishing them publicly. But since their crimes are of such a kind that it was not enough for them to commit them unless they themselves also became the authors and publicizers of their deeds, there is no reason for you to advise us to accuse them secretly. It is fitting that one guilty of manifest offenses should also repent publicly; and just as, when a disease yields to milder medicines, the knife or fire is applied, so, when all other remedies have been exhausted, public punishment is necessary for the obstinate minds of these men.’

“After this conversation they departed, leaving the bishop indignant. Fearing, however, that the enraged Wido might eventually plot something to destroy them, they sought support for their party. At that time Anselm, of the family of the Badagi, held the highest authority in Milan; the emperor had appointed him bishop of Lucca because of his innocence and virtue. Ariald went to him with his colleague.”

Thus far the fragment. The “Anselm” praised here had become bishop of Lucca in 1056. A contemporary—and on this matter the more trustworthy Landulf the Elder—teaches that he was rather the originator of Ariald’s undertaking of the preaching. In chapter 4 of his third book of Histories, he gives this title in Puricellus, p. 273: “How Anselm of Badagio, from the Ordinary clergy of the Milanese Church, urged Landulf and Ariald to preach that wives should be separated from priests”; and in chapter 5: “How Ariald began to disclose his purpose of preaching.” Further, in chapter 7 he says:

“‘At this same time a great terror invaded the Ambrosian clergy . . . . . Since the beginning and course of these events are still before our eyes, let us relate them as best we can. Let him provide the outcome who, being Alpha and Omega, wonderfully disposes all things.’”

And so Landulf enters upon the subject treated here by Andrea.] the filthy fornications of the clerics and their detestable marriages were so pursued and eradicated by the same people within a short time that no one remained who was not compelled either to abandon such utter wickedness or not to approach the altar.

15. At the same time the faithful decided to send Landulf to Rome [Col. 1447A] to the synod [Note: [Col. 1447B] In the year 1057 Pope Victor II celebrated a general council at Rome on the Kalends of May, in the Constantinian basilica, as is clear from the second letter of his successor Stephen. It is plausible that the council dealt with Nicolaitans and Simonians no less than the earlier council under Leo IX in 1051.

The aforementioned “Stephen,” consecrated on 3 August of the same year, is praised in his Life because, “after holding many councils in the city against concubinage and many other vices of the clergy, he reformed the customs of the Church”—clearly in that same year and at the beginning of the following one, when he died at Florence on 29 March. Baronius should be read under the year in question, no. 9, where those frequent synods are said to have been held during the four months that the pope remained in Rome, until the feast of St Andrew; and again, no. 16.

Landulf the Younger wishes “Ariald” to have gone to Stephen, not Victor, who had died on 28 June. He says that, because of the preaching of “Ariald” and “Landulf,” the clergy, first with the provincial bishops and then with the Roman pontiff, “complained repeatedly.” “At that time,” he says, “Pope Stephen presided in Rome, and he ordered a provincial synod to be assembled concerning this matter.”

It seems plausible to me that the matter, begun under Pope Victor and continued under his successor, may be attributed to both. At the command of one or the other, “a synodal assembly of bishops was held under Guido, archbishop of Novara” (another adds, “at a place called Fontaneto,” in the diocese of Novara, at the same distance from Milan as Novara itself). Read at Puricellus, p. 183, the passionate speech delivered by Guido, in the words of Landulf the Elder, who was excessively favorable to the corrupt clergy.

“When they had devoted three days to the matters mentioned,” Landulf the Younger continues, “it pleased many that Landulf and Ariald should be excommunicated in their absence; and this was done. Therefore Landulf, wishing to go to Rome, was severely beaten in the town of Piacenza, about thirty-six Roman miles from Milan, and thus returned to Milan.”], because their adversaries falsely accused them, saying that they were going there. He was not permitted to proceed beyond the city of Piacenza, because there he was struck by a certain profane man in the town, and so returned to Milan.

But Ariald, God’s servant, set out and knowingly avoided the plots of all the adversaries stationed everywhere to kill him; protected by God, he arrived safely in Rome. Presenting himself before the supreme pontiff, he reported to him the cause already begun. After showing him great honor, the pontiff ordered him henceforth to receive the divine mysteries from the priests from whom he should receive them, and under an unavoidable command instructed him to return to the work he had begun and to persevere in it with vigor until he either completely eradicated the abominable practices then existing among the ecclesiastical body or offered his own blood to be shed by his enemies for Christ [Note: [Col. 1448B] The same Landulf gives a much fuller account:

“Ariald proceeded to Rome and accused before Pope Stephen the adulteries and simony of the Milanese clerics. He explained how, through his preaching, the people were separating priests from their wives, and asserted that the priests were disobedient to the Roman Church, while he and Landulf were devoted to it and fighting for the truth.

“When these things had been heard, many supporters of the adversaries rose in anger. Among them Cardinal Dionysius rose and said much against Ariald. Then, when many others, favoring the adversaries, cried out against Ariald, Pope Stephen imposed silence. He spoke briefly, neither praising the cardinal nor condemning Ariald; indeed, he annulled the synodal sentence of excommunication, urged Ariald not to cease preaching integrity, and sent legates to Milan concerning these disputes—namely, Cardinal Hildebrand, Peter of Ostia, Anselm of Badagio, and Bishop Lucanus—so that through them the truth might be learned in the presence of the accused.

“When these legates reached Milan and had gathered an assembly of clerics, they investigated their offenses, called Guido a Simonian, and judged his clergy polluted by adulteries and evil morals. They declared that Ariald had reported the truth to the Roman pontiff and urged him to persevere in the purpose he had begun.”

These legates were men distinguished for holiness and authority: Hildebrand, later Pope Gregory VII; St Peter Damian; and Anselm, later Alexander II, as I have already said—all well known, whereas “Dionysius,” until then unknown, was passed over by Ciacconius and his interpolators. Puricellus, p. 187, asserts from Landulf the Elder that Dionysius had been “nurtured from childhood” in the Milanese Church and gives a long invective of his against Ariald. According to his account, Ariald “stood trembling and pale, almost frozen like a dead man,” recognizing that all those present sympathized with the Milanese Church.

I suppose Ariald was astonished that such things had unexpectedly been said to him at Rome and indeed before the pontiff; but the pope immediately restored his courage, as Landulf himself finally acknowledges.] He returned obedient in all things, pursued the oft-mentioned cause competently and steadfastly, and henceforth, together with his divinely granted companion, possessed a teaching as full in authority as in truth.

16. When the wicked secular clerics perceived this, they secretly gathered together, as it were. Because Landulf was of higher birth, they decided to kill him, thinking that Ariald, terrified by fear, could thus be silenced [Col. 1448A]. To carry out so wicked a deed, they approached a certain daring and impious cleric and made him confident through a very large reward if he would destroy the man already mentioned.

After obtaining a great executioner’s sword, which I myself often saw afterward, as well as a poison exceedingly swift in killing, he secretly pursued Ariald during the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, Holy Saturday, and the holy day of Easter [Note: [Col. 1448D] Easter was celebrated in the year 1050 on the 19th.]. I know that what I am saying is true; whether I am preserving the exact order of the events, I do not know.

Since he could not find Ariald during those days without causing disturbances, at last, on the second day after Easter, his wicked and long-desired wish was fulfilled. At twilight on that day [Col. 1448B] he found Ariald alone praying before a certain altar. He immediately mixed together the deadly instruments he carried—namely, the sword with the poison—and, coming secretly from behind, struck him heavily in the neck, then immediately fled. But, by God’s will, although he was exceedingly swift in flight, he was captured at the exit of the basilica by a certain lame man [Note: [Col. 1448D] Laxdulf adds “a beggar.”].

17. A great outcry was therefore raised; everyone ran together, and the cause of so great a clamor was investigated. When the reason became known, they surrounded the wicked cleric and found him carrying a horn filled with poison. They took up the wounded man and the man who had struck him, grieving, and went to Landulf’s house; there they immediately awaited his impending death.

But then almighty God displayed unmistakable evidence of a great miracle: the poison harmed his servant no more than water would have done. For the cleric himself confessed that he had tested it on several animals; as soon as they swallowed it, they all died shortly afterward. O wondrous power of the Lord! After touching this man, the poison could harm no one, even when swallowed.

Accordingly, giving God the praise due to him, Ariald released the cleric who had struck him unharmed, warning him never again to attempt so great a presumption. The cleric, seeing that his schemes, devised with such great effort, had plainly been brought to nothing by God’s power, and that the servant of God had repaid his evils with good, was pierced in heart, asked forgiveness, revealed the instigators of so great a crime, promised that he would never again attempt anything of the kind, and finally departed in this manner.

18. At the same time the suburban clerics gathered together and said to one another:

“What shall we do? Behold, Ariald, who has disturbed and dispersed us and our families, lives shut up in the city and surrounded by the people; therefore we cannot reach him in order to kill him. If we cannot do that, let us at least inflict upon him whatever harm and disgrace we can [Col. 1449C].

“Let us now return to our own places, obtain sharply honed swords, and gather again on another night. Let us go together to the place where he was born, where he and his parents still possess extensive property, and let us violate and destroy, to his disgrace, the church that he once built at his own expense. Let us strip the bark from the innumerable chestnut trees he owns, and cut down the vineyards in which he abounds.

“In the meantime, let some of us go there by day—those who have full knowledge of his property—and clearly mark his vineyards and woods, so that at that time there may be nothing in which anyone could make a mistake.”

19. They therefore gathered on the appointed night and found the church outside the village [Note: [Col. 1449D] I understand this to mean the village of Cotta, the saint’s birthplace.]. They entered it after breaking down the doors. [Col. 1449D] They broke and violated the altar and destroyed the other furnishings; and what the wretched men were unable to do to the servant, they did not hesitate to do to the Lord, to his disgrace.

When they wished to proceed to the marked trees and vineyards, as they later confessed at their deaths, they were struck by the just judgment of God with such fearful blindness that they could find neither where they were nor the object they had marked. O wondrous mercy of the Lord! He permitted them to demolish his house, but he knew perfectly well how to protect the house of his servant.

But lest the miserable men spend that night in vain, they entered vineyards and woods and cut down and stripped the bark from those belonging to others. Nevertheless, giving thanks to God, I declare that afterward I often saw those very trees yielding the richest fruits to their cultivators, and I still believe that they do so in the same way [Note: [Col. 1449D] I think this should be referred to the same year, 1056, concerning which Landulf the Younger reports at the beginning:

“When the translation of blessed Nazarius, on 10 May, was being devoutly celebrated by all the clerics and citizens, Ariald began openly to disparage the marriages and fornications of the clerics. Hearing this, a certain priest named Anselm said: ‘So you are the man who defames us priests before the people? Has virtue remained in you alone?’ After saying this, he struck Ariald with a slap.

“But Ariald said: ‘Not only this, but I am also prepared to suffer death for the truth.’”].

## CHAPTER III. The deeds of St Ariald against the Simonians, whom he taught must be shunned as heretics.

20. At the same time the servants of Christ, seeing that the entire people was extremely ready to follow whatever they said, began to speak openly about simony, which until then they had kept silent about. The first of them in the power of knowledge and holiness—namely Ariald, although Landulf was more eloquent than he—began to speak to the people about simony and against it as follows [Col. 1450B]:

“Beloved, we ought to give thanks to almighty God, who has given you the will to do what he himself wills. We wish you to know that the considerable labor we have undertaken until now against the insolence of married and adulterous priests was imposed upon us more by necessity than by choice. For whether heretics have wives or not, we consider it of little importance.”

When the crowds looked at one another and wondered why he was saying this, he added:

“You heard, beloved, when the book of the Acts of the Apostles was read, that Simon Magus came to blessed Peter the Apostle and sought the grace of the Holy Spirit for money. Luke the Evangelist, who wrote this, immediately added what blessed Peter answered him: ‘May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money’ (Acts 8:20).

“What does this mean? Is this not the same Peter to whom the Lord commanded that a brother who sins seventy-seven times must be forgiven? (Matthew 18:22.) It is indeed the same. But in this case he did not see Simon as merely sinning against himself or against a human being, but against God. For blessed Peter would have sinned greatly if, by remaining silent, he had allowed the author of so great a crime to prosper and had failed to condemn the estimation of such wickedness at its very root.

21. “I utter this with tears and profound grief. Behold the wickedness that the prince of the apostles consigned to eternal perdition in the very act of putting a value on it; it now holds such dominion throughout almost the entire world that no one reaches the pontifical or abbatial office, or any ecclesiastical office whatsoever, except through it.

“Who can hear what I am about to say and not grieve and be astonished? Behold Christ, the true Lord, the good Shepherd, gave his flock a solemn, salutary, and good commandment; it has been cast into such deep oblivion that no one seems now to dare remember it. Do you wish to hear what it is? ‘You have received freely,’ he says, ‘give freely’ (Matthew 10:8).

“On the contrary, the impious thought that once arose wickedly in the heart of the wicked Simon, and that was immediately condemned by so great an apostle together with its author, has been solemnly spread everywhere, so that scarcely anyone approaches the service of the altar unless he first carries out in deed what that man wickedly conceived in his heart; and the more deeply he subjects himself to that same curse, the worse the evil is known to be that he does than the evil he merely conceived.”

22. Would that this curse strike only those who presume, with bold and impious heart, to sell or buy the gift of God! Yet this guilt is so grievous that it binds not only those who do these things and those who consent to them, but also those who do not resist and oppose the perpetrators, so punishably that they are unquestionably not free from the curse pronounced by Peter against Simon. Lest you perhaps think that I am lying, hear what our patron, Blessed Ambrose, thinks about this matter [Col. 1451B]. For he says:

“For they also believe that they have received leprosy from the holy Elisha, together with Gehazi, who think that they can purchase the priestly rank with money. For just as, when the head is afflicted by more serious diseases, the rest of the body must necessarily be fatally drenched by the overflow of the disease above, so also those who appear to be the head of the Church corrupt the brotherly body with a pestilential disease, so that nothing from the structure of the whole body can escape uninjured. The virus of the wickedness of negligent priests has infected it, so that you may see throughout the Church men whom not merit but money has advanced to the episcopal order. Yet, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses (Deut. 17:6),” hear what blessed Gregory says about this matter [Col. 1451C]:

“Why is it not seen, why is it not weighed, that the blessing is turned into a curse for the man who is ordained in order to become a heretic?”

And again:

“Whoever, in consideration of the office entrusted to him, does not burn fiercely against this Simoniac and Neophyte heresy may have no doubt that he shares with Simon Magus, who first committed this abominable crime.”

23. Since that passage of Blessed Gregory’s sermon, where it is commanded that each person ought to burn against Simony in consideration of his own office, may perhaps not be fully clear to everyone, it is fitting that we explain it lucidly to you. There are three orders, after all, in the holy Church: one of preachers, another of the continent, and a third of the married. The first must burn against this evil through tireless exhortation; the continent through constant prayer; but you who are married and live by the labor of your hands must strive daily and fervently, through works of almsgiving, that almighty God may drive this evil from the holy Church and destroy it.

Therefore, whoever now among these three orders has not fought fervently against Simony, together with these works of justice, should by no means believe, according to the words of the Holy Spirit, who spoke these things through the mouth of Blessed Gregory, that he can escape at the end the punishment which Simon Magus now suffers.

For if those to whom the knowledge and office of preaching have been entrusted remain silent for any reason, not only must the continent—whose preaching ought to be all the freer and more truthful, since it is evident that they are detached from every worldly matter and instructed by constant meditation on the sacred law—but even you, who are uneducated and ignorant of Scripture, use the common words at your disposal to make one another cautious of this wickedness. Hence the Lord said: “If human beings remain silent, the walls will speak” (Luke 19:40). Does the prophet not say concerning this matter: “Cursed is he who restrains his sword from bloodshed” (Jer. 48:10)—that is, from the slaughter of this most wicked beast?

24. While Blessed Ariald was saying many such things and others like them, that salutary sword was undoubtedly sent into that place—the sword that divides the faithful from the unfaithful, and of which the Lord spoke: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.”

For Guido, who was called archbishop, and the greater part of the clergy and soldiers, together with many wicked men from the common people, seeing their position, said to one another:

“If this teaching succeeds, it will certainly not be advantageous for us or our sons to remain alive. For what is our life except the benefices of churches, which we constantly sell and buy? Therefore it is more useful for us to die resisting this new teaching than, as we have said, to allow it to succeed.”

But the faithful men of God cried out to them:

“We have heard from your assertion that those who are known to have bought sacred things are unquestionably Simoniacs and heretics. By this crime it is plainly evident that no one among the priests here is free from guilt, because there is no such person. But since we are called Christians, we cannot live without Christ’s sacrament. If we receive it from these men, you say that we receive condemnation rather than salvation; and therefore we are hemmed in on every side by these weapons, and truly do not know what to do” [Col. 1452C].

25. Blessed Ariald answered them as follows:

“See, beloved, while you say these things, lest what the Holy Spirit speaks through Blessed James come upon you: ‘A man double-minded is unstable in all his ways’ (Jas. 1:8). Therefore whoever sincerely desires to find the truth must steadfastly reject every falsehood.

“Accordingly, so that you may perfectly enjoy the truth, which is God, I beseech you by him to separate yourselves completely from the company of false priests, because there must be no fellowship, share, or partnership between light and darkness, between the faithful and the unfaithful, or between Christ and Belial. For it is written: ‘Come out from among them and separate yourselves, and do not touch what is unclean, and I will receive you, says the Lord’ (2 Cor. 6:17–18).

“How can it be that he will not grant you lesser things when you ask—that is, shepherds who will rule you justly—he who, before you existed, granted you greater things, namely himself for your salvation? Therefore, rejecting every association with heretics, confidently ask him for good and faithful shepherds; and know without doubt that you will receive them.”

Through these words many men and women were so inflamed that thereafter they not only despised the acts of the Simoniacs but also refused to pray with them in the same oratory under any circumstances. In those days, if you had walked through that city, you would scarcely have heard anything anywhere except disputes about this matter. Some were excusing Simony, others condemning it steadfastly. Nor is this surprising: one household was entirely faithful, another entirely unfaithful; in a third, the mother was a believer with one son, while the father was an unbeliever with the other. The whole city was filled and confused with this discord and contention.

26. In those days very many clerics began to abandon the fellowship of the wicked clergy and to adhere to Blessed Ariald. Among them was one of those priests who, moved by his exhortation, decided to relinquish a certain church which he had wrongly bought for a large price.

But by Christ’s arrangement, Miles, in whose legal possession it was, had already become one of the faithful, having been instructed by Blessed Ariald. Just as the purchaser had decided to abandon the church, so Miles chose by his own right to lose it as its mistress, although until then he had wickedly usurped it as a slave. When many faithful therefore gathered together with Blessed Ariald, Miles received from the purchaser a formal renunciation and, at the man of God’s urging, placed it upon the altar. He ordered Blessed Ariald thereafter to dispose of the church according to what he knew God desired.

Ariald immediately summoned three faithful and chaste clerics and ordered them together to take up the renunciation which Miles had placed on the altar.

27. When several people urged him to accept the church together with them, so that it might remain there for the benefit of many [Col. 1453C], he said:

“I shall remain with them for their instruction and the salvation of the others. Nevertheless, lest the word of God entrusted to me be hindered by the yoke of some earthly possession, and lest this Azo, in whose jurisdiction the church has been built, suffer any harm on this account, I will by no means take possession of this matter. For know without doubt that a time will come when no one will be permitted to live unless he drives me from his territory.”

How prophetic this speech was will become clearer than daylight to the reader’s mind in what follows. For while he remained in that church, no one can write—or indeed adequately relate—all the benefits he bestowed by word and deed upon the brothers themselves and upon the other faithful and unfaithful alike, nor all the evils he endured from them in return for his goodness over nearly ten years.

He immediately sent a messenger to his paternal home, took from it twenty pounds of silver, and built beside the same church a remarkably suitable dwelling [Note: [Col. 1453D] Landulf the Younger: “Here Blessed Ariald restored the church called Canonica, outside the walls of the New Gate of Milan,” and so forth, taken from this point onward.].

28. At last a new arrangement was undertaken, almost unknown in that place until then. The choir was enclosed by a high surrounding wall, in which a door was set; the sight of the clerics, laymen, and women, which had previously been one and common, was divided; all were compelled to live from one common chest; chatter at table was restrained, and in its place sacred reading was constantly brought forth there [Col. 1454A].

The other clerics used to mutter all the Hours of the day rather than chant them. But he, when the signal had been sounded seven times during the day, gathered the brothers together and sang the due praise of almighty God with great reverence. Whenever they happened to fail in that office, he urged them all, by word and deed, toward satisfaction.

Just as Blessed Ariald became exceedingly joyful because he had reached the long and greatly desired goal—namely, that he could live together with the brothers at the church—so many of the faithful became joyful because they had a suitable place where they could listen with free minds to the Lord’s words and receive the divine mysteries and sacraments.

Such a great multitude began to flock there, not only from the city but also from villages and castles, that the church itself, although quite spacious, could in no way contain them. The man of God instructed them with such steadfast and continual teaching that often he lost his voice so completely that he could scarcely be heard by some who stood beside him.

29–30. Moreover, because the “dumb dogs” had become unable to bark, the people at that time committed many evil and detestable acts. From the beginning of his preaching, Ariald condemned all of them so thoroughly that he undoubtedly made his own the statement uttered through Blessed Paul:

“I am clean from the blood of all of you; for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:26–27).

Throughout the entire Advent, he found them celebrating weddings solemnly without any opposition, even taking wives on the very vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, if it happened to fall on a Sunday. He began to oppose this abominable practice with such fervor and constancy, both by word and by deed, that by the time of his venerable death scarcely anyone could be found who dared to undertake so detestable a work.

On the very wedding day, when everything customary for a wedding had already been prepared, he would hurry anxiously with the brothers to the place where the wedding was being celebrated. He declared that those who were about to celebrate the wedding of the Lord of all things ought to be splendid, not defiled and preoccupied by their own sins. In this way he compelled them to abandon everything already arranged and to preserve it for a suitable time.

31. Two clerics had formerly received the clerical tonsure in a certain church called Saint Mary Secreta. Neither, however, could enjoy the benefit of it until the priest of that church had died, as was customary in that place; and during that same period the priest happened to die.

When the man who had first been designated was now to obtain the church, but only if he paid for it the dishonestly customary price, he delayed, having been won over by the words of the man of God. His wicked junior preceded him and, without blushing before God or man, was not afraid to acquire the church for himself with money.

When this was reported to the man of God Ariald, he summoned him and addressed him as follows:

“Wicked presumer, why, after hearing from my teaching that the buyer and seller of sacred things is a heretic, did you not fear to commit this iniquity?” [Col. 1455A]

32. The man fell silent, not knowing what answer to give in his defense. Since he was already regarded by his neighbors as exceedingly detestable on account of this, he finally replied:

“Having heard the manifest reasoning, I see that I have done wrong; but I have no idea at all what I should do now. The abbot of Saint Victor, to whom on this account I gave almost everything I possessed, does not fear God sufficiently to return to me the money he once received. If I do not have it, I will have no means by which to support my life even modestly.”

The man of God said to him: “What did you give?”

“Twelve pounds of silver,” he replied.

The man of God answered: “And if it is returned to you, are you willing gladly to relinquish what you wickedly purchased?”

He replied: “Most gladly.”

Then the good disciple, imitating his master’s piety, followed in action what he had said in words. From his own property he took twelve full pounds of silver and handed them all to him. Thus he enabled another man to possess the church freely—the man to whom it belonged by right [Col. 1455B].

[Note: [Col. 1455C] The first six sections are not marked by any indication of the time at which they occurred; the following sections refer to the pontificate of Alexander II. Between him and Stephen IX, whom Baronius preferred to call X, there sat for nearly two years and five months Nicholas II, until 24 June 1061. At the beginning of his pontificate, in April, Nicholas held a synod to which the saner part of the Milanese clergy, moved by the preaching of Ariald and Landulf, sent envoys, “humbly beseeching him to deign to have mercy and compassion on the afflictions of the Milanese Church,” as is read in the Vatican Acts of Nicholas apud Baronius. It is added that “for this reason Pope Nicholas sent there the venerable man Peter Damian, bishop of Ostia, and granted him his authority to correct and settle whatever pertained to that Church.”

Then Baronius says: “A full account of this embassy survives in the letter which Peter himself then wrote to Hildebrand” [Col. 1455D], who had recently been elevated from subdeacon to archdeacon of the Holy Roman Church by that same Nicholas. It is reckoned among Peter’s minor works as the fifth, entitled “The Proceedings at Milan concerning the Privilege of the Roman Church.” By this privilege, the things approved there made the Roman Church the mother of the Ambrosian Church, from which Ambrose himself had sought aid under Pope Siricius against the filth of the Nicolaitans and had requested legates, through whose judgment this ruin might be restrained.

The result was that the legate judged that pardon ought to be granted to those who repented, and that Guido, together with his associates, condemning their former excesses, promised to abolish the Simoniac and Nicolaitan heresies completely. When he had sworn this, Peter says, “he immediately prostrated himself on the pavement with all humility and begged that penance be imposed upon him for the commerce of that wicked sale; although he had not himself been the first author of that crime in that Church, nevertheless he had not eradicated it as he ought to have done.”

“I therefore imposed upon him,” Peter continues, “a penance of one hundred years and fixed its redemption at an amount of money assessed for each year. Soon afterward we entered the larger church and ascended the pulpit. Then, before the numerous people of the city and the clergy, he made his cleric swear, with his hand upon the Gospels, that the archbishop himself, as long as he lived, would sincerely and faithfully strive to eradicate these two heresies, so that he would permit neither priest, deacon, nor subdeacon to have a woman together with his rank; and that he would utterly prohibit every commercial transaction in the conferring of ecclesiastical sacraments.”

All the clerics were then admitted to swear likewise, and penance appropriate to the character of each one’s guilt was prescribed for them.

“After these men had thus been reconciled, it was decreed that the office should not immediately be restored indiscriminately to everyone, but only to those who appeared educated in letters, chaste, and honorable in the gravity of their morals. For the others, it was sufficient that, through divine grace, they had been inserted into the holy Church, from which they had previously been cut off by the sickle of divine judgment” [Col. 1456C].

The elder Landulf, approving none of this, says at Puricellus, page 205: “A crude decree was made, to which the archbishop, together with the ordinary clergy, subscribed unwillingly under pressure from the people.”

But how could he have been unwilling if, when summoned soon afterward to the Roman synod, he went there voluntarily? For this reason he was also “treated with distinction by the Apostolic Nicholas, at whose right hand he was placed in the synod.”

Speaking of this synod, Arnulfus says at Puricellus, page 211, that “Ariald” also went there and accused the archbishop, but was refuted by the bishops of Asti, Novara, and Turin. “When the archbishop promised obedience to the lord pope, having received from him the ring of apostolic favor and of all ecclesiastical dignity,” he returned to Milan.

Would that he had not also returned to his vomit, as will appear below! And in that synod “Ariald” most probably did only this: he proved that everything had been done at Milan by the legate Peter lawfully and in due order, not that he wished to persuade anyone that the archbishop ought not to be received again into favor.

Meanwhile, the other authors are silent about that journey of “Ariald,” as does Andreas also about all the matters noted above; and for that reason these things had to be related here at greater length.] 

**CHAPTER IV. The Approach of Saint Herlembald to Ariald, and the Office of Defender Entrusted to Him by Pope Alexander**

33. At that time Landulf died, leaving behind a surviving brother named Herlembald, a prudent and faithful man [Col. 1456A], although a layman. He had recently returned from Jerusalem and then wished to abandon the world and devote himself to the monastic life.

Recognizing his faith and steadfastness, Ariald began to promise him that he would acquire a more exalted standing before God if he delayed entering a monastery, defended the Catholic faith together with him, and resisted heretics and the enemies of Christ alongside him.

Wishing to test whether he might confidently trust what Blessed Ariald promised him, Herlembald took several faithful men and set out for Rome. He did not travel by the royal road, but went among worshipers of God living throughout the surrounding wilderness and monasteries, questioning them all about the matter in question.

When all of them, inflamed with true and pure faith, gave him a judgment agreeing with Blessed Ariald, he finally reached Rome. There, by an unavoidable command, Pope Alexander and the cardinals ordered him to return and, in defense of justice, resist the adversaries of Christ courageously with Blessed Ariald, even to the shedding of his own blood. They also gave him, on behalf of Blessed Peter, a marvelous standard, so that whenever the madness of the heretics raged beyond measure, he might restrain them by holding it in his hand.

How steadfastly he fulfilled this for nearly eighteen years, neither my tongue is fully able to express nor my pen adequately to describe.

34. In the sight of the world, the noble Herlembald was like a duke, dressed in costly garments; but in secret, before God, he was clothed in wool like a rustic hermit [Col. 1457A]. I saw him wash the feet of the poor—something I do not remember seeing in anyone else.

When he was moving through some part of the city, surrounded by a great multitude of faithful people who freely served him, and saw horrible-looking poor and disabled persons, he would secretly signal one of his servants to remain behind and bring the poor man home with him. After dismissing the outsiders, he would bring water, gird himself with a linen cloth, and wash and dry the needy man’s feet with the greatest reverence.

Afterward, with his body prostrate on the ground, he would place his head beneath the man’s feet, and in this way make the beggar and poor man tread lightly upon him, the rich man. Finally he would honorably and abundantly refresh him at table. I sometimes saw him perform this holy work for as many as twelve poor men.

Nevertheless, he was so inflamed with zeal for God that, often sighing in Herlembald’s absence, the man of God Ariald would say:

“Alas! Apart from Herlembald and Nazarius, I scarcely find any cleric who, under the pretext of false discretion, does not somehow urge me to remain silent, so that the Simoniacs and adulterers may freely carry out the works of the devil.”

I learned many good things about this man in familiar association. But because he has recently been crowned with martyrdom in the defense of justice, I leave them to another volume and writer, since I am eager to complete the Life of Blessed Ariald quickly.

**INTERPOLATION: On the Beginnings of Herlembald and the Death of Landulf**

[Col. 1457]

35. Since it is my intention to continue the Life of Saint Herlembald together with the Life of Saint Ariald, I cannot omit supplementing elsewhere the excessive brevity of Andreas in accordance with this purpose, following the authors supplied by Puricellus.

At page 221, from the Annals of Peter of Aruzzi, completed around the year 1402, he relates how, when the see of Milan was vacant through the death of Aribert, that most highly praised prelate—his epitaph records that he died “in the year 1045, on the seventeenth day of January, in the thirteenth indiction”—and when Lazo de Curte was in exile, the latter supporting the plebeian faction against the nobility in a city divided into parties, under the title “Captain,” the people’s party was reduced to nothing.

“Then,” he says, “the captains of the six gates, with their vassals, usurped control of the city. Gathering all their friends in the communal palace, they enacted two statutes out of hatred for the people.

“The first statute was this: that Ranzo de Curte, an outlawed knight, together with the entire family of those de Curte, should never be able to live in the city of Milan or in the county, nor possess property there forever.

“The second statute was this: that if any nobleman killed a commoner, he would pay seven pounds of tertioli and twelve denarii; once he had paid them, he would be free from every guilt and offense. For this reason countless people from the lower orders were slaughtered within a few days.

“For this reason the common people again elected another captain, a certain man from the number of the nobles, who was called Herlembald Cotta. He was a man of exceedingly distinguished birth, vigorous in arms, slender in body, and burning with a lion’s breast. His house, almost a royal house—with a magnificent court and delightful garden,” says Dacius, writing in the year 1080, “was opposite the church of Saint Victor at the Forty Martyrs.

“When the noble faction opposed Herlembald’s becoming captain, he nevertheless prevailed greatly against those nobles” [Col. 1457D].

36. Therefore, while the see was vacant, as I have said, Herebrald—thus writes the aforementioned Dacius, whose words, quoted at Puricellus, page 215, I continue—“arranged with the clergy that four men should be elected, and that the emperor,” Henry the Black, or rather the king—for he was first crowned emperor at the end of the following year, the seventh of his reign—“should confirm whichever of them he wished as archbishop.

“And four were elected. The first was Landulf Cotta, notary of the sacred palace and the natural brother of Hernebrald. The second was Anselm de Badagio, cardinal of the Milanese Church”—that is, an ordinary canon. “The third was Ariald, from the captains of Carimate,” plainly a different man from our saint. “The fourth was Atho, cardinal of the Milanese Church.

“On the other side, the noble faction elected Guido de Velate, the emperor’s secretary. After the matter had been reported to the emperor, he, excluding the others, invested Guido de Velate with the archbishopric of Milan by staff and ring. The pope, together with the cardinals, invested him with the archiepiscopal pallium” [Col. 1458C], perhaps brought to Rome in 1046 in the company of King Henry, who was about to receive the imperial crown on Christmas Day.

Alciatus supplied Dacius’s brevity in recounting Guido’s appointment in the fragment praised above and at the same time indicated the occasion of the disputes that followed with Saint Ariald and his companions. After saying that Henry “by the action and blandishments of the Milanese envoys who had arrived, induced them to approve his election,” he continues:

37. “The people took this exceedingly hard, as they rightly should, and could scarcely be brought not to repel the arriving prelate in disgrace. But after the leading priests had been corrupted by bribery, it was then very easily obtained that the common people themselves should acquiesce.

“They put forward religion and the claim that the authority of divine worship was not subject to secular matters . . . At that time the great famine still continued, together with its companion, the pestilence, which was not extinguished until the twenty-third year. Afflicted by these calamities, the Insubrians left everything to the priests.

“Recognizing Widon as the rightful prelate, they conferred the insignia of dignity upon him, increased his honors, and obeyed his commands. But Wido, naturally genial and generous, was not lacking to himself either. He willingly embraced priests, ministers, and all the initiated; he concealed their offenses and endured both the just and the unjust. By these actions he would have reconciled everyone to himself without difficulty, had Ariald not finally restrained this license.”

We have so far seen how that affair proceeded, as well as what has been preserved from the injuries of time in Alciatus’s words.

Concerning Herlembald we add that, once the archbishop was present and, according to custom, held the government of the city, and the clergy had to some extent reconciled the common people with the nobles, Herlembald, seeing that he was less necessary, went as a pilgrim to Jerusalem—perhaps so as not to become involved in the new disturbances which he foresaw would be stirred up on account of the measures being taken by Saint Ariald and his brother Landulf against incestuous and Simoniac men.

How he returned from there in the time of Alexander II and joined the same men, while the dispute over the judgments of Popes Stephen and Nicholas was at its height, may be learned from the younger Landulf, who continues the Life of Saint Ariald at Puricellus, page 140, as follows.

38. “At the same time Herlembald de Cotta, Landulf’s brother, had returned from Jerusalem, having become a knight. He was indeed a man of great nobility, always prudent in counsel and magnanimous. Ariald and Landulf considered him suitable for defending them against the clerics who were taking up arms.

“Therefore, when they had come to visit and encourage him, they began with these words:

“‘O Herlembald, venerable in every respect, we praise God together for your return and offer him immense thanks. For God in his kindness has arranged that you should return to us, shaken by many storms on sea and land.

“‘You were previously a soldier of the world’s vices; it is fitting that you should become a most valiant soldier of God and the Catholic Church. May your right hand accomplish what we have not been able to accomplish.

“‘Be for us like Mattathias and his sons, who died for the temple of God and the freedom of the people and, possessing eternal life in Christ, were happily crowned.

“‘Let us free the Church of God, besieged for many years and polluted by married priests—you by the law of the sword, and we by the law of God. You visited his tomb; free, therefore, his Church.’

“When he heard these things, Herlembald hesitated for a while, uncertain whether to involve himself in the clerics’ actions. At last, urged by Landulf, he set out for Rome with Ariald, promising that he would undertake the matter if Pope Alexander, who was from Badagio, confirmed it.

“For at that time, after the death of Pope Nicholas, Anselm, a citizen of Milan from Badagio and bishop of Lucca, was elected pope by all the cardinals and called Alexander II” [Col. 1460A].

39. “While he was an ordinary canon of the Milanese Church, he had been praiseworthy in learning and morals and powerful in speech; his eloquence and knowledge were greatly pleasing to the citizens. He then began in his sermons to condemn the life of the clerics and did not agree with the words of Archbishop Guido, who urged him not to make the clerics’ scandals public.

“Therefore the archbishop, concealing what he intended to do, went with Anselm to the emperor. On the archbishop’s advice, the emperor expelled Anselm from the city with considerable care, for he gave him the bishopric of Lucca.

“Thus Guido, thinking himself secure because of Anselm’s absence, was even more mistaken. For Anselm summoned Landulf, an ordinary levite, and familiarly urged him to denounce the clerics’ vices in his sermons. He did the same privately with Ariald, showing them the methods he had employed before he became bishop.

“And so this denunciation of lustful and Simoniac clerics, continued for a long time by Ariald and Landulf, took its beginning from the aforementioned Anselm de Badagio. Trusting, therefore, in this familiarity, Ariald went with Herlembald to Pope Alexander.”

40. “When the arrival of the two men was announced to Pope Alexander, he ordered them to be summoned to him in his bedchamber. There, throwing himself upon their necks, he rejoiced greatly, showing Ariald the old familiarity which friends who rise to high positions often neglect.

“But Ariald, displaying mutual affection while maintaining the proper reverence, began to speak as follows:

“‘Most holy father, I offer immense thanks to the Creator of all things, who in his mercy has chosen to raise and exalt you to so great a height of honor. Now my spirit, worn down by many anxieties, recognizes what your affection once promised me. Therefore, reverently I beseech Your Holiness, setting everything else aside, to give me this soldier, Herlembald, proven in war and most vigorous in counsel, established in every virtue and fortified by God’s favor and yours, as my defender. May he receive a standard from you, so that, serving as a soldier more securely, he may defend us and humble those who were formerly rebellious against you.’

“When he heard this, Alexander ordered Cardinal Hildebrand, formerly his colleague in the legation, to be summoned. With the other cardinals consenting and Hildebrand approving, Alexander gave Herlembald in a public consistory the holy standard which he called the Standard of Saint Peter and made him standard-bearer of the universal Roman Church.

“When these matters had been successfully completed, Ariald returned to Milan with Herlembald. Made secure by such a defender, he eradicated the clerics’ vices more fiercely” [Col. 1460D].

41. “When Herlembald saw the clergy taking up arms, he summoned both sides to a daytime debate, on the condition that whichever side was refuted by reason would submit to the other. The opinions of the doctors were brought forward, especially those of Ambrose, the protector of our most illustrious city. There, through Guibert the archdeacon, Antonius Bissus, and Andreas Decumanus, many arguments were advanced against Ariald and Landulf; they refuted the words of those three by the authority of the Apostle Paul and the saints” [Col. 1461A].

Thus far the younger Landulf.

Puricellus, however, in Book IV, chapter 92, examines at length the passage of Saint Ambrose taken from the final chapter of Book I, *On Duties*. He teaches that the defenders of clerical marriage had corrupted that passage and understood the corrupted text even more badly. According to him, the question then being debated among the Fathers concerned only whether a man who had been married twice before baptism should, after baptism, be considered bound by that fact and therefore excluded from the sacred orders. Saint Jerome thought that he should not be excluded, whereas Ambrose, Innocent, and Augustine held the contrary.

42. When Ambrose therefore says that clerics are permitted “only one union, not a repeated one” [Col. 1461B], he immediately explains in what sense he says this:

“Many people are surprised that even a second marriage contracted before baptism should create obstacles to the election to office and the privilege of ordination, since even sins ordinarily do not hinder a man if they have been forgiven through the sacrament of washing. But we must understand that in baptism guilt can be forgiven, whereas the law cannot be abolished”—namely, the law that permits only the husband of one wife to be ordained.

Puricellus shows from other passages of Ambrose that the chastity promised upon receiving the subdiaconate excludes even husbands of one wife from marital relations, much less permits them to take a wife, however virgin she may be.

He first explains that Dacius was the one who committed to writing a story thereafter commonly adopted by others concerning Ambrose, as though Ambrose, sent by Pope Damasus to Constantinople, had said that “the law permits priests to marry a virgin wife once, but not to repeat the marriage.” This is false: no Western bishop attended any council of Constantinople during the time of Damasus; nor is anything similar recorded among the Greeks, however much they may marry; nor, finally, is such a law found anywhere. Only the law permitting monogamous men to be ordained is found, together with the obligation to preserve chastity after ordination.

Adhering to this law, Alexander II had written to the Milanese after the Roman council of 1063 and had commanded:

“Let no one hear the Mass of a priest whom he knows to have a concubine or a woman living with him.” Moreover, “whatever priest or deacon, after the decree of Pope Leo or Nicholas, has openly taken a concubine, or has not abandoned a woman whom he has taken, shall not sing Mass or read the Gospel or the Epistle at Mass; he shall not remain in the presbytery for the divine offices, nor receive a portion from the Church” [Col. 1461D].

43. These matters concerning Herlembald and Alexander had to be supplied here. Andreas discusses Herlembald’s journey to Rome with Arialdus while recounting the death of Landulf, Herlembald’s brother, although that death occurred later than the journey—namely, in the year 1065. [Col. 1462A] Knowing this, the younger historiographer Landulf, after relating what we have prefaced concerning Herlembald, says: “When these things had been done, and the clergy had taken up arms, Landulf, the brother of Herlembald, died.”

Arnulf, the detractor of both men, speaks of this death in Puricellus, p. 223, as follows: “When it pleased the Most High, who searches the reins and hearts, he who had long meditated upon another’s weariness suddenly suffered his own unexpected illness; and, since he languished for two years from a disease of the lungs, he was deprived of the use of his tongue, so that in the very faculty by which he had afflicted many, he also failed.”

Thus speaks that malicious investigator of divine judgments. If something must be said about them by conjecture, it would be more plausible to say that this death was the punishment for delaying his entry into monastic life, to which Landulf had bound himself before God, as Saint Peter Damian had repeatedly urged him to do in book V, letter 16. [Col. 1462B]

44. Puricellus indeed attempts to excuse him by citing the example of his brother Herlembald, who had been drawn away from the monastic life for the sake of the greater public good; but the circumstances of the two men were plainly different. Herlembald had a plan or intention, not a vow, and the Church needed the assistance of an armed soldier, which a monk could not have provided.

The preacher Landulf, however, could have remained and become a monk. Locatellus writes in the history of his order, book I, chapter 68, that monks of this kind were also summoned from Vallombrosa to aid the Church of Milan. Peter wrote an exhortation to them, which is letter 14 in book V, addressed “to the holy brothers Rodulfus, [Col. 1462C] Vitalis, and Arialdus, and to Herlembaldus and the others who fight with unconquerable faith for the camps of Christ.” The order seems to have been preserved so that the monks are named first, then the cleric Arialdus, and afterward the layman Herlembaldus. Landulf, however, is not mentioned, either because he was already dead or at least useless because of the illness about which I would not wish to doubt Puricellus, since there is no obstacle to postponing that death until the year 1064 or even 1065.

Before Alexander wrote this letter, therefore, he had replied to the clerics Landulf and Arialdus in the words found in Ivo’s Decree, p. 12, c. 24: “We can extend the hand of mercy to those who have fallen into some crime of perjury; but we must not, as an example leading to future destruction, grant permission.” I believe that this refers to clerics who, after having sworn to amend their lives, were restored to their benefice and afterward relapsed; they were not to be restored to it again, although they were to receive sacramental absolution if they offered repentance.

With these matters inserted, I return, in order to continue the thread of the history, to Andreas’s narrative, which proceeds as follows.

45. “At the same time”—that is, when Arialdus and Herlembaldus were promoting the Catholic cause at Milan through their joint efforts—“after the death of Landulf,” presumably in the year 1064 or 1065, “the abbot of the monastery of Saint Celsus [Note: [Col. 1461D] Puricellus discusses this abbey of Saint Celsus at length in Dissertation Nazar., chapter 86 and following chapters. It was founded outside the city, between the Roman and Ticinese Gates, by Landulf II, in an uncertain year. He cites a monument concerning a decorated altar from the year 975, and in chapter 90 treats the event narrated here; but he adds nothing that would clarify this passage.] died. A certain cleric named Lanfrancus immediately seized his place, after rejecting the not inconsiderable stipend which he had annually received from the episcopal household for that service.” [Col. 1463A]

Against this wicked presumption the man of God Arialdus, together with Herlembaldus, his noble and faithful companion, resisted steadfastly for a very long time, until they made him an exile—not only from the administration of the abbey which he had improperly purchased, but almost from the boundaries of that parish. [Note: [Col. 1463D] Landulf adds that Arialdus “likewise expelled another man from the monastery of Saint Vincent in the same manner.” Jo. Antonius Castilioneus wrote an entire work entitled Florilegium of Memorable Antiquities of the Basilica of Saint Vincent, divided into ten fascicles; afterward he prefixed to it the more extensive title Antiquities of Milan Collected from the City’s Parishes. Yet nowhere did he undertake to compile a list of the abbots. Puricellus also discusses the matter in his Ambrosian Monuments, p. 389, and reports that the man later passed over to the nuns.]
