46. “At that same time, when the abbot of the monastery of Saint Ambrose had died, another cleric, a chancellor named Ariprandus [Note: [Col. 1463D] After showing on p. 431 that Landulf was still abbot there in 1053, the same author discusses this Ariprandus on p. 535. Finally, he judges him to have been the man who, as ‘Ariprandus, an unworthy deacon,’ signed in fourth place under Archbishop Wido, who detested the Simoniacal and concubinage heresies, in the year 1059; he also believes that Ariprandus was still abbot in 1064.], abandoned the clerical birrus, which he had until then worn disgracefully [Note: [Col. 1463D] The same author believes that “the clerical birrus was a shorter outer garment, by which only the arms and shoulders were covered.”], and wickedly usurped for himself the abbatial title of that monastery.

“Because he possessed such rank, and because of the natural pride of his haughty blood, he could not be expelled by force. The man of God Arialdus said: ‘If we cannot accomplish against this wicked man what we ought, let us at least do what we can.’ Thus, taking the brothers, he went to him. When he had come into his presence, he said: ‘What is this? Yesterday a cleric, today an abbot! You have made a great and rapid leap. Why were you not afraid to usurp this office against the holy canons and against the oath which you recently swore in the Roman Church?’

“He replied: ‘This has happened, as you see, and I can no longer abandon it.’

“The man of God said to him: ‘If you wish, you can; and, on behalf of God and the holy Roman Church, I earnestly beg you to abandon what you have taken against God’s will and seized to the peril of your soul.’

“But the other replied: ‘And I, under the same oath by which you adjured me, adjure you now to strip off your garments and have yourself beaten here before me with brooms.’ [Col. 1463C] [Note: [Col. 1464C] See the same author’s detailed discussion of this type of penance on p. 455. From Peter Damian he teaches that “brooms” means not only an instrument for administering blows, but also the blows themselves administered with brooms. It is said there that “the chanting of ten psalms permits a thousand broom-blows.”]

“Arialdus immediately ran, obtained rods, stripped off his garments, and had one of his own men beat him severely with them there before everyone. Seeing this, the false abbot, not knowing what more to say, rose from the place with his head bowed and, hardened like Pharaoh, withdrew elsewhere.”

## CHAPTER V. The virtues of Arialdus; his careful practice of fasting and psalmody

47. As many can testify as knew him intimately, his sole constant purpose and endeavor was to fulfill in practice whatever he read in the divine books. He was so generous that those who lived diligently with him often said of him: “If he possessed an ark full of gold, and if there were no lack of petitioners and needy people, he would undoubtedly spend it all in a single day.”

Whenever he was walking somewhere and poor people encountered him and begged him to give them something, he immediately borrowed from those following him the money which he never kept for himself, and thus mercifully relieved their need.

He loved purity of heart and body so greatly that, against the diabolical illusions by which people are accustomed to be deceived during the night, he remained awake and watchful for nearly every midnight and prolonged many nights until cockcrow, partly in prayer, partly in reading, and partly in council with the other faithful for the destruction of the Simoniacal heresy. [Col. 1464B]

48. He strongly condemned the gluttonous custom that compels carnal people, both clerics and laymen, on Holy Saturday to anticipate until the ninth hour the solemn celebrations of Mass and baptism which ought to be performed during that same holy night.

But since he could not prevail against others in this matter, he made provision for himself. While the entire city was dining, he awaited the holy night fasting with some of the brothers. With them he went out to a certain place called the Grove, isolated from the city by a mile. There still stands a church there, built and dedicated by Saint Ambrose. [Col. 1464C] [Note: [Col. 1464D] Saint Augustine, book VIII of The City of God: “Outside the camp of Milan lies a monastery full of good brothers, under Ambrose the nourisher.” We have stated, in the Life of Saint Placidus on 5 June, that it does not seem at all plausible to us that those three men were among them—men from whom the Ambrosian order there, and subsequently the order of the Apostolines, took their origin under the rule of Saint Augustine—although Morigia and Maurolycus write this: the former in his History of Religious Origins, the latter in his Ocean. Morigia locates it “in the suburb of the Comasine Gate.” Petrarch says in his book On the Solitary Life: “Although the forest has now been cut down, Ambrose’s grove nevertheless remains.”]

There, as is reported, the same Ambrose, fleeing the tumult of the people, was accustomed to spend his time and dictate books. In this church the man of God spent that holy night, suitably offering with the brothers the praises owed to almighty God.

He never wished to drink alone, never to eat without poor clerics, and never to cross the outer threshold without companions.

49. During days of fasting he did not celebrate the solemn offices of the saints at all. Conversely, on feast days he neither knelt nor fasted, nor did he allow anyone staying with him to fast.

He vehemently abhorred the three-day fast which has recently become customary, contrary to the statements of the ancient saints, during the holy days of Easter. [Note: [Col. 1465D] That is, the days called “the lesser Litanies,” or “Rogation Days,” on which people fast for three days before the Ascension of the Lord. This practice is not, as some think, the custom of the universal Church, since it is not observed at Rome or throughout Italy, but of all the churches beyond the Alps. It began with the Gauls and was instituted by Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, around the year 470. Henschenius, under 11 May, showed how highly Saints Sidonius Apollinaris, Gregory of Tours, Avitus, and Ado, bishops of Vienne, praised his zeal in this matter. Blessed Alcuin and many others may be added; they are cited by Du Cange in his Glossary.] He so greatly detested it that he would gladly have said that he wished to submit himself to death, if only he could persuade the people to change the time to one that was lawful and appropriate. [Note: [Col. 1466D] Perhaps this was done under Archbishop Guido, who was accustomed to this kind of observance before the emperor and thereby sought to win a reputation for religious devotion among the people.]

Therefore, on one of those days, when the entire Church had already assembled in order to proceed to the Litanies according to its accustomed practice, he climbed to the place from which he used to teach and began to address them in these words:

“Beloved,” he said, “according to the Apostle’s saying, our service to the Lord God must be reasonable (Rom. 12:1). It is suitably performed when our conduct is found to agree with the sayings of the saints.

“Know that I am completely unaware by whose inspiration this fast which you are now undertaking is being carried out. If it is from God, I am greatly astonished, since in the sayings of those saints through whom, without doubt, God spoke, I find that fasting on these days of Easter is forbidden.”

50. “There is another matter which makes me hesitate greatly about this. I see you afflicting yourselves so severely on these days—putting on woolen garments, walking barefoot, and fasting on bread and water alone—yet when you were rightly commanded to do these things, I see that you do them in no way.

“Know that, just as not one of the days of Lent, which signify this present life, ought to be interrupted in its fasting, so assuredly not one of these fifty days, which signify the future life, is to be observed as a fast, except the Saturday before Pentecost. And even that day is to be fasted not for the sake of affliction, as are the other fasts of the rest of the year, but in expectation of the new brothers who are reborn at the ninth hour; we ought to await their renewal while fasting.

“Nevertheless, to demonstrate that what I say is supported by full authority, the holy Synod of Nicaea—which must be received in the same way as the holy Gospels—decreed that during these days people should neither kneel nor observe fasts.

“It was sufficiently demonstrated to a certain venerable Father named Apollonius, who presided over approximately five hundred monks, that these were days on which fasting was not to be observed. After the rigors of Lent had passed, he prayed with the brothers that almighty God might deign to show them whether he wished them to fast during these days as usual. Immediately the Lord sent them, through unknown men, such an abundance of gifts of every kind suitable for eating that they could have sufficed them plentifully throughout all these days of Easter.

“And so that they might be entirely free from further doubt, those same gifts were measured out in such a way that they did not run out until the days of Pentecost had been completed; and when those days were completed, all the gifts were likewise entirely consumed. Blessed Benedict, seeing this, although he had prescribed fasting for the monks at every other time, in no way ordered them to fast during these days.” [Col. 1465D–1466A]

51. We must also recall what our patron, Saint Ambrose, said about these matters. He says (Sermon 2 on Pentecost):

“How should we observe this holy day of Pentecost, and why is there a continuous and uninterrupted festival throughout the number of these fifty days, so that during this entire period we neither prescribe fasts to be observed nor bend our knees in supplication to God, but, as we are accustomed to do on the Lord’s Day, celebrate the Lord’s Resurrection standing and at leisure?

“For the entire course of the fifty days is celebrated after the pattern of the Lord’s Day, and all these days are counted as though they were Lord’s Days. The Lord arranged it thus: just as we mourned his Passion through the fasts of Lent, so we should rejoice in his Resurrection during the festivity of Pentecost.

“Therefore we do not fast during Pentecost, because during these days the Lord remains with us. We do not fast, I say, when the Lord is present, because he himself said: ‘Can the children of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?’ (Mark 2:19).”

All this blessed Ambrose said. How his words are to be understood is known not only by us, whose patron he is, but almost by the whole world. Nevertheless, for the present let it suffice for your charity that we have merely recalled these things. In the future, if we live, with Christ’s help we shall say more about this matter. [Col. 1466C]

52. After this he dismissed the people and went to the body of Saint Ambrose in order to pray. Some people immediately ran to the greater church, where the whole city had already assembled, and reported all these things.

When they heard this, the sons of priests and many other detestable men seized the opportunity for which they had long been waiting. They began to rage and say: “Now it is plainly evident that this man, who condemns so holy a work, is a heretic and an enemy of God.”

Having said this, they raised their voices and clubs together. With the whole people stirred up, they rushed with great violence into the church of the holy man, which was called the Canonical Church. They plundered whatever they found and began to destroy the house. They did not kill the servant of God only because they did not find him. [Col. 1466D]

When the noble Herlembaldus and the other faithful heard this, they took up arms and rushed against the audacious and reckless crowd. They immediately routed them all as though they were the vilest beasts. Indeed, coming to the greater church with great strength and authority, they forcibly took from the wicked whatever they had stolen from the house of the Lord, and nearly everything was restored to the Church of God: Christ working through the zeal of the devout to restore what Satan, through the fury of the wicked, had caused to be stolen from it.

53. Just as Arialdus strove every day to raise up and exalt the causes of Christ, so Christ continually advanced Arialdus from strength to strength. I do not remember ever having seen anyone else so powerful in prayer. If I describe his qualities, I hope that it will please those who love God and benefit them.

I heard the names of so many saints proceeding from his mouth—not merely once a day, but two or three times—that I have never seen so many names written in a book, nor heard anyone else recite so many. Although he was so well instructed in sacred and liberal learning that scarcely could his equal be found anywhere, he placed no more confidence in his own knowledge than if he did not know a single letter.

When he was about to dispute publicly with someone concerning the faith, before the actual contest took place he would make it his concern, either personally or through brothers whom he sent, to search everywhere for the bodies of the saints and earnestly implore their patronage, in which he placed all his hope. Every day, surrounded by a brotherly host, he went around the bodies of the saints and poured out before them a groaning prayer to God.

54. When we left the house, we walked along individually and privately in prayer until we had passed through the tumult of the people. Once it had been crossed, we sang psalms antiphonally. He began them, and we continued in this way until we were near the doors of the church to which we were going.

There, after setting aside the psalmody and committing its final portion to memory, he took up whatever chants or hymns he knew to belong to the praise of that saint. He recited them in a moderate and gentle voice, so that we could hear what he was saying and say it together with him; and with this holy song we came before the sacred altar.

After venerating it, if the day was neither a solemn feast nor Easter, he placed both knees on the ground, stretched out his hands, fixed his eyes on heaven, and, standing before the altar in the form of a cross, entreated God with groans and tears for the supreme Roman pontiff, for peace, for the salvation of the universal Church, for the conversion of its adversaries, and for many other benefits of this kind. [Col. 1467D]

We, kneeling after him, listened to what he said and responded. Finally, he prayed silently for a little while and allowed each of us to do the same. Then he rose, reverently venerated the altar, and, already returning with us, said:

“Give us the angel of peace and the gifts of grace, Lord our God.” [Note: [Col. 1467D] I have not yet been able to find this prayer in an old Milanese missal or breviary. I would gladly receive it in full and learn where it was taken from.]

Then, at the exit from the church, he began to recite psalms—the same ones which he had left unfinished at the entrance. Whenever we came to another church, we did there what we had done in the previous one. It should be noted that, at the point where he ended the Psalter, he immediately began the same work again—even if only three psalms remained [Note: [Col. 1467D] That is, even if only the final three psalms remained.] and he was not permitted at that moment to recite the opening according to the order [or: “from the beginning according to the order”?]. For he always maintained that a cleric ought to be present throughout the psalmody.

## CHAPTER VI. The archbishop attacks Arialdus and the faithful with his men under arms, and is defeated

55. After he had spent nine years in such a great and admirable discipline, the tenth year arrived, in which he attained the long-desired goal. He ardently desired to die for Christ. Whenever he saw someone who loved God and himself purely, he would earnestly ask him in prayer, saying: “I beg you, for Christ’s sake, to pour out a prayer for me before him, so that I may deserve to bear witness with my own blood to the word which I preach.” This opportunity was granted to him in order that he might attain that end.

All the clergy, both of the greater and of the lesser order, had sworn to him, as had Guido himself, who was called the bishop, that they would condemn with him the Simoniacal and Neophytan heresies and thereafter persevere in the Catholic faith.

But whenever the administration of the churches appeared to Guido without rectors, he immediately consigned what he had sworn to oblivion and, like a dog returning to its vomit, went back to his former guilt. Seeing this, the man of God Arialdus sent a letter through Herlembaldus to the apostolic authority, asking him to determine what ought to be done with Guido, the adulterous, Simoniacal, and perjured man.

56. At that time two clerics from Monza [Note: [Col. 1468D] In antiquity “Modoetia”; at that time it was also called “Modica,” and now “Monza.” It lies ten miles north of the city.] came to the servant of Christ. They promised that they wished to abandon the works and fellowship of the devil and thereafter firmly to uphold and preach the works and faith of Christ. One of them had been so audacious and perverse that he was virtually the leader of the opposing party.

The man of God said to them: “There are so many who say this deceitfully that scarcely anyone now remains whose words can be believed sincerely. But if you want me to believe your words, go and make me certain through your deeds.”

They returned to their homes and immediately put away marriage. They began openly and steadfastly to profess that the words of Blessed Arialdus were full of truth, whereas they had previously professed them to be entirely false.

When Guido heard this, he immediately sent savage officers there and ordered them to be seized and taken to the Alps, to the fortress called Lecco. [Note: [Col. 1468D] “Leucum” appears to be Lecco, at the eastern end of Lake Como, thirty-nine miles from Milan.] [Col. 1468D]

There they were thrown into such a dreadful prison—as they later confessed to us—that they had never heard of saints suffering anything more severe at the hands of pagans.

When the servant of Christ heard this, he summoned the entire multitude of the city and said: “I want you, beloved, to know that a Christian ought to bear the sword for no cause except the defense of the faith. If this is so, you who are Christians and bear arms, consider what you ought now to do.

“For here are two clerics who, as long as they persisted in unbelief and followed the works of the devil, were honorably treated by the man who is called the bishop of Milan. But when they resolved to despise that same unbelief and diabolical wickedness and to follow Christ, then they were seized and then thrust into a dreadful prison.”

57. When the Christian citizens heard this, they were stunned. With a great outcry they began to condemn such faithlessness, run to arms, and go out against Guido to avenge so great a crime.

The servant of Christ, fearing that in the absence of Herlembaldus the people might be corrupted by reward or fear to the detriment of the faith, went ahead of them, carrying in his hand the banner of the holy cross.

Guido, relying on the hope inspired by a very large number of cavalry, came out to fight in the fields of Monza, about ten miles from the city. As both sides shouted, such fear immediately seized the faithless army that it had no hope of fleeing or fighting. They at once gave hostages and promised that they would promptly return the captured clerics.

Thus they returned on the same day, rejoicing and praising God.

On the third day after this, a voice sounded at the church of the man of God, saying: “Look, the inexperienced martyrs of Christ are now coming—the clerics who had been captured.”

The servant of Christ immediately went out with many of the faithful to meet them. He kissed them and received them with great joy. In a loud voice he began to sing “Te Deum laudamus” with the brothers, and thus led them into the church. [Col. 1469C]

They then consterna—[lacuna; the surviving word is incomplete] [Note: [Col. 1469D] Puricellus notes that two pages were missing from his manuscript. Until they could be restored from elsewhere, he ordered that the gap be filled from the Life written by the younger Landulf; this I now do.]

58. After Herlembaldus returned from Rome and brought letters of excommunication for the archbishop, the aforementioned archbishop suddenly sent messengers throughout the city on the Saturday before Pentecost, announcing to all the citizens that if they wished to hear something unheard-of, they should come to the greater church at first light on Pentecost. [Note: [Col. 1469D] Easter in the year 1066, with the Sunday letter A, was celebrated on 16 April, and therefore Pentecost fell on 4 June.]

He did this so that the people would rage against the saints of God, Arialdus and Herlembaldus.

In the morning the people gathered. Herlembaldus went above the chancel screen, so that he could be seen by everyone. Guido then began, holding the letter of excommunication in his hand, to complain to the people about Arialdus and Herlembaldus, saying:

“A destructive disturbance has been spread by these men, so that I see the ruin of all of us contained in these writings. This city, out of reverence for Blessed Ambrose, has never obeyed the Roman Church. Therefore let these sowers of words, who work every day to deprive this city of its ancient and proper liberty, be taken from the land of the living.”

At this the people began to shout: “Let them be killed quickly! Let them be killed!”

Having said this, Guido began to descend with a large crowd of clerics in order to crush the saints of God. But when the excessive density of the crowd prevented access to them, Guido began to shout:

“Let everyone who loves the honor of Saint Ambrose leave the church, so that our adversaries may be recognized more clearly and quickly crushed and destroyed.”

Immediately the church was emptied, so that of seven thousand men only twelve remained to support the servants of God.

Arialdus and Herlembaldus, standing above the chancel screen, knelt and entreated the Lord. The opposing party rushed upon them with a great shout: the laymen against Herlembaldus, and the clerics against Arialdus. They struck him and threw him down, and, having struck him, believed him dead.

Before Herlembaldus a military staff was held, on which he was accustomed to lean. With it he miraculously knocked down those who approached him, so that no one dared come nearer.

59. Rumor therefore began to fly through the city, announcing the death of Arialdus. His followers, stirred by anger, took up arms. They came not to the church, where the tumult was taking place, but entered the episcopal hall. They destroyed whatever they found and, through the entrance of the hall, entered the church [lacuna] …-ed and bloodstained (the surviving text reads “-tos cruentosque”).

They began to urge Herlembaldus to descend and overthrow the adversaries of Christ with them. He in no way consented: he neither descended nor lowered his hands.

They themselves immediately rushed upon the adversaries, and just as smoke vanishes before a powerful wind, so the entire faithless crowd immediately disappeared before them. They found Guido before the doors, on horseback. They rightly beat him and stripped him, and he scarcely escaped their hands, having been dragged rather than carried into a certain upper room. At that moment so many appeared to be fighting for the truth that it seemed there were no opponents left for them in the city.

Entering the church with a great victory, they made Herlembaldus come down. Indeed, they were made exceedingly joyful because they found Blessed Arialdus alive, whom they had believed dead.

Taking him to the courtyard of the church called Rozzoni, [Note: [Col. 1470D] “Which is now called the Church of the Holy Sepulchre,” says the younger Landulf, and therefore it must have been after the year 1100, when the structure was restored and rededicated. See the Ambrosian Monuments, pp. 477 and following, including the account of how it first received its name in the year 1036 from “Benedict, also called Rozo,” its first founder, under the title “Holy Trinity,” according to the document reproduced there.] they arrived there. Immediately such a multitude of armed men gathered that they could not only overthrow the bodies of their enemies but also freely demolish all their buildings. [Col. 1470D]

As they eagerly panted to carry this out, Herlembaldus, now holding the raised banner in his hand, said: “We must search for Lord Arialdus and determine whose house we ought first to destroy.”

When the martyr of Christ heard this, he ordered himself to be carried to a place where he could be heard by everyone. At his gesture a great silence was made. [Col. 1471A]

60. “Dearest brothers,” he said, “if all our limbs were changed into tongues, they would in no way be able to praise the mighty deeds of God which have been shown to you from heaven today.

“For today, as you know, there was an hour when not one of you was able to speak even a single word on behalf of the truth; now, however, there is no one who, as you see, dares even to mutter against you. Who has accomplished this, except Christ?

“If, then, the Lord has today acknowledged his servants in order to protect them, it is fitting that the servants should recognize the Lord as worthy of veneration. For if the enemies of God and of us had known the solemnity of this day, they would never have attempted what they did.

“We must both acknowledge the solemnity of God by venerating it and hear his commands by obeying them. For he says: ‘Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you’ (Luke 6:27).

“Therefore, through him, I beg you now to lay down your arms, come with me to the sacred body of Blessed Ambrose, and there give due thanks together to God. Let us allow our rivals to pass this day in joy, and let us also entreat God humbly for them.

“For those by whom such things are done acquire a lofty dignity, since, as Christ bears witness, from the sons of men they are made sons of God (John 12).”

When that multitude heard this, the wiser among them, looking upon Blessed Arialdus, covered in blood and half-dead, and hearing him ask for peace and life for his enemies, stood amazed in wonder. Others, however, more fervent in spirit, were in no way willing to accept these words.

Nevertheless, although they wished different things, all the martyr’s words were immediately fulfilled. [Col. 1471C]

## CHAPTER VII. The cruel murder of Saint Arialdus after he was betrayed by a priest who had hosted him

61. On the following night the perverse party again assembled with Guido and said:

“Let these reverses in no way cast us down. The popular crowd changes quickly and easily inclines to different sides. We are indeed certain that we cannot extinguish Arialdus in the city by any means. Let our ingenuity therefore discover another plan from which he will be entirely unable to escape.

“Let prudent men from our party be stationed in different parts of the city, possessing in abundance the money contributed to them by us; let them distribute it secretly among the people at night. During the day, setting aside every other business, let us meet continually and pursue this course until our numbers have increased so greatly that we can drive him violently from the city. Once that has been done, let him be captured by ambushes placed everywhere, and, once captured, let him immediately be killed. If we do not accomplish all this, we shall never have peace.”

What more need be said? For fifteen days, twelve—[the text is uncertain]—two powerful assemblies of the people were held continually in the city: one of the faithful at the church of Rozzoni, the other in the episcopal court.

The mad party grew excessively because of the money given to it at night. As it grew wickedly, the faithful gradually became weary and began to fall away.

Seeing this, the perverse crowd, elated, began with enormous shouts to prepare an assault upon Blessed Arialdus, so that it might kill him there and utterly desolate his place.

The servant of Christ was so strong and steadfast amid adversity that none of the brothers dared flee from there on the day of tribulation or carry anything away. When they heard the roar of the wicked approaching, they prostrated themselves before the altar and awaited death there.

62. On one of those days, when the doors had already been closed and the brothers were lying before the altar awaiting death, one of them secretly opened a door, carried away an object he valued greatly, entrusted it to the house of a certain civic friend, and immediately returned.

When the man of God heard this, he summoned the brother and addressed him as follows:

“Arnulfus, is this church not dedicated in honor and under the name of the one to whom we continually say, ‘We flee beneath your protection, Mother of God’? And have you not read: ‘Cursed is the man who places his hope in man’ (Jer. 17:5)? Why, then, have you dared to act against these words?”

The man fell silent in fear. To prevent both him and the others from presuming to do such things thereafter, this offense was immediately corrected with severe blows.

During those days such grave confusion and violent disturbance prevailed there that, at the appointed hour, many of the faithful despaired of taking food, expecting death to come upon them at any moment.

Yet although the wicked raged and went mad, they in no way dared to do what they threatened, because as often as they attempted to rise against the servant of Christ, sorrow turned back upon their own heads.

63. Therefore they issue an unjust and public decree that, for as long as Arialdus remained in the city, any cleric who publicly celebrated the sacred rite or sounded the bells, and any layman who permitted these things to be done in his church, should be deprived not only of his property but also of his life. These orders began to be observed not only elsewhere but also in the church where Arialdus himself was staying, under compulsion and out of extreme fear of the soldier to whom the church itself belonged. [Col. 1472D]

Considering this more grievous than everything that had hitherto happened to him, he said: “Far be it that those who, through fear of death, observe the impious institutions of heretics should any longer be counted as my companions and brothers!” Accordingly, without the other brothers’ knowledge, taking with him only one companion named Syrus, he secretly left the city by night and hid with him for two days at Saint Victor’s, beside the elm. [Note: [Col. 1471D] Henschenius said in his notes on Saint Victor’s Acts, under 8 May, that “Saint Victor” was beheaded at that place; it is a suburban locality, and a church still stands there.]

Finally, Herlembald, with many faithful soldiers, received them both and proceeded with them to Pavia. [Note: [Col. 1472D] “Pavia,” situated fifteen miles from Milan on the river Ticino, is absent from the account. The river, which gave the ancient city its name, flows into the Po a few miles below the city.] Sending some of the soldiers back but retaining others with him, they began to descend the Po by boat, [Col. 1473A] intending to proceed to Rome and, until another time, withdraw from such great wrath. [Note: [Col. 1473D] That is, into Emilia, so that they might take a safe route through the Papal States.]

On this voyage they were captured near a certain town. [Note: [Col. 1473D] Landulfus says “near a certain town of Piacenza.” For those coming from Pavia, after sixteen miles the first place encountered is “Parpanesius,” and not far beyond it, farther along the bank, is “the castle of Saint John,” to which the saint may have been taken.] From among his companions, who were grieving beyond words, Blessed Arialdus alone was violently seized and taken to a fortress. There, while he maintained his customary steadfastness in prayer and speech, the soldier who had captured him expressed his amazement and said:

“The archbishop of Milan promised me a great reward if I captured you and handed you over to him. He had informed me that you were a heretic; but, as I can see, that is entirely false.”

Thereupon he began to treat Arialdus and all his household with reverence, and hastened to return him to his sorrowful companions, who had already gone back to Pavia.

64. After this, knowing that the surrounding places were everywhere blockaded, they returned to a certain castle belonging to the faithful Herlembald. [Note: [Col. 1473D] Landulfus calls it “Legnano,” on the river Olona, fourteen miles from Milan; it was twenty miles from Cantù and only eleven from Lake Maggiore. [Col. 1474D]]

Then some brothers from Cantù sent word to him, saying: “We cannot live here because of the excessive persecution. If it pleases you, command us to come to you.” He replied: “Let anyone who is prepared to die with me for Christ hasten to come to me; whoever is not yet prepared should flee elsewhere and withdraw.” These words were spoken in my presence.

Afterward he addressed Herlembald and the others who were with him as follows:

“We cannot leave this land, because we know that every exit is blocked by deadly ambushes. Nor can we remain here, since the deranged populace is already threatening to persecute me here; and I am very much afraid that the innocent inhabitants of this place may be devastated on this pretext. Therefore we must find another plan: namely, we must seek some man who will conceal me in his house for several days, so that meanwhile either the fury of the populace may subside and I may be able to remain alive in this land, or the guards stationed everywhere in ambush may cease searching for me because they become overconfident; and thus perhaps I may be able to leave here.”

They replied: “Everyone approves what you say, if someone can be found who will faithfully do this.”

He said: “There is a certain priest near this place, recently returned from Jerusalem, who until now has seemed sufficiently trustworthy to me. If it pleases you, let a message be sent through him and let the matter be carefully investigated.”

Thus, with everyone willing, the wicked priest was sent for this purpose. [Col. 1473D]

65. After this, Arialdus entered the church. Since it was the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, he remained tirelessly in prayer from morning until about the ninth hour. [Note: [Col. 1474D] That is, 23 June.]

And behold, the detestable priest arrived. He was discreetly and carefully questioned as to whether he had a suitable place where Arialdus could be concealed for at least three months. [Col. 1474A] He promised that he had such a secret place beside the church that he could keep anyone hidden there for many years.

At last, in the middle of the night, after they had exchanged kisses, we proceeded with him, amid many sighs and tears, as far as the gate. For we had earnestly begged him to take one of us—whichever he wished—in his service and bring him along. But he replied: “By no means, because if two people are together, they speak, and what they say is overheard.”

Who could express how many good things Herlembald then promised the priest if he treated Christ’s servant well, and how many evils he threatened if he treated him badly? Thus, grieving, we allowed the two of them to depart; but in the morning we returned to the city.

66. As soon as the wicked priest had shut Arialdus in his chamber, he was touched by a diabolical spirit and hastened to inform the evil Guido, saying: “What will you give me, and I will hand Arialdus over to you without a crowd, without Herlembald, indeed without any man at all?”

Overjoyed, Guido immediately promised him a great reward and protection if he fulfilled what he promised. The priest then asked that several soldiers be given to him. Taking them, he stationed them by night between two walls, away from the dwellings, and said:

“Only one of you is to lie in the middle of the road, covered by a shield. When I come, I shall strike him with my foot. Then all of you must rise quickly and seize both me and Arialdus. Take care not to rise upon anyone else by mistake; know that this will be your signal.”

After this he entered the man of God and addressed him:

“Lord Arialdus, we must leave here quickly and return to the castle from which I brought you, because everyone knows that you are here. If we remain here, we shall undoubtedly be captured tomorrow.”

The man of God replied: “You know the way. Go ahead, then, and I will follow you.”

Thus, with the traitor leading, they both came to the soldiers. After he gave the agreed signal by striking with his foot, they all rushed upon the man of God at once, seized him, bound him tightly, placed him, still bound, upon a beast, and hurried silently and rapidly toward Lake Maggiore. [Note: [Col. 1474D] The “Lake” is called “Major”; formerly it was “Verbanus,” formed by the Ticino as it flows out of the Alps. It begins near the town of Saint Aurigio and, after it begins to stagnate and spread out, extends for nearly fifty miles as far as Sesto, where it is again confined within its banks. Sesto lies twenty-six miles from Milan.]

67. This became known throughout all Milan before the third hour of the day on which the vigil of Saint Peter is celebrated. [Col. 1474D] As a result, mourning and lamentation prevailed everywhere among the devout, while the wicked exulted in their madness.

When I heard this, I immediately left the tumultuous and confused city and followed him. Hurrying rapidly throughout that day and the following night, I reached the aforementioned lake at sunrise on the next day. As I was walking along its shore, [Col. 1475A] and had come near Stationa, where the relatives of the evil Guido lived, I encountered a man named Martin, who said that he was a priest. [Note: [Col. 1475D] The name “Stationa” has fallen out of use and was perhaps known only to the learned of that time. Thus, in the Life under 31 January, Saints Julius and Julian are said to have come “into the diocese of Novara, to the island of Lake Verbano which lies below Stationa”; by this name we have observed Angera to be meant. Others call it “Angleria”; Landulfus likewise uses that name. It is a town on the eastern shore of the lake, five miles above Sesto.]

He asked me where I was from and where I was going. Wishing to inquire safely of him about the truth, I lied in part, saying: “I belong to that populace, and my companions have sent me here so that they may learn for certain whether what has recently been reported among us about Arialdus, the enemy of the clergy, is true—namely, that he has been killed—and whether they ought to rejoice fully over this.”

He replied: “Come back with me; when you have returned to the church that you left a little behind you, you will be very well informed about this.”

68–69. As I returned with him, he said to me:

“On the day before yesterday, a joyful report reached our place from outside, saying: ‘Arialdus, the adversary of the clergy, is being held bound in a boat on the shore of the lake.’ I immediately ran there with many others, and, seizing a very sharp stake and raising my hand, I wanted to drive it into his chest, but I was not permitted to do so. Five men were immediately sent by the archbishop’s niece, [Note: [Col. 1475D] Landulfus the Elder, in Puricellus, p. 11, calls her “Oliva” and admits that she was “endowed with knowledge of every kind of wicked art, especially enchantments.” He adds that Arialdus, “represented to her face in the fortress of Arona,” which lay opposite Angera, “was immediately taken, at her command and in memory of the pain suffered by her uncle, to a certain island near Lake Maggiore, with the greatest secrecy.”] men whose ferocity she did not doubt, to separate him from the soldiers and take him to the place she had ordered them to use. This was done without delay, and he was taken into such a desolate place that scarcely any human beings ever reached it, except sailors—and the sole inhabitants were wild beasts of the forest.

“What more need I prolong the account with words? There they left his corpse without ears, without nostrils, without eyes, without the right hand, and without the genital member. If you have ever seen anyone live without all these limbs, do not believe that this man is dead; for I could scarcely rest at all until those who had done these things to him made me so certain that my mind could no longer have any doubt. But return to your people, report this to them, and make them secure and joyful.”

After this we parted from each other. Until he entered the church, I pretended to return; afterward, unwilling to trust the words of a treacherous man, I went back to the road I had left.

When I entered the village mentioned above, I found beside the road a church dedicated to Saint Peter. At that moment a crowd of clerics and laypeople was coming out in procession. [Col. 1476A] There I found two women apart, discussing and weeping over what had happened. I approached them and asked what was the matter and why they were crying.

One of them said:

“Truly, you belong to that order which, when it ought to raise everyone to heaven by its good words and deeds, instead plunges everyone into hell by its evil examples. In this place, through the plotting of your perverse order, such a crime has been committed in these days that we anxiously await the Almighty God’s casting us all into the abyss because of it—and you ask, ‘Why are we crying?’”

Seeing the women’s faith, I told them that I was a disciple of the man for whom they were grieving, and asked whether the things I had heard from the man mentioned above were true. They immediately became very friendly toward me and testified that everything was true, except that they were still uncertain about his death.

They showed me the road leading toward the desolate place mentioned above and earnestly begged me to return and tell them what I learned, since they still had doubts. But, hindered by enormous obstacles of rock, I could not reach the place by land; nor could I find anyone willing to convey me there by boat. Therefore I was unable to learn anything further about him beyond what has been reported.

70. Moreover, after I later investigated carefully how and with what words he departed from this life, I believe that it will be pleasing to those who love God if I briefly relate it.

From the place where he was captured, he sang psalms. At Stationa, as has been said, he was separated from the soldiers and handed over to five savage servants. As they were leading him to his death, they addressed him:

“Arialdus, why do you not reconsider and deny what you have said until now, and confess that our lord is the true pontiff? If you did this, perhaps you could still live.”

He replied:

“Far be it from me to lose, at the end of my life by lying, the crown that I gained in my life by speaking the truth! For I do not know whether you are now leading me to death; but if you are, know that my death will greatly harm your master, not only in the life to come but also in the present one.”

They said: “Do you see that great mountain? Even if it were entirely golden and belonged to you, and you gave it all away, you would still in no way live longer.”

Hearing this, he rose and began to sing in a loud voice the hymn of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. When it was finished, they reached the desolate place toward which they had been traveling. They lifted him from the boat and placed him, bound, upon a rock to sit.

Then, withdrawing a short distance, they began saying to one another:

“What shall we do? If we merely kill the man, our souls will never be able to obtain any remedy; and if we do not do so, we shall nevertheless die.”

While they were hesitating over this, they saw a small boat coming rapidly and carrying two men. They said to one another: “Let us wait for them; perhaps they are bearers of good news.”

71. The niece of the wicked Guido, thereafter called Jezebel and Herodias, had sent five servants to kill the servant of God. [Col. 1477B] She then summoned two clerics whom she knew to be especially eager for his death and addressed them:

“Take swords and pursue your enemy quickly, lest perhaps he deceive the others and live any longer.”

These were the men who were then coming in the boat. When they reached the others, they got out of the boat and said:

“Where is Arialdus?”

The others replied: “He is dead.”

But they said: “We have been ordered to see him, whether alive or dead.”

Looking around, they saw him at a distance, bound and sitting upon a rock. They rushed upon him anxiously, like hungry lion cubs upon their prey. Drawing their swords, one seized one of his ears and the other seized the other, saying:

“Speak, scoundrel: is our lord the true archbishop?” [Note: [Col. 1477D] The same Carolus says: “When Arialdus was asked whether he regarded Guido as archbishop, whom the Roman Church had confirmed with the pallium and the cardinals, he replied: ‘As long as I carry a tongue in my mouth, and my soul remains unharmed and my mind clear, I shall not regard him as archbishop nor call him one.’”]

He replied: “He never was, because the work of an archbishop neither exists in him now nor ever existed.”

Then the merciless men cut off both his ears. He, raising his eyes to heaven, said:

“I give you thanks, Christ, who have deemed me worthy today to be numbered among your martyrs.”

They asked him again whether Guido was the true archbishop. Maintaining his customary firmness of spirit, he said: “He is not.”

Therefore they immediately cut off his nose together with his upper lip, and then gouged out both his eyes. Afterward they severed his right hand, saying:

“This is the hand that wrote letters sent to Rome.”

Then they cut off his genital member at the root, saying:

“Until now you have been a preacher of chastity; henceforth you too shall be chaste.”

Afterward they pulled out his tongue from beneath his throat, saying:

“Now let the tongue that disturbed and dispersed the families of the clergy be silent.” [Note: [Col. 1477D] The same author says: “Pulling his tongue out from beneath his chin, they left him half-dead on the island.”] [Col. 1478A]

Thus that holy soul was released from the flesh. His body, somehow or other, was committed to the earth.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Transport of the Body, Uncorrupted for Ten Months, to Milan

72. After this, splendid lights began appearing there at night to the fishermen. When the impious Jezebel heard of this, she immediately ordered him to be transferred by night to another island. [Note: [Col. 1477D] Perhaps another of the aforementioned Isola islands, which, like that of Saint Victor, subsequently passed into the jurisdiction of Count Borromeo, according to the aforementioned Carolus a Basilica Petri; it was almost always without inhabitants.]

But when the same light repeatedly appeared there as well, she had him carried to a third place. [Note: [Col. 1477D] The elder Landulfus likewise says: “On the following day, at the command of that same Oliva, lest he be found even dead by her own people, and because she was being fiercely besieged by Herlembald, they buried the dead man most carefully in the fortress of Trevali”—commonly called Val Travaglia, says Puricellus—“in a storeroom of Saint Ambrose. After several days had passed, the stench of his corpse filled the entire castle, so that everyone fled in nausea.” If this last detail is not fabricated, it ought not to be attributed to the corpse but to another and higher cause, as a sign of abhorrence for the crime; for the corpse itself, even after ten months, was found to be exceedingly fragrant, as will presently be related.] Seeing, therefore, that she could not conceal the holy body either beneath the earth or above it, because an extraordinary light accompanied it everywhere, she became extremely angry and had enormous stones fastened around it and sank it into the depths of the lake. [Col. 1478B]

Nevertheless, at the place where it was thrown, the water is so deep—as I learned from men of that region—that scarcely anyone could reach the bottom with a rope one hundred cubits long. The lake is called Major because of its size, and it extends for more than fifty miles in length. It certainly contains such countless and enormous fish that in three months they could easily devour all the livestock in that parish.

But because all these things had been done secretly, there was everywhere considerable uncertainty and dispute about him. Some said that he was dead; others that he was secretly being held in chains. The whole populace then became so inflamed with love for him that everyone bound himself by oath either to have him back, alive or dead, or to fight for him to the death.

But Almighty God, whose cause Arialdus himself had made known, did not permit him to be defiled by a fish or to remain secretly in the deep lake.

73. After ten months had passed, a faithful man named Algisius began hurrying through the city, saying:

“Recently, on the feast of the Finding of the Holy Cross, [Note: [Col. 1478D] 3 May 1067. Some say that Herlembald had concealed the matter until then because the entire populace favored Guido while he was present in Milan; after Guido had departed, they say, Herlembald undertook to exact vengeance. But this is slander: he was content simply to recover Arialdus’s body, and the populace was moved by the miracles.] I was passing along the shore of Lake Maggiore on business of my own. And behold, that same eagle was flying over the shore, driving away all the other birds. When the shepherds who were grazing their flocks there saw this, they began hurrying toward the place; I ran with them.

And behold, most blessed Arialdus lay there, cast out of the water, whole except for the eight limbs that had been cut off from him with iron, and wonderfully white. When I saw him, I recognized him immediately and said tearfully to all who were present:

‘Look, he is safe here, for this is Blessed Arialdus, whom the entire grieving populace is seeking.’”

While we remained there for a short time, servants were suddenly sent from the fortress of Arona. [Note: [Col. 1479D] We have already seen that Landulfus calls it “the fortress of Trevali.”] They drove us away from the place and gently buried him in a ditch that was there.

When I, who have written this account, heard of it, I immediately went there with a companion. I found the shepherds and carefully and cautiously asked whether what I had heard was true. They replied and affirmed that everything was certainly true.

I asked: “If it is true, where is he, then?”

They replied: “Here is the place where he was placed in the evening, before our eyes. But when we returned in the morning, we found the place, yet nothing of him. We think only that he was carried upward by night into the fortress.” [Col. 1479B]

74. Hearing this, I quickly returned and related everything I had heard, in order, to the prudent man Herlembald. He immediately summoned all the citizens. Since they were already eagerly longing for the martyr whom they had heard had been revealed, he chose men from among them and sent them to seek the holy body.

They returned after two days and reported that the enemies of the truth had said: “We would rather die than return the body you seek.”

They said this because they had attempted to destroy it. On the night when they had brought it to themselves, seeing its integrity and beauty, they said to one another:

“If he is sought and is seen by the entire populace in such beauty, he will always be praised, while we shall always be held in disgrace. Therefore let us shave the skin and hair from his head; let us tear the whitening skin of his body with iron claws; let us cut off both his feet; and finally let us burn him in a very hot furnace, so that, if anyone is sent to see him, he may be rejected as hideous and unrecognizable rather than sought.”

75. But although they completed all these diabolical schemes against him, they fell into a disgrace worse than they had expected, because no one was sent merely to see him but to demand him.

When the messengers’ report was heard, and the bells and trumpets sounded with increasing force, the whole city gathered together. Then Herlembald said:

“Since the enemies of God and of us refuse without cause to return the holy body, it is fitting that we take it from them by force. But since the matter we are pursuing is believed and said to belong to God, I want us to proceed there justly and with the honor due to him. We should not go in a raid and at the expense of the poor and innocent; instead, we should carry with us what we need to live.

“Let messengers therefore hurry in every direction and urge everyone fit for battle to come with weapons, and urge the peasants to come with wagons, so that the former may fight alongside us and the latter carry our arms and provisions.”

Soon so many wagons had gathered that for nearly seven miles the crowd of foot soldiers and horsemen could scarcely move along the public road. An innumerable multitude flowed together from every direction, like the sand of the sea, carrying weapons and provisions upon the backs of servants or beasts of burden.

Proceeding in this way, on the second day toward evening we found a meadow, about four miles from the place from which we had set out, [Note: [Col. 1479D] Approximately halfway between Arona and the mouth of the lake, where it again narrows into the form of a river.] well watered and spacious. Since it was suitable for this purpose, we pitched camp there.

76. Here the prudent Herlembald again sent envoys [Note: [Col. 1479D] Landulfus the Younger says that envoys were sent “to Oliva.”] and courteously demanded the holy body.

Terrified by the alarming sound of the multitude roaring as it advanced upon them, the enemies no longer dared to prevent what was being demanded. And behold, at dawn on the following day, a joyful voice rang through the camp, saying:

“On the bank of the Ticino, the body of Blessed Arialdus has been placed in a boat.”

When they heard this, everyone seized the opportunity to run; the man who was readiest to run was then considered the most blessed. The body was lifted into a bier. [Note: [Col. 1479D] The same author adds: “At last, while everyone was waiting, the sacred body was cast out upon the bank along the Ticino”; but he says nothing about a boat. It is possible, however, that the body was carried by boat as far as the mouth of the lake and then cast upon the bank by those entrusted with it, since they did not dare wait for anyone to whom they might hand it over. [Col. 1480D]]

We began to return with such glory and praise that I could not express them even if I possessed an iron voice and tongue. For from the castles in which they had shut themselves up out of fear of the citizens came countless crowds of old men, young men, and women, carrying crosses, candles, and buckets filled with water for the thirsty. Everyone, according to his ability, gave immense thanks to God in a loud voice. Bells rang everywhere, and many people climbed trees so that they might at least see him.

77. When we drew near Milan, almost the entire city came out to meet us: matrons, noble and humble alike, carrying innumerable candles; children and old men, all giving praise to God. We even found the clerics who had been his rivals during his life prepared—not singing the office for the dead, but, as was fitting, that for martyrs.

Thus, on the holy day of the Lord’s Ascension, [Note: [Col. 1480D] Since Easter fell on 8 April in that year, the Ascension was on 17 May, and Pentecost, mentioned shortly afterward, on the 27th of the same month.] we placed him in the middle of the church of Saint Ambrose.

Then the noble Herlembald came forward in a prominent place and addressed all who could hear:

“You see, beloved, how powerful is the faith that Blessed Arialdus taught among us for ten years. Certainly, as you see, it preserved him unharmed after death in the depths of the lake, among countless and enormous fish, for ten months. Let that same faith preserve him here before you during these ten summer days, namely until the holy day of Pentecost, so that people of both sexes and of every age, from near and far, may come here and clearly behold our faith and the impiety of our enemies.”

Then, in our hearing, demons cried out to him:

“Why do you bark against us? You cannot bark so much that we shall not have you killed, as we killed your companion, and that fat and wicked bishops, abbots, and priests shall not be ours.”

78. During those days, an immense multitude came from every direction, bringing many gifts for the holy body. It was permitted to look upon him during the day; at night, a great crowd of clerics and monks came and kept vigil, singing psalms.

One of those nights, fearing greatly that, if he remained there throughout the summer, he might begin to stink, to the dishonor of Christ and his servants, I took a light and approached him while only a very few people were keeping vigil. I found an opening that his brother had made beneath his armpit in order to discover the condition of his internal organs, and I looked inside.

Behold, his entrails were white as snow, while his liver had the color of bronze. When I touched them and rubbed them with two fingers, then withdrew my fingers and held them to my nostrils, I call upon the Truth, who is God, as witness: I sensed such a great and remarkable fragrance issuing from those fingers as I do not remember ever having sensed anywhere else, or anything comparable to it.

As my conscience testified then and testifies now, if those fingers had possessed the edge of a double-edged sword, my nostrils could in no way have escaped without injury, because the sweetness of the odor was so delightful that my nostrils were stronger in drawing the fragrant fingers into themselves than my arm was in pulling them away. For many days I kept them free from every liquid, so that I might continue to enjoy that extraordinary fragrance.

79. On the holy day of Pentecost, an even greater multitude of men and women of every age gathered from near and far, so great that even the old men said they had never seen such a crowd. Thus, amid great glory and ineffable praise, he was carried to the monastery of Saint Celsus.

There he was given a burial place wonderfully suited for him: on one side it has the church in which the venerable body of Saint Celsus is now worshiped; on the other, a church [Col. 1481D] [Note: [Col. 1481D] Landulfus calls this church “small” and says that it was “the church of Saint Nazarius in the field,”] where, as is said, the holy Nazarius once remained for a long time in hiding.

From that time onward he has been worshiped and honored there by many faithful people; but not by unbelievers—not Christ, the Lord of all, nor Arialdus, his servant.

80. Blessed Levite and martyr Arialdus spent ten years fighting courageously for the law of Christ. Afterward he offered ten limbs to the hands of the wicked: eight when he was killed. For ten months he lay unharmed in the depths of the lake; the lake cast him up ten miles nearer to us than the distance at which it had received him.

For ten summer days Christ preserved him in the church of Saint Ambrose, in the sight of everyone. After this, in the tenth year, he joined to him, as I truly believe, his faithful companion Herlembald in the kingdom of heaven—Herlembald having been killed by the hands of those same wicked men. [Note: [Col. 1481D] Below I shall show that the years are counted incompletely and that Herlembald was killed in the year 1075.]

This was written in that tenth year, to the praise of Christ and of his servant Arialdus.

Blessed Levite and martyr of Christ Arialdus suffered on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1066, while the second Pope Alexander presided over the apostolic see, and our Lord Jesus Christ reigned with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen. [Note: [Col. 1481D] Puricellus thinks “the fourth” should be read; nevertheless, he acknowledges that “the fifth” is found in the other Life and elsewhere. Above I have shown that it should be retained. He also says that some maintain that the saint died on 29 June, but the authority of both Lives rightly prevails. [Col. 1482D]]

## CHAPTER IX. An Appendix of the Author’s Letters to Syrus, the Earlier Writer, and of Syrus’s Letter to Him, with Certain Miracles

81. ANDREAS TO SYRUS, VENERABLE AND FAITHFUL PRIEST.

When I formerly read what you had written about the venerable Arialdus together with your companion Herimbartus, [Note: [Col. 1482D] It is credible that this man too was a monk of Vallombrosa, and also Syrus himself.] I found that you had passed over many things that ought to be told. Therefore, at the command of Father Rodulfus of blessed memory, [Note: [Col. 1482D] In the Acts of Blessed Andrew, under 10 March, I said that Rodulfus died in the year 1076, on 12 November.] whose soul now rejoices with Christ, I have attempted to set down many things both from what you omitted and from what you related.

As I send these things to you, I beg you, by charity, to examine them carefully and, if they are true, to bear witness to them. For just as I had him as my teacher and commanded me to do this, so I want to have you as my defender, so that these things may be accepted as true. If, on account of the uncultivated style of this rot and worm who composed it, it is rightly despised, let it nevertheless be received out of reverence for two holy priests—one who commanded it, the other who confirms it.

You deserved to be his familiar brother for so long that you almost saw with your own eyes whatever I have said about him. Moreover, since you are a priest, you cannot lie; therefore I have rightly and justly chosen you to be a witness of this matter.

82. PRIEST SYRUS TO ANDREAS, SERVANT OF CHRIST.

My dearest, I am astonished that you ask for one witness concerning matters that can be attested not only by many thousands of the faithful but also by unbelievers. And if no other suitable witness to these things remained, who could be found so foolish as to say that you had written falsehoods?

He would know that you left the world for the purpose not merely of avoiding lying words but also idle ones, especially since you did not seek some worldly and lax monastery but the famous and renowned monastery of Vallombrosa, five days’ journey distant from your native land. [Col. 1483A]

Moreover, who is better informed than you about his secretly accomplished death, since you exposed yourself three times to the danger of death on this account? Once, somehow, you escaped capture. On another occasion, because it was said that he was being secretly detained in the supposedly impregnable fortress of Travallia, [Note: [Col. 1483D] I have already said that the fortress of Arona seems to be meant.] inflamed by the desire to see him, after completing a long journey and crossing many mountains, you presented yourself before its gates.

Because you dared to look inside, your identity was discovered; you were therefore captured and taken to the very highest tower of the fortress. Through an opening, with ropes, you were lowered into its depths, which seemed more like a tomb than a dwelling. The support of the bed was mud, and the headrest was stone. There was neither any place there in which bodily waste could be concealed nor a roof above to keep out the rain.

There, because of the excessive horror, your face and stomach became so weak and wasted that you could scarcely taste the food lowered to you by ropes. Therefore they dragged you out in the middle of the night and left you half alive.

On another occasion you crossed the lake, but were again recognized and captured. You could not escape at all until you bought your freedom with money.

Since these things are so, who could be so cruel and hard-hearted as to disbelieve your words?

83. Nevertheless, although I rejoice greatly over everything you have said, because it is true and useful for edification, I am nevertheless very sorrowful because you omitted matters of the greatest importance and most familiar to you. I am so surprised that you did this that I wish to disclose some of them to you and [Col. 1483C] learn why you left them out. Before he entered Milan to preach, he publicly summoned a great number of clerics to the people of Varese, pointed out the errors under which they were living, and kindly admonished them to abandon them. They despised his words, saying:

“You speak these things to us because you know us to be uneducated. But if you wish to be regarded as a credible teacher, go and do not be afraid to say these things in the city. If you dare to do what you are saying, you will prove that it is to be believed.”

He then entered the city and addressed the people, just as you said. At the very beginning of his preaching, he walked barefoot for a long time, together with some faithful companions, through venerable places, asking for the assistance of the saints, until his feet swelled so greatly that he could no longer stand upon them.

[Col. 1483D] 84. Finally, two highly learned clerics, having heard of his reputation, came to him from distant regions to discover how great his learning was. One of them challenged him to a disputation and, from morning until almost the ninth hour, while the other remained completely silent, resisted him as best he could. Then he was so utterly defeated that he could neither raise an unanswerable objection nor resolve the objections put to him. The other, however, because he found him exceedingly learned, he could not overcome on that day, but brought him down on the next.

Although he found both of them defeated, because he recognized that they were very learned, he loved them greatly, extended every kindness to them, and finally allowed them to depart.

It also happened that once he was passing along a certain street beside the episcopal residence. He began to admonish several men whom he found there. At that time Guido, the ordinary officials, and many other clerics were gathered together in that same house. When they heard this, they chose the wisest among them and sent him to confront Arialdo and declare that what he was saying was foolish. He was immediately so tightly trapped by a few words that he shamefully turned back in haste.

When his companions asked him what he had accomplished, he replied: “Know that either he is not a human being, or someone else is speaking through his mouth.”

Although you were not present, you learned all these things fully from Bonovisinus.

[Note: [Col. 1483] Here, and in the prologue, Bonvisino is written through an Italian idiom.]

85. Why did you not also mention that most famous zeal with which he drove a certain heretic away from the altar? Perhaps you feared that some people might be scandalized by it. Know, dearest friend, that the words and deeds of Arialdo—and indeed of Christ—are full of scandal to unbelievers and perverse people, but to the devout they are fuel for fervor and light.

Let us therefore disclose these matters to such people, and hear the Savior say concerning the others: “Leave them; for they are blind, and leaders of the blind” (Matthew 15:14).

As Arialdo, Christ’s servant, was passing through the greater church with his brothers, he heard that at that very hour a certain adulterer and Simonist had approached one of the basilica’s altars, pretending that he was going to celebrate Mass there.

“Let us go there,” he said.

When he reached the man, he said: “Since you are the sort of person before whom the doors of a church ought not to be opened at all, why do you, polluted as you are, presume to touch the holy altar and pretend to perform those mysteries that have been entrusted only to the innocent and chaste? Get away from here as quickly as possible, you rotten thing.”

When the man did not move away, the man of God seized his chasuble, pulled it from his back, and drove him away from the altar. At that time, both townsmen and suburban inhabitants had gathered around the church for purposes of trade.

The man went out and lodged a complaint in the marketplace. The people were stirred up; abandoning their business and raising clubs, they rushed through the doors to search for Arialdo and kill him.

Knowing what was about to happen, he had not fled. Instead, he had climbed onto the steps and was waiting there for the people. When they saw him standing on the steps and signaling with his sacred hand, they all lowered their clubs and prepared to listen, leaning upon them.

At last, when a great silence had been made, he delivered a sermon so sweet that the hearts which had been stirred and troubled by the words of the false priest, through the activity and instigation of the Adversary, were calmed and sweetened by the words of Christ’s true servant, through the activity and breathing of the Holy Spirit. The mouths that, as they entered, had madly shouted, “Let him die! Let him die!” said as they departed in prayer: “May Christ grant you to live for many years, for he has deigned to send you to this place for our salvation.”

[Col. 1485A] 86. What layman who had a blood-relative as his wife dared to enter the church in which Arialdo, Christ’s servant, was staying? For he drove such persons out of it in such a way that one is astonished not only that he did this, but that he even considered doing it.

He kindly received monks who fled the company of Simonist abbots and false brothers. But was any one of them daring enough to remain idle in his presence? They would not dare fail to read, pray, or do something else. For if they occasionally remained idle in his absence, as soon as they sensed him coming they hastened back to these activities—just as schoolboys who are idle return to their lessons when they sense the teacher approaching.

While he was preaching, did anyone dare even to mutter in that place? Whatever sort of person he might be, he would immediately hear: “Either you will be silent, or I will, because it is written: ‘Do not cast your pearls before swine’” (Matthew 7:6).

Yet although he was so severe toward wrongdoers, who was gentler in receiving penitents? When men who were called priests were caught in adultery, and no safe place elsewhere was open to them because of the people pursuing them, they fled to him. If he saw that they had made a sincere confession, he immediately made them his associates in every place whatsoever, except in the ministry of the altar; and thereafter no one appeared who dared to say anything against them.

On Good Friday, however, he would confess naked in a locked room before the other brothers whatever he had done wrong from the cradle onward, and he would have himself scourged most severely for every fault. No one was compelled to do this unwillingly; rather, anyone who wished to do so voluntarily was permitted.

Since these matters are known to you and useful for edification, why did you omit them? I beg you: do not keep silent, but reveal them to me, since I am exceedingly astonished about this.

87. ANDREAS THE SYRIAN.

Do you think, venerable Syrian, that I have said everything I happened to know about the blessed Arialdo? Hear still what three things I omitted, so that from them you may understand that I clearly knew many other things about him and deliberately omitted them.

On one occasion he had gone, at the invitation of the church of the city of Como, to reconcile the clerics of that city who were divided against one another. It was then the season of Lent. When we had gathered at one altar to perform the evening office, one item—I do not now remember whether it was from the antiphons or the responsories—slipped from everyone’s memory, so that it could not be found at all.

When a salutary plan had therefore been discovered, he made the sign of salvation upon his forehead, prostrated himself beside the altar, and asked the Lord for the lost item. He found it immediately, as though the thing being sought had been written down in the place where it had been hidden.

88. Another sign occurred when we were bringing him to the city after he had been thrown into the water of the lake. In a certain village there was a peasant who had been crippled by paralysis for many years. When he heard that Christ’s martyr was being carried along the road, he had firm faith and caused himself to be carried onto that same road and left there.

As the crowd preceding the bier passed by, the sick man waited for the martyr. When those carrying Arialdo reached him, they continued only after the sick man had earnestly begged them, and they set the bier down before him. Whether through sight alone or through touch, I do not know, but he was immediately restored to health, so that the man who could scarcely be carried by the hands of others at once walked firmly on his own feet.

I myself was then present among the crowd following behind. When I heard this, however, I quickened my pace so that, coming before the bier, I might see the man walking firmly and praising God.

89. The third miracle I shall relate I did not see myself, but learned it from the account of a highly trustworthy person.

Several men had gathered together at the Ticinese Gate. They began to converse both about Arialdo, Christ’s servant, and about those who worshiped his venerable tomb. Then one man, possessed by a proud and evil spirit, uttered this execrable statement:

“I have a greater desire to urinate upon him than to worship him.”

Immediately such a savage pain seized his inner organs that he could neither rest nor urinate until, compelled by his excessive suffering and likewise advised by the exhortation of the men present, he offered a gift at the tomb of the blessed Arialdo and worshiped there. Thus, humbled, he recovered the former health that he had justly lost through his pride.

If I wished to write down all the good things I know about him, the day and the paper would run out before my words. But since so much has been written about him, in which it can sufficiently be discerned who he was, from where he came, what he taught, and what he suffered for Christ, let us bring this to an end and bless the triune and one God, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1485]

## ANALecta concerning Saint Herlembald

From ancient chroniclers, in the account of Puricellus.

### CHAPTER ONE

Guido disturbs the peace laboriously established, with the Simonist Gothofredus substituted in his place; against him Herlembald leads out the Milanese.

[Col. 1485D]

1. At this point, after Andreas has finished, Landulf the Younger adds one further detail:

“Pope Alexander grieved over Arialdo’s death. Therefore, in the following year, namely 1067, when that same pope was going to the synod that he celebrated at Mantua, he came to Milan, made many statutes concerning the condition of the Milanese people and clergy, and entered the blessed Arialdo in the catalogue of holy martyrs.”

John Mabillon considered these words, transcribed from the original manuscript, worthy of inclusion in the first volume of his *Analecta*.

Sigebert of Gembloux serves as a witness to the synod of that year. Less than fifty years afterward, he says that, “while two men were contending for the papacy at Rome”—for Cadolus, bishop of Parma, whom the Romans had requested King Henry to send against Alexander, enthroned on 30 September 1061, had attempted, only a few months later, namely on 14 April, to occupy the see but had failed; and although condemned by various synods, he continued to act as pope—“while, then, the two were contending, a synod was assembled at Mantua. Through the agency of Anno, archbishop of Cologne, Alexander, clearing himself by oath of the charge of simony, was placed in the apostolic see,” that is, confirmed or declared to have been lawfully placed there. “But Cadolus was rejected as a Simonist.”

Francis Maria Florentius confirms the same year for this synod in his *Memoirs of Countess Matilda*, p. 88, from a letter of Alexander to Gervase of Reims, stating that Cadolus “oppressed the Roman Church for five years, now by crafty evasion, now by hostile invasion.” Thus Ptolemy of Lucca, who lived two hundred years after Sigebert and reports the event as occurring two years later, must certainly be corrected; nor should Baronius be accepted when he places it three years earlier.

Meanwhile, from Ptolemy we learn that Alexander held the aforesaid “council in the presence of the emperor”—evidently already reconciled through the efforts of Saint Anno—“and restored all the schismatic bishops, together with Cadolus, to the bosom of the Church, reconciled them to himself, won the entire people to his support, and prolonged his stay throughout that whole year for the greater security of peace and unity.”

2. With matters standing thus, it would not have been surprising if Alexander, returning from Mantua, had remained in Milan for a few days and, without any ceremony and perhaps merely by a declaration of his living voice, approved the veneration that the faithful offered to the blessed Arialdo as a martyr—at the urging of Herlembald and the other devotees of Arialdo. Even before the council, however, whether there or elsewhere, he may have received Archbishop Guido back into favor.

For Guido, as in the earlier judgment before Peter Damian, when he was “admonished,” in accordance with the profession that he was to submit to the legates, not only consented to sit on the left beside Cardinal Peter, while Alexander—then Anselm of Lucca—occupied the right; he also “readily offered of his own accord that, if Peter ordered it, he would sit without dispute on the stool beneath Peter’s feet.” With similar readiness he accepted, signed, and swore that he would fulfill whatever the same legate then ordered, as Saint Peter Damian himself relates at length.

Thus Guido, now with no less readiness to profess or feign repentance and obedience, may have seemed to deserve from a pontiff who was most desirous of peace the indulgence of being released from the bond of excommunication and being allowed to attend the assembly at Mantua and retain his rank there.

As for the statutes that Landulf says Alexander made at Milan, I think they were none other than those composed by his legates, who had been sent after the synod to put matters in order, and which the pope, arriving afterward, may have confirmed. No judgment was instituted concerning Arialdo’s case or the authors of the murder, lest the peace that had newly been formed should be dissolved.

3. How that peace was then established, at least to some extent, is briefly reported by the historian Arnulf in Puricellus, p. 248, in these words:

“Meanwhile there was no respite for the plunderers in their seizure of the clergy’s possessions.”
