That malicious writer interprets in this way Herlembald’s zeal in pursuing those responsible for the murder, in the exercise of his office as their defender, and in demanding from the clerics either the continence or the cessation from ministry that they had sworn to Saint Peter Damian they would observe—ministries that may be performed only by the undefiled.

“To settle this dispute at that time,” says Arnulf—Alexander was still present in Lombardy and directing affairs—“Maynard, bishop of Silva Candida, and Minutius, a cardinal bishop” (he himself signs as “John, cardinal priest”), “Roman legates, came to Milan. While they were proclaiming evangelical peace to all by the apostolic command of Alexander, they prudently arranged an agreement concerning Arialdo’s death. Then, judging between the clergy and the people, they established in an elegant written document what ought to be done in the future.”

In this document they say:

“Since certain matters in this city were formerly corrected through our brother, Lord Peter, bishop of Ostia, a man of reverend holiness, there is no need to repeat matters or earlier disputes that are known to everyone. Instead, we shall commit to writing, for the memory of future generations, the things now established by us according to canonical discipline.”

They also speak honorably of Guido as the true archbishop and therefore as one who had been reconciled, when article 15 orders:

“Any layman who knows that clerics under his authority are keeping a woman or have happened by chance to fall into the crime of fornication shall report them to the archbishop and to the ordinary officials of the church to whom this responsibility has been entrusted. But if the archbishop or his ordinary officials, after hearing of the matter, neglect it, that layman shall permit none of them either to perform his office or to retain a benefice until he abandons his fault and makes worthy satisfaction to the Lord through penance.”

Again, in section 18, it is ordered that “the bishop who now holds office, or whoever shall hold it thereafter, shall travel once or twice through all the parishes.”

The entire statute may be read in Baronius, or in the books of the Councils, where it is found as having been issued “in the year from the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1067, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Alexander II, in the fifth indiction, on the first day of August.”

4. “Nor was Herlembald content with these things,” says the aforementioned Arnulf in Puricellus, p. 257, since experience had already taught him how little or nothing could be trusted in Guido’s repentance, whether feigned or unstable. “Continuing to Rome” (in the year 1068, if I am not mistaken), “he entered into a new plan with the Romans.”

“It was an ancient condition of the Italian kingdom, continuing to the present day”—that is, the year 1077—“that when the rulers of churches died, the emperor or king would provide their successors, after being duly invited by the clergy and people. The Romans deny that this is canonical. But the archdeacon Hildebrand, who, while abolishing the old arrangement, attempted to introduce a new constitution”—more correctly, he should have said, “while abolishing the surreptitious arrangement, to restore the old one”—openly declared that the Milanese dispute could be settled in no other way than by having a canonical pastor, for whose election he said Roman consent would be necessary.

“Instructed by these assertions, Herlembald came to Milan and hastily carried out what he had heard. First, therefore, he secretly gathered a few of his friends. When he demanded from them a pledge to conceal what had been entrusted to them, he cautiously added under oath the matter concerning the future election of a pastor after the death of the present one. Then, laboring day and night, he bound every layman and cleric to the same oath. Meanwhile, however, he did not cease persecuting Bishop Guido and all the relatives of his blood.”

Thus Arnulf writes about Herlembald with envy and calumny. Nevertheless, he must be described further, so that the substance of the history may be retained and easily separated, by the judgment of a discerning reader, from the dross of a later hostility toward the jurisdiction of the Roman Church.

He continues as follows:

5. “But the archbishop, unable to endure so many pressures hanging over him, ripe for eternity and his whole body weakened by a long illness, perhaps thought it appropriate to forestall what that man”—Herlembald—“had anticipated should be done, namely, to surrender his own dignity to another while he was still alive.

“At that time there was a certain subdeacon of the Church’s ordinary clergy named Gothofredus, the sole person above all others admitted to his secrets. As soon as he had penetrated his master’s mind, he began by every means to strive to transfer the honor to himself.

“After a secret agreement had therefore been made with him, the bishop, with oaths of the mutual pact given on both sides, laid down his dignity”—the printed reading *abssas* is uncertain—“and sent the staff and ring to Caesar through legates. Gothofredus, who had long since won the king’s favor through much effort, nevertheless, by this recent agreement, rejoiced to obtain the episcopate from that Augustus.

“Yet, in accordance with the truth of Scripture, laughter was mixed with sorrow, and grief seized the end of joy” (James 4:9). Rejected by the citizens, he was received nowhere, either for the exercise of his episcopate or even for lodging; he became hated even by the farmers.

“The Roman lords immediately condemned him according to canonical law and apostolic authority, sending the Milanese their written judgment concerning him.”

If such letters survived, we could determine more certainly the year in which these events occurred. For the present, however, we seem unlikely to be far wrong if we say that they occurred in the year 1070 of the present century.

Arnulf continues in Puricellus, pp. 259 ff.:

6. “With this confidence Herlembald rises up more fiercely not only against him”—Gothofredus—“but also against all his supporters, destroying everything with sword and flames. Against him he had also exacted the oaths of many throughout the villages and castles.

“Therefore, whenever he attempts to appropriate anything from the church’s resources, he is completely forbidden by everyone, as happened in certain cases which it would be lengthy—and indeed unnecessary—to recount individually.

“Meanwhile Guido admitted that he had been deceived by Gothofredus’s plots, calling him a violator of the mutual agreement. When Guido wished to recover his lost honor, he joined a pact of peace with Herlembald.

“O blind mind of mortals! Coming to Milan under that man’s leadership, he was brought not into the city, as he wished, but to the monastery of Saint Celsus, made more private than a private citizen. There he lived for many days entrusted to guards, deceived more gloriously on this occasion”—by Herlembald—“than he had deceived many others.

“Gothofredus, however, having already been hemmed in by many obstacles, gathered with a number of his followers in a town called Castellio in the vernacular, a truly impregnable stronghold, fortified by its walls and by the nature of its location.”

7. “Frequently bursting forth from there, Gothofredus, who thirsted beyond measure for plunder and slaughter, provoked the Milanese to resolve to storm the fortress immediately.

“Without delay, they prepared an army and everything necessary for military use, and all advanced. They pitched their camp at the foot of the mountain”—for the place was a little more than twenty miles from the city—“then surrounded it on every side and attacked without interruption. They also urgently summoned all the farmers of that region to assemble, swearing to maintain a long siege.

“They set up stone-throwing engines and every kind of military machine; they prepared scorpions, ballistae, and a thousand snares of death.

“The besieged resisted as best they could, and much blood was shed each day, so that even during the venerable observance of Lent there was no abstinence from human slaughter.

“At this time, when few people in the city enjoyed their security, sudden disaster invaded the city that had seemed prepared for it. I shudder to relate it.

“For on the first Saturday of Lent”—this was in 1071, on 19 March, since Easter was then to be celebrated on 24 April—“the city was consumed in a great fire. When a violent whirlwind of winds was then blowing [lacuna]—oh, what buildings and what kinds of houses, and how beautiful were the walls that were burned! [lacuna] But, what was worse than every other loss, many basilicas of the saints were burned, both in the city and outside it [lacuna]”

For a fuller account, see Puricellus, *Ambrosian Monuments*, p. 461. I hasten to Herlembald.

8. “When such a dreadful report resounded through the camp,” says Arnulf, “many immediately abandoned the siege and went to the scant remnants left by the fire to visit the wretched household. Herlembald, however, together with the others, retained part of the army and persevered more resolutely, not ceasing to wage war each day.

“Gothofredus, who had now been besieged for three months, saw how small the army in the camp had become and secretly summoned his followers, carefully securing his friends. As the Easter holidays approached, they gathered together, immediately formed a battle line, and rose against the camp with a considerable assault and outcry. The besieged likewise broke through their barriers and rushed out on every side.

“Herlembald, placed in such danger, seized his arms and dared, with his few men, to resist to the best of his ability, himself becoming the standard-bearer. If he and his men had not fought with courage, that day would have been his last.

“When many saw the steadfastness of the few, they withdrew voluntarily, taking Gothofredus with them from the town. The Milanese pursued them for a long distance, suddenly massing together in the same way—both those who had been in the camp and those who had remained in the city. They did not cease the pursuit for several days and nights, until they forced those who had been reduced to the greatest necessity to enter Castellio again.

“After this, the Milanese returned to the city and determined by oath that Gothofredus should never be received, but that another should be chosen collectively from the catalogue of the greater church.

“By then that Archbishop Guido had departed from this world”—on 23 August—“and was buried in a place commonly called Burguli,” where the city of Alessandria is now believed to have been founded. “There, after the burning of the city”—having escaped from the custody of Saint Celsus, or having been allowed to leave it—“he ended his final day in bitterness of soul.”

## CHAPTER TWO

Herlembald secures a canonical election and restrains Gothofredus, the intruder and excommunicate; Pope Gregory VII assists him by letter.

9. “From that day Herlembald applies every effort,” sometimes dealing with the clergy, sometimes with the people, concerning the election of a bishop, having received new authorization from the Romans and rejecting the ancient provision of the kings.

“Nevertheless, the greater part of the city, consisting of clergy and prudent people, was intent upon the ancient custom and the honor of the monarchy. He, however, disregarding everyone and the common oath, listened only to the advice of that Roman Hildebrand.

“The day was therefore approaching which he himself had foreseen for carrying this out, namely the solemnity of the holy Epiphany. He diligently endeavored to summon those who were present, as well as absent clerics and laymen, abbots and monks, not omitting the rural crowd that was friendly to him.

“When the feast day arrived, a gathering of many people took place in the winter church. Those with whom he had sworn to conduct this election, however, were absent.

“After the solemn celebration of Mass, he first preached as he wished, saying much about the election of a pastor. With a certain Bernard, the Roman legate, standing by, he elected Atho, who was still only a cleric and a young man of tender age, against the will of the clergy and of many among the people, so that they returned from the church in anger.”

10. Here Puricellus rightly interrupts, at p. 265, and orders us to judge how bitterly Arnulf wrote these things in order to stir up hatred against Herlembald, from the fact that he calls Atho “a young man of tender age.”

Atho may have been young in comparison with Gothofredus, who was perhaps extremely old. Puricellus nevertheless firmly maintains that Atho possessed the age required by the sacred canons and was therefore more than thirty years old when he was elected.

He is moved to this opinion by the presence of the apostolic legate and by the character of Hildebrand. Later, when he had become Pope Gregory VII, Hildebrand refused in two letters to the bishops of Brittany to ordain to the archbishopric of Dol a certain young man, “quite distinguished by birth,” whom they had sent to him.

“To this request,” he says in one letter, “we could in no way give our assent, since the sacred canons oppose it.” In the other he says: “After examining his case as was proper, we found in him honorable morals, but not yet sufficiently mature or equipped to bear the burden of the episcopate.”

What clearer indication of Atho’s suitable age could be desired than the fact that Gregory himself refused to approve Theodaldus, elected in 1075, because Atho was still in possession of the see?

“We certainly know,” he says, “that he was elected in that same Church, but we have not yet been able to discover any reason why he ought to be rejected.”

Such a reason would certainly have existed if his age had been less than the canons permit.

Let us return to Arnulf, who brings his third book to an end in Puricellus, p. 27, with these words:

11. “When Atho and his followers were ascending to the episcopal hall for a banquet”—for a lavish meal had already been prepared on the tables—“the citizens, inflamed, suddenly attacked the house, searching its front rooms and outer areas.

“The newly elected man, hiding in a corner of one chamber, was found, seized, torn apart, and miserably mangled; finally, he was dragged by the calves and arms from top to bottom.

“When, fearing death, he stood prostrate before the altar in the church, the people shouted, and he climbed into the pulpit. There, after taking an oath in the hearing of all, he renounced the Ambrosian see for the present and for all time.

“Meanwhile his supporters fled through various hiding places. The Roman legate himself barely escaped, with his clothes torn and his body wounded.

“As for Gothofredus and Atho, both remained private citizens, content only with their own homes and possessions.”

After this, Arnulf begins Book IV as follows:

“Accordingly, when the aforementioned archdeacon Hildebrand heard what had happened to Atho, he immediately judged that the oath imposed by violence, relying on his authority as a cardinal, ought by every means to be considered invalid . . . Therefore it happened that, when a gathering of bishops had been assembled at Rome, at his insistence he declared Atho lawfully elected and cast an anathema against Gothofredus.

“Hildebrand repeatedly reported all these things in his letters to Herlembald . . .”

12. “Meanwhile, the suffragan bishops of the Ambrosian see, having received a mandate from the king, assembled at Novara and laid the hand of consecration upon Gothofredus, strengthening him as best they could.

“Although the royal command is said by many to have been obtained through substantial gifts, it is nevertheless clear that the king later repented and came to hate the intermediary completely . . .

“While these things were being carried out, the pope Alexander II died, in 1073, on 20 April. After an interval of only a few days—nineteen—Hildebrand succeeded him, taking the name Gregory VII. In him Atho’s spirit immediately revived, so that, going to Rome, he placed himself under Gregory’s protection.

“Since Gregory remained firmly fixed in his former resolve, he summoned a general synod at Rome and excommunicated Gothofredus together with his followers.”

Here Puricellus reports the letters Gregory wrote in this same matter to Beatrice, mistress of Tuscany and Liguria, and to her daughter Matilda, instructing them to abstain from communion with those bishops by whom Gothofredus had been consecrated; to William, bishop of Pavia, commending the Milanese cause and opposing the pseudo-archbishop and his supporters; and likewise to all the faithful of Saint Peter living in Lombardy.

All these letters are dated “in the eleventh indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, on the third day before the Kalends of July,” and “on the Kalends of July” themselves—that is, in the year 1072.

Passing over these letters here, the ones more directly relevant to our subject are those which Gregory wrote to Herlembald in the same year, “at Capua, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, in the newly begun twelfth indiction,” in the following words:

13. “GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HERLEMBALD, soldier of Milan: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Let your prudence know that, by God’s mercy, we are staying at Capua healthy and joyful, not without great benefit to the Church of God . . . Know also that King Henry has sent us words full of kindness and obedience . . . Moreover, some of his leading faithful promise us on his behalf that, concerning the matter of the Milanese Church, he will without doubt obey our counsel . . .

“Therefore, trusting entirely in the Lord and in your mother, the Roman Church, act manfully. Strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, know that the more violently the storm of disturbance now rises against us, the more pleasantly, with God’s favor, calm weather will smile upon us afterward.”

See Baronius, under the year 1073, no. 43, for the letters of the penitent Henry to Gregory. In them he confesses himself “guilty and unhappy,” having sinned “partly through the prompting of flattering childhood, partly through the freedom of a powerful and imperious authority, and partly through the deceptive seduction of those whose excessively misleading counsels he followed,” against heaven and before the pontiff.

“And now,” he says, “especially concerning the Milanese Church, which through our fault is in error, we ask that it be canonically corrected by your apostolic strictness, and that from there your sentence of authority proceed to correct the other Churches as well.”

Gregory again wrote to Herlembald, also from Capua, “on the seventh day before the Ides of October,” answering several of his questions at once:

14. “So long as you are occupied with the devoted concern of defending the faith and restoring religion, there will be no lack of willingness to hear your messages gladly and to help you. Because we are occupied with other matters, we intend to answer briefly your many questions.

“Concerning the associates of that excommunicated man who, after receiving money, wish to return to you; concerning the sons whose fathers, or the fathers whose sons, adhere to the excommunicated Gothofredus; and concerning those whose correction you do not wish to carry out without the payment of money—toward whom, nevertheless, we admonish you to show yourselves merciful if any wish to attach themselves to your party—we entrust the matter to your prudence, so that you may arrange it as you know and are able to do best.

“Let all of these, however, who repent of their error and desire to return to you for the sake of a remedy, know that they are to be received kindly and treated mercifully.

“As for the bishops who are attempting to support your enemy, do not fear them greatly. Beatrice and her daughter Matilda, together with certain of the kingdom’s greatest nobles, are working firmly to unite our mind and the king’s against him. We neither ought nor wish to exercise any hatred against that king, unless—God forbid!—he should choose to act contrary to divine religion.

“They confidently believe that the king will satisfy our will in the other ecclesiastical matters and, above all, will give his assent to our disposition concerning your affair.

“Finally, strive by whatever honorable means you can to win Gregory, bishop of Vercelli, to your side, because he declares that he obeys our command in everything.

“For the rest, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, asking for his indulgence through prayers, almsgiving, and purity of heart, so that he may deign to bring our desire and yours to completion.”

15. Likewise, writing from Capua “on the third day before the Ides of October” to “Albert, bishop of Alba”—one of Gothofred’s ordainers, but one whom he understood to have been excused by a trustworthy account—he declares his zeal for restoring the honor of the Milanese Church:

> “Your Religion can make St. Peter and us indebted to it in no matter more than this: that, armed with the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation, you fight with us against Simon Magus, who has miserably infected the Church of blessed Ambrose with the poison of his venality; and that you extend a helping hand to Herlembald, that most vigorous soldier of Christ, and to those things that pertain to the worship of God and to the religion of the holy Church.”

Likewise, to “William, bishop of Pavia,” on the same day and in the same place:

> “The letter of your fraternity sent to us, together with Herlembald’s words from Milan, clearly shows that you wish faithfully to render to the holy Apostolic See the obedience that you owe, and to obey our exhortations as is fitting. But there is nothing that we more readily enjoin upon your fraternity, nothing that we would more gladly have you do, than that you should strive, with pastoral vigilance, to defend your Church and the flock entrusted to you from the heresies that seem to be breeding pestilentially in the holy Church … and to recall the clergy from disgraceful conduct to chastity. Know also that you will render a matter highly commendable to your mother, the Roman Church, if you extend a helping hand to the aforesaid Herlembald in those things that he undertakes at our counsel—or rather, in fear of almighty God—and if you resist the enemies of the holy Church, who are about to wage God’s war with him.”

## CHAPTER III. The killing of St. Herlembald, the mutilation of the priest Liprand, and the intrusion of Tetald into the episcopate

16. With the integrity of blessed Herlembald thus approved by the judgment of the Apostolic See, he does not refuse to have his deeds—since no friend wrote them down—presented as written by the pen of an enemy and maliciously interpreted, for an impartial reader easily accepts them in a better sense. Let us therefore hear Arnulf, who, after the words quoted above in no. 101 concerning Hildebrand’s election to the pontificate, continues his account of the events of 1073 in Puricellus, p. 296:

> “While Gothofred remained in the sole fortress of Brebbia, Atho, having abandoned his own home and fatherland, lived in Rome, bound entirely to the service of the pope. Herlembald supported him at Milan with all his strength, laboring day and night and giving as well as promising gifts. Moreover, he persecuted the entire party of Gothofred with fire and sword, sometimes leaving nothing unattempted according to his ability, especially since he yielded neither to the will of the king nor to that of his equals and many others, relying solely upon and content with Roman confidence; and he went so far as to blaspheme the bishops of the Ambrosian consecration”—thus he calls the schismatic ordination—“asserting that they had been excommunicated by the Apostolic See and rejecting all their ministry. Hence it came about that on the holy day of Pentecost”—which fell that year on 19 May—“he prohibited baptism in the city.”

17. “Afterwards”—that is, in 1074, when Easter was to be celebrated on 20 April—he “trampled underfoot before the whole people the sacred chrism”—which one of them, in the mystery of the Lord’s Supper, had sent to the metropolitan church, as is customary when a bishop is absent—“after it had been poured out upon the ground. Bringing his own chrism forward, although it was unknown by whom or from where it had been prepared”—certainly by some Catholic, perhaps William of Pavia, mentioned above in no. 101—“he set aside the prerogative granted to that authentic Sabbath’s ceremonies and caused his own baptism to be celebrated on the Friday of the week in white garments … with the result that his Easter joy did not know its own washing, and long afterwards many catechumens lacked the grace of baptism.”

Puricellus strives to prove, in chapter 48, that Herlembald proceeded correctly in all these matters and in accordance with the judgment of the theologians. Meanwhile, the obstinacy of the clergy increased all the more the longer King Henry delayed fulfilling, as he had promised, the Apostolic See’s demands in the Milanese affair. For this reason Gregory finally saw himself compelled to employ a harsher remedy. Thus, as Arnulf writes, he “held a synod at Rome” during Lent of 1075, “at which he openly prohibited the king from thereafter having any right in the granting of bishoprics and removed all lay persons from investitures. Moreover, having pronounced an anathema, he condemned all the king’s counselors and threatened the same against the king unless he soon submitted to this decree.”

18. But the reverence due to the synod did nothing to move the Milanese schismatics, so that they continued to deliberate about receiving Gothofred, or whomever else the king might command. This certainly did not go unpunished. For “four years having passed since the aforesaid earlier conflagration, as the most holy feast of Easter approached—namely, on the second day of the authentic week, the third day before the Kalends of April—the wretched city again felt the divine anger and learned how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:31).

For when the solemnities of the Mass had been celebrated and the sun was already declining, a dense, dark smoke appeared in the middle of the city, flying through the air under the violence of an exceedingly strong wind. Indeed, many torches, like flashes of lightning, bursting from that immense and inextinguishable ball of fire, suddenly gleamed throughout the entire city, so that nearly everything in the city that had escaped the aforesaid conflagration was consumed by the flames now present … [lacuna] … What more can be said? Only that this fire was like another conflagration, yet more cruel in that it burned many more and larger churches … [lacuna] … whose ruined walls, I think, will remain visible for more than a thousand years …”

19. After reporting these events from Arnulf in the *Ambrosian Monuments*, p. 462, Puricellus, when he comes to Herlembald, continues the narrative at p. 300 in these words:

> “Amid such and so many afflictions, while the whole city was filled with mourning of every order and age and of both sexes, only Herlembald’s spirit remained fearless and unbending. For, as the baptism of Easter in white garments drew near”—Easter then fell on 5 April—“he was endeavoring, as he had done the previous year, to begin the mystery with unknown chrism. Since the cardinals of the Church, whose duty it was to consecrate the fonts, were unwilling to act contrary to custom, a certain Luitprand, called a priest, immediately appeared. A household servant by descent, he usurped the office of the ordainers by the command and power of Herlembald and baptized those who came, without due consideration.”

20. “This violence, added to the recent memory of the city’s burning, gravely offended very many citizens, especially the soldiers … Hence it happened” (p. 325) “that, going out of the city together for several days, they swore, with a large part of the populace, to obtain justice for themselves and the honor of St. Ambrose, and to receive a pastor from the king as a gift.

“When they entered the city together, Herlembald, as always unable to tolerate opposition, was haranguing those present in his customary manner. But when he could no longer restrain his fury, he and his followers made a charge with shouting; he hastily seized his arms and his banner, which he said belonged to St. Peter, carrying it in his right hand. As the citizens rose from every quarter, he burst armed into their midst. At the first instant and on the first line of battle, however, so great an attack overwhelmed him that he could accomplish nothing memorable. When he had been surrounded on every side, he was immediately pierced by repeated blows and, dying more quickly than one could say it, fell, while his small company was scattered in every direction.

“His lifeless corpse, thrown upon the ground, was stripped of its garments, and, once naked, was beaten on every side with clubs and stones, so that he who had been a terror to many while alive might, in death, be subjected to the sport of many. When it was carried away for burial, no devotion of funeral rites accompanied it. Afterwards, the priest Liprand”—who had gone forth with Herlembald, carrying a cross before him—“while fleeing, was deprived of his ears and nose, so that he who had presumed to usurp another’s office might lose what he seemed to possess. At that same hour, after this notable trophy, all the citizens sang triumphal hymns and, armed, went to the church of their patron Ambrose. On the following day, laymen and clergy together again proceeded in litanies and praises to St. Ambrose. There they confessed their former offenses to one another; and, absolution having been pronounced by the priests who were present, the whole people returned peacefully to their homes.”

21. If, however, there can be any peace for the impious—who were increasingly bound by still more impious priests to foster the schism—then, in a sense more accurate than Arnulf intended in Puricellus, p. 315, he says that he is proceeding to what followed, “the aforesaid matters not having been entirely settled, but rather entangled.”

What followed, then?

> “The Milanese, so often mentioned, sent an embassy beyond the mountains to King Henry to request a bishop, announcing the triumph of Herlembald’s killing. When that king learned of it, he rejoiced beyond measure and promised that he would give them whichever bishop they wished.”

A little later he writes:

> “Meanwhile, while envoys from the Milanese clergy and people were approaching the king concerning the aforesaid matter, a certain Tetald, a subdeacon of the Milanese Church, was serving in the royal chapel. The king, turning over many plans and counterplans, at last indulged his own judgment and gave him the Ambrosian episcopate, setting aside the investiture and anointing of that still-living Gothofred, as well as the election of Atho, who was then living in Rome. What more need be said? That prelate was received by the clergy and people … and the suffragans themselves—the very men who had consecrated Gothofred—laid hands upon him.”

This took place on 4 February 1076, as I have shown in the *Exegesis on the Milanese Bishops*. It occurred despite the fact that Pope Gregory, by a letter dated the seventh day before the Ides of September, had previously ordered Tetald to come to Rome to give an account of his election, and meanwhile not to receive holy orders. Likewise, in a letter written on the sixth day before the Ides of October to the bishops of Vercelli, Turin, Asti, Ivrea, Lodi, and the other suffragans of the holy Milanese Church, he had informed them what he had written to Tetald and ordered them not to promote him to holy orders.

Here Arnulf, however devoted he may be to the royal party, cannot restrain himself from exclaiming:

> “A remarkable thing, unheard-of in all former times: when one bishop has been elected and another consecrated for a single city, a third should emerge at one and the same time!”

22. Puricellus wishes Arnulf to be mistaken here, when he says that Herlembald was killed in the very year of the second fire, and before Tetald’s schismatic election and ordination, and maintains that the deed occurred shortly after Easter in 1076, that is, in April. But how could the man who was writing while the events were taking place, and who finished writing in the following year, 1077, have been mistaken?

For my part, I am not compelled to say this by the words of Andrew, who states in no. 80 that, after Ariald had gained the palm of martyrdom, God “in the tenth year afterward joined Herlembald, his faithful companion, to him in the kingdom of heaven, in which tenth year these things were written to the praise of God and of his servant Ariald.”

No, I say, these words do not move me. For there I see Andrew concerned to discover a number ten in matters relating to Ariald. To find it among the years lying between the two deaths, he could count incomplete years, counting as the first the very year in which Ariald was killed, although half of it had already elapsed. Thus “the tenth afterward” would be the very year assigned by Arnulf—and one that I cannot dispute with him—namely, 1075.

Two years later, after King Henry had been received into ecclesiastical communion, “the Milanese people, guilty through their association with Tetald”—since divine law forbade communion with an excommunicated man—“sent envoys to the lord pope and implored absolution. I myself,” says Arnulf, “was present at that embassy, making satisfaction for the past and promising correction in the future.”

Accordingly, had he needed or been able to write the same history again, he would have corrected the harsher things he had written against “the saints Ariald and Herlembald”—unless perhaps he still persisted in his former opinion, namely, that although those men pursued a just cause, they did not pursue it justly, because they exceeded the measure and limits assigned to each order.

This, certainly, was the opinion he retained, though by then somewhat amended, when he wrote in Puricellus, p. 329:

> “If there are good sayings or deeds of others, we do not reject them, nor do we in any way dissent from all those who condemn venal consecrations and the incontinence of the sacred orders, provided only that we do not depart from the authority of Paul. For he says: ‘Let all things be done decently and according to order’” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

23. Andrew judged that Herlembald had not sinned against this law, when he declared in no. 34 that he had been “crowned with martyrdom in defense of justice.” Nor did Pope Gregory think otherwise, when he wrote to “Wifred, a Milanese soldier,” whom he had learned, after Herlembald’s killing, “to have recovered his spirit and courage in order to strengthen the soldiers of Christ.”

He expresses his mind still more clearly and fully in his letter to the aforesaid Liprand, which Puricellus, p. 327, quotes from Liprand’s nephew Landulf of St. Paul:

> **GREGORY, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to LIPRAND, priest: greeting and apostolic blessing.**
>
> “If we venerate the memory of the saints, whose death and mutilation of limbs we read about; if we praise the endurance of those whom neither sword nor any punishment separated from the faith of Christ, then you too, whose nose and ears have been cut off for Christ’s name, are more worthy of praise, since you have merited to attain that grace which all should desire, and by which—if you persevere to the end—you are not separated from the saints.
>
> “The integrity of your body has indeed been diminished; but the inner person, who is renewed day by day, receives a great increase of holiness. Your visible form has become more disfigured, but the image of God, which is the form of righteousness, has become more pleasing through diminution and more beautiful through disgrace. Hence, in the Song of Songs, the Church glories, saying: ‘I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem’ (Song of Songs 1:5).
>
> “And if your inner appearance has suffered no loss through these mutilations, the priestly office, which belongs properly to holiness, has not been cut away from you. It is considered not so much in the integrity of the limbs as in the integrity of the virtues. Hence the emperor Constantine often kissed the eye of a certain bishop of Jerusalem”—namely St. Maximus, whose feast was discussed on 5 May—“which had been torn out for Christ’s name; and from the example of the Fathers and the teaching of our predecessors we have learned not to deprive martyrs of their sacred office because of such mutilation of their limbs.

24. “Therefore, martyr of Christ, take courage in the Lord. Believe all the more that the office of the priesthood is now in you: previously it was entrusted through the anointing of oil, but now through the staining of your blood. And the less you possess that can be taken away, the less you should fear to proclaim what is true and to sow what will be returned a hundredfold.

“We know that you have always been hated and afflicted by the enemies of the holy Church. But do not fear or be terrified of them, because, under the protection of ourselves and of the Apostolic See, we hold not merely you but all that belongs to you with great charity. And if it should be necessary for you in any matter to appeal to the Apostolic See, we grant you permission. If you come to us and to our see, we are ready to receive you with joy and great honor.”

Would that the letters also existed which Gregory is credibly believed to have sent, after learning of Herlembald’s death, to those who announced it—letters full of esteem and affection, as well as approval of his deeds. They could likewise silence the mouths of those who speak unjustly of him, just as they do of St. Ariald. For now, let us continue to gather from Puricellus whatever remains that we can collect to the honor of both men, introducing the words of the authors whom he represents.

## CHAPTER IV. Monuments erected to Saints Herlembald and Ariald at St. Dionysius

25. Pope Gregory VII died in 1085, the tenth year after Herlembald’s killing; Henschenius illustrated his life as a saint on 25 May. In that same year and on the same day, or at least on the following day, Tetald, the false archbishop of Milan, also died at Arona. Anselm succeeded him, while the Roman See remained vacant for nearly two years.

Puricellus does not dare to free Anselm’s appointment from the defect of the preceding elections. The very vacancy of the Apostolic See that I mentioned gave Henry—who was most eager to maintain investiture—a convenient opportunity to usurp the jurisdiction that Gregory VII had denied him.

It is unnecessary here to discuss how this Anselm conducted himself when he received ordination, from whom he received it, or when. It is enough to say that Berthold of Constance, a writer belonging to the papal party, says that he died in 1093 “most devoted to the cause of St. Peter.” He must therefore have been received and recognized as the true successor of St. Ambrose either by Pope Victor III, who was ordained at Pentecost in 1086, or by Pope Urban II, who subsequently governed the Catholic Church for eleven years and several months.

For a letter from Urban to Anselm is preserved in Ivo, part VI, chapter 406, in these terms:

> “It seems to our judgment that, in accordance with the tenor of our command, when, according to the custom of your Church, you begin to bless those to whom you are about to give holy orders, you should cause those whom your prudence determines ought to be reconciled to be present during the blessing and the laying on of hands. You shall complete for them all the other instruments of consecration except anointing, and thus reconcile them to the holy ministries.”

26. In 1095 Urban held a synod at Piacenza. According to Berthold of Constance:

> “The archbishop of Salzburg and the bishop of Passau from Bavaria attended it, as did the bishop of Constance from Alemannia; at the same time, by permission of the lord pope, they consecrated at Milan Arnulf, archbishop-elect of Milan, long elected but not yet consecrated.”

The pontiff himself then arrived there. What he did at Milan at that time was gathered by Puricellus from a certain marginal addition in a manuscript to the final chapter of book III of the *Annals of Landulf the Elder*. Nothing was more favorable to the memory of Herlembald than Arnulf himself.

After the marginal words “Herlembald is killed by Arnald of Raude,” the following is also read:

> “Verses over Herlembald’s tomb at St. Dionysius. Urban II entered him in the catalogue of holy martyrs; and, together with Archbishop Arnulf, he buried his body in the year 1091.”

Puricellus rightly thinks that “1095” should be read instead of “1091,” since Herlembald, standard-bearer and defender of the Church, was killed by the Church’s adversaries.

> Here lies Herlembald, a reverend soldier of Christ,  
> Who, slain, is said to possess heaven’s dwelling.  
> He condemns incest and damns simony;  
> The servants of Venus and wicked Simon kill him.  
> Urban, called the supreme pontiff and the Second,  
> And our Arnulf, a pious and gentle shepherd,  
> Bury the translated remains of this blessed man.

27. That the place of the first burial was none other than the place to which the pope later transferred him is indicated for us by Peter Azarius in Puricellus, p. 22. He first relates that:

> “When the noble soldiers proscribed from Milan heard the good news concerning the archbishop who had been given to them”—although in truth he had not yet been given, but only promised—“they were greatly encouraged. Gathering friends from every quarter of the city of Milan, they attacked the city. Herlembald Gotta, the first lord of the people, learning of this, went out to meet the enemies. In the field he was met by Herlembald”—called Arnald by others—“of Raude, a proscribed soldier, who threw him from his horse and beheaded him.”

Azarius then adds:

> “Thus he died in holy confession and was buried in the church of Saints Protasius and Gervasius—that is, St. Dionysius, among the martyrs.”

Hieronymus Montius, a Milanese jurist and orator, later also senator and superintendent of public health, in a panegyric delivered in 1547, after praising Herlembald for other reasons, also praised him because “he caused a law to be promulgated in the Milanese Church that clergy could neither take wives nor enter into marriage … For that reason,” he says, “I find in the authors that offended clergy”—he would have spoken more accurately of their noble supporters—“inflicted death upon the man. But we know that the people, in memory of so celebrated a deed, paid him divine honors, and that his body, enclosed in an iron chest, was preserved in the church of St. Dionysius down to our own day.”

28. Bernardinus Corius, chapter 9, calls it “a chest surrounded by iron plates.” Paulus Morigia, in his *Milanese Sanctuary* of 1603, lists among the bodies still resting at that time in the church of St. Dionysius “the body of St. Herlembald the martyr.” He does so, however, on the authority of ancient chronicles rather than from present observation, because:

> “In 1549 Ferdinand Gonzaga, governor of Milan, wishing to surround the city with walls according to the requirements of military art, began by constructing the fortress of St. Dionysius. Although the church had been newly built, he cut away a considerable part of it—namely, the entire apse together with the sanctuary or sacred crypt.”

Puricellus appears to acknowledge, on p. 384, that on this occasion the monuments of “Saints Ariald and Herlembald” were destroyed. He writes:

> “If someone should finally ask whether the bodies of the saints still remain in this St. Dionysius—if not in the underground chapel, which we have admitted was destroyed, at least in the church in some form—and whether they were ever transferred elsewhere, I still have no reason to doubt anything concerning Herlembald’s body.”

29. As for St. Ariald, Landulf the Elder, his contemporary but a historian hostile to him through partisan zeal, after reporting some account of the discovery or display of the body—Puricellus did not wish to publish the details—writes in Puricellus, p. 12:

> “After many had doubted, many had rejoiced, and very many had believed, he was finally placed upon a bier, with a pall laid over him. When he had been taken up and adorned like a Levite with a stole, amid the greatest litanies, great rejoicing, and the gathering of very many people, he was buried in the monastery of St. Celsus.
>
> “After these things had been done, Herlembald and all his people, celebrating him as a new martyr with great ceremonies, diligently and devoutly worshiped him, deceived by a phantom image—as later became apparent in the time of the fourth Archbishop Anselm. For when, two years after his consecration”—that is, in 1099 according to my calculation elsewhere, also approved by Puricellus on p. 382—“Lord Anselm discovered how badly Ariald’s bones and body had once been buried in truth, he proceeded ceremonially with a few clerics to the place, gathered the bones that he could find, and buried them in the church of St. Dionysius.”

These words seem to indicate that the body which Herlembald transferred and buried at St. Celsus was not the true body of St. Ariald.

30. Puricellus judges that Landulf “lied splendidly” in this matter, just as when he said that, “after some days had passed since the first removal to the fortress of Travalla, the stench of his corpse occupied the entire castle, so that everyone became nauseated and fled.”

Just as this is certainly false, as we saw above from the more truthful witness blessed Andrew, so too the account of bones secretly removed from the aforesaid fortress ought to be considered fabricated by the enemies. Perhaps the archbishop searched for one of the feet—which had been cut off from the dead man, no. 74—in the aforesaid place; or perhaps he sought the right hand, ears, and other limbs that had been cut off from the living man at the place of execution, and joined them to the rest of the body buried at St. Celsus, then transferred the whole to St. Dionysius, intending to give them a monument near the monument of St. Herlembald.

The copyist who transcribed the histories of this Landulf and then of Arnulf noted in the margin, in Puricellus, p. 11:

> “It is not surprising if this historian, and the one who follows, do not praise this Ariald, because they were supporters of married, concubinary, and simoniacal priests, by whom blessed Ariald suffered.”

Then, in the same margin, he copied the verses found “over the tomb of St. Ariald,” but as though they should be read consecutively as follows. It seems probable to me, however, that two or even three epigrams are present here: one of them may have been affixed or carved upon the chest, another upon the sarcophagus or apse, and the third may have been common to both, with an inscription written between the two monuments.

[Col. 1502C] 31. The writer seems to have indicated this when he adds: “These three verses speak of Ariald and Herlembald,” namely, the last three, copied as follows:

> Venerate in every way these three holy treasures,  
> These champions of Christ, O illustrious people of Milan,  
> Born from the blood of that saint.

I would assign the first three verses to the chest, adding to them one verse taken from Herlembald’s epitaph, which is very useful for completing the defective sense:

> The Levite-martyr Ariald lies in this urn.  
> He dies mutilated, but wins the gifts of life;  
> In this worthy mausoleum he is reverently laid;  
> He condemns incest and damns simony.

[Col. 1502D] Likewise, three other verses intended for placement over the sarcophagus seem to lack their beginning. I shall borrow it from the same epitaph of Ariald:

> While he restrains the servants of Venus and wicked Simon;

Then I shall append three verses that will at least yield some sense:

> For these twin causes Ariald suffered at their hands,  
> A Levite-martyr buried in this church.  
> Anselm the shepherd transferred the venerable body.

32. Whatever the exact truth of these matters may be, Puricellus cites on p. 14 a manuscript “concerning the archbishops of Milan, from St. Barnabas to John Arcimboldus”—that is, down to the year 1550—“to which certain materials collected by N. Fontana have been added.” Here, “from Andrea Alciati’s *Antiquarian*,” under the name of Archbishop Guido, it is noted as follows:

> “Under this Guido of Velate, a valvassor, there was the tomb of Ariald, from the family of Alciati. He was placed among the saints by Alexander II and buried in a marble tomb at St. Dionysius. But in 1508, by Louis XII, king of France, he was transferred to Paris in place of the body of St. Dionysius.”

The year 1509 would perhaps be more accurately recorded, since it is known that the king was then in Insubria, allied with the Emperor Maximilian and Pope Julius against the Venetians. Having fought a battle at the Adda, he won a great victory.

It seems that the king requested the body of St. Dionysius of Milan so that he might join it to two other St. Dionysiuses: the Parisian, whom the common people believed to be the Areopagite, and the bishop of Corinth, whose body was transferred there around 1215, as Henschenius discussed on 8 April. But when the Milanese pleaded that they not be deprived of their patron, he may have departed content with the body of St. Ariald. What happened to that body afterwards I have so far been unable to discover.

33. Puricellus, p. 15, also quotes another epitaph, although I do not know whether it was not composed by Alciati himself. It was certainly transcribed by Fontana in the highly praised *Antiquarian* of Alciati, and perhaps was never placed anywhere.

### TO ARIALD THE DEACON

> He, who better than any other conveyed  
> The mysteries of God in words, and alone was on the people’s lips;  
> Who dared to correct fallen morals  
> And the errors of Thyasus [reading uncertain];  
> Here is Ariald. Alas, the guilty life of the wicked,  
> Which cannot bear any censor!  
> Secretly seized and hung upon a millstone,  
> He was cast into the waves of Lake Verbano, to become food for swift fish.  
> Then, once found, with his body unharmed,  
> Later generations deemed him a new martyr worthy of the temples.

[Col. 1503]

# APPENDIX. ON THE VENERABLE PRIEST AND CONFESSOR LIPRAND

## § I. Grossulanus, Anselm’s successor, is convicted of simony by the judgment of fire

1. Since Landulf the Elder, in Puricellus, p. 13, charges the priest “Leoprand”—who accompanied Herlembald when he exposed himself to the utmost danger “with a few armed men”—with the crime that “he too carried the cross in his own hand, not to calm the combatants, but rather to incite his own combatants, himself an enemy to the enemies,” and since we have seen him mutilated in nose and ears and compared by Pope Gregory VII with the martyrs, I am pleased to pursue his deeds to the end, insofar as they can be gathered from Puricellus, and to refute Landulf’s abuse by the facts themselves.

Because of these deeds and because of the merit of his Catholic confession, Liprand was held in the highest esteem by all the faithful of the Apostolic See. The younger Landulf bears witness to this for us in Puricellus, p. 388, where he writes:

> “When his father Henry was still alive”—Henry being rebellious against the Church and excommunicated—“Cono, at the urging of Pope Urban II, through the intervention of Countess Matilda and the offices of Anselm of Chode”—the Milanese archbishop—“and Armannus of Brescia, was crowned at Monza in the church of St. Ambrose in the year 1093. He did not heed the ordination of these pontiffs, but, while reigning in the place called Borgo San Donnino”—a town midway between Piacenza and Parma—“he saw the priest Liprand, mutilated in nose and ears because of the Pataria, going to Urban, the Roman pontiff. The king himself said to that priest with devotion: ‘Since you are the teacher of the Patarines, what do you think of bishops and priests who possess royal rights but provide the king with no sustenance?’ And the priest himself, without any resentment, answered according to the good pleasure of God and of the king.”

2. First of all, it must be noted from Hugh of Flavigny, quoted by Du Cange in the *Glossary*, that “if there were anyone who communicated with Gregory”—and understand the same of Urban, his successor after Victor—“he was called a heretic, a destroyer of the kingdom, and by a certain invented name a Patarine.”

This name was subsequently transferred to the Waldenses and other heretics. See Du Cange at the cited place, where he supposes that the faithful were then first called by this name “because they adhered to the pope, whom they called father.”

It was in this sense that, on p. 300, Landulf the Elder accused Herlembald, saying that, through his power, which the schismatics who adhered to the king detested, “the number and strength of the Patarines increased so greatly in the villages and towns, and in certain cities under his own leadership, that he seemed to be lord of all his fellow citizens.”

I am not surprised that Landulf the Elder spoke in this way. But I am surprised that the younger Landulf, a Catholic writer and Liprand’s nephew, should use the term *Pataria*. The king, standing as though between his excommunicated father and Pope Urban, seems to have regarded those called Patarines in his father’s court with suspicion. He used the same name in his own court insofar as through them royal power appeared to be diminished and transferred in part to the pope.

Liprand, for his part, seems to have given the king who questioned him an answer that was not displeasing. “Nevertheless, on the following day, while he was traveling with the priest Arnald, master of the Milanese schools, and Syro, a priest of the church of St. Mary Podone, he was captured by the men of the bishop of Parma.” From this it is clear that the bishop was a schismatic, so that Ughellus, vol. II, col. 213, ought not to have been greatly distressed that “envious antiquity erased his name.”

3. Thus captured by his enemies, Liprand, as the younger Landulf continues, “was led away, enduring punishment, to a place whose name is absent or uncertain in the source; he was kept there and stripped for four days, and from there returned to Milan. The king himself, as I heard from those robbers, accepted compensation”—that is, a fine or satisfaction for the injury inflicted upon the priest—“and the priest’s mule.”

By doing so, he made himself an accomplice in the crime that he ought to have avenged severely. Nor did he escape punishment for this:

> “For he soon attempted to go into Tuscany, and when the king had reached Florence, he himself—a young man otherwise prudent, wise, and handsome in appearance … ended his life.”

Since Domnizo says in the *Life of Matilda* that this happened in the “third year after Urban the pope had passed away,” the injury must have been inflicted on Liprand in 1101, when he was going not to Urban—who had died in 1099—but to Urban’s successor, Paschal II.

It is easy and forgivable, however, to pardon this lapse of memory in Landulf, just as one may pardon his belief, based on rumor, that the king died “after receiving a potion from Avianus, Matilda’s physician.” Domnizo says instead that, after peace had been restored with Matilda, “Conrad was struck by a fever”—it was the month of July—“and died.”

If Cono nevertheless sinned by failing to avenge Liprand, he must have washed away that sin by final repentance, if—as Urspergensis writes—those who attended the dying man truly “testified that they had suddenly seen the sign of the cross appear on the arm of his lifeless body, and that his funeral rites had been honored by certain miracles.”

Nor was this undeserved, since he preferred due obedience to the pontiff to filial affection and reverence. Therefore, “with full faith and a good confession, he is believed to have passed from the transitory kingdom into the eternal kingdom.”

4. Meanwhile, it had happened that Archbishop Anselm undertook a pilgrimage to Jerusalem and appointed as his vicar a certain Grossulanus, the Elect of Savona. He “admonished the people to assemble every week on Monday at St. Ambrose’s and to sing litanies for that Archbishop Anselm and his army. He himself, however, not only on those weekdays but on every feastday, preached eloquently to the people of the great city, and in preaching he sought to win them to himself no more than by the harshness of his clothing and his own . . .” Thus “he labored for two years,” until “he received certainty of the aforesaid Anselm’s death,” which occurred at Constantinople in 1011, on September 30.

When he had received this information, he ordered “the primicerius and the ordinarii,” he said, “of the greater church, while I am present, to choose for themselves and the people a suitable archbishop before I returned to the bishopric of Savona. Then the primicerius, having taken counsel with the noble clerics and men of Milan, in the presence of the people and of Grossulanus himself, elected another of the Landulfi, an ordinarius of the Milanese Church, one of those returning from Jerusalem; but Grossulanus forbade an election to be made of an absent person. Therefore part of the clergy and people, at the command of Arialdus, abbot of the monastery [Col. 1506A] of St. Dionysius, shouted and acclaimed Grossulanus as their archbishop. As soon as he saw that he had been acclaimed by a large multitude of the common people and nobles and applauded by that abbot, he ascended the archiepiscopal seat and sat upon it; and he transferred that abbot from one abbey to another, namely to the greater abbey of Clavatense.”

5. “Before this transfer, however, it happened that certain Milanese men and clerics who seemed [superior] in life and conduct reported certain shameful matters concerning Grossulanus and his election to the priest Liprandus. The priest himself advised these men and clerics to send letters and two suitable clerics to Rome, asking the pope not to confirm Grossulanus in the archbishopric [Col. 1506B] until he had seen and heard the senders of the letters in the near future.

“But Bernard, abbot of Valle Ombrosa and a Roman cardinal, paid no attention to these letters and messengers before the pope and the Roman curia. Instead, having received the stole, he entered the court of Countess Matilda; and there, after taking counsel, at the pleasure of Ardericus of Carimate, who had gone to Rome on behalf of Grossulanus and with the stole, that abbot Bernard hurried to Rome. When Ardericus saw Milan from a distance, he carried the same [stole] on an extended staff” (perhaps “protensum” [extended] is a kind of umbrella) “to the greater church of the city, shouting: ‘Here is the stole, here is the stole!’ At this shout the entire multitude of the people gathered and acclaimed: ‘Let whoever contradicts it die.’ This great and continuous shouting [Col. 1506C] continued until that cardinal-abbot and Grossulanus ascended the pulpit of Milan’s greater church. And when both of them seemed there to be afflicted in body, downcast in face, and distinguished in speech, they heard such applause as though they were truly angels of God.

“There Grossulanus, clothed in the stole, and the abbot, rewarded in due course, rested and departed; and a few days later, in favor with the aforesaid Countess Matilda, that same abbot accepted the bishopric of Parma.”

He was plainly a holy man, as the Life to be read on December 4 will show; therefore, on his part we can suspect no vice of simony here.

6. Meanwhile Liprandus did not consent to accept Grossulanus. The latter, however, “tried to terrify with threats all whom he could not win over by flattery, especially the priest [Col. 1506D] Liprandus,” as is read in the *Monumenta Ambrosiana*, p. 493.

When Grossulanus had convened a synod to suppress the disturbances that were growing against him, and had summoned the people to an assembly, he said: “If anyone wishes to say anything against me, let him say it now; but if he remains silent at this time, he shall no longer have a hearing against me.”

When this was reported to the priest Liprandus, he himself summoned many citizens to the church of St. Paul on that day and said to them:

“You see me mutilated in nose and ears for the name of Christ; therefore a great reward has been promised me if I persevere to the end. For the love of Christ and for your salvation and peace, I ask you to attend to me and to what I shall say to you.”

After saying these and many other blessed and well-sounding things, especially against [Col. 1507A] simony, he proposed the following accusation:

“Grossulanus, who is regarded as archbishop, is a simoniac concerning the archbishopric of Milan: by a gift from the hand, by a gift from the tongue, and by a gift from service.”

As he continued with his charge, he very frequently urged everyone to assemble for the true examination of this accusation by divine judgment, confirmed in his life or death and manifested through him. But Grossulanus’s faction disrupted this through the authority of the bishops who had come to Milan to celebrate a synod with Grossulanus. Nevertheless, the priest himself, disputing against the bishops with arguments and examples, defended his position and did not abandon it.

Grossulanus, however, disregarding the priest’s words as though they had not been spoken in his presence, conducted his synod in the church of St. Mary for two days . . .

7. “Nevertheless, Grossulanus’s faction, fighting against the primicerius Landulfus, killed that primicerius’s cleric with a stone. Then, as though with the consent of the whole city, the priest was told to gather much wood for the ordeal in the field enclosed by a wall beside the monastery of St. Ambrose.

“The priest himself, filled with great spiritual strength, pawned the grain and wine that he had for food, and his tunic of wolfskin, to obtain the wood. He ordered that the rest of what he possessed in books and other goods be preserved for his nephew and pupil Landulfus” (the very man who would later write these things), “who at that time was studying at Orléans under the excellent master Alfred and the noble Jacob.

“He also ordered that, if he himself should die in that ordeal, whatever remained of his body should be carried to the church of the Holy Trinity, which he himself had founded on his own estate and given to Blessed Peter.

“After these things had been settled and arranged, the same priest went to St. Ambrose’s church. When he was about to undergo the ordeal, Grossulanus’s power prevailed: he scattered the wood that had been laid out in the field and disgracefully removed the priest from that arrangement.

“Afterward the priest kept silent and remained at rest in his own house and in the church of St. Paul, until shortly afterward boys and girls, men and women, shouted: ‘Out, out, Grossulanus!’

8. “Wishing to suppress this outcry, Grossulanus took counsel with his satellites and said to them: ‘Go yourselves and publicly choose men from the people to tell Liprandus either to come to me for satisfaction, or to leave this land, or to perform the ordeal that he promised to undergo.’

“His advisers therefore came from his side to the people’s assembly in the evening of Palm Sunday, on the Sunday of palm or olive branches” (that is, March 30; for the year was 1102, and Easter was to be celebrated on April 6), “and publicly announced what they had heard from their lord Grossulanus.

“Accordingly, not only did the men chosen at the assembly come to deliver this message to the priest, but an innumerable multitude of people came to confirm the message. At their outcry, as they shouted, ‘Let the priest Liprandus himself come!’ he came out humbly. When he heard and understood the message, he raised his hands to heaven, gave thanks to God, and asked the messengers:

“‘Does he himself wish and command what you tell me?’

“They all replied: ‘Indeed, he wishes and commands it.’

“And the priest said to them: ‘I shall not leave the land, but during these two days I shall fast, and on Wednesday, God willing, I shall perform the ordeal. But I have no means to buy the wood.’”

9. “Then the officials of Grossulanus and of the commonwealth bought oak wood, especially suitable for flame and heat, for thirty solidi of denarii. They arranged it in two piles facing one another in the field before the atrium of St. Ambrose’s church. Each pile was ten cubits long, while its height and width were four cubits, greater than a man’s stature; the path between the piles was one and a half cubits wide.

“When these things had been arranged and certain pieces of wood had been placed in the path between them, on Wednesday the priest, dressed in a hair shirt, tunic, and chasuble in priestly fashion, carried a cross barefoot from the church of St. Paul to the church of the Holy Martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and of the most blessed Ambrose. Since the other priests had failed, he himself sang Mass at their altar.

“When Mass had been sung, Grossulanus also entered the same church carrying a cross, and ascended the pulpit with Arialdus of Meregnano and Berardus, judge of Asti. When silence had been made among the people, and the priest was standing barefoot on the marble stone at the entrance to the choir that contains an image of Hercules, Grossulanus said to the people:

“‘Pay attention, because with three words I shall defeat this man and expose his disgrace.’

“And he said to the priest: ‘You have charged that I am a simoniac by a gift from the hand. Now say to whom I gave it.’”

10. “Then the priest opened his eyes toward the people and pointed his finger at those standing on the pulpit, saying:

“‘Look at the three greatest devils, who think that by their ingenuity and money they can put me to shame. Could not that devil who persuaded him to become a simoniac through money persuade him to give still more money, conceal the truth, and deprive me of worldly witnesses and judges? And do you not know that, to avoid the cunning of the devil and wicked men, I chose God as judge—God who cannot be bribed by money or deceived in judgment? If you wish to come to his judgment, I am ready to do what I promised.’

“Grossulanus said to him: ‘Now say: what kind of simony do you mean?’

“The priest replied: ‘Now you say: which kind is good?’

“Grossulanus leapt up somewhat and said: ‘It is simony when it does not depose a simoniac.’

“The priest said: ‘I mean that which removes an abbot from his abbey, a bishop from his bishopric, and an archbishop from the archbishopric in which he is.’

“When he had satisfied everyone with these words, he heard the people shouting: ‘Go out to the judgment! Go out to the judgment!’

“Amid this repeated shouting, the priest, although an old man, sprang down from the stone containing the image of Hercules and came with the people into the field where the piles of wood stood. While the fire was being lit beneath the wood, he said:

“‘You see no priest here except me to bless this fire; but you see this document that I hold, containing holy words and the signs of the holy cross. As minister, I shall say and make these signs below, and God, who is my Lord, shall bless the fire from above.’

“Hearing and understanding this well, they said: ‘Amen.’”

11. “After he had said these words around the fire, made the signs, and sprinkled blessed water and incense over the fire, while Grossulanus stood there, Grossulanus and Arialdus of Meregnano—who was virtually Grossulanus’s most powerful prince and the supervisor of the ordeal—began to doubt the proper ordering of the sacrament. Arialdus was waiting for the priest either to end his life by death in the fire or, through excessive terror, to turn to his lord.

“For he had said to Berardus, the judge of Asti, who condemned this law not only when it resulted in death but also for any burn injury inflicted upon the priest: ‘God forbid that there should be an injury; but I shall magnify the fire so greatly that, from a distance, the fire will tear his eyes out of his head, and he, burning in the fire, will rot into ashes.’

“Nevertheless, when the priest saw them doubting about the ordering of the sacrament, he said to them:

“‘Let me proceed; I shall order it properly. Nor shall I complete the sacrament until I have said as much as satisfies you.’

“Immediately, with their consent, he seized Grossulanus’s cloak and shook it, saying:

“‘This Grossulanus who is beneath this cloak—and I speak of no other—is a simoniac concerning the archbishopric of Milan, by a gift from the hand, by a gift from the tongue, and by a gift from service.’

“When this seemed sufficient to them, he added:

“‘And I do not enter this ordeal trusting in any magic, enchantment, or spell.’”

12. “After this sacrament had been performed, Grossulanus mounted his horse in agreement with everyone and went to the church of St. John called ‘at the Conch.’ Arialdus of Meregnano, however, inquiring into and awaiting the full effect of the fire, detained the priest. While detaining him, he felt his own hand injured by the heat of the fire; nevertheless he said to the priest:

“‘Priest Liprandus, I have seen your death in the fire. Turn to my lord the archbishop, with your life assured; otherwise go and burn under God’s curse.’

“The priest replied: ‘Satan, go back.’

“When Arialdus withdrew, the priest rose from the ground where he had fallen. After making the sign of the cross over himself, the great flame of the fire divided toward the south and north, and a path appeared, which the priest entered. As he passed through the burning coals, he felt as though he were walking on sand; and while he crossed by that path, the flame closed behind him.

“He himself told me, and I understood him clearly: ‘While I was on the path of this fire, I offered this prayer to God:’

“‘God, save me in your name, and deliver me by your power; God, save me in your name, and deliver me by your power; God, save me in your name, and deliver me by your power’ (Psalm 53:3).

“When he pronounced the word ‘save’ for the third time, he saw himself outside the fire. He felt no injury, either to himself or to his priestly garments of linen and silk, in which he was dressed, or to his hair shirt.

“Then the people, as though with one voice, offered praise to God and to this priest throughout the city, both outside it and within. Grossulanus, however, undaunted, abandoned the archiepiscopal see and the city, because it had been sworn by the common voice of the city that neither of them, nor anyone belonging to their faction, would suffer harm on account of this action, except whatever the Lord might do to him.”

Thus far Puricellus, p. 399 and following.

§ II. The Rest of Liprandus’s Life and His Death, Made Renowned by Miracles

13. So brilliant a miracle did not immediately produce every effect that had been hoped for. “But because the presence of the suffragan bishops did not fully grant their favor to this judgment and triumph; because the fire injured the priest’s hand while he was throwing water and incense upon it; and because the foot of John of Rode’s horse severely trampled the priest’s bare foot as he emerged from the fire, the crowd, saddened by Grossulanus’s downfall and ruin, soon became hostile to the priest and his judgment; and, by becoming hostile, at the urging of certain priests, committed many battles and murders.

“Meanwhile Grossulanus found Pope Paschal favorable to him. Landulfus of Vareglate”—one of the previously mentioned electors, rejected because of his absence—“returning from Jerusalem, arrived in Rome; and there he learned from Grossulanus, who had already returned” (as may be read in the *Monumenta Ambrosiana*, p. 596), “not only what had been done at Milan because of the dispute between the priest and Grossulanus, but also [Col. 1510C] how solemnly the Roman pontiff had received Grossulanus after other events . . . . . .

“Nevertheless, when that Landulfus of Vareglate came to Milan, he did not directly despise either the priest or his judgment. Rather, promising the Milanese clergy and people that he would depose Grossulanus from every ecclesiastical office according to the rule of the canons, he said:

“‘While you contend over the judgment of the priest Liprandus and Grossulanus, why do you wage battles and commit murders among yourselves? I tell you with complete certainty, and through John of Vicomercato I command Grossulanus, that before Lord Pope Paschal and his curia or synod I shall prove, with certain arguments and with just and holy canons, that he cannot remain among the bishops or priests, or even in any order of clerics.’

“The clergy and people, however, trusting this authentic man—who, with a certain novelty, was canonically provost of St. Nazarius and an ordinarius of Milan’s greater church—endeavored to reach the Roman synod together with Grossulanus.

“Then Amizo of Landriano, the stern and wise captain of the Milanese, said: ‘You wish to deny’” (that is, to drown) “‘the otter’” (that is, *lutra*, an amphibious animal) “‘in water’; that is, you are laboring in vain.”

14. “But Grossulanus, prostrate at the feet of the pope, again found refuge for himself and his followers. The priest Liprandus, however, since he was already an old man and two years had passed after the judgment he had performed”—and thus it was the year 1103—“being summoned and virtually compelled, came to the synod at Rome. At that synod the aforesaid Landulfus [Col. 1511A] of Vareglate, who after that synod became bishop of Asti”—perhaps corrupted by prayer or payment in favor of the accused—“did not utter a single dishonoring word against Grossulanus before the pope, his curia, or the synod,” contrary to what he had promised at Milan.

“But the priest Liprandus plainly reported the case that he had against Grossulanus. The pope did not praise the judgment given by the priest and marked by sacrament and fire; rather, he confirmed in him the grace and office of the priesthood and said:

“‘If this priest swore, and twelve priests swore together with him, affirming under oath that Grossulanus forced the priest to walk through the fire, Grossulanus would endure deposition.’

“He granted them one night to deliberate on this matter. After that night had passed, the pope received from Grossulanus before the synod an oath in which Grossulanus said:

“‘I, Grossulanus, archbishop by the grace of God, did not force the aforesaid priest Liprandus to go into the fire.’

“Then Ardericus, bishop of Lodi, also confirmed the same under oath. When Azo, bishop of Acqui, offered to swear the same on Grossulanus’s behalf, the pope excused him from doing so.

“Grossulanus then approached to receive restoration. As he approached to receive restoration, the *gabuta* and pastoral staff, which Grossulanus was holding in his hand, fell to the ground before the synod. This sign was, to many, an indication that his oath was an oath of death.

“Nevertheless, neither the pope nor his synod paid attention to this at that time. He restored Grossulanus—at the request of Azo of Acqui, Ardericus of Lodi, Jordan of Clivio, and the other Milanese, both clerics and laymen, indeed also the suffragan bishops of that Church—so that he might be archbishop, though without active authority.”

15. “That priest Landulfus, although because of this restoration he was suspected by the restored Grossulanus and by those who received him back, nevertheless remained a suitable priest in his office in the church of St. Paul and in his own house for seven years after that restoration,” until after the year 1115.

“But while each regarded the other with suspicion, it happened that Heribertus of Bruzano, severely afflicted with fevers, came to the said priest, begging him to give him a remedy against his illness. The priest’s servants supplied the sick man with suitable food and a bed, until the Lord of Hosts, through the laying on of that priest’s hands, provided the sick man with a healing remedy.

“Grossulanus, provoked by this, said to the priest:

“‘Because you have associated with Heribertus, my excommunicated man, I command you not to sing Mass until you have undertaken penance for it and satisfied me.’

“The priest replied:

“‘What I did for Heribertus was good and came from God; and I do not know how to repent of what was good and of God’s work. Although you have no authority over me, nevertheless, to avoid scandal, I shall obey you.’”

16. Furthermore, “through the favor of Guilielmus, abbot [Col. 1512A] of St. Ambrose, and Andrea, primicerius of Milan, and many other prudent men, both clerics and laymen, Grossulanus possessed neither the see nor any stronghold of the archbishopric after the first judgment performed by the priest or the restoration carried out by the synod.

“My often-mentioned uncle, however, within a year and a half, dismissed the men who were not contending out of love for divine law and ecclesiastical discipline, left their city, and settled in the Valtellina valley, more than seventy miles from Milan.”

What happened to him when he returned from there after some time, Landulfus relates as follows in Puricellus, p. 417:

“Having taken the horse of Anselm,” my brother, “and my own, I hurried with my said brother to my patron. When I had gone twenty-five miles, an angel met me and said: ‘The priest Liprandus, returning from Valtellina, lies ill at the monastery of Clivate.’

“Thus, sooner than I had expected, I found him sitting on a bed and eating milk. When he saw me, he raised both hands and gave thanks to God. When Arialdus, the abbot of that monastery, heard that I had arrived and had given consolation to the sick man, he called me and my brother outside the room. He indicated to us in many words that he feared for the loyalty he had sworn to Grossulanus; and, without the monks’ knowledge, he advised us to carry the sick man away from the monastery, at least two miles.”

17. “When the sick man perceived that my brother and I were concerned about his illness and removal, he said:

“‘Do not be troubled, because by God’s grace I am now much better, and tomorrow, with God’s favor, we shall travel to the city.’

“When morning came, he put on certain of his patched garments and took food, and, as though he had recovered, mounted a mule. His boy also had his own donkey loaded with skins. Although the boy was usually seized by a falling sickness two or three times a day, nevertheless, while the priest sat on the mule, the boy came with us in a single day as far as St. Damian of Baraza, without any hindrance from that illness.

“There, by the grace of God and of the most blessed Ambrose, whose cell this place is, we were well received and spent the night. We remained through half of the following day, and before sunset entered the church of St. Paul and our house, and made our household who were there joyful.”

At that time the Milanese were at war with the people of Lodi. Concerning this, Landulfus says in Puricellus’s *Monumenta*, p. 528:
