“Nor do I enumerate the innumerable evils that they brought about during the four years of that war,” he says; “but I mourn the death of my brother Anselm and of many other relatives and fellow citizens of mine, revealed through that war; nor do I entirely abandon the undertaking I began.

“For while that city of Lodi still stood and resisted the Milanese, who were attempting to destroy it, Grossulanus was exiled from Milan, and that Ardericus of Lodi very rarely entered his own city but frequently visited Milan. The priest Liprandus, however, awaited the consolation of the kingdom and of the Church in his house and in his church [near] the church of St. Paul.”

18. Nor did he wait in vain. In October 1111, because of the rivers swollen by continuous rain “so that they disturbed not only the villages but the city itself in a remarkable manner,” and because some people said that “the discord concerning Grossulanus was a wickedness deserving another Flood,” eighteen men were chosen to end it. All swore as follows:

“By the Kalends of next January we shall unanimously give a just and correct judgment, according to the canons, concerning the dispute over whether Grossulanus can be archbishop of Milan or not; and if he cannot be, on that same day we shall unanimously conduct a canonical election of another person.”

Those whom the eighteen expressly summoned for this purpose—priests and knights—likewise swore to uphold “the judgment.”

“But when on the last day of December,” Landulfus says in the *Monumenta*, p. 541, “that Ardericus”—left by Grossulanus as vicar in the city when Grossulanus had gone to Jerusalem—“and the other seventeen were in agreement to elect Jordan, I came to them at the command of Andrea, primicerius of the decanal priests and clerics of Milan. As that primicerius had ordered me, I told them that they had been badly advised.

“Nevertheless, they did not change their decision. When morning came, namely on the Kalends of January” of the year 1112, as is further read in Puricellus from Landulfus [Col. 1513C] in the *Life of Herlembald*, p. 412, “Ardericus, together with the vicedominus and the others bound to him by oath, ascended the pulpit. When silence had been made among the people, he spoke before that great multitude, saying:

“‘Saving the reverence due to the pope, according to the authority and justice of the canons we declare that Grossulanus cannot be archbishop of Milan.’

“After this declaration had been made and confirmed, he immediately elected the priest Jordan of Clivio as archbishop.”

19. “When the priest Liprandus heard this, he rose sick from his bed, and on the following day offered the elected man a fish, saying:

“‘Thanks be to God, for now you bear witness to me. But those who elected you archbishop did wrong, and may God have mercy on them; for you could have been a good cloistered priest, but now be a male’” (*masculus esto*, sic).

“When that elected man, or any of the many bystanders, gave no answer to the priest, the priest himself came closer and, having kissed Jordan as one of the other priests, departed.”

In February, Jordan was consecrated by the suffragans Landulfus of Asti, Arialdus of Genoa, and Mamardus of Turin, with Pope Paschal’s approval. Eventually Paschal also consented to Grossulanus’s deposition in a sentence by which he “forbade Grossulanus to disturb the Milanese Church, and told him to return” to the bishopric of Savona, which he had formerly occupied. The stated reason was that, although “the transfers of bishops” could occur “in two ways,” it was clearly apparent that the usefulness of Grossulanus’s “transfer” had been turned into harm to souls and bodies.

After Jordan’s consecration had been completed, “Mamardus of Turin immediately went to Rome and requested the stole. On returning, he brought back the stole and a document containing the oath that the pope required from Jordan; otherwise the pope had forbidden the stole to be given to Jordan, as the same Mamardus noted. Jordan, therefore, remained fasting for six months and did not possess the stole.”

20. Then, as is reported on p. 145, “the priest Liprandus, being at the extreme end of old age,” said to me, his nephew Landulfus:

“‘I see that you are somewhat ashamed on my account because of what I said and did against Grossulanus. But so that you may be less ashamed, I tell you truthfully that I reserve that entire matter for God alone, and, while hope remains, I greatly desire to end my life in this world in the hands of those under whose protection, by divine grace, my body and soul may be guarded from the hands of those who, by protecting Grossulanus, have wished and still wish to conceal the will of God.

“‘Concerning this Milanese Church, in which you advise me to remain and end my life, I say that, since I desire to go to Jerusalem, it is like a ship rotting in harbor without a captain or helmsman. If you live according to your age, you will experience it in such a condition.’

“Following the counsel of this teacher of mine, when I wished entirely to abandon the administration of Jordan, the priest himself was taken to the monastery of Pontida, without my knowledge.”

According to Puricellus, p. 419, this monastery lies beyond the river Adda, and is now called St. James; only its name is marked on maps, thirty miles from Milan. Its founder Albertus had died in 1095, and therefore the discipline there was still recent.

“When the priest Liprandus had been placed in the monastery of Pontida, news of Grossulanus, returning from Jerusalem, filled the ears of Jordan and his ordinarii. The bishop Mamardus of Turin again came to Milan; and the stole which he had refused—and did not give—to Jordan in the preceding June” (this is how the text must be read; the manuscript reading is impossible, as the event itself shows), “he now placed upon the altar of St. Ambrose on the feast of St. Nicholas, when the priest Liprandus entered Pontida. Jordan kissed it and took it from the altar. This placing and taking occurred in the absence of the ordinarii and primicerii.”

21. “The priest Liprandus, in that monastery, lived splendidly”—that is, with great edification—“before the monks and brothers from the feast of St. Nicholas until the feast of the Epiphany of the Lord,” in the year 1113. “On the night of that same feast, when he gave up his spirit, a great and gentle radiance illuminated the house in which he lay, to the amazement of those standing around him, just as he himself had foretold to the brothers.

“At the hour when his body was carried to the tomb, the brightness of the sun illuminated the air, and the cloud with snow ceased.

“While the priest himself was still alive, when Grossulanus and the other Grossulanists were slandering him and his judgment, a noble soldier of Piacenza was rescued from the jaws of death to his praise. For when that soldier was as though asleep, he felt this priest touch his throat, and immediately he vomited out a fish bone that was choking him.

“At the same time, when the house of a certain kinsman, adjoining his own, was burning, rain suddenly fell and completely preserved both the straw and the house of the priest.

“If I were to run through individually all the things he did to his praise, my breath would fail . . . But may God, who lives and reigns throughout all ages, bless his soul now and forever. Amen.”

22. Thus far Landulfus, the nephew through his sister of “the priest Liprandus,” transcribed by Puricellus partly in the *Monumenta of the Ambrosian Basilica* and partly, and chiefly, in Book IV *Concerning Saints Arialdus and Herlembaldus*. I have cited the pages of these books because the author himself remains unpublished to this day, as do the *History of the Elder Landulfus* and that of Arnulfus, which Puricellus promised and prepared for publication, but which, so far as I know, were never published.

For the rest, neither Puricellus nor anyone else mentions any cult offered to Liprandus as a blessed man after his death. Nor does any monument of the deceased seem to survive in the church of Pontida, or beside it, where one may suppose that he was buried; for Puricellus, who examined everything relevant to the matter with the greatest diligence, adduces nothing of the kind.

Nevertheless, on the preceding day, where the subject was St. David the solitary of Thessalonica, probably transferred to Pavia, I conjectured that the body—or certain bones—of “the priest Liprandus” had also been transferred there from Pontida. For among the relics found there near the tomb of King Luitprand on July 24, 1514, besides “the bones and ashes of St. David himself,” there are also said to be some relics of “St. Thomas the martyr and St. Liprandus.” It is not easy to find another person of this name to whom the title of saint could have been given.

[Col. 1515]

# In the Year of the Lord 1072

## SAINT ANNO, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE

[Col. 1517]

# LIFE OF SAINT ANNO

Written in a grave style at the command of Reginhardus, abbot of the monastery of Sigeberg, by someone who nevertheless suppressed his name; he sufficiently indicates that he was a monk of the monastery of Sigeberg.

(Surius, *Lives of the Saints*, December 4.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1517A] **The reliability of this history.** Since it is customary for some people to devote themselves more to criticism than to fraternal correction; and since there are others, partly envious and partly ignorant of the facts, who hold contrary opinions about the matters promised by the course of the present work, we have this consolation in describing the life of the holy Father Anno: that a not insignificant obligation of obedience compelled us to undertake it; and that the man who is to proclaim his praises in public is himself regarded as a witness whom both the purity of his devotion and his knowledge of the facts impel to this very task. His authority also strengthens him so greatly that he is by himself capable of establishing the credibility of matters for which other witnesses are lacking.

This man is, I say, Father Reginhardus, venerable administrator [that is, abbot] of the monastery of Sigeberg. When he provided the form for what was to be written, he subjected me, the last of his household, entirely to this work, so that although I use my own words, I follow his meaning in every respect—just as children attempting their first lessons customarily reproduce the sound that the teacher’s voice has first pronounced.

The reward for the labor imposed belongs to him; he alone will be crowned in a special way for the advancement of his readers. Nothing is owed to us here, except that, by agreeing in obedience to him who commanded us, we have some ground for hoping to share in his rewards.

Whoever, therefore, mindful of the brute animal that once divinely broke forth into human speech (Numbers 22), deigns to listen to this history, will, I believe, not be greatly troubled by the lowliness of the person or of the words, provided that the whole narrative serves him whom the Psalmist both admonishes and commands “young men and maidens, old men with the younger” to praise among his saints (Psalm 148).

Let no one complain about the length. He whom we love and venerate, by whose alms and patronage we are sustained and governed day and night, can never be repaid by us with honor worthy of him. We do not doubt that every devout person feels the same about his own patron.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 1517]

[Col. 1517B] **I. Saint Anno’s parents. Saint Anno is assigned to military studies as a boy. His uncle persuades him to become a cleric. He makes remarkable progress in learning.**

Anno, the glory of his family and homeland, superior even to the stars in his merits, originated among the Alemannic peoples. His father was called Uvalterus, his mother Engela: both were distinguished by their devotion to religion and, although they were not especially celebrated in this world, they greatly surpassed that renown in the nobility that is directed toward God, being themselves nobly born of noble parents. Their fruitful offspring, spread among sons and daughters, produced a sufficiently illustrious family for their descendants, some of whom rose to ecclesiastical disciplines and others to secular pursuits.

Moreover, Anno, commending the nobility of his excellent character by his conduct, intelligence, and appearance, began to be regarded with favor by all eyes and loved by every heart. His father therefore, greatly rejoicing, although very religious, nevertheless, as a secular man eager for an earthly name, began to train him for the world through military exercises [Col. 1517C]. Assigned as a boy to such studies, Anno meanwhile learned the noblest strength of moral discipline, enduring frequent hardships from cold, suffering hunger and thirst, and, in addition, burning with sleeplessness. All these things were necessarily preparing him for his future formation.

But the heavenly Father, who “calls those whom he predestines” (Rom. 8), mercifully fulfilled at the end of time what he had arranged in Anno before the ages. For of him it is said in the truthful word: “There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21). Accordingly, with God inspiring him, the boy’s uncle, a canon of the Church of Bamberg, came to visit his homeland, relatives, and acquaintances. When he learned of the father’s settled plan concerning Anno, he immediately grieved, distressed that a child of such outstanding character should first be consumed by worldly affairs rather than formed in ecclesiastical disciplines for what would one day be [for] the benefit of many.

Therefore, having found a suitable opportunity, he approached the boy privately, embraced him affectionately, and asked: “Anno, my son, what studies or occupations do you pursue?” When the boy smiled sweetly and innocently, his uncle first briefly spoke, in language suitable for so young a child, about the glory of the heavenly kingdom and the punishments of hell [Col. 1518C], and then continued: “Do the service of the Almighty and the discipline or habit of the clerical order please you?”

When the boy readily agreed, his uncle, in an excess of joy, offered vows of thanksgiving to God in heart and speech. Then, turning to him, he said:

“Look: at daybreak tomorrow I shall depart and, God willing, will soon reach the place of my profession and order. But you, my son, casting aside domestic impediments, must secretly leave your father and wait for me on the road as I pass. Keep this firmly in mind: you will never be abandoned by the one beneath whose protecting wings you now take refuge, until you have been more securely advanced into the hope and glory of your family—not only in temporal advantages, but also in eternal benefits and dignities in heaven.”

What more need be said? The boy Anno fled—not childishly, but as he had been instructed—and hid among willow thickets until his passing uncle secretly carried him away and placed him in the school of the people of Bamberg, who at that time surpassed all others in Germany in fervor for discipline, religion, and study. There he was assigned to learning, destined in due course to become a great instruction for the Church.

In that study, as time passed and his zeal for learning grew with it, aided and accompanied by the grace of that intimate teacher of whom Truth testifies, “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3), the young man of keen intelligence drew the greatest riches from human and divine books, so that later, at the proper time, he might bring forth for the peoples entrusted to him things new and old. Whatever was suitable for exercising the intellect, whatever could ennoble character, and whatever presented itself as pleasing to the ears or eyes, he immediately examined with the ingenuity of the wisest bee and carried into the hive of his heart. Thus, one day to slaughter the most unspeakable Goliath with his own weapons (1 Sam. 17), through constant meditation he mastered the torrents of secular eloquence as though by nature victorious.

**II. [Note: [Col. 1519D] In this chapter certain passages have been taken word for word from Lambert of Hersfeld.] Remarkable progress in learning. He is summoned to Emperor Henry’s palace. His bodily appearance.**

Growing upward through these and similar attainments like a cedar of Lebanon, when he entered the strength of mature manhood he became master of the schools there and began to extend the branches of his integrity and virtues far and wide through the mouths of many. Summoned to the bishops, he went to them, and he did not escape the notice of princes. Admitted by them into their friendship because of their respect for him, he soon became known to Henry III, Augustus of the Romans.

Henry summoned him to the palace, and within a short time Anno obtained from him, above all the clerics who kept watch at the palace doors, the first place in favor and intimacy. All good men especially loved this in him: he was exceedingly steadfast in justice and righteousness, and in every matter, according to his position, he defended justice—not by flattering, as others did, but by speaking out with great freedom.

Besides the glory of his spirit and character, he was also richly endowed in bodily qualities: tall in stature, venerable in appearance, ready in speech, exceptionally capable of enduring vigils and hunger, and, finally, abundantly equipped by nature for every exercise of good works. As he advanced from virtue to virtue, like the dawn in its ascent, so, as his holiness grew before God, he also advanced daily from glory to glory and from honor to honor, gaining authority among men.

This did not happen according to human judgment [or inclination], but through God’s customary providence. Knowing that his lamp was to be placed upon a most renowned lampstand so that it might shine for all the sons of the Church (Matt. 5), God first wished the light of Anno’s merits to be revealed to the world, lest the suddenness of his elevation produce merely wonder rather than joy. His promotion would thus be more fruitful because it would also be more welcome. And so it happened.

**III. Anno becomes bishop of Cologne in 1055. [Note: [Col. 1520D] Baronius, Marianus Scotus, and Sigebert place this in that year. Lambert of Hersfeld and Hermann the Contract place it in 1056.]**

Finally, after spending not many years in the palace, and amid the great expectation of the emperor and of all who knew him, Anno obtained the noble see of Agrippina, also called Cologne, after Hermann, the second bishop of that name, had been taken from this light a few days earlier.

When that same venerable man had been sent on an imperial embassy to Hermann, who lay on his deathbed, and had completed the king’s instructions after his greeting, he returned to his lodging. Those who were present report that the bishop then said that he too would soon undergo the laws of death and that Anno would receive Cologne in his place.

After Hermann died following these words, although the urgency of the royal business was already pressing Anno to return quickly, he nevertheless, mindful of his good custom, attended the funeral with great contrition of heart until Hermann was committed to the earth. For he had read—and throughout his life always fulfilled in deed—the words: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7). He impressed upon all a sufficiently laudable, indeed necessary, example, since, as it is written there, “in that house the end of all human beings is brought to mind, and the living considers what is to come” (ibid.).

**IV. The people of Cologne receive him reluctantly. How greatly the Church of Cologne grew under him.**

At that time the emperor was staying at Koblenz. Then the nobles and leaders of the people of Cologne appeared, returning the episcopal staff to the king and unanimously asking with humble prayers that a suitable successor be appointed in place of the deceased.

As is certain to happen in such matters, various men, according to their own inclination or advantage, pressed the king here and there with promises, counsels, or prayers. But God, the supreme judge, in whose hand the king’s heart is and who turns it wherever he wills (Prov. 21), directed the king’s judgment and will to no one other than Anno alone—some praising the decision, others protesting against it not without bitterness.

Thus Anno received from the king’s hands the pastoral staff, signifying the figure of a father and teacher. He also received the ring as the pledge of faith to be preserved toward God and toward his holy bride, the Church.

Without delay, entering Cologne like Moses as the leader of a people to be saved, he immediately heard them barking with doglike jaws: “Who is this man, or who appointed him ruler and judge over us?” (Exod. 2.) At the same time, with polluted and wicked lips they exalted the illustrious name of the blessed Archbishop Bruno, and, casting his deeds about as though in Bruno’s praise but in reality to Anno’s disparagement, they shouted tumultuously again and again: “Who is this man, and where are the things by which he is going to enlarge Cologne?”

They were the offspring and followers of those who, with a viper’s tongue, reviled the Lord and Savior as the son of a craftsman (Matt. 12–13). But to us and to all subsequent ages it is clearer than daylight that, since Cologne was founded, the wealth and glory of the Church of Cologne have never grown through the efforts of any one bishop so greatly—excepting Bruno’s privilege, so to speak.

But we shall speak of these matters more fully in their proper places. Following the tracks of the history, let us now attend to the narrative we have begun.

**V. Anno is ordained bishop on 3 March 1055.**

Accordingly, those who had vainly resolved to struggle against the mountain or the force of the river, pressed at once by the authority and fear of royal majesty, finally turned necessity into willingness and collectively consented to the consecration of the elected bishop.

An assembly of bishops and men of the entire ecclesiastical order was held, together with a great gathering of nobles in excessive display, and an immense multitude of every sex and age. On that day Christ the Lord had come with the angels to raise them all up through his servant Anno by his blessing and favor, while all the saints rejoiced in heaven with the one destined to be their fellow citizen.

Meanwhile the man to be ordained was brought before the altar, clothed in sacred garments, and drenched with the liquid of holy oil. Suddenly transformed into another man by the truly abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit, in the year 1055 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the fifth day before the Nones of March—that is, 3 March—he was placed in the episcopal chair to govern the holy Church and the entire people [Col. 1521A].

The hour of the singular sacrifice was now approaching. Behold, the supreme pontiff, adorned with pontifical vestments, approached the altar, truly a priest and victim of Christ. Who could adequately explain with what compunction and contrition of heart he performed that ministry? For he dissolved entirely into tears and received the power of so great a sacrament into himself. Some marveled at the immensity of his tears, and by his groaning, sighing, and beating of his breast they sought to discern the secrets of his heart.

No one doubted that heaven was then opened to his prayers, since the merciful and compassionate Lord had placed him there for this very reason: that, interceding for the offenses of his flock, he might become reconciliation in the time of wrath.

When the solemnities of the Mass had ended with the pontifical blessing and the assembly had dispersed, Anno thereafter conducted himself as equal to his received dignity in all ecclesiastical and public affairs. Just as he was distinguished by the eminence of his position, so he proceeded conspicuous among the other princes of the realm in every kind of virtue.

He rendered to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s and to God the things that are God’s (Matt. 22). For he displayed the majesty and secular pomp of the name of Cologne to the people almost more ambitiously than any of his predecessors; yet amid such storms of activity he never relaxed his unconquered spirit from devotion to divine matters.

He disciplined himself by fasts, though not beyond what was lawful, knowing what is written: “All things are clean to the clean”—“and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (Titus 1; 1 Tim. 4).

He often spent the night in prayer and, going through the churches barefoot with a few trusted companions—sometimes content with only one boy—proceeded in tears, at times wearing a hair shirt next to his skin. He spent the day arranging private or public affairs, but the entire night in the work of God.

For at that time the great pontiff did not blush to do penance, confess his errors, mourn his offenses, and humble himself, even for the chastisement of his body by corporal scourging, at the hands of an inferior person.

His kindness and remarkable generosity toward the poor, pilgrims, clerics, and monks were abundant. He did not leave a single religious community within his diocese without, at his death, having enlarged it by a special donation of estates, buildings, or stipends.

In judging the cases of his subjects he was diverted from the truth neither by hatred nor by anyone’s favor. Always following with unwavering constancy the line of equity he had set before him, he neither considered the person of the poor nor honored the face of the powerful in order to overturn judgment (Lev. 19). We shall add a sufficiently suitable and evident example of this.

**VI. A remarkable example of extraordinary humility and virtue in the emperor.**

King Henry, patrician of the Romans, held the royal scepters in a truly royal manner through his character, prudence, and glory, and administered them according to the most just laws both in divine and human affairs [Col. 1521D]. Yet he conducted himself outwardly toward the people in such a way that inwardly he did not forget himself.

Considering that the majesty of so great a name far exceeded his own merits, he never presumed to put on the royal insignia unless, secretly through confession and penance, and moreover through satisfaction by scourging, he had humbly earned permission from some priest [Note: [Col. 1521] When someone disapproved of this pious custom of the emperor, Peter Damian wrote an apologetic letter in its defense.]

Once, therefore, when a great feast was approaching and bishops, dukes, counts, and men of every other rank and order were hurrying from all sides to the royal court, custom and the honor imposed upon him required the king himself to appear wearing the royal robe. Henry, who knew that Anno was holy and the most exemplary in life among the bishops, began to approach him humbly and penitently so that he might preserve the practice of his custom [Col. 1522A].

At once the holy bishop, filled with authority and in such a matter thinking little of imperial magnificence, began to rage mercifully against the prince without mercy, just as he was accustomed to spare the poor and needy when he found the opportunity. Attacking him with the most vehement corrections, he freely and firmly said whatever presented itself to his mind, aroused on behalf of justice. He allowed the king, afflicted by the hardest blows of the scourge, to proceed crowned on that day only after Henry had spent thirty-three pounds of silver from his own hands on the poor.

The emperor did not refuse. With regard for the heavenly Judge, he both endured and did everything in the order in which it had been prescribed, and only then proceeded dressed in his customary manner.

The bishop’s constancy is truly astonishing, and the humility of the prince no less worthy of praise. In both of them there was a perfection of the fear of God worthy of imitation.

Since the occasion has presented itself, although by way of digression, I wish to mention the death of that same king, in which all the restraints of injustice were loosened [Col. 1522B], chiefly because Anno’s virtue appears here in no small degree, and Truth itself has spread the report that he sometimes flourished in the spirit of prophecy.

**VII. Saint Anno foresees the king’s death. Pope Victor comes to Goslar, a city of Saxony. The death of Emperor Henry. Saint Anno raises his son.**

When certain disputes arose between Anno and the king through the deceit of malicious men, and the king had disclosed the intention he had conceived against the archbishop in orders harsher than usual, the bishop came to an audience and tried to plead his cause by reason and justice. When the opportunity to proceed in this way was taken from him, he finally burst out with these words:

“Most excellent king, in the sight of the heavenly King, may the evil of any disagreement or hatred not prevail between us even this year, since what awaits us next year is now hidden in the inner recesses of our minds.”

In saying this, he tried to lead the king—whom he knew would die that very year—back to the path of amendment of life.

But as the thorns of disagreement grew day by day for one reason after another [Col. 1522C], Anno again went to the court at Goslar, where at that time the venerable Pope Victor, also called Gebhard, had gathered amid the great expectation of all the princes of the realm.

There, after restoring the minds of both men to their former friendship, the archbishop, preparing to depart, asked the king: “As I leave, may I now be certain of your affection and favor?”

When the king testified that this was indeed the case, Anno added: “I know, I know that from now on we shall not enjoy one another’s sight in this body. One of us will soon be carried away into death, while the other will be left still in the struggle. Therefore, wishing you farewell, because you will have arranged Cologne sufficiently fruitfully and healthfully for your soul, I, however unworthy its shepherd, promise this before God.”

The king immediately betrayed the fear he had conceived by the pallor of his face and persistently asked about the person to whom these words referred. Anno replied: “You are the one whom this very sad expectation awaits.”

The king himself, bringing his life swiftly to an end, showed that this was true.

When Henry had entered upon the way of all flesh, the holy bishop attended him with no less affection of faith and devotion than he had shown him while he lived. Through fasts, vigils, prayers, and almsgiving—in other words, spiritual remedies—he did not cease to reconcile his soul to divine goodness.

He also instituted that an annual commemoration of Henry should be celebrated at Cologne for as long as he himself lived, never forgetting him in a special way.

He took the king’s son, heir to his name and kingdom, into his care for upbringing and advancement in honor of the empire and the Church, thereby arousing the envy of many against himself. Yet he did not cease laboring in the hope of receiving fruit, raising the boy royally and educating him nobly, so that later, according to the boy’s own testimony, no man in the whole kingdom was found to have a deeper mind than he.

The holy pontiff Jehoiada once did the same for King Joash (2 Chron. 24), but, alas, Anno received a similar return for his goodness, as Jehoiada did.

But setting these matters aside, let us turn our pen to describing the practices of his life.

**VIII. He preaches frequently. Many flock to hear his sermons.**

From the earliest days of his ordination, taking up a work suitable and truly worthy of his office, and following the instructions of the teaching Apostle—“In all things labor, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry” (2 Tim. 4)—he traveled throughout every parish of his bishopric. Through constant preaching he instructed people ignorant of the faith and of almost the whole of religion, Christians in name only, in the practice of Catholic devotion. Briefly and clearly he explained what ought to be believed, hoped for, and loved.

Then, with pontifical authority, he commanded each listener, and with paternal devotion persuaded them, to evangelize these same teachings at home, promising them a good return from God for this.

He made such progress in this that even children who had not yet passed beyond the tender years of infancy learned the faith from one another, as they say, of blessed Anno, and taught it to one another. From their constant devotion to this good study, a kind of law grew up among them: each one was to recite it before God in the morning or evening.

He had this notable sign of his merits among men: whenever he came forth publicly to preach, he was suddenly drenched in such abundant tears that he moved every heart to compassion. Then he poured forth words sweet as honey and full of compunction, set forth God’s clemency without concealing his justice, urged the good to advance toward better things, urged the wicked to cease from their crimes, and exhorted everyone together to declare themselves guilty and invoke the common Lord for the needs of the whole world.

Whoever, even with a heart of stone, could hear Anno speaking in the church and restrain himself from tears?

Finally, from foreign and more distant provinces many people flocked to him solely because of the fame of his kindness and teaching. They preferred hearing Anno to every delight, considering it incomparable wealth to be released through his indulgence and fortified by his blessing [Col. 1523C].

Moreover, he was inferior to no one in devotion and works of mercy. When he learned that farmers and tenants owing rents had been burdened and almost stripped bare by the excessive demands or greed of his predecessors, he ordered the collectors to show mercy, remitting to each person all or part of what was owed, according to need.

His first and constant concern was for poor people, pilgrims, and the sick, in imitation of the one who said: “Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful” (Luke 6).

At the first glimmer of the rising day, behold, a swarm-like crowd of needy people flew in from every direction and daily besieged his doors, each person to receive sufficient food at the appointed hour.

Among all these, after the very poorest—twenty-four in number—had been identified, they were gathered separately. The supreme pontiff humbly prostrated himself at their feet [Note: [Col. 1523] Reader, observe that here “supreme pontiff” is used for “archbishop”]. After washing and drying them, he also impressed a kiss upon them with heart and lips, and poured water over their hands.

When this ministry of humility was completed, he turned to the work of charity, giving each person food, drink, and a coin.

When the hour and need arrived for him also to sit at table, as was customary, all the pilgrims who had come were brought before him to eat.

Then, gathering from each of the dishes set upon the table nearly a tenth portion, he set it aside in one place to refresh the sick scattered here and there throughout the city.

Finally, when the table had been removed, he rose as a true father of orphans and true judge of widows, as though saying: “Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matt. 19). Bending down, he personally fed the young, refreshed the orphans, and nourished the children of the poor with the more delicate foods he had reserved for this purpose from his own table. He also generously supplied what was necessary to their mothers, who more familiarly complained to him of their troubles.

Although he was merciful and compassionate toward all the needy, he was moved by a special kind of pity toward poor women and their little children. Learning this by experience, such women occasionally chose a suitable time and presented themselves in groups in the streets, throwing their little ones before him while pleading loudly.

Sometimes, as he passed by, he saw such children, emaciated and half-naked, who had fallen asleep from the weariness of their long wait. He would compassionately take one of them to himself, even one whom no one would have thought worthy of notice, and begin to kiss him as a mother would.

Some women who had no children of their own even sought out other people’s infants, uncertain whether Anno would be moved to pity toward them if they appeared before him burdened with such little bundles.

In addition, it was his solemn custom, every year from the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity until the Purification of his undefiled Mother, for forty continuous days to provide for a nursing mother. Giving water over her hands, he himself washed the infant’s feet and hands; then, after providing food, he gave one solid coin.

Besides this, he built a hospice at Cologne, bringing there the sick, the weak, and all who lacked every form of comfort, and assigning daily stipends for their support.

He never passed by a poor person crying out without mercy, and whenever he came to visit the needy, monks, or canons, he never returned without an abundant hand of charity.

Indeed, it is superfluous to mention how generous he was on the Lord’s Supper, since no parent on that day withholds his hand from almsgiving.

All these deeds are surpassed in number and wonder by those he performed during the darkness of night, with God alone as witness, except for only a very few of his most secret companions. With them, as has been said, he went by night around the thresholds of the saints, searching for pilgrims and those who had no shelter, in porticoes, corners, and wine jars set out in the streets. When he found them, he fed and clothed them, carrying provisions with him for precisely this food and clothing.

[Col. 1524C] **IX. A lamentable sight of a woman in childbirth.**

When, according to his custom, he had gone out during the silence of a certain night for a similar purpose, he encountered on the way a lamentable sight, full of every kind of compassion: a woman whom, because of her poverty, no one had deemed worthy of hospitality, and who, having just given birth and endangered by the delivery, was rolling herself tearfully upon the bare ground.

It was a misery to behold. Night had overtaken the wanderer with dense darkness. The muddy and rocky earth had received her, exhausted and half-naked. Hunger and thirst had consumed her, and the cold tormented her still more. No mortal was present. Then, as nature pressed upon her, she began to suffer, cry out, and draw frequent sighs. At last, having poured forth her offspring into the dust, she herself lay with her limbs miserably scattered here and there, expecting nothing more than death.

What misery could be more miserable than this?

The holy bishop then arrived, as has been said, and immediately, as though pierced through by an arrow, halted in astonishment, drawing back his steps before the horror and misery. But then, setting aside the dignity of his office, he hurried back like the swiftest runner. He placed a pallet with bedding upon his shoulders and returned with the same speed with which he had come.

At once, casting the burden from his neck, he bent down quickly toward the woman lying there. He wrapped the infant in cloth, lifted the woman from the ground, placed her upon the bed, and, removing his own garments, carefully covered them both.

After arranging provisions at that place for her support until she recovered, he departed, destined truly to obtain the effect of his prayers: through this humble and pious ministry, in the horror of the blind night, he had served in his least members the one who was once incarnate for us and whom the Virgin Mother “wrapped in swaddling clothes and laid in a manger” (Luke 2).

**X. Saint Anno visits Saint Ursula and her companion virgins.**

Another night had come, and the man devoted to God, avoiding the eyes of human estimation, began humbly to visit the venerable ashes of the holy virgins.

One of the accustomed little women, carefully foreseeing this, and equipped by both necessity and ingenuity, met him in his ignorance with this stratagem. Having nothing certain to meet her bodily need except her poverty, she secretly placed her little son, still fresh from the breast, in the middle of the road before the feet of the approaching man. Then she hurried away and concealed herself.

The priest soon approached. When he heard the first cry of the wailing infant, he trembled throughout with grief, entertaining various thoughts about how such a child had come to be there at that hour of the night.

Meanwhile, hastening eagerly as though to serve Christ lying beneath the hay, he bent down, lifted the child from the ground, and, remembering Saint Simeon—how he once embraced the Savior’s infancy in his devout arms (Luke 2)—prayed peace and salvation for himself and for the people.

Inspired by Simeon’s devotion, though recognizing that the situation and feelings were different, he went on joyfully under this burden, returning to his chamber, imitating the one who carried the lost sheep back to the fold upon his devoted shoulders (Luke 15).

Immediately, with paternal concern, he procured a nurse for the child whom he had not begotten in the flesh, but whom he regenerated more fully through spiritual rebirth in baptism. Receiving him from the sacred font, he named him Anno after himself, providing for himself through the child the hope of singular patronage before God.

**XI. Certain men plot his death.**

Such, then, was the daily practice of the man of God; such was his unceasing concern, his labor, and his devotion.

He could have said in the words of blessed Job: “I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame; I was a father to the poor” (Job 29)—“and I consoled the widow’s heart. When I sat like a king with an army surrounding me, I was nevertheless the consoler of the sorrowful; for from childhood compassion grew with me, and it came forth with me from the womb” (Job 31).

Yet certain rivals of justice conspired against him. Their wickedness is such that even today their accomplices cast doubt upon Anno’s holiness. One night, as he had gone out to perform the same works of devotion, he suffered an ambush.

Attacking him as he came in a furious assault, they accused him of being a thief and charged him with other offenses of which they themselves were conscious and by which they could easily vent their abuse of another.

When the bishop’s companions refuted these accusations and said that it was sacrilege to assail a cleric passing by for the sake of prayer with such insults, the attackers, in a most insolent reply, accused them of fabrication and added worse charges. Then, with poisonous tongues and hands full of blood, they attacked him without restraint, raging against the innocent like the fiercest beast. They violently stripped him of his cloak, seized him by the hair, dragged him through the mud, and struck him repeatedly with their fists.

After treating his companions no less brutally in a similar frenzy, they withdrew joyfully, satiated with madness, becoming participants in those of whom it is written: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in wicked things” (Prov. 2).

But once envy has been conceived, malice knows no limit. Thus the aforesaid criminals, breathing an even greater madness—I shudder to say it—plotted the archbishop’s death. They laid ambushes for him not once or twice, intending to complete, if opportunity allowed, a crime both detestable and no less lamentable, since they would not spare even the head of all good men.

When this became more certainly known to the bishop’s household members and friends, they alternated between rejoicing that he had so far escaped and shuddering at the thought of so great a danger. Under oath they declared that they would absolutely not allow him to go out in such a manner again, lest he should extinguish the lamp of Israel.

Persuaded by their counsels and prayers, Anno nevertheless continued to perform the appointed number of prayers at each place, reclining in bed or remaining in some church.

From that time onward he also devised a practice that could serve as an example not of concern for his own injury but of just zeal to vigilant pastors.

**XII. He takes action against depraved men.**

Knowing that certain profane and incestuous men roamed about at night in the works of lust [Col. 1526A], and inflamed by zeal for justice, he ordered that men caught in such wicked intercourse should be publicly shaved and flayed as an example to all. He granted this authority to a certain priest among his household, who, under the continual obligation of obedience, had to watch for such nocturnal excursions from the beginning of night until the first light of the following day.

Nevertheless, he summoned some of the women for whom, shamefully, chastity was a commodity, rebuked them in words, and also softened them with gifts. He led them either to a resolve of continence or to a respectable marriage, saving their souls from death (Prov. 10) through charity, which covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4).

### XIII. He visits the Church of the Eleven Thousand Virgins. What sacramental confession accomplishes. He protects, with extraordinary humanity, the reputation of a certain fallen woman.

There are very many who resemble whitewashed tombs: after the Pharisees’ manner, swelling outwardly with the appearance of holiness, while inwardly they are full of the bones of the dead (Matt. XXV), they treat sinners or any who are weaker—not with compassion, but with a certain abusive disdain. Anno, humble in his own eyes, never suffered from this plague.

One night, when deep darkness surrounded everything, he entered, as was his custom, the threshold of the holy virgins’ house. He withdrew into a corner, where, standing more privately, he might devote himself to prayer. There one of the sisters, lying face-down, was striking the ears of divine mercy with frequent sobs and inward groans, bitter tears, and blows upon her breast, grievously lamenting the carnal pleasure she had recently committed.

When the enormity of her offense had aroused in her the goads of remorse, the conception already swelling in her womb made them sharper still. Although she hoped, through the amendment of her subsequent life, in the kindness of the merciful Savior, she nevertheless declared in the most miserable complaints that she would bear the shame of human reproach throughout the ages.

Thus unspeakably distressed by this twofold tribulation, she gathered hope and recovered her strength. She appealed to the sole refuge of human misery—namely, to our merciful Lord, whom she had offended—knocking upon him with heart and mouth, while tears flowed like a stream. She prayed that he who had once been born for sinners and had deigned to die for sinners might, in his accustomed goodness, come to the aid of her misfortune and forgive the deed she had committed in such a way that she might escape the public mockery of disgrace.

O goodness of the Creator! O mercy of the Savior! He is good by nature and immeasurable in power, yet he cannot behold the tears of the human heart without mercy; and, in accordance with his magnificence, he also supplies consolation to those who have despaired.

While the afflicted woman was assailing heaven with such cries, the merciful priest, unaware to her, stood behind her as though sent by God. Applying his ear attentively, he heard all the words of the woman who was weeping and pleading. Nor was it difficult to infer the cause of such contrition.

At last, summoned by the ringing of the bells to the nocturnal hymns, she rose from the ground and went to the choir. The minister of divine goodness secretly followed her at once. From the place in the choir that she entered, he carefully determined her identity and then withdrew.

When daylight had returned, wishing to prove that “the Lord is near to those who are brokenhearted” (Ps. XXXIII), and that he had also bound himself by his own word, saying, “As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn and live” (Ezek. XXXIII), he sent for her through the sisters. She came with the fear suggested by her conscience before her eyes.

But the son of mercy received her gently, contrary to her expectations, and made her sit beside him. In the course of their conversation he inquired, as if indirectly, about the quality of her life, and, pretending ignorance, asked about the cause of the sorrow displayed on her face.

When she hesitated to offer the mortal wound to the hands of the spiritual physician, lest he strike it, he—who was not ignorant of the disease—applied the instrument. He declared that he knew the cause of her sadness and was not unaware of the prayers she had uttered in that place during the preceding night, repenting of what she had done. She needed only to confess her offense; through divine mercy, forgiveness and the possibility of escaping reproach were readily available.

To conclude the matter: she entered the path of confession amid tears and unexpectedly experienced the benefit of divine goodness in the misery of her situation. The consoler of the sorrowful, mindful also of his own frailty and following the Apostle’s warning, “Considering yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Gal. VI), sufficiently instructed her in a spirit of gentleness. He then entrusted her, under the oaths of fidelity due from him, to a certain soldier from Saxony, who, by his generous favor, was more highly regarded than the other members of his household.

He ordered the soldier, under the pretext of familiarity, to take her away with him and to attend carefully to all her needs until she had been freed from the unlawful conception. He was never to allow knowledge of the matter to pass beyond the threshold of his house, if he did not wish to be deprived of the bishop’s favor.

When the days of childbirth had passed, and the woman herself had recovered her health and returned to her former condition, he was to bring her back, together with the child, into the bishop’s presence. The soldier immediately obeyed the commands and faithfully carried out this task, which was known to no one except himself and the bishop. Afterwards he presented the woman and the infant to Anno.

The devout shepherd then entrusted the child elsewhere and sent the sheep that had strayed joyfully back to the dwelling of her fellow sisters. He sought no passing praise, wishing to be found worthy of heavenly reward.

### XIV. Having once tasted carnal pleasure, she was inflamed more fiercely in mind after her weeping. A truly astonishing miracle.

A matter not greatly unlike this occurred likewise at Cologne, which the venerable bishop used to relate as an example—a matter plainly worthy of remembrance and of being celebrated and frequently repeated by the mouths of all good people.

For just as this story can free the fallen from the great evil of despair, so it instills fear in those who stand, lest through presumption of a holier life they expose themselves to irreparable ruin. Let all who hear this therefore raise the ears of our hearts and consider, with hope and fear, how “terrible in his counsels toward the children of men is our merciful and just Lord” (Ps. LXV).

In the monastery of our most merciful Lady, the mother of God Mary, there was a nun who, from the beginning of her life among her companions, had grown up in complete moral integrity and holiness of life. The Almighty had granted her the special gift of the glory of virginity, like a diadem upon her head.

But when, at the instigation of the proud angel, a certain elation concerning her chastity began to creep over her, she came to disdain her fellow sisters and, as though she could never fall, admitted the company of men with excessive carelessness. Thus, according to what is written, “The heart is exalted before ruin” (Prov. XVI), she fell—alas!—into the pit of corruption, amid the great applause of the flattering enemy.

When the deed of her wretched intercourse had been completed, she came to herself and was almost driven mad by waves of immense sorrow. She considered, and hesitated as though deceived by a dream, over who she was and what she had done.

Then, when the purity of her former life touched her mind, she was struck in the heart as though by a thunderbolt. She uttered the bitterest groans and sighs, and, like a sudden rainstorm, poured herself entirely into tears with the wailing of a most miserable voice.

But once the deadly pleasure of the flesh had been tasted, when her weeping briefly subsided it stimulated her mind with still more violent fires. Fearing that afterwards, once the restraints of public shame had also been broken, she might rush headlong into every kind of immodesty, she looked toward heaven and groaned deeply. She prayed that, since she had already secretly clothed her soul in shame, she might also come into open disgrace through the conception and birth of criminal offspring, so that, subjected to public reproach, she might thereafter flee pride and lust in humility and repentance.

When she had prayed for this, and her swelling belly revealed to other eyes the signs of her violated chastity, she, deprived of every counsel and ignorant what to do or where to turn, avoided everyone’s gaze out of shame. She took pleasure neither in sleep, food, drink, nor even in life itself, for she was buried beneath the depths of incomparable sorrow.

She no longer reflected on satisfaction for her sin or thought about the punishments of hell. She desired with all her wishes to be freed only from the shame by which she was wasting away.

Thus, when no help of consolation appeared, she conceived in her whole mind a hope in the mercy of Christ, in accordance with the prophetic prediction: “Fill their faces with shame, and they will seek your name, O Lord” (Ps. LXXXII).

She fell before the image of Christ crucified for us and, entering the temple of his holy mother, lamented in these prayers:

> Most merciful Lord, may the calamity of my miseries penetrate the ears of your compassion. May you, the merciful Creator of your handiwork, not remain forgetful of me, offended though you are by my wickedness.  
>   
> Alas, I am defiled! Alas, I am a betrayer of the chastity I professed! Alas, I am the author of eternal shame! Now, deservedly and at the greatest cost to my salvation, I see myself beneath all others, though before, in my ignorance of myself, I—dust and ashes—gloried immeasurably above them all.  
>   
> What could more fittingly correspond to such presumption than the detestable impurity of this most shameful mire? I have no just complaint left against your goodness, O God, since I suffer all these things by my own will: I surrendered myself to the filth of incestuous lust, and then with my own mouth asked for the public reproach that threatens me—an audience unworthy of me, though would that it were only in this respect.  
>   
> I was heard, not as a sign of holiness, but as punishment for my preceding crime. Woe to me, wretched woman, who have lost the following of the heavenly Lamb (Rev. XIV), and who shall no longer hope for the glory of the virgin’s song.  
>   
> Let the path of indulgence alone be enough for me; and, if you show mercy, most gentle Jesus, let me be rescued from this shame.  
>   
> Behold, guilty and groaning, I cast myself at the feet of your devout mother. Through her intercession I humbly seek the grace of your consolation, promising the truth of complete conversion and, from now on, abstinence from and repentance for the crime I have committed.

While she continued these words with the greatest weeping, our merciful Lord, who looked upon Peter as he wept (Luke XXII), also looked upon her. He deigned to show by the clearest miracle how deeply he sympathizes with our miseries.

For when she stopped crying out and rose from the ground, her belly subsided and the wrongly conceived fetus disappeared. She herself wept even more abundantly for joy and did not delay fulfilling her promised conversion.

For many years she persevered continually in penance. Her body, weakened by vigils and prayers, was sustained only by bread and water. Without ceasing, she beat her breast with tears in humility, and, because of the crime she had committed, she placed the life that followed far above her former life.

The extent of her contrition can be understood from this: apart from her other private prayers, she always recited the Psalter three times between day and night—first lying prostrate on the ground, second kneeling, and third standing—so that, when her spirit failed, her limbs too might be wearied.

Pallor covered her face together with emaciation. The prolonged fasting and vigils, with her strength almost exhausted, presented the other sisters with a miracle. They suspected nothing except that, from longing for her heavenly bridegroom, his bride was wasting away through the languor of love; for no trace of her guilt was visible to them.

She did not entrust the confession of so great an offense to human confidence, which is sometimes nowhere to be found when it is most expected, but cried out trustfully to the Lord alone: “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, for my soul has trusted in you.”

[Note: This is not to be understood as sacramental confession made to a priest, but as meaning that she did not dare reveal her crime to anyone outside this confession.]

When, as has been said, she had devoted herself for several years to such works while seeking divine favor, and had already drawn some measure of hope for forgiveness, behold, the ancient plague of pride, lying beneath her feet, began again to raise its head against her.

She prudently foresaw this and recognized it as the cause of her earlier fall. Though fallen, she had nevertheless been beneficially instructed, and therefore did not consider the beginnings of this suggestion something to be neglected, as before. She hastened to the presence of the holy Father Anno and carefully recounted the entire sequence of her falls, asking with great sorrow of heart for the help of his counsel and prayers, lest, if she again plunged into similar things, the penance of so long a time should be lost.

Then the holy bishop, speaking at length words of consolation according to the wisdom granted to him, taught her to trust not in her own strength but in God, according to the saying, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). Nothing so crushes demons, he said, as to stand upon the foundation of humility: to prefer oneself to no one, even in thought; and to think humbly of oneself before all others. As for the guilt of past sin, she would not be held by it if she did not presume to repeat what was to be mourned.

When he had examined the innermost quality of her mind and learned that whatever she had undertaken in a more special way, as though holier than the others, had been turned into weapons of exaltation, he declared that the sound and holy path was not to exceed the limits of common life, but to remain within them if she did not wish to perish. She was not to take up any singular way of life contrary to her fellow sisters. She was to eat with those who ate, sleep with those who slept, abstain with those who abstained, and keep vigil with those who kept vigil.

This, he said, was truly the royal road: it deviated to neither side and led those who walked it into the homeland of eternal salvation.

Having been healthfully imbued with these streams of instruction and received his blessing, the servant of God returned to the monastery. She immediately entered upon the mother of the virtues, moderation—here called *temperantia*, which others call “discernment”—and burst forth into the fruits of complete moral integrity and religious devotion, content with the rule of common life. When she departed, she left no one in that community superior to her in virtues.

Until now we have been occupied with describing the life and character of the bishop beloved of God. It is now time to disclose how greatly the Church of Cologne prospered through him in the increase of divine service.

Although the slowness of our intellect presumes, in some fashion, to undertake this task, who, even by considering the matter with bodily eyes, would not see that all eloquence is unequal to the greatness of what occurred here? To trace fully the ardor of his mind toward God and neighbor is no small labor. So that we may not appear to boast falsely, let us take the beginnings of the following history from this point.

### XV. Saint Anno reforms the monasteries.

When he grieved that, throughout all the communities under his care, whatever their profession, the path of regular discipline had been largely lost—some wandering outside for the necessities of life, others for the desires of the world—he arranged generously for the prebends of all according to the calculation of their annual revenues, enlarging some from his own resources. Thus, by removing the occasion of freedom, he imposed upon everyone the necessity of continual enclosure.

In carrying this out he used the apostolic commands (2 Tim. IV), entreating as a father and rebuking as a teacher. At times he added goads to those who strayed from the path and resisted, and in his own time he restored to the world the school of heavenly discipline that had been so long neglected.

The more his love burned in these endeavors, the more diligently he persisted in them. Inflamed to greater works of divine praise, he undertook the construction of five monasteries, carrying them from the very beginnings of their foundations to completion and dedicating not only his soul but his entire body—with its five senses established by the Creator—to their service.

### XVI. He builds the monastery of Saint Mary ad Gradus.

Thus he first raised the monastery called ad Gradus, in honor of holy Mary, the mother of God, laying its foundations and consecrating it, beautifully distinguished by every kind of varied ornament. He abundantly assigned estates sufficient for the support of thirty canons, whom he had gathered there from every direction because of their excellence in knowledge, life, and character.

He himself, wholly devoted to the Lady whom he loved, entrusted his soul to her patronage. Still ignorant of what the future held, he also built his tomb for himself in that same monastery. As though he were about to depart at any moment, he frequently visited the place, spending the night in prayer and expiating his own sins and those of his people with rivers of tears.

Often, after passing the entire night without sleep, he would recline at the very rising of the light upon a mat, or upon the bare ground, and sometimes upon the steps at the entrance to the chapter house. After his eyes had closed in sleep for scarcely an instant, he would rise.

The virtue of such contrition and self-abasement was not easily believed to exist in him, since it was not always known even to his closest associates. Yet he walked surrounded by public honors and, in his very appearance, was formidable and glorious to the dignities of the world. Nevertheless, while living among Christ’s poor, he was always gentle and humble.

For, as we have learned from our brothers, when he was sitting with them he sometimes remarked with a smile:

> How great, and how terrifying to all courtiers, I become when I come before them! How I carry my head about on an upright neck, turn fierce eyes upon each one, and arrange my whole bearing like one at whose feet everything is about to fall! Yet amid all this I walk within, timid and afraid, far more abject than appears to anyone’s faith.

This is what he himself confessed about himself.

Moreover, whenever it was announced that he was about to be present at court, no layman, cleric, count, powerful person of any other kind, bishop, or even the king himself was excepted: each would alter his appearance, arrange his hair, and moderate his gestures in Anno’s presence.

### XVII.

Thus, after enjoying success in completing the church he had begun, and while burning more and more with desire for heavenly joy, he considered the labors of the past small and longed to grasp the summit of higher merit.

Accordingly, after assembling resources for a second time, he built outside the walls a church of Saint George the martyr, richly endowed with annual revenues, as the congregation of clerics assembled there required.

He longed with all his wishes for its dedication but was hindered by the need to acquire the martyr’s relics. Then, as he himself related and as was learned, one night, overcome by sleep, he saw that same martyr proceeding from the inner oratories of Saint Pantaleon amid a great abundance of light.

As he watched with astonished eyes, the martyr—clothed in a splendid mantle and suffused with a rosy face—directed his steps toward the new building of Anno’s devotion. When he had entered it, Anno immediately awoke.

Touched at once by the grace of divine inspiration, he perceived in the dream something consonant with his desires. As soon as the darkness had ended, impatient of every delay, he went to the shrine of Saint Pantaleon and, with God as his guide, received with the greatest reverence the arm of the illustrious martyr George, which had been presented to him.

Accompanied by a crowd, he carried it to the place where the martyr had entered, while a solemn procession followed the footsteps that the martyr had seemed to tread by night.

[Note: We have supplied “where he entered”; it seems to be missing in the exemplar.]

Then, when the clergy and the bishop proceeded according to the rite of consecration, the time and place demanded an appropriate sermon. Suddenly, a commotion arose. People hurried here and there, no one waiting for another, but each rushing to occupy the place thought to be nearer the bishop’s preaching voice.

Some climbed the walls, others houses and trees. Many gathered around two great beams by which an ascent had been arranged to the building from the wall, while innumerable people clustered beneath them.

Everyone’s ears were raised and their eyes fixed upon the mouth of the speaking bishop. But the beams, unable to bear the excessive pressure, collapsed with a great crash, and those who were upon them fell together toward the ground.

When the crowd standing beneath received the mass of those who fell, a tremendous cry and rush arose. No one doubted that the magnitude of the danger had caused the deaths of many.

But when silence had been restored, no sign of injury was found upon anyone. A greater voice of praise and wonder resounded from all. The power of divine virtue had revealed the merit of the martyr-priest all the more gloriously because it had done so all the more joyfully.

Filled with the sweetness of this joy, the holy bishop took the sacred arm in his hands and entered the church. The clergy sounded hymns and prayers on one side, the people on the other.

Meanwhile, a fiery splendor came down from heaven and accompanied the holy bishop as he entered with the saints. It visibly descended into the church, though only very few of those outside—and almost no one else—were granted this vision.

As everyone loudly expressed even greater joy because of this, the bishop, exhilarated by so many signs of divine presence, performed the entire ecclesiastical service with great confidence and devotion.

### XVIII. An unknown old man urges him to found the monastery of Siegburg.

Then, looking wholly toward what lay ahead and forgetting what was behind, one night, when everything was wrapped in profound stillness, he passed by the monastery of Saint Martin. With the ear of his heart and body he heard the monks laboring at the nocturnal vigils.

He sighed heavily and said to a certain priest, who knew his secret thoughts very well:

> Does it not knock at the door of your heart that, while everyone in Cologne is asleep, these alone, concerned for the service of God, are standing at this hour of the night to sing praise to God? Yet I, who offer nothing worthy to his ministers, have brought my misfortune upon myself by being negligent in everything. Until now I have lived as uselessly as possible to monks.

Having struck his breast and said this, he raised his eyes to the stars, stretched out his hands, and added with heart and mouth:

> I beseech you, ruler of life and death, supreme Father; I beseech you to grant me the respite of this life until, by your gift, I may accomplish something useful also for these men of religion.

As this voice pierced the heavens, he returned home. Early in the morning he went to the threshold of Saint Peter. While he was sitting more privately in the crypt and singing psalms, an old man who came upon him admonished him in these words:

> Do not delay, venerable bishop, in building the place of your rest, which, by God’s predestination, you will have on the mountain called Siegburg after the river flowing past it.

He had spoken, and the bystanders quickly drove him away as though he were a mocker. But the bishop received the force of his words more deeply than can be expressed.

From that point onward, his intention was occupied with nothing else. It remains to explain how he brought it to completion.

### XIX. Count Palatine gives the Siegburg mountain to Saint Peter.

Count Palatine Henry, a man of secular power and glory who at that time was exercising hostility against the innocence of the bishop beloved of God, ranged almost throughout the entire bishopric, relying upon the protection of the fortress on the summit of the aforesaid mountain, carrying out killings, plunderings, and burnings to the devastation of the country.

For just reasons, the archbishop struck him with the sentence of excommunication. At last he forced him to make satisfaction and took him captive.

When Henry came to Cologne, he fell suppliant and repentant at the bishop’s feet. Having received reconciliation and the place of communion and forgiveness, he gave the Siegburg mountain to blessed Peter as a grateful gift to the bishop who had reconciled him.

Then, seeing that the long-desired undertaking lay open before him, the bishop was stimulated and made more eager, as though already running, by certain portents that rumor had brought from the mountain. Among these the following is reported, with the support of many witnesses, and not implausibly.

### XX. The sign of the cross is seen in the air.

A village called Stieldorp lies almost a mile away from the mountain mentioned above. On the feast of the Lord’s Day, its inhabitants were drawn together during this same period and went to church. While, with the unrestrained freedom of a crowd, they conversed about various matters and directed their gaze in every direction, they looked toward the mountain and suddenly saw a sign of the cross close to the sky, as though hanging above its summit.

Each of them marveled at it as beautifully distinguished by a variety of colors. Those who were more discerning declared it to be a great portent, signifying that the triumph of the cross was to be honored and frequently celebrated there, with the inhabitants of the place always triumphing through faith in the cross, not through visible weapons.

### XXI. The vision of two pilgrims from Greece. In 1066 the church of the monastery of Siegburg is consecrated.

At about the same time, while two pilgrims from Greece were staying at Neron, which is also called Bonn, a ladder of great brightness appeared to them in a vision. It rose straight from the summit of the mountain to heaven, and through it little lambs of wondrous whiteness ascended with joyful movements and penetrated the heights of the sky.

Everyone interpreted this favorably. The bishop therefore went to the construction on the mountain, surrounded by craftsmen of various kinds. Some were cutting down trees, others carrying away what had been cut, others digging up the earth, others bringing stones; all, fervent with equal zeal in their different crafts, hastened the work, while the bishop and his overseers pressed them from above.

What more need be said? With help supplied from heaven, the completion of the church prospered. In the year 1066 of the Lord’s incarnation, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, he specially assigned it to the name of Saint Michael the archangel and consecrated it in honor of all the heavenly Virtues, under the protection of the glorious leader Maurice and his companions.

When he sanctified the altar of the holy Cross and placed relics upon it, a light shining from heaven with a fiery radiance seemed to enter at the same time.

### XXII. The vision of Saint Anno during the sacrifice of the Mass.

Taking this as a joyful omen, he dedicated a chapel of Saint Martin in the western part of the monastery, toward the north. After completing the rite of consecration, he stood vested at the service of the altar.

As, in contrition of spirit and compunction of heart, he sacrificed himself and accomplished the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, a fiery globe suddenly flashed between his eyes and hands and rolled about in a fearful vision.

Gradually gathering itself together, it slipped wholly into the chalice.

The priest was terrified and, as he himself related, was almost beside himself with fear, uncertain what to do. He thought it rash to extend his hands further in blessing over the chalice, which had been filled by the presence of such majesty. On the other hand, he feared guilt if, by stopping, he violated the rite of the universal Church.

At last it came to his mind, by revelation of the Holy Spirit, that it was his duty to continue the customary blessings, while what had appeared was the work of divine condescension, which also invisibly accomplished this every day.

Accepting with gratitude these and similar signs that heavenly election smiled upon his beginnings, he adorned the place with the most august buildings, illuminated it with the most exquisite ornaments of the church, and enriched it with extensive estates sufficient for the use of many brothers.

### XXIII. He brings monks from Italy to the monastery of Siegburg. How reverently he treated them. He observes silence like a monk and follows the other customs of the monastery.

[Note: This is taken almost word for word from the *Schafnaburgensis*.]

When he saw that in all the monasteries of the Teutonic kingdom the ancient fervor of regular discipline had greatly cooled and that the monks had turned all their attention and effort from common life to household affairs, his mind was oppressed by deep distress. He thought that, despite the immense expense, he would accomplish nothing worthy of God.

Meanwhile, it happened that he traveled to Rome on public business. As he passed through several regions of Italy, intending by his exhortations to strengthen the princes of that kingdom so that they would not defect from the king, he turned aside for the sake of prayer to a certain monastery called Fruttuaria.

There he marveled at the monks’ extremely strict way of life and their manner of living according to the precepts of the Rule. On his return he brought twelve of them with him, men whom he had found to be exceptionally proven in the work of God, and established them at Siegburg to transmit the pattern of that discipline to Gaul. The earlier monks whom he had summoned from elsewhere were honorably sent back to their own places.

The other bishops of Gaul imitated this action. Some summoned monks from Gorze, some from Cluny, some from Siegburg, and some from other monasteries, and each established a school of divine service in his own monasteries. So quickly did the emulation of this fortunate undertaking grow strong that we see few monasteries in Gaul that have not now accepted the yoke of this new institution.

He himself saw that his monks lived according to the strict disciplines he had discovered at Fruttuaria. Their reputation for religious life spread far and wide, inflaming many to despise the world and to place themselves under their instruction to be trained in the way of God. He gave great thanks to God that he had not been confounded in his expectation.

He also took every precaution to ensure that they suffered no lack of anything required to care for the weakness of the body. He honored and revered them as his lords. He was so submissive and obedient not only to the abbot but also to the deans of the monastery that, at their first command, no matter how deeply occupied he might be with weighty public or private business, he would immediately rise from his tasks and carry out whatever they ordered, like a worthless servant.

Every day, whenever he was able to be present, he himself brought them food prepared with the greatest care; he himself set it before them; he himself mixed their drink. Amid all this he kissed the hands of each of them as though they were divine, and, while they were eating, he stood ready and prepared for every service, more prompt than any servant. Once he had completed every ministry, he would sit contentedly on the stairway, on a sufficiently humble seat, intent upon the reader.

While he was among them, he observed silence and the other customs of the monastery with such attentive care that he seemed to be prepared to plead his case daily in their chapter for his offenses and to receive their sentence.

No father was ever moved by such affection toward his sons, nor any mother. Loving everyone as himself, he sympathized with each person and was ready to spend his soul for every one of them.

This was his zeal, this his custom, this his instruction at Siegburg, at Salevel, and at Grascaf—that is, at the places he later built.

### XXIV. At one time he is most beloved by the emperor, at another utterly hated. In dangers he turns to the monks’ prayers.

Although he often disagreed with the king in the most serious hostilities, at one time the king raised him to the greatest intimacy, almost making him a partner in the kingdom. At another time, because Anno vehemently detested and fiercely opposed what was being done wrongly in the kingdom contrary to justice and goodness, he was driven from the palace amid insults, and all the strength of the kingdom was stirred up to extinguish his name.

For several years he contended with the king amid these changes. Always turning, as it were, to a tower of strength, he called upon the prayers of the brothers of Siegburg for help.

Thus, on one occasion, when the king had been inflamed by the worst counsels against him, Anno went to the court. Finding the brothers generally occupied in cultivating the garden, he said:

> I am not unaware of the king’s agitation and indignation. As I go to the palace, I commend myself to God and to you. You are my shield; you are my protection; you, my most beloved sons, are everything to me. I place no hope in my soldiers, nor any confidence in their weapons. I speak in faith: I have greater trust in you than in all of them. Therefore, may it rest upon the kindness of the Savior and upon the power of your love how I shall be received by the king or by his people.

After saying this, he departed. Often, through the authority of him “who sets a boundary for the sea” (Jer. V), the king, abandoning the heat of his anger, rose when Anno approached and offered him the kiss of peace with great affection.
