Only a little earlier he had been threatening Anno and everything belonging to him with death and, if opportunity arose, utter destruction.

Those standing around were thrown into astonishment and whispered among themselves:

> Where is the anger now? Where are the threats now? Where are all the insults uttered only a little while ago?

In all this we must consider the Lord’s word, which promises: “Those who glorify me I will glorify” (1 Sam. II). And indeed, whether in our own times or in times past, it has been difficult to find anyone who displayed such majesty before the world and such humility toward God.

### XXV. What he established concerning the people of Siegburg.

After he had attained his desire and saw his monks flourishing in divine matters in a way worthy of imitation by all, he extended all his concern for them into the future. He pronounced the vengeance of public excommunication and eternal condemnation upon anyone who obstinately and maliciously persisted in harming them.

Then he prepared a document strengthened by the seal of his authority. In it, under the same solemn declaration, he decreed:

- No one should presume to alter the monks’ original custom.
- No one should compel the abbot to undertake any courtly service or any office not prescribed by the Rule.
- No bishop, nor any of his people, should have the power to take up residence in that place without the abbot’s permission.
- No advocate or sub-advocate should be appointed over the monastery or its goods except one whom the abbot himself wished to appoint.

To give these constitutions still greater authority, he went to Rome and sought a privilege from the Apostolic See. While the Church was still living in peace and harmony, he received the following written response:

## XXVI. Pope Alexander’s Privilege

“Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Anno, archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, his dearest brother in Christ Jesus.

“What you request from us, beloved brother in God, we owe, by virtue of the office we have undertaken and by apostolic authority, to all churches. But with you, beloved brother in God, I must act differently, since you are a religious man and, truly, a bishop both in your deeds and in your name.

“Therefore, on behalf of our Lord Jesus Christ, of holy Mary, Mother of God, of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and of all the saints and elect of God, we confirm and strengthen that abbey forever: let no person, great or small; none of your successors; no king or count—in short, no human being—dare to remove anything from it for the destruction of the place. Rather, let there be lasting and unshaken peace in all that has been or shall be bestowed there; let the original custom, according to which these things were established, remain among the monks, and let them have free election of their abbot.

“If anyone should rashly violate this privilege of ours, let him know that he will bind himself with the bonds of perpetual anathema, unless, repenting, he should make worthy satisfaction. But whoever strives to be its faithful observer shall obtain forgiveness for all his sins and shall merit the glory of eternal blessedness.”

From these words of the pope it is easy to perceive how highly this singular prelate of our age [Note: Here you have the date of the author of this history.] was esteemed in the heart of so great a pontiff for his holiness and veneration. For the pope attentively called him “a religious man and, truly, a bishop both in his deeds and in his name.”

We also set down part of the royal decree, lest the reader fail to know that the legitimate rights of the aforesaid monastery must not be lightly infringed:

[Note: Here you have the age of the author of this history.]

## XXVII. The Royal Decree

“Henry, by the favor of divine clemency king. Let it be known to all worshipers of Christ and to all our faithful, both those yet to be born and those living now, how our dearest Anno, archbishop, placed under our protection and defense the monastery that he built on Mount Sigeberg; and how he requested that the market, toll, mint, and estates, together with all the advantages obtained and granted for this purpose, or still to be obtained and granted, be confirmed and strengthened by our royal authority.”

And later:

“Therefore we receive the monastery and everything belonging to it under our protection, and, according to royal custom, we have strengthened with our own hand this charter written concerning it and have ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.”

## XXVIII. Saint Anno Builds Two More Monasteries

After this, the most prudent pontiff, seeing that he still had days of this life granted to him, added two communities of monks, because it is written: “Let the righteous still be justified” (Revelation 22).

One he established in the region of the Westphalians, at a place called Grascaf; the other on the border of the Thuringians and Slavs, at a place called Salvelt. The first was dedicated in honor of Saint Alexander the martyr and his six brothers; the second, consecrated by Anno himself, in honor of the prince of the apostles.

He abundantly endowed them with buildings and the revenues of estates, established them to live according to the rule of the Sigeberg community, and brought brothers from that same monastery to inhabit them.

Then, having been perfectly admitted into the number of the five wise virgins (Matthew 25), he was worthy neither in sight, nor hearing, nor taste, nor smell, nor touch to offend the face of the coming Bridegroom. He had assigned to each sense its own guardians, who, by perpetual prayers, vigils, and almsgiving, adorned him with the attire worthy of the heavenly King’s presence and cultivated him, living though already dead.

O truly happy, and exceedingly happy, was he who, supported by the intercessions of so many, could easily have any offense committed through the five senses erased by forgiveness.

Each of his disciples must take great care to consider what return they owe to his love. For he was wholly devoted to them, like a single mother dependent upon her only son; and sometimes, out of compassion for them, he endured bodily weakness because of the affection he bore them. One example will make this sufficiently clear.

## XXIX. The Cologne Fair. The Most Holy Man Suffers from a Violent Fever and Suddenly Recovers Miraculously

The singular and joyful celebration of the Paschal festival was approaching. Since crowds without number were flowing to Cologne for the fair, famous throughout the world, not only from nearly all the cities along the Rhine but also from overseas and from still more distant provinces, the very multitude brought the people of Cologne a double cause for rejoicing.

Yet something that could greatly mar the beauty of this happiness occurred: a fierce fever seized the bishop, and he took to his bed. When the day of the Lord’s Supper dawned, he was exhausted in every limb and despaired of being able to perform the sacred ministry, which he always attended at its proper time with particular devotion. From this distress an even greater illness penetrated the depths of his heart.

For he began to burn inwardly with various thoughts, just as he was burning outwardly with fever. At one moment he resolved by every means to rise and perform the duty, lest he be deprived of the fruit of so devout a service; at another, when he considered the strength of his weakness—barely sufficient for the first movement—he judged that it would be almost madness to attempt what plainly exceeded his capacity.

After the day had been consumed in this twofold conflict of the heart, the hour arrived when the supreme King, with the angels trembling, sought the feet of his servants and impressed upon his faithful ones, by deed and word, the example of his humility (John 13). The devout man contemplated this with the innermost eye of his mind and fell into the greatest anguish, fearing that, though infirm, he would be excluded from the companionship of the one whom he wished to imitate in this act.

Then, turning wholly to prayer, he asked the Lord of all—who is able to be present whenever he wills—that he might graciously attend to his desires and grant him the strength which his devout and suppliant intention required. He sent a boy ahead and instructed the brothers to wait for him there, saying that he would certainly come after a very short interval.

The brothers, detained from the sacred office by this unexpected message, began to offer the bishop’s presence only after some delay. The senior brothers, irritated by the weariness of waiting, sent word to him, saying:

“We do not know what we are waiting for. The hour has passed, and, with night already near, we shall certainly diminish, more than is right, the reverence due to this day by detracting from divine worship.”

At once, leaving his bed, the pontiff, whose charity’s fire had quieted the fevers’ flames, went to the brothers. Girded with a linen cloth according to custom, he proceeded, contrary to everyone’s expectation, to the ministry of the mystical washing.

How humbly, piously, and devoutly he fell before the feet of the Lord himself; how, weeping, he dried the feet of each one with the hair of his venerable head; and how he honored them with a suppliant kiss—I leave to the prudent judgment of the reader, since he always kept in the eyes of his heart that former penitent, Mary (Luke 7).

When each had taken his place in due order, the congregation of the ever-virgin blessed Mary, formerly established through his efforts, was likewise standing on one side according to his arrangement. When he had completed the work of charity and devotion toward the others, he came to that congregation. Fixing upon it the innermost eye of his love, he also remembered the other communities gathered by him in Christ.

Meanwhile his former illness returned. It happened that, when the desolation of his people struck his heart, it moved him so suddenly with compassion that, seized by grief, he fell to the ground. Already near death and deprived of the use of every limb, he was carried back to his bed in the arms of those who bore him.

He lay in the same illness for three days. But the Lord regarded his pious concern, by which he feared that his flock might be deprived of the nourishment of the sacred word during the holy solemnities, and he was miraculously healed during the very vigils of the Lord’s resurrection.

When the signals for Matins had sounded, he suddenly sprang from his bed, as though drawn by a divine impulse. His chamber servant, who suspected that he was being driven by the madness of pain, protested; but Anno scarcely managed to wrest his shoes and clothing from him and went joyfully to the church.

When all were filled with wonder, he sang with the others and recited the psalm concerning him “who ascends above the setting sun; the Lord is his name” (Psalm 67). He also came to the proclamation of the third lesson and read it with greater joy and cheerfulness than usual.

Thus the good shepherd of the sheep, expressing his delight in beautiful dances worthy of the Paschal worship, raised and increased the general joy of his people by his own rejoicing. He carried out every part of that solemnity so joyfully, devoutly, and diligently that no one could doubt that the right hand of the risen Christ had raised him from his bed of pain for the performance of these duties.

## XXX. Foreign Kings Also Honor Him. He Composes Certain Hymns

The stature of this man, whose fame and reputation for such great virtues among his own people extended also among foreign nations, can be judged from the following facts. He was joined in friendship with the kings of the English and Danes and was frequently honored by their gifts and embassies.

When he accompanied the emperor Henry into Pannonia and brought back the king of the Hungarians, expelled from his kingdom and homeland and taking refuge with him, Anno himself, by his own skill in subduing the enemy’s camps, accomplished and achieved more than all the others with their weapons.

He also sent his envoys with letters to the king of Greece. When they returned, they presented him with a considerable portion of the Lord’s Cross, together with other distinguished royal gifts sent by the king.

The queen of the Poles, of Teutonic origin and drawn by the fame of his name, hastened to visit him. She granted Salevelt and all its dependencies to his authority, receiving from him suitable prices in various kinds of goods and in payment for the tenure.

At this place, as was mentioned somewhat earlier, he built a monastery, which he always loved with a special veneration, both because he had experienced there the presence of heavenly grace and because of the conversion of the pagan people living in the surrounding region.

For he often avoided the uproar of Cologne by withdrawing there. Occupied with spiritual studies, he composed certain songs or hymns of divine praise, witnessed certain revelations, and, devoting himself to contemplation, tasted in advance the sweetness of the rest to come.

## XXXI. He Distributes All His Possessions to the Ministers of the Churches and to the Poor

Although he surpassed everyone in the kingdom in wealth and glory—a fact perhaps beyond belief—he often found that he had not even a coin, or scarcely the value of a coin, under his own control.

Whatever he had acquired from the rich of this world, whether by purchase, by receiving it on tenure, or in some other way, he immediately spent on the poor or on the ministers of the churches. His purpose was that, when he died, he should leave behind him not even the smallest object within the whole right of his property.

Thus, sometimes with many of our brothers present, sometimes with fewer, or even with only one, he would say:

“What is this? Why does human opinion celebrate me as though I were a great and wealthy man? Apart from the utensils of my little chapel, the equipment of the pontifical ministry, and this ring, I do not know that I possess even a single denarius today.

“For I do not accumulate the treasures of insatiable avarice in my cloisters, so that either the king or his people might be endangered or their gluttony satisfied. In this matter I oppose their greed sufficiently that, when I close my eyes, I shall not leave even one copper coin among their claws.”

The outcome of these words is evident from the fact that, in the illness of which he died, he was covered with garments belonging to others. Whenever the saints were carried in men's hands to visit him—since, now infirm, he could no longer visit them at their shrines and therefore often wished to have them brought to him—he lacked clothing of his own and meanwhile had to be covered by one of the canons.

How great a defender of the churches he proved to be, and how impenetrable a wall against the enemies of Christ! He was not one of those against whom the prophecy is directed:

“You have not gone up into the breach, nor built a wall for the house of Israel, so that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezekiel 13).

Rather, a good imitator of the supreme Shepherd, he offered his life for his sheep (John 10), never yielding like a hired servant when wolves attacked. He always pursued them either with the words of the most severe rebuke or with the sword of the most just excommunication. At times he even deterred the more shameless as though by military force; and against all of them he took up the invincible shield of prayer.

His countless labors for the Church remain. It would be impossible to recount everything he suffered from the impious. We shall mention only one event in which the power and efficacy of his prayer are especially recognized, as a warning to those who even now shamelessly oppose him, though he has been taken into heaven. Let them, even if late, repent and consider what one living with Christ can accomplish; they may perhaps marvel that, while clothed in flesh, he was able to accomplish so much.

## XXXII. The Count Palatine Becomes a Monk, Abandons the Monastery, and Ravages Saint Anno’s Territory. The Palatine Is Struck Mad

After Mount Sigeberg [Note: Sigeberg, in Latin Victorius, or Mount of Victory.]—which is interpreted as “victorious,” plainly victorious over vices—had passed into the jurisdiction of Saint Peter through the surrender of Count Palatine, that same man, a figure of great tyranny, came to Gorze as though the fire of his perversity had been smothered. There he laid aside the belt of worldly pomp and assumed the habit of monastic poverty.

The devil brought this about by his own art. As a creature of spiritual substance and angelic dignity, he sometimes perceives future things from what has gone before through the subtlety of his nature. By ensnaring those once made subject to hell with a thousand deceits, he made them his children in a twofold way.

Having used this deception against the man in question, after some time the devil cast him down from the profession he had deceitfully assumed. He persuaded him to resume conjugal relations and his former household affairs; then, joining to himself the seven spirits of his wickedness, he entered his heart and thereafter hurled him into every abyss of depravity.

This man, who hated all servants of God as a renegade, began wars and stirred up seditions. To complete his own destruction and extinguish the name of the then-famous pontiff Anno, he attacked the city of Cologne as an enemy after plundering and burning, after killing and mutilating many people.

There he sat close by with a multitude of armed men and ravaged everything around him like a savage boar, mingling fire and sword.

Meanwhile the holy pontiff, clothed inwardly in a hair shirt and burning with lesser concern for himself but the greatest concern for the flock entrusted to him, went one day to the wall. From a distance he saw a flickering fire; the flames and smoke of villages recently burned were rising upward, while the inhabitants fled from the enemies on one side and from the fires on the other.

The devout shepherd was pierced by this sight with inward grief and groaned as though he were being stabbed by the swords of all his enemies. He uttered a lamentable cry:

“Woe to me, wretched and sinful man! Woe to me, most unhappy man, whom an ungrateful age has prolonged to this hour as a spectator of so great an evil and so great a grief!”

Then he withdrew from the place, entered the threshold of the mother church, and fell before the memorial of his protector, Saint Peter. Mourning and wailing, he uttered these words:

“Alas, alas, Lord! What has your flock and sheepfold deserved, that, exposed in this way to the rabid teeth of wolves, it should be handled by their bites and devoured by their jaws?

“Those who injure them have not been injured by them; they do not repay injury with injury; they are slaughtered without cause, driven from their homes without reason. Whatever punishment the worst of men pays according to the dictates of justice, these people, under the sole command of cruelty, pay far more harshly.

“See how the cries of widows, the great misery of children and orphans, and the sufferings of so many poor people now necessarily call upon you, their protector and judge, to judgment.

“Have mercy, and breathe upon us a serene day of peace. Against whoever is responsible for such a storm threatening your Church, determine the sentence of your vengeance.”

Meanwhile, as the people of Cologne shouted for arms and watched the enemy’s attacks from here and there along the wall with the equipment of war for the city’s defense, the tyrant, seemingly unconcerned, withdrew to his castle, which they call Cochomo. More truly, he did so in order to gather there his strength and the multitude following him and openly engage in a bloody judgment against the bishop and his officials.

The bishop’s soldiers nevertheless armed themselves against him with all their strength. Some kinsmen joined the Palatine’s party, while others arranged themselves with the bishop, and the gravest suspicion of civil war threatened everyone.

The holy pontiff, weighed down by severe anguish of mind, did not know which of two tolerable courses to choose. If he decided to humble the enemy’s pride by force of arms, inhuman cruelty and a pitiable crime presented themselves, as brother would violently strike brother, son-in-law father-in-law, and father-in-law son-in-law. If he chose otherwise, he saw with the eyes of his imagination the misery of the city to be attacked, the destruction of churches, the insults inflicted on clergy and monks, the needs of widows and the poor, and finally the indiscriminate slaughter of young and old.

At this moment of necessity, he turned wholly to the Lord, his first, greatest, and most certain consolation. He organized litanies with fasts and visited various shrines of the saints.

The enemy, who was soon to appear, was already feared as though present. The priest went about with the people, meditating on sorrowful matters, yet he did not cease the chanting of the psalms.

When he came, in order, to Psalm 35, which begins, “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me,” and focused more intently upon it, the correspondence of the psalm caused the sorrow in his heart to increase.

When they reached the verse, “Let the snare come upon him which he does not know,” he seemed touched by some foreboding concerning his adversary. He growled in spirit, and, as tears burst forth with his voice, repeated it again while the deacon stood astonished, saying:

“Let the snare come upon him which he does not know, and let the trap which he has hidden seize him.”

Whether he uttered this in the emotion of prayer or rather in the spirit of prophecy—or, as I think more likely, in both ways—does not harm the historical account. For after only a few days had passed, the snare he had foretold so terribly entangled the enemy by the inscrutable judgment of the heavenly arbiter that, in a fury unknown through the ages, he killed with his own hands the wife for whose deadly sweetness he had apostatized.

While the commanders of the fighting forces were arranging their battle lines outside for the anticipated confrontation with the bishop, the Palatine himself sat in his chamber beside the companion of his desire. But the Lord was angered and could no longer endure the sufferings of the innocent. The man was driven mad; then, seizing a double-headed axe hanging nearby, he struck and severed the head of his beloved wife Adelheid.

He ran out through the doors and, clapping his hands and laughing loudly, explained what he had done in the manner of a madman.

Every age and condition of society shuddered at so grievous a sacrilege. The elaborate preparations for the battle ceased, and each person returned home.

The prince and author of the sedition was himself captured and bound by his own men. As long as he lived afterward, he remained furious and without control of his mind. Satisfied with his own calamities, he had neither the opportunity nor the will to inflict further destruction upon others.

Then the devout priest, the sole example in his time of heavenly teaching, fulfilled in deed the Lord’s command: “Pray for those who persecute you, and do good to those who hate you” (Matthew 5). He reverently and with excessive sorrow committed the pitiably slain woman to the earth, took her son into his own care, nourished him with the most kindly affection, and rewarded him most generously with many benefits.

Thereafter Cologne, filled with peace, rejoiced in the works of its shepherd. He was devoted not only to various acts of mercy, feeding the needy and clothing the naked, but also enlarged the splendor of ecclesiastical religion by building monasteries, providing what the ministers of God required, and always striving tirelessly to seek out and honor the ashes of the saints.

## XXXIII. Saint Anno Brings the Body of Saint Innocent the Martyr to the Monastery of Sigeberg

[Note: See Baronius, year 1070.]

At one time, driven by this desire, he entered Rome, both as archchancellor of the Romans and in order to consult for the benefit of his own devotion and of the Church. Having spent a considerable time there on this business and obtained permission to depart with the apostolic blessing, he quickly prepared himself and his companions to return.

While on this journey, he earnestly petitioned Adelheid, then marchioness of the Cottian Alps, that, by her authoritative order, he might obtain from the people of Agaunum relics from the Theban region, since that place belonged to her jurisdiction.

When he arrived there, he was received magnificently and with popular acclaim, as was fitting not only for the archbishop of Cologne but also for the archchancellor of all Italy. Nevertheless, he judged that he should proceed there more by counsel and prudence than by authority.

Accordingly, having won the custodian of the sacred buildings to his wishes through gifts and promises, and having removed the obstacles presented by other persons, he entered the church secretly at night with only a few of his men. There he reverently carried away the most sacred body of blessed Innocent the martyr, together with the head of Saint Vitalis. Moved both by the success of his vow and by fear that some disturbance might arise among the people, he ordered the journey to proceed more rapidly.

With Christ guiding the way, after traversing the sea of his pilgrimage, he reached the walls of the monastery of Sigeberg. Amid the great rejoicing of the people who had gathered there that day, he brought into it a treasure of sacred relics more precious than gold on the third day before the Ides of May. That day was then illuminated by the joys of the Lord’s Ascension; it was the seventieth year after the year 1069 from the Lord’s Incarnation. All the brothers solemnly celebrated with devout joy the heavenly patronage that had been bestowed and the presence of their long-desired father.

## XXXIV. A Memorable Pronouncement. A Fire Is Extinguished in a Wonderful Manner

The people of Cologne were also moved by this report. When the holy man afterward entered the city, a great multitude of clergy and common people received him.

He did not wish to share less generously with the citizens of his own see the wealth he had brought from the riches of Italy. Therefore he furnished a chapel of elegant workmanship, adjoining the church of Saint George, and placed in it the arm of the martyr Saint Caesarius, which he had brought from Rome and which was worthy of veneration.

To make the dignity of the apostolic name more celebrated, the venerable pontiff proceeded with the people to consecrate it in honor of Saint James. But suddenly a devouring fire, at the very moment when he had put on the episcopal vestments, invaded the city threateningly from the east, as custom required.

Then the crowds rushed eagerly to extinguish it, leaving the bishop surrounded by scarcely a few people out of the excessively large multitude that had gathered. Grieving at this great hindrance, he sat down for a little while with his head resting in his hands. Then, as though he had received a reply from heaven, he said:

“Today the fire that has arisen through the deceit of the malicious serpent will not exert the force of its own nature to endanger any part of this city. Let the people return without fear of this, so that, in the consecration of the daughter of our mother—the holy Church—we may render to the Lord the pleasing service of our ministry.”

At once the people returned, and the flame nevertheless died down and disappeared.

According to the rite established by the Church, everyone followed the priest joyfully during the dedication. When the proper time came, he sought the summit of a higher place and began to address those standing around him with honey-sweet exhortations full of contrition.

Suddenly, through the ambush of the envious enemy, the ravenous fire rose again and inflicted no small disturbance upon the listeners to the sacred word.

The bishop restrained them with a strong admonition not to move from their place. He declared that, in every danger, the first line of defense was to place no danger above the praises of Christ. If they would only decide to stand firm, they themselves would see how quickly the raging fire would perish without anyone resisting it.

While he was still saying these things, some acted otherwise, but the rest fixed their feet out of reverence for the word of God. As everyone looked on, the whole fire was suddenly overwhelmed in an instant, as though by a flood poured down from above.

And, for the greater glory of Christ, while the fire prevailed over those whom the ardor of greed had not permitted to remain and listen to the priest, those who had obeyed his words found not even the trace of a slight spark anywhere among all their possessions.

Taking this as the subject of his discourse, the bishop prolonged his sermon. He spoke at length of the snares of demons and at length of the mercy of God, asserting that Christians are judged by their end, not by their beginnings; and that to have begun a good work without completing it is liable not only to receive no reward but also to incur punishment.

Finally, lingering over the praises of the saints, he added the following matter worthy of being reported, while everyone sighed.

## XXXV. A Dead Man Returns to Life. What the Patronage of the Saints Accomplishes

[Note: Baronius, the same year.]

In the city of Rome there was a man named Andreas who, though not in conduct, abounded in wealth and the pleasures of life. He wore away the broad road of a loose manner of living, treating his soul as a burden and his body as a pleasure. Apart from the name of Christianity and a dead faith, he seemed to possess nothing of Christian religion, except that he was devoted to the blessed martyr Caesarius and regularly attended his church with candles.

Overtaken by the universal condition of death, he repented of himself too late and breathed out his final breath. Without delay, his body was placed in a bier, which was surrounded by the sad attentions of his weeping and lamenting friends. Because of certain obstacles, they postponed his burial until the following day.

After the watches had been prolonged until midnight and everyone had been overcome by deep stupor, the bier suddenly began to move. The man who had lain lifeless raised his head and, looking around in every direction, struck those who saw him with even greater terror. Some seized the protection of flight, while everyone else was equally overcome with fear. He sat up in the bier.

Meanwhile the more prudent, having somewhat recovered their confidence, stood at a distance for a while, then drew nearer. After carefully examining the man, they asked what had happened: whether they were being deceived by demonic phantoms, whether someone returned from the underworld had emerged according to a law unfamiliar to mortals, or—what seemed more likely—whether he had been taken for dead because of the violence of his illness, while only the eyes of those watching him had been deceived and he had not entirely lost his life.

At this he sighed heavily and said:

“I did not fall into the condition of death in appearance but in truth. Yet I would be paying the sentence of everlasting death in soul and body, alas, if the prayer worthy of God of the martyr Caesarius had not intervened.”

Then, answering according to the sequence of their questions—where he had been, what he had seen, and how he had returned—he said:

“Violently expelled from my body, I was led to the terrible and exceedingly fearful throne of Christ. There, while thousands of angels stood around trembling, I, most wretched and guilty in conscience, did not dare to raise my eyes in supplication toward any of them. Receiving only the grim sentence of the stern Judge, I was dragged without mercy by the most hideous and horrifying demons to the places of eternal condemnation.

Striking his breast and groaning most bitterly, he said: “The misery of that hour cannot be adequately expressed in any words; the memory of it will never escape my heart.”

“While I wept, the most shameless demons laughed, mocked my misfortunes, and drove me cruelly toward destruction, when the precious martyr Caesarius, moved with pity by my calamities, fell before the Lord, with the favor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy apostles and martyrs.

“He showed the marks of his wounds and said:

“‘Most merciful Lord, for the sake of your awesome name I once willingly accepted these things. In enduring them, although my flesh groaned, there was no resistance of mind, provided that, once my body had been slain by the harshness of temporal torments, neither soul nor flesh would thereafter, under your protection, be afflicted by any goads of sorrow.

“‘Why, then, while you look upon me in your goodness, am I again pressed down by fresh griefs in my heart? Behold, one who trusted in my patronage and entrusted his life wholly to me is being driven headlong to hell. He is now rightly accused of folly, having been deceived by an empty hope and having honored me as the guardian of his life, though I cannot even serve as his intercessor to lessen his punishments.’

“While he lay before Christ the King speaking these words, the most merciful Virgin Mary, Mother of God, joined herself to the other saints and bent her Son and Lord to the will of his martyr.

“By the martyr’s command I was snatched from the worst demons, now secure of pardon and life. I was ordered to put my body on again for this purpose: that, once these things were known, everyone might become more concerned for his own salvation.”

When the man had finished speaking, astonishment seized those standing around him. He gathered himself up on the bier and died.

The excellent teacher brought his account to an end with this conclusion. Everyone entrusted what they had heard to sighs and contrition. Then he addressed them:

“And you, brothers, and you, sisters, admit the consideration of this event into the hidden places of your hearts. Offer yourselves to the saints of God for every form of devotion and service, so that, when you are pressed by the distress of your final tribulation, each of you may experience one of the saints there as your patron with all the greater joy, the more devoutly you have lived here in his service.”

Having said this, we add a memorable statement celebrated by his own mouth, for the reason mentioned shortly before—namely, that he taught that in every danger the first line of defense is to place no danger above the praises of Christ. From this it may be established that we have not falsely testified that he taught this.

## XXXVI. The Very Ancient Monastery of Saint Cecilia at Cologne

There is at Cologne an ancient monastery, under the title of Saint Cecilia, virgin and martyr. Within it, among the religious women, a young girl of childish innocence and age was being nurtured with the sweetest affection. She was uniquely dear to everyone, and especially to the mother of the congregation.

But premature death, arriving unexpectedly, disturbed the joyful beginnings of her simple and cheerful character with the bitterest fate. She now lay as a burden to the eyes of everyone who had previously found her most delightful.

Truly, our condition is to be mourned: not only are we forced to endure within ourselves the unavoidable necessity of final separation, but, alas, daily slaughtered by the loss of those we love.

Thus all human beings suffer every day. So also those sisters suffered at that time. Since they were about to lose the girl, who was at the point of death, they went to the choir after the evening hymns, when the hour of Compline was already approaching, so that they might render their service to the Lord, grieving over their own loss.

The opening of the first psalms had not yet been fully completed when, at the sudden signal of the well-known bell, the sisters were summoned to the departure of the girl’s soul. With no small audacity of transgression, each of them abandoned the place she occupied, neglected the work of divine praise, and rushed to the dying girl as though to offer assistance—though they were more likely to bring danger upon her by doing so.

When they entered, the girl violently opened her eyes, which had been closed in the sleep of death. With a great rush, as though she had suffered no misfortune, she sprang from the bed, ran to the abbess, seized the insignia of her authority, and clung tightly to her, gnashing her teeth and trembling throughout her body.

“Bring protection, my lady; bring protection!” she cried.

The mother, trembling at the novelty of the extraordinary event no less than at the girl’s cries, and, like women, uttering a confused and constricted voice, asked:

“What is wrong, daughter?”

The girl replied:

“An enormous and terrible multitude of monstrous demons burst in as the sisters entered the doors. They threaten to carry me away with them to hell.”

When the mother, her face covered with tears, asked the cause of this evil, the girl said:

“I suffer this for no other sins, but because Christ holds me responsible for the loss of his service on my account. If the sisters wished to offer me anything, they ought first to have completed his praises with the proper ending.”

At once, on the mother’s command, all the sisters returned to the monastery. They began to devote themselves to divine praises with such greater devotion and such greater earnestness as they more clearly understood that, because they had neglected them, the girl had been endangered and they themselves had incurred the guilt of no contemptible transgression.

When they had passed beyond the threshold of the room, the girl returned to her little bed and lay down. While the sisters occupied the choir in singing psalms to God, she displayed no gesture of fear. Gradually, as the dying usually do, she weakened and died.

## XXXVII. Saint Anno Transfers Saint Agilolf, Bishop of Cologne, and Raises the Holy Evalds

But let us return to what came before. The most blessed Anno, honoring on earth those whom he was hastening with all his strength to join in heaven, gladdened the city of Cologne, long deprived of the body of its martyr and bishop Agilolf, by restoring his remains.

Taking them from the people of Malmedy, he transferred them to his monastery at the Steps, amid the great eagerness and rejoicing of the exultant city.

At the same time, instructed by a revelation of the two martyrs themselves, he raised from their tombs the precious bodies of the two Evalds. Long ago, the Rhine, flowing backward, had carried them from Saxony to Cologne for burial.

### XXXVIII. The Body of Saint Benignus the Martyr Is Found

It remains now to relate how, in Anno’s time, the body of the most blessed martyr and priest Benignus was either discovered or translated, for the perpetual glory and salvation of the people of Siegburg.

In a place of Swabia called the Cell of Saint Vitus, a certain duke of the Alemanni and Burgundians once founded a church and endowed it abundantly with his hereditary possessions for the support of the monks serving God there. Instructed alike by devotion and faith, when he had come to Dijon out of a desire for holy relics, he carried away with him, on his return, the body of the martyr Benignus, beloved of God. This martyr had been sent by divine providence from the East to Gaul and, after enduring many struggles, finally pierced by a soldier’s lance under the emperor Aurelian, had entered heaven in the form of a snow-white dove.

The same duke also, by Christ’s granting it, obtained the three brothers Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus—baptized by the aforesaid martyr and gloriously crowned at Langres—together with the body of Saint Mamertus, bishop of that city. Rejoicing, and returning to the regions of Alemannia with so great a pledge of heavenly patronage, he entrusted the desirable treasure to the church he had built. Out of fear of future dangers, the holy bodies were sunk more deeply into the earth in the sacristy, with their names inscribed.

After many years, when all the members of that generation had been removed from this life, and the same place had passed into the possession of the royal monastery called Ellwangen, the radiance of so many lamps, unknown to the world, lay concealed beneath the dust of a humble burial. Then, by the ordinance of God, who brings forth the Morning Star in its time (Job 38), the pavement above the holy bodies was opened by workmen for the purpose of some construction.

As they cut into the ground and vied with one another in removing the earth, the sarcophagi of the holy relics were unexpectedly found, each with its name distinctly marked. There the martyr and priest of great merit, Benignus—truly corresponding to his merits and his name, and more distinguished by name than the others—was discovered and raised up. At that time the monastery was being administered by Abbot Reniger, who was a kinsman of the blessed Anno.

Shortly afterward, King Henry celebrated the joy of the Lord’s Nativity at Bamberg. Since a gathering of many nobles and men of rank was taking place there, the same abbot also arrived. Because he was a relative of Archbishop Anno, as though wishing to congratulate him, he testified that he had discovered Benignus—the man who had come from Asia at the sending of Saint Polycarp, disciple of the blessed John the Evangelist.

The bishop seized the name itself from his mouth. “You claim,” he said, “that you possess Benignus? He is the special intercessor of my monks. You must grant him to my requests, if you wish me ever to receive from this any benefit of your affection.”

The abbot replied, since he was indebted to the king for a considerable sum of silver and was therefore liable to him in the matter of payment: “See, so that you may relieve me of concern for the money I owe, I shall satisfy your desires as you wish, sending you not another Benignus, but that very Benignus who truly suffered martyrdom at the fortress of Dijon under Aurelian.”

The bishop gladly accepted this promise; for he had no wealth that he would not willingly spend in such an exchange.

> **[Note: This should be understood piously. For it is not permissible to sell holy relics.]**

After they had pledged their faith to one another and each had returned to his own place, the bishop received the monks, who arrived after a month and a half carrying the relics of the precious body, with joy at Cologne. When they attempted to establish by public oaths that this was none other than the Benignus whom they had been asked to deliver, he did not permit it, saying that, in honor of the person in question, he would hold him without any doubt.

After sending ahead to Siegburg news of this joy, he himself mounted his horse with his companions. A considerable number of men and women from Cologne accompanied him. On the very evening of the Sunday night that marked the beginning of the Lenten fast, he reached the foot of the mountain. The brothers came down to meet him in processions with due reverence, and the sacred bones were received with praises during the night into the church beside the mountain.

In the morning of the Lord’s Day, which dawned as the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March amid universal expectation, the entire assembly was solemnly dressed, and the church shone with various ornaments and many lights. The holy bishop, together with Erpho, the abbot of blessed memory, placed their pious shoulders beneath the bier of the holy relics. As the people resounded and the bells rang, and as the monks went before them singing a hymn of great devotion, they presented their martyr and priest to Christ at the altar as an offering of sweet fragrance.

Then, intending to address the people, the bishop mounted to a higher place. His whole face streaming with tears of joy, he declared that no day had ever dawned more pleasing to him. Explaining who the man being carried was and what his merit had been, he indicated that he was called Benignus and said:

“Benignus means ‘benevolent,’ and rightly so. For he keeps his ears open to the prayers of all of us, and, most willingly hearing us, he himself approaches God to intercede for us. Now, therefore, beloved, since you have the presence of so great a patron, lift up your hearts, and let each of you humbly make known to him what is expedient for you. Believe me: if only faith is not lacking, because he is benevolent and is so named, he will benevolently grant whatever you ask and hasten to fulfill it.”

The year of the Lord’s Incarnation in which this translation was celebrated was 1073.

Afterward the bishop arranged two new little shrines on either side behind the altar, leaving an empty space between them. In the one on the right he placed the blessed Innocent, and in the one on the left the blessed Benignus. Overflowing with joy, and speaking as he often used to do, almost in play, he said:

“It will be according to my will how this matter proceeds, if one day a man worthy of the altar is received between you. Otherwise, you certainly must not expect any expression of gratitude from me.”

Although these words were spoken lightly, how seriously they were received by them we now contemplate with the eyes of faith. Though we have not yet seen him with bodily eyes, we rightly believe that he has already obtained a place among them.

Having brought to an end, with God’s help, this account of his life and deeds—short in proportion to their number, and written not as we ought but as we were able—we shall now take a brief rest, so that we may rise with greater lightness to elucidate the things that are proclaimed about his virtues.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1543]

### I. What So Great a Man Thought About Holy Relics. He Opened Without a Key the Casket Containing Saint Gregory’s Arm

With the intention of this work before me, undertaken for the sake of divine praise, I myself vehemently detest engaging in fabricated narratives. For if I have hope of drawing off at least a little of my sins from this source, a heavier iniquity would be added if I were shamelessly to put forward anything other than truth, or to assert anything as true. For God has no need of our lie (Job 13). Nevertheless, the man whom we have wished by this work to make known to the world is not pleased by the goodwill of our devotion if we honor him through false praises; for he will always be adorned by true praises, even while we remain silent, for as long as the world endures.

We have said this in order to answer those who, measuring the holy man according to the inclination of their own hearts, do not believe him to have possessed the merit by which such things as are reported could be done. For even the Savior himself was appointed as a sign of contradiction (Luke 2) to such people.

But we, knowing the holiness of the man of God and detracting nothing from Christ’s power, shall now undertake, for the knowledge of those who come after us, to gather at the outset those things concerning him that we have found credible either by hearing or in writing: signs, revelations, and the things he spoke prophetically, with the grace of the Holy Spirit guiding his understanding and speech.

In his monastery, situated on the mountain, a certain brother, when an affliction arose, fell ill, and no remedy appeared from which the sick man might have hoped for improvement. When this reached the ears of the man of God, who was then present, he sent a very swift messenger to Cologne with orders that the arm of the holy martyr George should be sent to him as quickly as possible. He asserted that the sick man would certainly be helped if, filled with faith, he took as a drink the liquid with which his most sacred mouth would be washed.

When the arm had been brought to him in a reliquary, just as he had ordered, he asked for the key with which to unlock it. Then the messenger, remembering for the first time, complained that he had left it at Cologne, since no one there had mentioned it to him.

The bishop, as though attempting to open the reliquary, lightly shook the lock with two fingers. In the presence of us who were there, at the first touch of his fingers the bolt sprang back, and a ringing sound arose, such as is usually produced by forcibly turning keys. It struck the ears of those present so sharply that it caused them no small astonishment. They saw that the man of God had performed the function of a key and opened the reliquary with complete ease, without a key.

### II. A Blind Man Is Given Sight by Touching His Garment. He Is Distressed at Being Praised

A certain man deprived of the light of his eyes, one day appealing humbly to him in the sacristy of Saint Peter, bowed earnestly at his feet as though hoping for some consolation. Gathering up a portion of the holy man’s garment at his side, and with only one of the bishop’s attendants observing the event, he faithfully rubbed the places of his eyes with it. Immediately the darkness was wiped away, and, at the rising of a new light, he healthfully experienced how great faith can accomplish. He could not contain himself for joy and wonder.

Thus, having obtained in the restoration of his sight riches that could not be equaled by any earthly price, the beggar concealed what had happened. From then on he neither sought nor expected the bishop’s kindness in order to receive some small charitable gift. Instead, as we have said, he departed, leaving knowledge of the event to one of the bishop’s servants.

This man reclined at table with the pontiff, who was dining in the midst of a considerable company of men. When the bishop asked where the blind man was, he replied that, having obtained what he had desired, the man had immediately departed.

When the man of God ordered him to explain what this meant, he said: “You have truly bestowed upon the man enough, and more than the customary generosity shown to mortals. For the blind man fell at the knees of your holiness, and rising from there, departed seeing. What gift could be greater than this? Rightly is the giver of so great a gift great; rightly is he blessed and called to such gifts. Although he seemed to ask for nothing comparable to what had been granted, he is believed to have brought the steps of faith for the purpose of obtaining only what he received, since, after receiving his eyes, he sought to receive nothing else.”

At these words the priest grew pale and suddenly became completely bloodless. He thus gave those present a clear indication of how unwillingly he heard such things and how gladly he would have been without the breath of popular esteem.

For he knew that the One who, by his own power, performed signs (Matthew 8), commanded certain people to conceal them. He judged that this command must be observed all the more strictly by himself, since he was a mere man and therefore more liable to fall in proportion as he might heedlessly sin even slightly in his heart against the example of the God-man.

Hence it happened that, although he had experienced the gift of divine grace, his mind did not transgress the measure of his weakness in such matters. Even if some event of this kind had occurred without his knowledge, or on the occasion of some great necessity, he did not neglect, so far as it lay within him, to remove it from human ears by every means.

This circumstance supplied us with the material for this account and gave envious people an opportunity to attack him, as though we had invented concerning a dead man things that had not even been suspected of a living one. But this is because, according to the judgment of a worldly man, each person readily accepts what he thinks easy to do; what lies above that he regards as fictitious and false. Nevertheless, we shall not be frightened by these objections into turning away from the remaining matters.

### III. He Regards It as Most Intolerable That a Miracle Should Be Expected of Him, and This Out of Modesty. Sight Is Restored to a Blind Man

One day the venerable bishop was about to celebrate the solemn Mass. Accompanied by his attendants, he began to enter the crypt of the church at Siegburg.

Here a man equally deprived of the office of sight judged that he had found a suitable time and place for his petitions. He humbly presented himself before the bishop and declared that he had gathered faith from the vision: he could be freed from the blindness by which he was condemned if the bishop would pour out some water for the use of his hands, and if he himself might obtain only enough of it to moisten his badly functioning eyes.

The guardian of humility did not receive this calmly. Fearing the opinion of those present more than he distrusted divine goodness, he assailed the man with the harshest rebuke. He accused him of being deceitful and an impostor who, for the sake of a tiny offering, had submitted himself to hateful fraud that kills the soul. He said that the man had spoken from the invention of his own heart concerning a fictitious vision; whereas, if his misery had demanded some benefit of divine mercy, he ought rather to have sought it through the patronage of those whose proven holiness had long shone throughout the world—not through that of a man stained by daily offenses, who himself stood anxiously in fear of the coming judgment and in need of every possible intercession.

Leaving the poor man at the doors full of confusion, he entered the crypt. The wretched man withdrew from his presence and went into a corner of the crypt. There he struck the ears of heavenly mercy with repeated prayers, neither disbelieving his vision nor being less bold in his faith in the evangelical words:

> “Everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to whoever knocks it will be opened” (Luke 11).

After he had prolonged his groans and sighs in humble prayer for a long time, one of the clerics serving there—who later testified to the whole matter—out of compassion secretly brought a basin of water to the one who desired it. He had received it from the hands of the priest as he approached the sacrifice and had reserved it for this purpose, not without the prompting of divine will.

The blind man immediately washed his entire face with it in faith. He no longer complained to anyone about the delay in fulfilling his expectation, for, when the darkness had been driven away, he rejoiced with loud applause that the day of the clearest light had then dawned for him for the first time.

Moreover, he thought that the bishop’s severity of mind would finally be softened if he, who had previously been blind and was now seeing, were brought before him. After Mass, as the bishop was leaving, he prostrated himself before him as though to offer congratulations, repeating his expressions of thanks and publicly recounting both the speed and the manner of the healing from the beginning.

At these words the bishop, already apparently stirred to the utmost, since he could not refute the matter by reason, at least made it unwelcome to those standing around him by the more insolent force of an inflamed heart. He repeatedly and threateningly asked:

“From where did this utterly presumptuous offender emerge? He has despised the reverence due to our authority and, though not ordered to do so, [or: though hateful to me,] administered that water. He did not fear, with the most reprehensible audacity, to investigate what either I—who have no part in this matter—deserved, or what divine favor might grant, although the Law says: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test’ (Deuteronomy 6).”

The cleric, trembling under this questioning and standing nearby, could not conceal what he had done. With words gathered as best he could, he satisfied the bishop that he had acted simply, while also earnestly asking pardon for his offense.

The bishop then gently slapped him and said:

“Do you wish to spread this rumor about me among the people, so that I may be celebrated everywhere, with vulgar levity, as a worker of new miracles? Do you wish people to say that I too, like the ancient Fathers, though lying far beneath them in merit, have in my own time displayed to the world a specimen of their works in signs and wonders?

“Do you want me, swollen for a moment by this passing breeze of empty praise, to be found at the last among those who will say to God, ‘Did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ and to whom it will be answered, ‘I do not know you; depart from me, workers of iniquity’ (Matthew 7)?

“This is truly a dreadful threat, and this temporal consolation is not proportionate to the greatness of that sorrow. Therefore I adjure you, and all of you who are present—and you above all—by the invocation of the One who sees all things, once and again and again, that you do not allow this deed, by which you have been illuminated not through our benefits but through divine benefits, ever to leave any trace of itself in the ears of others while I remain surrounded by the darkness of this mortality.”

This did happen. Though for the time being it lay hidden under silence, after the bishop had departed from the enclosure of the flesh, the report of the cleric mentioned above commended it both to us and to the hearts of other faithful people.

### IV. He Admirably Avoids Every Form of Display

A woman afflicted alike by poverty and blindness, under the scourges of divine punishment, came along the road toward the same monastery. As the high priest was leaving the church after Mass, she threw herself prone before him, suppliant and groaning.

He halted his step and, as he always used to do with the weaker sex, kindly stooped toward her, addressing her with gentle words and asking the causes of her complaints. She replied that she had been forewarned in a vision and had no doubt that, if the hands of his dignity touched her eyes in washing them, the darkness would be driven away.

Pretending to be disturbed because of those standing nearby, he immediately ordered that she be handed over to the guards, leaving her under the impression that he would multiply blows against her. In reality, he was avoiding public display and intended to care for her in secret.

When he had sat down to table and begun his meal, he sent the choicer foods from his own hands for her refreshment. After the meal was over, he secretly ordered that she be brought to his chamber.

Entering there, with two clerics and only one young chamber servant as witnesses, while the others had dispersed here and there, he did not wash her eyes as one presuming to perform a miracle, as she had requested. Rather, following the example of the humble Teacher and Lord, he bent his knee, washed her feet, and poured water over them with his hands (John 13). After this he also provided an abundance of food, plainly intending, through this path of humility, to profit both himself and the woman more greatly before God.

There can be no doubt that, amid these acts of compassion and self-abasement, he lifted his mind toward heaven and implored the help of the heavenly Physician for her. For when he had sat down after completing his service, as though he had obtained from heaven an answer to the prayer he had offered, he instructed her to taste a very small amount of the blessing that had been given.

As soon as she had barely moistened her palate with such a morsel, she felt the heavenly antidote. Her sight was fully restored, and she prostrated herself on the ground with immense thanksgiving, humbly venerating God in his servant Anno.

Then, as a test, various objects were presented to her. When she appeared to have distinguished each one with complete clarity, the blessed man gave her five solidi as alms and adjured her not to spread among the people a favorable opinion of him concerning such things.

Nevertheless, trusting her less than this, he arranged for one cleric to accompany her until she had left the village.

### V. Holy Water and the Sign of the Cross Drive Away Dropsy

Meanwhile, a certain young man, a native of the neighboring regions, had become useless both to himself and to his family because his entire belly was hideously swollen. Having learned by report of the merits of the blessed Anno, he was brought in a vehicle and climbed the mountain where it had pleased God to dwell. He approached Anno’s presence and miserably sought some remedy for so great a pain. Even if his tongue had been silent, the man’s very deformity and misery, set before the eyes, would easily have wrung it from him.

The holy bishop shuddered at the enormity of the illness and took pity on the young man. He blessed water, gave it to the dying man to drink, and sprinkled him with it. Then, impressing the sign of the cross upon his belly, he ordered him to return quickly to his own home, confidently promising him hope of perfect health. He followed the example of the One who, intending to cleanse lepers, sent them to the priests (Matthew 8).

That very night the subcutaneous fluid, which had been dangerously accumulating in disorder for a long time, was completely and healthfully expelled through a discharge of the bowels (Luke 7). Restored to his former health, the man ran back to the mountain on his own feet at daybreak and offered words of thanks to God and to his servant Anno with great joy and praise.

### VI. His Compassion for the Weak and Lame. A Remarkable Miracle

At a certain time, public business required each of the kingdom’s princes to prepare for a journey into Saxony, as each was making his way to the emperor’s court, which was then being held at Goslar. This high prelate of Cologne therefore had to undertake the same journey.

Having various stopping places according to the needs of the road, he came one day to the monastery of Corvey, compelled by the demands of the journey and the declining hour, intending to spend the night there. He had not yet reached the walls themselves but was already close to them. Suddenly he saw two poor men opposite him, pulling a cart in place of animals. A woman, weak in all her limbs, lay in it; in order to beg for alms, she was carried about in this manner almost everywhere.

When she passed the bishop of Cologne, whose reputation was famous, she learned who he was and cried out loudly, asking him in the name of Christ, with regard for Saint Vitus the martyr, to come to the aid of her distress by providing money to purchase a donkey. Thus, carried on it, she would be able to spare her companions their injurious labor.

At the woman’s voice the most pious priest checked his reins and handed five solidi to one of the clerics and to his chamber servant. He ordered them, without any delay, to find an animal worthy of so high a price wherever one could be found and quickly bring it to the woman. Having said this, he rapidly completed the remaining part of his journey.

While the attendants busied themselves carrying out his orders, a donkey suitable for their purpose finally appeared. When they presented it to the poor woman, they later became witnesses of the miracle that followed.

As she received the animal with words of thanksgiving and repeatedly spoke the name of Anno, the bishop worthy of God, praying that he might receive a reward for his benefactions, she suddenly felt such strength that, although previously she had possessed none, the stings of pain subsided. Leaping down to the ground, she walked on firm steps, completely healthy, and used her legs as she wished.

The same two men, astonished to see her running and giving shouts of rejoicing, while also explaining to everyone she met that she had received this through the merits and compassion of Bishop Anno, spurred their horses and pursued their lord to Corvey, following the tracks of his companions.

But knowing his agitation and indignation whenever such matters were brought before him, they were not bold enough to report anything of this kind to him. Nevertheless, when they later discussed the matter among themselves, it became clear that he was by no means ignorant of it—and rightly so. For he was one of those great lights of the Church to whom are given through the Spirit either the word of wisdom, or the grace of healing, or the working of miracles, or prophecy, or some other heavenly gift. The Holy Spirit distributes each of these to individuals as he wills (1 Corinthians 12), and he had wondrously bestowed almost all of them upon this man.

The reader who has the accounts of all these things written in their proper places, as far as our abilities allowed, will now hear, in a few narratives, how Anno foretold certain things through the spirit as one who knew the future, although the whole body of this book also speaks of the same matters in scattered passages.

### VII. He Predicts That Hildulf Will Succeed Him

Therefore, as it has been handed down to us through true testimony, the most blessed Anno, full of every kind of reverence, was at Goslar, a royal estate, attending the public assemblies of the great. A cleric named Hildulf, attached to the king and familiar with him, asked that the bishop give him as a gift the sacramentary commonly called the Missal, which the bishop possessed as an object of no small dignity.

The bishop replied: “For the present you will have to do without this request, until all the service owed to my little chapel within its cloisters has been transferred to your jurisdiction.”

### VIII. Benno, Bishop of Osnabrück

I think the following should also be received with no lesser reverence. One day at the Gradus, which are held in distinction at Cologne, Anno was sitting with the venerable Benno, bishop of the church of Osnabrück. When Benno’s archdeacon Sigewin was approaching them directly, Anno is said to have remarked:

“Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.”

The bishop recognized that these words had not casually escaped from the mouth of so great a man. Moved by affection and friendship, he pressed him to allow the meaning of his statement to become known.

Looking at him, Anno first explained what opinion concerning the man had moved him, and then added:

“You should certainly know that this man is one day to be received, by my right, into the see of Cologne.”

But since this statement, like the earlier one, was thought to have been spoken merely in a human sense and was therefore passed over with a kind of negligence, after Anno had departed from this darkness, Hildulf first and Sigewin second succeeded to his chair. Their succession showed that their most holy predecessor had truly foretold what concerned them.

### IX. He Indicates the Future in Writing to Egilbert, Bishop of Minden. Saint Anno’s Prophecy

Those who have before them a copy of the letter that Anno once sent to his teacher Egilbert as a token of affection—at the time when Egilbert was about to be placed over the church of Minden and had received the ring and the other insignia sent by the king—will easily be brought to believe that Anno shone in many ways through knowledge of the future.

For, bringing his writing to an end, he digressed into these final words:

“And you shall commend me to the earth.”

When Egilbert read this, though he received it unwillingly, the two later met. Bringing the letter into their midst, Egilbert said that he could not easily discover what faith he ought to place in its conclusion, especially, as he said, since advancing age was already denying him his strength and was compelling him to expect from Anno the very thing he had written.

To this the blessed Anno replied:

“Not at all. For, while you live, the outcome will contradict your words; and what the letter told you, the living voice now confirms anew: ‘You shall commend me to the earth.’”

### X. Some of His Servants Desert Him Like Judas the Traitor. Another Prophecy of His

Now, following the example of Judas the traitor, some of his servants—men whom he had richly adorned with benefactions according to their every desire—returned evil wickedly for good and completely deserted him.

One of them, still alive when these things were written and sharing in the sunlight of this world, raged fiercely in contempt of him. Living nearly a mile away, as though free and indebted to no one for any service, he sat there threateningly, trusting in the strength of his fortification, which the holy bishop had formerly built for this reckless man out of the indulgence of a kindly father.

Many people were indignant at his presumption. One day, as the priest of Christ was coming from the church, he directed his gaze toward the place from which the man’s evil pride had raised itself. Shaking his head, he spoke as follows:

“There is my man, now imagining himself to be a lord, swollen with royal pride. Secure in his own dwelling, he is comfortably protected and is pierced by no fear of the future. But I swear by the confidence that I possess in Saint Peter: all that stronghold in which he now boasts so proudly will be conquered and destroyed, not by battering rams, spear, or the shield of human arms, but rather by cowardly crowds of no steadfastness.”

After this the same man, full of hostility, became involved in the killing of a certain soldier of Cologne. The people of Cologne were aroused. Gathering a common force from the fields and villages, they surrounded the little fortification, captured it, and overthrew it, precisely as Bishop Anno had foretold.

### XI. He Has Great Confidence in the People of Siegburg. The Holy Man Most Truthfully Predicts Many Things About Himself

Who could be found so unbelieving as to deny that he spoke the words we shall now relate through a prophetic spirit, when he hears that they were fulfilled in what follows?

We have been induced by the authority of those who report them to set down these words, spoken familiarly to the brothers at Siegburg; for we consider it wrong to omit them. Sitting among them in good humor, as a father among his sons, he always made them acquainted with his secrets, and there was no hidden matter of his heart that he did not entrust to them.

In accordance with the apostle’s saying, “Love casts out fear” (1 John 4), this gave them the courage both to answer him and to ask him whatever they wished.

In this manner, as though setting serious matters aside, he often addressed them:

“That most renowned Simeon is gloried in as Trier’s illustrious patron, and likewise the most holy Bardo, the glory of the city of Mainz; commending the merit of their holiness by many proofs, they are rightly to be honored with every reverence. Yet because they are proclaimed great, and are great, they endeavor to be honored with lavish gifts.

“But since I am not equally associated with them in merit, after the burden of this body has been laid aside, I shall not find unwelcome the devotion of even the smallest gift. I shall accept the little gift of a very short candle and of linen.”

When the older men who were sitting with him smiled at this saying and persisted in asking whether he too wished to become abundant in signs after death, he replied with great confidence:

“I am certainly unable to disclose the greatness of this desire in words. Nevertheless, so that none of my secrets may be denied to your inquiries, know that this desire has always been, and still is, mine: that Christ may deign to display some signs through me before the eyes of those who persecute me and my life—both to increase the glory of his name and to remove my disgrace, when I appear pleasing to him before whom I am now placed under universal reproach.

“This will be the beginning of my signs. At the bank of the Rhine, they will bring my lifeless body on the shoulders of weeping and mourning men and place it on a ship amid sorrowful rites, before the memorial of the holy martyr Afra. The ship, once turned about, will make its way straight toward Saint Heribert, with no more exertion from the rowers than usual. It will come to rest at a place higher on the farther bank than on the nearer bank.

“But you, my only sons and most beloved brothers, who have always received me with joyful gestures, consider in what manner you will then come to meet me. Instead of song you will offer incomparable weeping, opening your mouths for psalms and hymns but uttering rather the cries of lamentation and sobbing. Whenever, restraining your tears by force, you attempt to sing psalms amid the enormity of your grief, you will fail each time in the attempt through new weeping and scarcely be able to utter even incomplete words.

“Meanwhile, both the younger and the older, rushing around my bier with miserable wailing, you will bring the greatest horror and distress not only upon human beings but also upon the angels. This is the funeral honor you will offer me; this will be the return of affection; these will be the marks of my obsequies.

“After my limbs have been committed to Mother Earth, you, covered in sadness, will leave the tomb. Then all my soldiers will enter, uttering their voices with groaning, and each will pour forth to God the supplication of the Lord’s Prayer for my repose.

“When they have departed, all my servants and those who serve me will burst through the door, joining their cries and sighs. They too will commend me to God in the same manner and return each to his own place, while you remain in sadness and mourning.

“But when I am brought before the presence of the heavenly King, at first I shall stand trembling and excessively fearful. Yet, having received a little confidence, with what persistence, with what urgency of prayer I shall strive to act on behalf of my monks—how shall I be able to express this to you?

“There will also be threats and terrors from poisoned tongues, by which sadness will be brought upon you. The destruction of the place and your dispersion will be proclaimed. Everyone, according to the inclination of his heart, will speak everywhere about the place, its possessions, and you. All these things will happen at the instigation of demons, so that on this occasion the ardor of your devotion may in some way be weakened.

“But do not fear any of these things. Believe the words of your father: everything will serve you in abundance and for every advantage, more fully when I am dead than while I am alive—provided only that, serving the Lord, you tirelessly continue along the path of the way of life you have begun.

“But if you evade it, throw off the yoke of regular discipline, subject your minds to frivolity, pursue amusements and idleness, love laziness and the pleasures of life, and devote yourselves to quarrels, murmuring, and detraction, know now that, however many monks you are, I would rather there be that many pagans devouring my alms.”

These words of the most blessed Bishop Anno are universally worthy of admiration, because they have already been preceded by the truth of events. For us personally, however, they are no less to be feared than embraced, since whatever in them sounds sweet or bitter concerns us above all.

They have been inserted here so that the holy man’s grace in foreknowing the future may be known, and so that the things he is said sometimes to have spoken as though lightly may not appear contemptible. For, so that we may understand their weight and force, certain further matters must be added, by which the same truth may still be demonstrated.

## XII. Saint Bardo shines through miracles. A remarkable miracle in the healing of a paralytic

At Mainz, the most noble and populous city of Germany, a royal command had brought about the celebration of a great and renowned festival for the princes of the kingdom and the prelates of the churches, who had assembled there from various provinces and were presiding over the court. At that gathering, Anno, distinguished above all others both by his inner merits and by his public authority, the supreme prelate of the people of Cologne, stood one day in the atrium of the principal church, surrounded by a very dense crowd, according to custom offering the sacrifice of the immortal mysteries near the tomb of Archbishop Bardo. He was delighted by Bardo’s sanctity, which meanwhile was being commended by fresh miracles.

As Anno was filled with deep contrition of heart and wholly flowed with tears [Col. 1551B]—for whenever he performed this ministry, tears did not pour forth as with most people under compulsion, but flowed spontaneously, so that one might believe living veins were springing forth from some fountain—he completed the customary prayers with his most pure lips and descended from the altar. He then saw a certain man miserably contracted throughout his entire body, clinging to the tomb of the blessed prelate. Anno knew who he was: he had been a serf of Bardo’s parents and, in addition, Bardo’s almoner; he was sitting beside Bardo’s ashes to guard them.

Following his usual practice, Anno stood facing the tomb and said:

“You swiftly regard those whom you do not know and who are almost devoid of devotion. But have you been able until now to despise with such obstinacy this man who always relies on your services, who is your own servant, who loves you and constantly troubles you with his prayers? If you wish us to attribute to your merits what, as report confirms, has been accomplished here in the healing of others, declare, before our eyes, the efficacy of your power in restoring this cripple.”

When he had said this before many listeners [Col. 1551C], without any intervening delay the sick man suddenly rose to his feet. His recovery was accompanied by another memorable sign: without any flow of blood or pain in his nerves, he was restored in an instant to complete health.

The servant of God, Anno, received this with wondrous joy and, loudly proclaiming the name and merit of Saint Bardo, began the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* in a high voice. People and clergy alike joined in the same devotion, while the bells rang solemnly. The report soon spread throughout the entire city and entered the royal residences. The nobles and the rest of the multitude alike proclaimed that, through Anno’s faith, Bardo’s power had shone forth, and that through the merits of both men health had been granted to the man. Yet even if Anno’s tongue had remained silent, Bardo’s sanctity would still have given its assent.

## XIII. Saint Anno’s exceptional zeal and devotion toward Saint Severinus

We shall relate no lesser matters. The most holy man [Col. 1551D] cultivated the heavenly patrons with great devotion, but he always kept Blessed Severinus, the prelate of his own see, especially in his speech and in his heart. His zeal was such that the man who was inwardly sweet and dear to him should also be held in veneration not only by his own people but by foreign peoples as well.

With this fervent intention, at a certain time he undertook with his companions the agreeable labor of a journey to the then wealthy and distinguished city of the Bambergers, in order to establish as a daughter of the mother Church a house under his jurisdiction in which he had once been reared as a boy, and to consecrate it to the name and honor of Severinus.

When this became known throughout the town, on the day appointed for the dedication the entire face of the sky was covered from the first hour of the rising dawn by such heavy rains that no shelter could sufficiently ward off the violence of the downpour.
