Since all who intended to hasten there were protecting themselves beneath their roofs, the bishop, violently prevented from carrying out his purpose, withdrew in silent prayer into the chamber of his heart, asking that the threatening deluge be interrupted [Col. 1552A], even briefly, for as long as the requirements of ecclesiastical procedure demanded.

But since this prayer achieved nothing in accordance with his wish, he seemed to gather his voice from the great disturbance already aroused and addressed threats of charity to Blessed Severinus himself, saying:

“If you do not swiftly assist me in driving away this flood, then, certainly provoked by such great adversities, I shall altogether refrain from consecrating the church to the honor of your name.””

A wondrous thing! He who spoke thus was still pressed by fragile flesh and sweating here on earth; the other, against whom the threats were directed, had already become one with God, free from every fear and heir to eternal security. Yet at the movement of the one who seemed inferior because he was also weaker, the more exalted one trembled. For as though he wished to be reconciled with an angry man, no sooner had Anno finished speaking than the winds grew calm, the clouds disappeared, and the rains ceased. Sudden rays of sunlight, glittering with rosy light, repeatedly struck the eyes of those astonished by the abrupt change in the weather [Col. 1552B]. Under the light of the serene day, everyone who had been drawn either by devotion or by curiosity followed the bishop as he proceeded to the joy of the new dedication.

Thus, with the serenity granted from heaven smiling upon his wishes, and with all who had come rejoicing, he completed the consecration he had undertaken with all the greater happiness because he understood more clearly that in this matter he was serving the divine will—since Severinus too desired the same thing, as the elements themselves testified.

## XIV. A miracle concerning a fly, worthy of the greatest wonder. Father Reginhard is a witness to this miracle

After all this, it is useless to ask how near the Lord Himself was to Anno’s lips, He “whose eyes are upon the righteous and whose ears are attentive to their prayers” (Psalm 33), “who is near to all who call upon Him in truth” (Psalm 144). Nevertheless, this inquiry will not lack a sufficiently remarkable proof.

On one occasion Anno stood before the sight of the Almighty, clothed in sacred vestments, offering [Col. 1552C] upon the altar the singular sacrifice of our redemption. This altar was considered especially distinguished under the title of Saint Michael, on the mountain now illumined by the glory of Anno’s precious body. The eyes of his heart were fixed upon the contemplation of heavenly secrets; outwardly, streams of tears flowed. As he touched the substance of the visible object with his hands, he sweetly embraced in the arms of faith Him who ascended the cross for us—both priest Himself and victim Himself.

Pouring out humble prayers to Him, Anno earnestly labored for bishops, kings, and all who held positions of authority, as well as for all worshipers of the Catholic Church and for its peace. Outwardly there was silence, but the inner man uttered great cries; penetrating the heavens, they were admitted to the throne of supreme Majesty.

Meanwhile, when the entire rite of the mysteries had been completed, the remaining portion was the breaking of the bread. One part was placed in the chalice, while the priest reverently held the remainder between his fingers. As he gazed upon it [Col. 1552D], he was filled with tears from the beginning, declaring himself unworthy to receive what none of the saints had ever dared to take without fear. Tears ran over tears; groans increased, and sighs multiplied. Nothing else was turning in his heart or on his lips except this one prayer: “Lord, I am not worthy that You should enter under my roof” (Matthew 8).

These were not, however, stimuli of some newly arising compunction in him: this was his daily custom whenever he stood at the sacrifice.

While his prayer was prolonged, an image of demons—a most filthy fly, whose very appearance produced nausea—hurled itself upon the Lord’s body and, biting off a particle, flew away and carried it off, causing the priest the greatest anguish. You would have seen Anno suddenly change color and take on the appearance of a dead man. He shuddered at the audacity of the unclean creature and, no less fearful for himself, considered that this had happened to him in order to increase his sins.

But from the greatest sadness there soon arose the greatest joy. From the very place where Satan was thought to insult him, Satan was most thoroughly confounded [Col. 1553A], by the merciful ordering of the Savior. What was most ignoble among creatures, and what had inflicted such grief upon the holy man, became the more glorious through the miracle by which the Savior triumphed over it, thereby revealing Anno’s merits.

Indeed, the venerable bishop, grievously constrained by this distress beyond the capacity of our style to express, finally fixed his heart and eyes upon God. Without revealing the matter to any of those standing nearby by any outward sign, he most earnestly implored help from the Almighty—not by movement of his lips, but through the contrition of his spirit and the humility of his tears.

What more is there to say? The creature friendly to every impurity, as though violently driven back, returned in precipitous flight, revealing by its buzzing and a kind of hissing the force it had suffered. It restored to the paten before the priest’s eyes the fragment it had seized in its most wicked theft. Then, lifting itself as though about to fly away, it fell lifeless to one side upon the altar, paying the fitting penalty for so great a crime.

The sorrow that had wounded the holy man’s breast was then wholly turned into joy [Col. 1553B]. I do not think anyone of such eloquence could fully express the words of thanksgiving or the jubilation of divine praise with which all his inner being resounded, as the priest marveled at the Lord’s immense compassion: that He had been so moved to mercy by the tears of one who was destined to become dust that He did not disdain to exercise His mighty power through so vile a creature; and that, by a miracle no less demonstrating His wisdom, so small a thing—although precious—had been preserved through those delays lest it perish, since He had certainly foreknown that it would be restored by every means.

Then Anno turned to the cleric who was standing nearest him and indicated that the fly should be consumed by fire. He himself received Holy Communion with great confidence and, accompanied by the joy of the Holy Spirit, brought that ministry to its proper conclusion.

So that no one may doubt this account, let anyone concerned know that we learned it from the testimony of Father Reginhard, to whom the holy bishop himself affirmed the matter in person—unless, indeed, someone were so utterly faithless [Col. 1553C] as to attempt to assert that the blessed man had fabricated falsehoods about himself.

## XV. An assembly of princes at Mainz. Two innocent young men are condemned to death. The Lord, appearing in Anno’s form, preserves and frees them from hanging. Anno attributes the miracle not to his own merits but to God’s mercy

Whatever doubt may arise concerning the matters being related will easily receive confirmation from one event, since we have published not doubtful things but certain things supported by reliable witnesses. The Lord, “wondrous among His saints” (Psalm 67), graciously deigned to act wondrously in order to confirm Anno’s merits.

The event is defended by such a witness that the truth of his account is proclaimed even to unbelievers by the gravity of the man’s conduct and words, and by his very gray hair. He relates the following sequence of the miracle’s origin.

At a certain time a celebration of royal service was to be held in the city of Mainz. In accordance with custom, the kingdom’s leading men had been summoned to court, and the venerable Anno, a man of universally renowned name, had then received from the king responsibility for the organization and administration of this festival [Col. 1553D].

As everyone hurried to the aforementioned metropolis, according to the king’s command, Anno himself likewise hastened his journey with his companions. He reached a certain region where a widely circulated report was being repeated everywhere: the king and his entourage were to take lodging there on the following night.

That day, after a council of the local inhabitants had been held, two young men, as can be understood from what follows, had been condemned despite their innocence. Their savage executioners, raging with the cruelty of beasts, immediately placed ropes around their necks and drove them toward the gallows.

There was no opportunity for excuse or pardon and no defense against those who “justify the wicked for gifts and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him” (Isaiah 5). They had only their hearts and eyes directed toward Him “whose judgments are all just and whose ways are all mercy and truth” (Daniel 3; Psalm 24).

Fear had already poured its coldness through their bones; already they stood lifeless from the mere expectation of death. Yet in the midst of their distress they were encouraged to implore [Col. 1554A] the Lord and uttered loud cries from the depths of their hearts, calling upon His omnipotence and His mercy, asking that through the intervention of any one of His servants, in whatever manner He willed, they might be delivered from death. For, since every form of human pity had been excluded, none of those present would spare them, nor was there anyone whom natural kinship might move to compassion.

The Lord heard and had mercy. Commanding invisible power to be visibly present, and wishing to provide mortal beings with testimony to His divinity through Anno, He chose above all to make that power appear in Anno’s likeness.

As the young men were dragged toward the gallows with their hands bound behind them, at the very moment of their death, when life and death engage in fierce combat, everyone standing nearby began mentioning the earlier report concerning the king. They caused the young men’s ears to be filled with the sounds of such conversation.

At once, as they were being dragged along, they perceived with their bodily eyes a likeness corresponding to the conversation they had heard—as they later reported. They seemed to see the king himself [Col. 1554B] approaching, surrounded by an imperial retinue and accompanied by a cleric of great dignity. The form of this cleric’s face expressed the entire likeness of the Anno whom they knew as merciful.

While all the others passed by, he alone fixed his gaze upon the unfortunate men. He quickly approached the place, placed himself between them, and, with one hand supporting the man on the right and the other the man on the left, restored each of them to his feet amid the darkness of night.

There was no delay or resistance in freeing them. He set them both down, restored both their hands and their lives to freedom, and exhorted them to flee in these words:

“Take whatever road you wish and depart from here, pitiable men. Your liberator [the text reads *veser*, apparently for *vester*], the powerful and merciful God.”

When he vanished from them with these words, the young men marveled at the manifest power of divine goodness within themselves. They resolved to flee toward whichever of the neighboring villages they could reach. Following a path determined now less by their own hearts than by heaven, they entered the place where [Col. 1554C] Anno, the minister of heavenly grace, had taken up his station for the night.

In a remarkable manner, although numerous houses were visible everywhere, they made directly for the house distinguished at that time by Anno as its guest, as though it had been inscribed upon their minds. Yet no knowledge either of his name or of his presence had reached them. It was plainly He who led them, who declares Himself to be the way and the life (John 14).

As soon as they encountered the unexpected face of the man of God among the curious circles of onlookers, they were shaken in all their limbs and quickly threw themselves at his feet. Through their tears and thanksgivings they proclaimed him the servant and friend of supreme Majesty, through whom Christ—who makes day and night and who had hung upon the wood—had preserved them through so long a delay lest they be strangled, and had restored them to life.

The strongest argument for believing them was that the marks of the ropes fastened around their necks could be seen beneath the emaciation that covered their entire faces.

The bishop, however, did not in the least alter his humble attitude. He angrily drove the men away, saying that they had been wickedly enticed by desire for gain [Col. 1554D] and had invented this story full of deceit.

Nevertheless, he signaled to some of the clergy to take the men aside and investigate the matter more fully through careful questioning. He also ordered them to inquire into the reasons for which the men had been condemned, so that they might either defend or disprove their innocence, since they claimed that a heavenly power had acted on their behalf.

And so it happened that, since they were equipped with no fraudulent devices and answered every question simply, both the virtue divinely wrought through the bishop became known and the young men were found free of guilt and unjustly condemned.

Then the holy prelate immediately raised his arms and eyes in praise of the Creator and said:

“It is not lawful to attribute this to my merits. These are Your works, O Christ; in these events the examples of Your goodness are certainly revealed. You are the true restorer and lover of innocence; as You willed, You had mercy on the innocent so that they would not perish.”

Afterward, having spent some solid coins from his alms on the men, he [Col. 1555A] and his companions resumed the journey they had begun. As Scripture says, he proceeded “from strength to strength” (Psalm 83), possessing also an abundance of revelations.

It is impossible to proceed through each revelation here. The reader’s attention will therefore be engaged by a few matters, some in this section and some in those that follow.

## XVI. His vision. A church must not be consecrated without an endowment

It happened that one day Anno was about to sanctify a small church of new construction situated within the territory of his administration, and he went there with his companions. But no endowment could be found at hand by which the church might properly acquire its legal status, since he had distributed as alms to other churches the estates he had acquired.

Troubled by many thoughts on this account, he prolonged the day until nightfall, knowing that ecclesiastical sanction forbade proceeding with such matters without the privilege of an endowment. Since the divine office would consequently be postponed there for some time, he was then deliberating whether to persist in the consecration [Col. 1555B] and afterward to work more diligently to secure an endowment.

After forming this decision in his mind through many reconsiderations, he fell asleep. And behold, in a vision he saw himself seated near a certain altar, splendidly surrounded by pontifical vestments, presenting such an appearance that he seemed just about to proceed to some celebration of dedication.

Immediately there stood beside him an angelic-looking man with white hair, rosy-faced, worthy of respect for both his radiance and his authority. When he said that he was Peter, he began to ask what Anno was waiting for.

The holy man, as though he were looking upon a very familiar person, remained unafraid and replied that he had come there for the consecration of a certain little shrine. The apostle immediately continued:

“Do you have the appropriate endowment assigned, so that you can lawfully carry out what you desire?”

The bishop understood that his conscience was being questioned. He said that he had deliberately resolved to proceed, although for the present he lacked the support of an endowment, lest he postpone any longer the blessing [Col. 1555C] for which he had come. He knew that delaying the endowment would not impede the divine services and that, while life remained, he would soon find an endowment and provide it according to custom.

The apostle said:

“Ecclesiastical law does not permit the bride of Christ to be joined to the bridal chambers without the endorsement of an endowment. Therefore, lest a graver sin be committed on account of this transgression, by the authority of our power we grant you permission that, whenever necessity requires it, the daughter may receive an endowment from what belongs to the mother Church.”

The bishop awoke at once. Repeatedly examining the sequence of his vision with the eye of reason, lest it have been produced by deception, he clearly recognized that he had been warned by God.

Thus, as the darkness retreated before the arrival of day, he proceeded joyfully and, certain from the vision what he should do for the rite of consecration, transferred to the daughter as an endowment an estate belonging to the metropolitan see, one that he had found could be given without harm to the mother.

## XVII. Many ancient buildings at Cologne. Three hundred and sixty Moorish martyrs slain at Cologne. Another vision of Saint Anno. [Col. 1555D] He is scourged by the holy Moors. The crypt at Saint Gereon’s is enlarged

As the preceding narrative has shown, all Cologne still bears witness to Anno’s zeal in divine matters. Filled with many assemblies of saints, the city preserves in each of them something of his monuments for posterity.

Among the many ancient structures by which the city itself is nobly distinguished, the remarkable building of blessed Gereon was formerly especially celebrated. Helena, that most Christian matron and mother of Constantine, erected it as a rotunda at royal expense. It shone both within and without with marble beauty and the radiance of gold, so that it was called “the Golden Saints.”

Within this circle of saints, as tradition relates, after the killing of blessed Gereon and his companions, three hundred and sixty soldiers from Mauretania were likewise slaughtered for the faith. Together with blessed Gereon, they deserved rest not only for their souls but also for their bodies [Col. 1556A]. Yet the people held them in less attentive veneration. Since they occupied, on the southern side of the church, a crypt dedicated to their memory that was quite low and, because of its narrowness, suitable for receiving only a few people, they had through the succession of generations and the rarity of visits almost been erased from memory.

This neglect, increasing over many years, continued during the time of Saint Anno until one night, while he was resting, he was seized by the salutary scourging of the following revelation.

Carried away in ecstasy, he saw the multitude of those same martyrs of Christ—the holy Moors—gathered in one place as if for a council, amid a great glory of light. As he gazed upon them in wonder and waited with intense expectation to see how the vision would end, he was suddenly carried into the middle of the assembled crowd, as though summoned for examination, while they all looked at him with grim expressions.

As a careful inquiry was conducted into his deeds or merits [Col. 1556B], a general cry of great complaint arose from that holy assembly. They complained that through the negligence of his predecessors they had endured contempt for so long and had until then received no honor of veneration from their fellow citizens. They were especially disturbed because, whatever the earlier bishops might have done toward them, the neglect shown by Anno—of whom they had hoped for greater zeal—was no less.

After these appeals from the saints, he was sternly questioned in a rebuke: how had he dared to hold so many witnesses of the truth in such contempt? Since no excuse was found, the judgment of all ordered him to undergo the scourge of just retribution.

His clothing was stripped from him, and he was severely beaten. Amid sighs and humble promises of every amendment, he pleaded under the torments that he be spared. At last he was released on this condition from a very deep sleep and awoke in great fear, trembling and conducting himself in every movement of his body as though he were still quivering beneath the lashes [Col. 1556C].

When he returned to himself, he understood the meaning of the dream not from any other source but from the blows inflicted upon his own body, which he could physically feel. He declared that those saints must necessarily be appeased, since their anger had contained such severity, and that he had much to fear lest, if he provoked them again, he would not be granted even the small opportunity to breathe that he had received before.

He therefore gathered skilled and ingenious men. At the same rotunda basilica, after breaking through the old wall on the eastern side, he continued a new building. Arranging its walls lengthwise, he raised it above with very handsome flights of steps leading to a splendid choir and with two carefully constructed towers; below, he laid out a crypt of great capacity.

Adding various ornaments of colors or metals, he also earned an excellent title of praise by having the following verses inscribed in the same paintings:

> Moved to compunction by the Lord’s command, Bishop Anno, [Col. 1556D]  
>   
> Offers to divine worship whatever he can possess,  
>   
> And ordered the attending fathers to be painted in due order,  
>   
> Of the city of Agrippina, lovers of holy virtue.  
>   
> For these things the faithful man himself will rejoice in heaven.

## XVIII. Saint George the Moorish martyr is discovered

When all these works had been beautifully completed, as can be seen today, Anno next devoted himself to searching out the bodies of the holy relics.

With this hope in mind, he uncovered the marble-paved ground within the church precincts and found, more carefully buried than the others, the leader of that holy fellowship, namely George, among the blessed Moors, while his companions rested around him. He was surrounded by a purple cloak whose edges ended in a distinguished golden weave.

Lifting him, together with some others, from the tomb and placing him above the altar with due reverence, Anno burst forth in praise of the one who was the author and giver of such treasures [Col. 1557A]. From that time onward, the name and memory of the holy Moors became more celebrated throughout every quarter of Cologne.

## XIX. Saint Eliphius appears to Saint Anno

Eliphius too was a martyr of great merit. After his head had been cut off, he traveled a very long distance carrying it with him. In a vision he appeared standing beside the blessed man and rebuked Anno for his negligence toward him. He reproached him because the devotion of mind that Anno, as a religious man, displayed toward the other patrons of his city was greatly obscured by the fact that, although he knew Eliphius to be second to no one in merit, he had placed him last in this matter and had never shown even the smallest sign of goodwill by enlarging his church.

When Anno replied that, if any new foundations were laid, the flooding of the Rhine would undoubtedly soon fall upon and destroy the entire monastery, Eliphius persisted, demanding that Anno undertake at least some small act of devotion, and then disappeared.

After resting, the priest rose from his bed [Col. 1557B] and went to the monastery of Saint Martin, where that martyr served as patron, to inspect the situation of the place. After taking counsel, he ordered two towers rising from the front of the sanctuary to be elevated into the air, thereby undoubtedly obtaining the praise and merit of the widow who offered two small coins (Luke 21).

## XX. A deacon’s negligence in chanting the psalms. Saint Anno’s vision

Making progress through many revelations of this kind, Anno was encouraged each day toward better things. He had with him a deacon who imitated a good master, and with him he had a constant custom: whenever the noise of public affairs ceased, they always returned to psalms and prayers.

Yet, as can sometimes happen through human weakness, this cleric, when chanting the psalms by turns with the bishop, was occasionally overcome by weariness. Through his increasingly careless and hurried enunciation of the alternating verses, he fell into the habit of always skipping the middle person [Col. 1557C]—namely the Son—in those hymns that resound with the glory of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit through their distinct personal designations.

No one noticed this faithless negligence, which ought altogether to have been avoided, and no correction was made for a long time. One night, the venerable bishop was lying in bed in the deepest silence, intending to rest. His eyelids had not yet been fully overcome by sleep when, from the direction above toward which his head was turned, he heard with his ears the sound of someone running negligently and corruptly through the words, “Glory to the Father and to the Holy Spirit,” and repeating the same words again while, because of the speed, omitting the middle expression.

Suddenly falling into a kind of ecstasy, he saw standing before him someone whose radiance and appearance exceeded human measure, in the majesty befitting the Son of God. With shining eyes, he gently and calmly presented himself to the astonished man. Extending before him three fingers of his left hand, he touched the first of them with his right index finger and said:

“Behold the Father.”

Then he touched the second:

“Behold the Son.”

After this he touched the third:

“Behold the Holy Spirit.”

Pausing his voice briefly [Col. 1557D] amid the words, he said:

“Behold the three Persons, equally worthy of worship in one Godhead, to whom glory is declared equally by the universal Church forever. The Son occupies the middle place between the Father and the Holy Spirit, and receives no division from the two through any diminution of the same majesty and glory.

“Since these things stand thus according to Catholic truth, why do you allow your cleric’s blasphemies to pass without correction? He takes away from Me the glory that I possess in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit, skipping Me—the middle Person of the Trinity—in the recitation of all glory, while naming the other two Persons.”

The priest immediately awoke, and the image that had appeared vanished.

As he reflected with astonishment upon so clear a vision, he considered the time he had to endure until the customary hymns were reached to be as long as years [Col. 1558A]. He was exceedingly eager to discern with the ears of his body what he had already received through understanding in his ecstasy.

Accordingly, he watched the mouth of the chanting deacon with the greatest attention and himself finished the final verse of the psalm more quickly than usual. The cleric then added the glory of the triune Godhead, but with his customary haste omitted the middle Person and named only the other two.

The chanting of the subsequent psalms did not proceed any further until the bishop rebuked him and, according to the sequence of the vision just described, taught him that he had incurred an offense by neglecting this matter for so long. From then on he possessed not merely an opportunity for correction but also a salutary opportunity for progress.

But now the Lord commands us to change our style. What follows is full of tears, full of miseries and sorrows—and perhaps all the more worthy of so great a man because it is also more grievous. For where the struggle is harder, the victory is more glorious. If Job is accepted after being scourged (Job 1–2), then here too we shall call Anno blessed, since after many tribulations he deserved to enter the kingdom of God (Acts [Col. 1558B] 14).

## XXI. The pious Lord, who reproves and chastises those whom He loves (Revelation 3), permitted this beloved soul also to be tested by many hardships before the day of his calling, so that the furnace of passing tribulation might burn away from him all the dross of earthly conduct

When the Saxon war broke out, a very severe storm of persecution engulfed his brother Wessel, Archbishop of Magdeburg, and his cousin Buccho, Bishop of Halberstadt. Since Anno did not offer the king—who was breathing out the destruction of the entire Saxon people—assistance with sufficient eagerness, being restrained, certainly, by the laws of nature and by carnal affection, he became hateful and suspect to the king and was accused of perjury and treachery.

## XXII. The bishop’s ministers are ill-treated by a certain merchant. Sedition at Cologne

[Note: [Col. 1557] This chapter is copied almost word for word from the Chronicle of Lambert of Hersfeld.]

Meanwhile, as the quarrels between him and the king increased from day to day, the citizens of Cologne—who shortly before had held him uniquely dear and acceptable—were, alas, urged to kill him [Col. 1558C]. An opportunity suitable for carrying out what they were wickedly plotting was supplied by circumstances.

The archbishop celebrated Easter at Cologne, and with him was the bishop of Mimigardevord—that is, of Münster—summoned in the bonds of familiar friendship to share the joys of so great a solemnity. When, after part of the Easter festivities had passed, the bishop was preparing to depart, those who managed the archbishop’s household affairs were ordered to provide a suitable vessel for transporting him. After examining and inspecting everything, they seized a certain wealthy merchant’s ship, since it appeared suitable for the purpose, and ordered it to be made ready at once for the archbishop’s service, after its cargo had been removed.

When the servants who had undertaken to guard the ship refused, they threatened them with violence unless they promptly carried out the order. The servants hastened as quickly as they could to report the matter to the ship’s owner and asked what should be done. He had a son of mature age, outstanding no less in boldness than in strength, and especially dear and acceptable to the city’s leading men both because of his family connections and because of his own merits. Taking his servants and as many young men from the city as he could gather to his aid amid the disturbance, the son hurried to the ship and violently drove away the archbishop’s ministers, who were insistently demanding that it be vacated.

Then he likewise repelled, routed, and put to flight the city’s advocate, who came to undertake the same task and renew the tumult. Soon the friends of both sides, each armed, rushed to their aid, and the affair appeared to be approaching great danger and an uncertain battle.

When news was quickly brought to the archbishop that the city was being thrown into confusion by a most violent sedition, he sent at once to calm the people’s agitation and, full of anger, threatened that at the next session he would punish the seditious young men with the penalty they deserved. He was, after all, a man flourishing in every kind of virtue, and his integrity had often been tested in matters concerning both the commonwealth and the Church.

The conflict was scarcely separated for a short time; but the young man, fierce in spirit and elated by his initial success, did not cease to disturb everything. Ranging through the city, he spread various speeches among the people about the archbishop’s insolence and austerity—[Note: [Col. 1559D] This is irony.]—claiming that he so often despoiled the innocent of their possessions and so often attacked the most honorable citizens with the most impudent words.

It was not difficult to transform people of this sort into whatever one wished, like a leaf carried away by the wind. Moreover, the notable and glorious deed of the people of Worms came to mind: when their bishop had begun to act too arrogantly, they had expelled him from the city. Since the people of Cologne were better supplied than the Wormans in numbers, resources, and arms, they were ashamed to be judged inferior in boldness and to endure for so long, like women, an archbishop who ruled over them with tyrannical arrogance.

The leading men devised foolish plans; the unrestrained mob raged, driven by a passion for revolution; and, swept through the whole city by a demonic spirit, it shouted for arms. They now conspired not merely to expel the archbishop from the city, as the people of Worms had done, but, if the opportunity arose, to slaughter him through every form of torture.

It was the feast of blessed George the martyr, which that year had fallen on the Wednesday of Easter week. After celebrating the solemnity of the Mass at Saint George’s, the archbishop had addressed the people. Unaware of the evil that threatened, but by some foreknowledge of future events, he had declared before his hearers that the city had been handed over to the devil’s power and would soon perish unless they hastened at once, through repentance, to turn aside the wrath of God that was already impending.

A celebrated vision of the following kind increased everyone’s suspicion. Several days before this disturbance, a man of good conduct saw in a dream a raven of terrifying size flying throughout Cologne. Croaking horribly, it drove the people, stunned by the spectacle, here and there. Afterward a man appeared, outstanding both in clothing and in appearance; he drove the raven, which was making a dreadful din, from the city and released the people, terrified in mind and already fearing the worst, from their vain dread.

When, shaken by terror, he asked those standing around him for an interpretation of the dream, he was told that, because of the people’s sins, the city had been handed over to the devil’s power, but that it had been liberated through the intervention of George the martyr and had escaped the necessity of the destruction that was already imminent and predestined by God.

Thus, after midday, when the day was already turning toward evening and drunkenness had added fuel to the fire of anger, the citizens’ conspiratorial band suddenly broke out. First, all the city gates were surrounded by guards. Then they rushed from every part of the city to the archbishop’s court [chortem]. They attacked him while he was dining with the bishop of Münster in a certain public place, hurled weapons and stones, killed some of those attending him [Col. 1559D], and put the rest to flight after exhausting them with blows and wounds.

During this, many people saw the demon who had kindled such madness himself running ahead of the raging people, helmeted and wearing a breastplate, flashing terribly with a fiery sword and resembling no one so much as himself. With a kind of military trumpet-call he urged the hesitant to follow him into battle; but in the very assault, as he rushed forward shouting to break the bolts of the gates, he suddenly disappeared from the eyes of those following him.

Then the archbishop was scarcely and with difficulty carried away from the ranks of his enemies and the cloud of missiles, and brought into the church of Saint Peter. They secured the doors not only with bolts and bars but also with great masses of material placed against them.

Outside, they raged, and like inundating water the vessels of the devil roared—full of the wine of God’s fury. Running through every inner part of the episcopal residence, they broke down doors, plundered the treasures [Col. 1560A], smashed the wine vessels, and, while they poured out with reckless haste the wines that had been laboriously stored for long-term use, they suddenly filled the cellar. The unexpected flood nearly suffocated them, trapped as they were in the waves—something ridiculous even to relate.

Others broke into the archbishop’s chapel, stripped the altar, handled the sacred vessels with polluted hands, and carried off the pontifical vestments. While they overturned all the furnishings of the sacred ministry with painstaking—or rather frenzied—zeal, they found there a certain cleric hiding in a corner of the altar out of fear. Believing him to be the archbishop, they killed him, not without jubilant reproach that they had at last put an end to the most insolent tongue.

But when they learned that they had been deceived by the resemblance, and that the bishop was protecting himself inside Saint Peter’s church both through the sanctity of the place and the strength of its walls, they gathered from every side and besieged the church itself. They deliberately attempted to break through the walls and finally threatened that, unless the archbishop were handed over to them at once, they would also set fire to the building [Col. 1560B].

Those inside, seeing that the whole people’s minds were fixed upon his death—not merely stirred by drunkenness, which time ordinarily dissipates, but also by hatred and a kind of frenzied madness—advised him to change his clothing and try to escape from the church, deceiving the besiegers. By doing so, he would free both the sacred building from fire and himself from the danger of death.

The time seemed favorable for flight. Since the sedition continued into the middle of the night, everything was shrouded in darkness and gloom, so that it would not be easy for anyone to distinguish the faces of those encountered. A narrow passage led from the church into the dormitory, and likewise from the dormitory into the courtyard and house of a certain canon adjoining the city wall. A few days earlier, that canon had obtained from the archbishop permission to make a small rear door for himself by breaking through the city wall. God, in his mercy, had thus provided this very means for the archbishop’s safety.

The archbishop was led out there. Four horses were harnessed to carry him and his companions, and he departed, making the greatest possible use of the darkness of the night so that he would not be recognized by those he met. After a short time he found the bishop of Mimigardevord, who was now surrounded by a fine group of companions, suitable for the crisis. They reached a place called Nussia.

Meanwhile, those around the church were shaking the walls with repeated blows of battering rams. There was a confused uproar of the rioters, who swore by the faith of almighty God that he would not escape their hands or deceive the vigilance of the besiegers, even if he transformed himself into the smallest creeping creature of the earth.

The besieged, on the other hand, now pleading and now promising that, if he were found after the most diligent search, they would hand him over to them, cleverly frustrated the efforts of the attackers until they supposed that the archbishop had been carried farther away and had reached a safe place.

At last they opened the doors and allowed them to enter and search wherever they wished. They added that they were searching in vain for him within the church precincts, since they had learned for certain that he had left the city at the first attack of the excited multitude, while it was still broad daylight, and might already have proceeded into distant regions [Col. 1560D]. This was all the more probable because, having gathered forces from every side during the delay caused by the night, he would come at first light to seize the city by arms.

They entered, and after overturning every recess of the church through a painstaking search, they scarcely at last accepted the belief that they might have been deceived. They then turned their attention from searching to defending the city and distributed the armed multitude all around the fortifications.

During this, they seized a certain man from the crowd and hanged him over the city gate as a disgrace to the bishop, satisfying in this way more the fury by which they were being driven headlong than any crime that they could produce against the wretched man as deserving hanging. They cut off another man’s legs. They also threw a woman from the top of the walls and killed her by breaking her neck [Col. 1561A], accusing her of this crime: she was said to have been notorious for driving people insane by magical arts. Yet they ought to have reserved punishment for this crime for a more suitable time and a calmer mind.

They had also conceived the plan—if he had not barely escaped by flight—of killing the abbess of Saint Cecilia, their sole reason for her death being that she was related by blood to the archbishop. They were prepared to undertake still more wicked acts, unless God, taking pity on Cologne, had shortened the days of their madness.

Furthermore, they ordered some energetic young men to go as quickly as possible to the king, to report what had happened and urge him to come as soon as possible and seize the city, now vacant because the archbishop had been expelled. The city’s salvation and the king’s greatest advantage, they said, depended upon his trying to forestall the archbishop, who was planning great things to avenge the injury done to him.

For three whole days they were driven by such madness. After it had been heard throughout the province and widely spread by public rumor that the people of Cologne had driven their archbishop from the city after subjecting him [Col. 1561B] to insults and abuse, everyone shuddered at the novelty of the event, the atrocity of the crime, and the spectacle of human affairs: that a man of such great standing, a man of such great virtues in Christ, could, while God looked on, have suffered such indignities.

His great generosity toward the poor, his great moderation in human affairs, his vigorous zeal in correcting laws, and his free severity in correcting those who acted wrongly were celebrated by everyone. The remembrance of these qualities won him no small measure of favor among the people.

Everyone cried out that the majesty of the pontifical name had been violated to their own greater injury, and that it would be better for them to die than to allow so great a crime of their age to go unpunished.

Thus, throughout the surrounding region for four or five miles, the call to arms was sounded. Many thousands of men assembled with extraordinary speed, and no one who was old enough to bear arms held back from so religious a military expedition. Gathering together [Col. 1561C], they begged the archbishop and compelled him by force, though he hesitated, to hasten as quickly as possible to recover the city. They would fight for him, they said, and, if necessity required, would gladly accept death as sheep for their shepherd and sons for their father. Unless the people of Cologne hastened to receive him on his arrival and made satisfaction according to his judgment for the offense, they would either consume the people and the city by setting fire to it, or demolish the wall and restore him to his episcopal chair over a mound of the slain.

Accordingly, on the fourth day after he had departed, the archbishop approached the city surrounded by a great army. When the people of Cologne learned this and realized that they could withstand the attack of so great and savage a multitude neither with their walls nor in battle formation, their fury at last began to die down and their drunkenness to evaporate. Struck by great terror, they sent ambassadors to meet him and seek peace, confessing themselves guilty and ready to pay whatever penalty they might be ordered to pay, provided they were allowed to keep their lives.

The archbishop replied that he would not deny pardon to those who truly repented. Then, after celebrating the solemnity of Mass at Saint George’s, he summoned to satisfaction under episcopal ban those who had expelled the pontiff from his own seat, polluted the church with murder, attacked Saint Peter’s church as enemies, and violated the remaining rights of religion with barbarous boldness [Col. 1561D].

At once they came barefoot and clothed in wool next to the flesh. They had obtained permission only with difficulty from the multitude surrounding the bishop to do this safely. For the people were also very angry with him because, by displaying clemency too immoderately in his desire to become popular, he seemed to encourage wicked men to undertake worse deeds by allowing this crime to go unpunished.

The archbishop, however, ordered them to be present at Saint Peter’s on the following day to undertake, according to the prescriptions of the canons, the penance for so monstrous a crime. He himself proceeded to Saint Gereon and decided to spend the night there outside the city. Fearing that, once the city had been handed over to him, the force of the excited multitude could not be restrained, and that, inflamed partly by injury and partly by a desire for plunder, they might rage more harshly against the people, he earnestly begged the provincial troops who were with him to return peacefully, each to his own home.

“I have made sufficient use of your service,” he said, “and you have given clear proof of what spirit sheep bear toward their shepherd and sons toward their father. The harshest part of the undertaking has been completed through your great valor. What remains can now easily be accomplished by private and domestic means. Therefore, may what is good, fortunate, and blessed attend you as you return to your homes. Take with you this hope: that, because of this benefit, your favor with me, whether I live or am dead, will remain forever.”

With difficulty he obtained this. He then ordered his soldiers—enough, as he thought, to suppress any urban disturbance that might perhaps be stirred up by the fickleness of the crowd—to enter the city ahead of him. He himself would follow at dawn, after the diligence of those who went before had taken precautions against any ambush that might be concealed in the city [Col. 1562B].

That night six hundred, or somewhat more, of the wealthiest merchants who had fled the city went to the king, intending to implore his intervention against the bishop’s severity. The others, after the archbishop entered the city and waited there for three days according to the agreement, did not appear at all to offer any form of satisfaction.

Therefore the bishop’s soldiers, unable to endure the indignity of the affair, seized their weapons—without the archbishop’s knowledge and, as most people assert, without his advice—raided the houses, plundered property, struck down some of those who met them, and threw others whom they captured into chains. They carried out the business of just vengeance much more fiercely than was fitting for the reputation of so great a pontiff, so that they compelled even those who resisted to acknowledge the truth.

But a more serious illness required a sharper remedy. The son of the merchant mentioned above, who had first inflamed the people to sedition, and a few others were deprived of their sight; some were beaten with rods and tonsured; all were punished by the gravest loss to their property. They were also compelled to swear that henceforth they would defend the city for the archbishop, against the violence of all men, with as much counsel and force of arms as they could provide, and that they would always regard those who had fled the city as their most hostile enemies until they had made worthy satisfaction to the archbishop.

[Note: [Col. 1561] Up to this point the account is taken almost entirely from Lambert of Hersfeld.]

Thus the city was held, according to the diversity of the parties, by grief and joy alike: some, upon the return of the expelled pontiff, paying the deserved penalties for their boldness; others establishing fitting choirs of consolation.

For not only in the city, but wherever an opportunity for a procession was offered, the confessor of Christ was received after this report with hymns and songs like an angel—and not without reason. For who could deny that he was one of those angels of whom it is said through Malachi: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi II)?

Afterward, the saints to whom service is rendered there both saw and pitied the tears he poured out while ascending or descending the mountain dear to him [Col. 1562D]. He complained to them of the insult he had suffered from his own people and drew all who happened to be present, whether from the clergy or from the people, to tears.

The monks also raised their voices together, and, as though contemplating his beloved face restored to them, all resounded:

“Our sighs called for you;
our abundant laments sought you;
you have become hope for the despairing,
great consolation in torments.”

These words were heard on high. It must surely be believed that Christ was truly present there, delighted both by the sweetness of what was sung and by the sacrifice of tears, just as he himself promised when he said: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew XVIII).

But since some good people are also scandalized that the vengeance upon so great a man is said to have resulted in such savage punishment, we have testimony from the most serious and trustworthy persons that he repeatedly affirmed under oath that his conscience was entirely free from this tyranny. For it had never been either his office or his will to extend vengeance for his injuries beyond the rights of ecclesiastical law (Exodus II).

Let the envious man, therefore, close his mouth. Whenever the matter is brought up, he is accustomed to object that, although the blind often return from the archbishop’s tomb with sight, he has taken away more eyes than he has restored. Nor is this surprising, since some also blaspheme holy Moses as a murderer (Numbers XVI).

## XXIII. The emperor comes to Cologne. A splendid encomium of Saint Anno. His steadfastness

[Note: [Col. 1563D] In this chapter also, much has been copied almost word for word from the Hersfeld account.]

Afterward, when the emperor had celebrated Easter solemnly at Bamberg and was preparing to go to Regensburg, he heard from a messenger bearing a fabricated embassy that William, surnamed the Bastard, king of the English, had been enticed by a vain promise from the archbishop of Cologne and was approaching with a great army, prepared to seize the royal seat at Aachen [Col. 1563B].

Terrified by so dreadful a report, the king hurried back to the Rhine and magnificently celebrated Pentecost in the city of Mainz. From there, when he set out to go to Cologne, breathing much anger and threatening against the archbishop of Cologne, the archbishop sent messengers to meet him. He instructed them to say that the story circulating against him was entirely false and like a theatrical fabrication. It had been composed by his enemies—namely, those who shortly before had expelled him from the city and who now, since they could not overpower him by arms, were attacking him with lies.

He was not so devoid of reason, nor so negligent of the common good, that he would wish to betray his homeland to barbarians in revenge for a private injury. Nor had he ordered his life from childhood with such frivolity that anyone possessing sound judgment could suspect anything so foolish about him.

After obtaining permission through his envoys to appear before the king, he met him at the royal estate of Andernach. When the king announced a most severe inquiry into what he had learned [Col. 1563C], the archbishop cleared himself by oath of the charge that he had betrayed the commonwealth. As for the other allegations that had been reported, the king said that he would forgive them out of regard for their old friendship and for the pontifical dignity, and that he did not wish to press his legal claim.

Thus, with his fury not extinguished but temporarily restrained, the king proceeded to Cologne. There, on the following day, he sat in judgment before the people, hoping that an accusation would give him the opportunity either to drive the archbishop from the city again by stirring up sedition or, because innocent men had been oppressed through slander, at least to make him guilty of treason.

But the archbishop tore apart all the devices of the accusations by the truth of his answers and the gravity of his judgments, like webs of spiders. When the king saw his innocence and integrity of life, and also that his counsels were secured on every side and that no opening for slander remained, he turned to another kind of injury.

He demanded from the archbishop—not by petition, as was proper, but with a certain imperious authority—that he grant the people of Cologne pardon for the rashness they had committed against him and reconcile the excommunicated to the Church [Col. 1563D]. In addition, to secure their perpetual loyalty to him, he demanded that the archbishop give him six hostages from among his own soldiers.

The archbishop firmly refused both demands. He refused the hostages because none of the earlier kings had ever made such a request of any predecessor of his. As for reconciliation with the excommunicated, he refused because ecclesiastical laws forbade receiving excommunicated persons into the Church without worthy satisfaction in penance.

The king pressed him vehemently, threatening to inflict every kind of harm and to destroy with sword and fire everything belonging to him. The archbishop remained fixed in his resolve. He said that he was indeed ready to die if he himself and the people of Cologne had conspired to kill the king, but that he would never, out of a desire to preserve his life, turn from right to wrong.

For a long time the contest remained undecided, and the soldiers on both sides were greatly shaken by anxiety as they awaited so grim a spectacle. At last, persuaded by those whose counsel he valued most, the king changed his position and said that he preferred to compete with the archbishop in benefits rather than in losses or enmities. If he found him faithful and devoted to him in the affairs of the commonwealth, he would henceforth count him first among his friends [Col. 1564A].

Reconciled with the archbishop in this way, he proceeded to Aachen and strengthened that part of the kingdom as much as he could against the rumored invasion of the barbarians.

## XXIV. The most holy man suffers many adversities. The Franks and Saxons fight among themselves

[Note: [Col. 1564D] This chapter too contains much from the Hersfeld account.]

Meanwhile, as Satan rose up against the man of God, two of his ministers, who were closely attached to his household, laid an ambush for him. If God’s mercy had not forestalled this evil, they would have murdered him while he suspected nothing.

To another man, whom he had made especially faithful and devoted to him by his benefactions, he gave familiar letters written by his own hand on tablets, for greater secrecy, to carry to the bishop of Halberstadt. In them he was to console and instruct his nephew [Note: [Col. 1564D] Above, he is called his cousin], who, assailed and tossed about by storms from every side, was almost shipwrecked [Col. 1564B].

But that man, inferring from the elaborate precautions taken to preserve secrecy that the letters contained something adverse to the king and the commonwealth, carried them to the king. Although the king saw that they contained no indication of disloyalty, contrary to his expectation, he nevertheless sent the archbishop a copy of them in order to frighten him, so that he might learn from experience that betrayals of his secrets were not uncommon in the king’s court.

Likewise, another of his ministers, whom the archbishop himself had acquired for the church of Cologne through his own efforts, whom he had always treated with the most indulgent affection for that reason, and whom he had enriched with every good thing beyond his birth and status, suddenly became elated with servile insolence. He began to reject the yoke of ecclesiastical service and, by a kind of violent legal claim before the secular court, shook himself free of it, with great insult to the archbishop, like an unbridled horse.

Then he was so embittered by the repeated deaths of his loved ones, and so cut by wound upon wound, that this violent storm of trial could have shaken even a heart of stone and a building founded upon rock [Col. 1564C].

To complete the fullness of his pain and sorrow, the misery of a new confusion, which was already beginning to spread through every corner of the kingdom, touched the innermost part of his heart all the more bitterly because the matter threatened a general danger to the whole Church.

For while the Franks and Saxons fought one another with barbarous savagery, the Suebi and the people of Bavaria, of uncertain allegiance, joined first one side and then the other. Throughout the whole German kingdom there were massacres, fires, and plundering.

Meanwhile, as the instigator of these calamities and as a kind of foundation for their continued endurance, there arose that ever-lamentable dispute between the king and the apostolic lord. Through the foul disease of a terrible schism it was throwing the holy Church into extraordinary confusion, and, alas, consigning the souls of many thousands to the underworld. It drove the unity of peace completely from the earth [Col. 1564D], dissolved the monks in shameful quarrels, brought the clergy into contempt, subjected ecclesiastical judgments to laymen, and overturned every rule of equity. The tearful ruin of so great an evil does not cease even today.

The man for whom nothing was dearer than God was so hemmed in and scorched on every side by these anguishes that he even grew weary of living. Thus he uttered words such as these with the Psalmist toward heaven:

“Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a long-time sojourner” (Psalm CXIX).

And saying, “desiring to depart and to be with Christ” (Philippians I), he would say: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm XLI).

Everything earthly had already become burdensome to him. Under the burden of the flesh he still burned out of necessity, not by choice. His body wasted away, and his spirit also grew weak. Like a widowed turtledove, he fed on mourning alone. He avoided public gatherings, delighted in solitude, and wept and grieved without ceasing [Col. 1565A].

The good Lord did not long leave the labors of his soldier unrewarded, nor did he allow him to be tested beyond what he could bear (1 Corinthians X). Rather, intending to snatch him away from these troubles, he first wished him, through the power of profound contemplation, to become a witness of future evils, so that he would not fail to know how many benefits God would grant him if, by dying, he escaped the necessity of sharing in such things.

The following page speaks of this. It alone is sufficient to reveal the merit of the man, who, while still dwelling in this mortal condition, became a participant in heavenly secrets.

## XXV. Saint Anno’s astonishing vision. He is seized by a most serious illness. He gives a general account of his vision to certain persons

After the wicked conspiracy of the people of Cologne described above, the days of winter arrived. The blessed bishop, leaving the city in search of some relief for his wounded heart, reached Salevelt, so that, by observing there the spiritual exercises of his sons, he might be refreshed as though by a draught of a healing antidote and moderate the bitterness of his grief [Col. 1565B].

After completing his visitation, he departed and solemnly celebrated at Hersfeld the feast called the Hypapante of the Lord. He then ordered his departure and traveled with his companions in a carriage along the road that is open to those heading toward Siegburg.

One day, while he was devoting himself to psalms and prayers and had lifted his mind to heavenly things, as the ninth hour was approaching, he saw the heavens opened above him—not in ecstasy or in a dream-vision, but as one ordinarily sees with bodily eyes. Like the distinguished prophet Daniel of old, he was shaken by terror and trembling and dissolved in all his limbs (Daniel X); all the strength of his spirit also collapsed.

After he had passed over the stages of the planned journey, he suffered no discomfort for two days while staying on a mountain, except that at times he became an object of wonder to some, as though he had gone beyond himself in his speech.

On the third day afterward, however, while he was dining, a powerful illness attacked him so terribly that all hope was lost that he would survive the night [Col. 1565C]. It was evening twilight, and the brothers, having finished Compline, had withdrawn to the dormitory.

As soon as news of this sort struck the abbot’s ears, he was thrown into confusion, and the report spread through every corner of the monastery. Brothers hurried here and there, while the signal calling them together sounded with increasing urgency.

An unbearable fear oppressed everyone. As though the life of them all hung in the balance, they went to the monastery, pondering the words in their hearts and repeating them with their mouths: “Lord, save us; we are perishing” (Matthew VIII).

Those who were permitted to leave the cloister hastened together to the bishop’s chamber. The others rushed into the choir and mournfully recited the seven psalms with the litanies. Everyone beat his breast; everyone gave forth tears and sighs; and each bore witness to himself concerning the love with which sons were devoted to their most beloved father.

Meanwhile, the man suffering under severe pain uttered increasingly unusual cries. But on the following day, when the violence of the pain no longer tormented him so severely and allowed him a little strength to recover his mental powers [Col. 1565D], the abbot sent three brothers of upright conduct to him. As the circumstances required, they were to urge him to confession and to the ordering of his affairs, and to encourage him not to neglect, insofar as was then possible, the welfare of his new foundation.

As they sat beside his bed and softened him with these exhortations, they asked him above all why he did not speak to his sons, for whom, after God, he alone was their hope. He forced out in his faint voice, as best he could:

“Where shall I begin to speak, brothers? What words can my sorrowful heart dictate that might relieve your sadness? Woe to the wretched world! Woe to every corner of the human condition because of those who are called bishops, who bear the likeness of me, a sinner [Col. 1566A], but possess the name of priests, not their life.”

Drawing a deep sigh from his breast, he answered those who were astonished and were investigating the root of this utterance with increasing eagerness:

“The sun was already declining toward the ninth hour, and I was sitting in my carriage, hastening along the road. As I cast my gaze into the air, the heavens suddenly split open, and everything above remained open and accessible to my eyes—not only to the eyes of my mind but also to those of my body. My heart was terrified, and I was dissolved; no strength remained in me. I am certain that I contracted the violence of this illness from that event.

“I saw that terrible vision no differently from the way I now look at you, directing my bodily eyes toward you. Nor do I think that any of the evils threatening the earth throughout all the ages to come, and throughout the age itself, escaped the sharpness of my eyes.”

Then, groaning more deeply with his heart trembling, he repeated:

“Woe to the wretched world! Woe to every corner of the human condition because of those who are called bishops” [Col. 1566B].

No amount of importunity from those who prayed and pleaded with him could persuade him to communicate even the smallest part of what he had seen. To all their questioning he brought forth only this, in sorrow:

“Woe, woe to the wretched world.”

As the illness increased day by day, and he suspected death daily, he summoned the leading clergy of Cologne. Under a solemn invocation of the divine name, he terrifyingly adjured them never to give their consent to anyone who might wish his body to be buried anywhere other than at Siegburg.

“If the result of your insistence fulfills my desire, and burial is granted to me here, then, although the reckoning of my merits resists it, through the mercy of our Redeemer, which surpasses all things, I hope that your ears will still hear from me that this will profit you and your Cologne as a protection of great consolation and great hope before God.”

Each of them gave him his pledge concerning this matter, and they departed.

He gradually recovered his strength and escaped that bodily weakness, but for a long time he was unable to regain the same mental memory that he had possessed before. So terrified and transported beyond himself was he by the majesty of that vision.

This is suggested by the fact that, although formerly he had received from Egilbert, bishop of Minden, a certain prayer to be recited perpetually as a confession, he could not by any means recall it until, after letters had been sent to him, he reconstructed its order from the annotations in the replies.

## XXVI. He Explains a Vision to One of His Household. Its Interpretation

**[Note: [Col. 1565D] This is truly word for word from the Schaffhausen account.]**

The days of Septuagesima, during which this revelation occurred, had already been followed by the Lenten weekdays, and the Lord’s beloved had not yet fully recovered from the weakness of his previous illness. Then, while he was lying asleep one night, he saw in the following manner a dream foretelling his most blessed departure:

He seemed to himself to enter a certain house shining with every kind of splendor, within and without. And behold, seated on judicial benches, as though solemnly summoned to a council, were Heribert, archbishop of Cologne; Bardo, archbishop of Mainz; Boppo and Everhard, archbishops of Trier; Arnulph, bishop of Worms; and many other bishops of Gaul. Some of these he himself had known in the flesh; others he had learned about only through report or reading. They were all dressed in pontifical stoles and wearing garments white as snow.

He himself also seemed to be dressed in exceedingly white and precious clothing. But part of the gleaming garment—namely, the portion covering his breast—was covered by a certain filthy and loathsome darkness, which greatly obscured the splendor of the rest of his attire by its foulness. He, suffused with extreme shame, tried to restrain and conceal it by placing his hand over it, lest it offend the eyes of those who looked upon him.

Moreover, he saw that a seat of wondrous beauty had also been prepared for him among them. As he hurried to occupy it, burning with joy and exultation, Bishop Arnold [Arnulphus] of Worms rose and stopped him in a gentle voice, saying that the revered Fathers who were seated there did not wish to admit him to their company, because this ugly stain defiled his garment.

When he was ordered to withdraw and went out weeping and utterly dispirited, the same bishop followed him and said: “Take heart, father. Order this stain alone, which has infected your garment, to be washed away without delay; for after not many days you will obtain, as you desire, fellowship in this blessed dwelling and a seat among the holy Fathers whom you have seen.”

When morning came, he related the vision to one of his household. That man, wisely interpreting the matter, said: “This stain imprinted on your garment, as I believe, is nothing other than the memory of the injury done by your fellow citizens, who expelled you from Cologne the previous year—an injury which, out of regard for divine mercy, you ought long ago to have forgiven them. This, if I may say so with your good leave, remaining too tenaciously in your breast, more than is right, consumes your mind with the bitterest grief contrary to divine law, and covers and obscures the remaining brightness of your most holy way of life with an oppressive darkness.”

The archbishop, convicted by the testimony of his conscience, did not deny what he heard but humbly acknowledged his guilt. Immediately he sent messengers in every direction and recalled to himself all the citizens of Cologne who had shared in his injury and had left the city. At the next Easter festival he most graciously restored to them everything of theirs that had been seized.

Thus that grievous storm, raised by a diabolical spirit and having shaken all Cologne, grew calm: father and sons recognized one another, the archbishop was freed from bitterness, the people from fear and anxiety, and the city from desolation.

# BOOK THREE

## I.

Thus the bishop, most beloved of God, as he was passing the final year of his life, frequented the mountain he loved more than usual. Every day and every night he visited each altar in turn, prostrating himself face down before each one, weeping and praying for the condition of the endangered Church, and commending his soul to the Creator.

He spent there the period of Septuagesima and part of Lent while ill. But when he had come again to celebrate Pentecost with festive joy, Anno, a boy and the son of his sister, whom he loved uniquely, was suddenly struck down by the violence of a premature death and brought him new pain and new mourning.

Nevertheless, he took part in the public gatherings of the common festival. While the choruses of monks went before him in gladness, with their songs and splendid garments, he followed them with a mournful expression, recalling the words of the holy Tobias: “Your festival days will be turned into mourning” (Tob. II). Everyone who looked into his face was wounded in spirit. For it had become very dark and had completely changed its former color (Amos VIII), presenting a kind of horror by which those who saw him might gather evidence of his inward grief.

## II.

**[Note: [Col. 1567] From this chapter to the end of the book, F. Laurentius Surius abridged most of the material in his own style in order to avoid excessive length.]**

A few days later Hermann, prior of the monastery of Sigeberg, an energetic man and most observant of the rule’s discipline, died. His death brought such grief to the blessed bishop that, compared with it, all the many bitter experiences he had previously endured seemed nothing.

For he had loved that man greatly and had shown him such veneration that whatever the other, trusting in his affection, might have wished not so much to ask as to command, Anno considered it something he must by no means neglect. He received the man’s words no otherwise than if the Holy Spirit had expressed them through his mouth.

Feeling himself therefore deprived of that man by the cruelty of death, and recalling with deepest sorrow his sobriety and integrity of life, he received the sacraments and, standing behind the bier, delivered the following prayer with profound grief.

## III. Commendation of Prior Hermann. Saint Anno Foretells His Own Death

“We have before our eyes the business of our miseries, and here we may already contemplate with our very eyes what the end of the human condition is. By this example we are most truly reminded that the Apostle said: ‘The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. For when they say, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labor-pains upon a woman with child, and they will not escape’” (1 Thess. V).

“Whatever can be thought in the mind or said in words about this matter is all set before our eyes here. Therefore, reducing a general discourse to a few words, I shall touch specifically upon my own bitter circumstances.

“Behold, alas! Anno the boy, than whom no one in this life was dearer to me, departed this life ten days ago. And while the grief I received from that event has not yet ceased even for a moment, behold, today I celebrate the funeral of one whom I must mourn in a very different way from my other friends.

“This man demands a greater flood of my tears, since he himself is such that this place ought not unjustly to accompany him with perpetual mourning. What hope can remain hereafter of preserving the condition of this place, when he lies lifeless here whose industry has hitherto advanced monastic discipline here?

“Whatever has afflicted me until now, by God’s permission, was in some way bearable. But what I now suffer reaches to my very inmost being, and the hand of the Lord could not touch me more harshly than by offering an opportunity for the enemy to ravage this place of mine.

“It remains, therefore, that death, which is owed to all, should also consume me. And whoever is present here today may learn from me that Bishop Anno will not survive many more days.”

At these words, while many wept, his body was buried according to custom.

## IV. His Saving Prayer. He Indicates the Place of His Burial. Why He Did Not Wish to Be Buried in the Choir

When the solemnities of the dedication of the church and of the most blessed Michael were being celebrated, he came at last to Sigeberg. He celebrated those two closely connected festivals there with such greater devotion and piety of spirit because he already knew through the Spirit that he would never return bodily to that place.

As he was about to depart, he bade farewell to the brothers with fatherly affection. Then, turning toward the monastery, he implored God with the most fervent prayers, invoking the patronage of the saints present there, for the protection of his body and soul, for the peace of the Church, and for the preservation of the place.

He prayed for the salvation of those sons of his, prostrating himself on the ground at each prayer, sometimes bending his knees, sometimes raising his hands and eyes to heaven, with tears continually flowing—so that heaven might rightly be thought to open before such earnest devotion.

At last, after marking them with the holy cross, as he was about to go out through the door, a small iron chain was brought to him, not without divine providence. Although it had been made at his command, it was displayed at that hour only because God had so ordained.

At that very moment the bishop turned back inside and marked the place of his grave with his staff, at the spot where it now is. He ordered the chain to be lowered beneath the floorboards so that a lamp might be raised.

When the soldier Suithard, not without amazement, asked him what he intended by measuring out the grave so carefully, he replied that he was marking out his burial place there.

When Suithard asked again what need of the body compelled him to do this, the blessed man answered: “The need which is certainly the greatest—namely, unavoidable death. For after this place will never again receive me alive.”

At once the soldier grew pale and repeatedly made the sign of the cross. Then he began to ask the bishop why he preferred not to be buried in the choir, the more sacred part of the church.

The bishop replied: “For this reason I do not wish it: so that you and others like you, who will come to my grave for the sake of prayer, may not cause disturbance to the brothers who are performing the divine offices.

“And also so that poor women may have access to my grave—women who come from the countryside out of devotion, bringing apples or eggs or some other little gift of holy simplicity. Since their devotion is more pleasing to God the simpler their lives are, my honor would be diminished if, after rejecting their tears and complaints, access to my monument were open only to noblewomen.

“Therefore, following the example of my Lord, who accepted the widow’s two small coins (Luke XXI), I too wish to embrace their little gifts and admit their prayers, and to have the place of my burial open to everyone.”

In this way, as was his custom, he revealed the secrets of his heart to the soldier almost as if in jest, and went outside.

Then he mounted his horse and repeatedly returned in sorrowful spirit to that monastery, deeply lamenting that he would no longer see that place so dear to him, and that he would leave his sons abundant cause for mourning.

Who, even if he had a heart of stone, could keep his eyes dry at the death of so great a man? Posterity will rightly mourn him, for, as Scripture says, “in his days he did not fear the prince, and no word overcame him” (Eccli. XLVIII); “in all his work he gave thanks to God” (Eccli. XLVII); “he cared for his people and delivered them from destruction” (Eccli. L); and “his good works are established in the Lord, and all the assembly of the saints will recount his almsgiving” (Eccli. XXXI).

A great man, a Catholic man, a champion of the Church, a persecutor of tyrants, worthy in word, deed, and conduct of the highest priesthood: after him no shepherd like him arose within our borders.

Yet even he did not escape the avenger of the first transgression. Rather, more cruel than usual, she wore down his life through prolonged torment more harshly than others, so that certain fools did not hesitate to apply to him also the words from Tobias: “Clearly your hope has proved vain, and your almsgiving has just now become apparent” (Tob. II).

## V. The Holiest Man Is Cruelly Tormented by Gout. He Foresees and Prophesies Many Things

When he had returned to Cologne, the pain of gout attacked his right foot. After he had been miserably tormented by it for about nine weeks, he was finally brought to the point of death.

At first, however, he seemed with a certain firmness of spirit to conceal those pains for about a week, until, while celebrating the solemn Masses in the church of Saint Gereon during the martyr’s festival, he was so weakened that, abandoning the sermon he had been about to give, he could scarcely manage to complete the sacraments.

That was his final sacrifice. When it was completed, he collapsed onto his deathbed, bringing pain and grief to all his people.

It would be a long task to recount the miseries and torments he suffered throughout that period of illness, both from the physicians and from the disease itself. It would be no less difficult to write down what he foretold in spirit and what he saw in ecstasy. Of these matters we shall relate only a few, insofar as the opportunity afforded by the history permits.

## VI. His Vision

When his flesh had already wasted away and his skin clung to his bones, he was once seized by sleep. On awakening, he burst forth in tears with words such as these:

“O martyr Ewald, what injury have I done to you, or what have I committed against you, wretch that I am?”

When others asked what he meant by these words, he replied:

“I truly saw the most holy martyr Ewald, whom they call the Black, standing beside the holy altars. While I was assisting him as he celebrated the sacrifice, after the sacrifice had been completed he was received into heaven, exceedingly beautiful in a purple chasuble and most radiant white garment, as though he had just come from the baptismal font.

“I followed him as he departed, and when we reached the gates of heaven I hoped that I too would enter. But alas! I was violently repelled by him, and I saw myself hurled back into this darkness.”

As he said this, he shed such abundant tears that those present, moved to pity, wept together with him.
