## VII. Saint Anno Foretells Many Future Events

During that adverse illness, for as long as he lived, he kept certain brothers of Sigeberg with him, and sometimes the abbot himself. Coming and going in turn, they brought him some refreshment by their presence.

When some were about to depart and others were taking their places, they asked him for his blessing. He followed them with a great wail, as though they would never return.

Reginhard, the prior—one of the senior brothers—also came to him. **[Note: [Col. 1569D] He was later made abbot.]** Among other matters, he spoke with him privately and said:

“Alas, father and lord, what hope will remain for us hereafter? What consolation will there be for our tears? Who will restore our place after its coming desolation? Behold, now that you have died before us, only your grave remains for you; and not without reason do we fear that, since we were unworthy to retain you alive, we shall also be deprived of you when you are dead.

“From this it seems likely that all our buildings will fall into desolation, and that we, who inhabit that mountain for the sake of God and of you, stripped of everything, will be scattered in a pitiable manner.”

To this the man of God quickly replied, having gathered his strength:

“Let that fear be utterly dismissed. I testify by that Truth who is God that my lifeless body will be brought to you, as I desired, although many will oppose it and appear to create great difficulty as to how and when it will happen. In the meantime, let there be an end to your grief: it is an absolutely certain hope that I shall have my burial among you.

“The good Lord will be present, and his grace will be present. I shall come to preserve the place, and through the place I too shall be preserved.

“Only persevere in the good things you have begun; indeed, increase what has been begun through better efforts, so that you may receive the fruit of your labor a hundredfold, both here and in the life to come.

“Let no suspicion concerning my successors terrify you. Among them there will be few who, at the sight of my tomb, will not bow their heads out of reverence for me. Indeed, even brute animals, if they pass close by, may appear endowed with some sense of the honor they ought to show.

“But if anyone should be so perverse as to treat me with contempt and insult, such a death will await him that it would have been better had he never been born.”

After these words, Father Reginhard, as he was about to depart, asked whether he wished any message to be conveyed through him to his sons.

At once, raising his voice amid many tears, Anno said: “My soul and my body.”

When Reginhard wished to go outside, he addressed him as follows:

“As you yourself have now seen, my affairs are coming to an end. Therefore I beg you, beloved brother, through Christ, do not abandon that mountain of mine, the unique support of my hope; but after my death, cherish and sustain it through your integrity and constancy.

“You will remove the occasion of great dangers from it if, with the strictness of the rule, you restrain in the brothers the license to sin, which overturns all religious life, in accordance with the saying of a certain wise man: ‘You have daughters: preserve their chastity, and do not show them your smiling face’ (Eccli. VII).

“Know that there are already there, and afterward there will be even more, whose minds and actions will aim at the destruction of the place, if—as God forbid—you begin to be more lax.

“See to it, therefore, that, constantly armed with the authority of the rule, you oppose the undertakings of the wicked, lest through your negligence that place of mine collapse.”

At that time the elder Reginhard did not understand what these words meant. But a few months after the blessed man’s death, he was elected by the brothers and compelled to assume the care of the entire monastery of Sigeberg. To this day he administers it, mindful of Blessed Anno, his unique intercessor, with great faith and diligence, sustained now for twenty-nine years not by his own strength but by Christ’s.

## VIII. He Insists Strongly on Being Buried among the People of Sigeberg

A few days later he summoned to himself the leading men whose opinion the rest of the clergy and people would certainly follow. Sitting on his bed, so that his words might carry greater weight, he placed a pontifical stole around his neck. Then, solemnly adjuring them and at the same time threatening excommunication against all who might act otherwise either by counsel or deed, he earnestly begged them not to allow the transfer of his body to the monastery of Sigeberg to be prevented.

Four weeks before his death, he wished Erpho, abbot of Sigeberg, whom he always called “father” out of reverence for his venerable gray hair, together with the fathers and brothers of other monasteries—no fewer than twelve in all—to sit beside him.

Reviewing with the eyes of his heart the entire course of his life, he publicly proclaimed himself guilty and a sinner, wholly unworthy to have been adorned until then with the titles of so great a priesthood. Then he removed the pontifical stole from his neck and offered it to them, saying approximately these words:

“Since I am far removed from deserving this, I return it to you in penitence and confession. My head, which I judge never to have used it worthily, will no longer abuse it.”

When everyone protested, Abbot Erpho was finally overcome by the one offering it and accepted the stole. Then, assuming authority from the confidence placed in him, he said:

“Great is your humility. All good men cannot fail to commend this act of yours: out of fear of God, you have submitted yourself so far to us, who are far inferior to you both in merit and in rank, that you wish us to be teachers to your episcopal excellence.

“Therefore, by the holy obedience owed to the Son of God, we command you to receive without hesitation the authority and privilege of your stole.

“For although by your own judgment you confess yourself unworthy of its eminence, it does not follow that God has lost sight of whatever good and whatever is worthy of a bishop you possess in the eyes of the supreme Judge. Indeed, since ‘the righteous man is the first accuser of himself’ (Prov. XVIII), and the Lord speaks through the prophet: ‘Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified’ (Isa. XLIII), you have greatly accumulated and increased this.”

The holy bishop did not dare resist him. He only arranged that a fixed number of Masses and other prayers should be designated, which each person would offer for the sins he had confessed.

And it was done so. For, as Scripture says, “the prayer of one who humbles himself penetrated the clouds, and it will not depart until the Most High looks upon it” (Eccli. XXXV).

## IX. The Holy Man’s Great Reverence for Sacred Relics

When he was already being pressed toward the end by increasingly severe pains, he did not forget the patrons from whom he had once drawn hope of obtaining the heavenly homeland. He wished them to be carried to the mother church, and, being placed on a chair, to be carried out to meet them. Since he did not possess one of his own, he was dressed in the elegant attire of a chief dean.

The ground was very wet from recent rains, and the place under the open sky where the sick man was sitting, through which the relics were to pass, was muddy and damp from water gathered here and there.

He reverently inclined his head toward each relic as it passed. But when he saw Saint Severinus approaching nearby, he burst into copious tears before his venerable shrine and threw himself face down from the chair into the mud, so that his white and costly garment was for the most part stained with dirt.

When the large crowd of both sexes that followed the sacred relics saw this, it uttered certain pitiable cries and accompanied him with such tears that even today many of them testify that they had never experienced mourning of that kind.

Everyone was moved because so great a prelate, so renowned in authority, cast himself out of devotion and humility into such filthy mud, weeping and wailing, even though splendidly dressed—mud which the most despised person would be unwilling to touch in the cheapest clothing.

From this they easily inferred how great was his devotion of spirit toward Blessed Severinus, and many considered it hardly doubtful that those two would be equal in glory whose merits were so illustrious.

After the sacred relics had been carried into the great church of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that night was spent with praises directed toward the heavenly treasures. The man of God was brought there, and, for the expiation of his sins, asked that the celebration of Masses be hastened.

After he had shown great honor to the sacred relics, and they were now to be returned to their places, he bade them farewell with tears, saying:

“I know, I know: whatever I have hitherto promised myself from your help in this valley of tears has now come to an end as far as preserving this life is concerned. But I have a firm hope and consolation in you: even though you are unwilling to help the body, you will always care for the salvation of my soul.”

## X. Holy Water Drives Away a Demon

Meanwhile, as the pain in his foot spread over his entire leg and part of his thigh, it frequently attacked his vital organs themselves. When he lay anxiously near death, he once saw the devil standing opposite him and said:

“What are you doing here, most wicked one? Yet it is not surprising if you lie in wait for us, so insignificant and reliant on no merits, since you were not deterred even by the holiness of the most blessed Martin from plotting against him at the end of his life.”

Then, crying out to ask whether anyone would come to his aid, and finding everyone ready, he requested holy water. As soon as it was brought, he flung it forcefully with a sprinkler at the demon, and the demon immediately vanished.

## XI. He Despises Wealth and Distributes Everything to the Poor

At the end, taking his stole, he absolved all whom he had bound for whatever reasons, and humbly asked forgiveness from everyone, charging them all not to conceal from him anything that he might have omitted in these matters.

He also summoned the administrators of the episcopal property and bound them by the oath they themselves had given, so that in paying his debts—which were not inconsiderable—they would carry out their duties without respect of persons and justly repay everything owed both to Jews and to Christians. He assigned them a definite sum of money, which he had carefully and prudently set aside from the resources of his household for these purposes and for almsgiving.

He could indeed have accumulated immense weights of gold and silver in his treasuries, from which dangers both to bodies and to souls would have been created for others. But this was not his concern or desire.

“For he dispersed,” as it is written, “and gave to the poor; his justice endures forever and ever” (Ps. CXI).

Finally, after his death, not even a single farthing was found that belonged to him. Neither the king nor any greedy associate of his could boast that, from Anno’s ample purses, this or that had fallen to him after his death.

Yet none of those from whom he had borrowed money was cheated of repayment. Nor did our age ever see or hear of almsgiving so abundant as that provided during the eight days of his funeral rites—God ensuring that nothing was omitted through negligence or malicious fraud by those to whom he had entrusted its administration.

## XII. He Again Foretells His Death. What He Attributes to the Patronage of the Saints. He Foretells the Death of Duke Godfrey

Three days before his death, of which he himself was aware, he summoned Count Gerlac, lord of the castle of Wichinrod, and said to him:

“You will now give certain proof of your loyalty to me if, obeying the final commands of your lord, you earnestly devote yourself to bringing Duke Godfrey to Cologne to speak with me before sunset tomorrow.”

When the count replied that there was no way he could be present within two days, since he was then said to be far away, and that it would be a great achievement if he could arrive even by the third day, the holy bishop immediately added:

“The third day is sought in vain, since before that day my words will come to an end, when my spirit returns to the Creator who gave it.”

Terrified by these words, the count said: “God forbid, my lord, that this should be so! By God’s favor, certain safety will be at hand.”

“You rightly say,” replied the bishop, “that lasting safety will soon come to me, since the merits of Blessed Severinus surround me, and the patrons of Cologne kindly intercede for me. Relying upon them with all my strength, I am now about to enter the eternal rest prepared for me by them.

“But you, whom the impossibility of fulfilling my earlier command excuses, will be considered to have broken faith if, after my death, you neglect to convey my commands to Duke Godfrey.”

When the count swore that he would carry this out diligently, the bishop, confident in his promise, said:

“I entrust to your loyalty the commands that are to be conveyed concerning peace and pardon for the Saxons before the king’s savage mind. You will deliver them to the duke from me, and he in turn will accomplish them with the king.

“You will remind the duke at every point of the love and loyalty that most closely united me and him. You will also add that he himself will die within the year.”

Thus spoke the holy bishop. But in that same year Duke Godfrey was killed by treachery.

On the following day the holy man was brought near death around the ninth hour, and sudden despair threw all Cologne into consternation.

The leading men of the clergy immediately came, devoting themselves wholeheartedly to his funeral rites. After consulting with the clergy, they considered what honor and devotion might be offered to him as he departed. They appointed messengers to be sent swiftly to all the monasteries of the city of Cologne. When the sign of his death was given, each messenger was to hurry to the monastery assigned to him and to order the bells and all other signals that were available in the parish to be sounded in service of his soul.

Meanwhile, as he lay at the point of death, four readers were present: two at his right and two at his left. They read in turn. If they made any mistake while reading, he corrected them immediately by moving his hand; and if they ceased reading even briefly, he opened his eyes with an effort and compelled them to continue.

Thus his senses remained lively and unimpaired right to the end.

## XIII. His Vision at the Point of Death. He Prays Greatly for Cologne. In 1075 He Happily Departs to the Lord

As he continued through the night and day in his struggle, he gazed with spiritual eyes upon that plague which we now see, by which the wretched world, deprived of all honesty and religion, lies oppressed.

Suddenly he raised his hands as high as he could and cried out piteously:

“Holy Mary, come to the aid of the wretched; come to the aid of Cologne; come to the aid of the city that is now on the point of perishing!”

Then, lowering his weary arms for a little while, he raised them again toward the stars and said:

“What are these, O Lady, the dreadful spectacles that present themselves to my eyes? By your singular mercy I implore you: become for me the door through which I may depart from here, lest I be forced to see such evils with my own eyes.”

After briefly restoring his failing spirit, he also called upon Saint Peter to come to Cologne’s aid, and at times invoked other saints as well.

At last, with a great groan, he burst into these words:

“O all you friends of the supreme King, admitted into his presence, come to the aid of Cologne through your intercessions!”

Having said this, he drew his final breath. As daylight dawned, he happily departed to the very source of light, bringing mourning to the world and joy to heaven by his death.

Thus, after a long illness by which the Lord refined him like metal in a furnace until he was pure, in the year of the Savior 1075, in the twenty-first year of his episcopate, on the day before the Nones of December, at dawn on the sixth day of the week, he passed from human beings to the angels.

## XIV. The People of Cologne Greatly Mourn His Death. Even the Jews Mourn. His Funeral Is Most Celebrated

A certain brother of his monastery, resting in the guesthouse, heard a voice of this kind:

“Why are you snoring so now, when mourning fills every house at the death of the archbishop?”

The brother immediately awoke and rose with great trembling. As he dressed, he heard the frequent ringing of bells announcing the bishop’s death, as had previously been arranged.

Soon afterward, as bells rang everywhere, it cannot be said how great a mourning and grief seized the entire city. Every age and every sex sprang from bed and showed its grief by clapping hands, beating breasts, and uttering various cries. Such a cry arose throughout the city as had never previously been heard there at anyone’s funeral, nor is it likely easily to be heard again.

Very many devout men from the people wept bitterly. The altered faces of the clergy testified to their grief. Monks, widows, and virgins all had one manner of mourning. A special grief filled our guesthouses, for we shall never have another like Anno.

From every side one could see pitiable crowds of the poor, orphans, and sick rushing together. Among them little women carried their children, ran ahead, beat their breasts, and tore their hair.

Nothing could appear more glorious than this spectacle to one who does not ignore the Savior’s saying: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. XXV). For he had hidden his almsgiving in their bosoms, and they, going before and following after him with little branches of olive and with prayers in his service, approached with him to the very seat of majesty.

Happy indeed is the man who prepared for himself such friends from the mammon of iniquity, so that they might receive him into the eternal dwellings (Luke XVI).

But these things are minor. Even in the synagogues of the Jews, the enemies of Christ, tumult arose at first light, together with shouting. They proclaimed the name of Anno, his goodness and integrity, and mourned his death.

Nevertheless, we are not unaware that many rejoiced at his death, some openly and others secretly. To them the saying rightly applies: “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John III). Of them the Apostle also says: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I).

This rather contributes to the blessed man’s praise: he wished to displease those who find no pleasure in ecclesiastical discipline.

It may seem sufficiently remarkable that although most of the people of Cologne who had expelled him from the city had hated him, the whole city was nevertheless so devoted to his funeral that no funeral like it had ever taken place in that city, nor will one ever take place again.

For even if Peter the Apostle, the shepherd of the whole Church, were to visit that city in bodily presence, he could not be received with greater glory and celebration than that funeral was attended for seven days—if it ought to be called a funeral, and not rather a heavenly gift, which Cologne carried around for six days for the protection of itself and the sanctification of its children, and then on the seventh day, with a vast company, sent with great honor and grief to Mount Sigeberg.

### XV. Description of His Funeral. The Wondrous Mourning of All. Many Endeavour to Keep His Sacred Body in Cologne. Count Gerlacus Opposes Them Most Vigorously

His lifeless body had been washed and, as befitted a bishop, arranged in a coffin; it was still being handled by the attendants when, before sunrise, the entire clergy of Cologne arrived with crosses at the royal court. Together with an enormous crowd, both from the city and from the suburbs, they surrounded the bishop’s residence—not as people preparing to receive a dead man, but as though they were escorting a living man in triumph to some splendid public celebration.

Soon certain venerable men, clerics and monks, lifted the most sacred burden onto their shoulders. The attendants followed them in mourning, and they carried it out toward the Bishop of Minden and the assembled clergy, preceded by two men bearing the bishop’s staff and the banner of the cross. When he came into the sight of the people, it is incredible to relate what tears and groans arose there.

From there, amid psalms and hymns, with a great peal and ringing of bells, he was carried into the atrium of the principal church and laid beneath a richly worked crown hanging there, on which many candles were burning. Soon numerous monks and women consecrated to God arrived. The office for the dead, which they call the vigils, was celebrated, and the whole church was filled with the voices of the singers.

At the hour of the sacrifice, when everyone had assembled, the Bishop of Minden in particular approached the altar with the sacred ministers, most reverently and devoutly, and all followed him, singing psalms and weeping indiscriminately. When the sacrifice had been completed, all the priests stood behind the coffin in their stoles. There mourning and groaning, grief and tears increased, and everyone said, more through feeling than through voice:

“May angels lead you into paradise; at your coming, may the martyrs receive you and lead you into the holy city, Jerusalem.”

Anyone who possessed even a spark of ordinary piety could not fail to be moved if he had witnessed the offices performed for the blessed man on that day. The very voices of the singers, the very sweetness of the hymns, the very meaning of the words, and even the ranks and multitude of those offering the sacrifice seemed to testify that his feast was already being celebrated in heaven. Everything was full of compunction, as befitted such a funeral.

Meanwhile, all the officials of the church of Cologne, in complete agreement, earnestly strove to ensure that the sacred body should have its burial in Cologne. Some did this from genuine goodwill; others, out of envy, sought the same end. Those clerics who had formerly been established by the blessed man in the church at the Steps in honour of the Mother of God claimed that public justice would be violated if, besides the tomb which he himself had measured out for himself among them, he—though dead—were to occupy another tomb, even if that second place had likewise been designated by him but at a later time.

Since nearly all the nobles also supported this view, only three opposed it most fiercely: Sigewinus, dean of the principal church; Hermannus, the steward—both of whom later succeeded him—and Count Gerlacus. They now denounced the others with the sharpest reproaches, asserting that those who followed this opinion would not only incur the crime of treachery but would also be struck by anathema.

For three days nothing was achieved. On the fourth day, however, when both sides, with increasingly obstinate minds, were pressing their respective plans, Count Gerlacus finally stood in the midst of the assembly and spoke:

“It would be proper to yield to the opinion of such eminent men if public justice did not stand on our side. But, if you wish to know, it binds you and us alike as lords bound to our lord, while he still possesses the free power to choose the place of his burial. Thus we cannot, without great danger to our salvation, do otherwise in this matter than he has commanded.

“You know what terrible imprecations he uttered against you, foreseeing your obstinacy—so terrible that anyone possessing understanding would prefer to lose this life rather than incur that curse. Yet such destruction of souls is being pursued.

“Even if none of these things moves you, I certainly am not free, following your example, to disregard the adjuration of my lord, to whom I have pledged my faith, since it is certain that by doing so I would rush headlong into the sword of excommunication. And even if divine vengeance did not compel me, human laws would nonetheless demand such fidelity from me, so that I would rather die nobly than ignobly disregard the injury done to any lord to whom I am bound by oath.

“If such fidelity is owed to every lord, how much more must it be offered to him who has already been received into the heavenly senate while it was still assembled, whose dignity is ennobled both by the nobility of this city and by the summit of the highest priesthood? His life was so holy that one who, in defending him, suffers insults or is compelled to shed blood is rightly proclaimed blessed.

“Let this therefore be known to you all: I am resolved, in order to preserve my fidelity to my lord, that, if no other course is permitted, I shall steadfastly remove his body with the help of my fellow soldiers and reclaim it by armed force, until the deaths of the vanquished establish each man’s right.”

While the count continued in this spirit and with such courage, the others, deterred by fear, fell silent. Only Rudolphus, provost of the church at the Steps, together with his supporters, still refused to abandon his position. But the count addressed him before everyone:

“It would indeed be ridiculous if you thought that your shameless speech could break us to such a degree that, defeated by cowardice, we would allow you, cowardly as you are, to seize our deposit—one for which we are willing even to fight with the sword. Therefore convince yourself completely that you will never attain what you desire by any device.

“For even if, while the outcome of this affair remains uncertain, necessity should force us to bury this body in this city without fault on our part, you will still be ashamed of having undertaken a useless labour. For it will necessarily have to be buried in the very choir or sanctuary of blessed Peter, where no one previously, however holy, has been laid in the earth.”

When that provost and his supporters had thus withdrawn, the whole dispute was quieted. God looked with favour upon His poor, who did not cease applying themselves to prayers, vigils, and fasts until they obtained the treasure they desired.

After the watches of the first night had been completed beside the body of the blessed man, and daylight had appeared, the people and a great crowd of clergy again gathered at the church of blessed Peter. New mourning and new lamentations arose, and the ministry of the saving Host was fervently performed.

Then certain men lifted the sacred body onto their shoulders, like the ark of divine reconciliation, and amid many tears and loud lamentation proceeded toward the gate facing south, which provides the route through the royal district for those going to Saint Martin’s. Soon the bells rang out, and the chanting choir went before the sacred body, while the magistrates and people followed behind.

The grief and mourning were again indescribable, and the devotion was no less remarkable. People continually displaced one another from carrying the coffin, since each person earnestly desired to bear the burden himself; and all competed to touch even the bottom of the coffin, promising themselves great resources of blessing from that contact.

Chaste matrons stood in the doorways of their houses along the route. Everywhere one could see people raising their hands to heaven, shaking their heads, and following the sacred body with their eyes.

When it was brought into the monasteries as well, truly exceptional honours were paid to it. The churches were illuminated by the light of candles and lamps; the altars shone with gold and gems; the walls were adorned with multicoloured tapestries. Even the bodies of the saints were removed from their places and carried out in processions—a thing never before seen at a funeral.

I do not think this was done without the force of some hidden inspiration. Just as blessed Anno, while he was still among the living, never failed to honour those blessed citizens of heaven with whatever he could offer in mind, speech, hands, and feet, so it was specially granted to him that, when he was being carried to the tomb, he should enjoy the company of the sacred relics.

Who, however, would dare to consider himself his equal in venerating the saints? Who ever burned with such zeal and love as he did, or took such delight in even the smallest fragments of sacred relics? Meanwhile everyone’s devotion to the blessed relics was fervent, and each person considered himself more glorious if he had spent something new or something greater than the others on their adornment.

Sacrifices were offered everywhere, and other religious offices were performed. No impediment of any kind ever arose in these matters, so that even the favourable outcomes themselves seemed to congratulate Anno’s holiness.

First, his body was carried from the principal church to the monastery of blessed Martin; from there to the monastery of Saint Mary, which they call the New; then to blessed Cecilia; and finally to Saint George, where vigils were celebrated beside it that night.

On the third day, after the sacrifice had been offered, the lifeless shepherd was brought to the church of his most gracious intercessor, Severinus. There, by a singular privilege, the sacred relics of so great a bishop were brought out to meet him.

After the sacrifice had also been offered there, they proceeded to the monastery of Saint Pantaleon, distinguished in religious observance and wealth; from there to the church of the Apostles, and afterward to that of Saint Gereon.

At Saint Gereon’s he was received with the greatest honour. Outside the doors of the basilica, the saint’s relics were brought out to meet him with great reverence; inside, lights glittered; various kinds of metal gleamed; the mixed ringing of the bells resounded; and the appearance of the entire church was no different from what it usually was on the most solemn festival.

That night vigils were kept there for the sacred funeral with psalms. On the fourth day, after Masses had been celebrated, the holy man was carried to the monastery of Saint Andrew, to the sacred virgins, and to Saint Cunibert, where he was placed between the two Evalds.

At last they came to the church at the Steps. There the grief was renewed, the tears increased, and no consolation was admitted, because in everyone’s sight the glory and ornament of Cologne lay extinguished.

There the nobles deliberated about paying still greater honours to the blessed bishop, as though nothing worthy had yet been done. It was therefore decided that on the following day a general assembly should be celebrated there, and that the relics of the saints should be brought from all the churches, each congregation honourably following its own patron.

This was done, to the immense amazement of many. The faith and devotion of the people of Cologne deserve to be praised throughout all ages, since they honoured the funeral of their shepherd with such splendour.

After those sacred relics had been brought into the church, the lifeless body of the blessed man was placed among them, so that it seemed to surpass those whom only the greatest could equal.

I do not know what others may think, but I can scarcely contain myself for amazement, since I do not remember that such honours were ever shown at any funeral to men whom, because of fear of their holiness, scarcely anyone had dared approach.

On the fifth day, the eternal and great treasures of the sacred bodies were lifted up. The blessed funeral was carried among them as a unique protection; tears and songs were offered together; they proceeded to the church of Saint Peter; and the sacred body was brought into it with such celebration and glory that scarcely any triumph of kings had ever been commemorated there with greater splendour.

Countless lamps and candles shone there. The vast church seemed narrow because of the excessive multitude of people. The staff of Saint Peter, a distinguished ornament, was brought out to meet him, together with many relics and crosses.

To summarize briefly what cannot be adequately contained in many words: nothing more worthy or more splendid could have been devised than what was performed there.

On the following day, at sunrise, it is impossible to say with what force both clergy and people pressed toward the doors, with what devotion the sacrifice and the commendations were performed, or how the procession was then organized toward the Rhine.

The responsory was sung with particular mournfulness:

“Look, Lord, for the city full of riches has been made desolate, etc.”

From this one may in some measure gather the grief with which Cologne then escorted its shepherd.

When the body of the blessed man had been placed on a ship and the banks of the Rhine resounded with the lamentation of the mourners, certain of those who had hated the man of God were also present. Then, by a most evident miracle, it was shown what merit he possessed before God.

For the ship, which was to cross to the other bank of the Rhine, ascended against the force of the river and, like an arrow, successfully reached the opposite shore—perhaps it would even have gone farther by that same force against the sailors’ efforts, had the church of Saint Heribert not stopped it.

The event was all the more astonishing because the sailors, overcome by the cold, scarcely seemed able to move their hands, while the Rhine, swollen by rains and ice, had risen higher than usual. As we mentioned above, the holy man had already foretold while still alive that this would happen.

When those standing on the nearer bank saw that the ship, contrary to the force of nature, had reached a higher place on the farther bank than the place where they themselves stood, they were greatly astonished and praised God. Others, who had burned with hatred for the blessed man, sighed, beat their breasts, and went home.

Then what is said in the Psalm was fulfilled:

“The upright shall see and rejoice, and all iniquity shall stop its mouth” (Psalm 106).

The sacred body was then carried into the church of the Mother of God, where Saint Heribert shines through his miracles, and that night was passed with hymns and psalms.

The next morning, so that the people of Cologne might make their faith and devotion a testimony for all ages even on the seventh day, numerous clerics, monks, nuns, and citizens crossed the Rhine and arrived there before daylight.

With many candles burning in the church, the sacrifice and the commendations were celebrated with all due reverence. Two bishops were present, Fridericus of Münster and Egilbertus of Minden, each an ornament of his age and worthy to oversee so great a funeral.

The leading men of Cologne were also present, together with very many nobles, groups of monks, and an innumerable people, all prepared to escort the heavenly pledge as far as Mount Sigeberg.

Throughout the journey the venerable funeral proceeded, surrounded by choirs of singers. The body was carried in turn by different people; for nearly four miles it was borne on the shoulders of none but the noblest men, travelling on foot along a route which, because the ice had melted, was extremely muddy and difficult.

No one of servile condition, nor anyone riding on horseback, was permitted to approach the coffin within a stone’s throw. Meanwhile, as long as the procession could be seen from Cologne, all the bells filled the air with their sound.

When they came within sight of the mountain, such mourning and grief again arose that no words can express it. The monks rushed upon the coffin and wept pitifully over the death of so great a man until their tears failed them. They could not complete the antiphon they had begun:

“Into paradise, etc.”

Then something extraordinary occurred. From the west, very numerous birds of a new kind flew in, covering the mountain and, by their density, for the most part blocking the sight of the sky. They remained there until the body had been buried and the people had departed.

Those who saw them thought that they were either angels or holy souls. Perhaps we shall interpret more correctly if we say that they signified the crowds of people who would come in the future.

At last the body of the holy bishop was committed to the grave. Wishing to calm the tears and lamentations of the people, Hermannus the steward said:

“Let all grief now cease. Our father and bishop has what he desired, and he sings and says:

‘Behold, I now see what I desired; I now possess what I hoped for. I am joined in heaven to the one whom, while on earth, I loved with complete devotion.’

“And he has heard that most joyful voice of his Lord:

‘Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord’” (Matthew 25).

For a short while the tears ceased. But not long afterward, first all the nobles, then the bishop’s attendants, and finally the poor entered and renewed the mourning, continuing throughout the day.

Let anyone who can now compare the glory and splendour of this funeral with the pageants and triumphs of any kings or princes.

The Lord also began to glorify His servant by signs of miracles, to refute the shamelessness of those who shortly before had gnawed at his most holy life with a dog’s tooth and attempted to obscure with false rumours the precious pearl destined for the diadem of the heavenly King.

### XVI. The Vision of a Certain Brother. The Saints Are Not Dead but Live. The Vision of Another Brother

After the death of the blessed man, the abbot of Sigeberg, fearing that the brothers might lack necessary provisions, began to distribute food more sparingly.

A brother who was then cooking vegetables saw himself, anxious and exhausted, standing in the kitchen in a dream on a certain day of his weekly service. Soon the blessed Anno entered and, according to his custom, tasted the food that was being cooked. He also asked why food was being distributed so sparingly, though it was intended for so many brothers.

The brother replied:

“After your death, Father, there is no hope for us, your dependants and beggars; fear of future want compels us to practise this economy.”

Then the bishop said, not without reproach:

“Do you consider me dead? Let that opinion disappear. I now enjoy that life most happily, which flows entirely in the eternity of supreme blessedness. Compared with it, if one considers what I was when you said that I was alive—almost as though I did not exist—I ought rightly to be considered dead.

“Go quickly and tell the abbot from me that, being certain of an abundance of supplies, he must not dare to reduce the brothers’ portions. For within a few days I shall make such abundance of provisions flow to you that, in your amazement, you will not even be able to contain it yourselves.”

At that time there was also a great shortage of candles, so that the brothers scarcely, and sometimes not even scarcely, had enough for private Masses.

The holy bishop therefore appeared to another brother who was sleeping and said to him:

“I am astonished at the stinginess of your keeper, who supplies the brothers with candles so sparingly. I wish to know the reason from you.”

The brother replied:

“It is not the keeper’s fault, most loving Father; it is want that compels him to act in this way.”

Then the blessed man smiled and said:

“If there is no other reason for this, you shall now be the messenger of my promise to the brothers. Tell them that within a few days they will have such an abundance of wax that they will not even be able to gather it without becoming weary.”

### XVII. A Woman’s Withered Hand Is Healed. The Monastery of Sigeberg Is Greatly Enlarged

When the brothers had been encouraged by these and similar events to hope for great things from the blessed man, a woman whose fingers were contracted brought wax shaped like a palm to his tomb. She prayed on bended knees, extended the wax together with her afflicted hand, and as soon as she touched the tomb she was immediately healed. Thus she carried away the first miracle as testimony to his holiness.

This happened on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, which that year was both Good Friday and the feast of the Annunciation.

The news soon spread throughout the surrounding region. Everyone was astonished and was reluctant to believe because of the novelty of the event; but the woman, well known both by her family and by her name, compelled belief even from the unwilling.

The fame of the miracle also travelled to foreign regions, and as crowds began to stream in from every direction, the abundance which the holy man had promised began to appear.

Reginhardus, mindful of the future and knowing that what begins with such splendour through the gathering of the common people often becomes diminished through familiarity, devoted himself to constructing buildings, acquiring estates, and adorning the church.

In the end, from the resources with which that place of the sacred body was then filled day and night, he achieved such growth that, although scarcely forty monks had previously been there, after he had first been made abbot their number soon exceeded seventy or eighty.

He also built the mausoleum of the blessed man, at whose summit this epitaph was written in golden letters:

> Cologne, adorned with many excellent fathers,  
> sent the mirror of the Church into this tomb.  
>   
> A new light shone upon the world in a second Anno,  
> who in every duty was equal to his own office.  
>   
> After ten months and twenty-eight years,  
> the fourth day of December took him from our midst.

### XVIII. A Blind Man Sees. Very Many Flock to His Tomb

Meanwhile, as the people came there in ever greater numbers, a certain Cologne craftsman, blinded by glowing iron, also approached. He poured out prayers at the man’s tomb and was healed before he rose. He compelled everyone, with raised voices, to extol so sudden a benefit with praise and proclamation.

A small girl was brought, miserable with a withered arm, and she too was healed.

Then it pleased all who lived in the surrounding area to go there on the day before the Nones of May, with the crosses and relics of their churches, and to seek the intercession of the new patron through a common supplication.

The day arrived, and an infinite crowd hurried there. In the midst of the crowd a lame man was healed, and everyone celebrated the miracle with an incredible tumult of voices.

How great the subsequent gathering of people on that mountain was may also be sufficiently established by this: Sigefridus, archbishop of Mainz, who came there at that time out of devotion, was unable to gain access to the tomb either by the dignity of his office or by the escort of his attendants. He was shut out for a long time by the crowds pressing in, until, through the abbot’s intervention, he was brought in by hidden passages.

It is neither possible for us nor agreeable for the reader to recount the miracles one by one. We shall faithfully record some of the most notable.

### XVIII*. Saint Anno Foretells the Future in Jest. A Lame Brother Is Healed

While the blessed Anno was still alive, a certain monk of Sigeberg had fallen from a high place in the church. His limbs were dislocated and broken, and he was carried away on a sheet, almost breathing out his soul.

After he had been placed on a bed, he lay there for a long time. Many treatments were applied, and, contrary to everyone’s hope, he was brought to the point where he could walk somehow with a staff, although he limped.

To this man, already advanced in age and religious life, the blessed bishop once said jokingly, as was his custom:

“You will lean on that staff until, healed by me, you throw it away.”

At the time no one interpreted this except as a jest.

But after Anno had begun to live in heaven, and miracles at his tomb had become frequent, this brother was keeping watch over it. One day an invisible force drove him from his seat and threw him face down upon the ground before the tomb.

Wishing to know by whose impulse he was suffering this, he looked around and tried to rise. He felt that his whole body was sound: his nerves were loosened and the joints of his limbs, which had long been disordered, had been restored to their proper places.

He therefore hurried from the church to the chapter house, threw away his staff, bent his knees, and repeatedly tested whether he could stretch out his body and kiss the ground—or make a genuflection—which had previously been impossible. He felt no difficulty whatsoever.

He ran eagerly to Abbot Reginhardus and handed him the staff, to be preserved as testimony to his healing.

The fame of so great a miracle quickly spread throughout the monastery and the neighbouring places. Monks and a great crowd of people gathered at the church; praises and hymns were offered to God; and everyone celebrated a particularly solemn feast.

### XIX. A Most Wretched Man Is Wonderfully Restored

There was at Bonn a certain man so afflicted and miserable that it could not be believed by anyone who had not seen him with his own eyes. His whole body trembled constantly. His teeth chattered; he uttered the most horrible cries, sounds which no one would believe could be produced by a human mouth.

Pain gave him strength to utter such cries, but otherwise the force of his disease so shattered him that he could speak nothing at all. He could neither lie down nor sit, much less stand. Whenever he moved a foot in order to advance, he was immediately driven backward. To see the man was itself an occasion of misery.

Some people told him that he would be well advised to go to Sigeberg, where new miracles were being proclaimed. They said this not because they wished to advise the man, but because, in their usual manner, they were mocking the blessed Anno.

Nevertheless, because Almighty God knows how to make good use even of evil men, an ass was brought to them at their insistence. The wretched man was carried on it to the monastery of Sigeberg and prostrated himself miserably before the sacred body. Everyone both marvelled at him and pitied him.

A little later, as though he had returned to himself, he repeatedly turned his eyes, addressed those standing around him, rose from the ground, rushed to the very shrine or coffin of the precious body, kissed it again and again, made his vows, and departed completely healed, while angels and human beings rejoiced.

We shall now add another remarkable miracle, one belonging to God alone. Although it is difficult to believe, its truth is so great that I would willingly submit myself to divine judgement if the matter is not as I shall report it.

Let those who know that God can do all things read and believe (Matthew 19). If they are pious and religious, let them rejoice that they have in blessed Anno a great patron; if not, let them fear the most powerful persecutor of his detractors.

### XX. A Wicked Man Joins Blasphemy to His Lie. The Devil Appears to Him. He Blasphemes Saint Anno. Another Punishment of a Blasphemous Man

Arnoldus, a brave and wealthy man, lord of the castle of Dollendorf, was once sitting to hear the cases and disputes of his people. He seemed to show anger toward guilty men, but he acted more mildly whenever the seriousness of the offence did not prevent it. For according to his way of life he was pious and possessed a very great faith in God.

At that time a thoroughly wicked man named Volbertus was accused before him of failing to repay a debt. But he was fierce in spirit and insolent in speech, and he gave no modest or sensible answer. Indeed, he began to accuse the judge himself.

He complained that he was being oppressed by the judge and by everyone else beyond what he deserved, that he was being dragged to the tribunal without any fault, and he broke out into impious words:

“Since I have hoped in vain for a just sentence from God, I must seek another judge and patron.”

Everyone shuddered. But the wretched man, invoking the devil, said:

“You be my protection. I surrender and dedicate myself to you as your servant with both hands. Avenge my injuries, since I have not obtained this from God.”

God endured the blasphemy of the impious man. But when the wretch also began to insult His saints, an unheard-of punishment followed, so that it might plainly be seen how true were the words:

“Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zechariah 2).

The judge and all the leading men rose, unable to endure such blasphemy. They dealt with the madman now by threats, now by entreaties, so that he might return to his senses; but he raged all the more.

The sun was already moving toward setting, and the evil man was looking for his horse in the pasture. When he came to a nearby forest, he saw among the shadows of the trees a horrible human figure and addressed it first:

“Who are you, and for what reason are you standing here?”

The devil replied:

“I have come here out of pity for you. You know whom, filled with bitterness, you invoked a little while ago and to whom you devoted yourself as a servant. I am that very devil. With me as your protector you will always be fortunate. Return home, but do not withdraw yourself from my service.”

The wretched man departed. The next day, sitting on his horse, he followed the judge with his fellow soldiers as the judge travelled elsewhere.

Again the judge, together with his men, as though changed by reflection during the night, invited him to settle the matter. He promised forgiveness for what had been done wrongly the previous day, provided that the debt was paid.

The man returned to insults and abuse. He said that he had now found a better patron, one who could defend his own people and crush their adversaries, and who had no equal.

When the others asked who this patron was, he answered without hesitation that it was the devil. He did not hesitate to hurl blasphemies and many abominable words against Christ and His saints.

Then the judge, overcome by religious grief, said:

“O wretched man, O prey of Satan, are you so mad as to rage against your Creator? Unless you were filled with the one whom you proclaim, you would never heap so many insults upon the Lord of the world and His saints.

“You appear to surpass even demons in impiety. ‘They believe and tremble’ (James 2); but you, utterly insane, fear nothing of God’s power, nor do you believe in the miracles by which the saints are glorified throughout land and sea.

“To pass over the others, it is established concerning the most blessed Anno, besides his other miracles, that he possesses great power to give sight to the blind; and there is no doubt that he can also deprive those who see of their eyesight. Take care, therefore, lest, struck with blindness, you be compelled, even too late, to implore him.”

At this the man held his head high, laughing and sneering:

“Who could believe that this man shines through miracles unless he were mad? I know the man while he is still alive, and surely it is contrary to faith that, once dead, he should perform miracles which he could not perform while alive.

“If I am lying, why does he delay avenging his insult? If he ever healed a blind man, may both my eyes be torn out by the roots.”

He had scarcely spoken these words when suddenly his left eye began gradually to dissolve completely like water, leaving behind an empty socket—a horrible sight.

The soldiers immediately rushed to him. They eagerly wished to inspect the man and could not wonder enough. They all proclaimed the name of the blessed Anno. Only the wretched man remained incredulous.

They all urged him to become cautious through experience and to win the blessed Anno’s favour by prayers. But, worse than before, he cried out again:

“As long as any portion of light remains to me, may I be far from wishing to become his suppliant. Let it be your error to call him a saint. If he can, let him first tear out my other eye as well before I will admit this.”

He spoke, and, as everyone watched, something like a thunderbolt seemed to be hurled against his head. By its blow the remaining eye was torn out by the roots.

Immediately his horse took flight, and the unhappy man was thrown from it onto the ground. One foot, however, remained caught in a stirrup, and he was dragged miserably for a considerable distance behind the horse.

The swiftest riders followed him, caught the horse, and freed the dying man. Everyone rushed to him, shaken with horror. He cried out and wailed from the pain, rolling himself in the dust.

Then everyone, seized with fear and amazement, invoked Saint Anno. Prostrating themselves on the ground, they repeatedly cried:

“Kyrie eleison”—“Lord, have mercy.”

As those cries spread through the woods and fields, a great crowd of people, together with priests, hurried from the nearby places. When they had learned the whole matter, they were profoundly astonished.

Everyone waited to see what would next happen to the wretched man. The judge and certain religious men approached him more closely and asked him what ailed him.

He replied that he was being tortured by such pains that he had abandoned all hope of living.

They urged him, while there was still time for repentance, to gather himself. If he would do so and sincerely implore blessed Anno, they promised him both forgiveness and health.

Then, driven by pain, he cried out:

“I confess that Saint Anno can, if he wishes, restore to me the eyes that were taken away.”

Stretching his trembling hands toward heaven, he prayed tearfully in the hearing of all:

“Spare me, most sacred bishop; spare me, rightly punished though I am in my misery, and do not deny mercy to one who has been converted—the mercy which the Lord offers to all who wish to repent, when He says:

‘As I live, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn back and live’ (Ezekiel 33).

“If you restore my sight, which I believe you are able to do, I shall always submit myself to you with all my heart, and throughout the whole world I shall proclaim what until now I impiously denied: that you are equal in merits and deeds to the saints who came before you.”

As he spoke, everyone was moved with pity. Judge Arnoldus urged them to win divine mercy for the wretched man by common vows and prayers and to cry out together, with raised hands:

“Kyrie eleison.”

He said that he could not escape the charge of impiety if they abandoned a fellow human being in such misery. He therefore first threw himself upon the ground and moved everyone else to do the same.

When they had risen from the earth, repeatedly invoking Saint Anno, in an unheard-of miracle new eyes suddenly appeared in the man’s head, brighter than those he had possessed before. The man rose healthy and unharmed, as though he had suffered nothing.

The surrounding people poured out tears from joy and proclaimed praises for a very long time with immense cries, as was fitting.

Afterward the man came to the tomb of blessed Anno and explained what had happened to him. But since no one believed him, Abbot Reginhardus arranged for him to be brought before the synod then being held at Cologne under the presidency of Archbishop Hildulphus.

There, before everyone, he unfolded the entire history of the matter, with many people confirming his words in their own testimony.

Finally, when the bishop Hildulphus sent messengers and required it, that most trustworthy Arnoldus—whom we have already mentioned frequently—gave the gravest testimony, confirming it by oath.

## XXI. Pilgrimage to Saint Peter. A cleric reviles Saint Anno. The blasphemer who slandered the holy man is punished. One who invokes Saint Anno is healed.

Certain people from the diocese of Trier, traveling to Rome to the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, according to a devotion already customary for centuries, had as their companion on the journey a certain cleric from Koblenz [Col. 1583A]. As they exchanged various conversations, as happens, to lighten the journey and refresh their spirits, they eventually began speaking of the most blessed Anno. Setting aside other topics, they spoke long and earnestly about the holiness of his life and the excellence of his virtues, and one after another they recalled his deeds.

The day had nearly been brought to evening by conversations of this kind when, behold, that cleric revealed his unbelieving heart. “You,” he said, “raise that ruined man to heaven with your empty praises, although I consider him to have possessed nothing beyond what ordinary dead men possess: a man, as they say, bad toward his own people and worst of all toward himself.”

When that accursed man blurted this out, he brought both pallor and silence upon his companions through horror. After they had paused for a little while and then resumed their journey, they said to him: “Who, even if utterly mad, would dare utter such words? Since no one ought to restrain him more than a cleric, on account of the authority of his office, the words have come from a cleric.” [Col. 1583B]

But he spewed forth even worse things. “If you think I ought to be reproved,” he said, “because I am a cleric, although what I say is not in accord with your faith but is not alien to the truth, listen to the end of the man whom you wish to claim as a saint. The most violent pain in his feet, and the previously unknown disease of gout, painfully tore his soul from him, as you have heard. Yet it would be most cruel for a man of any goodness to be consumed by that divine punishment, which not even the most wicked easily deserves. Vengeance bears witness that he did not live well; indeed, both life and the vengeance that followed his life show how badly he died.”

O tongue deserving to be cut out, when divine Scripture testifies in so many places that God reproves and chastises the one whom he loves (Apoc. III)! How great, how undeserved, and how monstrous were the sufferings endured even by the Son of God himself—and by the apostles and martyrs, whose death was the more precious the higher their life had been! “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV).

Therefore, far be it from the minds of the faithful to think that blessed Anno suffered any loss of his merits through the bitterness of death. Rather, let them understand that his glory was thereby increased. Let them hear what punishment overtook this blasphemer.

His companions warned him sufficiently and more than sufficiently to stop speaking so perversely, but the wretched man did not cease. Thus, while everyone was already seeking vengeance for such bitterness and such great rashness, the others suddenly continued freely along the road, but he stood motionless. He who had reproached the confessor of Christ for the pains in his feet remained fixed in place as though bound to his ankles by iron chains, while meanwhile he felt severe torments in his feet.

Soon he began to tremble, grow pale, groan miserably, and lament. The others looked back. They marveled at his shouting, scorned him for stopping, and with angry faces demanded to know why he was lingering while they were hurrying onward. With many groans he revealed what he was suffering. They did not doubt that this had happened because of the merits of the one whom he had slandered; they grieved out of compassion, yet rejoiced that the event had occurred.

At last they poured out common prayers for him. He venerated in them the faith he had previously condemned. He deeply regretted having spoken rashly and offered prayers and vows to blessed Anno for his release. Everyone prayed until he was freed and completed his undertaken journey unharmed [Col. 1584A].

After returning home, he considered nothing more urgent than to visit the venerable ashes of the most sacred bishop. Both the necessity of his vow and the advice of his friends urged him to do this. When he arrived there, he recounted the entire story with many tears and in complete truth, and left it with us to be written down.

## XXII. A crippled woman is healed.

A certain crippled woman brought a small wax candle to the tomb of the blessed man. As she was about to leave, she felt herself raised upright with astonishing speed. Distraught, she cried out:

“O supreme priest Anno, what has happened to me, most wretched and unsuspecting as I am? For my backbone and the ribs attached to it were restored with such a great cracking sound that one would have thought an oak was being broken.”

Many people came running, summoned by the woman’s cry and by the noise of the bones. They saw her standing upright beside the ark of that blessed treasure, offering thanks more gratefully than they had hitherto seen her, always bent over. They reported the event to others, and many people of both sexes rushed into the church and with one voice offered praises and thanks to the supreme Trinity.

## XXIII. The feast of the Assumption of Saint Mary celebrated throughout the world. A crippled boy is healed.

A common feast of the whole world was being celebrated for the most blessed Virgin and Mother of God, who had been assumed into heaven. That day is venerable, holy, and glorious; no solemnity of the saints can be compared with it. While the brothers were solemnly keeping the night vigil with hymns and psalms, a little boy known to everyone both by name and by appearance—for Father Reginhard had brought him from the Rhine, miserably crippled, to be supported through an act of mercy—came crawling on his hands to the tomb of blessed Anno.

Some people were then present there, intent upon the vigil in honor of the most sacred Virgin, the heavenly queen. They saw the boy grasping the top of the tomb once, then again, attempting to rise but falling back each time. On his third attempt, however, he rose to his feet. He did stand, although he seemed about to fall. Nevertheless, he succeeded in walking for a while while leaning upon a staff [Col. 1584C].

At last, having thrown the staff aside, he was safe and unharmed and recovered the full ability to walk. This event brought great joy on that day, when so distinguished a miracle was added to the glorious solemnity of the illustrious Virgin.

There are also many other miracles of blessed Anno, exceedingly worthy of being read. Passing over all of them, however, I have reached the desired harbor of my labor by means of these very few examples, so that I have, as I believe, portrayed a man most illustrious in merit and holiness, while I have not greatly exceeded the brevity required on account of tedious readers.

May almighty God grant that, if I have labored in this work at all worthily of his praises, it may benefit my soul in the life to come. May he who was the subject of my writing be a patron to me when I depart: Anno, thrice and four times blessed, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

On the wooden pastoral staff, or crozier, of Saint Anno, which is still reverently preserved in the monastery of Siegburg, the following verses are engraved in copper on its upper part [Col. 1584D]:

> Tityre, drive the flock together; being blind, do not lead the blind.  
>   
> Be grave in conduct; learn to be a gentle ruler.  
>   
> With the serpent’s cunning, preserve the simplicity of the lamenting dove.

[Col. 1583]

# Two charters of Saint Anno, archbishop of Cologne

## I. Concerning the castle of Saleveld belonging to the church of Saint Peter of Cologne, granted by Queen Richiza, and concerning the estates which Anno himself granted to the same queen on a precarial tenure. (Year 1057.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. III, col. 445, from a manuscript of the monastery of Brunweiler.]

[Col. 1583A]

[Col. 1584A] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Anno the Second, by the mercy of God archbishop of the Church of Cologne.

[Col. 1585A] We consider, therefore, that the Lord has done great things for me, he who is powerful; and I have become anxious because I could scarcely find what I might render to the Lord in return for all that he has rendered to me. As I was burning with these concerns, divine piety opened a way for me, by which I hoped, proceeding along it, to attain what I desired: namely, that by enlarging the Church of God entrusted to me, I might not fear to say that I had become equal to those men who preceded me, men conspicuous throughout nearly the whole world both for holiness and for possessions and for the distinction of their lineage—and, if I may say so without offending them, that I had worked more diligently than they.

Accordingly, when an opportunity arose, we approached the lady Richiza, queen, concerning certain estates at Salevelt-Kobins, so that, consenting to make a precarial grant from them, she might transfer them to Saint Peter of Cologne. When at the first approach this responded little to our wishes, it was nevertheless God’s will that, not long afterward, what we sought should have a prosperous and happy outcome.

[Col. 1585B] Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the Lord God and of Saint Peter, present and future, how a certain freeborn man and count, Starkhare, a knight of that queen, at the command and request of his lady, transferred to Saint Peter of Cologne, for the use of Archbishop Christian, the castle of Saleveld with everything belonging to it—lands and woods, forests and fisheries, meadows, pastures, dependants, and whatever she appeared to possess as property at Orla—excepting the servile tenants, to be held in perpetual right.

The arrangement was this: the queen herself was to retain the usufruct of the estate until the end of her life, with this firm prohibition, that no archbishop should ever alienate Salevelt or anything belonging to it from the archbishop’s demesne by exchange or by granting it to anyone as a benefice, except insofar as, with the advice of that queen, we might determine that something from it should be distributed among the monasteries of Cologne for the sake of our soul and of hers and of her parents [Col. 1585C].

The queen also assigned to the use of the monks at Brunweiler a tithe of clothing or of cloth of every kind, as well as coverlets, honey, and wax. We too, out of devotion to the most Christian queen, who was asking little from us but had herself proposed the amount, granted her the following estates of our demesne on a precarial tenure, handing them over to her to possess with every benefit until the end of her life: Sedekeback, Brezenheim, Vickolo, Moffendorp, Muoteresheim, Blasheim, and Znonoro. In addition, every year, one hundred marks of silver from our treasury.

If anyone—king, bishop, I myself, or any of my successors—should attempt to diminish anything of all this for her or to alter it in any way, unless at her own request, let him incur the hatred of God and Saint Peter. And let her have the power to receive Salevelt and everything belonging to it and to use them as her own.

[Col. 1585D] The queen also—or rather the aforesaid count Starkhare—at the command and request of his lady, transferred to the altar of Saint Peter all the male and female dependants belonging to these estates whom we excluded above, under an annual census of two denarii, so that they and all their descendants should remain under this law: that all should pay a similar census to the altar. He also firmly established [a provision concerning] free men, or *sinordi* hunters, or men of any kind belonging to this lordship who could prove that in their own time they had possessed rights and the best customs.

In the year 1057 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the tenth indiction, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, this transfer was made at Salaveldon according to the law and custom of that people. The witnesses to it, standing by and seeing the transfer, are these: Count Otto, Otlogh, Wetego, Romzezo, Herman, his son Herman, and again Herman, Reguhart, Gerwart, Aldeger, and again Aldeger, Gunthore, Rathere, Mazzo, Ruodolf, Herman, Adelart, Adelbert, Gerbort, Usito, Helinbolth, Ruozelin, Adeleich, Morlog, Vincho, and again Vincho, Hebo, Bubo, Gadelher, and Starkhare, when the lady queen, standing in the house of Saint Peter, acknowledged this transfer; and Count Starkhare, just as he transferred it at Salevelt, thus vested Saint Peter with it.

The clergy and people of Cologne are witnesses, together with those whom we shall name below: Berthold, Sicco, Ruotgher, Adolff, Christian, Ingram, Beringher, Adelger, Burghart, Thicmart, Herman, Arnolt, Godefrid, Berung, Sigebodo, Waltare, Nug, Goswin, Wecho, Cuno, Wigman, Herman, Herwart, and Bertholt.

## II. Foundation charter of the monastery of Saint Alexander at Graffshap in the diocese of Cologne, by Archbishop Anno. (Year 1072.)

[MARTENE, cited above, col. 490, from the original charter.]

[Col. 1586B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

Let it be known to all the faithful of Christ, present and future, that I, Anno, by the grace of God archbishop of Cologne, acquired a certain place in Saxony called Grafcaft from a certain noblewoman named Chuniza and her son Thietmo.

After this, with the permission of Pope Alexander and Emperor Henry, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1072, in the tenth indiction, with the counsel of the entire household, I established regular monks of the Siegburg order in that place [Note: [Col. 1585D] The monastery of Siegburg, Sibourg, situated two hours from Bonn and founded by the same Archbishop Anno, still exists; in it Anno wished to be buried [Col. 1586D]]. I confirmed and established them in every peace and justice enjoyed by the other abbeys of Cologne, and I prohibited all my archiepiscopal successors, binding them under the penalty of anathema, from exacting any secular service from that abbot.

Let the abbot choose an advocate who shall hold a court only twice a year and shall bring no more than twelve horses. In autumn and winter his service shall be two *maldra* of bread, two pork victims and one piglet, four chickens, one goose, four cheeses and twenty eggs, one *ama* of beer, and as much mead as is made from a quarter of a jar of honey. The horses’ fodder shall be three *maldra* of oats. In summer and spring, three victims and one lamb, and fodder for four horses, and so forth as above. If he wishes to hold court again on the following day, it shall be at the abbot’s discretion whether he wishes to provide him with a meal.

So that this disposition may remain stable and unshaken forever, I confirmed it under invocation of the holy and undivided Trinity, under the authority of the apostle Saint Peter, under the judicial enforcement of all the saints, under my pontifical ban, and under threat of perpetual anathema, and I authenticated it with the impression of my seal.

These are the names of the churches and places which I have justly and lawfully acquired and transferred for the sustenance and clothing of the monks of God and Saint Alexander: Worumbach, Attandarra, Luidolffescheide, Falebreht, Hertseido, Heslipho, Hademare, Hostervelden, Felmedo, Buodevelden, Brunscapellum, Ruothino.

These are the estates: Nuzlare, Clintfelden, Hademare; likewise Hademare, Amelinchusun, Pretinholo.

Ten hides given by Henry: Luidolfessceinde, Attandarra, Smerlecco, Alerenen, Holzhusun, Buodenveldum, Felmedo, Leno, Beigenchusun, Brunes-apella.

At Dietrinchegovan, one hide: Berendorff, Fatena, Suropo, Lannichofon, Gledorf, Harhincdorf, Werdincdorf, Wedirichueldem.

From the tithe at Suefacen, three and a half pounds; at Badelecche, eight pounds; from Luitbizo’s benefice, ten solidi; from Arnold’s benefice, twenty-five solidi: Gensingen, Allinchusun, Nescelestein.

At Thietbach, one vineyard; at Erpelle, one vineyard; at Erbinchusun, one house; Hasichenbruchum; the tithes of Warsten, Badelicke, Mulnheim, Anlagen, Bergheim, In Hare, Wlede, Usne, Hivenchusen, Thiedtvardinhusen, and Hiddinchusen.

Happily concluded.

Place of the seal.

## SAINT LEO IX, ROMAN PONTIFF

### LIFE OF SAINT LEO IX

Life of Saint Leo IX 457. Preliminary observations 457.

#### BOOK ONE

I. Bruno’s parents and lineage 467.  
II. He is born in the year 1011 467.  
III. His education; a eulogy of Adalbero, bishop of Metz 468.  
IV. Bruno studies together with him 469.  
V. He is wounded by a toad; while thereafter gravely ill, he is healed by Saint Benedict 470.  
VI. He obeys Hermann, bishop of Toul; he sympathizes with the afflicted monks of Saint Aper. He lives at the emperor’s court. He decides to prefer a poor bishopric to richer ones 471.  
VII. He leads soldiers into Lombardy 472.  
VIII. He becomes bishop of Toul 473.  
IX. The emperor opposes his election because of the poverty of the bishopric. Bruno obtains the emperor’s consent 474.  
X. He departs from Italy. He avoids the ambushes of the Lombards 477.  
XI. He arrives at Toul. He undertakes the reform of monasteries 478.  
XII. His ordination is delayed; he is ordained 479.  
XIII. He places Abbot Guidricus over the monasteries. His gentleness of character. He is skilled in music. His patience 480.  
XIV. He suffers envy. He falls ill and is healed by Saint Blaise 481.  
XV. The piety of Bruno’s mother. She falls ill and asks to be buried without adornment. She dies 483.

#### BOOK TWO

I. Bruno visits Rome every year. He heals his traveling companions from an epidemic. He sees Saint Peter in a dream. Another vision 484.  
II. At the assembly at Worms, the pope is elected. In the guise of a pilgrim he travels to Rome. He restrains the overflowing of a river. He arrives at Rome and is canonically elected pontiff 487.  
III. He assumes the name Leo. He is wonderfully enriched. His fame spreads everywhere 489.  
IV. A dog speaks. Leo gives to the poor what has been offered to him. He convenes councils. He comes to Cologne, then to Rheims, where he consecrates the church of Saint Remigius and celebrates a council 490.  
V. Council at Mainz. Leo frees a demoniac at Reichenau 493.  
VI. He returns to Rome. He restores a broken cup. He goes to Apulia. He heals a paralytic. Council at Siponto. He returns to Rome 493.  
VII. A bishop who contradicts him is punished; likewise the bishop of Ravenna 495.  
VIII. Leo frees a demoniac. He substitutes Udo for himself at Toul. He attempts to reconcile the Hungarians with the emperor. He foresees future evils. Council at Mantua. The dead visit sacred places 495.  
IX. The heresy of the Fermentarians. Leo writes against it. Nicetas Pectoratus comes to his senses. Michael, bishop of Constantinople, is excommunicated 498.  
X. Expedition against the Normans. The cruelty of the Normans 499.  
XI. The pope passes unharmed through the midst of the enemies. He cares for the funerals of the slain 500.  
XII. His devout exercises. He learns the sacred Scriptures in Greek 501.  
XIII. He places a leper in his own bed. By chance he frees demoniacs 501.  
XIV. He falls ill at Benevento. He comes to Rome. He is brought to the oratory of Saint Peter. He is fortified with sacred oil and the Eucharist. He dies and is buried 502.

LXXXII. Saint Leo IX orders the bishops of Venetia and Istria [Column 1600] to obey the patriarch of Grado, whose primacy, granted by the Apostolic See, he had confirmed by synod 727.  
LXXXIII. Letter of Saint Leo IX to Thomas, bishop of Africa. He shows that the archbishop of Carthage is primate of all Africa; that the bishop of Gummi cannot, without his consent, consecrate bishops or convene a provincial council; and that only the Roman pontiff can depose bishops and summon general councils 727.  
LXXXIV. Saint Leo IX praises Bishops Peter and John because, at his command, they held a council concerning ecclesiastical matters and defended the rights of the archbishop of Carthage against the bishop of Gummi 729.  
LXXXV. Saint Leo IX grants a ship for the use of the monastery of Cassino, with its captain and crew, free and exempt from every toll and payment 731.  
LXXXVI. Saint Leo IX presents Udalric, archbishop of Benevento, with the pallium and confirms his privileges 732.  
LXXXVII. Bull of Saint Leo IX confirming to the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Bari the church of Saint Nicholas, granted to it by Nicholas, bishop of Bari 733.  
LXXXVIII. Saint Leo confirms Dominic, formerly a monk and made bishop of Valva by him 734.  
LXXXIX. Letter of Saint Leo IX to Henry, king of the Franks 736.

XCII. Saint Leo teaches the clergy and people of Osimo that those who follow the perverse and utterly detestable custom of certain peoples must be anathematized—namely, the custom whereby, after their bishop has died, they invade the bishop’s house with hostile violence, seize his property, burn the houses on his estates, and, with a savagery more bestial than that of beasts, cut down his vines and orchards 739.  
XCIII. Saint Leo highly praises Peter Damian’s book, the *Gomorrhian*, against the fourfold pollution of cardinal contagion 740.  
XCIV. Saint Leo adorns with privileges Peter Damian’s hermitage “called Ocri, situated in the territory of Fucina” 740.  
XCV. Saint Leo IX gives Abbot Bernard of Farfa permission to summon any bishop he wishes to consecrate the Farfa church 740.

XCVIII. Letter or brief of Saint Leo IX concerning the cemetery of the priory of Saint Orientius of the Cluniac order 743.  
XCIX. Saint Leo IX confirms the foundation of the famous abbey of Saint Mary among the Santones 743.  
C. Letter of Saint Leo IX to Michael, patriarch of Constantinople, against his unheard-of presumptions and excessive vanities, and those of Leo, bishop of Acrida 744.  
CI. Letter of Saint Leo to Peter, bishop of Antioch. He congratulates him on his fidelity toward the Apostolic See. He confirms his ordination, provided that he was promoted according to the canons. He urges him to defend the dignity of his Church. He approves the faith written by him as the same faith held by the Roman Church, whose principal articles of faith he sends him 769.  
CII. Letter of Saint Leo to Michael, patriarch of Constantinople. He congratulates him on striving to reconcile the Greeks with the Latins. He rebukes him both for attempting to subject the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch to his authority and for usurping the title of universal patriarch, and for condemning the Roman Church, which celebrates the holy Eucharist with unleavened bread. He proves that Christ consecrated with unleavened bread 773.  
CIII. Letter of Saint Leo to Constantine Monomachus. He praises him for working to reconcile peace between Latins and Greeks. He urges him to defend the Roman Church. He complains of the arrogance of Michael of Constantinople and commends the legates 777.  
CIV. Saint Leo IX, at the request of Abbot Albuin, and for the love of God and at the petition of his faithful Richer, abbot of Cassino, with the intervention of Egbert, abbot of Fulda, confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Saint Salvator and Saint Mary of Nienburg 781.  
CV. Saint Leo grants to Albuin, abbot of Saint Mary of Nienburg, and his successors, at the request of Richer, abbot of Monte Cassino, that they may use dalmatics and sandals when administering sacred rites 781.  
CV bis. Saint Leo writes on the chastity of clerics against the letter of Nicetas, abbot of the monastery of Studios 781.
